**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the twelve earlier centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—one, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**First Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## [The Complete Works of Cassiodorus]

[Col. 0009]

# Preface of M. Aurelius Cassiodorus on the Psalter (C)

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009A] **1.** After I had at last cast off, in the city of Ravenna, the anxieties of public office and the cares of secular life seasoned with a harmful savor, and had tasted the heavenly honey of the Psalter for souls, I plunged into it as an eager investigator, as those who desire something commonly do, so that after my most bitter actions I might drink in its saving words with delight. But beginners encounter a familiar obscurity, woven through with various persons and veiled in parables. This is passed over in the life-giving words through a harmful concealment, although what is ambiguous is often found there to bear the secret of a great mystery.

Then I had recourse to the highly renowned reading of the most eloquent Father Augustine [Note: [Col. 0009D] The manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés reads, “the most eloquent reading.”], in which so great an abundance of sayings had been amassed that what has been thoroughly explained can scarcely be retained even after rereading. I believe that, when he wished to satisfy peoples excessively eager for ecclesiastical nourishment, the streams of so great a proclamation necessarily poured forth. Therefore, mindful of my weakness, with God’s mercy granting it, I have led the sea poured out from the fountains of his exposition of certain psalms into shallow streams, using a concise brevity: I have enclosed in one volume what he wonderfully unfolded in fifteen decades.

But, as someone says of Homer (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III, chapter 3): “To steal something from his meaning is like taking Hercules’ club from his hand.” For he is an outstanding teacher of all letters and—something rare amid such abundance—a most cautious disputant. He flows like a perfectly pure spring, polluted by no dregs; and, persevering in the integrity of the faith, he does not know how to give heretics anything by which they might defend themselves in some contest. He is wholly Catholic, wholly orthodox; and, shining in the Church of the Lord with the most pleasant radiance, he is illumined by the brightness of heavenly light.

Yet, after so marvelous a teacher, I have added certain things newly discovered, relying only on the presumption granted by the Lord, who gives confidence to little ones, sight to the blind, speech to the mute, and hearing to the deaf. I have also divided this book into three sections of fifty psalms each, with their prefaces, so that the clarity of the writing might open more beautifully to the eyes of the elderly [Note: [Col. 0009D] The printed edition reads, “to sounder eyes.”], and so that numerous volumes might be provided for the desire of the reading brothers. Thus one copy was left for the security of the library, and, for the study of the community, it is perhaps known to have been divided most conveniently.

[Col. 0009D] Therefore, trusting in the Lord’s command, let us knock at the gates of the heavenly mystery, so that he may open to our understanding flower-bearing dwellings, in order that, safely introduced into that heavenly paradise, we may pluck spiritual fruits without any transgression like that of the first man.

Truly a flashing book, a luminous word, the care of the wounded heart, the honeycomb of the inner man, a chart of spiritual persons, the hidden language of virtues—which bends the proud to humility [Note: [Col. 0010D] The manuscripts read, “bends the proud to humility”;], subjects kings to the poor, and nourishes little ones with graciousness. For so great is the beauty of its meanings and the medicine of its dripping words that Solomon’s statement in the *Song of Songs* may rightly be applied here: **“A garden enclosed, and a sealed fountain, a paradise full of every kind of fruit”** (Song of Songs IV, 12).

At one time, those formed by the salutary instruction of certain psalms turn troubled and stormy minds toward a clear and utterly peaceful life; at another, they promise that God will visibly become human for the salvation of believers and will come to judge the world; at another, they urge us to wash away sins with tears and cure offenses by almsgiving; at another, they are reverently awestruck by sacred prayers; at another, profound through the power of the Hebrew alphabet; at another, they proclaim saving things about the Lord’s passion and resurrection; at another, they are most compassionate in the lamentation of those who mourn; at another, by the repetition of verses they disclose certain mysteries to us; at another, they are wondrous in ascending the steps of the Songs of Ascents; finally, they cling joyfully to heavenly praises. Blessed abundance, inexplicable desire, astonishing depth! The faithful soul that has begun to be nourished there cannot be filled to satiety.

The psalms, finally, make our vigils welcome, when in the silent night the human voice bursts forth into music among singing choirs, and, through words skillfully modulated, makes us return to him from whom divine speech came for the salvation of the human race. The song that delights the ears and instructs souls becomes one voice of those who sing psalms; and with the angels of God, whom we cannot hear, we mingle words of praise—through him, of course, who came from the seed of David, the Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself says in the Apocalypse: **“I am the root and origin of David”** (Apocalypse XXII, 16).

From him we have received the salutary religion, and through him we recognize the revealed mysteries of the Holy Trinity. Hence one glory is rightly joined to them—to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that their perfect praises may be confirmed. They bring the coming day with morning rejoicing; they dedicate to us the first hour of the day; they consecrate the third hour to us; they gladden the sixth hour in the breaking of bread; they release our fasts at the ninth hour; they bring the final hours of the day to a close; and, when night arrives, they ensure that our mind is not darkened, as they themselves say: **“Night is my illumination in my delights, for the darkness will not be darkened by you, Lord”** (Psalm CXXXVIII, 11–12). Thus anyone who does not enjoy the delight of this gift may rightly believe himself alienated from true life.

To summarize their powers briefly, divine speech will say in the seventieth psalm (verse 22): **“But I will confess to you your truth in the vessels of the psalms.”** Truly they are vessels of truth, containing so many virtues, stuffed with so many divine fragrances, and heaped with so many heavenly treasures—jars that receive heavenly wine and always preserve its purity in its newness.

A marvelous sweetness, which does not turn sour through the corruptions of the world, but, remaining in its own dignity, is continually increased by the grace of the purest pleasantness. A very well-stocked storehouse, from which such great peoples of the earth drink, yet whose abundance knows no exhaustion.

How marvelous, moreover, is the sweetness that flows from the psalms themselves for singing! They rival the sweet-sounding organ with human voices; they reproduce the sound of trumpets with grandiloquent cries; they construct a sounding lyre through the mingling of living strings; and whatever formerly seemed to be performed by musical instruments is now shown to be expressed through rational substances.

Nevertheless, we must not sing like parrots and blackbirds, who, while attempting to imitate our words, are known in every way not to understand what they sing. A pleasing melody delights the mind, but does not compel it to fruitful tears; it soothes the ears, but does not raise the listeners to heavenly things. Yet we are pierced in the heart if we can recognize what we say with our mouth, as it is written in the Psalter: **“Blessed is the people that understands the shout of joy”** (Psalm LXXXVIII, 16). And again: **“For God is King of all the earth; sing psalms wisely”** (Psalm XLVI, 8).

The apostle Philip also (Acts VIII, 28), when he learned that the eunuch of Queen Candace was reading Isaiah, appropriately explained the Holy Scriptures to him. After he understood what he was reading, he immediately sought the grace of baptism and soon received the gifts of perfect salvation. In the Gospel the Lord also says: **“Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it—the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart”** (Matthew XIII, 19).

From this it is appropriately understood that such things cannot happen to those who deserve to perceive the Holy Scriptures with a pure heart. Concerning this, Father Jerome beautifully says: **“Divine Scripture is a certain pearl, and it can be pierced through in many parts”** [Note: [Col. 0011D] The manuscript of Saint-Sanger reads, “it can be formed from many parts.”].

Therefore, apostolic Father [Note: [Col. 0011D] It is uncertain to whom these words refer. This is discussed more fully in our preface.], who by God’s favor have restored the heavenly writings to holy conduct, summoned by your invitation [Note: [Col. 0012D] The printed edition reads, “summoned by your imitation.”], I shall enter the divine abysses—your invitation being the means—since you mercifully correct faults and, because you amend them, do not charge them severely against us.

But before I touch the spiritual treasuries, I think that certain matters, divided into chapters and numbering seventeen, should be sampled in advance, so that when the place of those matters arises, the drink of the great nectar may be drawn with the sweetest delights.

First: the various kinds of prophecy must likewise be discussed, so that we may be taught more distinctly what this Davidic prophecy is.

Second: why different names, as though of authors, appear in the titles of the psalms.

Third: what **“unto the end”**, which is frequently found in the titles, signifies.

Fourth: what the Psalter is, or why the psalms are so called.

Fifth: what a psalm is.

Sixth: what a song is.

Seventh: what a psalm-song is.

Eighth: what a song-psalm is.

Ninth: concerning the fivefold division.

Tenth: concerning the unified inscription of the titles.

Eleventh: what a *diapsalma* is.

Twelfth: whether the continuity of the Psalms should be divided into five books, or whether it should certainly be called one book.

Thirteenth: how Christ the Lord is to be understood in the psalms.

**3. Fourteenth:** how the exposition of the psalms has been arranged.

Fifteenth: concerning the eloquence of the whole divine law.

Sixteenth: concerning the distinctive eloquence of the Psalter.

Seventeenth: the praise of the Church.

Now, with the Lord’s help, let us proceed to the order set out above.

# Chapter One: On Prophecy

Prophecy is a divine breathing-in that announces the outcome of events, either through certain deeds or through words, with unshakable truth. Concerning it someone has aptly said: “Prophecy is a sweet heavenly utterance, composing the honeycombs of heavenly teaching and the sweet honeys of divine speech.” Hence David himself says in the hundred and nineteenth psalm: **“How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth”** (Psalm CXVIII, 103).

The gifts of this grace, however, were bestowed in many ways. To gather a few from among the many: it was enacted through human operations, as with Noah’s ark, Abraham’s sacrifice, and the crossing of the Red Sea; also through the births of the twins Esau and Jacob, who bore the mysteries of future things; through angels, as when they spoke to Abraham or Lot, Zechariah, and Mary; through visions, as with Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the other saints; through dreams, as with Solomon and Daniel; through a cloud and a voice from heaven, as with Moses.

It is therefore clear that holy David was filled not through human operations, not through the births of twins, not through angels, not through visions, not through a dream, not through a cloud and a voice from heaven, nor through any other modes, but through heavenly inspiration, as we read of him in the First Book of Kings: **“And the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day and thereafter”** (1 Kings XVI, 13).

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: **“If David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how do you say that he is his son?”** (Matthew XXII, 45). By this statement we clearly recognize that the psalms were prophesied through the Holy Spirit. It should certainly be known that every prophecy either speaks or does something concerning past, present, or future time.

It should also be observed that the Holy Spirit was attributed to the holiest prophets in such a way that, on account of the weakness of the flesh and the opposition of sin, he could nevertheless depart from them for a time when offended, and return again when appeased, at the proper time. Thus Saint Jerome, explaining the evangelist Mark at the passage where he says of John, **“He saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him”** (Mark I, 10), treated the matter with such evident reasoning that no one would dare oppose his judgment.

In the fiftieth psalm, too, after his sin, the prophet asks: **“Do not take your Holy Spirit from me”** (Psalm L, 13). For if, as blessed Jerome says (*On Ezekiel* XXXV, 1), divine speech were always in the prophets and had a permanent dwelling in their breast, Ezekiel would never so frequently write: **“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying.”**

Furthermore, in the Book of Kings the prophet Elisha says of the woman whose son had died: **“Leave her, for she is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not told me”** (2 Kings IV, 27).

The Apostle also says: **“I have no command of the Lord concerning virgins, but I give advice”** (1 Corinthians VII, 25). Again he states: **“This I command, not the Lord”** (ibid., 10). Elsewhere he says: **“What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord”** (2 Corinthians XI, 17).

Thus, similarly, among the other prophets, some things were spoken by the Lord and not by the prophets, and some by the prophets and not by the Lord. John the Baptist would not have said specifically concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: **“The one who sent me to baptize, he said to me: ‘Upon whoever you see the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’”** (John I, 33).

For the added phrase, **“and remaining upon him,”** would never have been a distinctive feature of the Lord Christ unless it showed that the Spirit sometimes departed from others. In Christ he remained because he had no sin; from others he rightly departed because they had received the stain of pollution. The Holy Spirit cannot have communion with sins, for it is written in the Book of Solomon’s Wisdom: **“For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding”** (Wisdom I, 5).

Prophecy, then, is a very magnificent and truthful form of speech, not composed by human will but poured forth by divine inspiration, as the apostle Peter says: **“For prophecy was not at any time brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit”** (2 Peter I, 21).

The apostle Paul likewise says: **“The one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation”** (1 Corinthians XIV, 3). A little later: **“The one who prophesies edifies the Church”** (ibid., 4)—plainly edifying it when, by the benefit of prior declaration, he makes unknown and exceedingly necessary matters thoroughly known.

Those who have been given the ability to understand or interpret the divine Scriptures well do not seem excluded from the gift of prophecy, as the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (chapter XIV, 32): **“The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.”**

But since we have perhaps suitably recognized what is read concerning the gifts of prophecy, let us now carefully investigate what remains.

# Chapter Two: Why Different Names, as Though of Authors, Appear in the Titles of the Psalms

In the First Book of Chronicles (chapter XXIII, 5) we read that, when the prophet David had grown old in devoted service to the Lord, he selected four thousand young men from the Israelite people to make the psalms which he had brought forth by the Lord’s inspiration resound with organs, lyres, *nablia*, tambourines, cymbals, trumpets, and their own voices, to the great delight of heavenly grace.

This harmonious union consisted of three parts: the rational part belonged to the human voice; the irrational part to musical instruments; and the common part was formed from both, so that the human voice might be produced in precise modulations and the melody of the instruments might be joined to it in consonant proximity. Thus that sweet and joyful music prophetically signified the Catholic Church, which, from diverse languages and varied harmonies, was destined, by the Lord’s favor, to believe in one concord of faith.

From this number we frequently find names inserted into the titles, such as Idithun, Asaph, the sons of Korah, and similar names. Not because they themselves, as some wish, were the authors of the psalms, but because they were placed over the musicians and proved to be reliable administrators of those matters, so that they might receive honor from such remembrance, since they served in a holy office with devoted minds. This is especially so because their names are also known to indicate appropriate meanings of the matters involved.

For the men mentioned above were not chosen to compose psalms; we read only that they were gathered to sing. No history testifies that they were psalm-writers, and it is presumptuous to say what cannot be confirmed by any authority.

That the psalms belong to the prophet David alone is established by sure indications. Finally, wishing this work to be understood in the Apocalypse, he mentions David alone, saying: **“Thus says the holy and true one who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts; who shuts and no one opens.”**

In the Gospel, too, the Lord himself says to the Pharisees: **“How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord’?”** (Matthew XXII, 43–44), and so forth.

Hence it is proved that all the psalms belong not to many persons, but only to him whom we know to have been named by the Lord. The practice of the Catholic Church, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, also holds generally and immovably that whenever one of those psalms marked by a different name is to be sung, the reader must proclaim nothing other than **the Psalms of David**.

If they were the proper works of Idithun, or of the sons of Korah, or of Asaph, or of Moses, their names would certainly be proclaimed, just as in the Gospels works are identified by the names of Mark, Luke, Matthew, or John. Following this view, Father Augustine also appropriately says that all the psalms are Davidic (*City of God*, Book XVII, chapter 14).

# Chapter Three: What “Unto the End,” Frequently Found in the Titles, Signifies

We speak of “end” in two ways. The first is common and moral: when something has been brought to its limit and can proceed no farther, so that it is understood to have reached the termination of its movement. Thus we speak of food as finished when it has been consumed by careful eating; of money as finished when it has been spent; and of other things that are expressed in this manner.

The second is called the perfect and everlasting end, which we are now seeking. This end begins to extend and expand for us when the devoted mind reaches it. The end, therefore, and the fullness of the Law is our Lord Christ, as the Apostle says: **“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes”** (Romans X, 4).

When we have reached him, we shall seek nothing further; but, content with that end of blessedness, we shall enjoy the fullest delight. Our love for him advances to the extent that our understanding, by the Lord’s favor, grows bright.

Therefore, whenever you find **“unto the end”** in the titles of the psalms, direct your mind’s gaze toward the Lord and Savior, who is the end without end and the completion and perfection of every good.

# Chapter Four: What the Psalter Is, or Why the Psalms Are So Called

The Psalter, as Jerome says, is a resonant hollow of wood shaped like the Greek letter **Δ** (*delta*), having a swollen belly in its upper part, where the strings are fastened in an orderly manner and, struck by the plectrum, are said to produce a most pleasing melody.

Its position seems to be contrary to that of the lyre: what the lyre contains at the bottom, the Psalter, in the reverse arrangement, bears at the top. This kind of resonant and distinctive instrument is adapted to the body of the Lord and Savior, because just as the Psalter sounds from the higher parts, so that body celebrates from above the glory of its institution, as he himself says in the Gospel: **“The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth; but the one who comes from heaven bears witness to what he has seen and heard”** (John III, 31).

Hence some have determined that this Davidic work is called the Psalms because it is known to resound from the heights above.

Know, however, that these alone are called Psalms on account of their excellence, namely, those contained in this volume. For the prophet Daniel testifies that the Psalter is also a type of musical instrument, saying: **“the sound of the trumpet, pipe, sambuca, lyre, psalter, and symphony, and every kind of music”** (Daniel III, 5, 15).

Chronicles likewise explains this (chapter IX, 11), when it speaks of the thyine woods, commonly called ebony, from which steps were made in the house of the Lord and in the royal house, as well as lyres and psalteries for the singers.

Among the Hebrews this is called a *nablum*, a term that nevertheless has been made familiar by frequent repetition in the book mentioned above. The word *psalm* itself is certainly Greek; some hold that it is derived **ἀπὸ τοῦ ψαύειν**, that is, “from touching.” We also call female lyre-players *psaltriai*, because with a trained thumb they produce musical modulations.

# Chapter Five: What a Psalm Is

A psalm is a certain sweet and tuneful modulation poured forth from the musical instrument alone, that is, from the Psalter.

# Chapter Six: What a Song Is

[Col. 0016A]

A song is what is sung to the honor of God when someone uses the freedom of his own voice and is not joined in harmonious modulation to any talkative musical instrument. This is what is also now performed in praises of the Divinity.

# Chapter Seven: What a Psalm-Song Is

A psalm-song occurred when, with a musical instrument leading the way, a singing choir acclaimed with joined voices, obeying only divine words.

# Chapter Eight: What a Song-Psalm Is

[Col. 0016B]

A song-psalm occurred when, with the choir singing beforehand, the art of the musical instrument was adapted in common accord to a single harmony [Note: [Col. 0015D] The manuscripts of Aud, Bec, and Fisc read, “was carried along as a companion.” The printed edition reads, “was carried along graciously.”], and the words of the divine hymn resounded in a sweet union.

# Chapter Nine: On the Fivefold Division

I shall point out this fivefold division, which we have described, in the most suitable places, according as each of its forms may be found in the titles of the psalms, where by mystical interpretation they convey a certain significance to the matters that follow.

But since there are also other titles of many kinds, which I do not think should be passed over, I judge that they should briefly be gathered into a single conclusion, so that the reader may neither incur weariness nor perhaps lose something necessary for understanding.

# Chapter Ten: On the Unified Inscription of the Titles

It is clear that certain superscriptions of the psalms are to be understood spiritually through a similar allusion. If you consider the letter, the title is foreign, since you do not find in the psalms the things contained in the titles. But if they are drawn toward a figurative interpretation, they appear exceedingly appropriate.

This is the case where events are signified, as in **“when he fled from the face of Absalom”**; where a place is indicated, as in **“when he was in the desert of Idumea”**; where a day is indicated, as in **“on the first day of the week”**; where Hebrew names occur, as in **“Idithun”**; where a comparison of events is made, as in **“when he changed his face before Abimelech”**; or where similar forms are indicated, as in **“for the winepresses.”**

Therefore, in the superscriptions of the titles, whether you find a psalm, a song, a psalm-song, a song-psalm, **“unto the end,”** or something from the sixth combination we mentioned, whether singly or with one, two, three, or four of them inserted, draw them toward the virtues that we shall say belong to each. For the remembrance of these matters is subtly placed by way of comparison with hidden understanding.

These things hang before the entrances of the psalms like sacred veils. If you direct the mind’s gaze through their thinning threads, you can easily behold their inner chambers. Who would think that so many causes and so many varieties of names are meaningless, since it is impious to believe that the divine Scriptures contain anything superfluous?

For it is written: **“Amen, amen, I say to you, not one iota or one stroke will pass away from the law until everything is fulfilled”** (Matthew V, 18).

# Chapter Eleven: What a *Diapsalma* Is

Among the interpreters of the Psalms, a certain diversity of opinion is known to have arisen concerning this term. Jerome, the most learned investigator of the Hebrew language, confirms that it signifies the continuation of the Holy Spirit (Letter 138), because *diapsalma* means “always.”

Blessed Augustine, however, the most subtle investigator of obscure matters, moving among difficult subjects without stumbling (*On Psalm IV*), is known to have chosen this interpretation instead: that it should rather be understood as a division, examining the quality of the word itself.

For *sympsalma* is a Greek term meaning a joined union of voices, whereas *diapsalma* means a broken continuation of words. It teaches that wherever it is found, a change has occurred either of persons or of matters. Therefore the term is appropriately inserted where either meanings or persons are shown to be divided.

Accordingly, we too shall make divisions wherever *diapsalma* may be found in the psalms; we shall investigate the remaining matters as far as opportunity permits, wherever the authority of this term may be found.

# Chapter Twelve: Whether the Continuity of the Psalms Should Be Divided into Five Books, or Whether It Should Be Called One Book

[Col. 0017C]

Blessed Jerome thought that the prophecy of the Psalms should be divided into five books (*Preface to the Psalms to Sophronius*), because the expression **“Let it be, let it be”** occurs for the fourth time in the text of this work; by the occurrence of this phrase, a certain division seems to be disclosed. Later generations have agreed with this view. I believe that he considered it a useful provision, since the tedious length was compressed into many parts.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, however, a most acute and profound investigator of divine matters, more suitably judges that it should be called **the Book of Psalms** (*Prologue to the Psalms*), because in Hebrew it is one volume, especially since in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter I, 20) we read: **“In the book of Psalms.”**

Therefore it is rightly called one book, since it is confirmed by such authority.

# Chapter Thirteen: How Christ the Lord Is to Be Understood in the Psalms

The psalms speak of the person of the Lord Jesus Christ in three ways, for the instruction of the faithful.

First, they speak according to what is known to pertain to his humanity, as in the second psalm: **“The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ”** (Psalm II, 2); and in the twentieth psalm: **“You granted him the desire of his soul, and you did not deprive him of the will of his lips”** (Psalm XX, 3).

Second, they speak in such a way that he is shown to be equal and coeternal with the Father, as in the same second psalm: **“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you”** (Psalm II, 7). And in the hundred and ninth: **“With you is dominion on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”** (Psalm CIX, 3).

Third, they speak from the members of the Church, of which Christ himself is the leader and head, as in the twenty-first psalm: **“The words of my sins are far from my salvation”** (Psalm XXI, 2); and in the sixty-eighth: **“God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you”** (Psalm LXVIII, 6).

We must understand this statement as being spoken on behalf of each of the faithful. In every other respect, sins are proved to be utterly alien to Christ. Therefore Tichonius discussed this matter at greater length and with care in his *Book of Rules* (see Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book III, chapter 30).

If we keep this in our minds, we are disturbed by no confusion, because the greatest error arises when what is clearly said concerning one matter is inappropriately applied elsewhere to another.

For if he had spoken in only one way, who could have recognized his twofold substance, when even now, despite so evident a distinction, some attempt by sacrilegious intention to confuse the divine and human nature of the Lord Christ?

He frequently admonishes according to the letter, frequently commands spiritually, and suitably changes persons suddenly, so that now Christ—God, the incarnate Word and made man, the head of the Church—seems to speak; now the Church herself; now the righteous man; now the penitent. In this way he touches upon and embraces everything necessary.

Everywhere the holy proclamation of heavenly things vibrates in its fullest richness [Note: [Col. 0017D] The manuscripts of Aud, Bec, and Fisc read, “balances the proclamation.”]; and through the manifold diversity of its virtues, the pious Redeemer insinuates the mysteries of his kingdom, which must be adored, for the purpose of granting salvation to the human race.

We have prefaced these matters so that, when we come to such passages, the reader may hear without fear what he recognizes that he has already learned for his salvation.

Nevertheless, this must be held with the firmest belief, on the authority of the Fathers and the most certain testimony of the truth itself: one of the Trinity, or one person of the Trinity—the Word of God—became man from the Virgin Mary through spontaneous power, out of compassion for mortals, not through any ministering necessity.

For he endured no change in his own nature, nor did the assumption of flesh increase the Trinity. But, as someone has said: **“He washed away our stains in blood, and also stretched out our wrinkles upon the cross.”**

Although this is the singular support of our hope, the blessedness of believers, and the great happiness of the righteous, heretics do not cease, through impious intent, to gnaw at what is known to have provided the human race with the cause of salvation.

# Chapter Fourteen: How the Exposition of the Psalms Has Been Arranged
First, with the Lord’s help, we must speak about the inscription of the titles, from which, as though from full breasts, the milky meaning of divine proclamation flows forth. Second, each psalm must be divided according to its character, lest either a hidden change of subject or the variety of speakers introduced confuse our understanding. Third, I shall endeavor, insofar as it is granted, to disclose the psalm’s mystery—partly according to spiritual understanding, partly according to historical reading, and partly according to mystical meaning—examining the subtleties of its subject matter and the proprieties of its words. Fourth, as the passage requires, I shall attempt briefly to demonstrate its power, so that the intention of the arranged poem may shine upon the inner eyes by divine gift. By the power of the psalm I mean the divine inspiration by which its heavenly intention is opened to us: through Davidic speech it removes us from vices and persuades us to live rightly. Fifth, when the matter requires it, we shall mention the order represented by the number of the psalms, which has been consecrated by the dignity of matters most worthy of reverence. We confess that it would have been difficult for us to do this for every single psalm, since even the authority of the Fathers has left the matter undetermined and unresolved. Let the diligent investigator seek out the remaining calculations for himself, since with the passage of time many things in the divine Scriptures become clear that now appear hidden. In the conclusions, we either briefly embrace the whole psalm’s substance or say something directed against heresies that must be destroyed. For this is the Lord’s sincere love: to hold his adversaries in perfect hatred.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Eloquence of the Whole Divine Law

The eloquence of the divine law was not fashioned in human speeches, nor does it proceed uncertainly through confused circumlocutions, so that it might either depart in forgetfulness from past events, be disturbed by the confusion of present things, or be mocked by the doubtful accidents of the future. Rather, speaking to the heart and not to bodily ears, judging all things with great truth and great firmness of foreknowledge, it stands established in the truth of its author. Thus it is said in the Gospel concerning the preaching of the Lord Christ: “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. VII, 19). For he speaks without uncertainty to whom all things are present, and to whom the outcomes of events are shown to be subject.

Eloquence, indeed, is speech that is fitting and appropriate to each matter. This chaste, steadfast, truthful, and eternal proclamation shines with exceedingly pure eloquence: its usefulness gleams, the magnificence of its power appears, and the working of salvation delights us. Thus also it will say in the hundred and eighteenth psalm: “For your eloquence will give me life” (Ps. CXVIII). And again: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet, and a light for my paths.” Truly it is light, because it always commands what gives life, forbids what is harmful, removes earthly things, and persuades us of heavenly things. Hence also the Teacher of the Gentiles writes in his Epistle to the Corinthians: “For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (I Cor. IV, 20). Likewise, in the Second [Epistle] to Timothy he says: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproving, for instructing, for correcting in the discipline that belongs to righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (II Tim. III, 16).

As the authority of Father Jerome testifies, among the Hebrews this [eloquence] consists either in rhythm or in a composition governed by meter; according to their own account, it is contained in *fastuciis* [the term is uncertain]. For a *fastucium* is a conception proceeding by cola, skillfully unfolded for the expression of meaning. If you, diligent reader, investigate its power, hear the Apostle speaking to the Hebrews: “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebr. IV, 12).

The sacred profundity of divine Scripture uses such common forms of speech that everyone accepts it without hesitation. Yet it conceals the truth’s meaning in a secret place, so that within it the life-giving judgment must be diligently sought. That it is truly divine may be understood above all from this: the unlearned seem to have been able to transmit the most subtle things, and temporal people eternal things, only because they were filled with the divine Spirit.

Finally, how many miracles were continually performed until Scripture itself, disseminated abroad, filled the whole circuit of the world? As it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5). This therefore belongs to the strongest proof: the divine law is known to have been received throughout every part of the world. It exercises many kinds of expression—compressed in definitions, adorned with figures, marked by the propriety of its words, made clear through the combinations of syllogisms, and sparkling with disciplines. Yet it does not receive from them an alien adornment; rather, it confers upon them their proper dignity.

When these things shine in the divine Scriptures, they are certain and most pure. But when they come to human opinions and utterly vain questions, they are tossed about amid the ambiguous waves of disputes, so that what is always most firmly true here is often rendered uncertain elsewhere. Thus, too, when our tongue sings psalmody, it is adorned with the nobility of truth; but when it turns to foolish stories and blasphemous words, it is excluded from the honor of integrity. As the Apostle James says: “With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the image and likeness of God” (Jas. III, 9).

The experts in worldly arts—who clearly came into existence much later than the beginnings of the divine books—transferred these things to collections of arguments, which the Greeks call *topica* [topics], and to the arts of dialectic and rhetoric. Thus it may plainly appear to all that what was first given to sound minds for expressing truth was later judged by the Gentiles to be adapted to human wisdom. These things shine in sacred readings like the brightest stars and fittingly illuminate the meanings of matters through most useful abbreviations. We shall briefly point them out in the most suitable places, since the matters themselves will most conveniently bring them into view, through which the conceived meanings will shine more clearly.

Father Augustine, too, in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine* (chap. 29), declared as follows: “Let the learned know that our authors used all the modes of expression that grammarians call by the Greek name *tropes*.” A little later he continues: “Those who recognize these tropes, that is, modes of expression, in the sacred writings are somewhat helped by their knowledge toward understanding them.” In other books of his he made the same point most explicitly. In the books he called *On the Modes of Expression*, he demonstrated that various figures of secular literature are found in sacred writings; but he also declared that there are other modes proper to divine speech, which grammarians and rhetoricians have in no way touched upon. Other very learned Fathers among us said the same thing—namely Jerome, Ambrose, and Hilary—so that we may appear not to be presumptuous inventors of this matter but rather its followers.

But someone may say: “Neither the parts of syllogisms themselves, nor the names of figures, nor the terms of the disciplines, nor anything else of this kind is found at all in the psalms.” They are plainly found in the power of their meanings, not in the utterance of their words. Thus, in our understanding, we contemplate wine in the vines, the harvest in the seed, leaves in the roots (*racidibus*, evidently *radicibus*), fruits on the branches, and the trees themselves in the kernels. From the deepest abyss, moreover, a delightful fish is caught, although before its capture it is not seen by human eyes. Therefore we rightly say that things exist when we nevertheless perceive their power to be present. The Apostle forbids us to be deceived by the vain wisdom of the world (I Cor. III, 18); yet he does not deny that such things exist in the divine writings. Certainly, let us approach the psalms and ask for the faith of realities, which is greater than every disputation.

This chief and salutary kind of expression generally reports certain matters, and often explains something quite different from what is heard. There is a simple, twofold, and guileless bilingual manner of speech, as Joseph did (Gen. XLII): although he had recognized his brothers by their very appearance and by their native speech, he seemed to speak to them in such a way that he could not possibly be recognized. This was not undertaken for the sake of deception but accomplished for the advantage of great usefulness. It employs Hebrew expressions that indicate profoundly hidden causes. It often places one matter in both evil and good, so that what appears common in name may be shown to differ in qualities. It compares heavenly things with earthly things, so that what the incomprehensible greatness forbids us to understand may be perceived through familiar likenesses. In the sowing of words, moreover, there is marvelous power, so that immense and incomprehensible things are suddenly explained to us in two or three expressions.

What could I say more briefly? Frequently even a single syllable demonstrates the Lord’s ineffable nature, as in the statement: “He Who Is sent me” (Exod. III, 15). Every word of this statement, subtly investigated, pours forth abundant meanings. For just as a most fertile field produces fragrant herbs suited to our health, so, whenever divine reading is examined word by word, the care of the wounded mind is always found there. Many Fathers have spoken more broadly and at greater length about the modes of this eloquence; we have judged that their names should be mentioned in introductory books. But this heavenly fountain, however constantly it is drawn from, does not know exhaustion.

And so that we may not linger any longer over generalities, let us, with the Lord’s help, touch upon the distinctive features of the Psalter, since the matter itself is clearly recognized when, after general matters have been set forth, it is subsequently described under some particular property.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Distinctive Eloquence of the Psalter

The first point is that only the psalms themselves are called *psalms* in the singular number. Having compared them, with the help of experts in this language, with their volume, we have judged that they should be rendered in their own verses while preserving the usage of those who sing psalms, lest authority, mixed into an assumed order, create confusion.

Next, no other work of divine authority is contained in one hundred and fifty sections. Where else are so many titles read, written with such varied diversity? Here the votive name *alleluia* began in the superscriptions. Here a historical remembrance drawn from the Book of Kings, placed at the very threshold, is known to indicate the powers of the psalms. Here also only *diapsalmata* [interludes between psalmic sections] are shown to have been inserted. Here the psalms hold numerical orders according to their powers.

The book begins with the blessedness of Christ, passes through the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments, and concludes with sacred praises and holy rejoicing. Thus the Church rightly finds consolation in such a gift, she who is known here to be wounded by the afflictions of many calamities. She knows, by the Lord’s benefit, how to triumph over her disasters even when they grow heavier. Through persecutions she makes progress; through afflictions she is always increased; she is watered by the blood of martyrs; through sadness she rises higher; through distress she is enlarged; she is nourished by tears; she is refreshed by fasts; and she grows all the more from the very source through which the world declines.

For what will you not find in that book from which the human race may gently console itself? It is a treasure continually increasing within a pure breast, a great consolation for the grieving, a blessed hope for the righteous, a useful refuge for those in danger. From it whatever is expedient is always taken, while its fountain is preserved in unfailing perpetuity. Blessed Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, in the book on the distinctive character of the Psalter that he sent to his dearest Marcellinus, says the following—to use his own words:

“Whoever recites the words of the Psalter sings words as though they were his own. Each person sings as if he himself had written them, and receives and reads them not as though someone else were speaking or signifying something about another, but as though he himself, speaking about himself, were uttering words of this kind. And whatever the things said may be, he seems to offer these words to God as though he himself were doing such things and speaking from himself.”

It is also distinctive of the Psalter that through it one enters into the holiness of the divine law. Beginners do not begin with Genesis, nor with the Apostle, nor is the holy evangelical authority struck at the very beginning. Rather, although the Psalter is the fourth book of divine authority, beginners who are commencing the sacred Scriptures properly make their beginning with it.

## CHAPTER XVII. Praise of the Church

O truly holy, O immaculate, O perfect mother Church, who, by the generosity of divine grace, alone give life, alone sanctify, and by your instruction restore the human race that has been ruined by its own faults: nothing can be added to or taken away from your devout confession. Throughout all the psalms and all the songs you insert praises of the holy Trinity, so that praise and the sweetest glory may always be rendered to them whose consecrated words we utter. You alone, in the likeness of Noah’s ark—which clearly bore your image—sail steadily and safely across the sea of this age and the fiercest storms of heretics, following an unharmed course of faith without danger from the flood. You yield to no errors, although you still remain amid the wickednesses of this age under the gravest necessity. Whatever is found outside your life-giving womb is clearly a deadly shipwreck.

For while detestable Sabellius errs concerning the Father, mad Arius commits offense against the Son, sacrilegious Mani denies the Holy Spirit, other criminals disparage the Old Testament, and some fail to follow the grace of the New Testament, you alone, with the Lord’s support, embrace all things without stumbling through faithful devotion. Teaching that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son; proclaiming one God and the holy Trinity, coeternal with itself and equally omnipotent; and [proclaiming] the Lord Christ remaining in his divinity and in the flesh of the humanity he assumed, while preserving the property of each nature, you confess one person. You bear witness to the New Testament through the Old, recognizing that the New has arisen from the Old. And, to embrace everything briefly, you do not know how to speak except what it is expedient to believe. For although you are afflicted here by various distresses and shaken by the opposition of the deceitful enemy, nevertheless, gathered from the whole circle of the world and shining in the form of a most beautiful pyramid, you are led to the eternal kingdoms.

You are not inappropriately compared with this figure, since, raising your precious summit from all nations, you send the souls of the righteous, like an extraordinary light, to the heavenly kingdoms: a boundary-marker full of heavenly grain; a blessed gathering of saints from diverse nations; a luminous assembly of serene minds; an indissoluble structure fashioned from living stones; the eternal happiness of all the blessed, brighter than the sun, whiter than snow, without spot and without wrinkle. Concerning her it is written in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army set in battle array?” (Song VI, 9). And a little earlier: “Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing; all bear twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your lips are like a scarlet thread” (Song IV, 1–2)—mother and virgin, fruitful and whole, mother and incorrupt, whose mouth breathes forth the fragrance of all virtues. Concerning her the bridegroom says: “The fragrance of your mouth is like apples” (Song VII, 8). And shortly afterward: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices. Your lips, O bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song IV, 10–11). Finally, you are worthy to kiss Christ and to guard that virginal beauty forever. For it is said to you: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments” (Song I, 1); and the other things that that divine book embraces in mystical proclamation.

Therefore, since the hearers have been made sufficiently astonished and inflamed by heavenly desire through a kind of *isagoge*—that is, an introduction to the work that follows, an index of heavenly mysteries and a herald of sacred speech—as I think, let us now, with Christ’s help, proceed to unfold what has been promised. Grant, O Lord, whose is everything that is expedient, that we may be worthy to be heard intelligently, willingly, and profitably. For we depend in every way upon your assistance, so that by the speech granted to us we may be able to explain, however inadequately, the words of your majesty. Amen.

## ORDER OF THE MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED

In the prolegomena—that is, the preliminary matters—before I taste the honey of the heavenly Psalter and, with the Lord’s support, touch those fields of the most glorious Passion, certain things seem to me to require explanation, arranged in chapters, concerning the text of the poem itself. In this way we may teach readers more distinctly, and we may proceed through the order itself without any impediment.

In the first part, the Lord’s bodily life is described.

In the second, the nature of his divinity is subtly indicated.

In the third, he speaks of the peoples multiplied against him, who were striving to destroy him.

In the fourth, the prophet persists in the same admonitions, so that the Jews may cease to think or do evil, since they should know that they will be destroyed by divine powers.

In the fifth, the Lord Christ cries out to the Father that his prayer may be heard and that, in his resurrection, he may grant what will benefit the world.

In the sixth, the words throughout the psalm belong to a penitent. Six others of the same kind are joined to it, although they are described in the conclusion of the fiftieth psalm.

In the seventh part, Christ humbly asks that the Father come to his aid, but he has confidence in the rightness of his conduct, which pertains more properly to his divinity. Yet, in the manner of the humanity he assumed, he asks that he be helped, lest the devil seize his soul through wicked presumption and, after his glory has been brought down into dust, it perish.

In the eighth, the following drama unfolds through gathered parables and figurative allusions, and everything is referred to the Lord Christ through allegorical comparisons. We shall point out these figures in the most suitable places, rendering them clearly, so that every ambiguity may be removed for the studious reader.

In the ninth, after many praises—which begin now from his divinity and now from his humanity—*Alleluia*, which means “Praise the Lord,” is placed with the persons and titles changed.

In the tenth, the gradual psalms follow, leading our soul to the Lord Savior through pure and humble satisfaction.

In the eleventh, with the words varied, it again celebrates the Lord’s praises in hymnlike exultation, now proclaiming the majesty of the Father, now of the Son, now of the Holy Spirit, so that no one may doubt that the holy Trinity is singularly omnipotent and wills to act in heaven and on earth.

In the twelfth, seven psalms are left at the end. Through hymnlike rejoicing they collectively celebrate the entire glory of the holy Trinity with devoted mind. Thus the text of the whole Psalter, divided into twelve parts according to the number of the apostles, concludes with wondrous praise, so that it too may do what we know Christ’s disciples did. There is also another, clearer mystery of the same matter: when the flood had covered the earth for one hundred and fifty days, the earth was cleansed of its crimes. In the same way, these psalms, extended to that number, fittingly render the human race, polluted by its sins, absolved. Now let us proceed bit by bit to explain the words of the Psalter.

## M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS’S EXPOSITION OF THE PSALTER. (C)

## FIRST PART

## EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST PSALM

### Why the First Psalm Has No Title

This psalm has no title because nothing ought to be placed before our Head, the Lord Savior, about whom it is going to speak in absolute terms; for he is clearly the beginning of all things, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, and therefore I speak to you” (John VIII, 25). Although other psalms also say many things about him, none speaks in this way about the life he lived on earth. And since everything that must be said here looks toward him, the head of the holy work is rightly placed here, for he is shown to be the prince of all things. Whatever this book says—whether it instructs us about past things, warns us about present things, or makes us more cautious about future things—all of it pertains to the instruction of the blessed man. Some have said that this psalm occupies the place of a title, others that of a preface. But although some may consider it suitably adapted to every righteous person, it can most truthfully belong to no one except the Lord Christ.

For if we say that it can apply to every blessed person, then what is said in the psalm is no longer established: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 11); nor what Job recalls: “No one is pure before you, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job XIV, 4); nor what is said elsewhere: “In truth, among those born there is no one who has not acted wickedly, nor among those who trust who has not sinned” [the manuscripts Aud., Bec., and Fisc. read: “nor among those who confess who has not sinned”]; nor this: “The righteousness of the righteous before you is like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. LXIV, 6). Therefore this statement cannot apply to every blessed person, but only to him of whom Scripture says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II, 22). And he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing in me” [the manuscripts Aud., Bec., and Fisc. read: “and he has nothing in me”] (John XIV, 30). Rightly, therefore, it is referred to Christ the Lord: “He did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. I, 2), and so forth. Wonderful is the order, truly a heavenly arrangement, whereby the beginning of the psalms came to us from him who is clearly the saving gate of heaven.

Therefore let us hasten to enter with the greatest joy, where we recognize that he himself is our open gate and Advocate, as the Apostle says: “For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses”; and a little later: “Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of his grace, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help” (Hebr. IV, 15–16). Now let us apply the keys that unlock the psalms, so that, with the Lord’s support, we may be worthy to enter the palaces of our King. And therefore, as we have stated above, a division must be made. If it is properly applied, it renders the speech so bright and clear to us that, before the text of the prayer is read, its intention may already shine before us.

### Division of the Psalm

The entire text of this psalm is narrated by the prophet. In the first part he explains the life of the holy Incarnation, since what is said about Christ cannot be made to fit if you wish to refer it solely to Christ’s majesty. In the second, he recalls that the wickednesses of sinners will receive the punishments owed to them at the future judgment, so that we may receive more gratefully what was set forth beforehand, whose subsequent matters seemed to be feared.

Consider also his intention, which is clearly to be sought above all. At the beginning, the blessedness of the Lord Savior is proclaimed so that life-giving examples may be offered to the human race, so that, just as an earthly human being brought death to us, so the one coming from heaven might give salvation. In the beginning, the condition of the deceived was exceedingly harsh, but afterward glorious redemption came to humanity. At first shameful captivity was imposed; afterward the freedom that had been desired followed. Humanity was expelled from paradise but received into heaven. It lost blessedness on earth but will be worthy to have the angels as companions. Mourning came from the devil; joy proceeds from Christ. Hence the Apostle also says: “For just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be constituted righteous” (Rom. V, 19).

At the very head of this psalm, the definition of the blessed man shines before us like the most beautiful diadem of the glorious King. It is a brief and lucid statement that shows in various ways what the proposed subject is. This beginning clearly contains two kinds of definition. In the first two verses, which say, “He did not walk, he did not stand, he did not sit,” there is the eighth kind of definition, which in Greek is called *κατ᾽ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου*, in Latin “by the removal of the contrary.” For it says what he does not do, just as he will say in the fifth psalm: “For you are not a God who wills iniquity” (Ps. V, 5). In the third verse, which says, “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night,” there is the second kind of definition, called in Greek *ἐννοηματική*, in Latin “notional.” It does not say what the thing is, but through what it does the particular thing we seek is indicated to us, just as he will say in the seventy-first psalm: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things” (Ps. LXXI, 18).

Remember, moreover, that every definition arises either from matter, which is body; or from form, which is quality; or from both, as in the case of a human being, set forth and arranged in wondrous order. For if he had first stated what the subject was, it would not have been necessary to say what it was not. Euclid, imitating this by reversing the order, did so when he said at the beginning of Book I of the *Elements*: “A line is length without breadth.” First he said what it is, and afterward added what it is not. So also do those who alter the statements of earlier writers through some variation, pretending to be their authors. Now let us come to the examination of the words, since within them, as within certain kernels, the sweetest fruit is found.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1. “Blessed is the man.”

An exceedingly beautiful and useful beginning: since the Holy Spirit was about to admonish the weakness of the human race, he seemed to begin with blessedness, so that through this hope he might invite the hearts of the fearful, lest the frail hearts of mortals withdraw themselves. Who would not be stirred toward any arduous undertaking when blessed happiness is proclaimed?

The blessed man is therefore so called, as the authority of our ancestors teaches us, as though he were “well-fitted,” to whom all desired things succeed. Yet the prophet recalls that this may be said in two ways in the hundred and forty-third psalm, where he writes: “They called the people blessed to whom these things belong” (Ps. CXLIII, 15); and again he adds: “Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.” Accordingly, the blessed person of this world is one who, as he supposes, supported by complete security, persists in continual joy and worldly abundance.

To this blessed man, who is removed from his purpose by no opposition, he fittingly added “man.” For a man is so called from his strength: he does not know how to fail through endurance or to throw himself into some pride amid prosperity; rather, fixed in steadfast mind and strengthened by contemplation of heavenly things, he always remains fearless. Our ancestors also called this a *veriloquium* [a truthful etymology]. For etymology is a brief statement that, through particular correspondences of sound, shows from what name the name under investigation has arisen.

Nor should you doubt that he calls the Lord Savior “man,” of whom the prophet Zechariah also says: “Behold, the man whose name is Orient” (Zech. VI, 12). Remember, however, that wherever he is so designated, the humanity he assumed is indicated. For “man” belongs to the sex of the flesh, which is in no way found in divinity. But because the nature of humanity had to be assumed by the Lord for our redemption, he fittingly used “man,” so that we might believe the one person of both natures.

“He did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of pestilence.”

Once the blessed man, that is, the Lord Christ, had been established, it was useful for him to explain him in consequence through his actions, according to the dispensation by which he suffered. Otherwise the teaching would be deficient if what belonged to the stated proposition were left unexplained.

Human errors clearly arise in three ways: in thought, deed, and speech. Here he denies them in order, saying: “He did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly.” First he rejects the detestable thoughts that the human race claims as its familiar possession, but which the Lord Christ did not have at all. And, so that we may not use examples from elsewhere, the thirty-ninth psalm plainly testifies that this must be understood of the Lord Savior, saying: “Then I said, ‘Behold, I come; in the beginning of the book it is written of me’” (Ps. XXXIX, 8).

“Walked” signifies that one departs from the straight road and slips into crooked paths. Next he excludes the acts of a vicious life, saying: “Nor stand in the way of sinners.” Certainly he came into the world, which is the way of sinners, but he did not stand there, because he passed through its vices in an immaculate life. By calling it “the way of sinners,” he wants it understood as broad, since the way of the righteous is known to be narrow.

In the third place he added: “Nor sit in the seat of pestilence.” This appears to refer to abominable teachings that disseminate the poisons of a pestilential doctrine. Such things are rightly denied of Christ, who healed the wounds of the whole world through his healing proclamation.

Someone has embraced this passage with the following distinction: he calls one “ungodly” who sins against God; a “sinner,” one who commits an offense against himself; and “pestilential,” one who plunders, oppresses, and injures his neighbor. But whichever of these you accept, you recognize that nothing of the kind existed in the Lord.

A seat is a sitting form composed from some material, which gently receives our bent backs and embraces us, lowered into its bosom, like a convenient case. Properly, it is given to teachers, as it says in the Gospel: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat” (Matt. XXIII, 2). We likewise remember that the tribunal belongs to judges and the throne to kings.

This order of the words must also be considered, and how it is entirely fitted against Adam. He “walked” when he departed from the Lord’s commandment; he “stood” when he delighted in sin, deceived into thinking that he would acquire knowledge of good and evil; and he “sat in the seat of pestilence” when he left his descendants examples of pernicious teaching.

Notice also how beautifully he assigned each word to its corresponding matter: “walked,” “stood,” and “sat.” This figure is called *hypozeuxis*, when different verbs are assigned to individual clauses. Therefore the general condition of sinners is rightly denied of the Lord Savior, just as Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world will come, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

#### Verse 2. “But his will was in the law of the Lord.”

It would not have been a great glory merely to have avoided what is vicious unless he had also said what deserves complete praise, just as he teaches elsewhere: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27).

The law of the Lord is therefore the holy commandment concerning the avoidance of sins, which Moses is clearly known to have received on Mount Sinai. The one who was wholly devoted to it with all the intention of his mind was he who had no sins. We, however, even if we think about the precepts of the law for a moment, do not remain in the law when the time of wrongdoing arrives.

“Will” is fittingly placed here to show the constancy of continual meditation. When it is taken up perseveringly, the weariness of labor is not felt. But lest you think that the will itself is idle, the effect of action follows, because for a holy purpose it was not enough merely to will good unless one also continually and devoutly satisfied the desire through labor.

Here a categorical syllogism may be found, which we ought not to pass over, lest what is the first element of the interpretation seem to have been improperly omitted. We shall state its definition and parts, so that nothing concerning these matters may remain ambiguous for the inexperienced.

A categorical syllogism, then, is one that dialecticians celebrate with the highest praise: a statement in which, once certain things have been posited, other things necessarily follow through what has been posited. It is formed from two propositions and a conclusion, as is evident here.

Its first proposition is: “Blessed is the man whose will is in the law of the Lord.”

Its second proposition is: “No one whose will is in the law of the Lord has walked in the counsel of the ungodly.”

The expected conclusion follows: “Therefore no blessed man has walked in the counsel of the ungodly.”

The diligent investigator will find this in various places, but we have judged that it should be presented more rarely, since many things must be said by us from different arts and disciplines together with the proposed exposition.

“And in his law he will meditate day and night.”

Notice that he says a second time, “in the law,” not “under the law,” because the one who despised sins was in the law. The rest of mortal humanity is rightly under the law, since they are bent beneath the weight of their transgressions. The law is so called because it binds our minds and holds them subject to its ordinances.

Yet he did not meditate on the law through letters but through the holiness of his purpose, as he will say in the thirty-ninth psalm: “I desired to do your will, O my God, and your law is in the midst of my heart” (Ps. XXXIX, 9). Thus both points have been established from one psalm: the beginning of the book must be understood as referring to him, and he is clearly shown always to have meditated on the Lord’s commandments.

In the seventy-seventh psalm also he says: “I will speak of propositions from the beginning” (Ps. LXXVII, 2). But when he says, “I will speak from the beginning,” he does not perhaps wish his own person to be passed over anywhere. Nevertheless, following the authority of various Fathers, we have assigned words both to the Church and to the prophet, and we have said that the most righteous people, as well as sinners, speak—showing them clearly in their proper places—so that the very variety of the matters may delight the hearing.

## Day and night

This phrase denotes continuous time [Col. 0030B]. But if one understands it literally, it is wholly inappropriate to suppose that someone should continually read or proclaim the law of the Lord day and night, since time must be allowed for the body to be refreshed and the necessity of sleep must be accommodated. Rather, the person is shown to meditate continually on the law who, conducting everything according to holiness, maintains heavenly purity in all things.

This certainly applies to the Lord Christ himself, the Head, although, as an example of his holiness, it also appears to be enjoined upon his members, as the Apostle says: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything to the glory of God” (1 Cor. X, 31). This continuity is also proclaimed elsewhere, as we read in Psalm 118: “Teach me your testimonies, O Lord, and I shall always seek your commandments in my heart.”

The pagans called the day *dies* from their divinities, that is, from the gods, from whom they are also known to have derived their name. Night (*nox*) is so called because it is harmful to our sight or to our activities.

## Verse 3

“And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters.”

Here an exceedingly glorious and singular happiness is now foretold: just as an admirable action has been described, so its prosperity is reported through a magnificent likeness. The Lord Christ is rightly, in my judgment, compared with a fruit-bearing tree, because of the cross which he undertook for the salvation of humanity. It is deservedly called the tree of life, since the Lord Christ, who is our life, was suspended upon it, and to the thief who confessed on that same cross it was said: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). Indeed, even today everyone who believes in it receives the gifts of eternal life.

Alternatively, as the historical account relates, there truly was a tree of everlasting life in paradise, had detestable disobedience not intervened. For how would death have gained entry if Adam had displayed the disposition of devotion? From this the most holy Fathers distilled the sweetest honey when they said: “He gave a command, so that he might discover free choice; he established a law, so that he might make him more cautious.” But Adam imprudently followed the enemy and unhappily abandoned the author of life [Note: [Col. 0029D] The manuscripts Aud., Bec., and Fisc. read: “and abandoned the happy author of life.”]. Then, deceived by a grievous fate, he lost the perpetual life which he was destined to possess and fell into the death which he did not possess.

But, to return to the principles of the comparison begun: when he says “planted,” that is, “established,” the tree of the cross was established by God, so that it might always flourish and grow in faith. This figure is called a *parable*, that is, a comparison through things unlike one another. Thus, in what follows, Christ is also compared with a mountain, a lion, and a worm.

### “Beside streams of waters”

He continues within the grace of the comparison. Just as flowing earthly water is the life of flourishing trees, so spiritual water inundates the sign of the cross, which is known to be the salvation of the souls of the faithful. This, then, is the water of which the Gospel says: “If you knew who it is who asks you for water, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John IV, 10), and so forth.

It is also worthwhile to consider why he said “beside streams of waters”: namely, so that neither excessive flooding would damage the tree nor, again, irrigation situated too far away [Col. 0031B] would dry it out.

## Verse 4

“Which shall give its fruit in its season.”

“He shall give fruit,” that is, he shall establish churches at the appropriate time—namely, when he received the mysteries of the blessed incarnation. O that wondrous fruit, which satisfied the human race with the sweetest faith! Hence, not to taste it is sin; indeed, it is rather a form of transgression to abstain from such food.

For *fruit* is so called from *enjoyment*. It should also be noted that he said “he shall give,” which belongs both to rational meaning and to the will of the one who offers. Although other trees also put forth and produce fruit, this one is properly said to give, because it is shown to bestow eternal rewards.

## Verse 5

“And its leaf shall not fall.”

That is, his word does not depart from the truth through any misfortune; rather, just as the leaves remaining on a palm tree endure, so these, fixed in the truth, persevere through sure promises [Note: [Col. 0031D] The manuscripts Aud., Bec., and Fisc. read: “so these too, fixed in truth.”], as it is written in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 15).

Observe also that the Lord’s words are compared with the leaves of a tree: just as those leaves protect the fruit, so these words preserve his promises. These are the spiritual waters; these are the salutary leaves, of which blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb; in the midst of its street, and on either side of the river, was the tree of life, producing fruit twelve times, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of that tree are appointed for the healing of the nations” (Rev. XXII, 1–2).

### “And everything whatever he does shall prosper”

This is most aptly set against Adam, whose deeds brought adversity upon us. For just as the Lord Christ bestowed the sweetness of salvation upon the world, so Adam inflicted the bitterness of death upon the human race.

This form of proclamation is therefore constructed in three ways: by saying what he avoided, by relating what he did, and, third, by indicating the end to which the fruit itself attained. But this has been stated briefly and moderately on account of the humility of the humanity he assumed. If, however, you wish to perceive his magnificence, hear the Apostle: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” [Col. 0032A] (Phil. II, 9).

And in the Apocalypse of John we read: “And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne, and of the living creatures and the elders; and their number was ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.’ And every creature that is in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that are in them, I heard saying: ‘To the one seated upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing, and honor, and glory, and power, forever and ever.’ And the four living creatures said: ‘Amen.’ And the elders fell down and worshiped” (Rev. V, 11ff.), and so forth.

The divine Scripture is full of such matters, because just as there was humility in the body he assumed, so after the Lord Christ’s resurrection his majesty was revealed. Now let us proceed to what remains.

## Verse 6

“Not so the impious, not so.”

He comes to the second part, where he recalls what the impious will suffer together with sinners, so that their conduct may be shunned once their punishment is known.

This figure is called *paradigm*. A *schema* is a figure of speech composed with elegance in the arrangement of words; a paradigm is a narrative through examples, encouraging or deterring someone. He encouraged when he said, “Blessed is the man,” and what follows; he deterred when he said, “Not so the impious, not so,” and so forth.

This is plainly a highly effective form of instruction: to invite through prosperity and frighten through contrary outcomes. Father Augustine likewise records this in his books *On Christian Doctrine*, saying (Book IV, chapter 4): “Therefore the interpreter and teacher of the divine Scriptures, the defender of right faith and the combatant against error, ought both to teach what is good and to unteach what is evil.”

He powerfully carries out this mode of instruction in Psalms 14, 36, 110, and 118, so that there may be distinction in the threatening of punishment and greatness always in the rewards.

Thus he says: “Not so the impious, not so,” because it will not be so with the impious as he said above. And so that you might believe it immovably, he demonstrated the firmness of the negation by repeating it. For if you inquire carefully into their place, hear John’s Apocalypse say: “And the devil who deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet are; and they will be tormented there day and night, forever and ever” (Rev.
