XX, 9–10)—which plainly concerns all the impious.

### “[They are] like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth”

The comparison is exceedingly appropriate. Dust is the disintegration of earth. And because an earthly human being, when puffed up by the deceptive wind of pride, is cast out from the solidity of the living earth like dust—since through his lightness he could not hold fast to the firmness of the commandments—he is rightly called dust, being driven about like a thin substance by the blasts of vices.

But we should not suppose that this most grievous condemnation is being compared with the playful tricks of winds, which transfer easily movable bodies into the ethereal breezes through sportive force. Here he wishes to show the ease of expulsion, not to lessen the severity of the peril.

The “face of the earth” signifies the surface of the land, where exceedingly fine dust can truly settle. The Greeks call this *epiphaneia* (“surface”), which possesses only length and breadth. It receives colors distinguished by varying qualities; it is capable of receiving the figures of geometrical science; and finally, upon it one may behold whatever can be seen by bodily eyes.

## Verse 7

“Therefore the impious shall not rise in judgment.”

The impious are those who, through the cruelty of their mind, in no way confess the holy Trinity, nor agree to obey the rules of the Old or New Testament [Note: [Col. 0033D] The manuscripts Aud., Bec., and Fisc. read: “through the belief of their mind”]; or, as the Apostle says, “Those who confess God in words but deny him in deeds” (Titus I, 16). These do not rise in judgment because they have already been condemned by their unbelief, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “But whoever does not believe in the Son is already condemned” (John III, 18) [Note: [Col. 0034D] The manuscripts Aud., Bec., and Fisc. read: “has already been judged.”].

For if to rise for judgment means to render an account to someone for his deeds, they are rightly said not to rise for judgment whom divine sentence is already known to have condemned. Catholic faith confesses that all will rise, as the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. XV, 51). The righteous will rise in order to judge; the sinner, in order to be judged; the impious, in order to be punished without judgment.

### “Nor sinners in the council of the righteous”

Sinners are those who are Christians by profession but are subject to lesser sins, from which the Lord’s Prayer is given to free them. The impious, however, are those who, ignorant of their own Creator, are polluted by various crimes—such as blasphemers, the impenitent, worshipers of idols, and those bound by principal vices.

There are therefore two kinds of sinners. The first remains in its offenses, with no atoning satisfaction having been completed; the other is forgiven its sins through the grace of confession, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1). The saints also belong to this number, since no one is without sin, as blessed John the Apostle says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I, 8).

Accordingly, he speaks of that first class of sinners, who were not worthy to be saved by any act of mercy. These will by no means judge with the righteous, a reward which the Lord promises by the evangelical word to his faithful alone. He says “in the council,” meaning “in the judgment,” because every right judgment takes place in council. *Council* is derived from *consulting*.

Above, however, “the council of the impious” was used improperly, because they too think that they are giving counsel, although they are known to handle each matter through a harmful scheme.

## Verse 8

“For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the impious shall perish.”

He said that the Lord knows the way of the good, but affirms that the path of the impious perishes—as though the Lord did not know both. This is spoken allegorically, so that the Lord knows what will remain in blessedness and does not know what will perish. For he himself will say to sinners at his judgment: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12).

If you wish to understand this literally, how could he fail to know those whom he created? Thus he also spoke to Adam after the sin: “Where are you, Adam?” (Gen. III, 9). This was not because God did not know that Adam was in paradise, but because Adam, having fallen, was rebuked as unworthy of divine knowledge.

“And the path of the impious shall perish.” For just as the way of the blessed is the Lord, so the path of sinners is known to be the devil, who will certainly perish when he is condemned to eternal punishment together with his followers.

A way (*via*) is so called because each traveler journeys along it. A path (*iter*) is as if “a repeated going,” because it is traversed again and again by walking. Yet you find both terms varied according to the character of the places. Above he spoke of the way of sinners, while “path” is used in a good sense in another psalm: “And there is a path in which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX, 23). Likewise the prophet Isaiah says: “I shall give the beginning to Zion, and I shall console Jerusalem on the way” (Isa. XLI, 27).

Now let us come to a kind of concluding mirror, so that the most beautiful face of the whole psalm may shine clearly before us.

## Conclusion of the psalm

This entire psalm belongs to moral instruction: through it the good are formed and the sinful mind is frightened. Nor is it without significance that the Lord Christ is placed at the beginning of the numbers.

Unity is singular, simple, and perfect; it needs nothing, remaining eternally in itself. From this fountain the multitude of numbers proceeds in such a way that, however multiplied, it is always recalled to unity; without it, calculation can neither begin anything nor advance.

Christ is therefore rightly placed at the beginning of calculation, because, as the Apostle says: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36). The Greeks call this Trinity a *monad*.

If a substance is incorporeal and immutable, it is understood to be God; if incorporeal and mutable, it is understood to be the soul; if both corporeal and mutable, it is understood to be the body. This monad, therefore, is explained by mathematicians through such a combination, as has been said.

Remember, however, that although the monad appears to be the source and beginning of number, it cannot itself be called a number. For whatever is more than one, as Nicomachus says, is already made countable. Number is a collection of units, or a heap of quantity poured forth from units. What we say is also made clear by the indication contained in the name itself: *number* is so called from multiplicity.

This discipline was not to be neglected even by our Fathers. It is true and immutable, and is diffused throughout all creatures according to the measure of their quantity. For it is written in Solomon that God made all things “in measure, number, and weight” (Wis. XI, 21).

I also think one should observe that, by a marvelous arrangement, all the succeeding matters ascend in sequence. In the first psalm, the bodily life of the Lord Christ is described; then the omnipotent nature of his divinity is subtly indicated. Third, he speaks of the multiplied peoples who were striving to extinguish him. Then the seven penitential psalms purify the hearts of the faithful. Afterward, through parables and figurative allusions, the succeeding drama proceeds, and nearly everything is referred through allegorical comparisons to the Lord the Savior; we shall point this out in its proper places [Col. 0035A].

After this, the prophet, celebrating the praises of the Lord Christ with marvelous variety, does not cease to proclaim the glory of his holiness until the end. Thus everything is known to have been spoken about him, for whose sake these matters have been undertaken.

# EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND PSALM

## A psalm of David

Although it is attested that in some manuscripts this psalm also has no title, which is why it is read in the Acts of the Apostles—“Why did the nations rage?” and so forth—as was said concerning the first psalm, nevertheless, if you pay close attention, there does not appear to be a contradiction.

It is said to have been placed as the first psalm, but it is first only by the inscription of its title. In sequence it is itself the second [Col. 0035B], while it is first in the title. By this example many things have been said which, although they differ from one another literally, are shown upon more careful investigation to be one—such as that broad field concerning the harmony of the Gospels.

Therefore it has been accepted by the approved practice of all the churches that the beginning of the titles should start here, where the text begins with a rebuke of the Jews. Consequently, it was fitting that this division should have its own title, since it is known to be separated from the preceding text.

But since it has been explained why this division received its title, let us now, with the Lord’s assistance, discuss its words.

A psalm is a hymn composed according to the law of a particular meter, which is known to indicate to us heavenly power in the likeness of the instrument mentioned above. As for David, although he appears through divine inspiration to be the author of this entire work, his name is nevertheless appropriately placed in particular passages.

But since, as we have said, the interpretation of names is shown to reveal more hidden matters to us, as the interpreters of Hebrew names have preferred to teach, *David* signifies “strong of hand” or “desirable.” This can suit no one more appropriately than the omnipotent Christ, who is truly most mighty and must be sought with the highest desire.

Accordingly, David here is to be understood as the Lord Christ, of whose passion the prophet speaks; and the Lord himself will speak his own words. This is found very frequently in the following psalms, so that in the name David the Lord Christ may be understood.

And lest the Christian mind, which must believe everything truly and firmly, waver amid heretical controversies, we shall conclude the definition of the name itself with a brief statement supported by the authority of the Fathers.

Let us therefore hear blessed and most learned Augustine speaking in his exposition of the Evangelist John (Treatise 78 on John): “Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father; and the human, by which the Father is greater than he. Yet both together, not two, but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity; and therefore Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh.”

When this truth has been recognized, we rightly avoid deadly errors.

## Division of the psalm

The form of this psalm has been elegantly shaped in four sections.

In the first, the prophet speaks about the Jews on account of Christ’s passion. In the second, the words are those of the deranged Jews. In the third, the words are those of the Lord the Savior concerning his omnipotent kingdom and his ineffable generation, insofar as human smallness can receive it. In the fourth, the prophet speaks, admonishing the peoples to come to the Christian faith once they have recognized the Lord’s majesty, knowing that they will perish from the righteous way unless they grasp the truest discipline of the Catholic religion. This is also narrated repeatedly in the speech of the other prophets.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1

“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things?”

This figure is called in Greek *erotema*, and in Latin *interrogatio*, “question.” It occurs in many ways. To mention a few: we ask when we wish to know something we did not know, as in the future psalm: “How many are the days of your servant, when will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me?” (Ps. CXVIII, 84).

We also ask about things we certainly know, as in: “Is there among the idols of the nations one who gives rain, or will the heavens give rain unless you will it?” (Jer. XIV, 22).

There is also a question used for accusation, as it is employed here. The prophet rebukes the peoples for raging against the Lord the Savior, although they had no grounds for anger. Raging is properly characteristic of wild beasts, and is rightly attributed to those who, setting reason aside, are inflamed by beastlike fury.

Since we will frequently need to introduce figures of speech, it is necessary at the outset to give a definition of the matter, so that when the term is mentioned it may be clearly recognized.

A figure, as the name itself indicates, is a certain shaping of speech removed from ordinary usage, which continually presents something with a face to the inward eyes. According to the tradition of our elders, we may call it display and form. Father Augustine also most beautifully counts these among the modes of expression.

Nor should it trouble us that, although the events concerned the Jews, “nations” and “peoples” appear to be set in the plural. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “For truly they gathered together in this city against your holy Son, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the nations and the peoples of Israel” (Acts IV, 27).

They “meditated on vain things” because they frequently repeated the divine Scriptures without the fruit of understanding. In countless passages it had been prophesied that the Lord the Savior, the Messiah, would come, but they, deceived by the greatest error, believed that he had not come and was still to come. They therefore rightly meditated on vain things, since they could in no way understand the fruitful character of his advent.

### Verse 2

“The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.”

“Stood forth” does not signify presence but intention. For it is certain that the Lord’s passion did not in any way take place in the presence of kings.

By the kings of the earth he wishes Herod to be understood, who, in persecuting the Lord, killed the infants; and the other Herod, his nephew, who agreed with Pontius Pilate in the Savior’s death. They are rightly said to have stood forth because, consenting with sacrilegious minds, they joined together in one crime.

By the rulers he means the Pharisees. This word sometimes signifies kings and sometimes those who are first. A ruler (*princeps*) is so called as if he were “taking the first place.”

“They gathered together” means into one will, not into one assembly, for they are read to have plotted this crime in various councils.

But so that you might understand that an injury against the Son can also affect the Father, he included both: “against the Lord,” that is, the Father; “and against his Christ,” that is, the Son, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V, 23).

### Verse 3

“Let us tear apart their bonds.”

These are the words of the deranged Jews. They called them bonds, although they rather loosened sins. They thought they would tear apart these bonds if, with criminal intent, they rushed against the teacher of the law and his apostles.

For “their” relates to Christ and to his apostles, who are shown to be bound by the Lord’s rule under the plural number.

### “And let us cast their yoke away from us”

They remained in a comparison worthy of foolish beasts: they did not cast off the yoke unless they had first torn apart its bonds, deceived entirely by their most vain will. For although the yoke of the Lord the Savior is easy and his burden light (Matt. XI, 30), they thought his rule exceedingly burdensome. Thus they unhappily hastened to cast away what could have contained and governed them.

### “He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them”

Here “the heavens” signifies holy men, just as he himself will say elsewhere: “The heavens declare the glory of God” [Col. 0037C] (Ps. XVIII, 2). He most appropriately chose to mention them, so as to confound all the more fully the pride and wickedness of the impious.

“Laugh” and “mock,” and similar expressions, are to be understood according to our customary usage. The Lord does not literally laugh with his lungs or mock with his face; rather, he accomplishes spiritually through his power whatever he determines.

This figure is called in Greek *metonymia*, and in Latin *transnominatio*, “renaming,” whenever we indicate the meaning of a thing in various ways through words that are foreign and transferred.

The prophet therefore rightly declares that the Jews’ faithlessness is to be mocked: they attempted to bring false witnesses against the truth; they preferred to crucify the Lord of glory; and, foolishly, they sealed the tomb’s enclosure after the omnipotent Christ was to rise again. Such a mass of crimes was undertaken against the Lord’s power, senselessly and in vain.

### Verse 5

“Then he shall speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he shall trouble them.”

But lest we think that the impious are merely to be mocked, he now recalls that they are to be gravely rebuked. “Anger” and “wrath” are terms similar to those used above.

For God judges with tranquility and troubles while preserving mercy—not growing hot through some movement arising within him against the wicked, but withholding from them the moments of his grace. The retribution of sins is therefore called God’s anger. The blessed Divinity does not suffer agitation, for it always remains the same, eternal, and immovable.

This change of condition belongs to human frailty, so that someone may be made sad from joyful, angry from placated, and offended from benevolent. “Then he shall speak” signifies the time when he will come to judge the world. Anger and wrath are therefore rightly mentioned when everything suitable to the merits of obstinate sinners is rendered to them.

### Verse 6

“But I have been established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain.”

Up to this point the prophet has spoken in his own person. Now, through a figure called in Greek *exallage* and in Latin *permutatio*, “change,” he reports the words of the Lord the Savior, who testifies that he has been established as king by the Father.

This was also written about him in the title of his passion: “The King of the Jews” (John XIX, 19). Pilate would not permit this to be erased, even though he handed him over to the Jews to be crucified. The Magi also professed this when they inquired: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matt. II, 2).

It follows: “upon Zion, his holy mountain.” This name is in itself richly capable of signifying many things. At one time it signifies the Church, at another the Lord the Savior himself, and at another the future Jerusalem. Since this term must frequently be repeated, it is more fitting that it be explained in each place with an appropriate account.

Here we must understand Zion as the Church, which he calls a mountain because of the eminence of its honor and the firmness of its faith. In Hebrew, Zion is said to mean “watchtower.” This is appropriately applied to the Church, because, sufficiently instructed concerning future hopes, it surveys the Lord’s promises through the foresight of the mind; it does not glory so much in present benefits as in future ones.

Zion is therefore rightly called the Church, because its contemplation is fixed upon that contemplative virtue. Christ is truly king over it, since it is governed and ordered by him.

### “Proclaiming the commandment of the Lord”

He did this by teaching the Gospel, so that through his manifestation he might complete the preaching of the prophets.

### Verse 7

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

“The Lord” signifies the Father, but he himself is also Lord, as he will say in Psalm 109: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1).

Let us also attend to the words he has set down: “He said to me, ‘You are my Son,’” which he was also to say to him after his baptism: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

And so that you might understand Christ to be one person—that is, the Word made flesh—he added: “Today I have begotten you.” This has nothing in common with the others; it belongs wholly to the only-begotten Son and could have served to designate and impress upon us the author of all things.

By saying “today,” he demonstrates the co-eternity of his majesty. For with God, “today” does not begin with any beginning or end with any end. There is no “was” or “will be” there; rather, he always remains and always is. Whatever you say, he is “today,” just as in Exodus he commanded Moses to say about him: “Go,” he said, “and say to the children of Israel: ‘I am who I am’; and ‘He who is’ has sent me to you” (Exod. III, 14).

Therefore he wished his eternity to be indicated by the designation of the present time. The present tense, expressed by “today,” is known to be used for perpetuity as a characteristic feature of the divine Scriptures.

“I have begotten you” signifies that birth of which Isaiah says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8). Light from light, omnipotent from omnipotent, true God from true God: “From whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things” (Rom. XI, 36).

Writing to the Hebrews, the Apostle says of him: “He is the radiance of his glory and the form of his substance, upholding all things by the word of his power; having made purification for sins, he sat at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” (Heb. I, 3–5), and so forth—the passage goes on to speak of the magnificence of the Lord Christ.

Therefore let empty disputes cease, and let the faithlessness of the Arian doctrine be silenced. This is what Catholic faith and a sound mind understand: the only-begotten Son cannot be separated from the Father by nature, by time, or by power.

It is also worthwhile to consider how, in these two verses, through the Father’s words, he wished to declare to human beings what he is. It was not possible to reach his proper nature substantially through genus and differences, since such a procedure appears to apply more suitably to creatures than to the Creator.

For how could any genus be found above his nature, when he is known to be the author of all things? This definition is therefore unlike the definition called substantial, which descends to the proper characteristic through established differences. It cannot be called substantial, since the substance of God cannot in any way be comprehended.

Nevertheless, as some have thought, God can be defined in this way: “God is an incorporeal, simple, and immutable substance.”

Let us now investigate the members of this definition in the finest detail. It first says: “But I have been established as king by him.” Yet earthly kings are also established by the Lord. It adds: “Upon Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the commandment of the Lord.” Prophets and preachers of the Church have also been chosen.

It follows: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son.’” Israel too was called a son, as in Exodus Pharaoh is told: “I said to you, ‘Let my firstborn son Israel go,’ and you refused” (Exod. IV, 23).

Thus nothing so far could have clearly designated the person of the only-begotten Son. But it is added: “Today I have begotten you.” This was declared of no other; only he was begotten without time, through whom all things were created.

In this way secular learning drew this most truthful and beautiful definition into its own schools, calling it substantial—a definition above which a genus could be found.

### Verse 8

“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.”

This is said according to an assumed condition and a servile form, because he is the Son of the Virgin. Whatever Christ received in time, he acquires according to his humanity what he did not possess. Here he is commanded to ask according to the lower nature and to possess what he receives.

According to the power of the Word, however, everything that the Father has the Son has equally; nor does he need to ask for what he is known to possess together with the Father.

“Nations” signifies peoples divided throughout the whole world, whom blood embraces as distinct and separate [Note: [Col. 0039D] The manuscripts read: “whom distinct and separate blood embraces.”]. A nation (*gens*) is so called from *genus*, “kind” or “stock.”

It follows: “Your inheritance.” When he says “your,” he shows that nature of perfect divinity in Christ. For the very word “your” demonstrates the incarnation of the Word, so that nothing is understood to be divided when all things are possessed by one majesty, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Everything that the Father has is mine, and everything of the Father is mine” (John XVI, 15).

Inheritance (*haereditas*) is derived from *heres*, that is, “lord,” because one rules over it with free authority.

### “And your possession to the ends of the earth”

Here it is revealed that all nations will believe in Christ’s name, through whom the world, its superstitions having been cast out, has been reconciled to God.

When he also says here “your possession,” human nature received what divinity had always possessed; for what he already had could not be given to his majesty.

“Boundary” (*terminus*) is so called, as some have wished, because the stone itself lacks something less than three feet. But I do not think “the ends of the earth” should be passed over casually. The ends of the earth are those which encircle and enclose the land, so that not only dry ground but also the surrounding substance of the entire air and the integrity of all creatures might be signified.

Thus he himself briefly comprehended the matter in the Gospel, saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18). The Apostle likewise says: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 10).

### Verse 9

“You shall rule them with an iron rod.”

The manner of his kingdom is now described. If this is understood literally, it is of little usefulness to perceive that something is to be broken and diminished. But first observe what he says: “You shall rule them,” so that he might remove the power of tyrannical domination. Those are ruled who attain the gifts of salvation.

The rod signifies royal power, by which the vengeance of correction is promised to sinners. It is “iron” not because God uses a metallic rod for vengeance, but because the hardness of iron is appropriately suited to the rigor of justice.

This is the same rod of which he will say in Psalm 44: “Your rod is a rod of uprightness, the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV, 7). What this rod does, however, he explains next.

This is the rod that breaks in order to give life; this is the staff that sustains the weak; this is the scepter that makes the living out of the dead. In ordinary human usage, a rod (*virga*) is so called because it governs by its force and does not allow those who lean upon it to bend or fall.

And like a potter’s vessel you shall break them. That is, through the zeal of conversion you will crush in them earthly desires and a life resembling the mire of the old man. Observe also how, in these comparisons themselves, the causes of things are aptly expressed in each individual word. He called the Lord’s power an iron rod; the proud peoples, a potter’s vessel, which, as soon as it has been struck, is scattered into the smallest pieces. The sinner is therefore rightly compared to a clay vessel, so that both his easy breaking and his clay-like life might be indicated. But he is then re-formed for the better, when, with divine grace assisting, he is led into the spiritual man. [Col. 0041A]

**Verse 10. “And now, kings, understand.”** He comes to the third member, in which the prophet now admonishes the human race humbly to obey the Creator, after the terrifying mysteries have been revealed. Here arises a most beautiful deliberative mode of speech. For when mortal hearts have been stunned by such a mystery being proclaimed, a most salutary and necessary exhortation follows: one must serve the true Lord with fear and trembling. He shows, by what is useful and honorable—matters of the greatest importance in deliberations—that what has been said is expedient.

The useful consideration is: “Lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way.” The honorable consideration is: “Blessed are all who trust in him.” Thus the deliberative mode of speech is completed by a perfect argument. Let us now return to the exposition of the words.

“Kings” means that we should understand dominators of vices, who, by the Lord’s help, are able both to understand these things and to carry them out. For it is not always necessary to understand “kings” as men clothed in purple. Those whose condition is private are also called kings, as the Apostle says: “Already you reign without us; and would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you” (1 Cor. 4:8) [MSS. A, B, F: *regnare possimus*, “so that we may be able to reign”].

**“Be instructed, you who judge the earth.”** To instruct is to teach; for the word itself signifies acquired knowledge: one who is *rudis* is called “new” or “untrained.” An *eruditus*—as though “raised up from the untrained state” [the edition reads, “from the countryside”]—is one who has been separated from ignorance and placed within the bounds of learning. This is appropriately said to those who have already subdued carnal sins. They judge the earth well when, with vices restrained, they impose the precepts of the law upon their bodies, with the Lord’s favor. [Col. 0041C] “Earth” (*terra*) is so called from *terere*, “to wear down,” because it is worn away by the footsteps of those who travel across it. [Col. 0041C]

**Verse 11. “Serve the Lord in fear.”** A brief and full admonition, by which God the Lord is served with loving fear. For just as careless security admits faults, so desirable fear continually excludes sins. And lest the service of God perhaps be thought too harsh or too sorrowful, he added:

**“And rejoice in him with trembling.”** For the fear of the Lord leads not to misery but to joy, since it makes people blessed and renders them holy. Again, lest this rejoicing become careless, he added “with trembling,” so that the two joined together might fittingly express heavenly reverence.

**Verse 12. “Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way.”** “Embrace discipline” is a magnificent expression, as though discipline were a shield’s defensive protection, destined to be useful against harmful vices. The prophet then added the benefit of this most excellent action, saying: “Lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way.” He said “lest,” because of the Lord’s patience, by which he long endures those who transgress. “And you perish from the right way” means: from Christ, the heavenly King, who is the Way of those who walk rightly toward life, the Leader of those who go forward, and the Path of those hastening toward blessedness. As he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He is the Way because of the incarnation, through which he offers the good an example of living; the Truth because of judgment; and the Life because of his divinity.

**Verse 13. “When his anger has blazed up in a short time.”** This is a metaphor drawn from a fire, which burns more fiercely when it has received fuel for its consumption. He said “in a short time” because, when he has decreed punishment, he vindicates. There is no indication in him of one disposition and another action; rather, what he decrees and what he does occur together. Observe also that above, concerning the present age and his endurance, he used “lest”; but concerning future judgment he said “in a short time,” so that his mercy might now be declared and his power then. In that judgment there will not be a separate examination of each person carried out successively; rather, all things will occur together in a single moment, just as he acts and judges. It is well said, “When he has blazed up,” because that end of his great patience is thereby declared, beyond which no one is permitted to hope for anything.

**“Blessed are all who trust in him.”** A fitting conclusion: after saying many things, he indicates toward what everyone ought to hasten. To trust in him is already a reward, because that very trust comes through God’s grace, as the Apostle says: “From whom comes both the willing and the accomplishing” (Phil. 2:13).

**Conclusion of the Psalm**

Now, after completing the exposition, let us briefly bring forward again this psalm, rich in heavenly mysteries, so that its power may clearly be understood once its members have been recognized. Let us consider how great is the grace of divinity with which the Psalmist is adorned. Before the Lord’s words he proclaimed; again, after the Lord’s sayings, he speaks. When he precedes, he is a prophet; when he follows, an apostle: for he predicted what was to come with complete faith, and, following after, agreed with perfect truth. The Lord himself, standing in the midst, as though resounding from heaven, disclosed to us the secrets of his power, so that, according to our capacity, we might learn profitably both the glory of his divinity and the mysteries of his incarnation.

In this second number, beautifully composed from two monads, the two natures—unconfused and perfect—are most fittingly set in the one person of the Lord Christ. One is the nature by which he reigns, the other that by which he serves; the first is creator, the latter created. Therefore the nature that assumed is impassible, while the nature assumed is passible. For, as the Fathers teach, let us attribute insults to the flesh and miracles to the divinity; let us distinguish the natures by understanding, and avoid harmful errors.

The divinity united humanity to itself in such a way that it could in no manner be confused with humanity, but that both should remain unconfused and united. For although the dispensation of the incarnation was glorified after the resurrection, it nevertheless remained in the truth of humanity. When, after the resurrection, he himself said to the apostle Thomas, “Put out your hand and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (John 20:27); when after the resurrection he took and ate a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb (Luke 24:42); and when it is read in the Acts of the Apostles, “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11); and when the prophet also says concerning sinners, “They will see the one whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10)—since they cannot behold his majesty, for that will be granted only to the blessed, as it is said in the Gospel, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matt. 5:8)—it is exceedingly destructive not to believe that the two perfect and united natures remain in Christ. Truth itself wished to proclaim this through so many examples.

This is affirmed by Father Athanasius of Alexandria, Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose of Milan, Augustine and Jerome, Cyril, and many other Fathers, in order also to remove completely the occasion for a most empty dispute. Pope Leo, together with the holy synod of Chalcedon, decreed and established this (Part II, session 2): whoever wishes to be Catholic must proclaim one Christ from two natures, and in two united and perfect natures. If, by the Lord’s assistance, we store these truths in our memory, we shall always walk according to ecclesiastical rules. [Col. 0043B]

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM III

**A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Abessalom his son**

While Abessalom was cruelly pursuing his father David, he was carried by the force of a mule into a dense oak tree; its branches caught his neck, and he was left suspended in the air, prefiguring in a certain way the Lord’s betrayer. Just as Judas, entangled in a noose, ended his life, so David’s persecutor expired with his throat constricted.

According to the testimony of the history of Kings, this psalm is fifty events later, since the persecution by his son Abessalom is known to have occurred after the sins of adultery and murder. Yet it is shown to have been suitably assigned its number because of its meaning. It ought to have held the third place because it contained within itself both the power of the holy Trinity and the mysteries of the three-day resurrection. For David’s deliverance fittingly signifies the Lord’s resurrection, so that, strengthened by such an example, the minds of Christians may rise steadfastly in adverse circumstances.

A similar case is that the Octateuch is read before Job [MSS. S., Aud., Bec., and Fisc.: “the Pentateuch is read,” etc.], although Moses is known to have lived many years after Job. Therefore the order of readings is often arranged not according to the sequence of historical times, but according to the character of what is said. Remember, however, that there are other psalms which briefly touch upon the Lord’s passion and resurrection, while others declare them more distinctly and openly; but the present psalm is the first of those that speak of these matters briefly.

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0043D]

This entire psalm is appropriately applied to the person of Christ the Lord. His person is the power of almighty divinity and the humility of the assumed humanity, subsisting not in a confused mixture but in an indivisible union.

First, therefore, he speaks to the Father, reproaching the persecutors who were uttering irreligious words against him. In the second place, the faithful people are instructed not to fear death, when he consoles them by the example of their author with the surest hope of resurrection.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1. “Lord, how many are those who trouble me?”** This appears to have an almost similar beginning to the second psalm. But there the question is one of reproach; here he marvels that peoples have been stirred up against him, though he is known to have come to save them. By saying, “They trouble me,” he shows that he grieved even more deeply over the blindness of those who rejected their salvation with obstinate minds, as he will say in the thirty-fourth psalm: “They repaid me evil for good, barrenness to my soul” (Ps. 34:12).

**“Many rise up against me; many say to my soul.”** There were so many that even Judas the betrayer, one of the disciples, was added to their number. By repeating “many” so often, he reveals the bitter multitude of the impious, who could not become fewer despite their most densely formed conspiracy. This figure of speech is called *epembasis*, repeating words in the interest of enumeration so as to increase the matter of which he speaks.

**“There is no salvation for him in his God.”** This refers to those words of the Jews: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27:42). The Father was thought not to love the Son whom he permitted to be killed according to the flesh. O most wicked and foolish saying of the impious crowd! Was the redemption of the world to be attributed to weakness? Insatiable death could not otherwise be conquered unless Life entered the gates of its tyranny. Thus darkness cannot remain when the presence of light has driven it out.

**Verse 2. “But you, Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.”** “Protector” is spoken according to the form of the servant; for the assumption of a human being is the Word made flesh. Therefore the flesh, which the almighty Word assumed, calls him its glory and the lifter-up of its head, so that the divine and human substance might be one person without any confusion.

This also applies to the destruction of the Pelagians, who think that a human being can accomplish something good by himself. For who, I ask, is sufficient for doing good without the generosity of divine grace, when human nature, through the grace by which it has been united to God, has been placed at the Father’s right hand? Blessed Augustine explained this more fully and usefully, in his customary manner, in the *Enchiridion* (chap. 35 and following).

A most beautiful figure is formed here, called in Greek *auxesis* (“increase” or “amplification”): by adding certain names, it gathers together increases of meaning in each member. For he says: “But you, Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.”

The Apostle also indicates this more extensively when he says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8:35), and so forth. Near to this is the figure called *climax*, in Latin *gradatio* (“gradation”), when, once certain steps have been set out, the expression continually increases, whether in praise or in blame. The difference between the two figures is that *auxesis* increases the matter without any repetition of the name, whereas in a *climax* it is necessary for the final word placed in the first clause to be repeated in every way in the following member, as in the Apostle’s words: “Knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance proven character, and proven character hope; but hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:4–5). [Col. 0045A]

**Verse 3. “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.”** When he says “my,” he demonstrates the most holy purity of his own prayer. No image of fantasy could obstruct its integrity, as weakness of the flesh often steals upon other mortals. What he says, “With my voice I cried to the Lord,” is explained by the Gospel words in which the Son says: “Father, glorify your Son” [the edition reads *Pater, clarifica Filium* rather than *Pater, glorifica Filium*] (John 17:1), and so forth. By saying “my,” he indicates that he himself also spoke through the prophets.

What follows, “and he heard me from his holy mountain,” is likewise explained by the Gospel text, where a voice came to him: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John 12:29). Through “mountain,” the Lord himself, his saints, and the Church are all most fittingly signified in different places. Here, however, it should be understood as the mountain—that is, the most exalted summit of divinity—as another psalm says: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 36:6). For it was fitting that the nature of the assumed humanity, which on earth displayed a singular example of patience, should receive in heaven supremacy over all creatures.

**Verse 4. “I slept and was overcome with sleep, and I rose, because the Lord received me.”** He comes to the second part, in which the hearts of those who doubt are strengthened so that they may believe that the one whom they were going to see crucified by the hands of the impious would immediately rise again.

“I slept,” he said, because he rose quickly. This sleep is the sleep of life, in which there is not the end of life but a temporary rest. “I was overcome with sleep” signifies a secure repose—not like that of the impious, who are shaken in death and continually disturbed by the consciousness of their sins. This sleep was the blessed slumber of the sacred body.

To rise means to rise with eagerness, since the flesh, having laid aside mortality, took on immortality and everlasting glory. But he clearly explains why he rose: “Because the Lord received me.” The nature of humanity could not have risen by its own power unless divine omnipotence had received it, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

**Verse 5. “I will not fear the thousands of people surrounding me.”** He could not fear the wicked people, since he had protection in his divinity. For it is written in the Gospel that, during his passion, a great multitude of people surrounded him. When he says, “I will not fear,” he does not mean that he would not die; rather, he could not fear the death that he knew would last three days and benefit the world.

**Verse 6. “Rise, Lord; save me, my God, because you have struck all those who oppose me without cause.”** This does not mean that God is awakened from sleep or from lying down. Rather, it is customary in the divine Scriptures to express a cause through *tropology*, speaking of God in terms drawn from our own custom. A trope is an expression transferred from the place in which it is proper to another place in which it is not proper.

“Save me, my God” is said concerning the resurrection. He who was destined to benefit the human race could not be permitted to decline into the setting of this life. “Those who oppose me” refers not only to death but also to heretical disputes, whose adherents, without any devotion to truth, attack Catholic rules with perverse doctrines. And rightly are such people struck with blindness of mind, since they have mingled themselves with perverse desires.

**“You have crushed the teeth of sinners.”** That is, the biting words of those who slander, who speak against divine power with wicked doctrines. “Teeth” are so called from *demere*, “to take away” [MSS. Aud., Bec., and Fisc.: “Teeth are so called from *edere*, ‘to eat’].” [Col. 0046B]

Therefore the teeth of slanderers are very aptly called tongues’ teeth: just as teeth take away pieces of food, so these people, by means of slander, gnaw away at human reputations. This may also be applied to the Jews, who said: “If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27:42). “You have crushed” means “you have reduced to nothing.” In truth, they were crushed when they recognized that the one whom they had attempted to slaughter, despising his humanity, had risen to glory.

**Verse 7. “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.”** This sentence is spoken against those whose teeth he previously said had been crushed. By declaring, “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” he confounds those who thought, with contemptuous presumption, that they could tear salvation away from Christ as though he were merely an earthly man. Why do you labor in vain, impious ones? How can eternal life be destroyed, or salvation in any way be taken away from the Savior?

“Your blessing is upon your people.” In one sentence he both commands human beings what they ought to believe and assures them of what they can receive from him.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This psalm is brief, yet it destroys the greatest error of the pagans, who think that the glory of heavenly majesty could not descend to the humility of suffering. They are fools, and their understanding is confounded by the very event through which the world is known to have been delivered, as the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1:15).

Let us now consider how the true order of heavenly philosophy has been set forth: the first psalm of Christ the Lord contains the moral part; the second, the natural part—that is, the substance of humanity and divinity; and the third, speaking of his resurrection, contains, in a certain sense, the contemplative part. This pattern runs through all the divine Scriptures.

Thus also the patriarch Isaac dug three wells, demonstrating that the Lord’s commandments are contained in a threefold teaching. Wisdom likewise admonishes us (Prov. 22:20) to inscribe these things for ourselves in the heart threefold, and so forth. In the subsequent psalms the reader will easily recognize these parts, whether mixed together or set out individually, even without being prompted. Do not frequently demand such explanations from us, since many things must newly be said.

The number of this psalm is taught by the holy Trinity. Although it possesses the nature of inseparable unity, it is nevertheless plainly constituted by three persons.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM IV

**For the end. A psalm of David. A song.**

Let us subtly examine what these words, which we have stated to be the most truthful indicators of the psalms, announce to us individually. “For the end” does not now signify the consumption of something, but the perfection of spiritual realities. For, as the Apostle says, “The end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4), and he is the glorious perfection of all good things.

Therefore, what is set down as “For the end” should be understood as referring to Christ the Lord. Or, as some prefer, it should be believed to have been said concerning us: “Upon whom, according to the same Apostle, the end of the ages has come” (1 Cor. 10:11). It must nevertheless be understood that it cannot refer to an ending, since the beginnings of the work itself still appear to be present.

A psalm is, as we have said, a musical instrument with a head of sounds, by which divine praises were sung. A song, however, is what resounded with human voices in praise of things above. These expressions therefore appear to have been joined because the songs were sung with harmonious voices both on musical instruments and by choirs of psalm-singers, as heavenly sacrifices. By all these words we are accordingly admonished that this song is to be understood as spoken about Christ the Lord.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the entire psalm the words are those of holy Mother Church. She is not formed in our hearts by a fantastic imagination, like a homeland, a city, or something similar that has no existing personhood. Rather, the Church is the assembly of all the faithful saints: one soul and one heart, the bride of Christ, the Jerusalem of the age to come.

Concerning her, the Lord Jesus says in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1) [Ms. Sang.: “Let him kiss me from the kiss of his mouth”]; and elsewhere: “Who is this who comes up, made white?” (Song 8:5); and: “My dove is one, my bride is one” (Song 6:8). Therefore it is impious to introduce any doubt here, where such truth is known to bear witness through so many testimonies.

Accordingly, under the figure of *mythopoeia* (“personification”), let us say that the Church speaks, since this figure is always known to be applied to quite definite persons. In the first part she asks that her prayer be heard, reproaching unbelievers because, while worshiping false gods, they neglected the worship of the true God. In the second part she admonishes the whole human race that, after abandoning deceptive superstition, it ought to offer a sacrifice of righteousness. And in order to convert the minds of the Gentiles through a promise, she recalls the great benefits that the Lord has granted to Christians.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1. “When I called upon you, you heard me, O God of my righteousness; in tribulation you enlarged me. Have mercy on me, Lord, and hear my prayer.”** [Edition: *Cum invocarem, exaudivit me Deus justitiae meae* (“When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me”).]

Let us consider what it means that Mother Church, in one and the same verse, both says that she has been heard and again asks to be heard. She signifies that this is the proper form of perfect prayer: even when the desires we have requested are granted, we should always be heard with worthy earnestness. We, however, should continually ask, as the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in all things” (1 Thess. 5:17–18).

“God of my righteousness”: the Church rightly speaks thus, since she confesses, in orthodox understanding, the unity and omnipotence of the Trinity. We also learn from sacred reading that her individual members may speak similarly. Thus Job says: “Attend to my innocence” (Job 27:5); the apostle Paul says: “He will render to me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4:8); and the prophet will say in the seventh psalm: “If there is iniquity in my hands” (Ps. 7:4). This does not mean that they were in every respect without sin, but that there are certain actions in which faithful people clearly appear innocent.

It follows: “In tribulation you enlarged me.” Tribulation is what always enlarges the Church, when at the same time confessors are made, martyrs are crowned, and the entire multitude of the righteous is continually increased through afflictions.

She added: “Have mercy on me, Lord, and hear my prayer.” The pious mother said that mercy should be shown to her if her prayer were heard on behalf of her children, because whatever is granted to the members is unquestionably granted to the whole body.

**Verse 2. “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?”** Since in the preceding verse she prayed for us, here she addresses the human race through *energia* (“forceful address”), so that it might not remain in the gravest error through the worship of demons, and so that the prayer poured out on its behalf might be heard. Otherwise, whoever does not abandon the fellowship of sinners renders the prayers offered for him ineffectual.

It follows: “How long will you be heavy of heart?” He rightly said that they had long been heavy of heart, since, after the preaching of truth, they chose instead to worship idols of falsehood. Such is the Gospel saying: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do what was required will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47).

At first the world was justly scourged with few blows, because it was shown to be ignorant of its Lord. After the coming of its Creator, however, it will most justly be beaten with many blows, because it continued to seek the songs of idols.

It follows: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” “Vanity” is indeed a general name for vices; but that is properly called vain which is judged alien to God. For just as trusting in divinity is fruitful steadfastness, so deviating from it is fleeting vanity, as Isaiah says: “Worshiping vain and false things, they have abandoned your mercy” (Isa. 2:8–9).

Those who burned with the most shameful love of idols are therefore reproved, and the words must be pronounced as though he were saying: “Why do you love the vanity by which you perish?” We ought to love what is beneficial, not what is harmful, since we should rather detest the things by which the punishment of eternal condemnation afflicts us. “You seek falsehood”—something you ought not to desire but to flee. This falsehood signifies idols, which rightly received such a name because they have been set up against the dignity of truth.

**Verse 3. “Know that the Lord has magnified his holy one”** [MSS. Aud., Bec., Fisc., and the edition read *mirificavit* (“made wondrous”) for *magnificavit* (“magnified”)] “the Lord will hear me when I cry to him.” He remains in his salutary reproach, so that he may turn the hearts of the foolish toward the devotion of true religion after their evil has been shattered. He announces to them the mystery of truth, so that they may not refuse reverently to receive the holy incarnation.

“His holy one” refers to the Lord Christ, just as the Truth elsewhere confesses concerning himself: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. 86:2). He added: “The Lord will hear me when I cry to him.” He rightly trusted that he would be heard, since he proclaimed to the peoples that the holy Lord should be magnified. “When I cry,” he says, that is, when I beseech the divinity through good works. For that is the cry which reaches God silently and causes those who steadfastly devote themselves to good works to be heard.

**Verse 4. “Be angry, and do not sin; what you say in your hearts, be pierced with remorse over upon your beds.”** This is appropriately applied to the Jews: if they happened to become angry, they should at least refrain from unlawful attempts. Yet it is also suitably understood in general. Anger is pardonable when it does not reach the execution of its indignation, as it is written: “Better is one who overcomes anger than one who captures a city” (Prov. 16:32).

Therefore an instruction for healing is applied: if we are already angry, we must not sin through unconsidered recklessness. Because of human frailty we cannot have the heated movement of the soul entirely under our control; yet, with God’s grace assisting, we restrain it through disciplined reason. Thus the blessed Prophet permitted what belongs to ordinary human custom, but prohibited what belongs to guilt.

For if we become angry and are not restrained by consideration of the Lord, but are prevented from fulfilling our intention by some obstacle of necessity, it is nevertheless clear that we bear the guilt of the deed, even if we are unable to accomplish what we wished.

Or, as some prefer, we ought to become angry at past sins so that we may escape present wickedness. For we cannot avoid recent offenses unless we condemn what is old through laudable hatred. What else is repentance than becoming angry with oneself, so that one may shudder at what one has done and exact punishment from oneself, lest the Judge, rather than oneself, become angry and inflict it?

He added: “What you say in your hearts, be pierced with remorse over upon your beds,” showing that the Lord knows the secret thoughts of human beings. He says, “What you say in your heart”—things you certainly do not think are heard—and therefore you believe them hidden because they have not been made public by the utterance of speech.

It follows: “Upon your beds be pierced with remorse.” The dwelling-place of wild animals is properly called a *cubile* (“bed” or “lair”), from *cubare*, “to lie down.” He therefore aptly calls fierce thoughts “beds,” although the expression is sometimes used figuratively in a good sense, as in the saying concerning the saints: “They will rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. 149:5).

“Be pierced with remorse” signifies, “Do penance.” For the desired conversion of souls occurs through a certain piercing of remorse, as though he were saying: “Abandon your evil thoughts before you commit crimes.”

Then follows the silence of the *diapsalma*. We have rightly placed a division here, since another subject is known to begin. Having laid aside the old man, we ourselves are salutarily commanded to offer ourselves as a new sacrifice.

**Verse 5. “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord.”** Since the most merciful mother previously admonished us to depart from ancient superstitions, in the second position she teaches that those who have been reborn should not devote themselves to sacrifices of animals, but should strive to offer themselves as a sacrifice to God. For it is not the same thing to offer the Lord a victim of beasts as to offer a human heart devoted to him.

If Christ himself was sacrificed for us, how much more fitting is it that we should offer ourselves as a sacrifice to him, so that we may rejoice in imitation of our King! He said, “Sacrifice”; and lest you understand this to mean animals, he added, “the sacrifice of righteousness”—that is, live rightly, and always offer your hearts, cleansed, to the divinity.

He also added, “And hope in the Lord,” so that a more blessed hope might follow a good life. For we cannot fully receive the reward here, even if we offer good works before the divine gaze. Rather, we are taught to hope in the Lord so that in the future we may obtain his saving promises.

But this hope does not deceive, and such a will does not come under condemnation, as the Apostle says: “Hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

**Verse 6. “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’ The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us.”** Through a kind of contest between opposing parties, the hearts of the faithful are salutarily built up. Many who still think carnally say what not even a few ought to say: “Who will show us good things?” They mean those things that the Church always proclaims: that the resurrection is to come, in which all the righteous will receive eternal rewards.

This should be read as an imputation, as though they were saying: “What is promised to us is something we do not see at all; we desire what we cannot obtain here.” In response to these people, the benefit that we possess even in the present age is indicated: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us.”

For just as an imperial coin bears the emperor’s image, so the marks of the heavenly Prince are impressed upon the faithful. By this protection the many-formed devil is driven away, and he cannot prevail through fraudulent plotting against one who has been tempted, whom he once held captive through the persuasion of the first man.

For the cross is the unconquerable protection of the humble, the overthrow of the proud, the victory of Christ, the destruction of the devil, the ruin of the underworld, the strengthening of the heavenly powers, the death of unbelievers, and the life of the righteous.

Concerning this, John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, flashed forth like a constellation of many definitions in his declamation on the cross, saying: “The cross is the hope of Christians; the cross is the victory of the Romans; the cross is the resurrection of the dead; the cross is the guide of the blind; the cross is the way of the converted; the cross is the staff of the lame; the cross is the consolation of the poor,” and so forth. These words flowed from him in this manner through divine inspiration.

Behold true gifts; behold present benefits, by which the tongues of slanderers are stopped in condemned throats. This figure is called in Greek *peusis* (“inquiry”), and in Latin *percunctatio* (“questioning”), where both a question is posed and a prepared answer follows.

He added: “The light of your countenance, Lord.” In the impression of the cross there is the light of God’s countenance, because it is always known to shine in those who do not choose to defile themselves with any wickedness, as the Apostle says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were marked for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30).

What this cross accomplishes, the Apostle has gathered in another place with beautiful brevity, saying: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18).

Therefore let us reject sacrilegious voices. The Lord’s gifts are great and fitting against the prince of darkness: the light of the Lord is present for us.

### Verse 7

“You have put gladness in my heart: at the time of their grain, wine, and oil, they have multiplied.” [Mss. A, B, F: “at the time of grain, wine, and his oil.”]

He continues to enumerate the benefits possessed by Christians. He does not mean the kind of gladness that we express by loud laughter, but the gladness of right faith, which the Lord customarily grants to a good conscience. For we truly rejoice when we both believe rightly and, with the Lord’s help, conduct ourselves in an exemplary manner. The statement is brief, but perfectly comprehensive. What more is sought from those who doubt than that we are known to serve our King under the sign of the cross and to rejoice, by the Lord’s gift, in perfect faith?

It follows: “At the time of their grain, wine, and oil, they have multiplied.” He returns to those who are demonstrably intent upon carnal things. Nor is it without significance that *their* has been added to these three—grain, wine, and oil. There is also the Lord’s living bread, which came down from heaven (John 6:42). There is also wine: “Your cup, which inebriates, how splendid it is!” (Psalm 22:5). There is also oil: “You have anointed my head with oil.” Therefore sinners do not possess these things of God, but their own things—that is, earthly things—from which the body may live, but the soul may not enjoy itself.

The word *grain* (*frumentum*) is derived from *frumen*, that is, from the upper part of the throat; for the ancients called the head of the throat *frumen*. “They have multiplied” through the worst actions, that is, they have been filled with worldly desire [ed., “pleasure”]. This is what we said in the preface: that the deepest causes are often indicated in a single expression, as here in the word *their*.

### Verse 8

“In peace, in the selfsame unchanging reality, I shall sleep and rest. For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.”

Against human tumults and fleeting successes, which the world considered supreme, he most beautifully set the peace of the heart—something those involved in worldly actions cannot possess. For this peace has a life of utter tranquility; it does not quarrel with its own mind but, persevering in the Lord’s benefits, enjoys pleasant serenity. Concerning this peace the Lord says in the Gospel: “I give you my peace; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

But lest you think this peace temporal, he added: “I shall sleep and rest in the selfsame reality.” The expression “in the selfsame reality” refers to what is changed by no alteration of circumstances; rather, remaining itself, it endures in unchanging eternity. “I shall sleep” is understood to indicate the end of life; “I shall rest” is shown to signify future blessedness, when rest and glorious repose will finally be granted to the saints.

The reason why he will rest follows: “For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.” The Church therefore has a unique hope in her members, because she alone receives the kingdom of God, which the people of Babylon cannot attain. When he says, “You have established me,” he signifies a worthy and deliberate sentence: here we possess it in hope, but there it is possessed in reality. Yet we shall truly deserve that gift of rest only if we trust that it will come about through the Lord’s help.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Having completed the discourse of the maternal proclamation, let us consider the beginning, middle, and end of this song; and through most reverent inquiry we discover the intention of so great a mystery. The power of a psalm is recognized in this way: when the circumstances of its wording are investigated and treated in such an order.

In the first verse the holy Church prayed to be heard on behalf of her members; and, so that her prayer might be heard, she admonished the human race to withdraw from the worship of idols, knowing that she has the Lord the Savior, to whom true worship is owed. Then she instructed the people how they ought to sacrifice and admonished them concerning what should be answered to blasphemers. Afterward she spoke of the singular blessedness that the Lord promised to his saints. Thus the instruction of the whole Christian discipline was completed, so that people might clearly recognize both what they ought to do and what they ought to hope for.

This number four also admonishes us to understand that he was proclaimed to the world by evangelical power. It was fitting that the entire expanse of the earth, established upon four cardinal points, should be urged to believe in the saving Lord, so that, called from diverse nations, the Church of the whole world might become one. The year itself is divided into four seasons; the air of the whole world is swept through by the four cardinal winds; and the dignity of the soul is likewise compared with four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. The Pythagoreans pursued this reckoning with such praise that they acknowledged it to be sacred.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM V

*For the end; a psalm of David, for her who receives the inheritance.*

Why it is placed “for the end” was recently declared in the preceding psalm. “For her who receives the inheritance” signifies the Church, whose person is introduced as speaking in this psalm. She approaches and possesses the good things of the Lord the Savior. She is said to receive the inheritance because, when Christ rose again, spiritual blessings came to her: the unconquerable foundation of faith, the most certain reward of hope, the gentle bond of charity, and so forth. Of these things she now holds images, and in the future she will possess their powers eternally.

Concerning this inheritance it is said in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth by inheritance” (Matthew 5:4). Again, the Lord’s Church is called an inheritance, as it was said in the second psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8). She is rightly called the inheritance of the one whose precious blood is shown to have purchased her.

Do not think this contradictory. Although different things may seem to be presented in the divine Scriptures, they nevertheless converge in one harmony and truth of understanding. The psalm itself, as we explained above, must likewise be referred to the Lord Christ, as must David himself.

### Division of the Psalm

This entire psalm is spoken by the person of the catholic Church. In the first section she asks that her prayer be heard, proclaiming that heretics and schismatics must be excluded from the Lord’s gifts. In the second section she prays, through understanding of the divine Scriptures, to be directed along the straight path toward that blessed homeland, asserting that the faithless are completely alienated from it. Finally, while recalling the rewards of the blessed, she both converts the wicked through the punishment announced beforehand and stirs the righteous through the promised rewards.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Give heed to my words with your ears, Lord; understand my cry.”

Through the figure of *mythopoeia*, which we discussed already in the fourth psalm, these words are most appropriately assigned to the Church: beloved, she awaits the Lord and, summoned, hastens, so that, passing through the wickedness of this age with his help, she may always cling to her Bridegroom immaculate and without wrinkle.

At the very outset, through the three parts of the prayer, the power of the Trinity is set forth in a manner suitable to the holy Church. By saying, “Give heed to my words with your ears, Lord,” she signifies the psalmody of the mouth. It follows: “Understand my cry,” so that she might open the affection of her heart, just as the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6).

The ears of the Divinity are described by analogy with the body, through which, when the air is struck, hearing enters human beings. The word *ear* (*auris*) is derived from *hearing* (*auditus*). Consider also that she asked for her cry to be understood. This voice was not the striking of the lips, but an utterance of the heart [ed., “affection”], which is accustomed not to be heard by the ears but to be understood by the light of the mind.

#### Verse 2

“Attend to the voice of my prayer, my king and my God, for I shall pray to you, Lord.”

Above he said, “Understand my cry”; now he says, “Attend to the voice of my prayer,” to declare that this prayer is perfect, being inflamed by the affection of the mind. Therefore we must examine why, with the words changed, he introduces the same sense.

“Attend,” he says, “to the voice,” which is accustomed to be heard. This is because God does not distinguish these senses by separate bodily members but accomplishes everything through one power. He hears what is seen by us, sees what is heard by us, and looks within upon what is thought by us; and there is nothing that can hide itself from his light.

This figure is called *metabole*, that is, the repetition of one thing under a variety of words. For through a threefold repetition he signifies one and the same thing. He said, “Give heed to my words with your ears, Lord”; then, “Understand my cry”; third, “Attend to the voice of my prayer.” All of this refers to one petition, as if he were saying, “Hear my prayer.”

It follows: “My king and my God, for I shall pray to you, Lord.” It is rightly accustomed to move some to inquiry why, in the middle of the verse, the blessed Church names the heavenly principate three times. For she says, “My king and my God,” adding, “For I shall pray to you, Lord.”

Yet to these three persons she did not say *attend, you all*, but *attend, you one*: for the catholic Church proclaims one God, the holy Trinity—not confusedly, like Sabellius, but distinctly and perfectly. The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one God. There is nothing more or less in this, except in Arian perversity, which after so many ages still does not recognize that it is in error.

Observe also the marvelous arrangement of the names themselves. He first places “King,” by which name the divine Scriptures frequently call the Lord Christ. He himself attests this order in the Gospel when he says: “Through me one goes to the Father” (John 14:6). Then he says “Father God”; third, “Lord,” referring to the Holy Spirit. Although the names appear distinct in order to express the persons, one God is nevertheless perfectly believed and proclaimed, as it is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

Therefore let this saving sentence be fixed in our minds: distinction in the persons; unity in the nature is to be believed.

#### Verse 3

“In the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I shall stand before you and see.”

“Stand before you” must be joined to both parts so that a complete sentence may be found. Therefore he prays in the morning who is recognized as living in a life of light. We call it morning when, after the darkness has been dispelled, the arrival of bright light shines forth.

The Church, which knows that she had possessed the darkness of sins and had been gathered out of the night of this world, rightly believes that she will then be heard when she has burst forth into the light of heavenly conduct. She repeats “in the morning” because she necessarily understood that a mind made luminous by the Lord’s gift must always stand before him in her prayers.

Consider why “in the morning” was said: namely, when, at the very beginning of good actions, the enlightened mind begins to recognize the truth. You should not think that after sins there is a delay during which one might be unable to be heard, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “On whatever day the wicked person turns away from his wickedness, none of all his wickednesses shall be remembered” (Ezekiel 18:21–22).

To stand before someone means always to be present before him. Through this word the continuity of religious devotion is indicated. For the one who is worthy to appear before God’s sight is rightly said to stand before him, as Elijah said of himself: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings 17:1).

Above he said, “You will hear”; here he adds, “And I shall see,” because in that resurrection he will behold the very one to whom here he has offered supplication in holy prayers.

#### Verse 4

“For you are not a God who wills iniquity. The malicious person shall not dwell near you; nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes.”

#### Verse 5

“You have hated all who practice iniquity; you will destroy those who speak falsehood.” [Mss. A, B, F: “all who speak.”]

#### Verse 6

“The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.”

In the first psalm we said that the power of an *ennoematic definition* is this: by denying what something is not, it appears to declare what it intends; and again, by saying what something is, it can plainly show what it proposes. Both effects are demonstrated in these three verses.

He says: “You are the God who is known not to will iniquity.” For what else can God will except what he himself is proved to command? As Isaiah says: “I am the Lord, who speak justice and announce what is right” (Isaiah 45:19).

It follows: “The malicious person shall not dwell near you.” Here he signifies that sinners are to be excluded from the kingdom of God—those who have not been changed by any conversion. For although those whom guilt envelops may see him only carnally, as it is written, “They will look upon the one whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10), nevertheless they cannot dwell near him, since they are to be condemned to the torment of Gehenna.

He added: “Nor shall they remain.” He showed that they will generally come to the Lord’s judgment; but they are rightly said not to remain before the Lord’s eyes, since they are to be sent into everlasting punishments. There is nothing God does not see, since he is known to be everywhere present and wholly so. Yet those who are to be deprived of his grace and gift are rightly said not to be before him.

Thus far the Lord has been indicated by saying what he is not. Now, in three other ways, he is shown by affirming what he is. He says: “You have hated all who practice iniquity.” He did not say “those who practiced,” because only those who stain themselves with the detestable crime to the end of their lives will be condemned in judgment.

But among the specific enumerations of crimes, a general name has appropriately been placed—“those who practice iniquities”—so that there you may understand everything that is known to be alien to the divine commandments.

He added: “You will destroy those who speak falsehood.” These sentences seem to admit of some difficulty, since he says that the Lord merely hates those who practice iniquity, but confirms that those who speak falsehood will perish—whereas, if one attends to the literal sense, practicing iniquity might seem more serious than speaking falsehood.

Here, however, he signifies heretics, who by speaking falsehood have destroyed the souls of their followers. For what can be more serious than to go astray in a place where one can also destroy another?

Finally he says: “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit.” The man of blood is one stained with human blood, but also one who deceives a living person. He added, “and deceitful.” Many wrong things are done that we do not undertake by our own deliberate will. But “the deceitful person” signifies those who, knowingly doing evil, strive to bring about another’s destruction.

When he says, “He will abhor,” he signifies that all those whom he mentioned above will be made strangers to the Lord’s kingdom. Those are to be abhorred who do not deserve to obtain his rewards.

The *ennoematic definitions* have been completed on both sides. These statements appear to have been expressed for the great benefit of humanity, so that sinners might briefly understand whom the Lord detests and rejects.

#### Verse 7

“But I, in the abundance of your mercy, shall enter your house.”

Since he had said that the wicked were to be abhorred, it followed that he should testify that, through divine grace, he would be admitted into the Lord’s house. For although the Church herself is here the Lord’s house, each blessed person who is one of her members can nevertheless say that he will enter the future Jerusalem.
