In this way we also speak of a homeland and a city, yet by these words we mean things that we know belong to their citizens. But because that future Jerusalem is believed to be constructed from the multitude of the saints as living stones, he aptly said: “I shall enter your house,” as though he were completing the perfect construction of that building.

#### Verse 8

“I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear.”

It must be considered that he did not say “in the temple,” but “toward the temple,” because it has already been stated that not even the syllables themselves are free from sacramental meaning. The holy temple is the body of the Lord the Savior, which the Church rightly worships, and through which she deserved to be honored. For he himself said concerning his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

It follows: “In your fear.” To declare the compunction of the heart, he introduced the mention of fear, because faith is solid when reverence for the Divinity is added to chaste love.

#### Verse 9

“Lead me, Lord, in your righteousness; because of my enemies, direct my way in your sight.”

After saying that his prayer was to be heard in the morning and also recalling the deadly rejection of sinners, he now enters the second section, asking the Lord that he may already be led to eternal joys, since here he was wearied by various distresses.

He says: “In your righteousness,” that is, while you spare those who confess and, when they condemn themselves through repentance, absolve them by the most equitable power of your mercy. For it is just that he who rejects rebels should wish to receive those who supplicate.

“Because of my enemies,” that is, because of heretics and pagans. One is hostile through perverse doctrine; the other is always opposed through unbelief. Because of them he asks to be directed in the Lord’s righteousness, since opposition does not believe his preaching.

“Direct my way in your sight,” that is, lead my life to the sight of your serenity. For by our own ability we cannot reach the one before whom we always walk along crooked paths.

#### Verse 10

“For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is empty.”

Since above he asked to be led by the Lord’s righteousness to his sight, so that by the Lord’s gift he might attain a share among the blessed, he is now understood to rebuke human deceptions. He shows that the obstinacy of stubborn heretics cannot reach the rewards that the Lord has prepared for his faithful.

It is rightly said that there is no truth in the mouth of those whose heart was possessed by emptiness. For the tongue follows the judgment of the mind, and the movement of the tongue naturally serves the authority of the heart.

#### Verse 11

“Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully.”

Through the figure of *parabole*, a highly appropriate comparison is made. The tomb of the dead is the throat of the liar, when he rolls in his throat the destructive emptiness that inflicts the evil of death.

He rightly added “open”; for if it were closed, it would stink less. Pay attention to what he said: “With their tongues they acted deceitfully.” Often they merely speak deceits and are not shown to bring them about. But here, to display more serious sins, he added “they acted,” so that the malice might be shown to exist not only in their tongues but also in their detestable deeds.

#### Verse 12

“Judge them, God. Let them fall from their own thoughts.”

It is the custom of prophecy to foretell the future. The Church did not wish for such things as a curse, since whatever appears to be acquired among good things is also shown to be added to her. But it was necessary to speak of the obstinate and foreknown, whom she knew the Lord could condemn.

“Let them fall from their own thoughts”: when they do not find themselves attaining what they believed they could deserve. For one is properly said to fall when one is deprived of one’s hope.

#### Verse 13

“According to the multitude of their impieties, drive them out, for they have embittered you, Lord.”

Through this statement we learn that each person is repelled by the Divinity to the extent that his sins accumulate. The quantity of the offense is the measure of rejection: the guilty person is made farther from him in proportion as he is enlarged by numerous crimes.

“Drive them out” is said because of their presumptuous thoughts: already deceived by a reckless will, they seemed to themselves to have been admitted among all good things. We call those driven out who are hurled from some interior place.

For they have embittered the good physician—the sick who rejected the remedies of their salvation through senseless hardness.

#### Verse 14

“And let all who hope in you rejoice; they will exult forever.”

After asserting the deserved retributions of the impious, the Church now returns to the saints, by whose congregation she is recognized as blessed, lest she be silent about the rewards of the good that she knew were to come.

Observe that what she asks as a supplicant in the first part of the verse, she promises in the following part, so that what was most certainly hoped for might not be thought ambiguous. And lest the joy be believed temporal, it was said, “forever”: there is no end to joy, since the rewards once received are continually possessed.

Notice that he says those who hope in the Lord will exult forever, because in this temporal existence the impious also seem to rejoice; but in the future only the Church will exult forever.

#### Verse 15

“You will dwell in them. And all who love your name will glory in you.”

This sentence depends upon the preceding verse. It can indeed be touched upon, but cannot be explained fully. For if you ask what that promise is which he said above—“They will exult forever”—hear it stated briefly: “And you will dwell in them.”

O great and ineffable generosity of the giver! What comparable gift can be given, when there the Lord of all things himself is known to be granted? For every generous person gives what he possesses; but God, who is ineffable goodness, gives himself as the reward. And what could be so comparable as this: that the author of all good things should begin to fill us?

He said, “They will glory,” because they enjoy the desired fulfillment. “In you,” because you are the inheritance promised to them; and therefore they will exult forever, because they will glory in the eternal Lord.

“All who love your name.” He signifies that in that happy homeland all will indeed glory through participation in the Lord, although, through an ineffable dispensation according to the quality of each person’s merits, the holy majesty appears to grant itself to each individually.

“For you, Lord, will bless the righteous.”

After the greatness of the reward and the immensity of the joys had been set forth, we are briefly taught why humanity is filled with so great a good without deserving it, lest anyone attribute to his own merits what is clearly bestowed through the blessing of the author.

“Lord, you have crowned us as with a shield of your good will.”

Consider how sweetly and fittingly the present psalm has been concluded: with one word it indicates the Lord’s benefits, which no volumes could explain. The Creator’s good will, which fills us with ineffable gifts, is called a shield, and truly protects us and grants splendid rewards.

A shield placed upon the head is a crown; fitted to the heart, it is a defense. This is the one who protects all the faithful; he himself covers the Church spread throughout the whole world; he also embraces heaven, under which all things are hidden: a fortress that no blow can break through; weapons through which no destruction can enter; by which, rather, conquered death has fallen, and humanity’s salvation, once despaired of, has risen.

“Of good will.” Since the Lord’s calling precedes every merit and does not find someone worthy but makes that person worthy, it is therefore gratuitous; otherwise it would be called just. This, then, is the good will that calls and draws us. We are unable to think or do anything beneficial unless we receive it from the author of goodness, as the Apostle says: “We are not able to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Let Pelagian madness therefore cease, lest, when it falsely tries to attribute some good to itself, it be deprived of the true giver.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How sweet was the prayer of the holy mother when it was heard—the mother who both gives us birth through faith and shapes us through religious instruction. She teaches the ignorant, cherishes the little ones, lifts up the afflicted, and gathers to be nourished at her own breasts those whom she recognizes as belonging to her doctrine.

For she supplicates so that we may learn to pray; she flees from the wicked so that we may abhor the worst; she trusts in the Lord so that we too may place our confidence in him. Thus, like a venerable mother, she gives words to her little ones for speaking, so that the affection of prayer, growing within us, may both provide psalmody as a consolation in human actions and produce conduct corresponding to the divine commands.

Let us therefore speak what she advises, understand what she believes, and certainly love what she loves, so that when we follow her mind we may without doubt be made her children.

The number five, in which this psalm is recognized as constituted, must be assigned to the Pentateuch, which the catholic Church alone truly understands, since she has received the promised and awaited fullness of the law.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM VI

*For the end; in hymns; for the eighth; a psalm of David.*

“For the end” is already known. A hymn is praise of the Divinity composed according to the rule of some meter. “For the eighth,” as some wish, signifies the Lord’s coming, when, after the week of the world has been completed, he will come to judge the world. Hence the psalm itself begins with the greatest trembling, saying: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

Saint Hilary, in the prologue to the Psalms; Saint Jerome, in his exposition of Ecclesiastes (on Ecclesiastes, chapter 11); Saint Ambrose, in his exposition of Luke the Evangelist (book 1, chapter 9), where the Lord was transfigured on the mountain; and Saint Augustine, in *The Sermon on the Mount*, where he discussed the eight beatitudes, have all spoken more extensively and carefully about this eighth day. Therefore the reader may choose whichever account pleases him. For this reason it is enough to have recalled such men, since their statements, if gathered into one sequence, could scarcely be contained in a very long volume.

Concerning this day the prophet Amos says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you want the day of the Lord? It is a day of darkness and not of light” (Amos 5:18). The prophet Zephaniah says the same: “The sound of the day of the Lord is harsh and bitter” (Zephaniah 1:14).

Accordingly, a penitent is now introduced, earnestly imploring through the several parts of his prayer that on that day of judgment he may not be accused of his own crimes. For what is more salutary, or more prudent, than that one who could have no hope in his merits because of the sins he had committed should, while placed in this world where there is a place for repentance, choose to implore divine mercy?

Some say that this day will come six thousand years after the creation of the world, because on the seventh day the Lord is read to have rested from his work in that creation of all things. They reckon a thousand years for each day, because it is written: “A thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Psalm 89:4).

Others think that after seven thousand years—that is, when the week of this age has passed—the eternal light will be revealed on the eighth day, just as our Lord’s resurrection is known to have taken place. But since the Lord himself says in the Gospel (Matthew 24:36; Mark 13:32) that neither the Son knows this day, it is exceedingly presumptuous to seek diligently what divine providence did not wish to reveal to us for our benefit.

Therefore, for explaining the title, it is enough to know that after the end of this age that day will come.

Now let us hasten quickly to understand the words granted to us. For if we ask with a pure heart, why should we doubt that we will be heard, when we come instructed by him and to him?

Grant, Lord, that in our satisfaction we may be pierced with complete charity—the one who provided us with a salutary rule for supplication.

Remember that this is the first psalm of the penitents. It is followed by the thirty-first, the thirty-seventh, the fiftieth, the hundred and first, the hundred and twenty-ninth, and the hundred and forty-second. Concerning these we shall speak in their proper places, as opportunity is given.

Do not think that they were brought to the number seven without reason, since our elders also said that sins can be forgiven in seven ways: first, through baptism; second, through the passion of martyrdom; third, through almsgiving; fourth, through forgiving the sins of our brothers; fifth, when someone converts a sinner from the error of his way; sixth, through an abundance of charity; seventh, through repentance. The communion [Mss. A, B, F: “reception”] of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ must also be added, provided that it is received worthily.

Other modes of forgiveness may perhaps also be found. For it is fitting that divine mercy should transcend the number of our supplications.

### Division of the Psalm

In this psalm the confessing and religious man implores in four ways.

At the beginning he makes the judge favorable to him. An exordium is a prayer that suitably prepares the mind of the hearer for what follows. Here it proceeds from the power of the judge, since he alone is the one whose decrees eternity preserves; from his own weakness, because he cannot endure as much as he deserves to suffer; and from the judge’s custom of sparing, because he does not wish to be entreated by the dead but confessed by living human beings.

In the second division he narrates his own hardships, by which he is recognized as afflicted and crushed. A narration is a clear and careful exposition of events, offered to make the case plausible.

There follows a salutary and exceedingly beneficial correction. He separates himself from the wicked, knowing that this is most pleasing to the good judge, so that his mind may be made alien to those to whom justice itself is shown to be opposed.

The conclusion remains, where something is now stated definitively, after which nothing further is desired. For he disturbs and rejects all the wicked, since he did not wish in any way to have a share with them.

Thus, through these parts, the purpose of fruitful repentance is accomplished. The psalm applies these things to God through words transferred from human custom, so that he may seem like a judge who hears, like an examiner who is informed, and like one ignorant of what has happened who comes to know it. This kind of figure is found in many places in the sacred writings.

This entire psalm is understood to have been written because of fear of the future judgment. It is certainly characteristic of a sound mind to fear impending calamities and to fear what one deserves to encounter. For if we keep before our eyes what is read in the prophet Malachi, we always return to right paths and are corrected by beneficial fear. He says: “Who will endure the day of his coming, or who will withstand his sight? For he enters like the fire of a furnace and like the lye of those who wash, and he will sit to melt and to purify silver” (Malachi 3:2–3).

Likewise Solomon gives this warning in Ecclesiasticus: “Before prayer, prepare your soul”; and shortly afterward: “Remember wrath on the day of completion, and the time of retribution at the turning away of the face” (Ecclesiasticus 18:23–24).

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.”

First we must know that the omnipotence of the Lord has enriched his eloquence so fully with various disciplines and arts that it both shines forth wondrously adorned for those who investigate it and, when carefully reconsidered, grants the seeds of diverse teachings.

This is why there are found in it matters that teachers of secular literature transferred into their own books. Among the other statuses that orators assigned to arising cases, they said that there is a status of concessive supplication: when the accused does not defend what was done but begs that forgiveness be granted.

Although this status may appear powerless before earthly tribunals and deprived of human resources, it is nevertheless surrounded by unconquerable protection before God, so that what no arguments can adequately defend may be vindicated by faithful confession alone. This is truly granted to penitents, who, while wishing to absolve themselves, strive instead to condemn their own deeds.

Isaiah likewise admonishes us: “You first declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26).

Now we must consider how fitting and salutary the placement of these words is. He does not, as some have thought, implore God the Father not to be rebuked, but not to be accused with the severity of judgment. For to many, being rebuked is salvation, as it is written in the Apocalypse of John: “I rebuke and chastise those whom I love” (Revelation 3:19). This also happened to David himself, when the prophetic denunciation corrected him.

The Son also rebukes, as it is written in another psalm: “I will rebuke you and set them before your face” (Psalm 49:21). The Holy Spirit also rebukes, as it is written: “When the Spirit, the Paraclete, comes, he will rebuke the world concerning sin” (John 16:8).

Speak now, you perverse people: where is the difference of nature and power here, when even the words themselves do not differ? Let Arian wickedness fall silent, lest those who wish to introduce sacrilegious divisions into the holy Trinity prove themselves to be cut off from the Lord’s kingdom.

“Nor correct me in your fury.”

The anger and fury of a judge toward the accused are the effects of condemnation—that is, an agitated movement of the mind provoking the infliction of punishment. Anger is prolonged indignation; fury is a sudden kindling of the mind.

These expressions, however, have been set forth allegorically through transferred words. In reality, the Lord is neither confused by anger nor disturbed by fury, but remains in the one and same tranquility of his glory.

Moses similarly says: “Just as the Lord rejoiced in building you and making you increase, so he will rejoice in afflicting and destroying you” (Deuteronomy 28:63).

He therefore asks to be corrected before the judgment, not in the judgment, because the one who is rebuked there is condemned without doubt. We must also keep in mind that the day of judgment is called anger and fury because of the fear inspired by its greatness, as it was said in the second psalm: “Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his fury he will trouble them” (Psalm 2:5). Another prophet likewise says of it: “That day is a day of anger, a day of tribulation and distress” (Zephaniah 1:15).

#### Verse 2

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak.”

The confession of weakness moves the mercy of the heavenly Physician, from whom remedies are easily obtained when manifest wounds are displayed. He did not say, “Because I deserve it,” but, “Because I am unable to endure your righteousness.”

O great mercy of the Creator! From the judge himself we learn what we ought to say; we are taught to ask for mercy, lest justice be able to destroy us. Who, then, would still doubt that he can hear his words—provided that the petitioner’s mind is such as he himself has deigned to command?

### Verse 3

Heal me, O Lord, for all my bones are shaken. In his supplication he perseveres in the same request. He tells the compassionate Physician that his wasting sickness has reached even his inmost parts, lest He delay help, since he recognizes that destruction threatens him. Here, allegorically, we should understand “bones” as the strength of the mind; when this fails, all vigor ebbs away, just as a body cannot be held together when its bones are shattered.

### Verse 4

And my soul is greatly shaken; and you, O Lord, how long? So that you would not understand the body—which he had called “bones”—he said that his soul was shaken. “Greatly” has rightly been added, lest the merciful hearer permit delay any longer if he did not recognize how greatly he had been shaken. “How long?” should be understood as “will you delay”—you who never customarily forget the prayers of suppliants even to the end? This supplication is commended by great distresses, so that the health restored may be recognized as more precious. Observe also that this penitent always flees the Lord’s justice and seeks the customary exercise of His kindness.

### Verse 5

Turn back and rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy. When one says to God, “Turn back,” the relaxation of vengeance is requested, so that His justice may not exact from us the punishments we deserve. Or, in our customary manner, “Turn back” is said to God as people ordinarily plead with those who have turned away—whether they are unwilling to look back or disdain to help. “Rescue my soul,” that is, from the impending punishment owed to those who go astray. He turns deserved penalties away from us when benevolent forgiveness releases them. Appropriately, “turn back” is placed in the prayer of the penitent, for the Lord promises this to those who make satisfaction, saying: “Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you” (Zech. I, 3). “Save me for the sake of your mercy.” How beautifully this supplication is explained in its own fitting and beneficial words! He asks to be saved not according to his merits, but for the sake of divine mercy; when hope is fixed upon this, pardon is more easily obtained.

### Verse 6

For there is no one in death who remembers you; but in hell, who will confess to you? It may be asked why he says that in death there is no one who remembers God, when the nearness of the Judge’s anger might cause greater trembling. Yet we rightly call the faithless forgetful of God, concerning whom Isaiah also says: “For those who are in hell will not praise you, nor will the dead bless you” (Isa. XXXVIII, 18). When the Apostle says, “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 10), this statement must be understood here of the unbelieving and obstinate alone, who are not worthy to possess any confidence in their confession.

He therefore rightly hastens to have himself forgiven here, because after the setting of the light nothing remains except the recompense of merits. “But in hell, who will confess to you?” The phrase “for forgiveness” must be supplied, just as Solomon says of the wicked: “They will say among themselves, repenting and groaning in anguish of spirit” (Wis. V, 3), and so forth. The rich man, too, who saw Lazarus established in repose, is shown to have confessed his sins (Luke XVI, 23), but he was not heard according to the desire of his supplication, because confession properly belongs to this world, where forgiveness is also found.

And if we should understand some distinction in these words, “in death” signifies the passage from life, whereas “in hell” signifies the confinement of the places which souls are known to endure according to their merits. In both cases, however, confession is absolutely denied admission. Thus far we have spoken of the opening; now let us consider the narrative.

### Verse 7

I have labored in my groaning. Having most carefully secured goodwill in the opening, he now comes to the narration of his deeds, asserting that his repentance has been completed through great torments; for repentance becomes especially capable of obtaining pardon not through idle words alone, but through credible affliction.

This groaning, then, is also said of what arises either from those bent down by excessive weight or from those wounded by an injury. But Christians must seek that groaning which is accomplished through contrition of heart, when we both remember our evils and are terrified by consideration of the future punishment. “Groaning” is so called as a doubled grief. The faithful rightly desire it, because it consoles those who mourn, cleanses penitents, drives away the devil, and reconciles us to Christ: a sweet bitterness, blessed tears, a saving affliction. Blessed John discussed this subject in two books with such eloquence that he deservedly received among the Greeks the name “Golden Mouth.”

I will wash my bed every night. If you wish to take this literally, he was indeed rightly washing with tears the bed he had polluted by night. But an impossibility presents itself: how could there have been such an abundance of tears that he was said to have washed not only his face but also his bed? Therefore it is better to understand “bed” as bodily pleasure, in which, as though in our couch, we relax through decaying pleasure [mss. A, B, F: burning pleasure]. A person can wash this with tears, however few, if heavenly inspiration should move him to lament.

A bed is so called from selected and soft herbs, upon which in ancient times the bodies of those resting were laid down to sleep.

I will water my couch with my tears. “To water” signifies something more abundant than “to wash.” But let us consider why, having previously said “bed,” he wished to repeat the expression “couch.” A couch signifies a heap of sins; he therefore waters it with tears so that, once dissolved by this most health-giving rain, a person may grow into a new harvest of virtue and become righteous from sinful, joyful from mourning, and completely healthy from sick.

For if you wish to understand “couch” as a collection of garments, the same impossibility arises as with the washing of the bed. Or this may be taken as a hyperbolic figure, by which certain things are customarily extended to an exaggerated magnitude. Thus, concerning those who sail, he will say in Psalm 106: “They go up to the heavens and descend to the abysses” (Ps. CVI, 26). And in Psalm 50: “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9), since nothing can be whiter than snow. In Deuteronomy Moses commanded Joshua, son of Nun: “Let this book of the law not depart from your hand; and you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may know how to enter upon your way” (Josh. I, 8). Likewise another penitent will say in Psalm 101: “I ate ashes like bread, and I mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI, 10), and similar statements.

### Verse 8

My eye is troubled because of anger. Since above he asserted that he had groaned and confirmed that he had wept, it is foolish to suppose that he has suddenly been thrown into confusion by his own indignation. Rather, because of the Lord’s anger, he confesses that the eye of his heart has been troubled. For what is more fearful than that He should grow angry who, unless He shows mercy, destroys? “Eye” is so called as though from *ocior lux*, “swifter than light,” because it quickly regards what is threatened; or because it is shown to be hidden by concealing eyelids.

I have grown old among all my enemies. “I have grown old,” that is, I have remained in the antiquity of the old man Adam, who, in distinction from the new man, Christ, is rightly called old. “Among all my enemies”: whether among demonic spirits or among our sins. For these truly are the adversaries that lead souls down to Tartarus and still flatter them in a deadly manner.

The promised narrative has been completed. It is, as required, brief and lucid, and also suitable for tempering the Judge’s anger. Now we must speak of the most health-giving correction.

### Verse 9

Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. Having enumerated his afflictions, he enters upon the section of amendment, so that the one who had sinned in the company of evildoers might appear most devoted to the Lord’s commandments after driving such people away from himself. This argument, drawn from the attributes of persons, is called an argument from conduct. He proves that he has arrived at complete correction by the manner in which he wished to separate himself from the company of the wicked. For see what follows.

### Verse 10

The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer. A supplication is frequent prayer offered with devotion, and it alone is appropriate when excessive and wins over even the importunate. “He has received” means “he has accepted,” as though he had taken something in his hands. Observe also the great mystery of exultation: he says that his prayer has both been heard by the ears of the Lord and received as some kind of offering. For joyful people customarily do this, repeating the same matter in different ways when they exult with a great surge of thanksgiving. Nor is it without significance that he says the Lord has granted him three things in one gift, namely, that he might show the holy Trinity to have been present to his supplications.

### Verse 11

Let all my enemies be put to shame and troubled; let them turn back and be put to shame very quickly. Having traversed three sections, he comes to the final conclusion. The conclusion is the outcome and determination of the entire prayer; here, as was fitting after being heard, he now exults joyfully.

For this is a certain formula of penitents: they begin with tears and end in joy, so that by such an example what is written may be recognized as true: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. CXXV, 5). Observe that the holy conscience of the penitent, freed from his sins and obeying ecclesiastical rules, immediately prays for his enemies, that they may be converted, so that, just as he received forgiveness, his carnal enemies too may return to the Lord’s grace.

When he says, “Let them be put to shame,” he wishes them to be enlightened by such great contrition that they themselves may blush for the things they were doing and understand that the actions they formerly thought useful to themselves were destructive. “Let them be troubled” refers to fear of the future judgment and to the terrifying preaching of the Scriptures, lest these most wretched of human beings fall into the punishments which divine law declares are to come upon sinners.

When he says “my,” he has relaxed the hatred to which the multitude of sins had given rise. It follows: “Let them turn back,” so that they may not be permitted to go where they are headed, but, when they return, may be freed from the pit of hell. This too was said to Peter when he was thinking in a human manner: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark VIII, 33), namely, so that you may not set your mind on the things you are setting it on. When the wicked turns back, he is corrected; when the righteous turns back, he gives offense. But since the subject here was sinners, a desired conversion was rightly wished for them.

And lest he perhaps seem to postpone their judgment for too long, he added: “And let them be put to shame very quickly.” O outstanding desire of a holy mind! Who could have asked more in his own case than this man, who made his request on behalf of his fiercest enemies? The Lord therefore has mercy on such people, who do not neglect the moments offered by mercy, as it is written in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall in turn obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7).

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Although in all the psalms we ought to devote ourselves to understanding, since from them we obtain the greatest supports for our life, nevertheless I judge the penitential psalms especially worthy of careful examination, for they are provided to the human race like an appropriate medicine. From them we receive the most health-giving washing of souls; through them we who are dead to sins come back to life; through them we who mourn arrive at eternal joys.

There is a certain judicial procedure in which the accused, presented before the sight of the Judge, stands there, washing away his sin with tears and dissolving it through confession, offering the highest kind of defense by condemning himself. Here there is no external accuser; he himself is his own prosecutor. He deserves pardon because he does not excuse himself from guilt. Nor can matters be conducted in this way before such a Judge when no one can prevail in denying his sins.

Here conjecture ceases; here no conclusion is sought; here the other kinds of legal status are absent, because everything is disclosed in clear truth. The only necessary form, therefore, is what is called concession, when the accused does not defend what has been done but pleads that he may be forgiven.

O immeasurable mercy of the Creator! The accused caused a sentence to be pronounced on his own behalf, because he accused himself all the more vehemently. Yet no clever advocate could have obtained from a judge what this man, full of simplicity, earned from the Lord’s mercy.

Nor is it without significance that he assigned the person of the penitent to the senary number, which is acknowledged to be perfect in the discipline of numbers. On the sixth day He created humanity; at the same age the Lord Christ deigned to come into this world to free humanity; and on the sixth day He decreed that He should be crucified for the salvation of humankind. Thus this reckoning appears most fittingly to contain both humanity’s beginning and the absolution of sins.

Regarding the usefulness, power, and grace of repentance, blessed Augustine, among his many books, did not think it right to neglect this subject wherever he found an occasion to address it; nevertheless, in a single volume he treated it wonderfully and briefly, with his customary vigor.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM VII

*A Psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the words of Chusi, son of Jemini.*

Although this episode is described more fully in the Second Book of Kings (ch. XV), it must nevertheless be explained briefly for the interpretation of the title. When David was being pressed by a cruel war waged by his son Absalom, he sent his friend Chusi to his camp in order to discover the plans, so that he might secretly report to him whatever was being done against him. Indeed, his very name indicates the matter just described.

For Chusi, according to Father Augustine’s teaching (*Enarration on Psalm VII*), is interpreted as “silence”; and he truly practiced this when he secretly communicated what would be beneficial to David. “Son of Jemini” is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” This aptly refers to Chusi himself, because by a necessary betrayal he took thought for David’s safety.

In this way our Lord sent silence into the midst of the Jews when He assumed the mysteries of the holy Incarnation. To the faithless it was like silence, whereas to the faithful it proved to be something proclaimed. Thus the prophet sang this psalm, in the likeness of Chusi, concerning the Lord’s future mystery: just as David endured the unjust persecution of his son Absalom, begotten and raised by him, so the Lord endured the fury of detestable presumption from the people whom He had freed and nourished.

We should know that this is the first of the psalms in which the Lord’s future mysteries are signified through David’s deeds. The twenty-sixth, thirty-third, and one hundred forty-third psalms follow in the same manner; they share the figure called allegory, that is, inversion—saying one thing and signifying another.

31. **Division of the Psalm**

The prophet, carrying his own situation forward into the future mystery of the Lord and Savior—to whom the very name David is also appropriately attributed through mystical interpretations—begs the Lord in the first division, in his own person, to be delivered by His power from all his persecutors.

A person is a rational substance, individual and distinguished from all other things of the same substance by its own properties. In the second section the same prophet asks that the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, once manifested, may come to his aid. In the third he introduces Him speaking according to the humility He assumed, so that He may be judged according to His justice and truth; terrifying the wicked with vengeance and promising the good gratuitous rewards. In the fourth part the prophet speaks again, admonishing the Jews to abandon the iniquity they have undertaken out of fear of the future judgment, lest they be forced to endure the punishments they deserve.

This must now be investigated with an attentive mind, so that by divine gift we may deserve to perceive the power of the psalm.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; deliver me from all those who persecute me and rescue me. Although the prophet’s situation appears to be presented on account of his son Absalom, he nevertheless begs to be delivered from all enemies, especially from spiritual wickedness, against which it is fitting to take the greatest care. Carnal enemies attack the body, but spiritual enemies strive to kill souls.

Deliver me from sin; rescue me from the devil. We are taken away from his power when, through the Lord’s mercy, we are cleansed from the filth of our sins. But why he ought to be rescued from his persecutors, he demonstrates by the preceding reasoning, since he confirms that he has hoped in Him.

### Verse 2

Lest at any time he seize my soul like a lion, while there is no one to redeem or save me. The devil is compared to a lion; Christ too is frequently compared to a lion: the former because he seizes for destruction, the latter because He rescues for salvation. Beautifully, he assigns the proper words to their proper authors: he asks the Lord to rescue him, so that the lion may not seize him.

He added: “While there is no one to redeem or save me,” that is, when you have ceased to come to my aid. For at that time the devil prevails in seizing us, when the Creator, because our sins stand in the way, delays coming to our help. He alone redeems the faithful who gave His Son as an immeasurable price for the human race. Salvation cannot come from anyone other than the author of salvation. Thus through these luminous words he has revealed the Lord Christ.

### Verse 3

O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands. Here he says, “If I have done this,” but below he explains what “this” is when he says, “If there is iniquity in my hands.” This figure is called *epexegesis*, that is, an explanation of what was said above.

But this must not be understood generally, since there is no human being who does not have some iniquity in his hands. Rather, “this” refers to the persecution of his son Absalom, by whom the prophet seemed to be unjustly afflicted. For the text of Kings shows how he treated even an enemy (II Kings XVIII, 5): when he sent an army against him, he commanded his officers above all to look after Absalom’s safety. When Absalom was dead, he mourned him with the deepest grief.

He therefore rightly says that in this particular matter there was no iniquity in his hands, since he had even wished to leave Absalom alive.

### Verse 4

If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil, may I deservedly fall empty-handed before my enemies. This is the second aspect of the patience mentioned above: he did not wish to avenge himself upon his persecutors. He also treated Saul with the greatest compassion, so that, although Saul had repeatedly been handed over to him for death, David sent him away to safety. The preceding passage likewise bears witness to this.

Saul and Absalom repaid evil, although they had first received from David a service of compassion. No one repays anything unless he has previously received something. But this man, full of God and strengthened by the virtue of patience, binds himself by the condition of perfect goodwill, so that, if he has repaid evil for evil, he may fall empty-handed before his enemies—that is, deprived of the fruit of great gentleness and unable to carry away from this contest anything which the Lord might credit to him as a crown.

If you consider these matters more deeply, they disclose signs of the Lord’s Passion, when the faithless Jew repaid evil, although he had continually received ineffable benefits from his own Creator.

### Verse 5

Let the enemy pursue my soul, seize it, trample my life into the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust. He calls the enemy the devil, who crushes the souls he has seized. Once he has become superior, he brings death, not salvation. Thus he treats the souls whom he conquers with the greatest cruelty, making their deeds be stained by earthly contagion.

Therefore the order of the words is appropriate: first he seized, and afterward he trampled. “And bring my glory down into the dust,” that is, the honor of the humanity assumed, which is known to have been made in the image and likeness of God. Let him bring it down into the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. Thus, while setting out a condition, he has described the ruin of sinners in a marvelous narrative.

Having explained these three preceding verses, we must show how the second mode of hypothetical syllogism appears in them. This mode is understood to proceed as follows.

A hypothetical, that is, conditional, syllogism is one which, taking its assumption from one or more conditional propositions, derives a conclusion. Its proposition, insofar as it concerns this wording, is as follows:

“O Lord my God, if I have done this; if there is iniquity in my hands; if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil, may I deservedly fall empty-handed before my enemies; let the enemy pursue my soul, seize it, trample my life into the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust.”

According to the rules of the dialecticians, the reciprocity of this proposition is as follows:

“If I do not deservedly fall empty-handed before my enemies; if the enemy does not pursue my soul and seize it; if he does not trample my life into the earth; if he does not bring my glory down into the dust, then, O Lord my God, I have not done this; there is no iniquity in my hands; I have not repaid evil to those who repaid me evil.”

The assumption arising from this reciprocal proposition is:

“Nevertheless I shall not deservedly fall empty-handed before my enemies; nevertheless the enemy will not pursue my soul and seize it; he will not trample my life into the earth; he will not bring my glory down into the dust.”

This assumption is followed by the conclusion:

“Therefore, O Lord my God, I have not done this; there is no iniquity in my hands; I have not repaid evil to those who repaid me evil.”

For the sake of brevity, we have touched on these matters summarily and simply. But if anyone wishes to know fully either the figures, or the modes of syllogisms, or what simple and compound syllogisms are, let him read Aristotle in Greek and Marius Victorinus in Latin, and each person will easily confirm for himself matters which may now seem difficult to judge.

### Verse 6

Rise up, O Lord, in your anger, and be exalted in the boundaries of your enemies. Rise up, O Lord my God, according to the commandment that you gave. He comes to the second division, in which he passes to the likeness he had established concerning the Lord Savior.

This petition ascends in three steps. The first is that He should rise up in anger, that is, in vengeance. But he is not provoking God to anger, whom he knew to be most gentle—especially since above he had said of himself: “If I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil.” Such expressions, however, are reported in human and figurative language.

This vengeance called “anger” must rather be understood of the devil, who is punished whenever a sinner, after being conquered by him, is rescued. “Be exalted in the boundaries of your enemies,” that is, be magnified in the possession of the devil, which he holds in sinners. For the Lord is exalted in them when praise is offered by those who are converted.

The second step is: “Rise up, O Lord my God, according to the commandment that you gave.” This is the same as what he said above, “in anger,” so that you may recognize it as vengeance rather than fury. The Lord gave the commandment when in the Gospel He said to His disciples: “On the third day I will rise and go before you into Galilee” (Matt. XXVI, 32).

When these things occurred, He was exalted throughout the whole world, which the devil’s power had possessed, and He took vengeance upon him when He took away from him what he held. Observe also that, in prophetic fashion, he speaks of future things as though they were past: “According to the commandment that you gave,” meaning, of course, the commandment He was still going to give. So it is in Psalm 21: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. XXI, 18), and so forth.

### Verse 7

And the assembly of the peoples will surround you; and on its account return on high. Above he asked that He should come; now he shows what might arise at His coming, as though he were saying: “You will indeed come to set free, but the Jewish people will persecute you with deranged minds.”

Here “assembly” signifies a gathering of the wicked, not a congregation of religious minds. For if the whole Jewish populace had believed in Him, it would certainly have received Him with devoted minds.

“And on its account return on high.” “On its account,” that is, on account of the assembly, which nevertheless was undevoted through its obstinate ways; He could not dwell in it, since He withdrew Himself from its unbelief. “Return on high” refers to the Gospel statement: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John III, 13). To return is to go back by a repeated journey to the place from which one came.

Concerning this glorious Ascension, he will say in another psalm: “And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds, and he made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 11).

### Verse 8

O Lord, judge the peoples. Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice and according to the innocence of my hands upon me. He comes to the third part, where the Lord Christ now speaks, according to the dispensation in which He suffered.

When he says, “O Lord, judge the peoples,” the majesty of the almighty Father is revealed. But when he says, “Judge me, O Lord, according to my justice and according to the innocence of my hands upon me,” the humility of His humanity is expressed, which is shown to have been assumed from the virginal womb of holy Mary. Thus the mysteries of such immense realities have been enclosed in a single verse.

Observe how the order of the whole truth is preserved. Previously the prophet had spoken of the innocence of his hands in one particular matter; now, in the person of the Lord Savior, the statement is made generally, since it is certain that He had no sin at all.

He rightly asks to be judged according to His justice, for He perfectly fulfilled the commandments as teacher of His divinity; He did not repay evil for evil; He, though holy [ed.: “the holy cross”], ascended the cross for the sins of others; He prayed for His persecutors with immeasurable grace and compassion; and there are other such things proclaimed by the most truthful text of the Gospel.

But since innocence is specially attributed to the heart, here it is said, “According to the innocence of my hands.” This kind of expression is recognized as characteristic of the divine Scriptures: they change the significations of words. Thus in Psalm 10 he will say: “His eyelids question the children of men” (Ps. X, 5), although questioning belongs not to eyelids but to the tongue.

### Verse 9

Let the wickedness of sinners be brought to an end, and direct the righteous. He asks that the coming of death be hastened, so that His ascent may quickly be glorified. For the wickedness of sinners was completed when the Lord was crucified. They could do nothing more, although they had raged with cruelty. He Himself spoke this word while hanging on the cross: “It is finished” (John XIX, 30).

The righteous was directed when He rose from the dead and ascended to the kingdom of heaven. Thus, in the zeal of compassion, that is sought through which the life of all is shown to be fulfilled.

### Verse 10

God is a just judge, searching hearts and kidneys. It is God’s distinctive power both to examine our hearts and to penetrate the strength of our spirit with the light of His power. Although the powers of heaven are far higher than we are, no creature has been granted to know fully the secrets of our thoughts. Only He who judges recognizes them perfectly in us.

For this reason I think it was said: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Rom. XIV, 4)—that is, you who do not understand his thoughts. We ourselves cannot be as fully manifest to ourselves as we appear before divine eyes, since it is written concerning humanity: “Who understands sins?” (Ps. XVIII, 13).

Let us also understand “hearts” as referring to thoughts, and “kidneys” to the most steadfast strength of the spirit, or to bodily pleasures.

### Verse 11

My help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart. That Incarnation which was assumed for our sake speaks to us in order to encourage us. Although He appears to say this concerning Himself because He was subject to the Father, He nevertheless grants immeasurable compassion as hope to those who believe in Him.

Since there is one and the same person of God and man, His humanity calls the power of the Word its help; the Word grants both pardon and salvation to those who are upright in heart. Observe also that in the preceding section the prophet asked to be delivered, whereas here Christ Himself promises the Lord’s help to Him, saying in the Gospel: “All things that the Father has are mine, and mine are the Father’s” (John XVI, 15). The former asks as a servant; the latter promises to Himself as Lord.

### Verse 12

God is a just, strong, and patient judge; will he be angry every day? He has nevertheless come to the fourth section, in which the prophet, singing praise to the Father in his own person, both greatly terrifies the obstinate Jews and promises hope to those who wish to return to Him.

God is called just because at the end He gives each person what he has done. He is strong because no one can resist His will. He is patient because even now He waits for repentance from those whom, according to the character of their crimes, He could have destroyed.

“Will he be angry?” must be spoken with astonishment, since this is a negative assertion. He is said to become angry in the manner of judges, who, when they wish to avenge offenses, rise up in stern indignation to pronounce sentence. But this does not apply to the divine nature, because where there is fiery vengeance, there is no tempered justice.

“Every day,” that is, at every moment, just as every sin is committed. For where would glorious patience be if punishment immediately followed offense?

### Verse 13

Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it. He terrifies the rebellious Jews who, having despised the Lord’s law, were serving idols with the utmost wickedness.

To them it is said: “Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword,” that is, He is about to send His only Son in shining glory. We call something “brandished” when it is seen to display now light and now trembling shadows.

This came about through the Incarnation of the Lord Christ, when He showed darkness to the faithless but the light of His divinity to the faithful. The Apostle too calls the Word a sword when he says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God” (Eph. VI, 17).

We appropriately understand the bow as the writing of the New and Old Testaments, which, as it were, through two curved bends embraces the necks of the devoted. To the faithful it displays a gentle yoke; to the obstinate it declares terrifying weapons.

“He has bent” was added so that His patience might not be thought lax. Finally he added, “and prepared it,” so that the custom of archers might be represented most fully: after they have bent the bow against the target, they place their hand upon the work of shooting and ready their arms. But let us see what arrows this prepared bow has sent forth.

### Verse 14

And in it he prepared the instruments of death; he made his arrows for those who burn. Here the distribution of the divine majesty [editorial reading: *law*] is shown: through the bow, that is, through the Old and New Testaments, as has already been said, both the effect of death comes and life is bestowed through its arrows.

From this bow arrows went forth, namely the apostles, who, with burning—that is, desirous—souls, transmitted saving commandments in the manner of arrows, so that the wicked might be wounded and effective care might come to the faithful.

“Made” means “worked,” a verb which Father Jerome also introduced into the text.

### Verse 15

Behold, he brought forth injustice, conceived anguish, and gave birth to iniquity. Let us examine carefully the words that have been spoken.

The Jewish people brought forth injustice when they saw the Lord performing miracles for human salvation but instead plotted His destruction. “He conceived anguish” when He rebuked them through various parables in order to turn them away from their perversity. “He gave birth to iniquity” when he said: “Crucify him, crucify him!” (Luke XXIII, 21). He rightly used the word “gave birth,” that is, as though he had produced the most wicked children.

Every fruit is shown to resemble its source, as it is said elsewhere: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII, 20). But since conception comes first and giving birth afterward, he appropriately placed “to give birth” in the earlier position, so that he might show that this iniquity had not been conceived from another’s evil but was its own.

### Verse 16

He opened a pit and dug it out, and he fell into the pit that he made. A pit is so called because its bottom lies hidden, while the surrounding enclosure confines one within a single cavity. With its level surface it flatters the eyes of those who look upon it with a false tranquility, but how deep it is remains concealed.

Such, then, was the pit of iniquity that Jewish depravity dug. “He opened it,” because he first wickedly began it; “he dug it out,” when he completed it in his own condemnation; “he fell into the pit that he made,” namely, the pit of death.

This statement can most appropriately apply both to a pit and to a grave, as Solomon says: “Whoever prepares a pit for another will fall into it himself” (Prov. XXVI, 27). An evil undertaking begins with oneself; and before it harms another, it first works destruction for its own author.

Vers. 17. His sorrow shall return upon his own head [ms. G. and ed., “upon his head”]; and upon his crown his iniquity shall descend. Here we must understand “head” as our soul, in which respect we are undoubtedly the higher. Sins are subjected to it when they are held in check. But if the soul should be overcome by transgressions, then those sins which overflow through their multitude of wickedness must necessarily rise above it. “Crown” is also so called because it turns the hair to the right and left; it signifies the summit of the head. We may rightly say that this is the meaning, because the summit of the contemplative soul is exalted; hence it also bears the image of the glorious Creator. If this soul should be bowed down beneath the weight of sins, then what has grown through the increase of iniquity must necessarily descend upon the crown—that is, above reason. For if we consider the very word, it is found to signify great mysteries. First, because when iniquity is hurled down from on high and descends, it strikes with violence. Then it powerfully explains how the wicked are tormented: for when their own sins have descended upon them, they are consigned to the punishments they deserve by their own evils and crimes. “Sorrow” is so called as if from *domabilis*, “capable of being subdued” [mss. A, B, F, *dominabilis*, “having power to rule”].

Vers. 18. I will confess to the Lord according to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High. Having set forth the virtues of the Father, by which he had terrified the Jewish people through the signs of his miracles, he gathers together in summary what he has said and declares with joyful mind that he will confess to the Lord. We speak of confession in two ways. The first is when we condemn our sins through humble penitence, as in the words of the prophet Daniel: “I will confess my sins and the sins of my people” (Dan. IX, 20). The second, which is the subject here, is when the praises of the Lord are celebrated with great exultation, as we read in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI, 25). Nothing there is said about sin, but only the occasions of grace are recounted. Thus this is to be understood as a proclamation of praise, offered to the Lord’s virtues with a joyful heart. “According to his righteousness”: because he both makes the proud endure their crimes and deigns to absolve the humble. To sing praise is also to carry out the Lord’s commandments in one’s deeds and to sing hymns with both voice and heart. The prophet promises that he will do this, because he knew that it was truly pleasing to the Lord.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0073C] If we examine it attentively, the mysteries of this magnificent psalm have become clear to us. In its first part it teaches fruitful patience, which is shown to make Christians perfect. Patience is the religious person’s willing endurance of all labors and sorrows, in hope of future things and in love of the Lord. In the second part the Lord himself promises salvation to those upright in heart. In the third, the wicked are terrified lest they be condemned when the erring are judged. O piety of the truly good Creator, who does not wish to abandon those whom you know will come before your judgment; and in the hidden treasury of your immeasurable mercy, while you spare those who confess, you yourself withdraw the guilty from punishment! For who could escape your justice unless your preceding mercy came to his aid?

The number seven also admonishes us to think of that eternal rest to which the present psalm extends our hope, so that, rightly received under such a number, it may be sung with joyful exultation. There is no doubt that, when the six days belonging to the active life have been completed, the seventh is assigned to rest; it is known to adhere to theological contemplation.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM VIII

**For the end; for the winepresses. A psalm of David.**

It has already been made known through the exposition of the fourth title that “for the end” signifies the Lord the Savior. A winepress is where grapes, pressed by many weights, with their hard seeds crushed and their skins emptied, pour forth the sweetest wines. This most aptly seems to apply to the Church, when, from stubborn habits and swollen pride, sweet tears are beneficially pressed out through the pressure of repentance. A similar comparison is also given in the threshing floors, where, under continual threshing, the chaff is separated from the wheat. Therefore it is fitting that we understand this psalm to have been uttered in the person of the ancient Church, in which there is indeed a winepress of bodies but the salutary fruit of souls. For if the Old and New Testaments are rightly called such, while nevertheless the law is taught to be one, why should we hesitate to affirm that the ancient and the new Church are one bride of the Lord Christ, acquired by his precious blood?

## Division of the Psalm

The ancient Church, which is most beautifully indicated to us by the winepresses, first, at the outset, joyfully sings the praises of Christ the Lord, proclaiming his majesty and his exalted works. Second, it comes more openly to the nature of humanity, which, from the most depraved condition into which it had been corrupted by Adam’s sin, it declares to have risen to the heights of great things. Thus the Lord Christ, from two natures and in two natures—unconfused and distinct—is recognized, with salvation and certainty, as one person.

It must also be borne in mind that this psalm celebrates with such great praise the human nature assumed by Christ the Lord that it most clearly testifies that this nature has been exalted above every creature, just as the Apostle says: “To which of the angels did he ever say, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’?” (Heb. I, 13). And elsewhere: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard being equal with God as a thing to be seized” (Phil. II, 6, 9); and shortly afterward: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name,” and so forth.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Vers. 1. “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!”

Although *Domine*, “O Lord,” is a vocative, *Dominus*, “Lord,” which is nominative, appears to have been joined to it contrary to usage. This figure is called *syllepsis*, whenever differing cases are gathered into a single meaning. Truly, therefore, she rejoices who says, “our.” For we must rejoice in the benefits of the one whose people we profess to be.

But when he says, “how,” he cannot express what he feels. Who could adequately comprehend either the creatures of earthly things, or the expanse of the sea, or the diffusion of this empty air, or the adornment of heavenly things, which the Lord has ordered by the power of his incomprehensible wisdom? Considering all these things, the Church, held fast and detained by the task of explaining them, exclaims: “How wonderful is your name,” and so forth.

“In all the earth,” because his holy religion is spread throughout the entire world; nor will there be any nation where the catholic Church does not rejoice. Therefore let the Jews and Donatists cease to claim for themselves in particular what they recognize to have reached the whole world.

### Vers. 2. “For your majesty has been exalted above the heavens.”

In the preceding verse he caused us to inquire into what he here appropriately explains. The mystery of the Lord’s incarnation is his majesty. Among its various miracles, this is known to have been bestowed upon us above all: that God deigned to become human and endured the cross for the salvation of all. This majesty, then, has been exalted above all the heavens and all creatures, when the Lord Christ, rising from the dead, sits at the right hand of the Father, as another psalm also says: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Ps. CVII, 6).

### Vers. 3. “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise.”

This prophecy is taught to have been explained in the Gospel by the mouth of the Lord, when the Jews forbade infants to proclaim the Lord’s praises, thinking that something childish was being done because such an act was undertaken by an age so young. Then he replied: “Have you never read, ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Matt. XXI, 16).

But lest you understand by “nursing children” those who are still nourished at their mother’s breast and therefore could not have sung the Lord’s praises, the apostle Peter also speaks of those advanced in age, saying: “Like newborn infants, desire rational and guileless milk, so that by it you may grow toward salvation” (1 Pet. II, 2). Hence the infants and nursing children are to be understood as those who, because of the beginnings and infancy of their faith, do not take stronger food but are nourished by gentler teaching. The meaning is therefore this: you are worthy of praise not only from the perfect, who understand you completely, but you are also proclaimed by the mouths of beginners and little ones.

### Vers. 4. “Because of your enemies, that you may destroy the enemy and the defender.”

“Enemies” designates pagans and blasphemers, lest the sacrilegious should say that the learned praise God for this reason: because they have been instructed through the study of books. He declared that infants also preach—those who have begun to come to the Lord through the newness of faith—so that this wisdom might appear to have been handed down divinely rather than gathered through human labor.

By “the enemy and the defender” he specially means the faithless Jew, who, while thinking that he is defending God the Father, proves himself an enemy of the Son. Thus it happened that one who appeared to be God’s most open defender was shown to be God’s adversary, because no one honors the Father unless he honors the Son, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V, 23).

This is also appropriately applied to all heretics, who, while thinking that they are defending the Scriptures through a bad interpretation, are shown by their hostile disposition to oppose the holy doctrines.

### Vers. 5. “For I shall see the heavens, the work of your fingers; the moon and the stars, which you founded.”

The Church, which before the Lord’s coming still existed in the patriarchs and holy men, rightly speaks of this in the future and in glory. For it says, “I shall see the heavens,” that is, the evangelical books, which are rightly called heavens because they contain the Lord the Savior, who said: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. XL, 12).

But he briefly defined what these heavens are by saying, “the work of your fingers.” For since we read in Exodus (chap. XXXI, 18) that the law was written by the finger of the Lord—which many have wished to understand as the Holy Spirit—I think that “fingers” was placed here to show clearly that the divine books were perfected through the cooperation of the Holy Trinity, as it is also read elsewhere: “He suspended the mass of the earth upon three fingers” (Isa. XL, 12). This must be received according to a similar mystery. For the finger of God is called the effect of divine operation, which most appropriately can be attributed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, to the one God.

It follows: “The moon and the stars, which you founded.” The Church says that it will see the moon’s increases and diminishings, which it undergoes: at one time growing through the faith of many, at another appearing diminished through the death of certain martyrs. Such comparisons are frequently given to the Church because of human opinions. In reality, however, it grows through afflictions and is always increased through crushing.

The moon is compared to many things differing from it. Sometimes it signifies the whole Church, as in the words: “Until the moon is exalted” (Ps. LXXI, 7); sometimes its most radiant member, as here; sometimes a foolish person, as Solomon says: “A fool changes like the moon” (Eccl. XXVII, 12).

He also added “the stars,” signifying righteous and religious people, concerning whom it is written: “As star differs from star in brightness, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. XV, 41–42). He added, “which you founded,” so that we might understand that all things are founded upon his judgment of predestination. Alternatively, this may refer to the divinity of the Word, so that he might be believed to have made all things in that original act of creation. In these three things he appears to have embraced the whole, as in the words: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1). Although he named two things, he embraced everything, arranging what was to be proclaimed in a wondrous order. Since he was afterward going to speak of the holy incarnation, he first had to demonstrate its divinity and omnipotence.

### Vers. 6. “What is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him?”

He comes to the second division, where in one verse, through two questions and answers, humanity is shown to be both insignificant and most powerful. This figure is called *peusis*, in Latin *percontatio*, “inquiry”: a question is posed and a prepared answer immediately follows. We have already used it in the fourth psalm.

“What is man?” This must be pronounced with contempt: that is, fragile and perishable, a follower of Adam, who, mingled with the ancient sin and enclosed within a shared depravity, has been bound by it. The Lord is mindful of him when he forgives his sins and bestows the gifts of his mercy, as he will say in another psalm: “But the sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV, 8). To be mindful, then, is to confer such saving grace upon those who offend.

“Or the son of man, that you visit him.” At this expression we must now rise, because it signifies the Lord the Savior, who was not born, like other mortals, from two human beings, but proceeded from the Holy Spirit and the womb of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, like a bridegroom from a glorious bridal chamber.

Consider also that above he said, “you are mindful,” but then added, “you visit.” He was mindful when he showed mercy from heaven to the patriarchs; he visited when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John I, 14). For we say that a physician “visits” when he enters the sickroom; and it is clear that this was fulfilled in the Lord’s coming.

### Vers. 7. “You diminished him a little below the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor.”

Here the humility and glory of the Lord the Savior are narrated. He was diminished, not by the necessity of servitude, but by the voluntary choice of his mercy, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7).

It follows: “A little below the angels,” because he accepted the cross for the salvation of all. In that respect, therefore, the Creator of the angels was made lower than the angels. He rightly said, “a little,” because although he assumed a mortal body, he nevertheless had no sins.

He was crowned with glory and honor when, after his exceedingly wondrous resurrection, God exalted him and received the faith of the whole world in him who had become human. A crown is appropriately fitted to the circle of the world, since the entire extremity of the world was formed in its likeness.

### Vers. 8. “And you established him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet.”

Above, his glory and honor were narrated; now his power is also presented, so that the perfect fullness of Christ the Lord’s majesty may be recognized. By saying, “over the works of your hands,” he shows that every creature has been subjected to him. For just as nothing is excluded from the Lord’s work, so nothing is shown to be divided from Christ’s power, since he is to judge the world.

By saying “all things,” he appears to have excluded neither earthly nor heavenly things. The Apostle, the heavenly interpreter of this passage, testifies concerning it: “For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him” (Heb. II, 8). In another place he also says: “Worship him, all his angels” (Ps. XCVI, 8).

He added, “beneath his feet,” so that every creature might rightly appear to honor and worship its creator. Observe that everything has been preserved in its proper place. The one whom he had first said was made a little lower than the angels because of the humility of the flesh, he now says, after the ascension, to have had all things subjected beneath his feet. This distinction removes doubt from those who waver and reveals the glory of the holy incarnation.

### Vers. 9. “Sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field.”

In this verse and the one that follows, what is said is an argument by enumeration. We must understand these and the other names that follow allegorically, lest he appear inappropriately to have placed beasts or animals after rational creatures.

“Sheep” signifies the chosen Christian people, as the Lord says to the apostle Peter in the Gospel: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 18). They are compared to sheep because, with the Lord’s help, they govern themselves in an innocent manner; and also because they relinquish the world’s coverings without any sense of pain. For just as a sheep does not reproach the one who shears it, so the righteous person does not accuse the greed that despoils him.

“Oxen,” however, designate preachers, who, plowing human hearts with heavenly commandments, caused the harvest of virtues to germinate. Nor is it without significance that he says “moreover,” since not only those holy people are subjected to him, but also sinners. Christ the Lord often triumphs with greater glory over such converts.

They are “beasts” while they feed in the freedom of the fields—that is, in the pleasure of this world; they are “sheep” when they are already enclosed within the Lord’s folds.

### Vers. 10. “The birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea.”

“The birds of the heavens” are proud people who, puffed up by the wind of boastfulness, are carried aloft as though through the empty air and despise humble things when they have been lifted higher. Birds are so called from their frequent flying.

“The fish of the sea” perhaps signifies philosophers, who investigate the nature of this world with wandering curiosity. For just as fish, with their heads forward, open paths for themselves through the sea’s confused waters, so these, with bowed heads, seek out the veins of reality through human reasoning and unceasing labor.

Although there are also fish of rivers, it is not without significance that he says “of the sea,” because of those who appear wise to themselves. Yet such people and those like them are happily subjected beneath the Lord’s feet when they come to embrace the Christian religion. For although all things have been bowed down to him by right of dominion, we say that those are properly subjected who have been judged worthy to come beneath his easy burden and gentle yoke.

### Vers. 11. “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!”

After the holy Church has joyfully sung of the incarnation of Christ the Lord and the glory of his resurrection, it repeats the verse of praise to the Lord that it uttered at the beginning. It is fitting that the beginning and the end be assigned to the same one who said of himself: “I am the Alpha and the Omega” (Rev. I, 8), that is, the beginning and the end.

But because the divine words are fertile, they produce other mysteries for us. They also signify those whose life, begun with divine gifts and religious beginnings, persevered in faith in the Lord. Therefore it must be borne in mind that this is the first among those psalms that repeat their verses through a sacramental repetition; we shall appropriately speak of this concerning the others in their proper places.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

The second psalm and this one have spoken of the two natures of the Lord Christ, although others follow as well: namely, the twentieth, seventy-first, eighty-first, one hundred first, one hundred ninth, and one hundred thirty-eighth. Thus, as we walk through the obscure path of this world, with many lamps kindled, we may by no means fall upon the rocks of heresy.

Therefore let us recognize the author of so great a benefit. There is one Lord Christ, begotten timelessly from the Father and born in time from his mother. First he created the world from nothing; afterward he delivered it from immense destruction. Such is the union effected between God and humanity that each remains entire, each remains distinct without any confusion. For neither could the impassible divinity be changed, nor did the humanity receive anything other than what allowed it always to remain improved.

Thus he became the true and almighty mediator: being equal to the Father in the form of God, he also became like us through the assumption of flesh. In himself he caused the joined natures to remain, which he willed to be peaceful. This is the singular protection of our hope, the unowed gift of redemption, the destruction of death, and the life of the saints.

For what kind of piety is this, I ask, that the Lord of the angels deigned to come even to the form of a servant, so that death might be conquered together with its author, the devil, who held the world bound by his chains? Therefore blessed Ambrose composed the hymn of the Lord’s Nativity with the most beautiful flower of his eloquence (Tom. V, hymn 24), so that the devout priest might offer a worthy gift to so great a festival. He says:

> Proceeding from his bridal chamber, the royal hall of chastity,  
> the giant of twofold substance, eager to run his course.

And the rest, which the holy man elaborated beyond human capacity.

For this number, the octave, is also recognized in the divine Scriptures as containing the mysteries of great things. Eight souls entered Noah’s ark and were saved while the world perished. David was the eighth son of Jesse, whom the Lord is known to have chosen. On the eighth day circumcision purified the Hebrews. On the eighth day—that is, the Lord’s day—the Lord rose from the dead; on that day the hope of the human race was raised from the hell of the wicked to the heights of heaven.

This is the number that mathematicians call the first square number in operation, and which the Pythagorean Philolaus calls “geometrical harmony,” because all harmonic proportions appear to converge in it.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM IX

**For the end; for the hidden things of the Son. A psalm of David.**

What this “end” signifies has often already been stated: it is not that in which something comes to an end, but that in which it grows; from it we are truly restored. It is the beginning of good things and the end of evils for us. The Jews do not reach it, because they fail through their unbelief.

“Of the hidden things of the Son” signifies the person of the Lord the Savior. For when no name is supplied to indicate to whom something belongs, it is necessary to understand the expression as referring to some exalted reality. Above, where he wished Absalom to be understood, he said “of his son”; here, however, because he wished the most exalted summit to be referred to the only-begotten Word, he said only “of the Son.” He is the almighty and infallibly the Son, coeternal with the Father, doing whatever he wills in heaven and on earth.

In the same way it is said in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John VIII, 36). The expression there is not followed by “of God”; the word itself, pure and without any addition, is sufficient.

“For the hidden things” is placed in the plural because the mystery here is understood to be not one but twofold.
