It signifies the incarnation of the Lord and the future judgment, concerning which this psalm is going to speak. The humanity of Christ has now been revealed, but his judgment is still awaited. When we hear “for the hidden things,” therefore, we must devote our attention to the reading, so that, with the Lord’s help, the hidden things that are proclaimed may be opened to us.

## Division of the Psalm

This entire psalm is drawn from the person of the prophet. In the first declaration he says that he will joyfully sing praise to the Lord because he has confounded the devil, whose worship he destroyed through the merciful dispensation of his coming.

Second, he admonishes the faithful to sing praise to the Lord who dwells in Zion, who avenges the blood of the poor and raises them up from the gates of death.

Third, he says that the end of evils will come upon sinners together with Antichrist.

Fourth, moved by the excess of those very evils, he turns to the Lord and says, as though the Lord had withdrawn from the defence of the poor, when the wicked are given licence for their presumption.

Fifth, he prays that the time of that dread judgment may arrive, so that all these things may quickly be brought to an end, lest the iniquity of any person prevail any longer. For the wickedness of that time will be such that no faithful person will wish the world’s duration to be prolonged when he has come to know that such evils are being committed.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Vers. 1. “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders.”

He confesses to the Lord with his whole heart who is not tossed about by any worldly thoughts. This is clearly characteristic of the perfect, who, by the Lord’s gift, have conquered both the defects of original sin and the wicked suggestions of evil spirits.

It follows: “I will recount all your wonders.” Who, I ask, can recount all the divine wonders that his power works daily in heaven and on earth? But it is the usage of Scripture, through the figure *synecdoche*, which signifies a part by the whole, to say “all” when everything cannot be comprehended.

Yet, to mention one thing among many, what is more wondrous than that God should become human without confusion for the salvation of the human race, and that the one who was judged here should come to judge the world?

### Vers. 2. “I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High.”

Not in this world, where joy brings death; not in the ambitions of the world, where bitter sins are made sweet; but in you, where secure joy continually increases. For to exult is more than to rejoice. To exult is to take delight with the movement of both soul and body, in the greatest and most joyful freedom.

He also promises that he will give thanks to the Most High, who is shown to be exalted above all things because he has deigned to free him from his enemies, whether fleshly or spiritual. As has been said, he promises that he will sing to the Lord both in his deeds and with his voice.

### Vers. 3. “When my enemy turns back, they will grow weak and perish from your presence.”

Although he had many enemies, here we appropriately understand Saul. He said “back,” because Saul could not obtain what he desired. Indeed, the more wickedly Saul persecuted him, the more righteous David appeared through his endurance of the wicked man.

Although he first said “enemy” in the singular, he now says “they will grow weak,” because the persecutor was a king who exercised his wishes through many servants. Therefore “they will grow weak” is appropriately said, because by God’s will they all became wholly ineffective.

“And they will perish from your presence,” while I flee to you with devoted mind. For the wicked person does not come before your face—that is, before your grace—because he persecutes the innocent.

### Vers. 4. “For you have carried out my judgment and my case; you sit upon the throne, judging righteousness.”

When two people contend from opposite sides, one must give offense when the other succeeds. Once the prophet’s case had been approved, it is clear that hatred belonged to the adversary, because the persecutor could not please the Lord when the Lord had determined to rescue the one who was being impiously oppressed.

But when he says, “my judgment and my case,” he testifies that the sentence turned out favorably for him. Sailors likewise speak of “their wind” when the outcome of prosperity has smiled upon them.

“You sit upon the throne” is said of the Lord Christ, who now sits at the right hand of the Father and from there will come to judge the living and the dead. “You sit” is spoken in the present through the power of prophecy, though it refers to the future. For it is clear that this sitting pertains to the Lord’s incarnation, which at that time had not yet appeared as accomplished.

The throne signifies the tribunal of the future judgment, upon which the Lord Christ will sit in the honorable power of his majesty.

“Judging righteousness.” Here also he used the present tense for the future. He will judge righteousness when, after the end of the world, he appears in splendor for judgment. This figure is called *idea*, when, by presenting the appearance of a future event as though before our eyes, we stir the movement of the mind. This will be explained more fully in what follows.

### Vers. 5. “You rebuked the nations, and the wicked perished; you blotted out their name forever and for ages of ages.”

Here the most sacred second coming of the Lord is now expounded, when the unbelieving nations will be rebuked and the devil, together with his schemes, will perish forever. His stormy wickedness will then no longer remain, when, by the Lord’s favor, all things will be tranquil.

For who will thereafter name either the devil or his followers in the kingdom of the Lord, when no adversity shakes the Lord’s city and no enemy invades it?

What “forever” means has also been appropriately explained by “for ages of ages.” The future age signifies the Lord’s kingdom, which will end in no age and at no time. And lest it be confused with anything else, it is called “of ages”—that is, following this age that we now use. This present age succeeds itself by returning and is repeated through annual revolutions after its times have passed; but the future age does not return to a beginning, and it endures continually without any change.

Therefore let heretics cease to say that the devil and his followers can at some time be restored to grace, when they hear so clearly that they are to be condemned forever and for ages of ages, so that not even a trace of their name can remain.

### Vers. 6. “The enemies’ swords have failed completely, and you have destroyed their cities. Their memory has perished with a crash.”

“Of the enemies” is a genitive expression, that is, “of the devil,” whose swords he testifies to have failed. *Framea* is a Hebrew word signifying a sword, with which that enemy rages.

By “completely” he means the consummation of the age, when the devil’s power is shown to be slain by that almighty sword concerning which he said in the seventh psalm: “Unless you repent, he will brandish his sword” (Ps. VII, 13), and so forth.

By “cities” he means the unbelieving peoples convicted at the final manifestation of the Lord Christ. In this age the devil possessed their hearts as though they were the walls of his city.

“But their memory has perished with a crash.” “With a crash” means with a very great outcry. This usually happens when prosperous circumstances are brought to a close by a most grievous end, so that neither their power nor their name appears to remain. Observe how he has maintained a most beautiful comparison: the cities that he had said were destroyed he now testifies to have been overturned with a crash.

### Vers. 7. “But the Lord remains forever. He has prepared his throne for judgment.”

A very beautiful and fitting contrast. Since he had said that the wicked perish, he now says that the Lord remains forever. Those who have resisted their Creator with wicked presumption do not wish to hear this. Let them therefore flee to the merciful Lord, lest they suffer the strict judge.

“He has prepared”—that is, God has become human—so that the one who was judged here in humility might come there to judge in his majesty.

These are the things that the title called “the hidden things of the Son”: for it is an ineffable gift that he should have raised human nature, humbled and cast down, to the heavenly kingdoms by the right hand of his power.

### Vers. 8. “And he himself will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge the peoples with justice.”

This is surely the Lord Christ, who, having suffered injustice here, is said there truly to demonstrate justice to the wicked.

We must understand “the world” as the holy men who are gathered from the universal Church, as though from the circle of a crown. These are to be judged in righteousness; because of the goodness of their faith and humility, abundant mercy will be granted to them, and they will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV, 34), and so forth. Hence: “They will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28).

“Peoples” should be understood as sinners who do not appear to have been stripped of their devilish works. They will be judged with justice and condemned for the wickedness of their deeds; to them it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41).

Thus, with the two words “righteousness” and “justice,” he describes the character of that judgment with wondrous brevity.

### Vers. 9. “And the Lord became a refuge for the poor, a helper in times of need and in tribulation.”

The poor have abundant hope and a great cause for joy when they have as their refuge the very one who is their judge. We have heard of “the poor,” but we must not think that every poor person is destitute. That person is God’s poor one who, emptied of earthly desire, longs to grow rich through heavenly generosity.

And lest the hearts of the faithful be frightened by their weakness, there follows a firm promise of great help: “A helper in times of need,” because the sweetest help is that which is provided in necessity.

He again expressed the very time of need clearly, saying, “in tribulation,” when the mind of the afflicted is more eagerly driven to the practice of penitence, as he will say in another psalm: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Ps. XLIX, 15).

### Vers. 10. “And let all who know your name hope in you, for you do not forsake those who seek you, O Lord.”

“Let them hope in you”: let them not look to the blandishments of the world, but trust in your promise.

“Those who know your name”—that is, those who venerate your majesty with the holiest devotion. Those who scarcely believe have also heard the Lord’s name; but only those who obediently submit to his commandments truly know it.

The reason follows why they ought to hope in the Lord: he does not permit himself to abandon those whom he sees have fled to him. For it is certain that the Lord, who is shown to be endowed with such a will, is always present.

### Verse 11

“Sing to the Lord, who dwells in Zion; proclaim his wonders among the nations.”

He comes to the second section, where the blessed prophet, contemplating the benefits of the present and future time, summons devout peoples to psalmody, lest, when such great rewards are conferred upon them, they grow sluggish through some torpor. First he says, “Sing to the Lord”; and lest the Gentiles think that they should sing amid their own superstitions, he adds, “who dwells in Zion” [Col. 0083B], thereby designating the Lord Savior, who, appearing bodily in those regions, embraced the whole world within the religion of his name. This is said concerning the holy incarnation; for where does he not dwell who is wholly everywhere? But if we also investigate the mystery of this name spiritually, Zion means “watchtower,” because God is truly found in devout contemplation. It is rightly said that he dwells there where, enlightened by heavenly grace, we behold him.

He also explains what he said above, “Sing,” because to sing to him truly is to proclaim his wonders to all the nations. Hence we can understand that in every action psalmody is appropriately spoken of as whatever can be applied to the praises of the Lord. It should also be observed that this has been suitably explained by a definition; for he says to which Lord one should sing, namely, the one “who dwells in Zion.”

### Verse 12

“For, when seeking their blood, he has remembered them; he has not forgotten the prayer of the poor.”

Because he had said above, “Preach to the nations,” and it is clear that many of them were killed, lest anyone think that what happened went unavenged, it follows that the blood of the martyrs is to be required of the impious persecutors, so that they may receive eternally what they inflicted in time. “He has remembered” is wonderfully used with reference to both parties: so that vengeance might terrify the persecutors, while a gracious promise might refresh the martyrs. “He has not forgotten” is said to strengthen the weakness of those who complain, who, because of the remoteness of the future judgment, suppose that God has in some measure forgotten their recompenses. [39] “The prayer of the poor” means the petition of the righteous, which he adds below in his own person, so that you may understand of every faithful person what the prophet asks to be granted to him.

### Verse 13

“Have mercy on me, Lord; see my humiliation because of my enemies, you who raise me up from the gates of death.”

This is the prayer of all the poor, suitably brought into the singular number, because this multitude is always led into the unity of the saints. He asks to be helped in such a way that he may be seen by the most merciful King, because his regard is truly assistance; and dark things immediately perish when they admit the serenity of so great a light. He therefore asks that his humiliation be considered in relation to the pride of his enemies, because Christ’s martyrs are humiliated in the flesh to the same degree that their persecutors appear to be exalted in time [Col. 0084A].

The gate of death, however, is the devil, or every worldly enticement, since through these one unhappily enters into eternal destruction. “You raise me up” means, “you remove me far from such things.” For since the gate of death is the sinful conduct of many, he rightly says that he has been raised above it, because he clung to life-giving commandments.

### Verse 14

“That I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. I will rejoice in your salvation.”

This repetition of “gates” is most pleasing, where there is one name but entirely different realities: in the former gates there is an entrance to death; in these latter there is found an entrance to life. Having therefore been freed from those mortal gates, he promises that in these gates of the Church—which bestow everlasting blessedness—he will proclaim the praises of the Lord [Col. 0084B], through which his eminent name is celebrated throughout the whole world.

For Zion gave birth to the remaining Churches of the world, because there was born there the source from which the beginning of our faith is known to have come, and this flowed more widely throughout the whole earth. Christ the Lord is the Father’s salvation, his power and wisdom, who grants us eternal rest and salvation. The prophet therefore rightly says that he rejoices in him, since in him there is no end to joy.

### Verse 15

“The nations are nailed fast in the destruction that they made. In the snare that they hid, their foot has been caught.”

In this verse and the one that follows, the retribution of sinners is powerfully explained, because each person is tormented by his own iniquity. He says that the nations are caught—those who are not held by fear of the Lord, but are shown to be fastened by certain nails of sin [Col. 0084C], so that they cannot shake themselves free, restrained as they are by bonds that appear to be harsh. We may properly apply this to the Jews, so that they are fastened to their evils just as they had determined to fasten the Lord to the cross with nails.

“They hid the snare” is said with reference to their intention; for nothing could be hidden from Christ, who foretold his passion through countless declarations. “Their foot has been caught.” He continues the metaphor of the snare, which he mentioned above. We call those “caught” whom a knotty capture constrains. The foot signifies the movements of the soul and the perverse desire that makes them walk toward vice, just as Solomon says in Proverbs: “Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed blood” [Col. 0084D] (Prov. 1:16).

### Verse 16

“The Lord will be known when he executes judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands.”

This is an exceedingly true and unequivocal statement, because the Lord will then clearly be known to execute judgments when sinners are given over to be tormented by eternal punishment. Here, because they have freedom for their crimes, they are perhaps thought to be left unpunished; but when that day of manifestation arrives, and the Lord Savior sits upon the throne of his majesty, then it will universally be recognized that he executes his judgments, when the human race has been separated according to his decision, whether on the left or on the right. For this truly is to execute judgments: to distinguish the merits of each person without any confusion.

An explicit explanation of this statement follows [Col. 0085A]. He says how it is known that the Lord truly executes judgments: namely, when the sinner is bound by the entangling works of his own deeds and receives a punishment worthy of the quality of his actions. For that interpretation must be avoided entirely which supposes that the sinner is tormented only by remembering his sins. If that alone were sufficient, why would it be said, “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41), and, “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24)? He does not deny here that places of torment are given to sinners; rather, he says that they are tormented according to the qualities of their works.

Let us therefore understand that a place has been prepared for the punishments of sinners; let us recognize outwardly the penal evil that we read is impending for the wicked [Col. 0085B]. Thus, so that we may truly understand that blessedness is divided from condemnations by certain boundaries, let us remember that the rich man lifted up his eyes and saw poor Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom, while he himself was assigned to avenging flames (Luke 16:23). This order of truth would in no way be stated if sinners were tormented solely by the memory of their evils. These are the hidden things of the Son, which the title foretold.

### The Song of the Diapsalma

A new diapsalma appears, and a song is shown to have been placed above it. This has led some people to observe that they should not think diapsalma means silence; for they say it is impossible that a song should be understood as silence. But this matter in no way impedes the definition given in the preface [Col. 0085C]. Here “song” does not remove an interruption of words; rather, it appears to indicate future joy.

### Verse 17

“Let sinners be turned into hell: all the nations that forget the Lord.”

He comes to the third section, in which he announces with an eager spirit that an end will come for sinners. “Let them be turned,” he says: let them be removed from the delight of this world, lest they be able to rejoice longer in their pleasure. He adds, “into hell,” lest they think they would be sent somewhere else. Hell is so called because souls are continually carried down there; or, as some wish, from its being a lower region. Here, however, “hell” is to be understood as perpetual death, which those who despise the Lord’s commandments will undoubtedly reach [Col. 0085D]. To forget the Lord is to be enveloped in the errors of superstition and the mire of pleasure; conversely, those remember him who do not seek such things.

### Verse 18

“For the poor will not be forgotten to the end; the patience of the poor will not perish to the end.”

The prophet sees that in this world the poor are despised by the rich and assigned to the most cruel oblivion. He therefore says that at the end of the age, when the Lord comes to judge the world, the poor are not to be despised; rather, they will come more fully into the Lord’s remembrance when the rich of this world are excluded from the gifts of his kingdom. He explains why those poor will be remembered by the Lord. For he says, “the patience of the poor,” which crowns the most faithful; for if patience is lacking amid any hardships, the soul cannot be perfect [Col. 0086A].

Therefore patience is thanksgiving continually maintained in the fear of the Lord amid the anxious tribulations of the world, all the way to the end of death, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Such is its power that even the Lord himself, who suffers nothing, is called patient.

### Verse 19

“Arise, Lord; let man not prevail; let the nations be judged in your sight.”

As the prophet was treating the end of the world, he foresaw the coming of Antichrist with the illumination of his heart and, terrified by the magnitude of the danger, proclaimed in a loud voice: “Arise, Lord; let man not prevail.” For this is the most wicked man whom the human condition cannot withstand; in him there will be such cunning or power that only the Lord’s strength can overcome his wickedness [Col. 0086B].

He also asks that the nations be judged by the swiftest coming—those that will commit great crimes together with that most savage one. For while the Lord now administers all things by hidden power, he is nevertheless asked to judge openly there, where the proud will no longer be permitted to do harm.

### Verse 20

“Set over them, Lord, a lawgiver, so that the nations may know that they are human beings.”

He now speaks more clearly about Antichrist himself, asking that such a ruler be given to sinners—not one who governs them, but one who perishes together with them. Finally he adds, “so that the nations may know that they are human beings.” This is spoken as a threat, so that those who presume upon the freedom of their crimes may instead be inclined toward conversion. The only truly authentic giver of the law is God. And because Antichrist will command many things against the Lord’s precepts [Col. 0086C], he is placed under a curse, so that a perverse lawgiver may be assigned to them—one who will not benefit the wicked unto salvation, but unto ruin.

### Verse 21

“Why, Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Do you despise us in times of need, in tribulation?”

After the insertion of the diapsalma, he comes to the fourth member. Treating the evils of that time, he says to the Lord, out of consideration for the afflicted and in the manner of human weakness: “Why have you withdrawn far away?” This does not mean that he abandons one place and transfers himself to another, since he is wholly everywhere; rather, he is believed to have withdrawn when he delays in giving aid.

But although he had said above, “For you will not abandon those who seek you, Lord,” here he adds, “You despise us in times of need.” The former statement is spoken truthfully and definitively; the latter is uttered from the anxiety of those who groan [Col. 0086D]. We think that we are despised if we are delayed even for the briefest time; but he then grants more abundantly, when he supplies us with the consolations of great patience (mss. A, B, F: “piety”).

### Verse 22

“While the impious man is proud, the poor man is set on fire; they are caught in the thoughts that they devise.”

This statement must be examined with particular care, lest it be thought that the righteous are burned because the sinner appears to be exalted in this world. It should rather be understood in this way: “the impious man is proud” when he has fulfilled the effect of his evil will. Then the poor man is more greatly inflamed toward the pursuit of virtue, because, when he sees the sinner excessively exalted, he readily knows that he will fall; and he more eagerly seeks humility, from which he trusts that he will be exalted.

But this condemnation comes upon those impious and proud people: that they are seized by deserved punishments, as though by certain hooks, so that those who are delivered over to dark deeds may not be permitted to emerge into the light [Col. 0087A]. Good God, how great is the horror of fearing what we cannot escape! Yet grant that here we may hate those things which by your command we are ordered to avoid.

### Verse 23

“For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who commits iniquity is blessed. The sinner has provoked the Lord.”

The reason is given why sinners are made captive by their thoughts. For when the wicked man is praised, he is exalted; nor does he think about correction when he finds a flattering praiser. The exaggeration of iniquity follows: the one who is known to act wrongly is blessed.

But this man, deceived by the falsehood of flatterers and raised to great pride of domination, is properly understood as Antichrist. He is brought so far by throngs of deceivers that he proclaims himself not only an earthly king but also the god of all things, just as the Apostle says: “So that he sits in the temple of God and exalts himself above everything that is worshiped and called God” (2 Thess. 2:4) [Col. 0087B]. But these things lead him to ruin; for he provokes the true Lord, so that the false god may be consigned to avenging flames.

### Verse 24

“According to the abundance of his anger he will not inquire. God is not before his eyes.”

He continues to explain the will of Antichrist, because according to his sins he will not seek the Lord. By saying, “according to the abundance of his anger,” he shows that he will do everything turbulent and cruel. The fitting cause of this wickedness is then given: he does not have God before his eyes [Col. 0087C].

O how profound is the blindness of not having God before one’s eyes! If it is considered the greatest evil not to see the lights of the sun, do those not suffer hell amid the heavenly beings who, because of their own blindness, do not look upon the author of the sacred light? The prophet Daniel also testifies concerning this most wicked one, saying: “The king will exalt himself against every god, and will magnify himself above every god, and will speak arrogance against the God of gods” (Dan. 11:36).

### Verse 25

“His ways are polluted at all times; your judgments are removed from his face; he will rule over all his enemies.”

Just as he will say concerning the righteous, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 118:1), so now it is said concerning Antichrist that all his paths are polluted [Col. 0087D]—that is, his thoughts and filthy deeds. For whatever is defiled by the guidance of the pestilential devil must necessarily be contaminated and polluted.

A further wicked crime is added: when he sees that vengeance against him has been delayed, he does not think that God intends to exercise justice. Thus God’s judgments are removed from the heart of the impious when he sees that what he deserved to endure swiftly comes more slowly. And what increases his destruction is that, while he serves his vices, he is said to obtain rule over all his enemies. Raised up by this apparent prosperity, he will be more inclined to crimes, since he knows that no one can oppose him.

He is described below with such precision that he seems already to be present rather than still future. This figure is called characterismos, when someone is described either by his appearance or indicated by his characteristic actions [Col. 0088A].

### Verse 26

“For he said in his heart: I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil.”

With these words he specifically designates the thought of Antichrist, or of those who serve according to his will, since it is written: “Thus they imitate him who belong to his faction” (Wis. 2:24). He will say to himself, prompted by his own wickedness: “I shall leave no nation untouched; but, having taken vengeance on this nation, I shall transfer myself again to another nation to exact vengeance,” so that he may afflict all who appear to oppose his efforts through his evil purpose. He defined his deeds in a single statement when he says that he will do nothing without evil.

### Verse 27

“His mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; under his tongue are toil and pain.”

His wickedness is described by a twofold perversity. In his mouth he will have blasphemous cursing when he falsely claims to be the Son of God; bitterness when he announces the penalty of death to those who resist him and orders those to be led to punishment who have scorned to worship him as a deity [mss. A, B, F: “an empty name”].

These are the things he will have in his mouth, which he will speak publicly. When he says “under his tongue,” he indicates that he will have savage thoughts, so that, though he himself is lost, he will hasten to destroy everything. The definition of these things is “toil and pain”: toil when he afflicts the innocent with various calamities; pain when he makes martyrs, since the crown of martyrdom cannot be completed without bodily toil and pain. Thus everything he says or thinks is polluted with the same filth.

[Col. 0088C] ### Verse 28

“He sits in ambush with the rich in hidden places, in order to kill the innocent. His eyes look toward the poor.”

When he says, “He sits in ambush,” he compares the actions of Antichrist to the custom of robbers, who lie in wait along hidden paths in order to kill the innocent. This figure is called phantasia whenever the mind of the hearer is led into visions while future events are being conceived. He says that the kingdom of Antichrist will be such that it is understood to have been permitted for the crowning of the martyrs and the ruin of unbelievers.

He adds, “with the rich.” Here he signifies the multitude of evils. For in the divine Scriptures the rich are often understood in an evil sense, just as the poor are understood in a good one. To kill the innocent is to turn a religious person into a sacrilegious one and condemn his soul to perpetual death. For when he says that his eyes look toward the poor, he does not look in order to protect them, but directs his gaze so that he may destroy them.

### Verse 29

“He lies in ambush in secret, like a lion in his den.”

He previously called Antichrist a lion in his den, because he will savagely and deceitfully tear apart the people of Christ. In the beginning, the persecution of the Church was so violent that the Christians were compelled by pagans, through proscriptions, tortures, and killings, to sacrifice to idols. The second persecution was fraudulent, and is now carried out through heretics and false Christians. The final one remains, which is foretold as coming through Antichrist. Nothing will be more dangerous than it, because it will be exceedingly violent through the power of a singular kingdom, and deceptive through miracles [Col. 0089A], so that, as the Lord says in the Gospel, it may deceive, if possible, even the elect (Matt. 24:24).

Accordingly, “lion” pertains to violence; “in his den” pertains to deceit. Thus both of his iniquities are indicated in their respective expressions.

### Verse 30

“He lies in ambush to seize the poor; he seizes the poor while he draws him. In his snare he will humble him.”

The repetition of the ambush shows the extreme cunning of the persecutor. To seize the poor signifies the sudden danger to the soul toward which that most wicked one strives to drag the innocent. Then, in explaining the preceding words, a fitting repetition follows. Lest you think that the poor man was seized either because of a financial debt or because of the prosecution of a civil case, he repeats, “he seizes the poor,” and immediately attaches the reason for the persecution [Col. 0089B]: “while he draws him,” that is, while he attempts to lead him from the truth of worship to veneration of his own name.

And lest you still have any doubt about the phrase “he draws him,” he adds: “In his snare he will humble him.” The snare signifies the deceit by which the hearts of the simple are captured and, as though by a knot of perversity, lamentably bound. “He will humble him” is well said, because those who are led to insane doctrines undoubtedly fall away from the true religion.

### Verse 31

“He will bend down and fall when he has prevailed over the poor.”

This is now said of the tyrant himself, who will rage against God’s servants with power that has been permitted to him. “He will bend down” means that, when he has relaxed his spirit through the excessive acquisition of the lost and, as though bloated by an abundance of evils, has reached some period of leisure after the sufferings and afflictions of the saints [Col. 0089C], then the most wicked one will fall from his presumption when sudden destruction overtakes him and his followers. For he does not know the end of the world, because the Lord has kept it within his own power.

### Verse 32

“For he said in his heart: God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so that he may not see to the end.”

This is an exceedingly foolish thought. He will believe that God is concealing himself, from whom the sacrilegious man attempts to take away honor, thinking that he does not wish to regard his faithful people, although they are taught to endure every punishment for his sake. Ignorant of the truth, he will be moved by the opposite suspicion; nor will he understand what follows: “Do not forget the poor to the end.” It does not say that they will suffer nothing, but that they will in no way be abandoned to the end.

[Col. 0089D] ### Verse 33

“Arise, Lord my God, and let your hand be exalted; do not forget the poor to the end.”

Having traversed the four parts, the prophet now turns exultantly to the fifth, asking that what he nevertheless knew was going to happen might take place. “Arise” means, “rise more quickly,” that is, “come swiftly.” “Let your hand be exalted”: the hand signifies an action, but this action of God is the judgment whose coming we await. He desired the coming of that moment when this proud one could perish.

“Do not forget the poor to the end” stands against what the impious man had said: “He has turned away his face so that he may not see to the end.” Now he asks that, contrary to the desire of Antichrist, God not forget the poor until the end of the age, when the recompense of merits will take place.

[Col. 0090A] ### Verse 34

“Why has the impious man provoked God?” (mss.: “the sinful man provoked the Lord”). “For he said in his heart: He will not inquire.”

In this verse, with marvelous brevity, both a question is put first and a fitting answer follows. It must be pronounced interrogatively: “Why has the impious man provoked God?” Then the answer should be given: “For he said in his heart: He will not inquire.” It is clear that the Lord was provoked for this reason: the impious man did not think that he could inquire into his deeds. But he will find him mindful whom he hoped would be forgetful, and he will perceive that the things which, because of the multitude of his sins, he believed would not be kept in memory are received in full measure.

### Verse 35

“You see that you consider toil and pain, so that you may deliver them into your hands.”

This must now be said to the Lord with rejoicing, once the matter has been proved [42; ed.: *probatori*, “to the One who proves”]: “You see that no one mocks you.” Above he had said, “Under his tongue are toil and pain.” He now repeats those words: “You see that you consider toil and pain,” which that treacherous man, while he had them under his tongue—that is, while he revolved them in his thoughts—did not believe could be completely known.

You certainly consider them when he, handed over into your hands—that is, into your judgment—does not escape, but receives what is deserved according to his deeds, since he did not think he should abstain from crimes. Thus all power is shown to belong to God, who himself both hands sinners over to punishment and punishes them. Where can one flee whom such power pursues? He may commit crimes and feed upon the overthrow of various people; whatever he does will not go unpunished, since he will be tormented by eternal condemnation [Col. 0090C].

### Verse 36

“For the poor man has been left to you; you will be the helper of the orphan.”

After bringing the impious and convicted into the midst, he returns to the righteous, so that just as the former receive what is worthy of their deeds, so the latter may attain the promised rewards. When he says, “The poor man has been left to you,” he shows that the one who is entrusted to him is deprived of no benefit, since to be left to a merciful ruler is to be handed over to every good thing.

The poor man is so called from *paululum lare* [“a little dwelling”]. He therefore says that the poor man has been left to God so that all may see what good things they can bring back from his judgment. The orphan, however, does not mean one whose earthly father has died, but one for whom the world has been buried as a father. You will find many orphans deprived of a visible father who are blasphemers, gluttons, and—what is especially common at that age—lecherous; and these are shown to be alien from the Lord [Col. 0090D].

But the help of God cannot be separated from those orphans whose father, the devil, is shown to have been extinguished in the practice of crimes. And observe what he says: “You will be the helper,” so that when you see them afflicted in the flesh, you may not doubt that they will be delivered.

### Verse 37

“Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man; his sin will be sought, and it will not be found.”

The wickedness of Antichrist returns before the prophet’s eyes, and he asks that he not be permitted to rage any longer in the blood of the blessed. “Break” means, “reduce to nothing.” His arm signifies the power by which sinners acted wickedly, because he committed impious deeds conspicuously; and he singularly deserved this name because he would have no equal in crimes [Col. 0091A].

He is “wicked” because he will be an unjust persuader: those whom he cannot pervert through terror, he will at least try to turn aside through harmful rewards. “His sin” means the things he has wrongly committed. Although it is expressed in the singular, his sins will undoubtedly be innumerable. All his deeds and words are sins, for his entire life is called sin. He adds, “and it will not be found,” because there is no doubt that the wicked power will perish, whose author is known to be condemned.

### Verse 38

“The Lord will reign forever and unto the age of the age; you nations will perish from his land.”

Once the general devastation has been extinguished, he turns to the order of future things, because after Antichrist has been killed, the Lord’s eternal, merciful, and generous kingdom will come. Wicked evil is permitted to advance too far so that the Lord’s desired kingdom may be received with greater gratitude [Col. 0091B]. There the security of the blessed, once attained, will rest, and they will no longer fear the ambushes which the holy man is forced to endure in this world.

He calls sinners and impious people “nations,” those who live like wild beasts and do not obey the Lord’s laws. “From his land” signifies the kingdom of the Lord Savior, which only the supremely blessed enjoy.

### Verse 39

“The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the longing of their heart.”

The vows of the righteous are fittingly expressed in suitable words. He says, “the desire of the poor,” which always arises from a love that has gone before, so that they desire to see him clearly there where they are now transported by the light of the mind [Col. 0091C].

He adds, “the longing of their heart.” This word is clearly the stronger. “Longing” is used where, with the powers of the soul somehow joined together, something is sought with the ardor of the mind. He continues, “your ear has heard.” We must understand as a rule that God possesses none of the bodily members, but that the effects of his power are called his ear, by which he hears; his eye, by which he sees; and his hand, by which he accomplishes.

Let these statements be committed to memory, lest, because they must often be repeated, we seem to cause weariness by repeating them.

### Verse 40

“To judge the orphan and the humble, so that man may no longer continue to exalt himself upon the earth.”

Behold, we are admonished by prophetic authority that not merely any orphan, but the orphan and the humble, are especially pleasing to God. For when he says, “to judge the orphan and the humble,” he signifies that a judgment can be rendered on his behalf. But when he is called humble, he is approved as most righteous.

A definitive promise also follows: the things that have been spoken are to occur so that no human being may thereafter be permitted to exceed these limits. Then all evils will indeed be brought to an end, when the author of all sinners is condemned together with his people.

These are the hidden things of the Son, which the title of this psalm sings. Although they frequently appear to be announced through certain signs, when they will come remains unknown to human beings. For concerning that day the Lord says in the Gospel: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone” (Mark 13:32).

Regarding this passage, the blessed Fathers Hilary and Augustine, holy lights of the Church [Col. 0092A], have said many profound and eloquent things, judging it wicked to suppose that the omnipotent human assumption of the Word was ignorant of something future which it declared the Father to know. For when Peter says in the Gospel, “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you” (John 21:17), the Lord himself likewise says, “All things that the Father has are mine” (John 16:15). Clearly, he would not have everything belonging to the Father if he did not know what the Father knew.

They therefore taught that this must be believed in a salutary and truthful way: through the figure of metonymy, that is, transnomination, which is frequently found in the sacred Scriptures. What is meant is that he usefully makes his subjects ignorant. For in Genesis God says to Abraham, “Now I know that you fear the Lord your God” (Gen. 22:12), that is, “Now I have made you known.” So here also it says, “I do not know,” meaning, “I make you not know.”

Likewise, the Lord says elsewhere, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12), although he certainly could not be ignorant of those whom he condemned. Finally, when asked about that specific moment, he says: “It is not yours to know the times or the seasons” (Acts 1:7). He did not say, “It is not mine,” or “It is not ours,” but said, “It is not yours to know.” Thus both things are preserved: human beings are ignorant of what it was not fitting for them to know, while the Son of God is in no way ignorant through the weakness of the flesh.

But if we suppose that that majesty—which it would be impious to say—concealed ignorance, then ignorance would be found stronger than the divine nature, which, to speak foolishly, would have been able to suppress providence, through which all things were created. Since these things are taught to be altogether absurd [Col. 0092C], it is worthy of belief that the whole Trinity, whose nature is one and omnipotent, always possesses unfailing knowledge of all things.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

The promise announced by the psalmist has been fulfilled; the hidden miracles of the Son have been disclosed. O mighty and wondrous causes, which, although they appear to have been explained, nevertheless remain undoubtedly secret! For when they are foretold, they are not unknown; yet while it remains unknown when they will come, they are shown still to be concealed. Thus what is spoken is both a secret and not withheld from those who seek.

Therefore let us pray more fervently to the Lord that he may deign to grant us a most salutary amendment, because the one who is told that the retribution of sinners will come sins without excuse [Col. 0092D]. It must also be kept in mind that this is the first psalm in which the coming of Antichrist is prophesied.

The present number also proves to disclose that hidden matter: the Lord gave up his spirit at the ninth hour. Since this psalm, among other things, also speaks of his passion, it is fitting that, through its numerical calculation, it announces the hour of his passing, since it is known also to have narrated the mysteries of his cross.

# Exposition of Psalm X

## To the End: A Psalm of David

Although “To the End” frequently appears in the titles and always directs the intention of our mind toward the Lord Christ, there is no doubt that it has been placed there because of various miracles. At one time it indicates his most glorious passion; at another, his triumphant and wondrous resurrection before all nations. Now it declares the holy faith in which heretics battle against the most faithful Christians. Thus it continually tends toward Christ, although it is found adapted to different meanings.

You recognize that the same must be done in the remaining psalms as well, if you direct the sharpness of your mind to them. Concerning the psalm and David, it is enough to remember what we know was said above. It must nevertheless be understood that this psalm was uttered to destroy the heretics.

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0093B] This entire psalm must be referred to the person of the prophet. In the first section he speaks about the heretical plotters who strive to convert Catholics to their own perversity. In the second he threatens the Lord’s judgment and clearly shows what they may have to endure in that retribution, so that, fearing the Lord’s justice, they may abandon their superstitious falsehoods.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“In the Lord I trust. How can you say to my soul: Flee to the mountain like a sparrow?”

This figure is called *coenonema*, that is, the sharing of counsel. It frequently occurs when we exchange words either with adversaries or with helpers [ed., “hearers”]. This speech is directed against the heretical persuaders who wish to say what is impious, so that through wicked disputes they may lead innocent souls astray [Col. 0093C].

The faithful man therefore says to them: “While I stand established upon the firm summit of religion, how can you advise me, ‘Flee to the mountain’—that is, to heretical perversity—lying that Christ is there where truth is shown to have no trace?”

For “mountain” is equivocal in the divine Scriptures: it is assigned to dissimilar things by way of some comparison. It is frequently used both in a good and in an evil sense. When it is used in a good sense, its firmness and honorable height are considered; when in an evil sense, it signifies mental stupor and exalted pride. Thus one name is suitably applied to different things when their qualities are taken into account.

There are also several kinds of sparrows: some delight in holes in walls; others seek dewy valleys; some desire barren mountains [Col. 0093D]. But here he speaks of those who, with a very light-minded will, are snatched toward the highest places of the earth, so that those who are transferred by the fickleness of an unstable mind to most wicked teachings may rightly be considered like them.

Verse 2. For behold, sinners have bent the bow. By “bow” we should understand the divine commandments, which the heretic, handling them and reshaping them according to his perversity, bends toward the infliction of a wound upon the soul, so that he may not pierce it for salvation but transfix it with eternal death. And the bow is appropriately employed in the most sacred Scriptures, because, joining the two Testaments into one, it grants either defense or ruin, as the Apostle says: “To some indeed we are an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:16).

Verse 3. They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. He remains within the comparison of an archer; for just as an archer has arrows in his quiver, so the other carries poisonous words in his heart. “In darkness” means either when the Church is thrown into confusion by persecutions, when carnal people are thought more easily to be changed through fear of danger, or in a hidden plan, when they think it more advantageous to deceive Christians because they judge that their designs are not seen by them. But when he says “the upright in heart,” he shows their ambushes to be futile and empty. For none are upright in heart except those whom no deceitful persuasion toward iniquity has been able to mislead.

Verse 4. For they have destroyed what you established; but the righteous one, what has he done? He says the same concerning the heretics themselves: they have destroyed the law of the Lord when they strive to tear apart the holy Scriptures by false interpretations, turning to the destruction of certain people what was prophesied by the Lord for salvation. The defense of the Lord Christ is also added. For he says: if human beings have wished to overthrow equity by an iniquitous interpretation, why do they accuse him who has spoken justly? They do not derive their errors from the commandment, but conceive them from their own utterly wicked will.

Verse 5. The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven. Having reproached those who think falsely about the truest religion, the prophet reaches the second section, in which he now says that the Lord’s judgments are to come, so that human perversity may at least correct itself when it considers the Lord’s severity. And lest anyone suppose that deceiving the innocent would go unpunished, he says that the Lord dwells in each religious person, as the Apostle says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3:17). Thus the heretic may know that he can be destroyed by God, by whom the hearts of those who believe rightly are known to be possessed.

“Heaven” signifies holy men, in whom the Divinity deigns to dwell through the presence of his majesty. O how beautifully praise arises from an unimpaired reality! For what honor, what glory it is to receive the Creator, whom there is no doubt continually visits the good!

Verse 6. His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the sons of men. Just as those from whom he turns away are wretched, so those upon whom God looks favorably are made blessed, because his gaze is a benefit. He who is illumined by such great brightness is not obscured by the darkness of sins. For Peter, after his fall, deserved to return when the mercy of the Divinity looked upon him.

And observe that he first mentioned eyes, and afterward eyelids. “Eyelids” are so called from fluttering. They are coverings of the lights, as it were, and something like bellows of the eyes, which we close when sleeping so that we may restore the little body wearied by labor. Therefore, because the ministries of the bodily members are frequently adapted allegorically to the Lord, he says that he examines—that is, considers—the sons of men not only when he directs his eyes toward them, but also when he is thought to neglect them, as though sleeping.

[Col. 0095A]

Verse 7. The Lord examines the righteous and the ungodly; but whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. No disparagement of the wicked should be inferred when the Lord examines both the righteous and the ungodly, for he distinguishes all things according to truth. This is said so that human desires and foolish opinions may not seduce people, but that each person may examine his own conscience, knowing that the Lord alone passes judgment upon it.

A brief and evident sentence follows. What is it to love iniquity? To hate one’s own soul. For the one who follows the devil persecutes himself, while wishing to travel those paths that lead to places of punishment which must be avoided.

Verse 8. He rains snares upon sinners; fire and sulfur and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup. “He rains” refers to the words of preachers descending from heaven. To the devout they are showers, but to the faithless fiery snares. The former, understanding them rightly, bear fruit from them; the latter, handling them wrongly, strangle their souls in the knot of perversity.

“Fire” is when a burning anxiety consumes them; “sulfur,” because their thoughts are soiled by a detestable stench; “the spirit of storms,” when they confuse themselves in a tumultuous mind; “the portion of their cup,” that is, the measure by which they become drunk with polluted acts.

“Cup” is also used in a good sense, as in: “Your cup, making drunk—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22:5). For a cup is the measure by which souls are given drink. It is called a cup because it is accustomed continually to receive a hot drink. Macrobius Theodosius likewise says in one of his works that a people called the Cylicrani was established near Heraclea; its name, formed from ἄπὸ τοῦ κύλιχος, *apo tou kylichos*, “from the cup,” was changed by one letter into *calix*, “cup,” the name for a kind of drinking vessel. Hence this name is evidently fixed in memory.

Verse 9. For the Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity. A fitting conclusion is made concerning the equity of the eternal King. He says that the righteous Lord loves righteousness because he knows how to look upon none except those who know how to preserve righteousness. He adds: “His face has seen equity”—namely, that equity which he himself nevertheless graciously grants. For human goodness possesses nothing from itself except what it has received from the Lord, the giver of all good things.

“Face” here signifies the Lord’s mercy. For in another psalm we read: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33:17). But since here he said, “he has seen equity,” he has made his grace understood through equity.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0095D]

How well this psalm has embraced, in marvelous brevity, the cunning of the heretics and their retribution, so that, recognizing the punishments destined for them, we may be kept away from their perversities! For in the number itself there is also the sacred power of the Decalogue, which has proved the most glorious founder of human life. Just as the Decalogue condemns human vices, so this psalm attacks the meaning of iniquitous preaching, freeing us from a danger all the greater because offending in faith is worse than sinning through the weakness of the flesh.

Therefore this psalm rightly also keeps this number, since it confirms our understanding in orthodox belief through the most perfect instruction. For in the Gospel (Luke 19), the good servant who offered ten talents was praised and received authority over ten cities as his reward. The Apostle also, as a great mystery, wrote the word of the Lord to ten churches, signifying that the fullness of sacred teaching embraces this quantity of number.

The number itself has also been gathered into great power and praise. Although it may be extended into a long and infinite reckoning, it nevertheless always turns back upon itself in a sum that continually increases; and rightly so, since, while it receives nothing foreign, it appears to produce from itself a great increase. It is also rightly called an ornament, since its name derives from beauty.

# Exposition of Psalm XI

## For the end; a psalm of David for the eighth day

[Col. 0096B]

As was already said in the sixth psalm, the eighth day pertains to eternal rest. This world does not receive an eighth day, but, when the seventh has ended, it always returns to the first. In these days the number is plural; that day, however, is understood as singular, since it is not changed by anything succeeding it.

Therefore the power of the psalm must be explained, so that through its intention the inscription of the title may more easily be understood. The prophet asks that the iniquity of this world be destroyed, so that one may reach the truth of the future promise. In this way that undisturbed kingdom is signified, when its blessedness is sought without interruption. Thus the eighth day is rightly fitted to this psalm, in which the corrupt custom of this age is abandoned and the innocence of that age is asked to come. The remaining words of this title are shown to be well known from the preceding expositions.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first part, the prophet asks to be saved from the perversity of this world, because the deceitful and proud were denying the Lord’s power through criminal insults. In the second, he proclaims that the Father’s promise is to be fulfilled through the almighty Son, praising the Lord’s utterances briefly, just as earlier he had accused impious speeches.

## Exposition of the Psalm

Verse 1. Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed; for truths have been diminished among the sons of men. Let us carefully examine this beginning of the psalm, since it has been formed with the beauty of great figures. The prophet suddenly cries out to the Lord, so that the magnitude of the danger may appear from the very fear. Then, through the figure *synathroesmos*, he gathers together, up to the division, many things that he feared. This figure is counted among the most violent figures, when numerous matters and many crimes are collected into one.

For when he saw this age weighing down souls in many ways, he asks to be saved by the Lord, with whom he knew true medicine to be found. He says that the holy one is absent from the world, where such a multitude of evils is known to exist. This is said with respect to human beings; otherwise, he is known to be present everywhere.

And lest there be ambiguity in what he said—“the holy one has failed”—he follows this by saying that truths have been diminished among the sons of men. The holy one could not otherwise have failed unless truth had been diminished among human beings. This argument is called one “from consequences,” when what is stated first is confirmed by the following expression.

But when he says “diminished,” he clearly shows that God’s gifts have been corrupted by human faults: people stain by their own perversity the benefits bestowed upon them. And observe that “truths” is placed in the plural, although truth is one. But since its power is bestowed upon each human being through heavenly dispensation, we testify that there are many truths. Just as we customarily say “the prophecy of David,” “the prophecy of Jeremiah,” “the Gospel of Matthew,” “the Gospel of John,” and so forth, honoring those who have flourished in this matter, so we also speak of “truths” when its quality is granted by the Lord’s generosity to human minds in their individual parts.

This may also appropriately be applied to the Jewish people, who, emptied of heavenly gifts, refused to believe—the people foretold by a multitude of such great seers.

Verse 2. Each spoke vanity to his neighbor; deceitful lips, with a heart and a heart, spoke evil. “Vanity” signifies falsehood, in accordance with what he said above: “Truths have been diminished among the sons of men,” when they sought testimonies against the Lord Christ and stirred themselves up by wicked whisperings.

“Neighbors” signifies those associated not so much by kinship of lineage as by participation in crime. For when he says “with a heart and a heart,” whenever we wish to portray deceitful people, we declare that they have divided hearts, as James says: “A man double-minded is unstable in all his ways” (James 1:8).

When, however, we wish to identify the simple, we testify that they have one heart, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Thus we also call those “double-tongued” who do not remain constant in one judgment.

And consider what sort of sentence follows the matters already mentioned: “They spoke evil.” They necessarily spoke evil, because they carried double hearts.

Verse 3. May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things. A general sentence follows, as is customary when a law is enacted: one person sins, and the severity promulgated condemns the universal evil.

“May he destroy” is spoken against the gathering of the Jews, so that those who had assembled themselves in one perversity might perish indiscriminately. The “tongue that speaks great things” is one that arrogates to itself some great power and does not understand that it was given by the Creator, while it thinks that the outcomes of events are subject to it. Thus the Apocalypse says concerning the Antichrist: “I saw in that horn which was higher than the others a mouth speaking great things” (Apoc. 12:5), and so forth.

And lest you be able to understand “the tongue that speaks great things” in a good sense, he first prefixed “deceitful lips.” Consider, moreover, the piety of the speaker: he does not curse human beings, since many of them were destined to be converted, but curses the vices themselves.

Verse 4. They said: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are from ourselves. Who is our lord?” He explains those who, swollen with excessive talk amid prosperous circumstances, presume to exalt their own glory and place in their own power what, in their madness, they do not understand they have received from God.

I ask them for a moment: why are they not talkative when, as cares descend upon them, they are bound by a stupid silence? Fixing their faces upon the earth, they close the doors of their lips; and as though they had lost their tongues, they fall silent with confused minds. Add the various circumstances of illnesses, so that frequently the person who seemed to boast of having power over his lips is not even able to ask for food.

Then let them say, if they can: “Our lips are from ourselves. Who is our lord?” But this phrase, “Who is our lord?” repeats the words of sacrilegious people. This figure is called *antisagoge*, that is, contradiction.

Verse 5. Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord. In these two verses the persons of the Father and the Son must be examined subtly, so that confusion of understanding may be removed from us.

After he had accused those who plotted the shedding of the Lord’s blood, he comes to the second part, in which the prophet, in the voice of the Father, promises the resurrection of the Lord and Savior. We can report another person’s words while nevertheless not changing the speech of our own person.

Let us understand what piety of the Creator is present here, when the Lord Christ was glorified because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, so that his faithful might not be burdened by prolonged tribulation. “I will arise” is said metaphorically of one who does not know how to lie down through human weakness. But when he says “I will arise,” he means: I will appear and be manifested in the Son. For there is one power and an undivided majesty. The Father appears and is manifested in the Son, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

Verse 6. I will place him upon my salvation; I will act confidently through him. The Father calls his Word, which became flesh, his salvation, through whom life came to mortals, since every believer receives salvation in abundant generosity.

And what does he place upon him? Consolation, namely, the consolation he mentioned above concerning the needy and the poor. It is evident that this came to the faithful when the Lord and Savior rose again.

“I will act confidently in him”: the power of the Father’s omnipotence is declared, because he truly acts confidently whose will no one prevails against. Thus it is also said of Christ in the Gospel: “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 7:29).

But the Father’s power is the Son’s confidence, just as the Son’s confidence is the Father’s power. This certainly belongs to the whole Trinity because of the unity of its nature.

Verse 7. The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances. After speaking of the Father’s words, he confirms those same words by praising them, for everything happened just as it was known to have been promised.

What, then, are the Lord’s utterances? It is defined briefly: pure utterances, possessing the utmost purity of virgin integrity, which no lie corrupts and no stain of falsehood infects. For just as chastity knows no pollution, so the Lord’s utterances do not know how to mingle with any impurity.

But do not understand this as incidental, since it is set against what was said above concerning the wicked: “Each spoke vanity to his neighbor,” so that, when the diversity of realities has been examined, we may be removed from an iniquitous custom. This figure is called in Greek *syndesmos*, in Latin *collatio*, “comparison,” when persons or causes are compared with one another, whether by contrast or by similarity. Here the divine utterances are praised; above, human speech is accused.

Verse 8. Silver tested by fire, purified of earth sevenfold. He continues to define by the likeness of shining metal what pure utterances are. Silver taken from the earth and tested by fire is ordinarily most pure when it has been cleansed by repeated smelting.

“Tested” or “purified” is set against what he said concerning sinners: “Deceitful lips, with a heart and a heart.” And so that you might recognize how greatly they differ, he added “purified sevenfold.” This number seems able to refer to the sevenfold Spirit: the fear of God, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom. Through these the divine Word, remaining as though in blazing furnaces, shines with the radiant brilliance of truth.

Verse 9. You, O Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever. Just as above he said, “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips,” so here he promises that the Lord will preserve those who have believed his utterances with a pure mind.

And observe the moderation with which the holy rule has been preserved. When he says, “You will guard us,” he cuts away the presumption of perishable humanity, so that no one may think he ought to rely upon himself in any way.

“From this generation” signifies either the Jews or the sinners of this world, from whom we cannot be guarded by our own power unless we are protected by his mercy. He also added “forever,” because here he consoles us in tribulations, while there he establishes us in eternal security; here he helps us, there he glorifies and crowns us. Thus the most merciful Creator preserves us here so that we may not perish, and there makes us blessed, so that we can in no way remain wretched.

Verse 10. The ungodly walk about on every side; according to your loftiness you have multiplied the sons of men. After he had rebuked the speeches of the ungodly in the first part with fitting execration, and praised the Lord’s utterances in the second part with marvelous proclamation, he comes to the conclusion of the psalm, in which he gives each part its due in a single verse.

He says in a very brief sentence that the ungodly walk about, so that they may never be able to reach the straight path. For crooked ways are always suited to evil habits, as Solomon says concerning the ungodly: “They abandoned straight paths in order to walk in crooked ways” (Prov. 2:13). And therefore they cannot reach the rest of the eighth day, since, like wheels, they are always turned back upon their own tracks.

It follows: “According to your exaltation you have multiplied the sons of men.” This pertains to those who have sincerely believed the Lord’s purest and chastest utterances. And observe how much is promised to them in this expression. He says: “According to your exaltation you have multiplied the sons of men,” not according to their merit, but according to that which does not know how to endure human limitations.

We often call “high” what we are unable to comprehend. The Creator is not subject to the measure that has been given to all creatures; nor can there be any dimension in him from whom number, weight, and measure are bestowed upon all things.

“You have multiplied the sons of men” refers to the promise made to Abraham in which he says: “Multiplying, I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven” (Gen. 16:10). It is evident that he has done this and continues to do it daily in his saints.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider how this psalm has revealed mysteries exceedingly useful to us. It said how people occupy themselves with vain and superfluous speech, wishing not to pursue the truth by which they may live, but falsehood by which they die. Then it explained in due order what the Lord’s utterance is, so that each person’s own impurity may become hateful if he recognizes how utterly pure the Lord’s words are.

Through these things a remedy is given, since it is evident that the sons of men can be freed according to the Lord’s power. And because the power of the number eleven, in which this psalm is established, is understood to indicate the evangelical mystery, let us beseech the Master of the household that, at least at the eleventh hour, he may graciously admit us into his vineyard, so that he may deign to grant us a reward not owed for our works, but given freely.

For blessed Prosper, in the second part of the book entitled *Before the Law, Under the Law, and Under Grace*, says this concerning the number eleven: “Nor was it without this mystery that eleven curtains of goats’ hair covered the tabernacle from above, thereby showing that the whole world is guilty before God and lives under penitence.” For the psalm of this number has as its beginning: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed; for truths have been diminished among the sons of men.”

# 47. Exposition of Psalm XII

## For the end; a psalm of David

Since the words of this title are already known from the preceding exposition, it is more fitting that we say something about the content of the psalm. For it speaks entirely of the charity of the Lord Christ, in which the perfection of the whole law is situated. Whoever possesses this charity sets aside all the allurements of this world, since, while it alone is sought with the whole heart, its opposite is not loved.

The charity of God is a kind of spring rain of virtues, beneath which both a blessed will germinates and holy action bears fruit: patient in adversity, temperate in prosperity, powerful through humility, most joyful in affliction, benevolent toward enemies, and overcoming the wicked through its own goodness.

The heavenly creation is also always kindled by it: a renewing flame, a desire growing toward salvation. And, to embrace everything in the Apostle’s words: “God himself is charity” (1 John 4:16).

Therefore it is fitting for us to seek charity itself and desire it without end, so that, since here we cannot be filled by it, we may at least be satisfied by it in the future recompense, as it is written in the one-hundred-eighteenth psalm: “My soul has failed in your salvation” (Ps. 118:81). For this failing consists in a blessed eternity.

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0101A]

When the prophet saw in the preceding section that the human race was occupied with deadly superstitions and was not hastening with pure understanding to the worship of the true Lord, he prays with great desire that his faith may be fulfilled by the coming of the holy incarnation, so that even then the confused Gentile world might salutarily abandon its wandering errors.

In the second section, in order to instruct our petitions effectively, he earnestly asks that his faith be enlightened, lest it succumb to any deception of the enemy, since he says that he has always trusted in the Lord’s mercy.

## Exposition of the Psalm

Verse 1. How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever? As has been said, the prophet is filled with the Lord’s abundant charity, by which he eagerly awaited his incarnation. Confidently pouring forth his words, he says that he has been delayed too long from the fulfillment of his expectation, since delay is exceedingly burdensome to anyone who desires intensely.

Although he believed through the illumination of faith that the Lord would come, he nevertheless complains of his delay, since he was not yet deemed worthy to see the advent for which he hoped. God does not forget; rather, he is believed to suffer forgetfulness by the one who desires, when he delays granting what is requested.

“Forever” here signifies the time when he foresaw that the Lord’s incarnation would come. Such a complaint strikes faithful souls: they desire heavenly things without end and always trust in the Lord’s promise.

And observe that throughout these four verses he places words of steadfast patience. He says “How long?” then “How long?” and “Until when?” repeating “How long?” again. This figure is called *epimone*, when similar expressions are repeated frequently.

Verse 2. How long will you turn your face from me? He asks for the appearing of Christ, which he already foresaw in the Spirit. For this is his face, which could appear to bodily eyes; and that holy man rightly desired to behold it with a universal affection, since it deigned to save the world through heavenly visitation.

Thus both the desire of divine love is shown and the charity fulfilled toward one’s neighbors is established, since he continually sought what he knew would benefit everyone. Both are joined and associated: neither can God be loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor be loved without the Divinity.

Verse 3. How long shall I place counsel in my soul? Here the greatest ardor of one who endures is expressed. He says that he lacks counsel by which he might mitigate his desire to see, since it is an immeasurable anxiety to long for a good and endure for a long time before it comes.

Verse 4. Sorrow in my heart by day. How long will my enemy be exalted over me? He continues in pious lamentation. “I will place,” from the preceding verse, is understood, so that the complete sentence is: “I will place sorrow in my heart by day,” that is, on each day, so that the continual passage of time may be understood without qualification.

And consider the first word of this verse, so that now not desire but the greatest sorrow may be perceived, aroused, as it were, by an elegant rising sequence. This certainly occurs when hope is prolonged.

“My enemy”: he speaks of the devil, who before the Lord’s advent rejoiced in human captivity. “Over me,” that is, over my faith, because he was earnestly worshiped throughout the whole world, while divine religion did not possess the devotion of faith.

Verse 5. Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God. Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death. He comes to the second section of his prayer. But what tears of piety should we believe that he poured out here, lest through prolonged delay the whole world perish, held captive by errors?

When he says “me,” he does not ask only for himself individually, but begs that all the faithful be helped; through love for them a universal remedy was being sought.

“Look upon me” must be referred to what he said above: “How long will you turn your face from me?” “Hear me” refers to what he says at the beginning of the psalm: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever?”

Here we must understand the eyes of the heart, which fall asleep in death when, with the light of faith buried, they are closed by carnal delight. This is the sleep in which the enemy rejoices.

Verse 6. Lest my enemy say, “I have prevailed against him.” Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am shaken. He says this concerning the devil and his angels, whose custom it is to insult people when they capture them, considering the ruins of their followers to be their victories.

He says: “If I am separated from you, I will give joy to those who, by their detestable custom, become happy when they know that those deceived by them have been taken possession of.” When he says “if I am shaken,” he signifies the mutability of the faithless soul, because anyone who withdraws even a step of his mind from the Lord’s firmness must place his foot in the devil’s snare.

Verse 7. But I have trusted in your mercy. My heart will rejoice in your salvation. Although he was being carried away by great desire, he nevertheless declared the moments of his patience, saying that, even if his personal prayers should still be delayed, he himself could nevertheless be found utterly firm in hope, with heavenly mercy assisting him, as the Apostle says: “Hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:5).

He says “in your mercy,” because whoever thinks otherwise empties all the hope of his faith. O power of faith, and great steadfastness of the believer! He rejoiced in the absence of the present, and the inner man had already seen God’s salvation, which the outer man still desired to behold with bodily eyes.

Verse 8. I will sing to the Lord, who has granted me good things; and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High. Although at the beginning he said that, through frequent complaint, he had been delayed from his desire, here he joyfully asserts that the Lord’s benefits have already been granted to him.

He says this either because, through the power of prophecy, he claims to have received what he knew would plainly come, or because believing this was itself already a reward, as it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6). Therefore he rightly says that he has received it, since such steadfastness of faith had been granted to him.

And observe that he first said “I will sing”; afterward, “I will sing praise.” “I will sing” with the heart, where he was filled with exceeding joy [ms. G., “contemplated”]; “I will sing praise” through good works, which the Divinity especially seeks. Thus “I will sing” pertains to the contemplative life, and “I will sing praise” to the active life. These two, joined most beautifully like twin eyes, produce a Christian filled with light.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us contemplate the prophet placed in blessed contemplation, and the desire with which he awaited the glorious incarnation of the Lord. From this let us perceive what a gift we have received, since we understand that he wished so earnestly to behold the powerful King and holy Prophet.

But we must beseech the Lord not to hand us over to the devil to be tested through abandonment, and not to make us unworthy of such a benefit, so that we may faithfully serve the one who has already come, just as that man most devotedly served the one who was still to come.
