The number twelve also admonishes us to remember the quantity of the apostles. Through the most perfect teaching of the commandments, they loved both the Lord above all things and their neighbors with the same charity with which they loved themselves. Thus this psalm rightly grants us such mysteries, since it is consecrated by the number of the apostles.

The people of the Hebrews are also known to have been divided into twelve tribes. The Lord likewise promises the apostles twelve seats in the coming judgment. The year itself is divided into twelve months. And the careful reader will find many other things of this kind, so that he may recognize this number to be filled with many mysteries.

# Exposition of Psalm XIII

## For the end; a psalm of David

[Col. 0103C]

Since the words of this title are now entirely familiar from the preceding expositions, memory of them is required rather than further discussion. In the titles, however, “the end” is frequently repeated with justice, so that the mind of the hearer may always be raised toward almighty Christ.

But this “end,” as was said, directs our understanding toward the Lord through various meanings: now through the confession of those suffering, now through the exultation of those rejoicing, now through the devotion of one teaching, now through the threat of judgment.

In the present case, however, this psalm chastises the madness of the Jews with vehement rebuke: harsh in its attacks, terrifying to the profane, bitter toward the unbelieving. Thus this rebuke is rightly given to the holy Church, against whose purpose mad unbelief strives to stir up wicked designs.

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0103D]

That face of the Lord which was sought in the twelfth psalm with desirous supplication is here introduced as having already arrived. Therefore, first, the Catholic Church rebukes the Jews, who did not believe after seeing Christ.

Second, it says that those who refused to recognize the fruitful fear of the Lord are thrown into confusion by empty terror. Finally, it foretells that their conversion will occur at the end of the world, when the fullness of the Gentiles, awaited through long ages, has come to pass, so that, when the Lord’s mercy is revealed in them, they may more readily be invited to the remedy of confession.

## Exposition of the Psalm

Verse 1. The fool said in his heart, “There is no God.” Seeing Christ come humbly in assumed flesh, the Jewish people foolishly said: “There is no God.” They did not understand that he was the one foretold by the prophets.

This was more serious because he did not say it with his lips but in his heart, so that unbelief might be joined to an even worse evil intention.

Verse 2. They were corrupted and became abominable in their desires; there is none who does good, not even one. “They were corrupted” when, departing from the soundness of the Scriptures, they were proved to have fallen into depraved understandings. Then follows the punishment of sin: stained by unspeakable unbelief, they made themselves abominable to the Lord through their errors.

“Will” is so called from *volatus*, “flight,” because the mind is carried with great speed wherever it wishes. It follows: “There is none who does good.”

What, then, shall we say about the patriarchs? Did Noah not do good when, obeying the Lord’s commands, he entered the ark to be saved? Did Abraham not do good when, obeying the divine commands, he offered his son for sacrifice? Did Job not do good when, struck by harsh suffering, he continually gave thanks to the Lord in all things?

What shall I say about the prophets and apostles, who, serving the Lord’s commandments, offered themselves in glorious deaths? Even today, by the Lord’s generosity, good works are accomplished through the activity of the righteous.

But so that this denial may shine forth as entirely true to you, consider what follows: “not even one.” Christ alone exists, without whom human weakness has no power either to begin or to complete any good. Therefore it was rightly denied that anyone does good unless, through his mercy, he has reached him.

For when one approaches him and does not depart from him, every good is accomplished without doubt. This, then, is the “end” that was promised [ed., *praemissus*, “prefixed”] in the title.

Verse 3. The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men. How did he look down? So that he might send us his only-begotten Son, through whom true faith could be recognized more clearly.

“Upon the sons of men” may be understood of the Jews, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:14). He called them “sons of men” more honorably because of their worship of the one God and in comparison with the Gentiles.

What was specially given to that people is known to have been made alien by their sacrilegious rejection of it.

### Verse 5

“That he might see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God.” “Might see” means “might cause to be seen.” This is the figure called *hypallage*, that is, inversion, whenever words that have been spoken are transferred to another meaning—as when someone is said to learn something in time although he knew everything before it happened. Thus the Lord also spoke to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord your God” (Gen. 22:12). So too he will say to sinners at his judgment: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:13), and similarly elsewhere. This manner of speaking is frequently found in the divine Scriptures.

He said “understanding” with reference to the assumption of humanity, since it would have been necessary to understand that it was God who, through many miracles, revealed the advent of his divinity [Col. 0105A]. By “seeking,” however, he meant whether they followed his commandments. For the one who does not depart from God’s will seeks God. Thus, in a single verse, the mystery of the holy incarnation has been revealed, so that through it both the faith of human beings might be understood and the remedy of the desired gift might be found.

### Verse 5

“All have turned aside; together they have become useless: there is no one who does good, not even one.”

All are said to have turned aside, although a considerable multitude among them believed. But the whole is to be understood from a part: there were so many wicked people that nearly all might be thought faithless and lost. Thus they turned aside from the grace of God and became useless to themselves.

### Verse 6

“Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully.”

These five verses, up to the second division [Col. 0105B], are not found in the Hebrew copies. But because long usage has received them into the practice of the Church, we shall expound them one by one insofar as permission is granted.

The present verse has already been spoken in the fifth psalm. Yet because the people and the cause were the same, the sentence is appropriately repeated against them. Their throat is rightly called a tomb, because they spoke words that brought death. For just as open tombs exhale foul odors, so their throat uttered poisonous speeches. And, lest they perish alone, they spread deceit with their tongues.

Remember also that in these five verses he has designated, through the second kind of definition—which in Greek is called *ennoematice*, and in Latin *notio*—those foolish people of whom he said above that they thought sacrilegious things in their hearts [Col. 0105C]. This kind of definition does not indicate substantially what something is, but clearly discloses them through the quality of their actions.

### Verse 7

“The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.”

The asp is acknowledged to be a monstrous kind of serpent which, through its natural obstinacy, is said not to admit the words of enchanters; nor can it be removed from its purpose, since it cannot be softened by any incantation. The Jews are most aptly compared with it. Against words that brought salvation they had brought upon themselves a wretched, deadly deafness, and they chose rather to follow poisonous counsels than to be led toward saving teachings. Thus it seems rightly said of them: “They loved darkness more than light” (John 3:19).

Poison is so called because it creeps through the veins. In the same way, the desires of the wicked advance through hidden thought. The following words also remain especially fittingly within the comparison with asps: even when soothing songs are sung to it, the asp continually threatens death. So too the mouth of the Jews was full of cursing and bitterness when, in response to good admonitions, they blasphemed the Lord Christ and plotted his death.

### Verse 8

“Their feet are swift to shed blood.”

He calls “feet” the advances of their plan, by which we move from an undertaking toward the outcome of events. By saying “swift,” he showed that their counsels lacked moderation. “To shed blood” is to be understood as referring to the blood of the Lord and Savior, so that the speed [manuscripts and edition: “the criminality”] of the deed might increase the enormity of the action. Thus, when this blood of the immaculate Lamb was shed by the Jews, it made them exceedingly guilty; but when it reached us, it consecrated us to blessedness [Col. 0106A].

### Verse 9

“Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace.”

The way of the wicked is most appropriately described as destruction, because it both wears down and is worn down. It is misery because by that way one never arrives anywhere except at disastrous punishments. Yet someone may be on the way of sinners and return again to the way of justice.

Here, however, he denies that they were freed by any conversion when he says, “They have not known the way of peace.” Their hearts were blinded, and they were in no way worthy to understand the Lord himself, who is the way of peace.

### Verse 10

“There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

A sentence has been added to the preceding matters that beautifully brings everything to a conclusion [Col. 0106B]. They did such great things because they did not have the fear of God before their eyes. Thus the Apostle says of them: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

We rightly say that the Lord of glory was crucified, although it is clear that he was killed only according to the nature of the flesh, not according to the nature of divinity.

### Verse 11

“Will all those who work iniquity not know, who devour my people like a morsel of bread? They have not called upon the Lord.”

The holy Church, whose person speaks in this psalm, has now come to the second mode, in which it threatens divine judgment against all the wicked. It says that at that universal recompense those who now practice wickedness under freedom will come to know vengeance.

The order of the words is as follows: “Will all those who work iniquity not know?” This should be joined to the following verse: “For God is in the righteous generation” [Col. 0106C]. They will certainly know at the future judgment, when they see the good summoned by God [manuscripts A, B, F: “of divinity”] to eternal rewards, while they themselves are sent to punishments that will never end.

“Who devour my people.” He speaks of those who, through a savage doctrine, swallow up simple Christians. The phrase “like a morsel of bread” seems adapted to the mind of sinners. Just as the hungry think their hunger will be satisfied by the sweetest food, bread, so these people hasten to be filled by the deception of Christians.

The reason for their increased destruction is added: they were unwilling to call upon the Lord. For it was necessary that those who refused to invoke the Lord and Savior with their proud minds should undertake desperate deeds.

### 50. Verse 12

“There they trembled with fear where there was no fear, because God is in the righteous generation.”

Just as fearing at the proper time is an act of foresight, so it is proved to belong to madness to confuse oneself with some senseless trembling. In the former case there is caution; in the latter, cowardice is always condemned.

They were therefore rightly shaken by empty terror, because in this world they had cast the saving fear of the Lord out of their minds. The Jews were saying: “If we believe in him, because of the novelty of this worship the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11:48). Thus it happened that, by not fearing the Lord, they were troubled by unnecessary terrors.

He added, “because God is in the righteous generation.” A sentence follows that corrects the unbelieving, so that they may remember that the restraint of divinity is absent from them when they see themselves rising through boastful prosperity [Col. 0107A]. All this is proclaimed with a devout mind, so that the sacrilegious mind of the wicked may be corrected.

### Verse 13

“You have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope.”

The reproach is directed at the Jewish people, to whom it is said enigmatically: “You have confounded the counsel of the poor,” that is, you refused to receive Christ, who had come to free you. He had determined, when believed, to give salvation; when despised, he brought retribution upon them.

“Poor” is said of the Lord and Savior, who was rich in himself but became poor for our sake (2 Cor. 8:9). The whole verse should be read as an expression of wonder: “You have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope.” The one from whom they ought especially to have derived reverence seemed instead to be despised and to endure reproaches.

You should not be troubled that, with reference to the assumed humanity, God is called the hope of the holy incarnation. For the humility of his humanity—which he assumed for the salvation of human beings—could not otherwise have been shown, just as in another psalm he will say: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:2).

### Verse 14

“Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion, when the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people?”

After the holy Church has spoken about the Lord’s advent, it now returns to wonder at so great a benefit, saying: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?”

When it says “who,” it wishes no one else to be understood except the Lord Father, who deigned to send and present the Lord Christ in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem [Col. 0107C]. He is indeed the Salvation of Israel—that is, the eternal salvation and boundless security of those who believe rightly.

It follows: “When the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people,” that is, when he has condemned the devil, who in ungodly cruelty persecutes God’s people and hastens to take them captive.

### Verse 15

“Let Jacob rejoice, and let Israel exult.”

A consoling answer is joined to the preceding question: “Let Jacob rejoice,” that is, the people of Jews and Gentiles gathered—or to be gathered—through the gifts of grace, who once wandered through their unbelief.

Here Jacob should be understood as the ancient people of the Jews, although his name also seems, in the manner of Scripture, to have been given to the new people in what follows. By Israel, however, we appropriately understand the universal Church gathered from all parts of the world [Col. 0107D]. It must exult when, through the Lord’s mercy, it reaches the kingdom of heaven.

Observe how words suited to different causes have been assigned! Jacob will rejoice because he has received medicine he did not expect. Israel will exult—that is, will be filled with indescribable joy—when it sees in reality what it had most ardently desired in hope.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

If we consider these words with a devout mind, the virtue proclaimed to us in this psalm is that, insofar as it lies within us, we should care for our enemies with a benevolent mind, lest, hardened by blind obstinacy, they be enslaved to an error from which there is no release.

The Church rebukes the sinful people so that they may not hasten toward their own destruction and, once their perversity has been laid aside, may not delay rejecting what can destroy them in every way. Therefore let us also, insofar as it is granted, follow these venerable teachings. Let us commend the right faith to heretics and proclaim holy humility to the proud. We confer these things upon ourselves if we are deemed worthy to benefit such people.

We should know first that this is the first of the psalms written about the rebuke and conversion of the Jews. We do not think it absurd to conjecture in this way about the number of the psalm: since the holy Church has been introduced as speaking, and since it receives the mysteries both of the five books of Moses and of the eight days associated with the Lord’s resurrection, her person may rightly seem to hold the number thirteen, because she embraces the mysteries of the New and Old Testament [Col. 0108B].

Or this number may be applied to the fact that thirteen days are reckoned from the Lord’s birth to his manifestation. Thus this reckoning has rightly been completed with reference to heavenly realities.

# Exposition of Psalm XIV

## To the end, a psalm of David

Since this title solemnly directs us back to the Lord, and there is nothing new that we need to say about its words, let us rather seek out what is most appropriate in the text of the psalm.

For it is not, like some psalms, veiled by a certain profundity. Rather, the Lord responds to a prophetic question in the form of the Decalogue: by ten virtues one reaches the courts of his blessedness. You should not look for these one by one in each verse, since one, two, and three are contained in each individual verse. At the most suitable points we shall indicate how they should be divided and understood.

Note also that this is the second psalm concerning the instruction of the faithful. In the first, he included the blessed man in a fivefold division, saying: “Who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his will was in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:1–2). Here, however, he says that such a man excels through ten holy virtues. Thus there, the virtue of the Pentateuch is shown, and here, that of the Decalogue.

## Division of the Psalm

The whole division of this psalm is understood to consist in a question and an answer. The question consists of one verse, while the answer is contained in six verses. Let us now come to the exposition of the words.

### 51. Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain?”

The prophet desires to know whom the Lord will judge worthy of his Church. Like a devout priest standing before him, he asks for an answer and longs to be made certain through his inquiry. This figure is called *erotema*, whenever an appropriate answer is given to one who asks a question.

He asks who might dwell in the Lord’s tabernacle. But let us examine a little more carefully why it is called a tabernacle. Our ancestors called the houses of the poor *tabernae* because they were covered only with beams and not yet with tiles, as though they were *trabernae*. And because people lived and dined there—since it was the ancient custom to eat only once—the word is said to have been formed from two names, *traberna* and *coenaculum*, as if *trabernaculum*.

From this we understand that *tabernacula* are appropriately called temporary and hastily erected dwellings. In the Old Testament also, the Lord commanded that a tabernacle be made for him (Exod. 26), when the Israelite people were in the camp, so that a kind of divine house might move together with the dwellings of the Hebrews.

Thus it came about that the Catholic faith, which has been spread throughout the world through the churches, is called the tabernacle of God. Josephus also discussed this at length in the third book of the *Antiquities*, chapter seven. We had it painted and placed at the head of the larger pandect [Col. 0109B].

The holy mountain signifies the Jerusalem that is to come. Observe how beautifully appropriate words distinguish different meanings. Of the tabernacle it is said, “Who dwells?”—referring to one who is still struggling in the contest of this world. Of the mountain it is said, “Who rests?”—when each of the faithful, after the labors of this world, is refreshed by the security of eternal peace.

### Verse 2

“He who enters without blemish.”

He comes to the second part, from which answers are now given, as it were, from the inner sanctuary. It is said in the person of the Lord Christ, both satisfying the desire of the questioner and revealing the adorable mystery of his incarnation.

His first glory was to enter the tabernacle without blemish, when he entered the temple of Jerusalem free from sins [Col. 0109C]. Although others entered the house of God for the sake of purification, he alone entered in such a way that he could stand without blemish before the presence of the Father. It was not the law that gave something to him; rather, as the best lawgiver, he fulfilled the law himself.

### Verse 3

“And practices justice.”

This is the second virtue that the Lord performed when he drove the buyers and sellers from the synagogue, forbidding human commerce in the divine temple. For he said: “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. 21:13).

### Verse 4

“He who speaks truth in his heart.”

This is the third virtue, which our Savior uniquely fulfilled. Truth is a matter that in no way becomes, has become, or is shown to be about to become otherwise than we have affirmed.

He spoke truth silently in his heart when he did not disclose the mysteries of his speech to those who deceitfully sought them. When he was pressed by the falsehoods of the Jews and by the voice of the governor, he answered him not a word, to the amazement of all. Yet in his holy conscience he spoke what those who appeared to inquire about him deceitfully were not worthy to hear.

### Verse 5

“And he has not acted deceitfully with his tongue.”

He comes to the fourth virtue. He himself testifies in the Gospel that everything he said was without deceit, when he says: “I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15:15).

For what is purer or simpler than that unchangeable truth should reach human ears in the utmost integrity, violated by neither addition nor suppression [Col. 0110A]?

### Verse 6

“He has not done evil to his neighbor.”

He enters upon the fifth virtue, which is likewise proved in the Lord. He not only harmed no one but also patiently endured everything.

By “neighbor” he meant the Jewish people, from whom he derived the origin of his flesh and for whom, even as he hung upon the cross, he prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

You see that no evil was done to the neighbor, since he even prayed for them so that they might be absolved.

### Verse 7

“And he has not accepted reproach against his neighbor.”

This is the sixth virtue, which designates Judas Iscariot. Although he knew that Judas would betray him, he did not wish to expose him through a public rebuke. He said only in general terms: “The one who puts his hand with me into the dish is the one who will betray me” (Matt. 26:23) [Col. 0110B].

Thus it happened that he neither concealed the power of his divinity from those who understood it nor attacked the reputation of his neighbor with a biting denunciation.

“He has not accepted,” that is, he did not regard it as pleasing. For we call those things “accepted” that we show to be pleasing to us.

### Verse 8

“The wicked has been brought to nothing in his sight; but those who fear the Lord magnify him.”

This is the seventh answer, in which he reduced the wicked one, the devil, to nothing in his sight when he said to him: “Go back, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. 4:7).

For to whom else can this apply except to one who is known to command all spirits by his own power?

A beautiful addition of the other part follows: just as the wicked one was reduced to nothing in his sight, so those who fear the Lord should always magnify him with a pure heart.

This figure is called *paradigma*, as was already said in the first psalm. It invites us through prosperity and frightens us through adversity.

### Verse 9

“He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive him.”

The eighth virtue is proclaimed. The Lord performed it when he promised his apostles with the most certain truth, saying: “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants” (John 15:14).

Let us examine what this sentence says at its beginning: “He who swears to his neighbor.” To swear is for human beings to promise something under divine attestation. But since God himself has also promised, it is more suitably said to be sworn when he makes the promise.

To swear is said as though it meant *jure orare*, “to speak justly.” Someone speaks justly when the things he promises are fulfilled. Thus for God to swear is to promise and fulfill, as he says elsewhere: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him” (Ps. 131:11). Again: “The oath that he swore to Abraham our father” (Luke 1:73). You will find this in many places in the divine text.

### Verse 10

“He who has not lent his money at interest.”

The ninth virtue is now touched upon, and we should investigate it more subtly. In the holy Scriptures, “money” is understood in two ways.

One is this metal currency, which is entirely forbidden to be lent at interest, since it is a fault of greed to wish to demand what one does not know oneself to have lent. The Lord Christ possessed this money, which he gave to Judas to distribute to the poor [52, Col. 0111A]. He did not lend it at interest when, in pious generosity, he granted it to those in need in order to instruct us.

The other kind is something which, according to the Gospel, we are urged to lend at interest: namely, the most holy proclamations and divine teachings. For he says: “You knew that I was a hard and austere man. Should you not have entrusted my money to the money-changers, so that when I came I might at least have collected what was mine with interest?” (Matt. 25:27).

Thus this ambiguous word is understood according to the character of the passages in which it occurs.

### Verse 11

“And he has not accepted gifts against the innocent.”

The tenth virtue, which remained, has been fulfilled. Here “against the innocent” is to be understood as “against the innocent.” It is clear that the Lord not only did not do this, but also proved himself to offer himself for the salvation of all [Col. 0111B], as he says in the Gospel: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10:12).

He accepted gifts from the magi, but not against the innocent. He also receives daily the offerings placed upon the sacred altars, but not against the innocent. Therefore we should understand that pious and small offerings, made out of love, are not to be rejected altogether. For if he had wished every gift to be rejected, the phrase “against the innocent” would never have been added.

### Verse 12

“He who does these things will not be moved forever.”

After the ten virtues that are appropriately understood of the Lord Jesus Christ have been explained, an answer has briefly and completely been given to the prophetic question: the one who does these things dwells in the Lord’s tabernacle and rests upon his holy mountain.

But observe that he said “does,” not “sings,” so that, by inserting this commandment, he might bind us to active virtue and prevent us from singing psalms vainly, intent only upon songs while neglecting so great a mystery [Col. 0111C].

“He will not be moved,” that is, he is not moved away from him—a gift granted only to the holy and blessed. For every wicked person will be moved away from him forever when deprived of participation in his kingdom.

This figure is called *zeugma*, that is, conjunction, whenever many dependent things are brought to a conclusion by one word or one sentence. Here it has occurred in the sentence; if it is found in a single word, we shall not pass over it in silence.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This is that heavenly Decalogue; this is the spiritual psalter of ten strings. Here is truly the crowned number, which only he could fulfill who overthrew the vices of the world together with their author.

But let us continually pray to his omnipotence that, although we cannot fulfill by ourselves the things that have been commanded, we may accomplish them when enriched by his gift [Col. 0111D].

Nor should the significance of his number be neglected. For the advent of the Lord and Savior shone forth in the fourteenth generation from the Babylonian captivity. Thus it is rightly seen that he himself spoke here, since he deigned to come in the same numbered generation.

# Exposition of Psalm XV

## The inscription of the title: “For David himself”

Although all the inscriptions attached to the beginnings of the psalms are called titles, this one is declared to be the first to contain something specially mystical.

We remember that when the Lord suffered, this title was written above his head: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19). Yet those Jews are to be understood in the true sense who serve Christ with pure devotion.

And because our King and Savior is about to speak of his passion and resurrection, the mention of this inscription was rightly made. It was destined, through the Lord’s ordering of events, to follow after so long a time.

And so that you might recognize that this inscription of the title ought to be referred not to some other person but to the Lord Christ, “for David himself” was added. We have frequently shown through exposition that this appropriately refers to the Lord and Savior.

It should also be known that this is the second of the psalms that briefly touch upon the Lord’s passion and resurrection [Col. 0112B].

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm, the person of the Lord and Savior is introduced. In the first section, according to his usual manner, he speaks to the Father from the humanity he assumed, asking to be preserved because he has always placed his hope in him. He diminishes nothing of his divinity but displays the nature of his humanity.

By “nature” I mean the origin of each thing and the power of its substance. He also explains how his saints are chosen not according to carnal desires but according to spiritual virtues, asserting that everything he endured was brought to the glory of his inheritance.

In the second section, he gives thanks to the same Father, who, by appearing at his right hand, overcame the iniquity of this world through the power of his omnipotence [Col. 0112C]. Hence he declares that his soul has been freed from hell and recalls that, after the glory of the resurrection, he has been placed in the delights of the Father’s right hand.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Preserve me, Lord, because I have hoped in you.”

About to enter human dangers and the wicked thoughts of Jewish obstinacy, he asks, in the nature of the humanity he assumed, to be preserved by the Father’s protection. To make the outcome of this request more certain, he says that he has always hoped in the Lord.

This figure is called *ethopoeia*, whenever speech is assigned to a definite person. Here the person is that of the Lord and Savior, a human being from two distinct and perfect natures [manuscripts A, B, F: “a perfect human being”], and the same Christ, one God who remains [Col. 0112D].

### Verse 2

“I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods.’”

He spoke not with his lips but with the affection of his heart, from which his holy conscience spoke.

“You are my God”: the Son, in the form of a servant, says this to the Father, so that you may clearly recognize two natures in the one person of the Lord and Savior [53]. One is humble through our weakness; the other is wondrous through his own power. Thus you understand that what he suffered belonged to the flesh, while what rose again belonged to his most powerful majesty.

To destroy the arrogance of the human race, which trusts that it can do something good by its own powers, he added: “For you have no need of my goods.” Let the Pelagians hear this, since they think that certain goods are to be attributed to their own powers. The humanity of the Word cries out that God has absolutely no need of its goods, referring everything to him who gave them, not to itself, which received what was bestowed [Col. 0113A].

### Verse 3

“For the saints who are on his earth, he has made all my desires wondrous among them.”

We must first set out the order of the words, so that, once the obscurity of the language has been removed, the meaning may shine more easily:

“For the saints who are on his earth, he has made wondrous”—that is, the Father has made wondrous—“all my desires.”

So that you might understand that Christ the Lord is to be loved by the elect, he added “among them,” that is, among the saints who are in the land of the living. He does not mean among just any people who parade themselves ambitiously in this world, but only among those who have been predestined for the kingdoms of heaven.

He signifies the innocent and just, among whom the desires of the Lord and Savior were made wondrous when, through his kindness, he made them eternal instead of mortal and heavenly instead of earthly, because they obeyed him and did what he commanded [Col. 0113B].

### Verse 4

“For their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened. I will not gather their assemblies from blood.”

He speaks of the saints who, under the Lord’s providence [manuscripts A, B, F: “through his mercy”], were freed by a most salutary affliction from the deceptive pleasure of this world.

At first their carnal weakness was multiplied through the severity of the law, so that they might reach the liberating grace of the New Testament with greater desire. He says that they were not to be gathered through the blood of cattle or the customary sacrifices, but through the offering of his body and blood, which, celebrated throughout the whole world, saved the human race.

When he says “from blood,” he designates the blood of cattle, which was then poured out abundantly in sacrifices. This rite was changed after Christ the Lord came.

The expression “from blood” is also plainly contrary to grammatical usage, since grammar does not recognize this plural number for the word. It is therefore to be counted among the *idiomata*, that is, the distinctive expressions of divine Scripture [Col. 0113C].

### Verse 5

“Nor will I remember their names through my lips.”

He says that those ancient names which the unbelievers had were changed by the grace that followed. For previously they were called sons of wrath, sons of the devil, and sons of the flesh. After the Lord’s advent, however, reborn through the sacred fonts, they were called Christians, sons of God, and friends of the Bridegroom.

Therefore he did not remember their names, since it is clear that new names were imposed upon new people.

The lips of Christ the King must here be understood as the two Testaments, through which we know that his wills have been proclaimed [Col. 0113D]. They are beautifully called lips because both proclaim the kingdom of God and, in harmony of a single sound, are joined together as lips are, while the remembrance is in the heart.

He says here: “Nor will I remember their names through my lips.” This should be understood among the distinctive expressions of divine Scripture, as was already said in the seventh and tenth psalms.

### Verse 6

“The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.”

Truly blessed is the teaching that chooses what never knows how to pass away through any exchange. It is as though he were saying: “Let others choose worldly desires and a life like one driven about by the winds; the Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup.”

Inheritance pertains to the faith of the Gentiles; the cup pertains to the venerable passion, which, when drunk with sobriety, bestows the most glorious resurrection.

We should observe that the Lord’s will and distribution are frequently called a cup. A cup is named from a warm drink, because just as a drink, when consumed, gladdens the human heart, so this cup, when drunk, perpetually delights holy souls.

“You are.” Maintaining the obedience of love, the Son says this to the Father—not inferior in divinity, but subject in humanity, as the Apostle also says: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things he suffered, and, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him” (Heb. 5:8).

“You will restore” is said because the human race had perished through the devil’s action. And in truth the inheritance was restored to the one to whom it had been granted in predestination before the creation of the world.

Inheritance is named from *herus*, that is, “lord.”

### Verse 7

“The boundary lines have fallen for me in excellent places; indeed, my inheritance is excellent for me.”

In ancient practice, land was divided by ropes, so that each person received an extent of territory proportionate to the amount of tribute and the rank of his person. Thus, in the Old Testament, Moses is read to have commanded Joshua to distribute the inheritance of the promised land among the children of Israel by ropes.

Hence he now rightly speaks of “cords,” because he has recalled the breadth and glory of his inheritance.

The cords may also be understood as the sorrowful bonds of this world. They too are called cords from funerals, because they were burned like candles before corpses. Without doubt, these cords were turned into excellent things when they reached the eternal gifts of the resurrection.

The inheritance of Christ is the predestined multitude of the saints. “For me” was added because he does not glory in himself according to his humanity but in the Father.

But since he said “excellent,” one may ask why he says that this inheritance fell to him, since the word is usually applied to adverse circumstances. Divine eloquence uses it for good things as well. For in the Acts of the Apostles it says: “The lot fell upon Matthias” (Acts 1:26), meaning that the honor of the apostleship came to him by divine judgment [Col. 0114B].

### Verse 8

“I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding; moreover, even until night my kidneys have reproved me.”

The second section has been reached, in which the holy proclamation must be understood more subtly. With what providence he excluded the heresies that were to come, by declaring that understanding had been given to him by the Lord in his incarnation—understanding, namely, by which he discerned all things true and holy.

He did this so that human weakness might not attribute anything to itself, since useful things are bestowed not through preceding merits but through the generosity of grace.

It follows: “My kidneys have reproved me,” as though he were saying: “In addition to the evils that the entire Jewish kinship inflicted upon me, those of the tribe of Judah are also known to have reproached me, from which the Lord Christ is shown to have derived the origin of his flesh.”

“Until night” signifies “until death.” The kidneys signify kinship, through which human generation is traditionally propagated [Col. 0115A].

### Verse 9

“I kept the Lord always before my eyes, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved.”

By explaining what he did, he gives us a unique remedy by which we may avoid sins. For the one who always looks upon him with the sharpness of the mind in no way turns toward transgressions. Thus, when truth dwells in the heart, it corrects the entry of falsehood.

He also states the reason why he was not moved. When the Lord helps at the right hand, the left-hand powers do not prevail; rather, the mind whom he guards remains most firmly established in him.

It was fitting for him to say that the Lord was at his right hand, because if he does not hold this place, the plotting devil will immediately occupy it. Thus it is written concerning Judas: “Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand” (Ps. 108:6) [Col. 0115B].

### Verse 10

“For this reason my heart was delighted, and my tongue will exult; moreover, my flesh will rest in hope.”

“For this reason”—namely, because he stood at the right hand—he testifies that delight arose in his thoughts and exultation in his tongue. This is perfect joy: it is conceived in a cheerful heart and expressed in lively speech.

Just as he said “moreover” concerning evils, so he repeated the same word concerning good things, so that his humanity might be understood to have received heavenly joys in proportion to the measure of its sufferings.

He says that his joy still increased beyond his former exultations, because that suffering flesh, which he assumed for the salvation of us all, deserved the truth of the glorious resurrection in an incorrupt state.

This figure is called *aetiologia*, that is, the assigning of a cause, whenever an appropriate explanation is added to a matter previously stated [Col. 0115C].

### Verse 11

“For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.”

Where are the Apollinarists, who falsely suppose that the Lord Christ did not possess a rational soul? Behold, he himself cries out; he himself gives thanks to the Father, because his soul was not abandoned in the underworld according to the common lot, but, glorified by a swift resurrection, reached the kingdom of heaven. In the Gospel he repeatedly attests this, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). And elsewhere: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

“Nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.” This must not be passed over lightly. For when in the twenty-ninth psalm one finds: “What profit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?” (Psalm 29:10), this seems, as it were, to contradict it. The matter is resolved in this way: there he says that he descends into corruption when he is pierced by the assault of the nails and the spear of those afflicting him, since the piercing of a solid body may rightly itself be called a kind of corruption. Here, however, he justly denies that corruption—that is, putrefaction—will occur, the corruption that generally destroys human flesh. For when the flesh came to life again on the third day, it was proved that it could not be corrupted.

### Verse 12

“You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence; delights are in your right hand forever.”

After everything concerning the holiness of his body had been completed, this verse is brought to its conclusion and also pertains to the righteous, who choose to obey his commandments.

“You have made known to me the ways of life”—that is, through me you have caused the human race to learn the life-giving path, so that, walking humbly in your commandments, they might avoid the poisons of deadly pride.

“You will fill me,” that is, “you will fill me completely.” For to fill completely is more than merely filling: here he who pours gives from what is already full. That joy fills in such a way that it is always possessed in its entirety. He also signifies that all the righteous are to be filled in that blessed joy of the Lord’s countenance; and because he himself is in them, he testifies that they can be filled with him.

But let us examine a little more carefully what he means when he says here that he will be filled with delights at the right hand of the Father, since earlier he said: “Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.” In this present age, where he assumed flesh, suffered scourging, was struck with blows, and was covered with spittle, yet was overcome by none of these adversities, it was fittingly said that the Lord was always seen at his right hand. For he conquered the world’s opposition because he never in any way departed from contemplation of the Father.

But after the glory of the resurrection he properly says that he delights at the Father’s right hand, where, with the adversity of this world now laid aside, his humanity has been completed by the clarification of its entire majesty, reigning, united with the Word, with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

“Forever” signifies perfection and eternity, because his glory, remaining in its own perfection, will never be brought to an end by any succession of ages.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

[Column 0116C]

Let us consider how great a gift of salvation this psalm provides us with: in sufferings it grants confidence, and in hope it promises eternal glory, so that, by teaching us what prosperous things are destined to come, we may not fear present adversities. It is a heavenly school, a life-giving instruction, an auditorium of truth, and a discipline of singular certainty, which occupies its disciples with fruitful perceptions, not with the empty allurements of words.

It is also appropriate to consider what the number fifteen signifies. For, as we think, it signifies the fifteen steps by which the marvelous breadth of the Jerusalem temple was ascended, indicating that, by the grace of the Trinity, the five bodily senses having been overcome, one reaches the courts of the holy Church through a blessed gift. This too will be granted through this psalm, if, with the Lord’s protection, we preserve its most salutary proclamation.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XVI

### A Prayer of David

Since many psalms contain prayers within their text, it may seem strange that this one has been given such a title. Yet although other psalms contain brief petitions mingled with various matters, this one is almost entirely a supplication throughout its composition. It is therefore rightly prefaced in this way, since its entire purpose is directed toward the practice of prayer.

Nevertheless, it must be called a prayer in such a way that it retains the name of psalm, for we find nothing placed in this book that ought not to be called by that name, especially since the book is read as the Book of Psalms.

The word “prayer” is used in two ways. When it occurs among human beings, it is called speech of the mouth (*oris ratio*); when it is poured out before the divine majesty, it is supplication, a wholesome and life-giving humility.

Note also that this psalm, the eighty-fifth, the eighty-ninth, the one hundred first, and the one hundred forty-first are all prefaced with the title “prayer.” Their distinctions and particular characteristics we shall suitably explain in Psalm 141, which is the last of them.

David, as has been said, signifies the Lord Christ for the instruction of the human race; the whole of this psalm is spoken in his person.

### Division of the Psalm

A threefold prayer is drawn from the humanity of Christ in this psalm.

First, he asks that what is due to him according to his justice be restored to him.

Second, he asks that his purity be freed from the plots of the Jews.

Third, he entreats a most swift resurrection, so that the perverse Jewish people may not be allowed to insult him any longer.

And, so that the faithful multitude might have no uncertainty concerning his majesty, he professes that he will remain in eternal blessedness.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Hear, O God, my justice; attend to my supplication.”

Before God, justice is certainly known to have its own voice, since he knows unspoken things by the power of his understanding. His is the perfect prayer whose cause and tongue, action and speech, life and thought all cry out together.

“Attend to my supplication.” These words have not been joined together incongruously. To attend belongs to the eyes, while admitting prayers belongs to the ears. The words have therefore been associated so that one result might be understood to arise from both actions. Whatever the ear hears, the eye sees, the hand touches, the palate tastes, or the nose smells is perfectly known to God through the sole power of contemplation.

#### Verse 2

“Give ear to my prayer, not spoken with deceitful lips.”

He develops what he said above. To receive means not to take something casually, but to accept human prayers with abundant graciousness.

“Not spoken with deceitful lips”: as the false sentence arose from the Jews, among whom the innocent was condemned and the robber was recognized as acquitted.

#### Verse 3

“Let my judgment proceed from your countenance; let your eyes behold equity.”

“Let judgment proceed from your countenance.” This is a mode of expression proper to divine Scripture and unfamiliar to us, since a judgment ordinarily proceeds from the mind. Yet it is suitably applied to the Lord through figurative expressions, because he sees what he judges while being the witness of his own examination. He does not seek testimony from anyone concerning another’s deed, since he alone knows the secrets of all with complete truthfulness.

Therefore he says, “from your countenance,” that is, “from your sight,” according to what you observe and know concerning me. He rightly asked this because he knew himself to possess no pollution of sin.

It follows: “Let your eyes behold equity.” Here we ought to understand equity itself as divinity, which he prays may always attend him without interruption, so that, by gazing upon it, he might have no stain of sin—as indeed came to pass.

Thus it was also said in the preceding psalm: “I kept the Lord always before my eyes, because he is at my right hand, so that I shall not be moved.”

O that saving sight! O those most pure eyes that behold equity! Surely they do not know how to be darkened by the shadows of this world, for they deserve to be filled with such great brightness.

#### Verse 4

“You have tested my heart and visited me by night; you have examined me with fire, and in me no iniquity was found, so that my mouth should not speak.”

He preserves an excellent order. First he says that he was tested, then that he was visited. But the testing signifies the Passion, while the visitation signifies the resurrection.

He was tested there, where, amid the many iniquities of the Jews and the dangers of death, he displayed proofs of wondrous patience. He was visited by night when his soul was not abandoned in the underworld, but reached that wondrous resurrection through the clarification of eternal glory.

“You have examined me with fire, and in me no iniquity was found.” A metaphor is introduced from furnaces blazing with fire, which customarily purge the defects of metals, consume them by smelting, and, once cleansed, restore them to the purity of their nature.

Thus the Lord Christ was examined by fiery tribulations, but no iniquity was found in him that any burning could melt away.

He fittingly added: “So that my mouth should not speak”—that is, “Even if I remain silent, you judge me to be pure.” For what need was there for him to say anything about the integrity of his conduct, when it is certain that everything is known by the Father’s majesty? Human ignorance must be instructed by words; divinity, however, knows everything with complete certainty, even when deeds remain unspoken.

#### Verse 5

“Because of the works of men, for the sake of the words of your lips I have guarded difficult ways.”

This verse requires its words to be arranged in the following order: “The works of men—that is, difficult ways—I have guarded for the sake of the words of your lips.” just as blessed Job says: “A bird is born for flight, and a human being for labor” (Job 5:7).

For when sins are avoided, the path is steep and the ascent always difficult; but when we slide into vices, the journey is easy and downhill.

Since the Lord Christ, visibly present in this world, displayed the laws of complete gentleness and self-restraint, he rightly says that, because of the Lord’s commandments, he walked the difficult ways of men with unstained feet.

Not that those ways could have been difficult for him. Concerning him it is written in Psalm 90: “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone” (Psalm 90:12). Rather, because they are shown to be difficult for the human race to imitate, they have been called difficult ways.

This verse contains the figure called parenthesis, that is, an insertion, because within the middle of the sense it receives certain words which seem able to interrupt the order of the sentence.

#### Verse 6

“Make my steps perfect in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be moved.”

“Make perfect,” he said—that is, preserve me to the end, where the entire perfection of merits and reward is found. We begin while we live in this world with commendable conduct; but when religious steadfastness reaches its end, there we are perfected, there we are filled with complete integrity, as the Gospel says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22).

“Steps” signifies human actions, by which we move through this world and walk, as it were, by successive strides.

“In your paths,” that is, in your commandments. In them the ways are truly straight, and if we follow them devotedly, we reach the gifts of our heavenly homeland.

But what is the meaning of his first saying “steps” and immediately afterward adding “footprints”? We call the movements by which we go from one place to another “steps.” Human actions are rightly compared to these, since they lead us from one undertaking to another and transport us through the various conditions of our life.

“Footprints,” however, are the marks of feet that we leave behind as we pass. The Lord Christ therefore asks that both his steps—that is, his human actions—and his footprints be guarded. We rightly understand the footprints as the faithful apostles, in whom, after his glorious ascension, he left the signs of the Catholic religion.

The sense is therefore this: “Guard me in your commandments, so that, by imitating me, they may not in the least be moved away from you.” For the follower proceeds well when the one who provides the example has walked uprightly.

#### Verse 7

“I cried out, because you heard me, O God; incline your ear to me and hear my words.”

He enters the second section of the holy prayer.

But it must be examined why, when it is customary to say, “You heard me because I cried out,” this sentence appears to have its order reversed. Whoever cries out because he is heard is recognized as pure, innocent, and undefiled. He prayed confidently because, from the purity of his conscience, he presumed that he could be heard.

Let us understand what he says: “Incline your ear,” because human weakness cannot by itself reach him. He hears in this way: when, in his kindness, he stoops toward us and first grants his mercy, so that he may receive the desires of those who supplicate him.

#### Verse 8

“Make your mercies wondrous, you who save those who hope in you from those who resist your right hand.”

He rightly entreats that the greatness and excellence of mercies be made wondrous in him, because nothing could be wondrous unless it appeared with some novelty.

He signifies the miracles that he was to perform in the flesh. Although the Jewish people did not all believe, nevertheless they beheld them with astonishment.

“You save those who hope in you,” that is, “you will establish them in eternal life.” For those who believed in his name were often slaughtered all the more in this world.

He beautifully says: “From those who resist your right hand.” The Son is the Father’s right hand, and the Jews attempted to resist him when they resolved to crucify him.

#### Verse 9

“Guard me, Lord, as the apple of the eye; protect me beneath the shadow of your wings.”

Through the figure called *icon*, which in Latin is called *imaginatio* (“depiction” or “imagining”), the Lord compared himself to the pupil of the eye.

The pupil is the transparent part situated in the middle of the eye, by which we distinguish the colors of bodies in their varied qualities. It is called *pupilla* because of its smallness, as though *pusilla* (“little”).

Christ is fittingly compared to it, since he has been given the task of separating the righteous from sinners in his judgment. He therefore most appropriately asks to be guarded as the pupil of the eye, since through it we distinguish visible things and nothing more precious is found in our body.

It follows: “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings.” Here another figure is introduced, called in Greek *parabolē* and in Latin *comparatio* (“comparison”), when a kind unlike another is joined to it in some shared feature.

Wings are compared to the Father’s protection. Mercy and charity are, as it were, the Father’s wings, and he fittingly asks to be protected by them. This comparison is drawn from birds, which guard their beloved young by spreading their wings over them.

[Column 0120B]

#### Verse 10

“From the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me; my enemies have surrounded my soul.”

This verse must be considered with particular care.

“From the face of the ungodly” signifies the demons, who drove the aroused Jewish people toward the Lord’s death with headlong zeal. Their face was their savage presence, as the Gospel says concerning Judas: “Satan entered into him” (John 13:27).

Thus it happened that, at the demons’ instigation, his Jewish enemies wished to take away his soul—that is, his temporal life. The very word “surrounded” also expresses the truth of the Gospel narrative, when a frenzied crowd surrounded him with swords and clubs.

#### Verse 11

“They have enclosed themselves in their fat; their mouth has spoken arrogance.”

They “enclose fat” who grow fat through excessive gluttony. Thus the Jews, fattened by the enormity of their crimes, lost the sharpness of true understanding.

It remained that those who had swollen with the grossest savagery should speak arrogantly. He rightly said here that they spoke only with their mouth, not also with their heart, because it is the custom of criminals frequently to defend in speech what they are known, with conscience as witness, to condemn.

#### Verse 12

“Casting me away, they have now surrounded me; they have set their eyes to turn toward the earth.”

“Casting me away” means casting him outside the city. “They have now surrounded me” does not refer to an act of obedience but of fury, when it is clear that they fastened him to the cross.

The word “now,” however, uses the present tense for the future, a usage known to be common among the prophets.

It follows: “They have set their eyes to turn toward the earth.” He describes the custom of the depraved, who look toward the earth when they turn over evil thoughts.

#### Verse 13

“They have received me like a lion prepared for prey, and like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding places.”

“They have received me”—that is, the Jews received him from Pilate when he said to them: “Take him yourselves and crucify him according to your law” (John 19:6). Since they eagerly received this command and fulfilled the desire of their cruelty, they are rightly compared to the ferocity of wild beasts.

We have said that the lion signifies the devil and is also frequently compared with Christ. This mode of expression must be accepted among the distinctive usages of divine Scripture; here, however, it clearly designates the devil.

The rulers of the Jews were rightly compared to him, since they raged at his instigation. Yet they became much worse, since the devil tempted the Lord, whereas the cruel madness of these men fastened him to the cross.

He calls the rest of the Jewish people “the lion’s cub,” because they made themselves children of the devil. Thus the Gospel says concerning them: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44).

“Dwelling in hiding places” means remaining in ambush. It is indeed the custom of detestable people to conceal evil desires, so that their plans may secretly reach their intended result.

#### Verse 14

“Rise up, Lord; go before them and trip them up; rescue my soul from the wicked one, your sword.”

The third section of the blessed prayer begins.

“Rise up” is said against sinners, who think that he can rest according to human custom, so that they may learn that he keeps watch when their iniquities are not permitted to grow.

He said “go before them” so that they might be overthrown before they complete their sins. We explained above that this sense is suitably applied to criminals, when they are not permitted to involve themselves in unlawful deeds. Those too are happily overthrown who are led back from depraved vices to the straight path.

“Rescue my soul from the wicked one”—certainly from the devil, who is rightly called wicked because he is always shown to be opposed to the godly.

“Rescue”—make it rise again. It is clear that this was fulfilled.

“Your sword.” The nature of the Lord Savior’s soul is briefly defined here. For it is the Father’s sword, since through it he conquered the devil; through it he cleansed the world from filthy superstition; through it the captivity that possessed the offspring of the human race was defeated.

We have said that “sword” has many meanings. At one time it signifies a spear, at another a cuirass, and at another a double-edged sword; nevertheless, all these clearly belong to the instruments of warfare.

Remember that in this verse there is the fifth species of definition, called in Greek *katà tēn léxin*—in Latin, “word for word.” For in a single word he defines what Christ’s soul is: the Father’s sword.

#### Verse 15

“From the enemies of your hand, Lord, separate them from the few upon the earth, and trip them up in their life.”

Here again a prayer is made for the Jews, who, bound by the devil’s power, were being driven toward criminal acts.

The demons are the enemies of the Lord’s hand; they continually tear the human race apart with a will opposed to the Lord.

He also prays that the unbelievers may be separated “from the few,” that is, from the apostles, while, separated from the vicious earth of this world, they are converted to the Lord.

Through the apostles’ preaching, with the Lord’s help, it came about that both Israelites and Gentiles, separated from earthly iniquity, followed Christ their author.

“Trip them up” is used here in a good sense. Those are to be understood as tripped up who, after their errors have been condemned, are transferred to straight paths.

“In their life,” which he added, means “in this world, while they live”: the place where there is opportunity for repentance; where one cries out to the Lord not so much with the mouth as with the mind; where those who supplicate are received in complete purity.

#### Verse 16

“From your hidden things their belly has been filled; they have been satisfied with swine’s flesh, and they have left what remained for their little ones.”

The hidden things of God can suitably be understood both in a bad and in a good sense. Every sin is abhorrent to him and foreign to his sight, although it does not seem to escape his knowledge, as was already said in Psalm 5: “The wicked shall not dwell near you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes” (Psalm 5:6). Scripture likewise says concerning Cain: “Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and dwelt as a fugitive in the land” (Genesis 4:16).

He therefore says that the Jews were filled with impurities that were hidden from the Lord—that is, known to be forbidden by him.

But if you understand this as having been placed in a good sense, consider the passage: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you, and perfected for those who hope in you” (Psalm 30:20).

Benefits are enumerated so that the offense of the ungrateful may be shown to be greater.

“From your hidden things” means from the law of the Old Testament and from the miracles that the Lord Christ was to perform in it through a glorious dispensation.

“Their belly” signifies an entirely carnal understanding, in which the Lord’s commandments have been stored as though in a belly.

Their understanding is aptly compared with the belly, from which spiritual foods were cast out like the vilest refuse, as they slipped away through their corrupted minds.

But although they had been filled with heavenly things, so that they ought not to have been able to contain anything earthly, observe what follows: “They have been satisfied with swine’s flesh.”

O execrable iniquity! Their understanding heard the commandments of God, yet they were satisfied with the filth of sins. In a novel fashion, they were nourished by heavenly goods but filled with the dregs of evil.

“Swine’s flesh” refers to polluted things, which are designated unclean among the other precepts of the Old Testament.

They passed the remnants of their sins on to their children when they cried out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25).

#### Verse 17

“But I, with justice, will appear in your presence; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed.”

He says that he will appear with justice in the presence of the Father because he had fulfilled his will when he saved the world from destruction and death by the shedding of his blood.

“I shall be satisfied.” This expression seems most appropriately to be repeated. Above he said that the Jews were satisfied with swine’s flesh, that is, with their own impurity; but he says that he will be satisfied with the faith of the human race that has been received, when the number of the saints is completed through blessed union.

The Father’s glory will be revealed in the judgment of the Lord Savior, when each person will receive according to his deeds, as the Lord himself says to the apostles: “On that day you will know that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10, 20).

Thus the one nature, the one power, and the one glory of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are revealed.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider, beloved, how many great mysteries of our faith this psalm embraces, so that whoever hears a human being supplicating may also recognize that same person as confessing the Creator.

Whoever today wishes to believe that there are two natures in Christ the Lord, unconfused and unchangeable, cannot be deceived by any falsehood.

Accordingly, blessed Cyril wonderfully and briefly explained this in a certain passage, saying (*Book V Against Nestorius*):

“Therefore, observing the manner of the incarnation, we see that the two natures have come together with one another through an indivisible unity, without confusion and without change. For flesh is flesh and not divinity, although it has become the flesh of God. Likewise, the Word is God and not flesh, although, through the dispensation, he has made flesh his own.”

This, however, proceeds without stumbling for one who finds in himself no bonds of his own error.

The number and prophetic measure of this psalm have also adorned it, so that the incarnation of the Lord may rightly appear to have been signified in this number, where the prophetic chorus is also understood to have assembled.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XVII

“To the end. For the servant of the Lord, David, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said.”

[Column 0123B]

There is no doubt that these three words—“to the end,” “for the servant,” and “David”—can be referred to our King and Savior.

For “servant” is also read in the prophet: “A child is born to us” (Isaiah 9:6).

“Who spoke to the Lord the words of this song.” After these words, others must be supplied in thought so that the sequence of the words may be fuller and complete.

As for the word “song,” it is clearly related to contemplation of heavenly things, so that the attention of our mind would not remain fixed merely on the historical David as king.

“On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said.” This event is well known from the reading of the Books of Kings, where it is described more fully how David was freed from the power of his enemies.

In accordance with this likeness, the resurrection of the Lord and the liberation of his members from demonic power are declared.

### Division of the Psalm

This psalm cannot belong to one person alone.

First, the prophet speaks, giving thanks that divine mercy was willing to free him from grave dangers.

Second, the Church speaks. Before the Lord’s coming she endured innumerable calamities; afterward, when he took pity on her, he granted the medicine of the holy incarnation and, through the benefit of baptism, gathered the Christian people from throughout the world.

Third, the voice of the Lord Savior descends like a shower of mercy, where his power and might are described through most beautiful allusions.

Fourth, the words of the Catholic Church are again brought forth, and with great exultation the gifts of the Divinity that have been granted are praised.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“I will love you, Lord, my strength.”

The one who devoutly obeys his commandments loves the Lord, as he says in the Gospel: “Whoever hears my words and does them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21).

For *diligo* (“I love”) is said as though from *de omnibus eligo* (“I choose from among all things”).

Consider also that this love is promised as something future, yet it never appears to have failed in the past.

“My strength.” The prophet, delivered from his enemies, rightly confesses that the Lord is his strength. Through the Lord’s gift it came about that he appeared stronger than his enemies.

Here is the twelfth species of definition, called in Greek *kat’ epainon* and in Latin “through praise.” By individual and various words, he declares through praise what the Lord is: at one time strength, at another firmness, refuge, deliverer, helper, protector, or horn of salvation. All these expressions beautifully show who the Lord is.

#### Verse 2

“The Lord is my firmness, my refuge, and my deliverer; my God is my helper.”

He rightly calls the Lord his firmness, since it was granted by him that he should stand firm against his enemies in battle and fight with vigorous courage.

“And my refuge.” Certainly, when counsel was needed, he withdrew into deliberation and, with divinity showing the way, found what could help him.

He rightly professes the Lord to be his deliverer, since he freed him from the wrath of the most savage king Saul as from the mouth of hell.

“My God is my helper.” Drawn by the sweetness of benefits received, he repeats in summary what he said above, because the Lord was present everywhere and guarded him with the protection of his strength.

But observe that he runs through each point in such a way that he does not presume to attribute the gifts received to his own merits.

#### Verse 3

“And I will hope in him: my protector and the horn of my salvation, my helper.”

After the examples of benefits, the one who presumes upon the Lord’s grace now asks confidently. He says that he will hope trustfully for the future because he had experienced the Lord as his helper in the past.

“My protector.” This pertains to the one who was being guarded because the plots of his adversaries sought him.

When he calls the Lord “the horn of my salvation,” this concerns the scattering of his enemies. Horns are the weapons of beasts, with which they defend their safety through vigorous struggle.

“My helper.” The sweetness of the benefit caused a repetition of the words. Above he called the Lord by this same name, and here he again names him his helper.

#### Verse 4

“Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.”

After his deeds of strength had been accomplished, the holy man did not boast with any elation. Since, however, he ought to rejoice with holy gladness over these very events, he said that he would call upon the Lord with praise and attribute everything to him, who had deigned to accomplish all things.

He therefore says that he will be saved from his enemies because he did not appear to attribute his victory to himself but to the Lord.

For whoever acts otherwise is made captive to his vices, even if he seems to have overcome his enemies.

#### Verse 5

“The groans of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me.”

After the prophet’s exultation, which he conceived in holy devotion, the second order is reached. Here, on behalf of the calamities of the human race that raged before the Lord’s coming, one person representing the righteous—who undoubtedly existed at that time—is introduced, and the devout supplicant pleads.

This righteous man rightly asserted that he was surrounded by groans, because, while there was an innumerable multitude of superstitions, the devotion of the faithful was rare.

And lest you think that the groans had been poured out because of the loss of possessions or some similar matter, he added “of death.” For there was truly death wherever the devil’s power reigned.

We have often said that torrents are rivers swollen by winter rains. Here, therefore, the rushing iniquities are compared with torrents, so that they might rightly have troubled the anxious people when they roared with the clamor of threatening waves.

#### Verse 6

“The pains of hell surrounded me; the snares of death came before me.”

Let the construction of this verse be understood through a reversal of the words, so that its meaning may be opened to us more clearly:

“The pains of hell surrounded me.” He speaks of the pagans, who will be the pains of hell—that is, those who will be tormented in hell with the punishment they deserve.

We say that something “comes before” us when it is known to anticipate us, as with the guilt of original sin, which makes us liable before we are born, from the very moment of conception.

For this reason the prophet will say in Psalm 50: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm 50:7).

The righteous man therefore rightly said that he had been anticipated, because he knew that his guilt had preceded him. But how he was freed from these things he explains below.

#### Verse 7

“And in my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and I cried out to my God.”

Among the many evils he had described, he declares that there is one singular remedy: calling upon the Lord in tribulations, when it is clear that what is desired in a time of need is sought with all one’s strength.

Observe that he first said “to the Lord.” But lest you think that he meant a foreign lord, he added: “I cried out to my God.”

To cry out is more than to call upon. As desire advanced, the speech grew, and the inflamed mind sprang eagerly into a cry of prayer.

[Column 0125C]

#### Verse 8

“And he heard my voice from his holy temple; and my cry entered into his presence, into his ears.”

We may suitably understand the temple as either heaven or the body of the Lord, which he foresaw was to come.

He therefore says that his voice was heard, the voice that he continually offered concerning the Lord’s coming.

But it must be examined how his cry was able to enter into God’s presence. This cry is the justice of his cause, which could indeed enter into God, because it was pleading on behalf of the world’s calamities.

It follows: “It entered into his ears.” This is said figuratively according to our custom, as though his cry, something corporeal, had entered the Lord’s ears, whereas he perceives everything spiritually and knows all things before they happen.

The quality of our actions always stands before him, as it were, with certain faces; and what is hidden among us is known to him as manifest.

#### Verse 9

“Then the earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because God was angry with them.”

Having passed through the sadness that the blessed people endured concerning the Lord’s coming, he reaches, through the spirit of prophecy, the mysteries of his incarnation and describes the very sequence in a wondrous narrative.

This figure is called *idea*, when, as though presenting the appearance of a future event before the eyes, we stir the movement of the mind. Its effect is evident here and in the verses that follow.

And so let us now listen to the mystery concerning the Lord Savior.

The earth was appropriately shaken at Christ’s coming, because it was fitting for sinners to tremble in the presence of the judge.

He preserved the order of the event by first showing that it was shaken and afterward saying that it trembled.

“The foundations of the mountains” signifies the presumptions of the proud—that is, riches, honors, and other human things on which they rely as though on enduring foundations.

All these things were troubled because the false hope of the world was removed when the true Lord came.

The words descend very appropriately: first, the foundations—that is, the hope of the proud—were troubled; afterward he says that they were shaken.

He added the reason why the foundations were shaken: “Because God was angry with them.” This means that human vices are hateful to the Lord, and he is angry with them.

From this it is shown that those who follow them will certainly be punished.

### Verse 10

“Smoke rose in his anger, and fire blazed from his face [Col. 0126B]; coals were kindled by him.”

Here “smoke” is used in a good sense: just as earthly smoke stirs up useless tears, so that other smoke, kindled by the heat of repentance, pours forth fruitful streams of tears. “In his anger”: at the time when he troubles sinners through fear of the coming judgment, so that he may lead them to the remedy of conversion. The fire, moreover, is the charity of God, increasing through the advancement of the virtues; the more earnestly it is desired, the more effectively it grows. He rightly said, “from his face,” since charity is granted by his illumination to those who abandon their sins.

By “kindled coals” he means sinners who, like dead coals, lie darkened in the blindness of this world, but are brought back to life when repentance again sets them aflame; from dead embers they begin to become living coals. He then continues [Col. 0126C] by explaining how they were kindled—namely, when the Lord Redeemer came.

### Verse 11

“And he inclined the heavens and descended; and darkness was beneath his feet.”

A great mystery is contained in this statement. The Word humbled himself, taking on, without sin, yet in the likeness of sinful flesh. For him to descend meant to come to us, as the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7).
