Here “darkness” is the devil, who clouds the minds of human beings, preventing those whom he possesses from seeing the splendor of truth. “Beneath his feet”: for, unquestionably, the accursed wickedness of demons is trampled beneath the majesty of the Lord and Savior, as he will also say in the ninetieth psalm: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC, 13). [Col. 0126D]

### Verse 12

“And he mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.”

This figure is called *hyperthesis*, that is, “excess” or “surpassing,” when we strive by our statement to exceed something known to everyone by common opinion. The same is found in the fiftieth psalm: “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. L, 9).

“Cherubim” is interpreted as “multitude of knowledge,” or “knowledge multiplied.” Elsewhere we read: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear” (Ps. LXXIX, 2). Thus he mounted upon the cherubim when, in the sight of the apostles, he ascended to the kingdoms of heaven. He now sits upon the cherubim, placed at the right hand of the Father; in heaven and on earth he reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Both realities are shown to surpass every measure of knowledge or wonder. For what creature could sufficiently reach the secret of so great a mystery—a mystery that placed earthly and mortal flesh in the eternal glory of heaven and made it worthy of worship by all creatures, although it had endured earthly sufferings? [Col. 0127A]

It continues: “And he flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.” This repetition suitably displays his immense speed: he swiftly traversed the expanses of the world, since, while he himself lay in the cradle, the radiance of the star announced him more widely. What can be said to be swifter than one who, as soon as he was born, was seen in another part of the world? Thus the speed of the winds was surpassed, although nothing in the world appears to be swifter than they.

That he repeats the word without the intervention of another word—“he flew, he flew”—is the figure called *epizeuxis*, which in Latin is called “joining,” as he will also say below: “Day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. XVIII, 3), and “God, my God.”

### Verse 13

[Col. 0127B] “And he made darkness his hiding place; around him was his tent; dark water was in the clouds of the air.”

By “darkness” he means the mystery of his incarnation: he who could not be seen in the nature of his divinity appeared to human eyes as the most merciful Redeemer beneath the veil of the incarnation. Hence the blessed John, bishop of Constantinople, spoke wonderfully and in a catholic manner: “Him whom, had he come in his naked divinity, neither heaven, nor earth, nor the seas, nor any creature could have sustained, the unharmed womb of the Virgin carried.”

Remember, however, that “darkness” can also be placed in a good sense, as in Solomon’s Proverbs: “He also understands the parable and the dark saying” (Prov. I, 6). For all divine things that we do not know are dark to us—that is, profound and obscure—although they are continually filled with light. “His hiding place” means the secret of his majesty, which he reveals to the righteous when they are granted to behold the glory of his divinity face to face. [Col. 0127C]

“Around him was his tent.” Here the glorious dignity of the blessed is explained: those who faithfully persevere in his Church dwell near him. “Around him” signifies proximity. For he surrounds and penetrates all things; he is not surrounded by anything, since he is inaccessible to place. It can also be understood as referring not to the designation of a place but to the protection and guarding of the tent.

By “water” he means the Lord’s utterance, which is dark in the clouds of the air—that is, in the prophets, the preachers of the word. For although someone may think that he understands their words, he can scarcely reach their full power as they truly are. Thus the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12), when he sees the very thing in which he believed and is understood to behold the very thing he hoped for. [Col. 0127D]

### Verse 14

[Col. 0127D] “Bright-shining clouds passed before his sight, hail and coals of fire.”

This verse must not be passed over lightly. “Bright-shining” (*praefulgorae*) is one part of speech, a plural nominative, and agrees with “clouds.” As stated above, the clouds are to be understood as the preachers of the divine word.

The meaning is therefore this: those clouds that contain God’s water—that is, the divine utterances—appear dark, namely obscure, in this air; but before God they are bright-shining, where the truth is always open. There it is not sought through prepositions or concealed beneath parables; it is revealed in manifest light.

These clouds, then—that is, the preachers—passed over to the nations, leaving the Israelite people, as was shown to have happened when the hardness of the Jews did not merit what had come to instruct them. [Col. 0128A]

“Hail and coals of fire.” Through allegory he explains what those clouds contain: he says one thing but wishes another to be understood. Thus divine eloquence is shown to be completely full of frequent figures. “Hail” means figurative reproofs by which the hardest hearts of the Jews were battered. “Coals of fire” means the fires of charity, by which the minds of the faithful are brought back to life through heavenly fire. These passed, as we have said, to the nations in the clouds—that is, in the preachers. [Col. 0128B]

### Verse 15

“And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice.”

For he was about to speak great mysteries. In the Gospel the voice of the almighty Father says: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII, 29). Hence many, as it is written there, believed that it had been thunder. The Most High gave his voice when it was said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

### Verse 16

“He sent out his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied his lightning and troubled them.”

By “arrows” he means the evangelists, flying along straight paths on the wings of virtues—not their own, but those of the one by whom they were sent. “And he scattered them,” namely, those to whom they were sent, receiving the faithful and rejecting the impious, as the Apostle says: “To some we are the fragrance of life unto life; to others the fragrance of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 16).

“He multiplied his lightning,” that is, he performed many miracles, which moved the hearts of those who saw them just as frequent lightning ordinarily terrifies those who behold it. “And he troubled them”: he speaks of those who were troubled when they recognized through manifest proofs that he had risen. [Col. 0128C]

### Verse 17

“And the springs of waters appeared, and the foundations of the world were revealed.”

That is, the truth of the preachers, who poured forth the springs of eternal life from the mouth of their holiness. When he came, what had been concealed by the obscurity of the divine utterance became evident.

“And the foundations of the world were revealed”: the prophets who had not been understood were made manifest. Upon them the world was built through holy construction in the form of the Church. Remember also that here “earth” (*tellus*) is placed in a good sense: it is the land of the living. [Col. 0128D]

### Verse 18

“By your rebuke, Lord; by the breath of the spirit of your anger.”

“By your rebuke” indicates the words of the prophets, who reproved sinful peoples with righteous reprimands. “By the breath of the spirit of your anger” displays the preachers of the word, who, inflamed by the Holy Spirit, rebuked peoples who were sinning.

Thus, through these shining parables and statements of words, he has announced, by the spirit of prophecy, the coming of the Lord to the peoples of the faithful, who constitute the holy Church.

### Verse 19

“He sent from on high and took me; he lifted me [Col. 0129A] from the multitude of waters.”

From this point the mother Church speaks about the Christian age. The Father indeed sent the Lord and Savior from on high, so that human beings might understand that what comes from on high glories in divine power.

The Church appropriately said, “He took me,” for she rejoices, joined to Christ the Bridegroom. The multitudes of waters may be understood either as innumerable nations; hence it is clear that the Church was gathered from the faithful, while the unbelieving Jews were rejected. Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, when the Jews opposed and blasphemed him, the most blessed Paul shook out his garments and said: “Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean. From now on I will go to the nations” (Acts XVIII, 6).

Or he says this about the sacred fonts, when the Catholic Church acquires a multitude of children through the regeneration of baptism. [Col. 0129B]

### Verse 20

“He delivered me from my strongest enemies and from those who hated me, because they were strengthened against me.”

By the strongest enemies he declares the savage persecutors who afflicted the Christian people with tortures and slaughter. For this reason he says that she was delivered all the more because her enemies had grown strong against her. The Church merited to grow when the enemy, granted power from above, afflicted her.

O truly divine providence: the enemy is destroyed by his own efforts, and the more he thinks he is inflicting harm, the more necessarily he performs his most savage persecution!

### Verse 21

“They came before me on the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my protector.”

This signifies the time when the pseudo-apostles tried to precede the true preachers, attempting to overthrow the hearts of the simple. It continues: “On the day of my affliction,” when the martyrdoms of Christians were being celebrated. “And the Lord became my protector.” God was protector because a human being had become the attacker. Yet the two realities, so utterly unlike, came together: temporal assault and eternal protection. [Col. 0129C]

### Verse 22

“And he brought me forth into a broad place; he saved me, because he desired me.”

[Manuscripts A, B, F: “he led me out.”]

No one is unaware that this is the custom of the faithful in the Catholic Church: the more they are confined by persecutions, the more they are enlarged through an increase of faith, as has been said. For then unconquered spirits rise up through God’s grace; then the fire of charity blazes, and, forming their ranks, they rush gladly upon the swords because they desire the rewards of eternal life.

The Church was therefore led out into a broad place when, through the savagery of the persecutors, the number of her faithful clearly increased. Let no one be troubled that he said, “he saved me,” using the masculine gender; for it is not absurd that this name should be applied to her, since she consists of a people. Rightly, therefore, that rejoicing company of the blessed says that it was saved, because it merited to reach the summit of the Christian faith.

“Because he desired me,” that is, because he chose me—the one who freely calls everyone and receives no benefit before he deigns to bestow one. As he himself says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). [Col. 0129D]

### Verse 23

“And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness; and according to the innocence of my hands he will repay me.”

He has preserved both points most appropriately. First he said, before she was taken up, “because he desired me”; now he says, “He will repay me according to my righteousness,” that is, according to my will, which after his benefits she held with a holy heart.

By “the innocence of my hands” he wishes to signify the work of piety, which the virtue of the saints exercises through a divine gift. But the repeated “he will repay” must be received carefully, lest the Pelagian heresy flatter itself deceitfully with some claim of its own.

For the Apostle says: “From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day” (II Tim. IV, 8). This does not mean that he attributed anything to his own merits in humility; rather, because of the Lord’s prior benefits, he confidently believed that a reward could already be owed.

The apostle James says the same: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James I, 17). [Col. 0130B]

### Verse 24

“Because I have kept the ways of the Lord, and I have not acted impiously against my God.”

The ways of the Lord are love of God and charity toward one’s neighbor. It is clear that those guard them most diligently who do not wish to abandon the Lord’s commandments.

He added: “And I have not acted impiously against my God.” Those who presume to disregard the Lord’s commands are marked by the word “impiety.” The devoted spirit of the Church rightly says that it has rejected this, since it knew that by such conduct it would offend the Creator.

### Verse 25

“For all his judgments are always before me, and I have not rejected his righteousness from me.”

He now gives the reasons why he guarded the ways of the Lord and did not act impiously, as he stated above: because he continually considered his fearful judgments.

He added: “And I have not rejected his righteousness from me.” This is what those do who are overcome by the weakness of the flesh: failing through prolonged observance, they sometimes abandon the justice they had begun to guard. But this blessed people never rejected the Lord’s righteousness, because it always remained in their heart. [Col. 0130C]

### Verse 26

“And I shall be blameless before him; and I shall guard myself from my iniquity.”

[Manuscripts A, B, F: “with him.”]

He has given the fruit of his blessedness and shown what benefit comes from not rejecting the Lord’s righteousness: namely, that one should be blameless. Yet not as that Lord who had no sins, but as one whom humble tears washed from the stains he had contracted.

All these statements, however, must be understood in the manner explained above, where he says “he will repay” with the word repeated, lest holy humility appear—far be it from us—to presume upon itself rather than upon heavenly benefits. [Col. 0130D]

It continues: “And I shall guard myself from my iniquity.” The life of the blessed is subtly described: whenever someone recognizes that he has attained some grace of the Lord, he takes care not to become entangled again in the calamities of his former iniquity.

### Verse 27

“And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the innocence of my hands before his eyes.”

He explains what he said above: “And I shall be blameless before him.” For when that has come to pass, this necessarily follows without doubt: that he will repay each person according to his righteousness—which he himself nevertheless deigns to give—and will return a worthy recompense according to the purity of his actions.

It was beautifully added, “before his eyes,” since this can happen only to the blessed: just as they always behold the Lord in their hearts, so the divine power continually looks upon them. [Col. 0131A]

### Verse 28

“With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent. And with the chosen man you will be chosen, and with the perverse man you will be overthrown.”

While speaking of heavenly justice—that he repays each person according to the quality of his actions—he now explains how what the law commands can be fulfilled. Our conduct derives its likeness chiefly from its former examples or leaders: each person delights in the character with which the one he follows has been endowed.

Hence we have been given a salutary and moral rule: that with the holy man, namely the Lord and Savior, we may, through his enabling, be holy. As he himself says: “Be holy, because I am holy, the Lord your God” (Lev. XIX, 2).

It is also commanded that through his innocence we may merit to be innocent. Thus it has already been said of him: “Innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. XXIII, 4).

A third point is added: that through his choosing we may be chosen. Thus Isaiah says of him: “My chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased” (Isa. XLII, 1). This happens to us when we obey his commands in a way that brings salvation.

It continues: “With the perverse man you will be overthrown,” that is, with the devil, who is perverse through his own iniquity. He makes those whom he turns to the obligations of his obedience utterly wicked.

This argument is called most noble in the *Topics*, under the category of a person attributed from outside, when someone is either accused on account of wicked friends or praised on account of association with the good. [Col. 0131C]

### Verse 29

“For you will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.”

Consider how this appropriately answers the preceding verses: the person devoted to the holiness, innocence, and choosing of the Lord is the one who will be saved, when he is placed at the right hand on the day of judgment.

The eyes of the proud, however, will be humbled. Together with their perverse leader, the devil, they will be overthrown, placed on the left and sent into eternal torment.

It is aptly said in the opposite direction, “You will humble the eyes of the proud,” because the more arrogantly they thought they would reach the heights, the farther they descend into the depths of hell.

### Verse 30

“For you illumine my lamp, Lord; my God, illumine my darkness.”

The Church—or that people of the blessed—continues to speak, with marvelous elegance of expression. The lamp of the Church is John the Baptist, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “He was a burning lamp, and you wished to rejoice in his light” (John V, 35). The same Gospel also says: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel” (Luke XI, 33).

The meaning is therefore this: he says to the Father, the Lord: “For you illumine my lamp,” that is, John the Baptist and the other apostles, or those known to shine with heavenly light. “Illumine my darkness,” that is, through them illuminate the remaining members of the believers, who still dwell in the darkness of the flesh.

A lamp is the light of night, and it is rightly given to sinners so that through the word of illumination they may flee the darkness of sin. Therefore remember that here the Father is said to illuminate; the Son also illuminates, as it is written in another psalm: “The Lord God has shone upon us” (Ps. CXVII, 27). The Holy Spirit also illuminates, as the prophet says: “I will no longer hide my face from them, because my Spirit has shone upon the whole house of Israel” (Ezek. XXXIX, 29).

Who, then, is so darkened by a clouded heart that he does not understand that the Holy Trinity has one nature, one co-eternity, and one power? [Col. 0132A]

### Verse 31

“For from you I shall be delivered from temptation, and in my God I shall leap over the wall.”

He taught the rule of faith with distinction. He said, “From you I shall be delivered,” not “from myself.” “Temptation” signifies the devil, who constantly tempts us in order to draw us away from a good way of life. “In my God,” that is, through his strengthening power, I shall leap over the obstacle of sins that the wickednesses of mortals have built between God and human beings.

That wall is one of death, not salvation. It is raised not for protection but prepared for eternal destruction. He rightly said, “I shall leap over,” not “I shall break in” or “I shall demolish,” because that wall remains immovable for the human race, even when the saints happen, through the benefit of the Divinity, to leap over it.

### Verse 32

“My God, his way is undefiled; the sayings of the Lord are tested by fire; he is the protector of all who hope in him.”

This verse is perceived to begin one thing and add another. Having begun, “My God,” he seems about to say something of a supplicatory character, but he adds to it an unexpected conclusion: “His way is undefiled.” For if the opening had agreed with what follows, he would have said “of my God,” not “my God.”

This figure is called *paraprosdokia*, in Latin “an unexpected conclusion,” when one thing is proposed and another is explained. “His way is undefiled” signifies that his path is utterly pure. Or this may refer to the incarnation of the Word, which is known to have had no pollution of sin.

It continues: “The sayings of the Lord are tested by fire.” By the flame of faith the heavenly law is examined when the divine utterances are searched out with the desire to know. [Col. 0132D] Thus the prophet Jeremiah concluded the Lord’s utterances with a remarkable definition, saying: “Are not my words like fire, says the Lord, and like an axe cutting a rock in pieces?” (Jer. XXIII, 29).

A general promise was also added to encourage human minds, lest it be thought that the one who had not been free from sin did not deserve protection. By saying “of all who hope in him,” he excludes no one except the person who has neglected to hope in him.

This very brief verse is unfolded through definitions of praise.

### Verse 33

“For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?”

This is said against the madness of the pagans, who fashioned gods for themselves with manifold vanity. He used “Lord” because we are his servants; “God” because we rightly worship and adore him.

But this God is the inseparable Trinity, distinguished only by the distinction of persons, not of substance. The praise of the Lord was appropriately stated briefly beforehand, since he himself was about to speak in the following section.

### Verse 34

[Col. 0133A] “God, who girded me with strength and made my way blameless.”

The third order has now been reached, in which the Lord and Savior explains his power. What he says, “He girded me with strength,” signifies both dignity and strength. It is clear that both belong to him, who by the power of his strength will judge the world.

Appropriately he continues, “He made my way,” that is, he established and strengthened it so that it would not be moved by any worldly ambition. By “blameless way” he means a life utterly pure and without the stain of sin—a life walked by him alone, who had no sins.

We appropriately apply all these allegorical and figurative expressions, both those already stated and those that follow, to the Lord’s incarnation.

### Verse 35

“He made my feet like those of a deer, and set me upon the heights.”

This animal is frequently placed in a good sense in the divine Scriptures, as in: “As the deer longs for the springs of waters” (Ps. XLI, 2). There the reference is to its great thirst; here, to its swift running.

Deer know how to leap over thorny places and cross dangerous chasms. In the same way he passed with holy steps through the sins of the world that prick human salvation and through the deepest pits of sins.

Observe how he remains within the comparison with deer: when they flee level ground, they climb the heights of the mountains. He signifies that he has been placed above all the eminence of creatures, as the Apostle says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 9–10). [Col. 0133B]

### Verse 36

“He teaches my hands for battle, and has made my arms like a bronze bow.”

To be taught means to be made cautious against imminent ambushes. “Hands” signify actions; “battle” demonstrates the conflict with the devil, against whom the spiritual struggle is waged, since he is always armed for unceasing contests.

The arms of Christ are the prophets and apostles, through whom he carried out the desire of his will. He compares them to a bronze bow because God’s servants do not grow soft in preaching; remaining in heavenly strength, they send forth saving words like arrows shot from afar and pierce the hearts of devoted people. [Col. 0133C]

### Verse 37

“And you gave me the protection of your salvation; your right hand received me, and your discipline itself will teach me.”

“The protection of salvation” signifies the glory of the resurrection, when, after laying aside mortal flesh, he took it up again incorruptible and glorified. “The right hand” is the power of the Divinity, which established the assumed humanity in eternal majesty.

He rightly says that he must be taught, in order to express the condition of a true human being.

### Verse 38

“You enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footprints were not weakened.”

He says that the most glorious acts of his incarnation, which were to be displayed through a most holy way of life, were enlarged. His footprints show the path of instruction that he left most firmly to the apostles, in which he himself walked, imprinting his steps through holy deeds.

He therefore rightly denied that these footprints could be weakened by enemies. Although the windy storm of the world had shaken him, it could not move his footprints, which he made firm so that Peter would not sink in the sea. [Col. 0133D]

### Verse 39

“I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them; I shall not turn back until they fail.”

### Verse 40

“I shall afflict them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet.”

There is no doubt that these two verses are understood of those who first rise up against the Lord and afterward, having been converted, bow before his feet. Those who had incurred death as rebels earn life as subjects.

He pursues his enemies, wearied by the varied devastation of afflictions, and overtakes those whom he has changed from their perverse zeal. But altogether blessed is the one who is captured; blessed is the one who does not deserve to escape those hands. He is made freer precisely when he has become captive in such a manner.

It continues: “I shall not turn back until they fail.” When the Lord does not turn back, the prey is captured; and the one who is conquered for salvation ceases from his perverse zeal.

He added: “I shall afflict them, and they will not be able to stand.” Afflicted by various calamities, they cannot stand in their stubbornness when they have lost the strength of wickedness in their undertakings.

Then what follows takes place: “They will fall beneath my feet.” Whoever falls beneath the feet of the Lord no longer suffers opposition from him, for he is now surrounded by his protection; but he is raised up again when he has been subjected to him through humble satisfaction. [Col. 0134B]

### Verse 41

“And you girded me with strength for battle; you cast down beneath me those who rose up against me.”

This is now said about unclean spirits, who stirred up wicked battles against him through the opposition of the Jews. He was girded with strength when, through the strength of patience, he overcame the adversity of the wicked.

Those who swelled up against him in mad conspiracy will nevertheless unquestionably be subjected to his judgment, so that they may perish with their instigator, because they refused to believe their creator. [Col. 0134C]

### Verse 42

“And you gave me the backs of my enemies, and you destroyed those who hated me.”

This verse contains the twofold mystery of the law. First, “backs” signifies the conversion of those who, having been driven from resistance to his name into a saving victory, suddenly emerged as Christians—just as the apostle Paul appeared, after the Lord’s rebuke, as a disciple from being a most savage persecutor.

Second, he declares that those who hate him will be destroyed, namely those who remained obstinate in their faithlessness, as must be observed concerning the Jews, who said with impious voice: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25). [Col. 0134D]

### Verse 43

“They cried out, and there was no one to save them, to the Lord, and he did not hear them.”

He means futile cries that the impious will utter at that judgment, as he says in the Gospel concerning those who are to be condemned: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XIII, 42).

These cries cannot save them, since they decided here to despise the author of salvation. “And there was no one to save them”: he says this because of the devil, at whose instigation they sinned. For who would save such people, when their instigator and prince himself is the first to be condemned?

When they see their hope in the devil collapse, they will indeed cry out to the Lord, but he will not hear them, because repentance is recognized as fruitless there, where just condemnation has already arrived. [Col. 0135A]

### Verse 44

“And I shall crush them like dust before the face of the wind; like the mud of the streets I shall wipe them away.”

Where is that grandiloquent tongue and windy pride? Let those who strive to oppose the Lord with perverse minds understand that they will be crushed into dust.

And lest they think that, once worn down, they could remain at rest, he added, “before the face of the wind,” so that they cannot rest once they have been reduced.

He aptly compares sinners to the mud of the streets, which is stained with the foulest filth and is not spared the trampling of the people, so that its stench is constantly renewed. “I shall wipe them away,” that is, I shall remove them from the midst—an expression that pertains to the mud of the streets.

Understand also the force of the comparison itself: he says “like the mud of the streets,” which is easily removed because it is shown to be extremely soft. [Col. 0135B]

### Verse 45

“You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will establish me as head of the nations; a people whom I did not know served me.”

He was plainly delivered from the contradictions of the people when, after the faithless Jews had been expelled, he was transferred to the faith and devotion of the nations. By “contradictions” he means the attacks that the criminal crowd repeatedly directed against him.

When he says, “You will establish me as head of the nations,” he indicates a sign of the Christian faith: for on the forehead of the nations the standards of the cross shone.

“A people whom I did not know,” that is, to whom I had not come—a new, untutored people, previously unreceived. “Served” means “believed,” since whoever believes also serves. This happened among the nations, who had not been sought out by Christ according to the flesh.

For what is there that he does not know, when he searches the inmost being of human beings and their hearts? [Col. 0135C]

### Verse 46

“At the report of the ear they obeyed me; foreign sons lied to me.”

This praise of the nations is a great reproach to the Jews: that those who had not seen should serve; that those to whose ears no sacred words had sounded from his mouth should hear. As it is written: “Those to whom he was not announced will see, and those who have not heard will contemplate” (Isa. LII, 15).

The sense requires us to add the contrast: the Hebrews who saw and heard, as he says below, did everything with an entirely contrary will. Isaiah likewise foretells this: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, or hear with their ears, or understand with their heart, and be converted and I heal them” (Isa. VI, 10).

This figure is called *aposiopesis*, that is, a statement whose ending is left unspoken, either to cause fear or to provoke the hearer’s desire.

“Foreign sons” means sons of the devil, to whom he himself says in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44). “They lied to me” when they said: “Teacher, we know that you have come from God and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. XXII, 16).

To lie means to speak against one’s mind: to bring forth with the tongue what it is clear that a person does not possess in the heart. [Col. 0135D]

### Verse 47

“Foreign sons grew old, and they limped from their paths.”

He rightly said that the foreign sons limped, because the sons of the Lord are known to walk with straight steps. Properly speaking, we call those people lame who are weak in one foot.

It is clear that this happened to the Jews, who, holding the Old Testament in a carnal manner, rejected the grace of the New; and thus they became weak in one part and limped in the steps of their mind.

Some assert that this was also foretold in that angelic struggle of the patriarch Jacob (Gen. XXXII, 24), when, after his sinew was touched, he became lame in one foot.

Nor is it without significance that he added “from their paths”: after abandoning the understanding of the law, they were driven by their own superstitions. Thus, refusing to receive the promised Lord and Savior, they raised insane accusations over the washing of hands and cups—truly filthy, but not to be cleansed by such observance. [Col. 0136A]

They could have been cleansed from their own filth if they had sought the washing of sacred baptism. [Col. 0136B]

### Verse 48

“The Lord lives, and blessed is my God; and let the God of my salvation be exalted.”

The gate of the fourth and remaining order is opened. Here again the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, speaks. In summary, she recounts the Lord’s benefits and pours forth a hymn with sweet delight.

She rightly said: “The Lord lives,” whom she discerned in her heart through continual contemplation. “He lives,” she said, because he is present and seen through firm belief.

God is called blessed when praise is offered to him with the greatest devotion of mind, as it is also written elsewhere: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest” (Matt. XXI, 10).

He is also properly understood as blessed because he himself blesses all things in his mercy, just as “the Lord lives” means that he himself gives life. These and similar expressions, as we have often said, are shown to be uttered through figurative allusions. [Col. 0136C]

“Let him be exalted” means: let him be believed throughout the whole world. For how else could he be exalted who is properly called the Most High?

### Verse 49

“God, who gives me vengeance and subjects peoples beneath me.”

[Manuscripts A, B, F: “and subjects.”]

In this world the Church is proclaimed to be avenged when blasphemers and unbelievers are led into the inner sanctuary of true religion, so that those who were previously rebellious become subject to the Church with fruitful devotion.

Behold the truly pious vengeance, the saving punishment, the glorious retribution. They are subjected to the Church who are shown to be free from vices; for those who depart from her immediately encounter the snare of harmful captivity. [Col. 0136D]

### Verse 50

“My deliverer from angry nations; from those rising up against me you will exalt me; from the unjust man you will deliver me.”

He added praise to the deliverer by saying “angry.” It is a lesser thing to deliver someone in danger from lukewarm enemies, but much more glorious to deliver him from enemies inflamed by fervent malignity.

A graceful contrast follows: the higher the enemies rose in anger, the more greatly she who endured it would be exalted.

By “the unjust man” he designates the schismatic, who rages through the wickedness of perverse doctrine.

### Verse 51

“Therefore I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord, and I will sing a psalm to you among the nations.”

“Therefore,” because of the things stated above. “I will confess you,” that is, I will praise you through the Christian peoples, whose tongue is certainly the voice of the Church. “Psalm,” as has been said, signifies an actual work; hence through the works of the faithful he gives thanks to God—thanks which the Divinity is known to hear more readily than voices. “Among the nations” indicates universality, since the Church was to be enlarged through the multitude of the nations.

### Verse 52

“Magnifying the salvation of his king, and showing mercy to his anointed, David, and to his seed forever.”

He explains what sort of psalm he had spoken above: one that magnifies his son throughout the whole world. Formerly every anointed person was called “Christ” in the sense of one anointed king; thus it was said of Saul: “Why did you dare to lay your hand upon the Lord’s anointed?” (2 Samuel 1:14). He showed mercy, therefore, to David, because, as the title stated, he delivered him from the ferocity of his persecutors. “And to his seed” signifies the Lord the Savior, who, according to the flesh, descended from his lineage. He therefore says that mercy was shown to his seed when, after three days, he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father. “Forever” is understood as “for eternity,” just as in the preceding psalm it was said, “to the end”; for these expressions signify the same thing, although they may appear to be varied for the sake of stylistic freshness.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

With what marvelous interweaving of words has the drama of this psalm unfolded! It is always produced through a variation of persons, while one speaker’s discourse succeeds another’s through reciprocal exchange. Let us understand how glorious is the fellowship of this chorus, since the Lord himself also deigned to mingle salutary words with it, for the sake of which he did not disdain to assume the humility of incarnation. The number itself, moreover, contains great mysteries of the Law. The number ten refers to the Decalogue of the Old Testament; the number seven refers to the sevenfold Spirit [editorial edition: “the grace of the Spirit”]. Joined into one fellowship, these produce seventeen. Thus the chief mysteries of the holy Law are contained in the number of this psalm.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XVIII

### For the end. A psalm of David.

This inscription has often been explained, referring the words of the psalm to the Lord Christ. The prophet is about to speak of his first coming, through which the enemy met his downfall and the human race received singular protection. Through him that tyrant was bound and groaned, while man—previously held captive by deadly bonds—was set free. Remember, however, that this is the first psalm here concerning the same subject; four others follow, namely, Psalm 79, Psalm 84, Psalm 96, and Psalm 97.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the words are those of the prophet. In the first section he praises the preachers of the Lord, himself also adding words about the Lord’s incarnation through most beautiful comparisons. In the second he praises the commandments of the New and Old Testaments. In the third he begs the Lord to cleanse him from hidden vices, so that he may make him worthy to be a psalmist. From this we understand that only those truly sing the Lord’s praises who know not how to depart from his proclamations.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands.”

Although this may also be understood literally—as the heavens having declared God’s glory when the star went before the Magi as they came to Bethlehem and, standing above his cradle, revealed the coming of the Lord and Savior (Matthew 2:10)—we more appropriately refer it to the apostles and prophets. By discussing his coming, they filled the whole world with holy admonitions. In them God dwelt as in the heavens, encompassing all things far and wide, entering them not partially but with the entire fullness of his majesty. For there is no part in God; he is wholly and fully present everywhere. To the impious it is said: “Who are you, that you recount my glory?” (Psalm 49:16).

It follows: “and the work of his hands”—that is, man himself, who was made by his hands. But this is said to the praise of the prophets: although they are his works, they deserve to announce the revered mysteries of their Creator. He added, “the firmament announces,” namely, the proclamations of his incarnation, through which the steadfastness of our faith becomes unshaken.

Notice that here it is said that man was made by God’s hands. Likewise we read: “And his hands fashioned the dry land” (Psalm 95:5). But this is an allusion to human activity, which cannot fashion anything without hands. Otherwise, God created all things by the command of his will, as we read: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148:5).

#### Verse 2

“Day pours forth the word to day, and night makes knowledge known to night.”

“Day poured forth the word to day” when the Lord was speaking to the apostles. Radiating with divine brightness, he communicated words of heavenly light to their purified hearts. He poured forth the word when he brought speech from the innermost chambers into the knowledge of the saints.

“But night made knowledge known to night” when Judas betrayed Christ to the Jews and handed him over to be killed (Matthew 26:48). “To make known” pertains to betrayal. For they had agreed among themselves that they would seize the one whom the most wicked man had kissed.

O utterly impious betrayer, rightly separated from the fellowship of the blessed! Through a kiss he caused the occasion of death to come; through it the disposition of the human race is revealed. The fact that he compared day with day and night with night is an example of what is called “from equality,” just as he will say in Psalm 41: “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts” (Psalm 41:8).

#### Verse 3

“There are no utterances or words whose voices are not heard.”

By denying that there were any words or utterances which the apostles had left unspoken, he seems to proclaim that they would speak in the languages of all nations through divine inspiration. Their words and utterances resounded throughout the world with the freedom of preaching. “Words” refers to ordinary narratives, and “utterances” to public exhortations; it is absolutely certain that the apostles did both.

#### Verse 4

“Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world; in the sun he has placed his tabernacle.”

Here we should understand “earth” as man, who is able both to hear and to believe. “Sound” is the fame of miracles, which, because of their novelty, spread among each of the nations with exceptional renown. “The ends of the earth” are kings, who guard their kingdoms like the boundaries of fields. Thus it is shown that the words of the Gospel reached not only the humble but also the rulers of the nations.

The prophet’s holy proclamation then proceeds to the incarnation of the Word, so that he might appear to have done himself what he had praised others for doing. The discourse passes from the apostles to the person of the Lord. This figure is called *exallage*, that is, “exchange.”

“In the sun” means in the manifestation of the world. “Tabernacle” means the dwelling-place of his body. I think he said that it was placed in the sun so that the one who possesses a perfectly pure eye of the heart might both endure and behold the brightness of that mystery. But whoever is confused by heretical perversity, struck by the radiance of his incarnation, is unable, because of the weakness of his error, to gaze upon the Lord’s holy light.

#### Verse 5

“And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course.”

“He himself” refers to Christ the Lord, who, like the bridegroom of his Church, came forth from his chamber—that is, from the virginal womb. He explained the mystery of his incarnation through a great comparison. For this reason he came forth from an untouched womb by a marvelous dispensation: reconciling the world to the Divinity, he joined the Church to himself in the love of a bridegroom. Therefore he was rightly born of a Virgin, since he was to be joined to the Virgin in holy union.

Appropriately, Christ is called a bridegroom from *spondendo*, “promising,” since he was so often promised through the prophets. And rightly our Christ is now compared with a giant, because, surpassing human nature by the greatness of his power, he overthrew all the vices of the world together with their most savage author.

By saying “to run his course,” he preserved what he said in the first psalm: “and he did not stand in the way of sinners” (Psalm 1:1). This “way” signifies the course of his life, which the Lord lived as a man born into the world: he was born, grew, taught, suffered, rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father. Therefore he rightly said that he “ran the way,” since his conduct could not hesitate in any worldly ambition. These things have been suitably expressed through allegorical comparisons, which say one thing while persuading us to understand another.

#### Verse 6

“His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its summit; and there is no one who can hide from his heat.”

If we examine this more carefully, the majesty of the whole Trinity is revealed here. “From the summit of heaven” signifies the Father. “His going forth” signifies the birth of the Son—not temporal, but co-eternal with the Father, existing before every beginning, since the Son himself is acknowledged to be the Beginning.

“His circuit” is spoken according to his humanity, because, after assuming flesh, Christ remained in both natures and came to the seat of the Father’s majesty. “To its summit” again refers to his divinity, by which the Son is always equal to the Father. When he came from the summit, he was inferior in nothing; when he returned to the summit, God-man, equal to the Father in the substance of divinity, he remained as he had come. His human humility took nothing away from him.

When he says, “there is no one who can hide from his heat,” he appears to signify the Holy Spirit, whom he sent to the disciples after his ascension. In the Acts of the Apostles we read that fire appeared (Acts 2:3), resting upon each of them and enabling them to speak in the various languages of the nations. He is therefore the heat from which no one can hide, since by the power of his divinity he knows the hearts of each person.

Thus, in this one verse, the immense mysteries of the holy Trinity are declared. Observe how, although he speaks of three persons, he nevertheless preserves their consubstantial unity. For he says “his,” as though speaking of one, because the holy Trinity is one God, as we read: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

#### Verse 7

“The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls.”

We have reached the second section, in which six verses define individual things through differing praise. This is the seventh type of definition, which the Greeks call *κατὰ μεταφοράν* (*kata metaphoran*), and the Latins call “by transference,” when we show what a thing is under a brief proclamation.

Let us now consider each item. That law which he gave through Moses is blameless, because it rests upon perfect truth. Through the Lord Savior it was not condemned but rather shown to be fulfilled; for he says in the Gospel: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17).

And lest the severity of the law bring us the destructive despair of terror, he added, “converting souls.” Fear of that strictness corrects the one who has gone astray and causes him to return to the grace of Christ when he begins to have no hope in his own merits.

#### Verse 8

“The testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to the humble.”

Here he speaks of the Father, since all the testimonies he gave to the people of Israel were certainly faithful, having been recognized as wholly true. They granted wisdom to the humble—not to the proud or to those who vaunt themselves with swelling arrogance, but to the humble. The humble are the lowly and innocent, as the Apostle admonishes: “Do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in malice” (1 Corinthians 14:20).

The Son also gives testimony, as the Apostle says to Timothy: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who bore witness before Pontius Pilate” (1 Timothy 6:11). The Apostle says the same concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit himself also bears witness to our spirit” (Romans 8:16). You see in that holy Trinity how little the divine Scripture wishes anything to be considered lesser or greater, since it does not even permit the names themselves to be divided.

#### Verse 9

“The ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts.”

They are truly right, because he is known to have acted no differently from what he taught. The righteousness of those people is not right whose speech differs from their deeds.

“Gladdening hearts”—understand, the hearts of the righteous, who rejoice in the judgment of God because they know that they will receive the rewards of the Lord’s mercy, as the Apostle says: “Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:8).

#### Verse 10

“The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes.”

It is truly radiant, because it is sincerely pure and undefiled, such as is taught to proceed from the Father of lights. It enlightens the eyes—not these bodily eyes, which even animals can possess in common with us, but those inner eyes which are spiritually illuminated by a divine gift.

#### Verse 11

“The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever.”

Let us see what this definition means. To fear God is not trembling confusion but undisturbed steadfastness, whose condition is not changed by any temporal alteration but perseveres unchanged in the sincerity of a good conscience.

Human fear changes with time and is not holy, because it cannot be beneficial. The fear of God, however, contains no disturbance. Although it rightly fears its author, it knows that he who judges is merciful to those who truly entreat him. Therefore the person who is known both to fear and to love his judge exists in complete holiness. Love mixed with awe is the fear of the Lord, which ordinary usage calls reverence.

#### Verse 12

“The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves.”

By “the judgments of God,” I think he means the commandments written in the Old and New Testaments, because they were truly issued from judgment. “That judgment,” in the singular, refers to the judgment in which good and evil are separated.

For what follows—“desirable”—prevents this from being applied to the future time of judgment, since we read: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord!” (Amos 5:18).

These judgments of both Testaments, once spoken, remain in unchanging truth. So great is the good in them that, when received by devout minds, they make people truthful and blessed. They give what they possess, since what makes the righteous must necessarily be filled with justification.

The sixfold variety of the proposed praise has reached its conclusion through the proclamation of the law of the Lord, the testimony of the Lord, and the judgments of God. This number is known to be perfect in the discipline of arithmetic. In each verse, as though in certain joined reeds, the works of the Lord are shown to have been sung in a spirit of praise, so that he might teach the perfection and harmony of the things proclaimed under such a reckoning.

O astonishing depth of immense realities! Who could have sufficiently distinguished or proclaimed the works of the Lord, unless they were shown to have been spoken by the Holy Spirit? For only the one who can know himself most completely is able worthily to speak about himself.

#### Verse 13

“They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

The judgments of the Lord are desirable, as has been said: the commandments of the New and Old Testaments. They are more desirable than gold, which human greed most ardently longs to possess, on account of which it often even despises the salvation of souls.

But since this was too little for so great a matter, he added “much precious stone,” since a very small pearl is of immense value and a tiny weight of metal surpasses a vast sum of money.

Yet since there could be disciplined people who restrained harmful greed through praiseworthy frugality, he also added flavors delightful for their exceptional sweetness: honey and the honeycomb. Thus no human being is excluded, however continent he may appear to be. In relation to the Old Testament, it surpasses honey; in relation to the New, it surpasses the honeycomb. The former merely tastes sweet in the throat; the latter becomes completely sweet to the mind.

This figure is called in Greek *auxesis*, in Latin “increase,” because it gradually grows toward superior things.

#### Verse 14

“For your servant will keep them; in keeping them there is great reward.”

When he says, “your servant,” he signifies the just and devoted person. “He will keep them,” having been drawn by that sweetness, since the judgments of the Lord are always bitter to wicked minds.

Notice that he says, “he will keep them,” so that he may not appear to receive an affection for these things only for a time, but to remain in such devotion throughout the final span of life.

After obedience, rewards follow: “great reward.” For the gifts of divine clemency are so great that they cannot be comprehended. Thus the Apostle says of them: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9). They are rightly called “many,” because they could not all be comprehended.

#### Verse 15

“Who understands offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults.”

Behold, the door of the third section is opened. In it the prophet begs that all his sins be cleansed, so that the words of his mouth may be made acceptable in the sight of the Lord.

Although human beings go astray in three ways—in thought, word, and deed—that immense sea of offenses is here compressed into a brief statement and declared to flow from two sources.

What is called original sin is hidden. In it we are conceived and born, and by a secret will we sin: when we desire what belongs to our neighbor; when we wish to take revenge on our enemies; when we want to become superior to others; when we crave sweeter foods; and in similar matters. These things spring up and steal upon us so subtly that, before the deed takes place, they appear hidden from many.

If these things are made manifest to someone, Solomon admonishes: “Do not go after your desires” (Ecclesiasticus 18:30). Nevertheless, we must recognize that there are many sins of which we are entirely unaware and whose origins and stealthy incursions we cannot discern. Hence we must understand: “Who understands all offenses?”

For when he is about to say in Psalm 50, “My offense is always before me” (Psalm 50:5), and elsewhere, “I made my offense known to you” (Psalm 31:5), how can it not be understood that the sinner is compelled to confess? But if you add “all,” then this question is shown to be resolved.

#### Verse 16

“And spare your servant from strangers. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense.”

In the preceding verse he placed “hidden,” which we call original sin. Now we must explain what “strange” means.

That is “strange” which is committed at the persuasion of wicked people or of the devil, but it becomes one’s own because punishable consent is added. From that corrupted mass of mortal beings, transmitted from generation to generation, a person is swiftly overthrown by the spiritual enemy without divine grace, since humanity is shown to have been corrupted through disobedience in the first man.

For how easily the ancient deceiver persuades the infected to do what is forbidden—he who was able by his cunning to deceive those who were free and incorrupt! Therefore the prophet asks to be cleansed from original sin, from which no living person is exempt until the end of the world, as though he had not yet been completely purified from carnal vices.

But when he says “your servant,” he already shows that he is bound by right to serve the Lord’s law. Errors rule over people when they presume upon them through a deceptive will; but they lose their dominion when, by God’s grace, people are withdrawn from them. The prophet therefore rightly trusts that he is made blameless when he has already been freed from their dominion.

The greatest offense is pride, through which the devil fell and dragged man down [manuscripts A, B, F: “laid him low”]. How great it is in evil may be understood from this: it made an angel into a devil, brought death upon man, and emptied him of the blessedness that had been granted. It is the mother of all evils, the source of crimes, the vein of wickedness. For it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15). Yet the Lord, when he came, cast it down through his humility.

#### Verse 17

“And the words of my mouth will be pleasing, and the meditation of my heart will always be in your sight, Lord, my helper and my redeemer.”

He says when the words of his mouth will be able to please the Lord: namely, if he is made free from the vices he mentioned above, in accordance with what is said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” (Psalm 49:16).

But what is the meditation of the heart that can reach the Lord? Hope, love, and faith—things that are certainly worthy of God. Those things deserve to ascend into his sight which he himself is known to approve.

He calls him his helper in good things and his redeemer from evil, so that no one may attribute to his own merits what he has received from heavenly generosity.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

With what marvelous order the most glorious prophet sang the whole psalm! He praised the preachers of the Lord; he himself also taught the coming of the most sacred incarnation, commending its greatness through a variety of definitions. Then, returning to the memory of his own frailty, he asked to be cleansed from sins, so that he might become worthy to relate such great mysteries—he who taught that the Scriptures of the Lord must be recounted from a most pure conscience.

The present number also seems to declare the power of the psalm. For just as in the Gospel, in the eighteenth year, a woman who was bent over was saved from her infirmity at Christ’s command (Luke 13:11), so in this psalm the prophet asked to be freed from his own sins. Through this reckoning he signified the most appropriate time in which he too might deserve the Lord’s saving benefits.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XIX

### For the end. A psalm of David.

Since the words of the title are already familiar, let us say something about the text of the psalm, so that it may be received more gratefully when its intention is briefly shown to be understood.

The prophet, filled with illumination concerning future things, uses the optative mood to pray that prosperity may come to the holy Church—prosperity which he knew with certainty would come to her after the Lord’s advent. Filled with immense love, he wishes prosperity for the one whose member he knew himself to be. Such desires always belong to the blessed: they show that their goods are placed where the vows of those who have deserved well rejoice together.

### Division of the Psalm

At the beginning the prophet prays that prosperity may come to the holy Church, so that, wearied by the world’s various tribulations, she may receive Christ the Lord when her prayer is heard.

Second, he prays that the Lord, through the mercy of his omnipotence, may confirm all her counsel and her right faith, promising that the faithful people will not be magnified by worldly power but by divine power.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.”

Through the figure of *prolepsis*, which in Latin is called “preoccupation,” the prophet, inflamed by great love, wishes for the Catholic Church to receive what he saw could take place only after a long time.

We are understood to be heard when we obtain something in every respect. By saying “in the day of tribulation,” he points to a time of the most severe affliction, when we beseech the Lord with great desire. For then we ask for what we seek to be granted not with our outermost lips but with a pure heart.

It must also be examined why the name of the patriarch Jacob seems to have been attached here. Jacob, by taking advantage of his elder brother, sought the grace of the entire blessing, so that his elder brother too, together with the rest of the people, might be subjected to him.

This likeness of the blessing is suitably applied to the Christian people. Following the nation of the Jews, they surpassed it through the religious devotion of a faithful mind, so that, by the gift of grace, they might be made first through the Lord’s giving.

When he says, “may the name of the God of Jacob protect you,” he wishes this kind of likeness to be understood as something granted by the Lord to the new people, which the holy patriarch received beforehand as a foreshadowing.

#### Verse 2

“May he send you help from the sanctuary, and may he protect you from Zion.”

He says “may he send,” in order to show that the Son was sent by the Father. But this word expresses love, not subjection, just as he himself says concerning the Holy Spirit in the Gospel: “It is better for you that I go; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7).

Zion, as we have often said, is a mountain signifying contemplation, which is fitting for the Divinity, since all things are known to him not through events as they become known to us, but through the glorious secret of his disposition.

#### Verse 3

“May he remember all your sacrifice, and may your holocaust become fat.”

The sacrifice of the holy Church is not to be understood as the offering of animals, but as this rite now performed: the solemn offering of the body and blood, which he foresaw would come, not something he knew was to be omitted.

It follows: “and may your holocaust become fat.” By the name “holocaust” he continues in the likeness of the former sacrifice. A holocaust was called something wholly burned; this must now be referred to the most holy purity of our communion. A holocaust is in itself burned and dry, but it becomes fat and pleasing when it is taken up by the grace of the Divinity [manuscripts A, B, F: “is consumed”].

#### Verse 4

“May the Lord grant you according to your heart, and may he confirm all your counsel.”

After the *diapsalma*, he comes to the second beginning, still wishing good things for the Church, which he knew would remain steadfast in orthodox religion.

He says: “May the Lord grant you according to your heart,” that is, according to the understanding you have concerning the Lord Savior: that you believe that one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh, hung upon the cross for the liberation of the world, rose again, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come to judge.

He also added: “May he confirm all your counsel”—namely, that, contemplating the Lord’s promise, you may despise the allurements of this world and not fear the dangers of the present age, while you always await with joy the rewards of the future resurrection.

This is the counsel of the holy mother Church: to believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one God, by whom all things were created and the universe is ordered. The prophet rightly prays that these things may be confirmed in the faithful people, through which he knows that they will reach eternal rewards.

#### Verse 5

“We shall rejoice in your salvation, and in the name of our God we shall be magnified. May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.”

When the most holy man was wishing spiritual goods for the Church, he appropriately joined his own person to hers, to show that he was one of her members.

For he declared that he would rejoice in the Church’s salvation, which is the Lord Christ, and testified that he would be magnified in his name, because Christians were to be called from Christ. To be magnified means to become great, especially since the name of the heavenly King has been bestowed upon his servant.

It follows: “May the Lord fulfill all your petitions.” Again he turns lovingly toward the Church, so that the greatness of his immense goodwill may be demonstrated through such frequent prayer.

#### Verse 6

“Now I know that the Lord has saved his anointed.”

From here to the end of the psalm he speaks in his own person. This figure is called *apostrophe*, that is, “turning,” whenever we repeatedly turn our words toward different persons.

By saying “now I know,” he displays the great power of prophecy, speaking as though he knew in the present what could be confirmed only after many ages. The Father saved Christ the Son through a glorious resurrection, when he also ascended into heaven.

#### Verse 7

“He will hear him from his holy heaven; salvation is in the powers of his right hand.”

The Father heard the Son after the incarnation had been assumed—that is, after the resurrection, when he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven to the apostles, whom he had promised to send upon the earth.

And to show that he himself is also omnipotent in his divinity, it follows: “salvation is in the powers of his right hand.” The salvation he himself created is recognized as our power, since that salvation is affected by neither illnesses nor wounds of pain, but makes us powerful by preserving us in its eternity.

The sense is therefore this: “The Father will hear the Son from his holy heaven,” because salvation is in his right hand; from his own divinity he possesses what he appears to request according to the flesh.

#### Verse 8

“These are in chariots, and these on horses; but we shall be magnified in the name of the Lord our God.”

Confident in the sincerity of his faith, which had been bestowed through the Lord’s gifts, the prophet rejoices, scorning those who ride in pompous chariots and place their confidence instead in temporal dignity.

Among the ancients there were two kinds of triumphs: one greater, in chariots, which was called the laurelled triumph; the other lesser, on horseback, which was called the ovation. But, leaving these things to worldly people, he confirms that he has been magnified in the Lord’s name.

Neither chariot nor horse magnifies a person, although they may appear to exalt him with honors in this world. It is the Lord’s name that magnifies, leading to eternal rewards.

This figure is called in Greek *syncrisis*, in Latin “comparison,” when through a certain comparison we demonstrate our cause to be more just than that of our adversaries.

#### Verse 9

“They were bound and fell, but we have risen and stand upright.”

He powerfully disclosed the outcome of the preceding matters. Those who presumed upon human honors, ensnared by their own depraved desires, fell into the pit of death.

Since he was going to say “they fell,” he first placed “they were bound,” which necessarily happens to those who appear to bind themselves in tangled errors.

A Christian is said to rise in two ways. First, when, by grace, he is freed in this world from the death of vices and perseveres in divine justifications, as the wisest Solomon says: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16). The general resurrection is also called rising, in which the righteous will obtain eternal rewards.

Here it is clearly appropriate to understand both meanings. He therefore added “we stand upright,” because in either resurrection the faithful rise from humiliation and are lifted up to divine rewards.

This argument is called in topical reasoning “from the things themselves,” when we say that our adversaries have fallen and testify that we have been raised upright.

#### Verse 10

“Lord, save the king, and hear us on the day when we call upon you.”

Drawn by his desire for future things, the prophet again asks that those things happen which he knew were going to come.

He says to the Father: “Save the king”—that is, may Christ the Lord rise from the dead, ascend into heaven, and intercede for us, so that our prayer may no longer waver, but that, with this Advocate, we may dare to pray. He taught us to supplicate the Father, lest the snare of death be able to hold us.

Then follows: “Hear us on the day when we call upon you.” This came to the human race when it firmly believed in and joyfully beheld the Lord’s resurrection.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

The most holy prophet taught us with what devotion we ought to serve Christ the Lord. He wishes for him the good things which he knew were going to come, because it is the practice of those who believe rightly to pray for the things they desire to arise.

Thus in the Lord’s Prayer we are also instructed: “May your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10)—something that will come even if we do not pray for it. Yet the devoted person (*devotus*; manuscripts G and the edition: *devotum*) does not wish to cease desiring what he believes will come.

Therefore let us be afflicted in his passion and rejoice in his resurrection. For we can rightly be called his if we deserve to be conformed to his dispensations.

We have not been able to discover the mysteries of the present number as a single total, but perhaps they may become clear to us when divided. The number twelve is therefore to be applied to the apostles. The number seven signifies the week, which certainly belongs to that first worship. Joined together, these contain the mysteries of both laws. Thus this prayer of the psalm to the Father contains the revered mysteries of the New and Old Testaments.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XX

### For the end. A psalm of David.

This title is equal to that of Psalm XIX because this psalm too will speak about the Lord Savior, though with some difference. The preceding psalm contains the prophet’s prayer and the confidence by which the Christian people will be delivered from the disasters of this age. Here a certain panegyric is spoken about his incarnation, and afterward deeds concerning his divinity are related, so that all may understand that the Son of Mary, ever Virgin, is the same as the Word of the Father.

For we rightly believe that there are two natures in Christ the Lord—the divine and the human—which remain unchangeably in one person throughout endless ages. This must frequently be repeated because it is always heard and believed as something vital to salvation.

### Division of the Psalm

In the first section of this psalm, the words of the prophet are addressed to God the Father concerning the Lord’s incarnation. The second describes his various virtues and glory, declaring that, from the condition in which he suffered, he reached—through his own gift—the summit and pinnacle of all things.

In the third, the same prophet turns toward the Lord Christ, where, in the manner of those who long, he wishes that the things he knows are going to come may take place in his judgment.

### Exposition of the Psalm
[Col. 0147D] **Verse 1.** “O Lord, the king shall rejoice in your strength, and in your salvation he shall exult exceedingly.” The prophet speaks to the Father: “in your strength,” that is, in the omnipotence of your majesty, in which the Son also reigns, as he himself says: “All things belonging to the Father are mine, and all things belonging to me are the Father’s” (John 17:10). “The king shall rejoice,” that is, Jesus Christ shall rejoice—of whom it is written in another psalm: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” (Psalm 71:2)—and in the title of his Passion it is written: “King of the Jews” (Matthew 27:37). It follows: “and in your salvation he shall exult exceedingly,” that is, your Son, who is the Savior, shall exult in that by which you saved human beings through him. He also added “exceedingly,” so that, just as the abundance of the benefit is great, so too might the magnitude of the joy be great.

[Col. 0148A] **Verse 2.** “You granted him the desire of his soul, and you did not deprive him of the will of his lips.” The prophet enumerates how great and glorious were the things bestowed upon Christ the Lord according to the flesh. The desire of his soul was as he says in the Gospel: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15). This figure is called *tautologia*, that is, repetition of the same expression, as in: “Blessing I will bless you,” and: “Multiplying I will multiply your seed” (Genesis 16:10). Yet he alone is the one who desired with desire to die, when he offered himself to be killed for the salvation of all, so that his precious blood might redeem the world, lest the devil should continue to ravage it through unlawful presumption. The will of his lips was manifested when he commanded unclean spirits, healed various illnesses by the authority of his word, and implanted his preaching in devoted minds. It is evident that his will was frustrated in nothing, since everything he commanded to be done was fulfilled, as it is written: “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Psalm 134:6).

[Col. 0148B] **Verse 3.** “For you anticipated him with the blessing of sweetness; you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.” After the silence of the *diapsalma*, he comes to a second mode of exposition, in which he describes the power of Christ’s incarnation with marvelous splendor. By saying, “For you anticipated,” he signifies that his humanity was always adorned by the grace of the divinity that preceded it, since no one first offers him anything good unless it is granted by this heavenly gift. Let the Pelagian be ashamed to call this a property of human beings, since the immaculate incarnation of the Word is clearly read to have received it. The “blessing of sweetness” was given when it was said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

“ You placed,” metaphorically, is said of those who, after very great labors, are crowned with a worthy reward. All of this pertains to the nature of his humanity, which received from the divinity what it did not possess. In the word “head,” however, we must understand the same expression with reference to bodily substance. The divinity, by contrast, has no limbs; it is everywhere whole and perfect.

The crown seems rightly to signify the gathering of the disciples standing around him, since the circle of the apostles who desired to hear him teaching surrounded him. This was the crown of his head, this the royal diadem—not something that adorned him when placed upon him, but something that was rather adorned by Christ the Lord. In this crown we may also rightly perceive the circle of the whole world, in which the universal Church is signified.

This figure is called *characterismos*, that is, an informing or description, which supplies to spiritual eyes either an absent thing or a person who is present. It is customarily used both in praise and in blame.

[Col. 0148D] **Verse 4.** “He asked for life, and you granted him length of days for ever and ever.” “Life” signifies the resurrection, which he requested when he said: “Father, glorify your Son” (John 17:1). “Length of days for ever and ever” means unending perpetuity, which is bounded by no end. But remember [Col. 0149A] that this and similar expressions are spoken from that aspect according to which he suffered.

**Verse 5.** “Great is his glory in your salvation; glory and great beauty you will place upon him.” At the beginning of the verse he states the idea that he explains below. The holy incarnation has great glory in salvation, that is, in the Word of the Father. But human understanding could not grasp this glory unless he declared it in what follows through a marvelous exposition. This figure is called *epexegesis*, in Latin “explanation.” For “glory and great beauty” seems to signify the time of judgment, when the Most High will appear in his divinity, possessing glory because of judgment and beauty because of majesty.

[Col. 0149B] **Verse 6.** “For you will give him as a blessing for ever and ever; you will gladden him with joy in your presence.” He proceeds gradually to clarify that glory which Christ the Lord, according to the flesh, received when glorified by the Father. He says that he is to be given as a blessing that can be bounded by no end. Yet these words must be weighed with devout discernment, so that the mystery of so great a matter may shine forth for us.

We have already said in many places that an expression must be understood as referring to the members when it cannot properly apply to the Lord and Savior himself, just as our Fathers are also shown to have expounded similar passages. Therefore, “you will gladden him with joy in your presence” must be understood of each of the faithful, concerning whom another psalm will also say: “And the upright shall dwell in your presence” (Psalm 139:14). For to be gladdened by the face of the Lord is recognized as belonging to another person; the Catholic Church does not permit this to be understood of Christ, since he is known to be so united to the Word that he is unquestionably one person.

[Col. 0149C] **Verse 7.** “For the king hoped in the Lord, and he shall not be moved by the mercy of the Most High.” He states the reason why he received so great a gift: because this king, who in his Passion was shown written in three languages, hoped in the Lord according to his humanity. Thus we recognize that, unless we approach through humble petition, we cannot attain his mercy.

There follows also a credible reason for this eternity: he knows not how to be removed from the Father’s mercy who perseveres in hoping in his glory, as Solomon says: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?” (Ecclesiasticus 2:11). And in another psalm he says: “He is the protector of all who hope in him” [Col. 0149D] (Psalm 17:31).

Since, then, a categorical syllogism was set forth in the first psalm and a hypothetical one in the seventh, we must now demonstrate an enthymeme. An *enthymeme*, which in Latin is interpreted as “a conception of the mind,” is a syllogism consisting of one proposition and a conclusion. Dialecticians call it a rhetorical syllogism, because orators frequently use it for the sake of brevity. It is explained as follows:

“Everyone who hopes in the Lord will exult and rejoice in his mercy; therefore I too will exult and rejoice in his mercy.”

This is the third species of syllogisms by which dialecticians, through very subtle arguments, demonstrate what they seek to prove. Nor should it disturb anyone that in these passages the words are not identical with those which dialecticians, at a much later time, fashioned for instructing the unlearned. In sacred preaching the argument itself is indeed present, but under freedom of wording. Now let us examine what remains.

[Col. 0150A] **Verse 8.** “Let your hand be found by all your enemies; let your right hand find all who hate you.” He comes to the third division, in which he wishes the Lord Christ to do what he knew he would do.
