For he says: “Let your hand be found,” that is, “let your activity be discovered”: convert the afflicted enemies who, because of their delight in the world, dissent from your laws. Of them the Apostle says: “For if, when we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved” (Romans 5:10).

But they are called enemies only so long as they are led on by the devil’s suggestions; when they return to Christ the Lord, they are called both servants and sons and friends.

It follows: “Let your right hand find all who hate you.” Here the time of judgment is understood, when the right hand of the Father, that is, the Lord and Savior, will judge the world; and those who hate him will be condemned to everlasting punishment.

**Verse 9.** “You will place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence.” A furnace is a rounded vessel of bronze, made for baking bread, which burns within under scorching flames. In this likeness sinners are rightly placed, since at the future judgment they will be tortured both by anguish of mind and by penal torment, because they lived with obstinate minds against the Lord’s commandments.

The “time of the Lord’s presence” is the day of judgment, when the Son of Man will be seen by all; but only the righteous will look upon him with contemplation of his divinity as well.

Remember, however, that above, in praise of the Lord Christ, he employed the figure *characterismos*, by which he described his honor and glory through various kinds of gifts. Now, through the same figure, he says that Christ’s enemies will be afflicted with various punishments, so that, as marvelous as he is, so terrible might they be made.

[Col. 0150C] **Verse 10.** “The Lord will trouble them in his anger, and fire will devour them.” The order of judgment is described in a most beautiful narrative. He says that those sinners who torment themselves because of the wickedness of their deeds will be troubled by the Lord’s anger when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41). They will then receive this sentence, that they be devoured by perpetual flame.

For no delay follows the Lord’s command; as soon as he distinguishes, it is fulfilled. Yet this fire consumes in such a way that it preserves; it preserves in such a way that it torments. Mortal life, and a preserving punishment, will be given to the wretched.

**Verse 11.** “You will destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed from the children of men.” Their fruit would have been in the land of the living if they had believed in the Son of God. But because they resisted his commandments with a rebellious spirit, they rightly lost that fruit of blessedness.

“Their seed” means the desires or deeds of sinners. They are rightly called seeds, since from them each person’s fitting recompense for his deeds is born. “You will make them strangers to the children of men,” that is, to the saints, whom you will send into an eternal inheritance through the generosity of your mercy.

[Col. 0151A] **Verse 12.** “For they turned evil against you; they devised plans which they were unable to establish.” We call “turning evil” the act of causing evils hanging over others to rebound elsewhere without a cause of iniquity—something which is shown to have occurred in the Passion of the Lord.

For when the Jews thought that Roman rule would be destructive to them if they accepted the King, the Lord and Savior, they appeared to turn against him the evils which they believed would befall them when the Romans took vengeance. They devised the plan when they said: “It is expedient that one should die for all” (John 11:50). “Which they were unable to establish” means that they could not bring it to the outcome they desired.

For, without knowing the truth, they spoke truly: one man had to die for all. The statement was true, but it was uttered with an evil intention. Therefore they will undergo punishment for such an act, because they did not possess a sincere conscience.

This figure is called *amphibologia*, that is, ambiguous expression, which leaves the meaning suspended in uncertainty. A plan is a deliberate reasoning about either doing something or not doing it.

[Col. 0151B] **Verse 13.** “For you will place them below; in your remnants you will prepare their face.” The Jews were placed below when, through their own fault, being earthly-minded, they were not worthy to contemplate heavenly things.

But their face, that is, their evil intention, was fitted to the Lord’s remnants, that is, to his Passion, so that, while they thought they were inflicting the loss of death upon him, salvation might become universally complete.

[Col. 0151C] **Verse 14.** “Be exalted, O Lord, in your strength; we will sing and chant your mighty deeds.” “Be exalted” means “be magnified through the resurrection.” For he is known to have been exalted from the lowliness he assumed when he was proved to have risen in his glory.

“In your strength” means “in the divinity of the Word,” through which you said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

To sing is to utter the Lord’s words with the mouth. To chant is to fulfill the divine commandments steadfastly through good works. These are the two things that are demanded from us in every way: that we faithfully sing the Lord’s praises with our mouths and carry out his commandments in our conduct.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

The image of the heavenly King has been shown to us through a marvelous description of truth, so that the world, by hearing, might believe that the one whom the Jews were not worthy to recognize when present had come.

Let us remember that this is the third of those psalms which we have gathered as speaking more explicitly about the two natures. Yet you should know that this rule is preserved throughout them all: that in these psalms both two natures and one person are declared to exist. Thus, by a saving and very brief summary, both those who falsely claim that there are two sons and those who craftily and perversely invent one nature in Christ the Lord are refuted.

Tell me, you who consider yourselves exceedingly wise: what is the meaning of what the Apostle says when writing to the Corinthians? “Then the Son himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

For if, as you believe, one nature had been made from divinity and humanity, what substance, I ask, can be subject to the Father eternally? It remains that the Arian error must swallow you up. For you must confess that the Word can be subject to the Father, although some of the Fathers have thought that this should be applied to Christ’s members.

Therefore, perhaps it seemed insufficient to you that you were held liable to the error of Eutyches, unless the Arian disaster also pressed you down under a joined burden? Each condemned the authors of his own errors; but what are they to do with you, whom a double fault condemns?

As soon as you come into conflict, you immediately call the Nestorian orthodox. We have your own judgments against you: you accuse others as a crime of what you are known to have persuaded yourself to believe.

Here there is a doubled association of the number ten: just as this equality marks out one total, so this psalm proclaims one Lord as the author of both Testaments. For there is an exceptional power in these decades, and whenever they are doubled, they disclose the mysteries of great matters.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXI

**For the end; for the morning reception. A psalm of David.**

What “for the end,” “psalm,” or “David” signifies has frequently been explained. It remains that we must explain “for the morning reception,” which is recognized as something still new.

The morning reception is the time of the resurrection, as it is said in the Gospel: “On the first day of the week, very early, Mary came to the tomb” (John 20:1), and so forth. The reception took place when the Lord Christ, having laid aside the mortal body under the condition of the old man, assumed it, glorified, into great glory; to him every knee is bent, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2:10).

It is called “morning” as though it were the primal dawn, and this time is shown in innumerable passages to have been applied to the Lord’s resurrection. But since this psalm clearly speaks at length about his Passion, let us consider why its title wished to commemorate only the resurrection.

Often what follows signifies what preceded—for example, when we say that morning has come, we understand that night also preceded it; similarly, when we say that someone has been freed, we understand that he was previously a slave; and likewise in other cases. This figure is called *synecdoche*, when through what follows we can understand what preceded. Therefore there is no doubt that the commemoration of the resurrection also indicates the most blessed Passion.

From this it is plainly understood what the power and brilliance of the psalm are, since he prefixed it with the name of the morning light: for the Passion of the Lord Christ, which it narrates, is clearly granted for the salvation of the human race.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the Lord Christ speaks. In the first section he cries out that he has been abandoned by the Father, since he had accepted the ordained Passion, commending his most powerful humility through the subjection of man [ms. G. and ed., “the abasement of human beings”].

In the second section he foretells the sacred Passion through various comparisons, praying to be delivered by divine protection from his raging enemies.

In the third he urges Christians to praise the Lord, because in his resurrection he looked upon the Catholic Church, so that, having heard of so great a miracle, they might remain steadfast in the most salutary faith, lest human hearts be disturbed when only the Passion had been foretold. Let us listen to this psalm with somewhat greater attention, for it is full of the wonder of immense realities, so that through the admonitions of the head itself we may recognize what is to be despised in this life and what is to be hoped for in the other.

For although many psalms briefly recall the Lord’s Passion, none has described it with such precision that it seems not so much prophecy as history.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0153A] **Verse 1.** “My God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me? The words of my sins are far from my salvation.”

The Lord Christ, foreseeing and arranging all things, for whom all future events are present, cries out as though already shaken by the approaching Passion: “My God, my God.” Yet these words must be understood as proceeding from the nature of his humanity. By “nature” I mean the power and vigor of a substance.

The repetition itself also displays the feeling of necessary prayer: the beloved Son invoked the one whom he knew would grant him not worldly salvation but the glory of eternal majesty, calling him by a repeated name.

Δέος is a Greek word, which in Latin is interpreted as *timor*, “fear.” For this reason, I think, our predecessors wished God to be named from fear. Hence one of the pagan poets said: “Fear first made gods in the world.”

When he says, “Look upon me,” he entreats that the help of the resurrection may come to him very swiftly.

It follows: “Why have you forsaken me?” This “why” is recognized to raise a certain question: how could that teacher of wisdom, consubstantial [ms. G., “consubstantial with the Father”] and the expounder of the Father, be so disturbed by the nearness of the death of his flesh that, as though unaware, he asks the Father why he had been forsaken by him?

Yet this and similar expressions concern the manifestation of his humanity. Otherwise, even in the Passion, we must not believe that his divinity was absent, since the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). But the impassible one suffered through the passible humanity he assumed; the immortal died; and the one who never dies rose again.

Concerning this passage, Father Cyril spoke beautifully as follows (Book IV Against Nestorius, p. 107): “The grace of God, indeed, tasted death for all, handing over to death his own body, although by nature he himself is life and the resurrection of the dead.”

Similarly, blessed Ambrose says (Book On the Incarnation of the Lord, chapter 5): “The same one suffered and did not suffer; he died and did not die; he was buried and was not buried; he rose and did not rise.” In the same way, even today we say that a human being suffers, dies, and is buried, although his soul is confined by no end.

Therefore he testifies under the form of a question that he was abandoned, because in truth he could not have been handed over to the hands of the wicked unless the power of his majesty had permitted such things to occur, as it is said in the Gospel: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

The human nature he assumed also cries out concerning what it suffers, rejecting blasphemous voices and impious murmurings. For he says [Col. 0154A] that the words which bring forth sins are far from him. The holy soul would have been safe if it had not possessed the words of those who sin; yet, through the power of patience, it willingly endured what it was to suffer by divine dispensation, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). And he added: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”

He also speaks of “the words of my sins” on behalf of his members. Therefore the one who had no sin calls our sins his own, just as in another psalm he himself will say: “O God, you know my foolishness, and my sins are not hidden from you” (Psalm 68:6).

Let us therefore hear the voice of the members from the mouth of the head, and understand that he spoke appropriately from our person, since he offered himself as a sacrifice for the salvation of all. Hence the Apostle says: “He who knew no sin, he made sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:21). In the Law also, the offerings made for sins were called “sins.”

[Col. 0154B] **Verse 2.** “My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it will not be reckoned as folly for me.”

The humanity of the Word cried out by day, for it was not surrounded by the darkness of sins; yet it is not shown to have been heard, although no offense seemed to obstruct it. Let the human race hear this kind of lament, since it desires its petitions to be fulfilled without delay.

The humanity of the Word asked, as has been said, and deserved to be heard; yet it is not shown to have been heard, so that the shameful crimes of the world might be washed away by his sacred blood. This is also taught by other examples.

Paul asks that the thorn of the flesh be removed from him (2 Corinthians 12:7–8), yet he is not heard [Col. 0154C] by the Lord. The devil asks that the holy man Job be struck by the most savage calamity (Job 2:5), and it is clear that this was immediately granted to him. But the Apostle was denied the fulfillment of his desire for his glory, whereas it was granted to the devil for his punishment.

Thus it is often beneficial not to be heard, although delayed desires distress us. He also added that he cried out by night, that is, in tribulation, when even sinners are often heard. He added: “And it will not be reckoned as folly for me”—“you will reckon,” which must be supplied.

There are two kinds of petitions. When we ask for honors, riches, vengeance upon enemies, and other things of this kind, we ask foolishly because we desire worldly things. But when we ask to be delivered from dangers and to be granted eternal life, we do not ask foolishly but pray appropriately.

Therefore Christ, the Mediator between God and human beings, asked not foolishly but wisely; yet he is not shown to have been heard, because the redemption of the world was to come in this way by the Lord’s dispensation.

[Col. 0154D] **Verse 3.** “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.”

After he had said that he had not been heard, lest anyone should think that God the Father did not love his own Son because he appeared not to hear him—although he himself testified: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17)—he added an indication of great love by saying: “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.”

By “you dwell in the holy place,” he declared his incarnation, as he also says elsewhere: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Psalm 85:2).

“The praise of Israel” is stated by way of definition as an indication of what the Father is: the praise of Israel. He is truly the praise of those who see God, since he grants all glorious things to the saints.

This is the third species of definition, which in Greek is called ποιότης, and in Latin *qualitativa*, “qualitative.” By saying what and of what quality the subject is, it clearly shows what the matter under discussion is.

[Col. 0155A] **Verse 4.** “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them.”

Lest anyone should think the Father harsh, since the Son, as has been said, declares that he was not heard, he briefly touches upon those things that were accomplished. For he rescued the people of Israel from the land of Egypt; he delivered the three boys from the furnace; he freed Daniel from the lions’ den; and there are countless other examples, whether things that happen or things that are read.

Yet although he has granted or grants such great things to those who petition him, he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (Romans 8:32), so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled and the salvation of the world might arise from his Passion.

When Christ the Lord calls them “his fathers,” this must be understood according to that aspect in which he also called his apostles his brothers. Thus in the Gospel, after his resurrection, he said: “Go to my brothers and say to them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father” (John 20:17).

[Col. 0155B] **Verse 5.** “To you they cried out, and they were saved; in you they hoped, and they were not put to shame.”

This is a most certain statement that demonstrates the result. For the one who cries out to the Lord must be heard for his own benefit. How many martyrs were thought by unbelievers not to be heard while bodily punishment consumed them; yet they were heard more powerfully, since they were deemed worthy to receive the martyr’s crown [Col. 0155C].

The Lord, therefore, always hears his righteous ones, but in the manner he knows to be expedient for them.

Nor is it without purpose that he repeatedly says “they hoped.” It is a figure called in Greek *epembasis*, in Latin “repetition,” whenever words are repeated in each clause for the greatest adornment.

“They were not put to shame”: they are clearly destined to come to their reward. For the one who is shown to be able to attain his good desire is not put to shame.

**Verse 6.** “But I am a worm and not a human being, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people.”

This is spoken through the figure called *tapinosis*, which in Latin is called *humiliatio*, “humiliation,” whenever marvelous greatness is compared with very lowly things, as the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of this world to put the strong to shame” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

A worm, though it seems contemptible because of its extreme lowliness, contains the mysteries of a great sacrament. It is born without sexual intercourse; it creeps humbly; it moves without sound. If you consider these things, you will rightly understand why the Lord Christ was called a worm.

He is a worm because he is mortal, because he was born from flesh without the mingling of human seed, and because his ways were silent and humble. The Creator compares himself with his lowliest creatures, lest you consider anything abject that is known to have been formed by him as its author, as it is written: “God made all things very good” (Genesis 1:31).

In the same way, David himself, following his teacher, compared himself to a tiny flea (1 Samuel 26:20). For the very power of religion is that the more each person humbles himself according to the example of the Creator, the more greatly he is exalted to glory.

“Not a human being,” that is, not a sinner—something that could not exist in him. He is called a human being insofar as this pertains to human nature. He is also called “not a human being” because he did not possess what is proper to a human being, namely sins.

The devil too is called a human being in the Gospel, as in: “An enemy, a human being, came and sowed weeds over it” (Matthew 13:25). Hence it is clear that this name is a homonym.

He was “a reproach of men” when they drenched him with countless spittings and struck him with sacrilegious slaps.

He was “an outcast of the people” when Pontius Pilate (Matthew 27:27) gave the crowds the power to have released whoever they wished. They chose Barabbas and rejected Christ the Lord instead.

[Col. 0156B] **Verse 7.** “All who saw me scorned me; they spoke with their lips and shook their head.”

“All” must be understood only of the wicked; for if you include the faithful, the statement cannot stand. This figure is called in Greek *synecdoche*, in Latin “a part from the whole.”

The Jews therefore scorned the Lord and Savior when they said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42), and so forth.

He specifically says that they spoke with their lips. Such people chatter with their mouths, not their hearts, and their speech does not arise from firm deliberation.

What, then, were they saying with their lips? “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (ibid., 40). Their lips seemed merely to resound with this, while their minds disagreed. And to prove that it was spoken in anger, not reason, he added: “They shook their head,” which is what people do when threatening, not when judging.

[Col. 0156C] **Verse 8.** “He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him. Let him save him, since he wants him.”

This was spoken by the Jews through the figure called in Greek *ironia*, in Latin “mockery,” which presents something other than what it attempts to show. These words are specifically those of the Gospel: the Jews were saying, while he hung upon the cross, “He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him now, if he wants him” (Matthew 27:43).

O heavenly integrity! Do we not seem here to be reciting the Gospel rather than the psalm, when everything has been fulfilled with such truth that it appears not to be future but already past? Rightly, so that nothing excusable might be left to the faithless or anything ambiguous to the faithful—

[Col. 0156D] **Verse 9.** “For you are the one who drew me from the womb; my hope is from my mother’s breasts.”

Certainly, it was from a virginal womb that he—already then set apart from the stain of original sin—came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber (Psalm 18:6). He says that he was drawn from there, from which humanity was held liable.

Alternatively, this may be understood as meaning that he rightly said he had been drawn by the Lord from his mother’s womb, so that he might show that that birth was accomplished by the Lord’s power. The birth of a virgin would have seemed incredible if it had not been completed by the Lord’s operation.

And to declare the perfect humanity which he deigned to assume and display, he says that from the beginning of his life he placed his hope in the Lord.

Yet here too an incomprehensible holiness and singular greatness are displayed. For to whom else was it granted to recognize the divinity of one whom breasts could still nourish with milk? The beginning of his age spoke of what the maturity of others could scarcely attain.

[Col. 0157A] **Verse 10.** “Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s womb you are my God.”

He spoke these words as a human being. For when he says that he was cast upon the Lord, he shows that he had been separated from human iniquity.

What follows—“from my mother’s womb”—concerns the error of the Synagogue, from which he is known to have been expelled by the Jews’ unbelief.

Nevertheless, even conception itself did not occur without God. For just as a human being is conceived in iniquities, so at the very origin of the incarnation of the Lord Christ the divine substance is declared to have been joined and united to humanity, as the angel also prophesied to Mary, the ever-virgin: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

[Col. 0157B] **Verse 11.** “Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near, and there is no one to help.”

These words too were spoken from fear of death, since he was about to say: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39).

He calls the thought of death “tribulation,” which was to threaten him after many ages. He therefore declares it near in order to show, through the assumption of true flesh, the grief of the Passion.

Or he calls it near because everything that will happen is near to him, as the prophet says: “For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed” (Psalm 89:4).

Or he calls the tribulation near because he was to suffer in his own flesh. For whoever endures loss of property, bereavement of children, loss of possessions, or other things of this kind is understood to suffer distant evils; but when someone suffers in his own flesh, then tribulation is joined closely to him.

When he says, “And there is no one to help,” the purity of the petitioner and the power of the divinity are shown: for if God does not help, there is no one who can rescue the one in danger.

Let us therefore consider whether we should ever be separated from the one by whose mercy alone we can be saved.

[Col. 0157C] **Verse 12.** “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me.”

Having completed the prayer which he always places before his sufferings—as the Evangelists’ accounts testify that he did at the time of his betrayal—lest the prayers of the faithful should perhaps rashly presume to rush ahead, he comes to the second section, where through allegorical comparisons he reveals the mystery of his crucifixion.

Note that he places future events in the past, so that he might convict the hardest hearts of the Jews as though the truth had already been accomplished. This figure is called *prolepsis*, in Latin “anticipation,” when something is reported in the past tense that is still believed to be future.

Everything was done in advance, so that the unbeliever might not perish; but he himself became guilty, since, despite being warned so often, he repeatedly refused to follow.

The “many calves” are evidently the Jewish people, who, ignorant of the yoke of God, frisk with heedless insolence—at once wanton and foolish. They do not regulate their steps with any moderation, but, wandering and unstable, rush through various leaps toward wicked counsels.

The “fat bulls” designate the leaders of the Jews, who, like bulls, puffed up their malice and pride with stiffened necks and poured out innocent blood with savage horns.

He appropriately added “fat.” The animal becomes especially restless when it is filled with much fat; and from gentle it becomes fierce when it is animated by the presumption of an overindulged body.

But if we weigh the words of the authority more deeply, “they surrounded me” can be applied to those who encircled him with swords and clubs; “they besieged me” to those who guarded his tomb so that he would not be secretly carried away by the disciples. For a siege is so called as though it were the occupation of enemies, that is, a hostile encirclement.

### Verse 13

“They opened their mouth against me, like a lion ravening and roaring.”

A metaphor is introduced from the behavior of wild beasts, which eagerly open their mouths when they strive to swallow something. But when he says “in me,” he means “against me,” since they were saying with detestable unanimity, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21). “Their mouth”—truly their own mouth—which wisdom did not open for them, but which wicked thought unfastened. Let the Pelagians hear both points: when the Jews spoke their wickedness, they themselves opened their mouth. In a good sense we read: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Psalm 50:17). But when he says, “like a lion ravening and roaring,” “ravening” refers to the most frenzied sedition, when they dragged him away after seizing him, to be heard before the governor’s tribunal; “roaring” refers to the blasphemous cries with which they shouted, “Crucify, crucify.” Both are rightly compared with wild beasts, since the mad populace had lost its reasonable judgment.

### Verse 14

“They are poured out like water [ed., ‘I am poured out’], and all my bones are scattered.”

This comparison contains no small mystery. “All his bones were scattered,” that is, the firm and faithful apostles, when he said to them: “Behold, I send you like lambs into the midst of wolves” (Matthew 10:16); then they were poured out like water. For when water is poured out, it both waters and washes; so they, satisfying the whole world with the divine rain, washed it from the filth of sins.

### Verse 15

“My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly.”

By “his heart” he means his will, which had been concealed and covered in the divine Scriptures; but when the Passion was fulfilled, every truth promised concerning his coming was revealed. The mysteries of Scripture are aptly compared with wax, which gives forth its brightness only when, melted and dissolved by heat, it is made useful for light. By “his belly” he means the catholic Church, where the words of the preachers, when the fullness of time had come, were laid open. Hence also comes the fact that the veil of the temple is recorded as having been torn at the Lord’s Passion: by that event, what had been hidden was revealed.

### Verse 16

“My strength has dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue has cleaved to my jaws, and they have brought me down into the dust of death.”

Let us not think that Christ’s strength has been inappropriately compared with a potsherd, because just as a potsherd hardens in a furnace and becomes stronger when baked by fire, so his strength was solidified through the Lord’s Passion, although previously it seemed, to unbelievers, like something made of clay. His tongue signifies the apostolic preachers, who cleaved to Christ’s jaws while they kept his commandments. For whoever preserves his preaching by divine assistance remains in the Lord’s jaws.

But how does he say that he was brought down into the dust, when his flesh did not undergo corruption? This is to be understood as referring to the desire of the savage Jews, who thought that they had inflicted upon Christ the common death in which he was believed to have been brought down even into the dust. Or rather, he may be speaking of his members, that is, of the Church, saying that he was brought down even into the dust, since this condition seemed to be common to human nature.

### Verse 17

“For many dogs have surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked has besieged me.”

Here he describes the mysteries of his Passion with marvelous precision. The nature of dogs is such that they do not at all tolerate strangers, but by untimely and incessant barking drive away those whom familiarity with domestic association does not recognize. The Jews are therefore most fittingly compared with them: they did not receive the Lord’s new teaching at all, but barked against him with savage cries.

The teaching is “new,” as the Evangelist says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34). The prophet Isaiah also bears witness to this, saying: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (Isaiah 45:19). The Jewish action is plainly described: there was an assembly of the wicked when they plotted to seize the Lord Jesus by deceit and hand him over to death. “Of the wicked” means, of course, those who were thinking wicked things. And he rightly confesses that he was besieged, because within it was the city of Jerusalem, which the enemies of the Christian faith seemed to be besieging in his person.

### Verse 18

“They pierced my hands and my feet.”

But before we come to the beginning of his Passion, we must examine why he chose such a death, when he said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

First, the very position of the cross is such that its upper part reaches toward the heavens, its lower part does not abandon the earth but, fixed, touches the depths of hell; and, as though with arms extended, its breadth reaches toward all parts of the world. Lying down, it indicates the four quarters of the world. Thus, set up in a small compass, it appears to embrace everything.

I am speaking of the Lord’s cross, which from the punitive evil of sins became blessed redemption; which afterward bestowed the good of salvation, although previously it brought death; a saving scaffold, a death signifying life; humility proclaiming divine exaltation. Thus, through the figure of the cross, you may recognize Christ in heaven, Christ on earth, Christ throughout the whole world, and Christ even in the depths below.

But if he had been cut down by the sword, consumed by fire, crushed by stones, drowned by the waves, or overtaken by any other kind of death, by what sign, I ask, would the devil have been driven away? By what standard would the Christian front have remained secure? By what figure would the weakness of body and soul have been strengthened? No death could have suited such majesty better than one that left us the tokens of perfect salvation.

This too was provided for our faith: that he should be fastened more conspicuously, seen by many, and believed by the greater number. And lest anyone doubt that he was God, since so many and such great miracles accompanied his Passion, “darkness came over the whole world, the earth quaked, and the rocks were split” (Matthew 27:45). Thus the world plainly bore witness to its suffering Creator. It was fitting that this crucifixion, which received the temple of the merciful Redeemer, should possess an entirely wondrous character. Therefore Christ rightly chose the cross, on which he could both die in a unique manner and die according to the common lot.

Although the account of the Lord’s Passion may here seem, in the literal sense, to be a simple narrative, this event also signifies something that we must understand spiritually. The Jews violated Christ’s hands when they preferred in every way not to believe in his miracles. For the hands signify the works which the heavenly Physician performed upon the illnesses of various people, so that their obstinate hardness might be softened by the power of the signs.

They also pierced his feet when they thought that his apostles, through whom the Christian faith walked among the nations, ought to be torn apart. Thus future causes were foretold in this crucifixion of the Lord.

We must not understand “they pierced” as something passing or superficial, because the earth then produces various fruits when it is known to have been ploughed by human labor. This happened in the body of the Lord Savior: fastened with nails and pierced by a spear, it brought forth for us fruit that will remain without end. Therefore we are no longer afraid to say that God suffered in the flesh, and that God died for the salvation of all.

For this reason Father Augustine wonderfully and, as usual, clearly explained the matter, saying (Sermon 39 on Time):

> It was an old thing that a human being should die; but, so that this might not always remain true in humanity, a new thing happened: that God should die.

As the Apostle also says: “But we preach Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 1:23). And lest you suppose that the Son of the Virgin was perhaps someone else, as certain madmen think, he added: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God; for what is foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weakness of God is stronger than human beings.”

What seems so foolish and so weak to unbelievers as this: that they hear that God, the Son of God, was crucified and likewise buried? Yet “it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (ibid., verse 21). The Lord’s Incarnation is indeed the wondrous height of his mercy, an immeasurable gift, an incomprehensible mystery. From it salvation comes to upright minds, while destruction is generated in perverse senses.

### Verse 19

“They counted all my bones; but they themselves looked upon me and saw me.”

The form of the cross is depicted with marvelous precision: the whole body is said to have been stretched out upon it in such a way that its bones could be counted by human eyes, since what the flesh spread over them had concealed became visible through the body’s extreme tension.

But let us consider whether this should be called a punishment or a tribunal, a condemnation or a hearing. There, established as though upon a royal throne, he left the accusing criminal guilty and immediately rendered the confessing one absolved. By this act that exceptional Compassionate One of the human race showed, in the thief’s sudden confession, what he would bestow upon his saints.

His bones were also counted—that is, the apostles or the remaining Christians—when, after the persecution had begun, they were sought out for destruction by the savage Jews, lest they grow strong in greater number. Their detestable obstinacy of unbelief follows as well, so that they may not seem to have acted casually or in passing. Rather, he says that they looked upon him and saw him, and that their stony heart was not softened by so many miracles. The rocks were split, the earth quaked, and the sun hid itself under a dark covering so that it might not see so great a crime; yet, alas, iniquity fixed in their eyes remained unmoved in its sacrilege.

### Verse 20

“They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.”

Although the whole Passion of the Lord contains great mysteries, here some greater hidden meaning is, I do not know how, brought forth: he says that some of his garments were to be divided, while another garment was likewise to be assigned by lot.

Those garments that were divided signify the writings of the prophets and the other heavenly readings. Heretics divide them by perverse interpretation and, through this wicked division, join themselves to Pilate’s soldiers.

But that tunic which came to be assigned by lot, which surrounded the holiness of his body, and which the Evangelist says was “woven from above throughout” (John 19:23), is shown to be the catholic Church. It is not given to be torn apart by human judgment, but, whole and inviolate, is always bestowed upon each person by divine generosity, as though by lot.

It is woven from above; no one divides it, no one tears it apart. Rather, in perpetual and most steadfast stability, it remains in the strength of its unity. Concerning it Truth himself says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

The Evangelist also testifies that this happened, saying: “After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots” (Matthew 27:35). Yet this lot is mentioned so frequently in the divine Scriptures that it seems to bear within it some great and mysterious secret of divine judgment.

For it is written in Leviticus that one lot was given to the Lord and one to the scapegoat, that is, to the one who bears away (Leviticus 16:8). Likewise, Moses divided the land beyond the Jordan among certain tribes by lot. Joshua, son of Nun, distributed the promised land among the children of Israel by casting lots (Joshua 18:10). The lot also exposed Jonah, who was hiding (Jonah 1:7). And in Solomon we read: “The lot restrains disputes and decides between the powerful” (Proverbs 18:18).

In the New Testament also, that is, in the Acts of the Apostles, the lot designated Matthias as an apostle (Acts 1:26). The Apostle Paul himself, writing to the Ephesians, says that he was called by lot according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1:11). And writing to the Colossians he says: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the portion of the lot of the saints in light” (Colossians 1:12).

Although many things are read as having been divided by lot in both the Old and the New Testament, no one has dared to deny that through it there was divinely shown what a devout mind had requested in humble prayer.

### Verse 21

“But you, O Lord, do not put your help far from me; look to my defense.”

Here he already entreats a very swift resurrection, so that the wicked credulity of the faithless may be destroyed by the glory that follows. “Help” signifies the resurrection itself, which certainly was not far off, since it came after three days. The text continues: “Look to my defense.” But what this defense is, he explains in what follows.

### Verse 22

“Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog.”

He asked to be delivered from the death he was about to undergo, through the assistance of the resurrection that was to be bestowed. *Framea* is a synonymous term, signifying either a spear, a sword, or any weapons whatsoever. Through these he wished the future destruction of the cross to be suitably understood, since death often follows through it.

At first he said, “Deliver my soul.” Now he asks that the Church, which is his only one—that is, the catholic Church—be delivered. Thus he is understood to have rejected new doctrines and the assemblies of the lost under the name of unity. Here he compares heretics with dogs: domesticated in a certain savage manner, yet brutally tame, they rush forth from our inner chambers to bite and tear the Church of God.

And so that you may know that dogs are most fittingly compared with such people, he says, “from the hand of the dog,” since it is a human being, not a dog, who has a hand. Or, as some wish, “the hand of the dog” signifies the power of this world, which always hastens to tear at the Church of God with a biting and deceitful wickedness. Dogs, however, are frequently placed not only in an evil but also in a good sense, as abundant examples testify.

### Verse 23

“Deliver me from the mouth of the lion, and my humility from the horns of unicorns.”

By “the mouth of the lion” he speaks of the power of the devil, who is rightly compared with wild beasts because he is always delighted by human destruction. But lest some difficulty perhaps arise for anyone as to why one and the same thing is frequently applied both to the best and to the worst persons, it must be said that it should be applied according to corresponding aspects.

It is certain that each thing possesses diverse qualities. Thus the lion, of which we are now speaking, has strength, on account of which it is called the king of beasts; but it also has savage cruelty, because of which it is called fierce. Therefore its strength and power are rightly compared with Christ, as in the passage: “The Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5). Its fierceness, however, is suitably associated with the devil, as the Apostle Peter says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8).

Thus one animal can reasonably be compared with things unlike itself when its qualities are taken into account. We may perhaps rightly call this kind of expression characteristic of the divine Scriptures. The logic of the present exposition likewise encompasses the remaining comparisons of this kind.

“From the horns,” that is, from the proud, who strike by the power of their lofty positions. But observe what he adds: “of unicorns,” that is, of those who raise themselves up in isolation. Rising through excessive arrogance, they cannot tolerate companions, since they think that whatever they wish should be done by themselves alone.

For such animals, armed with a single horn, are much stronger than those furnished with two, which the Greeks call *monókerōs* (“one-horned”). From the intolerable pride of these unicorns he requested that his humility, which could easily be crushed when left undefended, be delivered.

### Verse 24

“I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you.”

After the sacred Passion, he says that the glory of the Divinity will be proclaimed throughout the whole world. For “I will declare” means, “I will cause to be declared.” Those who love and are loved are called brothers. Since he came to suffer for the salvation of all, whom would he not call his brother?

Concerning this passage the Apostle plainly says:

> For it was fitting that he, for whom and through whom all things exist, who had brought many sons into glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering. For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.

For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Hebrews 2:10–11). He says likewise in the Gospel after the resurrection: “Tell my brothers” (Matthew 28:10); and elsewhere: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my father, and mother, and brother” (Matthew 12:50).

He praises the Lord in the midst of the Church, which has conducted itself in devout living. For the holiness of preserved conduct is his praise, since the flesh is unable to do anything good unless divine mercy is known to have granted it integrity.

By “in the midst” he means openly and in the company of many, where the work of an upright mind provides an example to the remaining faithful.

### Verse 25

“You who fear the Lord, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, glorify him.”

After narrating the Lord’s Passion at somewhat greater length, lest the hearts of the faithful be troubled by prolonged grief, he comes to the third part. Here he addresses the devout, so that, having recognized the Lord’s dispensation, they may praise him and celebrate his praises in universal rejoicing, since through his Passion came the salvation of the faithful and the life of the righteous.

Let us now consider how sweet an affection is declared in the fear of the Lord. Human fear does not produce praise but blame. The fear of God, however, because it is just and upright, generates praise, grants love, and kindles the ardor of charity.

“Praise,” he says, then, “you who fear God”—that is, you who have reverence for his name—for no one deserves to proclaim him unless he is known also to fear him. Understand “all” as referring to the company of the good, since he wishes only those to be understood who agree with the faith and devotion of Jacob, overcoming, through religious affection, the first birth of the old human being.

### Verse 26

“Let all the seed of Israel fear him.”

The seed of Israel does not signify the people of a single nation, but is understood as the fullness of all the nations, from which it is evident that the Church is to be gathered. Since above he had said, “Praise him, you who fear the Lord,” he now declares to whom fear may belong: to Israelites, certainly—that is, to those who see the Lord. For those who are blinded by heretical perversity or serve idols with a wicked mind do not know how to fear God.

### Verse 27

“For he has not despised or scorned the prayer of the poor.”

This is what those who glory in the honor of this world commonly do: they despise the poor, look down upon those who plead, and measure a case by the quality of a person’s clothing. If someone is splendidly dressed, he is considered truthful; if dirty in appearance, he is judged utterly mendacious.

But with God matters are altogether different. He does not judge by clothing, nor does he honor wealth; rather, he hears and assists the prayers of the poor faithful. The needy person is precious to him if he is nevertheless exceedingly rich in holiness.

### Verse 28

“Nor did he turn his face away from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me.”

Let us understand this verse and, with devoted minds, render thanks to God as far as we are able. For when he had said generally that thanks should be given because the Divinity deigns to hear the poor, the Lord Christ included himself, saying: “Nor did he turn his face away from me.”

Thus he made the cause of all his own; thus he wiped away the sins of the world through the holiness of his body. By drawing human weakness into himself, he caused the devil to lose what he held.

But what did he cry out, and what does he say was heard? Certainly, he cried out so that our death might be brought to an end by his death, and so that the sin of the old human being might be redeemed by the price of his most holy Passion.

### Verse 29

“With you is my praise in the great Church; I will fulfill my vows before those who fear him.”

“With you” means “from you.” “In the great Church” means, in the catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world. It is rightly called great both in extent and in honor.

By “vows” he prefers us to understand the mysteries of his body and blood, which are rendered in the presence of those who are subject to him in holy fear. Finally, see what follows.

### Verse 30

“The poor shall eat and be satisfied.”

These are the vows he mentioned above. Observe that he names only the poor, who have rejected the allurements of this world with the richest contempt; not the rich, who are filled with the prosperity of this age, but the poor—that is, those who hunger for the kingdom of God.

Therefore he added, “and they shall be satisfied,” for those alone could be satisfied whom such hunger possessed.

### Verse 31

“And they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their heart lives forever and ever [MSS A, B, F: ‘their hearts live’].”

He remains with the preceding statements. Once the poor have been satisfied, they will praise the Lord. The poor praise the Lord; the rich exalt themselves. The latter pile up earthly treasuries; the former grow rich through heavenly abundance. Their resources are different, but their consciences are utterly unlike. The latter are rich in the world; the former in God.

O how different are the vows that have fallen to their lot! The poor possess what they will never lose; the rich hold what they frequently lose not only when dead but even while alive.

The text continues: “Their heart lives forever and ever.” “Their heart lives” means that their hope is nourished in immovable vigor. For we truly call that alive which perseveres in the grace of the Divinity.

### Verse 32

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.”

Properly speaking, we call those people “remembering” who, after suffering the injury of forgetfulness, are known to have returned to the healing of memory. But how can this be understood of pagans, who before their conversion had received none of the sacraments of faith?

Nevertheless, we rightly say that they too remember, because every human being confesses God as his Creator. But when he is faithfully recognized as almighty God, they are rightly said to remember, so that they may truly return to the one whom previously, through perverse will, they had neglected.

The text continues: “All the ends of the earth shall turn to the Lord.” This is a prophecy of the universal Church, which is now known to be spread throughout the whole world.

### Verse 33

“And all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight.”

Lest anyone think it doubtful how he was to be worshiped by all nations, he inserted “in his sight,” since no one worships except the one who has relied upon sincere faith. For his sight belongs only to the most faithful and blessed.

By saying “all the families of the nations,” he excluded nothing, since he embraced everything. Thus, through their native peoples, the nations themselves also are believed to have become devout.

### Verse 34

“For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.”

Let us consider what this transposed verse compels us to understand: “God shall rule the nations because the kingdom is the Lord’s.” For the kingdoms do not belong to the nations but to the Lord, who by his power both changes kings and preserves them. It is necessary, therefore, that he be worshiped everywhere, since he is known to be Lord of all things.

Concerning this passage Father Augustine, in his letter to the presbyter Honoratus, said wonderfully in his customary manner (Letter 120, chapter 27):

> That one who was mocked, that one who was crucified, that one who was abandoned, acquires this kingdom and at the end hands it over to God and the Father—not so that he himself should lose it, but so that what he sowed in faith when he came in a state lower than the Father, he may bring to completion in the form in which, being equal, he did not depart from the Father.

The universal Church has been proved by these words. Let people cease to be confused by the vanity of the Donatists. Diabolical fraud cannot prevail more strongly than Christian religion. It is necessary to refute the wickedness of heretics wherever the passage is found, because while, with the Lord’s aid, we destroy them, we strengthen the convictions of the catholic faith.

### Verse 35

“All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped.”

What does this mean? Above he says that the poor are satisfied with the Lord’s body, but here he confirms that the rich of the earth alone have eaten and worshiped.

It means, of course, that you should understand not the humble but the proud—those who place no hope in the gentleness of preaching but presume upon riches. Although they have received the same mysteries of preaching, their devotion is nevertheless not equal.

The former eat until they are satisfied—that is, until perfection. The latter eat without being filled by great desires. For it is one thing to wish moderately to receive something, and another to seek it with the whole ardor of the mind. Therefore these are not called Christ’s poor, but the rich of the earth.

### Verse 36

“In his sight all who go down into the earth shall fall, and my soul shall live for him.”

Because above he had said that the rich of the earth are lukewarm Christians, he now says that those who fall before God—that is, who fall down—are those who descend into earthly desires through the frailty of the flesh and cannot appear before human beings.

“Descend” is well said, because every sin is proved to be an inferior part. Although the assemblies of the Church receive everyone without distinction, those are known to his sight who distinguish themselves by the quality of their merits.

He says that his soul lives for God because he passed through this world in blameless conduct.

### Verse 37

“And my seed shall serve him; the coming generation shall be announced to the Lord.”

By “seed” he means the works which he made manifest on earth during the time of his Incarnation, so that he might instruct the peoples, disclose the secrets of religion, and establish the apostolic preachers, who would proclaim the holy religion with sincere faith.

“Shall be announced to the Lord” means, according to some, by angels, who are remembered as bringing human prayers before the Lord. For it is written in the Book of Tobit: “I offered the memory of your prayer before the Lord” (Tobit 12:12).

But it is said figuratively: “It shall be announced to the Lord,” who knows and foresees everything. For it is written: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him,” says the Lord (Matthew 6:8). The angels therefore announce things to the Lord as a ministry, not to instruct him.

He speaks of “the coming generation,” which was to be brought forth by the Lord’s gift from water and the Holy Spirit. And to show that it is righteous, he says that it is to come for the Lord. For the generation of the wicked seems to come for itself, not for the Lord.

### Verse 38

“They shall announce his righteousness to a people that shall be born, whom the Lord has made.”

That is, the Evangelists will preach the Son of God; for he himself is the righteousness of the Father.

His righteousness is to be preached to that people which is to believe in God, which, having abandoned the death of sins, has come to life, and which is born through the benefit of God from faith in such a way that it may deserve to live eternally.

Therefore it is most aptly said that the Lord made the Christian people. He created it when he brought it forth from its mother’s womb; but he made it free from sins when he established the Christian through the water of regeneration.

It must also be firmly held in mind that this psalm and other psalms which speak of the Lord’s Passion reach their chief conclusion in the hope of Christians. Through this marvelous arrangement we understand that salvation has been granted to those who believe in such a mystery.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This is the psalm which the Church solemnly sings to us as an Easter gift, so that we may be salutarily instructed that, amid human affairs, even those who are blessed may be temporarily abandoned by the Lord in some measure, although by the power of his protection he leads them to eternal goods.

We hear him weeping with blessedness, through whom we can thus be refreshed if, with our minds fixed upon him, we may deserve to be afflicted in the same way.

O hard hearts of the Jews! O senseless minds of those who never believed at all! Should not this one psalm alone have been sufficient for belief in the Passion, which Truth himself so clearly prophesied concerning himself?

And lest any excuse be left to the hardest hearts, other psalms concerning this matter follow, written with evident and most unmistakable prophecy: namely, Psalms 34, 54, 68, and 108. Thus no one ought to doubt what is known to have been proclaimed by so many heralds.

The number of the present psalm also contains other mysteries of heavenly things. When the prophet Daniel had continually offered his prayer to the Lord for three weeks, so that he might learn what was destined to happen to the Israelite people, he received an answer through an angel’s voice: the angel had been sent at his first prayers, but was delayed by diabolical resistance; on the twenty-first day he had been able to descend to him and fulfill his requests (Daniel 10:12).

Therefore this psalm too is rightly understood to have been placed according to such a reckoning. Having destroyed the devil’s perversity, it disclosed the gifts of the healing Passion, through whose benefit the human race, liberated from eternal death, reached the gifts of everlasting salvation.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXII

## A Psalm of David

It is rightly passed over when there is nothing new that needs to be sought. This alone should be recalled: that we must bring the names in this title to the spiritual understanding, as we have said above.

Throughout the psalm, the most faithful Christian, regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit, speaks after laying aside the oldness of the first human being. He gives thanks because, through the Lord’s gift, he has been led from the dryness of sin to pasturelands and to the water of refreshment.

It should be noted that, just as he previously received the Decalogue of the Law, here he rejoices that he has been enriched with ten benefits. These are not stated in individual verses, but are briefly narrated in separate clauses.

## Division of the Psalm

This is indeed a short psalm, but it is known to consist of many parts. Its division is not by persons but by subject matter. Therefore, unlike in other psalms, we have perhaps appropriately attached not divisions but definite numbers to each of its several parts.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing.”

That most holy man, renewed through the grace of baptism and recognizing himself as the Lord’s poor man after rejecting the pomp of the world, joyfully exults in the chamber of his conscience and professes with the sweetest happiness that he is protected by the Lord.

For he says that he is governed by the Lord, where there is strong defense and great security, where no one fears an enemy, where no one is now disturbed by his own weakness. By adding, “I shall lack nothing,” that poor man recognized his riches, since he believed that the Lord would nevertheless confer spiritual substance upon him.

But let us hear in what follows how rich this poverty is, which is filled with such great goods that the treasuries of kings do not deserve to contain them.

This figure is called in Greek *synathroismos*, in Latin *congregatio* (“gathering”), whenever many things are collected into one and, as though formed into a weight, presented to the minds of the hearers. This figure is customarily considered extremely forceful among orators, whether in praise or in blame.

### “In a place of pasture, there he has placed me.”

This faithful man whom we have mentioned gratefully sets forth the first part of his gifts, which nevertheless we rightly recognize as pertaining to the universal Church of Christ.

He therefore asserts that he has been placed in pasturelands—not in places where flesh and body are fattened, but where the soul, refreshed by heavenly food, grows rich in the brightness of spiritual joy. For those are God’s pastures which do not disappear through the digestion of the belly, where troublesome hunger does not return; rather, once the soul has begun to be satisfied, it continues in the same state through the heavenly gift.

The place called that of pastures is the divine reading. For just as a grazed field gives fatness to the bodies of sheep, so the divine word knows how faithfully to fatten the soul that meditates upon it.

From these pastures he who said to God was satisfied and gave forth his words:

> “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118:103),

and similar passages.

### Verse 2

“Beside the water of refreshment he brought me up.”

He shows the second gift of his advancement, comparing divine gifts with the pleasant things of this age, in which human weakness commonly takes great delight. But let us consider what he wishes chiefly to be understood through these comparisons.

The water of refreshment is the bath of baptism, by which the soul, barren through the dryness of sin, is watered by divine gifts so that it may produce good fruits.

He rightly added, “He brought me up,” that is, “he gradually nourished me,” like little children and newborn infants, as the Apostle Peter says:

> “Like newborn infants, long for rational and guileless milk, so that by it you may grow toward salvation” (1 Peter 2:2).

### “He converted my soul.”

He comes to the third grace, where he asserts that his soul has been converted through the divine gift. He says “converted” because after baptism it has been made righteous from sinful, most clean from filthy, without wrinkle from contracted and deformed, as the Apostle says:

> “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Ephesians 5:27).

Therefore he rightly glories that his soul has been converted to Christ, since previously it was proved to be captive under the devil. But this conversion is salutary only if we do not relapse again into sins through the incitements of vices.

But observe what follows from this conversion.

### Verse 3

“He led me along the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” [Col. 0168D]. He recalls a fourth benefit, which must be investigated with particular care. For since it is a mark of pride to walk above the paths of righteousness, why does the holy man rejoice that he has been led to a place which seemed contrary to the Lord’s commandments? But “above” is to be understood here in the same way as when one says that someone has been placed over a people to be corrected, whom he ought to instruct in the paths of righteousness; as another prophet also says: “He set me upon the heights, that I might conquer in his glory” (Hab. III, 19). By saying, “for his name’s sake,” the servant of Christ rejoiced that he had attained to such knowledge that he could proclaim the Lord’s commands. For the paths of righteousness are the two saving commandments in which the Law and the prophetic word are summed up: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI, 5). Rightly, then, he rejoiced that he had been led above the paths of righteousness, since he had advanced through contemplation of the spirit. He added, “for his name’s sake,” so that no one might say that what divine grace clearly showed to have been granted had been bestowed on account of his merits.

### Verse 4

“For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because you are with me.” A fifth grace follows, which is truly acknowledged to have been granted to every steadfast Catholic. He says: even if I walk among heretics and schismatics—who are rightly called the shadow of death, since they bear the image of destruction when they lead people to the underworld—I will not fear their perverse persuasions, because you defend me by the protection of your presence; as it is written in the prophet: “I will not abandon you; I will not forsake you” (Josh. I, 5). In this world the Church walks among the wicked until the day of judgment, which separates the good from the evil, arrives; as the prophet says: “The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, under whose veil we live among the nations” (Lam. IV, 20). Or, absolutely speaking, the shadow of death is the devil, who secretly lays snares for us, so that, deceived by his mists, we may fall headlong into eternal death. But these things are not feared by the true believer, even if, relying on divine mercy, he dares to walk in their midst. For why should the righteous fear those who fear the saints and serve them against their own will?

### Verse 5

“Your rod and your staff, they themselves have consoled me.” He now rejoices in a sixth benefaction. The rod pertains to the justice and strength of the Lord the Savior, as he says in another psalm: “The rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom” [Col. 0169C] (Ps. XLIV, 7). The staff refers to human assistance, by which the foot is planted cautiously and the whole body is supported by the weight of those leaning upon it. The patriarchs used this: Jacob says, “With my staff I crossed this Jordan” (Gen. XXXII, 10). Likewise, in Exodus the Lord says to the children of Israel: “You shall gird your loins, holding staffs in your hands, and you shall eat in haste” (Exod. XII, 11). You will find this in many places in divine authority.

By these two things, then, the faithful person declares himself consoled: one is the discipline that crushes the vicious; the other is the governance that sustains the most faithful Christians. By setting “rod” and “staff” in the plural, he indicates the things he mentioned above. But let us see how both can console us, since the two things are altogether different. There is no doubt that the staff consoles, since it is always taken up to bring aid to human weakness. But what shall we say of the rod, which strikes, afflicts, and chastises our vices with judicial severity? It too plainly consoles the faithful when, through the correction it applies, it leads them to the way of the Lord. For we rightly call everything that helps us consoling, even if for a time it saddens us because of its severity. Hence the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “Every discipline for the present seems not to bring joy but sadness; afterward, however, it yields abundant fruit” (Heb. XII, 11).

### Verse 6

“You have prepared a table before me, against those who trouble me.” A seventh number of rejoicing is introduced when he says, “You have prepared before me” [Col. 0170A]—that is, you have predestined the holy altar, which the whole Church beholds and which the Christian people surround. The word *mensa* (“table”) is derived from *mensis* (“month”), because on that day banquets were celebrated according to the custom of the pagans. The Church’s table, however, is a blessed banquet, a joyful feast, the fullness of faith, and heavenly food.

But it is clear that this table is prepared against those who, sunk in some perversity, distress the Church of God by their grievous error. Of them the Apostle says: “Whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (I Cor. XI, 29)—the body given, that is, for the remission of sins and the possession of everlasting life. Remember, moreover, that “table” is used both in a good and in an evil sense, as the Apostle says: “You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” [Col. 0170B] (I Cor. X, 21).

### Verse 7

“You have anointed my head with oil.” An eighth generosity is presented. Christ the Lord is the head of the faithful, and he is rightly said to have been enriched with oil, since he has not withered through any dryness of sin. Therefore he declares that his own head has been enriched with oil, so that the other members might rejoice from it.

But what is this, that this very form of holy blessing is so often employed? It anointed prophets and consecrated kings. Not without reason, since that tree also provided an indication of peace, and its particular gift is known to be divine: the sap of the tree, a fatness that brings joy, the grace of great dignities, whose leaves remain in the beauty of their greenness. This too announced to Noah, through the dove, that safety had been restored to the earth (Gen. [Col. 0170C] VIII, 11), so that it may rightly seem capable of bearing such a great blessing, since it enjoys the fruit of its own tree with great beauty and usefulness. Another psalm says of him: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

“And your cup, making drunk—how glorious it is!” A ninth gift is the blood of the Lord, which so intoxicates that it heals the mind, restraining it from sins rather than leading it into them. This drunkenness makes the sober; this fullness empties out evils; and whoever is not filled by that cup is left fasting in eternal poverty. It is also found in an evil sense, as Isaiah says: “I received from your hand the cup of ruin, the cup of my anger and indignation” (Isa. LI, 17). He added, “how glorious it is!”—surely because it bestows such things as lead us to the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0170D]. Of this cup it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give will never thirst, but the water that I shall give will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John IV, 13–14).

### Verse 8

“And your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.” The tenth portion of the promised division has been fulfilled, where the greatness of his desire has satisfied itself in an accumulation of joy. For although the Lord’s mercy always goes before, here he says, “shall follow me”: it follows for protection, but goes before in order to confer grace. If it only followed, no one would receive what had been granted; if it only went before, no one could preserve what had been bestowed. The snares that the devil prepares from behind are more dangerous, and unless the Lord’s mercy follows [Col. 0171A], human weakness is very easily deceived. For when someone thinks that he has passed beyond a vice, he is then deceived all the more through careless ignorance. Hence it is exceedingly necessary that the Lord’s grace always go before us and his mercy follow us.

### Verse 9

“And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.” This conclusion depends upon what was said above. He professed that those things had been granted to him for the very purpose that he might attain to dwelling in the house of the Lord’s glory. For this is the consummating perfection of all good things, as he says in another psalm: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house! For ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). The house of the Lord signifies the future Jerusalem, which unquestionably endures for length of days. It is perpetual blessedness and joy without end.

Remember, moreover, that in the earlier verse of this psalm—“The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing”—he briefly stated what he enumerated more fully in what followed. This figure is called *epitrochasmos*, that is, “a running over of a statement,” when he touches briefly upon things that ought to be expressed more expansively. In this final verse, “that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days,” there is the highly distinguished figure *epiphonema*, that is, “acclamation,” which breaks forth briefly with an acclamation after the narration of events and, after everything, ends in the most emphatic climax. Thus the beginning, middle, and end of this psalm shine with the beautiful radiance of various figures.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us store in our minds what that heavenly pipe, fashioned from ten virtues, sang; how sweetly it sang its melody to the soul’s saving delight, so that in this celebration of the mystery not pleasure for the ears, but the health acquired for souls, may be recognized.

The number of this psalm also signifies the perfection of wisdom, since we know that there are twenty-two books of the Old Testament according to the letters of the Hebrews, which were clearly given to the human race for comprehending the fullness of divine knowledge. Therefore the heavenly mysteries are recognized as corresponding to this psalm in various ways.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXIII

### A Psalm of David, on the first day of the week

With the Lord’s help, let us cheerfully lift the veil of the present title, so that the innermost meaning of the psalm may become clearer to us [Col. 0171D]. “The first day of the week” signifies the Lord’s day, which is the first day after the Sabbath, on which the Lord rose from the dead. Because of the excellence of so great a miracle it is properly called the Lord’s day, or because on it he created the world. On that day the Lord is known to have helped this world by rising again, the world which he is also declared to have made. But because the whole psalm is sung after the resurrection, this title was placed before it so that it might fittingly admonish the hearts of the faithful.

### Division of the Psalm

After the Lord’s resurrection the prophet, having become more joyful, addresses the human race, which was suffering under varied superstition [Col. 0172A]. In the first part he declares that the whole earthly globe belongs to the Lord, so that, just as no one could prove himself excluded from his dominion, so no one should consider himself alien to the faith. In the second place he determines with what virtues those who are established in his Church are endowed. In the third he addresses the utterly foolish superstitious, so that, serving the true Lord, they may withdraw from the perversity that harms them.

### Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness; the world and all who dwell in it.” Although we know that “earth” is often used both in a good and in an evil sense, here we must understand the Church, which serves the Lord especially with a pure mind. For although all things were created by him, we properly call that his which venerates him as its creator. Therefore the Church is rightly received as the fruitful earth of good things, because it nourishes and contains the people of Christ.

It follows: “and its fullness,” that is, the holy multitude with which the Church is filled. But lest you should think that the earth he mentioned above meant some confined region, he now says, “the world,” that is, the universal Church, which is contained within the compass of the whole world. Consider carefully that he says, “those who dwell in it”—that is, not those who gather and depart, but those who persevere with a fixed stability of mind. For we call dwelling remaining; this does not belong to those who wander and is incompatible with mutability. Only the one who perseveres in the truest faith until his death dwells in the Church, as another psalm also says: “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” [Col. 0172C] (Ps. XXII, 6).

**Verse 2.** “He himself founded it upon the seas, and prepared it upon the rivers.” What is it to found it upon the seas except to establish the Church through the firmest faith above the trembling waves of the vices of this age, so that, anchored in faith, it may not fear the storms of any danger? Hence the Apostle also says: “Which we have as a sure and firm anchor of the soul” (Heb. VI, 19). In the same way he says that it was prepared upon the rivers, because the Church is evidently adapted to the turbulent wills of persecutors, so that their perverse intentions cannot harm it, although they rise against it in the mad rush of their minds.

**Verse 3.** “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?” After briefly teaching that all things which the Lord created belong to him, he now enters the second part by means of a question, answering what those must be like who desire to call themselves his own. This figure is called *exetasmos*, that is, “inquiry,” when, by investigating several matters separately through questions, we apply to each what is appropriate. He therefore sets the questions first, so that a suitable answer may follow.

“Who shall ascend?” Because he was about to speak of the mountain—that is, righteousness and the other virtues, toward which we strive with great effort, since we are hindered by sins that oppose us. But after saying, “Who shall ascend?” he now says, “shall stand,” because it is much more useful to stand in a holy place than to reach its summit.

**Verse 4.** “The innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain.” This is the expected answer: “innocent in hands and pure in heart,” that is, one whose action harms no one but strives to help as much as possible. And lest you should think that innocence of the hands could suffice, he added “and pure in heart,” because we often intend to harm but help unwillingly; and again, we desire good things but desist from putting them into practice. Therefore he does not say that anyone ascends there unless both qualities can be found in him.

He “receives his soul in vain” who thinks that things either transitory or perishable are to be desired. But he has not received it in vain who knows that he was created for understanding the Divinity, for keeping the Lord’s law, for thoughts of eternal life, and for whatever can merit heavenly grace.
