**Verse 5** [Col. 0173B]. “Nor has he sworn deceitfully to his neighbor.” By saying “deceitfully,” he seems to have permitted simple oaths; for it is written: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent” (Ps. CIX, 4), and we also read that the holiest patriarchs swore. Why, then, does he say in the Gospel: “You shall not swear, either by heaven or by earth” (Matt. V, 34)?

To swear truthfully was certainly not prohibited in the Old Testament. But because the occasion of perjury frequently arises for the human race from weakness of mind, in the New Testament he more usefully says that one should in every way refrain from swearing, just as with other similar matters which we recognize as not contrary but more cautious. For in the Gospel the Lord himself says: “It was said to the ancients, ‘An eye for an eye’; but I say to you, do not resist evil” (ibid., 38–39).

Therefore anyone swears deceitfully who intends to act otherwise than he promises, believing that he is not committing perjury while wickedly deceiving the error of the person who trusts him.

**Verse 6.** “He shall receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior.” He has prefaced pious observances; now he speaks also of rewards. “He shall receive a blessing”—not from anyone else, but from the Lord himself. The one who will judge blesses; the one who could have condemned unchangeably absolves. Thus he wanted the merit of the benefit to be recognized through the greatness of the giver.

Among rhetoricians this argument is called one from the person. It follows: “mercy,” so that the blessing may appear to have come not through merits but through the Lord’s forgiveness. There is no human being who does not need mercy for himself. Sins are forgiven so that the crown may come, just as freedom cannot be granted unless slavery has first been abolished [Col. 0173D].

Our Savior, therefore, is the Lord Christ, from whom both blessedness is granted and sins are loosened. Nor should it trouble us that he first said, “He shall receive a blessing from the Lord,” and afterward added, “and mercy from God his Savior,” since in the order of events he first pardons our sins and afterward the gifts of his blessing follow. You frequently find this order varied, so that mercy is placed first, as in the words: “May God have mercy on us and bless us” (Ps. LXVI, 2); and again the order is reversed: “May he illumine his face upon us, and have mercy on us.” This figure is called *anastrophe*, that is, “reversal,” when we express a statement in an altered order.

**Verse 7.** “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob.” Because above he had said in the singular, “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?”—lest you should think that this referred only to Christ the Lord, he now shows that it also applies to the Christian generation.

For when he says, “This is,” he indicates that this is the generation which seeks the Lord—that is, the generation reborn from the font of holy baptism and commending its faith through pious action. It follows: “who seek the face of the God of Jacob.” What does it mean that he repeats the same verb and adds another expression at the end? Previously he had spoken generally of those seeking the Lord, who do not strive to place themselves first but are content with their own order and end, so that they may deserve to receive even the smallest share in Christ’s kingdom. But because there are also others burning with an excessive warmth of faith, who wish to be placed before some by the goodness of their works, he added “of the God of Jacob,” so that he might do in them what is declared to have been done in Jacob, who, though born later, received the primacy belonging to his older brother.

**Verse 8.** “Lift up your gates, O princes.” He comes to the third part, where the prophet, having made the Christian religion known, commands the various wanderers with great exultation to open the former barriers through a faith appropriate to them, so that they may deserve to admit the King, the Lord, into their hearts.

For he commands the gates of death to be removed, gates which are shown to have been set up by the devil, the prince. They are called gates because through them human beings pass, carrying their deeds and diligently bringing in their provisions.

“And be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” In fitting opposition to the gates of death, the eternal gates are set forth, so that he might show the former to be perishable and the latter to remain without end. For what Adam lost by transgressing the law at the devil’s instigation, the Lord Christ restored by fulfilling the law. The eternal gates were lifted up—that is, the grace of baptism, the honor of chrism, the salvation of preaching, and the other gifts granted when Christ the Lord came. Rightly, then, they are called eternal gates, through which the King of glory deigned to enter.

**Verse 9.** “Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” The prophet asks this to refute the faithlessness of the Jews: “Who is this King of glory?” The answer is given through the third type of definition, which in Greek is called *ποιότης* (*poiotēs*), in Latin “qualitative”: “The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

If you examine the matter, it will be shown to apply to Christ alone. Earthly rulers too can be called glorious; no one except the Most High can be found to be the King of glory. To this question, therefore, as has already been said, the answer is appended, and in each word the unspeakable presumption of the Jewish people is rightly condemned.

He is called “strong” in opposition to their belief that he had to be seized with swords and clubs. He is “mighty,” whom they handed over to Pontius Pilate as though he were powerless. It is also added, “mighty in battle,” lest they be thought to have prevailed in their contest with him. Finally, when they came to seize him, they heard, “I am he,” and, as the Evangelist John testifies, they all immediately fell backward (John XVIII, 9). Thus the Lord and Savior was clearly proclaimed to us through his powers, as though he were disclosed by his very name [Col. 0175A].

**Verse 10.** “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.”

**Verse 11.** “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of powers—he is the King of glory.” Here too a most beautiful figure has been made, called by the Greeks *anadiplosis* and by the Latins “repetition of a word.” It occurs either within a verse or through the repetition of words. Since the same words have been repeated, the preceding exposition is more than sufficient here as well.

For in order to confound the Jews, he previously expounded the Lord’s majesty word by word, as was fitting; now he briefly added the summit of all praise and truth. He says that he is no longer merely strong, mighty, or great in battle, but the Lord of the powers themselves. He is the King of glory who makes those who glorify him glorious, as it is said through the Lord: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify” (I Sam. II, 30).

He grants to each person power, strength, and the other gifts as he wills. For “glory” means celebrated proclamation and frequently repeated praise. Indeed, by the Lord’s gift there are also glorious angels—Powers, Thrones, Dominations, and other exceedingly powerful creatures. But no one is the King of glory except the one who created and sustains those supreme beings.

A wondrous praise, an astonishing conclusion! Nothing worthy could have been said by another except by the one who alone is able to proclaim his own power. Learn from this, teachers of secular literature: from here came figures, from here arguments of various kinds, from here definitions, from here the teachings of every discipline, since you recognize that these writings contain what you perceive to have been spoken long before your schools.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

This entire psalm pertains to moral instruction. It admonishes us that, having abandoned superstitions, we should faithfully serve the true and devout Lord. For what is more just than to abandon the one who made us mortal in Adam? What is more blessed than to follow the one who enabled the human race to escape the death inflicted upon it?

But grant, Lord, that we who have entered through the washing of holy regeneration by the gates of your mercy may not depart from there, driven out by any sins. The number of this psalm may perhaps refer to the twenty-three letters of the Latins, which comprise the expressions proper to their eloquence. Although the Hebrews have twenty-two, the Latins—the language in which we are now speaking—twenty-three, and the Greeks twenty-four, an appropriate quantity of letters is used in each language to comprehend its meaning. Thus, in the reckoning of this psalm too, blessed perfection is discernible.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXIV

### To the end, a Psalm of David

Since the words of the title are already familiar, and this psalm is the first of the Hebrews to be written according to the alphabet, we must speak rather of its significance. Throughout the whole book there are two kinds of such psalms. One kind is shown to contain the complete alphabet, as do Psalms CX, CXI, and CXVIII. These, I think, indicate that the righteous sing the praises of the Lord with the perfect devotion of their merits, by his gift. Such was Nathanael, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John I, 47); and the prophet Jeremiah, of whom the same Lord says: “From your mother’s womb I called you, and in the womb I sanctified you” (Jer. I, 5).

Job likewise was praised by the voice of the Lord, for he says: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a righteous, simple, and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil?” (Job II, 3). There are also the others who are known only to God himself. But when we reach them, they will be explained more clearly.

The other kind shows, through the omission of certain letters, that people of such character sing in the Church that the integrity of all good works does not shine in them to the same degree. Such are the present psalm, Psalms XXXIII, XXXVI, and CXLIV, concerning which we shall speak more fully and distinctly in their proper place. For now, let us know that this psalm lacks the sixth and nineteenth letters; I have judged that the remaining letters should be painted in red ink in the text of the Psalter, so that no confusion might arise for readers.

The meanings of these alphabetic letters have been briefly gathered through the labor of Father Jerome; yet this is not unfamiliar in the divine Scriptures. For Jeremiah also lamented the captivity of Jerusalem through a fourfold alphabetic lament, teaching that the mysteries of letters indicate to us even mysteries of heavenly things.

### Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0176C]

Throughout the psalm, by the figure *ethopoeia*, the Church makes supplication with wondrous entreaty that she may not appear contemptible before the Lord’s enemies. In the first section she asks to know the Lord’s ordinances and ways. This section contains five letters of the alphabet mentioned above. In the second section she requests his benefits, which he has granted to the holy Fathers from the beginning of the age; this contains the following six letters. In the third place she says that those who keep the Lord’s commandments deserve eternal rewards, declaring that she remains continually in the same will; here she has the remaining nine letters. Thus the whole psalm is represented by the inscription of the letters mentioned.

### Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1. ALEPH.** “To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul. My God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame, nor shall my enemies mock me.” We say “to lift” in the sense of raising upward. Therefore the Church says that she has lifted her soul from earthly conduct and carnal vices to God—namely, to contemplation of heavenly things, by which the devout mind always beholds the Lord. For the one who has seen divine things easily despises human things.

To be put to shame means to be thrown into confusion by a sudden disturbance of mind and suddenly to look toward something other than what was expected to happen. She therefore asks not to be diminished in his sight, since she has trusted in his devotion. Enemies mock when they see that the confidence of the righteous has not been fulfilled, if things turn out otherwise than they had predicted. The mother Church therefore hopes that the Lord will fulfill his promises, so that her adversaries may have no basis for mocking her. To laugh is often the action of the kindly; to mock, however, is always that of the hostile.

**Verse 2. BETH.** “Indeed, all who wait for you shall not be put to shame; let the wicked who do vain things be put to shame.” To wait means to endure God manfully amid evils, so that, when he comes in his judgment, he may repay what the devoted heart desired. Thus another psalm also says: “Wait for the Lord, act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 14).

Notice also that through the figure *anadiplosis*, which in Latin is called “repetition of a word,” he repeats the phrase for the sake of beauty. In the preceding psalm the repetition occurred in the verses; here it is placed only in the words. He added, “let them be put to shame”: the very word that was placed at the end for the faithful he made the beginning of the section concerning the wicked. But there it is desired that shame not come; here it is requested that it arise. “Those who do vain things” means those who do what is shown to be alien to the Lord. For we call something vain when it is fruitless and empty.

**Verse 3. GIMEL.** “Make your ways known to me, Lord, and teach me your paths.” There is no small difference between ways and paths. We call “ways” those which the general freedom of travelers traverses; they are so called from *vehere*, “to carry.” Paths, however, are directed through a narrow track. They are not commonly known but are traveled by hidden routes. *Semita* (“path”) is so called as though it meant “half-way.”

Accordingly, let us understand “ways” as pertaining to the order of life, in which both the conduct of teachers and the multitude of the simple walk [Col. 0177C]. But “paths” should be understood as the meaning of the law, which is known to few and, because of its difficulty, is shown to be narrow. For it follows, “teach me,” an expression which is recognized as pertaining not to a track but rather to the law.

**Verse 4. DALETH.** “Guide me in your truth and teach me, for you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all day.” This verse embraces the meanings of the preceding expressions one by one. “Guide me” pertains to life; “teach” to knowledge. It follows: “For you are God my Savior, and I have waited for you all day.” He instructs us perfectly and briefly. For there are two things that make good Christians: first, that we believe God to be our Savior; second, that amid the endurance of our whole life we await his recompense.

“All day” is as though he had said “every day”—that is, the expression signifies not an interrupted period but the continuity of life.

**Verse 5. HE.** “Remember your mercies, Lord, and your compassions, which are from the age.” He comes to the second section, asking with the greatest piety and humility that, according to his custom, he may obtain the Lord’s mercy. In human usage, “remember” is said to one who can never forget anything. For whoever wishes to be helped thinks that the giver of the benefit has forgotten him when some delay has occurred.

He added, “and your compassions, which are from the age.” In these words a very clear and regular teaching seems to shine forth for us: no one comes to his grace through his own merits. By saying “your compassions, which are from the age,” he always approves the Lord as the giver of compassions, who does not first receive human merits but grants his own gifts beforehand.

All heresies have indeed been found through detestable speculation; but the danger of Pelagianism is shown by the fact that it is known to be refuted with such persistence. He says “from the age” when the age began to exist, when the world began to be administered. For the age is the course of the world’s order, which, tending toward future things, leaves the past behind. Some have thought that these ages should be defined in the likeness of weeks, by periods of seven years. Others have wanted them to be called ages because they continually revolve times within themselves.

And lest we seem to pass over distinctions of words: *miserationes* (“mercies”) pertain to acts of piety, whereas *misericordiae* (“compassions”) pertain to a compassionate nature. Hence he asks that the Lord remember both kinds of his own attributes.

**Verse 6. ZAIN.** “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance; according to your great mercy remember me, O God.” Some wish *delictum* (“offense”) to be lighter than *peccatum* (“sin”), and say that it is so called because it leaves the way of equity, though it does not yet involve the highest degree of criminal perversity. An offense is, for example, eating food too greedily, breaking into inappropriate laughter, devoting oneself to idle words, and other things of this kind, which do not seem to be the gravest sins but nevertheless are clearly forbidden.

By “youth” he means not merely the flourishing period of life but the rash boldness that is easiest in that age, when the heat of the mind exceeds the moderation of one’s conduct. For many young people are mature in the gravity of their behavior; conversely, some old people are stained by the fault of frivolity.

He said “of ignorance” because we do many things without knowing that they are evil. We often give advice unknowingly that harms another; we give a sick person, as though it were a remedy, foods that grievously afflict him. We frequently offend against the law itself through ignorance, although ignorance of it is not permitted, since the Divinity has willed that it be known and retained by everyone.

Others say that offenses of ignorance also pertain to little children, who, although sunk in sleep because of their weak understanding, are nevertheless shown to be subject to original sin. He therefore asks that he not wish to reserve the offenses of youth and ignorance for punishment, but that, as though they had slipped away from him, he not allow them to be brought to judgment [Col. 0178D]. Therefore the Church prays that he not remember the offenses but rather remember her according to his great mercy.

“Because of your goodness, Lord.” By saying “Because of your goodness, Lord,” he makes it understood that this is not because of my merit. Hence no one may ever presume upon himself, except one whom grave error has affected. This figure is called *emphasis*, that is, “exaggeration”; here it is that form of emphasis which signifies what it does not state explicitly. Rightly, therefore, his goodness is truly proclaimed, of whom it is written: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII, 19).

**Verse 7. HETH.** “The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will establish the law for those who offend in the way.” The Lord is sweet because, although he anticipates everyone with his benefits, he nevertheless awaits the conversion of the offender. For he makes rain fall upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V, 45), giving life to those who deserved to be extinguished. Rightly, therefore, he is called sweet, from whom pleasing gifts are bestowed, as another psalm also says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9). He is called sweet by analogy with sweet foods, in which humanity takes the greatest delight.

He is upright when, after frequent rebukes and very long periods of waiting, he withstands evils and humbles the proud and impious, so that at last they may come to their senses and repent that they have gone astray. But the fact that he establishes the law was an act both of sweetness and of uprightness, since he did not wish those whom he preferred to correct through the promulgation of the law to remain in error. And lest anyone should think that this discipline arose from harshness, he explains the purpose of the law that was enacted: namely, goodness and sweetness. “In the way” means in the present life, where the law is established, in which we are admonished to live rightly.

### Verse 8. THETH

“He will guide the meek in judgment; he will teach the gentle his ways.” That is, he causes those who are peaceful in spirit to attain the promised blessedness. For someone is called “straight” when he is made straight from being crooked. By saying “the meek,” he excludes the proud and haughty, just as he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5:4). He means the gentle, not the proud, who with harmful freedom kick against the easy yoke and light burden; rather, he will teach those who without murmuring do what they recognize has been commanded.

There appears to be this difference between the gentle and the meek: the gentle are those who are disturbed by no outbreak of anger but continually persevere in mildness of spirit; the meek are so called as though “accustomed to the hand,” that is, those who endure injuries and do not repay evil for evil. He said, “his ways,” but he subsequently explains what the ways of the Lord are.

### Verse 9. JOD

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.” Although the ways of the Lord are incomprehensible, he most suitably gathers them together in a brief statement. For who would be sufficient to recount his works, or the extent of the power with which he governs heavenly and earthly things? But since those ways could not be enumerated, they have been sufficiently comprehended in this statement: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” Mercy, because he anticipates all things with goodness; truth, because he judges everything with complete integrity.

But lest you think that this is to be applied indiscriminately, he adds to whom such things can properly belong: “to those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.” When “covenant” is expressed in the singular, either the Old or the New is signified. Here, therefore, we must understand the New Covenant; “testimonies,” however, means the sayings of the preceding prophets, for they were witnesses of the sacred promises, which the Lord fulfilled by the manifestation of his coming.

### Verse 10. CAPH

“For the sake of your name, Lord, you will be merciful toward my sin, for it is great.” This is appropriately referred to the person of the Church, whose congregation is understood to have arisen from various sinners. “For the sake of your name, Lord”: for he was to be called Jesus, which in our language is interpreted as “Savior.” The name itself, therefore, is understood to be a profession of salvation.

He continues, “for it is great,” that is, a sin which you could not pardon on its own account, but only for the sake of the holiness of your name. But when the sin is called great, it is shown to be exceedingly abundant, since it continually increases with the passage of time; and unless divine mercy comes to its aid, as long as life is prolonged, so long does human frailty continue to sin.

And remember that the Church speaks on behalf of a portion of her members when she says that her sins are abundant, so that those who proclaim themselves pure, such as the Catharists, may understand that they have no share with the holy Church.

### Verse 11. LAMED

“Who is the person who fears the Lord? He establishes a law for him on the way that he has chosen.” He comes to the third member, where it is specifically shown who it is that fears the Lord, or with what gift he may rejoice. As is his custom, he first sets forth a question, intending to give the appropriate answer: “He establishes a law for him.” This is the person whom he wished to describe.

He says that the person received the law, and that he wished fear to be added to it for this reason: so that he could not sin under the security of ignorance. “On the way that he has chosen,” that is, in the holiness of his purpose.

### Verse 12. MEM

“His soul will abide among good things, and his offspring will possess the land as an inheritance.” Since perfect blessedness is not immediately given to righteous people when they have been stripped of the body—the blessedness promised to the saints at the resurrection—he nevertheless says that their soul can abide among good things. For although those rewards are still deferred, “which no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2:9), they are nevertheless now nourished by the delight of the absolutely certain hope of the future reward.

He continues, “and his offspring will possess the land as an inheritance.” This now clearly signifies the future reward, when his offspring—that is, his good works—will be received in eternal security, and his possession will no longer be disturbed by any expulsion. For whoever holds something by inheritance rejoices in the firmest possession.

### Verse 13. NUN

“The Lord is a stronghold for those who fear him, and his covenant is given so that it may be revealed to them.” In this verse he carefully strengthened the spirits and minds of believers. First, because human custom is changeable, he says that the Lord will be their stronghold, so that they should not doubt themselves when they have been made secure by such a promise.

But observe that he says, “for those who fear him.” He does not promise these things to the proud and audacious. And consider what force the arranged words possess. Human fear produces distrust, whereas divine fear grants foundations of hope. The latter must be embraced, and is exceedingly necessary, so that his law may be disclosed to us by his own gift; without this, we can neither understand anything good nor succeed in accomplishing anything worthy of praise.

### Verse 14. SAMECH

“My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he himself will draw my feet out of the snare.” After the rewards of the blessed mentioned above, he now says that his contemplation was always directed toward the Lord. The resulting distinction is beautifully understood. For someone who does not look before his feet commonly falls into snares or into the openings of pits.

This, however, has been said wonderfully and truly: if we walk cautiously and direct our feet, if we continually raise our eyes toward the Lord, then that regard makes us strangers to every offense.

### Verse 15. AIN

“Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am solitary and poor.” He responds with an excellent comparison, because above he said, “My eyes are always toward the Lord,” and now he says, “Look upon me, just as I look upon you, and have mercy on me.” For whoever continually looks toward him demands that he himself look upon that person in mercy.

He also added the most abundant reasons for mercy: the solitary person is loved more, and the very poor person is pitied more. The Church appropriately says this of the person of the Christian people, who are solitary for her because they alone preserve the sacraments of the true faith. They are poor because, separated from the allurements of the world, they are filled with no worldly ambition.

### Verse 16. PHE

“The tribulations of my heart have been enlarged; rescue me from my necessities.” The Church’s tribulation has been enlarged while she stretches her thoughts through the calamities of the world in which she has been sown. For someone who suffers on behalf of many must necessarily be weighed down by a heavy burden.

He speaks of the necessities that she endured through the ambushes of persecutors and heretics. These are the people who desire to inflict death on Christians. She rightly called them “her own,” because she had taken them upon herself through the devotion of charity.

### Verse 17. ZADE

“See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins.” “See,” that is, look upon me favorably. The Church’s humility is shown when, by teaching, she endures the undisciplined and perverse, and permits what is concealed and hidden to be reserved for divine judgment.

Her labor is that she is exhausted by many persecutions and much struggle; and, continually harassed by the objections of the wicked, she finds here no rest in the peace she desires. Therefore, after enduring so much, she rightly begs that all her sins be forgiven, because the exceedingly hard labor of devout endurance always awaits the judge’s clemency.

### Verse 18. RES

“Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied, and they hate me with unjust hatred.” By saying, “Look upon my enemies,” she prays on their behalf, that they may return [manuscripts A, B, F: “believe”], because those whom he looks upon he converts without delay, just as in the Gospel the Lord looked upon Peter so that he might weep (Luke 22:61).

He added the reason why they should not perish: “For they have multiplied.” A few might perhaps be thought worthy of contempt, but the destruction of many could not be endured without the greatest grief. He continues, “because they have hated me with unjust hatred.” They truly hated the Church with unjust hatred, because while she poured out prayer for them, they nevertheless did not cease persecuting her without interruption.

For this reason he added “with unjust hatred,” because hatred can also be just, as in the statement: “I hated them with perfect hatred” (Psalm 138:22).

### Verse 19. SIN

“Guard my soul and rescue me; let me not be put to shame, for I have called upon you.” The Church asks that her faith be guarded as entirely upright, so that, preserved from schismatics, she may not be confused by any perversity, but may be offered to her Bridegroom, adorned with the virtues of faith, without stain or wrinkle.

A credible reason is added by which she ought to obtain her request: because she has called upon the Lord. Truly she does not deserve to be put to shame who is known to have placed her hope in such great power. For she chose to call upon him who does not know how to reject those who plead devoutly.

### Verse 20. TAU

“The innocent and the upright have adhered to me, for I have endured you, Lord.” Some understand “the innocent” as the little ones regenerated by holy baptism, who have not yet been stained by any worldly conduct, but pass onward in the very holiness which they have deserved to receive. They wish “the upright” to be understood as those who, converted at a mature age, have by divine favor been released from the snares of sins.

But since we have said that the Church is filled with the varying dispositions of human beings, how does he say here only, “The innocent and the upright have adhered to me,” as though she did not also have mixed among them those who are polluted by wicked conduct?

But consider the force of this expression: he says that the innocent and the upright adhered to her as though they had been joined and glued to her, which appears to be effected by the integrity of their conduct on both sides. The rest, however, were tolerated with difficulty rather than having adhered to her.

“I have endured,” he says: I have endured frequent hardships in this world with courage. But I had one consolation: to endure you as Lord. And observe the force of this verse, because he says that the innocent and the upright adhered to her for this reason: that she endured the Lord. Otherwise she could not have loved such people unless she herself also appeared to draw confidence from such great steadfastness.

### Verse 21

“Redeem me, God of Israel, from all my tribulations.” When she says, “Redeem me,” she calls for the coming of the Lord Savior, by whose blood she was redeemed and liberated from diabolical captivity.

“God of Israel,” that is, God of those who see you, because he truly regards as pleasing those to whom he grants the sight of his contemplation. By adding, “from all my tribulations,” she does not wish any stain to be found in herself, since the holy Bride cannot otherwise be joined to Christ unless she is, as was said, without stain or wrinkle.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us hear how the Church, still placed amid the tribulations of this world, cries throughout the whole psalm to her deliverer; and let us cease to bear our tribulations impatiently, since it is evident that the mother herself endures most grievous distresses on our behalf. Let us bear adversities courageously, with the Lord’s help; let us hope steadfastly in his mercy, because, if we remain in the Bride’s company, by God’s generosity we shall reach eternal joys together with her.

This number, twice twelve, discloses to us heavenly mysteries: the twenty-four elders celebrate the Lord’s praises with unwearied voices and sweet melody, admonishing us also, after their likeness, to sing this psalm with frequent devotion.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXV

### A Psalm of David

Since a psalm signifies the correspondence of spiritual realities in our actions, while David means “strong in hand” and “beloved,” this whole text must be applied to the perfect Christian, who, by the Lord’s generosity, perseveres with steadfast mind in his Church amid the praise of diverse merits and consoles himself with divine benefits. Yet, when such a hymn is sung, it must necessarily be referred to Christ the Lord by the power of understanding.

### Division of the Psalm

The saint of whom we have spoken, in the first division of the psalm, begs that his innocence be regarded, because he has had no share with wicked people. In the second, he entreats that he not be joined with heretics or schismatics in the Lord’s judgment, since he testifies that he has loved his house.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence; and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.” The request for judgment indeed seems perilous, but the separation from the wicked which takes place in the Lord’s examination is rightly recognized as something to be desired by one of good merit. Therefore this is not detestable arrogance concerning merits, but the just petition of one who faithfully serves: that he may be separated from the worst, lest he have a share with the wicked.

For the holy man asks for judgments because he was certain of God’s mercy, as the Apostle says: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:8). He walks in his innocence who, as he says below, hopes in the Lord and relies not at all upon his own powers, but upon divine generosity. A fitting proof of this follows: he declares that, by trusting in the Lord, he has not been weakened. For this is the innocence which he mentioned above: to trust in the Lord’s power, so that no weakness of sins may weigh him down.

#### Verse 2

“Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart.” “Test” and “try” are not said presumptuously, but he asks that this be done for the sake of correction. For when God searches and tries us, he causes us to recognize our sin and to attain the fruit of repentance. Otherwise, if no adversity in this world admonished us, we should leave unattended those matters for which we ought to make satisfaction.

He himself then explains why he desires to be tested and tried: namely, that his reins and heart may be burned, so that human pleasures and thoughts may be purified by the heat of the Lord’s word. Like furnaces, consuming the filth of vices, it brings human souls to the cleansing of most perfect beauty. We must inquire why here he asks to be tried, although the Gospel prayer contains: “Lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13). There are, therefore, two temptations. One is the Lord’s, by which he tests the good so as fittingly to instruct them, as is read in Genesis: “The Lord tested Abraham” (Genesis 22:1); or as Moses says: “The Lord your God tests you” (Deuteronomy 13:3). The other is the devil’s, which always leads to death; concerning this we pray that we may not, with blinded minds, be led into its domain. Rightly, then, the prophet asks, saying, “Test me, O Lord, and try me,” in that sense which belongs to the Lord, so that he might not be led into that diabolical temptation, after which follows, “But deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13), that is, from the devil himself.

#### Verse 3

“For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have pleased you in your truth.” This was why he did not fear the dangers of temptations: he could not forget God’s mercy. For the person to whom a benefit bestowed is always present before the eyes makes continual provision for his own help. For this reason he also says that he has pleased the Lord. To please God is to merit eternal grace with the Lord’s saints. “In your truth,” that is, in your Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). For no one can otherwise please the Father unless strengthened by such faith.

#### Verse 4

“I have not sat in the council of vanity, and I shall not enter in with those who commit iniquity.” He declares, in an exceedingly fine account, that he has pleased the Lord. He seeks to show his innocence in two verses by avoiding what is wicked, and in another two by doing what is right. This argument is called, in rhetoric, one from contraries. For the council of vanity and the congregation of the innocent are altogether opposites.

He now enumerates what, by the Lord’s generosity, he has done, on account of which he testified that he pleased God. He has not sat in the council of vanity who gives no consent or participation of his counsel to the deliberations of the wicked. A holy person may happen by some chance to come to a council of wicked people, where unsuitable or vain things are discussed. But once he recognizes such things, he neither sits with them nor remains through any delight, but either dissuades them from their wicked purpose or leaves it. Therefore, having first denied that he sat with the wicked, he now professes that he did not enter in with the worst. He first avoided their discussion, and afterward abandoned their deeds as well. Entry into crime occurs when something is boldly begun. Entry signifies the beginning of an action, and the holy man professes from his conscience that he is far from it.

#### Verse 5

“I hated the congregation of evildoers, and I shall not sit with the ungodly.” It would have been too little for the holy man to avoid the council of evil, unless he had also completely hated the congregation of the deceitful. For hatred signifies separation, just as fellowship exists in love. And although above he said that he had not sat in the council of vanity, he now professes that he will not sit with the ungodly. Both were altogether to be abandoned.

But some are vain and others ungodly. The vain are those occupied with transient inquiries and consuming their time in superfluous discourse. The ungodly are heretics, who endeavor by faithless questions to corrupt the divine Scriptures, as the apostle Peter says: “Twisting them to their own destruction and perdition” (2 Peter 3:16). He rightly warns that both sorts must be avoided, because the former love superfluities while the latter inflict the weapons of perversity.

#### Verse 6

“I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord.” One who follows Christ his head, despises earthly things, and longs for heavenly things may say this, as the Apostle says: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). He washes his hands among the innocent whenever he cleanses his own deeds by the practice of good conduct.

He appropriately added, “among the innocent,” because even the guilty can wash their hands, as Pontius Pilate did (Matthew 27:24): while he polluted his soul by the abominable betrayal of the Lord, he washed his hands with the water of this world. But one washes hands spiritually whenever he cleanses his actions by tearful satisfaction. “I will go around,” he says, that is, I will repeat it often, in order to show the constancy of most holy devotion. The altar is named from height, as though it were a high altar, where sacrifice is offered to the Lord, so that the gifts of his mercy may be displayed before the eyes of the people.

#### Verse 7

“That I may hear the voice of your praise and proclaim all your wonders.” Having advanced to heavenly things, he went around that altar in a spiritual mind in order to hear the harmony of the Lord’s praise. Perhaps he refers to that which is sung before him with unwearied voice: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isaiah 6:3). When he heard it and recognized it with the greatest devotion, he would proclaim to the peoples all the wonders which, even today, the blessed Church sings in the celebration of the holy Masses.

#### Verse 8

“O Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells.” That most blessed man of whom we have spoken enters upon the second division of the prayer, beseeching that, since he has loved the beauty of the Lord’s house, he may by no means be joined with those alien to it, but may persevere in his Church.

By “the beauty of the house” he means not the attractiveness of walls or the most precious furnishings of its ministrations, but the most blessed quality of the deeds themselves, in which the whole Church rejoices: in the jubilant singing of psalms, in the holiness of prayers, and in the most humble devotion of the Christian people. He first spoke of the universal Church; now he comes to the saints, in whom God’s glory is known to dwell. Of them the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17). By saying “the place of dwelling,” he signified the hidden recess of the human breast, wonderfully adding, “of your glory,” because wherever it dwells, there is glory. For it makes glorious whatever it deigns to inhabit, and the greatness of the lodging increases through the merit of its guest.

#### Verse 9

“Do not destroy my soul together with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood.” He rightly asks that his soul not perish with the ungodly in the future judgment, since he had no common activity with them here. He fittingly asks to be separated from them there, from whom he himself separated here. Men of blood are those who live carnally and desire none of the heavenly commands. Such people perish from the future Jerusalem, because they are to be condemned for their ungodliness.

#### Verse 10

“In whose hands are iniquities; their right hand is full of gifts.” He explains who the men of blood are, in whose conduct we see most wicked actions. Our hands signify the general actions which we perform while living in this light. Here he specifically declares the venality of a judge’s right hand, which he says is full of gifts because it is weighed down by the offerings of much money.

Consider that he execrates universally judges who accept such things. For one who sells justice fills his right hand with gifts; and one who acquits the guilty likewise fills his right hand by accepting gifts. Both, in my judgment, are fittingly to be applied to the man of blood.

#### Verse 11

“But I have walked in my innocence; redeem me, and have mercy on me.” Syncrisis is the figure in which someone endeavors to make his own case better than that of his adversaries. For while they rejoice deceitfully that their right hand has been filled by taking gifts, he says that he has entered into the riches of innocence. Having entered spiritual treasures, he has consoled himself far more truly than they could rejoice in worldly riches.

“Redeem me,” that is, make me free by the precious blood of your coming, by which the world, held liable by sins, was set free. “And have mercy on me,” namely in this world, where you spare those who faithfully entreat you.

#### Verse 12

“For my foot has stood in the straight way; in the churches I will bless the Lord.” Amid the shaking of heresies and the fiercely raging distresses of the world, the Catholic man fittingly professes this: his foot has remained unmoved. Though he is tossed by importunate tribulations, in the matter of faith he does not know how to be moved by any necessities.

Such people, and those like them, can say this—those concerning whom the Lord himself bears witness, as in the saying: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings 19:18). “In the straight way,” that is, in your commands, which are straight and make those who obey straight. Whenever “churches” is said in the plural, it signifies the Christian peoples of this world, who are shown to have been gathered from different nations. For there will be one perfect Jerusalem, purified by the separation of the wicked. Therefore the blessed man of whom we have spoken says that he will sing to the Lord not in the Church but in the churches, because the name Catholic is established throughout the whole world.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider what a pattern of life this religious man has handed down to us. He says that he avoided the worst people here in order that he might not be joined with the wicked in the Lord’s judgment, warning us that, fleeing the society of the unrighteous, we should always be united to Christ’s faithful by spiritual love, because from prolonged intercourse with people we always contract a quality of character.

The sixth psalm also admonishes this when it says: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Psalm 6:9); and so does the seventeenth: “With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the elect you will be elect; and with the perverse you will be perverted” (Psalm 17:26). Truly, this was so often warned against in order that the immense evil to be fled might be recognized. Therefore let us earnestly seek a most glorious and fitting fellowship, one that trains us in virtues and kindles us with desire for divine love, lest at the recompense of the wicked we deservedly be joined to the worst, having wished here to have fellowship with evildoers.

If we examine it more carefully, even the quantity of the number is not without significance. Evangelical authority records that Solomon’s five porticoes contained a crowd of sick persons in danger (John 5:2). That number, multiplied by itself five times, advances to the sum of twenty-five, so that the hearts of the faithful may be refreshed by the depth of this psalm, just as in those porticoes the sick bodies of those lying there were healed by the washing of the sheep-pool.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXVI

### A Psalm of David before he was anointed

The history of this title is indicated more fully in the book of Kings (1 Kings 16:13). For after Saul had sinned against God, David was anointed king at his father’s house through the holy prophet Samuel. But this title does not speak of that anointing; rather, it is recognized as recalling the occasion when, after Saul’s persecutions, he was brought to the kingdom by the people’s choice (2 Kings 5:3), since it is plain that he composed this psalm in testimony to those very events. For if you wish to understand the first anointing, no psalm is read as having been made by him before it. It remains, therefore, that we should understand this second anointing.

### Division of the Psalm

Since he was frequently delivered from his most bitter enemies before attaining the kingdom, the prophet speaks throughout the psalm. In the first division he says that he fears the Lord and dreads no other. But amid the adversities of the world he testifies that he has one refuge: although he was tossed by bodily dangers, he himself dwelt in the Lord’s house with the most steadfast devotion of mind. In the second division, delivered from manifold disaster, he gives thanks in diverse ways and, in the spirit of prophecy, promises himself hope of future blessedness. It should certainly be known that this psalm is the second among those which, through David’s deeds, signify the future mysteries of Christ the Lord.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

#### Verse 2

“The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? While evildoers draw near against me to eat my flesh.”

#### Verse 3

“My enemies who trouble me, they themselves have been weakened and fallen.” Let us hear these three verses rather more attentively, for they comprise a formula of a great argument, which the Greeks preferred to call an epicheirema, and the Latins “developments” or “proofs.” We use this argument whenever we endeavor to prove the matter at issue by some example.

For the proposition is set forth here in a verse and a half: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” In the other half-verse and one verse he adds the example why he ought not at all to have been afraid: those who attempted to persecute him fall instead. For he says: “While evildoers draw near against me to eat my flesh, my enemies who trouble me, they themselves have been weakened and fallen.” Thus the form of this epicheirema is briefly complete.

Let us now return to explain the words. The prophet exultantly says that he fears no human being, because he had been illuminated by God, showing that fear always has its own darkness when heavenly illumination is set against it. He continues, “and my salvation.” In this word he includes everything: both bodily health and the soul’s preservation. Both are indications of salvation when, that is, they endure most grievous sufferings. “Whom shall I fear?” That is, I shall fear no human being. Fear of the Lord had caused him to be unable to fear anyone else.

He continues: “The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” Many have lost God’s gifts through wicked actions. But those whose defender the Lord has been have lost nothing at all. “Of whom shall I be afraid?” is to be pronounced interrogatively, that is, “of no one,” just as he said above, “Whom shall I fear?” Such questions undoubtedly must be understood as denials.

He added: “While evildoers draw near against me to eat my flesh.” Here the desires of savage enemies are laid open; they desire not merely to destroy him but, in the greed of their rage, cruelly to devour even human flesh itself. The enemies’ great ferocity is thus revealed so that the grace of deliverance may be doubled. He added: “My enemies who trouble me, they themselves have been weakened and fallen.” This verse depends on the preceding statement, for it proves how he ought to fear no one. If persecutors, who might have been feared, have fallen, what fear, I ask, will there be when those who seemed to attack fall instead?

The words are also arranged in sequence: first came being weakened, afterward falling. Observe that here the benefits of the faithful are briefly explained: it is not those oppressed by sufferings who fall, but rather those who hasten to devour the blood of the innocent.

#### Verse 4

“Though camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear.” The saving proof having been completed, the joyful prophet exults, making a fine emphasis—that is, an exaggeration—that if a multitude of camps should gather against him alone, his steadfastness of mind ought not to be shaken, though people are accustomed to be terrified by the assault of many. A camp is a strong fortification which the onrush of an attacker cannot easily storm. Yet he says that all these things are contemptible to him when he is strengthened by divine aid.

#### Verse 5

“Though battle rise against me, in this I shall hope.” Camps could have stood without joining battle. But now he adds the fierce conflict itself, so that he might appear to fear none of those things which humanity thinks terrible. “Though battle rise,” that is, should a sudden conflict spring up against me like a boiling storm, I shall hope for victory in it instead. For in heated battles the glory of the victor always appears. Virtue that has not been tested by conflict can be shown to lie hidden, as he said above: “In tribulations you have enlarged me” (Psalm 4:2).

It should also be observed that this verse begins in the same way as the preceding one. This figure is called anaphora whenever one word is repeated at the beginnings of clauses; and it is clear that this has also been done at the beginning of the psalm, namely, “The Lord, the Lord.”

#### Verse 6

“One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek.” He says that he has asked one thing from the Lord, which he explains below. But let us see whether it is one thing and not rather everything. It is singular in numerical reckoning, but numerous in the usefulness of its benefits: a narrow petition, a broad reward; it is sought briefly, but obtained grandly. It is, therefore, the custom of the good to seek the Lord’s house alone, in which all good things are contained. But the wicked, torn apart by earthly desire, weary themselves by asking when they seek bodily health, pray for riches, and demand the overthrow of enemies; sometimes, in their seeking, they pursue things that will perish.

#### Verse 7

“That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life; that I may see the will of the Lord and be protected by his holy temple.” This is the one petition which he sought above. Observe that he had no need to fear any camp or battle when he had fortified himself with such a defense. For what cities are comparable, what armies stronger, than to dwell in the Lord’s house, where it is certain that nothing human and nothing diabolical is to be feared? And not for a short time, but for all the days of his life. When, I ask, would the person fear whose whole life is secure?

He also sees the Lord’s will who understands his commands and has subjected himself with all his mind to his purity. The prophet asks to be protected by the temple of Christ’s body, from which both the foundation of faith and the invincible strength of defense are received. By strength of mind he had reached that which he did not yet see in visible form.

#### Verse 8

“For he hid me in his tabernacle; in the day of evils he protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle; upon a rock he exalted me.” Let us examine this verse somewhat more carefully. He says: “For he hid me in his tabernacle in the day of evils,” signifying the time when Saul pursued him and he lay concealed in many places, through desolate caves and the recesses of mountains. That truly was a tabernacle to him because his mind never departed from the devotion of religion.

He continues: “He protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle.” Above he said “hid”; now he says “protected.” To be hidden is not to be exposed to the eyes of those seeking one; to be protected is to be freed from every fear and danger. “In the secret place of his tabernacle,” he says, that is, in the secret of divinity, to which his devout mind always hastened, because he seemed to himself to be where his attention persevered.

What he says, “Upon a rock he exalted me,” pertains to the Lord’s incarnation, because Christ, the corner-stone uniting peoples, was born from David’s seed.

#### Verse 9

“But now he has exalted my head above my enemies.” After he has spoken of the rewards that were to come from the Lord’s incarnation, he now speaks of present things, since he is known to have been delivered from his enemies, whether carnal or spiritual. By “my head” we rightly understand the eye of the mind, which is truly our head, by whose vitality we can see. For we often call “head” that which is shown to stand above. “Above my enemies” signifies sinful desires, above which our mind is fittingly raised when it is kept pure by divine benefit.

### Verse 10

“I will go around and sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation; I will sing and make a psalm to the Lord.” Having reviewed the benefits which he had learned that he had received both in the future and in the present, he now describes his joy in a marvelous account. “I will go around,” he says—that is, “I will search out in my mind by what power he made the heavens, established the stars, set boundaries for the seas, fixed the earth, and filled the whole world with the varied praise of his mighty works.” And when he has surveyed all these things in his mind, he says that he will sacrifice in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation—that is, offer in his Church a sacrifice of praise. For we call it “jubilation” from the fact that it brings us joy, when we strive to give thanks with delight and the greatest pleasure. We explained above that singing and making a psalm are different things. To sing is to utter praises with the voice alone; to make a psalm is to proclaim the glory of the Lord through good works. To sing and to make a psalm, then, is itself the sacrifice of jubilation.

### Verse 11

“Hear, O Lord, my voice, with which I cried to you; have mercy on me and hear me.” He comes to the second division, in which he fulfills through thanksgiving the duty of psalmody that he had promised, joining the present matters to those above. For he cried out when he said, “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” And although above he said that he would offer a sacrifice of jubilation because he had obtained various gifts, he now again asks to be heard. Nor is his desire yet satisfied unless he has asked this through repeated supplication, since there is no satiety in divine things: the more the Lord is tasted, the more sweetly he is desired, as he also says in another psalm: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm XXXIII, 9).

### Verse 12

“My heart has said to you: I have sought your face; your face, O Lord, I will seek.” The heart reveals a silent desire, which the Divinity hears more readily than the loudest voices of peoples, just as it is said to Moses: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus XIV, 15), although he is not read to have spoken anything. Thus the faithful man says that his heart speaks to the Lord, because what he was thinking seemed to be what he was offering. But he seeks the face of the Lord who has conducted himself in holy living; of such people it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V, 8). He also repeats what was said: “Your face, O Lord, I will seek.” It is one thing, but the prayer is repeated; for he knew how precious was that which he sought so many times with ardent devotion.

### Verse 13

“Do not turn your face from me, nor in anger withdraw from your servant.” He carefully and fittingly pursues his desires. In the preceding verse he professed that he eagerly sought the face of the Lord; and because it is not within human power to obtain one’s desire, he prays that the Lord not turn away the face which he was earnestly asking to see. For it belongs to the Lord’s own gift to make himself available to the most faithful for contemplation. It follows: “Nor in anger withdraw from your servant.” We have often said that “anger” signifies the time of judgment, when he will distinguish the wicked from the good. He is believed to be angry with those who are to be condemned by an unhappy separation. Therefore he asks that the Lord not withdraw from him at that time when he grants the saints the face of his majesty. The carnal man fears God lest, as sins grow heavy, he lose either his possessions or his children, or his abundance of gold and silver be diminished; but the holy man fears only that he may be rendered estranged from the face of the Lord.

### Verse 14

“Be my helper; do not forsake me, nor despise me, O God my Savior.” Where are those who say that something must be attributed to human merits? The king and prophet, full of grace and heavenly blessing, asks not to be abandoned by the Lord. For he knows that if the Lord abandons him, no power will be able to govern him. Nor is it enough for him to have asked this once, unless he repeats the same request. For to be despised is always to be given over, and no one can be made secure unless the judge’s serene eye looks upon him.

### Verse 15

“For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up.” He calls his father Adam, the first human being, and his mother his wife Eve, from whom the human race descended. They therefore abandoned him by mortal condition, and were unable to nourish him when they were transferred from this light. Although this may be understood of his actual parents, since he left his father’s and mother’s house when he was raised from among the Hebrew peoples to the height of kingship. It follows: “But the Lord has taken me up,” namely, in place of a true parent. He is father because he created and governs; mother because he cherishes and gives milk to the weak and the little ones. He said “has taken me up,” that is, he placed him in the kingdom from a private condition.

[Col. 0191C] ### Verse 16

“Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way, and guide me on a straight path because of my enemies.” The Savior rather prays that the Lord’s law be established for him—the law through which he is known to have freed debtors by grace. The law had already been given through Moses at that time; but the Lord’s law was expected to come, and he asks that it be established for him. “In your way,” that is, in your Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life (John XIV, 6). With his coming he rightly presumed that the law could both be taught and fulfilled by him. We have already said that the “path” refers to understanding the Scriptures. Therefore the prophet prays that he may rightly understand the books of the Old Testament and recognize that the Lord who was to come is present in them. “Because of my enemies,” he says—that is, because of heretics or unbelieving Jews who sought to subvert them with perverse intent.

### Verse 17

“Do not hand me over to the souls of those who persecute me, for unjust witnesses have risen against me, and iniquity has lied to itself.” Historically this can be understood of Saul, who persecuted him with the fiercest hatred. But since Saul was king and could not act alone in what he commanded, the plural number is suitably used here. Similarly, when Doeg the Idumean is read to have betrayed him, he used the plural, “unjust witnesses.” It could have happened that, when he accused him before the king, he wished to support his statements through other witnesses. Therefore the plural number is appropriately observed, since such a person could not easily be accused by only one man.

[Col. 0192A] The unjust witnesses, then, were Doeg the Idumean and his associates, who betrayed to Saul that the prophet Ahimelech had received David and that he had given him the sword and provisions; the king later exposed this by putting the priest and his sons to death. For they lied when they said that David’s plans had been made against King Saul and that God had been entreated on his behalf; the text of the Books of Kings explains this more fully (I Kings XXII). But he very beautifully said “to itself,” because the one who strives to give false testimony receives the penalties of his own lie. Or, as others say, it is an idiom of divine Scripture that a plural number is sometimes attached for a singular, as when it is said of Herod’s death: “They are dead who sought the life of the child” (Matthew II, 20); or when it is said to Moses concerning Pharaoh: “For they are dead who sought your life” (Exodus IV, 19).

### Verse 18

“I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Wait for the Lord.” After entreating the Lord in many ways not to be handed over to his persecutors, he returns to the support of his confidence and promises himself that he will see good things in the land of the living—that is, in the future life, where good things are everlasting. It is properly said that that land is the land of the living, since this one belongs to the dying. Among rhetoricians this mode is called “collective,” when what is not written is gathered from what is written, so that it is shown to be as though it had been written. Thus here too he believes that future rewards will come to him from the preceding benefits. Scripture itself speaks of the land of the living in a proper sense. It is added: “Wait for the Lord,” who does not deceive by promising and does not reproach when he bestows, as the apostle James says: “Who gives generously to all and does not reproach” (James I, 5).

### Verse 19

“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord.” Because in the preceding verse he had believed that he would see the good things of the Lord, he now says how he may see them. Let us believe that this word, “manfully,” is commanded not only to men but also to women. For men too, when they become soft, are womanly in spirit; and women become manly when they persevere in a good purpose with strength of mind. It follows: “Let your heart be strengthened,” lest, as though weary, you murmur and despair when weariness exhausts you. But to a confident and secure spirit he says: “Wait for the Lord,” who does not know how to withdraw what he promises. “Endure” and “wait” are said to the perfect Christian, as though he were admonished: endure what you suffer, and wait for what you believe.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Amid the many and savage afflictions, the most reverend prophet has disclosed what in particular we should desire: that we should seek by every means to dwell in the Church of Christ. Hearing this with open ears, let us implore it through continual supplication, since nothing shorter could have been said, nor anything more fully obtained. But in the numerical structure of this psalm and of certain psalms that follow, we have been entirely unable to discover a singular rationale of the numbers—namely, what creature is read as corresponding to the number twenty-six, or twenty-seven, or twenty-eight. We therefore leave this to diligent students, so that, following the examples that have been given, whenever they do not find a rationale in a single number, they may then investigate certain correspondences in a divided calculation, whether twice or three times. For example, twenty-six may be divided into twenty and six, and twenty-seven into three times nine. Then, with the numbers divided, a suitable rationale may perhaps be found more easily. What difference does it make if the vessels of the psalms hold two or three measures? But if you recognize nothing fitting even there, it is appropriate to believe that the Creator of heaven and earth distributed the powers of all things, without ambiguity, through different calculations—he who, as is written, perfected all things “by weight, number, and measure” (Wisdom XI, 21). For although drops of rain, the stars of heaven, or the sand of the sea cannot be numbered by us, it does not follow that they are not numbered with him. Even if they are hidden from us, they are nevertheless known to divine power. It remains that we ought to believe what was declared by the definition of our predecessors: that the powers of all the psalms correspond to the numbers assigned and determined for them.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXVII

### A Psalm of David

We have said that David signifies “strong of hand.” And when ought such a name to be given, if not when the glorious struggles of the Lord’s passion are recounted? He is truly strong of hand who by his endurance struck down the prince of darkness, who conquered death by dying, and who freed the human race, held captive, through the dispensation of his crucifixion. When “to him” is added, it is made clear that no other can be understood except Christ the Lord himself, the mediator, who speaks throughout this entire psalm: praying from the humility of the flesh he assumed and declaring the punishments due to his persecutors, not out of a desire for malice but as a testimony to vengeance. It must therefore be noted that this is the third of those psalms which briefly commemorate the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

### Division of the Psalm

In the first section, the Lord Christ, insofar as he is human, prays that his prayer may be heard at the future time of his passion. Second, he gives thanks because he has been heard in what he asked to take place. At the end of the psalm he adds that, just as he himself was raised by the power of his divinity, so his people may be saved when they believe in his name.

### Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“To you, O Lord, I cried; my God, do not be silent toward me.” Christ the Lord cries out to the Father at the time of his passion, asking that he not be silent toward him—that is, that he not refuse the one who asks [or, according to the edition, “the one who suffers”], but rather answer him. There is also a beautiful variation of the words. The human being cries out that God should not be silent, because through our silence he is silent, and when we are negligent we are not held in remembrance by him. Conversely, if, by the Lord’s aid, we look toward him, he looks toward us; if we cry out, he hears; if we love, we are loved.

[Col. 0194A] “And I shall be like those who descend into the pit.” That is, “If you are silent, I shall be like those who dwell in the depths of this world.” For this age is a kind of pit, which is believed to be pleasant and tranquil, but whose depths and engulfing dangers are unknown. It is called a pit because the earth lies hidden beneath it. Therefore the humanity of the Word prays that he not be like other human beings: for although he assumed the common condition of flesh, he obtained the excellence of all creatures through union with God. Of this the Apostle says: “To which of the angels did he ever say: You are my Son, today I have begotten you?” (Hebrews I, 5). Or he calls the grave a pit, where after the passion he was placed.

### Verse 2

“Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication when I pray to you, when I lift up my hands toward your holy temple.” He signifies the time of the most sacred passion and prays that his prayer may be heard, which he made before he was handed over. For after leaving the disciples, he withdrew and prayed, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew XXVI, 39). By “toward the holy temple,” as it seems to me, he perhaps wishes the custom of the Hebrew people to be understood: they had been commanded that, wherever they were located, they should always pray toward the direction in which they knew Jerusalem to be situated. We likewise read that Daniel did this three times a day in Babylon (Daniel VI, 10). Christ the Lord necessarily did this, since he had not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew V, 17).

Or by “toward the holy temple” he wishes heaven to be understood, as praying people are accustomed to do. For it is the desire of those who ask that, although they do not doubt that God is everywhere, they nevertheless trust that help will come to them from heaven. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew VI, 9). It is therefore not absurd to understand the temple as heaven, since divine Scripture shows that the Lord’s dwelling is there.

### Verse 3

“Do not hand my soul over together with sinners, and do not destroy me together with those who work iniquity.” Since he knew that he would die, he rightly asked that his soul, when handed over to the underworld, not be mingled with sinners or have any share with those who work iniquity. But this distinction is sought from him altogether for our salvation, so that our hope may be stirred toward such petitions; for in fulfilling this he prays that no human being become alienated from him. Where are those who think that Christ did not have a soul? But such people seem either not to read these things or entirely to forget what they have read.

### Verse 4

“With those who speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts.” He recalls the Jews, who said to him while testing him: “We know that you have come from God as a teacher” (John III, 2). Thus there was peace on their lips, but malice in their hearts. This figure is called irony, that is, mockery, whenever something said under the appearance of praise is shown to convey a meaning of blame. “With his neighbor”: he speaks of himself, because he was joined to them by the origin of his flesh. They were justly cursed, because they hastened maliciously to destroy their neighbor.

### Verse 5

“Give them according to their works, and according to the wickedness of their designs.” The Jews acted with the intention of doing evil, but unwillingly accomplished good: they sought to inflict death on Christ, by which death itself would be ended; they shed blood, by which the sins of the world would be washed away. Therefore he asks that they be given according to their works—that is, according to their will—for each person does what he wills. Frequently, those who strive to do harm also accomplish good, as the devil does: while he inflicts the penalties of death upon the innocent, he sends martyrs to their crowns. He also made explicit what he had said above by adding, “According to the wickedness of their designs,” that is, their evil ambition, by which they wished to harm the innocent and preferred to hand over to death the one who had come to save them.

### Verse 6

“Repay them according to the work of their hands; render their recompense to them.” There are four kinds of recompense. The first is when evil is given by human beings in return for good, as the Jews repaid Christ: although he had come to save them, they resolved to crucify him. The second is when good is repaid for good, when God will say to his elect: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34). The third is when evil is repaid for evil, when he will say to the wicked: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41), according to the saying: “With the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke VI, 38). The fourth is when he repays what is stated here: good for evil, so that those who were persecutors may become converts and afterward praisers.

Yet all these things that he foretells concerning his enemies are not wishes of malice but foreknowledge of the future. For in the Gospel he says: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). Both statements are pious. Here he threatens in order to terrify them, lest they complete their crimes in despair born of presumption; there, while suffering, he prays that he may bring their hearts to repentance. Nor is it without purpose that he repeated the sentence of terror so many times, so that their stony hearts might be saved by the fire of a great threat.

### Verse 7

“For they have not understood the works of the Lord, and they have not considered the works of his hands; you will destroy them, and you will not build them up.” He develops the preceding meaning. He says that they ought to be repaid because they have not understood the works of the Lord. His work was to teach the people the way of truth and faith and, from the mystery of his sacred incarnation, to reconcile humanity to God, so that, where corrupted nature could not ascend, humanity might arrive through the gift of the Lord’s visitation. And lest the obstinate mind of the Jews refuse to believe the Son of God when he taught the truth, he also confirmed this by the power of immense miracles: what they understood that an ordinary human being could not do, they should clearly recognize as accomplished by the power of the Divinity. But those madmen, believing him only human, could not endure to hear him called the Son of God, an outrage beyond measure.

It follows: “And they have not considered the works of his hands.” If they had considered them, they would have been struck with fear rather than contempt, wept rather than spat upon him, and worshiped rather than crucified him. Such sacrilege could happen to no others except those who had lost the understanding of truth. For God destroys some for correction and casts down others for ruin. He destroyed Paul in order to build him up for the better and make an apostle out of a persecutor; but when impious Pharaoh did not believe despite such great miracles, the Most High drowned him so that he might perish. Thus he says that they will be destroyed so that they ought not to be built up again. This statement, as we have often warned, seems to pertain more to prophecy than to a quality of anger.

### Verse 8

“Blessed is the Lord, for he has heard the voice of my supplication.” Knowing that everything he asked would be fulfilled, he enters the second section, giving thanks that he has been avenged upon his enemies, although this had not yet happened in any way. This figure is called prolepsis, in Latin *praeoccupatio*, “anticipation,” when future events are presented as past. But let us examine what this arrangement of words means: “Blessed is the Lord, for he has heard,” since he is blessed even if he does not hear. Properly, however, we call one blessed when we give him thanks—that is, when we bless him. Therefore “blessed” is fittingly applied to the one who has deigned to hear.

### Verse 9

“The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart has hoped, and I have been helped.”

### Verse 10

“And my flesh has blossomed again, and by my will I will confess to him.” “Helper” pertains to the dangers of life, which he overcame with the Lord’s assistance. “Protector,” because he surrounded him with his defense against diabolical snares. But after these things had happened, he faithfully says that he had hoped in the Lord. When he says “my heart,” he designates the hidden part of the soul, which is known to be the sacrifice of righteousness. He again added, “I have been helped,” so that as pure devotion increased, so too the greatness of assistance might increase.

He rightly said: “My flesh has blossomed again,” because it blossomed at first also: for, born from the Virgin without sin, it shone forth like the singular beauty of the most splendid flower, as Isaiah says: “And a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah XI, 1). “Has blossomed again,” therefore, signifies “has risen again,” as though it had burst forth into the ethereal breezes with wondrous beauty. It follows: “And by my will I will confess to him,” namely, after the resurrection, when human nature had been freed from corruption and, remaining in immeasurable glory, had been brought into union with the Word.

### Verse 11

“The Lord is the strength of his people, and he is the protector of the saved ones of his Christ.” A brief but great definition. What is the Lord? “The strength of his people.” Rightly so, since all adversities are overcome with his help. He is also protector, because he covers and frees them from impending evils. “Of the saving acts,” as though he were saying, “of the righteous,” whose salvation is the Lord.
