He rightly added, “of his Christ,” so that you should understand the Son of God. Others were also called *christs*, those adorned either by royal anointing or by priestly glory.

### Verse 12

“Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance; rule them and raise them up forever.” The humanity of the Word prays for the Christian people, for whose sake it is also shown to have been assumed, so that through faithful satisfaction they may be saved in this world, where they were exposed to the dangers of the Jews. “But bless your inheritance” pertains to the future judgment, when it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34).

And so that he might demonstrate more clearly the charity that he commands, he again asks that in this world he rule devoted peoples, lest they desire carnal things or choose crooked ways; but, illuminated by his governance, may they not know how to share fellowship with the worst. He added, “Raise them up,” so that they may advance with praiseworthy intention in understanding the Scriptures and in holy works, and, cleansed from earthly vices, may be brought upward to eternal rewards. He also asked that this be done “forever,” namely, throughout this entire world, where ages continue until that eternal age, which by its perpetuity is succeeded by nothing else.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

You have heard with what piety this psalm was concluded. He prayed for us, who is himself prayed to by the angels. The advocate of all creatures is our advocate; and so that we might be rescued from death, he himself chose rather to be put to death. In this psalm the previously announced pattern of the Lord’s passion has been fulfilled. He prayed before his betrayal, spoke of his own crucifixion and resurrection, and finally interceded for the faithful, so that those who were worthy to believe in him might rejoice in perpetual blessing.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXVIII

### A Psalm of David at the Completion of the Tabernacle

Since the preceding words are already known, we must now investigate somewhat more carefully the completion of the tabernacle. The completion of the tabernacle signifies the perfection of the Catholic Church, which is now shown to have been established throughout the whole world. By the name “tabernacle,” the Church placed in this world is indicated; because it wages war against carnal vices, it rightly received the name of a military dwelling. Therefore, after the perfection of the universal Church, the prophet sings this psalm, rich in the honor of Christian doctrine, in praise of the Holy Spirit. Since so great a reality was completed through the blessed preaching of the prophets and apostles, it was fittingly adorned with his praises.

The entire psalm is full of praise of the Holy Spirit, and through various allusions it renders proclamations of his majesty. This is what rhetoricians call the demonstrative genre, when someone is displayed and recognized through such a description. But what could anyone fittingly say about him except what he himself deigns to declare about himself?

### Division of the Psalm

When blessed David knew that the ends of the whole world were to be brought to the Catholic faith through the gift of the Holy Spirit by means of the prophets and apostles, as the apostle Peter says: “For prophecy was never brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit” (II Peter I, 21), he first addresses the whole human race, so that they may offer devoted sacrifices to him. Second, in a sevenfold account, through various allusions, he enumerates under a great proclamation the powers of that same Holy Spirit; frequent reading makes clear that this pertains especially to him. But so that you might recognize that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one power, in the third place he says that the Trinity dwells in holy baptism and that the Lord gives power and blessing to the Christian people who have been reborn from it.

### Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams; bring to the Lord glory and honor.” When the prophet looked forward spiritually to the multitude of nations coming to belief in the true faith, as had been foretold, and when the united confession of the whole world was to be joined with them, it was fitting to admonish the people who were now, as it were, believing, so that they might display the devotion of their faith through devoted sacrifices.

He invites the sons of God—that is, those who through the grace of regeneration have become his sons—as the Evangelist John says: “He gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I, 12). But although the whole Trinity is one God, and there is no difference in his majesty or nature, what is shown to apply to the individual persons is nevertheless spoken in different places. Here we must understand the Holy Spirit as specially called “the Lord,” whom he undertook to praise for the completion of the tabernacle.

Observe that at the outset they are not told what they should bring; rather, they are commanded to offer themselves—that is, their hearts shining with holy purity, which is shown to be acceptable to the Lord above every sacrifice. It follows: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” The rams are to be understood as the apostles, who, like leaders of flocks, led the Christian people into the Lord’s sheepfolds. He says that the sons of rams are to be offered—those whom the apostles begot through right preaching, not those who are shown to be outsiders through corrupt doctrine.

The apostles are aptly compared to rams, because these animals are particularly strong in the forehead and, by repeatedly charging against obstacles, knock them down. The apostles are known to have done this through preaching: with a kind of forehead of heavenly speech they broke apart various superstitions and the most firmly established idols. For *aries*, “ram,” is said as though from “rushing with the forehead.”

He added: “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” Here we are specially admonished that the Holy Spirit must suffer no injury. For whoever says that he is less than the Father or the Son is not shown to bring him glory. Nothing is glorious for anyone to hear—that he is less. Therefore we offer to the Lord our God, that is, to the Holy Spirit, pure, complete, and true glory when we proclaim him consubstantial with the Father and the Son, coeternal, and almighty, without any separation. Thus all heresies have been destroyed in various passages of divine Scripture through the preaching of the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 2

“Bring to the Lord glory to his name; worship the Lord in his holy court.” Above he said, “Bring glory to him”; now he says, “for his name.” Therefore he brings glory to the name of the Holy Spirit who makes him more widely known, when he converts the hearts of unbelievers and spreads his name through the multitude of the people and the throngs of nations. This seems especially to pertain to the prudence of those who teach.

But do not judge it pointless that he repeated “bring” for the fourth time. This figure is called *epimone*, in Latin “frequent repetition of speech,” which gathers many things through the repeated use of one word. It follows: “Worship the Lord in his holy court,” that is, honor him in your purest conscience. For this is the royal court and dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (I Corinthians III, 16).

### Verse 3

“The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is over many waters.” He comes to the second order, in which, through the figure *epimone* mentioned above, he repeatedly places one word at the beginnings of the verses and celebrates the praises of the Holy Spirit in sevenfold power. With the Lord’s help, I shall try to explain this in its proper places.

This is the first verse concerning the same subject: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters,” that is, the Spirit of wisdom. He established the law by which the multitude of believers was to be governed; for the tablets of the Testament are read to have been written by the finger of God (Deuteronomy IX, 10). The finger of God is specially understood as the Holy Spirit.

When he said “over the waters,” he signifies peoples, as another psalm also says: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Psalm LXVIII, 2); and in the Apocalypse we read: “The city sitting upon many waters” (Apocalypse XVII, 1). Therefore it is clear from these allusions that the Spirit of wisdom established the law for the peoples.

It follows: “The God of majesty has thundered.” This too pertains to the Spirit of wisdom. He says this when he proclaimed the day of judgment and foretold the punishments of Gehenna with immeasurable terror, so that he seemed not so much to speak as to thunder. He also added: “The Lord is over many waters,” that is, over the peoples of different nations whom he won through the preaching of the prophets and apostles. Thus in this clause too he signified peoples, whom he also preferred to be understood above.

### Verse 4

“The voice of the Lord in power.” A marvelous brevity: three words have filled out so great a meaning! By “the voice of the Lord in power,” he means the Spirit of understanding, who casts down and prostrates every adversary, as it is written: “There is no one who can resist your will” (Esther XIII, 9). Therefore the voice of the Lord is rightly said to be in power, since no obstacle can oppose it.

“The voice of the Lord in magnificence.” Here the Spirit of counsel is signified. For what is more magnificent than he who, illuminating the heart, makes it perceive what should be desired as good and what is most evil as something to be avoided? He brings it about that the impious becomes pious, the captive free, and the slave a son. There is no doubt that this happens to those whom the Holy Spirit visits with the power of his majesty.

### Verse 5

“The voice of the Lord breaking cedars, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.” Here the Spirit of strength shines forth. He breaks pride, which trusts in itself, and raises up humility, which presumes upon his goodness. We must understand the cedars as pride, which, lifting itself up to the heights, imitates the lofty crowns of this tree, especially since the wood itself is not useful unless it has been cut down. No one who remains in his own root produces fruitful growth; so too detestable arrogance, which brought sin into the world, produces nothing good.

The voice of the Lord breaks this pride by saying: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6). He repeats: “And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.” Although this may seem similar to what came before, the addition of one word, “of Lebanon,” appears to indicate no small difference. Cedars that grow elsewhere are not entirely lofty; in Lebanon, however, such trees are found that they seem to surpass the heights of all other trees.

Therefore divine power breaks the nobles and kings of this world, who despise the rest of humanity as though they were lowly shrubs, when it chooses the poor and humble. The former are overcome by this power; amid their riches, some groan in their thoughts, while others are dissolved in shameful ambition. Cedars are also taken in a good sense, as another psalm says: “The cedars of Lebanon, which the Lord planted” (Psalm CIII, 16).

### Verse 6

“And he will shatter them like the calf of Lebanon, and the beloved one like the sons of unicorns.” This verse too pertains to the Spirit of strength. In ancient times, calves of Lebanon were frequently offered in sacrifices; because of the abundance of sweet grasses, they were exceedingly fat and beautiful. He prefers to compare the worldly elite to these animals, which are to be shattered just as those appeared to be offered in sacrifice. They too are victims, when, converted, they are offered to Christ the Lord with purified minds.

But lest people complain that a harsh law had been imposed upon them, he also says that the beloved Son of God is to die—the one of whom it is written: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III, 17). Because of the incarnation he became like “the son of unicorns,” that is, like the Jews who exalted themselves in a unique manner. Or the Jews were called “unicorns” because they appear to accept only one Testament. Thus he says that Christ would die in the flesh, like the sons of the Jews; in immeasurable piety he assumed our condition in death, so that he might grant us a share in his immortality.

### Verse 7

“The voice of the Lord cutting apart the flame of fire.” He signifies the Spirit of knowledge, who, by cutting apart—that is, dividing and discerning—every opposing plan or heat, judges it. By the knowledge of his majesty he extinguished the burning and fiery tumults of the Jews, so that what the wicked had done as though merely to deny a human being might be turned toward human salvation and glory.

The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness; and the Lord will shake [Col. 0200D] the wilderness of Kadesh. Here he indicates the Spirit of piety, who, shaking false thoughts and the foolish desires of human beings, draws those who have been corrected toward the pursuit of truth. And rightly he called their errors a wilderness, since it has no inhabitant, God; nor can they themselves remain long in their perversities, since they either abandon them through a lamentable death or forsake them through a blessed conversion.

He continues: “And the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh.” This too still pertains to the Spirit of piety. But the narrative of the Book of Numbers explains this passage carefully (Num. XX, 1), relating that when the Israelite people had come to Kadesh and were suffering from extreme thirst because of the aridity of the place, Moses, at the Lord’s command, struck the rock and suddenly supplied them with an abundance of water; and in a wondrous manner the land that had lain parched and squalid in dry barrenness [Col. 0201A] became watered. Through this comparison, therefore, he says that the hardest hearts of sinners can be dissolved into the waters of wisdom, and that the example of Kadesh must again be enacted in human hearts. For “wilderness” is often used of a place where unbelieving peoples are known to gather, as the Gospel says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Matt. III, 3). John could not have preached in a wilderness where no one would hear; rather, those who had not yet received the gifts of faith were called a wilderness.

**Verse 8.** “The voice of the Lord preparing the stags, and he will reveal the dense thickets; and in his temple all will say, ‘Glory.’”

He speaks of the seventh Spirit, the fear of the Lord. For stags are timid, certainly, but they swallow poisonous things. And rightly those who fear the Divinity [Col. 0201B] yet devour every hostile thing are compared with them; such people cannot be deceived or harmed by those who are known to resist the Church of God with venomous disputation.

The sevenfold Spirit has been signified, as we said above; you may easily gather this by counting and recognize it by its operation. Yet we must understand this Holy Spirit as one and the same, whose seven virtues, as Isaiah testifies (Isa. XI, 2–3), are established as those we have mentioned: the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of understanding, the spirit of counsel, the spirit of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge, the spirit of piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord—“distributing to each one as he wills.”

Nor should it trouble us that everywhere he says that the voice is the speech of the Holy Spirit. For this word is evidently applied to the whole Trinity. We read of the Father’s voice when he says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17) [Col. 0201C]. Likewise, of the Son speaking: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4). Similarly, in the Acts of the Apostles we read of the Holy Spirit: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts XIII, 2). But Saint Augustine, writing against the Arians, collected this communion of words in one book with useful synthesis (*Serm.* 191, *On the Holy Trinity*), so that every prudent person might recognize the equality of substance and the indivisible power of the Trinity, since he shows that the very words are common.

The fear of the Lord also revealed the dense thickets, when, having laid aside ignorance, devout peoples gathered for understanding of the divine law. For this reason, in his Church they all render glory, according as each one has received the gifts of the aforesaid sevenfold Spirit [Col. 0201D]. For glory, as we often remember having been said, is praise produced through the celebration of many.

**Verse 9.** “The Lord inhabits the flood, and the Lord the King will sit forever.”

**Verse 10.** “The Lord will give strength to his people, and the Lord will bless his people with peace.”

Having passed through the virtues of the sevenfold Spirit, he reaches, in the third division, the unity of the Trinity by a wondrous arrangement. For by saying “the Lord” three times in these two verses, he shows that the Holy Trinity inhabits the flood—that is, the waters of baptism—as it is said in the Gospel: “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

But let us ask why “flood” has here been placed for the sacred fonts [Col. 0202A]. Rightly so, because what happened under Noah bore the image of holy baptism. For just as baptism cleanses souls from the filth of sins, so that flood wiped away the shameful crimes of the world. Thus “flood” has rightly been placed for baptism, since it is established that baptism was effected in its likeness.

Since the Lord is repeated three times without distinction of persons, the first statement may be understood of the Holy Spirit: “The Lord inhabits the flood.” It follows: “And the Lord the King will sit forever”; this we properly understand of the Son. “The Lord will give strength to his people”: we appropriately take this of the Father. “His people” signifies the Christian people, whom he acquired through the gift of sacred baptism.

He also added: “And the Lord will bless his people with peace.” He did not say “they will bless,” but “he will bless,” because our Lord God is one [Col. 0202B]. “With peace,” because of that saying of the Gospel: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27). For the peace of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is one.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us remember with what immense trumpet this psalm has thundered, so that those who disparage the Holy Spirit cannot defend themselves by pleading ignorance. For his power has been praised through a sevenfold distribution, so that you might recognize that nothing inferior and nothing divided exists there; because the unity of the Holy Trinity has been declared at the end. Let the insane perversity of heretics cease from stirring up empty accusations. Let them read Didymus, let them read blessed Ambrose, and the other Fathers who have spoken on this matter with the most complete exposition. Let them render glory [Col. 0202C] and honor to the indivisible Trinity, and let them not create a difference within equality, if they do not choose to be led to ruin.

# Exposition of Psalm XXIX

**A psalm of song at the dedication of the house of David.**

The meaning of “a psalm of song” is known. Let us now consider why “the house of dedication” has been placed. The house signifies the temple of the Lord’s body; the dedication, however, signifies the resurrection of that same Lord Jesus Christ. For then his body was brought into eternal glory and power, as he himself says in the Gospel: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

We say that something is dedicated when the newness of a house is assigned to the most solemn use. The house of David, however, has been named because of his seed, from whom our Savior took the origin of his flesh. This is the house [Col. 0202D] that now, with the doors of its lips opened, joyfully sings: “I will exalt you, O Lord.” It was built by being born, but is known to have been dedicated in the holy resurrection.

## Division of the Psalm

Our King, the Lord Christ, in the first account after his glorious resurrection, gives thanks to the Father because he delivered him from the adversity of this world, commanding the saints to sing praise to the Lord, since all things have been placed under his power.

In the second, he says that he will not be moved from his steadfastness, adding further that the praises of the Divinity should be offered by the living rather than by the dead.

In the third, he returns joyfully and [Col. 0203A] exultantly to his resurrection, since, having laid aside the frailty of the flesh, he remains in the eternal glory of his majesty; in his customary manner he speaks of the past as something he knew was to come.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me, nor have you made my enemies rejoice over me.”

The Lord Christ gives thanks to the Father through the dispensation by which he rose from the dead. For by “I will exalt” he means, “I will make more widely known” what was accomplished through the holy incarnation of the Word and his glorious resurrection. How many, before that time, could spiritually know the Lord, unless the promised truth had become clear through his coming?

But a human being was able to exalt the name of the Most High for this reason: it is established that he was assumed by the same One. For how could he [Col. 0203B] have disclosed the hidden things of God or foretold God’s future judgments, unless by the heavenly power through which he prevailed to reveal his own secrets and those of the Father?

A question follows: “Nor have you made my enemies rejoice over me.” For how were his enemies not made to rejoice, when they struck him and said: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is the one who struck you?” (Matt. XXVI, 68); and again, standing before the cross, they said: “Ha! You who destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days” (ibid. XXVII, 40)? How were they not made to rejoice when they cast lots over his garments?

But this fleeting and empty joy was turned into repentance and sorrow for them, when after three days they saw him rise again, whom they had hoped had met the common end. “You made [them] rejoice” is used [Col. 0203C] for “you caused [them] to rejoice.” This figure is called *hypallage*, whenever either the gender or the inflection of a verb is changed.

“Over me” he said after he had passed from this world. Then his enemies were made sorrowful, while the devout flourished in great joy.

**Verse 2.** “O Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.”

How was he healed, when he is not read to have been ill? Yet he was secretly ill when, through his incarnation, he assumed the whole human being, which was subject to diseases and deaths. But because we were healed in him, he himself declares that he was healed. The Lord Christ was then saved when, by rising again, he placed the flesh of our frailty in the joys of eternal life; and all were made safe who faithfully believed in him.

**Verse 3.** “O Lord, you drew my soul up from the underworld; you saved me from those descending into the pit” [Col. 0203D].

What shall we say of those who do not believe that the Lord Christ had a soul? Behold, he himself cries out so often that he was brought to the underworld according to human law, and that from there his soul was drawn out by the power of his divinity. And observe that he says it was “drawn out,” clearly because, once the bars of the underworld had been broken, it was brought all the way to heaven.

Those descending into the pit are people who are involved in the iniquity of this present age. And he rightly said “descending,” as though they were going into the depths: weighed down by the burden of sins, they are swallowed up in the deepest abyss.

But how was he saved, when it is established that he was killed? He was certainly saved from such people—that is, he was freed from their fellowship [Col. 0204A] when he rose from the dead, and death could no longer harm him.

**Verse 4.** “Sing psalms to the Lord, his saints, and give thanks to the memory of his holiness.”

After his resurrection, he appropriately commands the saints to sing psalms, so that when the head rose, the members might rejoice—especially since their hope had been strengthened through such a dispensation. For it is established that those who happened to believe in his preaching will themselves rise in joy.

He said “to the memory of his holiness” because he deigned to remember us, who were dwelling in the shadow of death, as though in the dense darkness of sins. We did not remember him who created us; rather, he remembered us whom he created, as he himself says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16).

Therefore the memory of his holiness must be acknowledged and glorified [Col. 0204B]. By bringing the human race into remembrance of himself, he made possible what could save us.

**Verse 5.** “For there is anger in his indignation, and life in his will; in the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning joy.”

Let us understand this verse in its parts. It recalls the recompense of the wicked, the rewards of the just, the sorrow of his passion, and the joy of his resurrection; and thus, when these are distinguished, the offense of confusion is avoided.

But since, as we read, our anger produces death, this is said of the Lord in the first clause by a figurative interpretation, because his indignation is truly the death of the sinner. Favor (*dignatio*) exists when he receives us mercifully; indignation when, being angry, he casts us away—not because he himself becomes angry, but because death arises from his [Col. 0204C] turning away, which proceeds from human anger.

It follows: “And life in his will.” Nothing more excellent can be said. For just as death is in his indignation, so life is recognized as being in his will; yet this rests not on our merits but on his will. This argument is called, in the *Topics*, “from contraries.”

He added: “In the evening weeping will remain.” We call it evening when, the day having ended, the sun sets and the darkness of night follows. This is understood to have happened to the Church when Christ our Lord was killed. Then weeping truly remained, while for three days the company of the faithful lamented together and the very nature of the world was shaken, so that the earth itself seemed to mourn the Lord’s death together with the human race.

We call it morning when, the darkness departing, the dawn begins to shine [Col. 0204D]. At that time, as the Gospel testifies, the Lord’s resurrection was made known; and from that event joy unquestionably increased for the blessed. Thus, in one verse, the immense fullness of so many matters has been unfolded.

**Verse 6.** “But I said in my abundance: I will not be moved forever.”

After giving thanks for his resurrection and salutarily commanding the saints to sing psalms, he returns, in a second account, to the most glorious cause of his passion and declares what he, the devout teacher, thought within himself at that time.

Let us now see what this “abundance” is, through which he professes that he cannot be moved in any way. The Son of the ever-virgin Mary possessed this abundance: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14). For what grace is more abundant [Col. 0205A] than that which merited to possess the fullness of the Divinity? As the Apostle says: “In him all the fullness of Divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. II, 9)—that is, most truly, substantially, and perfectly.

Rightly, therefore, he said that he could not be moved forever, since his own majesty bestowed upon him the gifts of confidence.

**Verse 7.** “O Lord, in your will you established strength for my beauty; you turned your face from me, and I became troubled.”

In this verse he clearly explains the source of that abundance which could not be shaken. For he does not say that he possessed strength from human nature; rather, he asserts that it was contributed to him from above. The beauty of that nature is proved by the example: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3).

But this spotless beauty of humanity, brighter than the sun [Col. 0205B], when joined to the Word, received the strength by which it performed great miracles, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John V, 26).

A proof of the preceding statement follows: “You turned your face from me, and I became troubled.” As though he were saying: “You gave me, according to the flesh, what I possess, so that when you turned away I became troubled.”

In saying this he cuts off the destructive arrogance of human beings. For how could a sinner dare to presume upon himself, when spotless holiness confesses that strength and beauty were bestowed upon it by the Lord? This argument is called, in the *Topics*, “from consequences.” For when the Divinity turned away its face, it followed that the weakness of the flesh would be troubled.

**Verse 8.** “To you, O Lord, I will cry, and I will entreat my God” [Col. 0205C].

What he now calls “Lord” and now “God” belongs to one statement. For what is it to cry to the Lord except to entreat God?

**Verse 9.** “What profit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?”

**Verse 10.** “Will the dust give thanks to you, or announce your truth?”

The spotless incarnation of the Word continues in the prayers it has begun. For from that same perspective it says: “If I descend into corruption”—that is, into putrefaction, to which all flesh is subjected by the universal law—“what hope will there be for the faithful who have believed that I would rise again with the speed of three days?”

He therefore asks not that he should not die, but that his flesh, dissolved by corruption, should not fail to display any sign of the promised majesty, because of [Col. 0205D] that saying elsewhere: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10); and that there should begin to be no benefit to the world in the saving blood of the Lord’s passion.

Here “thanksgiving” signifies praise, which those who are dissolved into dust by the common death cannot offer. It follows: “Or will it announce your truth?” Namely, that truth which after his resurrection he said to the disciples: “Go, preach this Gospel to every creature; whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark XVI, 14).

**Verse 11.** “The Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper.”

He comes to the third account, in which, now rejoicing over his resurrection, [Col. 0206A] he is comforted by the delight of eternal blessedness. But he himself explains in due course how he became a helper; and therefore we should not add our own words, so that the flow of the statements may disclose its own explanation more fully. This figure is called *epexegesis*, in Latin “explanation,” when earlier statements are explained by words that follow.

**Verse 12.** “You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore my sackcloth and girded me with gladness.”

Mourning refers to death, joy to resurrection; both are now established as fulfilled. Sackcloth is a very coarse and rough fabric assigned to human uses and labors, appropriately suited to the human body. The sackcloth was therefore torn—that is, his body—when he himself deigned to die for us [Col. 0206B].

Before his death, death surrounded us with twisted bonds and held us confined, like some grain, in an unbreakable prison. But so that you may understand that “sackcloth” was used for the sorrow of death, he says of the resurrection in contrast to it: “You girded me with gladness.”

Consider the word “girded.” It signifies a belt belonging to the dignity of a judge. For authority is understood to be established in the very word “girded.” Thus we speak of a judge as “girded” when we declare his insignia and honors.

And observe that he did not say “you girded,” but “you girded around”—that is, “you raised me above all powers and virtues,” because of the Apostle’s statement: “And he gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. II, 9).

**Verse 13.** “So that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced: O Lord my God, I will give thanks to you forever” [Col. 0206C].

This verse depends upon what precedes. For he said that he had been girded with gladness so that his humanity might sing to the Divinity, which is his glory. We have said that singing properly pertains to joy of mind.

The glory of Christ is the majesty of the Father, from whom he heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). And because he was once pierced—that is, crucified—for the salvation of the world, he declares that he will not thereafter be subjected to any passion; for he has laid aside the frailty of the flesh and remains in the glory of his majesty, as the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death will no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI, 9).

But lest you think that the song mentioned above is temporal, he says that he will give thanks forever. Here “I will give thanks” should be understood from the part of the members [Col. 0206D], as though it were “I will confess”—that is, “with the saints I will praise you with an eternal voice.”

This is absolutely believed to be destined to occur when that city, Jerusalem, has been dedicated, when unfailing psalmody is promised to all the just. For Christ frequently promises that he will do what the Christian people will certainly do, as in this passage: “I will give thanks to you, O Lord, in the great church; in a numerous people I will praise you” (Ps. XXXIV, 18).

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This psalm is small, certainly, but it is filled with the abundance of heavenly teaching: its verses possess the grace of brevity, while its meanings extend into immense breadth. Here the grace of the holy resurrection is proclaimed; here the glorious passion of the Lord is recalled [Col. 0207A], so that no tribulation of the passion may terrify those whom the great hope of the resurrection makes joyful.

And observe that, because of the grace of its novelty, the order has here been reversed, so that it begins with the resurrection, which is established to have occurred after the Lord’s passion.

# Exposition of Psalm XXX

**To the end: a psalm of David.**

We have often said that the words contained in the title are to be referred to the Lord Christ, to whom the entire psalm must be applied, since it celebrates his passion and resurrection. He deigned to speak from our lowliness, having also endured the passion of a human body; through his own words, the good Teacher instructs us, so that we too, imitating the discipline of heavenly things, may follow the words of our head in humility and devotion [Col. 0207B].

It should be noted that this is the fourth of those psalms that briefly mention the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the words are those of the Lord Savior. At the first entrance, he asks the Father to be delivered from the evils that threaten, and then exults with certainty that he has been heard.

In the second, he returns to his passion and describes the event in a wondrous narrative through various allusions.

In the third, he gives general thanks for himself and the faithful people, because he has bestowed the gifts of his mercy upon the universal Church; he also admonishes the saints to persevere in the Lord’s charity [Col. 0207C], since they have previously heard both the rewards of the good and the retributions of the wicked.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded forever. In your justice deliver me and rescue [Col. 0207D] me.”

We must examine how similar statements are so often repeated with pleasing variation. Christ prays to the Father from the nature of the humanity he assumed, so that, cast down from his hope, he may not suffer the insults of human mockery. He adds “forever,” where his contemplation remained fixed and unchanging.

“In your justice” means, “by which you are accustomed to assist those who pray,” who place their firmest confidence in your majesty. “Deliver” pertains to removing the dangers of this world; “rescue” refers to the swiftness of help, so that that resurrection, most beneficial to the world, might not be delayed. “Rescue” is formed from *rapere*, “to seize.”

Therefore he rightly implored the Lord’s justice, since he knew that he would suffer at the hands of the wicked. O truly wondrous and divine exchange! He received death and returned salvation; he endured insults and bestowed honors; he took upon himself pain and conferred healing—alone and supremely merciful, giving sweet things while receiving bitter ones.

**Verse 2.** “Incline your ear to me; hasten to rescue me. Be for me a protecting God.”

He said, “Incline your ear,” because of the lowliness of his members: since, by its own nature, the human condition could not reach the Divinity, the Divinity descended by inclining itself toward it. This came about through the incarnation of the omnipotent Word [Col. 0208A]. Hence he rightly asked for what had not yet been shown to have occurred.

It follows: “Hasten to rescue me”—that is, “hasten to grant a very swift resurrection,” not the delayed resurrection that the whole human race is still known to await. This repeated petition teaches us that we must not withdraw from prayer, even when we believe that certain things can be granted to us.

He also asks to be protected by divine power from the importunate ambushes of this age, so that a simplicity left exposed may not lie open to enemies; as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: “Like a lamb before its shearer, without a voice, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7).

**Verse 3.** “And into a house of refuge, so that you may save me.”

The house of refuge is the glorious resurrection, after which he is no longer shaken by any weakness but enjoys incorruptible majesty [Col. 0208B]. For he was then safe when death could no longer prevail over him. Thus what he fears comes from us; what he trusts belongs to his own Divinity.

Some say that “the house of refuge” also pertains to the Catholic Church, where, from the perspective of the members, he asks to be saved, since every Christian is truly made safe within it; just as, when the flood increased, only those who merited to enter safely into Noah’s ark were saved.

**Verse 4.** “For you are my strength and my refuge; and because of your name you will be my leader, and you will nourish me.”

“Strength” pertains to enduring what he suffered; “refuge” to the end of evils, when he overcame the iniquities of this age by the end of his glorious death.

It follows: “And because of your name you will be my leader.” Because of his name, the Lord was leader to the humanity [Col. 0208C], since he caused that name to be known more widely among all nations through the publication of saving preaching.

Or this should be understood from the perspective of the members, as has already been said above. For he is truly called our leader when we follow him and do not avoid the traces of his preaching. He also added that he had been nourished until the Catholic Church reached maturity through his gift.

**Verse 5.** “You will bring me out of this snare that they hid for me, because you are my protector, O Lord.”

The snare was indeed hidden by the enemies, but it was not hidden from Christ. He did not fall into death through deception; rather, he knowingly accepted it for our liberation.

The Jews therefore hid a snare for Christ because, believing him to be merely human, they plotted to destroy him through secret ambushes. Hence he says that he is to be brought out of it—that is, swiftly raised to the heights through the benefit of the resurrection [Col. 0208D].

But he says that all the plans of the Jews would be frustrated, because, with the Lord protecting him, no adversity can prevail.

**Verse 6.** “Into your hands I commend my spirit; you have redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth.”

Let us consider why the very words spoken by the Gospel text have been placed here. For there too he says: “Into your hands I commend my spirit”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (Luke XXIII, 46). This is so that here too you might recognize him as the one who, after so many ages, was going to speak the same words while placed upon the cross.

“Into your hands” means “into your truth,” by which you always act with kindness and justice. He therefore commends to the Father an incomparable treasure [Col. 0209A]: that soul, namely, which fulfilled his wills with pure intention. It was fitting, therefore, that such a spirit should be commended to so great a receiver.

He then bears witness that he was redeemed. But let us see at what price. At the price of which the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7). You see how great the price was: that he should incline his majesty to the flesh of a human being, and empty himself in order to fill human things with heavenly things.

But so that you might clearly recognize which Lord this was, he added who he was: “God of truth.” He is especially the God of those who love truth and do not mingle themselves with any falsehood.

**Verse 7.** “You have hated all who observe vanity in vain; but I will hope in the Lord.”

Those things are [Col. 0209B] always hateful that are proved to be contrary. Truth therefore rightly hated vanity, because vanity is concerned with falsehood.

He himself supplies an explanation of this by saying “in vain,” which is described not only as empty but also as superfluous. This is fitting, since, by removing fruitful understanding, it alienates people from the Lord.

When he first said that the Lord hated vanity—that is, the desires of this passing age—he now says that he loves what is most true. What are these most true things? “I will hope in the Lord”: there is nothing empty or superfluous there, but everything remains fixed and complete.

But what consequence follows from this matter?

**Verse 8.** “I will exult and rejoice in your mercy, because you have regarded my humility.”

In this verse and the preceding one, a categorical syllogism again arises [Col. 0209C]. We already explained its definition and parts in the first psalm; here too it is gathered together by reasoning:

“I hoped in the Lord. Everyone who hopes in the Lord will exult and rejoice in his mercy. Therefore I will exult and rejoice in his mercy.”

It is plainly a beautiful mode of expression, embracing in brevity what no adversity could break apart.

Let us now discuss the words of the psalm. To exult is to rejoice with great eagerness of spirit; to rejoice is to be comforted by a moderated affection of the mind.

But let us consider how often we are warned not to trust in human powers. For how, as was said above, should anyone presume upon himself, when the holy incarnation is read to have abstained from such presumption? Therefore the impulse of Pelagian perversity must be condemned, since it attempts to presume upon what it ought to have known that the Holy Spirit had so often [Col. 0209D] condemned.

Let us also attend to who says that his humility was regarded: the one who both created and sustains heaven and earth, whom the heavenly powers serve. Yet humility existed in the Most High for this reason: humanity also truly adhered to him, perfected from the very conception.

**Verse 9.** “You saved my soul from distresses, and you did not enclose me in the hands of the enemy.”

“Distress” is named from the fact that it is placed in death—that is, established in the straits of death. For when we are bound by the snares of sins and cannot be released from them by our own strength, this is called distress.

The soul of the Lord Savior was therefore freed from distresses when it was made wholly alien from sins [Col. 0210A]. It follows: “And you did not enclose me in the hands of the enemy.” This was the distress of which he spoke above: that he might be handed over to the power of the devil, made subject through sins.

Those surrounded by the hands of that most savage one are enclosed as though in a penal prison. Thus he says, “You did not enclose me,” because he was made free from the devil’s power, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

**Verse 10.** “You set my feet in a spacious place; have mercy on me, O Lord, because I am troubled.”

After completing his exultation over his liberation, he comes to the second entrance, where he will speak many things about his passion, so that he might recall it frequently and most devoutly—having accepted it for the salvation of all.

“You set” means “you established” [Col. 0210B], because he could not sustain a fall who possessed none of the world’s vices. “In a spacious place” means “in a free place, always exempt from the devil’s power.” For that is a free place which that enemy does not occupy; that is a spacious place which he does not possess.

And observe that he did not say “on the way,” but “in a spacious place”—that is, in the homeland of the virtues, in the region of the blessed. For the way of the just is read to be narrow.

By his “feet” he means moral virtues, by which he walked through this world with firm steps, which the devil’s opposition could not impede. But although he walked through the world without blame, it was necessary for divine grace to assist his weaknesses, lest frail flesh depart from the integrity of its heavenly purpose.

Therefore it follows: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, because I am troubled.” By the law of the human body [Col. 0210C], he asks that assistance be given to his distress, as he also says in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38), and similar things.

Or he calls his apostles his feet, who stood in a spacious place—that is, throughout the universal Church—with the utmost firmness of faith.

**Verse 11.** “My eye was troubled in anger; my soul and my belly.”

Across these four verses there is a figure called *diatyposis*, in Latin “expression,” in which, when persons or things are set before us, both their form and their condition are portrayed. He begins to describe the magnitude of the danger.

As though he were saying: “My mind was confused when the fury of those pursuing me attacked me.” He used “anger” for the indignation of the enemies [Col. 0210D].

The eye signifies understanding, which we continually trouble and confuse whenever we fear impending dangers. The belly is our abdomen, in which we store food that has been swallowed; it is appropriately compared with memory, because just as the belly receives food that has been transmitted into it, so the recesses of memory suitably receive knowledge of things.

He therefore says that his belly was troubled—that is, his memory, in which he had stored the things that the Lord had promised him concerning his glorification. But when the flesh saw that dangers threatened it, it necessarily became disturbed by trembling.

And note that he frequently says that he was troubled, but never that he despaired. He said this so that the heavenly Teacher might show us a pattern for imitation. For disturbance readily affects humanity, but despair cannot arise in divine holiness.

**Verse 12.** “For my life failed in pain, and my years in groaning.”

This is the source of that disturbance [Col. 0211A] and fear of the flesh: life had failed amid pains. The word “failed” itself signifies long and very severe sufferings. To fail is gradually to become less and, by losing strength little by little, to reach the end; it is clear that this can happen to human life, which is brought to the limit of death.

Clarifying what precedes, he adds: “And my years in groaning,” which certainly signifies a multitude of days. Consider that he said “in groaning,” because the pain was not slight where continuous groaning resounded.

Or this more particularly pertains to the sufferings of the martyrs, who are rightly understood in the head, since they are the members [Col. 0211B] of Christ. And consider that he placed it not in “voices” but in “groanings,” so that what seemed hidden to human beings might be made more fully known to God.

**Verse 13.** “My strength was weakened in poverty, and my bones were troubled.”

The strength of the soul is weakened in poverty, because human frailty lacks every good. For what is poorer than that which is recognized to possess nothing adequate of itself?

The bones signify the strength by which the structure of the body is supported. Both expressions are beautifully placed to portray the weakness of human substance, since no presumption should exist either in the strength of the soul or in hope placed in the flesh, as the prophet says: “Cursed is the one who trusts in man, who sets the flesh of his arm as his hope, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. XVII, 5) [Col. 0211C].

Verse 14. I have become a reproach above all my enemies, and exceedingly so to my neighbors, and a terror to my acquaintances. It is not without significance that he says “above all,” rather than “among all.” “Above all my enemies” is said by way of exaggeration, because although they were truly a reproach, Christ the Lord, innocent and immaculate, was regarded as a reproach among those who polluted themselves by their wicked crime. He continues: “I have become a reproach”—not because I was truly a reproach, but because I was thought by them to be what I was not; they had gone astray, deceived by empty persuasions. Against *probus* we say *probrum*, that is, something dishonest and disgraceful. But *opprobrium* signifies a highly detestable crime, which plainly befell the Lord and Savior among the iniquitous Jews when they said, “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16), and elsewhere, “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8:48).

By “neighbors” he means those who drew near to him by the proximity of faith—those who had not yet believed but were preparing to believe. Yet when they saw him hanging on the cross, they were removed from the neighborhood of faith, since they saw suffering the one whom they had thought should be worshiped. In their ignorance, although they faithfully saw the things previously foretold necessarily come to pass, they were then even more suspended from firm belief. Observe also that he first said “enemies,” then “neighbors,” and now, drawing still nearer, arrives at “acquaintances.” By “acquaintances” he signifies the apostles [p. 100], who were utterly shaken by his Passion. Of them it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7). Thus, as we have said, the rhetorical figure *diatyposis* is suitably completed through these four verses.

Verse 15. Those who saw me fled outside from me; I was erased as though dead from the heart. In this verse and in the one that follows there is the figure *metriasmos*, which is called in Latin *mediocritas*, whenever we present a great matter in a moderate form of expression. For he says: “Those who saw me fled outside from me”—that is, those who believed Scripture less fully, when they saw the Lord placed upon the cross, went outside his divinity, hoping that their hope had been ended by his death.

Alternatively, he signifies heretics, who hear the divine Scriptures in the Church and see its mighty works, yet go outside to wicked preaching, fleeing the truth in which they cannot bear to persevere. It appropriately follows: “I was erased as though dead from the heart.” He is not said to be dead from the faithful, for his divinity is rightly understood to be incapable of suffering. “I was erased from the heart,” that is, from the mind of unbelievers [MSS A, F, and B: “the faithful”]. This commonly happens to those who, by burying dead people, bury their memory and recollection together with their bodies.

Verse 16. I have become like a discarded vessel, because I heard the reproach of many who dwell around me. A discarded vessel is one that has been broken and is always thrown away as useless for every purpose. Thus Jesus, once dead, was thought by the faithless to be cast away like a broken vessel. For what could be expressed more moderately than that omnipotent majesty should be likened to fragile things? Yet consider these things as they were thought by the mad. In him, however, there was always a unique omnipotence and wondrous divine fullness, as the Apostle says: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2:9), that is, substantially and manifestly. Divinity, indeed, cannot be bodily.

It follows: “because I heard the reproach of many who dwell around me.” He signifies the faithless Jews, who dwell around the synagogue, not within it. The word “around” derives from *circuitus* (“a circuit”); he wishes sinners to be understood, of whom he says elsewhere: “The wicked walk around” (Psalm 11:9). Such people are therefore rightly called those who dwell around, because they preferred to regard God’s law not spiritually but carnally. Thus, through these luminous words, the dark crimes of the Jewish people are subtly indicated.

Verse 17. When they all gathered together against me, they conspired to take my life; but I hoped in you, O Lord. Let us restore the order of the words so that the connected statements may be understood more clearly: “When they all gathered together against me, they conspired to take my life.” He says that the greater part of the Jews conspired to hand the Lord over to death, since any crime is more serious when it is carried out by the counsel of many. By saying “all together,” he does not wish only a few to be understood, so that the due vengeance might overtake that criminal crowd. “To take my life” signifies “to deprive me of it,” or “to remove it.”

The order of expression is wondrous and most holy. While the enemies dwelt around the synagogue and placed their hope in their own strength, he says that he hoped in the Lord, knowing that their power was nothing and that by such plots they were striving rather to kill themselves.

Verse 18. I said, “You are my God”; my times are in your hands. Christ the Lord says, “You are my God,” but specifically from the standpoint of the humanity assumed, which, as he says below, was subject both to time and to death. He does not recall that his life was to be ended by their persecution, as the enemies supposed; rather, he places the times of his life in the Lord’s power. For it is by him that we exist as creator, by him that we are sustained as he orders, and by his command that we also depart. Therefore it was necessary that he should have fixed hope in the Lord, since he knew that both his life and his death were in his power.

[Col. 0213B] Verse 19. Free me and rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from those who persecute me; make your face shine upon your servant. He asks the one who can crush the life of his adversaries and, according to his wondrous dispensation, turn human hearts. Earlier he said “enemies,” that is, the Jews; he adds, “and from those who persecute me,” namely, the pagans or the various heretics who pursue the Church of God with deceitful schemes.

It follows: “Make your face shine upon your servant,” that is, “make me see that you deign to look upon me,” so that, just as they despair of him when he is dying, they may trust in him when he has risen. Do not be offended when you hear him called by the Lord “your servant.” All such words must specifically be applied to his humanity, as he says elsewhere: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Psalm 115:16). Where are those who refuse to acknowledge two natures in the Lord and Savior? For how else can this diversity be reconciled, so that in one and the same person you understand both the Lord of heaven and one subject to suffering?

Verse 20. Save me in your mercy, O Lord; let me not be put to shame, because I have called upon you. By saying, “Save me in your mercy,” he denies his own merit. For he continually repeats the same things to instruct us, and he is not satisfied with this loving confession, because the sweetness of truth does not produce weariness. He also adds: “O Lord, let me not be put to shame, because I have called upon you.” This is a wondrous and perfect proclamation, containing both humble supplication and the inviolable steadfastness of one who believes.

He therefore asks not to be neglected and put to shame. But how does he believe that he will be heard? “Because I have called upon you.” To call faithfully upon the Lord is a merit, not an offense; for the one who presumes that he will be heard by him cannot in any way be deceived.

Verse 21. Let the impious be put to shame and brought down to the underworld; let deceitful lips be made mute. In the preceding verse he said: “Let me not be put to shame, because I have called upon you.” Here, in an exchange of roles, he wishes instead that those who call upon idols, and all others who defile themselves with similar impiety, should be put to shame. It is fitting that those should blush whom eternal punishment awaits.

For while they do not believe here in God’s promised judgment, their deceitful lips are blasphemous and talkative. But when they recognize the manifestation of the resurrection and see themselves placed in grave danger, they quickly fall silent; they no longer rush into insolent speech, for excessive terror closes their mouths.

Verse 22. They speak iniquity against the righteous, in pride and contempt. He explains the deceitful lips which, as he said above, would become mute through the power of recognition. In this age they speak against the righteous, that is, against Christ. This is a worthy name and fitting designation, since he is rightly called righteous because he is proved to be “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

But against so great a name he suitably places “iniquity.” For just as light is opposed to darkness, so iniquity appears opposed to righteousness. Falsehood speaks against truth when the Jews proclaim that the Messiah is still to come; when the Arians call the Lord Creator a creature; and when the pagans foolishly declare Saturn, Jupiter, Venus, and the other monstrosities to be heavenly deities.

He adds: “in pride and contempt,” namely, because the proud argue about Christ’s humility when they say that the Lord of heaven could not have assumed the substance of flesh. Those who despise him consider it unworthy to believe in the passion of the immortal Lord. When they hear that he was struck with whips, beaten with blows, and handed over to the hands of the impious, they immediately burst into blasphemous speech, utterly failing to understand the saving purpose—not because the Most High was less able to appear most glorious amid the pompous honors of this world, but because it was fitting for him to avoid the very things by which the human race had wickedly despised its creator.

Verse 23. How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you! He comes to the third division, where he enumerates in various ways how many benefits the Lord bestows upon those who fear him. He admonishes all the saints to love the Lord, since it is established that he is both our judge and, in the future, the giver of all benefits.

Let us consider what the words of this verse contain. There is an “abundance of sweetness” because the Lord’s graciousness is indicated by many rewards. He is sweet when he corrects, sweet when he spares, sweet when he promises eternal rewards to believers. But understand that he is sweet only to those who have tasted his flavor. His sweetness cannot reach those who have not been worthy to experience his taste, as another psalm also says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9).

It follows: “which you have stored up for those who fear you.” This does not mean that it has been hidden from the saints so that they might not attain it, but that what is experienced here as hidden is promised to be revealed in the future judgment. We rightly understand it as hidden so that human desires may seek it more eagerly, since everything accessible is liable to become tiresome, and what is granted without difficulty is often considered worthless.

But the expression “you have hidden” is an instance of *homonymon*; it also signifies “you have denied,” as in the passage: “I give you thanks, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25).

Verse 24. And you have perfected it for those who hope in you, in the sight of the children of men. He perfects that sweetness which he had hidden for those who fear him in those who seek it eagerly with steadfast spirit. For this is truly to hope: to presume upon something with firm integrity of mind. He also adds: “in the sight of the children of men,” that is, in the general resurrection, when he will restore to his saints the rewards he promised and make all nations recognize that his words were wholly trustworthy.

Verse 25. You will hide them in the secret place of your face [ed., “in the hidden place”], from the disturbance of men.

Verse 26. You will protect them in your tabernacle, from the contradiction of tongues.

Verse 27. Blessed is the Lord, because he has made his mercy wondrous in the city of the surrounding region. He now proceeds to enumerate the benefits which the Lord, in abundant compassion, bestows upon his saints. This most noble rhetorical form is called *synatroesmos*, in Latin “gathering,” where many crimes or many benefits are collected into one. It is counted among the most forceful figures, because the gathering of things gives greater force to the case.

Continuing his exposition of the Lord’s sweetness, he says first: “You will hide them in the secret place of your face, from the disturbance of men”; second: “You will protect them in your tabernacle, from the contradiction of tongues”; third, he completes the fullness of this benefit with evident praise, saying: “Blessed is the Lord, because he has made his mercy wondrous in the city of the surrounding region.”

Let us now come to the explanation of the words. By “the secret place of the Lord’s face” he means the other resurrection, when all the righteous will receive the rewards of contemplating him, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

By “from the disturbance of men,” namely, evil men, he also says that the most faithful will be hidden when they have already been placed in eternal blessedness, where no one with a filthy will disturbs the purest truth, but the goodness of all things remains in its splendor. How beautifully he says that the royal presence is in a hidden place! Truly, because the impious will not see the contemplation of him in which the righteous will rejoice.

Here, all persecutors and schismatics are signified by “men,” for they are accustomed in this world to terrify the Christian people. But when that place has been reached, he says that the disturbances of the wicked will no longer have any place against God’s servants, since they are certainly to be separated from them. The wicked are sent into eternal punishment; the righteous are called to everlasting rest.

But lest the promise of so great a future reward disturb fragile hearts, he says in the second part that they are to be protected. For, as we have often said, “tabernacle” frequently signifies the Catholic Church, which endures struggles in this world and is called by the name of a temporary or campaign dwelling. Above he said, “you will hide”; here, “you will protect.” There they will be hidden, where they are not seen by the impious; here they are protected, where the wickedness of evil people is not at all permitted to harm them, since the unharmed souls of the righteous are preserved under every affliction of the body.

Thirdly, the heavenly man—the Lord Christ, who is also the Mediator—rejoices with spiritual joy, because through the incarnation of the Word saving gifts have come to the world. We should understand “the city of the surrounding region” as the earthly Jerusalem, which, established in the midst of the nations, was shown to exist like a temple of faith. From it the surrounding nations were deemed worthy to receive the rules of Christian doctrine; and, as though from a pure spring laid open, they were watered with the gifts of heavenly life.

In this city, therefore, the Lord made his mercy wondrous when he deigned there to teach, there to perform miracles, and there to suffer for the salvation of human beings. There also he displayed the glory of his resurrection, so that it was rightly said that he made his wondrous power manifest in Jerusalem, where he chose to reveal such great mysteries.

Verse 28. But I said in my fear, “I have been cast away from the sight of your eyes.” The Son says this to the Father in the form of a servant: “I hoped,” because I feared that your grace would abandon me when the anguish of the Passion prevailed, in the fear, certainly, of death. “From the sight of your eyes” means “from the presence of your mercy.” He beautifully attributes a face to the eyes, because the eyes especially signify the dispositions of the soul. The word “face” is derived from the fact that it reveals what the heart wills through its signs. Thus the eyes of the Divinity, when they look upon us, promise his grace.

Verse 29. Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer, when I cried out to you. He says that he was heard by the Lord because, humbly and not despairingly, in the manner of humanity, he said that he was despised. His grace could not be delayed, since of him the paternal voice was destined to say: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

“When I cried out to you”: when, in his Passion, he said with a loud voice, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). It is clear that he was heard through these cries, since he attained the glory of the resurrection and was placed at the right hand of the Father.

Verse 30. Love the Lord, all his saints. Having completed a hymn for the benefits bestowed upon them, he admonishes the saints to love the Lord, so that the members may love the author of so great a benefit, recognizing that it was bestowed upon them in their Head. “Love the Lord,” he says, now as friends, not as servants. It is the role of servants to fear, but of friends to love, as he himself says in the Gospel: “If you do what I command you, I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:14–15). He gives this command to the saints because loving the Lord belongs to them, since they do not love the world.

Verse 31. For the Lord will seek out truth, and he will repay those who act arrogantly in abundance. Lest anyone think that the Lord could disregard the blasphemies of heretics, he says: “The Lord will seek out truth,” which they do not know, being entangled in false errors. It follows: “and he will repay those who act arrogantly in abundance.” He investigates in order to avenge; he seeks in order to punish.

He appropriately adds “in abundance,” because he will not repay those who turn back through swift amendment, but the proud who sin copiously and despise the Lord’s commandments with wicked presumption must without doubt be cut off in those very things. Here, however, we must not understand “arrogance” as one single vice, since from arrogance arises whatever is committed in the perversity of morals. For it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15). It is therefore rightly established that this name is assigned to all vices, because he takes vengeance not only upon the arrogant but also upon all who attack the rule of holy conduct.

Verse 32. Act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord. Here the force of the entire psalm and the usefulness of the sacred Passion are gathered together. After saying, “Love the Lord, his saints”—the one who granted your Head both crucifixion and the glory of resurrection—he finally says by way of a definitive sentence: “Act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord.” This means that they should not be terrified by the Passion foretold above, but should strengthen their hearts for the glorious imitation of the faithful, knowing that it had been introduced beneficially for the healing of the world.

This figure is called *epiphonema*, that is, “acclamation,” which, after events have been narrated, breaks out briefly with an exclamation. Therefore this exhortation is directed to the good, so that they may not withdraw from their good purpose because of the weakness of the flesh. “Act courageously” means: persevere most steadfastly in good works, and do not fail through the softness characteristic of women, you who constantly offer your hearts to the Lord.

The breasts of those who endure are strengthened in this way, if they confirm their hope in the Lord’s power. This command, however, is common to men and women: every sex acts courageously when it does not allow itself to be changed by the softest concessions. Observe also how he has preserved those parts of the Passion throughout the entire psalm. First he spoke of prayer; then the Passion followed; finally he admonished the joy and steadfastness of the faithful, lest, after receiving such a gift, hesitation hostile to faith should prevail any longer.

Conclusion of the Psalm

The beneficial and beautiful composition of so great a psalm has been completed. In it the weakness of humanity is expressed and divine benefits are displayed, so that, considering his own fragility, no one may grow proud, while, looking upon divine mercy, no one may be terrified in any way.

The number of the psalm also reveals the summit of an elevated reckoning and promises rewards to faithful union, so that when the blessed soul joins itself to this teaching through a holy manner of life, it may grow rich through a thirtyfold recompense. Other mysteries also correspond to this number. Joseph is read to have been thirty years old when he was established as lord in Egypt. Our Savior, likewise thirty years old, consecrated vital baptism by being immersed in the waters of the Jordan. In these decades also there is the Holy Trinity, which grants the inviolable rule of our faith and salvation.

EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXI

David: Understanding

Since all the psalms are generally said to be directed toward understanding, so that our mind might recognize them and not remain ignorant of the rules of living, it is rightly asked why he placed “David: Understanding” in this title.

First, he mentions David on account of the Lord Christ, since whatever this penitent is going to say refers to him. Then “understanding” follows because, unless, with the Lord’s mercy assisting us, we understand our sins, we cannot devote ourselves to repentance. For it is said in another psalm: “Who understands offenses?” (Psalm 18:13). This is what “understanding” means: when the Divinity grants us understanding of our sins, we earnestly plead for them to be washed away. For who pleads concerning an error that he completely ignores?

Moreover, since the Lord Christ will speak in the fourth part, he begins in the first verse as follows: “I will give you understanding.” Thus, because of the merit of this penitent, “understanding” has been placed beforehand in the title, and it is also promised to him by the divine voice.

Although there are other psalms of penitents, they have nevertheless been marked by different meanings in their titles because of the subtlety of their distinctions. The first, which is placed as the sixth, contains the title “For the end, in hymns, for the eighth, a psalm of David,” because it pertains entirely to the fear of the future judgment. This one, however, is rightly marked with such a title because he realized only belatedly that he had deteriorated: he confesses that he remained silent for too long about sins that ought immediately to have been disclosed to the Lord.

The principal status of this case is *concessio*, which is granted to all penitents. *Concessio* occurs when everything is conceded to the adversaries and the defendant is defended solely by submissive tears.

Division of the Psalm

In the first part of the psalm the penitent speaks, plainly acknowledging his sin and imposing upon himself the punishment merited by strict judgment, because he believed that his guilty deeds should be concealed. Here the beginning and the narrative are briefly contained.

In the second part there is only correction: having condemned himself by his own confession, he believes that the Lord will spare him. In the third part, commending the good things of repentance, he also asserts that the saints plead with the Lord in this world, in whom he rightly testifies that his refuge lies; here the words of this penitent also end.

In the fourth part, the Lord Christ responds to his words and promises to surround those who hope in him with mercy, lest the integrity of the suppliant be thought to have been neglected through any dissimulation. These four parts are divided by intervening *diapsalms*. It is our purpose to follow them in the divisions.

Exposition of the Psalm

Verse 1. Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. This penitent, recognizing his own deeds and following the example of that tax collector who, beating his breast, did not raise his eyes to heaven (Luke 18:13), sighing with all his strength from a humbled heart, did not presume to invoke the Majesty. Instead, he calls blessed those whose iniquities have been forgiven, desiring the absolution of sins but not daring to ask for the same things for himself. He therefore rightly calls blessed those who had already been deemed worthy of these gifts.

This is the eighth species of definition, called in Greek κατὰ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου, “by the privation of the opposite.” For sins are contrary to blessedness. And because he says here “forgiven,” the blessed man is fittingly expressed under this formula of definition.

Saint Jerome makes this distinction between “iniquities” and “sins” in this psalm: he calls “iniquities” those committed before the reception of faith, whether through ignorance or knowingly; but he defines “sins” as those contracted after knowledge of the faith or the grace of baptism.

Verse 2. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin, and there is no deceit in his mouth. This blessed man is also embraced by the same species of definition. But we must know that there are some to whom sins are reckoned, as it was said to Paul: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4); and to the adulterous woman in the Gospel: “Go, and sin no more” (John 8:11).

It is equally clear that there are others to whom he does not reckon sins, such as Job, concerning whom it was said: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a just and simple man who fears God?” (Job 2:3); and Nathanael, of whom he says: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

Therefore he chose that portion which he desired, in which he would not be troubled by any anxiety. All nevertheless attain these gifts through the grace of divine mercy, as the apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

It follows: “to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin,” namely, in whose mouth there is no deceit. That is, he is one who gives himself no indulgence and, though a sinner, does not proclaim himself most holy—a disease from which humanity especially suffers—but rather recognizes his own offenses and continually perseveres in the humility of satisfaction. The one who displeases himself is pleasing to the Lord; for when we blame ourselves, it is truthful speech, but when we wish to praise ourselves, it is falsehood.

Thus far these were the opening statements, in which he desired to obtain the mercy of the good Judge through profound humility. But we do not place a division in this section, because we follow the *diapsalms*, which are known to be divided by the silence of the Holy Spirit; in this way we can preserve them and yet omit nothing here.

Verse 3. Because I kept silent, all my bones grew old while I cried out all day. Having completed the introduction briefly, as was appropriate, this penitent now comes to a very concise narrative. Some have rightly called the narrative the heart, others the soul, of a case, because through it everything contained in the substance of legal matters is recognized.

He says: “Because I did not confess my offense to you, all my strength grew weak through infirmity,” like a bodily wound which, if it is not opened for treatment, is kept concealed until it becomes putrid. As we have often said, bones signify the firmness of the soul; they are rightly said to have grown old because the ulcer had not been disclosed to the healing physician.

It follows: “while I cried out all day.” Above he says that he kept silent; here he again declares that he cried out. But he kept silent before the Divinity, to whom he ought continually to have offered supplication. He cried out because, over a long period of time, he spoke about his own justification. Thus he kept silent about what it was lawful to say and spoke about what he ought to have kept silent. In this way both became culpable, although they appear different.

Remember, however, that the entire force of this psalm is directed against this accursed vice of the human race, lest anyone think that what he hides in the innermost recesses of his conscience is concealed from the Lord.

Verse 4. Because day and night your hand was heavy upon me. For a sinner, the hand that scourges is heavy, and the hand that avenges is weighty. “Day and night” signifies continuous time; it was therefore rightly felt to be heavy, since it did not withdraw from the burden of correction. He could not otherwise have been beneficially humbled unless the hand of the Divinity had pressed upon him.

By a tropological interpretation, “hand” signifies action, because human beings customarily work with their hands. The Divinity, however, does not accomplish anything with hands; by the power of his will he orders and completes all things.

Verse 5. I have been turned into misery while my spine is being broken. This is what he said above: “Your hand was heavy upon me.” One who is miserable is described as utterly ruined. Ruin is so called as though it were a return to the depths.
