He had therefore been turned into misery because he had fallen from pride, so that the one who had previously cried out through arrogance might now confess to the Lord through humility. His hope of salvation returned for this reason: he recognized the death-dealing deeds in his own works.

The spine is what raises and holds together the entire body. It is appropriately set here for pride. When broken, it does not cast one down into destruction but rather raises one toward salvation. This argument is called one “from necessity,” when the gravest causes are placed first so that a corrected mind may be led to a fruitful confession.

Verse 6. I made my offense known to you, and I did not cover my iniquity. Just as he said above from what he had been wounded, so now, entering the second part, he reports from what he received healing, by the Lord’s generosity.

O ingenious simplicity, and purity more cautious than a thousand evasive arguers! He is said to have made his offense known to one from whom nothing is hidden, to whom the case cries out more loudly than the tongue, and who, even if he does not hear from a human being, knows everything more certainly than the one who does it. But “to make known” means to bring one’s offenses into confession.

To cover something is to conceal it deeply in silence or to hide it through dissimulation of the heart. Fools do this, believing that God can be ignorant of what they do. Those who know, on the contrary, that he has all things manifest descend to humble confession and the vows of repentance, lest they find the Judge hostile when they could have him as a merciful advocate.

Some have thought that an offense is a light sin, as though something carelessly abandoned, while iniquity is something enormous and savage that has been committed. Here, however, the purity of the confessor is shown: he did not conceal even what was believed likely to be venial.

Verse 7. I said, “I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord”; and you forgave the impiety of my heart [MSS A, B, F: “of my sin”]. Here the great mercy of the Divinity is shown: at the mere promise of devotion he suddenly loosened the sins, since he judges a pious intention as though it were the completion of an act.

He said in his heart that he would not remain silent before the Lord about what he had done; and, as though he had already disclosed everything, those things he intended to confess were forgiven him. This is rightly so, since mere intention can either absolve or condemn a person.

“I will declare” means “I will confess publicly,” so that a pious and faithful confession may draw others to imitation. There follows a salutary remedy in self-accusation, when the Judge spared the defendant because the defendant did not spare himself. The impiety of his heart lay in the fact that he had decided to remain silent, thinking himself concealed from the one who can know everything before it happens.

Verse 8. For this every saint will pray to you at an opportune time. Having completed his beginning, narrative, and satisfaction, he comes to the conclusion of his supplication. Here he commends the request for pardon in such a way that he says it is shared by all the saints: rightly so, because whoever is not free from sins ought to be included in supplications.

O saving medicine! Against the diseases of all sinners, various remedies are supplied to the sick; but if this one antidote is taken with a pure mind, the poisons of every sin are overcome. He adds: “at an opportune time,” namely, in this life of the world, where conversion is permitted. For in hell, as was said above in the sixth psalm, no one confesses profitably to the Lord.

Verse 9. Nevertheless, in the flood of many waters, they shall not approach him. After testifying above that the saints pray continually, he now denies that this devotion is granted to various superstitions. The “flood of many waters” is the error of very wicked people, who, tossed about by various depraved tendencies, establish multiple doctrines for themselves which they have in no way received from the true Teacher.

This judgment especially condemns heretics, who in the flood of their perversity raise stormy and shipwrecked controversies. They will not approach him, because they depart from true religion.

This figure is called *metaphora*, that is, “transference,” when a name or verb is moved from the place where it is proper to one in which either the proper term is lacking or the transferred term is better than the proper one.

### Verse 10

“You are my refuge from the distress that surrounded me; my exultation, redeem me from those surrounding me.”

A refuge is a place to which one flees so that dangers may be avoided. But this man did not hasten to inaccessible solitudes, fortified military camps, or human assistance; rather, he fled to God, who was able to disperse the spiritual enemies encircling him. Then he calls the Lord his joy, knowing that he would be spared by him. For when he says, “Redeem me,” does that one give gold in order to set him free? Rather, he gave precious blood, which cannot be compared with any riches or resources.

But let us investigate somewhat more carefully what these words announce to us. When he says, “My exultation,” he appears to be professing the benefit he has received. When he adds, “Redeem me,” he still indicates the fear of one who is in danger. But because he was already rejoicing in hope and still fearing in reality, the two expressions are appropriately joined. We can rejoice in spirit when we know that present evils are destined to end very quickly.

He added, “from those surrounding me,” whether these are carnal vices or unclean spirits, who hasten with headlong speed to destroy us. The conclusion of the penitent has ended in fear of present things and hope of those to come.

Come, advocates, who handle human cases with elaborate subtlety. See the accused washing himself clean with tears; hear the sinner absolved by confessions; understand that the sentence of the judge does not attack the salvation of the man, but rather condemns his sins. These are tribunals that no one bribes; this is a sentence that decides nothing ambiguously.

In this manner, then, defend your cases: you who, by denying the truth, are accustomed to mix your offenses with your crimes. Reverse the order of secular courts. Begin your plea with the epilogues; narrate your perverse wretchedness tearfully; immediately and truthfully announce your correction; and now you deserve to conclude joyfully what you began happily amid tears. From this you will understand how different this saving order is, since nothing opposed can withstand what ends in joy.

Now let us see, in the neighboring section, what the Lord himself answers him.

### Verse 11

“I will give you understanding, and I will instruct you in this way in which you will walk; I will fix my eyes upon you.”

He has arrived at the fourth section, where the Lord’s speech sprinkles us like a honey-sweet rain. But let us consider how fittingly and mercifully Christ is introduced as speaking, so that, with the judge himself making the promise, hope might appear more certain to penitents.

But what does he say first? “I will give you understanding.” You see that sinners do not possess understanding unless the Lord, propitiated toward those who have turned back, graciously grants it to them. For to understand means to act well and to turn one’s desires toward the commandments of God. This is the very understanding indicated by the truth of the title, which the Lord’s power mercifully pours into penitents.

He added, “And I will instruct you”: as though you were ignorant, I will teach you; as though you were unarmed, I will gird you with the sword of saving life. Previously, when he kept silent about his offenses before the Lord, he had been deprived of counsel; now he is instructed, when, by the Lord’s favor, he is admonished to pronounce judgment against himself.

O immeasurable medicine of repentance, which not only absolves from sins but also grants the blessed rewards of the saints!

The way is that in which he had entered to serve the Lord, after the wickedness of his former conduct had been condemned: the way that has no error except when one departs from it; the way of peace and truth, along which blessed virtues travel and to which no appearance of perversity draws near.

It follows: “I will fix my eyes upon you,” that is, “I will direct toward you the light of my understanding.” For whoever is rightly wise and fulfills the Lord’s commandments with a sincere mind is rightly said to have the Lord’s eyes fixed upon him. Therefore let us observe with what glory the humility of penitents is exalted, so that they hear that the Lord’s eyes have been fixed upon them when they hasten to desire to satisfy him.

### Verse 12

“Do not become like a horse and a mule, in which there is no understanding.”

### Verse 13

“With bit and bridle restrain their jaws.”

Here he admonishes the human race in general not to be subjected to wandering errors. But let us examine why these comparisons have been introduced.

A horse, without the rider’s discernment, serves the rider’s will, and wherever anyone mounts it, it rushes off. A mule, however, patiently accepts the burdens with which it has been loaded. For this reason neither has understanding: the one does not choose whom it should obey, and the other does not understand with what burdens it is being weighed down.

He therefore prohibits such people from being ensnared by diabolical deceits and oppressed by the burdens of vices, lest, through wrongful obedience, they become more committed to the party of pride.

But what does he say should be done to such people? Clearly, what is done to imprudent animals. Through these comparisons he has subjected foolish people to the truth against their will. For when he says “with bit,” he refers to the horse. The word *frenum* (“bit”) is said to derive from restraining a wild animal (*a fero retinendo*); for the ancients called a horse *ferum*. “With bridle” refers to the mule. Thus these two animals mentioned above are restrained by these reins, so that they proceed according to the will of the one giving orders and are not carried away by their own desires.

Jaws, moreover, are the animal’s instruments by which food is chewed so that the life of the body may be maintained. Therefore, by an allegorical figure, he says that the jaws of the disobedient must be restrained—that is, that supplies of food should be given more sparingly, so that, confined by the necessity of fasting, they may be subjected to the authority of the Creator.

For allegory is, as has often already been said, when one thing is said and another is signified. And since we have said that in this section the Lord Christ is speaking, he says to the Father, “Restrain,” because the Holy Trinity has one will, one power, and one cooperation.

### Verse 14

“Many are the scourges of sinners who do not draw near to you.”

He still continues with the comparisons mentioned above. For untamed animals must necessarily accept the bit and suffer the lash until they become accustomed to following the road by a straight course.

The order of the words is as follows: “Many are the scourges of those sinners who do not draw near to you.” But by saying “who do not draw near,” he shows that some sinners do draw near to the Lord. Although they sin through the weakness of the flesh, they nevertheless do not withdraw from devout prayers.

Those who depart from the Lord in a spirit of obstinacy, as though frightened by what is set before them and unwilling to travel along straight paths, endure many scourges, so that what they do not do willingly they may be compelled to accomplish when blows are applied. Yet these are scourges that heal us swiftly, free us quickly, and lead us onto the way of truth.

### Verse 15

“But mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord.”

Truly, divine justice promises scourges to those who do not hope, but mercy to those who hope in it, just as the prophet Ezekiel says:

“I am the Lord, who does not remember evils, provided only that a person turns away from his evil way and from all the iniquities he has committed, and he will live” (Ezekiel 18:28).

And he rightly said “will surround,” so that no place may be left through which the hostility of the devil could enter them.

### Verse 16

“Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright of heart.”

Here a categorical syllogism can be constructed, so that the rules of the dialectical art may be recalled, like runaway slaves, into a kind of service to the divine Scriptures:

Every righteous person rejoices in the Lord.  
Everyone who rejoices in the Lord is upright of heart.  
Therefore every righteous person is upright of heart.

Let us remember, however, that syllogisms should not be employed too frequently, since a diligent reader finds very often in the Holy Scriptures material from which he can draw them and place them into the form of comparison mentioned above. It is sufficient that, though more rarely, we have shown that the divine Scriptures contain this branch of the logical arts—not in outward form, certainly, but unmistakably in power.

He admonishes us according to rule not to rejoice in ourselves, but in the Lord. For whoever rejoices in himself is deceived by a deceptive presumption, as has often been said; but whoever rejoices in the Lord enjoys perpetual delight.

To rejoice (*laetari*) is to be soothed by the sweetness of a silent mind. To exult (*exsultare*) is to rejoice with the fervor of an excited spirit.

It follows: “And glory, all you upright of heart.” Here too, by the figure *ἀπὸ κοινοῦ* (*apo koinou*), that is, “from what is common,” the phrase should be joined as “glory in the Lord”: understand that you are subject to him, and entrust your freedom or your honor to his service, since you know that through it you attain the rewards of eternal blessedness.

It must also be considered that, for the sake of variety, he previously said “the righteous,” and now “the upright of heart.” All the righteous are upright of heart, and, conversely, the upright of heart are without doubt the most righteous. Therefore, since these terms cannot be divided, there is no doubt that the variation has been introduced for the sake of stylistic variety. Repetition of the same words is the mother of satiety.

Let us consider what this penitent deserved, so that the one to whom he had earnestly pleaded might answer him openly. The man who had shortly before lain prostrate, the man who had been crushed beneath the weight of his sins, is numbered among the righteous and received among the upright of heart, so that, the more he had previously been humbled by making satisfaction, the more exalted he might afterward appear once forgiven. Therefore he is already blessed, since here he is known to have been absolved by the sentence of the most merciful judge.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us now consider the power of this psalm: by pleading in ten verses, it merited a divine response without any delay. Perhaps it recalls the work of the Decalogue, so that, just as the guarded law calls one to a reward, so this prayer poured out from a contrite heart may lead us to the desires of forgiveness.

Let us therefore read attentively and lament with contrition of heart. For what should be meditated upon with greater eagerness than that psalm in which sins have been loosed by the voice of so great a judge?

This psalm contains something especially remarkable and unique: whereas other penitents rejoice at the conclusion of a psalm through the prompting of divine compunction, here he himself promises mercy, he himself promises joy—the very one to whom supplication is made with great longing.

Therefore he must be asked continually and with welcome persistence, since he also promises us in the Gospel by the preceding parable:

“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke 11:9–10).

Who, then, I ask, ought now to distrust the most faithful supplication, when royal mercy has deigned to strengthen us with a threefold promise?

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 32

### A Psalm of David

This title is entirely familiar, and therefore the reader should follow the earlier exposition concerning it. Nevertheless, we must necessarily point out that in this psalm the prophet exhorts the faithful Church to psalmody through certain comparisons, enumerating the power and works of the Creator, so that, when it recognizes his strength and mercy, it may hasten more eagerly to praise him.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. But in the first section he admonishes the righteous that they ought to rejoice in the Lord with complete gladness of mind, since he is recognized as sustaining his creatures with wondrous power. In the second section he exclaims that blessed is the one who has merited to belong to his worship, signifying the Christian times in which a multitude of nations was destined to believe.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord; praise is fitting for the upright.”

Blessed David, separating the Catholic Church from the contamination of heretics, admonishes upright Christians that they should not rejoice in earthly pleasures, but always rejoice in the Lord, where joys are perfected in continual sweetness.

For when the afflictions of the present age befit the faithful, it is said to the righteous: “Rejoice.” But with what joy, unless with that by which the Lord admonishes us:

“When people persecute you and say every evil thing against you falsely on account of me, rejoice and exult, because your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matthew 5:11).

So too the Apostle repeatedly affirms that we ought to rejoice. For he says: “Rejoice in the Lord; again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4:4). This repetition signifies that here we should rejoice amid afflictions, while in that kingdom we shall rejoice in perpetual peace.

Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

He also added: “Praise is fitting for the upright.” Who these upright people are, he will say in the second section. For by saying “praise is fitting for the upright,” he shows that it cannot be fitting for wicked heretics, just as another prophet says: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15:9).

“Praise” (*collaudatio*) is one praise from the mouths of many, spoken on account of the unity of the Church, which he everywhere teaches must be preserved. When he says “is fitting,” he signifies that it is suitable and appropriate: whoever sings the Lord’s praise should likewise please him through uprightness of faith and integrity of conduct.

### Verse 2

“Give thanks to the Lord on the lyre; sing psalms to him on the ten-stringed psaltery.”

These are the righteous whom he mentioned above, those who sing the Lord’s praises with devoted melody through holy actions.

The lyre, as has already been said in the preface, is a hollow cavity situated at the bottom of a wooden body, sending the strings upward and speaking through the sweetest sounds when struck. It received this name because it is struck with rapid repetition.

Works that are extended from earthly matters toward heavenly grace are rightly compared to it: when we feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and perform other acts which, although they may appear carnal, are nevertheless carried out for the love of the Divinity.

We also play the lyre when, amid our sufferings or losses, we say confidently or joyfully: “The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as it pleased the Lord, so it happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

We have said that the psaltery is ten-stringed. In reverse arrangement, it has the body of the lyre above, from which the sonorous strings descend toward the lower part. The commandments of the Decalogue appropriately correspond to it, because, according to the form of this instrument, we have received the Lord’s commands coming from above.

And consider that it is the only musical instrument called “ten-stringed” on account of its excellence. We do not remember reading this of the lyre or of any other such instruments.

The ten-stringed psaltery, as the ancients said, also indicates that mystery to us, so that we refer three commandments to God, who is Trinity:

First: “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:4).

Second: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image.”

Third: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain,” in which he also joins the commandment concerning the Sabbath.

The seven that follow, they said, pertain to love of one’s neighbor:

“Honor your father and your mother”; “You shall not kill”; “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not steal”; “You shall not speak false witness against your neighbor”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife,” and so forth.

Thus the complete power of the ten-stringed psaltery is shown to us as perfect and honorable.

We also sing with ten strings when we conduct ourselves commendably through the five bodily senses and the five spiritual senses. Yet these things of which we speak are not placed outside us, as in the discipline of music. The lyre is within us; the psaltery is within us. Indeed, we ourselves are the instruments when, by the Lord’s grace, we sing in imitation of them through the quality of our actions.

This is also made clear by that passage which says: “In me, God, are vows; I will render praises to you” (Psalm 55:12). These and similar expressions, as we have often said, are stated through figurative allusions.

### Verse 3

“Sing to him a new song; sing well to him with jubilation” [manuscripts A, B, F: “with shouting”].

He calls the incarnation of the Lord a new song, by which the world was filled with saving exultation, by which the angels resounded with melodious voices, praising and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

He therefore admonishes us that we too ought both to say and to believe the same thing.

It follows: “Sing well to him with jubilation,” that is, invoke God through good works. For jubilation is joy expressed with fervor of spirit and with a shout of indistinct voice. No one can sing well in this jubilation unless he adds a devotion to good conduct.

Observe the saving teaching that warns us to sing before God without offense, since he knows our kidneys and our hearts, lest we be able to offend more seriously by appearing to approach such great mysteries as criminals and deceivers.

### Verse 4

“For the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faithfulness.”

Here he begins, through the demonstrative genre, to traverse the Lord’s praises by various accounts, so that all his works and commandments might become sweet to us.

The word of the Lord is therefore upright, namely, for directing human beings. For he is truly called upright who makes people upright. This is a marvelous epithet, a truth-speaking word.

Through the divine law we are corrected; through it we are separated from our perversity. We live according to rule when we obey its commands.

This is the fifth kind of definition, which the Greeks call *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν* (*kata tēn lexin*), which in Latin we call “word for word.” The definition of what the word of the Lord is has been given in a single part of speech: namely, “upright.”

He adds: “And all his works are in faithfulness,” certainly when he works in those who have merited to be faithful through his gift, as he says in the Gospel: “Your faith has saved you” (Luke 7:50). For that woman would not have merited the works of the Lord unless faith had preceded through gratuitous generosity.

### Verse 5

“He loves mercy and judgment; the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.”

In this and the following verses, through the third kind of definition, which is called in Greek *ποιότης* (*poiotes*) and in Latin “qualitative,” he describes the Lord by narrating what he has done or what he does daily.

For we are said to love those things which we do more frequently. Thus the Lord is sung of here: “He loves mercy and judgment,” as though he did not also love prudence and temperance. But because he frequently grants this mercy to us, he is said to love it altogether.

In this world he loves mercy, where he spreads it far and wide: where he bears with sinners, patiently awaits blasphemers, grants life to the unworthy, and performs similar acts which clearly belong in every way to heavenly compassion.

He also loves judgment, when he separates the devout from the wicked and distinguishes their merits according to the quality of justice.

Next he states where he dispenses the mercy mentioned above: “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” This earth certainly contains the wretched: here we struggle under the devil’s assault; here we are held back from heavenly commandments by the weakness of the flesh.

When, then, can we seek mercy more appropriately than here, where we are already burdened by every kind of necessity? Let us seek mercy here, since the whole earth is filled with it.

### Verse 6

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power.”

Although this verse may also seem to concern the creation of things, it is nevertheless suitably understood in a spiritual sense.

“By the word of the Lord,” that is, by the Son of God, the heavens were established: namely, the apostles or saints were strengthened, those who would fill the world with saving preaching.

It follows: “And by the breath of his mouth all their power,” certainly because their teaching came from the Holy Spirit. Their power refers both to the miracles they performed and to the law of the Lord that they preached to the nations.

If we examine the passage more carefully, it also signifies the Holy Trinity. By saying “word,” he indicates the Son; by adding “of the Lord,” he names the Father; and by saying “the breath of his mouth,” he wishes the Holy Spirit to be understood, who proceeded from the Father before the ages.

And so that you might understand a manifest unity in the three persons, he said “his,” not “their.”

### Verse 7

“Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin; placing the depths in treasuries.”

When he says, “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin,” if you wish to understand it literally, he signifies the sea enclosed by shores.

But if you wish to recognize it spiritually, a wineskin is the stripped hide of an animal, which serves human purposes by collecting liquids. This wineskin is compared with the Church, because just as it contains the waters or something similar that it has received, so the Church encloses the unity of the believing people.

The waters of the sea signify the Christian people, who are shaken by alternating waves in the salt sea of the world.

We call the abyss something exceedingly deep, whose depth does not allow human sight to descend into it. Therefore he places profound depths in his treasuries—that is, in the treasuries of wisdom and knowledge—so that he may test whoever seeks his Scriptures with devout diligence.

### Verse 8

“Let all the earth fear the Lord; and let all who inhabit the world be moved by him.”

Here “earth” signifies, in every respect, the hardened sinner, who is rightly called earth because he is deprived of the abundance of heavenly grace.

Therefore let this earthly sinner, who does not know how to love, fear the Lord, so that, if he does not abstain from sins out of desire for rewards, he may at least be recalled by consideration of punishment.

By saying “by him,” he indicates that the sinner is also moved by the devil, of whom Isaiah says: “This is the one who shook the earth” (Isaiah 14:16).

Therefore the prophet rightly asks that everything be moved by the Lord, because everything arranged by his ordinance is always applied to useful purposes. But although he had first said “everything” in general, he now descends to human beings. For although all things require administration according to his command, this is especially true of the human race, which, corrupted from its nature by encroaching vices, is shown to be subject to sins.

### Verse 9

“For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created.”

He gives the reason why everything should be moved by the Lord: namely, because he himself is their creator, and the one who deigned to create existing things through grace must administer them beneficially.

“He spoke, and they came to be” signifies the beginning of things, when all things burst forth at the command of his Son.

“He commanded, and they were created”: he certainly commanded the law through the prophets, through which the faithful were created by the Lord’s will.

You see how savingly the prophet asked God that everything be moved, since he alone can be merciful toward his creatures.

### Verse 10

“The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations; he rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and he rejects the counsels of princes.”

He truly scatters counsels that are evil or very wicked; for he always assists and confirms what is good. The words are joined very appropriately to their subjects.

He scattered the counsels of the nations when he did not permit them to remain any longer in the worship of idols.

He rejected the thoughts of the peoples because, although the wicked will of the Jews was fulfilled in the Lord’s death, it is nevertheless established to have been rejected by his resurrection.

And because he had spoken of nations and peoples, lest he seem to leave anything untouched, he afterward also speaks of princes: either tyrants who attacked the Lord’s law through savage persecutions, or unclean spirits whose counsel is always directed toward evil.

### Verse 11

“But the counsel of the Lord remains forever; the thoughts of his heart from age to age.”

Just as he said that the wicked counsels of human beings would be frustrated, so now he says that the Lord’s decrees remain forever.

For sinful and mortal human beings understand transitory things, whereas the eternal Lord establishes nothing deserving of reproach, as Isaiah says: “All my counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish everything that I have thought” (Isaiah 46:10).

Jeremiah says the same: “If my covenant were not established by day and by night, I would not have appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 33:25).

We rightly understand his counsel as the mystery of the incarnation, which was granted for the salvation of the human race. This mystery is not dissolved by any age but remains forever, because the Lord’s triumphant death permanently extinguished the devil’s destruction.

“The thoughts of his heart” signify predestination, in which all things are stored: those that have been and those that will follow in the ages to come. It bears the order of things, which remains from age to age.

Those who falsely assert one nature in Christ the Lord rightly yield to this statement. For if his counsel is stable and the thoughts of his heart remain from age to age, and if the mystery of the incarnation was his thought and his counsel, then it is necessary that the form of the assumed humanity—the one Son in two distinct, perfect, and united natures—should exist forever, just as it began in the unity of his person.

### Verse 12

“Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord; the people whom he chose as his inheritance.”

He has come to the second member, in which he will state who the upright are, or whom the Lord’s praise befits, as he proposed in the first verse.

He therefore speaks of a nation belonging to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is known to be united from all nations. It is truly blessed, since God is rightly worshiped by it and the Lord of all is adored—that is, the one who protects and governs them.

An inheritance is so called both when something is transferred to another and when it is acquired. But the Christian people are an inheritance of acquisition, not of transfer, because their author possesses them, having acquired them through holy preaching and precious blood.

### Verse 13

“The Lord looked down from heaven and saw all the children of human beings.”

Here the future coming of the Lord is expressed through a figure called in Greek *ἰδέα* (*idea*) and in Latin *species* (“form” or “appearance”). Through it, as though presenting the likeness of a future event to our eyes, we stir the mind’s desire toward the effort of hearing.

“The Lord looked down from heaven” when he granted the coming of his own Son. For it was not the human being who looked toward the Lord; the Lord looked toward the human being.

To look down from above (*prospicere*) is to see what has been placed ahead. Humanity had truly been divided from God by sins and—something shameful to say—had been made distant from its Creator.

When he says “and saw,” he signifies the grace of the one who shows mercy. We say that he sees those to whom we also declare that something has been granted.

And consider that he does not say, “He saw sins,” but “the children of human beings.” When he looks upon sins, he punishes; when he looks upon the human being, he absolves. Thus he will say in Psalm 50: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Psalm 50:11), and elsewhere: “Do not turn your face away from me” (Psalm 142:7). Therefore this saving distinction must be understood and retained by us.

### Verse 14

“From his prepared dwelling he looked upon all who inhabit the world.”

He was speaking then of the future body of the Lord. For since all things that follow in their appointed order had been established in predestination, how much more is the miracle of his incarnation shown to have been arranged before the ages, since it could come to the aid of the world in danger, the world he had determined to create?

### Verse 15

“He who fashioned their hearts individually, who understands all their works.”

“He fashioned hearts,” to which he generously granted the gifts of his understanding. For we call those people *ceroplasts* who fashion certain forms according to the purposes of their work. In the same way, the Lord forms and arranges the minds of the righteous so as to lead them to the gifts of his mercy.

“Individually” means separately and distinctly.

“Their hearts” means the hearts of the saints who live under the fear of the Lord.

It follows: “Who understands all their works.” He understands them when he restores worthy rewards to the actions of the good.

By saying “all their works,” he signifies the thoughts, words, and deeds by which we continually perform either good or evil.

### Verse 16

“The king will not be saved by great strength, nor will the giant be saved by the abundance of his power” [manuscripts A, F: “will be saved”].

By “king” he means a self-controlled person who, although he rules his body by divine mercy, cannot be saved from carnal vices if he presumes upon his own strength.

Human strength is rightly abandoned when a good and perfect gift is attributed not to God, its giver, but to one’s own abilities.

He likewise wishes “giant” to be understood as one strengthened by the greatness of his virtues, who engages in continual combat against the devil’s monstrous power. He is rightly called a giant because he confronts such spirits.

But even this person, who, with God’s grace assisting him, already drives away many spirits, will not be safe if, lifted up by the vice of pride like a giant—which carries away fragile humanity—he presumes upon the strength of his merits.

Although *gigas* (“giant”) in Latin speech can mean “earthborn,” it is nevertheless clearly also used in a good sense. For it is written of Christ: “He exulted like a giant to run his course” (Psalm 18:6).

### Verse 17

“False is the horse for salvation; in the abundance of its strength it will not be saved.”

He uses “horse” for worldly prosperity, which carries human beings as though they were borne along by the prancing of horses.

This human hope deceives in the manner of a false horse: while it advances by tossing itself about, it suddenly encounters a fall that it does not expect.

He explains why the horse is false. While it seeks the open fields and mixes its feet together in hasty speed, it cannot preserve the safety of its rider, because things that are excessively impetuous are incautious. Whoever does not advance with moderation is always exposed to ruinous accidents.

The horse is called false because it is accustomed to deceive those who presume upon it.

### Verse 18

“Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, who hope in his mercy.”

“The eyes of the Lord” are used for the divine will, because we unquestionably look upon those whom we regard favorably; conversely, we turn our gaze away from those who have become hateful to our minds.

Therefore the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, because his compassion protects those whom he knows to fear him.

But since he has spoken of those who fear, he appropriately follows with those who love, because both are joined in love of the Lord. Whoever fears and loves God rightly loves and fears rightly. These things are divided in human actions; in heavenly devotion, however, they are joined together.

He explains who the fearful are: namely, those “who hope in his mercy.” This argument is called an argument from accompanying features, since fearing the Lord and hoping in him are joined things, connected by mutual and unbreakable fellowship.

### Verse 19

“To rescue their souls from death and feed them in famine.”

These are the two desires of the most faithful Christian: that at the future judgment he may be rescued from eternal death, and that here he may be sustained by spiritual nourishment.

He rescues the souls of the righteous from death when he removes them from the power of the devil, when through forgiveness he makes free those whom the condemnation of sin had made captives.

He feeds them in famine when, in this world, where there is a lack of good things, he does not cease to nourish with spiritual food those whom he has redeemed.

The word “nourishment” (*alimentum*) is derived, as it were, from “nourishment of the mind” (*mentis nutrimentum*). Those are placed in famine who continually kindle themselves with desire for heavenly things.

O famine that is greatly satisfied, and that is commendably always hungry without scarcity! The blessed hunger not because they are fasting from the Lord’s feast, but because by continually seeking they burn with desire, and because they advance through longing for the Lord, as the Evangelist says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

### Verse 20

“But our soul awaits the Lord, because he is our helper and protector.”

When he says “awaits,” he signifies the Christian’s patience, so that the righteous, invited by future rewards, may persevere with steadfast spirit.

But let us understand what sort of virtue this is, which we are so often admonished to preserve. It is patience that makes glorious martyrs, guards the good of our faith, and conquers every adversity—not by wrestling, but by enduring; not by complaining, but by giving thanks.

It restrains deceptive luxury, conquers fiery anger, removes envy, which devastates the human race, makes people gentle, appropriately smiles upon the kind, and prepares purified people for those future rewards.

It is patience that wipes away the dregs of every pleasure; it is patience that makes souls clear. Through it we serve as soldiers of Christ; through it we conquer the devil; through it the blessed reach the kingdoms of heaven. For it is written: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

It follows: “Because he is our helper and protector.” He is a helper when, with his grace supporting us, we strive to approach him; he is a protector when we resist the adversary.

Therefore the person who awaits God is secure when strengthened by such a promise. And consider that he places patience after all the commandments, so that we may endure everything courageously, since we trust in the gift of so great a reward.

### Verse 21

“And our heart will rejoice in him, and we will hope in his holy name.”

Lest anyone murmur about the patience that has been proclaimed, lest anyone be troubled by weariness of will, there follows a magnificent and most delightful gift: expectation itself has its reward, when the one who waits rejoices in the Lord.

He added: “And we will hope in his holy name,” that is, in Christ, whom the most holy prophet patiently awaited and rejoiced that he was destined to come.

“We will hope” indicates continuous time, because it is not right to cease there from which the weary soul can always be restored.

### Verse 22

“Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us, just as we have hoped in you.” With these words he desired the Lord’s incarnation to be fulfilled, which he was most eagerly awaiting with fervent spirit. But consider how abundant a gift it is: it enriched the human race, filled the choirs of angels with the joy of gladness, and was even perceived by the depths of hell. For he asks that his desires be fulfilled, so that he may be found most perfect. He added “in you,” in order to exclude every superstition and every depravity while he was entreating the true Lord.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How honey-sweet were the voices we heard! How healthfully the heavenly Psalter sang to us! Such, indeed, were the chords of the commandments that, if we receive them with inward ears, we too shall be cleansed by them through the healing power of David’s lyre. Saul’s cleansing will become ours, so that, when the unclean spirits have been driven away, we may serve the Lord with a purified mind. For the blessed have their own music, which enters the hearing of the faithful soul; its sound does not cease, nor does its attention grow weary. Therefore, lovers of spectacles, abandon your deadly pleasures; come rather to these joys, to these mysteries, where harp and organ arouse the virtues and do not incite the desires of wicked pleasure.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 33

**A Psalm of David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed.**

Since the history of this title is disclosed by the reading of Kings (1 Kings 21:13), it is unnecessary, within this brevity, to draw out the abundance of that source, lest an account spread over a single passage appear to fill and cover the entire little plot of our page. We shall briefly indicate the matter together with its names.

When Saul was persecuting David, he fled to Achish the king. There, while he was viewed with suspicion because of the hostility directed against him, he deliberately changed his appearance, filling his mouth with spittle, so that he might be regarded as possessed and, through the king’s pity, be dismissed unharmed. Yet this deed, like others, was accomplished through that man with the character of a great mystery. For the spittle signified the divine Scriptures, flowing in the beard—that is, in great strength. But, because of the symbolic significance of the events, the name Abimelech was substituted for Achish, to whom David had fled. Abimelech means “the kingdom of my father.” It is clear that this appropriately refers to the Lord Christ, through whom the glorious Father accepted the service of the world with most holy devotion.

But when he says, “he dismissed him,” he signifies King Abimelech. “And he departed” means that he withdrew to other regions, because, as we have said, he had begun there to be viewed with suspicion. The present psalm is the third of those in which the future mysteries of the Lord Christ are signified through David’s deeds, although it is recognized as the second among the alphabetic psalms. 110

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks, placing the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order at the beginnings of the verses, except for the sixth. In the first part he pledges that he will bless the Lord, exhorting the meek to persevere with him in the Lord’s praises. This part contains four letters of the aforesaid alphabet.

In the second part, the rewards of those who turn to the faith and merit well are not passed over in silence; it contains six letters. In the third, he admonishes them as sons regarding the sins from which they must abstain; this contains four letters. In the fourth, he says that the righteous will be delivered from every tribulation and that the wicked will suffer the punishments they deserve, so that they may not grow faint through any uncertainty in their dangers; here the remaining seven letters are set out.

And remember, as was already said in Psalm 24, that this incomplete alphabet indicates those who cannot sing the praises of the Lord with the fullest integrity of works.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1. ALEPH

“I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth.”

We know that time is diverse for human beings: at one moment harsh with tribulations, at another flattering with joy. Therefore the prophet declares that the Lord must be blessed at all times, both when we suffer adversity and when we rejoice in the happiness bestowed upon us, as the righteous have done and continue to do when aflame with love for the Lord.

Although it is both our duty and our advantage that creation should always praise its Creator, nevertheless, because human actions are various, it seems almost impossible for us continually to cause praises to the Lord to resound in psalmody. Yet the praise of God is always in the mouth of the righteous person when he either thinks or speaks such things that he cannot be blamed by any reproach. Whatever we say or carry in our minds from patience, charity, simplicity, and the other virtues is rightly applied to divine praises. For the heralding of the one who grants these things consists in meditating upon what is honorable with mouth and heart.

Praise derives its name from the laurel, which used to crown victors. These are the mystical spittles that the similarity of the title foretold: these words that seemed to express the power of the divine Scriptures.

#### Verse 2. BETH

“In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice.”

The love of the servant is expressed most beautifully in a single clause. He says that his soul is to be praised not in himself or in riches, but in the Lord. For then the faithful servant glories, when he is known to have a praiseworthy Lord; he knows that the good is attributed to him when his Lord has been proclaimed by the mouths of many.

If someone today were to disparage the Lord, with what fury would his devoted servant be inflamed, with what indignation would he be tormented? Faithful servants have been granted this: either to rage over the adverse reputation of their masters or to rejoice over their favorable reputation.

It follows: “Let the meek hear and rejoice.” He did not say, “Let those instructed in the law rejoice,” nor “those who fast,” nor “those who sing psalms,” but “let the meek rejoice”—those who, through outstanding charity, have made a habit of exercising moderation in all things.

#### Verse 3. GIMEL

“Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.”

Carnal utility desires to enjoy alone what it eagerly covets with greedy delight. Spiritual grace, however, does not wish to do alone what benefits many for salvation, lest detestable envy become mixed with the duties of holiness. This verse now explains that point.

For he calls his brothers and exhorts obedient peoples to magnify the Lord’s name in glorious fellowship. It follows: “And let us exalt his name together.” This is a gentle admonition and a most righteous rule: what is known to be offered to holy unity should be done by all as one.

“Together” signifies ordered choirs, when they respond to the Lord’s psalmody in alternating succession. This figure is called *energeia*, that is, “imagination,” which presents the action of a thing to incorporeal eyes.

#### Verse 4. DALETH

“I sought the Lord, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my tribulations.”

So that the people, invited to the Lord’s psalmody, might hasten to it, he now declares what good came to him from it. He sought the Lord—not across a long stretch of lands, nor through the breadth of widely extended places, but in his heart. When we contemplate his majesty there, we find him present there in every way.

And consider what he says: “I sought the Lord, and he answered me,” because his understanding embraces all things and he works not through bodily senses but through spiritual powers. He then shows how beneficial it was to seek God, since he delivered him from every distress. Who could have been sufficient to ask separately for all that this man deserved to obtain at once? By saying “from all,” he leaves nothing that you could suspect remained adverse.

#### Verse 5. HE

“Draw near to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be put to shame.”

Earlier he set forth the praises and arranged the choirs. Now, in the second part, he also exhorts the peoples to draw near to that very communion, so that the spiritual admonisher might instill the rite of the future Church.

“Draw near” is not said to drunkards, adulterers, or the proud, but to sober, chaste, and humble Christians, who may deserve to be enlightened through the sacred reception. As the Apostle testifies concerning this communion:

“Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (1 Corinthians 11:27).

Therefore one must strive that whoever approaches him should so govern himself with humble penitence that he may appear able to be enlightened rather than blinded. “Faces,” as we have often said, signifies presence, which can suffer shame through a change of color if heavenly gifts are withdrawn from it. The faithful, therefore, are not put to shame, because they obtain what they ask. To be put to shame belongs to the deceived person, who cannot attain his desires.

Some think that this must be understood in the following way, and they raise no small question on the matter. Since the Apostle says, “He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Timothy 6:16), how does this passage say, “Draw near to him and be enlightened”?

The answer is contained briefly in the truth itself. His light is called inaccessible when his unique and omnipotent nature is declared. But when the grace of the holy Divinity pours itself forth, one does draw near to him and blessed enlightenment is granted. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “He enlightens every human being who comes into this world” (John 1:9).

#### Verse 6. ZAIN

“This poor man cried, and the Lord answered him and delivered him from all his tribulations.”

By saying “this,” he designates the spiritual poor man, who is emptied not only of worldly riches but also of the abundance of vices. This is the poor man who, drawing near to God, is enlightened; this is the one whose face is not put to shame, who, whenever he cries to the Lord, is heard healthfully and appropriately. Thus it comes about that he is delivered not from one tribulation but from all worldly distresses.

This ordinarily happens to the righteous when, in holy conduct, they surrender their souls and are transferred from the confused ruin of this age to perpetual security.

Consider also that this is the letter of the Hebrew alphabet that has been skipped: the seventh has been placed in the sixth position. This should, I think, be referred to what I mentioned above: that this psalm signifies holy men who nevertheless are not proved perfect in all their works. For my part, I have not found a settled judgment of the Fathers on this matter.

#### Verse 7. HETH

“The Lord will send an angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.”

So that no one might believe that the Lord could neglect his faithful, he consoles them with the present oracle. Examine the medicinal word he uses: “He will send.” Because of the insolence of human frailty, he does not make it public but works through hidden interventions, so that, without your knowing it, you may receive what can be useful for your salvation.

The angel is the minister of the divine will. Therefore, if you wish to become an angel, do what he commands: free the endangered, assist the anxious, rescue the innocent, and perform the other things that divine authority orders. We are angels in spirit when we become ministers of the heavenly will.

#### Verse 8. TETH

“Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him.”

He returns to the Lord’s most holy communion and does not cease to say repeatedly where he knows that the joys of eternal life come to mortals. “Taste” does not refer to the palate but to the soul’s sweetest perception, which is nourished by divine contemplation.

To make you understand that very taste, he adds “see,” which certainly does not refer to the mouth but, without doubt, to the faculty of perception. Thus, when we receive such a body, we may trust that the grace of life is granted to us.

And so that you might not reduce this communion to an ordinary body, he says that the Lord is sweet, because in it he grants salvation to human beings according to his loving-kindness. For our life, which is truly God—the one who united to himself the flesh taken from the Virgin Mary and made it his own—declared that flesh to be life-giving, as he says in the Gospel:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have eternal life within you” (John 6:54).

Although it was taken from human nature, we must not regard it as the flesh of merely one human being from among us, polluted by the contagion of any sin. Rather, it is worthy of worship, saving, and life-giving; it forgives sins because of the Word to whom it has been united, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel:

“So that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Matthew 9:6).

And it leads us to the realms of eternal life.

He therefore adds an unqualified and firm judgment: blessed is the man who does not cease to hope in the Lord. This is the pre-eminent matter repeated so frequently, so that we may never cease seeking what is known to be proclaimed with such persistence.

#### Verse 9. JOD

“Fear the Lord, all his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing.”

He commands all the saints to fear the Lord, lest anyone, however deserving, depart from this most salutary purpose. But he immediately shows what benefit the fear of him possesses, saying: “For those who fear him lack nothing.”

O brief sentence, O immense promise! Those to whom riches, bodily health, and kingdoms are granted may still lack something. Only the one enriched by the fear of the Lord lacks nothing.

#### Verse 10. CAPH

“The rich have become needy and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.”

In a single verse he distinguishes the earthly rich from Christ’s poor through a magnificent contrast. For he says: “The rich have become needy and hungry.”

When are the rich in need? When they do not possess the right faith. When are they hungry? When they are not at all satisfied with the Lord’s body. Such rich people are in need; though their bellies are filled, they are always hungry in spirit. For what do those who do not possess God have?

It follows: “But those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing,” because those who enjoy spiritual desire lack no good. For when we love the Lord, we find everything in him. One is sought, but in him all things are contained.

O wondrous gain, O singular advantage! Why should we weary ourselves through many paths? Let us therefore hasten with one accord to him, after whom we seek no further good but possess all good, as the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8:28).

This argument is called one from contraries. For it is contrary that the rich should be in need and the poor should lack no good. An argument is an indication [*ed.*, “judgment”] of an ingenious mind, which establishes belief in a doubtful matter through probable inquiries.

#### Verse 11. LAMED

“Come, children; hear me. I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”

Having completed the solemn matters that pertained to the Church’s sacraments, he now comes to the third part, where he addresses those who are receiving the first rudiments of faith.

By saying “Come,” he indicates that they had not been within the Church. This is likewise said to those who now confess the faith when they come to the Christian faith. A father’s voice sounds; a voice of devotion admonishes us to listen willingly to one who speaks, though we ought to seek him when he is silent.

But how sweet and useful is the fear to which the son is invited! When he says, “I will teach you,” he warns us not to be terrified because we have heard the word “fear.” For this is not a fear that is dreaded but one that is loved. Human fear contains bitterness; this fear contains sweetness. The former compels service; the latter draws us toward freedom. Finally, the former fears prison, while the latter opens the kingdoms of heaven. Rightly, then, he declared this fear to be so useful that it should be learned with eager minds.

#### Verse 12. MEM

“Who is the person who desires life and longs to see good days?”

This question is posed in such a way that everyone should agree with it. For who could say, “I do not want life,” or, “I do not desire to see good days”? If only we sought eternal life as earnestly as we fix our hearts upon this temporal life.

By “good days” he does not mean those in which we are occupied with fleeting pleasures, but those that are truly good and are spent in complete holiness.

#### Verse 13. NUN

“Restrain your tongue from evil, and do not let your lips speak deceit.” 112

This is what it means to desire to see good days: that our tongue should speak nothing inappropriate. Everything forbidden is evil, and whatever opposes the truth is distinguished by this name.

But consider more subtly that he first says the tongue must be restrained, since when we wish to speak we move it first. He adds, “Do not let your lips speak deceit.” The lips immediately follow the tongue’s movement, and, joined together in a kind of harmony, human speech is produced through the modulation of both.

Deceit occurs when we deceive the listener, so that what is believed to be brought as assistance appears instead to inflict harm. This is rightly forbidden, because it is always opposed to a pure conscience.

#### Verse 14. SAMECH

“Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.”

To see good days, it is not enough merely to abstain from evil acts unless devotion also compels us to perform good deeds. The first step of virtue is not to seek what belongs to another; the next and higher step is not to refuse one’s own possessions to those in need. In the former we flee guilt; in the latter we gain the palm of devotion.

Not having harmed an orphan or stripped a poor person is abstinence, which by itself is not sufficient for a reward. For at that judgment only those will hear, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34), who, with the Lord inspiring them, have purchased his grace through diverse acts of generosity.

You see, therefore, that the addition “And do good” was necessary. This is what frees us and commends us.

Knowing that, in this struggle of the age, the most faithful have no peace with the body, and that they have an uninterrupted struggle here with their own vices, the prophet beautifully said, “Seek peace.” Although they do not have it here, they must nevertheless pursue it with the greatest diligence.

He did not promise that it could somehow be grasped here; rather, he commands, “Pursue it,” as though it were going before us. For why must it be pursued unless it is fleeing from here? In the future it must be hoped for, because there it remains in perpetual stability.

Let us therefore seek it diligently and follow it attentively, since we cannot find it there unless we seek it more carefully here. It will then be granted to be grasped when we behold the author of peace himself.

#### Verse 15. AIN

“The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers.”

He comes to the fourth part, where, to the end, he strengthens the people by a twofold proclamation: at one moment recounting the reward of the righteous, at another punishing the sins of the wicked, so that the people he has acquired may learn to serve the Lord after being admonished from both sides.

This figure is called a *paradigm*, plainly a most effective kind of figure, when what we ought to follow is commanded through a twofold benefit.

When he says, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,” he shows the continual grace of the Divinity, so that his gaze appears to remain fixed upon them. He also adds the swiftest speed of being heard, when he declares that the Lord’s ears are ready for their prayers.

What delay could there be for them in obtaining their request, when the one who can hear dwells within them? Although he frequently hears sinners, much more is promised to the righteous, since he is shown to have ears ready for their prayers.

#### Verse 16. PHE

“But the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.”

Having explained the grace given to the righteous, he now turns to the punishments of the wicked. Lest the worst of them should say, “He attends to the righteous but does not regard us; let us now act securely, since we do not deserve to be seen by him,” he declares that the face of the Lord—that is, his understanding—is upon the wicked.

He attends to them without approving them; he does not approve them, yet he knows their deeds. Let us therefore fear to do evil, since we know that it does not escape his knowledge.

And consider that here too he says, “against those who do evil,” so that the connected proximity cannot be misunderstood. Understand, however, that he sees both groups, but regards them with different outcomes: the righteous in order to hear them, sinners in order to destroy them.

“From the earth” means from the future homeland, which only those pleasing to God will possess. “Their memory shall perish,” because among the righteous there will be no remembrance of the wicked. We say that we keep those people in memory for whom we desire to provide something. But those who pass out of the Lord’s memory undoubtedly reach eternal punishments.

#### Verse 17. ZADE

“The righteous cried out, and the Lord answered them, and delivered them from all their tribulations.”

He returns again to the righteous and speaks somewhat more fully about them, so that the gifts he has recounted may refresh the people whom fear of the wicked’s punishment had terrified.

Let us examine what this statement means. He says that the righteous cried out to the Lord and always declares that they were heard. What, then, shall we say about the martyrs, whom it is quite clear were not delivered from the tortures of tyrants?

They were certainly delivered when, brought to the kingdoms of heaven, they were proved to have been freed from every tribulation. For the cry of the righteous is always heard not only for temporal but especially for eternal benefit.

#### Verse 18. COPH

“The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit.”

This verse too concerns the good things of the righteous. The custom of the Lord and human custom are different. Whoever wishes to become close to those who are higher is raised up; he stretches himself so that he may reach lofty heights.

But the Most High Lord cannot be approached except through bowed humility, nor can one reach his sweet joys except through bitter tears.

Or, as others have said, “near” signifies not proximity in place but assistance.

It must also be examined that he says, “those who are troubled in heart.” Many are troubled, but not in heart: complainers and fools, who do not grieve over sins but are distressed by worldly losses.

Those are troubled in heart who make the evils of others their own miseries, who mourn the world and are afflicted by the disasters of the whole human community. He will save these very people, who have subjected themselves to the humblest manner of life.

And observe that he does not say “humble in words,” which wickedness often possesses in sinners, but “in spirit,” as he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

#### Verse 19. RES

“Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from all of them.”

This verse and the following one still recount the good things of the righteous. It was appropriate to speak more about this side, lest the fragile hearts of mortals succumb again and again to fear.

In truth, the righteous have many tribulations, because the devil pursues them more vigorously and human beings frequently afflict them through envy. Moreover, an impious person can be troubled if he alone suffers some adversity; but the righteous are afflicted both by their own sufferings and by compassion for the sufferings of others.

When he adds, “And the Lord delivered them from all these,” the Creator’s power is shown, because the multitude of tribulations cannot prevent his deliverance. From this it follows that every righteous person is indeed burdened with many tribulations but is undoubtedly released from them all.

#### Verse 20

“The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken.”

By “bones” he meant the steadfastness of the faithful—that is, patience, meekness, and the other virtues—which cannot perish in the saints because they are preserved under the Lord’s protection. These are the things that cannot be crushed, even though bodily bones may be broken.

For if you consider the passage literally, no small question appears: how were the bones of the thief to whom the Lord had said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), not broken, when they are said to have been shattered by the soldiers? And how do you find that the bodies of many martyrs were violated in their physical condition?

All this blemish of doubt is removed if we understand the bones as the strength of faith and the firmness of the soul.

#### Verse 21. SIN

“The death of sinners is most evil; and those who hate the righteous shall offend.”

He speaks of that death of sinners which cannot be perceived by human beings, and declares it to be not merely evil but most evil. Truly it is most evil, because eternal punishment accompanies it.

For if you look at the death that lies open to our eyes, you will often find a sinful rich man carried out with fitting pomp and elaborate trappings, mourned by his household in such a way that they falsely represent him as having been good to human ears. His friends also accompany him with lavish tears, so that you might truly think that someone of great worth had been taken away, since he is mourned with such great lamentation.

Why should we mention the costly perfumes with which their bodies are embalmed so that they may remain after death? This is carried out with such care and such display that, at their funerals, the lives of the survivors are revived.

Where, then, is the “most evil death of sinners”? Clearly, in hell, where those received there suffer eternal punishments. With what pomp, as we believe, was that purple-clad rich man brought to the tomb, who asked the poor Lazarus for a drop of cold water (Luke 16:24)?

And note that the harshness of death itself is explained in this name. It is called *pessima*—“most evil”—as though derived from *pessumdata*, “ruined.”

He also adds: “And those who hate the righteous shall offend,” that is, those who, through wicked hatred, hated the Lord the Savior and refused to accept his commandments. The death of these people too is most evil, as is that of those whom he mentioned above.

#### Verse 22. TAU

“The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants, and he will not abandon all who hope in him.”

How fittingly this psalm ends in the hope of good things, so that, abandoning the company of the wicked, we may strive rather toward future blessings!

“The Lord will redeem,” namely, with precious blood, because whoever believes rightly in him will be redeemed from the deserved captivity of sins.

Scripture frequently uses “souls” for human beings, as it is written in Exodus: “Seventy-five souls went down into Egypt” (Exodus 1:5). The whole human being is rightly understood from his better part.

But observe that he says “of his servants,” not of those living in unlawful freedom. He also adds, “And he will not abandon,” namely, like the good Shepherd, who guards his sheep with attentive devotion.

But he doubled the safeguard of the promise. He does not say that no one will be abandoned, but “all who hope in him.” For he will abandon those who have placed their hope either in their own strength or in reliance upon some human being.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

The sacred mysteries of this psalm have been completed, and the order of the Mass has been so fulfilled that you might think it was written in Christian times. Here the order of the hymns has run its course; here the devoted people are commanded to draw near to communion; here those who receive the first rudiments of faith are invited to come, so that you may feel that nothing is lacking from so great a matter, although you know that none of these things had yet taken place.

Here, too, the human race is invited by the blessings of the righteous and terrified by the punishment of the wicked. This is what that title foretold, when David changed his appearance before Abimelech, so that we too, usefully changing our pleasure, should flee for refuge to the most secure Catholic Church of the Lord.

This calculation also concerns the age at which the Lord suffered, at which we too are believed to rise through the reading of the Fathers. Father Augustine treated this matter in many ways, as is his custom, and with care in his book *Enchiridion* (chapter 84 and following), so that no one may doubt that a psalm consecrated by such great virtues ought to be stored through frequent meditation in the repositories of our memory like a heavenly treasure.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 34

**For David.**

It is sometimes no burden briefly to repeat what has been said, so that the reader’s mind may be recalled to the studies necessary for memory. David, as we said, embraces two meanings: “strong of hand” and “desirable.” Both are certainly applicable to the Lord the Savior.

He is strong of hand because he struck down the captivity of our death together with its wicked author. He is desirable because his coming promises us unspeakable blessings.

This psalm, then, is sung from the person of the Lord the Savior, who asks to be delivered from the persecution of his enemies. The words “for David,” when they occur in the title, urge us to understand Christ, who is appropriately called David, since the entire exposition of this name applies well to him.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout this hymn are the words of the Lord Christ concerning the dispensation in which he suffered.

In the first section of the psalm he asks that retribution be rendered to his persecutors, wishing them adverse things which will nevertheless contribute to their conversion. In the second he rejoices over his resurrection and, reproaching the iniquities of the Jews, sets forth the event of his own passion.

In the third he promises that throughout the entire world he will confess the Father’s power in his members, since the Father delivered him from his enemies through the benefit of the resurrection. He prays that the persecutors [*ed.*, “sinners”] may be put to shame and that the faithful may exult in great glory.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me.” 114

The weakness he assumed for our sake cries out, so that those who harm him—that is, the devil and his ministers—may be condemned, which he knew was destined to occur. To judge the wicked is to condemn them, because those who are always proved entangled in wicked actions cannot be freed in the trial.

But, as has been said, this pertains to the devil and his followers, through whom the iniquity of the Jewish will came about. For since he himself commands, “Pray for your enemies” (Matthew 5:24), this sentence cannot apply to human beings.

Therefore he asks that those whom, through the power of his foreknowledge, he knows will not come to the remedies of repentance should be condemned. Later, when he comes to speak of human beings, he desires that they be converted, not destroyed.

He also added: “Fight against those who fight against me.” One who attacks strives to overcome; one who is overcome has already been utterly defeated. Thus the unclean spirits are rightly called fighters, because although they cannot conquer the saints, they nevertheless do not cease to contend with them through wicked determination.

The Lord fights against them because he alone prevails in accomplishing whatever he wills; his contest is triumph, and every battle is victory.

#### Verse 2

“Take up armor and shield, and rise to my assistance.”

“Armor” derives from the idea of warding off, because through it we repel the most violent enemies. Thus the expression is used according to human custom, which arms the hand so that it may crush the enemy.

But, properly understood, the armor and shield are the Lord’s will alone, by which he protects the endangered and defeats the adversary. The Apostle expresses this same tropology: “the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit” (Ephesians 6:16–17).

The shield is so called as though “sculpted,” because the ancients marked their deeds upon it. But when he says “take up,” is some foreign defense temporarily taken up by God? The outcome of all things is always ready for him who is proved omnipotent; nor is he thought to rise from rest, since he is shown never to have lain down.

The armor, therefore, pertains to the iron coverings by which human salvation is defended; the shield serves to repel the enemy’s blows, so that the weapons intended for human destruction fall frustrated.

The Lord Christ therefore prays from the nature of his humanity that his salvation should be fortified and that the enemy’s will should press on through its own bold attempts.

#### Verse 3

“Draw out the sword and shut the way against those who persecute me; say to my soul: ‘I am your salvation.’”

In the divine Scriptures, *framea*—“sword”—contains many meanings. It can mean a sword; it can mean a royal spear; it can mean deceit; it can mean vengeance. Here, however, he wishes his soul to be understood, for it truly was a sword against his adversaries.

Through it, idol worship in its sacrilegious form was brought to an end, the devil’s iniquity was defeated, and the power of death itself was struck down and forced to yield, though previously it had reigned throughout the whole world with unrestricted power.

For it has already been read in another psalm: “Deliver my soul from the wicked, your sword” (Psalm 16:13).

“Draw out the sword,” therefore, means: enlarge my soul through the gift granted by your mercy. “Bar [the way]” means: by my passion, and by your law having been fulfilled, which you foretold through the prophets. He also asks the Lord to say to his soul, “I am your salvation,” because he knew that the Lord’s words would be fulfilled without any difficulty.

#### Verse 4

“Let those who seek my soul be confounded and revere [me].”

#### Verse 5

“Let them be turned back and put to shame who devise evil against me.”

Here, when he has come to speak of human beings, he pours out not a curse but a request for correction. To be confounded is to be ashamed of one’s deeds and to change to a better judgment. Those who are convicted for punishment are also said to be confounded.

But so that you might understand this more as referring to conversion, he added: “Let them revere [him],” that is, let them, once corrected, worship the one whom they had thought ought to be persecuted.

“Those who seek my soul” is said in a bad sense: those who seek it not in order to honor it but hasten to separate it from the body. Yet seeking Christ’s soul is also used in a good sense, where he says: “Escape has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Psalm 141:5).

“To be turned back” is said only of those who are judged capable of correction. Thus he also said to the Apostle Peter, who was defending Christ’s safety in a human manner: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33)—not so that he might perish, but so that through a happy correction he might follow the Lord’s will.

Therefore, when he wishes those people to return behind him, he does not desire that they carry out the worst intention of their will, but rather that they follow him, where they are not proved to have gone astray.

“Those who devise evil against me” may refer to the Jews, to heretics, or perhaps to pagans. For all who hasten to assert something contrary to the Catholic faith with a wicked intention devise evil.

### Verse 6

“Let them become like dust before the face of the wind, and let an angel of the Lord afflict them.” Dust is indeed an earthly substance, but it is exceedingly dry and fine; when the wind blows, it is not allowed to remain in its place, but is lifted into the liquid air. Thus the wills of sinners, when they have been admonished by the inspiration of truth, are raised up from earthly vices and, with the Lord’s help, brought to heavenly virtues. In this way, then, he wishes for the wicked that through a happy correction they may attain heavenly life. We call an angel a messenger of heavenly power, through whom divine commands are fulfilled. This angel, then, afflicts the converted, so that by the gift of humility they may be brought to that blessed homeland. Yet this affliction is a benefit, when it is desired that they may emerge into the place of a great gift.

### Verse 7

“Let their way become darkness and slipperiness, and let an angel of the Lord pursue them.” He asks that everything be turned against sinners, so that the very way which appears to them bright or firm, while they linger in it with delight, may become dark for them, so that they dread it, and slippery, so that they cannot remain upon it any longer; as the prophet Jeremiah also says: “And for this reason their way became slippery in darkness; they shall be tripped up and fall in it” (Jer. 23:12).
