But if they should still decide to remain in their evils, let the power of the Lord pursue them, so that he may not allow them to persist in their crimes, since they are hastening toward the desires of their own destruction. O great happiness amid so many oppositions! With how many prayers it is sought here that the most prosperous adversity may be granted!

### Verse 8

“For without cause they hid from me the destruction of their snare; in vain they reproached my soul.” Without cause indeed, since he had done them no harm. This figure is called *syncrisis*, when by means of a comparison we show our cause to be more just than that of our adversaries. We call that “without cause” which is given without compensation for any matter. “They hid from me,” as they thought, because they did not believe in the power of his divinity. For what can be hidden from one for whom nothing is hidden? He both pointed out his betrayer at the supper and foretold his Passion before it occurred; nothing was hidden from him, since he endured everything by the dispensation of his will.

It is well said, “the destruction of their snare,” because that snare was not the destruction of the one who was dying, but rather of the sinner. What follows, “in vain they reproached my soul,” signifies “they falsely accused me,” when the Jewish people attributed truthful statements to the Lord and Savior as though they were some crime. For in their madness they falsely cried out: “This is the one who said, ‘I will destroy this temple’” (Matt. 26:61), although he had said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). For what is more vain than to try to turn into a charge of wickedness what was proclaimed to everyone for salvation?

### Verse 9

“Let the snare that they do not know come upon them, and let the trap that they concealed seize them; and let them fall into the same snare.” A pious retribution, a saving vengeance: since they had prepared a snare which they thought could remain unknown, let them fall into that little trap which the sinner’s understanding does not perceive; that is, let them be bound by the bond of truth and thereby rather be set free.

It follows: “And let the trap that they concealed seize them.” What is that trap except the death of the Lord and Savior, which is shown to have been contrived by hidden schemes of ambush? “Let it seize them,” as though it immediately pursued them while they were fleeing, and accomplish the whole purpose, so that, abandoned to their crimes, they would not be overwhelmed by them. Note that here he places “snare” in a good sense: captured by the Lord’s commandments, let them persevere in the same heavenly grace. Thus he prays—the one whose snare of destruction was concealed without cause, who did not repay evil for evil, but while hanging on the cross prayed for his persecutors.

### Verse 10

“But my soul shall exult in the Lord, and shall delight in his salvation.” After he had suitably spoken of the unclean spirits that were to arise for them, and had prayed for sinners according to his customary compassion, he comes to the second member, where he both sets forth the joy of his own mind and recounts the course of his Passion with the clearest truth.

For the first blessedness of the holy soul is to exult in the Lord, because everything is sought there when the purest mind is directed there. Whoever rejoices in the Lord neither has his joy ever fail nor finds anything sweeter that he could love. What, then, follows this exultation? Namely: “because he shall delight in his salvation.” “Salvation” is the majesty of the Lord’s Word, from which salvation proceeds and life is bestowed: the fountain of mercy, the remedy of those who plead, and the forgiveness of sins.

### Verse 11

“All my bones shall say: ‘Lord, who is like you?’” It is clear that bones possess neither understanding nor voice, but—as we have often said—they are to be understood as the strength of the soul and steadfastness of mind. They are rightly compared with bones, because just as bones contain the body, so this strength reinforces holy wills.

Let the bones, then, and not the flesh, speak this mystery—that is, firmness and not laxity—for only the strength of the mind can utter such a hymn. “Who” is negative, since no one can be like him, whereas the Holy Trinity is one and unique. The creature is vastly unlike the Creator: the former serves, while the latter rules.

### Verse 12

“Delivering the needy from the hand of the one stronger than he, the poor and needy from those who are plundering him” [ed., “from the hand of those stronger than he”]. In this verse he explains what he said above: “Who is like you?” For when the devil held almost the whole human race in his hand, it is clear that humanity was freed from that power to which it had been subjected through the incarnation of the Word.

He also added “the needy and the poor,” so that these three terms gathered together might indicate the condition of the human race, oppressed by calamities. He is called *inops* (“needy”) because he became mortal; *egenus* (“destitute”) because he sought bread through labors and sweat; and *pauper* (“poor”) because, cast down from that wisdom and purity, he possessed only a slight and shadowy reasoning faculty. For who would say that those truly possessed wisdom who were shown to lack knowledge of their Creator?

But how marvelous, how entirely unique, that he freed such a one through his incarnation, so that it is rightly said: “Lord, who is like you?” And remember that above, “from the hand of the one stronger” signifies the devil, who was certainly stronger than human beings. Below, “from those who are plundering him” is intended to mean the unclean spirits, who by wicked devotion serve alongside the devil’s power.

### Verse 13

“Unjust witnesses rising up questioned me about things I did not know.” After he had described the manifold calamities by which humanity was oppressed, so that he might not make himself alien to it—for in his compassion he deigned to assume it on our behalf—he now recalls his own Passion.

The witnesses, therefore, who rise up in a sudden, beastlike assault, and are not brought forward in a measured manner, are without doubt utterly false; he powerfully designates them with one word when he says: “Unjust.” Truly unjust, since they were going to speak against truth and justice.

He adds: “Things I did not know”—that is, things I was wholly unaware of having said. We speak in this way of those who, by the Lord’s favor, preserve themselves in an upright way of life: “He does not know how to lie; he does not know how to rob; he does not know how to oppress.”

The Lord was unaware of blaspheming, which the chief priest charged against him with his garments torn, when he said: “You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Father” (Matt. 26:64). Then the leader of the Jews continued: “He has blasphemed! What further need have we of witnesses?” But what sort of testimony it was, he made clear in what followed: he did not say that they had convicted him, but that they had questioned him, as though he did not trust his own integrity but was concerned about another’s testimony.

The evangelist Matthew speaks of this passage as follows: “At last two false witnesses came forward and said: ‘We heard him say, “I can destroy this temple”’” (ibid., 60), etc.

### Verse 14

“They repaid me evil for good, barrenness to my soul.” Nothing could have been said either more briefly or more elegantly. The Lord’s benefits and the Jews’ deeds are explained in these individual words: “evil for good”—namely, because while he had bestowed life upon believers, they preferred to return death; a kind of retribution that is shown to be the extreme of all evils.

There was also barrenness of soul when the good Teacher could find in them no fruit of faith; their breasts did not yield the shoots of belief, because they had been hardened by stony stupor. And lest the Jews think that they were only lightly condemned for this barrenness, he also cursed that fig tree, as the Gospel testifies, in which he found no fruit at all (Mark 11:13).

### Verse 15

“But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth.” Sackcloth is a rough, bristly covering made from goats’ hair. Goats rightly refer to sins, since at the Lord’s judgment they too are placed among sinners. Therefore the Lord, because he assumed sinful flesh, recalls that he clothed himself in sackcloth.

For if you take the statement historically, you never read that he used sackcloth. Therefore, while the Jews troubled him with insults and ambushes, he concealed his divinity beneath the veil of flesh from their darkened minds, because they did not deserve to recognize the one whom they treated with such impiety.

This figure is called *metriasmos*, that is, “moderation,” whenever we lower a great matter by a humble expression. An attentive reader will recognize this figure both here and in the verses that follow. Consider also the language of heavenly patience: he does not say, “when they persecuted me,” but “when they troubled me,” which we usually say of minor matters, when something is imposed upon us importunately and accepted with an unwilling disposition.

### Verse 16

“And I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer returned into my bosom.” The Lord’s fasting occurred when he found no one hardened by unspeakable obstinacy whom he could receive into spiritual feasts. This was the barrenness of his soul, and also his fasting. For fasting is so called as though from “lack of food” (*inedia*), because it brings those who abstain for a long time even to want of food.

The Lord therefore fasted because the unbelieving crowd had withdrawn itself from him. Bodily fasting may also appropriately be attributed to the Lord, since he fasted for forty days and nights on the mountain (Matt. 4:2); but this must be understood according to that perfected fasting of which Isaiah says:

“Release every bond of wickedness, undo the obligations of oppressive exchanges, set the afflicted free in release, and break every unjust repayment; break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor without shelter into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise those of your own seed. Then your morning light shall break forth, and your healing shall quickly arise. Your righteousness shall go before you, and the majesty of the Lord shall surround you. Then you shall cry out, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say: ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isa. 58:6–9), and so forth—the things that that wonderful text promises by a heavenly gift.

Thus the good Teacher showed by evident human examples what he had foretold in the books of the prophets. He also added a more hidden reason, which is aptly disclosed by an evangelical likeness. For the Lord says to his disciples: “When you enter a house, greet it, saying, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if that house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you” (Matt. 10:12–13).

Such also is this prayer that was poured forth by the Lord. Since the detestable Jews were not at all worthy to receive it, it returned into his bosom—that is, into the secret place of his heart—from which it had gone forth. For if it had worked within their hearts, it would certainly have been called not “returned,” but “poured out.”

### Verse 17

“As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing, as one mourning and sorrowful, so I humbled myself.” In accordance with Latin usage, we say that we have pleased a neighbor and a brother; but here the grammatical cases have been changed, since accusatives have been placed for datives. This figure is called *antiptosis*, when one case is used in place of another.

He says: “As for a neighbor, as for our brother, so I was pleasing”—that is, I rejoiced in the relationship of those who were hostilely persecuting me. For this is perfect retribution: that grace be offered for hatred, and a benefit for an injury.

The Lord was pleased with them when he taught them not to sin, and when, hanging on the cross, he prayed to the Father on their behalf. It follows: “As one mourning and sorrowful, so I humbled myself.” Although that holiness and devoted love of the Lord which he taught testifies that he loved the Jews as brothers and neighbors, he nevertheless rightly recalls himself as sorrowful, because he could not find in all of them the faith that he earnestly sought. For if someone wishes us well, he must be saddened when he cannot find in us what he seeks.

### Verse 18

“And against me they rejoiced and assembled; scourges were gathered against me, and they did not understand.” While Christ the Lord was sorrowfully compassionate, the Jews rejoiced with impious freedom. But their retribution will be different: Christ will rejoice over his sorrow, whereas the Jews will be tormented because of their own exultation. For blessed are those who mourn for the sake of righteousness (Matt. 5:5), and wretched are those who grow proud through foolish rejoicing.

He also explains the condition of the worst blindness: they were preparing torments against their Lord which, by a just recompense, were to return upon themselves. This is what he means by “and they did not understand”: what they appeared bodily to inflict upon the innocent was destined to turn against them.

### Verse 19

“They were loosened, yet were not pierced; they tested me and mocked me with mockery; they gnashed their teeth at me.” After the excess of impious boldness, he says what happened to the Jews; yet he does not suggest that their obstinacy could be converted.

They were “loosened,” certainly, when at the Lord’s Passion the sun was darkened, the earth shook, and the veil of the temple was torn (Luke 23:45); and although such great miracles were displayed, they were not converted because of their hardness.

They “tested” him when they said: “Tell us whether you are the Christ” (Luke 22:66). They “mocked” him when they attributed such words to him while he was crucified, as the evangelist Matthew testifies: “In the same way the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and Pharisees, said: ‘He saved others; he cannot save himself’” (Matt. 27:41–42).

That form of expression is used when something is shown to have been fulfilled in the fullest manner—for example, “Blessing I will bless you,” “Cursing I will curse you,” “Building I will build you,” and similar expressions. This device is called *notatio*, when a likeness of speech is drawn from the placement of a verb.

It follows: “They gnashed their teeth at me.” This is done by savage people when they are defeated by reason. When words fail them in defense of the truth, they angrily gnash their teeth and silently signal their intentions through an unspoken threat. But all this is referred to the great edification of the human race, so that the members may not think it burdensome to suffer what they know their head endured.

### Verse 20

“Lord, when will you look upon me? Restore my soul from their evildoings, my only one from lions.” “When will you look upon me?” is spoken according to the weakness customary to human beings, to whom whatever is future seems slow, and who, as soon as they desire something, hasten to accomplish it.

“Restore” means “return as though taken away”; that is, grant resurrection from evildoings, because he was unjustly killed. “From lions” signifies from bloody and cruel powers.

Some have wished “my only one” to refer to the Lord’s flesh. Although this flesh is common to us, it became unique because it was from the Virgin, because it was without sin, and because it was joined to the Word, that is, to the Son of God.

Alternatively, let us understand “my only one” as the catholic Church, which is one throughout the whole world and is called “only” because of its great love; from it the gatherings of heretics are entirely excluded. That this is indeed what “only one” means is shown by the following verse, which is about to speak of the Church.

Observe also that the order of events has been beautifully preserved: first he prayed for his resurrection, which has truly already taken place; afterward he prayed for the Church’s liberation, which at the time of judgment is to be protected from every disturbance.

### Verse 21

“I will confess you, Lord, in the great Church; in a weighty people I will praise you.” He comes to the third member, where, having already received the gift of resurrection, he declares that he will confess the Lord throughout the whole world.

We have said that there are two kinds of confession: one of praise and the other of repentance. Here you should understand confession as proclamation of praise, since “I will praise you” follows shortly afterward.

The great Church is the Christian people, steadfast in right faith, which by its vast extent embraces the whole world. It follows: “in a weighty people”—that is, a fruitful people, known to be established not in light chaff but in grains of wheat. When the breeze of temptation comes, it does not cast them away from Christ’s threshing floor; rather, they are purified by the winnowing and not thrown far away. Therefore the Lord is praised in the weighty people, while by those who are light and empty of faith he is certainly blasphemed.

### Verse 22

“Let those who unjustly oppose me, who hate me without cause, and who signal with their eyes, not insult me” [MSS A, B, F: “signal”].

The order of the words is: “Let those who unjustly oppose me, signaling with their eyes, who hate me without cause, not insult me.”

Heretics insult when the holy Church loses some people from the number of the faithful; they oppose unjustly when they rejoice over the error of those who perish. This is asked not to happen through the Lord’s pious intercession.

It follows: “who hate me without cause”—that is, those to whom I have done no harm. One curses in vain when no cause of injury precedes it.

“Signaling with their eyes” refers to what usually happens when we disclose our will by a silent and deceitful sign; when we do not wish to betray it by our voice, we warn someone through the gestures of our eyes.

### Verse 23

“For they spoke peacefully to me, but deceitfully plotted anger.” The Jews’ unspeakable deceit is foretold—not by our words, but by the words of the Gospel. They appeared to speak peacefully when they said: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. 22:16).

But even someone who does not intend to kill may devise deceit, as when someone plots to take away a neighbor’s money or property. Yet he added “anger,” so that their deceit might be shown to have been deadly. This refers to the time when they were devising their treacherous plan: “It is better that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50).

### Verse 24

“They opened their mouths against me; they said: ‘Good, good! Our eyes have seen it.’” They certainly opened their mouths when they cried: “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23:21). They were no longer signaling with their eyes or plotting deceitfully, but were condemning him with an open and uninhibited voice.

O criminal deed! The judge refused to do what the people were shouting should be carried out.

The words of the Jews rejoicing in a deadly way follow, as though they were saying: “Good, good! We see in you what we desire to accomplish: that, as one who dissuaded the people, you should hang on the cross with the robbers.”

Behold wonderful patience in the one who possessed supreme power! Could he not have descended alive from the gallows of the cross to confound his enemies, when, after dying, he was able to rise from the tomb on the third day? But it was not fitting for divine power to be provoked by the words of those who insulted him, so that they might be put to greater shame when everything foretold had been fulfilled.

Although the Gospel does not record that the Jews said “Good, good,” they nevertheless spoke similar words of insult, so that one event might truthfully be shown to have been narrated through different expressions. “Good, good” is spoken by the figure *epizeuxis*, when words are repeated in a single verse without any intervening expression.

### Verse 25

“You have seen, Lord; do not be silent. Lord, do not depart from me.” These three words also belong to what is recognized as having been narrated above.

“You have seen”—that is, you have proved completed the things which you had foreseen would be plotted against me. We speak in this way when we wish to recall something to memory: “You have seen how cruel he was toward me”; “You have seen how much the wickedness of the robber did against me.”

“Do not be silent”—that is, do not delay in giving judgment, which cannot be done by remaining silent but by speaking.

When he says, “Do not depart from me,” this is to be understood as referring in part to his humanity, which was subject to suffering.

### Verse 26

“Rise up, Lord, and attend to my judgment; my God and my Lord, attend to my cause.” As has often been said, “Rise up” is spoken according to human custom of one who is always watchful and always attentive. Although he continually regards everything, he is then thought to have attended when he takes vengeance.

“My judgment” is the judgment he endured from the Jews: judgment without justice, torments without crime, death without sin. He rightly said “my,” because he truly endured it.

Beautifully he said, “look upon my cause,” not “upon my punishment.” Punishment appeared similar to that of criminals, but no one else could share such a cause. What, then, is this cause to which God was asked to attend? Namely, that the one who had come to give salvation to the human race should be shown to have been killed by the insane and faithless.

### Verse 27

“Judge me, Lord, according to your mercy, my God; and let my enemies not insult me.” Although he who had committed no sins possessed the best cause, he nevertheless asks to be judged according to mercy, so that he might show us an example of prayer, since we could not possess such a case.

It follows: “And let my enemies not insult me”—that is, lest they say what the wickedness of those who insult can say: “We were able; we did it; we accomplished it.” Rather, he prays that they may mourn their evils with saving sorrow instead of rejoicing destructively that they have fulfilled them.

### Verse 28

“Let them not say in their hearts: ‘Good, good for our soul’; nor let them say: ‘We have swallowed him.’” He expresses the insult that he had earlier said was to be understood.

“Let them not say: ‘Good, good’”—that is, “well, well.” These are the words of those who rejoice with a criminal mind, but they can no longer speak them while they are afflicted by remorse. Let them therefore condemn their evil conscience, so that they may not undergo a punitive sentence.

O immense and immeasurable compassion of the Creator! He does not allow them to remain temporarily joyful, lest they should be struck by eternal calamity.

“To swallow” means to be transferred with sudden speed into another’s body. This happens to those who, swallowed up by certain superstitions, depart from the vitality of true faith. But he asks this for the instruction of the faithful. As for his ineffable purity, such things could not happen to him.

### Verse 29

“Let those who rejoice in my misfortunes be ashamed and filled with reverence at the same time.”

### Verse 30

“Let those who speak evil against me be clothed with shame and reverence.” A worthy vengeance, a sufficient punishment. For whoever is ashamed of his actions has been condemned by his own judgment, and he torments himself as his own avenger when he is wrapped in the bond of shame.

Someone may nevertheless be ashamed without feeling reverence. Here he added “and let them reverence at the same time,” so that he might indicate the signs of their conversion. Reverence is the fear of the Lord mingled with love; it comes to those who attain the gifts of confession with the sincerest will.

It follows: “Let them be clothed with shame and reverence,” as with a garment of penitence like sackcloth, as with mournful clothing. He sets shame against the boldness they displayed in their frenzy, and reverence against the shamelessness of falsehood, so that by two virtues they may remedy what they committed through two crimes.

For he said that they had spoken “great things”—that is, things exceeding the bounds of propriety through pride—as blessed John recalls in the Apocalypse: “I saw a mouth speaking great things against God” (Rev. 13:5).

### Verse 31

“Let those who desire my righteousness exult and rejoice, and let them always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified, who desire the peace of his servant.’” After he had spoken sufficiently about the persecutors, he comes to the part concerning the faithful: wishing the former to be tormented by salutary repentance, and the latter to be filled with the highest exultation of blessedness.

Observe also that their merits distinguish their very words. Persecutors are accustomed to say: “Good, good for our soul,” which is temporal joy and fleeting gladness. But the blessed say: “Let the Lord always be magnified,” which is eternal and perpetual.

The former bestow worldly pleasures upon their souls; the latter turn their own desires toward the Lord and place their exultation not in themselves but in his praises.

What he said, “his servant,” refers to the form of humility, because there is humility in the flesh he assumed, but power in his majesty. Thus both are perfect and wholly true: the one Lord Christ.

Who, then, desire the peace of his servant? Those, certainly, who are made strangers to vices and, by divine gift, live in the goodness of self-restraint with tranquility of spirit.

### Verse 32

“And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, all day long on your praise.” His tongue meditated on righteousness when he preached the New Testament to the peoples.

“All day long,” as has often been said, indicates the whole span of life. But since it seems impossible for human beings to praise God with an uninterrupted voice, let us transfer the expression to the understanding of good works: the one who considers God’s commands in every aspect of his will praises God always.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider how graciously the Lord Christ has deigned to speak to us throughout the whole psalm. He began with prayer, as in other similar psalms. Then he foretold the coming events of his Passion and resurrection. Finally, he concludes in the great hope of the faithful, so that there can be no doubt that this psalm too was completed according to the rule stated above.

Therefore let us rejoice in calamities and exult in dangers. For why should the faithful flee from what the Lord of all things endured for the salvation of everyone? It should also be noted that this is the second psalm among those that are known to disclose the Lord’s Passion and resurrection at greater length.

# Exposition of Psalm 35

**For the end; for the servant of the Lord: a psalm of David.**

All these names are rightly understood of the Lord and Savior. “For the end” itself signifies him. “Servant of the Lord” is said of him who, taking the form of a servant, became obedient even to death (Phil. 2:7), as the prophet Isaiah says of him: “Behold my servant; I will receive him” (Isa. 42:1).

“Psalm” and “David” are already familiar from frequent exposition. They are recognized as pertaining to the person of the Lord because the interpretation of these names shows that they are suitable to him.

## Division of the Psalm

The entire psalm is spoken by the person of the prophet. In the first member he vehemently accuses the despisers of the Law and says that they do not dwell with the Lord, recalling their impious wills.

Do not be troubled by the fact that after the title he chose to make such a beginning from the foolish: “There is no fear of God before his eyes.” For he commends the part of the good more forcefully when what is greatly dreadful is placed first.

In the second member, under the praise of the Lord, the rewards of the blessed are described; he says that they are filled with the abundance of the Lord’s house. The psalm is briefly concluded with the ruin of the wicked, lest anyone should perhaps think that what he knew had been accused with such great execration ought to be attempted.

Let us therefore examine its subtlety somewhat more carefully, for its arrangement presents some difficulty.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“The unjust man said within himself that he would sin: ‘There is no fear of God before his eyes.’” There are two kinds of sinners. One kind believes in the Law but, because of the weakness of the flesh, is unable to fulfill what has been commanded. Solomon speaks of them: “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

The other kind is bold, desperate, and blasphemous. It deliberately chooses to sin by its free will, despising everything and murmuring to itself that God does not care about mortal affairs. Therefore this man said to himself a wicked thing which he did not dare to profess publicly.

He thinks this way so that he may appear to grant himself permission to sin, and thus may sin without limit after deciding that the fear of the judge ought to be cast aside.

It follows: “There is no fear of God before his eyes.” He describes the thought of the wicked, who suppose that the fear of God is not before him—that is, that God does not care in such a way that human beings ought to fear him. Rather, as certain erring philosophers have said, they believe that the world is governed by chance instead of being ordered by heavenly administrations.

Alternatively, it is said of the unjust man that there is no fear of God before his eyes because, with sacrilegious will, he presumes to say such things. Finally, it follows:

### Verse 2

“For he acted deceitfully in his sight, so as not to discover his iniquity and hatred” [ed., “toward hatred”]. This wicked man of whom it was said, “There is no fear of God before his eyes,” neglected to apply himself to the Law, so that he might understand his belief to be entirely false. Instead, despising its saving words, he made every effort to remain ignorant of the truth.

He therefore acted deceitfully in God’s sight in order to avoid discovering his own iniquity and hatred, believing that through ignorance of the commandment he could defend himself.

It is beautifully defined that our sins are “iniquity” and “hatred,” since we ought to hate the very things through which we have reached eternal punishments.

### Verse 3

“The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he was unwilling to understand so as to act well.” A definitive summary is appropriately given of the speech of the wicked. Their words are iniquity and deceit. Thus what could not be counted is explained in two terms.

Iniquity refers to blasphemy; deceit, to deceiving one’s neighbor. But what remains for the one who does not refuse to sin against God and neighbor?

When he says, “he was unwilling to understand so as to act well,” he signifies those who have received from some quarter a spark of wisdom but, turning aside from true understanding through their own fault, have polluted themselves with perverse errors.

This also aptly applies to the utterly foolish Jewish people, to whom the Lord had come, but whom their detestable obstinacy despised healing. For ignorance is often granted pardon, but just vengeance always follows voluntary wrongdoing. This argument is called *ab ingenio*, when sin is committed not through ignorance but through malicious will.

### Verse 4

“He meditated on iniquity in his bed; he stood upon every path that was not good, but he did not hate wickedness.” He continues to describe the utterly wicked man. For he says: “He meditated on iniquity”—that is, he pursued error through prolonged reflection, composing perverse books, so that not only would he himself sin, but posterity too would sin under the authority of the same author.

“In his bed,” that is, in his own heart. A bed is so called from lying down, and there our mind, dwelling within, considers good and evil.

“He stood upon every path that was not good” means the life of this present world. He did not pass through it like the rest who confess, but remained and became fixed in it.

As an addition to the accumulation of sins, he says: “But he did not hate wickedness.” Here he wishes “wickedness” to be understood as the mother of all crimes, summing up in one word what appeared to have been spread out at greater length.

To pursue this is therefore a sacrilege. We are commanded not only to avoid it but rightly compelled to hate it, so that we may condemn so great a crime with perpetual execration.

Remember also that from the beginning of this psalm, through four verses, he employed the figure *synathroismos*, which gathers together many crimes in one continuous course and circuit.

### Verse 5

“Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds.” Having enumerated the thoughts of the worst human beings, he passes in the second member to the praise of the Lord.

Although his mercy is on earth, in the sea, and everywhere, here he speaks especially of it as being “in heaven”—that is, among heavenly creatures and holy human beings, where his gifts have flowed more abundantly.

He also mentions the truth of the righteous, which is engaged in the struggle of this present age. For above we said that the clouds are compared with the preaching of the prophets: just as clouds pour nourishing waters down upon the earth, so they send the rain of salvation upon faithful souls, so that they may produce the fruit of faith, which had been barren through the dryness of sin.

Thus we should truly understand that he shows mercy to the heavenly powers, while through the apostles and prophets we know that he bestowed truth upon the human race.

Observe that this praise has been introduced in common opposition to the reproach of the impious, so that the demonstrative mode may appear more clearly when both sides have been set forth.

### Verse 6

**Your justice is like the mountains, O Lord; your judgments are a great abyss; you will save human beings and beasts, O Lord.**

Although the customary reading is, “Your justice is like the mountains of God,” Jerome’s faithful translation is much more precise, since he wrote “O Lord” rather than “of God.” “Your justice” designates the blessed apostles, who became capable of the Lord’s justice through their devoted understanding. He rightly compared them with mountains, because, drinking in the light of the highest truth at its very sources, they poured it through holy preaching into humble peoples—just as mountains, when the sun rises, receive the rays of new light and transmit them to the valleys of the earth through the radiance reflected upon them.

Here he uses “abyss” in a good sense, comparing its depths with the divine judgments. An abyss is the depth of waters, which we are unable either to measure or fully to see within. Who, after all, could behold the interior of the great sea or comprehend its immeasurable expanses? So too we cannot encompass the divine judgments with our minds or define them by any reasoning, just as the Apostle says: “How incomprehensible are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). Yet one name has been applied to all these things: “abyss,” that is, an unfathomable depth.

He also explains why he called his judgments an abyss: quite properly, since he bestows the benefits of his kindness upon sinners who conduct themselves according to the disordered will of beasts. What mind or reason could comprehend this—that the entreaty of penitents should pass over into the rewards of the righteous? You therefore see that the Lord’s judgments are most appropriately compared with deep abysses.

### Verse 7

**How you have multiplied your mercies, O God! But the children of human beings will hope in the protection of your wings.**

Now, through various enumerations, he explains more fully what he earlier expressed briefly: “Your judgments are a great abyss.” “How” is an adverb of wonder; that is, how sublimely and powerfully, with marvelous generosity, you have bestowed your mercies, so that you might bring sinners also to their rewards and establish the righteous in hope of the promised gifts.

Notice that earlier he said “human beings,” whereas now he says “the children of human beings.” “Human beings” usually refers to those who, having not yet put off the oldness of the first human being, remain in the guilt of original sin. Adam himself, since he is the first, is called “a human being,” not “a son of a human being.” The children of human beings, however, are those who, having obtained the grace of baptism, are reborn by the Lord’s gift into a new lineage. Christ himself was also called “the Son of Man,” so that those who receive his rewards might truly be honored by his name as well.

The wings of the Lord are the commandments of the New and Old Testaments. Every righteous person is understood to hope in their protection, so long as he is shown to obey them. This comparison is appropriately drawn from birds, whose tender young customarily place their hope in the protection of their mothers’ wings. By this example both the simplicity of the one who hopes and the care of the most gracious benefit are made clear.

### Verse 8

**They will be intoxicated by the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight.**

“They will be intoxicated”: the expression is taken, in a good sense, from a vicious human custom: people who, having gulped down excessive wine, grow numb through the oppression of the mind. So this heavenly intoxication removes the memory of worldly things and makes carnal concerns depart from the mind as a drunken stupor from wine alienates human actions from our senses.

He next indicates from where such intoxication can arise: “from the richness of your house,” that is, from the spiritual storehouses of holy Mother Church. She is the house that does not know how to spend her stored goods in vain; she is sufficient for the whole world, so that she always overflows in fullness. It is a sober intoxication, a glorious drunkenness, in which the drinker sins if he scorns to seek it above all else.

We have said that a torrent is a swift river, which descends through the sudden flooding of rains. To this Christ’s wisdom is aptly compared, because it is sudden and so rapid that it reaches the end it desires without any delay.

### Verse 9

**For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we will see light.**

How salutarily he opens up, and how powerfully he explains, what he said above: “They will be intoxicated.” He says to Christ the Lord: “For with you is the fountain of life,” that is, the beginning of all good things and the source of the virtues, from which we are filled most perfectly whenever we receive any gift from his kindness.

For drinkable life intoxicates us when we have drawn the zeal for a good way of life from sacred preaching, as Isaiah says: “You will draw water from the fountains of the Savior” (Isa. 12:3).

In ordinary human experience, however, light is one thing and a fountain another; indeed, they are opposites, since a fountain of water extinguishes the light of flames. With God, however, they are one, because whatever you say of him is true and still falls short.

We call God light because he enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9); a fountain because he satisfies the thirsty and empty; a mountain because he is strong and exalted; a way because he is upright; a teacher because he is the teacher of eternal life; a rock because he is shown to be the foundation and support of the Church; and so forth, as these things are read in the sacred writings. Yet in all these expressions one Lord, Christ, is understood.

But so that we may understand this verse perfectly and carefully, we must know that the name “light” is common to the whole Trinity. For it is written: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him” (John 1:5). Therefore, since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, we rightly understand the statement, “God is light, and there is no darkness in him,” to have been spoken of the whole Trinity.

Hence this verse rightly says of the Savior, “In your light we will see light”—that is, the light of the Father and of the Holy Spirit—because through his preaching it came about that the whole Trinity was made manifest to us.

### Verse 10

**Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your justice to those who are upright in heart.**

“Extend,” he says—that is, grant beforehand, sow in advance, spread far and wide—so that those who know you may walk more safely in this world.

Those who know the Lord are to be understood in several ways. They know the Lord who confess the holy Trinity with the firmest heart; who do not distort the rules given from heaven through any perversity of their understanding; and, finally, who alone truly know God because they do not abandon the unity of the Catholic faith.

He asks that mercy be extended to them, so that they may live under the Lord’s kindness in this world and receive worthy rewards at the future judgment. This is what “your justice to those who are upright in heart” signifies: those who, by the Lord’s gift, have deserved to live here with an upright mind will there be most justly placed at the right hand.

### Verse 11

**Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me.**

He prays that the steps of his mind may not depart from the righteous path, lest the one who had stood firm in the safest humility fall when lifted up in pride.

Nor is it without significance that he used “foot” here in the singular. It is certain that we cannot continually stand on one foot; this foot is appropriately assigned to pride, since it cannot sustain an exalted person for long. The foot, however, is used for the disposition of the mind. For just as, when walking, we are transferred from place to place, so we are separated from the Lord when we divide ourselves from him through an exalted thought.

This is recognized as the greatest sin—the sin from which the angel fell and by which Adam is shown to have been expelled from paradise. The hand of the sinner, however, is the action of one who gives evil counsel; it moves us from the firmness of faith when it troubles us with wicked argument.

### Verse 12

**There all who work iniquity have fallen; they have been driven out and could not stand.**

“There,” where he spoke above: namely, upon the foot of pride and the wicked persuasion of evil.

He aptly said “they have fallen,” as though he were saying, “they have collapsed into a deep pit.” For upon that foot one does not stand but falls. Who could doubt that those can collapse who are lifted up by only one footprint, as I said above? Even if no one pushes such a person, his own weariness makes him most prone to ruin.

Yet he does not assign this foot to one vice alone, but to all who work iniquity. Although some slip through cruelty, others through lust, others through greed, and others through the devil’s envy, all nevertheless fall through the vice of pride, because they despise the Lord’s commandments.

For just as one is called obedient who complies with many commands, so one who despises the Lord’s manifold commandments is most truthfully called proud. This argument is called one from the genus. Pride is the genus from which all vices are known to arise, as Scripture says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Sir. 10:15).

Of such people it continues: “They have been driven out and could not stand.” They are indeed driven out because they will hear: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). “They could not stand,” because they will not be permitted to delay the Lord’s commands; rather, they will immediately be cast down by the angels into the punitive flame prepared for them.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

It is pleasant to repeat the earlier parts of the psalm and consider with what beauty they were expressed. For it says how much divine grace has bestowed upon his servants, so that they have reached the fullest satisfaction through blessed abundance.

O exceedingly praiseworthy intoxication! O drunkenness to be desired with every prayer, from which moderation is born and complete integrity of mind is obtained! Here there is no staggering, no confusion, no alienation of mind, no dark blindness; rather, the soul is made healthier in proportion to how fully it is filled by that intoxication.

Let us therefore eagerly drink this beverage—not with carnal lips, but with the purest devotion of heart. From it we do not obtain temporal joy, but seek the joys of eternal life.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXVI

**A psalm of David himself.**

There is no need for us to say anything new about the words of this title; rather, we must open up the psalm’s purpose in the fullest way. For it is entirely concerned with correcting morals. The Church, which is now introduced as speaking, instructs the human race through saving commandments, lest it become mixed with deadly errors: deterring the wicked by punishment and promising rewards to the good.

This kind of teaching is altogether most effective, so that the proud may be humbled and the humble may receive worthy consolation. The psalm is also arranged according to the order of the Hebrew alphabet, though it lacks the sixteenth letter. As has already been said above, we think this should be referred to those who lack something of the perfect conduct of the saints.

Since all the Hebrew letters have their own meanings, it may perhaps be considered reasonable to believe that whoever lacks one element also lacks its meaning. Let those who study these matters perhaps propose better explanations; yet, despite searching longer, we have not been permitted to discover anything other than what we have said.

Remember, moreover, that this is already the third of these alphabetical psalms, since they too tend toward the number seven. This will have to be discussed in its proper place.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the entire psalm, as has been said, the voice of the Church is introduced to correct the people.

In the first section she warns that no one should imitate those who do evil, but should ask the Lord for whatever good is to be hoped for—for he knows how both to grant what is beneficial and to provide what will endure forever. This section contains six letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

The second says that sinners are tortured here by the greatest torment of envy, because they recognize that they possess nothing comparably good in their actions. This section has seven letters.

The third declares that she has never seen a righteous person abandoned, mingling the punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the good in a useful exchange. This part contains the remaining eight letters.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1. ALEPH

**Do not be envious among those who do evil, and do not envy those who commit iniquity.**

The beginning of the psalm—namely, “Do not be envious among those who do evil, and do not envy those who commit iniquity, because they will quickly wither like grass, and like the vegetables of the field they will soon fall”—is constructed in the form of a categorical syllogism, as follows:

Those who do evil and commit iniquity will quickly wither like grass and soon fall like the vegetables of the field. All who will quickly wither like grass and soon fall like the vegetables of the field are not to be envied. Therefore, those who do evil and commit iniquity are not to be envied.

Through the figure of *ethopoeia*, holy Mother Church forbids us to take pleasure in the actions of the wicked and to mingle with their crowds in a harmful association. The impious multitude of sinners troubles many people, and we are deceived by a certain pleasure when we hasten to sin along with the majority.

Then it follows that we should not imitate the mad even individually, while perhaps believing those people happy who for a time enjoy the freedom of their crimes. Here “to envy” means to imitate evil actions, when those who sigh that permission for wickedness has come to them late think that they have lost their days.

The Apostle also uses this word in a good sense when he says: “Envy the better spiritual gifts” (1 Cor. 12:31).

### Verse 2

**For they will quickly wither like grass, and like the vegetables of the field they will soon fall.**

A plausible reason has been given why we should not follow those whom we know to be destined quickly to perish. Grass is beautiful while it is green and flowering; but once it has dried, it immediately withers after its color has changed. So are the impious: shining with a kind of flowering joy, they dry up through a premature end.

First they were compared with grass, so that they might wither; now with the vegetables of the field, so that they might fall. For he did not say “the vegetables of gardens,” but “of the field,” to signify rather those most worthless plants that grow spontaneously throughout the countryside. Vegetables are called *olera* from *olla*, the pot in which, after being gathered, they are boiled.

Therefore let us compare the grass of the world with the noble, who quickly advance and are clothed, as it were, with great verdure in the form of grace. Let the vegetables of the field represent the ordinary and humble, which rise in abundance through uncultivated places and retain the wild and bristling quality of their nature. Yet the former quickly withers and the latter soon fall.

Someone may ask, “When should we believe this will happen to them?” Clearly, at the time of judgment, when the splendor of summer smiles upon us, when every human being opens his fruits according to the custom of trees.

This present age is like winter, in which every shoot of our deeds is enclosed; nor can judgment be passed upon things that are shown to be hidden. Therefore, in these two verses there is also explained that outstanding argument called an *epichirema*—in Latin, an exposition or argument—which confirms the credibility of a doubtful matter through examples. For it has been shown through grass and vegetables that the impious soon fall.

### Verse 3. BETH

**Hope in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land, and you will be nourished by its riches.**

After carefully judging that those who do evil must be avoided, he now advises us how we ought to act. First he urges us to hope in the Lord. This is the entrance of faith; this is the beginning of salvation.

Then follows, “and do good,” because, as it is written, “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20).

“Dwell in the land”: that is, persevere within the heart of holy Church, since it is never fitting for the faithful to depart from her.

And lest someone perhaps say, “What benefit will there be if we do these things?” there follows the great recompense of the whole matter: “You will be nourished by its riches.” “You will be nourished” pertains to satisfaction and enduring sweetness. “By its riches” means by the contemplation of Christ the Lord, who alone is shown to be the Church’s immeasurable reward.

What a marvelous nourishment—not the deficient refreshment of the body, but the inexhaustible strength of the soul! From it the faithful are fattened: it is food which, the more it satisfies, the more it continually increases a blessed hunger.

### Verse 4

**Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the petition of your heart.**

Delight is spoken of both bodily and spiritually: the former nourishes vices, the latter virtues. When he says, “Delight in the Lord,” he wants the memory of him to be sweet to you: so that you may love the one whom you fear, desire the one whom you revere, and seek eagerly to pursue the one before whom you are afraid.

Then follows: “And he will grant you the petition of your heart.” Observe that he said “of your heart,” not “of your flesh,” which is ordinarily related to wisdom. The petition of the heart is faith, charity, understanding of God, and the performance of good deeds. It is this petition that he customarily graciously approves, since he ordinarily admonishes through devout preaching. Thus, through each individual saying, the Christian’s mind is formed for eternal life.

### Verse 5. GIMEL

**Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him; and he himself will act.**

The density of sins is a kind of veil; hence our way, that is, our life, is clothed and surrounded by the darkness of that covering. We reveal it when we confess our sins most readily.

The Apostle Paul revealed his way when he said: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). He hoped in the Lord when he cried out: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). “The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

He added, “and he himself will act”: he himself who is almighty; he himself who is strong of hand; he himself whose commands everything truly obeys. What he himself does is explained below through the figure of *epexegesis*.

### Verse 6

**And he will bring forth your justice like light, and your judgment like midday.**

He explains what he said above: “And he himself will act.” The light of the sun displays bodily colors to us; the splendor of God lays bare the qualities of our works, so that our justice—that is, the faith we have in Christ—may shine in such a way that it can appear to spiritual eyes.

To bring forth is to draw something from darkness into light. This means to lead it from the gloom of this age into the brightness of the future judgment, where all things are made public and are no longer concealed in dark hiding places.

Therefore our justice, which by God’s gift we now possess in faith, will then appear before human eyes and be brought forth like light, when Christ, our hope, is revealed, as the Apostle says: “When Christ your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

“Like midday” is spoken by hyperbole; it signifies the clearest and purest light. For then the sun floods the earth with extraordinary brightness and illuminates every part of the world with visible radiance.

### Verse 7. DALETH

**Be subject to the Lord and entreat him; do not envy the one who prospers in his way.**

Even one who appears to be alienated from the Lord’s faith is subject to the Lord by the power of his dominion, though not by the choice of his judgment. But so that you may recognize that this has been said about the saints, it follows: “and entreat him.” They certainly do not know how to do this except those who serve the Lord with devout dedication.

To entreat means to ask obediently. Notice that these two commands have been set down in due order, so that we may both act rightly and pray continually, as the Apostle says: “Be constant in prayer, sharing in the needs of the saints” (Rom. 12:12).

He also returns to the warning with which the psalm began: the faithful must not imitate a sinner who flourishes. For this reason “in his way” has been added, so that you should understand not the saints but the criminals. The way of Christ alone is good; our way is subject to sins. The following verse clearly demonstrates this.

### Verse 8

**In a person who commits iniquity.**

Here he has clarified what he said above: “the one who prospers in his way”—that is, “in a person who commits iniquity or wickedness,” whose conduct is disgraceful and whose dealings are filthy.

### Verse 9. HE

**Cease from anger and abandon wrath; do not envy so as to act wickedly.**

He says “cease” to the person who still mutters with the insane swelling of his spirit, who, inflamed by anger and indignation, pours forth blasphemous words and complains that the happiness of this age has been denied him, although he sees the worst people possessing it.

Anger is, as we have said elsewhere, what kindles the mind through a swift movement; wrath is what persists for a longer time. Therefore he commands us to abandon both, since through them we can arrive at guilt.

He added, “Do not envy so as to act wickedly.” The ancients defined wickedness as voluntary malice: we do not fall into it by accident, but willingly occupy ourselves in it with pleasure. He frequently forbids anyone to wish to imitate it.

For *nequam*—“worthless” or “wicked”—is said to derive from *nequaquam*, that is, “not at all,” because such a person is fit for nothing at any time.

### Verse 10

**For those who act wickedly will be exterminated; but those who wait for the Lord will themselves possess the land as an inheritance.**

A twofold reason is proposed, one of fear and one of reward, so that we may in no way desire to imitate the worst people. O human being, why do you wish to imitate those whom you see perishing? You hear from the mother who loves you why you should not rejoice with the good, lest you happen to perish with the worst.

“To be exterminated” means to be cast outside the boundaries—that is, to be deprived of the city of God.

But lest fear alone disturb the weak hearts of human beings, he also adds the hope of the good, saying: “But those who wait for the Lord will themselves possess the land as an inheritance.” These are those who despise the happiness of the impious and do not want the present gifts to be granted to them, but await the coming of the Lord and Savior.

They will rejoice in his inheritance—that is, in the inheritance that comes by law, which is secure and eternal. “They will possess the land”: that is, they will enjoy the future city of the Lord, which divine kindness promises to righteous people.

Therefore let us consider the order of the heavenly deed; let us await what has been promised in its appointed times, lest, while wishing to demand the promises hastily, we appear to be punished by the loss of our case.

This verse, however, depends upon what precedes; hence it says, “Do not envy the one who prospers in his way.” This figure is called *hyperbaton*, when the suspended order of the words is explained below.

### Verse 11. VAU

**And yet a little while, and the sinner will no longer exist; you will seek his place and will not find it.**

“A little while” signifies something small and slight, something that could be enclosed in the hand with the fingers closed. *Pusillum*—“a little thing”—is said to derive from *pugnus*, “fist.”

The Church promises this brief and final age as a remedy to those who labor, so that it may not seem long when the faithful are recognized as capable of growing weary. The “little while” is the time that remains until the day of judgment, which, compared with the days that have passed, is altogether very short.

“And the sinner will no longer exist”—not because the person who sinned will not exist, but because he will cease to sin. His place signifies this world, which favors sinners and is properly their friend, where it is clear that sins flourish as though in their own dwelling.

### Verse 12

**But the meek will possess the land, and they will delight in the abundance of peace.**

We call them “meek” who are accustomed to the hand—that is, patient and gentle people who tolerate the iniquities of others and do not presume to burden anyone themselves.

But observe how great the force of this name is: although it is fitting for a Christian to be capable of many virtues, the command is shown to have been expressed to explain the perfection of every good.

This says that they will possess the future Jerusalem, about which we have already often spoken. It is a city always filled with the sweetness of the good, where its inhabitants do not live by commerce but are nourished by divine delight.

There no one labors in order to live; rather, completely at rest, each receives what the blessed soul desires. There the blessed hunger of the heart’s eyes is nourished; there the soul is refreshed by sight alone, when everything belonging to its desire is supplied through contemplation of the Lord’s face.

Then follows: “They will delight in the abundance of peace.” Here the truth of perfect blessedness is already indicated, so that everything that exists may always be perceived with sweetness and what delights may never cease.

To show that this delight is dissolved by no opposition, he added, “in the abundance of peace.” The peace of the future age is where nothing adverse and nothing contrary can exist; rather, the joy once begun continues most sweetly in a single mode.

### Verse 13. ZAIN

**The sinner will watch the righteous and gnash his teeth at him.**

Although the connected meaning of this psalm appears to be composed throughout of references to sinners and the righteous, we will not inappropriately make a division here, since something new is perceived to have been introduced among the very comparisons. Therefore let this be a second division for us.

Earlier he had said that the faithful must not envy the impious; now he says that sinners are tormented by envy against the righteous. A different will prepares hatred for the righteous. For when a criminal sees him devoting himself to good morals, he believes that he is being specially accused. He gnashes his teeth and rages in his mind; and the one whose character he cannot subvert, he immediately tries to deprive of life itself.

“He will watch” means that he will look upon him with pain, as though from hidden ambushes. To gnash the teeth is characteristic of raging beasts, which the angry person imitates while threatening his neighbor with destruction.

Therefore it is shameful to emulate those who envy the good of others, since the one whom the charge of envy condemns considers himself the lowest.

### Verse 14

**But the Lord will mock him, because he sees that his day will come.**

A marvelous form of consolation is shown to us. For who should take pleasure in the pomp of one whose audacity he knows will perish? If we do not wish to be confused by some misplaced zeal, let us follow what the Lord does. Let us mock the one whose downfall we foresee; let us judge as miserable the things we discover to be destined to perish.

Let us believe these things with the greatest firmness, since they have been promised to us by the truth. Thus it will happen that the mocked sinner departs—the one who boasts of himself in a fleeting happiness.

### Verse 15. HETH

**Sinners have unsheathed the sword; they have bent their bow, to cast down the needy and the poor, to slaughter the upright in heart.**

The sinner’s sword is any deceit that seeks to injure another. For the person who strives to strip the needy also draws the sword of his perverse plan; and the person who desires through wicked persuasion to deceive innocent souls displays the sword of his worst thought.

“They have unsheathed” means “they have exposed.” What was previously hidden in thought, as though in a sheath, appears after being drawn out, when the thoughts have been revealed.

To bend a bow is not yet to shoot an arrow; it indicates that the bow is prepared and drawn taut. They await the time for their fraudulent work, when they may deceive the simple and innocent.

Then follows: “to cast down the needy and the poor.” We explained not long ago what distinction there is between “needy” and “poor.” It is beautifully said “to cast down,” as though they were standing and enduring through the strength of faith. They are cast down when a dark error, like death, is poured into them.

It is added: “to slaughter the upright in heart.” This may be understood of the martyrs, who are upright in heart but are slaughtered in the flesh.

### Verse 16. THETH

**Let their sword enter their own hearts, and let their bow be broken.**

Whatever attempts to destroy is properly called a sword, since the sword is the complete form of weaponry for producing death. A sword is called that which is made for the slaughter of enemies.

And so that you may know that this sword came from thought, he said in a reciprocal statement, “Let it enter their hearts”—from where it had come and where it had advanced through its perverse ambushes.

We have said that the bow signifies the hidden malice prepared against the most innocent. But he said that it should be broken because it was not going to harm the faithful in the part of the soul.

Observe that he repeated in punishment the very words he had used for crimes, because of that saying of the Gospel: “In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38).

### Verse 17

**Better is a little for the righteous than the many riches of sinners.**

The pious mother, as though kissing and embracing her good children, continues to console them, persuading them that a little for the righteous is better than the riches of sinners.

But let us consider what “a little” is, since it is precisely what makes people great. Here “a little” should be understood as humility. While our mind restrains itself in this, it rises above the precious things of the world.

By contrast, “the many riches of sinners” are the accumulation of crimes and the abundance of sins. Therefore let us judge how much better it is to receive that little of the righteous and not possess the mass of so many crimes. The former leads to the kingdom of heaven; the latter plunges into Tartarus.

This argument is drawn from opposites. For “a little of the righteous” is contrary to “the many riches of the sinner.”

### Verse 18

**For the arms of sinners will be broken, but the Lord strengthens the righteous.**

The arms of the wicked signify their proud actions, in which the impious presume while they are bent by no consideration of reason.

He did not say “they are broken,” which could happen through a single blow, but “they will be crushed,” that is, diminished through continual grinding, since it is always more grievous to be reduced piece by piece than to be destroyed by a sudden catastrophe.

But just as he weakens the impious through such a threat, so he strengthens the righteous through a good promise. To strengthen is to fortify someone placed in mental distress with a consoling word.

If you consider it carefully, the power of the entire psalm has been expressed in this statement. All these sayings are directed toward casting down the presumption of the sinner and lifting up the spirit of the righteous.

This figure is called *paradigma*, that is, an example used to encourage or deter. That is what has also been done here, when he invites the righteous through prosperity and terrifies sinners through adversity.

### Verse 19. JOD

**The Lord knows the ways of the blameless, and their inheritance will be forever.**

Human ignorance cannot see the ways of the blameless, because the narrow way of the virtues is imperceptible to the flesh. But the Lord, who created them, knows them in their complete quality and measure.

He explains what may come to such people: “Their inheritance will be forever.” Their inheritance is the heavenly Jerusalem, exceedingly rich in eternal peace. It is promised so often, rightly, that any doubt about the true promise may be removed.

“It will be forever” has been added in contrast with worldly inheritances, which cannot be eternal. That inheritance is granted perpetually because it is bestowed without end.

### Verse 20

**They will not be confounded in the evil time, and in the days of famine they will be satisfied.**

The “evil time” signifies the day of judgment, when all flesh anxiously fears the repayment and recompense of its deeds, as he says elsewhere: “In the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40:2).

At that time, therefore, the blameless will not be confounded, since their sins have been forgiven through the grace of satisfaction.

Then follows: “And in the days of famine they will be satisfied.” The days of famine signify the time of this world, when the blessed hunger and thirst for justice (Matt. 5:6). At the resurrection there is no time of famine for the righteous, but the eternal satisfaction of every good thing.

Therefore, in this world, where the righteous can hunger or seek justice, they will be satisfied—namely, through the holy Scriptures, through the Lord’s examples, and through the rewards promised again and again, by which Christ satisfies the faithful.

Thus perfect security is promised to the devout: in the future judgment they will not be ashamed, and in this world they will receive appropriate gifts.

### Verse 21. CAPH

**For sinners will perish; but the enemies of the Lord, though honored and exalted, will soon fail; failing, they will fail like smoke.**

It must be considered that one proof is placed in this verse and another immediately follows. For he says, “For sinners will perish,” and again, “But the enemies of the Lord, though honored and exalted, will fail.”

This figure is called *epexergasia*, whenever we add two proofs to a single cause.

At that judgment sinners will perish, since they are clearly not filled with spiritual food. Here they are considered satiated and wealthy by themselves, although their abundant satisfaction is utterly starved and empty—namely, a satisfaction that leads them all the way to perish.

Notice that he confirms that sinners will perish, that is, that they will be condemned in that judgment. For you will find impious people who enjoy worldly pleasures through almost the whole course of their lives. Why, then, does he say “soon”? Because whoever climbs a height destined to collapse immediately falls from the truth: he begins to perish when he strives to climb what is about to fall.

“Failing” could also have meant that they would fail in such a way that some trace of them might perhaps remain. He added “like smoke,” so that it might be understood that no remnant of their deeds would remain.

For just as smoke, emerging from flames, rises through the air in billowing masses and, the higher it flies, the more quickly vanishes, so dark and insubstantial sins, the more they raise themselves up, the more swiftly they are scattered.

The expression “failing, they will fail” is an argument called one from related forms. These words arise from one another and, deriving from a single source, proceed in corresponding similarity.

### Verse 22. LAMETH

“The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the righteous shows mercy and lends.”

The sinner borrows when he hears the word of God but does not put it into effect by his deeds. For this is what it means not to repay: to fail completely to fulfill the commands of the Divinity. He also borrows when he receives God’s various benefits but returns no expression of thanks; instead, insolent and as though he had received nothing, he remains perpetually ungrateful.

But the righteous person’s situation is different. Although he receives little in this life, he returns more through devout dedication: giving thanks to the one who bestows everything, he regards the poverty given to him as riches; he also embraces pains and calamities themselves, and through patience struggles even against death, in hope of the reward to come.

Observe that it says, “shows mercy and lends.” This refers to the giving of alms, where mercy comes first and benevolent humanity follows afterward. And consider that, through the figure of *diaphoresis*—by which a distinction between persons is made—it establishes a contrary separation between the righteous and the ungodly. [Col. 0264B]

### Verse 23

“For those who bless him shall possess the earth; but those who curse him shall perish.”

Just as above, through the figure of *diaphoresis*, he divided the will of sinners and the righteous, so now through the same figure he separates their recompense and rewards, lest he leave confused what has no point of agreement between them.

For those who bless the Lord—that is, those who give thanks in all things and keep his commandments—shall receive that land of the living as their possession, of which another psalm also says: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Psalm 141:6). But those who curse and blaspheme, or who disobey God’s laws, are removed from that homeland—not because they themselves will cease to exist, since penal fire will torment them, but because they will perish away from the blessedness promised to the righteous.

### Verse 24. MEM

“By the Lord a man’s steps shall be directed, and he shall greatly desire his way.”

Let us understand the matter being presented. Human steps are always crooked and perverse in themselves, since we have been conceived in iniquities and born in sins; but we are directed by the Father of lights when we receive the rule of faith in which we are to walk. We are plainly directed when we walk without error.

But where does this direction lead us? Clearly, so that we may come to perfect faith and eternal rewards. [Col. 0264D] Yet this Christian, who has already been directed in heart, “shall greatly desire his way”—that is, he will love the Lord and Savior himself above all things, for he truly is our way, truth, and life (John 14:6).

### Verse 25

“When the righteous falls, he shall not be shaken, because the Lord supports his hand.”

When he falls, do not understand this as falling into sin, since he has called him righteous, but as falling into the hands of sinners, in a harsh calamity of the kind that frequently comes upon the saints when the devil lies in wait.

But, so that you may seem satisfied with this explanation, consider that although the same verse says “he shall fall,” which refers to the feet, it immediately adds that the hand of the fallen man shall be strengthened. It would have been more appropriate to strengthen his step, so that he might be able to rise after his fall. Hence it is clearly evident that this “falling” means falling under the power of the ungodly. For he strengthens this man’s hand—that is, his counsel and action. And one who has determined fearlessly to undergo the adversities of this world cannot be shaken when he has been seized.

### Verse 26. NUN

“I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread.”

We have arrived at the third section, where, if you suppose that one man is speaking, a brief and narrow span of time is indicated, wholly insufficient for the praises of God. But rather let the voice of the Church be understood as having been introduced; from the beginning of the world to its end, it proves this statement true. [Col. 0265A]

She was young when, in the first ancestor, she received the beginnings of the law in its original form. She grew old—that is, she came to a more venerable age—when in the final times she was worthy to receive the Lord Redeemer. For the evangelist John also says in his Epistle: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

But throughout these periods, which extend over the whole circuit of the world, she does not say that she has seen the righteous forsaken. Thus it appears that a long period of time is designated through the words of the Church.

What, then, shall we say about those righteous people who fell into the hands of robbers, or even about the Righteous One of the righteous, who cried out on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)? But to escape every knot of contradiction, the righteous person was not forsaken in spiritual goods, though not—as is commonly supposed—in temporal aids. These spiritual goods were truly bestowed when they were able to overcome the torments of the world, as he himself testifies: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10). [Col. 0265C]

In the same way, he says that he has not seen the offspring of the righteous begging bread. If you take this literally, this too cannot be established. For we read that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob changed regions because of famine; thus there is no doubt that those whom necessity of place drove to seek foreign lands lacked bread.

But let us return to the inner person, and the true meaning will appear to us as a source of salvation. We have said that each person’s offspring is his work, which he sows and reaps, whether good or evil. Therefore the work of the righteous does not need bread—that is, the word of God by which it is satisfied, refreshed, and truly lives and is nourished within. In this way the statements that seemed contradictory will be brought into harmony.

### Verse 27

“All day long he shows mercy and lends, and his offspring shall be in blessing.”

By “all day long” he means throughout the whole time of his life. For the singular “day” is frequently used to indicate the periods of an entire life, as in the first psalm: “And on his law he will meditate day and night” (Psalm 1:2). Thus, when we say little, we may understand much.

“He shows mercy and lends”: either he is speaking of almsgiving, where mercy first touches the heart and then opens the hand. For that is perfect almsgiving which begins with itself and then hastens to bring aid to another. Or perhaps we should say that he lends spiritual goods, which the poor man of God possesses in abundance. Indeed, the righteous man lends from that in which he is altogether rich—from instruction, devotion, justice, patience, and the other goods with which that most holy mind enjoys itself. [Col. 0266A]

And lest you think that the righteous sometimes wishes to borrow, he says, “all day long.” O immeasurable riches, which throughout the whole of life pour out their abundance most generously! Rightly does he not grow weary of giving who has always been accustomed to receive from Christ.

It follows: “And his offspring shall be in blessing.” This passage resembles those above. For if you wish to understand “offspring” as children, many saints fathered dissolute and ungodly children. But by “offspring” he means the work which is scattered by a person as a gift from above, like seed. This is received in blessing because it was sown in good will. The Apostle understood our works as seed when he says: “He who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, and he who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Galatians 6:8).

### Verse 28. SAMECH

“Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever.”

Our devout mother establishes our life in two ways. The first is that we turn away from evil, since a sinner cannot suddenly acquire a desire for good things. The second is that we do good, because we have ceased from blameworthy action.

Let us therefore turn away from the evils that belong to us and do the good things that belong to Christ. For at the judgment the Lord does not call his righteous people to receive a reward because they took nothing from the poor; rather, he crowns them because they clothed the naked, visited the sick, and chose to feed the hungry and thirsty.

You see, then, that it is not enough for a Christian to abstain from evil unless he also strives by some action to accomplish good.
