But what follows these commandments? “And dwell for ever and ever,” so that, trusting in such a promise, he may already appear to possess future rewards through the surest hope. “For ever and ever” signifies the eternal kingdom, which will not be changed by any succession.

### Verse 29

“For the Lord loves judgment, and he will not forsake his saints; they shall be preserved for ever.”

Hearing this word, you too should love judgment and practice justice, so that, with the Lord’s help, you may maintain yourself in an upright will and rejoice together with your own good deeds. For the author of justice cannot forsake those who choose to fulfill his commandments.

And attend to the promise: he does not say that the righteous will never be abandoned in temporal matters, but declares that they will be preserved for ever. In this life they cannot be preserved visibly, since they are torn by tribulations and punishments. Let those who desire this life hear this—those who are known to ask for long years: those who strive to please the Lord will be preserved not in this world, but for ever.

### Verse 30

“But the unjust shall be punished, and the offspring of the ungodly shall perish.”

This meaning is frequently repeated, so that what is to come may be believed all the more firmly. For divine mercy, wishing us to escape the punishments of Gehenna, graciously admonishes us again and again.

And just as above he said that the offspring of the righteous—that is, their works—would remain in blessing, so here he confirms that the deeds of the ungodly will perish. They will indeed perish when both the sin itself and the place of sinners are known to perish.

We shall prove that the works of unbelievers perish not so much by our own words as by the words of Solomon. For they will say at the judgment: “What did our pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow” (Wisdom 5:8–9). You see that whatever destroys a person perishes, while only those things endure which make people remain in the Lord’s kingdom.

### Verse 31

“The righteous shall possess the earth as an inheritance, and they shall dwell upon it for ever and ever.”

Just as he continually rebukes in order to correct, so he frequently promises gifts in order to raise up. Both, as we have said, are highly effective instruments of instruction: punishment follows the wicked, and promised rewards follow the good.

This earth was so called because it is worn down by the feet of travelers. By analogy with it, that future earth is also called earth—not because it will be worn away, since it will remain perpetually unharmed, but because it does not lose its name, for it will remain with its qualities unchanged. We likewise believe that heaven and our bodies will be renewed; although they will be new, they will still be called by the same names.

He adds: “And they shall dwell upon it for ever and ever,” lest you think this is the earth that must someday be abandoned. Nor is it without significance that he did not say “in it,” but “upon it.” He seems, as we think, to be revealing the secret nature of that dwelling. It is said “upon it” because a spiritual body will not need to tread the earth with a heavy foot, as the Apostle says: “Then we who are alive, who remain, shall together with them be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:14).

### Verse 32. PHE

“The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment.”

This account, through the figure of *characterismos*, which in Latin is called *informatio* or “description,” indicates the time of blessed resurrection. For it does not say “he meditates,” but “he shall meditate,” using the future tense. Here we must understand “mouth” as thought, since what it will speak follows with reference to the tongue.

He will therefore meditate upon wisdom, not through reading the Scriptures, but through the purest vision of the heart. There wisdom is not gathered through letters, but is bestowed without labor by heavenly generosity. And his tongue shall speak judgment, because there speech will in no way disagree with thought. Just as the heart will meditate upon wisdom, so the tongue will speak justice in all things.

This is the heavenly condition of the blessed: that those who do not confuse themselves through any error may rightly be received into the fellowship of the angels. The tongue of the righteous therefore speaks judgment when he has been filled with the manifestation of the true light. “Judgment” is so called as though from *iuris dictum*, “the declaration of law,” because law is spoken through it. For the saints will not always judge, since it is certain that judgment belongs to the Lord alone. But those whom divine power truly embraces will speak justly for ever.

### Verse 33

“The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted.”

You see how the perfection of future blessedness is indicated to us: a person will receive nothing else in his heart except the will of God, by which he becomes blessed and through which he rises to such a height that he will give thanks without end.

“His God” signifies the one who freed him from the ruin of this world. This pronoun, “his,” indicates the grace of the Lord Savior. For although he is the God of all, he is properly called the God of the one whom he deigns to free.

When it says, “in his heart,” it signifies that the whole understanding of the blessed person is filled with such a good. No one, therefore, will be able to supplant his steps when original sin has already ceased and the devil no longer has permission to deceive.

For “to supplant” means to set pits beneath the soles of the feet, so that one walking cannot find firm footing. This cannot occur at all there, where everything is secure and eternal, as he will say in the fifty-fifth psalm: “For you have rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling” (Psalm 55:13).

### Verse 34. SADE

“The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to destroy him.”

These things are still being said about the future judgment. To watch means to observe something with deep deliberation and to penetrate to the very heart of matters. [Col. 0268B]

For on the day of resurrection the sinner will take stock of the righteous and say in his heart: “Is this not the one who was in need, whom we held in contempt and mocked? And now we see him chosen above us and established in the highest glory?” This is what it means for the sinner to watch the righteous.

“He seeks to destroy him” is said according to the habitual conduct of wrongdoers, because even in that world they will hasten to destroy the righteous, although it will already be recognized that they have no power to do harm.

### Verse 35

“But the Lord will not abandon him into his hands, nor will he condemn him when judgment is passed upon him.”

Consider how he has assigned this order to the future age: he says that the righteous will no longer be handed over to the power of his enemy. In this world it frequently happened that he left martyrs in the hands of their persecutors to be killed bodily. Then he will no longer abandon his servants to the decisions of the ungodly; rather, he will possess them, placed in eternal peace and freed from every danger.

“Nor will he condemn him when judgment is passed upon him.” He does not condemn the righteous when he judges the ungodly. Through the distinction of merits, blessedness will receive the righteous, while the other will be tormented by the punishment he deserves.

### Verse 36. COPH

“Wait for the Lord and keep his ways; and he will exalt you, so that you may possess the earth; when sinners have perished, you shall see.”

After carefully explaining the matters that could pertain to eternal blessedness, he returns to the righteous person, consoling him and saying: You who have now believed to what good things you may be raised, confidently wait for the Lord—that is, act patiently. And what that patience is, he does not leave unsaid.

For he does not say “wait” to one who is idle, but to one who labors, who keeps the ways of the Lord—that is, his most sacred commandments. He fittingly gives each person what belongs to him. No one can possess that earth unless he has been exalted, because it is so great, so holy, and so heavenly that no one can attain it unless he has earned it well.

It follows: “When sinners have perished, you shall see.” The joys of the righteous are increased in two ways. First, when they perceive the greatness of the delights in which they are to be placed; then, when they see the punishments of sinners, they will rejoice all the more that they have been freed from eternal torment. For the quality of a gift becomes more pleasing when its painful opposite has been seen.

Therefore he says, “you shall see”—that is, what you now believe, you will then know plainly and rejoice, when they have deservedly perished and you have been placed by the grace of the Lord in the highest blessedness.

### Verse 37

“I saw the ungodly greatly exalted and raised up above the cedars of Lebanon.”

Here the fullest medicine is provided against a very serious disease. Some say: If such things displeased God, such great happiness would by no means come to sinners. Therefore, through *energeia*, which represents the action of an incorporeal reality through imagination, he says that he saw the ungodly grow—not toward honor, but rather toward ruin.

Such people are raised above the righteous here because the righteous are humble and these people are proud. But these will fall in the judgment, while the righteous will be raised up in happiness. And because he had said “greatly exalted,” lest you think he had merely been raised above the humble, he added, “and raised above the cedars of Lebanon,” so that he might appear higher even than those lofty treetops. [Col. 0269B]

His advancement is exalted so greatly for the very purpose of showing his irreparable ruin. This may also rightly be understood of the devil, concerning whom the prophet Joel testifies, saying: “And him who is from the north I will drive away from you, and I will cast him into a thirsty and desolate land; I will destroy his face in that first sea, and his rear in the last sea” (Joel 2:20).

We give thanks to you, Lord, for your dispositions. For what would this one do if he were free—the one who, though bound, afflicts the world?

### Verse 38. RES

“And I passed by, and behold, he was no more; and I sought him, and his place was not found.”

This world is passed through in two ways: either when it is abandoned through a better way of life, or when it is left behind by the dead at the end. Therefore, whoever has passed over to God through a most holy way of life no longer sees the sinner as powerful, when he sees that all the things in which humanity boasts are weak.

“I sought,” he says—that is, “I recalled.” For the righteous remember sinners most of all when, through the Lord’s mercy, they are changed for the better, grieving that, wretched as they are, they are separated from those evil deeds.

The place of sinners is understood to be this world, in which they both carry out their crimes and are heaped with fleeting prosperity. But this place is dissolved together with their prosperity when the glory of the entire corruptible world comes to an end.

### Verse 39. SIN

“Keep truth and behold equity, for there are remains for the peaceful man.”

When he commands us to keep truth, he warns us not to devote our concern to worldly matters. For only one who is always constant, who thinks about it, speaks about it, and turns it over in his mind, and who is separated from that concern at no moment, is accustomed to keep something.

But what is this truth? Clearly, God, who said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Therefore, if you keep God, he undoubtedly keeps you.

He also says, “and behold equity”—namely, God’s equity. For he subsequently explains what that equity is, saying: “For there are remains for the peaceful man.”

Let us consider how we ought to understand this statement. There are remains for the peaceful man when his hope is fulfilled through the Lord’s reward. What remains is that after this life he should receive the rewards of eternal blessedness. Thus there are remains for the peaceful when they begin to possess the most certain hope at the very time they attain the Lord’s gifts.

A peaceful person is one who makes peace in this world among those who disagree and who, through a devotion to gentleness, does not himself become involved in disgraceful conflicts. And note that he is placed among the blessed, to whom this virtue is granted through the Lord’s loving-kindness.

### Verse 40

“But the unjust shall perish together; the remains of the ungodly shall perish.”

Statements suited to unequal persons are given here. For just as the righteous rejoice in the greatest hope after this life, so the unjust perish when the light of this life has ended.

Or, as some wish, “remains” signifies the memory of good deeds which a righteous man leaves behind in this world after his death, while he is praised for the integrity of his actions. This certainly happened to the martyrs, who happily surrendered their souls in testimony to the truth.

The ungodly can in no way merit this. They leave behind no trace worthy of remembrance, since when their destruction comes, their false praise and fragile life are dissolved.

### Verse 41. TAU

“But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation.”

Holy Church returns to her customary consolations, lest she seem harsh if she did not also possess the joys of a good promise. The firm promise and strong protection affirm that the salvation of the righteous comes from the Lord, not from any other power.

Here the meaning of another psalm should be mentioned: “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.” It follows: “And he is their protector in the time of tribulation” (Psalm 22:4).

The time of tribulation is twofold, but very different in character. Here there are temporal tribulations, which the Lord nevertheless does not entirely remove from his faithful. They bite rather than devour, prick rather than strike, afflict rather than diminish.

But the tribulation that comes upon the ungodly on the day of judgment is evil because it is eternal, grievous because it torments, and violent because it is exacting. In this time of tribulation, therefore, the Lord is a protector, because he rescues the righteous from it.

### Verse 42

“And the Lord will help them and deliver them; he will rescue them from sinners and save them, because they have hoped in him.”

He is speaking of faithful servants, whom he effectively helps in this world when they are wearied by opposing struggle. He delivers them by not allowing their faith to be perverted by wicked persuasion. He rescues them from sinners—that is, he preserves them unharmed from the opposition of this world.

He also adds the reason for their deliverance: “because they have hoped in him.” This is not because they have not sinned, but because they have placed their hope in the Lord’s loving-kindness. This may also be applied to that judgment, when he will deign to grant eternal rewards to his saints.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

How fruitful are the words spoken through the gracious condescension of the Holy Spirit! With what wondrous skill was that heavenly garment of the Lord Christ woven—not with threads, but with verses; not with warp, but with compunction; not with wool, but with grace! It surrounds the whole body and covers its members in the manner of a sacred vestment. The mad insolence of the soldiers could not divide it; nor can the multitude of heretics, who have been tearing at it throughout so many ages, rend it. Remaining firm in its integrity, it protects only those whom it knows to please the Lord.

Let us therefore ask the inseparable Trinity that this garment may also protect us and, through its gracious condescension, enclose us within its folds. At this point the words of Sedulius should be borrowed:

> “Great things indeed I ask, but you know how to give great things.”

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXVII

## A Psalm of David in Commemoration

By saying “in commemoration,” this title declares to us that, since we cannot avoid sin in every respect, we must at least always keep the sin itself in remembrance, so that, while we are mindful of our guilt, we may restrain ourselves from frequent sinning. [Col. 0271B]

So too in the thirty-first psalm it is written, “David’s understanding”; and in the fiftieth psalm he himself confesses: “My sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:5).

Although the prophet’s testimony concerning his own name speaks especially about future things, he does not leave aside the past, which he knows to pertain to the salvation of the faithful people. This psalm, as some have wished, relates entirely to the most vigorous suffering of blessed Job, who overcame mortal life, conquered his own flesh, and triumphed over immense punishments. It does this so that the burdens of penitents may be made light when examples of the gravest temptation are recalled.

For it is the custom of divine Scripture that, when Christ’s highly trained soldier is said to be afflicted, the spirit of the recruit may thereby be instructed more effectively. Therefore let us rejoice in harsh afflictions and be glad in the torture of our flesh, since what torments us here with momentary speed for the Lord’s sake is what frees us from eternal punishment. It should also be considered that among these psalms of penitents no one is read to have suffered so much that the quality of his joys may rightly be thought to correspond to the measure of his evils.

## Division of the Psalm

Through the figure of *ethopoeia*, a person is introduced—as has been said—as an unconquered soldier of Christ, pierced by the pain of wounds, swarming with worms, and further wounded by reproaches; yet amid so many calamities he remains completely healthy through the vitality of faith. We too rightly believe that this person should be identified with blessed Job, since the latter experienced calamities like these and the wording itself seems almost identical. Therefore, at each point we shall provide testimonies from his book, so that the sufferings themselves may appear altogether to correspond and agree with one another.

This psalm of the penitent is divided into four parts. First it contains an introduction, in which a life of suffering moves the merciful judge to compassion. A twofold narrative follows, in which he recalls both his body afflicted by various punishments and his spirit grievously wounded by the accusations of his friends, so that, when no consolation remains on either side, the Lord may be entreated with all strength.

Third comes the consolation of saving medicine, in which he says that amid manifold calamities he has placed his hope in the Lord. In the manner of a most devoted servant, he also testifies that he is prepared for the scourges, since he thinks that he still deserves more than he appears to have suffered.

After this comes the exultant conclusion that is always granted to penitents. Having now been freed from all calamities, he confesses God to be the author of his salvation, so that it may plainly be shown that the person who has been enriched by participation in such great joy has been established in the surest hope.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury.”

This most holy man, of whom the Lord said, “Simple, upright, fearing God, and turning away from evil” (Job 1:1), had been handed over to the devil’s temptations for testing. Amid his anxieties and pains, he was not so concerned about his own punishment as he was apprehensive of the Lord’s displeasure. He asks not to endure the torments he was suffering under an angry judge.

For a blow that comes from a peaceful mind is correction, as it is written: “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you” (Proverbs 9:8). But what comes from an offended judge is rightly feared. The former provides correction; the latter demands vengeance. Hence he asks not to be rebuked in anger or punished with eternal condemnation.

Thus, fearing this, he also says in his book: “His fury raged against me, and he treated me as his enemy” (Job 19:11).

Concerning the anger of the Lord, Father Augustine discussed the matter with beautiful brevity in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 13), saying: “When God is said to be angry, this does not signify a disturbance in him, such as occurs in the mind of an angry human being. Rather, through a word transferred from human emotions, his vengeance—which is nothing other than just—has received the name ‘anger.’”

Let what was said about such expressions of anger or fury in the sixth psalm suffice here.

### Verse 2

“For your arrows are fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand against me.”

A plausible reason follows: the person who has been severely afflicted by present evils ought not then to be punished at that judgment. For when the Lord punishes here, he spares there, since his clemency does not demand two acts of vengeance for the same matter, as it is written: “The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing” (Numbers 1:9).

But although this most faithful servant recognized that he was being tormented by the devil’s deceit, he nevertheless knew that the devil could not prevail against him unless he had received permission through divine commands. Therefore he addresses the one in whose power all things have been placed.

Arrows may be understood in both a good and a bad sense. In the good sense, as in the passage: “He made his arrows burning” (Psalm 7:14). Here, however, the arrows signify diabolical powers, which wound like missiles when they are directed by the Lord’s permission.

He rightly said “fixed,” because there could be no respite from his pains. Thus the blessed man himself also says: “For the arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation drinks up my spirit, and the terrors of the Lord wage war against me” (Job 6:4).

It follows: “And you have strengthened your hand against me.” Although divine power always works for the salvation and life of the faithful, here what he suffers through long and numerous calamities is attributed, as it were, to God’s hands—not because God himself had destroyed his children, ruined his possessions, and struck him with the pain of ulcers, but because he delayed removing the devil, who was shown to be inflicting such things.

Thus it is also written in Job’s own book: “Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?” (Job 7:21). This is fittingly said to the power of the judge, so that saving goodwill may be obtained.

### Verse 3

“There is no health in my flesh because of the face of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins.”

He also moves mercy through the weakness of his own person, since his flesh could not withstand the battle and had collapsed after so many blows.

“The face of anger” is the fear of future vengeance conceived with great dread. Therefore he asks God to free him from future anger, since he says that he is so terrified by the indignation to come that he has no bodily health at all.

He is like a shamefaced servant who, before suffering blows, is already grievously afflicted by the torments that are to come; one who is hardened in mind, however, does not shudder even at the punishments while they are being inflicted.

He also adds: “There is no peace in my bones.” What he previously called “health” he now repeats as “peace”—rightly, because health is the peace of the whole body and a balanced tranquility of its humors.

Here the excess of pain is expressed: the man who had said that his flesh was not sound now says that even his bones were disturbed. For the punishment that descends into the innermost parts is more severe; nothing remains untouched when the very supports of the body are shaken.

He signifies the consumption by worms that he was suffering, which could not grant the holy man any rest, because it did not cease consuming him, as he himself says: “Those who eat me do not sleep” (Job 30:17).

But above those bodily punishments he says that he is afflicted by “the face of my sins,” in the manner of a most holy spirit which, when it remembers its iniquities, believes that it will suffer more severe things.

### Verse 4

“For my iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden, they have been made heavy upon me.”

A third means of obtaining goodwill is added: he does not say that he has been struck unjustly, but seems to attribute what he suffers to his sins.

Let us now return to explaining the words. Our iniquities raise themselves above our head when they claim more for themselves than reason and justice can tolerate. For our head is reason, above which we possess nothing higher among the goods bestowed upon us. Guided by it, with the Lord’s help, we are directed; it leads us to good actions and useful pursuits. If iniquity oppresses it, reason immediately falls defeated.

But this reversal is assigned to such iniquities: those that raise themselves through lightness into swelling pride are weighed down by the heaviest afflictions. The opening principles have been constructed with the greatest truth; we must now examine how the narrative portion has been formed.

### Verse 5

“My scars have grown foul and corrupted because of the presence of my foolishness.”

We have reached the narrative, which is profitably added to every argument, since through it the accused person’s state and deed are made clear.

This narrative is formed in two ways. For in five verses he describes the punishments of his body; in the other five that follow, he recounts the violent sufferings of his soul, so that nothing seems to have been left out that is not shown to have been afflicted by harsh calamities. This argument is called one from necessity, when someone, after the harsh circumstances have been set forth, is led toward correction and the better part.

In the first verse of this section, therefore, the figure of *tapinosis* is recognized, since nothing more humble or abject can be found. Wounds are the healed traces of earlier injuries; it is known that they afflict a person more severely when they lead back to former dangers. A scar is so called because it reveals within itself a hidden wound.

Thus the body is frequently shown to have been wasted by wounds, so that this survivor of himself appears to have endured almost what lifeless corpses commonly suffer. So he himself says: “Only the grave remains for me” (Job 17:1).

He adds, “because of the presence of my foolishness”—that is, because of the presence of my folly. “Face” signifies presence, and unless it is present either to the mind or to the body, its appearance cannot be perceived.

He says that he has putrefied because of this very thing, so that the holy man would not attribute anything to the divine arrangements. For he himself recalls this in his own words when he answered the Lord: “Therefore I have spoken foolishly, and of things that exceeded my knowledge” (Job 42:3).

### Verse 6

“I am afflicted with miseries and bowed down to the end; all day long I went about sorrowful.”

He was rightly troubled, since he appeared burdened with such great pains. One is afflicted with miseries when he chastises his soul with pains and tears. As he himself says, insofar as it concerns consideration of his sufferings: “I have despaired; I shall live no longer. Spare me, Lord, for my days are nothing” (Job 7:16).

“Unto the end” either signifies the end of life or the Lord Savior, because each one of the faithful is troubled for as long as it takes to reach him through the mercy granted.

What follows, “all day long I went about sorrowful,” indicates the continuation of his pain. By saying “all day long,” he also designates the nights, which were not free from his torments, since his wounds are said to have putrefied. Yet amid these things he went about sorrowful and afflicted; and, as is characteristic of the faithful, he by no means despaired of the Lord’s loving-kindness.

### Verse 7

“For my soul is full of illusions, and there is no soundness in my flesh.” This was why he was sorrowful all day long: the devil, who had taken possession of his body in order to afflict it, did not cease to weary his soul with vain imaginings. He describes the vice by which human weakness suffers most: sometimes, prostrate in prayer, we desire to see superfluous things; sometimes, while reciting psalms, we think about earthly matters. But concerning this illusion that we suffer, enough has been said in the book that, according to my limited ability, I wrote on the Soul.

Since this especially tends to happen to the idle, he says that it also befell him, although he had no bodily health, so that he was battered on every side like a besieged city attacked by enemies. For although his flesh was being broken by various afflictions, it was not thereby considered exempt [ed., “believed to be exempt”] from its inherited vices. This is the illusion that will be healed at the Lord’s second coming, when we shall both be free from the vices of the flesh and no longer suffer demonic assaults.

### Verse 8

“I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly; I roared because of the groaning of my heart.” He repeats the very words, but they have become more forceful by being gathered together in a single verse. We can be bowed down in body without being humbled in spirit; but here the two are joined because manifold calamity leaves nothing free. He added something still greater: “exceedingly,” that is, on every side and in every respect, so that abundant calamity might be shown to have surrounded him from all directions.

There follows: “I roared because of the groaning of my heart.” Roaring properly belongs to beasts. Here, however, to show that his groaning was more powerful, he compares himself to those creatures that make their will known by a very strong bellowing. And observe what follows: “because of the groaning of my heart.” To demonstrate the strength of his patience, he asserts that he burst into a groan, not into words.

### Verse 9

“And all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you.” His desire was of such a kind that it deserved to be before God. For whoever asks forgiveness for his sins, and does all those things discussed above, places his desire before God. Whatever is before him is accustomed to be heard. For the Lord embraces whatever he does not reject.

That groaning is not hidden from God which is offered in piety for the liberation of the soul. Many groan when they lose their riches or pursue shameful desires; but that groaning and that weeping are, as far as the Divinity is concerned, shown to be hidden. The word “groaning” is used to express great pain, as though mourning were doubled.

### Verse 10

“My heart was troubled within me, and my strength deserted me; and the light of my eyes is not with me.” After traversing bodily hardships in a sorrowful account, he now comes to the gravest pains of the spirit, so that, after the flesh had endured much, the mind of the blessed man might also be tested by more severe affliction.

Observe how beautifully the words are arranged and illuminate one another. One depends upon the other: because strength deserted him, his heart was troubled. By “strength” he means the power of patience, which, as long as it remains, keeps our will firm in its own steadfastness; but if it withdraws, the troubled mind collapses. Thus he says that the firmness of his patience had been softened by the abundance of evils.

There follows: “and the light of my eyes is not with me.” The light of the eyes is an undisturbed power of judgment, and he could not retain it while enduring immense troubles.

### Verse 11

“My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me.” Friends are strangers to us by blood, but joined to us by affection. A friend is so called as though he were “equal in spirit” (*animi aequus*), because he is joined to us by an equal will. Friendship is a corresponding will to seek good things for someone for that person’s own sake—the person one loves.

Neighbors, on the other hand, are those joined to us by kinship. These are the two kinds of people in whose consolations human nature is accustomed to rejoice. Now he speaks of those who came to the holy man in order to console him, as the text of his book makes clear, but who wounded his spirit all the more with frequent reproaches:

“Now the scourge has come upon you, and you have fainted; it touched you, and you were troubled” (Job IV, 5), and so forth.

Let us consider how violent the affliction was, since he endured such things from friends and neighbors, so that those who ordinarily are a remedy for many calamities became an accumulation of sufferings. It was therefore fitting that the light of his eyes was not with him, since affliction came to him from the very quarter from which human beings usually receive relief.

### Verse 12

“And my neighbors stood far away; and they used force who sought my life.”

### Verse 13

“And those who sought evil for me spoke vanity, and all day long they meditated on deceit.”

They were indeed neighbors by blood, but they became most distant through the horror of the stench: what he endured in his wound, they could not endure in its odor. He himself says concerning his wife:

“My breath became abhorrent to my wife” (Job XIX, 17).

What, I ask, must have been the disgust of strangers, when even the affection of his wife could not endure the exhalations from him? He also says concerning his relatives:

“He has put my brothers far from me, and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me like strangers” (ibid., 13).

When he says, “And they used force who sought my life,” he signifies the devil with his ministers. The more they saw him persist in the love of God, the more they strove to inflict death upon his soul.

He added: “And those who sought evil for me spoke vanity.” He signifies his wife, who, driven on by unclean spirits, while desiring that he be freed from his punishment, urged the most holy man to speak insultingly against the Lord, saying:

“Speak a word against God, and die” (Job II, 9).

Those mentioned above also meditated on deceit, because, while they thought they were consulting his body, they were suggesting things contrary to his soul.

### Verse 14

“But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and I was like a mute who does not open his mouth.” Nothing can be stronger, nothing more excellent, than to hear harmful things and not answer with what is contrary. Although he spoke what was just, he was deaf to those things that the iniquity of his would-be consolers suggested.

He added: “and like a mute who does not open his mouth.” A mute, even if he says nothing aloud, sometimes mutters inarticulately. But he was like a mute who did not open his mouth: he did not stir his lips with any harsh speech or with any murmuring against God.

O tranquility of a holy mind! Outwardly he was being consumed by worms, but inwardly he was impassible; and, as though he were standing beside an altar [mss., “were becoming another”], he was recognized as being occupied with divine praises.

### Verse 15

“And I became like a man who does not hear, and who has no reproaches in his mouth.” The sense itself is repeated, so that an example of great patience may be impressed upon us more powerfully. He certainly possessed the truth of his case, by which he could have reproved those offering harmful advice; but the most patient man, attributing everything to himself, refrained from reproving them, just as he himself says:

“Was I not concealing it? Was I not keeping quiet?” (Job III, 26).

Although he could have reproved those who attacked him with false accusations, he chose to remain silent, as one customarily does who is recognized as not possessing the truth of a reply.

Now observe the remedies assigned to each circumstance. Against bodily pains he had said above:

“I roared because of the groaning of my heart”;

but now, against wicked suggestions, he set down:

“But I, like a deaf man, did not hear,” and so forth.

Thus the text of this account is brought to an end by a twofold interpretation.

### Verse 16

“For in you, Lord, I have hoped; you will hear me, Lord my God.” Having completed the account of his sufferings, he now comes to the help of saving medicine. Amid his harsh calamities his confidence did not fail; rather, he always hoped in the Lord, who can change sorrow into joy. He therefore considers that his petition will be heard, because he trusts that he has hoped in the Lord.

He himself also says:

“Even if he kills me, I will hope in him” (Job XIII, 15).

So too the three young men profess:

“God is able to free us from the furnace of fire. But if he does not wish to do so, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods” (Dan. III, 17–18).

Such is the will of the saints, such the decision fixed in their minds: they are captivated not by any advantage of the present age, but solely by the love of the Lord himself.

### Verse 17

“For I said: Let my enemies never exult over me; and when my feet are shaken, they have spoken great things against me.” He now enumerates the reasons why the Lord should deign to hear him. Amid the most grievous heats of affliction, that excellent man guarded this point with the greatest care: that the enemy should not exult over his fall.

They exult when they have turned a person toward the desires of their wickedness, thinking the downfall of the faithful to be a victory. Here “feet” signify the quality of our actions, by which in this life we walk with certain steps. But when these steps have been shaken by human frailty, they immediately encounter impious mockers who rise against them with great invective, as he says elsewhere:

“Those who afflict me will exult if I am shaken” (Psalm XII, 5).

The godly act otherwise: they are distressed by the misfortunes of others and desire to bring consolation to the fallen and relief to those who have been deceived, as the Apostle says:

“Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. I, 6).

### Verse 18

“For I am ready for scourges, and my pain is always before me.” Here is why the Lord deigned to hear the suppliant: because, knowing that he had sinned through his own frailty, he rightly seemed to prepare himself for punishment. Those who continually condemn themselves think in this way, so that they may be acquitted at that judgment—those who here have deserved to be accused by their own confessions.

Here “scourges” does not mean leather whips, but the harshest sufferings of pain. For it follows: “and my pain is always before me.” The pain of the most righteous man was directed against himself because he seemed to have departed from the Lord’s commandments, losing saving innocence and acquiring deadly errors.

This pain is worthy of imitation: sound judgment consists in a just person becoming angry with himself, since the wicked person who defends and favors himself proves to be the author of his own destruction [ed., “the maker of his own destruction”].

### Verse 19

“For I will declare my iniquity, and I will think upon my sin.” He disclosed from where that preceding pain could have arisen. For if he had felt no sorrow over his sin, the purity of such a great confession would not have appeared.

The virtue of perfect repentance is shown in two ways. First, we must declare ourselves sinners before the Lord, as he says in his book:

“I have sinned; what shall I do to you, O guardian of humanity?” (Job VII, 20).

Here is the declaration of the holy man; here is true confession, which did not take away his life but doubled the joys of salvation.

But lest you think that in confessions this declaration alone could always suffice, he added: “and I will think upon my sin”—that is, with your forgiveness, I will do such things as can wipe away my sin. I will shed tears, give alms, and, through observance of your commandments, you will purify me from what I have done wrong.

### Verse 20

“But my enemies live, and they have grown strong against me; and those who hate me unjustly have multiplied.” He calls his enemies spiritual wickednesses, which the most holy man endured by the Lord’s permission for his testing.

“Live” must be pronounced with sorrow: that is, they enjoy the freedom of their will and do not fear the death that we endure in the body. But it was not enough for him to say “they live” unless he also added, “and they have grown strong against me.” Then, expressing what he dreaded still more, he added: “they have multiplied.”

This figure is called *emphasis*, by which the expression gradually increases in order to stir the mind more intensely. “They have multiplied” refers to those who hated him unjustly, when the number of unclean spirits was increased against him. One laid waste his property, another tore apart his estates, and others slaughtered his children. It was therefore necessary that, amid so many calamities, his enemies should increase, since he was proved to have endured dangers so numerous.

“Unjustly” was added because the most holy man was always unjustly harassed by wicked spirits. This expresses the devil’s will, not any depraved and empty boast concerning the man’s merits.

### Verse 21

Those who returned evil for good slandered me, because I pursued righteousness. He returns to the friends who tore him apart: they charged the holy man with his harsh circumstances and slandered him, when they should rather have praised his patience. His wife also slandered his righteousness when she said:

“Speak a word against God, and die” (Job II, 9).

He rightly said that he had pursued righteousness, because he was never proved to have abandoned it. For he himself testifies:

“You will not find in my tongue iniquity, nor will folly resound in my mouth” (Job VI, 30).

The testimony that this declaration proceeded from the complete purity of his heart is the Lord’s sentence, pronounced at the end of his book, where he says concerning his friends:

“My wrath is kindled against you, because you have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job XLII, 3).

The comparison that, as we said, belongs to the third part has been completed; it is without doubt a healing medicine. Now let us consider the conclusion, the end of the entire discourse.

### Verse 22

“Do not abandon me, Lord my God; do not depart from me.” This most holy penitent, released by the Lord’s forgiveness from his former dangers, now joyfully cries out to the Lord not to be abandoned by the one whose grace had freed him. For it is a graver fear for one of good conscience to go astray after forgiveness, so that one who owes gratitude incurs offense again.

When he departs from us, we follow trackless errors, because, when the straightest path is absent, it is necessary always to go astray.

### Verse 23

“Attend to my help, Lord, God of my salvation.” Earlier he asked not to be abandoned by the Lord; now he begs more earnestly that the Lord deign to attend to his help, because he knew that he was engaged in combat with the one who had said:

“I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13).

By what strength could that most savage enemy be conquered unless the Lord attended to him? If the Lord looked upon him, he could avoid perishing [ed. and ms. G., “obeying”].

And so that you might recognize that he had offered complete thanksgiving, he added:

“God of my salvation”—

the one, certainly, who restored him to safety after so many wounds and sufferings, and granted health to his soul, which that ancient tyrant could not take away.

Here the rule of the penitent has been fulfilled: the one who had earlier rotted with the corruption of ulcers now rejoices, saved. This is how the Lord’s soldiers reach victory when they are attacked.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

How strong, how triumphal over himself this Davidic Job became, that amid so many bitter wounds he did not cease to pour forth restrained words! His body lay on a dung heap, but in spirit he dwelt in heaven. He was consumed by worms, yet he overcame the unclean spirits. What he endured is small if you consider what he received.

This is how the pious Lord is served profitably; this is how the Divinity’s clemency is recognized: when we offer him his own gifts, we again demand exceedingly abundant rewards.

O blessed security of penitents! O wondrous exaltation of those who humble themselves! By confessing, the one who condemned himself by his own judgment returns to grace. Certainly, let us understand what dignity belongs to penitents, since not even the one who was praised by the voice of so great a judge is excluded from it.

# Exposition of Psalm XXXVIII

## A song of David for Jeduthun, for the end

This title has introduced a new name to us. Therefore let us investigate more carefully the reason for this designation and what it signifies. It has already been said in the preface that these men were not the authors of the psalms. But because they were outstanding singers, it is clear that they were included because of the meaning of their names: both so that they might receive the honor of their highly approved service through such a commemoration, and so that the hidden meanings of the psalms might be disclosed through interpretations of their names.

“Jeduthun” is a Hebrew name which in Latin is called *transilitor*, “one who leaps across”—not someone who crosses something by walking or passes over gaps by a bodily leap, but one who has already attained such purity above the variations of this world that he seeks only the rewards of future blessedness.

Thus in this psalm a person of holy conduct is introduced: one who had leapt over human enticements but was still seeking future joys. And because the most holy man enumerates some of his afflictions, lest you think this psalm should also be applied to penitents, he added “song,” which certainly cannot befit such persons. Singing belongs to one who rejoices, and sometimes to one who grieves, but never to one who is doing penance.

## Division of the Psalm

This Jeduthun, whom we have called the one who leaps across harmful vices, presents us with the form of a righteous person. In the first section of the psalm, he declares that, for the greatest benefit and remedy, he kept silent against his plotting enemies, asking to know the end of his life, in case he might deserve to see the Lord’s incarnation even with bodily eyes.

Second, through a five-part syllogism, he proves that mortal fear is vain, since everything has been established under the Lord’s power.

Third, he asks that his harmful offenses be forgiven, so that his life may be brought to a prosperous end.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“I said: I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.” It is characteristic of human beings that, when someone has conducted himself in a praiseworthy manner, he is immediately attacked by the plots of slanderers. Thus this Jeduthun, who had incurred the envy of the wicked because of his good reputation, deliberating with himself, says that it is better to keep silent than to say anything to malicious people.

For who is so cautious that, if he speaks among rivals, none of his words will give rise to some accusation?

Let us now examine each expression separately.

“I said”—that is, within myself, in my heart, where wise people deliberate before they speak.

“I will guard my ways.” He does not say, “I will abstain from crimes,” because he was already holy, but “from superfluous words,” which even a self-controlled person can rarely avoid, as the Apostle James says:

“No human being can tame the tongue. It is a small member, but it boasts great things” (James III, 8).

It is indeed difficult to keep the tongue, situated on the slippery ground of the throat, within the measure of strict truth. If its reins are carelessly loosened, it frequently speaks against itself. Guilt is more easily avoided by keeping silent than by speaking.

### Verse 2

“I placed a guard over my mouth while the sinner stood against me.” This is a figure of *epexegesis*, that is, an explanation of the preceding statement. He explains how he might sin with his tongue. The mouth is rightly regarded as the door of the tongue, and that door will be well kept closed if its entrance is guarded.

Solomon says:

“Make a door and a lock for your mouth, and a yoke and a balance for your words” (Ecclus. XXVIII, 28–29).

A lock is so called because it is applied to doors late (*sero*). But after introducing such great vigilance, he explains when it must especially be exercised: namely, when an envious person stands against someone, seeking to hear something from which he can construct a slander.

### Verse 3

“I was mute, and I was humbled, and I was silent concerning good things; and my pain was renewed.” The plotters were prudently deceived: while they sought to elicit speech by trickery, they found silence. But those whose mouths are often closed by excessive rage can also become mute.

He added, “and I was humbled,” so that you would understand this silence to be not deceitful but completely pure. “Humbled” signifies “prostrated on the ground.” He also says that he was silent concerning good teachings, so as not to instruct one who despised them.

But because it is characteristic of the wicked that, however much good they hear, they never consent to it, he says that he was compelled to be silent concerning good things: those who were seeking the seeds of quarrels could not receive a salutary admonition. For the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII, 6).

When he says, “my pain was renewed,” he signifies that it had existed in him earlier as well, when by the power of understanding he recognized the desires of the wicked. But now, when he saw human iniquities being exercised against him, his pain was renewed through compassion, as he made another person’s sin his own affliction.

### Verse 4

“My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire burned; I spoke with my tongue.” After the silence he says he endured unwillingly, since he could not preach things that would be salutary to people, he turned, in the great heat of charity, to speak to the Lord.

But let us hear how powerfully the ardor of his deliberation is explained. “Grew hot,” he says, “my heart”—that is, it was inflamed on every side, so that this great movement might reach the contemplation of heavenly things.

“Within me”: namely, in the inner person, where silent reason speaks and is graciously heard by the Lord.

There follows: “and in my meditation the fire burned.” Lest you think that the fire was seething with irrational movements, he said “in my meditation”—that is, in his counsel and deliberation, where the ardor of the mind is prudently kindled under the control of moderation, and a disciplined flame circles around the enlightened mind.

For what burns more intensely than charity? Yet that fervor is tranquil: a gentle inflammation, a blameless movement, a measured haste. Therefore this most holy man did what happens to the most perfect: he kept silent appropriately and spoke suitably. He who had been silent before deceitful enemies proclaimed with the tongue of his conscience to the truthful Lord.

Nor is it without significance that he says “with my tongue”: that is, with the tongue by which, in a pure mind, he was accustomed to confess to the Lord and to await his coming with the devotion of loving affection.

### Verse 5

“Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, so that I may know what is lacking for me.” After such great patience and the exceptional strength of an unconquered spirit, it is absurd to believe that the holy man asked to know the number of years of this life out of a desire for the present life.

Rather, filled with desire for the Lord and Savior, whom it was fitting to seek with his whole mind, he wished to know what limit of light had been prepared for him: whether his longevity might reach that holy incarnation which he carried in his mind.

He therefore asks to know his end—that is, the Lord and Savior. For he himself is our end, and to reach him is likewise life without end, provided that we do not make him hostile to us through subsequent sins.

Then he desires to discern the number of his days, so that it might become clearer whether he would deserve to behold him even with bodily eyes. He also added: “so that I may know what is lacking for me.” Once he had recognized his end, he could know how much time might remain until his coming. And “what is lacking for me” is rightly added, because he judged that life would be lacking for him if he did not deserve to see his presence.

Thus the desire of that great ardor is shown to have been expressed by the character of this speech.

### Verse 6

“Behold, you have made my days old, and my substance is as nothing before you.” You see that the presence of Christ the Lord was rightly requested before he declares his days to be old. For although he conducted himself in a manner pleasing to God, he was nevertheless in old days, since he had not yet come to the grace of the new regeneration.

Those days were old because they led the human race directly to the decline of death; there was nothing new in them, since the coming of the Lord and Savior had not yet shone forth. Hence the Apostle says:

“Old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V, 17).

There follows: “And my substance is as nothing before you.” He does not say that his actions are nothing before God, but his substance. For how could it be that one who had leapt beyond the world and overcome the vices of his flesh should be regarded as nothing before God?

But he rightly says that his substance is nothing before God, because it was condemned when Adam sinned. Unless the Divinity confers something upon it, it has nothing from itself in which it may presume.

### Verse 7

“Nevertheless, all is vanity; every living person.” When this one who leaps across vices had been filled by beholding the true light and had seen the future coming of the Lord and Savior with the eye of his heart, lest anyone think that holy men are free from temptations, he returns to his weakness, which he endured amid outstanding virtues because of the defect of the flesh, saying:

“Those things we have said are indeed great, and those things we believe are great. Nevertheless, because we live in this mortality, where human frailty strikes our mind, and that one eternal reality has not yet come which will make us stand firm in its own steadfastness, all is vanity; every living person.”

For vanity, as we have often said, signifies mutability, which every human being clothed in this flesh endures, except Christ. The most holy man reproaches the evil custom of worldly life, desiring to reach that eternal blessedness where he understood that he would share an inheritance with the angels.

### Verse 8

“Although a human being walks in the image of God, yet he will be troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.” After having kept commendably silent and spoken religiously, he comes to the second section, where by a five-part syllogism he proves that, after the transgression of the first human being, the human race was subjected to vanity apart from hope and expectation in God.

By saying “although,” he wishes something great and distinguished to be understood: although a human being bears something exalted, he is nevertheless occupied by vain desires. He next explains what this exalted thing is:

“A human being walks in the image of God.”

The image of God is that which human beings received in the creation of things, when it was said:

“Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26).

This statement will become clear to us if we first understand that “image” (*imago*) is one thing and “likeness” (*similitudo*) another. An image possesses the likeness of the thing whose image it is. A likeness, however, does not always possess the image of that to which it is like.

Therefore the inner person—who, as the Apostle says, “is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV, 16), and in whom there are rational understanding, recognition of truth, and immortality conferred by the Divinity—is rightly said to possess the image of God, because he is superior through the spiritual ordering of his actions.

The outer person, about whom the same Apostle says that he “is being corrupted” (ibid.) and is weighed down by the diverse burden of sufferings, nevertheless possesses some likeness of the Creator because he lives, sees, exists, and turns toward the mind that governs him, and because he is said to be very good among the remaining creatures. Yet these qualities exist in God in a far different and supreme manner from that in which they are said to exist in creatures.

But why speak of the outer person? A worm is compared with him, a lion is compared with him, and a stone is compared with him—not in the dignity of substance, but in some aspect of likeness. Thus it is rightly understood that God made the human being according to his image and likeness, if these are distributed according to their respective parts.

Father Augustine treated this more subtly and carefully in the second title of his book of Questions (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 51).

But although this image is great, and although it glories in some likeness to so great an author because it lives, is rational, and is immortal, the human being, since he has already become subject to sins and has become unlike the purity of the first father before his transgression, is nevertheless disturbed and confused by perishable desires. At one moment he thinks about food; at another, because of bodily necessity, he seeks clothing; and there are countless other things by which humanity is held subject in this world.

He rightly said, “he will be troubled,” because those who are occupied by temporal desires lose purity of mind.

He added: “He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.” Here foolish vanity is proved: he desires to preserve things destined to perish and to guard what is transient, especially since possession of them is shown to be uncertain. Someone who thinks he is leaving his possessions to his dear children does not know whether the most hostile enemies may come to possess them.

And observe that, although there are many similar matters in which human mutability is accused, avarice has nevertheless been selected as the object to which these things should chiefly be attributed, so that it might hear the designation of a conspicuous evil and lesser vices might recognize themselves. For it is written:

“The desire for possessions is the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI, 10).

### Verse 9

“And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is before you.” Having described the exceedingly vicious vanity of the human race, he now returns to his own person, declaring that his expectation is the Lord Christ and that he places no confidence in perishable desires. Rather, he awaits the one who is already known to have come salvifically into the world.

This expectation can also signify the judgment in which the saints are known to merit everlasting joys. For this outstanding one who leaps across vices necessarily ought to have awaited the time when eternal rewards would crown him.

Here, however, he does not call “his substance” the substance of Adam, which he mentioned two verses earlier. That substance was mentioned in an evil sense, while this is mentioned in a good sense, because the word is ambiguous. Therefore here we must understand “substance” in a good sense: namely, the possession of conscience, by which he was sustained, nourished, rich, and master of a household.

“Before you,” he says, not in my purses, as was said above concerning the avaricious; in your sight, not in my hidden places, where riches are proved to be impenetrable. Of the substance that was blameworthy it was said, “as nothing before you”; of this substance it is said, “it is before you,” since nothing can be there except what has been perfected by glorious action.

### Verse 10

“Deliver me from all my iniquities; you have made me a reproach to the fool.” Although this holy man conducted himself with commendable devotion, he nevertheless asks to be freed by the Lord’s mercy from all his iniquities, so that we may recognize that no one here is secure, even if he has received divine benefits.

When he says “from all,” he signifies that iniquities have various lesser forms, as it is said in the eighteenth psalm:

“Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Psalm XVIII, 13).

There follows: “You have made me a reproach to the fool.” It is customary for fools to mock those whom they recognize as devoted to good morals. Thus the holy man was a reproach to fools, because they rejected him as unlike themselves. The wicked praise only those things that they see to be common to them.

### Verse 11

“I was mute, and I did not open my mouth, because you made me.” He returns to what he said earlier, asserting that he did not answer his enemies, and adding this reason: “because you made me.” It was he who made him patient, since he granted the gifts of patience. He would not have possessed such salutary silence unless heavenly generosity had bestowed it.

### Verse 12

“Remove your scourges from me, for I have failed under the strength of your hand.” Having stated the basis of his devotion, Jeduthun fittingly asks forgiveness, so that he who had followed the Lord’s commandments might deserve to be heard.

The scourges are corrections that come from the rod; through them we are most justly beaten for our sins. The most holy man therefore desires those scourges to be removed which were owed for the faults he had committed.

A strong hand scourges severely; and it was necessary for anyone to fail whom an exalted hand struck.

### Verse 13

“You chastised a man with rebukes because of iniquity, and you made his soul waste away like a spider; nevertheless, every living man is troubled in vain.”

Here the Lord’s compassion is clearly shown: he does not love rebukes except so that human beings may be corrected. For the iniquity of mortals would wander endlessly, like a spreading corruption, if medicinal rebuke did not cut it away. We are converted, and we turn away from an evil intention, when we realize that we can be reproved by the Lord’s commandments.

A spider has a delicate body; it does not live in the earth, but in higher places it weaves certain very fine webs from the digestion of its own entrails [Col. 0285A], just as silk is said to be drawn out by certain worms. The soul of the one converted and afflicted is rightly compared to this tiny body: worn out by prolonged observances and vigils, abandoning earthly things, and wasting away through divine fear, it produces the most delicate works of virtue.

After this he returns to the beginning of his proposition: although a person is rebuked and wastes away, nevertheless, through the frailty of humanity, he is confused by the variety of different things. But the one who is transferred with a pure mind to divine contemplation alone is exempt from this disturbance.

The five-part proof of the rhetorical syllogism called an *epichirema* is complete, as I judge; let us now render it, as best we can, in its members and verses. Its proposition is: “Although a human being walks in the image of God, nevertheless he will be troubled in vain.” The proof of the proposition is: “He amasses treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it.” Then follows the assumption, extending through four verses: “And now, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?” and so forth.

Let no one be offended that the assumption appears so long. For we have said that the masters of secular learning later compressed the brevity of these members. Here, however, one must seek not so much their explicitly expressed traces as those indicated by them. The proof of the assumption is added: “You chastised a man with rebukes because of iniquity, and you made his soul waste away like a spider.” The expected conclusion follows, if I am not mistaken, fittingly answering its proposition: “Nevertheless, every living man is troubled in vain.” Thus, as I think, the proof of the five-part syllogism has been completed [Col. 0285C].

### Verse 14

“Hear my prayer, O God, and my supplication; give ear to my tears.”

The more mysteries this Idithun had learned, the more fervently he poured out his supplication before the Lord. He therefore comes to the third division, where he humbly and confidently pleads that his sins be forgiven before he ends his life. For this reason it is necessary to consider why the man who was said to have transcended the vices of the world still appears to groan so grievously.

The reason is that no one’s victory over vices is sufficient unless it is preserved by continual supplication. Thus he first said “prayer,” and afterward “supplication.” Prayer (*oratio*) is the ordering of the mouth, by which, bending low, we disclose our vows. Supplication (*deprecatio*), however, is frequent and constant pleading, brought forth secretly from the depths of the heart [Col. 0285D].

Hear what follows: “Give ear to my tears.” We have often said that God hears what he sees and sees what he hears, because he is not distinguished by bodily members but accomplishes all things through the power of his divinity. And lest you think that only words were offered in supplication, he said, “my tears,” which are always forceful in prayers and bring the mind of the merciful one toward healing clemency.

### Verse 15

“Do not be silent toward me, for I am a sojourner with you on the earth and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were.”

He said, “Do not be silent,” that is: “Let me hear you say what the Gospel bears witness to: ‘Your sins are forgiven you’” (Luke VII, 47). Or that which the psalm says elsewhere: “Say to my soul: I am your salvation” (Psalm XLIII, 3); or: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34). Accordingly, whichever of these meanings you wish to understand is appropriate.

A sojourner is one who cultivates the land, a stranger arriving for a time, not one who remains in the territory of his own homeland. This happens to every saint who is received into the divine city. Sin made all of us strangers and held us captive in a wicked land. But when his mercy receives us, we are sojourners, because we have arrived there—that is, we are transferred from Babylon to Jerusalem, he himself drawing us onward.

For this reason he said, “with you,” so that you would understand that he was a sojourner not in the city of the devil but in the city of the Lord. He added, “and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” [Col. 0286B]. He expressed what he had said above: every person who is received into blessedness is called a pilgrim, because he begins to be where he was not. A pilgrim is so called as though from *pergens longius*, “going farther.” And so that you might recognize this as a universal judgment, he says, “as all my fathers were,” lest anyone be thought exempt from this condition.

### Verse 16

“Forgive me, that I may recover my breath, before I depart and exist no more.”

A prudent man, filled with the illumination of truth itself, asked here that he be forgiven, so that he might reach the future judgments with confidence and receive a certain refreshment in the [p. 135] present life, having obtained security regarding that kingdom. He confessed that he was burning with consuming anxiety, since he asked to be tempered by the rain of mercy, just as he says elsewhere of himself [Col. 0286C]: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire burned.”

He therefore rightly asked here to be refreshed, since he had been inflamed by the heat of so great a desire. He added, “before I depart,” that is, before I leave this light. And “exist no more” means, certainly, in this world, where aid is given to sinners while they correct themselves through the humility of conversion received from the Lord.

Or he says, “I shall exist no more,” if you cease to aid me, because to remain in eternal afflictions is not truly to exist. Properly speaking, existence belongs to the blessed. Thus he rightly said that he would not exist if he did not understand himself to have a share among the elect.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Behold how greatly this excellent transcender of vices has admonished us, with the saving benefit of a most blessed instruction: to maintain restraint of tongue among blasphemers and wicked people, to avoid harmful conflicts, and to suppress quarrels with the greatest moderation [Col. 0286D]. Silence is indeed praiseworthy when it does not lead us into guilt, reveals the wise, makes people serious, nourishes counsel, and shows speech itself to be especially welcome.

Therefore, let us drink deeply of this most health-giving remedy, so that, recognizing how profitably the saints kept silent, we may not love the immoderate license of the tongue in sinners.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XXXIX

### For the end. A psalm of David.

We have often said that “the end” and “David” signify Christ the Lord, to whom this psalm must be applied. But at its beginning the Church speaks—that is, the heavenly bride, the members of Christ, the multitude of the faithful. Then it comes to our head, the Lord and Savior, so that the whole composition of the psalm may fittingly correspond to one body [Col. 0287A].

### Division of the Psalm

In the first narrative, the Church that came from the nations gives thanks, because, freed from the ancient sorrow of this world, she has deserved to attain the joys of the New Testament.

In the second part, the Lord Christ himself speaks, setting forth the holy incarnation and the righteousness of his preaching. For this reason he implores the Father’s aid, so that he may overcome the dangers inflicted by the Jews; he asks that his enemies be confounded and that all who hope in him rejoice [Col. 0287B].

### Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me; and he heard my supplication.”

The Catholic Church, which was to be gathered from all parts of the world, proclaims the virtue of patience, which a Christian ought to possess among his highest praises. For how could anyone either endure tribulations or escape the burden of dangers unless he were strengthened by the divine gift of the power of endurance?

Here, however, the doubled expression must be considered, because such an elegant repetition is not superfluous. We can indeed wait—and do so ungratefully. But when we “wait with waiting,” we patiently endure something with great desire.

This argument is called *a conjugatis*, “from related forms,” when we variously alter one word derived from another, as *sapiens* and *sapienter*, “wise” and “wisely,” *prudens* and *prudenter*, “prudent” and “prudently,” and similar examples.

“He looked upon me,” because he anticipates all our good. We cannot possess the light of truth unless we are deemed worthy to be seen by his radiance. It follows, “he heard me,” so that she may appear to have waited piously and effectively. “Supplication” likewise signifies, as has been said, the most frequent prayer, since she who endured while awaiting the Lord could not pray only rarely [Col. 0287C].

### Verse 2

“And he brought me out of the pit of misery and from the mire of filth; and he set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps.”

Just as he commands a Christian to work in two ways—turning away from evil and doing good—so he says that the Lord grants beneficial things in a twofold manner [Col. 0287D].

The first is that he brings us out of the deepest calamity of this world, whose malign breadth is aptly signified by “the pit of misery” and “the filthy mire.” And to express the corporeal thickness of sins, he added the mire contained in the pit, so that you would not understand sins merely by comparison with waters, however dense they might be.

For just as the mire of a pit is foul and heavy, so human sins are muddy: they horrify through their stench and drag down through their weight. Then he sets our feet upon a rock when we walk according to the commands of Christ the Lord. For he is our spiritual rock, fixed in himself and not allowing our footsteps to sink.

And notice that just as sins are contrary to virtues, so their paths are proved to be unlike one another [Col. 0288A]. Sins, being soft and dissolute, roll about in the filth of their own way. Virtues, however, just as they are firm and immovable, possess a rocky path, where feet walk not soiled but clean.

### Verse 3

“And he put a new song in my mouth, a hymn to our God. Many shall see and fear, and shall hope in the Lord.”

The earlier parts of the psalm refer to the fact that God transferred the human race, sunk in the mire of this world, to the firmness of the rock, namely, to the Christian religion. This verse now discloses that meaning, saying: “And he put a new song in my mouth,” that is, the most holy preaching of the New Testament.

It is rightly called “new,” because no earlier age saw the Lord’s incarnation with bodily eyes. Nothing is new to God, since before the foundation of the world he foreknew all the arrangements of his plan.

“Hymn” is a Greek word, meaning praise composed according to the law of song. And because the pagans also sang hymns to their idols, he added, “to our God,” so that we might clearly understand what kind of hymn he meant.

“Many shall see and fear.” He speaks of the miracles performed at the time of the holy incarnation. For when the Jews saw such things, they were afraid, and multitudes of peoples believed the preaching of Christ the Lord.

“They shall hope in the Lord” when they began to become Christians, so that, converted after that fear of the miracles, they might be shown to possess the firmest hope in the Lord [p. 136].

### Verse 4

“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.”

This blessed man is expressed through the second kind of definition, which in Greek is called *ennoematice* and in Latin *notio*, “notion.” It attempts to show each thing by what it does, not by what it is.

For who this blessed man is is defined by the determination that follows: “whose hope is the name of the Lord.” Hope is so called as though it were a stable foot. Those who ask the Lord to give them temporal goods are also said to place their hope in him. They seem not to love God for his own sake but for the sake of what they ask.

But the one who truly has hope in the name of the Lord is the person who eagerly desires his contemplation alone. The name of the Lord, among its other meanings, is the eternal Savior; and the one who places his hope in his name is the person who believes that he is saved not by his own merits but by the Lord through his grace [Col. 0288D].

They are also called blessed eight times in the Gospel, as in: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V, 3), and so forth. The same is likewise found in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy XXXIII, 29), when the Israelite people were entering the promised land. This is said in many ways because blessedness is granted in diverse ways. But the diligent reader will find all these things carefully expressed through the individual kinds of definitions.

### Verse 5

“And he did not look upon vanities and false insanities.”

This verse depends upon the preceding sentence, for it explains whose hope is in the name of the Lord: namely, the one who did not look upon vanities and false insanities [Col. 0289A].

For it is written: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew VI, 24), and this passage also recalls that teaching. Whoever places his hope in the Lord, who has power over all things, ought not to look toward things that perish.

Vanity is to be changed suddenly from holy religion and to turn the mind aside through deceptive illusion. False insanities are to form a god from stones for the pagan world to worship, while it falsely sought to discover the order of future things in them.

“Falsity” is a most appropriate epithet for insanities. For insanities deceive the mind because they dissent from the truth. This can also be applied to those who are captivated by the delight of deceptive spectacles. For this reason “insanities” is placed in the plural, so that we may range more broadly through analogous examples.

### Verse 6

“You have done many wonders, O Lord my God; no one is like you in your thoughts.”

While he was speaking about the insane works of human beings, he appropriately introduced divine miracles. For how much better it is, instead of being inflamed by competing charioteers or softened by dancing pantomimes, to contemplate heaven and earth formed with most beautiful diversity, possessing both a pleasing appearance and an altogether wondrous subject for reflection!

It follows: “No one is like you in your thoughts.” He continues to overthrow those superstitions that people either devised for a perverse religion or invented, moved by some pleasure, in the celebration of spectacles.

Is running along a rope with one’s foot suspended anything like Peter’s treading upon the back of the sea with a firm footstep? Is playing with burning torches in a theater anything like the three boys walking amid the fires of the furnace [Col. 0289C]? Is listening to theatrical tragedies anything like learning the life-giving psalmody in the choirs of the Church?

We ought rather to behold these things by reading them—things that we do not foolishly seek and that we always hear to our benefit. By saying, “Who is like you?” he reproves the inventors of evil things, who, wickedly exalting themselves, boast that they are authors of deceptive arts.

Thus far the holy mother Church has spoken. Now let us hear the Lord and Savior speaking, so that what was said—“Who is like you?”—may be made clear to us by the exposition that follows.

### Verse 7

“I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number.”

This is the second narrative of the psalm, but through the figure of *exallage*, which in Latin is called “alteration.” Mystical words are spoken from the person of the Lord, in which he makes known his coming and his gracious preaching to the nations [Col. 0289D].

To announce is to proclaim things that are to come, which he did through the mouths of the prophets. “I spoke” means that, when he dwelt among us, he preached after assuming the mystery of the blessed incarnation.

He added, “They were multiplied beyond number,” namely, because the multitude of sinners was increased beyond the reckoning of the blessed.
