How many are the great peoples, and how few are the faithful! Not without reason: while many are occupied with the vanities of this world, you will rarely find people who are truly wise.

And observe that he says “beyond number.” He indicates that only those are counted in the book of the living who are known to have been predestined for that Jerusalem above.

### Verse 8

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you fashioned a body for me; you did not ask even for burnt offerings for sin” [Col. 0290A].

This verse encompasses the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments. It says that God finally rejected the sacrifices and offerings that had previously been made in the Lord’s honor through the slaughter of animals, from which the priests also ate.

At first he deigned to accept such things, because through those sacrifices a certain prefiguration of Christ’s body appeared to be present. But after the Messiah himself, who is the Lord Christ, had been foretold and came, and had offered himself as a sacrifice of mercy for all of us, it was no longer necessary that, once the reality had been completed, that preliminary figure should remain.

The Apostle explains these verses in this way when writing to the Hebrews: “He takes away the first,” he says, “in order to establish what follows,” where “body” must be understood. “By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews X, 9–10), and so forth—those passages that are recognized as belonging to the beautiful clarification of this matter.

It follows: “But you fashioned a body for me.” Here he clearly shows, according to the Apostle, his holy incarnation, saying that the body which had previously been promised through the images of sacrifices was now completed by his own coming.

He added, “You did not ask even for burnt offerings for sin.” Burnt offerings are things wholly consumed by fire, which were placed upon sacred altars for sins and afterward burned, so that their devouring might become the abolition of sins.

He says that the Lord no longer asked for these things—rightly so, because he seeks from us what is read in the fiftieth psalm: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm L, 19). You see that the Church truly said: “Who is like you?”

### Verse 9

“Then I said: Behold, I come; at the beginning of the book it is written concerning me.”

“Behold” immediately signifies and promises swiftness, guaranteeing speed in every way. And you, Jew, since you do not possess your own sacrifices, whom are you, deceived, awaiting? He has already come; the Word has already become flesh; he has filled the world with saving preaching.

But you still dream—I know not what—in your chambers. What more are you seeking? Why are you fixed in amazement? In this book of psalms he says that he himself is written of at the beginning, so that you ought to believe that our blessed one has already come, whose life, as has now happened, is known to have been set forth [p. 137].

Where are those who see that they have no sacrifices, just as it was promised here? And as though they did not possess this statement in the sacred books, they remain stunned and plausibly fall silent before the words set before them [Col. 0290D].

### Verse 10

“To do your will, my God, I desired; and your law is in the midst of my heart.”

The words of the Son are directed to the Father. For he desired to do the will of the one who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of pestilence (Psalm I, 1–2).

When he said, “I desired,” he declared the power of foreknowledge, saying in the past tense what was certain to come. The divine law also remained in the midst of his heart, since his will was in the law of the Lord and he meditated on his law day and night (Psalm I, 2) [Col. 0291A].

### Verse 11

“I proclaimed your righteousness well in the great Church; behold, I shall not restrain my lips, O Lord; you have known.”

He proclaimed the Lord’s righteousness well when it was said: “Not so are the ungodly, not so, but like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth” (ibid., 4).

By “the great Church,” as we have often said, he means the Catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world. Of it he said there that it would give its fruit in its season (ibid., 3).

It follows: “Behold, I shall not restrain my lips, O Lord; you have known.” The Son speaks as one subject to God. Although it was dangerous to preach the truth among the obstinate, since he knew that his death would follow from it, nevertheless he did not cease to admonish the faithless people, saying: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly shall perish” (ibid., 6) [Col. 0291B].

In this passage he had the Father as the witness whom he invokes, because he feared no dangers when he preached spiritual goods to a carnal people. Thus the most truthful text of the first psalm now appears to be repeated in the Lord’s own remembrance.

### Verse 12

“I did not hide your righteousness in my heart; I declared your truth and your salvation.”

It is the will of the righteous person, whenever he can be of benefit, not to hide the truth. There is no doubt that the Lord and Savior did this when he reproved the crowds, rebuked unbelievers, and preached many things of this kind, which the text of the Gospel recounts.

Yet there was a time when he was silent in his passion, as it is written: “But Jesus answered him nothing,” when Pontius Pilate said to him: “You do not speak to me?” (John XIX, 9–10) [Col. 0291C].

He declared the truth when he said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). Christ is shown to be salvation by the confession of the blessed Simeon, who, when he saw him, said: “Now dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples” (Luke II, 29), and so forth.

### Verse 13

“I did not conceal your mercy and your truth in the great Synagogue.”

He continues to expound his works. He did not conceal the Father’s mercy when he said: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Luke XI, 13).

He also declared the truth “in the great Synagogue,” that is, in the most densely gathered assembly of peoples, when he received the book of Isaiah and read it, saying: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke IV, 21) [Col. 0291D].

Do you hear, unbelieving Jew, your own prophet agreeing at last with our Gospel? Whom do you continue to await, now that you know that Christ the Lord has come, unless your heart is still covered by a harmful veil?

### Verse 14

“But you, O Lord, do not remove your mercies far from me; your mercy and your truth have always received me.”

After recounting his holy works, he comes to the glory of his passion, so that the integrity of his whole life and life-giving death might be made known.

Here he rightly prays that the Father not remove his mercies far from him, since he was to die in the reality of the humanity he had assumed [Col. 0292A], just as he says elsewhere: “My God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm XXI, 2).

Mercy was shown in saving human nature, wounded by the vice of transgression, through the holy incarnation. Truth was shown when, through the benefit of the promised resurrection, he sat at the right hand of the Father, from there to come to judge the living and the dead.

“They have received me” means “they have received me to be glorified.” We are said to receive into a good sense those whom we acknowledge to have been accepted by our grace.

### Verse 15

“For evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have seized me.”

He says this of his members, whose head is Christ, so that he might profess himself to suffer what the multitude of the faithful endured, as in the saying: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4) [Col. 0292B].

“Of which there is no number” means, among human beings; for all things are numbered by God, who knows the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the multitude of the stars with a comprehensive reckoning.

He added, “My iniquities have seized me.” He speaks in the same manner as above, where he said: “Evils have surrounded me.” The Lord and Savior neither committed evils nor was subject to iniquities; but this is appropriately said from the perspective of his members, who endure such things.

For it was an act of compassion by our head that, although he had spoken much about himself, he also deigned to make mention of the faithful, lest they think themselves excluded when they realized that they had been passed over.

### Verse 16

“And I could not see; they were multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart abandoned me” [Col. 0292C].

This must be referred entirely to the members; such things cannot apply to the Lord Christ. “I could not see” means: surrounded by my iniquities, which the faithful person can truthfully say.

Although the hairs of a person’s head appear to be innumerable, their sins are nevertheless proved to exceed all reckoning. Nor were hairs brought into comparison with sins without reason. In the Old Testament, priests were shaved according to this very comparison, so that, cleansed by such purification, they might appear to have put away the vices of the flesh.

The heart abandons us when, sick with sins, it does not seek what would benefit it.

### Verse 17

“Be pleased, O Lord, to rescue me [ms. G.: ‘save me’]; O Lord, look upon me for my help.”

After the preceding enumerations, he comes to the most health-giving conclusion, from which every adversity is attacked and everything harmful destroyed: may it please the Lord to rescue the one who was surrounded by the oppositions of this world [Col. 0292D].

And observe what he says: “Be pleased,” that is, “let it please jointly.” For here the harmony of the Trinity is shown: what pleases the Father also pleases the Son and the Holy Spirit. He added, “you,” so that you might understand the holy Trinity to be one God.

It follows: “O Lord, look upon me for my help,” so that we may understand that his regard is our protection, as in the Gospel: “He looked upon Peter, and he wept bitterly” (Luke XXII, 61–62). For we cannot be freed in any other way unless the propitiated Divinity looks upon us.

### Verse 18

“Let those who seek my soul to take it be confounded and revere together” [Col. 0293A].

He comes to the remaining narrative, where the Lord and Savior desires confusion and reverence for the ungodly, while he asks that exultation and joy come to the devout.

But observe how much concern for piety this prayer contains. “Let them be confounded,” he said: let them be disturbed by the working of miracles. “Let them revere”: let them be corrected by the glory of the resurrection, so that they may confess him to be God whom earlier they had thought must be slaughtered.

“Together” means: just as they persecuted him, so may they also be freed through the gift of conversion that was predestined for them.

It follows: “Those who seek my soul.” The soul is sought in two ways, either for honor or for death. But to show here those who pursued it with an opposite desire, he added, “to take it”—not to love it, not to venerate it, but to attempt to separate it from my body by the intervention of death [Col. 0293B].

### Verse 19

“Let those who devise evil against me turn back and be ashamed.”

We have often said that good may be wished for the wicked in such a way that they turn back from their pleasures and do not persist in evil works. If they suffer confusion, they escape; if they enjoy the world’s happiness, they perish.

That this “turning back” is meant in a good sense is attested by the Gospel passage in which he answered Peter, who loved this life with excessive affection: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark VIII, 33).

What he added, “those who devise evil against me,” signifies the wicked intentions of the Jews. Their thoughts were not evil to the Lord but to those who conceived them. For thoughts (*cogitationes*) are so called from *cogere*, “to compel” [Col. 0293C].

### Verse 20

“Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ immediately bear their confusion.”

They immediately bear their confusion when they reach the point of recognizing that they have wickedly gone astray. He said, “Let them bear,” as though it were an immense weight.

“Immediately” means as soon as they begin to sin, lest, by proceeding farther, they become more dangerously burdened.

“Their confusion” means an evil thought convicted by the truth.

It follows: “Those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done.’” Here he reproves false praisers, who strive more to deceive by flattery than they could wound through criticism.

“Well done” is indeed a word of acclamation; but when it is not spoken with an upright intention, it is twisted into an insult of mockery. This figure is called *ironia*, that is, “mockery.”

### Verse 21

“Let all who seek you, O Lord, rejoice and be glad, and let those who love your salvation always say: ‘The Lord is magnified’” [Col. 0293D].

Just as he asked that his enemies be confounded—the enemies who mocked him with false praises—so he desires the devout, who are known to have placed their hope in the majesty of the Lord, to rejoice sincerely.

He asks that they not merely be glad but also exult. What this exultation is, he then explains: “And let them always say: ‘The Lord is magnified.’”

This is the confession that makes Christians rejoice eternally. Although it is said continually, it is nevertheless always desired.

Job also lived upon this statement in this world, when he had been grievously afflicted in body, saying: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21).

He exulted when he rejoiced in the Lord, in whom all things truly beneficial are found [Col. 0294A]. But lest you think that this exultation is granted to just anyone, he added: “Those who love your salvation,” that is, those who seek me through spiritual love and obey my commandments with devotion.

### Verse 22

“But I am needy and poor; the Lord takes care of me.”

After he had said that those who wished to love the divinity of the Word were to be filled with gifts of joy, the Lord Christ speaks from the form of the humanity he assumed, so that no one might claim the glory of merit for himself: “I am needy and poor.”

“Needy,” because humanity always needs help from the Lord. “Poor,” because, unless it is glorified by divine grace, it is known to be altogether frail in itself.

But lest you regard this poverty as vile and contemptible, he added: “The Lord takes care of me,” namely, the one of whom he was to say: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew III, 17).

O poverty richer than all treasures! He is poor from what is ours and rich from what is his. For this reason he assumed the want of humanity, so that he might make us participants in his abundance [Col. 0294B].

### Verse 23

“You are my helper and my deliverer; O Lord, do not delay.”

Secure regarding help and protection, he asks for the necessary speed, so that, since death could not now be avoided, at least the resurrection might quickly follow.

When he says, “helper and deliverer,” he shows his endurance of various passions—the very subject from which the psalm began. Therefore the whole psalm is rightly assigned to the virtue of patience, since it is also concluded by that same theme [Col. 0294C].

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Magnificent and exceedingly sweet words have penetrated the marrow of our understanding, when we hear teaching from the very one whom we worship as their author. Although we venerate all the psalms with great honor, something nevertheless seems sweeter when a passage concerning the holy incarnation is brought forth. For every faithful person receives with the greatest gratitude the means by which he is known to have been freed.

Observe also the order in which the composition of this psalm is arranged. At first the Church speaks, as though teaching the inexperienced, comforting the fearful, and preparing the disordered, so that the prepared people might hear with willing hearts the saving words that follow from the Lord and Savior.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XL

### For the end. A psalm of David.

[Col. 0294D]

These words ought by now to be thoroughly familiar to us through frequent use; nevertheless, let us touch on them briefly. Everything is directed toward Christ the Lord.

This psalm is made especially significant by its placement at the number forty, a number frequently applied to cleansing and purification. For after the flood had poured forth for forty days, the earth was cleansed of human iniquities. For forty days also holy Moses abstained from bodily food so that he might be deemed worthy of divine converse. In the same way, Elijah, in his flight, abstained from bodily nourishment. The Lord himself likewise fasted for that many days and nights, so that he might show us the pattern of blessed purification [Col. 0295A].

We are also taught by his example concerning Lent itself. A period of abstinence is set beforehand, so that, with the stains of sins washed away, we may approach the Lord’s resurrection with purified minds.

Therefore let us judge this psalm to have been placed among those mysteries that cleanse our souls through heavenly purification, especially since the prophet is about to speak of almsgiving, through which the cleansing of sins is known properly to take place. For it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus III, 33).

### Division of the Psalm

At the first entrance the prophet speaks, proclaiming blessed the giver of alms and celebrating him with a manifold blessing [Col. 0295B].

Second, the Lord recalls his glorious passion.

Third, to confirm the hope of the faithful, the same Lord Christ foretells his own resurrection.

### Exposition of the Psalm
### Verse 1

“Blessed is he who understands the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him.”

Here again the hypothetical syllogism shines forth in this form: If every blessed person understands the needy and the poor, the Lord will deliver him on the evil day. But every blessed person understands the needy and the poor. Therefore, on the evil day the Lord will deliver him.

A hypothetical—that is, conditional—syllogism is one which, from conditional propositions and a categorical assumption, draws a conclusion. Let us now consider what follows.

[Col. 0295C] The second species is the definition called in Greek *ennoematice* (“conceptual”), and in Latin *notio* (“notion”). This shows each person what he is by his actions. For he says how sins are expiated through the most salutary works of almsgiving, so that the most glorious blessedness may be found.

The dignity of the subject would certainly have urged us to make some digression by way of a common theme, so that we might praise almsgiving, the reconciler of the human race. But since it has been celebrated by the most holy and eloquent mouths of many Fathers, let it suffice to refer the hearts of our hearers to their books, so that their desire may be more abundantly fulfilled and we may vigorously complete the work we have begun, with the Lord’s help.

[Col. 0295D] Yet although many Fathers have written much about this matter, some disagreement nevertheless arises among them concerning this point. For it is written: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6:30). It is also written: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find a righteous person to whom you may hand it over.” But if we seek only the righteous, we restrict the generosity that has been commanded.

In truth, this matter rests solely upon pious intention, because it is not our task first to investigate people’s conduct and only then to assist their need. It is enough for us to ensure that we do not knowingly give anything to evil practices, nor bestow alms out of pride while seeking to win human approval; rather, we should act solely from the desire to help, which the Divinity commands us to regard above all else. Whoever gives in this way, even if he does not give to the righteous, will nevertheless distribute justly to everyone.

[Col. 0296A] Still greater effort must be made so that we may assist holy men in some need, for the sake of Christ our Lord, who will say concerning his poor at the judgment: “He who did it for one of these least ones did it for me” (Matthew 25:40). For what could be said more sublime or glorious, when either those whom we have neglected send us into the fire, or those whom we have rewarded place us at the right hand?

But observe that he says “understands,” so that such people may also be offered assistance when they do not ask. For the one who gives to someone asking performs a good work; but the one who understands someone who remains silent acquires blessedness without any doubt.

He adds: “On the evil day the Lord will deliver him.” He certainly means the day of judgment. But some are troubled because he so frequently calls it “evil.” Every person rightly regards God’s judgment as evil and fearful for himself, because the punishment owed by sinners is dreaded. For even though we are delivered by his mercy, we rightly fear the force of his judgment.

[Col. 0296B] ### Verse 2

“May the Lord preserve him, give him life, make him blessed, and cleanse his soul upon the earth; and may he not hand him over into the hands [manuscripts A, B, F: ‘into the soul’] of his enemy.”

This request of the prophet is a firm promise, because it must happen—provided that the needy and poor person is raised up by a pious gift.

He says, “preserve”: that is, may he not allow him to perish amid the evils of the world, but may he bring him unharmed, through holy conduct, to his reward. Those are properly called living who do not separate themselves from the Christian faith. For concerning those who live in error it was said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9:60).

[Col. 0296C] Therefore, when he says “give him life,” he means: let him live among the elect in his portion. He adds, “and make him blessed,” namely, so that he may be placed at the right hand in the resurrection and sent, by the pronouncement of the great Judge, into that homeland of the blessed.

But after what he had said above, he touches upon something exceedingly necessary: while a person remains in this world, he must be cleansed through the forgiveness of sins. Forgiveness is received there when sin is mourned with devoted supplication.

He also adds that he must not be handed over into the hands of the enemy. The enemy is the devil; his hands are his unrighteous power. For what hands could one who has no flesh possess? The “hands,” therefore, are the very power by which he chastises God’s servants through manifold temptation.

And notice how often he has placed *and* in this verse, in order to display, through the frequent repetition of this conjunction, the rhetorical figure *polysyntheton* (“many conjunctions”).

[Col. 0296D] ### Verse 3

“May the Lord assist him upon his bed of pain; you have turned his entire bed in his sickness.”

Lest you think that this blessed person possesses unshaken rest in this world, he prays that his pains may be mitigated, so that the multitude of evils may be overcome through the benefit of moderation.

A bed is given to us for rest, in which the weary limbs of human beings may recover. Likewise, the person who acquires a patrimony, takes a wife, begets children, and forms friendships rests, as it were, upon a certain bed for the sake of pleasure.

[Col. 0297A] But the Lord frequently makes these things bitter and full of pain for his servants, lest those who place their hope in temporal matters fail to desire future goods. Therefore the prophet wishes the Lord to comfort the pain of one who is wounded amid his pleasures, as though upon a little bed.

He adds: “You have turned his entire bed in his sickness.” He develops the cause he mentioned above: divine providence brings it about that the worldly pleasure of God’s servants is turned into distress and pain, so that, afflicted here by various calamities, they may attain the rest of eternal blessedness.

This happened to Job, whose worldly goods were turned into sickness; yet he became more fortunate because worldly prosperity withdrew from him. Accordingly, he asks the Lord to assist such people, lest human frailty, pressed down by harsh labors, be overcome.

[140] ### Verse 4

“I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.”

[Col. 0297B] Having recognized that the tribulations of the faithful occur by divine judgment, the prophet cries out in pious fear, so that he too may obtain the Lord’s mercy. For he who recognized that he had sinned rightly feared being handed over to temptations.

Every sin is a disease of the soul, and as it increases, the health of the inner person is destroyed. The one who cried out to the physician felt his sickness, but he was sound in understanding because he recognized himself to be ill.

Thus he desires his soul to be healed—that is, through the forgiveness of sins. By this we are truly healed, when the sins that strangle us are loosened.

### Verse 5

“My enemies spoke evil against me: ‘When will he die and his name perish?’”

[Col. 0297C] Until now the prophet has spoken about the affliction of the blessed. Now, in a second movement, the Lord and Savior is going to speak about his passion, so that when the servants of God are afflicted by various events, they may not believe themselves abandoned by God, since they recognize that Christ the Lord endured such things. He said: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours” (John 15:20).

His enemies “spoke evil” when they uttered falsehoods. For it was necessary that the impious devise lies, since they raged under the devil’s instigation.

The text continues: “When will he die and his name perish?” These are the words of the deranged Jews. For they said: “If we let him go on like this, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11:48). Caiaphas likewise said: “It is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish” (John 11:49).

His name did perish—but only from those who refused to believe in him.

### Verse 6

“And they entered in order to see; their heart spoke vanity.”

[Col. 0297D] ### Verse 7

“They gathered iniquity for themselves; then they went out and spoke.”

He explains that period of the Lord’s passion, when Judas entered deceitfully, not to honor the Lord but rather to destroy him. The plural expression “they entered” also signifies those who dared to lay hands upon him.

The Jews spoke vanity when they cruelly deliberated about the death of the one known to be the life of all. The text continues: “They gathered iniquity for themselves.” Their assembly was certainly the gathering of sinners, when all crimes were perpetrated in a single deed, as they resolved to crucify the Lord of all things.

[Col. 0298A] They went out, because they could not remain inside, having departed from the hidden reality of faith. Both things were wretched; both were deadly. They entered to commit the crime, and then went out from the boundaries of truth.

### Verse 8

“All my enemies whispered together against me; they devised evil against me.”

A whisper is the very faint sound of the mouth, confused without any clear distinction of voice. The word is derived from bees, whose emitted sound is a whisper. This is what happened among those who delighted in murmuring to one another in one another’s ears.

Those joined together in a partnership of crimes do not dare to disclose their plans. He adds: “All my enemies devised evil against me.” He expressed the madness of raging and foolish peoples. Usually only a few are the authors of crimes; here all are said to have devised evil, so that no one may be less guilty, since the equality of their crime condemns them all.

[Col. 0298B] But when he says “evil against me”: if you seek the outcome, it was against themselves; if you seek their intention, it was against me. The punishment of the righteous is the envy not of the one who suffers, but of the one who acts.

### Verse 9

“They established an iniquitous word against me: ‘Will not one who sleeps add [this], that he may rise again?’”

He speaks of an “iniquitous word” when they cried out to Pilate: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19:12). “They established” means that they decreed or determined it, namely, when they pronounced judgment concerning the Lord and Savior.

[Col. 0298C] To sleep is to rest from the senses of the flesh, with the mind’s attention relaxed, and then to return again to the activities of life with the strength of the spirit restored. This is beautifully applied to the Lord’s death, because the resurrection occurred with such speed that he may be thought rather to have slept than to have died: he rose in strength, though he had died as one weak.

And lest heretics flatter themselves any longer, let them hear the one who sleeps himself add that he will rise, just as he says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

### Verse 10

“For even the man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, magnified his treachery against me.”

He calls the disciple Judas “the man of his peace,” because he gave him peace when he betrayed him. [Col. 0298D] We speak of peace when we kiss one another. But if you refer the matter to tranquility of soul, there could be no peace in the heart of one who prepared ambushes while making flattering approaches.

He adds: “In whom I hoped,” that is, in whom I was thought to hope. For how could he have hoped in the worst of men, when he was able to recognize him before he was born? To understand that Judas had been foreknown, listen to the Lord himself: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:60).

The text continues: “Who ate my bread.” This may mean either that he listened to my teaching, by which we feast spiritually, or that he placed his hand with mine in the dish, as the language of the Gospel makes clear.

He rightly said “magnified” when Judas had revealed who he was to those who did not know. O deaf disciple! O one utterly hardened in an unteachable heart! For who could believe that he had received any virtue in his mind from such great piety, when he proved to be so cruel a murderer of his own master?

[Col. 0299A] ### Verse 11

“But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them.”

After describing the passion, he comes to a third movement, in which he asks that the miracles of his resurrection be accomplished according to his humanity.

Why do you prick up your ears, heretic? Why do you think you have found something that can excuse your unbelief? If you seek his power, listen to what he says in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

Here humanity asks; there divinity promises. Stop making accusations, for both are united in the Lord and Savior: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

He said, “I will repay them,” not with the pain of vengeance, but with the expectation of patience. Even today, by enduring them, he converts a large part of them through the working of his mercy.

[Col. 0299B] ### Verse 12

“By this I know that you have desired me, because my enemy will not rejoice over me.”

He says that by this he has recognized the Father’s love: because a glorious resurrection is to follow. “You have desired me”—understand, to glorify and exalt me.

Both these words and similar ones can appropriately be applied to this passage. He adds: “Because my enemy will not rejoice over me.” This explains what he had said: “You have desired me,” namely, because the enemy was not permitted to rejoice over him, since what they had planned was in no way fulfilled.

[141] For they wished to kill him, as was said above, so that they might utterly erase his name from the earth. But, on the contrary, they see the Church of Christ spread throughout the whole world and recognize that his name is celebrated everywhere. Thus they cannot rightly rejoice, since events have turned out so contrary to their desires.

[Col. 0299C] ### Verse 13

“But because of my innocence you received me and established me in your sight forever.”

Truly holy innocence; truly simplicity; truly blessed humility: after suffering so many evils, he defended himself with no contention. With a peaceful spirit he went to the cross, about to die with a tranquil mind.

He fulfilled with perfect truth all the words previously foretold by the prophets. He grieved over the misfortunes of his persecutors, and, placed upon the cross, he mercifully prayed for his enemies, because he had decreed that this too should be done by his faithful. He rightly gave the command, having first provided the example.

[Col. 0299D] The text continues: “And you established me in your sight forever.” Here the blessedness of his holy incarnation is expressed: having laid aside the weakness of a dying body, the God-man remains in eternal glory, from two natures and in two distinct and perfect natures. His name is above every name; his power rules heaven and earth; to him “every knee bends, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Philippians 2:10).

### Verse 14

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from the age and unto the age; let it be, let it be.”

After explaining what pertained to the passion and resurrection of Christ the Lord, a laudatory conclusion follows beautifully, because the one who fulfilled our hope through the glory of his dispensation ought to be blessed at all times.

We also call a human being blessed when he is blessed; yet if no one blesses him, he is not blessed, and in a certain sense this blessing is celebrated according to another’s judgment.

[Col. 0300A] God, however, is blessed even if everyone is silent, because he does not receive all goodness as something external, but goodness proceeds from him himself.

When he says “from the age,” he signifies the present world, from the time when all things began to be administered. “And unto the age” is to be understood of the future, where all things already remain eternal and do not pass away through any change of time.

For although this present age comes to an end, God’s blessing nevertheless remains unchangeable.

He adds, “let it be, let it be.” This repeated word urgently declares that it must be done by all. It is not to be understood as though the Lord becomes blessed—so that, if he is not praised, he would not be blessed. Rather, “let it be” refers to what benefits us, as we continually devote ourselves to his praises.

[Col. 0300B] Some interpreters, because of the unusual occurrence of this word—which appears here and in the seventy-first, eighty-eighth, and one hundred fifth psalms—thought that the Psalter ought to be divided into five books. But our preface has sufficiently shown that we must not agree with them. For in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:20), the psalms are read as constituting one book.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

In the preceding psalm, the holy Church spoke in the first part, and the Lord’s words followed; so also here the prophet goes before. At the very beginning, blessed David taught us moral disciplines through holy almsgiving. Secondly, through his passion, the Lord pointed out the natural paths. Thirdly, through the miracle of the resurrection, he completed us with contemplative brightness, so that the truth of heavenly philosophy might be shown to have been narrated in three parts.

[Col. 0300C] If you examine this carefully, you will frequently find the same arrangement in the remaining psalms. Therefore, having received the benefit of this psalm, it must be said with great exultation:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from the age and unto the age; let it be, let it be.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM XLI

“Unto the end; an understanding for the sons of Korah; a psalm of David.”

Among the customary words, he introduces the sons of Korah afresh. These are the names of singers, not of psalm-writers, as has already been said concerning Jeduthun in the thirty-eighth psalm. They had been chosen by David for psalmody, but because of the significance of their names they seem appropriately to have been placed in the titles. We must investigate this with great care, so that it may appear to us like a very white kernel, properly stripped of its covering.

[Col. 0300D] In Hebrew, *Korah* is said to mean “Calvary.” Calvary is the place where the Lord and Savior is known to have been crucified. Therefore they are rightly called the sons of Korah, because they deserved to receive the sign of the cross as the most glorious trophy of the heavenly King.

For this reason the psalm applies to every Christian who is kindled by love for the Lord with the flame of the Lord’s charity. Without that charity, everything regarded as excellent in human affairs is worthless.

[Col. 0301A] This is the first psalm concerning this subject; the eighty-third and eighty-fourth follow it. But concerning these names we must remember what blessed Jerome says (*On the Exposition of the Title of Psalm LXXXIV*), as he surveys the entire Psalter with an attentive mind: “I never find that the sons of Korah sang anything sorrowful. For in their psalms there are always joyful and pleasing things; despising worldly matters, they desire heavenly and eternal things, in accord with the interpretation of their name.”

### Division of the Psalm

The son of Korah, whom we have said is marked by the honor of the cross, declares at the first profession of this psalm that all the desire of his mind has been transferred to the Lord.

In the second part, through a five-part syllogism, he speaks to his soul, saying that it ought not to be troubled in the sea of this world, because God is its refuge by fixed deliberation.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0301B] ### Verse 1

“As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

Here there is a figure of comparison—that is, a comparison between things dissimilar in kind. A human being is understood to be compared with a deer. This kind of argument is called “from the lesser to the greater.”

But the faithful are not compared with this animal without reason. First, it is harmless; second, it is exceedingly swift; third, when its desire is inflamed, it becomes thirsty. It draws serpents in through its nostrils, and after devouring them, driven by the heat of their venom, it hastens to a spring of water with all possible speed. For it loves to be satisfied with sweet and utterly pure water.

[142] This beautiful comparison ardently stirs up our desire: when we drink in the poisons of the ancient serpent and burn with his flames, we should hasten immediately to the fountain of divine mercy, so that what is contracted through the hostility of sin may be overcome by the purity of the sweetest draught.

[Col. 0301C] Nor is it insignificant that he says “to the springs of water,” not “to the waters.” For Christ the Lord is the spring of waters, from whom flow all things that refresh. Streams can often dry up; but a spring of water is always irrigating. Therefore it is rightly said that we must hasten to the fluid of the sacred source, where our desire can never experience thirst.

### Verse 2

“My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?”

So that you might recognize that the desire he mentioned earlier belonged to divine charity, he says that his soul thirstingly seeks the sight of the Lord. By this kind of longing, human weakness is especially inflamed.

[Col. 0301D] Thus he continues: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” For he will appear manifest to us when he graciously regards us in his judgment.

Instructed by these things, we understand that the soul has its thirst when, moved by heavenly desire, it seeks the divine streams that are always poured forth in abundant irrigation: waters most plentiful and salutary, which not only refresh the thirst of souls but also remove every need arising from weakness.

This thirst continually burns in blessed hearts in this world and does not rest, satisfied by any limit, because in future blessedness it is granted to find what it desires. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

The word “when” should be pronounced with weight, so that the delay may appear burdensome to him.

[Col. 0302A] ### Verse 3

“My tears have been my bread day and night.”

Let those who do not desire to weep for the Lord hear that continual tears bring not starvation but rather satiety. And rightly so, because that weeping is food for souls, strengthening of the senses, release from sins, refreshment of minds, and cleansing from faults.

Through these continual tears he signifies that the Christian people can be instructed by afflictions. We should understand “day” as prosperity and “night” as sorrow. Through these two, the whole period of human life is indicated.

### Verse 4

“When it is said to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’”

The son of Korah gives the reason why he shed continual tears. During the time of persecution, this was constantly said to Christians: “There is no one to avenge you. Certainly endure what we want and what we command.”

[Col. 0302B] Who would not weep in such affliction—to possess a clear conscience and yet be subjected to the insults of the wicked? For nothing exceeds this pain: to see an insulter whom you know to be defiled by a corrupt conscience.

And observe the correspondence of the elements: just as he marked out his continual tears, so he says that the accusations were continual, so that everything contained in the sacred readings may agree with itself.

### Verse 5

“I remembered these things, and I poured out my soul within me, because I was entering the place of the tabernacle.”

That is: while I was thinking about the offenses charged against me, I poured out my soul in tears, as though from a full vessel, in a sudden flood, asking God not to be tortured any longer by such reproach.

[Col. 0302C] A person pours out his soul within himself, in a certain sense, whenever, stirred by a full desire, he casts himself before God in sincere supplication. Notice also that every pouring-out, once motion has occurred, proceeds toward neighboring places. The soul, however, is poured out within itself whenever, impelled by compunction, it returns to itself.

He then explains why he poured out his soul within himself: namely, because he was entering the place of the tabernacle—that is, the present Church. While entering there, he wept and groaned all the more because that Jerusalem which the Lord promised to his saints was still being delayed.

What is awaited must necessarily be desired more vividly when some likeness of it is seen.

[Col. 0302D] ### Verse 6

“Wonderful even unto the house of God, amid the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting.”

Here we must supply what he said in the preceding verse: “into the place of the tabernacle.” He was entering the wonderful tabernacle because he did not know how to yield to such unjust accusations.

For it was said to him: “Where is your God?” But he desired God all the more intensely as the wicked insult against him increased.

From this tabernacle to that house of God belonging to the future age, the devout inhabitant hastened, lest the desires of this world should appear acceptable to a holy man.

But how did this most holy person long to go there? Through “the voice of exultation and confession.” Exultation refers to psalmody; confession to mourning over sins. These two joined together certainly make a perfect Christian.

[Col. 0303A] The text continues: “the sound of one feasting.” This is a brief definition of exultation and confession: the sound of one feasting. For the sound itself nourishes the soul and grants it a banquet with sweet delight.

What is sweeter or more salutary than to praise God and always accuse oneself as guilty?

The part that speaks of thirsting for the Lord is complete. But in the following part he repeats the same point through great and subtle arguments, lest he appear to cease from the desire he had conceived with a commendable ardor because of mental sorrow.

### Verse 7

“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord” [edition: “in God”].

Let us listen to these verses with somewhat greater care, because unless they are treated more subtly, they are obscure.

[Col. 0303B] After the accusations he had heard—“Where is your God?”—and after the outpouring of his soul, which he had brought about through excessive tribulation, the son of Korah comes to the second part. Through the true proof of a five-part syllogism, he speaks to his soul up to the end of the psalm, saying:

“Why, my soul, are you weighed down, wounded by the savage accusations of your enemies? Why do you trouble me by your affliction?”

It is necessary that human weakness, sad and sorrowful, should be troubled. Against this comes the salutary remedy: “Hope in the Lord.” For hope changes everything for the better and leads to eternal joy those whom the sorrow inflicted by this world has enclosed, as it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.”

Nor should it seem strange that a person speaks to his soul after introducing it as a character. For elsewhere we read: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” (Psalm 102:1); and elsewhere: “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Psalm 145:1). In the forty-second psalm he repeats the same words: “Why are you sad, my soul?” (Psalm 42:5).

[Col. 0303C] ### Verse 8

“For I will confess to him, the salvation of my countenance.”

[143] Lest the soul perhaps say, “How can I hope in the Lord, while your weakness frequently obstructs me?” the Son of the Cross says: “Hope in the Lord, because I will confess to him”—that is, I practice repentance for my sins, so that I may not be able to hinder your devotion.

He also indicates to whom he will confess: to the one who is “the salvation of my countenance.” Christ the Lord is the salvation of our countenance. He deigned to come in the form of a servant, which we bear, yet without sin, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “The breath of our countenance, Christ the Lord, was seized; under whose veil we live among the nations” (Lamentations 4:20).

[Col. 0303D] ### Verse 9

“My God, my soul is troubled within me; therefore I will remember you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan.”

The one who gave counsel to his soul and rationally corrected his mind now returns to the condition of humanity and confesses, saying that his soul is troubled by himself.

Indeed, unless the vices of the flesh caused this, the purity of the mind would remain in its own tranquility. I think that this reasoning has been introduced very appropriately, so that a human being might clearly recognize from what diversity he is constituted.

But the son of the cross whom the title mentioned shows the remedy by which everyone can escape the disturbances of his soul, saying: “Therefore I will remember you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan.”

[Col. 0304A] “Therefore”—that is, because of these disturbances by which my soul is greatly afflicted. “I will remember you, Lord,” as though he were saying: I hasten with the greatest speed to you, where arrival is the remedy and where the appropriate exclusion of carnal evils is found.

He also says from where he will remember him: from the land of the Jordan, that is, from the place where the Lord first consecrated the benefits of baptism. For the very name of the river Jordan is interpreted as “their descent.”

He descended into the height of the springs who desires to be renewed by that sacramental gift. Even today we say of a baptized person: “He descended into the fountain.”

Alternatively, this descent signifies the humility that a baptized person must possess when following the ordinances of our Lord. Therefore, while we remember these things—our received baptism and the humility we have stored in our memory—we are not disturbed by any confusion arising from the evils that come upon us.

[Col. 0304B] “And from Hermonim, from the little mountain.”

Hermonim is a small mountain situated beside the Jordan, as is known from the reading of Deuteronomy: “At that time,” he says, “we took the land from the hands of two Amorite kings who were beyond the Jordan, from the torrent of Arnon to Mount Hermon” (Deuteronomy 4:47–48).

But let us see what significance this name also seems to convey to us. Hermonim is said to mean “anathema,” the word a person says to the devil when he comes to God.

He rightly said “from the little mountain,” because God is not sought from the height of pride; rather, his memory is found in modest humility. Therefore, while we remember the baptism we have received and humility, we obtain, by the Lord’s gift, the rules of the faith we have accepted in a saving manner.

[Col. 0304C] ### Verse 10

“Deep calls to deep in the voice of your cataracts.”

### Verse 11

“All your heights and your waves have passed over me.”

Jordan, Hermonim, “deep calls to deep in the voice of your cataracts”—these have produced the figure called *sardismos*, which is always formed through a mixture of languages.

For “Jordan” and “Hermonim” are Hebrew names; “deep calls to deep” and “cataracts” are Greek; “calls” and “in the voice” are plainly Latin. Thus this figure is beautifully composed in this passage through the intermixture of languages.

[Col. 0304D] By the two deeps he signifies the two Testaments, namely, the New and the Old, which confirm each other by mutual testimony: the Old Testament foretells the New, while the New recalls the readings of the Old Testament. Thus they call to one another when each bears witness to the confirmation of the other.

Elsewhere also the Psalmist says: “Your judgments are a great deep” (Psalm 35:7). The Testaments of the Lord are deep, because they rest in the bosom of his wisdom, founded upon profound truth.

By “the voice of your cataracts” he means the prophets and apostles. For just as a multitude of waters is vomited forth through cataracts, so streams from the Lord flowed from their mouths.

We appropriately apply “heights” and “waves” to the sacred Scriptures. They are the very things he previously called “deeps,” where the wave of certain parables plays and the height of meanings grows greater through devout investigation.

Therefore the righteous person says that these have passed over him, because in his eagerness he had immersed himself as an investigator in knowledge of them.

[Col. 0305A] ### Verse 12

“By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it; with me is prayer to the God of my life.”

Let us understand “day” as a time free from distraction, in which the Lord’s commandments are learned. His law is absorbed during a period of tranquility; one has leisure to learn when there is nothing that ought to obstruct.

The text continues: “And by night he declared it.” What is learned in quiet is declared in tribulation. First, during a time of leisure, the words of the law are learned; but their fruit is displayed in affliction. As it is written: “The mercy of the Lord is beautiful in the time of tribulation” (Ecclesiasticus 35:26). Thus what is learned by day is declared by night.

He adds: “With me is prayer to the God of my life,” as though he were saying: within me is the sacrifice that I will offer to God.

[Col. 0305B] What sacrifice is this? Prayer, certainly—the prayer God does not despise and which he chooses above sacrifices, provided that it is offered with the devotion of a pure mind.

But this Lord is the God of our life, because while we die through the actions of our sins, we are saved through the forgiveness of his mercy.

### Verse 13

“I will say to God: You are my protector. Why have you forgotten me? Why have you rejected me? And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?”

The son of Korah had said above: “With me is prayer to the God of my life.” Now he declares that he will speak to the Lord the prayer he previously introduced.

That is: since, through the divine grace of baptism, you received me, to be placed in that homeland through your benefits, why do you then permit me to be tormented by various calamities through the devil’s deceit?

The most holy man had sensed how great the sweetness of that rest would be, and he greatly dreaded the rough roads of this world.

[Col. 0305C] He also speaks in human fashion: “Why have you forgotten me?” because that promise which the Lord makes to his saints in the future homeland was still being delayed.

“Why have you rejected me?” Because he could not yet reach that rest which he desired with such fervor.

“And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” We are sorrowful when we receive scourges in this world, when we are tempted by the enemy’s deceitful ambush, and when we endure the vices of the flesh with an unconquered and resisting spirit.

This figure is called *erotema*, when we magnify something through repeated questioning as we grieve.

[144] ### Verse 14

“While all my bones are being broken, those who afflict me reproach me.”

We have often said that bones refer to firmness of mind. Therefore, while the strength of our patience is afflicted, our bones are broken, as it were.

[Col. 0305D] The enemies see this and mock it; they abhor him as though he were disgraced, because they recognize that no worldly happiness smiles upon him.

### Verse 15

“While it is said to me every day: ‘Where is your God?’”

This is the reproach by which the bones of patience were broken as though by a hammer.

Persecutors and mockers are accustomed to say this to afflicted Christians: “Where is your God? Let him avenge you, if he can.”

How often did the martyrs hear this? How often did confessors hear it, those who could not yield to various tortures? For this is a celebrated cry, constantly addressed to those who suffer for the name of Christ.

### Verse 16

“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?”

[Col. 0306A] **Verse 17.** “Hope in the Lord, for I shall yet confess him: the salvation of my countenance, and my God.” We must ask what this repetition of words signifies, since in these writings nothing is superfluous and nothing is demonstrably confused. It seems to me, however, that a five-part syllogism may perhaps be found here, of the kind which Cicero considers applicable to orators; so that it may clearly appear that they were imitators, not authors, of such rules. Let us now set out distinctly the members of this argument. The proposition is: “Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord, for I shall confess him, the salvation of my countenance.” The proof of the proposition is undoubtedly contained and attached in the four verses that follow. Then comes the assumption: “I shall say to God, You are my protector: why have you forgotten me? Why have you cast me away, and why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” The proof of the assumption follows in two further verses. Finally, under the repetition of the first verse, there is introduced the beautiful conclusion of the proposed syllogism: “Why are you sorrowful, my soul?” etc. This repetition is still regarded as especially famous in the rule of the five-part syllogism. Nor should it disturb us that in the proposition this statement seems to be extended over two verses, whereas here it is compressed into a single verse; for it was fitting that what above seemed to have been proposed at greater length should be gathered together at the end.

**Conclusion of the psalm.**

This Son of the Cross, wishing at the beginning of the psalm to display his eminent desire, compared himself with an extraordinary example, so that he might be believed to love in an exceptional way, since he was known to have longed for the Lord with so great a desire. But since, in ordinary human experience, a good intention is always opposed by evil conduct, when an iniquitous mind cannot deceive someone by flatteries, it tries to overthrow him by crafty reproaches, and says that, once stirred by repeated insults, he is driven to continual tears. And lest the sorrow of the world occupy his mind or he reach the dangers of despair, he addresses consoling words to his own soul, so that he might drive away from himself the disturbance of this world, hostile to the faithful, lest the weariness of despair take possession of him. For it is written: “For the sorrow that is according to God produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10). Therefore he rightly attempted to drive away from himself that from which he knew perpetual destruction threatened him. And for this reason the Church still fittingly chants this psalm for those being baptized, as a persuader and instructor in good desire, so that, alienated from the sorrow of this world, they may hasten to the Lord with complete purity of mind [ed., “sigh”]. Grant, good King, that—since your mercy has not one single mode—just as you wash them through the water of holy regeneration, so you may also purify us from the dregs of sins by the gift of your clemency.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 42

**A psalm of David.**

Although some titles contain much and other titles contain less, all nevertheless lead to the gifts of heavenly contemplation, so that their very variety neither causes weariness nor ceases to remind us of what is necessary. Thus a psalm—as has often been said—signifies the melody of heavenly words, which is perceived to resound to us from above, as this one is about to say: “Distinguish my cause from an unholy nation,” etc. David, however, indicates Christ as strong and desirable for us, to whom this psalm is directed in the person of the most faithful Christian, while his mind and intention are eagerly fitted toward him. For just as the preceding psalm teaches that everything must be despised so that the desire for the Lord may be sought uniquely, so this one forewarns us not to be confounded by worldly tribulation, but says that we must rejoice in the courts of the Lord, proving how greatly necessary to our illnesses is the potion that the merciful physician so often administers to us.

## Division of the psalm

Each of the faithful will fittingly apply this psalm to himself. In its first section he entreats the Lord that, at the final advent when he will judge the world, he may be freed from the company of unbelievers. Secondly, he confidently declares that he will enter the Lord’s altar, where only the blessed have access; and therefore, amid the troubles of this world, he says that the soul must not be disturbed, since it already rejoices in hope of the heavenly gift.

## Exposition of the psalm

**Verse 1.** “Judge me, God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.” When the faithful man was troubled by the iniquities of this world and was still mingled in habitation with unbelieving peoples, he suddenly broke into speech, asking that at the Lord’s judgment his cause be separated from the wicked, when he will place the sheep at his right hand but set the goats at his left. For he does not ask that his sins be examined, but to be freed from the company of the wicked. It would indeed be dangerous to say, “Judge me,” unless he had added, “and distinguish my cause”—that is, separate my mingling, which I endure in this world, and at some time, once I have been separated from the wicked, establish me among the chosen people. He added, “from an unholy nation,” that is, from the perverse and those who live evilly. Truly, his conscience was holy, since it could not even observe in another what was proved contrary to the divine commandments.

**Verse 2.** “Rescue me from the iniquitous and deceitful man.” A good desire, but it does not yet have its proper time. What this holy man now asks for is found by the faithful at the future judgment. Yet those who are known to be peaceable desire such things even here: they wish to be separated from restless ways, lest they be corrupted by any perversity. It is the same iniquitous and deceitful man of whom he earlier said, “from an unholy nation.” For the iniquitous man is one who does evil openly; the deceitful man is one who proceeds by secret plotting—such are all who are shown to be alienated from the Lord’s commandments.

**Verse 3.** “For you are my God and my strength: why have you cast me away? And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” Often the reason precedes the matter, and often again follows in conjunction with it; here, however, it cries out at the beginning after the matter has been proposed. Since God is his strength, he wonders why he still seems to be rejected from the advent of the Lord, at which he will judge the world—the advent he endured with great desire because of the hardships he suffered on account of the world. Strength is the endurance of considered dangers and the unfailing proving of labors. For the most holy man knew that he could no longer be saddened if he reached the eternal rest of the age to come. It is the custom of those who desire something to think themselves driven away from the thing to which they are not permitted to come quickly. A fitting explanation of this also follows: “And why do I go about sorrowful while the enemy afflicts me?” The saints certainly go about sorrowful in this world when they suffer the most savage scourges of their enemies. But when the day of judgment arrives, they will suffer nothing of the kind, because the enemy and his followers will be utterly condemned. Therefore the holy man longed eagerly for those times in which he knew blessedness would be bestowed upon him.

**Verse 4.** “Send forth your light and your truth: they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacle.” Here he gives the reason why sorrow must be removed: that the Father may send the Son to judge, who is light and truth. For he himself said of himself, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and elsewhere, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). When this one comes—for he is Christ the Lord—all the grief of confusion departs from his saints, when they attain the glory of eternal blessedness. Thus this faithful man whom we earlier said was speaking declares that he has been led and brought to the holy mountain—that is, to firm belief in the Lord the Savior—offering everything to his glory and attributing nothing to his own powers. What he added, “and to your tabernacle,” signifies the Catholic Church established amid the contest of this world, which is still harassed by the enemy’s varied weariness. But when we hear “tabernacle,” let us beware the adversary’s snares; for while the Church is in tabernacles, we can by no means possess secure leisure. The text of Exodus depicts this tabernacle with such an evident description (Exod. 26:1) that it is offered not only to our ears but almost to our very eyes.

**Verse 5.** “And I shall enter the altar of God, to God who makes my youth rejoice; I shall confess to you upon the lyre, God, my God.” He comes to the second section. But since the Church also has an altar here, he does not without reason say after the tabernacle has been mentioned, “I shall enter the altar of God.” There is a certain sublime altar, invisible to us now, where only the righteous are permitted to approach. For among the other parts of the tabernacle that the Lord commanded his servant Moses to make, he also clearly indicated this, saying: “Look and make it according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40). Here an indiscriminate crowd surrounds the Church’s altar; but to that altar which he says he will enter in the future, only those pleasing to God can attain. The altar is so called as if from *alta ara* (“high altar”), or *alta res* (“high thing”). He continues, “to God who makes my youth rejoice.” Here he uses “youth” for the newness of life on account of the Lord the Savior, who, restoring all things that had failed through old age, gave believers the strongest firmness of youth. Behold, this man, saddened by the disasters of the world, made joy for himself from a good understanding. He confesses upon the lyre because, while enduring the adversities of this world, he does not depart from the praise of the Lord.

**Verse 6.** “Why are you sorrowful, my soul? And why do you trouble me?”

**Verse 7.** “Hope in God [ed., ‘to God’], for I shall confess him: the salvation of my countenance, and my God.” Let us remember that these verses were also written in the preceding psalm, where we said that there was a five-part syllogism. But we must consider that he both frequently warns us to flee this sorrow of the world and urges it with the greatest force—not undeservedly, since it is always opposed to good things. Through it the strength of patience is broken; through it the light of charity is extinguished; through it the desire and power of our hope grow weak; and all life is thrown into confusion wherever this malignant iniquity rages. But that life-giving sorrow, the peace of good minds and perpetual joy, is to be sought with the greatest desires of the blessed. Of it the Apostle says: “Brothers, I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance; for you were made sorrowful according to God” (2 Cor. 7:9). The name is one, but the condition of the realities differs; for just as the former nourishes toward death, so the latter directs toward perpetual well-being.

## Conclusion of the psalm

In the preceding psalms we read that many persons were introduced to raise the minds of the perfect to the summit of virtue: now the Church, now the penitent, now the prophet, now Jeduthun, now the sons of Korah, speaking with great virtue of patience. Here, however, a moderate and gentler discourse is employed, one appropriate to a devout Christian, so that no one, even if weak, may distrust his own lowliness, since each person finds the goal toward which he may hasten with an inclined mind through the grace of God. Moreover, the forty-second number is fittingly applied to this person who desires to reach the courts of the Lord. For by such a number those Hebrew stations in the wilderness were consecrated. Also, in the forty-second generation from Abraham, the Lord the Savior came and saved the world by his visitation. Thus it is rightly believed that this faithful man will also reach the kingdom of the Lord, since he is recognized as joined to that earlier number. Here, therefore, the faithful soul finds all virtues and all delights, so that whoever has received that little spark of divine charity may be able, through God’s grace, to console and refresh himself. 

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 43

**For the end; for the sons of Korah; for understanding; a psalm of David.**

146 What the sons of Korah signify was sufficiently stated recently in the forty-first psalm. Here, however, “for understanding” seems to have been added in a new but not pointless order, in order to remind us that this psalm must be examined more carefully. We are about to hear martyrs or confessors—that is, sons of the Cross—declare that, while their fathers had their enemies subjected to them without any difficulty, through God’s favor, they themselves have won victories through the divine gift amid the most grievous sufferings of martyrdom. But here a deeper understanding is needed, so that we may refer the Lord’s deeds to glorious purposes. At first, miracles of the Red Sea and effortless victories over different nations occurred, so that so remarkable a miracle might invite uncultivated peoples to belief in divine power. Then the land of Canaan was promised to those who were, of course, under the Law. But now, as faith grows, worldly prosperity has been withdrawn from the martyrs, lest human weakness seek the goods of the age to come with insufficient fervor. The heavenly kingdoms have been promised to those who are known to be under grace. Therefore this understanding must be sought and this grace contemplated, since the things now brought about by the Author of all things for the salvation of everyone are generally ordered by hidden movements [ed., “ways”].

## Division of the psalm

Whether you receive these as the words of martyrs or of confessors, consider the psalm, formed with wondrous construction. In the first section they say that they have heard that their fathers, through the Lord’s favor, visibly achieved victories among innumerable nations; but they themselves profess that, at the Lord’s judgment, they will rightly see vengeance taken upon their enemies. There the enemy is not conquered by bow or sword but is overcome by the Lord’s judgment alone. Thus the two kinds of benefits are set out distinctly, benefits that the Lord deigns to grant his servants. In the second section they enumerate the sufferings of the various necessities they endure in this world, yet they profess that they have not forgotten the divine commandments, and that they persevere in the virtue of patience. Third, they pray for help, so that those who are grievously afflicted here may be aided at the time of the resurrection.

## Exposition of the psalm

**Verse 1.** “God, with our ears we have heard; our fathers have declared to us the work that you worked in their days, in ancient days.” First he placed “God,” which either a joyful person utters at the beginning or one wounded by excessive affliction. But lest what they were about to say be thought ambiguous, they declare that they heard it with their own ears, so that greater credibility might be gained for the matter. And consider that they do not say that young men or adolescents related to them what happened, but fathers, who by the significance of their name could possess an affection for truth [ed., “piety”]. “Our” was added, since they could have spoken what was altogether certain from their own experience. “They have declared to us”—that is, they related the benefits that they wished to be made known to their descendants for the praise of the Lord. Although God’s daily work consists in sustaining the world by his benefits, so that everything proceeds according to the law established for it, we nevertheless say that he “worked” when he displays some sign of novelty. Thus they testify that their fathers related the work that God worked in their days—that is, in ancient days—when he led the Israelite people unharmed through the waters of the Red Sea and made them conquerors of their enemies without effort of their own. This argument is called “from the words and deeds of the ancestors,” when the weight of testimony is strengthened by the very great authority of the fathers.

**Verse 2.** “Your hand destroyed nations, and you planted them; you afflicted peoples and drove them out.” From this point a beautiful enumeration proceeds, showing how great a power the divine power bestowed upon the Israelite people, so that the Lord’s benefits, both in prosperity and in the adversities he is about to mention, might shine forth more clearly. As has often been said, “hand” signifies power, because through trope the nations are said to have been afflicted by the Lord’s hand, by which we especially customarily act. When the Amorites and the others departed from their own lands, the Hebrews are read to have been planted in their settlements. They were truly planted, since as the days passed they were increased by the Lord’s gift through continual growth. He afflicted the hostile peoples when, as the priests’ trumpets sounded, the walls of Jericho collapsed with a crashing roar (Josh. 6:20); and it is evident that they were driven from the city, since they could not withstand such great miracles.

**Verse 3.** “For they did not possess the land by their own sword, and their arm did not save them.” Lest the Hebrews, as conquerors, think that they had prevailed by their own powers, they profess that they had not been victorious by their own sword, nor claimed the lands of the nations through their own strength. “Arm” signifies strength, since battle is fought by the arm engaged in combat. But this arm was unable to free them from their enemies; it was the special power of God that saved them. Thus, while the deeds of the Hebrews are expounded, a profitable lesson is provided for the human race.

[Col. 0311C] **Verse 4.** “But your right hand, and your arm, and the illumination of your countenance, because you were pleased with them.” “But your right hand, and your arm, and the illumination of your countenance” must collectively be supplied with “saved them.” The right hand signifies the prosperous side, the arm strength, and illumination counsel—things that the Lord grants to those who fight when he deigns to give victory. But lest anyone say, “Your fathers pleased God by their own merit, and therefore they obtained such great things from the Lord,” he added that it was not given because of merits, but because it pleased God to give it; everything he bestows is gratuitous. He was also pleased with them when, from the whole world, the one chosen nation was selected from which the Lord the Savior would come.

**Verse 5.** “You are he himself, my King and my God, who commands salvation for Jacob.” When the sons of Korah—that is, the people of the blessed—had said, “You are he himself, my King,” meaning the Lord and Savior, to whom the name “king” plainly belongs, he added, “and my God,” lest you doubt that the Lord Jesus Christ, who graciously transmitted salvation also to our father Jacob, made him wrestle with an angel in a glorious contest. For he commanded salvation for him when he heard through the angel: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel” (Gen. 32:28). For whatever that power of our will may be, we customarily commission it not through ourselves but through another person.

**Verse 6.** “In you we shall winnow our enemies, and in your name we shall despise those rising up against us.” The martyrs have come to that extraordinary kind of liberation which is known to be granted to the faithful at the time of judgment. Those who had been worn down by excessive affliction recover courage and console themselves with future prosperity, saying: “In you we shall scatter our enemies like chaff.” The enemies are to be winnowed by divine judgment, when our Savior, shaking his threshing floor with the winnowing of judgment, separates the chaff from the grain. It follows: “And in your name we shall despise those rising up against us.” Then those rising up are despised—that is, unclean spirits—when they will no longer be able to inflict harm. Now they despise those whom the righteous will later judge worthy of contempt. What the Lord’s hand did in scattering the nations, planting the Hebrews in their settlements, and granting them the power to overcome their enemies without any labor belongs to that earlier time. But the scattering of the enemies and the contempt for the ancient enemy belong to the future judgment, where victory will be achieved in such a way that all conflicts will be proved to have been overthrown.

**Verse 7.** “For I shall not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me.” With their customary faith and humility, the multitude of the saints says that it will not place its hope in earthly weapons. The bow is the protection of the warrior, in which the human mind trusts. Worldly fighters, however, rely more upon the sword. An arrow is often shot in vain, but the sword produces the effect of certain death. Therefore he says that he will not even claim for himself that aid which people in war believe to be most effective for protection.

**Verse 8.** “For you have delivered us from [mss. A, B, F: ‘of’] those afflicting us, and you have put to shame those who hate us.” With confidence in faith they speak of the future as though it were past, since for them there is no doubt about what they know will certainly come. They therefore say that at the Lord’s second advent they will be delivered from the persecution of the most evil spirits, who do not cease to afflict them here with manifold ambushes. They will plainly be delivered then, when they are removed from the spirits’ power, so that it will no longer be permitted to them to rejoice in the harassment of the innocent—something that certainly cannot generally happen in this world. Those who hate the blessed will also be put to shame, when they are condemned to eternal punishment while the righteous receive the kingdoms of heaven.

**Verse 9.** “In God we shall be praised all day long, and in your name we shall confess throughout the ages.” Those who say, “we shall be praised,” profess that they will be celebrated in the future; yet they designate their glory without arrogance, since they testify that they will be praised in God. “All day long” indicates perpetual time, which has no night, as will occur in that eternity where the continual praise of the blessed is known to exist. But lest you think that those who said they would be praised in God would be idle, they also profess that they will continually resound the praises of the Lord. For the blessedness of the righteous is to praise the Lord forever: a satisfaction that never knows satiety; a hunger that is not born from the mother of abstinence; an eagerness that is not created by fasting.

**Verse 10.** “But now you have cast us away and put us to shame, and you do not go forth with our forces.” After that ineffable reward of the age to come, the devout martyrs come to the second section, saying in the following eight verses what afflictions they endure in the present time and that they never in any way depart from reverence for the Lord. This figure is called *emphasis*, that is, exaggeration, when we allege some matter with many sorrows gathered together into one, so that by enumerating calamities we may obtain the judge’s goodwill. By saying “but now,” they indicate that just above they spoke of future times. And observe how everything proceeds in a wondrous order. “You have cast us away” signifies the delay that undoubtedly comes to the saints, because perfect blessedness is promised to them not here but in the future. “You have put us to shame” signifies the glorious shame that martyrs undergo when they are afflicted with insults, beaten with clubs, and, as though liable for crimes, continually handed over to death. The Apostle also speaks of such people: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11:38). But observe that in this world martyrs are put to shame among wicked men, whereas the impious will bear the weight of eternal disgrace before the true Judge. Yet this shame will lead to glory; that shame will lead to everlasting destruction. “Now God does not go forth with the forces of the martyrs” when he subjects them to tribulations and delivers them to various sufferings.
