He then went forth with the forces of the Hebrews when those who attempted to rise up against the chosen people were struck down without effort. This certainly pertains to the consolation of the holy people, lest anyone take it hard that their fathers were supremely happy while he himself is afflicted by the Lord’s permissions.

**Verse 11.** “You have turned us back before our enemies, and those who hate us plundered us for themselves.” They testify that in this world they have been turned away before their enemies, since they avoided the dangers of their pursuers. To be turned away is to flee a bodily enemy, as it was commanded: “If they persecute you in this city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23). It follows: “And those who hate us plundered us for themselves.” This commonly happens to fugitives: those who could not resist their enemies fall into plunder and spoil.

**Verse 12.** “You have given us like sheep for food [ed., ‘foods’], and you have scattered us among the nations.” When they say, “You have given,” they signify that everything is distributed by divine power. They say that they were handed over to the nations like wolves, which are accustomed to devour gentle sheep. The meek simplicity of sheep is food for wolves; it is rightly compared with the martyrs, who submit to being killed by their persecutors without engaging in struggle. It follows: “And you have scattered us among the nations.” They indicate the various faithful whom the compassion of the martyrs now mourns—those who, handed over to the nations, lost their freedom together with their possessions. This was accomplished at various times among Christian peoples by divine dispensation, so that through the temporal evils of tribulations they might attain the goods of glorious blessedness, which are eternal.

**Verse 13.** “You have sold your people without price, and there was no multitude in their exchanges.” We must not take this as spoken by way of reproach, but as expressed, as usual, through a mystical allusion. God seems to receive a price when he subjects unbelievers to peoples who have deserved well. For he hands over the irreligious in order to acquire the most devout. But God sells without price, as it were, when he hands the Christian people over to foreigners to be afflicted. This frequently happens by a hidden judgment, either for the merit of testing or for the purpose of correction. And note that this manner of expression is to be counted among the distinctive features of divine Scripture: something is said to have been sold where no price is shown to have been paid. He added, “and there was no multitude in their exchanges.” Human beings who make exchanges receive something equal to what they have handed over; but here no multitude of price arose for God in compensation for so great a thing, when Christians were handed over even though their persecutors were not proved acceptable to the Lord. For how could they truly have been pleasing to God, entangled as they were in profane superstitions?

**Verse 14.** “You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a derision and a contempt to those who are around us.” They enumerate how great the affliction was by which they had been struck, so that amid manifold hardships the quality of their devotion might increase. The affliction we suffer from neighbors is severe, because what is attributed by those standing around us is not said to be transitory but continual. For when he says, “You have made us,” he reveals an immovable suffering. Someone is believed to remain there for a long time when he is shown to have been placed there. “Reproach” is set against “upright,” for just as all upright things are beautiful, so all indecent things are displayed as reproachful. But this reproach was not before the Lord’s sight; it was before the eyes of neighbors who knew how to judge the things that a corrupted understanding had been taught to notice. “Derision” is a confused expression of joy, declaring their insult through immoderate hilarity. “Contempt” signifies the most abject degradation that the martyrs of the Lord, handed over to various sufferings, endured. “Those who are around us” explains that they are unbelievers and treacherous people, who always walk in every direction and do not walk with us according to right doctrine.

**Verse 15.** “You have made us a likeness among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples.” Observe the figure of *anaphora*, which in Latin is called *relatio*, the repetition of the same word: namely, “you have made,” which was already said at the beginning of the preceding verse, so that frequent repetition might intensify the force of the suffering. The martyrs were evidently set before the nations as a likeness of Christ when the nations afflicted them with comparable punishments and tortures. The shaking of the enemies’ heads also happened to the martyrs, and it occurred in the passion of the Lord the Savior, as it is written: “They spoke with their lips and shook their head” (Ps. 21:8).

**Verse 16.** “All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my countenance has covered me.” Shame usually comes for a moment and departs after being calmed in a short time. This shame, however, was exceedingly grave, since it continued without interruption. For before the eyes of the holy people there was immoderate shame and violent confusion when they continually saw those whom they knew to be impious insulting them. And observe how fittingly the description of shame follows. For he says that his face was covered by a kind of cloak of confusion, while his face, inflamed, glowed with a bloody cloud. But when he says, “it has covered me,” he indicates not only an alteration of the face but also the horror of the whole body.

**Verse 17.** “At the voice of the one reproaching and insulting, at the face of the enemy and persecutor.” The description of that confusion continues up to this verse. Now it is said from where came that rosy covering which clothed the naked face in the veil of its color. To reproach is to curse someone to his face, as though hurling indecent accusations. To insult is to disparage someone in his absence and to wound him with deceitful speech. “At the face of the enemy”—that is, when he sees the person who hates him with deadly hatred. And lest you think the adversary insignificant, he added, “and persecutor,” which proves the hatred to be most bitter, since they desire not only to extinguish the body but by their depravity to slaughter the souls themselves.

**Verse 18.** “All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, and we have not acted wickedly against your covenant.” The sons of Korah have come to the most glorious firmness of their confession, to show us that no evils whatsoever ought to separate us from the grace of Christ, as the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness?” (Rom. 8:35), etc. By saying “all these things,” they gather into one what they had said throughout the preceding passage, so that, if scattered matters were received more lightly, they might grow greater when collected into one heap. This argument is called “from tortures,” when the soul of the faithful cannot be changed by so many evils. “They have come upon us” like a terrifying wild beast, like a turbulent river. And because grave tribulation often casts down from the soul what someone previously seemed to have believed, they add that they had not forgotten the Lord amid such manifold hardships. Rather, stirred by the persecution of the wicked, they continually sought help from the Lord. It follows: “And we have not acted wickedly against your covenant”—that is what they said when they said, “we have not forgotten you.” For those who retain him in their minds cannot forget his covenant. But although Latin usage allows us to say, “we have not forgotten you” (*obliti non sumus tui*), it is characteristic of divine Scripture to say, “we have not forgotten you” (*obliti non sumus te*).

**Verse 19.** “And our heart has not turned back, and you have turned our paths away from your way.” The heart of those who despair of the Lord’s goodness turns back and thinks that the one who is known to help even those who do not ask will not come to the aid of one who has been entreated. These people certainly did not do that, since they were proved to have hope in the Lord. Here he uses “paths” in a negative sense when he says “our,” as though they were shady and pleasure-filled tracks worn down by frail humanity. We travel them when we depart from the Lord’s command. But “way” is named from violence, and is rightly called Christ’s, since his faithful walk in hardships and tribulations just as he himself did. Therefore human paths are most fittingly said to be divided from the heavenly way: those lead to detestable death, while this unquestionably bestows the well-desired well-being. Hence the sons of Korah were truly sons of the most holy Cross, since they felt such things.

**Verse 20.** “For you humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us.” They give the reason why they said that the way and the paths had been divided: because they testify that they had been humbled in a place of affliction—that is, in this world—which is a place of affliction for the faithful, from which compunction arises and repentance follows. It continues: “And the shadow of death covered us.” They refer to the passage of this life, which is shown to be common to saints and sinners alike. But true death is that by which the impious are punished with eternal condemnation.

**Verse 21.** “If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god.” This is the meaning that the title plainly attributed to the faithful: they do not know a foreign god, nor do they forget the one to whose name they have been consecrated by the imprint of the Cross. When they add, “And if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god,” they describe a person praying who, with hands extended, reproduces in the form of his body the very Cross that he receives upon his forehead. The most faithful certainly did this not for a foreign lord but for their own Lord, so that their perseverance might prove them faithful, since they had not been changed by so many adversities.

**Verse 22.** “Will God not require these things? For he himself knows the secrets of the heart.” “Will he not?” must be pronounced with emphasis, because it is an exceedingly grave matter before the Lord if one sins in his religion. We customarily “require” something when we desire to know what we know our conscience does not contain. God, however, requires knowingly—not so that he himself may learn something new, but so that he may make us recognize things buried in forgetfulness. Thus it was also said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear your God” (Gen. 22), as though he had learned something in time, although he had foreknown everything before the ages. It follows: “These things”—that is, the things he had said above: “If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god.” And because the discussion concerned religious devotion, which is practiced not only through bodily devotion but more especially in the hidden chamber of the heart, they hastened to the knowledge of the Divinity, where all integrity presses forward, saying: “For he himself knows the secrets of the heart.”

### Verse 23

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.”

The most blessed interpreters explain what was said secretly: they were not dying for any crime they had committed, but out of divine love, so that the saving belief in the Trinity might increase among the nations. To be subjected to death means to find the end of the present life through prolonged sufferings. This is what perfect Christians do, being afflicted by strict observances. To make this clearer, he added, “all day long”: he thereby declares that the death of the faithful is not momentary, but prolonged throughout the entire span of life.

Attend to what follows: “We are regarded as sheep for slaughter.” A sheep, because it possesses no weapons with which to resist, proves contemptible to its predators. It cannot fight with its horn, contend with its teeth, or rely on flight; rather, it patiently submits to the robber’s hands, defending itself with no resistance. Thus Christ’s servants were regarded as sheep destined to die, since they seemed to be slaughtered without any struggle.

### Verse 24

“Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not reject us forever.”

After recounting the multitude of their sufferings, the sons of Korah came to the third division, where they seek help with such longing that they even declare that the Lord has fallen asleep. This is a figure called *catachresis*, which we properly call “abuse” (*abusio*), since it lends a name belonging to one thing to another. For it is not fitting to say that God rises, since he is never known to be able to sleep. Yet we say that he sleeps in human usage when our expectation is delayed by the divine dispensation.

For if you inquire into the power of his majesty, you have the clearest statement: “Behold, he neither sleeps nor slumbers who keeps Israel” (Psalm 120:3). “Rise up” is repeated so that he may not pretend not to help those whose dangers he sees increasing. It follows: “and do not reject us forever.” If you still think that the matter must be delayed here, do not reject us forever—where the whole perfection of your gift is established, where the rewards of the blessed are found, and where crowns are prepared for the martyrs.

### Verse 25

“Why do you turn your face away? Will you forget our poverty and our affliction?”

Burdened by present evils, they persist, after the manner of the blessed, in tearful supplication, saying: “Why do you regard us as being delayed for so long that you seem unwilling to look upon us, since you have postponed coming to our aid?”

It follows: “Will you forget our poverty?” That is: the poverty to which you were accustomed to give aid, which you love so greatly among others that you call yourself poor. For you came, supremely rich, to help our need. He added, “our affliction,” of which he is always the merciful observer, as he will say in the fiftieth psalm: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm 50:19). Such causes have the greatest force before that merciful Judge, although they are judged contemptible by human judges.

### Verse 26

“For our soul has been humbled in the dust; our belly has clung to the earth.”

After the delay in being heard, devout minds did not turn toward the audacity of despair, but toward the salutary vows of continual prayer. Here the fulfillment of constant supplication is described. Those who scatter ashes over themselves and torment their souls by recollection of sins bend down into the dust.

It follows: “our belly has clung to the earth.” This is what those customarily do who, prostrate in prolonged prayer, stretch themselves out with the full extension of their bodies. To cling to the earth means to remain longer in prayers, through which sins are powerfully overcome. For great weapons against the devil are not to trust in one’s own strength, but to beseech God, who is able to crush the adversary.

### Verse 27

“Rise up, O Lord; help us, and redeem us for the sake of your name.”

The sweetest conclusion is applied to these great afflictions: they ask to be freed by the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, in which the hope of all Christians is recognized. “Rise up” should be understood here not as referring to sleep, but rather to the resurrection. Above, when they wished to rouse him as though he were sleeping, it was said: “Why do you sleep?” Here, however, they simply say “rise up,” so that we should understand that resurrection in which the captivity of humanity is recognized as destroyed.

When he rose, we were helped; when he ascended into heaven, we were freed. Yet he bestowed all these things upon us not because of our merit, but for the sake of his name. For this reason he is called the Savior: because through the grace of his mercy he saves the weak.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Behold, the salutary sayings of the sons of Korah have shone forth for us; behold, the ecclesiastical order has flashed forth, revealed by the Lord. We have learned that our fathers were visibly freed from their enemies by miracles; now we have learned that the faithful reach eternal rest through bodily sufferings and the sorrows of their souls. Thus, in its proper time, each event would be recognized as beneficial to the human race, and no one should complain when he realizes that he is being weighed down by worldly troubles.

With the freedom of innocence, the voices of the martyrs also rise up when God is said to sleep and to forget. This statement should not be received as a rebuke, but expressed with affectionate devotion. Such expressions are also found very frequently in the Book of Job; unless one examines them with prudent inquiry, one will understand not supplications but complaints. Yet this measured presumption of the righteous seems to express the purity of a sincere heart, so that the simplicity of the soul appears to set forth the weight of the suffering inflicted upon it. Thus, whenever we find something of this kind in the divine Scriptures, both the mercy of the ruler is displayed and the purity of the supplicant is indicated.

## Exposition of Psalm 44

**For the end; for those who will be changed; of the sons of Korah, for understanding; a song for the beloved.**

[Col. 0318C]

Let us see what these words, examined one by one, bring forth for us, since the title of the psalm is extended by a gathering of many names. “For the end” has often been said to signify perfection, that is, the Lord the Savior.

“For those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah” declares this: that the sons of the cross, remaining in the Church, will pass from the sorrow of this world to everlasting joy.

“A song for understanding” signifies the text of the psalm, which must be drawn toward heavenly understanding, in which the spiritual mysteries of future realities are contained.

“For the beloved son” is meant to indicate the Lord Christ, concerning whom the Father’s voice resounded: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). His spiritual marriage is now related; the vows of his wedding song are celebrated with praise. His power surpasses all powers, his beauty all beauties, his strength is ineffable, and his mercy unique.

O blessed bride, who are shown to be joined to such majesty—not by bodily association, but by an inviolable union of charity! When will you be recognized as united to him who has illumined you with his most splendid light? Therefore, let us devoutly beseech the Godhead that, raised by a most pure heart toward the light of contemplation, we may spiritually hear the marriage of the holy Bride.

### Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0319A]

Filled with heavenly banquets and completed by the quality of future rejoicing, the prophet promises that he will pour forth the Lord’s praises, so that the faithful people might be nourished most abundantly from the same source by which he himself had been satisfied through heavenly generosity. He celebrates, as has been said, a kind of heavenly wedding song with nuptial exultation.

“Epithalamium” is interpreted as “praise of the bridal chamber,” which, according to human custom, is offered to the heavenly Bridegroom. The first part contains the praises of the Bridegroom—that is, the Lord the Savior—in four modes. In the second, likewise in four mystical sections, the Bride, the Church, is proclaimed in her virtues; namely, the Church that consists in the gathering together of holy people.

The wisest Solomon also described this in the book called the Song of Songs [Col. 0319B] in a passage familiar to all. Therefore, in the present psalm, wherever the context requires, we join examples from that book, so that although the preachers are separated by time, they may nevertheless appear to have spoken as one through the harmony of prophecy.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the King.”

#### Verse 2

“My tongue is the pen of a ready writer.”

When the prophet recognized that his understanding had been suffused by the brightness [edition: “charity”] of the divine gift, he was compelled by the greatness of his rejoicing. He praised beforehand what he was about to say—not out of a desire for exaltation, but moved by the impulse of truth.

We say “has uttered” when an abundance of food, through healthy digestion, gives off vapor. But with what great spiritual banquets had this man been filled, that he should utter such a secret of good fragrance! “My heart” means the inner chamber of the mind.

“A good word” means the Son of God, concerning whom John the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Truth itself also says of itself: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

“My works” means that the prophet’s task was to offer, through the service of his voice, the beautiful composition of this psalm and to cause divine words to resound through the organ of his tongue, as through certain pens. He desired to speak this proclamation to the King, which he had conceived from the King’s wondrous brightness [manuscripts A, B, F: “charity”].

But lest anyone suppose that he was going to speak something from his own will, he compared his tongue to a scribe’s pen [Col. 0319D]. It was to speak the words of the Holy Spirit faithfully, just as a pen records the desires of our minds on paper. He added, “of a ready writer.” We should understand this more as a secretary or recorder, who receives words swiftly and transcribes what he has heard even more quickly.

It must be considered that here the power of prophecy is displayed: it does not deliberate under human torment, but proclaims the commands of the Godhead without any labor. Let us now hear the prophet announce the praise of the wedding song without flattery—a praise that does nothing but magnify the truth, that flatters while preserving integrity; and although it says great things, it does not, nevertheless, enumerate everything sufficiently.

#### Verse 3

“You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips. Therefore God has blessed you forever.” [Col. 0320A]

When the prologue had been completed and the peoples had been suitably stirred to eagerness for hearing, the beginning of praise was made concerning the Lord’s incarnation, so that through the one by whom we were worthy to know the mysteries of the Godhead, we should also hear the praises of such great majesty.

This kind of praise is called *forma* (“form” or “beauty”) among rhetoricians. But since it is written in Isaiah: “We saw him, and he had no appearance or beauty; his facial appearance was rejected and without honor before all men” (Isaiah 53:2), one may ask why he is here described as most beautiful above the human race.

It is not because his appearance shone with the beauty of a milky complexion, or gleamed with blond hair, or excelled in notable stature; rather, he was truly more beautiful than the human race because he had no sins. That is rightly called beautiful which is adorned with the grace of the purest purity [Col. 0320B], although Father Augustine says that the appearance of his body was praiseworthy.

He referred the example placed above from Isaiah to the time of Christ’s passion, when he is read to have been struck with blows, crowned with thorns, and covered with spittle.

The Church, however, which bears the image of the Lord the Savior, is described in the Song of Songs as follows: “I am dark and beautiful” (Song of Songs 1:4)—that is, dark in bodily flesh, beautiful in heavenly merits. It shows why he called him beautiful: because, when Christ spoke, the world was reconciled to God through grace.

What, then, could have been comparable in the human race to seeing him incarnate, through whom the whole world received the gift of redemption? For Solomon’s aforementioned book likewise says of him: “Your lips and your speech are beautiful.” It follows: “Therefore God has blessed you forever” (Song of Songs 4:3).

“Therefore,” he says, because of his outstanding proclamations and entirely singular mercy; for he bestowed nothing on anyone according to merits, but rather granted everything through his own goodness. He is blessed forever, whose kingdom will have no end.

The statement is rightly made concerning the form of a servant: “God has blessed you,” since he both endured suffering and reached the kingdoms of heaven.

#### Verse 4

“Gird your sword around your thigh, O most powerful one, with your appearance and your beauty.”

The second mode of praise of the Lord the Savior is introduced; it is called praise “from power.” The prophet, lifted toward some indescribable joy, begs the Lord, who was awaited by the nations, finally to appear as their most salutary deliverer.

He says: “Gird your sword.” This is a metaphor taken from a warrior who girds himself with a sword when he is about to fight, so that he may overthrow the enemy. Here, however, we should understand the sword as the word of preaching, concerning which he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34). The Apostle also says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17).

The word of God is called a sword because, by the blow of its power, it penetrates human hearts grown gross with vices. Human weakness cannot resist where that glory of strength deigns to enter.

The thigh signifies the incarnation of the Lord the Savior, as it is written in Genesis: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs” (Genesis 49:10). In the same mystery, Abraham also made his servant swear (Genesis 24:2), when, touching his thigh, he commanded him not to take a wife for his son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites.

He added to “thigh” the word “most powerful,” so that you might believe the incarnation, already worthy of reverence, to have been assumed by the power of the Godhead. Likewise that very wise writer said: “His sword is upon his thigh” (Song of Songs 3:8).

He added: “with your appearance and your beauty.” Here we clearly recognize both natures: “appearance” refers to humanity, and “beauty” to divinity. That appearance is rightly called beautiful in which he appeared as the world’s salvation; that beauty is most appropriately proclaimed from which all beautiful and comely things come.

#### Verse 5

“Attend, proceed prosperously, and reign, because of truth, meekness, and righteousness; and your right hand will guide you wondrously.” [Col. 0321B]

The activity of the most sacred incarnation is still being explained, and the miracles of his power are proclaimed in each word.

“Attend” was said so that, in pity from heaven, he might look upon the human being who was perishing, as it is said in the thirteenth psalm: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men” (Psalm 13:2).

“Prosper,” because he was about to bestow upon the human race the benefits of liberation.

“Proceed,” like a bridegroom from the virginal womb, as it is written: “And he himself, like a bridegroom proceeding from his bridal chamber” (Psalm 18:6).

“Reign,” that is, display the power of your majesty in the belief of human beings. For the Son unquestionably reigned with the Father and the Holy Spirit even before the foundation of the world.

“Because of truth” indicates that truth would arise from the earth, cleansing our falsehood by its illumination.

Meekness was shown when, hanging upon the cross, he prayed for his persecutors.

Righteousness refers to the fact that the merciful teacher infused saving commandments.

“Your right hand will guide you” means that it will preserve you, through the course of your entire life, in an unblemished conduct.

“Wondrously,” because, contrary to the world’s unimaginable custom, he was to rise from the dead on the third day; and this miracle filled every region of the world.

“Your right hand” signifies the power of the Word, by which he accomplishes everything he wills in heaven and on earth.

Let impious detractors hear this statement. He says “your right hand,” that is, the impulse of his own will. For if he does everything by his own power, as it is manifest that he does, how can he have anything greater?

Against this sickness, however, that remedy should be applied to diseased minds: “All things that belong to the Father are mine, and all things that are mine belong to the Father” (John 17:10). He would not possess all the Father’s things unless he were equal to him and of the same nature.

#### Verse 6

“Your arrows are sharp and exceedingly powerful; peoples will fall beneath you in the heart of the King’s enemies.”

The sharp arrows are the words of the Lord the Savior, which salutarily pierce human hearts. They wound in order to heal; they strike in order to free; they overthrow in order to raise up.

But let us see by what comparison this weapon is likened to the word of God. An arrow is a piece of wood armed with iron, whose first part is feathered. Thus the word of God, proceeding from the wood of the cross, possesses both the strength to penetrate and the speed to reach wherever it wills.

Above, he mentioned the sword, which wounds at close range; here he mentions arrows, which are directed from far away—clearly so that incomprehensible power might be displayed through this comparison.

“Sharp” refers to the speed of the piercing. “Exceedingly powerful” means that no material, however hard, is shown capable of resisting them, since they have been endowed with the power to accomplish the effect of their will.

“Peoples will fall beneath you” signifies the conversions of human beings: believers happily fall into humility, though previously they had stood upright through the vice of presumption. This happened to the Apostle Paul, who, pierced by the arrow of the Lord’s voice, fell face down as a persecutor, but was immediately raised up by the Lord’s right hand as an apostle.

“In the heart” explains what he said above—“will fall”: not with the feet, by which bodies are supported, but with the heart, by which the unbelief of souls is sustained. There, the one who falls in repentance rises again; cast down from his iniquity, he is transferred to the Lord’s saving commandments.

“The enemies of the King” means the enemies of Christ, who dissent from the heavenly law with a contrary will. This is what the title of the psalm foretold when it said: “For those who will be changed, for the sons of Korah.”

#### Verse 7

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of your kingdom is a righteous rod.”

He comes to the third mode of praise, properly called praise “from the cause of judgment.” Here God’s throne pertains to the future judgment, in which the eternal Ruler examines and judges all things truthfully.

“Forever and ever,” because whatever he establishes can be dissolved by no succession of time.

The rod signifies the rule of divine equity, which is truly called righteous because it is bent by no perversity. This rod rules the righteous, strikes the impious, and truly sustains those who plead.

Yet this rod does not emerge from the trunk of a tree [p. 152], but proceeds from the power of the Godhead itself: unconquered strength, perfectly upright equity, inflexible discipline. Concerning it another psalm will also say: “The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies” (Psalm 109:2).

Antiquity called this rod, the insignia of royal honor, a scepter, thereby designating in it the King of virtues, the Lord the Savior.

#### Verse 8

“You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you.”

This is the righteous rod: to love equity and hate wickedness. No one perfectly loves righteousness except the one who also detests evil deeds, since there is no place for contrary qualities in one person at the same time. Nor can blackness be seen in the very moment when brightness has taken its place.

The presence of light is likewise the absence of night; so the love of truth is the hatred of falsehood. Hence some have beautifully defined the matter thus: “Substance is capable of contraries, but not at the same time.”

What rewards have been given for these things he explains below: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.”

“Anointed” (*Christus*) signifies both king and priest, since these dignities were assumed through sacred anointings; indeed, the very name “Christ” is derived from the holy chrism. But he is called anointed with respect to that dispensation in which he is truly said to have been born, to have died, and to have risen as Christ. His divinity, however, needed assistance from no gift and no honor.

The repetition in the phrase “God, your God” displays the proclamation of great love.

#### Verse 9

“With the oil of gladness above your companions; myrrh, drop, and cassia are from your garments.” [Col. 0323A]

He indicates in two ways that this holy anointing came about. The oil of gladness is the absence of the stain of sin. Hence the conscience is always made joyful when it is not bitten by any harshness of recollection.

“Above your companions” means above the sons of men, whom he himself also calls brothers in the Gospel. It is said “above your companions” because he is recognized to have received this blessing above the whole human race, so that, being uniquely anointed, he should anoint the others.

In him is the fountain of blessing, from which, according to his own will, it suitably flows throughout all the elect. But all these things pertain to the flesh, to which the most merciful and glorious Word was united for the salvation of all.

It follows: “myrrh, and drop, and cassia are from your garments.” We have often said that the forms of earthly things display indications of heavenly virtues, because we could know nothing about that majesty unless something concerning it appeared to us through worldly likenesses.

Therefore let us explain the latter part of this verse first, so that the preceding names may shine forth more clearly. The holy body of the Lord is recognized as a kind of garment of the Godhead. For just as the limbs of mortals are covered by clothing, so the majesty of the Word seemed hidden from the eyes of unbelievers by the veil of flesh.

Accordingly, myrrh, drop, and cassia are suitably said to have come from this garment—that is, from the mystery of the incarnation.

Myrrh signifies the death which he accepted for the salvation of humanity.

The drop, which is called ammoniac, cures hardnesses contracted from some necessity. It is beautifully compared with the Lord’s incarnation because, through holy preaching, it dissolves the hardness of the human heart.

Cassia, which our people call *fistula*, signifies the redemption of the human race through the water of baptism, since this kind of plant is said to be found in watery places.

These things also possess a sweet fragrance, so that both the power of the herbs and the sweetness of their scent may rightly be compared with the holy incarnation, as the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “We will run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song of Songs 1:3).

#### Verse 10

“From ivory houses, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor.”

In the fourth mode, praise of Christ is taken from the person of the Bride. The prophet says from where comes the Bride’s most glorious beauty, she who stands stationed at the Lord’s right hand: namely, from ivory houses, which signifies decorated palaces clothed with abundant ivory.

Let us not understand ivory as referring only to wealth. The elephant, whose bones it is, is said to possess extraordinary chastity: among four-footed animals it is especially intelligent, mates temperately with its female, and does not use a second consort. This is suitably applied to chaste women, since those are known to have dwelt in ivory houses who followed the commandments of Christ the Lord through chastity.

The most learned Fathers Augustine and Jerome approved this interpretation.

“From which they have delighted you” means that they did not run to you by their own judgment, but were led to you by your delight.

“The daughters of kings” may mean either faithful men who rule their bodies and bring forth daughters generated through holy baptism, or rulers themselves. It frequently happens that, abandoning the rule of a palace, the offspring of princes choose divine service.

He therefore added “in your honor” to designate a religious mind by such an indication. They were not delighted in the honor of their fathers, but in the honor of the Lord the Savior.

#### Verse 11

“The Queen stood at your right hand in a gilded garment, clothed all around with variety.”

Everything is described through a marvelous account. This figure is called *characterismos*, which in Latin, as we have often said, is called “description” or “depiction.” It presents before the eyes of the understanding things that are not seen with bodily sight.

First the Bridegroom’s beauty was praised; afterward his power was asserted; third, his throne and authority were recounted. Since nuptial joy was being celebrated, forms of the sweetest fragrance were introduced through mystical interpretations.

Fourth, the source of the Queen’s own wondrous beauty is described. Then she is placed at the divine right hand, adorned with precious virtues, so that every faithful soul, stretched out toward heavenly contemplation, may behold its heavenly vows and know what reverence it ought to show her on earth, since it understands her to be so honored in heaven.

She is the Queen who says in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1), along with the other things that the text expresses through mystical riddles.

Consider also that above he praised the throne of the Lord the Savior; here, however, he says that the Queen stood at his right hand, because the right hand is the honorable side of the Bridegroom, who is acknowledged to be the head of the Church.

It follows: “in a gilded garment.” We should apply gold to the splendor of charity, by which virtue the holy Church shines when surrounded. And lest you understand that charity alone is present there, he said “in a gilded garment,” not “a golden garment.” We call something “gilded” when a layer of gold’s appearance is fastened onto some material.

Charity appears above the other virtues because its radiance surpasses them all.

He added: “clothed all around with variety.” Let us investigate why the Church of God is praised for the variety of its clothing, although simplicity and unity suit it in every respect.

Here, “variety” signifies either many languages, because every nation sings praise to its author in the Church according to its own homeland, or the most beautiful diversity of virtues. The Church is adorned with the gold of the apostles, the silver of the prophets, the gems of virgins, the scarlet of martyrs, and the purple of penitents.

This, then, is the variety of unity, woven together from all nations to please the Lord through devout conduct.

#### Verse 12

“Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house.”

After the Bridegroom’s praise has been sung, the praises of the Bride are now offered in as many modes, but much more modestly and humbly. It was fitting not to leave unpraised, even in a secondary place, one who had been deemed worthy to rejoice in such a great union.

The first mode of this praise is “from appearance,” as the following verse makes clear.

Let us now come to the words. To her standing at the Lord’s right hand, where the place of the blessed is, he says: “Hear”—that is, hear the prophets, who sang of the Lord’s incarnation in a true promise—so that she might believe what she heard and soon see what she believed.

The prophet rightly calls her “daughter,” because the Christian people were generated through her holy proclamations.

“And see” should be said with rejoicing, because the Bridegroom who was promised to you has arrived; in him are your love, glory, and joy.

It follows: “incline your ear.” This was necessary for the Church to do, so that she might receive the prophets’ words with honor.

“Forget your people,” he said—that is, abandon them and make the gatherings of the pagans, or the utterly insane superstitions of the Jews, alien to your mind.

He signifies the Babylonian house, which delights in its most wicked inhabitants against the Church of Christ and, possessing the mind of the confused multitude in this world, claims for itself a share of the lost.

“Your father” means the devil, who is truly recognized to possess that house of confusion according to the interpretation of his name.

But consider that the Church then dwelt there when she did not yet possess the grace of the heavenly Bridegroom; hence she is also read to have been dark. She was then suffused with the splendid adornment of beauty when the Lord deigned to choose her from among the nations.

#### Verse 13

“For the King has desired your beauty, because he himself is your Lord and God; and they will worship him.”

This is the mode of praise that we said above was “from appearance.” This King, then, is the Lord the Savior, who desired the Church, established through the guilt of transgression in the devil’s lot. He himself made her most beautiful; he did not find her so.

She was foul when the invader held her; she became beautiful when she returned to her creator. Concerning her it is written: “Who is this who ascends, made white?” (Song of Songs 8:5).

Consider that this Bride is praised with a similar beginning to that used above concerning the Bridegroom: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.” But he is said to possess a unique beauty in his own appearance; she is beautiful because the Bridegroom joined her to himself.

Thus everything is said distinctly and variously, although the Bride herself is praised in the same lines.

It follows: “because he himself is your Lord and God.” Not the one whom you used to call father, nor the one who had made you dark, but this one is your Lord and God. Removing your former foulness, he bestowed nuptial beauty upon you.

A saving sentence is also added: “and they will worship him”—that is, all the peoples who, through their own gathering, made you the holy Church. They will worship not you but the Lord, because your honor is in him, and your blessedness is his everlasting glory.

#### Verse 14

“The daughters of Tyre will entreat your face with gifts; all the rich of the people.”

He comes to the second mode, in which he said above concerning the Bridegroom: “Press forward, prosper, and reign.” Here, however, the dignity of the Church is that devoted peoples supplicate the Lord; and just as the Bridegroom’s power is described there, so here the glory of the Bride is made clear through Christ’s honor.

Tyre is a city situated not far from Jerusalem. But by the name “daughters” of this city, he prefers to signify the souls of the faithful. For Tyre alone did not produce faithful daughters; rather, the united diversity of the whole world did so. Therefore this figure is called “from the part, the whole” (*a parte totum*).

The daughters of the nations entreat the face of the Church with gifts when they distribute alms with devout intention. These are the gifts that are especially pleasing to the Godhead.

We look toward the face of the Church—that is, toward the face of the Christian people—when we beseech the majesty of Christ with devout tears.

“All the rich of the people” must be joined to what precedes, so that the passage forms a *hyperbaton*, that is, an inversion or transposition: “The daughters of Tyre—all who are rich among the people—will entreat your face with gifts.” The order is explained by reversing the arrangement of the words.

#### Verse 15

“All the glory of the daughter of the King is within; she is clothed around with golden borders and variety.” [Col. 0326B]

You see how he persists in proclaiming the Church. The glory of the Church is present when the daughters of princes—or of the righteous—are converted to the Lord and desire to offer themselves in the secret devotion of their hearts.

“Within” signifies the hidden places of the senses, not the noise of the lips: the place where the inner person silently turns over in thought what is known to pertain to the divine mysteries. Thus it is also said of the Church in the Song of Songs: “The King brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs 2:4).

Count this expression, “the daughters of the King within,” among the proper expressions of divine law; you will not find it in ordinary usage [edition: “common”].

It follows: “clothed around with golden borders and variety.” Borders are the edges of garments, gathered in the warp and hanging down like crops of hair. Through them the final state of human life is signified.

She is not said to be gilded, as above, but is now declared to be golden, because all perfection is at the end, where charity is not seen as merely gilded but is found already completely full, like gold.

“Clothed around with variety” refers to the various virtues of the faithful, which, as is clear, were explained above. Since she is clothed in these diversities, it is necessary that the catholic Church be dressed in a multicolored garment.

This was also signified by that garment of Aaron, which was woven from gold, purple, fine linen, scarlet, and hyacinth.

#### Verse 16

“Virgins will be brought to the King after her; her companions will be brought to you.”

Just as the Bridegroom was proclaimed thirdly from judgment, so here, in the third place, the Bride is praised through her members.

Observe how powerfully he preserves the order: “Virgins will be brought to the King after her”—after the Church, certainly—because it was first necessary to speak of her unity, and afterward to present a distinct enumeration of her parts.

Notice also that he said “will be brought,” so that the grace of the Lord might be declared, for it is his grace that brings us to him when he looks upon us in mercy, as it is said in the Gospel: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John 6:44).

But which virgins are brought before the Lord’s sight? The faithful, naturally, who conduct themselves with chaste minds. For what benefit is it for someone to preserve an untouched body if she happens not to possess integrity of faith?

It follows: “her companions will be brought to you.” “To you” is said to God.

Her companions are those close to the Church: chaste widows, who are joined at a lower rank. For while virginity possesses the hundredfold fruit, these women glory in a sixtyfold abundance.

Observe that there is no small distinction in the names themselves. He says that virgins are “brought,” since they are strong in bodily integrity; widows are “carried,” since they are often weakened by various cares and wearied by bodily frailty.

#### Verse 17

“With joy and exultation they will be brought into the temple of the King.”

To show that abundant gifts are to be bestowed upon the holy Church, he says that she will be brought with the ministries of the angels in joy and exultation—not only into the presence of the King, but also into his inner chambers, that is, into Jerusalem, where blessed joy and glorious security are found.

It was therefore rightly said, “they will be brought with joy and exultation,” because that fragile sex conquered the gravest sufferings of the body.

### Verse 18

“For your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth.”

He has come to the fourth mode, in which it was described above that the Church had come from the ivory steps and stood adorned at the King’s right hand. Now it is powerfully explained how greatly this Bride has advanced: in place of the ancient fathers—that is, the worshipers of idols—sons have been born to her, namely the apostles, whom he sent throughout the whole world as princes of preaching. But to the extent that these things differ, to that extent the Church is praised. The former were deceivers of error; the latter, teachers of truth. The former sowed destruction; the latter exhorted people to life. O praise worthy of such great joy: how blessed was it to flee the embrace of the enemy and find the marriage of the Thunderer! This passage is rightly called “praise from offspring,” since here holy posterity is proclaimed.

### Verse 19

“They will remember your name throughout every generation and lineage; therefore peoples will confess to you forever and unto the age of the age.”

By “they will remember,” he means the Christian peoples, who in her preachings persevere with devout intentions through the various generations of humanity. What wondrous glory, and what supreme praise: amid such manifold successions of human beings, never to receive an end to praise! It follows: “therefore peoples will confess to you.” For every Christian, after professing the sacraments of the creed, confesses in the presence of the Church; and this confession is eternal, because it is true and devout. For what he added, “unto the age of the age,” signifies the future, when every adversity comes to rest and justice alone reigns, the opposition of the devil having been destroyed.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Behold, the glorious epithalamium of the psalmist has been completed in exultation. Behold, the praise of the Bridegroom and the Bride has been celebrated in wondrous variety: spiritual union, marriage continuing in virginal purity, chaste love, eternal charity, a bond dissolved by no end. Here the holy drums of the prophets resound in exultation; here the instruments of the apostles respond in sweetest fellowship; here the lyres of the martyrs sing not with strings but with virtues; here the choir of the saints delights the ear most pleasingly with spiritual pipes; here such music is performed that all human joy is surpassed.

We have been fed, O good King, drawing heavenly delights from the wedding feast. Grant us, wondrous Bridegroom, that we who have rejoiced here in hope may in the future be filled with perfect joy. Blessed Jerome also treated this psalm, writing to the virgin Principia (Epistle 140), with marvelous brilliance, as is his custom. We have therefore thought that he ought to be mentioned, so that whatever may perhaps have been explained less fully by us might be supplemented by the explanations of that most learned man.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 45

**For the end; for the sons of Korah, a psalm concerning hidden things.**

“With regard to the end,” it is known how this can be referred to the Lord Jesus Christ. We say that the sons of Korah signify Christians, from whose person this psalm is sung. “Concerning hidden things,” however, signifies the advent of the Lord the Savior, which he arranged, through the wondrous secret of his divinity, for the salvation of human beings.

### Division of the Psalm

The sons of Korah, who are to be understood as the faithful Christians, first declare in the opening section of the psalm that they do not fear the disturbances of the world, because God is proved to be their refuge and strength. Secondly, they say that Christ appears in the midst of his Church, which he deigned to build in himself as upon the most solid rock. Thirdly, the multitude of believers in general is invited to behold the mighty works of God: they say that the almighty God breaks the weapons of wickedness, removes wars, and changes the sadness of the faithful into eternal joys.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Our God is refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations that have found us exceedingly.”

At the very beginning of the psalm, a categorical syllogism delights us. For he says: “In the tribulations that have found us exceedingly, our God is refuge, strength, and helper.” “In tribulations we will not fear when the earth is disturbed.” Therefore, in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly, we will not fear when the earth is disturbed.

Let us now examine the statements one by one. What a beautiful and concise formulation! It is as though they were asked, “What is our God?” They answer: “Refuge, strength, and helper.” This is the fifth kind of definition, which in Greek is called κατὰ τὴν λέξιν (“according to the wording”) and in Latin *ad verbum* (“word for word”): whenever we show by individual words what each thing is.

“Noster”—“our”—has been added on account of the most false Christians, whose God is not accustomed to be their refuge. Refuge, therefore, belongs to the faithful when he frees them from danger to their soul. Strength belongs to them when he steadfastly guards their minds from the wicked error of the world. It follows: “a helper in tribulations.” Here the mercy of the heavenly majesty is expressed through various definitions: in tribulations it both receives and defends us. Tribulation, however, makes God merciful toward us, releases guilt, and then especially comes to our aid when he recognizes that we wish to trust in him, as the Apostle says: “For the sorrow that is according to God produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

And lest you should consider these tribulations light, he added, “that have found us exceedingly,” so that you would understand that nothing mediocre was meant, but something you would recognize as excessive. The dangers are suitably magnified so that their all-powerful destroyer might appear.

#### Verse 2

“Therefore we will not fear while the earth is disturbed, and the mountains are transferred into the heart of the sea.”

That time of the tribulation foretold above is explained here: when, at the advent of the Lord the Savior, the hearts of the Jews were troubled by the novelty of so great a miracle, the holy men who trusted in his name and power could not fear.

It follows: “and the mountains will be transferred into the heart of the sea.” This certainly happened when the mountains—that is, the apostles—left the unbelieving Jews and passed into the heart of the sea, that is, to preach to the Gentiles, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you; but because you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

From this example we understand that those mountains, towering with devout summit and most firm in the solidity of faith, were transferred into the heart of the sea, that is, to the faith of all nations. It should also be observed that he compared the faithlessness of the Jews to dry land, but the belief of the Gentiles to salt waters, so that you might recognize those hearts as hardened for evil, while you might rightly judge these to have been seasoned with evangelical salt. For the sea does not have a heart; human beings do.

#### Verse 3

“The waters of them roared [editorial reading: *sonuerunt*, ‘resounded’], and were troubled; the mountains were troubled by his strength.”

He remains with the preceding sense. For the disturbance caused by the advent of the Lord Christ is still being explained. He says that the apostles’ preachings roared, like the strongest voice of some crash, which resounded not so much in ears as in minds. At that time he asserts that the waters were troubled—that is, the innumerable nations of this world, which had been terrified by amazement at such a thing.

This figure is called *parabole*, that is, comparison, when we associate things differing in kind through a qualitative comparison. Yet one must observe that this has been said through the beauty of a most splendid comparison. For waters are then disturbed by great confusion when the mass of constructed things is thrown down into the sea’s depths; and they produce a great sound when the streams have been struck by a great weight. This indeed happened when the whole world trembled at the apostles’ resounding preaching and afterward returned to belief in the Lord with a heart cleansed.

It follows: “The mountains were troubled by his strength.” Here he means other mountains, that is, the powers of the world. For mountains are understood both in a good and in an evil sense. The mountains of God are stable and beautiful; the mountains of the devil are changeable and squalid. The worldly powers were troubled when pagan rulers brought sacrilegious laws against the religion of God.

#### Verse 4

“The river’s rushing stream makes glad the city of God; the Most High sanctified his tabernacle.”

Above he spoke of the terrors that the world received from the new preaching. Now the benefits bestowed upon the Church through the advent of the Lord the Savior are proclaimed, so that the change of meaning may rightly have received the division of the *diapsalma*.

Consider what is said and with what distinct precision it has been expressed. The city of God, gladdened by the river’s rushing stream, came to rest. And so that you might recognize this river as one that irrigates souls, he does not say that it satisfied the city but that it made it glad. This is the river of which Truth itself says: “Whoever believes in me will never thirst, but in him there will be a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:13–14).

And he rightly said, “the river’s rushing stream,” because its course tolerates nothing marshy and nothing sluggish when the power of Divinity has poured itself in. It is added: “The Most High sanctified his tabernacle.” The tabernacle of the Most High is either the Church or the glorious reception of the human heart; both are plainly shown to have been sanctified when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).

#### Verse 5

“God is in her midst; she will not be shaken. God will help her with his countenance.”

God is not said to be in her midst as though he were enclosed within the extent of some place. He is enclosed by no space, since he is wholly everywhere, not with unequal but with equal benevolence. He is therefore said to be in the midst because he always attends to the faithful. Accordingly, God is rightly said to be in the midst of the Church according to his justice, because he regards all with equal will; and no one will be deprived of his sight except the one who has made himself alien from him.

“She will not be shaken” is said of the Church, to which that singular promise was given: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). The Church cannot be shaken because it is known to have been founded upon the most solid rock, that is, the Lord Christ.

It follows: “God will help her with his countenance,” that is, with the presence of his incarnation, when his saving countenance shone forth. For he said “will help,” that is, the Church laboring under worldly adversity.

#### Verse 6

“The nations were troubled, and the kingdoms were bowed down; the Most High gave his voice, and the earth was moved.”

The nations were indeed troubled when, although they were wholly devoted to idols, they suddenly heard the rules of a religion unknown to them. The operation of many miracles converted many; the terror of the judgment preached afflicted many; and although they were being led toward the good, they could not help having a troubled mind.

It follows: “and the kingdoms were bowed down,” that is, they were humbled for worship, not for falling, because each person is raised up to the degree that he is bent in that submission.

He added: “The Most High gave his voice, and the earth was moved.” He did not say that he brought forth his voice, but that he gave it, as a wondrous gift and as a reward-bearing benefit. By “voice” he means the holy preaching which the almighty Teacher, both through himself and through the apostles, made resound throughout the whole world with thunderous power. Sinners who heard the terrible commands of the eternal Judge necessarily trembled at it.

#### Verse 7

“The Lord of hosts is with us; our protector is the God of Jacob.”

What omnipotent Christ is, namely “the Lord of hosts,” is briefly explained: he whom the heavenly powers serve, whom every power obeys. Hear, you hard-hearted; hear, you senseless. Why do you wish to perish utterly, presuming to sin against such majesty?

It follows: “with us,” because, having assumed flesh, he dwelt on earth. It is added: “Our protector is the God of Jacob.” He is a protector because he deigns to apply his power to the infirmities of others. Properly, the God of all is called our God and our protector when he assumed flesh for the salvation of the faithful. For “our” is rightly said by the children of the cross, because he is the protector only of those who have deserved to come to his faith.

The phrase “the God of Jacob” should be understood to mean that he will bestow upon those who believe well as much as he also granted to Jacob. For he is not the God of Jacob alone, but of all who are devoted with similar faith.

#### Verse 8

“Come and see the works of the Lord, who placed wonders upon the earth.”

After the interposed *diapsalma*, he comes to the third section, where he invites the peoples to see the mighty works of the Lord the Savior, which he performed through the wondrous dispensation of his incarnation.

When he says “come,” he urges them to draw near to the Lord in faith, whom they could not see as distant. For when he added “the works of the Lord,” the whole world is summoned to some great spectacle. Therefore let us approach with eager spirit, because by seeing such things in faith we conceive those realities that lead us to everlasting joys.

“He placed” means that he set down certain signs, so that the world, beholding them, might hasten toward the remedies of its salvation. A *prodigium*, “wonder,” is so called because it points forward: through certain signs the disclosure of a coming novelty is made known. This occurred at the Lord’s birth, when the Virgin gave birth, the star appeared to the Magi, and the choir of angels proclaimed the birth of their Lord.

#### Verse 9

“Removing wars to the ends of the earth.”

Behold, those works of the Lord that had been promised have been proclaimed; and so great a promise must explain some great hidden reality. Rebellion against God occurred when the Gentiles worshiped carved images through various superstitions. These images, together with their worshipers, fell at the Lord’s advent.

Therefore he removed the wars of faith to the ends of the earth—wars that were waged throughout the whole world—and restored those to his peace to whom he granted the gifts of true religion. Or this may be understood according to historical truth, since it is read that at the Lord’s birth, while Augustus was reigning, the world was at peace. This is shown to have been accomplished not by human strength but by the bodily presence of Christ the Lord.

#### Verse 10

“He will shatter the bow, break the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.”

The bows are the ambushes of unbelievers; they will be shattered by the power of truth when their insane desires are reduced to nothing. Here the weapons signify the superstitious contests of pagans; they are rightly said to be broken when they are overcome by the struggle of the faithful. The shields signify the defenses of the faithless; these are burned up in the fire of heaven for the liberation of humanity.

But this soldier is the devil, for whose salvation the bow is shattered, the weapons broken, and the shields consumed in fire. For he could not otherwise have escaped unless he had lost the defenses he thought were his. Or, as some maintain, everything that has been said can refer to incentives to vices.

Strip from us, good King, the devil’s weapons, by which we are not defended but burdened; and gird us with that spiritual sword which may bring us both salvation and protection.

#### Verse 11

“Be still, and see that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, and I will be exalted on the earth.”

The sons of Korah, carried along by the spirit of prophecy amid their own words, proclaim this verse in the person of the Lord. This figure is called *apostrophe*, in Latin “conversion,” when by a sudden change we turn to another subject.

It is rightly said to those who were armed with worldly illusions and were carrying out the devil’s warfare in a destructive struggle: “Be still.” They could not hear unless, having laid down their wicked weapons, they gathered with quiet and restful minds for saving instruction.

For he says: “I am God”—not the one who armed you, not the one who led you into abominable struggles, but “I am God, who will be exalted among the nations,” whose religion is true and whose exaltation is not fragile.

And lest you should perhaps think that he was to be exalted only among certain nations and not also among the Jewish people, whom he compared above to the earth, he added: “and I will be exalted on the earth,” that is, among the Jewish people. As the Apostle promises: “For I say to you, do not be wise in your own eyes, because a partial hardening has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25).

You therefore see the Lord exalted and to be exalted both among the Gentiles and among the Jewish nation.

#### Verse 12

“The Lord of hosts is with us; our protector is the God of Jacob.”

The sons of Korah return to their own persons, and the psalm receives a beautiful conclusion through the repetition of the verse. They repeat this profession a second time so that through it they might declare that liberation has been granted to us. The title “God of Jacob” is added frequently so that the victory of the Christian people might be declared: although later in time, it nevertheless surpasses the first people in faithful devotion.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us contemplate the text of this psalm, brief in words but not in powers. For the number itself also reveals great mysteries to us. In a mystical interpretation, we read that the Lord’s temple at Jerusalem was completed in the forty-sixth year. These years, however, were used by the ancients for days; multiplied by the number perfected six times, they produce 276 days, the length of time our Lord is shown to have dwelt in the virginal womb in the likeness of the human race—that is, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April to the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

Thus the whole psalm is rightly understood as spoken especially about the Lord, since its number also aptly corresponds, in the manner described above, to the mystery of his conception and birth.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 46

**A psalm for the end, for the sons of Korah.**

All the names in this title have indeed been retained and explained. But always attend carefully, diligent reader, so that you may understand the meanings of these names as suited to the subjects of the psalms. For if you examine the text of the psalm more attentively, you will discover that not one of them can be without significance.

Accordingly, it happens that sometimes the diversity and sometimes the similarity of the titles appears to direct our attention to the Lord the Savior. When they are diverse, they relieve weariness; when they are one, they consolidate the sharpness of our understanding with steadfast firmness. Thus both are known to be beneficial, since the whole arrangement is established for the salvation of all.

The sons of Korah also speak in this psalm; the mother who marks them with the banner of the cross is the Church.

### Division of the Psalm

Although this whole hymn is sung in the person of the sons of Korah and is compressed into very pleasing brevity, it is nevertheless divided by the interposition of a *diapsalma*.

First, the nations are admonished to make praises resound for the Lord, because he subjected all things to the people of his possession and, as a merciful Judge, placed them in his inheritance. Secondly, the Lord’s ascent and his kingdom are described briefly; the saints will likewise possess these without end.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“All nations, clap your hands; shout joyfully to God with a voice of exultation.”

Since it is customary for revelers to make music by striking their hands and, for the delight of their ears, to express through them a kind of melody without the service of speech, we must understand this clapping spiritually, in the manner that the children of the cross were able to describe and that we ought to hear.

Those who give alms clap their hands; those who serve the sick out of compassion clap their hands; those who carry out some commandment through honorable actions clap their hands; and so does anyone who performs some similar act that can pertain to the Lord’s grace.

To shout joyfully (*jubilare*) is to rejoice. The word is said to derive from *juvare*, “to help,” that is, “to delight,” when we express our joy not in articulated speech but with an inarticulate voice.

And lest we remain attached only to such joys, he added, “with a voice of exultation,” signifying the psalmody that is offered to God in accordance with the majesty of his name. He most perfectly admonishes us to let the hands perform God’s praise in such a way that the human tongue does not remain silent about his glory. For it is fitting that the tongue should sing the commands of its Lord and the hands should perform them.

#### Verse 2

“For God is most high and fearful, a great King over all the earth.”

He gives the reasons why the Lord ought both to be applauded and to be praised with joyful shouting. This figure is called *epexegesis*, that is, an explanation of the preceding statement.

First, because God is most high. Fearful, because he himself will judge the world. A great King, because he is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16). He is the one of whom it was written in the title of the Passion: “King of the Jews” (Matthew 27:37).

It is true that he was their King, but he is also the King of all nations, because he is the Creator and Administrator of all things. Therefore, lest he be thought to have been only the King of the Jews, he says that he is King of all the lands.

Let the Jews recognize that the Lord’s power extends far beyond their narrow confines, and let them not cease to worship the one whose dominion they hear is everywhere.

#### Verse 3

“He subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet.”

This pertains to all Christians who have deserved to possess divine grace. “Peoples” and “nations” signify those who are known to lurk outside the Church. For all are spiritually subject to the righteous, since they cannot equal their merits.

But we must understand this more spiritually, lest any arrogance—God forbid—appear to affect holy men. “Feet” signify the most holy preachings, to which the peoples were rightly said to be subject, being held bound by their rules, as the prophet Isaiah says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Isaiah 52:7).

#### Verse 4

“He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved.”

“ He chose for us” should be understood as “to give,” so that the one who had come to save the Israelite people might grant this even more generously to the Gentiles in pious largesse.

It is necessary to recall this comparison so that the truth of the matter may be recognized more clearly. Esau, attracted by the delight [editorial reading: *vanitate*, “vanity”] of bodily food, asked his brother Jacob for lentils (Genesis 25:30). Jacob replied that this would be done if Esau would yield to him the glory of the firstborn.

That eager seeker of earthly things surrendered his honor. As a result, Jacob, through a fortunate exchange, offered the carnal so that he might obtain the spiritual. This is the beauty of Jacob, which the Lord loved exceedingly, wishing his faithful servants to do the same things that Jacob foreshadowed as worthy of pursuit through mystical meaning.

Thus we are truly called Christians if, while offering earthly things, we seek heavenly ones.

#### Verse 5

“God ascended with joyful shouting; the Lord with the sound of the trumpet.”

The sons of Korah come to the second section, where they celebrate with devout praise that time when the Lord’s ascension was seen with bodily eyes in glorious reality.

It is said to have been “with joyful shouting” because the apostles, amazed, were filled with inexpressible joy of heart at such a miracle; their blessed eyes were granted the sight of the Lord the Savior going to heaven.

We have said that joyful shouting is an exceedingly great joy, but one that cannot be explained in words. “The sound of the trumpet” signifies the words of the angels, which rang out with great noise, like the crash of air struck by a blow. For then, when the apostles were amazed at such a vision, the angels said to them: “Men of Galilee, why do you marvel? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11). Thus the world might believe more firmly what was proclaimed by such heralds.

#### Verse 6

“Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises.”

It is not without significance that this expression is repeated so many times. We recognize how useful and saving the work is which he wished to repeat with such frequent reiteration. This figure is called *epembasis*, whenever words are repeated to enhance beauty.

To sing praises is to sing praises to God through good actions. If this is properly carried out, it is shown to be something we share even with the angels, who continually celebrate God’s proclamations with spiritual exultation.

It follows: “Sing praises to our King, sing praises.” By “our King” he means Christ the Lord, not some alien king to whom this praise might be due, because he alone rightly receives praises, since he both creates all things and continually governs what he has created.

#### Verse 7

“For God is King of all the earth; sing praises wisely.”

This is said against those who made different deities for themselves in different places: Venus at Paphos, Mars in Thrace, Jupiter in Crete. The omnipotent King must be worshiped universally, since he alone is proved to be the Creator and Liberator of all.

He added, “sing praises wisely,” so that we should sing praises not only by chanting but also with understanding. No one does anything wisely that he does not understand.

#### Verse 8

“God has reigned over all the nations; God sits upon his holy throne.”

The sons of Korah have come to the perpetual happiness of the future age, where they now say that the Lord will reign over the nations. For although he also reigns over all now, he is then properly said to reign when he is shown to dwell more manifestly in his faithful ones.

“Over all the nations” designates the heavenly Jerusalem, which is gathered from all nations. It follows: “God sits upon his holy throne.” This signifies the Lord the Savior, who sits at the right hand of the Father and reigns forever and ever.

Observe that he calls the throne itself holy, so that you would not understand it as something senseless or devoid of reason, but as the powers and thrones upon which that glorious Ruler sits. This can also be understood of the saints. For if anyone possesses the benefit of a good way of life, he too undoubtedly becomes a royal seat.

If you direct your attention more deeply, the whole passage is spoken against the faithless, so that, hearing of his power, they may submit—those who think his humanity is to be despised.

#### Verse 9

“The princes of the peoples have gathered with the God of Abraham.”

“The princes of the peoples” means the leading men of various nations, of whom the beginning of the psalm sings: “All nations, clap your hands.”

“They have gathered,” as though he were saying, “they have believed.” To gather means for many to come to one place. “With the God of Abraham” means with Christ, who is the God of Abraham.

After the unbelieving Jews were expelled—those who were sons of Abraham only in the flesh, not in their deeds—he admitted the fullness of the nations to possess the blessedness of the promise that he had made to Abraham and his seed. They became his sons through holy faith, although they were not sons by the seed of the flesh.

#### Verse 10

“For the strong gods of the earth have been greatly [manuscripts A, B, F: ‘exceedingly’] exalted.”

This sense depends upon the preceding verse. The princes of the peoples gathered with the God of Abraham because the strong ones of the earth, who were the people of God, have been greatly exalted—that is, the Jews, to whom power among the nations had been given, rose up against God and swelled with a criminal mind. Through pride they became last, although through humility they could have been foremost.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us contemplate the text of this psalm, which is brief in words but not in powers. The number itself also declares great mysteries to us. For in a mystical interpretation, we read that the Lord’s temple at Jerusalem was completed in the forty-sixth year.

These years were used by the ancients for days; multiplied by the number perfected six times, they produce 276 days, the amount of time our Lord is shown to have dwelt in the virginal womb in the likeness of the human race—that is, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April to the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

Therefore the whole psalm is rightly understood as spoken especially about the Lord, since its number also corresponds suitably, in the manner stated above, to the mystery of his conception and birth.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 47

**A song-psalm for the sons of Korah, for the second Sabbath.**

We placed the explanation of “song-psalm” in the preface. “The sons of Korah” has likewise been discussed frequently. Now let us see what “the second Sabbath” signifies.

We must understand the Sabbath as the synagogue, that is, the assembly of the Jews, which appeared to observe the Sabbath. The second, however, is its Catholic Church. Therefore the words of this psalm are attributed to priests for the instruction of Christian peoples. There is no doubt that these can be regarded as the children of the cross, and we recognize by clear reasoning that they are second in time after the synagogue.

### Division of the Psalm

Since a devout people had to be instructed concerning the faith and the preservation of the ranks of the Church, the words of this psalm are rightly given to pious priests. In the first section they praise the Lord because he has extended his Church and shown the power of his majesty to all the kings of the earth. In the second they give thanks for the advent of the Lord the Savior, admonishing future bishops to distribute the ranks within the Church through which the Lord God and Savior may be recognized, who guards his servants with eternal protection.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1
