“Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.”

We must consider how these words ascend through definite stages of wondrous arrangement. This figure is called *emphasis*.

First he said, “Great is the Lord”; “worthy of praise” was added. But lest you should think that this too was to be done moderately, he adds “exceedingly,” which has neither limit nor end but continually increases through its own persistence.

He is great because he made all things powerfully. He is worthy of praise because he made beautiful and wondrous things. Yet it is not enough to say that the Lord the Father is exceedingly worthy of praise unless they also state where he is to be proclaimed: namely, “in the city of our God,” that is, in the Catholic Church.

For there is also a city that is not the city of our God, such as that Babylon of the devil, where God is not worshiped but rather blasphemed with most accursed madness. Therefore it was necessary to state where the Lord was to be praised, lest anyone think that he should be proclaimed amid heretical superstitions or in the ancient synagogue.

But lest you doubt where the Church in question had been established, he added, “on his holy mountain.” The holy mountain is Christ the Lord, the foundation and summit of his Church. This is the holy mountain of which the prophet Daniel says: “The stone grew and became a mountain, so that it filled the whole face of the earth” (Daniel 2:35).

Let us consider that here he calls the Lord the Father great, but the Son is not left unmentioned as great also. Concerning him the Apostle writes to Titus: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13).

The Holy Spirit is also read to be great, as it is written in the Book of Kings. The Lord says to Elijah: “Behold, the Lord will pass by, and a great and powerful spirit” (1 Kings 19:11).

Let the insane persuasion of the Arians be ashamed. Who, I ask, is lesser, when the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are all read to be great?

#### Verse 2

“Extending the joys of the whole earth, Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King.”

Lest you should have understood the mountain mentioned above as a local one, he says that it grants joys to the whole earth. For who is this mountain except the Lord Christ, who has been able to extend beneficial joys throughout the universal Church of the world?

Here understand “earth” in a good sense. It signifies the righteous, who receive abundant and eternal rewards. Mount Zion, as has often been said, designates the Church, which is fulfilled through the power of holy contemplation, in keeping with the interpretation of its name.

The sides of the north signify the unbelieving peoples among whom the devil’s iniquity reigned. For he himself said: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13).

But because sinners, who had been held subject to the devil, were converted through God’s mercy, now Mount Zion and the sides of the north—that is, the nation of the Jews and the peoples of the Gentiles—have become “the city of the great King,” that is, the Catholic Church, which is known to have been gathered from the whole world.

This is the second Sabbath referred to by the title. Earthly rulers are indeed called kings, but no one can truthfully be called the great King except God alone.

When he said “Mount Zion” and added “the sides of the north, the city of the great King,” the figure is *exergasia*: that is, whenever something is proposed briefly and then explained subtly and at greater length.

#### Verse 3

“God will be recognized in her ranks when he receives her.”

The future time of that great judgment is shown, when the Lord receives his Church and is himself recognized in her ranks—that is, in her most holy and approved members.

Then God will be recognized: that is, his power and strength will be declared, when the Church is shown, by his gift, to offer him blessed men. The holy people will be placed at the right hand according to the degrees of their merits, as the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:42).

Then she is received into eternal blessedness, when perpetual joys are granted to her. There God is recognized: that is, his power and strength are declared, when he grants his Church such rewards, distinguished according to ranks, that they never decay or come to an end. Here it is believed; there it is bestowed in manifest vision.

#### Verse 4

“For behold, the kings of the earth have gathered, and have come together as one.”

These are the sides of the north that he mentioned above. Although they came with minds conspiring against God, many of them are nevertheless known to have believed.

The kings of the earth here signify the rulers of the Jews, whom Herod gathered together and asked where Christ the Lord was to be born. They answered appropriately and unanimously, according to the Holy Scriptures, that he would certainly be born in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:5).

They gathered, therefore, in order to say what they had read. They came together as one because they all gave one answer.

### Verse 5

“They themselves, when they saw, were amazed, were troubled, and were shaken.” “They themselves” means the Jews, of course, who told Herod that the Lord would be born in Bethlehem. For they had seen what they had read as having been prophesied [ed., “in the prophet”]; and it was necessary that amazement should arise from such great glory. But this amazement was neither slight nor idle. They were troubled because they knew themselves to be sinners. They were shaken because they had been deemed worthy to learn of such great majesty. For we call those “shaken” whom we also testify to have believed.

[Col. 0338B]

### Verse 6

“Trembling seized them there: pains like those of a woman in labor.” The order of events has been preserved most beautifully. First it is said that they saw, afterward that they were amazed, then that they were troubled, and finally that they were shaken by trembling. For it is vehement fear itself that brings people to trembling; the mind must necessarily be deeply agitated when the body has been seized by trembling. Nor was this alone sufficient in so great a matter; repentance immediately followed, when pains torment them like women in labor. For grievous is the pain that is imposed upon women as punishment for sin. But since we have heard of women in labor, let us suppose that a fruit is to be born from this through humble confession.

### Verse 7

“With a vehement spirit you will shatter the ships of Tarshish.”

[Col. 0338C]

The event of the Lord’s birth itself is being explained. For, as some have wished to say, there was a vehement spirit (Matt. II, 8) when Herod, anxious about his kingdom, had sent the Magi to see the king who had been born and to report to him what they had learned. But when they did not return to him, he necessarily was stirred by a vehement spirit and shattered the ships of Tarsus in Cilicia, which were believed secretly to have transported the aforementioned Magi into their province. This is what kings who bring false accusations are accustomed to do: whenever they cannot fulfill their desires, they rage through the losses and sufferings of the humble. Consider how greatly this narrative has grown—from what beginning it started and to what summit it has reached.

### Verse 8

“As we have heard, so also have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God.”

When everything that took place at the birth of the Lord and Savior has been traversed, a fitting conclusion follows: it was seen to have happened just as it had previously been prophesied. The words “so also” carefully express the truth of the events, because everything was established as having happened just as it had been promised. “In the city of the Lord of hosts” has been added because there both the truth is heard and every promise is seen. “In the city of our God” is repeated so that you might understand it to mean the Catholic Church alone, lest assemblies of heretics also claim this name for themselves.

[Col. 0338D]

### Verse 9

“God founded it forever.”

Lest you should have understood this city of God as temporal, he says that the Church, which alone is truly called the city of the Lord, has been established forever. Let Christians rejoice and celebrate with the exultation of their whole mind when they hear that it was founded by the Lord, in which they do not doubt that they can stand firmly. For although they are shaken by the storm of this age, what is shown to be transitory is rightly not feared, as the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

[Col. 0339A]

### Verse 10

“We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.”

The devout priests have come to the second part, where they exult with great joy of heart. “We have received” should not be understood generally, because not everyone believed; rather, it applies only to Catholics who followed his commands. They call the Lord Christ “mercy,” because he had pity on the world that had strayed beyond the bounds; and he wished to be seen for this purpose alone: so that every believer might be absolved. The name is appropriate and the promise certain, since the one who is truly called Savior and Redeemer is called “mercy.”

“In the midst of your temple”: they wish the synagogue to be understood, to which he had come in order to set it free. But because that people did not believe, the nations who were called received the gifts of mercy. “In the midst of the temple” was said so that the wickedness of those who did not believe might be more gravely reproved: they refused to follow the one whom it is clear had been seen in their midst.

[Col. 0339B]

### Verse 11

“According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth; your right hand is full of justice.”

The name of God is unquestionably believed to be worthy of worship throughout the whole world. Some may not know how he should be worshiped, yet there is no one who does not consider himself subject to this name. Thus they say: Just as reverence for your name is spread throughout the whole world, so also devotion offers you praise in the Church, which extends throughout the entire world.

It follows: “Your right hand is full of justice.” He indicates the place where these people are to be situated; for all who attain eternal rewards come to his right hand. His right hand, therefore, is full of justice, because those who have deserved to be righteous by his gift are received into that part.

[Col. 0339C]

### Verse 12

“Let Mount Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult, because of your judgments, O Lord.”

By Mount Zion the Catholic Church is signified, which is understood to have been established in contemplation of the people according to the interpretation of its very name. She is desired to rejoice because by his gift she will possess eternal joys.

“Daughters of Judah” designates all holy women. Through Judah the race of righteous women is shown, because the Lord Christ descended from that tribe through the propagation of his flesh. They ask these women also to exult, so that they might show that the Lord’s Church would rejoice in both sexes. They add, “because of your judgments, O Lord.” This itself is the great cause of joy: that they should exult because of the Lord’s judgments, where they recognize that they will come to eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0339D]

### Verse 13

“Surround Zion and embrace her; tell it in her towers.”

After the devout priests have admonished both sexes, they come to the ecclesiastical orders, which surround the house of God with loving devotion. “Surround” pertains to the honors that are to be offered; “embrace” pertains to charity, which embraces the Lord’s name in the bosom of the heart. “Tell it in her towers” has been added so that those who serve the holy orders should not cease from religious discourse.

And because the Church is the city of God, towers are appropriately fitted to it there—that is, heights and defenses against heretical enemies. But because they were persuading unbelievers who remained outside the Church to listen, they say that preaching should take place not from houses or porticoes, but from lofty towers, from which the outsider people might be able to hear.

[Col. 0340A]

### Verse 14

“Set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her ranks, so that you may recount them to another generation.”

Lest the souls of the faithful, on hearing of joy and exultation, should grow slack through some relaxation, they say that hearts must be placed in the Church’s strength—that is, in charity, than which nothing can be more excellent in strength. As the Apostle teaches: “Faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII, 13).

He distributes the ranks of the Church who arranges her offices in a distinct order. For in her there are readers, subdeacons, deacons, presbyters, and bishops; and although the Church is one, she contains offices distinguished by a variety of dignities. The devout priests therefore admonish that these ranks ought to be distributed, so that through them the mighty works of the Lord may be preached to another generation.

“Another generation” signifies the Christian people, who are recognized as second after the Hebrew people whom the Lord first chose.

[Col. 0340B]

### Verse 15

“For this is God, our God forever and unto the age of the age; he himself will rule us forever.”

[Col. 0340C]

This is what they wished to recount to the faithful people through the ecclesiastical orders, as is done today. The statement is indeed brief, but it embraces everything: “This is God, our God” signifies Christ, pointing him out with the finger as though he were present.

This figure is called *idea*, in Latin *species*—“form”—when, by presenting something future as though before our eyes, we stir the movement of the mind. Here “this” is an articulating pronoun, which is used when someone is indicated with an outstretched hand. For the one who is pointed out here is the one who also wished to appear to bodily eyes. Concerning him the prophet Baruch likewise says: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him” (Baruch III, 36).

It follows: “Forever and unto the age of the age.” This must be said against those who foolishly dreamed that temporal men were gods for themselves—Mars, Mercury, Saturn, and the rest, which ought rather to be called monstrosities than divinities. Therefore the Lord Christ must be proclaimed as immortal, everlasting, supremely powerful without end, for he continually protects and defends those who believe in him.

It continues: “And he himself will rule us forever.” He will indeed rule us, because Christ is properly and truly called our King. “Forever” signifies without end, because those whom he has received to govern—provided, of course, that they do not depart from him—he guards in glorious perpetuity.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Paternal and priestly words have resounded for us, so that, struck from every side, we may deserve to be led onto the straight path. How great is your care, good King, for human beings, upon whom you deign to pour such manifold medicine through your commands! You do not wish to say only once what you do not permit humanity to ignore. From every side you admonish; from every side you teach; and you make our faith cry out through the persons introduced, so that the place of ignorance may seem to have been utterly cut away. The holy Job rightly says: “What shall I do to you, O guardian of men?” (Job VII, 20). You admonish us concerning what we ought to seek; you grant what we do not know we can deserve.

# Exposition of Psalm XLVIII

## For the End; a Psalm for the Sons of Korah

The words of this title, as has often been said, refer everything to the Lord Savior. For he is signified by “the end,” understood through the sons of the cross, and is without doubt proclaimed through the psalm; so that we may rightly understand that the voice of the one is to come whose luminous discourse is promised by so many indications.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the entire psalm are the words of the almighty Son. In the first section he says what he will speak or accomplish for the faithful at the time of his incarnation. In the second he recalls what great things are to come upon the foolish and senseless. In the third he says what will follow for the righteous and the wicked. In the fourth he admonishes the faithful not to fear the rich of the earth, because they leave all their power behind with the light.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Hear these things, all nations; perceive them with your ears, all who inhabit the world.”

The whole human race is admonished to come indiscriminately to listen, because God is good without respect of persons; he does not wish to benefit only a few while neglecting, under a pretense of concealment, others who nevertheless seek him with a pure heart. Moreover, since such a mystery of the Lord’s incarnation ought to be heard by the whole world and not by anyone less than the whole world, a universal benefit plainly demanded a universal hearing.

It follows: “Perceive with your ears, all who inhabit the world.” Here they are already more earnestly admonished to grasp the words with the greatest devotion and to store them in the recesses of their memory. By “nations” let us understand pagans; by “inhabitants of the world,” Christians and the righteous, who know that the earth must be inhabited in such a way that they do not become entangled in its wicked errors.

And consider the good teacher, how he stirred everyone’s eagerness to listen, so that the one who did not wish to profit for himself might himself be held guilty. Rhetoricians transfer this device to their own discipline: they make judges attentive when they promise to say something new or extraordinary.

[Col. 0341D]

### Verse 2

“And you who are earthborn, and sons of men; together in one, rich and poor.”

The Lord continues in the same eagerness, so that an assembly of everyone who should listen might be formed, lest anyone think that he was going to say something ordinary. The earthborn should be understood as sinners who pursue earthly vices. These are rightly counted among the portion of Adam, the first man, because he is declared to have been not a son of man but the first man himself.

Opposed to this is what he said, “sons of men.” By this expression we ought to recognize the righteous, who come into the lot of Christ, since Christ himself is also proclaimed to be the Son of man. And remember that he is always set against Adam—rightly so, since what was lost through that one was saved when this one came.

It follows: “Together in one, rich and poor.” Behold, the sentence promised above has shone forth. For it is said of Christ the Lord: “Together in one, rich and poor”—rich because he is God, poor because he is human—as the Apostle says: “Remember the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who for your sake became poor, though he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (II Cor. VIII, 9). The promises are therefore rightly so great, since such important and salutary words follow.

This is a brief explanation of the preceding words. “Rich” pertains to the earthborn, because he is shown to be wealthy in numerous sins; “poor” refers to the sons of men, because they are poor in the life [ed., “ambition”] of this age, so that they may fully obtain future riches, as the Gospel says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3).

[Col. 0342A]

### Verse 3

“My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding.”

He develops what he began above: he will speak not human but divine wisdom and understanding—that is, the Lord Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24). Solomon likewise bears witness (Prov. I, 2) to knowing wisdom and instruction and understanding words of prudence.

Wisdom pertains to the declaration of divine mysteries; understanding, to the instruction of worthy conduct. Thus every divine discourse is shown to be completely filled with these two virtues. From this point he began what he was going to narrate, first describing his words with a marvelous combination, so that everyone might eagerly seek what they sensed was being promised under such a proclamation.

[Col. 0342C]

### Verse 4

“I will incline my ear in likeness; I will open my proposition on the psaltery.”

After the true preacher had said that the power of his eloquence was contained in two distinguished qualities, he now promised that he would incline his ear, so that he might know whether the devoted people were fulfilling his preaching and how his commands could be received by the human race. But observe that the pious teacher used the word “likeness.” A likeness is an imitation of a true thing, so that what has been given to us as an example we may perform through devoted emulation, with the Lord’s help.

But so that the most serene instructor might invite everyone to fulfill his commands for salvation, he said that he would open his proposition on the psaltery—that is, he would declare the commands of the Divinity through the holiness of his own body, so that he might be proved to teach by example rather than merely by word. For the psaltery, as we have often said, is a fitting likeness of the Lord’s body; just as the psaltery sounds from above, so the Lord’s incarnation celebrates the heavenly commandments.

[Col. 0342D]

### Verse 5

“Why should I fear on the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me.”

This verse is to be read as a question followed by its own answer, because he says that everything that was going to happen would occur without his fear. This figure is called *peusis* and *apocrisis*—“question and answer”—when an appropriate response follows a preceding question.

For he says, “Why should I fear?” That is, “Why should I be confounded by fearful thought?” “On the evil day,” namely, on the day of the Passion, which was evil for the Jews but good for the faithful. The one who should fear the end of life is the one who is tormented by the recollection of sins. But Christ could not fear death, since he had no sins whatsoever.

He says: “Why should I fear on the evil day? Will the iniquity of my heel surround me?”—as commonly happens to a sinner, whose end is closed by a wicked conclusion. Others, however, because of the excellence of the holy incarnation, have said that this should rather be understood from the perspective of his members.

[Col. 0343A]

### Verse 6

“Those who trust in their strength, and those who glory in the abundance of their riches.”

These words depend on the preceding verse, to which they should be joined: such people are surrounded by the iniquity of the heel. For they presume upon their own strength, those who seem to trust in some ability—those strong in bodily power, preeminent in strength of mind, and distinguished by eloquence of tongue.

But after he spoke of inward attributes, he now comes to riches, which come from outside and by which humanity is especially inflated. For rarely does a rich person understand that he shares the same lot with the poor. And such people must fear the end, since they are unwilling to leave worldly things and, with conscience as their witness, fear the punishments of their sins.

[Col. 0343B]

### Verse 7

“A brother does not redeem! Will a human being redeem? He will not give God his propitiation.”

After speaking of sinners, whose iniquity surrounds the heel, he comes to an outstanding form of healing. This too must be read with astonishment: “A brother does not redeem!” That is, the Lord Christ, who said in the Gospel: “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matt. XXVIII, 10), and in the psalm: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. XXI, 23).

If he does not redeem—the one who shed precious blood—will a human being redeem, that is, Adam, who wounded the human race through the fault of transgression? “He will not give” belongs to the language of denial, because no offering and no propitiation can compensate for what the Divinity has deigned to redeem in us.

[Col. 0343C]

### Verse 8

“Nor the price of the redemption of his soul; and he will labor forever.”

The first part of this verse refers in meaning to the preceding statement: the human being who has been liberated will not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul. For a price is the compensation of some thing. But what can a human being give as a price, when he has received everything that he could offer?

It follows: “And he will labor forever.” He has spoken of the faithful, who, although they cannot give the price of the redemption of their soul, nevertheless labor forever, while they do what benefits them for the rewards of eternal life.

[Col. 0343D]

### Verse 9

“And he will live to the end, because he will not see destruction.”

He is still speaking of those who labor forever. They, living at the end—that is, in the Lord Savior—will not see destruction, because although they die in the body, they have been enriched with the gift of eternal life.

Others judge that these verses should be applied to sinners, saying that “they labor forever”—those who are to be condemned to perpetual punishment—and that they “will live in this world at the end,” luxuriating in their freedom when all hope has been abandoned. Therefore it will be for readers to choose what they will follow. We, however, have understood that what has been said up to this point concerns the faithful. Now let us hear what great things the faithless will suffer.

[Col. 0344A]

### Verse 10

“When he sees the wise dying, together the senseless and the fool will perish, and they will leave their riches to strangers.”

He comes to the second mode of teaching, where he says that sinners will perish together with the wise of this world and that their riches, which they loved so greatly, will have to be left not to their own people but, more painfully, to foreign successors. Thus, for the sake of which they had committed every sin, they would rejoice neither in possessing those riches nor in having their own successor, as Solomon says: “In the things in which they sinned, they could not even rejoice” [ed., “hide”] (Wis. X, 8).

“When he sees”: the sinner sees, of course, that the wise men of this age are not freed from destruction, such as Solon of Athens, Philo of Lacedaemon, Aristippus, and the others who flourished with the most celebrated praise of worldly wisdom. He sees those whom he considered participants in divine Wisdom dying in common with all.

It follows: “Together the senseless and the fool will perish.” The senseless and the fool must perish in despair when they have learned that their own wise men have perished. But so that we may understand these things more spiritually, the senseless are those who refused to obey the preaching of the prophets; fools are rightly called those who did not even wish to receive the Lord Christ when he came. These, therefore, will perish together, since they are to be condemned in the future judgment.

But the Jews left their riches to strangers, because, while they despised the Lord Savior, the rewards of their salvation passed to foreign nations.

[Col. 0344C]

### Verse 11

“And their tombs are their houses forever; their dwelling places are for generation and offspring; they will invoke their names in their own lands.”

The pomp of dying rich men is described: they build tombs for themselves, designed with great effort and refinement. We see certain mausoleums gleaming with the most beautiful marble, so that they may be considered eternal houses constructed with massive structures.

After this he comes to their dwelling places, which are supported by abundant generosity, so that they may be carried through successive generations and descendants with enduring beauty. He also adds the rite that paganism customarily performs at funerals, when in foolish superstition they invoke the names of the dead in their lands—that is, in their tombs—and believe that this benefits the dead, since they appear to be honoring their memory.

[Col. 0344D]

### Verse 12

“And a human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”

He is still speaking of those who flourished in the honor of this world. For although a sinner is in honor while he lives, because he bears the image of God, he is rightly said not to understand his dignity when he does things that appear wholly opposed to the Creator himself.

It follows: “He was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.” A fitting likeness is given to the foolish, so that those who do not understand that they bear the image of God may appropriately be compared with senseless beasts. For when they do not display the reason they have received through the Lord’s commands and instructions, they have rightly lost it as unworthy of so great a gift. Take away from a human being the consideration of God, and he is altogether a senseless animal—vain presumption and transitory pride.

But although it is said of mortals, “And a human being, when he was in honor, did not understand,” the transgressing angels who were cast from heaven may also be understood here, because they too did not understand their honor when they were shown to have grown proud against their Creator. “Human being” is also used for the devil, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel (Matt. XIII, 25): “The enemy who sowed the weeds over it is the devil.”

This is the tenth species of definition, which the Greeks call *hōs typō* (ὡς τύπῳ), while the Latins call it *veluti*—“as it were”—when the characterization of something is such that it appears applicable not only to the one thing about which it is said but also to others, as has already been read in the thirty-fifth psalm: “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. XXXV, 7). For the Lord is accustomed to save not only these but also the rest.

[Col. 0345A]

### Verse 13

“This is their way, a stumbling-block to them; and afterward they will bless with their mouth.”

Here the preceding enumerations are gathered together into one heap, like scattered grains. After what has been said, it is declared in summary: “This is their way.” We ought to understand “way” as the life in which we walk through this age by the traces of our deeds.

But what this way does to the wicked is not concealed: it is a stumbling-block to its authors—that is, a goad and a pain. For a sinner achieves nothing for his own security when he is tormented by the result of his own action.

It follows: “And afterward they will bless with their mouth.” Here the custom of sinners is described. After they have fulfilled the desire of their wicked intention, they immediately give thanks to the Divinity, because they have been brought to what they wanted. Miserable people that they are, they do not know that it is by that author alone that one reaches holy desires. But they will bless with the mouth, not with the heart; hence the sentence is usually feigned, as Isaiah says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX, 13).

[Col. 0345C]

### Verse 14

“Like sheep they have been placed in hell, and death will feed upon them; and the righteous will rule over them in the morning.”

He comes to the third section, where he says that recompense is to be given to the righteous and the wicked according to their merits. For eternal death feeds upon sinners placed in hell. Just as sheep continue perpetually through the loss of their wool, so in those people it always finds, without diminution of their substance, something for punishment to torment.

“For death will feed upon them” is drawn from beasts, which do not tear up grasses by the roots but rather cut off their upper portions.

It follows: “And the righteous will rule over them in the morning.” “Will rule over them” means “will surpass them,” which will certainly take place in the resurrection of the blessed, so that they may rise above the wicked. In this life the righteous are ruled by sinners; in that judgment, however, the righteous will surpass the faithless in every way.

“In the morning,” as though he were saying, “on the dawning day, when the glory of the resurrection has shone forth,” when the radiance of blessedness is already revealed and the day begins that is ended by no night.

[Col. 0346A]

### Verse 15

“And their help will grow old in hell, and they have been expelled from their glory.”

He continues to describe the unhappiness and misery of sinners, whose helps grow old like rotten rags. For what will riches provide for the dead? What will human presumption provide for the departed, who lose everything in which they delighted here and arrive at eternal punishments that they never believed they would suffer?

It follows: “And they have been expelled from their glory”—from the world in which they gloried, or from those things in which, deceived by an unhappy lot, they presumptuously trusted. As it was said in the Gospel to the rich man: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and whose will the things be that you have prepared?” (Luke XII, 20).

[Col. 0346B]

### Verse 16

“Nevertheless, God will free my soul from the hand of hell, when he receives me.”

After the errors of sinners have been explained, the Savior’s statement is rightly introduced, so that just as human frailty has been cast down by terror, it may rise again, lifted up by hope of a future reward.

Whether the Lord Christ says this about himself or, as is customary, speaks from the perspective of his members, it is suitable. For in descending he freed his own soul from hell, and at the same time the souls of those who steadfastly believed in his coming. By “the hand of hell” he means the power of the devil, who before his coming held souls subject to him.

### Verse 17

“Do not fear when a human being has become rich, and when the glory of his house has been multiplied.”

The fourth part of the psalm proceeds from the mouth of Truth, so that a most salutary medicine may be supplied to us. For this is the one complaint of the whole world: Why do people flourish in this age whom we know to be alienated from the worship of the Lord?

But these things have been promised to sinners. Therefore the pious teacher addresses true Christians, so that they may not fear the rich of the earth, since wealth is rightly feared in general when the desire of human beings to serve it is taken into account. “Rich” is derived from *divus*, “divine,” because a rich person is thought to need nothing, as though he were a god.

Here we ought to understand an impious person, who makes himself frightening to those subject to him while he disregards the laws of equity.

It follows: “And when the glory of his house has been multiplied.” Join this with “do not fear.” This figure is called *apo koinou* (ἀπὸ κοινοῦ), that is, “from what is common,” when the preceding words correspond to those that follow.

And observe with what purpose everything advances. It would have been less to become rich, since you frequently find this among merchants and among lowly people. He added: “And when the glory of his house has been multiplied”—that is, when he has been celebrated with honors, possessions, and the praise of all people, so that he thinks nothing is lacking to him except sole dominion.

And see that he said “his house,” so that not only he himself but also all who belong to him may appear to flourish in great pomp. But why such people should not be feared follows beautifully.

[Col. 0346D]

### Verse 18

“For when he dies, he will not take [ed., ‘they will perish’] all these things, nor will the glory of his house descend with him.”

Here the reason is given why the glorious man of this world should not be feared. Why should we fear a rich man who dies poor? Our stumbling-block is not everlasting for him, nor can he carry anything else with him except that from which he may burn.

How deformed you will see him in that homeland whom here you admire as most splendid in precious clothing. And he rightly said that dead sinners descend as though into deep abysses, as though into the deepest pit—but without worldly glory, without a crowd of attendants, without the presumption of treasures. That house which you admired remains entirely behind; but it sends forward immense burdens that you did not see.

[Col. 0347A]

### Verse 19

“For his soul will be blessed in his life; he will confess to you when you have done good to him.”

Here “will be blessed” does not refer to obtaining sanctification but to the favorable voices of those who indulge themselves. He will be blessed, it is said, because of the speech of his attendants, who amid chatter and banquets are accustomed to wish their patrons well; his soul is praised not for a good deed but because of the preparation of luxuries.

It follows: “He will confess to you when you have done good to him.” The wicked bless God when they receive temporal goods; but the good person praises the Lord even when weighed down by a burden of evils, as Job and his other saints did.

It is therefore said to the Father: “This sinner will confess to you—but only when you have done good to him.” What if he suffers something contrary? He does not cease to blaspheme. And therefore this custom, which is found frequently among the wicked, must be avoided.

Let us, however, praise the Lord with a devout heart at all times, for he always works our salvation both in adversity and in prosperity.

[Col. 0347B]

### Verse 20

“He will enter into the generation of his fathers; forever he will not see the light.”

Those who imitate the worst fathers are to be condemned in their company; and therefore he says that sinners have entered into the generation of their fathers. He called them their fathers not so much because of the seed of the flesh as because of those whom they followed in imitation of their conduct, as he says in the Gospel to unbelievers: “You are from your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

He added: “Forever he will not see the light,” because just as sins are dark, so they take away the light of wisdom from sinners. And therefore he said, “forever he will not see the light,” since he was not enlightened even in this world, whose harmful heart the darkness of error possessed.

In the same way, he will not see the light forever, because here he did not deserve to possess it through the fault of his perversity. The true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John I, 9), is the Lord Christ, whom only the saints are able to see in his Divinity.

[Col. 0347C]

### Verse 21

“And a human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them.”

After he had given prior notice of everything that had to be said, he concluded this most beautiful psalm with a repetition of the verse in equal form, so that the sinner might remove himself from his evil purpose when, through repeated rebuke, he recognized his marked deformity.

[Col. 0347D]

## Conclusion of the Psalm

The psalm should be read very often and stored in the treasury of memory, since at its beginning it admonishes us to hear with the ears of the heart. It itself has testified to the merit of the one who urged it to be heard diligently by all parts of the world. It contains everything that belongs to contemplative and moral discipline, just as that verse promised: “My mouth will speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding.”

Holy Truth has fulfilled for us what it promised. May it now make sweet to our senses and cause to cling within us what it commands.

[Col. 0348A]

# Exposition of Psalm XLIX

## A Psalm of Asaph

Asaph was the son of Barachiel, who is read about in Chronicles as having been chosen among the four masters of the singers, so that he might sound the psalms to the Lord on musical instruments (I Chron. VI, 39). He deserved to be included in this title because of the meaning of his name—not as the author of the psalm, as has also been written concerning others, but as an outstanding musician who might indicate something to us through his name.

For the meaning of this name, which among the Hebrews is always full of mysteries, signifies the Synagogue that speaks in this psalm. But here we must understand that faithful Synagogue of the Lord which both believed in the Christ who was to come and received his coming with glorious expectation. Its members included the patriarchs, the prophets, Nathanael, the apostles themselves, and the others who believed with sincere devotion.

It must be clearly understood that this psalm prophesies both the first and the second coming of the Lord, although the ninety-fifth and ninety-seventh psalms are also known to proclaim the same things. Thus every excuse is completely removed from unbelieving Jews, since they do not accept what the Synagogue itself also bears witness to. What, I ask, do they worship if they even refuse to listen to the very thing they claim to venerate?

[Col. 0348B]

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0348C]

In the first section the faithful Synagogue speaks—now present among Christian peoples—about the first and second coming of the Lord Christ. In the following section Christ himself, the King, speaks, admonishing the peoples that, having abandoned sacrifices of cattle, they ought to offer a sacrifice of praise. In the third section the devout Synagogue mentioned above speaks again, charging sinners with their wickedness.

## Exposition of the Psalm

[The supplied source ends here.]

### Verse 1

“God of gods, the Lord has spoken, and has summoned the earth, from the rising of the sun to its setting.”

So that no one might regard the Lord’s incarnation as something to be measured by an ordinary standard, his power is proclaimed beforehand, so that every perverse unbelief might be removed. Human beings are called “gods” when, through upright conduct, they receive the grace of the heavenly Majesty, as he says in another psalm: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81:6). Thus they are called sons, just as they are called gods, because both titles are granted by grace, not by nature.

Christ the Lord, however, is God of gods. For he, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is truly called God of gods. Yet this name is not wholly proper to divinity; human language, as we have already said, cannot indicate his supreme height beyond this. For in the Greek language God is called “fear,” and because he alone is to be feared, such a word has come to stand in place of his name. For it is read in Exodus: “I have not made my name Adonai known to them” (Exodus 6:3), so that we may understand this to be a secret name, which was not made known even to the chosen servants.

He therefore spoke through the prophets, through the apostles, and—what is more powerful—through himself. It follows: “and he summoned the earth.” Here we must understand “earth” as the human race, which is seen to be spread throughout the whole world. But because the dwelling place is intended, the inhabited thing is named. For how could he have summoned what was unable to hear? This figure is called metonymy, when what is contained is declared through that which contains it.

He added: “from the rising of the sun to its setting.” By the course of the sun he signifies the whole world, because its brightness rises and sets over every land. This is what the advent of the holy incarnation accomplished: the merciful Physician invited all nations, wounded by corrupt errors, to the remedies of faith, as he himself said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

### Verse 2

“From Zion, the perfection of his beauty.”

Jerusalem is signified here, within which city this mountain shines like a mass of gold to pure minds. For from this city the apostles went forth and proclaimed the beauty of Christ throughout the whole world, as Isaiah says: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3).

Venerable city, holy summit: we may rightly call it the distinguished dwelling of our King, the citadel of the earth. And observe how appropriately we are instructed. In the preceding verse he had said that Christ the Lord calls all nations forth; now he also indicates from where his teaching flowed, like a stream from the purest and most abundant spring, across the regions of the whole world.

The evangelical words agree with this statement: “to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47). From there Christ began to be preached, whose beautiful appearance is known, as another psalm bears witness: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3). There it has been sufficiently explained why he is specially called beautiful.

### Verse 3

“God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not keep silent. Fire will burn before him, and around him a mighty storm.”

After the faithful Synagogue had said much about the first advent, it comes to the second advent of the Lord and Savior, which it describes figuratively through various comparisons and with marvelous imagination, so that he appears not so much as one who will come as one who is already present.

By saying “he will come manifestly,” it indicates that he was not manifest to everyone in his first advent, because his majesty was concealed beneath the cloud of flesh, as the Apostle says concerning unbelievers: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). But he will then come manifestly, when he will no longer be fastened to the cross but will judge the world.

The expression is drawn from sacrifices, for the whole day was devoted to a festival. “Manifestly” is said as though from “a festive day beginning in the morning.” He repeats “our God,” lest unbelievers think that he is a common god to them. The God of Christians is himself the God of gods, who will come manifestly and will not keep silent.

He is now silent while this world is being completed: while he does not condemn blasphemous and sacrilegious voices with the severity of judgment, but patiently endures sinners so that they may be healed by conversion. Then he will not keep silent, when he says to the wicked: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). Hence elsewhere he also says: “I was silent, I was silent; shall I always be silent?” (Isaiah 42:14).

As for what follows—“fire will burn before him”—the glorious advent of the great Judge is described, as has been said, through a mystical image. Fire is said to go before him, so that whoever is straw may fear that he will be burned.

He added: “and around him a mighty storm.” This storm is not driven by winds, nor raised by raging tempests. Rather, a vehement spirit will arise through divine power, so that the Lord’s threshing floor may be winnowed by the sentence of his justice. Then he will separate the grain from the chaff—that is, he will distinguish the good from the ungodly.

This judgment is rightly called a storm, because it will come unexpectedly and will sweep people with extreme speed into its reckoning. “Mighty” is also appropriately added, for its power is shown by the fact that it will distinguish every kind of human being according to their merits with instantaneous speed, as the Apostle says: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

The phrase “around him a mighty storm” is also fittingly understood because the righteous will sit with him and, as the Gospel promises, will judge.

### Verse 4

“He will summon heaven above, and the earth, to judge his people.”

Certainly this is what he will do in that judgment. Yet perhaps “earth” is reasonably said to have been summoned upward, since it is now known to be established in a lower place. But since heaven is above, where did he summon it upward?

Here “heaven” must be understood as every righteous person, and “earth” as the sinner. The former purifies himself through a spiritual way of life, by the Lord’s favor; the latter is stained by the earthly quality of vices.

Observe that at the first advent he had summoned everyone without distinction, so that, being admonished, they might correct themselves in this world, as the Gospel says: “And they went out to the roads and summoned everyone whom they found, both good and bad” (Matthew 22:10). At the end of the world, however, he summons heaven so that he may then distinguish the righteous from the ungodly, lest they continue, as here, to be mixed together in confused dwellings.

### Verse 5

“Gather his holy ones to him, those who establish his covenant above sacrifices.”

Here the Synagogue speaks the words of Christ to the angels, who, in their ministry, will gather the holy ones from the whole world at the end of the age, as is written. For the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “He will send his angels, and they will gather all nations before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats” (Matthew 25:32).

It follows: “those who establish his covenant above sacrifices.” We say that those establish the covenant who restore through good deeds what they have learned in the text of the covenant: receiving the stranger, giving alms, and devoting themselves to love. For it is established that the Lord values this above the sacrifice of animals, so that the goodness of deeds may be offered to him instead.

Or, as some have wished, this may also be understood ironically of the Jews—that is, by way of mockery, when something contemptible is reproved through praise—as though he were saying: “Gather to the Lord those who remain in the practice of holiness,” while, on the contrary, they do impious things; and because they celebrate the sacrifices customary to God, they judge themselves worthy to be sanctified.

### Verse 6

“And the heavens will proclaim his righteousness, for God is judge.”

He develops the preceding interpretation, signifying righteous men by “the heavens,” upon whom the dispensation of the heavenly word is bestowed. He added, “for God is judge,” as though he were saying: he cannot be deceived; and just as he knows all things openly, so he distinguishes them without error.

This is truly and properly said of God, from whom nothing is concealed or withheld, from whom no deed is hidden, and from whom nothing that is judged can be concealed.

### Verse 7

“Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you: I am God, your God.”

We have reached the second section, in which Truth itself now speaks in its own person. God does not wish his words to be received in vain, lest, as it is written, swine scatter precious things. Therefore he says to the people: “Hear,” that is, receive my words devotedly.

We call those people hearers who fulfill the commandments, as it is written: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8). “My people” signifies the devoted community.

“And I will speak”—understand, things that will be beneficial. If you do not listen, then, to your destruction, I will be silent.

We have often said that “Israel” is interpreted as “seeing God.” Therefore, if you see me, do not neglect to hear, because contemplation of me grants obedience to the one who hears.

To testify is to give testimony. God will certainly do this in the judgment, when he distinguishes the deeds of each person. Then he will give testimony to his faithful, when he says: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matthew 25:35), and similar words to them.

It follows: “I am God, your God.” This was what he had earnestly warned the people to hear: that the universal God of both the willing and the unwilling might be especially the God of the one who loved him with a pure mind. For when he says “your,” he shows that the person was faithful to him.

The repetition “God, God” strengthens the mind, so that the words once spoken might not slip away.

The expression “I am” is the proper word of divinity. It is not changed by time, but is always present and remains eternal, as Moses was told: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14); and again: “He who is has sent me.”

But we must examine why God alone claims this name of being for himself. At the time when this was said, angels existed, heavenly things existed, and all earthly things existed, just as they had been decreed to exist. But because only God is the uncreated and eternal nature, which never began in time, and because the one divinity subsists in three persons, he alone is rightly said to be. For in order to exist he needs nothing, but always stands through the strength of his own power.

There is also another mystery here: one syllable is contained in three letters, so that the holy Trinity may be taught to be one God.

### Verse 8

“I will not rebuke you on account of your sacrifices; but your burnt offerings are always before me.”

The glorious teacher and perfect instructor, wishing to draw the Jewish people away from carnal things and lead them to spiritual mysteries, now says that sacrifices of animals are no longer to be sought. He testifies that the people cannot henceforth be rebuked if they do not sacrifice animal victims. Rather, he recalls that burnt offerings are to be given before him—those which are offered upon holy altars with a humbled heart.

Burnt offerings were sacrifices which, after being slaughtered, were consumed by fire coming down from above; in Latin they are called *tota incensa*, “wholly burned.” Christ rejected these when he came, because he himself was the true victim.

There is another kind of burnt offering, which the Lord declares to be always before him: namely, when our mind, kindled by divine love, purifies its sins through tribulation and, after the likeness of that burnt offering, consumes all its vices by bodily suffering.

### Verse 9

“I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.”

Through this verse and the two that follow, he briefly lists what he declares that he rejects. This figure is called *brachylogia*, that is, brief expression, when many things are embraced in a few words.

But lest the human mind, on hearing of a burnt offering, return to the ancient sacrifices, he openly rejects the former custom, so that what was represented in the preceding likeness might be understood spiritually. When he rejects these two things, he signifies that all the sacrifices of the former age are to be excluded in every way. The whole is signified by a part.

### Verse 10

“For all the wild beasts of the forests are mine, the animals upon the mountains, and the cattle.”

He gives the reason why he does not expect the slaughter of four-footed animals from the people, saying: “I do not wish to ask from you what I know to be mine.” Perhaps a poor person does not possess an animal, either because he was unable to catch one or because he could scarcely feed it. But God asks for right faith and devoted confession, which all can offer by his mercy, even those who possess no earthly property.

The same meaning continues through the remaining enumerations. He added “the animals upon the mountains, and the cattle,” lest anyone, relying upon his possessions, devote less attention to his conscience, believing that he could atone for what he had done with an evil mind by sacrificing animals.

The passage may also be understood in another way. “The wild beasts of the forests” signify the nations that lived amid the woods of this age in the most savage superstition. “The animals upon the mountains” are the simple people established in the Catholic Church, who are known to dwell upon the summit of faith. “The cattle” indicate the apostles and prophets, who labored continually in the Lord’s field.

Thus, through these appropriately placed allusions, he prefigures the Catholic Church, which was to be gathered from the various regions of the world.

### Verse 11

“I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me.”

Do not interpret “I know” according to our weakness, by which someone knows something in time when an opportunity presents itself. The Lord knew everything before he made it, and in his presence was everything that could ever exist.

For who can know all the birds of heaven except the Majesty alone? In this verse he has embraced everything, since he knows all the birds of heaven by their number.

He professes that he possesses the beauty of the field with him—truly with him, because he is wholly everywhere, as the prophet says of him: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24).

But we must treat these things spiritually. The birds of heaven refer to the higher and wondrous powers, such as the angelic authorities, which are spiritually carried by swift movement in accordance with the holy will.

“The beauty of the field” refers to the nations that were to believe in Christ the Lord—truly “beauty,” because through the human being all the beauty of the earth is aptly understood.

### Verse 12

“If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world and its fullness are mine.”

The God of gods, as we have often said, deigns to express his will through human customs for the sake of our understanding. Thus he says that he is hungry, although he nourishes all flesh; the contemplation of spiritual substances is his sweetest food and contemplative refreshment.

It follows: “for the world and its fullness are mine.” Here, having supplied the reason, he rebukes needless curiosity by saying: Why should I ask you for sacrifices of animals when the whole world is known to be mine?

“Its fullness” signifies the diversity of created things. Let human beings therefore cease their needless concern with contemplating the slaughter of animals. The Godhead prefers that we offer it a right heart, by which one is also known to have sinned, so that what was formerly made foul by sins may become utterly pure through saving cleansing.

And remember that through these allusions he signifies the number of the predestined, which is to be completed not from the Jewish Synagogue alone but from all nations.

### Verse 13

“Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?”

In how many ways he deigns to give the reason for his will! How can things that are unnecessary be pleasing? Does God feed on the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?

Yet these rejected things can benefit us when the needy receive them—when the hungry are fed and the thirsty are given drink. In the poor God receives what he does not permit to be offered to him in sacrifices.

### Verse 14

“Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.”

Up to this point he has said what he rejects; now he says what he requests. The statement is narrow in words, but in meaning it is shown to be exceedingly broad.

For who offers a sacrifice of praise except one who has been separated from earthly vices, who dies to the world so as to become a victim for Christ? The Lord is not pleased if an unworthy person sings his praises. He seeks a deed worthy of approval, not a melodious voice.

Let us therefore sacrifice to the Lord by praising the wisdom with which he orders all things, the mercy with which he spares sinners, and the strength with which he conquers the devil.

A sacrifice is not to be understood only as the slaughter of animals, but as every sacred deed by which a devout offering commends us. The one who prepares and offers such things to the Most High as he himself, in his favor, commands also fulfills vows to him.

He added “your,” so that you would not perhaps seek something external—a fat goat, the blood of calves, and other things which rational understanding recognizes as existing outside us. “Your” refers instead to the secret place of the heart, which lies in the inner chambers of the soul, which is not sought outside, and which the poor and the rich possess equally.

There the richer person is more needy; there the one who is known to be humbled in heart is much higher.

Let us also consider this carefully, and we shall find here a kind of distinctive expression which ordinary eloquence cannot possess. God says: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you”; and shortly afterward, without changing persons, that same speaker says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise”; then he adds: “But to the sinner God said.”

The order of our ordinary speech would have required him to say: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you,” and so forth; “offer me a sacrifice of praise”; and “to the sinner he said: Why do you recount my righteousness?” Thus one and the same speaker, speaking about himself, appears to introduce the person of another. This is rightly counted among the distinctive features of divine Scripture.

### Verse 15

“And call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.”

After saying by what sacrifice he is pleased, he now promises the reward of that offering. He commands: “Call upon me,” so that no one may place his hope in earthly assistance, where everything is perishable and comforts are even more fragile.

“In the day of your tribulation” means when another afflicts you, not when you are stung by having escaped an enemy. Our tribulation is that which arises from fear for our own salvation, not that which is shaken by fear of bodily things, as the Apostle says: “Godly sorrow produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, but the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

“I will deliver you”: as though you were surrounded by the devil’s attendants, I will free you with the greatest speed.

“And you will glorify me”: you will declare me great for eternity, since I free you from punishment and place you in blessed rest.

Some wish to apply this verse, richly filled with an immense promise, to the final moment of our life, when the soul, passing from this light, is troubled by the conflict of unclean spirits, just as it is read that they opposed the soul [Editorial reading: “body”] of Moses.

See how little the Lord asks from us, when he is prepared to grant such immense things.

### Verse 16

“But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses, and take my covenant upon your lips?”

We have come to the third section, where Asaph—that is, the devoted Synagogue—speaks again.

Since the Lord had said above that he could receive human praise in place of sacrifices, sinners might perhaps rely upon this promise and say: “Only praise, and not a commendable action, is known to have been commanded of us.” He therefore explains the matter with necessary reasoning, forbidding their tongues to presume to sing praise to God when an evil conscience could oppose it.

This figure is called *percunctatio*, an interrogation that does not allow the other person to await an answer. The wicked are forbidden to presume to mingle themselves with divine speech.

But understand the matter more deeply: this is said about those sinners who are described below, of whom he says: “Understand this, you who forget the Lord.” Divine mercy does not forbid praise to those who have turned and repented.

Those whose hearts have become hardened and who do not cease from the perversity of their crimes are forbidden to recount the Lord’s righteousnesses—that is, even to say anything about that Majesty in ordinary speech. For the mouth that presumes to recount the Lord’s righteousnesses must itself be righteous.

It follows that unworthy presumption must not handle his covenant, lest holy and venerable words appear able to proceed through a criminal and blasphemous mouth, as it is written elsewhere: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Sirach 15:9).

The covenant signifies both the Old and the New Testament; while one is mentioned implicitly, both are recalled. This may also be said of heretical teachers, who presume to teach God’s law. “To take” signifies the presumption of the irreverent. Yet he does not appear to forbid the reading by which he has especially deigned to admonish sinners.

### Verse 17

“But you hate discipline, and have cast my words behind you.”

He begins to enumerate those from whom the word of God is known to be withheld.

A person hates discipline when, through wicked presumption, he protests against just corrections and does not wish the Lord to punish in him what he has done wrong. A saving cleansing—or, according to the editorial reading, “correction”—comes to us when we love more what corrects us. It is better to be afflicted briefly here than to be condemned in that judgment.

He also casts God’s words behind him who despises the divine commands, for whom that which he ought always to contemplate is not before his eyes.

### Verse 18

“If you saw a thief, you ran with him; and with adulterers you placed your portion.”

He who forbids lesser crimes condemns still more strongly the greater ones. For what is theft compared with murder? What is adultery compared with sacrilege? The passage should therefore be understood so that, through these two forbidden acts, he appears to have forbidden every crime.

This figure is called “from a part, the whole,” and it has already been shown to occur earlier in this psalm.

He rebukes the sinner for running together with the thief—that is, for joining himself to the commission of a crime with a shared will—so that what the thief perhaps could not accomplish alone might reach completion through the sinner’s assistance.

As for the words “with adulterers you placed your portion,” they must be examined carefully. If someone assists an adulterer by giving money, offering advice, or praising him, so that he may accomplish his desires, he is clearly recognized as having a portion in the deed.

If someone has the means to intervene but does not turn back the person who is transgressing, he too is proved to be a participant in the error. We must have such love in our conscience that we allow neither ourselves nor others to perish.

### Verse 19

“Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit.”

Earlier he accused sinners of theft and adultery; now he also accuses them of the perversity of conscience and the deceits of the tongue.

Here we must understand “mouth” as the thought of the heart, because he will speak about the tongue afterward. The wickedness of thought abounds when the human mind advances into the pleasures of this age and, through various kinds of sin, acts according to an evil will.

It follows: “and your tongue fashioned deceit.” This must be understood in many ways. One who praises falsely commits deceit; one who offers malicious counsel participates in the same iniquity; one who speaks well while acting badly is stained by this perversity; and, finally, whatever is not true and simple is applied to deceitful conduct.

“Fashioned” is most aptly used, because it is the custom of deceivers to arrange falsehoods in such a way that, through some charm of words, they flatter the ears of those who hear them, as will be said in Psalm 54: “They have softened their words more than oil, yet they are arrows” (Psalm 54:22).

### Verse 20

“Sitting, you slandered your brother, and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block.”

To sit is to remain. Therefore the person who persists in disparaging another is blamed more seriously—not one who slipped into it by some accident, but one who remained for a long time as a slanderer of his brother.

Here “brother” must be understood as every neighbor related to us by flesh, because he will also speak of a spiritual brother.

But observe with what abhorrence he condemns this vice, so that one who becomes involved in such perversity may be counted among the greatest sinners, as the apostle James says: “Whoever slanders his brother slanders the law and judges the law” (James 4:11).

It follows: “and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling block.” “The son of your mother” means a child of the Church, to whom we are joined by fraternal love through the birth of regeneration.

He therefore places a stumbling block before his brother who devises heretical perversities or other snares by which an innocent person may be caught. Concerning such people the wise man himself says: “One who speaks sophistically is hateful” (Sirach 37:23).

He specifically said “you placed,” because of the treacherous snares hidden by the art of words, so that unwary simplicity may be bound by concealed knots.

### Verse 21

“You did these things, and I was silent; you thought that I was like you in wickedness. I will rebuke you and set them before your face.”

Consider how here, in a single statement, he gathers together the things that had been explained at greater length. He says that, although sinners were committing many offenses, the just Lord did not unjustly delay judgment, so that time for conversion might be found while the punishment of condemnation was suspended.

But he explains what opinion of the Creator’s benevolence arises in depraved minds. He says: “You wickedly supposed that I would be like you.” It is the custom of mortals that whenever we allow evil to be committed without openly resisting it, we appear to agree with them through similarity of conduct.

Here he confirms that the wicked mind thinks this unjustly about the Lord: because he delays punishment, they believe that human crimes have pleased him.

But a just sentence is given against this perverse understanding. Above he said that sinners had cast his words behind their backs; now, in the opposite manner, he says that their sins will be placed before each person’s face.

Through this sentence we learn the nature of the future judgment: every sinner will see standing before him what he thought had passed away through the benefit of forgetfulness. It will be an immense horror and immeasurable dread to see the things by which they will know that they have reached eternal punishments.

### Verse 22

“Understand this, you who forget the Lord, lest he suddenly seize you, and there be no one to deliver you.”

Here there is an apostrophe—that is, a turning toward those sinners whom he had forbidden above to recount the Lord’s praises.

He says: “Understand,” that is, obey faithfully. And lest you think this was said to all sinners, he added: “you who forget the Lord.” A sinner who supplicates and chastises himself with humble satisfaction does not forget the Lord.

He therefore briefly shows to whom this was said. It is an immense crime, an intolerable negligence, to forget the Lord, who gave the soul, nourishes the flesh, and defends the faithful from every adversity. It is certainly madness to be without memory of the one who is always known to be present.

But who forgets the Lord except those who, through wicked presumption, despise his commandments?

It follows: “lest he suddenly seize you, and there be no one to deliver you.” When the devil seizes someone, there is one who can deliver that person to salvation. When the Lord drags someone to punishment, there is no one who can free the condemned person, especially since the very author of crimes is himself condemned to eternal torture.

### Verse 23

“A sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is a way by which I will show him the salvation of God.”

This is set against those who presumed, though unworthy, to sing the Lord’s praises.

“A sacrifice of praise will honor me”: not the kind sung by the wicked, but the kind that a pure mind is accustomed to offer. The sacrifice of praise honors the Lord when it has been offered with purity of faith and uprightness of deeds.

It follows: “and there is a way.” He calls blessed psalmody a way. But he explains where this way leads: “by which I will show him the salvation of God.”

It is a glorious path that leads to the Creator of heaven and earth. Yet this way is traversed not with feet but with holy minds. If we walk upon it with a pure heart, it leads us to Christ and becomes for us that ladder of Jacob by which those ascending were brought to the heavens (Genesis 28:12).

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This psalm would be altogether beneficial if the wickedness of the Jews were willing to recognize it. At its beginning it spoke about the Lord’s incarnation. The Savior himself also admonishes the devout people to abandon animal victims and offer the sacrifices of the heart instead. He excluded from the preaching of divinity the sinner who did not believe in Christ. Then he showed what kind of sacrifice of praise should be offered. Finally, he revealed how the sinner would be judged.

Why, then, do you still act foolishly, Jews? Why do you not fear your destruction? Hear the Synagogue sounding forth concerning the Lord’s incarnation and the future judgment. Believe now that the one who was foretold has come. The remedies you seek are not far away. The following psalm absolves you, if you hasten to the benefits of repentance.

Why do you separate yourselves from the universal remedy? The same one saves you too [manuscripts A, B, F: “may absolve”], who also frees us. Let us say together: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

Seek baptism. Receive the flesh that you crucified. Drink the blood that you poured out. Devout confession can absolve what impious vows are known to have committed.

# Commentary on Psalm 50

“Toward the end; a psalm of David, when the prophet Nathan came to him, when he entered in to Bathsheba.”

It is worthwhile to examine this psalm somewhat more carefully, so that, with the Lord’s assistance, we may be found worthy to understand the depths of its mysteries of virtue.

Since the king and prophet, as the history of Kings testifies (2 Kings 12:13), prostrated himself in humble satisfaction and, when rebuked for his sin, was not ashamed to confess it publicly, the most holy Fathers rightly judged that he should be honored through a most sacred figure.

Among others, the blessed Jerome demonstrates that Bathsheba bore the figure of the Church or of human flesh (Commentary on Amos, chapter 8, verse 14). David, as is evident from many passages where he is suitably interpreted, he says bore the image of the Lord Christ.

Just as Bathsheba, while she was washing in the spring of Kidron, was pleasing to David after she had removed her clothing and was compelled to enter the embraces of the king, while her husband was killed by royal command [Editorial note: “In the place where he was to be killed by the enemies, he was stationed”], so also the Church—that is, the assembly of the faithful—is known to have been joined to Christ the Lord through the washing of holy baptism, after the stains of sins had been cleansed.

It was certainly fitting in those times that the future mysteries of the Lord should be indicated through such an action, and that what appeared to be culpably committed among human beings should be proved spiritually to refer to a great sacrament.

For God also commanded the prophet Hosea to take a prostitute as his wife (Hosea 1:2), so that the Church of the nations, filthy with its sins, might be signified as being cleansed through union with the Lord.

We also find that this was enacted figuratively in Judah and his daughter-in-law Tamar, and in other similar cases, as the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

The holy Augustine also discussed this figure of David and Bathsheba very carefully, among other matters, in the books he wrote against Faustus the Manichaean (Book 22, chapter 87). Therefore, whether this likeness or another was intended, it was of great benefit to the world that David sinned in such a way as to make satisfaction, so that from one temporal wound the human race might receive eternal healing.

How great, I ask, was the blessed man’s humility in acknowledging his fault, since after forgiveness he showed such constancy in making satisfaction? The crime of adultery is shown to have been foreign and unusual to him, since he mourns it with such intensity of mind.

The sudden confession of the thief invites us; we rejoice that Peter’s tears were immediately regarded; the publican’s momentary humility wins our favor. David, however, while striving to cleanse his sins at greater length, provided a means by which the whole human race might be absolved. He caused his tears, as they flow through the mouths of later generations, never to dry up through any length of time.

Let us also consider what humility there was in the prophet. The voice of a private person terrified the heart of a ruler, and he was angry rather with himself, recognizing that he was rightly condemned by the rebuke.

The ruler of such immense peoples became his own most severe torturer, demanding from himself punishments that he could scarcely endure when imposed by another’s command. It is customary among ordinary people to excuse their sins with clever arguments; but the most powerful king chose instead to condemn himself in the sight of everyone, making himself liable to judgment whose authority the people had been accustomed to fear.

Therefore he deserved to be absolved by the Lord because he did not defend his vices.

O sins that must be feared more when they occur amid the greatest joys! In Saul’s persecution David exercised numerous virtues; when established in the security of kingship, he sinned. By this we are taught that the prosperity of this world ought not to be sought, since one makes greater progress in affliction and sins in prosperity.

We must also remember that this psalm has the character called *concessio*. For *concessio* occurs when an accused person does not defend what he has done through any dispute, but simply asks to be forgiven. There is no doubt that this can generally be found in all the psalms of penitents.

## Division of the Psalm
[Col. 0359B] We see this psalm composed in five sections, arranged with a highly appropriate structure: just as every sin is gathered together under the five senses, so the iniquity contracted through them is expiated in an equal number of parts. The first is the satisfaction of the most perfect humility. The second is confidence in the Lord’s mercy, which it is always beneficial for the faithful to possess. The third asks that the Lord turn his gaze away from his sins, but that the Holy Trinity, in pity, look instead upon the sinner himself. The fourth encourages all sinners more and more earnestly toward the desire for supplication, if so enormous a transgression could be forgiven him. In the fifth section, the cause of the Church is recalled, since it was to be built through the Lord’s coming from his offspring; and there he joyfully promises that calves will be offered upon his altar. Thus the devout supplication is brought to a close, and the joys of the salvation to come are announced.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1. “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

### [Col. 0359C] Verse 2. “And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.”
