That most powerful king, an outstanding conqueror of many nations, when he heard himself rebuked by the prophet Nathan, was not ashamed publicly to confess his sin, nor did he flee to the harmful excuses to which shameless human nature most readily hastens. Instead, suddenly cast down by saving humility, he offered himself to God and, a penitent clothed in purple, pleaded with devout tears. For the faithful servant does not resort to hardened denials, but quickly recognizes the sins he has committed.

What a remarkable beginning! By saying to the Judge, “Have mercy on me,” he is seen to have removed the occasion for an examination. This utterance is not subjected to interrogation, but is always heard in tranquility; and it is the sole means by which we guilty persons can be defended without any opposition. He was asking for mercy, which he could not define; yet he felt in every way that it was greater than his sins. For how great it is, as the most holy Fathers have said, who could sufficiently relate it? It brought the Creator of the world down from heaven and clothed the Maker in an earthly body; it made him who remains equal to the Father in eternity equal to mortals; and for our sake it imposed the form of a servant upon the Lord of the world—so that bread itself should hunger, the fountain of life should thirst, power should grow weak, and omnipotent life should die.

What mercy, finally, is greater than that the Creator should be created for us, the Lord should serve, the Redeemer should be sold, the Exalter should be humbled, and the Life-giver should be killed? This was that great mercy of the Lord, which the holy man could not explain; yet through it he easily believed that he could be absolved, since through it he already understood that the human race could be liberated.

When he said, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy,” this is an argument *A conjugatis*—“from related words”: for *misereri* (“to have mercy”) derives from the source of *misericordia* (“mercy”). He continues: “And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.” What could he not give, when the Lord was asked to forgive according to his own nature? [170] The multitude of divine indulgence surpasses every possible magnitude of sins; and no offense could prevail against such mercy when it was invoked to come to the sinner’s aid. This argument is called *A parte majori*—“from the greater part.” The Lord’s mercy is far greater, however enormous our sins may seem.

Accordingly, in all his offenses he prays for an abundance of compassion, because through the prophet he had received forgiveness for his present wickedness, so that he might also deserve to escape those sins which he remembered committing at various times. Most prudently, he wanted no trace of his offenses to remain, since only the one whose sins are all blotted out is inscribed in the book of life.

### Verse 3. “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity [manuscripts A, B, F: ‘transgression’], and cleanse me from my sin.”

He who has been darkened by the poison of crimes must be washed diligently, since one who has been stained by a shadowy pollution is not cleansed through carelessness. “Thoroughly” means from every side and in every respect, so that he might also receive forgiveness for those things he knew he had previously committed. Someone may indeed be washed in such a way that he is still not completely pure. Therefore he added, “Cleanse me,” so that nothing unclean might remain in him.

This washing, which removes the stains of sins so completely that what is filthy can be made whiter than snow, is understood to signify the purity of saving baptism. In baptism both original sins and personal transgressions are so cleansed that it restores us to the purity in which the first Adam is known to have been created. If only we preserved the dignity of so great a gift, so that sins sprouting up again would not darken us.

The prophet therefore asks, in a prefiguration of holy baptism, to be cleansed from his iniquity, lest, having been released into security, he should appear negligent after receiving forgiveness. For we must take the greatest care that the things adjoining us not be made liable to guilt, as Solomon says: “At his end every man will be praised” (Ecclesiasticus XI, 30).

### [Col. 0360D] Verse 4. “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.”

Knowing that the Lord is merciful, yet does not cease to be just, the prophet suitably mingled equity with his supplications, so that what was requested with justice intervening might more readily be heard. He knows that sin must be punished; but he says that the Lord should therefore spare him because he confirms that he has condemned it in himself, as Solomon says: “The just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs XVIII, 17).

Let us therefore attend to what he says: “I acknowledge.” Those sins are stronger when we knowingly commit them, not those that we perpetrate through ignorance. Or he means this: everyone can know his sins, but only those are proved to acknowledge them who appear to condemn them by their own execration.

Perfect repentance is to avoid future sins and mourn past ones. At first, after the deed itself, the crime occurred when, in response to the prophet’s question, he answered that the man who coveted the poor man’s sheep deserved death (II Samuel XII, 6)—at a time when he did not believe that his own sin needed to be mourned. Now, however, he repents, when he groans in humble prostration and says that his offenses stand against him, as though presenting a figurative image.

He added “always,” that is, what he continually beholds, even when he closes his eyes. This constant contemplation of sins shows the perseverance of devout supplication; for whenever we look upon such things in our hearts, we lament our committed offenses. The Lord said in the preceding psalm: “I will rebuke you and set it before your face” (Psalm XLIX, 21). This the most holy man did to himself here when he says: “And my sin is always before me.”

He therefore justly asked to be absolved, since he already appeared to have formed in himself the image of the future judgment. This figure is called *procatalepsis*, that is, anticipation. For here, as though already placed in the coming judgment, he trembles at the most dreadful sight of his offenses.

### Verse 5. “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.”

Here again an enthymematic syllogism appears, which we discussed in the twentieth psalm. Its proposition is: “The Lord is justified in his words, and he prevails when he is judged.” To this, by way of conclusion, is attached the preceding statement: “Therefore against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you.” In presenting syllogisms, the ancients permitted this practice without fault.

Let us now return to the exposition of the words. If someone from the people goes astray, he sins both against God and against the king. But when a king sins, he is guilty before God alone, because he has no human being who can judge his deeds. Rightly, therefore, the king says that he sinned against God alone, since God alone could examine his transgressions. And because he knew that God was everywhere, he rightly lamented that he had done evil before him, reproving his own madness in not fearing to sin while so great a judge was present.

The Lord’s words are rightly said to be justified, since without doubt his declarations are always fulfilled, as he himself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew XXIV, 35). He continues: “And prevail when you are judged.” God possesses such justice that he is willing to be judged together with human beings. For he himself says: “Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isaiah V, 3); and elsewhere he says: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I grieved you? Answer me” (Micah VI, 3).

Thus the prophet now confesses that the Lord has such justice against him that he will plainly prevail when judgment has been rendered. Baruch says likewise: “You shall say to the Lord our God: To you belongs justice, but to us confusion of face” (Baruch I, 15). For he had in mind that he had been made king from a shepherd, that he had received peoples to govern, and that he had transgressed without considering his dignity. It was therefore necessary that the prophet be defeated in another’s judgment, since he was already known to have been defeated in his own examination. Some apply this also to the Lord’s Passion, when, having been judged and having condemned the world, he absolved it.

### Verse 6. “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.”

Here the odium of the sin is diminished when the personal crime is compared with sins common to all, so that the multitude and confession of sins themselves might move the good Judge to mercy. The sense, therefore, is this: What shall I say that I have now done, for which I am accused, when I am shown already to have been conceived in iniquities through original sin—so that I contracted sins before I had encountered the beginnings of life?

This argument is called *Ab antecedentibus*—“from antecedents.” It is not strange that one sins who was conceived in iniquities and begotten in sins. What is more humble, what more straightforward, than to be reproved for one sin and at the same time confess all?

He therefore appears rightly to have been forgiven so readily, since after the gift of absolution he strives in many ways to show himself guilty. Let the Pelagians hear this and be ashamed to oppose manifest truth. For how can it be that at any age we should not need to be absolved, when we enter this world burdened with sins that weigh us down?

Job likewise professes in similar words: “No one is pure before you, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job XIV, 4). The Apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, also recalls this among many other things, saying: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians II, 3). The same Apostle Paul says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans V, 12).

The Truth itself also testifies in the Gospel with a definitive judgment: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III, 3). Therefore I ask why infants are excluded from the kingdom of God, when they cannot be blamed for a sin personally committed. It remains, then, that infants are held liable to original sin, since before they commit personal sins they are shown to carry with them the sins of the first human being.

There are also other entirely true proofs. Therefore let human arrogance not seek sacrilegious errors for itself. Their second wickedness remains: they place free will in human powers in such a way that they think human beings can, by themselves and without God’s grace, conceive or perform some good.

If this were so, why would the prophet say: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Psalm LVIII, 11)? When you hear that you have been preceded by the Lord’s mercy, you must understand that nothing of yours preceded it. In another psalm he says: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm CXXVI, 1). He says the same: “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will greatly desire his way” (Psalm XXXVI, 23). Elsewhere the Psalmist testifies: “The Lord raises up those who are bowed down; the Lord releases those in chains; the Lord gives sight to the blind” (Psalm CXLV, 8).

When you hear that the Lord goes before, builds, directs, raises up, absolves, and enlightens without preceding merits, what do you recognize as having begun from yourselves, except that by which you are justly condemned for your pride?

But perhaps you say that the prophet Isaiah confirms free will: “If you are willing and obey, you shall eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah I, 19). And again Ezekiel says: “Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit” (Ezekiel XVIII, 31). And again: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm XCIV, 8).

But you understand these and similar passages with the worst intention, so that you believe human beings begin good will from themselves and afterward receive the help of Divinity; with the result—something impious to say—that we are the cause of his benefit, rather than he of his own. How, then, will what John says be true: “From his fullness we have all received, and grace upon grace” (John I, 16)? Or how can grace be called gratuitous if the prior swiftness of some good anticipates it?

Hear the Apostle, who refutes your utterly false doctrine by true preaching, saying: “Who has given to him first, so that he may be repaid? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Romans XI, 35). The Apostle also says: “From whom are both willing and accomplishing, according to his good pleasure” (Philippians II, 13). And the Apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I, 17).

There follows another absurdity, much worse. If the beginning of good will came from us, we would be the ones to lay the foundation upon which the Lord would build. Certainly no sound mind can approve this. Therefore stop asserting what you cannot accomplish.

Those obey willingly whom he himself makes able to hear; those desire profitably who receive the gift of Divinity. For after the nature of the human race had been corrupted, the Lord both granted the salutary element of free will and, in his mercy, granted its operation. Blessed Augustine, learned Jerome, and Prosper taught these things by divine gift with the agreement of the whole Church. But an accursed heresy has caused us to encounter matters that are shown to be exceedingly contrary to our salvation.

### Verse 7. “For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

Just as in the preceding verse he demonstrated through common sin that no one is exempt from sins, so now again, through his own confession, he begs for assistance, because in confessing his sin he has spoken the truth, which the Lord God seeks above sacrifices. For God is not pleased by our punishments, but seeks confession of error, as it is written: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel XVIII, 32).

“Uncertain” are things that cannot be discerned at all but are grasped through certain ambiguities. “Hidden,” however, are things that neither the eye sees nor the human mind judges. He says that these two things were not merely revealed to him but made manifest, so that what had been difficult even to suspect came to him plainly in disclosure.

Notice also how beautifully he gathers together the gifts bestowed upon him by means of a definition. For by saying, “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom,” he shows what prophecy is. He adds another burden to his guilt, so that when he counts his benefits, his fault may continually increase.

The uncertain and hidden things, therefore, are those which God revealed to him in the manifestation of his Son: first, that he might recognize that God had a Son; then, that he might know that the Son was to come from his offspring by assuming flesh; that he might also foretell his future Passion and announce the glory of his Resurrection. Thus he says that he ought not to have sinned after being judged worthy to recognize such things.

O holy simplicity! Who could have labored so earnestly for his own defense as this man labored for his own condemnation? This argument is called *A causis*—“from causes.” He says that, after so many benefits had been bestowed, he ought not to have proceeded to such sins.

### Verse 8. “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.”

Having been cast down by his preceding supplication, he rises in confidence in the Lord’s mercy to the second section, lest he appear to have despaired of the clemency of the almighty Lord, which would be graver than all sins.

Although hyssop is a very small plant, it is said to penetrate with its roots into the innermost parts of rocks. It is also considered suitable for wounded human interiors. In the book of Leviticus, after being dipped in sacrificial blood, it was customarily sprinkled seven times over the body of a leper (Leviticus XIV, 6–7), signifying that the stains of sins are effectively washed away by the precious blood of the Lord the Savior.

By this likeness the prophet begs to be liberated, so that through the saving blood of Christ—which he believed in a devout heart was to come—he might deserve the gifts of absolution. For by hyssop he signifies the sacraments we have mentioned, which not only wipe away defilements but also reveal the soul’s purity shining more brightly than snow.

Nothing white can be found in bodies whiter than snow; but he said “whiter than snow” because the spiritual soul, once cleansed, shines far above bodies. [172] This figure is called *hyperthesis*, that is, “excess” or “superlative expression,” when we claim that our statement surpasses something known to everyone by common opinion. The same is found in what was already said in the seventeenth psalm: “And he flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm XVII, 11).

### Verse 9. “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will exult.”

Here devout confidence in Divinity is displayed, so that he says he will hear such things as multiply joy and gladness. Joy pertains to absolution; gladness to the possession of eternal rewards.

To hear joy and gladness means what is promised to those who have been absolved: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34).

He continues: “And the humbled bones will exult,” that is, when they have heard the voice we have mentioned. This argument is called *A consequentibus*—“from consequences.” For when these things have been heard, joy must follow.

By the bones are signified the firm foundations of the soul, which had necessarily to be humbled as long as this penitent could obtain absolution. He said “humbled” on account of the consciousness of his error, which always profitably makes people humble.

### Verse 10. “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.”

He comes to the third section, asking the merciful Judge not to look upon the sins that also seemed dreadful to him. Consider, however, how beautifully rules are given from opposites.

If we turn our faces away from our sins, it is harmful, because we forget and neglect what we ought to wash away with continual weeping. If the Lord does not turn his face away, he destroys sin, because he judges the offenses upon which he looks.

He prays similarly elsewhere: “Do not turn your face away from me, and I shall be like those who descend into the pit” (Psalm CXLII, 7). Rightly so, because if we are looked upon, we are absolved by the Savior’s mercy, as it is said of Peter in the Gospel: “And the Lord looked upon Peter, and he went outside and wept bitterly” (Luke XXII, 61–62).

He continues: “And blot out all my iniquities.” Called to account for two crimes, the supremely prudent petitioner asks forgiveness for all his offenses. For he knew that he had committed many more things than the justice of the present occasion accused him of; therefore, in a saving brevity, he asked that whatever could be charged against him be forgiven in a single act of mercy.

When “blot out” is said, “forgive” is signified, because every offense of ours is written, as it were, on tablets when it is contained in divine knowledge.

### [Col. 0365B] Verse 11. “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”

We must examine these verses subtly, word by word, so that their meaning may become clearer to us. We say “create” when something new is instituted, so that what did not exist appears to come into being.

How, then, can we say that David did not possess a clean heart before his sin, when the Lord said of him: “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man according to my heart, who will do all my will” (Psalm LXXXVIII, 22; Acts XIII, 22)?

Here “create” must be understood as “restore what has fallen away.” The prophet therefore asks that such a clean heart be created for him that, once urged on by sins, it could no longer be moved toward guilt, but, fixed in stability, could not change its good purpose.

This will certainly be given to the saints after the Resurrection. But this penitent, eager for good things and set aflame by love of the reward to come, asked that what could occur in the future be granted to him in the present.

By the “right spirit” he means the Word, the Son of God, of whom it is recalled in another psalm: “The rod of your kingdom is a right rod” (Psalm XLIV, 7). He rightly called him “spirit” according to the nature of Divinity, because it is written: “God is spirit” (John IV, 24).

“Renew” is placed by the figure *hypallage*—a transposition—not because the Son himself needed to be renewed, but because he can renew David, who had been made old by sins, through grace. For he renews us when, having put off the oldness of the ancient human being, he changes us into the gifts of his new regeneration.

For just as through Adam we became old, so through the benefits of Christ the Lord we are renewed (Ephesians IV, 22), as the Apostle says: “Putting off the old human being with his deeds, put on the new, who was created according to God” (Colossians III, 9–10).

He added “within me,” because he knew that the detestable crime of adultery had emerged from within him. He was seeking a remedy for both parts, since he had sinned in both respects. And observe with what vitality he desires to be purified, so that you may understand that he wished never again to commit such an offense.

For just as severed limbs cannot be joined again into their former structure, so past sins cannot return to the true penitent.

According to some, however, this passage is rightly explained in another way. The prophet asks God to create a clean heart in him, not requesting something he did not possess, but asking that what already existed be made clean. For we also say “create” in the sense of “renew.” It is said elsewhere of the faithful: “Behold, now there is a new creation” (II Corinthians V, 17)—not as though something came from another thing that did not exist, but because a new illumination had arisen in what already stood established.

### Verse 12. “Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.”

A person is cast away from someone’s face when he is refused healing. And what is a sick person to do if the medicine withdraws? He knew that from the Lord’s face came health of mind and the light of wisdom; and he believed that he would be handed over to the enemy if he were judged expelled from the Lord’s countenance.

Here he wishes to be looked upon only insofar as he had previously cried out that his sins ought not to be looked upon. O mind of the prophet, extraordinary even after human errors! He said nothing about power and made no plea concerning emotions. He asked only that the spirit of prophecy not be taken from him, which the king valued above all things precious.

The prophet Jeremiah likewise testified to its power, saying: “The Lord stretched out his hand to me, touched my mouth, and said to me: Behold, I have given my words into your mouth; behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, demolish, destroy, exterminate, build, and plant” (Jeremiah I, 9).

Rightly, therefore, he asked that what he recognized as more magnificent to him than all riches be preserved for him. Observe that he did not say, “Give me,” as though he did not possess it, but said, “Do not take it away”—clearly because such a great and powerful supplication could not occur except through the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 13. “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a principal spirit.”

He returns to the Son of God. To show that he is speaking of Christ, he says, “of your salvation,” through whose birth salvation came to the nations, and what had previously been known to a few through exceptional faith became known throughout the whole world.

Therefore, when he says, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation,” he signifies Christ. By contemplating him, he was joyful even amid his tears, and through the gift of his prophecy he was nourished during the fasts of his repentance.

He said “restore,” because he had felt that some grace had been diminished in him; for a person withdraws from saving grace to the extent that he conducts himself in a blameworthy manner. When he says, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation,” he undoubtedly recognized that he had lost the grace of the Holy Spirit, which human frailty cannot possess while it sins.

He continues: “And strengthen me with a principal spirit.” That most holy king and marvelous prophet did not consider it the supreme gift to dictate laws to his subjects or to subdue foreign nations by war. Transported wholly into contemplation, he sought more earnestly to be established in princely understanding than to remain at the summit of kingship.

“Strengthen me,” he said, “so that I may not sin again, so that I may not depart from you through the mutability of my soul.”

Nor should we think it accidental that the holy man, radiant with illumination of heart, mentioned “spirit” three times, unless because, devoted to the undivided Trinity, he asked forgiveness to be granted to him by it.

For with respect to the essence of Divinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are rightly called one God. But in the distinction of persons, it is proper to the Father that he naturally begot the Son without beginning, before the ages; it is proper to the Son that he was naturally generated from the Father; and it is proper to the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Through their ineffable love and cooperation, their consubstantial eternity and power accomplishes all that it wills in heaven and on earth.

Although these matters are incomprehensible and inexpressible, and although we now know them to be as they are, some Fathers nevertheless propose the following likeness from bodily things that exist together. In the sun we find three properties: first, its bodily substance itself, that it is the sun; second, its radiance, which remains in it; third, its heat, which proceeds from its radiance even to us.

This is how I think the comparison should be understood—if any likeness to so great a matter can be found: what the bodily substance is in the sun may in some way be understood as the person of the Father in the Trinity; what the sun’s radiance is may be understood as the person of the Son in the Trinity, as the Apostle says: “The radiance of his glory” (Hebrews I, 3); and what the heat is in the sun may be understood as the person of the Holy Spirit in the Trinity, as it is written: “Who hides himself from his heat?” (Psalm XVIII, 7).

Another example is also given from incorporeal things, namely from the soul, which is known to have been made in the image of God. The soul, then, is itself an incorporeal, rational substance in which understanding and life are present.

Therefore what substance is in the soul may be understood—if it is permissible to say so—as the person of the Father in the Trinity. What power and knowledge are in the soul may be understood as the Son in the Trinity, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God. And what the property of giving life is in the soul may also be understood as the Holy Spirit in the Trinity, through whom the work of giving life is proclaimed to be accomplished in many passages.

Thus the Apostle Peter says in his Epistle: “Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit” (I Peter III, 18). The Apostle likewise says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (II Corinthians III, 6). And in the Gospel the Lord says: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John VI, 63).

These three things, considered individually and separately, are nowhere found entirely apart, although our understanding can perceive them as distinct. Rather, they are naturally united in such a way that whenever one of them presents itself, all three always appear together.

Through these likenesses, then, some conception of the truth concerning so great a matter is opened to us. There are other discussions of the Fathers very similar to these, but the weakness of the flesh now prevents us from understanding them fully. They will be grasped much more excellently when all who are blessed behold the Divinity in its majesty.

Whoever desires to know these matters more fully should not cease reading the books on the Trinity by Saint Hilary, Saint Ambrose, and Saint Augustine. This subject is as great for discussion as it is extensive. Blessed Jerome also discussed the Trinity in this psalm lucidly and briefly against the heretics.

### Verse 14. “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the impious will turn back to you.”

He enters the fourth section of the supplication. Once he has been heard, he shows what glory belongs to the one who spares, so that he too, now wholly cleansed, may be gained when he converts another from unbelief. For it is written: “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James V, 20).

There are two kinds of teachers: one instructs by examples, while the other is known merely to admonish sinners with words. Both are understood here. He says, therefore, that if the prophet is spared, the greatest hope of forgiveness is granted to those who sin. For who would not turn his mind toward conversion when a king and prophet offered an example of the forgiveness granted to him?

Or the passage can be understood in a second way: having been delivered from great destruction, he could preach to the nations the Lord’s various great deeds, as the text of the following psalms shows. He also promises a profitable shortcut: because one man had been forgiven, many impious people would be shown to be gained through him. This is not said out of pride, but is prophesied through the power of providence.

How many people are made free from guilt by supplicating the Lord through these words, and happily released from their bonds?

### Verse 15. “Deliver me from blood-guilt, O God, God of my salvation, and my tongue will exult in your justice.”

In “blood-guilt” the plural number appears to have been adopted contrary to Latin usage. But because this expression is contained in the Greek manuscripts, the translator must be praised in every way: he chose to place something contrary to the art of secular usage rather than depart from the truth established in the text.

For if he had said “from blood,” he might perhaps have appeared to indicate a single sin. But by using the plural number, he undoubtedly confesses that there are many sins. This may be called an idiom of divine Scripture. The figure is called *exallage*, that is, “alteration,” whenever, contrary to customary usage, either gender or case is changed.

The prophet therefore asks to be delivered from carnal sins, so that he might cease sinning in this frailty. “Blood” is used for the human body, because among its other fluids it appears to be the chief [editorial reading: “the earlier”]. In the Gospel, too, it is said to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matthew XVI, 17).

“God of my salvation” signifies the Lord Savior, through whom salvation is given to those who devoutly believe. He also added, “And my tongue will exult in your justice,” that is: if you deliver me from blood-guilt—which is understood as sins—my tongue will rightly speak your praise, in accordance with what was said in the preceding psalm: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justices?” (Psalm XLIX, 16).

Once absolved, he could rightly speak, whereas divine law had silenced the sinner.

Some people also seem to raise a question about why, after the forgiveness of his offense, he said, “I will praise your justice,” rather than using the more suitable expression, “I will praise your mercy.” For the one who prayed to be mercifully absolved ought to give thanks for mercy.

But if you consider the matter with profound reasoning, it was also an act of divine justice for God to hear the one crying out to him, spare the supplicant, and receive the one confessing. Or it was because these two things are always joined in the Lord’s judgment, as he will say in the hundredth psalm: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm C, 1). We shall explain this more clearly in its proper place.

### [Col. 0369A] Verse 16. “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise.”

The prophet declares that his lips, which had been closed by the condition of sin, must be opened through the benefit of absolution. For the mouths of those placed under guilt are condemned, as Isaiah also says: “Woe is me, for I am unclean; although I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell among a people who have unclean lips” (Isaiah VI, 5).

The mouth is also said of the secret place of the heart, from which divine praise is effectively sung. Rightly, therefore, after the forgiveness of his sin, he declares both that his lips must be opened and that his mouth can proclaim the Lord’s praises.

### Verse 17. “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; but you will not delight in burnt offerings.”

Recognizing himself as guilty because fault intervened, the humble petitioner indicates that, as a king, he could easily have offered sacrifices of animals, which at that time were still offered for the expiation of sins, if the Lord willingly accepted burnt offerings.

When he says, “But you will not delight in burnt offerings,” he signifies the sacred rites involving the sacrifice of animals, which were to be rejected at the Lord’s coming. It is therefore clear that the prophet had been wholly turned toward the Lord in mind, so that he did not believe himself to be cleansed by the sacrifices performed at that time, but rather by the offering he describes below.

### Verse 18

“A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”

After saying which sacrifices God rejects, he now states those which he seeks. For this is the sacrifice we give to God: a spirit of pride slaughtered by the humility of confession, from which not blood flows forth, but streams of tears run down. For this spirit, when it is joyful, binds us; when it is contrite according to God, it releases us.

He expresses this through the fifth kind of definition, which in Greek is called *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν* and in Latin *ad verbum* (“word for word”), indicating what sacrifice is more acceptable when offered to God—namely, a contrite spirit. There follows also the unquestionable promise of this statement, by which pardon is no longer requested for himself, but promised by God to those who humble themselves before him: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”

By “contrite” he means one severely afflicted by the labors of repentance. By “humbled,” humbled before God, so that what previously had been proud through arrogance might become devout through pious confession. And observe how the order of things has been preserved. The heart could not have been humbled unless it had first been crushed by frequent tribulation. For when he said, “God does not despise,” this is already the authority of a holy promise, which is proclaimed rather than requested.

It is clear that God does not despise such offerings, just as he is known previously to have rejected those sacrifices. It should certainly be investigated why, throughout the divine Scriptures, the heart is so often used to signify understanding. For he says in the Gospel: “From the heart come evil thoughts” (Matt. XV, 19). The Apostle Peter also says to Simon: “Your heart is not right before God” (Acts VIII, 21). Isaiah likewise testifies: “The heart of this people has been hardened” (Isa. VI, 10). And in the fourth psalm: “How long, O you heavy of heart?” (Ps. IV, 3). In the seventh: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. VII, 10). Here too, above, he said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” so that it might unquestionably appear to all that the heart is the source of our thoughts, and that good and evil deliberation proceed from it.

Indeed, that very bodily organ is the seat of thought [ms. G and ed., “is conoid”], and it bears the image of fire; so that it was fittingly fashioned in such a position, from which counsel can come to us.

### Verse 19

“Deal favorably, O Lord, with Zion according to your good pleasure, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.”

The fifth and final section now begins. The anxiety of his calamities has been laid aside, and, mindful of the divine promise, he joyfully asks that what the Lord had deigned to promise may come to pass. He therefore entreats that, since the Synagogue placed under the Law sinned, Zion—that is, the Catholic Church—might be established, with the grace of Christ succeeding it.

Accordingly, it is said: “In your good pleasure, deal favorably with Zion,” as though that mountain had not yet come into being. But consider that Zion signifies the Church, through which the world could, of course, be adorned.

O region, patroness of all lands! O city of the great King, which bears both the image and the name of the heavenly homeland! Who would dare call you local, when you are shown by your most holy faith to have filled the boundaries of the whole world? If you wish to consider the historical reference, it perhaps signifies the time of Theodosius, when his most religious wife Eudoxia, the most devout of women, enlarged that worthy city and crowned it with a better circuit of walls.

### Verse 20

“Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar.”

Holy men frequently make an assertion in such a way that a votive promise is added, as in the passage: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXV, 12).

Thus here also it is said to the Father: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness”—that is, the most glorious passion of your Son, who offered himself as a sacrifice for all, so that the world might receive the salvation which it did not deserve by its own works. It is beautifully defined what the Lord’s revered passion is: “the sacrifice of righteousness.”

There follows: “Offerings and burnt offerings.” This now refers to the faithful Christians who were to believe after the Lord’s coming. It signifies that the living hearts of human beings were to be sacrificed, not the limbs of dead animals. The former were consumed by destructive fire; the latter are tormented by a life-giving conflagration. The former were immediately reduced to ashes; the latter, by burning souls through temporal tribulations, lead them to the eternal joys of the pleasant paradise.

There follows: “Then they will place calves upon your altar”—namely, the priests, when the Catholic Church has been established through the Lord’s passion. Since he said above, “You will not be pleased with burnt offerings,” it must be asked why here he again promises that calves will be sacrificed.

This was spoken through an allegorical figure, which says one thing and signifies another. He placed “calves” either for innocent adults, whose age is still in its first stage and whose neck is shown to be free from the yoke of sin. For this reason he retained that expression, so that the action of the former Law might be shown to have been an image of future realities.

Or perhaps he promises the preachers of the Gospel, whose image the Evangelist Luke assumed in the figure of the calf—men who would not strike the air with lowing, but would fill the whole world with the preaching of faith in the Lord.

Or perhaps we should understand those calves more particularly as the people who offered their souls as a sacrifice of sweet fragrance upon the sacred altars. For Father Augustine too, when he was discussing those Gospel figures (Sermons 70 and 190, *On Time*), says in one passage that the Lord himself is the calf who offered himself as a victim for the salvation of all.

Therefore, whether the reference is understood as adolescents, preachers, or martyrs, the prophet could nevertheless promise to the Lord’s altars such calves as he knew to be fitting for the Christian religion.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This psalm, exceedingly sweet, has poured forth from the bitter fountain of compunction. But what tears should we believe the Israelite people shed at that time, when so great a prince was lamenting under such affliction? Who would not weep while he wept? Who would not groan while he grieved, when the king wore ashes upon his head instead of a jeweled diadem, gray with dust rather than with age?

He did not wish to appear outwardly adorned when he knew himself to be utterly foul within. He was more beautiful in his filth, because in his sins he rejected the pomp of the world. The pain of one heart was plainly the correction of the city, when he who had presumed at that time to be joyful incurred the crime of madness.

Happy indeed—three and four times happy—is the city where the Lord of the world was permitted to repent before God, and where the heavenly King received the glory of crucifixion.

Hence, although this book teaches that there are seven psalms of penitents, it has rightly become established through the practice of the Churches that whenever pardon for sins is sought, the Lord should especially be entreated through this psalm. First, because in none of the psalms is found such profound humility of spirit—the quality most necessary for penitents—as here: a powerful king, established at the height of prophetic dignity, hastened to lament his sins as though he were the lowest of men.

Then, after the promise of absolution, he bound himself to such a necessity of tears as though this had by no means been unknown to him. A moderate and readily accessible form of supplication has clearly been chosen, one which every truly wise age ought to seek and which anyone can quickly fulfill in an emergency.

For here, unlike the other penitential psalms, nothing difficult is prescribed, such as that in the sixth psalm: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI, 7). Nor that which he says in the thirty-first psalm: “Your hand has been heavy upon me; I have turned in my anguish, while the thorn is fastened” (Ps. XXXI, 4). Nor that which he says in the thirty-seventh psalm: “My wounds have become foul and festering because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6). Nor that which he says in the hundred-and-first psalm: “For I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. CI, 10). Nor that which he says in the hundred-and-twenty-ninth: “From the depths I cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. CXXIX, 1). Nor that which he says in the hundred-and-forty-second: “For the enemy pursued my soul; he humbled my life to the ground. He placed me in darkness like those who have been dead for ages, and my spirit was anguished within me” (Ps. CXLII, 3).

Instead, having been rebuked by the prophet and terrified by recognition of his sin, the king asks the most merciful Judge that, washed by his mercy, he may be made completely clean from the filth of all sins.

Thus the excellent teacher gave severe forms of satisfaction elsewhere to stronger powers, while granting this moderate form to the weak. The pious mother Church has rightly chosen it, so that in every way she might invite her children to the grace of the most gentle confession.

Perhaps this too can be understood here: that he says in this psalm, “I will teach the wicked your ways, and sinners will turn back to you,” because he foresaw that later peoples would seek through this psalm the abundant gifts of repentance.

Let us clearly consider, however, what it means that we may repeat this psalm through frequent meditation without being prevented from seeking ecclesiastical honors, whereas, if a penitential vow is pronounced over us by a priest, we are rightly forbidden by the canons to advance any further, because it is bestowed in another’s person.

Whatever we receive in the name of Christ ought to be for us an inviolable and definitive judgment. Thus it comes about that everyone may continually perform repentance privately, but when it has been imposed through a priest, it does not permit us thereafter to advance to ecclesiastical honors.

Nor is its number without significance. It pertains to the jubilee year, which among the Hebrews dissolved ancient obligations and contracts, and which the Lord commanded in Leviticus to be called the year of remission for all the inhabitants of the land.

It also pertains to Pentecost, when, after the Lord’s ascension, the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles, performing miracles and granting the gifts of the charisms. Thus this psalm too, established by the number fifty, if recited with a pure heart, loosens sins, cancels the written record of our obligation, and, like a year of remission, renders us free from the debts of our sins, through the Lord’s favor.

# PART TWO

### 176. Title of Psalm 51

“To the end; an instruction of David, when Doeg the Idumean came and reported to Saul, and said to him: ‘Behold, David has come to the house of Abimelech.’”

To explain the title, the circumstances must briefly be related. When David was fleeing from Saul, he came to the priest Abimelech. Abimelech received him and gave him the bread of the Presence and the sword with which he had killed Goliath. The bread of the Presence signified the priest; the sacred sword signified the future most powerful king.

Doeg the Idumean, chief of the mules, happened to be there and reported everything to King Saul (1 Reg. XXII, 10). Then Saul, enraged, had Abimelech and the other priests of that city killed by his own command.

This Doeg, through whom such events occurred, was called an Idumean by the name of his homeland. These two words taken together, as the authority of the Fathers teaches, indicate earthly disturbances. This interpretation of the words is not improperly applied to the deeds of Antichrist.

Doeg the Idumean was an adversary of David, just as Antichrist will be an adversary of Christ. Doeg extinguished priests; Antichrist will make martyrs. Doeg, by the meaning of his name, indicates earthly disturbances; Antichrist will shake the whole world, compelling it through sacrilegious presumption to worship his name.

Therefore Antichrist is rightly understood under the name of Doeg the Idumean, to whom he is shown to be similar in so many comparisons. Accordingly, this entire title is rightly referred to the Lord’s second coming, in the time of Antichrist, since everything is appropriately directed toward the manifestation of Christ, so that the title may appear not to differ from its psalm but rather to correspond to it.

## Division of the Psalm

Illuminated by the Holy Spirit, the prophet looked ahead to the judgment of the Lord and saw the abominable dominion of Antichrist arising. To strengthen the hearts of the faithful, he rises in the first part of the psalm with an attack against him, so that he might not exalt himself excessively in his iniquities, while the gravest end was approaching.

In the second part, still rebuking him, he says both that he will be swept away by a swift end and that he will have no portion with the Lord’s saints.

In the third part, he describes the astonishment that will come upon the saints when the devil, who has raged in this world with excessive presumption, is seen at the end as utterly wretched and cast down.

In the fourth part, trusting in God, the prophet considers that in the future world he will possess a most blessed portion with the saints.

Some, however, have thought that this psalm was generally spoken against sinners. But since we are rather commanded to pray for such people, who have by no means lost hope of conversion, it follows that the psalm should more properly be understood of Antichrist and his followers, who are already known to be condemned through the cruelty of their obstinacy—especially since, as is said below, he will be destroyed at the end of the world.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity all day long?”

Since divine Scripture does not say that one should glory even in good works, but commands that “the one who glories should glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. I, 31), the prophet now rebukes with indignation a wicked man who boasts only of his malignity. Why does he wish to glory in evil deeds, by which he ought rather, with conscience as witness, to be confounded?

This is a form of *energeia*, since he addresses an absent person as though present. Through the following verses, after making his attack, he describes him with remarkable precision, so that the one who is believed to come after a long time may seem visible through his character.

A person is also powerful in iniquities when, having been permitted to act in evil, he is able to accomplish what he strives for. But to the extent that he is strong in wickedness, to that same extent he is to be detested by those of good character.

And so that this might not seem to happen only momentarily, “all day long” is added, signifying the period of his entire life: he both performs and conceives evil continually, without any interruption.

### Verse 2

“Your tongue has devised injustice; like a sharpened razor, you have practiced deceit.”

The custom of the worst people is described with remarkable brevity: they do not think before they speak, as the most wise Solomon says: “Their heart is in the mouth of fools” (Ecclus. XXI, 29).

Here he says that the tongue devised it, not the heart, so that the tongue, which ordinarily serves the counsel of the prudent, might appear to have devised its words within its very utterances. It produced them without deliberation because it had not refined them through prior judgment.

“Your tongue has devised” makes both things clear: the easy willingness of a mind that is exceedingly light and the utterly thoughtless haste of its speech. We can sometimes think evil without speaking it with the tongue. Here, however, the wicked man’s worst habit is condemned.

He adds: “Like a sharpened razor, you have practiced deceit.” A razor is a broad piece of iron, stretched into a certain thinness and prepared with an extremely sharp edge for shaving hair. Although, when pressed against the beard, it cuts through its growth, it leaves the substance of the body unharmed.

He therefore suitably compares the deceit of the most savage man to a sharp razor. For just as the razor does not injure the man, so this man does not strike the soul of the righteous under any affliction. He can shave away everything externally attached, like hairs; but when he attempts to remove worldly things, he actually makes the inner soul more beautiful.

### Verse 3

“You loved wickedness more than goodness, iniquity more than speaking righteousness.”

The one who is known to love what he sins by never abandons evil. We unequivocally abandon those things which we condemn when hatred intervenes.

This most wicked sinner is said to love his vices because, corrupted by a detestable disease, he judges most desirable what good morals always accuse. And to multiply the additions to his guilt, he adds: “More than goodness,” so that, even if goodness should at some time touch his mind, it might immediately be rejected like a detestable vice and lie in disgrace [ms. A: “rejecting it”].

There follows: “Iniquity more than speaking righteousness.” Often people who commit sins conceal themselves beneath the beauty of carefully composed speech. They do not wish to be found guilty of what they know is condemned by the universal judgment of mankind.

But this man has openly professed evil, so that he is not ashamed to speak what the intentions of the wise reject.

Observe also how he has briefly conveyed many things in these three verses. This figure is called *leptologia*, that is, subtle speech, when individual matters are indicated minutely and precisely.

### Verse 4

“You loved every word of rashness, O deceitful tongue.”

After an interval (*diapsalma*), he comes to the second part. But even if we imagine some exceedingly wicked person, whose deceitful words could descend as though from the precipice of a mountain, who would he be?

Yet this is truly said of Antichrist, who loves iniquity with ways turned backward and confused. He runs toward every word of rashness; he commands what benefits no one; and he speaks everything deceitfully, so that nothing he says is judged beneficial to anyone.

### Verse 5

“Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from his dwelling, and your root from the land of the living.”

In this life God most prosperously destroys those whom he has determined to build up again. But the one who is destroyed forever is assigned to eternal punishments.

Because of the things said above, that tyrant will be punished at the end of the world by the mouth of the Lord, so that such enormous wickedness may be destroyed by the coming of the supreme Judge. The prophet Daniel also determines the duration of his power, saying: “For in a time, times, and half a time, all these things will be completed, when the dispersion has been brought to an end” (Dan. XII, 7).

There follows: “He will tear you away and remove you from his dwelling.” A great punishment, a terrifying condemnation: to be torn away from the Lord’s most delightful dwelling and handed over to everlasting fires, where no one is permitted to grow green or flourish, but where, like a great old tree torn up by its roots, he will dry up in eternal sterility.

It may also trouble some readers that these words cannot seem to apply to Antichrist. For it says, “He will remove you from his dwelling,” although that most pagan man does not appear to have been planted there.

But this can be understood of his members, who appear to be in the Church bodily but not in spirit. For just as the faithful are members of the Lord the Savior, so he gathers his accomplices into one fellowship of wickedness.

He adds: “And your root from the land of the living.” The roots of Antichrist will be his supporters and servants of the devil. Therefore he says that his root is to be torn away with him from the land of the living, because neither the devil, nor Antichrist, nor their followers will have any portion with the Lord’s saints.

Let the person who thought his power here worthy of admiration consider his punishment. It is necessary that the one whose dominion he does not doubt will be cut off should be held in the utmost contempt.

### Verse 6

“The righteous will see and fear; and they will laugh over him, and say.”

He comes to the third part, in which the prophet’s spirit foresaw what was still to occur after long ages. Although the righteous continually fear God and never cease to regard his power as something great, they will then see such things that they will dread them far more intensely than human thoughts can comprehend.

“They will fear” therefore refers to divine glory, not to fear of punishment, for he is speaking of the blessed.

There follows: “They will laugh over him, and say.” In this world the righteous rather mourn those whom they know to be in error, as the Apostle says: “That I may mourn many of those who have sinned and have not repented” (2 Cor. XII, 21).

But since there will be no place for repentance at the future judgment, the righteous will rightly laugh over him, because the holy patience of the Lord was despised by the faithless through an iniquitous will. And lest we think that this laughter is frivolous, as it often is here, the words they will speak are added, so that their agreement with the Lord’s judgment may be shown.

### Verse 7

“Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity.”

When “behold” is spoken with an outstretched hand, the sinner’s wicked fate is displayed. It becomes clear to what end the deeds which that most cruel man considered glorious have led.

Here we must understand “riches” as all the pomp of the world, in which that most wicked one will abound, as the prophet Daniel recalls: “He will rule over the hidden treasures of gold and silver, and over all the desires of Egypt” (Dan. XI, 43).

For he will be rich not only in gold, but also in the multitude of nations and the domination of lands. He will rejoice in the display of miracles, boast in the exaltation of an evil honor, and be filled with the other vices that appear to be signified by the name of Egypt.

But all these things will be vain, because they are shown to be alien to the Lord. That is called vain which is empty, fragile, or fleeting, and separated from the most firm truth itself.

Although all worldly things may seem able to serve his rule, he nevertheless prevailed in vanity, because he acquired nothing that could benefit him. As the Teacher of the Gentiles says of him: “Puffed up without cause by the madness of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, joined and extended through its connections, grows with the growth of God” (Col. II, 19).

### Verse 8

“But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God forever and unto ages of ages.”

The prophet comes to the fourth part, in which he now exults joyfully—that is, in the coming of the far-distant future. And rightly he compares himself to an olive tree, because from its shoot the Lord Christ blossomed, anointed with spiritual oil above his companions.

This most blessed olive tree produced such fruit that it would make the whole human race, dried up by sins, grow rich through the abundance of its mercy.

He also adds: “In the house of God,” where indeed the fruit of this happy tree grew. But that marvelous fruit appeared because he hoped in the mercy of God, whereas Antichrist will hope in the abundance of his riches.

This is placed in opposition to the other, so that it may be clear what fruit comes from hoping in divinity, and what destruction follows from not having hope in the Lord.

This figure is called *syndicasmos*, that is, comparison, when different things are set against one another in contrast.

And lest this confidence be thought to have been assumed only for a time, he adds: “Forever,” which is “unto ages of ages.” This expression is repeated so that he may be judged to have possessed a hope wholly fixed in that eternity.

### Verse 9

“I will confess to you forever, because you have done it; and I will await your name, because it is good before the sight of your saints.”

As the most salutary preacher declares the good things of his confession, he shows us how we ought to act. Here it has been granted to confess, so that there we may deserve to be absolved.

He adds: “Because you have done it.” Here an omission (*ellipsis*) is to be understood through a figure: namely, the mercy in which he testified above that he had hoped.

There follows: “And I will await your name, because it is good.” The one awaits his name who believes that he will be saved by the Lord Savior’s mercy at the judgment, while he considers that such a name will be fulfilled in him.

It is rightly called good, since there both the hope of salvation and the victory of the whole life are received. He also adds: “Before the sight of your saints,” when the general joy of the righteous has arrived and the Lord’s praise will be sung without end in harmonious exultation.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

After the blessed tears of the fiftieth psalm and the most blessed expiation of sins, the prophet, freed from the adversity of sins, joyfully bursts forth against the adversary of the Lord out of love for his divinity, and most devotedly pursues the enemy of his King.

Although praise and blame are found in different places and belong to the demonstrative genre, in this psalm he has most beautifully embraced both parts. From the beginning up to the statement, “He prevailed in his vanity,” he carries out the part of blame. From there to the end, the form of praise is displayed. Thus the perfection of the demonstrative genre is completed on both sides.

It is also fitting for us to remember that this psalm, which prophesied the coming of Antichrist, is the second and is joined to the preceding psalm by a marvelous arrangement. For just as he will be destroyed at the end of the world by Elijah and Enoch, those two most holy men, so through these twin psalms Antichrist is indicated, so that he may not terrify us while remaining hidden.

Therefore this psalm has appropriately been placed after the fiftieth, because the son of iniquity of whom it speaks, exceeding the limit of remission, is known to have no pardon.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 52

“To the end; an instruction of David for Amalek.”

Since this psalm is known to correspond in large part to the thirteenth in the similarity of its verses, the meaning of those verses has been changed as much as possible through the difference of the titles.

For while that psalm has “A psalm of David,” this one contains: “To the end; an instruction of David for Amalek.” Thus, without changing the verses, the former announces that one thing will come, and the latter another.

The former is brought forth against the Jews; this one is generally directed against all sinners. The former speaks of the Lord’s incarnation; this one will speak at the end of the psalm about the coming of judgment.

This is plainly a beautiful mode of expression, arising through allegory: to say the same things while understanding what has been said in another way. In a marvelous manner, diversity is found in the meanings where the wording has not changed.

Let us now explain the words of this title: “To the end; an instruction of David for Amalek.” What “to the end” signifies is already known from frequent exposition.

Amalek was a nation that fought against God’s people with extreme and repeated hostility. The interpretation of this name is “for one giving birth” or “for one grieving.”

We now appropriately apply this to the Church of the Lord, which, like a woman grieving and giving birth, admonishes the people of the faithless to cease from their iniquities, lest they perish in the divine judgment, as the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19).

### 179. Division of the Psalm

In the first section of the psalm, the Church speaks, rebuking those who refuse to turn their hearts toward spiritual goods, but instead pollute one another through mutual imitation in filthy deeds.

In the second section, it says that they will receive the evils which they have inflicted upon the Christian people.

In the third, it urges the faithful peoples to endure the troubles of the world with equanimity until the judgment of Majesty arrives, when all the blessed will unquestionably receive the good things which the Lord promises.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“The fool said in his heart: ‘There is no God.’”

### Verse 2

“They are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires; there is no one who does good, not even one.”

If we examine this again, a categorical syllogism arises for us in the following form:

The foolish are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires.

All who are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires say in their hearts: “There is no God.”

Therefore the foolish say in their hearts: “There is no God.”

Let us now proceed to explain more precisely what has been set forth.

The verb “to speak” properly belongs to the tongue, not the heart. But because the power of the divinity understands our thoughts, it is rightly said that the heart of the fool speaks—something that could reach the Lord’s ears, not for pardon but for vengeance [ed., “judgment”], just as the Lord says in Genesis: “I will descend and see whether they have fulfilled by their deeds the cry that has come to me” (Gen. XVIII, 21), and so forth.

For whoever detracts from the omnipotent Word on any pretext and does not submit to Catholic principles is certainly a fool, because he has despised the gifts of true wisdom.

This person therefore denies God in his heart. For if he truly believed in God, he would commit no sin against him through any depravity.

And so that you might recognize this fool through his manifold errors, he appropriately adds the plural number, saying: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires.”

All heretics are marked by this one statement. To have failed to believe rightly in God is corruption, because those who become entangled in deadly persuasions depart from the life-giving sense.

The most just punishment follows them: they become abominable in their desires because they obey corrupt perceptions.

He adds: “There is no one who does good, not even one.” This figure is called *anaphora*, that is, repetition, whenever one word is repeated frequently.

This was the labor of the Church, full of grief, as she gave birth: that amid such a multitude of the lost there was no one able to do good.

This should be understood only of those who, placed outside the faith, persist in detestable obstinacy. For you can recognize that this is what is meant by what he will say below: “Those who devour my people.” There he designates those who openly persecute the faithful people with ravenous mouths.

### Verse 3

“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.”

Truly the Lord looked down from heaven—that is, from each of his preachers, whom he inhabits as though they were heaven. He looked upon the children of men when he caused himself to be beneficially preached by the apostles and prophets, so that the Gentiles, who had been ignorant that he was God, might recognize him through them by manifest truth.

And truly he looked upon the children of men with great compassion, so that he might not destroy those who were erring, but save those who repented through pious confession.

There follows: “To see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.” Since God knows hidden things and knows everything before it happens, it is said here that he “sees”—that is, makes visible—as was also said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear the Lord your God” (Gen. XXII, 12).

This figure is called *hypallage*, that is, transposition, whenever we say that one sees or knows who in fact makes us see or know.

This was said so that unbelievers might have no excuse, since the Lord Christ had been made known to all nations through preaching long beforehand.

### Verse 4

“All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one.”

He speaks of those who, with hardened hearts, remained in a criminal purpose. We can understand “all” partially, so that it applies only to those who are blinded by wicked persuasions.

The words descend in a beautiful order. First they turned aside; then it followed that they became useless to themselves.

He adds: “There is no one who does good, not even one.” That grief of the thoughts, like a birth bursting forth, has poured out. He repeats the words because he could find no fruitful remedy in their obstinate perceptions.

Therefore the Church rightly declares her grief on behalf of those from whom the faithful people could receive no improvement.

When he says “not even one,” all are denied. For if he had wished one person to be understood as good, he would not have said “not even one,” but “except one.”

Observe that he removed the five verses of the thirteenth psalm which are appropriately applied to the Jews, so that he might transfer the entire meaning generally and absolutely to all unbelieving peoples.

### Verse 5

“Will they not understand, all who work iniquity, who devour my people as though eating bread? They have not called upon God.”

He comes to the second part, where the Church of God rebukes those who transgress against the Christian people.

By saying, “Will they not understand?” he confirms that they will understand, because they ought not to do what they presume to do through criminal iniquity. The very word makes this clear through its inverted syllables: it should be understood as “lest they not understand.”

This figure is called *anastrophe*, in Latin *perversio* (“inversion”), whenever words are spoken in an altered order.

They “work iniquity” who strive to tear apart the Lord’s faithful, who oppress widows and strip orphans contrary to his commandments.

He says “who devour,” that is, swallow down and consume them with the full speed of their crimes.

Nor is it without significance that he says “my people,” showing that all the preceding statements were spoken about the worst people, since he testifies that they devour his people as an increase of their wickedness.

For if you wish to understand that statement generally of the human race, as some do, this distinction will appear unsuitable.

And to show the avidity of their tearing apart, he adds: “As though eating bread,” namely, something that is always desired and used. Although at different times we are satisfied with a variety of foods, bread nevertheless remains our constant nourishment.

He also adds: “They have not called upon God.” He returns to the consolation of the faithful, because the things sinners do against the Lord’s will are quickly destroyed in the end, and whatever exists apart from him vanishes into the ethereal air like smoke.

### Verse 6

“There they trembled with fear where there was no fear.”

The sinners of this world, thinking about the good things of the present life, are more afraid in this world that they may be deprived of the happiness they have obtained, that they may not fully enjoy the riches they have discovered, and that they may lose the honors they have acquired.

Here the living fear losing what they nevertheless know they must leave behind according to the human condition. They do not think about those things by which they will be tormented with true fear, when there will be weeping and the gnashing of teeth.

Therefore “where there was no fear” must be understood as “where there was no just fear.”

### Verse 7

“For God will scatter the bones of those who please themselves; they were confounded, because God rejected them.”

This verse was not spoken in the thirteenth psalm, but has newly been added here to confirm the time of judgment, because he is going to say everything concerning that subject—something which, as has been said, does not seem capable of fitting there because of the difference in the title. For in the future judgment God scatters their bones, that is, their extremely hardened obstinacies, whose insolence he knows to have become terribly hardened. He also added, “of those who please themselves,” which is recognized as applying particularly to criminals. For the just man is always displeasing to himself, while he chastises the vices of his flesh through heavenly reflection. He understands that the part from which he knows he will arrive at eternal punishments must not be indulged.

But with sinners the opposite is true: they love what will destroy them; they desire what will condemn them; and they take pleasure in the evil through which they will endure everlasting punishments, as was already said in the tenth psalm: “But the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6). He added, “They were confounded, because God rejected them.” Such people, who please themselves, must be confounded, because it is certain that they are shut out from the kingdom of Christ almighty.

### Verse 8

“Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion, when the Lord turns back the captivity of his people?”

The joyful mother Church now comes to the third section, returning to the text of the thirteenth psalm, so that, just as she made the beginning similar, she might also conclude it with an ending corresponding to that one. “Who will give” must be understood as “unless you, Lord?” These are the words of one who believes, not of one who doubts.

By “from Zion” he means that blessed vision in which the Lord is seen and the Majesty itself is received by the true light of the heart. This is the salvation of Israel, that is, the salvation which grants life to the faithful people who behold God. He added, “when the Lord turns back the captivity of his people.” This means: while the devout people still appears in this world to be captive amid the anxieties of tribulations, since it has not yet been able to reach the remedies of the promised freedom. For as long as he liberates his faithful from this world, he also gives salvation to Israel here from Zion, when he consoles the labors of the saints with his benefits.

### Verse 9

“Jacob will rejoice, and Israel will be glad.”

This verse recalls the future happiness, when the Lord’s faithful will rejoice in complete freedom. And observe that in the general resurrection the patriarch Jacob is frequently mentioned, because of the words: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I, 2–3). It is entirely fitting that the beloved one is placed in such a commemoration of time, where joy is without end.

He added, “and Israel will be glad.” We have said that Israel is interpreted as “the man who sees God.” This is undoubtedly granted to the Church at that time, when, as was promised to her, she will be happily established in the eternal homeland.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

We must consider with the greatest care this variation and equality of the psalms, when they are shown to agree in their words but to differ in their meaning. For they most fully reveal the radiant dignity of divine speech, so that, while preserving the faith, we ought to understand different things in the same expressions.

For if the colors of precious stones have been given the capacity to shine with varied light; if certain birds have been granted the ability to gleam with different colors; if human eyes see the chameleon in one and the same body now green, now blue, now rose-colored, now pale, why should divine utterances not possess a diversity of interpretation, since they are often compared even with the depths? For the sea shines with varied light through its trembling movement.

This is also why the orthodox Fathers say different things about one passage, and yet all are heard profitably. Hence one of our authors has said: “The divine word is indeed a pearl, and it can be pierced from every side.”

We should also remember that this is the psalm which was uttered concerning the rebuke and conversion of the Jews. Just as they are now continually rebuked through both Testaments, so the remnant of them will be saved at the end of the age.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 53

“To the end; in songs: David’s understanding, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: ‘Is not David hidden among us?’”

“To the end” is well known to signify Christ. “In songs,” that is, in the work of the present psalm. A song is something that proceeds according to the feet of a particular meter and is contained within established rules, just as the whole Psalter is composed in the Hebrew language. This song, therefore, signifies the praises of Christ.

“David’s understanding” announces the Lord Savior, whom David, always understanding him profitably (*proficue*; ed., *perspicue*, “clearly”), desired with intense longing to come for salvation.

It follows: “when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: ‘Is not David hidden among us?’” Here again the history of the Books of Kings is introduced (1 Kings XXIII, 19), for the Ziphites were so called from the village of Syria in which Ziph dwelt. They came to Saul and betrayed that David was concealed among them. But, displaying (*exerentes*; ed., *exercentes*, “practicing”) their malice, they were entirely unable to harm the holy man.

Now let us see what peoples these names signify, so that the mysteries of this psalm may become more evident. The Ziphites signify “flourishing ones,” which is what is granted to sinners in this world. David, however, bore the figure of the Lord the Savior, through whom the Christian people is represented. In this likeness, therefore, it is fittingly expressed that here the faithless are flourishing and free, while the faithful are hidden and confined. Hence the prophet now prays to be delivered from such people, lest he be betrayed into the hands of his enemies through their treachery.

### Division of the Psalm

Delivered from Saul’s danger, the prophet gives thanks to the Lord throughout the whole psalm, because the treachery of the Ziphites was unable to harm him. In the first part he prays that his most powerful enemies may not prevail in oppressing him. In the second place he entreats, with spiritual piety, that his adversaries should be converted. This is fitting for every Christian to ask: that he may be liberated from the flourishing ones of this world in such a way that the grace of conversion is not denied to them.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“O God, save me by your name, and deliver me by your power.”

The figure is a *hirmos*, that is, a joining or correspondence, which occurs when the sequence of a prayer preserves its continuity all the way to the end. This figure is recognized as extending through the whole section of the psalm.

The prophet prays to be delivered from the malice of his persecutors in the name of the Lord the Savior. Many in this world seem to themselves to be saved for the present, but not in the Lord’s name—for example, when someone appears to be relieved of certain present illnesses by amulets or sacrilegious incantation; or when someone is freed from a crime he has committed through the mass of money offered to a corrupt judge.

This man, however, asks that the kind of safety which comes from the Lord be granted to him, so that, persevering here in wholly sincere faith, he may be saved from the plague of this world through the soundness of mind bestowed by God.

It follows: “and deliver me by your power.” Above he asked that in this world he might receive healing in the Lord’s name; now he asks that in the future judgment he may be delivered by the Lord’s power. For just as here he came in the weakness of the body, so there he will appear in the powers of his majesty.

Thus, in one verse, these two things are fulfilled which religious people chiefly ought to seek. Every faithful person rightly says this; the Christian people rightly says it.

### Verse 2

“O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.”
