He repeats the name of the Almighty, so that, when God is invoked frequently, help may not be delayed. But because he could hear a silent prayer, he added, “give ear to the words of my mouth,” so that he might hear not only the prompting of the heart but also the utterance (*affatum*; ed., *affectum*, “feeling”) of the voice.

The word “give ear” is especially well placed, because we are properly said to perceive those things which we store in the secret chamber of the mind.

### Verse 3

“For strangers have risen up against me, and the strong have sought my life; they have not set God before their eyes.”

The cause of the prayer mentioned above is now explained. But since the Ziphites are known to have been from the tribe of Judah, from which the prophet also derived his origin, why did he say that strangers had risen up against him?

Here, however, he does not wish “strangers” to be understood as men of foreign origin, but as those who have made themselves strangers to the Lord by their deeds. Rightly so, because when he sought from them help for his defense, he found among them instead the ambushes of treachery.

By “the strong” he wishes Saul and his servants to be understood: royal power raised him up, while the jealousy of a mad mind armed him.

It follows: “they have not set God before their eyes.” The one who sets God before his eyes is the one who believes that God is present everywhere and easily recognizes what the human will strives to accomplish.

But the lost do not set God before their eyes because they believe that he does not know what they conceive in their criminal minds. This is the devout prayer he desired to have heard: that those whom it was clear did not have God before their eyes might not be permitted to carry out their wishes.

### Verse 4

“For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul.”

He comes to the second section, where, after the most devoted holiness of prayer, he promises himself the Lord’s help through spiritual confidence.

He said, “helps,” namely, the one who is laboring, so that he might be able to bear what the impious were striving to gather against him.

He then explains what this help is: “and the Lord is the protector of my soul.” The one whom he protects he not only helps in labors but also, in his mercy, absolves from all sins.

Observe that he says, “my soul,” so that, even if the body is exposed to dangers, the soul’s salvation may nevertheless remain unharmed. God knows how especially to guard it in his saints, and through it he is believed to crown a person in the judgment with abundant mercy.

### Verse 5

“Turn away evils from my enemies; in your truth destroy them.”

When the prophet recognized that he had been freed from the persecution of his enemies through the Lord’s mercy, he is shown to offer this sacrifice of good will: he strives to pray for his enemies in every way, something which divine mercy customarily receives gladly.

He therefore prays that evil will may be removed from his enemies, by which he knew they were being burdened.

It follows: “in your truth destroy them.” When the wicked come to the truth, they perish from their former intention; and unless someone departs from his purpose of iniquity, he will have no place among good deeds.

Let the Ziphites therefore perish, lest they betray the one who is hidden; let Saul perish, lest he persecute the innocent.

### Verse 6

“I will sacrifice to you willingly, and I will confess your name, O Lord, because it is good.”

The one who prays for his enemies out of devotion to piety sacrifices willingly to the Lord. For the person who asks vengeance on his enemies, who desires to avenge himself through the calamities of others, or who prays on account of other desires of the world, does not sacrifice willingly to the Lord, because he does not pray out of love for him but appeals to his power because of some necessity concerning worldly affairs.

To sacrifice willingly to the Lord is to offer the purity of a good will, and for this reason alone to worship, fear, or love him: because he is God, because he is the Creator, because he is shown to be the merciful disposer of all things.

Those who continually give thanks amid the distress of sufferings also sacrifice willingly to God, as the holy man Job is remembered to have done.

It follows: “and I will confess your name, O Lord, because it is good.” This responds very appropriately to what came before: in whose power he had been saved, to that one’s name he would offer the sacrifice of confession.

Here “to confess” means “to praise,” because this word, as we have often said, is a homonym. He added, “because it is good.” To wish to praise him is an immeasurable good; through it the holy mind is refreshed and the adversity of this world is escaped.

### Verse 7

“For you have delivered me from every tribulation, and your eye has looked upon my enemies” [MS A: “my eye”].

Just as in the first section he gave the reasons for his prayer at the end, so now he adds the reason for his confession. Although he seemed to have sacrificed willingly to the Lord, God had nevertheless granted what he knew would be beneficial.

The prophet testifies that he was delivered from all tribulations through the Lord’s power. This cannot happen in this world except to those who persevere in the Lord’s love.

The Lord’s eye looked upon his enemies, the Ziphites, when he did not permit them to fulfill their wicked plans. For God frequently, in his mercy, does not permit us to carry out evil deeds, so that, pierced with remorse, we may be compelled to pray concerning our errors. Thus Saul was prevented when he was sent by the priests to Damascus to devastate the Church of Christ with the fiercest persecution (Acts IX, 1). He was not permitted to act with such great success that he could thereby have reached eternal punishments.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This prophetic supplication and the devoted simplicity of holy prayer offer a most useful example for our life: when we are oppressed by the Ziphites, that is, by the flourishing ones of this world, we should not be provoked into petty quarrels, but, sacrificing willingly to the Lord, we should be freed from every tribulation through his benefits.

Let us strive to confess him with complete sincerity, so that, even though ignorant, we may deserve to be released from our chains. A great model of petition has plainly been expressed, so that, whenever any dangers threaten, we may pray with a calm and confident mind [MS A, F: “confessing”], since he knows how to deliver us from all tribulations—provided that he understands it to be beneficial for us here.

For we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should (Rom. VIII, 26); we are surrounded by the darkness of ignorance and confounded by harmful sins.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 54

“To the end; in songs: David’s understanding.”

“To the end” has indeed been said frequently. It will nevertheless not be tiresome to repeat it, if it can be explained in another way as well.

Christ is rightly called the End, because whatever we do rightly and faithfully is unquestionably to be referred to him; or because he came at the end of the ages, as the Apostle says: “In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son” (Heb. I, 2).

This was also signified by what Moses said: “You shall kill the lamb at evening” (Exod. XII, 6).

“In songs” means “in praises.” For he admonishes us, whether in sorrow or in joy, continually to sound forth the Lord’s praises—as this psalm is going to do—and never to depart from his praise. For with a father’s affection, when he chastises, he corrects; when he consoles, he comforts. Both things therefore benefit us, if thanksgiving does not depart from our mouth.

It follows: “of understanding, of David.” This is certainly David’s understanding: according to the flesh we call him the Father of the Lord Christ, just as the blind man cries out in the Gospel: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Luke XVIII, 40). But according to his divinity we confess him to be a servant, just as he himself says in the hundred-and-ninth psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1).

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm, with two *diapsalmata*—like twin eyes appropriately set in place—the words of the Lord the Savior are presented according to the form of a servant. By declaring that form in its complete particularity, he has given us a most salutary example of humility.

In the first section he asks that the prayer of those placed in tribulation not be despised, entreating the swiftness of deliverance which he was shown to seek from the weakness of the flesh.

In the second place he asks that the iniquities of the Jews be destroyed, because contradiction of the truth existed in their city.

In the third place he says what he knew would happen to the obstinate Jews on account of their crimes.

After this, a pious consolation is introduced, lest any of the faithful be terrified upon hearing the Judge’s severity.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Hear my prayer, O God, and do not despise my supplication.”

The Lord Christ, who came to us in merciful compassion to save us, giving us a pattern of life and salvation, voluntarily placed in the disturbances of the world through the dispensation in which he suffered, first asks in the opening verse that his prayer be heard. Then he asks that his supplication not be despised.

But all this is said because God was willing to be man. For he could first be heard and afterward be despised. This happens to those who desire the good things of this world: they receive what they ask for, and yet afterward are despised, because they did not seek eternal rewards.

### Verse 2

“Attend to me and hear me; I am sorrowful in my exercise, and I am troubled.”

First comes attention, then the hearing of the suppliant’s voice. No one who has turned away hears; rather, the one to whom a tranquil gaze is granted is also provided with the most peaceful ears, as it is said in another psalm: “Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God” (Ps. XII, 4).

Then the reason for the complete prayer is supplied: “I am sorrowful in my exercise, and I am troubled.” In one beautiful statement the course of the Lord the Savior’s life is explained.

We call an “exercise” something that rests through no relaxation and no leisure, but, intent upon continual labor, perseveres in the glory of virtue. He was exercised through miracles; he was exercised through the holiness of his teaching. But he was especially sorrowful because the faithless were not shown to produce the fruit of righteousness, as the evangelist says: “And he was sorrowful over Jerusalem, and he wept” (Luke XIX, 41).

O goodness of the most merciful Creator! He says that he was sorrowful and troubled because the madness of the obstinate people did not believe his saving preaching.

### Verse 3

“Because of the voice of the enemy and the tribulation of the sinner; for they have turned iniquity against me, and in anger they troubled me.”

“Because of the voice of the enemy and the tribulation of the sinner” must be understood as “deliver me,” so that the division of the verses may agree with the authority of the Hebrew wording.

He asks to be delivered from the voice of the enemy when the Jewish people said of him: “If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. XXVII, 42). He therefore asks that this voice of the faithless be overcome when the resurrection is seen.

The tribulation of the sinner occurred when they spat upon him with sacrilegious mouths, struck him with slaps and whips, and multiplied insults upon the blows.

It follows: “for they have turned iniquity against me, and in anger they troubled me.” The rush of the raging people is described as the course of a river. They turned iniquity against the Lord because, unwilling to accept any reason, they desired the shedding of innocent blood.

Observe how great causes are explained in individual words. He says that the Jews were vehemently inflamed, whom burning anger was driving headlong toward crime. As for what concerned himself, he said, “they troubled me,” which is what ordinarily happens to us when we are made restless by excessive insolence.

Let the foolish Jews hear that they troubled the Lord alone, but brought perpetual ruin upon themselves.

### Verse 4

“My heart was troubled within me, and the fear of death fell upon me.”

Here again the humility of his humanity is expressed. For although his mind was troubled according to the law of the flesh, nevertheless, through the protection of his divinity, he conquered the pains and torments of the body.

If God’s power accomplishes this in his martyrs, how much more, in the dispensation of his flesh, could the violent sensation of torments not prevail over him?

By suffering he fulfilled the reality of a human being; but by conquering such things through himself, he also declared that he was God.

He added: “and the fear of death fell upon me.” The corresponding things are appropriately attributed to him. For it followed that the one whose heart had been troubled would also be invaded by the fear of death.

Let us examine his words: “the fear of death fell upon me.” It truly fell, when it came upon him, but could no longer prevail thereafter as it had been able to do. For by the Lord’s momentary death, perpetual death was conquered—the death that claimed dominion over the human race—as the Apostle says: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. XV, 54–55).

### Verse 5

“Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me.”

He describes the manner of our departure with the most exact particularity. We fear death first, then tremble, because this separation of body and soul cannot occur without the greatest disturbance.

It follows: “and darkness covered me.” The nearness of death brought the appearance of darkness beforehand, because we frequently perceive in our minds the things concerning which the fear of what is coming usually troubles us.

### Verse 6

“And I said: Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I will fly and rest?”

After the mortal disturbances and the need of true humanity, it was necessary to seek the deliverance which he knew was to be bestowed upon him.

For he says: “Who will give me”—that is, unless you, Father, who, bringing human nature all the way to the realms of heaven, will place it at your right hand?

Wings are so called from *pendere*, “to hang,” because they suspend the bodies of birds in the ethereal air with lofty lightness.

But observe that he does not ask to be given the wings of an eagle, hawk, or swallow, which fly more swiftly than all these, but those of a dove. The dove is so called as though it were “the nursling of a cell,” because it lives without burdening another. It is an innocent and gentle bird, which attacks no animal with a savage will and in no way consents to filthy foods.

Therefore the Lord Christ rightly desired the wings of a dove, in whose form the Holy Spirit also appeared above him when he was baptized (Matt. III, 16).

It follows: “And I will fly, and I will rest.” “I will fly,” that is, “I will transport myself with the swiftest speed.” This signifies when he avoided the troubles caused by the Jews, so that he might rest from their iniquity. The following verse also shows this.

### Verse 7

“Behold, I have fled far away, and I remained in solitude.”

He recalls those passages in the Gospel when, through frequent miracles, he provoked seditions against himself among the faithless in every way.

Mark says: “And rising very early, he went out and departed into a deserted place, and there he prayed” (Mark I, 35, 45); and shortly afterward it follows: “so that he could no longer openly enter a city, but was outside in deserted places.”

He went far away from his persecutors in order to remove the occasion of anger from their mad minds. He remained in solitude so that he might enjoy the purity of undisturbed seclusion. By such an action he admonishes us that, when we are weighed down by some burden of iniquity, we ought to rest in the secrecy of our conscience.

Alternatively, it can be understood in this way: departing from the faithless Jews, he remained in the solitude of the Gentiles. The prophet testifies that the Gentiles are called “solitude,” saying: “Rejoice, thirsty desert; let the desert exult, and let it flower like a lily; let the deserts of the Jordan flower and exult” (Isa. XXXV, 1).

### Verse 8

“I awaited the one who saved me from faintness of spirit and tempest.”

He comes to the second section. After the intervening *diapsalma*, he has also changed the subject. He had said that he rested in solitude; now he declares that he awaits the Father’s protection, who was able to save him from bodily weakness [MS A: “heal”].

He did not consider himself secure because of solitude, since he still relied upon the Father’s protection. He thus offers us an example of a most salutary instruction: we should place our confidence not in the help of anyone else, but solely in his deliverance.

And because he had earlier said that he was troubled, he now testifies that he had been faint-hearted. These and similar expressions must be referred to the nature of his humanity.

“Little” is derived from *pugillo*, “a fist”: something small and very brief, as much as the capacity of a closed hand can contain. By “tempest” he means the storms of seditions, which the headlong Jews stirred up like waves.

### Verse 9

“Cast them down, O Lord, and divide their tongues, because I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city.”

Here he prays for the Jewish people in a salutary manner, that through the division of their tongues they might not bring their malice to fulfillment, just as happened at that tower which men attempted to extend high into the sky out of fear of a renewed flood, where the division and confusion of tongues first occurred (Gen. XI, 4).

Previously, as we suppose, the world used only the Hebrew language. But it must especially be fixed in the mind that God divided the tongues in anger, while in mercy he united them in his apostles: there, so that they might not fulfill their vain desires; here, so that all nations might recognize the preaching of the truth through their own language.

He said, “Cast them down,” so that they might not fortify their thoughts through wicked plotting. “Divide,” so that they might not flow together into a destructive unity.

It follows: “because I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city.” He rightly asked that those whom he foreknew to be wicked in their sacrilegious gatherings should be divided. And he rightly sought solitude, because he knew that iniquity existed in their city.

### Verse 10

“Day and night iniquity will surround it upon its walls; and labor in its midst, and injustice.”

### Verse 11

“And usury and deceit have not ceased from its streets.”

In these two verses, the appalling character of ancient Jerusalem is reasonably accused in three ways.

He says: “Day and night,” that is, at all times, “iniquity will surround it upon its walls,” so that, to the extent that the structure of the walls could rise upward, arrogant malice would stretch itself out there even more.

It follows: “and labor in its midst, and injustice.” First he mentioned the walls, so as to include all the inhabitants; now he mentions the middle of the city, designating the nobles and leading men, who always wish to appear established in the center, in an honorable seat.

They were possessed not by law or reason, but by labor and injustice. “Labor” refers to the practice of oppression; “injustice” concerns wicked judgments.

He adds a third mode: “and usury and deceit have not ceased from its streets.” Let us note that he did not say “secretly,” but that such things were committed in the streets—things which the heavenly law condemned.

Concerning usury it is said: “The one who has not given his money at interest” (Ps. XIV, 5). Concerning deceit: “And let not your lips speak deceit” (Ps. XXXIII, 14). They did not commit these things secretly, but practiced them, as it were, with open iniquity. For every evil becomes more execrable when it is practiced publicly and presumptuously.

Remember, however, that figure of speech which signifies the whole by a part. For many people were found there who received the sacred preaching with devout minds.

### Verse 12

“For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him.”

In this verse and the two that follow, the treacherous Judas is reproached, because he could have been guarded against if he had been an open enemy. For how could one regard as suspect someone who appeared to be a disciple?

He says: “For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it,” because he truly would have come forward to hurl insults, and what is not unexpected ought to be accepted patiently.

And understand how humble a word he used when he said, “I would have endured it,” a word which custom has derived from human footwear. It is therefore not unusual that he should say, “I would have endured it,” since he also compared himself with beetles and worms.

This figure, as has often been mentioned, is called *metriasmos*, that is, moderation or restraint.

It follows: “and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him.” Here too an example of extraordinary patience is shown: he did not burst into quarrels against enemies speaking great things, that is, arrogant things, nor resist with some altercation, but yielded ground to their mad words.

And lest the speech of the malevolent continue to pursue his holy mind, he said that he would hide himself, so that their insolence would necessarily cease when they no longer saw their adversary.

### Verse 13

“But you, a man of one mind, my leader and my acquaintance.”

This verse and the following one are indeed to be read as reproaches. But let us consider with what patience: he is still called “of one mind,” still “a leader,” still “an acquaintance,” although he was known in every respect to be a future enemy and most cruel betrayer.

“Of one mind” refers to the fact that he was among the apostles. “Leader” refers to the fact that he was sent ahead to villages and towns so that he might imbue inexperienced minds with the preaching of the word. A leader is properly called the one who goes ahead on a journey.

“Acquaintance” refers to the fact that his betrayal was not hidden, since the Lord Christ foretold at the banquet (*convivii*; ed., *communi*, “common”) meal that he was the betrayer; and elsewhere he says: “Did I not choose you twelve? Yet one of you is a devil” (John VI, 71).

### Verse 14

“You who together with me received sweet foods; with one accord we walked in the house of God.”

Guilt to which [ed., “when”] exceptional benefits are reckoned grows greater. This figure is called *emphasis*.

For every kind of malignity is softened by the eating of food, and the one who is soothed by the pleasure of a sweet table is not usually savage.

It is therefore fitting that we understand bodily foods to have been charged against the foolish man, which alone he could consider sweet. For if he had wished to retain the doctrinal foods which he had previously received, he would not have proceeded to such sacrilege. Concerning these foods it was said to the faithful: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9).

It follows: “in the house of God we walked with one accord,” that is, in the Jerusalem temple, where he appeared to be among the Lord’s disciples, so that he might be summoned and proceed with them and follow their fellowship together.

The agreement of the treacherous man concerns gatherings and processions, not the firm holiness of his purpose.

And so that the connection of the words may stand clearly, “Why did you betray me?” must be joined to this verse and the preceding one.

### Verse 15

“Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell, because wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst.”

Although above he spoke of Judas individually, he now turns, through a sentence concerning common punishment, to the Jews.

But it may be asked why he said, “Let death come upon them,” and added, “and let them descend alive into hell,” since it cannot happen that someone both dies and descends alive to the underworld.

This must rather be understood spiritually, because according to his custom he asks that correction rather than destruction come upon his enemies.

Death is called the end of life; and the one who is converted to a better way is rightly judged to have found the end of his former manner of life.

The living descend into hell, as our smallness seems to understand it, when they dread their worst thoughts and are transferred by divine grace to the path of better instruction. Thus we descend alive, as it were, into hell when we are terrified by the remembrance of our evils.

By such an interpretation we escape the question mentioned above.

He also rightly asks that those be converted who have received wickedness in their breast as though in a lodging place. He appropriately said “lodging,” to show that malice is not natural but received through a kind of temporary hospitality.

By saying “in their midst,” he designates their innermost hearts, so that the most destructive thought might be shown to possess the human heart.

### Verse 16

“But I cried to God, and the Lord heard me.”

After the rebukes of the wicked had been given first, as was fitting, he returned to his own desires and prayers, bringing forth words in the form of a servant.

For he continually cried to God, conducting himself in a divine manner of life; and it was fitting that he should be heard, since he could not be separated from his own majesty.

This figure is called *prosphonesis*, in Latin “exclamation”: whenever, amid other things that we are saying, we suddenly turn our words toward God.

### Verse 17

“Evening, morning, and midday I will recount and announce, and he will hear my voice.”

Let us attend with the mind, because these words announce great mysteries to us.

“Evening” signifies the time of the betrayal, when Judas is known to have handed him over to the cohorts that were seeking him.

“Morning” refers to when he was brought before Pontius Pilate to be heard.

“Midday” refers to the sixth hour, when, as the evangelist says, he was suspended on the cross. Midday is so called as though it meant “the middle of the day.”

The following words correspond to these times. “I will recount” pertains to evening, because it is clear that he spoke of everything which the most wicked Judas was planning to do.

“I will announce” corresponds to morning, when, after Pilate said, “You are the King of the Jews” (John XVIII, 33), he announced: “For this I was born,” and the other things which the Lord says there.

He also joined the words, “and he will hear my voice,” which pertains to midday, when on the cross he said: “It is finished,” and gave up his spirit (John XIX, 30).

O wondrous brevity! In this single little verse so great an action has been narrated that what is known to be explained at length is shown to have been gathered together in this brief statement.

### Verse 18

“He delivered my soul in peace from those who draw near to me, because they were with me among many.”

This is what he said above when he declared that his voice had been heard: that through the benefit of the resurrection his soul might be delivered in peace.

He then appropriately explains from whom it was delivered: namely, from those who draw near to him. He speaks of those who appeared to render service through feigned praises, while nevertheless favoring his enemies in their hearts; from them he rightly says that his soul was delivered.

For it was a most grievous kind of hostility to be adversaries in the heart while pretending to be devoted with the tongue.

### Verse 19

“God will hear, and will humble them, he who is before the ages.” He will certainly hear the things stated above [Col. 0391A]. He will humble them, that is, so that they may believe; so that those who through pride had turned away from the Christian faith may again recognize the light of truth through humility. For when it is added, “he who is before the ages,” the Word is indicated as coeternal with the Father, lest he appear to have come into existence at some point in time who created all the ages. Time itself began when the world received its beginning. Let the insane rashness of the Arians therefore cease from proclaiming the Creator of times as existing under time, while the only-begotten Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, remains unchangeably with the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 20

“For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God.” After the insertion of the *diapsalma*, he comes to the third section. Previously, in his customary piety, he wished the erring to be converted; now, knowing by the power of his divinity what would come, he says that the understanding of the faithless is unchangeable, because the hardness of their mind could not receive the truth. We must understand “change” in two ways: either the change that takes place here, when one passes from an obstinate will to a devout confession; or the change of which the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. XV, 51). Therefore whoever is not changed here cannot be changed there.

But the reason why such people will not be changed follows: “because they did not fear God.” For the one who fears God is changed from his faithlessness, choosing to obey the Lord’s commands through fear of judgment and devotion to charity. Notice that in this verse and in the two others that follow, he likewise states both their punishments and their faults.

### Verse 21

“He stretched out his hand in requital: they polluted his covenant.” These things are now spoken allegorically of what will be done with the faithless at the future judgment. “Hand” here signifies power and action, which will occur when that separation between the good and the evil has taken place. He also adds why the Jews will be overtaken by a most just punishment: because they polluted the Lord’s commandments by their wicked deeds and refused to believe what the truth of the Scriptures is known to have proclaimed to them. For, insofar as it depends on him, the one who does not obey God’s commands pollutes God’s covenant.

### Verse 22

“They were divided from the anger of his countenance; and his heart drew near.” He says what will happen at that judgment. The faithless are divided from the faithful people and, like straw destined to burn, separated from the grain. “From the anger of his countenance” expresses the time of judgment. For “anger” here means the vengeance that the impious will endure for their deeds. In all other respects, he decides everything unchangeably and calmly [ed., “discerns”].

He adds, “and his heart drew near.” He still explains that time when the heart of the Lord—that is, his will—will be made known to all. His heart drew near at that time when the whole human race will see with complete clarity what he foretold here through his prophets and proclaimed through the Apostles. But he subsequently explains why he does the things that have been mentioned.

### Verse 23

“They softened their words more than oil, yet they are arrows.” The faithless Jews softened their words when they said: “Teacher, we know that you came from God and teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. XXII, 16). For what in the world is gentler than oil? Yet he says that the words of the faithless were softened beyond oil by an extraordinary excess, so that nothing equal to such a crime could have been found.

They were also arrows when they said: “He is worthy of death” (Matt. XXVI, 66). Those words are shown to have accomplished what arrows do. O accursed contradiction—that human beings could speak gentle words while preparing to do such harsh things!

### Verse 24

“Cast your thought upon God, and he himself will nourish you; he will not permit the righteous person to waver forever.” While heavenly justice was speaking about the faithless Jews, it gave sound counsel to our weaknesses. The thought of this world continually afflicts us; if we do not cast it away, we are worn down, as Solomon says: “As a worm harms wood and a moth clothing, so sadness harms the heart” (Prov. XXV, 20).

But when the thought is cast upon the Lord, it not only does not consume us; it also nourishes us, so that what ordinarily diminishes us may seem to bring us increase.

It follows: “he will not permit the righteous person to waver forever.” The Lord’s judgment is true and unchangeable, provided that we understand with what integrity it was spoken. In this present life he does not remove the righteous from the world’s disturbances, because here he tests them temporarily, so that there he may find those whom he will crown. But forever, as he says here, he permits no one who is truly righteous to waver, when he is known to reign with them in eternity in perpetual peace. There the waves will never be stirred, where the harbor is always perfectly tranquil.

### Verse 25

“But you, God, will lead them into the pit of destruction.” [Col. 0392C] Since he has spoken about the righteous, he now speaks about the impious, who are to be plunged into the depths of Gehenna. A “pit” properly means an open chasm excavated in the hollows of the earth and containing water assigned for human use. But lest you understand this as a life-giving pit, he added “of destruction.” Concerning it we read elsewhere: “Nor let the pit open its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII, 16).

It is a deadly pit, a terrible plunge, where no space is granted and no breathing-room is afforded the wretched; instead, a dark obscurity surrounds them and removes the sight of pleasant light. By the likeness of the pit he warns us to fear the torments of Gehenna. O unheard-of mercy of the Judge! Everything is foretold to human beings so that punishable guilt may be avoided.

### Verse 26

“Men of blood and deceit will not complete half their days.” The Latin language does not accept the plural of *blood*, but we say that this is especially characteristic of divine Scripture. Properly speaking, “men of blood” does not refer to those who innocently shed human blood, since even righteous judges, constrained by the necessity of discipline—which restores peace to peoples—sometimes punish the guilty; and the person who repels violence sheds the blood of a most savage enemy, especially since we read that just wars were commanded by the Lord for holy men.

Therefore he added “and deceitful,” so that you would understand as guilty only the person who seeks another’s destruction through ambushes and the most wicked deceit. He does not say that such people complete their days, because while they promise themselves a long life, they encounter the end of the swiftest death.

[Col. 0393A] The days of all people are known to have been determined in predestination; but their days are “halved” whose end is shown to occur contrary to their own plans. For this reason “their own” was added, so that you would understand the days to be those they had planned for themselves, not ones established by the Lord.

“But I will hope in you, Lord.” It is beyond doubt that such people, whose end comes with extreme swiftness, hoped in themselves. But it is clear that the Lord and Savior, whose words these are, hoped in the Father in the form of a servant. Concluding the psalm of the Passion in his customary manner, he says that he hoped in the Lord, signifying that the hearts of the faithful must always be fixed in hope in the Lord.

For frequently the Head speaks in words that we must apply to the members. Therefore, as was already said in the thirty-fourth psalm, we must also seek the established structure of this hymn. First, because it was spoken from the person of the Lord Christ. Second, because it began with prayer. Third, because it recalled the events of the Lord’s Passion. Fourth, because it agreed with the words of the Gospel in harmonious truth. Fifth, because it concluded with great hope for the faithful, so that there is no doubt that the present psalm conforms to the prescribed rules.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

We have heard that the life-giver of creatures laid down his soul for the salvation of mortals. We have heard that the impassible God took on flesh and suffered for sinners. We have heard that the one coeternal with the Father underwent the punishment of death. O immeasurable price, which redeemed the human race! O holocaust, which enabled us to escape eternal flames! Destruction that removed destruction; an end that bestowed a good destined to remain without end.

For when the sting of death came upon the innocent, it happened that death justly lost those whom it held liable. Hell swallowed its own destruction in the manner of fishes; and although it believed that it had seized its prey, it received its own predator instead, deceived.

For this reason Pope Leo, worthy of his own see, spoke beautifully when he said (Epistle 97, to Leo Augustus, ch. 2):

“Although the death of many martyrs was precious in the sight of the Lord, nevertheless the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of sins. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the courage of the faithful were born examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness. Their deaths were individual deaths, each one his own, and no one paid another’s debt by his own end. Among the sons of human beings, however, there arose one alone, Christ, who was truly the spotless Lamb, in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised.”

Grant, most merciful God, that you who in the flesh you assumed deigned to suffer for us may bestow on us a share in your kingdom. It must also be kept in mind that this is the third of those psalms that speak at greater length about the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM LV

“To the end, for the people who have been made far from the holy ones, David, in the inscription of the title, when the allophyles seized him in Geth.”

This title contains two mysteries. One part is from the Gospel up to the words “in the inscription of the title”; the other is from the Old Testament up to the end of the title. First he says, “To the end,” which has frequently been explained to signify Christ. Then: “for the people who have been made far from the holy ones, David, in the inscription of the title.”

We said in the Passion of the Lord that the inscription of the title was not erased because it had been prophesied long beforehand: “Do not destroy the inscription of the title.” But the Jewish people pressed Pontius Pilate to alter the inscription of this title contrary to the prophecies of the prophets, unwilling that their King should be called the one whom they rejected with deranged minds. This desire made them far from the holy ones, when the faithful eagerly hasten with their whole mind to have Christ called their King.

“When the allophyles seized him in Geth”: this is what the text of Kings relates (1 Kings XXVII, 2–3), namely, that David, terrified by Saul’s pursuit, believed he should hide himself among the allophyles in the city of Geth. But since we have said that all these things must be explained through mystical comparisons, Geth signifies a winepress, that is, the pressure which every Christian suffers. Yet it yields the richest fruit when it has been pressed down beneath the burden of tribulations.

Therefore it is fitting that the Church should speak in such a superscription: burdened by the persecutions of the allophyles, that is, of foreigners, she pours forth the abundant merits of the saints with generous freedom, like nectarous liquids.

## Division of the Psalm

Burdened by various afflictions, in the first section of the psalm Mother Church prays, nevertheless confident that she will be liberated from her raging enemies. In the second section she enumerates her own sufferings, giving thanks because she has been rescued from frequent dangers; nor does she say that she fears evils which she knows will quickly pass. In the third place she says that, in that future blessedness, she will continually sing praises to the Lord, who has liberated her from the adversity of this world.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Have mercy on me, Lord, because a human being has trampled me down; battling all day, he has afflicted me.” The virgin mother Church, who gives birth to faithful peoples and does not depart from her integrity, asks her heavenly Bridegroom with devout tears not to allow her to be oppressed by enemies, since she is still known to dwell amid the calamity of this world.

“Has trampled me down” refers to the winepress mentioned in the title, because as much wine is expressed as the grape is vigorously trodden. “Human being” here signifies the devil in an unqualified sense, just as the Lord says about him in the Gospel: “The enemy who sowed the weeds over it is the devil” (Matt. XIII, 28).

It follows: “Battling all day, he has afflicted me.” He describes what the holy Church suffers in this world, because she is known to endure the devil’s conflicts without any interruption, as the Apostle says: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of these darknesses” (Eph. VI, 12).

The war is grave because it is hidden; the struggle is difficult because one fights with a stronger adversary. For what is it like to engage an enemy and not see his ambushes? Our adversary neither grows weary through labor nor ever departs defeated; rather, he returns more savage in proportion to the degree to which he has happened to be overcome by divine grace.

We call this “war” a figure of speech, specifically *antiphrasis*, just as we call a grove a *lucus* although it does not shine, and a pool a *piscina* although it has no fish. Therefore let no one of the faithful complain that he is harassed by the devil’s continual machinations, because if we wish to belong to Christ, we must always endure the devil as our adversary here.

### Verse 2

“My enemies have trampled me all day; from the height of day, because many who battle me will fear.” It is certainly a most grievous kind of insult to reach the humiliation of the feet; yet from this comes what is offered upon the holy altars. Wine does not flow unless the grape is crushed beneath the feet. Thus the enemy tramples the Church in her members so that glorious merits may be born from them.

He repeats “all day,” so that you may truly understand that in this world no time is entirely free from such temptations. When he says “from the height of day,” he signifies this world, in which the height of pride swells. For just as Christ’s rule commands humility, so the devil’s practice urges the summits of ruinous exaltation.

But in order to express the great weight of her oppression, she says that she was trampled down from the height of pride, so that you would not think the weight light when she was pressed by so great a mass.

It follows: “because many who battle me will fear.” It is not without significance that he says “many,” rather than “all,” will fear: namely, because many of those who battle the Church are converted to the Lord and begin not to fear eternal destruction when they are added to the company of the blessed. But those who persist in their obstinacy will all fear the judgment of punishment for themselves when the Lord’s coming is revealed.

Happy is the change by which the faithful fear chastely here for a short time and are secure in that perpetual rejoicing. On the contrary, the lot of the unhappy is utterly harsh: here to rejoice briefly, and there to be tormented throughout eternity.

“But I will hope in you, Lord.” He states why she should not fear in the way the impious will fear: because she hopes in the Lord, who never disappoints [ms. A: “despises”] those who trust in him, as Solomon says: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been confounded? Or who has remained in his fear and been forsaken?” (Ecclus. II, 11–12).

### Verse 3

“In God I will praise my words all day; in God [ed., “the Lord”] I will hope; I will not fear what a human being can do to me.” She praises her words in God when she is known to attribute everything she speaks well—not to herself, but to divine gifts. “My” must therefore be understood not as words uttered by her own will, since such words are always evil, but as words granted by the Lord’s generosity. We rightly call things ours if we recognize that they have been granted to us as gifts of the Lord.

This must be done “all day,” that is, throughout the whole period of life, both when we are weighed down by adversity and when we are lifted up by prosperity.

It follows: “In God I will hope; I will not fear what a human being can do to me.” Unless it is examined carefully, this statement seems contrary to what came before. For after saying that she had been trampled down and attacked by a human being, and after requesting the Lord’s mercy in fear of the impending dangers, she now again asserts that she does not fear a human being.

Both statements are true. Previously, while she was looking upon present calamities—that is, those of this world—she feared; now, as she contemplates what is to come, she has cast off fear. For what could a human being inflict upon one who had placed her hope in that retribution of judgment? Let the hands of executioners rage and furnaces of fire be prepared: the Church, in her members, scorns every torment while she awaits the gifts of the Lord Savior.

### Verse 4

“All day they were cursing my words; all their plans [ms. A: ‘all their thoughts’] against me were for evil.” He comes to the second section, where she complains sorrowfully that the words of her preaching have continually been cursed by the faithless. Although she spoke the truth, she encountered detestable slanders. This applies to heretics or to Christians who conceal their wickedness, who, while hearing the Lord’s words, despise sayings that bring salvation.

It follows: “All their plans against me were for evil.” Plans ordinarily anticipate what is beneficial; the word derives from consulting. But so that you might understand that their deliberations rested on no goodness, he added “for evil,” lest you think that they had considered anything good in that deliberation.

### Verse 5

“They will dwell and hide; they themselves will watch my heel, as my soul has expected.” These deceitful Christians appear to inhabit the Church publicly, to follow her assemblies and the gatherings of peoples; but they conceal the poison of their perversity. They do not dare openly to reveal that they lack what they know to be the apostolic rules. It is an internal evil, an incurable wound, which, the more it is covered, the more it is injured by incurable corruption.

It follows: “They themselves will watch my heel.” This is the custom of the devil, or of those known to be his ministers: to look upon our heel—that is, our last or final part—with treacherous cunning, as the Lord said to the serpent: “She will watch your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. III, 15).

For the devil knows that our extremities are judged, and he wishes to overturn them so that we may reach the dangers of guilt. He added: “as my soul has expected,” that is, as I foresaw beforehand, as I was instructed, as I received from the Lord the rule of preaching.

### Verse 6

“For nothing you will save them; in anger you will break the peoples, God.” Those whom he earlier called plotters who concealed themselves under poisonous pretense, he now promises will easily be saved through the Lord’s grace, so that no one among the erring should be despaired of, even when he is known to be guilty.

When he says, “For nothing you will save them,” he signifies that God grants everything freely under his mercy [ed., “under his own mercy”], and does not demand anyone’s merit by which that person might be saved through his own labor. For what did the thief deserve, that he should enter paradise so quickly? What did the tax collector deserve, who suddenly departed justified from the temple? He gave the sudden vow of confession, and he who granted the reward also granted the confession. It is therefore clear that sinners are saved for nothing, since conversion is granted by free generosity.

It follows: “In anger you will break the peoples, God.” Previously he had said that the wicked crowd was to be liberated; now he explains how it can be saved. The Lord’s justice, which is considered anger, breaks rebellious peoples. For when he has shaken their hearts through tribulations and filled them with a multitude of various distresses, they are recalled from iniquity and compelled to confess the Lord. It appears to happen through his anger, although he is calm and unchangeable and is known to bring about the causes of our salvation.

### Verse 7

“I declared my life to you; I placed my tears in your sight, as in your promise.” He declares his life to God who confesses his own sins, as the Apostle did when he said: “Previously I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man” (1 Tim. I, 13). For this is to give glory to God: publicly to declare what sort of people he has deigned to endure and bring to conversion, though our sins deserved that we perish.

Observe that he says “my life,” which is always shown to be blameworthy. For when do we not sin either by thought, offend by words, or commit wrongdoing through unstable action? Therefore, just as the faithless conceal their life, so the faithful declare theirs—not to make it known to God, who can in no way be ignorant of anything, but so that, by condemning themselves more fully, they may deserve absolution, as the prophet says: “First declare your sins, so that you may be justified” (Ps. XXXI, 5).

It follows: “I placed my tears in your sight.” Tears placed in God’s sight are pleasing, because they do not torment but free from torment. He poured out devout tears who prayed for his enemies, and for this reason deserved to obtain his request, because he is shown to have fulfilled the Lord’s command.

He added: “as in your promise.” For the Lord’s promise is that he will not reject devout tears, as he says in another psalm: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will rescue you, and you will glorify me” (Ps. XLIX, 15).

### Verse 8

“My enemies will turn back; on whatever day I call upon you, behold, I have known that you are my God.” He says that the enemies will turn back so that, by persevering on their path, they may not be taught to complete their worst errors. For the one who turns back from evil abandons the guilt of his faithlessness. Thus the Lord speaks graciously, not angrily, to the Apostle Peter: “Go back, Satan” (Mark VIII, 33). When this happens to the erring, the error of their former perversity departs.

It follows: “on whatever day I call upon you.” Here he proclaims the Lord’s mercy and wondrous compassion: whenever he is called upon, he always forgives in mercy. “On whatever day” signifies satisfactions made at different times. One person entreats the Lord for nearly his entire life; another is converted in middle age; another is saved at the end of life. This is what “on whatever day” means, because the Lord in merciful patience awaits whatever time we choose for conversion. Therefore he tolerates the guilty and waits for the erring, saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 23).

The only opportunity is to confess every sin in this life, where we fall through human weakness. He added: “Behold, I have known that you are my God.” It is a sweet confession and a true proof, so that he himself might recognize that what he had sought with great desire had been fulfilled.

It follows: “for you are my God.” Although the Lord is generally the God of all of us, we confidently say “my God” when we rejoice that he is able to look upon us.

### Verse 9

“In God I will praise the word, and in the Lord I will proclaim the saying.” These are truly recognized as the words of the orthodox Church. In the Father she promises to praise the Son, so that whatever is said about the one may likewise be understood of the other. For when we proclaim the Father eternal and omnipotent, we undoubtedly confess the Son eternal and omnipotent. Their praise is one, because their power is one and their glory undivided, since their nature is indivisible.

Finally, he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10–11). What, I ask, does the Father lack of the Son, since he has the nature of the omnipotent Son? Or what does the Son lack of the Father, since he has the nature of the omnipotent Father? Their substance is truly one, because nothing unlike or discordant is found in their essence. You find neither more nor less here, except what the Arian heresy invents for itself.

This rule of unity and equality also unquestionably embraces the Holy Spirit as consubstantial with the Father and the Son, because the Holy Trinity is one God. Nor can anyone give glory to one person who has not understood that he offered it jointly to all.

It must certainly be known that the most learned Augustine, in the fifteenth book of *The Trinity* (ch. 17), says:

“The Holy Spirit, according to the divine Scriptures, belongs neither to the Father alone nor to the Son alone, but is established as belonging to both.”

Therefore the love of the Father and the Son is united, although the Spirit himself is also perfect love. He proves this in many ways in his exposition of the Epistle of Saint John, saying more openly in the seventh homily: “For whoever does not have love of his brother certainly does not have the Holy Spirit.”

It follows: “and in the Lord I will proclaim the saying.” Here he comes to the Lord Christ, who, one of the Trinity, is “the Word made flesh and dwelling among us” (John I, 14). The Church rightly promises to praise his sayings—that is, his teachings—because he gave the human race a rule for living and salvation. Truly, his sayings are to be proclaimed everywhere, through which the salvation of the world could be restored by heavenly compassion.

These are the two holy realities that the mother promises to proclaim, which grant eternal preservation to our faith: namely, the power of the Word and the humanity of that same Lord Christ.

But lest anyone among the wicked judge that the names “God” and “Lord” must be understood with some distinction, as though the title “Lord” did not entirely apply to the Father and the Son, the prophet testifies in the hundred-ninth psalm, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX, 1).

### Verse 10

“In God I will hope; I will not fear what a human being can do to me.” Truly, one who does not fear losing worldly things cannot fear a human being. For what can an enemy take away except what the holy mother is shown to cast from her mind? Here, as was said above, we must understand “human being” as the devil, who always persecutes the holy Church with wicked intent.

This verse is also the concluding verse of the first section, and it appears to be repeated here, so that, like pearls shining on certain threads, the symmetry of the sections might display a harmonious beauty.

### Verse 11

“In me are your vows, God, which I will repay as praises [ed., ‘praise’] to you.” He comes to the third member, where the Church, already freed from the evils of this world, declares that she will praise the Lord. For she says that vows of praise are in her, although they have been contributed by God’s gift, and that they are to be repaid in that eternity when the saints will render the service of praise with tireless voices.

These are the things that we always have within us when we love God; they do not depart from us in any way. But we repay them in that eternity, when we always discharge what we nevertheless always owe. The following verses demonstrate that we must understand this verse as referring to the future, since it cannot in any way apply to this world.

### Verse 12

“For you have rescued my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.” He gives the reason why she will offer vows of praise through devout sacrifices: namely, because he has rescued the soul of the faithful people from eternal death. This figure is called *aetiology*, that is, a giving of the cause.

The holy mother rightly says that her soul was rescued from death, since she rejoiced in the liberation of her children. It follows: “my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.” He assigns each thing to its corresponding part. He says that the soul was rescued from death, the eyes from tears, and the feet from falling.

But these three things will be granted in the future age, when the soul will no longer die by sinning, the eyes will no longer weep over their evils, and the feet will no longer fall. For in this present age, from whom are tears taken away among the blessed, when he himself says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. V, 5)? Nor are the feet of the righteous made free from falling in this world, because while they walk in this world they are always in danger of falling; but they are restrained by divine mercy, as it is written: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. XXIV, 16).

### Verse 13

“So that I may please God in the light of the living.” He says how the Church can please the Lord in the manifestation of the saints—that is, in the light of the living—in whom she herself is made beautiful, without blemish, and without wrinkle. Whatever happens in them shines forth in her face.

Just as healthy internal organs make a person’s face more beautiful, as Solomon says: “A joyful heart makes the face flourish” (Prov. XV, 13), so the beauty of the holy Church’s countenance is sprinkled with what is found in the merits of the blessed.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

The words of the holy virgin and mother, the Church, have been completed. For she gives us incorruptible birth and brings us forth from a chaste womb into perpetual light. But would that the end of this life should find us such as she produces us through baptism, lest we share a portion with the most wicked people, who—as the title says—have been divided far from the holy ones.

Indeed, may the winepress of this world press us while we rejoice, so that it may pour forth abundant wines from us. Therefore, though afflicted, let us give thanks; though saddened, let us by no means despair, since those torments are beneficial which lead us to blessed rewards.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM LVI

“To the end, do not destroy David, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.”

[Col. 0400A]

We have frequently said that “the end” signifies the Lord, because our perfection is to reach him successfully. For just as, when you reach the end of your appointed journey, you rest after your labor in the place you most desired, so, when you come to the Lord, you seek nothing further.

“Do not destroy David.” David is forbidden to be destroyed by Saul, since he had been prepared for the kingdom by the Lord’s will, as is clearly shown to have happened.

It follows: “in the inscription of the title.” It is clear that this did not happen to David but to Christ the Lord in his Passion, so that the title written by Pontius Pilate would not be changed. But since we have said that David bore the person of our Lord and Savior, this is now said of David himself: that in the Passion of Christ the Lord it was to happen that David would not be destroyed from the kingdom assigned to him, just as the inscription of the Lord’s title could not be altered.

He added: “when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave.” This event appears very similar in David and in the Lord. For just as David, fleeing from Saul, hid himself in a cave, so the divinity of the Lord and Savior is shown to have been hidden from the faithless Jews within the temple of his body. Thus the individual deeds that occurred in David and Christ are common to them under this allusion.

These images of events anticipate what follows in the title because the whole psalm will speak about the Lord’s Passion. Thus David endured the savage Saul, just as Christ endured the most wicked Jews. It is therefore necessary to remember that this is the fifth of those psalms that briefly commemorate the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first order of the psalm, the Lord Christ, troubled concerning his Passion, prays according to the fact that in immeasurable compassion he deigned to become human for our sake. Having been made—as I might put it—God humanized, he did not cease to be God even in the assumption of flesh: remaining unchangeable, assuming changeable humanity, he did not diminish his own nature but exalted the condition of mortality.

For one and the same is the Lord Christ, who, in the form of God, worked great miracles of power, and, in the form of a servant, underwent the cruelty of the Passion.

In the second order he describes the glory of his Resurrection with astonishing variety. Third, after his most blessed Resurrection, he promises to sing praises to the Father and Lord; these members are also separated by the insertion of a *diaplasma*.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Have mercy on me, God, have mercy on me, because my soul trusts in you.” Christ the Lord, made human, cries out to the Father because he fears the Passion that is to come, so that, although he willingly accepted death, he might plainly declare the fear of his soul.

The Son of God asks for the mercy of God, who has mercy on all and descended to us with such great humility to free us that you might think one of the faithful was crying out, while the Creator of the world pleads through the weakness of the flesh he assumed.

For when he says, “Have mercy on me, God, have mercy on me,” this repetition reveals the danger of the death to come, so that he who was about to undergo the trials of the Passion might repeatedly ask for the miracle of the Resurrection.

It follows: “because my soul trusts in you.” This prayer is a model for the faithful, so that the compassionate teacher who endured such things for our salvation might also instruct us by his prayers. He prayed in order to show us the rule of holy prayer. He suffered for us so that no one would refuse to wish to suffer for him. He rose again so that the hope of our weakness might also extend toward his Resurrection.

For he did not lack these things himself; rather, he accepted everything for the sake of our salvation.

### Verse 2

“And in the shadow of your wings I will hope, until iniquity passes away.” Let us understand the most pure holiness of this prayer. In the first verse he asked above all that the Lord have mercy on him. In the second he says why he ought to obtain it. In the third he explains how he can be freed from the persecution that threatens him.

The shadow of wings is the protection of a mother, which cherishes tender young ones with a kind of affection and guards them from an approaching storm. Since such defenses reveal the great help of maternal compassion, this comparison is frequently found in the holy Scriptures, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. XXIII, 37)!

This figure is called *parabole*, that is, comparison, whenever things different in kind are compared with one another.

It follows: “until iniquity passes away.” He remained within the comparison, so that he might rest beneath the same shadow until heated iniquity burned fiercely.

### Verse 3

“I will cry to God Most High, to God who has done good to me.” A great order of devout proclamation is revealed: to cry out to the Most High, to whom one reaches not by a powerful voice but by purity of conscience. He cried out from the humanity he assumed, from whom the heavenly creatures never cease to request help.

When he says, “to God who has done good to me,” he indicates the outstanding mystery of the Incarnation, which divine grace bestowed upon the human race.

### Verse 4

“He sent from heaven and delivered me; he gave those who trampled me over to disgrace.”

The nature of humanity, united to the Son of God, confesses that it has been delivered from human weakness, since after the resurrection it merited to receive the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0401D]. When he says “he sent,” he does not mean an angel or any creature—for they were able to serve of themselves, not to deliver—but “he sent,” understand, the aid of his heavenly power. For the Father delivered his Son, as the Apostle says: “For this reason God also exalted him and granted him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). The Son himself also testifies that he is able to deliver himself, saying: “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18). Yet these expressions show the cooperation of the holy Trinity, which wills one thing and always accomplishes one thing.

He added, “He gave those who trampled me over to disgrace.” It was a disgrace to the persecutors when they saw the faithful peoples rejoicing in the resurrection of the one whom they had believed they would destroy [Col. 0402A]. An evil conscience judges its own disgrace when it sees that its own plans cannot be fulfilled.

### Verse 5

“God sent his mercy and his truth.”

He enters the second part. Although he spoke similar words in the preceding verse, here he nevertheless bursts forth into thanksgiving, in order to strengthen the hope of believers concerning his prosperity. For when he says that he was sent by the Father, he speaks of the humanity he assumed, just as he says in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished, the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). Mercy, therefore, is present because he has compassion on the human race in the flesh he assumed, when he cries out: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), or words to this effect. Truth [Col. 0402B] is present because he repays each person according to his deeds.

### Verse 6

“He snatched my soul from the midst of lions’ cubs; I slept in distress.”

With his body crucified, he says that his soul was snatched away—the soul about which he especially commands us to be concerned. Everything is restored to safety when it is saved. For the body will rise to spiritual glory if the soul has not been wounded by the injury of obstinacy.

By “lions’ cubs” he signifies the people of the Jews, whom the rulers and priests brought forth with a beastly will, so that the lions are those who plotted evil counsels concerning the Lord’s death. The cubs are their peoples, who followed what had been wrongly devised.

He added, “I slept in distress.” The Lord’s death is described with marvelous precision: distressed by the Jews’ roar, he slept in the deepest peace, showing that the persecution of the wicked was so insignificant that, once killed, he was brought to sleep [Col. 0402C]. For sleeping is not the act of one who is distressed—except of the one who, placed upon the cross, gave up his spirit by his own will.

### Verse 7

“Human beings: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword.”

He says this concerning those who raged with impious intent in the killing of the Lord. He himself explains who these “human beings” are, whose teeth were weapons and arrows: namely, those who, as it is written, gnashed their teeth against him. This is expressed by the fifth species of definition, which in Greek is called κατὰ τὴν λέξιν, in Latin *ad verbum*, “word for word.” For each word defines what the teeth of furious people are: that is, weapons and arrows.

He referred weapons to their most evil counsels, and arrows to words that fly, but are discharged toward the accomplishment of death.

He added, “and their tongue is a sharp sword.” Those voices that said, “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21), are compared to a sharp sword. For just as a sharp sword produces the effect of death with great speed, so those words fulfilled the sentence of destruction swiftly. They seemed to kill with a single attack, just as exceedingly sharp weapons usually cut through things. Yet through this he subtly warned that a raging tongue can also kill, as Solomon says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.”

### Verse 8

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth.”

While Christ’s humanity was suffering such things on the cross, and the Jews appeared to hold the Lord of heaven up to mockery, he cries out from the form of a servant that he assumed for us: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God” [Col. 0403A], so that you who hang upon the cross may be recognized as always reigning in majesty.

God could not be exalted above himself, because there is no height beyond which he could grow; but he was plainly exalted among human beings when the glory of his majesty appeared to minds that had been converted. He said “above the heavens” because the Lord is known to have the heavenly powers subject to him.

It follows: “and let your glory be over all the earth.” Both parts have been fulfilled. He was exalted above the heavens when he sat at the Father’s right hand; he was glorified over all the earth when the Catholic Church filled the whole world, in which praises are continually sung to the Lord, as the Lord says: “As I live, says the Lord, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory” (Num. 14:21).

### Verse 9

“They set snares for my feet and bent down my soul.”

### Verse 10

“They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it.”

He signifies the Jews as plotters, who believed that they could attach deceit to righteous teachings, as the Evangelist says concerning the Pharisees when they set an adulterous woman before him, saying: “We found this woman caught in adultery. Now Moses commanded us to stone such women; but what do you say?” (John 8:3), and other words of this kind, which that malicious question provoked.

Christ’s feet are the rebukes of the wicked and the promises to the faithful, by which, while evangelizing in this world, he walked as if with certain feet.

It follows: “and they bent down my soul.” Here the Lord’s compassion and holiness are described. For the wicked Jews bent down Christ’s soul when they refused to believe. In compassion for them—as he also says elsewhere—he was made hungry and sterile. His soul could not be bent in its own actions, since it had no stain of sin.

He added, “They dug a pit before my face.” The pit is rightly understood as the sentence of death, which sends a person into the pit. For they directed it against his face when they said: “He is liable to death” (Matt. 26:66); and therefore they are said to have dug a pit because they appeared to hand him over to death.

He added a general statement: “and they themselves fell into it.” Every unjust word first condemns its own authors; before it harms another, it condemns itself. Solomon says something similar: “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (Eccl. 10:8).

### Verse 11

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord.”

After speaking of the deserved punishments of the wicked, he now comes to the third part, in which he promises that after the resurrection he will give thanks. Yet he gives thanks through that by which he also rose from the dead. In every other respect, Christ’s deity, coeternal with the Father, always provides, is always omnipotent, and is always equal.

Although the enemy had prepared snares and the ungrateful one had opened a pit, he says that he is ready to give thanks because he knew that the glory of the resurrection would in every way be present for him.

But what he is ready for is declared by the following words: “I will sing and make melody to the Lord.” We have said that to sing is to return thanks with the voice; to make melody is to praise the Lord through an action worthy of proclamation. These two expressions seem appropriately matched to the preceding doubling, since in both he professes himself to be ready.

But while he says these things about himself, he instructs us how we should confess. The Apostle Paul too, following his teacher, professes himself ready when he says: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, and endurance produces tested character” (Rom. 5:3–4), and so forth.

### Verse 12

“Awake, my glory; awake, harp and lyre; I will awake at dawn.”

Through tropological interpretation, “awake” is said as though it meant, “Rise to perform a miracle,” as it is also written in the eleventh psalm: “Now I will arise, says the Lord” (Ps. 11:6). This expression has been transferred to divine power in order to express matters arising from human weakness.

He also doubles the expression: “Awake, harp and lyre.” This figure is called *epembasis*, that is, repetition of a word. He did the same in the preceding verse when he said: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” [Col. 0404B].

Here the nature of the humanity assumed is expressed. He was the harp when the flesh carried out the divine commandments, conducting itself in holy behavior. The lyre signifies the glorious passion, which, with its strings stretched and its bones counted, sounded forth the power of endurance through a kind of intellectual song.

He added, “I will awake at dawn,” that is, between the darkness of night and the brightness of day. The sacred Gospel reading testifies that he rose at that time; for it says: “Very early at dawn Mary came to the tomb” (Luke 24:1), and what follows.

### Verse 13

“I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord; I will make melody to you among the nations.”

This is now said from the standpoint of the members, because it is evident that the one who is understood to be the head and leader of the Church confesses to the Father among the peoples [Col. 0404C]. When he says, “I will make melody to you among the nations,” he signifies the heavenly activity of the universal Church, which among all nations renders psalmody to the Lord with devoted mind and varied tongues.

### Verse 14

“For your mercy has been magnified to the heavens, and your truth to the clouds.”

This is the reason for confession; this is the promise of psalmody: “For the Lord’s mercy has been magnified to the heavens”—that is, because the Son’s humanity has been brought to the kingdom of heaven.

To the endangered human being, who was held liable under sins, he showed his mercy, so that through a wondrous dispensation he might make exalted the one whom the judgment of an impious people thought to be the lowest.

It follows: “and your truth to the clouds” [Col. 0404D]. The clouds signify the prophets, whom the truth watered by the Holy Spirit filled like abundant rain. They are rightly called clouds because they were satisfied from a heavenly spring and poured out gifts of spiritual abundance upon barren sinners.

These two expressions have been placed in an inverted order. Truth is earlier in time, whereas mercy is later in the advent; yet they have been exchanged so that one glory and one author might be recognized in them without any difference.

### Verse 15

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God; and let your glory be over all the earth.”

He has already spoken this verse in the second part, confirming our faith by such a promise: the glory of his name will reign over all creatures.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0405A]

Who could adequately express the power of this psalm, or its benevolence? Christ prays in order to teach us; he rises in order to raise us up; he praises the Father in order to instruct us. Rightly is he our way, rightly our redemption, rightly is he read as our Advocate with the Father.

Let us love the merciful defender, lest we suffer the severe judge. It is clearly the height of madness not to desire with all one’s heart the accused one who is known to invite us to eternal joys by such frequent admonitions.

# Exposition of Psalm 57

**For the end: “Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title.”**

Although these words are frequently repeated, I shall not hesitate to explain them in each place, so that the dignity of the psalms may be appreciated [Col. 0405B]. We confidently enter houses whose inner chambers we recognize from their very façade.

“For the end” signifies Christ, who will speak in this psalm.

“Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title.” We have often said that David signifies Christ, because he was also a king, and his name is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable,” which is also fittingly applied to the Lord.

Pontius Pilate is therefore warned not to destroy the written title that declared the Lord to be King, because what was known to have been written by divine command could not be rendered void. For who could abolish that King whom we know to be the creator of heaven and earth? This is repeated so frequently that an excuse is removed from those who might contradict it.

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0405C]

The Lord Christ, both as Savior through his powers and through his admonitions, is understood in the psalm’s first narrative to reproach the Jews for their wickedness. Yet while he charges them with what they did, we are warned not to do similar things.

In the second narrative he declares their punishments through highly appropriate comparisons. In the third, the correction of the righteous through the vengeance inflicted on sinners is recalled.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“If indeed you speak righteousness, judge justly, sons of men.”

The Lord Christ attacks [MS A: *convenit*, “addresses”] the Jews for things they would do in a distant age. They falsely speak the righteousness of the law, since they are not going to judge rightly. Those who are going to do just things truly speak what is equitable; for right speech ought to resemble one’s life [Col. 0405D].

Here, therefore, he censures those words of the Jews when they deceitfully said: “Teacher, we know that you have come from God, and you teach the way of God in truth” (Matt. 22:16). These statements were indeed just, but they were not speaking them sincerely. For if they had been uttered with complete conviction, their judgments could have been beyond reproach; and afterward they would not have said to Pontius Pilate: “Crucify, crucify, because he claims to be the Son of God” (John 19:6, 8).

They judged in such a way that they are shown to have spoken righteousness not rightly but falsely. This argument is called *a contrario* in the topics. For the contrary is to speak rightly and to act perversely.

Some, however, raise a question here, saying that a commandment is given: “Judge justly,” whereas the Gospel says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Luke 6:37). But this statement does not altogether take away from us the freedom to judge.
