When he says, “Do not judge,” he wishes it to be understood of those actions which our perception is not able to discern.

There are certain intermediate matters whose motive we do not know, because they can be done both well and badly; concerning these it is rash for a human being to judge. Here, however, he commands us to judge justly those matters that are manifest. Thus, when these statements are carefully examined, they do not appear at all to contradict one another. Father Augustine treated this passage more fully and carefully in the second book of *The Sermon on the Mount* (chapter 28).

### Verse 2

“For in your heart you work iniquities upon the earth; your hands fashion injustice.”

As though he were saying: How could you judge me, when you work iniquities in your heart, where the crime is complete before it is committed, and every evil becomes punishable when the desire of an evil will accuses it? By “upon the earth” he means either the hidden place of the heart or the people over whom the rulers and Pharisees appeared to preside.

Observe that above he attributed iniquities to the heart; now he also signifies actual deeds through the hands, so that he may show that the crime is not only conceived but completed. “They fashion” is appropriately said of iniquities. For fashioning signifies that perversity has been gathered together and united from many parts into a harmonious whole.

### Verse 3

“Sinners are estranged from the womb [ed., ‘from the vulva’]; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods.”

He rightly calls sinners like aborted children, cast out from the womb of the Church [Col. 0406C], because they have not been perfected by any doctrinal formation. Like the feeble softness of a young animal made foolish, they are shown to have been cast not into the vital light but into the darkness of faithlessness.

The Church is rightly said to have a womb, since through sacred baptism she brings us forth into perpetual light. But woe to those who have come prematurely from her inner parts!

It follows: “They have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods.” They have indeed gone astray from the belly because they followed teachings contrary to their mother and do not revere the holy womb with pious devotion. They too have spoken falsehoods because they have wandered from her holy traditions.

### Verse 4

“Anger belongs to them according to the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf viper that stops its ears.”

The Jews’ anger is defined by a highly fitting comparison. The anger of obstinate people is irreconcilable because, in order not to hear the preaching of their teachers, they deliberately arrange a voluntary deafness for themselves [Col. 0406D].

The habit of the viper is compared to this evil. To avoid hearing the words of the enchanter and leaving its hiding places, the viper is said to stop one ear by bending its tail over it and to press the other into the earth. The Jews are deservedly compared to it because, with the ears of their hearts stopped, they refused to hear the salutary command of sacred Scripture.

The practice of stopping the ears was taken from the priests, who filled their ears with incense so that, when foreign words intervened, the confused memory of the chants would not be disturbed.

### Verse 5

“Which will not hear the voice of enchanters, nor the spells that are chanted by the wise.”

He continues the explanation of the comparison. He speaks of the viper that does not hear the voice of enchanters: it has become deaf because its ears have been condemned, and it has not allowed itself to hear the voice that could have drawn it into the light.

O human race! Unless it is illumined by divine mercy, it is utterly blind: created in the image of God, it wishes to bear the likeness of a serpent.

We call this “wise” person an operator of worldly skill, who, with the Lord’s help, completes a task he has undertaken through cunning ingenuity. Note, therefore, that people are called wise even in evil, concerning whom it is written: “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe?” (1 Cor. 1:20), and similar passages.

### Verse 6

“God will crush their teeth in their own mouths; the Lord will break the molars of lions.”

The opening of the second narrative is presented. It describes the evils that those who despised divine preaching will suffer, refusing to be saved like vipers.

First he says that their teeth will specifically be crushed, when their deceitful words and crafty questions were reduced to nothing. This happened to them when they slyly asked to whom Caesar’s coin should be paid. But they received such an answer from the Lord that, when they had tried to bite, they appeared to withdraw with their teeth crushed. For he said: “Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

It follows: “The Lord will break the molars of lions in their mouths.” Here something seems to increase, since he has named both lions and molars. He signifies those who attempted to rise against the Lord’s death not with crafty words but with the roar of beasts.

They were vipers when they insidiously said to him: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” (ibid., 17). They were lions when they cried out with bloody mouths: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21) [Col. 0407C]. Thus their madness is described as resembling not only the venom of serpents but also monstrous beasts.

The molars in their mouths were broken when they could not answer his most truthful words.

### Verse 7

“They will come to nothing like running water; he bends his bow until they become weak.”

He has spoken of vipers; he has spoken of lions. Now he turns to torrents, which, stirred up by winter rains, descend in sudden floods. They are terrifying because they are unexpected; they are dangerous because they rush headlong. But as soon as, with their force spent, they have lowered their savage necks, they fail beneath a clear sky, although they had swollen through clouds pouring down rain.

This figure is called *synathroismos*, that is, “gathering,” where we collect many things and crimes within a single narrative [Col. 0407D].

O unheard-of savagery of the Jews! So many enormous evils are compared with them, from which we know that immense dangers arise.

He added: “He bends his bow until they become weak.” Here the mercy of divine power is displayed, whose bow is drawn for salvation. God directs the weapons of his power against the wicked, and terrifies them until, weakened, they yield and turn with an improved mind toward the salvation of confession.

### Verse 8

“Like melting wax they will be carried away; fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.”

Above he spoke of those whom he declares will be converted through the Lord’s terror. Now he explains the case of those who, because of faithlessness, have become hardened in their obstinacy. A fitting recompense is given to them, so that the hardness of their heart may disappear like melting wax [Col. 0408A].

“They will be carried away,” he says, from the sight of the Lord, when they are to be sent into the torments of Gehenna.

Thus he continues: “Fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.” By fire he means the burning of an evil mind, which they drank in during this age with senses blinded. It darkens rather than illumines; it does not open but closes the sight.

Such fire falls upon the impious so that they cannot see the true sun, that is, the Lord Savior. They themselves will also say at the future judgment: “The sun did not rise for us, and the light of righteousness did not shine for us” (Wis. 5:6). For no one can behold that sun except those who contemplate him with pure and holy minds.

### Verse 9

“Before your thorns produce the thornbush: as living beings, so in anger he will swallow them.”

The *rhamnus* is a very troublesome kind of thorn. At first it grows into a very soft plant, but when it has grown hot in mature age, it produces pointed branches; afterward its spikes harden into the strength of a tree.

The present sentence therefore threatens the Jews with this: they will be swallowed up before their wickedness grows strong through long age. As he says elsewhere concerning such people: “Men of blood and deceit will not divide their days” (Ps. 54:24).

The swiftness of their destruction follows: “As living beings, so in anger he will swallow them.” He rightly says “as living beings,” because they appear to live but are dead. Every sinner who dwells in wickedness dies to the truth, as the Apostle says: “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6).

What he added—“as in anger he will swallow them”—signifies that the Lord appears to strike sinners as though he were angry, though he is not angry. Concerning him it is written: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with calmness” (Wis. 12:18).

The statement “he will swallow them” signifies their sudden destruction. For as great as the Lord’s patience is in enduring, so great will be the blow in the swiftness of judgment.

Observe that just as above he made an increase (*auxesis*) in sins over two verses, so here he increases the punishments over four.

### Verse 10

“The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance of the wicked; he will wash his hands in the sinner’s blood.”

He enters the portion of the third narrative, in which he says that the joy of the righteous and the vengeance of the wicked arise even in this age.

The righteous will see the vengeance of the wicked when he observes them doing things for which they ought always to be afraid. Every evil carries its own punishment at the moment it is committed, because, when conscience torments it, it is shown to fulfill vengeance within itself [Col. 0408D].

The righteous, by contrast, is joyful even when weighed down by a burden of troubles. He is free in spirit, from which true joy always rises. Thus both kinds of people bear within themselves the qualities of their actions.

It follows: “He will wash his hands in the sinner’s blood.” What does this mean, when the one who commanded us to pray for our enemies declares that the hands of the pious are to be washed in sinners’ blood?

But if we examine this more carefully, it offers an example of correction rather than cruelty. When a sinner’s blood is shed, the hands—that is, the actions—of the righteous are corrected. When the wicked perish, the innocent person is warned to conduct himself more cautiously and carefully.

Thus the blood of the sinner cleanses the hands of the righteous not cruelly but piously, as Solomon says: “When the fool perishes, the wise person becomes wiser” (Prov. 21:11).

### Verse 11

“And the human being will say: ‘If there is indeed fruit for the righteous, then indeed there is a God judging them on earth.’”

When the things mentioned above occur, the faithful person understands and says: If the righteous receive the rewards of their goodness even here, it is clear that the Lord also judges concerning them on this earth, since he does not permit them to live in unfruitful holiness.

He wishes it to be understood that the wicked are not entirely free from punishment in this age, although they may appear to flourish; nor are the good deprived of benefit, although they are weighed down by worldly burdens [p. 194].

This argument is called *a consequentibus*, “from consequences,” since, when rewards are given to the righteous, the Lord is shown to be just.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0409B]

Behold the true Sun, who, dispersing our darkness and gloom, has shown us what we ought to think in truth. Let no one now be doubtful; let no one murmur. For we know that in this world God secretly examines human affairs, and it is clearly demonstrated that he does so in this age.

Therefore we rightly call him the truest Sun and the true day: through the twelve apostles, corresponding to the number of the hours, he poured the light of his truth into us. For he himself says: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

This is the day of good minds; this is the day of the righteous. No cloud’s darkness hinders it, and no gloomy night ever follows it.

# Exposition of Psalm 58

**For the end: “Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title”: when Saul sent and guarded his house in order to kill him (1 Sam. 19:11).**

[Col. 0409C]

“For the end” has already been explained as “without end.” “Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title”—this too is frequently placed there, so that the Lord’s Passion may be revealed through these indications.

The madness of the Jews was attempting in vain to destroy what divine authority had so often forbidden. Through the incorruptible inscription of this title, he reveals the unchangeable firmness of the Lord’s kingdom.

It follows: “when Saul sent men and watched his house in order to kill him.” This too is appropriately applied to the Lord’s Passion. The house indicates the tomb where he rested through a death of three days. The rulers of the Jews sent men to guard it, as though to destroy the glory of his name [Col. 0409D], lest it be said deceitfully that he had risen, since they had heard Christ previously proclaiming this.

But it was better that the enemies themselves preferred to revile it, so that the whole world might recognize the event with greater certainty. For the testimony provided by an ungrateful person is indisputable; and what is confirmed by the guilty party cannot be called a favor.

Therefore let no one doubt that these matters pertain to the Lord’s Passion, concerning which this psalm is about to speak.

But we must understand this carefully: when the Lord Christ speaks, some statements must be received as coming from the humility of his flesh and others from the excellence of his divinity. We must not imagine two sons, as the sacrilegious wickedness of Nestorius dreams [Col. 0410A]; rather, we must hold that the Lord Christ remains in two united and perfect natures, as the authority of the holy synod of Chalcedon, taught by the most learned Fathers, testifies.

It says as follows (Part II, Session 5):

> We are all instructed and taught to confess harmoniously one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same one perfect in divinity and the same one perfect in flesh; truly God and truly the same human being, himself truly consisting of a rational soul and a body; ὁμοούσιον, that is, of one essence with the Father according to divinity, and the same one ὁμοούσιον, of one essence with us according to humanity, in every respect like us except for sin alone.
>
> Before the ages, indeed, born from the Father according to divinity; but in the last days, the same one, for us and for our salvation, born from the Virgin Mary, θεοτόκον, that is, the Mother of God, according to humanity. We acknowledge one and the same Christ, Son of God, the only-begotten Lord, to be recognized in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation.
>
> Nowhere is the difference of the natures removed through the unity; rather, the distinctive property of each nature is preserved, and the two come together into one person and one subsistence. We confess one and the same only-begotten Son, true God, Jesus Christ the Lord, not divided or partitioned into two persons.
>
> This is holy faith, inviolate truth, and a preaching to be embraced. The Catholic Church throughout the whole world rightly confesses that it has been fittingly poured out through the Holy Spirit.

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0410C]

At the psalm’s opening, the Lord Christ prays—not as God born from the Father, but as a human being made from the Virgin Mary—that his enemies may not prevail against him. He rises like material light from the depths and gradually ascends toward the most exalted summit of his resurrection.

Second, he explains how the Jews are to be converted at the end of the age, and a prayer is offered for them with wondrous compassion.

Third, he indicates what they will do after their conversion and testifies that he rejoices in his holy ones. These parts are divided by the conclusion of the *diapsalma*, so that they may be shown to be not so much highly elaborate as not neglected.

## Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0410D]

### Verse 1

“Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those rising up against me.”

While the humanity of the Lord Savior asks to be snatched from the plots of spiritual enemies, to whom it was nevertheless not liable—as he himself says, “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30)—he shows us what we necessarily ought to ask.

He, without the stain of sins, humbly pleads that the devil or his ministers, the Jews, be turned away from him. We, however, make this request so that, as captives and guilty, we may be freed from unclean spirits by divine mercy.

Our Head asks this, but without the law of sin; his members likewise ask, but as those liable to offenses [Col. 0411A].

Through this verse and the next he clearly shows that there are four kinds of enemies. First he says that he is delivered merely from “enemies,” who could have the intention of harming him but did not desire with greater eagerness to injure him immediately.

A second kind is added: “and free me from those rising up against me.” He says “those rising up,” as though they had already been stirred by the storm of their iniquity and, in the indignation of their minds, prepared for future calamities.

### Verse 2

“Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and free me from men of blood.”

He names a third kind: those who had risen up with hardened minds and also completed their crime in action. They showed their iniquity not only through their thoughts but also through the completion of the deed itself.

It follows: “and free me from men of blood” [Col. 0411B]. He comes to the fourth kind, so that these enemies appear to seek not merely insults but also to hasten to shed blood itself.

Here he signifies the Jews, who condemned the blood of the innocent through sacrilegious crime when they said: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 23:21), and again: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). They are rightly called men of blood because they unjustly took upon themselves the burden of death.

He therefore asks, on account of human weakness, to be snatched and freed from them, although he was willingly enduring everything. Observe that through the figure *epembasis*, which is called repetition, he doubled the words in these two verses: “Deliver me” and “free me.”

### Verse 3

“For behold, they have seized my soul; the strong have rushed upon me; neither is there my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord.”

Here “soul” means bodily life. Otherwise, no adversity could seize the soul of the Lord Savior, who, united to God, conducted himself in an unstained manner. But when it is said that his soul was seized, the time of the Passion is indicated.

It follows: “The strong have rushed upon me.” “The strong” signifies the devil together with his ministers, as he himself says in the Gospel: “No one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark 3:27).

They themselves entered Judas’s heart so that the Savior might be handed over to death. They themselves incited the people through the worst instigations, so that they might condemn the Redeemer of the human race with faithless intent.

They are called “strong” because they overcome the fragile weaknesses of mortals. But they could not be strong against Christ’s power, since he bound them with divine strength [Col. 0411D].

He added: “Neither is there my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord.” Although demonic strength rose against the Lord Savior—at one time setting him on the pinnacle of the temple, at another offering him riches—they nevertheless dared not presume against him anything like the temptations of vice that they effectively customarily bring upon us.

Here “iniquity” is to be understood as ill will; “sin” refers to the carrying out of a crime. Both are proved to have been wholly foreign to the Lord.

The nature of the humanity assumed by the Lord is shown to be present, not guilt. Yet he endured the strong tempter because he assumed the flesh of our weakness. Nor could it otherwise have happened that the one who justly destroyed him might justly lose his own claim, unless he had reached the author of life [Col. 0412A].

Thus sad cold is dissolved when warmth arrives; thus dark night departs when the brightness of serene light has come.

But our Head truly says these things concerning himself. This profession, however, cannot apply to the subordinate members.

### Verse 4

“Without iniquity I ran, and I was directed; arise to meet me, and see.” A person can run without being directed, like those whose life is entangled in crooked paths; and those who are directed by no truth do not reach the straight road. Christ, however, passed through worldly life by a straight course; nor could iniquity obstruct him, since it always twists human actions. Concerning him the eighteenth psalm says: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven [Col. 0412B], and his meeting-place is even to its summit” (Psalm XVIII, 6–7). To be directed meant that he should return to the place from which he had come. Yet he came from the Father in such a way that he did not depart from the Father; he departed from the world in such a way that he did not abandon the faithful, as he himself says: “I will not leave you orphaned” (John XIV, 18); and, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20).

It follows: “Arise to meet me.” Here, through figurative allusions, the power of the resurrection is expressed, so that he asks the Father to meet him—that is, to come toward him—although the Father had never at any time departed from him, nor had he come to the Father, insofar as his heavenly nature is concerned, with the face of something new. Rather, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11). What he added, “and see,” means “cause to be seen,” just as it was said to Abraham [Col. 0412C]: “Now I know that you love the Lord your God” (Genesis XXII, 12)—that is, “I have caused it to be known.” This is a figurative expression, and it is scattered throughout the divine Scriptures with very frequent usage.

### Verse 5

“And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel,”

### Verse 6

“Attend to visit all the nations; do not have mercy on all who practice iniquity.”

These two verses must be expounded together, since they are evidently dependent upon one another. After the remarkable account of the resurrection, therefore, the merciful Advocate intercedes for us, saying to the Father: “And you, Lord God of hosts, God of Israel”—you who are thought to be the God of Israel alone, that is, of one nation—“attend now to visit all the nations,” so that the number of those who believe in you may increase from among the nations [Col. 0412D], since you have found barrenness of faith among the Jewish people.

Notice that he says “all the nations,” because people from every nation were going to believe, with the Lord’s help, as in the passage: “And I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm II, 8). But when he turns back to the Jews, he says: “Do not have mercy on all who practice iniquity.” This prayer, if it is properly considered, disagrees in no respect with his commandments. By saying “do not have mercy on all,” he shows that mercy is to be shown to those who will plead with sincere devotion. For although all human beings practice iniquity, there is no doubt that those who have been predestined and flee to him with devoted mind are to be spared.

[Col. 0413A]

### Verse 7

“They will return toward evening, and will suffer hunger like dogs, and will go around the city.”

We have reached the second door of the psalm, in which the future conversion of the Jewish people is revealed. Thus it signifies that at the end of the world innumerable Jews will believe in the Lord. The Apostle also says this: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Romans XI, 25), and so forth. You see that there also it was promised that, although late, they would nevertheless at some time be saved by a saving conversion. Therefore the evening of the end of the world is suitably expressed by comparison with the day.

It follows: “And they will suffer hunger like dogs.” This signifies the intention of the Jews of that time. Just as now they have been hardened by the most savage obstinacy [Col. 0413B], so then they will suffer the most eager desires for faith. They are rightly compared with dogs, because, carried away by the warmth of faith, they will pursue that most savage beast, Antichrist, with religious barking. Dogs are so called from *canere*, “to sing” or “to bark.” At that time the dogs will be better than human beings are now, when they strive faithfully to defend [196] the law against which they now offend. By “hunger” he signifies eagerness for the heavenly word, as the prophet says: “Behold, I am bringing hunger upon the land, not hunger for bread nor thirst for water, but hunger to hear the word of God” (Amos VIII, 11).

He added: “And they will go around the city.” He remains within the same comparison. It is the habit of dogs to defend those places in which they know that they find nourishment. Thus the Jews, once converted, will defend the city—that is, the holy Church [Col. 0413C]—which they will surround with corrected preaching. Scripture of the Gospel testifies that dogs are compared with the faithful. For the Canaanite woman says: “Yes, Lord; for even the dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” (Mark VII, 28). This figure is called an *aenigma*, that is, an obscure saying, which itself also belongs to allegory: it says one thing and signifies another.

### Verse 8

“Behold, they will speak with their own mouth, and a sword is in their lips; for who has heard?”

Certainly then they will speak with their own mouth what now they are not worthy to have in their heart, and they will turn others toward good, although they themselves previously refused to believe it.

It follows: “And a sword is in their lips.” There will certainly be in their lips a heavenly sword, which is read to be two-edged, striking from both Testaments [Col. 0413D] and bringing fortunate souls to health through its wound. Concerning it the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI, 17).

He added: “For who has heard?” He rightly first said that the sword would be in their lips—that is, that the preaching in their mouth would be exceedingly frequent—because, while they remain in the wicked religion of Antichrist, a Gentile will rarely be found to hear it. “Who,” when it must be understood with emphasis, means “almost no one,” “almost exceedingly few.” This syllable frequently signifies “no one,” as in: “Who is like you?” (Micah VII, 18); and sometimes “one,” as in: “Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion?” (Psalm XIII, 7).

[Col. 0414A]

### Verse 9

“And you, Lord, will mock them; you will regard all the nations as nothing.”

He declares that those who refused to hear upright preaching will be mocked, as in Solomon’s saying: “You did not attend to my reproaches, but made my counsels void; therefore I also will laugh at your destruction, I will rejoice when ruin comes upon you” (Proverbs I, 25–26). They will be objects of mockery when, empty and foolish, they are driven away from entry into the eternal kingdom.

It follows: “You will regard all the nations as nothing.” It is well known that “nations” can be used both in a good and in a bad sense. Here, however, he means those who persist in their wickedness with cruel obstinacy. The Lord regards as nothing those who do not venerate him as the Creator of all creatures. For if this is understood universally, from where will the Lord’s Church be built? But it is the custom of divine Scripture to say the whole with reference to a part [Col. 0414B], according to the Lord’s saying: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8). And if you wish to take this generally, to whom should it be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34)?

It remains, therefore, that here you understand “all the nations” to mean those who, because of their unbelief, are destined to be condemned. Some will perish from every nation, just as it is established that the righteous are gathered from every people.

### Verse 10

“I will keep my strength toward you, because, O God, you are my protector.”

Above we said that the devil and his ministers are strong: placing their strength in themselves, they fell from eternal exaltation. But the Lord Christ, displaying the form of truth to human ignorance, says that the strength of his humanity [Col. 0414C] must be attributed to the Lord’s benefits. Thus, just as through that treacherous enemy we learned what is harmful, so through the true Redeemer we may recognize what is profitable for us.

What he says, “toward you I will keep,” by a change of syllable signifies “through you I will keep my strength”; this is found frequently in the divine Scriptures. This figure is called *prothesios parallage*, when one proposition is put in place of another.

It follows: “Because, O God, you are my protector.” He rightly declares that his strength must be attributed to the one whom he knew to be his protector.

### Verse 11

“My God, his mercy will precede me; my God, show me among my enemies.”

He explains what he said above: “I will keep my strength toward you.” For the human condition [Col. 0414D] offered him nothing worthy by which it might deserve to rejoice in the abundance of his gift. O truly astonishing piety of the Creator! He teaches us about himself what we ought to understand and preserve within ourselves.

But woe to those who, deviating from this rule, think that it lies within human choice to deserve to attain some of God’s gifts! He himself grants that we should desire good; he himself brings it to completion so that we can attain his rewards. The Apostle made this perfectly clear: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians IV, 7). Let the Pelagian heresy cease reviving its old accusations. We can possess no good from ourselves unless we have received it from the Lord.

It follows [Col. 0415A]: “My God, show me among my enemies.” He speaks of a second gift of divine favor: that the power of his majesty may also be displayed among his enemies, so that the blasphemers may become devout and those of wicked conduct become most righteous.

### Verse 12

“Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your law; scatter them by your strength, and destroy them, my protector Lord.”

This is what he said above: “Show me among my enemies,” because anger is held back from these enemies who, by God’s generosity, will believe, so that they may not seem to be ignorant of the Lord’s law until the end of the age and begin to perish in such a way that no good fruit can emerge from them.

The person who does not fulfill its commandments forgets the law, even though he may seem to retain its words in his mind. He therefore prays that the Jewish nation not perish utterly, but rather recognize through [Col. 0415B] glorious repentance that it has gone astray.

He added: “Scatter them by your strength.” That this was said of the Jews is confirmed by their actual dispersion, since they are seen divided and scattered through almost the entire world. For although they are subject to Roman law [*ed.*, “to the Roman yoke”], they nevertheless live everywhere scattered according to their own custom.

This is the meaning: “Do not kill them.” For if they had been extinguished as they deserved, the hope of their conversion would have perished utterly. The Jews were therefore scattered either so that they might be summoned to pursue conversion, or—as some wish—as a result of the disputes among heretics, so that the Church might have testimony prepared by the enemies of the ancient law, since what is confirmed by an adversary’s support is believed without hesitation.

It follows: “And destroy them, my protector Lord.” He continues in the same supplications [Col. 0415C], so that the Jews, having been destroyed, may be rebuilt for the better, and a saving elevation may follow their fall. For the Apostle Paul would not have risen to salvation unless he had deserved to fall at the Lord’s voice.

[197]

### Verse 13

“The sins of their mouth, the word of their lips; let them be seized in their pride, and they will be torn away from cursing and falsehood.”

“The sins of their mouth”—that is, they were the madness of their thoughts—when they formed a plan to hand the Lord and Savior over to death. The word of their lips was also detestable when they said: “He is guilty of death” (Matthew XXVI, 66). They were seized in pride when those same people said: “Who gave you this authority? And by what authority are you doing these things?” (Ibid., XXI, 23). They were plainly captured in their pride when they later saw rising again [Col. 0415D] the one whose miracles they had previously rejected.

It follows: “And they will be torn away from cursing and falsehood”—that is, when, after their conversion, the disgrace is removed from them which they are now known to possess among all the nations. They will be torn away from falsehood when they come to know the divine Scriptures through true illumination, although now they receive them under a false interpretation.

### Verse 14

“In the wrath of consummation they will not be; and they will know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.”

The wrath of the Lord is spoken of in two ways: either when he chastises for salvation, as in the passage, “For he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews XII, 6); or when he sends someone into eternal fire, concerning which another psalm says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Psalm VI, 2; XXXVII, 2) [Col. 0416A].

It has been transferred abusively from human beings, since when we avenge some fault, we are improperly said to be angry with evil deeds. God, however, judges everything in tranquility, because he does not experience the confused disturbances of agitation.

He calls that “consummation” which each person suffers when, mindful of his sins, he torments himself by inward chastisement. The proud will certainly no longer exist, since it is clear that they will come to the repentance of humility.

It follows: “And they will know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth.” When the Jews have been truly instructed in perfected religion, then they will recognize that the Lord Christ is the God of their patriarch Jacob, which at first they did not believe. “And the ends of the earth,” that is, the Catholic Church, which has been spread throughout the whole world—a truth they do not now understand because their hearts are hardened.

[Col. 0416B]

### Verse 15

“They will return toward evening, and will suffer hunger like dogs, and will go around the city.”

After the insertion of the second *diapsalm*, he comes to the third entrance, where once again the conversion of the Jews and the resurrection of the Lord and Savior are shown. Since the present verse, already placed in the second part with the same words but not the same meaning, is repeated—as we have often said is found in the divine Scriptures—its successive statements reveal the difference between the two.

The first belongs to the end of the age; this one belongs to the Lord’s Passion. Thus the intention of each must be sought according to the causes stated above. In the earlier division we said that evening signifies the end of the age. Here, however, the beginning of the sixth age itself [Col. 0416C] is shown, which is evening, when the Lord and Savior came for the world’s salvation.

Thus Moses speaks of him: “You shall kill the lamb at evening” (Exodus XII, 6). After the miracle of his resurrection, a multitude of Jews believed.

It follows: “And they will suffer hunger like dogs.” The dog, a most voracious and importunate animal, customarily defends with its barking those houses in which it knows that its greed will be satisfied with bread once it has received it. The Jews are rightly compared with these dogs: nourished by the gift of the Christian faith, they will hasten to defend the Church of God with clamorous preaching. This happened in the case of the Apostle Paul, who had formerly been a persecutor of the Christian name but afterward, by divine generosity, was joined to the apostles.

He added: “And they will go around the city.” The city signifies Jerusalem, which is known to have been spread universally throughout the world. That Paul went around it is testified by his letters, which resounded throughout all the nations like sacred divine proclamations for the human race [Col. 0416D].

O blessed dog, who pursues unbelieving peoples, drives away thieves, and guards the holy sheepfolds; whose barking resounded throughout the whole world like a mighty trumpet!

### Verse 16

“They will be scattered to eat; and if they are not satisfied, they will murmur.”

Those, therefore, who deserved to possess true doctrine are scattered in order to eat, namely, spiritual food, so that the nations may be converted as they come to the Catholic faith, just as it was said to the Apostle Peter in a vision: “Kill and eat” (Acts X, 13).

It follows: “And if they are not satisfied, they will murmur.” Teachers are satisfied when they see peoples eagerly [Col. 0417A] receiving their preaching. But if they do not recognize their words bearing fruit in the minds of unbelievers, they murmur while fasting. He therefore says that these distributors of the Lord’s word can murmur if they are not satisfied by the people’s belief, as he himself says in the thirty-fourth psalm: “They repaid me evil for good, barrenness to my soul” (Psalm XXXIV, 12).

### Verse 17

“But I will sing of your strength, and in the morning I will exult in your mercy, because you have become my protector and my refuge on the day of my tribulation.”

After speaking of the conversion of the Jews, he suddenly turns his words to the Father. This figure is called *prophonesis*, in Latin “exclamation.” He himself will sing in his saints, while his members rejoice. And what joy it is to rejoice continually in the contemplation of the Lord [Col. 0417B]! For just as divine power never fails, so neither does the joy that comes from contemplating it.

It follows: “And in the morning I will exult in your mercy.” In the morning, that is, when the dark night of this age has passed, when the Lord’s mercy already shines forth in the reward of the saints. There he will exult as King and Lord, where he sees his people rejoicing in him.

He added: “Because you have become my protector.” He explained why humanity exulted in Christ the Lord: because he became my protector. He is received when the whole Church is saved, as in the passage: “Whoever has done something for one of the least of these has done it for me” (Matthew XXV, 40).

He added: “And my refuge on the day of my tribulation.” O how welcome is refuge when it is granted in the time of tribulation! Every human being is in suspense as long as he hears: “Come, blessed of my Father” [Col. 0417C] (Ibid., 34), and so forth. But then it becomes an eternal refuge, when one reaches that most desired summons. As we also said above, this must be understood with reference to the members.

### Verse 18

“My helper, to you I will sing praise, because, O God, you are my protector, my God, my mercy.”

We said that the psalm refers to active virtue, which the holy and venerable activity of the flesh of the Lord and Savior also displayed in this world. He frequently repeats his benefits in order to show us how we ought to give thanks.

[198] The Word is the one who assumed our humanity: he deigned to join and unite it to himself in the womb of the Virgin Mary, without any confusion or mixture of substances [Col. 0417D], while an ineffable and indescribable unity remained.

He added: “My God, my mercy.” A marvelous and worthy saying. For although he had said many things, and yet not everything had been included, in the end he summed it up in one word: “What is my God?” That is, “My mercy.” All benefits are there, where every gift is designated. For what good is not experienced where mercy is recognized as having been bestowed?

## Conclusion of the Psalm

We have learned, Lord Christ, how many things you endured in the flesh, and that you always prayed for your persecutors. O truly merciful Judge [Col. 0418A], under whom no one who confesses need despair! O equal kindness and power! For if you pray for your enemies, which of your own could fear that he will perish? Grant us to do what you command; grant us to fulfill what is beneficial, because just as apart from you we are nothing, so with you we can accomplish completely whatever good we strive for.

# Exposition of Psalm LIX

“To the end; for those who will be changed; in the inscription of the title; by David himself, for instruction: when he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Zobah, and Joab returned and struck Edom [*ed.*, Idumea] in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.”

This title, unless we seek a summary, is altogether lengthy in its interpretation of names and commemoration of wars. First it says: “To the end, for those who will be changed.” Those are changed [Col. 0418B] for the end who, having laid aside the error of the old person, serve the Lord and Savior with pure intention of mind. Concerning them it is said: “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Ephesians V, 8).

How they can be changed, he explains below: “In the inscription of the title, David, for instruction.” The inscription of the title signifies Jesus Christ as King. Thus let them be changed so that, abandoning the devil, they recognize Christ as their King. As we have often said, David signifies the Lord.

“For instruction”: add, namely, Christian instruction, because it is not enough for anyone to call him his King unless he also strives to obey his commandments.

It follows: “When he burned Mesopotamia of Syria,” and so forth. The history of Kings records that David achieved these victories [Col. 0418C] after he succeeded Saul in the kingdom (2 Samuel VIII). It seems inappropriate to set them forth here in detail, since they are narrated there at great length. We must nevertheless observe that these wars are presented figuratively on account of the victories of the Lord and Savior, which he wins throughout the world over pagans and unbelievers, whose words this psalm is about to proclaim. Thus, truly destroyed with respect to their former superstition, they may deserve to be changed by the grace of the new person.

## Division of the Psalm

That people which had been bound by ancient errors, coming into the new grace of holy religion, first supplicates that after the affliction it suffered in making satisfaction, it may be restored by the novelty of divine favor.

[Col. 0418D]

Second, after an interposed *diapsalm*, the same people asks that, after the tribulations it has endured, it may be led by the Lord into a most strongly fortified city, requesting that help in its tribulation be granted to it—something which is shown to be possible for the Lord alone.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“O God, you have rejected us and destroyed us; you have been angry, and you have had mercy on us.”

That people which had been bound by ancient errors recalls, with thanksgiving, that it was rejected and destroyed, so that the slaughter of the nations conquered—which the title foretold that King David had carried out—might instead be declared to have been accomplished throughout the whole world by Christ, strong and desirable, not with the sword but through the zeal for conversion; not by visible fire but by the ardor of charity. This is how Divinity habitually conquers and defeats invisibly [Col. 0419A].

That people supplicates that, having been destroyed with respect to its ancient superstition and changed into a holy purpose, it may obtain the grace of a new rebirth. Nor should it trouble us that the plural number has been added. For when “people” is spoken of, there is no doubt that many persons can be signified within it. When they say, “You have rejected,” they show that by divine favor they were recalled from the pursuit of crimes, lest their life should end in wicked doctrines.

It follows: “And you have destroyed us.” This destruction rightly becomes an act of thanksgiving: it overturns in order to build, lays down in order to raise up, and humbles in order to lead to the kingdoms of heaven. Recognize these words not as those of the ungrateful, but rather as those of people rejoicing.

He added: “You have been angry, and you have had mercy on us.” By “angry,” we must understand that he opposed them, overthrowing their superstitions and vices by the power of his justice [Col. 0419B]. The people very appropriately call the Lord angry with them when they were sinning, and merciful when they fled to the remedies of conversion. Thus he caused both grounds to be understood through the individual expressions.

This figure is called *emphasis*, that is, exaggeration, providing a clearer understanding than the words themselves express: merciful anger, saving indignation, liberating captivity, fruitful opposition. He was angry, therefore, when he overthrew their superstitions; he had mercy when he led them to the worship of true religion.

### Verse 2

“You have shaken the earth and troubled it; heal its breaches, because it has been shaken.”

By “earth” we must understand the universal sinner, who was shaken by the Lord’s coming, as he will also say in another psalm [Col. 0419C]: “He saw, and the earth was shaken” (Psalm XCVI, 4). Sinners were shaken when they recognized that their religious rites had proved abhorrent to God, when at last they understood that their idols were made of stone. They also noticed that riches and honors, and the other things of this world, were of little account with God, although previously they had considered them supremely important.

They were also troubled when, amid other teachings, they heard: “Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry, and you perish from the righteous way” (Psalm II, 12).

Observe the order of the psalm, arranged in a most beautiful narrative. First it was necessary that they be shaken; afterward, that they be troubled.

It follows: “Heal its breaches, because it has been shaken.” Wounds are disclosed to the heavenly Physician, so that suitable medicine may come to the aid of the afflicted sick. But [Col. 0419D] let us understand for how long he says that they were afflicted: until they appear to have reached the point of brokenness.

This is the brokenness that makes us stronger; this is the weakening that restores health. We are broken in mind when we descend into humility with the whole intention of our soul, as it is said in the fiftieth psalm: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Psalm L, 19).

And in order to obtain the mercy of the most compassionate Judge, he added: “Because it has been shaken”—that is, it has been transferred from its former error, so that what previously served idols might now obey you, Lord.

### Verse 3

“You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of compunction.”

After the saving victories that the Lord accomplished through grace for the reconciliation of this world, he says “your people,” that is, those subjected and devoted to you [Col. 0420A]. He showed hard things to his faithful when he acquired bands of martyrs through savage sufferings. He showed the righteous hard things in this transitory world in order to make them precious in that eternity. For he does not command his servants to remain idle or to occupy themselves idly in ease; rather, exercised by hard labors, they deserve to be brought to the palm of his mercy. Thus Paul also says: “No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy II, 5).

He added: “You have given us wine of compunction.” Virtue is compared with wine: it changes the zeal of our will toward a good purpose and makes us understand what is right, after people have deserved, by divine generosity, to fill themselves with it. In contrast, the human drink that shakes the health of the mind admits words of vanity.

But that drink is not of the mouth [Col. 0420B], but of the mind; nor is it prepared by human effort, but granted by divine inspiration, as it was said above: “And how excellent is your cup that intoxicates!” (Psalm XXII, 5). What this cup is has been beautifully and briefly defined: it is wine in which there is not vicious abundance, but abundance of compunction.

### Verse 4

“You have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they may flee from the face of the bow.”

He gave a sign to those who fear him when, through his Scriptures, he taught that in this world his most faithful servants would endure many sufferings, as he says in the Gospel: “For they will hand you over to kings and governors, and they will scourge you in their synagogues, and you will be hated by all nations on account of my name” (Matthew X, 17–18). The Apostle Peter also says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God” (1 Peter [Col. 0420C] IV, 17).

You see, therefore, that he gave a sign to those who fear him. These things happen so that the punishment of the future judgment may be escaped. The reason itself follows: “So that they may flee from the face of the bow.” The face of the bow clearly displays the day of judgment, where the whole people is judged under the two bent arches, as it were, of the New and Old Testaments.

But the one who has prostrated himself in humility of confession with devoted intention does not receive from this bow the arrow—that is, the sentence. Let us therefore give thanks to the Lord, who through the signs of preaching caused this bow to be feared, by which every unbelieving person is struck in the Lord’s judgment.

### Verse 5

“So that your beloved may be delivered; save me by your right hand, and hear me.”

That people of the faithful, now subjected to divine powers, enters the second part of the supplication, asking that God’s power [Col. 0420D] transform their tribulations into the joy of gladness. This people rightly prays to be saved by the right hand, because those who will rejoice in perpetual happiness will stand on that side.

It could have asked to be saved in this age, as people ask in sickness and petition amid tribulations. But it prays to be saved by the Lord’s right hand, where there is eternal salvation and joy without end.

### Verse 6

“God has spoken in his holy one: I will rejoice, and I will divide Shechem, and I will measure out the Valley of the Tents.”

God the Father spoke in his holy one, that is, in Christ, when the Word became flesh and appeared as the Savior of the world. “He spoke” signifies the evangelical truth, through which the redemption of the faithful and the blessedness of the saints [Col. 0421A] came.

He added: “I will rejoice, and I will divide Shechem.” The people rightly rejoiced, to whom the Lord had spoken prosperously. But these Hebrew names, throughout this verse and the three that follow, mixed with Greek and Latin expressions, form the figure called *sardismos*, which arises from the commingling of different languages.

Let us now come to the explanation of the words. Shechem is interpreted as “shoulders.” Since shoulders are appropriately fitted for carrying a burden, he says here: “I will divide Shechem,” that is, the burden of divine devotion, which is granted to each person by heavenly distribution. This is the burden whose absence causes us to fall, while carrying it raises us up. Concerning it, it is written: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew XI, 30).

The joyful people therefore says that it will divide among its shoulders the grace of servitude and faith, which it knows how to carry as a very light load.

He added [Col. 0421B]: “And I will measure out the Valley of the Tents.” The patriarch Jacob, exceedingly rich in possessions and flocks, when he decided to migrate from his father-in-law Laban, came to a valley of Syria. There he settled, and his sheep are said to have rested, the place itself receiving the name “tents” from his dwelling there. Since Jacob’s sheep suitably correspond here to the Jewish people, he says that the people which bears the type of the holy Church will measure out the Valley of the Tents—that is, that from the Jewish gathering he will possess no small portion.

For it is established that the Lord’s Church is formed from various nations, like a single crown made from different flowers. A valley is so called as though it were a hollowed valley.

[Col. 0421C]

### Verse 7

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim [MS A: Ephraim] is the strength of my head; Judah is my king.”

Let us examine these names, since, as we have already said, it is clear that they contain the meanings of things.

Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” which can doubtless be referred to the martyrs. For in the Greek language witnesses are called *martyres*. That heap of testimony, gathered from the multitude of heavenly grains, signifies a great assembly of martyrs. A heap rises from below and stretches toward the summit; it is rightly compared with the martyrs, because, brought to immortal gifts, they attain the heavenly height.

The faithful people therefore rightly calls this heap its own, since it is constituted from it.

It follows: “And Manasseh is mine.” Manasseh is interpreted as “forgotten.” During those persecutions of the faithful, the Church seemed to endure great disgrace, when any [200] Christian who was found was condemned to death [Col. 0421D] by the order of pagan rulers. This disgrace is now shown to have been abolished and consumed by a happy forgetfulness, since it is now a glory in the Roman world to be a Christian.

The faithful people therefore rightly says that this forgetfulness is its own, since it was to arise from the abolition of crimes, as Joseph says: “God has made me forget my grief and my father’s house” (Genesis XLI, 51).

He added: “And Ephraim is the strength of my head.” Ephraim is called “fruitfulness”; but what this fruitfulness is is explained in what follows: “the strength of my head.” Who else is this but the Lord and Savior, who by dying in the flesh, through his most glorious resurrection [Col. 0422A], bestowed the richest fruit upon our hope? As the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John XII, 24).

He added: “Judah is my king.” Judah signifies Christ, who according to the flesh descended from the tribe of Judah. This people therefore does not differ from the inscription of the title, since it testifies that Judah—that is, the Savior—is its king.

And it must be said with exultation: “Judah is my king,” because this is the glorious confession of the faithful.

### Verse 8

“Moab is the vessel of my hope; into Edom I will extend my sandal; the foreigners are subjected to me.” Moab stands for the nations, from which he foretold that the Church would be gathered. “The vessel of hope” signifies tribulation—but that tribulation which the most holy Christians endure in this world and which, by the Lord’s providence, extends toward the hope of eternal life, as the Apostle says: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance; endurance, proven character; and proven character, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:4), etc.

The vessel is also used in a negative sense, because in a perverse mind it seethes like a wave of boiling liquid. Concerning this it is written: “A boiling vessel from the north” (Jer. 1:13); this certainly signifies the devil’s schemes, for he said: “I will set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14:13).

It follows: “Into Edom I will extend my sandal.” Edom signifies earthly things, by which the world is held in bondage. The Gospel reached these things when divine mercy came to the aid of sinners. We rightly understand the sandal as the preaching of the Gospel, because just as protection for our feet in the form of sandals repels the discomforts of thorns and other injuries, so the Gospel’s authority fortifies the glorious ordering of our life—which is often compared with one’s steps—so that, strengthened by such a benefit and with the Lord protecting us, we may pass through this world without suffering any wounds. For it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isa. 52:7), and “with your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel” (Eph. 6:15).

This, then, is the sandal that protects us against vices; this is the defense that rises above the thorny things of this age, so that they cannot wound us, though they are shown to be armed with sharpened ambushes.

He added: “The foreigners are subjected to me.” Here the Christian people likewise speak of “foreigners,” that is, alien peoples subjected to them, whom we know already to have confessed the faith. But he wishes these foreigners to be understood as fictitious Christians, who associate continually with the faithful, yet because they live with a perverse mind will not reign with the Lord.

### Verse 9

“Who will lead me into the fortified city? Or who will lead me as far as Edom?” The faithful people, longing for future blessedness, cry out to the Lord: “Who will lead me?”—that is, no one except you alone, God. He calls the future Jerusalem “the fortified city,” because it will be so fortified and perfected that it will no longer be shaken by any persecution, nor will it have mixed among it the foreigners whom the Church now patiently endures.

It follows: “Or who will lead me as far as Edom?” As we said above, Edom signifies earthly things. “Who will lead me?” must be read as a question, with the answer understood to be “he,” namely God, whom he mentions below. For he also desires those peoples to be joined to him who have not yet deserved to be perfected, so that, when the number of the predestined has been completed, they may arrive together at the joys of eternal blessedness.

### Verse 10

“Are you not, O God, the one who rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?” By saying, “Are you not, O God?” he shows whom he meant above by “who.” You truly, Lord, will lead us to your kingdoms—you who made us condemn idols—so that it may profit us to have followed you, whom we have clearly recognized as our only Creator and as the only one who ought to be propitious toward us.

He says: “The one who rejected us,” that is, you prevented us from evil, so that we would not wander astray according to our own will. For the Lord rejected from a perverse religion the one whom he deigned to lead to Christian doctrines, just as it was said in the first verse of this psalm: “O God, you rejected us and destroyed us; you were angry, and you had mercy on us.”

It follows: “And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?” The sense is this: although in the future we rejoice greatly in the hope of your mercy, in the present age we do not see ourselves helped in such a way that, with your assistance, we may conquer our adversaries. Since these things do not happen, but rather we are exposed to afflictions, our enemies suppose that you do not go forth with our armies. Yet this concealment is a saving and glorious test, as the Apostle says: “For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure” (2 Cor. 4:17).

### Verse 11

“Give us help from tribulation, for human salvation is vain.” After the holy congregation had said that in this world it was not at all avenged upon its enemies, it turns to a consoling prayer, asking that the Lord’s help proceed from the tribulation of this world, which it continually endured. It knew that each person would be consoled there in proportion to the severity with which he had been afflicted here for the Lord’s name, as the Gospel says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10).

It follows: “For human salvation is vain.” One who lacks salvation cannot provide salvation; therefore no one should hope in a human being who is shown to be weak in his own strength. Hence the prophet Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5).

### Verse 12

“In God we shall perform a mighty deed, and he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us.” The people of the blessed, having abandoned human confidence, say that in God they can perform a mighty deed. For one must not contend with the devil by fire and sword, but with those virtues by which Christ himself fought, so that we may conquer pride through humility and overcome the riches of the world through poverty.

Finally, he performs a mighty deed in God 201 who, persevering continually in his commandments, tramples upon diabolical temptations by the Lord’s mercy. It follows: “And he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us.” What need have you of weapons, most faithful one, when you are shown to possess such auxiliaries? He himself fights for you, whom no one resists; he himself pursues, whom no one evades. Indeed, he brings the enemies of his faithful to nothing, because he erases them from the book of the living, where they had seemed to themselves to be written in exaltation.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Behold the blessed crushing of this world, if it is endured according to the Lord’s command. Behold humility, higher than earthly summits, when the one to whom help has come in tribulation cannot fail; and in the very danger he finds a benefit that had been accustomed to crush him.

Without you, God, the entire principate of the world is guilty. Every power is anxious for itself, while humility rejoices through you. Your treasures, Lord, are hidden; one thing appears outwardly, while inwardly you make it possess another reality. Who could recount your magnificence? You know how to turn temporal tribulations into eternal joys. And that which appears rejected in this world by criminal men is precious with you.

# Exposition of Psalm 60

**For the end, with hymns; of David**

The Latin wording and the brevity of the title clearly indicate that this is a concise and straightforward psalm. For, unlike the preceding one, it is not filled with obscure names and historical material, so that it may plainly appear that the indications of the titles truly proclaim the psalms as heralds of salvation.

No one is unaware that “for the end” signifies the Lord the Savior, since this has already become clear through frequent exposition. “With hymns” is a Greek expression; it is interpreted as “with praises,” because the entire psalm will resound with praises of Christ. “David” signifies the Lord Savior himself, whose praise is sung by the Christian people spread throughout the whole world.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first part of the psalm, the faithful people, from the ends of the earth, beseech that their prayer be heard, so that, persevering in the holy Church, they may be protected beneath the covering of his wings.

In the second part, they give thanks because the merciful Compassionate One has granted his inheritance to the righteous and consecrated his name to eternal glory. For this reason they promise that they will continually render praises to the Lord.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer.” The faithful people, who are nevertheless members of the Lord, inflamed by holy love, ask that their prayer be heard. But let us consider what it means that they ask for their supplication to be heard and their prayer to be attended to, if we can distinguish these matters with some subtlety.

A supplication is a continual and common entreaty, which we frequently offer even to human beings from whom we request something; he asks that this supplication be heard by the Lord. But he asked that attention be given to his prayer, which we properly offer only to the holy Trinity—that is, that it be regarded and met with mercy—because he presented it in complete purity before the divine presence. Its power is such that, when it is faithfully expressed, it is shown to obtain an acceptable desire.

### Verse 2

“From the ends of the earth I cried out to you; when my heart was anxious, you exalted me upon the rock; you led me.” The holy congregation of the righteous, which is the Lord’s inheritance, weighed down by the evils of the age and groaning among all the nations, cries out to the Lord. It was subject to the needs of the flesh, yet it hastened with the whole desire of its mind to cease from the flesh’s vices.

It cries out “from the ends of the earth,” that is, from the whole globe of the earth, where the Church of the omnipotent Lord has been established. But this cry does not arise only from the ends; it also arises from the interior regions and from the very center of the earth, as was said in Psalm 18: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5).

This people, therefore, which was mentioned above, cries: “Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer.” It also says when this cry is offered to God like a sacrifice: when one cries out to the Lord with greater urgency, as the necessities of the endangered soul seek remedies.

Then follows the hearing of the cry and the singular reward of the righteous: “You exalted me upon the rock.” The rock signifies the Lord Savior, as the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). He declares that he has been exalted upon this rock, upon which every Christian has been built. For the one who is known to be founded there is plainly exalted.

He added: “You led me”—namely, into that future rest which the Lord promises to his blessed ones. For when he said, “You led me,” this is the usage of prophecy: to speak of things that are to come as though they had already occurred, just as it was said in Psalm 21: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:18). This figure is called prolepsis, that is, anticipation of future events.

### Verse 3

“For you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy.” The reason is given why he has been led to the reward: because he had established the Lord as his hope—the one who builds up those who trust in him and always exalts those who place their confidence in him—as the Apostle says: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance; endurance, proven character; and proven character, hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Rom. 5:3–5), etc.

There follows an altogether great comparison: “A tower of strength against the face of the enemy.” By the tower of strength he signifies the Lord Savior himself. A city’s tower protects its walls and wounds attacking enemies from above; so the Lord’s power defends his people when he has openly struck down their enemy by the contradiction of his mouth.

But that tower is filled with virtues, not swords; it fights by speech, not by battle; it commands all things rather than contending. No battering ram shakes it, no siege machinery weakens it, and it does not defend in one particular place; rather, throughout the whole world it guards its servants with unconquered protection.

### Verse 4

“I will dwell in your tabernacle forever; I will be protected beneath the covering of your wings.” Here too a categorical syllogism arises, which is assembled in this manner: The righteous person dwells in the Lord’s tabernacle. Everyone who dwells in the Lord’s tabernacle is protected forever beneath the covering of his wings. Therefore the righteous person is protected forever beneath the covering of his wings.

Now let us return to the explanation of the words. The holy mind of the Lord Christ trusts that benefits will be bestowed upon it, so that amid the dangers of this world it may remain most securely in the Lord’s tabernacle—not for a short time, but until, by divine administration, the ages of this life have run their course. Thus the people of the faithful, succeeding one another as their allotted time passes, are contained in the Lord’s tabernacle throughout the ages.

But let us consider why the Lord’s covering of wings is so often compared with sacred defenses. First, because the wings of birds extend like palms, resembling exceptionally beautiful ribs. Second, because they defend in such a way that they cannot weigh down those whom they protect. Third, because with loving protection they drive away from their beloved young the harshness of heat and cold.

So the Lord’s protection, if we piously flee to him, makes the aerial powers strangers to us, so that neither their blazing fury may harm us nor their cold poison strike us with viperous force. The Lord’s protection is rightly compared with wings, since they neither burden those subject to them nor fail to remedy every hostile injury.

### Verse 5

“For you, O God, have heard my prayer; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.” After the diapsalm, the faithful people come joyfully and exultantly to the second part, rejoicing that their prayer has been heard. By the figure of aetiology—that is, the explanation of a cause—it adds the reason why it rejoices in the protection and covering of the Lord’s wings: rightly so, because its prayer is shown to have been heard.

It follows: “You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name.” The inheritance signifies the kingdom of the future age, which he promises to his blessed servants. It is an inheritance that is not left behind through death, but possessed as an everlasting gift together with its giver; it comes to the children without the testator abandoning them. This inheritance has no end; once it has been received, it never departs from us through any exchange.

### Verse 6

“You will add days upon the days of the King; his years unto the day of the age and the ages.” He signifies the eternity of the Lord Savior, who is truly called our King because we are ruled by him and saved by his power.

“Days upon days” is expressed according to human usage, since many days are mentioned because nights are also shown to follow them. In that eternity, however, there is one day that will end at no limit, as he says in another psalm: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). We should understand the same concerning years, since such things are spoken tropically of the Lord Christ.

Finally, the verse itself continues, “unto the day of the age and the ages,” to show that there is one day with the Lord that transcends these ages. They are called “ages” because they roll times back within themselves.

### Verse 7

“He will remain forever in the sight of God; who will seek his mercy and truth from them?” Behold, the eternity of that day has been clearly expressed. But this is now appropriately understood as referring to the members, as is established in many passages of the exposition, because what follows cannot apply to the Head.

For he says: “He will remain forever in the sight of God.” This is more appropriately understood of the faithful people; the following words also make this clear. He added: “Who will seek his mercy and truth from them?” Why would mercy be sought where no one is wretched? Why truth, where everyone will see God? None of them will be needy of such goods, since they will possess the kingdoms of heaven forever, as the Lord himself says to his apostles: “Now you have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22). “On that day you will ask me nothing.”

Thus it comes about that none of the saints seeks mercy or truth, since he enjoys the immeasurable gift of that contemplation.

### Verse 8

“Thus I will sing psalms to your name, O God, forever and ever, so that I may fulfill my vows from day to day.” “Thus” means “in the manner that he will explain in what follows.” The people of the blessed say that they will sing psalms to the everlasting name; but this will not be for a short time, rather “forever and ever,” signifying that their devotion will remain with unchanging perpetuity.

It follows: “So that I may fulfill my vows from day to day.” The same meaning is repeated with a graceful variation. What “forever and ever” signifies, “from day to day” declares—that is, always—so that here we may fulfill our vows and there sing the Lord’s praises with perpetual joy.

He promises that he will fulfill his vows to the Lord, so that he may adequately repay him with eternal thanks, just as another psalm says: “I will fulfill my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people, in your midst, Jerusalem” (Ps. 115:18–19). Let us therefore fulfill our vows in this transitory day, so that in that perpetuity we may deserve, by his granting it, to sing the Lord’s praises.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let the Donatists hear the Church crying out from the ends of the earth, and let them immediately cease to call it local. Who could be heard against the voice of the world? It is utterly shameless to speak against the testimony of three, and they do not blush to arm themselves shamelessly against the universal judgment. Why do they weary souls with new inventions? Let them accept what they should believe, not what they pervert through their own iniquity.

The faithful people pray from the ends of the earth because the Lord has become its hope; afterward it rejoices with hymnic exultation that it has been heard, because it will continually appear in the sight of the Lord. What could satisfy one if this does not satisfy? We see daily what he promised being fulfilled; we see the world conforming to the standards of the Christian faith. And, alas, falsehood strives to conceal what truth has resolved to reveal.

The reckoning of this psalm is not without significance either. For the number sixty pertains to the continent and widowed, as the mutual insertion of their fingers indicates [ms. A, F: “bending”]. Hence this psalm promises the Lord’s faithful rewards of sixtyfold—not because martyrs or virgins are absent there, those who glory in a hundredfold fruit, but because, within the congregation of many, it can specially indicate certain persons who are continent in this manner.

# 203 Exposition of Psalm 61

**For the end; a psalm of David, for Idithum**

Among the very familiar words of the title, “Idithum” is repeated; concerning him we have already spoken recently in the thirty-eighth psalm. Under the meaning of this name something exceptional is always declared. Its interpretation is “one who leaps over them,” namely, the lovers of this age, whom the soldier of Christ transcends after despising the world’s pleasure.

But since this leaping over appears to signify a blessed purpose for us, a certain holy person is introduced who had abandoned the desires of the world and remained established in the Lord with the firmest hope. Such a person places first “the end,” that is, the Lord Christ. The psalm follows, meaning a commendable life that obeys the Lord’s ordinances. David is also joined to them, so that a praiseworthy life may seem to tend toward the Lord Christ, in whom there is saving and complete perfection.

## Division of the Psalm

This leaper over secular vices, whom we have mentioned, saw the whole world filled with savage errors: some persecuting, some heretical, and others entangled in empty desires.

In the first section of the psalm, he professes that his soul is subject to God, because through the only-begotten Son he has received the gift of salvation, reproving those who desire to be called Christians in name only.

In the second part, he again says that his soul is subject to the Lord Father, because through his Word he acquired saving endurance. He strengthens the people by a faithful confession, so that they ought always to hope in the Lord with the whole affection of their heart.

In the third section, he warns wandering peoples that they ought to place their trust in God rather than in the fleeting happiness of this world.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.” Throughout the psalm, one of the faithful is introduced on behalf of the universal body of the saints. Having abandoned the vices of the age, he recalls that he is subject to God alone.

For to be called subject to the Lord means to be free from worldly vices and filled with holy faith. This is an interrogative or reproving manner directed against those who think that he is idle because of excessive prosperity and, as it were, inactive in a certain leisure of joy.

The expression must be inverted so that it becomes clearer. Let us say: “Will my soul not be subject to God?” This figure is called anastrophe, that is, inversion. The person who always performs humbly and energetically what he has learned belongs to the Lord’s commandments is certainly subject to God. He delights in him, is refreshed in him, and the most blessed mind desires nothing apart from him.

“Will be” signifies an endless time, one that is to be closed by no end. There follows the most just reason why the blessed person’s soul is subject to God the Father. He says: “For from him is my salvation,” that is, the only-begotten Son, who rightly exists as salvation for believers.

When he says “from him,” the Son is signified. For the holy Trinity, the one God, possesses this distinctive order: the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. This the whole faith professes; this the catholic Church professes.

You therefore rightly profess, Idithum, that you are subject to God, from whom you testify that you have received an immeasurable benefit. But so that the holy Word may be honored with one uniform and equal veneration, attend to what follows.

### Verse 2

“For he himself is my God and my Savior; my helper, I shall not be moved any longer.” Above he had called the one begotten of the Father the author of salvation; now, in a threefold confession, he embraces who this Savior is.

First, lest you believe him lesser, he says: “He himself is my God,” just as above he calls the Father God. The equality of the supreme name demonstrates the unity of substance and power. Hence Father Augustine says in the fifteenth book of *On the Trinity* (ch. 3, middle):
