“Once the reasoning has been supplied for those who understand, it is clear, in the substance of truth, not only that the Father is not greater than the Son, but also that the two together are not something greater than the Holy Spirit alone; nor are any two in that same Trinity something greater than one; nor are all three together something greater than each individually.”

Thus he demonstrated with wondrous truth the perfect and singular nature of the holy Trinity.

He repeats: “My Savior.” For the salvation of the human race, which had perished in Adam, was restored through the Lord Christ. It follows: “My helper,” because, when he was entangled in the struggles of this world, Christ alone provided assistance so that he could transcend the world’s vices.

“I shall not be moved any longer” is not an arrogant assertion. For the one whose God, Savior, and helper was the Lord Christ could not be moved. Here perhaps we can recognize the figure called epidiorthosis, in Latin “correction of what has been said above.” For by adding “any longer,” he signifies that he had once been moved. There was a time when this Idithum, weighed down by the weakness of the flesh, stumbled. But after he had been filled with the illumination of true doctrine, he could not be moved, since, with the Lord’s help, he stood firm in the strength of faith.

### Verse 3

“How long will you rush upon people, killing them all, like a leaning wall and a battered fence?” After proclaiming his faith in a threefold declaration, he turns his words toward the persecutors of Christians.

He says: “How long will you rush in formation upon innocent people?” Does divine fear not restrain you, so that you become more savage because you recognize that the worship of demons has been rejected? And lest you think that this persecution was carried out either by privations or by light tortures, he added: “Killing them all,” so that they would bring to death those whom they perceived to be devoted to God. By “all,” we should understand the devout.

There follow highly appropriate comparisons: “Like a leaning wall,” which falls even if it is not pushed, because whatever has been inclined away from its solidity tends toward collapse.

He added: “And a battered fence.” A fence is a dry construction of stones, assembled and raised high without any binding material. And lest you think that its novelty gave it some firmness, he said “battered,” so that what had been shaken either by blasts of wind or by some impact might easily fall to the ground.

But these comparisons are recognized as indicating this meaning to us: Do you think, sacrilegious persecutors, that the Christian people have no firm defender, whom you slaughter so indiscriminately with impious intent?

### Verse 4

“Nevertheless, they planned to drive away my honor; I ran in thirst; with their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed.” The preceding verse concerns the pagans; this one concerns Jews and fictitious Christians. The Church suffers in two ways: either when pagan error persecutes it, or when heretics tear it apart through perverse contention.

The honor of the holy man was the catholic and faithful Church, and Christ himself, who is both head and dignity to his members. Unbelievers planned to drive him away when, so that he might not be worshiped with a pure heart, they opposed him with sacrilegious doctrines.

Then the holy man passed through the course of his life in the barrenness of thirst, because he could find no one to give drink. For thirst acts so that it desires to draw external moisture into its members. Hence the Gospel saying, “I thirst” (John 19:28), and “Woman, give me a drink” (John 4:7). He did not ask her merely to receive water from her, but to pour into her the drink of faith by which she herself would be satisfied.

The cause of the thirst also follows: “With their mouth they blessed.” This happened to those who pass through the Lord’s law with deceptive meditation and do not demonstrate through their works what they proclaim with their mouth. It was added: “And with their heart they cursed.” Those curse in their heart who interpret the holy Scriptures through the vice of perverse novelty.

### Verse 5

“Nevertheless, my soul will be subject to God, for my endurance is from him.” After the pause of the diapsalm, Idithum comes to the second section of the psalm, repeating what he said above: that his soul is subject to God, so that this repetition might impress the strength of faith upon our mind.

But let us examine this more carefully, because, as far as the words are concerned, the reason for rejoicing does not appear to be the same. There he says, “My salvation is from him”; here he says, “My endurance is from him.” Yet although it is expressed in different words, we understand that it is one and the same thing if we examine it more deeply.

For Christ the Lord is our endurance. Because of him we willingly endure adversity and rejoice in observing the rule we have undertaken. Thus it is also sung in Psalm 70: “For you are my endurance, O Lord” (Ps. 70:5). So that you may perceive the same meaning in this statement, the following words are clearly seen to explain it.

### Verse 6

“For he himself is my God and my Savior; my helper, I shall not depart. In God are my salvation and my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God.” In these two verses the Lord Christ is indicated, the one whom he called above “my endurance.”

And as if someone had said to him, “Who is this endurance of yours?” he replied: “He himself is my God and my Savior,” because even then he knew that salvation would come to his soul through the Word who was to become incarnate.

He added: “My helper,” so that he would not attribute to his own powers what he had escaped. It follows: “I shall not depart,” namely, from the faith that I hold, just as it was said in Psalm 10: “I trust in the Lord; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10:2).

Therefore he says that he will not change his judgment, because he had recognized that what he held was beneficial to him. He repeats that salvation is in God—not like the gods of the nations, who bring everlasting death. He also added, “And my glory,” so that it might be not only salvation but also glory to have believed in him.

He says as well, “God is my help,” so that human weakness would not attribute anything to itself. Finally, summing everything up, he said: “My hope is in God,” so that he might attribute to the Lord both the things he had received in the past and, in every respect, the holy man’s future blessedness.

### Verse 7

“Hope in him, all the assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him; God is our helper.” After proclaiming the mysteries of his faith, he turns to the people, who were afflicted by the varied emptiness of superstitions, and urges them to place their hope in the Lord’s power.

He says: “Hope in him”—namely, in the one whom he had professed to be his God and salvation, along with the other things mentioned above.

“All the assembly of the people.” In addressing the people, he does not exclude the powerful, because it is the custom of divine Scripture to speak to one part in such a way that it does not appear to pass over the rest.

He added: “Pour out your hearts before him.” A person pours out his heart before the Lord when he confesses his sins with the most abundant tears. The heart cannot otherwise be poured out except by a frequent rain of tears, as was said in Psalm 41: “I remembered these things, and I poured out my soul within me” (Ps. 41:5). We rightly count this among the distinctive expressions of divine Scripture.

### Verse 8

“Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they themselves may deceive from vanity unto the same thing.” After the second diapsalm had run its course, he comes to the third section, reproaching human beings for their wickedness. For this reason the saving mysteries of this psalm have been proclaimed, so that they might abandon their perverse convictions with their will corrected for the better.

He gives a frequently repeated judgment: “Nevertheless, the sons of men are vain,” so that humanity, recognizing its vice, may hasten with the swiftest supplication to the author of salvation and truth. Thus it was said in Psalm 38: “Nevertheless, every living person is utter vanity” (Ps. 38:6). That wise man also frequently repeats it, saying: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:2).

Some people are accustomed to wonder why the Psalms read, “The sons of men are vain,” while Solomon says, “All is vanity” (ibid., 14). Do the heavenly and earthly things that God created, all of which are very good, consist entirely in vanity? Certainly not. Rather, when compared with greater things, they are judged to be exceedingly small and empty.

As blessed Jerome says: “A lamp is nothing in comparison with a torch; a torch does not shine in comparison with a star; compare the star with the moon, and it is blind; join the moon to the sun, and it does not glow; compare the sun with Christ, and they are darkness.”

Thus all things become vain when, compared with better things, they are diminished in their own splendor. Thus human beings, when they come into comparison with the heavenly truth, are reasonably called vain.

But he added to this matter the vice with which humanity is especially afflicted: “The sons of men are liars in the balances”—whether he is referring to those who deceive the simplicity of buyers with unjust weights, or to people who please themselves and wish to appear just and immovable, though they are deceitful through deceptive instability.

“In the balances” signifies that they are placed, as it were, in the scales of justice and are not believed to love deceit. It follows: “So that they may deceive themselves together through vanity.” They could avoid deceiving if their wickedness could be detected; but 205 when they are believed to be just, they more easily deceive through their concealed perversity.

“Together” means in the equity that faithless people are falsely thought to possess.

### Verse 9

“Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder” [ms. A: “and do not desire plunders”]. He still admonishes those whom he had shown to be corrupted by a detestable habit. He teaches that they must not hope where the fruit of a good desire cannot be found.

One who hopes in wickedness deceives himself, because no benefit arises from it; rather, eternal punishment is procured, as was already said in another psalm: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

He then turns to the poor, who, driven by the necessity of subsistence, desire something obtained by theft. He says: “And do not desire plunder.” Need cannot remove the crime of plunder, nor can it excuse what is subject to punishment. Rather, the one who sends rain upon the just and the unjust, who gives food to every creature, restrains us.

It is therefore exceedingly foolish to abandon the Creator’s power and rush toward hope in crimes. But lest you think that only the poor have been admonished, in the following verse he turns to the rich, so that, with a saving moderation introduced, neither may this one covet nor that one become proud.

### Verse 10

“If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.” He does not condemn abundant riches when they are administered with proper moderation. For if the heart is not set upon them, so that they are regarded as the sole source of happiness, they are plainly necessary. Through them assistance is given to the needy; through them the sick are restored; through them the nakedness of the poor is covered; through them many reach the kingdoms of heaven.

But, on the contrary, one who sets his heart upon riches does not wish to spend gold but to hide it; he always desires to increase his patrimony. And while all hope is placed there, the hunger for those things continually grows.

Therefore he rightly commands the rich not to love what they possess, as the Apostle says: “Command the rich of this world not to be proud in mind, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us with all things for enjoyment. Let them be rich in good works; let them give readily” (1 Tim. 6:17–18), etc.

**Verse 11.** God has spoken once; I have heard two things: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy; for you will repay each according to his works. Just as the beginning of the psalm began with the Father and the Son, so now its completed sequence reaches its conclusion. For he says: “God has spoken once.” If one attends to the literal sense, a considerable question arises. God spoke frequently to our fathers—Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and his other saints—but he spoke once and in a special way to his Son, as the second psalm says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). It is clear that the Father spoke this to no one else. And, as some have wished to understand it, God spoke once because before the ages he begot one Word, consubstantial with himself, immeasurable, coeternal, and equal in power. For true God was begotten from true God, light from light, immortal from immortal, invisible from invisible, almighty from almighty, and so forth—all that incomprehensible unity is truly believed to possess in common.

Let us also examine what these two things are that Jeduthun says he heard. After he had trampled human vices, advancing to divine contemplation and listening through the ear of the mind, he understood that the Son possesses power in himself, as in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). The second follows: “and to you, Lord, mercy”—with “power” to be supplied. Both belong to the Godhead: both that he may be able to act [manuscripts A and F: “be beneficial”] mercifully, and that he may show mercy powerfully. But so that you might more clearly perceive this as spoken of Christ the Lord, the time of judgment follows: “for you will repay each according to his works,” as it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us look in this psalm upon the lights of its sentences, as though certain lamps were shining forth. Faith burns brightly; truth flashes forth—what the Christian people ought to contemplate—lest, blinded by the darkness of this world, it fail to follow the path of right faith. Let pagan error depart; let the murmurs of heretics fall silent; let human vanity and deceit be abandoned. Let no confidence be placed in ingenuity or in the doctrines of the age; rather, let hope be placed in true wisdom, which habitually gives such things as no one can condemn. Grant, Lord, that we too may leap over our vices, so that with purified minds we may be able to come to you.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 62

**A psalm of David, when he was in the desert of Idumea.**

“Psalm” and “David” frequently indicate the Lord Christ, and frequently the Church, because Christ is in his members, and the members are contained in their head. For if the head suffers in any way, the members suffer with it; and again, if the members are afflicted, the head undoubtedly suffers with them, as the Apostle also says: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; or if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26). Therefore the words spoken by the Church in this psalm are rightly presented as signifying the Lord the Savior.

This Church, then, dwells in the desert of Idumea—that is, in the aridity of this age—where it thirsts, longs, and earnestly seeks the Lord’s mercy until it may deserve to come to that eternal glory. Idumea is the place where David is known to have hidden while fleeing Saul’s persecution. Its name is interpreted—as we have often said—as “earthly,” so that we may clearly understand this desert to signify earthly actions, which are altogether stripped of spiritual goods. Hence the Church keeps vigil for the Lord at dawn, praying that it may not become entangled in the errors of this world.

### Division of the Psalm

That spiritual Bride, which contains the members of the Lord the Savior, first says that it has been carried away by an insatiable desire, so that it might behold the Lord’s power; it longs for its soul to be filled with the richness of every good, so that it may be found worthy of his praises. In the second part it gives thanks because, beneath the shelter of the Lord’s wings, it has escaped the storms of this world; it declares that its enemies will be condemned to the lower regions of the earth, while it proclaims and rejoices that Christ the King will rejoice in God the Father together with the saints.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0434B]

**Verse 1.** “O God, my God, I keep vigil for you at dawn; my soul has thirsted for you.” The repetition itself of the revered name first displays the affection of a devout prayer. By saying, “O God, my God,” she somehow calls him her own, so that she may show herself to be moved by such desire all the more. She adds: “I keep vigil for you at dawn.” One keeps vigil for him whenever one sleeps amid the world’s ambition; for we attain the former only if we hasten to abandon the latter. She rightly added “at dawn,” when the time of the Lord’s resurrection dawned, so that she might sing his praises at the moment when he encouraged the human race by the example of his resurrection.

It follows: “My soul has thirsted for you.” “Thirsted” is used with reference to the water of which he says in the Gospel: “Woman, if you knew the gift of God, and who it is who asks you for water, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10). The soul of the faithful therefore thirsts for God when it longs for his commandments and eminent virtues, when it desires to see him from whom all the streams of good are known to flow. This, then, is the soul which, adorned with heavenly things, regards the world as a desert; which is always burning with desire and always thirsty until it may deserve to reach that fountain of divine mercy.

**Verse 2.** “How manifoldly [does] my flesh [thirst] for you! In a desert, and in a trackless and waterless place.” Above he said that his soul thirsted for God; now he testifies that his flesh likewise has a similar desire in many ways, so that, just as God is the author of both, he may be sought by both. But let us consider that, by saying “in many ways,” he says that the flesh thirsted for God more intensely: the more fragile it is, the more ardently it appears to have sought the merciful physician.

The soul of the blessed people thirsts for the virtues commended by Holy Scripture; but there are also innumerable things that the flesh is known to request from God. Both need to be saved, but the flesh has greater need of food, drink, clothing, transportation, sleep, the proper balance of bodily fluids, healthy air, expense, and other things that the soul does not need; yet bodily necessity is shown to seek these. He adds where his flesh thirsted in many ways: namely, “in a desert,” as the title also said—that is, amid the needy and barren hunger of this world.

It follows: “and in a trackless place,” because the world has no way within itself except the Lord the Savior, who is the way of the blind and the saving straight path for those who wander by themselves. He adds: “and in a waterless place,” that is, a barren and unfruitful place. We call that “watery” which abounds in flowing waters; “waterless,” however, means dry and barren, so that his soul may rightly grow hard through excessive dryness. Thus the necessity of this world is indicated by these three names.

**Verse 3.** “Thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory.” By enduring the thirst of flesh and soul that he had mentioned—in the desert, in the trackless place, and in the waterless place, which we understand to pertain to the barrenness of this world—the Church says that she appeared in a holy and faithful purpose when she recognized Christ to be the true God. Let us note what she says: “I appeared to you, that I might see your power,” because no one sees the truth unless he has first been able to appear before God. For if this sun enables us to see when it shines upon us with the light of its brightness, how much more does divine power, without which we can neither receive nor retain anything good!

**Verse 4.** “For your mercy is better than life; my lips will praise you.” By “mercy” he means the Lord’s rewards, which he promises to his saints in generous compassion, and which are far better than the present life. Innumerable miseries possess the present life; eternal tranquility accompanies the other. It is as far removed from worldly light as torments can be distinguished from eternal rest. Hence the hosts of martyrs gladly desire the death of this age, because they know that, in exchange for this temporal destruction, they will live forever, as the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

It follows: “My lips will praise you.” After the benefits he has mentioned, he promises the service of devoted praise, which he knew to be most pleasing to God. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel, after healing ten: “Were not ten cleansed? And none was found to return and give glory to God except this Samaritan” (Luke 17:18). For the holy mind did not wish to conceal what it had recognized ought to be condemned.

**Verse 5.** “Thus I will bless you in my life, and in your name I will lift up my hands.” Thus he looks back to what he had said above: “Your mercy is better than life.” A brief utterance in syllables, but an immense promise in its meaning. For what greater thing can a human being give than to offer his soul willingly to his Creator? Each person perfectly blesses God in his life when he lives by good works in this light. He adds: “And in your name I will lift up my hands.” He lifts his hands in the Lord’s name who, persevering in holy works, prays to the Lord with outstretched hands, so that the prayer itself may represent the form of the holy cross.

We are often urged to pray in this manner. Moses too, when he fought against the Amalekites, supplicated with his hands extended toward heaven (Exodus 17:11). It is also written in another psalm: “I stretched out my hands to you” (Psalm 142:6); and the Apostle says: “Lifting up holy hands without anger or dispute” (1 Timothy 2:8). Understand that by this extension of the hands we are reminded that our conduct must be most holy—commended by holy faith and stained by no foulness of actions.

[Col. 0436A]

**Verse 6.** “May my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness; and lips of exultation will praise your name.” We know that the divine Scriptures frequently display heavenly mysteries through earthly comparisons. “Fat” therefore means the thick coverings of the inner organs that cover and enclose the liver’s interior. “Fatness” is the corpulence of a fattened animal nourished by food. Such an animal was worthy of sacrifices and appropriate for offerings. By this comparison the Church asks that her soul be fattened with the richness of virtues, so that she may be worthy to be offered to the Lord. For the soul cannot be fat unless it has flourished after being fed by the Lord.

The soul’s fatness is knowledge of divine things, right faith, unshaken patience, and whatever else overcomes the fasting thinness of this age. It follows: “And lips of exultation will praise your name.” Dry lips, parched by sin, could not occupy themselves with divine praises, as it is also written in another psalm: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts?” (Psalm 49:16), and so forth. But when the devout soul has received the fatness of the Lord’s mercy, it will praise his name with worthy exultation.

**Verse 7.** “If I remembered you upon my bed, I will meditate on you at the morning hours.” In this verse and the following one, a hypothetical syllogism appears to us in the following form: “If I remembered you upon my bed, and I will meditate on you at the morning hours, because you have become my helper, and in the shelter of your wings I will exult.” Yet the meaning is: “I remembered you upon my bed, and I will meditate on you at the morning hours, because you have become my helper. Therefore, in the shelter of your wings I will exult.”

After listing the difficulties of this age, which the holy Church endured in the desert, in the trackless place, and in the waterless place, he comes to the second part, where she declares that her security is subject to the Lord, because beneath the shelter of his wings she was able to avoid the enemy’s wiles. This signifies that he must be sought in tribulations and that his name must be sung in times of security.

When he says, “If I remembered,” he shows that she always possessed remembrance of the Lord and did not forget him amid prosperity, when human hearts commonly fail to keep bestowed benefits in memory. By “bed” he signifies rest, where we usually release our bodies into sleep and attain the joys of refreshment. It should be applied to prosperous and peaceful circumstances, when we scarcely retain God in our memory. For he returns to what he said above: “I keep vigil for you at dawn.” The faithful person rightly keeps vigil in the morning, since even amid prosperity he could not forget the author of light. To such people the Apostle says: “You are sons of light and sons of the day” (1 Thessalonians 5:5).

**Verse 8.** “For you have become my helper, and in the shelter of your wings I will exult.” This verse contains the benefits that had been bestowed upon her by the Lord’s generosity. He was her helper in dangers, when she was in the desert, in the trackless place, and in the waterless place. The Church exults beneath the shadow of his wings when she is upon her bed—that is, when she has been placed in prosperity. Thus, in the brief compass of a single verse, he concluded the intention of the entire psalm.

**Verse 9.** “My soul clung after you; your right hand upheld me.” Let us consider the vow of the one who desires: the Church does not say that she is near the Lord, but that she has clung to him. This word is understood to indicate a kind of adhesion, so that the one who clings to the Lord may never depart from a good purpose. Excessive love and excessive affection produce this result: that we love in such a way that, clinging to God, we may always be able to remain with him, as the Apostle also says: “The one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

He adds: “after you,” because the Apostle Peter sinned when he wished to go before the Lord, and the Lord said to him: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33). It is characteristic of divine Scripture that those whom the Lord wishes to save he commands to return behind him, where there is no room for error.

It follows: “Your right hand upheld me.” Christ the Lord is the Father’s right hand; he upheld the Church, which was to be protected by the shelter of his wings.

**Verse 10.** “But they sought my soul in vain; they will enter into the lower regions of the earth.” By “they,” he signifies those who attempted to extinguish Christ through criminal opposition—Christ in whom all are most certainly proven to be healed and to live. They sought his soul in vain when they resolved to shed his blood through false accusations, although he was destined to rise after three days into everlasting glory.

The punishment of sinners follows: “They will enter into the lower regions of the earth,” because they were not raised to the heavens; rather, the earth’s depths below swallowed them. Evil thoughts incline toward the depths of the earth, because they emerge from there and roll back into the same filth. This clearly happened to the Jews when they were involved in blasphemies and in the blood of the innocent.

**Verse 11.** “They will be handed over to the power of the sword; they will become the portion of foxes.” The Jewish nation was handed over to the power of the sword when the Roman commanders Vespasian and Titus devastated it with slaughter and fire. Among wild animals the fox is wholly deceitful: it seeks food through tricks and protects its safety by cunning deception. Deceitful people are rightly compared with these animals, since through feigned cunning they strive to carry out their iniquities.

This applies well to Herod, concerning whom the Lord said: “Go and tell that fox: A prophet will not be seized outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13:32). And in the Song of Songs he says: “Catch for us the foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Song of Songs 2:15). This kind of small animal is frequently used negatively because, as we have said, it is cunning through excessive craftiness.

The Jews refused to believe heavenly things and became the portion of foxes—that is, they passed into the wickedness of the deceitful. Or “they will become the portion of foxes” signifies what happened when, in that devastation of Jerusalem, the corpses of the Jews became food for foxes and other wild animals. Or, as others have thought, the Jews are the portion of foxes when by perverse will they join themselves to the deceitful and fraudulent.

**Verse 12.** “But the king will rejoice in the Lord; all who swear in him will be praised.” He calls the Lord the Savior “the King.” He is the King forever, as the unchangeable title of his passion specifically indicated. When Pilate questioned him about himself, he also said: “For this I was born” (John 18:37). He says also, “He will rejoice in the Lord,” that is, in the Father, as he himself testifies: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

He adds: “All will be praised.” When God’s saints praise Christ, they themselves undoubtedly become praiseworthy, because no one can worthily proclaim his praises unless he has deserved to attain the palm of forgiveness. He adds: “those who swear in him.” He did not say “those who swear through him,” lest you think an oath had been commanded, since elsewhere he is known to have forbidden it. For he himself says: “Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth” (Matthew 5:34), and so forth.

But they “swear in him” who bind themselves to him by an inviolate service of the mind. Elsewhere too this word signifies a faithful promise, as it is written in another psalm: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not revoke it” (Psalm 131:11). The Godhead could not swear by another, since it had no equal.

“For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.” He gives the reason for the joy: why the king rejoices in the Lord, and why all who faithfully fulfilled their devotion to him in their promise are praised. “For the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped.” In this world those who are shown to devote themselves to wicked speech do not fall completely silent. But the time of that judgment is better understood here, when all iniquity, convicted universally, will fall silent and will speak no further, recognizing that it can in no way benefit itself.

Observe that in the two preceding verses the vengeance of sinners was related, while the blessedness of the saints with the Lord was proclaimed. This figure is called in Greek *syndiasmos*, in Latin “comparison”; I think it is suitably applied here, since the good and evil of different parties are presented by comparison.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

O truly holy mother Church, who nourish the faithful for God with sacred breasts and make them bear without pain what you willingly assert that you endured amid the struggle of this world. You also say that thanks must always be rendered to the Lord, so that tribulation may never overwhelm us, while you set before us within those very tribulations something that we may love. Then you show what may befall the wicked and what may befall the good, so that, every doubt being removed, the true Prince may be served with the full efforts of devotion. Grant, eternal King, that we who now rejoice in the preaching of the holy mother may enjoy the future gift of your forgiveness.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 63

**For the end; a psalm of David.**

The words of this title, as has often been said, refer plainly to the Lord Christ, who will speak throughout the whole psalm. They have been written without any narrative of historical events, so that the clarity of the title itself may seem to breathe light upon the psalm that follows. For the Lord is about to speak of his passion, which granted life to the world and infused the light of belief. Let us therefore listen with attentive minds, because although it is often repeated, we always receive new benefit from it. This psalm is recognized as the sixth among those that touch briefly upon the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

### Division of the Psalm

The Lord Christ, our King and head, declaring that he is about to assume true humanity, first prays to be freed from fear of the Jewish people. He recalls their deceit and wicked deeds as though they had already taken place, teaching that they failed in their persecutions while he reached the glory of the resurrection. In the second part he mocks the savagery of the Jews, because they themselves were more deeply troubled by their crimes when, after the Lord’s resurrection, his power was proclaimed. Then the joy of the righteous and the virtue of right faith appeared.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0439B]

**Verse 1.** “Hear, O God, my prayer when I am troubled; rescue my soul from the fear of the enemy.” From the standpoint of the humanity he assumed, in which he was destined to suffer, the Lord Christ asks that, when he is placed in tribulation, his prayer be heard, since one asks with all one’s strength for what one perceives to be beneficial.

But let us carefully hear what he asks. He adds: “Rescue my soul from the fear of the enemy.” He does not ask that he should not die at all for the salvation of everyone—hence he rebuked Peter when Peter said, “Be favorable to yourself, Lord; this shall certainly not happen to you” (Matthew 16:22)—but that his soul, rescued from fear of the persecuting people, might complete the passion of his holy dispensation. Proposed goods reach their fulfillment in this way, when the persecutor is not feared. For if human weakness gives way, iniquity is not conquered but rather strengthened by increase.

**Verse 2.** “You have protected me from the assembly of the wicked, from the multitude of those who practice iniquity.” Let us consider how he can say that he was protected, although he suffered, and let us not grieve over the death that the will of criminals attempted to inflict upon the Lord’s faithful. He was plainly protected from the assembly of the wicked, because, while they thought that he would die along with everyone else, they were shown to have been confounded by the glory of his resurrection.

Finally, he was protected by the power of his divinity, because he was the Son of Man and likewise the Son of God: in two natures, yet unquestionably one person, possessing the power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10:18). He was therefore protected because through the power of his might he overcame the plots of the wicked. He adds: “from the multitude of those who practice iniquity.” Above he said, “from the assembly of the wicked,” which may refer to their counsels; now he says, “from the multitude of those who practice iniquity,” so as to express the deed of his own passion.

**Verse 3.** “For they sharpened their tongues like a sword; they bent the bow against a bitter matter.” Through these four verses, up to the division, he signifies the persecution of the Jews by various allegories. Here, however, the most just reason is given why he was protected from the multitude of those who practiced iniquity. For as much as they sharpened their tongues like a deadly sword, so much was their iniquity broken, so that they might turn upon themselves the evils they were preparing against innocent blood.

This is the custom of sinners: those who hasten to burden another first harm themselves. But let us consider what he said: “They sharpened their tongues,” indicating that moment when they cried out with one voice: “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23:21). The sentence itself was the deed of the crime; it makes no difference who kills if someone pronounces that an innocent person ought to be killed.

It follows: “They bent the bow against a bitter matter,” that is, against hidden plots which, as they thought, would not be perceived at all. They enticed the treacherous Judas, by giving him thirty pieces of silver, to become the betrayer, though he appeared to have been his disciple. O bitter matter, more grievous than every gall: that a table-companion should suddenly have been corrupted into a betrayer, a disciple into an agent of death, and the keeper of money into one bought by a reward!

**Verse 4.** “To shoot in secret at the blameless; suddenly they will shoot him, and they will not fear.” This little verse depends upon what precedes: “They bent the bow in order to shoot in secret at the blameless.” “In secret” should be understood as the Jews imagined it. In reality, their deed could not be hidden from Christ, who had been frequently foretold before it happened.

We speak of the blameless in two ways. There are ordinary blameless people who, washed by the Lord’s mercy, are made altogether pure, as it is said in the fiftieth psalm: “You will wash me, and I will be whiter than snow” (Psalm 50:9). But Christ alone is truly called blameless, since he contracted no stain of sins and is proven to be utterly pure through heavenly purity, alien from every offense. Therefore he rightly signified himself by saying: “To shoot at the blameless,” so that greater fear might grow among the Jews who hastened to shed innocent blood.

It follows: “Suddenly they will shoot him, and they will not fear.” Here too “suddenly” must be understood as the utterly foolish Jews imagined it. For how can that be considered sudden which is known to have been foretold to the disciples? As it is written in the Gospel: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matthew 20:18), along with similar statements that he foretold about his passion.

When he said, “They will shoot him, and they will not fear,” he showed the outcome of their wicked thought, so that it might appear that not only had the crime been planned but also accomplished.

**Verse 5.** “They established an evil word for themselves; they planned to hide snares; they said: Who will see us?” They established an evil word for themselves when they said: “He is deserving of death” (Matthew 26:66), or when they declared: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25). “Established” here means established by the most stubborn obstinacy, not solidified by the support of truth.

It follows: “They planned to hide snares; they said: Who will see us?” Here the habit of sinners is described. Anyone who prepares a deception thinks that he is deceiving a human being, so that he may reach his wicked purposes. Thus the Jews, confused by criminal intent and thinking Christ merely human, did not believe that their wickedness was recognized by him to whom all heavenly and earthly things are more truly open than they are known even to themselves.

**Verse 6.** “They searched out iniquities; those searching out the investigation failed. A human being will approach a high heart, and God will be exalted.” This verse is divided into these two sentences. It says how wicked counsels confuse themselves, and how the evil mind fails in the work of its own thinking. In contrast, it shows what progress a good will and an enlightened understanding may possess: the closer one comes to God, the more one recognizes the Divinity as exalted.

The Jews searched out iniquities which they ought rather to have passed over, since they could find no fruit of salvation there. For they said: “If we let him go on this way, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11:48). They also searched out iniquities when they heard the Lord say to the paralytic: “Your sins are forgiven” (Matthew 9:2); they immediately thought that he was blaspheming, and the Lord said to them: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” They also searched out iniquities, as the Gospel says, when they brought various questions in ambush, seeking to discover some basis on which they could accuse him.

The punishment of sinners follows: “Those searching out the investigation failed,” because those who strive to reach the worst things always fail in their thoughts. Of them it is also said elsewhere: “They were weakened, and there was no one to help them” (Psalm 106:12).

The second part of the sentence follows: “A human being will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted.” When he says, “A human being will approach a deep heart,” he signifies those who seek divine things with devout intention. The heart is high when it thinks about heavenly things and avoids earthly ones. Such a person does not fail like those who investigate their investigation; rather, he grows more and more, until he reaches the point at which the supreme and almighty God is believed to be present in him—not because God becomes higher, but because, when divinity is contemplated in the heart of a holy person, it continually grows greater there.

Note that above he spoke of the faithless Jews, saying that they failed in their thoughts; now he speaks of the apostles and all the faithful, in whose hearts God was exalted to the extent that true and most holy thoughts entered their purified minds.

**Verse 7.** “The arrows of little ones became their wounds.” After enumerating the Jewish wickedness that they attempted to carry out against the Lord’s death, he comes to the second part, where he mocks their uproar and harsh counsels by a most fitting comparison. This figure is called irony.

For what is lighter or emptier than falsely judging the true Judge, than wishing to kill the one who raised the dead, than handing over the one who was loosening the world’s bonds while he himself was bound? The arrows of little ones are empty weapons: in the desire to play, children customarily throw fragile reeds in the manner of arrows.

Thus the Jews’ intentions, raging with most savage but ineffectual wickedness, did not inflict a death to be mourned, but rather brought about a most glorious passion. They gave wounds by which death itself would die and the promised salvation of the world would swiftly be fulfilled.

**Verse 8.** “And their tongues were weakened against them; all who saw them were troubled.” In this verse we should follow Origen’s translation, so that the complete sense may be clear to us. The tongues of the Jews were truly weakened when they said: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40). Later they saw rising from the tomb the one whom they had believed unable to come down from the cross’s gibbet.

Where is your unbelief now, Jews? You were still saying of the living man: “If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross” (ibid., 42). I appeal to you yourselves; I ask you yourselves to judge: how much more wondrous is it that a dead man should be able to rise than that one still living should wish to come down from the cross! You asked for little things, while greater things came to pass. But your unbelief could not be healed by signs far more powerful than those you requested.

It is added: “All who saw them were troubled”—that is, they were convicted and confounded, against whose tongues Christ’s glorious resurrection prevailed. O new and astonishing hardness of mind! Others were troubled by their confusion, yet their own insolence could not be bent toward repentance. Some of them were indeed troubled and believed when they came to the apostles and said: “What shall we do, men and brothers?” (Acts 2:37). Receiving saving instruction from them, they deserved through holy baptism to be cleansed from eternal condemnation.

**Verse 9.** “And every human being feared; and they proclaimed the works of God, and understood his deeds.” We have often said that a universal expression may be used for a part. “Every human being” here should not be understood as every person without exception, but as the person who fears the future judgment after considering the Lord’s power.

To understand that this is spoken only of the faithful, observe what follows: “And they proclaimed the works of God”—namely, the glory of the resurrection, recognition of him in the breaking of bread, his ascension into heaven, the disciples’ speaking in various tongues, and the other things that the Lord the Savior displayed through his apostles after his resurrection. They proclaimed these things by preaching to different peoples; and, alas, the nations believed after hearing the miracles to which the Jews had refused to give their minds even when they saw them.

It is added: “And they understood his deeds.” They understood them to be divine, since human weakness could not accomplish such things.

**Verse 10.** “The righteous will rejoice in the Lord, and will hope in him; and all upright in heart will be praised.” We have heard the Lord’s promise and the sentence of the one who judges most truly. He says that the righteous will rejoice in the future, because he knew that his disciples would here be weighed down by the afflictions of various sufferings. But they will rejoice when they sit in judgment, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. They were saddened for a time, but they will rejoice forever, because the Lord’s rewards are greater than those which the faithful are shown to offer him, although even that offering comes from his gift.

But lest you think this is said only of the apostles, a general sentence follows: “And all upright in heart will be praised.” Those are upright in heart who walk along the Lord’s straight paths. Whoever wishes to remove his foot from that rule is crooked; no one can be called upright except one who agrees with that truth and preaching. Such people are always made praiseworthy, because they praise the Lord and are praised by Truth itself.

For what is more praiseworthy than to hear from the Judge himself, gloriously and with longing, in the presence of all the angels: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25:34), and the rest that the text of the Gospel has taught us?

### Conclusion of the Psalm

The Lord Christ has instructed us most profitably through his own person, so that he himself might explain his passion, whose meaning no one can refute. For when we say to the Jews, “The Catholic Church is speaking,” they perhaps receive it carelessly. When we confront them with their own prophet, they nevertheless resort to false interpretations, so that some argument may arise in defense of their assumption of falsehood.

But now what will the obstinate say when they hear the Lord himself speaking about what was to happen to him—the Lord upon whom they presumed to inflict a most savage passion, whose resurrection, accomplished among them, the world acknowledged, and who promises due punishments to unbelievers but eternal rewards to the faithful?

Pray, Jews, while there is time; seek while you can to be received among the lambs at the right hand, lest you should happen to be driven away to the left with the goats.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 64

**For the end; a psalm of David, a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel concerning the people of the migration, when they began to set out.**
Toward the End; a Psalm of David—the words are already familiar; it remains for us to say what follows. When the Hebrew people were led captive by the Chaldean nation because of their disobedience, the prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel said (Jer. 25:11) that after seventy years they would return to their own country and restore Jerusalem, overthrown by its enemies, to a better condition. He added: “Of the people of the transmigration,” that is, of the Hebrew people who migrated to the city of Babylon. Spiritually, this signifies the time when, because of our sins, we are transferred into the power of the devil. For Babylon, as has often been mentioned, is interpreted as “confusion,” which is clearly especially applicable to the devil.

This people, therefore, which, after its captivity, was leaving Babylon and hastening toward the city of Jerusalem, the Lord’s city, represents those who, having rejected the confusion of this world, strive to come to the Church of Christ. By the authority of the Fathers, this entire psalm must be applied to them, since when this people was returning to Jerusalem, Jeremiah and Ezekiel had already been overtaken by death. But to avoid the difficulty of this question, let our ordering of the words be as follows: “Toward the End; a Psalm of David, a song concerning the people of the transmigration, through the prophecy of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, when they began to set out.” This is correctly understood, so that the words appear to belong more to the people than to Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

## Division of the Psalm

This people, which has abandoned the sins of the world and is returning to the Lord the Savior, recognizes at the beginning of the psalm that it has been delivered by its Creator and asks that its prayer be acknowledged, declaring blessed only the one who has deserved to reach his courts. In the second section it says that the Lord is the hope of all the ends of the earth, describing his various praises and power through allegorical comparison, and that his saints rejoice in him with hymnic exultation.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“You are worthy of a hymn, O God, in Zion; and to you the vow shall be paid in Jerusalem.”

The people, having returned to the Lord from the captivity of sin, burst forth in great exultation, affirming that God alone is worthy of a hymn, not the throngs of demons, as the gentiles had previously thought. They had possessed songs that they poured out to unclean spirits and idols; but, brought to the light of truth, they say that he alone ought to be praised, since he is acknowledged to be the Creator of all things. Yet this takes place nowhere except in Zion, that is, in contemplation.

This contemplation, however, reveals the light of right faith. In it the true hymn is spoken to the Lord in a disciplined song, not in the perverse shouting of the tongue. But to make this more explicit, he added: “And to you the vow shall be paid in Jerusalem.” Vows were paid by unbelievers to Mars, Venus, and the other demons. If someone had been delivered from battle, he sacrificed to Gradivus; if someone had entered into a shameful adultery, he regarded the goddess of lust as worthy of worship.

Now, however, with truth recognized, he says that in Jerusalem a vow is to be paid to God alone from good works. Jerusalem is the vision of peace, in which fixed and immovable happiness remains.

### Verse 2

“Hear my prayer; to you all flesh shall come.”

This people, which had previously said, “You are worthy of a hymn, O God, in Zion,” now cries out to the Lord in a hymnic supplication, saying, “Hear my prayer,” so that it might first do what it had declared must be done by others. It is this people, of whom we spoke above, that asks for its prayer to be heard.

Knowing that it would die, it begged the one to whom it knew it would come after this life, asking him to spare it here, so that he would not judge it there. The Apostle speaks of that judgment as follows: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10).

Here we must understand “flesh” to mean not only the saints but every human being, since it is certain that all will come to him, whether to be condemned or to be placed in eternal rest. Observe also that in the divine Scriptures both the soul alone and the flesh alone are frequently used for the human being, as in Genesis: “And they entered Egypt with Jacob, seventy-five souls [ms. A: two]” (Gen. 46:27). And here: “To you all flesh shall come.”

At this point it is very useful to remember the figure of synecdoche, which signifies the whole by a part.

### Verse 3

“The words of the wicked have prevailed against us, and you will be merciful toward our iniquities.”

The words of the wicked certainly prevailed when pagan parents persuaded their children to follow the ancient rites and sacrileges that they themselves worshiped. Drawn into this through childhood, they seemed to follow what they had absorbed with their unformed minds.

“The words of the wicked have prevailed against us” was said as though of some exceedingly deep sea whose abundant currents overwhelm everything placed in their way and do not permit anything it has swallowed to swim out. But divine mercy came to the aid of these errors when, through the coming of the Lord the Savior, it granted salvation to the world.

We must investigate what is meant by “being propitiated.” We properly say this of priests whenever, through sacrifices offered, they render the Divinity propitious for our sins, so that the wrath owed to transgressions is changed into the grace of salvation, and those who were most justly guilty because of their deeds are released through the gifts of the Divinity.

Thus the Divinity was reconciled to the human race when he gave us Christ himself as both priest and victim, as the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them” (2 Cor. 5:19).

### Verse 4

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up; he shall dwell in your tabernacles [ms. A: courts].”

Some consider this verse to be applicable to the Lord the Savior; but we say that it should rather be referred to the blessed person in general. For above he had said, “You will be merciful toward our iniquities”; now he continues, “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken up,” so that it may be understood that he did not say this specifically of the one who was sinless, but absolutely of the sinner.

Blessed, therefore, is the one whom the Lord has chosen. But observe what he says: “you have chosen,” so that no one might attribute this election to his own merits, as he himself says in the Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16).

“To be taken up” means to be placed in eternal rest, which the merciful Lord promises to his saints. But what happens to such people he immediately explains: “He shall dwell in your tabernacles.” We say that those dwell who do not abandon the place they have obtained through any change of residence.

What this dwelling is like, he says in another psalm: “My soul has desired and fainted for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3). There, to dwell is already the reward, since no one can enter there except those whom heavenly mercy deigns to choose.

### Verse 5

“We shall be filled with the good things of your house; your temple is holy.”

If the human mind should wish to examine fully the good things of the house of God—that is, of the future Jerusalem—it would not suffice. Concerning these the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

But since it is permissible to speak of what has been heard in part, the good things of his house are the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit that the Lord promises there to his faithful saints. There are also good things of his house here, which the Apostle describes: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretations of words” (1 Cor. 12:8–9), and so forth.

Observe also that he said, “We shall be filled,” as though according to our measure: we shall be given to drink as much as we are able to contain. This signifies what the same Apostle says: “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7).

It follows: “Your temple is holy.” This may refer either to the house of God, which is the Church, or to the Lord’s incarnation, as it is read in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). A little later the Evangelist says: “He was speaking about the temple of his body.”

[Col. 0446A]

### Verse 6

“Wondrous in righteousness. Hear us, O God our Savior.”

What he said, “Wondrous in righteousness,” refers to the temple mentioned above, for it can be wondrous in many ways. But he added “in righteousness” so that you should understand his coming, when he separates the good from the wicked and repays each according to what is deserved.

Yet, so that we should understand this as referring to him, it follows: “Hear us, O God our Savior.” He himself is God our Savior, who brought salvation to the world and in his mercy came to the aid of the human race.

### Verse 7

“Hope of all the ends of the earth, and of the distant sea.”

After that people had been converted, poured out its prayer with a simple heart, and declared itself filled with the Lord’s good things, it comes to the second section, in which it describes the Lord’s praises and powers.

This meaning cuts away with the sickle of truth the persuasions of the Jews and the perverse doctrines of heretics. For the Lord is not a local hope, nor the hope of one nation, but the hope of all the ends of the earth, since humble vows are poured out to him throughout the whole world.

He is rightly the hope of all, since he has promised eternal rewards to all the faithful. But so that you would not understand this only of the earth that they call the great land, he added, “and of the distant sea.”

This may refer to the islands, which he did not seem to include within the ends of the earth; or to the distant sea, that is, the habitation of the whole world. Concerning it he says elsewhere: “This sea is great and spacious in its reaches” (Ps. 103:25). It is distant because its habitation contains innumerable nations.

The Lord himself also testifies that the sea is to be understood as the world, for he said to his disciples: “I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19). Where are fish found most of all, if not in the sea? This world is rightly compared with the sea, because it is bitter with falsehoods, shaken by demonic waves, and stirred up by the storms of vices.

### Verse 8

“Preparing the mountains by your strength, girded with power.”

Let us examine this verse somewhat more carefully, for it is profound in the subtlety of its wording. What is said, “preparing the mountains by your strength,” does not refer at all to earthly elevations. We do not speak of preparing anything unless it is provided with the necessary quality for suitable uses. Therefore, through allegory, we appropriately understand the prepared mountains as the apostles, who were chosen for the word of preaching. They possessed the strength of faith and the height of holiness, humble in their way of life but exalted in merit.

The Lord prepared them by his strength, because through them he performed great miracles: by the greatness of their word they converted unbelievers, and by the wonder of their deeds they softened the hardest hearts.

He then explains how he prepared them: “girded with power,” that is, clothed with his majesty. The humanity of the Lord the Word was girded with power, so that divine strength might supply what humanity did not possess.

We gird ourselves with the honor of a belt, although the dignity of the belt differs from the nature of the one who wears it. Thus it is also said in the forty-fourth psalm: “Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one” (Ps. 44:4); and elsewhere: “You have girded me with gladness” (Ps. 29:12).

These and similar passages indicate the Lord Christ’s two natures, both completely full and perfect, in one and the same person, as the entire Catholic Church confesses.

### Verse 9

“You disturb the depth of the sea; who can endure the sound of its waves? The nations shall be troubled.”

After he had said allegorically that the mountains were the apostles who had been prepared, he now explains what the Lord accomplished through them.

When the apostles preached, he disturbed not only the surface of the sea but the bottom of the sea, that is, the hearts of the gentiles, which had been sunk more deeply. When they saw their own divinities fall silent and felt that they had been annihilated, they were rightly troubled in heart, since they realized that their hopes had come to nothing.

Since the world is called the sea, the hearts of the foolish are appropriately compared with the sea’s bottom. From there rises what stirs up the waves of sinners; from there comes the unexpected disturbance that strikes innocence and exhausts the saints.

It follows: “Who can endure the sound of its waves?” Here he signifies the persecutors. Although they themselves are stirred up like the highest waves, their sound—that is, their cruel words—cannot be endured by human beings unless, by divine grace, their insolence is broken and overcome.

“Who can endure?” is said with regard to human weakness. For, with the Lord’s gift supporting them, the martyrs were able to overcome their violence. Hence the nations were especially troubled when they saw the most faithful performing miracles while alive and fulfilling the petitions of those who prayed even after death; they saw their own divinities and their power grow fearful and refuse to give responses.

Then Delphic Apollo also fell silent; then Diana departed from Delphi; then Cytherean Venus blushed with shame. But what, I ask, could the nations do when they saw their own divinities trembling?

### Verse 10

“And all who inhabit the ends of the earth shall fear because of your signs; at the rising of morning and at evening you will rejoice.”

Here he signifies the time when the apostles performed various signs. It was necessary that the whole world tremble, since it appeared to inhabit the globe of the earth, when it saw such signs as neither their writings had disclosed nor any vision had shown.

He himself indicated the source from which that fear could arise: “because of your signs.” He added: “At the rising of morning and at evening you will rejoice.”

The rising of morning occurs when someone is converted from the happiness of this world to the Lord the Savior. The morning hour always grows bright and, as the day advances, acquires the grace of illumination.

When he says, “and at evening you will rejoice,” he signifies that for those suffering heavy things it is always dark; yet they come to the Lord the Creator, who turns their sorrows into joy.

Thus the Lord will rejoice at the outcome of both conditions, because through the abundance of his generosity he gains devoted people from every direction.

### Verse 11

“You visited the earth and intoxicated it; you multiplied it to enrich it.”

Here we must understand “earth” as the human race, which was satisfied and refreshed when the Lord deigned to come. But another psalm explains with what this earth was intoxicated, saying: “And how splendid is your cup, intoxicating!” This is a blessed drunkenness, a saving fullness, which, the more abundantly it is received, the more it deigns to bestow sobriety upon minds.

For this reason, this kind of expression is characteristic of the divine Scriptures, since it is often used in a good sense. In secular writings and common stories, however, drunkenness is never understood favorably.

He adds: “You multiplied it to enrich it.” These words reveal an immeasurable mode of giving. For when he says “you multiply to enrich,” he does not seem to express any limit; rather, what is promised by such words is extended into infinity. A person is called “rich” because he possesses many places.

This is the earth that he deigned to take up, not the earth that he trod according to the manner of human beings. We read that the earth on which we tread is not to be enriched but rather transformed, as Isaiah says: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 65:17).

[Col. 0448B]

### Verse 12

“God’s river is filled with waters; you prepared their food, because such is your preparation.”

The Lord’s mercy is rightly compared with a river filled to overflowing. It cannot be diminished by any drought, since it does not know how to be exhausted by frequent drinkings.

Worldly water receives increase from rains or diminution from drought; but God’s river is always full and always equal. Concerning it it is said: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:13).

Let it not disturb you that rivers are placed elsewhere in the singular number and elsewhere in the plural. The power of unity embraces many things. For although we speak of “Churches” in the plural, it is nevertheless certain that there is one Catholic Church, as has been recognized on countless occasions.

But after speaking of the river’s drink, he added a spiritual food, so that the Lord’s most abundant banquet would not leave his friends hungry in any respect. He says: “You prepared their food.”

That food is not chewed by the teeth but devoured by the soul’s hunger. Concerning it it is said: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25). Thus the whole passage is appropriately referred to sacred communion, since we drink his blood and are nourished by his body.

And so that you would not think that anything happened by chance, as the mockery of the gentiles supposes, he added: “Because such is your preparation.” Everything happened just as it had been arranged by him, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies, and not one of them will fall to the ground without the will of your Father?” (Luke 12:6).

### Verse 13

“Intoxicate its streams; multiply its generations; in its showers it will rejoice when it rises.”

Here also he calls the apostles, or other faithful people, “streams,” because they drank from that river of God which is always full. But so that you would not think their drink to be exceedingly slight, he says that the streams themselves are to be intoxicated, so that they may reach such fullness as is sufficient for them in abundance and may grant what will benefit others.

He returns, therefore, to the singular number, which we have said is appropriate to ecclesiastical unity. He says: “Multiply its generations,” that is, those of the stream which flows from the holy river, so that through succeeding generations the blessed preaching may not fail but may be multiplied, and thus the Catholic Church may always grow. Those who are now instructed in sacred doctrine may then be seen teaching others after them. We clearly recognize this happening every day.

He spoke of the streams, which pertain to those who are advanced [ed.: perfect]. Now he speaks of the showers, which refer to Christians who are beginners. For the broadest doctrine cannot enter confined beginnings. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

Showers are drops that fall from roofs. They penetrate not by their weight but by their persistence. How far they differ from streams is also clear to us by ordinary observation.

Therefore, at the outset, every believer rejoices when he rises from water and the Holy Spirit, when we are truly reborn and are prepared by the Lord’s gracious favor for glory. Great joy is ours then, when, having laid aside the oldness of the ancient person, we are changed into the joys of new birth.

Although these gifts of God may appear to be set forth in the text in another manner, when their order is reversed they seem to show the certain order of our progress. First, the aridity of faith is enlivened by certain showers; afterward we are watered by flowing streams; then, as the preceding verse says, with the Lord’s help we reach the fullness of that river. Through these three stages, therefore, the order of the divine gift is revealed.

### Verse 14

“You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance.”

The crown of the year is appropriately understood as the whole world, through which the Catholic Church is extended. The Lord blesses those whom he truly makes Christians through the river, the stream, and the shower, which he mentioned above.

Then observe what follows: “And your fields will be filled with abundance.” By “fields” he means faithful and righteous people, who are compared to the levelness of fields because of their most equitable hearts. Such people are filled with abundance because, with the Lord’s generosity, they will produce thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or hundredfold fruit.

### Verse 15

“The ends of the desert will grow fat, and the hills will gird themselves with exultation.”

The ends of the desert are the peoples of the gentiles, to whom no prophet had been sent; all the prophets preached within the nation of Judaea. These ends of the desert, therefore, were enriched by the great gift of the Divinity when the holy preaching of the apostles reached them, and they were made beautiful by the Lord’s grace through faith. Previously, the dreadful emaciation of unbelief had disfigured them.

At first, sowing through the prophets took place in the nation of Judaea; afterward, among the gentiles, it was spread far and wide through the apostles. Yet the Lord’s power gathered more grain from these ends of the desert than appeared from those lands that seemed cultivated, as the prophet says: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

The hills, however, must be understood as the multitude of martyrs, because after the apostles they are the higher ones. This is signified by the words, “They will gird themselves with exultation,” because, through endurance of sufferings and with the Lord’s help, they reach eternal joy.

[Col. 0450A]

### Verse 16

“The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys will abound in grain; for they will cry out and sing a hymn.”

“They are clothed” signifies that nuptial garment with which the rams of the sheep—that is, the apostles and the other saints—will be clothed. They became leaders in good doctrine (doctrinae bonae; ms. G: doctrinae bono, an inflectional variant) for the Christian people.

It follows: “And the valleys will abound in grain.” The valleys signify humble peoples, since nothing is more humble than things that descend into a certain hollow of the earth.

These humble people, therefore, will abound in grain, like that publican who neither dared to raise his eyes toward heaven nor trust in any presumption of merits. He abounded in grain because he was a humble valley. He was raised up because, with the Lord’s help, he cast himself down; and he became stronger because he confessed that his own strength was weak.

He added: “They will cry out and sing a hymn.” This final conclusion shows us that the allusions he made above are to be received through mystical comparison. For neither the ends of the desert, nor the valleys, nor the rams of the sheep, nor the other things he mentioned earlier will cry out. Rather, those to whom these things are referred through an appropriate comparison will cry out and sing a hymn.

He first said, “They will cry out,” and, so that you would not think the cry itself confused, he added, “and they will sing a hymn”—that is, praise, which is known to belong sweetly to rational creatures.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us understand how pleasantly that blessed people rejoiced when it came to the Lord Christ, and let us know that the benefit celebrated with such exultation is beyond estimation.

How richly he adorned the hymn that he had promised in the first verse of the psalm with a variety of graces! Describing the praise of his incarnation with marvelous brevity, the faithful teacher instructed us concerning what he had bestowed upon the world. Finally, he says that at the resurrection to come all his saints will rejoice in him with hymnic exultation.

Thus he narrated the present with marvelous brevity and promised us future rewards in order to stir us to the greatest hope.

Grant, heavenly King, that we too, rescued from the aridity of sin and more abundantly watered by the river of your mercy, may deserve to grow rich, so that we may continually sing a hymn to you with your saints.

# Exposition of Psalm 65

“Toward the End; a Psalm of David; a song of resurrection.”

[Col. 0450D]

Although the names placed at the head of the title may seem to be already thoroughly familiar from the exposition given above, it will nevertheless not be out of place to repeat them occasionally for those who know them, so that the intention of the entire inscription may be recognized more clearly.

“Toward the End,” as it is said, refers to the Lord the Savior, as the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

“Psalm” announces him without ambiguity, because the psalm resounds from what precedes, just as his works and words resounded.

“David” is interpreted to mean “desirable” and “strong of hand.” These words apply especially to our King and Lord Christ.

It remains for us to say what follows. This general song, which the preceding names have taught us is spoken concerning the Lord the Savior, proclaims his glorious resurrection. Through it the Church admonishes the gentiles, whom it knew beforehand would believe through the Lord’s grace, to rejoice together, since they were to be restored in their Head.

But because the Jewish nation thought that it alone would come to the rewards of blessed life—since, among the other nations still devoted to idols and serving them, it alone seemed to possess the law of the true Lord, though it was destined to fall through the fault of its unbelief—the holy Church poured forth this song through the spirit of prophecy. It affirmed that the hope of resurrection would belong not only to the faithful from the Jews but to the whole world from every nation, as the Lord says: “As I live, says the Lord, the glory of the Lord shall fill the whole earth” (Num. 14:21).

Accordingly, this psalm also begins in this way: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.”

## Division of the Psalm

Against the persuasion of the Jews, who claimed that they alone, above all others, belonged to the blessed life, mother Church joyfully sings the hope of the general resurrection, with three intervening diapsalms.

First, she urges the whole world to rejoice with the Lord’s resurrection, which was to provide eternal rewards for all the faithful.

Second, she invites everyone to come and contemplate God’s works, so that one faith may join together those who seemed to await one reward.

Third, she again exhorts the gentiles to bless the Lord, who, although he tests us with various tribulations, nevertheless leads us to the rest of his mercy.

Fourth, she again invites the whole world, so that, reminded (commonita; ed. communita, “fortified”) by the example of its deliverance, it may trust more fully in the Lord, blessing him because he has deigned to hear its prayer.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.”

As we have said, holy Church tells the whole earth that it ought to rejoice, since it was destined to believe in Christ the Lord.

“Jubilation” means exultation of the heart, which cannot be expressed in words because of its immensity. Therefore he rightly began with such a word, so that the joy of the incomprehensible benefit might be shown.

When he says “all the earth,” he does not mean the soil but the faithful and devoted, who could rejoice at such a miracle. This figure is called metonymy, that is, transference, whenever what is contained is announced by means of what contains it.

By such preaching he refutes the Jews, who thought that the hope of blessed resurrection had been promised to them alone.

It follows: “Sing a psalm to his name.” After that inexplicable jubilation, it was fitting for him to urge the peoples who were to believe toward psalmody, so that they might express through spoken praises what they had conceived in their minds.

The former was known to God alone; the latter was also to be heard by human beings, as it is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

When he says “to his name,” he signifies the Lord the Savior, at whose coming the wounds of the world are shown to have been healed.

Let us also attend to what is said: “Give glory to his praise,” and let us draw the heavenly antidote into our thirsty souls. The one who gives glory to his praise is the person who celebrates the Lord’s praises with repeated exultation, attributing everything to him and judging that nothing should be assigned to human strength.

For human frailty must avoid and flee with every effort the desire to be raised up by its own praises; rather, it ought to be censured by just reproach.

### Verse 2

“Say to God: How terrible are your works! In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.”

Let us hear what the Church teaches the gentiles to say in a single brief statement, and how it compresses a great matter of religion into a few words: “How terrible are your works!”

Although it says that the Lord’s works are terrible, it does not state how great their terror is. But I think the Lord’s works are to be feared for this reason: we must consider what could happen to us if that majesty which looked upon the world in mercy should, because of our sins, become hostile.

For God deigned to become human for our sake, as Pope Leo, the apostolic teacher, says in his letter to Flavian (Letter 10 to Flavian, chapter 4):

> The Creator of angels consented to be one of mortals; invisible in his own nature, he became visible in ours; incomprehensible, he willed to be comprehended; remaining before time, he began to exist in time. The Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, while the immensity of his majesty was veiled. God, impassible, did not disdain to be a passible human being and to be subject to the laws of death, though immortal.

If we consider these things, the Lord’s works are terrible for us, since we cannot offer even that which heavenly mercy deigns to urge us to offer for our salvation in response to such condescension.

Thus it is also read elsewhere: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Hab. 3:2).
