But this fear is affectionate and devout. It possesses sweetness, not bitterness; it generates hope, not distrust; it increases desire, not extinguishes the ardor of charity.

It follows: “In the multitude of your power your enemies will lie to you.”

The multitude of his power was shown in his healing people afflicted with various illnesses. Yet in this power his enemies lied when they said: “He performs these signs by Beelzebub” (Matt. 12:24).

They also lied in the multitude of his power when he said: “You will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven” (Matt. 26:64–65). They replied: “He has blasphemed; why do we still need witnesses?”

Finally, they lied in the multitude of his power when, after the glory of the resurrection, they gave money to the guards and said: “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep” (Matt. 28:13).

Thus the venerable mother, with concise brevity, declared the mysteries of the future holy incarnation.

### Verse 3

“All the earth shall worship you and sing to you; let it sing a psalm to your name, O Most High.”

Since above he said that the enemies had lied, the whole world is now admonished to worship the Lord Christ truthfully.

He added: “And sing to you,” which truly ought to be offered to divine powers.

It follows: “Let it sing a psalm to your name, O Most High.” Earlier he had said, “Let it sing to you”; then he repeated almost the same words. But to those who inquire carefully, the meanings are very different.

Previously he intended psalmody to be understood; here he admonished the works of holiness. When he says “to your name, O Most High,” he signifies, as was said above, the Lord the Savior, who is rightly called Most High, because he is known to have nothing above himself—not even the Father and the Holy Spirit.

This name was placed especially to convict the pride of the Jews, who believed him to be so abject that they did not shrink from crucifying him. The Arians too are convicted by this name: he who is Most High in his divinity cannot have anyone greater.

### Verse 4

“Come and see the works of the Lord, how terrible he is in his purposes concerning the children of men.”

In the second order, the Bride of the eternal King invites the gentiles to contemplate with devoted minds the miracles of the Old Testament, so that they may recognize that what happened figuratively to the Hebrew people has been truly fulfilled in themselves.

“Come” is appropriately said, as if to those still far away, as if they were still dwelling in the city of Babylon.

“See” means “recognize with the light of the heart.” They could not see with bodily eyes the things that were already past.

He does not mean by “the works of the Lord” those things that everyone sees together—the heaven, the earth, the sea, and everything in them. Rather, he invites them especially to contemplate those things that the most faithful recognized spiritually: that the sea was divided and opened before the fleeing Hebrews; that for forty years the people were fed to satisfaction in the desert; that the waters of the Jordan provided a passage on dry feet; and the other things that happened figuratively to the Jews.

He added: “How terrible he is in his purposes concerning the children of men.” He made the children of men terrible and fearful when he displayed great miracles through them [ms. A: “he became terrible and fearful when, through them, etc.”].

What these works are that he wishes the gentiles, still unformed, to recognize, the following verses will explain.

### Verse 5

“He turns the sea into dry land; they will cross the rivers on foot; there we will rejoice in him together.” These are the works of the Lord of which the preceding verse gave warning. He turned the sea into dry land when he made the Hebrew people have a solid path through the midst of the waves. He crossed the rivers on foot when, with the Jordan divided to the right and left, he led the Jewish army into the promised land.

But it may be asked why he used “rivers” in the plural, when we read that this happened only in the Jordan. Not without reason: although it happened only in that river, it is nevertheless shown to have occurred there frequently. Elijah too had such a crossing there, and the waters of that same river were similarly opened for his disciple when he was returning (IV Kings 2:8, 14). Alternatively, it is because divine Scripture has the custom both of saying one thing for many and of calling many things by the name of unity.

He continues: “There we will rejoice in him together.” Here he hastens to disclose the mysteries of those works, because the Christian people truly rejoiced afterward in their prefiguration. For the fact that the Jewish nation passed through the seas announced the baptism of Christ that would follow. The fact that it crossed the rivers on dry feet, without danger from their depth, signified that it could safely pass through the currents of this world and reach the safest refuge of repentance. Hence it was necessary for the Church, together with holy men, to say that it would rejoice there in him together, where the fountain of our joy and the source of eternal salvation have been prepared. What he says—“there, in him together”—should be counted among the distinctive expressions of divine Scripture. [Col. 0453D–0454A]

### Verse 6

“He rules by his power forever; his eyes look upon the nations.” He explained what he had said—“We will rejoice in him together”—namely, “He rules by his power forever.” Earthly rulers too can exercise dominion, but not by their own power, nor forever. Therefore these two additions were made so that the power of the omnipotent King might be displayed.

And lest the still-blind Gentiles consider the promises mentioned above empty, he added: “His eyes look upon the nations,” so that what they could not see by themselves they might behold when touched by the sight of the true light. For the Lord illuminates those whom he regards; those whom he intends to visit, he also delivers. [Col. 0454A–B]

### Verse 7

“Those who provoke him to anger—may they not exalt themselves.” The custom of our frailty has been described with fitting brevity: when we do things by which we provoke the Lord to anger, we exalt ourselves within ourselves, desiring rather to defend our sins. But he forbids these people to exalt themselves, since they ought to be found humble. The faithful ought to be exalted not in themselves but in Christ, where exaltation is secure and the ascent can never fall.

### Verse 8

“Bless God, you nations, our God, and hear the voice of his praise.” He comes to the third member, in which he urges the nations to glorify the true God with harmonious preaching. He continues: “And hear the voice of his praise”—that is, receive with faithful belief what the Father says about the Son. His voice of praise is: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

This must be heard with the purest and most devoted minds, so that the one and same Lord Christ may be believed to have been begotten from the Father before the ages, consubstantial with him, and to have been born from the Virgin Mary, graciously becoming like us in the humanity he assumed. For the holy Church lives by this faith and progresses in this faith, so that in the Lord Christ neither humanity without true divinity nor divinity without true humanity may be believed.

### Verse 9

“He has appointed my soul for life, and has not allowed my feet to be shaken.” Now he enumerates the reasons for which the Lord’s mercy is proclaimed. These are the two mysteries of our liberation. First, through the gift of baptism he leads us to life. We did not reach it by our own merits; rather, we are drawn there by the benefit of his mercy. Then he does not permit us to be expelled from it, although we are shown to be burdened with grave vices.

He himself appoints us to life, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He does not allow our steps to be shaken, who extended his hand to Peter lest he sink (Matthew 14:31). And lest you think that these things are said idly, he lists below the dangers from which she was delivered. [Col. 0454C–D]

### Verse 10

“For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire.” Until this point the Church seems to have prophesied in the singular; now she speaks in the plural through her members, explaining in these three verses by how many tribulations the Lord’s faithful are afflicted.

God causes us to be tested when, through various kinds of temptation, he grants us the endurance of blessed suffering for the confession of his name. He does not come to know us by testing us; he knows us beforehand.

The diverse punishments of the martyrs follow. The blessed conscience is examined by the fire of charity: it is so kindled by love of Christ the Lord that it overcomes the torments of burning flames. But this fire is not consuming; it is purifying. The example of silver is given because it is refined by fire so that it may be rendered purer. The mass of silver would remain with its impurities unless, through the benefit of great heat, it laid aside its native defilements. [Col. 0454D–0455B]

### Verse 11

“You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back.” “You brought us into a snare”—that is, you made us enter the chains of imprisonment, which the martyrs deserved to endure. It was a snare that did not deceive but tested; that bound the body but loosened the soul’s chains; that did not lead to guilt but granted the gifts of acquittal.

He added: “You placed tribulations upon our back”—namely, the blows that Paul endured and the rest of the company of the faithful suffered. They were humbled by blows so that they might reject diabolical pride together with the pleasures of this world. For when he says, “You placed tribulations upon our back,” he signifies the bodily pains that they endured from the blows inflicted upon them. [Col. 0455B–C]

### Verse 12

“You placed men over our heads; we passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment.” He says “you placed,” so that it might be clear that everything happened by his will, just as the Lord says to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

He continues: “men,” so that you might understand sinners—those who, in savage persecutions, afflicted the holy martyrs with various tortures. “Over our heads”—that is, so that you gave them power to pronounce a capital sentence against us.

He added: “We passed through fire and water.” This happened when fire consumed some of the martyrs, water devoured others, and their deaths were shown to have been accomplished through different elements.

Then follows the blessed promise of that age: “And you brought us into refreshment,” so that you might understand that all these things which the Church suffered in her members were conferred not as detestable punishment but as the blessedness of rest. Refreshment is the delightful and pleasant security that follows burning cares; those who deserved to suffer for the Lord’s name receive it in that recompense. [Col. 0455C–D]

### Verse 13

“I will enter your house with burnt offerings; I will repay you my vows.” Here the members of Christ return to the singular number. His body says that it will happily enter his house—that is, the future Jerusalem, where not the burnt offerings of animals but the purity of souls is sought.

And observe that, just as in the preceding three verses he spoke of the punishments of the martyrs, so now in another four verses, up to the end of the division, he recalls the good things of the blessed, so that he might strengthen the faithful amid harsh afflictions by promising them such great rewards.

A burnt offering is so called because it is entirely burned. And because he had said above that he was examined by fire like silver, he rightly says that he will offer himself as a burnt offering—that is, his soul purified from sins.

He continues: “I will repay you my vows”—that is, so that I may sing your praises continually and, with the angels and powers, thrones and dominions, always proclaim a hymn of your mercy. These are the vows of the faithful, these the desires of simple Christians: that they may be received into that fellowship, having joined themselves to it through the holiness of faith and works. [Col. 0455D–0456A]

### Verse 14

“Which my lips have distinguished, and my mouth spoke in my tribulation.” He explains those vows that he mentioned above—namely, “which my lips have distinguished.” For the faithful, although placed in affliction, as Job was, praise the Lord and continually accuse themselves.

Therefore they are shown to distinguish their vows with their lips, because there is no doubt that what is attributed to humanity has been divided from what is always offered to divinity. And consider the blessed holiness of endurance: after the resurrection, he says that he will repay those vows of praise which he sang in tribulation, when the weakness of the flesh frequently leads to sin, and the soul, overcome by pains, is often prevented from accomplishing the worthy things it has resolved upon. Here, however, by God’s gift, such an abundance of charity is displayed that it is shown to have overcome every adversity. [Col. 0456A–B]

### Verse 15

“I will offer you burnt offerings rich in marrow, with incense and rams.” He continues to explain the vows that he mentioned above. Burnt offerings rich in marrow are sacrifices that we give before the divine presence with a pure and inward heart.

For when, in place of a burnt offering, we offer contrition of heart, it must contain within itself the purest faith; within itself it must contain the works of faith, which, in place of marrow, render the offering exceedingly rich. What we sacrifice before the divine presence must not be dry and empty.

Therefore he promises to offer such burnt offerings as possess the firmness of marrow and the richness of saving faith. He added: “with incense and rams.” Incense signifies prayers, which are offered before the divine presence like fragrant incense, as it is read elsewhere: “Let my prayer enter like incense in your presence” (Psalm 140:2).

Rams signify the apostles, who became leaders of the Christian people through their devout preaching. And observe that he joined the two together when he said, “with incense and rams.” Truly, that incense is most pleasing to the Lord which is shown to have been joined to the traditions of the apostles.

Remember, however, that this verse and the following one are spoken allegorically; through the significations of the animals, the offering of the devoted is explained. [Col. 0456B–D]

### Verse 16

“I will offer you oxen with goats.” Oxen are understood as preachers, who happily ploughed human breasts and planted the fruitful seeds of the heavenly word in their understanding.

Goats are understood as those who devote themselves to diabolical perversions and are clothed in shaggy vices. For *hircus*—“goat”—is said as if from *hirsutus*, “shaggy.”

But the Church offers these together with oxen when converts confess Christ the Lord. That thief who hung on the cross was a goat; but he soon became an ox when, with the Lord looking upon him, he reached conversion to the truth. For he said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). [Col. 0456D–0457A]

### Verse 17

“Come and hear, and I will tell you, all you who fear the Lord, what he has done for my soul.” He comes to the fourth division, where he summons not the inexperienced but the faithful and devoted. He now recalls nothing of his sufferings, but will speak entirely about the liberation of his soul.

Let us hear what he has done for his soul, so that we too may learn to seek what we have recognized the Lord to have bestowed upon our Mother. [217; Col. 0457A]

### Verse 18

“To him I cried with my mouth, and I exalted him beneath my tongue.” When these two things are carefully fulfilled, the Christian becomes perfect.

First, he must cry out to the Lord with his mouth—that is, with a right conscience, not with a perverse will. Thus we speak of those who are deceived in some matter: “He does not possess his own mind; what he says belongs to another.” Therefore he cries out with his own mouth who entreats the Lord purely, because whatever is known to be perverse is not ours at all but wholly diabolical.

The second follows: “And I exalted him beneath my tongue.” By “beneath my tongue” he means in the conscience, because our heart is beneath our tongue. There, with silent thought, we praise him, and we seem to exalt him who is always shown to be the Most High.

And observe the order of events. First he mentioned the cry of the mouth; then he came to the purest affection of the heart, from which even when silent we are accustomed to be heard. [Col. 0457A–B]

### Verse 19

“If I have seen iniquity in my heart, may God not hear me.” He carefully explains what he had said: “I exalted him beneath my tongue.” For whoever praises God in his heart ought not to confuse his understanding with varied imaginings or to contemplate any iniquity, but ought to devote his entire mind to him with the greatest vigilance, so that the devil cannot find a place in it.

Thus the purity of the one praying is recognized: it is not stained by any defilement of thought. For he says: “If I did this, may God not hear me,” showing that those who do such things are mocked by empty visions. [Col. 0457B–C]

### Verse 20

“Therefore God heard me and attended to the voice of my prayer.” Because he had not seen iniquity in his heart, he says that he was heard. The cry that ascends to the Lord is the one that contains no pollution of human affairs.

When we attend to him, we receive a corresponding return, so that he too, having mercy upon us, may attend to us. Finally, this follows: “And he attended to the voice of my prayer.” Let us therefore ask that he grant us the purest prayer, so that, having been faithfully entreated, he may hear us completely from the sanctuary of his mercy. [Col. 0457C–D]

### Verse 21

“Blessed is the Lord, who has not removed my prayer and his mercy from me.” These two things are connected. When God does not remove our prayer, he undoubtedly grants his mercy. For when our prayer is suspended, his mercy too is prolonged.

Let us also consider how the beginning of the fourth section was conceived in truth. He said: “Come and hear what he has done for my soul.” At the end came the fulfillment of a most truthful promise, because he is recognized neither to have removed his prayer nor to have shown himself to suspend his mercy.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0458A]

This psalm has indeed run its course through a successive exposition, but now its structure must be gathered together for us, so that the power of this song may be clearly recognized.

First, the holy Mother Church addressed the nations in a salutary way, so that they might devote themselves generally to the praises of the Lord, and thus heavenly desire might remove from us our attachment to the world.

Then she invites them to learn that the miracles of the Old Testament were granted to them as prefigurations, so that the people who followed might be stirred to the greatest hope, since the benefits granted to the ancient people announced the blessings of future regeneration.

She also taught us that the Christian people are delivered, by the Lord’s mercy, from the various disasters it endures here, and that, by his generosity, it reaches that blessed homeland. It is a singular promise and a desirable pledge: here to be guarded under his protection, and there, through the generosity of the same Lord, to be placed in eternal reward.

If we always fix our attention upon this with steadfast mind, we shall never fear the dangers of this world. Rather, with the greatest joy we shall sing what is written at the end of this psalm: “Blessed is the Lord, who has not removed my prayer and his mercy from me.”

# Exposition of Psalm 66

*To the end; with hymns, a song-psalm of David.*

The two names “hymn” and “song,” unless they are examined carefully, seem almost to indicate one and the same mystery, because both are shown to signify the praise of the Lord.

We said that a hymn is a poem composed according to the rules of some meter, as all the psalms are known to have been formed in the Hebrew language. Whenever these words occur alone in titles, they signify that the compositions were performed with instruments and tambourines.

But this hymn, which the prophet now sings, placed “to the end” before it because the whole prayer is directed without doubt to the Lord Christ.

A “song-psalm,” however, is one sung only with the modulation of the human voice. But now, through these names, it is understood that the two could be joined, so that the composition might be sung both with musical instruments and with the human voice. Thus every song is also a hymn, but not every hymn is a song.

The distinction is indicated to us by this fact: psalms that do not have “song” could be sung with musical instruments alone. [Col. 0458B–C]

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0458D]

After the song of Resurrection in Psalm 65, the prophet wonderfully added his prayer, so that we might deserve to be led to divine knowledge—a knowledge which our merits cannot reach.

Therefore, in the first part, speaking to the faithful, he entreats that he may deserve to be blessed by the Lord together with them, so that, enlightened in heart, they may recognize that the Lord Christ must be proclaimed among all the nations.

Then, turning to the Lord, he says in the spirit of prophecy that the peoples will confess him, because he judges the nations with equity.

Third, he repeats the same verse that he spoke above, adding this mystery: the earth has already yielded its fruit. Therefore, by repeating the word, he asks that we ought to be blessed. [Col. 0458D–0459A]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“God have mercy upon us and bless us; may he illuminate his face over us and have mercy upon us.” Directing his supplication, the prophet hastened to the help of the necessary name. He rightly first asked for mercy, since he did not presume upon the work of his merits.

For it was first necessary that he have mercy upon those who were wandering, and afterward bestow the gifts of his blessing. The Lord’s blessing always increases us: when we bless him, we make absolute progress; and when he blesses us, he grants what will benefit our souls.

But let us ask what blessing he requests, since many blessings are granted by the Lord’s generosity. He blessed Adam before the sin, saying to him: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and rule it” (Genesis 1:28). He blessed Abraham when he said: “Blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea” (Genesis 22:17). He also blessed the lands with various fruits, so that he might remove the need arising from our frailty.

But here he asked for the blessing that he explains below: that, removing the darkness of our mind, he might illuminate us with the brightness of the Lord Savior. For it follows: “May he illuminate his face over us.” This was the request for blessing: that he might illuminate his face over them, because they could not see him, lacking in their own powers the benefits of light.

Human understanding cannot see him unless it has been suffused with the brightness of his splendor. He repeats: “And have mercy upon us.” The repetition is necessary, because we begin to make progress through the Lord’s mercy and are preserved in good hope through his generosity.

This figure is called *epembasis*, that is, frequent repetition of speech. [Col. 0459A–C]

### Verse 2

“So that we may know your way on earth, your salvation among all the nations.” He clearly expressed what he had said above: “Bless us,” and, “May he illuminate his face over us.”

These things have this effect: that in this world we may know that way of truth, namely the Lord Savior, who leads us to life. No one can go astray on it except one who presumes to depart from his rules.

And lest we need to establish by other examples who the way is, he explained it next: “Your salvation among all the nations.” Thus this way would not be thought to belong to only one place, and the benefit it brings to the world could be recognized through the testimony of its name.

This name was clearly applied to Christ the Lord when that blessed man Simeon, taking him into his arms, said: “Now dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples” (Luke 2:29), and so forth.

Consider also that in the first verse he speaks to the faithful people and suddenly turns to the Lord Christ. This is not inappropriate, because speaking to the members is speaking to the head.

This figure is called *prosphonesis*, that is, exclamation, whenever, amid other things that we are saying, we suddenly turn our words toward the Lord. [Col. 0459C–D]

### Verse 3

“May the peoples confess to you, O God; may all the peoples confess to you.” After the prophet had prayed that faith might come to the peoples, he came to the second part, saying to the Lord: “May the peoples confess to you, O God.”

The word “confess” is equivocal, for confession is known to indicate both praises and lamentations over sins. Here both meanings must be understood: let the peoples confess their sins and not cease to proclaim the Lord’s glory.

Finally, the word itself is doubled in one verse, so that you might understand that everything must be done by the faithful people [ms. A., F.: “for the faithful people”].

For when he added “all,” he struck down the perversities of the Donatists, who think that the Church of the Lord is not spread throughout the world. [Col. 0460A]

### Verse 4

“Let the nations rejoice and exult, because you judge the peoples with equity and direct the nations on earth.” We must ask why he urges the nations to rejoice and exult when he says that the Lord will judge. A guilty conscience can fear when it hears that the truthful Lord will judge.

But he speaks of those who, having already confessed their sins, cannot fear the coming judgments. For Christ is not their judge but their advocate: they have condemned themselves by their own confession.

Therefore let the nations exult and rejoice, since they have deserved to anticipate his face in confession. The reason for their joy follows: they are shown to have confessed before a merciful judge, who knows how to heal the hearts of the humble and crush the necks of the proud.

And so that you might understand that confession in the sense we have explained, he says: “And direct the nations on earth”—that is, in this world, where you make them confess their own sins, so that they cannot be overthrown by diabolical error. [Col. 0460A–C]

### Verse 5

“May the peoples confess to you, O God; may all the peoples confess to you.” He comes to the third narrative, in which he repeats the verse of the second part but adds an entirely different matter below.

In the preceding verse he said: “Let the nations rejoice and exult.” Now, however, he says: “The earth has yielded its fruit.” Thus, although the beginning sounds the same, the meaning itself, because of what follows, does not appear to be directed toward similar causes.

Some have wanted to understand these peoples, whom he frequently repeats, as the twelve tribes that will receive the grace of recompense in that judgment.

### Verse 6

“The earth has yielded its fruit; may God, our God, bless us.” “The earth has yielded its fruit”—namely, the confessions of the peoples, which he mentioned above as coming forth through necessary repetition.

Truly it is its own fruit, which it received through the pious generosity of the Lord, not the fruit which it produced when the devil sowed. The earth also yielded its fruit when a crowd from different nations received the Lord Savior.

That earth, which had been full of the thorns and thistles of Adam’s sin [ms. G.: “the thorns and thistles of sins,”] bore vital fruit when it obeyed the Lord’s commands. Then the faith of the apostles burst forth into various languages when the Holy Spirit filled them. Then the world recognized immeasurable powers. Then truly the earth brought forth its fruit, when it abandoned the thorns and thistles of the devil.

And because fruit was able to come forth, blessing is rightly requested. For he says: “May God, our God, bless us.” He had said “God” once; but lest he be thought to mean the god of the Gentiles—for they too say that they worship God, although they are entangled in empty errors—he nevertheless added “our God,” so that the one God whom the holy catholic Church worships and confesses might truly be believed to be the only God worthy of worship: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0460C–0461A]

### Verse 7

“May God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.” He repeats “May he bless us,” which must often be repeated and is plainly to be desired without end, because it is always necessary and always shown to be beneficial.

This figure is called *tautologia*, that is, repetition of the same expression.

Let us also observe how the fear of God is requested among great gifts, since after the blessing has been sought, a prayer is made that his fear be granted to the ends of the earth. It is among God’s first gifts, because those who know how to fear him do not cease to love him.

Thus Solomon also says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclesiasticus 1:16), and in another psalm: “Let all the earth fear the Lord” (Psalm 32:8).

But this fear does not arise from human trembling; it is bestowed through divine inspiration. The prophet therefore, in his mercy, desired this fear for the ends of the earth, so that they might begin to believe and carefully preserve what they had believed. [Col. 0461A–B]

## Conclusion of the Psalm

What vast fields of faith this psalm has embraced in its most delightful brevity! It supplicated the Lord Christ to deign, at his coming, to bless us through his abundant mercy, so that the salvation awaited by the nations might become known to the world and they might receive the fruit of his mercy through complete devotion.

Let it therefore be sweet to us in its brevity and illustrious in the dignity of its prophecy, since so many ages ago it foretold what the world has now come to know for its salvation.

Grant, eternal King, that just as we have recognized that you came in the humility of the flesh, so also, in the power of your divinity, we may experience you as the merciful judge granted to us. [Col. 0461B–C]

# Exposition of Psalm 67

*To the end; a song-psalm of David.*

We must understand the force of this name from the fact that, although “end” is what it means, it is always placed at the beginning. For it signifies the head and eternal beginning of things, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, for which reason I speak to you” (John 8:26).

There follows “a song-psalm,” which, as has been said, is usually sung only with the human voice. David signifies the Lord himself, whom that “end” also proclaims.

This is a long psalm, marked at the outset by five *diapsalmata*—musical or sectional pauses—to relieve weariness; through them we have appropriately indicated the divisions. Although in other psalms human diligence may investigate these divisions as far as the Lord permits, these cuts must nevertheless be followed absolutely, since divine authority made them through the *diapsalmata*.

It should be known that throughout the psalm the psalmist speaks through mystical comparisons. He is entirely filled with evangelical mysteries and is shown to be especially devoted to describing Christ’s ascension. [Col. 0461C–D]

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0461D–0462A]

Filled with the spirit of providence, the prophet fittingly declares at the beginning of this psalm, in the optative mood, what will happen to the Lord’s enemies and what will befall the faithful in the future judgment. Thus he may terrify the faithless with punishment and gladden the Lord’s servants with the promised reward.

In the second section he signifies the powers that he bestowed upon the Jewish people, and then says how he formed the Church from them.

Third, through the image of a mountain, he signifies the Lord Savior, asserting what benefits he granted to the Church when he raised it up through the gift of his resurrection.

Fourth, he declares that the pride of the Lord’s enemies must be shattered, and says that conversions and martyrdoms will arise from both sexes, even from the worst people, when the Lord’s saving coming has shone upon the world.

Fifth, he says that the Lord must be blessed in the churches, where the apostles and Christ himself preached, and he supplicates that the gifts he gave to his faithful may be preserved. He also urges those who dwell in this world as in Egypt and Ethiopia to come swiftly to the Lord.

In the sixth section he urges the whole assembly to sing psalms to the Lord Christ, who has now revealed the miracles of his resurrection; then he concludes the psalm with praise of the Lord. [Col. 0462A–B]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him flee from his face.” The prophet confidently appears to desire what he knows is going to happen. He asks for Christ’s resurrection, in which his adversaries would be scattered—namely, the Jews, who, seeing the power of his resurrection, feared the crimes of their wickedness.

Their vengeance is described in a single word. For that people was not gathered into one nation; rather, it was dispersed throughout the world in an outpouring of charity. There follows the immeasurable punishment of the accursed: let them flee from his face whose presence is known to be everywhere.

For what is it to flee forever and not escape the presence of an angered judge? He added “those who hate him” to signify those who persisted in their stubbornness. We ought to hate those things to which we profess that we can in no way assent. [Col. 0462B–C]

### Verse 2

“As smoke vanishes, so may they vanish.”

### Verse 3

“As wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God.” In these two verses the punishment of sinners is foretold through a twofold comparison.

Smoke is a dark mass rising from this corruptible flame; the higher it is lifted, the more it is thinned into emptiness. Sinners are rightly compared to it, because from the flame of their wickedness they produce smoky deeds. Although these deeds rise to greater heights through pride, they must necessarily weaken through their own exaltation, like smoke.

Another comparison of them follows. Wax is a tender and soft substance gathered from honeycombs; it is dissolved by the heat of fire so that its solidity is entirely consumed. This likeness is suitably applied to wrongdoers, because in God’s judgment sinners perish from his face just as wax, melting before a nearby fire, is consumed.

Observe that he does not say that sinners can be consumed in their substance, since they are to be tormented by everlasting fire. Rather, he says that they will perish from the face of God, because they will never come to his grace and benefits, as certain misguided people have attempted to say.

Note that in these verses the figure is *parabole*, that is, a comparison of unlike things; sinners are known to have been compared with smoke and wax. [Col. 0462C–0463A]

### Verse 4

“And let the righteous feast, and exult in the sight of God; let them delight in joy.” Just as the punishment of sinners was described above, so now the future reward of the righteous is recounted.

We call “feasts” the choice and abundant supplies of food by which the body is refreshed and the desire for eating is often increased. The nourishment of the faithful and the abundance of the righteous are compared with these: when satisfied, they still desire, and they are insatiably filled with heavenly delights.

But where these delights are found is added next: namely, in the sight of God, where true and desirable joy always exists. What is it to exult beneath the sight of so great a judge, so that the one whom we rightly fear here may, after delivering us by his gift, become the one in whose presence we rejoice?

He added: “Let them delight in joy,” so that it might delight them precisely that they are joyful. Since they know that their joy will not be enclosed by any end, they delight in it more sweetly, unaware that they will ever lose it.

Thus the coming happiness of that blessedness is indicated through certain glimmering patterns. [Col. 0463A–B]

### Verse 5

“Sing to God, sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends above the setting; the Lord is his name; exult in his sight.” After recounting the future punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the righteous, the prophet urges the peoples to celebrate God’s praises with hymnic exultation, trusting in their faithful hearts what they have heard.

He sings to God who always beholds him with a pure and faithful mind. He sings a psalm to his name who performs the works that God has commanded.

He continues: “Make a way for him”—that is, prepare your purified hearts, which the holy Lord may deign to enter. Or else: fill all people with blessed preaching, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Prepare the ways of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isaiah 40:3).

But for whom this way is to be made is declared: “for him who ascends above the setting.” The Lord Christ surely ascended above the setting by rising from the dead, so that he might lead our captivity captive, and death might leave free those whom, bound by sins, it had held in subjection.

For it was necessary that the dark setting should yield, above which the Sun of righteousness had been shown to rise.

And lest anyone doubt who ascended above the setting, he says: “The Lord is his name,” so that no one might doubt that the Lord Savior is God—the one whom the wicked Jews thought should be slain as an ordinary human being.

He continues: “Exult in his sight,” not in the presence of human beings, where joy is fleeting, but in his sight, where purity of mind continually delights itself. Whatever hardships it suffers here, it is always lifted up by consideration of the future reward. [Col. 0463B–D]

### Verse 6

“They will be troubled before his face, the Father of orphans and Judge of widows: God in his holy place.” After saying that the blessed should rejoice in the sight of the Lord, he now asserts that plunderers and wicked people will be driven away from his face—those who tear orphans and widows apart through savage greed.

Such people are driven away, troubled and exceedingly fearful, from the face of God when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

But he explains who the one is from whose face they are driven away: “the Father of orphans and Judge of widows.” Of him it is also read elsewhere: “You will be the helper of the orphan and widow” (Psalm 9:14).

What, then, will the plunderer be able to suffer, since he has violently destroyed those entrusted to his judge through impious cruelty?

He used the genitive cases “Father” and “Judge” so that what God is might be displayed through these constructions. He also added: “God in his holy place.” One should understand: he preserves an unchangeable and firm judgment, as Father Augustine said of him: “You change the times, but you do not change your plans” (*Confessions* 1.4). [Col. 0463D–0464B]

### Verse 7

“God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house; who brings out the prisoners by his strength.”

In this verse and the two that follow, by the twelfth kind of definition—which in Greek is called *κατ’ ἔπαινον* (*kat’ epainon*), and in Latin “by praise”—it is declared who God is: namely, “He who makes those of one mind dwell in a house,” as it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Or this may refer to the fact that the prophets and evangelists, agreeing in the house of the Lord, spoke the word of truth with harmonious proclamation [Col. 0464C], as he himself will say elsewhere: “How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one!” (Psalm 132:1). For they dwell in his house who join themselves to one another in mutual love. By “house,” however, he signifies the Church.

It follows: “who brings out the prisoners by his strength.” Here he signifies the human race, which he freed, by the power of his strength, though bound by the law of sin. For after the devil had been bound, he brought out the prisoners whom that one held captive. It is well said “brought out,” because, freeing them from hell, he raised them to the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

### Verse 8

“Likewise those who provoke to anger, who dwell in tombs.”

He continues to enumerate those whom he brings out as prisoners by his strength. They provoke the Lord to anger: blasphemers, who conduct themselves in the most wicked manner. These are indeed the living who dwell in tombs [Col. 0464D], that is, those who have been buried in foul and carnal behavior. Of them it is also said elsewhere: “Their throat is an open tomb” (Psalm 5:11). For although he visibly raised the dead, he nevertheless snatched the human race from tombs when, through true faith, he restored to them the desired joys of life.

### Verse 9

“God, when you went out before your people; when you passed through the desert.”

This verse must be joined to the word “you will be recognized.” For he is still persisting in praising God’s works. God did indeed go out before the Israelite people when he appeared in the pillar of fire and when he satisfied them in the desert with the abundance of manna. But this more properly concerns the Christian people. He goes out before the people when he brings out the prisoners by his strength [Col. 0465A], and when those who dwell in tombs are raised. The faithful behold him when, in his great works, they recognize his mercy and power. He also passed through the desert when he came to the nations, to which no prophet had come; they had been rendered, as it were, a desolate wilderness, alienated from the word of the Lord.

### Verse 10

“The earth was shaken; for the heavens also dripped before God, Mount Sinai before God, the God of Israel.”

After the interposed *diapsalma*, he comes to the second entry, where he enumerates the things that divine power granted to the Israelite people. “The earth was shaken,” that is, earthly human beings believed when they saw such great miracles. “The heavens dripped before God” when manna descended, like drops of rain, before God, because his presence was made known through the pillar of fire and cloud [Col. 0465B]. Mount Sinai also smoked before God when blessed Moses received the law there on two tablets. For it is likewise written in Exodus: “The whole of Mount Sinai smoked, because the Lord had descended upon it” (Exodus 19:18).

### Verse 11

“Dividing a willing rain for your inheritance, O God; for it was weakened, but you perfected it.”

He explains what he said above: “The heavens dripped.” This is the willing rain which that people, eager to eat, then obtained. For, in order to satisfy its desire, the world received an unprecedented miracle. That rain was indeed “willing,” unlike the rain that is generally poured out everywhere. Thus he continues: “Dividing it for your inheritance,” because the Lord did not give other nations what he then mercifully granted to the Hebrew people [Col. 0465C]. The Hebrew people were his inheritance, as it is written: “The Lord’s portion became his people, Jacob the measured share of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9).

Although this inheritance was weakened for a time by refusing to believe in the Lord Savior, he perfected his inheritance when he admitted the remaining nations as an addition to the faith.

### Verse 12

“Your animals will dwell in it; in your sweetness you prepared for the poor, O God.”

Because he had said above concerning the Lord’s inheritance, “but you perfected it,” he now adds how he would perfect it. The nations, emptied of true religion, were animals; but when they came to the Lord, they became his. They now lack nothing, but are filled with rational and complete light. They will dwell in the Church when, through his mercy, they have received the worship of true religion [Col. 0465D].

He again explains what these animals are, for he says: “In your sweetness you prepared it for the poor, O God.” “You prepared” signifies the predestined, who, through his mercy, were prepared from the beginning of the world. “In your sweetness” means not in this age, where they suffer bitter things, but in that sweetness in which God’s poor surpass the richest kings.

### Verse 13

“The Lord will give the word to those proclaiming the gospel, many powers” [ms. A: “with great power”].

The order of this verse is as follows: “The Lord will give many powers to those proclaiming the word.” For he gave many powers to the apostles, who preached his word with venerable confession, when they were granted the ability to heal crowds of the sick [Col. 0466A]. The Gospel itself, moreover, is manifestly full of many powers. For what is stronger than saving souls that could have perished through the vices of their errors? As the apostle James says: “He should know that whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way saves his soul and covers a multitude of sins” (James 5:20).

### Verse 14

“The King of the powers of the Beloved, and the beauty of the house to divide spoils.”

This verse must be examined with particular care, for it is entangled by the subtlety of its wording. Here we must understand “the Beloved” as the Father’s Son, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). This figure is called *antonomasia*, that is, “substitution of a name,” when another name is placed in such a way that the name intended as necessary is nevertheless understood [Col. 0466B].

The Father of the Beloved, therefore, is the King of angels and powers, who commands the powers. This may also suitably be understood of the Son, of whom another psalm says: “The Lord of powers is himself the King of glory” (Psalm 23:10). Yet it is certain that this applies to the holy Trinity. Here, however, he wishes the Father to be understood, because he says “of the Beloved,” that is, of Christ.

It follows: “and the beauty of the house to divide spoils.” The beauty of the divine house is recognized when the spoils of the devil—that is, wicked human beings—are transferred into the Lord’s Church. The devil’s spoils are the peoples whom the Lord freed after binding the strong man, as he himself says in the Gospel: “No one can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his house” (Mark 3:27). With these spoils he adorned the house of his power [Col. 0466C], caused the holy Church to rejoice, and frustrated the desires of the savage enemy.

### Verse 15

“If you sleep between the two lots, the wings of a silvered dove, and the hinder parts of its back in the appearance of gold.”

The words “they will receive you” must be supplied. Here “to sleep” does not signify the stupor of sleep or the forgetfulness of things that we customarily experience while sleeping. Rather, he calls those “sleeping” who rest in the Lord’s commandments and possess rest in the same place.

By “lots,” according to the authority of the Fathers, we should understand the two Testaments, between which he urges Christians to remain and rest. The meaning, therefore, is this: he admonishes the faithful, “If you sleep between the two Testaments”—that is, if you commit your soul to its final sleep in the divine Scriptures. That “sleep” is used for death the Lord confirms in the Gospel when he says: “Lazarus our friend sleeps, but let us go so that we may awaken him from sleep” (John 11:11).

It follows: “the wings of a silvered dove.” Through these clauses, as we said above, “they will receive you” must be supplied. The wings signify the swiftness that carries us to that homeland, if here we deserve to rest in the law of the Lord.

The silvered dove signifies the Church, which is rightly called a silvered dove because it possesses the dove’s innocence and shines with the silver color of divine utterances. Of her it is written: “My dove is one, my beloved is one” (Song of Songs 6:8). The hinder parts of this dove, that is, its final parts, shine, glorified in the appearance of gold, because after she has departed from this world, her grace will gleam above gold [Col. 0467A]. Observe that in this world she is compared with silver; but in that resurrection he says she will be adorned in the appearance of gold, as has already been said in the forty-fourth psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a gilded garment, wrapped in varied adornment” (Psalm 44:10).

### Verse 16

“When he distinguishes the heavenly kings over the earth, they will be whitened with snow on Salmon.”

After the silence of the *diapsalma*, he comes to the psalm’s third member, where he enumerates the gifts that the Lord, through the glory of the resurrection, bestowed upon the Church. The heavenly kings are the apostles and holy bishops, or the other faithful, who by divine gift deserved, with good judgment, to rule their bodies. “King” is derived from ruling. This name was rightly imposed upon them, because by divine power they were able to restrain worldly desires, as the Apostle says when rebuking certain people: “Already you are reigning without us—and would that you were reigning, so that we also might reign with you!” (1 Corinthians 4:8).

While the Lord harmoniously distinguishes and distributes these kings over that dove whom he mentioned above, “they will be whitened with snow on Salmon,” that is, they shine above the whiteness of snow, those who are known to rule and order the Church faithfully.

The phrase “on Salmon” is interpreted as the name of this mountain, “shadow.” Here it suitably signifies divine power. For it both defends and refreshes us from the heat of vices, and grants us heavenly gifts, as the angel announced to holy Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). Elsewhere: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16:9). This is the shadow that is understood in a good sense. Indeed, in the following verse he will speak of the mountain’s praise.

“Whitened” is also used in a bad sense, as it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Lord will strike you, whitewashed wall!” (Acts 23:3). The Gospel likewise bears witness: “You are like whitewashed tombs, which are full of the bones of the dead” (Matthew 23:27).

### Verse 17

“Mount of God, fertile mountain; a congealed mountain, a fat mountain.”

By the fifth kind of definition, which in Greek is called *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν* (*kata tēn lexin*) and in Latin “word for word,” the prophet explains what that Salmon mountain is which he mentioned above, as though he were saying: “I call it a mountain”—that is, the Lord Savior himself, of whom the prophet Isaiah sang: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it will be raised above the hills, and all nations will go to it” (Isaiah 2:2) [Col. 0467D].

He adds: “a fertile mountain,” from which perpetual and pleasant streams descend, which has waters for irrigation, seasoned with heavenly sweetness. He adds: “a congealed mountain,” namely, for nourishing little ones, who are to be given not solid food but congealed milk to drink. He also adds: “a fat mountain,” because through its fertility it is always exceedingly abundant.

O mountain briefly praised, yet rich in the quality of heavenly things! From it living waters flow; milk is prepared for the salvation of little ones; spiritual richness is recognized; and whatever is believed to be supremely good is established in the grace of this mountain [Col. 0468A].

### Verse 18

“Why have you received fertile mountains?” [ed.: “Why have you received us, fertile mountains?”] “The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell in it.”

Above he said that the mountain should be understood as the Lord Savior. But now the prophet reproves anyone who might understand these mountains to be those compared with the eminence of the apostles, although we also know that they are made fertile by God’s grace. For he adds: “the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell in it.”

He clearly indicates which mountain we ought to understand. Christ is the one mountain who pleased the Father, so that he might dwell in it, as he himself testifies: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). What he says—“to dwell in it”—is common both to the Father and to the Son, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

When he says, therefore, “in which it pleased God to dwell in it,” the expressions “in which” and “in it” are not suitable to ordinary speech; let us say that this is characteristic of the divine Scriptures, just as he also said in the sixty-fifth psalm: “There, in the same place” (Psalm 65:6).

### Verse 19

“For the Lord will dwell there to the end.”

After those mountains which he had said should not be understood as being compared with the eminence of the apostles—because he was speaking of the Lord Savior, who is the mountain of mountains, the Holy One of holy ones, the King of kings, and the Lord of lords—he returns to the Author of salvation, saying that the Lord Christ will dwell in those mountains, that is, in the apostles, to the end [Col. 0468C]: namely, to the most perfect consummation of his majesty, which is an end without end and the perfect fullness of every good thing.

### Verse 20

“The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them, on Sinai, in the holy place.”

It is customary for the divine Scriptures to speak allegorically, so that while they say one thing, they intend another; you will frequently find this in this psalm. Here, therefore, the chariot signifies a joined association of human beings, because charity binds the saints together just as animals are joined by straps and yokes. Hence the Lord also says: “My yoke is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

The unanimity of the saints is therefore the Lord’s chariot. He sits upon it like a charioteer and governs it, by a saving law, for the service of his will [Col. 0468D]. But to show that this chariot was not devoted to horses but assigned to human thoughts, he says: “ten thousandfold,” which is rightly understood to refer to innumerable peoples, not horses. He adds: “thousands of rejoicing ones,” which must certainly be understood of the faithful.

To show the fullness of joy, he says: “the Lord is among them,” which is the culmination of great exultation and the wondrous sweetness of all good things.

It follows: “on Sinai, in the holy place.” Sinai is a mountain of the desert where Moses received the law, and it is interpreted as “commandment.” There the Lord truly rests, because his presence is accustomed to be contemplated in his holy commandments.

### Verse 21

“He ascended on high; he led captivity captive.” [Col. 0469A]

How beautifully, through the figure of *idea*, the action of the triumphant one is described! *Idea* is a form of expression in which, by presenting a future event as though before our eyes, we stir the movement of the mind. For he who was crucified descended into the underworld and led those freed from captivity to the heavens. Death had to perish, whose kingdom life had invaded.

These are the spoils mentioned above, by which the holy Church is adorned and with which the Lord’s kingdoms [ed.: “camps”] are to be filled. He certainly ascended who descended for our sake in order to rescue us [ed.: “to instruct us”]. He ascended “on high,” namely, above the heavens of heavens; and, as he is recognized to be above all heights and honors, he sits at the right hand of the Father. Who among the faithful could now doubt the liberty granted, when destruction has been extinguished and captivity itself has been taken captive?

### Verse 22

“He gave gifts to human beings; for the Lord God [converts] those who do not believe so as to dwell [there].”

He continues in that likeness of triumph, when a festival is proclaimed to stir up immense joys and gifts are bestowed. The Lord’s gifts were the great works of the Holy Spirit granted to the apostles, or what the Teacher of the Nations says: “To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4:7).

It follows: “for those who do not believe him to dwell there, the Lord God…” Here “he converts them” must be supplied, so that the sentence may stand complete. For “those who do not believe so as to dwell [there],” that is, those who neglect to reach the Lord’s inner chambers so that they may be able to dwell with the faithful in his house—the Lord God converts them, since in his mercy he grants faith to the human race [Col. 0469C]. This is the grace that is given freely, because his gifts precede us, while we are also granted the will to desire what is good.

### Verse 23

“Blessed be the Lord from day to day; our saving God will make the journey prosperous for us.”

After that triumphant description, a brief but great praise is offered. “Blessed be the Lord from day to day,” that is, he must be blessed on every day and at all times. He who ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings will also “make the journey prosperous for us.”

The journey signifies the course of life, which has now been made prosperous because the world has recognized its Redeemer. He adds: “our saving God,” so that no one would doubt the prosperity of the journey when the Lord Christ is its saving guide.

Let those who delight in human spectacles tell me: what comparable thing do they see in the pompous public shows of consuls? Let them turn their minds and faces here; let them look upon this savingly in their hearts, so that from here they may be destined not for fleeting joy but for eternal exultation [Col. 0469D].

### Verse 24

“Our God is the God of salvation; and the Lord’s is the way out from death.”

After the division of the *diapsalma*, he comes to the fourth entry, where he says how he made us safe through his death. He says: “Our God is the God of salvation,” with the words “he has the power to make us safe” understood here.

Therefore the one who saved us is our God, Jesus Christ the Lord [ed.: “God”], who deigned to die for us, who ascended on high, and who did the things that have been described [Col. 0470A]. Thus he continues: “and the Lord’s is the way out from death.”

The path out of death that belonged to the Lord himself frees us; it makes us come out from perpetual death. I think this was beautifully added so that human weakness would not ask: “Why do I die? Why do I fail?” Great healing has been applied to our complaints: “The Lord’s are the paths out of death.”

The Lord’s way out from death is, that is, the desired resurrection of the faithful. Truly, his departure was unique and wondrous, because he himself emerged from the underworld and by his gift enabled us to emerge from it as well.

### Verse 25

“Nevertheless God will shatter the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins.”

So that the evils of the obstinate would not be thought to remain unpunished, he says: “Nevertheless God will shatter the heads of his enemies.” Thus, concerning the faithless and obstinate, you should understand that vengeance too will come upon them [Col. 0470B].

The heads of the enemies are the authors of the Jewish rebellion, and without doubt also the teachers of the heretics. The former persecuted Christ in the flesh; the latter rage even against the Godhead itself—if it is permissible to say so—with greater cruelty.

It follows: “the crown of the hair of those who walk,” that is, those who seek such minute points of accusation that they seem able to walk over and scrutinize the very crowns of hairs. He signifies the clever tricks of empty questions, which abandon what would be useful and investigate what is unnecessary with detestable disputation.

To demonstrate the emptiness of their pursuits, he added: “in their sins,” where foolish thinking was present, which led to guilt. Such are the Manichaeans, Priscillianists, Donatists, Montanists, and the others who mingled themselves with the stench of muddy doctrines.

### Verse 26

“The Lord said: ‘From Bashan I will turn; I will turn from the depths of the sea.’” [Col. 0470C]

In this verse we must follow absolutely the authority of the most learned Jerome, because his translation, clear in its meaning, removes every question for us. “The Lord said.” Let us ask what he said, since the Lord is making some very great promise.

“Bashan” is interpreted as “dryness,” which had possessed the human race through the aridity of sin. But the Lord turned it toward his own greenness when he poured rivers of salvation into it and caused it to bring forth the fruit of life, though previously it had produced destruction.

He adds: “I will turn them from the depths of the sea,” namely, the peoples whom he freed from the depths of this world. It is already well known from frequent reading that the sea must be understood as this world, which is both bitter in taste and disturbed by the waves of vices [Col. 0470D].

### Verse 27

“So that your foot may be dipped in blood; the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.”

He now explains for what purpose the people whom he had earlier said would be turned from the depths of the sea are led: namely, so that its foot—that is, the action of its good resolve—might reach the blood of glorious martyrdom.

For those who had previously walked in a pleasure-filled sea, he afterward caused to walk in blood. This is a difficult path for the flesh, but a blessed way for the soul, which we cross by his mercy if we place our hope and our hearts in him.

A dark but most worthy statement has been added: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.”

“Dogs” are used in a bad sense, as the Apostle says: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” (Philippians 3:2), and in a good sense, as here: concerning them the Canaanite woman says in the Gospel, “Yes, Lord, for even the dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” (Mark 7:28). In another psalm it is said: “They will return in the evening and suffer hunger like dogs” (Psalm 58:7).

These dogs do not cease to bark for the Lord, and with the utmost vigilance and skill they guard his house. Here, therefore, he says: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him,” because those who were previously enemies afterward defended the Lord’s Church with clamorous barking.

But he added from whom this could take place: namely, “from him.” From the Lord himself, of course, who changes bitterness into sweetness, turns sadness into joy, and transforms detestable illnesses into salvation.

### Verse 28

“Your footsteps were seen, O God; the entry of my God and King, who is in his holy place.”

This entire verse signifies the incarnation of the Lord Savior. He says: “Your footsteps were seen, O God,” either through the form of the body he assumed or through the traces of his preaching, by which he walked innocently in this world with holy steps.

To show clearly that he meant the Lord Savior, he added: “the entry of my God and King,” because he himself, the King, entered this world in a distinctive manner. Of him it is written in the title of his passion: “The King of the Jews” (Mark 15:26).

He also clearly expressed his body when he said: “who is in his holy place.” The temple of the Lord Christ’s body was holy; in it was the fullness of divinity, which the faithless could not see.

### Verse 29

“The princes went before, joined with those singing in the midst of the young women with tambourines.”

“Princes” signifies the apostles, who are both princes of believing peoples and went before all in the holiness of their teaching. For this reason they became leaders, because the peoples afterward followed them.

He adds: “joined with those singing.” So that you would not think there were only a few, he suitably adds a multitude of singers joined together, who now resounded with the Lord’s praises not only in voice but also in good deeds.

It follows: “in the midst of the young women with tambourines.” So that you would not think the female sex had been disregarded, he says that this action took place in the midst of young women with tambourines—that is, young girls flourishing in the first stage of life—who turned their tambourines, that is, the tension of their bodies, toward the Lord’s praise and glory [Col. 0471D]. They mortified themselves through fasts and rejoiced more in the affliction of the flesh. This is what divine power still works today in many virgins.

Others have wished “young women with tambourines” to be understood as churches, whose courtyards, as though with certain tambourines, celebrate the Lord’s praises together with the rejoicing of the peoples. He will speak of them in the following verse.

### Verse 30

“In the churches bless God the Lord, from the springs of Israel.”

After the interposed *diapsalma*, he has been transferred to the psalm’s fifth section, in which he says where the Lord should be blessed. He says to the faithful: “In the churches bless God the Lord,” because the Lord should be blessed not in the various meeting places of pagans or in the caves of heretics, but in the Catholic Church [Col. 0472A], where there is right faith and true confession.

He is rightly praised there where he is not cursed. For how can he receive praise from one who defiles himself with impious superstition?

It follows: “from the springs of Israel,” that is, from Christian teaching, which the apostles poured into the nations. From there the spring of religion flowed out among the other peoples. A spring is called a *fons* from *fovendo*, “refreshing,” because it refreshes our bodies, wearied by labor.

### Verse 31

“There is Benjamin, the younger, in fear; the princes of Judah are their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.”

We have said that this manner of expression is characteristic of the divine Scriptures, when they insert Hebrew names for the sake of some mystery of meaning. There is no doubt that all the prophets desired the blessed time of evangelical preaching. The Psalmist, fervently longing for it now, is shown through the names of the tribes to have indicated both the Lord Christ and the apostles themselves.

“There is Benjamin, the younger, in fear.” “There,” namely, in the temple of Jerusalem, where Paul heard the words of the Lord, as the text of the Acts of the Apostles clearly recounts. Or, as some wish, “there” means in the Church, where he said that praise should be sung.

Benjamin designates the apostle Paul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin. He himself says: “For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin” (Philippians 3:5).

“The younger in fear,” because he was young in age, as Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the passion of blessed Stephen: “The false witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a certain young man named Saul” (Acts 7:58) [Col. 0472C]. Although he was young in age, he proved the younger in fear when he fell at the voice of the Lord, who mercifully thundered to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

“Adolescent” is derived from *adolere*, that is, “to grow.”

“The princes of Judah” indicates the Lord Savior, who descended from the tribe of Judah, as John says in the Apocalypse: “The Lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).

He adds: “their leaders,” that is, the leaders of the peoples who had been established in the Church. This applies not only to Paul or to the Lord but also to those whom he later called “the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.”

Zebulun and Naphtali were tribes established among the Jewish people, from which the other apostles are read to have derived their origin. All of these were rightly called princes, because a crowd of the faithful followed them, as men worthy of honor and primacy.

For those who are not kings are also called princes, as it is read in Exodus concerning the dedication of the tabernacle, how twelve princes offered gifts, one from each of the tribes of Israel (Exodus 35:27).

It is also appropriate to state the meanings of their names, since these too prove to be applicable to the Church. Judah means “confession”; Zebulun, “dwelling of strength”; Naphtali, “my expansion.” If you examine these carefully, you will suitably apply them to the Catholic Church.

### Verse 32

“Command, O God, your power; strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us.”

After that most blessed proclamation concerning the Lord’s coming, as though he had already received an immeasurable gift, the prophet turns to the Father, saying: “Command, O God, your power.”

The power of the Father is Christ the Lord, as the Apostle says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). “Command” pertains to the distinction of persons; their willing is one, and their ability is eternally one.

He then states what is to be commanded: “Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us.” It is a great request that God strengthen in us the faith which he deigned to give. For it was the Lord’s work that blind paganism, struck by the light of truth, was able to recognize the true Lord Savior, according to the Apostle: “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in him” (Ephesians 1:3–4).

### Verse 33

“From your temple, which is in Jerusalem, kings will offer gifts to you.”

Although gifts are customarily offered in the temple, here he says that they must nevertheless be offered from the temple of Jerusalem. From the temple of Jerusalem, therefore, kings offer gifts: those who live in God’s Church with upright conduct offer the purity of their hearts when they come to the reward, when the grains are separated from the chaff, and when Jerusalem becomes one—the mother of all who have lived under Christ’s law.

We can understand “kings” in both ways, because emperors themselves offer themselves as gifts to God, and because they are faithful people who have deserved, through Christ’s grace, to rule their own bodies.

Observe that he calls only Jerusalem the Lord’s temple, where there is both the vision of peace and no hostile opposition of quarrelsome heretics is mixed in.

### Verse 34

“Rebuke the beasts of the forests; the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples.”

So that that holy faith might be strengthened by the protection of confession, the prophet says: “Rebuke the beasts of the forests,” that is, accuse proud and savage people who persist in perverse persuasion, so that the rebuke of these people may become a solid defense of the faithful.

He uses “beasts” for wicked people or for the devil, as it is said in another psalm: “The boar from the forest ravaged it, and a solitary beast devoured it” (Psalm 79:14).

He adds: “the assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples.” He must likewise be understood to say that the untamed heretics are to be rebuked. They seduce innocent souls with stiffened necks and draw to their own herd those whom they deceive by their wretched persuasion [Col. 0473D].

The cows of the peoples are also women, extremely fickle in their yielding will, who follow the teachers of faithlessness like bulls. Of them the Apostle says: “For among them are those who enter houses and take captive little women weighed down with sins, led by various desires, always learning and never able to come to knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 3:6–7).

Why such people should be rebuked is added below.

### Verse 35

“So that those who have been tested by silver may not be excluded; scatter the nations that desire wars.”

The usefulness of that rebuke has been demonstrated, because while falsehood is condemned, truth is nevertheless confirmed. It is necessary to rebuke the beasts of the forests, cast out the bulls, and reproach the cows of the peoples, so that those who have been approved—that is, those whom spiritual charity, after burning away the filth of vices, has brought to the purity of the soul like the purest silver—may be strengthened and advance [Col. 0474A].

A sentence has also been added that would scatter the heretics. They are the nations that desire wars, that is, those whose disputes do not strive for the soul’s progress but seek, through perverse persuasions, to take innocent souls captive.

### Verse 36

“They offer swiftly from Egypt; Ethiopia hastens to give its hands to God.”

There is no difficulty in accepting this verse according to the translation of Father Jerome, whom we must follow both because of the Hebrew truth and because he resolves the connection of the ambiguity for us.

Egypt and Ethiopia are always used in a bad sense because of the dark blackness of their inhabitants. This figure is called *synecdoche*, that is, “the whole from a part.” It signifies the world, which was oppressed by the dense darkness of vices and subjected to the devil. Having been illumined by the Lord’s light, it deserved to attain the gifts of eternal life [Col. 0474B].

The prophet therefore urges the peoples of the nations to offer gifts swiftly to God from Egypt—that is, their souls cleansed of worldly filth. Ethiopia likewise should hasten to give its hands to God.

This is a metaphor drawn from combatants, who, so that they may not perish cruelly, surrender their hands to the victors; laying down their weapons, they escape the danger of death. Thus Ethiopia is admonished not to delay handing itself over to God, so that, once conquered, it may flourish, though in its freedom it had been defiled.

### Verse 37

“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord.”

He also concluded this section with a beautiful exhortation. By saying “kingdoms of the earth,” he wished to signify the entire human race. For although there are nations that have no kings, this expression nevertheless encompasses whatever is understood to belong to the nations.

What he says, “sing,” refers to purity of soul; “sing praises,” to the holiest works, which are judged acceptable to the Lord.

### Verse 38

“Sing praises to God, who ascends above the heavens of heavens from the East; behold, he will give his voice, the voice of his power.”

After the insertion of the fifth diapsalm, the prophet comes to the sixth section, admonishing the faithful to sing psalms to God, who rose from the dead. For he explains to which God they should sing: to the one who ascended above the heavens of heavens—namely, the Lord Jesus, who descended from heaven [Col. 0474D] to set free the weakness of our nature. He himself also ascended above the heavens of heavens, and sits at the right hand of the Father.

It should be observed, however, that you will frequently find the heavens named in the plural number in the divine Scriptures, even though it is written, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), while nevertheless heaven and earth are read in the plural as well. This manner of expression extends more broadly, so that, by an improper usage, we speak of singular things in the plural and plural things in the singular.

By “from the East,” he clearly indicates Jerusalem, which is situated in the regions of the East. From there the Lord ascended into the heavens while the apostles watched: a land filled with many miracles, where the faith of believers is instructed more by what is seen than by what is read. Concerning this, [Col. 0475A] blessed Leo, truly an apostolic father, beautifully said:

“And what elsewhere may not be believed, there cannot fail to be seen. For what difficulty is there for the understanding when sight itself is its teacher? And why should things read or heard be doubtful where the mysteries of the whole of human salvation present themselves both to sight and to touch?”

Nor, therefore, do I judge that this too should be passed over: in his Epistle to the Hebrews, the blessed apostle Paul wonderfully applied to that triumphant ascension the very image of the tabernacle, saying:

“But Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, and not through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 4:11).

And again:

“For Jesus did not enter into holy places made with hands, [Col. 0475B] copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf” (ibid., 24).

Thus this magnificent deed, now described through splendid joys, is shown to have been fittingly prefigured by that tabernacle.

It follows: “Behold, he will give his voice, the voice of his power.” This can be understood in many ways. He gave his voice when he said to the paralytic, “Rise and walk”; when he raised Lazarus; and when he commanded the demons to leave those they possessed. He will also give the voice of his power when, on the last day, he commands the human race to rise again. For what is more powerful than to recall ashes to a living body and living substance, and to lead that mortal nature to the gifts of eternal life? As it is read in the Gospel:

“The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth” [Col. 0475C] (John 5:28).

### Verse 39

“Give glory to God over Israel: his magnificence and his power are in the clouds.”

He continues to persevere in these exhortations. For when he says, “Give glory to God,” he chiefly exhorts them to be honored themselves; for whoever gives praise to God makes himself praiseworthy, and likewise whoever gives him honor undoubtedly acquires dignity for himself.

When it says, “over Israel,” the catholic Church is signified, in which God is truly perceived when he is understood with right faith. For Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” Therefore he cannot be seen elsewhere except where a people is proved to confess him most truly.

It follows: “His magnificence and his power are in the clouds.” Magnificence pertains to the fact that he always does great things; power, because the effect obeys his command. [Col. 0475D] For “he does everything that he wills in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 134:9).
