But this magnificence and power of the Lord are said to be in the clouds—not in those visible clouds which either pour down waters or are condensed into a bodily mass, but in certain powers endowed with heavenly understanding, which serve the Lord’s commands in an intellectual order. Concerning them it is said: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6). This expression is filled with many meanings; it also has reference to the apostles and prophets.

### Verse 40

“Wondrous is God in his holy ones, the God of Israel.”

Lest you understand those clouds to be aerial, he says, “Wondrous is God in his holy ones,” whether in angels or in human beings who obey his commands. Again he repeats “the God of Israel,” so that he might impress upon human hearts where the wondrous God would appear. [Col. 0476A]

“He himself will give strength and power to his people [ed., ‘of his people’]; blessed be God.”

Lest anyone distrust human weakness or believe that he could attain such great rewards, he is strengthened by a true promise: the Lord will give his faithful the strength of patience and the power of faith, so that they may attain eternal rewards.

And to indicate more clearly who can give what he has said above, he added, “Blessed be God”—that is, he who ought always to be blessed by every mouth. Just as he never ceases to bestow benefits, so may he always receive blessings.

We should not suppose that his praise can be briefly expressed in only two words. The one who meditates on his Scriptures blesses the Lord; the one who fulfills his holy commands through action blesses the Lord; and the one who faithfully confesses him blesses the Lord. Thus it comes about that this brief praise is rendered continually throughout the whole course of our life. [Col. 0476B]

## Conclusion of the Psalm

The abundant psalm has flowed forth like an immense river, which, the more land it occupies, the more abundantly fertilizes the fields. It is a river that is drawn in not by the mouth but rather by the ears; a river drunk by the mind, not by the body; a river that, without any moisture, is always irrigating, intoxicating pure minds and bringing those drunk with sins back to sobriety of mind.

It is water that removes thirst and hunger at once, which is not poured out through digestion but, once received, is always increased. Let us pray that this river may possess us without interruption. We shall not be barren sand but fertile soil if, through the Lord’s favor, its channel continually holds us occupied.

[Col. 0476C] Remember, however, that this psalm described the Lord’s ascension with a splendor surpassing all others.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 68

*For the end; for those who will be changed; of David.*

[Col. 0476D] No one is unaware that “for the end” refers to the Lord and Savior, who is going to narrate his passion in this psalm, so that both the authority of the Gospel testifies to his words and the Apostle is taught to take an example from him.

For it is read in the Gospel: “And they gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (John 2:17); and elsewhere: “Zeal for your house has consumed me.” The apostle Paul also says: “Let their table become before them a snare, and a recompense, and a stumbling block; let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bow down their back continually” (Rom. 11:9).

As a mindful reader, you will find these verses placed here. Who, therefore, could doubt that this psalm pertains to the Lord’s passion, when such great and authoritative testimony supports this interpretation?

It follows: “For those who will be changed.” This change signifies the Christian peoples, who, having laid aside the depravity of the old man, have been changed through the gift of new regeneration. What is said “for those” is to be understood as showing that the Lord’s passion was truly undertaken for all the faithful. “Of David” is also added, so that both the end and the beginning might correspond to Christ the Lord, just as he says of himself: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8). [Col. 0477A] Thus the force of the entire psalm is disclosed by the arrangement of this title.

Remember, moreover, that this is the fourth of the psalms that speak at greater length of the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

## Division of the Psalm

Up to this point I have fearlessly noted the divisions by means of the diapsalms, knowing that a separation is rightly placed wherever divine silences have occurred. But now let us pray to the Lord that he who grants a way on earth may himself provide safe paths in the depths.

Throughout the psalm, as we have said, Christ speaks in the form of a servant. In the first section he begs to be saved by the Father, because he endured many tribulations and persecutions from the Jews without cause. [Col. 0477B] In the second section, speaking on behalf of his members, he asks that the hope of the faithful, which rests upon his resurrection, not be deceived; he says that he endured calmly everything that the wicked seemed to inflict. In the third he prays that his own prayer may be heard, so that his blameless way of life may be freed from the mire of this world. For he says that God knows by how many snares of his enemies he was assailed, so that he might reach the end of the Passion through a danger deliberately contrived.

In the fourth, by the power of his foreknowledge, he declares beforehand what would happen to his enemies. In the fifth, in the form of a servant, he professes himself poor; therefore he says that he will return praises to the Father’s mercy. He exhorts the faithful to trust in the Lord, who freed his Church from the adversity of this world and provided his holy ones within it with perpetual happiness.

## Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0477C]

### Verse 1

“Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul.”

Every sound understanding confesses the divinity of Christ to be incapable of suffering; yet he assumed our weakness, which could be subject to destruction. From this dispensation he now cries out: “Save me, O God.” Since he ought not to flee the death that he voluntarily endured, he sought the help of resurrection, so that his humanity might be saved more swiftly.

He suffered because he willed to suffer; martyrs suffer even unwillingly. Thus the Lord himself said to the apostle Peter: “When you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18).

The reason is now given why he asked to be saved: “For [Col. 0477D] the waters have entered even to my soul.” Divine Scripture frequently testifies that waters should be understood as the seditions of the people and the disturbances of nations, as in the passage: “Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive like water” (Ps. 123:4). And it continues: “Our soul has passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water.”

Therefore that Jewish people entered even to the soul of the Lord and Savior when, with criminal intent, it dared to crucify him.

### Verse 2

“I am fixed in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance; I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has submerged me.”

First it must be understood that the figure is *characterismos*, which in Latin is called “formation” or “description.” For the Lord was describing his future passion through certain [Col. 0478A] allusions.

But let us examine this verse carefully, since it is recognized to be of no small depth. In the original ordering of things, God created man indeed from the clay of the earth, but not from the deep. Human beings became the mire of the deep when they were held subject both to original sins and to daily sins.

The Lord was fixed in this mire of the deep when the mad crowd of the Jews cried out: “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6). Their flesh, given over to original sin, was mire; but their criminal cunning had added for itself the name of “the deep.” For *limus*—mire—is so called as if from “binding earth.”

It follows: “And there is no substance.” No evil is a substance, because what was not created by the Lord cannot be called a substance. It does not subsist but occurs; [Col. 0478B] it does not remain externally but only appears to exist while it arises.

He therefore truthfully denies that corrupted nature was a substance, since he knew that it had not been created by him. So also it is read in another psalm: “And my substance is as nothing before you” (Ps. 38:6)—not, of course, the substance that God was able to create, but that which, persuaded by the devil, was corrupted and brought low.

Or we should understand it simply in this way: “I have been crucified by the iniquity of the Jews, and there is no strength of the flesh by which to escape this deadly passion.”

He added: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has submerged me.” How does he who walked upon the sea with fixed steps, and who extended his right hand to Peter lest he be submerged, say that he was submerged by a storm?

Here the depth of the sea signifies the abundant madness of the people. Likewise, the storm is the stirred-up sedition of the deranged; [Col. 0478C] for it submerged the Lord and Savior when it brought him to the cross.

### Verse 3

“I have labored, crying out; my throat has become hoarse. My eyes have failed while I hope in my God” [ms. G. and ed., “the living God”].

It must be asked how he says here, “I have labored, crying out,” when it is read in the Gospel: “He did not answer them a word”; and Isaiah likewise says: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).

Both are true; both were fulfilled. He was silent when he was handed over, so that his dispensation might reach its saving conclusion for the world; and he cried out openly when he said: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John 17:25); or: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” [Col. 0478D] (Matt. 26:39); and again: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

He also cried out in his labor when he said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees”; and: “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 23:13; likewise, 18:7), and similar things.

He therefore labored while crying out when he was not heard by the faithless. For “labor” signifies an unheard cry, because we do not say that those labor who, as we testify, have fulfilled their desire.

Finally, it follows: “My throat has become hoarse.” When hoarseness possesses our throats, our words reach alien ears in confusion. He rightly says that his throat became hoarse, because the sacrilegious people did not listen at all to his words.

He added: “My eyes have failed while I hope in [Col. 0479A] my God.” Let us understand these eyes to be the bodily eyes of the Lord, which were closed in death; for he always kept the eyes of his heart fixed upon his divinity, and never sinned according to the law of the flesh.

### Verse 4

“Those who hate me without cause have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.”

We know that our hair is granted for the adornment of the head. Likewise, the apostles have been bestowed upon the Church so that, just as hair adorns the head, they may be shown to adorn all the faithful and the Church.

Therefore, to show that the number of unbelievers was greater than that of the devoted, he says that the faithless Jews had multiplied beyond the number of hairs—that is, beyond the number of those who rightly believe.

If you wish to take it literally, it is spoken by *auxesis*, an amplification, in order thereby to indicate the crowd of the Jewish multitude.

It follows: “Those who hate me without cause.” [Col. 0479B] Clearly without cause, when they persecuted the one whom they ought to have desired as propitious. We are said to hate someone without cause when we curse a person without any offenses on his part, as was also said earlier in the thirty-fourth psalm: “For without cause they hid their destructive snare for me” (Ps. 34:7).

### Verse 5

“My enemies who persecute me unjustly have grown strong; what I did not take, then I repaid.”

Above he said that enemies had multiplied beyond the hairs of his head. And lest you believe that they were merely numerous and not also harmful, he added, “They have grown strong”—when they are shown to have accomplished what they were attempting.

And so that you might recognize that those enemies were stirred up by their own guilt, he added: “Who persecute me unjustly”—that is, what he said above, “without cause.” It was truly unjust that he who had come to save the [Col. 0479C] Jewish peoples should instead find them as enemies.

He continued: “What I did not take, then I repaid.” Adam took what he had been persuaded by the devil to take, when he presumed to touch what had been forbidden him by command. And rightly he was condemned to death, because he chose to despise the Author of life.

But Christ did not take sins; he knew no offenses. Nevertheless, he accepted the cross as though he had committed some offense, and paid for us what he did not justly suffer on his own account. And, to cancel the bond of our death, he himself paid the due amount for the whole of guilt.

### Verse 6

“O God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you.”

He comes to the second section, where he now speaks on behalf of his members. Christ cannot be foolish, of whom the Apostle says: [Col. 0479D] “The power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). But he is said to possess foolishness on behalf of those who, as the title says, are known to have been changed.

For they were made truly wise from being foolish, because after great crimes they received the grace of true religion. Concerning them the same Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of this world in order to confound the wise” (ibid., 27).

In a similar way, Christ the Head speaks on behalf of his body, saying: “My offenses are not hidden from you.” Certainly, everything we do is manifest to God, while what we commit through sins that steal upon us is often unknown to us.

Of human ignorance it is said: “Who understands offenses?” (Ps. 18:13). [Col. 0480A] These offenses therefore rightly must be referred to those who are to be released from their debts.

The Lord Christ, however, had no sins, as he himself says: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30). Isaiah also says of him: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53:9). Rather, as the Apostle says: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us” (2 Cor. 5:21)—that is, the Father appointed his Son to be sacrificed as an offering for sins.

Father Augustine carefully grasped and discussed this in his *Enchiridion*, chapter 41. Therefore we must understand “foolishness” and “offenses” as placed on behalf of the members. This figure is called *tapinosis*, that is, “humiliation,” when the greatness of a matter is diminished through very humble words.

### Verse 7

“Let those who wait for you, Lord God of hosts, not be put to shame because of me; let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be disgraced on my account.” [Col. 0480B]

This verse has made clear that what he said above was spoken on behalf of the members. Jesus Christ prays that those who endured the glorious expectation of his resurrection might not be put to shame because of him, since they could not behold it with bodily eyes. As the Lord himself said: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear” (Matt. 13:17).

The weakness of the flesh therefore asks that matters not turn out otherwise than the Holy Spirit had foretold through the prophets. When he says, “Lord God of hosts,” he shows that nothing is impossible for his omnipotence. For the one who commands the hosts has nothing that he cannot accomplish according to his will.

Observe also how this is transferred to the mystery of the resurrection. For he says: [Col. 0480C] “Let those who seek you, God of Israel, not be disgraced on my account”—that is, let those who are proved to seek you not endure human insults for a longer time because of my sleep.

And he rightly added, “God of Israel,” so that those who were able to behold his divinity would not be led astray by bodily weakness.

### Verse 8

“For on your account I endured reproach; shame covered my face.”

Through these six verses, almost to the end of the section, he returns to his own person, enumerating the various insults he endured from the Jews. This figure is called *synathroismos*, “gathering,” in which we gather many things into a single heap in order to arouse hatred.

He endured reproach when the Jews said to him: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (Matt. 12:24); [Col. 0480D] and elsewhere: “Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (likewise, 11:19); and elsewhere: “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. 13:35); and similar things.

It follows what usually happens to good causes when they are attacked: those involved are known to become temporarily sad in proportion to how much more they recognize that unjust things are being fabricated against them.

### Verse 9

“I have become a stranger to my brothers, and a foreigner to the sons of my mother.”

Here he calls the Jews brothers, since they were joined to him by closeness of blood. He became a stranger to them when they refused to believe in him.

For although he himself was descended from Abraham according to the flesh, they, rejected because of their evil deeds, were separated from the origin of the patriarch, as he says in the Gospel: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” [Col. 0481A] (John 8:39).

He added: “And a foreigner to the sons of my mother.” We call anyone a guest who lives in our house for a time, received not by the name of blood relationship but as a stranger.

He calls the Synagogue his mother, since he was born from it when he deigned to be born among the Jewish people. Therefore he calls those whom he previously called brothers the sons of his mother.

But if these had been true sons, they would not have treated him as a guest; they would have received Christ the Lord as their dearest brother.

### Verse 10

“For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me.”

This is the very sentence that the evangelists commemorate. Therefore no one should doubt that this psalm foretells the truth of the Lord’s passion, since the incarnate Son of God himself spoke these words.

Zeal for God’s house [Col. 0481B] consumed him when, after making a cord, he overturned the seats of those selling doves and the tables of the money-changers (John 2:15), teaching that the holy temple was one thing and commercial activity another.

But what followed from this zeal is plainly added: “And the reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me.” After they had been rebuked as unworthy of saving admonitions, they hurled reproaches at him like a mass of weapons, returning quarrels for holy warnings.

For they said: “Is this not the son of Mary and Joseph?” (Luke 4:22). And elsewhere: “But we do not know where this man is from” (John 9:29), along with similar things spoken by the mad crowd of the Jews.

But when he says, “of those reproaching you,” we must ask why he says that the Father was reproached, since we do not read that the Jews committed anything of this kind at the [Col. 0481C] time of the Lord Christ’s passion.

The Father was reproached by them, as he will say in the seventy-seventh psalm: “And they spoke evil against God and said, ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?’” (Ps. 77:19). Or when the mad people said of the fashioned calf: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 32:5).

Therefore Christ the Lord rightly now says that the reproaches which they had formerly directed against God the Father had fallen upon him, so that you might understand that this resulted from an impious habit rather than supposing that something new had happened.

It follows: “They have fallen upon me,” so that he might show the outcome of death, which he accepted through the dignity of the cross. For evils fall upon us when we cannot avoid them. [Col. 0481D]

### Verse 11

“And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me.”

We call it fasting whenever we abstain from bodily foods and do not satisfy our hunger with any eating. In a similar way the Lord Christ says that he fasted, because he could not find the faith of human beings, which he greatly hungered for, as it was also said in the thirty-fourth psalm: “But when they troubled me, I put on sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. 34:13).

In the same way he said that he thirsted when he came to the Samaritan woman and asked for water, saying: “I thirst; give me something to drink” (John 4:8)—that is, so that he might recognize from her the faith he was seeking.

But because this fasting arose from human lack of devotion, [Col. 0482A] he said, “I covered my soul,” as though he had wrapped it in some cloak of sadness.

It follows: “And it became a reproach to me.” The good are always a reproach to the wicked, because they do not consent at all to their crimes, while they deliberately slander those with whom they have no fellowship.

The reproaches, blows, scourging, and spitting that the Lord and Savior endured from the mad crowd testify to this.

### Verse 12

“And I made sackcloth my garment, and I became a byword to them.”

Through sackcloth, sadness and tears are signified, as when the Lord, moved by the weakness of the human race, wept before raising Lazarus. For nowhere is the Lord read to have actually used sackcloth.

He also became a byword to the Jews when he seemed to teach the carnal people through certain comparisons, as it is read in the Gospel: [Col. 0482B] “The Lord spoke a parable to the crowd” (Matt. 13:34); and in another psalm: “I will open my mouth in parables” (Ps. 77:2).

A parable is a comparison made between things that differ in nature through some likeness, according to the manner of divine providence, so that those who could not grasp heavenly things might receive what they heard through earthly comparisons.

### Verse 13

“Those who sat at the gate were attacking me [ed., ‘were talking about me’]; and those who drank wine sang psalms of me.”

Those who mingle with human gatherings in diligent curiosity sit at the gates. For just as a gate receives the crowds of those going and returning, so various crossroads and public streets are filled by the multitude of the people. A gate is so called because everything is carried through it.

He says that his passion was [Col. 0482C] the subject of the Jewish people’s conversation, so that no one was excluded who would remain apart from such discussion. The Gospel passage in which Cleopas was questioned by the Lord, not yet revealed to him, bears witness to this matter. He replied: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?” (Luke 24:18).

All the citizens are shown to have shared the same story when the one thought ignorant of this matter is called a stranger.

Up to this point he has spoken of the reproaches and insults of the Jews; now, as it seems to me, he speaks of the faithful.

“And those who drank wine sang psalms of me.” Those who are directed by commendable conduct sing psalms to God, and by their works render what they receive as heavenly commands through his warnings.

And so that we should understand this of the faithful, he says: “Those who drank wine.” Not the wine [Col. 0482D] of drunkenness, but that spiritual wine of which it is read: “How excellent is your cup, which inebriates!” (Ps. 22:5). For they sang psalms who, through heavenly understanding, were drinking the saving nectar.

Others apply this to the faithless Jews, who, as though their intention had been fulfilled, babbled drunkenly about the Lord’s death.

### Verse 14

“But I direct my prayer to you, O Lord, in the time of favor, O God, in the abundance of your mercy.”

He comes to the third section, where, in opposition to the curses of the Jews, the heavenly Teacher sets forth the holiness of his prayer, indicating that human quarrels should be met not with inflamed strife but with devout prayers.

Let us now see what “the time of favor” is. It is the time of favor when, through the benefit of his incarnation, he freed the world, which was in peril, [Col. 0483A] from imminent destruction. This is the time of favor of which the Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

It is the time that conquered all ages; the time that restored the falling world; the time that bestowed eternity and salvation.

But he suitably explains how this time came about, for he says: “In the abundance of your mercy.” For if there had not been an abundance of mercy, we who were subject to sin could by no means have been redeemed. It was no small mercy that overcame such enormous sins.

There was indeed an abundance of sin; but much greater was that mercy which conquered it, as it is also said in the fiftieth psalm: “And according to the abundance of your mercies, blot out my iniquity” (Ps. 50:2). [Col. 0483B]

### Verse 15

“Hear me in the truth of your salvation.”

Having recalled the time of mercy, in which through his passion he granted salvation to the world, it was fitting that he should also pray for the resurrection to occur for him, which he had truly promised through the prophets.

Therefore it is not the nature of his divinity, by which he is always equal to the Father, that prays to the Father, but the weakness of the assumed human being, in which he is less than the Father.

### Verse 16

“Rescue me from the mire, so that I may not cling to it; deliver me from those who hate me, and from the deep waters.”

Through the weakness of the assumed flesh, in which the human race lies in misery, this is powerfully explained. We are taught to ask God in the same words in which we recognize that our Head prayed.

This must be examined carefully: why did he say above [Col. 0483C] that he was fixed in the mire, and here entreat that he might not remain clinging to it?

He was indeed fixed in the mire because he was held by the weakness of the flesh he had assumed, and from this he also accepted the death of the cross. Here, however, he suitably asks that his soul be made foreign to muddy desires, that is, to the desires of this world.

This is rightly understood on behalf of the members, because he could not cling to the mire who had no stain of sin.

“Deliver me from those who hate me.” This plainly pertains to the Jewish people, because when Christ rose, their hatred was frustrated and disappeared. When he says, “From the deep waters,” there is no doubt that he refers to that people itself, which was deep in the wickedness of its counsel and turbulent with seditions.

### Verse 17

“Let not the storm of water submerge me; [Col. 0483D] let not the deep swallow me; let not the pit close its mouth over me.”

This verse is placed in a similar way to the one above. For in the second verse of the psalm he says: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has submerged me.” Here he asks not to be submerged by the waves—that is, by the most savage storm of this world, which overwhelms souls like a sea when it entangles them in the vice of depravity.

Finally, he makes this clear throughout the whole treatment, saying: “Let not the deep swallow me.” The deep is certainly the depth of sins, which with a kind of greed devours the souls of the wicked, so that those who despair of the iniquity of their deeds cannot return to repentance. As it is written: “When the sinner comes into the depths of evils, he despises” [Col. 0484A] (Prov. 18:3).

He repeats the same meaning again in words different from those he used above: “Let not the pit close its mouth over me.” A pit is a depth excavated more deeply in the earth. By allegory, sinners truly fall into it when they do not withdraw themselves from a vicious will. Its mouth presses upon them to close them in when they persist in an evil will until the time of their death.

He therefore asks that all this be made foreign to him, since he had no contagion of sin, so that his members might recognize the dangers to which they would be subject unless they drew breath through the mercy of the most compassionate Lord.

This figure is called *metabole*, that is, “repetition,” when one matter is repeated with a variation of words.

A pit is also read in an evil sense, as in the book of Genesis: “The valley of the forest had many pits of bitumen” (Gen. 14:10). [Col. 0484B] The sacrilegious and profane are cast into these.

Pits are also mentioned in a good sense, signifying the divine Scriptures stored in the highest depth, as were the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, or the well from which Moses, by the Lord’s command, satisfied the Hebrew people in the wilderness.

Thus the two kinds of pits have one name but different functions: the former lead into hell; the latter send people onward to the kingdom of heaven.

### Verse 18

“Hear me, O Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the abundance of your compassion [ed., ‘mercies’], look upon me.”

Having exposed, as was appropriate, the dangers of human frailty, he returns in the voice of the members to that saving prayer. For he says: “Hear me, O Lord,” and adds the reason [Col. 0484C] why he should be heard: not because humanity deserves it, but because the Lord’s mercy is kind and always ready to do good, provided that he is devoutly asked and entreated with complete purity.

And to explain that kindness more fully, the devout teacher added: “According to the abundance of your compassion, look upon me.” He always returns to that mercy, which he knows to be the patron of the weak, to which all sins yield, however numerous they may be proved.

Observe that whenever mercy is requested, a human being is always said to be looked upon. For if he looks upon sins, he condemns us without hesitation.

### Verse 19

“Do not turn your face away from your child, for I am afflicted; quickly hear me.”

The form of the assumed human being is preserved. For just as he prayed that he himself might be looked upon, [Col. 0484D] so now he begs that the Lord not turn his face away from his servant.

The Lord Christ is frequently called a child because of the purity of his innocence. Simple childhood grants this benefit: that it does not love the vices and wickedness of the world. As he himself testified: “For of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:14).

He is also read as “the child” in the passage: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased” (Isa. 42:1); and elsewhere: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (ibid., 9:6).

He therefore rightly asks swiftly for a remedy, since he recognizes that he has been placed in tribulation. Salvation is sought with all one’s strength when it is desired in a time of necessity.

### Verse 20

“Turn your attention to my soul [Col. 0485A] and deliver it; because of my enemies, rescue me.”

“Turn your attention,” he says, “to my soul,” so that it may truly obtain deliverance when the appeased Divinity has looked upon it.

He also gives the reason why attention should be paid: “Because of my enemies, rescue me.” Because of his enemies he sought the swiftest help of resurrection, so that those who had despised him crucified would be obliged to believe in him when he rose on the third day; and, freed by such a benefit, they might be spared everlasting condemnation.

### Verse 21

“For you know my reproach, my confusion, and my shame; all those who afflict me are before you.”

The Lord the Savior assumed reproach, confusion, and shame on behalf of the human race, just as he assumed death. He endured these things not on account of any guilt of his own, but bore them all innocently, so that, as a good Teacher, he might mercifully instruct those placed in such circumstances by the example of his patience. [Col. 0485B] He endured reproach when the Jews said, “He has blasphemed; what further need have we of witnesses?” (Matt. 26:65). He endured confusion when the mad Jewish crowd cried out, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (ibid., 27:42). He endured shame when he was struck and scourged, and when the immaculate Lamb was handed over to Pontius Pilate as though he were guilty.

It follows: “All those who afflict me are before you”—that is, those who were doing such things had already been placed before the presence of the Divinity, although they did not yet appear to have been brought before the tribunal of judgment. This serves to arouse indignation: they committed their unspeakable crime in the presence of Majesty.

### Verse 22

“My heart expected reproach and misery; I waited for one who would grieve with me, but there was none; and for one who would comfort me, but I found none.” [Col. 0485C]

His heart expected reproach and misery when, of his own will, he endured the Jews’ transgressions and the various sufferings he underwent, and when, in consideration of human peril, he graciously accepted his Passion, as it is written in the Gospel: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15). That crucifixion could not have occurred otherwise unless he himself had desired it; against whose desire and will the madness of the Jews could in no way have prevailed.

It follows: “I waited for one who would grieve with me, but there was none.” If you seek the Lord’s Passion, you will find his disciples grieving when he was handed over to Pilate, and many other believers grieving when he was led to the cross. But here we should not understand that grief of the faithful, since they certainly possessed it in every way—for the sake of which Peter heard, “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33): [Col. 0485D] rather, here we should discern the grief of the persecutors, which their irreverent minds unanimously rejected when they seemed happily to be accomplishing their crime. For them, too, the Lord, while placed in his Passion, prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). In their grief he had no companion, since he saw them obstinately determined to carry out their crime.

He added: “And for one who would comfort me, but I found none.” That people comforts the holy teachers in whom the words of their preaching make progress. But because the obstinacy of the Jews resisted the Lord and Savior, [Col. 0486A] he rightly found no one to comfort his spirit.

### Verse 23

“And they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

This is the verse that brought the Lord’s venerable Passion to completion. For Matthew reports (chap. 27:34) that, when the Lord said, “I thirst,” gall mixed with vinegar was offered to him, so that the Jews’ deeds might truly indicate the bitterness and harshness of that drink. He said, “I thirst,” because he could not find in them the faith he desired. They offered their bitterest character, for they were converted by no remorse.

### Verse 24

“Let their table before them become a snare, and a retribution, and a stumbling block.” [Col. 0486B]

After he had set forth his future Passion in his prayer, he came to the fourth mode—not pronouncing a curse as a wish, but predicting what would emerge—and throughout the entire division he declared that things deserving of the Jews’ deeds would come upon them.

The Lord’s table is the spiritual banquet of both Testaments. At it, like banqueters, those are nourished who hunger with the mind’s eagerness for the Lord’s delights and are filled with the most health-giving intoxication of the Holy Spirit. It is that table at which the circle of apostles, gathered around it, consumed the fare of the heavenly gift.

“Table” is used both in a good and in a bad sense, as the Apostle says: “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:21). The Jews possessed that holy table when they observed the Lord’s commandments in their entirety. But after they began to fast from faith, their table was handed over before their eyes to the Gentiles, so that they might grieve more bitterly as they watched their happiness taken away, just as the Lord rebukes them in the Gospel, saying: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:43). [Col. 0486C]

But lest anyone be troubled by his saying, “their table,” although it is truly known to be the Lord’s, the Lord himself similarly says in the Gospel: “In your law it is written” (John 8:17)—not because it belonged to the Jews, but because it is established that it had been delivered to them.

It follows: “As a snare”—that is, so that, from the letter by which the Jews tried to bind others, they themselves might instead fall into it and be bound. “And as a retribution” was added because the table, taken away and handed over to the Gentiles, was a retribution for their evils: since they refused to feast at it, they are rightly seen to be excluded from it. “And as a stumbling block” is added because, having abandoned the author of peace, they stirred up quarrels and perverse pursuits against themselves. [Col. 0486D]

A grave vengeance, a vehement punishment: to have lost the nourishment of the human race with famished throats.

### Verse 25

“Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see; and always bend their back.”

It is clear that this was the punishment of the cruel Jews: with their eyes darkened, they would not see the truest Sun. Since they refused to look attentively, the very punishment is wished upon them: that they may not see.

He added: “And always bend their back.” This happened to those who, weighed down by the excessive burden of their sins, always bend their necks toward the earth, stooping forward. Those burdened by the weight of sins are not granted the ability to look toward heaven. “Back” is so called as though it were “descending downward” (*deorsum*). For when he said “always,” [Col. 0487A] he signified the wicked, who were converted by no act of satisfaction.

### Verse 26

“Pour out your wrath upon them, and may the indignation of your wrath seize them.”

When he says, “Pour out,” the greatness of the wrath is signified: it descends abundantly, like a river. “Upon them” also indicates that it should not merely touch them but should even be shown to overwhelm them.

It follows: “And the indignation of your wrath.” The indignation of wrath arises when vehement vengeance rises in the sinner’s destruction and brings about what is feared. He added: “May it seize them,” as though it were to seize condemned and terrified people with certain hands, so that they could not escape what they were given to endure for their crimes.

### Verse 27

“Let their dwelling become desolate, and in their tents let there be no one who inhabits them.” [Col. 0487B]

It is evident that both of these things happened to the Jews when that city, Jerusalem, was destroyed by repeated captivity. Private houses became desolate, and the tents—that is, the Lord’s temple or the king’s palace—remained without an inhabitant.

Notice that he used “dwelling” for private houses, but “inhabiting” for the Lord’s temple. In the former we dwell with bodily residence; in the latter we inhabit wherever we frequent with the devotion of the mind.

### Verse 28

“For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds.”

Among the most just punishments of the unbelievers, the cause of the Lord’s Passion is set forth: they persecuted the one who had been struck and, after he had been handed over to them, killed him with detestable savagery, as he himself said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). [Col. 0487C]

It is also written: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32). It is stated even more plainly that God frequently strikes for salvation, as in Deuteronomy: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. 32:39).

Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ says that he was struck by the dispensation through which he suffered. But in this the Jews became detestable, because what had to be done for the world was shown to have been fulfilled through them by a cruel resolve.

It follows: “And they added to the pain of my wounds.” This sentence is expressed in the same way. The pain of the pious Lord was that he did not satisfy his thirst and hunger from the unbelieving people. The Jews added a Passion glorious for the Lord but most destructive for themselves, inflicting a detestable death on the one who had come for the salvation of all. [Col. 0487D]

### Verse 29

“Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness.”

The first iniquity of the Jewish nation was that they destroyed the prophets sent to them. Iniquity was added upon their iniquity when they also chose to crucify our Lord Jesus Christ. This is attested by the parable of the tenants and the vineyard spoken in the Gospel: “A certain man had a vineyard, and he surrounded it with a hedge” (Matt. 21:33), continuing to the place where it says: “And after throwing him outside the vineyard, they killed him.” [Col. 0488A]

Thus it is said, “Add iniquity,” by a figurative expression, just as it is written: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 10:20)—not because the Lord added an evil thing, but because he permitted what he judged advantageous for the salvation of many to occur.

The punishment of sin is added: “Let them not enter into the righteousness of the Lord”—that is, let them not become participants with Christ in that kingdom of righteousness. For those who contemplate righteousness here with the clear light of the mind reach righteousness—that is, the Lord’s kingdom. This cannot happen to the faithless, who have been blinded by the obstinacy of their hearts.

Or in this way: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity,” because they killed the prophets and slew the Lord.

### Verse 30

“Let them be erased from the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous.” [Col. 0488B]

That such words are spoken of God by a figurative expression is well known from frequent reading. For erasing, writing, and possessing a book were assigned to human beings for the sake of memory, so that what they could not retain because of the mind’s weakness they might later recognize, when circumstances demanded it, with the help of writing.

Thus Moses also says to the Lord: “If you do not spare this people, erase me from the book of the living” (Exod. 32:32). But this book is the Lord’s unchangeable knowledge and firm judgment. Therefore it is said of the Jews: “Let them be erased from the book of the living”—not because they had been written in it, but because they judged themselves to be written there. For what is written there cannot be erased, since everything has been established in predestination; and no event can change what that heavenly providence has decreed.

It follows: “And let them not be written with the righteous.” The same mode of expression is used, so that God is said to write what he will do in that judgment, just as he says in the Gospel: “But rather rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). [Col. 0488C] He denies that this can happen to those who, as the title says, have not been changed by acts of pious repentance.

### Verse 31

“I am poor and grieving, and the salvation [ms., ‘your salvation’] of your face, O God, has received me.”

After he had fittingly wished upon the Jews, by prophetic proclamation, the things that were to emerge, he came to the fifth section, in which he explains in many ways the holiness of his purpose in the dispensation of the Incarnation.

For he says: “I am poor and grieving.” Poor, as the Apostle says: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich” (2 Cor. 8:9). Grieving, because, as Isaiah says: “He himself bore our weaknesses and grieved for all” (Isa. 53:4).

And why does he say, “I am,” when many people are poor and grieving? [Col. 0488D] He assigned this characteristic to himself because no one else endured this grief for the guilt of the whole world.

But this is said through the figure *metriasmon*, that is, “moderation,” when we lower a great matter through a humble expression. This is frequently applied to the person of the Lord Christ.

It follows: “And the salvation of your face, O God, has received me.” The omnipotent Word certainly received humanity when he deigned to reconcile the world to God. “The salvation of your face” is the form of the Only-Begotten Son, in which he is equal to the Father. It is rightly called salvific, through which healing is bestowed upon the faithful.

“He has received me” is said from the aspect in which he is less than the Father, so that, placed at the Father’s right hand, he might lay aside both poverty and grief.

[Col. 0489A]

### Verse 32

“I will praise the name of God with a song, and I will magnify him with praise.”

This can properly be understood of those who have been changed—that is, from the perspective of the members. In the Church, he praises the name of the Lord, our head, with a song when a great union of the faithful is formed through hymnic exultation. For he himself praises and magnifies in us what he knows we truly praise.

If he hungers when we hunger, and thirsts when we thirst, how would he not also praise together with us when we praise?

### Verse 33

“And it will please God more than a young calf producing horns and hooves.” [Col. 0489B]

Here the power of psalmody is explained: praise poured forth from a pure heart is much more pleasing to God than the slaughter of animals can be. The earlier practice of offering was to present a young calf for sins.

This victim signified the gifts of innocent and new life that were to follow. It would have defense in its horns and protection for its feet in its hooves, by which we would trample the harshness of this world’s way of life with the utmost holiness.

By saying “producing horns,” he signifies that the Christian people continually increase day by day through the Lord’s power.

### Verse 34

“Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul will live.”

After saying that sacrifices of praise are greater than the slaughter of animals, he turns to the poor, urging them to rejoice, since the offering is no longer placed only in material resources but in the disposition of the mind, where even a poor person can be exceedingly rich. [Col. 0489C]

Therefore, rich people, do not glory—you who can possess calves producing horns and hooves—for God rejects these things and requires the purest heart. Those who do not seek your riches with a subservient mind possess such a heart more fully.

It follows: “Seek God, and your soul will live.” He urges the poor to seek food for the mind, not for the body, and to desire that bread of angels by which the soul may rather be nourished.

Let us consider what he says: “Your soul will live,” even while the sinner’s soul lives. But we properly call that “living” which consists in the joy of blessedness. Although the other thing lives, we rightly consider it to be dying when it is burdened by perpetual sadness and the gravest pains.

### Verse 35

“For the Lord has heard the poor, and has not despised his prisoners.” [Col. 0489D]

We gladly hear that the poor are heard, but let us inquire more carefully who these poor are. They are Christ’s poor, as we have often said: those who despise the riches and pleasures of this world and choose the deprivation of human things so that they may be filled with spiritual banquets.

The Lord Christ says that these are heard: those who have been filled with the world’s deprivation and who rejoice in the security of their poverty as though they possessed everything, just as the Apostle urges: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10).

When he says, “And has not despised his prisoners,” we are all commonly prisoners under the law of sin and entangled in certain fetters, because we pursue human desires. But the Lord does not despise his prisoners—that is, those who are bound by his laws. [Col. 0490A] He frees from bodily snares those whom he recognizes as bound to his rules.

### Verse 36

“Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all that are in them.”

A brief and complete statement is given concerning great things: at the mention of heaven, all heavenly beings should praise him; at the mention of earth, all earthly beings; and at the mention of the sea, all that swim in it. And, to make the conclusion complete, it is said, “and all that are in them.”

Thus whatever is recognized as belonging to creation is invited to the Lord’s praises. So also the Apostle embraces all things, saying: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:10).

### Verse 37

“For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah will be built; and they will inhabit them, and acquire them as an inheritance.” [Col. 0490B]

The greatness of the work of the Lord in building his Church is powerfully perceived from the magnitude of these praises, when heaven, earth, sea, and all that are in them are urged to praise the Lord, because he will save Zion, which here is wearied by many persecutions and afflicted by many hardships.

Zion is joined to the Jerusalem temple—a very small hill, but made great by the quality of its name. For it signifies contemplation, by which alone God is regarded, in which the hearts of the faithful are directed, and in which there is one happiness for all rational creatures if they contemplate the Lord as Creator.

The cities of Judah were built when the Catholic Church was spread throughout the whole world through humble piety. The Lord does not rejoice in buildings of walls, which will certainly perish through age, [Col. 0490C] but in the devotion of the faithful—that is, in living stones—from which the future Jerusalem is built.

And it is rightly said, “the cities of Judah,” that is, of the Lord and Savior, who descended from the origin of Judah through the propagation of the flesh, as it is written of him: “The Lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. 5:3).

But lest you understand that only cities, and not also future dwellings, are intended, he says: “And they will inhabit them.” This is properly the inhabiting of the faithful: to dwell where they continually remain in purity of mind. Christians inhabit this Church here.

They will acquire it as an inheritance when, through the Lord’s mercy, they reach that eternal Jerusalem. For that inheritance is the one which, as has already been said, will be granted not through the death of the testator but by the testator who lives forever.

### Verse 38

“And the offspring of his servants will possess it, and those who love his name will inhabit it.” [Col. 0490D]

A blessed promise concludes this psalm. But as great as the reward is, so great must be the effort we apply to understanding it.

Here we should understand “offspring” as holy conduct, not bodily descent. For those who boasted that they descended from Abraham are plainly shown to have been rejected. The Lord said to them: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39).

If we understand “offspring” as good deeds, as has been said in many places, the meaning can remain complete for us. For whoever imitates those who pleased God by the excellence of their deeds will possess the future land, which will no longer be changed by any end—that is, the Lord’s kingdom, which he faithfully promises to his saints. [Col. 0491A]

And lest you perhaps reduce this offspring to bodily descent, from which the Jews chiefly glory, he added a general command: “And those who love his name will inhabit it.” This is the same thing he said above, “the offspring of his servants,” which he here expresses as “those who love his name.”

“Inhabit it” means that they will enjoy perpetual happiness. It is a land that no longer produces thorns and thistles, that does not feed human beings through toil, that does not bear poisons, that never loses its inhabitants, and that will shine continually not alternately through the sun and stars, but—what is more blessed—from its own Creator.

Notice also that this psalm has been concluded in its proper order. First, it was uttered from the person of the Lord Christ. Then it began with prayer. [Col. 0491B] Third, it recalled the events of the Lord’s Passion. Fourth, it agreed in harmonious truth with the words of the Gospel. Fifth, it concluded with statements concerning the hope of the faithful people.

Thus this is the fourth psalm that prophesied the Lord’s Passion according to the law foretold.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

We have heard a psalm wondrous in its heavenly dispensation, in which there is as much humility in humanity as there is power in divinity. The holy Word assumed the nature of our weakness, as the title says: “For those who will be changed,” so that through his undeserved death he might free us from the death we justly deserved.

He entered the barriers of the underworld [ms. A., “of the air”], so that the lower regions might be opened. Death was conquered by the Savior’s arrival, and it rightly lost its perpetual darkness after it received the eternal light. [Col. 0491C]

He conquered the devil through the human nature that the devil held subject to himself. Through the weakness of the flesh, the strong one was overcome, when he exalted above all rational creatures that which was weaker than all spiritual beings.

For to which of the angels did he say, as the Apostle states, “Sit at my right hand” (Heb. 1:13)? No other nature has been united to Christ; only the glorified assumption of our flesh has been united to him.

Truly omnipotent, truly merciful is he who blessed those who had been condemned, restored those who had been lost, freed those who had been enslaved, made our miseries foreign to us, and granted that the human being whom the devil had caused to perish, though created immortal, might live through his death.

Grant, omnipotent God, that you who deigned to suffer in the flesh for us may give us what you may deem worthy to crown.

## 233 — EXPOSITION OF PSALM 69

**For the end; of David; for remembrance, that the Lord saved me.**

[Col. 0491D]

“End” and “David,” as has often been said, signify the Lord and Savior, to whom these words of the faithful are directed, because this entire psalm is spoken from the person of the martyrs, who suffered under varied persecution but did not cease to have their hope firmly fixed in the Lord.

“For remembrance” was added. We remember in two ways: when, by recalling our sins, we fear heavenly justice, and again when we retain granted benefits with the purest heart.

Thus, in Psalm 37, where these words are placed, there is fear of the future judgment and remembrance of sins; here, however, there is hope of liberation and the secure promise of a future reward. To show this remembrance, he added, “that the Lord saved me,” so that it might be proved that this memory arose not from fear but from an accepted benefit. [Col. 0492A]

It was fitting, then, that since in the preceding psalm the Lord Christ had narrated his Passion and added the hope of the resurrection, after the head the members should likewise speak, so that the faithful might both declare their sufferings and embrace the hope of the resurrection for which they pray.

## Division of the Psalm

The people of martyrs and confessors, who suffered manifold but blessed affliction, first entreat the Lord to free them from the dangers of their persecutors and to make their mockeries ineffectual, so that, when converted, they may salutarily blush for what they have said. [Col. 0492B]

In the second part they ask that the faithful crowd may exult while magnifying the Lord, because he deigns to help and free his poor and needy.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“O God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me.”

A pious confession begins from the Lord, from whom it knows that aid comes to those in peril. To show the hardships of the blessed company of martyrs, it says: “Attend to my help.” [Col. 0492C]

We seek help when we are subject to dangers, so that, lifted up by some remedy, we may be able to overcome the calamities of various sufferings. “Attend,” he says: look upon me favorably, because the Lord recognizes everything even when he is not asked. But this is the custom of those in peril: to believe that they will be freed if they know that they can be regarded by the Lord.

And lest the benefit he knew was going to come be delayed any longer, he added: “Lord, hasten to help me.” “Hasten” is said as though divine mercy were delaying and the torments were becoming more severe through the delay of its arrival.

Therefore he says “hasten” to the Lord, since he was hastening to be freed from the destruction of this age. For will and perfected accomplishment are joined to him and accelerated, while all things serve the Creator, because everything ministers at his command.

Thus many things have been enclosed in a single verse. This figure is called *epitrochasmos*, that is, “the turning or rolling of an expression,” when matters that ought to be understood at greater length are explained briefly. [Col. 0492D]

But the most eloquent Cassian should not be followed generally in everything here. In the tenth Conference (chap. 10), he discusses its usefulness at length and celebrates it with such honor that whatever monks undertake, they do not begin without the threefold repetition of this verse. By repeating it and doubling it with frequent praise, he proves its remembrance to be exceedingly useful.

### Verse 2

“Let my enemies be confounded and put to shame, those who seek my soul; let those who think evil against me turn backward and be ashamed.”

The people of martyrs, imitators of their head, seeking the correction of their enemies, says: “Let my enemies be confounded and put to shame.” [Col. 0493A]

To be confounded is to be disturbed by the perversity of one’s deed when an evil conscience recognizes its own intentions in the light of truth. To be put to shame is to recognize that justice has been violated by our action and to fear that we will suffer punishment for these things.

This happens to those who, after condemning their perversity, hasten to return to the Lord’s mercy through a desire for conversion.

It follows: “Those who seek my soul.” The faithful crowd rightly placed “soul” in the singular, since they have, as Scripture says, “one soul and one heart” (Acts 4:32).

Their enemies sought the soul of the faithful not for veneration but, to satisfy their hatred, to separate it from its body. This happened in the sufferings of the martyrs, when the enraged persecutor slaughtered them. [Col. 0493B]

“To seek” is also read in a good sense, as in: “My escape has perished, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Ps. 141:5). Since this word is homonymous, he added, “to take it away,” so that you would understand that it had been placed in a bad sense.

He added: “Let those who think evil against me turn backward and be ashamed.” The one who turns backward is the person who, as has often been said, withdraws from an evil thought and follows the Lord’s commands.

The meaning, then, is this: let those who think evil against me receive this retribution, so that they may not persist in their iniquity.

O piety of the saints—even that which is thought to be adversity! They seemed to wish better things for their enemies than they appeared to seek for themselves while established in prosperity.

### Verse 3

“Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ turn backward at once in shame.”

This is an elaboration of the preceding meaning: those who are known to rebuke the most faithful with false praises are to be compelled to depart swiftly, ashamed of their purpose. [Col. 0493C]

“Well done” is the speech of one who praises. But here it must be understood as spoken ironically—that is, mockingly—since it appears to have been uttered by enemies.

Or he rebukes those who applaud the afflictions and punishments of the martyrs and do not refer to the glory of the author what has been granted to them through abundant mercy. For both things are vicious: either to mock the calamities of others or to praise people for what they are able to endure.

### Verse 4

“Let all who seek you, Lord, exult and rejoice in you, and let those who love your salvation always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’”

After speaking of the iniquity and conversion of the persecutors, he entreats in the second section that all who love the Lord Christ may exult and rejoice.

Confusion and shame are wished upon the former; perpetual exultation and joy upon the latter, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46). [Col. 0493D]

But he suitably indicates the character of genuine joy. By saying “in you,” he confesses that the joy that boasts in human presumption is transitory.

It is added: “All who seek you, Lord”—not sought by their own powers but sought by your mercy. For, so that the human race might seek you, you mercifully sought it by looking down from heaven. He himself came to us so that we might deserve to return to him.

Yet those who seek the Lord are salutarily instructed what they should say: “Let the Lord be magnified.” “Always” indicates continuous time, because one must never cease from the Lord’s praise. [Col. 0494A]

And so that the meaning itself may shine more clearly for us, the order of the words should be restored. It is this: “Let those who love your salvation always say: ‘Let the Lord be magnified.’”

Let us understand that this word was borrowed from human custom. A person is magnified when he grows through praise and becomes great through a good reputation. But God has no increase, because he is understood in himself as complete, singular, and ineffable fullness. He cannot grow from another source, since he customarily grants increase to all creatures.

But by magnifying him, we ourselves make progress, and when we render praises to God with a holy mind, our conscience continually grows.

### Verse 5

“But I am needy and poor; God helps me. You are my helper and my deliverer, Lord; do not delay.”

When the faithful crowd imitated the example of the Lord’s Passion, it also transferred his words into its own psalmody.

For in another psalm the Lord says from his own person: “But I am needy and poor; the Lord cares for me” (Ps. 39:18), just as it is also said here from the person of the blessed. [Col. 0494B]

But when he says, “I am needy and poor,” he signifies that those who are worldly were rich. Of them he says: “Let my enemies be confounded and put to shame, those who seek my soul.”

Yet let us consider: although it is exceedingly rich in the heavenly treasure, glorious poverty everywhere calls itself needy and poor. This is because it does not possess worldly resources, while inwardly, where it is rich, it always strives, always desires, and always receives, as the Apostle says: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended” (Phil. 3:13); and again: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2). [Col. 0494C]

You see that such people are rightly called needy and poor: they continually desire to acquire the grace of the Divinity. We are needy when we are continually in need; poor when we always hasten toward his benefits with eager minds.

It follows: “God helps me”—that is, in worldly tribulation, where we struggle against the opposition of vices, where we suffer unclean spirits as enemies and are freed by the Lord’s mercy.

He added both things together, so that the Lord may be a helper in necessities and a deliverer from this world’s destruction.

And observe that he says, “You, Lord,” so that all our hope should look fixedly toward him. [Col. 0494D]

It follows: “Do not delay.” It is the custom of those in peril to judge help slow, even when it is supplied most swiftly. He does everything appropriately and in due measure; but we consider slow what we seek with great desire.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This entire psalm shines with the light of heavenly philosophy, for it has been formed with moral excellence. It asks for relief in afflictions and for the most salutary confusion of enemies, so that, ashamed, they may abandon their evils—those who obey wicked deeds.

Then it promises joy to the good and eternal happiness, and, since the greatest protection in affliction is for the Lord to come swiftly, it entreats him to remove the oppressive hardships of this world by the visitation of his coming. [Col. 0495A]

When he is seen, the devil’s pride collapses—that pride which once reigned through impious domination. He who bound the world with the chains of sins has been fettered, and through the Lord’s power he has been brought to such a state that he now fears the saints, although previously he ruled the human race with the utmost wickedness.

Therefore it should be said frequently and with longing: “You are my helper and my protector, Lord; do not delay.”

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 70

**A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the former captives.**

“David” and “psalm” are well known through constant repetition. But by saying “of the sons of Jonadab and of the former captives,” he indicates the power of the psalm through historical causes, warning in the vestibule that it must be sought in the inner chambers.

For the prophet Jeremiah reports (Jer. 8:9) [Col. 0495B] that Jonadab was a priest of God who commanded his sons to dwell in the temple and to conduct themselves with commendable sobriety. They are known to have done this and to have found great favor with God for their obedience. They are now presented as representing the faithful and devout.

The name itself also indicates the reason. For Jonadab is interpreted as “voluntary of the Lord,” that is, one who served God with an unforced desire, as it is written: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. 53:8).

It follows: “And of the former captives.” The text of the Books of Kings recounts this history. When the Israelite people despised the divine commandments, they had been decreed to undergo a first, second, and third captivity.

But so that, recognizing their fault, they might return with a corrected mind to supplication before the Lord, God announced to them through the prophet, before the first captivity occurred, that this evil was going to come. [Col. 0495C] They, however, remained in their customary wickedness and obstinacy.

These people, then, are now set in the place of the stubborn, who, although frequently admonished, refused to correct themselves.

We are therefore instructed by this title to possess the devotion of the sons of Jonadab, not the obstinacy of the Jews, who deserved to be captives. For the entire psalm concerns the faithful person who rejects the world’s hope and trusts in the Lord with pure devotion, commending the grace of the Divinity to us with complete attention, through which we may be released from the bonds of our sins.

## Division of the Psalm

Through the figure of *ethopoeia*, a general character is introduced: one who, liberated from the captivity of sins, adhered to the divine commandments. He proclaims to us the exceptional love of Christ the Lord, which is always freely bestowed without preceding merits. [Col. 0495D]

In the first part of the psalm, this person continually asks to be freed from human iniquities, so that he may deserve to give thanks to the Lord. In the second section, he pleads not to be deprived in his old age of the benefits of the one whose help protected him in his youth. In the third, enumerating his gifts, he promises to give thanks continually.

## Exposition of the Psalm
### Verse 1

“God, in you I have hoped; Lord, I shall not be put to shame forever.” Here again the pleasing form of a hypothetical syllogism smiles upon us in this manner: If, O God, I have hoped in you, Lord, I shall not be put to shame forever; but, O God, I have hoped in you; therefore I shall not be put to shame forever. Now, with the Lord’s help, let us discuss what follows.

A certain faithful person is selected—one who existed in the earliest times, who does not cease to exist in the present, and who will remain firm in the Lord with perfect steadfastness of mind until the end of the age. Placing all his hope in the Lord, he commends to us the mysteries of divine grace, lest, presuming falsely within ourselves, we be deprived of the prosperity bestowed by his gift.

Let us understand what he means by asking not to be put to shame forever: namely, in that judgment of retribution where being put to shame is altogether penal. In this life we are often put to shame beneficially, when we are recalled from a wicked intention and, being led toward what is good, blush commendably—though previously we rejoiced in our crime. He therefore first stated the reason why he should not be put to shame forever: namely, because he hoped in the Lord.

### Verse 2

“In your righteousness deliver me, and rescue me; incline your ear to me, and deliver me.” When he says, “In your righteousness,” he asks for divine mercy, for it belongs to that righteousness to spare the one who pleads. It is pleasing to God’s equity to forgive the person whom he is known to condemn for his deeds.

He says “deliver me” from impending dangers; “rescue me” from the power of the devil, lest he be condemned with him for eternity. When he says “incline,” he professes himself to be lying prostrate in humility, because unless divine grace inclines itself toward delivering a human being, that person cannot attain by his own merits the mercy that he desires. No one’s merit can reach him unless he himself, in his mercy, comes near to sinners.

### Verse 3

“Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me; for you are my strength and my refuge.” If this is not carefully examined, it may offend some people that, after mentioning divine protection, he is understood to have added a fortified place—as though a place could defend someone whom heavenly power does not vindicate.

But the first statement asks that his soul be protected from spiritual enemies; then he also asks for the preservation of his body, which is defended from the darts and swords of enemies in a most strongly fortified place. The metaphor is drawn from castles, because we escape our adversaries when we are defended in the strongest of places. Yet this place is divine protection, as he says in another psalm: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16:9).

For when we are with Christ, we fear none of the devil’s ambushes, because that most wicked enemy is cheated of his own desire wherever divine protection is present. And observe how beautifully each expression is matched with its corresponding expression: “strength” belongs to “protector”; “refuge” to “fortified place.” He rightly believed that both came to him from the Lord, because he contributed nothing through his own strength.

I think another meaning should also be understood here: the Lord is called “strength” in this present age, where endurance is sought; and “refuge” in that eternal blessedness where no danger is any longer feared.

### Verse 4

“My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the lawbreaker and the unjust.” That general human figure cries out—because he had been captive under the law of sin, but trusted that he would be released through divine grace—that he might be rescued from the harmful power of the sinner, who always desires to do what is known to be contrary both to the divine law and to equity.

But because he had spoken universally of “the sinner,” he now explains him in two parts, saying: “From the hand of the lawbreaker and the unjust.” The lawbreaker is one who, having received the law, acts contrary to the rules of the commandments—as do the Jews, who are known to have received the law among the other nations. The unjust are the pagans, although also those Jews who are restrained by no law of the Lord but, like wild beasts, do whatever they please. Thus he is shown to have embraced every sinner under these two categories.

The Apostle likewise speaks of both kinds of sinners: “Those who sinned without the law will perish without the law, and those who sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Romans 2:12).

### Verse 5

“For you are my patience, Lord; my hope from my youth.” He explains why he should be rescued from the hand of the sinner: namely, because the Lord was his patience, so that when he directed his attention toward him and believed that he would be saved through him, he might endure everything willingly.

Patience is the voluntary and prolonged endurance of difficult and arduous things for the sake of honor or usefulness. He continues: “My hope from my youth.” He placed patience first, and his hope rightly followed, just as the Apostle says: “Tribulation produces patience, patience produces proven character, and proven character produces hope” (Romans 5:3–4). First, we must be tested through patience by God’s grace; then, by his gift, we shall deserve to possess that fruitful hope.

For what he added, “from my youth,” signifies the age at which he believed in the Lord. Whatever time a person comes to him, it is rightly called our youth, because in it we are strengthened with our fullest vigor. Or “from my youth” signifies the time since he began to fight against the devil’s cunning. That is the age directed toward combat and prepared with the liveliest vigor for arduous struggles.

### Verse 6

“In you I have been established from the womb; from my mother’s womb you are my protector; in you is my song always.” Let us examine this verse somewhat more carefully, lest some absurdity confront us. For he said, “My hope from my youth.” Could his establishment in God have existed when, in his mother’s womb, he was nourished without any rational support—especially since we read: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm 50:7)?

Here, however, we must understand the womb of holy Mother Church, where we are first conceived through the rudiment of faith and then born from water and the Holy Spirit. Our establishment can then be the Lord, when we have come to him through the gift of faith.

He added, “You are my protector,” because he himself protects and defends us against the devil’s wickedness and grants that we escape in this world, so that we may not perish beneath the burden of our sins.

A repayment of rewards follows, so that just as his benefits are always present, so also the psalmody offered to him should be continuous. For if no time is free from his gifts, why should anyone withdraw from glorifying him? This signifies both the present age and the age to come. Here we sing to him for deliverance; there we offer thanks for eternal recompense. Thus the Lord must always be praised, because everything he bestows is continuous.

### Verse 7

“I have become like a portent to many; and you are a strong helper.” The faithful person becomes a portent in this world when he pursues what the multitude of sinners cannot love: they seek riches, while he seeks poverty; they seek feasts, while he seeks fasting; finally, they seek joys, while he seeks sorrow.

How, then, could one not appear to be a portent who is known to conduct himself contrary to the consensus of the many? This is what orators have called the humble [editorial reading: *humilis*] type of case: it is believed to be so contemptible that it is considered rather a portent.

But human accusations must be disregarded when divine virtues are shown to favor us. Everything opposed to us is fleeting when the helper is proved to be most powerful. Yet by saying “helper,” he admonishes us that, with God’s grace supporting us, we too must strive and contend for what is good, lest we be found opposed to divine benefits.

### Verse 8

“Let my mouth be filled with your praise, so that I may sing your glory, your magnificence all day long.” Thus far he has told the human race how many different benefits God has conferred; now he also asks this from the Lord, that he may be able to give him fitting thanks. For if the Lord does not fill our mouth, neither is the tongue moved nor are honorable desires kindled.

If we consider it, our happiness is great: to ask for everything, and not always to shrink from asking. Our Creator is offended all the more if we cease from the devout persistence of supplication.

He then gives the reason why he desired his mouth to be filled with praises of Christ: “So that I may sing your glory.” Glory is praise celebrated by the mouths of many. But he added permanence to this good, for when he says “all day,” does he mean that we should cease from the Lord’s praises during the nights—especially since the catholic Church consoles herself with the Lord’s praises at that time? Then evening, night, and morning services are performed while the faithful people keep vigil.

By saying “day,” he included night also, just as we read in Genesis: “There was evening, and there was morning, one day” (Genesis 1:5). This figure is called synecdoche, that is, the whole by a part.

He says “magnificence” because the Lord has done great things: he has inclined his ear toward the humble; protected the endangered; rescued him from the hand of the sinner; established him from the womb; and determined to protect him from his mother’s womb. Thus, under the single name “magnificence,” the praise of all the benefits mentioned above has been gathered together.

### Verse 9

“Do not cast me away at the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not abandon me.” He has come to the second part, in which he more urgently pleads not to be cast away by the Lord in the time of his old age, when the body’s exhausted strength needs greater assistance.

But we should understand this old age not only as the age near life’s end, but also as the time when, through frequent tribulations and martyrdoms, the strength of the soul grows old. This is what he means by “when my strength fails”: when the firmness of patience, shaken, grows weak and can no longer bear by its own strength the burden of tribulation imposed upon it.

He therefore asks not to be abandoned at that time, because with the Lord he could endure everything.

### Verse 10

“For my enemies have spoken against me, and those who watched over my soul have taken counsel together.” The reason is given why the Lord’s mercy should be stirred to come to his aid: weakness has been detected, and the fervor of those lying in wait has been kindled, since they believe that the person whom failing strength prevents from resisting can easily be deceived.
