And lest his enemies be thought insignificant, he says that they were those who watched over him—not with the desire for his salvation, of course, but with a determination to deceive him. He continues: “They have taken counsel together.” The assembled gathering of enemies is always more savage, and what is not divided is carried as a heavier single burden. He subsequently explains what sort of counsel this was, for he says:

### Verse 11

“Saying: God has abandoned him; pursue and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him.” This is what that most faithful man feared, whether placed amid afflictions or in old age. For carnal enemies, looking rather to worldly things, when they see a person worn down by repeated calamity, believe that he has been abandoned by God; they think that divine grace consists only in bodily strength.

“Pursue him,” they said, because he could not flee. “Seize him,” because he was unable to resist those exceedingly violent men. They judged that he had been abandoned by the Lord because they perceived that he had been handed over to their savagery.

Some have thought that this should also be applied to the Lord and Savior. But a more appropriate order of expression is maintained if we do not suddenly change, through an incongruous variation, the person whom we introduced. He continues: “For there is no one to rescue him.”

Utterly deranged were those who judged by what they saw, as though God abandoned with rewards those whom he exposes to injuries, rather than wishing to crown those whom he allows to be tested. Such is the reasoning of one who judges by outward appearance. He denied the Lord’s presence because he did not think that visible help would come to the faithful, believing that the one whom he considered absent from human sight did not exist.

### Verse 12

“God, do not be far from me; my God, look upon me for my help.” Human weakness supposes that God becomes distant when his help is slow to arrive. He does not advance by movement or transfer himself from place to place; rather, filling all things ineffably, he governs everything through the powers of his will.

He therefore asks that God’s grace not depart from him and that he not be exposed to the more serious ambushes of the wicked. He added: “God, look upon me for my help.” Knowing that he would be afflicted, he prays that worthy patience be granted to him through the Lord’s help. For the person whom the Lord assists does not fail under the crushing of evils; rather, he is lifted up by hope precisely when he is weighed down by the burden of tribulations.

### Verse 13

“Let those who slander my soul be put to shame and fail; let those who seek evils against me be covered with shame and embarrassment.” He has come to the most salutary rebukes, such as the catholic Church is accustomed to make.

He says, “Let them be put to shame,” when they see that what you have established is not changed. “Let those who slander my soul fail”: that is, those who speak vainly against it and habitually attack a right course with biting disparagements.

He teaches that such people are to be overcome by the virtue of patience. He commanded that they be endured to such an extent that they themselves might appear rather to fail in their slanders—so that, if they cannot cease because they have been refuted by reason, they may at least cease when wearied by their own excess.

He continues: “Let them be covered with shame and embarrassment.” In beautiful language the future correction of the wicked is portrayed. He said “let them be covered,” as though their faces were veiled by a rosy covering of shame—a thing that usually happens to those who condemn their former actions by a better life.

He added: “Those who seek evils against me,” like the woman who said to her suffering husband Job: “Say a word against God, and die” (Job 2:9). Such are the things that wicked persuaders are accustomed to do: under the appearance of bodily well-being, they seem to attack souls with a hidden wound.

### Verse 14

“But I shall always hope in you, and I shall add to all your praise.” Having completed the correction that he prayed might befall sinners, he turns to his own delight and welfare: just as they despaired of divine power, so he says that he will always hope in the Lord.

This figure is called syncrisis, that is, comparison, when someone demonstrates that his own case is better than that of his adversary.

He continues: “And I shall add to all your praise.” This is obscure unless we look at it carefully. Nothing can be added to divine praises, since admirable perfection admits no increase. Yet there is something that can be celebrated by human beings in a new proclamation.

If I say that the Word of the Father made heaven and earth and everything in them, I have praised the Lord with perfect devotion. But if I add that he became incarnate for the salvation of all, I have added a culmination to complete praises. The things that follow testify that this addition of praise refers absolutely to the incarnation of the almighty Word.

### Verse 15

“My mouth shall proclaim your righteousness, your salvation all day long, because I have not known commercial dealings.” The Savior is the Father’s righteousness, and he promises that he will proclaim him to the nations. Lest you think that another righteousness is intended, he added, “your salvation.”

What else could the faithful person proclaim except that from which Christian faith arose? From what else did the Churches spring up fruitful throughout the whole world? From what else did the salvation of the world proceed through a glorious incarnation?

As has often been said, “all day” indicates continuous time. He continues: “Because I have not known commercial dealings.” Unless this part of the verse is carefully examined, it appears to invite a question. For if every merchant is altogether to be condemned, then those who practice other occupations would also not escape this punishment. What else is commerce than wanting to sell at a higher price what can be obtained more cheaply [editorial reading: *comparari*]?

Moreover, in the *Lives of the Fathers* we read that the most holy man Paphnutius was compared by revelation to a merchant, and even today we find people in God’s Church who conduct trade yet possess the highest faith. It is the most wicked action, not an honest occupation, that is condemned. Likewise, we read that a rich man does not enter the kingdom of heaven, although Job, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the patriarchs, were also wealthy in possessions.

Those merchants, therefore, are considered detestable who, giving no consideration to the Lord’s righteousness, are defiled by immoderate greed for money, burdening their goods more with perjuries than with prices. The Lord drove such people from the temple, saying: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce, a den of thieves” (John 2:16).

This meaning must therefore be understood as follows: “My mouth has proclaimed your righteousness, because I have not known commercial dealings”—namely, those dealings that are defiled by wicked actions.

### Verse 16

“I shall enter into the power of the Lord; Lord, I shall remember your righteousness alone.” People think that they acquire power through commerce and become prominent in this world. This blessed man, disregarding such an aim, says that he will enter into the Lord’s power—that is, into the heavenly kingdoms, where true happiness consists in having arrived.

He said “I shall enter” to show that the heavenly Jerusalem is closed to the faithless and open to the faithful. He then explains what he will do there: “Lord, I shall remember your righteousness alone”—namely, at that time when he separates the lambs from the goats, when with momentary equity he distinguishes all the peoples of the nations, when he sends the impious to Gehenna and the faithful into everlasting rest.

Then he will truly remember the Lord’s righteousness alone, because he will recognize it as both wondrous and unique.

### Verse 17

“God, you have taught me from my youth; and until now I shall proclaim your wonders.” We have said that “youth” should be understood as the time from which a person begins to attain divine grace, because then the soul is firm in its powers and begins to be strong.

“You have taught me” refers either to the divine books or to faith infused from heaven. And lest you think that this knowledge was acquired only at the beginning, he says what usually happens to blessed minds: “And until now,” so that his teaching might appear to have grown through the passage of time.

He continues: “I shall proclaim your wonders.” Truly they were wonders: that the unlearned should be taught; that the faithless should become devout; that the sinner should become most righteous. These, then, are the things he declares that he will proclaim—those which divine mercy had accomplished in him.

### Verse 18

“And even into old age and advanced age, God, do not abandon me, until I announce your arm to the generation.” Among the Greeks these two names are different: they call *senectus* [old age] “gravity,” and *senium* [advanced age] the age near the end. But because Latin did not possess these two words as distinct from one another, two ages are here designated by nearly the same name: old age and advanced age.

The meaning, therefore, is this: since he had said that he was taught from his youth to proclaim the Lord’s righteousness alone, he now asks not to be abandoned by the Lord either in mature age or in old age, so that, strengthened by his power, he may be able to unfold the praises he owes until the end of his life.

But let us see to which periods these ages should be assigned. The youth of the Church was when Christ the Lord was crucified, when the multitude of martyrs fought, and the strength of the Church appeared in the faithful who died.

We call “old age” the period now approaching its end, when faith advances and the people of God increase throughout all the Churches, while the fleeting times of this world diminish.

I think “advanced age” should be understood as that final period when that savage tyrant will arrive and the multitude of martyrs will bring this life to its desired conclusion.

He continues: “Until I announce your arm to the generation.” The faithful man who has been introduced speaks, asking the Lord that he may remain in the congregation of the Church until old age and advanced age, until he should proclaim the arm of the Father—that is, the Lord Savior—to the succeeding generation of human beings, as we read: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1). Thus the Christian religion may be spread through the devotion of the whole world, especially when, at the end of the age, the predestined number of the saints is completed.

### Verse 19

“To every generation that is to come: your power and your righteousness, O God, reach to the highest.” “To every generation that is to come” must be joined to the end of the preceding verse: “to the generation.” And lest you perhaps think that the Lord’s arm—that is, the Lord Christ—was to be announced only to those who lived at the same time as he, when he deigned to become incarnate for us, he added “that is to come,” so that you might understand that this proclamation must continue until the end of the age.

He continues: “Your power and your righteousness, O God.” Here too it must be supplied: “until I announce.” “Power” refers to the grace of the incarnation, through which he deigned to free humanity; “righteousness” refers to the judgment in which he is known to have brought death upon disobedient Adam.

Nor should it trouble us that these have been stated in reversed order, since you frequently find this in the holy Scriptures. “To the highest” declares that both are wondrous and both glorious: humanity, previously justly condemned through righteousness, has been restored through grace.

Let us extend our understanding “to the highest,” because God made man sits at the right hand of the Father, reigning with him and with the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages.

### Verse 20

“What great things you have done! O God, who is like you?” After saying that the Creator’s grace and righteousness had advanced to the highest, he comes to the third part, where, in a hymn of exultation, he celebrates how great a righteousness the Lord showed toward sinners and how, when they were converted, he again bestowed the clemency of his kindness.

For he immediately deprived disobedient Adam of the delight of paradise, but swiftly admitted the confessing thief into its pleasant places. These are the great things that he testifies the Lord accomplished, for he is shown to be uniquely powerful in judging, and no one like him is found in delivering.

“What great things!” must be read with wonder, because no one can comprehend them and no one is sufficient to praise them worthily. They are called “great things” from their greatness, because by their magnitude they appear to produce astonishment in human minds.

He also added: “Who is like you?” because he is shown to be unique by his works. The greatness of the deed bears witness to the power of its author.

### Verse 21

“How many great and evil tribulations you have shown me! And, having turned, you have restored me to life.” “How many” must likewise be read with wonder, as though he were speaking of innumerable sufferings.

Observe also that he says “you have shown”: for he shows harsh tribulations to the faithful in the present, and although they may seem evil or numerous, they nevertheless turn out for good because they strive to benefit them. “Many” therefore indicates quantity; “evil” indicates quality.

He continues: “And again you have restored me to life.” If you consider the nature of the Word, he is always unchangeable and always shown to be immovable. But “you have turned” is spoken tropologically, that is, “you have caused me to turn,” because I had been twisted by the law of sin.

The tribulation of the faithful leads to life, as the Gospel says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

### Verse 22

“And again you have brought me back from the abysses of the earth; you have multiplied your righteousness, and, having turned, you have encouraged me.” We read of abysses as the depths of divine understanding, as the Psalmist says elsewhere: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

But here “of the earth” has been added so that we should understand the deep measures and chasms of sins, from which he professes to have been frequently recalled to the joys of life.

Let us consider what is meant by the fact that he says “again.” “Again” is used for “frequently,” because something is repeated in many ways. In the sixth psalm, following the authority of our predecessors, we said that the Lord grants us remission of sins in seven ways: first, through baptism; second, through martyrdom; third, through almsgiving; fourth, when we forgive the debts owed to us by our debtors; fifth, through the conversion of brothers; sixth, through an abundance of charity; seventh, through repentance.

Perhaps our weakness is also relieved by other remissions. Nevertheless, “again” is said here to indicate that his medicine is applied more frequently.

For when he says, “You have multiplied your righteousness,” he is shown to be explaining the preceding meaning: the Lord multiplies his righteousness when he deigns to help us through various forms of affliction. The Lord’s righteousness is often spoken of when he shows mercy, and again his mercy is called righteousness, because the two are always joined together in him, as it is written in the hundredth psalm: “I shall sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Psalm 100:1).

He continues: “And, having turned, you have encouraged me.” We should notice how fatherly this word is: although he chastises his servants with the severity already mentioned, he nevertheless does not allow them to remain sad, while he consoles them with the holy address of the divine Scriptures.

“Encouragement” should be understood as consolation: it composes the spirit, relieves affliction, and heals the mind wounded by various illnesses.

### Verse 23

“But I shall confess your truth to you in vessels of psalms.” Since the Lord has promised eternal rewards to his faithful through pious encouragements, that general righteous person now joyfully confesses that he will sing the truth—that is, because the Lord’s promises are trustworthy, since what eternal Truth promises cannot deceive.

It is beautifully defined that psalms are vessels of truth, like spiritual jars preserving the Lord’s wine with an incorruptible flavor.

### Verse 24

“I shall sing to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel.” We have often said that faithful Christians possess two greatest virtues: the spiritual virtue of believing rightly and the practical virtue of acting rightly. Here he promises to offer both to the Lord under musical forms.

As regards spiritual virtue, he promised in the preceding verse that he would sing a psalm; as regards practical virtue, he says that he will praise the Lord on the lyre. For the psalm, as has often been said, sounds from above; the lyre sends melody from below toward things above.

But he says to whom the psalm or lyre-playing is offered: to the Holy One of Israel—not to the one whom pagan error imagined, but to the one whom true faith had revealed to our fathers.

### Verse 25

“My lips shall rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed.” He calls the lips the mouth of the inner person. The mind too has its own voice, with which it silently cries out to the Lord.

To make you understand this spiritually, he added: “And my soul, which you have redeemed.” It is therefore the soul that rejoices in its inward lips, knowing that it has been redeemed.

### Verse 25

“But my tongue also shall meditate on your righteousness all day long, when those who seek evils against me have been put to shame and have been confounded.” Just as above he said, “I shall sing your truth in vessels of psalms and on the lyre,” wishing to signify the virtues of soul and body, so he promised that the lips of his heart would sing.

Now he added that his tongue would meditate on God’s righteousness—that is, the substance of his body, which will meditate on the Lord’s praises most fully when it has received his kingdom in that resurrection.

But so that you should recognize the end of the age, he continues: “When those who seek evils against me have been put to shame and have been confounded.” This will certainly happen most fully when the righteous have been placed on the right and the impious on the left.

Enemies are put to shame and confounded in two ways: either when they do penance here and recognize that they have gone astray, or at the Savior’s coming, when they see with their own eyes those things made manifest that they did not believe would happen.

Then the time of secure exultation will belong to the saints, when the impious will no longer possess a place of dominion. The righteous will rejoice when the end of all evils has arrived and the Lord has granted good things without end. In this the unceasing petition of Christians remains.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Since this entire psalm commends the Lord’s grace—which is given freely—with the greatest earnestness, it also admonishes us to declare the incarnation of the Word, through which salvation came to the human race, with a fortunate proximity: like the sun, which, rising with the approach of light, sends ahead a rosy dawn, so that the eye may be prepared to behold the splendor of the brightness that is about to appear.

Our fathers believed that the number of the psalms should be divided among the mysteries of the Old and New Testaments in this way: they assigned seven decades to the Sabbath, which unquestionably pertains to that first observance; but they assigned eight to our time, since every week we honor the Lord’s resurrection on the eighth day. Therefore, through both reckonings, this sacred number is recognized as containing the psalms of the Old and New Testaments.

For what one hundred and fifty can signify as the total number of individual units, fifteen decades signify in the order of tens. Thus this calculation of the psalms is suitably adapted to the New and Old Testaments.

It must plainly be understood that, in the first part of the Old Testament, he also mingles the mysteries of the new dispensation. For in the number seven he speaks both of the passion of the Lord Christ, and in the reckoning of eight he places many things from the Old Testament, so that in every way it may be perceived that both accord with our religious observance.

We must also remember that the psalms frequently mention arithmetic and other disciplines. In what follows, whenever appropriate, we shall briefly mention something about these matters themselves, so that, although they are treated briefly, they may not appear to have been passed over.

The essential point is that we should avoid sacrilegious astrology with the utmost determination; even the judgments of distinguished philosophers have condemned it.

Therefore let us bring the present work to an end, so that a brief rest may restore the reader’s zeal and the next organized portion of the psalms may suitably begin from the significance of the New Testament. Amen.

# EXPOSITION OF THE EIGHT DECADES CORRESPONDING TO THE NEW TESTAMENT

## Preface

Having completed the seven decades—as was said—in the figure of the Old Testament, let us now come to the remaining eight. Their number is recognized to indicate to us most fully the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, so that, when these sections have been carefully examined, the Book of Psalms may truly appear to embrace the treasury of all divine Scripture.

For although everything is full of spiritual riches and illuminated by great lights, nevertheless, as I think, you will find scarcely any other volume among them that is taught to be so completely filled with heavenly matters.

Nor should it trouble us that the section we said belonged to the mystery of the Old Testament begins with the blessedness of the Lord Savior, and that again in the subsequent psalms we find things that clearly took place in the earliest times. These matters should not be judged wholly contradictory, because the Old Testament is also full of the New, and the New frequently makes mention of the Old.

Let us now come to the title, which is known to pertain, through the interpretation of its name, to the mystery of the New Testament. It is entitled:

# PSALM 71: “FOR SOLOMON”

“Solomon” is interpreted as “peaceful.” But who is truly peaceful except the Lord Christ, who recalled to the service of his Creator the human being deceived by the devil’s cunning and made him worship the author of salvation, though previously, in his misery, he had followed the author of death?

For he himself, the Mediator of God and human beings, still intercedes for us today. That we rightly call him peaceful is testified by his own words when he says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27).

But this is not a peace that wars can disturb, nor one that any unrest can shake. Rather, remaining forever undisturbed and eternal, it cannot be dissolved by the opposition of any enemy. It is the peace of which the prophet says: “I shall give you true consolation, peace upon peace.”

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks, signifying the coming of the Lord Savior. In one and the same person he clearly displays, in alternating sections, now Christ’s humanity and now his divinity.

In the first part he speaks to the Father, asking that judgment be given to the Son for judging the peoples—although this is known to have been predestined before the ages.

In the second, he says that, at the Lord’s judgment, the sons of the poor will be saved and the devil’s pride will unquestionably be humbled. He is also understood to indicate, through certain comparisons, the very birth from the Virgin.

In the third part he recounts what good things occurred through the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary when the Lord Christ was born.

In the fourth he says that Christ is to be worshiped by all kings, because he freed the human race from the devil’s power.

In the fifth he declares that, having been seen by human eyes, Christ was the strength of believers and unquestionably the advancement of the righteous.

In the sixth he affirms that praises are to be offered to the eternal Lord by the agreement of the whole world.

In the seventh he offers a hymn to the Lord Christ with most joyful devotion.

Thus, through the sequence of this psalm, the clear and manifest beginning of the New Testament is shown to have been expressed.

## Exposition of the Psalm
### Verse 1

“Give the king your judgment, O God, and your justice to the king’s Son.” When it says, “O God,” this name does not appear to designate any particular person; but since it follows with “give to the Son,” it is certainly understood that the Father is being invoked. For the latter name is relational and indicates the former, though it does not say it, just as the designation “servant” implies a master. We should know, moreover, that these names alone are sufficient to distinguish and declare the persons of the holy Trinity. For when you have said, “God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit,” you appear to have fully declared the persons of the holy Trinity [Col. 0506D]. These names alone are proper to the holy Trinity; the remaining terms—namely, nature, power, eternity, omnipotence, and the like—are shown to be common to all three.

Therefore the most blessed prophet, inflamed with glorious desire, asks the Father that judgment be given to the Son, which he knew was destined to come, as it is read in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). *Judgment* is so called as though it were *juris dictum*, that is, “a declaration of law,” because law is declared in it. And so that the petition might be proved most truthful, he repeated it once more in the following clause. For this is what he says: “and your justice to the king’s Son,” which he had said above: “Give your judgment to the king.” In the divine Scriptures you frequently find the same thing repeated in order to express the point, as in: “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Psalm 2:4); and: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands” (Psalm 18:2). The following verse, too, is expressed in the same way.

This figure is called *epimone*, that is, the frequent repetition of a proposition, whenever one matter is repeated in different words in order to impress the point. We must also remember that whenever the Lord Christ himself asks that something be given to him, or another person requests that it be granted to him, the nature of his humanity is plainly being shown. The almighty Word, however, since he possesses the whole of the Father, needs nothing to be given to him, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Everything that belongs to the Father is mine” (John 16:15).

### Verse 2

“To judge your people in your justice, and your poor in judgment.” He explains the reason why he had asked that judgment be given to the Son: namely, that he might judge the world through the Father’s justice, which is undoubtedly also the Son’s. For this reason he says to the Father, “in your justice,” so that no one might sacrilegiously suppose that the holy Trinity differs from itself in anything.

He continues: “and your poor in judgment.” He also calls them the Father’s poor, although they are declared to be Christ the Lord’s as well, so that it may be understood that in that majesty no power has been divided, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). The poor of God, therefore, are those who, having abandoned worldly pride, have surrendered themselves entirely to humility. For if a poor man is proud, he is not God’s poor man; and if a wealthy man loves humility, he is not rich in the world’s sense. The dispositions of such people must be examined, not their names [Col. 0507C].

### Verse 3

“Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills justice.” We have often said that the mountains signify the apostles and prophets, who, firmly raised toward heavenly things, draw near to heavenly grace. Let such men, then, receive peace—that is, Christ—to be preached to the faithful people. For that is the Lord’s people which has believed in him and conducted itself in a spiritual manner.

He continues: “and the hills justice.” By the hills he means the other blessed men, at a lower level, who rightly appear to preach the Lord’s commandments. Both “peace,” which he mentioned above, signifies the Lord and Savior, and “justice” undoubtedly designates him himself, as it is also read elsewhere: “Justice and peace have kissed” (Psalm 84:11). He is truly called Peace because through him humanity has been reconciled to God [Col. 0507D]; and Justice because he will judge the world with equity, having also overcome the devil through justice more than through the exercise of power.

### Verse 4

“He will judge the poor of the people in his justice, and he will save the children of the poor, and he will humble the accuser.” Up to this point he has spoken in the form of a wish. Now, by the power of prophecy coming to the second part, he recalls through a most beautiful variety of different parables what is to be accomplished at the Lord’s coming.

For above he said to the Father, “in your justice”; now he says of the Son, “in his justice,” so that you may hold firmly that there is nothing there either differing or divided, but that what is the Father’s justice is likewise, without doubt, the Son’s justice.

It can also be understood in another way. The poor of Christ are shown to be rejected by the judgment of this world, since they are excluded from testimony and removed from honorable assembly [Col. 0508A]. God, however, will judge the poor not by human justice but by his own, because he has chosen precisely those whom proud mortality has despised. He also added “of the people,” where “faithful” must be understood. For the Lord did not choose just any poor people, but those whom he himself describes: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

He continues: “and he will save the children of the poor.” Christ’s poor are the apostles or prophets, who despised the wealth of this world through the poverty chosen by the Lord. Of him it is written: “Though he was rich, he became poor for our sake” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Their children are the Christian peoples; they were generated by the apostles’ preaching, and through the teaching of those men they merited to believe, as the Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19); and again: “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4:15). He will therefore save those whom he recognizes as the children of the apostles.

He adds: “and he will humble the accuser.” The accuser signifies the devil, proud, cruel, insatiable, and the prince of all evils. Let us examine why he is called an accuser. Ancient judges affixed the letter *K* to condemnations; and because the cruel adversary favors the condemnations of others, they wished to call the soldier of the letter *K* an accuser. An accuser, therefore, is one who strives by carefully devised machination to turn another’s innocence into guilt. This seems aptly applied to the devil, who for so many ages has been shown to attack the human race by his deceits [ms. A., “to hinder”]. What is more calumnious than to be the author of crimes and to claim for himself the worship of the earth?

The Lord will humble this spiritual tyrant when, after he has been condemned together with the faithless, the faithful see themselves reigning with Christ [Col. 0508C].

### Verse 5

“And he will remain with the sun, and before the moon, forever and ever.” Here the honor of the holy Incarnation is explained: it remains united with the Word. For he sits at the right hand of the Father, reigning in everlasting glory.

The sun is understood to be the Father’s Word, the Son of God: Christ, God and man, one from two and abiding in two distinct and perfect natures. Of him the impious will say: “The sun did not rise for us, and the light of justice did not shine upon us” (Wisdom 5:6).

He continues: “and before the moon, forever and ever.” The verb “he will remain,” which he said above, must be supplied. Christ remains before the moon—that is, before the sight of the Church, which continually beholds him with the lights of the heart. The moon is rightly compared to the Church, since it does not possess native brightness but receives light from the sun according to fixed phases; astronomers explain this carefully among other matters.

It is altogether wondrous, and deserving of deeper amazement, that the courses of so many stars and the lofty, subtle measurements of such immense things have been able, by the Creator’s gift, to reach human understanding. Thus the Church received light in measured fashion from that true Creator: at one time she appears diminished by persecutions, and then, having recovered tranquility, she is filled with the joy of the most brilliant light [Col. 0509A]. For when he said “forever and ever,” he indicated an entirely perpetual time, as it is written: “And there will be no end of his kingdom” (Isaiah 9:7).

### Verse 6

“And he will descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling gently upon the earth.” Here the mystery of the glorious birth is explained. For that Lord of hosts, before whose presence the earth trembles and is shaken, and every creature is thrown into confusion because he cannot in any way be endured when he wishes to make himself known through manifest power, chose to descend gently into the virginal womb without any disturbance, like rain upon a lamb’s fleece. In this way he showed his power even more, if he tempered that ineffable might.

As the Apostle says: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man” (Philippians 2:6–7).

But let us consider what sort of likeness has been employed for so great a matter. Fleeces are the wool of sheep. They receive water without being torn apart by any division, and they give it back while remaining in their own wholeness. Hear this, whoever among you are still unbelieving, and be ashamed not to believe this concerning the supreme Divinity when you see the smallest creatures indicating it.

He continues: “and like drops falling gently upon the earth,” that is, drops which descend with the utmost gentleness like dew. If you consider these things with a pure mind, you will have no hesitation concerning the Virgin’s childbirth. He confirmed that immense miracle, so that it might be believed without any doubt, by a double example.

Here that Ambrose, a kind of candle of the Church, shone with wondrous brilliance, saying (Tome 5, hymn 24):

> Come, Redeemer of the nations,  
> Show forth the Virgin’s birth;  
> Let every age marvel:  
> Such a birth befits God.

From this also the speech of the most blessed Pope Leo shone forth, like a flash of lightning. For he says (Epistle 10 to Flavian, chapter 2):

> He was conceived of the Holy Spirit within the womb of the Virgin Mother, who brought him forth while preserving her virginity, just as she conceived him while preserving her virginity.

Worthy Fathers, and men distinguished by the eminence of the pontificate, whose most gracious teaching and eloquence were sufficient to declare so great a miracle [ms. A., “mystery”].

### Verse 7

“Justice will arise in his days, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted.” Now he comes to the third part, in which, in order, the various great things the Lord accomplished at his birth are described [Col. 0509D].

Let us therefore understand what he said: “Justice will arise,” as though it had not existed before, although it had always reigned in an adorably majestic manner [ms. A., “in a majesty worthy of adoration”]. But he says that it will arise from the time of the holy Incarnation, when it was about to be born through the Virgin’s childbirth.

For Justice is the Father’s Word, which made every creature and all times. Of him it is written: “Truth has arisen from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Psalm 84:12).

He added: “and an abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted.” Here too “will arise” must be understood. The abundance of peace exists while the religion of the Christians is spread throughout the whole world. “Until the moon is exalted,” he said—that is, as long as the Church is extended and grows, or until the number of the predestined is completed [Col. 0510A].

### Verse 8

“And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.” By saying “he will rule,” he indicates that the Lord Christ, of whom the preceding verses sing and the following verses will speak, is made widely known through the worship of religion.

This cannot in any way refer to Solomon, son of David, who is known to have been king only among the Jewish people. By “sea” we should understand the Ocean, which, as some say, surrounds and encloses the surface of the whole earth with its rim. For if you wish to understand this as our local seas, you will not be able to grasp the circuit of the whole world that this verse signifies.

He continues: “and from the river to the ends of the earth.” This is a beautiful brevity, but it has poured out immense mysteries for us. By “the river” he means the Jordan, from which the most salutary rule of sacred baptism flowed throughout the whole world. This was expressed through the figure of *periphrasis*, that is, by circumlocution, signifying the circuit of the whole world through the seas and the river.

### Verse 9

“Before him the Ethiopians will fall, and his enemies will lick the earth.” We should understand the Ethiopians as sinful peoples. For just as they are clothed in a very dark skin, so the souls of sinners are darkened by the obscurity of their crimes.

These Ethiopians, therefore, who are sinners, fall before him when they prostrate themselves in the humility of repentance.

He added: “and his enemies will lick the earth.” He said that those who are to be spared by the Lord’s mercy fall before him. But these others are called the obstinate enemies, the Jews, who will remain in their stubbornness.

What punishment is theirs? “They will lick the earth,” that is, they will taste the earth; for each person tastes what he licks. For them, like a serpent, the ground is their penal food [Col. 0510C]. We rightly refer this to their humiliation, since those who refused to believe Christ to be God are to be condemned to such punishment.

### Verse 10

“The kings of Tarshish and of the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring presents.” Tarshish, according to Father Jerome (On Isaiah, chapter 29, verse 1), is interpreted as “contemplation.” There is no doubt that this should be referred to the faithful, who are fixed in divine contemplation.

The kings of Tarshish, therefore—that is, rulers of vices—offer gifts to the Lord when they are shown to serve him with devoted spirit.

The islands are those who have excluded from their bodies the vices flowing around them in the world, so that the worldly sea, which is poured into the hearts of the faithless, does not rule in them. It is called an “island” because it is situated in the open sea.

They are therefore gifts of a pure heart, offered upon the divine altars—the very sacrifice which the Lord graciously accepts when it is offered.

He continues: “the kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring presents.” Arabia stands for people who delight in sweet and earthly pleasure. For just as that country soothes the sense of smell with various spices, so such people are invited to the softest pleasures by worldly allurements.

The kings of Arabia, therefore, are those who subject the blandishments of the body to a rigorous discipline.

Likewise Sheba, from which the Sabaeans are called: although it excels in bodily pleasure and is filled with pleasant fragrances, its converted peoples offer more pleasing gifts of virtue [Col. 0511A].

When he says “they will bring,” he refers to the people themselves as being offered, because after the Lord’s coming the sacrifices of animals ceased.

### Verse 11

“And all the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him.” He comes to the fourth section, where he says that the Lord is to be worshiped by all nations, and then sets out his benefits.

By “all kings,” he wished us to understand all nations, because there is no nation in which some part of its people does not worship its own Creator. And so, lest you understand this as having been said only about kings, he added: “all nations will serve him”—namely, those divided throughout the whole world both by languages and by homelands [Col. 0511B].

Thus the error of Donatus is shown to have been refuted: he considers the Church local, although it is established that she has been spread throughout the whole world.

Notice that he said “the kings will worship,” since kings are thought to be objects of worship, but “the nations will serve,” since they are known to have earthly lords.

### Verse 12

“For he has delivered the poor from the powerful, and the needy who had no helper.” He gives the reason why all nations serve the Lord Christ: because he delivered the poor—that is, the faithful people—from the powerful devil, whom he earlier called the accuser.

Elsewhere he calls him “the strong man,” as in this Gospel passage: “No one enters the strong man’s house to plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Matthew 12:29). These terms signify his wickedness, not his honor; his unspeakable cunning, not a praiseworthy rule.

He continues: “and the needy who had no helper.” Here too “he delivered” must be supplied from the common construction. We have said that the needy person is more than the poor person: the needy has no aid for life and cannot sustain himself by his own resources.

The Lord Christ delivered such people when, coming into this world, he most justly crushed the devil’s cunning and freely bestowed the gifts of spiritual abundance upon the poverty of the human race.

He rightly added “who had no helper,” because the human race had turned with abominable superstition to the worship of idols. And what help could it receive from things that did not even possess the understanding of animals?

### Verse 13

“He will spare the poor and needy, and he will save the souls of the poor.” When he says “he will spare,” he indicates all sinners in general. Those are spared who are held in some guilt.

He will therefore spare even his elect, who, although they shine through a holy manner of life, nevertheless need something to be forgiven them [Col. 0511D].

But lest it be thought that the Lord spares only to the extent of freeing the poor from deserved torments, he added: “he will save the souls of the poor,” so that to those whose sins he forgives he may also grant future rewards. For those who will possess the kingdom of God will be saved.

This, therefore, cannot apply to Solomon: he could not save souls, a work which certainly belongs only to the Divinity.

### Verse 14

“He will deliver their souls from usury and iniquity, and their name will be honored before him.” Usury is named from use, because it continually causes an increase in money that has been lent.

Thus, for those living in sin, the usury of evil increases when they receive in eternal punishment what they committed during their temporal life.

Faithful souls are delivered from these usuries, or from the obligation of sin itself, when through repentance they are released and restored to divine gifts.

He continues: “and their name will be illustrious before him.” Truly an illustrious name: to be called Christians, to shine forth from their King, and to glory in the dignity received through that name.

Isaiah is known to have foretold this while rebuking the Jews, saying: “The Lord God will kill you, but he will call his servants by another name” (Isaiah 65:15)—namely, Christians.

He also added “before him,” because they will live before him and in his kingdom. Blessed is that presence: always to be before God, whom you no longer fear offending.

Add to this that it is such a reward to see him whom not even thought itself can now reach [Col. 0512B]. Thus, in these very few words, some indication—though veiled—is given to us of that blessedness.

### Verse 15

“And he will live, and gold from Arabia will be given to him, and they will worship him continually; all day long they will bless him.” Behold, the fifth mode of the vision already foretold, in which he says that the vow of faith and the foundations of the earth have brought about the Lord’s presence.

When he says “and he will live,” he shows the eternity of his majesty, as it is frequently read in the Old Testament: “The Lord lives.” He lives, therefore, not with the life of some creature, which even the angels possess, but with that singular blessedness which the holy Trinity alone enjoys.

He continues: “and gold from Arabia will be given to him.” Gold from Arabia is said to be purer than that of other lands and precious for its supreme brilliance. This is appropriately referred to wisdom, since we read: “Receive prudence as silver, and wisdom as tested gold” (Proverbs 8:10).

A gift will therefore be given to the Lord from that wisdom signified by the gold of Arabia, when the devoted come to him with a most purified heart.

Alternatively, perhaps it signifies the gifts of the Magi, which are rightly compared with the gold of Arabia because they were offered with purity of heart.

The ancients called the color of gold most beautiful; therefore they wished gold to be named from *aura*, because it shines with an exceedingly pleasing color. Even today we call something “golden” when we wish to judge it beautiful.

He continues: “and they will worship him continually.” This is clearly referred to his humanity, since with his own mouth he instituted the manner in which he should be prayed to. The benefit of the Lord’s Prayer is well known, and the Church always makes use of it. The most holy Father Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage, was the first to expound it and expanded that profound brevity with the marvelous beauty of eloquence [Col. 0512D].

He added: “all day long they will bless him.” “All day long” indicates the whole period of our life, which is rightly called a day because the hearts of the faithful are not darkened by any shadows.

### Verse 16

“And there will be firmament on the earth upon the heights of the mountains; his fruit will be exalted above Lebanon.” The heights of the mountains signify the excellence of the prophets, whom we frequently say should be understood as mountains.

The firmament of these mountains is certainly the Lord Christ, because what was foretold about him through them is shown to have been fulfilled when he came.

He continues: “his fruit will be exalted above Lebanon.” Since above he compared God’s saints with mountains, and since he himself is the mountain of mountains, here a chosen mountain is presented whose fruit may be compared with the Lord Christ.

For in Lebanon, as we have often said, outstanding cedars grow, possessing the greatest height. But what can be found like the Lord’s fruits, from whom the lofty saints are produced? For it is not the same thing, even if tall trees grow to whatever height or touch the clouds, as for the blessed to reach the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

### Verse 17

“And they will flourish from the city like the grass of the earth; may his name be blessed forever.” This appears to raise some difficulty, because now he makes grass of the earth resemble eternal life, although grass is frequently compared with the impious. But this should not disturb us at all.

Just as Christ is called a lion because he is a powerful king among beasts, while on the other hand the devil is understood as a lion because he is known to be fierce and savage, so grass, because it is the earth’s first fruit, green and pleasing, is not unfittingly compared with the Lord’s saints; but in the respect in which it quickly withers and is cut down, it is rightly likened to sinners.

Thus, when different qualities are considered, one and the same thing may be compared most appropriately in different ways [ed., “in diverse ways”].

The righteous will therefore flourish from the city—that is, from the Church of God—like the grass of the earth. It is not the age of the grass but its beautiful greenness that is compared with the saints.

Observe that he says “they will flourish from the city,” not “in the city,” because from this city of the present age they will flourish in that eternal blessedness [Col. 0513C]. Here they are afflicted by tribulations, so that there they may be crowned with perpetual rejoicing.

He continues: “may his name be blessed forever.” After describing the blessedness of the saints, he returns to the praise of the Lord, through whom they are blessed, as though he were saying: “May God be glorified forever, for he is recognized as the one who will bestow eternal glory.”

### Verse 18

“His name remains before the sun, and all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him; all nations will magnify him.” The gate of the sixth section is opened. Here both the Lord’s eternity and the universal service of all the earth are signified.

And lest anyone, with blasphemous thought, regard the holy Son of God as temporal, he declared that his name remains before every creature, as the Gospel says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2).

Behold the name that remains forever. And so that you may understand that this Word was placed before the sun, it follows: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (ibid., 1:3). You see, therefore, that his name existed before all creatures, since he is the creator of all.

“Name” is so called because it makes a thing known. Here he places the sun for all creatures, because it shines more agreeably to our sight. This is the figure called *synecdoche*, which signifies the whole by a part.

He continues: “all the tribes of the earth will be blessed in him.” By “in him” he means the Lord Christ, just as it was said to Abraham: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

And because he mentioned “tribes,” lest you understand this of only a few nations that had their people divided under that name, he added: “all nations will magnify him.” “They will magnify him” means, certainly, that they will praise him. For who can make greater the one whom all powers and heights serve? Yet by proclaiming him we are magnified, because we advance through his praise. No perverse interpretation can deny that this is said to the proclamation of his divinity.

### Verse 19

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does great wonders.” The seventh section, which remains, now begins. After everything has been traversed, the Lord Christ is praised with great exultation.

When we proclaim the Lord, we are indeed said to bless him—not because he is sanctified or increased by us, but because when he sanctifies us through his blessing, protection arises and growth proceeds.

He indicates who this Lord is through the fifth kind of definition: “the God of Israel,” that is, the God of the whole earth, as another prophet says: “He who redeemed you, the God of Israel, will be called the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 54:5).

He added: “who alone does great wonders,” because he needs no helper. For although angels and many righteous people perform miracles, they accomplish them not alone but with the Lord’s help.

### Verse 20

“And blessed is the name of his majesty forever and ever; and the whole earth will be filled with his majesty. Let it be, let it be.” In the preceding verse he says that God is blessed; in the second, the name of his majesty—that is, because Christians were named from Christ, and this title has filled the whole world’s boundaries with sacred reverence.

For just as he himself is eternal, so the proclamation of his name endures.

When it follows, “and the whole earth will be filled with his majesty,” he means the saints, who have been filled by his glorification. Here we must understand “the whole earth” as the whole body of the faithful, whom the Lord truly deigns to fill.

He added: “Let it be, let it be.” It belongs to one who wishes to say “let it be,” but to one who desires greatly to repeat it. We should understand this as having been placed for the mystery of certain psalms, not—as some have thought—to divide the unity of the book into many sections.

A magnificent psalm, followed by doubled petitions: the Lord’s coming most certainly ought to have been desired with longing.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0514D]

Let us consider, distinguished listeners, that against the wicked battles of Eutyches and Nestorius the weapons of the true faith were once provided for us, so that God, the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, may be believed to exist and remain in one person in two most true and perfect natures. Thus we may labor to suppress those errors, being admonished by the strength of so great an authority.

When we find both natures expressed in this psalm, the perverse doctrine of Eutyches, who defended one nature, is driven out. But when the one person of Christ the Lord is proclaimed, the poisons of Nestorius are condemned, because although this psalm speaks of two operations, it is nevertheless understood to proclaim one person of the Lord [Col. 0515A] Christ.

It said nothing in the plural number, because it wished one Son to be believed. He is the one who was born from the Father before the ages; who assumed in the Virgin’s womb the flesh of our mortality; who is *homoousios*—of one substance—with the Father according to divinity, and likewise *homoousios* with us according to humanity; invisible in divinity, but made visible in humanity.

As man, he deigned to suffer for us; in himself, as God, he is impassible—not diminishing the height of divinity, but exalting the humility of the flesh.

This is what holy prophecy says; this is what the text of the Gospels frequently indicates; this is what the blessed Church sings throughout the whole world. Thus anyone who has not been established upon such a foundation is shown to be an outsider to the catholic faith.

Remember, moreover, that this is the fourth of those psalms which, as we foretold, would speak about the two natures.

# Exposition of Psalm 72

## “The praises of David son of Jesse have failed; a psalm of Asaph.”

Although in the preceding titles only David appears to have been written, here he added “son of Jesse,” so that we should understand this David as the father of Solomon. This was appropriately added to express the person of the prophet.

This is the ninth kind of definition, which the Greeks call *kath’ hypotýpōsin*—καθ’ ὑποτύπωσιν—and which the Latins describe as a kind of imaginative representation [ed., “image”]. It occurs when, by naming the mother or father, our understanding is led to an individual person.

Many details may also be gathered together in order commonly to identify persons, as in the description: “Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, whose mother is Phaenarete, bald, pot-bellied, and snub-nosed.” All these details are known to indicate and define Socrates alone. But in such a matter one must include as many details as can separate the individual being sought from all others.

He therefore says that the praises of this David have failed. Unless we investigate the matter, this is entirely contrary to reason: that in the middle, almost, of the prophet’s work he should say that his praises have failed.

Let us therefore seek the reason for this saying from the beginning. When the Israelite people were freed from the land of Egypt through miracles visible to human eyes, they rendered praises to God for the benefits bestowed, through sacrifices of animals and the harmonious sound of musical instruments. These things were performed figuratively until the fullness of time, when Christ the Lord would come.

Those temporal praises, therefore, which were offered for divine benefits, failed and were changed, because now the catholic Church performs the offering of the body and blood of Christ and sacred psalmody.

He continues: “a psalm of Asaph.” The Hebrew language testifies that Asaph signifies the Synagogue. The Synagogue did indeed worship the Lord, but, seeing the wicked flourish, it fell into very evil thoughts. In this psalm Asaph himself speaks in its person, and in his own name he contains the meaning of the Synagogue.

He will say many things about the peoples of the Gentiles and about those who received the law—things usefully spoken for our correction, so that we may not be polluted by such thoughts.

## Division of the Psalm

As we have said, Asaph speaks throughout the psalm typologically on behalf of the Synagogue.

In the first part he says that he envied worldly happiness, seeing the peace of sinners. He wonders why such prosperity has come to the enemies of God and to pagans that they appear to raise their mouths even to heaven.

In the second part he says that his people will return to salutary counsel and blush at the perversity of their former thought, until they merit to understand and behold the final destiny of the impious.

In the third part he testifies that evils come upon the impious because of their deceits, since they appeared to scandalize holy men by their prosperity; nevertheless, he asserts that by the Lord’s favor he was freed from these evils.

In the fourth he explains how, through the Lord’s mercy, he reached perfect understanding.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“How good is the God of Israel to those who are right in heart” [ed., “to the upright in heart”]!

Asaph remembered that he had envied those who were fortunate in this world and had reached excessive sadness because the Lord permitted sinners to flourish in this age. Condemning himself, he burst forth with a true and gracious judgment, saying that God is good—but to those who are right in heart, that is, to those who understand his works with devoted reverence.

From this it is perceived that his ordering of things displeases crooked and distorted mortals in their sacrilegious thoughts. Thus the serene sun shines most brightly upon healthy eyes; by contrast, it appears obscure to those whose sight is held by weakness.

### Verse 2

“But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out.” In order that you might understand that the holy man had uttered the preceding judgment against himself—a practice always familiar to the righteous—he confesses his own error, saying that he had almost fallen because the Lord’s governance irrationally displeased him [Col. 0516C].

Scripture frequently calls the foot, by *tropology*, the mind’s judgment, by which a person stands through a fixed will. He says that this foot was almost moved when his mind differed from the true understanding.

When he says “almost,” he recalls that he quickly returned to the way of truth, so that he might condemn the error which was hastening to steal upon him.

He continues: “my steps were almost poured out.” We have said that steps signify human actions, by which we walk along the paths of our life. These steps of good conduct therefore almost slipped away in another direction when it seemed, amid an ungrateful state of mind, that so much had been granted to the impious.

Observe that he says his steps were “almost poured out,” not “fallen,” so that you may understand that the strength of our mind can be dispersed like a liquid element when it begins to differ from true thought [Col. 0516D].

Hence we understand that even holy men are often overtaken by evil thoughts, but that they return again to their former soundness when, through the Lord’s help, they are quickly corrected by themselves.

### Verse 3

“For I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners.” The reason followed why his steps seemed to be poured out: he was so envious of sinners that he was deeply distressed by their tranquility.

O incongruous jealousy—to envy those who are perishing and to regard as happy those whom it is certain will be struck by eternal condemnation!

He continues: “seeing the peace of sinners.” Truly, this peace is not understood but seen: it deceives our sight while growing toward its own destruction. For when sinners appear wealthy, to rule over many peoples, and to have nothing in the world to fear, they are thought to possess peace.

But this peace is always at war with conscience; it quarrels inwardly. And when it has no external enemy, it fights against itself.

### Verse 4

“For there is no decline toward their death, and there is no firmness in their affliction.” He still speaks of the prosperity of the wicked. For he says: “For there is no decline toward their death,” that is, they do not quickly decline into death, nor are they immediately driven to their final day; rather, while they are granted time in life to repent, they are shown to increase their crimes all the more. He continues: “and there is no firmness in their affliction.” The sense requires this to be understood: even if some adversity happens to touch them here, their sorrow does not seem to remain long-lasting; and therefore they do not turn back to the physician, because they have never lain for a long time in worldly illnesses.

### Verse 5

“They are not in the labors of men, and with men they will not be scourged.” Here we should understand “men” to mean holy men, who endure labors in this world and suffer the scourges of various afflictions, so that, once corrected, they may deserve to return to the Lord. What is granted for the salvation of the devout does not befall obstinate sinners. But if we judge that the statement is directed against spiritual wickedness, it can appropriately be understood of those powers, which in this world do not receive punishments corresponding to their crimes. Nor are they scourged with men, since by divine command they are to be condemned together with their followers. The tribulation of this world is a desired correction for the faithful, which the wicked do not receive, because they will be shut out from future rewards.

### Verse 6

“Therefore their pride took hold of them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety.” Let us consider how far the unrestrained security of sinners has carried them, and let us cease to envy the joys of those whom we know to have rushed into the pit. The freedom of the wicked produces pride in the fullest sense, since unpunished insolence continually nourishes contempt; and the person who has feared nothing capable of opposing him does not believe himself subject to evils.

He says “took hold,” that is, it seized them as though with certain hands, so that they cannot escape once they have been bound fast. He says “their pride,” which is truly the devil’s, for it was through him that this crime arose—the crime that condemned him to eternal torment. He continues: “they are covered with their iniquity and impiety.” If he had said “clothed,” perhaps their heads would still have been free; but when he says “covered,” we should understand them to be wholly submerged. Iniquity can be moderate; but he added “impiety,” which is shown to be the extreme of every evil. Consider also that this verse and those that follow describe the crimes and conduct of the wicked.

### Verse 7

“Their iniquity came forth as from fatness [ms. G., ‘arose’]; they passed over into the disposition of the heart.” Evil arises from leanness when someone, stripped of worldly resources, devises some crime. But iniquity proceeds from fatness when those who, by the Lord’s favor, have been filled with the abundance of the present age commit some offense against divine honor. For a sin is fat and strong when it is committed by choice rather than necessity. To intensify their guilt, he says that they sinned amid an abundance of possessions, rather than devising some crime that poverty might excuse.

He added: “they passed over into the disposition of the heart.” “They passed over,” as though they had wandered from straight paths. Even today we say, “It passed us by,” when our understanding has wandered from some truth. For sinners “passed over into the disposition of the heart,” that is, they went astray, when, by a most terrible fate, rational human beings served senseless idols.

### Verse 8

“They thought and spoke wickedness; they spoke iniquity against the Most High.” It is a double evil to think wickedness and then openly present it as something good. For the person who ought to repent of having conceived a crime doubles his guilt by publicizing his imagined offenses. What is most especially wicked to have conceived is sacrilege to have spoken.

He continues: “They spoke iniquity against the Most High.” This is what the treacherous mind was bringing forth: blasphemous words against its own creator, so that insulting speech might provoke to anger the one whom no one is sufficiently worthy to praise.

### Verse 9

“They set their mouth in heaven [ed., ‘toward heaven’], and their tongue passed over the earth.” He sets his mouth in heaven who thinks that Jupiter, Mercury, and the other monstrosities are gods comparable to God. He also sets his mouth in heaven who, having transgressed human limits through tyrannical will, thinks that none of his evils will have an avenger; but, enslaved by proud iniquity, believes that God does not know what he delays avenging in due time.

He continues: “and their tongue passed over the earth.” They pass over the earth, certainly, who speak beyond the measure of humanity; and although they themselves are fragile through weakness, they consider themselves to possess immortal dignities.

### Verse 10

“Therefore my people will return here, and full days will be found among them.” After describing the license and practices of the worst people, he now comes to the second part and says that the people will therefore return to the way of truth, because they must be filled by the Lord’s illumination.

But since we say that those who have left their ancestral places are “returned,” it is appropriate here to understand those peoples who once remained in the law received from the Lord, but were scattered through various worldly desires and, corrected once again, returned to the Lord’s commandments. Therefore Asaph says that this people has returned to him, having returned, by the Lord’s favor, to the knowledge of truth.

He continues: “and full days will be found in them.” The days are full when Christ the Lord deigned to come in the fullness of time that the prophets foretold, as the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Galatians 4:4). Thus the full days found the Jewish people emptied by their unbelief when some among them, with unveiled heart, were granted to behold Christ the Lord.

### Verse 11

“And they said: ‘How did God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?’” He now clearly explains from what thought those whom he previously mentioned as having returned proceeded, so that the Lord’s mercy might be declared: he makes the blasphemous righteous and turns the foolish of the people into wise and devoted persons.

They doubted that God knew that the most wicked had committed so many crimes, since they saw everything prospering for them in the world. They did not know that those who had been awaited so long and had been proved to remain in their obstinacy were incurring heavier punishments, as the ninety-third psalm also says of such people: “And they said, ‘The Lord does not see, nor does the God of Jacob understand’” (Psalm 93:7).

He continues: “And is there knowledge in the Most High?” This is a blasphemous thought, conceived in a foolish will: to doubt that there is knowledge in the one who bestows wisdom upon human understanding, and who enriches the angels themselves and the powers of heaven with the light of his providence. For he is called *scitus*—“knowing”—as though from *scire citius*, “to know swiftly.” Hence the psalm mentioned above says: “He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not observe? He who chastises the nations, will he not rebuke?” (ibid., 9).

### Verse 12

“Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in the world, they have acquired riches.” What wearied the hearts of the foolish has been exposed: their reasoning is without reason, their deliberation without counsel, their thought without understanding. They therefore did not think that God knew what was happening because sinners possessed riches—as though he had promised such things to the just and faithful, rather than having willed those to be poor in the world to whom he promised the kingdoms of heaven.

### Verse 13

“And I said: ‘Then in vain have I justified my heart, and washed my hands among the innocent?’” Asaph confesses that he too was deceived by foolish thoughts, just as he said above: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out,” so that, by confessing that he rejected such thoughts, he may prevent perverse thoughts from entering our minds at all.

Therefore the statement should be pronounced as a rebuke: “Then in vain have I justified my heart?”—as though someone might think that he had been deceived by an empty hope if he did not perceive in this world that the fruit of righteousness had been granted to him.

For *causa* (“cause”) is derived from *casus* (“chance”), because it is often good and often bad. This kind of cause is called “ambiguous” by orators, since it especially arises in deliberations, when the mind is uncertain what course to follow.

He added: “and washed my hands among the innocent.” He continues to explain what he began. It is as though he were saying: “What benefit was it to me to conduct myself in a commendable manner, if those who do not abandon their vices possess riches?” He washes his hands among the innocent who performs pious works according to a praiseworthy discipline. For Pilate did not wash his hands among the innocent when he handed the scourged Lord over to be fastened to the cross.

### Verse 14

“And I was scourged all day, and my guide [mss. G. and F., ‘my chastisement’] came in the morning.” He seems still to be recalling his punishments, which he thought he was enduring without purpose, so that this scourged man was poor while the wicked securely possessed their riches. It is a very bad judgment, but one close to correction, as happens with the sick, who are freed from a prolonged illness only when, at the end of their disease, a more abundant flame of fever has attacked them.

He continues: “and my guide came in the morning.” Behold, he has already returned to the moderation of health, he who was burning with diseased fevers. He calls the Lord Christ his “guide,” because through evangelical preaching he showed us the way of truth; and, rising in the morning and taking away our hope from this world, he extended it toward the kingdom of heaven.

### Verse 15

“If I said, ‘I will speak thus’: behold, the generation of your children, for which I made provision.” Now warned by the truth that was near, he deliberates with himself; having been brought to so great a matter, he wavers amid many thoughts.

For he was saying: If I were to announce to the people that God does not care for mortal affairs, his earlier preaching would confront him—what he had previously proclaimed to the Israelites: that they should worship God, creator of heaven and earth, who arranges all things through his wisdom and repays good and evil according to the quality of their deeds. How, then, could he speak otherwise, when he seemed previously to have taught such things?

### Verse 16

“I considered how I might understand this; it was labor before me.” The first step of knowledge comes when we begin to understand that we do not know at all what we had previously thought we knew. He had first persuaded himself that God did not care for mortal affairs because he saw sinners possessing riches. Now, however, he considers that the matter must be investigated so that he may deserve to recognize the truth.

It is therefore clear that his former opinion has been rejected, since another is being sought for recognition. He continues: “it was labor before me.” Truly, for one who was burning with uncertainty, it was laborious to understand so great a matter in the clear light of truth, so that he might despise the prosperity of sinners and praise the Lord’s patience through contemplation of the truth itself.

The words “before me” show the strength of the difficulty. For who could break through this mass of ignorance except through the grace of divinity? As it is also read in another psalm: “And in my God I shall leap over a wall” (Psalm 17:30).

### Verse 17

“Until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny [ed., ‘in their final destinies’].” Asaph eventually perceived what he had been hastening to understand. He repeats that he could not recognize the truth of the question stated above in any other way than by contemplating the divine law, which is the sanctuary of God, and understanding the final destiny of sinners: human happiness, which is shown to flourish here for a time, will be condemned in the future judgment.

By this remedy all hesitation was removed, for a pious mind ought not to be offended when it realizes that it is being instructed more deeply through such matters. This kind of speech is called deliberative, when the alternatives that make us uncertain are set forth and a judgment is chosen that accords both with usefulness and with propriety.

He stated what was disturbing his scruple: “If I said, ‘I will speak thus.’” That shameful inconsistency naturally confronted him: “Behold, the generation of your children, for which I made provision.” Finally, the judgment that would preserve everything is chosen: “This was labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny.”

Thus the deliberative genre is completed according to its parts and its regular arrangement. It should certainly be known that all arguments proceed from topics; but when they are stated generally, they belong to dialecticians, whereas when they are expressed individually and specifically, there is no doubt that they belong to orators.

### Verse 18

“Nevertheless, because of their treacheries you set evils before them; you cast them down while they were being lifted up.” Asaph has come to the third section, where he recalls the punishments of sinners, which he had previously said would be inflicted upon them severely in the future.

And lest the wicked be thought entirely exempt from evil in this world, or their crimes be believed in every respect to go unpunished, he says: “You set evils before them.” Although they enjoy worldly prosperity, they bear guilt within themselves, and guilt cannot wholly abandon criminals. Such people also frequently suffer here reversals that they had not even suspected.

He continues: “you cast them down while they were being lifted up.” By saying “you cast them down,” he indicated that they were struck down from on high. To make this clear, he added “while they were being lifted up,” that is, while they were climbing into the buskin of pride by a height that leads to ruin. Consider that he signifies the very time of their elevation as the time of their fall. He did not say, “after they had been lifted up,” but “while they were being lifted up”: their being raised is their falling, and their being lifted is their sinking, because they are striving toward that summit which collapses through sudden downfall. As it is also said in another psalm: “I saw the wicked exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Psalm 36:35), and so forth.

### Verse 19

“How they have become desolate! Suddenly they have failed; they have perished because of their iniquity.” The expression is one of astonishment: how has someone who possessed such great prosperity suddenly appeared desolate? He is desolate, certainly, having been abandoned by those things that surrounded him like a numerous family. There is no doubt that this can happen to the wicked when they incur the debt of dreaded death.

He continues: “Suddenly they have failed.” He also explains how they reached desolation, those whose earlier prosperity had amazed us. By saying “suddenly they have failed,” he signifies the arrival of sudden death. And lest you think that they died an ordinary death, he added: “they have perished because of their iniquity,” because the wicked fail in this world in such a way that they nevertheless die again through everlasting ruin in that condemnation.

### Verse 20

“Like the dream of one who rises, Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.” A beautiful comparison. He says that the happiness of the wicked is like the dream of those who awaken. Deluded by certain illusions, we often dream that we attain those things we pursue with excessive desire. A poor man suddenly becomes rich; a criminal is found to be honored; another enjoys the marriage he desired; someone else obtains the power he longed for. Yet, when all these things are suddenly abandoned, with open eyes we do not look back upon what we saw with closed eyes.

Behold, that wondrous happiness of the wicked has become a dream. The dead cannot possess riches any more than those who have awakened retain their joys. In this clause, however, a complete punctuation must be placed, since it depends upon what precedes.

He continues: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.” Here he says how, in that heavenly Jerusalem, the wicked cannot appear before the divine presence. Just as they defiled the Lord’s image within themselves in this world, so in that future homeland their likeness will not be seen, since they are to be sent into the separation of Gehenna.

Their image will therefore perish when the very truth, having withdrawn itself from them, deprives them of its presence. Nor can they retain the likeness from whose blessedness they will possess nothing. For an image is the formed likeness of some existing thing.

### Verse 21

“For my heart was delighted, and my kidneys were dissolved.” Above he prophesied that the wicked would be removed from the Lord’s kingdom. Now he gives the reason: it had been through them that his heart had come to envy worldly prosperity with a harmful delight. Hence it is evident that this is an extremely serious sin, when someone provides the occasion by which another person’s conscience is polluted.
