Nor is that a small matter which, with the Lord’s help, provides the good with an example.

He added: “and my kidneys were dissolved.” We have often said that the kidneys signify constancy of mind. For just as the kidneys contain the body, so they guard the stability of the soul. He therefore said that his kidneys had been dissolved because he had sought the prosperity of worldly things with an incautious will.

### Verse 22

“And I was reduced to nothing, and I did not know; I became like a beast before you.” He had rightly been reduced to nothing, since he clung to such desires that, by envying sinners, he seemed to wrong his creator. For the person recognized as emptied of the fruit of true understanding reaches nothingness.

He also says that he did not know this. It is profound ignorance not to know that one is sinning. Hence it is said in another psalm: “Who understands his transgressions?” (Psalm 18:13).

He continues: “I became like a beast before you.” He rightly calls himself a beast, since carnal rivalry possessed him like an irrational animal. Before God, those who resist his commandments and wish to think something other than what is contained in the sacred rules take the place of cattle, as it is said in another psalm: “Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9).

### Verse 23

“And I am always with you; you have held my right hand.” When he says, “And I am always with you,” he shows that, in a pure mind, he believed in the Lord his creator, having turned away from idols. But he was mistaken in this respect: he did not know how to discern the Lord’s judgments concerning the prosperity of sinners.

Therefore a complete punctuation must be placed here, since the sentence is complete. He continues: “you have held my right hand.” He said, “you have held my hand”; and lest you think he meant the left hand—for that part of the body also has a hand—he added, “my right hand.” Whoever’s right hand is held by the Lord is always absolved and delivered. Thus, when Peter was sinking, the Lord held his right hand and made him secure in the fluid element, fixing his foot firmly.

### Verse 24

“In your will you have led me, and with glory you have taken me up.” Here too the Lord’s grace is signified, by which he redeemed sinners. He did not say, “By my merits,” but “In your will you have led me,” namely, to the most salutary understanding, to which, after his deadly thoughts, he returned, as from a tomb, with the Lord giving him life.

He continues: “and with glory you have taken me up.” Here he announces the future incarnation of the Lord, in which, through his mercy, he deigned to assume humanity. For what is more wondrous than that mortal nature should, through the incarnation of the Word, be placed at the right hand of the Father and judge the living and the dead—the nature that, after the first man’s sin, had been subject to diabolical temptations?

Hence John, bishop of Constantinople, says most aptly and explicitly (*Homily on the Ascension*): “Let us recognize what nature it is to which he said, ‘Be a participant in my throne’: that nature which heard, ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall return’” (Genesis 3:19).

### Verse 25

“For what remains for me in heaven, and what did I desire from you upon earth?” After saying how he had been freed from his perverse understanding by the Lord’s will, he comes to the fourth stage, where he now enumerates the good things of that mercy by which he was delivered.

When he says, “What remains for me in heaven?” we must understand, “What more shall I ask for?”—that is, what more than what you are going to give the world? Namely, the benefit of your holy incarnation: that God-man, one Christ from and in two distinct and perfect natures, might appear and, through the grace of redemption, absolve those condemned by the law of sin.

He speaks the next words as a rebuke of himself: “and what did I desire from you upon earth?”—as though he were saying: “Ignorant as I was of the truth, what things on earth was I hoping for, that I should desire to share in the goods of sinners, when you were preparing benefits destined to endure forever?”

These, rather, are the riches that we ought to desire for our salvation; this is the happiness in which a Christian should rejoice to be rich: to be poor in this world and rich in heaven.

### Verse 26

“My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion forever.” It is called “failure” because the effect is lacking in it. And rightly carnal thought had failed, since it recognized that it had gone astray. But he confesses this to the one to whom revealing guilt is a remedy: to confess transgressions is security.

Notice also that in a single verse “heart” is used both in a good and in a bad sense. “My heart has failed” signifies evil thought; “God of my heart” signifies good understanding, since he beneficially realized that he had gone astray.

It should also be noted that divine Scripture frequently says that counsels proceed from this bodily part, as it is written: “From the heart of man proceed evil thoughts” (Matthew 15:19). Although some say that the seat of wisdom is in the brain, we should rather believe the one who speaks of our heart, since he formed our hearts.

He continues: “and God is my portion forever.” God is the portion of the person who joins himself to his majesty through faith and commends himself through honorable action. By adding “forever,” he promises that he will always cling to him. This truly belongs to the perfect: never to wish to depart from him without whom one continually goes astray.

### Verse 27

“For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed all who fornicate away from you.” He remembers those of whom he said above: “Suddenly they have failed; they have perished because of their iniquity.” They distanced themselves from him by serving idols and showing no reverence to the true God.

This man, who believed in God, had withdrawn for a short time so that he might return, when, as has often been said, he had contracted perverse thoughts from the prosperity of sinners.

He continues: “you have destroyed all who fornicate away from you.” To fornicate away from the Lord means to deviate from his chaste love through adulterous thoughts and, preferring the luxury of the world, to reject the discipline of heavenly commandments. It is clear that those who pursue the worship of idols and the empty superstitions of impiety do this; and, finally, whatever is believed contrary to the catholic faith fornicates through polluted senses.

### Verse 28

“But for me, it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in God, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.” Behold, the meaning we stated has been made clear: although he polluted himself with a perverse thought, he nevertheless did not withdraw from the worship of the Lord.

For he says that it is good for him to cling to the Lord. The person clings to divinity who joins himself to it through true faith and upright conduct. Just as he says that the wicked have distanced themselves, so he professes that he clings to the Lord, so that by doing the opposite of them he may find a different recompense.

He continues: “to place my hope in God.” He explains the word he used above. The person clings to God who places his hope in the Lord, because nothing can be more blessed than to entrust everything to him who knows how to provide what is fittingly beneficial to his worshipers.

He added: “so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion.” As we have often said, Zion is the mountain situated in Jerusalem, which in our language is interpreted as “watchtower” or “vision.” Its daughter, therefore, is clearly the catholic Church, where the person who believes with a pure mind truly offers praises to the Lord.

By “the gates,” he prefers us to understand the very entrance into Christianity, when the people of the new birth are brought to receive the true faith.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

How wondrously this Asaph, whose name signifies “Synagogue,” both rejected former errors and embraced the good things of future faith! He deliberated wisely and chose excellently, so that, not undeservedly, after the saving promise of the Lord’s coming in the preceding psalm, the number of the seventy-second psalm seems to have suited him: weighing both sides of his thoughts as though on a just balance, he considered the whole with even moderation.

Through these admonitions the instruction of the Christian has been completed, so that the person who hastens to commend himself to the Lord may not sin even in his thoughts.

Grant, Lord, that you do not make us envy those whom you condemn by your truth, but that we may detest those whom you abhor and certainly love those whom you love; for they cannot have a portion with you except those who follow your will with the most devoted mind.

# Exposition of Psalm 73

## The Understanding of Asaph

“Understanding” signifies divine inspection, which this psalm beholds in every way with devoted zeal. Asaph, as has often already been said, is interpreted as “Congregation,” which is now called the Church.

This congregation laments the future disasters of the city of Jerusalem with pitiable mourning. What remarkable devotion and astonishing clemency: to make an impending evil present to oneself through lamentation, and to grieve over things to come as though they had already been suffered! You will find this kind of speech, full of charity and pierced by love of one’s neighbor, sung in this psalm, in the seventy-eighth, and in the one hundred thirty-sixth.

We should know the difference between penitents and mourners, since sorrowful tears are common to both. Penitents pray for their own sins or for the transgressions of the community, asking the Lord to forgive their offenses and not punish their errors when he judges. Mourners, however, out of regard for compassion, lament the ruins of a city and the destruction of their fellow citizens, which they have either already suffered or are certainly going to suffer. Hence the Apostle, persuading us to love our neighbor, says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).

Let us now consider the order and arrangement of the psalms themselves. The seventy-first psalm promised that the Lord’s incarnation would come. In the seventy-second, after setting aside his errors, Asaph chose what should be followed. In the present psalm, the overthrow of the city is lamented, so that the hardest heart of the Jews might be terrified by the calamities of its own city.

The good physician did everything, if only the sick person had wished to recover his health. Let us remember that ecclesiastical authority teaches that Jerusalem was devastated in those days when the most savage Jewish people crucified Christ the Lord, so that there can be no doubt that it received the evil of that time as punishment for its presumptuous transgression.

Now let us proceed to what follows.

## Division of the Psalm

The people of Israel, who contain the figure of the most devoted Synagogue, speak throughout the psalm.

In the first section, they lament why they were handed over to the nations, so that the audacity of their enemies profaned the Lord’s sanctuary. They recall that the impenitent heart of certain Jews provoked the Lord’s judgment, though he prophesies that these people will nevertheless be converted at the end of the age.

The second section says that, at Christ’s coming, the superstitions and iniquities of human beings were destroyed. It enumerates the various mighty deeds he performed and, among them, asks that he come to the aid of the erring Jews.

In the third section, it asks that, mindful of his promises, he rescue the seed of Abraham from destruction and that the pride of the Romans, who exalted themselves savagely [ms. A., F., “vainly”], may ascend to him.

Let us listen to this psalm with attentive minds, for it is a remarkable lament over the destruction of Jerusalem.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Why, O God, have you rejected us forever? Has your fury been angry against the sheep of your flock?” The Jewish people are introduced as supplicating God to turn away from the Israelites the destruction that threatened them.

“Why?” expresses a question, not an accusation. Terrified, he rightly asked why the Lord’s sanctuary was destined to suffer such unspeakable devastation, fearing that, since the temple’s destruction had been permitted, the Jewish people too might perish utterly. For who is now believed capable of being preserved when reverence is not shown to holy places?

“You have rejected” means “you have cast away,” as though you had made them strangers to your protection. “Forever” here signifies the destruction and captivity that Jerusalem is said to have suffered from the Romans in the time of the emperors Vespasian and Titus.

He continues: “Has your fury been angry against the sheep of your flock?” He calls the Jewish people “sheep,” so that the name of the flock might move the compassion of the merciful Shepherd. He added “your,” because we always take vengeance more moderately upon those whom we remember once to have been ours.

### Verse 2

“Remember your congregation, which you created from the beginning; you redeemed the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion, in which you dwelt.” Observe carefully the many ways in which he seeks the goodwill of the Judge; here you may see the origins of the arguments of orators.

The gifts bestowed are enumerated so that the mind of the good Judge may be invited to his customary benefits. Therefore he asks that the Lord prefer to consider his own benefits toward them rather than their errors.

The congregation of the Jews clearly prevailed through his assistance, when he caused them to grow under the Egyptian people and, when he pleased, deigned to free them through remarkable miracles. For although he creates and orders all things, he is said to have created the Jews in a special manner, since he gave them the law, granted them prophets, and bestowed great miracles upon them.

“From the beginning” refers to the faith and worship that were established and that the Hebrew people received through Moses.

He continues: “you redeemed the rod of your inheritance.” The Jewish people were the Lord’s inheritance as long as they served him with a pure heart. He called this inheritance a “rod” because of Moses, his servant, who was commanded to perform mighty deeds with a rod, so that, strengthened by divine power, they might leave the land of Egypt without fear.

By this rod the hardness of Pharaoh was shaken; by it the waters of the Red Sea were divided; through it rivers flowed from dry stone. And rightly this inheritance was called a rod, since it was powerful enough to accomplish such miracles. It is recalled here so that through it the magnitude of what he had bestowed might be shown.

He also added a notable culmination of perfection: “Mount Zion, in which you dwelt.” The miracles that came before reached their fulfillment in the gifts of this mountain. There is no doubt that everything in the Old Testament was done for this purpose: that the promised truth of the New Testament might follow.

For when he says, “Mount Zion, in which you dwelt,” he certainly signifies the city of Jerusalem, in which the Israelite people dwelt, and where he declares that the bodily presence of Christ the Lord had dwelt, so that he would not allow those places to suffer the most terrible devastation in which he had deigned to appear to human eyes.

It was a land plainly shining with miracles, made venerable by the Lord’s visitation, where carnal eyes were permitted to see what is the highest blessedness even to believe. This argument is called an argument from praise of the injured object, so that the envy of the enemies might increase all the more because the holy places were to be devastated through their presumption.

### Verse 3

“Lift your hand upon their pride, to the end; how greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in your holy places!” These words are not spoken by one who is angry, but by one seeking rather a remedy through correction. The Israelite’s petition truly prevailed.

For where did the worship of the Christian religion flourish more greatly than in the city of Rome, which had previously claimed superstitions for itself above all other lands? The Lord’s power was therefore lifted up among them when he changed their pride through the grace of humility, leading them “to the end,” that is, to the Lord the Savior.

For how many unspeakable signs of temples were there in that place! How many gifts of heavenly Churches and blessed martyrs shone forth! When both are seen, the power of Christ the Lord is truly understood: from such a superstitious people he produced a most holy city.

He continues: “how greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in your holy places!” “The enemy” signifies the Roman people, who at that time, as has been said, were regarded as distinguished worshipers of idols. He acted wickedly in the Lord’s holy places when the priests and all the temple’s ministries were exposed to plunder, and the entire Hebrew people either fell beneath the sword or served under the yoke of captivity. The history of Josephus, celebrated in seven books, describes this exceedingly fierce war.

### Verse 4

“And those who hated you exulted in the midst of your court; they set up their standards as standards, and they did not understand.”

From this point, through contempt for the most sacred temple, greater resentment rises against those who dared to presume such things, so that he seems in a certain sense to have despised Divinity itself, when he is accused of violating sacred religion. But since every crime ought to be followed by repentance, the words “they exulted” have been placed here, so that they might seem not only to have sinned, but also to have turned the very evil into their glory. He added “those who hated you,” so that what is known to have been perpetrated by enemies should not be endured patiently.

It follows: “in the midst of your court.” This serves to express the magnitude of the contempt: they are said to have committed sacrilege not in some remote place, but in the middle of the court. As for what he added, “they set up their standards as standards, and they did not understand,” this may refer to the eagles, dragons, and other devices customarily used by the Roman army in battle; or certainly to statues, monuments of victory, which generals erected above the arches of gates in praise of themselves.

What follows is also said with grief: “standards,” so that the repetition itself might move the just Judge to swift vengeance. This figure is called *epembasis*, whenever the same words are repeated from a neighboring expression in order to produce amplification, showing that what had been permitted by divine dispensation had been carried out by human strength.

For you to understand that this meaning is intended, he adds: “and they did not understand.” If they had understood, they would certainly have offered sacrifices to you; they would not have chosen to return to the worship of demons. This captivity or ruin occurred many years later, and is known to have been prophesied. For when these things were being said, the temple at Jerusalem had not yet been established—indeed, it is read that it was built by Solomon, his son. Thus the great power of heavenly prophecy truly appeared: its destruction was foretold before its construction could have taken place.

### Verse 5

“As upon a road, at the summit: as in a forest of trees, with axes they cut down its gates together; with a double axe and an axe they overthrew it.”

The more fully the contempt of the enemies is expressed, the more urgently a swift vengeance is demanded. In these two verses the mind of the grieving speaker is shown with great force. He says that they set up their standards in your temple just as statues of rulers are customarily placed in elevated locations in public squares, so that the memory of passers-by may be instructed by the sight of such things.

For what could be more detestable than that they dared to do this in the inner sanctuaries of the temple, which sacrilegious men presume to do in public squares?

There follows another pitiable complaint by way of comparison: he says that those doors of the most revered temple were shattered with axes just as forests offer license to woodcutters, where no guardian and no opposing force is found. The ancients, moreover, wished doors to be called *januæ* from Janus, because, as they thought, through him an entrance into the year was provided.

He also added “together,” that is, in the temple itself, so that the nature of the deed might be felt as all the more grievous because of the reverence due to the place.

It follows: “with a double axe and an axe they overthrew it.” A double axe is an iron implement fashioned with a blade on both sides, suitably adapted for cutting beams. It was called *bipennis* because it is sharpened twice. The ancients called a sharp thing *pinnum*. An axe is iron curved in the manner of a hooked nose, by which the craftsman’s hand more carefully follows what has been determined should be cut away into smaller pieces.

Thus, to show that that city had been utterly devastated, he says through these instruments of the smith that both great and very small things were overthrown together. Whatever the double axe could cut down or the axe pursue, the savage hand cast down.

At this point, to express the prophet’s grief, that saying of Jeremiah should be inserted:

> “See whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which has come upon me. The Lord has delivered me into hands, and I cannot stand” (*Lamentations* I, 12, 14).

### Verse 6

“They burned your sanctuary with fire; on the ground they polluted the tabernacle of your name.”

The grief increases when the calamity of the overthrow grows greater. The double axe and the axe could cut down the wood alone, but in the end fire happened to devour everything together. But what, I ask, could have happened to private houses, when hostile fury spared neither the Lord’s sanctuary?

As for the wording “they burned it with fire,” in secular literature this figure is called *pleonasm*, where something superfluous may also be added. In the divine Scriptures, however, as it seems to me, this figure does not properly apply, since everything is useful, everything necessary, and everything complete. Rather, we should understand that it is expressed in this manner of speech just as we commonly say, “I heard with my ears” and “I saw with my eyes,” although no one can see with another’s eyes or hear with another’s ears.

It follows: “on the ground they polluted the tabernacle of your name.” The tabernacle of his name was the temple that Solomon constructed with marvelous workmanship. At its dedication, while praying, he said: “But I have built a house for his name” (III Kings VIII, 21), and so forth.

Thus this tabernacle, which heavenly power visited, was polluted by the hand of the devastator, and he brought down to the ground its summits, which had been built for the praise of the Lord.

And note that in these four verses that most celebrated figure, *auxesis*, which in Latin is called “increase,” is employed. The atrocity of the deed continually grows, so that the all-powerful Judge must confront those who have exceeded all bounds with such monstrous wickedness. This figure is very usefully and appropriately employed both in praise and in blame, as the Apostle did when he said: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience probation, probation hope, and hope does not put to shame” (Romans V, 3–5), and so forth.

### Verse 7

“They said in their heart, their kindred among themselves: ‘Come, let us suppress all the solemnities of the Lord from the earth.’”

The evils listed above might have moved the Lord’s mercy, had obstinate pride not still remained in the Jews. For although they had suffered such things, their minds did not withdraw from their blasphemies. “They said in their heart.” And lest they seem to have been few, he added, “their kindred among themselves,” so that calamity was rightly not suspended from an impenitent heart.

It follows: “Come, let us suppress all the solemnities of the Lord from the earth.” Here the words of the enraged Jews are reported. When they saw their city overturned and God’s sanctuaries profaned, they foolishly and furiously said: “Let us cast away the law of the Lord, who has disdained to avenge us.” They did not consider that those who dared to crucify the Lord Christ could have deserved punishments far more severe.

Asaph could not have said such things in his own person, since the meaning conveyed by the preceding title adorned him.

### Verse 8

“We have not seen our signs [ed., *we do not see*]; there is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us.”

Most foolish of men were those who thought that, after their guilt, signs such as they had seemed worthy to receive before so monstrous a crime could still be granted to them. It surely came to their minds how many nations their fathers had struck down with the Lord’s help, and how many kingdoms they had subdued in a momentary conflict; yet, established in the greatest guilt, they said that the signs they knew had been granted to their devout fathers had themselves been taken away.

It follows: “There is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us.” These too are the words of the despairing Jews. For whenever the Israelites in ancient times were oppressed by some calamity, they went to the prophets and were instructed by them, at the Lord’s command, what they ought to do; yet their hardness of heart scorned obedience to them.

But when, after the Lord’s coming had been fulfilled, they no longer had such prophets, they said that they had been abandoned by the Lord, because they did not see those through whom they had been accustomed to receive admonition. Of such people it is written: “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Proverbs XVIII, 3).

All these things could have been said only by the Jewish people, because they were contrary to the Romans, who at that time served detestable idols. Truly, Asaph, understanding and distinguished in holiness, poured out a wondrous supplication for the Jews. But lest the Divine compassion be thought lacking because he is not shown to have been heard on their behalf, he added the Jews’ sins and despair, so that they might justly receive due punishments, since amid so many crimes there was no appropriate repentance.

### Verse 9

“How long, O God, will the enemy reproach you? Will the adversary provoke your name to the end?”

He cries out like one seeking a helper; he groans like a wounded man seeking a physician, saying to the Lord: “How long will you endure these reproaches that the unbelieving Jew directs against you?” He does not say this in order to destroy those whom he judged worthy of being mourned, but so that through the benefit of confession he might change them for the better.

It follows: “Will the adversary provoke your name forever?” This explains what he said above. The Lord endures the murmuring of the faithless until, in his mercy, he brings his adversaries to confess his name. For he is powerful enough to correct those who disparage him, so that those who previously spoke mortally may afterward be heard preaching salutarily.

The word “provoke” (*irritat*) is derived from dogs, whose barking gives especially strong expression to the letter *r*. “Forever” signifies the evening of the world, when the Jewish people will believe for the most part.

### Verse 10

“Why do you turn your face away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever?”

He speaks as though the Lord were offended and angry, unwilling to look upon sinful peoples, who thus appear still to persist in their wickedness. For those whom he regards in his wondrous dispensation, once appeased, he corrects; those upon whom he looks favorably, he reforms.

It follows: “and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever.” Another mystery of the Old Testament is touched upon here. For just as Moses had been given power to perform miracles with a staff (Exodus IV, 6–7), so he was commanded to put his right hand into his bosom; when he drew it out, it was seen to be leprous. He was then ordered to put his hand again into his bosom, and immediately it was healed.

This signifies that the Jewish people, departing from the Lord Christ, would become unclean, but that, turning back to him, they would recover their former health. This event is recalled in order to foretell that the Jewish people would return to their former health.

This argument is called one from the event, when the supplication tends toward that which it knows will be reached through the sequence of events. But lest he linger too long in such an account, he hastens to the praises of the Lord, declaring that all things are possible for him who is known to perform such mighty works.

### Verse 11

“But God is our King before the ages; he has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.”

That meaning of Asaph announced by the title has arrived at a second section. By the prophetic spirit he foretells that the Lord and Savior will come, enumerating, through the demonstrative mode of discourse, how many miracles he performed in heaven and on earth.

Since he was about to speak of his incarnation, lest anyone believe him to be a temporal Lord, he testifies that he was already King before the foundation of the world, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “For this I was born” (John XVIII, 37). The ages are so called because they turn times within themselves.

It follows: “He has worked salvation in the midst of the earth.” Although this may also be understood of the miracles he performed, which he is known to have worked visibly before human beings, let us better understand it of the salvation of souls, which he worked through life-giving preaching.

“In the midst of the earth”—that is, before all the peoples who are understood through the name “earth.” This figure is called *metonymy*, when what contains is used to signify what is contained.

### Verse 12

“You established the sea by your strength; you crushed the heads of dragons upon the waters.”

To show truly what he said above—that the Lord and Savior was King before the ages, and that he deigned to suffer for us so that by dying he might destroy death, grant freedom to captives, and bestow rewards upon the guilty—he recalls the miracles he once performed among the Jewish people.

For he established the fluid abysses of the Red Sea when the water was fixed on the two sides, so that the navigable sea became a land route.

It follows: “You crushed the heads of dragons upon the waters.” He fittingly explains the mystery of the earlier miracle, because that prefiguration of the crossing of the Red Sea indicated the waters of holy baptism. There the heads of dragons—that is, of unclean spirits—are brought to nothing, when the saving fountain cleanses the souls that they pollute with the filth of sins.

And note that in this and the four following verses he gathers individual praises through the figure of *synathroesmos*, an accumulation, so that the enumeration itself might temper the spirit of the offended and most powerful Judge.

### Verse 13

“You crushed the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the people of the Ethiopians.”

Although above he said “the heads of dragons” in the plural, wishing to signify spiritual wickednesses, he now places “dragon” in the singular, so that he appears to indicate Satan himself, who is as much more powerful as he is more wicked. When he is named in the singular, he is entirely denied to have an equal place among the wicked spirits.

His head was crushed when his pride was cast down from heaven. He did not deserve to retain his original brightness, since he stained himself with voluntary darkness.

He added: “You gave him as food to the people of the Ethiopians.” We properly understand the Ethiopians as sinners, who had previously been most dreadful in their darkened minds; but after turning to the Lord, they began to have the devil as food, since they are satisfied by vilifying him.

Even today, when we wish to indicate someone as utterly wicked, we call him a devil. For he is reviled for all the sins that have been committed and is called the author of every error; and just as he persecutes Christians, so he is torn apart by all with detestable horror.

Thus it comes about that he who was formerly revered by pagans is now gnawed by Christians with the bites of reproach.

Alternatively, the converted faithful may have the devil as food when they advance through his contrivances and temptations. For through his persecution they become martyrs; through his affliction they are crowned with the reward of patience. Therefore the devil is rightly called the food of those whom, through repeated hardships, he brings to their desired hopes.

### Verse 14

“You split open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan.”

He says all this allegorically about sinners. He calls them “springs” whose evils flowed continuously; “torrents” are those who, suddenly stirred up, rushed in rapid courses. The Lord will split apart these two kinds of sinners when he separates them from the service of the devil.

It follows: “You dried up the rivers of Ethan.” He develops the preceding meaning, so that he not only splits apart and divides the rivers—that is, the floods gathered by diabolical wickedness—but also dries them up and removes them. For when a river is dried up, it is without doubt brought to nothing.

This is clearly what happens when, by forgiving the multitude of sins, it is established that the devil’s swelling plans have perished. *Ethan* means “strong” in the Hebrew language, a term we have already said often signifies the devil.

### Verse 15

“The day is yours, and the night is yours; you made the sun and the moon.”

This verse and the next are clear to everyone in their literal sense. The Lord is indeed the creator of all things; but they appear more fitting if they are sought spiritually.

Let us call “day” righteous men, upon whom the light of wisdom always shines; and “night,” earthly people, who are darkened by the things they do through sins, as it is said in another psalm: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night announces knowledge to night” (Psalm XVIII, 3).

But when he says, “The day is yours and the night is yours,” he signifies that God performs great miracles in both: he illuminates the one through the gift of his mercy, and, when the other has been corrected from sins, he makes him a participant in his kingdom.

He added: “You made the sun and the moon.” All these names are explained more clearly through examples. The sun signifies the wise person, the moon the foolish person, as it is written: “The wise man remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus XXVII, 12).

It is a beautiful account, in which the wondrous greatness of the Almighty is declared through comparisons drawn from created things. In all things, however, we must understand that the Creator and Lord displays his customary and abundant mercy.

### Verse 16

“You made all the boundaries of the earth; you made summer and spring—you made them; remember this creature of yours.”

It is not inappropriate to call all the apostles and prophets “the boundaries of the earth.” For just as the boundaries of fields distinguish their limits [ed., “ropes”], so the preachers of Christ preserve the rights of true faith.

It follows: “You made summer and spring.” Through these seasons he signifies the faithful distinguished by different qualities of character. Some are like summer heat, fervent with the warmth of faith and carried even to martyrdom; others, tempered by gentleness like spring, serve the Lord with an even devotion.

He himself made all these things, and things like them, since by his grace that which is displayed in the good will of human beings is granted.

He added: “Remember this creature of yours.” He gives the reason why that enumeration was introduced: namely, so that he who is accustomed to perform great deeds might mercifully forgive the Jews also when they sin. And in order to arouse the benevolence of the good Lord, he frequently enumerates his benefits, so that he may deign to remember those whom he deigned to create.

### Verse 17

“The enemy reproached the Lord, and the foolish people provoked your name.”

He recalls those words that he said above: “Come, let us suppress all the feast days of the Lord from the earth,” and so forth.

This enemy was certainly the Jewish people, who spoke such things against the Lord that they seemed to reproach the one to whom no creature can sufficiently give thanks, even in part, for any benefit.

It follows: “And the foolish people provoked your name.” They were foolish indeed, since they acted unworthily by listening patiently to things they ought altogether to have rejected. And by this they provoked the Lord to anger, because they did not say that such things had happened to them on account of their sins; rather, they thought God unjust, as though he permitted destruction to rule over those who did not deserve it.

Let us therefore consider the most salutary order of the one who supplicates. He prays for the guilty in such a way that he always confesses their errors. If the Jews had done this with a devout mind, they could have avoided the punishments generally due to them.

### Verse 18

“Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you; do not forget forever the souls of your poor.”

Asaph has come to a third section. The meaning announced beforehand is appropriate to it: he confessed the people’s sins above in such a way that he nevertheless presumes that those devoted to the Lord will be delivered.

The holy man begs for what he knew was going to happen, namely, that he not hand over the souls of the faithful, lest the devil attain his desires. Even then there were vessels of mercy among that people, among whom were Simeon, Nicodemus, and Nathanael, of whom the Lord bears witness, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John I, 47), together with the others who pleased the Lord through purity of heart.

He called the devil and his ministers “beasts,” whose heads, as he said above, he crushed upon the waters.

It follows: “And do not forget forever the souls of your poor.” He speaks of those who, rejecting the pride of the world, have betaken themselves to the most holy humility. He asks that the benefits of the Lord and Savior not be denied them; rather, because they have become his poor, may they grow rich through his generosity.

### Verse 19

“Look upon your covenant, because the dark places of the earth are full of houses of iniquity.”

He says “look upon” so that you may deign to fulfill what you are known to have promised beforehand, as it is written: “Behold, the days will come, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I established with their fathers” (Jeremiah XXIII, 5).

In that earlier covenant there were temporal promises, such as the promised land and the subjection of enemies. Such things had to be granted to an unformed people, so that they might thereafter hasten fearlessly toward spiritual things.

But in the New Covenant are promised untroubled life, a kingdom without end, everlasting blessedness, and the glorious contemplation of the Lord.

In this covenant, therefore, he says that the Lord must look, so that he may quickly grant what will be beneficial to the erring people. Truly Asaph had become understanding, since he asks for things through which the whole world could have been absolved.

And observe with what wisdom he proceeds through everything: since there were no good deeds that he could recall concerning the delinquent people, he remembered the Lord’s promise, which is always fulfilled.

There follows another reason for showing mercy, which is called an absolute quality: “because those who have been darkened have been filled”—that is, sinners who have been submerged in the darkness of ignorance. He himself also pleaded for them while hanging on the cross, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

But let us repeat this verse, so that the connection of the words may appear more easily. He said: “Look upon, because those who have been darkened have been filled.” They had indeed been filled with iniquities, and it was necessary that darkness follow them who are rightly compared with darkness, since they had lost the light of wisdom.

He added: “the earth of houses of iniquities.” These are “the earth of houses of iniquities,” that is, earthly people from the house of iniquities. And lest you perhaps wish to understand “earth” in a good sense, it is beautifully defined what the body of unbelievers is: a house of iniquities, because those who are polluted by evil actions receive all vices as though in a kind of lodging.

### Verse 20

“Let the humble and disgraced person not be turned away; the poor and needy will praise your name.”

In the place of those who seemed likely to offend, he places those who are accustomed to possess the Lord’s grace, so that the love of the devoted might temper hatred of the obstinate. This is a very fitting argument, when a beloved person is placed in the position of someone detestable.

To be confounded does not belong to the humble, but to the proud person, who, not acknowledging God’s glory, attributes to human merits whatever good he has received through the Lord’s provision. In contrast, the humble continually praise God and always accuse themselves, understanding that whatever they know belongs to Divinity, while whatever they do wrong is properly their own.

He asks that these people not be confounded, since whatever good they have received they understand to be attributed to the Lord’s gifts.

It follows: “The poor and needy will praise your name.” Let us consider how glorious this poverty is, how blessed this neediness is, since it praises the Lord even in silence and celebrates him through the strength of its patience.

The proud person is mute even if he sings psalms; the poor and needy praise the Lord even when they appear to maintain silence. O immeasurable good, if it is weighed inwardly! The man who is poor for God is so called; the rich man of the world is so named. The former belongs to the eternal King, the latter, of course, to fleeting time. The one who is rich outwardly possesses nothing for himself; rather, the one should be called truly capable who is shown to have stored up outstanding virtues in the treasuries of his soul.

### Verse 21

“Arise, O Lord; judge your cause. Remember your reproaches, those spoken by the foolish all day long.”

After everything he has said, he now presents the Judge’s cause, so that he might move him more effectively by making the nature of his case known. Now he turns his words to the Lord himself, asking him to judge his cause against those who do not cease to resound with wicked murmuring.

He judges his own cause when he makes the erring understand clearly, so that, having been converted, they may proclaim what they had rejected in foolish thoughts.

It follows: “Remember your reproaches”—namely, those spoken above: “There is now no prophet, and he will no longer know us.”

He added: “those spoken by the foolish all day long.” This too depends upon what precedes, since these reproaches came from the foolish. And lest they be thought to have been poured out only for a time, he added “all day long,” so that the very continuity might indicate the gentleness of the most patient Judge.

### Verse 22

“Do not forget the voices of those who seek you; let the pride of those who hate you continually rise up to you” [ed., “rises up”].

In the first clause he again combines the prayers of the faithful, asking that he not reject the prayers of those who are known to cry out to him with their whole-hearted devotion, so that they may find the one whom they seek and may deserve to behold the one whom they desire [ms. G., ed., “certainly”].

It follows: “Let the pride of those who hate you continually rise up to you.” We appropriately understand this to have been said of the Romans, concerning whom he said above: “They set up their standards in the midst of your court,” so that he might move the all-powerful Judge most vehemently against the enemies of Jerusalem.

For pride is the vice that the Lord especially detests; through it the angel fell, and through it the blessedness of the first man departed.

And consider how prudently this most savage vice has been placed at the end, so that after everything else he might say what would be stored away in the final boundaries of memory. Thus those who are devoted to the Lord with a pure mind lament simply and prudently; thus, despite their excessive grief, those who obey pious rules do not know how to be deceived.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

You have learned, distinguished hearers, how pleasing are the duties of devotion to faithful men: how they do not wish their neighbors to endure sorrow, and therefore are afflicted with such tears over the disasters destined to come upon them.

This is truly the holy perfection of charity: to present to oneself the future dangers that are feared for one’s neighbors. What would this man have done over the calamity he saw [ms. A: “when”], which he is known to have mourned as future with such a stricken heart?

Let us therefore consider with what truth the Holy Scriptures agree with one another: how Asaph lamented Jerusalem while it was still flourishing, before Jeremiah, many years later, grieved over it after the captivity had taken place.

Both were devout, both glorious; but this one is recognized, I do not know by what greater measure, as more merciful, since while still established in prosperity he is known to have been struck by the bitterest grief.

Therefore we ought to consider that, with the text shining forth in varied patterns, the whole Psalter is adorned now with the jubilation of those rejoicing, now with the groaning of repentance, now with salutary instruction, now with the grief of those lamenting, now with the salutary incarnation foretold, now with the promise of rewards, now with the terror of punishments, and now with praises of the Lord.

Just as a crown woven from the sweetest flowers gives off a pleasing fragrance, so this book too is perceived to exhale the varied fragrances of virtues.

## 254. EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXXIV

### “For the end, do not corrupt; a psalm of song of Asaph.”

The words of this title are obscure unless they are considered in their proper order. Asaph, as we have often said, signifies the Synagogue—that is, the congregation that believed, not the one that remained obstinate.

For after the Lord’s resurrection, we read that many thousands of Jews confessed the faith, as the Acts of the Apostles testify among other passages. Therefore this Asaph now admonishes that people not corrupt their faith “in the end”—that is, in the Lord and Savior, who was worthy to receive their belief and found the fruit of salvation.

For as long as these gifts are not scattered, we remain unharmed; when they have been corrupted, we are made strangers to the sight of the King.

We have said that this is a “psalm of song” when we discern present realities through spiritual contemplation. You, diligent reader, will find all of this in the present psalm.

## Division of the Psalm

At the first entrance, the faithful Jews declare that they will confess all his wonders. In the second, the King himself, Jesus Christ, speaks, promising that he will judge with justice when the time of the general resurrection arrives. He also warns that no one should dare to presume anything against the divine commandments, lest eternal punishment be able to torment him.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“We will confess to you, O God; we will confess to you, and we will call upon your name; I will recount all your wonders.”

In this one verse the rule of holy devotion is set forth in order. That Jewish people which was going to believe in Christ the Lord, whom the title admonishes, “Do not corrupt in the end,” breaks into speech and most devoutly promises in its confession.

To confess is, as we have often said, to profess something through the confession of many [*confatione*, sic]. For even if one person is said to have confessed, he is understood to have been joined to others who preceded or followed him in the faith.

It follows again: “We will confess to you.” The repetition itself testifies to the firmness of the promise, which is never made in passing except where steadfastness of mind is indicated, as in the words: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Psalm LVI, 8), and similar passages.

“To you” is said so that the worship of others might be rejected, because true devotion is that which venerates only the author with complete justice.

And let us observe that confessing crimes even once to an earthly judge generally produces death, whereas frequent confession to God does not bring forth danger but salvation.

The order of the words proceeds beautifully. First he says that he will confess—that is, mourn his sins—then that he will call upon the Lord’s name. For it is fitting that, by his gift, we first cleanse our hearts through confession, and then call upon the Lord’s name in order to receive help.

For to whom could he come except to those whom he recognizes already as his own? But if an undevout person calls upon him, he seems to be asking for judgment, not pardon. Such things must therefore come first, so that we may confidently invoke divine mercy.

He added: “I will recount all your wonders.” Although above he said “we will confess” in the plural, here he says “I will recount” in the singular, because both ways belong to the people of God: to speak in the singular and to think as part of the plural.

But this account is introduced as the voice of the faithful, because no one deserves to recount divine greatness unless he recognizes that he serves God with pure devotion. Thus it is read in another psalm: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” (Psalm XLIX, 16), and so forth.

But who could recount all heavenly wonders except one who briefly professes the Holy Trinity to be the author of all things, and attributes to its indivisible will whatever is carried out in heaven and on earth through ineffable governance?

### Verse 2

“When I receive the time, I will judge justices.”

The change of person has shown us another section. From this it is understood how Asaph, in the first verse, grasped the rule of perfect religion, so that he might deserve to be heard so quickly.

For the Lord Christ is now speaking: “When I receive the time,” he says, referring to what he became as man, just as he says in the Gospel: “He gave him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John V, 27).

But hear what he says according to the nature of his divinity: “All things that the Father has are mine, and mine are the Father’s” (John XVI, 15). Yet both the nature that receives and the nature that gives are one Lord Christ, as the Apostle says: “And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (I Corinthians VIII, 6).

It follows: “I will judge justices,” so that the hearts of mortals, pierced with repentance before the time of judgment, might strive more earnestly in this world to be absolved, lest, when they come to that future inquiry, they suffer the Judge’s unforeseen sentence.

### Verse 3

“The earth melted, and all who dwell in it; I established its pillars.”

The Lord says that, before his coming, the earth is the human race, which has dissolved from that solidity of truth into the mire of sins, since, having abandoned its creator, it served detestable idols.

But how he came to the aid of the melted earth through his saving incarnation follows: “I established its pillars.” We must understand the apostles as the pillars. They were strengthened through the resurrection, when they faltered during the Lord’s Passion.

He himself also strengthened them when he said to the Apostle Peter: “Peter, Satan has sought you, that he might sift you like wheat; and I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII, 31–32).

And observe the exceedingly fitting opposition of the words. The pillars, once established, were rightly able to come to the aid of the melted earth. The apostles are rightly compared to pillars, because they press earthly vices down into the depths and raise heavenly virtues toward the grace of the celestial kingdom.

### Verse 4

“I said to the wicked: ‘Do not act wickedly’; and to sinners: ‘Do not exalt the horn.’”

This is what he said above: “I established its pillars.” Through the prophets and apostles he gave the admonitions of the New and Old Testaments, so that the wicked should not act badly, but should quickly turn to the Lord with humble satisfaction.

Truly, the merciful physician provided a regimen conducive to health, lest human weakness reach harmful diseases.

It follows: “And to sinners: ‘Do not exalt the horn.’” Here too “I said” must be understood. But first he says “to the wicked,” in order to include every sin.

Now he comes to the greatest vice of excuse-making, from which humanity suffers greatly: when someone does not allow himself to be called guilty, he invents all sorts of foreign causes for himself in his offense, “to make excuses for excuses in sins”—sometimes accusing the devil, sometimes tearing apart the words of the tempter.

Such a person seems to raise his horn because he strives to excuse his own sin through others [ed., “otherwise”]. Therefore such people cannot return to pardon, because they have lost the remedies of confession.

[Col. 0537D] **Verse 5.** Do not raise your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God. The repeated warning displays fear of great vengeance, because what is commanded by repeated instruction is always punished more severely. For when he says, “Do not raise your horn on high,” he urges that blasphemous thought be abandoned, since the one who murmurs against God with conceived wickedness raises his horn on high. For see what follows: “Do not speak iniquity against God.” He continues to address the vice of making excuses. Someone speaks iniquity against God when he judges that things were so constituted that he could in no way have avoided sins, saying that he came to some disgraceful deed not through his own fault but through the necessity imposed by the stars, thus imputing more to the Creator because he sinned by his own will. But how much more truthful and beneficial it is for one to confess his own crime, when, while committing a wicked deed, he neglected to call upon the Redeemer of all in order to be freed from guilt.

**Verse 6.** For neither from the East, nor from the West, nor from the desert mountains. This verse requires something to be supplied mentally, so that its meaning may become clear to us. It says: “For neither from the East, nor from the West, nor from the desert mountains”—we must add, “is the Lord absent,” so that he may recognize you, although it is evident that he is wholly present everywhere, as it is read elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1:7). In secular literature this figure is called *eclipsis*, that is, “omission,” whenever some words are withheld from a complete meaning. But this was done not because the language was deficient, but so that what had been suppressed by necessary silence might be sought with greater diligence. Therefore let blasphemers cease to conceive sacrilegious words, when the Judge declares himself present, to whom it belongs to know all things truly.

And lest anyone wonder that only two regions of the world were mentioned, let us explain this more spiritually, if we can. By the East, let us understand people already made visible through divine brightness; by the West, sinners from whom the light of truth is still hidden; and by the desert mountains, perhaps we should understand false preachers, who, although they usurp for themselves the place of mountains—that is, of preachers—are nevertheless deserted by truth, as are all heretics and pagans. Therefore, since God is shown to be present and all-knowing among every class of human beings, no one should presume anything of such a kind as could condemn him in that judgment.

**Verse 7.** For God is judge: he humbles one and exalts another. Behold, every profane question has been removed from the midst: “For God is judge”; and since he is judge, there is no doubt that he is just. For when someone is called a judge, he is understood without doubt to be perfectly equitable. And so that this may be shown to be contained in the word itself, the reason for the judgment is given plainly: “He humbles one and exalts another.” Certainly he humbles the proud and exalts the humble, because the former trusts in himself, while the latter trusts in the Lord. Thus it is also read in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). [Col. 0538D] You therefore see that the just Judge pronounces a sentence appropriate to the parties.

**Verse 8.** For there is a cup in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine with mixture; and he has poured from this into that. We have often said that the cup is a measure of drink by which bodies weakened by thirst are restored; it is named from the hot drink with which we frequently refresh ourselves at banquets [ed., “drink together”]. Thus the law of the Lord is beautifully called a cup, which, eagerly drunk and stored within, grants souls the sweetest health.

It follows: “It is full of unmixed wine with mixture.” In the divine Scriptures wine signifies the heavenly mystery, as in the case of those jars which the Lord caused to be filled with water, so that the waters of the springs, changed in quality, might receive the redness of wine, which it did not possess by nature. [Col. 0539A] Hence blessed Ambrose magnificently proclaimed this in the hymn of the holy Epiphany, with words of extraordinary brilliance (Tom. V, p. 356).

By saying “unmixed,” he indicates purity, because it is always pure and always clear. For it brings people who have been refreshed to the glory of virtue, not to the vice of drunkenness, as he says in another psalm: “And your cup that intoxicates—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22:5). The Lord’s cup is certainly “full of mixture”; therefore, although it is drunk continually, it is never exhausted.

By saying “with mixture,” he signifies the New and Old Testaments, which, mixed together, produce a most health-giving drink for souls. The Jews drank wine, but not mixed, because they refused to receive the health of the New Testament. Likewise, the Manichaeans did not drink mixed wine, because, accepting the New Testament in part, they rashly rejected the sacraments of the ancient law. He added, “and he has poured from this into that.” Here he plainly signifies two peoples, namely the Jews and the nations, because from the mouth of the unbelieving Jews he took away what was to be drunk and poured it toward the converted peoples of the nations. Happy and secure is the refreshment of receiving the cup of salvation from him who always knows how to provide what will be beneficial. This mode of expression is proper to sacred writings, since, as I believe, it is scarcely found in secular literature.

**Verse 9.** Nevertheless, its dregs have not been emptied; all the sinners of the earth will drink from it. Dregs are called the remains of wine that settle into the thickest consistency, which the liquid ordinarily reaches when the upper portion has been consumed. But since we previously called the cup full, he rightly denied here that its dregs had been emptied, since they could not be reached [ed., *pervenire*, “to reach”], because its fullness does not fail for all who drink.

Here we must understand by “dregs” not filth, but the lowest and final portion of the wine. For how could that which he previously declared to be unmixed and pure have dregs? But so that you might know that this dregs had by no means been reached, he returns to the full cup, saying: “All the sinners of the earth will drink from it.” Here he signifies—as we have often said—that the Jews will drink from this cup at the end of the age together with the other sinners, when they will have been deemed worthy to believe and will have been joined to the Catholic Church in united faith. For all belong to that portion which, by the Lord’s granting, will have been deemed worthy to believe. Many sinners, however, will remain in their obstinacy. [Col. 0539D]

**Verse 10.** But I will rejoice forever; I will sing to the God of Jacob. “I will rejoice” and “I will sing.” Christ speaks concerning his members: he rejoices when they rejoice in him, and he sings to the God of Jacob when the Church sings the psalm. For whatever members conduct themselves well are—as has often been said—reasonably applied to the Head.

**Verse 11.** And I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous will be exalted. Behold the voice of the Judge; behold the voice of the Almighty resounding. For he who previously sang in his members now breaks the horns of the sinner. In that judgment, all the power of the wicked will be humbled, and those things will perish when broken which here are raised up to great heights. Let the proud therefore consider how shameful it is here to imitate a mutilated animal, and let them be ashamed to exalt themselves by that from which they are known to face future deformity.

It follows: “And the horns of the righteous will be exalted.” This figure is called *catachresis*, that is, “abuse,” whenever names belonging to other things are applied to things that lack them. For the horns of the righteous are the gifts of the future judgment, which truly are raised up firmly, since they will remain in eternal beauty. Here we see the horns of sinners, which will not be there; here we do not see the horns of the righteous, which there will be granted as an everlasting gift. O humility deserving exceptional adornment, which here you are seen bereft! What greater value could your beauty possess than that he should have taken it up here, from whom all blessedness will rejoice without end?

### Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0540B]

We have heard the words of the Lord, not from the height of heaven, but from the holy writing of the Psalter; let us obey it all the more willingly because he has deigned to admonish us all together. For when the Lord spoke to Moses (Exod. 19:16), flashes of lightning appeared, thunderclaps resounded, Mount Sinai also smoked entirely, terror of death seized everyone, and the life-giving command reached the peoples in such a way that they thought they would perish in great danger.

Behold the benefits of the Lord the Savior, benefits to be continually admired if they are understood: every day we carry his tongue in our hands. The Lord’s will, enclosed in the divine writings, lies open to us, and through bodily sight it grants instruction, so that the eye of the heart may be beneficially enlightened within. He is never silent if we hasten to consult him in his Scriptures; he is always ready with saving answers, and is never rendered absent if we seek him with pure minds. Therefore let us cast away—as the psalm admonishes—pride, which separates sinners from him; let us love humility, which joins the saints to him in heavenly charity.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 75

**For the end, among praises; a psalm of Asaph, a song for the Assyrians.**

All the words of this title ought to be thoroughly familiar from the preceding expositions. It remains, therefore, to explain what he has introduced as new: “for the Assyrians.” The Assyrians are interpreted as “those who direct,” namely those who, already instructed in the rules of faith, strive to walk along straight paths. Asaph addresses these people, singing the praises of the Lord in wondrous variety.

### Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0540D]

Asaph—whose name, as we have said, is interpreted as “Synagogue”—addresses in the first part the “directing,” that is, the faithful Jews, indicating where the name of the Lord became widely known through the revelation of his powers. In the second part he declares the wondrous deeds he performed. In the third he admonishes all the devout not to cease offering gifts to the terrible God, who purifies the spirit of rulers through salutary correction. These parts are divided by the insertion of *diapsalmata*.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0541A]

**Verse 1.** God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel. This verse may raise a question: why is God said to be known in Judea, where it is rather evident that Christ the Lord was crucified? But we must inquire what “Judea” is, so that the truth of the meaning may shine upon us.

Although the people were distributed among twelve tribes of the Jews, it is evident that the Jews were called after Judah, the son of Jacob. From his lineage they created kings for themselves by divine dispensation, so that that royal vein, originating in the flesh, might continue until the coming of the heavenly Prince. Therefore it is clear that the true Judea is Christ’s Church. For “Judea” is interpreted as “confessing”: believing in that King who came through the Virgin Mary from the tribe of Judah.

Those who made themselves strangers to Christ—that is, to the lineage of Judah—are not properly called Jews, and from this their name is known to have been imposed. For at the Lord’s trial they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). How, then, can those truly be called Jews who professed that they had Caesar, not Christ, as king? [Col. 0541B]

It follows: “His name is great in Israel.” We have said that Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” And how can those reasonably claim this name for themselves who, not recognizing God, determined to crucify him as a human being, as the Apostle says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8)? Therefore they also lost this name, because they were unwilling to believe in his majesty in any way. Most wretched of human beings! Along with the sacred gifts, they also lost their names.

This psalm, therefore, speaks—as we have said—to those who, illumined by true light, have been distinguished from the wickedness of the faithless. [Col. 0541C] For them the name of the Lord is truly great when with a pure heart they confess him as King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16).

**Verse 2.** And his place came to be in peace, and his dwelling in Zion. A wondrous and concise statement, since it declares that the Lord’s place is peace, because he does not know how to rest in anyone except one who knows how to conduct himself—with the Lord’s help—in tranquil behavior, as it is written: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

But the one is shown to have peace with the Lord who does not quarrel against his commandments with a contrary will, who follows the commands of the ruler, and bends his own will to every divine precept. For true peace is to be in harmony with good conduct and to quarrel with vices.

It should also be examined how he gave the Lord a place, although the Lord is not confined by place. Since he is wholly everywhere and enclosed by no spaces, he is nevertheless said to be locally present in those whom he deigns to attend with favor.

It follows: “And his dwelling in Zion.” Zion, as we have often said, is a mountain situated at Jerusalem, whose name is interpreted as “contemplation,” through which God is perceived in the hearts of the faithful [ms. A: “he looks upon the hearts”]. For although the revered Godhead does not reveal itself to bodily eyes, the supreme Divinity does not deny itself to the purest thought; it is seen precisely in that part in which we bear his image. The mountain itself becomes Zion when it has been deemed worthy to behold him with a sincere mind. He dwells, therefore, in the one by whom he is understood; [Col. 0542A] and in a wondrous manner he is said to rest only in holy minds, although he embraces every place with spacious generosity.

**Verse 3.** There he broke the horns of bows, the shield, the sword, and the war. “There,” namely in that peace and in that contemplation of the Godhead which he mentioned above. For where the Lord of peace deigns to dwell, these things are broken, nor can such things prevail except where human conflict is shown to inflame itself.

The horns of bows signify the malice of the proud, from which wounds and unspeakable dangers come upon the innocent. The shield here is to be understood as referring to the most wicked conflicts undertaken through diabolical fraud. The sword refers to dangerous and manifest wounds. Finally he introduced war, which is plainly shown to be contrary to peace.

It is well known that all these things depart broken and shattered wherever the author of peace is certain to come. This figure is called *energia*, that is, “imagination,” by which the action of a thing is supplied to incorporeal eyes.

**Verse 4.** You illumine wondrously from the everlasting mountains. He comes to the second part, where he successively expounds the Lord’s various miracles. And lest anyone ask from where this illumination could have proceeded, he added: “from the everlasting mountains,” that is, from the preachers, who are truly everlasting mountains because they stand in perpetual and unchangeable sublimity.

Earthly mountains are temporary and lifeless; those mountains, through the Lord’s gift, know how to remain ever wise and everlasting. Beautifully he preserved the order of truth. He said that the Lord illumines through the everlasting mountains because he gave to the prophets and apostles what was proclaimed throughout the whole world by holy preaching. And remember that through this epithet, “everlasting,” he separated true preachers from heretical false ones. Those cannot be called everlasting who teach the fleeting things of perversity and are abolished together with their doctrines.

**Verse 5.** All the foolish in heart were troubled; they slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands. Above he said that the faithful were illumined by the Lord through the mountains; now he presents the foolish in heart as troubled and confused. Not without reason: from the holy preaching through which the righteous were illumined, the foolish were troubled; and, withdrawing from the true light, they followed the dark desires of the world.

These people slept while awake, and possessed sleep in their good works; they were always disturbed by confused errors. He rightly called the life of unbelievers “sleep,” because to be awake is not to neglect what will be beneficial and pursue what is fleeting. He rightly added “their own,” in order to distinguish them from the rest of the blessed. For this sleep is deceptive and misleading: now they rejoice that they have acquired riches, now that they have been joined in the most noble marriage, now that they have been elevated by distinguished honors.

But see what confusion follows them: “And the men of wealth found nothing in their hands,” so that they alone among human beings lose what they did not possess, and grief becomes theirs in their senseless loss, since they had no joy in enjoying what they possessed [ms. A, *quaerant*, “seek,” for “lose”]. Observe how he identifies and defines the greedy. For he says, “men of wealth,” namely those who, with a mind held captive, serve their money. [Col. 0543A]

A beautiful emphasis follows: let them still seek in their hands what they recognize they held nothing of. For emphasis is a twofold exaggeration: one that signifies more than it says, and another that also demonstrates what it does not say. Here it is the latter part, which signifies even what it does not say. For by designating them “men of wealth,” he indicates that they possessed the desires of the whole world, so that, in the likeness of a dream, they were deceived by various perceptions of their desire.

**Verse 6.** At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell asleep. Although rebuke ordinarily makes energetic men cautious and watchful, here he says that unbelievers fell asleep at the Lord’s rebuke—he is the God of Jacob—because they heard the holy admonitions negligently and with dull minds.

But he next explains who those who fell asleep are: “those who mounted horses,” that is, those who, growing in pride, roam through the enticements of this world as though riding swift horses. And if you examine the cause of such great haste, that ardor grows drowsy, that hurry snores, and the very action, so headlong, lies buried in sleep. Such was Pharaoh, who, mounting chariots and horses, stubbornly disregarded the Lord’s rebukes and, sleeping, arrived at eternal sleep, where no rest is found.

**Verse 7.** You are terrible, and who can resist you? Then from your anger [ms. A: “from then your anger”]. Let us look somewhat more attentively at what this verse declares. Above he said that the Lord rebukes those who mount horses, that is, those who leap into pride. In that judgment, however, he declares him terrible to all, when, coming in the glory of his majesty, he condemns the proud and bestows perpetual dignity upon the humble in heart.

Here many resist his commands when they desire more strongly those things that are forbidden by his admonitions. But then who will resist you? This must be read negatively, because none of the wicked can resist him there, when they recognize that the Lord condemns all crimes. “Then” means at the time of judgment, which is also called the day of anger and fury, because nothing will any longer be passed over through patience, when vengeance is already taken upon the wicked.

**Verse 8.** Judgment was hurled (*jaculatus* [ms. A, *jaculatum*]) from heaven; the earth trembled and was still. Here the power of the judgment itself is expounded, because from that summit of power judgment descended like a missile launched by a very strong and certain hand. But that spear inflicts a temporal wound; the judgment, however, will pierce the wicked with an eternal wound.

It follows: “The earth trembled and was still.” Earth, as has often been said, here signifies the gross and exceedingly weighty sinners who are to be condemned by the authority of the divine sentence. They will tremble when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). They will be still when they are received into everlasting condemnation. But this stillness is without rest: they will be still from evil works, but they will not rest in punishment, since they will be tortured by eternal flame.

**Verse 9.** When God arose for judgment, to save all the quiet ones [mss. G., A: “the meek ones”] of the earth. This verse must be joined to what precedes. For it says: “The earth trembled and was still when God arose for judgment.” He is rightly said to arise in his judgment, since here he endured everything quietly when Christ was judged, although there also he judges all things in tranquility.

But “arise” is taken from the judges of the world, who, whenever they determine something with strict severity, are said to arise, because they appear, moved by anger, to avenge the crimes committed. And lest you think that judgment was to be carried out only for the condemnation of the wicked, he added: “to save all the quiet ones of the earth.”

The quiet ones of the earth are those who are not seized by any vice of this world through a will inflamed by desire, but who, conducting themselves with even moderation—as was said above—are shown to possess tranquil peace of mind. These are saved when, by the Lord’s gift, they receive the promised rewards.

**Verse 10.** For the thought of man will confess to you, and the remnants of thoughts will keep a festival for you. He comes to the third part, urging that, since the Lord alone is owed the highest festival, they should fulfill their vows [ms. A, *reddantur*, “may the vows be fulfilled”] to the terrible God, who can convert the pride of rulers to the most humble holiness.

Our thought first confesses to God when it condemns past sins with humble penitence. But because human frailty must always mourn what it sins, he added: “And the remnants of thoughts will keep a festival for you.” The remnants of thoughts are, after poured-out tears and continual contrition of heart, the remembered destruction of past crimes. These keep a festival for the Lord when they sense that they have been freed by him from that destruction of sins. [Col. 0544C]

For this reason the Hebrews, cleansed from the filth of sins, are commanded to offer a festive gift to the Lord; the fiftieth psalm also seems to touch on this. For when it says, “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. 50:4), it confesses to the Lord, in fear of the coming judgment, the destruction of the past.

Do you also wish to hear the prophet keeping a festival in the spirit? After many things he continues: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and whole burnt offerings; then they will place [ms. G. and ed., “I will place”] calves upon your altar” (ibid., 21). Thus the blessed kinship of the psalms agrees with itself in mutual truth.

**Verse 11.** Vow and repay to the Lord your God, [Col. 0544D] all you who around him offer gifts to the Terrible One. Since it is fitting that we fulfill all the Lord’s commands, and since we must hear the voice of his command, Asaph here admonishes us that we ought first to make vows and afterward repay them.

Not without reason, because there are many things that we ought to fulfill even without promising them, such as: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Exod. 20:13), and the other offenses which we are forbidden to commit. There are other things which, unless we vow them, we are bound by no law to fulfill: preserving virginity, seeking the desert, and binding ourselves by daily mortification through fasting.

He therefore invites us to promise such things, which we absolutely ought not to undertake unless we make a pledge. For it is permitted both to seek marriage, to remain in the holy Church, [Col. 0545A] and to enjoy suitable refreshment; yet when better things have been promised, he commands that these be fulfilled, as the Apostle says: “He who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better” (1 Cor. 7:38).

He added, “your God,” to signify the faithful, who rejoice in the worship of the holy Trinity.
