It follows: “all you who around him offer gifts.” These are all those to whom he said, “Vow and repay”: certainly not heretics or pagans, but those who hasten, according to Catholic instruction, to return gifts to his altar. For the matter takes place “around him” when the gifts of the faithful are offered upon the most sacred altars.

When he says “to the Terrible One,” this refers especially to the devout, to whom he is also known to be gracious, as it is written: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11). For he is not terrible to the perverse and contemptuous; if they feared the Lord, they would certainly conduct themselves honorably.

**Verse 12.** And to him who takes away the spirit of rulers, terrible among the kings of the earth. The faithful preacher continues to expound the Lord’s magnificence. He says that vows should be made to that Terrible One who takes away the spirit of rulers, that is, their pride or arrogance. And to make clear that he means those who have been converted, he added, “among the kings of the earth,” namely those who, by the Lord’s gift, have been deemed worthy to rule and govern their own bodies.

Here we should understand kings emptied of the spirit of pride, not swollen with power, because in this respect the greater miracle is that those swollen with pride were not punished but rather freed through the conversion granted to them.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Here is that Asaph who, in the title, was said to admonish the directing ones, and who has reached the mysteries of the Lord Christ, declaring him terrible to kings—the one whose crucifixion the madness of the Hebrews demanded. Therefore understand, obstinate ones, that you are not directing ones but rather erring ones, because you were unwilling to hear so salutary a monitor in all things.

And therefore you live scattered through foreign kingdoms; you have no sacrifices, because you were unwilling to love the ancestral scepter but chose the Roman one. For although Jews are called by a Latin expression meaning “confessing,” how can you, so gravely obstinate, be called by that name? Why do you not perceive such great vengeance, since after everything else you have also lost the very name?

Half of the text of the Psalms has now been completed, and we know that as many as we have passed through by the Lord’s generosity remain for us until the end. Let us pray that he who granted us grace in the past may himself effectively grant us help in what lies ahead.

## 259 EXPOSITION OF PSALM 76

**For the end, concerning Jeduthun; a psalm of Asaph.**

“For the end” is known to signify the Lord the Savior. In the preceding titles we also said what the name Jeduthun—“one who passes beyond them”—ought to indicate. It is clear that Asaph means “congregation.” Once the interpretation of these names has been handled, the congregation should be understood as that which has passed beyond the vices of this age with glorious steps and has reached that end to which nothing can be found comparable. This entire psalm, therefore, will be sung by the faithful congregation, which is contained under the name Asaph.

### Division of the Psalm

Asaph, whom we said was one who passes beyond vices, testifies in the first narrative of the psalm that he cries out to the Lord, and shows himself—something that commonly happens to the faithful—to have been instructed more deeply through his tribulations. In the second narrative he enumerates the thoughts that commonly assail the hearts of those who labor in this world. In the third he declares that, through the benefit of the Godhead, he has been changed to a better understanding, so that with steadfast mind he might contemplate God’s work and power; through these things he is recognized as having advanced by continual exercise. In the fourth narrative he proceeds to explain how divine miracles were performed among the peoples through the Lord the Savior.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0546B]

**Verse 1.** With my voice I cried out to the Lord; my voice [ms. A: “with my voice”] to God, and he attended to me. This Asaph, an exceptional one who passes beyond worldly desires, cries out to the Lord not for bodily health, not to acquire riches, not to obtain honor, but out of love for the Lord, which is poured into those who are already perfect, so that in this gymnasium of confession the contemplation of the Godhead may spiritually console him.

For what he says, “with my voice,” is that mode of expression which we already presented in the seventy-third psalm, where it says: “They set fire to your sanctuary” (Ps. 73:7), and similar passages. In secular literature this figure is called *pleonasm*; we too may employ it without fear, since Father Augustine is known to have mentioned it very frequently among the modes of expression.

But it must be observed that only the one who asks the Lord for such things as he promises to give the faithful truly cries out to the Lord. For one who asks him for transitory things is not recognized as crying out to the Lord, although he may appear to be asking him.

He repeats, “and my voice to God”—we must understand, “reached him.” Yet he does not specify what he sought; rightly so, because it is not necessary for one to say what he should provide when he alone knows how to bestow what is beneficial. Therefore those who entrust themselves to the power and ordering of the Godhead are truly wise; they seek him alone and obtain all favorable things. Thus the prophet Isaiah says: “Lord our God, give us your peace; for you have granted us everything” (Isa. 26:12).

It follows: “and he attended to me.” Behold that brief voice, but magnificent in devotion, sent to the Lord so that he might deign to attend. Yet what did he not grant there, when in his mercy he bestowed such things? For his looking upon someone is liberation, and it is to confer such great things as the eager petitioner cannot manage to request.

**Verse 2.** In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived; I refused to let my soul be consoled. Those occupied with worldly desires ordinarily wish in tribulations to be freed from the necessity they endure: if one is sick, he seeks health; if a traveler, his homeland; if poor, expenses.

This man, in order to gather into a brief petition everything that would be beneficial, did not cry out about his distress or impatiently thrust forward what he was suffering. [Col. 0547A] Rather, like one tranquil and unaware of his own misfortunes, in the day of his tribulation he sought the contemplation of the Lord with his whole desire.

He added, “with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived.” Here he embraces how he sought the Lord courageously and what fruit appeared from his action. By “my hands” he means good works, which are known to accord with divine commands. By “night” he signifies the life of this world, which, although it appears to possess light, is darkened by the obscurity of sins. “Before him” means not before the faces of human beings but in secret, as he himself says: “Do not perform your righteousness before human beings” (Matt. 6:1), and so forth.

It is done in his presence when no human gaze is sought, lest someone swell with empty praises while spreading the report that he has done something good. [Col. 0547B]

It follows: “and I was not deceived.” Truly, the one who is not deceived is the one to whom the promises are fulfilled. But we must inquire more carefully why he says, “I refused to let my soul be consoled,” since he was already rejoicing in the contemplation of the Lord.

The holy man rightly refuses to let his soul be consoled by those things that are sought by human desires: if he is wearied by vigils, he does not seek relaxed wandering; if by fasts, he does not refresh his body with suitable cheerfulness; if he is sad, he is not diverted by the conversations of friends. His one consolation was always to place his attention upon the Lord.

**Verse 3.** I remembered God and was delighted; I exercised myself, and my spirit failed for a little while. Behold how he was refreshed who denied that his soul had been consoled by worldly things. For when we remember God, we are filled by the gift of complete sweetness; nothing can be equal when divine grace begins to satisfy us.

It follows: “I exercised myself, and my spirit failed for a little while.” He says that he exercised himself in that divine contemplation while considering with what wisdom God arranges all things and with what power he sustains the universe—doing everything at once and distributing so many things in wondrous order. His understanding necessarily failed when, in a single reflection, it gathered together things so innumerable and so immense, as it is read elsewhere: “I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Hab. 3:2). He rightly added, “for a little while,” because although he seemed to fail for a time, shortly afterward he is understood to have been able to recover.

**Verse 4.** My eyes anticipated the watches; I was troubled and did not speak. He comes to the second narrative, in which he enumerates the heat of his thoughts. For he says that his eyes anticipated the watches that he regularly kept in the praises of God. Our usage commonly calls these “night offices.” This must happen to those who are always intent upon spiritual thoughts. Care makes the senses fully watchful, and only those who are emptied of every concern fall asleep.

It follows: “I was troubled and did not speak.” He shows that it truly was nighttime, when a person reflecting searches out the secrets of his own mind. He was troubled by the recollection of sinners, because the human race was rushing headlong into offenses, and he was tortured with compassionate grief on behalf of others, although he had already passed beyond the vices of the world. [Col. 0548A] Therefore he remained silent, because in the deep night he had no comfort of human conversation; at that time whoever deliberates thinks more cautiously.

**Verse 5.** I considered the ancient days and the eternal years. He enters upon a deliberative mode of speech, which, once carefully unfolded in its parts, we will display at the end of this section. For he says why he was troubled: because he considered the ancient days, namely those of Adam, in which the human race was held liable through sins. Concerning these he says elsewhere: “Behold, you have made my days old” (Ps. 38:6).

But these days are temporal, fleeting, and fugitive in their unstable variation. In contrast to the ancient days, he sets eternal years, because just as the former perish in a moment, so the future ones endure in perpetual longevity: in the former, death rules; in the latter, everlasting life reigns; the former are gnawed away by consuming sadness, while in the latter the righteous will rejoice in secure happiness; finally, in the former everything that comes passes away, while in the latter whatever arrives will stand.

But what is this? This man, already devoted to God, sets the eternity of years against ancient days. He was considering why humanity desires and seeks so greatly those fleeting days which no one can retain, while we neglect, despise, and refuse to believe in those eternal years that alone ought especially to be sought by us, because we cannot see them in the present. Rightly, therefore, he was troubled, since he knew sinners to be subject to such perverse convictions.

### Verse 6

“I kept the eternal years in mind; and I meditated during the night with my heart; I was exercised and sifted my spirit within me” [Col. 0548C].

The beginning of this verse must be joined to what precedes. It is as follows: “And I kept the eternal years in mind”—not like fools, who neither believe what they hear nor store it in their memory, but consign to oblivion what they have received too carelessly. He kept the eternal years in mind because he believed that they would come. He also meditates with his heart who makes his soul consider something rationally. With it we speak in silence; with it we are exercised in quiet; nor are we alone when, having undertaken an inward dispute with it, we struggle.

It follows: “I was exercised and sifted my spirit within me.” The act of deliberation itself is properly expressed. We are exercised when, through countless reconsiderations, we burn with concern and, as in a gymnasium, are wearied by spiritual combat in the soul. The spirit is sifted [Col. 0548D] when it is carried here and there by the swiftest thought, like the wind. For the spirit is the soul’s power, which strives to fulfill its intentions.

### Verse 7

“And I said: Will God cast off forever, or will he not further grant that it may still be pleasing to him?”

When this Asaph, who leaps beyond the vices of the whole world, was considering its distresses, and his spirit was being exercised by divine meditations, he said: “Will God cast off the human race forever, so that he will not look favorably upon it through the mercy of his coming?” For he was already sensing the Lord’s future benefits, since he was considering the promise of heavenly mercy.

It follows: “Or will he not further grant that it may still be pleasing to him?” This *not* is by no means a denial; rather, it is an affirmation. For he will grant that the human race be pleasing to him [Col. 0549A]—that is, he will grant that the human race be pleasing to him—when he deigns to reveal the mysteries of his incarnation. But when he says “again,” he is waiting, not grieving. For although he believed that it could happen, he nevertheless trusted that it would emerge at a later time.

### Verse 8

“Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from age to generation?”

The Lord’s mercy is that he deigned to be born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary for the sake of our weakness. The Lord did not cut off this mercy, which he had proclaimed through the prophets as destined to come for the salvation of human beings.

Concerning this passage, Bishop Stephen, writing in his circular letters to the emperor Leo, says admirably: “The Son put on a garment of flesh—that is, the complete human being—from the holy Virgin, whom the Holy Spirit wove ineffably: inexpressibly at his entrance, comprehensibly at his departure. The Invisible One entered; the Visible One departed. God the Word entered; the same One, both God and man, departed.”

“Forever” signifies the fullness of time, when he deigned to come. Of that time the apostle John said: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). He added, “from age to generation”: “from age,” in which it had been decreed that he should come; “from generation,” namely the Jewish generation, whose members, by kinship of flesh, he also deigned to call brothers.

O glorious promise! O saving attainment [mss., “command”], if only they had deserved to recognize what was being granted to them as a singular gift!

### Verse 9

“Will God forget to show mercy, or will he restrain his mercy in anger?” [Col. 0549C]

We can forget what comes to us and departs from us; but how can God, in whom mercy exists substantially, forget what cannot be taken away from him? Hence he was foretelling that God would show mercy, because he foresaw his coming. For what mercy is stronger than that by which the world’s ruin is understood to have been removed?

It follows: “Or will he restrain his mercy in anger?” Observe in what wondrous order this coming has been described! Mercy is placed everywhere, because so great a thing is granted to the wretched. It is easier for the Lord to restrain anger, which is recognized as alien to his tranquility; but he should rather be believed to be inclined toward mercy, which is never separated from his majesty, as he says through Isaiah: “I will not be an avenger forever among you, nor will I be angry with you for all time” (Isa. LVII, 16) [Col. 0549D].

Therefore he will not restrain mercy in anger; rather, in mercy he will restrain anger, provided that devoted conversion arises in this world. And remember that anger is spoken of with reference to the Lord abusively, not properly.

The deliberative mode of speech has been completed; let us now bring its members into correspondence with their verses. His thought compared the ancient days and the eternal years according to their qualities and effects. He stored these distinctions in his mind and sifted his spirit through prolonged fluctuations. Yet he chose, as commonly occurs in deliberations, a definite and decisive judgment belonging to the third division. For he said: “Will God cast off forever, or will he not again be pleased with him?”—and the remaining two verses, which appear and are shown to agree with the judgment stated above [Col. 0550A].

### Verse 10

“And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High.”

After the second *diapsalma*, he comes to the third narrative. Here, after meditating on good things and being transferred to a most salutary understanding, he appropriately declares that he has been changed. First he says: “Now I have begun”—as though to understand, as though to possess wisdom, as though to have reached the most splendid light; for he was about to rejoice in the works of the Lord.

But what “Now I have begun” means is explained by the following statement. This figure is called *epexegesis*, that is, an explanation of what was said above. For he says: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” The word “change” is ambiguous. We are said to have been changed when, through some error, we slip into the worse direction [Col. 0550B]. But lest anything of that kind be understood here, he says that a transformation has taken place in him, such as the Lord’s right hand is accustomed to effect.

For the right hand of the Most High is Christ the Lord, through whom we have been so transformed that, from a servile condition, we have even become worthy to be called his sons. He perceived this transformation taking place in himself, and rejoiced that it would one day be granted to the Christian people.

### Verse 11

“I remembered the works of the Lord, for I shall remember your wonders from the beginning.”

He says that the transformation made in him remains in his memory, because one who deserves to receive better things is not shown to lose the benefits bestowed upon him from his heart.

But lest he appear to rejoice only over himself, he continues: “For I shall remember your wonders from the beginning”—namely, those which the merciful and compassionate One graciously bestowed upon the human race [Col. 0550C]. First, that he made Adam according to his image and likeness; then, that he accepted the offering of righteous Abel; that, as the Flood increased, he saved various animals in Noah’s Ark as a mystery of the Church; that, when Abraham offered his son, he displayed by heavenly compassion a type of his own coming; and finally, that he himself deigned to come to free humanity.

These, I believe, were the wonders from the beginning that delighted the holy man through their remembrance.

### Verse 12

“And I shall meditate on all your works, and I shall exercise myself in your observances.”

Let us learn how far this excellent man who leaps beyond the world has advanced. For, with the Lord’s mercy assisting him, he promises that he will meditate through constant reflection on his works—that is, on the divine Scriptures [Col. 0550D]. In them there is no weariness and no satiety; rather, the more one drinks in, the more one seeks sweet meanings. Hence the one-hundred-eighteenth Psalm will have much to say.

But since it is not enough for the faithful merely to read unless they also display the fruit of good works through diligent devotion, he says: “I shall exercise myself in your observances”—that is, I shall humbly and devotedly occupy myself with your saving commandments. Our exercise is rightly so called when, through his mercy, we carry out the Lord’s orders.

### Verse 13

“O God, your way is in the holy place; what god is great like our God?”

He comes to the praises of the Lord, in which he recalls his strength and gentleness, so that they might more easily obtain the favor of the most compassionate Judge through repeated proclamations [Col. 0551A]. It is evident that the holy man had been assured of the promises. For it is clear that he was instructed both by books and by works, since he burst forth in devoted exultation into the praises of the Father.

He says: “O God, your way is in the holy place.” The Holy One is Christ the Lord, as he himself says: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. LXXXV, 2). He likewise says that he himself is the way, as in the statement: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). But since he gave human beings the faith by which the Father might be known most perfectly, he is rightly called the Father’s way, because through him we have learned how the Trinity is to be worshiped. For he himself said: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

It follows: “What god is great like our God?” Now, as one who has been instructed, he rejoices exultantly in the Holy Spirit and places the Lord’s power above all the images that were worshiped on earth through false persuasion [Col. 0551B]. Those images were utterly worthless, weak, and contemptible; but our Lord is great, strong, and fearful, doing whatever he wills in heaven and on earth.

Therefore this verse is spoken against those who must be rebuked, who were still blinded by the error of superstitions, so that the unhappy might recognize the one they flee and those whom they follow. This figure is called *syndyasmos*, which is interpreted in Latin as “comparison” or “joining.” It arises from a comparison of opposites, when persons or causes are compared either in contrast or in similarity.

### Verse 14

“You are God, who alone performs wonders; you have made your power known among the peoples.”

When he says, “You are God,” he displays the essence of the divine Majesty, as he himself says: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14). Being properly belongs to the One who depends on no assistance in order to exist, but by the power of his own nature remains always great, always exalted, and always unchangeable.

Therefore he alone is the one who performs wonders. For although he has often granted his saints the ability to perform such things, he alone brings wondrous works to fulfillment according to his will.

But let us see why he said “alone,” since the Son and the Holy Spirit also cooperate in everything. He said “alone” because we truly confess the holy Trinity to be one Lord and one God, as he himself says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI, 4).

It follows: “You have made your power known among the peoples”—that is, when he sent into this world the Lord and Savior, who, as the Apostle says, “is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24) [Col. 0551C].

He made him known when those who knew him only outwardly recognized him, and those who believed with faithful minds that he was the Son of the Father contemplated him more deeply. Thus he became known to unbelieving peoples only in the flesh, but to the faithful also in his Divinity, as the Gospel says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

### Verse 15

“You redeemed your people by your arm, the sons of Israel and Joseph.”

He develops the preceding meaning. For he says what the Father’s clemency accomplished for the human race: that by his arm—that is, by the Lord and Savior—he redeemed his people, as it is written: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1) [Col. 0552A].

And lest there be any ambiguity about which people he redeemed, it follows: “The sons of Israel and Joseph.” We have often said that “people,” although expressed in the singular, contains a plural meaning. Therefore we should understand “the sons of Israel” as the Jewish people who nevertheless believed, and Joseph as the other people that came from the nations.

But whether it is the people from the Jews who believed or the people gathered from the calling of the nations, there is one people of God, although it may appear divided during the time of its believing, as the Gospel says: “There are other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 16).

For in the name of Joseph we may suitably understand the faith of the nations. Although this Joseph was the son of Jacob, who was first called Israel, nevertheless, because he was handed over by his brothers and reached the nations, where he was held in honor and power—so that the land of the Egyptians was governed according to his will—the nations that believed in the Lord and Savior with devoted minds are reasonably indicated by his name [Col. 0552B].

The name “Joseph” itself signifies “increasing,” which is appropriately applied to the nations, from whom the Church of Christ continually grows.

Therefore the meaning is this: He redeemed those who chose to believe in him with pure hearts, both from the people of Israel and from the gathering of the nations, by his arm—that is, by the Lord and Savior.

### Verse 16

“The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and they feared, and the abysses were troubled.”

He comes to the fourth narrative, in which he now joyfully recounts what powers the majesty of Christ the Lord accomplished. For whereas earlier he had said, “You have made your power known among the peoples,” he now says of him: “The waters saw you, O God.”

Divine Scripture frequently testifies that peoples are signified by waters, since it also speaks of them as seeing and fearing. These are the waters that were able to recognize or fear the Lord with rational understanding. For observe what he added: “The waters saw you, and they feared.” This could not have occurred in a lifeless element, namely, that it should recognize and fear such a manifestation of miracles.

It follows: “And the abysses were troubled”—that is, here too we must understand peoples, now in greater numbers, who are stirred up like a liquid element by the blasts of vices. Yet they were happily troubled when they came to the pursuit of conversion [Col. 0552D].

And note that what follows, all the way to the end of the psalm, is spoken through the figure of *parabole*, in which things unlike in kind are compared with one another.

### Verse 17

“The multitude of the sound of the waters; the clouds gave forth their voice; for your arrows passed through.”

There is a multitude of the sound of the waters when sweet psalmody is offered, when guilt is washed away through groans and tears, and when thanks are returned for a gift received. And, like a stormy sea, diverse vows of the peoples resound in the holy churches.

But why was the sound of the multitude of the waters produced? He beautifully added the reason: “For the clouds gave forth their voice.” We have often already said that clouds signify preachers, concerning whom it is written: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V, 6).

They release their great voice when they proclaim the Lord’s commandments throughout the whole world, just as another psalm previously proclaimed: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5) [Col. 0553A].

From this came the sound of the waters; from this the abysses were troubled, because these words of preaching brought the pursuits of devotion to peoples who had been wandering.

It follows: “For your arrows passed through.” Here we appropriately understand the evangelists as arrows. Through their preaching they pierced devoted peoples medicinally as far as the innermost recesses of the heart—not by inflicting a wound, but by bringing salvation.

### Verse 18

“The voice of your thunder is in the wheel; your flashes illuminated the world; the earth was moved and trembled.”

This too is spoken comparatively, because the voice of thunder seems to roll around as though it were heard coming from rumbling wheels [Col. 0553B]. For when it is poured down from the highest place, it passes through the expanse of the heavens with rolling murmurs, so that the sound itself is perceived as revolving and winding.

Or, better, by “the wheel” we should understand the world, which is enclosed in the form of a wheel by its perfectly rounded shape. Therefore, in the wheel—that is, in the world—the voice of his thunder went forth when the preachers of Christ filled the whole circle of the earth with thunderous words.

But what did those clouds and thunders do? It follows: “Your flashes illuminated the world.” Divine benefits are narrated through fitting comparisons, so that heavenly realities may be explained through heavenly likenesses. By “flashes” he means the divine commandments radiant with the light of truth, which dispelled the darkness of human beings throughout the world by a saving illumination.

He says what these thunders and flashes accomplished: they moved and made the earth—that is, our bodies—tremble when such a great miracle was heard [Col. 0553C]. He calls those “moved” and “terrified” who, faithfully hearing the word of God, came through Christ’s gift to the pursuit of conversion.

### Verse 19

“Your ways were in the sea, and your paths in many waters; and your footsteps will not be known.”

If you wish to take this literally, his way was in the sea when, visibly walking upon the surface of the waters, he summoned the apostle Peter to come to him.

Or it should rather be understood as follows: “Your ways were in the sea”—in the thoughts of human beings, which fluctuate like a faithless sea. Yet he has ways there when he has subjected them to himself through abundant mercy.

“Many waters” is likewise the multitude of the converted nations [Col. 0553D]. The Lord’s paths—that is, his ways—are among them, since he deigns to come to them.

It follows: “And your footsteps will not be known.” This should be read with the sense of an accusation: although he came openly and manifested himself through so many miracles, he was nevertheless not recognized by the unbelieving Jews. He rightly reproaches those who refused to believe in such majesty and in benefits so present.

For “footsteps” signify bodily presence; a footprint is the mark made by the sole of the foot as we walk.

### Verse 20

“You led your people like sheep, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”

Since this miracle cannot be applied to anyone else, there is no doubt that the accusation made earlier—that they did not recognize his footsteps—also pertains to the Hebrew people [Col. 0554A].

They were led by the hand of Moses and Aaron—that is, by the activity through which they performed various and wondrous miracles. And he rightly said, “like sheep,” but not “sheep,” because through unbelief they became goats. Here “like” does not signify truth but appearance.

Moses is interpreted as “taken up,” because he was taken from the river by Pharaoh’s daughter. Aaron means “mountain of strength.” These names also appear to express the very powers they exercised.

Among other things, Moses worked in the waters at the Lord’s command, when he made a dry path for the Hebrews through the Red Sea, signifying that the faithful people would be liberated through the gift of baptism.

Aaron bore the image of the Church, which he aptly compared to a most powerful mountain: it stands above others in holy honor and endures in the solidity of faith [Col. 0554B].

Under these leaders, we read that the people of Israel were liberated by divine power.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

O Idithun, truly excellent man who leaps beyond human affairs! You sang the psalm with wondrous structure. Exercised by tribulations, you denied that you were consoled in any way. Then your deliberation is recognized to have arrived at a perfect judgment. Third, you feel that you have now been happily changed; yet you do not relax your spirit amid prosperity. Rather, while you always profess yourself intent upon the great works of the Lord, you are recognized to have continually advanced through a certain increase of wisdom.

Fourth, you celebrate the miracles of Christ with great exultation; and as you pass through them one by one, you show the Christian people the instruction by which they may be saved [Col. 0554C].

Grant, Lord, that in your customary compassion you may command us to be cleansed, so that, although we differ in the quality of our deeds, your mercy may make us fellow-sharers.

## Exposition of Psalm LXXVII

### The Understanding of Asaph

Whenever “understanding” is found in titles, it declares the significance of some great matter. For although we generally call “understanding” whatever enables us to discern good and evil, here the term is used when our perception, through perfect intelligence, is directed toward the Lord.

We have said that *Asaph* signifies “synagogue” in the Hebrew language, and “collection” in Latin. But because “understanding” precedes it, he has indicated that the faithful synagogue is able to speak. For only faithful hearts can reproach the wicked [Col. 0554D].

### Division of the Psalm

The longer this psalm proves to be, the more diligently it must be opened through numerous divisions, so that its meaning may become clearer through distinction and the division of its parts may remove the weariness of its length.

In the first part of the psalm, only two verses are shown to belong to the person of the Lord, so that reverence might increase for the words that follow, where he himself appears to make the beginning.

In the second part, Asaph speaks at greater length, accusing the Jews of having proved ungrateful for the Lord’s great benefits. Yet, twisted by their perversity, they did not at all bring their hearts close to the Lord’s commands [Col. 0555A].

In the third, the many gifts that divine power bestowed upon the people of Israel are enumerated; yet they did not cease from murmuring.

The fourth tells what sort of vengeance came upon them and how the sentence was softened by the Lord’s mercy.

In the fifth, punishment was inflicted upon them because of their murmuring; but again they returned to supplication of the Lord, recognizing his great works.

In the sixth, they once more spoke deceitfully and followed their customary errors. Yet the Lord’s mercy did not allow them to be scattered, although this could justly have been inflicted upon them for their wickedness.

The seventh tells how they provoked the Lord in the wilderness, even though, because of them, the people of Egypt had been severely afflicted by ten plagues.

In the eighth, the Lord’s benefits are recounted, and again the guilt of Jewish obstinacy is added [Col. 0555B].

In the ninth, the gravest vengeance follows, so that he handed the people over to captivity and rejected the tabernacle at Shiloh, in which he appeared to dwell among human beings. Afterward he chose Mount Zion and David his servant, from whose seed Christ the Lord would be born and come into the world as its saving physician.

Thus, throughout this psalm, events are described from the beginning of the election of the Hebrew nation up to the coming of the Lord and Savior.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Attend, my people [ms. A., ‘O people’], to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth.”

At this beginning God speaks, the God who gave the law to the Hebrews through Moses. When he says, “Attend to my law” [Col. 0555C], he does not merely wish what is said to be received by the ears, but for the truth of what is said to be contemplated by the eyes of the heart. One attends to what is heard when one regards the matters spoken with a devoted mind.

When he says, “My people,” he clearly signifies those who were obedient to his commands. For neither the prophets nor the other righteous can be said to have been alien to our faith, since they received spiritually the deeds of the earliest period, as the Apostle says: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud”; and shortly afterward: “And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (I Cor. X, 1, 3).

It follows: “Incline your ear to the words of my mouth.” Here the disposition required for hearing is commanded, because one who wishes to receive what is heard with his whole heart is known to incline his ear, so that, humble and ready, he may accept what proceeds from the mouth of holy authority [Col. 0555D].

But note that the one to whom such care in listening is assigned is already understood to be among the faithful.

### Verse 2

“I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall speak propositions from the beginning.”

He made his hearer attentive by saying that he would speak in parables, so that the one who promised to utter such great things could not be heard carelessly. A parable, a Greek word, means a likeness: it occurs when we indicate what we wish to be understood through certain comparisons.

Thus we call someone “iron” when we wish him to be understood as hard and strong; and we compare someone swift to winds or birds.

Observe that the Lord calls his mouth Asaph, who is about to speak below. Therefore “understanding” rightly preceded him, since such a great privilege of testimony was to be conferred upon him [Col. 0556A].

It follows: “I shall speak propositions from the beginning.” He himself speaks—the one who causes speech. For although the utterance is brought forth through another’s ministry, the Holy Spirit speaks, whose commands are proclaimed, as the apostle Peter says: “For prophecy was never brought forth by human will; but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit” (II Pet. I, 21).

“Propositions” signify obscure and hidden questions, which must be solved through discussion. We shall explain these more suitably in their proper places.

“From the beginning” means from the beginning of the Old Testament, as Asaph will speak below.

### Verse 3

“How many things we have heard and known, and our fathers have recounted to us.”

Having established the person of the Lord at the honorable head of this psalm, he comes to the second part, where Asaph is introduced as speaking. We must receive his words not as merely human words but as a heavenly command.

“How many things” indicates a multitude of matters. “We have heard” pertains to the prophets; “we have known” looks toward the New Testament. They were heard when they were prophesied; they were known when they were fulfilled through the Lord Christ.

It follows: “And our fathers recounted them to us.” He calls Moses and the other prophets of the Old Testament his fathers, because they spoke much about the Lord’s coming and, enlightened, proclaimed what this man also foresaw would take place. For the righteous would not be righteous unless they were shown to believe what they said.

### Verse 4

“They were not hidden from their sons, in another generation” [Col. 0556C].

He says that the great things which, as he reports, his fathers had proclaimed concerning the Lord’s coming were not hidden from their sons—that is, from their spiritual sons, who were their imitators.

When he said “in another generation,” he no longer signifies the gathering of the Hebrews but that of the nations, because they are regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit through the gift of the undivided Trinity. Hence they too have been filled with the true light of understanding.

### Verse 5

“Recounting the praises of the Lord and his powers, and his wonders that he performed.”

The order of the words is as follows: “Our fathers announced them to us, recounting the praises of the Lord.” To recount the Lord’s deeds is to praise him, since whenever his works are related, his glory is increased.

“His powers” signifies the liberations he accomplished among the Jewish people when he freed them from the impious power of Pharaoh.

“His wonders” refers to the fact that he fed them with great deeds in the wilderness and subjected mighty nations to them through the lightest of contests.

He added, “that he performed,” so that they might appear to have been not merely promised but also completed.

All these things are drawn from the history of the Old Testament. For history is a faithful recollection of past events removed from the memory of our own age.

### Verse 6

“And he raised up a testimony in Jacob, and established a law in Israel.”

He comes to what he said above: “I shall speak propositions from the beginning.” The beginning is the Old Testament, from which he will speak below.

Perhaps he recalls the testimony raised up in Jacob when, wrestling with the angel, he was touched and limped in one thigh as a prefiguration of future events. This signified that the people of Israel would stand partly in firmness of faith and partly depart from their own salvation.

This was the testimony concerning the people who would wander or believe, which that struggle of Jacob foretold. He said that it was “raised up,” as though it had been brought into the light, although it seemed to have been oppressed by the sleep of ignorance.

This is what he promised above: “I shall open my mouth in parables,” namely, because he was going to speak such things from this beginning.

It follows: “And he established a law in Israel,” in order to remind them to be devoted to their Lord, lest, left to their wandering will, they slip into misguided errors.

He properly said “established a law,” as though it were a yoke for sinners, a burden for the frivolous, and an example of warning for those who would wander [Col. 0557B]. Hence he says elsewhere: “The law is not laid down for the righteous” (I Tim. I, 9).

This is what he said above: “I shall speak propositions from the beginning.” But, diligent reader, you will appropriately apply these matters to their places, since it is tedious to recall them everywhere.

### Verses 7–8

“Whatever he commanded our fathers to make known to their sons, so that another generation might know.

The sons who will be born will rise up and recount them to their sons.”

These verses signify that the Lord’s commands were transmitted through successive generations of human beings, so that no one might think that what is known to have been assigned to all was given to one alone.

The Jews received what there is no doubt came to the Christians. For this reason it was added, “so that another generation might know”—not, certainly, the Jewish generation, but the generation that is known to have been chosen from the nations.

For “another” here signifies outsiders, not relatives [Col. 0557C]. When it follows, “The sons who will be born will rise up and recount them to their sons,” it undoubtedly wishes Christians to be understood: they handed on the holy proclamations to their descendants, so that they might bring salvation to souls.

### Verse 9

“So that they might place their hope in God, and not forget the works of their God, and seek his commandments.”

The benefit of their fathers’ preaching is clearly shown here: their descendants should place their hope not in the law that punishes but in the grace that has been granted and redeems.

It follows: “And not forget the works of their God,” as the faithless Jews did, who, forgetting their Creator, turned to the worship of demons.

He added: “And seek his commandments.” For this is the true remembrance of the Most High God: that we fulfill his commandments with devoted minds.

### Verses 10–11

“Lest they become like their fathers, a crooked and exceedingly bitter generation” [Col. 0557D].

“A generation that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God.”

In these two verses the faithlessness of the Jews is marked out through beautiful definitions.

He says: “Lest they become like their fathers,” who were a crooked and exceedingly bitter generation. Crooked, because they refused to receive the truth. Those who do not follow the straight rule must necessarily remain distorted.

He said “exceedingly bitter,” that is, harsher than every bitterness, so that they armed themselves for the destruction of the one who had come to save them.

It follows: “A generation that did not direct its heart”—that is, what he previously called “crooked.” For if it had directed its heart, it would neither have been crooked nor have been made alien from God [Col. 0558A].

The person who directs his mind is the one who corrects himself according to the divine commands. When he recognizes that everything is governed by the administration of Divinity, he devises nothing through the pride of human presumption.

When he repeats the word “generation,” he refers only to those who remained in their obstinacy. There were, after all, Jews who served the Lord with pure minds.

He added: “And whose spirit was not faithful with God.” The spirit of one who does not understand that God’s visible works are to be applied to spiritual mysteries is not considered to be with God; rather, he wishes to refer everything only to what is seen. This is what the Jews did: intent only upon present miracles, they brought nothing beneficially into spiritual understanding.

### Verse 12

“The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting arrows, turned back on the day of battle” [Col. 0558B].

Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitful” or “abundance.” He was the younger son of Joseph, whom his grandfather Jacob is read to have blessed in the foremost place, with his hands crossed, in the Old Testament (Gen. XLVIII, 15).

His sons, rich in divine gifts and endowed with their father’s blessing, fell through a failure of faith. For they bent the bow and shot arrows when, at Moses’ admonition, they said: “Whatever the Lord our God has spoken, we shall do and we shall hear” (Exod. XIX, 8).

But they turned back on the day of battle when they said to Aaron: “Make gods for us that we may worship” (ibid., XXXII, 1).

You see that everything is explained through parables and propositions. For this meaning pertains to those who promise something in precipitate haste but nevertheless do not wish to persevere in that decision, as happened to the apostle Peter, who denied him three times, although he had promised to die with him (Matt. XXVI, 35).

### Verses 13–14

“They did not keep the covenant of God, and they did not wish to walk in his law.

And they forgot his benefactors [ed., ‘benefits’] and his wonders that he showed them.”

The reason is given why the sons of Ephraim turned back on the day of battle: namely, because “they did not keep the covenant of God, and they did not wish to walk in his law, and they forgot his benefits and his wonders that he showed them.”

This is so clear that it requires no explanation.

### Verse 15

“Before their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis” [Col. 0558D].

He comes to the third part, in which, after the crossing of the Red Sea, the benefits bestowed are described.

These are the people whom he earlier called “a crooked and exceedingly bitter generation.” He recounts the miracles performed before their fathers—that is, before Moses, Aaron, and the other elders—so that they ought to have believed more firmly in manifest events, since the testimony of fathers is usually sweet and trustworthy.

And to remove every scruple of doubt, he names both the province and the place where the events mentioned are known to have occurred.

Nor is it without significance that he says, “in the field of Tanis.” For Tanis signifies “humble command,” which Christ is known to have taught while he was on earth, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 29) [Col. 0559A].

He also did this before their fathers when he proclaimed the commandments of the New Testament.

### Verse 16

“He split the sea and led them through; he made the waters stand as though in a wineskin.”

Although the sea is a liquid element, he preferred to say that it was “split” rather than “divided,” because it was truly split when it remained on two sides with an unfamiliar solidity, so that they might have thought that not the sea but cliffs had been cut away.

“He led them through” refers to the security of the promised land, where they now seemed to walk without fear of the sea, sharing a common path.

For what follows—“He made the waters stand as though in a wineskin”—belongs to what he said, “He split the sea,” so that the wave stood motionless, as though it had been enclosed in vessels.

And note how the promised parables are unlocked.

[Col. 0559B] **Verse 17.** “And he led them out in the cloud by day, and throughout the night by the illumination of fire.” He explains what he said above: “And he led them in the cloud by day,” since “day” signifies the Lord Christ. For although he himself was the true day, he was nevertheless hidden from the faithless by the cloud of his flesh. Hence a remarkable mode of expression emerges: ancient events are narrated in such a way that they seem rather to express what is to come; so that they must be heard in one way and nevertheless understood in another. Yet there is no uncertainty in this, because both senses are entirely true. These are the promised parables arranged with heavenly integrity [ed., “set aside”]; these are the most certain indications of the truth.

It follows: “and throughout the night by the illumination of fire.” Here he signifies more clearly Christians, whom, in this night of the world, he guards by the brightness of his own light. For the Apostle testifies that everything happened to the Jews figuratively, saying: “For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea [mss. A, G: ‘by the sea,’] and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:1–2), etc. Therefore we must always render great thanks to him, because through such great and such remarkable miracles he foretold what he was to bestow upon us undeserving ones as rewards.

**Verse 18.** “He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them water as though from a great abyss.” Let us consider how miracles were displayed through contrary things. At first he caused the wave of the sea to hang like a rocky cliff; now he says that the rock poured forth irrigating springs, in order to show that all creatures obey his commands, although they seem naturally to exist in opposition to one another. When he says “in the wilderness,” he doubles the grace of the gift bestowed, since he performed such a miracle where there was no other remedy in necessity. He used “gave them water” so that he might seem to be signifying beasts rather than human beings, who did not know how to give thanks for such great benefits. But when he said “as though from a great abyss,” he declared the abundance of the exceedingly copious stream, which flowed forth in such quantity as though from the abyss of the sea. Note also that, following the Greeks, he everywhere uses *abyss* as feminine in gender.

**Verse 19.** “And he brought water out of the rock, and led waters forth like rivers.” He repeated this in order to emphasize the grace with which such great wonder had been shown: water came forth from something that had been hardened by its natural dryness. And lest you think that only a little had flowed out, he added “like rivers,” which proceed in a copious flood from the abundance of the mountains. [Col. 0560A] For he signified to us that water would flow from the rock—that is, from Christ—and would not fail through any diminution, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst, but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14). The Apostle says that the rock signifies Christ: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

**Verse 20.** “And they continued still to sin against him; they provoked the Most High to anger in the dryness.” By “continued,” he means “added”: amid so many miracles they did not believe, even though the transformed nature of the elements themselves proclaimed the truth. He said “to sin,” meaning “not to believe,” which is plainly a most wicked offense: to ask benefits from God and, after receiving them, not to return the thanks that are due. It follows: “they provoked the Most High to anger in the dryness.” We have often said that these are figurative expressions, which attribute to the Lord words reflecting human weakness, so that difficult and arduous matters may be explained more clearly to our understanding. They provoked him to anger when they did not believe that he could do difficult things for them, although they saw that he could accomplish such great deeds. For this is recognized as the gravest sin against God: to say that anything is impossible for him who is supremely able to accomplish whatever he determines to fulfill.

It is rightly said “in the dryness,” not merely of the earth but of the mind. Although they had been flooded with so many miracles, they were dried up by the barrenness of their faithlessness. For, applying themselves entirely to carnal desires, they were filled only in their bellies, not in their understanding.

**Verse 21.** “And they tested God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls.” To ask by testing is one thing; to ask by confession is another. These people certainly asked by testing, since after they received what they requested, they spoke unworthily. We call it “testing” when something is sought through deceitful words, so that simplicity seems to be present in speech while wickedness lies in the heart. Thus they cunningly requested not spiritual but bodily food for their souls. We speak in the same way of food being given to the sick “for their souls,” so that they may be kept alive in the body—not because food is nourishment for souls, but because through it the body’s strength appears to be maintained in this life.

**Verse 22.** “And they spoke wickedly concerning God; they said, ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?’” Wickedly indeed, because they spoke falsely. What they said he explains next: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” “Can” is to be read as an imputative expression, since it has been placed in the sense of “no.” O heinous crime, not to believe in the Almighty, who is daily and everywhere proven to accomplish such things! For it is written: “He gives food to all flesh” (Ps. 135:25). What, then, is more contrary to him than refusing to believe that he can fulfill what he has commanded? Their guilt was therefore especially grave, because such distrust touches divine majesty.

The table signifies the nourishment by which we, when hungry, are refreshed. And when he says “prepare a table in the wilderness,” it is as though what is ordinarily done in abundance could not be provided amid the solitude of the wilderness. It was utter foolishness and absurd madness to transfer human impossibility to divine power!

[Col. 0561A] **Verse 23.** “For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed; can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” It was an exceedingly foolish thought to cite an example of a great miracle and then suppose that its author might fail in other matters. For if he commanded waters to flow from a rock, why would he not also cause food to be supplied from the air to a hungry people? As though he had been able to do the former with some assistance, but could not accomplish the latter by himself! Yet this guilt of foolishness was soon followed by the most just punishment, so that no one would thereafter presume to think such things.

**Verse 24.** “Therefore the Lord heard and delayed, and prolonged it, and fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger rose up in Israel.” He has reached the fourth section, in which, through the figure called *synathroismos*, “gathering” in Latin, the crimes of the Jews are collected. God knows the thoughts of those who murmur, even when their tongues are silent. He alone can hear an inward and secret deliberation as though it were the cry of a loud voice.

But observe that he first said “he delayed”; now he adds “he prolonged it,” lest, if he had punished them immediately, it might be thought that he had been unable to satisfy the murmurers. He delayed the punishment to show patience; he prolonged the delay to manifest power. He then exacted punishment appropriately, when he had convicted their faithless minds through the fulfillment of the events themselves.

It follows: “and fire was kindled in Jacob.” Jacob signifies “supplanter,” and the name is often applied to the Gentiles, who, coming to Christ, are shown to have supplanted the Israelite people, since when the former entered, the latter were expelled. Thus in those Gentiles whom we have said are signified by the name Jacob, the fire of charity was kindled; and in proportion as the Jews were profaned by murmuring, so the Gentiles advanced through the fervor of confession.

He added: “and anger rose up in Israel.” Just as he says that charity was kindled in Jacob, so he declares that anger rose up in Israel, so that the former might be inflamed toward grace, while the latter were led into guilt.

**Verse 25.** “Because they did not believe in God, nor hope in his salvation.” Above he said: “Anger rose up in Israel,” in order to show their obstinacy; now he explains the cause of that stubbornness. He says that they did not believe in their God. And lest you think that there is another God, it follows: “nor did they hope in his salvation,” that is, in the Lord the Savior. Thus that murmuring not only brought them into disfavor but also condemned the hardness of mind that followed from it.

**Verse 26.** “And he commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven.” At the beginning he himself testified that these things are spoken through parables and propositions. Therefore, although they appear to have happened historically, they must nevertheless be referred to the Lord the Savior, so that the meaning foretold may be clear to us. The clouds were commanded—that is, the preachers—so that through the doors of heaven, namely, the holy Scriptures, glorious preaching might announce the coming of the saving Lord [ed., “of the Savior”], who is truly consumed as manna when he is received in venerable communion.

**Verse 27.** “And he rained manna upon them to eat; he gave them the bread of heaven.”

[Col. 0562A] **Verse 28.** “Man ate the bread of angels; he sent them food in abundance.” The beginning of this verse depends on what precedes. He said: “He opened the doors of heaven,” and then continues: “He rained manna upon them to eat.” He said “rained” in order to show the excessive abundance of the food, which descended from heaven like rain. And lest you doubt what that rain was, it follows: “manna to eat.” *Manna* is interpreted as “What is this?”—an interpretation that we appropriately apply to holy communion. For while this food is sought with wonder, the gifts of the Lord’s body are declared.

He added: “he gave them the bread of heaven.” What other bread of heaven is there than Christ the Lord, from whom heavenly beings receive spiritual food and enjoy an immeasurable delight? Accordingly, it follows: “man ate the bread of angels.” Christ is therefore rightly called the bread of angels, because they are truly nourished by his praise. Angels are not to be thought to eat bodily bread; rather, they are refreshed by that contemplation of the Lord by which the sublime creature is nourished.

This bread fills the angels in heaven and feeds us on earth: it delights them through contemplation and refreshes us through holy visitation. He added: “He sent them food in abundance.” He continues with the preceding interpretation, calling that manna “food,” not “grain,” in order to express the abundance that surpassed the people’s appetite. Hence it follows: “in abundance.” For that is abundant which no appetite can consume.

**Verse 29.** “He brought the south wind from heaven, and by his power brought in the southwest wind; and he rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.” As far as the historical sense is concerned, he says that these winds were provided as vehicles, carrying the commanded abundance to the appointed camps. But since they must also be interpreted spiritually, let us now examine them as presented under certain figures.

We know that the south and southwest winds are southerly winds, arising from the brighter and hotter quarter. When they blow, sluggish cold is driven away and a temperate atmosphere is produced. Thus the words of the Lord, burning with the fire of charity, provided the world with saving moderation in the likeness of the south and southwest winds; and they rained nourishment upon the peoples, by which the souls of the faithful might be abundantly satisfied.

The dust signifies the subtlety of understanding, which, stirred toward heavenly thoughts, continually rises upward. The sand signifies the innumerable abundance of prudence seasoned with the salty flavor of the sea. The winged birds signify heavenly desires, by which the devout soul, as though filled with flesh, grows rich. “Sand of the sea” is a fitting epithet, since there may also be sand belonging to rivers, which does not have this flavor.

**Verse 30.** “And they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents.” To remove from the murmurers even the difficulty of obtaining food, he says that what they sought with great desire fell not only around their tents but also in the midst of their camps. Camps are called *castra* from chastity, because an army occupied with warfare would have no leisure for foul luxury.

For us this signifies that within the boundaries of the holy Church we can receive all heavenly gifts, if we ask that our good desires be fulfilled through divine grace. Thus the power of the expression is immeasurable: it both completes the credibility of the historical account and conveys matters to be understood spiritually.

[Col. 0563A] **Verse 31.** “And they ate and were exceedingly satisfied, and he brought their desire upon them.” Behold, those who thought that something was difficult for God have been convicted. They fulfilled the desire of the flesh, though starved in understanding: their bellies were full, but their minds were empty. This figure is called *synchoresis*, that is, “concession,” whenever things are granted to those who desire them improperly, although those things cannot contribute to their benefit.

**Verse 32.** “They were not deprived of their desire; while their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose up against them.”

**Verse 33.** “And he killed many of them, and hindered the chosen of Israel.” He has reached the fifth section. This is what he said above: “He delayed and prolonged it,” so that they would not be deprived of their desire; otherwise, the impotence of God that they had conceived in their sacrilegious minds might perhaps seem to be confirmed by the difficulty of obtaining what they desired.

“To be defrauded” derives from “fraud”; for fraud is so called as though from “faith broken.” They were therefore satisfied to their own ruin—not so that they might live from it, but rather so that they might perish. For see what follows: “while their food was still in their mouths,” namely, while they were eating manna and quail meat. Food is called *esca* from *edendo*, “eating.”

He added: “and the anger of God rose up against them. And he killed many of them, and hindered the chosen of Israel.” Here he touches upon the history in Exodus (Exod. 32:1). In the absence of Moses, who was receiving the Lord’s law on the mountain, the maddened people rose up against Aaron, demanding that gods be made for them, as the entire Gentile world seemed to possess. Then that unspeakable calf came forth, whose worship they themselves were destined to bellow for.

At that time God, angered, told Moses that the Jewish people had sinned gravely. When Moses came down and the assembly had been convened, twenty-three thousand of them are said to have been killed; and Aaron, who was chosen by the Lord, fell into guilt on their account. For Scripture says: “The people were struck because of the sin of the calf that Aaron made.”

Their wicked murmuring also hindered Moses himself, when he said: “Can we bring water for you out of this rock?” (Num. 20:10). Because of this word he was forbidden to enter the promised land. Thus it happened that the insolence of those who sinned hindered the chosen of Israel.

**Verse 34.** “In all these things they still sinned, and they did not believe in his wonders.”

**Verse 35.** “And their days failed in vanity, and their years in haste [ms. A: ‘with hastiness’].” Those sins aggravate God which continually increase through grave additions. And because they refused to believe in his wonders, he says that their days failed, as though they had been consumed by a wasting disease. The days of sinners pass swiftly, as it is written elsewhere: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Ps. 54:24).

[Col. 0564A] **Verse 36.** “When he killed them, then they sought him; and they returned before dawn, and came to him.”

**Verse 37.** “And they remembered that God was their helper, and that the Most High God was their deliverer.” It was not those whom he says were killed who sought God; rather, the remaining multitude pleaded by the example of such people. It is therefore the practice of the righteous to seek God faithfully, whether before they suffer evils or while they are suffering them. The wicked, however, rush toward him with an unstable will only when some necessity disturbs them.

The Jewish people therefore feared God’s anger when they saw their companions being destroyed—that is, at the time when fire descended from heaven and killed fourteen thousand seven hundred, as is recorded in the Book of Numbers (chap. 16:49), because they had stirred up unjust rebellions against Moses and Aaron on account of the destruction of Korah and his companions.

What follows—“and they returned before dawn, and came to him; and they remembered that God was their helper, and that the Most High God was their deliverer”—signifies the time when, as the Lord was angry, the outer parts of the Jewish camp were consumed by divine fire. After this happened, they asked Moses to supplicate the Lord on their behalf. The pious asks in the light; the impious asks before dawn, as it is written: “It is vain for you to rise before dawn” (Ps. 126:1). Yet they seem to have done this out of fear of danger, not out of heavenly reverence, since he will speak further below about their faithlessness.

Note also that here the Father is called the deliverer, while the Son likewise delivers, as it is written in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36). The Holy Spirit also delivers, as the Apostle says: “The Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has delivered me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:2). Therefore there is no doubt that the holy Trinity possesses equal power and equally fulfills whatever it wills.

**Verse 38.** “And they loved him with their mouths, and with their tongues they lied to him.”

**Verse 39.** “But their heart was not right with him, nor were they faithful to his covenant [ms. A: ‘nor were they held faithful’].” He has reached the sixth section, where he recalls that the Jews again returned to their sins, yet declares that God had mercy on them.

He says: “And they loved him with their mouths, and with their tongues they lied to him.” This happened to those who think that they can believe through fear alone. For unless God is feared together with love, he is not sought with the whole heart. It is an especially serious sin when the tongue says that one confesses him while the depths of the heart disagree. Surely he does not fail to know everything that is done within, he who, as we read, is “the searcher of heart and kidneys” (Ps. 7:10), and does not hear only what the tongue proclaims according to human custom.

Whoever faithfully believes his testimonies loves him truly. For *faith* is so called because words are made true. The Lord himself also testifies to this, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). The prophet Isaiah rightly bears witness concerning them, saying: “Your neck is an iron sinew, and your forehead bronze” (ibid., 48:4).

[Col. 0565A] **Verse 40.** “But he is merciful and becomes propitious toward their sins, and he will not destroy them.”

**Verse 41.** “And he abounded in mercy, turning away his anger from them, and he did not kindle all his anger.” This example is appropriately introduced here: when Moses, pleading for the transgressing people, said to the Lord, “I ask you, forgive the sin of this people; but if not, erase me from the book that your hand has written” (Exod. 32:32–33). The Lord Christ also prayed for them while he was on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Through these supplications it came about that the Lord’s anger toward them was appeased. He became propitious toward their sins, since, for his satisfaction, not all but many of them deserved to return to him.

[Col. 0565B] **Verse 42.** “And he remembered that they were flesh, a spirit that goes away and does not return.” The fragility of sinners moved the merciful Judge: their carnal blindness did not see the light of heavenly wisdom. For this reason he says that they were to be awaited, since if their spirit had been immediately taken away, they would have lost the opportunity for repentance.

They are called “flesh” because flesh is dear to its own soul. In remarkable brevity, human death is defined as “a spirit that goes away and does not return”—that is, it is understood, “in this world,” since it is certain that the spirit will return to its own body in the resurrection.

**Verse 43.** “How often they provoked him in the wilderness and angered him in the waterless land!”

**Verse 44.** “And they turned back and tested God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel.” He has reached the seventh section, in which he briefly indicates their obstinacy and bitterness. He then enumerates how much divine power had provided for them in the wilderness and among the Egyptians, showing that although he continually provides for those who sin, they nevertheless do not cease to sin, forgetful of his benefits.

**Verse 45.** “They did not remember his hand, on the day when he delivered them from the hand of the one who afflicted them.” Tribulation ordinarily fixes memory firmly; but among the faithless even remembrance itself could not remain, although sorrow fixes it most firmly in our hearts. “To remember” means “to call back to the heart.”

It is beautifully said “the hand of the Lord” and “the hand of the one who afflicted them.” By this name the activity of both is signified. Yet how different are the things that seem to share one name! The one was able to deliver the people; the other attempted to retain them for their destruction.

**Verse 46.** “As he placed his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Tanis.” He designated one event by two names. In Egypt he performed the signs that he himself will mention below; but he also displayed wonders there, in the field of Tanis. Tanis is a city of Egypt where the wonders that are recorded took place.

The signs were, as it were, traces impressed upon the hard hearts of the Egyptians, like the marks of a seal. The wonders were things “speaking farther ahead,” that is, things prefiguring what was to come. For all those plagues occurred in ancient times with some further significance. They were therefore rightly called signs and wonders, since they are shown to have taken place in Egypt.

We have said that Tanis is interpreted as “a humble command,” which is understood to be necessary and saving for us in this present age, where we must be humble and prostrate, continually seeking the assistance of pardon. The righteous, however, will be raised up when, in that resurrection, they receive good things that will endure forever.

**Verse 47.** “He turned their rivers into blood, and their rainwaters, so that they could not drink.” Here he begins the first plague of the Egyptians. For just as water is read to have been changed into wine in the Gospel (John 2:9), signifying the transformation of peoples for the better, so here its transformation into blood announces that sinners perceive the causes of spiritual things carnally.

Blood is used to express the flesh; there is no doubt that this referred to the Jewish people. He says that both their rivers and their rainwaters were changed into blood (Exod. 7:17), so that those occupied with carnal perceptions would not understand the heavenly preaching spiritually. These and the following events are entirely clear according to the literal sense, and the text of the divine history shows that they occurred in Egypt.

**Verse 48.** “He sent against them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them.”

**Verse 49.** “And he gave their fruits to rust, and their labors to locusts.” The dog-fly is the stinging punishment assigned to the insolence of the wicked. The frog is the extremely talkative vanity of heretics, which, dwelling in muddy perceptions, does not cease to chatter with wicked cries. Rust is shameful love, consuming integrity through hidden diminishment. The locust is malicious and persistent detraction, gnawing away at the deeds of others through envious slander.

**Verse 50.** “And he killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.”

**Verse 51.** “And he delivered their cattle to hail, and their possessions to fire.” Hail is the Lord’s threat, which scourges the stubborn and strips them of the shelters of their own delight. Frost is malice that runs ahead and anticipates, preventing the labors of others from reaching their fruits.

It follows: “and he delivered their cattle to hail.” The death of foolish beasts signifies the downfall of fools, who, struck by innumerable evils, are poured out like worthless animals. He added: “and their possessions to fire.” Fire is used both in a good and in an evil sense. But because here it is clearly inflicted as an expression of indignation, we should understand fire as ignoble desire, which devastates our possession—that is, the state of our mind—with detestable ambition.

The tenth plague, concerning the firstborn, remains; we shall discuss it in its proper place, since two verses are known to have been inserted here to intensify the evil that follows. It should be noted, however, that these three plagues—rust, frost, and fire, which he has mentioned here—are not read at all in Exodus. There fire is said to have descended mingled with the hail, so that it damaged the fruits, not that it could have burned up their possessions. In their place, three other plagues are given there: gnats, boils, and darkness.

You frequently find this kind of variation in the divine Scriptures according to the appropriate understanding of events, as in the title of Psalm 33. It says: “A psalm of David, when he changed his face before Abimelech, who dismissed him, and he departed.” Yet in the Book of Kings Abimelech is not recorded as having been king of the Philistines; rather, the king was Achish. These names, as we have said, were changed according to the character of the mysteries, and we should understand the present passage in the same way. It is also clear that Augustine gathered similar examples in his *Harmony of the Gospels*.

**Verse 52.** “He sent against them the anger of his indignation: indignation, anger, and tribulation; sending through evil angels.” The order of the punishment is narrated with a most truthful description. First the Lord is angry at our sins, when we are not converted by any contrition. Then he abandons a person’s wickedness to his own indignation, anger, and tribulation, so that those who disdain to obey divine commands may be afflicted by their own adversities. Thus it is written: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity, to do what is not fitting” (Rom. 1:24), etc.

In a wicked person, indignation belongs to swollen pride, anger to criminal boldness, and tribulation to confused despair. Then they are driven by evil angels into unlawful actions, and, as though stripped of divine protection, they fall as prey to the most destructive beasts.

It must also be examined that he says these attacks were made through evil angels, as though God had not also destroyed sinners through good angels. Through good angels he overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:1), whom Abraham and Lot were worthy to receive as guests. A transgressor was also tested through an evil angel, as the Book of Kings says: “And an evil spirit from God entered Saul” (1 Kings 18:10). The righteous too were tested by the devil, as Job and the Apostle Paul were, along with others of this kind. For it is certain that all created things are subject either to the Creator’s permission or to his command.

**Verse 53.** “He made a path for the way of his anger, and he did not spare their souls from death; and he shut up their cattle in death.” When he says that the Lord made a path by which he could reach the punishment of the unhappy, he shows that he would not come against them unless they had first been deprived of the Lord’s protection. The Lord’s anger is spoken of tropologically; it is the same thing he mentioned above: “sending through evil angels.” The devil is not permitted to do this unless it is allowed by the Lord’s will.

What this anger did he explains next: “and he did not spare their souls from death.” “Their souls” must be understood as “the people,” whom it is known he killed in that disaster. For Scripture itself testifies that the soul alone may be placed for the whole person, as has already been said: “All the souls that went forth from the thigh of Jacob were seventy souls” (Exod. 1:5). Thus this expression arises through the figure of *synecdoche*, in which a part signifies the whole.

It follows: “and he shut up their cattle in death.” Consider how he says that everything belonging either to human sustenance or to human comfort was laid waste, so that punishments might rightly be judged to have come upon the impious and hard-hearted.

[Col. 0568A] **Verse 54.** “And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the first fruits of their labor in the tents of Ham.” Behold, the tenth plague, that of the firstborn, which the anger of God had threatened through evil angels, is explained. It was so great and terrible that it compelled the Egyptians, who had been unwilling to release the Israelite people, rather to drive them out voluntarily.

The firstborn are those things that first and reverently present themselves to our understanding, such as the supreme commandment to love God with the whole heart and to show love toward one’s neighbor in every way. When these perish, we are struck by the loss of the firstborn, and in the offspring itself we are deprived of reason.
