Let us observe carefully that he afflicted the Egyptian people with ten plagues and adorned the Hebrew nation with the gift of the Decalogue, so that in the mystery of the number you may find both the punishment inflicted and the grace bestowed.

It follows: “the first fruits of their labor.” This is what he said above: “every firstborn.” The first fruits of labor refer to everything that human ability could possess. And just as above he said “in the land of Egypt,” so here he repeats, “in the tents of Ham.” Ham was the father of Canaan, whose descendants are known to have possessed that land.

**Verse 55.** “And he took away his people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the wilderness.”

**Verse 56.** “And he led them out in hope, and they did not fear; and the sea covered their enemies.”

[Col. 0568C] **Verse 57.** “And he brought them to the mountain of sanctification, to this mountain that his right hand acquired.” He has reached the eighth section, where the Lord’s benefits are recounted and the guilt of Jewish obstinacy is added. Although these verses seem to be connected with what precedes, here it is nevertheless shown what that tenth plague accomplished: namely, that the Lord’s people, freed from impious servitude, might reach the promised land unharmed.

A question may arise here, because those whom he took out of the land of Egypt were not the same people whom he brought to the mountain of sanctification. The mountain of Zion is signified, where Jerusalem is known to have been established. But since the subject was the Jewish people, it is clear that those who were brought to this city were their descendants, who succeeded their fathers and preserved both the name and the race of the Hebrews.

Yet the passage signifies, as truly happened, that many of them reached the Catholic Church—which he prefers to have understood here—through the grace of conversion. For this is the Church that our Christ, who is the Father’s right hand, acquired.

It is clear that we must also understand the preceding verses figuratively. For when he said “sheep” and “flock,” he signified the Christian people, who are fed in this world as in a wilderness, provided that they do not pursue the desires of worldly things. We have been led out in hope from the land of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of sins—because we have received the light of faith. And he covered our enemies, namely, the devil and his ministers, with the sea, when the waters of holy regeneration washed us. Thus those things happened to them figuratively—as the Apostle says—because they announced signs of our salvation.

**Verse 58.** “And he drove the nations out from before them, and divided the land among them by lot, with a measuring cord of distribution.”

**Verse 59.** “And he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents.” The nations are driven from before us when barbarous and savage errors are expelled from us. He divides that promised land among us when, in his graciousness, he gives each person a blessed portion. The “cord of distribution” derives from those who divided the land by stretching out a cord.

It follows: “and he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents.” The divine Scriptures have handed down to us that an elect people was to be gathered in their place and number, from which the proud angels are shown to have been expelled. Therefore he will give tents to the tribes of Israel—that is, to those who see God—which the angels, still innocent before their fall through pride, once possessed.

**Verse 60.** “And they tested and provoked the Most High God, and they did not keep his testimonies.”

**Verse 61.** “And they turned away and did not keep the covenant, like their fathers; and they turned into a crooked bow.” He now speaks of the Jews’ defiance and consequently explains what happened to them when the Lord was angry, so that the disobedient may fear such examples.

A crooked bow is the wickedness of sinners, which does not shoot wounds from a distance but instead turns the arrows directed outward back upon itself. This plainly happens to the deceitful: while they try to inflict blows upon others, they are shown to turn their own plots against themselves.

[Col. 0569C] **Verse 62.** “And they provoked him to anger on their hills, and with their carved images they rivaled him.” The hills signify the proud and swollen thoughts of human beings, against which the Lord is always found to stand when, through wicked presumption, they rush into the worship of demons. They rivaled him when they bestowed the Lord’s honor upon detestable images. This rivalry must be understood in a bad, not a good, sense; for see what follows.

**Verse 63.** “The Lord heard and rejected them, and reduced Israel to utter nothingness.” The ninth section, which remains, now begins. In it the forms of punishment are enumerated, and afterward the coming of the Lord the Savior is proclaimed.

Some people are accustomed to raise the question why, when only certain individuals had sinned, he is nevertheless said to have punished all of them. This should not trouble devout minds. For although he handed the nation over to captivity, he preserved those who pleased him in the integrity of their consciences. Rather, he exercised through tribulations those whom he had determined to crown with eternal honor. For if we search deeply into the truth, those who were inwardly free did not suffer captivity, nor were those delivered to the internal enemy whose conscience could not be torn away from the Divinity.

Verse 64. “And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle, in which he dwelt among human beings.” Shiloh was a city where the Lord’s ark is said to have been established; from there the Hebrews received divine responses through priests who made supplication, before the Temple had been built at Jerusalem [Col. 0570A]. He therefore says that the Lord rejected this tabernacle, in which he deigned to dwell among human beings, as we read in another prophet: “See what I did to Shiloh, where my tabernacle was” (Jer. VII, 12). But we must fear lest, offended, he abandon the tabernacles of our bodies, which the Holy Spirit inhabits when, by God’s gift, we care for ourselves properly, as the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III, 17).

Verse 65. “And he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy.” He recalls the time when the Hebrews were defeated by the Allophyles and lay exposed to slaughter and plunder. Therefore “strength” and “beauty” signify the ark of the covenant, through which they seemed invincible among the nations [Col. 0570B] and distinguished by the highest praise of beauty.

Verse 66. “And he enclosed his people in the sword, and despised his inheritance.” It followed that the people fell by the sword into shameful ruin, once the dignity of the ark had been taken away from them. For he annihilates those whom he despises; nor can anyone help the person from whom divine consolations are shown to withdraw. He despised his inheritance when he cast away, because of the enormity of their crimes, the people whom he had chosen from among many nations. “Inheritance” is derived from *heres* [heir], since the Lord is known to possess it by legitimate right.

Verse 67. “Fire devoured their young men, and their virgins were not mourned.” Here we should understand “fire” as the anger of the combatants, which, like a consuming flame, devoured those delivered into its power [Col. 0570C]. It follows: “and their virgins were not mourned.” To mourn is characteristic of one who has leisure to do so. For when everyone feared the dangers hanging over them, no one was permitted to perform the proper rites for another’s funeral. “Lamentations” are so called from the household shrines, which served as tombs, as was the ancient custom of burial.

Verse 68. “Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not mourned.” Thus, during that very captivity, the sons of the priest Eli are read to have been killed by the sword of the Allophyles; one of their wives, having become a widow, was overtaken by death after a sudden childbirth. Thus it happened that his widow was not mourned at all, since a common destruction had overtaken everyone. For we must believe that many such things happened in that people, since sacred authority used the plural number, and is known to report nothing superfluous.

Verse 69. “And the Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine.” We have said that these human ways of speaking are often attributed to the Lord in order to explain matters. He is described from the viewpoint of foolish people, who think that, when he does not help those in danger, he is as though overcome by wine. But he sleeps only for the negligent and unbelieving, who awaken Christ by no psalmody and by no good works. And rightly he is made alien to those who foolishly understand him as sleeping, so to speak, for them. He is also aroused to vengeance when provoked by evil deeds, though his patience was thought to have been asleep; this is what we should understand here more particularly. For the Allophyles aroused him when they placed his ark of the covenant among their idols [Col. 0571A]. What happened to them because of this deed follows. We must also examine why he said “like a mighty man,” because people are then quick to anger and powerful in strength when they customarily rise from sleep after drunkenness. Accordingly, blessed Jerome, a truthful interpreter among others, rendered “mighty” as “strong.”

Verse 70. “And he struck his enemies on their rear parts; he gave them everlasting disgrace.” This is read in the First Book of Kings (I Reg. V, 6): because of the insult done to the sacred ark, the Allophyles were struck on their rear parts, so that even while alive they were gnawed by mice in an accursed punishment. This disgrace remains everlasting for them, because no one else was punished in such a way. Thus he strikes sinners in the life to come, when he does not forgive them their debts, and they are, as it were, consumed by mice while the hostile cohort of devils surrounds them.

Verse 71. “And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim.”

Verse 72. “But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved.” The judgments of the Lord are also declared by the testimony of the names themselves. Joseph signifies “increase,” a term used both for evil and for good; here, however, it must be taken in the contrary sense, since he is clearly said to have been rejected. Ephraim is interpreted as “fruitful” or “abundance”; Judah as “confessing” or “glorifying.” We should also bear in mind that through Hebrew names Holy Scripture often discloses hidden causes to us [Col. 0571C]. There is no doubt that this manner of expression is proper to sacred writings, since nothing of the kind is found in worldly literature.

Thus he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph because, although Joseph himself had been righteous, his descendants, who belonged to the seed of the flesh, are known to have desired worldly increase and [271] carnal advancement. He did not choose the tribe of Ephraim because they relied upon the carnal abundance of the harvest of this world. But he rightly chose the tribe of Judah, which was humble in confession and praiseworthy in conduct; from it the Lord and Savior came to us according to the flesh. It follows: “Mount Zion, which he loved.” This signifies the catholic Church, of which the Lord says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my beloved is one” (Cant. VI, 8).

[Col. 0571D]

Verse 73. “And he built his sanctuary like a unicorn, on the earth which he founded forever.” “Unicorn” signifies those who have one hope in the most holy Trinity, toward which the consecrated minds of the faithful are humbly raised and stand firm, as though upon a very powerful horn, through the steadfastness of faith. It follows: “on the earth which he founded forever.” Although the Jerusalem predestined for the future age endures, nevertheless it is shown to be founded on earth—that is, in holy human beings—under eternity [ed., “in the hope of eternity”], as it was said to Peter in the Gospel: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18). See how it is known to be founded on earth for eternity. Elsewhere too it is read concerning the Church: “God founded her forever” (Ps. XLVII, 9).

[Col. 0572A]

Verse 74. “And he chose David his servant, and took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the nursing ewes he took him.”

Verse 75. “To shepherd Jacob his people [ms. A., ‘his servant’], and Israel his inheritance.” A very suitable and beautiful narrative has been introduced. Since he had said, “he chose Judah,” he now says “David,” who was related to Christ the Lord through the humanity He assumed. But we understand this better of the Lord and Savior himself, for in the Gospel the blind cried out: “Son of David, have mercy on us” (Matt. XX, 30). And because they had spoken the truth confidently, they were immediately healed.

It follows: “And he took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the nursing ewes he took him.” Through this likeness, David son of Jesse—as in other passages also—the mysteries of the Lord and Savior are disclosed to us [Col. 0572B]. For David was taken from the sheep and reached the kingdom; our Lord, having fulfilled the office of shepherd, sits at the right hand of the Father, who is truly “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Apoc. XIX, 16).

Nor is it without significance that he said the sheep were nursing ewes. The Lord’s flock, fruitful through spiritual grace, is known to have many children, as is read concerning the Church in the Song of Songs: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep ascending from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none is barren among them” (Cant. IV, 2).

He added: “To shepherd Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.” Here we recognize more clearly that this was said of the Lord and Savior, who alone was able to satisfy his flock with heavenly bread and rescue his inheritance from all dangers to the souls [Col. 0572C]. We may understand Jacob as the Christian people who dwell here on earth. Israel, however, is the future assembly that is to be nourished by contemplation of the Lord; this cannot in any way pertain to a temporal king.

Verse 76. “And he fed them without malice of heart, and guided them by the understanding of his hands.” Everything belongs absolutely to the Lord and Savior; for he alone had no sins. By saying “without malice,” he shows that sins are rightly called malice. That purity, that holiness, that Majesty coming from heaven was shown to have taught what it did, and without doubt did what it taught. For the excellent teacher fed those whom he deigned to teach, as he himself testifies: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. [Col. 0572D] IV, 4).

“Without malice of heart,” as he says elsewhere: “Nor was there deceit in his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 9). “The understanding of his hands” signifies active holiness, to which he led his faithful, insofar as he granted it, through glorious imitation. Nor can this in any way suit David as a temporal king; but when everything is referred to Christ the Lord, all the details agree with one another in fitting harmony.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

In some psalms we customarily inquire what the heavenly authority admonishes us to do. Here he made such an opening that the exposition seems to be more than the beginning of the psalm. For he said that he would speak in parables and propositions, so that each person might quickly recognize the character of the psalm once the form of its expression had been made clear [Col. 0573A].

Therefore he asserts that the Hebrews were expelled because of their sins and that Christians were admitted, in such a way that he made the intention of both laws hang, as it were, in the beauty of a single cluster of grapes. Let us therefore love its length, in which, while history is recounted, the grace of the New Testament is revealed: like a fluctuating abyss that reflects as many lights as it has produced ripples. At one moment brightness flashes there; at another, a shadowy image moves around; and within the same element different appearances are seen, although no color is added or removed. So the wondrous variety of this psalm both narrates history and suggests very different things to be understood spiritually. The hundred and fourth psalm follows its likeness as well. And just as the future mysteries of the Lord are declared through David’s deeds [Col. 0573B], so through the miracles granted to the Jews the mysteries of the Christian people are disclosed.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXXVIII

## A Psalm of Asaph

As we have often said, this meaning of the name pertains to those deeds that relate to the Lord’s commandments and grace. Asaph, however, signifies the Synagogue, though the term may also apply to the catholic Church. For those who shone with the brightness of the Lord’s grace must not be considered alien to Christians. Add the prophets, patriarchs, and that people already devoted to Christ before the Christian era. This psalm too is therefore wholly composed as a lament, like Psalm seventy-three; it mourns future times as though they were past [Col. 0573C], and, because of the hardness of its heart, earnestly begs Christ the Lord to help the nation that is to be severely afflicted.

## Division of the Psalm

Before speaking of the division, we ought briefly to indicate knowledge of the events, so that, once the cause has been set forth, the text of the psalm may be heard more intelligibly. The First Book of Maccabees tells us that when King Antiochus came to [272] Jerusalem, he stripped the city of its wealth by hostile action, placed idols in the temple of God, and, while compelling the Hebrews to sacrifice to his gods, made many martyrs. Therefore Asaph—whom we have said represents the faithful peoples—speaks throughout the psalm.

In the first part he enumerates how much the people of Jerusalem and the Jews suffered during the time of the aforementioned King Antiochus [Col. 0573D]. In the second part he asks the Lord to pour out the anger of his indignation upon their powerful enemies and to deign to be merciful toward the sins of his servants. In the third, he asks by the spirit of prophecy that vengeance be taken—not with a desire for destruction, but with a purpose of correction.

## Exposition of the Psalm

Verse 1. “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance.” Although David lived long before Antiochus became king, he nevertheless, in his customary manner, reports as already completed everything that, filled with the Holy Spirit, he foresaw would happen. Hence Asaph, suddenly lamenting, cried out to the Lord: “The nations have come,” as though they were already breaking through the walls and the dreaded captivity were entering. A nation is so called because it is produced from one stock [Col. 0574A].

“Into your inheritance” signifies Jerusalem, where God’s inheritance was established in holy people: such as Mattathias, Eleazar, the seven brothers with their holy mother; such as the thousand who, so as not to violate the Sabbath, all allowed themselves to perish at the hands of the enemy without resistance; and the others whom our knowledge does not encompass. He added “your” in order to stir the judge’s mind against the savage adversaries, saying that they had come to harm what belonged to the judge. Orators have expressed this point more broadly and at length when they tried to arouse hatred and hostility against their adversaries.

Verse 2. “They defiled your holy temple; they made Jerusalem like a fruit-keeper’s hut.” The injury done to the consecrated temple most appropriately first occurred to the holy man, so that at the outset he might lament what he knew belonged to divine insult [Col. 0574B]. “They defiled,” he said, that is, they polluted; for at that time the Lord’s sanctuary was not destroyed, but impious nations, with abominable presumption, placed idols in the most holy places, so that where the true God was worshiped, an unclean spirit might be adored.

Thus we read concerning Antiochus in the Book of Maccabees: “He ordered the holy places and the holy people of Israel to be defiled; he ordered altars, temples, and idols to be built, so that they might sacrifice swine’s flesh” (I Macc. I, 49–50), and so forth.

A deeply mournful and insulting comparison follows: “They made Jerusalem like a fruit-keeper’s hut.” This figure is called a *parabole* [parable], when things dissimilar in kind are compared. Fruit-keepers’ huts are shelters that cultivators of gardens reinforce with branches and *liscis* [ed., *foliisque*, “leaves”] in order to ward off the sun’s harm and protect against the wicked hands of thieves [Col. 0574C]. As soon as the season of the fruit has passed, they abandon them as useless.

Therefore the nations that devastated Jerusalem regarded the singular beauty of the Temple as contemptible, like a little fruit hut that, worthless and despised, is abandoned after summer has passed. Hence Isaiah also says: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard and like a hut in a cucumber field” (Isa. I, 8).

Verse 3. “They gave the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth.” After complaining about the injury done to the divine temple, he turns to the slaughter of human beings, so that, after the crimes of sacrilege, he might accuse them of the guilt of homicide. Something still more serious is added: they cast those slaughtered with cruel savagery to wild beasts, unburied [Col. 0574D].

The contempt shown toward dead bodies is no small insult [ms. A, “injury”]; for if burial is an act of piety, casting bodies to the birds of heaven is plainly an example of great cruelty. By saying “your servants,” he signifies the martyrs who flourished in that captivity amid extensive persecution, as the same book records: “Many from the people of Israel held firm and strengthened one another, so as not to eat what was unclean; and they chose to die rather than be defiled by foods forbidden by the Lord” (I Macc. I, 65).

It follows: “the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth.” One event is described with twofold variation, so that the judge’s hearing might be made to feel the magnitude of the cruel deed. For it was not enough to deliver the dead to the birds unless they also allowed wild beasts to tear their bodies apart [Col. 0575A].

Verse 4. “They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.” He still lingers over the same amplification, so that what had been committed in so atrocious an example might not quickly pass from the mind. By saying “like water,” he increases the condemnation of their cruel deeds, as though they had believed it permissible to pour out human blood just as water ordinarily flows without anyone’s guilt.

What he added—“around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury”—shows the unspeakable abundance of the sinful slaughter: destruction had occurred not only within the city but also around its walls, so that no one could fulfill the duty of burial, since the same fate encompassed everyone [Col. 0575B]. Thus he says in the preceding psalm: “Fire devoured their young men, and their virgins were not mourned” (Ps. LXXVII, 63).

Verse 5. “We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and scorn to those who are around us.” He says that the glory of Jerusalem, once wondrous throughout the whole world, had come to be a reproach among its neighbors, so that the greater the nobility with which it had previously shone, the greater the abomination with which it afterward became foul. Jeremiah likewise says in the Lamentations: “How the city that was full of peoples sits alone! She has become like a widow, she who was multiplied among the nations; she who was a princess among the regions has become subject to tribute” (Lam. I, 1). And shortly afterward: “This is the city that was called the crown of glory, the joy of the whole earth” (ibid. II, 15).

It follows: “a mockery and scorn to those who are around us.” By repeating the same idea with variation, he intensifies it, so that what he had called a reproach might be shown more clearly. For he says that the Hebrews were a mockery, though previously they had been revered because of their devotion to the Lord. They were held in scorn when people saw them delivered into captivity, though they had formerly known so many kingdoms to have yielded to them [Col. 0575C].

Nor is it without significance that he added “those who are around us,” because reproaches known to one’s neighbors are always more grievous: constant reflection forces one to endure what distance would scarcely allow. Thus the whole text, growing from the beginning onward, produces that most distinguished figure called *auxesis*, or in Latin “increase.” Where are the orators who transferred the duties of truth into the art of plausibility? [273] Behold the arguments by which ingenious simplicity, not malicious cunning, operates [Col. 0575D].

Verse 6. “How long, O Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your zeal burn like fire?” He comes to the second part, in which he asks the merciful judge not to remain angry with the Jewish nation forever, since he had announced through the sacred proclamations of the prophets that he would come. For although holy men suffered evils, they knew that they would not be abandoned by the Lord, as another psalm says: “The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not delivered me to death” (Ps. CXVII, 18).

By the spirit of prophecy he also announces that what he foresaw would happen was taking place. During that captivity, Mattathias, one of the Hebrews, inflamed by zeal for the tradition of his fathers (I Macc. II, 23), saw the population of the city being drawn toward the worship of idols [Col. 0576A]. He gathered the remaining faithful and attacked the army of King Antiochus with his sons in such indignation that he both threw off the yoke of servitude and most gloriously rejected the commanded sacrifices. Indeed, out of love for holy devotion, he killed a certain Jew who was sacrificing to idols upon the very altars.

Verse 7. “Pour out your anger upon the nations that did not know you, and upon the kingdoms that did not call upon your name.” After recounting the most grievous disasters of the Hebrew nation, he now asks the just judge that their devastators should suffer afflictions, since they utterly did not know his name. “Pour out your anger,” he says—that is, send your indignation abundantly upon the adversaries, so that, just as they oppress us, they may be overwhelmed by your powers.

For he knew that human victory could prevail only so long as divine power permitted it [Col. 0576B]. When he says “that did not know you,” he mitigates the guilt of the Jews, since, although many had sinned, there were nevertheless among them those who obeyed the Lord’s commands. He says that those who utterly ignored the Lord’s name deserved to be persecuted. Thus guilt that cannot be excused is lightened by comparison with a greater crime.

Nor is it without significance that he first said “upon the nations,” and afterward “upon the kingdoms”: first he invoked punishment upon the peoples, then upon the kingdoms that cruelly ordered such things to be done.

Verse 8. “For they have devoured Jacob, and they have desolated his place.” Instead of the sinful nation, the name of the most beloved patriarch is brought forward, so that remembrance of the holy man might mitigate the people’s offense. This figure is called *anteprosopon*, when a most beloved person is placed in the position of an ungrateful human being [Col. 0576C].

By saying “they have devoured,” he means “they caused to be devoured.” He shows the savagery of the impious nation, since they exposed the corpses of the dead to be eaten by wild beasts. Alternatively, “devoured” signifies those who, having abandoned the Lord’s law, were swallowed up by impious superstition.

It follows: “and they desolated his place.” He laments the overthrow and desolation of the most beautiful city, when, through impious domination and the persuasion of pagan citizens, it was stripped of its inhabitants.

Verse 9. “Do not remember our former iniquities; may your mercy quickly anticipate us, because we have become exceedingly poor.” By confessing their sins, he makes the judge favorable to them, so that one who could not defend himself by justice might expiate his guilt through necessary supplications.

But since Asaph knew that in the time of King Antiochus some Jews [Col. 0576D] would be led astray, abandoning the worship of the Lord to follow abominable idols, he could not pray only concerning ancient sins, since he knew that they would also commit great crimes in future times. Here, however, I think “former” should be understood as “like ancient sins,” sins committed through the abominable wickedness of the world over countless years; as another psalm says: “Behold, you have made my days old” (Ps. XXXVIII, 6).

It follows: “May your mercy quickly anticipate us.” Whoever fears the Lord’s judgment rightly desires to be anticipated by his mercy, because unless pardon comes before the sinner, it will not acquit the erring person in judgment.

He added: “because we have become exceedingly poor.” Poverty in us is the smallness of good works, and we have nothing that we can offer to justice if the force of equity begins to examine us [Col. 0577A]. He adds “exceedingly,” lest anyone presume upon the uprightness of his deeds when he recognizes himself to be exceedingly poor in good merits.

Verse 10. “Help us, O God our Savior, for the glory of your name.” When he says “Help us,” he perhaps signifies the struggle that Mattathias was about to undertake in order to free the Hebrews from the devastation of superstition, so that a cause desperate from the standpoint of human strength might be aided by the Lord’s power. He rightly understood his weakness and invoked the Savior as physician with all his strength, so that the Jews, having been rescued, might return glory to his name. It is useful that he says he is to be helped for the Lord’s glory, not for any merit of his own.

[Col. 0577B]

Verse 11. “Lord, free us, and be merciful toward our sins for the sake of your name.” Whoever despairs of his own strength necessarily runs to the help of the omnipotent judge, so that what cannot be granted through one’s own deeds may be bestowed through the mercy of the holy name. He is called Savior for this reason: because he saves those who hope in him and changes the impending punishments of sinners into rewards.

Verse 12. “Lest the nations say: Where is their God? And let it become known among the nations before our eyes.” He gives the reason why he asked that the Lord’s people should be delivered: namely, lest the faithless utter the familiar saying, “Where is their God?” For although the faithful suffer various scourges, they cannot endure this, when the Creator of all creatures is mocked. By saying “Where is he?” they are thought either to imply that he is not present or that he cannot defend them [Col. 0577C]. See how necessarily, amid their calamities, he recalls that reproach which concerned divine insult.

It follows: “And let it become known among the nations before our eyes.” We must supply “vengeance” here—the vengeance that the Lord usually takes upon the faithless when he compels them to condemn their perverse desires. When he says “before our eyes,” he asks for the vengeance to come quickly, so that he may see happen what he had known could at some time be granted.

Verse 13. “Avenge the blood of your servants, which has been poured out.” He carries out the third part that remained, asking that vengeance be taken for the blood of the faithful who suffered martyrdoms for his name. Vengeance is the means by which violence and injury are defended through just recompense.

But here he seems to desire something that pertains to the conversion of the enemy [Col. 0577D]. For when punishment is inflicted upon them temporally here, they escape the destruction of eternal damnation. Thus we read in the Apocalypse (Apoc. VI, 10) that the souls of the martyrs beneath God’s altar ask to be avenged by divine judgment. This vengeance must be understood in the manner we have described, because the blessed do not cruelly seek vengeance when they have received the command: “Pray for your enemies, do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V, 44), and similar instructions.

Finally, the Lord himself, the most powerful fulfiller of his commands, said while hanging on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

Verse 14. “Let the groaning of the prisoners enter into your sight; according to the greatness of your arm, [Col. 0578A] possess the sons of those punished by death [ms. A., ‘of those put to death’].” He speaks of those whom irreligious paganism had bound for the Lord’s name, and who, with frequent groans, begged the omnipotent Lord that his Church might not fail in their brothers, even if the punishment threatening them should consume them. For holy men always ask for things that advance the increase of faith.

It follows: “According to the greatness of your arm, possess the sons of those punished by death.” A deeply pious and affectionate prayer arises: that the Lord should not cast away from his possession the children of those who had been punished by death for his religion. For at that time there was an innumerable crowd of martyrs there, whose descendants desire to possess the Lord, lest they be corrupted by any error. For whenever he possesses us, the devil’s claims over us have no power.

[Col. 0578B]

Verse 15. “Repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom: their reproach with which they reproached you, O Lord.” “Repay” has the same meaning as the “avenge” mentioned above; although it inflicts affliction upon bodies, it nevertheless brings salvation to souls. By “neighbors” he means those living nearby, concerning whom he said above: “We have become a reproach to our neighbors.”

“Sevenfold” signifies the perfection of the heavenly gift, which we receive when we are filled with the illumination of the Holy Spirit; concerning this it is said elsewhere: “Silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold in the earth” (Ps. XI, 7). There is no doubt that this pertains to their conversion, since they receive the recompense in such a way that they are changed into the better part.

“In their bosom” should certainly be understood as referring to the secret place of their souls, where glorious conversion always takes place [Col. 0578C]. It follows: “their reproach with which they reproached you, O Lord.” Let them who inflicted injuries speak praises; let those who were unbelieving become devoted; let those who were proud become humble. For the Lord is gloriously avenged when he is praised by the mouths of those who cursed him.

Verse 16. “But we, your people and the sheep of your flock, will confess you forever.” He speaks, I think, of those survivors who, gathered through Mattathias’s efforts, deserved to keep the Lord’s law. These truly are the Lord’s sheep, who, confessing his glory, remained firm in faith. This may also be understood generally, so that the Christian people may be seen to be included there, since, as has often been said, one assembly of holy people has been formed from two peoples.

We should note with what sweetness he concluded his lament [Col. 0578D], saying that the flock belonged to the Lord, for which he prayed most devotedly that he not remain angry with those whom he remembered to be his own.

“And forever and ever we shall proclaim your praise.” Here he touches upon the most blessed psalmody of the future age, which the choir of the saints will utter without cessation—not to instruct others, since there will be no ignorant person there, but so that, while returning the honor that is owed, they may themselves be nourished by the sweetness of their praises.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This is now the second psalm that has mourned Jerusalem, worthy of honor, in pious lamentation. But we should know that Psalm seventy-three contains the captivity it suffered under the Romans [Col. 0579A], whereas this one mourns the sacrilegious and most cruel devastation of King Antiochus.

We must also consider and fix deeply in our minds that we are admonished, through the zeal of charity, to rejoice in the prosperity of God’s Church and, again, to be deeply afflicted by its calamities. For it is written: “Blessed are those who rejoice in your peace, and blessed are all who will grieve over all your scourges!” Therefore it is fitting that whatever happens to each of the faithful we should transfer to our own sorrows through the closeness of fellowship, as the Apostle says: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer together; if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice together” (I Cor. XII, 26).

From this lofty charity is acquired; from this the proclaimed unity is found. And if you examine more deeply the cause of this good, from this also arises that heavenly affection [Col. 0579B] which is shown to enrich the Lord’s Church.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM LXXIX

## “For the End; for Those Who Will Be Changed; a Testimony of Asaph; a Psalm”

If someone tries to repeat familiar matters to learned men who have been salutarily instructed in Christ’s assembly, he gives offense. Since all the words of this title are already known, we must inquire into what it newly says: “a testimony of Asaph.”

This Asaph, formerly fearful and anxious, who in the preceding psalms seemed to plead for the sins of the Synagogue, is now filled with such confidence that, with things changed for the better, he appears to offer a testimony of conversion. For he speaks of the first coming of the Lord and Savior, who led the human being, deteriorated by the law of sin, [Col. 0579C] to the gifts of holy conduct, and who strengthened the transplanted vine from Egypt with the root of his power.

This is what is meant by “a testimony for those who will be changed.” This hymn is therefore sung concerning the coming of the husbandman and the Lord’s vine, so that his coming may now be requested not with obscure but with manifest prayers. This psalm is recognized as the second concerning the same matter.

## Division of the Psalm

This Asaph, whom the title announced as changed, asks for the Lord’s coming in the first section. In the second he testifies how the vine, which is the Church, has been spread throughout the whole world. In the third he asks that the Church be visited through the benefit of the Lord’s incarnation, by means of the comparison with the vine, and he asks to cling to the Lord.

## Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0579D]

Verse 1. “You who rule Israel, give heed; you who lead Joseph like sheep [ms. A., ‘a sheep’]; you who sit upon the cherubim, appear.” Through the second kind of definition, called in Greek *ennoematice* (“conceptual or suggestive”), and in Latin *notio* (“notion”), Christ the Lord is asked to come with great desire, so that he may be seen to be fully indicated by what he does.

For this kind of definition is known to indicate each person not by substance but by his acts. Rightly, therefore, it is said to the King of heaven and earth: “You who shepherd Israel,” by whose will all things were created and are governed. But although everything has been placed under his power, he is said to govern those who know how to conduct themselves in heavenly ways [Col. 0580A]. For this reason “Israel” has been added: he governs graciously those who look upon him with a pure heart. Israel is interpreted—as has often been said—as “a man seeing God.”

“Give heed,” as though he said: Pour the light of your mercy upon us, so that we who are darkened in ourselves may be made conspicuous by the brightness of your sight.

It follows: “You who lead Joseph like sheep.” We should understand Joseph as the faithful people, who are led into the Lord’s folds as sheep are gathered for pasture. The name Joseph itself signifies “without reproach,” which certainly suits a devoted people.

And note that proper words have been assigned to the individual persons: the one who is Israel is governed; the one who is Joseph is led. He added: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear.” Cherubim is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” and it is manifest that Christ the Lord sits in this fullness [Col. 0580B]. But since he was still hidden in the secret of his majesty, he asks that he appear through the benefit of holy incarnation, so that he may strengthen his faithful with the firmest belief.

Observe also that the verse is composed with a threefold invocation, signifying that the holy Trinity cooperates in all things.

## Verse 2

“Before Ephraim, and Benjamin, and Manasseh. Stir up your power and come, so that you may save us.”

These names are plainly those of a Hebrew people, before whom he spiritually beseeches God to appear; that is, so that—as had been promised through the prophets—he might be born from the Jewish people. But since these names do not seem to have been fitted together in vain, according to the custom of Holy Scripture, let us diligently seek their interpretations.

Ephraim means “fruitfulness”; Benjamin, “son of the right hand”; [Col. 0580C] Manasseh, “forgotten.” These virtues are certainly present in the Lord the Savior. He was fruitful when, after his body had been put to death for a time, he rose to the eternal kingdoms of heaven. He is the Son of the right hand, that is, the Son of the almighty Father. “Forgotten” indicates the time when, having forgotten his injuries, he prayed on the cross for the Jewish people.

Thus he prayed that he might come in these virtues, which he had no doubt he would accomplish. It follows: “Stir up your power and come, so that you may save us.” The more he knew how great a benefit was to be bestowed upon us through the Lord’s incarnation, the more earnestly he prayed that the Lord would stir up his power and come to wash away the sins of the human race. What desire, what prayers, what vows could suffice to seek that which is able to save the world from its impiety?

[Col. 0580D] ## Verse 3

“God of hosts, turn us, and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

Because he believed that wondrous things were to be accomplished in him, he rightly invoked God as the God of hosts, who alone prevails in freeing us from the death of unbelief. And because he knew himself to be distorted, he earnestly asked to be turned. For to whom would this be fitting except the Lord of hosts, who alone is powerful enough to accomplish everything he wills?

After the benefit of conversion there appropriately follows: “Show your face,” because the Divinity is accustomed to look upon people once their hearts have been converted. What he added—“and we shall be saved”—clearly signifies the Lord the Savior, by whose incarnation we have truly been saved.

## Verse 4

“Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant?” [Col. 0581A]

This must be understood of the time when Asaph was asking that the Lord come. And because, in accordance with the divine dispensation, this had to be deferred for a while, he says: “How long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant,” so that you do not now bring about what you are known to have promised?

Observe also the compassion and desire of the one who is pleading. He believed that the Lord was angry with him because the Lord was delaying assistance to the human race.

## Verse 5

“You will feed us with the bread of tears, and will you give us drink in tears by measure?”

After he had perceived that the matter might be delayed, he enumerates the evils that the Hebrew people would suffer. For he says, “You will feed us with the bread of tears,” signifying that they would live under affliction. The bread of tears is a life full of sorrows; nevertheless, in it we are fed by the Lord’s mercy, when we are not destroyed by disasters [Col. 0581B] and sufferings but rather instructed by them.

It follows: “And you will give us drink in tears.” First he spoke of bread; now he speaks also of drink. These are the two things by which all humanity lives, with bread standing for every kind of food and drink for every beverage. For what period could be free from tears, when even the refreshment itself seemed to be an occasion for weeping?

“By measure”—that is, according to an allotted portion—he says, as the Apostle declares: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide your way out, so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13).

## Verse 6

“You have made us an object of contention to our neighbors, and our enemies have mocked us.”

That opposition by the Gentiles must be understood which rose up against the preachers of Christ through perverse arguments, believing [Col. 0581C] that they could defend what the Gentiles appeared to worship in their temples.

Or rather, it seems to recall the period mentioned above: when, under King Antiochus, certain Jews were sacrificing to idols, they opposed those who appeared to keep the Lord’s law. Therefore, we should understand “neighbors” as relatives, who were attached to them by kinship.

It follows: “And our enemies have mocked us.” The enemies mocked them deservedly, seeing among them so impious a conflict that one party remained steadfast in its ancestral religion while the other was compelled to serve idols.

## Verse 7

“Lord God of hosts, turn us, and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

The verse is repeated, and it has already been shown that it was placed above, before these three verses. For it is characteristic of one who desires something frequently to repeat what he asks to come about with fervent prayers. This face, therefore—that is, the presence of Christ—is the very face through which we have been saved, through which we have escaped the snares of death; finally, it is the face that bestows the kingdoms of heaven both upon the undeserving and upon those who confess.

## Verse 8

“You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.”

He comes to the second section, in which he recalls through mystical figures the events that took place. This rhetorical figure is called *metabole*, the frequent repetition of one matter under varying forms of expression. Through these six verses [276], up to the third division, this vine is described.

By the vine he means the Hebrew people, which is plainly set forth as a type of the Church, from which the congregation of the faithful peoples was born. [Col. 0582A] The vine is so called from vines. He led it out of Egypt through great and famous miracles and, after driving out the nations—that is, the Amorites, Hittites, Jebusites, and the other neighboring peoples—planted it like a wondrous cultivator.

This is the testimony given concerning the Hebrews’ transformation, which is contained in the title. The vine of the Church is also beautifully compared to this: for just as that vine bears necessary fruit among falling leaves, so this one is adorned with the fruit of the saints amid the shadowy crowds of sinners. The saints, pressed as though in winepresses by the affliction of this world, know how to pour forth the sweetest flavor.

Or this may be because a vine prospers more when it is dug around and multiplies when pruned—something attributed solely to the merit of the Church, which is accustomed to grow through the sickle of suffering and to increase continually in the holy people through the blows of persecution. But how this vine has been spread throughout the whole world is declared below.

## Verse 9

“You made a way before it, and planted its roots, and it filled the earth.”

The Lord made a way for this fruitful vine, which embraces the expanses of the world, when he deigned to appear before it. For this was the cause of its progress: that it should see its cultivator and receive from him the rain of preaching, so that it might produce exceedingly sweet fruits.

It follows: “And you planted its roots, and it filled the earth.” Its roots are the prophets, planted through the operation of the heavenly King. From them it extended its fruitful branches and occupied the whole world like pleasant shelters of faith.

## Verse 10

“Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God.”

The breadth and height of this vine are fittingly explained. It knows how to cover those whom it nourishes, because its shadow makes fruitful and causes to grow more abundantly what it is proved to protect more completely.

But what kind of vine is this that covers the mountains? Certainly, it is heavenly, since every height of the earth is beneath the sky.

It follows: “And its branches the cedars of God.” Since he speaks of cedars, he rightly uses the word *arbusta* (“vine-trained trees”); for when vines climb into trees, they are called *arbusta*. Although in the thirtieth psalm we said that cedars were used to signify pride, nevertheless, since “of God” has been added here, we must understand martyrs, who have been established at the loftiest heights in the Church of Christ. The Church protects these also, since they are proved to dwell in her embrace.

## Verse 11

“You extended its branches to the sea, [Col. 0582D] and its shoots to the river.”

The branches signify the Lord’s disciples, to whom he says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John 15:5).

By “the sea” he wishes the most holy faith of all the nations to be understood. He says, “You extended,” because this vine was extended from Jerusalem through the preaching of the apostles into every part of the world. We cannot take this locally, since it has already been said: “You planted its roots, and it filled the earth.”

By its shoots he means the children of regeneration, who flowed forth from the river Jordan, where the Lord deigned to be baptized as an example of our salvation.

## Verse 12

“Why have you torn down its wall [mss. A, F: ‘destroyed it’], and all who pass along the way gather its grapes?” [Col. 0583A]

He wonders why the protection of this vine, which derives its origin from the Jewish people, has been overturned—that is, why the Lord’s defense has been withdrawn. A wall is a protective enclosure constructed solely of stones, which is customarily built around vineyards for their defense. And rightly this word has remained in the earlier translation.

It follows: “And all gather its grapes.” Here “gather its grapes” must be understood in a negative sense, just as Jeremiah says: “See, O Lord, and consider, for you have gathered our grapes. Priest and prophet have perished from your sanctuary” (Lam. 2:20).

Thus “they gather its grapes” means that they plunder and trample it. This is what is usually done by passersby, who, eager to seize spoils, strive to take away the labors of others. The vintage is called the time when the grape is removed from the vine. God also threatens this vine through the prophet Isaiah: “I will destroy its wall, and it shall be for plunder; I will destroy its fence, and it shall be for trampling” (Isa. 5:5).

He added: “Those who pass along the way.” He signifies the nations, which, while passing along the way—that is, Christ the Lord—remained continually in the sacrifices of idols.

## Verse 13

“The boar from the forest ravaged it, and a solitary wild beast devoured it.”

“He ravaged it”: he scattered it everywhere outside its borders and its homeland. This happened to the Jewish people; it is what he said above: “They gather its grapes.”

By the boar we should perhaps understand Vespasian, who proved both strong and savage against them. Through this name it is signified that he was hostile to the Jews, who appeared to regard this animal as unclean among the other animals.

“From the forest,” that is, from the nations, which are rightly compared to rough forests, since they had not yet been cultivated by a fruitful shoot. The boar is so called because it dwells in rugged places.

By “a solitary wild beast” he recalls Titus, his son, who crushed the remnants of the war through such devastation that he consumed the people and city, as though they were grass for pasture, by a terrifying devouring. This necessarily happened to the vine whose wall had evidently been torn down.

Spiritually, however, the boar may be understood as the devil because of his extreme ferocity and strength. He said “from the forest” because his thoughts are always wild and savage.

Observe also that in these six verses mentioned above this vine is described according to the fourth kind of definition, which is called in Greek *hypographikē* and in Latin *descriptionalis*. By using a circumlocution concerning the things said and done, it declares the matter under discussion with appropriate significance.

## Verse 14

“God of hosts, turn; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vine.”

## Verse 15

“And perfect it, which your right hand planted; and upon the son of man whom you established for yourself.”

After recounting all that had happened above, Asaph comes to the third section, in which he asks that the almighty cultivator visit the scattered vine that he had deigned to plant, and look upon the son of man whom he had established for himself.

Having been changed for the better, he sought this singular remedy for all things: that he should entreat Christ the Lord. When he says, “God of hosts, turn,” he asks that the Lord look upon his suppliants with serenity and come to the aid of those in danger.

It follows: “Look down from heaven and see” [Col. 0584A] [277]—namely, with what waves humanity struggles, by what sins it is dragged to the underworld, and how it delights in vices, by which it is plainly extinguished in everlasting death. When he says, “Visit this vine, and direct it, which your right hand planted,” he asks for the coming of the holy incarnation, so that, when its cultivator is present, the planted vine may prosper. Without him it could neither bear fruit nor have a fruitful cultivation.

He added: “And upon the son of man whom you established for yourself.” This makes entirely clear what he said above: “Visit.” The Son of man is Christ the Lord, born from the Virgin Mary and begotten by the Father before all ages. He was established when the truth of the Father’s voice sounded concerning him, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3:17). [Col. 0584B]

## Verse 16

“Burned with fire and dug up, they will perish at the rebuke of your face.”

By “burned with fire and dug up by hand,” we must understand human vices to be signified. Someone is burned with the fire of desire or with the heat of pride when he commits wicked crimes. They are dug up by hand when, through criminal action, we prepare ambushes for others and wish to deceive those who are unaware, while we ourselves fall more deeply into that very pit.

These sins, then, will perish at the rebuke of the Lord’s face, when it is said to them: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:14). They will no longer see the one whom, because of their crimes, they have lost.

## Verse 17

“Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, [Col. 0584C] and upon the son of man whom you established for yourself.”

A great mystery and a great gift of the Divinity are set forth here: for it might perhaps have been doubted for a long time that Israel would be saved, until the saving Lord should come. When he came, the entire promise was fulfilled, and the Church no longer departs from him, being joined to her Bridegroom by spiritual love.

For when he says, “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand,” he asks for the operation of the holy incarnation. He is the right hand of the Father, of whom he says elsewhere: “For I will not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me; but your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your face” (Ps. 43:7, 4).

Then, according to his custom, he repeats for the sake of explanation what he said above: “And upon the son of man.” It should be joined to the preceding words in this sense: “Let your hand”—that is, let the holy operation bring the promise to fulfillment. For the Son of man is the same Lord Christ, who is also the right hand of the Father.

It follows: “Whom you established for yourself.” He was established among human beings—as has already been said—when the voice of the Father’s truth sounded concerning him, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3:17). It is not burdensome to clarify this by repeating the same example, since the same words are plainly repeated in the authority cited.

## Verse 18

“And we shall not depart from you; you will revive us, and we shall call upon your name.”

This part of the verse looks back to what came before. For it says: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand”—that is, deign to send your Son, who will free the guilty world from the crime of sins.

“And we shall not depart from you”: that is, having once conceived him in our mind, may we continually behold him with the eyes of our heart; nor may we be able to withdraw our devotion from you, whose Son we are known to have earnestly desired to come.

The benefit of not departing from him is then explained: “You will revive us, and we shall call upon your name.” You will revive us when, having laid aside the death of sins, we are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit.

“And we shall call upon his name” signifies that, through the saving institution of the Lord Christ, we continually invoke the Father’s name in daily prayer.

## Verse 19

“Lord God of hosts, turn us; and show your face, and we shall be saved.”

The sweetness and usefulness of this verse may be understood from the fact that he mentioned it three times in this psalm, so that, like the expanse of a flowering meadow arranged in ordered rows, the delight of its rosy color might adorn it.

In this brief passage he sets forth the rule of the whole religion. First, the Lord must turn us; second, he must show his face; third, he must make us safe. For he does not show his face before he turns us, nor does he save us unless he has first looked upon us with the light of his mercy.

Therefore, this verse must be stored in the mind, because through it, in brief, we ask for whatever is shown to be beneficial for us.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

It is evident that Asaph was greatly changed for the better, since he saw Christ’s pardon extended throughout the whole world and saw his branches overshadowing the mountains and the cedars. [Col. 0585C]

A truly blessed spectacle, whose beauty is itself a refreshment when contemplated: one vine casting the shadow of its leaves over the whole world, so that none of the faithful might be darkened by the sun. Of them it is written: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120:6).

Indeed, this vine produces holy fruits instead of clusters rich in must; it creates martyrs, raises up prophets, brings forth apostles, and produces countless faithful. Whatever is gloriously accomplished in the holy Church is fittingly applied to this likeness.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 80

**For the end, for the winepresses, of Asaph, on the fifth day of the week.**

That “for the winepresses” signifies the Church was indicated in the preceding titles. But since there we placed this prefiguration in the pressing of grapes, let us now explain it through the harvest of olives.

When a beaten heap of olives has been subjected by the farmers’ skill to weights and begins to be tortured by excessive pressure, both muddy lees and oil of the richest purity flow forth. There is no doubt that this can happen in the persecutions of the Church, when it both reveals pure minds to God and clearly exposes consciences full of dregs.

“The fifth day of the week” signifies the fifth day after the Sabbath, when the Lord, in the creation of the world, created the animals from the waters, as the reading from Genesis testifies: “God said: Let the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls” (Gen. 1:20).

This is joined by an attractive likeness to the grace of baptism, which truly produces living creatures through its fecundity, when the sanctified waters make spotless those whom they received polluted by their own crimes.

But, to gather the matters explained in separate parts [278] into a single sequence, the intention of the title is as follows: “for the end” designates the Lord Christ; “for the winepresses,” the Church; Asaph, the congregation; and “the fifth day of the week,” the baptized. Hence it follows that the psalm speaks in the Lord’s Church to the congregation that has been regenerated. For here Asaph speaks historically to the Jews, but it is better understood spiritually of the Christian people.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first part of the psalm, Asaph speaks to the faithful, so that they should sound forth the Lord’s praises through various musical instruments, since he has deigned to bestow many benefits upon his people.

In the second part, the words are those of the Lord threatening that idols must not be worshiped, but that he alone must be adored, since he is accustomed to provide useful gifts.

In the third part, Asaph again speaks in his own person, reproving the unbelievers for having proved faithless, although the Lord’s gifts had been bestowed upon them with abundant generosity.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob.”

This Asaph, whom we have often said signifies the Synagogue, exhorts the faithful peoples not to cease praising God with the greatest joy, since he has deigned to rescue them from the most savage dangers.

By the word “helper,” the true God is indicated: a false god is not a helper but a destroyer; not one who heals but one who wounds; not one who lifts up but one who plunges down deeply.

When he says “our,” he testifies that he is exhorting the devout. “Shout for joy” derives from helping, that is, from delighting, so that those for whom verbal rejoicing could not suffice might leap into an overflowing and indescribable joy. He teaches that those who rejoice in spirit ought to give thanks to the Lord, not sing while confused by some anxiety.

For if we despise earthly things, we are always glad in him, toward whom a mind that is uncertain and wavering cannot attain.

Jacob signifies the Christian people, to whom the earlier Synagogue consents, since what was taken away from the former has plainly been transferred to the latter through grace. These are those whom he called “the fifth day of the week,” namely, those who are born through sacred regeneration.

### Verse 2

“Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine; the pleasant psalterium with the lyre.”

These are both musical instruments, but they are shown to contain remarkable meanings. For he says: “Take up the psalm, and perform good works.”

The psalm concerns the proclamation of divine words, since its melodious structure—as we have often said—has its resonant body in its head. This rightly refers to the psalm, which always resounds with heavenly mysteries.

The tambourine is an instrument that, with stretched hide, is accustomed to sound when struck, as though joined across two—so to speak—boundaries at its pointed side. Thus the human body, when shaken by tribulation for the Lord’s sake, is more sweetly tuned to heavenly commandments.

He therefore exhorts us that, after receiving divine words, we ought to offer earthly things to the Lord. We give God the tambourine well when we give alms, when we afflict the body with fasts, and when we despise the vices of the world together with their author.

He added: “The pleasant psalterium with the lyre.” He also admonishes us that these two should be joined most agreeably: the words of God contained in the psalterium and the lyre, which is understood to signify human actions, ought to come together in one fellowship. For each melody, joined to the other, is proved acceptable to the Lord.

The psalterium signifies the same thing as the psalm, and the lyre the same thing as the tambourine; but through different names he briefly included the same matters. For how the lyre is formed in relation to the psalterium has often been explained.

In this and the following verse, an enthymematic—that is, rhetorical—syllogism again becomes apparent to us in the same manner: “Singing was commanded in Israel, and judgment belongs to the God of Jacob; therefore the trumpet must be sounded at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of their solemn feast.” Let us now examine the remaining matters.

### Verse 3

“Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of your solemn feast.”

Among other commands, the Jews had been instructed to sound the trumpet for seven days from the first day of the seventh month. They still do this literally today, not understanding that it had been commanded because the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit was to be preached throughout the world to those being baptized.

Therefore he now admonishes the faithful Christians that they ought to sing the Lord’s praises with a herald’s voice when they have received the joys of new regeneration. For when the trumpet is mentioned, it indicates that something is being proclaimed with loud and powerful cries. Thus another prophet also says: “Cry out and lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1).

It should also be considered that through the instruments of musical discipline we are commanded both to sing to the Lord and to complete the day of the solemn feast. Just as those instruments are brought into sweet melody and gently gathered into one harmony, so all our actions should be brought into conformity with the Lord and offered to his ears in the most delightful modulation.

This discipline possesses great power and delightful knowledge. The teachers of secular literature—through God’s generosity, since he grants everything useful—made it known through instruction in their writings, although it had previously remained hidden in the nature of things.

The first division of this discipline is harmonic, rhythmic, and metric. The second division concerns its instruments: percussion instruments, stringed instruments, and wind instruments. The third is divided into six symphonies. The fourth is divided into fifteen tones.

Thus the power of this most beautiful discipline is explained through such ancient distinctions. In secular books we read that many wonders were displayed through these modes. But, to leave aside perhaps-fabulous stories, we read that David drove out a demon from Saul with his melodious lyre (1 Kings 16:23); and Holy Scripture testifies that the walls of Jericho immediately collapsed at the sounding of trumpets (Josh. 6:20). Thus there can be no doubt that musical sounds—when commanded and permitted by the Lord—have often accomplished great deeds.

### Verse 4

“For it is a commandment in Israel, and judgment belongs to the God of Jacob.”

He gives the reason why they should sound the trumpet: because the law was given through Moses among the Israelite people, and once it was known, no one ought to have sinned.

“Judgment belongs to the God of Jacob,” that is, to the God of Christians. For he judged rational creation by heavenly truth [ms. A: “power”], as he says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

Through this wondrous dispensation, therefore, the Lord is plainly to be praised: he both gave the law and made known the future judgment of his majesty. We have said that Jacob signifies the people who follow, who, having been adopted through the grace of Christ, surpassed the commands of the former severity.

### Verse 5

“He established it as a testimony in Joseph when he went out from the land of Egypt; he heard a language that he did not know.”

Joseph signifies increase; the interpretation of this name is a testimony concerning the Hebrew people, who came out of the land of Egypt in great numbers.

But this is aptly applied to our regeneration. For just as that people was brought out safely through the waves of the Red Sea, so we, released from the land of Egypt—that is, from carnal vices—are reborn through the sacred water of regeneration.

Nor is the very name “Red Sea” without significance. For just as it is called Red, so this water may now also be called red, since water came forth together with blood from the side of the Lord the Savior.

It follows: “He heard a language that he did not know.” Here we must understand the commandments of the New Testament as the language. For if you understand it as ordinary speech, how could the Hebrew people have heard a language it did not know, when Christ the Lord is known to have spoken Hebrew?

This therefore means that through the Gospel they heard a language—that is, commandments—that their previous knowledge did not possess. Or it signifies the time when the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in unknown and various languages (Acts 2:4).

### Verse 6

“He turned his back away from burdens; his hands served in the basket.”

Although this appears to be said historically, referring to the time when the Jewish people in Egypt served under various demands—sometimes making bricks, sometimes carrying earth in baskets—we apply it more carefully to the Christian people. God turns the burdens of sins away from their backs when they prostrate themselves in blessed humility, as he himself says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

We call “baskets” the vessels by which we throw out refuse so that the purity of a place may become visible. Their hands, therefore, are held in them by those who are occupied with the filth of sins. But the Lord frees us from this servitude when we are cleansed from the pollution of our crimes.

### Verse 7

“In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction.”

The words of the Lord the Savior are now being reported. There could have been a division here, unless a *diapsalma*—a musical or sectional pause—followed this verse; we believe the division should more appropriately be made there.

But since the speaker has changed, this figure is called *ethopoeia*, whenever we introduce someone as speaking. The benefits are charged against them so that the offense may be judged more serious.

He himself delivers us from tribulation; he himself hears us in the hidden place of the distress of our storm [mss. G and F: “in the hidden distress”] [ms. A: “temptation”]. But he tests us amid the contradictions of heretics, when we are stirred up by various disputes, like winds blowing upon us.

If you refer it to history, he calls it “the water of contradiction” when, in the wilderness, the Israelite people sought watercourses with unbelieving minds.

### Verse 8

“Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you: Israel, if you hear me, there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god.”

After the *diapsalma*—which must be carefully preserved in our divisions—he comes to the second part. But although speaking logically precedes hearing, “Hear” is placed first here, so that you may recognize that the word refers to understanding rather than to the passing sound of the ears.

He also says, “my people,” in order to separate it from that dregs which, like a foul portion of the Church’s winepresses, is cast away. For that is the people of God which does not know how to be mixed with the wicked through any fellowship of morals, but remains most pure in the richness and purity of the oil of Christ’s grace.

It follows: “Israel, and I will testify to you.” Since witnesses are customarily brought before a judge, the Lord himself declares that he is the witness of truth in the judgment, so that no one might doubt the recompense for his deeds when such an advocate was present. Yet he explains this subsequently.

The Lord testifies when, in the judgment of his majesty, he gives each person a sentence according to the quality of his deeds. There witnesses will not be needed for judgment, but the judgment itself will provide testimony concerning our actions. For he will say to the righteous: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25:35), and so forth. To the impious he will charge that they did not do such things. Thus his judgment appears not to be without testimony.

He added: “Israel, if you hear me, there shall be no new god among you.” He repeats “Israel” so that it may recognize itself as his familiar people and turn its desires obediently toward the Lord’s commands.

A great mystery is enclosed in one word, so that the heresy of the future might even then be overcome by the judgment of truth. For he said, “There shall be no new god among you,” lest anyone think that the Father’s Word came into existence in time. One is “new” if he has someone older than himself. Therefore, if he cannot be called new, soundness of mind must confess him coeternal.

And so that no one might call Christ a recent God because he is known to have been born from the Virgin Mary, whose humanity is proved to have come into existence in time, he says: “There shall be no new god for you.” For he is the one who, begotten from the substance of the Father before every beginning, subsists with him in equal coeternity, reigning through infinite ages of ages.

Therefore, in a wondrous and holy brevity, our Fathers preferred it to be said and believed that two natures remain united and perfect in the one Lord Christ, so that the diseased and foul belching of all heretics might be closed, like a deadly opening, by a saving remedy.

When he said “among you,” he signifies “in your heart,” where truth rather than falsehood ought to be found.

He added: “Nor shall you worship a foreign god.” Having forbidden above the worship of a new god, he here forbids the worship of a foreign god, so that it might be understood that it is nearly the same crime to think that God is new and to serve idols with wicked devotion. Let the Arians, therefore, understand with whom they have allied themselves, since they separate themselves from Catholic soundness.

### Verse 9

“For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.”

He gives just reasons why a foreign god should not be worshiped. First, because our God is immutable and eternal, who said of himself: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14).

Then, so that we might understand that everything beneficial that comes to us is accomplished by him, he says: “Who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

This is the second species of definition, called in Greek *ennoematice* and in Latin *notio*, “notion.” It is always formed in this way, when each person is judged by his own deeds, which appear to happen to him alone and not to others.

Although this is said historically concerning the Jews, the whole body of Christians is admonished. For he brings us out of the land of Egypt when, through the grace of regeneration, he frees us from the most dreadful sins to which we were enslaved, when our hands—as he said above—served in the basket.

It follows: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” “Open wide” means “proclaim, disseminate,” namely, by confessing or admonishing, so that you may wish to speak the things that appear worthy of hearing.

For the understanding is filled with spiritual grace when the mouth is known to have been opened in the praises of the Lord, so that by his grace we may begin this and by his gift bring it to completion, as the Apostle says: “You also be enlarged. Do not be yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6:13–14).

### Verse 10

“And my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me.”

[Col. 0590C] ### Verse 11

“And I let them go according to the desire of their heart, and they shall walk in their own wills.”

Although the Lord had filled the mouths of the prophets when they opened them, he says that they were not heard by the Israelite people, since it did not at all fulfill his commands.

He spoke to his people as to oil, so to speak; but the dregs could not hear, since it was like something useless that had to be rejected.

He added: “And I let them go according to the desire of their heart, and they shall walk in their own wills.” Then follows a punishment deserved for sin. For the one who is abandoned from the Lord’s protection is not abandoned without punishment. He afflicts those whom he leaves, because to be deprived of such great goodness is the recompense for all evils.

The sinner thinks it a kind of benefit if he is permitted to fulfill his own desires, while the Apostle says: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity” (Rom. 1:24), and so forth.

**Verse 12.** “If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have reduced their enemies to nothing, and upon those who afflicted them I would have sent my hand.”

It must be asked why he called the people his own, since they were not going to listen to him. He called them his own because he gave them the law and displayed great miracles to them, so that their guilt might increase when the chosen people sinned against him. Observe how, in this first verse, the words that follow explain one another. What he called “my people” signifies Israel. What he said, “had listened to me,” is to be understood as “if it had walked in my ways.” For the one who is not found opposing his commands both listens to the Lord and walks in his ways.

Observe also that the proper order has been preserved. First we must be taught, and then what we have heard must be fulfilled. The reward that the disobedient could not deserve follows: “I would have humbled their enemies for nothing, and against those who afflicted them I would have turned my hand.” These words are to be understood generally, because he resists our enemies when we have become devoted to him through humble submission. For if by doing evil we resist God, he does not in turn oppose our enemies, nor does he place the hand of his protection over those who have withdrawn from him in proud opposition. Hence we must understand that, when he turns away from us, this is not a failure of mercy but the sting of a great punishment.

At times he suspends his protection of the saints when they are tested by tribulations and affliction. But he allows the righteous to be tested in such a way that he does not abandon them; the wicked, however, he permits to suffer in such a way that he makes himself alien to them.

**Verse 13.** “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him, and their time will be everlasting.”

After the Lord’s words, Asaph returns to the third section, rebuking his enemies with a fitting curse. Those lie who, having bound themselves by good promises, relapse again into the worst errors. This could not have been said of the pagans, who had not been constrained by any promise of the Lord.
