And lest, perhaps, when you see them flourishing in this world, you should think that they have already been abandoned, he added: “Their time will be everlasting”—that is, the time of their punishment, when it will be said to them, “Go into the everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41). Of them it is also written: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. 66:24).

The figure called in Greek *eclipsis* (ἔκλειψις), and in Latin *defectus* (“deficiency” or “absence”), is not the kind of deficiency caused by ignorance, but one in which something conceals itself so that it may be sought with particular attention.

**Verse 14.** “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.”

Here the Creator’s mercy is expounded: he filled with his benefits the enemies—that is, the ungrateful—whom he had earlier said were liars. “With the fat of wheat” signifies either manna or the body of the Lord Christ. We call the fleshy fatness of animals *adeps* (“fat”); this name has been transferred figuratively to wheat to signify that some inner goodness resides in it.

“With honey from the rock” means from the wisdom of Christ, because he is the Rock from which the honeys of heavenly teaching flowed. He said “he satisfied them,” that is, he filled them with holy preaching. But the faithless were hungry in faith, for, with their ears made dull, they were unwilling to hear [mss.: “they heard to satiety”].

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us now return to the preceding thought and, like bees settling upon the sweetest flowers, let us pluck pleasant honey through continual repetition; for whenever a salutary matter is repeated, something necessary is always drawn from it.

Therefore let us seek with the greatest diligence why it was said: “There shall be no new god among you,” if we truly wish to be Israel. In this word the most holy power of the whole faith is contained; in this statement that ineffable nature of the divine majesty has been revealed. For if “a new god” is not admitted, the holy Trinity, coeternal with itself, is understood without doubt, because there is no younger where no older is found.

The Father, therefore, is eternal; the Son is eternal; the Holy Spirit is eternal. There is distinction in the persons, but unity is recognized in the nature. The Father is almighty, the Son is almighty, and the Holy Spirit is almighty: a threefold name, but one power and one might. The Son is incomprehensibly begotten from the Father; the Holy Spirit ineffably proceeds from the Father and the Son. The power is not accidental but remains indivisible. It is the supreme greatness shared in communion, the kingdom without end, the everlasting glory—alone creating, alone forgiving sins, and granting the kingdoms of heaven.

It follows: “Nor shall you worship a foreign god.” A foreign god is one who has come into sacrilegious worship through the perversity of foolish people—not possessing the essence of divinity, but receiving the honor of a false majesty; not one who created human beings, but one who was fashioned by human beings. He is truly foreign, since he is found in an alienated mind.

If we reject both of these things, we merit the grace of the true God, because he knows how to cast away those who think wrongly about him and to bestow fitting benefits upon those who believe rightly.

# 281. EXPOSITION OF PSALM 81

**A Psalm of Asaph**

It was said in the preface that all the psalms are Davidic, but that those marked beforehand by a diversity of names were assigned titles because of the meaning of their names [ms. A: “written out beforehand”]. Here Asaph is placed, signifying the Synagogue, which was worthy to behold the Lord Savior also in bodily presence, when the Word deigned to become flesh and to be slain for the sake of our restoration to life.

Indeed, the psalm itself begins in this way: “God stood in the assembly of gods.” Nor should I omit to determine why the ancients called that body a *Synagogue* which in Christian times we now call the *Church*. *Synagogue* generally means an assembly, without sufficiently expressing a gathering of human beings; *Church* (*ecclesia*), however, means a convocation, gathered together from diverse nations. Being summoned together belongs to those who excel in reason, so that we may understand that the Church of God has continually grown both in name and in merits.

## Division of the Psalm

Asaph, who is evidently placed in the title because of the meaning of his name, speaks throughout the psalm against the Jews concerning the coming of Christ. In the first section he warns them that God has stood in their midst, and therefore that they ought not to enter into fellowship with sinners. In the second section he admonishes them to understand that this is Christ, who in the assumption of flesh seemed poor and needy. In the third place he says that they were honored so that they might become sons of God, but that through their own fault they fell into the snares of death.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst he distinguishes among the gods.”

In one remarkable phrase Jesus Christ is declared to us with extraordinary brevity. The God who stood in the assembly is himself the one who sits at the right hand of the Father. These positions are bodily ones. For if you consider his majesty, he is wholly everywhere and fully everywhere; nor can one say that he stands or sits according to the nature of divinity, since he is confined by no determination of place.

But this Asaph, illuminated by divine vision, proclaims that God—Jesus Christ—stood in the Synagogue, whom the crowd of the wicked attempted to resist, so that with paternal affection he might correct those whom he knew to be raging rather against themselves. Thus John the Baptist also says of him: “But there stands among you one whom you do not know” (John 1:26).

He also added “of gods,” so that you might recognize more clearly that this was spoken of human beings, among whom Christ is known to have dwelt bodily, just as the prophet Baruch foretold: “After this he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:38). For we frequently find this said of human beings; hence he also says to Moses: “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7:1). And later the psalm itself will say: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’” For we also call human beings sons of God.

But if you refer this to the nature of divinity, there is one Word who should truly and properly be called by this name. Sometimes we call even the higher powers “gods” figuratively, as the Apostle says: “Although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—yet for us there is one God, the Father” (1 Cor. 8:5–6).

It follows: “But in the midst he distinguishes among the gods.” Here too his incarnation is declared through bodily location. For when he says “in the midst,” he signifies a local space surrounded by crowds. “He distinguishes among the gods,” that is, among the apostles and the righteous who followed the admonitions and faith of his majesty. Distinguishing belongs to divine foreknowledge and understanding, which rescues us from the mass of sin and leads us to the kingdoms of heaven. Hence the Apostle also says: “For who distinguishes you?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

**Verse 2.** “How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to sinners?” [ms. A: *peccatorum*, “of sinners,” for *peccantium*]

By saying “How long?” he accused them of a depraved habit of long duration. They had fiercely resisted the law they had received; they had inflicted the worst deaths upon the prophets sent to them; and they preferred to crucify the Son of God when he came rather than honor him. Thus “How long?” was rightly said, since, insofar as their will was concerned, they had even resolved to kill the Creator himself.

“You show partiality to sinners” was said of those who did not distinguish themselves in that rebellion of the crucifixion, but raged with the raging and shouted with the insane, putting on the face of sinners with grim expressions. For if they had been separated in face, they could also have been separated in their actions.

**Verse 3.** “Judge for the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor.”

After the *diapsalm*—the intervening refrain—he comes to the second section, in which he more earnestly admonishes the Jews that they ought to have understood whom they were seeing and recognized that he had been made humble for their sake, he to whom the powers and dominions of heaven minister; that he had been an orphan, though he is the ruler of all; needy, though he cannot be exhausted by giving; poor, though all things created in heaven and on earth belong to him.

He therefore admonishes them to justify the very one whom the Jews’ insolence desired to destroy. It is beautifully said, “the orphan,” since an earthly father did not provide him with human assistance. For just as before the foundation of the world the Word was without a mother, so at the time of his incarnation that same Lord Christ existed without an earthly father.

**Verse 4.** “Rescue the poor, and free the needy from the hand of the sinner.”

These words are understood to be addressed to those who did not themselves take part in the Lord’s death, but were unwilling to oppose the criminal presumption of others, so that they might both free him from bodily destruction and remove themselves from complicity in wickedness. Of such people it is also said elsewhere: “They are mute dogs that do not know how to bark” (Isa. 56:10).

They are therefore admonished not to cease rescuing the one unjustly handed over, since they were about to sin through an iniquitous crime. For when you are able to oppose the wicked, if you cease resisting them, that is consent to error.

That the poor and needy can be spoken of as the Lord Savior has often been expounded: when he assumed humanity, he also assumed the deprivation of our poverty, as it is said elsewhere: “I am poor and in pain” (Ps. 68:30).

**Verse 5.** “They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness. All the foundations of the earth will be shaken.”

A true conclusion and a brief statement: they did not understand the author of light, although they walked in darkness. Of them the Apostle says: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

It follows: “All the foundations of the earth will be shaken,” so that you may recognize more truly of whom the preceding words were spoken. He refers to the sign that is known to have occurred at the Lord’s crucifixion, as the teaching of the Gospel testifies: “The earth was shaken, the rocks were split” (Matt. 27:51), and so forth. If this were transferred to other causes, as the faithless Jews wish, it could in no way fit.

But “the earth was shaken” can also be understood spiritually, because at that time many sinners—that is, earthly people—believed when they saw so great a miracle. Among them the centurion exclaimed: “Truly this was the Son of God” (ibid., 54).

**Verse 6.** “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’”

He comes to the third section, turning his words toward the apostles and the other righteous. This honorable name is given only to the faithful, of whom he said above: “God stood in the assembly of gods.” They had therefore received promises such that, if they kept the Lord’s commands, they would be called sons of the Most High—by grace, certainly, not by nature.

For the Word alone is substantially and properly called the Son of God, as in the passage: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son’” (Ps. 2:7). All who obey his holy commands are called his sons, as it is written in the Gospel: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

Observe also that, through the thirteenth species of definition, which the Greeks call *kat’ analogian* (κατ’ ἀναλογίαν, “by analogy”) and the Latins *juxta rationem* (“according to reason”), human beings are called gods and sons of God. This arises when an inferior thing is defined by the name of a greater thing. This argument is also a comparison from the lesser to the greater, for human beings are lesser than gods.

**Verse 7.** “But you will die like human beings, and like one of the princes you will fall.”

In the preceding verse he spoke to the righteous; now he turns his words toward the wicked. He rebukes unbelievers who preferred to die through pride rather than live through obedience. By saying “like human beings,” he signifies sinners, who were redeemed at no price and were not made free from their bondage.

He added: “And like one of the princes you will fall.” “One of the princes” signifies the devil, who fell when he was cast down from heaven and received the punishment for his perversity.

**Verse 8.** “Arise, O God; judge the earth, for you will inherit among all the nations.”

To whom is “Arise” said, except to the one who was foreseen as destined to be killed? “Judge the earth” is said to that same one of whom it is written: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all the nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. 25:31–32).

“You will inherit among the nations”—that is, the earth mentioned above, the earth which the blessed will possess and from which they will receive the eternal joy of great happiness.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Hear, O Jews; understand, O obstinate ones, how much this Asaph has spoken concerning the Lord’s coming. What do you worship if you do not know the words of your prophets? Come to Catholic priests; let your ears be opened so that, by the Lord’s gift, you may escape your long-standing deafness.

You also, who burn with the deadly vapor of Nestorius and Eutyches, should be healed by the first verse of this psalm. Of whom is it said, “God stood in the assembly of gods,” and it follows, “but in the midst he distinguishes among the gods”? He stood in respect of his humanity; he distinguished in respect of his divinity. One and the same Lord Christ is both: both are true, both are perfect.

To profess two natures divided according to two persons in the Lord Christ is an error of the same kind as believing in one nature confused, even though there is unity of person. To you must be spoken that verse of Sedulius:

> *Ambo errore pares, quanquam diversa sequantur.*

“Both equal in error, although they pursue different things.”

For if he did not raise the human being to the heavens, tell us whom he redeemed. For you read that the form of a servant was assumed, not absorbed. But no one was then allowed to perish, when he received it so that it might never be able to perish.

For if, as you Eutychians think, one nature has now been produced through your confusion, how is the Son of Man still foretold as coming to judge? Or how will the wicked see the one whom they pierced (Zech. 12:10)?

Finally, so that this conviction might be utterly removed, after the resurrection he himself answered Thomas in his doubt: “Put out your hand and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (John 20:27; Luke 24:39).

Consider also the absurdity that follows from your position. For when you say that one nature has been made from two, you either believe that confusion has resulted, or you shamelessly maintain that one nature has perished. Why do you refuse to confess what pleased our Fathers when the Holy Spirit revealed it to them?

Certainly, if you do not wish to believe in two natures—unconfused, unchangeable, undivided, and inseparable—then say “two substances,” say “two forms,” as the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped; rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:6–7).

The only point is this: do not, by rejecting the saving doctrine, prepare eternal destruction for yourselves.

It should be known, moreover, that this is the fifth psalm among those which, as we have stated, were written concerning the two natures of the Lord Christ.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 82

**A Song of the Psalm of Asaph**

We explained the significance of “a song of the psalm” in the preface and frequently stated in the titles, wherever the passage required it, that the force of these names draws us toward that understanding by which, amid practical matters, we continually lift our minds toward divine contemplation.

There is no doubt that *Asaph* means “assembly” in Latin. But this Asaph, whenever he is introduced, is not himself the author of the song, as we have already said; rather, because of the meaning of his name and the virtues of the psalms, he has appropriately been placed in the titles.

## Division of the Psalm

Asaph, who had already foretold much concerning the Lord’s incarnation in the preceding psalms, now speaks in the first section about his second coming. He asks that, since at the end of the age his enemies will be raised up excessively through the Antichrist, his judgment may come quickly, lest the prolonged license of so great an enemy be able to devastate the whole Church.

In the second section he entreats that vengeance be taken upon them through certain likenesses expressed in names—not from a desire to curse, but from a wish for correction.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “O God, who will be like you? Do not remain silent, and do not be restrained, O God.”

This figure is called *epanalepsis* (ἐπανάληψις), that is, the repetition at the end of a verse of the word placed at its beginning.

We must consider what this beginning means, since in the greatest brevity it encloses the mysteries of great things. Who, indeed, will be like the one who completed heaven and earth, and all that is in them, with instantaneous speed? For although the Lord Christ, who lived among the Jews, was believed by the faithless merely to be someone like them—to such an extent that they scourged him and condemned him by a perverse judgment—this outstanding man, who contemplated Christ in the greatness of his power, rightly professes that no one is like him. Clothed in the reality of flesh, he did not diminish the rights of his divinity, but, while always remaining with the Father, deigned to dwell among us.

Thus it is truly said: “Who will be like you?”

It follows: “Do not remain silent, and do not be restrained, O God.” Here the power of the future coming is already declared, when the one who judges will not be silent, nor will the one revealed through the manifestation of his power be restrained.

It is evident that such things did not occur at the first coming, when “he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). He also restrained his power when he allowed himself to be held as though guilty and offered no resistance to Pontius Pilate. These things will cease in the future judgment, where the power of his divinity will shine forth.

**Verse 2.** “For behold, your enemies have resounded, and those who hate you have lifted up their head.”

He matches each statement with its counterpart. Against “Do not remain silent,” he adds, “For behold, your enemies have resounded”; against “Do not be restrained,” he gives the reason: “Those who hate you have lifted up their head.”

But this whole passage is more fittingly applied to the times of the Antichrist, when the Lord’s enemies will resound with tumultuous rebellions. He rightly did not say “they spoke,” but “they resounded,” so that words might be denied to those who, by the standard of human beings, had no rational voices.

Observe also that he said “those who hate” in the plural, and then follows, “they have lifted up their head,” although he could have said “their heads.” But all the insane have one head: the Antichrist. He says that it has been lifted up because he will boast of great power, even daring to call himself the exalted god.

**Verse 3.** “They have cunningly devised a plan against your people, and they have plotted against your saints.”

This is more a mocking than a sorrowful complaint: that those destined to perish have plotted against the Lord’s people and, through cunning falsehood—that is, through a deceitful will—have attempted to deceive those who are known to be fortified by devotion to the truth.

But to expose their frivolity more fully, he added: “Against your saints,” so that they might attempt to bring destruction not only upon ordinary people but, in a certain sense, upon the heavenly men themselves.

**Verse 4.** “They said: ‘Come, let us destroy them from the nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.’”

He reports the empty words of madmen, which he rightly said above to have “resounded” rather than “been spoken.” For the persecution of the Antichrist will be carried out with this intention: that the Christian name might be utterly removed from the face of the earth as though it were some evil thing. They do not know that, while they desire to kill Christ’s servants, they will complete the number of the saints through continual persecution.

By saying “from the nation” in the singular, he signifies the Christian people. Although it is taught to have been gathered from many nations, it is rightly called one nation because it is known to have been generated from the one fountain of baptism.

Alternatively, that persecutor may have said “one nation” of those whom he recognized as joined together in one will. Or it may be understood through the figure of *exallage* (ἐξαλλαγή), that is, alteration, when the singular is placed for the plural.

**Verse 5.** “For they have plotted together in agreement; against you they have established a covenant.”

In the divine Scriptures, *testamentum* (“covenant” or “testament”) does not refer only to the covenant of the dead, but also to an agreement made between the living, because Scripture bears witness to the minds of those who enter into a pact. Thus we read that Laban and Jacob made a covenant (Gen. 31:44), since they are shown to have made an agreement with each other while still alive.

The wicked are likewise said, in a certain sense, to have made a pact when, united in purpose, they persecute those who dissent from their error. Observe that by saying “against you” he aroused envy against the adversaries. Orators, transferring this kind of argument to their own purposes, are accustomed to move the minds of judges in every way.

**Verse 6.** “The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites” [mss. A, F: *Ismahelitae*, “Ishmaelites”].

**Verse 7.** “Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek; and foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.”

**Verse 8.** “For Assur also came with them; they became a support for the sons of Lot.”

The enumeration of these names, which these three verses contain, reveals the enemies of Christ. Let us explain their meanings, so that everything may appear to correspond to the times of the Antichrist.

Edomites means either “bloody” or “earthly.” Ishmaelites means “obedient to the world, not to the Lord.” Moab means “from the father,” signifying a sinner in such a way that his disobedience is referred to the father Adam. Hagrites means “sojourners” or “newcomers.” Gebal means “empty valley.” Ammon means “turbulent people.” Amalek means “licking people,” that is, flattering deceitfully. Tyre means “narrowness.” Assur is placed here for the devil himself, who truly came with them to attack the faithful. Lot means “the one who turns aside.” Hence that name is fittingly placed at the end, as though he were saying: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3).

This crowd of the lost, which is to be gathered under the Antichrist, is clearly expressed through an allusion to such names, so that you may rightly understand that the names of so many evils have been heaped together in that people.

We must also remember that these verses proceed through the figure of *polysyndeton*, “the use of many conjunctions.” If you read them carefully again, you will find that they are joined together by many conjunctions.

**Verse 9.** “Do to them as to Midian and Sisera; as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon.”

**Verse 10.** “They perished at Endor; they became like dung upon the earth.”

He comes to the second section, where, in the spirit of prophecy, he prays that they may receive their recompense according to the order of future events. Since above he had described their character through the collected names, now he also prays that retribution may be made upon them through comparisons with nations whom the Israelite people overcame with the Lord’s help.

Midian means “turning aside from judgment.” Sisera means “exclusion from joy.” Jabin means “wise,” but this Jabin is worldly; of him the Apostle says: “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe?” (1 Cor. 1:20). All of them perished in the torrent of Kishon and at the spring of Endor. They became like dung upon the earth when their corpses dissolved in bodily decay, as it is written: “You are earth, and into earth you will go” (Gen. 3:19).

A similar end is therefore desired for those who will remain in their obstinacy: for just as those former enemies fought against the Israelite people, so these will fight against the most faithful people of that time, namely, Christians.

**Verse 11.** “Set their princes like Oreb and Zeb, and Zebee and Salmana, all their princes.”

He continues in the same enumerations, where only an explanation of the names is necessary. As for the reasons for which they were used, we retain what we recently stated.

Oreb means “dryness.” Zeb means “wolf.” Zebee means “victim.” Salmana means “shadow of disturbance.” All these things he desires for the army of the Antichrist, who are not to be saved through any conversion. Their detestable destruction is already perceived in the dark meanings of their very names.

We say that this manner of expression is proper to the divine Scriptures, so that through interpretations of names we may perceive the force of what is said.

**Verse 12.** “They said: ‘Let us possess for ourselves the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’”

This is the same thing he had said above: “Come, let us destroy them from the nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.” Here the princes of evil counsels are signified as their authors.

“Let us possess as an inheritance” is set against the fact that the inheritance belongs to the Lord, so that they might strive to seize the inheritance which the Lord rightly claimed for himself. What this inheritance is, however, is explained next: “the sanctuary of God,” that is, the Christian people, of whom the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

**Verse 13.** “My God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind.”

**Verse 14.** “Like a fire that burns forests, like a flame burning up mountains.”

We have joined these two verses because of the similarity of their subjects; in them manifold calamities are foretold for unbelievers.

The wicked, while they revolve in evil thought, become like wheels, which, with their rear portions raised, seem to send their fronts backward; they accomplish nothing, while they are worn down by their own turning.

A second comparison follows: the fickleness of sinners is carried away like something borne along by the wind, flying here and there and always moved by an uncertain will. “The face of the wind” means the presence of the wind itself. The wind is not marked out for us by some figure; we perceive it as bodily only in this respect, that we are struck by its force and its courses.

He also placed fire and flame for the time of judgment, when both the thick forests of sins and the mountains of pride will be burned.

**Verse 15.** “Thus you will pursue them in your tempest, and in your wrath you will trouble them.”

“Thus you will pursue them” refers back to what he said above, so that they must be destroyed in the manner described by the preceding comparisons.

Other comparisons are introduced: “In your tempest, and in your wrath you will trouble them.” “In your tempest,” that is, at the time of judgment, which is rightly compared to a storm: first, because it is unexpected; then because it suddenly disturbs with a crash, and the sudden magnitude of danger removes the possibility of deliberation.

A tempest of rain is a kind of agitated disturbance of the air, in which we are violently shaken while we are afflicted by an excess of waters.

It follows: “And in your wrath you will trouble them.” We have often said that wrath cannot properly belong to the divine nature, but that the term has been taken from human beings, who, when they judge criminals, are stirred by a fervor of spirit. They do not come to condemn people in any other way than by being aroused by the crimes they have committed.

**Verse 16.** “Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord.”

Up to this point he has prophesied future punishments for those sinners who remained obstinate in their crimes. Now he turns to those who, by the Lord’s favor, are destined to believe.

The faces of those who find no praisers of their sins are filled with disgrace; rather, in the present life they are held accountable for what they have done in evil action. Reproach often corrects such people when they see themselves condemned by the community at large.

**Verse 17.** “Let them be confounded and troubled forever and ever; let them be ashamed and perish.”

He returns again to the obstinate, who will not possess God’s gifts. Some can be profitably confounded and ashamed in this age, when they receive the gifts of conversion. But those who are to be condemned to eternal punishment are confounded and troubled forever and ever.

It follows: “Let them be ashamed and perish.” The meaning is the same as he expressed above: there they do not advance through shame, but perish, since they are destined for eternal punishment.

**Verse 18.** “And let them know that your name is ‘Lord’; you alone are the Most High over all the earth.”

“Let them know” refers to both kinds of sinners: those who will perish through their obstinacy and those who will be freed after offering satisfaction. All recognize the Lord’s omnipotence, because he alone is the Most High, when they come to know that he both spares those who are converted and condemns the hardened to eternal punishment.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us remember that this Asaph was not introduced without purpose in the preceding eleven psalms, so that the hardest hearts of the Jews might be softened by the repeated voice of their own Synagogue, and so that they themselves might grow in devotion to the very name to which they seemed dedicated.

Therefore the preachers have a responsibility, provided that the obstinacy of the lost does not obstruct them. Everything concerning the Lord’s incarnation has been fulfilled; everything concerning the faith of the nations has been made manifest. The time of judgment remains, which we all generally await. But first it is necessary to believe, lest the punishment foretold there be able to condemn the wicked.

# 285. EXPOSITION OF PSALM 83

**For the end; for the winepresses; of the sons of Korah; a psalm**

What “for the end” signifies has often been explained. And since, in connection with the preceding titles, we have said that “for the winepresses” pertains to the Church, it is nevertheless worthwhile to examine carefully why the Church appeared to receive such a name.

A hanging, untouched grape and an olive berry set upon the tree do not reveal the quality of their most pleasant flavor. But when both reach the winepress and, compressed under great weight, are emptied of their bulk, then the fruits of their sweetest liquid flow forth—fruits whose contents, stored within their skins, had not previously been visible.

So, when the Church of God is crushed by afflictions and persecutions, the merits of the saints are revealed, merits that were not known in times of peace. The pressure of this winepress therefore sanctifies, its crushing improves; its labor is heavenly fruit, and its present punishment is everlasting rest.

Nor is it without significance that “for the winepresses” is placed only in the eighth psalm, the eighty-eighth, and here. It signifies that this mystery of the Church belongs to the holy Trinity, since it has been consecrated by the repetition of the threefold number.

We have already stated above that Korah is interpreted as “baldness.” The interpretation of this name announces the place of Calvary, where Christ the Lord is known to have been crucified. Therefore the sons of Korah signify Christians in every respect, and this psalm is sung in their person.

Observe also that this is the second psalm concerning the Lord’s most precious charity, which joins us above all else to divine grace.

## Division of the Psalm

One general person is introduced in the name of the sons of Korah, whom we have said, through the signification of Calvary, belong to Christ the Lord. At the beginning of the psalm this person displays the Church’s immeasurable desire.

In the second section he declares blessed the one to whom the Lord grants assistance and enables to attain the grace of confession. In the third he says that it is far better to dwell as an outcast in the house of the Lord than to enter the tents of sinners with whatever worldly honors.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts!”

The son of Korah, regenerated through spiritual fruitfulness and appropriately pressed in the winepresses of the Church, longs to reach the future Jerusalem. There there will no longer be burdens of tribulation, but he will enjoy secure blessedness and undisturbed happiness.

By saying “How,” he could not express the greatness of the matter; rather, he left it to be understood as something wholly beyond measure. For who could comprehend with what breadth either an afflicted person seeks rest or mortal existence longs for eternity?

For when he says “Lord of hosts,” I do not know how great a power he sensed to be present there. Although he could not set forth such a gift in words, he nevertheless showed that some immense good was present. This figure is called *emphasis*, which leaves more to the understanding than it actually says.

### Verse 2

“My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God.”

Whatever is undertaken beyond human strength necessarily involves languishing in proportion to the greatness of the matter. For one must languish toward that which the mind, directed toward the present, cannot yet attain. This most holy man was contemplating the Lord’s powers and rewards, those heavenly blessednesses and joys, and Jerusalem rejoicing immortally from mortal peoples; and it was necessary that his very senses should succumb amid their joys, since he could not immediately reach the object of his desire. But how vigorous this languishing is, how extremely powerful this weariness, he appropriately explains by saying: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God.”

Although both seem to pertain to the flesh, there is no doubt that “heart” can refer to understanding. For when we wish to proclaim someone’s wisdom, we praise that person’s heart without hesitation. He says that both elements of which humanity consists—that is, body and soul—have burst forth into heavenly joy. Yet we should note how distinguished this man was in holiness: not only his soul but even his flesh, which is demonstrably more liable to the fault of transgression, burst forth in the Lord’s exultation by a blessed lot, foreseeing the good things of the future age, which he believed he would attain through the Lord’s gifts.

### Verse 3

“For indeed the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest for itself where it may place its young.”

After saying above that soul and body rejoice in the Lord’s exultation, he is here recognized as having introduced these two kinds of birds to commend a certain likeness. The sparrow is exceedingly swift in its speed. It cannot tolerate dwelling in the forests, but eagerly seeks a house for itself in holes in walls. When it has found one, it exults with immense joy, because it believes that it will no longer be exposed to the snares of various adversities. So the soul rejoices when it realizes that its dwelling has been prepared in the kingdoms of heaven.

The turtledove, however, is most chaste through its moderation in abstinence. Content with a single union, it is known to build a nest for its young. Unlike the sparrow, it does not find a prepared house but strives to construct a new one for itself from various small pieces. Our flesh is not improperly compared to it, since it rejoices to have placed its works under the Lord’s command. Through it, sacrifices of fasting are offered acceptably; we give food to the poor; we bury the dead; we serve the sick; we visit those held in prison; and we perform the other works of piety that are known to be accomplished through bodily ministries.

Others have applied the turtledove to the holy Church, because apart from Christ the Lord it knows no other companionship.

### Verse 4

“Your altars, Lord of hosts, my King and my God.”

This verse responds to what precedes. For he says, “Your altars, Lord of hosts,” to which must be joined what was said in the first verse of the psalm: “How lovely they are!” This figure is called *ἀπὸ κοινοῦ*, that is, “from the common,” when words stated above respond to what follows.

But since he had previously spoken of the sparrow’s house and the turtledove’s nest, he now shows what we ought to understand in them. In these altars, as in a most welcome house, the faithful soul rejoices [ms. G. and ed., *fritinnit* (uncertain reading)]. In these altars the works of the flesh—provided that they are holy—are stored. In that altar the firmest hope is placed, where the souls of the blessed feast on heavenly banquets as though at an everlasting meal: where satiety stimulates desire all the more, and blessed hunger never departs.

He also added, “My King and my God.” He is called “King” from ruling; “God,” clearly, from creating, although this name also appears to signify fear.

### Verse 5

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; they will praise you for ever and ever.”

He has already stated what gift those altars bestow. For if someone is considered blessed when everything favorable proceeds well for a time and no adversity shakes him, what should we think of that blessedness in which nothing comparable is found, either in quality or in perpetuity? Yet although this good cannot be explained in human words, its source is nevertheless not concealed. He says, “They will praise you.” From this comes that wondrous blessedness; and so that you might understand it as eternal, he added, “for ever and ever.” But what, I ask, will the joy of that age to come be like, where one will be granted abundant rejoicing and will never be able to depart from it?

### Verse 6

“Blessed is the man whose help is from you, Lord; his ascents are in his heart.”

Having completed his contemplation of future happiness, he comes to the second mode, in which he also shows God’s servant to be blessed here, lest the faithful be thought to have been entirely deprived of rewards in this life. By saying, “whose help is from you, Lord,” he revealed the difficult labors and struggles involved here. He added, “his ascents are in his heart.”

Certainly, for the blessed man whose help is from the Lord, ascents are in his heart, because he always progresses and always rises; and to the extent that the Lord grants help, he is lifted higher toward heaven. It is like what we say, for example, when someone conquers lust with the Lord’s help: he has climbed the first step. When he has mastered pride, he leaps to the second. When he has overcome greed, he ascends the third. He is raised by as many steps as he has been freed from vices.

Thus, by the fifth species of definition, which in Greek is called *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν* and in Latin “word for word,” the definition of the blessed person has been established. For it embraces what it means to be blessed: to have help from you, Lord.

### Verse 7

“He has appointed in the valley of tears, in the place that he appointed; for he will give blessing, the one who gave the law.”

The valley of tears is the humility of the penitent. From it a person ascends to higher things in proportion to how deeply he has descended in that satisfaction. But lest you perhaps ask where one ascends, he added, “in the place that he appointed.” That appointed place signifies the future kingdom of the Lord, which we shall deserve to reach by a blessed lot if we desire to attain it according to the rules appointed by the Lord.

For he himself appointed both the steps and the place, since he ordered them. Whoever wishes to receive the reward should hear what is commanded. It follows: “For he will give blessing, the one who gave the law.” Since the time of prophecy was established under the Lord’s law and the gift of grace had not yet come, he says that the same one who gave the law before righteousness would give the blessing—that is, his grace. He thereby teaches clearly that the Lord Christ is the author of both Testaments, when he says, “He will give blessing, the one who gave the law.”

### Verse 8

“They will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion.”

Strength was first in the law; now strength is in grace. Grace is more pleasing, for it redeems [ms. F., “remits,” *remittit*], whereas the law judges. May he himself, who gave both, grant that, since we do not deserve to receive good things through the law because of our sins, he may deign to bestow absolution upon us through grace.

Yet let the Christian understand that he must walk from strength to strength, lest he surrender himself to idleness. It follows: “The God of gods will be seen in Zion.” Behold, he says that those two strengths come together in the one person of Christ. For he himself was seen at Jerusalem on Mount Zion, the one who gave both law and grace.

But how should we understand “the God of gods”? This was recently explained in the eighty-first psalm, since divine Scripture does not cease to call holy men “gods.” Thus he is called “God of gods” in the same way as “King of kings,” “Holy of holies,” and “Lord of lords.” He said, “will be seen,” not “will be understood,” because the former was for all, whereas the latter is for few.

### Verse 9

“Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer; listen with your ears, God of Jacob.”

So that you might truly understand that there is one God of those strengths which he mentioned above—“They will go from strength to strength”—he himself also cried out and confessed: “Lord God of hosts.”

And who is this God of hosts? “The God of Jacob,” that is, the Lord Christ, who is recognized as the most merciful supplanter of his enemies, since he causes their perverse wickedness to arrive, directed, at the paths of virtue.

Or the meaning may rather be that, just as Jacob was made to be called Israel because he had seen God, so he might also cause this most faithful man, who speaks here, to behold the eternal glory of his majesty.

### Verse 10

“Our protector, look upon us, God, and look upon the face of your anointed.”

He comes to the third mode, in which he prays that the Lord Savior be made known to the world. The most holy man does not desire these things as though he were uncertain; rather, he asks that what he knew was to come might happen quickly.

And because he knew that the world would be saved through our Redeemer, he asks that the Father look upon the human race in such a way that he looks upon the face of his Christ—not because he ever fails to look upon him, but so that through the presence of the incarnation he might make him known to the nations, to whom he had previously been unknown by face.

This figure is called *hypallage*, in Latin “permutation,” whenever the one who looks is spoken of as being looked upon, or something similar occurs—usages frequently found in the divine Scriptures. Thus it is said: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 52:3). For he said “to see,” that is, “to cause to be seen.” The same applies to: “Understand my cry.” This does not mean that the one being entreated should himself understand, since he knows all things as they are, but that he should cause them to be understood by those who are known to be ignorant.

### Verse 11

“For one day in your courts is better than thousands.”

### Verse 12

“I have chosen to be abject in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”

These are the Lord’s courts in which, as he testified above, he had longed and languished, and in which one day is rightly desired. For it is always eternal: it does not arise with the sun’s arrival or end with its setting; tomorrow does not follow it, nor does yesterday precede it. Remaining immutable, it stands in perpetual unity.

“Than thousands” signifies this world, where thousands of days come to an end, and that one day surpasses whatever is amassed through the multiplication of these. Therefore it is rightly sought with such desires, since nothing comparable is found.

This figure is called *parison*, that is, “equalization of a statement,” when two things are set in opposition but one is preferred—as he did here, above, and will do below.

It follows: “I have chosen to be abject in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.” The wise man did not judge by the eyes of the flesh but by the sight of truth itself, choosing to be abject in the Lord’s house rather than to live in the glory of the world as a criminal.

O beautiful abjection! O most shameful sublimity! This is surely what is called above the valley of tears, unquestionably higher than all palaces. Although one mourns there for a time, from there one rejoices without end.

A person is called “abject” who is regarded as lowest in human estimation. But before God the one is judged more honorable who, because of his name, appears despised among human beings.

### Verse 13

“For the Lord God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory.”

The reason is given why the Lord’s house should be loved more than the tents of sinners. In his Church there is first mercy, because he makes the righteous out of sinners, and he has not denied them the truth of the promised reward. As the Apostle says: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13). And shortly afterward: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is reserved for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

Behold, he has embraced both the Lord’s mercy and his truth. He also adds: “The Lord will give grace and glory.” Lest you think that the saints have received grace alone in this age, it follows: “And the Lord will give glory.” Here he first grants grace, so that sinners may be converted to life; in the future he will give glory, so that those justified by the divine gift may deserve to become companions of the angels.

Grace is called “freely given,” as the Apostle says: “But if it is by grace, it is not by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Rom. 11:6). This is indeed the grace of the Lord Christ, which prepares us, assists us, strengthens us, and crowns us.

### Verse 14

“He will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things.”

It is punishment for the wicked alone to be kept away from the divine gift. It is clear, however, that innocence is full of God’s gifts, but this innocence must be understood from the end of its name: an innocent person is one who harms no one.

Such a person, therefore, cannot be deprived of God’s gifts, since he has already received here the gifts of blessed conversion [ms. A. and ed., “conduct,” *conversationis*]. The innocent person is one who is appointed here in the valley of tears, who chooses to be abject in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners, and who does the other similar things he mentioned above.

### Verse 15

“Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.”

He could not explain all the good things that his holy soul perceived, and therefore this should be read with wonder: “Lord God of hosts,” who do such great things that human beings cannot recount them.

Finally, he introduced something different from what he had announced: “Blessed is the man who hopes in you.” This figure is called *paraprosdocia*, in Latin “an unexpected ending”: that is, when one thing is proposed and another follows.

Let us therefore understand, as far as we can, how the divine meaning shines forth with manifold beauty, so that what he could not explain in many words he might conclude in a few. Blessed is the one who has placed his hope in eternal happiness. Blessed is the one whose good things do not perish. But ultimately, perfectly blessed is the one whose hope continually remains in the Lord.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

A wondrous psalm, sweeter than every worldly delight, which has made the Church’s winepresses altogether sweet for us, so that we prefer to be pressed down beneath such a burden rather than lifted up by the world’s felicities. Hence we now rightly say: “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord.”

Let us therefore ask the holy Trinity that, just as the sweetness of the present reading has affected our senses, so what it has mercifully poured into us may remain continually within us.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 84

## For the end, a psalm for the sons of Korah

“In the end” is clearly understood in the titles to signify the Lord Savior, as the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

“A psalm for the sons of Korah.” What Korah signifies, we have often already said. For the present, it is enough to recall this in brief: this psalm is spoken about those who have already believed sincerely in the Lord Savior. The present psalm is approved as the third concerning his first coming.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first part of the psalm, the prophet briefly gives thanks to the Lord because, from the ancient condition of the Jewish nation, a people has come to the worship of the Lord Savior.

In the second part, he recounts how the Lord deigned to mitigate his anger against the Jewish people, while seeking the coming of Christ, in whom human blindness received the clearest light of faith.

In the third part, he turns his words toward himself and, in the spirit of prophecy, clearly proclaims the coming of the incarnate Word.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“You blessed your land, Lord; you turned away the captivity of Jacob.”

Foreseeing future miracles, the Psalmist rejoices as though over something past, declaring that the land was blessed by the Lord’s coming—that is, the flesh which he himself deigned to assume.

As we have often said, the patriarch Jacob signifies the faithful people, who were freed from the captivity of the devil when they deserved to be saved by the Lord’s mercy. By saying, “You turned away the captivity,” he shows that it had indeed been thickened by human iniquities but was removed by divine mercy.

### Verse 2

“You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sins.”

To forgive is to release a debt, not through the intervention of some cause but out of regard for compassion. Thus the Lord forgave guilt when he brought the guilty to pardon. This is what he said above: “You turned away the captivity of Jacob.”

The captivity was that of sin when the world, enslaved to idols, lay subject to them. But when the Lord Savior came, there is no doubt that it was covered—that is, blotted out. At his coming, our freedom lifted its head, and the devil’s pride was broken and fell.

It follows: “You covered all their sins.” The Lord’s propitiation is clearly recognized when our sins are shown to have been covered. Their abomination is our absolution, and we are made secure when those sins are not summoned to judgment. This was granted to the human race when the Lord Savior deigned to come.

Note also that in these two verses there is the figure *homoeoteleuton*, because many words end with similar letters. He said: “You blessed” (*benedixisti*), “you turned away” (*avertisti*), “you forgave” (*remisisti*), “you covered” (*operuisti*).

### Verse 3

“You mitigated all your anger; you turned away from the anger of your indignation.”

After the insertion of a *diapsalma*, he comes to the second part, recounting how the Lord deigned to mitigate his anger and how salvation would come to those over whom despair threatened because of the nature of their deeds, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

But observe the measure expressed by the word “mitigated.” He again pursues the offenses which the Jews’ wicked stubbornness, with perverse determination, committed against the Lord Savior.

From “the anger of his indignation,” one must understand that he turned away the destruction of the Jews, while the physician came to the sick and the author of salvation came to those filled with disease. This should be applied not merely to one nation but to the benefit of the whole world.

### Verse 4

“Turn us, God our Savior, and turn your anger away from us.”

Although above he said, “You covered all their sins,” he now seems to ask anew: “Turn your anger away from us.” Yet both statements agree if we consider the times of their sins.

For the iniquities that the Jewish people had previously committed, he first gave thanks, because all things were shown to have been mitigated by the Lord’s coming. Here, however, he asks again concerning future offenses, because he foresaw that they would commit savage crimes again in the Lord’s Passion.

Finally, he says, “Turn,” so that persecutors may become defenders, blasphemers preachers, and opponents disciples. By saying “us,” he assumes the person of the people about whom he speaks. “Turn your anger away from us” should likewise be understood as a prayer that the Jewish nation might not be struck by the punishment it deserved.

### Verse 5

“Do not be angry with us forever, nor extend your anger from generation to generation.”

He knew that the Lord’s patience bore with human beings’ impious sins, and therefore he asks that he not strike them with eternal condemnation but gently attract them, gain them by enduring them, and correct them by admonishing them—something he knew the Lord would indeed do.

We must examine the fact that he speaks of two generations. The first, as some think, extends from Adam to Christ; the second, completed through the grace of baptism, extends to the end of the age.

He therefore asks that, although the Lord was justly angry with the first generation according to the quality of its obstinacy, he should not likewise be angry with the second generation. Although it cannot be free from sin, it nevertheless desires to be cleansed from the stains of its faults through the grace of baptism and the satisfaction of confession.

### Verse 6

“God, when you turn us, you will give us life, and your people will rejoice in you.”

With wondrous mercy he entreats the Lord, proving that we do not possess our conversion through our merits but that it comes from his gift, whenever the soul healthfully desires something for his sake.

For he says: “God, when you turn us, you will give us life,” that is, because you first inspire the desire for conversion, so that we may be able to reach the entrance to life. When you have granted this, then that people will rejoice prosperously in you—the people that had rejoiced disastrously in itself. This comes to the converted when they begin to receive the Savior’s benefits.

### Verse 7

“Show us, Lord, your mercy, and give us your salvation.”

He knew that the Lord would come, but he asks that he might see these benefits not merely with bodily eyes, as the other unbelievers did, but with the purest vision of the heart.

The Father’s mercy is the Savior Lord, whom the blessed company asked to be shown to them through the illumination of true faith—not merely covered with the veil of flesh but visible in the splendor of his power.

For when he spoke of him, he added, “Give us,” that is, grant us your salvation as something to be embraced, possessed, and enjoyed as a gift of eternal glory.

To the faithless he merely appeared; he was not also given to them. Therefore he says, “Give,” so that when he is received in our minds as a heavenly gift, he may not be taken away by any temptations.

### Verse 8

“I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me, for he will speak peace to his people and upon his saints.”

He comes to the third part, in which, through a most beautiful figure, he proclaims the coming of the Lord Savior. After he had prayed that the Lord might appear to him, as though his petition had been granted and he had suddenly been filled with illumination, he says: “I will hear”—that is, I will not hinder myself by speaking, since I already feel that I have received what I am to believe.

We recognize this kind of expression as characteristic of divine Scripture, since, as I think, nothing similar is found in secular writings. You see that the power of prophecy was revealed by this statement.

The Lord speaks within, that is, the Holy Spirit, so that the Psalmist may appear able to speak outwardly. He hears inwardly, so that he may be heard outwardly. The prophet silently says what can be heard by the peoples when the air has been struck by his voice.

It follows: “For he will speak peace to his people and to his saints.” The peace of God is Christ the Lord. He says that the Holy Spirit will speak it because he is going to speak of Christ’s incarnation.

He said “to his people,” not to an undevoted people, but to his own—that is, to the saints who have pleased God the Lord by an exemplary manner of life. For them the Lord Christ is peace; to unbelievers he is a stumbling block and foolishness. They suffer war in their sacrilegious minds because they do not follow the author of peace along straight paths.

But let us examine this verse more carefully, since it convicts wicked minds by the testimony of truth itself. Here it is clearly expressed what the Holy Spirit is: the Lord God.

Where are those who say that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father and the Son, and so subject to them that he is thought not to possess judgment of his own will? Let us hear the Holy Spirit, who spoke spontaneously through his prophet, declaring that the Lord is God.

In the Acts of the Apostles it is also plainly read that the Holy Spirit is God, when Peter says to Ananias: “Why has Satan tempted your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5:3). Shortly afterward, wishing to show who the Holy Spirit is, he says: “You have not lied to human beings but to God” (ibid., 5:4).

The same Peter says in his Epistle: “By the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into whom angels long to look” (1 Pet. 1:12). If he were not equal, he would not be ranked with the Father and the Son in baptism, with the most reverent honor, in the name of the Godhead, as the Truth himself declared: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

This single testimony ought to be more than sufficient for the human race, because where he speaks of one name of the Godhead, there is no diversity either of nature or of power.

### Verse 9

“And to those who turn to him; nevertheless, his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land.”

“Those who turn to him” signifies penitents who, having abandoned the world’s destructive freedom, choose to submit to his blessed service.

When the whole world was burning with the most shameful devotion to idols, only the Jews were thought to fear the Lord closely. Having received the law through Moses, they appeared devoted to the one God. But they are said to fear him “closely” because, conducting everything carnally, they stubbornly provoked him by various offenses.

They were not said simply to fear but to fear closely, because they received his law carnally rather than spiritually. To understand that this was spoken about them, the Apostle likewise says: “He came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near” (Eph. 2:17).

Although they were such, the Lord Savior nevertheless chose to be born according to the flesh from their race. From there came the Virgin Mary who bore Christ; there the Lord lived; there the miracles were performed that are both read and believed by the faithful.

### Verse 10

“Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have embraced one another.”

This figure is called *somatopoeia*, that is, “attribution of a body,” when bodies are attributed to incorporeal things. For mercy and truth, peace and righteousness are incorporeal, yet he gave two of them feet and two of them an embrace, which is plainly bodily.

After saying from which nation the Lord was to be born, he now explains what the coming of the holy incarnation accomplished. Through his action, the two Testaments were brought into a single sequence of union. In the New Testament there is mercy, through which the human race is freed by grace; in the Old there is truth, in which the law and the announcement of the prophets are contained, as was already said in the seventieth psalm.

These two met one another, not to exercise opposition, but to fulfill the grace of the promised perfection. What had been divided by the times is shown to have become one.

And so that he might express the very nature of the covenant clearly, he repeated the idea with various names, saying that through an embrace of love two things—righteousness and peace—immediately came into mutual harmony. This usually happens when people see one another after a long time and, out of affection, bind themselves together in the clasp of their arms.

### Verse 11

“Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.”

Truth arose from the earth when the Word became flesh from the Virgin Mary, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Righteousness looked down from heaven when the Son of God, through a wondrous dispensation, came to the aid of the human race in peril.

This meaning can also be understood in another way. Truth arises from the earth when a sinner’s confession is offered; righteousness looks down from heaven when sins are forgiven. This occurred in the prayer of that tax collector. Truth arose from the earth when, looking down into the depths, he confessed his sins and begged God; righteousness looked down from heaven when the tax collector descended justified rather than that Pharisee.

### Verse 12

“For the Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit.”

This verse too can appropriately be applied to the humility of the penitent. By his goodness he grants the disposition to confess—that is, a most fruitful rain of tears—so that our flesh, watered by devout weeping, may be able to bring forth abundant rewards.

### Verse 13

“Righteousness will walk before him, and he will place his steps on the way.”

We say in the same way that this verse should be applied to those who are corrected by the Lord through devout supplications.

Righteousness will walk before them when, having recognized the truth of their evils, they humbly ask that what they have perpetrated through criminal boldness be forgiven them, and that what they had joyfully bound through wickedness may be released through the benefits of devout lamentation.

Then they truly place their steps on the way—that is, in Christ—those who previously wandered along detestable paths.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

We have heard, blessed David, what the Lord spoke within you. May this peace that reigned in your heart also come upon us.

Behold the true King, whom such virtue governed; the temple of righteousness; the palace of compassion; the treasury of mercy. The earthly realm rightly lay subject to you, since such a Lord commanded you.

Behold what can surpass every empire and stand above every proclamation: from your offspring the almighty Word took flesh, through whom the human race received the saving gift of redemption.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 85

## A Prayer of David

“Prayer” (*oratio*) is a homonym. Its etymology is *oris ratio*, “the expression of the mouth.” When it is spoken in human courts, it is composed by eloquent people with exceedingly artful refinement; when it is poured out to God, it is expressed in simple and humble supplication.

Yet this humility and purity of petition appropriately belong to the holy Word if we confess—as the Church, our mother, teaches—that there are two perfect and wholly genuine natures in Christ the Lord, namely, that of God and that of man. Then we will not be troubled by any contradiction in truthful words if we assign them to the properties appropriate to each nature.

For if you wish to know the power of his Godhead, hear the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

And if you wish to know the weakness of his humanity, hear the Apostle Paul saying: “He was made in the likeness of human beings and was found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:7–8).

Therefore, when he speaks from the standpoint of his humanity, the weakness of his Godhead should not be supposed [ed., “the weakness of his humility should not be imputed to the Godhead,” *humilitatis fragilitas non imputetur*; mss. A., F., “the weakness should not be imputed to the Godhead,” *Divinitati fragilitas non imputetur*]. For he exalted what was human in such a way that he in no respect diminished what was divine.

Thus the same and one Lord Christ is prayed to, because he is the Son of the Father; he prays, because he is the Son of man. From one standpoint he is Creator; from the other, created. From one, Lord; from the other, servant. From one, he is the conqueror of death itself; from the other, a participant in our mortality.

For this reason, throughout the divine books he always shows his two operations in highly appropriate passages. If you preserve these things, devout reader, with faithful mind, you will understand that everything can truly stand firm for you.

We must further acknowledge and hold firmly in our minds that when prayer is poured out by the Lord Christ, it is the holy instruction of the faithful, the pattern of good conduct, and an example of sincere humility. When it is offered by those subject to him, it is satisfaction for offenses, confession of crimes, and the washing away of faults.

There it is the instruction of the teacher; here the abolition of error is sought. For the innocent man prayed just as he endured the cross without any fault. He wept for Lazarus to show us the love we owe our neighbor. He fled from persecutors to remove from us the rashness of ill-considered presumption.

The provident Teacher did these and similar things so that he might show the truth of the holy incarnation and forestall future Manichaeans and others of their kind.

“David,” however, as it is written here, signifies the Lord Savior—either because its interpretation, as has often been said, is understood as “strong of hand” and “desirable,” or because he descended from David’s lineage. In his humanity he is David’s son; in his divinity, Lord and Creator.

If you foolishly abandon this rudder, you will undoubtedly dash the ship of your faith against the most jagged rocks. Note also that this is the second psalm whose title is prefaced by “A prayer.”

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the entire psalm the Lord Christ prays. In the first section he says things that are shown to apply to him alone. In the second, he prays more humbly on behalf of his members, of whom he himself is the head. In the third, he speaks again from his own person, and you should understand that this pertains especially to him.

Yet all these things are spoken by one and the same God-man, Christ.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Incline your ear, Lord, to me, and hear me, for I am needy and poor.”

From the form of a servant, as we have stated above, Christ supplicates the almighty Father that his prayer may be heard.

By saying “Incline,” he shows that the human condition could not extend itself to him unless he, in his great compassion, inclined his majesty. He speaks of an “ear,” not a bodily ear, but that spiritual hearing by which he knows the desires of those who ask. Through tropology, such things said about God are already familiar from frequent exposition.

“Listen to me” signifies: let my desires be fulfilled, so that I too may be saved through the resurrection, since it is established that the world is to be saved through his death.

By saying that he is needy and poor, he shows the condition of the humanity he had assumed, which can possess nothing of itself except what it has received through the generosity of the Godhead.

Let the needy and poor hear this and console their souls with such glory, since the Lord of all things says this about himself—something which the fainthearted often think should be applied to their miseries.

Yet he does not exclude those who serve the Lord with pure mind amid their riches. For whoever has deserved to be emptied of this world’s perversity is needy and poor before God.

### Verse 2

“Guard my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.”

He forcefully explains who is poor and needy: namely, the Lord Christ, who truthfully calls himself holy because he trampled the enticements of this world by the conduct of heavenly life. Let the Apollinarists hear that the Lord Christ possesses a soul and assumed the nature of a complete human being; for he could not fail to possess the very nature he is specifically shown to have come to save. No one liberates what he does not snatch from the power of its captor; and even if what he claims to defend is not present in the defender, the condition of the captivity undertaken still remains. And consider what a saving pattern is set before us. He who had truthfully said that he was holy and alien to the enticements of the world begs to be saved by Divinity, so that he might instruct us that salvation is not established in human powers, just as the prophet Jeremiah also says: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man and whose heart departs from God” (Jeremiah XVII, 5), and so forth.

### Verse 3

“Have mercy on me, Lord, for I have cried to you all day long.”

The one and the same Christ Jesus, God and man, asks for mercy who grants mercy, teaching that through perseverance in supplication the Lord’s compassion must be obtained by every means; as he himself teaches in the Gospel: “It is good to pray and not grow weary” (Luke XVIII, 1).

Let those who despair, through perverse unwillingness, of doing penance at the end of their lives hear this passage; let those who impiously turn to excuses for making excuses hear it, when they know from the Gospel reading that the thief already fastened to the cross was helped with instantaneous speed—and other similar examples, which the text of divine Scripture grants with wonderful kindness to nourish the hope of mortals.

It is always fitting for us to plead, since we offend through frequent fault. It is an immeasurable evil for people themselves to take away the most salutary hope from themselves, when divine clemency commands us to plead with it without ceasing. Let us ask this in the flourishing season of life; let us ask while placed in youth; let us ask also when we have reached declining old age. The one who has sinned by a perversity deserving punishment must never cease from prayers, lest, while we seek a time for supplication, we take away the Lord’s mercy from ourselves by such an argument.

For when it says “all day long,” it indicates the whole span of life, so that through many periods and cycles of years an unbroken cry may be shown to be like a single day. Indeed, he cries out to the Lord with a great voice who, although silent with his tongue, cries out perseveringly through good works.  
[Col. 0613A]

### Verse 4

“Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul.”

He asks that his soul be made joyful—the fountain of gladness and source of delight—from that aspect by which he is a servant. He rightly called himself a servant because he was born from the Virgin Mary, who professes herself a handmaid. For when the angel announced to her that Christ the Lord would be born from her, she replied: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I, 38). Thus also he says in another psalm: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Psalm CXV, 16).

Therefore he asks that his soul be gladdened, because he did not incline it downward toward earth but always lifted it up to the Lord, where there is true joy and security without end. Thus, as the Head of the Church recounts his own deeds, he granted examples to the remaining members.  
[Col. 0613B]

### Verse 5

“For you, Lord, are gentle and mild, and abundant in mercy toward all who call upon you.”

God is shown to us most beautifully—not substantially, which no creature can comprehend, but through the fifth kind of definition, called in Greek *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν*—“according to the expression” or “in the wording.”

He is gentle because, after the bitterness of this world, he is sweet to those who return to him. He is mild because he long endures sinners. He is abundant in mercy because, although our sins are numerous, his compassion is far more abundant, for it releases so many offenses. It remains for us to plead with him continually, since we have heard that he does not deny help to all who call upon him.

[Col. 0613C]

### Verse 6

“Give ear, Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication.”

Let us observe how appropriately the order of this prayer proceeds. First, the voice of supplication had to rise, and then the one asked had to hear. But when it says “give ear,” it does not request that something be received only temporarily; rather, it prefers that the prayer be stored in the recesses of that majesty, just as something is shown to be impressed upon human memory through the ears. It adds, “attend to the voice of my supplication,” so that an attentive mind might open its hearing. All this is said allegorically, so that the power of Divinity may be intimated through human customs.

### Verse 7

“On the day of my tribulation I cried to you, for you answered me.”

Earlier he said, “I have cried to you all day long.” Here he seems to make a certain increase in his great petition by saying, “On the day of my tribulation I cried to you.” For although holy men continually plead with the Lord, they ask more earnestly in a time of tribulation, when help is urgently required.

We must consider this manner of expression, which occurs very frequently in the divine Scriptures: he says that he cried out because he was heard, although the cry precedes, so that God may be able to hear. This figure is called *anastrophe*, that is, inversion; it occurs whenever either the sense or the words are turned for the sake of some elegance.

### Verse 8

“There is none like you among the gods, Lord, and there is nothing according to your works.”

A great praise is contained in a brief definition. By saying, “There is none like you among the gods,” he signifies the idols of the pagans, which were still being worshiped in the world with wicked devotion; as he also says elsewhere: “For all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm XCV, 5). This can also be applied to human beings, who have been called gods.

But observe that he does not say what God is; rather, he denies that anything is like him. This kind of definition is called in Greek *κατ’ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου*, “through the removal of the contrary” of the thing being defined. He also added, “and there is nothing according to your works,” that is, nothing like them. This clause too he included under the definition mentioned above. For who could, as he did, complete heaven and earth and all that is in them with instantaneous speed, or sustain their existences?  
[Col. 0614A]

### Verse 9

“All the nations that you have made shall come, and they shall worship before you, Lord, and they shall honor your name.”

While only the Jewish nation still seemed to worship the one God, he foretells that all the nations held under the power of idols will come to his worship; for the one who honors the Lord Christ truly worships the Father. He completely destroys the error of those who think that the Lord’s religion has not been spread throughout the whole world.

By saying, “All the nations that you have made,” he proves the universality absolutely, because no nation exists except one that he himself formed, as he says elsewhere: “He made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them” (Psalm CXLV, 6).

He also added, “and they shall honor your name.” When it is said to God, “they shall honor your name,” it figuratively signifies that the devoted will be honored because of your name, since human worship does not make God honorable—he who is unquestionably known to be the giver of every good thing.  
[Col. 0614C]

### Verse 10

“For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God.”

He brought to completion, at the end of this verse, the hymn to Divinity that he had begun above. For the devil too thought himself great when he said: “I shall set my throne toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV, 13–14); and proud people still consider themselves greater than all others.

Yet no one can truly be called great except God alone, whose power nothing can in any way equal, who is changed by no mutability but always remains in the glory of his nature. He added, “and doing wondrous things; you alone are God.” Although we read that Pharaoh’s magicians also performed various miracles, here it is said that he alone can perform miracles.

This is a truthful statement if we weigh the quality of the deed by the truth of the word itself. Those things cannot truly be called miracles which, offering no benefit, flatter deceived eyes through contrived illusion. “Alone” is said because the holy Trinity is one God, distinguished only in persons and not separated by a division of nature; as it is also said elsewhere: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy VI, 4). Isaiah likewise says: “For you are just, and there is no God besides you” (Isaiah XLV, 21).  
[Col. 0614D]

### Verse 11
