“Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth; let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.”

Having completed the prayer and appropriately fulfilled the praise of Divinity, he comes to the second section, in which he prays for his members, so that the Lord may grant them what will benefit them. When he says, “Lead me, Lord, in your way,” it is shown that he was not yet there; and this cannot apply to Christ the Lord, since he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

But this is more fittingly understood of the faithful, whose Head is the Lord: unless they are led into the way—that is, into Christ—they cannot walk in truth.

It follows: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name.” What the fear of the Lord is is declared in a marvelous order. In worldly fear, the cause of danger or of some distress comes first; but in the fear of the Lord, gladness of heart is set first, so that someone may deserve to arrive at the sweetness of that fear. And truly such a fear deserves to have this entrance, since humanity perceives that it has been granted for its salvation.

The one who dreads this judge is guilty; the one who fears that Judge is holy. Therefore both must be mingled, so that we may fear under hope and rejoice under fear, as it is read in another psalm: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Psalm II, 11).  
[Col. 0615B]

### Verse 12

“I shall confess to you, Lord my God, with all my heart, and I shall honor your name forever.”

This is appropriately said of every Christian, because that is true confession which is uttered from the whole secret place of the mind, as the Law also teaches: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy VI, 5).

But the one who places all his hope in the Lord also confesses with his whole heart; he does not rely upon the fleeting consolations of the world, since he has transferred himself to the Lord with complete integrity of mind.

For what he added, “forever,” signifies that among his saints he will continually resound with praises of the Lord, when he has received the promised rewards in that blessedness.  
[Col. 0615C]

### Verse 13

“For your mercy is great over me, and you have rescued my soul from the lower underworld.”

An acknowledgment of praise is offered, and the cause of mercy is added. By saying, “For your mercy is great over me,” he declares some great benefit. By adding, “you have rescued my soul from the lower underworld,” the cause of the benefit is explained.

But let us consider that, when he says “the lower underworld,” he shows that there is an upper underworld as well. Such arguments are called *conjugates* in topical reasoning: they arise from one name and are variously changed, as here with *infernum inferius*, “the lower underworld.”

Perhaps it is not unreasonable to think that the underworld is beneath the earth, since in the Old Testament we read concerning Dathan and Abiram: “The earth opened and swallowed them, and they went down alive to the underworld.” But by what route souls are transferred there remains uncertain to us, since it is not stated in divine authority.

That the underworld has a lower part is attested by the passage in the Gospel (Luke XVI, 23), which says that, while the impious rich man was being tormented by avenging flame, he lifted up his eyes and saw Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom. Hence it appears that both were in the underworld, since they were able to see one another, and that the rich man lifted his eyes from a lower place to higher regions.

Although both seemed to be in the underworld, however, the teacher Augustine judges that, according to the distinction of their merits, the higher place should be assigned to the saints and the lower place to sinners. Therefore the faithful people now give thanks, saying that their soul has been freed from the lower underworld—that is, from the place of punishment.

### Verse 14

“God, the unjust have risen up against me, and the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul; and they have not placed you before their eyes.”

He comes to the third section, where he explains the mystery of his Passion and the glory of his resurrection. God the man speaks from the form of a servant, through the fact that he was born from the Virgin Mary.

When he says “the unjust,” he signifies the Jews, who repaid him evil for good. By saying “against me,” he means that they called the innocent guilty and that the mad populace slaughtered its own king.

The “assembly of the powerful” is the gathering of the proud. With bestial roaring and deceitful plotting, they cast justice aside and sought to take away his life.

He added what always occurs to criminal minds: “For they have not placed God before their eyes.” Whoever commits a crime in no way sets God before his eyes; for if he believed him to be present, he would immediately be recalled from the crime he had conceived.  
[Col. 0616B]

### Verse 15

“But you, Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and abundantly merciful, and truthful.”

Through each word of praise the Father’s majesty is defined. This is the twelfth kind of definition, which the Greeks call *κατ’ ἔπαινον*, and the Latins “through praise.”

He is compassionate because he shows mercy to each individual thing. He is merciful because the nature of Divinity itself is always loving. He is patient because he endures sinners and invites them to the desire for conversion.

It follows: “and abundantly merciful.” He added this expression because our weakness always receives more of it when it merits it through frequent remission. He continued: “and truthful,” because he does not know how to withdraw his promises through any weakness.

Yet this is said of the Father in such a way that we understand the whole to be present also in the Son and in the Holy Spirit.  
[Col. 0616C]

### Verse 16

“Look upon me and have mercy on me; give power to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid.”

From the aspect in which the Son suffered, he asks the merciful, patient, and truthful Father to look upon him and come to his aid through the swiftest resurrection. For he showed mercy in such a way that, in him, he raised mortal nature itself to the glory of resurrection and eternity. Yet he requests this from the Father in such a way as to declare that it was accomplished by himself.

For in the Gospel he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up” (John II, 19). So that this might not be understood otherwise, the evangelist follows: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (ibid., 21).

It follows: “Give power to your servant”—the power he himself testifies to when he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22).

In the sacred Scriptures, “servant” is often applied to Christ because of the innocence of his mind, as Isaiah says: “For a child is born to us, and a Son is given to us” (Isaiah IX, 6). And again: “Behold my servant; I shall receive him, my chosen one; my soul has been pleased with him” (Isaiah XLII, 1).

He added: “and save the son of your handmaid”—of the handmaid, certainly, because he was truly and properly to be born from Mary, ever-virgin, who—as we said above—when the angel announced her childbirth, professed herself the Lord’s handmaid.  
[Col. 0617A]

### Verse 17

“Work with me, Lord, a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see and be put to shame; for you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me.”

A sign is so called because it signifies what is to come and because, from what is seen, it urges us to perceive something else. Therefore we may perhaps understand here the event of Jonah (Jonah II, 1), who remained three days in the belly of the sea creature and, as an image of the Lord’s resurrection, was vomited out safely upon the shore.

For it is also said in the Gospel: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet” (Matthew XII, 39). You see, therefore, that one thing was denied, but only this one was promised.

We can also fittingly apply the sign he requested to his resurrection, especially since it follows: “for good.” What is more excellent than that good by which divine power was declared and the hope of believers was strengthened by a truthful promise?

It follows: “so that those who hate me may see and be put to shame”—namely, the Jews who hated Christ. He asks that they see the miracle of the resurrection, so that their hardness may be obliged to change.

“For them to be put to shame” refers to a good outcome, because whoever is put to shame here on account of his evil is undoubtedly transferred to a better condition. In this world, if we are put to shame, we are corrected; but those who are not put to shame will be condemned at that judgment.

He added: “for you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me.” The order of the words is as follows: “So that those who hate me may see—for you, Lord, have helped me and comforted me—and be put to shame,” namely, when they see me glorified, whom they thought ought to be despised.

“You have helped me” refers to the contradiction of disputants and to the Jews’ unjust contests, in which they were always overcome by the testimony of truth. “You have comforted me” refers to the most savage persecutions of the mad, which he endured with the greatest patience, as though they were a storm’s assault.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider how humble is the prayer poured out to the Father by the Lord and Savior from the aspect in which he suffered. He had no sins at all, yet, instructing our weakness, he asked to be rescued from the dangers of this world.

Therefore let human presumption blush to be proud, since it does not hesitate to acknowledge itself guilty. Christ prayed for his enemies and patiently accepted death; yet we wish to avenge our injuries if we are attacked by the words of those who slander us. May he himself grant the gift of patience, who gave us the example, so that, following in his footsteps, we may be able to avoid errors that bring death.

# Exposition of Psalm LXXXVI

**For the sons of Korah, a psalm of a song.**

For the sake of restoring your memory, let us briefly recall what has often been said already: for almost nothing is thought to have been recounted usefully if whatever was transmitted has been consigned to oblivion. “The sons of Korah” signifies the faithful Christians, to whom the prophet proclaims the city of God, so that their affection for such great glory may be increased all the more.

For when he said “for the sons of Korah,” he showed that the psalm was to be spoken to them, not by them. It follows: “a psalm of a song,” so that we may be raised from the tabernacles of this world to an understanding of the city above. A psalm, sounding of things above, reminds us to think of heavenly realities and to rejoice in them with hymnic exultation.

## Division of the Psalm

A short psalm, but it is recognized as divided by two *diapsalmata*; mindful of our purpose, we explain its division in a manner corresponding to its own boundaries.

In the first part the prophet speaks to the faithful, proclaiming the heavenly city. In the second, the Lord and Savior declares that it will be believed in through an allusion to various names, reproving the Synagogue for not having recognized God, while the devoted faith of the nations has believed in him.

In the third part the prophet touches, in a single verse, upon the blessedness of the age to come. Thus the distinct alteration of speakers removes every obscurity of confusion from us.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Its foundations are in the holy mountains.”

It is characteristic of human thought that, when it has gathered itself through extensive inquiry, it breaks forth into some conclusion of its deliberation. Such seems to be the beginning of this psalm: although the prophet has not previously said anything about the city of God, he appears to discuss its foundations as though he had already said something about its summit.

A new order of exceptional praise has been established, so that the prophet seems to take his beginning from the foundations of the heavenly city, in order that the great solidity of the whole structure might appear, whose foundations were praised first.

This is not without reason, because its foundation is Christ the Lord, who contains his Church in such a way that it cannot stagger through any shaking, as the Apostle says: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Corinthians III, 11). Rightly, therefore, he took his beginning from him who is clearly the principle of all things.

Josephus also—as someone has said, a native Jewish writer—spoke at length in the eighth book of the *Antiquities*, in its third section, about the construction of the temple, which is known to have been built by Solomon. We too had the tabernacle painted, which was originally its image, and the temple itself, and had them placed in the body of our larger *Pandect*, so that what the text of divine Scripture says about them might be displayed more clearly when rendered visible to the eyes.

By “the holy mountains,” he signifies the apostles and prophets, who are called mountains because of the solidity of their faith and the excellence of their holiness. Rightly, therefore, they have been designated by this name, since the true Church of God has been established in them.  
[Col. 0618D]

### Verse 2

“The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob.”

Now he speaks of that city whose foundations he praised earlier. This figure is called *anastrophe*, that is, inversion: it occurs whenever what ought to be said earlier is placed later.

He says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion.” Zion—as we have often said—is the Jerusalem mountain, interpreted as “watchtower,” through which that future Jerusalem is appropriately understood. The Lord loves its gates—that is, faith, charity, baptism, penance, and whatever admits the peoples acquired for that city.

Or, as some wish, they signify the twelve apostles, whose holy preaching opened the palaces of the eternal King to the faithful.

We must carefully examine what he added: “above all the tabernacles of Jacob.” The tabernacles of Jacob signify the Catholic Church, which is now being built. It continually struggles against the adversities of this world through the disciplined exercise of a campaign.  
294

And because this Church bears the image of that future Jerusalem, where there is blessed life and eternal happiness, it is rightly said that the spiritual Jerusalem is loved above it, since in that city no confusion or disturbance is shown to exist. Observe that the future city is said to be loved more, in such a way that this present one is nevertheless undoubtedly understood to be loved also.  
[Col. 0619B]

### Verse 3

“Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.”

As is his custom, he places future things in the past tense. For this city will be praised in the second part through the testimony of the Lord; appropriately, therefore, glorious things are reported of it, since it is known that it will be proclaimed by the voice of its Creator.

### Verse 4

“I shall remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me; behold, the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were in her.”

The second part of this psalm opens like a kind of cloud. From it the Lord, thundering, promises the faithful the gifts of his remembrance, signifying through allusions to names that they will be gathered from various nations.

Rahab was a prostitute who secretly received the spies of Joshua son of Nun when they came to Jericho and sent them out by another route so that they would not be discovered. Her name signifies pride, which, converted by divine generosity, deserved to obtain the Lord’s clemency.

She therefore bears the figure of the Church, which receives souls endangered by the vice of pride and sends them to life by another route—that is, by humility and patience.

Babylon too is a city of the world, and its name is interpreted as “confusion.” It indicates the peoples of this age who served shameful idols with blinded minds; but, enlightened by the Lord’s mercy, they became Christians.

Therefore he says that he will remember Rahab and Babylon—that is, the peoples of this world who nevertheless humbly transferred themselves to his worship. Thus he himself replied to the proud Pharisees in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XXI, 31).

It follows: “Behold, the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were in her.” He continues in the same sense. The foreigners are those who are indeed outsiders to the Jewish people; but when the Jews did not believe, the foreigners were received into the inner sanctuary of the Church, as he says in the Acts of the Apostles: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you; but because you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts XIII, 46).

Tyre signifies the distress produced by the affliction of penitents. The people of the Ethiopians had been extremely darkened by the obscurity of their sins; but they were gathered into this city of the Lord, so that the number of the radiant saints in that homeland might be completed from them.

These are precisely the things that the preceding verse foretold: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.” For what is more glorious than that such great foulness of peoples previously wandering should come together into the single beauty of the holy city?

And remember that we have already said that this kind of expression is proper to divine Scripture: namely, that the intention of an utterance may be understood through the interpretations of names.  
[Col. 0620A]

### Verse 5

“Mother Zion will say: ‘A man, and a man was made in her; and the Most High himself founded her.’”

Here we may perhaps not inappropriately understand the Catholic Church’s mother to be the Synagogue, which, as we have often said, is to be understood through Mount Zion. For the greater part of its people it called the Lord and Savior merely a man, because it did not deserve either to believe or to understand that he was God.

A pause must be placed here, because what follows introduces another sense. For it continues: “and a man was made in her,” which must now be read as confirmation. It does not say here that a man was made in the same way as the Synagogue said above. The Synagogue, in error, thought him merely a man; but now the Lord confirms of himself, in a definitive statement: “and a man was made in her.” For in truth, having assumed flesh, God became man, as the Evangelist also says: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14)—that is, the Son of God became man—not so that anything might be diminished from Divinity, but so that he might graciously raise up the nature of humanity, which he had predestined to save.

And lest you should perhaps believe that the Lord Christ was temporal, he added: “and the Most High himself founded her.” The one who was thought to be merely the man Jesus Christ himself founded the Synagogue by his own disposition. He not only gave the Law through Moses, but before the beginning of the world he is also known to have been the beginning, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, which is also why I speak to you” (John VIII, 26).

He was rightly called the Most High, so that no heresy might say that the Father was greater.  
[Col. 0620C]

### Verse 6

“The Lord has recounted the writings of the peoples and the princes: these who were in her.”

He foretells what he himself would say at the time of the Incarnation by recalling the ancient Scriptures. For in the Gospel he frequently reminds us of what Moses foretold about him and what the prophets foretold, both to instruct those who believed less and to show that he was their author.

The princes are Moses and the prophets who were in the Synagogue, whose testimony he was going to recount. And lest you should perhaps understand other princes, he says: “these who were in her,” that is, in the Synagogue.  
[Col. 0620D]

### Verse 7

“As the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you.”

He comes to the third part, in which the prophet speaks again. He both begins and ends it in one verse, briefly encompassing what could not be explained even in lengthy speeches. This figure is called *brachylogia*, that is, brevity of expression, when we embrace many things in few words.

Do you wish to hear how incomprehensible that joy is? The Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him.” Therefore it is beautifully said here: “as those who rejoice,” because that joy will not be of the kind experienced here: now we rejoice in the adoption of children, now we take pleasure in the gift of wealth and honors, and in the other things that produce exultation when they are acquired through great temporal effort.

But that joy is so much greater that even the fullest joy of this world can scarcely be called any image or likeness of the age to come.

He added: “the dwelling of all of us is in you.” “All of us” signifies the faithful, who have believed either that the Lord Christ would come or that he has come. “The dwelling is in you”: he speaks to Jerusalem, to which he earlier said, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.”

But in this dwelling the affliction of the righteous has ceased. Prayer passes away, but praise succeeds it. Perpetual security remains, because no perversity is mingled with it. Eternal joy endures, because it is in no way established to be violated by any opposition.  
[Col. 0621B]

## Conclusion of the Psalm

That city of the faithful has been praised through demonstrative discourse. It is not marvelous because of temporal goods but because of eternal happiness. It seemed that little had been said about it, yet the minds of all are shown to have been filled with wonder.

This praise is not extended through argumentation of words, nor does it grow through human effort; rather, it is compressed into great brevity, so that it may seem possible to grasp at least something from it.

Truly blessed is the one who, with the Lord leading, reaches that place where every thought is conquered and every desire surpassed. And this is the form of the sweetest security: there one receives a happiness that cannot be lost through any opposition.

Grant, Lord, that what we cannot explain here in words, we may behold there by your gift.

This Jerusalem, too, which still exists on earth and bears the type of that heavenly mystery, was praised in the second division; rightly so, since it is the visible dwelling of such great realities and powers.

There the swimming pool, as a figure of sacred baptism, was stirred by an angel descending to heal the sick. There, at the Lord’s command, the pool of Siloam washed away the blind man’s darkness and restored the gift of light to his condemned eyes.

There the table of Christ, filled with heavenly delights, spiritually satisfied the apostles; and lest we be left unfed by that supper, the sacred cup granted us both communion and salvation.

There the hardest stone displayed the footprints of the merciful Redeemer when he stood before Pilate the judge to be heard. There the column bears witness to the lashes inflicted upon the Lord when he was bound to it.

There the crown of thorns is seen, which, as is known, was placed upon the Savior so that the thorns of the whole world, gathered together, might be broken.

There the reed is preserved that struck the Lord’s head, so that it might proclaim to all the earth that he himself is the beginning of all things.

There that cross of salvation and glory consecrated the reverence of the place. There remains the lance that pierced the Lord’s side, so that its healing might come to our aid.

There believers today are brought to life by his very tombs. There the place of the resurrection raises the hearts of the faithful to heaven.

There is that chief of the mountains, Zion, where, while the disciples were seated in the upper room with the doors closed, the Savior miraculously entered; and there are the other things that that rich homeland gained through the Lord’s Passion.

But when it shines adorned with so many miracles and possesses another heaven in the manner of the stars, who would dare call it small, when it is proven to have filled the boundaries of the world with the most holy faith? There, indeed, the faith of the blessed nourishes human sight.  
[Col. 0622A]

# Exposition of Psalm LXXXVII

**A song of the psalm, for the sons of Korah, to the end, for Maheleth [manuscripts: Meleth], to respond; an understanding of Heman the Israelite.**

Since I do not doubt, most diligent reader, that your memory has been formed through frequent exposition, and that you retain what “A song of the psalm, for the sons of Korah, to the end” signifies, it remains for us to investigate what is new in the following part of this title.

“Maheleth” is interpreted as “a chorus singing divine words.” He added “to respond,” signifying that musical instruments went before and that the chorus solemnly answered. It follows: “An understanding of Heman the Israelite.”

“Heman” is interpreted as “his brother.” By this name the Lord Christ calls those who are devoted to his commandments and works, as he says in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matthew XXVIII, 10).

“Israelites” means “those who see God,” which clearly happens to those who, through the mystery of obedience, are radiant with the holy light of the Lord.

But since this psalm is going to speak about the Passion of Christ the King and draws the most faithful Christians toward imitation, the chorus for responding was therefore placed first: so that, just as they make one harmony from many voices, so the united gathering of the devoted might respond to Christ the Lord. These too are Israelites, who by heavenly generosity have deserved to be called his brothers.  
[Col. 0622C]

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the entire psalm the Lord and Savior speaks from the dispensation by which he suffered.

In the first account he implores the Father’s help; through various comparisons he recounts the contempt that the Jewish people were going to inflict upon him.

In the second he enumerates what he is going to suffer, asserting that the dead cannot be raised by physicians so that they may confess to the Lord.

In the third account he denies that those buried proclaim the Lord’s mercy or that the lost resound with the Lord’s praises; therefore he begs that the resurrection come to him with the greatest speed.

Continuing along the path of his prayer, he speaks from the perspective of his members, recalling various sufferings, which both he himself endured and his devoted people sustained.  
[Col. 0622D]

## Exposition of the Psalm
### Verse 1

**Lord, God of my salvation: by day I cried out, and by night before you.**

In the eighty-fifth Psalm we said that Christ prayed through the fact that he was born of the Virgin Mary, thereby indicating the humility of human weakness that he deigned to assume. In the same way here, when he prays to the Father, he shows us how we ought to supplicate. For by professing God to be the author of his salvation, he has explained fully and briefly everything that needed to be said. Thus the excellent teacher frequently does not cease admonishing us about what he knows will benefit the human race.

By “day” he signifies joy, and by “night” he declares adversity; since both periods together encompass human life, he thereby makes clear that he cried out continually to the Lord.

### Verse 2

**Let my prayer enter into your sight; incline your ear to my supplication, O Lord.**

Here the great power of the most sincere prayer is displayed: truthful words are not scattered into the thin air, but seem to enter, as a kind of person, into the Lord’s presence and to carry out a task that our flesh cannot accomplish. The Lord inclines his ear when, in his mercy, he deigns to hear—not by any bodily part of himself, for we have frequently said that he does not possess such a thing, but through the wondrous operation of his power.

### Verse 3

**For my soul has been filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell.**

It must be considered that he asks to be heard in a new way because he says that his soul has been filled with evils—obviously not with his own evils, since he had no sins, but with the transgressions of the world, under which humanity labored. In his compassion, the merciful one had drawn these into the distress of his own soul, since he grieved for everyone, just as he said in the thirty-fourth Psalm: “They repaid me evil for good, barrenness to my soul” (Psalm 34:12)—not because he himself was barren, but because he declared himself fasting on account of their unbelief.

The statement may also be applied to his own sorrow, if you refer the word to the iniquities that the Jewish people inflicted upon him. It follows: “And my life has drawn near to hell.” This refers to the time of his glorious Passion, as he says in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). For he grieved on our behalf, and on our behalf endured our death.

### Verse 4

**I have been reckoned among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without help.**

He reproves those who generally thought that he had died. This figure is called a *parabola*, that is, a comparison between things differing in kind. It was a very inappropriate comparison to liken that singular and miraculous Passion to the deaths of other human beings. This figure extends through many of the verses that follow.

By “the pit” he means either the place of the tomb or the deepest depth of hell. It follows: “I have become like a man without help.” “I have become,” that is, in the eyes of those who, with deranged minds, did not believe in his divinity and thought that he had perished together with the rest of mortals.

### Verse 5

**Free among the dead, like the wounded lying asleep in the tombs [ms. A: in the sepulchres], whom you remember no longer; and they themselves have been cast away from your hand.**

Here he specifically designates his own person. He alone among the dead was free, for he broke even the barriers of death itself. His death alone was free because it was voluntary: he had power to lay down his soul and to take it up again (John 10:18).

Yet although he was free among the dead, he was nevertheless regarded by the senseless as one of the wounded lying asleep. Truly the Lord was called “free,” for he deigned to set the human race free.

He still speaks of those utterly vain men who thought that the Lord had been wounded by a spear, killed, and likewise buried, as though he had passed away, like one of the wicked, in the common course. But to distinguish his own condition, he added: “whom you remember no longer,” that is, “for whom you have no care,” since, because of their sins, they are made alien from you. The same thing is said elsewhere in the Psalm concerning the impious: “Their memory has perished with a crash” (Psalm 9:8).

He added: “And they themselves have been cast away from your hand.” A just punishment is returned for their insolence: those who had thought that the Lord Christ was without the help of divinity were themselves proved to have been cast away from the Lord’s hand, since their sins made them exiles from his governance.

### Verse 6

**They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness [mss. G, F: in dark places] and in the shadow of death.**

The estimates of the deranged Jews are still being reported. “The pit” is used for hell, for a burial hollow, and for the deepest calamity of this present world. Here it is understood to mean that his persecutors placed him in the degraded condition of death: although they unjustly judged him to be dead, they did not believe that he would be avenged.

“In darkness,” that is, abandoned and passed over beneath the blindness of oblivion, so that no one would seek him and no one would save him.

“In the shadow of death” indicates the place of sinners, because the death of transgressors has shadowy and dark shades, since joy does not shine upon those who have been submerged in the perpetual darkness of their sorrow.

“Shadow” is also used in a good sense, as in: “Under the shadow of your wings” (Psalm 16:9), and elsewhere: “We shall live in his shadow” (Lamentations 4:20). Therefore, according to the character of the places involved, this word varies in its many meanings.

### Verse 7

**Your wrath has been confirmed against me, and you have brought all your surges upon me.**

So thought those who, to their own destruction, were rather permitted to prevail: they supposed that Jesus Christ had reached the dangers of the Passion through God’s wrath, just as the Evangelist reports the unbelieving people saying: “Let him rescue him, if he wishes” (Matthew 27:43).

It follows: “And you have brought all your surges upon me.” This is still spoken with reference to the wicked deliberation of the Jews. They believed that God had brought his surges—that is, his greatest indignation—upon Christ when he allowed him to be crucified. They thought that death was a punishment because they did not see the glory of his providential dispensation.

### Verse 8

**You have put my acquaintances far from me; they made me an abomination to themselves; I was delivered up, and I did not go out.**

He comes to the second narrative, in which he recalls the course of his Passion through the increase of his sufferings. Earlier he had spoken of the most impious contempt of his persecutors; now he speaks of his “acquaintances” [ed., “those driven away,”], signifying the apostles.

He calls them “acquaintances” because they were worthy to behold him with clear perception. He knew all of them by the power of his divinity, while he himself was known by only a few. These acquaintances were put far away when they were scattered by his Passion, as it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7).

He was then made “an abomination” when the scribes and Pharisees, passing by the crucified one, taunted him, saying: “Ah! You who destroy the temple of God and build it in three days” (Matthew 27:40), and so forth.

It follows: “I was delivered up, and I did not go out.” A remarkable and subtle statement. He was delivered up by Judas to the bands of madmen, but was held because he permitted himself to be held. The most powerful Lord endured feeble hands; he who cannot be confined by place was bound with chains; he heard accursed insults, though the angels praise him with trembling.

Yet he did not emerge from that cloud of his body, nor did he wish to reveal what he could do, since he endured everything that the cruelty of Jewish perversity inflicted. He did not go out when he showed least of all what power he possessed.

Or he speaks of the custody into which Pontius Pilate shut him away as though he were a weak human being.

### Verse 9

**My eyes have grown weak from want; I cried out to you, O Lord, all day long; I stretched out my hands to you.**

Since we nowhere read that the bodily eyes of Christ the Lord were weakened, still less should we think that his inner eyes grew sick, for they always shone with holiness. It remains, therefore, that we should understand Christ’s “eyes” as the apostles, who in his body—that is, in the Church—flourished like eyes with heavenly light.

Yet they were weakened by want because they had not yet received the Holy Spirit. Once strengthened by him, they thereafter feared no human torments. “Want” is spoken in contrast to abundance, where no abundance exists.

It was added: “I cried out to you, O Lord, all day long.” A division must be placed here, so that this continuation through the whole day may refer to the cry—that is, to prayer and the performance of good works.

“I stretched out my hands to you.” In his customary manner, he prefers this to be understood as works, which he constantly extended toward the Lord through good deeds. For if we suppose, as some wish, that this should be joined to the cross, what follows will be entirely inconsistent.

### Verse 10

**Will you work wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up and confess to you?**

This must be read as a negation. But we must examine what he says: “You will not work wonders for the dead,” although it is certain that innumerable dead have been raised. Yet he means the dead—that is, unbelievers—for he worked no wonders for those who did not believe, since their unbelief prevented them from being brought to conversion. Wonders are performed for those who behold the Lord’s mighty works with faith.

It follows: “Or will physicians raise them up and confess to you?” This too is spoken negatively, because the physicians whom humanity has believed capable, through the benefit of their art, of giving health to the sick cannot raise the dead, so that they ought to confess to the Lord—even though without God’s gift they cannot give bodily health itself to the sick.

Or this may be understood more subtly: physicians, while caring for bodies, are nevertheless unable to raise souls dead in sins, so that those whom the wounds of their unbelief have struck may be brought to life through a most truthful confession.

### Verse 11

**Will anyone declare your mercy in the grave, or your truth in perdition?**

He comes to the third narrative, where in this verse and the one that follows he introduces the figure called *emphasis*, whose meaning here must be understood from the part that makes us notice what he does not say.

He says: “Will anyone declare your mercy in the grave?” This must be read negatively, so that it may be understood that living and faithful people are accustomed to declare his mercy.

For “the grave” signifies the minds of unbelievers, concerning whom it was said above: “Their throat is an open grave” (Psalm 5:11). And rightly it is called a grave, where the soul dead in sins is confined. He therefore wishes those people to be understood who will not believe in the Lord, since no one seems to have declared the Lord’s mercy to them—something they were unwilling to receive with devoted minds.

We say that an action has occurred wherever someone, hearing it, produces an effect [ed., “affection”]. The same applies to what follows: “or your truth in perdition,” because no one is thought to have spoken the truth if he appears to neglect it and pass it by. Perdition is rightly named where truth is not admitted and only obstinacy is preserved.

### Verse 12

**Will your wonders be known in darkness, or your justice in the land of forgetfulness?**

Everything proceeds according to the same pattern, with the wording varied, so that by denying what does not exist, what does exist may be understood in contrast. The Lord’s wonders are not seen by darkened minds, because those who neglect God have lost the lights of wisdom.

Nor can his justice be known in earthly forgetfulness—that is, in the thickest blindness of the body, which abandons spiritual admonitions while its desires are occupied by carnal vices.

Remember, however, that all these things are said so that his soul might not be left in hell, but that the swiftest resurrection might come to him, so that the Lord’s praise could be acknowledged through his benefits.

### Verse 13

**But I cried out to you, O Lord, and in the morning my prayer will come before you.**

In opposition to what was said above, the Lord Christ, through the fact that he was to rise again, says that he cries out to the Lord together with his faithful people. He enumerates the most glorious qualities of various tribulations, so that Christian peoples, warned by such examples, might be strengthened.

By saying, “But I,” he indicates that he cried out together with his members, whose head is Christ. For when he himself cries out and teaches the Church, when he prays together with the faithful, he reveals one body.

Remember, therefore, that until the end of the Psalm he enumerates various calamities that he himself endured in his martyrs. Here I believe the figure of *synathroesmos* should be applied, when many things and many dangers are gathered together into one.

It follows: “And in the morning my prayer will come before you.” These words must be handled carefully, lest they appear contrary to that most truthful rule that the grace of the Lord precedes all things.

He says that the prayer of his body, the Church—which is made bright in the morning, that is, by good works—comes before the Lord’s coming, namely, the day of judgment. Yet this prayer was granted by the Lord’s generosity.

Therefore it is rightly said that his prayer has come beforehand, since many ages ago there was continual petition for what we still await as destined to come. He will come at the fitting time, but our desire must be shown through fervent petitions. He does not judge us to be his own if he does not come greatly desired by us.

Yet since it is said so clearly that he himself is the one who comes, he cannot speak this in his own person unless we understand the words as spoken by the members of the Church.

### Verse 14

**Why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer [ed., “have you rejected”]; why do you turn your face away from me [ed., “have you turned”]?**

Here the desire of the most holy mind is expressed, since it endured impatiently the delay of that through which the world could rightly be saved. The Lord is thought to reject our petition and turn his face away when he postpones our requests; and although he does what will benefit us, we are nevertheless deeply saddened by the delay.

This is also appropriately spoken from the person of the martyrs, who are wearied in this world by such desires. They are delayed for their increase and postponed for their glory, because being heard is not as beneficial as being delayed for the increase of their reward. Thus fire is driven back by a gust of wind so that it may be kindled more vigorously.

### Verse 15

**I am poor, and in labors from my youth; but, having been exalted, I have been humbled and confounded.**

The Church rightly says this, for she is wearied by the poverty of the world and by labors from her youth, as it is written in another Psalm: “They often attacked me from my youth” (Psalm 128:1).

She grows through persecutions and is lifted up by the pressure of the times; through humility she is always exalted. Her longer age is not a weak weariness but a mature perfection.

It follows: “But, having been exalted, I have been humbled and confounded.” This is shown especially to apply to the members, not to the head.

“I have been exalted,” he says, when each of the faithful formerly considered human affairs with a proud heart.

“I have been humbled,” when, through the mercy of divine grace, he reached the healing gift of confession.

“Confounded,” when he condemned by a profession of penitence the things he had wrongly done.

O blessed confusion, which removes eternal reproach! For whatever guilt has come upon penitents is absolved throughout the ages.

### Verse 16

**Your wrath has passed through me; and your terrors have troubled me.**

“Have passed through” is beautifully said, as though they had come upon him without remaining for long. For when a faithful person afflicts himself, he escapes the Lord’s anger through chastisement.

By saying “upon me,” he testifies, in his customary manner, that the affliction of the faithful has been imposed upon him.

It follows: “And your terrors have troubled me.” These are certainly the terrors of the coming judgment, which every sinful flesh is known to fear. It is clear that this applies to the members alone.

### Verse 17

**They surrounded me like water all day long; together they encompassed me.**

These are certainly the sins condemned by the strictness of the law. They surround human beings like water when they are known to spring up from every side. From what side, indeed, should we believe that sins do not come, when they are not made foreign to us even for a moment of the hours?

They are rightly compared with waters, for they enclose us in a most abundant flood. This is appropriately understood entirely from the person of the members.

### Verse 18

**You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances from misery.**

These things frequently happened to pious martyrs, from whom human services were withdrawn through fear of death. By “friends” he signifies those joined to us by honorable pursuits and likeness of character; by “neighbors,” those associated with us by the order of kinship; by “acquaintances,” those who are neither friends nor neighbors, but have learned of us only by reputation or sight. The feared calamity of persecution frequently drove these classes of people far from the faithful servants.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This is the chorus of Christ, which the prefixed title foretold through the interpretation of the name *Maheleth*, when his faithful people, following his most holy Passion, responded with exceedingly glorious imitation. From this came the prison that held the confessors enclosed; from this came the blood of the martyrs, more precious than purple and fine linen; from this came the words of the apostles, resounding throughout the whole world; from this, like a purest sun, holy faith advanced; from this, even today, people hasten toward temporal deaths in order to seek the rewards of eternal life.

Therefore let no one fear the miseries that make people blessed; let no one dread the torments that grant perpetual salvation; let no one fear the sorrow that bestows everlasting joy. How much is it to die temporally, so that eternal life may be acquired? How much is it to endure a human sentence, so that we may deserve to obtain divine absolution? Who would be ashamed of the punishments that Christ the Lord deigned to endure? Who would regard as disgrace what the Creator of all chose to suffer? Therefore let us undergo worldly calamity for his sake, if we wish to have an everlasting portion with him.

# Exposition on Psalm LXXXVIII

## The Understanding of Ethan the Israelite

The words he set down should be expounded not so much according to the order of the title as for the convenience of understanding, so that the truth of the matter may shine forth more easily for us. *Ethan* is interpreted as “strong”; *Israelite*, “seeing God.” And because this Psalm was going to recount the praises and promises of the Lord, it is clear that such a name was assigned to him to indicate the unchangeable firmness of faithful words.

“Understanding,” as we have often said, must be referred to things above, where the one who truly understands directs the gaze of his mind. He is going to speak at length about the hope of Christians and the magnificence of the Lord; through these things no one is deceived if the mind of the one who supplicates is strengthened in the most steadfast will of this Ethan.

## Division of the Psalm

This Ethan, whom we said signifies “strong,” was filled with such illumination of mind that he could most truly be called an Israelite. At the Psalm’s opening he says that he will sing of the Lord’s mercies, because he promised many things beneficial to the faithful people. In the second part he describes the Lord’s praises and power in various ways. In the third he enumerates the paternal promises concerning Christ the Lord. In the fourth, Christ the Lord is remembered as having been handed over to enemies because of the Passion he endured. In the fifth he asks that help be given to human frailty, because he asserts that the children of human beings were not fashioned by him in vain. In the sixth he asks the Lord to fulfill his promises, which he is declared to have made to his servant David, and to remember what insults his servants endured from the impious.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

**I will sing your mercies, O Lord, forever; from generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.**

He is rightly called strong, since he is going to speak of things so firm. This Ethan is going to sing of the Lord’s mercies, which both stand in eternal stability and must be celebrated with everlasting praises. For he showed wondrous compassion toward the human race, seeking what had perished and saving what had been wounded.

When he added “from generation to generation,” he signifies two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, to whom he testifies that he will proclaim the truth that he states below. It follows: “And your truth with my mouth,” truly speaking with his mouth what he had grasped in understanding. And “with my mouth” is rightly said, because what proceeds from the mouth quickly dissipates, whereas what is turned over in the mouth is celebrated with enduring devotion.

### Verse 2

**For you said: “Mercy shall be built forever; your truth shall be prepared in the heavens.”**

This is the truth that the holy man had foretold he would proclaim. And he preached it confidently with good reason, since the Lord had promised it unequivocally; for the one who follows the words of truth cannot be deceived.

But let us see what “Mercy shall be built forever” signifies. There are structures that cannot rise unless destruction has preceded them, such as the worshipers of idols and the followers of the worst customs. Unless these people have been destroyed in their evil ways, they cannot be built up for good, as was said to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have appointed you to build and to destroy” (Jeremiah 1:10). This mercy, however, is not destroyed; it always flourishes and always increases.

It follows: “Your truth shall be prepared in the heavens.” The heavens, as we have often said, signify the apostles, through whose preaching it came about that Christian religion was proclaimed among the nations.

All these words, however, must be extended through the intermediate distinctions as far as the *diapsalma*, because everything refers back to what he says: “For you said.” This figure is called *ἀπὸ κοινοῦ* (*apo koinou*), that is, “from what is common,” when what precedes responds to what follows.

### Verse 3

**I have established a covenant with my chosen ones; I have sworn to David my servant.**

Now he reports the words of the Lord, which he had remembered him saying above. For although he seems to have announced these things to everyone, he established them only for his chosen ones, who preferred to believe in him through his own gift, lest those also be bound to such a promise who preferred to descend bodily from David’s seed.

He added: “I have sworn to David my servant.” A divine oath is known to be the security of a promise, because only one to whom the fulfillment of what he has said is subject promises justly and definitively. Human frailty is therefore forbidden to bind itself by oaths to promises, because it does not lie within its power to accomplish what it promises.

God, then, most justly swears when he promises by his right. For the word itself indicates the reason: we say *juravit*, “he swore,” as though *jure oravit*, “he spoke justly.”

### Verse 4

**Forever I will prepare your seed, and I will build your throne for generation upon generation.**

We have reached the things that the Father promised to his servant David. The Lord Christ was prepared, for he was to descend from David in the origin of his flesh, forever King of kings and Lord of lords. But what he said, “I will prepare,” pertains to Christ’s humanity, not to his divinity, by which he is consubstantial, almighty, and coeternal with the Father.

It follows: “And I will build your throne for generation upon generation.” This entire promise pertains to the Lord the Savior. A throne was then promised to him that was afterward to be established in the breasts of the saints. Every saint is the Lord’s throne, upon whom, like a most splendid throne, he has seated himself by the condescension of his majesty; as it is read concerning the Holy Spirit: “And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and it sat upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:3).

### Verse 5

**The heavens shall confess your wonders, O Lord, and your truth in the assembly of the saints.**

He comes to the second part, in which he is going to speak of the mysteries of divine power. The heavens, which are the true preachers, will confess with how many miracles the Lord governs the world as it pleases him: how every creature obeys his commands; and they proclaim that changes in things are not carried out accidentally, as certain utterly foolish people have thought, but are contained within his ineffable power.

He added: “And your truth in the assembly of the saints.” He said that the wonders were to be proclaimed everywhere, but that the truth was to be confessed in the assembly of the saints, where it is believed that “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), where the Holy Trinity is received in such a way that the one God, as he is, is praised by the mouth of all as Lord of all.

### Verse 6

**For who in the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?**

We have frequently said that the clouds are preachers of the Word of God, who through the Holy Spirit watered the peoples with divine grace. Yet they were subject to the law of sin: powerful in miracles and terrible in preaching.

But who among them could be like Christ, even though he too was covered by the veil of flesh? For one thing is he who possesses power from himself, and another is he who is glorious from another. Similarly, no one among the sons of God could have an equal to him, because he is Son by nature, whereas the saints are sons by grace; he is without any sin, while they are shown to have been stripped of sins through him. These things were said so that no one might sacrilegiously regard him as merely a human being.

### Verse 7

**God, who is glorified in the counsel of the saints, great and to be feared above all who are around him.**

He explains what he said above: he could not have anyone like him, because he contained all things. The Lord Christ himself, who is preached by the saints, is called great because he is God and to be feared because of his wondrous power.

“Above all who are around him” means the saints, whom he called above the sons of God, who draw near through the gift of his grace. But he is rightly shown to be exalted above them, through whom all are known to be glorious.

Consider, moreover, that through the twelfth species of definition, which in Greek is called *κατ’ ἔπαινον* (*kat’ epainon*) and in Latin *per laudem*, “by praise,” the verses subject to the division continue, and through various praises the identity of this Lord is indicated.

### Verse 8

**O Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are powerful, O Lord, and your truth is around you.**

After what he said above, the sentence “Who is like you?” appropriately follows, that is, because you are Lord of powers. The saints are enriched with powers, but they do not rule; you command those things through which they are glorious because of your gift.

“Who is like you?” is rightly repeated. You are powerful from yourself, while they are powerful from you; they have been illuminated by your truth, whereas your truth is indivisibly present in you forever.

### Verse 9

**You rule the power of the sea; you still the movement of its waves.**

Now he gives many enumerations through which he clearly shows the Lord’s singular power. “The power of the sea” is the honor of this age, which has frequently risen against Christ’s martyrs with swift swelling.

Yet lest it be thought that this willfulness rages by its own power, he says also of these powers: “You rule,” when you turn their fierce movements to the advantage of the saints, as he himself says in the Gospel: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11).

And because he had said, “You rule,” a fitting proof follows, since he himself stills its waves. Observe that he said “stills,” not “removes,” because if he had taken it away completely, the martyrs would not have crowns.

If you wish to understand this historically as well, that the Lord stills the waves of the sea is testified by that Gospel passage (Matthew 8:26), when, as the disciples were in danger, he commanded the wind to cease and the sea to become calm.

### Verse 10

**You humbled the proud as one wounded; by the strength of your arm you scattered your enemies.**

Some are humbled for destruction, others are bowed toward grace. But so that you might understand that this was spoken in an evil sense, he added: “As one wounded, the proud.”

He signifies the devil, who, exalted above what he could be, was humbled through his own fault within what he was not by nature, struck in mind and not in body. Thus that most wicked one, like a wounded man, fell from heaven into this thickest density of the air, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

By “enemies” he means the unbelieving Jews, who were scattered throughout countless nations by the power of Christ the Lord, whom divine authority testifies to be the Father’s arm, as we have often said.

### Verse 11

**The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness.**

Because above he had spoken of two kinds of miracles, he now confirms them by the proof of this verse. He triumphed in heaven over the proud devil and on earth over the faithless Jew because heaven and earth were his.

Why would the devil or the Jew grow proud in what belonged to another, when both were shown to have him as their author?

It follows: “You founded the world and its fullness.” This rebuke still pertains to the Jews. The sense, then, is: Why did fools wish to rage against you in this world, whose founder you, Christ, are, so that in their extreme madness they might presume things that are proved to exceed human strength?

“The world” refers to the entire expanse of the universe; “its fullness” refers to all the creatures known to exist within it. Thus, by recalling such things, he briefly embraced everything.

### Verse 12

**You founded the north and the sea; Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name.**

“North” still signifies the devil, who said: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13–14).

We aptly understand “the sea of this age” as the exalted and wicked powers of human beings, which rise against the Lord’s commands through sacrilegious desires, not so that they may prosper, but so that they may fall utterly. He rebukes both for placing presumption in themselves, since it is clear that they were fashioned by their own Lord.

A creature ought not to grow proud against its Creator, since it received from him the ability to exist.

It follows: “Tabor and Hermon shall rejoice in your name.” Tabor and Hermon are mountains of the province of Syria, whose names give rise to great mysteries. *Tabor* is said to mean “coming light,” which particularly refers to the advent of the Lord the Savior, concerning whom it was said: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

*Hermon* signifies “his anathema,” that is, the anathema of the devil, which he received from Christians when the Lord came. For it was fitting that the dark devil should be conquered in the presence of the light.

These mountains, therefore, will rejoice in the Lord’s name, just as the faithful say elsewhere: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 113:1, 8).

### Verse 13

**Your arm is with power; let your hand be strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted.**

We frequently read that “arm” signifies human strength, as the prophet says: “Cursed is the person who places flesh as the hope of his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jeremiah 17:5). But it cannot possess as much power as has been assigned to it for the time being.

Here, however, to signify the Lord the Savior, it is said: “Your arm is with power,” that is, for him being and being able are the same; his power never grows cold, since he continually does everything he wills in heaven and on earth.

He added: “Let your hand be strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted.” Hand and right hand, if we examine them carefully, are very different. He asks that the hand—that is, the operation—be strengthened against the proud, so that those bowed down by tribulations may be led swiftly to the pursuit of conversion.

But “let your right hand be exalted” may perhaps mean here: let the number of the predestined be glorified, the number that is to be placed on the right.

### Verse 14

**Justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne; mercy and truth shall go before your face.**

The Lord’s throne is indeed always eternal, but it will appear prepared for us when we see him judging in justice. At that time sacred equity will be revealed to us, and the true Judge will be shown, when the mysteries of the angels are seen.

His throne is prepared when these things are observed by human beings at the general resurrection.

It follows: “Mercy and truth shall go before your face.” This is appropriately applied to the time of the present world. “Your face,” that is, the manifestation of his judgment, will be preceded by mercy and truth.

There is mercy because he spares those who have converted; there is truth because he restores what he promised. Thus both periods are clearly indicated by these words.

### Verse 15

“Blessed is the people that understands the joyful shout; Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance.”

That most holy Ethan, whom the title introduced, after appearing to have proclaimed the mysteries of God, undertakes the manifold praises of the blessed people through what rhetoricians call the demonstrative genre of discourse. For he exclaims: “Blessed is the people that understands the joyful shout”—that is, the people recognized as having placed their immeasurable joy not in their own strength but in the power of God. A joyful shout is an abundant exultation of the mind that cannot be expressed in words. Thus it belongs to the blessed people to search out this joy in the secret place of the heart; and we perceive it as blessed when we confess its author with a pure mind.

It is also entirely useful to understand the sentence in this way: that blessed people are those who not only sing the praises of God with their mouths but also understand them by the light of the mind. To understand means to search the Holy Scriptures according to Catholic principles; to grasp the sayings of the Fathers through saving doctrine; and to direct everything toward the devotion of right faith, rather than yielding to the perversities of heretics.

He added the reward that follows such people: “Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance.” That blessed people whom he said understands the joyful shout walks in the light of his countenance when it continually perseveres in the contemplation of the Holy Trinity. For “walks” signifies “lives,” because this present time of our life is completed through a kind of passage.

### Verse 16

“And in your name they shall exult all the day; and in your righteousness they shall be exalted.”

He still continues with that reward which is given to the people who understand the joyful shout. For when he says to the Lord, “In your name they shall exult,” he forbids rejoicing in presumption upon oneself, lest deceived mortality place its joy where everything is perishable. It follows, “all the day,” which indicates the entire period of life, since one ought never to cease from that source from which perpetual and abundant joys are known to proceed.

When this has taken place, it comes about that they are exalted in the Lord’s righteousness, when in that resurrection they have been placed at his right hand. [Col. 0633D] Behold what gifts he says are prepared for those who understand the joyful shout. Therefore let us cast away harmful negligence and hasten toward the blessed pursuits of understanding, so that here, by the Lord’s gift, we may be nourished by the sweet feast that follows from it, and there may enjoy the gift of perpetual joy.

### Verse 17

“For you are the glory of their strength, and by your good pleasure our horn shall be exalted.”

Their horn—that is, their power—is rightly exalted because they have placed their strength and glory in the Lord the Savior, of whom the Father says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). For when everything that has been given is referred to him, he himself becomes our praise and perfect joy.

And note that in this passage he has placed “horn” in a good sense, but elsewhere in an evil sense, as in: “And from the horns of unicorns my humility” (Ps. XXI, 22). This is not without reason, since a power that is given can produce both good and evil.

### Verse 18

“For the taking-up belongs to the Lord, and to the Holy One of Israel, our King.”

He explained why the horn of those who believe in him is exalted: “For the taking-up”—that is, the glory of the incarnation—has been shown to be fulfilled by the Holy One of Israel. Through it all who have hope are raised up from the depth of sin, while, by his mercy lifting us, we are placed in eternal joys.

Behold, the gifts promised to the people who understand the joyful shout have been explained. The admirable praise of the demonstrative genre has been completed, so that in each matter his power might be narrated and we might more clearly establish who this Lord is. Now let us learn something about the third division.

### Verse 19

“Then you spoke in the presence of your sons, and said: ‘I have placed help upon the mighty, and exalted the chosen one from my people.’”

Until now Ethan has spoken in his own person. Now he comes to the third part, proclaiming the words of the Father, which were spoken concerning the Lord the Savior, so that the preceding praise might be taught to be beyond doubt, since paternal authority also confirmed it.

We have often said that the saints are called children of God not by nature but by grace. To these children, therefore—that is, to the prophets and preachers of the word—the Lord spoke “in the presence,” making them behold what they were saying. Through this expression it is shown that whatever the prophets said, they did not speak in ignorance; rather, established in most certain contemplation, they saw inwardly what they proclaimed with their mouths. Hence the prophets are also called “seers.”

It follows: “I have placed help upon the mighty.” Let us ask what is meant by help being placed upon the mighty. For one who seeks help is not mighty, while one who is mighty does not need to be helped. But this statement may reasonably be understood either of the universal body of the Church, which everyone knows to be mighty and chosen; and to it Christ the Lord is said to have been given as help, since he said of himself in the second psalm, “But I have been established as King by him upon his holy mountain of Zion” (Ps. II, 6).

Or certainly, if we wish to understand this of Christ the Lord, when it says, “I have placed help upon the mighty,” it should be taken as though he were saying: “The Father bore witness to the Mighty One, that is, to the Son,” as the voice addressed to him in the Gospel testifies: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII, 28). This is perhaps what he means by “help placed upon the mighty.”

[Col. 0635A] He added: “I have exalted the chosen one from my people.” The prophet Isaiah recalls that the Lord Christ is called chosen, saying: “Behold my servant; I will receive him, my chosen one; my soul has been well pleased in him” (Isa. XLII, 1). He was exalted, as the Apostle says: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 9).

“From my people” signifies the Jewish nation, from which it is established that the Lord Christ was born.

### Verse 20

“I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him.”

When he says, “I have found David,” he clearly indicates Jesus Christ, whom he previously called “the Mighty One.” For this name is frequently shown to refer to him, since he is called strong of hand and is found to be desirable—especially when what follows can in no way apply either to David or to any other righteous person except the Lord the Savior. Concerning him it has already been said in another psalm: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of exultation beyond your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 9).

### Verse 21

“For my hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him.”

This is said according to the form of the servant that was assumed in the Virgin’s womb. The divine hand helped it in its sufferings, and the Lord’s strength fortified it, so that the holy Redeemer, having assumed the passion for the salvation of the world, might complete the passion set before him.

This figure is called *characterismos*, which in Latin is called “formation” or “description,” when we make an absent person appear present to the observer through certain indications. This figure, therefore, embraces the whole part of this division with an elegant variety.

### Verse 22

“The enemy shall profit nothing against him, and the son of iniquity shall not harm him.”

How can this certainly apply to David, who endured stronger enemies and sinned at the instigation of the devil? But it is necessary to understand this truly of Christ. For although the devil, the insolent enemy of humanity, raged against him; although Judas, the son of iniquity, presumed to harm him, nevertheless none of them found in him a sin for which they could justly accuse him, as he himself says: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

[Col. 0635D]

### Verse 23

“And I shall cut down his enemies before his face, and turn those who hate him to flight.”

Christ’s enemies are cut down before his face when, through the benefit of conversion, his presence separates them from their own crimes and sins. For when his face deigns to look upon sinners, they are cut down from their wickedness; and those who come, by the Lord’s mercy, into the presence of the true light can no longer offer consent to their dark offenses.

Those who hate him are turned to flight when, abandoning their impious life, they begin to hasten toward his remedies. Mindful of sin, they flee from their own deeds and turn with salutary haste to the Lord’s benefits. Blessed, therefore, is the flight from crimes that seeks refuge in the Lord, as has already been said in another psalm: “You are my refuge from the distress that surrounds me” (Ps. XXXI, 7).

### Verse 24

“And my truth and my mercy are with him, and in my name his horn shall be exalted.”

The Father says of the Son, “My truth and my mercy are with him,” so that we may understand that nothing is divided, but that the virtues possessed by the Father are possessed together by the Son, as he himself testifies: “All things of the Father are mine, and mine are the Father’s” (John XVII, 10).

Truth pertains to judgment, by which he will judge the world; mercy pertains to compassion, by which he forgives sins and grants everything he bestows through generous kindness.

It follows: “And in my name his horn shall be exalted.” Here “horn” signifies unconquerable power, concerning which he himself says in the Gospel: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

### Verse 25

“And I shall place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers.”

The sea signifies all the nations, among which our Savior received the glory of dominion when they believed in his name with minds humbly devoted to him. “Upon the rivers” perhaps signifies the streams of springs, where the people of regeneration are acquired for the Lord the Savior. Or he uses the Jordan River for “rivers,” in which the Lord consecrated the example of his baptism.

So also we say “heavens” for “heaven,” “lands” for “land,” and “seas” for “sea”; and, if you wish to seek further examples, Athens, Thebes, Mycenae, and similar names.

### Verse 26

“He himself shall call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.’”

### Verse 27

“And I shall place him as firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.”

In these two verses the iniquity of the Jews is utterly refuted. What could be clearer or plainer than that he should be believed to be the Son who calls upon the Father, and again believed to be the Father who addresses the Son? Although these two names are relational and one would suffice for the power of both to be understood, nevertheless, to exclude every scruple of ambiguity, he placed both and confirmed both; yet the Jews’ insane obstinacy still does not cease to wander, even though the cause of their error has been removed.

This is the fourteenth species of definition, which the Greeks call “according to relation” (*κατὰ τοῦ πρός τι*) and the Latins call “relative” (*ad aliquid*), whenever one name is spoken in such a way that another appears to be understood from it.

It follows: “And I shall place him as firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.” We must also examine why he said “firstborn,” as though the Father had begotten the Son substantially in such a way that another would follow. But this mode of expression is clearly proper to divine Scripture, as is also the Gospel passage concerning Joseph and Mary, where it says: “And he did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son” (Matt. I, 25). Will it therefore follow that the virgin Mary is to be believed to have borne another after the Lord Jesus Christ? Yet “firstborn” is rightly said, although he alone is shown to have been begotten from the substance of the Father.

For he himself says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end, the prince and origin of David” (Rev. XXII, 13, [Col. 0637A] 16). Thus this expression should rightly raise no question, since he is established as both beginning and end.

“I shall place” means “I shall establish,” just as he says in the second psalm: “But I have been established as King by him.” “Exalted above the kings of the earth” is as it is said in the seventy-first psalm: “And all the kings of the earth shall worship him” (Ps. LXXI, 11).

### Verse 28

“I shall keep my mercy for him forever, and my faithful covenant with him.”

This too is said according to the form of the servant, because he received the Father’s mercy in eternal honor, and perpetual power in heaven and on earth was given to him. The covenant is faithful to him when whatever the prophets foretold about him is fulfilled with complete truth.

### Verse 29

“And I shall establish his seed forever and ever, and his throne like the days of heaven.”

“Forever and ever” signifies eternity. The seed of David is Christ the Lord, who, established in eternal glory, reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. His throne is the power of the future judgment, which will be carried out with such truth that it will shine with heavenly splendor before all the saints.

We must understand that the days which succeed one another in alternating cycles are one thing, and the future day, everlasting in continuous light, is another. Concerning the latter it is said in the eighty-third psalm: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII, 11). It is rightly called “the day of heaven,” since it cannot have nocturnal darkness caused by the interposition of the earth.

### Verse 30

“If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments;

### Verse 31

“if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments.”

He speaks these two verses concerning the Christian people, who are truly called the sons of the Bridegroom, since they are regenerated through the Church, their mother, from water and the Holy Spirit. If they forsake the Lord’s law, if they do not walk in his judgments, if they profane his ordinances, and if they do not keep his commandments, a punishment worthy of them is promised to follow.

### Verse 32

“I shall visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with blows.”

He comes to the sentence threatened by the preceding words. He visits with a rod when he avenges strictly; thus the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV, 21). He also visits with blows when punishment is inflicted upon us more lightly. A rod strikes in one way, whips beat in another. It is clear that both occur among the Christian people according to the character of the sin, yet they contribute to salvation, as Solomon says: “For whom the Lord loves, he reproves; but he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. III, 12). For see what follows.

### Verse 33

“But I shall not scatter my mercy from him, nor shall I harm him in my truth.”

After speaking above of the members, he now returns to the head. The Father says that he will not scatter his mercy from Christ, but will bestow it in its entire fullness, as the Apostle says: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. II, 9)—that is, substantially and manifestly.

Or this may be because the fullness of divinity is recognized as dwelling in the Lord’s body; hence it was also said earlier in the thirtieth psalm.

It follows: “Nor shall I harm him in my truth.” For above the Father had promised: “My hand shall help him, and my arm shall strengthen him.” How could he harm one to whom he appeared to have made such promises? Consider what is said: “Nor shall I harm him in my truth.” Even if the enemies were permitted to harm him, the Son was not injured in the Father’s truth, whose passion gloriously completed the salvation of the whole world.

### Verse 34

“I shall not profane my covenant, and I shall not make void the things that proceed from my lips.”

This is what he said above: “Nor shall I harm him in my truth,” since everything is known to have been completed according to the order of truth. For he did not profane his covenant by lying; rather, he made it honorable through the faithfulness of events, since the things that proceeded from his lips—that is, what he proclaimed through the holy prophets—were destroyed by no falsehood.

The prophets are appropriately called the Lord’s lips, since through them he deigned to speak.

### Verse 35

“Once I swore by my holiness: I shall not lie to David.”

It is the custom of human beings to swear frequently so that someone may believe them; God swears once, because he is not changed by any variation of time. We have said that God’s swearing means his promising future things. For by what religious obligation could one who has no superior bind himself?
