He also says, “By my holiness”—that is, by Christ, who said: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Ps. LXXXV, 2). He also added: “If I lie to David.” “If” is used with negative force, as common usage also has it.

### Verse 36

“His seed shall remain forever, and his throne like the sun in my sight.”

The seed of Christ consists of all who believe in him with faithful minds, because the future kingdom has been sown in them, which the coming harvest will reveal. Thus he himself says in the twenty-first psalm: “My seed shall serve him” (Ps. XXI, 31).

The saints, therefore, shall remain forever, those who dwell in an excellent and blessed way of life. Hence we do not properly say that those remain who are rejected from the Lord’s kingdom.

The throne of God here should be understood as the faithful soul, in which he truly sits when he has filled it with the illumination of his majesty. Thus it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” He added, “like the sun in my sight.” That soul of the righteous will be like the sun—the soul which we have said is the seat of the Lord the Savior. By saying “like the sun,” he makes a comparison with visible things. For if it is a great thing to shine from a creature, it is much better to shine from the Creator.

### Verse 37

“And like the full moon forever, and a faithful witness in heaven.”

Above he spoke of the sun, which we said pertains to the soul of the righteous. Now he speaks of the moon, which is appropriately applied here to the human body, because it is diminished and grows through the various stages of life. But he added “full” so that in that spiritual body you would understand nothing temporal, but would perceive only complete eternity.

Our body itself will likewise be filled with glory forever, like the full moon. That moon—that is, the structure of our body—will be a faithful witness, namely, the body in which the promises are fulfilled. But observe what he added: “in heaven,” that is, in the holy man. Their bodies will shine in this way, whose souls also shine through divine illumination, as Solomon says: “The righteous will shine, and will run to and fro like sparks through stubble” (Wis. III, 7). For the moon is frequently compared with the Church.

### Verse 38

“But you have rejected and spurned, and delayed, your Christ.”

Until now Christ has been praised in the Father’s voice. Now Ethan comes to the fourth part, in which, speaking in his own person, he presents something apparently contrary to what preceded. There the Father asserts that Christ will be vindicated from his enemies, and confirms this by an oath’s promise; here he is remembered as rejected and handed over.

This should be understood in two ways. We may take it as referring to the glory of the resurrection; or, more appropriately, we may say—as Father Augustine found—that the former refers to the Lord the Savior, while this refers to David his servant, who is shown to have been afflicted by many calamities. For the name “Christ,” which comes from anointing, is certainly applicable to both.

“You have rejected” pertains, as I think, to the parable that the prophet Nathan told him, in which he was rejected from royal dignity and compared with an unjust man who devoured a poor man’s sheep. He was rightly called rejected, since he is also shown to have been condemned by his own judgment.

“You have spurned” means that you made him contemptible, when, expelled from the kingdom and fleeing from his son Absalom, he walked barefoot and endured the reproaches of the son of Jemini [Col. 0639C] amid the harshest insults.

“You have delayed” does not refer to forgiveness, to which the prophet immediately replied: “And the Lord has taken away your sin” (II Kings XII, 13). Rather, he was delayed in his tribulations until he could restore the kingdom that had been seized.

“Your Christ” signifies “your anointed one,” since at that time the leaders of the Hebrews were anointed as kings.

### Verse 39

“You have turned aside the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his holiness on the earth.”

This now pertains to the Jewish nation, a subject he pursues to the end of the division. It is said in the manner of human beings: “You have turned aside,” that is, “you have transferred to another side,” so that what had been promised to the Jews might in fact reach the benefit of the nations.

A priest did not remain among them, nor a temple, which is known to have been overthrown; but Christians have obtained everything in complete fullness. Thus it is rightly said: “You have turned aside,” when what was taken from the faithless is shown to have been granted to the faithful.

He said “the covenant of your servant,” not because David made the covenant, but because the dignity of the Lord’s birth had been committed to him by the covenant.

It follows: “You have profaned his holiness on the earth.” “Profane” means irreligious—something that was driven away from a shrine, that is, from reverence for the temple. The sacrifice of animals and observance of Sabbaths, which had previously been performed figuratively, were removed when the truth came.

By “on the earth,” we should understand the whole world, where the Catholic Church has been established.

### Verse 40

“You have destroyed all his walls; you have made his fortifications a cause of fear.”

A wall is a structure that fortifies places prepared for some useful purpose as a means of defense. It is not built by mixing in another material, but is constructed, like a wall, by joining stones alone.

In accordance with its likeness, he describes that simple and unconquerable divine defense which had to be removed so that the Jewish nation could be devastated by the invasion of enemies. It is beautifully said, “You have made his fortifications a cause of fear,” so that, because of their sins, they might fear the very Lord by whose fortification they had been accustomed to be enclosed.

And note that through these three verses different words have ended with similar sounds. He said: “You have rejected,” “you have spurned,” “you have delayed,” “you have turned aside,” “you have profaned,” “you have destroyed,” “you have made.” This figure is called *homoeoteleuton*, when many expressions end with similar letters.

### Verse 41

“All who pass by the way have plundered him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors.”

That state of the Jewish kingdom is known to have been plundered both in faith and in resources. For those passing through it violently transferred to themselves the resources of its religion after stripping away its possessions—people who believed more readily in those whom the Lord had not come bodily to instruct, as he himself said: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII, 45).

The Jews therefore rightly became a reproach to their neighbors, because they refused to believe in the Lord of glory.

### Verse 42

“You have exalted the right hand of his enemies; you have gladdened all his enemies.”

These things undoubtedly happened when the Jews, handed over to their enemies, endured the most devastating plunderings and massacres. For an enemy becomes joyful when his adversary is humbled according to his desires.

### Verse 43

“You have turned aside the help of his sword, and you have not helped him in battle.”

The sword rightly offered him no help, since he had lost the strength of divinity. Although iron may appear to be a human defense, it accomplishes nothing unless the heavenly right hand strengthens it, as has already been said in another psalm: “For I shall not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me” (Ps. XLIII, 7).

Thus that armed people was rendered unarmed, so that when the few had conquered the many, the many were unable to resist the few.

### Verse 44

“You have dissolved him from purification, and struck his throne down to the earth.”

Divinity frequently purifies those whom it scourges, so that it may receive back as cleansed the one whom it had rejected as filthy with sins. But those whom it dissolves from purification—that is, removes from it—it has already determined to condemn.

Therefore he signifies here the Jews, who in the obstinacy of their minds preferred to spurn Christ. Their throne was also struck down to the earth when, rejecting the King, the Lord the Savior, they no longer deserved to have a ruler from their own nation.

“Throne” stands for kingdom. It is rightly said to have been struck down to the earth when the people, divided and shattered, were dispersed piecemeal throughout the whole world.

### Verse 45

“You have shortened the days of his times; you have drenched him with confusion.”

That state which we have described as the Jewish kingdom, to which eternity had been promised if it served the Lord, was certainly shortened into limited days, because it did not deserve to obtain the promise made to Abraham. It was rightly reduced to brevity, since it vainly promised itself a long succession of years.

He also added, “You have drenched him with confusion,” because it bears the filth of its unbelief upon its face even today, carrying disgrace in its countenance while it is confounded among all the nations by an abhorrent horror.

This mighty Ethan narrated these things with marvelous variety. Yet in all of them he did not acknowledge that the Lord had lied. For what he promised to David—that is, to his Christ—he bestowed upon all Christians. Nor do the Jews have any just grounds for complaint, since they preferred to separate themselves from the most truthful promise [ms. A: “from truth”].

[Col. 0641B]

### Verse 46

“How long, Lord, will you turn away forever? Will your anger burn like fire?”

Ethan comes to the fifth part, where he briefly asks the Lord to show mercy and pardon the Jewish people, since there is no one who can free the soul from hell.

“Forever” here should be understood as the end of the age, when, as has often been said, the countless conversion of the Jews is awaited, because the Apostle says: “For a partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. XI, 25).

He therefore asks that the Lord not turn away forever, since the faithful recognition of the Jews is awaited.

He added: “Will your anger burn like fire?” We are moderately angry when we rebuke someone in speech; but we burn with anger when we decide to take vengeance. He also added, “like fire,” which consumes whatever is placed before it.

### Verse 47

“Remember, Lord, what my substance [ed.: righteousness] is; for you did not establish the sons of human beings in vain.”

That Ethan, strengthened by firmness of mind, asks the Lord to deign to free this flesh, subject to sins, through the glory of his coming, since it was not created for him to permit it to perish as something vain.

For when he remembered our substance, he both rescued the sons of human beings from death and placed them in the hope of great blessedness.

### Verse 48

“Who is the person who lives and will not see death? Or who will rescue his soul from the hand of hell?”

“Who is?” must be read interrogatively. This figure is called *erotema*, that is, interrogation, where “no one” is to be understood.

For all human beings, whether righteous or sinners, will see death, which was inflicted upon the first human being by the law of sin. As the Apostle says: “Therefore, just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

He recalls this now so that the human condition may merit the Creator’s mercy through its calamities. Hence those who refuse, through an evil presumption, to believe in original sin, the more they claim to be free from this condition, the more they are bound by a pitiable fate.

It follows: “Or who will rescue his soul from the hand of hell?” Here too “no one” is to be understood. “From the hand” means “from the power of hell.” Since it happens that all human beings die, it is necessary that they cannot remove their souls from the power of hell except through the one who rescued us from the devil’s dominion and, by dying, struck down death.

### Verse 49

“Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth?”

He comes to the sixth part, where he entreats the Lord to come to the aid of the afflicted nation and of the human condition, which is exceedingly fragile [ms. A, F: “of the human condition”], and to fulfill the promises he knew had been made to David.

“Where are” is not spoken in grief, but as though the Lord were being asked why he delays. For how could he doubt the one to whom it is said, “in your truth”—that is, so that he may quickly grant what he was known to be going to do?

He calls them “ancient mercies,” remembering those he had shown to the patriarch Abraham. He would not call them ancient unless he recognized that they had been performed before David’s time.

### Verse 50

“Remember the reproach of your servants, which I have held in my bosom, from many nations.”

The order of the words is: “Remember the reproach of your servants,” that is, “of many nations,” “which I have held in my bosom.”

This is said to the one for whom past and future are present. Yet it is spoken in the human manner, because when the Lord delays granting something, he is judged to have forgotten.

Reproach came upon the servants of God when, among nations seized by love of idols, Christians were regarded as criminals and judged worthy of persecution because they were known to be devoted to a new form of worship. This was in the bosom of Christians—that is, in the secret affection of the mind—because they feared to speak openly, and therefore were proved to be extinguished.

[Col. 0642C]

### Verse 51

“With which your enemies, Lord, reproached; with which they reproached the exchange of your Christ.”

He explains what he said above: “the reproach of many nations.” “They reproached” must be read in the sense of imputing—that is, they charged them with what they ought rather to have believed and proclaimed.

But lest you be uncertain who was saying these things, he added, “your enemies, Lord,” that is, the worshipers of idols, who hastened in every way to oppose the holy proclamations.

He repeats “with which they reproached” to intensify their crime, since they attributed to the faithful the exchange of Christ, which they ought to have honored with the highest reverence.

The exchange of Christ is so called because he called the old human being into the new grace of regeneration and led him from the darkness of sins into the light of true faith; because he prepared the joys of everlasting life for mortal humanity; and because he deigned to grant sinners these and similar gifts.

This is the exchange of Christ, by which he abandoned the obstinate and admitted the faithful through the gift of his compassion.

### Verse 52

“Blessed be the Lord forever. Let it be; let it be.”

After that most fortunate and most holy exchange [ms. G: “most faithful and holy”], it was fitting that praise should be added to the Lord, who is recognized as having bestowed it upon mortals who did not deserve it.

Beautifully, in opposition to the temporal curses of the nations, it says: “Blessed be the Lord forever,” since what they say is perishable. The Lord’s praise endures forever because he knows how to give things that are enclosed by no end.

It follows: “Let it be; let it be,” so that no one would doubt such great promises when repeated confirmation followed, like the signature of a good ruler added to sacred commands.

But we should understand this rather as belonging to the praise of the psalms, not, as some have thought, to some division of the book.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

O truly strong Ethan—not strong in bodily vigor, but steadfast in firmness of soul—who, like the most faithful steward of the human race, explained for us the commandment of life inscribed upon those sacred altars.

Now let us pray that what we perceive with our ears we may store within our minds. For our victory is accomplished if, after such sacred words, we contend not against outsiders but against our own vices; and if, rejecting earthly things, we seek heavenly things without any hesitation.

For the interpretation of this name admonishes Christians—“faithful” and “patient”—not to be broken by any adversity, as the Apostle says, providing the greatest example of this virtue. For he says of himself: “In many labors, in prisons more abundantly, in blows beyond measure, in deaths frequently. From the Jews I received five times forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck; I spent a night and a day in the depths of the sea” (II Cor. XI, 23–24).

There follow also the other sufferings that fulfilled this Ethan more by his deeds than by his name. Behold, blessed Apostle, an exchange of honor has been granted to you: just as you confirmed your holy preaching through the testimony of the psalms, so the psalms are explained through your deeds.

# Exposition of Psalm LXXXIX

## The Prayer of Moses, the Man of God
There is no doubt (as we have often said) that such names are applied to titles which seem, by their interpretation, to disclose the text of the psalms. First of all, prayer is set forth, through which the Lord’s anger is suspended, pardon secured, punishment avoided, and generosity of rewards obtained: through it he speaks with the Lord, converses with the Judge, makes present to himself the one whom he cannot prevail to see, and by it appeases the one whom he vehemently provokes by his deeds [edition: “exacerbates”]. In a certain sense, prayer provides the Lord’s secret place; it offers room for petitions; through it the sinner is admitted into the Judge’s inner chambers. And no one is rejected from there except the one who is found lukewarm in prayer. He obtains what he prefers, beyond what he deserves; he comes to it sad but departs joyful. Holy prayer, indeed, saves the devoted in such a way as to make them blessed, while receiving them as criminals. The examples of this goodness are innumerable; but this one is sufficient: the Lord himself, giving us life-giving examples, deigned to pray. Therefore prayer is rightly placed before such a great man, who frequently appeased the indignant Lord by the marvelous example of his supplication.

Let us recognize this psalm as the third of those shown to contain prayer in their titles. It is clear that Moses—that most celebrated man through whom the Lord gave the Law to the Israelite people—was a minister of the Old Testament and a prophet of the New. For concerning him the Gospel says: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). And because this psalm has joined both Testaments, a name was rightly assigned to it which, by the force of its meaning, would indicate the two mysteries. For Moses is interpreted as “the one taken up,” because he was lifted from the waters by Pharaoh’s daughter. In relation to the Red Sea, this signifies the Israelites; but in relation to the grace of baptism, it pertains to the Christian people.

“Man of God” was also added, lest you perhaps think of another person, rather than the one who, honored by divine conversations, deserved to be foremost—so that he might now be called not merely a servant but God’s own man. We use this expression not of servants but of sons and friends, as it is written in Exodus: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exodus 33:11).

## Division of the Psalm

Moses, a most holy man, marvelous in his works and venerable in his divine conversation, begins the first section with praise of the Judge, briefly recalling his benefits and power. Then he asks that our weakness—which he himself also displayed in many ways—be aided. Third, he entreats that the coming of the Lord Savior, whom he knew would bring benefits to the human race, may be made known more quickly.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1. “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation.”

That venerable Moses, in the type of the holy Church which he carried in prefiguration, pours forth a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord because the Lord had become his distinguished refuge amid the sea of this world. First, he had been cast away among the children of the Hebrews so that he might die; then he endured the wicked conflicts of the king of Egypt; third, the unheard-of miracles of the Red Sea; finally, the terrifying insolence of the murmuring people. Yet amid all these things the Lord became a refuge for him, since Moses is known to have been delivered from every danger.

Therefore, remembering his dangers, he is rightly understood to have made such a beginning. But so that we should understand this not merely of one man but of the universal Church, he used “our,” not “my,” because the Lord is always the safest refuge of the entire Church, which lives amid the storm of this world. For see what follows: “from generation to generation.” “Generation” signifies the time from which the human race began to be generated. “Progeny” signifies the period extending to the end of the world, as one generation of the human race succeeds another through the ages—as though he were saying, “always.”

### Verse 2. “Before the mountains were made and the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are.”

Because in the first verse he had said, “You have become our refuge,” lest you should understand the Godhead to be temporal, he now discusses its eternity. But so that we may perceive this everlastingness most clearly, the mountains here signify not something earthly but the eminent powers of heaven, since what follows speaks of the whole earth. Thus it is truly and fittingly said to the Lord: “You are before you formed heavenly and earthly things.” This “before” has no beginning; rather, it is declared to be immense and incomprehensible, since it is recognized as existing before even those beginnings themselves.

He continues: “from age to age you are,” as though God were not God either before the age or after the age. Here, however, “from age to age” must be understood as eternity. The Greek copies have “eternity,” which our fathers translated as “from age to age.” “You are” is fittingly said of God, because he has neither past nor future. Thus it was also said to Moses himself: “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘I am who I am’; and ‘He who is’ has sent me to you” (Exodus 3:14). Therefore the holy man rightly wrote “you are,” which he remembered hearing from him.

There is no doubt that this pertains to the Father, to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. For the essence of the undivided Trinity—which is truly and properly said to “be” from the fact that it is—always possesses the present, whereas among us we call things either past or future.

### Verse 3. “Do not turn man toward humiliation; and you said, ‘Return, children of men.’”

He comes to the second section, in which the holy man asks from the Lord what he knows the Lord has commanded. For he says: “Do not turn man toward humiliation,” that is, do not cast him into the desire and ambition of this world. Here we must understand “humiliation” as earthly desire, which before God is rejected and contemptible—not that glorious humility by which we confess our sins to the Lord.

Thus the holy man entreats what the Godhead commands: that the human will, cast down from heavenly sublimity, not be permitted to love the lowest things of the world—things that are indeed low because they are stained by their own worthlessness [edition: “humility”]. He continues: “and you said, ‘Return, children of men.’” Here *et* (“and”) is used in place of *quia* (“because”), so that the joined sentence may open a single sense for us. You see how plausible the preceding petition is: since the Lord commanded the children of men to return, they ought to be saved by his mercy. For who else can free them from the ambition of the world except the one who taught the faithful to seek the kingdoms of heaven? He therefore rightly asks that human beings not be abandoned in slippery falls, to whom it was said: “Return.”

### Verse 4. “For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed, and like a watch in the night.”

The reason is given why the ambition of the world ought to be avoided: because a thousand years are not merely few in God’s sight but are regarded as wholly past, like yesterday. This figure is called *tapinosis*, that is, humiliation, when the greatness of anything is reduced to a very small measure. For so immense an order of ages is compared not even with the present day itself but with a day already past.

He used “a thousand”—a finite number—in place of an infinite number, perhaps designating the age of the ancients, who were filled with great longevity. He continues: “and like a watch in the night.” So that you might recognize those thousand years mentioned above as annulled, they are compared not only with a past day but also with the very brief period of the night. A night watch, during which human guards customarily keep vigil, is divided into three-hour watches, where nothing distant or prolonged is accomplished by the relieving companies.

He beautifully compared human life with nocturnal watches, in which everything is carried on amid darkness and trembling, when the human mind, surrounded by carnal vices, is assailed. Distinctions must be placed within this verse, because the fullness of the sentence follows.

### Verse 5. “They are regarded as nothing; their years will be. In the morning may it pass away like grass.”

This is what depended on the preceding verse: since, just as the two things he mentioned above—the past day and the night watch—are regarded as nothing, he added: “Their years will be.” And therefore, just as he said shortly before that we must pray, “Do not turn man toward humiliation,” he added: “In the morning may it pass away like grass.”

Here again the fleeting and transitory things of human life are being compared. Grass is frequently consumed in an instant either by the feeding of animals or by some threshing; so are the years of human beings, which are regarded as nothing. “In the morning,” that is, in the very life which they enjoy, they pass away and are completed; nor can there be satisfaction in their length, when their end is received with hurried speed.

### Verse 6. “In the morning may it flower and pass away; in the evening may it fall [printed: *aecidat*, probably *decidat*], grow hard, and wither.”

The weakness of the flesh is rightly compared with the fleeting ages of grasses. “Morning” signifies the whole of human life, in which a person is recognized both to flower and to pass away. “Evening,” however, which indicates the setting of the light, refers to the time when a person passes from the world. As soon as he has fallen into death, he grows hard as a corpse, and afterward withers [edition: “grows”] into dust—a condition known to be common to both grasses and human bodies.

But here, in my view, “morning” and “evening” should not be understood as one day. These parts should not be joined, since each has been placed separately to convey brevity. They are developed with such care so that no one may flatter himself about having a very long life.

### Verse 7. “For we have failed in your anger, and in your wrath we have been troubled.”

The holy man, mindful of former deeds, recalls that anger of God which he endured because of the Jewish murmuring, when the Lord said to him: “I see that this people is stiff-necked. Leave me, so that my anger may burn against them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation” (Exodus 32:9–10).

Therefore he was troubled by a terrifying remembrance, since he was pleading for such a people. “We have failed” means that we have been wearied by human weakness. “We have been troubled” refers to the fearful thought of death, which they dreaded because of the punishments they deserved.

### Verse 8. “You have placed our iniquities before you; our age in the illumination of your face.”

He speaks of the age of past time, when the Jewish people were visited both with miracles and with punishments. Because they did not believe what they saw, they endured the sight of the avenging Judge. For elsewhere he says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31:1). Those things were covered which attained forgiveness; those things were illuminated which immediately endured vengeance.

### Verse 9. “For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed; our years were meditating like a spider.”

He says that the brevity of human life arose from the Lord’s anger, because people sinned through presumption upon a longer life. He will state below to what brevity they came after the numerical abundance of the former age. When he says, “All our days have failed,” this pertains to years diminished. What follows—“and in your anger we have failed”—refers to the tribulations and hardships which we endure within this very short life, because our insolence could not otherwise be corrected unless we were proved and afflicted by the Lord’s scourges.

A very apt comparison follows: “Our years were meditating like a spider.” The comparison reveals the malignity of our life. A spider is a weak and extremely delicate creature that deceitfully weaves certain nets to obtain food for itself from passing flies. So the years of those devoted to wicked works are occupied with empty and deceptive contrivances. The spider is so called because it is dry and exceedingly fine.

And observe how the verb, placed with the action itself [edition: “of the creature itself”], makes the point clear. He said “were meditating,” not “were working,” to show that those years passed without any usefulness—people who lived not under the fruit of good works but under hesitant and dangerous reflection.

### Verse 10. “The days of our years are seventy years; but if in strength, eighty years; and most of them are labor and sorrow.”

If we wish to understand these years literally, we will find many people vigorous even in their nineties, and again others exhausted by weakness before reaching seventy; so what is said here seems scarcely able to stand. But we should adapt the number seventy more suitably to the Law, which commanded that the seventh day, the Sabbath, be observed. We most appropriately assign eighty to the Christian people, who venerate the eighth day, the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, with holy celebration. Thus it seems that the two Testaments are signified by this number, as we already said in the seventieth psalm, where we divided this work.

These are the commandments by which faithful souls are governed with the most healthful soundness of mind. To the number eighty he added “in strength,” because we truly began to possess strength when the Lord Savior appeared to us. These, then, are the days of our years which confer on us the brightness of a credible life. They are rightly called “days,” because through them, with minds illuminated, we behold the Lord in his words.

And attend to what follows: “And most of them are labor and sorrow”—that is, whoever goes beyond these two Testaments is entangled in the greatest labors and sorrows. For there is nothing there, as the heretics do, of thinking more or less, where moderate distinction preserves the heavenly rule.

### Verse 11. “For gentleness will come upon us, and we shall be corrected. Who knows the power of your anger, or can reckon your anger according to fear?”

Because he had said, “Most of them are labor and sorrow,” he now develops the point, saying that the precepts of the Law must not be surpassed. For Jesus Christ, who is perfect gentleness [the supplied text reads *per fecta*], coming upon us, rebukes and corrects us if we stubbornly neglect his Testaments.

And because he said, “we shall be corrected,” he placed “gentleness” beforehand, so that we may understand that all the Lord’s corrections arise from an intention of mercy toward the faithful. He continues: “Who knows the power of your anger, or can reckon your anger according to fear?”

Moses rightly cries out—Moses who had experienced what the Lord had repaid to a sinful people when that people provoked him with repeated murmurings—that no one’s consideration reaches the measure of his vengeance, and that it cannot be reckoned how much he can accomplish when angry. Note that in both parts the immensity of his power is proclaimed. For just as the Lord’s rewards cannot be fully understood, so the measure of his vengeance cannot be grasped. He aptly added “according to fear,” as another prophet likewise says: “I considered your works, and I was afraid” (Habakkuk 3:2).

### Verse 12. “Make your right hand known to us, and make us learned in heart in wisdom.”

That most holy man, an outstanding interpreter of both Testaments, comes to the third section, in which he beseeches the Father that Jesus Christ might appear salvifically to the Jewish people and to the nations. To embrace both peoples, he used the plural “to us,” just as was already done in the first verse of the psalm.

By the “right hand” he means the Lord Savior himself, concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “Your right hand, Lord, has shattered the enemies” (Exodus 15:6). He asks that the one through whom all beneficial things are learned may be made known to them.

“And make us learned in heart in wisdom.” His desire is not satisfied with asking for the Lord’s coming, because many who saw him bodily did not believe him to be God. Therefore he added: “Make us learned in heart in wisdom”—that is, grant us understanding concerning the Lord Christ. A person is called “learned” (*eruditus*) as though drawn out of complete rawness (*ex omni rude elicitus*). For he is the power and wisdom of the Father, whom the psalmist asks to know not with bodily eyes but with a learned heart. Truly, seeing him benefited those who deserved to behold him with an illuminated mind.

### Verse 13. “Turn, Lord, for a little while, and be entreated concerning your servants.”

The holy man follows his customary practice, for in Exodus he says: “Be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people” (Exodus 32:12). With the same feeling and the same grace, he asks the Lord to temper his justice with some gentleness, so that he may be entreated by sinners against whom he was justly known to be angry.

It should be observed that he did not say “turn completely,” but “for a little while,” because this is more beneficial for us when some goad of tribulation afflicts us: thus, being frequently admonished, we may be able to obtain forgiveness of sins through a most salutary conversion.

### Verse 14. “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we have rejoiced and delighted in all our days.”

No one is unaware that the Lord Savior is called “mercy,” since he was given to the wretched so that through him they might live—those who were known to have utterly perished through themselves.

He therefore says that he was filled with this mercy “in the morning,” that is, in bright contemplation, because the holy man foresaw the coming of Christ the Lord. It was necessary that his heart should exult in praise and delight in contemplation throughout all the days of his life. His soul, filled with such a gift, rejoiced with heavenly exultation. This figure is called *idea*, when, as though setting a future thing before our eyes, we vividly stir the movement of the soul.

### Verse 15. “We have delighted in proportion to the days in which you humbled us, and the years in which we saw evil.”

He had weighed with truthful judgment the tribulations which divine providence grants to human beings, so that he could say that he delighted in them, through which he perceived that the people were salutarily humbled. For he knew that pride was harmful to faithful men, and therefore he gives thanks to the Lord for that by which he recognized believers to have progressed.

Accordingly, he confesses that he delighted in those years in which he had seen evil—evil, that is, which humanity considered grievous while suffering it. But for the holy man who contemplated the truth, they were not merely grievous; he confessed that they had even become sweet to him.

### Verse 16. “Look upon your servants and upon your works, Lord; and direct their children.”

A holy conscience does not cease to do for another’s work what it practiced for its own. Everyone knows how he pleaded with the Lord in prayer for the Israelites. Now he concludes with a similar ending, asking that he spare the sinful Jews and correct their children through holy belief, so that, if they have been scattered because of their iniquity, at least their offspring, converted at the end of the age, may deserve to attain forgiveness. He knew through the spirit of prophecy—as we have often said—that this was to be done.

Consider also by what words he invited the goodness of the good Judge. First he said, “upon your servants”; then, “upon your works,” so that even if they did not deserve to receive forgiveness on account of their deeds, the Creator’s highly praiseworthy work might obtain it for them. Among rhetoricians this argument is called an appeal based on praise of the judge.

### Verse 17. “And may the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us; and direct the works of our hands upon us.”

The splendor of the Lord is upon us when we are adorned with the imprint of his cross and carry the banner of his triumph on our forehead, as the Apostle says: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

Hence it is also said in another psalm: “The light of your face, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4:7).

He continues: “And direct the works of our hands upon us.” He directs our works upon us when he grants us forgiveness of sins, so that, when we have been perverse, we may through his correction become completely upright.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider, most prudent men, how many mysteries of the divine Law are indicated to us through various numbers: here he gathers the course of human lives by calculating the numbers seventy and eighty; the entire order of the Psalms is comprehended by a mystical reckoning; all the divine books are enclosed by a secret number; and other mysteries of the divine Law are contained through manifold calculation.

We read that the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the hairs of human beings are subject to number. And so that we may learn, in brief summary, the praise and power of this discipline, Solomon says: “God has made all things in measure, number, and weight” (Wisdom 11:21), so that it may plainly appear to all that the discipline of arithmetic is diffused everywhere.

The authors of secular literature, examining this discipline more carefully, divided it into many parts: even and odd, perfect and imperfect, excessive and deficient, and the other categories which are set forth most clearly in those authors. Our own forebears likewise permitted students to read these works and consider them with sound judgment.

Let us nevertheless ask God in all things to open our understanding and lead us by his illumination to true wisdom. Whatever you read, whatever you think out, can become sweet to you if you are seasoned with the savor of the heavenly gift.

# EXPOSITION ON PSALM 90

## Praise of a Song of David

When “praise of a song” is said, we should not understand something ordinary. Praise can mean human commendation; but “praise of a song” cannot be understood except as divine praise.

Here we must understand David himself, the prophet, who is about to speak the first part of this psalm in a pleasing account. It is exceedingly beautiful and especially sweet because of the variety of its promises. The devil, when he tempted the Lord Savior, brought its eleventh and twelfth verses against him. With devout confidence we always oppose this hymn to demons, so that they may be defeated by us precisely through the words with which they deceitfully attempted to say something against their Creator.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first section the Psalmist declares that every truly faithful person is surrounded by divine protection. In the second he sings praise to the Lord Savior. In the third, the Father speaks to every faithful person whom he knows to hope most devotedly in him, promising him protection in this world and rewards in the future.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1. “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven.”

Here again a categorical syllogism raises its head:

- The just person dwells in the help of the Most High.
- Everyone who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven.
- Therefore the just person will abide in the protection of the God of heaven.

Now let us treat the words of the psalm. With holy David placed in heavenly contemplation, a certain person suddenly appears—one wholly devoted in purity of mind, continually rejoicing in heavenly protection. The psalmist asserts that many benefits have been divinely bestowed upon him, so that our mind may be more ardently stirred toward devotion to the Lord when great hope is promised to the faithful.

This figure is called *diatyposis*, that is, an expression of condition, in which, when persons or things are placed before us, we express both their forms and their conditions.

“He who dwells” should be pronounced affirmatively, that is, “he who continually abides.” To dwell is characteristic of one who remains, not of one who departs. But whoever places his entire hope not in his own powers but in the will of the Most High, receives the definite promise that such a person will be protected by the Lord in every way.

It should also be examined that he says “in help,” so that he may designate the intention of the true Christian: to serve the Lord through arduous struggle. And observe how great matters are conveyed through individual words. He says: “He who dwells here will abide there”—that is, whoever does not depart from him in this world will remain forever in that eternity.

### Verse 2. “He will say to the Lord: ‘You are my protector and my refuge, my God, and I will hope in him.’”

This is said by the one who casts away harmful presumptions from his heart and considers only that useful to him which heavenly mercy deigns to provide.

For whoever says, “You are my protector,” confirms that he has cast his entire self upon the Lord’s benefits, so that he may glory in a kind of fortunate intimacy. Likewise, whoever says, “And you are my refuge, my God,” declares that he has no other help, but when he is shaken by the storms of this world, he testifies that he wishes to flee to the harbor of divine mercy.

And lest you believe that, after blessed protection and saving refuge, nothing further should be desired, he adds: “And I will hope in him.” No one should ever presume upon himself, who is exceedingly fragile, but should always trust in him who is proved to contain all things. If Adam had followed this, he would neither have acquired guilt for himself nor transmitted destruction to his descendants.

### Verse 3. “For he has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.”

He states the cause of the divine gift: the Lord can free us from the tricks of enemies, whether spiritual or carnal. He makes a comparison with hunters, who set snares of nets to catch wild animals, so that the unsuspecting may be entangled in deceitful ambushes.

He continues: “And from the harsh word.” A harsh word is every statement which is offered against the divine rules like a deadly cup. Even if we are diverted from a good purpose through insults or mockery, it is certainly a harsh word, and extremely hard because of its bitterness. Again, if a flattering speech, seasoned with poisonous honey, is heard, we ought to receive it harshly, because it is proved to oppose the divine commands.

For the things communicated in the softest words frequently deceive more. The Lord therefore frees us from this most grievous harshness and bitter sweetness when we walk in his way and do not turn aside to the right or left, where we recognize that snares have been set by the devil. For in the way—that is, in Christ himself—no one dares to lay snares, where he cannot prevail to wound the faithful.

### Verse 4. “He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you will hope; his truth will surround you with a shield.”

Through this verse and the two that follow, how beautifully the prophet promises the Lord’s benefits to that most holy person whom he introduced above, using the loveliest allusions! Since he had previously approved that person’s character, he now narrates the rewards worthy of him. Our curiosity ought to investigate these things, if, with his grace supporting us, we can discover anything worthy.

The Lord’s shoulders are the works of his wonders, through which divine power is displayed as though upon certain shoulders. The wings are the admonitions of the prophets; if received with a pure mind, they carry faithful souls all the way to heaven.

Perhaps you will ask what this overshadowing will provide, so that the sun may not burn you by day, nor the moon by night. What, likewise, do the Lord’s wings confer? Certainly, the protection of the Lord, which you recognize as a motherly tenderness amid the dangers of the world, as it is also written elsewhere: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37).

“His truth will surround you with a shield.” A human shield covers only that part against which it is held; but the divine shield surrounds us on every side and protects us as though with a wall of fortification. “Truth” here must be understood as the incarnation of Christ the Lord, as it is written: “Truth has risen from the earth” (Psalm 84:12). This truth overshadows us with its shoulders, makes us hope under its wings, and guards us with the protection of its shield.

### Verse 5. “You will not fear the terror of the night.”

### Verse 6. “Nor the arrow flying by day, nor the affair that moves about in darkness, nor ruin and the noonday demon.”

Just as he previously named kinds of protection, so now in these two verses he announces the forms of danger, because salvation is much more welcome when the multitude of dangers avoided is recognized.

The terror of the night is therefore the dark persuasion of heretics. The arrow flying by day is the manifest persecution of tyrants. The affair in darkness occurs when something is sought with wicked zeal, by which the eye of the hearts of believers is blinded. The noonday demon is an enormous danger kindled by the heat of persecution, where ruin is often feared when human weakness is overcome. “Ruin” is so called as though it were a return to the lowest places.

Through all these allusions and definitions of things, however, this is clearly shown: we can fear none of them when, with the Lord protecting us, we are saved.

### Verse 7. “A thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand; but it will not approach you.”

While he was speaking in the first section about the most faithful man, he now comes in the second section to the Lord Christ, since the members are joined to their head. He shows that those whom he had said lay in wait for the servants of God will undergo the retribution for their sins.

But let us investigate this verse somewhat more carefully. Those who are already known to have been predestined among the blessed cannot fall from the Lord’s side or from his right hand. Rather, this is rightly said of presumptuous people who believe they will obtain what they do not deserve.

He said “they will fall,” as though they would tumble from the lofty blessedness which a rash, not faithful, soul had promised itself. The Lord Savior’s “side” is the crown of the righteous, which, together with him—as he promised the apostles—will judge in the resurrection.

Even today, when we ask an emperor or king for judges, we say to them: “Send from your side,” that is, someone who, with most faithful devotion, shares counsel with you. “Side” is so called because it lies hidden under the arm.

And because human hope vainly promises itself lofty things, he says that those who make such promises to themselves beyond their merits will fall from that glory. Since those who are known to possess such a great and remarkable hope are few, he asserts that a thousand will fall from his side—that is, from that height of judgment.

“At your right hand,” however, because many think they will be placed at the right hand, he declares that ten thousand will fall from there, since they too had conceived the false opinion that they possessed what was not found in their merits.

This sentence especially strikes those who are inflated by some favorable success and think themselves holy when they are not. He uses “a thousand” and “ten thousand,” finite numbers, in place of an infinite number.

He continues: “But it will not approach you”—that is, no one among those who falsely promise themselves the kingdom of God. In truth they will be far from the Lord, because, while they place their hope in their own merits, they do not have recourse to the remedies of repentance and satisfaction.

### Verse 8. “Nevertheless, with your eyes you will look on, and you will see the retribution of sinners.”

“With your eyes” refers to that divine, lucid, and penetrating sight by which human merits are judged. Through divine justice human beings who are to be placed on the left or on the right are examined.

He continues: “And you will see the retribution of sinners.” This is what he said above: “With your eyes you will look on.” That examination will be the retribution of merits. “You will see” means “you will cause to be seen,” as in the passage: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood or sought God” (Psalm 52:3).

### Verse 9. “For you are, Lord, my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.”

When he had been speaking above about the retribution of sinners, he suddenly introduced: “For you are, Lord, my hope,” which the preceding sense did not contain. This figure is called *paradoxon*, when an unexpected or unforeseen conclusion is introduced.

Let us examine carefully what the prophet means by saying: “For you are, Lord, my hope.” When the Lord rose again, the remaining members received the hope of resurrection—those members which had been placed in the death of sin. What ought to be hoped for by the remaining body preceded in the Head.

This hope of resurrection was given to the holy man because the Lord Savior himself, insofar as he died, is recognized to have placed his refuge in the Most High, as was already said in the thirtieth psalm: “Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge, so that you may save me” (Psalm 30:3). Therefore he rightly follows the example of the one through whom he knew that he himself would live forever.

### Verse 10. “Evil will not approach you, and the scourge will not come near your tabernacle.”

Here the blessedness of the assumed humanity is powerfully explained. Although in this world he endured both insults and scourges from the Jews, it says that no evil could approach his tabernacle—that is, his holy body.

Rightly so, because the scourge is divine vengeance, which customarily cuts away human crimes, as it is written elsewhere: “Many are the scourges of sinners” (Psalm 31:10). It is therefore most truthfully said here that this did not come upon him, since he was proved to conduct himself in an immaculate manner.

Here “scourge” signifies that which chastises offenses and avenges wicked actions. Therefore sin is denied to have approached Christ the Lord through the scourge. This kind of expression is called the figure *hypallage*, which is frequently found both in secular writings and in the divine books.

### Verse 11. “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.”

### Verse 12

“They will carry you in their hands, lest you ever strike your foot against a stone.”

In these two verses are words that the devil, doubting the Lord Christ’s divinity, presumed to set before Him when he attempted to tempt Him. But where he fell, let us walk attentively, since another’s preceding fall is a warning to the one who follows.[Col. 0654B]

We have often said that in the Lord and Savior two natures—that is, those of God and man—remain united and perfect in one and the same person, so that He is proclaimed and believed by all to be one Son of God, just as our fathers also taught, enlightened by the truth itself, saying: “The Son alone of the Trinity took the form of a servant, and that form was joined to Him for the unity of the person”; that is, so that the Son of God and the Son of man might be one, almighty Jesus Christ, lest not a Trinity but—God forbid—a quaternity be proclaimed.

Hence, whenever humble things are said of Him, they must without doubt be assigned to His humanity; whenever something more powerful thunders forth, it must be applied to His divine powers. Both principles have been observed here and below. For the statement that angels were commanded to guard Him pertains to the weakness of His humanity, as the Gospel also testifies: “And an angel from heaven appeared to Him, strengthening Him” (Luke 22:43). And to declare the very nature of man most perfectly, he added, “lest you strike your foot against a stone”; that is, lest you stumble against the Law, which appeared written on stone tablets, and which He had come to teach the nations and to confirm by the saving integrity of its fulfillment.

### Verse 13

“You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon.”

Here the divine power is now expressed, which commanded such savage beings. All these names are appropriately applied to the devil: he is an asp when he strikes secretly; a basilisk when he spreads his poisons openly; a lion when he persecutes the innocent; a dragon when with impious greed he swallows the negligent.[Col. 0654D]

Yet all these things lay prostrate beneath the Lord’s glorious advent, crushed under His feet. For only He was able to subdue such ferocity, who is shown to exist, according to His divinity, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father. If we carefully consider these matters in the preaching of the holy Fathers, and are not disturbed by any insane heretical perversity, everything will stand before us in complete truth, just as it has been said.

### Verse 14

“Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he has known my name.”

He comes to the third section, where the Lord the Father responds with most just and gracious regard to that blessed man whom we recognize as having been introduced in the first section, so that He might strengthen the hearts of the faithful by such a promise. He therefore promises that He will deliver this blessed man, who dwells in the help of the Most High, from the evils of this present age, because he has placed his hope in His power.[Col. 0655A]

It follows: “I will protect him, because he has known my name.” He explains how He promised that he would be delivered: namely, so that, protected from all the devil’s ambushes, he might be kept apart from them. He also adds the reason for this gracious deliverance: “because he has known my name.” He knows the Father’s name who does not think the Son inferior, nor judge Him to be a creature—as certain utterly foolish people wish—but rather professes Him, with an undivided mind, to be the Creator.

### Verse 15

“He will call upon me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation, I will rescue him and glorify him.”

To this blessed man who trusts in His protection, the Lord promises a singular reward: when called upon, He will hear him and grant him what will benefit him in two ways. For He says, “I am with him in tribulation,” which refers to this present world, where the devoted mind is more fervently afflicted by hardships. Thus He Himself also promises in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

And see what follows: “I will rescue him and glorify him.” The just man, rescued from this world, will certainly be glorified when he is placed in that blessedness where tribulation will no longer have any place.

### Verse 16

“I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation.”

He continues to unfold the rewards that He promises to the blessed man. The length of days is eternal life, which no end brings to completion but which endures with stable strength in its own permanence. The conclusion of the whole reward follows—a conclusion that has no end: “and I will show him my salvation.” For this is what is promised to the faithful as the highest recompense: they will behold Christ the Lord, the Savior.

When He appears and is seen by the illumination of the heart, He will fulfill the entire hope and desire of the righteous. Thus He also promises Himself in the Gospel to those who believe well: “I will show myself to them” (John 14:21). This, as some would have it, could not be said of Christ Himself, who is both the saving Lord and the hope desired by believers; but it is better—as has often been said—to understand it as spoken from the perspective of His members.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Wonderful is the power of this psalm, which puts unclean spirits to flight. For from the very point at which the devil wished to tempt Him, he departs from us defeated.[Col. 0655D] The wicked one remembers his presumption; he remembers the divine victory. For he himself conquers in us who overcame him in himself by His own power.

Therefore let it be said by us after all the activities of the day, at nightfall; let him recognize that we belong to the One before whom he recalls that he once yielded. Nor do I judge it without reason that so great a glory has been placed in this psalm’s number: through the thrice-threefold revolution of the number ten, it is known to point toward the omnipotent and indivisible Trinity.

## Exposition of Psalm 91

### A Psalm-Song for the Sabbath Day

The psalm-song admonishes us that in all our actions we ought to give thanks to the Divinity. For the psalm—as has often been said—signifies spiritual works that rise upward toward the Lord Christ. In these we ought to sing and always give thanks, when by His benefit we are made free, although through ourselves we are bound by the chains of sins.

He sings in the psalm who establishes his entire life in thanksgiving. The Sabbath day is interpreted as rest, by which we are admonished to cease from every wicked action and to render our tranquil souls free from vices through the holiness of heavenly works.

The Jews do not rightly observe this, since they have transferred its observance to the literal meaning. But for those who lead the Lord’s commandments toward the significance of the New Testament, and truly understand that what was said was spoken as a prefiguration, there is rest on the Sabbath day. Therefore we ought to understand in this psalm the words of the Church, which is known to announce to us the rest that is to come through the Sabbath day.[Col. 0656B]

### Division of the Psalm

At the first entrance the Church speaks, recalling that it is good to proclaim praises to the Lord, and declaring that the foolish and irreligious person is wholly ignorant of this. Second, it asserts that sinners will quickly perish like grass. Third, it says that the righteous will flourish like a palm tree and grow like the cedars of Lebanon, so that it may correct the obstinate through fear and enable the devoted to rejoice in a happy promise.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“It is good to confess to the Lord and to sing praises to your name, O Most High.”

Holy Mother Church says that it is good to confess to the Lord, so that at the very beginning she might briefly assess what would be beneficial. We confess—as has often been said—in two ways: when, condemning our sins, we continually ask for the Lord’s mercy; and also when we always attribute the benefits we receive to His gifts, refusing to say that what is granted through His compassion is due to our merits.

Therefore, whichever of these is done, it is good to confess to the Lord. Then, turning her words toward the Lord, she says: “and to sing praises to your name, O Most High.” The phrase “it is good” is to be understood from the common construction. To sing praises means to carry out the Lord’s commandments through devout works, so that, just as the psalter gives forth its sound from above, our action may rise to the ears of the Divinity. Thus, in a single verse, she has embraced what was to include holy and manifold actions.[Col. 0656D]

#### Verse 2

“To proclaim your mercy in the morning, and your truth by night.”

Our life is wonderfully enclosed in two expressions. Morning signifies joy, while night is understood to indicate sadness. Therefore, when we are joyful in His benefits, we ought to proclaim His mercy, because He is good and grants benefits to the undeserving and the wicked.

By night—that is, in tribulation—when certain hardships are known to chastise us, we ought likewise to proclaim His truth, because we rightly suffer what we endure beneath the weight of our sins. Thus, in both periods, we ought most justly to confess the praises of the Lord.

#### Verse 3

“Upon the ten-stringed psaltery, with song and lyre.”

It is evident that the ten-stringed psaltery signifies the ten commandments of the Law, since the strings themselves are those commandments. If we touch them through the quality of good deeds, they produce a saving melody and lead us to the kingdom of heaven.

We ought to know why this number appears to have been added to so great a matter. It is the number that the Pythagoreans call τετραδαξάτην (*tetradaxatēn*), that is, the divine quaternity, because it briefly embraces what is known to be capable of expansion through infinite sums. One, two, three, and four make ten; when this sequence is continually revolved and repeated, it extends into vast and infinite calculations.

For in any sums whatsoever nothing new is found beyond this order; rather, it is shown to be so constituted that it is always itself countable, without being altered by any novelty.[Col. 0657B] Properly, therefore, such a calculation contains the pattern of our entire redemption. Through its oblique lines it imitates, in its written form, the figure of the holy cross, and on the fingers it is enclosed in the rounded beauty of a graceful circle.

He added: “with song and lyre.” Song and lyre signify the joy of good work—that is, the cheerful giving of alms—as the Apostle says: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). The lyre signifies practical deeds, which, although performed with labor and tension, will nevertheless have the greatest fruit if they are completed with joined joy. He sings with the lyre who accomplishes good works without the harshness of sadness.

#### Verse 4

“For you have delighted me, Lord, in your work, and in the works of your hands I will rejoice.”

Observe that this rule of truth is preserved everywhere: what has been bestowed by divine generosity must not be attributed to human strength. Harmful exaltation and pride hostile to God arise when human weakness presumes upon something from its own ability.

Therefore Mother Church says that she has been delighted in the Lord’s work, because whatever good she had received she attributed in every way to that holy purpose. And to preserve the integrity of the rule mentioned above, she professes that she rejoices not in her own happiness but in His works, as the Apostle also says: “For we are his workmanship, created for good works” (Ephesians 2:10).

#### Verse 5

“How greatly your works have been magnified, Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep.”

All the works of God are known to be deep beyond human understanding, and whatever one seeks among them is recognized without doubt to be most profound.[Col. 0657D] But it is better to learn about these works through His own words, lest we seem to introduce something foreign into the discussion.

After saying, “in the morning your mercy, and your truth to be proclaimed by night,” and “upon the ten-stringed psaltery, with song and lyre,” he marvels with still greater astonishment at the Lord’s works and at the miracles of His ordering of things, and he pursues His magnificence with the deepest wonder. Thus formed by such imitation, we may be able to escape safely the dangers of this world.

In this matter, His thoughts have become exceedingly deep: just as the devil fell through pride, so the human race might be set free through the benefit of humility. By saying “exceedingly deep,” he indicates that this estimation rises all the higher the more diligently and intensely one is able to consider it.

Therefore, this is the kind of perfect knowledge: to know that God accomplishes such great things as human understanding cannot reach, as is read in the prophet Habakkuk: “I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Habakkuk 3:1).

#### Verse 6

“The foolish man will not know, and the fool will not understand these things.”

These statements are suitably related to different causes. For just as he said of himself, “For you have delighted me, Lord, in your work, and in the works of your hands I will rejoice,” and so forth, so he declares that unbelievers cannot know the Lord’s benefits.

This figure is called *parison*, that is, the balancing of a statement, which is often composed of equal elements and frequently of unequal ones. The foolish man is one who, emptied of heavenly wisdom, is shown to be full of human cunning. Such a person will certainly not know the works of God, because he believes that what happens occurs by chance, as certain philosophers have said.

He added: “and the fool will not understand these things.” The fool is one who knows neither divine things nor the very actions of the world, which we commonly call brutish. It is rightly said, therefore, that such people do not understand the things stated above, because they are not inflamed in any way by heavenly contemplation.

#### Verse 7

“When sinners spring up like grass, and all who work iniquity appear, that they may perish forever and ever.”

He comes to the second entrance, in which he says that sinners flourish in this world for a brief time like grass; but at that judgment where they receive what their deeds deserve, he asserts that they will quickly perish, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Every man is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

When he says, “and all who work iniquity appear,” he indicates the future time of judgment. Although many may here be understood to be guilty of crimes, all who work iniquity cannot appear to us here, especially since we cannot see unclean spirits. There, when they come to judgment, they will appear to human sight.

He then gives the reason for their appearing: not for glory but for ruin, that is, “that they may perish forever and ever.” The punishment of the condemned has been beautifully explained. They do not perish in such a way as to cease to exist; rather, they perish forever and ever, because they are never stripped of their afflictions.[Col. 0658D]

#### Verse 8

“But you, O Most High, Lord, are forever.”

“Remain” must be supplied—not, as the Jews have thought, that He should be slaughtered like a mere man according to the common lot. It is appropriate to understand this of the Lord and Savior, so that the wicked faithlessness of the Jews may be refuted by contrast.

#### Verse 9

“For behold, your enemies, Lord, will perish, and all who work iniquity will be scattered.”

The enemies of God are worshipers of demons, or anyone shown to oppose His commandments. This hostility is called hostility toward God, but it is proved harmful rather to the one who resists. He persecutes himself who does not follow the Lord’s commands.

For the pious Creator does not know how to be angry except when we seem to set ourselves against Him. Finally, he adds who these enemies are: those who work iniquity. They will be scattered when they have been separated from the Lord’s flock, when they have not deserved to enter His kingdom, because no one can be gathered there except those who have pleased the Lord with the most devoted intention.[Col. 0659A]

#### Verse 10

“And my horn will be exalted like that of the unicorn, and my old age in abundant mercy.”

The unicorn sometimes signifies pride, as has already been said in another psalm: “and from the horns of unicorns, my humility” (Psalm 21:22). Here, however, it signifies the exaltation of unity, by which the Church is rightly said to be exalted at the end of the age, when the faithful are shown worthy to receive their rewards.

That unity is lofty strength. Just as horns adorn animals in this age, so there the glory of the saints adorns the Church. He said, “it will be exalted,” because, when sinners have been humbled in Tartarus, its exaltation will appear higher still.

It follows: “and my old age in abundant mercy.” Old age has a white head. This likeness, as I think, is rightly given here to the Church, since all the merits of the saints will shine with the purest light, like the whiteness of the head.

He did not add “my” without reason, because human old age, wounded by the gravest illnesses, moves toward its end; burdened with complaints, it is disfigured in color. By contrast, the old age of the Church leads to perpetual life, marvelous blessedness, and singular beauty, so that they may shine like the angels of God when they have deserved to be numbered in that assembly.[Col. 0659B]

He also added “in abundant mercy,” so that you might understand both many gifts and benefits and their perpetuity without doubt. All this is said in contrast with the old age of this world, which is weighed down as evils grow heavier.

#### Verse 11

“And my eye has looked upon my enemies, and my ear has heard the evildoers who rise up against me.”

The enemies are, of course, those of the Church, whom he earlier said worked iniquity. They will then be seen openly, at that judgment, when those who were hidden here will appear there together with their works. She looks upon them in anger when she recognizes that they have been separated to the left-hand side.

It follows: “and my ear has heard the evildoers who rise up against me.” Those who rise up are the wealthy evildoers of this age, who here despise the Church’s poverty with impious arrogance. The ears of all the faithful will hear them when, in their own reproaches, they condemn their desires and deeds. For they will say—as Solomon says: “What did our pride profit us, or what did the boasting of riches bring us?” (Wisdom 5:8), and so forth.

There they are heard condemning their own wishes—those who in this world considered themselves supremely blessed.

#### Verse 12

“The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon.”

At the third entrance holy Church appears. Here she recalls the rewards of the blessed through comparisons, just as above she said that the deeds of sinners could be condemned.

Sinners are compared with grass, which rises in pleasing greenness but quickly dries up at the end; the righteous, however, is most appropriately compared with a palm tree. The palm is so called, as it were, *alma pacis*, “nourishing peace”; it is the prize for those who conquer in the contest, as the Apostle says: “I press on toward the palm of the heavenly calling” (Philippians 3:14).

Above the ground the palm is rough and uneven with certain swellings; but when it rises toward the heights, it is filled with the sweetness of the most delightful fruits and spreads out as though adorned with rays. So the conduct of the righteous in this world is full of harsh labors, but in the heavenly realm it is shown to be most beautiful.

A second comparison follows, that of the cedars, which are shown to be much taller than palms. Cedar is a sweet-smelling wood, very strong for bearing weights. Although it grows tall everywhere, it is found still taller on Mount Lebanon. Thus the righteous, celebrated with manifold praise, is said to possess both the height of the cedar and the beauty of the palms.

This figure is called *ison*, that is, equality, when certain things resembling one another in parity are joined with praise or blame.[Col. 0660B]

#### Verse 13

“Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God.”

Since he compared righteous men with chosen trees, he now designates, in a very brief statement, the pleasantness and beauty of the Catholic Church. In saying “planted,” he signifies the Lord’s predestination, because unless someone has been planted in her, he will not have the most blessed growth.

Consider also that he declares those planted in the house of the Lord to flourish in the courts: namely, those who are planted in this Church by the Lord’s grace will flourish in every way at that entrance into Jerusalem.

The court is called the beginning of a dwelling; the house signifies its inner members. The two cannot simultaneously refer to one and the same thing. Here the righteous is properly called planted, since he is firmly held by the roots of virtues in earthly bowels.

He will rightly flourish in the courts when, at the beginning of that resurrection, he rejoices in the happiness of the promised gift: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

#### Verse 14

“They will still multiply in a fruitful old age, and they will be well enduring.”

Human old age is dry and barren; but the Church then begins to be most fruitful when, by the Lord’s mercy, she has been brought to the end of the age. O green old age, and maturity compared with flowers!

It is evident that this house is covered by heaven, in which human beings are planted so that they may flourish. Indeed, at the end of the age the number of the saints grows, and they are driven by frequent persecutions so that the number of the predestined may soon be completed.

Thus he also said above: “And my old age in abundant mercy.” He added, “and they will be well enduring,” because the sufferings of the blessed win the kingdom of heaven.

#### Verse 15

“To proclaim that the Lord our God is righteous, and there is no iniquity in him.”

The saints whom he earlier said would be well enduring will proclaim, when they have begun to receive the divine rewards, that the Lord is righteous—that is, He who has fulfilled the gifts promised to His servants.

“And there is no iniquity in him,” since in this world He permitted those whom He will adorn there with the crown of martyrdom to endure danger on His behalf.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Holy Mother Church has admonished us concerning how sinners perish like grass and the righteous flourish like the palm. She has also said with what reversal those rejoice who here are weighed down by continual afflictions.

This is the Sabbath day announced by the title, on which the righteous will celebrate the praises of the Lord with exultation and, freed from the persecutions of this world, will rejoice in tranquil security. He has promised good things so that we may not despair; He has issued grave threats so that we may not sin. Thus everything is done for our sake, since He graciously deigns to admonish us.

## Exposition of Psalm 92

### A Praise-Song; To David; On the Day Before the Sabbath, When the Earth Was Founded

We have often said that a song pertains to the praise of the Divinity. For what he added, “to David,” is shown to apply to Christ the Lord, who is rightly called both strong-handed and desirable, since He alone can accomplish what He wills and is desired by His worshipers with a unique affection.

It follows: “on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.” The day before the Sabbath signifies the sixth day, which unquestionably precedes the Sabbath. But since Genesis says that dry land appeared on the third day (Genesis 1:9), we must inquire why he says that the earth was founded on the sixth day.

Here we must understand man, who is appropriately signified by earth, as in the saying: “You are earth, and into earth you will go” (Genesis 3:19). We read that the Creator formed him on the sixth day, at the beginning of created things. And just as He made him in the light of the sixth day, so, coming in the same age, He restored him.

The first age, according to the authority of the Fathers, is understood to extend from Adam to Noah. The second from Noah to Abraham. The third from Abraham to David. The fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity. The fifth from the Babylonian captivity to the preaching of John. The sixth age extends from the preaching of John to the end of the world. It was in this age that the Lord and Savior is manifestly understood to have come, when, in His mercy, He granted foundations for faith to man, tossed about by various misfortunes.

Then the earth was founded, when the faith of the human race was established in Him. Therefore the praise of His holy incarnation is sung through the composition of this psalm.[Col. 0661C]

### Division of the Psalm

The first point concerns His beauty; the second, His strength; the third, His works; the fourth, His power; the fifth, the praises of the universe; the sixth, the truth of His words; and finally, the praise of His house, which ought to rejoice with eternal exultation.

Thus, through these seven seats of argument belonging to the demonstrative genre, the praise has been formed. But instead of divisions, as we have done in other psalms, it is sufficient to give the number, since the number itself is suitably arranged to separate continuous matters.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty.”

Here is the first point of the argument, which we said proceeds from beauty. For, looking upon what was to come, the prophet celebrates the Lord who was to reign with great exultation—not because He began to rule at a particular time, but because the eternal King became known to the human race through the manifestation of His holy incarnation.

It follows: “he has clothed himself with beauty,” that is, He displayed the beauty of His majesty, as is read in the Gospel when He was transfigured on Mount Tabor before His disciples: “And his face shone like the sun, but his garments became white like snow” (Matthew 17:2), such as no fuller can make on earth.

“The Lord has clothed himself with strength, and he has girded himself.”

This is the second point, which we said proceeds from strength. Observe that the preceding clause ended with the same word with which the following one began.
