This figure is called *epembasis*, whenever a word is repeated for the beauty of expression, as in: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises,” and similar examples.

He clothed Himself with strength when, during His passion, He answered the Jews who sought to seize Him: “I am” (John 18:5–6). But they went backward; and struck with great terror, those who had come to use force themselves fell down instead.

If we understand these two statements spiritually, they fit perfectly. He clothed Himself with beauty for those to whom the Son of God appeared in the truth of faith; but He clothed Himself with strength against those who refused to believe in Him, foretelling through threats of judgment the punishments due to the wicked.

“He girded himself” perhaps signifies the occasion when He girded Himself with a linen cloth and washed the disciples’ feet (John 13:4). That humility possessed beauty, because the Lord of heaven deigned to offer the humblest service to His servants. It also possessed strength, because through humility He overthrew the devil’s wickedness and pride.[Col. 0662C]

#### Verse 2

“For he established the inhabited world, which will not be shaken.”

The third point of the argument arises here, which we said proceeds from works. He established the inhabited world—that is, the Church—when in the Gospel He said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

True praise, wondrous proclamation: that earth signifying the Church, spread throughout the whole world, should not be shaken in any way, although it is battered by frequent upheaval.

#### Verse 3

“Your throne is prepared, O God, from that time; you are from everlasting.”

This is the fourth point, which we said above proceeds from power. Whether he wishes us to understand the throne on which He sits at the right hand of the Father, or the throne He possesses in the minds of the faithful, as it is written: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

“Prepared” signifies predestination, because everything that occurs in the ordering of the world rests upon that truth. “From that time” signifies Christ’s incarnation, which was from the Virgin Mary, when He taught His apostles and the other faithful through the fullness of His majesty.[Col. 0662D]

“From everlasting” signifies His divinity, by which, reigning coeternally with the Father, He knows nothing of subjection to time.

Through these words one person, but two natures, are signified in the Lord Christ. Therefore it is necessary to recall this rule frequently in appropriate places, as the authority of the Fathers confirms. Would that the perversity of foolish heretics might grow quiet, so that we would seem to repeat this more importunately than necessarily.[Col. 0663A]

#### Verses 4–5

“The rivers have lifted up, Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices, at the voices of many waters.

The surges of the sea are wondrous; the Lord on high is wondrous” [manuscript A: “the Lord in the heights”].

This is the fifth point of the argument, proceeding from the praises of the universe. Here the prophet, rejoicing in the contemplation of divine love, says that the rivers pour forth the Lord’s praises.

This figure is called *prosopopoeia*, whenever words are attributed to inanimate things. The device is found very frequently in the divine Scriptures. But it is good for us to ask what these rivers are that raise their voices in a cry.

They are the apostles, who drank from the Holy Spirit, as the Lord Himself testifies in the Gospel concerning the head of rivers and the fountain of waters: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

These rivers therefore poured forth irrigating words; in their preaching they raised most holy voices. They are rightly called “lifted up,” because they offered their praises to the Author for salvation. For worldly rivers do not raise their courses but rather plunge them into lower places.

After speaking of the apostles’ preaching, he now explains how the Church progresses through the Lord’s generosity. “At the voices of many waters” signifies the nations, who come together to the Lord in praise, entering the Catholic faith.

From these voices, therefore, “the surges of the sea” have become wondrous—that is, from the salt sea of this world there arises a saving ascent of souls. The sea is a great gathering of salt waters; so the Church embraces wise peoples within Catholic unity. Their wondrous surges occur when they stand firm in mind upon the Lord’s commandments.

They refer all these things to Him, through whom all that is good comes, as the Apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

He says, “The Lord on high is wondrous,” because the life of mortals is not praiseworthy unless it belongs to those whom He Himself makes exalted.

#### Verse 6

“Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy.”

The prophet spoke of the Lord’s advent, which he foresaw would most truly take place. Now he explains the very kind of praise involved: the testimonies of the prophets became exceedingly trustworthy when the incarnation of the Word, which had been foretold, appeared as salvation for the world.[Col. 0663D]

For through His glorious advent, the things held hidden in the sacred books were revealed. Who among the wise could doubt the promise of the gifts when the very fullness that had been promised arrived?

#### Verse 7

“Holiness befits your house, Lord, for length of days.”

The seventh and remaining point has been added, which we said should be marked by praise of His house. The house of the Lord, therefore, is the universal Church, known to have been established throughout the whole world.

Holiness befits her—that is, the abundant blessing of Your advent. For this is the adornment that can surpass every ornament: it adorns in such a way that it never abandons; it arranges in such a way that it is never dispersed.

Yet this holiness, which is the most excellent adornment, is not granted for a moment but bestowed under eternity. For “length of days” signifies eternity, which cannot be enclosed by any end. As someone has said, “That in which there is an end is not long.”

Thus, through the seven parts of the demonstrative genre, the perfection of the Lord’s advent has been praised.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Behold, the sixth weekday, before the Sabbath, foretold in the title has been revealed in the Lord’s incarnation. Let the foolish hear this psalm, those who think that the Lord’s splendid advent ought to be darkened by some derogation.

Through Him the most holy power of the Trinity was declared to human beings; through Him the washing of sacred baptism came forth; through Him the gifts of blessed communion were bestowed; through Him the diverse gifts of the charisms blossomed; through Him death was destroyed and life arose; through Him the devil was conquered; through Him man is known to have been set free.

The angels rejoice, the heavens glory—and, alas for the impiety!—man is still rendered ungrateful, although singular aid is shown to have been given to him.

## Exposition of Psalm 93

### A Psalm to David; The Fourth Day of the Week

Although the words that precede are familiar, we ought to examine more carefully what “the fourth day of the week” means. The fourth day of the week is the fourth day counted from the Sabbath, on which day, at the beginning of the world, the Lord established the lights of heaven by a wondrous ordering.[Col. 0664C]

This must be applied to the holy men about whom this psalm is going to speak. They are rightly compared with the lights of heaven, because on earth they shine through a heavenly way of life.

With great mystery he marked this psalm and the two preceding ones by the mention of such days, so that through the significances of the things he might appear to indicate the power of the psalms.

### Division of the Psalm

When the prophet saw the human race confused by a detestable persuasion, imagining that God had no care for mortals, since he saw the righteous oppressed by adversity while the wicked were raised up by prosperity, he asks the Lord in the first section to repay the proud, through whom he recognized that the world had been corrupted by such an opinion.

In the second section he attacks those who blasphemed with foolish murmuring, imagining that God had no concern for human affairs, even though He is shown to have granted intelligence to His creatures. He calls blessed the one who, despising the happiness of this world, perseveres in reverence for God.

In the third section, to invite their hearts, he says that the Lord has been his refuge and will be the future avenger of sinners.

### Exposition of the Psalm
### Verse 1

“God of vengeance, Lord; God of vengeance acted freely.”

Seeing that the wickedness of blasphemers had burst forth into great license, the prophet threatens them with the Lord’s severity as though with terrifying thunderbolts, so that, frightened by fear of such majesty, they might be brought to abandon their perversities. For he says, “God”—a terrible name, since it derives from fear. And so that you may understand “God” as the Savior, he adds, “Lord of vengeance,” that is, the one who will judge the world and will come to afflict the obstinate with just punishments. Who, then, would not be terrified by such a pronouncement? Who would not tremble before the avenger [ed., judge], if he recognizes himself to be a sinner?

He repeats, “God of vengeance acted freely,” that is, he judged without anyone impeding him, as he did when he charged the Pharisees and those in authority with their wickedness. He also acted freely when he taught the crowds in the temple as one having authority. Thus, in another passage, the Father says of him: “I will place him upon my salvation; I will act confidently in him” (Ps. 11:6). Therefore it is clear that he acted freely, since neither could his truth be censured nor could anyone oppose his authority. In him there was voluntary humility, not the necessity of endurance.

[Col. 0665A]

### Verse 2

“Rise up, you who judge the earth; repay the proud according to their deserts.”

“He who was humble” is told to rise up, for he is known to have been seized by the ungodly and crucified. Yet although he endured these things for our redemption, he was exalted before his disciples in his majesty when he rose, as is known, to everlasting glory. The most holy prophet therefore prays for what he knows will come. These are not imperative words; rather, through them the conviction of a certain mind and the devotion of one who desires are displayed.

He continues, “you who judge the earth,” so that he might openly demonstrate that the Lord Christ will judge “the earth”—that is, earthly human beings—by the dominion of his majesty. And so that you should understand this as referring to the ungodly, he adds, “repay the proud according to their deserts.” The proud are those who fail in their wickedness and do not appear to reach the Lord’s mercy through any satisfaction. The devil is also called proud, as is anyone who complies with his perversities. To these, then, repayment is due when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

[Col. 0665B]

### Verse 3

“How long, Lord, how long will sinners exult?”

Continuing in the preceding sense, he speaks of those sinners who grow hard through obstinate will. By saying, “How long will sinners exult?” he signifies this age, in which they have no limit to their pride. For on the day of judgment they cannot exult, since they will receive the punishments they deserve. The repetition displays the pain of prolonged expectation, because the ostentation of criminals is always grievous to the innocent when they behold it.

[Col. 0665C]

### Verse 4

“They will proclaim and speak wickedness; all who practice injustice will speak.”

To proclaim is to relate something publicly, in a loud voice, before others. He speaks of those who not only conceive evils in their hearts but also disseminate them with freedom, so that they destroy themselves and infect others whom they have deceived.

He continues, “and they will speak wickedness.” Since proclaiming is speaking, this seems to me to signify that we should understand proclamations as public exhortations, while “speaking” may refer to private conversations, so that no time would remain free from the offenses of the wicked. There is no doubt that “wickedness” applies to both, since it is said of those who are carried away by perverse loquacity.

But lest you think that “speaking” refers only to words, he adds, “who practice injustice,” so that they might continually appear detestable both in speech and in action. Observe carefully how, until the end of this division, he continually increases the escalation of crimes. This figure is called *climax*, that is, gradation. For when things are being intensified toward what is higher, an elegant ascent is produced.

The Apostle did the same with virtues when he said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or persecution, or the sword?” (Rom. 8:35), and so forth.

[Col. 0665D] [Col. 0666A] [Col. 0666B]

### Verse 5

“Your people, Lord, they have humbled, and your inheritance they have harassed.”

By “your people” he means faithful men [ed., true men], whom he likewise declares to have been humbled because they heard insults being directed against God. A devoted servant must necessarily be tortured by grief when something profoundly irreverent about the Lord is heard.

By “inheritance” he signifies Christian peoples, whom he says were harassed because proud persecutors tried to crush them with countless disasters. Observe how moderately he says that they were “harassed,” not destroyed, because the faithful always advance through temptation; and the more human force is brought to bear against them, the more abundantly heavenly protection is provided. As Solomon says: “Fire tests silver, and tribulation tests acceptable people” (Ecclus. 27:6).

[Col. 0666C]

### Verse 6

“They killed the widow and the sojourner, and they murdered the orphans.”

We also read: “Be as a father to the orphan, and as a husband to their mother” (ibid. 4:10). Concerning the sojourner, the Pentateuch likewise commands: “You shall not harm the foreigner or sojourner, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deut. 10:18).

Here, therefore, to intensify the crime, he says that widows, sojourners, and orphans were killed, so that the criminal hand would spare none of those whom the Lord had commanded to be protected and helped. Here is the argument that orators call “from the praise of the injured thing”: how well truth then expressed what human subtlety now turns to plausible uses.

[Col. 0666D]

### Verse 7

“And they said: ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’”

The proud intensified their wickedness, adding blasphemous words to the murder and oppression of the innocent as a culmination of evil. This figure is called *sarcasmos*, as though it were a hostile mockery penetrating as far as the flesh.

For they said that the Lord did not see what they were demonstrably doing in wickedness, judging that their evils were not being noticed because they did not feel themselves struck down swiftly. They were madmen who stretched the Lord’s patience into an accusation of weakness, saying that he could neither see nor understand their deeds, while that merciful governor cries out: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 18:23).

By “God of Jacob” he means the God of the Christian people. Sacred Scripture commonly repeats this name because through it the succeeding catholic Church is signified.

[Col. 0667A]

### Verse 8

“Understand now, you who are foolish among the people; and, you fools, learn wisdom at last.”

Having described the custom of the wicked, he comes to the second part, in which he admonishes them finally to abandon their abominable persuasion. He calls “foolish” those who, established within the Church, are stung by the prosperity of this age. He added “among the people” because they publicly denounce their perverse ideas in their assemblies and seem to teach what they themselves have learned with the worst intentions.

He calls “fools” those who, lacking true religion, blaspheme through open contradiction, saying that God neither sees what human beings do nor understands their offenses. He continues, “and, you fools, learn wisdom at last,” that is: you madmen, recognize the Lord’s mercy, although you think that the Lord neglects such things as he is known to forbid by his commandments.

[Col. 0667B]

### Verse 9

“He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, will he not observe?”

### Verse 10

“He who corrects the nations, will he not rebuke—the one who teaches human beings knowledge?”

In these two verses, a supremely beautiful and complete proof proceeds through each successive statement; nevertheless, it must be read as a rebuke. He says:

The one who gave ears to his various creatures denied hearing to himself! The one who formed the eye will not possess sight! The one who rebuked the nations through the preaching of the prophets will himself not judge at all! The one who taught human beings knowledge will remain without reason!

Rather, the maker of all things, distributing to each its proper measure, has given none of his creatures as much as he is known to possess in himself. Let empty presumption therefore cease imagining such falsehoods. For only the Divinity truly knows all things and is able to know all things perfectly.

Let us also examine how beautifully the order of expression proceeds. He says, “He who planted the ear,” and does not continue, “does not have an ear,” but says, “will he not hear?” Likewise, he says, “He who formed the eye,” and does not say, “does not have an eye,” but says, “will he not observe?” Thus he shows that the powers of hearing and seeing exist in God, not bodily members.

Dialecticians have wished to call such brief and lucid arguments *enthymemata*, that is, conceptions of the mind. Because of their brevity, orators have often adapted them with their own divisions. Here, however, the syllogism consists of a proposition and a conclusion that are nevertheless contrary to each other; 317 this is what has happened here. For he proposed, “He who planted the ear,” and concluded contrariwise, “will not hear”; the other statements that follow in that verse are of the same kind.

[Col. 0667C] [Col. 0667D]

### Verse 11

“The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain.”

After what he had said, a true judgment follows: the thoughts of such people are altogether most vain. And “the Lord knows” is well said, because those occupied by wicked thoughts cannot know themselves by themselves. We call anything vain that departs from truth or bears no profitable fruit.

[Col. 0668A]

### Verse 12

“Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law.”

“Blessed” is rightly set against the vain. Just as the former are deceived by their fleeting thoughts, so the latter are strengthened by the truth of heavenly teaching. He therefore comes to those whom he compared in the psalm’s title to the lights of heaven. He subsequently explains how this kind of blessedness comes about, saying: “And whom you teach from your law.”

These people are not deceived by vanities; they are filled with the true quality of teaching and become truly blessed because they have received the gifts of heavenly wisdom.

### Verse 13

“To give him relief from evil days, until a pit is dug for the sinner.”

This is clearly already a benefit of holy law: that in the adversities of this age the Christian may learn patience, by which adversities are always softened. For we read: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he regarded me” (Ps. 39:2), and similar passages.

The evil days are those when the unjust are seen to insult others and worldly prosperity favors persecutors. But observe what follows: one must wait until a pit is dug for the sinner—that is, until the day of his burial arrives, when the wicked will no longer be proud or rejoice further in prosperity. Then they receive what they postponed correcting here.

[Col. 0668B]

### Verse 14

“For the Lord will not reject his people, and he will not abandon his inheritance.”

Since he had earlier said, “to give him relief,” he now asserts that the person whom he has described as wearied for a short time on account of the reward of the crown will not be rejected.

By “his people” he designates the most faithful Christians, who hasten toward the Lord with pure intention of mind. He continues: “and he will not abandon his inheritance.” An inheritance is human: it passes to a successor when the former lord departs. Christ’s inheritance, however, although acquired by his blood, never loses its author; rather, it is possessed together with him.

[Col. 0668C]

### Verse 15

“Until justice is turned into judgment; and all who hold it are all who are upright in heart.”

Human justice will then be turned into judgment when the apostles, or those who are close to them in merit—as was promised to them in the Gospel—sit upon twelve thrones to judge (Matt. 19:28) with Christ.

For this justice of the faithful, which in this world is subjected to the scrutiny of the wicked, will there judge all the insolent and proud, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this life?” (1 Cor. 6:3).

And lest you perhaps doubt who these people are, the question is posed: “who hold it,” that is, justice. He answers: “all who are upright in heart.” Those upright in heart are all the saints who, joined to the divine rule, do not follow wandering errors.

[Col. 0668D]

### Verse 16

“Who will rise up for me against the wicked, or who will stand with me against those who practice injustice?”

He comes to the third part, in which he testifies that God alone is his helper against evil spirits. Since no human being is able to contend against them by his own strength, the question must be read as: “Who will rise up for me?” That is: no one stands forth to fight the demons on my behalf, while human beings instead follow them through evil imitation.

“To oppose” belongs to an enemy, not to a follower. He adds: “Or who will stand with me against those who practice injustice?” It is as though he were going to fight in battle formation, as though he were to be wounded by various missiles—not conquering by laying hands upon them, but reaching victory rather through suffering. For this contest is such that the one who endures wins, while the one who wounds loses.

The Apostle expresses the same meaning: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

[Col. 0669A]

### Verse 17

“Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul had almost dwelt in hell” [ed., “would almost have dwelt”].

First attending to human weakness, he found no helper anywhere; but when he turned to the Lord, he immediately found one who could assist him. For he says: “Unless the Lord had helped me,” I would at once have fallen into that pit in which sinners are certainly able to sink; that is, “my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.”

He could have been deceived by vain persuasions had he not deserved to be freed by the Lord.

[Col. 0669B]

### Verse 18

“If I said, ‘My foot has slipped,’ your mercy, Lord, was helping me.”

Here the benefit of a very swift confession is displayed: when he declared himself fallen, he immediately experienced the divine gifts. Liberated by a fortunate outcome, he was able to escape guilt because he did not deny his fault before the Judge.

Thus Peter, when he had been called and was walking upon the waves of the sea, became afraid (Matt. 14:30). But he deserved to be freed quickly because he immediately cried out that his weakness was overwhelming him. Divine mercy was instantly present: the outstretched hand rescued the one whom dangerous distrust was engulfing. So powerful is confession hastened at the beginning that forgiveness comes to the aid of a person before punishment strikes.

[Col. 0669C]

### Verse 19

“According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

There were many wounds, but entirely sufficient medicine, since he says that consoling remedies came in proportion to the harshness of his sorrows. By saying “in my heart,” he signifies his most salutary thoughts: when he revolved eternal rewards in his mind, he despised temporal evils without hesitation. Strengthened by this, he took his remedy from the very place from which he judged that he would reach Christ.

These are the consolations that gladden souls, even though bodies appear afflicted.

[Col. 0669D]

### Verse 20

“Does the seat of iniquity cling to you, you who fashion pain in the commandment?”

The question must be answered negatively: “Will the throne of ambushes be your accomplice?” For nothing can draw near to the just Lord except what is known to conform to his ordinances.

Thus, through the eighth form of definition, which in Greek is **κατ’ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου**, and in Latin *per privantiam contrarii* (“by deprivation of the contrary”), Christ the Lord is defined by denying what he is not.

The seat of iniquity is the pleasure-filled possession of this world, which cannot cling to the Lord, since he warned his servants not to be captured by such things. His commandment states: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted”; and again: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:5, 10).

We understand *fingere* (“to fashion”) to mean “to form.” Hence we properly call a potter the maker of vessels; and even a liar seems to be able to fabricate something for himself. For this reason the word is applied to many things, but it is understood appropriately when it is suitably adapted to circumstances or persons.

[Col. 0670A] [Col. 0670B]

### Verse 21

“They will lie in wait for the soul of the righteous, and they will condemn innocent blood.”

We often read that this happened to martyrs: savage persecutors attempted by some deceit to ensnare innocent souls. He says “they will lie in wait,” as though they will deal deceitfully, because they cannot find a genuine cause of accusation in such people.

What follows must be read as a curse: “and they will condemn innocent blood,” so that wickedness may not refuse to attribute to virtues what was inflicted through crimes. Blood is demanded in exchange for the suffering of the holy person, to whom praise and service ought to have been offered.

This may also be referred to the Lord the Savior, who, truly innocent and undefiled, accepted the sentence of an unjust condemnation for our redemption.

[Col. 0670C]

### Verse 22

“And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope.”

To show that human persecutions are powerless, he says that divine refuge came to him all the more at the very time when human pride was inflated by persecution. Through this the palms of the holy martyrs grow; through this that crowning blessedness is prepared; through this the wedding garment is granted; through this the kingdoms of heaven are opened; and whatever is sought with great desire is granted precisely when persecution rages most fiercely.

He continues: “and my God the help of my hope.” By saying “help,” he shows that he will still suffer. For this reason he adds, “of my hope,” because here we still have hope and do not possess the reality itself. But when that time of revelation dawns, we will abandon hope, because we will then possess our desire, as the Apostle says: “For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

Therefore, just as above the prophet expressed the cry of the saints, saying, “How long, Lord, how long will sinners exult?” so now, by placing the words “The Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope,” he cuts off the cause of all hesitation.

[Col. 0670D]

### Verse 23

“And he will repay them for their iniquity, and in their wickedness the Lord our God will destroy them.”

Behold, every doubt has been healed by a most salutary conclusion. Those whom the Lord was said not to see or understand, he will repay at the proper time according to their deeds.

But let us understand what he means by “he will repay them for their iniquity”: he will repay the wicked according to the desires of their wickedness, not according to the good that they seem unknowingly to accomplish. Those who persecute the saints send them indeed to the kingdom of heaven, but they believe that they are destroying those whom they have resolved to slaughter with wicked intent. Such people, however, must be judged according to the part in which they are known to have conceived their wickedness.

Note that the word “wickedness” is said to be capable of containing every crime. For just as charity contains manifold virtues, so wickedness encompasses various crimes.

“He will destroy them,” that is, he will make them strangers to his kingdom, where the wicked endure incomprehensible punishment when they are made outsiders to so great a gift.

[Col. 0671A]

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider with what beauty this psalm shines and how appropriately it is set against that murmuring with which humanity is especially afflicted. Let no one envy those who are perishing; let no one consider happy those who are destined to be condemned eternally. Rather, let us love the afflictions that make people happy forever.

For if we do not reject a bitter medicinal potion in order to deserve temporal health, who, possessing a sound mind, ought not desire that which he recognizes he can undergo for the sake of eternal joys—especially since, amid those very miseries, the Creator’s right hand gives us even greater assistance? Therefore we should not be anxious, because the one who attacks us is not such as the one who avenges us.

[Col. 0671B]

# Exposition of Psalm 94

## The Praise of the Song, to David

The power of this psalm is proclaimed neither through an obscure interpretation of names nor explained through the likeness of some historical event; rather, what is found within is read openly and briefly at the entrance.

“Praise” signifies devotion of voice; “song,” cheerfulness of mind. Both ought to be joined in the work of psalmody, so that the service of our tongue may be completed with corresponding joy.

“To David” signifies the Lord the Savior, to whom this praise is sung. For the opening words of the psalm sing of him, while the latter words are spoken by the Lord himself.

Consider that human praises are heightened and intensified by additions and exaggerations, whereas divine praise, however great the excellence with which it is spoken, is always found to be greater when reconsidered.

[Col. 0671C]

## Division of the Psalm

Foreseeing that the Jewish people might resist Christ the Lord, the prophet first invites the Hebrew peoples to enter into psalmody, describing the Lord’s praises with the sweetest truth.

Second, the Lord Christ himself speaks, warning the same Jewish people not to harden their hearts and not to suffer what happened to their ancestors, who did not deserve to enter the promised land.

Thus, by a marvelous dispensation, the prophet first encouraged the people with gentle invitations; then the Lord himself admonished the most obstinate, so that, considering the majesty of their Lord, their stony hearts might soften.

[Col. 0671D] 319

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us shout for joy to God our salvation.”

Like a herald of the judge, the rooster that awakens the people of the Church invites those who pray to awaken from the sleep of this age and sing praises to the Lord with joyful exultation.

“Come” is said to those who are understood to be far away, who have not yet been joined in the integrity of faith. Although we are not made absent from the Lord, since he is wholly everywhere, we become distant when we are removed by the quality of our actions, as the Lord says through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

Then he shows to what banquet he invites them. He says, “Let us exult.” But since there is also an exultation of this age, which especially occupies the minds of unbelievers, he adds, “in the Lord”: in him one rejoices with true confidence, where exultation finds edification and not destruction.

He continues: “Let us shout for joy to God our salvation.” We have often said that to shout for joy is a great movement [ed., manner] of gladness which, although it cannot be expressed in words, is nevertheless declared by the fullest voice, indicating an inward joy for which speech is insufficient.

When he says, “our salvation,” he signifies the Lord the Savior, who granted us salvation by dying, gave us an example by suffering, and bestowed saving gifts by rising again. This word has shown clearly and abundantly to whom this praise is addressed.

[Col. 0672A] [Col. 0672B]

### Verse 2

“Let us anticipate his presence in confession, and let us shout for joy to him in psalms.”

To anticipate is to do something before the one believed to be coming can be seen. By “face” he means his presence, when he will appear terrifying to all the ungodly at the time of his judgment.

We have said that “confession” must be understood in two ways. We confess when we offer God’s praises with religious devotion. We also confess when we condemn our sins through the satisfaction of repentance. He admonishes us to do this here, so that before the judicial coming we may confess our crimes, lest, when he comes, he examine what we condemn without hesitation.

He continues: “and let us shout for joy to him in psalms.” Observe with what balance he arranges everything: he assigned tribulation to confession and joy to jubilation, so that, purified through both changes of circumstance, the devout spirit of the faithful might be offered. Nor is it without significance that he again says “let us shout for joy,” so that you might recognize the great necessity of the matter from its repetition itself.

[Col. 0672C]

### Verse 3

“For the Lord is a great God, and a great King over all gods.”

From here through three verses, reasons are given why the Lord should be praised with joyful acclamation. This figure is called *aetiologia*, that is, the giving of a reason.

By saying, “For the Lord is a great God,” he shows that there is no one superior. For one is called great only when he is shown to hold the summit of supreme power.

He continues: “and a great King over all gods.” We often read of gods fabricated by human beings, such as Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, and the other idols, as he will also say in the following psalm: “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95:5).

We also read of gods as holy men appointed by the Lord, as in the passage: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst he distinguishes gods” (Ps. 82:1).

Over all of them—whether those fabricated by human beings or those whom he himself made—the almighty Christ is a great King. He surpasses them more than royal power can rise above private authority. He is properly called King because he both creates all things and governs the universe.

[Col. 0672D]

### Verse 4

“For the Lord will not reject his people; for in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his.”

After the Lord’s greatness has been proclaimed, he comes to his wonderful and infinite clemency. For he says that the Lord does not reject the Jewish people, whom he is known to have chosen for himself.

From that people came the prophets, the apostles, and many of the faithful who believed in the Lord with sincere minds, as the Apostle says: “What shall we say, brothers? Has God rejected his people whom he foreknew? Certainly not. For I am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. 11:1–2).

He continues: “for in his hand are all the ends of the earth.” This refers to all the nations, which are subject to Christ the Lord in faithful devotion. One wall was the Jewish people, and the other was the calling of the nations; coming together in the cornerstone—that is, in Christ the Lord—they joined their mouths, so to speak, by an unbreakable charity. Concerning this it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 97:21; Matt. 21:42).

He adds: “and the heights of the mountains are his.” The heights of the mountains are the powers of this age and earthly honors. He says that these belong to the Lord so that we may not be troubled by their exaltation. For although the sea swells under raging winds, it nevertheless has its shore as a boundary; similarly, the powers of this age receive a measure of dominion, even though they boast heedlessly of their power.

[Col. 0673A] [Col. 0673B]

### Verse 5

“For the sea is his, and he made it; and his hands formed the dry land.”

The sea signifies the nations, which are stirred in this age by the diverse winds of vice. He says that they were made by the Lord so that you might recognize that all things are subject to his will. For everyone who produces something has in his power the things he makes, as another psalm also says: “All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, Lord” (Ps. 86:9).

He continues: “and his hands formed the dry land.” He said “the sea”; now he says “the dry land,” which is rightly understood as the earth, since by itself it is always dry unless it is watered by the flooding of rivers or rains.

So also our hearts are barren and dry with respect to good fruits unless they are watered by the Lord’s mercy, and unless he deigns to establish us, unstable and wavering as we are, by the gift of his mercy. Therefore, as was said above, all these words should be joined to the summons: “Let us shout for joy to him.”

[Col. 0673C]

### Verse 6

“Come, let us worship and fall prostrate before him; let us weep before the Lord, who made us.”

At the beginning of the psalm he invites the people to jubilation; now he urges them toward the saving health of repentance. This is appropriate, because at first he invited inexperienced peoples to exultation, lest he impose upon those still trembling something that might cause them fear.

But after the Lord’s glory and power had been described, he suitably added the confession of weeping, since an instructed mind could not reject a most salutary potion.

Observe that here a form of holy prayer is given. “Let us worship” means that we should bow by bending our bodies. “Let us fall prostrate” means that we should cast ourselves down before him and stretch ourselves out in the complete surrender of our limbs. This is customary when the spirit, inflamed by intense compunction, is brought low through the humility of prayer.

He adds: “and let us weep before the Lord, who made us.” Great confidence is shown by groaning before the one who in his mercy deigned to form us. He quickly recognizes his own work if he sees that our hearts have turned toward him.

To weep before the Lord, therefore, is to pour out pious tears and condemn our worst deeds, so that we may deserve forgiveness for the things we abandon through fear of the Lord. For if we pray with complete purity of heart, the one who made us will easily also restore us.

Thus, through the figure of *characterismos*, the image of those praying has been described.

[Col. 0673D] 320 [Col. 0674A]

### Verse 7

“For he is the Lord our God; and we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture. Today, if you hear his voice.”

A threefold reason is given why the Lord should be worshiped.

First: “For he is the Lord our God,” so that the gift of worship may rightly be offered to him.

Then: “because we are his people.”

He continues: “and the sheep of his pasture.” This is the third point, which is clearly promised. It is again stated what the faithful are: certainly, the sheep of the Lord’s pasture. Pastures signify heavenly gifts by which the soul is fattened through a sweet feast.

It is rightly defined that the Christian people are “sheep of the pasture,” because they are filled by a fortunate lot with eternal delights. Sheep signify simplicity of heart, which the people possess when they follow their shepherd with gentle devotion.

But one condition is set before all these things: “Today, if you hear his voice”—the voice that he is about to speak below. For whoever does not hear his voice is neither called his flock nor placed in his pastures, as it is written in the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice, and my sheep follow me, and I know them, and no one snatches them from my hand” (John 10:27–28), and so forth.

“Today” signifies always, because the one who gives salutary admonition must be heard continually. The Apostle powerfully expressed the force of this saying: “But exhort one another every day, while it is called ‘today’” (Heb. 3:13).

Thus far the prophet has spoken; let us now consider what follows.

[Col. 0674B] [Col. 0674C]

### Verse 8

“Do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, according to the day of testing in the wilderness.”

We have reached the second entrance, where the Lord the Savior addresses the Jews, warning them not to imitate the obstinacy of their ancestors and thereby become strangers to the Lord’s rest.

He says: “Do not harden your hearts,” because the hearts of unbelievers are altogether stony and truly comparable to flints. They do not receive the rain that produces fruit, because they grow hard through the dryness of their sterility.

He also presents famous examples, so that he might frighten those whom he knew to be obstinate with the memory of a well-known calamity. For, as we read in Exodus, the Jewish testing rose up against Moses with serious murmuring, saying that food was not being given to them in the wilderness, nor drinkable water being granted through divine generosity (Exod. 16:3).

They were asking for something necessary, but their will was detestable because they did not believe in the power of the Divinity. Therefore the fault of their ancestors is necessarily recalled to them, so that they may fear the punishment they deserve.

[Col. 0674D]

### Verse 9

“There your fathers tested me; they proved me, and they saw my works.”

“There,” as he said above, signifies “in the wilderness.” There human frailty tested God; but the power of the Divinity immediately appeared when food came from the air and drink from the rock.

The rock produced water, but the hearts of the unbelievers hardened into stony dryness. What madness, then, is it still to follow the perversities of those upon whom punishment is known to have fallen so severely?

When he says “your fathers,” he also indicates that they were obstinate, because each person has as a father the one whom he is known to imitate. Thus the Lord himself says to the Jews in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44).

He continues: “they proved me, and they saw my works.” They proved him, certainly, when manna rained down for the hungry, when a multitude of quail was supplied to them, and when welling waters flowed from the dryness of the rocks.

By adding, “and they saw my works,” he rebukes their unbelief: with bodily eyes they looked upon what they did not at all believe with the light of the heart. Therefore he said “they saw,” not “they believed.”

[Col. 0675A]

### Verse 10

“For forty years I was near this generation; and I said: ‘They always err in heart, and they have not known my ways.’”

This period is shown to have been mentioned as a great mystery. For although the Lord fasted for forty days according to the mystical number, and remained with the apostles for another forty days after his resurrection so that the whole world might believe, the obstinate Jews were found unwilling to be satisfied with the benefits of forty years.

For this reason a greater ruin is prepared for them, because prolonged pride grows greater within them.

[Col. 0675B]

[Col. 0675C] **Verse 11.** “To whom I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest.” God is said to swear in two ways. He swears when calm and gentle, as is read in another psalm: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: I will not lie to David” (Ps. 88:36). Here, however, he is said to swear in anger, because he is known to threaten vengeance. Yet this oath clearly pertains to the firmness of his promise. For if human beings swear in order to keep their promises, how much more is God said to swear, so that the things foretold may stand with necessary stability! He swears by himself who has no one greater, as he himself also says to Abraham: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord: unless, blessing, I bless you” (Gen. 22:16–17). Humanity, however, calls upon God because it knows him to be the avenger of faithlessness. Hence human beings are forbidden to swear, [Col. 0675D] since by their own ability they are unable to fulfill their promises.

What, then, does the Lord swear? That the obstinate will not enter into his rest; but eternal death will receive those who have not deserved to attain the gifts of his satisfaction. Rightly, indeed, those who offend Christ himself, the door of tranquility, cannot enter into rest. Yet we must examine what he means by saying, “They shall not enter into my rest.” The Doctor of the Gentiles explains this passage in the following manner, saying: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works” (Heb. 4:4). Therefore, whoever has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God did from his. For it signifies that time of blessedness when the righteous, after the struggle of this age, enjoy eternal rest; but this [Col. 0676A] will certainly not be given to the wicked, who through their own malice have fallen away.

**321 Conclusion of the psalm**

Hear, Jews hardened by sacrilegious minds: if you do not recall the benefits, at least fear the punishments that are due. What else is it not to enter into the Lord’s rest than to receive perpetual torments? Do not, we ask, let another’s error entangle you; change the desires of your fathers for a better condition. If you ask for water in the wilderness, come to the Lord’s fountain; if you desire manna, receive the body of the Lord the Savior. Those things brought punishment to your fathers; these things bestow everlasting rest upon you. Indeed, surpass your predecessors in faith; reject their unbelieving hearts; believe, as you hear with divine illumination, what they, even while seeing, refused to receive with their blinded will. Do not dissemble while there is time; for afterward you will endure the Judge, if now you refuse to acknowledge the one who admonishes you.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 95

*The Song of David, when the house was being rebuilt after the captivity.*

As far as the literal sense is concerned, that time is signified in the title, when, under Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, the Jerusalem temple is known to have been restored after the captivity—after the hostile hand of the Chaldeans had destroyed it down to the surface of the earth. But since he says nothing of this kind in what follows, and since the title never departs from the psalms’ narrative, it remains that we must seek its meaning spiritually. The destroyed house is rebuilt when the soul, after the captivity of sin, begins, with the Lord’s help, to return to an understanding of the truth. For this house, that is, the universal Church in which Christ dwells, is always built of living stones, because every day it receives growth in its construction from those who confess; nor does it cease to be built until the number of the predestined is completed at the end of the age. We must bear in mind that this psalm is the second among those that speak of the Lord’s first and second coming.

## Division of the psalm

In the first part of the psalm the prophet urges all humanity to sing to the Lord and to announce throughout the whole world [Col. 0676D] the coming of the Lord’s incarnation, because he alone is the true Lord above all gods. In the second part he admonishes various nations first to offer themselves and afterward to render the offerings of preaching, commemorating both comings of the Lord: when he was judged by humanity, and when he will come to judge the world.

## Exposition of the psalm

**Verse 1.** “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” In the preceding psalm the prophet admonished the Jews to lay aside their hardness of heart and come to faith in the Lord Christ. But because obstinate wickedness was going to remain in them, he now appropriately admonishes the nations that they ought to sing a new song to him. For the one who sings a new song to the Lord is the person who, having laid aside the old human being, is happily renewed through the grace of baptism. Then the house of the Lord is built from him, when, after the devil’s dominion, he is acquired for the number of the blessed congregation. This is the song that consoles the purest mind; this is the melody that delights to the marrow, when the soul truly sings because it believes that by God’s grace it is to be freed from sins.

It follows: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” The repetition itself is pleasing, and in such a word there can be no weariness, where no affection is able to exhaust itself. By saying “all the earth,” he signified the catholic Church, which is known to be spread throughout the whole world. In a brief summary he both refuted the Jew, because he admitted the nations, and overthrew Donatus, because he did not deny grace to the universality of the confession. For so that you might understand that human beings are meant, he said “sing,” namely those who truly can sound forth the Lord’s praises; and then, because he fitted a plural number to “earth”—which certainly would not be suitable if he intended the physical ground to be understood.

**Verse 2.** “Sing to the Lord, and bless his name; proclaim his salvation from day to day.” It is not without purpose that this repetition has been constructed with a threefold elegance. For the praise of Christ is the honor of the whole Trinity. We bless his name whenever we confess him in every respect to be our salvation. This figure is called *epimone*, that is, frequent repetition of a statement; when appropriately employed either in praise or in blame, it adds great force to amplification.

It follows: “Proclaim his salvation from day to day.” “Day from day” signifies two days in the plain sense; we judge this to pertain to the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, because both shine with the brightness of the eternal Sun. Through them the Lord the Savior is rightly proclaimed, since through them he is shown both to be coming and to have come. The prophets promised his coming; the evangelists declared that he had come. Thus the two heavenly days are shown to have announced his glory.

**Verse 3.** “Declare his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples.” Having said above, “Proclaim his salvation,” he here says, “Declare his glory”; and both expressions are most appropriately placed. The Lord the Savior was to be proclaimed, but his glory was to be announced among the nations because it proclaimed the author of so great a miracle. Let the Jew hear and understand that he has been despised because of the wickedness of his obstinacy, since he does not say to the Hebrews, “Declare,” but to the nations. And lest you be able to understand this otherwise, he also added, “among all peoples”; by this expression he comprehended all the nations according to a complete reckoning.

It follows: “His wonders,” that is, the mystery of his incarnation: although he is most high, he became most lowly in order to free us. Let us also understand how greatly the building of the holy house has advanced, since it is known to have embraced the whole world.

**Verse 4.** “For great is the Lord, and exceedingly worthy of praise; he is terrible above all gods.” Here he says why his wonders and glory ought to be proclaimed: “For great is the Lord.” This figure is called *aetiology*, that is, the giving of a cause. “Great” pertains to power, because he is more powerful than all things. “Worthy of praise” pertains to mercy, because, while we were captives, he redeemed us with precious blood. “Exceedingly” suits both, because it could not be explained how great he is, nor how worthy of praise. But since evaluation fails before one who considers him, he beautifully added “exceedingly.” Thus, without explaining what he intended, he signified it most abundantly, and by failing to comprehend what he willed, he made it clear.

It follows: “He is terrible above all gods.” Here we must understand the gods whom impious paganism fashioned for itself through presumptuous invention. For he makes them manifest in the following verse: although they may seem worthy of adoration and fear to foolish minds [ed., *exorabiles*, “to be entreated”], the Lord is far more terrible, whose multitude of miracles cannot be understood and whose fullness of majesty cannot be grasped.

[Col. 0678B] **Verse 5.** “For all the gods of the nations are demons; but the Lord made the heavens.” Wonderfully, through the fifth species of definition, which in Greek is *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν* and in Latin is called “word for word,” it has been comprehended what the gods of the nations are: demons. For demons are beings who benefit no one; rather, they always deceive and mock those who believe in them. Although demons are called *daemones*—“knowing ones”—in Latin, as though they were gods who know [ed., Greek *δαήμονες*], in human speech this is nevertheless an insult, since we thus name those whom we judge worthy of execration. And rightly so, because true knowledge is not in them, since it does not obey the will of its Creator.

So too we call philosophers “wise”; but the Apostle’s definitive sentence applies to them: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 1:20). [Col. 0678C] Hence we must regard these “knowers” as people without understanding. The substance of demons, then, was indeed created by God, just as was that of the good angels, and was superior to human beings; but, because pride acted through its own agency, it reached the point that, having abandoned its natural dignity, it persisted always in evil works. These are the demons who destroy others and deceive themselves. These are certainly the gods of the nations, who through fruitless prophecies and empty illusions concerning the future hasten to deceive the souls of those who consult them.

It follows: “But the Lord made the heavens.” Behold a praise truly worthy of the Lord! For when he says, “He made the heavens,” he sufficiently shows that all creatures were made within them. Thus we comprehend lesser things within greater things when we say that a city has been built or a house constructed; for the remaining parts are included wherever the general name is used. And consider where the expression leads: “He made the heavens.” The false gods were discovered through human imagination; but God made the heavens, where they neither deserve to approach nor to dwell. Or, by “heavens” he signifies the apostles and holy men, who by the Lord’s gift have been accustomed to command demons. Thus the demonstrative manner of speaking has been completed in brief form. Above he censured the gods of the nations, and afterward added the praises of the Lord, because the brightness of day is more welcome when dark night has preceded it.

**Verse 6.** “Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary.” The universality whom he had undertaken to admonish demonstrates the usefulness of the catholic religion. For he says how those who have deserved to attain the forgiveness of sins are made both beautiful and magnificent. Beauty rightly follows confession, because no one can be beautiful except one who has been cleansed by the Lord’s mercy. Our sins make us ugly, but the baths of repentance make us comely. Therefore he says that the purest beauty stands before the Lord’s sight when it has been cleansed by faithful confession.

It follows: “Holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary.” He develops what he said above. For the beauty given to the faithful is holiness and magnificence, that is, perpetual honor and blessedness. “In his sanctuary” signifies that voice which the elect will hear: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). Behold the beauty that is neither darkened by the sun nor worsened by age: it always shines, it is always new, and it suffers nothing adverse, since it has no defect throughout eternity. By saying “and magnificence,” he signifies that those who have deserved to be honored in his sanctification are always great and always exalted.

**Verse 7.** “Bring to the Lord, homelands of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor.” After proclaiming the Lord’s great deeds and the gifts of the blessed, in the second part he more earnestly admonishes the nations, having laid aside all hesitation, to “bring to the Lord glory and honor.” For when he says “homelands of the nations,” he signifies more than if he had said only “nations.” A nation may contain some foreigners, but when a people is named, we do not include newcomers; rather, we indicate only a people of one blood. Here, however, he says “homelands of the nations,” so that no native, no guest, and no foreigner might be excluded. *Patria*—“fatherland”—is so called as though it were “the halls of the father.”

It follows: “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” He also admonishes that this universality should bring glory and honor to the Lord. The Lord’s glory exists when someone conducts himself in praiseworthy behavior. The Lord is glorified in such people when he is praised because of the conduct of the faithful, as he says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). The Lord’s honor, however, exists when we give him thanks for his gifts and confess that whatever good we have received was bestowed by him, as it is read in the Gospel: “Were not ten cleansed? And was no one found who would give honor to God, except this Samaritan?” (Luke 17:17–18).

**Verse 8.** “Bring to the Lord glory to his name; lift up sacrifices and enter his courts.” Just as above he said “sing” three times, so here he places “bring” for the third time, so that you might always recognize the mysteries of the Holy Trinity as present in Christian doctrine. Those, then, bring glory to his name who are changed for the better through devoted zeal and confess in every respect the Trinity, consubstantial with itself and almighty, distinguished only by its persons and not by a difference of nature.

It follows: “Lift up sacrifices and enter his courts.” By sacrifices he does not mean victims of cattle, but the pure offerings of conscience, [Col. 0680A] from which not blood flows but pious tears. These are the sacrifices of which he said in Psalm 50: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19). But consider that he first placed “lift up” and then “enter,” because those who do not carry such sacrifices are not judged worthy to enter the Lord’s courts.

Nor should it be received without purpose that he used the plural “courts.” For the Lord’s courts are the apostles or prophets, through whom the faithful people enters to the Lord.

**323 Verse 9.** “Worship the Lord in his holy court; let all the earth be moved from his face.” The Lord is truly worshiped when the sacrifices he mentioned above have been carried, so that the supplication of the one who confesses may deserve to reach the ears of the Creator. It is not without purpose [Col. 0680B] that in the preceding verse he used the plural “courts,” while here he says “court” in the singular, because from those courts—that is, from the patriarchs, apostles, and prophets—one arrives at this court of the catholic Church alone, where his power and majesty are worshiped.

It follows: “Let all the earth be moved from his face.” Since he had said to the faithful, “Lift up good works and enter,” he now says that lovers of the world are to be removed from his presence. For he did not say, “Let all the earth be moved before his face,” but “from his face”—just as today we say this of those whom we render alien from our sight. They are rightly called “earth,” because they do not abandon earthly vices. Yet others have said that this should be understood in a good sense: the earth is moved when, by God’s mercy, the sinner is brought to repentance. Thus the incomprehensible depth of the divine Scriptures is understood in different ways and shown to stand in one truth.

**Verse 10.** “Say among the nations: The Lord has reigned from the wood; for he has set the world firm, and it shall not be moved; he will judge the peoples in equity and the nations in his wrath.” He admonishes those whom he commanded to worship the Lord in the holy court to proclaim the revered mysteries to the nations: among the nations they must say that the Lord will reign from the wood of the cross—not from that wood of paradise by which the devil seemed to hold the human race captive, but from this wood from which freedom raised its head and life arose. On that wood the death of transgression hung; on this one the faith of confession shone forth. The former led to the underworld; the latter sends to the heavens.

“Has reigned,” however, let us understand as “has been made known,” when the Lord the Savior appeared to the world. For when did he not reign, who always continues with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the power of his omnipotence? Some translators do not have “from the wood,” but for us it is sufficient that the expression has been confirmed by the authority of the Septuagint Translators.

The Lord’s cross set the crooked and distorted world straight, while through the rule of faith it converted the hearts of pagans. Here we must understand “earth” in a good sense, since in the divine Scriptures you frequently find the term varied according to the character of the places. He says that this earth is not to be moved completely—the earth that perseveres in the solidity of faith—not like the one of which he said above, “Let all the earth be moved from his face.” That earth is moved so that it may be converted from evil works; this one is not moved, because it stands firm in the solidity of true faith.

It follows: “He will judge the peoples in equity.” Here he prefers “peoples” to be understood as faithful human beings, who will be judged under the tranquility of heavenly mercy, when he restores to them the promised rewards. But by adding “the nations in his wrath,” he designates the proud and wicked, who receive their portion with the devil. And observe how in two expressions he designates the mysteries of such great things: equity pertains to the blessed; wrath to the everlasting punishments of the wicked. Note also that throughout all the clauses of this verse it must be joined to the opening phrase: “Say among the nations.”

**Verse 11.** “Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult; let the sea and its fullness be moved.” Since above he said, “He will judge the peoples in equity and the nations in his wrath,” by which he displayed the time of the future judgment, there now follows a most beautiful and delightful digression. For he says that then the heavens will rejoice, the earth exult, and the sea be moved. By “heavens” he signifies—as has often been said—the apostles and prophets, or the remaining faithful, whom divine majesty is known to inhabit as heaven. “Earth,” however, indicates sinners who nevertheless have deserved, through the benefit of satisfaction, to return to the Lord’s grace. That earth can exult at the coming of its Judge which understands itself to have been absolved from its own sins.

It follows: “Let the sea and its fullness be moved.” Here he uses “sea” for the peoples, who, set in the salt waters of this age, are tossed by various storms. They are moved to joy when they have received the gifts of conversion. And so that you might understand the totality of the nations, he added, “its fullness.”

**Verse 12.** “The fields will rejoice, and all that is in them; then all the trees of the forests will exult.” Here likewise we must understand “fields” in a good sense, because we call those things fields that are stretched out in the most beautiful equality. Thus he calls fields men distinguished by the praise of justice, not swollen with pride, not rough with anger, but made perfectly level by gentle meekness.

It follows: “Then all the trees of the forests will exult.” “Then” refers to the second coming, when he will judge the world. The trees of the forests naturally bear bitter and barren fruits; but when grafted, they grow rich with the sweetest abundance. Thus the nations, which had previously been like trees of the forests, brought to fruitful cultivation, will rejoice before the Lord with the great gift of joy. But when he says “all the trees,” he wishes that part to be understood which could be grafted into good commandments and changed.

**Verse 13.** “Before the face of the Lord, for he has come; for he has come to judge the earth.” Because he had said that believers would rejoice, he does not say “in corners” or “in secret places,” but “before the face of the Judge”—when joy is immeasurable and abundant, when rewards are granted and security without end is bestowed. And lest you think that he meant the first coming of the Lord’s incarnation, he says, “For he has come,” and then adds: “For he has come to judge the earth.” For if he had ended the statement with that first clause, you might perhaps have understood the coming that has already passed; but when he added, “For he has come to judge the earth,” he wished us to understand only that coming which we are still known to await. The prophet Ezekiel also bears witness to it: “Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you shall live. And I will put sinews upon you, and bring upon you the inward parts of flesh, and stretch skin over you; and I will put my spirit in you, and you shall live, and you shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. 37:5–6). Daniel likewise says: “And many of those sleeping in the earth will rise through fissures, these to everlasting life and these to reproach and confusion” (Dan. 12:2). Here he calls the whole population of the world “earth,” so that he may restore eternal rewards to the good and punishments to the wicked.

**Verse 14.** “He will judge the world in equity and the peoples in his truth.” First a general summary was set down, because divine equity will judge the world, that is, the whole human race. Then he explains how it will be judged by saying, “the peoples in his truth,” because in that separation of the right side and the left there will be two peoples, to whom he will give the sentence [ed., *sententia*, nominative for *sententiam*] of his truth: [Col. 0682B] those who faithfully believed in him will enjoy the blessedness of his kingdom; but those who stubbornly followed the vices of the world will endure their deserved punishments with their author.

It must certainly be investigated why here too he speaks of the world, while in the following psalm he says, “His lightning flashes have illuminated the world,” and in many other places by the same figure he declares the earth to be enclosed; and again Psalm 106 comprehends the expanses of the earth by its four cardinal points, saying: “From the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. 106:3). There is also a very clear example of this in the Gospel, where it says: “He will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and he will gather” [ed., “they will gather”] “from the four corners of the earth” (Matt. 24:31).

Therefore I rightly judge that it must be investigated how both a square and a circle can suit the earth, since the figures themselves, as geometers say, appear to be different. Scripture calls the shape of the earth a circle because, for those looking toward its extremity, a circle always appears; the Greeks call this circle *ὁρίζων* (*horizōn*, “horizon”). But it says that the earth is formed by four cardinal points because the four cardinal points signify the four corners of a square, which is contained within the aforementioned circle of the earth. For if you draw one straight line from the eastern cardinal point toward the south and another toward the north, and likewise draw one straight line from the western cardinal point toward those same points, namely the south and the north, you make a square of the earth within the aforementioned circle. But how this square should be demonstrated as inscribed within the circle, Euclid clearly explains in the fourth book of the *Elements*. Therefore Holy Scripture rightly calls the face of the earth a circle and says that it is contained by four cardinal points.

## Conclusion of the psalm

Let us hear what the prophet admonishes us: “Sing to the Lord; bring living sacrifices to him.” Let us have no part with the devil, and without doubt we shall have a part with Christ. Then, as the title says, after the captivity of sins, the Lord’s house can be built from us, if we deserve to be found living stones. Let us beseech continually; let us pray without ceasing. He will recognize the humble when he comes to condemn the insolent, and he will not punish the sinner when he has found him continually confessing.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM 96

*The psalm of David himself, when his land was restored.*

“The psalm of David himself” is clearly to be referred to the Lord Christ. It follows: “when his land was restored,” that is, when sinners who had turned away from him through the error of wickedness returned to him, with the grace assisting them, in purified sincerity of mind. This happened among the Jews, who after that wickedness of the crucifixion obtained the grace of conversion. It may also be understood otherwise, so that “the land restored” indicates the mysteries of his resurrection. His body indeed died according to the common law, but it was restored in the singular gift of glory. Therefore let us remember that this is the fourth psalm concerning his first coming, through which the world is known to have been freed.

## Division of the psalm

In the first part of the psalm the prophet, describing the Lord’s virtues through his resurrection with varied proclamation, rebukes the worshipers of idols with a fitting reprimand. In the second he turns his words toward the Lord, rejoicing that the catholic Church rightly believed in its author. He also urges the faithful to rejoice in the Lord, because he is accustomed to rescue those who appear to lie under the assaults of the cruel.

## Exposition of the psalm

**Verse 1.** “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult; let the many islands rejoice.” Seeing the world confused by the detestable superstition of human beings, the prophet describes the Lord’s praises with marvelous variety, so that unbelievers, recognizing the true God, might no longer place their hope in utterly vain things. And he made a beginning that would both briefly encompass everything and remove all delusions: “The Lord has reigned.” Who else, then, should be worshiped except the one who alone is known to rule?

It follows: “Let the earth exult.” What remains now for idols, if the whole earth venerates the name of its creator? Sensible earth ought not to worship the most brutish stone, because the one who seeks help from insensible things denies the effect [ed., “affection”] to himself. Yet there is one cornerstone that ought spiritually to be worshiped and feared.

He added: “Let the many islands rejoice.” Since the Lord reigns throughout the whole world, let the established Churches rejoice. They are rightly compared with islands, because, surrounded by the waves of the world, they are battered by the multitude of persecutions that rage around them. But just as islands are not harmed by raging waves, so the holy Churches are not diminished by the disturbances of their adversaries; rather, they shatter upon their rocks those who rush against them with billowing crests. And observe that he says “many,” not “all,” because of heretical perversions, which impose the name of churches upon their errors.

**Verse 2.** “Cloud and darkness are around him; justice and judgment are the correction of his throne.” In this verse the Lord’s character is described both to the impious and to the devout. He appears cloudy and dark to the irreverent, since he shines with no brightness upon a darkened heart, just as the sun appears shadowed to bleary eyes. For those clouds do not arise from the source of light, but from the bodily weakness that has been contracted, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:40).

In contrast, it follows: “Justice and judgment.” This is what the Lord appears to be to those who are most pure of heart, whom he rightly called “correction,” because, stripped of the error of wickedness, they are the seats of the Lord the Savior; he already possesses them by his majesty, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” The order of the words is: “the correction of his throne”; truly so, because justice cannot sit upon twisted minds. And note that through this verse and the four others that follow, the Lord’s first coming is indicated by various allusions. This figure is called *characterismos*, which in Latin is called “formation” or “description.”

**Verse 3.** “Fire will go before him, and it will burn his enemies round about.” Fire preceded the Lord’s coming when, through the preaching of the prophets, the hearts of unbelievers raged, so that, inflamed by the heat of anger, they plotted the death of the preachers. It is therefore the fire that will go before him, but it consumed its own authors instead, as the prophet Isaiah says: “And now fire will consume the adversaries” (Isa. 26:11).

It follows: “And it will burn his enemies round about.” “Will burn,” as we have said, pertains to indignation and the sudden heat of spirit which the enemies of the holy Church inflicted at that time. “Round about” must be understood as “on every side,” because, although the preachers were few, the multitude of the adversaries surrounding them was innumerable.

**Verse 4.** “His lightning flashes have illuminated the world; the earth saw and was moved.” A most beautiful and appropriate comparison has been made. For just as clouds, when stirred and struck together, hurl lightning, as natural philosophers say, so the words of the prophets flashed forth indications of the truth. Indeed, in the divine Scriptures you frequently read that they are compared with clouds, as in the passage: “And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

Let us also attend to the fact that here again the figure of the earth, as was already said in the preceding psalm, is described as a circle. For it is the circle that is also called the world. A circle, as geometers have defined it, is a plane figure contained by a single curved line, to which all straight lines drawn from one point among those established in the middle of the figure are equal to one another. Once this configuration has been recognized, the shape of the earth becomes very familiar to us.

The whole world is also signified by the straight line of the heavens, which astronomers call the diameter of the world, as in the passage: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112:3). A line is an intelligible length without breadth, beginning at a point and ending at a point. A point, however, is that of which no part exists.

We must therefore remember that all these things—whether a point, a line, a circle, a triangle, a quadrilateral, or other theorems of this kind—whenever they come before the eyes, are enclosed by bodily definitions, that is, by sensible ones; but whenever they are grasped by the mind alone, there is no doubt that they are merely intelligible. A diligent reader will find fuller knowledge of these matters in books on the discipline of geometry.

It follows: “The earth saw and was moved.” “The earth saw” signifies that human beings recognized the Word of the Lord with the light of the heart. “Was moved”: it was terrified by the novelty of the great preaching, so that it discovered that it was worshiping senseless idols, while it had the supreme Creator, the Lord worthy of worship.

**Verse 5.** “The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord; before the face of the Lord the whole earth trembled.” Here “mountains” signify people who both seek the heights of this world and grow hard through senseless superstition. They are marvelously compared with melting wax, because they flow into repentance all the more readily the more firmly they had believed themselves to be immovable in their hardness [mss., “the more”]. For when he says “before the face of the Lord,” he shows from where the mountains melted like wax; and the same is read in another psalm: “There is no one who can hide from his heat” (Ps. 18:7).

But when he repeats, “Before the face of the Lord the whole earth trembled,” he signifies those who, having been regarded by his mercy, attained the remedies of satisfaction. We see this happening even today, when the powers of the world, whether called pagans or heretics, condemn their superstitious vow and choose instead to submit to divine service.

**Verse 6.** “The heavens declared his justice, and all peoples saw his glory.” After the clouds mentioned above, which we said should be understood as the prophets, he comes to the heavens, whom we must understand as the apostles. Through their holy preaching the Lord’s justice, salutary to the world, was made known.

It follows: “And all peoples saw his glory.” Here “saw” must be understood not with bodily eyes but with the light of the heart. For glory is usually heard, not seen; elsewhere too it is written in a way that must be understood in this sense: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten” (John 1:14). Or, as some wish, the Lord’s fore-visible [ed., “visible”] coming is signified.

Let us also observe how the first coming of this Lord is indicated in different ways. He mentioned fire, lightning, mountains, and heavens; [Col. 0685D] and through all these there is one intention: to announce the Lord the Savior. This figure is called *aenigma*, that is, an obscure statement, when one thing is said but another is intended.
