**Verse 7.** “Let all who worship idols be confounded, those who glory in their images; worship him, all his angels.” Having prophesied the Lord’s coming, he rebukes the worshipers of idols, who, despite so great a manifestation, are still not ashamed to worship I know not what absurdities. An idol is so called because it is itself a deception, that is, something discovered through human falsehood. An image is composed from a simulation of sacred things, and an alien honor is bestowed upon it. Thus both are shown to be things to be avoided through the interpretation of their very names.

And because unclean spirits desire to be worshiped, claiming for themselves false honors [Col. 0686A] which their wickedness does not deserve to receive, see what follows: “Worship him, all his angels.” For a good angel worships the Lord because with an upright heart he recognizes his creator; nor does he permit himself to be worshiped by human beings, as the angel says to John when John fell at his feet in the Apocalypse: “See that you do not do it, for I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers” (Rev. 19:10). But evil beings command that they be worshiped, as Satan said to the Lord Christ in the Gospel when he had taken him up onto a mountain and shown him the kingdoms of the world: “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

### Verse 8

“Zion heard, and rejoiced; and the daughters of Judah exulted because of your judgments, O Lord.”

He comes to the second member, in which the prophet, turning to the Lord, exults joyfully: because Zion—that is, the catholic Church—received the Lord’s judgments with a pure heart. For the one who is going to believe rejoices that he has heard the word; but the one who receives it with a deceitful mind departs in sorrow, because he heard against his will what he was not going to believe.

Zion, as we have often said, is the mountain established at Jerusalem, whose interpretation signifies “watchtower” or “contemplation.” This is rightly attributed to the holy Church, because in the virtue of contemplation she continually beholds the Lord who is present.

It follows: “and the daughters of Judah exulted.” The daughters of Judah signify religious minds and approved persons. They are called the daughters of Judah because they preferred to believe in Christ and are shown to have descended by origin from Judah [ms. G: *qui, etc., monstratur*], from whom the Jews also received their name. And why Zion rejoiced is subsequently explained: “because of your judgments, O Lord”—that is, because you turn the sorrow of your servants into joy and overthrow the proud devil by the virtue of humility.

### Verse 9

“For you are the Lord Most High over all the earth; you are exceedingly exalted above all gods.”

By “over all the earth,” we rightly understand sinners here; by “above all gods,” we appropriately understand righteous human beings, who have been shown by frequent exposition rightly to be called gods. Or else, through these two expressions, he signifies that the Lord rules both earthly and heavenly creatures, just as another psalm says: “For all things serve you” (Ps. CXVIII, 91).

### Verse 10

“You who love the Lord, hate evil. The Lord guards the souls of his saints; he will deliver them from the hand of sinners.”

Here too a categorical syllogism seems able to be formed as follows: The saints love the Lord, because the Lord guards their souls and snatches them from the hand of sinners; all who love the Lord, because the Lord guards their souls and snatches them from the hand of sinners, hate evil; therefore the saints hate evil.

Now let us examine the words of the psalm. Here he addresses the good and the faithful, so that they may be separated from the malice of the devil; for he is rightly called evil, through whom all sin comes. What, then, is it to love the Lord? To hate the devil, because, as it is written: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24). This figure is called *parison*, that is, an equality of sense consisting of unlike members.

And so that no one might fear offending the devil, it follows: “The Lord guards the souls of his saints; he will deliver them from the hand of sinners.” Let no one now doubt that evil must be hated, when the Lord is known to guard the souls of his saints. But observe that he says “souls,” lest you should confine the statement to their bodies [ms. A: *ne tenderes*, “lest you should stretch yourself”], which he freely hands over to punishments in order to bestow crowns upon the martyrs. For he delivers souls from the hand of sinners when he does not allow them to be overthrown by any wickedness, but rescues them unharmed in such a way as he knows to be pleasing to himself.

### Verse 11

“Light has arisen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.”

He says that light has arisen for the righteous—that is, the truest faith—so that, once illuminated, he may believe such things as will lead him to the kingdom of heaven. There is indeed also that common light of the saints, which human beings and animals alike see indiscriminately. But their own proper light is that which is bestowed by Christ the Sun. Concerning it the impious will say: “We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine for us, and the Sun did not rise for us” (Wis. V, 6).

For the upright in heart, joy rises without doubt when, with God’s help, they do such things as they know will benefit them. Thus it is indicated in this passage that lovers of the world enjoy neither steadfast joy nor the true light.

### Verse 12

“Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord, and confess to the memory of his holiness.”

Having said above what good things the righteous receive through the Lord’s favor, he now again admonishes them that they ought to rejoice in the Lord, not in human desire or in the ruinous boasting of this age, as the prophet Isaiah says: “There is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVIII, 22).

The righteous, however, confess to the memory of his holiness when they have been placed in that everlasting kingdom, remembering from how great a destruction of this age, through the Lord’s mercy, they have been withdrawn.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider how salutarily this psalm forms us by its instruction. It prohibits the worship of idols, through which we might have incurred eternal death. It appropriately commends the praises of the Lord, from which our life will undoubtedly proceed. It teaches us not to fear afflictions or dread the evils of this age. [Col. 0687D] For we can escape all dangers, all things that bring death, with great advantage if we love the author of our salvation, as the Apostle says: “In everything we suffer tribulation, but we are not distressed; we are at a loss, but we do not perish; always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh” (II Cor. IV, 8–10), and the other things which the distinguished Teacher is known to have spoken for the salutary instruction of the human race.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCVII

## A Psalm for David

These simple titles smile upon us with the clearest arrangement of words. For they refer to the Lord the Savior, concerning the glory of whose incarnation and second advent this psalm is going to speak. These events are described with such a wealth of variety that, although they have often been foretold, they always shine forth as new and marvelous to human understanding. There is no doubt that this is the third of these accounts. But these titles, which have gathered both advents of the Lord into a single statement, disclose great mysteries to us. In the one, they admonish us to seek the merciful Lord; in the other, to fear the Judge who is to come. Thus this salutary and precious conjunction gives us grounds both for hope and for fear.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. In the first part he admonishes the Christian people to rejoice with the exultation of a new song when the wondrous advent of Christ the Lord is granted. In the second part he says more fully, in various ways, that there should be rejoicing, because the judgment expected by the righteous is known to have come, in which they will receive the Lord’s worthy rewards.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Sing to the Lord a new song.”

The prophet admonishes the Christian faithful that, receiving the mysteries of new birth, they should celebrate with a new song the incarnation of the Lord. The new man ought to sing a new song—not that old man who, not yet laying aside Adam’s sins, persists in the transgression of the old man. It is truly new because the world has never heard anything like it. New, because no antiquity sullies it, but it always remains in the glory of its dignity. But from where this new song comes is disclosed below.

### Verse 2

“For the Lord has done marvelous things; his right hand and his holy arm have saved him.”

The cause of the new song is given: “For the Lord has done marvelous things”—namely, when he gave sight to the blind, movement to the lame, hearing even to the deaf, and other things of this kind which the text of the Gospels presents as having been done contrary to the ordinary course of human nature.

But his saints also did these things. Hear what follows, so that you may truly understand that something unique was granted to the new song: “his right hand and his holy arm have saved him”—that is, Christ the Lord—when he knew no sin of this world and rose from the dead with the swiftness of three days.

But who saved him? What follows: “his right hand,” that is, the omnipotent Word—not because Christ is one and the omnipotent Word another, as Nestorian madness fabricates, but so that you might understand that the one who saved him is the very one who said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X, 18).

As for the arm, Isaiah the prophet likewise speaks of the Son: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1). The right hand pertains to wondrous works; the arm to singular strength.

### Verse 3

“The Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness.”

“The Lord has made known his salvation,” that is, the Lord Savior. For he is the salvation whom Simeon, receiving him in his hands in the temple, says: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29).

To express also the most manifest truth of the matter, it follows: “in the sight of the nations,” just as Jeremiah says: “Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III, 38).

He added: “he has revealed his righteousness,” because previously he had been proclaimed through the prophets under a certain veil; when that veil was removed at his advent, the very face of truth appeared.

And note that the same one is called the right hand, the arm, salvation, and the Father’s righteousness, so that you may understand that there is one substance and one power in that passage. For in what respect can he be divided who is affirmed to possess not merely similar things [ms. A: *dissimilia*, “dissimilar things”], but everything belonging to the Father, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “All things that the Father has are mine, and all mine are the Father’s” (John XVII, 10).

### Verse 4

“He remembered his mercy toward Jacob and his truth toward the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God.”

“He remembered” is said because he fulfilled his promises. This is the promise that Isaiah foretold, saying: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. LII, 10).

A fitting name was given to this promise—“his mercy”—so that the Creator of heaven and earth might deign to become human and, by the benefit of his advent, free the human race, bound by the chains of sins.

By Jacob, as we have often said, we may not improperly understand the people of the New Testament. For just as Jacob preceded his brother in blessing, although he was born later, so the Christian people preceded the earlier people of the Synagogue by the steps of faith.

And so that the differing variation of the names may not confuse our understanding, let us examine why it was added: “and his truth toward the house of Israel.” Thus we may understand that this was given not only to the people who after the Lord’s advent were called Christian, but also to those who believed that he would be born of the Virgin. Israel signifies every faithful person who has seen God with a pure mind.

He placed mercy in Jacob and truth in Israel. Mercy existed when he came to free the human being; truth will exist when the saints see face to face the one whom here, as the Apostle says, they behold “in a riddle through a mirror” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

He added: “all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God.” By this statement all the depravity of the heretics is excluded, for they think that the worship of the Lord Savior was granted to the earth in a merely local way. “They saw,” he says—that is, they perceived with the mind—what is known to have been accomplished throughout the whole world. For how many were there who could see him with bodily eyes among the Jewish people? But since he says here “all the ends of the earth,” there is no doubt that this must be referred to faith, so that the truth of the words may be established for us.

### Verse 5

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing, exult, and sing psalms.”

He comes to the second part, in which he admonishes the devout to rejoice in various ways. These words, however, are appropriately referred to the Lord’s judgment, at which this psalm is also known to end.

“Shout joyfully” means: leap forth into the joy of the voice with great delight, so that what speech cannot express through confused utterance may be declared by the outburst of the devout person rejoicing.

“All the earth” designates the universal Church, which placed her hope in the Lord’s advent with undivided devotion.

It follows: “sing, and exult, and sing psalms.” Although these words appear similar, they are nevertheless distinguished by a certain difference. To sing is for the mouth of the most serious Christian to resound with praises to the Lord; to exult is to express the desires of the soul with great affection; to sing psalms is to fulfill the Lord’s commandments through good works.

He admonishes that this be done in many ways because there is a diversity of virtues in which one should rejoice. This figure is called *homoptoton*, because different words end in similar sounds: “shout joyfully,” “exult,” “sing,” and “sing psalms.”

### Verse 6

“Sing psalms to the Lord with the lyre, with the lyre and the voice of a psalm.”

These words have been joined together in a most beautiful combination, so that they themselves seem to create a kind of harmony. Instruments of musical art are employed to perform a heavenly work, which is necessarily said so that that perfection may be indicated through certain likenesses.

He sings psalms to the Lord on the lyre who performs the commandments of the Godhead through bodily action: who breaks bread for the hungry, clothes the naked, offers consolation to the abandoned, and does the other things that can be applied to heavenly commands.

It follows: “with the lyre and the voice of a psalm.” He added the same words in inverted order, so that, whichever of them you do first, you may nevertheless understand that the whole belongs to the Lord’s grace.

### Verse 7

“With trumpets of beaten silver and the voice of a horn; shout joyfully before the Lord the King.”

Let us observe that all these words are filled with divine mysteries. The Book of Numbers indicates that among the Hebrews there were two kinds of trumpets, expressing certain likenesses (Num. X, 2). One was formed from beaten silver; this is suitably applied to the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets.

Silver is so called from the purity and brightness of words, as he himself says elsewhere: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, purified of the earth sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 7).

“Beaten” signifies that the faithful, being struck by various sufferings, make progress through the Lord’s gift, and grow all the more the more frequently they are struck by the blows of hard hammers. For the hammer is the devil, concerning whom the prophet says: “The hammer of the whole earth has been crushed” (Jer. L, 23).

The voice of the horn is the fixed endurance of patience, which, like a substance of horn, perseveres in faithful men through love of the Lord.

Therefore he sings psalms to the Lord with these trumpets who rejoices devotedly in both virtues: who proclaims the Lord with a pure heart and endures his mercy through the virtue of patience.

It follows: “Shout joyfully before the Lord the King.” In this clause the sentence that seemed suspended in the preceding sections is completed. Here he says where one should shout joyfully, where sing, where exult, where sing psalms, where play the lyre in a psalm, where sing a psalm on the lyre, and where shout joyfully with beaten and horn trumpets—namely, “before the Lord the King,” when, at that judgment, the righteous receive the promised rewards.

Through these various expressions it is signified that one should rejoice before the Lord through diverse holy works and diverse gifts. Or else, he says that these things should be done here in such a way that the mind’s attention is always directed toward him.

### Verse 8

“Let the sea and its fullness be moved; the world and all who dwell in it.”

Here the terror of the future judgment and the dread of the impious are described. The sea that is in the breasts of the impious is moved by the recollection of their sins.

Its “fullness” is rightly so called, because many sins raise immense waves; and it is most fully shaken when the guilty person knows that he is to be condemned.

It follows: “the world,” which itself must be shaken when it is foretold that it will come into a new form, as it is written: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. LXV, 17).

He added: “and all who dwell in it,” so that you might truly understand this to have been said of human beings, of whom above he spoke figuratively as “the sea.”

### Verse 9

“The rivers will clap their hands together; the mountains will exult before the face of the Lord, because he has come to judge the earth.”

We have often said that the divine Scriptures speak through various likenesses, so that what is said may be hidden from the impious while the faithful are more diligently encouraged to seek it out.

Thus here too, through manifold allegories, he says that a song should be sung to the Lord. For allegory is saying one thing and signifying another.

Above he compared the sea to sinners; now the rivers signify holy men, whose good works flowed forth with heavenly abundance. “Together,” that is, in the Lord Savior, for whom they are shown to have performed the service mentioned above.

But observe that all these things are expressed by allusion. For when do rivers have hands, unless they have been compared with holy men? Concerning these it was said: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38).

It follows: “the mountains will exult before the face of the Lord.” It is evident that mountains are often used both in a good and in a bad sense. The impious swell with proud efforts and, with hearts hardened by obstinacy, reach the hardness of rocks.

The meek, however, are most firm in the solidity of their minds; and although they bow in pious humility, they are raised to the most solid summits by hope of future blessedness. These are the ones who will rejoice when the Lord comes, because at the future judgment they will receive the gifts of his promise.

He added: “because he has come to judge the earth.” Here we appropriately understand “earth” as every sinner, because they always desire earthly vices. You see that the entire sense has been brought to that time of judgment, so that you may understand that everything said can correspond to it.

### Verse 10

“He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity.”

Here too “the world” must be applied to the impious, who are frequently designated by the term “earth.” They are to be judged according to justice, since their stubbornness leaves them no possibility of pardon.

“The peoples” signifies those who have been approved as faithful from among the Hebrews and those who have come devoutly from the nations. Concerning them he says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 16).

These peoples, therefore, are to be judged in equity, because there they will receive rewards—those who here endured the gravest dangers for the Lord’s name, as the Apostle says: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V, 10).

Where this judgment will take place is also clearly stated. For the prophet Joel says: “I will gather all the nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and there I will contend with them on behalf of my people and my inheritance Israel” (Joel III, 2).

## Conclusion of the Psalm

What is the meaning of this, that we frequently find musical instruments placed in the psalms, instruments that seem not so much to soothe the sense of the ears as rather to summon the hearing of the heart?

But since that sound and the modulation of pipes have nevertheless departed from our age and from the sacred mysteries, it remains that we must seek the meaning of this matter spiritually.

Music is the discipline that investigates the differences and correspondences of things fitting together—that is, of sounds. It is rightly introduced to explain likenesses of spiritual things, because harmony exists through the power of agreement among things that are otherwise discordant.

For whether we utter a psalmody or diligently [ed.: voluntarily] devote ourselves to the Lord’s commandments, we are tempered by the grace of the sweetest harmony. And if you weigh the causes of this matter in profound reflection, no rational creature is shown to be excluded from this concord, provided that it lives under the rule of its Creator.

Rightly, therefore, we are continually commanded to sing psalms to the Lord, to play the lyre in a psalm, to sing psalms on the lyre, and to shout joyfully with beaten and horn trumpets, so that there may be no doubt that these sweet-sounding instruments signify to us the harmony of worthy actions.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCVIII

## A Psalm of David

I cannot admire sufficiently the dignity of this name, which, always attached in the titles, raises the focused gaze of our mind toward Christ the Lord. For his honor and power are sung in this psalm.

But what praise is due to the most holy man, that through his distinguished name the mystery of such great majesty should be signified? For through David we perceive both the person who speaks and Christ, whom we understand to be strong of hand and desirable.

Therefore, recognizing the distinguished herald, let us await the coming of the great Judge.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first section the prophet admonishes all peoples to confess Christ the Lord, because he is declared to have carried out judgment and justice in Jacob.

In the second he admonishes the people to worship the Lord Savior, who is known to have been gracious to Moses, Aaron, and Samuel because they are shown to have kept his commandments.

Therefore he says that the Lord, who deigned to hear his faithful, must be exalted and worshiped.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry. You who sit above the cherubim, let the earth be moved.”

When he says, “The Lord has reigned,” he explains that he displayed the glory of his resurrection—not as though he had previously been believed unable to reign, whom the Jews seemed to extinguish; rather, the time is here indicated when, after his resurrection, he himself says: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII, 18).

It follows: “let the peoples be angry,” though they will do no further harm. For they are mocked with great weight of seriousness, since their deceit and cunning are shown to have done absolutely no harm.

When he said “let them be angry,” the prophet does not command the peoples to be stirred up to some crime; rather, he means that they should be angry with themselves, since they have been proved to have done a wicked deed, so that they may quickly come to the salvation of conversion when, by their own will, they begin to condemn their actions.

If you wish to take the statement literally, it seems to be a kind of urbane irony, just as in the Acts of the Apostles Paul is read to have said to the high priest, after being struck: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall.” Shortly afterward, when reproved, he said: “I did not know, brothers, that he was the ruler of the people.” For it is written: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people” (Acts XXIII, 3, 5; Exod. XXII, 28). He did not say this because he did not know, but because, with a certain urbanity, he denied that he was the ruler of the people.

So here too it is said: “The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry”—that is, they will do no further harm. This seems to pertain not to exhortation but rather to mockery. This figure is called *astismos*, in Latin “urbane expression,” composed for the sake of elegance and wit.

It follows: “He sits above the cherubim; let the earth be moved.” “You who sit” is the indicative mood, second person; for, turning the words toward the Lord himself, he brings the sentence to an end.

“Cherubim” is a Hebrew name signifying “fullness of knowledge,” and it shows the Lord seated there as though upon his throne. He also sits upon human beings [ed.: “sit”] who are filled with complete faith and integrity of works.

He added: “let the earth be moved.” Either this signifies what he said above, “let the peoples be angry,” or it more especially calls sinners to be moved toward conversion. As has already been said, they are rightly called earth because they desire earthly vices.

### Verse 2

“The Lord is great in Zion, and exalted above all peoples.”

So that you might clearly understand the God whom he said sits above the cherubim to be Christ the Lord, he expressed it as: “The Lord is great in Zion,” who deigned to appear as a human being in the regions of Jerusalem.

Pay attention to the words he says: “the Lord is great,” lest anyone should think him contemptible because of the humility of his passion.

He added: “and exalted above all peoples,” because the one whom they had despised with irreligious minds stood forth as the exalted King above all peoples.

Zion is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” which is the Church, in whom the Lord is shown always to be spiritually present through reverent contemplation.

### Verse 3

“Let them confess your great and fearful name, for it is holy.”

After the appearance of the flesh that took place in Zion, he says that the peoples should confess the Lord Savior—those of whom it was said above, “let the peoples be angry.”

Thus we see this happening daily in the catholic Church: those who were previously blasphemers are shortly afterward corrected through the Lord’s favor.

His name is called great because it has been spread everywhere; fearful because he himself will come to judge the living and the dead; holy because he remained in an immaculate and heavenly way of life. Thus it is also said elsewhere concerning him: “For the Lord has magnified his holy one” (Ps. IV, 4); and the angel said to Mary: “Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35).

### Verse 4

“And the honor of the King loves judgment; you have prepared equity.”

Above he had said: “Let the peoples confess your name.” Now he clearly explains how they ought to confess. For the honor of the King is glorious preaching, which we always offer to him by confessing.

“He loves judgment”—that is, we ought to love the Creator by deliberating and considering. For he is not to be worshiped with a wavering will or a fleeting mind, but with a firm and discerning judgment, as he always appears to pure hearts.

It follows: “you have prepared equity,” so that human beings might recognize that this gift is attributed to him, by which they may steadily understand or practice equity.

Finally, the following verse makes this sense clearer. Or else, as some prefer, “the honor of the King” is the just condemnation of the guilty, since the king’s glory is always increased when iniquity is punished.

### Verse 5

“You performed judgment and justice in Jacob.”

He performed judgment in the faithful people when he gave them the ability to distinguish good from evil; and justice when, having abandoned idols, they deserved to serve their Creator with humble devotion.

By “Jacob” he means each faithful person, because through the recollection of this name the devout people are displayed.

“You performed” is said because no one other than he established and confirmed [ms. A., “formed”] the Church, as the Apostle says: “For no one can lay another foundation besides what has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (II Cor. III, 11).

### Verse 6

“Exalt the Lord our God and worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy.”

The prophet comes to the second section, in which he admonishes devout peoples not to cease magnifying the Lord’s name, so that, by proclaiming him, they may themselves rather be seen to exalt him.

For the rest, he does not need to be assisted by human powers, as has often been said: he is supreme power and the perfection of the whole Majesty, which must be worshiped.

It follows: “and worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy.”

Since blessed Augustine, the most diligent investigator, asserted that the body of the Lord, which he took from the Virgin Mary, should be understood as the footstool of his divinity (Augustine, *Exposition of Psalm XCVIII*, before the middle), because of the nature of the humanity he deigned to assume, we must recognize that this body is subject and united to that power which all creation agrees is higher than everything, as the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. I, 25).

And elsewhere, concerning the same Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, the Apostle says: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 9).

Now we must say what his “feet” seem to signify in this verse: namely, the stability of the Godhead, which always persists in the omnipotent glory of its nature like the unfailing stability of feet.

Therefore, although the assumed body of this Word is glorious, great, and adorable, nevertheless, because of the humility of the humanity, we appropriately understand it as the footstool of his feet.

For when he himself says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI, 1), the earthly body that he took from the Virgin Mary is, in my opinion, rightly understood by the same likeness as the footstool of his feet.

And note that he did not say, “because he is holy,” but “because it is holy,” so that you might distinguish the body from the Godhead through the contemplation of the mind, while referring both to one person: the Word “who became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

He also speaks of the feet of the Godhead by a tropological figure, just as “footstool” was spoken figuratively. Perhaps we should also understand it in this way: that it designates the final period of time, when the Lord deigned to become incarnate.

Thus the evangelist John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18); and the Apostle Paul likewise says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. IV, 4).

### Verse 7

“Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name; they invoked the Lord, and he heard them.”

He placed here great men of ancient authority and asserts that the Lord’s grace was granted to them, in order to incite the faithful people to similar devotion.

And note that here he calls Moses a priest, although he is not so called in the Pentateuch. Even though he did not offer sacrifices, as his brother Aaron did, he nevertheless always presented the prayers of the people before God, which is shown to be the office of a priest.

Therefore he is rightly called a priest here also, since, when the Lord was angry, he pleaded for the people with great prayers.

Samuel, however, lived in the temple of the Lord with a holiness worthy of praise, and he anointed David as king. But because he did not receive the office of priest—since he was from the tribe of Ephraim, from which priests could not be made—he added concerning him: “among those who invoke his name,” because he could not name individually those whom an infinite multitude encompassed.

He added: “they invoked the Lord, and he heard them.” The power of sincere prayer is shown in its brevity, because he effectively heard those who supplicated faithfully.

### Verse 8

“In the pillar of cloud he spoke to them, because they kept his testimonies and his commandments, which he gave them.”

It is not without significance that it says “in the pillar of cloud,” because this is always placed in the construction of a house as a sign of strength and beauty.

In this form, therefore, the Lord spoke to them, a form that announced the future construction of the Church. But because at that time he spoke words to them through a cloud, to us he deigned both to speak more clearly and to appear through his holy footstool—that is, through the incarnation.

O footstool higher than all temples, far more excellent than all spiritual creatures! As the Apostle says: “But to which of the angels did he ever say: Sit at my right hand?” (Heb. I, 5).

But what wonder if he is called a footstool who compared himself to a worm, a scarab, a fuller’s herb, and the cornerstone—not with a view to lowliness [ed., “utility”], but out of affection for humility? By assuming humility he made it as exalted as it had previously been insignificant in this world.

It follows: “because they kept his testimonies and his commandments, which he gave them.” He gives the reasons why the Lord would deign to hear them: because the one who truly loves him is the one who keeps his commandments, as he himself says to the disciples: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XIV, 15).

A testimony is a signification established through certain signs of a preceding matter, as he says in the Pentateuch: “This will be a testimony for you.”

The commandments pertain to the law which they are seen to have received through Moses. Thus it is shown most effectively that God is pleased when his command is fulfilled by us.

### Verse 9

“O Lord our God, you heard them; God, you were gracious to them, and taking vengeance upon all their endeavors.”

By saying, “you heard them” and “you were gracious to them,” he shows that the desires of the saints were fulfilled in their good requests and that they received the benefits which they seemed necessarily to seek.

But he added: “and taking vengeance upon all their endeavors.” This was placed here so that we would not always expect to be heard, since both things appear to have been fulfilled in them.

For we recognize that they were sometimes heard when they asked for prosperity, and again that vengeance was taken upon their endeavors, lest human elation should be able to steal upon them.

For although some may be faithful and worthy of veneration for their great devotion, it is necessary that vengeance sometimes be taken upon them, lest their hearts appear able to be led into pride, just as the Apostle says: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. Because of this I besought the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 7–9).

Therefore we have heard that they were heard, and in them we should understand that vengeance was also taken, so that we may recognize that merciful Christ performed both acts graciously.

### Verse 10

“Exalt the Lord our God and worship on his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.”

The first part of this verse is also read above, where the division was made; but there it was followed by “and worship the footstool of his feet.” Here, however, he commands that the Lord be worshiped not at the mountain, but “on his holy mountain.”

There is no doubt that this can be referred to Mount Zion, which is the Church. She is the mountain of mountains and the holy of holies, whose inhabitant is Christ himself.

Thus he says that both things must be done in the holy Church. It should be noted, however, that he commands the holy Lord to be worshiped on the holy mountain, because just as his praise does not befit a perverse mouth, so the disgracefulness of a place cannot be appropriate to his worship.

## Conclusion of the Psalm
Let us contemplate the face of this psalm as though it shone with two most beautiful lights. It terrifies unbelievers, so that they may be led to the most devoted supplication; it commands the faithful to adore Christ the Lord, because he himself knows how to hear those whom he loves. Blessed is the people that rejoices in such a command: for it is a life-giving desire to recognize and love the Creator. Therefore, may hearing the Lord Christ stir us to exultation. It belongs to a faithful servant to love the one who rules. For whoever does not hold his master as most dear declares himself to be terrifying. It is indeed the nature of things that you cannot possibly suppose yourself able to be loved by one whom you do not seek with an affectionate heart. Let us therefore love, so that we may be loved; let us seek, so that we may find; let us knock, so that we may be able to approach him. It is opposed to every madness to seek lukewarmly the one whom you know can bestow eternal blessings upon you.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM XCIX

## A psalm of confession

[Col. 0697B]

Although confession is frequently placed in the psalms as circumstances require, here it is nevertheless shown to have been expressly assigned in the title: and rightly so, because this entire psalm belongs to both kinds of confession. One kind occurs when, lamenting our sins, we acknowledge ourselves guilty and liable, and with devout tears beseech the Lord to grant us mercy. The other occurs when we either praise the benefits conferred upon us or venerate, with great exultation, those bestowed upon others. For *confession* is so called as if from *confatio*—whether it is repentance or praise celebrated by the mouths of many—and it is called this in order to show that it belongs to a multitude.

## Division of the psalm

[Col. 0697C]

In the first part of the psalm, the prophet admonishes the whole community that it ought to praise the Lord with great joy, because gloomy service is not fitting for so great a Lord. And lest a Christian think that this kind of confession must always be used, in the second part he says that, repenting of our evil deeds, we should merit entry through the gates of his forgiveness, because his mercy endures forever.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1. “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth.”

The prophet, concerned for the faithful people lest they suppose they should serve Christ the Lord under the burden of anxious sadness, began with joyful shouting, because it is the perfect devotion of the righteous to serve the Lord with gladness of mind, just as the Apostle also exhorts: “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things” (I Thess. V, 16–18). And lest anyone think that he had not been summoned at all, he added, “all the earth,” so that no one among human beings might seem to exist who refuses to hear this voice.

For joyful shouting is—as we have often said—to be stirred by great gladness of mind, though not to burst forth into articulated words. When he said “shout joyfully” and added “all the earth,” he frequently indicates great meanings even through differing grammatical cases. For although “earth” is announced in the singular number, he says “shout joyfully,” which certainly belongs to the plural number, so that you may understand this “earth” to refer to human beings rather than to the soil itself; this is clearly to be understood allegorically. For allegory is a figure that says one thing and signifies another.

### Verse 2. “Serve the Lord with gladness; enter his presence with exultation.”

Although the services of the Lord may appear to be carried out through various forms of ministry—such as ecclesiastical orders, monasteries of the faithful, solitary hermits, and devoted laypeople—all of them nevertheless properly refer to these three words: the Lord is to be served with gladness, not with grumbling or bitterness of mind, as happened in the desert when the Jewish people grumbled against the Lord.

But this gladness is certainly charity, which, as the Apostle says, “is not puffed up, does not behave improperly, is not ambitious” (I Cor. XIII, 5), along with the other qualities by which he describes this outstanding virtue in a marvelous account. Therefore, those serve the Lord with gladness who love him above all things and regard one another with fraternal charity.

O free service! O service more excellent than all dominions, to which such gladness is granted as is not found in the glory of kingdoms! But consider what reward follows the gladness commanded in this world. For he says: “Enter his presence with exultation.” It is much more difficult, and much more excellent, to rejoice in the presence of so great a judge, where conscience is admonished to come together in such a way that it may then receive joy from humility, at the very moment when he is shown to be terrifying to all the proud.

### Verse 3. “Know that [ms. A: ‘because’] the Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves; but we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.”

At the beginning of this verse he speaks against the faithlessness of the Jews, who, by not believing the Lord the Savior to be God, dared to lay hands upon their Creator. “Know,” he said—understand—that this Lord whom you have in no way believed to be the Son of God is himself the God who made heaven and earth, who also formed us according to his own image and likeness.

And lest they think that the creation of human beings should be attributed to the seed of their fathers, he added, “and not we ourselves.” For although the activity of the flesh supplies the service required for our birth, nevertheless it is he who is shown to bring us into this world, he who causes all things to come into existence.

He continues: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” He comes to the faithful people through beautiful comparisons, showing what they are. They are sheep because they are simple, and he himself is their true shepherd. “His pasture” means the abundant and sweet feast of the divine Scriptures. These are the pastures by which the faithful soul is nourished and led to the pleasant places of future blessedness. Thus, in these three verses he has summed up what a Christian ought to do, believe, and understand.

### Verse 4. “Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns of confession. Praise his name.”

He comes to the second part, so that, since he had said above that one should shout joyfully in the praises of the Lord, he might now teach how each person ought to confess to him. The gates of the Lord are humble repentance, holy baptism, sacred charity, almsgiving, mercy, and the other commandments through which we can reach his presence.

Therefore the prophet urges us first to enter through this confession of humility into the gates of the Lord’s mercy, lest the rapacity of the raging wolf find us outside the sheepfolds. He added: “his courts with hymns of confession.” With “his courts,” understand here also “enter.” For he signifies the prophets, evangelists, and all who, with the Lord’s help, have taught. Their words are clearly the Lord’s palaces, when he is found in them if he is sought with a devoted mind.

But in order to distinguish this confession from the former, he added “with hymns,” as in that confession of the Lord the Savior when he said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 25). He did not confess anything on account of his own sins; rather, he rendered praises to the Father with sincere love. A fitting order has been preserved, because when the former is offered first, the latter follows in security.

He added, “Praise his name,” where a minor division should be placed, because the phrase is clearly joined to the following verse.

### Verse 5. “For the Lord is gracious; his mercy is forever, and his truth is unto the age of the age.”

Lest anyone think that he would grow weary from praising, or weaken through constant labor, he gave the reason why his name must be proclaimed: namely, “because the Lord is gracious.” When does weariness arise from graciousness, or can the spirit be filled where desire is always making progress? This delight does not know satiety, where the mind is refreshed by consolation in such a way that its desires nevertheless are never laid aside.

And lest you think that the graciousness he mentioned is temporary, he says that his mercy remains forever, because once he has bestowed future blessings, they are nevertheless preserved by him perpetually unharmed. He added: “and his truth is unto the age of the age.” “The age of the age” signifies both what is now taking place and what we believe is to come: for here too there is the truth of the Lord, as it is written, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV, 12), and in that age in which the gifts of his promises are fulfilled and he will reign with his saints in glorious eternity.

## Conclusion of the psalm

This psalm has marvelously taught us both kinds of confession, so that we may shout joyfully to the Lord with alacrity and continually lament the wounds of our sins. Both are necessary in this world, so that God’s servant may neither despair in sadness nor, again, become elated by prosperity. For just as human health consists in the harmony of the bodily humors, so the Christian is perfect who remains unwaveringly balanced amid the vicissitudes of these things.

Let us therefore receive with an eager mind what has been said. The character of this lamentation is shown by the fact that the Lord is commanded to be praised within it; rightly so, because from it comes advancement, not guilt; rewards, not punishment; beautiful freedom, not degrading servitude.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM C

## A psalm of David

Although titles drawn from histories appear to indicate the force of the psalms, they are also known to contain simple meanings. This is indeed a marvelous text, enclosed in the form of perfect holiness, which ought to await the hundredfold fruit of rewards. But it is known to have prefaced the most familiar words for this reason: that its simple and evident force might indicate meanings that are most lucid and most honorable.

For “psalm” signifies holy action. Where “of David” is placed, everything is applied to the virtues of Christ, so that you should understand nothing concerning that earthly king, but recognize that everything was spoken concerning the heavenly one.

## Division of the psalm

That holy congregation which the catholic Church continually brings forth and multiplies throughout the whole world says in the first part of the psalm that it will sing of the Lord’s mercy and judgment and avoid association with the worst people. In the second part it declares that it loves the faithful and dwells with them in most welcome fellowship; but it drives demons, together with their assaults, from its heart, knowing that they have no share whatsoever with God’s servants. Thus, formed by such instruction, we ought both to desire good things and to reject evil.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1. “I will sing of mercy and judgment; to you, Lord, I will play the psalm.”

The multitude of the blessed, heavenly upon earth, brought forth a beginning that would briefly encompass everything. For the Lord’s power always either shows mercy or judges. Yet neither is his mercy found without judgment nor judgment without mercy; the two are joined together in mutual fellowship, and no act of his occurs that is not perceived to be full of every virtue.

For just as he says here, “mercy and judgment,” elsewhere he uses, for these two names, “justice and peace,” and again “mercy and truth,” or “justice and judgment are the preparation of your throne,” so that everywhere he may demonstrate God to be compassionate and just. There is no doubt that this kind of expression can be numbered among the characteristic forms of divine Scripture.

For even at the glorious time of his advent, he first performs mercy when he says, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV, 34), and so forth—but not without equity, because he restores what he promised to his faithful. Then judgment follows when he says to the wicked, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (ibid., 41); yet this too is not without compassion, since he is known to bring forth vengeance only after great patience.

You see, therefore, that these two things both agree with one another and shine forth when placed in their proper order. Let sinners who wickedly despair of their salvation hear the merciful Lord; let the proud understand the Judge, who do not consider that their evil ought to be punished. Thus everything has been sung here most concisely and most fully, because in these two expressions the whole work of the Lord and the building of the entire Church are shown to have been narrated.

He added: “To you, Lord, I will play the psalm.” One plays the psalm to the Lord who strives to please him through his good deeds. For this is the sweetest virtue of harmony: when the voice is known to accord with one’s actions. If these two things disagree with one another in discordant variety, they can in no way produce a measured song of psalmody; nor does what confounds itself through mutual contradiction reach the ears of the Lord.

### Verse 2. “And I will understand in the blameless way when you come to me.”

This verse depends upon what precedes. For if that disciplined psalmody is properly directed toward the Lord, see what it provides: that he may understand in the blameless way when the Lord deigns to come to him, the one whom he was awaiting with the greatest longing.

“I will understand” means, “I will believe with a pure affection of heart,” so that what he did not see with bodily eyes he might vividly behold through the effort of a desiring soul. And because such desire belonged already to one who was seeing spiritually, he says how the Lord intends to come: namely, “in the blameless way,” because Christ the Lord had no sins and walked through this world with blameless steps.

This is what he says: “And I will understand in the blameless way when you come to me.”

### Verse 3. “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.”

A hypothetical syllogism is again disclosed: If the righteous walks in innocence of heart in the midst of the house of the Lord, he does not set an evil thing before his eyes; but the righteous walks in innocence of heart in the midst of the house of the Lord; therefore he does not set an evil thing before his eyes.

Let us now examine what follows. By saying “I walked,” he shows that he did not pursue the life of this world with the greatest zeal, but passed through it as something transitory. Then, in a few words, he completes what innocence can accomplish: that he might merit to dwell in the midst of the house of God, both offering a good example to the rest and shining through an honorable way of life.

The power of innocence is understood from this: because of its most welcome simplicity, the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove; and because of blessed gentleness, the Son of God chose to call himself a Lamb, signifying that heavenly and true wisdom rests in peaceful and humble hearts.

### Verse 4. “I did not set an evil thing before my eyes; I hated those who commit transgressions. It did not cling to me.”

Because he had said above that he walked in the midst of the Church in innocence of heart, he now explains this in two ways through the figure called *aetiologia*, which in Latin is called “giving the reason.” First, up to the division placed below, he says that he had no fellowship with the vicious; then, to the end of the psalm, he asserts that he nevertheless placed his portion with the faithful and drove the devil’s craft from his heart. Thus this figure is known to encompass the greater part of the psalm.

Let us return now to the explanation of the words. Whoever believes that God is an avenger does not set an evil thing before the eyes of his heart, because it is necessary for one who is known to contemplate heavenly things to despise earthly ones. But since he was in the world, how could he not have an evil thing before his eyes, unless such things displeased him and he was not captivated by their vicious delight? Rightly, therefore, the holy congregation said that it had not placed before the eyes of its heart the wickednesses that it had excluded from the inner chambers of its mind. Indeed, we are rightly said not to see those things upon which we do not gaze with any delight.

He continues: “I hated those who commit transgressions.” He explained how evil could not reach the inner eyes of his heart: because he continually held human transgressions in hatred. Each person is said to regard those things which he is also judged capable of loving. For although such things come before our face, they are not in the sight of our mind if we flee them with detestable abhorrence.

He added: “It did not cling to me.” This clause is altogether suspended; it requires the beginning of the following verse, namely, “a perverse heart,” as we frequently find in the verses of the Psalter according to the Hebrews. For a perverse heart cannot cling except to those distorted by the iniquity of sins. Things with equal desires are glued together with one another, while whatever is contrary is separated in the opposite direction. Nor does what is perverse agree with what is upright, since it disagrees through the diversity of its morals.

Here, however, the status of conjecture arises, in which it is asked either with whom he associates or how he lives.

### Verse 5. “A perverse heart; those who turn aside from me, the wicked, I did not acknowledge.”

We said that “a perverse heart” must be joined to what precedes, so that the complete sentence may follow: “The wicked who turn aside from me I did not acknowledge.”

By “the wicked who turn aside from me,” he means heretics, who disagree with catholic preaching through perverse doctrines and, turning aside from straight paths, lead themselves and their hearers along the worst roads. “I did not acknowledge” means that, although they assert that they have been baptized and signed, divine love is not recognized in them, since they are shown to be blasphemous toward the Lord. For those are truly recognized as Christians who do not defile themselves with perverse faith.

### Verse 6. “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued.”

A heretic slanders a Catholic when he tears apart an absent person through some form of verbal abuse; and he does not dare to contend openly, knowing that he is defending irrational positions. He says that such people must be pursued, so that they may be stirred toward the study of truth—people who, deceived by various questions, are led astray.

For we call “neighbor” both one joined to us by kinship of flesh and one associated with us through some proximity of the law. For although certain of them appear to accept the Old and New Testaments with us, they nevertheless contemptuously reject the divine Scriptures through a detestable will, refusing to understand them correctly.

### Verse 7. “With one who has a proud eye and an insatiable heart, I did not eat together.”

He says that there are two kinds of faithless people. One, as he stated above, slanders his neighbors; but he has now shown how that person may be healed. The other, with a proud eye—that is, with an arrogant will—and an insatiable heart, does not withdraw from blasphemies. He says that this person must be avoided in such a way that we ought not even eat with him, lest the ears of Christians be polluted by abominable speech.

Yet even this is a more severe kind of remedy that has been granted, so that when the impious mind sees itself made detestable to holy men, it may correct its error by offering satisfaction. For if the Apostle says of Christians who live badly, “with such a one do not even take food” (I Cor. V, 11), how much more fitting is this regarding savage and obstinate heretics!

Alternatively, this may be understood spiritually of the body of the Lord the Savior: communion should not be shared with those by whom the Christian faith is torn apart.

And observe that both the things said above and those to be said in the second division all belong to the status of conjecture, in which the eloquence of orators exercises its powers most fully.

### Verse 8. “My eyes are upon the faithful of the earth, that they may sit with me; the one walking in the blameless way, he ministered to me.”

That holy congregation comes to the second part. Just as above it made unbelievers abhorrent to itself, so now it desires to have the fellowship of men who believe rightly. The eyes of the heart that it turned away from the worst, it now declares that it joins to the saints.

By “the faithful of the earth” he means the Christians who dwell throughout the whole world. “Let them sit with me” means, “Let them remain in the unity of faith.” Through this posture both rest is signified and steadfastness of mind is shown.

Some wish, on account of the excellence of the words, to apply this clearly to Christ the Lord; but no sudden alteration should be made where the person introduced alone is able to explain the passage.

He continues: “The one walking in the blameless way, he ministered to me.” This is truly the evident proof of faithful Christians: both to shine through their own life and to be radiant through the conduct of their ministers, just as it was said already in the seventeenth psalm: “With the holy man you will be holy, with the innocent man you will be innocent, with the chosen man you will be chosen, and with the perverse man you will be overthrown” (Ps. XVII, 28).

Although this does not appear to be excluded from laypeople, it is nevertheless shown to have been imposed especially upon priests, so that they may have as ministers those who do not oppose the divine rules.

### Verse 9. “He who practices pride will not dwell in the midst of my house.”

He still perseveres in the statements above. For he denies that he had any portion with the proud, lest anyone think that he approved those whose familiarity he appeared to join to himself.

By what he placed here, “in the midst of my house,” he wishes this to be understood: such a person had received no office, had been advanced to no honor, and had rejoiced in no authority, so that the one whose mind the head of the household regarded serenely might appear to be in the midst of the house.

From this we learn that we ought to exercise such judgments concerning those entrusted to us that we never favor the worst people; nor should those appear pleasing to us whom the perversity of their morals requires us to avoid.

### Verse 10. “The one who speaks wicked things did not prosper in the sight of my eyes.”

This verse too responds to what precedes. For he says that he did not please the person who was known either to pursue wicked slanders or to devote himself to perverse conversations. “Wicked” applies to everything that divine mercy abhors.

“Did not prosper” signifies “did not advance.” For we say that those people prosper who improve by progressing or become better through some prosperity; but this does not usually happen to those who devote themselves to walking along crooked paths.

### Verse 11. “In the mornings I was killing all the sinners of the earth.”

After saying that he had fled the company of the wicked, from which sins can generally arise, he now turns to the interior of his mind and fittingly explains how he expelled from its inner chambers that tyrannical plague, the destroyer of the human race—that is, the perverse suggestion of demons.

“In the mornings,” he says, meaning at the very beginnings, when diabolical suggestions begin to appear within us like uncertain twilight: then they must be driven out through prayer, then thrust away with detestable abhorrence, lest, gradually growing harmful, they seize us like an extremely dark day.

The “sinners of the earth” are demons, who lead all flesh to guilt through evil assaults. They are rightly called sinners because they make others sin. Therefore, when they are killed together with their works, human souls are undoubtedly saved.

This is clearly accomplished when, through the mercy of the divine dew, the compunction of tears is granted to us. For we cannot prevail upon ourselves to offer it whenever we wish; rather, it is bestowed when it is granted by his generosity.

### Verse 12. “That I may destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity.”

The Fathers said that the city of the Lord is the devout soul; therefore the devil is destroyed when he is removed from his purpose.

O cruel iniquity of tyrannical will! It was not enough that you caused human beings to die; you still press on fiercely so that, even after they have been restored, they may not be able to live. But you, Lord, who see the most shameless enemy, grant powerful defense, lest he reach his desire—the one who hastens, with insatiable cunning, to make you hostile to us.

We beseech you with your own words and your own admonitions: “Judge, Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me. Take hold of weapons and shield, and rise to my help.”

## Conclusion of the psalm

[Col. 0704C]

We have learned what sort of most holy person this was, who sang of the Lord’s mercy and judgment with a pure mind in the midst of the divine house; how he absolutely avoided the wicked, while he was joined to the good in most welcome fellowship; and how he cast away the desires of his heart through a most salutary deliberation. Thus he appears rightly to have obtained this number, which, through the bending of the fingers of the right hand, depicts the form of a desirable crown.

This is the gift of martyrs; this is the offering of virgins; and whatever is outstanding in the Church is shown to reach its reward through such fruit, as the Apostle says: “As for the rest, the crown of righteousness has been laid up for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (II Tim. IV, 8).

The whole orb of the earth is said to be enclosed by this figure. We read, on the authority of innumerable writers, that heaven is vaulted. We see the stars shining with spherical roundness; the sun itself radiating with the beauty of a circle; and it is certain that the moon too assumes this form when it is known to be full.

Therefore, let us consider the merit of the person represented here and the elegance with which he is approved, so that he may seem to have been placed in a calculation that contains both the dignity of immense rewards and the image of the heavenly creatures. For it is shameful to say that someone subject to sins has advanced through the fruitfulness of the number one hundred, and that what we have said was applied to the merits of the saints was granted to me, an unworthy person.

But may divine power grant that, at his judgment, he make us rejoice through the remission of sins beyond all doubt, and that he not condemn us according to our merits—the one who alone has power to free those who confess.

# PART THREE

[Col. 0705]

## 336 TITLE OF PSALM CI

“Prayer of the poor man when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.”

[Col. 0705A]

Although some have thought that the present psalm should be applied to the Lord the Savior, it nevertheless seems more appropriate in this account to introduce the person of an afflicted and groaning poor man, as the title itself contains, because there are many things that cannot suitably apply to that spotless and holy incarnation.

First, the Lord Christ is nowhere read to have been anxious. For one is anxious who, placed in grave danger, does not know which course he ought to choose. Then there is what the text of the psalm says: “I forgot to eat my bread,” and “because I ate ashes like bread and mingled my drink with weeping”; “because of the face of your anger and indignation, for you lifted me up and dashed me down.” There are other statements as well that are defended only with the greatest difficulty if we agree to apply them to the Lord himself.

But since it was fitting for one gravely wounded and full of harsh calamities to pour forth continual prayer, the person of an anxious poor man has been appropriately introduced—a person whose voice neither shame could restrain nor the necessity of want could suppress. For when he says “before the Lord,” he wishes such a prayer to be understood as pours forth from the purses of the soul before royal feet, like a beautiful abundance of gold.

You will scarcely find—as someone has said—that, when anyone is praying, some empty obstacle or foreign thought does not intrude and divert or break the intention by which the mind is directed toward God. Therefore, it is a great and salutary struggle to remain constantly attentive to the prayer that has been begun and, with God’s help, to resist vigorously the enemy’s suggestions, so that the mind may always strive toward God with steadfast intention; thus it may rightly say what the Apostle said: “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the race, I have kept the faith” (II Tim. IV, 7).

Such are the poor of Christ, who are shown to intercede not only for their own evils but also for the calamities of the whole world. They are needy in this age, but rich before God; empty of vices, but full of virtues; despised by human beings, but acceptable to Christ [ms. A: “to God”].

For this man, who first torments himself with lamentable affliction, shines afterward with such glory of prophecy that it can clearly be recognized with what reward he will be crowned there, since already here he is refreshed by such great hope [mss. A, F, B: “what gift he will be crowned with there, since already here he is refreshed by such great hope”].

And note that, although names are placed in the titles everywhere, here the poor man is introduced to speak without a name, so that, when it is given to one person, all the poor of Christ may recognize that it has been assigned to them. It should also be firmly kept in mind that this psalm is the fourth among those marked “Prayer,” although it appears to be the fifth among the penitential psalms.

It must plainly be understood that there are two kinds of prayer. One occurs when the Lord Christ prays to the Father—not for his own sins, which he certainly did not have, but asking that the human nature he deigned to assume be delivered from the adversities of this age—as is shown in the sixteenth psalm and clearly accomplished in the eighty-fifth.

The other occurs when, in Psalm LXXXIX, the revered person of Moses is introduced in a priestly type; he prays for both his own sins and those common to all. Likewise, in the present psalm the person of a poor man is introduced, who, anxious under the humility of repentance, cries out to the Lord.

Therefore, all repentance is prayer, but not all prayer is repentance, since even one prayed who had committed nothing that could be attributed to guilt. Thus these psalms, which are marked beforehand by the title “Prayer,” are shown to be explained according to their particular characteristics.

## Division of the psalm

[Col. 0706B]

This poor man, needy of worldly riches but abundantly wealthy in heavenly virtues, repeatedly asks the Lord at the beginning of the psalm that his cry may merit to reach him, because, crushed by continual affliction, he says that his bones have been crushed as in a frying pan.

There follows a very mournful and grievous account, which reveals his necessities and gives a credible statement of their causes. And lest, after so many harsh calamities, he appear ungrateful for his chastisement, in the third part he pursues the Lord’s praises with an exceedingly sweet devotion. He says that, at the Lord’s coming, the Church is to be built; and although all things are to be changed, he himself will nevertheless remain forever.

A highly joyful and deeply desired conclusion is also added: the seed of the saints is to be directed to the place where the Lord dwells in everlasting glory. Thus that regular law of penitents is known to have been fulfilled most completely: it began with tears and ended in joy.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1. “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.”

Seeing human errors increasing without cease before the Lord’s advent, the prophet appropriately assumed the person of a poor man who would lament the calamities of the world with the humility of repentance, so that the merciful one might quickly help him whom so many evils pressed down under a united burden.

For he says: “Lord, hear my prayer”—namely, the prayer that the devout advocate poured forth for the liberation of the whole world. It is the custom of the saints to grieve over the calamities of others as over their own, as the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (II Cor. XI, 29).

He continues: “And let my cry come to you.” This poor man, learned in divine law, knew that a kind of cloud is frequently placed before the prayers of sinners. Jeremiah speaks of it: “You have placed a cloud, so that our prayer may not pass through” (Lam. III, 44). The prophet Habakkuk says the same: “How long, Lord, shall I cry, and you will not hear? I shall cry out to you while suffering wrong, and you will not attend” (Hab. I, 2).

Therefore, mindful and anxious about these matters, he hastened for his cry to reach the Lord, lest, with sins obstructing him, he be delayed in receiving a remedy from the Lord, since he was shown to lie under many calamities.

First he placed “prayer”; now he added “cry,” so that you might recognize that his efforts at supplication had increased, and perceive that his prayer had burst forth into a very great cry.

Let the most devoted Christian understand that this manner of holy prayer must be observed: he should think about the very thing for which he is praying, direct his mind toward the one whom he entreats, exclude all superfluous thoughts, and admit nothing foreign, lest—as someone says—he seem to release unwary boars into the purest springs.

Hence that rose-colored hymn of the sixth hour by Saint Ambrose, composed according to the Apostle (I Cor. XIV, 15), also gave forth its fragrance. He says:

> “I will pray to the Lord with my mind; I will pray also with the spirit, so that the voice alone may not sing to God while our sense, led elsewhere, wanders astray, distracted by empty circumstances.”

[Note: This hymn of Ambrose is missing.]

Then the prayer of those who sing is acceptable to God, if a pure mind performs the same thing that the voice of the hymn expresses.

### Verse 2. “Do not turn your face away from me on whatever day I am afflicted.”

This most blessed poor man recalled that the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah, had rejected the stubborn sinners’ offerings, when he says: “I do not want the blood of calves and lambs and goats. When you come before my sight, who sought these things from your hands?” (Isa. I, 11–12).

Fearing and reconsidering such things, he asks that the sacrifice he was offering—that is, his repentance—not be despised in the way mentioned above concerning the sacrifices of the worst people. Thus Psalm L also says: “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L, 19).

He therefore begs not to be made alien from the Lord’s presence. This is the rule of a right petition: that, while he looks upon us, he may look away from our sins. For he absolves us in compassion if he does not look upon them, as was already said in Psalm L: “Turn your face away from my sins” (ibid., 11).

Therefore, it is not inappropriate to borrow examples from the penitential psalm of the penitent, since the meaning is shown to be similar and the cause comparable.

He added: “On whatever day I am afflicted.” “On whatever day” does not signify uninterrupted continuity, but declares that there were intervals of time when he was pressed by the greatest wounds of sins, when the detestable enemy weighed upon him, so that the most compassionate Liberator might come to his aid as though he were placed beneath a savage beast.

[Col. 0707D] **Verse 3.** “Incline your ear to me; on whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly.” There are indeed many expressions, but one petition: that the Lord may deign to hear the prayer of the poor man. This figure is called in Greek *epimone*, in Latin “repetition,” whenever the same thing is stated repeatedly in different words. This is shown to have been done from the beginning through these three verses.

“Incline your ear”—that is, “lend,” he says, “your hearing.” Hence *ear* itself is named from hearing, because there were no merits by which he could have raised himself to Him. The Lord’s ear, however, is used for His clemency, by which He mercifully hears the prayers of supplicants. For although He hears all and sees all, He is said to hear only those whom He deigns to favor.

It follows: “On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly” [Col. 0708A]. To the extent that this penitent had prostrated himself with a humble spirit, to that extent he grew in his very supplication. For whereas he had first said, “Incline your ear to me,” he now asks more confidently that he may deserve to be heard more quickly. Anyone who asks for speed is assured of obtaining his request.

**Verse 4.** “For my days have vanished like smoke, and my bones have been scorched as in a frying-pan.” He added the reason for his supplication, so that the immense desire for prayer might be recognized as having arisen from many miseries, and so that he might more easily obtain the goodwill of the merciful Judge by alleging the necessity of great calamities.

We see smoke emerging from a flame, yet dispersing very thinly into the liquid air; its substance does not remain, although it appears to have been generated from a bodily burning [Col. 0708B]. Thus deservedly are the days of sinners compared with smoky globes, which deceived men have lost amid entangled and foul actions. This especially pertains to the world’s pride, which, the more it is exalted, the more greatly it vanishes.

For this poor man was intensely devoted to the saving humility of Christ [mss. A, F: “had clung to”], who condemned the devil’s arrogance and pride.

It follows: “And my bones have been scorched as in a frying-pan.” Just as, according to the favorable opinion concerning the virtuous, their bones—that is, the strength of their spirit—grow fat when their conscience rejoices in a happy recollection, as Solomon says, “A good reputation fattens the bones” (Prov. 15:30), so, through the contrary recollection of sins, virtue contracts as though it had been fried, while he dreadfully fears the reproaches of men and the judgments of his own conscience [Col. 0708C].

Or the sinner is scorched here because he fears future fires and burnings; for one who dreads being burned is already scorched by the terror of that very burning.

It is commonly asked what it means that penitents say they suffer such things as human nature cannot endure. First, the greatness of the offense can properly be understood through the exaggeration employed, since such immense satisfaction appears to be offered for it. In addition, those who recognize that they owe so much for past sins are not drawn toward new vices.

**Verse 5.** “I have been struck down like grass, and my heart has withered, because I forgot to eat my bread.” Having secured the Judge’s goodwill through very humble actions, he came to the tearful narration of his miseries, so that he might quickly obtain a remedy if he did not conceal his suffering from the merciful physician [Col. 0708D].

The human race is rightly compared with transient grass, which possesses the temporary joy of greenness and easily feels injury when struck down. Thus, as long as we remain in the law and commandments of the Lord, we are invigorated like green grass; but as soon as we have been cut down from His precepts by the devil’s sickle, we immediately wither, and our heart is dried up by the barrenness of sin. The soul cannot possess the nourishment of His benefit when it is shown to have been separated from Him by its sins. Those who do not depart from the Lord’s commands, however, are always cheerful and always pleasant.

It follows: “Because I forgot to eat my bread.” He gives the reason why his stricken heart had withered [Col. 0709A]: because he had forgotten to eat his bread, by which he had known that he could be spiritually satisfied. Of this bread the Lord says, “I am the bread of life, which came down from heaven” (John 6:51). For how could he complain about the loss of bodily bread, when he rejoiced to be afflicted by fasts? Here the nature of sinners is expressed: while sin is desired, contemplation of the Lord is absent.

**Verse 6.** “At the sound of my groaning my bones have clung to my flesh.” We must examine what is intended by “at the sound of my groaning.” There is a sound of groaning in one who loses a son, whose property is seized, or from whom the pleasant delight of this world is taken away. But this is not the groaning of the blessed. They groan over such things as please the world, because they desire what is destined to perish and do not hasten toward the Lord’s promises [Col. 0709B].

This most holy man was afflicted by that kind of groaning which lovers of the world would rather mock. For this reason he added “my,” to show that he was excluded from worldly desires.

It follows: “My bones have clung to my flesh.” If you understand this literally, it cannot properly apply to those who are exceedingly afflicted, since this also happens to the fat and luxurious, so that their flesh is known to cling to their bones.
