Here, however, we may reasonably take “flesh” to mean skin, since skin too is flesh, so that the extreme emaciation may truly be displayed when the skin is said to have clung to the bones. Thus the prophet Jeremiah also says: “Their skin was fastened to their bones; they dried up and became like wood” (Lam. 4:8) [Col. 0709C].

But to ascend more fully to the spiritual understanding, he calls his bones the firmness of faith by which we stand and have strength. He rightly says that this firmness clung to flesh on account of the weakness of the brethren, who were not yet established and remained in confidence in the Lord Christ. He clung to these people when he was continually anxious and concerned for them, lest they be made strangers to the Lord’s kingdom.

**Verse 7.** “I have become like a pelican of solitude” [ed.: “in solitude”]; “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” Through these names of birds, as I think, different kinds of penitents are indicated to us.

The pelican is an Egyptian bird, similar to storks in bodily size. It is always afflicted by natural emaciation because, as naturalists maintain, with its intestine stretched through its viscera, it passes along whatever food it receives without any digestion [Col. 0709D]. Hence it is not at all stuffed with its own fat, since it is restored by only the smallest amount of nourishment. It does not fly in flocks like other birds, but consoles itself through solitary enjoyment.

One kind is said to inhabit marshes; another, as has been said, dwells in deserted and secluded places. Through this species of bird, therefore, hermits are beautifully signified: having abandoned human society, they torture themselves in secluded affliction through fear of the Lord.

It follows: “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” Another kind of penitent is introduced [ed.: “of penitents”]. *Nycticorax*, a Greek word, means “night-raven.” Some have said that it is an owl; others, a night-owl. Still others say that it is more similar to a raven in size and color and testify that it can be found especially in the regions of Asia [Col. 0710A].

Just as the brightness of day conceals it, so the arrival of night brings it forth. Contrary to the habits of birds, it then begins to keep watch and seek food, when all living creatures settle into sleep. Thus this penitent also seeks food for his soul during the night with watchful care: sometimes devoting himself to psalmody, sometimes giving alms, sometimes secretly visiting prisons. He wishes to have God alone as his witness, for the darkness of night does not remove anything from His sight.

Note also that just as the pelican signifies the hermit and solitary, so the night-raven indicates one who keeps himself within his dwelling and remains removed from public view.

**Verse 8.** “I kept vigil and became like a solitary sparrow on a building.” He comes to a third kind, which is indicated by the likeness of a sparrow, so that he who mourned the crimes of the world might seem to pass through every form of satisfaction [Col. 0710B].

The sparrow is a small bird, but watchful with extraordinary cleverness. It is neither easily caught in snares nor deceived by an appetite for food through the gluttony of its belly. Because of its weakness, lest it itself be caught by a predator or its young be devoured by serpentine ambushes, it alone among birds, armed with caution, hastens to the high roofs of houses, so that it may be kept apart from suspected dangers, though it is known to be exposed to many perils.

He is rightly compared with this bird who, fearing the devil’s treacherous snares [mss. A, F: “ambushes”], betakes himself especially to the enclosure of the Church and, keeping watch upon its height, remains there in the greatest safety.

He said “solitary” on account of charity, which makes one out of many. “On a building” refers to the height of faith and the strength of the mind.

It must also be considered how this supplicant began with larger birds, the pelican and the night-raven, and reached the very small size of the sparrow. For as penitence descends by stages, it is great in the first place, moderate in the second, and in the third, through habit itself, entirely bearable.

These birds are compared with human beings by the figure of *parabole*, that is, comparison. They differ in kind but are similar in the quality of their habits. This argument of comparison is called “from the greater to the lesser,” for a human being is much greater than a sparrow.

**Verse 9.** “All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.” It is clearly the devil’s malice that, when it cannot crush God’s servants through tyrannical presumption [Col. 0710D], it deceives them instead through artful illusion, so that those who do not yield to open terrors may be bent by mocking reproach.

This figure is called *ironia*, that is, mockery, which displays something other than what it attempts. Accordingly, sinners gravely mocked this man as he afflicted himself and seemed to labor in vain. And to increase the magnitude of his disgrace, he says that they swore while expressing their detestation.

For it is customary for the perverse to say: “May I not live such a life as this man endures—he who now seems to resemble corpses rather than living people.” They had previously praised him when he enjoyed secular life; afterward they detested him with oaths, when they judged him similar to the dead.

**Verse 10.** “For I was eating ashes like bread [Col. 0711A], and I was mingling my drink with weeping.” He gives the reason why he was cursed by enemies or acquaintances upon seeing his face, just as Job is clearly known to have suffered, whose life appeared filthy with the most grievous squalor to his neighbors and friends.

This verse must be treated with particular care, lest we suppose that the ashes of wood are food for penitents, contrary to human custom. We know ashes to be the remains of burned coals, and we rightly compare them with sins, so that even the smallest remnants of offenses may be consumed by the pain of afflictions. For however little of sin remains, it does not lead to life. Hence in the fiftieth psalm the prophet cries: “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Ps. 50:4).

Thus deservedly the most holy penitent hastened to consume even the ashes of sins [Col. 0711B], lest anything remain that would prevent him from deserving the kingdoms of heaven.

It follows: “And I was mingling my drink with weeping.” Although this may sometimes seem able to happen literally, I nevertheless believe that this too must be understood spiritually. The drink of souls is that satisfaction of which the seventy-fourth psalm says: “A cup is in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine mingled, and He poured from this into that” (Ps. 74:9). This, then, is the drink that we rightly temper with tears; this is the cup that our tears make sweeter. For that heavenly drink enters the innermost chambers of the soul when they are watered by devout weeping.

This was the cup that seemed unworthy to mockers; this was the food judged dreadful by the luxurious. But the good Christian ought rather to love that by which he may reach the banquets of the heavenly King.

Observe that the entire verse is spoken through the figure of *tapinosis*, which is recognized as having the power to lower a great matter, through an attitude of humility, to the most insignificant smallness. This figure is very frequent in the holy Scriptures, as the Apostle says: “God chose the weak things of this world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27).

**Verse 11.** “Because of the face of your anger and indignation, for while you exalted me, you struck me down” [mss. A, B: “cast me down”]. This clause is connected with what precedes, so that the great magnitude of the penitence might arise from the Lord’s anger and indignation.

He says: “Because of the face of your anger and indignation.” Anger and indignation do not possess a bodily face, but they always appear under an imagined form to those who fear. Thus the very force of the one who fears is powerfully expressed, because he knew that the Lord threatened sinners, as Jeremiah says: “The lion from the forest devoured them, and the wolf toward evening ravaged them” (Jer. 5:6). The Apostle Peter also warns: “Keep watch,” he says, “and pray, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

Thus he rightly feared the face of the angry Lord, since he knew that through His prophets He had foretold such things to sinners. Anger pertains to vengeance; indignation, to a moderate movement of the mind. We become indignant even with our children, but we grow angry with those who deserve punishment through a greater impulse.

He added: “For while you exalted me, you struck me down.” Although the person of one poor man seems to have been introduced, nevertheless, as we have often said, the most prudent enumerator of the human race’s good and evil implicitly indicates all humanity [Col. 0712A].

The Lord frequently exalts sinners through His benefits: He grants them wealth, gives them life, bestows worldly glory, and causes them to move amid universal renown. But when the swollen hearts of mortals have risen into pride, the excellent governor withdraws what He had granted, so that they may carefully recognize that the goods suddenly taken away had not been their own.

There is no doubt that this striking down is a fortunate one, as it is said elsewhere: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes” (Ps. 118:71). From this comes compunction; from this the medicine of souls is supplied. This penitent too, not ungrateful but rather corrected, recounts it [Col. 0712B].

**Verse 12.** “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.” Most beautifully did the man after Adam’s transgression say that his days had declined like a shadow, because the true Sun, the Lord Christ, had left them. Without Him all life is shadowy, and, as though it possessed no substance, our days perish in useless conduct.

His days therefore declined because he himself declined from the Lord. The more anyone is separated from that fullness, the more he is diminished.

It follows: “And I have withered like grass.” It was consequent that, since his days had declined, he should wither like grass. For when the life-giving benefit that invigorates us and makes us green and flourishing has been withdrawn, we are brought wholly into the dryness of sin, unless we sprout again into new grace through the dew of divine mercy [Col. 0712C].

The sorrowful enumeration of immense afflictions is complete. Now let us see what the third section appears to indicate to us.

**Verse 13.** “But you, Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from age to age.” After worthy satisfaction and the fitting lamentation of general evils, that penitent, as though now lifting his head and breathing with some freedom, enters the third section, raised up and refreshed. To the extent that he had humbled himself while condemning himself, he now confidently rejoices in the Lord’s praises.

Accordingly, he very properly begins his praise with the Lord’s coming, through which he knew that the world would be saved.

It follows: “And your memorial from age to age” [Col. 0712D]. The memorial is the saving promise concerning the Lord’s future incarnation, which no ages and no forgetfulness can alter. Stored in the bosom of memory, it remains immovable forever through endless ages.

**Verse 14.** “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, because the time has come to have mercy on her.” This most holy poor man teaches us how much the prayer of a simple and faithful man can accomplish: the man who previously did not consider himself worthy even of human eyes or of enjoying the freedom of daylight, who ate ashes like bread and mingled his drink with weeping.

Now, if one may say so, he almost compels the Lord Himself to fulfill His promises, so that He may look upon the laboring world through the mercy of His coming.

He is said to “arise,” as though speaking of one who was sleeping, because He had delayed assisting for so long [Col. 0713A]. And so that the Lord might be understood to do everything according to the order of His will, he says, “The time has come to have mercy on her”—not because time admonishes Him, but because He Himself arranges times with the most fitting deliberation.

This was the time of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4:4). And elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

This argument is called “from time”; among orators it is usually regarded as exceedingly effective. For what could hinder us when a suitable time invites us?

Zion is a mountain situated at Jerusalem, through which, as has often been said, the Church is signified. He truly had mercy on it when He gathered it from the Gentiles and established it through a most sacred institution [Col. 0713B].

**Verse 15.** “For your servants have been pleased with its stones, and they will have mercy on its earth.” This verse must be treated subtly, so that it may be understood whom he intends allegorically by the servants, the stones, and the dust.

By the Lord’s servants he means the apostles and prophets, who fulfilled His service with devoted minds. They were pleased with these stones—that is, with Christians, who flourished through divine firmness—when they saw their preaching bearing fruit in them.

They also had mercy on the earth, that is, on sinners who were to be gathered into Zion from the Gentiles. They resembled earth because they minded carnal things.

Observe how precisely the words are fitted to the things. He says that the stones were pleasing because, by the Lord’s favor, they were secure in their solidity [Col. 0713C]. He added, “They will have mercy on the earth,” because those who were soiled with earthly filth were to be cleansed through Christ’s mercy.

**Verse 16.** “And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.” These words are directed against the wicked superstitions of this world. The true Lord was not feared when the devoted world served idols; but after His saving coming shone forth, the nations were converted through fear. Of them he said above, “They will have mercy on its earth.”

The kings of the earth also believed in His glory—that is, those who, restraining their bodies by divine regulations, were able, by the Lord’s favor, to become rulers of themselves. These are the ones of whom he said above, “For your servants have been pleased with its stones” [Col. 0713D]. For those who stand firm in the faith they have assumed now truly recognize the Lord’s glory.

**Verse 17.** “For the Lord has built Zion, and He will be seen in His majesty.” This verse depends on what precedes: all the nations will fear the Lord and the kings will dread His glory because Zion has been built—that is, the mother Church has been fashioned from living stones. In it the worship of the Lord will advance without interruption until the end of the world.

This Lord who built Zion will likewise be seen in His majesty in the truth of the body He assumed, when He separates the goats from the lambs, sending the wicked into Gehenna and granting everlasting blessedness to the just.

[Col. 0714A] **Verse 18.** “He has looked upon the prayer of the poor and has not despised their petitions.” He calls the faithful of Christ “the poor,” because, as has often been said, they are poor in the world but rich in Him alone.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, like the speaker here, they poured out their prayer to the Lord, asking Him now to command His coming, lest He delay the desires of the saints any longer. He says that the prayer of the poor has been regarded because He sees all incorporeal things, and nothing is hidden from His eyes. For this is what His regarding means: not to despise.

**Verse 19.** “Let these things be written for a later generation, and the people who will be created will praise the Lord.” That poor man, crushed by the recollection of sins and worn out by vigils and anxiety, now adorned as though with prophetic honor, commands that the future age learn through the testimony of Scripture what he knew he had proclaimed in the present [Col. 0714B]. Thus it would not be uncertain to those who saw it, since they would recognize that it had been foretold so many ages before.

The “later generation” signifies the Christian people, who are second in relation to that earlier one. For see what follows: “And the people who will be created will praise the Lord.” He said “will be created” in the future, that is, “will be regenerated through the grace of baptism.”

Without doubt, this people will praise the Lord, for whose salvation He came, for whom He endured being killed, and in whose hope He rose from the dead on the third day. This people will praise the Lord with a new song, as it is said in another psalm: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. 97:1).

**Verse 20.** “For He looked forth from His holy height.” “The Lord looked forth from heaven upon the earth.” This is what he said above was to be written. To make you recognize the power of the truth itself—what was to be performed in future ages—he has already said that it was accomplished. For “He looked forth” signifies past time.

But let us ask: From where did He look forth? “From His holy height,” that is, from heaven. He looked forth upon us when He assumed the frailty of our humanity, because through Him we have been made free, made immortal, and placed in the greatest hope, if we deserve to turn toward Him with a humble mind.

And so that the meaning itself might appear more clearly to us, it follows: “The Lord looked forth from heaven upon the earth.” For it is written: “The Lord is in heaven; His throne” (Ps. 10:5). From there, then, He looked upon the earth—that is, upon the frailty of our body, which was held subject to the vices of the world.

Observe that he used “looked forth” in both places, so that through the very similarity of the words he might show that there is one meaning [Col. 0714D].

**Verse 21.** “To hear the groaning of the imprisoned” [mss. A, B: “of those in fetters”], “to release the sons of the slain.” He gives the reason why the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth: namely, “to hear the groaning of the imprisoned.”

Here “imprisoned” does not signify those bound by human chains, but holy men who, bound by legal restraints, are shown to have abandoned the errors of harmful freedom. Concerning them Solomon says: “Listen, my son, and receive my judgment; do not reject my counsel; put your foot into his fetters, and place your neck in his collar” (Ecclus. 6:24–26). A little later it follows: “His fetters will be for you a protection of strength, and his collar a robe of glory” (ibid., 30), and so forth [Col. 0715A].

These, then, are the imprisoned, whose groaning and cries to Him the Lord deigned to hear, so that He might free the world, entangled in its own sins, through the benefit of His mercy. He also freed the sons of the slain—those who had been killed through the devil’s deceit—from their ancestral errors by divine strength. This is shown to occur daily in the Church through the solemn gifts of grace.

**Verse 22.** “So that the name of the Lord may be proclaimed in Zion, and His praise in Jerusalem.” He described with marvelous brevity what was to come. The name of the Lord Christ was proclaimed in Zion when the apostles were first shown there to have spoken of God’s mighty works in various languages.

From there it came about that, as from a purest fountain, the Lord’s devout commandments flowed through the universal Church from local Jerusalem [Col. 0715B]. The groaning of the imprisoned was therefore heard so that the saving Lord might come and establish His Church in the most holy religion.

**Verse 23.** “When peoples and kingdoms” [mss. A, B: “kings”] “are gathered together, to serve the Lord.” He continues to enumerate the reasons why the groaning of the imprisoned was heard: namely, so that the people, gathering together as one, might resound with the Lord’s praises.

By saying “as one,” he displays the power of catholic unity. Although this people is gathered from different parts of the world, they come together as one because they are held together by one rule of faith.

Thus the prophet Ezekiel testifies: “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will take the whole house of Israel from among the nations into which they have entered; I will gather them from all those around them, and I will bring them into their own land, and I will make them one nation” (Ezek. 37:21–22).

And the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in us all” (Eph. 4:5–6).

Accordingly, those truly come together as one who hasten with devoted minds to believe in the undivided Trinity, that is, in the one God.

There follows a fortunate transformation: the kingdoms of earth and heaven serve the Lord, and they are then freer, when they have been bound to their author in faithful service.

**Verse 24.** “And He answered him in the way of His strength.” How well these two words express what Christian religion is: the way of strength, in which we walk amid pains and travel through tribulations, but endure all these things in Christ’s name with the greatest hope [Col. 0715D].

To this strength, then, which the Lord Christ proclaimed, the congregation of the saints responds in devotion. For when He calls to the good life, the one who is obedient to His commands is recognized as answering Him.

Accordingly, one responds to Him not with the tongue but with life; not with the voice but with faith; not with shouting but with the heart. All this clearly pertains to the catholic Church.

**Verse 25.** “Declare to me the fewness of my days.” Amid the praises of the Lord, traversed in manifold variety, this poor man now desires to know the end of the world, so that he may quickly deserve to approach the blessedness the Lord promised to the saints.

He does not desire to know the end out of love for the light of this life, but so that, persevering in these very confessions, he might swiftly reach that rest of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0716A]. He therefore said “the fewness of my days,” because it was certain that they would eventually end. Compared with eternity, even the age of the whole world appears exceedingly brief; for whatever is destined to end ought not to be called long.

**Verse 26.** “Do not recall me in the middle of my days; your years are from age to age.” The intention of his earlier petition is made clear: he was not supplicating from a desire for life who asked not to be recalled to the middle of his days—that is, to the age already passed.

A person is recalled to the middle of his days when he returns to his former sins. This signifies youth, in which a slippery will is usually pursued and the crimes of the age’s fervor are loved all the more [Col. 0716B].

But the one who prays this understands that he has already been freed through a great benefit and does not wish to lose what he recognizes he has acquired by divine gift.

It follows: “Your years are from age to age.” He had rightly asked not to be recalled to the middle of his days, since he was hastening with great desire to reach the Lord’s eternity. There the saints will rejoice with the Lord in perpetual delight, when, as the Apostle says, “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

The Lord’s “years” are said tropologically, because years properly belong to those for whom times also change. But he explains the Lord’s eternity below in three verses, which we therefore present together, so that the Lord’s eternity and His work upon the world may be declared under one exposition.

**Verse 27.** “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands.”

**Verse 28.** “They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment.”

**Verse 29.** “And like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail.”

When he says, “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord,” he shows what sound minds cannot deny: that the Creator is known to have existed before His creatures, without any beginning.

Observe that here he destroyed, with marvelous brevity, the opinions of philosophers. The first is that the world was created by no one; the second, that it will remain without end. When it is said, “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands,” that first impious persuasion is refuted. When it is declared, “They will perish,” he shows that they have an end, so that no one may trust in the stars through pagan error, when he realizes that they too are subject to change [Col. 0716D].

But I think we must examine more carefully why, although all things were made through the Word, he said that the heavens were founded as the works of His hands. Here we must understand “hand” as the power of command. Elsewhere he says: “For He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5). Thus Scripture is not perceived to contradict itself when words are given the most suitable interpretation according to their contexts.

He added, “But you remain,” so that just as he showed the Lord’s eternity when He created all things, so he might say that, after the heavens have been changed, He Himself remains in the glory of His majesty.

When he says “all things,” as I think, he does not designate the angels or spiritual creatures, which will remain in their own dignity, but those things that are shown to be subject to change. This figure is called *synecdoche*, that is, “the part from the whole,” and is very frequent in the divine Scriptures.

As for “They will grow old like a garment,” this seems to apply to the frailty of the flesh, which is likewise compared in the Gospel, where it says: “Is not the soul more than food, and the body more than clothing?” (Matt. 6:25). That grows old which, in the manner of clothing, is consumed by death.

He added: “And like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed.” Perhaps we should understand the heavens as the covering, since they cover the earth like a veil and, like other things, are changed.

And to show that the Lord’s works would now remain under eternity, he says, “You will change them, and they will be changed,” because they will never again return to corruption. For if they were afterward subject to corruption, they would not be said to have been changed, as the prophet Daniel testifies: “For wisdom and strength and understanding are His, and He changes times and ages” (Dan. 2:20–21).

He added: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” This is set against what was said above: while those things are changeable, the Lord remains forever unchangeable. “He Himself is” designates His omnipotence, because He truly is when He always performs works worthy of Himself.

“Are” briefly declares His nature: He alone knows how to exist through Himself, needing no other helper in order to be. Thus in these three verses the change of creatures and the Lord’s eternity have been described with marvelous brevity.

[Col. 0717C] **Verse 30.** “The sons of your servants will dwell there, and their offspring will be established from age to age.” Having completed his prayer with the greatest prudence and usefulness, that most holy poor man, rejoicing in the remission of his sins and in the hope of the future resurrection, comes to the end of the psalm. Summing everything up briefly, he rejoices that he will dwell with the Lord’s saints, where there is the glorious hope of the faithful and the eternal rest of the just.

By “the sons of your servants” he means the disciples of the prophets and apostles, whom they begot through holy preaching in the womb of faith. The Apostle says to them: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor” (Gal. 4:19). Writing to Timothy, he likewise began his Epistle: “To Timothy, my dearest son” (2 Tim. 1:2), whom he had certainly begotten in faith, not in the body.

“They will dwell there” signifies the place of blessedness that the Lord possesses, concerning which He says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24)—namely, in that perpetual kingdom where joy is eternal and security never comes to an end [Col. 0717D].

But understand that the sons of the servants are there with the Lord in such a way that you should not doubt that the servants themselves—that is, His apostles and preachers—are there as well. For if a place of blessedness is given to the disciples, is it perhaps to be denied to their teachers?

It is a custom of Scripture sometimes to mention lesser things so that greater things may also be understood as included there, as it is said in another psalm: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (Ps. 49:18). There lesser offenses are mentioned so that greater crimes may also be understood together with them.

It follows: “And their offspring will be established from age to age” [Col. 0718A]. Their offspring signifies the works of the faithful, which are sown in this world so that their praiseworthy fruit may appear in that eternity.

Observe why the word “established” has been placed: because whatever is received there is placed in eternal straightness, where nothing crooked and nothing distorted can exist. Rather, His saints will rejoice with the Lord Savior in a right and steadfast will.

**Conclusion of the psalm.**
How happily this anxious man lamented, until by tormenting himself he reached joys! Earlier he was like a pelican; in what follows he is to be compared with the phoenix. Earlier he was a night-raven, afterward an eagle; at first a sparrow, then he became a splendid dove. Such transformations [Col. 0718B] belong to those who submit themselves to the Lord with a pure mind. Let kingdoms be spoken of: they are insignificant. Let purple robes be praised: they have often become soiled for those who use them frequently. Behold, the world is vanquished in rags; the devil is overcome by weeping; and he against whom no armies are sufficient to resist is brought low by the prayer of one poor man. These are the wise, these the eloquent, these truly are to be called glorious orators: victors, they receive such a possession that they can in no way be excluded from it by the hostility of their enemies. Finally, they receive such an inheritance as they may always possess without labor and never abandon through death. O blessed condition of the penitents, which makes the guilty righteous, the sorrowful eternally joyful, and mortals absolutely everlasting! Here they endure the company of the wicked for a time; there they will receive the fellowship of angels in eternal happiness. [Col. 0718C] Therefore, let us recognize this man as the fifth of the penitents: he defended himself by not defending himself, washed himself clean by not washing himself, and purified himself by not purifying himself. If we should merit to come to his poverty, we shall unquestionably surpass all the kingdoms of the world.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 102

*A psalm of David.*

After the exceedingly humble prayers of that blessed poor man and the groans of such great repentance have been set forth, this entire psalm is filled with praise of the Lord [mss. A, B, F: “with laudation”], so that, by a pious arrangement, the joys of proclamation might follow the preceding tears. And therefore, as we have often said, it is ascribed to David, so that we should not refer anything in it to that earthly king, since [Col. 0718D] heavenly praise is explained with manifest meaning. It is clear and similar to the brightness of its title, so that we may understand the contents of the psalm’s words without difficulty.

## Division of the psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. In the first section he addresses words to his own soul, so that it may bless the Lord and in no way forget his benefits. In the second section he says what the Lord granted to Moses and to his other faithful servants, so that he may be understood to have always been generous throughout the ages. In the third section he turns his words toward the angels, addresses the heavenly powers, and invites the other rational creatures to devote themselves continually to the praises of the Lord.

### 343 Exposition of the psalm

[Col. 0719A]

**Verse 1.** *Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name.* Knowing that human minds are subject to various illusions and are not always fixed in true contemplation, the prophet addresses his own soul, so that, once it has been freed from various calamities, it may remember the author of all benefits and not think that what has clearly been granted by the Lord alone should be attributed either to itself or to anyone else. It is a pleasing and most fitting manner of speaking to converse with one’s soul, so that everyone may understand that what the prophet is known to have given himself as a salutary counsel is in every way to be desired.

It follows: *and all that is within me, his holy name.* The inner parts are the soul, its manifold thought, and the power of reason. He wished this power to agree with the soul, so that, in faithful harmony and with united strength, praise of the Lord might resound. Often the soul wishes to do something but is deceived by fantastic imaginings. But the holy man did not wish anything in himself to deviate from the Lord’s praise; rather, he wished everything to sing in one concord whatever might otherwise culpably be at odds within him.

**Verse 2.** *Bless the Lord, my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses.* He repeats the first verse with an elegant repetition of words, so that the doubled statement might arouse the greatest zeal, lest the soul appear sluggish in undertaking such a task through a harmful dissimulation. Above all, he warns it to remember that it has received everything from the same source. For the one who cannot forget the benefits bestowed never ceases to praise him.

Consider also what is meant by *recompenses*: for one thing was owed to human transgressions, and something else is known to have been repaid [mss. A, B: “to be repaid”] to those who have been set free. This is what no one is permitted to forget: that one who was liable to punishment should soon become worthy of honor. What these recompenses of the Lord are, he next recounts; if a person reflects upon them, he praises the Lord’s benefits with his whole mind.

**Verse 3.** *He who is gracious toward all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases.*

**Verse 4.** *He who redeems your life from destruction, who satisfies your desire with good things.*

**Verse 5.** *He who crowns you with compassion and mercy; your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.* In these three verses, under a fivefold division, [Col. 0719D] the recompenses of the future age are explained, which the Lord grants to his saints in pious compassion [mss. A, B, F: “mercy”]. This figure is called *synathroismos*, that is, “gathering,” when harsh crimes or exceedingly sweet benefits are collected into a single heap.

First, he is gracious toward their sins, when, after their transgressions have been forgiven, he deigns to receive sinners into peace. Second, he heals all the illnesses of the faithful, when eternal security and immortality are granted in the resurrection—that is, when “this corruptible thing puts on incorruption, and this mortal thing puts on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:54). Third, he will redeem our life from destruction, when he removes us from the calamity of eternal death, so that we do not hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). Fourth, he satisfies the desire of the blessed with good things, when they are told: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (ibid., 34). Fifth, he crowns them with his compassion and mercy, when he restores worthy rewards to those who are already blessed [ed., “will restore”], as the Apostle says: “From now on a crown of righteousness remains for me, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:8).

Perhaps the five loaves signify this, by which he satisfied the people after their long fasting, since these and similar things are known to have preceded as part of a great mystery. But we must investigate why the example of the eagle is introduced. It is said that, in this bird, when advanced in age, the upper beak, hooked by a horny curvature, grows so much that it is no longer free to pluck food in its customary manner. Realizing where danger to its life might arise, it is said to rub its beak against a rock until it removes every impediment. Once this has been done, it returns to the former health of its body by taking food as usual. So the soul returns to its former health if it does not cease to polish away its sins on the rock that is Christ the Lord. It returns to salutary nourishment when, by the Lord’s grace, it rejects its transgressions, which are impediments to eternal life.

**Verse 6.** *The Lord performs acts of mercy and judgment for all who suffer injury.* After speaking of the Lord’s recompenses, which he is believed truly to be able to grant in that age to those who have been converted here, he now says briefly that the Lord shows mercy to those who hope in him and provides vengeance for all who suffer injury, so that no one can doubt what has been said when he recognizes that the Lord himself has been displayed through such a definition. This verse is expressed in the form of a definition, since someone is identified by what he uniquely does. For when someone asks you, “What is the Lord?” you answer: “The one who performs acts of mercy and judgment for all who suffer injury.” Therefore, the Lord God has been abundantly identified, since what is said cannot apply to anyone else.

He shows mercy to those who have shown mercy, as he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). It follows: *and judgment for all who suffer injury.* This is promised to those who are adorned with the gift of patience, of whom he says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. 12:19; [Col. 0720D] Heb. 10:30). For those who desire to avenge themselves by their own hand and strive to satisfy their fury through the persecution of an enemy do not reserve vengeance for the Lord, because they believe that they themselves can exact what they ought to request from the Judge [ed., “await from the Judge”]. You have given your soul, most holy prophet, a salutary counsel in which the world also may feel itself consoled. Thus you spoke to yourself that you might speak to us; thus you benefited yourself that you might unquestionably save us as well.

**Verse 7.** *He made his ways known to Moses, his intentions to the children of Israel.* Above he had said what recompenses the blessed people would merit in that age. Now, coming to the second section, he proves through the example of one person how much he also granted here to his servants, [Col. 0721A] so that no one could doubt the future recompense.

But observe how Moses and Israel are distinguished by the wording: *He made his ways known to Moses*, when he disclosed to him the justice of his power [ed., “piety”], so that he might write down the law, teach moral conduct, and walk in the ways [ed., “in the way”] of the Lord by steps of perfect faith. It follows: *his intentions to the children of Israel.* Here he used *intentions*, not *ways*, because not all Israel, after receiving the word of the Lord, walked in his commands. We know what rebellions that people committed, so that by the voice of the Judge it deserved to hear: “This people is stiff-necked” (Exod. 32:9). Therefore he says that the Lord’s intentions, not his ways, were made known to them, because a large part of them presumed to turn aside from the Lord’s way. Understand the example of Moses placed here in such a manner that you nevertheless recognize the Lord as acting daily and able to act until the end of the age.

**Verse 8.** *The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and very merciful.* He is *compassionate* who is shown to be most gentle by nature. He is *merciful* when he bestows the gifts of his mercy. Someone may be compassionate and merciful in one or two matters, but no one except the Lord can be compassionate and merciful by nature. Here *compassionate* is therefore placed first so that you may recognize the Lord as merciful not temporarily but continually. This figure is called *paronomasia*, that is, “denomination,” which stirs the listener’s feeling through similarity of expression.

He added *patient*, which must accompany the compassionate; for no one is compassionate unless he is also patient. Thus the Apostle says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience? Do you not know [mss. G, F: “not knowing”] that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” (Rom. 2:4). He himself says of himself: “You did these things, and I was silent. You thought that I was altogether like you in wickedness” (Ps. 49:21).

It follows: *and very merciful.* Truly very merciful is the one who, hearing wholly blasphemous voices, makes his sun rise over the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the impious [ed., “unjust”] (Matt. 5:45); who bestows the life-giving spirit with great compassion; who waits for those who wander, so that they may condemn the wrongs they have committed [mss. A, B, F: “the wrongs perpetrated”].

**Verse 9.** *He will not be angry forever, nor will he be indignant eternally.* This applies, of course, to those who recognize [this] with devout satisfaction, who love to return to him, and who despise the enticements of the world together with their author. Against those, however, he will be angry forever to whom he will say: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). Great is the unhappiness of perishing under a merciful Lord: to delay satisfying the one whom you acknowledge yourself to have offended, especially when you do not find your supplication fruitless, provided you recognize that you have offered it with an undivided heart.

This may also be understood of the Jewish people, who are known to be converted at the end of the age. Concerning them the Apostle says: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

**Verse 10.** *He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities.* [Col. 0722A] This is a general statement, because there is no one who does not possess his grace freely, since the law encloses everything under sin, as the Apostle testifies: “God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he might have mercy on all” (ibid., 32). Yet he gives spirit alike to the good and the evil, grants salvation, removes their needs, and is generally good. He added: *nor has he repaid us according to our iniquities*, because he is so gracious toward those who supplicate him that he is especially pleased to absolve each person when that person strives, by making satisfaction, to condemn himself.

**Verse 11.** *For as high as heaven is above the earth, so the Lord has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him.* Let us examine more carefully what this comparison means. He says that the Lord’s mercy toward the faithful is greater than their merits by as much as the height of heaven can be raised above the earth. This comparison also signifies that, just as heaven covers the earth and at its appointed times grants suitable benefits to humanity—sometimes pouring down rain, sometimes providing clear weather, sometimes tempering the air with health-giving winds—so the Lord’s mercy is known to provide varied assistance to our frailty. He sustains us in order to correct us, scourges us in order to instruct us, tests us in order to benefit us; and through the various works of his benefits there is one will: to aid sinners.

But so that the force of the entire statement may be understood, it must be said briefly: if it is possible for heaven not to cover the earth, then it can happen that the Lord does not protect those who serve him with complete purity.

**Verse 12.** *As far as the east is distant from the west, so he has removed our iniquities from us.* [mss. A, B: “sunrise”] He has given another most beautiful comparison expressing divine benefit. The east is the beginning of our good life; the west is the inclination toward an evil manner of life. We were in the west when we were held bound by the chain of sin; but we are in the east when the true Sun visits us through the water of regeneration and causes the darkness of our sins to depart. Thus our iniquities are as far from us when our sins are forgiven as the bright day can be distant from the dark night.

Or, by the east he signifies the kingdom of God and by the west Gehenna, which is separated from the dwelling of the blessed as far as that poor man says, seated in Abraham’s bosom: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke 16:23).

[Col. 0722D]

**Verse 13.** *As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him.* Behold, the comparison is no longer made with things foreign or distant; rather, words drawn from the very entrails of compassion are joined together. He has compassion as a father, but toward those for whom he himself is father; he corrects as sons, but those who have deserved to be heirs of his kingdom.

It follows: *so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him.* When he says *so*, he indicates to us the affection of paternal correction. A human father who wishes to train his son in good actions frequently corrects him and frequently scourges him, as Solomon says: “If you love your son, frequently chastise him while he is still tender” (Sir. 30:1), and so forth. Parents truly love their children when they are strict with them out of devotion. So our Lord also scourges every son whom he receives and leads those who fear him toward the pursuit of good will.

**Verse 14.** *For he himself knows our formation. Remember, Lord, that we are dust.* This clause is to be joined to what precedes. The reason is given why he has compassion as a father: namely, because we have cast ourselves down from that natural dignity and, rejected from the Creator’s workmanship, are shown to be a formed thing. Rightly, therefore, the one who had no hope in his own strength asks to be helped.

It follows: *Remember, Lord, that we are dust.* He says, “Remember, Lord”—not because you created us from clay [ed., “formed us”], not because you made us immortal by your generosity, not because you deigned to fashion us according to your image and likeness, since all these things could rather provoke envy in the sinner, but because we have now been reduced to dust by the dryness of sin. Have mercy on those who have unhappily struck themselves down; help those who were entirely unwilling to remain in that gift of yours. For you alone are compassionate toward sinners, because those who transgressed have grievously struck themselves down.

### 345

**Verse 15.** *Man’s days are like grass, and like the flower of the field so he will flower* [mss. A, B, F: “will flourish”]. There are forms of definition that are explained through certain comparisons with things, as in the statement: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). This verse and the following are formed in the same way. If you ask, “What is man?” the answer is: “His days are grass,” which springs up with the greatest cheerfulness but dries with the swiftest speed. Grass raises its head rapidly into the breezes after the rains, but lowers its neck in the heat.

And lest you perhaps think that this comparison possesses any durability, he added: *and like the flower of the field so he will flower.* The flower of the field passes much more quickly than the greenness of grass is seen to endure. Yet although it appears most beautiful while it is in bloom, it is seen to be exceedingly fleeting when it falls. So human weakness grows beautifully; so the honors of the world and its riches are exceedingly pleasing, but they are not carried through to the farthest end. Humanity is therefore truly compared with these transitory things, because, deprived of robust strength, it always hastens with swift momentum toward the fall of death.

**Verse 16.** *For a spirit will pass through him, and he will not be; and he will no longer know his place.* The comparison of the preceding verse is expressed through this likeness. He describes what man is: a spirit passing through the world—namely, the present world—in which he cannot remain for very long. Let those who grow proud and rejoice that they have been carried along by worldly prosperity hear that the spirit leaves our little bodies as streams usually pass through flooded places. Those spaces that seem full when torrents occupy them—how empty they are when the waters withdraw!

One must not therefore presume upon a fleeting breath. Rather, one should do here what one knows will be profitable in the future. And lest anyone perhaps believe through metempsychosis that souls will return to this world—as certain madmen have supposed—he added: *and he will no longer know his place*, that is, he cannot return to this age in order to repeat his life there. Human frailty has been convicted by its own weakness. You have heard, human being, what you are; hear what you will be if you disdain to fear the Lord. This figure is called *parison*, that is, “equality of statement,” whenever good or evil is joined together in corresponding but dissimilar members.

**Verse 17.** *But the mercy of the Lord is from the age, and unto the age of the age, upon those who fear him; and his righteousness is upon the children of children.* Human condition was first truthfully explained because of the unlawful presumptions of the arrogant. Now he introduces the hope that ought to console the faithful: although we are fragile and perishable in ourselves, through the Lord’s mercy we are made absolutely everlasting, so that we may both recognize how fragile we are and hear what we attain through the Lord’s grace.

Observe that he said *from the age*, that is, from the time when the world began to be ordered and the various creatures burst forth through the gift of their Creator. Hence it seems to me that this may appropriately be understood here: Adam, as many of the Fathers have said, was recalled by the grace of the Lord [ms. G, ed.: “recalled to the grace of the Lord”] when he was the first person in the world, as were Abel, Noah, Abraham, and the other Fathers, who were indeed in the world but not from the world.

For what follows, *and unto the age of the age*, absolutely designates the Lord’s eternity, since he is shown to be merciful before the age, in the age, and after this age. Consider also what he added: *upon those who fear him*, lest those who disdain to obey him through criminal audacity should think that this ought to be done for them as well.

It follows: *and his righteousness is upon the children of children.* By *children*, as has often already been said, we ought to understand each person’s actions; by *children of children*, the most just recompense of our works. For just as we in a certain sense beget our work, so our actions beget recompenses for us. Every just person will receive this when he has been placed in eternal blessedness.

Many of the faithful have not had children, either because of the occurrence of sterility or through devotion to virginity. If you wish to understand this literally—which God forbid—very many saints are deprived of this promise. The following passages, moreover, make clear that it is spoken spiritually.

**Verse 18.** *For those who keep his covenant and remember his commandments in order to do them.* These are the children whom he mentioned above: those who keep the Lord’s precepts and remember his commandments by their deeds, not merely through the practice of singing. Even if someone recites the Psalter aloud, he is not mindful of it unless he does what is commanded. They were spoken in order to be done, not to be sung only with the voice.

Therefore the most learned Father Augustine, discussing this psalm, professed that he did not hold the Psalter, nor recall the words of the whole law, clearly intending to stir everyone’s zeal not merely to hear but especially to act. Memory is that by which the mind recalls what it has heard, seen, and done.

**Verse 19.** *The Lord has prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all.* He has come to the terrifying proclamation of the future judgment, lest the minds of sinners grow arrogant when they do not fear the vengeance that will come upon evil deeds. He says: *He has prepared his throne.* This refers to the time when the Lord Jesus ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father, from there to come to judge the living and the dead.

And lest you be troubled by any supposed weakness of the Lord, he says that the one who is going to judge the world himself prepared his throne. He added: *and his kingdom will rule over all.* Lest the pagans think that their demons would rule in any way, he says that the one who prepared his throne—namely, the Lord Christ—will rule.

**Verse 20.** *Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, who do his word, obedient to the voice of his words.* After the prophet had spoken above about human beings, he came to the third section, in which he addresses the heavenly creatures so that they may celebrate the Lord’s praises. And because there is great distinction even among the angels, he says that only those are worthy of the Lord’s proclamation who are shown to obey his commands. He demonstrates that neither human beings nor spiritual substances can approach the service of such majesty unless they comply with his wishes.

Thus he admonishes: *all his angels.* They are called his who in no way wished to depart from his command. It follows more explicitly: *mighty in strength, who do his word.* Those are mighty in strength who obey his commands. The devil also can be powerful, but not through virtue, rather through perversity; not through honor, but through presumption. [Col. 0725C] Those who strive to obey the word of the Lord are truly to be called mighty.

And lest anything remain ambiguous, he makes the point more forcefully: *obedient to the voice of his words*, that is, let them be humble, not proud. Those are worthy to bless who both recognize and honor their own Creator.

**Verse 21.** *Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will.* He judged that a great and altogether sublime matter should be strengthened by a repeated invitation, so that human weakness might recognize how salutary it is to obey the Lord, when the strength of heaven serves his will.

Observe how the words are precisely chosen. First he said: *who do his word.* And lest you understand *word* as something customarily produced by human beings through the striking of air, he added: *who do his will.* For the angels, the word of the Lord is his will, because that sublime and spiritual substance of the blessed angels, when it beholds the Lord, recognizes there the truth of his will. There is no need for speech among those to whom the Divinity, in its favor, reveals itself. God does not speak to them by striking the air; rather, by his inspiration he turns their wills toward his own will. So, as we believe, blessed human beings will be after they have obtained the rewards of the eternal kingdom.

**Verse 22.** *Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion; bless the Lord, my soul.* The word *bless* is now doubled through a third repetition. This figure is called *epembasis*, a becoming pattern, namely, to repeat a word more frequently in praises or reproaches in order to raise the spirits of those being addressed.

First he said that those who fulfill the Lord’s commands ought to bless him. Now he admonishes that the Lord’s work itself ought to praise its Creator, so that he might include earthly and heavenly things together. Since everything is his work, everything ought to bless its Creator.

It follows: *in every place of his dominion.* Just as no creature is commanded to be excluded from the Lord’s praises, so no place is left out that might be separated from such a duty. When it says *in every place of his dominion*, nothing is excepted, because he rules everywhere. Perhaps this signifies the Catholic Church, which, by the Lord’s grace, was destined to believe throughout the whole world. For it blesses the Lord everywhere, praises him everywhere, and celebrates the greatest thanksgiving with hymnic rejoicing.

He added: *Bless the Lord, my soul.* This same statement concludes the psalm that made its beginning so beautiful. But since all things in the divine Scriptures grow rich with the abundance of mysteries, this likeness—as has already been said—in the eighth psalm indicates, in my opinion, those who have entered the courts of faith with sincere minds and, by the Lord’s grace, bring their lives to a glorious end. It is a worthy admonition by which the faithful soul may console itself, taking it up like an unconquerable shield against every misfortune. For if we always bless him, we are continually guarded by him.

## Conclusion of the psalm

We have recognized with what great generosity the Lord’s blessing is granted to those who fear him. Let us hasten to fulfill the commandments, so that we may merit to reach the rewards. We have the Lord, compassionate by nature and exceedingly generous in the gifts of his mercies. Who would hesitate to ask him, when he is offended if he is not asked? Let us therefore all together bless the Lord and celebrate his works with hymnic rejoicing.

For what sacrilege it would be if, when every creature is commanded to bless the Lord, a human being should cease to praise the Lord, who is known to have been created in his image and likeness! We have heard to what virtues the Lord’s blessing is applied: to the chaste, the most humble, those full of charity, and those who fulfill the Lord’s other commandments. Therefore, let everything that is perverse be driven away from here; let all the wickedness of the world be excluded; let its enticements be corrected; let the devil be cast out with his followers.

Therefore, having heard of so great a gift and filled with so great a hope, let us bless the Lord with holy works and sing to the Author through religious deeds. The Judge’s choice will not reject us if he recognizes that here we have accomplished what he commanded.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 103

*A psalm of David.*

We have often said that a psalm signifies those actions of mortals which, on account of their goodness, look toward the understanding of divine things. The instrument itself is adapted to their likeness; it is specifically called a psalm, having a tympanum above, where the sweetest melody is modulated in sonorous sound. David, however, is used only as the person who speaks. [Col. 0727A] Otherwise, it is clear that everything is to be narrated about the Lord the Savior, who in the beginning made heaven and earth.

This psalm is perfected with such an arrangement that here you may understand certain things which you recognize were left unspoken in the book of Genesis. Therefore, we shall expound literally whatever is suitable to be taken literally; but whatever can disclose knowledge of our faith, we shall explain through spiritual understanding, as we have received it from our predecessors. Hence we must be attentive and ready to listen, since that most eloquent Father Augustine himself says that this psalm must be diligently investigated and discussed with the greatest labor.

## Division of the psalm

The prophet, wishing to show that the conditions of created things signify divine mysteries, first indicates certain doctrines to us through the construction of heaven and earth [ms. G: “dogmatic teachings”]. We are to recognize that all things can truly be understood as created in harmony by one Author, since they are shown to disclose certain likenesses of one another. Second, he enumerates the Lord’s works, covered by various figures. Third, he declares that in that eternal age he will continually proclaim the Lord’s praises, which he had also sung during the brevity of this life.

## Exposition of the psalm

**Verse 1.** *Bless the Lord, my soul; Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified. You have put on confession and beauty.* The prophet invites himself to bless the Lord. And because he knew that, in the Catholic faith, the grace of unity is exceedingly powerful, he speaks only to himself in a way that ought to admonish everyone.

To bless God is to confess his mighty deeds, so that whenever something great is said about him, each person may render service to the truth. This statement therefore looks toward the entire text, where the length of this psalm comes to an end.

But while, as has been said, he was speaking to his soul, he suddenly turns and says: *Lord my God.* This figure is called *proanaphonesis*, when, amid other things that we are saying, we suddenly turn our words toward God. He confidently asserts that the universal Lord is his God, so that, when he professes himself to be the Lord’s servant, he may prove that he has no share whatsoever with the devil. Thus that transgressor might find nothing in one whom he recognizes as alien to himself.

It follows: *you have been greatly magnified.* We must diligently investigate the force of these words. For when is he not great, so that he should be magnified by human praises? Or what can be added to him who is the wondrous and incomprehensible fullness of virtues? Yet the Lord is magnified among human beings when he becomes clear to them as great and exalted, so that they recognize him as Creator, giver of all good things, Redeemer, and finally Judge.

From this it follows that the Lord of the redeemed is rightly said to be magnified, since he daily becomes wondrous through the devotion of believers. He is likewise said to be sanctified, glorified, blessed, and similarly described.

He added: *greatly.* Truly greatly, when he is praised by the mouths of the converted and those who once polluted themselves with unspeakable crimes enter the assembly of the saints. *Greatly* is most appropriately said of what is accomplished with the whole effort of the heart.

But how he has been greatly magnified is explained next: *You have put on confession and beauty.* To put something on is to assume something one did not have. And when did God lack beauty, since he always bestows all that is beautiful upon his creatures? Here, however, the incarnation of the Lord Christ is clearly expounded: he assumed it in time, through which the bestower of his own mercy found the confession of mortals.

Human beings had withdrawn from the worship of the true Divinity while serving the cults of idols and empty religions. But when he came—although in his Divinity he was never absent—the confession and beauty of the heavenly Majesty became known, and the Lord is said to have been clothed in those things with which the Catholic Church is known to be adorned.

**Verse 2.** *Clothed with light as with a garment* [ms. G and ed.: “light as a garment”], *stretching out heaven like a skin.* These twenty-two verses, up to the forthcoming division, are explained through the figure of *parabole* with the most beautiful allusions. This occurs when things dissimilar in kind are compared with one another.

Light signifies the Church, concerning which it is written: “Who is this that ascends, made white?” (Song 3:6). “Made white” is understood as “illuminated.” It is rightly regarded as the garment of the Lord the Savior, having neither spot nor wrinkle. For it is itself white and made white; concerning its members the Apostle says: “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). It was also signified by that tunic which could not be divided at the time of the Passion. This is the one of which it is said: *clothed with light as with a garment.*

It follows: *stretching out heaven like a skin.* The Lord is rightly said to stretch out the heavens where it is established that he admits prostitutes and tax collectors. For although, through justice, they are the heavens of the righteous, they have also been made so through the abundance of grace for sinners.

Nor was skin compared with heaven without reason: just as skin covers all our limbs, so the surrounding circuit of the heavens encloses the creatures within it. Some have understood heaven also as referring to the just person, whom he is shown to stretch out through grace just as a stretched skin can expand.

### Verse 3

[Cols. 0728D–0729B]

“He covers its upper parts with waters; he makes the cloud his ascent; he walks upon the wings of the winds.”

Although this may seem to explain the order of creation—for waters have been placed above the heavens, as is also read in Genesis, and elsewhere he himself says, “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4)—nevertheless, an indication of sacred baptism is also disclosed to us. Thus, as has frequently been said, we ought to understand “heaven” as every righteous person, whose upper parts—that is, the amendment of the faithful soul—are watered with saving waters. For all these things have been arranged by that author in such a way that heavenly statements seem both to indicate ecclesiastical actions and, again, to testify to the conditions of things through a most truthful account.

It follows: “He makes the cloud his ascent.” This is certainly understood appropriately in the literal sense, when, after the resurrection, the Lord ascended into heaven before the eyes of the apostles; for thus it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “When he had said these things, a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1:9). But we are also most suitably permitted to understand the cloud as the preacher of the Lord’s word, through whom Christ ascends in his members, when he has cleansed the minds of sinners from the perversity of this world.

He added: “He walks upon the wings of the winds.” Winds are known to fly amid this movement of the air as though upon wings of their own; but the Lord walks upon their wings, since he accomplishes his wills much more swiftly than the course of the winds can be. Or rather, we ought to understand the winds as the souls of the righteous, because, instructed through both Testaments, they are transferred to the joys above as though on two wings. The Lord is rightly said to walk above them, since in them he displays the mercy of his action.

And note that in this verse, as also in those that follow, he prefers to show the Lord through what he has done. Among the Greeks this second kind of definition is called *ennoematice*; in Latin it is called *notio* (“conception” or “recognition”). For although the Lord cannot be defined according to his nature, he is beautifully known through that which he uniquely accomplishes.

### Verse 4

[Col. 0729C]

“He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire.”

It should be impressed upon the mind that here he speaks specifically about angels, 348 a subject that is not presented so clearly in the Book of Genesis. The very words, moreover, must be examined more carefully. “Spirit” is a general name for an incorporeal and powerful substance that operates visibly or invisibly, and that is divinely breathed into it.

The name “angels” does not signify nature but obedience. In Greek, *angelos* means what is interpreted in Latin as “messenger”; for when angels are sent, they become angels, although by nature they are known to be spirits. He added “his” in order to indicate those who obey the Lord’s wills with a right mind. The order of the words is therefore: “He makes his spirits angels.”

It follows: “And his ministers a burning fire.” Every person who carries out the divine wills and is always enflamed with the fervor of charity is a minister of God. Such a man becomes heavenly fire when he is shown to be capable, through the word of preaching, of burning and consuming the wickedness of sinners. Thus the Lord himself says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49)—a life-giving fire, certainly, a fire of salvation, which, while consuming sins, nourishes souls.

### Verse 5

[Cols. 0729D–0730A]

“He founded the earth upon its [mss. A, B: ‘his’] stability; it shall not be shaken for ever and ever.”

This verse does not seem able to stand in the literal sense. For since we have read that this earth is to be changed, how can it be that it will not be shaken for ever and ever? But here let us understand instead the earth as the Church, made firm and solidified. It is called “earth” because it is shown to have been gathered from earthly human beings, as he says elsewhere: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm 23:1).

The stability of this earth is rightly called Christ, who is the immovable foundation and inviolable rock. Concerning him the Apostle says: “For no one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11). If we remain continually upon him, we shall never be shaken. For things placed upon a foundation do not know how to totter, since what supports them is fixed. Thus the truth of this statement will stand established for us by a complete interpretation.

The Holy Spirit sometimes speaks things that are extremely difficult in the literal sense so that we may seek the spiritual meaning with greater breadth. What has therefore been said—“It shall not be shaken for ever and ever”—must be understood as applying throughout the clauses of the preceding three verses. This figure is called *hyperbaton*, because the order of the words is extended over a greater distance.

### Verse 6

[Cols. 0730B–C]

“The abyss, like a garment, is its covering; upon the mountains the waters shall stand.”

Nor can this verse be referred to history, although it seems to speak of the flood that was brought over the earth. The time of the flood is past, whereas the prophet now proclaims that something future is to occur. We must therefore investigate this more spiritually, since the times cannot agree in the literal sense.

The abyss is the name given to a most abundant multitude of waters, and it is generally placed both in a good and in an evil sense. Here it is deservedly compared with superstitious people and persecutors, because, just as a garment covers what lies beneath it, so they covered the world with the most foul superstition. They seemed to overwhelm with bodily tortures not only ordinary people but even holy and most eminent men, to their own destruction.

Here, however, the abyss is placed in an evil sense, although it is also read in a good sense, as in: “The judgments of the Lord are like a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). This kind of expression is rightly reckoned among the distinctive forms of divine Scripture.

Finally, the passage continues: “Upon the mountains the waters shall stand.” They did indeed stand over those who were called “mountains” because of the firmness of their faith, when they inflicted various punishments and deaths upon them. Here we should understand the waters and abysses as the impious, who hasten to overwhelm holiness just as a mass of waves can cover what lies beneath it.

But so that you might more clearly recognize that this concerns the proud and the wicked, the following verse demonstrates it. Some also wish to maintain a literal interpretation, saying that the abyss surrounds the margin of the earth; for just as the exterior parts of our bodies are covered by a garment, so the globe of the earth is said to be enclosed by the circuit of the Ocean.

### Verse 7

[Col. 0730D]

“At your rebuke they will flee; at the sound of your thunder they will be afraid.”

Who will flee, except the abysses, except the waters that seemed to tower above Christ’s mountains? For although they had afflicted his saints with various massacres, when rebuked by the voice of the apostles they nevertheless abandoned their superstition and were driven away; and, what is the greatest kind of victory, they experienced the opposite of what they had desired.

It follows: “At the sound of your thunder they will be afraid.” The preaching of the saints is described under this most beautiful allegory. He says, “At the sound of your thunder,” so that you might understand that it was not a human utterance but the sound of heavenly power. People everywhere feared the thunder of preaching when the terror of judgment was proclaimed, when they heard that the devil would perish together with his followers; and although they had enjoyed license in this world, they condemned their own crimes with a reformed mind.

### Verse 8

[Cols. 0731A–B]

“The mountains ascend; the plains descend to the place that you founded for them.”

He continues in the figurative allusions, since, for as long as he wished, the Lord permitted the proud and the impious to grow into mountains; and again, when it pleased him, he made them settle in the humility of valleys. So too a time was granted to the persecutors to rise up high, and then, brought low, to lie beneath the Christian people. He teaches that all things occur by the ordering of the one whose will cannot be opposed, just as the Lord himself said to Pontius Pilate in the Gospel: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given (*data*; edition: *datum*) to you from above” (John 19:11).

Observe also that here the mountains are placed in an evil sense, whereas above mountains signify men most faithful. We have said that this is often found in the divine Scriptures.

It follows: “To the place that you founded for them.” Those who have now become plains descend to the place of the most firmly founded Church and will remain in her inner chambers. For even a limit has been set for sinners themselves; they are not permitted to go beyond the extent to which they have been granted license to loosen the reins of their freedom.

Thus it is read: “The iniquity of the Amorites has been completed” (Genesis 15:16), so that you may understand that all things have been placed beneath the Lord’s will. The following passages also explain this clearly.

### Verse 9

[Col. 0731C; p. 349]

“You set a boundary for them which they will not cross, nor will they return [ms. G: ‘turn back’] to cover the earth.”

If you wish to take this literally, he is speaking of the abundant waters which, once the flood has receded, can no longer occupy the lands, as it is written in Genesis: “I will establish my covenant with you, and never again shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of the flood, nor shall there ever again be a flood to devastate the earth” (Genesis 9:11).

But if you seek a spiritual interpretation, this can also appropriately be understood of the practice of the pagans. Although they have departed from their perversity, they will never return to that license, with God opposing them, so as to cover the human race with the flood of their superstitions. Their coming to an end was the coming of the Lord Christ; as devotion to him increased, all idols [mss.: “idolatry”] fell together with their authors.

Let us also consider under what rebuke these things are related, so that rational human beings may think that they ought not to despise the Lord’s commands, when even the elements are known to obey his orders.

### Verse 10

[Cols. 0731D–0732A]

“He sends forth springs in the valleys; the waters will pass through the midst of the mountains.”

When the nature of the lands is described, a more hidden cause is indicated to us through the most beautiful allusions. It is certain that valleys abound in plentiful waters and that springs are frequent there where the flat fields lie. But we should attend rather to the fact that divine waters always surge within the humility of human beings, who are placed in the position of valleys.

Spiritually, however, we must understand the mountains here as heretics and the proud, among whom the divine Scriptures flow with perpetual abundance, since in this world hearing them is shared by the good and the wicked alike. “They will pass through” is rightly said, because such men are not perceived to have been made fruitful by any benefit. For if, as some say, he had wished the mountains here to mean righteous preachers, he would have said that the waters flowed from those mountains, not that they could pass through while situated among them.

### Verse 11

[Cols. 0732A–B]

“All the beasts of the forests will drink from them; the wild asses will await their thirst [mss. A, B, F: ‘for their thirst’].”

Here we should understand the beasts of the forests as the nations, who came out of the worship of idols as from shadowy forests, casting aside their fiercest ways, in order to drink the waters that the Lord promised in the Gospel to the Samaritan woman, saying: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:13–14).

It follows: “The wild asses will await their thirst.” Although he said that the beasts of the forests had been given drink from the flowing waters, he placed the wild asses alone as awaiting their thirst—namely, the Jews, who neglected to drink in the streams of divine mercy.

A wild ass is a woodland ass. Among the other animals it is said to have an especially fat heart; and this creature, to the extent that it is patient when domesticated, becomes equally savage when it grows wild in the forests that retain it. The obstinate Jews are rightly compared with them: they have been hardened by the fierceness of their mind and their calloused folly, and they do not readily consent to be satisfied with the cups of life.

The word “await” signifies what has frequently been said: that at the end of the world, when Elijah and Enoch come, the multitude of the Jews will believe. Wretched are those who thirst for so long and do not at all desire to be satisfied. Their life is punitive, since they are tormented by such prolonged expectation.

### Verse 12

[Cols. 0732C–D]

“Above them the birds of heaven will dwell; from the midst of the rocks they will give their voice.”

Above those things, namely, of which he earlier said, “He sends forth springs in the valleys,” the birds of heaven will dwell. These birds are known to love both valleys and irrigated waters (*aquas irriguas*; mss. A, B, F: *aquis irrigata*, “waters irrigated”). Yet it is not without purpose that he added “of heaven.” For if he had wished merely to indicate birds, it would have been sufficient to say “birds.” Rather, he prefers us to understand the holy souls of bishops, conducting themselves in a heavenly manner, who dwell above the peoples of the Lord through holy preaching.
