He added: “From the midst of the rocks they will give their voice.” These birds, which have been called heavenly, will give their voice not from the earth, not from trees, but from the midst of rocks, when they are known to proclaim something according to the examples of the apostles and prophets.

All the faithful are rightly called rocks, because Christ himself is also called a rock. Thus the Lord himself said to the apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). Therefore all who confirm their words through the traditions of the apostles and prophets preach from the firmness of rocks.

### Verse 13

[Cols. 0732D–0733A]

“Watering the mountains from his upper chambers, the earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works.”

Above he had mentioned the lofty mountains and the very low valleys watered by springs; now he proclaims that the mountains themselves have also been drenched (*complutos*; mss. A, B, F: *completos*, “filled”) with waters from above, lest anything seem to have been excluded from the Lord’s gift.

Paul, previously a great and lofty persecutor of the Church, was watered with spiritual water—and how fruitful were the works he proved able to produce for Christians! This is what the Lord does daily, making teachers of the pagans teachers of the faithful after their conversion. Such men are watered from above when, after their conversion, they acknowledge that they had gone astray.

It follows: “The earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works.” When the earth produces fruit, how can this trampled earth be satisfied from fruits? The earth is satisfied with fruits when sinners, changed for the better, receive from the giver things that are exceedingly useful and saving. Thus the earth is satisfied when someone, freed from obstinacy, is recognized as having learned the Lord’s praises.

### Verse 14

[Cols. 0733B–C]

“Bringing forth grass for cattle, and plants for the service of human beings, that he may bring bread from the earth [mss. A, B, F: ‘that you may bring’].”

He develops what he said above, so that the earth, satisfied with heavenly rain, may bring forth grass for cattle—that is, may perform acts of almsgiving for those who ask everywhere. Concerning them it is said: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6:30).

They are called cattle because, lacking modesty on account of the greed of their bellies, they burst forth shamelessly into the voices of the needy like animals which, when hungry, are entirely unable to restrain their own cries.

“Plants for the service of human beings” means that what is necessary may be given to those of whom it is written: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find the righteous person to whom you may give it.” Here they are called “human beings” because, full of reason, they conceal their need beneath the strength of endurance. Thus two kinds of needy people are expressed through such allusions.

It follows: “That you may bring bread from the earth.” Bread is brought forth from the earth when the Lord’s commandments are fulfilled, so that from these carnal and visible things food may be made by which the soul is nourished with heavenly refreshment.

For Christ is truly our bread, and he is produced from the earth when something is provided for the needy out of consideration for him. Or this may be said of preachers, who mercifully supplied the needs of ignorant people from heavenly riches.

### Verse 15

[Cols. 0733C–0734A; p. 350]

“And wine that gladdens the human heart, to brighten the face with oil, and bread that strengthens the human heart.”

Above he had said, “That you may bring bread from the earth.” But lest you understand this as ordinary bread, by which our flesh is refreshed, he adds these three things, which must be understood spiritually.

Scripture frequently testifies that the heart signifies rational understanding. Therefore wine gladdens the human heart when it has been consecrated into the blood of the Lord Christ. We may be inebriated by this, as it is written: “And your cup, making drunk—how glorious it is!” (Psalm 22:5). This is truly pure wine that gladdens the mind, not wine that leads to guilt and vices. It is a sober drunkenness, a blessed fullness, which is rightly said to gladden because nothing culpable is found there.

The face is also brightened with oil when the royal chrism is prepared—but it is that face of which it is said: “Draw near to him and be illumined, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm 33:6).

It follows: “And bread that strengthens the human heart.” Again, “heart” is used so that it may be understood as having been spoken of wisdom. For if you wish to consider the bodily sense, does bread strengthen the human heart but not the other members as well? Examine the properties of the words, so that you may recognize that these things were truly placed here for the understanding of heavenly realities.

Of wine he says, “It gladdens the human heart.” If you wish to understand worldly wine, it is known to gladden not only the heart but the whole body for a time, although it frequently also incites quarrels and urges a person toward some excess of presumption. But “heart” has been placed for “mind,” from which we are said to be wise and through which we perceive and understand good and evil.

Likewise, if we suppose this to be the oil generally used by the world, how can it brighten the face, when the joy of the mind is continually expressed in the features? And how can bread strengthen the heart alone, when it is received for the refreshment of the whole body? These things must rather be referred to the parts of the soul, which make Christians perfect.

### Verse 16

[Cols. 0734B–C]

“The trees of the forests will be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which you planted.”

The trees of the forests signify the common people of vast nations, who came to the Catholic Church from thorny and uncultivated peoples. These plainly indicate people of modest status. The cedars of Lebanon, however, signify the noble and powerful, who are known to rise above the human race like cedars.

But in order to separate these people also from the heretics and pagans who have been raised to the greatest power in this world, he added, “which you planted”—that is, those who by your predestination have been established in the most lovely garden of religion. Thus he says in the Gospel: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matthew 15:13).

Nor should the interpretation of the name itself be passed over, since it is shown to reveal some significance to us. “Lebanon” is interpreted as “whitening” or “whiteness.” The power of this world, however, seems to be a kind of festivity, where rich and powerful people, lofty and tall, are born as though upon Mount Lebanon; nevertheless, they have reached the true religion through the Lord’s gift.

### Verse 17

[Cols. 0734C–0735A]

“There the sparrows will build their nests; the coot’s house is their guide.”

There, namely in the cedars that you planted, the sparrows will build their nests. The sparrow is a small and exceedingly cautious bird, signifying the lowliness of monks. In the cedars of Lebanon—that is, in the resources of powerful Christians—they are shown to build monasteries for themselves like nests upon certain branches. Sustained by their strength, they sing the praises of the Lord with unceasing voice like sparrows.

This is a heavenly life on earth: the imitation of the faithful angels; living spiritually in the flesh and not loving the vices of the world; despising the present life and always seeking the joys of future blessedness; and, finally, becoming the temple itself, whose image human nature has received.

Truly this is a delightful paradise, in which such fruits of virtues flourish. For these people have made it their purpose to conquer their enemies not by resisting but by enduring. Every triumph for them lies in the suffering of their own bodies; and they effectively overcome their adversaries when they yield with praiseworthy humility [mss. A, B, F: “flourish”]. Truly they are soldiers of Christ, who place no presumption in human strength but trust that they can overcome all adversity by the Lord’s power.

They do not quarrel with others but always contend with themselves. They have compassion on everyone and spare only themselves. Enflamed with heavenly charity, they strive to share with others the good things they desire to happen to themselves.

Great indeed is the glory of that tree in which this nest is built. Let it hear from the Lord that it has been planted by him, since it is known to contain such an institution.

It follows: “The coot’s house is their guide.” The coot is a tame and black bird, smaller than a duck but similar in the position of its body, and it dwells delightfully in ponds. This appropriately refers to those who are baptized and persevere in the grace of the most sacred font.

Their dwellings, therefore—that is, perseverance in baptism—are the guide of the sparrows who nest in the cedars. For the sacred font of all Christians is their guide, since it leads them to the kingdoms of heaven.

### Verse 18

[Cols. 0735B–C]

“The high mountains are for the deer; the rock [ms. G and edition: ‘rocks’] is a refuge for the hedgehogs.”

The deer is, as we have said, a devourer of poisonous serpents; it leaps over thorny growths and is endowed with the greatest agility. It loves to dwell in the highest mountains.

The faithful are rightly compared with it. They devour the devil when they turn his wickedness toward the Lord’s praise and glory; they leap over the vices of this age as though over thorns through a good way of life; and they dwell in the mountains—that is, in the apostles and prophets, who through their holy preaching have deserved to be solid peaks in this world.

The hedgehog—called *hericius*—is an extremely timid animal, always armed by nature’s foresight. Its skin is protected in place of bristles by very sharp and densely packed spines. Yet its natural defense is not enough for it; lest it be caught by some trick, it always has refuge among the rocks.

This fittingly applies to one who, bristling with his sins and fearing future judgments, is known to have Christ, the firmest rock, as his refuge.

These animals therefore rightly indicate for us such men, who never separate themselves from the Lord’s solidity. Observe that the sparrows seek the heights of the cedars; the coots defend themselves by dwelling in the waters; the deer choose the mountains; and the hedgehogs fortify themselves under the protection of the rocks. Thus, through different birds and animals, the diversity of Christian lives is indicated to us.

### Verse 19

[Cols. 0735D–0736A; p. 351]

“He made the moon for appointed times [ms. G and edition: ‘time’]; the sun knew its setting.”

He passes from earthly things to heavenly things, but these too are indicated through certain allusions. The moon, as we have often said, signifies the Church, which was made for appointed times, since it happens to diminish and increase; yet it diminishes in such a way that, with its integrity continually returning, it is always restored.

Here we rightly understand the sun as the Lord and Savior, concerning whom the impious will say at the end of the world: “We went astray from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wisdom 5:6). This could certainly not be said of the ordinary sun, since it is written: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matthew 5:45).

This sun, therefore, knew its setting—that is, he recognized the glory of his passion—when he said to his disciples: “The hour has come, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners” (Mark 14:41).

It is therefore fitting that, after those forms of Christians which above appear to have been expressed through various significations, the passage proceeds to the increase of these matters, speaking of the Church and of the Lord himself.

### Verses 20–21

[Cols. 0736A–B]

“You appointed darkness, and night came; in it all the beasts of the forests will pass through.

The young lions roar, seeking to seize and seeking their food from God.”

Here we have joined the two verses together for the necessary connection of the words. He appointed darkness when, at the sixth hour during the time of the passion, the world received obscurity.

Then night truly came for the disciples and believers, when Peter, confused by anxious error, lost the brightness of faith by denying him three times. It was night also for those who, looking carnally, generally supposed Christ to be dying upon that cross.

In this night, therefore, the beasts of the forests—that is, demons—and the young lions, whom the devil begot through a corrupted will, went out seeking some people to devour, so that, with the Lord permitting it, they might find food for their wickedness.

For nothing can be done by anyone except what he himself, by a secret judgment, permits to be done either for testing or for vengeance. They are called “young lions” because they are skilled in the sense of smell.

Let it not trouble you that above we said that the beasts of the forests must be understood as multitudes of nations, whereas here the devil with his ministers seems to be signified. In the divine Scriptures it is an extremely common practice for one thing to be applied to persons differing among themselves, as we said concerning the mountain and the lion.

### Verse 22

[Col. 0736C]

“The sun rose, and they gathered together; and they will lie down in their dens.”

When darkness had come upon the Lord’s passion, the demons, with the Lord permitting it, burst forth to seek food for themselves, because they could find wavering hearts.

But when the sun rose—that is, when the holy Resurrection was revealed—they could not endure his majesty and hid themselves trembling in their dens; that is, they settled in the breasts of the obstinate. Since they could not persuade everyone, they at least possessed those whom they had deceived.

The sun is so called because it alone shines in such a way that day comes from it.

### Verse 23

[Col. 0736D]

“Man will go out to his work, and to his labor until evening” [mss. A, B, F: “he went out”].

Since above he had said that the sun rose, he appropriately added that each human being in this life goes out to perform his works.

This is the practice of mortals: for as long as we are in this world, when day comes we are occupied with activities of various kinds. One cultivates a field, another exercises himself in warfare; one studies, another teaches; some rule, many serve. Whatever fragile mortality does is shown to be brought to an end by evening—that is, by the end of the world.

### Verse 24

[Cols. 0736D–0737C]

“How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your creation.”

After the figurative enumeration of things and the mysteries of our faith that have been recounted, the prophet comes to a second mode of expression, where, after such great miracles, he fittingly cries out the praises of the Father.

By saying “How,” he confesses that he can marvel at them more than explain them. And rightly does his praise begin in this way, since no creature is sufficiently capable of completing his praises.

For this is shown to be immense not only for human beings but even for the angels themselves. How greatly his works have been magnified is made clear by what follows.

It continues: “You made all things in wisdom.” This Wisdom is therefore the Son, as the Apostle says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, through whom all things were made, and without him nothing was made” (1 Corinthians 1:24; John 1:3).

And to show the cooperation of his power [edition: “and his power”], he says to the Father, with the Son working: “You made.” The same Apostle says this also concerning the Holy Spirit: “All these things are effected by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). From this it may be gathered [edition: “understood”] that the cooperation of the Holy Trinity can plainly be recognized through these examples.

He added: “The earth is filled with your creation.” The earth is not filled everywhere with similar things. Nevertheless, although a wilderness may seem empty of living creatures because of the heat of the sun or excessive cold, the earth is filled with the Lord’s creation in whatever forms it may have.

Or this should rather be understood: the creation of the Catholic religion, which the Lord Savior established, has filled the whole earth, since the universal Church serves the Lord. Concerning it the Apostle says: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). And elsewhere: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new, who was created according to God in righteousness” (Ephesians 4:22, 24).

The whole world has been filled with this creation. Hence another psalm also says: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:8).

### Verse 25

[Cols. 0737C–D]

“This sea is great and spacious in its extent; there are creeping things without number, small and great animals.”

In this section too, up to the division, there is the figure of *parabole*, which is explained through varied and beautiful comparisons.

Although at the beginning of this verse he seems to speak of a sea suitable for navigation, it is nevertheless appropriately understood as this world, where the devil’s snares are shown to creep about without number, and where the unstable will of souls is shaken by the wickedness of demons as though by certain waves [edition: “immeasurable”].

They make the world into a sea when they compel people to suffer shipwreck. For there is no doubt that the one who is submerged in the whirlpool of sins suffers enormous waves.

The sea is called *mare* from *meando* (“going”), because it continually goes and returns [mss. A, B, F: “approaches and withdraws”]. But these innumerable spirits are comprehended by God, who counts the sand of the sea and the drops of rain. And lest they be left altogether incomprehensible, he defined them by quantity, not by quality.

Finally, it is said of them: “Small and great animals,” because among them there are proved to be both the greatest forms of wickedness and the lesser ones.

### Verse 26

[Cols. 0737D–0738B; p. 352]

“There ships will pass through; that dragon which you formed to mock him.”

“There,” namely in the world, which he earlier called “the sea.” The ships rightly signify the Churches, which escape the dangerous waves of the world through the wood of the glorious cross, carrying the peoples who have believed through the sign of faith. In these ships Christ dwells; if he is awakened by believers, he says to the most violent storm that it should be still, and it becomes still.

It follows: “That dragon which you formed to mock him.” Here he openly signifies the devil, who is truly called a dragon because of the poison that he breathed into Eve, the first woman, through his deadly persuasions.

This being was created good, as it is read in Genesis: “God made all things very good” (Genesis 1:31). But after he sinned by his own will, he was so formed by God that he might be mocked by the angels, since, on account of his execrable perversity, he was deprived of his native dignity.

Thus the Lord says in the Book of Job: “There is nothing made upon the earth like him” (Job 41:24). He was formed “to be mocked by my angels.” He is mocked by the angels of God either through most just rebukes, since he who was created for the service of the Lord is seen to be entangled in foul perversities; or, rather, he is mocked when, by heavenly command, the souls of those who confess are taken away from his destructive power.

He is also mocked by faithful men when they flee from the incentives of his vices with detestation and horror. You hear of a dragon, but do not fear him as wholly terrible; for he was formed in such a way that, by the Lord’s favor, he can be mocked even by human beings.

Invoke the one who treads upon him, and you will begin not to fear the one who devours. For it is written: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90:13).

### Verse 27

[Cols. 0738C–D]

“All things await you, that you may give them food in due season.”

This verse signifies what is also said elsewhere: “In your will, O Lord, all things have been placed, and there is no one who can resist your will” (Esther 13:9).

For when he says “all things,” he shows that everything lives by God’s command, by whose authorship it was also created. Even the spiritual dragon, whose food is the deception of human beings, cannot accomplish anything by its own power unless the Lord permits it.

For the person whom God casts away because of his evils becomes the devil’s food. Therefore, if we do not wish to be given as food to the enemy, we must not be earthly, because he was cursed at the beginning so that he might eat the earth. As it is written: “Upon your breast and belly you shall walk, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:14).

But if the Lord’s mercy makes us heavenly, we are entirely removed from being the devil’s food.

He also added “in due season,” so that the Lord may be understood not only to give food to his creatures but also to bestow it at the appropriate time.

The devil wished to test Job, but he could not accomplish this unless the Lord’s power permitted it. That most holy man also knew that he was being tested by the Lord’s permission, and he responded to everything: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

This is the true and firm judgment: that, as has been said, all things are placed within the Lord’s will.

### Verse 28

[Col. 0739A]

“When you give to them, they gather; when you open your hand, all things will be filled with abundance.”

He continues to explain the preceding statement, so that when we are troubled by diabolical wickedness, we may not believe that the devil presumes to do this by his own power. Rather, let us return to the one without whose permission he can do nothing, and he departs more swiftly when defeated.

For he says: “When you give to them, they gather,” so that you may understand that unless something has been given to them, they will be unable to gather anything.

It follows that the statement can also be applied to prosperity: “When you open your hand, all things will be filled with abundance.” It is clear that the causes of all things are located there, whence abundance is granted and unfailing plenty is bestowed.

The hand signifies power, through which he fills all things abundantly and orders everything wondrously.

Verse 29. But when you turn your face away, they will be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and return to their dust. He is now speaking of those who, not acknowledging in the least the gifts granted by God, applied to their own strength whatever abilities they possessed. Against them the Apostle says: “For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7). And in another psalm we read concerning such a person: “I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever” (Ps. XXIX, 7). Therefore, when the Lord turns his face away from such people, they are undoubtedly troubled, stripped of their great protection; and as soon as that spirit of pride which they had conceived from the abundance of their possessions has been taken away, they utterly fail and return to the most salutary conversion [ed., confession], having gone astray in their presumptions. Let such people therefore seek remedies and expose their own wounds, so that they may be healed, and let them say: “Hear me, O Lord, for my spirit has failed; do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. CXLII, 7). The Lord provides them with a beneficial medicine. For once the spirit of wickedness by which they were inflamed in their error has been removed, they must return to their own dust [Col. 0739C]—that is, to humble confession, in which they acknowledge the neediness of their frailty—and they begin to be more fortunate when they depart from their presumption. Here, however, the Lord’s administration by which the world is governed must be examined: with what brevity, or with what precision, it has been described [mss. A, B, F: “everything has been described”]. For when he regards us, all things that will profit us follow; and when he turns away, human need, stripped of salutary protection, is overcome.

Verse 30. Send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth. Behold, the medicine that was awaited has come forth. Those who humbly acknowledged themselves to be dust have indeed been restored; this happens to those who, repaired by divine grace, are shown to have escaped the dangers of death. The Lord creates us as often as he deigns to restore us from the oldness of sin into the new man, as it is read in the fiftieth psalm: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. L, 12). Observe also that where we failed, he called us “our dust”; but where we are restored, he professes it to be the Spirit of the Lord, so that no one may claim for his own merits what he has received as a gift from the Creator. Let the sacrilegious hear that the Holy Spirit is the Creator; for he says: “Send forth your spirit, and they will be created.” Hear also elsewhere where the Holy Spirit is declared to be the Creator; Job says: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job XXXIII, 4). For by calling him divine, he clearly demonstrates that the Spirit is both God and Creator.

Verse 31. May the glory of the Lord be forever and ever; the Lord will rejoice in his works. The good teacher still teaches this very point, lest we go astray in exaltation, desiring that he may be what can never at any time fail. For it says: “May the glory of the Lord be”—not that of anyone else. “Forever and ever,” that is, eternally, because there is no end to his praise: in this age the Lord has perpetual praise among the faithful, and after this age eternal praise will be rendered by the blessed. “He will rejoice” is a promise of the future, not of the present. Observe also that wherever he mentions “works,” he says “his,” not “your,” lest, after so many admonitions, we follow the mad error of Pelagius, whose unspeakable poison we recognize clearly here, against which the heavenly antidote is so often administered, lest future dangers spread.

Verse 31. He looks upon the earth, and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they will smoke [ed., “will give off smoke”]. He is now speaking of those who, illuminated by the Lord’s grace, tremble at their past sins when they recognize that they have grievously gone astray. But the trembling of the humble is more secure than the insane presumption of the proud. Peter deserved to return to pardon when he was terrified at having committed a great crime. Thus another prophet also says: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2). The Apostle likewise gives this admonition: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II, 12). You see, therefore, how desirable and how firm this trembling is, since it both gives birth to pardon and produces salvation. But observe to whom these things happen: namely, to those whom he himself has deigned to regard. It follows: “He touches the mountains, and they will smoke” [ed., “will give off smoke”]. Here we should understand the mountains as sinners swollen with excessive pride. When they have been struck by the Lord’s indignation and deprived through the loss of worldly possessions, then they hasten to salutary tears and emit from themselves certain smoky clouds of grief, like an incense of sweetness; ascending toward the heights, they are shown to obtain the mercy of the Lord Christ. For here smoke is used in a good sense, since it causes us to reach the grace of absolution.

Verse 32. I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist. Having traversed two sections through various verbal allusions, he comes to a third mode, in which he says that he will sing the Lord’s praises throughout eternity. For when he says, “I will sing to the Lord in my life,” he signifies the time when he seemed to dwell in this world. This life truly becomes life-giving if the Lord’s praises are sung with continual rejoicing. And lest you think that these praises could end with death, he added: “I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist”—that is, in the future age, where existence is perpetual and psalmody has no end. “As long as I exist” is beautifully expressed; for once made immortal, he desires to sing psalms for as long as he exists, and is thereby shown always to wish to proclaim the Lord’s praises. By this indication it has been declared what those will do who have deserved to be happily admitted into that homeland. They will praise the Lord continually, because they will always see him, while that indescribable beauty awakens praise without end from the one who loves.

Verse 33. May my praise be sweet to him; but I will delight in the Lord. These are indeed two things, but both agree with one another in equal partnership. Our praise is sweet to the Lord if we delight in the Lord; and the sweeter he becomes to us, the dearer we become to him [mss. A, B, F: “the more dear”]. For each person discovers within himself what he may be before that Majesty. The one who loves is loved; the negligent person is rejected; the one who desires is sustained. Let the Divinity therefore be most sweet to us, so that our life may also be made acceptable to him. For we are commanded, for our own sake, to love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, so that by that same measure we may deserve, through his gift, to receive love.

Verse 34. Let sinners perish from the earth, and the unjust, so that they are no more. Bless the Lord, my soul. Sinners perish from the earth when, deprived of earthly desire, they are stirred by God’s grace toward better pursuits; and the wicked likewise perish when they cease to be evil. This is more a prayer than a curse, because every righteous person, desiring the Church of God to increase, undoubtedly wishes sinners to be converted—especially when he knows that the desirable coming of the Lord can be delayed until the number of the predestined has been completed. It follows: “Bless the Lord, my soul.” A worthy beginning of the psalm, and a worthy ending: always to bless the one who never ceases at any time to grant benefits to the faithful. This similarity of expression also, unless I am mistaken, like the preceding one, should refer to those who, through the Lord’s favor, have joined the religious beginnings of their life to a glorious end.

## Conclusion of the psalm

We have heard, good king, how many mysteries from the hidden treasury of truth you have poured forth for us. You taught how heaven is stretched out, how waters have been placed above the heavens, and how the moon was made for appointed times [ed., “in time”]; you taught that the sun has recognized its setting as a great mystery. Let those who pursue superfluous studies and are deceived by vain calculations concerning the courses of the stars learn instead that this is the truthful condition of things. Let them hear the heavenly teacher, the truthful instructor, the narrator of his own creation—those who rush after foolish inquiries and, wishing to be disciples of false opinions, have lost the time for learning the truth.

# Exposition of Psalm 104

## Alleluia

This splendid word first made its beginning with the present psalm, and before this you do not find it placed by anyone, although there were many writers among the Hebrews from the beginning. We must know, however, that *Alleluia* is defined as a neuter noun; Saint Jerome also clearly indicates this in his exposition of the same psalm, which we believe he found in the Hebrew sources. Therefore, wherever the occasion arises, we shall follow the rule established by that most learned man, since what has not been altered by the presumption of any language ought to remain one and undivided.

Among them *Alleluia* is said to mean “praise God”: *allelu*, “praise”; *ia* signifies the invisible God. Jerome is said to explain in his letter to Marcella that this is one of the ten names of God. He says:

The first name of God is *El*, that is, “strong.” Next are *Eloim* and *Eloe*, both of which mean “God.” Hence the name is frequently doubled, as in: “God, my God, look upon me” (Ps. XXI, 2); and: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”; and: “God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the dawn” (Ps. LXII, 2), and similar passages. The fourth is *Sabaoth*, which means “of hosts.” The fifth is *Helion*, which we call “the Most High.” The sixth is *Esereheie*, which is read in Exodus: “He who is sent me” (Exod. III, 14). The seventh is *Adonai*, which we generally call “Lord.” The eighth is *Ia*, which is applied only to God and sounds as the final syllable in *Alleluia*. The ninth is the *Tetragrammaton*, which is called ineffable. The tenth is *Saddai*, that is, “strong” and “sufficient for accomplishing all things,” and so forth.

A wholly new title, distinguished by the brevity of its expression; this is votive for the Churches, and fittingly suited to holy festivals. By it the tongue of singers is adorned; the joyful hall of the Lord responds to it, and like an inexhaustible good it is renewed through ever-varying tropes. Therefore the sweet words of the psalms are to be awaited [ed., “desired”], words preceded by so sweet a proclamation. What can follow is clear from this, since the title itself is already praise.

It should further be noted that throughout all these twenty psalms that bear the title *Alleluia*—namely, the present Psalm 104, 105, 106, 110, 111, 112, 113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 134, 135, 145, 146, 147, 148, 149, and 150—the mighty deeds of the Lord are described, and they rejoice in abundant exultation over them [mss. A, B, F: “there should be rejoicing”]. Their number may perhaps, by a corresponding relationship, signify the glory of the New and Old Testaments, so that the power of the Creator ought always and everywhere to be praised. We find no more evident reason why *Alleluia* has been placed in these psalms alone.

## Division of the psalm

Knowing that the Hebrew people had frequently offended the Lord, because they placed their hope in temporal things and benefits, the prophet in the first part admonishes the faithful always to seek him spiritually. In the second, he strengthens their hearts through the examples of the patriarchs, showing that those who served the Lord’s command were not abandoned by him. In the third, he counts how many and what kinds of benefits divine power had bestowed upon their ancestors, describing Joseph’s dangers and honors and recalling the Hebrews’ entry into Egypt. In the fourth, he relates how the Israelite people, at the Lord’s command through Moses and Aaron, were delivered from their enemies by the various plagues inflicted upon the Egyptians. In the fifth, he describes how many benefits the Lord bestowed upon the Hebrews in the wilderness, so that they might not rejoice in temporal goods but, softened by great gifts, might guard his justifications and law with devoted hearts. Thus the length of the psalm is sweetened by the concise division into its several parts.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1

Confess to the Lord, and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. The order of the statements in this verse consists of three parts. First he says, “Confess to the Lord,” that is, praise him, and obtain the favor of the Divinity for yourselves through good deeds. For to praise the Lord is precisely to offer him honor with the mouth and to carry out his commands through one’s works. Here “confession” must be understood as that which never ceases to celebrate the Lord’s praises, since the following words also declare such a vow and action.

Then he urges that the Lord be invoked, so that after the ministry of most holy praise we may be graciously heard. Something good must be offered first, so that the Judge may hear us with favor. Third he says, “Proclaim his works among the nations.” This can suitably apply to glorious evangelists, most holy apostles, and now to priests, who are known to proclaim his mighty deeds throughout all the nations.

### Verse 2

Sing to him and sing psalms to him; tell of all his wonders. He explains what he said above, “Confess to the Lord.” “Sing” refers to hymns being offered; “sing psalms” refers to pious works being carried out. He says that the wonders are to be recounted only after these two things have first been offered. “All” signifies the things he is about to mention. It is not within human power to recount everything that divine power does, as he will say in Psalm 105: “Who can speak of the powers of the Lord or make all his praises heard?” (Ps. CV, 2). But this figure of speech is called “the whole from a part,” which you will frequently find in the divine Scriptures. Otherwise the Gospel statement could not rightly be understood: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14), as though he had not also assumed a soul, which he specially deigned to save.

### Verse 3

Glory in his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Lest anyone perhaps claim credit for himself when he does something good, the careful teacher warns the frail, saying that one must glory not in oneself but in the Lord, so that they may avoid false boasting when they recognize that these things have been granted by the Divinity. Thus it is also read in another psalm: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. XXXIII, 3).

He does not forbid us to be praised, since such a thing cannot be denied to good actions; rather, he commands that we be praised in the Lord, who grants the things we perform well. And so that they might draw consolation from this, he added: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice”—that is, let it rejoice because the Lord is praised, not because anyone is praised for his own ability. It should indeed be our chief and glorious concern when the name of the one who bestows upon us benefits that will profit us is exalted. Hence it was the height of shamelessness for certain people to speak against this; against them not merely frequent testimonies but almost the whole law has been brought forward.

### Verse 4

Seek the Lord, and be strengthened; seek his face always. He urges those who have chosen to seek him to strengthen themselves for future rewards. But this desire and this seeking must not end here at any particular time, since he added, “always,” especially since it is written: “The one who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke II, 10). When he says, “Seek his face,” he signifies his presence, which only the humble and devoted person seeks. No one can desire the Judge unless he trusts in his goodness; and when he desires his presence, he restrains himself from evil action.

The Apostle sought the face of the Judge when he said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will render to me on that day” (II Tim. IV, 7–8). Such a person therefore rightly sought the face of the Judge, having foreseen that he would be crowned through the Lord’s mercy.

### Verse 5

Remember his wonders that he performed, his signs, and the judgments of his mouth. He comes to the second part, where he recounts the names and benefits of the patriarchs, so that the devoted people may perceive that no one served the Lord with empty devotion. The “wonders” refer to the division of the Red Sea; the “signs” to the plagues he sent upon Egypt; “the judgments of his mouth,” because he fulfilled everything that he is recognized to have promised to his servant Moses. Thus, in a single verse, he briefly presents in advance, as a proposition, what he will discuss more fully below. Yet he prefers this whole passage to be understood of Christ the Lord. This argument is called one from the person.

### Verse 6

The offspring of Abraham, his servant; the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones. What he said above, “Remember,” must be supplied. It must be carefully examined that the prophet, with great discrimination, calls the offspring of Abraham “servants,” while he declares the sons of Jacob to be the Lord’s chosen ones. The contumacious Jews, whom he prefers to have understood here, were the offspring of Abraham according to the flesh; he rightly calls them servants, since, because of their unbelief, they refused to be sons. To them the Lord himself says: “If you were Abraham’s sons, you would do the works of Abraham” (John VIII, 39). By the sons of Jacob he signifies the most faithful Christians, who are known to be heirs of the Lord.

### Verse 7

He himself is the Lord our God; his judgments are throughout all the earth. The offspring of Abraham and the offspring of Jacob are admonished to believe that our Savior is not the God of one nation but the Lord of all the earth. For just as the Church has been spread everywhere, so his judgments have undoubtedly been propagated throughout the world. By saying, “He himself is the Lord,” he urges us to understand the one whom the Jewish people decreed should be crucified. But those who do not heed this statement thereby declare themselves specifically alienated from the patriarchs.

### Verse 8

He remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations. “He remembered” when he fulfilled his promises. “Forever,” that is, unto eternity, because whatever the Lord has promised will remain with perpetual firmness. “His covenant” signifies the preaching of the prophets, who foretold the incarnation of the Word. It follows: “that he commanded.” To command is to speak something through another person, which certainly happened when the prophets were given the task of prophesying future things. “For a thousand generations” uses a finite number for an infinite one, although it is enclosed within the end of this age, in which one human generation succeeds another in its appointed time.

### Verse 9

Which he established with Abraham, and his oath with Isaac.

### Verse 10

And he established it for Jacob as a commandment, and for Israel as an eternal covenant. This responds to what he said above, “his covenant.” For the things that were promised or sworn to the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac in the Old Testament, he established—that is, confirmed—for Jacob and Israel, namely, in the New Testament, which is eternal. It has often already been said that Jacob and Israel frequently signify the Christian era. The New Testament is properly called eternal because no other covenant will ever succeed it; in it the perfection of all the promises has been completed.

### Verse 11

Saying: To you I will give the land of Canaan, the measuring-cord of your inheritance. Canaan is interpreted as “humble.” Therefore he suitably signifies that Christians will receive the land of the humble. This is what he said above, “the eternal covenant.” For the land of humility and submission is received by the faithful in such a way that it is held as an eternal gift.

The measuring-cord of the inheritance signifies the twisting constraints of this world, which the Lord dissolved through his passion for the salvation of all. His assumption of flesh is our inheritance, in which we receive the eternal patrimonies of heavenly life, if we deserve to believe these things firmly and wholly. This comparison is drawn from those among whom fields and possessions were divided by a stretched cord.

### Verse 12

When they were few in number, very few, and resident aliens in it.

### Verse 13

And they passed from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people. He comes to the third part, in which he consequently enumerates how many benefits divine power bestowed upon the patriarchs. Indeed, observe what follows.

### Verse 14

He did not permit anyone to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake.

### Verse 15

Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets. Here he signifies the time when the king of Egypt was divinely warned not to presume to harm Abraham; it is clear that the same thing also happened with Isaac. Thus divine protection is plainly demonstrated, so that their safety was provided not by human strength but by heavenly favor.

It must also be carefully examined that he chose to call the patriarchs mentioned above “anointed ones,” although anointing had not yet been instituted. This matter began with Saul. But since they were Christians in spirit and are shown to have been devoted to Christ’s faith—as the Lord says concerning Abraham, “He desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII, 56)—they were rightly called by the sacred name, since they were already shown to love the faith of Christ. Indeed, the Lord’s own words are recorded: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

### Verse 16

And he summoned famine upon the land, and destroyed every support of bread. He signifies the time of Pharaoh, when savage famine raged in Egypt for seven years. Although famine is not a substance but merely the departure of abundance, just as night is called the absence of the sun, it is nevertheless said to have been summoned as though it were some subsisting person who could hear. But it is the custom of the divine Scriptures to speak in this way, as in the Apostle’s statement: “He calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. IV, 17).

It follows: “and he destroyed every support of bread,” that is, he brought the grain harvest to nothing. This is recognized to be the support of human beings, just as he said in the preceding psalm: “And bread strengthens the human heart” (Ps. CIII, 15).

### Verse 17

He sent a man before them; Joseph was sold into slavery. Before the patriarchs whom he mentioned above, he sent Joseph, whom he rightly called a man because, after suffering much, he endured everything manfully. It must also be considered that he says the Lord sent him, although he was sold through the wickedness of his brothers. God knows how to make good use of the evils committed by others; and just as sinners turn his commandments into abominations, so, by his ordering, the deeds of the wicked are transferred to prosperous outcomes.

Joseph, though sold, reached glory through servitude, and afterward showed mercy to the very brothers who had cruelly determined to destroy him. Thus all the adversities that befell him turned out favorably, so that the sending was the Lord’s, while the sale of Joseph was deceitful. He himself said to his brothers: “For your salvation God sent me into Egypt” (Gen. XLV, 5); and again he says: “You indeed intended evil against me, but God turned it to good” (Gen. L, 20).

What he suffered he explains in sequence. The order of the words is as follows: “He sent before them the man Joseph, who was sold into slavery.” Here we must supply “who,” so that the sentence may be understood as complete.

### Verse 18

They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul [ms. F: “his soul”]. Joseph was indeed confined in prison by Potiphar, Pharaoh’s prefect, but it is not recorded that he received fetters. Yet it could have happened that one who was shut up in a dungeon was also bound with iron chains, especially one who had been accused of so serious a crime. Nor is there any contradiction with the account that he was placed over the prisoners through the jailer’s compassion; these things could have occurred first, and those later.

Therefore, the person who believes that truth is present in each individual passage understands the divine Scriptures reasonably. For in Psalm 103 also it is said: “He makes his angels spirits,” although this is not read in Genesis. But the Holy Spirit omits certain things in an earlier account so that what follows may find room for grace, declaring something new while preserving the truth of the matter.

Thus he reports that his feet were humbled in fetters, to indicate the affliction of his body. He added: “Iron passed through his soul,” so that his soul also might not be shown to have been exempt from punishment. Although it is subjected to suffering through its sympathy with the body, it has its own punishments as well, when it is tormented by grievous thought.

His soul passed through iron when he was reduced to these straits, lest, amid the evils he suffered unjustly, the charges of falsehood should prevail against him. Here iron indicates the tribulation of harsh necessity, which ranges through the fevered soul while, anxious about the future, it already suffers the evils that it never ceases to fear.

There is a similar expression in the Gospel, where Simeon says to Mary: “And a sword will pass through your own soul also” (Luke II, 35), signifying that the glorious mother would have the sorrow of the Lord’s passion. We believe that this kind of expression should be noted among the distinctive features of the divine Scriptures.

### Verse 19

Until his word came. The utterance of the Lord inflamed him. This verse is joined to the preceding statement. For he says that Joseph’s anxiety was most grievous until the time came when his word would be sought by King Pharaoh for the interpretation of a dream. Then he found glory and joyfully escaped the prison gates.

But when he said “his word,” he indicates the personal voice of the speaker. Yet what was bestowed upon him by divine inspiration was not his own. Hence it follows: “The utterance of the Lord inflamed him.” It inflamed him by stirring him vigorously to speak, so that he might declare future things before the prince with confidence in the truth. Within, he received the light of a heavenly flame, so that he might foresee things surpassing the wise men and teachers of that kingdom.

### Verse 20

The king sent and released him; the prince of peoples, and he dismissed him. “Sent” signifies the ministers who obey royal commands. He calls him “the king,” namely Pharaoh, in whose kingdom Joseph had been imprisoned. “Released” means from the guilt by which he had been held bound.

It follows: “The prince of peoples, and he dismissed him.” This prince is Pharaoh himself, whom he previously called king; but for the grace of expression he varied the words. “He dismissed him,” that is, he caused him to leave the prison gates, so that the one who had freed the ruler of the lands from the straits of his thoughts would now in no way suffer confinement. But lest it appear that only release had been granted to him, he also states with what honor he was endowed.

### Verse 21

And he appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possession.

### Verse 22

To instruct his princes as he himself did, and to teach his elders wisdom. In these two verses he clearly explains what authority Pharaoh gave Joseph. He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possession when he made him ascend into the chariot and had it proclaimed in a most celebrated herald’s voice that he was second lord after the king. This authority is still retained by prefects today, who judge in the place of the sacred authority and are known to possess the greatest power over all the provinces.

In these matters he gave Joseph authority equal to his own. But in the following verse, what he granted is recognized to be above him, for he says: “to instruct his princes as he himself did.” We must understand this according to the pagan interpretation of Pharaoh, who believed that the leading men of his people could attain such wisdom that they too might deserve to be interpreters of dreams, and that their knowledge could be brought to such a level of learning that, consulted about a doubtful matter, they could speak with certainty.

For if he had handed them over to the holy man as disciples in faith—whereby it would be clear that he pleased the Lord—the order of the Synagogue would have been newly established for them. But since no such thing is read, he should be considered to have desired not religion but only the glory of Joseph’s divination, in the manner of the pagans. They are eager for future things but do not seek to understand from where the revelation itself proceeds [ms. G and ed.: “eager for future things”].

### Verse 23

And Israel entered into Egypt, and Jacob dwelt in the land of Canaan. He appropriately follows the order of events, because after the things that have been mentioned, at Pharaoh’s command Joseph’s kinship was led into the lands of Egypt, under the same ordering authority. The graceful text of Genesis explains this (Gen. XLVI).

But the one called Israel is also Jacob. Yet lest he repeat the same words, he varied the expression of his account by using different names. For Israel, after departing from Egypt, dwelt in the land of Canaan. Canaan was the son of Ham and grandson of Noah, from whom the Egyptians are read to have drawn their origin.

### Verse 24

And he greatly increased his people, and strengthened them above their enemies. He increased his people through the fertility of childbirth, when scarcely any woman there was without bearing a child. But he strengthened them above their enemies when, as they increased, the Egyptian multitude was grievously afflicted by the well-known plagues. Here, by way of a summary proposition, the things that happened are stated in brief. How they occurred individually he explains next.

### Verse 25

He turned their heart so that they hated his people and dealt deceitfully with his servants. He comes to the fourth part, in which he recalls that the Egyptians had the fiercest envy toward the Hebrews and subjected them to the harshest labors.

By granting prosperity to the Israelite people, the Lord turned the hearts of the Egyptians toward hatred and deceit—not because he himself is the author of evil, but because, by granting benefits to others, he stirred minds inclined toward evil. For it is necessary that wicked people swell with envy at the prosperity of others when they know that they cannot deserve similar things. Thus it happened in the sacrifices of Cain and Abel, when he rejected the sacrifice of one and gladly accepted that of the other.

It follows: “that they might deal deceitfully with his servants.” It was inevitable that, after hatred had been conceived, the savage people would proceed to deceitful schemes. This refers to the time when they commanded them to make bricks, while straw was withheld even though the labor was doubled, and to the other sufferings that the Hebrew people, devoted to the Lord, endured under that most savage domination.

### Verse 26

He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he himself chose. It is clear that the Lord sent these men to Pharaoh as witnesses, so that he might permit the people pleasing to him to depart unharmed.

O immeasurable compassion of the Almighty! He asked a frail human being to accomplish what no creature could oppose according to his ordering, so that he might truly teach us, who are weak, with what moderation we ought to live, since the holy Creator is known to have carried out his will with such clemency.

Let us also attend to this manner of expression as proper to the divine Scripture. It would have been enough to say “whom he chose,” but he added “himself,” so that this too might be explained more clearly. This form of expression is found very frequently in the divine Scriptures, as in the statement: “In whom he dwelt, in him” (Ps. LXXIII, 2).

### Verse 27

He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Canaan. “He placed” means that he set within them—namely, Moses and Aaron—the words of signs and wonders which they proclaimed that the Lord was going to perform.

Signs are like traces of future or past events; wonders, however, refer to marvelous occurrences that had not previously existed in the order of things. A *prodigium*—“wonder”—is so called from the fact that it speaks of what lies ahead. But these signs and wonders were performed among the Egyptians so that, as the authority of many Fathers says, they might foreshadow something for the Christian people who would follow. We shall point this out most suitably in its proper places.

### Verse 28

He sent darkness, and it became dark for them, because they embittered his words. It is indeed read that the Egyptians endured the darkness of the air among the other plagues. But we should understand more suitably that their hearts were darkened, since they despised the Lord’s commands.

“Embittered” means that they received them bitterly, or certainly rejected them with insulting abominations. For in the enumeration of the plagues themselves he made an appropriate beginning. They could not have proceeded to the remaining plagues unless, with their senses darkened, they had fallen into the deepest blindness. The conduct of sinners shows that the same thing still happens today.

### Verse 29

He turned their waters into blood, and killed their fish. He speaks of the second plague, which is recorded as the first in the history of Exodus; but the plagues themselves announced signs of future destruction.

“He turned their waters into blood,” because they were destined to perish among the streams of the Red Sea. Their fish were killed, so that no hope of life might appear to remain for human beings, when what had been nourished in its native element was found dead amid the waters.

### Verse 30

He sent frogs into their land, and into the chambers of their kings. This is the third plague. He gave them the company of frogs, because they too were shown to be destined to receive a watery place. Their kings also—that is, their rulers—were not exempt from this sign, since they were destined to die by being submerged in the depths of the abyss.

But this appears more marvelous than the other things: that not even the houses of the kings were seen to be exempt from this plague, although the services of many attendants could have removed such portents from them. This clearly demonstrates that no resources and no forms of assistance can oppose the divine commands.

### Verse 31

“He spoke, and the dog-fly and gnats came throughout all their territories.”

The fourth plague follows: “He spoke, and it came.” These two expressions are joined together with great significance, because no obstacle of delay can withstand the command of the Divinity. For, if you pay close attention even to the very words that seem to be joined together, some delay is nevertheless extended through their syllables. The Lord’s command, however, does not prolong the time, since the will itself is already the effect.

*Cynomyia* signifies a dog-fly, which is altogether more biting than other flies and more violent in its persistence; hence it received a derivative name from an offensive and most savage animal. *Ciniphes* is a kind of gnat, exceedingly troublesome because of its fixed stings, which the common people customarily call *zinzalae*. Let those who swell with foolish pride recognize that that fierce and harsh Pharaoh could not even equal flies, although he boasted of himself because of the great exaltation of his kingdom.

But when he says “throughout all their territories,” he means that no place among the Egyptians was to be regarded as exempt from the destructive calamity.

### Verse 32

“He made their rains hail, and fire consuming in their land” [ms. E and ed., “the earth”].

### Verse 33

“And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered every tree of their territories.”

The fifth vengeance is related. This expression resembles the preceding one, where he says, “He placed among them the words of his signs.” “He placed” signifies “he established and decreed.”

The enumeration of the Egyptians’ plagues still continues: the rain that is given for the fertility of the earth was turned into the harmful devastation of hail, whose blows destroy no less than when a dense mass of stones has fallen. This is shown to be a burning of the fields’ moisture, when, through its harmful impact, it dries out whatever fruits the stony torrent has struck.

“Fire consuming” signifies lightning, which, when raised by a storm, is accustomed to rage. The text continues: “And he struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered every tree of their territories.” What he says—“he struck”—refers back to the preceding matters, whether hail or lightning, which the heavenly power hurls against the earth like hostile weapons.

And lest you think that only fig trees or vines were struck, he added, “every tree of their territories,” so that you would not doubt that the crops too were overturned, once you recognized that even the strength of the trees had been shattered. For greater things contain the meaning of lesser ones.

### Verse 34

“He spoke, and the locust and the young locust came, whose number there was not.”

### Verse 35

“And it consumed every grass of their land and every fruit of their land.”

The sixth plague begins. This expression too is shown to resemble the preceding one: “He spoke, and the dog-fly and gnats came.”

The locust is the parent of the young locust, which it produces through an evil fertility; and this offspring descended with it upon that prey like a summoned army. And lest you think that it had been brought forth without purpose, he says that they consumed every fruit of that land.

### Verse 36

“And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labor.”

He comes to the seventh plague, which, insofar as this psalm is concerned, is the final one; by it the Egyptian people, already defeated by the multitude of their calamities, gave way. For how could those who had lost every pleasant thing and found themselves deprived even of their provisions endure anything further?

Thus one who thinks that the divine commands ought to be resisted perishes grievously, piece by piece.

Here a question seems to arise: why does this psalm mention only seven Egyptian plagues, when ten are described in the account of Exodus? We have frequently said that in the divine Scriptures the whole must be understood from a part, just as it is read in the Gospel: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), as though he had not also assumed a soul, which he graciously undertook especially to save. Thus, when the flesh is mentioned, the soul too is understood to have been assumed along with it; and you find this proclaimed in many passages.

Moreover, the number seven is proved to be perfect through the power of the Holy Spirit. Therefore he rightly enclosed the ten plagues within the relation of the number seven, so that you might understand the whole to be perfect, although you recognized that only a part had been mentioned.

Furthermore, it was appropriate to describe a familiar matter in varied expression, since he was proclaiming both the punishments of the Egyptians and the same number of benefits bestowed upon the Hebrews. Thus the variation does not make the account different; rather, the cause of the variation makes it especially beautiful.

Or else—as Father Augustine prefers—the praise is free from the law governing narrative. One who composes history must mention everything in full; but one who praises is sufficiently served by touching upon a few things from among many. Therefore he speaks briefly of the earlier events, because here he is not teaching those who do not know, but recalling matters to those who retain them.

And since, in the division that follows, he is going to say that the Lord bestowed seven benefits upon the Hebrew people, he first stated that the Egyptian enemies received seven plagues, so that the number itself—as I may suppose—might establish in this psalm a correspondence between good and evil things.

### Verse 37

“And he brought them out with silver and gold, and there was not a feeble person among their tribes.”

After enumerating the plagues that he inflicted upon the Egyptians, he comes to the fifth section, in which he says that an equal number of benefits was conferred upon the Hebrews. For he says: “And he brought them out with silver and gold.”

The first benefit, therefore, was that a people exhausted by long servitude should not depart destitute and empty-handed. We read that, at the Lord’s command, the Israelite people received gold and silver from the Egyptians as they departed, so that this might appear not to have been a sudden theft but the reward of long labor. And since there can be no doubt that the Lord commands all things justly, what is known to have been fulfilled at his command appears to have occurred without guilt.

Therefore the second benefit follows: amid the necessity of that migration, no one could be afflicted by bodily weakness, so that they might vigorously fulfill everything the Lord commanded them.

### Verse 38

“Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them had fallen upon them.”

We must examine this verse carefully. It is clear that, when the Hebrew people departed, Egypt did not rejoice, since it judged that they ought to be pursued. But after those who had decided to pursue the Hebrews had been drowned, then those who remained in Egypt rejoiced greatly, because they themselves had not suffered a similar fate.

For he gives this reason when he says, “because fear of them had fallen upon them.” That fear itself was such that the elements seemed, in a certain way, to have fought in favor of the Hebrew nation.

Observe also that, through the rhetorical figure of metonymy, which in Latin is called *transnominatio*, he says that Egypt rejoiced, not the Egyptians. Through the thing that contains, the thing contained is indicated.

### Verse 39

“He spread out a cloud for their protection, and fire to give them light by night.”

Both gifts are shown to have been granted against the harshness of the weather. The cloud was given to temper the heat of the sun; fire was granted so that it might remove the darkness of night. This is the third benefit that is known to have been granted to the Israelite people.

### Verse 40

“They asked for meat, and quail came, and he filled them with the bread of heaven.”

Consider how the desires of those who asked were surpassed. The Hebrew people asked for meat and received quails. For it is clear that, both among birds and among four-footed animals, meat is undoubtedly sweeter. Moreover, they asked for one thing, and two came in abundance.

For the text continues: “And he filled them with the bread of heaven.” These events are well known from the reading of Exodus, when quails poured down in the manner of a very dense rain, and manna too was received so that the Jewish people might be satisfied.

But to show that these things had been done as a prefiguration, he did not say “manna,” but “the bread of heaven,” so that the coming of the Lord Savior might be perceived in that gift. For he is the living bread who came down from heaven (John 6:51).

Indeed, “manna” means, as was explained in Psalm 77, “What is this?” Removing the question contained in that name—that is, expressing what the question about manna sought—he said, “He filled them with the bread of heaven.” Thus both the Lord of heaven is indicated, and what manna is becomes clearly understood [ed., “shown”].

### Verse 41

“He split the rock, and waters flowed; rivers went through the dry land.”

This too was carried out as a figure of the Lord Christ, so that the rock might pour forth abundant waters. For Christ the Lord is the spiritual rock who sends forth life-giving waters, so that the satisfied desire of the soul may no longer endure thirst.

“Rivers went through the dry land” signifies the sinners among the nations, who are rightly called dry because they are dried up by burning sins. These, made green by the Lord’s rain, sprouted into the new person; concerning them the Lord says: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

### Verse 42

“Because he remembered his holy word, which he spoke to Abraham his servant.”

### Verse 43

“And he brought out his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness.”

In these two verses the reason for the miracles mentioned above is related. They are said to have been done because they had been promised to Abraham.

Observe also that he says he brought out his chosen ones with gladness, because those who murmured were struck by the Lord’s anger.

### Verse 44

“And he gave them the territories of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples.”

### Verse 45

“That they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

He comes to the seventh benefit. First, he said that they were brought out with gold and silver; then, that none among them was weakened; third, that the cloud was spread out, providing light in darkness and removing the sun’s heat during the day; fourth, that quail was given; fifth, he relates that they were satisfied with heavenly bread; sixth, that abundant waters flowed forth in the driest places; finally, that the truth of the promises was fulfilled, so that he gave them the territories of the nations and, in his most abundant mercy, granted them the labors of their enemies.

What he calls “the territories of the nations” appears to refer to possession of lands; “the labors of the peoples” refers to riches gathered over a long period.

And lest mortal hearts cling to present things, he added spiritual goods, so that they ought both to seek and to keep his commandments, lest they place their hope entirely in those things. For although such things may delight them for a time, they do not lead them to the kingdom of heaven, as the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all people the most miserable” (1 Corinthians 15:19).

His ordinances are that we love God with our whole heart, love our neighbors as ourselves, honor our father, cherish our son, and observe the other acts of righteousness commanded in the various circumstances of life. He urges them to keep these [ed., “to be kept”], because their command is clear and absolute.

His law, however, was that one ought to rest on the Sabbath, sacrifice a year-old lamb at Passover, have the priests approach the altar in sacred vestments, and observe the other commands known to have been given by the Lord in this manner. But these things and those like them must be sought not bodily but spiritually.

For this reason he added “seek,” since he knew that the commandments of the law are a shadow and mirror of future things.

### Alleluia

Do not regard as insignificant the fact that, in some psalms, “Alleluia” is placed at the beginning and the end, while in others it is written only as a title. Those that agree at the beginning and the end should, as I think, be referred to the interpretation that we said applies to psalms which likewise conclude at beginning and end, such as the preceding Psalms 102 and 103.

Or perhaps this is because what is repeated as a sentence is always poured forth more expressively, as in: “Not so the wicked, not so”; and “Let it be, let it be”; or “Amen, amen, I say to you”; and “Abba, Father”—for *Abba* means “Father.”

Perhaps there is also another reason that remains hidden. Concerning this matter we have been unable to learn anything else from our teachers, nor have we been permitted to think anything further.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Behold, both alleluias have been sung. The course of the psalm is complete, a psalm filled with heavenly praise, which truthfully recounts past events and salutarily admonishes us concerning the future.

The Egyptians suffered punishments fully deserving of them; the Jews received heavenly gifts. Now let each of us await the recompense of those whose example he imitates.

We must examine with the light of the heart what has been placed at the end of the psalm, so that with the whole attention of our mind we may be directed toward the Lord’s ordinances and his law. For even if we receive temporal goods, like Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other faithful men who flourished in abundant prosperity, we ought rather to direct our attention toward that by which we may be led to the kingdoms of heaven.

Those things that make the world appear delightful have no place in eternity.

We must also remember that this psalm is the second among those which, while describing the miracles bestowed upon the Hebrews, declare through the allegorical figure—one that says one thing but signifies another—the mysteries that were to come for the Christian people [ms. G. and ed., “allegorical”].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 106

### Alleluia

Behold, once again the joys of *Alleluia* have returned to us; behold, it is briefly commanded that the Lord be praised with the jubilation of the entire psalm.

But let us observe that, in comparison with the preceding statements, neither the title nor the reason is known to have changed. The title is *Alleluia*; the reason is confession, which in a marvelous way is entirely fertile in the praises of the Lord.

How many mouths have been opened by this! Through it Moses with the men, and his sister Miriam with the women, celebrated the crossing of the Red Sea with divine praise. Through it Deborah sang beforehand with joyful exultation. Many prophets too poured forth various songs in acknowledgment of so great a miracle.

And rightly so, because these great deeds bear witness to the mysteries of the whole of human redemption. We are rescued from the Egyptians when, by God’s gift, we are freed from the works of the devil. We cross the Red Sea when we receive the mysteries of baptism. We are fed in the desert when, by the granting of divine grace, we are satisfied with the abundance of good things in this world. We are led into the promised land when, by the gift of heavenly mercy, we enter that blessed homeland.

Thus such a reason is rightly proclaimed again and again, since it is adorned with the prefiguration of so many great deeds.

### Division of the Psalm

A confessing Hebrew people is introduced, one that, having abandoned the unbelief of its fathers, was led by the Lord’s mercy to piety, so that we may understand that, once converted, they too rightly sing *Alleluia* for their redemption.

In the first section, therefore, the prophet asks that he be joined to the people pleasing to God, which was to be gathered from the nations through the coming of the Lord Savior.

In the second, he enumerates the sins of their fathers, which they committed in Egypt: they did not perceive the Lord’s miracles with an upright heart, yet he affirms that the merciful Lord freed them from their enemies.

In the third, he relates that they returned to their eagerness for sin, but says that the Lord was appeased by the prayers of his chosen servant Moses.

In the fourth, he asserts that their iniquities were repeated, and that the Lord had decided to destroy them unless he were appeased by the supplication of his servant Phinehas.

In the fifth, he recalls that Moses was provoked by them at the waters of Contradiction, and afterward that they cruelly killed their sons in the worship of idols. Therefore the Lord, more intensely angered, handed them over to the servitude of the nations; then, taking pity on them, he made them glorious in the sight of their enemies.

In the sixth, he prays concerning what he knew would come to pass: that the Catholic Church would be gathered from all nations and celebrate the Lord’s praises together in eternal exultation.

Now let us walk through the sections of the psalm along the clear paths of its divisions.

### Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

Just as the preceding psalm declared in its first verse that confession ought to be directed toward the praises of the Lord, so this one too indicates that confession is to be applied as a remedy for repentance.

But there is no doubt that this also pertains to the Lord’s praises, since it is a greater glory of mercy to spare one who confesses than to preserve one who lives without offense.

The repentant congregation of the Hebrews, corrected by divine inspiration, speaks to the rest of the people, so that, condemned for the perversity of their ancient error, they may return to divine clemency.

And lest anyone be frightened by the multitude of his sins [ed., “the multitude of his sin”], he added, “For he is good.” Who would hesitate to return to one whom he hears can help him most quickly?

The Lord is rightly called good: he feeds the one who sins, awaits the one who goes astray, “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” [ms. G. and ed., “the impious”] (Matthew 5:45).

This is also declared by the voice of Truth himself: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

He added, “For his mercy is forever.” Once the good Lord has been heard of, lest human negligence withdraw from diligent and earnest supplication, he states the reason for the remedy, so that one ought to hasten by his gift toward swift confession of the Lord.

“Forever” signifies the course of this life, in which all who sin are wretched, and in which it is permitted for our hearts to be converted and to seek mercy. For confession of sin is condemnation there where judgment is already established.

### Verse 2

“Who can speak of the powers of the Lord? Who can make all his praises heard?”

This people, whom we have described as filled with the contemplation of divine works, denies that the human mind can comprehend what it ought to narrate fully concerning that Majesty.

For “who” signifies “no one.” Who possesses either the intellect to conceive or the tongue to express such immensity, so that it could be narrated by a single mouth? Here one may rightly say: “Not even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, a voice of iron.”

He also added, “Who can make all his praises heard?” Here too “who” must be understood, so that the sentence may be complete.

The wording is beautiful in its variation: “Who can make all his praises heard?” For only those things can be heard that are shown to have been spoken. This too is to be regarded as one of the proper modes of expression.

### Verse 3

“Blessed are those who keep judgment and practice righteousness at all times.”

After denying that the Lord’s praises can be comprehended, he gives a statement by which the human race may console itself: since it cannot fulfill that task, it should at least hasten to keep this command.

For one keeps judgment who judges rightly among others; one practices righteousness who acts impartially. Or he calls blessed those who keep judgment in faith and demonstrate righteousness in their works.
