But observe that he added “at all times,” just as the Gospel says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13).

They are rightly called blessed, then—those who keep the Lord’s commandments with a pure mind.

This is the third kind of definition, which in Greek is called *poiotēs* [ποιότης], and in Latin *qualitativa* (“qualitative”): by saying what something is like, it shows what it is.

### Verse 4

“Remember us, Lord, in the favor shown to your people; visit us with your salvation.”

The devout pray that they may be counted among those who have pleased the Lord through faithful works. For we know that the Israelite people were partly rebellious and partly steadfast in the Lord’s commandments.

Therefore these people earnestly pray that they may be numbered among those to whom eternal blessedness can be attributed by the grace of the Divinity.

And so that their faith might be recognized as most perfect, they desire to be visited by the Lord Savior, through whose coming they knew they would be saved.

He is the Savior of whom blessed Simeon says:

“Now you release your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the nations and the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2:29–31).

### Verse 5

“To see the goodness of your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of your nation, that you may be praised with your inheritance.”

This is what they were asking: to be visited by the saving Lord, so that they might see his goodness, which he was to bestow upon the chosen through the gift of his coming, and so that they might rejoice with the Christian people, who were to rejoice over his incarnation [ed., “who was to rejoice”].

For this is the Lord’s nation, gathered from the diversity of the nations, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd.

The most delightful fruit of these things follows: that the Lord should be praised with his inheritance. The two are joined together, because in the praise of his Lord the faithful servant [ed., “people”] is undoubtedly praised, just as it was said in the preceding psalm: “Praise the Lord in his holy name.”

Therefore this faithful people hastened toward the sight of the Lord with such desire and joined itself to the Christian people with such love that it is wrong to think that it did not behold in spirit the one whom we know it sought with such grace, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

### Verse 6

“We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity.”

He comes to the second narrative, in which the people mentioned above prostrate themselves in humble satisfaction, so that the confession declared at the beginning of the psalm may be seen here.

For he says that he sinned with his fathers because he was constituted in their loins and origin. Although a long period had elapsed, during which their fathers had received the miracles performed in Egypt bodily, without responding to the Lord with any satisfaction, and although the generation of the present psalm was much later, there is no doubt that they lamented those sins whose burden they were shown to bear because of the wickedness of their parents.

The Pelagian heresy does not accept this, since it thinks that original sin could in no way reach Adam’s offspring. Those sin with their ancestors who do not separate themselves by the Lord’s grace from their ancestors’ offense.

Father Augustine refuted this through the most diligent argumentation in his books (*Book I Against Julian*).

But now, when the mind had repented after being stirred by the Lord, it rightly wished the sins of its parents to be wiped away from itself, since it had begun to separate itself from their obligations.

And so that the firmness of the purest confession might be evident, he confirms the same point through a threefold repetition. “We have sinned” means “we have acted unjustly”; “we have acted unjustly” means “we have committed iniquity.”

For each person is absolved more quickly in proportion as he vigorously condemns himself.

This figure is called *schēsis onomatōn* [σχῆσις ὀνομάτων], that is, “a multitude of joined names,” signifying one thing through different words.

Another interpretation has also been handed down to us at this point: one sins with his ancestors when he does not avoid similar offenses but commits the same things he recognizes his predecessors to have committed; nevertheless, the guilt of original sin cannot be excluded from posterity except through the grace of the Lord.

### Verse 7

“Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders, and they did not remember the multitude of your mercy, and they provoked him as they went up to the Red Sea.”

There are two things that commend the benefits bestowed: understanding and memory. Both are denied to the faithless.

“They did not understand” is expressed with beautiful precision. They saw what was being done, but they did not recognize the reason for which it was being done.

For the Egyptians were struck by ten plagues so that the Hebrew nation, devoted to the future Decalogue, might serve it. They were dismissed by Pharaoh so that they too might leave the devil with his ministers.

But, looking at what had been done only in bodily terms, they did not seek the rewards of spiritual grace.

They did not remember the Lord’s mercy when, seeing Pharaoh’s army before the Red Sea had been divided, they believed they had lost the means of escape and spoke against Moses, saying that it would have been better for them to remain subject to harsh servitude than for the entire people to perish in the wilderness.

After this it naturally followed that they provoked the Lord as they went up to the Red Sea, since they did not believe that what they heard his omnipotence promise could happen.

Thus it came about that they neither understood the Lord’s power nor retained his benefits with devoted hearts.

“Provoked” is well placed, as though they had made one who was quiet and appeased become hostile and angry toward themselves.

“They went up to the Red Sea” is evidently expressed according to the position of the lands, since Egypt is said to be lower than all the surrounding regions, and those who departed from it seemed to seek higher places.

### Verse 8

“And he saved them for his name’s sake, that he might make known his power.”

By saying “for his name’s sake,” he seems to me to indicate the Lord Savior, whose very name is fittingly associated with saving those in danger. For when God frees sinners, he does so not because of their merits, but in order to display the power of his name, so that he may plainly appear merciful when he bestows abundant benefits on the undeserving. When he says, “he made known his power,” this is not to eyes of flesh, of course, but to those who see by spiritual reflection. For if he had made it known to all, the stubborn people would by no means have sinned through unbelief.

### Verse 9

“And he rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up; and he led them through the deep waters as through a wilderness.”

He called the hidden command of the Divinity a “rebuke,” because nowhere in Exodus is the sea read to have been rebuked by the Lord’s voice. He accomplishes by hidden movements everything that he commands, and, as though speaking to hearers, addresses things that have not been given understanding. So great is the power of his command that things unable to hear nevertheless have power to obey.

We must not understand the sea’s being dried up as applying to its whole extent, but only insofar as it opened a way for them. Indeed, the miracle was greater because the liquid waves stood with their sides cut away, and the waters did not flow but stood fast with a kind of mountainous solidity. The words, “and he led them through the deep waters as through a wilderness,” follow. A wilderness is especially that which is made desolate by an inundation of waters, so that no animal can live there because of its innate peril of dryness. The Hebrews were therefore led through the abyss as through desert places parched by excessive barrenness, showing that that path through the waters was so dried up that it could become a dusty roadway.

### Verse 10

“And he saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and redeemed them from the hand of their enemies.”

Even if he had merely freed them from another’s power, this would have been a benefit; but he increased the greatness of the gift by saying, “from the hand of those who hated them,” for they could certainly not spare those whom they attacked with cruelty. They plainly dreaded those on whose account they had suffered so many plagues and were deprived of their possessions.

This is also understood of the united host of demons, which both hates and strikes the human race with the spur of sins. The text continues, “and redeemed them from the hand of their enemies.” If you wish to take this literally, it does not seem capable of fitting: to free the Hebrews, he gave the Egyptians no price; rather, because of their obstinacy he doubled harsh plagues upon them. But let us believe that this was said in the spirit of prophecy concerning Christian times, when the Lord Savior redeemed sinners, held liable, from the devil’s rule by his precious blood.

### Verse 11

“And the water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained.”

This indeed appears, without controversy, to be understood literally, since the familiar account is recorded in Exodus. But “not one of them remained” does not refer to the entire Egyptian nation, but only to the multitude that pursued them, which is shown to have perished there to the last man. Egyptians remained who rejoiced at their departure, as he said in the preceding psalm: “Egypt rejoiced at their departure”; but these were, of course, those who had not shared the same disaster.

### Verse 12

“And they believed his words, and sang his praises.”

By saying, after so great a miracle, “they believed,” he shows the hardness of their heart: they preferred to believe not before the event but after the miracles had been accomplished. Although it is good to assent to things seen, it is far better to have believed promises, as he says to Thomas in the Gospel: “Because you have seen, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

What he adds, “and they sang his praises,” signifies the hymn of Exodus which says, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exodus 15:1), and the other things which the Hebrew people sang with great exultation after the miracle had been performed, as was related in the exposition of the title.

### Verse 13

“They acted quickly, and forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel.”

He comes to the third narrative. “They acted quickly” is as though he said: they were changed with the utmost speed, so that those who sang the Lord’s praises for the miracles bestowed upon them shortly afterward took up impious murmurings against him. “They did not wait for his counsel” when they conceived despair before his prepared benefits had arrived. The Lord, who had freed them by such great and numerous miracles, had allowed them to suffer no lack of provisions. But they anticipated the heavenly counsel, because they were unwilling to await what he had arranged, in the manner of human frailty, which, while thinking to provide for itself through excessive haste, rashly anticipates the ordering of the Divinity.

### Verse 14

“And they desired desires in the wilderness, and tempted God in the dry place.”

This was how they failed to wait for his counsel: in the wilderness they sought food in distrust, and asked that water be given them amid murmurings. This figure is called *cacozelon*, that is, “bad affectation,” whenever talent lacks judgment and precipitate speed is deceived by hope of good.

“They desired desires.” This manner of expression is exceedingly frequent in Holy Scripture, as in: “With desire I have desired to eat the Passover with you” (Luke 22:15); “Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die” (Exodus 21:17); and “The Lord has chastened me severely” (Psalm 117:18), and similar examples. The doubled placement of the words displays the excessiveness of the desire.

### Verse 15

“And he gave them their requests [mss. A, B, ‘their request’], and sent satiety into their souls.”

Because they sought temporal things, they rightly received carnal benefits. For we speak of the soul as being satisfied in two ways: when it is refreshed with bodily food because of the weakness of the flesh, and when it is filled with spiritual joy. But here he says that their souls were fattened with meat and drink, so that the very will which had sinned through despair might be overcome when the desired things appeared.

### Verse 16

“And they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord.”

Rebellion followed fullness of belly, which often produces causes from which destructive dangers arise. We say that someone is provoked when he is stirred to anger either by the wicked actions of others or by most bitter words. This signifies the occasion when Dathan and Abiram, through stirred-up disputes, claimed for themselves an honor in opposition to Moses and Aaron. Their punishment follows, for they provoked holy men to their own destruction: they spoke from envy, which is known to have displeased the Lord. This is fittingly placed among the Lord’s praises, because he is declared to have avenged his servants.

### Verse 17

“The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the assembly of Abiram.”

As the book of Numbers testifies (16:31–32), these things plainly happened to those who attacked with the poisoned teeth of envy the heavenly grace bestowed upon Aaron and Moses, so as stubbornly to claim for themselves an honor which they knew the Lord’s mercy had conferred upon the aforesaid men. A similar end befell them because the cause of their schism was one: they were swallowed by the earth because they savored earthly things, so that the very character of the punishment might testify to their wicked deeds.

### Verse 18

“And fire blazed up in their assembly, and flame consumed the sinners.”

This happened to the two hundred and fifty accomplices of Dathan and Abiram, who unhappily followed their designs and presumed to hold censers, as the same text of Numbers relates (Numbers 16:35). Here *synagoga* does not mean a temple, but an assembly, which is known to have been burned by divine fire, so that those who had sinned by presuming to offer incense might be consumed by heavenly flame. He added “their” so that you might understand it to have been separated from the Lord’s people. Flame is so called from the lash-like movement of its hair.

### Verse 19

“And they made a calf in Horeb [mss., Coreb], and worshiped a carved image.”

This too is made clear by the account of the well-known history: unable to endure Moses’ absence, the Jews, with monstrous judgment, made for themselves a metal god on Mount Horeb in the wilderness. Yet how much worse than the very beasts were those who did not even judge living cattle worthy of worship by their ridiculous devotions!

Horeb is interpreted “Calvary,” where afterward the Lord is known to have been put to death in the flesh on the gibbet of the cross. Thus, in that very same name, already then in the wilderness of Horeb, the faithless violated the worship of the Lord by their impious presumption—those whose descendants were to crucify the Lord Christ at the place of Calvary.

I also think it should be considered that he said, “they worshiped a carved image,” because in Exodus we read that a molten calf was formed from contributed ornaments by a certain monstrous device. But we must observe that two matters are spoken of here: they worshiped a calf in the wilderness, and afterward worshiped carved images in the land of promise, as he himself will say in what follows.

### Verse 20

“And they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass.”

Their glory was the Divinity whom they worshiped. Losing him in an unhappy exchange, they deserved to reach the point of abandoning the Creator of heaven and earth and making for themselves a god in the likeness of a calf that eats hay. O unspeakable crime—that those who had been heaped with the sight of so many miracles could have been so deceived! For what an offense it was to believe that a dumb animal was like God—something that would have been sacrilegious even if it had been compared with human beings. But all this was caused by the impatience of the light-minded, which always leads to sins and plunges them into ruin. For if you examine the matter truthfully, there is no crime that impatience does not produce as its mother. Against this there is one true remedy, one firm and unquestionable defense: “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined toward me” (Psalm 39:2).

### Verse 21

“They forgot God, who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham [ms. G and ed., Canaan], and fearful deeds in the Red Sea.”

The charge of forgetfulness grows greatly against the Jews: what benefit could they have retained in their minds, when they were unable to keep their deliverance in their memory? And lest what seemed to have been excluded from the mind be thought insignificant, he says, “great things.” Even if their treacherous minds could not retain these as benefits bestowed, they certainly ought to have recalled them at least because of the greatness of the events [ms. G and ed., “be recalled”]. He also added “wonders,” which they ought in no way to have excluded from their minds, however changeable they were. Finally, he added “fearful deeds,” which normally remain more vividly impressed upon human minds; when their terror is recalled, their memory is not erased.

But what stupor, what madness is condemned here—that amid so many great deeds they could have turned away from the works performed by so great an author! And consider how many things he has accumulated by adding one word after another. This figure is called *auxesis*, that is, “increase,” gradually ascending toward higher points. Whether in praise or in blame, it is altogether very powerful.

### Verse 22

“And he said that he would destroy them, if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood in the breach before him, to turn away his anger, lest he destroy them.”

All this is related in the text of Exodus, when the Lord spoke to Moses and would have allowed his anger to consume the people who were sinning so grievously. But Moses stood “in the breach,” that is, in the destruction which the people deserved to suffer, and stood before the Lord, saying: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from your book” (Exodus 32:31–32).

O holy man, worthy of every praise! When he descended from Mount Sinai to the camp and saw the people rejoicing in their impious revelry before the idol, he was moved against them, broke the tablets, and ordered them to kill one another with the sword. But when universal calamity threatened, he prayed that he himself rather might be extinguished, lest he should suffer the nation to perish altogether. Both acts were pious; both were glorious. Rightly, therefore, could he speak with divine clemency, since he loved to carry out its decrees.

At the same time, this virtue is also displayed: through the prayers of the saints we often escape the punishments due to death—not because anyone can change what the Lord has ordained, but because he should know that these events were foreknown by him as they come to pass.

### Verse 23

“And they regarded the desirable land as nothing; they did not believe his word.”

He comes to the fourth narrative, in which he says that the Jews regarded neither the future promises nor the miracles already accomplished as having any value. They seemed worthless because they always thought carnally about what they saw and heard. Bodily desire, once satisfied, soon grows weary. But observe how great the land was to those who understood, since it was called desirable; yet to them it seemed worthless because they perceived nothing spiritual in it.

It follows: “They did not believe his word.” He signifies the Son, in whom the most impious people did not believe. Or the statement may appropriately be understood literally, since they murmured because they preferred not to believe his promises. Their faithlessness makes many things about them intelligible, but everywhere there is guilt.

### Verse 24

“And they murmured in their tents; they did not hear the voice of the Lord.”

While they practiced murmuring, they did not hear the Lord’s voice at all. This generally happens to those who, while occupied with other voices, cannot hear another. And note that the verb “to hear” in the sense of heeding is ordinarily applied only to suppliants, not to those above them. Thus, because he says here that the Lord was not heeded, it is clear that this should reasonably be counted among the distinctive expressions of divine Scripture. The word for being heard (*exauditio*) is ordinarily applied to suppliants, not to superiors.

He added “in their tents,” so that this might appear to happen not to people laboring but to people at leisure. The gravity of the crime increases when people at leisure are found to have murmured.

### Verse 25

“And he raised his hand over them, to strike them down in the wilderness.”

### Verse 26

“And to cast down their offspring among the nations, and to scatter them throughout the lands.”

Here the Lord’s justice is placed first, so that the mercy that follows may be perceived with greater glory. He says that the Lord’s power rose up in order to punish those who transgressed and to strike down in the wilderness those who refused to hear the Lord’s commands. Then he says that he would humble their offspring, that is, the survivors of them, among the nations—those who had previously been renowned among all peoples. Finally, he would scatter them, bowed down and despised, throughout the lands, so that they would no longer presume anything concerning their assembly.

### Verse 27

“And they consecrated themselves to Baal-peor, and they ate sacrifices offered to the dead.”

### Verse 28

“And they provoked him by their practices, and ruin was multiplied among them.”

In these verses a greater transgression and more vehement anger are added, so that they appear not merely to have sacrificed for a time, but also to have consecrated themselves to the idol of the nations, Baal-peor. They had passed over into the worship and rites of demons so completely that they were shown to be servants not of the Lord but of demons.

It is beautifully said, “sacrifices offered to the dead,” because the worship itself was shown to have been offered to dead human beings, whom paganism judged to be immortal gods.

But attend carefully to the fact that he says ruin was multiplied upon those whom he intended to spare through the prayers of his holy one. He called what was owed “multiplied” because of the mass of their sin, so that the clemency might be greater toward those whose offense was more numerous.

### Verse 29

“Phinehas [mss. A, B: ‘and Phinehas stood’] stood, and he made supplication, and the plague ceased.”

### Verse 30

“And it was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation, forever.”

“Stood”—the word itself shows firmness of mind, since amid that general disturbance he alone dared to assume the confidence of one making supplication. For although we read that he pierced with a weapon the Israelite who was joining himself to a Midianite woman against the Lord’s prohibition (Numbers 25:7–8), nevertheless, because he is known to have done this out of divine zeal, the act is called a prayer rather than a deed. Whoever is occupied with good deeds makes supplication. His homicide did not arouse horror, because he avenged the stain of adultery. Indeed, after shedding blood he remained so innocent that he deserved to be praised even by the voice of the judge himself.

### Verse 31

“And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses was afflicted because of them, because they embittered his spirit. And he made a distinction with his lips.”

He comes to the fifth narrative, where that offense is related: after so many miracles had been displayed, water was demanded amid impious murmurings. It was sought in such a way that the request seemed more like contradiction than petition. There Moses, as we read in the Book of Numbers (chapter 20:10), inflamed by the excessive importunity of the Jewish people, spoke out distrustfully, saying: “Hear me, rebels and unbelievers: can we bring water for you from this rock?”

By this speech he too sinned, since, after having received so many miracles, he did not believe that the Lord would do what he had done. By that utterance of his lips he wholly marked himself off and separated himself from his former constancy, when he spoke ambiguously, although he had previously made those promises with the greatest certainty. We say that this kind of expression belongs properly to divine Scripture, since neither secular literature nor common usage employs it.

Moses, however, while his holiness was preserved, deserved to be struck by this one punishment: he was not to enter the land of promise, because he had not presumed to make a great promise concerning the Lord. For after his death, when the Lord spoke to Joshua the son of Nun, he said: “Therefore be strong and very courageous, so that you may keep and do all the law that Moses my servant commanded you” (Joshua 1:7). By saying “my servant,” he showed that the grace of his favor had remained in him.

### Verse 32

“They did not destroy the nations of which the Lord had spoken to them [mss. A, B, ‘which the Lord said’].”

### Verse 33

“And they mingled among the nations and learned their works; they served their carved images, and it became a stumbling-block for them.”

As though it had been a small matter that the Hebrew people had sinned in the wilderness, after they entered the promised lands they forgot the Lord’s commands and joined themselves, through a forbidden association, more closely to those nations whom they had been commanded to destroy because of their worship of idols. They added evil to their crimes by defiling themselves with the superstition of those peoples. The land of promise, which had been granted by the Lord as a great reward, became a stumbling-block for them [ed., “became a stumbling-block”].

Wretched human beings, who turned God’s gift into sins, so that what he had given for grace became a cause of ruin to those who transgressed. Thus we are warned to use rightly the benefits granted by divine generosity, lest we perish more greatly from the very source from which we are known to have been raised up.

“Stumbling-block” is a Greek term, *skandalon*, meaning “a thing on the left”; it led their minds toward the left-hand side through perverse imitation.

### Verse 34

“And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.”

### Verse 35

“And they shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and their daughters.”

Although in the divine Scriptures it is not recorded that human blood was shed by the Hebrews who entered the promised land in sacrifices to demons, nevertheless there is no doubt that this could have happened in a later age, since the present Scripture is also shown to be a witness to the truth.

And observe how, by a truthful account of the sinners, their wickedness is intensified. First he said: “They shed innocent blood.” And lest they be thought to have been strangers, he added: “the blood of their sons and their daughters”—those whose safety is most precious in human society—so that they did not spare those for whom pious parents would not refuse even to be killed.

### Verse 36

“Whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.”

### Verse 37

“And the land was slain with blood, and it was defiled by their works; and they prostituted themselves in their practices.”

He continues to persist in *auxesis* in these two verses. This figure is called in Greek *climax*, and in Latin *gradatio*, “gradation,” because our understanding rises by certain steps, whether in praise or in blame. We have just mentioned it, but we are not reluctant to repeat frequently what the authority of Scripture itself is known to repeat.

And because he had said that the blood of sons and daughters was shed, the charge still increases, the crime still grows greater, when those memorials of affection are recalled as having been sacrificed to horrifying carved images.

We must therefore understand “the land was slain” of cruel people who slaughtered themselves through their wicked devotion. By killing their sons, the parents themselves seemed rather to be extinguished through such a dreadful crime. “The land was slain” is a figurative expression, since earthly people are said to have been killed by evil deeds. He explained how he said that the land was slain: carnal and foolish people had been overwhelmed by their most wicked action.

For those who polluted themselves with adulterous superstitions are seen to have prostituted themselves against the Lord.

### Verse 38

“And the Lord was angry in spirit against his people, and he abhorred his inheritance.”

### Verse 39

“And he handed them over to the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.”

### Verse 40

“And their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands.”

This too is expressed figuratively, because disturbance of mind is not thought to fall upon the Lord. Rather, the power of his vengeance was aroused, and in accordance with human usage it is called anger.

But what did he do when angry? He turned away from them—which is plainly the extreme of all evils. Thus, when what contains is withdrawn, the ruin of what is contained must immediately follow. They were handed over to the disgrace of servitude, although they had seemed to glory in idols.

It follows: “and those who hated them ruled over them” [ms. G and ed., “ruled over them”]. Although every rule exercised by the nations seems most grievous, he added “those who hated them,” so that it might be more severe when they served one who was hostile. No services can please such a master, for whoever always hates is always angry.

Finally, see what follows: “Their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands.” Such, then, is the recompense they received: those who refused to serve the Lord who loved them were justly shown to be subject to enemies who hated them.

### Verse 41

“He often delivered them. But they provoked him by their counsel, and they were humbled by their iniquities.”

### Verse 42

“And he looked upon them when they were afflicted, when he heard their prayer.”

Here the mercy of the Divinity [ed., “of the Lord”] is explained in two ways. He set benefits before them, and human wickedness did not cease; he brought punishment, and again deigned to grant clemency to the afflicted. Thus we understand that he both goes before them with good things and comes to the aid of those who have been scourged. You will find this in these verses if you attend carefully.

### Verse 43

“And he remembered his covenant, and he relented according to the multitude of his mercy.”

He gives the reason why the Israelite people, although they sinned repeatedly, were heard and did not, through the Lord’s mercy, reach the destruction they deserved: namely, because of the New Testament, which is eternal, in which the Lord’s coming shone forth and which will not be changed by any succession.

He was promised to Abraham, since he was to be born from his offspring. This had been hidden in the prophets but was revealed in the time of the Gospel.

“He relented” is spoken in accordance with human usage, since when human beings repent, they ordinarily change what they had determined. With the Lord, however, all things proceed according to fixed arrangements; nothing new occurs contrary to his foreknowledge, since he knows everything that is to be done.

It was necessary for him to speak to us in our own manner, since he assumed mortal nature in order to make us alive forever. But consider that this repentance of the Lord is said to occur when he also recognizes us as repentant. He becomes for us what he finds us to be toward him.

He added: “according to the multitude of his mercy.” This is what surpasses all sins; this is what deigned to come even to our flesh. It is rightly called the multitude of mercy, through which the world is known to have been delivered.

### Verse 44

“And he gave them into mercies, in the sight of all those who had captured them.”

He says that they were given “into mercies” because they received diverse gifts of grace. From that very people of the Lord, some became prophets, others apostles, others martyrs, others confessors, flourishing through his mercy, so that later the nations revered through the sight of their miracles those whom they had previously possessed as rejected slaves.

Or the expression may more appropriately be referred to the devil or his ministers: they were made free in the presence of those whose wickedness had previously made them appear captive. Hence the Apostle says: “The prince of the power of the air, who works in the sons of unbelief” [ed., “in the children of unbelief”] (Ephesians 2:2); and elsewhere: “That they may recover their senses from the snares of the devil, having been taken captive (*captivati*) by him according to his will” [mss. A, B, F, *capti*, ‘captured’] (2 Timothy 2:26).

### Verse 45

“Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations.”

### Verse 46

“So that we may confess your holy name and glory in your praise.”

That people to whom we gave the words of this psalm at its beginning, after filling itself with the abundance of the Lord’s praise, now, in the sixth narrative, beseeches the Father and Lord to perfect his Church from the gathering of the nations.

It adds: “and let us glory in your praise”—not in human boasting, but in you, where glory is truly fixed and joy is without end.

Observe also that here the Father is said to save; the Son is likewise read to save, as in the statement: “The Son of Man came to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). The Holy Spirit is also proclaimed to save, as in the passage addressed to Titus: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). Thus the equality and unity of the undivided Trinity are indicated by similar words and by similar powers.

### Verse 47

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age; and all the people shall say: Let it be, let it be.”

This is the praise which the people gathered in the preceding verse desired to utter [ms. G and ed., “which the gathered peoples desired to utter.”] The holy Church also sings this now, taking consolation in the present time from so great a good.

But it says that this is to be done from this age to the age that endures forever, so that continuous praise may never grow tiresome.

Yet when the devout people of the Jews sing the hymns mentioned above, who is this other one who says, “Let it be, let it be”? It is, as I think, the people of the uncircumcised, who were not yet in the faith when this psalm was sung, but who was destined to be introduced by the power of prophecy, so that, out of love for the whole community, it might say: “Let it be, let it be.”

Thus even today, when priests pray in the churches, the response is “Amen,” that is, “Let it be.” Even in those times they were being indicated who now do the same. For it is more fitting to draw these words toward such an interpretation than to attend to the divisions of the books, as some prefer.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

The festive “Alleluia” was sung, and all the parts answered to their title. For although different things were said, they are nevertheless known to have come together in one grace, like the voices of a harmonious instrument.

Therefore let us beseech him with the greatest desire to grant that we may be a people pleasing to him—he who is accustomed to make straight things from crooked, sweet things from bitter, and eternal things from temporal—so that we too, glorying together in Christ the Lord, may deserve to say:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age.”

We must also remember that although this psalm contains the words, “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity,” it should nevertheless not be applied to penitents.

First, a festive “Alleluia” is placed before it. Second, it speaks of the Hebrew people, while individual persons are assigned to penitents. Third, it contains more history than it laments offenses. Moreover, in many psalms one finds brief mention of satisfaction for sin, although they do not appear to be applicable to that particular subject.

# Commentary on Psalm 106

## Alleluia

Since this psalm, like the two preceding ones, is marked beforehand by the same title, we think it appropriate to recall their interpretations together in one exposition, so that the meaning of so great a mystery may be understood more easily.

In the first “Alleluia,” the Jewish people are commended, and there is no complaint against them. In the second, those are recalled who, within the same nation, went astray through very frequent offenses and returned to the Lord’s grace through his mercy. Here, however, the Christian people are admonished to sound forth the Lord’s praises for the benefits bestowed upon them.

Thus it can briefly be understood what should be sought in each of them. Therefore now the prophet, as has been said, admonishes the Christian people, who have been saved by the Lord’s redemption, to sing a new “Alleluia” by confessing their past deeds.

This is a sweet voice; this is a festive speech. Therefore let us reverently hear the wondrous great deeds announced by the splendor of so great a title.

## Division of the Psalm

After the confession of the Hebrew people, of whom the preceding psalms spoke, the prophet turns to the Christian people, who had wandered throughout the expanse of the whole world in the desolation and error of superstition.

In the first section, he admonishes them to confess the Lord’s praises, because, redeemed by his glorious blood, they received Churches; previously they had been foolishly carried away to the altars of demons and in sacred groves.

In the second, he says that thanks must be given to the Lord, who satisfied with the abundance of his religion the souls of the Gentiles, which had been hungry for the food of truth, and who tore apart, by his unconquerable power, the bonds of their sins.

In the third, he commands that thanks be offered to the Father, because the Lord Christ, when he came, broke the bronze gates and iron bars of the devil by the majesty of his omnipotence.

In the fourth, he admonishes priests to offer to the Lord Christ a sacrifice of praise. These priests are known to preside over the governance of the Churches amid the immense waves of this world, as though over certain ships; he describes how divine power also deigns to assist them in their temptations.

In the fifth, he again says that the Lord is to be praised by priests and elders, because by a heavenly gift he changed the world, made barren by the dryness of sin, into the most delightful beauty. Seeing this, the upright of heart will rejoice with immense exultation.

It should also be considered that the sections mentioned above are known to begin with similar verses. Secular teachers call this poetic form *intercalare*, “intercalation,” in which repetition is so frequently doubled that necessary admonition is made sweet by repeated return.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

The prophet foresaw that the Christian people would receive grace through the Lord’s coming. Lest security arising from so great a benefit produce any negligence, he admonishes them both to disclose their sins and to sound forth the Lord’s praises, because, as we have said, the word “confess” applies to both.

The one who salutarily takes up the Lord’s praises is the one who has first appeased him by confessing his sins. It follows: “for he is good,” so that after satisfaction sinners may have confidence in entreating the gracious Lord.

“Forever” here signifies “for eternity,” because no time is found to be excluded from his mercy. Here he is accustomed to spare, and there he will deign to bestow eternal rewards upon the faithful. Thus he is always shown to be good to his suppliants and always merciful. Even when he judges, he is good, because justice is good.

### Verse 2

“Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy.”

Let them certainly say “Alleluia,” as the title declares, and let those who have deserved to come to the Lord’s grace console themselves with joyful exultation.

He refers especially to the peoples of the nations, who were redeemed by the Lord’s blood and lifted by his mercy from the devil’s power. That hand was so hard, rigid, and senseless that it could never have been loosened except by the shedding of sacred blood.

The following verses make clear that this refers to them.

### Verse 3

“From the regions he gathered them: from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.”

By the figure of *periphrasis*, called in Latin “circumlocution,” he explains how far the power of the devil’s right hand was spread throughout the whole world, so that the benefit of the holy Incarnation might be made known to human beings. By the power of its majesty, the Incarnation both bound the destructive author and rescued from him, once he was bound, the vessels of death.

He first said, “from the regions.” And lest you think that they were gathered from only a few provinces, he added: “from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.”

Having designated three quarters of the world, he set the sea in place of the fourth, that is, the south. By this he wished the Ocean to be understood, which is said to surround the whole circumference of the world.

There is a similar description in Genesis, where he promises the whole world to Abraham’s offspring, saying: “Lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you now are, toward the north and the south, toward the east and toward the sea, which is the west” (Genesis 13:14).

“Setting” is so called as though from “the falling of the hours.” Thus the sea, which he placed here for the south, is clearly named there for the west. This term can suitably be applied to any part of the world, since the sea is said to enclose the whole earth within the circle of its wandering.

Hence it is clearly perceived that this universal gathering is not spoken of the Jews but of the Catholic Church, which is known to have been gathered from the whole world.

### Verse 4

“They wandered in the wilderness, in a dry place; they did not find the way to a city of habitation.”

### Verse 5

“Hungry and thirsty, their soul failed within them.”

Although the various nations rejoiced in the multitude of their peoples, they were living in a wilderness, since they were shown to have no true teachers and no Church. For pagan superstition had not yet found the way to the city of the Lord where it ought to have dwelt, since it was sacrificing to idols.

“Hungry and thirsty” signifies the curious men of this world, who sought the paths of truth through diverse opinions. But because they had not believed in its Author, they could not be found in true wisdom.

It follows: “their soul failed within them.” “Within them,” that is, their spirit, wearied by their labors and pursuits, collapsed, because they desired to seek God in a manner by which they could not find him.

### Verse 6

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

### Verse 7

“And he led them into the right way, so that they might go to a city of habitation.”

Just as in the preceding two verses he described those who were wandering, so now in two other verses he relates their return to the Lord’s gifts.

“They cried” signifies that they sought with great desire. Yet this compunction comes from the Lord, so that what is known to be profitable may be sought eagerly.

And to indicate the force of the word itself, he added: “when they were afflicted.” At that time the cry of the heart is aroused with all its strength, when impending danger is feared and human presumption is removed.

But see what this cry accomplished: they were delivered from their necessities and came to recognize the paths of truth, so that those who had previously wandered in trackless error, having received the way of the holiest religion, might happily reach the courts of the blessed Church.

### Verse 8

“Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.”

He comes to the second section, in which he now admonishes the faithful not to cease giving thanks to the Lord, who has bestowed upon them his abundant benefits.

It is truly and salutarily said that they ought to confess to the Lord his mercies, because whatever appears praiseworthy in us is evidently due to his clemency. He forgives sins, grants hope, and leads us to the gifts of his goodness.

When he says “mercies” in the plural, he signifies that he grants many gifts, but different ones, as the Apostle says: “Each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Corinthians 7:7).

Therefore it is always fitting to confess to the gracious Lord, who both delivers us from dangers and illumines us with the splendor of his goodness.

The miracles he performed at the time of his Incarnation, he says, are to be proclaimed to later generations through evangelists and apostles, as has indeed been accomplished.

Remember also that this verse is repeated without any alteration through four divisions up to the end. Just as he says that the Church was gathered from the four parts of the world, so praises of his mercies are offered by devoted minds from the same four quarters of the earth.

### Verse 9

“For he satisfied the empty soul, and he filled the hungry soul with good things.”

The soul is empty when, occupied with the perversities of the world, it does not hasten by any devotion to return to its Creator.

He calls the soul “hungry” when, already visited by divine grace, it desires to come to the Lord’s healing [mss. A, B, F, “to the healing from the Lord”].

This happened among the nations, which at first occupied their minds with the empty desires of idols. They were then empty and void, when they were deprived of good fruits and deceived. Second, they were filled when, admonished by the Lord’s mercy, they turned their vows toward the practice of repentance.

### Verse 10

“Sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in chains, in misery and iron.”

The life of the nations that existed before the Lord’s coming is described in this verse. They sat in darkness because, emptied of the light of faith, they were rendered obscure by the blindness of unbelief [mss. A, B, F, “when emptied of the light of faith”].

When he says “sitting,” he shows that they had remained there for a long time.

The shadow of death was the vicious life of this age, which bore the most dreadful image of the death to come.

They were bound in chains because, under the devil’s domination, they were held fast by the bonds of sins.

“Beggary” (*mendicitas*) refers to the lack of good. Here the deprivation is altogether more serious, since it is shown to afflict not the body but, what is more grievous, the soul.

“Iron” signifies the hardness of evils, since we commonly call something iron when we show that it is hard.

### Verse 11

“Because they embittered the words of the Lord, and they provoked the counsel of the Most High.”

### Verse 12

“And their heart was humbled by labors; and they grew weak, and there was no one to help.”

It must be observed that in these two verses there is the figure *parison*, that is, “equality of statement.” In the first verse he explains how they sinned, and in the second what they received. An attentive reader will frequently find this figure in this psalm.

He speaks of those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death because, acting against the Lord’s words, they refused to live according to his ordinances. It was necessary that they suffer the anger of the one whom they judged worthy of contempt.

Finally, see what follows: “They provoked the counsel of the Most High.” They certainly provoked it, so that those who had been proud in prosperity might be humbled in tribulations and distress. It was a just counsel and a most salutary medicine, so that the disease of the world might be cured by the contrary remedy.

He added: “they grew weak,” that is, they were cast down from the presumption of the world, so that they might reach the remedies of repentance more easily if they had lost the incentives to stubbornness.

It is added: “and there was no one to help,” with “another” understood. No one assists a person in danger unless almighty God has commanded him to give help.

### Verse 13

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

### Verse 14

“And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and he broke their chains.”

Behold why they were humbled and why they grew weak: namely, so that they might cry to the Lord, confessing their own sins. While placed in arrogance, they were silent; like senseless animals, they uttered no saving word. Compunction arose, and then they gave forth a profitable voice.

Observe also by what distinctions the Lord’s mercy is explained.

First, he delivered them from their necessity [ed., “necessities”], since they were oppressed by the devil’s slavery.

Then he led the souls of sinners, stained by the filth of superstition, out of the darkness of their superstitions.

Third, he did not say that he loosened their chains but that he broke them. Thus the devil’s tyrannical power was shattered when Christ came, so that it could never prevail to return to the domination it had possessed.

### Verse 15

“Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.”

He comes to the third section, where he repeats the verse that he already spoke in the second part. These are intercalary verses, as though placed in the middle of the road, that is, established along the course of the poem.

He admonishes the liberated (*liberatos*) to give thanks [mss. A, B, F, *liberatori*, ‘the liberator’], because divine power has broken open the gates of sins and the barriers of every evil.

### Verse 16

“For he shattered bronze gates, and he broke iron bars.”

This is the reason he says that the Lord must be confessed: for our liberation he broke the bronze gates and the iron bars, so that, with him providing the way for us, we might pass through this life in safety.

The bronze gates are the vicious habits of human beings, which shut us within the courts of sins so tightly that they cannot grant permission to go out.

By the iron bars we may rightly understand unclean spirits, who are known to bolt (*obserare*) those gates of sins so that those surrounded by them may not be permitted to leave [mss. A, B, F: *observare*, ‘to watch’].

These two metals appear to have been employed because of the strength of sins. But divine power, which human strength had despaired of overcoming, broke them when, in compassion, it looked upon those in danger through the light of his coming.

### Verse 17

“He received them from the way of their iniquity, for because of their injustices they were humbled.”

Although the Lord appears to fill all things through the presence of his majesty, he becomes so distant from sinners that they do not draw near to him except when, moved by his mercy, they come to him in compunction.

How harmful this abandonment is is plainly explained. He says that they were humbled because of their injustices—not with that life-giving humility, for there is one humility that raises up, and another that casts down.

One is humbled unto destruction who has not deserved to reach that healing.

### Verse 18

“Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near [mss. A, B, F: “drew near” (*appropinquaverunt*)] to the gates of death.”

As far as the literal sense is concerned, the condition of the sick is being described: through their loathing of food, they are evidently brought into danger of death. But here we should rather understand spiritual food, that is, the law of the Lord and his saving commandments, by which the faithful soul lives and is refreshed by heavenly abundance. The mind of the ungodly is empty of this food through a destructive hunger, while the soul, being sick, is known to endure a scarcity of good things. It is a grave illness and an accursed calamity not to desire the divine law; for how could one live if one began not to love one’s own life? Hence they came to those deadly confines [ms. G. and edition, “one came”]. They did not enter them because they were to be liberated by the Lord’s mercy.

### Verse 19

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

It is clear that this verse has been repeated, since in a similar circumstance one statement was fitting.

### Verse 20

“He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions.”

Here we recognize what sort of illness it is to loathe spiritual delights, since only the presence of the heavenly Physician could have removed such a peril of sickness. For the Lord the Savior came to refresh and heal us, lest the fasting from spiritual food consume the hearts of sinners. When he says, “He sent his word,” this refers to the Father’s love, not to an inequality of power. The Holy Spirit, too, is sent by the Son, as he himself says in the Gospel: “It is expedient for you that I go; for if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). Again, the Son is sent by the Holy Spirit, as Isaiah says concerning Christ: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isaiah 61:1). One who is greater is also sent by one who is lesser, as Tobias sent the angel. Yet the Son is not lesser when he is sent by the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit lesser than the Son because he is sent by him. This expression concerns concord, not a difference of power; for the equality of power or nature in the Trinity is frequently asserted in the divine Scriptures. Among others, our father Augustine is known to have collected this appropriately in the Book of Testimonies (also Sermon 181, On Time).

### Verse 21

“Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.”

The fourth section is introduced with repeated verses, for which the preceding exposition will suffice. He admonishes the priests to offer sacrifice to the Lord and never cease proclaiming his wonders to the peoples.

### Verse 22

“And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, and declare his works with rejoicing.”

One renders sacrifice to the Lord who joyfully offers a sacrifice of praise, since it is far more excellent to offer him, together with good deeds, the jubilations of psalmody than to sacrifice victims of cattle. He subsequently explains what sort of sacrifices are to be offered: namely, that the 368 preachers must not be silent about his benefits, so that they may render what is owed and suitable instruction [mss. A., B., F., “medicine”] may be shown to the faithful. What this declaration should be like is expressed by a most fitting word: “with rejoicing”—not sadly, not distrustfully, but joyfully and most eagerly, so that the confidence of the preacher may be understood by his hearers. We more readily consent to believe those things which we see teachers proclaiming with a steadfast and joyful mind.

### Verse 23

“Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters.”

When he says, “They go down to the sea,” he signifies the priests who descend into the stormy conditions of this age. By saying “they go down,” he shows that the places of this world are lower, to which one can descend. By “ships,” as we have often said, he signifies the Churches, which sail through the storms of this world by means of the wood of the cross. Thus one descends into and crosses the sea if one sits in the safest ships, where Christ is the helmsman, the apostles are the rowers, and the blessed company of the holy bishops is gathered.

He continues: “doing their work upon many waters.” He remains within the same comparison. For the priests are those who work upon many waters, that is, who preach to Christian peoples. There is no doubt that “many waters” signifies peoples, since when John asked what the waters were in the Apocalypse, he received the answer: “They are peoples” (Revelation 17:15). What interpretation could be truer than one confirmed by the authority of such great truth?

### Verse 24

“They saw the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep.”

These preachers recognized his works through spiritual understanding: they understood that the Red Sea signified baptism; that Jonah’s three-day, unharmed dwelling in the belly of the beast signified the Lord’s tomb; and that similar events prefigured the things accomplished in the divine Scriptures. Thus those who contemplate his works through spiritual discernment behold his wonders in the deep.

### Verse 25

“He spoke, and a storm-wind arose, and its waves were raised up.”

### Verse 26

“They rise up to the heavens and descend to the abysses; their soul was wasting away in evils.”

So that those whom he previously said could behold the Lord’s work in the deep would not swell with some kind of exaltation, he now explains their storms and waves in turn. “He spoke, and the spirit of the storm stood still” signifies the time when the Lord, in compassionate mercy, suspends the storms of our tribulations, lest we be overwhelmed as evils increase, nor again be delivered unless he protects us. This delay becomes for us the cause of greater danger.

For the waves are raised up in human minds when we suppose that what we seem able to escape only by divine grace is attributable to our own merits. But these waves are described with the greatest beauty. They rise up to the heavens when they are lifted by the exultation of this world; they descend to the abysses when they have reached despair and fear. And see what follows: “Their soul was wasting away in evils,” precisely because, under the effect of fear, they had descended to the deepest abysses. “Was wasting away” is also used in a good sense, as the thirty-eighth psalm says: “And you made his soul waste away like a spider” (Psalm 38:12). But here “in evils” has been added so that the sense in which it is used should be understood without ambiguity.

### Verse 27

“They were troubled and shaken like a drunkard, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.”

He is still speaking of those of whom he previously said, “Their soul was wasting away in evils.” “They were troubled” refers to confusion of mind; “they were shaken” refers to the immediate eruption of anger. Therefore he says that the wisdom of such people has been swallowed up, because wisdom can be found only among tranquil and undisturbed minds. Their wisdom is rightly said of those who had previously seemed to themselves to be teachers; yet it is clear that the wisdom which cannot appear to disturbed minds has been swallowed up.

By these examples, therefore, the priests are admonished to entreat the Lord, so that he may strengthen their hearts in humility and prevent them from being tossed about by diabolical temptations.

### Verse 28

“And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

### Verse 29

“And he made his storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent.”

Those who were like drunkards, whose wisdom seemed to have been swallowed up, returned through a salutary cry to life-giving counsel. Turning to the Lord, they began at last to become sober. What the cry for help accomplished is explained: “And he delivered them from their necessities.” The manner in which these necessities were removed is narrated through allegorical description. It follows: “And he made his storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent.” That exceedingly fierce storm, which human frailty could not endure, disappeared when it was commanded to become breezes; and immediately the uproar of those raging evils fell silent at the command of the Ruler.

### Verse 30

“And they rejoiced because the waves were silent; and he led them into the harbor of their desire, and he delivered them from their necessities.”

He describes what commonly emerges after dangers, when those wearied by labor rejoice that they have been delivered from a great catastrophe and begin to reach an utterly safe harbor. A harbor is so called from *portare*, “to carry,” because it carries ships.

A repeated but exceedingly pleasing conclusion follows: the soul in turmoil is delivered from all its necessities.

### Verse 31

“Let them confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.”

He comes to the fifth section, where he admonishes the holy Church to give thanks to the Lord, because the compassionate one has graciously bestowed various benefits upon the human race. But observe that he repeated the same verse for the fourth time, so that the fourfold division of the world mentioned above—by the rising and setting of the sun, by the north, and by the sea—might be rendered concordant with these sections, so that the faithful confession might everywhere be sung as one and everywhere with the greatest renown. It was fitting that one religion, one people, and one Church should also contain one holiness of proclamation.

### Verse 32

“And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders” [ms. G. and edition, “of the old men”].

He says that the Lord is to be exalted because he is higher than all the powers of heaven and earth—not because anything can be added to him, but so that we should increase through his exaltation. For when we contemplate and praise him, the Most High appears immense and incomprehensible.

Here we should understand “people” not as just any despised class of human beings, but that noble people endowed with true religion, which always exalts the Lord through religious deeds. When he says, “and let them praise him in the seat of the elders,” he commands all teachers to make the praises of the Lord resound—those who are known to sit in the seat of the elders, that is, those who have deserved to become successors of the ancient bishops. That a seat is given to teachers was sufficiently explained in the first psalm. 369

### Verse 33

“For he made rivers into a desert, and springs of water into thirst.”

He gives the reason why the multitude of the faithful should confess the Lord: because, when the unbelief of the Jews was rejected, the whole fullness came to the Christian people. Those rivers—that is, the prophets or apostles—passed over to the deserts of the nations when the Jews did not believe. For when the stubborn Hebrew people refused altogether to receive the words of God spiritually, the divine word, like a well-watered spring diverted into another channel, was transferred to all the nations, and those who had previously been dried up by the aridity of sin became exceedingly fruitful.

It is wonderfully said, “springs of water into thirst,” that is, toward the nations that would thirstily drink the heavenly waters, unlike the Jews, who rejected them with destructive contempt.

### Verse 34

“A fruitful land into a salt marsh, because of the wickedness of those who dwelt in it.”

Because he had previously spoken of the calling of the nations, which pertains to Christians, he now speaks of the expulsion of the Jews, which he declares came upon them because of their pride. The land was fruitful when it flourished in heavenly religion; but it became a salt marsh when it despised the Lord’s commandments. Salty moisture is hostile to fruits, since wherever it has prevailed, it interrupts the grace of fertility. But the reason why this happened to them follows: namely, because of the wickedness of those who seemed to dwell in that fruitful land—that is, in the Lord’s tabernacle—with deceitful minds [edition, “deceitful”].

### Verse 35

“He made a desert into pools of water, and a waterless land into springs of water.”

### Verse 36

“And he settled the hungry there, and they established a city as a dwelling place.”

This verse concerns the Christian people, whose thirst was given the saving water of holy baptism. I think that “pools” has been used for the fountains of the Churches, from which the water received is held in a quiet basin until the dignity of the new birth is completed. Pools are so called from *stare*, “to stand.”

The waterless land signifies the unbelieving hearts of the nations, which, watered by the stream of baptism, flourished through holy preaching. But those who embraced the Lord’s glorious gifts with exceedingly great eagerness were settled in this benefit. The city as a dwelling place is the Catholic Church, in which those who obey the commands from above establish themselves firmly.

### Verse 37

“And they sowed fields and planted vineyards, and they produced the fruit of birth.”

### Verse 38

“And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly, and their cattle did not diminish.”

They sow fields and plant vineyards who purify their bodies of the thorns of sin through heavenly instruction, so that they may find those fruits known to please the Lord. Blessed is the labor, wonderful the yield: to work in such a way that the Redeemer of the nations may be recognized as appeased.

A field is so called from *agere*, “to act,” because various means of obtaining food are carried out there. He adds: “And they produced the fruit of birth, and he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly.” Fruit is derived from *frui*, “to enjoy”; therefore those who produce spiritual fruit enjoy the Lord’s blessing. But those who happen to be unfruitful are cut off, like the fig tree in the Gospel which, though luxuriant in leaves, was seen to be barren of fruit.

They multiplied when the blessed faithful brought forth holy works [mss. A., B., “riches”] and became more glorious through the fecundity of merits granted by God. It follows: “And their cattle did not diminish.” By “cattle” we should understand simple people—endowed indeed with the excellence of faith, but not distinguished by eloquence; better in life than in speech, possessing great strength not in words but in the heart, like the Paul whom we read of as simple, yet one who commanded demons. Such people did not become fewer; rather, they appear to have obtained the Lord’s great grace. Thus the holy Church is shown to possess these two kinds of people.

### Verse 39

“They became few, and they were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and by sorrow.”

### Verse 40

“And contention was poured out upon their princes; their vanities led them astray, and [he] led them into a trackless place and not into the way.”

In these two verses he describes those who, deceived by heretical depravity, abandon the Lord’s Church. Concerning them the Apostle John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

These people are few, although they may seem to themselves to be many; for when compared with that universal Church, they are proved to be utterly insignificant. “They were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and by sorrow”—afflicted, certainly, when diabolical snares struck them. For sorrow and tribulation must follow those who are known to have abandoned the author of salvation.

It follows: “And contention was poured out upon their princes.” In brief, the priests of the heretics are designated and condemned. Contention is rightly said to have been poured out by them, because they contend not through saving doctrine but only through deadly loquacity: they accept the divine Scriptures in certain passages but abandon them for the most part. Since they were led astray by their own vanity, they slide through trackless places of error, having abandoned the way of salvation and lingering in twisted paths. Let them therefore hear where they are walking and learn where they may arrive.

### Verse 41

“And he helped the poor man out of poverty, and established families like sheep.”

### Verse 42

“The upright will see and rejoice, and all iniquity will shut its mouth.”

Above he spoke of the arrogant heretics; now he returns to the humble Catholics, abandoning their starving princes and refreshing their poor with heavenly assistance. This poor man is one among all [ms. G. and edition, “in all”], who, having abandoned worldly enticements, continually knocks at the door of heavenly mercy, so that he may deserve admission into that family which is adorned with the honor of harmless simplicity, like sheep.

When the holy see this, they will undoubtedly rejoice, because they recognize that a faithful person has been added to their fellowship. Once this has happened, the iniquity of the devil will fall silent, since it will have nothing that can be brought against the Lord’s elect.

### Verse 43

“Who is wise and will keep these things, and will understand the mercies of the Lord?”

The marvelous psalm has been brought to its conclusion with a fitting ending. “Who is wise?”—as if he were saying: Whoever is truly wise keeps these things that have been said, preferring to be Christ’s poor man rather than a prince of the heretics, and choosing to knock at the door of the heavenly King rather than teach harmful words. Whoever can make this choice and judge in this way will then receive the mercies of the Lord, which can never come to an end.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Although all the contents of this psalm have been recounted through a delightful proclamation, that passage especially delighted my soul which says, in a brief summary, that God’s Church is to be gathered from all the regions of the world. It says: “He gathered them from the regions: from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.”

It is worthwhile to examine this verse somewhat more carefully, for it is an excellent indication of astronomical learning. By naming the four cardinal points of the world, he depicted the globe of the earth in the form of a quadrangle.

I discovered that this psalm had been divided by the most learned Father Augustine, who is said to have explained it to the people in such a way that he no longer considered it in need of further exposition. Imitating him insofar as permission has been granted, we have judged that all the psalms should be divided into sections. We consider that the authority of so great a Father has provided no small support for our explanations. 370

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 107

### A Song, a Psalm of David

In this psalm a certain novelty is recognized as requiring investigation, since it is evidently woven together from portions of Psalms 56 and 59. Although the very words that had already been spoken in those psalms have been set down here, they nevertheless lead to a different understanding, because the changed title—which is always shown to indicate the content of the psalm—persuades us to understand these portions differently from the way they were understood above.

We have often said that “song” refers to contemplation of divine things, while “psalm” refers to active works, which nevertheless are known to conform to divine commands. The psalm itself testifies to this in the first verse: “I will sing and I will recite a psalm to the Lord.” David signifies Christ the King, who will speak in this psalm.

Therefore we must investigate each point with great attention, since the psalms in which he deigns to speak in his own person are profound, with the most reverent subtlety, so that the dignity of so great a mystery may be protected by a denser veil.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm, as has been said, the Lord Christ speaks. First, in relation to what he is as man, he offers praise in repayment for the grace of the Father’s glory, because, having received the wondrous mystery of the Passion, he rose into everlasting glory.

Second, he continually humbles his humanity, while nevertheless displaying the power of his own majesty, so that you may truly recognize two natures in the one person of the Lord Christ—not that Christ is divided into two sons, as the impiety of certain people maintains, but that one and the same Son of God speaks now according to the flesh assumed for us, and now according to the power and glory of the Word.

Distinguish the natures, both of God and of man, and you will pass through everything without offense, as the Fathers briefly instructed: “Attribute sufferings to the flesh; attribute miracles to the Divinity.”

### Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and recite a psalm to the Lord.”

The holiness of that glorious incarnation, while proclaiming its own purity, shows how praises are to be offered to the Lord. He was always ready for such things, since he had no discord with sins when proclaiming the Father. The repetition itself also shows the confidence of the promise, because what is known to be reinforced by repeated profession is established most firmly.

But what he truly promises concerning himself, we rightly say concerning ourselves if we trust that our sins are forgiven through his gift. It follows: “I will sing and recite a psalm to the Lord.” He rightly spoke such things about himself, since both his speech and his deeds accorded with divine ordinances. In his psalter there was no defective string, nor did his voice resound with any hoarseness caused by evil deeds. Rather, works were joined with joyful exultation and spiritual song; and that psalter was truly sweet-sounding, consonant with holy melodies.

### Verse 2

“Awake, my glory; awake, psalter and lyre; I will arise at dawn.”

After the Lord Christ has said that, according to the flesh, he sings and plays the psalms to the Father, he now says, “Awake, my glory,” which is signified by the psalter and the lyre. The psalter pertains to uprightness of conduct; the lyre to bodily affliction and suffering. Through these he displays both praiseworthy actions and his most glorious Passion.

He adds: “I will arise at dawn.” A most beautiful order follows in what is said. After the signification of the Passion, this is necessarily understood of the Lord’s resurrection, because, as the Gospel bears witness, he rose from the dead at that time.

If you wish to understand this also of his members, it applies fittingly to every believer: for he always rises at dawn who attends in the Church to praise the Lord through pious works. Even if he keeps vigil through the deep night, the one illumined by so great a splendor of proclamation does not know how to endure darkness.

### Verse 3

“I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord; I will recite a psalm to you among the nations.”

These words signify the universal Church, because, as has often been said, many first believed from the Jewish people, and afterward the fullness of the nations was admitted. Observe how fitting words distinguish the individual reasons.

He says that he will confess among the people of the Jews, where he spoke with his own voice; but he will sing psalms among the nations, to whom the apostles were sent and among whom they fulfilled his commands through holy preaching. He says that he truly sings psalms because he is known to have accomplished this through his ministers.

### Verse 4

“For your mercy has been magnified up to the heavens, and your truth up to the clouds.”

This, too, is said to the Father. His mercy has been magnified up to the heavens, when the heavenly powers enjoy his benefits. For although the highest dignity belongs to the good angels and the various powers, they are blessed nevertheless through his gift.

His truth has been magnified up to the clouds when the preachers of the word, like rain-bearing clouds, have drenched unbelieving peoples.

### Verse 5

“Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth.”

This develops what he said above: since he first declared that the Lord’s mercy had been magnified up to the heavens, it followed: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God.” Since it is evident that his mercy contains the heavenly things, he ought rightly to be exalted above the heavens.

And again, because he said, “Your truth up to the clouds,” it is rightly added: “And your glory above all the earth.” These statements themselves clearly explain one another through their mutual declaration. 371

### Verse 6

“So that your beloved may be delivered. Save with your right hand, and hear me.”

He comes to the second narrative, which we said was the final portion of Psalm 59. Hence the division has rightly been made here, where a portion of another psalm is known to have been joined.

And so that you may understand clearly that the Lord’s Passion was undertaken for the benefit of the faithful people, he prays that he himself may be saved, so that the multitude of believers may be delivered. There is no doubt that this occurred at the time of the resurrection, when the apostles and all believers perceived the divinity of the Lord the Savior through such a manifestation.

### Verse 7

“God has spoken in his Holy One: I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and I will measure out the valley of the tents.”

Through this verse and the following three, a figure called *sardismos* is formed, which arises from a mixture of different languages, as we have already said in Psalm 59. Let us now return to explaining the words.

When he says that God spoke “in his Holy One,” he clearly signifies himself. Understand the force of “in his Holy One.” He did not say “through his Holy One,” as through the prophets, the apostles, and others who pleased the Lord. Rather, he says “in his Holy One,” so that the Word made flesh might speak with the Father in one will.

It follows: “I will rejoice and divide Shechem.” We must diligently seek the meanings of all these names, since they are shown to reveal the mysteries of hidden things. Shechem is interpreted as “shoulders.” The shoulders signify works, through whose support and direction we habitually perform something with our hands.

The sense, therefore, is this: he says that after his resurrection he will rejoice, because he divided his work—that is, his grace—among the apostles and the faithful, who followed the glory of his Passion and preaching.

He adds: “And I will measure out the valley of the tents.” “Valley” signifies humility. He speaks of the tents of the Churches, whose special holiness is clearly established.
