The Lord measured out this humility when he distributed the gifts of charisms to each of the faithful according to his will, as the Apostle says: “But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4:7).

### Verse 8

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the strength of my head. Judah is my king.”

In Latin, Gilead is said to mean “migration,” which truly belongs to the Lord when the nations, pierced by remorse at his calling, happily migrated to him.

Manasseh is interpreted as “forgetfulness.” By this word the Jewish people are signified: having forgotten the divine benefits, they crucified Christ the Lord in sacrilegious presumption; nevertheless, afterward, through his mercy, they returned to his religion and worship.

Thus, by mentioning these names, he testifies that both peoples are his own.

It follows: “And Ephraim is the strength of my head. Judah is my king.” He spoke this concerning his Passion. Ephraim is said to mean “fruitfulness”; it signifies the crown of thorns that he received when it was placed upon his head in his Passion. This crown was fruitful beyond all other fruits, so that through that humility he might win the whole world.

He rightly called Judah his king, because he descended from Judah’s origin through the propagation of the flesh.

### Verse 9

“Moab is the pot of my hope. Upon Idumea I will extend my sandal; the foreigners are subject to me.”

As Jerome prefers, Moab signifies “from the father,” which is “without a father.” Hence he wishes the devil to be understood: through evil works he does not have God as father, but as a just judge.

He is therefore compared to a pot, which boils the flesh placed in it and brings it, through fiery heat, to a certain tenderness. In the same way, the devil chastises those handed over to him through unceasing consumption [edition, “completion”], and, against their will, brings them through continual persecution to the humility of confession.

Thus, in human fashion, the Lord says that he has hope in the devil’s persecution, because many whom the devil hastens to afflict, once converted, strive to return to the Lord’s benefits.

It follows: “Upon Idumea I will extend my sandal.” Idumea signifies what is earthly and bloodstained; the Lord indicates that he will possess it through the preaching of the Gospel. In Psalm 59 we said that the sandal signifies the Gospel, which the Lord extended even to earthly human beings, filling the world with universal preaching through his law.

He added: “The foreigners are subject to me.” “Foreigners” is the interpretation of *allophyli*. They signify the Christian people, gathered from various nations through his mercy. By saying that they are subject, he testifies that they will be believers.

### Verse 10

“Who will lead me into the fortified city? Or who will lead me as far as Idumea?”

From the standpoint of his humanity, a most fitting question is placed first, so that the answer may follow. For he denies that he can be led onward by human assistance to the place where he desires to arrive in order to liberate his faithful.

It is that very nature which humbly says: “O God, my God, look upon me; why have you abandoned me?” (Psalm 22:2). It is that same nature which said: “The one who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28). Finally, it is that nature which said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39).

Everything is humbly understood according to that aspect, so that the God-man may be understood as most perfect.

The fortified city perhaps signifies hell, which no human power could open except the one who is known to have broken its gates. Hence it was said in the preceding psalm: “For he shattered gates of bronze and broke iron bars” (Psalm 106:16).

The city stands open for receiving and closed for releasing. It lost the law of its fortification when the Redeemer of the nations entered it. That gates are placed in both a good and a bad sense is testified by Psalm 24, which says: “Lift up your gates, princes of yours” [edition, “prince of yours”], “and be lifted up, eternal gates” (Psalm 24:7).

We have said that Idumea signifies what is earthly. The Lord came to it after the resurrection, when, with his immeasurable glory revealed, he became known to all the nations as the omnipotent ruler. He asks for this to happen in the same way as what he said above.

### Verse 11

“Is it not you, O God, who have rejected us, and will not go forth, O God, in our strengths?”

The confession that had been suspended in the preceding verse now follows in completed form, since the things accomplished in the resurrection could be fulfilled only by divinity. Who could break the prison of death? Who could open the gates of the fortified city except the Lord Christ himself, who rose from the dead on the third day contrary to the order of human nature and displayed the glory of his majesty?

Observe carefully that above he proceeds in the singular number; here, however, he says that he was rejected in the plural, so that the head may be understood to speak such things together with his members.

“You have rejected us” signifies “you have delayed us,” because it is clear that he himself was also delayed until his glorification while he remained in this life. The glory of all believers is likewise suspended even today, until we come to the rewards of the resurrection.

It follows: “And you will not go forth, O God, in our strengths.” This signifies the time when he was seized and handed over by the Jewish crowd, when he was beaten with scourges by the governor and endured the spittle of the mad Jews. If the divinity had then wished to repel these things, every adversity would have been shattered and fallen. But he delayed displaying the miracle of his power in order to fulfill the beneficial order of the Passion as it had been dispensed.

The same thing happens by experience to the faithful when they are afflicted with various calamities for their testing.

### Verse 12

“Give us help in tribulation; human salvation is vain.”

Here the humanity of the Lord cries out together with his members, asking that security through the resurrection be granted from the tribulations of this world, so that at last the storm of this age may come to rest. He does not ask for help from pleasures, but from tribulation, from which he knows that remedies come to human beings through divine clemency.

And lest any hope remain in the powers of this world, he adds: “Human salvation is vain,” because such presumption is truly weak and transitory.

### Verse 13

“In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us.”

This is the voice both of the Lord the Savior and of all the faithful, since spiritual and bodily enemies are effectively opposed by divine powers.

Let those also hear this psalm who say that the flesh and divinity of the Lord are of one nature. The heavenly orator Ambrose rightly rebukes them in his book *On the Incarnation of the Lord* (chapter 6), saying:

“What hells have spewed forth so great a sacrilege? The Arians are now more tolerable, for through these people the strength of the Arians’ own perfidy grows, so that they assert with even greater insistence that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not of one substance. For these people have attempted to say that the Lord’s divinity and flesh are of one substance, along with the other things that this remarkable passage is known to contain.”

Therefore let them understand that they are especially called more wicked than those whom the universal Church renders strangers to itself. And rightly so. For since the Word made flesh received the name Christ, and the Word is one thing while the flesh is another, if Christ is said to exist in one nature, as they wish, no more wicked perfidy—unless I am mistaken—can be found among all heresies.

Although different heresies touch upon the injury of the divine majesty in separate ways, this one alone, alas, has dared to presume something that strives to abolish the very name of our faith from its foundations.

It should certainly be known that this is the sixth among those psalms which, as we stated, will speak of the two natures.

## Conclusion of the Psalm
How well are those things joined together which descend from one source for the working of the salvation of the human race! For who would not marvel that what was said in earlier and different psalms is shown here to have been brought into such complete harmony [Col. 0782A]? Thus David himself, in Chronicles (1 Chron. XVI), having joined together portions of the psalms—that is, the hundred and fourth, the ninety-fifth, and the hundred and fifth—and filled with the Holy Spirit, resounded the praises of the Lord with great rejoicing before the ark of the covenant, so that, as it were, sweet incense made from different spices might arise and happily reach the sight of the Lord. For what is shown to be in no way contradictory to itself is joined together without difficulty. Therefore, let us also believe that this psalm was composed from others for this reason: so that the hungry soul, nourished by a variety of flavors, might be refreshed. Hence I think that even today it is permitted for singers to join together something from portions of the psalms. For I judge that this too suits the present passage: the Lord’s work made one Church from two peoples [Col. 0782B].

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 108

**For the end, a psalm of David.**

The title of this psalm is already known from the exposition of the preceding words, and therefore it should be referred to the heavenly King, since all its words tend toward the Lord Christ. For in this psalm he will speak of the iniquity of Judas and of the Jewish people, and, foretelling the mysteries of his Passion, will proclaim them.

### Division of the psalm

Throughout the entire text, as has been said, the Lord Christ speaks. In the first part he rebukes the Jews, who preferred to repay their Creator evil for good. In the second, the iniquity of Judas the betrayer and of the faithless people is recounted [Col. 0782C], and the things that were to come upon them [ed., “will come upon them”] for so great a detestation are foretold. In the third, he prays, in respect of the fact that he is human, that, once delivered from the danger of his Passion, he may quickly attain the glory of the Resurrection.

### Exposition of the psalm

**Verse 1. “O God, do not be silent about my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man have been opened against me. They have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue.”**

Our Lord and Savior asks this in respect of the fact that he deigned to assume the form of a servant: that the Father should not cause the praise of his Resurrection to be silent [ed., “to be silenced”], although, according to the lowliness of the flesh, he was to suffer the harsh insults of the Jews. For this is what is meant by, “Do not be silent about my praise”: that is, “Do not cause it to be silent” [ed., “to be silenced”]. There is an appropriate contrast here: since the enemies were speaking lies, testimonies of the truth should be sung against them throughout the whole world. For he desires them to be convicted by the glory of his Resurrection, so that they may recognize the guilt of their own perversity and return more quickly to the remedies of confession, lest, persisting in their insolence, they perish forever.

This figure is called syncrisis, that is, comparison. It occurs when, by a certain comparison, we demonstrate that our cause is more just than that of our adversaries. But this praise was certain, because it flowed from the truth. That other speech, however, was recognized as utterly false, since it was shown to proceed from the mouth of a deceitful and faithless man. For how can that be called true which is taught to be opposed to truth itself?

The “open mouth” therefore signifies the insults he endured from the Jews. But here he uses the singular number for this reason: because, as has often been said, the people may rightly be designated in both ways. Although it is heard as one in name, it is nevertheless understood to be many in number. He continues: “They have spoken against me with a deceitful tongue.” They spoke, therefore, with a deceitful tongue when they attacked the Lord’s holy simplicity with the most deceptive words, saying, “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” and also, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful” (Mark XII, 14). For they uttered these words with a treacherous intention.

**Verse 2. “And they surrounded me with words of hatred, and they fought against me without cause.”**

By saying, “They surrounded me with words of hatred,” he signifies the time when, in an evil conspiracy, they said to Pilate, “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke XXIII, 21). For those were words of hatred, not of truth, which seemed to demand the death of the innocent man [Col. 0783B]. “They surrounded me” signifies the mad crowd, which was shouting its most wicked words on every side. “They fought against me without cause” refers to the time when, before the governor, they attacked the innocent man’s blood with false accusations.

He said “without cause” because their action could bring them no advantage, but rather caused a detestable destruction to spring up among them. For just as the righteous love the Lord without cause when they love him solely for his own sake and do not seek him for any temporal benefit, so the wicked hate without cause because they cannot find a reason for their righteous hatred, as is also said in the sixty-eighth psalm: “Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head” (Ps. LXVIII, 5).

**Verse 3. “Instead of loving me, they slandered me; but I was praying.”**

**Verse 4. “They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love.”**

In these two verses, the things stated must be separated according to their distinct meanings, so that what has been spoken obscurely may become more clearly known.

Every sin is contracted in three ways. The first degree of wrongdoing is not to return good for good. The second is to return evil for evil. The third and most extreme form of vice is to repay evil for good. Conversely, praiseworthy conduct is carried out according to the same order: to bestow good for good; secondly, not to return evil for evil; thirdly, the most perfect kind of virtue is to bestow good for evil.

And observe that, just as the Jews resolved to commit that final and most vicious act—when they ought to have loved, they rushed headlong into wicked hatred [Col. 0783D]—so the Lord, in perfect devotion, returned that supreme good: while hanging on the cross, he prayed for those who had resolved in their impious will to slaughter him.

**Verse 4. “Appoint a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.”**

He comes to the second part, in which he will first say much about Judas, who was capable of every evil. Then, using the plural number, he includes the impious Jews who became his sons through imitation of his crime.

Therefore, with absolute certainty concerning the future, he foretells that the devil is to be appointed over Judas the betrayer. The devil is rightly called a sinner because the sin of betrayal took its beginning from him. And lest you perhaps doubt of whom this is said, it is added: “And let the devil stand at his right hand”—namely, because he deserved to be saved by no confession, but died strangled by the noose of evil through despair. Nor could he have a free right hand who was wholly devoted to the crimes of the left.

For this is how each person is shown to be of the character of the one who holds his right hand, as in the evil passage: “Their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Ps. CXLIII, 11); and in the good passage: “I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand” (Ps. XV, 8). Thus, by these meanings, the quality of our whole life is indicated.

**Verse 5. “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin.”**

This is spoken of the future judgment, when sinners will be condemned by the most just sentence, as in the Gospel: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

And consider that he says, “Let him go forth”—namely, from the assembly of the righteous; for everyone who goes forth from it is joined to the party of the impious. His prayer, which he had undertaken to recite among the other apostles, is shown to have been turned into the gravest sin for him when it contains the words: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12). But what would he forgive those who owed him, when he was betraying the author of every blessing? Therefore the holy prayer was rightly turned into sin for him who sinned by a detestable example.

**Verse 6. “Let his days be few, and let another receive his episcopate.”**

He says that Judas’s days should be few, as though his long life appears to have been shortened by his most cruel sin, just as he says elsewhere: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. LIV, 24).

But this seems rightly to occur when younger men are compared with older ones. For when some live a hundred years, the life of those who do not live even fifty years appears to have been halved. So Judas’s apostolic days became few when other apostles remained after him, preserving the Lord’s will.

And lest that most sacred number of apostles be broken by Judas’s death, it was foretold even then that another should be made in his place, so that the number twelve might remain intact.

“Episcopate” is the highest rank in the Church. An episcopus is called a superintendent—*superinspector*—because, with the help of the Lord’s grace, he guards the Lord’s flock from a lofty seat like a most vigilant shepherd, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “I have appointed you as a watchman over the house of Israel” (Ezek. III, 17). And observe that this name is first used in the Old Testament in this passage.

The Apostle clearly indicates the dignity of this office when he says: “Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work” (1 Tim. III, 1), and so forth. Therefore this name signifies not so much honor as labor. For whoever has undertaken to watch over others must observe himself with continual vigilance, lest what the Apostle says happen to him: “Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. IX, 27).

We should also remember that it is very clearly declared in the Acts of the Apostles that this verse was written concerning Judas. Peter says: “Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became the leader of those who arrested Jesus” (Acts I, 16) [Col. 0785A]. A little later it follows: “For it is written in the book of Psalms: ‘Let his dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one who inhabits it’ [ed., ‘who may inhabit it’]; and ‘Let another receive his episcopate.’” Thus no one can doubt that this must in every respect be understood of Judas himself.

So we recognize that this psalm was prophesied concerning the Passion of the Lord through both the words of the Gospel and the testimony of the apostle Peter. In this verse, the figure called *hypexaeresis*, which in Latin is called *exceptio* (“exception”), is to be understood, because Judas is excepted from the honor of the episcopate, that is, of the apostleship.

**Verse 7. “Let his children become orphans, and his wife a widow.”**

Although it is not read elsewhere that Judas had a wife or children, this prophecy nevertheless allows us to understand that he was a husband and a father. When he died, such things undoubtedly happened to those attached to him: the wife who was left behind became a widow, and the children became orphans because they had lost their father [Col. 0785B].

But if you wish to refer this to the spiritual meaning, the children may be understood as those who followed him in that betrayal; the wife as the will, which is always joined to us like a spouse, from whom we bring forth children when, as though from a certain womb, we generate our deeds.

**Verse 8. “May his children be violently removed and beg; may they be cast out of their dwellings.”**

What has been said may apply to both possibilities, whether to bodily children or to our deeds. “Violently removed” signifies that they are expelled by force, so that they suffer unwillingly what is inflicted upon them. “Let them beg” signifies the lack of good things, so that it may be evident to all that those who followed such ways possessed no resource of reason [Col. 0785C]. They are cast out of their dwellings when they are made strangers to the assembly of the Lord’s people, where previously they seemed to have dwelt not in mind but only in body.

**Verse 9. “Let the moneylender search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder all his labors.”**

This verse must be explained through the comparisons it contains, so that the obscurity of the whole matter may be removed for us.

When a debtor is unable to repay what he owes, his moneylender, having received authorization from the judge, enters the house of the person under obligation, seizes everything he can find, and satisfies his claim from the money that was lent. So also, when the devil has gathered many sins in people and they have persisted in them with obstinate will, he receives power to plunder the substance of the person under obligation [Col. 0785D] and, according to his own desire, to satisfy himself by tearing apart the human being.

This is now wished upon Judas: that, handed over to the devil’s power, he may be stripped of every good. “Strangers” are also unclean spirits, whom the devil commands like slaves to do harm. They are rightly called strangers because they are shown to be outsiders from the Lord’s kingdom. These spirits plunder the labors of those who transgress the Lord’s commandments, when, having received permission, they deprive them of every good.

**Verse 10. “Let there be no helper for him, and let there be no one who pities his orphans.”**

Good men too are struck by the devil’s temptation, but they do not cease to have the Lord as their helper, so that they may be delivered from the danger threatening them. He says that the wicked are to be abandoned to such a condition, so that iniquity may remain without hope, deprived of the most salutary medicine [Col. 0786A].

They are called orphans as though they were “little ones,” because, through the smallness of their age, they are shown to be weak in governing themselves. Hence the pupil of the eye is also so called, because it appears exceedingly small in our body.

**Verse 11. “Let his offspring be brought to destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out.”**

He calls them the same offspring whom above he called orphans. And because some sinners are accustomed to extend their kind through a long succession, he also cuts off their hope of posterity, so that wicked minds may not console themselves with any good [mss. A, B: “with any good whatsoever”].

Or “one generation” should rather be understood as the time when we are born in sins. Therefore he asks that they not reach the second generation, that is, regeneration—though they have been rejected in predestination—but perish in the first filth of their sins and not escape the snare of death through the benefit of a second birth [Col. 0786B]. But these things, and others like them, are said of those who are to be condemned in the Lord’s judgment.

**Verse 12. “Let the iniquity of his fathers return to the memory of the Lord’s presence, and let the sin of his mother not be blotted out.”**

By a tropological interpretation it is said that the sins of his ancestors return to the Lord’s memory, so that the impious Judas may be tormented both by his own new offenses and by the errors of his parents [mss. A, B, F: “by his own offenses”]. For, as we have often said, one is guilty of the sins of earlier generations when one is found to be their most devoted follower.

“In the presence of the Lord” means in the deliberation of judgment, since, when the Lord looks upon sins, he unquestionably strikes their authors. Hence the prophet also cries: “Turn your face away from my sins” (Ps. L, 11).

“The sin of his mother” is the notorious insolence of the Synagogue, which killed the prophets and did not abstain even from sacrifices to demons. He calls that part the mother of Judas the betrayer—not the part that brought forth holy men, but the part that shed the blood of the innocent.

**Verse 13. “Let them always be against the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth.”**

Now he uses the plural number because he prefers the Jews to be understood as contumacious. For just as in one holy person we perceive many blessed people, as in the saying, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 18), so again in one most wicked person many detestable people are contained.

Peter bears the type of the Church, whereas Judas carries the image of Babylon destined for condemnation. Therefore, after speaking of Judas, he rightly speaks of the faithless, since wicked people follow him in evil deeds [Col. 0786D].

Sinners are therefore always “against the Lord” when, having been alienated from his kingdom, they are to be sent, by the operation of justice, into the opposition of Gehenna. Since the Lord is eternal blessedness, one who is condemned to everlasting punishment is rightly said to be made “against” him.

But the person who is not seen in the blessed homeland perishes from the land of the living. Nor do such people come into remembrance, since they obtain no further mercy. For we are said to remember those to whom we are about to grant something.

**Verse 14. “Because he did not remember to show mercy.”**

He states the reason for the most just punishment: the one who despised showing mercy to others cannot find mercy, as it is written: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. V, 7).

Although he has returned to the singular number, we must still understand the Jewish people, who did not show mercy to the apostles or to Christ’s faithful when, after the Lord’s Passion, they harassed them with wicked persecution. For this cannot be understood of Judas, since he departed from this life before the Lord’s crucifixion and did not have time to persecute his faithful.

**Verse 15. “And he pursued the poor and the beggar, and put the brokenhearted man to death.”**

This too must still be understood of the Jewish people, who, with unspeakable presumption, slaughtered both Christ and his disciples.

People are generally moved to persecute by either the pursuit of riches or the hateful ostentation of pride. But to pursue a poor and needy man is pure savagery, since neither honor is sought from him nor an abundance of possessions desired.

In his customary manner, the Lord recalls, from the nature of the humanity he assumed, that he was poor and a beggar. He is a beggar from what is ours and rich from what is his own, as the Apostle says: “Though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich” (2 Cor. VIII, 9).

But I do not think that “brokenhearted” can be spoken of the Head himself, because no such example occurs. Rather, I judge that “brokenhearted” should be referred to the sinner who is pierced by the recollection of his sins, so that he may deserve to return to making satisfaction; Scripture testifies to this in countless places. It must therefore necessarily be understood of the members, since Christ the Lord had no sins [Col. 0787C]. For the Jewish people persecuted those who were brokenhearted, as is shown to have happened in the case of blessed Stephen and the apostle Paul.

**Verse 16. “And he loved cursing, and it shall come to him; and he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” [mss. A, B, F: “it shall be removed from him”].**

He continues to speak of the faithless people, because they loved cursing—namely, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25). It is clear that this came upon those who persisted in an impious will against the Lord.

The people referred to did not desire blessing when the man healed of blindness asked them: “Do you also wish to become his disciples?” (John IX, 27–28). But they, as though provoked by an extremely bitter curse, replied: “You are his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses.” By saying this, the blessing was removed from them, when, after abandoning them, it came to the faith of the Gentiles, as the Apostle says: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46).

**Verse 17. “And he put on cursing as a garment, and it entered his inward parts like water, and into his bones like oil.”**

We must carefully observe how the quality of the sin itself is indicated by certain expressions.

First, the people mentioned above put on cursing like a garment when, at the devil’s instigation, they gave their consent and preferred to hand the Lord over to Pontius Pilate. For there he was clothed with a certain burden of vesture, where he is known to have been wrapped in such a will [Col. 0788A].

Second, the curse entered his inward parts like water when he resolved to do what had been suggested to him by a most wicked inspiration. For when water is received into diseased entrails, it always enters in order to cause harm.

Third, iniquity flowed into his bones like oil when he completed the deed with unheard-of perversity, so that it seemed to have penetrated not merely the inward parts of the flesh but the very bones themselves. By saying “oil,” he signifies the pleasure of the crime, which enters our body softly and gently, so that it caresses us with a certain delight. This is known to happen to wicked minds when they take pride in some pleasure within their crime.

**Verse 18. “Let it be to him like the garment with which he covers himself” [mss. G and ed., “with which he shall cover himself”], “and like the belt with which he always girds himself.”**

He continues with the same comparisons, so that the sin in which he preferred to be wrapped may be indicated by the likeness of another garment. Above he said, “He put on,” which pertains to a tunic; now he says, “He covers himself,” which seems to suit a cloak, so that the doubled clothing may signify the immense burdens of sins.

He continues: “And like the belt with which he always girds himself.” The belt here is not to be understood as the feminine girdle, but the belt with which we gird our loins, as is read in the Gospel concerning John, and in the Book of Kings concerning Elijah: “And a leather belt around his loins” (Matt. III, 4; 2 Kings I, 8). This word has been granted both meanings. By this comparison he says that the man was bound by sins like a belt, so that he would never be stripped of his burdens, weighed down by the faithlessness of obstinacy [Col. 0788C].

O unhappy people—how badly clothed they are! These are the garments that make sinners burn, not grow warm; that cast them into the flame, rather than protect them from the necessity of cold.

**Verse 19. “This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord and speak evil against my soul.”**

We should indeed understand this verse as directed against all the faithless, but it nevertheless appears especially to attack two heresies.

The Arians slander the Son before God the Father when they testify that the Son is lesser and shamelessly call inferior the one whom they jointly confess to be the Creator of all. The Apollinarists also speak evil against the Lord’s soul when they say that his divinity assumed only human flesh, not a soul; nor does their faithlessness depart, defeated by so many examples [Col. 0788D].

Therefore, what has been said above is to be understood not only against these people but against all heretics, who will have no share in the Lord’s kingdom.

**Verse 20. “But you, Lord, Lord, deal mercifully with me for your name’s sake, because your mercy is sweet. Deliver me.”**

He comes to the third part of the account, in which he prays, in respect of the part in which he suffered, that the glory of the Resurrection may be hastened and that his enemies may be clothed with the disgrace of confusion.

When he says, “But you, Lord,” this is joined to what was said above: “If Judas betrayed, if the Jew crucified, then you show mercy, so that a glorious Resurrection may arise in opposition to what was done” [Col. 0789A].

Or the Son says to the Father, “You act,” in order to display the power of their cooperation. For everything that the Father does, the Son also does, as he himself says: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does”; and, “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself,” so that “all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John V, 19, 26, 23).

When he repeats, “Lord, Lord,” he shows the affection of his most gentle prayer. This figure is called *epezeuxis*, because in one verse he doubled the expression without any intervening word.

“For your name’s sake,” so that the worship of his name may be spread throughout the whole world. Here the great clemency of the Godhead is asserted, because no human merits could bring it about that mortal nature should be shown to have been exalted by such immense miracles [Col. 0789B].

He says “mercy” because he deigned to assume flesh, through which the most merciful author might assist the human race. He continues: “Deliver me”—obviously from the most savage Passion inflicted by the Jews.

**Verse 21. “For I am needy and poor, and my heart is troubled within me.”**

He calls himself needy and poor in the humility of the flesh, as has been explained above. Let the poor hear this, let the needy hear it, and let them recognize that it is glorious for them that Christ is called such.

His heart could indeed be troubled, since his flesh was known to be extinguished for our sake, as he confessed when his Passion was near: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XXVI, 38). All these things are recounted according to a saving plan, so that, for the sake of the heretics, both the complete nature of humanity in Christ the Lord may be shown and we may be taught how to pray [Col. 0789C].

**Verse 22. “Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away, and I have been shaken like a locust.”**

Here he shows the ease with which he was persecuted: for he was snatched from the midst of the disciples by the Jewish crowd with as much speed as a shadow at night commonly departs when the light of the sun arrives.

He was “shaken like a locust” when, amid repeated persecutions, he seemed to change from one place to another: namely, when he went from Nazareth to Capernaum, from Capernaum to Bethsaida, from Bethsaida to Jerusalem, traveling around these places with greater concern for sinners, lest the persecuting people fulfill their crime.

A locust avoids the hand that tries to seize it and flies away in certain leaps. He compares himself to it both on account of his smallness and because of the speed of its departure. This cannot seem unbecoming to his humility, since he also compared himself to worms, saying: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI, 7) [Col. 0789D].

**Verse 23. “My knees have grown weak from fasting” [mss. A, B: “before fasting”], “and my flesh has been changed because of the oil.”**

Although the Gospel testifies that Christ the Lord fasted for forty days and forty nights (Matt. IV, 2), we do not read that his knees grew weak; only that he was hungry is declared. Therefore, if you refer this hunger to the knees—that is, to the stability of the body, upon which we always stand—it can be fitted to the passage with some difficulty, unless this objection troubles you [Col. 0790A]. It is better to refer the knees to his members, which truly grew weak when his apostles were scattered during his Passion.

For what could have been weaker than that Peter should deny him and the rest of the faithful multitude should hide [ed., “should have hidden”]? He continues: “And my flesh has been changed because of the oil.” Here “oil” signifies divine grace, as has already been said of him in the forty-fourth psalm: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

For it is this grace that changed the weakness of the flesh into the glory of immortality. This also seems not improperly to be applied to Christ’s members.

**Verse 24. “And I became a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads.”**

He touches upon the things that the Jewish people were to say in derision, as the Gospel says: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. XII, 24). And elsewhere: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter?” (Luke IV, 22). Again they say: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days!” (Matt. XXVII, 40), along with the other things which seemed to be insults to their mad minds, but which themselves proved to bring us healing.

They shook their heads according to the custom of those who are excessively angry. For whenever we are inflamed with rage, we threaten with turbulent movements of the head.

**Verse 25. “Help me, Lord my God; save me according to your mercy.”**

The weakness he assumed prays to be helped. For he himself asks for mercy who also grants assistance. He asks as a human being and provides as God. No one who healthfully confesses the two natures in the Lord Christ can be confused by this. For countless such passages are found, which cannot stand in any other way.

**Verse 26. “So that they may know that this is your hand; and you, Lord, have done it.”**

So that the Jewish people would not arrogate to their own power the persecution of the Lord and Savior, he says to the Father, in respect of what he suffered: “Let people know that this dispensation was prepared by you, Lord, so that fools may not attribute to their own strength what you determined in great devotion to be done for the salvation of the world.”

He says, “So that they may know,” meaning the persecutors, who certainly did not know. For when he rose, they recognized this most clearly, because, unless the Lord had permitted it to happen, it could in no way have been accomplished.

He continues: “Because this is your hand,” that is, your power; and we should understand that it “has done” this.

**Verse 27. “They will curse him, and you will bless; let those who rise up against me be confounded” [ed., “will be confounded”], “but your servant will rejoice.”**

This is through the figure of syncrisis, which was placed at the beginning of this psalm.

“They will curse him” signifies those of whom the evangelist Matthew says: “Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads” (Matt. XXVII, 39). The Father blesses the Son when he says: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (John XII, 28).

But observe who those are who curse: they are full of falsehood, they raged cruelly, and they hastened to repay evil for good. The Father, however, is the source and origin of truth, the author of all goodness, and the fullness of every virtue. There is an admirable proclamation on both sides: the faithless people cursed, while Christ the Lord was praised by the glory of the Father [Col. 0791A].

He added: “Let those who rise up against me be confounded.” These are the Jews who rose up against the Lord and Savior in order to hand him over to death, though he had come to save them through his mercy. They were confounded when they learned the miracles of his Resurrection.

He continues: “But your servant will rejoice.” Let us recognize which nature is speaking, since it calls itself a servant. Can God be anyone’s servant? Yet he is a servant in the sense in which the Apostle says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7). So too the prophet Isaiah speaks of Christ: “Behold my servant; I will receive him; my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased” (Isa. XLII, 1), and so forth.

Therefore, let heretics cease to regard the Son as lesser in his divinity when they hear such an explicit statement of the humility of the flesh that even the name of servitude is assigned to him [Col. 0791B].

**Verse 28. “Let those who slander me be clothed with reverence, and let them be covered, like a double cloak, with their confusion.”**

Here, since the matter concerns a people who are to believe, the words are given as a prayer rather than a curse. For one who is clothed with reverence is already almost rejoicing in the gift of conversion, so that he fears as God the one whom previously he believed to be a contemptible man.

*Diplois* is a double kind of cloak. He therefore asks that those who have now been stripped bare through the action of their double faithlessness may be clothed with an understanding of both laws. The confusion of the Jews is that they do not understand the law, which so often foretold that the Lord and Savior would come.

Or he wishes to express the kind of thing that is commonly said in proverbs: that they be clothed in a double cloak of confusion, while they are ashamed before God and human beings.

**Verse 29. “I will confess the Lord exceedingly with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him.”**

This is spoken in respect of the members, because, after the manifestation of the Resurrection has been spread throughout the whole world, he himself prays, and through the mouth of the Catholic Church a fitting confession is offered to the Father.

“In the midst of many” designates the universal Church, which does not cease to confess the Lord’s praises while the faithless still surround it. For as long as the world continues, Christ’s Church is girded about by a crowd of slanderers.

**Verse 30. “For he stood at the right hand of the poor man, to save my soul from those who persecuted me.”**

He states the reason why, in his members, he ought to confess the Father: namely, because, once his persecutors had been confounded, he himself was saved [Col. 0791D].

Above he said that the devil stood at Judas’s right hand because Judas was polluted by the filth of sins; but here he says that the Father stood at his own right hand because he had no sin. Thus he also stands beside the faithful when he forgives their sins [ed., “when he will have forgiven them”].

He continues: “To save my soul from those who persecuted me.” His soul was indeed saved from his persecutors when it did not consent in any perversity to the wickedness of the persecutors.

This also suitably applies to his members, who do not know how to yield to their persecutors, although they are afflicted by various tortures [Col. 0792A]. For the soul is not saved when it is withdrawn from temporal death, but when it is freed with the greatest blessedness from the prison of this age, as the Apostle says: “I am hard pressed between the two: my desire is to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I, 23). And elsewhere: “Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. VII, 24–25).

### Conclusion of the psalm

This is the fifth of those psalms which, according to the rules stated above, speak at greater length about the Lord’s Passion: namely, the twenty-first, the thirty-fourth, the fifty-fourth, the sixty-eighth, and the present one, the hundred and eighth.

First, all began from the person of the Lord Christ; second, they are shown to have begun their speech with prayer; third, they related the events of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 0792B]; fourth, they agree with the words of the Gospel in harmonious truth; fifth, they ended with great rejoicing in the hope of the faithful. Thus the dignity of the present psalm joined itself to this mystical number, which was given to the five virgins and assigned to the five books.

Yet although those too are great miracles of our salvation, nothing is clearer, nothing more acceptable, than to receive with worship the Passion of the incarnate Lord. Everything fits; everything corresponds to everything else with radiant equality. A virgin gave birth, the Messiah came, the immaculate Lamb was slain, the Redeemer rose from the dead, the world heard and believed—and still the Jew pretends not to know what the whole world has recognized.

Grant, Lord, conversion to the obstinate, light to the darkened, and faith to the unbelieving, so that you may deign to assist those in danger for whom you prayed while hanging on the cross [Col. 0792C]. For when we cannot persuade them of what is just, we rightly beseech you, Lord, on their behalf.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 109

**A psalm of David.**
These words are indeed very well known, and are affixed to the doors as though inscribed on a royal document. But this title does not say, “Read and depart”; rather, “Read and draw near.” Therefore, let us reverently enter upon the Lord’s mighty works, because this psalm will speak most fully and briefly both of the Lord’s sacred incarnation and of his omnipotent divinity. At certain points it may even seem to have been uttered with a similar sublimity or beauty to the beginning of that Gospel where it says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Therefore, so to speak, it is a certain sun of our faith, a mirror of the heavenly mystery, a treasury of the sacred Scriptures: here is summed up everything narrated in the preaching of both Testaments. Therefore it must be held with love; its sweetness increases toward merit, and it is gathered together in a concise brevity. Now, since it is distinguished by a variety of persons, let us courageously hear its division.

## Division of the Psalm

The most holy prophet, raised into the secret place of the loftiest contemplation, reports in the first verse words beyond estimation: what the omnipotent Father said to the omnipotent and coeternal Son, simultaneously displaying the nature of divinity and humanity. For when he declares, “The Lord said to my Lord,” he shows the nature of his divinity. When he adds, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool,” and, “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power, and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies,” the substance of his humanity is made clear, which was able to receive what it did not possess.

In the second division the Father begins, in a manner proportionate to our capacity, to indicate something of the nature of his divinity. For he says: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones: from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” In the third section the prophet speaks to the end, again displaying the form of his humanity when he says: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent,” and so forth, so that in these passages the Word made flesh, who is the Lord Christ, might be recognized through a threefold illumination.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1. “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.”

It seems appropriate first to set forth a figure by which we may inwardly grasp the beginning of this psalm. A figure is what in Latin is called a *species*, through which invisible realities are offered to the senses for contemplation. He says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.”

One divinity, one power, one eternity. The Father says to the Son what the one did not utter with his mouth, nor the other hear with attentive ears [ms. G. and others: “attentive”]. The Father wills, and the Son knows; the Son wills, and the Father knows. Yet neither that will itself is comprehensible to us, nor can that knowledge itself appear to human senses. Therefore, appropriately, there has been a descent to the level of our customary understanding, so that weak humanity might be instructed, since human thought could not reach that secret perfection.

“Lord to Lord.” These names declare equality of substance and the power of might. This repetition of one name fittingly expresses both the persons and clearly reveals one nature of divinity. Nor should it disturb us that Jesus Christ himself is sometimes called both Son and Lord of David. For if you examine the reasons, both statements are entirely true. He is Son according to the origin of the flesh, as it is written at the beginning of Matthew: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matthew 1:1); and elsewhere the blind cried out: “Son of David, have mercy on us” (ibid., 20:30).

Here, however, he is called Lord of David according to his divinity, by which he is David’s creator. The same thing even happens in our present society: a son who has become a bishop may be called his father’s father—not according to the order of birth, but according to honor. For what was born from David’s seed was so honored and exalted that it was both Lord of David and his son.

It follows: “Sit at my right hand.” To the victorious Son, and through the holy incarnation the triumphant conqueror of the whole world, an honored seat is offered after the glory of the resurrection, so that through this position the glory of the humanity he assumed might be revealed. For this word indicates that our Head has been placed at the Father’s right hand. In that place are to be placed those who are separated from the gift of divinity by their unbelief, in accordance with: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

For if you consider the nature of divinity, what place can belong to the left or right side of him who embraces all things everywhere in the fullness of his majesty? When it says that the right hand was given to the Son, this was not so that anyone should believe him greater, but so that the Arians might not, in their criminal conception, falsely proclaim him lesser.

He added: “Until I make your enemies your footstool.” A *scabellum*—a footstool—is so called from being mounted, that is, ascended. Consider that here “until,” which has a temporal sense, is used for the infinite—as though he would not sit at the Father’s right hand after his enemies had been bent beneath his feet like a footstool. It is the usage of divine Scripture both to use this word for a short period and to express eternity.

It is used temporally, as in Isaiah: “Close your little door until the wrath of the Lord passes by” (Isaiah 26:20). But elsewhere, as here, “until” signifies eternal time. Thus in the hundred and twenty-second Psalm he will say: “So our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he have mercy on us” (Psalm 122:3). Similarly, in the Gospel it is said of Joseph: “He did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son” (Matthew 1:25)—as though he knew her afterward, although she remained a virgin. We shall treat this at the appropriate place with renewed care; this idiom, that is, this characteristic usage, may be called proper to divine Scripture.

By the Lord’s feet, eternal stability is signified: there he stands, as though with his footprints planted, by the power of his omnipotence. Those are evidently to be placed beneath these feet who, abandoning the opposition of their vices day by day, return to the Lord and, like a footstool beneath his feet, bend before his teachings.

O blessed stool placed beneath holy feet, raised above all kingdoms, to which such submission is granted! For when a footstool is placed beneath one seated at the right hand, there is undoubtedly reference to those enemies who, once converted, are placed at the right hand.

### Verse 2. “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your power, and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies.”

In this verse also the prophet speaks in his own person, offering praise to the Lord Christ. The rod of power is the scepter of royal authority, by which the faithful are supported, unbelievers afflicted, and the ungrateful terrified. To show that the Son lacks nothing, he said “your,” because that power of his divinity is proper and eternal to him.

But so that you may perceive this more clearly, he added that the Lord would send forth this rod from Zion—namely, the omnipotent Father. The Lord is said to be from Zion, and so is the Son, as Isaiah says: “For from Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3). Let the heretic hear the Father speaking of the power and majesty of the Son. Once he has spoken, how can that person be instructed if he does not believe the very author?

He added: “And you shall rule in the midst of your enemies.” He explained what the rod of power sent forth would do: namely, that you would rule in the midst of your enemies. Consider the most merciful wording: he says that Christ rules over his enemies, not that he takes vengeance on them, because he rules them when the multitude of sinners is converted to him. In one way he rules the faithful, and in another he reigns over the ungrateful: the former he trains through benefits and correction; the latter he strikes with the severity of vengeance.

He said “in the midst,” that is, in the soul and in the inmost heart, where the Lord rests after the filth of sins has been cleansed. Or he says that Christ rules in the Church, which in this world is situated amid the rage of heresies and superstitions.

Thus far the prophet has spoken of the nature of his divinity and humanity. Let us now examine the beginning of the second section.

### Verse 3. “With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones.”

He has arrived at the second heading, where these two verses are to be understood as the words of the Father, since he is about to speak appropriately of the holy generation of the Son. To demonstrate his coeternity clearly, the omnipotent Father says of his omnipotent Son: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power.”

The Father himself is also the beginning, as in: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). There he indicates that the Father is the beginning, where the Word was. The Son too is declared to be the beginning in the Gospel, when he says: “I am the beginning, for this reason also I speak to you” (John 8:25/26). Yet there are not two beginnings; just as there is one God, so there is evidently one beginning. The same must undoubtedly be understood of the Holy Spirit.

For when Scripture spoke of the beginning, it added: “And the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters” (Genesis 1:2). But the holy ones cannot behold how he is the beginning in the Beginning. When Philip saw the Son, he said: “Show us the Father.” The Integrity replied to them: “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:8–9). Then, when through the Lord’s grace they begin to shine with the fullest splendor, they see Christ the Beginning existing in the Beginning with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore let Arian unbelief cease to arise. The Father and the Son are both called the beginning so that their coeternity may be declared. For if there had been a time when the Son did not exist, only the Father could have been said to be the beginning.

It follows: “In the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones.” Consider how much force and honor each word possesses. “In the day” signifies eternity: there is one day, in which the blessed now behold divine brightness and power. Of this it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). And of the wicked it is read: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isaiah 26:10).

All will see the Son of Man judging the living and the dead, but only the most blessed will gaze upon his divinity. Where are those who even now refuse to confess two natures in Christ the Lord? The sinner sees the humanity; the blessed simultaneously behold the divinity. If there were one nature, as they fabricate, sinners could not look upon only the flesh they pierced in the resurrection without also seeing his divinity.

The “splendors of the holy ones” are present when, in the resurrection, they will shine like the angels of God and will be so purified and transparent that they can behold that majesty with the eyes of the heart. They cannot see that light unless they have been changed for the better, as the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51).

### Verse 4. “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

After saying that the Son was begotten in the splendors of the holy ones, he now intends to speak of his holy generation. Although it is indescribable, it is nevertheless touched upon by some recollection: an ineffable account, an incomprehensible understanding, a thought beyond the powers of all creatures, surpassing even the perception of angels—and yet he graciously discloses himself to us insofar as we are able to comprehend.

For God, eternal and unchangeable, remaining in his own nature, deigned to assume our humanity, so that he might renew the old man, make the mortal immortal, the sinner righteous, and command the alienated to share in his kingdom. Thus the gracious one would not allow his image in those who confess him to perish—an image that the cruel enemy wished to annihilate.

Let us now come to the words of this verse. The Father says to the Son: “From the womb I begot you,” that is, from the secret of my substance, from divinity itself: wholly from the Whole, omnipotent from Omnipotence, light from Light, the Highest from the Highest—something that no investigation and no sense can reach. For how can it be comprehended of whom it is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). Wonderful brevity, and a measure sufficient for our weakness: we are unable to grasp more, and it is entirely enough to have believed this much.

When he says “before the morning star,” he shows the immensity of eternity. The morning star is placed for all the stars, the part standing for the whole; it signifies the day that is to come. To indicate some incomprehensible reality, he says that he was begotten before that existed which customarily announces the coming day to the world. For the beginning of him by whom all things were created cannot be comprehended.

Let us now come to the beginning of the third section, in which the prophet again speaks.

### Verse 5. “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Here again the prophet, as has been said, recalls the Father’s promise. He swore to the Son—but now to Christ, who was born of the Virgin Mary. For what could he promise the Word alone, since he is known always to possess all things together with him? To swear is to promise something firm under attestation. And to whom could this apply better than to him who fulfilled the effect of his word through divine power? As the Apostle says in the Epistle written to the Hebrews:

“To show the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, God interposed an oath, so that through two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest consolation, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us, which we have as a sure and firm anchor of the soul” (Hebrews 6:17–19).

This is why, as has already been said, human beings are rightly forbidden to swear: they rashly promise under God’s attestation what they are unable to accomplish. God, however, swears by himself, as he promised Abraham: “I live, says the Lord: because you have heard my voice and have not spared your only son for my sake, surely blessing I will bless you” (Genesis 22:16–17), and so forth.

“And he will not repent,” certainly because all things rejoiced in such a great and such a dispensation. You also read: “It repents me that I have made man” (Genesis 6:7), when, before the coming of the Flood, the hearts of mortals had plunged into a whirlpool of sins. This is said according to human custom, since a person is thought to have had something in mind when what he hoped for turns out otherwise.

It follows: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Here too the prophet recalls that the Father promised this to the Son. For to whom can it truthfully and clearly be applied except to the Lord Savior, who sanctified his body and blood for salvation through the distribution of bread and wine? As he himself says in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have eternal life” (John 6:54).

But let the human mind conceive nothing bloody or corruptible in this flesh and blood, lest, as the Apostle says, “whoever eats the body of the Lord unworthily eats judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29). Rather, let it conceive a life-giving and saving substance, made proper to the Word himself, through which the forgiveness of sins and the gifts of eternal life are bestowed.

This order the most righteous king Melchizedek instituted through a mystical likeness, when he offered the Lord the fruit of bread and wine. It is clear that the victims of animals, which belonged to the order of Aaron, have perished, whereas the institution of Melchizedek remains—the institution celebrated throughout the world in the distribution of the sacraments. The obstinate Jews still do not understand this, although both their priesthood and their sacrifices are demonstrably taken away.

Christ is especially called a priest because he offered himself once for us as a sacrifice. Of him the Apostle says: “For such a high priest was fitting for us, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens” (Hebrews 7:26). He explains this meaning with marvelous clarity. When it says “forever,” the Lord Christ is signified, who remains in everlasting glory.

### Verse 6. “The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings in the day of his wrath.”

What the Father is said to have done, the Son and the Holy Spirit are likewise, without doubt, established to have accomplished. Yet this may cause difficulty: at the beginning of this psalm the Father said to the Son, “Sit at my right hand”; now the prophet again says that the Father’s power acted at the Son’s right hand.

This was said so that, when this equal reciprocity is presented, no greater or lesser status might in any way be imagined. “He has shattered kings” refers to those of whom the second psalm says: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2:2). He shattered these when, by the power of his omnipotence, he cast down their pride; for unless they had been shattered, they would have remained fixed in the harmful rigidity of their wickedness.

### Verse 7. “He will judge among the nations, he will fill the ruins; he will crush many heads in the plentiful land.”

Observe the particular force of the words. In the preceding verse he said that kings would be shattered on account of tyrannical pride; now he declares that peoples are judged on account of common sins. Yet both fall happily from their former aims when they withdraw from their prior wickedness and turn toward a good purpose.

Consider how he says here that he will judge in order to fill the ruins. He fills the ruins when he causes sins to fall from human hearts and causes harmful offenses to perish through the most salutary correction. This may be understood through the example where he says: “You will destroy them, and you will not build them up” (Psalm 27:5). This would certainly not be said unless some were destroyed in order to be renewed more successfully.

It follows: “He will crush many heads in the plentiful land.” These are surely the heads of those who do not have Christ as their head. For when those who follow the devil through various errors have been corrected, their head is undoubtedly crushed.

The head is called the elevated and honorable summit of our body. It is named from *capere*, “to take,” because it receives all our senses—that is, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—which our other members do not receive, except touch. Therefore we can rightly call our head the one whom we decide to follow.

He calls it a “plentiful land” because it nourishes abundant sinners, like a harvest and growth of vices.

### Verse 8. “He will drink from the torrent on the way” [mss. A, B, F: “he drank”]; “therefore he will exalt the head.”

The torrent was the turbulent persecution of the Jews, from which the Lord Christ drank on the way—that is, in this life, while he endured it in the body. But when it says “on the way,” the violence inflicted is displayed, and the swift passage is indicated by which travelers are accustomed to be carried toward another dwelling.

He is the one who heard, “Sit at my right hand.” He is the one to whom it is said, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” He is the one who crushes the heads of sinners. Because of the merit of his glorious passion, he was given the name that is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2:9–10).

You hear that he suffered, pagan or Jew; read also that he will himself be the judge, so that you may tremble before the omnipotent God whom you judge to be unworthy of attention.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This is the seventh psalm which, as we have stated, was preached concerning the two natures of the Lord Christ. But since the Apostle writes to Timothy: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke with all patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4:2), I wish to continue a conversation with you who still think that one nature was made in Christ the Lord.

Certainly, you believe with us that in the womb of Mary, ever-virgin, the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14); and you preach without qualification that he suffered and was buried in the humanity he assumed, that he rose from the dead on the third day, that he was then seen bodily by the apostles and by those who believed in him, and that he also ascended into heaven with the flesh in which he rose from the dead.

But what earthly notions do you retain for the future, you who have reached the heavenly things? Where, then, is that nature with which the Lord ascended into heaven? It could no longer perish by death, as the Apostle testifies: “Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead [ed.: ‘rising’], dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died to sin, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6:9–10).

Why would he say “he lives to God,” and not “he lives as God,” if there were one nature that lives? But there is another reality: he lives to God—namely, that which once died to sin.

Finally, you hear that he sits at the Father’s right hand, and you hesitate to retain in him what can belong only to his humanity? Permit us, we ask, always to call Christ the Lord the hope of our salvation. He may rightly be called by this name, since, in two united and perfect natures, he remains in the glory of the Father forever and ever.

For if you weigh your statements with careful examination, whenever you say that Jesus Christ is of one nature, you deny that he is the son of the holy Virgin. And consider from where salvation can now come to you, if the perversity of your confession cuts off the Lord Savior from you.

## Exposition of Psalm 110

Alleluia.

Although this name of praise seems to be general, it is especially added where there is rejoicing with great exultation. For his people praise the Lord, having been freed from the ruin of the world and knowing no longer how to endure slavery to vices. This praise is known to bear the figure of future joy, where the Lord is seen by his faithful without interruption and praised without end, as is read in another psalm: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ages upon ages” (Psalm 83:5).

This psalm too is adorned among the Hebrews with alphabetical order, marked at the beginnings of its clauses or divisions by all the letters in sequence. It indicates to us those righteous persons who, through the bestowal of divine grace, shine with perfect virtues. For just as the preceding alphabetic psalms, lacking certain letters, signify those who are not filled with every merit, though they are nevertheless known to dwell in the holy assembly, so this one, with all the letters completed, seems to indicate the merits of outstanding righteous persons.

There is also another reason for the use of this alphabet, as Father Hilary says (*Prologue on the Psalms*): we know that children and beginners are taught by letters so that they may seek the precepts of wisdom; similarly, psalms of this kind are given to children and beginners, that their first principles may be formed, as it were, by the instruction of certain elements. For although we read that some learned the divine Scriptures even without letters, it is nevertheless easier for our frailty, by God’s grace, to learn wisdom through letters than to undergo that miracle. We are therefore admonished by this mystery to hasten most eagerly to the pursuits of learning, since the very order of the letters is set forth to show that we ought to meditate upon and learn the elements.

## Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0800A]

The people of the blessed, gathered from different parts of the world, say at the psalm’s opening that they will confess to the Lord in the assembly of the righteous, where there is eternal praise and proclamation without end. This section contains six letters of the aforesaid alphabet. Secondly, he says that his faithful are satisfied with abundant provision, pledging the Lord’s advent so that they may seek the promised inheritance with most eager attention; in this section another ten letters are arranged. Thirdly, he declares that Christians have been redeemed and that the New Testament has been consecrated by eternal grace. This section, receiving the remaining six letters, completes the whole alphabet in beautiful perfection.

## Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0800B] ### Verse 1. ALEPH, BETH. “I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the congregation.”

“Confess,” as we have often said, is an equivocal term, understood differently according to different contexts. Those who lament their sins confess, and likewise those who give thanks to the Lord confess; but the former is in tears, the latter in joy; the former is known to be in affliction, the latter in holy cheerfulness of mind. Hence the faithful people here exult in overflowing joy, portraying a certain image of the age to come, where these voices are continual and the praises of the Lord are celebrated with a devout mind.

To show the sincerity of his intention, he says that he will praise him with all the affection of his heart, so that no contrary thought may steal in, nor the devil’s wiles seem to darken a splendid and luminous mind. It follows: “In the council of the righteous and in the congregation.” If you wish to seek the council of the righteous and the congregation here, it seems altogether difficult to find all the elect in this world, where the Church is made up of a mingling of good and evil. But those who confess here with their whole heart already seem to sing in that congregation of the righteous which the Lord will manifestly gather in the future from all nations.

Let us see what these words announce to us. The council of the righteous is when the blessed will judge with the Lord at the time of the resurrection, as was said in the first psalm: “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous” (Psalm 1:5). For in the Gospel the Lord specially promised this to the apostles and his saints, saying: “You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). The congregation, however, signifies the blessed crown of the whole Church, gathered from different parts of the world.

### Verse 2. GIMEL, DALETH. “Great are the works of the Lord; sought out in all his wills.”

Here he enters upon the fullest enumeration of sincere confession and displays the great immensity of goodness. For what is more magnificent than to make a righteous person out of an ungodly one, a son out of an enemy, a free person out of a captive? Thus is fulfilled in them what the Apostle says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans 5:20). “Sought out,” that is, singular and exact, such that nothing similar can be found. For he permits the devil to rage, so that from the latter’s wickedness he may find for himself persons most faithful; and in a new manner joy is born from affliction, eternal security from temporal persecution. And lest you should think that he is praised only in part, he added: “In all his wills.” Whatever he does, he works excellently and incomprehensibly, as is written in Genesis: “God made all things very good” (Genesis 1:31). Thus that unsearchable and inestimable praise is contained in brief compass.

### Verse 3. HE, VAU. “Confession and magnificence are his work, and his righteousness remains for ages upon ages.”

He now explains again how the works of the Lord, of which he spoke above, are to be understood. For glory and beauty, as Father Jerome translated it, are his work, since the things he does are both exceedingly praiseworthy and beautiful. We have said that “confession” here is to be understood as that expressed in words of praise. It follows: “And his righteousness remains for ages upon ages.” Here we must understand the Lord’s righteousness as the sentence of the future judgment, which is altogether everlasting. For his righteousness remains for ages upon ages when he says to sinners: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). Again, his righteousness remains for ages upon ages when he calls the faithful, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world” (ibid., 34). Thus the Lord’s righteousness remains perpetual and unchangeable in both cases.

### Verse 4. ZAIN, HETH. “The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders.”

He comes to the second section, where he shows that the most faithful have been fed with heavenly food, that is, certainly by the advent of the Lord Savior. He therefore made a memorial of his wonders when he showed many new and unprecedented things. For then it could be clearly perceived that God governs all things, when the customary course of events was seen to be changed by sacred commands. No one can truly change the order of things except one who is known both to have made and to govern them. To show who made the memorial of his wonders, he adds: “The merciful and compassionate Lord.” “Merciful” displays the nature of his loving-kindness; “compassionate,” the time when by his advent he showed mercy and aided the human race with lavish pity.

### Verse 5. TETH, JOD. “He gave food to those who fear him; he will remember his covenant forever.”

What he says, “He gave food to those who fear him,” certainly signifies spiritual food. For who would suppose that common food was given to the faithful as a reward, when it is plainly bestowed everywhere even on sinners? But so that you might understand this more fully of the advent of the Lord Savior, it follows: “He will remember his covenant forever.” “He will remember” is said according to human custom, because one is thought to have something in mind when one fulfils what was promised. “Forever” signifies eternity, because he keeps the words of his covenant with most steadfast truth. For just as the Lord Savior was promised in the Old Testament, so he deigned to come in the New, in which food was given to those who fear him: namely, participation in the sacred body and blood, which is the salvation of the nations and the remission of sins.

### Verse 6. CAPH, LAMED. “He announced to his people the power of his works, that he might give them the inheritance of the nations.”

Here is the meaning completed which is contained in three verses. The power of his works was that of which he says in the Gospel: “The blind see, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, the dead rise; and blessed is he who shall not be offended in me” (Matthew 11:5). “He announced,” that is, he made manifest, to the Christian people whom he redeemed by precious blood. But those who believed in him in holy faith before the Lord’s advent say this in the spirit of prophecy.

He gave them the inheritance of the nations when he built the Catholic Church from living stones out of all nations. This is the inheritance promised to Abraham: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea” (Genesis 22:17). For he disclosed the reason why he would announce the power of his works to his people: namely, that he might give them the inheritance of the nations. For the purpose of the miracles was that they might believe and, by believing, receive the promised rewards.

### Verse 7. MEM, NUN. “The works of his hands are truth and judgment; all his commandments are faithful.”

In this and the following verse the Lord’s praises are described in most beautiful and varied statements. This is the twelfth species of definition, which the Greeks call *kat’ epainon* (“according to praise”) and the Latins *per laudem* (“by praise”). The work of his power is when he spares those who confess and makes blessed persons out of the ungodly, and then renders due punishments to the obstinate. Therefore it is properly said: “His work is truth and judgment.” It is truth when he fulfils his promises to the faithful; it is judgment when he carries out what he threatens to the ungodly, since those who neglect to perform his commandments here will suffer everlasting vengeance there.

It follows: “All his commandments are faithful.” It is written: “Keep the commandments, and they will keep you” (Ecclesiasticus 15:16). They are faithful because what they say is altered by no falsehood; rather, they unfailingly preserve us when, by the Lord’s gift, we hasten to keep them.

### Verse 8. SAMECH, AIN. “Confirmed for ages upon ages, made in truth and equity.”

Human words, sent forth in vain, come to nothing; but the Lord’s word, once confirmed, remains forever. For what Truth speaks cannot waver. It follows: “Made in truth and equity.” The commandments of which he spoke above—so that you might believe them to be full of the most certain effects—he said to be made rather than [Note: [Col. 0801D] Here some conjunction seems to be lacking. EDITOR.] merely spoken. To make their dignity appear still greater, he added: “In truth and equity.” There is truth because what is said is fulfilled; there is equity because they are pronounced with the weight of justice. It is clear that his commandments contain these virtues.

### Verse 9. PHE, SADE, COPH

“He sent redemption to his people; he ordained his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name.”
