Here a syllogism in enthymematic form, already frequently encountered by us, arises. Its premise is: “He sent redemption to his people; he ordained his covenant forever.” The expected conclusion follows: “Therefore his name is holy and awesome.” Let us hear the rest that follows.

We have reached the third entrance, in which he declares that the Lord and Savior is to come—one who is to be feared, loved, and praised with continual rejoicing. Appropriately, however, it says, “He sent redemption,” since captives seemed to require this. Yet such was the price that the tyrant would not take it; rather, the one who was being freed received it. The captive gained his own redemption, and the one who had been held liable was thereby enriched still more.

It follows: “He ordained his covenant forever.” We say that one “ordains” when he sends words to those who are absent through intermediary persons. This plainly occurred when he transmitted the New Testament to the nations through his apostles and evangelists. “Forever” is rightly said, because it signifies that no other covenant will succeed it, just as this is shown to have happened with the Old Testament. For this is what brought everything to completion, because it restored the fullness that had previously been promised. It is therefore rightly called eternal, since it is understood to require no other.

He added: “Holy and awesome is his name.” “Holy” refers to the incarnation, as he himself says: “Preserve my soul, for I am holy” (Psalm 85:2). “Awesome” refers to the omnipotence of the exalted Godhead, as it is said in another psalm: “You are awesome, and who will resist you?” (Psalm 75:8). These two qualities pertain to this: we should love our advocate, but fear him as judge. Both have fittingly been joined together, lest either love alone make us negligent or fear alone render us despairing.

### Verse 10. RES, SIN, TAU

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Good understanding belongs to all who practice it” [manuscripts A, B, F: “him”]. “His praise endures forever and ever.”

The nature of the fear of the Lord has been beautifully defined: it is “the beginning of wisdom.” Through it one enters to the Lord, as though through certain doors. For if fear of his judgment is unknown, the remedy of conversion is neglected. Let us fear the one who takes vengeance, so that we may deserve to find the grace of the Redeemer [edition: “redemption”].

It follows: “Good understanding belongs to all who practice it.” Lest you suppose this to be human wisdom, which wavers and fluctuates amid uncertain circumstances, he says of this heavenly wisdom: “Good understanding”—that is, true and saving understanding, which is plainly absent from the wisdom of which it is written: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). This understanding, therefore, which is shown to be intent upon the fear of the Lord, is useful and fruitful, because it arises from that which appears to lead to everlasting glory.

He added: “His praise endures forever and ever.” Behold, the whole purpose of the psalm has been made clear. That faithful people, delivered from the devil’s wickedness and giving thanks to the Lord, expressed the judgment of a devout mind. Those who are devoted ought to do the same here, and it is established that this will be accomplished by the blessed in that heavenly Jerusalem. For his praise is not enclosed within a limit, since his benefit can have no end. Here he is praised because he frees sinners; there he is proclaimed because he crowns the devoted. This psalm is therefore rightly understood to have received “Alleluia” in its title, since it both began with the Lord’s praise and ended in his praise.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How fittingly this most faithful people rejoiced! It was also our joy to hear it rejoicing. For the mind’s gladness increases when the words uttered by another who is rejoicing are sweetly received.

Nor should this be considered meaningless: after the hundred-and-ninth psalm, this exultation of the faithful is placed at this particular number. Consider the sweetness and security of those who sing, and you will find here an image of that reward which the Lord promises to the laborers in the Gospel, whom he invited to the labor of his vineyard by the gifts of his calling. For this is the denarius that will be given both to those who come in the morning and to those who come in the evening. It is a denarius because it is a crown; it is one because it will have no end at all.

This psalm has also been given the graceful perfection of the alphabet, so that the structure of letters might be joined to the grace of such great exultation.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 111

### Alleluia, of the return of Haggai and Zechariah

Since he has often previously placed only “Alleluia,” let us see what this addition of names is intended to mean. Haggai and Zechariah were prophets who prophesied after the Babylonian captivity, under King Darius, long after these songs had been sung. When they had returned to Jerusalem, their homeland, and saw the temple being restored, they poured forth the Lord’s praises with great exultation.

In a similar way, this psalm is also known to be woven together with the letters of a complete alphabet, as though with golden rules. After the absolution of sins, a Christian ought to sing it with the most perfect joy. And remember that this is the fourth psalm instructing the faithful: for it shows, after liberation from sins, what great blessings belong to the faithful and what recompense awaits the faithless.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. In the first admonition he shows what the blessed man does and how great are the blessings he merits through the Lord’s grace; this section contains six letters. The second signifies the coming of the Lord the Savior, through whom human beings, formerly sinners and impious, merit becoming blessed forever; this division is known to contain thirteen Hebrew letters. In the third part he testifies that the opposite will befall the impious; it contains the remaining three letters.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1. ALEPH, BETH

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly desire his commandments” [manuscripts A, B, F: “he desires”].

“Blessed is the man” is introduced in various ways, so that his desire may not be neglected through any concealment. It is fitting that we frequently turn over in our minds the source from which we are proved capable of rejoicing eternally. But since no blessedness exists under worldly fear, which rather makes people wretched, it is nevertheless clear that no eternal joys are found except those prepared by the fear of the Lord.

Under the compulsion of this fear, we desire what can make us blessed. Thus it follows: “He will greatly desire his commandments.” This is certainly able to occur through the fear of the Lord, when we fear the Lord by loving him, lest he make us strangers to his kingdom.

“Blessed, therefore, is the man who fears the Lord,” and so forth, is called in Greek the twelfth species of definition, κατ’ ἔπαινον, in Latin “by praise.”

#### Verse 2. GIMEL, DALETH

“His offspring will be powerful in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed.”

The rewards of that blessed man whom he mentioned above are now described. But since he himself declares that the humble are especially pleasing to him, so that his righteous ones are called poor, let us ask in what land those who are here shown to be objects of ridicule are said to become powerful.

It is, of course, that land in which the saints will reign with the Lord, where human riches and temporal honors do not make people powerful, but rather the contemplation of the Lord and praise without end. This truly is a power that is not followed by weakness; whatever one has merited to be, it preserves through eternal happiness.

“Offspring” signifies the works of good things, which are cast like seeds in this world so that the fruit of the future harvest may grow. “The generation of the upright” is rightly said—not the generation of the flesh, but that which is recognized as propagated through imitation of the righteous, by the likeness of their works. Hence the devil is also remembered as having sinners as his children, to whom it was said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44).

#### Verse 3. HE, VAU

“Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever and ever.”

The preceding description of the blessed man’s blessings continues. The house of the blessed is the secret place of the mind, where whoever fulfills the Lord’s commandments stores holy riches and everlasting glory. That glory has no end; those riches do not perish through malicious theft, but come from the Lord’s commandments. Whatever is acquired is therefore preserved in perpetual integrity.

Thus it follows: “And his righteousness endures forever and ever.” It is called a person’s righteousness, but it is bestowed by God’s generosity. Although the word is general, it is nevertheless understood in a particular sense when, by divine dispensation, the granted gift reaches each individual person. And lest anyone suppose that he becomes blessed only temporarily, he added: “It endures forever and ever.”

Up to this point the blessings of that blessed man have been recounted. Now it is declared from what source he can become blessed, lest the text seem merely to have aroused such a desire without also teaching its cause.

#### Verse 4. ZAIM, HETH

“Light has risen in the darkness for the upright in heart; the Lord is merciful, compassionate, and righteous.”

He comes to the second admonition, in which the Lord’s first coming is signified—the coming by which he made the confessing blessed and condemned the proud on account of their wickedness.

Yet the Lord’s coming is described with marvelous precision. Light came, surpassing every light; and to make it more welcome, he added, “in the darkness”—not the darkness caused by the sun’s absence, but that which is darkened rather by the presence of sinners. These darknesses are within the heart, where the worldly sun cannot enter. That light drives them away; it has conquered death and crushed sins.

But when it says “for the upright in heart,” the perverse are separated from this light.

It follows: “The Lord is merciful, compassionate, and righteous.” The words are few, but they embrace the actions of all rational creatures. Those who confess him have a merciful one [manuscripts A, B, F: “mercy”]; those who despise him will undoubtedly endure the just one [same manuscripts: “will undoubtedly endure judgment”].

#### Verse 5. TETH, JOD

“A good man is one who shows mercy and lends; he will order his words in judgment.”

He calls him “good” not so much because he is accepted by human beings as because he is pleasing to God. He “shows mercy,” that is, he gives to those in need. He “lends,” however, when he lends in this world to those hoping to receive something in return, in their necessity, as he says in the Gospel: “Give to everyone who asks you, and do not refuse the one who wishes to borrow from you” (Matthew 5:42). For even this is no small reward: to rescue the one in danger for the present, and faithfully to receive back only the amount of money that was given.

It may also be understood in this way: what he does in showing mercy—that is, what he gives to the poor—may be regarded as lending, when a person gives temporal things in order to receive eternal ones.

Although both actions seem to concern manual works, he is nevertheless not speaking only of showing mercy to the poor with money or lending to those who hope for it. He is speaking of every benefit that the deprived person is known to need. Therefore we must eagerly do everything that can help another.

It follows: “He will order his words in judgment.” The ordering of words signifies an undisturbed and tranquil arrangement, narrated according to a sound reason. For when the master of the household comes, one must say: “Lord, you gave me five talents; behold, I have gained five more” (Matthew 25:20).

He therefore orders his words in judgment who proves that he has doubled the Lord’s gifts—not like the one who preserved the buried talent through sterile caution and harmful parsimony. This can also pertain to the person who, having examined the divine Scriptures through the Lord’s gift, either retains them in unfruitful silence or spreads them abroad with devout purpose.

#### Verse 6. CAPH, LAMED

“For he will not be shaken forever; the righteous will be in everlasting memory.”

He gives the reason why the righteous man orders his words in judgment: namely, because “he will not be shaken forever”—that is, he will in no way be separated from the Lord’s glory.

It follows: “The righteous will be in everlasting memory.” The righteous will indeed be in everlasting memory because he is called to his reward. To the impious it is said: “I do not know you” (Luke 13:25). Therefore, just as those assigned to punishment are said to depart from remembrance, so these are said to remain in the Lord’s memory in order to receive blessedness.

#### Verse 7. MEM, NUN

“He will not fear an evil report; his heart is ready to hope in the Lord.”

He calls “that evil report” the one that the impious will hear: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41), and what follows. It seems evil to those who will be punished with just severity, although it is not lawful to say anything except that the Lord’s judgment is always just.

And lest you suppose only that the blessed do not fear harmful punishments, it follows: “His heart is ready to hope in the Lord,” so that they may receive his promises—those who, with his help, have trampled underfoot the enticements of the world. To them he himself will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34).

The heart is set here for the affection of a righteous mind, which knows without any hesitation to seek the promises.

#### Verse 8. SAMECH, AIN

“His heart is steadfast; he will not be shaken until he sees his enemies.”

Because the blessed man’s heart had been ready to hope in the Lord, it is consequently added: “His heart is steadfast.” For the person who has been filled with that delight despises all perishable things. The righteous man’s heart is therefore strengthened when it is softened by no worldly happiness; and, looking here upon the power of sinners, he awaits rather their downfall.

In this world he is compelled to see his enemies powerful, so that there he may behold them humbled. But although here we see that our enemies are fleshly persons who contend with us through some adversity, he wishes spiritual wickednesses to be understood—wickednesses that we do not see fully here, but that we shall certainly recognize in that judgment.

When he says, “until he sees his enemies,” we must supply “humbled and crushed.”

O holy ordering [edition: “dispensation”] of the Creator, who then makes them appear broken when they can be objects of ridicule rather than of fear!

#### Verse 9. PHE, SADE, COPH

“He has distributed; he has given to the poor. His righteousness endures forever and ever; his horn will be exalted in glory.”

This sentence pertains to that dominical command: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21). This is the distribution that gathers together felicitously; this is the expenditure that purchases the kingdom of heaven.

Whoever does this practices righteousness, because he has fulfilled the Lord’s commandments. He always remains in this righteousness, since he receives eternal gifts from the author who created the ages.

It follows: “His horn will be exalted in glory.” It has often already been said that “horn” is used for power, as the prophet Daniel testifies when he says: “The four horns are four kingdoms” (Daniel 7:17). How necessary it is that power be given there to those who here seemed to have been cast down in devout humility!

Up to this point he has spoken of the blessings of the blessed; now he concludes the psalm with the affliction of the impious.

#### Verse 10. RES, SIN, TAU

“The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away; the desire of sinners will perish.”

After defining the blessed man and describing his rewards, in the third part he noted the envy of sinners. This figure is called a paradigm whenever we urge people by the blessings of the blessed and deter them by the examples of the wicked. This scheme is found throughout these psalms that speak of the instruction of the blessed, although it is sometimes adapted elsewhere as well, as is also established in the first psalm.

“He will be angry,” he said—that is, angry with himself, because he did not wish to be restrained from wickedness. For they see [edition: “see”] that they once presumed upon fleeting glory and fugitive power, while others receive a blessedness that does not know how to cease. It is a just anger, a true indignation, but one that brings no benefit in the time of vengeance. They could have avoided that indignation if here they had become hostile to their own vices.

It follows: “He will gnash his teeth and waste away.” The sinner and the envious person are described as wavering amid their own malignity: he retains the evil of his anger, but will no longer harm anyone else. Here he was wickedly agitated in order to injure another; there he is justly angry with himself, because he is punished for his wickedness.

Isaiah likewise says: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 57:21). His gnashing works to make him waste away; his violent impulse works to make him fail. He now bites himself with his own teeth and chastises himself with his own pain, exacting from himself the torments that here he compelled the innocent to endure.

He added: “The desire of sinners will perish,” because just as the wishes of the blessed, planted in the Lord’s kingdom, will flourish there, so the desires of sinners, cut off, will wither.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How beautifully this blessed man has been described through the descending alphabet, so that his deeds and rewards might be recounted together! Who would not believe that he sees what holy truth promises? But may he himself cause us to receive what he has already granted us to hear.

There is no doubt that this alphabet, with which the poem has been completed, pertains to the perfection of wisdom. Through it the understanding of divine things is recognized and the fault of ignorance avoided. Thus the psalms are shown to be varied with different kinds of sweetness, so that human weakness in learning may not be overcome by weariness.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 112

### Alleluia

Behold, the following psalm explains the words of its title. Since the title is “Alleluia”—“Praise the Lord”—the true teacher and excellent instructor begins in the same way. His speech cannot deceive, because it plainly flows from the fountain of truth. For what can be stated with greater certainty than where the teacher of realities proves to be their proper interpreter?

### Division of the Psalm

The prophet David, passing briefly through the text of the psalm, first admonishes the devoted to offer praises continually to the Lord and not to cease proclaiming him throughout the whole world. In the second part he himself does what he urges others to do, so that, as a true teacher, he may appear to teach not so much by word as by example.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Praise the Lord, servants; praise the name of the Lord.”

It is clear that this name is given to the simple and most pure, since the Lord himself is also called a child, as in the passage: “A child is born for us” (Isaiah 9:6). The Lord evidently chose this age because of its innocence, for he says to his disciples: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew 19:14).

The prophet therefore rightly admonishes these people to sing praises to the Lord, since they appear to approach them with a pure heart. It is not age that is chosen here, but purity.

Consider also that a certain distinction is present in the repetition. The one who commends himself by worthy action praises the Lord; the one who celebrates his virtues through holy proclamation praises the name of the Lord.

#### Verse 2

“May the name of the Lord be blessed, from this time forth and forever.”

Lest the servants suppose that a momentary praise has been commanded for them, he says that the Lord is to be proclaimed now in this world and also praised in that eternity. But lest even this be understood locally, he states below how he is to be praised everywhere.

#### Verse 3

“From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord.”

Here he designates the universal Church, so that throughout the whole world—whose maker is Christ—his praises should not be silenced. This is a just admonition of the Lord, a saving injunction: that creation should recognize its Creator and magnify him, so that it may continually increase through his praises.

This scheme is called *periphrasis*, in Latin “circumlocution.” In some places the world is indicated “through the globe”; in others, through the four cardinal points; here it is declared through the sun’s course, as though the world were traced by a certain line.

#### Verse 4

“The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens.”

Through these two parts he wishes all creatures to be understood. By “nations,” let us understand all earthly things; by “heavens,” let us attend to all heavenly things. He is shown to be exalted above everything, and even the heavens are subject to him, as it is read in another psalm: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Psalm 107:6).

Or we should understand “nations” as fleshly human beings and “heavens” as spiritual beings, so that the Most High may be understood to be above all creatures, since he is recognized as the creator of all things.

#### Verse 5

“Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high?”

He comes to the second part, in which he now joyfully offers the Lord’s praises on the basis of his works. When it is said, “Who?” no one other than the one who glories in the majesty of his own power is signified.

“He who dwells on high” means that he dwells in his exalted creatures, which he makes great when he deigns to dwell in them. Such are the good angels, his saints, and the remaining powers, which grow great through the dignity of his presence.

But lest you suppose that this greatness intends to despise the lowly, see what follows.

#### Verse 6

“And he looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth.”

What was said above—“who dwells on high”—is explained. He himself looks upon the lowly so that, by his gift, they may always become most exalted. Above devout humility there is a seat for him; he visits that humility which hopes for nothing in itself but relies upon the Lord’s generosity alone.

Understand this humility as a quality of the mind, not as a position in the lands. For it follows: “in heaven and on earth.” What humility is there in heaven except that in which the holy angels have pleased God through their humility? All the powers of heaven are exalted by this very praise, and whatever is faithfully humble is found there to be God’s dwelling and eternal power.

When he says “on earth,” he signifies the holy men of whom it is written: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

Thus humility pleasing to God is found in heaven and on earth, just as pride is shown to be hated—the pride through which the devil fell and through which human beings are plunged into the innermost regions of Tartarus. Let the haughty be ashamed and, having accepted reason, convict themselves. Where do they suppose pride can have a place, when they see heaven and earth occupied by humility?

#### Verse 7

“Raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dung heap.”

The needy and destitute should not claim this benefit for themselves alone. Whoever is lifted by God’s grace from the stain of the body is raised from dung and poverty.

Indeed, the worldly king himself is needy of God’s gifts and rolls in dung when the vices of the flesh dominate him. Therefore the Lord raises people of every rank and every age from these conditions when he bestows the gifts of his mercy.

#### Verse 8

“To make him sit with princes, with the princes of his people.”

He declares what the raising of the poor and needy can attain: namely, that he may be seated with the princes of his people. The princes of the people are the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all who have pleased God through a worthy manner of life.

But do not suppose that this is the principate—not the honor acquired through human approval, but the one bestowed by the Lord’s generosity: exalted through humility, secure through faith, and strengthened through firmness of mind.

For what he added, “of his people,” signifies the Catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world.

#### Verse 9

“Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a rejoicing mother of children.”

Here the conclusion of the preceding meanings is made, together with the descending beauty of the words. For what he said—“raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dung heap, to make him sit with princes, with the princes of his people”—he explains by showing where this can occur: namely, in the Church.

Before the coming of her Bridegroom she had been barren; but she became a joyful mother of children when, through the preaching of the apostles, she brought forth abundant children from water and the Holy Spirit throughout the whole world. Once dark, now beautiful, she gives birth through the most fertile water and guards her virginity in glorious integrity.

She, therefore, was the barren woman whom the Lord makes dwell joyfully in his house, rejoicing in the birth and number of the saints.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

I am exceedingly astonished whenever I encounter this number, so full of the honor of mighty mysteries. This number embraces the apostles; it divided the people of Israel into tribes; and, as Father Jerome says (on Ezekiel 31), it signifies that future blessedness is distinguished by the number twelve.

For example, the apostles may hold the first place, the prophets the second, the martyrs the third, infants taken after baptism the fourth, virgins the fifth, and those who rightly repent the sixth, proceeding in this way through twelve divisions according to the different degrees of merit.

The Apostle seems to touch upon this when he says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars” (1 Corinthians 15:41); and elsewhere: “Star differs from star in glory; so also will be the resurrection of the dead.”

386 Therefore this psalm, placed after the hundredth as number twelve, promises us an image of future blessedness, when, in likeness to that eternal joy, he commands the Lord continually to be praised by the servants.

## EXPOSITION OF PSALM 113

### Alleluia

Since many psalms have already preceded and others marked “Alleluia” will follow, it is not without purpose that so many psalms appear adorned with this heading. Just as, in melody, this compound name receives various tones, so it also takes up multiple causes for the force of its proclamation.

For “Praise the Lord” is not said in only one way. Rather, just as this praise is gathered from different actions, so “Alleluia” is applied to various circumstances and appropriate narratives.

The purpose of this psalm is to announce that, from the beginning of the Hebrew people, the fullness of the law—which is Christ the Lord—was bestowed upon the world through great miracles, and to show through these likenesses of events that even today every Christian is delivered.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. First, he recalls what miracles the Lord performed for the Hebrews and for the Christian people. Second, by way of questioning, he says why the sea fled and why the Jordan held back [edition: “retained”] its course, adding the most welcome answer: that the earth was moved at the presence of the Lord. Third, he demonstrates to their worshipers the uselessness of the nations’ idols and then explains how useful and health-giving the worship of the Lord is to his own worshipers.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people.”

We should understand this exodus as the time when we are enabled to leave the bonds of sins. For then we are freed from the Egyptians—that is, from the multitude of demons—when we no longer endure the laws of that barbarous severity. We truly become Israelites when the pomp of this world begins to depart from our minds.

“Barbarian” is said to derive from *barba* (“beard”) and *rus* (“countryside”), because one who had never lived in a city was recognized as having always dwelt in the fields like a wild animal. We truly become the house of Jacob when we observe the precepts of Christian doctrine.

#### Verse 2

“Judah became his sanctification, Israel his power; Israel will reign in it.”

Let us understand these three clauses of the verse through their divided exposition. We have said that Judah belongs not only to the nation of the Hebrews but can also refer to all the faithful. The true Judah is the Lord the Savior, in whom the kingdom and power of the Israelites—that is, of those who see God—is known to be perpetual. Thus those who follow him with circumcised hearts are truly called Jews.

His power is called Israel because in him he displayed the great miracles of his own power. For where does he not have power who does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth?

It follows: “Israel will reign in it,” namely because the person who sees God will reign in that blessed assembly where the saints are to be gathered in every way.

#### Verse 3

“The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back.”

Seeing himself overwhelmed by the mass of such great miracles, the prophet condensed the causes of all vices into two allusions of the fullest brevity.

We have often said that the sea should be understood as the sinners of this world, who, like swelling waves, fluctuate amid proud thoughts. The Jordan, however, should be understood as any river that carries human beings away through various desires and, with wicked haste, leads them into that great sea.

These two things, which carried the human race away through different pleasures, returned in retreat from their accustomed ways when the Lord’s coming was perceived. Although this history is related in the Old Testament, it is indicated here through other words and likenesses, so that we might clearly perceive that those ancient events announced, through spiritual understanding, signs of our salvation.

#### Verse 4

“The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.”

Little by little he descends more clearly to Christian times. It is evident that the mountains can be understood as the apostles and evangelists, or as all preachers of the word, who were the first, before the rest of the earth, to receive heavenly light.

They are rightly called mountains because of the lofty summit of their holiness and the most solid firmness of their faith. They leaped in their works like rams, who, with divine assistance, led the most faithful flock to the Lord’s sheepfolds.

The hills signify the moderate multitude of believers, whose hearts effectively received the seeds of faith. They are called hills from *colere* (“to cultivate”). Reason itself compels us to understand these things spiritually, since they are altogether absurd if taken literally. Therefore consider with what sweetness the earlier likenesses appear to have been brought to this interpretation, so that everything may answer everything else in a most beautiful comparison.

#### Verse 5

“What is the matter with you, sea, that you fled? And you, Jordan, why did you turn back?”

He enters the second mode, in which an elegant question is placed first so that a most pleasing answer may follow. This figure is called *peusis* and *apocrisis*, in Latin “inquiry and response.”

The sea is questioned, and the river is examined as to why they have lost their customary ways, as though those very things that previously swept everything away had fixed their steps. “Back” has rightly been added, because all corrections come to us when, through the Lord’s gift, our ways are changed.

The fact that he nearly repeats what he said above—“What is the matter with you, sea, that you fled? And you, Jordan, why did you turn back?”—is another figure, *epanodos*, that is, a repetition of matters stated together.

#### Verse 6

“Mountains, why did you leap like rams, and hills, like lambs of sheep?”

He preserved the order of the preceding verses. They have been placed here in another form just as they appear to have been narrated in the first division.

He questions the world, represented by the sea or river, about what caused its bonds to be loosened. And since one answer was about to follow, he also questions those who seemed especially to have leaped. One Author made the former marvel and granted the latter to rejoice with fixed prosperity.

#### Verse 7

“At the presence of the Lord the earth was moved, at the presence of the God of Jacob.”

The fitting answer prepared for both questions followed. Hear, you who have been converted; hear, most faithful Christians: hear this movement—that is, this transformation—which happily occurred in the earthly human race. It was not produced by the trembling of mountains, but by the prosperous conversion of peoples.

If you ask who the Lord is, hear: “the God of Jacob.” When he mercifully appeared, the earth was moved beneficially by his presence—that is, by his saving presence. The earth had grown sluggish and rigid through the stupor of death; yet it was moved from its superstition in such a way that it remained fixed with eternal strength in the worship of the Lord.

#### Verse 8

“He turned the rock into pools of water and the cliff into springs of water.”

The rock, as I think, should be understood as the hardness of the Jews, which he turned into pools of sacred baptism when he brought them to a tranquil religion. The Lord says this likeness in the Gospel: “The Lord is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3:9).

Likewise, he caused the cliffs—that is, the dry and hard hearts of the nations—to pour forth well-watered springs of divine speech, so that those who had previously been dried up by barren superstitions, after hearing the word [auditi; manuscripts A, B, F: avidi, “eager for the word”], might cause abundant proclamations of heavenly teaching to flow forth.

Up to this point the preceding verses are known to have proceeded through the figure of parable.

#### Verse 9

“Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory. On account of your mercy and your truth” [source: super misericordiam tuam et veritatem tuam; edition: super misericordia tua et veritate tua].

After he had recounted the many benefits that Christ the Lord granted for our advantage, a very true and heartfelt petition follows: that, for the sake of his name, he might bestow useful things upon the human race, since he could find no worthy merits in sinners.

When he generously gives good things to the undeserving, what he grants is shown to belong to his own glory.

It follows: “Because of your mercy and your truth.” He asks that the Lord’s glory be granted on account of these two things. It is mercy when he forgives the sins of the wretched and the transgressors; it is truth when he restores the promises of future blessedness—or, as others wish, when he judges the impious.

It is clear that both actions—whether he spares or judges—belong to the glory of the Lord.

### Verse 10

“Lest the nations say: Where is their God?” The reason has followed why the Lord deigns to bestow the gifts of his mercy upon the devout. This figure is called *aetiology*, that is, the giving of a reason. For he asks that the unspeakable charge be removed which Christians very frequently suffer in this age. For whenever the bodies of martyrs are afflicted with various torments, it is the very voice of tyrants, the very voice of the pagans: “Where is their God?”—as though he could not rescue those whom, in order to crown them, he permits to endure torments.

### Verse 11

“But our God is above in heaven; in heaven and on earth he has done whatever he willed.” Against the senseless words of the pagans, who say, “Where is your God?”, there is introduced a most truthful and decisive statement: that our God does everything he wills in heaven and on earth. When it says “above in heaven,” it shows that he is powerful above all creatures. It follows that he does whatever he wills to work either in his least or in his greatest creatures, so that you may recognize him as omnipotent, since everywhere he displays the effect of his will.

### Verse 12

“The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.” He comes to the third mode, in which the prophet mocks the idols of the nations and celebrates the Lord of Israel with fitting praise. This kind of argument is called *demonstrative*, because it is recognized to contain both blame and praise. For in five verses he censures the gods of the pagans, but in ten he praises the exalted God, so that even in the quantity of his words he might show the difference between the two things. But since above he had called God invisible and said that he does everything he wills, here he rightly speaks of idols as objects of mockery: fashioned in the form of humanity, they are shown to be alien even to the bodily senses themselves.

For although bronze and wooden idols are also found, he nevertheless more usefully chose that material which the pagan world judged more worthy of reverence and worship, so that it might blush to venerate cheaper objects whose costly counterparts are also shown to be mocked. But lest you should think that these images possess some living substance of nature, he says—so as to express their baseness—that those gods of the pagans were fashioned by mortal hands. It is shameful to say that an image is worshiped by the one who could himself be found to have been its maker. What can it offer to a mortal, when the idol could not have existed unless a human being had wished it to?

Jeremiah likewise summed up such ravings in a beautiful definition, saying: “It will be nothing other than what the goldsmiths wish it to be” (Jer. 10:9). To these words the verses of Sedulius, the poet—if I may call him so—of truth should also be repeated:

> Wooden one, you ask for wood: you seem to be shouting at the deaf;  
> You seek answers from the mute.

For if you wish to know what God truly is, hear Isaiah saying:

> “I am the Lord; this is my name forever. I will not give my glory to another, nor my powers to carved images. Behold, the things that were from the beginning are coming to pass; and the new things that I shall announce, before I revealed them I made you hear” (Isa. 42:8–9).

“For I am he. Before me there was no other God, and after me there shall be none” (ibid. 43:10).

### Verse 13

“They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see.”

### Verse 14

“They have ears, but they will not hear; they have nostrils, but they will not smell.”

### Verse 15

“They have hands, but they will not touch; they have feet, but they will not walk; they will not cry out with their throat; for there is no spirit in their mouth.”

In these three verses, too, those people are marked out by a most truthful description who wished vainly to assign human limbs to their false divinities. For what need, I ask, did one who could not speak have of a mouth? What need of eyes, when it could not see? What need of ears, when it was not going to hear? What need of nostrils, when it could in no way perceive fragrance? The nostrils, moreover, are so called from *gnaritas*—“knowledge”—because they make us recognize by smell. What need of hands, when it knew nothing of tangible things? What need of feet, when it was utterly unable to move?

And so that the mockery might be increased by such details, he added that they should not even be compared with creatures lacking reason, since they do not possess in their throats even a confused cry such as cattle habitually emit in their own particular voices. Then follows the statement that sums everything up: they are found to be incomparable both with human beings and with cattle because there is no spirit in their mouths. There is no doubt that voices—whether articulate or confused—belong to living creatures; in these verses a suitably long enumeration has been made, lest the reproaches against the pagans should end too quickly. 388

### Verse 16

“Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them.” Perhaps the pagan hears this and rejoices that he has been compared with his own divinities; but let him understand how much he has been able to gain from such patronage, since he has deserved to pass from being a rational human being to becoming like lifeless metals. Let him understand that his worship has been turned into his own condemnation, and let him shrink from worshiping that from which he is known to have received a punishable judgment.

For those who have resolved to follow such things become like them. Nor should it be omitted that both the makers and the worshipers of this object are shown to have been struck by the same sentence. It is equally wickedness to deceive others by one’s works and to bind oneself by the worst forms of worship. The Apostle also speaks of these people: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:25).

Here too the figure called *sarcasmos* is shown to be appropriate—that is, a violent mockery of an adversary, which is recognized to penetrate even the faults themselves.

### Verse 17

“The house of Israel hoped in the Lord: he is their helper and their protector.” Having condemned the wickedness of the faithless, he gladly proceeds to celebrate the Lord’s praises. The house of Israel is understood to signify the Church of peoples who believe. For it is she who hopes in the Lord, continually rejecting worldly desires and delighting solely in him. And he consequently explains what comes to her: he becomes her helper and protector, to whom all things are shown to serve.

He is a helper because, while they labor in the flesh in this world, he helps them insofar as he knows it to be useful; he is a protector because he does not permit holy souls to be overthrown by any demonic deception.

### Verse 18

“The house of Aaron hoped in the Lord: he is their helper and their protector.” What he stated generally in the preceding verse he now unfolds concerning the priests by a beautiful repetition, so that the exalted order of pontiffs might be praised not in a general commemoration but with a particular proclamation. Aaron was the first priest chosen among the Jewish people, and by recalling him the order itself is rightly indicated.

### Verse 19

“Those who fear the Lord, let them hope in the Lord: he is their helper and their protector.” [The edition reads: “they hoped.”] He explains what he said above: “the house of Israel” and “the house of Aaron.” These are the people who fear the Lord and hope in the Lord. For these are the two things that make people blessed and happy; and what he said above follows for them, namely, that the Lord is both their helper and their protector.

### Verse 20

“The Lord remembered us, and he blessed us.”

### Verse 21

“He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron.” [Col. 0816A]

He repeats the same point with beautiful variety, so that we may believe, through this reiterated argument, that the Lord’s blessing is bestowed upon such people. For when he says, “he remembered us,” he reveals the grace of divine compassion. What merits did they have that the Lord Christ should come, he who would both teach peoples who had gone astray and save those who had been converted by his blessing?

For he blessed the house of Israel by being born from the virginity of holy Mary. He also blessed the house of Aaron, girded with the honor of the priesthood, as it is said of him in another psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

### Verse 22

“He blessed all those who fear the Lord, the small together with the great.” After the specific enumerations, he rises to the blessing of universality, where all those who have chosen to serve the Lord with pure mind are blessed together. This he did among fishermen; this he did among kings. No class of human beings who believed in him is shown to have been excluded or alienated from his gifts.

This figure is called *anacephaleosis*, that is, recapitulation. It occurs when things that were previously said at greater length are afterward recalled briefly to memory. [Col. 0816B]

### Verse 23

“May the Lord add to you—to you and to your children.” “May he add” seems to be understood in two ways: either that the Lord may add the blessing which in this age he grants his saints in part, or that he may add faithful peoples to your number. He does this also in our own times, and does not cease to work until the end of the age, so that the Church, predestined from the nations and gathered into one flock, may rejoice and enjoy the glorious rule of one shepherd. [Col. 0816C]

### Verse 24

“You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” Since above the prophet had wished that the faithful might be blessed, now, trusting in that very predestination, he says that they are most justly blessed. And observe the kind of blessing he names: “by the Lord,” because perfect blessedness consists in no one being prepared for himself, but for the Lord. By this word both the hearts of the faithful are strengthened and the source of future blessedness is shown.

“Who made heaven and earth”: either it signifies the Word, by whose operation every creature was perfected, or it signifies the small and the great whom he mentioned above—those who by his mercy have reached the joys of the catholic religion.

### Verse 25

“Heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the sons of men.” Since the righteous are called heaven, the Lord Christ is fittingly understood as the Heaven of heavens, just as “Holy of holies,” “God of gods,” and the other expressions that are magnificently spoken in this manner. It is called heaven because it conceals all things within itself.

Since the Heaven of heavens was given to the Lord, as it is read in the sixty-seventh psalm, “who ascended above the heavens of heavens from the east,” the earth was assigned to the sons of men, where, through the grace of the Lord and amid manifold struggles, they may purify themselves and reach eternal life after the contest of this world.

“Gave” pertains to the humanity of the incarnation. For what could be given to the Word, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit has always possessed and possesses all things? [Col. 0817A]

### Verse 26

“The dead will not praise you, Lord, nor all those who descend into hell.” Here he calls “the dead” those who are to be afflicted by everlasting torments. The Lord does not receive their voices, because only the blessed will resound with his praises, as Solomon says: “From the dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17:26). And shortly afterward: “But we, the living and the healthy, praise your name.”

By saying, “nor all those who descend into hell,” he shows that the saints also descend to the underworld, but rejoice in the Lord’s exultation. Death is shown to be common to the righteous and sinners, but they are separated by a very great distinction, as it is said in the eighty-fifth psalm: “And you delivered my soul from the lowest hell” (Ps. 85:13).

### Verse 27

“But we who live will bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.” 389

After the condition of the condemned had been explained, it was fitting that the blessed should conclude the beauty of the psalm with good things. The Lord is the God of the living, not of the dead, as it is read in the Gospel: “For he is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:32).

“Of the living,” however, must not be understood as meaning those living this present life, which the saints plainly share with the wicked, but that life of which it is read in another psalm: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9). And lest the human mind should descend to earthly goods, it fittingly rises to those heavenly realities which can have no limit in praise and are shown to suffer no decline in their rewards.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

The most beautiful little fragments have glistened for us like pomegranate seeds; when revealed from the skin of the historical account, they have exuded the sweetest honey. For as many as there are verses, so many are the graces; as many words, so many are the fruits of the soul.

Through the likenesses of the ancient people, we are admonished to leave the Egyptian domination of this world, so that we may be able to reach the promised land by the journey of baptism. Let us hasten without fear: at the coming of the Lord our adversities have been dissolved. The sea fled; the Jordan turned backward in fear; the idols of the nations were despised like senseless metals. But the glory of our Lord is worshiped everywhere and proclaimed everywhere.

Therefore, with God’s help, let us seek out the powers of the psalms with the greatest zeal, since they reveal themselves to the faithful and always conceal themselves from unbelievers. [Col. 0817D]

## Exposition of Psalm 114

### Alleluia

A solemn and true admonition awakens us from the sleep of this age and, like a kind of spiritual cock, compels us to come to the works of the faithful. Let us hear the holy voice, let us follow the pious command [in manuscripts A, B, and F, *imperium* is absent], and let us abandon the impious [in the edition and manuscript G, *et relinquamus impium* is absent]. For the praise of the Lord is the dignity of our works and the reward of our labors, since nothing sweeter can be spoken and nothing more healthful can be practiced.

### Division of the Psalm

The prophet, liberated from the deep pit of sins and established upon that rock of mercy, first gives thanks in the first section, because he knows that he has been heard and testifies that he effectively called upon the Lord against all the dangers of death. In the second, he again cries out to the Lord, so that, once liberated, he may reach that everlasting rest which the Lord promises to grant to the faithful as a gift.

### Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“I loved, because the Lord heard the voice of my prayer.” It is clear that love of the Lord arises among human beings in two ways.

The one occurs when, on account of benefits bestowed, he is loved and praised even by unbelievers, as it is said of the sinner in another psalm: “He will give thanks to you when you have done good to him” (Ps. 48:19).

The second is utterly certain and perfect: when the mind devoted to God is not cast down by any adversity arising from evils, but in its miseries is kindled by hope of the future and remains always inflamed with love of the Lord, as the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness?” (Rom. 8:35), and so forth.

The prophet explains this second mode below. He loved amid his tribulations and distresses, because those tribulations and pains enabled him to deserve to call upon the Lord. Therefore David does not rejoice exultantly in the greatness of his kingdom, nor congratulate himself on worldly prosperity, which he knew would pass away. Rather, he rejoices that his prayer was received in his distress by the most merciful Lord, something which he felt would profit him forever.

And observe how concisely he both states the cause and immediately adds the reason for the cause. This figure is called *epitrocasmos*, that is, “the rotation of a statement,” because it briefly and succinctly touches upon the things that must be said.

### Verse 2

“Because he inclined his ear to me; and in my days I will call upon him.” As has already been said, the ear is named from hearing. God is rightly said to incline it toward us, because no human merits appear capable of reaching him so that he may deign to hear us. The authority of truth itself handed this down at the Lord’s coming, when, moved by pity for the crimes of the world, he bestowed the medicine of blessed incarnation.

And because he had begun to experience his abundant compassion toward him, he professes that, while he was troubled by many tribulations in his days—as he says below—he had called upon the Lord. For we call those “our days” in which we sin through our own iniquity and endure anxious pains through wicked thoughts. A marvelous statement, a blessed exchange: the faithful continually seek benefits, and the merciful Lord continually bestows them by his goodness.

### Verse 3

“The pains of death surrounded me, and the dangers of hell found me.” He continues to give the most suitable reasons why the holy man loved the Lord—not those in which humanity thinks itself loved when it is raised up by inflated honors or grows great through the mass of riches, but because he says that divine grace visited him when he was shown to be afflicted by pains and dangers. This is rightly so, since the former lead to glory, while the latter plunge people into ruin.

And examine how simple words are filled with great meanings. He says that he was surrounded by pains; and lest you should think them ordinary, he added, “of death.” He also added “the dangers of hell,” which are known to be more grievous than all torments. Then follows “they found me,” as though he had been caught unawares, as though he had been secure, as though he had been set apart from the Lord’s protection—so that he could easily have been captured after being separated from so great a defense.

### Verse 4

“I found tribulation and pain, and I called upon the name of the Lord.” You hear “tribulation and pain,” and perhaps you are offended; but recognize what riches this treasure carries hidden within. These are the tribulations that made him cry out to the Lord; these are the pains that wounded hearts medicinally, so that the sick person might cry out to the true physician, from whom help is unquestionably known to come.

And observe what these changed words produce. Above, when he was captured, he says that he was found by pains; here, when he discovered the remedy, he asserts that he found the pains themselves. For the person who understands himself to have been afflicted so that he may be converted recognizes the causes of his calamity. A physician is also sought when some disease is felt to weigh upon the human entrails.

It follows: “and I called upon the name of the Lord,” by whose help both pain and tribulation would swiftly be overcome.

### Verse 5

“O Lord, deliver my soul! The Lord is merciful and just, and our God will have mercy.” [Manuscripts A, B, and F read *miseretur*, “has mercy.”]

Having enumerated his sufferings, the prophet comes to the second section, where he cries out to the Lord that his soul may be freed from the depth of sins, as the Apostle says: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

This figure is called *proanaphonesis*, in Latin “exclamation,” whenever, amid other things that we are saying, we suddenly turn our words toward God.

Therefore let us examine our tribulations and pains with the greatest care by divine gift. They lie hidden more deeply and are often lulled to sleep under the veil of worldly pleasure. Unless we seek them with divine assistance, we cannot inwardly bring forth this saving cry. For when he says, “Deliver my soul,” he confesses that it is always captive without the Lord.

It follows: “The Lord is merciful and just, and our God has mercy.” In the preceding clause he asked that his soul be delivered; here he promises that the Lord is merciful and just, so that he might neither appear to have doubted in that petition nor make others remain anxiously suspended in uncertainty.

He is merciful because he inclined his ear to him; just because he rebuked the sinner so that he might seek forgiveness. He will have mercy when he receives the son whom he scourges. Hence understand that these three qualities are mentioned to instruct the weakness of the human race, which, while gazing eagerly at worldly pleasures, considers harsh the pains that are inflicted for the soul’s salvation.

### Verse 6

“The Lord preserves the little ones; I was humbled, and he delivered me.” He has placed the order in reverse for a profound reason. Above he first asked that his soul be delivered and afterward generally professed that the Lord is merciful; now, however, he says universally that he is the guardian of the little ones, and afterward proclaims that he was humbled and delivered. Through this order of events he shows what is read in the Gospel: although gathered from many nations, there is one flock of the Lord and one shepherd over it.

The little ones are those who most certainly consider themselves insignificant; but by the Lord’s generosity alone they grow great. And observe what word is used: “preserving,” he says, like an outstanding shepherd who defends his flock from the attack of a ravenous wolf.

But consider that, while preserving the appropriate order, he first says that he was humbled and afterward delivered, so that wounds cannot remain painful once they have reached health through the gift of the heavenly Physician. [Col. 0820B]

### Verse 7

“Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you.” [Manuscript G and the edition read “with me.”]

Let the soul that wanders away from the Lord sing this with the prophet. Let that sheep sing which had gone astray and, carried back on the shoulders of its Guardian, deserved to return to the sheepfolds of the Shepherd. Let that son sing who had been dead and came to life again, who had been lost and was found. Let the devout people sing this, who, redeemed by precious blood, have deserved by the Lord’s generosity to reach the desired rest.

Therefore the prophet urges his soul to return to the Lord, from whom tranquil rest and the abolition of sins have come to it. He calls it “his rest,” then, because it was given to him by grace, not possessed as a compensation for merits. Hence the following words:

“Because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you.” [Col. 0820C]

### Verse 8

“Because he delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling.” The reasons are explained why he said above, “Because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you.” Let us understand the prophet to be speaking here of the future through the power of foreknowledge, since these things cannot yet apply to those living in this present age.

He says: “He delivered my soul from death.” For when the souls of the righteous depart from this world, they are freed from that death of which it is said in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Luke 9:60). When he says “he delivered,” he shows the benefit of divine power, since he could not have been freed from perpetual death except through its might.

It follows: “my eyes from tears.” The tears of the saints certainly cease when the death of the soul is no longer feared. One does not weep in security, but in this contest, where coming calamity is feared.

He added: “my feet from falling.” By saying “from falling,” he shows that sin is slippery and prone to failure. But ruin is not feared where eternal prosperity already exists. For those established in this age—as has been said—both fear the death of the soul and continually pour out tears, and do not believe their feet to be in any way free from falling.

Here there is a struggle, and therefore everything is subject to fear. Hence we understand that the human race, which is still engaged in the struggle of this life, is subject to these three dangers. For observe what follows.

### Verse 9

“I shall please the Lord in the land of the living.” We must investigate why he spoke of the future: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living,” as though the saints do not also please him here, in the land of the dead, since they have been praised by the mouth of the Judge. For it is also read in Genesis: “Enoch pleased God, and God translated him” (Gen. 5:24). Job too was praised by the voice of the Lord (Job 1:8). And in the Gospel the Lord himself says of Nathanael: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

But here he says, “I shall please,” now secure, now unable to displease, and no longer enduring anything doubtful, when, as the Apostle says, “Death will have been swallowed up in victory, and this corruptible will have put on incorruption, and this mortal will have put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:54). Then the righteous will please the Lord in such a way that they will no longer fear anything arising from the opposition of sins.

“In the land of the living,” he says—in the assembly of the saints, where every living person is truly gathered and separated from the lot of the dying, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me will pass from death to life” (John 5:24). [Col. 0821B]

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Having treated the saving purpose of this psalm, we ought to set courage of soul against the pains of the world. Let us say, as the psalm begins: “I loved, because the Lord heard the voice of my supplication,” because there is no punishment that leads us forward, no pain that brings us to rest; nor should that weeping be considered harsh which supplies eternal joys.

Let us fix our attention not on what we suffer but on what we hope for, and temporal evil will undoubtedly grow mild, since its end is understood to be most prosperous. Let us therefore ask the omnipotence of Christ, who alone is able to overcome these things by immeasurable power, so that, once the edge of wickedness has been broken, even those things that now appear harsh may not prove altogether bitter to us.

For we shall please the Lord in the land of the living if, in this age, we hasten to mortify our bodies for the sake of his glory. [Col. 0821C]

## Exposition of Psalm 115

### Alleluia

The praise of the Lord ought at times to increase within us so greatly that we cannot grow weary of alleluiatic joys. It is the voice of the faithful, the speech of the blessed, the sacred melody of those who sing; through it bodily hearing is sweetly soothed and the weary soul is refreshed by heavenly delight.

The words of the martyrs must be introduced—those who both flourished through glorious confession [manuscripts A, B, and F read “the glory of confession”] and obtained the Lord’s gifts through an extraordinary passion.

### Division of the Psalm

Throughout this psalm the words of the unconquered martyrs are recounted. In the first section they recall the Lord’s benefits. When they hesitate over what worthy return could possibly be made to him, that glorious cup of martyrdom presents itself—although even it is bestowed by the Lord’s generosity.

In the second, the chorus itself professes that it is the Lord’s servant and a son of the catholic Church, lest anyone should suppose that, apart from the most faithful men pleasing to God, the martyrdom of some heretic could also be acceptable.

### Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“I believed, and therefore I spoke; but I was humbled exceedingly.” That venerable people of the martyrs, observing the order of true doctrine, says that it first believed and afterward spoke, specifically in order to destroy those who, not truly believing, aspire to proclaim something about its glorious deeds.

For after true faith, holy confession ought to follow, lest one hear that unwelcome reproach: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” (Ps. 49:16).

It follows: “But I was humbled exceedingly.” Do not understand this as meaning that the most truthful proclamations were humbled, since they shine all the more brightly the more thoroughly the persecutors strive to suppress them. He says that he was humbled because, while holy religion was growing, the martyrs themselves appeared to be subjected to temporal punishments.

### Verse 2

“I said in the ecstasy of my mind” [manuscripts A and B read “in my ecstasy of mind”]: “Every human being is a liar.” Lest anyone think that the most truthful confession which he had received through the Lord’s help could be attributed to human powers, he himself declares what belongs to humanity: namely, that every human being is a liar.

But observe that he could not easily arrive at this consideration unless he had been raised to heavenly contemplation through an ecstasy of mind, when the soul, cleansed of bodily impurity, looks upon the causes of things through clear perceptions. Great prudence is shown when someone considers himself imprudent. For just as the frivolous and foolish falsely claim to be utterly truthful, so the enlightened recognize themselves to be liars.

Therefore let this certain rule constrain us: whenever we are liars through the weakness of the flesh, let us acknowledge that this belongs to us; whenever we are truthful, let us attribute it to divine gifts.

This statement belongs to the figure called *paroemia*, because this proverb is celebrated through frequent use in human speech. Such is the saying addressed to Saul in the Acts of the Apostles: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5)—truly hard, because the one who is shown to have struck against what is sharp is wounded by his own efforts.

It should be noted, however, that “ecstasy of mind” is also used in a bad sense, as in Chronicles: “And you gave them over to ecstasy,” that is, “to a lapse of mind, and to agitation and destruction” (2 Chron. 29:8).

### Verse 3

“What shall I repay the Lord for all the things he has repaid me?” [The edition has *nostra* (“our”; its exact syntactic relation is uncertain in the supplied text).]

Humanity rightly hesitated over what it could repay, since it possessed nothing good of its own. For when he says “what?”, great hesitation is shown. What can be returned to him by a human being, when we are always known to be sustained by his gift? He therefore rightly hesitated, since nothing worthy arose from his own resources.

Yet, lest he should remain altogether sterile, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, he subsequently explains what he will repay. But this must be investigated very carefully: he says that God repaid us with the things he bestowed, as though we had first given him something good and then received from him what he bestowed, although the Apostle cries out: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

The Lord repaid us good for evil, so that he might demonstrate by example what he preached in word. He was struck with blows; he was handed over to the judge; he was scourged with undeserved lashes. Yet he gave us the hope of resurrection and promised the kingdoms of heaven.

### Verse 4

“I shall receive the cup of salvation, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord.” A worthy promise indeed, but if it is placed in human strength, a dangerous presumption. For who can give confessors patience amid torments except the one who deigned to receive the cup of suffering for us?

To show absolutely that this was impossible for human strength, he continued: “And I shall call upon the name of the Lord.” Trusting in whose help, he believed that he could accomplish what he did not think his fleshly weakness sufficient to achieve.

Very beautifully and briefly the death of the martyrs is defined as “the cup of salvation”: a cup because it is drunk in measured portions; salvific because, by the Lord’s grace, it is offered for eternal salvation. The Lord also spoke of this cup in the Gospel: “Can you drink the cup which I am going to drink?” (Matt. 20:22).

### Verse 5

“Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” It is rightly called “precious,” since it is known to have been purchased by the Lord’s blood. It was glorified by his passion, so that it might be exceptional in his sight. For we know that the Lord bestows this upon his servants with great abundance of grace, since he himself deigned to undertake it.

O life-giving death! O destruction to be desired! O glorious passage, which makes the members of Christ imitators of their head! And for it to be precious, it is not made so by riches offered, but is purchased by the shedding of blood.

### Verse 6

“O Lord, for I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid! You have broken my bonds.” He comes to the second section, where, having received an extraordinary gift, he cries out, saying: “O Lord, I am your servant?” 392

He marvels that he has received such benefits as the Lord himself deigned to undertake for the redemption of the world. For how could the servant not marvel when, bound by the condition of the first human being, he has come to those things which so great a Majesty deigned to choose? It is frightening to speak of the benefits received by one who, through his actions, deserves offense.

To reveal the increase of this wonder, he repeats: “I am your servant.” He added, “and the son of your handmaid,” to indicate his humility through a threefold confession. “The son of your handmaid” seems to have been added in order to signify the catholic Church in every respect: she is a handmaid when she serves, a bride when she is joined to him.

And therefore we rightly understand that there is no martyrdom except that which the Lord’s servant and the son of the catholic Church deserves.

It follows: “You have broken my bonds.” Here we perceive the power of martyrdom being explained: by its triumphal force all the bonds of sins are broken. No stain can remain in a human being which pious blood has washed away.

It should be noted, however, that this verse was believed to possess such power that some said that sins could be forgiven human beings if, at the end of their life, they repeated it three times as a confession.

### Verse 7

“To you I shall sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.” Because the bonds of sins had been broken, he says that he will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise; this sacrifice appears to be exceedingly acceptable to the Lord. For he himself teaches in the Gospel: “Ten were cleansed, and no one was found who would give glory to God except this Samaritan” (Luke 17:18).

For he was not one of those who suppressed the Lord’s benefit in ungrateful silence. Rather, he promises to restore to God the thanksgiving owed for the good he had received.

### Verse 8

“I shall repay my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord.” After he had said that he would offer a sacrifice of praise, lest it be thought that it could be paid anywhere whatsoever, he says: “in the courts of the house of the Lord”—that is, in the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, which contains all true Christians, not heretics who are separated by empty perversity.

For when he says, “I shall repay my vows to the Lord,” he clearly promises to offer himself. The vow of all the faithful is to offer themselves to Christ and to remain in his Church with right belief.

But so that you may recognize what this house of the Lord is, observe what follows.

### Verse 9

“In the sight of all his people, in your midst, Jerusalem.” Behold, he has explained what house of the Lord he meant in the preceding verse: “in the sight of all his people.” For it is fitting that the one who deigned to suffer for the salvation of all should be praised publicly. The Lord certainly knows this perfectly even if it takes place in the secrecy of the heart. But this pertains to the edification of the people, so that a good confession may be absorbed by the ears of all, as he says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32).

He added: “in your midst, Jerusalem,” where the peace of the Lord rests and the unity of the holy people rejoices in the contemplation of the Lord.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

This psalm has been consecrated to the magnificent honor of the martyrs. It has been given to us both as an example and as a means of obtaining protection. Let us venerate the sufferings of such people; let us desire punishments of this kind for ourselves through the zeal of love, so that, if we do not deserve to be crowned by such a consummation, we may at least be found in similar efforts.

Why would a Christian wish to escape such sufferings, through which he knows that he will reach the joys of heaven?

## Exposition of Psalm 116

### Alleluia
With only two verses, yet the full dignity of a title is appended [Col. 0824D], so that we may understand that however few the words, they are always entirely full when they praise the Lord. For who would doubt that something should not be called insignificant from which heavenly magnificence can be praised? To this is fittingly added the figure called in Greek *hirmos*: for it preserves the sequence of the discourse to the very end, and is seen to have changed neither its person nor its subject; rather, it carries through to its conclusion, with a single meaning, what it began.

## Structure of the Psalm

Although this psalm, because of its few verses, does not admit division, it surpasses all others in the compactness of its expression. For it is indeed the first atom of the psalms, possessing the dignity of a point, from which a line arises [Col. 0825A] and the various kinds of figures are formed with the most learned diversity.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1. “Praise the Lord, all you nations, and praise him together, all you peoples.”** We must also apply this psalm to the person of the martyrs. For the holy men speak as though they had already undergone their glorious passion, so that all nations should be stirred to the praises of the Lord, who granted such things to his servants that they might instead be imbued with his own examples. Where are the Donatists, who falsely claim that faith has been granted only to their own congregation? That chorus of saints cries out that all nations ought to praise the Lord; and would that they might do with us what they falsely claim to do alone!

It follows: “and praise him together, all you peoples.” The common praise is the praise of all the faithful gathered into one; [Col. 0825B] this is recognized as appropriate to the Catholic Church, which is assembled from the various regions of the world. For all nations are generally admonished in their peoples, lest anyone say that he has been passed over in the Lord’s judgment.

**Verse 2. “For his mercy has been confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever.”** The reason is given why the Lord should be praised throughout the whole world: because he fulfilled, through the visitation of his coming, the promises that he had made through the holy prophets. His mercy has indeed been confirmed in the Christian people, and it will not be shaken forever, since he who bestowed it himself also guards us, as is worthy of belief, by his compassion.

He added: “and the truth of the Lord remains forever.” Here the Son is signified as the truth of the Lord, just as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and [Col. 0825C] the life” (John XIV, 6). For, according to the utterly foolish Arian—an assertion that it is impious to make—there was a time when the Son did not exist; there must therefore have been a time when the Father existed without truth, without the way, and without life. But since we must believe that the Father never existed without these things, it is fitting both for our salvation and for truth itself to confess that the Son is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father in all things.

Then it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3). For if time was made through the Son, how could time have existed when its author did not exist? Thus absurdity always follows perverse errors.

They also add a third falsehood: that the Father is always proclaimed before the Son. And where is that found? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” [Col. 0825D] (ibid., 1). You see that nothing was placed before him there; indeed, in many passages the Son is named first, as in the Apostle’s words to the Ephesians: “Or do you not know that every fornicator and unclean person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians V, 5)? And to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Galatians I, 1). And to the Thessalonians: “But the Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us” (II Thessalonians II, 13). And in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God” (II Corinthians XIII, 13).

And so that you might understand this equality as belonging to the whole Trinity, he added: “and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” It is also read that the Holy Spirit was called “Lord” and was named first; [Col. 0826A] for Paul says to the Thessalonians: “But may the Lord direct your hearts in the love of God and in the patience of Christ” (II Timothy III, 5). The Holy Spirit is prayed to, that he may direct the hearts of believers both in the love of God and in the patience of Christ.

Therefore, when one of the Trinity is named before or afterward, this can offer no prejudice to the hearer, since human speech cannot otherwise express itself. For in God no inequality or diversity is to be considered: where one God is rightly believed, no lesser or greater can be found. Unity does not know number, nor does equality admit rank, as it is written: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar” (Exodus XX, 26).

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0826B] This little psalm has been concluded in the fullest brevity. For what more could have been said than that the Creator ought to be praised throughout the whole world? Fruitful brevity, compressed abundance, narrow vastness, and infinity confined. O sweet and admirable diversity! At one time to speak salutary things in a few statements, at another to recount great matters in an extended discourse, so that wearisome mortality would not endure boredom even in its very devotion, when pleasing variety [mss. A, B, F: “truth”] supplies its appetite.
