Perhaps it may be asked why this psalm contains only two verses, whereas, by contrast, the hundred and eighteenth is shown to extend to one hundred and seventy-six verses, while many others have likewise been formed differently according to the nature of their subjects. But this matter may perhaps be understood to indicate the following: just as harmony—that is, the beautiful modulation of musical art—makes one perfect song from diverse [Col. 0826C] sounds and accents, so these psalms, at times brief, at times moderate, at times extremely long, are brought together into a single concert by the sweetest agreeableness. Or, as is worthy of belief, the future kingdom of the Lord is signified, where the diverse merits of the saints will shine according to the quality of their deeds, while one blessedness and eternal sweetness will nevertheless be granted to all.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXVII

## Alleluia

We read in the Apocalypse of the apostle John (Chapter XIX, 1, 4) that a great multitude sings “Alleluia” in heaven; the four living creatures and the twenty-four [Col. 0826D] elders also say this while adoring the Lord, and the entire heavenly host celebrates together with hymnic exultation in the voice of a loud-sounding trumpet. Therefore let us also approach this service of praise eagerly. If we sing with a pure heart, we are joined to the holy virtues in devout dedication; and the honor and grace of earthly beings become what is proved to be the blessedness of heavenly beings.

Accordingly, let us contemplate this psalm shining with a beautiful face. At its very beginning he concluded four verses with the same ending, so that, by a fourfold exhortation, corresponding to the evangelical number, he might remind the whole world that it owes praises to the one Lord. We cannot call these intercalary verses, since he introduces no others among them, but perhaps we may aptly call them *unifines*, because they end with a similar concordance of words [Col. 0827A]. He will do the same absolutely throughout every verse of Psalm 135; we shall explain more clearly in its proper place how this is arranged.

## Division of the Psalm

The faithful people, freed from the bonds of sins, generally exhort in the first section that everyone ought to confess to the Lord: having been heard in tribulations, they declare that no human being should be feared. In the second section they say that one must trust in the Lord alone, through whom they are shown to have escaped the hostility of the nations and to have reached the remedies of truly sound life. In the third section they say that the gates of righteousness must be opened to them, where they also speak of the cornerstone, that is, of the Lord the Savior. In the fourth, they persuade the other Christians to frequent the courts of the Lord, rejoicing with sweet delight at the coming of the holy incarnation.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1. “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”** That blessed people, which had been delivered from its own ruin, admonishes the remaining faithful to devote themselves steadfastly to the praises of the Lord. This confession plainly pertains to praise, whether because “Alleluia” has been placed before it, or because the people rejoice that they have been rescued from various afflictions by the Lord’s mercy.

The reason for praise is also added: “for he is good.” This name certainly and properly belongs to God. For when Christ the Teacher was called “Good Master” by the unbelieving Jews according to the appearance of the flesh, [Col. 0827C] he himself replied: “Why do you ask me about the good” (Matthew XIX, 17, and Mark X, 18), when you do not believe that I am the Lord of heaven? Adding: “No one is good except God alone.”

But since we read, “The good person brings forth good things from his good treasure” (Matthew XII, 35), this may seem to be contradictory. Yet we call a person good because he has been made so by the Lord’s grace; for he alone is properly said to be good in himself who makes others fulfill what is good in them.

It follows: “for his mercy is forever.” The explanation of that goodness of which he had spoken is also made clear: for he not only grants benefits to the undeserving, but bestows the gifts of his mercy eternally. “Forever” signifies the coming perpetuity, where there is one age and one day, and no change follows.

**[Col. 0827D] Verse 2. “Let Israel now say: for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”**

**Verse 3. “Let the house of Aaron now say: for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”**

**Verse 4. “Let all who fear the Lord now say: for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”** Since similar endings are read in these verses, the preceding exposition appropriately embraces them. Yet we must investigate more deeply why he varied only the names at the beginnings of the verses.

For he says: “Let Israel now say,” which embraces the whole people of the blessed. In the second verse appears: “Let the house of Aaron now say,” signifying the priests, whom he judged worthy of being mentioned separately because of the reverence due to their honor. The third verse likewise says: “Let all who fear the Lord now say,” [Col. 0828A] so that he might indicate those whom he had called in Psalm 113: “the small together with the great” (Psalm CXIII, 13), those who are devoted with pure mind to Christ the Lord in one fellowship. Thus this diversity of names plainly embraces the universality of the faithful.

**Verse 5. “In tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in a broad place.”** A personal example is offered to stir the minds of the hearers, since it is a great incentive to belief to hear someone giving thanks who has himself endured the experience.

But consider what he added: “in a broad place.” For he frees us from the narrowness of this world, but in the great breadth of his rewards he mercifully receives us. He snatches us from temporal evils, but is powerful to fill us with eternal goods. Therefore let passing dangers rage as much as they wish, and let perishable adversities swell up [Col. 0828B]; what the faithful people endure in the briefness of this world is repaid with the greatest breadth.

**Verse 6. “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.”**

**Verse 7. “The Lord is my helper, and I shall see my enemies.”** Although these verses appear almost identical, they are entirely distinguished by their individual words. When he says that, with the Lord’s help, he does not fear a human being, he designates bodily enemies who visibly persecute the purpose of the devout. But when he says, “I shall see my enemies,” he wishes spiritual wickednesses to be understood, which he says will be seen at that judgment where the devil, already destroyed and condemned together with his other ministers, will appear before human eyes.

For although now the greater part of humanity sees [Col. 0828C] its bodily enemies, he should be understood to have desired especially that which he could not see here. Or he prays that he may be able to behold the hidden enemy, so that, becoming more cautious, he may be made free from that enemy’s snares.

And note that he repeated the same words at the beginnings of both verses. This figure is called *anaphora*, and it is also found in the verses that follow.

**Verse 8. “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in a human being.”** That blessed people, liberated by divine favor, faithfully and devoutly teaching, comes to the second section, saying: One must trust in God alone, not in a human being—in him, that is, who truly makes promises, not in one who deceives himself through deceptive presumption.

For how many fools say, “I do what I want, [Col. 0828D] and I have no master of my will,” thinking that human advantage is to be carried out through free choice? The apostle James rebukes them, saying: “Do you not say in your desires: Tomorrow we shall go into that city, and we shall trade and make a profit,” instead of saying, “If the Lord wills, and if we live, we shall do this or that” (James IV, 13, 15), and so forth.

There is indeed, in the evil sense, an accursed freedom of choice: when the transgressor abandons the Creator and turns to shameful vices. But in the good sense we lost free choice when Adam sinned, and we cannot return to it except through Christ’s grace, as the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Philippians II, 13).

Therefore we must pray continually that a perverse will [Col. 0829A] may not seize us, but that divine inspiration may possess us; for whatever we devise from ourselves, we arouse against ourselves with deadly boldness. Rightly, then, he forbade trusting in a human being, since no one by himself is able to provide a remedy either for another or for himself, as Jeremiah also says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jeremiah XVII, 5).

Therefore let presumptuous people cease to assume for themselves those positions from which the divine sentence may more justly condemn them. For this reason Father Augustine also argued wonderfully and at length in many books against the heretics Pelagius, Caelestius, and Julian, and shattered the weapons of their poisonous doctrine.

**Verse 9. “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope [Col. 0829B] in princes.”** Two changed words have made an entirely different meaning. Above he says that he trusts; here, that he hopes. There he speaks of a human being; here, of princes—so that there he seems to have spoken of bodily enemies, here of spiritual ones.

For the devil is also called a prince, as in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). A good angel is likewise called a prince, as it is read in Daniel: “Michael, your prince” [ed., “the great prince”] (Daniel XII, 1). Therefore he says that human hope must be placed neither in good nor in evil angels, but in the Lord alone. For although we love the good angels because of the kindness they show us, in them we praise the Lord’s benefits, not the rights of their own power.

**Verse 10. “All nations surrounded me, and in [Col. 0829C] the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them.”** This was rightly said by that people which had placed its hope in the Lord’s protection. It signifies the labors of the Church, which it first endured in its Head, that is, in the Lord Christ, and afterward bore in its own passions.

For when the Christian religion first became known, all the nations, rising in persecution against it, inflicted various disasters upon the most faithful men. Yet, with the Lord’s help, they took vengeance on their persecutors when they subjected them by a marvelous conversion, so that they might impose upon themselves the penalties of repentance for the evils they had formerly inflicted upon the innocent.

When he says “nations” and then adds the masculine form, “I took vengeance on them,” this either pertains to the meaning, because the peoples are signified by the nations, or it is the figure *exallage*, that is, alteration, because [Col. 0829D] here he has altered the grammatical gender of the noun.

**Verse 11. “Surrounding me, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them.”** The details of the words must be examined, because when they are investigated—as we have often said—they produce for us no insignificant mysteries.

First he said “nations,” which pertained to the Church because of the people of the martyrs, who, devoted to the worship of demons, were everywhere tearing apart the faithful people. Now, however, in this repetition of the words he did not wish to say “nations,” so that he might indicate more subtly the Lord’s passion, which is known to have been accomplished especially by the Jews alone. Yet in them also vengeance was taken in the name of the Lord, when many of them repented of the evils they had committed and were found worthy to take the name of Christians.

[Col. 0830A] These verses too should be called *unifines*, like those placed at the beginning of the psalm. And it should be noted that just as the Head often speaks of the members, so now the members speak concerning their Head.

**Verse 12. “They surrounded me like bees surround a honeycomb, and they burned like fire among thorns; and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them.”** These verses too still speak about the Lord. Surrounded by the raging Jews, he poured out the honey of his passion throughout the whole world.

Bees surround a honeycomb when, in waxen houses, they store the sweetest liquids; and when they think they are laying up provisions for themselves, they make something by which human beings can satisfy their desires. It is evident that the Jews fulfilled this image when [Col. 0830B], through bitter efforts, they made something that was most sweet for the entire world.

Bees are said to have received their name as though from “feet,” because they are born without feet. The thorns of the world signify sins. The people of the Jews, fiercely goaded by them, seethed in their transgressions like crackling fire. Yet in them also the Lord’s grace took vengeance, when, converted to the Lord, they were most sweetly filled with that honey which, without knowing it, they had stored up.

**Verse 13. “I was thrust and shaken so that I might fall, but the Lord received me.”** Now the entire body of the faithful bears witness to this about itself with a most truthful voice. The person who is thrust falls when the Lord’s strength is withdrawn from him. And observe the force of the words: he says that he was thrust and turned so that he might fall, but that he was strengthened by the Lord’s receiving him.

For those who are assailed [Col. 0830C] do not fall, provided that they are held fast by Christ’s virtues, as often happens when those who have merited well are handed over to punishments. They seem to be handed over so that they may fall—that is, so that they may be changed from right belief—but, strengthened by the Lord’s right hand, they do not fall, because they remain established in the holiness of faith. Otherwise unbelievers fall even when they are seen standing in the obstinacy of their stubbornness.

**Verse 14. “The Lord is my strength and my praise” [mss. A, B: “praise”], “and he became my salvation.”** One who has been thrust cannot fall when the Lord’s help is seen to offer strength. But lest it be thought that the one whom the Lord’s gifts protected merely avoided dangers, he added: “he became my salvation,” because through him they receive eternal [Col. 0830D] life, through whom they also deserve to escape the ruin of this world. For he himself is both the eternal strength and the praise of the blessed.

**Verse 15. “The voice of joy and salvation is in the tents of the righteous; the right hand of the Lord has wrought might.”** That chorus of the faithful rejoices joyfully, because, while their persecutors thought that they were being consumed by grief and exhausted by tribulation, they, rejoicing in divine contemplation, took delight in their own punishment, which they knew would benefit them for eternal joys.

Here “the tents of the righteous” designate the hidden places of the human heart, where they are always joyful, although they are afflicted outwardly. And so that you might know from where this joy comes, he added: “the right hand of the Lord has shown strength,” that is, Christ, through whom the Father [Col. 0831A] displayed his power in the exaltation of the saints; he himself will say this below.

**Verse 16. “The right hand of the Lord has exalted me.”** The right hand of the Lord exalts when he grants the kingdoms of heaven to earthly human beings. For what is more powerful than to give mortals immortality, to give the corruptible incorruption, to give sinners blessedness, and to give victory over the strongest enemy to the weak?

**Verse 17. “I shall not die, but live; and I shall recount the works of the Lord.”** These words are spoken against the things that the insane insolence of persecutors habitually utters against the Church of Christ. When it thinks that it is destroying the Christian name, it seems rather to provide for its increase.

The faithful person rightly says to it: “I shall not die, as you suppose; rather, I shall live with a life unknown to you,” a life to which the proud in mind [Col. 0831B] cannot attain. He also promises that he will recount the works of the Lord, so that the Church may continually grow through such widespread preaching. What can cruelty accomplish against those whom it sees always increasing through persecutions? How much better would they themselves live if, converted, they lamented their own deeds!

**Verse 18. “The Lord chastening has chastened me, but he has not handed me over to death.”** So that the pride of the persecutors might claim nothing for itself, he confirms that their tortures and most savage cruelty are the Lord’s chastening, so that all that wicked power may seem to have been granted for the correction of the faithful.

Why do they boast about their power, when nothing is granted to them for their own benefit? Their cruelty is our correction; the flame of their fury is a test. [Col. 0831C] Let them not consider themselves better because they commit offenses: the son is not spared, so that he may be seen to be capable of instruction. But this is proclaimed by one who has been chastened well; only the person whose committed faults are cleansed here is not handed over to death.

And note that he says, “chastening has chastened.” This kind of expression is frequently found in the divine Scriptures, as in: “Blessing I will bless you. Multiplying I will multiply your seed,” and similar expressions. This device, as we have often said, is called *derivation from cognate words* (*a coniugatis*).

**Verse 19. “Open for me the gates of righteousness, and entering them I will confess to the Lord.”** That people of the faithful [ed., “faithful”] comes to the third section. Desiring to enter Jerusalem, it asks in spiritual fervor that its gates be opened to it.

To whom, then, is “Open” said, except to the prophets and apostles, who received the keys of heaven through mystical powers [Col. 0831D]? Having been brought in through these gates of teaching, and now standing within, we truly confess to the Lord. Moreover, whatever is done outside the Catholic Church is in no way applied to the praises of the Lord.

The prophets and apostles have rightly been called gates by allegory. Gates are so called because provisions are brought through them into cities, just as through these men the nourishment of souls is evidently brought in.

**Verse 20. “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.”** Since above he said “gates,” it must be asked why here he wished to use the singular “gate.” It was evidently to indicate that the prophets and apostles are indeed gates of heaven, but that all of them can lead to one gate, since they have all been accustomed to admit people to the Lord the Savior, who can also be called the gate [Col. 0832A], as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the door of the sheep” (John X, 7), and so forth.

It follows: “the righteous shall enter through it.” Let us also examine subtly why above he said “the gates of righteousness,” while here he wrote, “the righteous shall enter through it.” He signifies, as I think, that this no longer refers to the divine Scriptures, through which even the unrighteous pass, but to that Jerusalem which has the Lord the Savior as its gate, through whom only righteous people will enter. He has well embraced both meanings, so that he might seem to signify both this age and the age to come.

**Verse 21. “I will confess to you, Lord, for you have heard me, and you have become my salvation.”** We must understand this confession not as belonging to an afflicted people, but to a rejoicing one. It gives thanks because the Lord who saves has shone upon it, [Col. 0832B] and the Redeemer of the nations has appeared to human eyes.

Hence we truly understand that the Lord’s coming was continually desired even by the righteous of earlier times, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and to hear what you hear” (Matthew XIII, 17), and so forth.

**Verse 22. “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.”** Under the allusion to builders, the fruitless work of the Jews is explained. They alone among human beings, while still in the world, appeared to worship one God and therefore to build, whereas the other nations were destroying themselves through the worship of idols.

Builders always extend toward a corner, so that the solidity of the joined walls may be completed. But the Jews did not complete the structure of their faith [Col. 0832C], because, like madmen, they thought that the very one who was the strongest cornerstone should be despised.

The Lord Christ is called the cornerstone in a tropological sense—as is established in the exposition of countless passages—because he joined two peoples coming to him from opposite directions, Gentiles and Jews, like twin walls, into one grace of solidity [ed., “placed”]. The prophets said many things about this stone, the apostles said many things, and various others said many things.

The word “corner” (*angulus*) is derived from the Greek word γόνυ (*gónu*), which in Latin is called *genu*, “knee.” This bent form reproduces the shape of a corner through corresponding form; for among the Greeks the origin of the word is fully preserved in its derivatives, as in *tetragonus*, “four-cornered,” *pentagonus*, “five-cornered,” and similar words.

**Verse 23. “This has been done by the Lord, and it is marvelous [Col. 0832D]” [mss. A, B, F: “this marvelous thing has been done”] “in our eyes.”** Lest you think that this stone was hewn from rocky mountains, he says that it was made by the Lord for the salvation of the world. But when he mentions that it was made, the nature of the humanity is shown, which is also demonstrated to have been created.

Thus the Apostle likewise says: “Made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being” (Philippians II, 7). And elsewhere: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans I, 3).

This stone, which is the beautiful joining of the structure, the clasp of the walls, and an everlasting strength in the foundations, is marvelous in the eyes of the faithful, who see him not only bodily but also perceive him with an enlightened mind. The Jews too saw him, but not as marvelous, because they looked only upon the flesh, which they saw to be ordinary.

But to the senses of the faithful [Col. 0833A], who professed him to be the Son of God, he appeared marvelous and terrible, as to the apostle Peter, who said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew XVI, 16).

**Verse 24. “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.”** O how sweet are the words that holy faith is proved to pour forth! Although God created all days, nevertheless he is said to have made one day in a special sense—the day consecrated by the birth of the Lord Christ. In it we rightly ought to exult and rejoice, because on it the devil lost his power and the world received salvation.

**Verse 25. “O Lord, save me! O Lord, prosper me!”** These interjections reveal the desire of a great petition: that they may be freed here from the ruin of this world and placed there, by the most prosperous lot, at the right hand [Col. 0833B].

For these are the two things that the faithful Christian desires: to be rescued here from the death of sins and to be placed there in everlasting rest. Those afflictions that they suffer here, those pains that they endure here for love of the Lord, will undoubtedly prosper there, when they have already reached eternal joys. To prosper is to make something harsh tranquil, so that past evils become pleasing to us because we believe they will be changed into eternal joys.

**Verse 26. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; we have blessed you” [mss. A, B, F: “to you”] “from the house of the Lord.”** The remaining fourth section is entered, where a sweet offering of praise is made concerning the Lord’s coming, and the wicked presumption of the Antichrist is subtly condemned.

This [Col. 0833C] figure is called *emphasis*, which signifies even what it does not say. By saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” it is clear that the one believed to be coming in his own name is accursed. And so that you might recognize Christ as the almighty Lord, he says that Christ came in the name of the Lord, lest the human mind think of him in a merely carnal way.

The Gospel text also shows this, saying: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V, 43).

It follows: “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord.” This is said by that faithful people whom we mentioned earlier to the other Christians, who, as though raised to priestly dignity, speak to the people, showing that the Lord’s blessing is salutarily given to the devout people through their bishops.

And lest you receive this doubtfully, [Col. 0833D] he says: “from the house of the Lord,” that is, from the Catholic Church, from which saving baptism comes, from which holy communion proceeds, from which we are cleansed by the anointing of consecrated oil, and from which, finally, every true blessing is bestowed.

**Verse 27. “God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us; establish the feast amid the throngs, up to the horn of the altar.”** When he says, “God is the Lord,” he responds to what precedes, so that you may understand it as follows: “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord”—or rather, not we, but God the Lord.

For he blesses through the mouth of the saints, and he shines upon us when he separates us from the darkness of sins. It follows: “Establish the feast amid the throngs, up to the horn of the altar.” This is now said to those who have been blessed, who were able to celebrate feast days solemnly.

“Establish,” he says—that is, preserve by deliberate decision the solemn day that has been consecrated by the honor of the Lord and the confession of the saints. “Amid the throngs,” that is, amid the frequent processions which the crowd of the people thickens and makes most celebrated through festive devotion.

But by adding “up to the horn of the altar,” he perhaps forbids certain people—as is customary among many—to leave after hearing the Gospel reading. For those who are not filled with the grace of communion do not approach the horn of the altar.

In my view, we may fittingly understand this as referring to the visible altar, which gives us the body and blood of the Lord through solemn participation. But that altar is before the sight of the Lord, where we are commanded to approach with purified minds through holy contemplation, so that in this present celebration we may always behold it, as has already been explained in Psalm 42, where it says: “And I shall go in to the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my youth” (Psalm XLII, 4). The horn signifies power, which the holy altar plainly possesses.

**Verse 28. “You are my God, and I will confess to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you.”** How appropriately this truth of confession is repeated, so that we may say that the Lord whom we do not cease to worship with a pure mind is ours!

In the first clause he says, “I will confess to you,” which pertains to thanksgiving. In the second, “I will exalt you,” because the Lord Christ is exalted through the preaching of the blessed among all nations. He returns good for evil; although he is able to destroy his enemies, he patiently [Col. 0834C] waits for them; and to those who are converted he gives such things as his free mercy promised to his saints.

**Verse 29. “I will confess to you, Lord, for you have heard me, and you have become my salvation.”** Since this verse has been repeated, it has already been shown above to have been explained in the third section. We shall nevertheless state briefly that we must understand this confession as an exceedingly joyful one, poured forth after benefits have been received, just as the title “Alleluia” also reminds us.

**Verse 30. “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”** This verse too has already been shown to have been spoken at the beginning of the psalm, so that, just as the psalm began from Christ, its conclusion might also appear to agree with him. For he himself says in the Apocalypse: “I am the Alpha and the Omega” (Revelation I, 8).

Rightly, therefore, the confession has been placed at the beginning and repeated at the end, because throughout our entire life we ought to take it up and end in its delight.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 0834D] Let us remember that this psalm has not been woven together without purpose, as though with certain shining colors. At its beginning he placed four verses with the same ending, and again at the end he doubled the first verse of the psalm through a beautiful repetition. He also repeated almost at the end the verse that he had placed as the twenty-first, so that it might shine like the vestment of the high priest, woven with golden threads and embroidered with a variegated beauty.

That vestment had bells on its fringes; these bells echo at the end the same things that sounded at the beginning. Therefore, when the high priest [Col. 0835A] entered the Holy of Holies, he wore this garment so that the arrival of the venerable priest might in no way go unnoticed, even when he walked silently, yet with a voice [mss. A, B: “with words”].

This psalm has likewise been arranged with such beautiful variety that the proclamations of the holy incarnation may be perceived through certain most beautiful indications. May this garment of your eloquence cover us, pious King, and, by your granting it, may our deeds echo what your commandments, Lord, have ordered [mss. A, B: “may our deeds perceive this while the present garment remains”].

Let us remember that this is the fifth of those psalms that were produced with marvelous narration concerning the Lord’s first coming—perhaps to be compared with the five loaves that filled the hunger of the watching peoples with heavenly abundance.

# EXPOSITION OF PSALM CXVIII

## Alleluia

[Col. 0835B]

A desirable *Alleluia* is prefixed to this festive psalm, so rich in the power of divine things, that the worth of the sacred song may be recognized by the honor of its title. For it is exceedingly lofty in the depth of its meanings and composed, as it were, through the repetition of similar words: at one point confessing what it has received, at another again hoping for the same things that it has merited. It is seen to move gently, like the great rivers, although it is known to be exceedingly deep; nevertheless, with God’s help, we must traverse it according to the measure of our undertaking, lest we who have hitherto restrained ourselves be overwhelmed by a sudden flood.

It is also depicted according to the Hebrew alphabet, for the instruction of peoples who are uneducated yet teachable in the school of Christ, in such an arrangement that the letter assigned the first verse is affixed likewise to the following seven, perhaps signifying that mystery in the circumcision of the heart. Thus this psalm, running in its own language through the individual letters in groups of eight verses, is brought to completion by the equality of its parts, each section corresponding throughout to the others. We say that this was arranged both for the sake of division and so that it might indicate the perfect number of the righteous. For through these letters Hebrew wisdom is learned, and the sacred number of the divine books is contained. We know, as blessed Jerome testifies, that these letters possess their own meanings; to repeat them here now seems superfluous, since they have already been collected through the labor of another. Josephus further reports that this psalm, Psalm 144, and the song of Deuteronomy [Col. 0835D] were composed in elegiac meter.

## Division of the Psalm

With respect to this moral psalm, we may appropriately say that the Hebrew letters have contributed divisions that illuminate it according to their number [ed., “according to its number”]. Each letter, claiming eight verses for itself—as has been mentioned above—describes the whole song with the most beautiful equality. The song is not confused by any mixture; rather, it explains new subjects through letters changed in relation to one another.

Throughout the psalm, therefore, the universal chorus of the saints speaks: those who have existed, now exist, or are believed to be destined to exist from the beginning of the world. Among them are apostles, prophets, martyrs, confessors, the ecclesiastical orders, and all who serve the Lord with holy integrity [Col. 0836A]: “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition” (1 Peter 2:9), to be gathered from the origin of the human race until the end of the age. Although their multitude is countless, one person is nevertheless introduced everywhere as speaking, so that the power of unity in the concordant Church may be recognized [mss. A, B, F, “in concord”]. Let us now see what spiritual fruits are born in this heavenly paradise.

## 398. Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1 — I. ALEPH

**Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.**

Since everyone’s desires are carried away by the ardor of this name, and no one can be found who does not wish to attain the rewards of blessedness, it was fitting for the holy men to point out the way by commendable prayers [Col. 0836B], lest the confused mind of mortals, ignorant of the way, should go astray. For even those who are deceived by the ambitions of the world consider themselves blessed.

But lest anything of that kind be thought worthy of choice, he first used the plural form, “the undefiled,” so that this might be understood of the faithful, not of Christ. He alone is naturally undefiled, because he had no sin. The saints, however, become undefiled when they receive the gifts of forgiveness, as the prophet says in Psalm 50: “You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 50:9).

It follows: **in the way**, that is, in the Lord himself, the Savior, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). To walk there is the activity of the righteous—not with bodily feet, but with the steps of commendable conduct. And so that you might understand that he did not mean that way in which one can go astray, he added: **who walk in the law of the Lord**, that is, those who either do not sin or, through heavenly grace, provide themselves with appropriate satisfaction.

Nor is it without significance that he says, **in the law of the Lord**. There is also a law of sin, as the Apostle says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Romans 7:23). Therefore “of the Lord” has been added, so that it might be distinguished from the law of sin.

### Verse 2

**Blessed are those who examine his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart.**

This sentence still belongs to the preceding meaning. Although the undefiled who walk in the way—that is, in the Lord himself, the Savior—and proceed with devoted mind in his law are blessed, this virtue is nevertheless added to them: **those who examine his testimonies**. What this examination is, is subsequently explained: namely, those who have chosen to seek the Lord with their whole heart.

Heretical evasive disputants also seem to examine his testimonies, but they do not seek the Lord with their whole heart, because through human cleverness they strive to discover new accusations. Someone who is transferred by punishable error into the pursuit of falsehood cannot rightly be said to have placed his entire heart upon the holy Scriptures. Hence the holy Primasius, an eloquent bishop of Justinianopolis, is known to have composed a book under the title *What Makes a Heretic*.

Nor do those appear to have placed their whole heart upon the Lord’s testimonies who, neglecting the discipline of his commandments, desire worldly joys. And observe the order of holy and true teaching: first he says that those are blessed who walk [Col. 0837A] in the law of the Lord; then those who examine the testimonies of the sacred writings. For no one is worthy to investigate these things unless he is known to conduct himself through commendable action.

A third mode of definition embraces both statements; in Greek it is called *poeotes* [ποιότης], and in Latin, “qualitative.” What a blessed man is, is here shown through the quality of his actions.

### Verse 3

**For those who practice iniquity have not walked in his ways.**

Since the truthful words of the Apostle John are: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8), the saints too seem not to walk in his ways, since we know that they have sins. Yet this question is resolved by the voice of Truth itself.

There are unlawful desires that we commit because of the necessity of original sin, but we are not held by the consent of the mind in these things. The blessed mind does not walk in them; rather, by the gift of the Lord, it overcomes them through integrity of heart. Such things include, for example, suddenly desiring something beautiful, eagerly craving food, being stirred by pleasant scents, becoming confused by a sudden wicked suggestion, and similar impulses, which are destroyed by holy prayer and the sign of the cross.

Thus it happens that the saints possess sins arising from the suggestion of the flesh, and yet, since their fulfillment is in no way granted to them, they are truly judged not to practice them. This is more clearly confirmed by the testimonies of the Apostle Paul. He walked in the ways of the Lord when he said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7), and so forth. But he committed an involuntary sin when he cried out: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want is what I do” (Romans 7:19).

His following explanation removes every stain of doubt: “But if I do what I do not want,” he says (ibid., 20), “it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” You see that only those are accused who consent to the works of sin with abominable delight. Therefore those who practice iniquity are rightly said not to walk in the ways of the Lord. The practice of iniquity is the consent of the wicked, and this, by the Lord’s gift, is shown to be alien from the hearts of the saints.

The Apostle himself also gives this warning: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires; and do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Romans 6:12). Solomon likewise says: “Do not follow the desires of your heart” (Ecclesiasticus 18:30). He therefore forbade obedience to sin, not the suggestions that the flesh cannot avoid by its own powers.

Let us also consider why he used the plural here, **in the ways**, whereas above he said in the singular: **Blessed are the undefiled in the way**. There he signifies the Lord and Savior, who is the definite way by which those who come to the Father proceed, as he himself said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). But what he says here, **in the ways**, designates the prophets and apostles, or anyone who has taught the people through true preaching.

### Verse 4

**You commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly.**

He had said that the person to whom such things lend their aid is blessed: that he is undefiled, walks in the law of the Lord, examines his testimonies, and—as the most perfect way of life—seeks the Lord with his whole heart. And lest these great things seem worthy of neglect, there follows the venerable command of the Lord’s injunction: his commandments are to be sought not only diligently but exceedingly.

One is called “excessive” who is doubtful in nothing and always remains intent upon the task set before him. Here is the saying of the pagans celebrated throughout the whole world: “Nothing in excess.” Behold, the Truth commands excess of us; behold, the Ruler of all things decrees that something must be done without defect. For this “exceedingly” signifies much and without limit, as he says in another psalm: “Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Psalm 91:6). And elsewhere: “You have been exceedingly exalted above all gods” (Psalm 96:9).

Alternatively, we are commanded to keep the Lord’s commandments exceedingly when we are judged to have to prefer them even to the health of our bodies. Therefore to exceed the powers of our human capacity is a divine service, because everything there ought to be excessive, since that too is infinite which we ask to be granted to us.

The distinct meaning of these terms must also be investigated, lest anyone think that they are confused. In the preceding verse he said, **the law of the Lord**. The law of the Lord is, as the Apostle says, “a shadow of things to come” (Colossians 2:17), and it is not fitting that it be observed according to the letter but according to a spiritual order. Such are the law of sacrifices, observance of the new moon, the rite of circumcision, and other things of this kind, which plainly possessed more a typological representation than a definitive form of truth.

In the second verse he introduces **testimonies**. A testimony is an evident and predetermined condition; when reminded by its ordinance, we cannot forget past events. Thus Jacob says in Genesis: “This hill shall be a testimony for you” [ed., “for us”], and “This stone shall be a testimony” (Genesis 31:52). It is also written in the book of Joshua: “Take twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, so that these may be for a testimony to your children” (Joshua 4:5–6).

So the divine commandments are testimonies for us when they warn us that we ought not to sin, as the Apostle Paul says: “I testify before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus and the elect angels, that you keep these things” (1 Timothy 5:21).

In the present verse he places **commandments**, which are not shadows of things to come, as the law is, but have the evident effect of present action. The Lord declares this plainly in the Gospel, saying: “The first commandment is, ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength’” (Matthew 22:37), and so forth. This was spoken to one person in such a way that it must be kept by everyone and throughout all times.

Therefore, whether the law, the testimonies, or the commandments of the Lord are kept, it is certain that one reaches the sure rewards of blessedness. These words, together with their definitions given above, must be committed to the mind, because we frequently find them placed in the verses that follow.

### Verse 5

**Would that my ways might be directed toward keeping your justifications!**

Having clearly expressed above the life of the blessed man, the faithful people now also ask, through intercessory prayers, that good things may come to them. **Would that** is always the word of one who desires, so that what we cannot attain by our own powers we may deserve through the generosity of divine mercy.

When he says, **may my ways be directed**, he shows that, insofar as human weakness is concerned, they are crooked. **My ways** signify the actions we perform in this life. He adds, **toward keeping your justifications**. Here he has disclosed what he desired above: no one can reach the Lord’s justifications unless his ways are shown to be directed by the Lord.

But let us examine what the justifications signify. Among the ancient people there were many and various justifications of the Lord: that a Hebrew servant should serve for only six years; that a son should be instructed with the affection and discipline of a father; that a father should be reverently honored in all things; that God should be worshiped with the highest fear and love; that the priest should be held in honor; that one’s neighbor should be loved as one’s own advantage; and similar things that Holy Scripture commanded to be done. These things cannot be kept unless they are shown to have been bestowed through the Lord’s mercy.

### Verse 6

**Then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments.**

The reason is given how the Lord’s justifications can be kept continually: namely, if all the commandments are regarded. But when he says **all**, he warns that one must sin in nothing, since it is written: “If anyone fails to observe the least commandment of the law, he is guilty of the whole law.”

To look upon the commandments means always to keep those that have been commanded before one’s eyes, so that if anything crooked is committed, it may immediately be corrected by salutary amendment. Otherwise, whoever does not look upon the commandments will remain entirely unaware in what way he has gone astray.

The Apostle James offers this same comparison, saying: “If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man who looks at the face of his natural birth in a mirror. For he looked at himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he was like. But the one who has looked closely into the perfect law and has remained in it—not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work—this person will be blessed in his deed” (James 1:23–25). Those, therefore, are praised from whose sight the commandments of the Lord do not withdraw.

### Verse 7

**I shall confess to you, Lord, with an upright heart, in learning the judgments of your justice.**

Here confession signifies the praise that it is fitting for the people of the blessed to utter. Uprightness of heart is the holy rule of the catholic faith, because one cannot confess him through the distorted cunning of heretics.

By saying **in learning**, he indicates that the discipline was handed down to him by the blessed Fathers, not—as some do—discovered through a zeal for perversity. The judgments of God’s justice are those by which he deigns to free his servants when they are suffering under diabolical persecution.

### Verse 8

**I shall keep your justifications; do not utterly forsake me.**

The beautiful structure of the proposed blessedness is complete. He asks the Lord to deign, through his gift, to preserve the devoted people in the justifications that have been granted. What the justifications signify has already been explained above, in the fourth verse.

And because he knew that diabolical temptations surround us on every side, as it is written, “Your adversary, like a lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8), he asks to be guarded everywhere and on every side, lest the enemy’s ferocity find a place to cause harm.

Let us now see what the second letter contains.

### Verse 9 — II. BETH

**By what means does a younger man correct his way? By keeping your words.**

In the first letter the faithful people indicated the aspects of blessedness in which they asked to be preserved. Now, in the second letter, the same people show the time of conversion, also explaining in what delights they rejoice in the Lord’s words.

Therefore, through the figure of a question, he asks: **By what means does a younger man correct his way?** The chosen age belongs to the New Testament, not the Old, since from the old man we have been renewed into a vigorous age. He is called **younger** in comparison with the ancients, because the comparative degree frequently possesses the force of the positive.

How, then, has this younger man corrected his way? He confirms it in the following answer, saying: **By keeping your words**—that is, when the Christian people received evangelical discipline. At that time humanity was corrected, when, after its former perversity had been condemned, it reached the gifts of the right faith. Whoever keeps the Lord’s words does not merely retain them in memory but restores them through the goodness of his actions.

### Verse 10

**With my whole heart I have sought you; do not cast me away from your commandments.**

This too is a gift of the Lord: he asserts that he sought him with his whole heart. For he would not seek him unless he had first been sought, as it is written in Ezekiel: “What was lost I shall seek, and what had gone astray I shall bring back” (Ezekiel 24:16).

In every good thing we are anticipated by the Lord’s grace; and, so that we may wish to ask, he himself deigns to pour himself into us. It follows: **do not cast me away from your commandments**, as though I were unworthy of your benefits; since you have made me seek you with my whole heart, may you also deign to hear me.

He casts away from his commandments those who ask deceitfully, as it is written in another psalm: “The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Psalm 5:7). Solomon also says: “For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding” (Wisdom 1:5).

He therefore asks not to be rejected as unworthy of understanding the divine law, so that we may recognize that this understanding is deserved only by those known to beseech him with their whole heart.

### Verse 11

**I have hidden your sayings in my heart, so that I may not sin against you.**

Although we read that the works of the Lord must be proclaimed, as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles, “We cannot refrain from speaking about what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20), here he says that the Lord’s sayings were hidden in his heart so that he might not sin.

Both statements are true. Just as it is fitting for the faithful to proclaim these things at the proper time, so it is fitting to hide them from unbelievers, as it is said in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7:6).

Another psalm says: “I placed a guard over my mouth while the sinner stood against me. I was silent and humbled, and I kept silence from good things” (Psalm 38:2). Thus we understand that proclaiming the Lord’s sayings to the obstinate is a kind of sin. Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition” (Titus 3:10), and so forth.

### Verse 12

**Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your justifications.**

Lest anyone apply holy instruction to his own powers, he begins: **Blessed are you, Lord**, that is, “you who grant freely,” because you cannot find in a human being anything that you might choose.

Here, however, “blessing” signifies the Lord’s praise. When we bless God, we praise his deeds; when he blesses, he deigns to sanctify us.

It follows: **teach me your justifications**. Although above he said, **I have hidden your sayings in my heart**, now he says, **teach me your justifications**, as though he had learned nothing previously. Yet for the holy congregation that hungers and thirsts for justice, it is not enough to have learned the Lord’s commandments in words; it asks to be able to display them in deeds, knowing that there it will find the fullness of grace.

Thus he says: **Teach me your justifications**—that is, “grant me to do what you have been accustomed to use in justifying your chosen ones.”

### Verse 13

**With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth.**

That chorus of saints says that it has proclaimed the judgments of the Lord’s mouth, which he spoke through his prophets and apostles, when it recounted them with its lips and preached them to the people.

**All the judgments** signifies everything that has been written or spoken. Yet he cannot literally proclaim them universally, since no human knowledge is capable of apprehending everything, as it is said in another psalm: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 36:6). The Apostle also testifies: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). And, when his passion was near, he said to the apostles: “I have not told you everything.”

Therefore, figuratively, the whole is frequently said in place of the part in the divine Scriptures.

### Verse 14

**I have rejoiced in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches.**

The way of the testimonies is Christ the Lord, because the things that speak about him lead to him: a sure way, an unfailing journey, a profitable labor, where whoever arrives is delighted and comforted by the enjoyment of immeasurable riches.

And we must attend to what follows: **as in all riches**. Here we should understand spiritual riches, of which the Apostle says: “For in everything you have been enriched in him, in all speech and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed among you” (1 Corinthians 1:5–6).

The holy chorus, however, could not have compared worldly riches with the Lord’s testimonies, since it is known to have cast worldly riches away as though they were refuse.

### Verse 15

**I shall exercise myself in your commandments, and I shall consider your ways.**

The order of ecclesiastical discipline has been preserved. First it was necessary that he be exercised in the divine commandments—that is, that through frequent action he should carry out the requisite works with continual labor—and thus reach the innermost chambers of understanding.

No one deserves to behold so great a secret unless he has been granted, through good conduct, to draw near to heavenly benefits. And observe that exercise in the divine Scriptures is most often used in a good sense.

### Verse 16

**I shall meditate on your justifications; I shall not forget your words.**

Forgetfulness does not come to us by nature but descends from the weakness of original sin. Meditation is set against it as a remedy, lest wicked forgetfulness destroy the summit of memory.

He says that he will meditate on the Lord’s justifications so that he cannot forget what he desires to retain. He knew by what defect the human mind was oppressed, and he found against it an aid by which violent forgetfulness could be excluded.

Consider how the appropriate words have been attached to different subjects. In the preceding verse, **I shall exercise myself in your commandments**, he spoke of the sphere in which action is required. The Lord’s commandments include: “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not bear false witness” (Exodus 20:14, 16), and so forth. These things had to be not merely heard but done; therefore he said, **I shall exercise myself**.

Here, however, he says, **I shall meditate on the justifications**. The justifications, as was explained above, include the provision that a Hebrew boy should serve no more than six years, signifying the blessed people who serve in this age so that in the resurrection they may be freed from every form of subjection. Since this was established in an enigma, he said, **I shall meditate**, so that frequent repetition might make the understanding of the future reality clearer.

### Verse 17 — III. GIMEL

**Reward your servant; I shall live, and I shall keep your words.**

He comes to the third letter, in which he confesses human need and commends the Lord’s grace in all things. He declares that the proud have been rebuked, those who persecute the Lord’s faithful with wicked impulses.

For **reward** does not mean “repay according to merits,” but “give again,” so that you who have granted the inclination to ask may also grant the fulfillment of the petition. Finally, the following phrase makes this meaning clear, when he says, **your servant**.

No one can be called Christ’s servant unless he attributes to divine grace, not to his own merits, whatever good he is known to have done. To keep the Lord’s commandments truly belongs to one who lives. Conversely, the one proved disobedient is rightly called dead, as we read concerning unbelievers in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9:60). To bury the dead was the task of the living; but because the unbelievers appeared to be dead, we rightly understand that they were called dead.

And observe the holy confession: he judged that he would live if he could keep the Lord’s words. Rightly so, because whoever keeps them is undoubtedly kept by them, and death will not rule over him—the death that rages in the destruction of the impious.

### Verse 18

**Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law.**

This verse sets forth both human weakness [Col. 0842D] and the benefit of heavenly majesty. To reveal means to remove a veil. An inner vision is covered by a kind of garment of ignorance; and unless his mercy removes this veil, we cannot contemplate the holy Scriptures with the light of the heart.

He therefore asks that the blindness of ignorance be removed from him, so that, enlightened by divine grace, he may be able to see the Lord’s wonders. What these wonders are, he himself indicates by saying, **of your law**.

We said above that the law was a shadow of things to come and contained the significance of the fullness that was destined to arrive. An undefiled lamb was sacrificed at the Passover festival, signifying Christ the Lord being put to death. The priest was covered with a splendid and shining garment, announcing signs of the future High Priest and heavenly [Col. 0843A] King.

There were also the Lord’s promises, that the Israelite people would be led into a land flowing with milk and honey. There is no doubt that this pertains to that future age in which the joys of supreme blessedness are abundantly sweet.

That holy people therefore asks to contemplate these things with a revealed heart, which it could not see while the veil lay over them.

### Verse 19

**I am a sojourner with you on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me.**

The righteous are sojourners on this earth, for they have no permanent dwelling in the world. They are placed bodily on earth, but dwell in heaven through commendable conduct, as the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

They are rightly called sojourners, because they have no attachment to a foreign homeland but inhabit the earth of their body for a time. That rich man was not a true sojourner who built barns and placed the length of his life in the accumulation of many things. Rather, these are truly sojourners who store their treasure in heaven, so that their heart may always long for the homeland to come.

The faithful people therefore asks to be made aware of the Lord’s commandments, because it is not found to be dwelling in Babylon’s portion [ed., “conducting itself in Babylon’s portion”]. Anyone can know the desire of the one whom he is also known to wish to serve.

We have said that the commandments are: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 6:5), and so forth. He asks that these not be hidden from him—that is, withheld and denied—since he knew that from them the salvation of his soul would come. He therefore asks that those things not be concealed from him which are shown to be hidden from sinners, although they appear to have been proclaimed generally.

### Verse 20

**My soul has desired to desire your justifications at all times.**

Desire is used both in an evil and in a good sense: in an evil sense, “You shall not desire your neighbor’s property” (Exodus 20:17); in a good sense, “The desire for wisdom leads to the kingdom” (Wisdom 6:21). So here too it is said: **My soul has desired to desire your justifications**.

This is a powerful force, exceedingly strong in either direction. What is bound by the roots of desire does not easily slip away. And to show the full force of the expression, he added, **at all times**, so that no interruption and no period might be able to resist this desire.

An unbeliever too can desire something good for a time; but the holy people attributes to perfect desires the fact that it desired this at all times. To desire is the same as to long: no one longs unless he desires, and again no one desires unless he longs. Therefore the doubled declaration indicates the fullest willingness.

### Verse 21

**You have rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn away from your commandments.**

Although human crimes are innumerable, here he declares that the proud have been rebuked, since they are always proved hateful to God. Pride is what caused the angel to fall and caused Adam to be cast down from the dignity of his nature. For just as humility is proved to be the peace of all virtues, so pride is recognized as the mother of vices.

It is written concerning them: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). To rebuke means, as it were, to break forth from silence and rush into biting words. God frequently does this through the divine Scriptures when he displays to them the terror of his indignation.

A general and absolute judgment follows: those are cursed who attempt to turn away from his commandments. For human frailty’s failure to fulfill the Lord’s precepts is a lesser evil; but it is wicked to turn away through pride from the means by which one might free one’s soul from the bonds of sin.

Adam too, who turned away from the Lord’s commandment, is known to have been cursed; and even today those who are polluted by a similar crime are cursed. What the commandments are has already been stated above.

### Verse 22

**Take away from me reproach and contempt, for I have sought your testimonies.**

Behold, the words of that chorus of saints and martyrs have sounded: subjected to various punishments [ed., “overcome by various punishments”], they seemed to be a reproach and a contempt to the proud and wicked. Now they ask that, through the manifestation of the Lord’s mercy, their derision and degradation be removed.

The same is read in another psalm, where it says: “For we have been greatly filled with contempt,” and “Our soul has been greatly filled with reproach from the prosperous [ed., ‘of the prosperous’], and with contempt from the proud” (Psalm 123:4).

They sought the divine testimonies in order to suffer such things, since it is written: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10).

But we must examine more carefully why the martyrs ask that reproaches be removed from them, when they knew that through the Lord’s gift they were crowned by those very reproaches. This prayer is poured out for their persecutors: when the persecutors have been converted to the Lord, the martyrs’ reproach is removed, since the persecutors too have begun to practice the religion that they had thought ought to be persecuted in others. By the Lord’s provision, we know that this has frequently happened.

### Verse 23

**Indeed, princes sat and spoke against me, but your servant was exercised in your justifications.**

The chorus of martyrs explains that it was heard by princes who sat in judicial fashion and deliberated over the destruction of the innocent. And, so that they might terrify them more gravely, those very men were both accusers and judges.

He rightly calls himself the Lord’s servant, since amid the dangers of life he reflected on the Lord’s justification and on what the person who endured the gravest temporal sufferings in this life would receive in the life to come.

He was being exercised for his advancement, not tortured as punishment. Such souls conquered the world; they softened the awareness of their pain through thoughts of their eternal reward.

### Verse 24

**For your testimonies are also my meditation, and your justifications are my consolation.**

A counsel has been found against the counsel of the wicked: meditation upon the Lord’s testimonies is sufficient against the fury of the impious. The thought of these testimonies alleviates every pain and leaves no room for fear when one is continually occupied with the Lord’s promises, as the Apostle says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

He declares that the Lord’s justifications are his consolation—the justifications that he promises to his martyrs. They are consoled amid the afflictions of present things by the hope of rewards to come.

### Verse 25 — IV. DALETH

**My soul clings to the pavement; revive me according to your word.**

The faithful assembly comes to the fourth letter. In it, it says that it is indeed constrained by bodily necessity but must be saved solely by the Lord’s mercy. It asks him to remove from it the ways of iniquity, since it has chosen the way of truth.

The human condition is explained through very beautiful allusions. A pavement is a solid surface constructed with great smoothness upon some ground; it is rightly compared with our body, since the body too is polished with a similar smoothness. He therefore says that he has clung to his flesh, which is undoubtedly a sinful thing. If the soul clings to the body, it favors sins; if it is separated from the body in its will, it favors virtues.

Therefore he rightly asked to be made alive through the word—that is, through Christ the Lord—because he knew that he was being extinguished through the consent of the flesh.

But we must investigate why that assembly of the blessed, which above had said, **your servant was exercised in your justifications**, here confesses that its soul has clung to the pavement. We are thus truly to understand that although the saints enjoy the Lord’s grace and shine with a great variety of virtues, so long as they are in this mortal flesh there remains something for which they must ask to be absolved.

The best of teachers says this in the Gospel: “After you have done everything, say: ‘We are useless servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17:10). Elsewhere Scripture says: “The righteous man is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs 18:17).

### Verse 26

**I declared my ways, and you heard me; teach me your justifications.**

Those who confessed that they had clung to the pavement rightly disclosed their sins in what follows; and therefore it says, **you heard me**. What a wondrous compensation, what an astonishing exchange: to tell one’s own evils to the Lord and to receive from that same Lord the rewards of salvation!

Who would not be stirred by such blessings to confess to the one who grants the reward, to whom you cannot deny what you have done?

We must also examine that he said, **Teach me your justifications**, not merely so that he might hear them, but so that he might do them. For the person who is shown to be learned in divine things is the one who is shown to have done what was entrusted to him.

Alternatively, he asks to perceive those justifications that appeared to have been prescribed in a figurative manner.

### Verse 27

“Teach me the way of your statutes, [Col. 0845D] and I shall exercise myself in your wonders.”

The holy company rightly sought to understand the way of the statutes, since it had disclosed its own ways—that is, its sins. For unless we condemn those ways, we cannot reach this one. “Teach me” pertains to understanding, so that he might perceive what has often already been said: by what mystery, after six years, the Hebrew slave was to be released; in the seventh year the produce of the earth was to be given to cattle and the needy; after the fiftieth year whatever it was was commanded to be restored to its former owner; and similar matters, which are shown to accord with the Lord’s statutes. For he rightly desired to recognize these things, since they are proved to contain mysteries of our future hope.

It follows: “and I shall exercise myself in your wonders.” Certainly the person who draws the Lord’s words toward spiritual significance exercises himself in exceptional understanding and prudence. He calls “wonders” the very things he previously called statutes. For understood in this way, they produce a miracle, since they are set forth in the present in such a manner that they seem to signify things far in the future.

### Verse 28

“My soul has slumbered from weariness; strengthen me according to your words.”

After that holy petition, we understand that he was delayed, when he says that his soul slumbered from weariness—as happens to those who are held back by prolonged waiting—in order that we might understand that divine help comes to us through the virtue of patience. The soul therefore slumbers when it grows slack in its purpose and, exhausted, withdraws into idleness, while it is shown to be unable to reach what it had been pursuing.

And observe that he says “has slumbered,” not “has slept.” To sleep belongs to the forgetful and sluggish; to slumber belongs to the weary and the one who is waiting. Another psalm also uses this word: “If I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids” (Ps. CXXXI, 4). And elsewhere: “Behold, he shall neither slumber nor sleep who keeps Israel” (Ps. CXX, 4).

But in order to remove this failing also from the weary soul, it follows: “strengthen me according to your words,” so that, if the waiting still had to be prolonged, the soul might remain fixed and unchanging in the Lord’s words. We learn that every delay, every weariness, and every labor can be wholly consoled by this remedy, if we meditate on the Lord’s law through frequent repetition.

Cassian, that excellent instructor of the servants of God, calls this slumber of the soul *acedia* (Institutes, Book X, chapter 4), and strongly urges the monks [Col. 0846C] to flee it.

### Verse 29

“Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to your law.”

Raised up to that contemplation of truth, he asks for what was necessary in this present age: that the way of iniquity—that is, the devil—might be removed from his assaults, and that he might find the mercy he desired in the Lord’s law.

For no one will be justified through the law, as the Apostle says: “Knowing that no one will be justified by works of the law, but through faith in Jesus Christ” (Rom. III, 20). And again: “For through the law comes knowledge of sin” (ibid.). Therefore he rightly asks for mercy there, where he did not believe that he could be released through the bonds of the law.

### Verse 30

“I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments.”

The Lord Christ is the way of truth, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John [Col. 0846D] XIV, 6). The most holy choir said that it had chosen the worship of the Lord and Savior amid the various superstitions of the world, to which worldly peoples foolishly devoted themselves.

For to choose means nothing other than to select one thing from many. But let us see why he says that he chose, when the Gospel says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). The blessed people therefore rightly said this, since they had already been chosen, so that they could choose; as it says in another place: “I have chosen to be despised in the house of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 11). Therefore he rightly said that he had not forgotten the Lord’s judgments, since he rejoiced in such a choice.

### Verse 31

“I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame.”

The one who had previously said that he had clung to the pavement [Col. 0847A] now recalls that he has clung to the Lord’s testimonies, to show that he had received advancement in life through a divine gift.

But since everything depends upon divine protection, he asks not to fall away from the gifts bestowed, lest he come to shame and confusion. Holy consciousness had not relaxed into careless security; rather, in humility, he feared losing what he had received. For he could be put to shame if he lost what he held.

### Verse 32

“I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.”

How variously this way is described, and with what differing treatment it is presented! For above he said: “I have declared my ways”; then: “Teach me the way of your statutes”; and again: “Remove from me the way of iniquity.” He repeats: “I have chosen the way of truth”; finally, [Col. 0847B] “I have run the way of your commandments,” so that we may be instructed in every respect whether the way of good or of evil life is intended.

Maintaining the order of truth, he says that he has run the way of the commandments because he asserts that his heart was enlarged by the Lord. He could not have walked or run unless his heart had been extended in the breadth of knowledge. For although the way of his commandments is read to be narrow, no one runs in it without an enlarged heart.

When the soul has received the light of truth, it opens itself to manifold forms of understanding and becomes broader through the virtues it has learned, whereas it had previously been narrowed by sins. He rightly said “I have run,” to show that, by the Lord’s gift, he reached the true faith swiftly. The righteous man ran the way until, as the Apostle says, he reached “the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. [Col. 0847C] III, 14).

### Verse 33 — V. HE

“Establish for me, Lord, the law, the way of your statutes, and I shall seek it always.”

The blessed people have advanced to the fifth letter, asking in many ways that they may be kept in the Lord’s law by his gift. It must plainly be investigated what law this people asks to be established for it, since above it said, “and have mercy on me according to your law.”

That earlier statement concerned the Old Testament. Now, however, it asks that a new law be established for it, with the coming of the Lord Christ, so that, once that advent of holy incarnation had been completed [*expleto*; ms. G. and ed.: *expletus*, “completed”], it might be strengthened by the perfect firmness of Christian faith. As it is said: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 3).

Finally, he says that he continually seeks it. For that which is sought with burning desire is always sought—the thing whose coming is requested with great prayers.

### Verse 34

“Give me understanding, and I shall search your law; and I shall keep it with my whole heart.”

We must consider what is meant by his asking again for what he previously remembered having received, namely: “I have run the way of your commandments.” The reason is that the Lord’s gifts must continually be requested. For the one who preserves what has been given is always providing it; and with an approved desire we continually ask for what we request to remain perpetually in us.

He searches this law to whom understanding is granted by the Lord. And to show the constancy of holy perfection, he says that, by the gift of the Divinity, he keeps it with his whole heart, declaring in every subtle detail that all good is bestowed by the Lord, preserved by him, and continually increased by his grace.

Observe how beautifully everything proceeds in order. First he asks that the law be established for him—that is, the law of the New Testament, since he already possessed the Old. Then he asks to deserve to understand the purpose of that law, so that he might keep it with an undivided heart.

### Verse 35

“Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it.”

Although in the fourth letter he says that he ran the way of the commandments, here he again asks to be led along that same way. We must understand these commandments as those of the New Testament, into which he earnestly begged to be led, since he had run the way of the Old Testament.

Thus the desired perfection of faith is fulfilled, and holy Scripture appears to have said nothing contrary to itself. For when he says, “I have desired it,” he is proved to seek the spiritual grace of the New Testament, by which he knew that he would reach the kingdom of heaven.

### Verse 36

“Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to greed.”

These words must be treated carefully. He asks that his heart be inclined toward the Lord’s testimonies, to which one comes not through rapacious greed but through praiseworthy humility, with the Lord’s help.

When we are inclined, we see more clearly what is shown to be before our eyes. Those who stand erect and lie back in vanity cannot at all behold what is placed before their eyes. He added, “and not to greed.” Knowing that greed is capable of producing every vice, the holy company asks that it be removed from it, so that it might beneficially incline toward the most sacred Scriptures with its whole heart.

Greed is an ardent desire for temporal things. From it the first man sinned and left his descendants incentives to vice. Hence the devil also accused Job, saying (Job I, 10) that he loved the Lord because of the wealth the Lord had given him, not because of the contemplation by which he was good. The subsequent outcome refuted this, when the holy man continually gave thanks to the Lord amid every adversity.

The blessed people therefore ask that he remove this greed from their hearts and invite them to the Lord’s testimonies by the affection of integrity alone.

### Verse 37

“Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity; give me life in your way.”

Many wise men of this age restrained themselves by the law of continence in order to please human judgment more than the Lord’s. But they wasted their efforts through vain zeal, for it is written: “Do not practice your righteousness before human beings” (Matt. VI, 1).

Therefore the blessed people now implore the Lord to deign to turn the eyes of their hearts away from such a purpose, lest through a perverse habit they become entangled in worldly pleasures. For there is no doubt that we sin through our eyes as well, when we are led astray by desire for the things we have seen.

He asks to be made a stranger to this vanity because he knew that the greatest sin comes from it. Hence those who are occupied with various spectacles are censured; hence those who are seized by foul love of women; hence those who wickedly covet possession of another’s property.

But this petition is also joined to perfection: that he may deign to give him life in his way—that is, in the Lord Christ—in whom he is truly given life, because death is overcome by his power.

### Verse 38

“Establish your word for your servant in your fear.”

“Establish,” he says: make it stand—that is, implant, strengthen, and confirm it, so that the holy word may not slip away through fleeting forgetfulness, but may always remain firmly fixed in our understanding.

He rightly added “fear,” so that we might always pray not to lose the gifts we have received, and so that it might be a more serious matter to have learned a sweetness that then perishes. He added “your,” which is far removed from human fear.

This fear is such that it loves; it seeks in such a way that it never ceases to love the one it fears. And because many receive the Lord’s words negligently and shrink from hearing them as though they were useless stories, he rightly added, “in your fear,” where guilt is neither sought nor one brought to the dangers of indolence.

### Verse 39

“Cut off my reproach, which I have suspected, because your judgments are pleasing.”
