This sentence exposes a grave human vice. Many fall into reproach by suspecting things otherwise than truth has them; he desires that this fault be cut away from him.

We often give good testimony about many evils, and again speak evil of good things without knowing the truth. Necessarily, the person who asserts something in ignorance incurs shame. Suspicion is very often proved uncertain, and such suspicion does not suit a Christian man. This suspicion therefore leads to reproach, which arises from sin.

He rightly asked that it be cut away from him, since through it he could be found guilty. First he confessed his weakness; now he is known to praise the Lord’s judgments, whose word is true and whose sentence is firm.

Therefore the lover of truth rightly said that the Lord’s decree was pleasing to him, through whom he knew that he would find both rest and a crown, as the Apostle says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (II Tim. IV, 7).

### Verse 40

“Behold, I have desired your commandments; in your righteousness give me life.”

Above, the holy company asked that various benefits be bestowed upon it. In this verse it says that it has attained the fullness of graces, because it had desired the Lord’s commandments, which confer true prudence and salvation.

He asks to be given life in the Lord’s righteousness, although he still appeared to be alive, so that we may understand that there is no truly genuine life except the life which the Lord Christ has deigned to bestow.

The Father’s righteousness is the Word made flesh, to whom he gave all judgment, so that the whole world might stand to be judged at his tribunal, as the Apostle says: “Who was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (I Cor. I, 30).

### Verse 41 — VI. VAU

“And let your mercy come upon me, Lord; your salvation according to your word.”

The holy congregation has reached the sixth letter, in which it asks that the saving Lord be granted to it, so that he may confound its enemies through so great a reward and enable it to advance through constant meditation on the Lord’s law.

It therefore prays that the Lord and Savior may come upon it, he who is the mercy of sinners and the life of the faithful. And so that you might understand that this mercy specifically refers to him, what follows is added: “your salvation”—truly, through him salvation came to the nations, and he bestowed the medicine of his compassion upon the sick world.

“According to your word,” he said—that is, according to your promise, which you are known to have made through the prophets.

### Verse 42

“And I shall answer the one reproaching me with a word, because I have hoped in your words.”

This clear statement teaches us that when the cunning of opponents is brought against us, if they are capable of receiving a rational answer, we must not remain silent but answer courageously, lest the presumption of the malicious seem to prevail over us.

They reproach with a word who say that the Son is inferior, or who absolutely refuse to believe that he suffered in the flesh, as the Apostle says: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8).

Such people must be answered with the Lord’s authority, since they do not listen to saving doctrine with reverence but instead turn it into an occasion for insulting reproach.

It follows: “because I have hoped in your words.” He therefore says that one must answer because he has hoped in the Lord’s words, who says: “When you come before rulers and authorities, do not consider how or what you will speak; for what you should say will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 19–20).

### Verse 43

“And do not take the word of truth entirely from my mouth, because I have hoped in your judgments” [mss. A, B, F: “I have hoped greatly”].

He asks that no punishment and no terror extort from his mouth the confession of truth, but that, whatever tortures may be inflicted, he may persevere in one steadfast utterance, because he is known to have hoped not in human strength but in divine judgments.

But when he says “entirely,” he indicates that for a time the word of truth was taken from some people, as happened to the Apostle Peter, who denied the Lord three times before the cock crowed (Luke XXII, 37). Yet the word of truth was not taken entirely from his mouth, since he washed away his guilt both with tears and with the shedding of blood.

The reason why the truth of confession should not be removed from his mouth follows: “because I have hoped in your judgments.” The Lord’s judgments were being carried out when crowds of martyrs were subjected to various torments. But he professes that he placed even greater hope in these, because it is written: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6).

The wicked despair when they are troubled; holy men, when afflicted, receive greater hope of the Lord’s love. Up to this point, the letters of this verse have contained a prayer; those that follow to the end are presented in narrative order.

### Verse 44

“And I shall keep your law always, forever and ever.”

This and the other verses to the end of the letter contain not a petition but a narrative. Above he asked to receive; here he already gives thanks for the benefits received.

He affirms that he will always keep the Lord’s law, because it is impious to vary from it. He can keep it in this way if, as he said above, the Lord does not take the word of truth from his mouth.

Sometimes “always” refers to the end of this present age. But here, when he says “forever and ever,” he signifies that eternity which has no end.

Yet since we said above that the law was a shadow of future things—that is, sacrificing an unblemished lamb, practicing circumcision on the eighth day, and similar matters—how does he say that he will keep the law forever, when these things will not only be unnecessary after the future resurrection but already seem to have been abolished here?

There will be another law of the Lord there, which the most holy people promise to keep. They know that through this shadow of the law one ascends to the mystery of the eternal law. They also know that angels and powers customarily praise the Lord without end. They know that the solemnity of supreme blessedness consists in continually beholding the Lord. Finally, they know that there are laws for the faithful there, which they have professed they will keep without end.

### Verse 45

“And I walked in breadth, because I sought your commandments.”

This is the breadth of which he spoke in the fourth letter: “I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.” It is the manifold and saving knowledge that he deserved because he sought understanding of the commandments.

We rightly call this love, of which it is written: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5).

By contrast, the hearts of sinners are constricted in goodness. The Apostle touches on this when he says: “You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (II Cor. VI, 12). For a constricted—that is, polluted—mind does not receive God; he is received in the breadth of the mind, by whom heaven and earth are filled.

The dwelling place must be spacious, so that it may deserve to receive such majesty.

### Verse 46

“And I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame.”

He spoke of the Lord’s testimonies because he had asked and received the ability to answer those who reproached him with a word. Strengthened by this firmness before the kings of the world, who could terrify him through their exalted power, he says that he was not put to shame, but proclaimed in fearless speech the truth he had conceived in his mind.

The person whose words are defeated by argument is put to shame. The one strengthened by the testimony of truth itself cannot come to shame. He must not be denied under any compulsion, for he says: “Whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X, 33).

### Verse 47

“And I meditated on your commandments, which I loved exceedingly.”

Here he shows the ardor of frequent meditation. No one can meditate on the commandments unless he has traversed them through constant reading. And to make this frequency clearer, he added: “which I loved.” A person can never neglect what he loves.

But lest you perhaps consider this love lukewarm, he added “exceedingly,” beyond which no love can be found. The commandments of the Lord cannot be loved in any ordinary way; they must be loved exceedingly, as is sought here.

Therefore he rightly loved the Lord’s commandments exceedingly, through which he walked confidently in the breadth of his heart.

### Verse 48

“And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I loved greatly, and I exercised myself in your statutes.”

In the preceding verse he said: “I meditated on your commandments,” which pertains to the contemplative faculty. Now he says: “I shall wash my hands,” which pertains to the active life.

To lift up one’s hands means to be occupied with good works. The person held by evil actions does not lift up his hands but lowers them.

Observe that in both passages he includes “which I loved”: there, “exceedingly”; here, “greatly.” Both works must be performed with great zeal, so that, by the Lord’s mercy, which brings them to completion, they may bear fruit.

He added: “and I exercised myself in your statutes.” There he meditated, where he was transported by the intention of his mind; here he exercised himself, where he sought to advance through the frequent practice of works.

Note also that in the divine Scriptures “exercise” is generally used in a good sense; in secular writings and ordinary speech it is used in a good sense either never or rarely. We therefore say that this expression belongs properly to the divine Scriptures.

“In your statutes” pertains to both: that he might meditate on the Lord’s commandments with delight and complete the works of his hands with love. These are the two things, as we often say, that make Christians perfect.

The narrative associated with this letter is finished; it began, namely, with the fourth verse.

### Verse 49 — VII. ZAIN

“Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope.”

That choir of saints has reached the seventh letter, in which it commends the hope of the Lord’s promises wholly to our understanding, so that what glorious truth promises may remain firm in our minds. It asserts that because of this hope the faithful endure the adversities of this world patiently and most willingly.

Who would fear temporal death when eternal life is promised to him? Who would dwell on the loss of children when he knows that he will be joined to the choirs of angels? Who would fear the labors of the flesh when he knows that he will be placed in everlasting rest?

According to human custom, “remember” is said to God, who can in no way forget anything—not because it was fitting to attribute the injury of forgetfulness to that majesty, but because he prays that God may soon grant his servant the fulfillment of his most merciful promise.

You will frequently find such figures of speech in the divine Scriptures, as in Genesis: “I will remember my covenant” (Gen. IX, 15); or in Exodus: “And the Lord remembered what he had covenanted with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Exod. II, 24).

“Your word” perhaps signifies the promise that he makes in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 5). And elsewhere: “I will not leave you orphans” (John XIV, 18), and similar sayings.

“Your servant”: supply “fulfill the promise.” For if you wish to attach what is said to the preceding words without any addition, the words cannot fit together. This figure is called *ellipsis*, that is, deficiency, whenever a word is suspended so that it may be sought with greater liveliness.

It follows: “in which you gave me hope”—namely, in that promise of your word, which the faithful people rightly expected to be fulfilled by the truthful Lord [ed.: *exspectabat*, “awaited”].

### Verse 50

“This has comforted me in my humiliation, because your word has given me life.”

The hope which he says arose for him from the Lord’s promises is the very thing that he testifies comforted him in the necessities of this world, since amid every calamity the spirit of the faithful is restored whenever such a recompense is considered.

Who would fear temporal ambushes when he looks toward the Lord’s eternal promises? When he says “it has comforted me,” he shows that amid the afflictions of the world this was his consolation: to suffer in the present life and rejoice in the promise of future hope.

This is also signified by “in my humiliation,” because true holy humility is proved by bearing everything patiently and everything with thanksgiving. The Lord also granted this hope in the Gospel when he said to the apostles: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19).

It follows: “because your word has given me life.” He explains why his humiliation was comforted. The promise of so great a Judge strengthened the spirit of the one who endured; and so that he might not fear temporal death, the hope of consolation gave life to the afflicted.

### Verse 51

“The proud acted wickedly against me exceedingly, but I did not decline from your law.”

He indicates the time when the humble Church was severely harassed by proud persecutors. But he says that all these things were frustrated, since the wickedness of the malicious could not harm her.

Observe that the faithful people says that its humility was given life, while it recalls that the proud—that is, the malicious and tyrants—acted cruelly. They are not to be given life but rather put to death.

Through these two words he designates the human race. The humble are those who strive to obey the Lord’s commandments; the proud are those who swell up through diabolical suggestions.

It follows: “but I did not decline from your law,” namely, as those who persecuted the innocent supposed. When he says “I did not decline,” he signifies that he continually remained in the judgment of truth.

### Verse 52

“I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord, and I was comforted.”

The person who remembers punishments does not presume upon punishable deeds, because fear of penalties restrains the one inflamed by the incentives of wickedness.

When he says “from of old,” he signifies the time when the world began to be governed. This could be said by that company which is known to have existed through long ages and successive generations. If he had wished to indicate eternal time, he would have said “forever and ever,” as he frequently indicates elsewhere.

Through this thought he says that he was comforted, because divine strength does not abandon its servants, as he also says elsewhere: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken” [main text: *Juvenior*, “younger”; mss. A, B: *Junior*, “younger”].

### Verse 53

“Despondency held me because of sinners who abandon your law” [ms. G., F.: “on account of sinners”].

Here the piety of holy conduct is set forth: he says that he fainted from grief because he saw sinners abandoning the Lord’s law.

A holy man must be saddened by another’s guilt, since a pious spirit desires that everyone be saved. He is distressed when he knows that punishment threatens one whom he does not wish to transgress [ms. G: *excidere*, “to perish/fall away”].

For he knows that an evil inflicted without cause weighs more heavily upon its author. Hence the holy company was troubled not so much by its own punishments as by the excesses of tyrants.

### Verse 54

“Your statutes were songs for me in the place of my sojourning.”

When he says “songs,” he signifies that psalmody is to be performed with great delight, as the Apostle says: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to God” (Eph. V, 19).

Song always lightens labors and does not allow weariness to steal over the spirit, since it is soothed by the great sweetness of contemplation.

For what he added—“in the place of my sojourning”—signifies this world, as we have often said, where everyone devoted to Christ the Lord lives as a stranger. For having been expelled in Adam from the seat of paradise, we sojourn on this earth because we do not possess the blessedness of that homeland.

Thus we appear to be strangers in this world, as the Apostle also says: “As long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V, 6).

### Verse 55

“I remembered your name in the night, Lord, and I kept your law.”

There is no doubt that “night” can signify this world, in which the darkness of sins reigns. Would that it merely closed the bodily eyes and did not more dangerously blind the lights of the heart.

The Lord dispels this night when, coming at the time of judgment, he illuminates the hidden things of darkness and reveals the purposes of the heart (I Cor. IV, 5), which are now nourished by unlawful excesses.

But in this night he says that he remembered the Lord’s name, since he attributed all his benefits not to his own merits but to divine gifts, as it is also read in another psalm: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. CXXIII, 8). The Apostle likewise says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (II Cor. X, 17).

In this way the faithful person is not enveloped by the darkness of this night, because he is illuminated by the light of his heart. A fitting profession follows: he kept the Lord’s law because he remembered his name in the night. For he could not have kept the Lord’s law if he had attributed anything to his own merits.

### Verse 56

“This has happened to me because I sought your statutes.”

“This has happened to me”—supply “as consolation.” This should be understood more of the night than of the law, so that what is blindness to sinners may appear to be illumination itself for holy men.

In this way believers do not suffer darkness, even though they live amid the blindness of this world. The reason why night became consolation for him follows: “because I sought your statutes.”

If he had said “my statutes,” he would still have endured the densest blindness. But because he said “your statutes,” he could not be blinded by the darkness of the world.

### Verse 57 — VIII. HETH

“The Lord is my portion; I said that I would keep your law.”

The blessed company has reached the eighth letter, in which it desires to see the face of the Lord because it is known to have obeyed his commandments.

“Portion” is derived from “part.” We belong to the part whose wishes we obey. You frequently find this word used, as in the saying: “The sons of Levi shall have no portion or inheritance among their brothers, because the Lord God is their portion” (Deut. X, 9).

Therefore God is rightly called the portion of the pious, since they will live in the blessedness of his kingdom.

It follows: “I said that I would keep your law.” “I said” means: I established, determined, and promised to keep the Lord’s commandments. Thus he came to be in the Lord’s portion—that is, in blessed Jerusalem—not in the portion of confused Babylon.

### Verse 58

“I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your word.”

The Lord’s face can properly be understood in two ways. Desiring with unwavering thought the Christ whom he believed would come, he sought to behold his incarnation, which could appear as salvation for the world, as it is also said in another psalm: “God of hosts, restore us, and show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX, 8).

“With my whole heart” means without any hesitation, so that he would not seem suspended in uncertainty about the future but, as though he were present, would ask with complete confidence.

He also asks that the mercy of his coming be fulfilled, since through the prophets it is known to have been promised by countless announcements. Or he seems rather to pray that at that future resurrection he may be able to behold his face, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). And the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

But because he knew himself to be a sinner, he asks that mercy be shown to him, so that, freed by grace, he may see what he could not behold by his own merits.

“According to your word”—namely, the word by which he promises his saints the supremely blessed and incomparable vision of his Divinity in every respect.

### Verse 59

“Because I considered my ways, and I turned my feet toward your testimonies.”

He explains the order of human conversion [mss. A, B, F: “conduct”]. First we must accuse ourselves strictly, and then turn toward the Lord’s commandments.

He had accordingly considered that glorious examination of his ways—that is, human actions. But because they displeased him in every respect, he turned his feet to walk in the Lord’s testimonies, in which, if anyone walks, he can have firm footsteps.

He saw that sins existed in human actions, but that righteousness flourished in divine commandments; and wisely he abandoned what he perceived to be exposed to danger.

By saying “I turned my feet,” he shows that they had previously been perverse.

### Verse 60

“I am ready, and I was not disturbed, to keep your commandments.”

When he says “ready,” he shows that he had resolved to endure every danger for the sake of the Lord’s commandments.

The person testifies that he is ready to keep the Lord’s precepts who neither fears persecutors nor allows the allurements of this world to enter his senses, as the Apostle Paul also says: “For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of Jesus” (Acts XXI, 13).

Hence it is similarly said in another psalm: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. LVI, 8).

It follows: “and I was not disturbed.” Sudden events perhaps cause disturbance. A settled decision does not make the spirit afraid. Therefore the Lord, warning in the Gospel, says: “Let not your heart be troubled” (John XIV, 1), since the person whose thoughts are trembling and confused cannot be called ready.

He also indicates what he said he was ready for: namely, to keep the Lord’s commandments. They are kept properly and completely when no adversity is feared.

### Verse 61

“The ropes of sinners have entangled me, but I have not forgotten your law.”

When he says “the ropes of sinners,” he shows that there are as many snares as there are sins we commit. Ropes are tangled and twisted bonds by which delinquents continually bind themselves, as Isaiah says: “Woe to those who drag sins like a long rope” (Isa. V, 18). And elsewhere: “Each person is bound by the bonds of his own sins” (Prov. V, 22).

But this must be referred to the perversity of the body. For when he says, “I have not forgotten your law”—which belongs to the blessed—why does he say that he himself has been entangled in the bonds of sins?

It could happen that the flesh was bound and entangled by the ropes of transgressions, while the holy spirit, resisting the incentives of vice, had not forgotten the Lord’s law, as the Apostle says: “I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. VII, 25).

### Verse 62

“At midnight I rose to give thanks to you, because of the judgments of your righteousness.”

It is not without purpose that he says, “At midnight I rose.” For he knows that at this time the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck down (Exod. II, 4–5); he also knows that at that hour the chains of Peter, Paul, and Silas, who had been placed in prison, were loosened (Acts XII, 6); and he knows that the bridegroom will come at midnight (Matt. XXV, 8). Therefore he rises at that same hour for praises, lest he remain outside when the door has been shut among the foolish virgins.

Nor is it without purpose that he says, “I rose,” since one is always rising when one hastens to the proclamations of the Lord. Here “to give thanks” means “to praise,” because what follows is, “because of the judgments of your righteousness.” For if he had wished the confession of repentance to be understood, he would have said, “because of your mercy,” not “because of the judgments of your righteousness.”

### Verse 63

“I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments.”

Here he stated more explicitly what he had placed above at the beginning of the letter: “You are my portion, O Lord.” For he was the Lord’s portion in such a way that he also proved to be a companion of his servants. And observe how he displays the virtue of ecclesiastical unity: he says that he is a companion of all the faithful—not of one Church alone, but of the Church spread throughout the whole world.

And rightly does he say that he has a share everywhere, since the universal assembly was speaking such words. Whatever could please God throughout the whole world was his portion. And observe how humbly he calls himself a companion of those who fear God, although we read in the Apostle: “We have become partakers of Christ” (Heb. III, 14). We also remember that certain people are signified as partakers of Christ in the forty-fourth Psalm, where it says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8). Whoever walks in newness of life will be a partaker of Christ.

Thus he spoke humbly, yet directed the mind of the attentive hearer toward the very meaning of what it is to be a partaker of Christ. And because he said, “of all who fear you”—lest one should suppose that he meant those who dread the Lord’s judgments with servile fear—he added, “and who keep your commandments,” namely, those who are shown to be most devoted through the purest fear and reverent love.

### Verse 64

“The earth is full of your mercy, O Lord; teach me your justifications.”

When he says, “The earth is full of your mercy, O Lord,” he certainly reveals the expansion of the Christian faith, which God filled so mercifully that the name of the most empty superstition is shown to have been everywhere abolished.

And note how earnestly he asks to learn the Lord’s justifications, although he has often professed that he kept them. He does this to show that the Lord’s commandments must be sought tirelessly, so that our progress may continually increase under such desire, just as he said in the first verse of the fifth letter: “Establish for me, O Lord, the law, the way of your justifications, and I shall always seek it.”

### Verse 65 — IX. TETH

“You have dealt well with your servant, O Lord, according to your word.”

The blessed people enter upon the singing of the ninth letter. In it they give thanks that they have been humbled, so that they might reach the Lord’s justifications with the greatest devotion, asserting that his testimonies are, for them, above all riches.

When he says, “You have dealt well with your servant, O Lord,” he professes the gifts bestowed upon him. For the good Lord grants goodness to his servants. But he explains below what this goodness is, saying: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications.”

He is not giving thanks for worldly happiness, but for saving affliction. For he remembers that the discipline which corrects is a pious one. He understood that goodness ought to be called that from which one makes progress, not that in which one rejoices with empty exultation.

Thus a physician acts well when he cuts wounds; thus a father acts well when he beats his son. Although they inflict punishments for a time, they nevertheless provide remedies through affliction. Therefore he knew that the Lord should be honored with devout prayers, since by his clemency our tribulations are changed into joy, although they may appear grievous for a time.

It follows: “according to your word,” namely, that word which says: “He who humbles himself will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. XXIII, 12).

### Verse 66

“Teach me goodness and discipline and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments.”

It must be asked why he still asks to be taught what he has already professed above to have received. The reason is that there is no satiety in good things. Like a blazing fire, the more abundantly it runs through dry wood, the more fiercely it burns.

The Apostles, too, burning with the heat of faith, said: “Increase our faith” (Luke XVII, 5). God therefore teaches goodness by inspiring the desire for charity. He teaches discipline when he grants patience in tribulations. He teaches knowledge when he himself is recognized as the giver of saving things.

But God teaches in one way, and a human teacher in another. The human teacher offers words, but cannot provide understanding of the matters he commands; God, however, first illumines the heart, so that his words may descend into the understanding of his elect.

It follows: “because I have believed your commandments.” Since commandments are proclaimed so that they may be carried out, it must be asked why he said, “I have believed your commandments.” This is because of the Lord’s promise, which says: “Everyone who hears my words and does them is like a wise man building his house upon rock” (Matt. VII, 24), and so forth. He therefore rightly added, “I have believed,” because he promised the greatest rewards to those who obey him.

### Verse 67

“Before I was humbled, I sinned; therefore I kept your word.”

Let us observe how human life is described in this verse. First he says that he sinned, since he was held liable to original fault. Afterward he professes that he was humbled, so that he might be free from the guilt he had contracted at its root. Finally, he kept the Lord’s word, because he deserved to be humbled, as the Apostle James says: “But he gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV, 6).

And in order frequently to restrain the license of those who transgress, he says that after his humiliation he kept the Lord’s word—that is, the holy Scriptures—with the whole exertion of his mind, by the Lord’s gift.

### Verse 68

“You are good, O Lord, and in your goodness teach me your justifications.”

He asks the good teacher to deign, in his goodness, to teach the disciple. This figure is called *paronomasia*, in Latin *denominatio*—“designation”—which turns the affection of the hearers toward itself through the similarity of the word.

### Verse 69

“The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but I shall search out your commandments with all my heart.”

He appropriately asks goodness for help, since he was about to undergo the uncertainty of combat, so that he might make manifest in his own struggle the Lord’s justifications, which he had learned through reading. For commandments are learned perfectly when they are practiced.

He says that the iniquity of those pursuing him has been multiplied against him. Therefore he asks that his devoted humility not be stained by the severe punishments of the proud. But observe what follows against that most savage faction: “But I shall search out your commandments with all my heart.” To the extent that they strove to lead him astray, he appeared to cling all the more firmly to the Lord’s commandments.

In this way those who attempted to conquer the saints through temporal punishments are gloriously overcome. The more they tried to separate them from the Lord’s law, the more they made them investigators of his commandments.

### Verse 70

“Their heart has been curdled like milk; but I have meditated on your law.”

“Curdled” is used both in a good and in a bad sense. It is used in a good sense, as was already said in the sixty-seventh Psalm: “A curdled mountain, a rich mountain” (Ps. LXVII, 17). Here, however, we must understand it in a bad sense. For he wishes the iniquity of the proud, which he testified above had been multiplied against him, to be understood as hardened—constricted by wicked deliberation into a thicker substance, in the manner of milk.

Milk is so called from its liquidity, because it flows from the inner substance by a natural liquid. The letter *a* changes into *i*, as in *amicus*, *inimicus*, and similar forms.

But to the extent that they hardened in evil, he could not separate himself from the Lord’s law, so that their cruel obstinacy might be overcome by pious perseverance.

### Verse 71

“It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications.”

He called it good for himself that he was subjected to savage punishments, thinking not of present things but desiring future ones. For he had begun to taste that sweetness which is known to surpass all delights.

This humility touches the glorious heights of Jerusalem. For just as pride plunges one into Tartarus, so humility raises one to heaven.

What kind of struggle this humiliation entails is explained in what follows: “so that I might learn your justifications”—that is, so that I might do what you have taught. For one learns perfectly only when the Lord’s commands are demonstrated through faithful action.

### Verse 72

“The law of your mouth is good for me above thousands of gold and silver.”

How often in this letter that company of saints remembers goodness—the goodness it requested so frequently because the sweetness of goodness was increasing in it more and more.

Let us consider the force of the expression “of your mouth.” He does not testify that the words of prophets or apostles, but the evangelical commandments, are most precious to him—those which Christ the Lord spoke with his own mouth.

It follows: “above thousands of gold and silver.” Gold and silver appear to be especially prized by human desires. But because that goodness could find no comparable object, he first said “above thousands,” which signifies something infinite and incomprehensible, so that the comparison with gold and silver might be cheapened by such an addition. Whatever you name, “above” always surpasses it.

Thus a comparison without likeness has been made, a price without measure, a love without end. Such love deserved to be indicated [mss. A, B, F: investigated] as something to which no other thing could be equal.

### Verse 73 — X. JOTH

“Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments.”

The glorious company advances to the tenth letter. In it, it asks that understanding of the commandments be granted to it, so that it may enjoy the gift of a most true life. It asks that, by the Lord’s mercy, it may become without blemish, lest it be confounded in that judgment.

If, therefore, we wished to gather discussions about this verse, we would produce the bulk of individual books rather than relate anything within the brevity we have promised. But, with the Lord’s help, it is enough for us to disclose the meaning in concise reflections.

For we read: “The heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. CI, 26). We also read: “And his hands fashioned the dry land” (Ps. XCIV, 5). The same is said here: “Your hands made me, and fashioned me.”

But all these things are said figuratively. To have hands is a bodily attribute. If, however, you wish to consider the proper manner of the Lord’s operation, hear: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5). Therefore the power of his operation is called “hands” in human fashion, since by our hands we customarily work.

Some wish “made” to refer to the soul, and “fashioned” to the body, which is known to have been formed from the clay of the earth. His creature rightly cries out to the Author: “Give me understanding,” from whom I am known to have been fashioned.

But what kind of understanding was he seeking—an understanding which, by the reasoning of human nature, he could not find? It was that pure, contemplative, and devoted understanding which Adam’s uncorrupted simplicity possessed before sin—not the kind by which human beings appear wise to themselves and in some respect superior to animals.

He therefore asks for understanding so that he may know the Lord’s commandments, in order that what Adam lost through disobedience might be recovered by the holy company through devoted service.

### Verse 74

“Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped greatly in your word.”

A most beautiful occasion for mercy has been offered to the loving Lord. For if he grants something to anyone from the holy congregation, he will fill the hearts of all with great gladness.

He knew that the Lord’s clemency wished to do what would strengthen the hearts of the faithful, and he asks that such things be done in him as may increase everyone’s devotion. For the holy conscience makes progress by seeing another’s rewards, while examples set before it of praiseworthy things always advance it toward imitation.

He also added why he ought altogether to obtain what he asks: because he professes that he hopes in the word—that is, in Christ the Lord. Hope never deceives there, nor can the mind, which deserves to be fixed in such truth, be deluded by transitory desires.

### Verse 75

“I have known, O Lord, that your judgments are just, and in your truth you have humbled me.”

Since we read elsewhere, “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV, 7), and again, “The judgments of God are unsearchable” (Rom. XI, 33), it must be asked why he says here: “I have known, O Lord, that your judgments are just.”

But whenever something immense and incomprehensible is read, we must understand that eternal judgment which we cannot fully apprehend here. This judgment, however, belongs to the present world, as he testifies that he has known it: it corrects a person who sins through the swelling of his spirit by humbling him, and divine mercy receives the one who supplicates it.

For who would doubt that it is a judgment of supreme justice that those who offend through pride should be cleansed by devoted humility? And observe that he does not say here, “I have believed,” but “I have known”—that is, “I have experienced”—so that he might show that he had come to know this equity of the Lord through his sufferings and benefits.

### Verse 76

“Let your mercy now come, that it may comfort me, according to your word to your servant.”

He rightly asked for mercy, since he had previously confessed in his humility that the Lord’s judgments were just. Amid manifold hardships and savage struggles of torment, he asks for mercy as the comforter of these things, so that he might be able to endure the adversities of the age, which he knew had been beneficially assigned to him for the purification of his faults.

For he did not ask that such things be taken away from him, but that he might be comforted in them. There is consolation when God grants patience amid miseries, tempers savage torments, and strengthens the sorrows of the afflicted spirit with the promise of blessedness.

It follows: “according to your word to your servant.” Supply from the common construction, “Let it be”—that is, according to the promise by which he pledged in the Gospel that he would in no way abandon those troubled in their sufferings.

### Verse 77

“Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation.”

It has been sufficiently expressed what we attain through the Lord’s mercy: eternal life. Since he said that this was to be granted to him, he asked that he might deserve to live truly. For only that is properly called life which no trouble disturbs and no fear of death saddens. Of this life it is said in the Gospel: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX, 17).

Nor should it trouble us that he did not add “eternal.” Such is the force of this name that when “life” is said alone, eternal life is understood instead.

He says, therefore, that he must merit this life because his meditation was shown to be occupied with good works. Here do not understand meditation as reading alone, but rather as the works of the law. We do not become blessed merely through that meditation which is pursued by repeating what has been read. That meditation makes blessed which obtains the kingdom of heaven through holy works, as the Apostle says: “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified” (Rom. II, 13).

### Verse 78

“Let the proud be confounded, because they have acted wickedly against me unjustly [ms. G and edition: ‘because the unjust have acted wickedly against me’]; but I shall exercise myself in your commandments.”

It is not fitting for the holy people to leap forth against their adversaries with a wish for a curse, since the Lord himself says: “Love your enemies and pray for those who slander you” (Matt. V, 44).

He also added: “But I shall exercise myself in your commandments,” so that we might recognize that he had done nothing against the rule. The words “let them be confounded” refer to correction, not to eternal punishment.

The conscience of the sinner is rightly confounded when past evils are condemned by his own will, and he begins to hate what he had previously seemed to love. This is what he prays may happen to the proud, so that they may no longer appear to rage in unlawful boldness [mss. A, B, F: “in unlawful practices”].

The reason why the proud ought to be confounded follows plausibly: “because they have acted wickedly against me unjustly.” For what could be called more unjust than their wishing to persecute those who appeared to be occupied with the most sacred commandments?

It follows: “But I shall exercise myself in your commandments.” Against the ambushes of the enemies and against pride flaunting itself in an overbearing iniquity, he sets a saving remedy: the practice of the commandments.

He did not fight against the treacherous and cruel by some physical struggle, nor did he involve himself in contentious disputes of words. Rather, as though lashed by a blowing wind of empty words, he pursued his purpose with a tranquil mind, so that his adversaries might fall all the more quickly because he had resisted them with no human strength. This kind of patience unquestionably adorns Christians.

### Verse 79

“Let those who fear you and who know your testimonies turn to me.”

The words have been marked according to the distinctions between persons. Above, it was said of the proud, “Let them be confounded”; here, however, it is said of beginners, “Let them turn to me”—that is, to you.

One is rightly understood to turn to the Lord when one begins to take one’s place in the ecclesiastical congregation—namely, those who have already begun to fear but have not yet turned with the full attention of their minds.

He added: “and those who know your testimonies,” meaning those whom divine reading has already imbued, but whom saving practice has not yet instructed. “Let them turn” could not be said of the perfect, who shone both through sacred reading and through pious action.

### Verse 80

“Let my heart be made without blemish in your justifications, so that I may not be confounded.”

He asks that his heart be made without blemish through the remission of sins, not through the quality of merit. For as it was said at the beginning of the Psalm: “He whose sin is forgiven is without doubt cleansed.” Nor can anyone put on the nuptial garment unless, by divine grace, he has deserved to receive the purity of forgiveness.

There alone is the one who is not confounded—the one whose sins are forgiven. And observe that after those extraordinary virtues the company of saints prays that its heart be made without blemish, so that no human being might presume to possess what certainly belonged to Christ the Lord alone: holiness.

For the one who had confessed that he was made and fashioned by the Lord’s hands; who had said that he was justly humbled through repeated sufferings; who had been exercised in the Lord’s commandments and had meditated on his law—this one does not dare to say that his heart is without blemish. Rather, he asks that it become what he had not yet received in that resurrection where they will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34), and so forth.

And observe how one word is applied to different causes. Above, he asked that the impious should be confounded so that they might be corrected; here he asks that he himself should not be confounded, so that he might escape the destruction of condemnation.

### Verse 81 — XI. CAPH

“My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have hoped in your word” [mss. A, B, F: “I have hoped greatly”].

The people who are pilgrims in this world sing the eleventh letter. In it they joyfully confess their immense desire for the Lord’s coming. They also recount how many persecutions of the proud they have endured. Finally, they ask that by the Lord’s gift they may persevere in his commandments.

“Failure” is used for the end of something, as in: “The weapons of the enemies have failed completely” (Ps. IX, 7). It is sometimes also used to express the extremity of desire, as in: “My soul has desired and failed for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 3).

Here too the holy congregation says that its soul has failed in its most ardent love for the Lord the Savior. It is a human custom that when we desire something exceedingly, we seem to grow weary and fail in it, suspended by delay and unable to reach what we long for.

If a most compassionate father were to endure the delayed arrival of his dearest son with an eager soul, or if a most chaste wife were to await her sweetest husband, would they not, exhausted by love, fail while longing to see those whom they earnestly demand?

Therefore, “My soul has failed” means, “It has grown weary and exhausted”—something that ordinarily arises from excessive desire. Let us therefore consider the greatness of this most holy desire: he wearied himself with such intensity of mind that he reached a most blessed state of exhaustion.

But lest this failure appear to be the collapse of faith, he says that he failed “for salvation,” which in the Hebrew language is called *Jesus*. And lest anyone perhaps doubt that it should be understood in this way, he added: “and I have hoped in your word”—that is, in the only-begotten Son, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. I, 24). Of him it is also read elsewhere: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

### Verse 82

“My eyes have failed for your word, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’”

A saving and strengthening failure is repeated here—a failure that does not arise from weakness of mind, but rather proceeds from the glorious strength of the spirit.

Above he said that his soul had failed through an excessive desire for the Lord the Savior; now he recalls that the eyes of his heart have failed through such longing. These are the eyes that can speak inwardly, as it is written: “I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord.”

Although the tongue ordinarily speaks, here the eyes are said to have said: “When will you comfort me?” It is clear, therefore, that these eyes are intellectual eyes—that is, the inward lights of the heart [mss. A, B: “inward lamps”], which effectively supplicate the Lord and cry out in a kind of silent speech.

For eyes to say something is not ordinary or customary speech. But we must acknowledge that this mode of composition belongs properly to divine Scripture. And observe the force of the preposition: he says “in your word,” not “away from your word.”

For to fail away from the Lord’s word is truly the deprivation of every good; but to fail within his word is always to increase. He says that he endured this most powerful failure until the awaited incarnation of the Lord appeared to the eyes of his heart.

From this we clearly recognize that although righteous men did not see the Lord’s coming with bodily eyes, they continually beheld it through the light of faith, just as the Lord himself says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII, 56).

### Verse 83

“For I have become like a wineskin in frost; I have not forgotten your justifications.”

Since above he had asked to be comforted, he now gives the reason why the Lord ought to help him. A wineskin deprived of its natural warmth contracts in the icy cold. In the same way, the body of the saints, emptied of the heat that incites vices, is drawn together through the benefit of conversion. And when it has been thus happily emaciated, what follows comes about: it is able in no way to forget the Lord’s justifications.

The wineskin signifies the mortal body; the frost displays the benefit of conversion, through which our wanton flesh is contracted by the affliction of repentance. The heat of faith increases to the degree that bodily flame has been withdrawn.

This wineskin, however, belongs to the blessed, who make the confessing soul advance through contrition concerning itself. Do not consider it improper that living human beings are compared with wineskins, since the Lord, speaking in the Gospel about the preaching of faith, says: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matt. IX, 17).

### Verse 84

“How many are the days of your servant?” [servi tui; edition: servo tuo—both ‘of your servant’]; “When will you execute judgment upon those who persecute me?”

The assembly of the saints knows that, until the end of the age, the members of the Lord are subject to diabolical temptations. It asks when this world will end, so that the vengeance prepared against the persecutors—that is, the devil together with his ministers [mss. A, B, F: “diabolical ministers”]—may be completed.

He does not ask because he wished to know the length of his own life, but because he sought the swift arrival of the future judgment, in which there will already be rest for the blessed and joy that will endure without end.

It may be asked why he desired to know the end of the age, since we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts I, 7).

First, because the disciples themselves asked Christ the Lord about this matter, and it was fitting that, in the figure of the Apostles, the holy company should speak what they were going to say. Further, it must be understood in this way: the blessed people desired the end of evils, which they could not see except after the conclusion of this world.

### Verse 85

“The wicked have told me stories, but not like your law, O Lord” [“O Lord” is absent from mss. A, B, F].

The wicked are clearly heretics or Jews, whose perverse loquacity appears to tell itself some kind of foolish tales when, abandoning the order of truth, they are shown to devote themselves to the falsest inventions.

These things are entirely opposed to the Lord’s law. The law teaches truth, while they strive to persuade people of deceptions. Understand, you madmen who depart from Catholic truth, that your doctrines are comparable to empty stories.

Whom do you think you are pleasing, when you realize that the Holy Spirit has branded you with such a name?

### Verse 86

“All your commandments are truth; the wicked have persecuted me. Help me.”

Against what he said of the heretics—“The wicked have told me stories”—he here professes that all the Lord’s commandments are truth. Truth speaks what is true, but the treacherous strive to obscure it with certain clouds.

It follows: “The wicked have persecuted me,” namely, by commanding perversities, persuading people of falsehoods, and by whatever means the iniquity of persecutors customarily rages.

He added, “Help me,” as though against a monstrous beast, a most savage enemy, a fierce lion, and the other things that fearful apprehension compels us to avoid.

### Verse 87

“They almost consumed me on the earth; but I did not abandon your commandments.”

When he says, “They almost consumed me,” he both reveals the excess of the persecution and declares that, nevertheless, by the Lord’s gift he did not fail.

The word “consumed” signifies both perfection and destruction. If you carefully attend to the force of the matter, you will recognize that they were more truly brought to perfection, as the Gospel says: “It is finished”—that is, “It is perfected”—and, saying this, he gave up his spirit (John XIX, 39).

But if you think of the slaughter of those who were dying, you will judge that they were mercilessly almost consumed. “On the earth” means in this age, where the martyrs suffered.

He added, “But I did not abandon your commandments,” so that his steadfastness might continue to the end, as it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

### Verse 88

“According to your mercy, give me life, and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.”

After the singular desire for the Lord the Savior, after the affliction of the body expressed through the likeness of the wineskin, and after the glorious punishments of suffering, he appears to ask to be given life, as though he were not yet living. He promises that he will keep the testimonies of the Lord’s mouth, as though he were not yet keeping them.

But when he said, “Give me life,” he meant: Establish me in that eternal life where life belongs to the saints, because they are struck by no opposition.

As for what he said, “I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth,” he did not mean that he was not keeping them in the present. Rather, with the Lord’s help, he promised that he would keep such testimonies to the end of his life.

Alternatively, as some think, this is the voice of the saints who desired martyrdom. A little earlier they said: “The wicked have persecuted me; help me.” It also follows: “They almost consumed me on the earth.” Therefore, they judge that the verse should be referred to the desire for martyrdom.

They were asking to be given life through a glorious death, so that by losing this life for the sake of faith they might earn eternal rest. They would then receive eternal honors precisely when the treacherous believed that they had been consumed.

Yet, considering human weakness, he says that this must be granted according to the Lord’s mercy, since he gives life to the dead and strengthens the weak.

### Verse 89 — XII. LAMED

“Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven.”

The heavenly people arrive at the twelfth letter. In it, describing the Lord’s power and deeds, they say that all temporal things can come to an end, but that his commandments can never find an end.

But because he had said above, “They almost consumed me on the earth,” he marvels at the Lord’s power, who does not permit the condition of the Church to be destroyed, however savage the persecution. He therefore bursts forth in a devout exclamation, saying that the Lord’s word remains in heaven.

This means: it remains in each of the saints, whom he makes live from death and rejoice from tribulation, those who serve his commandments with devout humility. For heaven is present in those who are known to conduct themselves with a heavenly manner of life—or in the angels, archangels, and heavenly powers, which holy majesty inhabits because of the sincerity of their will.

The Word always remains in them, since they too continually stand in the Lord’s service with the firmest resolve.

Here, however, some raise a question: How does the Word remain in heaven forever, when the Lord himself says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Luke XXI, 33)?

Although these things are changed, the word remains in heaven because, by the graciousness of his majesty, he inhabits all heavenly things.

### Verse 90

“Your truth is from age to age; you founded the earth, and it remains.”

“From age to age” signifies the times in which, by the Lord’s gift, the two peoples believed. One is the people of the Law and the Prophets; the other is the people of the Gospels and the Apostles. In them is the Truth—that is, the Lord Christ himself—who both granted them faith and enabled them to remain in the foundation of faith.

But he explains afterward why truth was not absent from those ages, saying: “You founded the earth, and it remains.”

This is better understood of holy people, who were so founded that they remain in faith in Christ the Lord. For if he had not founded them, neither the first age in the patriarchs nor the second in the Apostles could have believed or remained.

For if you refer this to the universal earth, which is read to have been suspended by its wondrous mass, how can we say that it remains when divine Scripture confirms that it will be changed, together with heaven?

### Verse 91

“By your ordinance the day continues, because all things serve you.”

Whenever “day” is placed in the singular number, that coming day is signified which is one and eternal and has no night. Of it it is written: “The Lord will be their everlasting light” (Isa. LX, 19).

And lest anyone think that such a great miracle should be debated, he added [edition: “he added”] that all things serve the Creator, who by his will disposes both temporal and eternal things.

A question may arise concerning unbelievers, who do not appear to serve the Lord when they are separated from his devotion. But they too serve him when they are judged. For the one who is shown to deserve punishment is not dismissed free.

Alternatively, we should understand “all things” to mean those of which he was speaking—those for whom the day will be perpetual, since they suffer the darkness of unbelief at no time.

### Verse 92

“Unless your law had been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation.”

If he had not possessed the benefits of meditation on the law—so that he would not yield to punishments and would preserve the constancy of faith by scorning dangers—he asserts that he might have perished amid the calamities he endured.

Thus we understand how much the meditation on the law provides for us: it was able to free him from such immense dangers. For the meditation of the law consists in what it has commanded one either to think or to do. Formed, as it were, by an inner counselor [mss. A, B, F: “comforter”], he can overcome raging torments without fear.

“In my humiliation” means “in the afflictions” which he endured with pious purpose. He rejoices that he was rescued from them when he deserved to attain holy martyrdom.

Humiliation is both undergone by necessity and embraced by choice. The guilty endure the former; the most holy practice the latter in purity.

### Verse 93

“I shall never forget your justifications, because through them you have given me life.”

After the gifts which he deserved to obtain through the Lord’s clemency, he makes an unqualified promise of devotion.

Other things may perhaps fall from the memory, but none of the faithful forgets the benefit through which life is granted. Therefore it was necessary always to remember those justifications from which he is known to have received the gift of life.

The justifications are—as was already said above—the understanding of future meanings through temporal events: the slaughter of the spotless lamb at Passover; the Red Sea providing a path to salvation; the people receiving the promised land after being brought into it by Jesus son of Nun.

All these things clearly provided signs of the perfection that was to come. Therefore we must in no way forget these justifications, which supplied us with the beginnings of faith. No one can perfectly recognize the grace of a gift unless he also remembers the beginnings of things and why they appeared to have begun.

### Verse 94

“I am yours; save me, for I have sought out your ordinances” (Psalm XXIII, 1).

Although it is written, “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness; the world and all who dwell in it” [Col. 0867A], this company, trusting in some special recompense of the Lord’s grace, says: “I am yours.” For one who is known to engage in some disgraceful conduct cannot truly say, “I am yours.” A servant of vices does not deserve to have the Lord of the saints. The Apostle Paul could use this expression without impropriety [ms. F., “wisely”], for he cried out: “For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians I, 21); and: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians II, 20); and similar statements.

We must also consider that, although he has professed himself to be the Lord’s, he still asks to be saved—obviously in that future judgment when the blessed are admitted to everlasting rest. But why this salvation is continually requested, he added below: “for I have sought out your ordinances” [Col. 0867B]. Others pursue honors, seek marriages, and desire the joys of the world; this man considered himself to possess immeasurable riches if he were proved to seek the Lord’s ordinances with unremitting zeal. We must also investigate why he repeats these ordinances so often: namely, so that no one might think the foreshadowings of the Old Testament could be disregarded.

### Verse 95

“Sinners waited for me in order to destroy me; I understood your testimonies.”

“They waited in order to destroy me” refers to the fact that evil persuaders acted by flattery so that they might wound his soul with the injury of depravity. For if punishment had been hastened, it would not be said, “they waited,” but “they hastened.” More grievous is this persecution, which both suspends the martyr’s crown and never ceases to persuade the soul toward death.

But he shows by what remedy he could have avoided it: understanding the Lord’s testimonies, he could not be led into abominable vices. Hence it is clear that only those are rescued who have been freed from such danger by the Lord’s illumination [mss. A, B, “martyrdom”]. By “I understood,” let us take it to mean “I practiced,” just as he says in another psalm: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm XL, 2). For what good could it do the poor man if he merely understood that he was needy and did not support him with any gift? Therefore, understanding the commandments is holy action.

### Verse 96

“I saw the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad.”

He had entered into the riches of the height of God; he had seen what could not be explained piecemeal; finally, in a brief statement, he summed up what had to be said. For he professes that he had seen the end of the whole consummation [Col. 0867D]. Consummation is the completing perfection of all virtues; Christ is the end of this consummation. He rightly says that he had seen him, because with enlightened mind he then believed that he was to come.

If, however, you wish to understand this literally, it may also be taken in this way: worldly affairs always seem to have an end imposed upon them, whereas the Lord’s commandments have no end, because they extend themselves with exceedingly great breadth of virtue. This was stated so that no one would eagerly desire the ambitions of this world, sensing that an end had been assigned to them, and so that he would seek the Lord’s commandments with great urgency, recognizing them to be exceedingly broad.

Nor is it without significance that he said, “your commandment is exceedingly broad” [Col. 0868A], thereby signifying the charity that we are commanded to have toward God and our neighbor. For what can be called broader than that which encompasses the whole Law and the sayings of all the prophets? Concerning this the Apostle also says: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans V, 5). 413

### Verse 97 — XIII. MEM

“How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long.”

The blessed people, who had advanced through abundant meditation on the prophets and the Gospel, are introduced in this letter as speaking. They assert that they have understood the divine commandments better than their teachers and elders; and therefore they testify that the sweetness of the divine Scriptures has come to their mouths, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

By saying, “How,” he promises that he will explain how he loved the Lord’s law with exceptional devotion. He therefore loved the law; he did not fear it, because holy men ought to carry out the Lord’s commandment through love, not through worldly fear. It is more acceptable to do something out of love than merely to fear it in unbelief.

He next explains how he loved it, saying: “It is my meditation all day long.” By “all day long” we must understand continuous time, just as it is read elsewhere: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise is always in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII, 2). A holy conscience always possessed day, because with its heart illumined it knew nothing of the darkness of unbelief.

O unfailing meditation, for which the day of this world is not enough! And so that we may believe that human weakness could have been sufficient for continual meditation [Col. 0868C], this will, as I think, become clear to us in the following way: if someone orders every kind of activity with regard for the Lord and with moderation; if he takes food temperately; if he obtains sleep appropriately—then he meditates on the Lord’s law in everything, because he commends himself by honorable and commendable action, just as the Apostle says: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians X, 31).

### Verse 98

“Above my enemies you have made me prudent through your commandment, because it is mine forever.”

The enemies are to be understood as obstinate Jews, heretics, or pagans, who either did not understand the Lord’s precepts at all or are not shown to practice them with a right intention. He says that he was made prudent above them because he both received the Lord’s commands devotedly and preserved their true integrity [Col. 0868D] [ms. G. and ed., “he served them with true integrity”].

But from what source he became prudent above his enemies, he added: “through your commandment,” because by faithfully obeying it he surpassed all who were in error without hesitation. Behold, truly blessed honor: to surpass the proud, to rise above the powers of this world, and to remain fixed in mind in holy humility.

He added, “because it is mine forever”—that is, your commandment. But let us ask what commandment it is that remains when this world passes away: namely, love of God and neighbor. For there we love the Lord above all things, and then we love our neighbor perfectly as ourselves. Rightly, therefore, he said that this commandment was to be kept by him forever, since the blessed continually enjoy it with a holy conscience.

### Verse 99

“Above all who teach me I have understood, because your testimonies are my meditation.”

It seems utterly contrary to the most holy humility of the blessed if we take this statement as referring to Moses, the prophets, or the apostles, who taught the Lord’s Church with completely sound faith. But let us attend to the preceding verse, and every malicious objection disappears. He did not say “above the fathers,” but “above my enemies”—that is, those who taught the Lord’s law with a perverse intention.

Here he censures, not rejects [ed., “approves”], the teachers, specifically indicating the Pharisees, who clung to the letter and neglected spiritual understanding. The Lord also frequently censures them in the Gospel; but their stony heart did not deserve to perceive the reason of truth [Col. 0869B]. Above all such teachers, therefore, the Gospel company rightly says that it understood better, because, having rejected their perversities, it received the sincere teaching of the Lord the Savior.

But why did it understand better? He identifies the reason: “because your testimonies are my meditation.” For the Lord’s testimonies were not a meditation to those who, through utterly false persuasion, understood something far different from what had been said.

### Verse 100

“Above the elders I have understood, because I sought out your commandments.”

This is not proud boasting, but truth. By “elders” we mean both those distinguished by maturity of wisdom and those who precede us in length of years, concerning whom it is said: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 7).

We also call elders those who are mature in age but exceedingly light in their pursuit of vices, such as those of whom it is written in the Gospel: “The priests took counsel with the elders in order to hand him over to death” (Matthew XXVI, 3–4). These are the elders he now speaks of—not gray in mind, but in body.

He therefore rightly says that he understood more than these, since the one whom they despised with sacrilegious mind he revered as his creator. Frequently, younger people understand the divine Scriptures better than elders: for example, Jacob, who presented himself for blessing and received the promised fruit of the first blessing instead of his brother; Samuel, who understood better than the priest Eli; or Daniel, who understood better than the false elders whom, filled with the Spirit of God, he condemned to death.

The new people certainly understood better than that Jewish elder who faithfully [mss. A, B, “happily”] received Christ the Lord, rather than the one who fatally believed that he should be rejected. And to confirm this very point by the testimony of truth, he continues by explaining why he understood more than the elders: namely, “because I sought out your commandments.” For if they had sought the Lord’s commandments, the younger could by no means have been wiser than they.

And observe how he preserves the order of truth. He says “your commandments,” not those of perverse men, of whom it is said: “For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans X, 3).

### Verse 101

“I kept my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your word” [mss. A, B, F., “your words”] [Col. 0870A].

From this verse it clearly appears that those previously called enemies did not know the Lord’s law, that the teachers were held captive by the blindness of ignorance, and that the elders did not possess the gravest firmness of faith, since he says that he kept his feet from all their evil way lest he be overthrown by their perversity. This is the more certain explanation, since the authority itself, like a flash of light, makes the matter clear.

But let us see what the words of this verse bring forth for us. “From every evil way” signifies the wicked and thoroughly evil persuasions of heretics, by which they flatter others with a destructive sweetness. He also added, “I kept my feet,” as though they desired to go there, where they could fall into a dark pit. For the guilt of original sin continually draws us toward vices; and unless we are fortified by the Lord’s grace, we are very easily deceived by perverse persuasion. With the Lord’s help, prohibition is salutary when we do not allow what is found to be full of dangers to take place.

“my feet,” however, signifies the assent of the mind, which by a kind of footprint leads us toward guilt and drives us toward evil ways, unless the mercy of the Divinity draws us away. He continues: “so that I might keep your word.” For the Lord’s word could not otherwise be kept unless that deadly persuasion had first been expelled, as the Apostle says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians X, 20–21).

### Verse 102

“I did not turn aside from your judgments, because you established your law for me.”

He explained what he had said above: “I kept my feet from every evil way,” namely, so that he would not in any way turn aside from the Lord’s judgments [Col. 0870C]. Thus the integrity of perfect blessedness is preserved when the wickedness of heretics is rejected as perverse.

He therefore says, “from your judgments”—that is, those which your holy will established and which gave us a rule for living. Not to turn aside from them means to remain on the right path; it means to reach the joys of heaven.

He follows with a credible reason: “because you established your law for me.” Since the Lord gave the law through Moses and commanded that it be observed inviolably, we appropriately understand the Gospel here when he says, “You established your law for me.” The law he gave through Moses presented us with the office of a pedagogue; this one, however, granted the effect of complete fullness. Rightly, therefore, the holy people rejoiced in that law which it had already received through faith. Finally, see what follows.

### Verse 103

“How sweet your utterances are to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” [Col. 0870D]

Although these comparisons seem to possess some special force, they cannot be made equal to spiritual realities unless “above” is always understood, as was already said in the ninth letter: “The law of your mouth is good for me above thousands of gold and silver,” so that you may understand that, although these things are preeminent among human beings, they are inferior to divine delight.

Thus, the blessed people, richly nourished by spiritual delights, exclaim: “How sweet your utterances are to my throat!” By saying “How,” he professes that they are a great sweetness to him, but one that the tongue could not express.

Since every taste is perceived on the palate, we must consider why he says here, “to my throat” [Col. 0871A]. The throat is the passage of our gullet, where sweetness is no longer perceived once it has been swallowed. But since he was about to speak explicitly of the Lord’s utterances, he wonderfully named that part so that the sweetness might quickly reach the inner chambers of our heart. For the Lord’s utterances do not taste sweet on the palate; rather, they become sweeter once they have been swallowed.

He continues: “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” Honey pertains to the Old Testament, and the honeycomb to the New Testament. Although both are sweet, the flavor of the honeycomb is sweeter, because the grace of newness is added in greater abundance.

Honey may also be understood as the open teaching of wisdom, while the honeycomb signifies what is found stored in certain deeper chambers. There is no doubt that both are found in the divine Scriptures.

He added, “to my mouth,” since in truth he proclaimed with his mouth the very wisdom that he had swallowed with his throat. Thus the prophet Ezekiel also says of the Lord: “And he said to me: Son of man, eat what you have found; devour this scroll, and go and speak to the house of Israel. And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey” (Ezekiel III, 1–3).

### Verse 104

“From your commandments I have understood; therefore I hated every way of iniquity.”

Having been taught the Lord’s law, he had received this instruction: “My son, do not walk in the way with the impious; turn your foot away from their paths, for their feet run toward evil, and they are swift to shed blood” (Proverbs I, 15–16).

He had also heard: “You have destroyed all who fornicate away from you” (Psalm LXXII, 27). And elsewhere: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Psalm XCVI, 10). And the other statements of this kind that are brought forth in divine reading for this purpose [Col. 0871C].

When he had heard such things among the Lord’s commandments, he understood the way of iniquity to be utterly detestable, since it could not please the just Lord. The things of the world ought to be hateful, so that the whole of our desire may be devoted to heavenly realities.

It is fitting for us to abominate evil things, because at times we are prevented from them by the necessity imposed by the wicked; for the mind of one who has consented to such things with some pleasure appears to be conscious of them. The will of the faithful, however, is separated from those things that it had condemned through hatred, so that the one who purifies his mind by such abhorrence may defile himself neither by desire nor by action.

### Verse 105 — XIV. NUN

“Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.”

After the thirteenth letter, the blessed company reaches the fourteenth, in which it rejoices that the light of the Lord’s word shines upon its feet [Col. 0871D], commending its soul by most humble penitence and seeking the Lord’s rewards out of desire for recompense, not from fear of punishment.

Knowing that the night of this world is entangled in various offenses—containing snares in one place, cliffs in another, and elsewhere the deepest wastes—it testifies that the Lord’s word shines upon its feet, lest, in the absence of true light, it fall into a ruin that it could not avoid by its own foresight.

Here, however, “word” must be understood as that which was sown through the Scriptures by the mouths of the prophets. He rightly called it a lamp, since it was given for human use to dispel the deepest darkness of night, as the Apostle Peter says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Peter I, 19).

Thus the Lord himself also says to the apostles: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII, 35). He rightly added “burning” on account of the foolish virgins, who, when their oil failed, could not await the Bridegroom’s arrival.

The Word who is consubstantial with the Father according to the nature of his divinity cannot be called a lamp, for he illuminates every person coming into this world (John I, 9), just as he himself says of himself: “I am the light of the world” (ibid., VIII, 12). This distinction is also made in the Gospel, where it is said of John: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (ibid., V, 35). And again: “He was not the light, but was sent to bear witness to the light” (ibid., I, 8).

He continues: “and a light to my paths.” He remains in the same translation, saying that the word of the Lord—that is, the sayings of the prophets—provided light for his paths. For along these paths, while we are instructed in the course of a good life, our hearts are illumined and we walk with upright [ed., “directed”] steps.

### Verse 106

“I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness.”

After that illumination of the word which he professed to shine upon his feet, let us see whether the blessed people could swear contrary to the commandment, since it is written in the Gospel: “You shall not swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by Jerusalem, nor by your head” (Matthew V, 34), and so forth. But “to swear” does not always mean to make an oath, in which, by invoking the Divinity, we promise that we will not change our promises.

Thus holy devotion also decreed and resolved for itself that, amid every danger, it would keep the Lord’s judgments.
