The word itself indicates the reason: to swear is “to pray by right” (*jure orare*), that is, to speak equity, so that no one might turn aside what he had promised to another side after being led astray.

Thus the saints swear—that is, they firmly resolve—when they have already been strengthened by the Lord’s gift. In the Gospel, however, the Lord prohibits this to the weak, since he came to save the little ones and the wounded, lest they rashly promise what they could by no means fulfill through their own strength.

The judgments of righteousness are present when he exalts the humble, casts down the proud, and by the gift of his mercy raises up those who have been prostrated in humble penitence. The following verse demonstrates this.

### Verse 107

“I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; give me life according to your word” [Col. 0872D].

When those who call themselves members of Christ say that they have been humbled exceedingly, they show that they have endured the dangers of many persecutions; and therefore they ask to be given life according to the Lord’s promises, since in their carnal condition they seemed to have been placed in death [mss. A, B, F., “carnal”].

“According to your word” means that promise which says: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew XI, 28), and similar statements.

They also know that through this humility the Lord Christ conquered the devil’s pride; they know that through the endurance of his death strong things were overcome; they know that the Lord endured everything that he commanded his saints to endure. Rightly, therefore, they seek remedies through their humility, by which they knew they would be saved [Col. 0873A].

Through this, then, the faithful advance above kingdoms; through this, tyrannical pride is overcome; through this, martyrs live forever. No one can be called perfect who is deprived of this virtue.

### Verse 108

“Make the willing offerings of my mouth acceptable, O Lord, and teach me your judgments.”

Since he had said above that he was humbled exceedingly, lest you think that this inclination arose from necessity rather than willingness, he added that the voluntary sacrifices of his mouth could be most pleasing to the just Lord—sacrifices that a devout spirit offered amid raging afflictions.

It is most pleasing to offer praises to the Lord even in times of ease; but they are shown to be more exceptional in tribulation, when the weakness of the body, pressed by pain, is not overcome, but the blessed soul is then stirred even more strongly to the Lord’s praises.

The voluntary sacrifices of the mouth are the offering of devoted praise, not with regard for any worldly advantage, but out of consideration for one’s own devotion, so that we may love the Lord for his own sake; that we may venerate the Creator, who sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew V, 45), who is good beyond measure.

He therefore asks that his devotion be made acceptable to the Lord, so that, pleased by this offering, he may teach him his judgments, which he deigns to disclose to faithful minds.

But let us consider the glorious ardor of his heart: he always eagerly seeks what he repeatedly recalls having received, as he says in the ninth letter: “You have dealt kindly with your servant.” And again: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.” By this manner, both things are proved to be understood. For one must continually hope wherever one continually acquires by asking.

### Verse 109

“My soul is always in your hands, and I have not forgotten your law” [Col. 0873C].

When the iniquity of thieves was pursuing the soul of the righteous and wanted to entangle it in various snares, he most wisely says that it had been placed in the Lord’s hands, where no force of those who inflict harm could approach, as it is written: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of death will not touch them” (Wisdom III, 1).

And again: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X, 27–28); and shortly afterward: “No one snatches them from my hand.” He added “always,” so that he would seem to leave no time for deceitful attacks.

When he says “in your hands,” he signifies “under your power,” because the Lord knows how to govern beneficially the one who has entrusted himself to his judgment.

He then explains why his soul is believed to be established in the Lord’s hands: namely, because he is taught not to have forgotten his law [Col. 0873D]. Thus we are under his protection when we do not deviate at all from his saving precepts. This is commanded everywhere and this is what we are specially admonished: to return to the law in such a way that we do not depart from the law.

### Verse 110

“Sinners have set a snare for me” [ms. G. and ed., “snares”], “but I have not gone astray from your commandments.”

“They have set” signifies “they have stretched out and armed,” for they could not merely have been placed idly. A snare does not catch a bird if it has no bait; rather, that snare deceives more effectively which entices by some pleasure.

The devil’s snare was armed with thirty pieces of silver (Matthew XXVII, 3) when it seized Judas and suffocated him in destruction; the same devil bound Saul with the zeal of pride (1 Samuel XV, 20); the same restrained Cain through envy of his brother (Genesis IV, 8); and there are similar examples of the demonic madness that continually rages throughout the long life of this age.

In the forest of this world you find as many snares as you behold vices. But nothing earthly could prevail against this holy company, which conducted itself in a heavenly manner, as it says in another psalm: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare was broken, and we were freed” (Psalm CXXIII, 7).

He next gives the heavenly antidote known to fight against the poisons of this age: namely, that he did not deviate at all from the Lord’s commandments. Whoever does not deviate from them is not caught by any deception, because snares lie beside them, not within them.

### Verse 111

“I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart” [Col. 0874B].

Possession acquired for gain is said to be acquired in many ways; but the honorable son is considered to be the one who glories in his paternal succession. This is the lawful name, this is the highest sign of love: to receive the judgments of one’s elders and to rejoice in a most secure possession.

The testimonies are the Lord’s most holy precepts, which Moses recalls in the book of Deuteronomy under the form of testimony, saying: “I call heaven and earth to witness against you today” (Deuteronomy XXX, 19). And elsewhere: “You are my witnesses, and I am your witness, says the Lord” (Isaiah XLIII, 10). Thus also the Apostle says: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus and his chosen angels” (1 Timothy V, 21).

Therefore these are the testimonies which the blessed people rejoiced to have acquired forever as an inheritance, since such an inheritance is possessed forever, not entered into for a brief period.

He continues: “because they are the rejoicing of my heart.” Rightly he called the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom the rejoicing of his heart, acquired for everlasting times. For the one who is proved to rejoice in such an acquisition deserves to attain it.

### Verse 112

“I inclined my heart to do your ordinances forever, because of the recompense.” 416

This most holy company, continually instructed by frequent meditation, had heard: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew XI, 29). It was therefore necessary for it to incline its heart in every way toward doing the Lord’s ordinances. Instructed by such teaching, it salutarily rejected the proud heights of the world.

For to do the ordinances means to put the Lord’s commandments into practice through humility: to break bread for the hungry, to clothe the naked, to grieve over the calamities of others, and the other things that the Creator’s mercy has deigned to commend to the human race [ed., “to humankind”].

But we must consider that he says “forever,” although everything mentioned above can be done only as long as we are afflicted by the calamities and needs of this world. For who will show mercy to the afflicted in the future, when in that kingdom there is proved to be no misery?

But the one who does these things here out of zeal for charity is shown to do them forever, because he will receive the fruit of these deeds for eternity. He added, “because of the recompense”—namely, that which the saints will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34), and so forth.

Great is the recompense, although it will nevertheless come from the Lord’s generosity: to become an inhabitant of the everlasting kingdom, a companion of the good angels, to receive a homeland that always delights and is never abandoned through any exile. They will remain fixed in that contemplation so that they may continually desire him in whom they always rejoice.

### Verse 113 — XV. SAMECH

“I hated the wicked, and I loved your law.”

At the fifteenth letter the Catholic company arrives, in which he says that he hated the wicked—that is, the adversaries of the law—but recalls that he loved the Lord’s law. He asks that, received by the Lord’s mercy, he may escape the evils of the world, and he also requests that his flesh be subjected to the fear of the Lord [mss. A, B, F., “to fear”], lest he be condemned in the divine judgment for his transgression [Col. 0875B].

Here too that question raises its head: why does the faithful people seem to have pronounced something contrary to the commandments of the Gospel? For he says, “I hated the wicked,” although it is commanded: “Pray for your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matthew V, 44).

But if you consider the times, you will recognize that everything agrees. When he commanded us to love our enemies, the heat of opposition and the fervor of injury are tempered, so that we may not appear to return evil for evil and may be patient toward every insult, like the one who endured spitting and received blows.

But when the time of martyrdom arrives, we are commanded to hate wicked persuaders. At that time we must even disregard sons and parents, if they are opposed to us, with an estranged will. Often those whom flame did not terrify and iron did not subdue have been swayed by the blandishments of family ties. Therefore it is said: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 26).

No person may be preferred to God. But once love of God has been placed first, it is fitting to love one’s family relations when no opposition to the faith conflicts with them. Therefore, when the times are taken into account, both statements can stand for us in complete truth. For it is written: “A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing” (Ecclesiastes III, 5); and after many other statements: “There is a time for every matter.”

We must also know that this verse contains the argument called in the topics “from contraries,” when we conclude our proposition from diverse realities in a single statement [Col. 0875D].

### Verse 114

“You are my helper and my protector, and I have hoped in your word.”

“Helper” pertains to fulfilling the commandments, because without his help we can neither begin anything good nor succeed in completing it.

He became our protector through the mystery of the holy Incarnation [mss. A, B, F., “the protector of our soul”]. Through it, he took up the human being so that humanity might not perish utterly under the law of sin.

Finally, observe what follows concerning this protection: “and I have hoped in your word.” That is, I have placed my highest desire in the protection of your divinity, where it is permissible to hope and where firmly established hope does not deceive, as it is written: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?” (Ecclesiasticus II, 11). And again: “Mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord” (Psalm XXXI, 10).

He therefore hopes that the Redeemer of the nations will come, who can wipe away the stains of the world, give life to the dead, heal the sick, and dissolve by death itself—when death dies—what had been bound by the law of sin.

Thus, in a single verse, the complete perfection of our whole religion has been summed up.

### Verse 115

“Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God.”

Just as heretics, while desiring to know the truth, often profitably exercise us in the Lord’s commandments, so the obstinate are known to clamor against and hinder us in searching the sacred readings. He declares that those who strive to tear apart the Lord’s Scriptures through senseless disputes must be avoided [Col. 0876B].

For what can human speech accomplish there when their desire is that no one should believe such things? To them it is said elsewhere: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Psalm VI, 9). When you do not see someone wishing to be converted, the remedy is to avoid him if you can.

While such people are present, continually fighting with contentious malice and fabricating accusations with studied vanity, we cannot be found fit to search out the Lord’s commandments, in which we ought to be occupied with all the powers of our soul [ed., “mind”].

### Verse 116

“Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not let me be put to shame in my expectation.”

After the faithless have been driven away and he has been cleansed from association with evil people, he asks the Lord to receive him, so that he may be saved by the promise of his word.

It might perhaps be presumptuous to say to the Lord, “Receive me,” unless he added the promise, which never knows how to deceive. But when he says, “I shall live,” he indicates the future tense; for here one does not truly live, where one sins through the weakness of the flesh.

His expectation was also that he would find the mercy of Christ with the deepest devotion. He asks to attain this hope in the coming judgment, lest, deceived by shame, he be deprived of his expectation.

But when he says, “from my expectation,” he assigns no time at which he ought not to hope. This reality has no end in holy hearts except when the heavenly promise arrives. Thus he also says elsewhere: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he looked upon me.” Blessed, therefore, is the expectation (Psalm XXXIX, 2) in which there is a sure promise.

For how could faithful hope endure failure when the one who promises does not know how to change? The expectation of the saints, therefore, is to earn the kingdoms of heaven, the fellowship of angels, and—what is above all—to see continually the one who always grows sweet in the hearts of the blessed [mss. A, B., “the whole”].

### Verse 117

“Help me, and I shall be saved; and I will meditate forever on your ordinances.”

Although these words seem often to be repeated, they nevertheless reveal great mysteries of continual devotion. This must be applied to the soul’s greatest desire, which could not be suspended by any interruption. For although we receive from the Lord, we must always ask him continually to give, lest the benefits bestowed upon us depart from us in the course of faith.

We must not regard the repeated word as pointless, lest we seem carelessly to have omitted what it is useful for us to know [Col. 0877A].

He added: “and I will meditate forever on your ordinances.” He gives the reason for his obedience, lest, after receiving salvation through the gift bestowed, he should appear ungrateful. But when he promises to meditate forever on the ordinances, he desires his salvation to be continually preserved. By doing this, he completely removes a place for the devil.

We can understand ordinances in two ways: either as those which we perform here daily in confession of our sins, as in that passage of the Gospel (Luke XVIII, 13–14), when the tax collector, confessing his sins, went away justified from the temple. For as long as we are in this world and cannot be free from sins, it is fitting that we should continually prostrate ourselves in this justification.

But because “forever” follows—a term understood to extend beyond every span of time [Col. 0877B]—you should not think that this applies only to this age; rather, it should lead you to conceive something concerning that eternity.

The saints meditate forever on the Lord’s ordinances when they join their desires to the choirs of angels; when they sing the Lord’s praises in everlasting rejoicing; when, as the Apostle says, “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (1 Corinthians XV, 54).

### Verse 118

“You have rejected all who depart from your statutes, for their thought is unjust.”

It has been explained why frequent and constant meditation on the Lord’s statutes was undertaken. Such a sentence, which was to follow, rightly inspired fear, since those who depart from the Lord’s statute are despised by him. For since the statute is the pure confession of the mind’s sins, the proud are rightly despised by the Lord when they disdain to heal themselves by such a remedy. Their thought is indeed unjust: they both wish to sin and refuse to satisfy the most just Judge. Such people are therefore rightly removed from the grace of absolution, since, though so often admonished, they have attempted to entreat the merciful Lord here.

### Verse 119

“I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved your testimonies.”

Unless this statement is examined carefully, it may seem contrary to the Apostle. For he says: “Those who sinned without the law will perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12); but here he declares that all the sinners of the earth are transgressors. For how can anyone be without the law if all are to be considered transgressors? To transgress is nothing other than to violate an established law.

Yet both statements are true, since both descend from one source of truth. The Apostle speaks of those who will perish without the law only with reference to that ordinance which is shown to have been written on stone tablets on Mount Sinai by the finger of the Lord. There are also other laws, through which peoples will be subject to divine judgment: such is the transgression of Adam, from which the human race, unless it is freed by Christ’s benefit, is destined to be judged.

The nations too are bound by the natural law, so that they should not do to another what they do not wish done to themselves. Hence the same Apostle says: “When Gentiles who do not have the law by nature do what belongs to the law” (Rom. 2:14). You see, therefore, that it is rightly said here that all who could fall into some error are transgressors. Whether they have transgressed the first law or the one given through Moses, everyone becomes a transgressor, since no earthborn person is proved to be exempt from these laws.

It followed, moreover, that he should love the Lord’s testimonies with greater eagerness, since he appeared to condemn all sinners under the name of transgressors. For he believed that through those testimonies a remedy could come to him, and through them he hastened with longing toward the grace of Christ. For although the law condemns us, grace alone absolutely sets us free; it is grace that releases the shackled and makes children out of servants.

### Verse 120

“Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments.”  
[Manuscripts G and F: “Fix my flesh with your fear.”]

The congregation of spiritual men, knowing whence the transgression of the law described above came to the human race, implores, in a new and unusual supplication, that its flesh be not merely bound but also pierced, as though it were a savage robber or an untamable beast. The vices of the flesh are earthly sins, which make us transgress the commandments of the law by drawing us away from our commitment to the truth.

How rightly, then, he begs that the flesh be pierced by the fear of the Lord, so that it may not be released by a harmful freedom from him! In a single word he indicated how a Christian’s flesh must be treated, and he explained with what devotion he prayed excessively and forcefully against his own body: namely, through fear of the future judgment, so that what is mortified here may be made eternal there; what is sorrowful for a time here may there be most joyful forever.

Consider also what he says: “with your fear”—that is, with chaste and perfect fear, which not only keeps the terror of punishment before its eyes but vehemently fears the loss of grace, in which the faithful person lives and through which every Christian is renewed.

But let us see what nails are those which pierce us in the Lord’s crucifixion. They are certainly love, which makes us disregard our torments and love the dangers of death itself more deeply. Blessed is the one who is pierced by this nail and wounded by such a wound. He was pierced by this very nail who said: “For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). By this same compunction was pierced the one who prayed: “Now dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29). Finally, in the Song of Songs the Church confesses: “I am wounded by love” (Song 2:5).

The holy people therefore implores that it be pierced by the fear of the Lord, so that by dying it may live—having previously been dying while living.

### Verse 121

**XVI. ʿAyin.** “I have done judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who persecute me.”

The living members of the Lord have reached the sixteenth letter, in which with one voice they ask for the advent of the sacred Incarnation, declaring that the time had come for divine power to be displayed in order to destroy the proud.

Let us therefore attend to the words that have been spoken, so that no perverse thought may attribute to the saints the arrogance they hate. Whoever judges against himself and condemns his own perversities before the Lord’s tribunal with righteous abhorrence performs judgment. But lest you think that this judgment is flattering rather than true, he added: “and justice,” because we judge ourselves through justice when we become the avengers of our sins.

This, then, is the equity that acquits us from punishment; it is the equity that frees us from guilt, provided that we acknowledge ourselves to be entangled in crimes. And since the completeness of devout satisfaction had been accomplished, he now asks not to be handed over to sinners, he who has condemned sins.

This is what he requested above: “Fix my flesh with your fear,” so that the harmful thing might be subjected to the judgment of the soul and serve after being fastened, though it could have run wild in unrestrained wantonness.

Those who persecute are the devil and his ministers. They pursue us with tireless malice and, once we are handed over to them, tear us apart with cruel rending. We remember what that most holy man Job endured and how patiently he submitted to so many calamities, because he knew that he had been handed over to them. We also know how much Joseph and Susanna suffered when they were delivered into the hands of the wicked.

For this reason, instructed by admonition, we also pray daily: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13). Sinners too are handed over, so that they may suffer punishments worthy of what they have committed, as the Apostle says of the wicked: “God handed them over to a debased mind, to do what is improper” (Rom. 1:28). And elsewhere he says of sinners: “Those whom I handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20).

The holy people therefore asks not to be handed over to those who persecute it. For this reason unclean spirits were enraged against them: they saw their own suggestions and instigations being condemned by them. This is the hatred that merits Christ’s love; for no one can be loved by him unless he is hated by Christ’s greatest enemies.

### Verse 122

“Receive your servant for good; let not the proud slander me.”

“Receive me”: he seems to have said this as one driven by the devil’s arm, lest he fall. We are received by the Lord’s mercy when we are struck by the force of our sins. It is therefore aptly said: “Lord, receive me for good,” because he knew that the opposing side had driven him toward evil.

“Servant” is an indication of liberation. A servant is so called from being saved, because the hand of his master, moved by compassion, preserves him when he has been captured from imminent destruction. Thus this man rightly calls himself a servant, since he had been freed from the soul’s deception.

Accordingly, here “servant” is recognized both as a profession of liberation and as a title of honor. No one is his servant except one who has been joined to the assemblies of the saints.

The proud slander when they thrust heretical disputes upon us with the violent weight of falsehood. He therefore rightly begged to be received by the Lord, lest he be overthrown by their quarrels.

Or this is better understood of unclean spirits, which slander us shamelessly. Although they themselves are chiefly guilty of our crimes, they do not want us to be freed by the pardon granted to us. They deceive us, yet they are always accusing us.

But what is surprising if the devil slanders sinners, when he attempted to say to the Lord Christ: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9)? And also: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

He is therefore rightly called a slanderer: while he performs cruel deeds, he continually accuses the devout. Scripture says of him elsewhere: “And he will humble the slanderer, and he will remain with the sun” (Ps. 71:4).

Most justly, therefore, he asks that the humble not be handed over to the proud, the simple to the slanderer, or the devout to the ungrateful, since they rage most savagely against those whom they have been least able to seduce.

### Verse 123

“My eyes have failed in your salvation, and in the word of your justice.”

Some are accustomed to wonder why he uses the plural “eyes,” when there is only one sight of the heart. Nor can this refer to bodily eyes, which at that distant time could not have seen anything of this kind.

But since the holy company is speaking, and it is established that this company is the Church, he rightly speaks in the plural: “My eyes,” just as elsewhere it is read of the same Church: “Your eyes are like doves over an abundance of waters” (Song 5:12); and elsewhere: “Your eyes are like doves outside your silence” (Song 4:1).

He therefore says that these eyes failed in the Lord’s salvation because of the holy advent of the Incarnation, which he awaited with such longing that he could admit no rest. He rightly failed, since he received no time of respite.

“Salvation” signifies the Lord Savior, of whom it is written: “Save your people, Lord, and bless your inheritance” (Ps. 27:9). It follows: “and in the word of your justice,” that is, the evangelical words that he was going to speak to the believing people.

### Verse 124

“Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes.”

He perseveres in continual prayers, since there ought never to be weariness in asking where the generosity of the giver cannot fail. He asked for infinite things when he requested that good be done to him according to the Lord’s mercy. For just as that mercy is eternal, so its gifts are proved to be everlasting.

He rightly added: “your servant,” because he will immediately fall who wishes to belong to another. As usual, he continually asks for the statutes that he has already devoutly received.

The Lord’s Prayer also indicates this persistence when it says: “Give us today our daily bread” (Luke 11:3). It is right that the one who is offended if not asked should be entreated continually.

Observe also with what precision these matters are distinguished by their wording. He asked that mercy be shown toward him; but he humbly requested that the statutes be taught to him.

### Verse 125

“I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies.”

Although everything that is necessary must be requested from the Lord in continual prayers, the understanding of the divine Scriptures must above all be sought unceasingly. The more it is received, the sweeter it is found to be by holy minds.

But because he knows that the almighty Lord is most generous toward his subjects, he says: “I am your servant; give me understanding”—you who are accustomed to grant what is rightly and confidently requested.

Although all things recognize themselves as subject to obligation, it is nevertheless a great merit to be called his servant. No one can truly be called his servant except one who serves according to his will.

And see what he says: “that I may know,” that is, “that I may retain what I have received.” To know something means that, once it has clearly entered our awareness, it is erased by no forgetfulness.

### Verse 126

“It is time to act, Lord; the wicked have broken your law.”

The devout people foresaw that in the time of Antiochus the law of the Lord would be polluted by the Jewish people through the worship of demons. Like a sick person crying out to a physician, it says that the time for help has come, lest the people’s salvation be consumed as the diseases grow worse.

It says: “It is time to act,” not to postpone what is necessary. Through the law and the prophets he had commanded that the true Lord be worshiped with the deepest devotion. But because the obstinacy of the Jews despised this to its own destruction, the faithful people cries out: “It is time to act”—that is, it is time for you to appear as salvation to the world, dissolve sins, conquer death, and overthrow the devil himself with his host.

For this is the Lord’s act: to come at the foretold time. Hence it was said through the prophet: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8). And the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

Everything the Lord does is completed according to the most fitting arrangement, so that it ought not to happen beforehand, except when he, in his mercy, grants it. Hence it is always useful for us to have patience, to await what has been commanded, and to ask for what is beneficial [Manuscripts A, B, and F: “what has been promised”]. The one who is ruler knows the time for acting.

He added the reason why he should do what is requested: the Jews have broken the law that he had commanded them to keep inviolably. To break the law is to live otherwise than its commands instruct, and especially to do what it is known to have condemned under every curse.

Rhetoricians place this argument among the most forceful appeals, when the most suitable timing helps prayers to be heard.

### Verse 127

“Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz.”

To the extent that wicked presumption had broken the Lord’s law, to that extent the devout spirit hastened to fulfill his commandments. The fervor of religious devotion grows great whenever the audacity of the wicked attempts to attack it. For this reason “therefore” was added.

For the most holy company, preserving reverence for the Lord’s commandments was worth more than gold and gems, which humanity considers most precious. Gold and gems flatter human eyes only temporarily; through the commandments the blessed mind is led to eternal rest.

Topaz, as some writers have wished to record, is a kind of stone as rare in discovery as it is precious in commercial value. It is said to possess two colors: one of the purest gold, the other shining with an ethereal brightness. It has a rosy richness and modest purity and is close to the chrysoprase in size or color. It shines most brightly when struck by the sun’s radiance, surpassing the precious brilliance of all gems and uniquely inviting the eyes’ eager delight.

If you wish to polish it, you obscure it; if you leave it to its natural state, it radiates. It is said to be astonishing even to kings, so that amid their riches they recognize that they possess nothing comparable.

It is said to be born on the island of Topaz, which belongs to the province of Thebaid, and from this it received its name. Not much more need be said about it, lest we make desirable through affected praise what Scripture calls contemptible.

### Verse 128

“Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every false way.”

He who loved the Lord’s law above gold and gems necessarily appeared most upright in relation to all his commandments. Only someone corrected by divine inspiration could neglect such things, treating gold as earthly filth and gems as worthless pebbles.

To love what is not beneficial is the mark of a madman; but it is fitting for the holiest men to desire what can bestow rewards that never perish. It was therefore appropriate that he should hate the perverse way, since he had been worthy to love the most upright one.

The unjust way is the way that leads us to vices; the straight way is the way of virtues, which grants us forgiveness and salvation. But how carefully and how frequently this is impressed upon us, so that we may understand by what kinds of delights blessed men are nourished: they regard as sweetest above all things whatever they believe should be repeated most often.

### Verse 129

**XVII. Pe.** “Your testimonies are wonderful, Lord; therefore my soul has searched them out.”

The prayer of the holy people enters the seventeenth letter, declaring that it opened its mouth and drew in the spirit, so that its prayer might be heard, and that streams of water had passed through its devout tears because the law of the Lord had not been kept by the Jews.

Observe how he compressed the definition of the matter into a single phrase by saying: “Your testimonies are wonderful, Lord.” They are plainly wonderful, because through them heavenly power was made known to earthly human beings, and they gave little ones knowledge of that in which the sublime nature of the angels is filled with blessed delight.

They may always be searched out and investigated through constant meditation. Here, however, it is not appropriate to fear the saying: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not search out what is stronger than you” (Eccl. 3:22). They were proclaimed to us for this very reason: so that our spirit might always investigate them devoutly and carefully.

Things that are “higher” and “stronger” cannot be understood in this way, since they were expressly commanded to be investigated. This is the fifth species of definition, which in Greek is called **κατὰ τὴν λέξιν** and in Latin **ad verbum**, “according to the word.” For what the Lord’s testimonies are has been explained: they are “wonderful.”

### Verse 130

“The exposition of your words gives me light and gives understanding to little ones.”

The Lord’s words are those which the authority of the prophets foretold. Thus it is written: “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). And elsewhere: “All flesh will see the salvation of God” (Isa. 52:10).

But the Lord’s advent, by its illumination, disclosed these words, which had been concealed under the obscurity of a long period, because through him those things were made manifest that had been hidden in the sacred writings.

Then the Word became flesh and the Virgin gave birth; then the mute spoke, the deaf heard, the lame walked with an upright step, and the other miracles that served the Lord’s works of power took place.

This revelation deigned to illuminate by the force of its power the obscurity of our nature, which lay in darkness. It gave understanding to little ones—that is, to those who acknowledged themselves humble and lacking in their own powers.

These “little ones” are not measured by age, but by simplicity of conscience. Of them it was said: “Let the little ones come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:14). To these he grants here a pure and most innocent understanding, to whom he will grant there an eternal reward.

### Verse 131

“I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit, because I desired your commandments.”

If you wish to understand this literally, the speaker’s custom is expressed. First the mouth is opened, the breath is drawn in, and then the mobility of the tongue is employed to produce the sound of the voice.

But if you understand it spiritually, as is appropriate, “mouth” signifies the entrance of the mind, which is opened whenever we hasten to learn something. He draws in the spirit when the desire for salvation is already filled by a divine gift, and he begins with firm intention to will what previously he appeared to have desired only through the Lord’s grace.

The weak and little one therefore opened the mouth of his heart and drew in the spirit—that is, the power to act, which he could not attain by himself.

But so that you may recognize that this has been said for the benefit of understanding, not for the act of speaking, it follows: “because I desired your commandments.” He first expressed the ardor of his will, and then explained the desire for the commandments. He could not logically say that he would first speak and afterward desire what is beneficial.

### Verse 132

“Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.”

The Lord often looks in anger and more frequently looks in order to destroy, as when he looked upon Sodom and Gomorrah and upon the camp of the Egyptians. He also looks favorably, as he did upon Abel in his offerings. He looked upon the children of the poor and did not despise their prayers (Ps. 101:18).

Therefore, lest he be received into the opposing side, he immediately added: “and have mercy on me.” As has often been mentioned, this is rightly called mercy because it is generously bestowed upon the wretched.

The poured-out prayer did not stop there. He added: “according to the judgment of those who love your name.” It is the Lord’s judgment to grant the help of mercy to those who love his name, so that the expectation of the faithful may not be deceived—an expectation that is always received through consideration of him.

### Verse 133

“Direct my steps according to your word, and let no injustice rule over me.”

“My steps” signifies the movements of the soul. Just as by bodily steps we move from place to place, so by certain steps of the soul we advance either toward better things or toward worse.

The holy company asked that these steps be directed according to the Lord’s word, lest, seduced by the perversities of vices, it fall into deadly errors. “According to your word” means according to the commands that you prescribe for the correction of the human race.

It follows: “and let no injustice rule over me.” For if the Lord deigned to direct his steps according to his word, it was necessary that no injustice be able to prevail over him.

Observe how cautiously he asks that injustice not rule over him. It could not be excluded so completely that it would never again be able to knock at the door; but when it does not rule, we escape, because that slavery plunges us into ruin.

Nor is it insignificant that he says “all injustice.” He knows that if any one of these injustices rules, it destroys us. It is of no benefit to keep the law in many respects if we seem to offend against it in one part. For it is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (Jas. 2:10).

### Verse 134

“Redeem me from the slanders of men, and I will keep your commandments.”

“Slander,” by antiphrasis—that is, by an expression that says the opposite—is called **capitis alumna**, “nursling of the head,” although it more truly seeks another’s head and is hostile to it. So too war is called what is not good, and a grove is called **lucus**, though it has no light.

Slander is an invention of dangerous falsehood brought against good people through perverse zeal, attempting to disfigure what has been done with a righteous conscience.

The just clearly endured this, so that people might turn them from the path of equity through a zealous campaign of attack [Manuscript G and the edition: “through a campaign of denial”]. How much did David endure, to say nothing of the ancients, when he spared Saul and, before an unjust king, became guilty for that very reason—because he was shown to have been favorable toward him?

What kind of slander, I ask, was stirred up against him when the young women said: “Saul has killed his thousand, and David his ten thousand” (1 Sam. 18:7)?

Slanders, therefore, are disputes raised by men against the honor of truth. The holy company rightly prayed that they be removed from it, so that, once adversities had been taken away, it might investigate the Lord’s commandments.

### Verse 135

“Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes.”

We read that the face of holy Moses was so glorified by the Lord (Exod. 34:35) that the Israelite people could not look upon it. Hence, after a veil had been placed over it, he spoke to them, because they were unable to see the heavenly splendor in him.

The face of Moses was the radiance of the law, which they could not endure because they heard it with veiled hearts.

The holy people therefore asks to be able to behold the Lord’s illuminated face, not a veiled one, so that it may deserve to be breathed upon by the grace of pure light [printed *puri*, “of pure”; edition: *pura*, “pure”] and no longer suffer any obstacle, since it desired to behold the truth itself.

More likely, the holy company may be longing for the advent of the Lord Savior, whose illuminated face has shone upon the darkness of sin, giving life to the dead and the most certain remedies to the despairing.

### Verse 136

“Streams of waters have passed through my eyes, because they did not keep your law.”

“Streams of waters” signifies abundant tears, which he says were so great that they even surpassed the flowing waters of springs.

They plainly surpass them when those waters run without feeling, while these are poured out through the anguish of the heart. What they could not surpass in quantity, they surpassed in the quality of most blessed compunction.

We pour out such tears when we are pierced by the remembrance of our sins. For if we kept the Lord’s commandments, we would have joy rather than the burning of lamentation.

But since we cannot avoid such things by the necessity of the flesh, may the Lord grant us tears by which we may be washed from the filth of our sins.

I also think this should be considered: he says that satisfaction came through the eyes, through which we are generally known to draw in the attractions of this world. It is therefore right that guilt should be cleansed through the same organs through which excess is committed.

This pattern is very frequently found in the divine Scriptures, as the sixth psalm says: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6:7). And elsewhere: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 42:4).

This figure is called hyperbole whenever the quality of a statement is presented with greater force through exaggeration. The holy company had to weep in such a way as to wash away all sins with an abundant rain of tears.

### Verse 137

**XVIII. Ṣade.** “You are righteous, Lord, and your judgment is upright.”

The company of saints, triumphant over its flesh, comes to the eighteenth letter. In it, it confesses the Lord’s justice and says that it continually venerates his fiery words with love, finally asking for understanding of his testimonies, through which it is to be made alive forever.

After saying above that its sins had been washed away by flowing tears, it now praises the Lord’s judgments with faithful understanding, saying: “You are righteous, Lord, and your judgment is upright.” You continually command sinners to afflict themselves, so that your medicine may save them. For otherwise they would never be shown to be corrected under joy, nor could divine benefits be recognized in any other way.

A sinner would think that he had received prosperity through his own merits if he continually flourished unharmed. Yet both are just and both are most fitting: the offender is corrected through satisfaction, and the Lord’s judgments are declared through humble confession.

When Daniel spoke these words, he was saved from the most savage mouths of lions. By this statement the flame was overcome for the three youths. Jeremiah frequently repeated this judgment in his Lamentations.

Let us therefore say this verse in every danger; let us say it also in times of joy, because such confession both rescues us from hardships and preserves us in prosperity.

### Verse 138

“You have commanded your testimonies in justice and in your truth exceedingly.”

“You have commanded” signifies “you have ordered.” The testimonies, as has already been said, are things proclaimed under testimony. They contain justice and truth: justice, because they distinguish everything equitably; truth, because they grant what has been promised.

He therefore rightly loved and repeated these testimonies so greatly, since through them the incomprehensible and venerable power of the Lord was made known.

“Exceedingly” may commendably apply to both justice and truth: for the Lord to command justice exceedingly is beneficial strictness, while to impress truth exceedingly upon minds is a safeguard.

### Verse 139

“Zeal for your house has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words.”

“Wasting away” is the debilitating effect of a disease, which causes us gradually to decline as it consumes the body’s solidity through painful affliction. He testifies that this happened to him because of his zeal for the Lord’s house, which he could not endure seeing violated by the tearing apart of the faithless.

“Zeal” is used both for evil and for good. In an evil sense, as in: “Zeal and envy devour the house of Jacob.” And in the Acts of the Apostles it is read: “When the Jews saw this, they were filled with zeal and laid their hands on the apostles” (Acts 5:17). This kind of zeal always leads to guilt, weaves snares, and blocks the way of salvation.

But it is used in a good sense in: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 69:10). Elijah also says: “With zeal I have been zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have abandoned your covenant” (1 Kings 19:10).

Phinehas the priest likewise, when he saw a Hebrew joining himself to a Moabite woman, was zealous for the Lord’s commandment and pierced them both with the sword (Num. 25:8). His zeal accomplished so much that he alone turned away the Lord’s anger.

This zeal grants salvation, preserves faith, guards chastity, and protects the Church of God with glorious vitality.

### Verse 140

“Your word is exceedingly fiery, and your servant has loved it.”

The Lord’s word is refined by fire because it purifies the hearts of mortals stained by worldly filth. Just as the heat of a blazing furnace smelts metals and consumes their impurities through necessary purification, so the Lord’s word, wiping away the stains of sins, cleanses the understanding of the humble.

By this fire the heart of Cleopas was burning when he said: “Was not our heart burning within us when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). Jeremiah, kindled by this fire, also declares: “And there was a flaming fire in my bones” (Jer. 20:9).

The others who flourished in triumphant love were likewise kindled by this fire. Therefore this fire is Christ’s word, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and whom I desire should burn” (Luke 12:49) [Edition: “and what do I desire?”].

He added “exceedingly,” so that you would understand this intensification as referring not to death but to salvation.

It follows: “and your servant has loved it.” He certainly loved what he knew bestowed life, and he honored what he knew had been given as a remedy for the human race.

### Verse 141

“I am younger and despised; I have not forgotten your statutes.”

This verse may fittingly apply to many saints. We may rightly understand it as spoken in the person of Joseph, who was despised by his older brothers and sold as a worthless slave to slave-dealers. Yet he did not forget the Lord’s statutes accomplished in him, since he conducted himself piously in all things.

The one who is shown to obey his commands is recognized as remembering his liberator. David too can say this in his own person. Because of his youth he was not thought capable of attaining the height of royal power among his brothers. Yet he held the Lord’s statutes in his memory with such devotion that the Lord himself said: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man according to my heart, who will do all my wills” (Acts 13:22).

Finally, this may be said by the adopted people, the people of grace, the new people, who come later in age but precede in the dignity of faith. This people is the foundation of the whole Church.

It is therefore fitting that the blessed company of saints be understood as speaking throughout the psalm, a company that embraces all the faithful and all those proved most blessed.

### Verse 142

“Your justice is justice forever, and your law is truth.”

This verse distinguishes the Lord’s justice and the law with appropriate precision. Human justice, however great it may be, is without doubt temporary, such as the justice of philosophers, who seem to conduct themselves with moral goodness but whose virtue, without the worship of God, is truly called empty glory.

The Lord’s justice, however, remains forever, because whoever keeps it will rejoice in eternal happiness. There also appeared to be the justice of the Jews, who looked chiefly to the letter and thought that there were no future mysteries in it.

But the Lord’s justice, as the Christian people has understood it, is kept forever, because it is itself always eternal.

The same, I think, must be understood of the law: whoever has been worthy to understand it has been filled with heavenly truth. For the truth of the law is the Lord Christ, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Therefore it is rightly stated definitively: “Your law is truth,” which means: the Lord Christ.

### Verse 143

“Tribulation and distress have found me, but your commandments are my meditation.”

Tribulation and distress are great gifts to holy men, because they know that, compressed beneath their weight, they sweat out their sins and move toward joys that have no end, as the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine?” (Rom. 8:35), and so forth.

For blessed men this is like an antidote: although it is drunk harshly, it produces remedies of salvation [manuscript G: *momenta*, “moments”; edition: *monimenta*, “memorials”].

It follows: “have found me,” as though he were waiting for them [Edition: “as though they were attacking him”], as though fixed in place, as though prepared for their contests.

He also adds the assistance by which he undoubtedly knew himself to have been healed amid his various sufferings: “Your commandments are my meditation.” By what tribulations or distresses could one who rejoiced in such meditation be oppressed? Even if his frail body were afflicted and his suffering flesh tormented, he was known to have been transferred into rest, since his mind was occupied with the divine Scriptures.

### Verse 144

“The equity of your testimonies is forever; give me understanding, and I shall live.”

Again, by way of definition, he identifies the virtue of the testimonies. If you ask what the Lord’s testimonies are, the answer is: “Equity forever.”

Beautifully, against tribulation and distress—which are known to be temporary—he places equity that is eternal, so that each person might despise what he recognizes as temporary because of such hope.

Thus in the preceding letter too he defined them: “Your testimonies are wonderful, Lord.”

He added: “Give me understanding, and revive me.” Earlier he had said that he was young and despised; now, more mature than the elders amid adversity, he asks for understanding, so that he may recognize the dangers of this world as passing winds.

He could be made alive in this way: by judging such things unworthy of concern, so that he might live through the death of martyrdom and rejoice in perpetual exultation.

O life-giving death! O blood more precious than every purple dye, which deserves to bring tribulations and distresses to an end and, beyond that, awaits receiving the kingdoms of heaven!

### Verse 145.—XIX. QOPH

“I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord: I will seek your ordinances.”

The most reverent chorus enters upon the nineteenth letter, in which it promises to seek the Lord’s ordinances and to rejoice in his word through an anticipated confession, adding that it has learned that the Lord’s testimonies are founded forever. Let us now return to the verse. The cry of the faithful, therefore, is the devout emotion of the mind, which is expressed not merely in speech but uttered with the heart’s intense concentration. The murmuring Jewish people cried out, yet were not heard by the Lord. Moses was silent, and the Lord said to him, “Why are you crying out to me?” (Exod. XIV, 15)—namely, because the Most High hears those thoughts that are revolved with pious intention. “With my whole heart” has been added, lest you should suppose that something else ought to be contemplated when one cries out to the Lord. For the whole spirit ought to be occupied in religious thought alone, lest a divided mind be unable to obtain the result it seeks.

And consider what he sought with his whole heart and with all his strength: not the riches of the world, not marriages with noble women, not transient dignities, but the Lord’s ordinances, which the holy mind always desires and always seeks above gold and topaz. For when he said, “I will seek,” he surely meant ordinances that he ought to perform, not merely those that he might know by reading. For no one truly seeks the ordinances unless he has fulfilled them with a devout mind.

### Verse 146

“I cried out to you; save me, and I will keep your commandments.”

He explains the cry that he mentioned above. “I cried out with my whole heart” is the same as “I cried out to you.” For no one cries out to him unless he directs his petition with the whole affection of his heart. But when he says, “Save me,” this must be understood of the soul, not of the body—for it was through the soul that he could truly keep the Lord’s commandments. Indeed, he could not have been asking for the salvation of the flesh when he willingly submitted to bodily sufferings.

### Verse 147

“I anticipated the dawn and cried out; I hoped in your word.”

Whoever anticipates maturity anticipates the sobriety of old age in the years of childhood and assumes the gravest state of mind before he can grow gray through the number of his years. What praise is there for old men if, weakened by prolonged luxury and wearied out, they merely rest? Conversely, what glory belongs to young men if, in the very ardor of youth, they are restrained by disciplined conduct? As Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man who has borne the heavy yoke from his youth. He will sit alone and be silent, because he has borne the heavy yoke” (Lam. III, 27–28).

It follows: “And I hoped in your word.” This is precisely what he had anticipated in maturity and for which he cried out to the Lord, because he did not cease to hope with fixed mind in his word—that is, in the coming of the Lord the Savior. For holy men, although they burn with great desire, continually add ardor to their expectation: the more their expectation is prolonged, the more eagerly they desire the happiness that is to come.

### Verse 148

“My eyes anticipated you at dawn, that I might meditate on your words.”

In the preceding verse he says that he anticipated maturity, signifying the period of youthful age; now he speaks of the hour of the day. “My eyes anticipated you at dawn” signifies, of course, that the eyes of his heart believed in the coming Lord the Savior before his coming had shone upon them. For dawn signifies the beginning of light, that is, the advent manifested at the beginning of the day, when, after the darkness of sins by which this world was held captive, the life-giving presence of the Lord shone forth. Or it signifies the Lord’s resurrection, which took place at dawn; for the Gospel says: “When it was very early, Mary came to the tomb” (Luke XXIV, 1), and so forth.

It follows: “That I might meditate on your words.” The reason is given why the devout mind rose before dawn: not to cultivate a field, not to anticipate the greetings of the powerful, but to meditate on the Lord’s words, which can never reject pious desires, since their sweetness always seems to increase, as was said in the thirteenth letter: “How sweet are your words to my throat!”

### Verse 149

“Hear my voice, O Lord, according to your mercy, and according to your judgment give me life.”

Let us observe with what remarkable humility the true servants of the Lord entreat their Lord, and let us understand that we must presume on nothing if some prosperity has smiled upon us through God’s grace. He who, overcoming childhood, cried out to the Lord in his early years, who rose at dawn, always asks for mercy in his praises and begs to be given life, because nothing is to be presumed upon in any works except the Lord’s compassion alone.

For when he says, “Hear my voice, O Lord, according to your mercy,” he has nothing that he can confidently set against his sins. He asks only for that mercy which makes the blessed out of the wretched, the free out of captives, the living out of the dead, and the eternal out of those who are temporal. It follows: “According to your judgment give me life”—that is, according to the judgment by which you spare those who plead and mercifully absolve those who condemn themselves. And when he adds, “Give me life,” he confesses that he is dead under the law of sin. For no one can be given life who does not possess life in himself.

### Verse 150

“Those who persecute me unjustly have drawn near [ms. G and ed.: appropiaverunt; main reading: appropinquaverunt]; but they have gone far from your law.”

The prophetic spirit knew what grave dangers threatened the blessed, and first asked for mercy, so that they might not be overcome by any violence within those dangers. Persecutors draw near when, after everything else, they are seen to approach even to the tearing of the flesh, as it is said in the twenty-first Psalm concerning the Lord’s Passion: “Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near” (Ps. XXI, 12). And in the Gospel: “Rise, let us go; behold, he who betrays me has drawn near” (Matt. XXVI, 46; main reading: appropinquavit; ms. G: appropriavit).

He appropriately added “unjustly” for the sake of distinction, since even those who are guilty can suffer persecution—those in whom crimes are punished, as the Gospel also says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” (Matt. V, 10), but adds, “for righteousness’ sake.” Here, however, “unjustly” is rightly said, because they were suffering evil for good, so that those to whom they preached salvation might think them worthy of being handed over to death.

It follows: “But they have gone far from your law.” These persecutors, the nearer they came to the sufferings of the saints, the farther they withdrew from the Lord’s law. For those who hasten toward crooked paths and wickedness must abandon righteousness, because no one can draw near to the Lord except one who obeys his ordinances.

This figure is called syncrisis, whenever we show that our cause is better than that of our adversaries. He says that he endured persecution unjustly, while his adversaries had gone far from the Lord’s law.

### Verse 151

“You are near, O Lord, and all your commandments are truth.”

Against the closeness of that most violent persecution, he says that the Lord’s nearness is his remedy, knowing that the help of salvation would come from it. He says, “You are near, O Lord,” because you are wholly everywhere and fully everywhere—not confined by spaces, but yourself filling and encompassing every space. When the prophet wished to show that his presence is everywhere, he says elsewhere: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before the dawn and dwell at the farthest end of the sea, even there your hand will lead me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 8–10; ed.: “you are there”).

But when he says, “You are near, O Lord,” he confesses that the Lord does not fail to know when we act perversely, nor withdraw when we flee. There is therefore one means of salvation: to hasten toward him whom you cannot escape.

He also adds: “And all your commandments are truth.” One who has believed in the truth—that is, in the Lord Christ—and has received his commandments for salvation can say this. The Jew, however, cannot speak in this way, since he refused to believe the truth.

### Verse 152

“From the beginning I learned from your testimonies that you founded them forever.”

“From the beginning” signifies from the world’s beginnings, when the name of the saints began with righteous Abel (Gen. IV, 8), who, innocent, was killed by his wicked brother as a foreshadowing of the Lord the Savior. He also learned from the beginning when the offerings presented by Melchizedek the priest were received as a foreshadowing of the Lord’s body. He likewise learned from the beginning when Abraham offered his son to be sacrificed as a mystery of the Lord the Savior, and similar events contained in the readings of the sacred writings (Gen. XXII, 10).

These things were undoubtedly founded forever, since they are confirmed by the testimony of truth itself. And he appropriately said “founded,” since they pertained to the foundation of the Lord Christ. For he himself is the unique and solid foundation, as the Apostle says: “For no one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11). Hence it is clearly apparent—something often stated—that the faithful perceived the Lord Christ in their minds and recognized his holy coming in the foreshadowings of the Old Testament.

### Verse 153.—XX. RES

“See my humiliation and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law.”

Behold, the people victorious over vices now enter upon the twentieth letter, in which they ask to be given life, since they have sought the Lord’s commandments with the greatest zeal. He also declares that salvation is far from sinners, because they have not done such things. He testifies as well that the beginning of the Lord’s words is truth.

But, to return to the beginning of this letter, he says: “See my humiliation.” This appears to concern the martyrs, whose bodies are afflicted by such enormous torments that not the nature of human beings but, as it were, the worthlessness of animals is judged in them. The following Psalm will speak of this humiliation: “For we have been filled exceedingly with contempt” (Ps. CXXII, 4); and, “Our soul has been filled exceedingly with reproach from those who abound, and with contempt from the proud” (Ps. CXXII, 4). Hear also the Apostle humbling himself: “But I am the least of the apostles” (I Cor. XV, 9).

But to clothe this humiliation in a kind of purple mantle, the Lord also says: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. XXI, 7). Through this humiliation the devil’s pride was conquered, so that he might fall from the opposite side and not rejoice in having presumed that he had accomplished anything profitable.

It follows: “And rescue me.” From what, unless from the necessity of the punishments pressing upon them, from the danger of death, and from whatever the blessed martyrs could endure in that contest? For the holy people could not be asking to be freed from an idle humiliation, since their profession was bowed down and devout.

Here he calls “law” that saying which declares: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11). Therefore he rightly said that he had not forgotten it, since he persevered in it to the very end of life.

### Verse 154

“Judge my judgment and redeem me; give me life because of your word.”

This verse must be sought with careful piety, lest—God forbid—the company of the saints appear to have sought judgment out of arrogance. Of them it is written: “The righteous man is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. XVIII, 17). But by “his judgment” he means that by which he believed in the word and received the Lord’s incarnation with a pure mind—a secure judgment, one by which no one need fear the Lord’s judgment.

For in those matters that the saints judge rightly through God’s grace by believing, they are always made secure; and rightly they ask for divine examination in those matters, because they know that they will be glorified in them.

And observe how beautifully a denominative expression has been made. This rhetorical argument is called an argument from cognate words, when one word is formed from another by a harmonious similarity of sound.

It follows: “Redeem me.” Whom could he redeem except one who believed? Or for whom would he pour out the blood of redemption most fully, if he had not been a faithful servant? He adds: “Give me life because of your word”—the word in which he promises: “Whoever believes in me will not die, but will have eternal life” (John XI, 26).

### Verse 155

“Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your ordinances.”

In the first verse of this letter he had said that he must be rescued from persecutors because he had not forgotten the Lord’s law. Now, with most fitting contrast, he says that salvation is far from proud persecutors, because they did not seek the Lord’s ordinances at all, both to encourage the devout through the hope of a good way of life and to terrify the faithless by the condemnation set before them.

I think this is to be understood especially of the Jews, who, by refusing to believe in the Lord the Savior, made salvation—that is, the Lord the Savior—farther from themselves. For if they had been willing to believe, they would have sought the ordinances of the Old Testament, in which, as has often been said, the coming of the Lord the Savior was foreshadowed.

Therefore they were rightly made far from salvation, since they rejected the author of salvation. For when the Lord Christ was offered to them by Pilate, they chose, with hardened minds, to have Barabbas the robber—such as they themselves were—released to them (Matt. XXVII, 17).

### Verse 156

“Your mercies are many, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life.”

The Lord’s mercies are those by which he deigns to aid the afflicted and wounded in various ways: Joseph, for example, who was confined in prison bonds; Jonah, whom the sea-monster swallowed; Susanna, whom Daniel’s judgment absolved when she was suffering under a false charge; and the robber, whom he saved through a momentary confession—along with the other kinds of mercies that no human knowledge can enumerate.

It follows: “According to your judgment give me life.” Everywhere we must observe with the greatest caution what sort of judgment is being requested, since it is not an act of human confidence to ask for that of which it is said: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. CXLII, 2).

The judgment we ought to seek is that which we ask for when we prostrate ourselves in humble satisfaction, when we confess our sins after removing our excuses. For then it is the Lord’s judgment to show mercy to such people; and the one who asks to be given life according to the Lord’s judgment asks well when he presents himself as humbled and suppliant.

When he judges, he shows mercy; when he shows mercy, he also judges, because he neither shows mercy without judgment nor judges without mercy. To him the Psalmist says: “I will sing judgment and mercy to you, O Lord” (Ps. C, 1). It is clear that all virtues are present in him; they do not come to or depart from him, since they are known to exist in him substantially.

### Verse 157

“Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I have not turned aside from your testimonies.”

The injustice of savage persecution is greatly intensified when one man says that he has suffered what many detestable people inflicted. Hence the Church has received a numerous crown; hence the blood of the martyrs has been consecrated throughout the whole world, because the fury of the raging did not rejoice in persecuting the innocent. The number of the elect increased to the extent that the anger of tyrants was inflamed.

Yet amid all these things he testifies that he did not turn aside in any way from the Lord’s testimonies. For devotion is received with greater favor when it is preserved amid the dangers of life.

### Verse 158

“I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your words.”

A covenant is a condition established between people divided in affection through the gift of grace; it is derived from peace, as though it were an act of peace. Hence the arrangement established by both laws is rightly called a covenant, since it recalled the human race, separated from divine grace, to the Lord’s peace and harmony.

Therefore the Lord’s covenant is that whoever overcomes persecutions must be crowned with a glorious election. Those who, yielding through frail slackness, turned and fell into the joy of their persecutors did not keep this covenant at all. When the holy company saw this, it was afflicted that it had lost companions in the faith.

To show the excess of its grief, it said, “I was wasting away,” as happens to bodies exhausted by prolonged illness. But he shows the cause of his wasting away: the transgressor had in no way kept the Lord’s words. The Lord’s words are: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

Or he may mean the covenant of the Old Testament, when the Hebrew people, hearing the Lord’s words, said: “Everything that the Lord has spoken, we will both hear and do” (Exod. XIX, 8). But when the people worshiped foreign gods and stained themselves with the foulest service of demons, they abandoned that covenant of the first promise through detestable forgetfulness.

The holy men necessarily grieved over this even to bodily wasting, since they saw their fellow citizens and relatives neglecting the Lord’s words, and with most devout sorrow they mourned those who had been handed over to a reprobate mind.

### Verse 159

“See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life.”

Observe how he has adorned both matters through a similarity of words. In the preceding verse he said: “I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I was wasting away.” Now he says: “See that I have loved your commandments,” so that he might deserve to be seen by the Lord because he had regarded his enemies with a zeal for piety.

But after recalling the savagery of the persecutors and the punishments inflicted, he comes to the love that commends everything. For if he suffered such things without loving the Lord’s commandments, the crown would not be blessed but a vicious boast, as the Apostle says: “If I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 3).

Someone who endures the tortures of martyrdom with murmuring appears, in a sense, ungrateful toward the Lord’s law. He ought instead to love the very thing by which he believes he will reach eternal joys. For the Lord regards the qualities of souls more favorably than he attends to the torment of bodily suffering, just as he accepts as pleasing those alms that are given with gladness of spirit.

Therefore he rightly asked the Lord to give him life, since he had despised the life of this world for the sake of true religion.

### Verse 160

“The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your righteousness endure forever.”

“The beginning of your words” seems to me to signify the beginning of the divine Scriptures. And what is this other than the beginning of Genesis, which says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I, 1)? There, however, everything is understood to be contained and signified: heavenly things are contained by heaven, while earthly things, created through the signification of earth, must be understood as earthly.

Thus that beginning of the words is proved to be the perfection of the whole truth. For truth speaks truly from the beginning and carries its words through to the end of truth. Of these words it is written: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35). Whatever descends from that source of truth remains established with unchanging power.

For just as it is said, “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Ecclus. I, 16), so here this order of speech has been formed: “The beginning of your words is truth.”

And since he had touched upon what was done in the beginning, he adds what is destined to occur after the end of this world, when the Lord’s judgments will remain in the eternal age. For he will say to the righteous: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.” But to the wicked he will say: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 34).

Those judgments of his righteousness will undoubtedly be everlasting, since neither time will alter his sentence nor any circumstance overturn it. Thus, in a single verse, he has brought together both the beginnings of our faith and its still-future consummation.

### Verse 161.—XXI. SIN

“Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart feared your words.”

The company of the saints enters upon the twenty-first letter, in which it says that the persecutions of those who rage are most welcome to it because of the Lord’s love. It also recalls that it spoke praises to the Lord seven times a day and professes that its ways are known to him.

Here too we must understand “princes” as persecutors, who carried out bloody assaults upon Christians by the authority of rulers, as had been foretold: “They will hand you over in their synagogues, and they will scourge you, and you will stand before kings and governors because of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations” (Matt. X, 17–18). In the same way we call the devil a prince, since he claimed primacy for himself in crimes.

“Without cause,” because the Christian religion harms no one; rather, in obedience to the Lord’s command, it prays for all who strive improperly to afflict it. For it is written: “Pray for your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V, 44).

They truly suffered assault without cause from princes, since they were neither commanded to despise them nor to withhold taxes from them. For he says: “Be subject to all higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII, 1). And when asked about the tribute, the Lord said in the Gospel: “Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII, 21). He himself also paid the tribute from the mouth of a fish for himself and Peter (ibid. XVII, 26), so that it might be entirely clear that the most shameless persecution was inflicted without cause upon those who preferred to conduct themselves innocently.

But, without fearing such things, he says that he feared the Lord’s commandments. When the persecutors threatened him with temporal destruction, he feared eternal destruction, lest, acquitted by a human sentence, he should incur eternal judgments. He feared those words that the Lord spoke in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. X, 28).

### Verse 162

“I will rejoice over your words, like one who finds abundant spoils.”

The comparison is drawn from combatants, who rejoice both that they have conquered the enemy and that they have found much booty. But let us consider in what respect that devout mind appears to have compared itself with savage men.

The martyrs, although they died in a lowly condition, found abundant spoils when they both received divine rewards and rejoiced that their persecutors themselves had been converted through the Lord’s mercy. Thus those who had taken the lives of the innocent themselves became the spoil instead.

Therefore he says that he rejoices in the Lord’s words—that is, in the admonitions given—like a victor who hastens with excessive eagerness to seize the spoil of the slain. This comparison is applied to the joy of those who triumph; it is not compared with an appetite for bloodshed. Such language is frequently found in sacred writings to express various meanings.

The Hebrew people despoiled the Egyptians when, through the Lord’s favor, they were freed from long slavery. David took spoils when he overthrew the pride and wickedness of Goliath. The Lord himself triumphed over the devil when, after binding his strength, he rescued the vessels of death and transferred them to salvation. Finally, the Christian people rejoiced as one who had found abundant spoils in the Lord’s words, which it seized from the unbelieving Jews for the advancement of its own salvation.

### Verse 163

“I have hated and abhorred iniquity; but I have loved your law.”

We must firmly retain in our minds that he demonstrated his love of good things by his hatred of evil things. For if our mind wishes to admit iniquity, it cannot be joined wholly to the Lord’s law, as the Gospel says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24).

True love is that which guards its affection for the truth with such firm deliberation that it utterly abhors whatever can be opposed to it. Therefore he says that he hates not the wicked person but iniquity—which is right—and that he abhorred it in such a way as to make it entirely alien to himself, so that he might love the Lord’s law with perfect willingness.

This argument is drawn from the contrary diversity of things. The Lord’s law is, as has often been said, that which was enacted under enigmas: that a Hebrew servant should serve for six years, that a year-old lamb should be sacrificed, and similar things that can signify the New Testament. He rightly recalls that he loved these things, lest anyone think that they should be heard with neglect.

### Verse 164

“Seven times a day I have praised you for the judgments of your righteousness.”

If we wish to attend to this number literally, it signifies the seven times by which the devout observance of monks consoles itself: at morning prayer, terce, sext, none, the lighting of the lamps, compline, and the night offices.
