The hymn of Saint Ambrose also testifies to this in the singing appointed for the sixth hour.

But if you attend to it spiritually, you will wisely understand it as referring rather to continual praise, as in: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII, 2). So too there is the week, which continually revolves in this number and extends for us the longest span of time, since everything that occurs in the age of this world is enclosed within this number.

It is also used for the infinite where it says: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. XXIV, 16). The number of falls is not fixed for the righteous; rather, whenever he falls, it is necessary that he rise again.

The same is true of: “Repay our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom” (Ps. LXXVIII, 12)—that is, many times. And in Moses: “Everyone who kills Cain will be punished sevenfold” (Gen. IV, 15)—that is, many times—and similar passages.

But so that you should understand these praises as continual, he added below: “For the judgments of your righteousness,” because he spares the one who pleads and is so gracious to the humble that he not only forgives their faults but also grants them eternal rewards.

### Verse 165

“Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them.”

Since God is tranquil in undisturbed purity, it is necessary that the joys of peace be granted to those who love his law. But “great peace” must be understood as purity of mind and abundance of faith, which we fittingly set against vices.

Nevertheless, in this world the one who professes to be the Lord’s servant is subject to tribulations and dangers. To the apostles, who were destined to be torn apart by various persecutions, the Lord says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV, 27). Thus it plainly appears that the Lord’s servants always enjoy tranquility of mind, although they may seem to be weighed down by various afflictions of the body.

It follows: “And there is no stumbling-block for them,” because whoever truly loves the Lord’s law does not suffer a stumbling-block in it—that is, anything sinister—as did the Jews, of whom it is written: “A stumbling-block to Jews, but folly to Gentiles” (I Cor. I, 23).

A stumbling-block is a mind offended because it thinks something different from what it is instructed; this is shown to be foreign to those who love the Lord’s law [ed.: “God”]. We must love everything in the law that it is known to contain; otherwise, one who is offended by even the smallest part of it does not love the law.

But we must pray that, through the Lord’s mercy, we may understand what our weakness does not permit us to see. To suffer a stumbling-block there means to be separated from the Lord’s elect, as happens to all heretics, who cut themselves off from the unity of the holy Church through the fault of their perversity.

### Verse 166

“I awaited your salvation, O Lord, and I loved your commandments.”

This verse suits both the faithful of ancient times and those of the present, if we understand it as referring to both comings of the Lord. It pertains to the ancient faithful if you understand that they awaited the coming of the Incarnation. It also suits the saints who began to believe after the evangelical command, while they still await the coming of the future judgment.

For neither group could love the Lord’s commandments unless they desired the fullness of the commandments; nor could the latter love the commandments unless they awaited the coming of the Lord the Savior with the purest fear.

The Lord’s “salvation” is the salvation granted to the Gentiles, which was foretold by the angel to Joseph and which Simeon recognized when he was to be dismissed in peace.

### Verse 167

“My soul kept your testimonies, and loved them exceedingly.”

“Kept” pertains to endurance in martyrdom, lest he appear to lose what his religion contained. “Loved,” however, pertains to love stronger than every torment, which conquers flames, overcomes swords, and transcends all things by heavenly power.

But this love is not to be carried out casually; it must be carried out “exceedingly,” which is expressed through the exertions of the whole soul, so that it neither withdraws at any time nor grows sluggish through spiritual torpor.

Thus he reaches what the Apostle says: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness has been reserved for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give me on that day” (II Tim. IV, 7–8).

### Verse 168

“I kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you, O Lord.”

In the preceding verses he set down the commandments and testimonies separately; here, bringing the letter to a close, he joined them together, so that you might understand that both were kept at once.

He therefore says that he kept the commandments and testimonies, but below he adds why he was able to keep them: namely, because the Lord deigned to regard all his ways, so that he attributed his ability not to his own strength but to divine power. They would have been confused in blind night unless the true light had deigned to look upon them.

But this is wholly the voice of the blessed: to confess that their ways are before the perpetual Sun and eternal Light. He denies that error could have prevailed over one who professes that the Author of light looks upon him.

Adam hid his way after his sin; Eve hid hers; Cain hid the murder of his brother. None of them could say, “All my ways are before you, O Lord,” since they knew that, though known, they were perishing.

### Verse 169.—XXII. TAU

“Let my prayer draw near before you, O Lord; according to your word give me understanding.”

With the Lord’s help we have reached the twenty-second letter. In it the chorus of the saints, being as near to the end of the Psalm as it is, desires to draw nearer to Christ. Everything pertains to the coming of the Lord the Savior, which the devotion of the faithful awaited with ineffable desire, so that he might deign to restore the lost sheep through the gift of his mercy.

For when he asks that his prayer draw near to the Lord’s presence, he shows that the presence of sinners is very far from him, since nothing comes near him unless it has been purified by the most spotless holiness.

It follows: “According to your word give me understanding.” He therefore asks to have wisdom according to the Lord’s word, lest he be submerged in vanity through human prudence, cleansing himself more diligently from vices in proportion as he already enjoyed the nearness of virtue.

For he did not ask for worldly understanding, but understanding according to God’s word, which always advances toward life and whose knowledge is true and whose wisdom is eternal.

There is also the understanding of this age, such as the unfruitful labor and empty disputation of certain people. They investigate the courses of the stars, placing human lives under the power of the constellations. If this could be admitted or taught, there would be no recourse to the power of the Creator, to whom every form of understanding is known to flee and in whom it is perfected.

### Verse 170

“Let my petition enter before you, O Lord; according to your word rescue me.”

The holy petition ascends by degrees. For the one who had earlier said, “Let it draw near,” now says, “Let it enter.” First it had to draw near; then it had to be able to enter into the Lord’s presence. Thus we attribute nothing to human virtue, but recognize that everything is accomplished through his grace.

This presence shows how great is the power of devout prayer: through it we are presented, since it is known that prayer can be offered before the Lord’s presence, as it is also said elsewhere: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your presence” (Ps. CXL, 2).

And whereas above he said, “According to your word give me understanding,” here it says, “According to your word rescue me,” so that there he may see the heavenly things he desires, while here he may be cleansed from the stain of earthly desire.

The Lord’s word provides both, for it knows how to save us through manifold power, as it is written: “Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?” (Ecclus. II, 11).

### Verse 171

“My lips shall pour forth a hymn, when you teach me your statutes.”

The word *ructare* (“to belch forth”) is derived from *rumpere* (“to burst”), because a kind of digestion, bursting through the barriers of our stomach, is emitted into the ethereal air with the sound of the mouth. But how richly must that prophet have been nourished with divine delights, who belched forth the Lord’s hymn with joyful exultation! For this vaporous outpouring comes from the depths of the mind. When the Lord has inwardly nourished the needy understanding, his hymn emerges as a salutary drunkenness.

It should also be noted that the language of prophecy is frequently signified by this word, as in: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. 44:2); and: “I shall pour forth what has been hidden since the foundation of the world” (Matt. 13:35); and elsewhere: “Day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. 18:3). A hymn is therefore poured forth when the tongue, filled with the Spirit of the Lord, does not serve the judgment of the human mind—as ordinarily happens in common speech—but speech is ordered according to the heavenly understanding of the divine meaning.

The text continues: “when you teach me your statutes.” The order of the words is: “When you teach me your statutes, my lips shall pour forth a hymn.” For he promises the grace of devotion when he has received the Lord’s gifts. This kind of argument is considered especially distinguished among rhetoricians.

[Note: Here and elsewhere we consistently find this word written *eructuare* in Cassiodorus; but, in accordance with the most customary usage among authors and with the reading of the Vulgate edition, we have everywhere restored *eructare*. — Editor.]

### Verse 172

“My tongue shall proclaim your word, because all your commandments are righteousness.”

The holy company, knowing that an account must be rendered for every idle word, says that it proclaims the Lord’s words to those who seek them. Thus the soul’s salvation is gained, and the dangers of offense are avoided.

For it is exceedingly blameworthy that, when the divine Scriptures—filled with such great gifts—are offered to us, and when the Lord’s great miracles shine everywhere, we should abandon the life-giving word and turn to the foolish tales of the world; and that we should be anxious about harmful things, as though some good seemed capable of being gained through them. Hence Scripture threatens, saying that we shall render an account for an idle word (Matt. 12:36).

Therefore the holy mind proclaimed the Lord’s words, so that it might gain glory rather than discover the disgrace of guilt. The reason why the Lord’s words must always be proclaimed follows: namely, because all his commandments shine with the honor of righteousness. This should be proclaimed in one continuous utterance, since it both assists the speaker and edifies the understanding of the hearers.

### Verse 173

“Let your hand come to my aid, that you may save me, because I have chosen your commandments.”

When he says, “Let your hand come,” he designates the Lord Savior, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3), through whom all things were made and are governed.

Here we must understand “hand” as the right hand, because the Lord himself is signified by various names, as Isaiah says: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). And elsewhere: “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. 117:16). Therefore, whether one says “hand,” “arm,” or “right hand,” the Lord Christ is signified.

This manner of expression is frequently found in the Psalms, and we may rightly call it characteristic of divine Scripture, as in: “Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant” (Ps. 129:2). This is called the optative mode of expression. He therefore asks that the Lord Savior come, through whom he knew that he, together with the rest, would be saved.

When he says, “I have chosen your commandments,” he testifies that he has placed every danger after the love of the Lord. For no one chooses anything good unless he is shown to have rejected the things opposed to it.

### Verse 174

“I have longed for your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation.”

The saints’ more manifest and complete prayer has reached Christ the Lord. The united company of the blessed has disclosed what previously it seemed to request through riddles. For it had longed to see the very one whom, in those earlier times, it believed would come from a virgin’s womb.

And to show that this knowledge had come to it from the divine Scriptures, the text continues: “And your law is my meditation.” In the prophets it had longed for Christ the Lord, since from them it had learned that he had been prophesied as the one who would be born. It was necessary that he be sought with great love, since many ages before he had been revealed as destined for the salvation of the human race.

### Verse 175

“My soul shall live and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.”

He speaks to the very one whom he had desired to behold, promising that his soul would live forever—the soul which he had rightly known to have believed.

“And it shall praise you”: namely, with the new song, which that person, having been renewed unto salvation, ought to sing.

By “judgments” he means those deeds which the Lord promised to perform among his servants: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). He then believes that he will be helped perfectly, when the number of the righteous is placed at the right hand.

### Verse 176

“I have gone astray like a sheep that had perished; seek your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments.”

Although this psalm contains various persons speaking—sometimes the most faithful of the Old Testament, sometimes the elect of the new regeneration, some enduring martyrdoms and others persevering in continual meditation on the Lord’s law—it has nevertheless been made clear that the Catholic Church speaks in the members of Christ, since at the end of the psalm a statement is made that is shown to belong to the Lord’s bride.

For that universal human being who had gone astray in Adam under the law of sin, and who could not return to the Lord’s folds by his own strength because he had lost the gift of wisdom that he possessed, says:

“I have gone astray”—as though he were saying, “I have departed from your way and, blind, entered the trackless wildernesses of vices,” so that the one who does not have the protection of his Shepherd may easily lie open to plunder.

He adds the Gospel comparison: “like a sheep that had perished” (Matt. 18:12). For its shepherd left the ninety-nine on the mountains and, seeking it, was pursued by Jewish ambushes. Yet, through his cross, multiplying it, he does not cease to seek it, nor does he stop gathering it.

The one sheep is the holy congregation of all the faithful, because there is one flock and one shepherd.

Consider how weak a thing human beings are compared with when they are abandoned by Christ’s grace: like a wandering sheep exposed to dangers and to the ravages of wolves, which neither flight can rescue nor bodily strength defend. Whatever the ambusher wishes, it must endure, since no physical power protects it.

And it is rightly said, “that had perished,” so that you may recognize that it was found by the Lord’s mercy, who gathers back those who wander and, through the goodness of his compassion, takes possession of those who are lost.

But that nature, made weak and shown to be more fragile than everything else, conquered and overcame all things through the Lord’s incarnation. It was restored above all things, although previously it had seemed lower than everything, as the Apostle says: “But to which of the angels did he ever say: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet?” (Heb. 1:13).

The text continues: “Seek your servant.” Christ is told, “Seek,” because human weakness cannot seek you out. What has often been said is added, and rightly concludes everything: this righteous person is sought because he is not shown to have forgotten his commandments.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This psalm, which ended with such a confession, must be embraced with complete affection. In length it is immense; in the wonder of its depth, an Ocean; in the beauty of its excellent themes, a paradise. Adorned with the flowers of the virtues, it was sung through the alphabet as an unfading crown of all the Hebrew saints.

And if we seek some comparisons from nature: cranes depict their flights in Greek letters. Such is the force of this practice that, although the birds do not know the letters, they nevertheless arrange them by natural instruction.

Thus we have seen its statements set like brilliant stars in the highest heaven. We have seen a vast sea filled with those fish whom the nets of the apostles drew at the Lord’s command.

Let us also consider that the very order of the psalms reveals no small mysteries of the age to come. It was fitting that songs of ascents should follow the Church gathered from the whole world and dwelling amid the praises of the Lord, so that the likeness of what will occur at the end of the age might be indicated.

For after the entire number of the blessed has been gathered by the Lord’s favor, it is necessary that the blessed people, raised up, ascend to that heavenly Jerusalem.

Therefore we must remember that among those alphabetic psalms which are marked by completing the letters, this psalm is the third: namely, the 110th, the 111th, and the present psalm. Marked by a threefold honor, they are recognized as indicating to us the Trinity of perfect faith. And rightly this reckoning is assigned to the Jerusalem to come, since it is fortified by the strength of complete integrity.

The four other alphabetic psalms—the twenty-fourth, thirty-third, thirty-sixth, and one hundred forty-fourth—which are formed with diminished letters according to the four quarters of the world, are not inappropriately understood to indicate the Catholic Church, which still exists in this world. For it is still imperfect until it suitably obtains the number of the predestined.

Thus the collection of these psalms is recognized as indicating the mysteries of great things.

This psalm is also the fifth instructor of the faithful, as has already been said in the earlier psalms. In it the blessed company sang everything that pertains to ecclesiastical discipline; and it is rightly understood to have been placed in this number. For Noah’s ark itself, which especially bore the type of the Church, is read to have been built over one hundred years.

The Greek letters *Iota* and *Eta*, as they are written among the Greeks, have the value of the number eighteen. Thus this number is shown to contain both the reward of a crown and the honor of the holy name.

## 429. Exposition of Psalm 119

### A Song of Ascents

New and remarkable titles are beginning, but they have already been encountered in the explanation of the preceding psalm. That psalm sang the blessedness of faithful peoples through a unified diversity of merits; these psalms explain it as a mystery of the New and Old Testaments through fifteen ordered steps.

The number seven, as has often been said, signifies the week because of the Sabbath of the Old Testament. The number eight signifies the Lord’s day, on which it is evident that the Lord rose again, and which belongs to the New Testament. Joined together, these numbers are understood to complete the fifteenth number, with the renunciation of the world already begun, since the person has come to detest worldly conduct as the burden of his evils.

Ascending through certain steps of merit, he reaches the perfect and eternal love of the Lord, which is understood to be placed at the summit of the virtues. We shall explain this more clearly in its proper place.

I nevertheless think it should be pointed out that, by divine grace, fifteen steps are placed in these psalms with varied significance according to merits, just as in that temple at Jerusalem which is known to have been completed by Solomon. Thus the present order of the psalms appears to have been prefigured and foretold in that construction. That earthly structure seemed to bear the likeness of the heavenly temple.

Therefore, when we hear of steps in the psalms, we must not imagine that something earthly is to be approached by bodily footsteps; rather, we must understand an ascent of the mind. For “song” has been placed first so that we may apply this chiefly to the soul’s progress.

This step, however, is an ascent of humility: a confession of sins, as was said in Psalm 83: “He has arranged ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:6–7). We shall deserve to climb these steps if, prostrate on account of our offenses, we continually beseech the Lord.

It must be understood, moreover, that these steps are thought to have an ascent only, and not a descent as well. For what we call “songs of ascents” is known to be expressed in Greek as **ᾠδὴ τῶν ἀναβαθμῶν** (*ōdē tōn anabathmōn*), “song of the steps,” signifying steps that extend only toward heavenly things.

Therefore they must be believed already to belong to the blessed, who, by the Lord’s favor, cannot be submerged by any deception. Hence we may perhaps rightly compare these steps in part with Jacob’s ladder. That ladder had both those ascending and those descending; in these steps of the blessed there is ascent alone.

Some also adapt to this comparison the fifteen years added to King Hezekiah’s life, so that the same number may be shown to indicate there as well the course of a perfect life.

## Division of the Psalm

The prophet speaks throughout the entire psalm. In the first part he cries out to the Lord to be delivered from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue. In the second he is deeply afflicted because, while dwelling longer in this life, he is burdened by the mixture of evils as he endures the vices of others.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“To the Lord, when I was troubled, I cried, and he heard me.”

The first step of the virtues begins. In it the prophet, abandoning earthly vices, asks with tearful confession to be freed from the tribulation of this world. The beginning of progress is to abandon carnal offenses and thus beseech the Lord.

For whoever climbs one step certainly leaves the earth and is received in a still somewhat lowly place, where the first elevation is granted. Yet undoubtedly the one who can be found even on this step already possesses the merit of the blessed, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Ps. 31:1).

Therefore he says that he was heard because he had cried out in tribulation. The Lord does not know how to delay when he perceives someone beseeching him with a contrite heart, as is read in Isaiah: “While you are still calling, I shall say: Here I am.”

Observe how beautiful the order of the statements is: first tribulation is placed, then crying out, and thirdly being heard, so that it may be clear that the prayers of the faithful reach the Lord through definite stages.

### Verse 2

“O Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

Placed in that valley of mourning—which is nevertheless now recognized as the steps of faithful souls—he asks to be delivered from harsh accusations and from flattering words composed by crafty persuasion.

For the person who begins to abandon the world because of the abomination of its vices suffers unjust lips at the very beginning of his conversion, when his purpose is mocked with wicked insults.

The wicked say to him: “Why do you torment yourself by fleeing the honors of the world and abandoning human pleasures, so that you lose this world and never attain there what you desire?”

But these things are established on deceitful lips, since they are evidently supported by no firm deliberation of the heart.

When these arguments have achieved little, the persuaders turn to deceitful flattery, saying: “Do not shut yourself away; do not weary yourself with fasting. There will be time for you to do these things.” While they think they are speaking on behalf of the body, they are recognized to burden the interests of the soul in every way.

These, then, are the unjust lips and the deceitful tongue that the person experiences at the very beginning when he is transferred to the Lord’s commands.

Although he may think the words spoken trivial, it was through them that the human race fell and received the condition of death. For when the serpent came to Eve, it first said to her through unjust lips: “Why did the Lord command you not to eat from this tree of paradise?” (Gen. 3:3). When she replied that the Lord had forbidden it, the serpent said through a deceitful tongue: “Eat, and you shall be like gods.”

You therefore see why it was rightly sought with all one’s strength that the prophet be freed from these persuasions, since he knew that through them the human race had been deceived.

### Verse 3

“What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?”

After the preceding cry and fear of impending dangers, the prophet returns to his question, as people commonly do when they think deeply. He hesitates and asks what remedy he should believe could be provided against so monstrous a crime, so that, with some defensive protection set against it, he might safely escape the weapons that had been sent against him.

Although he previously named two things—“from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue”—here he says only, “against a deceitful tongue,” which embraces both. For a deceitful tongue always assumes unjust lips as well.

But so that help might not be delayed, the requested medicine follows. This figure is called *erotēsis*, that is, “question,” when someone proposes to himself, for the sake of practice, what he himself answers.

### Verse 4

“The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with desolating coals.”

Behold the remedy that the anxious man sought; behold the appropriate benefit that destroys unjust lips and confounds the deceitful tongue by the Lord’s power.

“The sharp arrows of the mighty one” are the words of divine law, by which the hearts of heretics and of those who flatter deceitfully are pierced as though by darts, as it is written: “The arrows of the little ones have become their wounds” (Ps. 63:8).

They are “of the mighty one” because no one may resist one whom divine power wills to save.

They are “sharp” because of the swift effect of their operation, since no delay intervenes where that medicine is supplied.

Some have wished to understand the “desolating coals” as the most frightful sinners, extinguished by evil deeds, whose fear and memory are recognized to lay waste our vices, since we fear committing the things we know they endured.

The expression may also be understood in this way: by “desolating coals” we may understand prayers kindled by the fire of charity. These cleanse and purify us from vices in such a way that what the devil had built in us is perceived, by divine favor, to have been laid waste and overturned.

Or perhaps the passage more particularly means what Isaiah says: “And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand he held a burning coal, which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips; and he said: Behold, I have taken away your iniquities and cleansed your sins” (Isa. 6:6–7).

This is now accomplished through the benefit of the holy cross, when we mark our lips with remembrance of the Lord. Perhaps we do not improperly call the sign of the cross a desolating coal, since it drives away the sins of believers, although to the faithless it may appear extinguished.

### Verse 5

“Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar.”

He comes to the second part, where, condemning the vices of the world, he regrets that he has a life of such length.

“Woe is me” is the speech of one who grieves because he is wearied by the length of this world. There is no doubt that various saints uttered this complaint, as Ecclesiastes says: “And I praised all the dead who have already died above all the living who are still alive” (Eccl. 4:2). The Apostle Paul also cries out: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

The prophet therefore rightly groaned in this passage, since he burned with a love very like the Lord’s.

“Sojourning” signifies pilgrimage. We call those people “sojourners” who inhabit foreign lands for a time but are separated far from their homeland. This is rightly said of those whose manner of life is always in heaven, although they are still detained here in the body.

When he says, “has been prolonged,” he expresses the intense feeling of one who desires. For to someone longing to see a blessed homeland, even though the time spent here may be judged short, it is long.

The text continues: “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar.” *Kedar* is a Hebrew name that our language interprets as “darkness.” This refers to the lovers of this world, who, wrapped in dark deeds, love more eagerly the things by which they are known to perish.

To understand briefly the origin of this word: Kedar was the son of Ishmael, who gave his name to his people. Their territory extended as far as the Medes and Persians; they are now called Saracens. By this name he appropriately signifies sinners, among whom he sighs that he still dwells.

A good spirit must necessarily be afflicted whenever it is enclosed within a mixture of wicked people. He says this appropriately because, established on the first step, he has despised the earth and abandoned it through a blessed transformation.

### Verse 6

“My soul has been a long-time sojourner with those who hate peace.”

He repeats with grief what he had said above about sojourning, so that it might appear not only long but also burdensome. And lest you think that this pilgrimage concerned the body alone, he adds, “my soul,” because the mind of the saints undergoes sojourning here, where it is recognized as dwelling without any true delight.

The reason why this sojourning was so harsh follows: the suffering and benevolent person appeared to dwell in this world with quarrelsome people, distorted by heretical perversity.

The one who does not love Christ hates peace, because Christ himself is recognized as our peace, as the Apostle says: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). And what can it be like to hear the one whom we ought always to approach in humble prayer being blasphemed?

### Verse 7

“I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.”

The one who had said above, “My soul has been a sojourner with those who hate peace,” adds this lest he be thought angry or turbulent because of some disputes: “I was peaceful”—with the enemies of peace, with his adversaries, with those who hated him—fulfilling what was spoken through the Apostle: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18).

Then the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44). This is surely the supreme virtue of a Christian: to be found always gentle amid the turbulence of the present age.

Nevertheless, lest this peace itself appear harmful to those who were going astray, because they might not be restrained from evil, he adds: “When I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause.”

For he spoke as a peaceful man—not persecuting, not insulting, but honoring them with words that were exceedingly gentle and comparable to the sweetest drink. Yet those whose minds had hardened in obstinacy attacked him without cause, as though he were an enemy, a foe, or one giving bad advice.

“To attack” is derived from fighting, which truly suits the furious and the proud. He was attacked without cause when, amid inflamed wickedness, he endured utterly false disputes.

We say that something is suffered “without cause” when we endure it without preceding faults, while only a wicked will rages against us. These are the very people from whom he asked to be delivered, of whom he said: “From unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

## Conclusion of the Psalm

You see the prophet abandoning earthly things and already holding the glorious ascent of virtue, yet still groaning because he recognizes that he dwells with the wicked.

Therefore let us see what the progress of the second step is, since the first has already been shown to us with the Lord’s help.

## 431. Psalm 120

### A Song of Ascents

Just as there is nothing new that we can say about these titles, so it remains for us to speak about the psalms that ascend step by step.

At first the prophet was placed in tribulation. Following the example of that publican who, beating his breast, did not dare to lift his eyes toward heaven, he asked to be delivered from unjust lips and a deceitful tongue.

Now, drawing breath as he advances to the second step, he lifts his eyes toward the mountains—namely, toward the holy intercessors—by whose intercession he might merit heavenly gifts.

The prophet speaks this in his own person, although he himself was also a mountain and a remarkable patriarch. But he appropriately reported that he had ascended through these steps so that he might show us, in an ordered account, the distinct kinds of heavenly virtues, which we do not know.

## Division of the Psalm

The prophet, as we have said, ascending by divine generosity toward the heavenly Jerusalem, says in the first section that he lifted his eyes toward the merits of the saints, so that through their prayers he might merit the help he requested and his mind might not succumb to hostile assault.

In the second section he confidently promises himself what he knew he had asked for completely, teaching that whenever we ask for good things with a steadfast heart, we should believe without any doubt that they will be granted to us.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verses 1–2

“I lifted my eyes toward the mountains: from where will help come to me?”

“My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

From this a categorical syllogism is hatched, after the fashion of a bird nurturing its young, as follows:

“My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Everyone whose help is from the Lord who made heaven and earth has help from the true God. Therefore my help is help from the true God.”

Let us now examine the words of the psalm.

Although he was already placed on the second step, the prophet nevertheless hastened to climb higher. He says that he lifted his eyes toward the mountains, to show that the rewards of the Lord are desired all the more in proportion as they are granted with generosity, as was said among other things in Psalm 118: “My soul has longed to desire your statutes at all times” (Ps. 118:20). And in Psalm 83 it is written: “My soul longs and languishes for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3).

When he says, “I lifted,” he shows that he had advanced toward some contemplation. For to lift is to transfer something to higher things.

“My eyes” means the sight of the heart, of which it is written: “Reveal my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18); and: “The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18:9).

For if you understand these as bodily eyes, what benefit could he have gained by choosing to gaze at mountains planted with forests or covered with barren rocks? But if you seek the spiritual meaning, it is entirely profitable to believe that he lifted the eyes of his heart either toward holy men, or toward the divine books, or toward exalted angels. By their greatness and firmness they are truly mountains, from which appropriate help could be sustained.

But lest we perhaps place our hope in the mountains just mentioned, the second verse shows from where help can truly come. Arranging everything in a salutary order, it teaches that we should hope in the mountains while recognizing that through them the Lord provides help to us. From him comes the necessary benefit and saving protection, unshaken happiness, as the Apostle says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

And lest you think that there is another Lord—for this is an equivocal name—he says, “who made heaven and earth,” signifying the Word through whom all things were made.

### Verse 3

“May he not allow your foot to be moved, and may the one who guards you not slumber.”

Having previously asked that protection come to him from the Lord, he suddenly turns and speaks to his own soul, so that it may persevere with steadfast strength in the saving petition.

The foot is the final part of our body, carrying us from place to place at the command of the mind. By analogy with it, we also call our thoughts “feet,” since through them we approach good and evil directions.

Speaking to his own soul, the prophet therefore wishes that these feet—from which the devil fell and through which the first human being collapsed—not be turned by the slipperiness of sins, so that, while the body remains standing, he might not be seen to suffer ruin in his heart.

This fall is pride, which frequently drives servants of God who have already advanced into guilt. While they appear to themselves to be something, they slip into the worst error.

The text continues: “May the one who guards you not slumber.” This is said through a transferred figure drawn from human custom. Tired watchmen commonly suffer theft when heavy sleep overtakes them; with their eyes closed, they cannot see when the flock suffers loss.

Subtly, he wishes for his soul not to be laid waste by the plundering of an enraged enemy through the Lord’s negligence.

The Lord is said to slumber when we grow lukewarm in faith in him. For wherever faith does not sleep, Christ keeps watch.

But if we withdraw from contemplation of him, he too withdraws from our defense, as happened in that boat when the Lord was sleeping while the disciples were negligent (Matt. 8:24). But when their faith was awakened, the Lord also rose from sleep and immediately removed the dangers of the sea from them.

He therefore prays that the Lord may always keep watch, so that he may deserve to have the lights of his shepherd’s eyes fixed upon him.

### Verse 4

“Behold, the one who guards Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.”

This statement is a likeness of the preceding one. Earlier he wished this for his own soul; here he declares that it must be observed by the faithful people.

Israel, as we have often said, is interpreted as “a man who sees God.” Therefore the Lord is not said to slumber over those who see God. For in us his appearance truly becomes such as the gaze of our mind has been toward him.

Those truly see God who contemplate without hesitation not only his humanity but also the power of his divinity.

His incarnation is, as the Gospel says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). His divinity, as the same evangelist testifies, is: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1).

Whoever believes this will be a most genuine Israel; and the Lord, guarding him, shall neither slumber nor sleep.

### Verse 5

“The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection, over the hand of your right side.”

He comes to the second section, where he confidently promises himself what he appeared faithfully to have sought.

It should also be noted that, although we have said these words were turned toward the soul, they are nevertheless most suitably referred to the members of the Church.

He says: “The Lord guards you”—that is, the one who made heaven and earth. And lest this guarding be able to contain any uncertainty, he adds: “The Lord is your protection.” For where there is divine protection, who could doubt that there is secure guardianship?

When he says, “The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection,” the figure is *epembasis*, which in Latin is called “repetition.”

He clearly shows where this protection can be: “over the hand of your right side.” “Hand” is a common term, for there is both a right hand and a left. But “right” is rightly placed here, where the Lord is shown to have promised all prosperous things.

For it is written in Proverbs: “Length of days and years of life are in his right hand” (Prov. 3:16), which signifies eternal happiness.

“In his left hand are riches and glory,” signifying the goods of this world, which there is no doubt can also be given by him.

His right hand is also the place to which the saints are separated to receive rewards. His left is the place where sinners are to be condemned to eternal punishment: the former because they desired heavenly things, the latter because they pursued worldly things.

We also read that sinners made a right hand for themselves, although it is in fact a left hand. Concerning them the same prophet will say in Psalm 143: “Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Ps. 143:8).

That alone is truly to be called the right hand where the Lord’s grace is shown to have been bestowed.

### Verse 6

“By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night.”

These elements indeed have the nature of scorching our bodies when they are heated by the warmth of summer. But since this is not the prophet’s intention—that we should understand the passage entirely in terms of the body, when he wishes provision always to be made for souls—we should understand “day and night,” that is, “sun and moon,” as adversities and prosperities, through which the life of the human race is contained in varying alternation.

Thus it is said elsewhere: “By day I cried out, and by night before you” (Ps. 87:2). This signifies the whole span of life, because one must always cry out to the Lord.

Therefore the Lord does not permit such people to be led into guilt or to be scorched when scandal intervenes, since he provides them the help of his protection.

In this way he guarded the Israelite people by the gift of his benefits: by day he protected them with a cloud, and by night he illuminated them with a fiery column. He now does this secretly in his servants when he defends them from the fiercest enemy amid prosperity and tribulation.

### Verse 7

“The Lord guards you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul.”

Divine protection is promised in various ways. It not only rescues from adversities, but also makes people blessed and leads them to the kingdom of heaven.

He adds, “from every evil.” But this evil must not be understood as mortality understands it: suffering bereavements, being weighed down by the greatest losses, being oppressed by poverty, and the other things that lovers of this age consider most grievous.

Rather, he means the evil that removes divine grace, destroys the soul, and empties all the Lord’s promises.

And because he knew that holy men had been tortured by enormous sufferings and had reached the rewards of martyrdom through the loss of the body, he added: “May the Lord guard your soul”—the only thing he preserves in the saints, who, through the loss of the body, attain the gifts of eternal light.

**Verse 8.** “May the Lord guard your going in and your going out, from now and forever.” After the prayer had been expressed in various and diverse ways that the Lord’s mercy might guard him, he came to the end of the psalm [Col. 0908D] and brought everything to a close. For he says: “May the Lord guard your going in.” We properly understand this as said of the martyrs, whose entrance must be guarded by the Lord, lest they yield either to the violence of torments or be led astray by the enticement of flatteries. Therefore the prophet rightly desires that their entrance be guarded, since without the Lord they can in no way be most cautious, as it is said in the Gospel: “When you come before rulers and authorities, do not consider how or what you shall speak; for it will be given to you in that hour how or what you shall speak” (Matt. X, 19). He adds also, “and your going out,” in which there is complete perfection, when true and irreproachable confession remains in them until the end of life, as he says in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end, this one will be saved” (ibid., 22). He therefore protects the entrance; [Col. 0909A] he also guards the exit, so that the martyrs may both profess the truth and not be overcome by any excess of punishments. But observe what he added to this consummation: “from now and forever.” For whoever perseveres will possess eternal benefits; nor can there be an end there, where joy will be without end.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How well did the second prophetic degree contain its feet with unwavering firmness! How well did he grow above himself, who climbed toward stronger merits! Let us see what he undertakes in the third degree, since here he sought the Lord’s protection with great desire.

# Psalm 121

### A Song of Degrees

[Col. 0909B]

We have heard of a degree; let us understand an ascent toward higher things. Yet this ascent is firm, being preserved while the Lord guards it: the more one advances in merits, the more one prostrates oneself in submission of mind. Behold, the prophet is now raised up to the third degree, made higher than the second, and he declares that he has taken the beginning of the psalm from that very joy.

### Division of the Psalm

In the first part the prophet rejoices that he has been summoned and is destined to come to the heavenly Jerusalem, where the saints already dwell in secure prosperity and, with the Lord’s mercy granting it, will judge together with him. In the second part he speaks to the citizens of Jerusalem, wishing them an abundance of peace, which he says he proclaimed out of love for the brethren and [Col. 0909C] love for the Lord.

### Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord.” A very fitting and salutary cause of joy is placed first, so that it might make the hearers both cheerful and attentive. But lest you think that this was an ordinary human joy, he shows over what perfect good he declares himself to rejoice, since he testifies that he is going into the house of the Lord. O worthy exultation, to hasten there from which no one would ever wish to depart! Yet we must investigate who said these things to the prophet. Clearly, the Holy Spirit, who spoke to his heart with a silent voice. The prophet therefore heard not with the ear but with the mind, not through speech but through divine inspiration; [Col. 0909D] inwardly forewarned, he burst forth into these words of exultation. It follows: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” This is the house that receives only the righteous, contains angels, and is worthy to behold the very Author of all creatures; the desirable house, the house built of living stones. Of it another psalm says: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI, 4).

**Verse 2.** “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem.” Since the prophet had said that the eternal house had been promised to him, he now says that, through this foreshadowing of future things, he is standing in it—the place he desired with utmost zeal to reach—so that we may recognize that holy men [Col. 0910A] already stand in spirit in that Jerusalem when they are proved to remain in the Lord’s commandments. In truth, one is said to stand in that place in which no one can fall. Finally, consider what he says: “Our feet were standing.” For one stands where one always remains with firm resolve. Yet this standing has no defect and is not exhausted by any labor; persevering in its own strength, it is wearied by no fatigue. It follows: “in your courts, Jerusalem.” Here he uses “courts” for the inner chambers; a court is the entrance of a house, in which the inhabitants cannot remain. But this is spoken figuratively, with the part standing for the whole.

**Verse 3.** “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same.” Lest you suppose that the Jerusalem he had mentioned was earthly, he indicates, with marvelous subtlety of distinction, that it is the heavenly [Col. 0910B] city. For he first says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.” It is indeed being built, since daily, up to the consummation of the world, it is constructed through spiritual work from living stones—that is, from confessors, martyrs, and those devoted to the Lord with sincere minds. He adds, “as a city,” in order to show that the likeness of a city exists in it. For although every city is said to derive its name from citizens, that city is more truly so called which is shown to contain citizens of one mind.

We must understand that the city now in progress contains undifferentiated and mixed peoples; but the city that is to come receives, without doubt, only the perfect. This city is shaken by conflicts; that one rejoices in continual security. This one is full of penitents; that one knows no tears. This one believes in hope; [Col. 0910C] that one sees God face to face. Thus, although there are two cities, the faithful are believed to be one future people.

What follows is a very appropriate but obscure statement: “whose participation is in the same,” that is, the participation of this city is in the Lord the Savior, who is properly “in the same.” “In the same” signifies eternity, which never ceases to be what it is but always remains in one and the same condition: unfailing virtue, unchangeable power, substance existing in itself, effectively able to do all that it wills. Thus he also said of himself to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14); and shortly afterward: “He who is has sent me to you” (Ps. CI, 27, 28). In another psalm it is said to him: “All things will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail.” Therefore [Col. 0910D] it belongs to the Creator alone to be “in the same.” For the angel who thought that he was this immediately fell; he was not, from himself, what he was, and therefore could not be “in the same.”

This was also said in the fourth psalm: “In peace, in the same, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV, 9). We recognize this kind of expression as proper to the divine Scriptures. The participation, therefore—the fellowship and communion—of this city is, as we have said, with the Lord the Savior, just as he himself also testifies in the Gospel: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24). In that city the Lord will be, and the saints will be participants in him without doubt, insofar as he himself grants it.

The prophet Isaiah also describes this city with marvelous [Col. 0911A] praise, saying: “Your walls shall be called Salvation, and your gates Joy. The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the rising of the moon shine for you by night; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your glory. For your sun shall not set, and your moon shall not fail; for the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed, and all your people shall be righteous, and they shall possess the land as an inheritance forever” (Isa. LX, 18–21).

The apostle John likewise distinguishes the astonishing mysteries of this city in his marvelous proclamation in the Apocalypse, so that you may almost believe yourself to be present, while nevertheless recognizing that you are situated elsewhere. As for the fact that he placed “Jerusalem” at the end of the preceding verse and repeated it in the present chapter, this is the figure called anadiplosis, that is, the repetition of a word. It differs from epembasis, which we discussed in the preceding psalm, in this respect: there, a word may be repeated after some intervening words; here, it is repeated without anything else intervening.

[Col. 0911B]

**Verse 4.** “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord: the testimony of Israel, to confess your name, O Lord.” By saying “there,” he signifies the city of Jerusalem, which above he called “whose participation is in the same.” And so that you might recognize it as heavenly, he added, “went up.” The blessed always ascend to it, because they advance through continual exercise.

He added “tribes,” among which the Israelite people were distributed. For that nation had twelve tribes according to the number of Jacob’s sons, just as the Roman people had thirty-five curiae. In these tribes, therefore, he signifies the saints who confessed that the Lord the Savior is God. For, in order to distinguish these tribes of the faithful [Col. 0911C] from the unbelieving, he added, “the tribes of the Lord.” They could not be his unless they had believed in him with pure minds. For it is evident that other tribes belonged to the devil, choosing to be separated from Christ by impious will; to them he said in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

434 “the tribes of the Lord.” They could not be his unless they had believed in him with pure minds. For it is evident that other tribes belonged to the devil, choosing to be separated from Christ by impious will; to them he said in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII, 44).

He briefly indicated what sort these tribes of the Lord would be: “The testimony of Israel,” that is, those who bear witness to holiness and are a proof of those who see God. Testimony provides confirmation for those who do not know, so that they may believe that those who have seen blessed men distinguished by the uprightness of their deeds are truly servants of God. Lest this remain doubtful to you, he added: “to confess your name.” For “to confess” means “to praise,” since all the saints will celebrate the Lord’s praises with the angels. This is the true testimony of Israel, when the Lord’s praises are sung with most devoted love. Thus that future city has been described with shining blessedness and bestowed honor.

[Col. 0911D]

**Verse 5.** “For there the thrones sat in judgment, thrones over the house of David.” Speaking of those whom he had previously said had gone up there, lest you perhaps think that they would receive less honor, he says: “For there they sat.” There, certainly, where they went up, and where they will judge with the Lord. Such great honor is promised to the saints that they will even be worthy to judge with that heavenly Judge, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28). An honorable [Col. 0912A] session, an astonishing dignity: by God’s grace, human beings become judges, though they had been made guilty by sins!

But since the Lord says both things that are written—“Go into eternal fire,” and “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV, 41, 34), and so forth—how will the saints judge with the Lord? They will truly judge with him when, having already been purified in mind and established in the most perfect contemplation, they will undoubtedly judge that what they know to have been established by the Lord ought to be done. For the will of those hearing alike makes the judgment one, even though the others are known to have remained silent.

The statement “they sat” uses the past tense for the future, because all God’s words are so firm that, although they are believed to be still to come, you may judge them already accomplished by the stability of their nature. But let us investigate [Col. 0912B] what it means for him to say that thrones sat. It is appropriate, because holy men are God’s thrones; while he sits in them, his grace illuminates them with the majesty of his presence, as it is written: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Isa. LXVI, 12); and elsewhere: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?”

It follows: “in judgment.” In what judgment, if not that future judgment of which it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22)? Although he did not specify which judgment he intended, we nevertheless understand by sound reasoning that it is the one in which the saints will sit and judge together with the Lord.

You frequently find this said in the divine Scriptures: the thing itself that is meant is not expressed, yet what can reasonably be understood is left for people to infer. Thus it was said in another psalm: [Col. 0912C] “Who is the man who desires life?” (Ps. XXXIII, 13). And in the Gospel the Lord says: “If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX, 17). He did not say “eternal,” although that is what must be understood in every respect. This figure is called ellipsis, and because a necessary expression is lacking from it, it is called deficiency.

Yet he subsequently explains by praise what these thrones are, saying: “thrones over the house of David.” By “over the house” he means over the family of Christ, because some of the saints will be more illustrious there than the remaining faithful, just as the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. XV, 41–42). If it is glorious here for one servant, among his fellow servants, to know something more of his master’s mind, how much more remarkable may it be in Christ’s house to possess a greater contemplation of the Lord, so that one differs from another to the extent that one has been granted to behold his divinity more fully.

“David,” moreover, signifies Christ, taking the name from his human [Col. 0912D] parentage. Observe how the description of that city has been constructed: he says what is to be done there, how it is built, who will ascend there, and what they will do there. This figure is called characterismos, which in Latin is called *informatio* or *descriptio*—“formation” or “description.”

[Col. 0913A]

**Verse 6.** “Ask for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem, and abundance for those who love you.” The prophet has reached the second section, where he addresses those who, by the Lord’s favor, will judge. This word is equivocal. In this place, “ask” means “inquire,” not “supplicate.” It is fitting for the judge to investigate and examine everything; but this does not happen there through words or spoken questioning, but through silent consideration of the mind.

All will judge with the Lord, as has been said, when, enlightened and sanctified, they will truly recognize that to be the truth which the Lord will declare with his own mouth. For the Lord seeks the peaceful; the entire company of the saints also seeks the peaceful—those who are completely filled with charity, who abound in moderation, and who are exalted by devout humility. For the saints also wish to seek what they know the Lord can love.

But whose peace does he say this is? Jerusalem’s, certainly—that is, the faithful people who are received into the eternity of peace at the time of judgment. The prophet therefore [Col. 0913B] announces what he knows is to come, so that those who will judge with the Lord may rejoice with such men in that homeland: men who love peace here and there receive the rewards of eternal peace.

And because he placed “Jerusalem” at the end of the sentence, he turned to it and embraced it in a very brief declaration: “Abundance for those who love you.” It is clear that all good things abound for those who love Jerusalem. Those who were poor here will there be rich in every good; those who were fragile here will there be unfailing; those who were temporal here will there be eternal. Whatever can be good appears to be contained in this heavenly abundance.

**Verse 7.** “Let peace be within your strength, and abundance in your towers.” He still speaks to Jerusalem, wishing for it such things as he knows are to come. For its strength [Col. 0913C] is, without doubt, the peace of the saints, which is also called charity, concerning which it is written: “God is charity” (1 John IV, 16). Through it they become one; through it they are deemed worthy to be the Creator’s temple; and whatever is promised to them is granted with regard to it.

This is the peace shaken by no wars and disturbed by no sedition; what is bestowed there through Christ’s mercy will be possessed without end. Peace is so called either from *parcere*, “to spare,” or from *pascere*, “to nourish.”

It follows: “and abundance in your towers.” This is the abundance of which he said above: “and abundance for those who love you.” But here something more significant seems to be expressed through “towers,” so that you might understand this abundance as not equal for all, but greater for some. Towers defend cities by their position and height and receive approaching enemies [Col. 0913D] at the first line. Hence we rightly understand the martyrs to be signified: by the opposition of their bodies they defend the city of God through devout confession, and, like lofty buildings, they are known to resist the enemies of the faith.

**Verse 8.** “For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I was speaking peace concerning you.” In the manner of perfected men, he proclaims peace and displays the signs of his own peace. For he says that he proclaimed this peace of the Church for the sake of his brothers and neighbors, so that, instructed in this virtue of concord, they might love and seek unity.

He therefore did what he taught: out of love for the brethren he proclaimed what he urged would benefit all [ms. G. and ed., *sciebat*, “knew”]. He thus admonishes us that no one should teach for the sake of his own praises or advantages, but should labor for his brothers [Col. 0914A] and neighbors with a merciful spirit, as the Apostle says: “Not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many” (1 Cor. X, 33).

He does not therefore say that he spoke of that peace of the future age for his own temporal advantage, but for the sake of his brothers and neighbors, so that, desiring it for their salvation, they might bind themselves together in the bond of unanimity [ed., *colligerent*, “might gather/bind themselves”; base text, *colligarent*, “might bind themselves together”]. When he says “concerning you,” he still indicates that he is speaking to Jerusalem, in which the assembly of the saints exists—that is, the most blessed uniting of peoples.

**Verse 9.** “For the sake of the house of the Lord my God [mss. A, B, *nostri*, ‘our’], I sought good things for you.” Lest anyone think that affection ought to be directed toward some other thing in such a way that the love of the Lord seemed to be neglected, he added why he sought good things for Jerusalem: namely, because it is the house of the Lord, to whom whatever love is expended is rightly referred.

[Col. 0914B]

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider what words of charity the prophet poured forth in the third degree, and let us rejoice in his progress, with the Lord granting it. For the more any of the saints advances by ascending, the higher and sweeter are the words he brings forth.

# Psalm 122

### A Song of Degrees

It is pleasant to observe how this prophetic ascent progresses and, seeking higher things little by little, displays to us the signs of its perfection. For the one who previously raised his eyes toward the mountains has now lifted the eyes of his heart toward the Lord himself, so that he who was striving to ascend to higher places by spiritual steps [Col. 0914C] might happily draw near to divine mercy.

A beautiful spectacle: human beings rising toward God and lifting this sluggish mass toward the rewards of heavenly grace! Yet this is accomplished only by him who commanded Lazarus to come forth from the tomb (John XI, 43), who rescued Peter when he was sinking by extending his right hand (Matt. XIV, 31), who translated Elijah and Enoch while they were still alive (2 Kings II, 11; Gen. V, 24), and who performs similar things daily through the power of the Divinity.

Those who are one here in charity ascend these degrees. For they cannot hasten to the Head unless they have been deemed worthy to be members of Christ. Therefore, just as we have contemplated this marvelous ascent with the heart, so now let us examine the height of the psalm with attentive mind.

### Division of the Psalm

[Col. 0914D]

The prophet, fearing to lose what he held and cautious in the very part through which he had grown, devoutly carries out the perseverance of his prayers at the outset, so that the gifts he has received may be preserved for him by the divine reward. Second, he begs the Lord to grant him mercy, because, at the devil’s instigation, he suffered many adversities from those who attacked him; although they could not defile him by their association, at least they might wound him with proud contempt.

### Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “To you I have lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven” [mss. A, B, F, “in the heavens”]. Humanity is salutarily admonished to seek help from the place from which it believes an unconquerable [Col. 0915A] defense will come. For those who are presumptuous in heart and boast of worldly power, if provoked by some injury, run back to riches and flee for refuge to perishable patronage, so that they may exact punishment from the enemy who presumed to inflict an outrage. But God’s servants, governing themselves in a most patient way of life, whatever scandal or tribulation they endure, lift their eyes to the Lord and look toward him, trusting that they can truly be saved by him.

It follows: “who dwell in heaven.” We read that the Lord dwells in many ways, as in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10). He is also said to dwell in the saints, as it is written in Leviticus: “I shall dwell among them, and I shall walk in them, and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (Lev. XXVI, 12). Of these the Apostle [Col. 0915B] also says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. III, 16). The Gospel likewise testifies concerning both: “That all may be one, and I in them, and you in me” (John XVII, 21). We also read that the Lord sits in heaven, as in the words: “Heaven is my throne; but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI, 1), and elsewhere: “Heaven belongs to the Lord, but the earth he gave to the sons of men” (Ps. CXIII, 16).

**Verse 2.** “Behold, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters.” Let us look inwardly at what these comparisons signify for us. Servants attend to the hands of their masters, either when they desire to be nourished by them, so that they may escape the necessities of every want, or when they are ordered to be beaten for their faults until they hear, “Spare me.” For both things lie within the power of masters: either the hope of restraint, or the eventual end of punishment. It is fitting for us to do both, so that we may always lift our eyes to the Lord, both when we suffer some want and when we are beaten for certain excesses.

This verse and the following are expressed through the figure of [Col. 0915C] *homoeosis*, by which the explanation of a less-known matter is made clear through the likeness of something better known.

**Verse 3.** “And as the eyes of a maidservant are toward the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” [mss. A, B, F, “our”]. Some wish to apply this verse also to the Lord in such a way that they say that God himself is the Lord, on account of the example: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I, 24). But lest the difference of sex [Col. 0915D] offend anyone, it may perhaps be understood in the following way. Above he made a comparison between servants and masters; and lest the female sex think itself excluded, other likenesses are added here also, because a maidservant attends to the hands of her mistress just as servants do to the hands of their masters.

The following statement, however, includes both sexes: “so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.” Thus, when this is said, the preceding comparison is explained, so that whether we seek something prosperous from the Lord or endure torments of mind or body, we may always lift our eyes toward the Lord. He also added “our,” so that either sex might understand this as spoken of itself. He added, “until he has mercy on us,” to show that women and men alike must seek divine benefits [Col. 0916A] under patience [mss. A, B, F, “under repentance”] and continually entreat him.

The word “until” is equivocal in the divine Scriptures. Sometimes it signifies that something is done temporally, as in the hundred-ninth psalm: “Until I place your enemies as the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1). But sometimes it signifies “always,” as the present psalm declares: “until he has mercy on us”—as though our eyes ought not to be in his hands even after he has shown us mercy. The same is true of the Gospel saying: “He did not know her until she bore her firstborn son” (Matt. I, 25), although it is established that he never knew her as a wife. Therefore “until” is rightly understood here to mean “always,” although it may appear to have been spoken temporally. This kind of expression must be counted among the distinctive features of divine Scripture.

[Col. 0916B]

**Verse 4.** “Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we have been filled exceedingly with contempt” [mss. A, B, F, “with disdain”]. He has reached the second entrance, where he begs for mercy by considering his contempt and reproach. For that servant who was beaten by continual affliction from evils, and had fixed his eyes on the Lord’s mercy, breaks forth into a necessary cry and laments that mercy must be shown him in a doubled petition, because his body suffered from torments while his soul labored under reproaches. This properly refers to the martyrs, who, by God’s granting it, overcome the injury of sufferings through the vitality of their spirit.

The reason for this repeated appeal for mercy is then added: “for we have been filled exceedingly with contempt.” God’s servants are filled with contempt [Col. 0916C] when they are torn by blows, when they are burned by raging flames, and when they are drowned in the deepest waters. For unless they were despised exceedingly, they could not endure such things. “Filled exceedingly” signifies an abundance of sufferings, which nevertheless they testify that they endured eagerly and willingly.

**Verse 5.** “And our soul has been filled exceedingly: with the reproach of the prosperous, and the disdain of the proud.” Since above he had said that he was filled with the contempt of those who seemed happy to themselves, and had asserted that his body was torn by painful beating, he now says that his soul too was filled with reproaches and disdain, so that nothing remained that was not subjected to the outrage of the most grievous suffering.

He placed “the reproach of the prosperous” [Col. 0916D] because, while the persecutors were rich and joyful, they charged holy men’s poverty and humility against them in an unjust attack, saying: “What benefit is it to you not to possess the riches of the world and to pursue some future things—I know not what—while abandoning present joys and loving sadness more? Behold, I possess what I see; you hope for what you vainly imagine.” It follows: “and the disdain of the proud.” The proud despise the humble when they hear such exhortations from them, which they disdain to obey. For while the proud love present things and do not consider the future, they rise more fiercely in the wickedness of their perversity against those who strive to serve the Lord’s rules.

Yet at the coming judgment an opposite reversal [Col. 0917A] will occur for these people: the prosperous and the proud will come into reproach and disdain, as Solomon says of such men: “What did pride profit us, or what did the boast of riches bring us?” (Wis. V, 8), and so forth.

It should plainly be understood that the order of ordinary eloquence would have required him to say: “Our soul has been filled exceedingly with the reproach of the prosperous and the disdain of the proud.” But when he says, “Our soul has been filled exceedingly, the reproach of the prosperous and the disdain of the proud,” this seems to be characteristic of divine Scripture. Yet it should not be attributed to a fault, but rather to the fact that it has not yet been grasped by human rules.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Rightly did this man, who had already ascended four degrees, endure the envy of the foolish, since prosperous circumstances always bite their adversaries, when one who is shown to devote himself to the advancement of the soul is believed to be hindered by vain accusations. Let us contemplate a man marvelous in his perseverance in prayer and not made numb by any mockeries, but curing diverse troubles and diverse wounds with one medicine: he always lifts his eyes to the Lord.

# Psalm 123

### A Song of Degrees

[Col. 0917B]

The prophet testifies that he ascends these degrees both as many in one and as one in many, since he is shown to have spoken in these psalms sometimes in the plural number and sometimes in the singular. Not without reason: the people of God are one body of Christ, and the devoted people are again shown to be poured forth through each of the [Col. 0917C] faithful. Therefore, whether one person or many are speaking, the Church nevertheless sings as one. These degrees, however, are established on that journey where the King himself is known to have offered himself as the way for us. If, by his granting it, we walk along it faithfully and humbly, we arrive at his holy tribunals.

### Division of the Psalm

The holy confessors, remembering how many dangers they escaped through divine mercy as though from the force of a torrent, first confess that they were delivered from so many raging calamities by God’s mercy alone. Second, they give thanks because they were not deceived by their persecutors; rather, in a reversal, the plots were crushed upon the plotters themselves, and they were certainly rescued.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0917D]

**Verse 1.** “Unless the Lord had been among us, let Israel now say.” Sudden joy arising from remembrance of past danger customarily fails to maintain the normal order of words. The confessors marvel at how they escaped their pursuers, how torments did not overcome human frailty, how, when the body failed, the mind strengthened by faith did not yield; and they placed at the beginning a small portion of the words that had arisen from a profound meaning. Yet they explain them subsequently, so that neither admiration at such great dangers might be removed nor the completeness of the speech be delayed for long.

The usual sentence would have been: “We could in no way have overcome the dangers inflicted upon us, unless the Lord had been among us” [Col. 0918A]. At the same time, the pernicious habit of human presumption is removed, since it is said that neither our riches, nor counsel, nor strength came to our aid, but that the Lord’s mercy alone delivered us.

It follows: “let Israel now say.” It is recognized as exceedingly salutary that the Lord’s authority decrees that such things be done [ms. F. and ed., “that such a thing be done”]. For since they themselves had been saved, the remaining blessed were rightly urged to give thanks. This is the power of charity and unity: if something favorable is granted to one person, all rejoice as though it had come to them; and, conversely, if something adverse occurs, all grieve as though it had happened to them. Therefore he added below [Col. 0918B] what Israel should say. And so whoever wishes to be Israel should not refuse to say such things with a pure heart.

**Verse 2.** “Unless the Lord had been among us, when men rose up against us.” The devout confessors who began speaking at the beginning of the psalm urge Israel to say both this verse and the three that follow, since, although each person may be released from particular dangers, he is delivered by the almighty Lord.

Although one sentence extends through all these verses, we nevertheless set down the individual verses according to our custom, so that we may indicate what must be supplied from one verse in order to explain the meaning of another. The second verse accordingly begins with the sense still pending, [Col. 0918C] as happened already in the first, saying that Israel was delivered by the Lord’s grace when wicked men were savagely pursuing them.

For how could fragile flesh suffice, or the changeability of the human mind remain firm, unless the Lord were among them? For when he is in us and does not depart because of the fault of our perversity, we remain always safe and always unharmed, because the wickedness of our persecutors does not prevail against the one for whom the grace of divine power sets itself in opposition.

Therefore we must observe that in these two verses just mentioned, and in the three that follow, there is the figure of anaphora, since the same words are known to be repeated at the beginnings of the verses. This figure is especially effective in moving the emotions.

**Verse 3.** “Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive, when their anger was kindled against us.” The middle part of this verse answers the preceding material. The sense must be joined in this way [Col. 0918D]: “Unless the Lord had been among us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”

Here we must place a full stop, so that what follows may answer us again with a complete connection of words. For when he says “they would have swallowed us alive,” ordinary human practice does not consist in swallowing enemies alive. We are swallowed alive when we are plunged, through abominable perversity, either into heretical depravity or into the deep plunge of sins. This could have happened to holy men unless heavenly power had delivered them.

The remaining half of this verse, however, is clearly to be joined to the lower sentence. For he says: “When their anger was kindled against us.” He said “was kindled,” because they had no just causes. Anger and envy lack judgment when they pursue their desires with a headlong mind, as Job also says: “Anger kills the fool, and envy slays the simple” (Job V, 2).

For what just cause could they have had against the servants of God, when they presumed to despise in them the Author of all things? “Mind” is a Greek expression [Col. 0919A], derived from *anemos* (ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνέμου), that is, because its mobility is compared with the swiftest winds; or from *anaimos* (ἄναιμος), “bloodless,” since it is not corporeal—as we explained in the book that, with the Lord’s favor, we wrote concerning the Soul.

### Verse 4
