“Perhaps they would have swallowed us like water: the torrent passed over our soul.”

These verses too are joined together in a similar way. For, if it is read thus, the sentence is complete and beyond doubt: “When their anger was kindled against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us” [Col. 0919B]. Here he wishes the water to be understood as the wicked peoples of the pagans, who seemed, as though by an exceedingly great flood, to have occupied earthly hearts with the worship of idols. They desired to swallow the servants of God when they tried to lead Christians into their own rites. But divine power delivered them—the same power that extended its hand to the apostle Peter so that he would not sink.

The ancients, however, called water that from which all things came into being, believing that everything had been produced from it. It follows: “The torrent passed over our soul.” A torrent is—as we have already said—a river suddenly roused by winter rains, known both for its swiftness and for its muddy character, because it does not pour forth from a pure spring but is sullied by earthly contaminations. To this the turbid course of this age is rightly compared: it does not flow from any spring of truth but is formed by the storm of every evil [Col. 0919C].

This is the torrent from which the Lord also drank, concerning which it was already said: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Psalm 109:7). Thus Israel is rightly said to have passed over it, since its head was foretold to have drunk from it. Yet throughout all these things there is one true confession: that we are delivered from such great dangers solely by the Lord’s mercy.

### Verse 5

“Perhaps our soul would have passed through intolerable water.”

We must be attentive in asking why this part of the prayer, “perhaps,” is repeated so many times, since it is not fitting for the faithful to doubt that we could not pass through the dangers of the world by ourselves, unless the Lord were within us. This is what the true, catholic Church confesses. Yet it is the custom of great danger that, whenever we are delivered from the greatest calamity, we say with apparent hesitation [Col. 0919D], “Do you suppose we have escaped?”—although we have no doubt whatsoever that we have escaped.

Thus elsewhere, in a matter that is certain, it is said: “Had not your law been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation” (Psalm 118:92). The prophet Tobias likewise says: “Turn back, sinners, and do justice before the Lord; who knows whether he may desire you and show you mercy” (Tobit 13:8)? And elsewhere it is written: “Lift up your eyes to heaven with weeping; perhaps the Lord will have mercy on us and save you” (Judith 7:18, 24).

You see that “perhaps” is placed in so many passages where there was no room for uncertainty. Therefore we rightly call this verbal hesitation not a defect but the great and complete constancy of faith proper to divine Scripture [Col. 0920A]—something that worldly usage customarily employs only in doubtful and uncertain matters. Accordingly, an expression of this kind is not a weakness of the strongest faith but a great intensification of danger.

For why would they doubt that their souls had escaped intolerable water, when just above they had confessed: “The torrent passed over our soul”? He added, “intolerable water.” In the same way, he calls the water “intolerable” which he confessed that they had endured. For it could not otherwise have been escaped unless, strengthened by God’s grace, they had endured everything.

Water is therefore called intolerable when our weakness is being considered. The abyss of sins and the storm of crimes cannot be endured when they find us separated from the Lord’s protection. Conversely, everything becomes tolerable when God dwells in his saints. Then neither error steals upon us, nor lust drags us away, nor windy pride prevails, nor the malicious suggestion of the ancient enemy rages [Col. 0920B].

### Verse 6

“Blessed is the Lord, who has not given us as prey to their teeth.”

The devout confessors have reached the second part of their account, in which they give thanks to the Lord because they did not fall according to the wishes of their enemies; rather, those who preferred to destroy them were themselves crushed. And observe how savagely the enemies’ will is portrayed: they seemed, after the manner of wild beasts, to attack human innocence with their teeth. The same is said of the devil: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8).

### Verse 7

“Our soul, like a sparrow, has been snatched from the snare of the hunters” [Col. 0920C].

### Verse 8

“The snare has been crushed, and we have been set free.”

The saints rightly say this, since although their body was afflicted, their soul was preserved under the Lord’s protection. For the sparrow—as we have often said—is an exceedingly cautious bird that lives on walls, skillfully avoids traps that have been set, and is not easily caught; it is always known to come anxiously in search of food.

The snare of the hunters is any sweetness of this world set before us. We are caught in it when it is judged to be pleasant, as it is written concerning women: “The eye of a prostitute is the sinner’s snare” (Proverbs 7). The same must be understood of avarice, pride, and all vices.

But observe what they added: that the snare was crushed and that they had been set free. Truly, [Col. 0920D] the one who hastens to burden another burdens himself; and, as it is written: “He falls into the pit who strives to prepare it for another” (Ecclesiasticus 27:29).

Moreover, observe that he says not that the snare was broken but that it was crushed. We do not call anything made of leather or hemp “crushed,” but only what is shown to possess the hardness of some metal. Therefore it is called “crushed” so that it might reveal both the force of the suffering and the power of the deliverer. Accordingly, once the snare has been crushed, they rightly say that they have been set free, when those who lay ambush are brought to nothing because they cannot capture those whom they tried to deceive.

### Verse 9

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

They give the reason why that snare was crushed: nothing can prevail against the one whom divine power assists [Col. 0921A]. Why, fools, do you seek to lay ambushes against his servants, when you have heard that by a momentary command he established heaven and earth? It is easy for him to destroy your [ed., our] snares, since, whenever he wills, he is accustomed to scatter every evil.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How fittingly blessed devotion ascended in the fifth stage of the confessors, so that those who, with the Lord’s help, had been able to overcome bodily senses might rejoice in the advancement of the fifth place! But so that they would not fall or stagger through bodily weakness, that remedial humility of the human race provided protection: they were to place all their hope in the Lord and attribute no good to themselves through ruinous presumption.

## Psalm 124

### A Song of Ascents

[Col. 0921B]

Knowing the unstable step of human weakness, the Lord constructed this path of virtues with certain stages, so that our desire might advance more securely toward difficult heights when its foot was placed on level ground. Thus we tread upon the backs of the steps without suffering an uneven ascent. Yet although this saving staircase seems to have been constructed as a suitable remedy, we stand firm by no strength unless we are held there by the Lord’s governance [mss. A, B, F: “guarded”]. This ascent, however, takes place in the mind, not in the body. For, sitting in one place and confined within a cell, we ascend these steps more effectively than if we flew about on human lips [Col. 0921C]. Therefore the prophet cries out that we must trust in the Lord, lest we labor in vain.

### Division of the Psalm

As the prophet ascends the sixth step, which is considered perfect in the discipline of numbers, he strengthens the faithful people with his first exhortation, saying that those who have placed their confidence in the Lord’s power can in no way be shaken. He gives the reason why he does not permit sinners to increase above the lot of the righteous. Secondly, he prays that prosperity may come to the upright and punishment to the wicked.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he shall not be shaken forever who dwells in Jerusalem” [Col. 0921D].

The prophetic utterance addresses everyone in general, since those who remain steadfast here in true religion and place their hope in the Lord’s protection stand with the firmest solidity, like Zion, the mountain of Jerusalem.

But the meaning of the name must be investigated. Zion is called “watchtower” (*speculatio*), which suits the Shepherd, the Lord Jesus Christ. Nothing insensible could be compared with such majesty unless under some credible signification, something you will frequently find in the divine Scriptures. Elsewhere too it is said: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep” (Psalm 113:4), and similar expressions.

He therefore says of the person who trusts in the Lord that he will not be shaken forever, like Mount Zion, although we believe that even it will be changed at the end of the world [Col. 0922A]. But that Zion—that is, the Lord Christ—will not be shaken; it is Christ who is indicated by this signification.

And consider that above he used the plural, “those who trust,” and afterward said in the singular, “he shall not be shaken,” namely so that he might display the unity of the numerous Christian people.

He added, “who dwells in Jerusalem.” Since we know that earthly Jerusalem was completely overthrown by different nations and that its citizens were frequently led into captivity, how does he say here that its inhabitants will not be shaken at all? Here too, however, we must understand Jerusalem as the heavenly homeland, which signifies “vision of peace.” No one can in any way be shaken from it who has deserved to be established in its firmness.

Thus the truth becomes clear to us and the reasoning is fully coherent if we transfer such names to an appropriate signification [Col. 0922B].

#### Verse 2

“Mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people, from now and forever.”

The form of earthly Jerusalem is described in the present verse so that the heavenly homeland might rather be indicated to us. For this Jerusalem, although it too is situated on a mountain, stands in the midst of surrounding mountains and is encircled by lofty peaks like a kind of arena.

This form of expression is called in Greek *topothesia*, in Latin “description of a place.” Mountains are used both in a good and in a bad sense, since in either case they are seen to rise above the common nature by their great height.

They are used in a bad sense: “In the Lord I trust; how then do you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Psalm 10:2). In a good sense [Col. 0922C]: “Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills righteousness” (Psalm 71:3).

So here too the mountains designate holy men, who inhabit that heavenly Jerusalem on every side. And so that you might understand that blessed men are intended, it follows: “and the Lord surrounds his people.”

For he surrounds only the one whom he knows to be faithful to him. He surrounds him to provide eternal protection and to bestow the fullness of every honor. By his ineffable nature he is wholly present everywhere, penetrating all things and containing everything. He does not depart from one place to be elsewhere, as creatures do. Yet although he fills all things, he is recognized as present to the good and absent from the wicked.

We must understand and believe without hesitation that this is true of the whole Trinity. For when he added, “from now,” he signified this age, concerning which the Lord says [Col. 0922D]: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). “Forever” refers to the time when he will appear to the saints in the most powerful majesty of his light. But why this protection is provided is explained next.

#### Verse 3

“For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands toward iniquity” [mss. A, B: “leave”].

The rod signifies power, whether good or evil. Thus it is said in a good sense of the Lord Savior himself: “The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength from Zion” (Psalm 109:2), “and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies” (Exodus 7). Moses too received a rod with which he performed numerous miracles.

It is also given in an evil sense [Col. 0923A] to those who always afflict the faithful through their zeal for wickedness. Persecutors are a rod to the martyrs, and angry masters are a rod to their servants, as were Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, and the others who ruled with the harshest domination.

But the Lord does not permit this wicked power to rage in prolonged freedom, so that the faithful may understand that it was granted to the proud for a very brief time as a test of their patience. For the servants of God might perhaps have stretched out their hands toward iniquity if they believed the persecution would continue for a long time.

The lot of the righteous is the Lord’s inheritance—that is, the Christian religion—against which he does not permit cruel tyrants to rise for long, lest they crush the Lord’s Church through an excessively prolonged persecution.

By saying “he will not leave,” he indicates that although trial may be permitted for a time, it is nevertheless not left free in its own power. Rather, an evil end and lamentable destruction are prepared for it [Col. 0923B].

#### Verse 4

“Do good, O Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart.”

After strengthening the people and solidifying them in the firmness of faith, he comes to the second part, in which he briefly entreats the Lord concerning what he knows he will do: that he restore good things to the good and fitting things to the wicked.

People are good when, preceded by divine grace, they begin to desire and fulfill what has been commanded. For we read: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

Yet both statements are true, and both are complete. For if we are left to our own strength, we are undoubtedly shown to be evil; but if we are regarded with the support of divine mercy, then, so long as we are obedient, we are certainly found to be good.

It follows: “and upright in heart.” The upright in heart are those who follow the Lord and do not strive to go before him, as was said to the apostle Peter in response to his human understanding: “Get behind me, Satan” (Mark 8:33).

Those who wish to go ahead never cease to err; those who desire to follow are undoubtedly shown to be upright in heart. The prophet therefore wishes good to be done to those who do not know how to separate themselves from the Lord through a perverse will [Col. 0923C].

#### Verse 5

“But those who turn aside toward bondage, the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity; peace be upon Israel.”

Just as he asked that good be done to the good and upright in heart, so now he says that those who turn aside toward bondage can be led away. The work of iniquity is beautifully defined as bondage, namely that which binds us with the chains of wickedness, so that we cannot be free when we are [Col. 0923D] constrained by such snares and such bonds.

And note that he says “those who turn aside,” that is, those who do not follow the Lord’s commands. Those perish by an equal judgment who strive both to turn aside from the commands of their ruler and to practice wickedness.

A definite promise is added: “peace be upon Israel.” In this peace, all extraordinary things are promised—things that surpass the whole understanding and transcend every desire. To encompass much in brief, this peace is the Lord himself, the Savior.

But those who quarrel with unity and are shown to be hostile to the catholic people will by no means possess this peace.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us consider how well this step has been made firm: the prophet recalls past evils and says [Col. 0924A] that in all things the Lord has provided. For the one who recognizes that the Lord was present to him in the past prepares an ascent toward better things. He could not have ascended farther if he had wished to presume anything about himself [440].

Therefore let us embrace this saving rule with the whole affection of our mind, so that he may grant us to ascend these steps—the one who has caused us to hear his mighty works.

## Psalm 125

### A Song of Ascents

How sweetly the voices of the blessed who ascend are offered after the captivity of all sins, so that, placed on a difficult journey, they may console themselves with a holy song! It is a most blessed journey, a fruitful labor, never deceiving, if the one toward whom we are striving is always held in the heart.

Therefore let us apply the ear of the soul and offer a most pure mind. We receive something of that blessedness if we draw the holy song into the innermost parts of our hearts [Col. 0924B].

### Division of the Psalm

The most holy men, delivered by divine mercy, give thanks in the first part of the psalm because they have been received from the fiercest bondage of sins into such great grace that they are judged praiseworthy among the nations.

In the second part they pray that their captivity may be changed into joy, adding this wonderful and true statement: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.”

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are consoled” [Col. 0924C].

Here a spiritual exposition proves necessary. Since it is declared that Zion suffered no desolation in David’s time, it remains to investigate what sort of captivity this verse seems to indicate—namely, that of the devil, by which the world was held in bondage.

The captivity of Zion existed when the wickedness of idols oppressed the Church of God, which at that time consisted of only a few. But it was changed into freedom when, at the Lord’s coming, the bonds of hell were shattered.

It follows: “we became like those who are consoled,” because although that captivity, which truly existed, was driven away from us by the help of the Divinity, it makes us like those who are consoled, not entirely secure. Certain consolation exists there where the promise will also already be fulfilled.

Nevertheless, amid these uncertainties of the world we possess the greatest consolation when we believe that the one whom we recognize as having freely spared us will preserve his gifts [Col. 0924D].

#### Verse 2

“Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation.”

Then, namely, when the coming of the Lord Savior—as has already been said—changed our captivity into joy, vices into virtues, ignorance into knowledge of divine things, and destruction into everlasting life [ed., “to live eternally.”] Thus our mouth was rightly filled with joy and our tongue with exultation, since such things were bestowed by the Lord’s gift.

But here “mouth” signifies the hidden place of the heart, where joys are first sown and grow together, then burst forth through the service of the tongue into the fruit of speech. Of this mouth it is said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9).

Even with closed lips it cries out to the Lord, and from an inactive mouth the voice of a contrite heart is effectively heard [Col. 0925A].

#### Verse 3

“Then they shall say among the nations: ‘The Lord has magnified what he has done with them.’”

This is an entirely certain praise, which adversaries themselves profess; and it is a great weight of truth when the one who is shown to have thought otherwise gives this good testimony.

And observe carefully that he does not say “the nations” but “among the nations.” For at the Lord’s coming the nations did not believe universally; rather, among the nations there were those who, being pierced to the heart, could say such things.

Seeing religion flourish among the Christian people, they understood well and confessed that the Lord was truly with those who, devoted to an upright conscience, wished to pollute themselves with no superstition.

And because they saw them also performing miracles, they said: “The Lord has determined to do great things with them,” since they saw what they sought fulfilled through their prayers [Col. 0925B].

#### Verse 4

“The Lord has magnified what he has done with us; we have become joyful.”

So that they would not leave the preceding words of the gentiles in doubt, they now apply their statements to themselves and confirm them. For the Lord was doing great things with them when he graciously deemed it worthy to hear them.

And note the form of expression: “The Lord has magnified what he has done with us,” that is, “he has determined to show us great to the nations through the gift of virtues.” We appropriately recognize this as a form of expression proper to divine Scripture.

It follows: “we have become joyful,” certainly because of such great grace [Col. 0925C]. Their joy was indeed abundant when they saw themselves specially loved, having been delivered from the worst captivity.

This figure is called *diatyposis*, that is, “expression of a state.” We call a state a constant and complete perfection of mind or body in some matter.

#### Verse 5

“Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the south.”

After the redemption proclaimed at the Lord’s coming, the faithful people come to the second part, praying that their sins may again be forgiven.

For it is written: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs 18:17). And again: “You first declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26).

They therefore rightly both rejoiced in the general remission and prayed that forgiveness be granted to them.

A beautiful comparison follows [Col. 0925D]: “like a torrent in the south.” The south wind is warm; by the power of its heat it loosens waters bound by cold and causes a torrent to run through the ardor of its blowing.

So sins, bound by the frost of death—for they have no life in themselves—are dissolved by the warmth of heavenly mercy and, like a turbid torrent, flow away swiftly.

But so that the full meaning may be clear to us, it should be pronounced thus: “Turn back our captivity, O Lord, as a torrent in the south is turned into liquid.”

#### Verse 6

“Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.”

We know, as the Apostle teaches, that there are two sowings in this age, just as he himself says: “The one who sows in the flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh; and the one who sows in the Spirit shall reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Galatians 6:8).

Spiritual sowing is therefore always in tears [Col. 0926A], because although the faithful, through the Lord’s gift, practice virtues, they either lament past sins or fear becoming entangled in future faults. Thus it was said of them: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

Such people, therefore, who sow in tears, obtain the joys of the future promise. The prophet Hosea also says to them: “Sow for yourselves for righteousness, and reap mercy” (Hosea 10:12) [441].

Their sowing is to seek peace, to endure all things through devotion to charity, to subdue the body by fasts, to refresh themselves through almsgiving and piety, and to do whatever may pertain to the discipline of the faithful.

By contrast, those who desire temporal things and seek the empty pleasures of the world sow with joy when they commit adulteries, love avarice, pursue luxurious banquets, practice idolatry, and commit the other sins brought about by the devil’s instigation [Col. 0926B].

But on the day of judgment they will reap their deeds with sadness and weeping. Concerning them it is written: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12).

Thus in one verse both the compensation of good things and the repayment of evil things are declared. This figure is called *antistathmisis*, that is, “recompense,” when the one who has conducted himself either rightly or wickedly receives according to his deeds.

#### Verse 7

“Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds.”

#### Verse 8

“But coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” [mss. A, B: “with”].

Although this verse too seems to concern good works in general [Col. 0926C], it is nevertheless understood to exhort especially to almsgiving, as others have also thought. Hence it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33).

When he says “going,” the progress of a most holy life is signified, in which one continually advances by walking well. They wept when they saw the poor exposed in nakedness, constricted by cold, and wasted by cruel want, so that they first practiced compassion in their hearts before their generous hand supplied anything.

It follows: “casting their seeds.” “Casting” means sending them ahead into that age where our deeds arrive before we can go there, as it is written: “But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves [Col. 0926D] do not break in and steal” (Matthew 6:20).

Nor is it without purpose that he added “their own,” so that we might give alms from our own labors, not from robberies. That is mercy from which another does not groan and from which no one departs saddened, because what can be acquired through piety must be offered to the Majesty.

Since the Lord says that it is given to him, consider whether anything arising from wickedness could be offered to him.

He added: “But coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.” Those who have divine mercy prepared for them come with exultation; they are the ones who have acted here as the heavenly commands prescribe. Those who have polluted themselves here with the most wicked deeds do not come to joy.

Coming is common to all, but reaching joy belongs to the blessed [Col. 0927A]. These are called “conjugate terms,” which are formed from verbs of the same kind.

And because above they had said that each person would reap his own work, they persevere in the same metaphor with a truthful statement. They also added: “carrying their sheaves.”

After their work is completed, reapers carry in their laps to the threshing floor what they have bound together in the field from the gathering of ears. Thus the blessed carry their most fruitful deeds into the Lord’s threshing floor.

But blessed is that lap which is weighed down by wheat-bearing burdens, lest the lightness of straw deceive the reaper’s hopes, and he discover the emptiness of his labor when he no longer has the power to work.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How fittingly this seventh of the gradal psalms [Col. 0927B] prophesied the Lord’s first coming to us in the figure of the Old Testament and foretold that saving joy would be bestowed on the peoples, so that an octave might remain for the rest, which we have said pertains to the Lord’s resurrection.

The following title also makes this distinction clear, for it is written: “A Song of Ascents of Solomon.” Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” a name that especially pertains to the Lord Christ, who reconciled the world to God and said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

Finally, the psalm itself is now shown to indicate not a future prophecy but the fruit of the womb itself, so that it may plainly appear to all that in the seventy-first psalm the indications of the whole work of the New and Old Testaments are contained through the decades, whereas here the same things are shown to have been declared through a single number [Col. 0927C].

## Psalm 126

### A Song of Ascents of Solomon

We have said that it is not without purpose that Solomon’s name has also been added to this title; in Latin its interpretation is “peaceful.”

And to whom could this word be more fittingly applied than to the one who gathered the people of circumcision and of uncircumcision for the sake of unity, and, like a cornerstone, strengthened the walls coming to him from opposite directions with the power of stability? Concerning him the Apostle says: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14).

It is also added that this is the eighth psalm, extending to the end of the gradal psalms. This number pertains to the resurrection of the Lord Christ, concerning whom he is certainly about to speak, indicating the New Testament, to which these preceding mysteries refer [Col. 0927D].

And note that here and in the seventy-first psalm Solomon’s name is evidently written because of the distinction between the Testaments, so that you may recognize that the two correspond to one another.

### Division of the Psalm

The prophet rejoices that, filled with the Holy Spirit, he had foreseen the grace of the New Testament. Yet, lest harmful presumption steal from him or others any part of so great a gift, he teaches the most holy men at the outset that no one should attempt to attribute anything good to his own powers, since everything has been placed under divine authority. No one should wish to anticipate the time that he understands [Col. 0928A] to have been arranged by the Lord’s ordinance.

Secondly, he speaks of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, of his apostles, and of all who fulfill his commands.

### Exposition of the Psalm

#### Verse 1

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain.”

It is clear that the Psalmist is speaking of certain builders. But it is not fitting for us to believe that this was said of builders of cement or cutters of squared stones. Rather, we must understand as builders those who strive to construct each Christian through the truth of faith.

They are the house concerning which the Apostle says: “For you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 1:16).

But if these people [Col. 0928B] strive to build by their own powers, they appear to labor in vain unless the Lord’s grace grants the disposition [ed., “result”] of the truest belief, just as the Apostle says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (ibid., 7).

We must apply diligence to doing these things, but in such a way that we believe the Lord can complete them. Otherwise, deceived by empty presumptions, we may seem, to our own destruction, to neglect the Author and Perfecter of all things.

Let us remember that this verse and the following one are expressed under the category called “from necessity.” For the Lord’s building is necessary; without it, nothing good is brought to the summit of perfection.

#### Verse 2

“Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it will watch in vain” [Col. 0928C].

He passes from the house to the city, so that neither detestable arrogance may steal upon individuals nor pernicious boasting prevail in the holy Church.

The city of the Lord is understood as the heavenly Jerusalem, part of which is still journeying on earth. In it bishops strive to keep watch, so that with tireless care they may guard the flock entrusted to them.

The same is said to them: they must not be stirred up by harmful thoughts or believe that human vigilance can prevail over anything, since only the Divinity can ward off the dangers of invasion.

We understand how shameless Pelagian presumption is, and how wicked, since the Holy Spirit so often decreed that this should be said against it—yet it did not endure hearing it.

#### Verse 3

“It is in vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down.”

He still addresses the teachers themselves, so that the people may be corrected more effectively when they see that their teachers too have been warned [Col. 0928D].

For it is said: “It is in vain for you to rise before the light.” The one who rises before the light is the person who desires to attain blessedness in this age, although the true Light, that is, the Lord Christ, endured many things here and graciously consented to reach the gallows of the cross for our salvation.

This is shown by a most beautiful comparison. The one who rises before the light still walks in darkness and cannot make his journey successfully because of the obscurity of night. So too are those who strive to live here in security before they attain the joys of the resurrection.

To them it is said: “Rise after you have sat down,” that is, first endure humiliation, and afterward seek the rewards of joy in the ascent [Col. 0929A]. Here sitting signifies humility, not honor.

The following verse shows that this must be understood in every way. To instruct us through clear examples concerning our Head, he sat when he said: “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matthew 26:38). He rose when he said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (ibid. 28:18).

“Before the light” is also used in a good sense, as Jeremiah says: “I spoke to you before the light, and you did not hear me. And I sent all my servants the prophets to you before the light, saying: ‘Return, each one of you, from his evil way’” (Jeremiah 7:13, 25).

But if you direct the attention of your mind to the passage, both statements concern Christ, although they seem divided. The present psalm says that no joys should be presumed before the light—that is, before the Lord’s second coming [Col. 0929B].

Jeremiah, however, by “before the light”—that is, before Christ’s first coming—admonishes the peoples to depart from wickedness, so that they may not be found on crooked paths. Thus both prophets touched upon the Lord’s coming in its twofold aspect.

#### Verse 4

“You who eat the bread of sorrows, when he gives sleep to his beloved.”

He has shown to whom he said, “It is in vain for you to rise before the light”: perfect Christians, as he himself testifies, eat the bread of sorrows. Another psalm says concerning them: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 41:4). And elsewhere: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure” (Psalm 79:6).

For them sorrow itself is truly bread, since they are nourished by affliction and find consolation in worldly sadness. Bread pertains to nourishment, which occurs in that purity when the faithful do not regard the punishments given to them as leading to destruction but to salvation [Col. 0929C].

It follows when those who were first commanded to sit should rise: namely, at the time when the faithful are received into rest, for whom death is sleep and secure repose.

God’s beloved are those who seek him with extraordinary love. But how much is bestowed upon them can be understood from the fact that they have received such a name. For whoever is called God’s beloved is undoubtedly enriched with eternal prosperity.

#### Verse 5

“Behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons, the reward, the fruit of the womb.”

To show that the prophet had spoken above about Christ’s faithful, he comes to a second mode, in which he now indicates the Lord Christ himself.

For he says: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord,” namely, the sons of the Church, generated from water and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0929D], who are recognized as the Lord’s inheritance.

And who these sons are is explained in what follows: “the reward, the fruit of the womb.” The whole of his inheritance is the reward of the fruit of this womb—that is, of the offspring of the virginal womb—which, rising again, is brought into possession of the heavens and will rejoice in eternal happiness with the Lord.

The reward is said to have been given to his humanity, concerning which the second psalm also says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8).

And the Apostle says afterward: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

His divinity, however, received nothing by which it might grow; rather, it bestowed upon the world the means by which it might escape the danger of death.

Thus we also speak of a “people of acquisition,” and confess that the souls of converts are “gain” [ed., “gained”]. In the same way he is said to receive a reward, although we testify that he acquired it at some time.

These and similar expressions are appropriately understood according to that part of him which suffered [Col. 0930A].

### Verse 6

“As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of the searchers.”

An arrow is a weapon that quickly reaches its appointed targets and flies altogether in a perfectly straight line. When it goes forth from the hand of a mighty man, it travels with great speed and strikes what it aims at. For the one who directs it is not mighty if the arrow’s course goes astray. Therefore “from the hand of a mighty man” has been added, so that you might neither doubt its effectiveness nor distrust its speed. The apostles are rightly compared to these arrows, because, sent forth from the hand of the mighty one—that is, from the Lord Savior—they were quickly brought to their appointed destinations [Col. 0930B] and faithfully fulfilled his commands.

For the passage continues, “so are the sons of the searchers.” We rightly call the prophets searchers (*excussores*), because, searching out the Lord’s inner chambers, they prophesied wondrous miracles to the peoples. To shake out means to investigate something hidden and to make it public; and there is no doubt that this happened to those who, through a commendable life, deserved to be filled with the truth of holy light. The apostles are deservedly called the sons of these searchers, since believers were in a certain manner generated by their faith through their preaching. For blessed Paul plainly testifies that a kind of generation proceeds from teaching, saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19); and elsewhere: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (I Cor. IV, 15).

[Col. 0930C] **Verse 7.** “Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them.”

The sons of the searchers—that is, the apostles—had this desire: that the Christian people should believe and serve the Lord. He therefore calls them blessed when their labor reached its glorious hopes; or rather, because they themselves desired to enter the Lord’s courts without delay, as has already been said in the forty-first psalm: “As the deer longs for the fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. XLI, 2). Thus the Apostle too burned with this desire when he said: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). Therefore they are blessed three and four times over who deserved to attain such hopes. Yet this desire was not fulfilled through human haste [Col. 0930D]; rather, the one who grants its accomplishment stirs up such a hope.

**Verse 8.** “They shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies at the gate.”

This too pertains to the sons of those who have been shaken out, who filled the ends of the world with holy preaching. The gate of the city Jerusalem, however, is Christ the Lord, as he himself says: “I am the door” (John X, 9). The one who rightly preaches about the Lord Savior speaks in this gate, so that those who enter through his baptism and repentance may possess the kingdoms of heaven.

But we must also examine why such a place was chosen for preachers: namely, so that the one who does not believe may go out, while the one who assents may enter. At such a place, therefore, the devout preacher both makes unbelievers go out and permits the devoted to enter [Col. 0931A]; or because the voice that speaks at the gate is public, since it is always heard by those passing through.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

How well he ascended to the heights, even to the true Sun, like another Elijah—not carried aloft in a fiery chariot, but raised by the steps of the virtues; not snatching at the air through bodily movement, but ascending in spirit to the holy summit! Glory to the Lord Savior, who displayed various miracles in his servants. That mortal body of Elijah traveled through the air, while the prophet, without leaving the earth, ascended to what is above. Let us ask him to lift us on the wings of his mercy, for we are weighed down by the frailty of the flesh. Nothing is difficult for him, except when it is thought that something good cannot be accomplished by him.

Let us therefore diligently search the divine Scriptures: let us turn over the books of the New and Old [Col. 0931B] Testament, if we wish to be sons of the searchers. For there we find the Lord, if we deserve truly to shake out and investigate these things.

## PSALM 127

### A Song of Ascents

How magnificent the ninth step is, the number itself declares: extended through a triple multiplication, it displays to us the holy summit of the Trinity. But since we read that the fear of the Lord is “the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. I, 16), we must inquire why the prophet judged that it should be remembered at such a place.

There are two fears that pierce our hearts. One is human fear, by which we fear either to suffer dangers to the flesh or to abandon the goods of the world. But this fear is known to be temporary, because we fear these things only as long as we remain engaged in the conduct of this age. Divine fear, however, rises with us through every advance in this life. For when that dread of this age is abandoned with the world at the first step, this fear always remains with us and is taken up at every ascent as a most faithful companion, as has already been said in the hundred-eighteenth psalm: “Fix my flesh in your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII, 120). Rightly, then, at this step and everywhere we are commanded to possess the fear of the Lord, since it is shown to be a necessary guardian for us.

### Division of the Psalm

In the first section, the prophet, through certain allusions, enumerates the blessings of those who fear God, so that he may kindle the minds of the devout with the warmth of the heavenly reward. In the second, he blesses them so that they may receive eternal joys, lest anyone fear this most delightful fear.

### Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.”

In his first statement he distinguished the fear of the Lord from the terror of this age. By saying, “Blessed are all who fear the Lord,” he showed that those are not blessed who anxiously fear the dangers of this world through the loss of temporal things. Those dangers make people wretched when they torment them with empty fear; they do not bring advancement, but change; they know not ascent, but ruin.

By contrast, the fear of the Lord descends from love, is born from charity, and is brought forth from sweetness. Devout fear consoles the one who fears and restores the afflicted; it does not know how to be deprived of joy except when such fruit has been abandoned. Of this it is written: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII, 12). How profitable is the fear by which children are taught! What kind of discipline is this, which is bestowed with sweet affections [editorial reading: “effects”]! Elsewhere the same thing is commanded: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, except that you fear the Lord your God with all your heart, and walk in all his ways, and love him, and keep his commandments with all your heart and with all your soul, so that it may be well with you?” (Deut. X, 12). It is also said of the same fear: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. XVIII, 10).

But lest you perhaps think that the Lord is to be feared only when he thunders, flashes lightning, shakes the earth with trembling, and threatens criminals with destruction, he added, “who walk in his ways,” so that we might not merely be restrained from evil deeds but also be proved to walk most directly in faith. Those fear the Lord who walk in his ways and carry out his commandments with devout minds.

But let us see why elsewhere “way” is put in the singular and elsewhere in the plural, as it is here. When the Lord Christ speaks of himself, he calls himself the Way, as in the saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life”; and again: “For no one can come to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6). When he speaks of many ways, he signifies the apostles and prophets, through whom one comes to the one Way—that is, to the Lord, unquestionably the Savior. Jeremiah testifies to both meanings when he says: “Stand in the ways of the Lord, and ask about the everlasting paths of God, and see which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. VI, 16). We have also noted elsewhere that this should be understood in the same way.

**Verse 2.** “You shall eat the labors of your fruits; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.”

In this verse and the two that follow, he enumerates the blessings of those who fear God. But first we must consider why above he used the plural, “blessed,” and now has spoken in the singular, “you shall eat.” It is characteristic of divine Scripture to reduce to the singular what appears to have been stated in the plural, namely because Mother Church—as has often been said—although she contains very many blessed people, rejoices in holy unity.

Next, let us examine what he wishes to say by “the labors of your fruits,” since fruits do not come from labors, but fruits unquestionably arise from labors. He wished “labors” to signify good works, which are performed in this world in such a way that they grant a delightful banquet in the future recompense. To eat is to be refreshed by some food and to rejoice in the satisfaction it provides.

These labors, therefore, which are good works, are received in that resurrection when it will be heard: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34). Blessed is that eating, which is not digested by the belly but preserved in imperishable eternity. Another psalm also shows that souls have their own nourishment, saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9). And lest you think this nourishment is bodily, he added: “You are blessed.” No one is made blessed by bodily eating except one who is fattened by spiritual gifts. And lest you think that this blessed person possesses only a modest fruit, he added: “and it shall be well with you.” Where it is well, all good things flow together and lead to the joy of sweetness. He signifies those rewards that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man,” which God has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II, 9).

**Verse 3.** “Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house.”

**Verse 4.** “Your children are like young olive trees around your table.”

Here too, in the same way, a literal understanding must be avoided. For when you observe that many most holy men have neither wives nor children, while wicked people possess all these things, how will you apply to this side of blessedness what you recognize as often taken away from the good and given instead to the wicked?

A wife is so called, as it were, “like a sister.” Therefore here we should understand the wife of the blessed man as wisdom, as Solomon says: “Whoever wishes to take wisdom as his bride” (Wis. VIII, 2); and elsewhere: “Love her, and she will embrace you; surround her, and she will guard you” (Prov. IV, 6). She, then, is the wife of the righteous, who embraces her husband with chaste affection.

A vine, however, is the mother of grapes, pouring forth sweet wines that refresh our hearts. So too this wife—that is, wisdom—bearing pleasant fruits, gladdens us with delightful joy. Our house is rightly understood as our own thought, when, fixed within it, we dwell as though in a certain building. The walls of this house are the two Testaments, in which the holy mind is strengthened and made firm as though by solid bricks.

The passage continues: “Your children are like young olive trees around your table.” Children are rightly said to be born from the wife Wisdom, and not daughters. The masculine gender generally indicates firmness of mind; or because this gender, when named, embraces both sexes, just as it is said elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Ps. CXI, 1). For not only is the man blessed who fears the Lord, but the woman who fears the Lord is also blessed.

These children, therefore, surround the spiritual table—that is, the altar of the Lord—when they are nourished with heavenly bread. But it is called “your” table so that the honor of the bishop might appear more clearly. Thus we say of them: “He presides over his Church”; “Return to your Church.” This expression is plainly in common use among all.

We must also examine why he preferred to compare the children of the blessed to young olive trees. They are greener and stronger, and firmest in every respect; they also produce fruit more abundantly. From this fruit food is prepared, a light is kindled, and relief is given to the weary body.

Nor should you think that the olive and the vine were joined in these comparisons without reason. For we read that the man who had been wounded by robbers in the Gospel was cured by wine and oil being poured in (Luke X, 34), because these two provide the mystical supports of our life: in wine there is the austerity of justice, and in oil the gentleness of mercy. The former may refer to the Old Testament, the latter to the New [Col. 0934A] Testament. The fact that he compared the wife to a vine and the children to olives is recognized as a figure of parable, since he compared things different in kind.

**Verse 5.** “Behold, thus shall every man who fears the Lord be blessed.”

The perfect conclusion of the blessed man who fears the Lord follows. For when he says, “Thus shall he be blessed,” he signifies—as has already been explained—that this is how the one who fears his Creator deserves to be blessed: the one who ceases to fear empty things and is filled with chaste fear of the Lord.

Observe the order of the words. He first says: “Behold, thus shall every man be blessed”; and lest the insolent and foolish claim this blessing for themselves, he added: “who fears the Lord.”

**Verse 6.** “May the Lord bless you from Sion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.”

He comes to the second section, where with most holy devotion he asks that those be blessed who are inflamed by the fear of the Lord toward every good pursuit, so that we may recognize how profitable this fear is, since holy blessing is doubled for it.

He says: “May the Lord bless you from Sion,” that is, the Lord Christ, who deigned to appear to human beings on this mountain and, in accordance with the meaning of his name, is always designated as the best shepherd. For Sion—as has often been said—is interpreted as “watchtower” or “contemplation.”

The passage continues: “and may you see the good things of Jerusalem.” We must frequently explain these words, because the meaning of the passage is known to depend especially upon them. Jerusalem is understood as “vision of peace.” Here peace is an invisible reality, which will then be seen when its author, Christ the Lord, is viewed by a blessed mind. He therefore wishes the person to see in Jerusalem all the things that are good.

There the Lord himself is seen, who both makes those who behold him eternal and displays himself in unceasing perpetuity. Thus, by the spirit of prophecy, that which is known to be able to happen to the saints is wished for them. But lest you think this temporal, he added: “all the days of your life,” so that the fullness of eternity might be added to the ineffable gift.

**Verse 7.** “And may you see the children of your children: peace [MSS A, B, F: *pacem*, ‘peace’] upon Israel.”

He added this verse to his blessings, so that the one who fears the Lord here may see, in that blessedness, the children of his children. There is no doubt that this too can happen to eunuchs. Children are—as has already been said—those who are generated through spiritual teaching. But it would have been a lesser joy to acquire spiritual children if those who had been taught were not also seen to have generated other children.

“Children of children” signifies grandchildren, which can certainly happen to blessed men who have been accustomed to instruct peoples through holy preaching. Observe that he mentions this among the highest joys as something to be seen. For it is necessary that an acquired believer produce great joy for the one who acquires him, since the latter is thereby shown to be destined for a great reward. To this refers the talent that the master of the household gladly found doubled.

The sentence that follows declares the summit and sweetness of that blessedness: that above that blessed Jerusalem peace—that is, the Lord Savior—may dwell and make blessed all that he embraces by the power of his majesty [Col. 0935A]. This is what he said above: “May you see the good things of Jerusalem.” For this is the peace that every devout person desires, for which he sighs and groans, and for which he willingly pours out his very soul.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

In the present psalm we have learned what has been promised to those who fear God, and what fruits are received by the one who fears the Lord with a sincere mind. Let us therefore pray with the greatest zeal that we may deserve to receive this fear, which is sought not for punishment but for salvation; from it come such things as never arise from the pleasures of the world.

For it is fitting to seek with excessive supplication what is supreme. Therefore, as has been said, let us continually seek the Lord, so that by his generosity we may deserve to attain such gifts. For he who commands sinners to pray at suitable and unsuitable times has promised that he can also hear us, though unworthy.

## PSALM 128

### A Song of Ascents

This tenth step is now advanced by a tenfold ascent, abandoning earthly things and joining itself to what is above through glorious nearness. Let us hear it singing more sweetly, placed on high, since the height of the psalmic steps provides us with an ascent toward understanding. The one who draws nearer to the sight of the Lord has rightly risen. Yet humility provides all these things, for it fittingly exalts the servants of God.

Let us see what has been placed in this number of reward, for it is the denarius that the rich Lord, in his loving generosity, grants to those laboring in his vineyard (Matt. XX, 9). The prophet teaches us patiently to endure the troubles of the age, since he proves that the Church has often suffered.

### Division of the Psalm

Filled with the Holy Spirit, the prophet first warns Israel to say what struggles and what kinds of ambushes it has suffered from its enemies, lest any of the faithful appear to despair over their own tribulations. In the second section, in the spirit of prophecy, he calls down through certain parabolic comparisons what he knew would come upon the obstinate enemies of the Church in the future judgment.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0935D] **Verse 1.** “Often they have fought against me from my youth; let Israel now say.”

Israel—that is, the Church of God—is admonished to say that it has often been attacked, and attacked from its youth. “Often” signifies the frequency of its sufferings. “From my youth” refers to the first period of life, when from its very beginnings it endured the most savage opposition at the devil’s instigation.

Thus another psalm says: “I was young and have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring begging bread” (Ps. XXXVI, 25). He joined the masculine gender to the neuter gender, which is to be counted among the idioms of divine Scripture. “Begging bread”: neither a child nor an adolescent had seen what he was describing.

“From my youth,” therefore, signifies the time when righteous Abel was killed by his perverse brother. It also endured in the days of Lot, when a faithful man experienced the many iniquities of the Sodomites. It endured in Job, when those famous and repeated calamities were suffered, and the devil’s machinations yielded, overcome by the glorious endurance of his suffering. The people of God also endured the bitter domination of Pharaoh.

Many most holy people, attacked by tribulations and dangers and enduring the fiercest struggle, earned the crown of martyrdom when their conflict was completed. The Church was also attacked through the passion of Christ the Lord, when it seemed to the undiscerning that it had lost the Lord whom it proclaimed the author of its life. Yet from that very point it grew from which unbelievers thought it was being brought low.

Nor is it without significance that the passage continues: “let Israel now say”—that is, in this age, when it is the time of repentance, so that the remaining faithful may be instructed. For after the general resurrection the Church will always sing only the praises of the Lord. The expression “let Israel now say” is to be understood throughout each of the three following verses.

**Verse 2.** “Often they have fought against me from my youth; yet they have not prevailed against me.”

A similar beginning also occurred in the fifth of the preceding gradual psalms. This figure is called anaphora, that is, the repetition of the same word at the beginnings of several verses.

Here the old age of the Church must be understood, as the Apostle says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). Whatever happens at the end of the world is most appropriately called old age. Therefore the Church rightly says that she has been attacked from her youth, so that you may understand that she has never come to an end, since she has always been attacked.

She grows through the persecutions of the wicked and becomes mature through her own crushing. For although she may appear to lose holy men in this life, she is nevertheless shown to acquire them for the homeland to come. Therefore she cannot come to an end, since it is clear that she is increased by her losses.

The following words also make this clear: “yet they have not prevailed against me.” She says that those whom she previously recalled attacking her have not been able to overcome her. An attack is incomplete when it returns again to the contest; nor should it be called victory once it is clear that conflict can arise again. The verse that follows explains this clause.

**Verse 3.** “Sinners built upon my back; they prolonged their iniquity.”

It is the most wicked practice of the faithless that, when they cannot publicly impose something upon the whole people, they secretly try to persuade individuals of various things, so that they may deceive at least a few [MSS A, B, F: “because” (*quia*)]—those whom they could not overturn from the Church of God through any perversion.

The Church testifies that sinners built upon her back because those who hasten to devise plots do so from that side: those who can be seen from the front are not at all perceived from behind. Hence the assault of enemies is greatly feared when they strive to disturb the back by a sudden attack.

And to show the strength of her patience, she describes the very kind of struggle that is sometimes feared more than the trials mentioned above. Moreover, lest you think these sudden acts of stealth insignificant, she says that the ambushes were prolonged [Col. 0937A], which the enemies of the faith continually thrust upon armed minds.

**Verse 4.** “The just Lord will cut the necks of sinners.”

Although the Lord is patient, magnanimous, and long-suffering toward sinners, this should rather be understood of those transgressors who desire to return to salutary satisfaction through his mercy.

Scripture testifies that “necks” signify pride, saying: “I see that this people is stiff-necked” (Exod. XXXII, 9). Blessed Stephen also, in his passion, reproving the Jews, says: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts VII, 51).

To these, therefore, this recompense is returned: the necks that they fatally raised against the Lord are subjected to his yoke through a salutary humility that is sweet. We often remember this happening to persecutors, so that those who previously defended idols with most wicked persuasions [manuscript G and the edition: “persecutions”] became preachers of the most holy religion.

**Verse 5.** “Let all who hate Sion be put to shame and be ashamed.”

He comes to the second section, where, through the figure of a parable, he foretells until the end of the psalm, by certain comparisons, what will come upon the obstinate adversaries. It is clear that this can happen to them in the judgment of the Lord.

“They shall be put to shame” when they see their faithlessness condemned by that truth. “They shall be ashamed” before the judge whom they thought should be despised here. Those hate Sion—that is, the Church—who rejected the incarnation of the Lord with deranged minds.

**Verse 6.** “Let them become like the grass of buildings, which withers before it is plucked up.”

Abandoned buildings commonly produce on their highest points fleeting grasses that dry up and perish before the time of gathering, because they have never grown strong with any firm root. Obstinate sinners are joined to these in a most fitting comparison, since they too frequently perish here before they are removed from this light. They are born on the heights of pride, where they possess no stability.

For if they were to germinate in the valley of tears, they would bring their fruits to maturity, with the Lord’s help.

**Verse 7.** “Of which the reaper has not filled his hand, nor the one who gathers sheaves his bosom.”

He continues with the image of grass. Just as he says above in another psalm concerning the fruits of the blessed: “But coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV, 6), so now he declares concerning sinners that nothing of them is to be carried either in the hand or in the bosom by the reapers—that is, by the angels who will gather the peoples for the judgment of the Lord.

That former harvest was spiritual and brought forth fruit; this one, however, is carnal and rejoices in no abundance of wheat’s bounty, so that it can neither fill one hand nor manage to load the bosom. Such is the harvest that is not sown in the Lord’s field, but grows in the breasts of the proud as upon fleeting heights.

For what fruits could it have produced when it withered before it was plucked up? Nor is it without significance that he mentioned both the hand and the bosom: the hand pertains to action, the bosom to conscience. In the deeds of the wicked, nothing fruitful could be found in either.

**Verse 8.** “Nor did those who passed by say: ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord.’”

It was customary among the Hebrews that if travelers found people laboring at some work in the fields, they would bless them in gratitude for the favor granted, as is read in the book of Ruth: “Boaz said to the young man who was in charge of the reapers, ‘The Lord be with you.’ They answered him, ‘May the Lord bless you’” (Ruth II, 4–5).

From this custom the splendid contrary meaning of the present passage is derived, because no blessing is bestowed upon the wicked while they labor in vain.

By “those who passed by” he signifies holy men who, despising the confusion and disorder of this world, hasten toward the peaceful and tranquil things of the age to come. Thus they truly appear to pass by the things they despise for love of the Lord.

If you wish to have these passers-by confirmed for yourself by divine authority, hear Moses: “I will pass over and see this vision” (Exod. III, 5). And it was said above in another psalm: “I saw the wicked exalted above measure and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Ps. XXXVI, 35). You see that this word is often attributed to holy minds.

But lest the blessing itself be thought to be applied through human strength, the passage continues: “We have blessed you in the name of the Lord.” That is the firm and true blessing which is bestowed with the Lord’s name invoked, from whom comes everything that is beneficial.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us contemplate this psalm as though carried aloft on two wings, having ascended the tenth height. Its right wing is the conversion of the proud, announced to the Church after many persecutions. Its left is the desired shame of those who hate Sion.

The prophet does not speak from a desire to curse, but under the impulse of future truth. Although we are commanded to pray for our enemies, he has explained what truth held in store for the obstinate and perishing. These words, however, were not spoken without the fruit of great compassion. Many correct themselves because of the punishment foretold, when they learn that such things threaten the obstinate.

## PSALM 129

### A Song of Ascents

Unless the Church’s vigilant practice is recalled, a certain question may arise: why, placed on the eleventh step, does the prophet prostrate himself in penitential satisfaction? Established at such a height and raised to everlasting glory, could he still feel trepidation, though not fall?

A similar explanation was given in the hundred-and-twenty-seventh psalm, when we said that the fear of the Lord is appropriate to the saints at every step in this world. The Church also says in the hundred-and-twenty-eighth: “Often they have fought against me from my youth”; and shortly afterward: “Sinners built upon my back.” That people, as it ascended, enumerated many calamities that it still endured in the world.

So here too, whatever the prophetic mind strives toward on high, it prostrates itself all the more in devout humility, so that, though still bent down in mind, it might ascend because it had no presumption based on its merits. Conscious of the human condition, it bowed and subjected itself more humbly than before, because no one can escape sin who is shown to be established in a fragile body.

For when do we not either sin in thought, offend through excessive speech, or fall through an imprudent action? There is therefore one security for the person living in this age: to bow continually in devout prayers, so that although we cannot be free from fault, we may deserve to be absolved through acts of devotion.

### Division of the Psalm

Seeing more with his mind than with his body, lest he be overwhelmed by the great waves of sins, the prophet begins by crying out to the Lord to be freed from the depths of sin, seeking the goodwill of the good Judge on account of the calamities he has revealed. For no one can be saved unless he has been absolved by divine clemency.

A concise conclusion follows, omitting the narrative and the other material, because such things adorn a discourse when introduced appropriately, but when inserted incongruously they are repellent. The good teacher therefore followed a useful and devout brevity: he quickly came to the joys of thanksgiving, so that penitents might recognize with what great grace they are received and how swift a remedy is provided for them.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 0939D] **Verse 1.** “From the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my prayer” [manuscripts A and B, and the edition: “my voice”].

“Depth” is as though one were to say “the farther bottom,” whose lowest parts are completely submerged. From this depth the prophet cried out to the Lord, so that he might more easily be heard.

From this depth Peter poured forth glorious tears. From this depth the tax collector beat his guilty breast; he had risen so high in sins that he did not even raise his eyes toward heaven. From this place Jonah, finally, cried out silently to the Lord: placed in the belly of the sea creature, he had entered alive into the underworld.

The sea creature was the prophet’s oratory, a harbor for the shipwrecked, a house amid the waves, a fortunate refuge in despair. He was not swallowed as food, but to possess rest; and, in a marvelous novelty, that beast’s belly returned its nourishment unharmed, not consumed by the customary violence of digestion. As he himself testifies in his book, saying: “And the Lord commanded a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish for three days and three nights, etc.” (Jonah II, 1), where he also narrated his prayers with prophetic truth.

O exceedingly and wholly glorious repentance; humility that knows not how to fall; mourning that gladdens hearts; tears that water the soul! This depth, finally, does not know the underworld, for it sends one on to the heavens.

Therefore attend to the power of holy prayer: for the prophet believes that he will be heard all the more quickly because he cried out to the Lord from the innermost depths. Thus the passage continues: “Lord, hear my prayer.” Those who have hidden themselves in the entrails of holy humility are nearer to the Most High. Thus, when he prayed from the depths, he quickly reached the gifts of the Most High Redeemer.

[Col. 0940A] **Verse 2.** “Let your ears be attentive to the prayer of your servant.”

With this most beautiful supplication he makes the Judge favorably disposed toward him, so that the most merciful one may grant a gracious hearing to his petitions. But although “to be attentive” pertains to the eyes, here it is attributed to the ears, because the unique power and strength of his nature neither hears with ears, nor walks with feet, nor sees with eyes, nor tastes with the mouth, nor smells with the nostrils; rather, through incomprehensible power he accomplishes the things that have been named.

For although God is spirit, as is read of him: “God is spirit” (John IV, 24)—eternal, omnipotent, penetrating and containing all things created by him, wholly present everywhere, wholly everywhere, shining from and through himself—yet, following our customary manner of speaking, the power by which he sees is called his eyes, the power by which he hears is called his ears, the power by which he accomplishes things is called his hands, and likewise with the other expressions that are applied allegorically to divine operations.

When he says, “of your servant,” the mercy of the good Judge is moved [editorial reading: “reminded”], so that he may not cast away one whom he recognizes as faithfully invoking him.

**Verse 3.** “If you observe iniquities, O Lord, Lord, who will endure?”

Behold, that depth from which he cried out to the Lord has now been disclosed. By “iniquity” he wishes every sin that can be committed through some form of wickedness to be understood. For that which is not just is iniquitous.

And who could be found exempt from such a condition, except the one who alone was continually able to fulfill righteousness? Even holy men, although they may appear to conduct themselves in a devout manner, cannot avoid faults altogether: an idle word is guilt; to think about tomorrow is sin; to be deceived in sleep, to be filled suddenly with an unsuitable thought, and other things of this kind are also faults.

The prophet therefore sees that there is no one who does not either go beyond measure in superfluous thoughts, offend through empty speech, or occupy himself with futile actions. Terrified, he cries out to the Lord that the human race is not sufficient for his justice unless he supplies the help of his mercy.

“Who will endure?”—as though it were an immense weight, an intolerable mass, a consuming flame. Rightly did he call the Lord’s justice unbearable for himself, since, considering his own actions, he feared the Lord’s judgments.

This figure is called in Greek *diaporesis*, and in Latin “doubt,” when we are uncertain whether what is sought can be found.

## Verse 4

“For with you there is forgiveness, and because of your law I have waited for you, O Lord.”

Terrified by the Lord’s justice, through which no one may lawfully escape punishment, he fled to the patronage of mercy. For it does not lie in our actions that we deserve to be acquitted; rather, it belongs to his forgiveness that he deigns to free the confessing guilty person. But if you examine this name more carefully, forgiveness was granted when God came to the aid of the perishing world through the incarnation of his Son, so that he might absolve the human race, which was bound by sins that fettered it.

He continues: “and because of your law, I have waited for you, O Lord.” The law seems contrary to forgiveness, because the law exposes sin, identifies the guilty, and makes the whole person liable to itself, as the Apostle says: “I did not know sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. 7:7).

But here we must understand that law as the evangelical commandment, which says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). This, then, is the law which the prophet says he endures, through which he rightly believed that he would be saved. For the very fact that he says “I have waited” indicates charity, which “endures all things” and “suffers all things,” and eagerly awaits its hope; it beneficially inflames the hearts of the faithful and makes them fully Christian.

## Verse 5

“My soul has waited for your word; my soul has hoped in the Lord.”

This repetition explains the preceding meaning, so that you may recognize that the law mentioned in the earlier verse was the law of the New Testament, since here the Word itself—that is, the Son of God—is clearly set forth. He therefore “waited for the Word,” because he believed that the Lord’s incarnation was to come. No one waits except one who desires to receive what has been promised.

And lest you should think that this “word” was some transitory utterance, he added: “my soul has hoped in the Lord.” For the Word of God is the almighty Son, of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2). In the latter days, taking flesh from the Virgin Mary in order to remove the destruction of the human race, he deigned to be born.

## Verse 6

“From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord.”

## Verse 7

“For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.”

Having completed his opening statements with every adornment, he comes most joyfully to the conclusion of the psalm. For, having been made secure concerning his sins, he now proclaims to the peoples that throughout their whole life they ought to hope in the Lord Christ, because he can transform the most grievous sufferings of his Church into eternal joys.

The “morning watch” is that manifestation of the Lord Savior when, while the Jews guarded the tomb, he rose in the reality of his restored body. “Night,” however, signifies the end of this age, so that the universal Church ought to persevere in hope of the Lord until the end of the world. But while this is said generally to Israel, each most faithful person is reminded of his own end.

And consider that he said “from the watch,” so that from the Lord’s advent, when his name had been revealed, he should be obeyed more fully. He continues: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.” A marvelous reason is given why Israel ought to hope in the Lord: because mercy is in his hand, and it can make the righteous out of the perverse, the immortal out of the weak, and one like the angels out of the fleshly. This is what he habitually displays in us, something to which human nature cannot attain by itself.

He also added “abundant redemption,” so that the precious blood might have been so richly provided that it could redeem the sins of the whole world and, as though by a saving flood, cleanse the earth from its uncleanness. We have placed the two verses together because they are so closely joined that their mutual connection makes their meaning clear.

## Verse 8

“And he himself will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.”

The one whom he previously called merciful and abundant is now shown by what he will do. He will therefore redeem Israel with precious blood: blood that purifies without staining, that does not defile but cleanses, as the Apostle John says: “The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7).

But when it says “he himself will redeem,” it shows that there was no possibility in human beings by which they could have escaped. These are the very iniquities which he earlier did not wish to be considered; for if they had been taken into account, this person could in no way have been redeemed.

Alternatively—as some have wished to say—the redemption of Israel signifies that time at the end of the age when, after Elijah has been seen, the multitude of the Jews is expected to believe, just as the prophet Malachi also recalls, saying: “And I will send you Elijah the prophet, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes” (Mal. 4:5). But what benefit will this bring them when another has escaped, if the one who is found alone guilty among corrected descendants will be punished more severely? It would be much better if those who were first in time had preceded them in faith.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This psalm certainly began from the depths, but it rose, like the sun advancing, to a great height, so that we may recognize what benefit repentance possesses, since it is seen to have been placed at such a summit. Let us therefore consider how harmful pride is, since a frequent remedy never ceases to oppose it.

A violent disease is not treated with a single medicine; rather, it is treated against with manifold care. For that tree too is repeatedly cut with axes which luxuriates with great freedom through the light airs. This evil of pride was struck by the sixth penitential double axe, and the trembling limbs of its branches quaked; but in the following seventh penitential psalm it is cut down so that, immediately dashed against the ground, it is broken.

I return to those who disdain to practice repentance at the end of their lives. Behold, nowhere do you read that what is said by ruined people to be neglected has been prohibited; indeed, we are always admonished never to cease from it because of sloth. Let us therefore shudder at pride, which cast the angel out from the grace of heavenly sweetness; let us love humility, which raised the faithful to heaven; let us confess quickly what we have done wrongly, lest we incur what we deserve.

# Psalm 130

## A Canticle of Ascents

When the careful farmer has cut through the dense soil of fertile fields with curved plows and entrusted fruitful seed to the cultivated land, he joyfully climbs the crown of a tree with songs of consolation; then, by cutting branches, he supplies his beasts with leafy fodder, so that what the labor of continual sowing had exhausted may be restored by abundant nourishment.
