Thus the prophet, carried upward by the ascent of spiritual steps after completing the labors of repentance, sends us the sweet nourishment of his songs. For this entire psalm is sung about gentleness and humility; and so it happens that those whom the labor of the preceding confession had afflicted are refreshed by the sweetness of glorious devotion. Let us therefore receive the food transmitted to us and taste the gifts of so great a benefit. Would that we were oxen who plow the field of our Lord with regular furrows!

Remember, however, that this entire psalm, as we have said, concerns the destruction of pride and the building up of humility in every way, just as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). This saying embraces the highest aspects of both realities. In pride it designates the devil; in humility, the Lord Christ. Thus, in the brevity of his words, it clearly indicates both what human beings ought to desire and what it is fitting for them to shun.

## Division of the Psalm

First, teaching the Christian people humility and gentleness by his own example, the prophet imposes a very severe penalty upon himself if he should not receive the Lord’s commandments with the greatest humility. Second, turning to Israel, he urges it to hope continually in the Lord, so that, strengthened by such hope, it may be able to endure all the adversities of the world.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Lord, my heart has not been exalted; nor have my eyes been lifted up.”

### Verse 2

“Nor have I walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me.”

A hypothetical syllogism arises in this way: If my heart has not been exalted, nor my eyes lifted up—that is, if I am shown to be alien to pride—yet my heart has not been exalted, nor my eyes lifted up; therefore I am shown to be alien to pride.

Now let us examine what follows. This psalm indeed proclaims humility, teaches self-restraint, and exhorts to patience. But when the prophet denies what is vicious, he altogether confesses what is worthy of praise. This figure is called *anastrophe*, when, by rejecting the contrary side, he wishes those things to be understood which the divine admonitions commanded.

For he will say that his heart was not exalted, as happened with Pharaoh, when, presuming upon the multitude of his people, he cruelly afflicted the most devoted Hebrews through Moses, despite having been forbidden so many times. He continues: “nor have my eyes been lifted up.” The eyes of that rich man were lifted up who is read of in the Gospel as having considered destroying his small barns and wishing to build enormous ones in order to gather abundance (Luke 12:18).

He added: “nor have I walked in great matters.” Pilate walked in great matters when he said to the Lord Savior: “Do you not know that I have authority to release you, and authority to crucify you?” (John 19:10).

Finally, as the crowning point, he added: “nor in things too wonderful for me.” Simon Magus walked in things too wonderful for him when he believed that the Holy Spirit could be bought from Christ’s apostles with money, so that he might purchase at a price what his merits did not possess.

Thus, while he denies such things, those which he did with the Lord’s help are understood. The following verse finally shows that this is how the passage should be understood.

### Verse 3

“If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul.”

### Verse 4

“As a weaned child upon his mother, so you will requite my soul.”

The statement “If I did not think humbly” is most aptly expressed, because the highest form of wisdom is not to persuade oneself of something through arrogance, but to perceive with a devoted spirit what is expedient. He therefore declares that he meditated upon the divine Scriptures with a simple and pure heart—not as the Arians, Manichaeans, Donatists, and others who separated themselves from the true religion did.

For if they had wished to think humbly, they would not have chosen to defend their own perversity; instead, coming to the truest and holiest teachers, they would have deserved to receive an understanding of the correct faith. He therefore says that he thought humbly, as the Apostle exhorts: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20); and elsewhere in the psalm: “He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100:7). Again, praying against this vice, he asks the Lord’s aid, saying: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. 35:12).

He continues: “but I exalted my soul.” Here he denies that his soul was exalted—that is, raised to the summit of pride, where ascent is ruinous and advancement dangerous. Holy men, however, exalt their souls when they strive to lift them toward divine preaching. For how can we understand anything about the Holy Trinity, or think soundly about the blessed incarnation, unless with great humility we raise our soul to the Lord?

That it is lawful for the soul to direct itself toward heavenly things is attested by another psalm, where it is said: “To you I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24:1). In those matters it is right for the soul to be lifted up from which it may live, flourish, and be nourished with heavenly bread. But in these perverse inquiries, swollen with unhappy teaching, the soul ought not to be exalted, for there it finds death, enters hell, and is condemned to eternal misery.

He added a very beautiful and subtle comparison, saying that he desired the Lord in this way: “As a weaned child upon his mother.” It is the custom of a small child, whenever he is being prepared by advancing age for other foods, that the milk on which he used to feed is withheld from him by his loving mother, so that he may pass to more solid nourishment and his substance may not remain in a certain tenderness and grow soft.

But then, with what purity, desire, and grace he seeks his mother, so that her loss is almost mourned when his spirit is moved to lamentation! By comparing this desire and longing to himself, the prophet shows how great hope, simplicity, and ardor there ought to be in the Lord.

Those who have been deprived of milk are called “weaned.” The comparison is fitting: just as infants suck their mothers’ breasts, so little believers are nourished by the simplicity of divine Scripture until they are prepared for solid food, as the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

Nor is it without significance that he added “upon his mother,” while they are still tender and are carried above their mother’s breasts. For the habit of food being withdrawn is more burdensome to those who do not know how to console themselves with other foods [editorial reading: *quia*, “because,” for *qui*, “those who”].

He added: “so you will requite my soul.” This is spoken according to human usage. We ourselves impose a penalty upon ourselves when, on some ground, we trust rightly [editorial reading: *justa*, “just,” for *juste*, “rightly”], as is also said in the seventh psalm: “Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:4–5).

But the order of the words must be arranged for us, so that the verse’s poetic composition may seem to explain itself more clearly:

“If I did not think humbly, as a weaned child upon his mother, but exalted my soul.”

There follows the compensatory condition: “so you will requite my soul.” When this is said, it signifies that if I presumed to despise you, you would rightly appear to cast me away.

Alternatively, the passage may perhaps be understood as spoken against those who, placed in certain tribulations and adversities, act impatiently and refuse to endure the divine remedies. Against these the humble and faithful person says that, although he was delayed in being heard, his heart did not leap into contempt; nor does he say that his eyes were lifted up, since this is especially done by little children who, in a mad willfulness, presume to despise their parents.

The comparison itself can also be taken in a negative sense: a weaned infant exalts his soul against his mother when he presumes to tear at her breasts with his hands and acts with wailing and tears, so that his indignation may be recognized. Then there follows the penal condition, namely that if he did the things mentioned above, he would be cast away by the Lord, just as a weaned infant is proved to be excluded from his mother’s breasts.

But so that we may understand this psalm to have been uttered for the virtue of patience and humility, as has been said, he added: “Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time forth and forever,” lest our headlong despair should appear rightly comparable to that of weaned infants.

### Verse 5

“Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time forth and forever.”

After he had suitably taught that humility and gentleness must be followed, he turns, like a good teacher, in the second part and admonishes each of the faithful to place his confidence always in the Lord and to persevere in it throughout all ages. For in this world it is possible to hope; there, however, the desired rewards will be seen.

Sometimes “age” signifies this world; sometimes it signifies that kingdom of the Lord which we believe is to come. He says “from this time forth and forever,” that is, from the present time to the future eternity, when there will be one age and the succession of times will happily be changed into perpetual unity.

Thus he brought the text of the psalm to its conclusion with a concise ending, so that even the brevity of its wording might befit holy humility.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Humility is exceedingly marvelous, since it is commended at the highest summit. If some hermit devoted to his cell were to say such things, he would nevertheless shine with great praise for his patience. But this was said by one clothed in purple, by the outstanding one among the prophets, so that the more brightly he shone with the splendor of honors, the more earnestly he might shun pride.

But what is required of us, if such things were demanded of him? Grant, O Lord, the humility of a king and the patience of a prophet, since in whatever person these qualities are found, they are truly your rewards. They are not acquired casually by human will, but bestowed by the generosity of your mercy.

For this reason humility rises honored above all the eminent virtues: your majesty’s condescension has assumed it. Finally, let us consider how greatly humility has been honored, since, opposed to pride, it is recognized as having been placed on the twelfth step. Pride plunges into Tartarus; humility leads to heaven.

# Psalm 131

## A Canticle of Ascents

Although all the Canticles of Ascents have raised the prophet to the advancement of a higher hope, this one lifted him in every respect, because it describes the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation. It was fitting that, after the number twelve of the apostles, the thirteenth himself should arrive as the head of all. I do not think this can fit the person of the prophet, because the glory of so great a psalm cannot reasonably be applied to anyone other than the Lord Christ.

For the humble man who had hitherto cried out from the depths could not suddenly have raised himself to such great praise that he would seem to exceed human measure. Therefore that desirable David, that strong-handed David, is here to be understood by us: in him the humility of assumed incarnation is present, and the omnipotence of Deity excels.

## Division of the Psalm

Although the prophet frequently spoke in the psalms about the Lord’s incarnation, in this ascent he declares so great a mystery most clearly. He was therefore rightly able to ascend to the glory of perfection, since he never ceases to reveal the salvation of the human race.

In the first narrative, then, he reports the words of the Lord Christ, by which he is known to have promised his Father that he would take no rest at all unless he had infused the affection of true religion into human hearts.

In the second narrative, he says that what had truly been promised by the Lord Savior has become known, adding his prayers that he may quickly provide the saving advent whose arrival was still delayed by the postponement of the future.

In the third part, he asserts that the promise made to him by the Father will be fulfilled: the fruit of the virginal womb will sit eternally upon the throne of dominion, so that he may bless his Church, feed the poor, glorify the priests, and extend his power; may clothe his enemies with confusion; and may eternal sanctification of righteousness flourish over him.

Therefore let us hear this psalm with attentive minds, for it is profound in its meanings and rich in the significance of its very words.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness.”

The prophet frequently uses human customs when entreating the Lord. “Remember” is said to one who was never able to forget anything. The Divinity is not reminded so that something may return to memory, since before him all the present, past, and future are present.

“David,” however, signifies the Lord Christ, who descended through the seed of the flesh from the origin of his creation. We place the names of grandfathers and great-grandfathers in a later generation in order to declare someone to have been the son of his ancestors.

That Jesus Christ is called David is attested by Jeremiah, who says: “And I will raise up David their king for them” (Jer. 30:9); and again: “I will raise up for them David, the righteous East” (Jer. 23:5), and so forth.

Likewise Ezekiel says: “And I will raise up over them one shepherd, a lofty one, and my servant David will feed them; he will be their shepherd, and I will be their God, and David will be prince in their midst” (Ezek. 34:23).

It is therefore clear that this was not said of David the son of Jesse, since these prophets are declared to have lived long after him, and their prophecy is known to speak of the future. Moreover, he could have said, “Remember me”; but in order to signify another, he said, “Remember, O Lord, David.”

Therefore it must confidently be accepted that this meaning is confirmed by such great testimonies. For what follows—“and all his gentleness”—shows the virtue of immense patience. Of him Isaiah says: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7).

Certainly, how could the prophet have said this of himself, when he remembered that he had cruelly killed Uriah the Hittite because of his wife (2 Sam. 12:9)? Hence the glorious example of his repentance also remains.

### Verse 2

“As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.”

“Swore” is said of Christ the Lord, whose mystery is a firm promise. The very etymology of the word, as has already been said, signifies *iure oravit*—“he prayed by right,” that is, he promised truly and firmly. This was when the Lord himself said to Peter, who was thinking carnally: “Put your sword back in its place. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John 18:11).

And again, lest he seem to depart from his purpose, he said to Peter elsewhere: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me” (Matt. 16:23).

But lest you think less highly of the one whom you know to have sworn, hear about the Father himself: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent” (Ps. 109:4). And: “The Lord swore to Abraham” (Deut. 30:20). The same thing is said of the Father below: “The Lord swore truth to David.”

Moreover, the statement “The Lord swore” shows that another person, not his own, must be understood. The vow of the Son, therefore, was that by the advent of his own incarnation he would reconcile the human race to the Father, a race made hostile by the effects of sin.

Yet this vow was not divided from the Father. For everything the Father wills, the Son also wills, and the Holy Spirit wills, since one nature, one power, and one will are recognized. What this vow is, however, is explained below.

### Verse 3

“If I enter the tabernacle of my house, if I ascend upon the bed of my couch”  
[manuscripts A and B: *strati* instead of *stratus*].

In this verse and the two that follow, the words of the Lord Christ are to be understood as reported by the prophet from the standpoint of Christ’s humanity. He denies that he will enter the tabernacle or ascend the bed of his couch until he is known to have fulfilled what he promised to the Father.

By “tabernacle,” unless I am mistaken, he means the heavenly dwelling, where after his resurrection he ascended, with the flesh he had assumed, before the eyes of the apostles. He declares that he will not enter it beforehand, until he finds for the Lord Father a dwelling-place of devout hearts.

For this reason he added “of my house,” in order to signify the heavenly dwelling, as he says elsewhere: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1).

He continues: “if I ascend upon the bed of my couch.” In his customary manner, he makes heavenly realities known through human practices. Our bed, when spread, gives us rest and an end to our labors; hence his bed—that is, his rest—must be understood as the completion of his most blessed Passion.

The very phrase “if I ascend” signifies the Ascension, when he ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father. Then the vows of his oath—that is, of his promise—were fulfilled. He himself also said this in his Passion, when he had been given vinegar to drink: “It is finished”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John 19:30).

### Verse 4

“If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples.”

Although even the earlier statements we have discussed cannot seem to be applied to the nature of his divinity, this statement is recognized as entirely different, since it would appear to attribute sleep to the eyes or slumber to the eyelids of the power of Divinity. Yet all these things are reasonably understood to belong to his humanity.

He says: “If I give sleep to my eyes.” This sleep must be understood as the rest of death, concerning which another psalm has already said: “I slept and was overcome with sleep; and I rose, because the Lord received me” (Ps. 3:6), and so forth.

He continues: “or slumber to my eyelids.” The practice of sleep is powerfully expressed. Eyelids are so called from *palpitare*, “to flutter,” since unless they come to rest through a certain trembling relaxation, sleep cannot enter the eyes.

He continues likewise: “or rest to my temples,” because in truth the temples of our head cannot have rest when the eyes, driven by frequent movements, are known to remain awake. First he placed “sleep,” and afterward explained how that sleep itself is fulfilled.

It was truly sleep, because it was received only as a three-day pause, which brought no corruption to the body but rest.

### Verse 5

“Until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.”

The promise that was sought while suspended in the preceding statements has now been reached. For he says that his vow had always been directed toward this: until the steadfastness of the Church had been founded through the order of holy preaching.

The Lord’s place is the tabernacle of the Christian heart and the courts of the Catholic Church, which he inhabits as heaven itself. These were found after they had been established and had grown strong through the Lord’s advent.

They were plainly found when he himself sought us, himself found us, and himself built us by his mercy; and when he made a tabernacle for himself from us and in us, restoring us to eternal life by his own compassion.

Remember also that, just as above he said that Christ promised this to the God of Jacob, so here he asserts that Christ fulfilled the vow to him, so that the truth of his oath might appear to have been accomplished.

But lest the perfidy of the Jews should cause this addition to disturb what has been explained—since it presumes, to its own destruction, to divert the divine Scriptures from the path of truth by certain other inventions, so that it may seem to conceal the integrity of the matter—let it hear what follows, and at last, confounded, come to its senses.

### Verse 6

“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest.”

After the mystery of the Lord and after his work, which he completed in all truth, the prophet comes to the second narrative. In it, speaking in his own person, he asserts that he found in the fields of the forest the Lord’s promise which he had heard in Ephrata.

In Latin, Ephrata is said to signify “mirror.” The fields of the forest signify the hearts of the Gentiles, which, cleansed by the Lord, opened out with the spacious purity of a plain from sins that were like forests and thickets.

Fields are so called from their capacity and broad extent. For from rough they became polished, from wild they became gentle, from barren they became fruitful, and from dens of demons they became temples of the Ruler.

Therefore he says that what had been promised to the Jews in the image of prophecy was discovered in the fields of the forest—that is, among the Gentiles.

Bethlehem itself, where the Lord was born, was also called Ephrata, as the prophet Micah says: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrata, are you indeed least among the tribes of Judah? From you will come forth a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel” (Mic. 5:2).

And it is written in Genesis that Rachel was buried beside Ephrata, which is Bethlehem (Gen. 35:19). Hence it is clearly apparent that the Lord was heard to be destined to be born in Bethlehem, but that, for the sake of the faith of the Gentiles, he was discovered in the fields of the forest.

### Verse 7

“We entered his tabernacles; we worshiped in the place where his feet stood.”

Since above he said that in Ephrata he had heard what he found in the fields of the forest, he now, to confirm the effect of complete devotion, says that he entered the Lord’s tabernacles, so that he might profess in every way that he had entered into what he held in the firmest hope.

The statement above must plainly be examined: the Lord promised a tabernacle in the singular, whereas here the prophet, together with the faithful Christians, asserts that he enters tabernacles in the plural. Christ the Lord promised the Catholic Church in the singular, but the prophet used the plural because he then joined himself in faith to the Christian people, when innumerable churches had already been promised throughout the whole world.

Yet it is not enough for him to profess merely that he entered the churches unless he also says that he worshiped where the most holy feet of the Lord Christ stood.

The feet signify the evangelical commandments, as it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Isa. 52:7). His feet stood there where the truth of faith is shown to have been founded.

For we must stand eternally in that place where the fullness of the law and the prophets—the Lord Christ—stands firm. “To stand” often refers to steadfastness, as it is written in the Gospel: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him” (John 3:29).

Standing belongs to a most solid mind; hence it is written: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). Another psalm shows that sinners cannot remain steadfast in faith, saying: “There they fell who work iniquity; they were cast out and could not stand” (Ps. 35:13).

If you wish to refer this also reverently to the historical event, it perhaps signifies the holy cross, where he stood bodily when he appeared fastened upon it. He is rightly said to have stood there where his body is shown to have been fixed.

Therefore the prophet deservedly says that this place must be worshiped, since it provided us both the sign of faith and salvation.

### Verse 8

“Arise, O Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification.”

After the prophet recognized that the promises of the Lord Christ mentioned above had been fulfilled, so that nothing remained unpaid, he cries out to the Lord: “Arise into your rest,” so that he might declare the outcome of events according to the order of perfect truth—that is, that he should rise from the lower regions into the everlasting blessedness of his divinity.

And observe that he added “your,” meaning the rest which your majesty has assigned to you, which reigns with the Father in equal power and everlasting glory.

And lest you think that the head could abandon its members, he added: “you and the ark of your sanctification,” that is, the Church, which he deigned to sanctify by making it his members.

For he did not say Noah’s ark, nor the ark of the covenant—although both appeared to bear the type of the Church—but specifically designated the ark when he added “of your sanctification.” Finally, see what follows.

### Verse 9

“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness”  
[manuscripts A and B: *justitiam* instead of *justitia*],  
“and let your holy ones rejoice.”

He is still speaking about those members whom he asks the Lord to receive into eternal rest. But let us see what “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” signifies: let them be clothed, as it were, with heavenly armor, just as the Apostle says: “Clothed with the breastplate of righteousness and charity, so that you may be able to extinguish the flaming darts of the enemy” (Eph. 6:14–16), namely, so that they may be able to confront the darts of heretics without fear.

Alternatively, “righteousness” itself signifies the Lord Christ, as the Apostle says: “Who was made for us by God wisdom and righteousness” (1 Cor. 1:30). The priests ought therefore to put him on and carry him always in their hearts. Yet he is put on in such a way that he deigns to be within, as the same Apostle says to the baptized: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

He continues: “and let your holy ones rejoice.” It was fitting that the holy ones should rejoice when they had put on Christ the Lord himself. For if worldly joy arises from putting on a costly garment, what joy can arise from that majesty which both makes one honorable and surrounds one in every way for salvation?

### Verse 10

“For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.”

Remembering what evils the Jewish people had committed in the wilderness, and afterward how greatly they had sinned against the Lord, and foreseeing also the Passion which they were about to inflict—a Passion indeed salutary for the world, but lamentable for them—the prophet prostrates himself in supplication before God the Father, asking that he not turn away the face of his Christ, that is, his presence, from the Jewish people whom he had once promised through the prophets, so that the one who was to reconcile the world might also wipe away the offense of the Hebrews  
[editorial reading: “Jews”].

[Col. 0951A] **Verse 11.** “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not disappoint him: From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.”

After that prayer which, briefly but with great longing, sought the Lord’s coming, the prophetic discourse enters upon a third narration, in which it joyfully enumerates what had been promised by the Father to the Son. For what can be said that is firmer or more constant, when he swears by whom oaths are sworn, and he promises who cannot be deceived? But this does not refer to that David, Jesse’s son, since he could have said, “The Lord swore to me,” as he also said at the beginning of this psalm. For when he says, “The Lord swore to David,” he indicates another—the one of whom it was already said in another psalm: “I have placed help upon the mighty, and exalted the chosen one from my people. I found David, my servant; with my holy oil I anointed him” [in is absent from manuscripts A, B, F]. And shortly afterward: “He will call upon me: You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation. And I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth” (Psalm 88 [89]:20–21, 27–28). This is what he has placed here: “He will not disappoint him.” For to disappoint is to reduce promises to nothing; and here he rightly denies that this can occur, since there could be no room for deception where the promise is declared by its utterly truthful author.

It follows: “From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne.” The fruit of the womb is the heavenly teaching of the Lord and Savior, from which the Christian people is known to have been generated. We have often said that, through faithful instruction, believers may be generated as though from a certain womb. The Father therefore promises that these will be placed upon the throne of the Lord Christ, when they are shown, after being converted to the commands of their author, to teach similar things. For someone is rightly said to sit upon another’s throne when he is also shown to teach that person’s commandments.

**Verse 12.** “If your sons will keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine, which I will teach them, their sons also will sit upon your throne forever and ever.”

He has explained what he said above. Here too he speaks of the apostles and the other faithful, who merited being called Christ’s sons through the integrity of their faith. To them it is said: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). The Lord’s thrones, therefore, will be given to those who merited becoming participants in his kingdom, just as he himself says in the Gospel: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). And lest you doubt to whom they should be given, he says that they are given to those who preserve the Lord’s covenant and testimonies, and every teaching, with pure devotion. But lest you suppose that this reward is perhaps temporal, he says: “They will sit upon your throne forever and ever.” That age will have no end, because every reward there endures in unchangeable eternity.

**Verse 13.** “For the Lord chose Zion; he preferred it as a dwelling for himself.”

**Verse 14.** “This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, because I preferred it.”

This cannot in any way be claimed according to the literal sense, since we know that ancient Jerusalem very frequently endured overthrow and desolation. Concerning it, Scripture says: “Zion shall be plowed like a field” (Jeremiah 26:18). But by this name the Jerusalem above is revealed: harmonious among its peoples, united by the power of charity, purified by the grace of forgiveness, and enjoying through an eternal contemplation the divinity and power of its Lord. For that majesty, supremely good, supremely blessed, and supremely powerful, although wholly present everywhere and possessing the hearts of the blessed, makes dwellings for itself—those whom it has preferred through the power of its mercy. This is indeed the Lord’s rest: for that special tabernacle to dwell within the most devout hearts of human beings, and to be everywhere in such a way that he is said to dwell in them as immeasurable and incomprehensible.

**Verse 15.** “Blessing his widow, I will bless her; I will satisfy her poor with bread.”

Christ’s widow is called the Church, because, deprived of every worldly assistance, she places her only hope in the Lord. She endures what a widow endures from the wickedness of evil people and the most savage plunderings of the impious. As though deprived of marital assistance, she continually mourns and is continually worn down, yet enjoys the unaltered steadfastness of a most chaste mind. In her likeness the Apostle praises the widow, saying: “But she who is a widow and desolate hopes in the Lord” (1 Timothy 5:5). Although this appears to include both married women and virgins, she is nevertheless called a widow because, deprived of secular protection, she has placed her hope in her heavenly Bridegroom, who made her beautiful from dark, upright from wandering, devout from cruel, and most firm from frail.

Or, as some prefer, the widow is the Synagogue, which is now the Church, because, when the law ceased—the law under which she was subject as though to a husband—she was undoubtedly joined to Christ when grace came. As though freed from her former condition, she merited heavenly marriage while preserving her chastity. The Apostle also made this comparison, saying: “Or are you ignorant, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives? For the woman who is under a husband is bound by her husband’s law while he lives [Latin, *vincta est lege mariti*; ed., *juncta est legi*, ‘is joined to the law’]; but if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband is alive, she will be called an adulteress if she joins herself to another man,” and so forth (Romans 7:1–2).

Let us also consider what he says: “Blessing, I will bless.” One who blesses once testifies that he brings his blessing to an end with that one blessing; but “blessing, he will bless” refers to one who sanctifies with continual blessing, now granting grace in one direction, now in another, through the generosity of his gift. This figure is called *A conjugatis*, because the joining of the words themselves is recognized as conjoined; and it is likewise shown to occur in the following verse.

It follows: “I will satisfy her poor with bread.” Truly, Christ’s poor are nourished with heavenly bread, since they always hunger amid worldly riches, as it was said in the preceding psalm: “The rich have lacked and hungered; but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing” (Psalm 33:11). These, then, are Christ’s poor: they lack earthly possessions, but enjoy heavenly abundance.

**Verse 16.** “I will clothe his priests with salvation [Latin *salutari*; ed., *salutare*], and his saints will exult with exultation.”

Priests are clothed with salvation when they receive the Lord Savior with the utmost integrity of faith and are clothed in his honorable mercy, as the Apostle says concerning the baptized: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). Although we have said this just above, we are not reluctant to repeat what can disclose the divine mysteries to us. Teachers ought to be such that they themselves are first irreproachable, and thus instruct the hearts of the other faithful, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever teaches and does these things will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19).

When he says, “They will exult with exultation,” he wishes to signify the perpetual joy of the saints, since he says that they will not merely exult but rejoice with everlasting gladness. Anyone may leap forth in great delight of spirit and later cease; but those exult with exultation who are never removed from the rewards bestowed upon them.

**Verse 17.** “There I will bring forth David’s horn; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.”

When he says “there,” he signifies that rest of blessedness of which the Father said above: “This is my rest forever and ever.” For the Father’s rest is the Son’s, and the Son’s is the Holy Spirit’s, since the Holy Trinity, which is one God, is neither separated in blessedness nor divided in power or nature.

It follows: “I will bring forth David’s horn.” Here too David is to be understood, as we said above, as the Lord Savior, whose horn—that is, the strength of his power—will be manifested at that judgment where eternal rewards are granted to the saints by him. David could not have said this of himself, since he too, among the other blessed, will not be the giver of the gift but will receive his reward from the Lord.

And so that you might understand that the Lord Christ is intended, it follows: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ,” that is, the light of the preaching of John the Baptist, who was truly Christ’s lamp, displaying heavenly light to the darkness of the world. Concerning him the Lord himself said: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). A lamp plainly shining—not for bodily eyes but for spiritual ones—and sending throughout the whole world an exceedingly abundant brightness, nourished by the oil of its Lord.

**Verse 18.** “I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him my sanctification will flourish.”

“His enemies” signifies heretics and pagans, or whoever has lived against his institutions. The one referred to in what follows as “his” designates the adversaries of Christ the Lord. And just as the Lord’s priests are clothed in the glory of salvation, so his enemies are clothed in a garment of confusion, when the former hear: “Come, blessed of my Father,” while the latter are told: “Go into eternal fire” (Matthew 25:34, 41).

And so that you might recognize that the Father does what the Son performs, here he says that the Father confounds his enemies, although this is known to be something the Son will do. For he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). Yet the glory of the Son is fittingly explained by the testimony of the Father. Elsewhere too, concerning the unity of their cooperation, it is said: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). There is no doubt that this must also be understood of the Holy Spirit. For what is said frequently of one person is understood of the power of the whole Trinity.

It follows: “But upon him my sanctification will flourish.” “Will flourish” is said to express the holiness of his glorious incarnation, which flourished in such a way, as the Apostle says, “that every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10–11). This is clearly said by comparison with fields: a great beauty rises before those who look when the loveliness of the countryside is clothed in flowering colors.

But how can such praise of continuous flowering apply to anyone else, since the prophet is read to have been driven from the kingdom by his son and is shown, in certain respects, to have committed extremely serious crimes in a human manner? The Lord Christ, however, whatever he did and whatever he endured, always had the Father’s sanctification flourishing within himself. Therefore this present psalm is rightly applied to him, since he is known to have been without any offense.

**Conclusion of the Psalm**

You have heard what this ascending man accomplished; you have heard with what joy he has filled us. For although all the Songs of Ascents grow in grandeur from the beginning, and although these may be called loftier because they have shone with the clearest light concerning the Lord’s coming, once the Creator had been prophesied, it was necessary for the step to grow by which all things are known to receive their increase.

What remains for us in the following gradal psalms is love of neighbor and charity toward God. If we ascend these with a pure mind, then we shall reach his most glorious vision.

# Psalm 132

## A Song of Ascents

After the most holy preaching of the preceding psalm, the prophet, now placed at the fourteenth step, proclaims to the peoples the blessed unity, so that those who bind themselves together in the Christian religion may persevere in one harmony of charity. Although some have judged this to apply to monks, we nevertheless say that it also pertains to universal concord, since it is proclaimed not only to monasteries but to the whole Church, gathering together with a spiritual trumpet whatever belongs to Christ’s soldiers throughout the entire world.

I do not resist its being said of blessed monasteries, but neither do I think it should be withheld from the whole body. It is therefore a worthy place to contain the gathering of the faithful people, which clearly came into being before the Lord’s incarnation acquired it from the nations with precious blood. And it is rightly placed after that psalm through which it is declared to have been bestowed upon the world.

## Structure of the Psalm

Behold another psalm that is recognized as having no division. It was fitting, indeed, that one speaking of unity should not receive a division into sections: remaining simple, without any diversity of subjects, like what we rightly call atoms. It does not change its person, subject, or manner of speech toward something else; for these three things appear to generate divisions in psalms.

These atoms perhaps pertain to those two small coins which the woman, placing them in the treasury, is shown to have received as gifts of fullest mercy (Matthew 21:2). So too, if we draw the power of these psalms into devout minds, we receive remission of all sins. The one invites us to the praises of the Lord; this one urges us toward love of neighbor.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together!”

“Behold” belongs more to one who is showing than to one who is speaking; it is the gesture ordinarily made with an outstretched hand through great concentration of mind, rather than explained in words. “Good” refers to charity, because perfect men encourage one another by common examples and, by imitating each other’s virtues, are seized by the fire of mutual love. We often do good while disagreeing through inner adversity. Perfect virtue consists in this: that the good you have done should itself please you.

“To dwell” means to remain in a good purpose. This is the dwelling the Lord seeks—not roofs and walls that bring bodies together, but what joins souls in religious fellowship. By such a saying he prohibits the *circumcelliones*, who wander through different monasteries with fickle intention.

By saying “brothers together,” he signifies those who are established under one Father through the fellowship of faith, of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that they had “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Those who wander through the solitudes of the desert also dwell together. Although they appear to be separated in body, they are not shown to be divided in the harmony of faith.

If you understand it according to the literal sense, this too is a good fellowship, which is gathered in assemblies of brothers, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “It was distributed to each according to his need; nor did anyone (*aliquis*, ‘anyone’; ed., *aliquid*, ‘anything’) call his own property among them, but everything was common to them” (ibid., 4:35, 32). Yet this part will be praised only if that harmony of mind which we mentioned above is not denied. And so that you might understand this union to be not merely some moderate good but a remarkable one, praise worthy of it follows it through mystical comparisons to the end, so that a most precious reality might be joined to the grace of its proclamation.

**Verse 2.** “Like oil upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descends upon the hem of his garment.”

The explanation of the preceding verse, made through subtle comparisons, now begins. In ancient times some were anointed as kings, others as prophets, and others for the most revered dignity of the high priesthood. Yet these proclaimed a likeness of the Lord Christ, as did many other things performed figuratively in those times.

Coming invisibly and incorporeally, the Lord Christ was anointed. Otherwise, the almighty King, the wondrous Prophet, and the eternal High Priest, who offered himself immaculate to be sacrificed for sinners, is not read to have been anointed bodily.

Concerning this oil the forty-fourth psalm says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44 [45]:8). If you still seek more clearly what this oil of gladness, or spiritual anointing, is, it is not beside the point to observe that the Holy Spirit, according to the Gospel reading, descended in the form of a dove and remained above the baptized Lord Christ (John 1:32). He is the head of the body of the Church, crucified, raised on the third day, ascended into heaven, and seated at the right hand of the Father.

It follows: “which descends upon the beard,” that is, the Holy Spirit, who descended upon the apostles with the power of his immeasurable might (Acts 2:4), when they spoke in the languages of different nations with their various forms. We rightly call the apostles “the beard,” since this is an indication of robust manhood and remains fixed beneath its head. Having overcome many sufferings by divine favor, the apostles proved themselves exceedingly steadfast men through God’s grace. By preserving the rules they had received from the Lord, they showed that they had remained beneath their head.

But lest you understand this beard as belonging to just anyone, he added “Aaron,” who, bearing the appearance of Christ, already represented Christ himself in his priesthood under a certain figure. We frequently use transferred names for Christ himself, such as Solomon, David, and Samson; so too here, Aaron.

He added: “which descends upon the hem of his garment.” The hem of the Lord Savior’s garment signifies the Church, because the Holy Spirit descends to its very extremities when, through his gracious mercy, he sanctifies the baptized to the end of the age. This is the Church, also represented by that tunic which could not be divided at the time of the Passion.

Our fathers therefore spoke spiritually and abundantly about this garment. Josephus, in the third book of the *Antiquities*, chapter eight, disclosed the mysteries of great realities arising from it, demonstrating that its four colors—that is, fine linen, purple, hyacinth, and scarlet—reasonably signified the elements of the world. Jerome also, writing to Fabiola (Letter 128), did not fail to offer useful material concerning this subject.

**Verse 3.** “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.”

He comes to another comparison for praise, which again, as is customary, reveals great mysteries to us through the meaning of names. Dew is thin and light rain, not falling in drops but permeating the hardness of earthly dryness through extremely minute particles. Through it all growing things cohere and are brought to various fruits by the gift of tempering.

Hermon is the Hebrew name of a mountain situated beyond the Jordan River. Its interpretation, as handed down by the Fathers, signifies “anathema,” that is, a curse. The dew of this mountain, therefore, nourishing sinners who lay under the curse of anathema, descends upon Mount Zion when, through the Lord’s gift, they arrive at the remedy of conversion.

For Zion signifies the catholic Church, which receives the nations that had been placed under the danger of anathema. Perhaps you will ask why he said “which descends,” when he could more appropriately have said “which ascends,” since it has been transferred to better things. But it is common usage to speak of those who come *tarde* (‘slowly’; ed., *trahendo*, ‘by being drawn’) to some knowledge in this way: “He descended to truth; he descended to justice”—as though they came from that summit of pride to a level and lucid understanding.

This is what it means for dew to descend from Hermon to Mount Zion: for the nations to pass from the seat of impiety to the pleasant places of blessedness. This is also what the first verse proclaimed: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together!”

**Verse 4.** “For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever.”

“There,” namely, on Mount Zion, that is, in the Church, which consists in the union of the brothers, he commanded blessing—that is, he sent the Lord Savior, who is the life of believers and everlasting blessedness.

In truth, we have often said that this name of the mountain signifies that heavenly Jerusalem, of which the earthly city bears an image. It is she who contains life without end and joy without interruption; and, surpassing every kind of happiness, she is ruled and possessed by her author through his beneficence.

By saying “there,” where concord is signified, he shows that no blessing is granted to those who are divided. You see with what comparisons and how greatly that congregation has been praised, so that no one may doubt that it is a great gift, since it is praised by the one who will give the reward.

It should also be considered how this psalm proceeded (*cucurrerit*; manuscripts, *concurrerit*, ‘run together’) with one sense and one continuous construction. This figure is called *hyrmos*, when the sequence of speech preserves its continuity to the end, with neither another person nor another subject being changed. We recognize that we also placed this structure in Psalm 116 because of its indivisible continuity.

**Conclusion of the Psalm**

The usefulness of unity has been shown to us, and it has been declared what brotherly affection can accomplish. Let us love our brother as ourselves; let us love the Lord above ourselves, so that this love of neighbor may lead us to that Lord’s perfect charity. For what can be more pleasant than to imitate here what is known to be bestowed there in that blessed homeland as the highest gift? Let those who are greatly to be loved there be carried here.

Let this be proclaimed to monasteries, to churches, to cities, to villages, and to the deserts. No one who is shown to possess the affection of holy religion is separated from this brotherhood.

Nor should we leave unexamined the fact that here the charity of brothers is placed first, and divine love follows, whereas the commandment gives first place to: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 6:5); and afterward follows: “and your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37). Teachers have the custom of most suitably reversing the order of statements in order to explain the usefulness of their subjects. Since these psalms always involve ascent, it was fitting that what is declared superior to all things should be placed at the summit, after everything else.

# Psalm 133

## A Song of Ascents

Let us look with the attentive eye of the heart at how the prophet has climbed, through successive steps, the highest traces of virtue. To that blessed brotherhood which he had said was to be gathered together, he now salutarily persuades what remains: that the happy union should be stirred to the praises of the Lord by the most ardent zeal of charity, so that perfect action may follow the faithful, and here they may imitate the sweetness believed to remain in the minds of the saints in that homeland.

It is fitting that blessing should be rendered to him to whom ascent has clearly been made with the highest devotion. We must now discuss the power of this commandment, so that, once its meaning has been understood, its usefulness may be opened to us through examination.

The commandment is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matthew 22:37, 39–40).

What an admirable summary: to say in one heading what you can find throughout the holy Scriptures! For one who loves God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength leaves no room for vices. Where could wickedness enter when the mind is wholly occupied with God? The devil seeks what is vacant and searches out what has been stripped bare; but when he finds God present, he departs in great confusion.

Thus, if we love God with our whole heart and surrender ourselves to his power with devoted affection, we can neither give room to sins nor fail to walk continually along the straightest paths. Vessels that are already full of some liquid cannot receive an increase poured into them; so, if divine charity fills us completely, there will be no place for crime to enter.

It follows: “and your neighbor as yourself.” We love our neighbor as ourselves when we do harm to no one but treat everyone with the same affection with which we treat ourselves. No one is willing either to wish calamities and dangers upon himself or to be enclosed by deceitful ambushes; everyone wishes to be protected in such a way that no adversities attack him. If we preserve this toward others with equal willingness, and do for our brothers what we wish to be done for us, every offense, every disgraceful act, and every sin unquestionably cease. Such people the present rule makes us, as the heavenly Teacher commanded us to be.

This commandment perhaps also embraces the good angels, who, by wishing that what they themselves possess may come to us, gain us as companions in that eternal fellowship.

Remember, moreover, that this is the third psalm of the Lord’s charity, so that from the number itself the virtue of the Holy Trinity may be recognized.

## Division of the Psalm

In the first part the prophet invites people to bless God; here he is recognized to admonish the people in the plural. Then, turning, he blesses the people individually, because holy unity is the glory and virtue of the Church.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord; you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

**Verse 2.** “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places, and bless the Lord.”

We have placed the two verses together because they are joined to each other by mutual connection, so that the complete meaning might appear more clearly to us.

First let us ask why he has placed “behold” both here and in the preceding psalm: namely, so that not only speech but also a demonstrative gesture might be supplied for certain and completed realities. Here it is said because, after so many steps had been climbed, only the one who granted so much ought to be praised. The first thing was that he had ascended with progress; then, beyond this ascent, he had no further ascent. The Lord is to be proclaimed with greater devotion when, through his generosity, he makes people secure.

Or, as others prefer, this time signifies the present world, in which the mind must be trained so that there it may be occupied with eternal and perpetual praises.

“Bless the Lord” signifies “praise,” because by blessing him we praise him, while by blessing us he sanctifies us. You heard “servant,” and, lest you think anything base was intended, he added “of the Lord,” so that the dignity of the servant might grow from the power of the supreme ruler.

Paul made himself honorable to the nations by this title, for his Epistle begins: “Paul, servant of Christ” (Romans 1:1); and again: “If I were still trying to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). Of Moses also, in another psalm: “He sent Moses, his servant” (Psalm 104:26). Therefore this is now properly said of the perfect, who are without doubt also called friends.

It follows: “you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.” He had first called them servants for the sake of honor; but lest uncertain human hearts apply this also to others who are known to be undevoted, since all creatures are subject to the Lord by the condition of their creation, he added: “you who stand in the house of the Lord,” that is, whose mind perseveres in the Lord with the firm step of religion.

“Standing” is said of those who do not slip from a good purpose through the fault of fickleness, as it was said of the devil, who had been an archangel but “did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44).

Having named the house, he concludes with the courts, since a court is the entrance to a dwelling. He signifies either those who are already in the inner chambers of the Church or those who have merited being at its entrance. The Church is known to have different places beneath the grace of unity.

To these words he also added another kind of firmness: “of our God,” that is, not the one whom the nations worship, but the one whom the true catholic religion confesses.

He added: “In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places, and bless the Lord.” “In the nights” signifies the most dreadful time of this world, which is continually darkened by very frequent tribulations. In this age, therefore, hands must be raised where good action deserves the Lord’s assistance.

Thus, as long as Moses held out his hands, the proud audacity of Amalek was oppressed (Exodus 17:11), foreshadowing the cross of the blessed Passion. Perhaps the fact that he extended his fingers signified the Decalogue. When he lowered his arms, the enemy’s pride, which had been despaired of, rose again. Therefore our hands must be raised to the Lord through good works, so that the adversary, the devil, may be conquered by heavenly majesty.

But consider what “lift up” signifies: give alms more generously. The Lord does not demand pious words from us alone, but deeds as well. He added “in the holy places,” so that the hand of the Christian might sow almsgiving there. If heretics or pagans perform it, their hands are not lifted up in the holy places, since Christ accepts only that almsgiving which a faithful Christian offers in his name.

Yet in this action, lest anyone claim anything for himself, he says that the Lord is to be blessed, since it is he who grants both a merciful spirit and more abundant means. Thus he teaches that the Lord’s charity is to be completed both in sacred praises and in pious action.

When these things have been done, consider what worthy repayment follows.

**Verse 3.** “May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.”

Once he has completed the exhortation in which he said that we must persevere in the Lord’s praises and good works through zeal for charity, he comes to the second part, in which, in one verse, he blesses the people who persevere in unity and love of the Lord.

Previously he said everything in the plural; now he concludes the psalm in the singular, so that the people whom he had earlier gathered as faithful brothers into unity may now receive the gifts of blessing as a people already loving the Lord.

Therefore, if we wish to be blessed, let the love of the Holy Trinity and the unity of the blessed Church embrace us. And observe how fittingly a perfect ending embraces this psalm: the one who climbed as far as the heavenly Jerusalem has received heavenly blessing as his reward.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

It is pleasing to recount how these steps have reached the heavenly Jerusalem.

The first step signifies the horror of the world, after which one hastens to the pursuit of every virtue. The second explains the power of divine protection, which nothing is shown capable of resisting. The third says that it is a great joy to dwell in the Lord’s Church with a pure mind. The fourth teaches that, amid every kind of distress, one must steadfastly hope in the Lord until he hears in mercy. The fifth advises that, once freed from dangers, we attribute nothing to ourselves but everything to the Lord’s power. The sixth compares the confidence of the most faithful Christian to the most solid mountains. The seventh says how abundant are the fruits harvested by those who sow in tears. The eighth says that nothing endures which each person has done by his own will, but only those things are most firm which are built with the Lord as their author. The ninth declares that a person becomes blessed through fear of the Lord and is granted everything that will benefit him. The tenth pours patience into the devoted, commending it through the words of the Church. The eleventh has the penitent cry to the Lord from the depths, so that the greatness of the divine power may be perceived in the liberation of human beings. The twelfth displays the virtue of gentleness and humility. The thirteenth approves the promise of the holy incarnation and the truth of the words. The fourteenth proclaims spiritual union to the brothers, upon whom the Lord’s blessing and eternal life are shown to come. The fifteenth awakens that perfect charity in the praises of the Lord, above which nothing can be said that is greater or found that is more glorious, as the Apostle testifies: “God is love” (1 John 4:8).

Therefore let us continually contemplate the mystery of so great a miracle, so that, always beholding such things, we may avoid the deadly errors of the world. This number also contains another mystery: when the five bodily senses, through which frail humanity contracts every sin, have been overcome by the power of the Trinity, it leads us to the summit of the fifteenth of the gradal psalms, so that, once bodily weakness has been removed, everlasting rewards may be granted to the victorious.

# Psalm 134

## Alleluia

After the most beautiful construction of the gradal psalms, which has reached that summit that makes people secure and happy forever, “Alleluia” is very fittingly placed, so that the holy Church may delight in the Lord’s praises, since such a gift is known to have been prepared for her. Therefore, let us hasten to say “Alleluia” with joyful and sincere minds, so that by divine grace we may be joined to that holy people.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. At the beginning, because of the power of the Lord’s name, he says that praises are to be rendered to the Lord, because he has done whatever he wished in heaven and on earth, recalling his various great works. Second, since the perfect praise of truth is to destroy falsehood, he rebukes the worshipers of idols with ridicule. Third, he admonishes different orders not to cease praising the Lord. Thus the demonstrative genre is completed in both parts with marvelous execution.

## Exposition of the Psalm

**Verse 1.** “Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants of the Lord.”

[Col. 0961C] **Verse 2. “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”** After the preceding psalms—as has been said—in which, by divine mercy, the prophet ascended to the summit of every virtue, he addresses those standing in the house of the Lord, so that, after receiving such immense benefits, they may not cease to praise the Creator of heaven and earth.

Observe also how these commands increase through the distinction of these two verses. First he said, “Praise the name of the Lord.” And lest you think this was enjoined upon just anyone, he added, “Praise the Lord, servants”—that is, you who are devoted to him with willing obedience, and recognize as your Lord the one whom you do not despise through any superstition. Third he says, “You who stand in the house of the Lord”—that is, you who remain with steadfast and unwavering will in faith in his holiness [Col. 0961D]. This is said, of course, against those who, having suffered a failure, fell from an honor suddenly bestowed upon them.

It follows: “In the courts of the house of our God.” A court (*atrium*) is said to be the first entrance of a very spacious house, where the inhabitants were accustomed to make hearths for themselves to drive away the cold; and antiquity says that the courts were called *atria* from the very dark clouds of smoke, as though they were *atra*, “dark.” And because no expression is without meaning, and every expression seems to contain some mystery, he also says that those must praise the Lord who appear to have entered the first section of the Lord’s house.

**Verse 3. “Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing praises to his name, for he is gracious.”** Consider that he placed “praise” three times, so that by the similar quality of praise he might show us the indivisible unity of the holy Trinity. For he recounts a manifold reason for the Lord’s praise, extending it even to division. Since all the things he made are very good, one perceives whose goodness it is, from whom such things are known to have proceeded.

He also added “gracious,” so that you might understand him to be not only good but also sweet. Thus he says elsewhere: “Taste and see that the Lord is gracious” (Psalm XXXIII, 9). But when “sing praises” is used, it refers to good bodily actions, so that in this worldly life we may appear to praise the Lord for our upright conduct.

**Verse 4. “For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.”** This verse too still belongs to the section explaining why the Lord should be praised. Some people are known to be troubled by the question why Abraham is not mentioned here, since this possession is first declared to have been promised to him by the Lord.

But the name “Abraham” did not seem to signify what could be understood from this name. “Jacob,” indeed, has often already been said to mean “supplanter,” because he seized his brother’s blessing with exceedingly glorious eagerness. This appropriately applies to the multitude of the nations called forth, which, drawing the coming of the Lord the Savior to itself through faith, received the gifts promised to the Synagogue and surpassed the earlier people in religious haste.

But after that mystical struggle of the patriarch, which Jacob steadfastly carried on with the angel, he himself also deserved to be called Israel, because he endured the weight of so great a contest with resolute mind. “Israel,” moreover, is interpreted as “a man seeing God,” which pertains to that significance by which the Lord possesses the blessed.

Therefore he chose Jacob when he united the people of the Church through the gathering of different nations. He possesses Israel when, in that resurrection of the blessed, he is proved to dwell in all.

**Verse 5. “For I have known that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods.”** Every account is made certain when the one giving it testifies that he has proved what he says. Thus the prophet says that he has come to know what he proclaims—not through any bodily vision, but because, placed in that height of knowledge, he contemplated the Lord’s greatness there.

The most holy man saw that wondrous Majesty commanding all powers and the forces of heaven; and it was necessary for him to say, “For I have known that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods”—not because there is any other God besides him, as we read in another psalm: “For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God?” (Psalm XVII, 32), but because this name is known to have been applied improperly to various powers, as it is written in Exodus: “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exodus VII, 1). The Apostle also says: “For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (I Corinthians VIII, 5–6). Therefore God is rightly called great above all gods: he from whom all things were created.

[Col. 0963A] **Verse 6. “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses.”** After what he said above, the true and exceedingly lofty proclamation rises still higher. This figure is called *epiphonema* (ἐπιφώνημα), that is, a judgment which, after the matters narrated, rises to greater things.

For although the works of the Lord are indescribable, and the whole world is unable to recount what he does in the world, here everything is enclosed in astonishing brevity: God made everything he willed in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in the abysses. Thus you might recognize that the created things you see were made by his will, and understand that those things which cannot appear to human sight can nevertheless be held within his power.

“Heaven” is used for all heavenly things; “earth” for everything produced on earth; “sea” may be said to refer to those gulfs visited by the movement of travelers; and “abyss” designates the Ocean, which is unknown to us and, as some report, deep to a great depth. In all these things the Lord’s will is fulfilled without any uncertainty. What the Lord did he recounts next.

[Col. 0963B] **Verse 7. “He brings clouds from the end of the earth; he made lightning into rain. He brings winds from his treasuries.”** If you attend to this literally, it testifies that the hidden processes of nature are fulfilled under the Lord’s administration. But since below he speaks about the Hebrew people, it is also fitting to apply this to human beings.

He brought clouds from the end of the earth when he caused prophets to advance from humble purpose to the heights of preaching. They are rightly compared with clouds, because by the rain of their speech they defend us from the heat of the future judgment while bringing forth what will benefit our souls. Scripture testifies that clouds are to be understood as prophets—as has frequently been said—when it declares: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon her” (Isaiah V, 6).

It follows: “He made lightning into rain.” The prophets’ proclamations are therefore lightning when they strike enemies; they are rain when they wash the devoted from sins and pour upon them the shower of salvation, so that spiritual fruits may spring up and, by the Lord’s provision, grow into a mature harvest.

He added: “He brings winds from his treasuries.” We may properly understand the winds as the apostles, whose preaching sped through the whole world like a swift wind. Of them it is written elsewhere: “He made his arrows into burning things” (Psalm VII, 14). Wings are also attributed to the winds because of the speed of their movement; for he says: “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm XVII, 11).

He adds, “from his treasuries,” from which spiritual riches could truly proceed. Note that through these eight verses he describes the Lord’s mighty works with a most pleasing variety, in various modes of an increase of praise. This figure is called *auxesis* (αὔξησις), in Latin “increase,” because it continually ascends by successive stages. Therefore one need not hesitate to repeat the explanation of the meanings frequently, since the authority of Scripture itself is also shown to take up the same things without weariness.

**Verse 8. “He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man to beast.”** Prophetic speech frequently repeats these miracles in order to make the Lord’s power understood, so that we may perceive that they were not performed by chance, but were set forth for the great understanding of a later age.

For if we consider the matter more deeply, such things happen even today. Egypt here is the world, which afflicts the Christian people with various calamities, but is terrified by the Lord’s strength and power. “Egypt” signifies affliction, which does not release faithful souls unless they are weighed down by hard labors within it [variant: “he does not release” / “it does not release”]. It strikes the firstborn of the world, as though of Egypt, when by the inspiration of his power he corrects human beings born in original sin.

“From man to beast” means from the more prudent of this age to gentle and simple men. For unless all are delivered by the Lord’s grace, they are oppressed by the devil under a wicked domination like that of Pharaoh.

[Col. 0964B] **Verse 9. “He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.”** He sent signs and wonders when, at his Passion, the earth trembled, the rocks were split, and many of the saints came to the Lord’s city, having overcome the law of death. It is clear that this happened in the midst of the world—that is, openly and visibly.

A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance it presents to our senses, causes something else to come into our thoughts from it; for example, when we see a footprint, we think of the animal whose footprint it is and that it has passed by. It is called a “sign” because it signifies. “Wonders” (*prodigia*) are, as it were, *porro digia*, “things proclaiming from afar.” He does this also today when he converts faithful souls through certain signs set forth beforehand.

“Pharaoh” is interpreted as “dissipation.” To whom could this be more appropriately applied than to the devil, who persecutes the human race with cruel intent? “Against all his servants” signifies human beings who obey his desires. We are called the servants of the one whom we serve with a consenting mind. Therefore the devil is submerged with his ministers when the Christian people are freed from wicked error through the saving font.

**Verse 10. “He struck many nations and slew mighty kings.”** By “nations” he means the harmful hordes of vices, which continually afflict us within, like barbarous powers. He says that these are struck when they are wounded by the satisfaction of penitents. For what is salvation to us is a wound to them.

He also slays mighty kings within us when he makes the unclean spirits that rule through the stain of sins strangers to us by cleansing our offenses. They are rightly said to have been slain in their will, because they were utterly unable to extinguish us.

[Col. 0964D] **Verse 11. “Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan he slew.”** Although the children of Israel, with the Lord’s favor, struck down many kings, only these two are mentioned, so that through the interpretation of their names we might be led to that meaning which is at work in us today.

“Sihon” is interpreted as “temptation of colors”; “Amorites” signify “those who make bitter.” For the vices that lead us away from that most joyful blessedness are bitter. They have the devil as their king, who is “temptation of colors,” when he transforms himself into an angel of light (I Corinthians XI, 14), so that through the appearance and color of goodness he may overthrow the souls of the devoted by continual temptation.

This divinity [i.e. divine power] will slay these things in us when it frees the minds of the faithful from such servitude.

It follows: “And Og, king of Bashan.” “Og” is said to mean “conclusion,” and “Bashan,” “confusion.” The king of confusion is therefore rightly called “conclusion.” For when the devil closes that saving path for us, he abandons us in wicked confusion, in which that most dreadful one reigns. Hence his city is also called Babylon, which likewise means “confusion.”

But divine power destroys all these things when it leads us to the gifts of its mercy.

He added: “And all the kingdoms of Canaan he slew.” “Canaan” is interpreted as “humiliation,” but not the humiliation that leads to the Lord. For those who fall from holy honor and sink into the worst way of life are also said to be humbled, as it is said in another psalm: “And he will humble the accuser” (Psalm LXXI, 4). For if humiliation did not also pertain to punishment, it would not be written: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Matthew XXIII, 12). Therefore he alone slays this humiliation, which is to be understood in an evil sense, who accepted the cross for the salvation of all.

[Col. 0965B] **Verse 12. “And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance for Israel his people.”** This verse declares that the preceding statements should not be accepted literally, but understood through spiritual interpretation. The land of promise was not given as an inheritance to the Israelite people, because they lost it through their offenses; but, under the prefiguration of that people, the land of promise is unquestionably given to Christians, for them to possess in eternal peace.

To make you understand this, he repeats: “An inheritance for Israel his people.” “Israel,” as has often already been said, is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” “His people” means, of course, the Christian people, who will deserve to be called his when they have kept his commandments with saving devotion.

[Col. 0965C] **Verse 13. “O Lord, your name is forever; O Lord, your memorial is from age to age.”** After the Lord’s benefits, worthy praise follows. He says: “O Lord, your name is forever,” as though we were wishing for him to have something he does not possess, or as though he might advance through our prayers. But this is the custom of mortal beings: to wish God what it would be impious to think could happen otherwise.

Thus we say: “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew VI, 9), although it is certainly holy; “Your kingdom come,” although his kingdom will unquestionably come. But when we say such things, we declare our own will. He therefore prays that his name should always remain among the human race, so that from the coming of Christ onward they may perpetually be called Christians.

It follows: “O Lord, your memorial is from age to age.” The Lord’s memorial is whatever is contained in the Holy Scriptures as a most salutary reminder. It always remains in us when it is preserved with most faithful devotion, as it is written: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew XXIV, 35). “Age to age,” as has often been said, signifies the everlasting day.

[Col. 0965D] **Verse 14. “For the Lord will judge his people, and he will take comfort in his servants.”** The reason for the preceding praise is stated: “For he will judge his people”—namely, the Hebrew people, to whom he granted great miracles, to whom he gave his prophets so that they would not sin, and to whom he sent his own Son, so that its criminal hardness might at last be dissolved.

But because that people remained hardened in detestable obstinacy, he will indeed judge it, because it refused to belong to him, though he had chosen it from all the nations as his possession. To it he says: “Hear, O my people, and I will speak” (Psalm XLIX, 7); and elsewhere: “My people, what have I done to you?” (Micah VI, 3). These, therefore, he will judge.

But hear what follows concerning the faithful: “And he will take comfort in his servants”—that is, when he restores the rewards promised to those who here were afflicted by arduous contempt [manuscript F and printed edition: “struggle”] for his name. Of them it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.” Thus it is also said elsewhere concerning them: “Whoever believes in me will not be judged, but will pass from death to life; whoever does not believe has already been judged” (Matthew V, 5; John III, 18).

You see what that gradation achieved, as we said: by enumerating the Lord’s mighty works, it arrived at his holy and terrible judgment. Let us now examine the statements of the other section.

[Col. 0966B] **Verse 15. “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.”** After he had sufficiently filled himself with the praises of the Lord, prophetic speech turns, in its second movement, to destroying the error of the nations. Among grammarians this figure is called *sarcasmos* (σαρκασμός), that is, hostile mockery, which penetrates to the bone when it refutes by manifest truth.

Therefore he mocks the rites and idols of the nations, lest anyone worship golden images and silver gods, and lest what began from a human being be thought superior to a human being.
