How much better would they serve their purpose if, having been smashed, they were broken? They truly become useful if, converted into money, they are reduced to that form. Accordingly, their god does not hear as a whole, but is rather made more useful by being diminished.

Observe also that through the forms of various definitions the most beautiful order of the statements descends. Here idols are designated by the material from which they are made—that is, gold and silver—formed from the quality of metals.

**Verse 16. “They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see.”**

**Verse 17. “They have ears, but they will not hear; they have nostrils, but they will not smell.”**

**Verse 18. “They have hands, but they will not touch; they have feet, but they will not walk; they will not cry out with their throat; for there is no spirit in their mouth.”** He now comes to other forms of definition, signifying and determining idols by what they are unable to do.

For he says: “They have a mouth, but they will not speak.” What benefit is a mouth that does not speak? What benefit is an eye that does not see, an ear that does not hear, nostrils that do not smell, hands that do not touch, feet that do not move? These are empty words, not useful functions; names without realities; fleeting presumption, not enduring truth.

Why do you seek, for your own destruction, harmful delusions? Why do you manufacture things that destroy you? How much more fitting it would be for you to submit to your Creator and cease worshiping the error you made.

Thus the prophet Jeremiah, admonishing the Jews in his letter, says: “For their tongues have been polished by the craftsman; but they themselves, gilded and silver-plated, are false and cannot speak” (Baruch VI, 7). And again: “The beasts are better than they, which can flee under a roof or benefit themselves” (ibid., 67).

Observe that in these verses, and also in Psalm CXIII, the idols of the nations have been mocked at length, so that those whom the first admonition had not corrected might be moved by renewed shame.

[Col. 0967A] **Verse 19. “Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them.”** After the falsehood of the gods of the nations had been mocked, a fitting sentence was pronounced: those who made senseless gods for themselves should lack their corresponding senses.

What has been said truly applies to such people. For the person who reaches the point of appearing to worship not what is beneficial but rather his own destruction is abandoned by every form of reason and emptied of all prudence. Observe that one condemnation embraces both the makers and the worshipers of idols.

**Verse 20. “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord.”**

**Verse 21. “House of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.”** After mocking the idols of the nations, in the third movement he declares that the praises of the Lord must be celebrated by the mouths of the saints.

But in these two verses, moving through different offices, he admonishes us that the praise of the faithful should resound for the true Lord. In “Israel,” every righteous person who rejoices in divine contemplation is named generally; afterward he counts them specifically: in “Aaron,” the priests; in “Levi,” the remaining ministers; finally, those who serve the Lord in any worthy manner of life.

Thus the entire people, through its different parts, is commanded in devotion to praise the Lord.

[Col. 0967C] **Verse 22. “Blessed be the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.”** Above he commanded others to celebrate the Lord’s praises; now, following the example of a good teacher, he himself also fulfills what he advised. For he says: “Blessed be the Lord.” And he clearly identifies which Lord he had mentioned: namely, Christ the King, who visited Zion—that is, his Church—by his holy incarnation.

He is the one who dwells in Jerusalem, which is built from the congregation of different saints and rejoices in eternal happiness through the presence of its King.

**Conclusion of the Psalm**

This is a marvelous psalm for instructing the most devout peoples. After such great benefits, we can render nothing except—as was said at the beginning—to proclaim our Lord with a threefold confession [Col. 0967D]. Let us praise the Father, praise the Son, praise the Holy Spirit, the one and almighty God, so that just as there is no distinction in that nature, so there may be no difference in its praise.

This is truly the praise that refreshes us; this is the nourishment by which the devoted soul is fattened. It is our reward and also our work, in which we are so refreshed that no pleasure seems comparable to it. Let us therefore proclaim him now, so that we may deserve to praise him eternally with the angels. But may he himself grant the vow here who will bestow the reward there.

---

# PSALM CXXXV

**Alleluia**

Again we must say “Alleluia”—always new through grace, though entirely familiar from the preceding expositions. This psalm follows, and it is sung with a similar assonance of words. For it begins with different subjects but rises into a single harmony of proclamation. We may properly call its verses “single-ended,” as we already said in Psalm CXVII, where four verses end with a similar meaning.

Whatever is said is referred to the mercy of the Lord, without which we can in no way endure. It is therefore rightly repeated so often, since it accomplishes everything in us through its most indulgent gifts. For if you examine the cause of so great a mystery, the Lord’s clemency is everything we live, and his mercy is everything we are able to do. Therefore it ought neither to depart from our mouths nor from our hearts, so that it may itself deign to preserve us by continual protection.

Imitating this, poets composed little flowers of assonant verse, transferring the sounds of heavenly powers to worldly pursuits. But since all the psalms seem to contain manifold virtues, this one may properly be judged to proclaim the perfect life of the righteous: they begin salutarily with the Lord’s commandments and persevere continually in his mercy.

Let us therefore recall inwardly that similar verses have subtly indicated different virtues for us in Psalms VIII, XXIII, XLI, XLV, XLVIII, LVI, LXVI, CII, CIII, and CVI, as is clear from their expositions. What virtue the present psalm represents, however, we shall explain more fully in its conclusion [Col. 0968C].

**Division of the Psalm**

Throughout the psalm the prophet speaks. Although the whole psalm appears woven like a heavenly basket with beautiful repetitions, as though with golden bars of ornament, so that spiritual goods may be offered like sweet fruits to the guests of the Church, nevertheless, in those principal verses that are variously expressed, the first part explains the Lord’s magnificence and declares the creation of the whole world.

In the second part, the miracles he performed in Egypt and among the Jewish people are recounted. The third descends to Christians, successively enumerating the Lord’s benefits, so that through this repetition you may recognize that there is one author of all things.

**Exposition of the Psalm**

[Col. 0968D] **Verse 1. “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”** We said that the beginnings of the verses contain a most beautiful variety, while at their ends there is a similar repetition; therefore only the beginnings of the verses need to be explained, whereas their endings, repeated in one continuous form, need to be expounded only once.

This, however, must be firmly retained in the mind: the Lord’s mercy is fittingly joined to all the works mentioned below. We have often said that “confession” commonly refers both to praising the Lord and to lamenting sins. Here it must be understood as both, not merely one of the two. For he teaches blessed men both continually to offer praise to the Lord and to mourn their past sins.

Thus we understand the righteous: when they have turned from evil, they condemn what they once did, as the Apostle Paul says concerning his past: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (I Corinthians XV, 9).

It follows: “For he is good”—he who mercifully hears his praises and compassionately forgives those who beseech him. He added: “For his mercy is forever.” By “forever,” he means perpetually, because his mercy occupies eternal time. Here he grants it in order to restore; he spares in order to correct; there he grants mercy to the good in order to crown them.

[Col. 0969A] **Verse 2. “Give thanks to the God of gods, for his mercy is forever.”** In the preceding psalm he shook the hearts of the nations by mocking their idols; now, by proclaiming the truest majesty, he shows how great and what kind of being the almighty Lord is. Thus he is believed to be not merely a god in the sense in which an angel is called one, or a man of exceptional virtue is often so styled; rather, he is the God of gods, like whom none is found.

A creature can indeed be called “god” on account of the excellence of honor. For it is written in Psalm LXXXI: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Psalm LXXXI, 6). And in Exodus: “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh” (Exodus VII, 1). But “God of gods” can be called nothing other than the holy Trinity alone.

[Col. 0969B] **Verse 3. “Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever.”** This expression resembles the preceding sentence. He is called “Lord of lords” in the same way as “God of gods.” We also call the holy angels “lords”; but he alone is Lord of lords, to whom all things are subject.

He is also the Holy of holies, the King of kings, and ineffably the exalted summit of all powers. For who would doubt that he is above all things, since he is able both to create all things and to sustain the universe?

**Verse 4. “He alone does great wonders, for his mercy is forever.”** Just as “give thanks” was placed in the three verses above, so throughout all the verses that vary until the end, “give thanks” must be understood. This figure is called *apo koinou* (ἀπὸ κοινοῦ), “from the common,” because it allows the complete meaning to stand, especially since the psalm ends with this same construction.

He is therefore said to have done great wonders alone, as though he had not displayed signs of various powers through angels and apostles, his servants [Col. 0969D]. But he is said to have done them alone where he is shown to have fashioned the structures of things through his Word, since there is no doubt that he also created those ministries themselves. The following statements make this understanding clear.

[Col. 0969D] **Verse 5. “He made the heavens with understanding, for his mercy is forever.”** To the end of the psalm, praise is drawn from a laudatory narrative. For a narrative is a collected exposition of accomplished deeds. To narrate the Lord’s deeds is to praise him.

This is therefore the same as what he said above: “He alone does great wonders,” because he performed this not through creatures but solely through the power of his divinity. When he says that he made the heavens “with understanding,” he expresses the power of his ordering.

He does not make things by seeing them, nor by imitating the works of others; rather, whatever he has ordered in the understanding of his majesty, he brings instantaneously into effect. For the perfection of things is his will, and what he has decreed admits no delay. Thus it was said in the preceding psalm: “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Psalm CXXXIV, 6).

Therefore he made the heavens with understanding because they were created without confusion, disorder, or formlessness; rather, they are carried out distinct and ordered according to the will of their Creator.

Nor should it trouble anyone that he called them “heavens” in the plural, since elsewhere we read: “Praise him, heavens of heavens” (Psalm CXLVIII, 4). The Apostle also says: “I was caught up to the third heaven” (II Corinthians XII, 2). Therefore we cannot determine their number, since Scripture does not explicitly explain it.

[Col. 0970B] **Verse 6. “He established the earth upon the waters, for his mercy is forever.”** After speaking of the heavens, it followed that he should also speak of the earth, for he made it with understanding as well. It is that understanding which embraces all things and fulfills them through the power of its ordering.

But let us inquire why he said here that the earth was placed upon the waters, when Job says: “He hangs the earth upon nothing” (Job XXVI, 7), and elsewhere: “Who hung the mass of the earth by three fingers—what is his name?” (Isaiah XL, 12).

Neither statement is contrary to the other, because he could say that the earth is upon the waters even when it appeared to be separated from them by a great distance. Thus we also say that heaven is above us, although we know that great expanses of air lie between us.

Or, as others think, “upon the water” should be understood as “beside the water.” Even today we say that a city is situated upon the sea when it has been established not in the sea but beside it.

Alternatively, it must be understood spiritually: our earth—that is, our body—is restored upon the water of sacred baptism, while it is formed through the stability of religion.

[Col. 0970C] **Verse 7. “He alone made great lights, for his mercy is forever.”** Although literally the lights of heaven, the stars, appear to be meant, it is nevertheless fitting to investigate them somewhat more deeply. “Great lights” may perhaps signify angels, powers, thrones, and dominions, who shine with heavenly light through most holy devotion. By saying “great,” he seems to place them before all things that shine bodily.

**Verse 8. “The sun for the governance of the day, for his mercy is forever.”** The sun’s arrival is the power of the day, because through it every visible creature is revealed. It is the usage of the divine Scriptures to speak in this manner, as it says elsewhere: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John I, 12).

Spiritually, it can be understood when he mercifully pours the sun of wisdom upon his saints, so that they may see those things which certainly pertain to his commands.

[Col. 0970D] **Verse 9. “The moon and stars for the governance of the night, for his mercy is forever.”** Hear this, astrologers, who attribute the governance of the universe to the operations of the stars: the moon and stars were granted authority over the nights. Were these things created for command or for service? For what would the Creator do if he had permitted human lives to be governed by the stars?

The philosophers themselves rightly reject you, since you say that such great power resides in visible things that you remove free will from the Creator.

For us, however, another spiritual meaning is disclosed through these things. Perhaps we should understand the Church as the moon, and its various orders that shine with holiness as the stars: bishops, presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and the others who are known to radiate like stars through their heavenly manner of life. All these have been given authority over the night—that is, the darkness of this age—so that through them the obscure hearts of mortals may shine with light.

[Col. 0971A] **Verse 10. “He struck Egypt with its firstfruits” [manuscripts A, B, and F: *primogenitis*, “firstborn”], “for his mercy is forever.”** Up to this point the things that the holy Divinity created by itself have been described. Now, in the second section, the sort of things it brought about in the world through the angels and servants of its mercy are recounted.

This is the twelfth type of definition, which the Greeks call *kat’ epainon* (κατ’ ἔπαινον), and the Latins call “through praise.” It is carried through these twelve verses and continues until the division.

Since the history is well known, let us see what may be understood here more spiritually. He struck the first things of Egypt when he condemned the glory of this age, which was thought to be preeminent. Luxury, pride, and greed are, as it were, the firstfruits of the world. For the most wicked belly first produces these and embraces them like dear children, while rejoicing in the desire for such things.

The Lord struck them when he excluded them from the laws of his divinity. For those things that have been removed by the Author of life lie dead.

[Col. 0971C] **Verse 11. “He brought Israel out through their midst, for his mercy is forever.”** He leads Israel through the midst of the Egyptians when he frees his saints from association with the wicked and brings them from the most dreadful dwelling of this world into the light of his truth.

**Verse 12. “With a strong hand” [manuscripts A and B: “powerful”] “and an exalted arm, for his mercy is forever.”** The strong hand pertains to invincible action; the exalted arm to the Lord’s unique omnipotence. For strong action comes from the exalted arm, since the outcome of things always reveals their author.

[Col. 0971D] **Verse 13. “He divided the Red Sea into divisions, for his mercy is forever.”** Men of ancient authority said that the Red Sea was divided into twelve sections, corresponding to the number of tribes the Jews are known to have had. The phrase is placed here in the plural—“into divisions”—so that we would not think the Red Sea was crossed by a single route.

But this can also fittingly be understood spiritually. The Red Sea is the mingled depth of this age, which we cross by many divisions when, converted toward the land of the living, we hasten by the Lord’s gift. One crosses through almsgiving, another through continual prayer, another through virginity, another through supreme charity. Thus by many divisions the sea of this age is crossed toward the Lord.

[Col. 0972A] **Verse 14. “And he led Israel through its midst, for his mercy is forever.”** In this verse, since “for his mercy is forever” is repeated, the explanation given above is sufficient.

**Verse 15. “He shook Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea, for his mercy is forever.”** He shakes the devil and his ministers into the font of salvation when, by the power of his strength, he removes them from us. He said “shakes out” as though he were throwing away dust, so that through this speed he might both show the power of his divinity and demonstrate that they are earthly filth.

### Verse 16

“He led his people through the wilderness, for his mercy endures forever.”

He leads us through the wilderness when he enables us to pass unharmed through this world; for only those who pass beyond the evils of this world escape. Whoever becomes entangled in these things, however, does not attain the divine rewards. The world is called a wilderness because it has been deprived of divine election. And it is rightly so called, because it did not receive the Creator who came to it.

### Verse 17

“He brought water from the rock, for his mercy endures forever.”

He brings forth water from the rocky crag [the manuscript G and the editions read “casts out”], when he causes the barren hearts of mortals to produce life-giving streams of tears, so that those made barren by their own dryness may, through divine generosity, become capable of flowing. “From the rock of the crag” is placed by way of amplification, since the reference is not to small stones but to immense and hard rocks raised to the size of a crag.

### Verse 18

“He struck down great kings, for his mercy endures forever.”

He strikes down great kings when the heavenly Merciful One extinguishes impious desires in our hearts. For then we live, while those desires die; and by the opposite fate we must perish if they happen to prevail over us.

### Verse 19

“And he slew mighty kings, for his mercy endures forever.”

He slays mighty kings when he drives out from us the demons that rage through various assaults. Their wicked will is extinguished when the souls of the faithful are removed from their power. Slay the mighty kings, Lord, that you may free humble servants; rescue those devoted to you, lest that most wicked one make them subject to himself.

### Verse 20

“Sihon, king of the Amorites, for his mercy endures forever.”

These matters already seem to have been expounded in the preceding psalm; nevertheless, it will not be burdensome to repeat them when sacred authority is shown to have repeated them for our salvation. Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of colors,” or alternatively as “unfruitful tree”; Amorite means “exasperation.” All these meanings seem to refer to the devil: for he is the unfruitful tree, and he is exasperation. The Lord kills these things within us when he leads us to his ordinances through holiness of conduct.

### Verse 21

“And Og, king of Bashan, for his mercy endures forever.”

Og is interpreted as “heaping up,” and Bashan as “confusion.” Whoever heaps up our sins is plainly the devil. He is also rightly called “confusion,” because he confounds his followers, and he himself departs confounded by the Lord’s judgment. Yet these and similar things lie slain by the Lord’s power when he deigns to rescue us from such a wretched bondage.

### Verse 22

“And he gave their land as an inheritance, for his mercy endures forever.”

He enters upon the third part of the narrative. Although the history seems to speak of the Hebrews, it is nevertheless most appropriately referred to the Christian people as well: for, once those who fell through their own iniquity have been expelled, the rewards of the promised inheritance are bestowed upon the holy and faithful Christians—the blessedness that had been promised to those earlier people. Let us also remember that in this division too, across five verses, the twelfth species of definition remains, as we explained in the second part.

### Verse 23

“An inheritance for Israel his servant, for his mercy endures forever.”

When he says, “his servant,” he separates those who resisted the Lord’s commands through wicked efforts. In this sense both the devout people of the Jews and the Christian people are included.

### Verse 24

“For the Lord remembered us in our humiliation, for his mercy endures forever.”

Humiliation properly belongs to the Christian era; it began to be more widely desired when the Lord Savior displayed it in himself. For he showed both the way of humility and the discipline of patience. Therefore he remembers the humility of his servants, he who is also recognized as their teacher. “He remembered” signifies the mystery of the holy incarnation, when he deigned by his coming to free believers.

### Verse 25

“And he redeemed us from the hand of our enemies, for his mercy endures forever.”

If you attend to the historical account, he paid no price to the Egyptians when he deigned to free the Hebrews from their hands. But because we were held in bondage under the power of the devil or his ministers, he then paid a great price by sacrificing himself, in order to set us free from them. He redeemed us through his various injuries and sufferings: he endured confinement, was struck with blows, and was beaten with scourges. He certainly redeemed us by his precious blood; and finally he redeemed us by displaying the miracle of his resurrection, as the Apostle says, embracing the whole matter: “You were bought with a great price” (1 Cor. VI, 20). This was a price for which no price could compare.

### Verse 26

“He gives food to all flesh, for his mercy endures forever.”

By “all flesh,” he did not intend us to understand only human beings, but also everything that swims, everything that flies, everything that creeps, and everything that walks, since all are satisfied by his generosity. For just as he is the Creator of all things, so he is proved to be the shepherd of every living creature. He also feeds all spiritual beings with the incorporeal food of his mercy. Since all generally stand in need, it is through his gift that all are shown to be sustained and to exist.

Or perhaps “he gives food to all flesh” should be understood as referring only to the faithful, whom he deigns to nourish with his body and blood.

### Verse 27

“Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his mercy endures forever.”

### Verse 28

“Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy endures forever.”

Although he previously spoke these verses in the same words, here he is shown to have changed only “to the God of heaven”; previously he had “to the God of gods.” Thus it appears that everything could be encompassed by the designation “heaven.” And so that he might seem to recall everything to the confession of God, at the end he again mentions that thanks must be given, lest anything be thought capable of being done apart from his praise and mercy.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

This is a wondrous psalm, profoundly deep in its immense power, everywhere recognized as radiant with the Lord’s mercy, like gleaming stars. Its virtue and power are shown in Chronicles, where it says: “When they began to praise the Lord and to say, ‘Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is everlasting,’ the house of God was filled with a cloud, so that the priests could not stand and minister because of the gloom. For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of God” (2 Chron. V, 13–14).

What, then, can we say that is comparable to this, when the authority itself is known to testify concerning it? Although it is certain that, if they are sung purely, the divine presence is with us in all the psalms, this is nevertheless believed more evidently here because it is confirmed by the authority of Scripture.

# PSALM CXXXVI

## A Psalm of David

The order of the titles has returned to its former custom. For it signifies that merciful and most holy deeds are to be referred to the Lord Savior. It should be observed that this hymn is not uttered by those who rejoice, but is sung in the compunction of sorrow alone. This history was fulfilled, as the prophet Jeremiah relates, when the captivity of Jerusalem was accomplished upon the coming of King Nebuchadnezzar. There survives concerning this matter a most compunctive book of piety, marked out by a fourfold alphabet. But we must receive these matters spiritually, since, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. X, 11), it is certain that all these things happened to them as figures.

## Division of the Psalm

The Hebrew people, who through the fault of their obstinacy were to suffer captivity under King Nebuchadnezzar after long ages, are introduced speaking, so that they may bewail their future evils as though they already appeared to be past. In the first section they enumerate their calamities, adding that amid whatever straits of this world they will never in any way forget Jerusalem, although it was evident that she was to be overthrown. In the second section they turn their words to the Lord, asking him to remember those who rage with most wicked purpose in their insults against the Church, and declaring blessed those who, beginning with their heart, cast away evil thoughts.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, while we remembered you, Zion.”

The remembrance of one’s homeland is exceedingly sweet when one finds oneself in an enemy land; for as much as this is felt to be bitter, so much sweeter does that become. Love for one’s own dwelling increases from the place of exile. But although the prophet seems to expound the captivity of the Israelite people which occurred under the Assyrians, we ought nevertheless to understand it spiritually. For we learn by frequent reading that there are two cities in this world: one is the Lord’s, called Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace.” Here it suffers oppression and is wounded by the onset of many evils: humble, afflicted, and placing its hope in that eternity which has never known subjection to decay. Conversely, the city of the devil, called Babylon, whose interpretation means “confusion,” is flourishing, proud, and most joyful here; it is watered by the vices of this age as by great rivers. Above these rivers, therefore, sit the faithful who suffer captivity in this world and, sighing with longing for their homeland, pour out bitter tears because they cannot attain here that promised peace.

It should also be considered that he does not say “in the rivers,” but “by the rivers.” For those still in these rivers are carried away by the flood of sins, whereas those who sit above the banks of the channel have already been freed from those waves by the divine gift. Observe also the moderation of the very posture: he does not call them standing erect, lest arrogance be sought; nor lying down, lest collapse be courted; but sitting, in humility, and sending pious tears over the impious streams of sins.

### Verse 2

“On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.”

Here the bitterness of grief is intensified: the people hung upon trees, as though unnecessary, the source of delight by which they could have consoled themselves. For what were sweet instruments doing there, where the times of life were occupied by bitter laments? Yet let this history be transferred to a spiritual understanding. Willows are trees which rejoice in the richest verdure along riverbanks; frequently, when stakes have been cut from them and buried in moist ground, they send down the deepest roots. They cannot be drowned by streams, though satisfied by abundant watering. Holy and faithful persons are compared to them, as Isaiah says: “They shall spring up like grass amid water, and like a willow beside flowing water” (Isa. XLIV, 4). Therefore we hang our instruments upon such men when, grace having been shared, we confer upon the reading of the divine Scriptures. For these are our instruments: they both furnish the grace of psalmody and cheer us by reciprocal discussion.

“In its midst” means in the midst of the city of Babylon, not of the river, because the most holy Christian must be in the midst of the world, although in mind he seems to have been borne up to the things above.

### Verses 3–5

“For there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs; and those who carried us away said: ‘Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.’ How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

They add another weight to their sorrows, bewailing that they had reached even this mockery: that they should pour out God’s venerable songs everywhere for men’s pleasure, and that pagans should be compelled to say what only the Lord’s people were accustomed to hear. For the proud and arrogant victor wishes to have entertainments and delights supplied from God’s songs. They must be answered: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

But, to pursue more fully the interpretation we have begun, the Apostle testifies that the desire of the world holds us in bondage, saying: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. VII, 23). These desires, therefore, which ensnare us by the law of captivity, frequently urge us to sing words of psalmody in profane places and spectacles with most wicked gesticulation. But the present teaching declares that one must not consent to them, when it warns that in a foreign land—that is, amid vicious acts which are alien from God—the Lord’s hymn must not be sung. For the Lord’s holy words ought to belong to the holy; for it is written: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII, 6). Thus it warns that they must never be assented to.

### Verse 6

“If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me.”

The prophet promises never entirely to forget the Church of God, imposing upon himself a most severe condition: it must necessarily happen if Jerusalem should cease to be loved. For the right hand of the good is Christ the Lord, as was said in the fifteenth psalm: “I set the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved” (Ps. XV, 8). The prophet therefore binds himself with harsh, though by no means novel, bonds: that he may fall away from the remembrance of the Lord Savior if Jerusalem should depart from his mind. She is the mother of the faithful, the homeland of the happy, the country of the blessed; whoever forgets her here is by no means placed there in the Lord’s kingdom.

### Verse 7

“May my tongue cleave to my jaws, if I do not remember you; if I do not set Jerusalem before the beginning of my joy.” [MSS A, B, and F read “set before” (*proposuero*) for “prefer” (*praeposuero*).]

A second penal condition is proposed: that he may become mute in the Lord’s praises if he has forgotten Jerusalem, which Christians hold as a great reward. For what is shown to be worse than being unable to speak by that through which healing was customarily bestowed? Psalmody is consolation for those who weep, treatment for the suffering, health for the sick. It is the remedy of the soul, the refuge from all miseries. Whoever is deprived of such a gift is excluded from every benefit of consolation.

It follows: “if I do not set Jerusalem before the beginning of my joy.” There are beginnings of worldly joy: for the miser, finding gold; for the lustful man, a beautiful woman; for the proud, boasting. But far be it that such beginnings of joy should suit prophetic holiness. Rather, let us name things that are honorable, yet must in no way be preferred to the holy Church. For serious men, who conduct themselves with the highest honor, the beginning of joy is a son’s birth, as happened to Zechariah concerning John, who was promised to him by an angelic voice (Luke I, 13). There is also the son who returned after a long time, of whom the Gospel records the same thing in a parable, when the most joyful father killed the fattened calf for his feast (Luke XV, 18, 23). Or it may be health of body restored after illness, as happened to King Hezekiah, to whom, after a most severe sickness, we read that a further span of fifteen years was granted (4 Kings XX, 6).

The wording itself must also be weighed. For the beginning of joy is always strong and always most ample, when at the very outset the will is kindled with gladness, while in warmth of spirit we are carried into a joy which we scarcely believed would come about. For all sudden things are violent, and whatever has been prolonged in this world grows lukewarm. Therefore, to heighten the fervor of faith, he says that she whom it is fitting to love more than all things is to be preferred to the beginning of joy. Yet this verse and the preceding one may also apply to those whom we said above were captives.

### Verses 8–9

“Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom, in the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Empty it, empty it, even to its foundation within her.’”

The Hebrew people come to the second section, where, turned toward the Lord, they pray that he not allow those who tear apart the Church of God with most savage reproach to depart unavenged. Some have thought Edom should be interpreted “bloody,” others “earthly”; yet there is no doubt that either meaning can be referred to carnal vices. These, then, are the sons of Edom who have persecuted the Christian people most grievously and have not turned through any satisfaction. The people pray that, in that separation of the good, these should be brought to remembrance so that they may receive their deserved punishment. This is said, as has often been mentioned, from prophetic feeling, not from a wish to curse. For our pity is not sought in the case of those who are to be condemned by the Lord’s judgment.

He added: “who say: ‘Empty it, empty it, even to its foundation within her.’” In these words, “let us come” must be supplied, so that the sentence may stand complete for us. This figure is called by teachers of secular letters *ellipsis*, that is, omission, when we deliberately suspend words so that what has been passed over may be sought more eagerly. These, then, are the words of the sons of Edom persecuting the Christian people, drawn from the likeness of a cistern: if water is diligently drawn out, one undoubtedly comes down to its foundation. But what profit was it to them to remove from such people the light of this age, when, killed in the very foundation, they seemed rather to possess eternal life? For the foundation of the faithful is Christ the Lord, who cannot be taken away from the righteous, though all things of this age are proved to be stripped from them. Thus, while persecutors desire to drain the Catholic religion dry, they bestowed most happy and abundant crowns upon the martyrs.

### Verse 10

“Wretched daughter of Babylon: blessed is he who repays you your repayment, which you repaid to us.” [MS G and the editions read “repays” (*retribuit*) for “shall repay” (*retribuet*).]

Our flesh is aptly called the daughter of Babylon because it is shown to bring upon us the confusion of sins. To this was added its proper epithet, that it should be called wretched. For what is more wretched than that a fragile thing should become insolent with such audacity and, through unlawful desires, wound souls with the injury of sin? As the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. V, 17). But after speaking of Babylon’s daughter, he declares that the most just recompense must be rendered to her: as luxury incites us to vices, so, subdued by fasts and tribulations, we may make her subject to virtues. We render her a worthy repayment when, compelled, she does what in indulgence she neglects to fulfill. It belongs to the blessed to render such repayments to the flesh: that what drew us to guilt may, with the Lord’s help, be brought to glory.

### Verse 11

“Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock.”

He still speaks to the flesh itself, declaring blessed the one who seizes her children—that is, harmful vices—because he has already advanced so far as to hold them. For whenever we hold something, we reduce it to our power, and what has begun to be captive to us ceases to be free. He added, “and dash [them] against the rock,” so that the one holding them may not delay, lest flattering pleasure steal in. “He shall dash [them],” he says, “against the rock,” namely, against the Lord Savior, of whom it is written: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X, 4), so that, broken at once, the things which urged us by most foul impulses may perish.

It should be carefully considered that he said “your little ones”: namely, the errors of the flesh, born of their wretched mother. While they are little, they are held more easily and are effectively dashed against that heavenly rock; for if they have already begun to be grown and to flourish in most vigorous youth, a graver struggle arises against them, and they are not easily overcome by our weakness. The hundredth psalm is also shown to have warned us of this matter, where it says: “In the mornings I slew all the sinners of the earth” (Ps. C, 8). Yet although this psalm has softened our minds with pious lamentation and in its first part has also narrated our captivity by mystical exposition, in this present verse it has disclosed the secrets of a most savage and hidden vice, so as both to reveal the plague and not to conceal the remedies. For, at the devil’s instigation, what we do not wish is sent into our mind; we receive what we condemn in our judgment; and by a kind of tyranny of sin we are undoubtedly made captive to our own abhorrence. But while these thoughts are little, let them be struck against the rock, let them be crushed, as has been said, against the cornerstone, where every evil is quickly dissolved if it is dashed firmly against him.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

The most pious and praiseworthy devotion of the lamenting psalms is complete. For above, in the seventy-third and seventy-eighth psalms, Jerusalem’s future captivity is read as lamented; but this is the third psalm on the same matter, so that the piety of most devoted compunction may be offered to the most sacred number of the Trinity. It is indeed a great kind of charity which the Lord commands to be shown to our neighbors, provided that grief is kept in such a manner and measure that neither the hope of resurrection can be taken away nor may we suspect that the Lord has done anything unjustly. For though we are kindled with affectionate grief, we must not exceed the limit of moderation. What is offered through devotion to piety ought to be humble and gentle. For the Lord Christ bears witness to the disposition proper to righteous tears: considering the frailty of the human race, though he was about to raise Lazarus, he wept, so that, as a good Teacher, he might both teach pity and show the reality of the humanity he had assumed (John XI, 35).

# PSALM CXXXVII

## Of David Himself

Although in the preceding titles we have said that David signifies “strong of hand” and “desirable,” which has been proved to suit the Lord Savior properly, yet here he indicated Christ more plainly when he added this pronoun. For *ipsi* (“to himself”) is to be pronounced more reverently, as of the Most High, the Almighty, the heavenly King. Then this David must be joined to it, a name not taken from his divinity but shown to derive from the origin of the assumed flesh. Yet he, the incarnate Word, is the one Lord Christ, to whom the entire confession of this psalm is referred.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the whole psalm the Catholic people speak, gathered from the whole world. In the first narrative they praise the Lord’s benefits bestowed upon them, asking for patience in things to come, so that by his gift they may endure the adversities of the world. In the second they pray that the kings of the earth may confess the exalted Lord, because in all things he deigns to show the miracles of his majesty; they pray that he may not despise sinners who have turned, whom he deigned to create.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“I will give thanks to you, Lord, with all my heart, because you have heard all the words of my mouth; and in the presence of angels I will sing psalms to you.”

How strong and complete this confession is is shown by the gathering of the whole heart. For when it says, “with all my heart,” no part is left occupied with the ambition of this world, but the whole and undivided heart is devoted, as is fitting, to the praises of the Creator alone. Heart signifies the inner sanctuary of the mind, from which we silently cry to the Lord, and our prayers are heard much more effectively than if we resounded with loud cries. Whether the voice strikes the air, from there one must sing; whether the tongue is silent, from there one must cry out. For the Lord gladly hears what he is known to have worked in us after his image and likeness.

It follows: “because you have heard all the words of my mouth.” To show the Lord’s mercy, the Psalmist chose first to say that holy men had been heard, and afterwards that they sounded divine praises. He judges this also applicable now to the faithful people, as was said in the hundred and seventeenth psalm: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, because you have heard me” (Ps. CXVII, 21). But consider the merit of the prayer: he declares that all his words have been heard. For the petitions of the righteous were that Christ the Lord should come, through whom they are known to have grown by immense increase. Rightly, therefore, all the words of that people are proved to have been heard, through whom the redemption of the world is known to have been obtained.

He added, “and in the presence of angels I will sing psalms to you.” Here the power of psalmody is shown: one who sings psalms among people with a pure heart seems also to sing above with the angels. He also added “in the presence of angels,” so that the angels are shown not merely to hear it but also to attend to it. For we say that we look upon what can be beheld with serene minds. Or it signifies the time when, after the resurrection, the people of the blessed will sing praises to the Lord in fellowship with the heavenly creatures.

### Verses 2–3

“I will worship toward your holy temple, and give thanks to your name, for your mercy and your truth; because you have magnified your holy name over us.”

The holy temple is the coming of the Lord’s blessed incarnation, which the Church even now worships daily when it venerates his body and blood in the sacraments of the highest mystery. But that worship is perfect which blessed confession accompanies; for it says that thanks must be given to the Lord for mercy and truth. Mercy is that he deigned to come to free us without anyone’s merits. Truth is that he fulfilled the promises of his prophets. Whoever confesses these things with a pure heart is truly known to have worshipped his temple.

He added, “because you have magnified your holy name over us,” so that this people may be shown to have been gathered from every part of the world. Though above he spoke in the singular, he now used the plural, “over us,” because, just as the voice of all saints is one, so the words of the faithful people are those of many. For below they return again to the singular number; this plural usage must be observed as disclosing the mystery. For the Lord’s name was magnified over us when the power of his worship became known to us. He designates all ages: his name was magnified in our holy fathers, and most especially in Christian times, when our forehead was marked by the anointing of sacred chrism. Observe that we have set the two verses together because of the connection of the words, so that one construction might contain what one meaning embraces.

### Verse 4

“On whatever day I call upon you, hear me; you will multiply great strength in my soul.”

The day here signifies a bright and sincere petition, not clouded by desire or darkened by any avarice, but shining from that Sun who dispels all the darknesses of mortality [the editions read “cleanses” (*emundat*) for “corrects” (*emendat*)]. In such petitions the devout people pray to be heard, so that, filled with the Lord’s strength, they may deserve to escape the snares of persecutors. For if you wish to take it literally, are we not to pray at night, especially when then we are attacked by diabolical deceits? But for the faithful Christian it is always day when he strives to be heard with bright and clear supplications. When he says, “You will multiply great strength in my soul,” he shows that he will suffer countless things, against which he has asked for equally manifold help.

### Verse 5

“Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth.”

He has come to the second part, in which the people of the blessed pray that the kings of the earth may give thanks to the Lord in humility, because all pride is shown hateful to him. The kings of the earth are those who rule their bodies by the gift of divinity. For the one who is shown to serve vices is not truly called king. But by adding “all,” he specifically designates religious and self-controlled men, since we see many kings of nations either subject to deadly vices or stained by perverse religion. He added, “because they have heard all the words of your mouth.” He states which kings ought to give thanks to the Lord: namely, those who have deserved to hear his words. For hearing belongs to those known to be obedient; we do not say that those have heard whom we recognize as stubborn against sacred commands. Consider also that one does not seem to withdraw from devotion without great evil if one has been able to hear the glory of his preaching. Therefore let the Jews understand how great the guilt is by which they are bound, since they preferred not to grasp his words with the mind but to hear them only with the ears.

### Verse 6

“And let them sing in songs to the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord.”

The Lord’s songs are the mercy and truth mentioned above, as he says elsewhere: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10). He therefore commands the kings of their bodies to sing these songs, having rejected the pomp of the world and devoted themselves with all desire to the Lord’s mercy. He adds, “because great is the glory of the Lord.” The Lord’s glory is that, rejecting the world, they should not cease to sing his praises, having abandoned the pathless ways of the first man and passed over to saving rules.

### Verse 7

“Because the Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly, and knows the high from afar.”

Care for the preceding statement follows. For he says that, although the Lord is exalted, he regards the lowly, lest any of the subject people should think that the exalted Lord does not regard them when they know themselves to be prostrate in great devotion. Divine power is not like the human condition. Here one who is humbled and cast down is despised, because he is separated by a great distance; but before the Lord, one who bows with great effort is made nearer. And so that you might perceive this humility to be precious in his sight, it follows: “and he knows the high from afar.” “The high” signifies the proud, who are known from afar because they do not draw near to his grace. To terrify the proud, he used “knows,” lest in their folly they think that what they do with malicious thoughts is unknown to God. This is an argument gathered from contraries by a most beautiful contrast: the humble draw near to him, and the proud become altogether distant.

### Verse 8

“If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will make me live; and over the wrath of my enemies you have stretched out your hand, and your right hand has saved me.”

When the blessed people say that their tribulations are to be overcome by the Lord’s power, they show that his faithful are pressed by many disasters in this age. They know that gold is purified by fires, that a reward is given to a soldier after greatest labors, and that faith itself is to be crowned after the struggle has first been undergone. For if wickedness is suspended for a time in the age of persecutors, people are nevertheless continually subject to diabolical temptations; and thus the Christian, longing for the future homeland, sighs for joys deferred. Therefore the people are made to live while placed amid such afflictions. “You will make [me] live” must be understood as “you will make [me] glad,” which is the opposite of affliction; for in truth that person is called living who is to be filled with the gladness of eternal joy.

It follows: “and over the wrath of my enemies you have stretched out your hand, and your right hand has saved me.” He speaks of persecutors, who, though in anger they do many things against the faithful people, receive far greater things in return through divine justice. For even when converted, they are afflicted more severely than they had afflicted others, and begin justly to persecute themselves, since formerly they had been unwilling to spare the innocent. Yet they declare themselves to be saved when no adversity could overcome them amid the punishments of persecutors. The right hand signifies power: the Lord Christ himself, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. I, 24).

### Verse 9

“Lord, you will repay for me; Lord, your mercy is everlasting: do not despise the works of your hands.”

This is an altogether perfect prayer, of the kind we are instructed to offer: to commend one’s cause to the Lord, who knows how to repay each person what is due. But lest you should understand angrily what was said and appears contrary to prayer, there follows: “your mercy is everlasting”—may you show it also to those who persecute us savagely, so that, as they seem to afflict us for your name, they too may be tormented by the gift of confession unto salvation. For they receive a beneficial punishment when they too are tortured for eternal life; and everything is mercifully bestowed upon those to whom this medicine of confession is granted.

It follows: “do not despise the works of your hands.” He expressed the intention that above seemed to be held in suspense. The devout people pray for their enemies, whom they knew would be joined to them. Although they seem to have become perverse through their own fault, there is no doubt that they are divine works. For when they ask that he look upon his own work in them, they entreat him, in mercy, to pardon. His work in us is good, but our deeds are altogether perverse. Therefore he has mercy when he sees his own creature; but he condemns when he beholds our works. Thus the prayer is brief and cautious: it shows both the piety of the petitioner and that they are to be converted.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us attend to the teaching with which the holy people have instructed us and the impulse of piety with which they prayed. For, to exclude from the heart every zeal against enemies, they prayed that those whom they seemed to have as adversaries might become their companions. Let us follow this pious judgment; let us rather love those who afflict us. We ought not to consider enemies those who benefit us; for, if borne with equanimity, they frequently bestow upon us what sweetest friends cannot provide. The latter often lead us away from virtue by flattery; the former establish us in it by affliction. Therefore love patience, and in an enemy you will find more to love.

# PSALM CXXXVIII

## For the End, a Psalm of David
After so many psalms, this phrase *In finem* is repeated, so that it rightly appears to require explanation again. For prolonged distance is close to oblivion. We have said that *In finem* is understood in two ways. One is the mortal setting and end of certain things, which, once its span has been completed, brings them to a close in a manner very like the human condition. The other is perfect and eternal—that is, the Lord Christ—who, as the end, does not look toward setting but attends to the summit of complete perfection. For when one has reached him, there is nothing further that we ought to seek, since he himself is sufficient for everything, in whom is the whole perfection of majesty and the fullness of every virtue. Therefore this entire psalm, as the most learned Father Hilary also judged (*In the Preface to this Psalm*), must be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord Christ.

But lest his humility seem to disturb or confuse anyone, let him return to the rule of catholic teaching and remember that two natures, united and perfect, exist in the Lord Christ: one, by which he is God and coeternal with the Father; the other, by which, born from the Virgin Mary, he deigned to become, in time, one and the same man for our salvation. Therefore, what he says humbly must not be applied to his divinity, but understood in relation to the mystery of his holy incarnation. When this principle has been applied, we recognize the divine mysteries without offense.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the Lord Christ speaks. First, he speaks to the Father about his own repose and resurrection, declaring to him that all his thoughts are known. Second, he sets forth the power of the Father’s divinity, since, in what he is as man, he cannot hide from the Father’s knowledge in any place or distance; he adds that, with the Father protecting him, he was preserved from his mother’s womb, and that he overcame the vices of the world through glorious holiness. Third, he professes that he will praise the Lord the Father in the aspect in which he is subject, whose work in him has been shown to be powerful and wondrous; he also says that his own preaching and the desires of all the saints are known to the Father. Fourth, he asserts that the primacy of all the blessed has been confirmed, ordering the impious and obstinate to depart from him, although they were not to be saved by any humility of repentance. I think this psalm must be heard with much greater attentiveness, for it is filled to overflowing with the profundity of mysteries.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

**“Lord, you have tested me and known me; you have known my sitting and my rising.”**

“Lord,” Jesus Christ cries to the Father from that aspect in which he is a servant. He “tested” him—that is, he made his humility manifest—when he wished to be baptized by John, although he had no sins. For he was not a sinner; rather, he undertook to heal sins, as the prophet says: “He took up our sins and bore our infirmities” (Isaiah 53:4).

He “knew” him—that is, he showed him forth—when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 17:5), namely, when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

There is another appropriate understanding of these words. He was tested when the devil tempted him in the desert; he was acknowledged when, after the temptation had ended, he received the ministry of angels. A third instance occurred, which he himself attests in the Gospel: he was tested at the time of his passion, when he displayed what kind of piety he possessed by praying for his enemies while he was hanging on the cross; he was acknowledged when he revealed the glory of his wondrous resurrection. Then his divinity became known even to those who had previously doubted whether they should believe in it. For the evangelist says: “This was the third time Jesus revealed himself to his disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, after he had risen from the dead; and his disciples believed in him” (John 21:14).

“His sitting” has rightly been called the death of the Lord Savior, in which there was not punishment but repose. Or, as others think, “sitting” refers to the teaching that the Lord preached with heavenly holiness, just as he also says in the Gospel, indicating the teachers: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat” (Matthew 23:2).

“You have known” is expressed through the figure of *hypallage*, which in Latin is called *permutatio*, “exchange”; that is, “you have made me known,” because to the Divinity all things are manifest—not only when they come to pass, but also in predestination.

### Verse 2

**“You understood my thoughts from afar; you investigated my path and my course.”**

### Verse 3

**“You foresaw all my ways, because there is no deceit on my tongue.”**

In these two verses the foreknowledge of the holy Divinity is displayed. “From afar” is proved to signify not place but time, because he foresees not only our deeds but also recognizes our thoughts before we ourselves exist. All this is appropriate if it is suitably applied to the Lord’s incarnation. By his divinity he was Creator; by his bodily substance he was created.

Let no one therefore bring forward foolish accusations, but let him understand with devout attention what is most certain, lest we fall from the very place from which we received the hope of salvation.

It follows: “You investigated my path and my course; you foresaw all my ways.” The paths refer to silent thoughts, the course to righteous judgments, and the ways to human actions. He completed all these in immaculate purity, whom the catholic faith confesses truly to be one and the same existing in both natures.

For when he says, “You investigated,” he displays the righteousness of his action, since, although he was examined with the utmost care, nothing blameworthy is found to have existed in him.

“You foresaw my ways.” They were foreseen to such an extent that they are also known to have been prophesied. For it is written concerning his gentleness: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

He added, “because there is no deceit on my tongue”—certainly because truth has no deceit. For he himself declared: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He did not speak anything under any false pretense; rather, just as he received from the Father, so he proclaimed it beneficially to the peoples.

For he says, from the nature of his humanity: “He who sent me is greater than I” (ibid., 14:28). He also spoke of the equality of his majesty: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Both statements are true, and both were uttered without deceit: thus he both displayed the majesty of his divinity and truthfully revealed the humility of his holy incarnation.

### Verse 4

**“Behold, you, Lord, have known all things, the latest and the ancient; you formed me and placed your hand upon me.”**

Observe how truthfully it was said above, “There is no deceit on my tongue,” so that here he might clearly express the two natures. For he says to the Father: “Behold, you have known all things, the latest”—which pertains to his incarnation, accomplished in the last times, as it is written: “A lamb slaughtered at evening” (Exodus 12:6). And the Apostle says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

He added, “and the ancient.” There is no doubt that this pertains to his divinity. Hence it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and so forth.

For “the ancient” means the eternal, which is bounded neither by beginning nor by end, as we read in Daniel: “Thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down” (Daniel 7:9), and so forth.

And to make this clearer once again to human understanding, he repeated the same point with a change in the character of the words. “You formed me” means “you begot me.” This expression is also customarily used of the divinity, as the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6).

It follows: “and you placed your hand upon me.” The Father placed his hand upon him when he displayed the power of his majesty in him, as it is said in another psalm:

> “I have found David my servant;  
> with my holy oil I have anointed him.  
> For my hand will help him,  
> and my arm will strengthen him.  
> The enemy will accomplish nothing against him,  
> and the son of iniquity will not add to harming him”  
> (Psalm 88:21–23).

Behold how the Father placed his hand upon him.

### Verse 5

**“Your knowledge has become wondrous through me; it has been strengthened, and I cannot attain to it.”**

He speaks of the Father’s knowledge, which was proclaimed through him throughout the whole world. It was strengthened in human hearts, although previously it had been doubted with uncertain belief. He expresses the same meaning in the Gospel: “Father, I have manifested your name to the people” (John 17:6).

For through his revelation it came about that the unity of the holy Trinity could appear worthy of reverence. Through Jesus Christ the Father’s wondrous knowledge was made known, when the mysteries of the holy law were recounted to earthly inhabitants.

And to disclose the truth of the human condition, he added, “and I cannot attain to it,” because the nature of man, which he deigned to assume, could not equal the divine substance. The Gospel voice likewise makes this clear: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28); and again: “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19).

But let the utterly deranged Arian understand this: it could not have been said otherwise by the flesh, which was also expected to be put to death.

### Verse 6

**“Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?”**

He comes to the second mode, in which, through mystical enumerations, he shows that the divine presence cannot be eluded by any creature. Since he is wholly and completely everywhere, where could the person who thinks he can avoid him hide?

Someone can be concealed only where the one from whom he flees is not present. By saying, “Where shall I go?” he signifies that the nature of his humanity has nowhere to flee, since the Holy Spirit is wholly everywhere, as Solomon says: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7).

But this is spoken through the figure called *diaporesis*, when we ask what we ought most properly to do. Since, however, this proclamation teaches us that the Holy Spirit is everywhere, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit is found coeternal and coequal with the Father and the Son. For nothing can be everywhere and wholly present except the Trinity alone.

Therefore let irreligious presumption cease; let no one fabricate anything greater or lesser here. Let us return to that saving remedy: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the omnipotent and incomprehensible Creator, are one God.

“Face” is used tropologically for “presence,” because, just as our face sees, so the whole substance of the Lord knows, embraces, penetrates, and observes all things through a vision that is perceptible and indescribable.

### Verse 7

**“If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.”**

### Verse 8

**“If I take my wings before the dawn [manuscript A: ‘at daybreak’] and dwell at the farthest part of the sea.”**

### Verse 9

**“For there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.”**

Here, it seems to me, there is that argument called a dilemma, which is formed from two or more propositions, whichever of which is chosen necessarily leading to the contrary conclusion. Thus in the Gospel Christ also questions the Jews who were making accusations against him, saying: “The baptism of John—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?” (Matthew 21:25). For whichever answer they wished to choose would nevertheless have turned against them.

The Apostle also uses this concerning good things: “Having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for you” (Philippians 1:23–24). And he added: “I do not know what I should choose” (ibid., 1:22).

So here too, concerning three contrary possibilities, his humanity was uncertain what it should choose. Let us now proceed to explain the words, since they are exceedingly profound in their height.

For he says, in that which he is as man: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there,” namely, where he was to be placed at the Father’s right hand. But to understand that the Lord is present everywhere, hear the prophet Jeremiah: “I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God from far away. If a man hides himself in a hiding place, shall I not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:23–24).

It follows: “If I descend into hell, you are present.” This was accomplished according to the law of humanity: when his body had been crucified, he descended to break open the bars of hell, and the most merciful Redeemer came to the aid of the human race in its distress.

He also adds, “you are present,” because he rose with the speed of three days.

He added the third part: “If I take my wings before the dawn and dwell at the farthest part of the sea. For there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.” This figure is called *aetiology*, that is, the giving of a cause, for he gives the reason why he could not escape God’s presence.

He calls his wings the most effective swiftness of the divine majesty, which raised his holy body to the things above through the power of the Deity. But when you hear “my,” understand the glory of his own power.

When, therefore, he takes these wings before the dawn—that is, at the time of the resurrection—and dwells at the farthest part of the sea, that is, above the vast limit of this age, there the Father’s hand will lead him.

And to show their cooperation, it follows: “and your right hand will hold me.” The right hand is indeed the omnipotent Word of the Father, who will preserve the humanity assumed and united to himself throughout the eternal ages.

And if it seems hardly fitting that, since he himself is the Father’s right hand, he should say that he is held by the Lord’s right hand, this should rather be understood as spoken from the perspective of the members. This form of expression is frequently employed.

Nevertheless, the following rule must be held consistently: whatever expresses uncertainty should be understood as belonging to the humanity; whatever expresses presumption or confidence should be understood as belonging to the Deity.

It follows:

### Verse 10

**“And I said: Perhaps the darkness will trample me, and night will be illumination in my delights.”**

The first part of this verse must be pronounced ironically. We frequently utter certain things as though under ambiguity, although we cannot doubt them, as it has already been said in another psalm: “Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Psalm 123:3), and so forth.

For how could darkness trample him, when it had no power over such great glory? For he himself says of himself: “I am the light of this world” (John 8:12). Rather, he trampled the darkness, overcoming by the light of his mercy the blindness of the first man as it passed to his descendants.

Therefore, in the clause where he says, “Perhaps the darkness will trample me,” those who could imagine in him some cloud of fear are mocked.

The explanation of its meaning follows when he says: “And night will be illumination in my delights.” How could he be trampled by darkness for whom night was illumination in his delights?

“Night” signifies the prison of hell, which he truly illuminated when he crushed the devil’s power and freed, through his mercy, the man whom he had deigned to fashion in his own image and likeness.

“In my delights” signifies paradise, from which sins drove the first man, but to whose pleasantness the souls of the saints returned through the Lord’s provision and by the benefit of confession.

For this is what was said to the believing thief: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Paradise signifies a most pleasant place and the eternal security of the happiest joy.

### Verse 11

**“For darkness will not be darkened by you, and night will be illuminated like day; as is its darkness, so also is its light.”**

The reason for the preceding statement is given: why night is illumination in his delights—namely, because darkness will not be darkened by you but will rather be illuminated.

By “darkness” he means the mystical and profound things of the divine Scriptures, according to what we read in Proverbs: “He also understands the parable and the obscure saying” (Proverbs 1:6). Likewise, in another psalm we read: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Psalm 17:12).

Therefore these darknesses will not be darkened but rather illuminated by the Lord, because the preaching of the prophets was fulfilled when he came. He customarily refers to the Father what he himself does, so that the cooperation of the holy Trinity may be understood.

It follows: “And night will be illuminated like day.” Those things which, as night, had been obscure under a mystical covering were illuminated like day when, at the coming of the Lord Savior, the words of the prophets became clear.

And the two statements are rightly joined: “As is its darkness, so also is its light,” because truth was present in both—whether the things appeared obscure or whether, once illuminated, they became clear.

### Verse 12

**“For you possessed my kidneys, Lord; you received me from my mother’s womb.”**

The kidneys signify bodily strength. When they are healthy, our body is invigorated through their service; when they are injured, it collapses in extreme weakness and fragility.

Therefore he rightly says that his kidneys were possessed by the Father, since, established in the strength of heavenly righteousness, he knew no sin belonging to fragile flesh.

By “from my mother’s womb” he means from the boundaries of the synagogue, because through the flesh he assumed he was generated from the synagogue, when we know that he was circumcised according to Jewish custom on the eighth day. He thus declares himself received by the divinity of the Father—or by his own divinity, since the two are one.

If, however, you wish to understand this only of the virginal womb, he is shown to have been assumed by the Lord not only when he emerged from it but also when he was conceived by the Holy Spirit; from this the Nestorian impiety is destroyed.

“For the womb” signifies “in the womb,” just as the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in the womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5).

In truth, all these statements are referred to the honor of the holy Father from the perspective of the human nature that was assumed, as the Gospel text shows. It was the Father’s purpose that he should proclaim the Father, fulfill his will, drink the cup received from him, and in no respect depart from the glory of that divine dispensation.

### Verse 13

**“I will confess to you, Lord, because you have been wondrously terrible; your works are wondrous, and my soul knows them exceedingly.”**  
[Manuscripts A and B: *magnificatus es, mirabilia . . . cognoscit*—“you have been wondrously magnified; wondrous [things] . . . knows”; the variant contains a lacuna.]

He comes to the third mode, in which he praises the Father, who displayed such great miracles in him.

The Father was wondrously terrible when darkness followed the passion of the Lord Christ, the earth trembled, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and the dead rejoiced in resurrection; and when he himself was seen again in the same body through the holy resurrection, entered to his disciples while the doors were closed, and ascended into heaven before human eyes.

Although he accomplished these things through his own divinity, according to his custom he attributed them to the Father’s powers, in order, as has often been said, to reveal the unity of their holy cooperation.

It follows: “Your works are wondrous, and my soul knows them exceedingly.” He knew the Father’s wondrous work because, as he said above, night was illumination in his delights; because the Father had possessed his kidneys; because he had received him from his mother’s womb.

It was necessary that he should recognize as wondrous the one whom his humanity, filled with the brightness of divine light, saw as the most devoted giver of such great benefits. For, as he says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27).

Alternatively, he knew the Father’s work exceedingly because, as he himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11). For one who is separated externally cannot know in this manner.

This knowledge is immeasurable, unique, and incomprehensible: it occurs when the two are known to dwell in one another.

### Verse 14

**“My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret; and my substance was in the lower parts of the earth.”**

Here *os* does not mean “mouths,” but that which comes from bones—that is, “bone.” This was truly made in secret, since it is established that it is hidden within the interior of our bodies. For who can see the bones in a human being, when flesh covers them and the skin laid over it conceals them?

If, however, we wish to understand this more spiritually, what has been said is communicated to us more easily. After Eve had been formed from Adam’s rib in the creation of the world, her husband said: “This is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” (Genesis 2:23).

Speaking to married people, the Apostle explains what mystery this may signify, saying: “This is a great mystery, but I am speaking of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:32). Hence it is clear that “the bone of the Lord” must here be understood as the Church.

And to apply what has been said more fully to the example just mentioned: before the Lord’s coming, certain mysteries of the Church were hidden, such as holy baptism, the body and blood of the Lord, and the other things that became clear when fullness arrived.

He added: “And my substance was in the lower parts of the earth.” The lower parts of the earth were the filthy practices of the nations, which at that time stood far apart from the religion of the Jews.

But the substance of the Lord Savior became known to those peoples when, understanding the divinity of the Word in him, they received it with devoted minds through apostolic teaching.

Although they were different nations and, through their superstitions, were the lower parts of the earth, they were nevertheless raised above the Jews when they absorbed the saving rules of the Christian religion.

### Verse 15

**“Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all will be written; by day they will be established [manuscripts A and B: ‘will be formed’], and no one among them.”**

That nature of man which, in the Gospel, declared that it did not know the end of the world, and which said, “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matthew 26:38), and similar things, testifies that the Father saw its imperfection.

Its imperfection is that the Church is still being gathered until the end of the age; that in the resurrection he will give the blessed the rewards promised to them; and that he will be “all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

But the Deity has already seen these things, which are still reserved for the distant future.

The following words make clear that this is said concerning the blessed people. For he added: “And in your book all will be written,” namely, all who will rejoice in eternal blessedness.

Just as what is written in a book is preserved by the writing that contains it, so what is held in the Lord’s memory remains much more firmly fixed.

It follows: “By day they will be established, and no one among them.” These are the blessed whom he mentioned above. “By day they will be established”—that is, they will be filled with the perfect brightness of light from that true Sun, so that what was said may come to pass: “As star differs from star in brightness, so also will be the resurrection of the dead” (ibid., 15:41–42).

Notice that he did not say, “They will be glorified by day,” but “They will be established by day.” For if he had said, “They will be glorified,” it might perhaps also be understood of a brief period. But when he says, “They will be established,” he bears witness that the benefit will remain eternally.

He added: “And no one among them”—one must understand, “will become weak,” because all the fragility of flesh will now be cast off and depart, and all mortality, consumed, will perish.

### Verse 16

**“But to me your friends have been greatly honored, God; their principalities have been greatly strengthened.”**

The fourth remaining mode of the psalm begins: he asserts that the honor of the saints is praise of both himself and the Father.

When he says, “to me,” he indicates himself; when he says, “your friends,” he declares the Father, as he himself says in the Gospel: “All things that are mine are the Father’s, and all things that are the Father’s are mine” (John 17:10).

We read that the Lord’s friends were first called the patriarchs, namely Abraham and Moses. Later the Lord Savior said to his apostles: “I no longer call you servants, but friends” (ibid., 15:15).

These, then, are the Father’s friends, whose honor returns to the Lord Savior, because no one venerates his saints unless he is devoted to the Lord Christ with a pure mind.
