He added: “Their principalities have been greatly strengthened.” “Greatly” means “very greatly.” By their strengthened principalities he means the episcopal seats of the apostles, which they established through the work of holy preaching when they founded Churches and distributed their seats throughout the world.

For, by God’s provision, they are read of as the leaders of the Churches, the rams of the flocks, and the princes of faithful peoples; rightly so, since, through their labors and by the gift of the Holy Spirit, the devotion of the whole world has been united and consolidated.

### Verse 17

**“I will number them, and they will multiply beyond the sand; I have risen, and I am still with you.”**

In the promises that the Lord made to Abraham in Genesis, it is written that his offspring would be multiplied “like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven” (Genesis 22:17). Here, however, he says, “and beyond the sand of the sea,” so that there he appears to make an equal comparison with the sand, whereas here he appears to surpass it.

The sand of the sea signifies the Jews, on account of their earthly understanding and the sterility of their faith. Sand is so called from its dryness.

The stars of heaven, however, refer to the Christian people, on account of the brightness of their religion and the splendor of their faith.

Christ the Lord therefore promises that he will number the faithful people, which is found to be far more numerous than that Jewish people. For it was necessary that the multitude of gathered nations should overcome one nation.

He added: “I have risen, and I am still with you.” Here, in wholly hidden and very brief words, he indicates his second coming, when he will judge the world.

“I have risen” signifies the time of his resurrection. “I am still with you,” while he sits at the Father’s right hand as though in concealment, while human beings are not yet able to see him, until that time when his kingdom becomes most clearly known to humanity.

“Still” signifies a future time—not that he will at some point be separated from the Father, but that he who is now invisible to us will later appear to all the nations.

### Verse 18

**“If you kill sinners, God: men of blood, depart from me.”**

### Verse 19

**“For you say in your thoughts: They will receive their cities in vanity.”**

In these two verses, let us first identify a *hyperbaton*, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may explain their meaning more easily in parts.

The order of the words is as follows: “If you kill, God, sinners.”

Above all, we must be careful not to think that the Lord Christ is praying for the destruction of sinners, since he came without doubt to save sinners, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:13).

If, however, we investigate this spiritually, every difficulty is removed from us. He therefore says: “If you kill, God, sinners.”

God kills the sinner when the sinner dies to sin in order to live for the Lord, as the Apostle says: “I died to the law, that I might live for Christ” (Galatians 2:19).

Sinners are therefore killed when they are transferred from evil thoughts to a disposition toward the good. When this has emerged in them through the benefit of conversion, then they receive their former cities in vanity—that is, their most vicious superstitions, which pertain to Babylon—once, by God’s grace, they have reached the boundaries of the catholic Church.

And since not everyone deserves to reach the catholic faith, what follows in the middle is said to those faithless and hardened people who refused to believe: “Men of blood, depart from me, for you say in your thoughts.”

These men are “men of blood” because they live according to the flesh and carry out the works of blood. They are rightly told to depart, because they did not desire to find a place in the Church.

It follows: “For you say in your thoughts”—that is, you murmur against those things that have been preached to you through the power of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, if you preserve the order stated above, you remove from yourself every darkness of confusion.

### Verse 20

**“Did I not hate those who hate you, and was I not wasting away over your enemies?”**

### Verse 21

**“With perfect hatred I hated them, and they became enemies to me.”**

It does not seem superfluous to inquire why we are commanded to love our enemies, while it is considered devout to hate the enemies of God, since there is a great difference between the two.

Our enemies sometimes rise against us in justified indignation and become angry because we do not provide them with the services owed to them, because we slander them, or because we envy their good endeavors. We are therefore rightly commanded to love our adversaries, whom we happen to offend through our own fault.

But the enemies of God, when they are obstinate, are condemned with appropriate and religious detestation, because, although they were created by him and owe him everything by which they live, they nevertheless become defiant toward their Creator.

Such people are therefore rightly to be regarded with horror, since they have not remembered such great benefits.

The distinction in the words must also be considered. First he said: “I hated those who hate you.” Hatred may first turn secretly in an evil heart; but the one who declares himself an enemy already possesses the strongest wickedness.

He signifies open and obstinate persecutors who tear the saints of God apart through criminal presumption. Holy piety rightly says that it wastes away over them, because, while they are endured here for a longer time so that they may be corrected, they pursue the Church of God with reckless assaults, as it is also said elsewhere: “Zeal for your house has made me waste away” (Psalm 118:139).

This expression is an indication of great grief. We say that people are wasting away when they are afflicted by unceasing cares and, as the body fails, reach almost to the destruction of life itself.

The second verse follows: “With perfect hatred I hated them, and they became enemies to me.”

Perfect hatred is to love the people while always abhorring their vices. Insofar as they are God’s creatures, there is no doubt that they are to be loved, since, considered as God’s work, they are good. But insofar as they are in the iniquity with which they have polluted themselves through shameful crimes, they are to be dreaded, since they can please only those who are entangled in similar deeds.

And to show you the unity of his divinity, he says that those became enemies to him who stood opposed to the Father’s commands.

Notice that, by the fifth species of definition, which in Greek is called **κατὰ τὴν λέξιν**, “according to the wording,” or in Latin *ad verbum*, he defines the hatred with which he hated the Father’s enemies: it was perfect hatred, generated not by human resentment or carnal envy, but by the Lord’s love.

The word *odium* (“hatred”) is said to derive as though from *oris repudium*, “rejection by the mouth.”

### Verse 22

**“Test me, God, and know my heart; question me, and know my paths.”**

### Verse 23

**“And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me into the eternal way.”**

No one else can say this of himself except the one who also said: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30).

For he alone is recognized as being without sin who is also proved to have borne the sins of human beings.

“Test me” demonstrates patience. “Know,” because I did not know how to transgress amid so great a turmoil of circumstances.

“Question me” refers to the most minute investigation, since no one who is questioned by one who knows can deny what has been done.

The “paths” likewise refer to the actions that he continually carried out in heavenly holiness.

It follows: “And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me into the eternal way.”

Consider, good teacher, how he teaches a perfect order. First he said that he should be tested and known, then questioned, so that, when no iniquity had been found, he might be led into that way where he reigns with the Holy Spirit in wondrous power and everlasting glory.

The way of iniquity is a diabolical act, which the devil does not cease to practice through evil instigations in the course of this age. He rightly denied that this way was in him, because he is the rock, and the footprint of the ancient serpent could in no way be found in his firmness.

The human substance therefore rightly asked to be led into the eternal way, in which the path of the devil could not be found.

For the Lord Christ frequently asks the Father for things that properly belong to himself, so that the unity of their love, power, or nature may be recognized.

## Conclusion of the Psalm
Behold, the eighth psalm concerning the two natures has now appeared for us; by these the presumptuous unbelief of those who err is beaten back. Let them at least be healed by that example of circumcision, so that, just as the Jews removed their foreskin on the eighth day, so these, admonished [ed., fortified] by the eighth psalm, may abandon the superfluous excesses of their obstinacy. For, as has been said, the psalms concerning this matter are the second, eighth, twentieth, seventy-first, eighty-first, one hundred seventh, one hundred ninth, and this present one hundred thirty-eighth. And although the deepest deafness threatens them, and does not depart even when overcome by so many heralds [Col. 0993B], nevertheless, if they still remain hardened by their wicked persuasion, let us present them with syllogistic proofs, since they especially wish to appear dialecticians.

The first proof, therefore, is that Christ the Lord consists of two natures, as follows: If Christ, one and the same, is perfect God and perfect man, as the agreement of all the holy Fathers confesses, he consists of deity and humanity united and perfected. Whatever, however, consists of deity and humanity united and perfected must necessarily consist of two united and perfected natures, namely, divinity and humanity. Therefore Christ, one and the same remaining, consists of two united and perfected natures, namely, deity and humanity.

The second proof is that the Lord Christ is in two natures, as follows: If Christ, one and the same remaining, consists of two united and perfected natures, as has been demonstrated, namely, of deity and humanity, then whatever consists of two united and perfected natures—of deity and humanity—also has its essence in two united and perfected natures. Therefore Christ, one and the same existing, has his essence in two united and perfected natures.

The third proof is that the Lord Christ always has two natures in himself, as follows: If Christ, one and the same existing, has his essence in the two united and perfected natures of deity and humanity, as has been demonstrated, then whatever has its essence in the two united and perfected natures of deity and humanity has two perfected and united natures in itself. Therefore Christ, one and the same remaining [Col. 0993D], has two perfected and united natures in himself, namely, of deity and humanity.

The fourth proof shows that if someone confesses Christ as perfect God and perfect man while denying two natures, he destroys both right doctrine and what he has confessed—that is, Christ as perfect God and perfect man—as follows: If Christ, one and the same, is perfect God and perfect man, he has in himself two perfected and united natures, of deity and humanity. For if he does not have in himself two perfected and united natures, of deity and humanity, as certain madmen say, he is not perfect God and perfect man, but either God alone, or man alone, or neither God nor man. But since that is inconsistent and impious, while Christ, one and the same, is perfect God and perfect man, as the common confession holds, he therefore has in himself two perfected and united natures, of deity and humanity.

For this reason also the venerable Bishop Facundus, a destroyer of heretics by penetrating subtlety, recently wrote to the emperor Justinian and treated the two natures of the Lord Christ with great caution and clarity in two books, which I have left transcribed for you, so that you might lack neither ancient nor modern writers.

Therefore, let us at last abandon the unlawful disputes of our opponents. No one, perhaps, will dare to call us blameworthy if, after the eighth correction, we say to them what the Apostle judged should be done when writing to Titus after the second rebuke; for he says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, and is condemned by himself” (Tit. III, 10–11).

But one of the Fathers beautifully defined what a heretic is: “A heretic is one who, driven either by ignorance or contempt of the divine law, or stubbornly inventing a new error, or following another’s sect, prefers to oppose Catholic unity rather than submit to it.”

# PSALM CXXXIX

*To the end, a psalm of David.*

Although this title seemed to have been explained in the preceding psalm, it is nevertheless not burdensome briefly to repeat what we know is always salutary for us to hear. “To the end” signifies the Lord Christ, as the Apostle says: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). Let us raise our hearts toward him with all our strength, because in this psalm a terrible, almighty, merciful, and greatly desired Judge is foretold as coming to us, as though by the voice of a herald.

## Division of the Psalm

Throughout the psalm the holy Church speaks. In the first section she entreats the Lord to deign to free her from the wicked devil, who tries by many deceits and ambushes to overthrow the devotion of the faithful people. In the second she asks not to be handed over to the most wicked tempter, from whom it is already clear that she has been freed by his protection amid bitter dangers. In the third she says that vengeance will come in the future judgment upon those who persecute his poor with insane assaults.

## Explanation of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; free me from the unjust man.”

The mother Church, knowing how much affliction from the devil her members suffer, cries out anxiously to the Lord, who alone can overcome his wickedness, asking to be freed from his manifold temptation, lest, exhausted by it for too long, she succumb. We have learned from the Gospel that “the evil man” is placed for the devil, since it says: “But the evil man is the devil” (Matt. XIII, 39). And rightly is he so called, because he is polluted by the contagion of sins, so that he now seems not a heavenly angel but a man, so called from *humus*, earth. Yet they succeed one another by an exchange of names. For even today we call the devil an evil man, and conversely, as was proved above, we call an evil man the devil.

Then, for the sake of distinction, he says “the unjust man,” so that he may specifically designate an earthly being, as though the devil’s soldier, and thus may pray with perfect supplication to be delivered both from the author of crimes and from his followers. For the very different designations indicate different persons. The devil is called “malignant”; his human follower is called “unjust.” Two epithets could not belong simultaneously to one person, which is prohibited by the rule of eloquence.

### Verse 2

“Those who have devised evil in their heart have established battles all day long.”

The dangers that are hidden are always more serious, because they burst upon us suddenly, when, like overflowing rivers, they descend without warning. He signifies those who, coming forth from the Church’s innermost parts, have burst into sacrilegious conflicts with perverse doctrines. He rightly asks to be delivered from them, lest he be wounded by their perversities. And to show that their wickedness is continual, he says: “All day long,” so that no weariness and no length of time might soften them.

### Verse 3

“They have sharpened their tongues like serpents; the poison of asps is under their lips.”

Here the malice and deceit of heretics are beautifully described. “Tongues” signifies words which, polished on the whetstones of wickedness, seek to wound the hearts of the simple. They are rightly compared with serpents, because they spew out venom through their speeches; hence they are likened to deaf asps. They strive with such an intention that, through the obstinacy of their minds, they never wish to be overcome by the truth. This figure is called a *parabole*, because things dissimilar in kind are compared by reason of their harmful qualities [Col. 0995C].

### Verse 4

“Guard me, O Lord, from the hand of the sinner, and free me from unjust men.”

Here again “the sinner” signifies the devil, who was the first of all creatures to transgress and is known to have wounded Adam through his injustice. The holy Church asks to be guarded from his most wicked power—for he is exceedingly strong and is therefore even called the prince of this world—because he deceives by many tricks and many ambushes, insinuating himself under a slippery disguise so that he cannot be easily avoided. His ministers also follow, because what he cannot steal by inspiring our minds he tries publicly to accomplish through his followers.

### Verse 5

“Those who planned to trip my steps have hidden proud snares for me” [Col. 0995D].

Properly speaking, we say that someone is tripped when the ground is taken from beneath our feet, so that we fall heavily into dark caverns. This is what the enemy does to us: for those walking in the Lord’s way he prepares nearby pits of sin, so that, once he has led us away from that most direct intention, he may plunge us, deceived and mocked, into destruction. They do not dare approach that path, which belongs to the righteous alone.

But the proud are the exalted heretics who, abandoning the Lord’s way, hasten to deceive peoples with perverse doctrines rather than teach them. They set snares for the holy people when they strive to bind them with empty riddles.

### Verse 6

“They stretched out ropes as a snare for my feet; beside the path they placed a stumbling-block for me.”

He continues to explain the perversities of the heretics [Col. 0996A]. They set out ropes—that is, deceitful and twisted objections—by which they capture human understanding, so that, just as a snare is stretched for the feet, a stumbling-block is shown to be stretched for the mind. A snare is made of rope because it always tightens its bonds more severely, and its embrace does not slip away with any gentleness when it encloses the trapped person in certain knotted loops.

“Beside the path” is properly said, because they catch only those who depart from the straight road of virtues. Then follows the first *diapsalma*, where a pleasant pause grants us a division.

### Verse 7

“I said to the Lord: You are my God; hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.”

After the cruel snares prepared, after the twisted ropes laid out, after the unjust stumbling-blocks contrived by the devil’s fraud, he comes to the second section, turning his words toward the Lord so that he may not be handed over to the worst ambushes. The Church, shining with pure faith and standing firm in unchangeable virtue, says: “I said to the Lord: You are my God.”

Certainly this cannot be said by one who is proved to be entangled in perishable errors. The Arian congregation, the Sabellian, the Manichaean, the Pelagian, the Apollinarian, the Eutychian, the Nestorian, and the other monstrosities—which should be called portents rather than doctrines—cannot truly say to the Lord: “You are my God.” Let the Catholic Church say it; let the Bride called from the nations say it, she who confesses the holy Trinity with truest faith.

Then follows: “Hear, O Lord, the voice of my supplication.” It would have been sufficient to say, “Hear my prayer,” unless he had wished something deeper to be understood. The “voice of supplication” is the purity of prayer, that silent cry which rises to the Lord. To the silent Moses it is said: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. XIV, 15). To Cain it is said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. IV, 10). Therefore the voice of holy action is the most eloquent cry of the deeds themselves, unknown to human beings but known to God alone. For this reason she asks that the voice of her supplication be heard, because she knew that she was offering the most righteous gifts of petition.

### Verse 8

“O Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of battle.”

The repetition “Lord, Lord” displays the affection of devout prayer. This figure is called *epizeuxis*, that is, the doubling of the same word in the same verse without any interval. This figure, as has often been said, is highly effective in moving the emotions [Col. 0996D].

When he says, “Strength of my salvation,” he demonstrates his patience and perseverance. In the struggle of tribulations there can be no salvation unless the Lord’s mercy has been granted as the strength of endurance. “Strength” derives from *viriditas*, greenness, because it does not know how to wither under any labor.

Then follows: “You have overshadowed my head in the day of battle.” When the Church says that her head was overshadowed in the day of battle, she signifies the blessed passion of the Lord, who on that day of his crucifixion was so overshadowed and defended that neither did his soul suffer any confusion nor did his flesh endure the injury of corruption. At that time he himself also asks for help in the twenty-first psalm. After his passion had run its course he says: “But you, O Lord, do not keep your help far from me; look to my defense, etc.” (Ps. XXI, 20).

The Lord’s passion is rightly defined as “the day of battle,” namely, when, after the devil had been defeated, the prisons of hell were shattered, captives were freed, and he alone triumphed by dying—he who in a new manner destroyed death.

### Verse 9

“Do not hand me over, O Lord, from my desire to the sinner; they have plotted against me [mss. A, B, F: ‘against’]; do not forsake me, lest they ever be exalted.”

Anyone is handed over from his own desire to the sinner when, through the desires of the flesh, he is abandoned to the devil to be possessed. Concerning these the Apostle says: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity” (Rom. I, 24).

But lest this happen, what follows is entirely credible: just as the enemies devise a plan for evil, so may divine power deign to provide help. Finally, the most just reason is given: lest they truly be exalted through the destruction of the righteous, those who glory in the overthrow of the faithful people.

Then follows the second *diapsalma*, where, as usual, we shall place a division.

### Verse 10

“The head of their circuit is the labor of their lips; it will cover them.”

After offering prayers that he not be handed over to the enemies, the holy mother Church comes to the third section, in which she indicates the inexplicable errors of the wicked. For just as above she said that her head was overshadowed by the Lord on the day of battle, so she reports that their head—that is, the devil—has a remarkable circuit, since he never reaches the straight path; returning along his own tracks, he always entangles himself.

The order of the words is: “Their head is circuit.” The Apostle Peter says something similar: “Your adversary, like a roaring lion, goes around seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. V, 8).

This is a most beautiful form of definition: to declare in one word what the thing being sought is. In Greek this is called κατὰ τὴν λέξιν, and in Latin *ad verbum*, “word for word.” The “labor of the lips,” however, is the lie uttered by the mouth, which is laboriously fabricated because it is formed through elaborate contrivance. Truth is spoken without labor, because it is uttered simply and without difficulty. Therefore the lie of their mouth covers them when the faithless are defeated by their own assertion. For malice is never so cautious that it does not speak against itself.

### Verse 11

“Coals of fire will fall upon them; you will cast them into the fire; they will not endure in miseries.”

First he called their errors inexplicable [Col. 0997D]; now he recalls punishments that are entirely salutary. The coals of fire are the torments of repentance. Yet this fire arises from a rain of tears, as is also said in the one-hundred-nineteenth psalm: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals that lay waste” (Ps. CXIX, 4).

First, mournful compunction falls upon them; afterward they are cast into the fire, when, through the Lord’s mercy, they have already been kindled by the flame of charity. They begin to burn with holy works, though previously they had lived in excessive sluggish tepidity. It happens to such people that they do not remain in their miseries, when by divine gift they are transferred to what is good.

### Verse 12

“A man of many words will not be established upon the earth” [mss. A, B, F: “in the earth”]; “evil will seize the unjust man unto destruction” [ms. F: “in destruction”].

Although those who are eloquent through an abundance of speech can also be called “men of words,” this name is especially established for those who are verbose in inconsiderate speech. They are opposed to the wise and conduct themselves in an opposite manner. For the Apostle James admonishes: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak” (Jas. I, 19).

Such people are not at all established upon the earth, since they frequently exceed the limits of their levity. For it is difficult for an unconsidered speech to be right, as it is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. X, 19).

The unjust man, however, is one who, despising the divine rules, is carried away by the fervor of his own will. He is seized by his evils and submerged in the deepest abyss by an exceedingly devouring force, because he always thinks what is harmful to himself, since he rejects the Lord’s commands.

### Verse 13

“I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy and vengeance for the poor.”

The holy Church speaks briefly and truly about the sort of people whom she ought indeed to condemn as men of many words. Through faith, by God’s gift, she says that she has learned this—that it is most certainly believed to be accomplished.

He will therefore execute judgment for the needy when, in that judgment, he restores the things promised; and he will avenge the poor, concerning whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “I saw beneath the altar of the Lord the souls of those who had been slain.” And shortly afterward: “Crying out: How long, holy and true one, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?” (Rev. VI, 9–10).

### Verse 14

“Nevertheless, the righteous will confess your name, and the upright will dwell in your presence.”

This is shown to be destined to happen amid every kind of grave and bitter pressure. For it is then a great virtue to praise the Lord, when the allurements of this age withdraw from us. Job was good when, while wealthy, he worshiped the Lord; but how much better was he when he praised him under manifold affliction!

Therefore let us desire all the more to give thanks when the tempter tries to afflict us. The enemy departs more easily when he sees that he cannot overcome those whom he oppresses.

For see what follows: those who are upright do not cease to dwell in his presence. It is an inexhaustible and perpetual vision always to see him by whom every rational creature is accustomed to be refreshed, as was already said in the fifteenth psalm: “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Ps. XV, 10).

That presence is the gift of all rewards, and whoever has deserved to behold it cannot lack any goodness. But since it is written, “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18), this must be referred to that time when the blessed behold the Lord not through a mirror but, as the Apostle says, “face to face” (1 Cor. XIII, 12).

## Conclusion of the Psalm

How salutary, how sweet were the words we heard from the holy mother! She prayed for us, that we might be stripped of the devil’s temptations, which she knew to be exceedingly violent for us. Once freed, she promises us the Lord’s presence, so that we may fear nothing burdensome and nothing sad, since such a gift, so great a promise, is offered to us.

Grant, O Lord, that just as you are desirable to your servants, so you may show yourself through the brightness of your mercy. Let not the sins which we condemn by our own execration hinder us. We confess our faults so that we may have you reconciled to us. For you alone are the Judge who grants pardon to the one who confesses; and although nothing is hidden from you, you nevertheless seek that it be declared by human beings, thereby showing that you know it far more truly.

# PSALM CXL

*A psalm of David.*

Since the words of the title are already known through frequent repetition, we ought to raise our intention toward the Lord the Savior. For what is said once can sometimes be doubtful; but what is proclaimed through frequent repetition is entirely certain and beyond doubt. For this reason we are warned by certain preceding heralds, so that we may prepare the attention of our mind with suitable devotion for future events, lest, while the things being said are unfamiliar, they perhaps be heard carelessly [Col. 0999B].

The prophet entreats, as those who have judged more cautiously think, that amid these worldly activities he may be freed from various errors, lest he fall into the snare of sinners, with whom he does not wish to have any share.

## Division of the Psalm

The prophet, understanding human frailty to be entangled in various bonds of sin, first asks the Lord that his prayer be heard, adding from which errors he especially begs to be freed. In the second section he chooses to be rebuked by the righteous rather than praised by the sinner, asking to be guarded from the snares of sinners, since he testifies that he has no communion with them.

## Explanation of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“O Lord, I have cried to you; hear me. Attend to the voice of my prayer when I cry to you.”

Here let us seek an enthymeme. He proposes: “O Lord, I have cried to you”; the conclusion follows: “Therefore hear me.” Thus the force of that enthymematic syllogism is completed in a brief formulation.

The prophet, wishing to instill in the human race an affection for continual prayer, seems to have set down two apparently differing times. He speaks of the past: “I have cried,” which signifies a completed prayer. Then he repeats, “when I cry to you,” which clearly refers to the future, so that, just as no time is free from faults, so no time may be left idle with respect to devout prayers.

Against continual sins, the saving remedy is to supplicate the devout Lord continually. For what will it profit for past sins to be forgiven if future ones seem to bind us? The Christian’s good end is therefore sought: that he may pass away at the end with forgiveness, lest his life be the last thing to sin.

Observe that here and in the following verse he has made his prayers fourfold, because for a holy man so great a matter could never produce satiety. Prayer is what frees us from faults, wins the judge’s favor, and cleanses offenses; nor can mercy be absent from the one who prays, since humility urges us to supplicate continually.

But the merciful Lord does all this because he does not wish to condemn those whom he warns. For the maker of all things cries out: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII, 32).

### Verse 2

“Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting of my hands an evening sacrifice.”

Incense is the sweet burning of fragrant spices which, consumed by coals, sends forth most pleasing smoke upward and delights those who smell it with agreeable pleasure. Thus the prayer of the blessed, kindled by the fire of charity, is offered before the divine presence; it is raised still higher by the weight of humility and compunction.

For the Lord delights in our virtues as in good fragrances. That the Lord receives holy prayer as a most pleasant odor is also read in the Apocalypse, where it is said: “An angel stood before the altar of the Lord, having a golden censer; and the smoke of the prayers rose from the angel’s hand before the Lord, that he might give from the prayers of the saints what is before God” (Rev. VIII, 3).

Then follows: “The lifting of my hands an evening sacrifice.” The lifting of hands signifies a pious work, which is exercised either in almsgiving or in some commendable way of life. The evening sacrifice perhaps signifies that offering which religious devotion customarily offers to the Lord at the end of life, when we practice repentance and cleanse ourselves through humble supplication, as it is said in the fiftieth psalm: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L, 19).

Our evening is when, as death approaches, we leave this light. Behold, we have often warned that no one should despair if at the end he cleanses himself rather by a fountain of tears.

### Verse 3

“Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door around my lips.”

The most holy prophet asks not to say anything that ought to lead to guilt. But he begs to be fortified by a double protection, so that neither may his thought savor of iniquity nor may a wicked will burst forth into foolish words.

For he knew that there was sin in both, and he asks to be made free from it, as Solomon says: “Fence your possession with thorns; establish your silver and gold, and make a door and a bar for your mouth, and impose a yoke and measure upon your words” (Sir. XXVIII, 28–29).

A door is so called from *obstare*, “to stand against,” because when it is closed it obstructs those entering. The holy man saw that the place from which he knew sin could come so easily had to be fortified by great prayers. For shortly before, in the preceding psalm, he had said: “A man of many words will not be established upon the earth” (Ps. CXXXIX, 12).

### Verse 4

“Do not incline my heart toward evil words, to make excuses for sins.”

A second prayer follows: even if it should happen that he say something for which he must repent, he should not strive to excuse himself through the most wicked falsehoods. This is the greatest vice with which humanity struggles: after its sin, it flees to excuses rather than prostrating itself in a confession of repentance.

This crime must clearly be numbered among the greatest sins, because it arises from the very source that makes the guilty person appear slow to come to repentance. As it is said in the First Book of Kings: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to acquiesce is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. XV, 23).

When he says, “to make excuses for sins,” he signifies the custom of the shameless, who, when caught, are known first to excuse themselves with some falsehood; and when they have been refuted in that, they continually adopt other excuses, lest their brazen obstinacy ever yield to the truth—at one time attributing what they do to circumstances, at another to necessity, and at another to other causes.

This figure is called *metastasis*, that is, transference, when we strive to transfer our guilt to someone else.

### Verse 5

“With men who work iniquity; and I will not be joined with their chosen ones.”

The third petition is that he be freed from the company of those who work iniquity, lest he become entangled with them as though joined together [Col. 1001B]. The guilty are called “joined together” when two are bound together in one bond, so that, each hindering the other, they cannot have free flight.

The prophet therefore prays not to be bound to such people, who are known to hinder one another through mutual entanglement. “I will not be joined” refers both to the men who work iniquity and to their chosen ones. And observe that he added “their,” lest you think that they were truly the Lord’s chosen ones, though they were called by that name. For those who appear foremost among the wicked are much more criminal—as though leaders of crimes, princes of robbers, and the head of all the lost.

### Verse 6

“The righteous will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but the oil of the sinner will not fatten my head.”

After requesting protection of the tongue and condemning excuses for crimes, he comes to the second section, in which the holy man chooses the rebukes of the righteous rather than the flatteries of sinners. He briefly indicates what the correction of the righteous is by saying “in mercy,” since the holy man does not rebuke in anger but approaches the rebuked person out of love.

Even if he displays the face of an angry person, he always assumes the heart of one who has been reconciled, as the Apostle admonishes: “Brothers, if a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI, 1).

Therefore it is the custom of the good to prefer being corrected by the good rather than being praised by the flattery of criminals, as it is written: “The wounds of a friend are better than the willing kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVII, 6).

Then follows: “But the oil of the sinner will not fatten my head.” Oil is generally used both in a good and in a bad sense. In a good sense, as in the Gospel: “But when you fast, anoint your head with oil and wash your face” (Matt. VI, 17); and in the forty-fourth psalm: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

Oil in the good sense is a cause of radiance, fuel for light, providing both splendor and health. In the bad sense, as it is used here, “the oil of the sinner” is the feigned affection of words which, entering our minds gently through flatteries and caresses like the richness of oil, softens the rigor of truth and leads us toward harmful thoughts through the display of a fictitious love. As it is said in another psalm: “They have softened their words above oil, yet they are arrows.” And Solomon says: “The words of flatterers are soft, but their end reaches the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. XVIII, 8).

Therefore those admonitions must always be chosen which do not draw us toward love of the world but invite us to the commandments of the Divinity.

The Gospel parable of the ten virgins can also suitably be applied here (Matt. XXV, 1). The five virgins who devoted their most approved deeds to the Lord, preserving clear consciences and filled with the oil of charity, offered themselves before the Lord’s presence like exceedingly bright lamps. These, as he says here, must rightly be believed to have been corrected by righteous people and nevertheless reproved in the spirit of mercy.

The other five virgins, who in their unhappy lot believed the voices of flatterers, had their heads made exceedingly fat through their deception; and therefore, when their lamps had gone out, they were not received, since a dark life was not fit to be offered before the Lord of true light. Blessed Augustine explained this parable more fully and suitably in the fifty-ninth book of his *Questions*. Let us therefore consider how dangerous flattery is, since it is shown to exclude people from the Lord.

### Verse 7

“For my prayer is still in their good pleasures.”

This little verse depends upon the preceding sense. He said: “The oil of the sinner will not fatten my head,” and then added: “For my prayer is still in their good pleasures.”

When he says that his prayer is still in their good pleasures—that is, in the pleasures of the wicked—he indicates that he had not yet been perfectly converted, since, even while praying for himself, he desired such things to come to him as he knew were the objects of their wishes.

He was praying to be made alien from all these things, lest his head be fattened by the oil of the sinner—that is, by the flattery of evil persuasion [Col. 1002C].

### Verse 8

“Their judges have been swallowed up beside the rock; they will hear my words, for they have been able.”

Here, as in many places, the rock signifies the Lord Christ. Beside him the heretical teachers stand—as judges of their own people—and are swallowed up by sudden voracity; they fall into the depths because they do not choose to stand upon the rock.

For what does it profit them to stand beside solidity when they are not seen to stand upon that very strength? This is the rendering which the translator Jerome employed, and which Father Augustine, the expositor, followed, so that no one may dare to criticize what has been approved by the authority of such men.

This translation of the word seems especially to signify the faithlessness of heretics. For when they baptize, when they share communion, and when they read the sacred writings with us, they are said to stand beside the rock, not upon the rock. Only those stand upon this solidity who do not place fragile foundations upon sand.

Then follows: “They will hear my words, for they have been able.” He says that his words have been heard by the heretics; the text of the present book declares them. In how many places are they accused, in how many admonitions rebuked, so that they ought to be corrected and not remain in their perversities?

By this statement we are taught most fully that those who hear the Lord’s words yet perversely refuse to do them are guilty in every respect. Since they have been admonished so many times, they were able to understand—if they had not determined to cling instead to their own persuasions.

### Verse 9

“As the thickness of the earth is spewed out upon the earth, so our bones have been scattered beside hell.”

Having previously spoken of the heretics and tyrants who refused to hear the Lord’s words, he now comes to the martyrs, whom they were tearing apart with savage persecution.

For when the thickness of the earth spews forth, it produces diseases, corrupts the air, and spreads a pestilence dangerous to human beings far and wide. Thus the wicked pride of tyrants wounded the bodies of the martyrs with the corruption of its own malice. The prophet appropriately called them “his bones,” because it is clear that they are the strongest supports of the Christian faith. Their constancy, worthy of proclamation, was neither overcome by punishments nor softened by prolonged persecution, with the Lord’s help.

And observe how the particular meanings of the words flow like the sweetest honey. He did not say “into hell,” because although they seem to die according to the common lot, eternal life is granted to them.

### Verse 10

“For my eyes are toward you, O Lord, Lord; in you I have hoped; do not take away my soul.”

After speaking of the frailty of the human race, he now flees to divine remedies, asking in reversed order that, because he has placed his hope in the Lord, his soul should be delivered. You will frequently find this in the divine Scriptures, as we have often said: sometimes the reason precedes, and sometimes it immediately follows.

But since it is the custom of the blessed to wish to be freed from this world, as another psalm says, “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. CXLI, 8), and, “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better” (Phil. I, 23), how does the prophet here ask: “Do not take away my soul”?

“Do not take it away,” that is, from your good things; rather, let my hope be continually in you, and let my eyes always look toward you.

### Verse 11

“Guard me from the snare which they have set for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity.”

Through “snares” and “stumbling-blocks,” the prophet has briefly embraced the evils of the whole world. He asks to be guarded from them, lest he be caught through their ambushes.

The snares are the various desires of the flesh, by which human minds are bound in pleasing bonds. The stumbling-blocks arise through restless brothers who, through quarrel and pride, reject holy charity.

What will they have in common if they happen to lose so distinguished a gift? And observe that he places stumbling-blocks after snares, because that most wicked ancient enemy, whenever he cannot deceive us through snares, strives through stumbling-blocks to take away from us the grace of the Divinity.

### Verse 12

“ sinners shall fall into his net; I alone am until I pass over.”

Here is what he was asking earlier to be delivered from, so that he would not have to be joined with such men. And observe how the appropriate words correspond to the comparison that has been made. Those who are enclosed by the circling of sins will fall into the devil’s net. Yet we also read of those good nets which, at the Lord’s command, enclosed one hundred and fifty-three fish; these are evidently proved to be a type of the holy Church. Blessed, then, are those who are numbered among those fish; wretched are those who fall into this number of the lost.

For *nets* are so called as though from “holding fast.” He adds: “I alone am until I pass over.” He is alone who—as he said above—does not walk joined together with the worst of men; who confesses the holy Trinity to be one God and Lord; who places his hope in no one else, but only in the Lord. “Until I pass over,” that is, for as long as I remain in this world. For the blessed are said to pass through this age like travelers, because they are occupied by none of its attractions.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 1004B]

We have learned, dearest brothers, what danger there is if we speak incautiously; we have learned how greatly we ought to fear what the most holy prophet fears. For when does either idle speech not creep in, or a desire for falsehood arise? [Note: [Col. 1003D] A question mark would better be placed there. EDITOR.] It is the tongue that frequently drags us toward vices, and we overcome it most safely in one way: by always occupying it with the praises of the Lord. Let it always speak of that in which it does not know how to err; let it perform work profitable to the soul; let it reverently serve its Creator. For then we place a guard upon our mouth if we continually meditate on the Lord’s commandments. One is silent concerning evil who does not keep silent concerning good; and error does not creep in where heavenly truth has poured itself forth. For if evil thought is removed from us, if the most shameful deed is kept apart, if we are separated from the company of the wicked, then—as the prophet says—we shall become solitary for the Lord, when we are least entangled in wicked thoughts.

## PSALM 141

*Understanding of David, a prayer when he was in the cave.*

The subject of the psalm is indeed contained in the present title; but through likenesses drawn from bodily events, an indication suitable to a spiritual reality is offered to us. David, son of Jesse, fled from Saul the ruler, and while he was hiding in a cave he prayed (1 Kings 24); this signified beforehand that the Lord Christ would do the same in the body before his Passion. For when *understanding* is prefixed to this prayer, it is shown that such a comparison ought to be referred to the one who, avoiding his persecutors by prayer, was concealed through changes of place, so that the Son of God might both fulfill what he had promised about himself through the prophets and reveal the truth of the incarnation he had assumed.

There are in this psalm words of the Lord and Savior, as he avoided the most criminal madness of the Jews. Hence it rightly happened that, to signify the persecution of the Hebrews, David’s flight was placed in the title. For David—as we have often said—indicates both an earthly king and a heavenly one. Thus the signification of two realities is contained in one name. We must also remember that this is the fifth psalm among those entitled *Prayer*.

### Division of the Psalm

[Col. 1005A]

In the first part, the Lord Christ cries out to the Father, exposing the wicked deceits of Jewish persecution. In the second, he implores deliverance from the prison of hell, since the faith of all the saints depended upon his resurrection.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 1005A]

#### Verse 1

“With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I pleaded with God.”

That holiness of the venerable incarnation says that, according to ordinary usage, it cried out to the Lord with its own voice. This figure is called *pleonasm*, that is, abundance, as when we commonly say, “I did it with my hands,” “I heard with my ears,” and similar expressions. And lest the cry be understood as momentary, he added, “I pleaded,” which is carried out through repeated supplication.

[Col. 1005B]

#### Verse 2

“I will pour out my prayer in his presence, and before him I declare my tribulation.”

How pure, how sweet was the prayer that was poured out in the Father’s presence, like the abundance of a clear spring! It was truly poured out—not so as to seek the depths below, but so as to reach the height of heavenly compassion. It is said, “in his presence,” because the Divinity regards good prayers as something bearing a countenance; and although our will cannot be seen by human beings, it is nevertheless certain that the Divinity observes it.

But what this prayer is is explained below: namely, tribulation, which makes prayers sincere and continuous. And observe that he says with the security of innocence, “I declare my tribulation before him.” For only those afflictions could be declared before him which were proved to have been inflicted unjustly. Thus the merciful advocate declares his tribulations before the Father, so that he may obtain pardon for our sins.

And observe that in these two verses prayer is offered in four ways, as the Apostle says: “Therefore, first of all, I urge that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Timothy 2:1).

#### Verse 3

“When my spirit failed within me, you knew my paths.”

This part of the verse depends upon what precedes. For when he says, “When my spirit failed within me,” it is to be understood as though he said: “I declare my tribulation before him when my spirit fails within me.” He wishes many and very grievous tribulations to be understood, which he professes to declare before God.

But since we never read that his spirit failed, because he completed all things through a voluntary Passion, this must rather be understood as referring to the members of his body. This type of interpretation is evidently an invention of our predecessors, used when someone speaks in a way that cannot properly apply to his person, as in the statement: “My iniquities are not hidden from you” (Psalm 68:6). The faithful likewise spoke in this manner in Psalm 83: “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83:3). And elsewhere: “My eyes have failed while looking for your word, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’” (Psalm 118:82). And in the following psalm he will say: “Hear me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed” (Psalm 142:7).

[Col. 1006A]

#### Verse 4

“On this way in which I walked, they hid snares for me.”

The devil—as has often been said—hides a snare beside the way, so that he may deceive those who presume to depart from the straight paths. But because the Lord Christ never departed from his holiness, it was necessary that on the very path of his righteousness he endure ineffectual temptations, from which he was in no way proved to have departed.

He touches upon the time when the kingdoms of the world were shown to him by the devil, when his hunger was being tested, and the other events which diabolical deceit and the wickedness of evil men presumed to undertake. For it was necessary that the Lord Christ speak in this way, so that even then the truth of the flesh he was to assume might be revealed.

#### Verse 5

“I looked to the right and saw, and there was no one who knew me. Escape has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul.”

When he says, “I looked to the right,” he refers to the time when he was going to the cross, because he was able to look upon none of the faithful there. They were not seen standing at his right because they had been scattered by carnal fear, as it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7).

It follows: “And there was no one who knew me”—that is, who knew the divinity within him, which was voluntarily enduring all these things in the flesh he had assumed, and which said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). For if they had known the Lord Christ in that confusion, they could certainly also have been seen at his right.

He added: “Escape has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul.” He says that escape had perished when he allowed himself to be killed by the hands of the impious. For when escape has perished, the danger of death can in no way be avoided. No one, however, sought his soul, since no consolation was offered him; he was left alone for his Passion, though he was to die for the salvation of all.

Thus, under this brief and subtle signification of the words, the whole sequence of his betrayal has been narrated.

#### Verse 6

“I cried to you, O Lord; I said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living.”

He has come to the second part, in which he asks to escape the ambushes of his enemies, so that the hearts of the faithful may rejoice in the gift of his resurrection. He cried out while placing his hope in the Lord, when he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

It follows: “My portion in the land of the living.” This is especially proved by that passage in which, hanging on the cross, he said to the thief: “Amen, I say to you: Today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid., 23:43). Paradise is the land of the living, which only the blessed will happily enter, those who will live under eternity and security.

He speaks humbly and generally when he says that his portion is in the land of the living, although it is known that the whole of it belongs to him. Similar is the statement made concerning the apostles: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

#### Verse 7

“Attend to my prayer, for I have been humbled exceedingly.”

He rightly says, “I have been humbled exceedingly,” since, as the Apostle says, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Philippians 2:7). To this he was humbled still further, for “he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.”

For if he had not bowed down that marvelous height of his divinity through the reality of the body he had assumed, how could he have been crucified for the salvation of all, he who governs heaven and earth through wondrous powers?

#### Verse 8

“Deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown stronger than I.”

When he says, “Deliver me,” the weakness of his own divinity is not being shown; rather, the Father’s love is being revealed. For although he had the power—as he himself says—to lay down his soul and take it up again (John 10:18), nevertheless, for our instruction, while retaining the reverence due to the beloved and well-pleasing Son, he appropriately displayed honor toward the Father’s majesty.

For he says in the Gospel: “Father, glorify me” (John 17:5). He also cries out from the cross: “God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that he might clearly show the humility of the flesh and thereby refute the wicked doctrines of the Manichaeans.

He therefore prays to be delivered by divine power from the Jews who persecuted him, who had become so much stronger in bodily terms that they laid hands upon him and rejoiced in his death. But these most wretched men attempted all these things because they did not perceive in him the power of the Divinity, but only his bodily appearance. Of them the Apostle says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

#### Verse 9

“Bring my soul out of prison, so that I may confess your name.”

The earlier authorities wished to understand “prison” here in two ways: either as the penal confinement of this age, which we suffer while established in this body; or, rather, as the custody of hell, from which it is not permitted to escape under the weakness of human condition.

But it is better in this passage to refer it to the underworld, because of the hope of resurrection, which he implores may come about through frequent supplication, as he asks in another psalm: “May the pit not close its mouth over me” (Psalm 68:16).

For *prison* is said as though from *arcer*, because it keeps those enclosed from going out. But why he desires to be freed from this prison follows: “so that I may confess your name.” For confession of praise was then offered to the Father by all the faithful, when he was clearly brought out of the prison of hell by the miracle of his resurrection.

The word “bring out” itself signifies that he was dead: he was transferred from the innermost depths to the heights.

[Col. 1007C]

#### Verse 10

“The righteous await me until you reward me.”

This is the confession concerning the Lord’s resurrection that was mentioned above. For while all Christ’s apostles had been confounded by his death, they were certainly waiting until they recognized the glory of the promised resurrection and strengthened the hearts of all who were trembling.

But observe that it says, “until you reward me,” because the glory of the one rising again was the reward of his most blessed Passion. Concerning this reward the Apostle says: “For this reason God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:9–10).

The word “until” indicates the period of the three days, when the devotion of the righteous rejoiced in his resurrection. This was certainly granted to Christ the Lord uniquely in respect of the humanity he had assumed, whose resurrection strengthened the hearts of the righteous.

Now let us consider, if we can with some spiritual contemplation, the mercy of our Lord, who both redeemed us from the enemy and does not cease to teach us how not to be taken captive again. Behold, he makes his own rule our daily medicine, when he deigned to humble himself for this reason: lest that diabolical spirit of pride be desired in any way.

There is ruin there; here there is always ascent. From the former comes death; from the latter eternal life follows. Let us therefore ask the almighty Son that he who provided the saving example of prayer may mercifully grant us the result of imitating this most holy example.

### Conclusion of the Psalm

[Col. 1008B]

The sequence of psalms designated by the title *Prayer* has indeed been completed. Now, at their conclusion, it is necessary to gather a few things briefly, so that, with the Lord’s assistance, we may be salutarily urged to hasten toward our remedy.

First of all, let us do what has been commanded, and, marking our lips with the sign of the cross, beseech the Lord to wash our mouth, polluted by human filth. For Isaiah says: “I have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5).

Next, we must pray with words—not words supplied by human desires, but those which the Divinity itself has granted for the remedy of our perversity. The prayer itself must proceed from a humble, gentle, and sincere heart: confessing its sins without excuse, and amid bitter tears trusting in the Lord’s sweetest mercy.

Let it not seek earthly things, but desire heavenly things. Let it be separated from bodily desire and joined only to the divine. Let it be wholly spiritual, possessing only the tears of the flesh.

For contemplate whom you are praying to and desire, as far as permitted, to behold him with the mind’s eye; and recognize how you ought to be offered prostrate before him. For he is, as the Apostle says, “blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Timothy 6:15–16).

Therefore we ought to approach such a great Lord with all fear and love, and direct the gaze of our mind toward him in such a way that you recognize God to be beyond all that the human mind can conceive of splendor, brightness, radiance, and majesty—he who distributes all his creatures with incomparable goodness.

Let us imagine nothing for ourselves through false presumption, since the hidden substance of God, who made all things, cannot be comprehended by the knowledge of creatures as it is in itself. For there is no form in God and no limitation. His nature is beyond estimation, his power incomprehensible, his mercy unique.

Of him it has been very appropriately declared: “God can be said to be what he is not; what he is cannot be comprehended.” To this almighty One, without beginning and without end, who permeates and fills the whole world and every creature of his, yet in such a way that he is wholly everywhere in himself, while he abandons the wicked not by his presence but by the power of his grace, Father Augustine gave a fuller explanation in writing to Dardanus (Letter 57, response to Question 1).

The prophetic word salutarily urges us to hasten, saying: “Come, let us adore and fall down before the Lord; let us weep before God” (Psalm 94:6). And lest we be left altogether wavering and fearful, it added: “who made us.” Thus, when we recognize that we were created by him, we may confidently entreat our Maker.

Then what must be said by us humbly in the praise of God is almost felt within the prayer itself, when we are mercifully heard by the Lord—provided, however, that it is beneficial for us to obtain what we ask. For no ungrateful person is excluded from heavenly generosity if he is permitted to ask with a simple and devout mind. A person feels that he has obtained forgiveness to the extent that he recognizes that he has poured out devout tears.

There is also another indication of our progress: the more someone recognizes that he loves and fears God, the more necessary it is that divine assistance draw near to him. Thus every diabolical deception is conquered by the Lord’s beneficence; thus, through his mercy, sins are overcome.

These things have been said about prayer to the extent required by the modesty of my intellect and the character of the place. But if anyone desires to be satisfied with the fullest abundance on this subject, let him read the eloquent Cassian, who in the ninth and tenth Conferences discussed the kinds of prayer with such fullness and insight that the Holy Spirit seems clearly to have spoken through him.

## PSALM 142

*A Psalm of David, when his son was persecuting him.*

[Col. 1009C]

This history is very well known from the reading of the Books of Kings (1 Kings 15). For David’s son Absalom is known to have impiously persecuted his father, who had been driven from the kingdom. This likeness—as some wish—extends to every Christian, who, when sins rage, is harassed in the harshness of this world as though by his own children.

But against these things the healing remedy of repentance is set forth, which this psalm is shown to contain. Remember, however, that this history was already presented in the third psalm; but there Absalom was named because he wished his example to refer only to Judas. Here his name has not been placed, so that, as we said earlier, each of the faithful might understand it to have been spoken concerning his own vices.

### Division of the Psalm

[Col. 1009D]

Although the prophet had been exercised by the meditation of many penitents, the nearer he came to future praise, the more he turned, with heartfelt remorse, to the cleansing waters of repentance, so that, washed appropriately in this saving refuge, he might appear most pure before the Lord’s sight. Rightly so, lest he hear that sentence of condemnation: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds?” (Psalm 49:16).

Accordingly, in the first petition he asks the Lord Christ not to enter into judgment with his servant, but implores his mercy to come to the aid of his distress. In the second, he asks to arrive quickly at forgiveness, so that, led into the way of truth, he may be freed from the ambushes of his enemies.

### Exposition of the Psalm

[Col. 1010A]

#### Verse 1

“O Lord, hear my prayer; listen with your ears to my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness.”

Unless we examine the matter more deeply, the clauses of this verse seem to contradict one another. For when the prophet first humbly asks that his prayer be admitted, afterward he begs to be heard in God’s righteousness.

But there is no doubt that the whole belongs to a tearful confession, especially since this psalm is shown to have been adapted to the humility of penitents. His truth and righteousness consist in this: that he not dispute with the one who is praying, and that he not bring to judgment the one who first condemns himself here.

For the Lord brings the proud to examination, those who think that their affairs are good; and only the one who has recourse to prayers is proved to escape judgment. [Col. 1010A] The divine majesty is not severe with an austere power, as though it wished to afflict those who here torment themselves through remembrance of their sins. For observe what follows.

#### Verse 2

“And do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight.”

It is clear with what intention he had asked for the Lord’s righteousness, since he now says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant.” For if righteousness had signified judgment, he could not have asked for what he feared.

Nor should it trouble us that it is said to the Judge, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant.” For he himself shows this form of speech when he says: “Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isaiah 5:3).

It follows: “For no living person will be justified in your sight.” The reason has been given why he did not wish to come to judgment with the Lord: so that it might be seen that not only the majesty of his power but also the very standard of righteousness was feared.

For it is written: “God has enclosed all things in disobedience, so that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11:32). But when it says, “every living person,” it signifies humanity in general, including the life of infants, who are liable to original sin unless they are washed by the water of regeneration.

Hence Job also says with complete truth: “No one is pure before you, not even an infant whose life is but one day upon the earth” (Job 15:14). And it was already said in the fiftieth psalm: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth” (Psalm 50:7).

Who possessed such righteousness that he never sinned at any time or at any age, since we are held liable both through the transmission of sin and because we add to it by daily lapses, so that we can never be free through ourselves, but only through divine grace?

Therefore let the Pelagian heresy cease its folly. It was condemned beforehand by so many sentences of divine Scripture, even before it began.

#### Verse 3

“For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to the earth.”

Although the title seems to speak of Absalom, “enemy” is properly placed here without a personal designation, so that we may understand this of the devil. He is humbled to the earth whose life is polluted by carnal actions—not by an approved humility, but by a vicious deviation.

The penitent rightly expresses this especially because of his affliction, having said in another psalm: “For I ate ashes like bread, and I mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10).

#### Verse 4

“He has placed me in dark places like the dead of the age; and my spirit was anguished within me; my heart was troubled within me. I remembered the days of old.”

“He has placed” means “he has assigned,” in the manner of raging enemies who despise a hated person as though they already judged him and considered him buried.

He was truly placed in dark places, since, after the heights of the kingdom, he suffered the injury of persecution. And he was treated like one dead in the age, in whom neither prophetic reverence, nor royal honor, nor even paternal affection was taken into consideration.

The dead of the age are those who are known to have failed in their sins. Therefore this man, endowed with so many virtues, rightly laments that he was despised in such a way that he was thought in no way to be avenged.

It follows: “And my spirit was anguished within me; my heart was troubled within me.” An anguished spirit reveals the nearness of danger; a troubled heart testifies that human wisdom has been thrown into confusion, so that he might place his hope more fully in the Lord when he had no confidence in his own strength.

He added: “I remembered the days of old.” His heart had rightly been troubled, because he remembered his enormous sins. These are the days of old, darkened by the antiquity of the old man. For just as newness reveals innocence of life, so antiquity bears witness to deeds of wickedness.

#### Verse 5

“And I meditated on all your works, and I meditated on the deeds of your hands.”

He returned to salutary recognition, so that, when he recalled the divine works, he would not retain the memory of his own troubles. He calls the Lord’s works those by which he established heaven and earth in wondrous order; those by which he did good to the patriarchs; those by which he led the Hebrew people across the sea.

He says that he frequently repeated these things, so that the sweetness of reading might exclude the bitterness of the world. We ought to accept this example as a supreme remedy, so that a similar medicine may also save us.

#### Verse 6

“I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is like dry land before you, without water.”

Although he prophesied the coming of the Lord Savior in countless passages, here too, by the extension of his hands, he depicted the form of the holy cross. For one who prays with outstretched hands imitates the cross of the Redeemer, which, although it was given as a punishment by the faithless Jews, was nevertheless granted to believers for salvation.

Thus Moses also, when he was fighting with the Amalekites, brought this about: he conquered when he stretched out his hands, and he lost when he lowered his arms (Exodus 17:11).

The comparison follows, in which he says that his soul desires God just as dry land is accustomed to receive abundant rains. Similar is the beginning of the forty-first psalm: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41:2).

Observe that he said, “to you,” not “to another,” lest you apply this desire to evil wills.

#### Verse 7

“Hear me quickly, O Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn your face from me, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit.”

After completing the opening portion, he comes to a most mournful account, asking that the rain of mercy come to his aid with the greatest speed, lest, rejected by the Lord, he be reduced to dust and, scattered by the wind of pride, be made alien to the land of promise.

And so that he might be heard more quickly, he says that his spirit has failed within him. This commonly happens through excessive tribulations to those weighed down by the burden of various sufferings, as the same penitent says in the thirty-seventh psalm: “My heart was troubled within me, and my strength abandoned me” (Psalm 37:11).

It follows: “Do not turn your face from me, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit.” God had previously turned his face away because of the insolence of sins, but now he asks that he look upon him, since he was bowing before him with contrite supplications.

For it is appropriate to his mercy that he look upon the humble, while he despises the hearts of the proud. By “the pit,” we should understand the lower place of hell, where the impious will be plunged into eternal punishment.

Those who rejected the divine power are therefore like them. By corrupting the image in which they were created, they have put on the form of the devil’s condemnation. It is well said, “those who descend,” because those who will deserve to enter there are plunged into the depths.

He therefore asks not to become like the proud, since he laments his sins with humble satisfaction.

#### Verse 8

“Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you.”

“Your mercy heard” means the Lord’s clemency, known throughout the whole world, by which he grants to those who supplicate and shows indulgence to the afflicted. Thus he himself may hear what was said in the Gospel: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Mark 2:5).

“Morning” designates the time of forgiveness. For it dawns upon the mind when it has reached it through a fortunate outcome. After the night of sins, it is rightly called morning, when guilt is released.

Or it refers to the resurrection that was to be heard, when the angel said to Mary: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter: For, as he said, he has risen from the dead” (ibid., 16:7).

The reason that ought to secure the request also follows: hope was placed in him, and he does not fittingly deceive those who trust in him. Observe also that he confirms his other petitions in what follows by a similar argument. This figure is called *aetiology*, that is, the giving of a reason.

[Col. 1012D]

#### Verse 9

“Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you, O Lord.”

When he asks God to make known to him the way of life, he shows that this way is unknown to human beings. The lamp of that one displays this path; the light of that one opens these paths—he who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9).

Likewise, it was already said to the penitent in the thirty-first psalm: “I will give you understanding and instruct you in this way in which you will walk” (Psalm 31:8).

Therefore the prophet rightly asks the Lord to show him the way of salvation, so that he may always know it and it may never depart from his heart. The solemn confession is also added: our petitions make us worthy to receive what we ask if we do not incline our soul toward the world under the burden of the flesh, but continually raise it to the Lord with spiritual assistance.

#### Verse 10

“Rescue me from my enemies, O Lord; I have fled for refuge to you.”

Although, according to the title given, the prophet seems to speak of bodily enemies, this must nevertheless be referred to the hostile demons, who continually surround the faithful so that they may take away their hope in the Divinity. As the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the powers of this darkness” (Ephesians 6:12).

For he says, “I have fled for refuge to you,” which is done only by those who obey his commands. Adam, after he had been disobedient, fled from the Lord. Here, therefore, the indication of a religious mind is declared in the opposite way: after the guilt of sin, he says that he did not flee from the Lord, but fled for refuge to the Lord.

#### Verse 11

“Teach me to do your will, for you are my God.”

He did not at all wish to err, since he desired to be the disciple of so great a teacher. For he says, “Teach me,” as one ignorant, as one inexperienced, as one presuming nothing upon his own ability.

The Apostle expresses this meaning when he says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know how he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2).

He added: “For you are my God.” This is a faithful petition and a fitting reason: to ask a benefit from the merciful Lord because he himself is the Lord of the one who supplicates.

#### Verse 12

“Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way.”  
[ed., “land”]

Let us consider what is meant by his saying, “Your good Spirit.” Through this name, God the Holy Spirit is designated. For it is written: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

The Father is also called good, as in the words: “Good Father” (John 17:11). The Son is likewise called good, as in the words: “I am the good shepherd” (ibid., 10:11).

Thus, through this sharing of names among the holy Trinity, its equality and power are continually declared.

The good Spirit will lead us into the right way when he subjects our body to his rules and makes that which had been distorted by the perversity of sins follow those instructions without deviation. But this cannot be accomplished by human power. For he makes those straight by restoring them who both is and deigned to create them.

Or “the right land” signifies that of the age to come, where the upright will walk and rejoice forever with the Lord in great exultation.

#### Verse 13

“For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness; you will lead my soul out of tribulation.”

Here the grace of the most merciful Divinity is revealed, which returns nothing according to our merits, but grants everything through the generosity of its indulgence. For the prophet does not say that he will be given life on account of his own deeds, but on account of the name of the Lord Christ, whose name truly has the power to save those who faithfully ask.

But although grace is commended, the force of righteousness is wonderfully mingled with it. For although he gives everything freely, it belongs to his righteousness to give life to those who supplicate, whom he sees cruelly attacked by unclean spirits.

It follows: “You will lead my soul out of tribulation.” Holy souls are led out of tribulation as from prisons when, forgiveness having been granted, they are commanded to leave this world.

Here the devout are afflicted and the righteous are tormented; but the end of this light is the end of their labors for the saints. Therefore the Apostle cries out: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23).

#### Verse 14

“And in your mercy you will scatter my enemies, and you will destroy all those who afflict my soul, for I am your servant.”

The fullness of that marvelous joy has been completed. Enemies are scattered in mercy when, through the zeal of contrition, they are drawn away from wicked thoughts. There is no doubt that this applies to those who escape the punishments they deserve through the remedy of supplication.

He added: “And you will destroy all those who afflict my soul, for I am your servant.” Here he says that at the time of judgment the devil and all the impious who die in their obstinacy will be destroyed through justice.

He says that they afflicted his soul because he himself remained in God’s service. Those who are proved to assume such dispositions must necessarily perish in judgment, since they persecute innocent men precisely because they recognize them to be servants of God.
