Behold, that rule of the penitent has been fulfilled: after afflictions and tormenting hardships, it has ended in exultation.

### Conclusion of the Psalm
The supplication of the petitioners has indeed come to an end, and that fortunate course of tears. But we must examine more carefully what the seventh prayer of these penitents signifies. For he began with Psalm 6, came to Psalm 31, then to Psalm 37, from there to Psalm 50, then to Psalm 101, next to Psalm 129, and finally to the present Psalm 142. Perhaps this is because, just as we sin during this week through which the course of this world’s age runs, so in the same number we might also be saved through the gift of remedial repentance. But this must be observed with the greatest care—as we have often warned—namely, that the psalms themselves begin with afflictions and end in joys, so that no one might despair of pardon, since he would recognize it as placed within these very prayers. They are the most holy intercessors, heavenly patrons who open the way of salvation for those entangled in the bonds of sins.

Yet although these intercessors individually admonish us to mourn our sins and lead us by the Lord’s promise toward the hope of joys, there also remains that most effective example of the Ninevites’ supplication, where every age groaned, where every animal experienced the fast; and the general affliction had such power that it was able to surpass the truth of the prophetic word. Those who had become fearful became secure, the sorrowful became joyful, and those who were judged condemned to death were restored to life. Therefore let us desire repentance as the salutary remedy of the human race, the consolation of those who weep, and the seed of future joys—repentance which grants the surest hope to each individual and, as a common gift, bestows heavenly grace upon those who supplicate.

# PSALM 143

## David against Goliath

[Col. 1015A]

Although the historical event of the present title took place in the prophet’s earliest days—that is, before his reign—nevertheless, because of the greatness of its mystery, it is called forward at appropriate points, so that you may understand that everything in the psalms has been mystically both spoken and placed there; we shall explain this more explicitly in the conclusion. Yet we should remember that this battle of David was set forth to signify the contest of the Lord Christ: just as David struck down Goliath in combat with a stone missile, so by the rock, who is the Lord Christ, the strength of the devil was to be conquered. Hence these likenesses have also been preserved in this psalm. For here the victory described is not merely that contained in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 17), [Col. 1015B] nor is thanksgiving offered only for that victory; rather, there are many things that correspond to the contest of the Lord Christ, which we shall explain suitably in their places. Therefore let us know that this is the fourth of those psalms in which, through David’s deeds, the future mysteries of the Lord are signified, so that, consecrated by the honor of the Gospel reckoning, they might become revered and wondrous throughout the whole world.

## Division of the psalm

After the slaying of Goliath—which we have said was completed through a mystical operation—the prophet, in the first part, gives thanks to the Lord for having been delivered from the danger of the completed battle. He entreats that the Lord’s coming may quickly be revealed, through which the devil was conquered and, as it were, the perfection of the spiritual battle symbolically represented by Goliath followed; for then the faithful were delivered from great danger. In the second part, the prophet promises that he will sing to the Lord in the New and Old Testaments, having been delivered from the worst enemies, who placed their blessedness in the prosperity of this age; and he defines as blessed only those whose God is the Lord.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1

**Blessed is the Lord, my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.**

The conqueror of a most savage enemy and vanquisher of monstrous vices, after his triumph had been accomplished, when human wickedness was at its most insolent, did not boast with any proud elevation born of self-confidence; rather, applying everything to the Lord’s powers, he celebrates his praises with devoted exultation. For he added the reason for the blessing: [Col. 1015D] **who teaches my hands for battle.**

He taught his hands for battle when he arranged everything so opportunely that the outcome of the desired victory was achieved. For he is not shown to have been trained through the practice of arms or any preliminary exercise; rather, he suddenly appeared excellent to his enemy, although previously he had seemed despised even in his father’s house.

It follows: **and my fingers for war.** Just as above we may understand the hands as an operation, so here we may perhaps understand the fingers as salutary counsels, which leap forth from our heart like rays, while through a certain subtlety they strive to secure necessary ends. This word has many meanings, but it is recognized as needing to be understood according to the variety of contexts. Thus Isaiah says: **Who weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers** (Isaiah 40:12), which some judge should be referred to the Holy Trinity. And in Exodus: **This is the finger of God** (Exodus 8:19), which the Fathers wished to understand as the Holy Spirit. Likewise there: **Moses received two tablets written with the finger of God** (ibid. 31:18), along with the other passages that you will find varied in this manner.

Or **my fingers for war** means the same as **my hands for battle**. This figure is called *epimone*, in Latin, “frequent repetition of a statement.” We too rightly use it when the ancient enemy is destroyed by the sign of the cross and shattered by the solidity of the rock.

### Verse 2

**My mercy and my refuge; my supporter and my deliverer; my protector, and in him I have hoped, subjecting peoples beneath me.**

These names undoubtedly arise from benefits bestowed, so that, since it would have been lengthy to trace multiple causes in a single psalm, they might be presented in a concise summary. This figure is called *hypozeuxis*, when different verbs are appropriately assigned to individual causes.

The Lord showed him mercy when, through the prophet Samuel, he chose him, the last among his brothers, for royal eminence. He was his refuge when, against so monstrous an enemy, he gave him the strategy by which the rock might overthrow one whom he could not engage with the weight of weapons. He was his supporter when he caused Saul to receive him as a son-in-law, so that he might be joined to his own lord, although previously he had been subject to him in the condition of a servant. He was his deliverer when he rescued him from the danger of the king’s anger. He was his protector when, while hiding in a cave, he received the right of vengeance against Saul the king. Thus each name appropriately expresses what had been granted to him through the Lord’s generosity.

And see what follows: **and in him I shall hope.** After so many benefits, the holy man knew that he must not cease from such hope; rather, the more he had received from him, the more he desired. He added: **subjecting peoples beneath me.** Either he says this concerning the future, because he was going to rule peoples; or rather he recalls that peoples were to be subjected to him—those whom he saw in the spirit as destined to be subjected to his offspring, that is, to Christ the Lord, as he says in the second psalm: **Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance** (Psalm 2:8).

### Verse 3

**Lord, what is man, that you have made yourself known to him, or the son of man, that you take account of him?**

Let us hear the king more masterfully controlling his own impulses, so that, after being protected by such great grace of the Lord following so many distinguished acts of virtue, he may confess not only that he himself is insignificant but also demonstrate that the human race is unworthy of divine benefits.

For he nullifies it when he says: **What is man?**—as dust carried away when the wind blows; as clay dissolved into fluid earth, which cannot possess stability. Therefore **What is man?** must be pronounced as both a question and an expression of contempt.

To this is added a laudatory answer: **that you have made yourself known to him.** For what is more remarkable than that the maker of heaven and earth should have deigned, through the reality of the assumed body, to come even to the knowledge of human beings, and that the immeasurable mystery of his divinity should have become known to those upright in faith? This figure is called *erotesis*, that is, a question posed in opposition to the contrary.

In the same way one must ask: **or the son of man?** The same answer should be given: **that you take account of him**—certainly among your sheep, among the number of the predestined, in that blessed Jerusalem where the righteous will always rejoice in contemplating the Lord.

### Verse 4

**Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow.**

He explains definitively what he said briefly above: **What is man?** That is, he has become like vanity, not been fashioned as such. For when Adam was created, he was truthful, simple, pure, and immortal; but after he sinned at the woman’s prompting, he became like vanity, since he became both changeable and mortal.

We call that “vain” which, falling from its own substance, vanishes into thin air, like smoke or a shadow. He supplied the comparison himself, [Col. 1017B] saying: **His days pass away like a shadow.** Properly, when a shadow is seen, it is indeed seen, but it has no stability of continuance; for when the body through which it is made departs, the shadow itself also vanishes and disappears. Such, then, is human life after Adam’s sin, unless it has been restored by the Lord’s favor through confession.

### Verse 5

**Lord, incline your heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they will smoke.**

He has burst into open prophecy concerning the Lord Christ, expanding somewhat more fully the statement he made briefly above, namely, **that you have made yourself known to him**. He became known to human beings by sight when he appeared in the humility of holy incarnation; for although he remained in the form of God and was coeternal and equal with God the Father, **he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant** (Philippians 2:7).

Hence it is rightly said: **Incline the heavens and descend**, because these things could not occur unless divine power had inclined itself. The inclination of the heavens occurred when the honor and power of the heavenly beings descended to set humanity free.

Here we must understand the mountains as proud people, swollen with diabolical wickedness, whom the Lord touched when he granted them the compunction of a devout conversion. They smoked when they wept over their sins with frequent sighs and continual groans. For thick smoke is vomited from the mouth when the structure of the mortal body stirs itself into life-giving lamentation.

### Verse 6

**Flash forth your flashes, and you will scatter them; send forth your arrows, and you will trouble them.**

Now the battle of Christ is being spoken of, and the manner in which the diabolical throng was overcome is related. Yet although he says that the battle was fought with flashes and arrows, it was the rock who accomplished this, the Lord Christ.

He came in opposition against the devil’s forehead, since he is always opposed to his commands. That exceedingly hard, shameless, and aggressive forehead was shattered—the forehead that before the Lord’s coming had resisted the truth undefeated. This is truly to be called Christ’s battle, because David’s battle was figurative, carrying the image of this fulfilled truth.

He says: **Flash forth your flashes, and you will scatter them.** This figure is called *a conjugatis*, “from related words.” He flashed forth his flashes when, through the preaching of the prophets, he poured the light of his truth into sinners living in darkness. **He scattered** means that he dispersed them, so that those who had previously been devoted to the worship of idols subsequently fled for refuge within the bounds of the Catholic Church.

It follows: **send forth your arrows, and you will trouble them.** The arrows signify the apostles, who, like feathered darts, pierced human hearts with the truth of their preaching, producing the healing of minds through sacred wounds. **Them** must be referred to the mountains mentioned in the preceding verse.

### Verse 7

**Send your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters, from the hand of foreign sons.**

Here he turns his words toward the Father. By “hand” he means the Lord Savior; for he is the Father’s hand, through whom all things were made and stand. He entreats him to come, so that the human race may be delivered [mss. G, A: “so that he may deliver it”].

**From on high** means from the height of power, where he reigns with the Father in equality of might and unity of substance.

The prophet therefore asks to be delivered from the multitude of waters—that is, from watery peoples, stirred up like a most savage storm. It is well known that waters signify peoples, as Isaiah says: **Therefore, behold, the Lord will bring upon you the water of the river, strong and abundant, the king of the Assyrians** (Isaiah 8:7).

But from which people he asks to be delivered he adds, saying: **from the hand of foreign sons**—that is, from the power of those who do not know how to spare the faithful, because they are born from a hostile father. Although this may appear historically to refer to the Philistines, it is better understood of those who are begotten by the devil as father; concerning them it is said in the Gospel: **You are from your father the devil** (John 8:44). These are the foreign sons, who are regarded as strangers by the Church, the mother of Catholics.

### Verse 8

**Whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.**

He continues to speak about those peoples from whom he asked to be delivered, so that the more cruel and wicked they are, the more quickly he may be heard.

Their mouth speaks vanity, because they presume to differ from the divine ordinances. For everything contrary to the truth is vain.

And although “right hand” is very often used in connection with good things, he describes the right hand of the wicked as so iniquitous that it seems rather to be a left hand. For when they consider worldly things to be excellent and desirable, they regard as prosperous whatever is contrary to virtue.

### Verse 9

**O God, I shall sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psaltery I shall sing to you.**

He comes to the second section, in which, after being delivered from spiritual wickedness and monstrous peoples, the prophet promises to give thanks to the Lord through a new song. Here there is the institution of the new human being and the fulfillment of the old law.

The new song is the one of which it is said in another psalm: **Sing to the Lord a new song** (Psalm 97:1). And to show its very newness, he added: **Sing to the Lord, all the earth.** It is rightly called new because, although it had been promised to the Jews that he would come, he was not received by them and passed over to the Gentiles.

It is also new that he deigns to nourish us with his body and blood. It is new that through the water of regeneration he absolves us, along with similar things that became manifest through the Lord’s coming under a new institution.

It follows: [Col. 1019A] **on a ten-stringed psaltery I shall sing to you.** The ten-stringed psaltery is the Decalogue, which was given to the Hebrew tribes. And to show that both Testaments have one author, he promised to sing to Christ the Lord in both.

### Verse 10

**Who gives salvation to kings, who rescues [mss. A, B, F: “redeemed”] David his servant from the evil sword.**

“Kings” signifies just and truthful people, who, as we have said, rule their bodies with the Lord’s assistance. The Lord gives salvation to these kings when he makes them free from bodily vices. Concerning them it is said in Wisdom: **He gives kingship to kings** (Wisdom 9:7).

**Who rescues David** looks back to the battle with Goliath, so that he who had been delivered bodily might also be spiritually victorious over monstrous vices.

**From the evil sword** signifies the power of the devil. For the Lord’s sword is also mentioned in Scripture, but there is no doubt that it is benevolent, as he says in the Gospel: **I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword** (Matthew 10:34). Therefore the devil’s sword is evil because it separates from the good; but the Lord’s sword is benevolent because it separates from evil.

### Verse 11

**Rescue me and deliver me from many waters, and from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.**

He already spoke this verse in the first part. He repeats it in order to make wicked people more detestable through the repetition itself.

### Verse 12

**Whose sons are like young plants, established in their youth.**

In the first verses, while discussing the evils of the wicked, he makes them detestable; now he also condemns the things that seem good about them, so that they may be disgraced everywhere, since even their glory is rejected as loathsome.

He calls their sons those who are begotten through the preaching of a perverse doctrine. They are compared with young plants because they have not flourished through any teaching handed down by the Fathers; rather, they have sprouted from newly contrived errors and, badly established, are fixed by the worst root. They are not grounded in the prophets, the apostles, or any divine authority; instead, through the voluntary perversity of novelty, they have been separated from the unity of the holy Church.

It should be observed that in Psalm 127 he gave the faithful this comparison, but there he says that the sons of the saints are established around the Lord’s table; here, because these people have no proper communion, the most sacred altar is removed from them.

### Verse 13

**Their daughters are adorned, decorated like the likeness of a temple.**

Let us consider how subtly and repeatedly he separates heretics from Catholics. In the first comparison he took the altar away from them; now, in the second, he introduces daughters whom he did not grant to the Catholic Church in the psalm just mentioned.

First, this sex is frequently given over to various and unstable thoughts, because it lacks the strength of constancy, being often led into different desires. Then he says that they are not naturally beautiful, but arranged by human will. Third, he does not say that their thoughts or teachings—which he had compared to women—possess the true Church, but only the likeness of a temple. A likeness does not possess truth; it bears the image of some existing reality.

### Verse 14

**Their storehouses are full, belching forth from one thing into another.**

The storehouses, which the common people call cellars, signify the hearts of heretics, where various kinds of things and foods are stored. To the extent that these are stuffed full, they emit that many different belchings of the worst exaltation [Leg. “exhalation”].

If you overcome them by authority, they turn to wicked interpretations. When they have been overcome there as well, with the Lord’s help, they turn to the tricks and calumnies of sophists—wandering and unstable, because they cannot possess the root of truth. Thus they are rightly compared with harsh odors, since they deceive simple hearts with foul speech.

### Verse 15

**Their sheep are fertile, abundant in their exits.**

We understand this more appropriately according to the literal sense, because the prophet’s purpose is to show that such people possess only perishable and temporal things. They seem to have fertile property, although they are taught to be barren in faith.

“Abundant” is derived from *unda*, “wave,” as though overflowing. He also did not say that the sheep they are seen to possess are in their entrances, but in their exits, because everything goes out from them, when they themselves too are shown to be destined to perish.

### Verse 16

**Their oxen are fat [ms. F and ed.: *crassae*, feminine form]. There is no breach in the wall, no passage, and no outcry in their streets.**

Here the abundance of their resources is displayed. Their oxen are not lean from constant labor, but extremely fat from luxurious idleness; yet they themselves are shown to be thin and fasting in truth.

It follows: **There is no breach in the wall.** The prosperity of the wicked is still being described, although it is shown to exist in transitory things. A wall is a structure made solely by arranging stones, which either encloses vineyards or protects cultivated gardens. Thus their prosperity is said to be so great that even those structures which appear to have been erected for some useful purpose do not collapse.

He adds: **no passage, and no outcry in their streets.** This too is intended to belong to the prosperity of this age: when heads of households wish to refresh themselves through rest, there is no movement through their houses and no turbulent shouting arises in the streets, lest their sleep be broken by untimely talk. Rather, there is silence when they wish to rest, and meeting when they order themselves to greet their friends. This figure is called *climax*, when an expression rises step by step toward what is higher.

### Verse 17

**They called the people blessed to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.**

This verse is shown to contain two statements, indeed, but different ones. One belongs to those who seem happy to themselves; the other to the blessed.

He says: **They called the people blessed to whom these things belong**—namely, the things stated above. Those who were not disciples of the truth judge in this way: they prefer the riches of the world and despise the heavenly kingdoms, thinking it blessedness either to see fertile sheep or to possess extremely fat oxen.

Listen, badly misled ones; listen, mad ones: the things you think magnificent are placed on the left. For it is written concerning wisdom: **In her right hand are years of life; in her left hand are riches and glory** (Proverbs 3:16).

Now let us hear what is said about the company of the faithful: **Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.** After that mockery directed against the wicked, he comes to the inner chambers of wisdom, that is, to the very voice of the most holy truth.

He defines truthfully who the blessed people are: namely, those **whose God is the Lord**. By saying **whose is the Lord**, he signifies holy men who conduct themselves in a commendable way. The Lord is not said to belong to those who in no way heed his teachings. These people have Christ as their Lord, and they are also specially called his servants.

He also added **their God**, that is, those to whom he deigns to be gracious. We often read the faithful saying: **My God and my Lord** (John 20:28). For if we are rightly called his servants, he is truly named our Lord. Thus, in a few words, the definition of the blessed people has been completed with the fullest truth.

## Conclusion of the psalm

This psalm has indeed been heard as a triumphal one; but let us see what this victory signifies, since it is clearly fulfilled as a likeness of the Church. Although through this holy man the Lord displayed many mysteries of his religion, this event is nevertheless evidently shown to refer to the battles of the Church, which it endures spiritually, so that the proud man might fall upon the pastoral rock while boasting in confidence in his own strength.

Therefore we should receive this model as pregnant with the whole of faith. Let Goliath refer to the devil together with his ministers; let David refer to the whole Christian people, who are known to have overcome their terrifying enemy through the solidity of the rock.

This too must be considered with the greatest care: after such a very long series of psalms, this psalm seems to have had placed upon it a kind of boundary of worldly affairs. For after it there is no account of the persecutions of the Church, the bitterness of the age, the sufferings of martyrs, the tribulation of penitents, the lamentation of the faithful, or the detestable exaltation of Antichrist. Rather, the remaining seven, fitted to a great mystery by divine praises, seem to be completely filled with heavenly joy. Now, with the clouds of sins driven away, let us approach the praises of the Lord with serene minds.

# PSALM 144

## A praise to David himself

[Col. 1021D]

We have shown, both through the interpretation of the name itself and through the descent of flesh from his ancestor, that David signifies Christ the Lord and was so called. But although this may seem established for us, I believe we must inquire more carefully why this title alone contains the phrase **A praise to David himself**, when his glory is proclaimed in all the psalms.

It is placed here as more distinct and clearer for this reason: after everything by which human ignorance had to be instructed has been completed, the command is now given to devote oneself solely to the praises of the Lord. These praises are wonderfully unfolded, with a certain distinction and according to their individual virtues, in the following seven psalms. Their particular character is revealed in their conclusions, as also happened in the preceding psalms.

Nor is it without significance that the praises of the Lord are completed here by the number seven: the confession of penitents is marked by this number, and the Holy Spirit himself is proclaimed through a sevenfold power. Perhaps it indicates that mystery when the Lord commanded Moses to place in his tabernacle seven lamps shining with perpetual light (Exodus 25:37).

But since nothing in the divine Scriptures is shown to be idle, I judge that the order of the Hebrew alphabet has also been preserved here, not without purpose, at the beginnings of the verses—the order which, in Psalm 24, we said must be understood as applying to two classes of people.

For when the alphabet is set out in its entirety, it designates the righteous, in whom no virtue is shown to be lacking through the Lord’s grace. But when it is marked with not all its characters, it seems to indicate those who are indeed in the Lord’s Church, but are not proved to be perfect in all good works. For concerning this mixture it is written: **Sheep and oxen, all of them, moreover also the beasts of the field** (Psalm 8:8).

Thus in this alphabet only one letter is withdrawn, so that it does not seem to indicate the highest members. The Lord also said in the Gospel to a man who conducted himself in a commendable manner: **One thing is lacking to you; but if you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and follow me** (Mark 10:21). But since not everyone does this, they are known to possess something less than perfection.

Therefore, giving thanks to the Lord, let us continually supplicate him, since here he has shown us such a mystery of his goodness, so that we too, who have been healed in the greatest part of our merits, may dare to ask for similar things and thus, through the gift of his indulgence, deserve to arrive at his eternal praises.

Or rather, as I later discovered, incomplete alphabets indicate the Church as it is conducted here, not yet purified by the separation of the wicked; whereas complete alphabets signify the future Jerusalem, where the assembly of the perfected saints will be completed through election. The psalms themselves, which are marked with Hebrew letters, are also known to indicate this, if you examine them carefully.

## Division of the psalm

The praise of Christ proposed by the blessed prophet proceeds according to the order of the Hebrew alphabet and is explained in three accounts.

The first is an infinite promise of his praise, containing three letters of the alphabet mentioned above. The second says that the praise of the Lord must be carried out in nine ways and contains four letters. The third explains somewhat more fully and clearly what it briefly proposed in the second concerning the praise of Christ, concluding by reminding us that the Lord must be praised by all flesh; this section retains fourteen letters.

Above all, however, we must attend to this: the psalm speaks in such a way as to indicate how the Lord may be praised, while nevertheless making those very sections appear inexplicable. For example, it says that he is to be praised in his works; but who can explain his works as they deserve? It speaks of his power; but who could successfully recount his power? There is therefore one truth: the Lord’s praise is spoken in sections in such a way that you should nevertheless not believe it can be sufficiently completed.

## Exposition of the psalm

### Verse 1

**ALEPH. I will exalt you, my God and King, and I will bless your name forever and ever.**

The blessed prophet, filled with the divine Spirit, burst into speech, not presuming upon human wisdom but illuminated by heavenly contemplation. For he says nothing local or particular, but something by which all the frailties of the world may be saved.

**I will exalt you** means, “I will make you known by proclaiming what you are.” For how could God be thought to become higher through some praise, when divine perfection cannot be increased?

**My King** is a profession of faith, since he said that he was ruled by the one whom he knew he served with a pure mind.

To bless his name **forever** is to supplicate him here through the grace of psalmody; whoever is worthy to do this will also deserve to praise him in that eternity. For it follows: **and forever and ever**, where there is already no end, but what is begun happily is preserved in perpetual joy.

### Verse 2

**BETH. Every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name forever and ever.**

Above he said: **I will exalt you, my God.** And lest human negligence perhaps think that this should be done only once, the necessary reminder was added: **every day**. Here indeed the days succeed one another in mutual alternation. But whoever blesses the Lord here through these individual days will praise him there with continual exultation on that one eternal day which is to come with the blessed.

As for the remaining words of this verse, since they are similar, let the exposition given above suffice.

### Verse 3

**GIMEL. Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness.**

A remarkable combination, a true proclamation: to praise the Lord in such a way that, however great he is, you do not suppose that his greatness can be explained. The understanding of the whole creation falls short, and yet that further reflection continually grows.

For just as he is confined by no place, so his praises cannot be brought to an end by any eloquence, however extensive. His power is inexplicable, his compassion incomprehensible, his wisdom ineffable; his true definition is that he has no end in the praises of the saints.

And observe that when it is said, **There is no end to his greatness**, you are never commanded to cease proclaiming him. We also give thanks silently when we conduct ourselves in a commendable manner.

Although he cannot be encompassed by any praises, he is nevertheless indicated by individual expressions when it is said: **Great indeed**, and again, **There is no end to his greatness**. This is the fifth mode of definition, called in Greek *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν* (*kata tēn lexin*), in Latin “word for word,” when we convey the thing we seek to know through individual terms.

### Verse 4

**DALETH. Generation and generation will praise your works, and they will proclaim your power.**

### Verse 5

**HE. They will speak of the magnificence of your majesty and your holiness, and they will recount your wonders.**

### Verse 6

**VAU. And they will speak of the power of your awesome deeds, and they will recount your greatness.**

### Verse 7

**ZAIN. They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will exalt your righteousness.**

He comes to the second account, where the forms of the Lord’s praise are marked out by a sacred reckoning. Although this repetition of generations may seem to indicate infinite time, since the Lord’s works are always established as worthy of praise, **generation and generation** should rather be applied to two peoples: one to the Hebrews, who were chosen through the sign of circumcision; the other to the people that came from the Gentiles.

These are the peoples who received the Lord’s benefits. They are rightly said to sing his praises, since they are proved to have received the gifts of his devotion.

But since these nine things—works, power, magnificence, holiness, wonders, the power of awesome deeds, greatness, memory, and righteousness—are here stated in the form of a proposition, so that praise of the Lord should subsequently be sung along the same lines, it is fitting that we speak of them more clearly where authority has judged that they should be explained more fully. We might perhaps call them by these names: the cataracts of divine eloquence, the fountains of heavenly words, the blessed breasts of praise, from which the human race is refreshed through devout confession and the angels receive blessedness without end.

I believe these arguments should be defined in summary as follows: an argument is a line of reasoning that makes mention of something incomprehensible and most exalted in a summary and concise manner, insofar as it can—not as much as the thing itself is. For nothing external, nothing merely plausible, and nothing ambiguous seems to be brought forth from here; rather, everything proceeds as truth speaks and as things are spoken concerning the truth.

I also believe that these nine places from which the praises of the Lord arise have been apprehended as a great mystery, so that the honor of the Trinity may be recognized in a number tripled within itself. This number is also contained in the sacred books which the holy Church of the Lord reads and venerates: in the Octateuch [mss. A, B, F: “Pentateuch”], in the Books of Kings, in the Prophets, in the Psalter, in Solomon, in the Hagiographa, in the Gospels, in the Epistles of the Apostles, and in the Acts of the Apostles together with the Apocalypse. Thus this number is fruitful through its recollection of heavenly things.

### Verse 8

**HETH. The Lord is merciful and compassionate.**

The third remaining account begins. In it he develops at greater length those places of argument that he briefly indicated in the second part. Let us now investigate them individually with attentive minds.

He began from the Lord’s works, so that he might be called compassionate. For the fact that he is called **merciful** is a power belonging to his nature; the fact that he is called **compassionate** is the cause of salvation for our weakness.

He is merciful when he creates, because he is not induced by any benefits to bestow them, but by the disposition of his clemency he brings all things into existence. He is also compassionate when, through his goodness, he rebuilds things that are falling, so that those who fall through guilt may be raised up through grace.

For who earns the gifts of the Lord Savior through his own actions, when it is plainly written: **All have sinned and lack the glory of God** (Romans 3:23)? **Merciful and compassionate** is a figure of *paronomasia*, which is also called *denominatio*.

**Patient and greatly merciful.**

He comes to the second place of argument, which is called “from power.” He did not praise God because he suspended the lands, restrained the seas, and painted the heavens with stars; rather, he called him patient because he tolerates human excesses, so that those who could be punished according to the law of justice are shown not to perish through the Lord’s patience, as it is written: **I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live** (Ezekiel 18:32).

### Verse 9. TETH

“Gracious is the Lord to all, and his mercies are over all his works.”

The third division of the argument is drawn from magnificence. For what is more magnificent than that he should be gracious to all, though only those who have tasted him with devoted hearts through his gift have experienced this? As the Apostle Peter says: “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Peter 2:3). He cannot be called sweet except by those who have spiritually taken in his goodness.

[Col. 1025B] What, again, is more magnificent than to bestow mercies upon all his works, which glory in having him as their author? Someone may say: “Why, then, are sinners to be condemned, when there is no doubt that they are his creatures?” But observe that he says that mercies are to be bestowed upon the works of the Lord. What he grants in us by a hidden judgment, with grace taking precedence, crowns the person himself; what is constructed through the devil’s contrivance, he condemns. The force of the words resolves the question with complete clarity. For the works of the Lord are always chosen, whereas what is ours or the devil’s is without doubt condemned.

### Verse 10. JOD

“Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord, and let your saints bless you.”

The fourth division is described as arising from holiness. This is the holiness that he mentioned above, so that his saints ought to give thanks to him—that is, the good angels, dominions, powers, and principalities, or righteous human beings, and whatever is known to be blessed.

But since not all creatures are exalted to intellectual dignity—for example, animals, stones, trees, earth, and things of that kind—how can every creature praise him? It gives thanks plainly in this respect: by existing, it causes its author to be glorified, since he perfected all things through an admirable ordering. Thus either the creatures themselves praise him, or the works of the Lord are proclaimed exceedingly good through rational substances.

### Verse 11. CAPH

“They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom, and they shall proclaim your power.”

The fifth division proceeds from marvelous works. For how marvelous is God, who made heaven and earth and filled them with an astonishing variety of diverse goods! In small things there is sufficient measure; in intermediate things, balanced proportion; in great things, an abundant profusion of gifts.

And everything must necessarily be marvelous, since he is acknowledged to be the omnipotent author of all things.

### Verse 12. LAMED

“To make your power known to the sons of men, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom.”

The sixth division, which arises from virtues, now begins. This is what he said in the second part: “The power of your awe-inspiring deeds.” Through the proclamation of the saints [ed.: “through holy preachers”], the power of the Lord and the glory of his kingdom have been made known, lest, remaining unknown, they should perhaps be sought less earnestly.

His power was also made known when Peter and John caused the lame man from his mother’s womb to walk, saying: “Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this, as though by our power or piety we had made this man walk?” (Acts 3:12). A little later they say: “That he has been made whole in the name of Jesus Christ.” The power of the Lord was also made known when the apostles performed various miracles after invoking his name.

### Verse 13. MEM

“Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, O Lord, and your dominion is in every generation and lineage.”

He comes to the seventh division, which is drawn from greatness. For if it is great to rule for a time, how much more magnificent is it to have no limit to one’s dominion? First he praised the Lord for perpetuity; afterward, for the effect of his dominion.

There are human kingdoms, but they are not eternal; some are powerful in comparison with others, but they do not rule for long. Therefore this perpetuity is recalled, [Col. 1026B] so that you would not suppose it to be such a kingdom as you perhaps know to exist in the world.

### Verse 14. SAMECH

“The Lord is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works. The Lord raises up all who fall, and lifts up all who are crushed.”

489 The eighth division is opened, which is called “from abundance.” This is the passage: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness,” which he mentioned above in the aforementioned second part.

He is therefore called faithful because he fulfilled the promises of his coming—not in a few words, but in all his words. This truly belongs only to the one who said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). Just as he is recognized as truthful in his promises, so also he is holy in all his activity.

This too undoubtedly belongs to the Lord’s abundance: that those who are falling are raised, the guilty are released, and the crushed are lifted up. For the memory of his sweetness is then retained, when the power of such deeds is seen and poured forth in praises of him who deigned to rescue the sinner from the devil’s power.

And observe that here, too, two things are ascribed to the Lord. He raises those who are falling, who have not yet completely fallen; he lifts up those who are crushed, who are known already to have suffered a collapse. Rightly so: we are defended by him as guardian lest we fall; but so that, once prostrate, we may be able to rise, we are likewise lifted up by his power. For there is no doubt that these and similar things can happen through the abundance of his sweetness.

### Verse 15. AIN

“The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them [mss. A, B: ‘their’] food in [Col. 1026D] due season.”

### Verse 16. PHE

“You open your hand, and you fill every living creature with blessing.”

Behold, the ninth division is entered, which is called “from justice.” This is explained more fully in these two verses and in the one that follows, so that those who hear that the Lord is merciful may also fear him as the just judge.

For it belongs to his justice that those who do not cease to hope in him should receive from him the gifts of satiety. But this food should be understood as the sustenance appropriate to each thing. Some seek to be governed bodily, others spiritually; yet for all of them there is one food: the generosity dispensed by the Creator.

And lest you believe that whatever is requested must always be given, he added, “in due season.” Many ask, but their requests are profitably deferred. [Col. 1027A] Therefore let us continually pray for this one thing: that the Lord in his mercy grant us what he knows to be beneficial. For we do not know what we ought to pray for, as the Apostle says (Romans 8:26).

We also recognize that everything is established within his power, since, when he opens his hand, every living creature is filled with blessing. Yet it is better to understand “living creature” here as referring to the rational creature, which truly is capable of being blessed.

### Verse 17. SADE

“The Lord is just in all his ways, and holy in all his works.”

That aspect of justice has been made manifest when we also recognize that the very name is mentioned. The ways of the Lord are his dispositions and wills; if we truly understand them, we perceive that they are always just.

For when he scourges us, [Col. 1027B] he acts equitably, because he repays what our sins deserve. Therefore, while asking him to spare us, let us first confess his justice, and thus await from him the gift of mercy.

“Holy” also signifies merciful, patient, and the giver of every good, since whatever is brought about by him is filled with the praise of virtue. “Ways” refer to dispositions; “activity” to the result. But this distinction is made on account of our weakness. Otherwise, with him, to will is to do, to dispose is to command.

### Verse 18. COPH

“The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.”

### Verse 19. RES

“He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers and save them.”

These statements, too, are shown to belong to the justice of the Lord. He is called near when he is merciful, and distant when he is angry. His presence, however, is always and everywhere, as it is said in the preceding psalm: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm 138:8), and so forth.

But since those who wish their vain desires to be fulfilled also call upon him, “in truth” was added, excluding every superfluity. For only that person calls upon him truly who asks him for what he himself has established should rather be requested. Indeed, he hears the one to whom things proven beneficial are granted.

For what sense is there in demanding an excess of prayers for something whose receipt would make the importunate petitioner regret it? This happened to the children of Israel when they asked that a king be given to them according to the custom of the nations (1 Samuel 8:8).

### Verse 20. SIN

“The Lord preserves all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners.”

The part concerning justice is now brought to a brief conclusion, since both belong to the equity of the Lord: that he should preserve those who love him and destroy sinners because of their iniquity.

When he says that all sinners are to be destroyed, he means those who persist in their obstinacy. For those who turn to the Lord with a pure heart cease to be sinners, as it is said in another psalm: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Psalm 31:1).

### Verse 21. TAU

“My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord; and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.”

Having set forth all the divisions that he judged capable of generating and producing the praise of the Lord, he now repeats its briefest conclusion, so that what cannot be explained by any books or by human powers may be shown to have been brought to completion with marvelous brevity.

He promises that his mouth—that is, the secret of his heart—will utter the praise of the Lord, by which the prophet knew that he himself was gladly heard. He also urges all human flesh to bless the Lord the Savior. This statement is clearly made by the figure of synecdoche, that is, taking the part for the whole.

By “flesh” he means human beings, just as he means human beings when he mentions souls alone, as in the passage from Exodus: “All the souls that entered Egypt were seventy-five souls” (Exodus 1:5). For it is this flesh that can bless the Lord with worthy praise.

If a diligent investigator should find, either in the psalms that follow or in those that preceded, any portion beyond what we have discussed that ought to be applied to the praises of the Lord, let him not doubt that it belongs to one of the modes mentioned above, at least as we understand it. Nor should he accuse us of failing to grasp completely what we acknowledge to be immeasurable.

Aristotle, with his keen intelligence, seems to me to have imitated this method by collecting the divisions of secular arguments with marvelous subtlety, so that, just as all discourse is enclosed by letters, so all human thought, expressed in a judgment [mss. A, B, F: “approved judgment”], might be enclosed by that arrangement of arguments.

From this, dialecticians compressed their disputations into concise collections; from this, orators flowed like certain rivers; from this, poets are surrounded by flowers of ornament; from this, satirists, historians, comedians, and tragedians were enriched, so that almost nothing seems to have been left out of human speech that has not been separated from this arrangement.

He gave this subject the name *Topics*. The *Topics*, however, are the seats of arguments, from which, as though from certain elements, the intention of the speaker is constructed for the purpose of establishing belief. No religious scruple condemns reading and discussing this, since whatever is not proved contrary to the sacred writings may be investigated harmlessly.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

We have heard, briefly gathered together in one psalm, things that are widely dispersed throughout the holy Scriptures. For where is there no mention of his work, or his power, or his magnificence, or his holiness, or his marvelous deeds, or the power of his awe-inspiring acts, or his greatness, or his abundance, or his justice? It may rightly be called a heavenly storehouse, in which such a repository of celestial things is shown to exist.

For all these things are not usually placed together at once; but, as we think, the praise of the Lord cannot be found without some one of them. Since he has carefully expressed here the pattern of the Lord’s praise, he has evidently indicated that the following psalms also undoubtedly belong to his praises, since such a rule and arrangement has been set forth beforehand.

Do not think it accidental that the praises of the Lord are contained in seven psalms. This may be what is said in Psalm 118: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118:164). Perhaps they are the seven lampstands mentioned in the Apocalypse, which shine before the Lord (Revelation 1:12, 11). They are also the seven churches to which the Lord’s book was commanded to be sent. Finally, they are the sevenfold Spirit who granted these praises through heavenly generosity (Isaiah 11:2).

Therefore let us rejoice that the Lord has given us abundantly what we may offer to his ears, provided only that it be presented with a pure conscience. For who would doubt that what he himself commands to be sacrificed to him is graciously received?

O immeasurable mercy of the Creator! He both commands that he be praised and, lest we offend through our words, shows how he is to be proclaimed [ed.: “how it is to be commanded”]. This is not because he needed such things, but because he foresaw that they would be useful to us. He has said everything and instructed us in everything, so that we might not wish to go astray. Finally, he assumed human nature itself, lest fragile humanity perish. But let us consider whether, if we receive such immense gifts, we ought to sin against such great grace.

# PSALM 145

## Alleluia

[Col. 1029B] Behold, once again heavenly authority resounds in our ears and strikes upon the doors of the heart with “Alleluia,” lest we be occupied with empty and futile thoughts, since it is not fitting for a soldier of Christ to have idle time.

The tongue, too, has its fruits. Indeed, an exceedingly rich harvest is gathered from it if it is moved by a pure mind to the praises of the Lord. It is a spiritual member when it serves its author; it also commends the soul itself when it speaks the truth.

Therefore let us fill the air with the sweetest sounds. For this saving music not only delights the hearing of mortals but also pleases the angelic understanding.

## Division of the Psalm

Desiring the praises of the Lord to be sung with the whole heart, the prophet says at the outset that one must place no confidence in human beings, lest anything be asked lukewarmly if another were believed capable of providing it.

Second, he declares that all hope must be placed in the omnipotent Lord. Since this is the Lord, he is most beautifully defined by his works, so that the Gentiles, convicted by such frequent reasoning, may abandon their errors with faithful devotion.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Praise the Lord, my soul.”

So that the will might not remain idle in earthly desires and the mind’s attention might be occupied with foolish concerns, as commonly happens, the prophet gives himself salutary counsel, by which he knew that the whole community should be counseled [mss. A, B, F: “the Gentiles”]: let the soul praise the Lord, not merely the sound of resounding lips.

Often we utter words after reflecting in such a way that, carried away by foreign thoughts, we do not realize that we have said what we are speaking. The soul is a power kindled by spiritual vigor, ranging through diverse regions and investigating with searching reason the causes of heavenly or earthly creatures, at one moment mingling with higher things, at another with lower.

But how these matters stand, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it, seems to have been explained more fully by us in the book *On the Soul*, which is the thirteenth book contained in the work *Variae*. Therefore the Psalmist urges his soul to praise the Lord, so that, having expelled superfluous thoughts, it may devote all its strength solely to this task.

### Verse 2

“I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am” [mss. A, B, F: “as long as I shall have been”].

Let us consider what this repetition means. First he commands his soul to praise the Lord; now, assenting, he promises that he will praise him in a twofold manner.

To praise in life means to confess the Lord in that eternity which is more truly called life, since it is not crushed by the pressure of any anxiety. Therefore he said, “I will praise,” in order to indicate the future time, when this lot is shared by angels and righteous human beings.

Of the present life, however, it is said, “I will sing psalms,” which, as we have often said, clearly refers to good works. Thus it should be understood that there he is to be praised perpetually, and here continually.

The expression “as long as I am” also signifies this age, since the time would come when he could no longer be here.

### Verse 3

“Do not place your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.”

The heavenly physician first cleanses human hearts of destructive concerns, so that he may pour in saving remedies appropriately. He says that confidence must be placed neither in demons nor in human beings, who cannot give salvation, since they are known not to possess it by their own right.

Here we should understand “princes” as spiritual wickednesses, concerning which the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against princes and powers of this darkness” (Ephesians 6:12).

“Sons of men” unquestionably signifies mortals, who cannot give salvation because they succumb to the death owed to them. For there is only one Son of Man—that is, the son of the holy Virgin—who grants salvation, since he is established as the Savior of the human race.

### Verse 4

“His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts will perish.”

491 He gives the reason why he said that one must not place confidence in human beings. Here we should understand “spirit” as “soul,” as it is said in the Gospel: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

When the soul has gone out from the confinement of its body, the flesh, as it decays, returns to the earth from which it took its beginning. He therefore added “his” in order to signify that it was created from there, as it is written in Genesis: “God made man from the clay of the earth” (Genesis 2:7).

At the time of death, therefore, human thoughts perish—thoughts that continually extend themselves into various pursuits: at one moment striving after possessions, at another accumulating wealth, at another seeking honors with the greatest eagerness. But all these things disappear when the desires directed toward them are frustrated, as we read that the rich man in the Gospel was rebuked: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; whose will the things be that you have prepared?” (Luke 12:20).

### Verse 5

“Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God.”

Having expelled the harmful thoughts by which the human race is infected as though by the gravest diseases, the prophet comes to a second entrance, in which he offers human minds a saving drink to consume.

For he did not merely prohibit useless presumption; he also gave warning about what ought to be desired. He says that the person who hopes in the Lord is blessed through this very act of thought.

We have often said that Jacob the patriarch is mentioned here because, after his struggle with the angel, he was the first to be called Israel, [Col. 1031A] that is, “a man seeing God.” This name is appropriately applied to all the elect.

“Helper” is used so that the understanding of the name might stir us toward good efforts. He is a helper to those who, with his gift, strive through good intentions to ascend the degrees of virtue.

It follows: “whose hope is in the Lord his God.” This continuation belongs to the preceding statement, since blessed is the one whose hope is known to be in the Lord his God.

By saying “hope,” he signifies endurance of present things and desire for future things. Whatever a Christian may suffer in this world, he is refreshed by the thought of eternal blessedness.

But since the worshipers of demons could also have hope in their own god, he designates the Lord Christ through each of the various clauses, by one consistent mode of definition, until the end of the psalm. In him the hope of the faithful must reside.

### Verse 6

“He who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them; who keeps truth forever, who executes judgment for those suffering wrong, who gives food to the hungry. The Lord raises up the crushed.”

We said that Psalm 144 contained the divisions from which the praise of the Lord would be formed; now we think that the same divisions are to be recalled in especially suitable places.

He says: “He who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them.” There is no doubt that praise proceeds from his works. For what could be more glorious or more magnificent than to have made heaven and earth and everything that is in them?

Moreover, the statement “he executes judgment for those suffering wrong; he gives food to the hungry” clearly belongs to his justice, since he grants his equity to human beings, as he wills, through the gift of his judgment.

This is the second type of definition, which is called *ennoematice* in Greek and *notio* in Latin. For he does not say substantially what God is, but what he does or has done. His acts, at least in part and insofar as he himself permits, can be grasped by our understanding; but our inquiry cannot prevail over his substance.

He says first: “He who made heaven and earth.” He is the one in whom Christians ought to place their hope. Although he enclosed everything under the names “heaven” and “earth,” he nevertheless added, “and all that is in them,” lest you suppose that anyone else is the creator of even the smallest things.

It follows: “who keeps truth forever.” He is evidently the Lord Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). It is necessary that the one who is acknowledged as heavenly truth should speak truth in this age.

Of human beings who are under sin, however, it is said: “Every man is a liar” (Psalm 115:11).

He added: “who executes judgment for those suffering wrong.” Christ is the true judge and eternal governor, who vindicates those afflicted for his name and shows mercy to the innocent. These are the ones who suffer wrong—that is, injustice—when, while proclaiming the truth, they are afflicted with severe punishments.

He continued: “He gives food to the hungry.” He gives food to the hungry because he is the Creator of the world. But we ought to seek spiritual food, lest, like the Jews, we take pleasure only in the satisfaction of the belly.

For the prophet Amos says: “Behold, I am bringing a famine upon the earth—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8:11).

He added: “The Lord raises up the crushed.” There is no doubt about this either, because he raises the crushed: the devil casts them down, but the Lord lifts them up. Therefore hope must be placed in him, who is accustomed not to crush but to raise up.

### Verse 7

“The Lord releases the chained; the Lord gives sight to the blind. The Lord loves the righteous; the Lord protects the stranger.”

In this verse and the following one, the division “the memory of the abundance of his sweetness” must be applied. For what is sweeter than for deeds of his mercy to be remembered, so that it may be said: “The Lord releases the chained; the Lord gives sight to the blind; the Lord loves the righteous; the Lord protects the stranger; he will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the way of sinners”?

The Lord Christ certainly releases the chained, as it is said in the Gospel: “Was it not necessary that this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, should be released from her infirmity?” (Luke 13:16).

But this may be understood not only of the oppression of an unclean spirit, but also of all the vices by which our mind is bound as though by certain ropes. For just as the devil binds by fastening sins together, so Christ releases by forgiving transgressions.

It follows: “The Lord gives sight to the blind.” All vicious people are blind because they are entangled in the darkness of sins. But only he gives sight to these people who in the Gospel anointed the eyes with clay (John 9:6) and led the darkened man to the joy of perfect health.

Of him it is also said: “He gives light to every man coming into this world” (John 1:9).

He added: “The Lord loves the righteous.” For whose role is it to love the righteous except that of the one who can establish them in eternal blessedness? For just as the devil desires the impious, so the Lord loves the righteous.

He also added: “The Lord protects the stranger,” that is, the one who has come from the city of Babylon, the devil’s city, to Jerusalem, the city of the Lord Savior. He protects this person, provided that he remains in the dwelling-place of the elect, as it is said in another psalm: “I am a sojourner with you on earth, and a pilgrim like all my fathers” (Psalm 38:13).

### Verse 8

“He will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the way of sinners.”

The orphan and the widow are those who look toward the Lord with a pure mind, deprived of human assistance. Christ receives them so that they may be defended by his protection.

[Col. 1032D] But when he has received them in accordance with his mercy, he will destroy the devil, who is the way of sinners—that is, he will make him an alien from the boundary of his kingdom. This is what will happen to every impious person in that holy judgment.

Thus, through these ten proclamatory statements, it has been abundantly shown in whom the hope of the faithful ought to be placed.

And lest you perhaps think it contradictory that in the preceding psalm we said that nine divisions of the Lord’s praise had been arranged, whereas now we have mentioned that a tenfold enumeration has been completed in his proclamations, you should understand that the seats of arguments are one thing and the rules of definitions another.

There, each item was set out according to a general distinction; here, under a single form of definition, what the Lord is is indicated through various statements. And, as commonly happens, two or more definitions have been gathered from a single seat of arguments [the printed text reads *siut*, evidently corrupt or uncertain].

### Verse 9

“The Lord will reign forever, your God, O Zion, from age to age.”

This is shown to be understood as arising from the magnificence of the Lord. For what is more magnificent than that the Lord should reign over Zion from age to age, whose kingdom will have no end?

“Will reign” appears to indicate the future time, when our hearts already stand in him with the firmest stability. At present Christ is not said to reign most fully in his members, because their hearts are sometimes occupied by empty thoughts.

But when this mortal body has put on immortality and has left behind these harmful thoughts together with the loss of this world, then Christ will reign perfectly in the saints, when, as it is written, “God will be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

Whose Lord this is is made clear by the words: “your God, O Zion.” It has often been said that Zion signifies the Catholic Church, on account of the contemplation that it offers to the Christian people. He will reign both with it and in it—the one who is blessed forever and ever.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Through the gift of contemplation, the prophet, established as though near the end of the age, where the world’s perversity is now recognized as especially liable to condemnation, taught the whole human race to occupy itself with the praises of the Lord, lest it seek fleeting desires whose imminent end is certain.

But when that time is said to be coming for us, our own time is undoubtedly being announced. We are at the end of the world when, not after a long interval, we abandon it through the reception of death. Let fleeting desires pass away from us; let worldly enticements depart. Let us desire instead what we know to be eternal.

# PSALM 146

## Alleluia

The following text explains the words of its title, so that it has no need of foreign phrasing, since the declaration of its own speech makes it clear. Read the beginning of the psalm, and you have explained the title.

For “Alleluia” means “Praise the Lord.” The two correspond with such harmonious speech that you might think the title is the beginning of the psalm, while you may reasonably regard the beginning of the psalm as its title.

Therefore let us enter this psalm confidently and joyfully, since we recognize its saving meaning plainly even at the very doorway.

## Division of the Psalm

First, the prophet urges the devout people to praise the Lord, who raises up the humble and cuts down the necks of the proud.

Second, he declares cheerfully that one must sing psalms to the Lord, who grants beneficial gifts to those who entreat him, since those who presume upon their own strength cannot please him.

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let praise be pleasant to our God.”

Every human work demands that a reward be repaid to it, so that we may console ourselves with hope of the promised gift for what we carry out laboriously.

In the praises of the Lord, however, the act itself possesses its reward, since the very thing that is now an exercise will then be the recompense. For since it is good to proclaim the Lord, each person is thereby known to receive the promised gifts.

He receives them plainly when, in that angelic fellowship, the singular gift of the saints is to undertake the Lord’s perpetual proclamation. Let us therefore praise him with whatever devotion we can, and here meditate upon those blessed gifts.

For what is happier than to practice now what you hope to be able to perform in future blessedness?

The psalm, as it has been handed down by our predecessors, is a musical instrument, like the lyre, the *pandurium*, and other instruments that respond to our voices in the sweetest modulation. We have often said that this refers to our most approved actions.

Therefore he commands the praise of the Lord and the psaltery to come together in one harmony: just as we proclaim the praises of the Divinity with our tongue, so let us praise him through the activity of good works.

It follows: “Let praise be pleasant to our God.” Praise is pleasing to the Divinity when our actions do not differ from the character of holy words.

For what sense is there in a psalm speaking of chastity while its singer does not withdraw from obscenity? Or in its proclaiming humility while its reciter swells with the blasts of pride?

Therefore what is known to struggle against itself in mutual opposition cannot be rightly received by the Lord. Praise is pleasing to the Lord when voice and life come together in one fellowship.

### Verse 2

“The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersed of Israel.”

Through this verse and the two others that follow, the Lord is rightly praised for his marvelous and glorious deeds. For when it says, “The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersed of Israel; he heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds; he numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names,” he is shown to be marvelous through his works.

In the first verse, however, it is demonstrated that the Lord does not love division, since he is known to gather what has been dispersed. For how could he tolerate different actions and a different song in us, when he gathers the peoples of the whole world into holy unity?

Thus the Lord builds the city of Jerusalem from living stones when he gathers the dispersed of Israel, who are known to dwell throughout the whole world, as it is said in the Gospel: “And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and he will gather [ed.: ‘they will gather’] his elect from the four corners of the earth” (Matthew 24:31).

### Verse 3

“He heals the brokenhearted; he binds up their wounds.”

A marvelous kind of healing is proclaimed: if we wish to be restored, we must crush ourselves most vigorously. But this crushing belongs to restoration and leads to solidity; and, better than every good, it brings in the physician who grants eternal health.

It follows: “He binds up their wounds.” This is a metaphor drawn from those skilled in healing, who, when they wish to make broken and crushed bones solid, bind them with strips of cloth, so that the limbs, returning to their proper place and recovering their former strength, may grow together.

[Col. 1035A] Thus the heavenly physician binds and consolidates the hearts of penitents, crushed by severe affliction, as though applying a bandage of his mercy, and leads them to the firmest hope of healing, as it is also said in Psalm 50: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

The tax collector who repeatedly struck his breast (Luke 18:13) is also shown to have brought about this very contrition within himself, which he did not cease to inflict upon his guilty breast.

### Verse 4

“He numbers the multitude of the stars, and calls them all by their names.”

Although this too may appear literally to display the power of the Lord, saying that the innumerable stars are numerable to the Divinity and that they are called by their proper names, since everything is comprehensible to him, to whom the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the hairs of human beings are known to be counted, nevertheless, when he says “by his name,” he censures the astrologers who call them by foreign names, such as Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, and similar names.

Yet it is more fitting that we should understand this in a deeper sense. For above he had said that the brokenhearted are to be saved; after the medicine of forgiveness, we ought to understand them as stars. They shine like stars in the night of this age, those who have deserved to be gathered among the number of the saints.

Although the Church may seem to contain many here, they are numbered by the Lord—those who will rejoice in participation in his kingdom.

That we can understand the stars as holy men is attested by the passage in Genesis that says: “I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven” (Genesis 22:17). Solomon also says: “The righteous will shine like the stars of heaven” (Wisdom 3:7).

We know that the names of the saints can be called by the Lord, since we read that they have been written in heaven, as he says in the Gospel: “Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you; but rejoice and exult because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

### Verse 5

“Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number!” In this and the following verse, praise worthy of the Lord’s greatness is sung. For by saying, “Great is the Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number,” he declares his greatness without qualification: “The Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners to the ground.” For when earlier the prophet had ranged through various aspects of praise, filled with wonder he exclaims: “Great is our Lord!”—that is, the one whose deeds cannot be counted and whose praise cannot be adequately grasped: gathering Israel’s dispersed, healing the brokenhearted, numbering the multitude of the blessed, and calling them all by name. Who could comprehend how great is the praise gathered from all things, when each individual thing possesses a wondrous greatness? By saying “our,” he excludes the worship of utterly senseless paganism. His power is great because he is unique, omnipotent, and the governor and creator of all things. [Col. 1035D]

It follows: “And of his wisdom there is no number.” Here we should understand “number” as an end or limit, since calculation numbers and defines everything that exists. But how could God’s wisdom have a number, when it is known to be the author of calculation? For if it could be numbered, it would already seem to fall under number. And if even number itself in its entirety cannot be known by us, how, by what means, could divine wisdom be comprehended? The Creator is incomparably superior to his creatures, and therefore it is truly said: “Of his wisdom there is no number.” For concerning what he created, the Wise Man says: “God made all things by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. XI, 21). [Col. 1036A]

### Verse 6

“The Lord receives the meek, but humbles sinners to the ground.” The meek are those whom he earlier called broken by tribulation and made patient through the habit of affliction. Observe how beautifully the contrast has been fashioned: the meek are received into heaven, while the proud are cast down to earth, so that through reciprocal change, where the humble has been lifted up, the proud may fall; and where Satan, exalted, fell, the faithful human being may be raised and ascend. [Col. 1036B]

### Verse 7

“Begin to the Lord with confession; sing psalms to our God on the lyre.” He comes to a second mode, where he urges those who linger, drives on the hesitant, and rebukes the negligent. “Begin” is said to those who are still known to be silent. “To the Lord with confession” should be understood as “sing.” Yet this confession urges praise and encourages virtuous action. The lyre signifies moral virtues sounding forth together in harmonious action; it becomes a true lyre when they join together in allied fellowship. For just as an instrument cannot be called a complete lyre if one of its strings is removed, so a holy man cannot be considered perfect if any virtue in him is diminished. [Col. 1036C]

### Verse 8

“He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth. He produces hay on the mountains and grass for the service of human beings.” In this and the following verse, the Lord’s works are again recalled. He says:

“He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth. He produces hay on the mountains and grass for the service of human beings. He gives their food to the beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon him.”

For what is more powerful than that the Creator should aid his creatures according to a fitting measure? [p. 494] Divine Scripture frequently embraces this kind of definition, so that through what the Lord does his virtue and power may be displayed. This is now accomplished through this verse and the next. For whereas earlier he had said, “Begin to the Lord [Col. 1036D] with confession,” he now clearly shows to which Lord confession must be made.

Although these words may rightly be understood literally, it is better if we recognize them as spoken allegorically. Here we appropriately understand heaven as holy prophecy. Divine providence covers it with an obscurity like that of clouds, so that it stimulates our minds to seek, since what is reached through wearied desire is received with greater gratitude. It follows that we should ask what these clouds bring forth: namely, that they appear to provide an abundance of rain, that is, well-watered fountains of divine preaching. But for what earth is this rain prepared? Certainly, for the thirsty. For he effectively receives the word of the Lord who has eagerly offered himself for hearing through a heavenly gift.

Nor is it without significance that he says “prepares,” since unless he himself has prepared it, no one can reach it by his own merits. [Col. 1037A]

It follows: “He produces hay on the mountains and grass for the service of human beings.” This too must be understood spiritually. The mountains signify holy men, in whom the Lord produces hay and grass, by which the simpler people in the Catholic Church may be fed like simple beasts. Hay belongs to stronger preaching, grass to gentler admonitions. Hay was present when the Apostle said: “I would that all men were even as I myself” (I Cor. VII, 7). Grass: “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (ibid., 9). And again: “I desire the younger widows to marry” (I Tim. V, 14). And once more: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III, 2). These lesser commandments are rightly compared with grass. For when he says “for the service of human beings,” he signifies that they have been appointed for human use. Thus it is plainly understood that the things said above are to be referred to human beings. [Col. 1037B]

### Verse 9

“He gives their food to the beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon him.” The beasts signify ecclesiastical flocks, which are fed with suitable nourishment: some with milk, others with solid food, according to what the steward considers appropriate—the one who alone knows what benefits it is useful to provide.

Ravens are irreligious men, who are inseparably clothed in the blackness of sins and do not shine forth with any brightness of conversion. The young of ravens, as the natural philosophers maintain, feed on heavenly dew and, because of their age, do not yet know their fathers’ food—that is, the stench of corpses. Therefore he gives food to the sons of pagans and the perverse, because they do not follow the life of their fathers through the gift of innocence.

And observe what he adds: “that call upon him.” For only those call upon him who do not overthrow the rules of Scripture through any heretical perversity. Unless you refer this to human beings, how can “calling upon the Lord” be fittingly applied to the young of ravens? [Col. 1037C]

### Verse 10

“He will not take pleasure in the strength of the horse, nor does he take pleasure in the encampments of a man.” After recounting what the Lord has done, he now says what can in every way displease him.

The horse is generally used to signify pride. The animal itself, presuming upon its neck, continually strains against the reins and hastens toward rapid running in foaming exertion. The proud and excessively presumptuous man is compared with it. Divinity cannot be pleased with such a man, because it chooses the meek and devoted, as another psalm also says: “The horse is deceptive for salvation” (Ps. XXXII, 17). And elsewhere: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. XIX, 8). [Col. 1037D]
