The encampments of men are the meeting places of foolish pagans, which continually extend themselves toward the worst forms of worship. Consider the force of the words: he says “the encampments of men,” not divine encampments—that is, unlawful presumptions that bold men establish for themselves by their own will. “Man” is also used in a bad sense, as in: “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V, 7).

### Verse 11

“The Lord is pleased with those who fear him, and with those who hope in his mercy.” Earlier he said who could displease him; now he says what kind of people please him.

The Lord therefore loves those who fear him, but not with a degraded fear. Many fear; but because they despair of his mercy, they are by no means loved—like Judas, who, after recognizing his guilt and fearing it, judged that he should not plead for mercy but rather despair. The fear that is approved and accepted by God is joined with the greatest love and devout confidence. Let each person therefore fear lest he sin, and love in order to plead for mercy. For if he is not going to ask, he acts like one who does not fear. [Col. 1038A]

### Conclusion of the Psalm

There is no doubt that this psalm too pertains to the end of the age, when Israel’s dispersed people are gathered into one people, so that there may be “one flock and one shepherd” (John XI, 16). O blessed time, when those living stones, more precious than every pearl, are gathered into the heavenly structure and eternal blessedness! [Col. 1038B] Then each of the saints will find his labor most sweet: mourning will bring them consolation, persecution eternal rest, and poverty the pious gift of heavenly kingdoms. Whatever they endured here with hardship, there they will rejoice that they endured such things.

Grant us here, Lord, patience amid evils, so that there you may make our joy everlasting.

# Psalm 147

## Alleluia

We return indeed to the customary “Alleluia,” but we never grow weary of repeating it: a taste that is always desired, a sound that does not produce weariness, an understanding received without labor. Such is the honor of this word that, although it is preserved in the Hebrew language, it is nevertheless found translated into no other language. The Greek, Latin, Chaldean, Syrian, Persian, Arab, and every nation of the earth retains it; and whatever is devoted to Divinity venerates the dignity of this name with devout dedication. It sounds strange to no one and absurd to no one; rather, all celebrate their joys expressed through the sweetness of this name. [Col. 1038C]

Let us therefore sing it with a pure mind and devote all our strength to it, so that just as the sweetest sound is presented to bodily ears, it may also be uttered with the sincerity of the heart.

## Division of the Psalm

[p. 495] In the first section the prophet speaks briefly to Jerusalem—that is, to the heavenly city—so that, now restored to security in its citizens, it may praise the Lord with continual exultation. In the second, through broader mystical allusions, he enumerates how much the merciful and devout Lord has granted to his people. [Col. 1038D]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion.” From the first verse to the end, this psalm recalls that the Lord’s power must be proclaimed, as you recognize from the psalm’s own account.

Jerusalem, as has often been said, is interpreted as “vision of peace.” This properly belongs to that city which will have no fellowship with vices and scandals. But this vision of peace will be contemplation of the Lord the Savior, which no one will attain except one who has been freed from every disturbance of mind. Thus these two names rightly belong to that future city: the gift of the reward it has attained, and the exalted title of the shepherd. [Col. 1039A]

### Verse 2

“For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you.” The cause of future blessedness is openly indicated. Although this matter was promised through the mouths of many prophets, it is nevertheless declared most clearly in the present account.

When he says that the bars of the gates have been strengthened, he shows that the doors of the blessed city have been closed. For *sera* (“bar”) is derived from *sero* (“late”), the time when it is inserted into the doorway so that permission to enter is denied. This will occur when the bridegroom has entered, as the Gospel says concerning the virgins: “Those who were ready entered with him into the marriage feast, and the door was closed” (Matt. XXV, 10).

It was closed not as a punishment of confinement, but for everlasting blessedness, because no holy person will ever leave from there, nor will anyone new enter afterward. [Col. 1039B] O secure blessedness of the righteous, received under such a law that it can never be lost! Rightly so, because that city has within it the God who can be seen. No one therefore desires to depart from it, since nothing like him can be seen apart from him.

It follows: “He has blessed your children within you.” The blessing of children is indeed great, but it is much more pleasing when it is bestowed within the mother’s womb. What could be more delightful for a mother than always to see her children flourishing? What could be more delightful for children than continually to behold the grace of their mother? It is therefore said, “within you,” because those who are consecrated by an eternal gift will never be able to leave that Jerusalem.

### Verse 3

“He has established peace within your borders, and satisfies you with the richness of grain” [manuscripts A, B, F: “he satisfies you”]. How great and inestimable is that city, described in so few words of praise! For what could be said to be superior to it, whose borders are enclosed by the gift of peace? From this it can plainly be inferred that it enjoys eternal tranquility, since it is shown to dwell within. [Col. 1039C]

By contrast, whatever exists outside it is hell; and just as blessed Jerusalem possesses peace, so unhappy Babylon will undoubtedly endure the conflict of sorrows. Through defining one side, he clearly disclosed the character of the other cause. This figure is called *emphasis*, which signifies even what is not said.

But how this peace comes about is subsequently explained, when the faithful are nourished by contemplation of Christ the Lord. By “the richness of grain” he means the very Deity who can be seen, by which the understanding of the righteous is so refreshed that it is known to surpass every satiety. [Col. 1039D] He is the true bread who descended from heaven (John VI, 41). For if here he refreshes us through participation in his body, how will he satisfy there those whom he will fill with the full light of his divinity?

Truly, it will be secure peace and inviolate tranquility, when no need wages war against us, no weariness exhausts anyone, cold does not sadden, hunger does not oppress, and the other things that here continually inflict battle upon our weakness are absent. There the fellowship of body and soul will be such that they will not disagree with each other through any adversity, but both will consent to one another in glorious will.

### Verse 4

“He sends forth his word to the earth; his speech runs swiftly.” Having described the city of the future age, the prophet comes to a second section, in which he foretells the gifts to be bestowed upon us here, so that the truth of the future reality may already be recognized through present benefits. [Col. 1040A]

The Lord’s utterance is the Word of the Father, which descended to earth when he assumed the humility of a pious incarnation. By saying “he sends forth,” he indicates the present time through the spirit of prophecy, although he may seem to be speaking of the future. But when he says “he sends forth,” he does not reveal him as lesser; rather, he shows the harmony of holy unity.

The speech of this omnipotent Word ran so swiftly that the recognition of the holy Trinity filled the world with astonishing speed, converting the worship of idols through the manifestation of the truth itself.

### Verse 5

“He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes.” [Col. 1040B]

### Verse 6

“He sends his ice like morsels of bread; who can stand before his cold?” [manuscripts A, B: “who will endure?”]

After prophesying the coming of Christ the Lord, he now explains in sequence what his benefits accomplish through figurative allusions. This figure is called *parabole*, because things dissimilar in kind are compared.

Thus all these things—snow, mist, ice, and cold—are evils of this age. They constrict mortal hearts with the frost of sins and make them remain in stony stupor unless they are dissolved by the Lord’s warmth. But let us see how a fitting remedy is provided for each thing.

He says: “He gives snow like wool.” “Gives” signifies “makes,” just as we commonly say, “He gave us an indication,” when we declare that something has been shown and taught. Therefore he makes snow like wool, so that what was previously frozen by the severity of cold may be brought to woolen softness. This happens when he leads hearts of mortals, chilled by sins, to the warmth of repentance. [Col. 1040C]

Snow is a human being when he departs from the Lord; wool, when he has been worthy to come to the Lord’s healing.

Mist signifies every sin, which is always carried out in obscure darkness. But it is scattered like ashes by the Lord’s favor, when its accumulation is dispersed through the grace of confession.

Ice is a liquid substance hardened like glass through many winters and brought to the hardness of stone. Obstinate sinners are rightly compared with it: bound by the chill of unbelief, they grow colder day by day.

The Lord also sends these people forth like morsels of bread when he makes converts proclaim his mighty deeds, so that the hungry people may feed on heavenly bread. [Col. 1040D] [p. 496] We call “morsels” the parts of some body. They signify the various gifts of teaching that the Lord has often deigned to display through sinners in his saints.

It follows: “Who can stand before his cold?” “Before the presence of his cold” is said—not that the cold comes from him, but that he perhaps permits it to occur. Such is the statement: “God hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. X, 20). And elsewhere: “I am the Lord, making good and creating evil” (Isa. XLV, 7).

Therefore no one can stand before that cold, which he does not remove, because it can condemn people through sluggish stupidity. The danger is magnified so that greater gratitude may be owed for the most glorious deliverance.

### Verse 7

“He sends forth his word and will melt them; his spirit blew, and the waters flowed.” When the Word comes, no darkness, no cold, and not even hardness itself should despair, because those who are summoned are released from their evils and brought into the most health-giving fluid. [Col. 1041A]

Thus what had been held fast by the frost of sins flows away through the Lord’s mercy into healing, as it is also said elsewhere: “There is no one who can hide from his heat” (Ps. XVIII, 7). For through his spirit, like a south wind, the hardness of dangerous cold vanishes, while heaps of crimes are dissolved, bowed necks sink into the grace of humility, and, brought into most health-giving liquids, pour forth streams of spiritual benefit.

This happened with Saul the persecutor; it happens today with many, so that those who are now dry through obstinate will may afterward become well-watered through the flow of preaching. [Col. 1041B]

### Verse 8

“He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel.” Through Jacob and Israel the Church is signified. These two names belonged to one person, just as one people was made from two. He is rightly called both Israel and Jacob by a particular designation. For even now whoever is faithful is an Israelite, and the one who pleased the Lord through pure devotion was formerly Jacob. To them, then, he is known to have declared his word, his statutes, and his judgments.

### Verse 9

“He has not done so for every nation, and he has not manifested his judgments to them.” This verse appears to be understood as follows. Although the Christian religion has embraced all nations, he nevertheless spoke face to face with none of them, divided the sea for none of them, rained manna upon none of them, filled the tabernacles with a cloud for none of them, or consumed their burnt offerings with heavenly fire—along with the other things that were visibly granted to that people through a heavenly gift. [Col. 1041C]

For us, the things that appeared bodily before their eyes take place spiritually.

## Alleluia

It is customary to be moved by the fact that we find “Alleluia” placed at the end of certain psalms. Perhaps it signifies that they belong wholly to the Lord’s praises and are not mixed with any reference to another cause; but just as they begin from the beginning, so they end in the Lord’s praise. Yet we cannot assert this, because in such matters it is dangerous to define anything.

It is better for a person to confess that matters exceed him than to be condemned for some presumption. Therefore, whatever we have thought should be offered concerning this matter or other novelties, with the Lord’s assistance, let it remain to the judgment of the reader to follow what he chooses. [Col. 1041D]

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Thus far, in the conclusions of the four psalms that preceded this one and concerned the praises of the Lord, it has been said with what intention they were composed, so that they may appear to have been placed entirely as a preparation for what follows.

The very order of the psalms is known to indicate a marvelous arrangement of subjects. It was fitting that first there should be a discussion of the commandments of divine proclamation; afterward, of the perversity of the world that must be fled; third, of the gathering of the Church; and fourth, in the psalm now completed, that Jerusalem, gathered together and established in eternal rest after being liberated from the various dangers of this world, should be commanded to celebrate the Lord’s praises. [Col. 1042A]

Therefore he adds threefold rejoicing to that most holy choir, gathered from the regions of the world, so that the grace of the Trinity might shine everywhere in the most holy work.

# Psalm 148

## Alleluia

This portion of the prayer is compressed into few syllables, but when considered it continually expands. It pours forth the sweetest discoveries when the mind’s attention examines it. When it is spoken by the reader, it is a proclamation of praise; when it is answered by the people, it is a hymn. Thus one voice produces a mystery so diverse, although nothing in it appears to have been changed. [Col. 1042B]

This psalm must be treated subtly, because through the mention of a few creatures the prophet urges all creatures to sing the Lord’s praises: rational and intellectual creatures by themselves, and those lacking understanding or sensation through those creatures that praise the Lord together with wise reflection upon his works.

## Division of the Psalm

Considering that all the works of the Lord are contained in heavenly and earthly things, the prophet first urges the heavenly things to praise; in the second part, through allegorical allusions, he admonishes earthly things to celebrate the Lord with devout mind. He adds one plausible reason for both: it is fitting that the creature should praise its Creator. [Col. 1042C]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.” Since all heavenly things continually pour forth hymns to the Lord, we must investigate why the prophet first admonishes them to do what they are continually shown to be doing.

This is ordinary human usage: when we see people working in a field, we say, “Work”; when they are reading, “Read”; when they are building, “Build.” Thus such an exhortation seems to be spoken more to increase zeal than to begin something.

But what are these things from the heavens that are summoned to praise? Certainly those that, by his generosity, are capable of contemplating the Lord with the purest understanding and, inflamed with perpetual love, [p. 497] celebrate their Creator with sweet rejoicing. For just as they are immortal, so their praises are not enclosed by any end.

“In the heights” signifies the more excellent substances, which human weakness rightly calls exalted because it is weighed down by the frailty of the flesh. For it is fitting that each thing should praise its Maker according to the measure of the gift it has received. [Col. 1042D]

### Verse 2

“Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers.” What is called *angelus* in Greek is rendered *nuntius* (“messenger”) in Latin. But when a heavenly power is sent to accomplish something, it assumes this name from its office. “Angel” is derived from the name of an office, not of a nature.

It follows: “Praise him, all his powers.” This is a general designation, for it includes all those who are exalted by the dignity of the heavenly army. Perhaps angels are placed before the powers here because the one through whom the Lord’s commands are fulfilled should be considered more honorable.

Most beautifully, he began the Lord’s praises with the angels, who are considered eminent among creatures. [Col. 1043A]

### Verse 3

“Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light.” The sun, moon, and stars, as some say, although they may be governed by some spirit of their own, are nevertheless visibly accessible to bodily eyes. It may reasonably be inferred that they are inferior to the unseen powers, although they appear to adorn the appearance of the heavens with beautiful light.

For those things to which our sight reaches, although luminous and subtle, are nevertheless plainly bodies; and it is necessary that they yield to those that subsist through invisible power. [Col. 1043B]

Therefore the prophet commanded the sun, moon, and stars to praise the Lord, whether through their own rational faculty or through other perceptible and describable substances, because they were worthy to exist through the Creator’s gift. The contemplation of so many lights can arouse immense wonder, since they cause mortal eyes to see and themselves persist in such splendid brightness.

“Light” has been generally added to these things so that it might urge toward the Lord’s praises all the other things that possess light within themselves but have not been enumerated individually.

### Verse 4

“Praise him, heavens of heavens, and the waters that are above the heavens.” Although we read in Genesis that one heaven was made, the Apostle Paul also called them by the plural number. He reports that he was caught up to the third heaven (II Cor. XII, 2), where he learned things that it was not permitted for a human being to utter. Here too they are named in the plural, perhaps in harmony with that account. [Col. 1043C]

We say that there is one palace, although it is surrounded by many chambers and many spaces. In the same way, perhaps we call the parts of heaven “heavens,” while its structure and interior remain one.

Genesis also reports that there are waters above the heavens, for it says: “And he divided the waters that were under the firmament from those that were above the firmament” (Gen. I, 7). Both things indicate a mystery of immense praise: that the subtlety of the heavens should remain firm, and that the waters placed above them, although heavier, should not flow down unless commanded.

Although the substance of heaven should be considered pure, luminous, excellent, and worthy of such great inhabitants, I have not discovered that it is an animate being. [Col. 1043D] It is rash to say, on the basis of human opinion, what the authority of the heavenly writings does not transmit.

As for the waters that are above the heavens, I think there is no doubt that they are those that pour down, as Genesis testifies: “The floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights” (Gen. VII, 11–12), and so forth.

There is no great need to investigate this, since all things are admonished to praise the Lord either by themselves or through rational substances.

### Verse 5

“Let them praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” In this verse he commands that the Lord be praised for his works. For what is more worthy than that the creature—that is, the created order—should praise its own author? [Col. 1044A]

And to refute the opinions of philosophers by the very voice of truth, he says: “For he spoke, and they were made.” By saying “he,” he signifies the Lord the Savior. For he is the Word made flesh, by whose command all things were created, as the Gospel truth says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 3).

The Apostle also says: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him” (Col. I, 15–16).

Therefore let the most false opinion of the philosophers fall silent—those who think that the world could have existed of itself as coeternal with Divinity. [Col. 1044B]

He “spoke,” then, when he said: “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. I, 3). “He commanded” signifies “he established and confirmed,” as another psalm also indicates: “He commanded his covenant forever” (Ps. CX, 9).

“Made” and “created” have a certain distinction if we inquire more closely. We too can make, although we cannot create. But because he had used a general word, he added what was proper to Divinity, so that you might understand “made” in such a way that you would recognize that they were created.

### Verse 6

“He established them forever and unto the age of the age; he set forth a commandment, and it shall not pass away.” Here too the passage declares the Lord’s power and strength, saying: “He established them forever and unto the age of the age; he set forth a commandment, and it shall not pass away,” so that there may be no doubt that the Lord is omnipotent, since what he establishes is not overturned by any change. [Col. 1044C]

A conclusion has been made concerning the heavenly things. But since we read concerning the future age, “There will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. LXV, 17), how can it be said of this heaven, “He established them forever”?

There is no doubt that all things are established by God. Even a human being, although he dies, is established by Divinity when he rises again. So heaven and earth remain established by God when they are renewed. For, as the Fathers say, after their harshness or corruptible quality has been removed, their very nature remains, improved, when it has been commanded to exist in eternity. The Apostle likewise speaks of the transformation of our body: “When this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 53). [Col. 1044D]

“Commandment” means law or condition, so that all things may be known to be under his power. What the omnipotent God establishes, and what the truth promises, cannot pass away.

### Verse 7

“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses.” Having passed through the heavenly substances, the prophet comes to the second part, where he admonishes earthly things, whether animate or inanimate, to express the Lord’s praises through their most wise natures.

The dragon is a very corporeal mass, [p. 498] furrowed with scales and extended in the form of a serpent. Kindled by natural heat, it inhabits watery caves as a remedy for regulating its condition. It does not crawl upon the ground, but when it wishes to move, it is said to fly. A torn [manuscripts A, B: “snatched”] elephant is its food; by its marvelous strength it binds the limbs of enormous beasts in its coils and takes away their vital breath as though they were flies. [Col. 1045A]

The considered depth of the abysses—that is, of the sea’s waves—should stir all rational beings to the Lord’s praises. And observe the order of the wording: he placed one substance among perceptible things and another among insentient things, so that the Lord should be praised through the power of all creatures.

But since, on the authority of the Fathers, we have said that this psalm is the hymn of the blessed, sung after the transformation of this age, here we should understand the dragons and abysses as fierce and powerful persons who, having been converted here, are honored in that homeland with the Lord’s praises.

### Verse 8

“Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, which perform his word.” Fire, hail, snow, and ice signify allegorically—as has been said—human beings who in this age have come from turbulent and exceedingly evil conditions to the most peaceful pursuits of devotion. [Col. 1045B]

Finally, observe what follows: “storm winds, which perform his word.” Who are they that perform his word, if not those who have merited coming from tempestuous and wicked ways to the grace of confessing him?

### Verse 9

“Mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars.”

### Verse 10

“Beasts and all cattle, serpents and winged birds.” Mountains signify human beings exalted by excessively proud power; hills, those who conduct themselves with moderate equality; fruitful trees, those who, converted from the hardness of sins, have brought forth the sweetest fruits of conduct. [Col. 1045C]

Cedars plainly signify the proud and exalted; beasts, the cruel and untamed; all cattle, the common and innumerable multitude. By serpents he means the poisonous and crafty. Winged birds signify philosophers, who are accustomed to traverse the natures of things with the speed of their thoughts.

From all these kinds of human beings Christ prepares chosen ones, who may be joined to the assemblies of angels in that resurrection.

### Verse 11

“Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth.”

### Verse 12

“Young men and virgins, elders with the younger.” We have often said that the kings of the earth are holy men who rule their bodies, commanding their own flesh and not allowing it to fulfill the enticements of its will. [Col. 1045D]

“All peoples” signifies the crowds who come together to the Lord with a numerous and united will. We may appropriately understand “princes” as the exalted powers of the world. And so that you might understand them as noble and powerful, observe what follows: “and all judges of the earth.” We know that it often happens that people suddenly abandon the power of the world and choose to undertake the Lord’s service.

He calls “young men” those who, burning with the heat of age, turn toward the moderation of self-control. “Elders with the younger” signifies mixed ages, because the Lord is powerful enough to summon those whom he chooses from every sex and every age. For so that you may refer all these things to human beings, observe what follows.

### Verse 13

“Let them praise the name of the Lord, for his name alone is exalted; his praise is above heaven and earth.” This passage too praises him for his magnificence and uniqueness. For when it says, “His name alone is exalted; his praise is above heaven and earth,” it undoubtedly declares his magnificence throughout the whole world. [Col. 1046A]

The preceding words were suspended until this statement so that the faithful people might praise the Lord, established in that homeland—those who are now known to have been freed from the bonds of sins.

The most just reason why the Lord should be proclaimed follows: namely, because his name alone is exalted. It is exalted because, as the Apostle says, “every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 10).

He adds: “His praise is above heaven and earth.” Here “praise” signifies that praise which, after the renewal of this age, is rendered to him by all rational creatures. He said “above heaven and earth” because neither heavenly nor earthly things can be found equal to those proclamations of praise. [Col. 1046B]

### Verse 14

“And he will exalt the horn of his people; a hymn for all his saints, for the children of Israel, the people drawing near to him.”

Here the hymn is poured forth without qualification from the holiness of the Lord. For when he says, “He will exalt the horn of his people; a hymn for all his saints, for the children of Israel, the people drawing near to him,” there is no doubt that the holiness of the Lord and the gifts he bestows are being praised: he will deign to glorify his saints through participation in his gift.

As we have often already said, “horn” is used for power. Here that power has been humbled because of the afflictions and sufferings endured by the faithful people; but there it will be exalted, where complete glory is bestowed openly: first, [Col. 1046C] because they deserve the right hand; then, because they will judge with the Lord; third, because they will pass into eternal peace and joy. Thus they are rightly said to be exalted, since by his wondrous compassion they attain even to the contemplation of the Lord himself. This happens—as the Apostle says—“when he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule, and every authority, and power” (1 Cor. 15:24). For “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.”

It continues: “a hymn for all his saints.” This expression is a promise and the consummate perfection of complete blessedness. For what the saints will deserve is the hymn of the Lord, which they sing when they are also crowned with an eternal gift. Once this has been received, they will lack nothing further; but there will be found there whatever cannot now be grasped: heavenly manna, unfailing fullness, an incomprehensible gift—to do this continually and always to burn with eagerness for it.

[Col. 1046D]

The hymn, then, is the song of the saints, established in praise of the Lord, to which soul and body consent in perfect purity. Although here we now seem eagerly to desire to utter it, we cannot perform it without failing. He adds: “for the children of Israel, the people drawing near to him.” He shows to whom that hymn is to be granted: namely, to the children of Israel, who are shown to possess this name not only by descent but also by faith. We truly call those Israelites who, by believing rightly, have deserved to behold the Lord with the light of the heart.

They are Israelites who are shown to draw near to Christ the Lord through obedience to his commandments; for those who do not carry out his orders are far from him. No one, therefore, is near him except one who is also his member. [Col. 1047A] For a member does not know itself to be separated from its head.

### 499

Concerning the final “Alleluia,” which we discussed in the preceding psalm, it must also be understood here, since repeating what is nearby produces weariness in the listener more than understanding.

## Conclusion of the Psalm

Let us contemplate this psalm and the beauty and power with which it shines forth. For heavenly voices are recounted here—voices that, because of our bodily weakness, cannot yet be heard. The heavenly creatures proclaim praise to the Lord; earthly beings proclaim it; and the work proceeds through melodic songs, so that the Lord may be praised by the harmonious rejoicing of his creatures.

At the very beginnings of things he established that remarkable discipline of astronomy, which the teachers of this age, investigating it with the greatest precision, thought should be defined as follows: “Astronomy is the discipline that contemplates the courses of the heavenly stars and all their figures, and investigates by a method of inquiry the positions of the stars in relation to one another and to the earth.” By its solemn operation, they say, the year is completed through a fourfold division of the seasons. From it, they maintain, come the rains; from it earthly things are produced; from it the cold arrives; from it, they say, comes the moderation of the air. Whatever is shown to be necessary for the earth, they assert, can be supplied through the service of these things by the Lord’s command.

[Col. 1047B] Our predecessors did not say that this science should be wholly rejected, so long as it is recognized as a discipline and investigates the movements of the stars according to their natural regularity. But when unstable error has insinuated itself into astrology, and someone supposes that the lives of mortals can be inferred from the course of the stars, then such people are detestable—then rather they are blind—when they imagine that they can foresee what the Creator has usefully decided to conceal from us.

They also say that the planets move against the pole by very certain courses. They say, too, that the structure of heaven, which sustains itself through ceaseless rotating motion, possesses a certain delight of harmony, which is sweet and unending. But let us refer the services of natural things to the authority of their author, who commands his creatures to obey him by the very power through which he brought them into existence.

[Col. 1047C]

# PSALM 149

## Alleluia

We are urged in every way to keep this name in use, since we know that it has been suitably applied in both the New and the Old Testament. In the Old Testament it is prefixed to Psalm 104, where the miracles of Egypt and the benefits of the Red Sea are described; here it is placed before a new song, where the complete perfection of the whole religion is set forth. Thus it is placed everywhere, since it is always established as something that must be said.

O name worthy of veneration with great devotion, which the angels sing and which the vows of the faithful on earth frequently take upon their lips.

[Col. 1047D]

## Division of the Psalm

In the preceding psalms the prophet commended the praises of the Lord through countless exhortations. Now, in the first section, he says in various ways that a new song must be sung to Christ the Lord, who by his compassion built the universal Jerusalem from the whole world. In the second, describing the joys and virtues of the saints, he says that the vengeance of sinners is the glory of the righteous.

[Col. 1048A]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the assembly of the saints.”

In this verse and the three that follow, the greatness of the Lord is praised on the basis of his works. By saying, “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is in the assembly of the saints,” and so forth, he says that the Lord must be proclaimed on account of his works.

For the prophet, though established in this world only in the body, was united in understanding and faith with the angelic multitude in that homeland where he exhorts the blessed people to sing a new song. The new song is the mystery of the holy incarnation: the wondrous birth, saving teaching, passion—the teacher of endurance—the resurrection, the surest proof of our hope, and his sitting at the right hand of the Father, signifying unique power and might.

[Col. 1048B] And lest you believe that this praise could be celebrated anywhere or by just anyone, he continues: “his praise is in the assembly of the saints.” Whether you understand this as the catholic Church, which truly belongs to the saints, or as that heavenly Jerusalem, it too is without doubt the assembly of the saints. For “church” is interpreted as “assembly,” and it is clear that this may refer to both.

### Verse 2

“Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the children of Zion [mss. A, B, F: daughters] exult over their king.”

Israel and Zion are different names, but they signify one virtue of the saints. For Israel is interpreted as “a man who sees God”; Zion is called “contemplation.” It is clear that both names belong to the blessed people, who are urged to rejoice and exult in their King, Christ the Lord, when they see him as almighty and as the giver of eternal reward—the one whom here they believed would come in his majesty.

[Col. 1048C] Who could measure the joy of seeing the Lord of all things, who was believed here to have died for the salvation of everyone? We rightly do not know the measure of this joy, yet we are confident that it exceeds every good, since such great truth makes this promise.

### Verse 3

“Let them praise his name in the chorus; let them sing psalms to him with the tambourine and the psaltery.”

In the preceding verse he says that one must rejoice in the Lord Christ; now he says that the Lord’s name must be praised in the chorus. This is the chorus that suffers no dispersion, no weariness, and no scandal, but, gathered through the excellence of its merits, remains forever in the dearest unity.

Another psalm explains what kind and how great this chorus is: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112:3). It is the chorus gathered from the multitude of the nations from the beginning of the world, and it cannot be gathered in its entirety except in that homeland.

[Col. 1048D] He continues: “let them sing psalms to him with the tambourine and the psaltery.” Here we understand the tambourine and the psaltery as exemplary actions that are referred to divine gifts and that do not seem to exist there in that homeland; nevertheless, they will exist when there is rejoicing in their exultation. For what causes sorrow here brings joy there; what crushes us here raises us up there, as it is written: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10).

Thus all these things—whether the tambourine or the psaltery—sing to the Lord there, because here they are known to have been practiced or endured for his name. [Col. 1049A]

### Verse 4

“For the Lord is well pleased with his people, and he will exalt the meek unto salvation.”

It is indeed written that the Creator was pleased with all his works in the establishment of creation; yet, in accordance with changes in the condition of things, God is also said to repent and to rejoice, as in the statement: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. 6:6). Elsewhere: “I will rejoice over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7).

We apply these changes to the Godhead through figurative expressions arising from our weakness. He says: “For the Lord is well pleased with his people”—that is, when he has made them rejoice in perfect sweetness, when he has made them equal to the angels, when he has truly made them his own, whom he will judge worthy of being crowned with so great a gift. [Col. 1049B] Then there will be “well-pleasing,” when, as the Apostle says, “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

By “the meek” he means the patient, who endured various forms of wickedness in this world but were content with the most holy devotion for the sake of God’s kingdom. “Unto salvation” means unto eternal life, which the just Lord will restore to them in that judgment.

### Verse 5

“The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice in their dwellings.”

From here to the end of the psalm the power and might of the Lord are proclaimed. For what could be stronger than to grant his saints such power that, by his generosity, they may win victories over their enemies?

But when he says, “The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice in their dwellings,” he now enters the second section, which contains the joys of the saints and the power of those who believe in Christ.

[Col. 1049C] Let us consider how the exultation of the saints is described. Glory is the repeated praise of good actions. In this the righteous rejoice in their dwellings—that is, in the secrecy of the heart—as the Apostle says: “For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). They rejoice there where the only one who knows them is the one who has deigned to bestow the gift.

They rejoice when they understand that the good Lord is such that he grants pardon to the guilty, grace to sinners, and everlasting glory to those who do not deserve it. By contrast, in this age the fool, going outside himself, exults in the stories of men and thinks he has earned whatever false speech raises him up.

[Col. 1049D] The saints therefore possess a discipline of glorying and a proper measure of joy, so that their good things may be referred to the one who bestows everything. For if joy lacks measure, it is not joy but ruin.

### Verse 6

“The exultations of God are in their throats, and two-edged swords are in their hands.”

### Verse 7

“To execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples.”

We must observe how beautiful and useful this distinction is. Above he said that the saints have their exultation in their dwellings; now he says that the exultations of the Lord are established in their throats, signifying that whether in thought or in speech they do not cease to praise the one from whom they receive eternal gifts.

He also proceeds to explain their power, saying: “and two-edged swords are in their hands.” [Col. 1050A] The two-edged sword is the word of the Lord and Savior, concerning which he himself says in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34).

It is two-edged because it contains the two Testaments. First it separated the Jews from the nations; afterward it separated and divided Christians from the allurements of the whole world. It is one sword, but it has two cuts, which it grants to the chosen peoples at the appropriate division of time.

He says that these swords are in their hands—that is, in the power of the saints—as it is written: “The word of the Lord came to the hand of Haggai the prophet” (Hag. 1:1). Receiving this power, then, the blessed will judge with the Lord, as it is written: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

[Col. 1050B] For see what follows: “To execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples.” These things truly take place when they judge with the Lord.

### Verse 8

“To bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with iron chains.”

### Verse 9

“To execute upon them the judgment that has been written. This glory belongs to all his saints.”

He explains what that double-edged sword does. It binds the kings of the earth in fetters from which it is not permitted to escape. It also places iron chains upon the nobles of the world, so that they are heavy to carry and so that no power can prevail to break their bonds.

This is truly the new song: that those poor people who were mocked in the world should be able to judge the princes of the earth.

[Col. 1050C] He continues: “To execute upon them the judgment that has been written”—namely, what the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). Who could estimate such a miracle? Who could encompass in the mind such glory, that those proud and wicked sinners should endure being judged by those whom here they regarded as worthless cattle destined for slaughter?

And lest you perhaps think that only the apostles would judge, to whom the Lord made this promise in the Gospel, he adds: “This glory belongs to all his saints.” [Col. 1050D] For all who do not oppose Christ’s rules judge with Christ, since whatever pleases him, they too accept with pious willingness.

Although the power and glory of the saints have been recounted in many ways, none of them is found to possess the entire reward of the virtues in its fullness. For Jesus Christ alone possesses this, concerning whom the Apostle says: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9)—that is, substantially.

For since the Lord possesses all good things perfectly and supremely, he gives to each person as he wills; and he himself is, according to John, the manifest fullness of all the saints (John 1:16).

## Conclusion of the Psalm

We must examine carefully how the preceding psalm has been joined to this one in the duty of praise, yet divided from it by a certain distinction. In the former, he urged all creatures to proclaim the Lord; here, more distinctly and specifically, he signified that Israel must sing a new song and rejoice in its own Lord, who gathered it from the multitude of the nations.

[Col. 1051A] The power that will be granted to the saints in that judgment is also recalled, so that the Lord’s power may be recognized in their glory. Thus the psalm has been divided both by the common duty of praise and by the particular character of its subject matter.

### 501 PSALM 150

## Alleluia

Behold, that salutary herald is sent forth again, now to speak not of carnal nourishment but of heavenly abundance. The city of God is admonished to sing both with its mouth and with its spirit, having been gathered from the circuit of the world.

[Col. 1051B] Therefore let us sing this Alleluia with the fullest devotion, since by the Lord’s dispensation it has carried the entire psalmody to its exalted summit. For just as this mortal fire, hastening upward, raises its gleaming locks to the peak, so this song, gradually increasing, has flown upward by steps of virtue to the heights of heaven.

If we too ascend with it through the devotion of the spirit, with the Lord’s right hand lifting us up, we shall be granted to reach that saving end which is bounded by no limits.

## Content of the Psalm

This psalm, raised to the harmonious unity of all the saints, ought not to have a division, because it has brought the end of the entire work to the power of the inseparable Trinity. It proceeds throughout with a single meaning, so that it seems neither to change its person nor its subject.

[Col. 1051C] This figure is called *hyrmos*, when a sequence of speech preserves its own tenor to the very end. The psalm is brief, so that it would not cause weariness; it is full of musical instruments, so that it might be especially suitable for spiritual chambers and be sung with nuptial sweetness in the assembly of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Its purpose is that the Lord should be praised through the congregation of the saints. Restoring them to his image, he has made them lay aside the frailty of flesh and blood. He has placed them, already conformed to his glory, in that blessedness, so that they may be filled with an abundance of all good things, concerning which the Apostle says: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing, so that we might be holy and without blemish before him” (Eph. 1:3–4).

[Col. 1051D]

## Exposition of the Psalm

### Verse 1

“Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power.”

We must carefully examine with what sweetness this book of Psalms ends and how it looks back to its beginning. The prophet says that, having received his saints into that Jerusalem, one ought to praise the Lord—namely, those to whom he himself showed the form of right conduct. Concerning this it was said: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1:1), and so forth.

They are the saints who, by his generosity, have deserved to become his imitators. But what kind of veneration is owed to the saints is suitably explained: it is not they, but the Lord, who must be proclaimed on account of their justification. He must be glorified first, since he grants the things that are to be proclaimed. Reverence is owed to the righteous because they have received divine gifts.

He continues: “Praise him in the firmament of his power.” The firmness of his power is shown in this: undergoing death for the salvation of all, he overcame death itself, together with its most wicked author, by the strength of his power; he shattered the gates of hell, healed the wavering through the resurrection, and led those who firmly believed into the kingdoms of heaven.

[Col. 1052A]

### Verse 2

“Praise him in his mighty acts; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.”

Here he commands that the Lord be praised on account of his power and greatness. He says: “Praise him in his mighty acts; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.” He then explains, through mystical allusions, how he ought to be praised, continuing to the end of the psalm.

His might is what was said in Psalm 8: “You have subjected all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field” (Ps. 8:8). The Apostle says likewise: “To him every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10).

Let us also consider what a great command is given to the blessed people. He continues: “Praise him according to the multitude of his greatness.” Who, I ask, could praise him according to the multitude of his greatness, when it is said in Psalm 144: “The Lord is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 144:3)?

[Col. 1052B] But observe to whom these words are addressed, and no doubt will remain: to spiritual beings, who are capable precisely of this work of praise. For since the Lord’s power has no end, he is praised according to his greatness when he is praised without end.

### Verse 3

“Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with the psaltery and the lyre.”

Here the musical instruments are arranged in order in a meaningful way: let the trumpet sound for the King, the psaltery sing to God, and the lyre, together with the others, sing to the Bridegroom.

It is clear that these instruments do not literally exist there; nevertheless, all these things are evidently to be referred through mystical allusions to Christ the Lord.

The trumpet is a small tube formed from joined horn sections or fashioned from some metal. It begins with an open circular mouth and ends in a narrow opening. When filled by drawn-in breath, it expands into a terrifying sound; it is used either in times of war or prepared for royal arrivals.

[Col. 1052C] The psaltery is an arrangement fashioned in the shape of a lyre. At its upper end it carries certain resonant wooden sides, where the sounds of the strings, rising from below, are drawn upward and answer with a most pleasing modulation, as it is said.

The lyre, with a kind of fiery belly positioned below, receives the sounds produced by the strings descending from above and releases them in a single pleasing harmony. All these things, compared with human actions, are figuratively said to resound with the praises of the Lord.

[Col. 1052D]

### Verse 4

“Praise him with the tambourine and chorus; praise him with strings and organ.”

These verses too, as has been said, belong to the nuptial hymns all the way to the end. The tambourine is a resonant object made as though two wooden vessels were joined at their rims, with stretched hide over them. Musicians strike it according to disciplined measure and produce a modulated sound through its doubled resonance.

The chorus is an assembled group of many voices tuned to sweetness.

He continues: “Praise him with strings and organ.” Since, besides the psaltery and the lyre, other instruments could be found—as some say—that resound through the tension of strings, he used the general term “strings,” so that every musical instrument might be assigned to the Lord’s praises.

The organ is like a kind of tower constructed from various pipes, to which a very abundant voice is supplied through the blowing of bellows. [502] To regulate its melody attractively, it is furnished on the inside with certain wooden tongues, which the fingers of skilled musicians press according to disciplined measure, producing a loud and very sweet song.

[Col. 1053A]

### Verse 5

“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with ringing cymbals. Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

So that we might understand the earlier instruments as having been spoken of through certain allusions to the saints, he now comes also to the human mouth. But the distinction made in these words must be considered, so that we should understand the “well-sounding cymbals” as our lips. They are not improperly placed among the musical instruments, since there is a certain likeness to cymbals and since human voices are shown through them to produce a most harmonious sound.

[Col. 1053B] Harmony is the joining together of different things brought into a single agreement. This also occurs in the human voice, when both the durations and the syllables are brought into a single concord of sound.

Our cymbals, then, are lips struck so as to regulate the sound of the voice with the greatest clarity. They sound beneficially when they are moved with the deepest devotion to the praises of the Lord.

The “ringing cymbals” are very small bowls made from mixed metals, with little bellies on their sides. When struck together through an artistic modulation, they return a very sharp sound in a pleasing consonance.

But since the holy prophet wished everything that has been said to be understood spiritually, he brought the book to its most appropriate conclusion: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” Not flesh and blood, [Col. 1053C] not the circuit of the world, not worldly allure; rather, let that which is higher in the nature of things praise the Lord—that which savors heavenly things and longs for eternal rewards.

Therefore he gave the entire work a brief and perfect statement, so that all things should spiritually praise the Lord and Savior.

With these matters reviewed, the perfection of the entire musical discipline has been assigned: breath in the trumpet, striking in the lyre, ringing in the cymbals, voice in the chorus—the sweetest harmony, which is not heard by fleshly ears but perceived through the contemplation of a pure mind.

For the discussion of syllogisms, begun in the first psalm, should also be brought to a corresponding close. We began with the categorical syllogism, which is the purest and chief of all syllogisms, as was appropriate; now we conclude our work with it as well.

[Col. 1053D] For the end ought to answer to its beginning, since everything in sacred writings should be found to correspond with everything else. The categorical syllogism is gathered for us in this form:

Every spirit should praise the Lord.  
He whom every spirit ought to praise is the true God.  
Therefore the Lord is the true God.

It is an astonishing mode of argument, drawing a person through confession to what he had previously refused to accept.

Behold, we have shown that the sequence contains material from grammar and etymologies, figures of speech, rhetorical art, topics, dialectical art, definitions, music, geometry, astronomy, and the distinctive expressions of divine law—all to the extent that the Lord has deigned to grant it. Thus those who read such things may acknowledge them gratefully, while those who are still inexperienced may receive the clearly expressed material without offense.

[Col. 1054A]

## Conclusion of the Psalms

The beautiful and wondrous order of the Psalms has been completed. It is brought to an end by a mystical number, yet is infinite in its sacred virtues; it is known in its full measure only to the one who embraces, in a countable quantity, the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the natures of all creatures.

Although we cannot comprehend it in its entirety, it is nevertheless beneficially sought, because whatever is examined is always found to be more abundant. How many new things will still have to be said from this work, and how many minds of the faithful will labor with diligent curiosity until the end of the age!

Yet this truth will be recognized most fully when the Lord himself deigns to grant us his contemplation.

[Col. 1054B] The entire order of the Psalms, insofar as human ingenuity has been able to investigate it, is recognized as proceeding through a twofold mystery.

First, as has been stated on the authority of the Fathers, it embraces the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments. Seven decades are referred to the Sabbath, which plainly belongs to that first worship. Eight decades are assigned to our own time, in which we venerate the Lord’s resurrection with pious devotion on the eighth day.

Second, by the Lord’s generosity we have observed that, when the flood had prevailed for one hundred and fifty days, the earth was cleansed of its crimes. In the same way, the spiritual abyss of the Psalms purifies the hearts of mortals polluted by sins through perpetual cleansing until the time of judgment. Thus the flood itself becomes saving for us, rendering our sense, soiled by transgressions, washed clean.

[Col. 1054C] What could you fail to find in this heavenly treasury of the divine Scriptures? If you seek Genesis, here the manner in which the world was fashioned is explained. If you name the prophets, who spoke so much about the Lord’s incarnation? If you desire the Gospel, it clearly displays in countless places the passion and resurrection of Christ the Lord. If you want the Apostle, listen to the teacher, listen to the compassionate one, who proclaims future judgments for the sake of correction and frequently pleads for sinners.

And, not to delay longer, whatever is done in heaven, on earth, in the sea, or among the underworld beings, if you read with the greatest care, you will recognize that everything has been suitably placed in its proper locations.

A witness is the magnificent discourse of Bishop Athanasius (*Tom. I, epist. ad Marcellinum*, p. 959), who, investigating the virtues of the Psalms with unsearchable truth, proves that everything contained within the scope of the sacred Scriptures is present there.

[Col. 1054D] He also causes the nature of God, if it is permissible, to be understood in two words: “I today”—something that no books or volumes can fully contain. Thus what is briefly said is explained, while what is silent becomes perceptible in some measure.

For in the second psalm the Father says to the Son: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). In these two words he subtly signifies something that seems capable of transcending human understanding.

The book embraces the New and Old Testament with such precision that you may truly understand a spiritual library to have been constructed within it. For if paradise is considered delightful because the courses of four rivers are known to beautify it [ed.: “flow forth”], how much more blessed is the soul watered by the fountains of the one hundred and fifty Psalms?

[Col. 1055A] Nor did divine power operate only within this number. Much more extends beyond it, whether things partially understood or various miracles that are still entirely unknown. For in the one hundred and fifty-three fish that the apostles’ nets drew from the depths of the sea (John 21:11), the number of the saints is understood and explained.

The ark of Noah, as a type of the holy Church, is read to have been constructed with a length of three hundred cubits, a width of fifty, and a height of thirty (Gen. 6:15). From this Origen, as usual, developed many mystical interpretations.

Therefore it plainly appears that the Creator and Maker of all things, when arranging all things heavenly and earthly, made everything that was created according to measure, number, and weight, as the Most Wise says: “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21).

[Col. 1055B] Now, for the sake of memory, let us briefly recall what above seemed to have been set forth at greater length.

First, we should remember what was related concerning the various diversity of titles. We should also recall how fittingly the persons in the text of the Psalms are changed, and how their conclusions were formed especially against heretics.

We should remember why the Hebrew alphabet is placed in the Psalms; why one psalm seems to have been composed from parts of psalms; why intercalary psalms have been placed there; why the repetition of verses is found in the Psalms; concerning the interpretation of Hebrew names; concerning those who are called *unifines* [“single-ending” psalms]; concerning the fifteen Gradual Psalms; why seven psalms are taught to belong to penitents; why the words of those lamenting for the city of Jerusalem are poured forth with tears; and why the order of the Psalms has been brought to an end in the praises of the Lord—where it is explained in how many ways he is proclaimed, although his praises can be explained by no books and no human powers.

[Col. 1055C] This variety of the Psalms may perhaps suitably be compared either to the most precious topaz or to the most beautiful peacock, which display so many different colors of their bodies as often as the eye of the observer is fixed upon them.

These matters, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it, have been traversed according to our modest ability. But you, teachers, who grow rich through abundant reading of heavenly writings, spare the inexperienced, pardon the one who confesses, and be favorable.

[Col. 1056A] It is difficult to find a human work that does not suffer some question, as the Apostle James testifies: “If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2). If some people prepare accusations against the sacred writings, what will they not do against the weak, whom they boldly accuse?

Things brought forth should always be adapted to the mind of the speaker. For if we wish to destroy everything through contentious dispute, we condemn pious devotion by an unwary contradiction instead.

But now it is time to turn our hearts toward the Lord, toward whom every attention ought rather to be directed and toward whom the end of our labor ought to proceed.

## Prayer

You, Lord, true teacher and bestower, advocate and judge, giver and admonisher, terrible and merciful, reprover and consoler, who give sight to blind minds; who make possible for the weak what you command; who are so compassionate that you wish to be entreated continually; so generous that you permit no one to despair:

[Col. 1056B] Grant what, with you enabling us, we seek well—and especially those things that in our weakness we do not know. Receive what we have said from you; pardon what through ignorance we have uttered from ourselves; and lead us to that contemplation where we can no longer err.

Grant that I may do the things I have presumed to speak under your inspiration; grant that the things I have urged others to observe may be fulfilled, so that you who have granted a pious discourse may also bestow upon your servants an approved way of acting.

Deliver us, lover of humankind, from the danger that, as the Apostle says, while preaching to others I myself may be found disqualified (1 Cor. 9:27). How weak we are, you truly know; what kind of enemy weighs us down, you recognize.

[Col. 1056C] An unequal contest seeks you; mortal weakness longs for you. For the glory of your majesty is shown if the roaring lion is overcome by a weak sheep; if the most violent spirit is conquered by the feeblest flesh; if the one who fell from heaven is subdued here while you fight on our side—so that, even if by your permission we endure his power for a time, we may in no way be swallowed by his insatiable jaws.

Make him sorrowful because of human joy, him who always exults in our offense.

Amen.

Thus far, by the Lord’s generosity, we have traversed what seemed to pertain to the exposition of the Psalms [ed.: “discussed”]. Now let us consider the words of Solomon, which are known to have their own interpreters.

[Col. 1055]

# EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF SONGS ATTRIBUTED TO MAGNUS AURELIUS CASSIODORUS

*(C, G, S)*

## Notice

[Col. 1055C]

[Col. 1055D] The name of Cassiodorus is prefixed to this little work both by manuscript codices and by printed editions—at least those that I have been able to see. All the librarians, if you except one, and also many authors of better repute, without any controversy ascribe it to our author.

Nevertheless, it does not seem certain to me that it is by Cassiodorus. The preface that I placed before the beginning of this work will sufficiently show by what arguments in particular I have been led to this opinion. If you wish, consult it, friendly reader.

## Prologue

[Col. 1056C]

[Col. 1056D] Solomon, inspired by the divine Spirit, composed this little book concerning the marriage of Christ and the Church, and in a certain sense made it a wedding song for Christ and the Church—that is, a song over the bridal chambers.

Hence he called this work the “Song of Songs,” because it surpasses all songs. For just as one says “King of kings” and “Lord of lords” (Rev. 17:14), and “solemnity of solemnities,” so it is called “Song of Songs” on account of its excellence and dignity.

This little book is more obscure because no persons are identified in it, and it has been composed, as it were, in comic style.

## Chapter One

### Verse 1

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

This is the voice of the Synagogue desiring the coming of Christ. It is as though she were saying: “So many times he has promised me his coming through the prophets; let him come now, therefore, and kiss me with the kiss of his mouth”—that is, let him speak to me through himself.

Because your breasts are better than wine. Suddenly turning her words to the one for whom she was burning with desire, she adds: “Because your breasts are better than wine.” By the breasts of Christ the sweetness of the Gospel is understood, since the infancy of believers is nourished by it as by milk. Wine, however, signifies the austerity of the Law. But Christ’s breasts are better than wine, because the sweetness of the Gospel is better than the austerity of the Law. For in the Law no penance is granted; rather, it is commanded that whoever sins be put to death. But the Gospel says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner” (Ezek. XVIII, 32), and so forth.

## Chapter I

### Verse 2

“Fragrant with the finest perfumes.” The perfumes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or also the works of the virtues, concerning which the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (II Cor. II, 15).

“Your name is poured-out oil.” Your name, O Christ, is poured out. *Chrisma* in Greek means *unction* in Latin, whence comes “Christ.” The name “Christ” is derived from anointing. The Holy Spirit is customarily called by the name of oil, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with oil” (Ps. XLIV, 8), that is, with the Holy Spirit. This oil was poured out when the grace that Christ possessed uniquely was given to all the elect. Hence Christians are also named from Christ, sharing in Christ’s name. And it is rightly called not oil that has been dripped out but oil that has been poured out, because this grace has been given abundantly to all who recall the faith of Christ.

“For this reason the young women loved you.” The young women are called the souls of the elect, who in baptism abandoned the filth of the old person and were renewed in Christ. They are rightly designated in the feminine gender, because the more the souls of the saints are conscious of their own fragility, the more greatly they love Christ.

### Verse 3

“Draw me after you; we shall run.” This is the voice of the Church. Here there is a change of speaker: until now the Synagogue has spoken; here the Church from the Gentiles begins to speak: “Draw me after you; we shall run.” Since, she says, I recognize my weakness and see that I can accomplish nothing good by my own strength, draw me by your grace to imitate you; or even, when you have ascended into heaven, “Draw me after you,” so that I may deserve to follow you.

“The King brought me into his chambers.” Here the Church speaks of Christ her bridegroom to faithful souls. The chambers of God are eternal blessedness and the joys of the heavenly homeland. The Church has already been brought into them through faith and hope, and one day she will be brought into them in reality.

“We shall exult and rejoice in you.” In your gifts, she says, we shall exult and rejoice. But because we know that this is not our merit, we shall exult in you, not in ourselves. This is what the Apostle says: “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

“Remembering your breasts above wine.” That is, remembering your grace and the mercy by which we have been saved. The breasts are the very grace by which we are saved. We also remember that you deigned to temper the austerity of the Law with the breasts of evangelical teaching.

“The upright love you.” Those who are upright of heart, she says, love you; that is, those who attribute nothing to their own merits but ascribe everything to your grace. No one loves you except the upright, and no one is upright except the one who loves you.

### Verse 4

“I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” Here the Church again speaks of her afflictions to holy souls. “I am black” because I suffer persecutions; “but beautiful” in virtues, O daughters of Jerusalem, that is, faithful souls. “I am black,” that is, disfigured by the persecutions and hardships I endure; “but beautiful” in the splendor of virtues. How she is black, and how she is beautiful, she shows when she adds:

“Like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.” The distinction is therefore this: “I am black like the tents of Kedar, beautiful like the curtains of Solomon.” Kedar was a son of Ishmael, whose name is interpreted as “darkness.” The Ishmaelites, moreover, were always accustomed to live in tents and did not have houses. The Church therefore says that she is black like the tents of Kedar because of the persecutions she suffered from the sons of darkness, which is what “Kedar” signifies. Hence the Psalmist says: “I dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar” (Ps. CXIX, 5), that is, I lived among persecutors and sinners blackened by unbelief.

But she says that she is beautiful like the curtains—that is, the tents—of Solomon, whose name is interpreted as “peaceful,” because amid her afflictions she was worthy of a visitation and consolation from her bridegroom Christ. And just as tents are made from the skins of dead animals, so the Church, namely the tabernacle of God, is built from those who mortify themselves with their vices and desires (Gal. V, 24).

### Verse 5

“Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.” O faithful souls devoted to God, do not look at me because I am dark, that is, because I am afflicted by tribulations and oppressed by persecutions; “because the sun has discolored me,” that is, the heat of persecution has in some way obscured my brightness. It is as though she were saying: Consider my inner beauty and attend to it, not to what I seem outwardly to suffer. The Apostle says something similar: “Do not lose heart over my tribulations for you, which are your glory. For the sufferings are not commensurate” (Eph. III, 13), and so forth.

The sun, however, has many meanings in Scripture. At times it signifies the Mediator himself between God and human beings; hence it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. IV, 2), that is, Christ. It also signifies the Church, as the Lord says: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matt. XIII, 43). At times it signifies the heat of persecution, as here and in the Gospel, where it is said of the seed that fell upon the rock and, when the sun rose, was scorched. The Lord himself explains this: “When persecution occurs because of the word, they are scandalized” (Matt. XIII, 6, 21).

“The sons of my mother fought against me.” He shows from whom this persecution began when he adds: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” This is the voice of the primitive Church, whose mother is the Synagogue, to whom it is said through the prophet: “And you shall be called the faithful city” (Isa. I, 26), and the mother of the cities, the daughter of Zion. Her sons are the Jews, who fought against the primitive Church when they stirred up persecution against the believers, and all were scattered throughout the regions of Samaria (Acts VIII, 1).

“They made me keeper of the vineyards.” There was one vineyard, the primitive Church in Jerusalem. But because of the Jewish persecution, when all the believers had been scattered, many vineyards came into being, that is, many churches were established throughout the whole world. The primitive Church therefore says: “They made me”—namely, the apostles and teachers—“keeper,” that is, so that I might be guardian of the churches. Hence the Greek text rightly says “they were disseminated” where we read “they were scattered” (Acts VIII, 1); for they were divinely dispersed for this purpose, so that more churches might arise throughout the whole world.

“I did not guard my vineyard,” that is, I did not guard that one Church which was in Jerusalem. This is not to be understood with reference to desire or intention, but to place: “I did not guard it,” meaning, so that it would remain there where it had begun.

### Verse 6

“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday.” This is the voice of the Church to her bridegroom Christ. O bridegroom, whom my soul loves—that is, whom I love with the whole attention of my mind—tell me where you pasture, that is, where you cause your sheep to pasture. For he is the good shepherd, as he himself says in the Gospel (John X, 14). Tell me where you pasture and where you lie down, that is, rest—and this at midday, that is, in the heat of persecution or temptation. For the Church, laboring amid persecutions, begs her bridegroom to tell her in whose minds he rests. For the bridegroom’s lying down means resting, as he himself says: “Upon whom my spirit rests” (Isa. LXVI, 2), and so forth. So that the saints may not wither in the heat of temptation, he lies down and rests in their hearts, and protects them from every heat of temptations and persecutions. Why is this?

“Lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” He calls the gatherings of heretics “the flocks of companions,” because they too are Christ’s companions and pasture their own flocks. The sense is: O bridegroom, show me your saints and elect, lest I stumble and fall among heretics, thinking that you might be found there. Heretics wrongly divided this verse, as though the bride asked, “Where do you pasture? Where do you lie down?” and he replied, “I lie down at midday, and in the southern region.”

### Verse 7

“If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out and follow the footsteps of the flocks.” This is the voice of the bridegroom to his bride, the Church. It is as though he were saying: You complain that you have been abandoned by me and darkened by the heat of persecutions; yet you do not consider how beautiful you are among women, that is, you do not attend to the beauty of spiritual virtues by which you are adorned above all others, although you may be darkened by temptations. If, therefore, you do not know yourself—that is, if you do not recognize this dignity and beauty of yours—go out from my fellowship and follow the footsteps of the flocks; that is, follow and imitate the teaching of wandering heretics, who, having rejected the true Shepherd of the one flock, have heaped up many flocks for themselves.

“And pasture your kids,” that is, sinners and erring hearers, “beside the tents of the shepherds,” that is, according to the doctrines of the heretics. For Christ is the one shepherd, and he has one flock, namely the unity of the Catholic Church. Heretics, however, are many shepherds who gather a flock of deceived people to themselves and feed them to the devil. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Like sheep they are placed in hell” (Ps. XLVIII, 15). They are called sheep in this passage not because of simplicity or innocence, but because of dullness, since they do not know how to resist perverse teaching; rather, they endure everything imposed upon them by wicked teachers with an endurance that is not good.

### Verse 8

“To my cavalry I have compared you, my beloved, in the chariots of Pharaoh.” He calls his cavalry the army of the children of Israel, namely the six hundred thousand who went out of Egypt and crossed the Red Sea (Num. II, 32; Exod. XIV, 22). He calls that multitude his cavalry because, just as a charioteer presides over a chariot, so God presided over that people, protecting and defending them and bringing them into the promised land. He compared his beloved to this cavalry of his, because just as that people was saved through the Red Sea when Pharaoh was submerged (Exod. XIV, 27–28), so the Church of the Gentiles was freed through baptism from the service of the devil and brought into the true promised land and evangelical freedom. Thus she who had been a slave of vices became Christ’s beloved, cleansed and washed through baptism from the filth of sins.

### Verse 9

“Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” It is the nature of the turtledove that, if it happens to lose its mate, it does not seek another thereafter. The Church is therefore compared to the turtledove, because from the time Christ left the world in bodily presence and went to heaven, the Church has persevered most steadfastly in his love and accepts no adulterous lover. She despises the world and all its desires and contemplates in her mind the beauty of her one bridegroom.

He compares the cheeks of the Church to the cheeks of the turtledove because modesty appears especially in the cheeks, and through this the Church’s modesty and shame are shown: she blushes at everything foul and fears to commit anything displeasing to her bridegroom. The sense is: Do not fear that you will wander among the flocks of your companions, because I have endowed and fortified you with such modesty of love for me and such shame that I am certain you cannot abandon me or turn aside to others.

“Your neck is like necklaces.” By the neck of the Church the holy teachers are signified, for through the neck food is supplied to nourish the body. The words by which the secrets of minds are disclosed also proceed through the throat. Thus the holy teachers both show us the food of saving doctrine and reveal to us the secrets of Scripture. This neck of the Church is therefore like a necklace, because the holy teachers are adorned with the gems of chaste doctrine and the ornaments of virtues. A necklace is an adornment of maidens or married women.

### Verse 10

“We shall make golden necklaces for you, studded with silver.” Literally, necklaces are ornaments for a maiden’s or girl’s neck, namely rods of gold woven together, sometimes interlaced with the beautiful variety of the finest silver threads. This is what he says: “studded with silver,” that is, arranged and joined together in the manner of earthly worms, which are called *lumbrici*. The necklaces are called by analogy with a sea fish called the *muraena*, or moray eel.

Mystically, the necklaces are the intricate doctrines of Scripture, joined together from the diverse opinions of the holy Fathers. Gold signifies the radiance of spiritual meaning; silver signifies the brilliance of eloquence. The bridegroom therefore makes golden necklaces for his bride when Christ equips his Church with the doctrines of the holy Fathers, shining in meaning and expression, and kindles her to imitate their faith and virtue.
