It should be noted that he says in the plural, “we shall make for you,” as though Christ joined himself to the persons of the teachers through whom the necklaces themselves are linked together, so that the Church might be adorned by them.

### Verse 11

“While the king was on his couch.” The bride calls her bridegroom Christ “king,” because through his divinity he rules all things and, also according to his humanity, was born from the royal line of David. The king’s couch was his incarnation. To recline means to lean back or sit at table. Christ reclined when, for our redemption, he stooped even to assume our nature. And then—

“My nard gave forth its fragrance,” when the virtue of the Church shone forth more brightly. For when she considers that God became human for her sake, she is kindled more greatly to pursue spiritual virtues and to love her Creator. Nard signifies the fragrance of spiritual virtues. There were holy people of God before the incarnation, but, as has been said, holiness increased more greatly from the time of the incarnation. Then, in a certain sense, the nard of the Church—that is, the fragrance of her virtues—gave forth its scent more powerfully.

Literally, nard is an aromatic plant with a thick, fragile root and a small, dense leaf, whose tops spread out into spikes. In the Gospel it is read that Mary Magdalene anointed the Lord’s feet and head with this perfume in the house of Simon (Matt. XXVI, 7; Mark XIV, 3; Luke VII, 38; John XII, 3).

### Verse 12

“My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me.” Myrrh is an aromatic substance of extreme bitterness, with which the bodies of the dead are embalmed. In this passage the passion and burial of Christ are signified. For after the Lord’s body had been taken down from the cross by Nicodemus and Joseph, it was embalmed with myrrh and aloes, wrapped in linen cloths with spices, and committed to burial (Matt. XXVII, 59; Mark XV, 46; Luke XXIII, 53; John XIX, 40). The Church therefore says to her bridegroom: “My beloved has become a bundle of myrrh to me,” because he died and was buried for me.

“He will remain between my breasts.” No one doubts that the place of the heart is between the breasts. She therefore says: “He will remain between my breasts,” that is, he will be held eternally in the memory of my heart, and I will never forget such great benefits of his. Whether I am in prosperity or adversity, I will nevertheless remember him who loved me so greatly and died for me.

### Verse 13

“My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi.” Cyprus is an island said to have noble vines that produce enormous clusters. Engaddi is likewise said to be a place containing little trees that exude the liquid of balsam. The bride therefore speaks of the resurrection of Christ her bridegroom: “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me,” as though she were saying: My bridegroom, who tasted the bitterness of death for me and was like a bundle of myrrh to me, became for me, in his resurrection, a cluster of Cyprus when he gladdened me with the joy of his resurrection. “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII, 15). And this occurred “in the vineyards of Engaddi,” because through his resurrection he spread his fragrance throughout the whole world like the sweetest scent of balsam and widely dispersed the fragrance of his faith.

Engaddi is interpreted as “the spring of the kid,” by which baptism and the sacrifice in which all sins are washed away are signified. For the kid signifies sinners. Baptism, therefore, is the spring of the kid, because it receives sinners but makes them immaculate and cleansed from every sin.

### Verse 14

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful.” This is the voice of Christ the bridegroom to his bride, the Church. He repeats twice that she is beautiful, because of the perfection of her work and the purity of her thought. “Behold, you are beautiful,” that is, you are perfect in good works, living holy, piously, and justly according to the Apostle (Titus II, 12). “Behold, you are beautiful,” possessing a pure and simple intention of heart, because you do good not for earthly advantages or the glory of the world, but so that you may please the eyes of God alone.

“Your eyes are those of doves.” The dove is a very simple bird, and through it the simplicity and innocence of the Church are represented. She has, as it were, the eyes of doves because she keeps herself free from every deceit and pretense. Or she has the eyes of doves because she understands the knowledge of the divine Scriptures with a chaste and simple gaze, seeking spiritual and divine meanings in them. Since the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove (Matt. III, 16), heavenly doctrine is rightly understood through the eyes of the dove.

### Verse 15

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely.” It is as though she were saying: You indeed say that I am beautiful in work and thought, but I believe and recognize that I have all this beauty from you. For you are beautiful and comely; you are the source of every good, and whatever good I possess, I possess through your grace. He is called beautiful and comely because he is wondrous both in the eternity of his divinity and in the dignity of the humanity he assumed.

“Our couch is flowering.” The Church’s couch is whatever tranquility or rest belongs to the present life. The Church is as though in a war while she endures various struggles for Christ; yet she rests as though on a couch when she enjoys whatever small measure of peace has been granted to her. This couch is flowering, however, that is, the Church’s rest is marked by a variety of virtues like spring flowers. At such times she devotes herself more freely to divine contemplation; at such times she more freely carries out fasts, vigils, and the other practices of good works.

### Verse 16

“The beams of our houses are cedars; our ceilings are cypresses.” The houses of the Church are the gatherings of the faithful dispersed throughout the whole world. The beams and ceilings are the faithful themselves, from whom the Church is composed. It should be observed, however, that beams provide a house with support, while ceilings provide ornament. Thus the beams signify the teachers, whose doctrine supports and sustains the Church; the ceilings signify the saints who rejoice in simplicity and adorn the Church with their virtues, though they do not fortify it through doctrine.

It should also be observed that the ceilings are attached to the beams. So the life of the faithful in the Church depends upon the teachers, because it is instructed and strengthened by their doctrine. The beams are rightly called cedars and the ceilings cypresses, for both trees are of an imperishable nature and signify the saints, who burn with an unfading desire in love of their Creator and, despising transient things, hasten toward eternal realities. Cedar also drives away serpents by its fragrance; likewise, the holy teachers repel demons or heretics through the fragrance of their doctrine.

## Chapter II

### Verse 1

“I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” After the bride had shown what sort of house she and her bridegroom possessed, the bridegroom himself also shows what he is like, saying: “I am the flower of the field,” and so forth, because I spread the fragrance of my virtue across the breadth of the whole world. “I am the flower of the field,” that is, I am the beauty of the world. For just as a field is adorned and made fresh with flowers, so the whole world is beautified by the faith and knowledge of Christ.

“I am also the lily of the valleys,” because I grant my grace especially to those minds that, having no hope in themselves, submit to me with humble devotion. Valleys signify the humble or the minds of the humble; their lily is Christ, because he himself is the beauty of humble minds, the one who said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

What he says, “I am the flower of the field,” can also be referred to the incarnation. A field is not plowed, cut open, or furrowed by any plowshare. He therefore says, “I am the flower of the field,” that is, the son of the Virgin. He does not call himself the flower of the countryside but of the field, because he is the fruit of virgin flesh, according to Isaiah’s prophecy: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI, 1).

The lily of the valleys is likewise Christ, that is, the son of humble parents. The valleys signify his humble and poor parents. For when the Son of God came into the world, he deigned not only to become human but also to become a poor human being for us. He chose to have not rich but poor parents, so that, having become a participant in our poverty, he might make us participants in his riches and glory.

### Verse 2

“As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters.” Seeing his bride hastening toward rest, fleeing from eternal labors, and moving through the rest of the present time toward eternal blessedness, he warns her by this comparison and praise that she must know she will reach that destination through the pressures and labors of this age. “As a lily among thorns,” he says, “so is my beloved among daughters.”

The thorns that prick and tear signify every kind of wicked person, whether within or outside the Church. The sense is: You must live in the world for a time, and you must be prepared against every adversity, just as a lily exists among thorns and yet does not cease to flower and emit its pleasant fragrance. So is my beloved among daughters, because you suffer evil not only from those who are outside the Church but also from those who, regenerated through baptism, seem to have entered into adoption as children of God.

Note that above the bridegroom called himself the lily of the valleys; now he says of his bride, “As a lily among thorns.” For he who is truly the lily, by grace makes his Church a lily, whitened by virtues and free from every stain of vices.

### Verse 3

“As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.” Now, having been praised by the bridegroom, the bride returns the favor and says what he is like. “As an apple tree,” she says, “and so forth.” Just as an apple tree possesses the beauty of its fruit and a pleasant fragrance among the wild trees of the forest, so also Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings (I Tim. II, 5), shines with a special grace among the sons, that is, among the elect. He alone is the Son of God by nature; the other elect are sons by grace, having received power from the one Son of God to become sons of God. Hence John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John I, 14)—not just any glory, but glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father.

“Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat,” because I trust in his protection and hope to be guided by him amid adversities. The shadow of Christ is the protection of his divinity, by which he guards and defends the elect.

“And his fruit is sweet to my throat,” that is, the contemplation of his divinity, by which I trust I shall be satisfied. This is the expectation of the saints, this is their reward and satisfaction: the vision of their Creator. The Church therefore desires the shadow of her Creator because she longs for his protection amid the adversities of the present life. His fruit is sweet to my throat because I await the enjoyment of the sight of him and satisfaction with the sweetness of his love.

### Verse 4

“The king brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered love in me.” The wine cellar is the Church, in which there is the wine of evangelical doctrine. The bride, beloved of the bridegroom, is brought into this cellar when the faithful from all nations are united into one Church.

“He ordered love in me,” she says. Among all virtues, love holds the primacy, and the Church itself subsists through it. Love is therefore ordered in the Church, because the love of God and of human beings must be maintained neither rashly nor confusedly, but in due order. God must be loved above all things with the whole heart, the whole soul, all one’s strength, and the whole mind. Finally, one’s neighbor must be loved as each person loves himself (Deut. VI, 5; Matt. XXII, 39; Mark XII, 30–31; Luke X, 27).

For the person who places love of neighbor before love of God wishes to confuse love. The Lord speaks of such people in the Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37).

Or “he ordered love in me” means that he loved me first. Then he taught me how I ought to love him; hence he himself says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV, 16). And John says: “Let us love God, because he first loved us” (John IV, 19).

### Verse 5

“Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, because I am sick with love.” After the Church, or the soul beloved of God, had spoken of the ordered love within her, she shows how she wishes to rest and on what bed she wishes to repose with her beloved bridegroom, saying: “Strengthen me with flowers,” and so forth.

She addresses souls already perfectly attached to divine love. The flowers signify the beginnings of holy conduct; the apples signify the perfect examples of good works. The sense is: O holy souls who cling to love of your Creator, strengthen me with examples of good works. Show how you have lived at the beginning, in progress, and in the perfection of virtue and good works, because I am sick with love.

The soul is sick with the love of God when it places nothing before his love; indeed, it becomes weak and feeble toward secular works, and nothing delights it except meditation on heavenly things and contemplation of its Creator.

### Verse 6

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” When, she says, I have lain on such a bed, his left hand—that is, the bridegroom’s—will be under my head. By the left hand the prosperity of the present time, or also the gifts of God bestowed upon the saints in the present life, are understood. By the right hand the blessedness of the heavenly homeland is understood.

God’s left hand is the pledge of the Holy Spirit, the understanding of the divine Scriptures, and other such gifts and charisms by which the holy Church is consoled in the present. The head signifies the ruling faculty of the mind. The bridegroom’s left hand is therefore under the bride’s head because the Church receives all these gifts for this purpose: that through them she may learn to sigh for eternal realities.

The bridegroom’s right hand embraces her because the whole intention of the Church, or of the faithful soul, is to reach eternal blessedness at last and rejoice in the sight of her Creator. It is rightly said first that the left hand is under the bride’s head and afterward that the bridegroom’s right hand embraces her, because no one can reach the embrace of eternal blessedness unless here he strives to become a participant in the heavenly mysteries and divine gifts.

### Verse 7

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the stags of the fields, do not arouse or awaken the beloved until she herself wills it.” This is the voice of the bridegroom adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, his friends intent upon eternal desires and seeking the vision of peace, not to arouse or disturb the resting bride.

“I adjure you,” and so forth, not to disturb the beloved—that is, the soul devoted to divine contemplation and occupied with prayers or divine readings—or awaken her to external works until she herself wills it. This means: until, when the time of contemplation has been completed and the frailty of the body gives its warning, she herself wishes to be awakened from the sleep of eternal rest and proceed to temporal tasks.

Let us see, then, by what he adjures the daughters of Jerusalem: by the does and the stags of the fields. Does and stags are clean animals, hostile to serpents and poisons. They signify the virtues of the saints, which shine with spiritual purity and not only avoid the poisons of diabolical deceit but also pursue and destroy them.

The sense is: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by your virtues, in which you rejoice as gifts bestowed upon you by divine grace, not to disturb the soul devoted to my contemplation until, the hour of contemplation having ended, she herself wishes to do something else.

### Verse 8

“The voice of my beloved.” This is the voice of the Church. “The voice of my beloved,” that is, this is it. Rejoicing that she is loved so greatly by the bridegroom that he even adjures the daughters of Jerusalem on her behalf not to disturb her while she rests, the Church says: “This is the voice of my beloved speaking on my behalf.”

Desiring to see her beloved but unable to do so, she adds:

“Behold, he comes leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.” The mountains and hills signify all the perfect saints, raised above earthly things by the loftiness of their way of life and, as it were, surpassing the level ground of the fields through the merits of a better life. Concerning these mountains Isaiah says: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills” (Isa. II, 2).

The bride therefore speaks of her beloved: “Behold, he comes leaping over the mountains and bounding over the hills,” that is, even according to his humanity he surpasses all the excellence of the saints and all purity of divine contemplation. He is said not to stand on the mountains but to bound over them because, although he visits the hearts of the saints for a time through inward inspiration, he nevertheless suddenly withdraws in order to kindle them to love of him.

This may also be referred to the incarnation of Christ, in which he made certain leaps: he came from heaven into the Virgin’s womb, from the Virgin’s womb into the manger, from the manger to baptism, from baptism to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and from the tomb to heaven. Hence the Psalmist says: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. XVIII, 6), and so forth.

### Verse 9

“My beloved is like a doe and a fawn of the stags.” Although does and stags possess many features in their nature that suit allegorical meanings, they have this particular characteristic: they do not remain on level ground but are accustomed to make leaps in steep and elevated places. Christ is therefore rightly compared to them because of the subtlety of contemplation and because no understanding can comprehend the majesty of his divinity.

He is compared not to stags but to does, namely smaller animals, because of the humility of his incarnation. For he deigned not only to become human but to become a humble human being. He is said to resemble a fawn of the stags because, according to his humanity, he derived his origin from stags, that is, from the patriarchs; or also because of the variety of his virtues and his innocence he is compared to a fawn of the stags.

“Behold, he himself stands behind our wall.” The wall is called our mortal condition, because a kind of thick wall has been established between us and God and does not allow us to enjoy his contemplation. The first human being was created so as to enjoy the vision and conversation of God (Gen. I, 26); but after he sinned (Gen. III, 6), a wall was added, namely mortality itself, by which we are weighed down. For, as the Wise Man says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that considers many things” (Wis. IX, 15).

The bride therefore says that her bridegroom, whom she earlier compared to does or fawns of stags, now stands behind her wall, because Christ sometimes becomes near when he permits himself to be contemplated as far as the human mind is able to grasp him; at other times he withdraws and, like a doe or stag, escapes by certain leaps.

Since a wall stood between us and him, and we could not see him, he deigned to make windows and lattices in that wall, through which he might in some measure be sensed and in some measure perceived. Hence it follows:

“Looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.” Windows and lattices are made in the wall, as it were, when he permits himself by his grace to be contemplated, although in a mirror and in an enigma.

What he says, “He himself stands behind our wall,” can also be referred to his humanity. He stood, as it were, behind our wall when he joined our flesh to himself, in which his divinity lay hidden. But what follows—“Looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices”—is referred to his divinity. For the one who looks through windows or lattices sees everything that takes place outside, yet is himself seen by no one. So God, although he sees all things, cannot himself be investigated or comprehended.

### Chapter II

**Verse 10.** “Behold, my beloved speaks to me”—he urges me to preach, saying: “Arise, hasten, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one, and come.” This is the voice of the bridegroom calling her to the works of public ministry. “Arise, hasten, my beloved,” through faith and love; “my dove,” through innocence and simplicity; “my beautiful one,” hasten and come through the beauty of virtues. It is as though he were saying: “Arise from that sweetest bed of yours”—that is, from the repose in which you desire to please me alone through psalms, hymns, and prayers—“hasten and come,” that is, hasten for the benefit of your neighbors, so that through the ministry of preaching and the example of good works you may make them imitators of you as well and lead them with you to salvation.

It should be noted that above he adjured the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken the beloved; here, however, he himself rouses her and urges her to arise for labor, because everything has its time, and there is a time for every matter under heaven: a time for contemplation and also a time for action. At one time holy preachers must devote themselves to divine contemplation and delight their minds in heavenly repose; at another time, through charity, they must care for their neighbors, offer them examples of good works, and impart the teaching of divine contemplation. [Col. 1065B]

**Verse 11.** “For now winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed.” By the names of winter and rain, the harshness of unbelief is expressed, which held the whole world until the coming of Christ. The bridegroom therefore says: “Arise, my beloved, and come, because winter has passed,” with the Sun of righteousness appearing; “and the rain” of unbelief “has departed,” and the serenity of true faith has shone forth in the world. The Apostle says something similar: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12).

**Verse 12.** “The flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come.” When winter and rain had ended, flowers appeared in the land—namely, the beauty of virtues and chastity. As the harshness of unbelief passed away, the springtime mildness of faith followed; the time of pruning came, that is, of the purification of the saints. The pruning of the vineyards signifies the purification that is in Christ and through Christ, concerning which he himself says: “I am the vine, you are the branches” (John 15:5).

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” This means the voice of the apostles who preached. The turtledove is an exceedingly chaste bird; and because it habitually dwells and builds its nest in lofty trees, it signifies the apostles and the other teachers who can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Its song is also a lament, and this signifies the weeping of the saints, who urge their own people to tears and mourning, saying: “Be miserable and mourn; let your laughter be turned into mourning” (Jas. 4:9). “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land,” that is, the voice of the apostles who preach; “in our land,” that is, in the Church, of which the Psalmist says: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1). [Col. 1065D]

**Verse 13.** “The fig tree has put forth its unripe figs.” The fig tree signifies the Synagogue; the unripe figs are so called because they are the first and immature figs, unfit for eating and easily blown down by the force of the wind. When the voice of the turtledove sounded, the fig tree put forth its unripe figs, because, while the apostles were preaching, many emerged from the synagogue of the Jews who believed in Christ yet wished to observe the law carnally, taking greater delight in the authority of the law than in the sweetness of the Gospel. They wished to observe circumcision, the sabbath, and the other precepts of the law according to the letter. Concerning them the Apostle says: “They are zealous for you, but not well; rather, they wish you to be circumcised, that they may boast in your flesh” (Gal. 6:13).

“The flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.” After the voice of the turtledove had been heard, after the fig tree had put forth its 511 unripe figs, the flowering vines gave forth their fragrance, because the multitude of Churches was spread throughout the breadth of the world, scattering far and wide the flowers of virtue and the fragrance of good works. [Col. 1066A]

“Arise, hasten, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come.” “Do not,” he says, “my bride, whom I have made my beloved through faith and love, grow sluggish in idle torpor; but arise and come, and display the examples of your virtues openly to your neighbors.”

**Verse 14.** “My dove in the clefts of the rock.” If the rock is Christ, according to the Apostle’s statement, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4), the clefts of the rock are the wounds that he received on the cross for our salvation—namely, the piercings of the nails and the thrust of the lance (John 19). In these clefts, therefore, the dove—that is, the Church—dwells, because she places the whole hope of her salvation in the passion of her Redeemer. There she lies hidden, secure from the ambushes of evil spirits as from the attack of a hawk; there she builds her nest, that is, she gathers the offspring of good works.

“In the hiding-place of the wall.” Walls are commonly made from dry stones to protect vineyards and repel foxes and other harmful creatures. By the wall, therefore, the guardianship of heavenly virtues is signified—namely, angelic protection—as Isaiah says concerning the Lord’s vineyard: “He surrounded it with a wall and dug around the vineyard” (Isa. 5:2). She dwells in the hiding-place of the wall because she is surrounded on every side by the protection of angels and guarded from the temptations of the devil. [Col. 1066B]

“Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.” “You,” he says, “my beloved, who rest most sweetly in the bed of contemplation, come and show me your face”—that is, leave the secrecy of repose for public action, and display the beauty of your good works to others as an example. He says, “Show me,” as though the Church shows her face to God when, through works of virtue performed for the benefit and progress of her neighbors, she reveals how great is the beauty she possesses within. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). “Let your voice sound in my ears”—namely, the voice of preaching or of divine praise, by which you cause others to advance. The Church’s voice sounds in the Lord’s ears when God rejoices in the conversion of many through preaching.

He rightly says, “Show me your face, and let your voice sound,” not another’s: “Show me your face,” namely, the face I gave you in baptism, when I cleansed you from every sin. “Let your voice,” he says, “sound in my ears,” so that it may proceed from the sincere intention of love for me, and so that you may preach for no other reason than for me. [Col. 1066C]

**Verse 15.** “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has flowered.” This is the voice of the bridegroom commanding his bride and the daughters of Jerusalem—namely, the holy teachers or faithful souls. “Catch for us,” he says, “the little foxes.” The fox is a crafty and deceitful animal, living in caves and dens and moving not along a straight but along a crooked path. It therefore designates heretics or schismatics, who destroy the vineyards—that is, the Church of God—and never cease to tear apart and deceive the people of the faithful.

He therefore commands that the little foxes be caught: that is, that they should not cease to fight down and destroy heretical depravity at its very beginning, lest, once it has grown strong, it attack with greater force. “For our vineyard has flowered,” that is, the Church has sent forth the flowers of virtues throughout the whole world. Note that above he used “vineyards” in the plural, but now says in the singular, “our vineyard has flowered,” because from many Churches there is one chosen Church. [Col. 1066D]

**Verse 16.** “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” This is the voice of the bride. “My beloved is mine”—understand: let him be joined to me by the bond of charity and love, and let me be joined to him and consent through the reciprocal exchange of love.

Or understand it thus: “My beloved” should speak words of exhortation and divine promise; and “I” should show him my face. Or again: may “my beloved” deign to be joined to me by the bond of charity, and may I be joined to him by the bond of worthy obedience, obeying his commands. “Who feeds among the lilies,” that is, he delights and rejoices among the bright and fragrant virtues of the saints.

It should be noted that above “lily” was said in the singular, but here “lilies” is plural, because the virtues of the saints are many, whereas there is one faith and one charity, in which God chiefly delights. Or “he feeds among the lilies” means that he delights most sweetly among choirs of virgins. The whiteness of lilies is rightly compared with virginal purity.

“Until the day breathes,” that is, until the clouds of the present life pass away and the day appears—until the clarity of eternal blessedness arrives. The meaning is this: my beloved grants me assistance, and I offer him worthy obedience; he delights in the virtues of the saints until, when the night of the present life has passed—the life in which he is seen “through a mirror and in an enigma”—the day of heavenly glory appears, so that he may be seen face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). [Col. 1067A]

**Verse 17.** “Return; be like, my beloved, a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel.” This is the voice of the Church desiring the appearance of her bridegroom.

“O my beloved, who commands me to rise from the bed of repose and urges me to show you my face, return”—that is, permit me to contemplate the glory of your divinity, and permit me, while I am still in this pilgrimage, to possess at least in figure and in an enigma what you perfectly promise me in the other life—namely, blessedness and knowledge of you.

“Be like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of Bethel.” It was said above that gazelles look down upon the plains and strive toward the heights of the mountains. Christ is therefore compared with gazelles because, rising in the flesh from the dead, he sought the heights of heaven.

He is called a fawn of the deer—that is, the son of the ancient Fathers. The deer are the patriarchs and prophets, from whom Christ derived the origin of his flesh. It is said that the fawn has this nature: when the sun is hot, it seeks shady and shadowed places where it may be protected from the heat. So Christ rests in the minds of those who are cooled by the dew of the Holy Spirit from the heat of carnal pleasures.

It is as though she were saying: “O my beloved, return”—that is, make me glad by frequently illuminating me through your visitation—you who, through the flesh you assumed, have already penetrated the heights of heaven.

The mountains of Bethel signify the minds of the saints, raised above earthly things by heavenly desires. Bethel is interpreted as “the rising house” or “the house of watchfulness,” and it signifies the watchful minds of the saints, which rise up to desire heavenly things and keep watch in order to receive them. They have within themselves God as an inhabitant, who says through the prophet: “I shall dwell in them and walk among them” (Lev. 26:12). Upon these mountains of Bethel, therefore, the beloved is like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer, because he deigns to visit those who strive to be the house of God.

### Chapter III

**Verse 1.** “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.” This is the voice of the Church gathered from the nations. “On my bed,” she says—that is, while I was still resting in carnal desires and still placed in the darkness of unbelief and ignorance—“I sought him whom my soul loves.”

Many philosophers, although they did not know God, nevertheless sought him with the greatest zeal, wishing to know the Creator through creation. Such was Plato, who discussed the soul at length in the *Timaeus*, and such were Aristotle, Socrates, and the others, who spent the whole of their lives in study for the purpose of seeking the truth. “I sought him and did not find him,” for God could not be known through worldly wisdom.

**Verse 2.** “I shall rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I shall seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.” “I shall rise,” she says, “from the bed of the body and of carnal pleasure, and I shall go around the city of this world, traversing seas and lands. Through the streets and squares I shall seek him whom my soul loves”—that is, I shall look upon those who walk along the broad roads of this age and are devoted to its pleasures, to see whether I might perhaps find the footprints of my beloved.

Although this may be said by way of example concerning many, it was fulfilled especially in the eunuch who came from the ends of the earth to worship the God of heaven in Jerusalem. Philip found him and showed him Christ in the prophecy of Isaiah (Acts 8:27). It was likewise fulfilled in Cornelius, who, while still a pagan and ignorant of God, gave alms and devoted himself to prayers; Peter baptized him and his entire household (ibid. 10:22). She repeats the difficulty of finding him and says: “I sought him and did not find him.” [Col. 1068A]

**Verse 3.** “The watchmen who guard the city found me.” The watchmen are the holy apostles and the other teachers of the Church, who guard the city—that is, the holy Church—and defend it from the attacks of unbelievers and spiritual enemies. She asks them:

“Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” The Church questions the watchmen when she receives their preaching with attentive ear. [Col. 1068B]

**Verse 4.** “A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.” To pass by the watchmen means diligently to examine their words and teaching. We commonly say, “I went through a book while reading,” or “I passed through it.” “When I had passed them,” she says, “I found him whom my soul loves,” because, when we seek the sayings or writings of the saints with attentive meditation, we immediately find the beloved: we find God in their teachings.

This may also be understood as follows: “When I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves”—that is, when I understood that Christ surpasses every sublimity and grace, then I found him whom my soul loves; that is, then I truly understood how far he stands above the merits of all the other saints.

“I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into the house of my mother and into the chamber of my mother.” This means: I clung to him with the most ardent faith and devotion; I will not let him go, but will persevere in his love and faith until I bring him into the house of my mother and into the chamber of my mother—that is, until I preach him to the Synagogue, which is spiritually my mother, and bring it also to faith in him.

This will happen at the end of the world, when, as the Apostle says, “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered; then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26). The Church therefore promises herself so much through the charity of her bridegroom that she even believes she can convert the Synagogue.

When she says, “until I bring him in,” it should not be thought that she will abandon him once she has brought him into her mother’s chamber. Rather, “until” means forever: I shall always cling to him and always persevere in his faith and love. The Psalm says something similar: “So our eyes are toward the Lord our God until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122:3). Will our eyes not be toward him after he has had mercy on us? Certainly they will. [Col. 1068C]

**Verse 5.** “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the deer of the fields, do not stir up or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.” This verse is repeated twice; it has already appeared above. There, however, it referred to the primitive Church gathered from the Jews; here it refers to the Church gathered from the nations and more closely joined to Christ by the bond of love.

For God has one and the same care for the saints, whether they pleased him in circumcision or in the time of baptism, when the grace of the Gospel shone forth. Since this verse has already been expounded, it must now be considered why the Church is introduced as though sleeping, and why he adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken her, when shortly before he introduced her not as sleeping or resting but as engaged in the labor of a most arduous search, seeking the bridegroom.

If she was seeking the bridegroom, how was she resting? Yet seeking Christ is the sweetest and most delightful sleep. The Church therefore sleeps and seeks Christ: she sleeps with respect to earthly desires and the activities of the world, but she is awake and seeks the bridegroom because she clings to his contemplation, desires him alone, and strives to reach him.

The bridegroom therefore adjures the daughters of Jerusalem—namely, souls clinging to desires for their heavenly homeland—not to awaken her from this sleep of most sweet repose and contemplation until she herself wishes. Sleep is rightly called love, because just as a sleeping person closes his eyes to visible things and contemplates invisible things, so one who devotes himself to divine contemplation sleeps, as it were, as a stranger to outward things and sees only spiritual and heavenly realities.

Nor is it surprising that love is called sleep, since in what follows love is called death: “Love is strong as death.” When he says, “until she herself wishes,” he shows that the Church from the nations will voluntarily prepare herself to endure labors and persecutions for Christ. [Col. 1068D]

**Verse 6.** “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense and every kind of perfumer’s powder?” This is the voice of the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, of the saints of the primitive Church—marveling at the beauty of the Church gathered from the nations.

“Who is this?” they say. “Who”—that is, what kind of person? How worthy of praise and wonder is she, who, cleansed by circumcision and not yet sanctified by baptism, is already running to God?

“She comes up through the wilderness.” This is said in imitation of the ancient Jewish people, who, freed from Egyptian slavery, passed through the wilderness and, after crossing the Red Sea, came to the promised land. So the Church was already ascending through the wilderness of the nations, freed from Egypt—that is, from the confusion of idolatry—and with Pharaoh, that is, the devil, drowned, so that she might be fed with heavenly manna and enter the true promised land.

“She comes up,” she says, to the mountains of virtues, or even to heaven itself, raised up by virtues. In the Psalm she says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120:1), and elsewhere: “To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 122:1).

These mountains are the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and other saints of God, who are called mountains because of their virtues. First the Church—or the faithful soul, which considers their teaching and deeds—raises her eyes to the mountains, that is, to the saints, and rejoices to be fortified by their example and intercession. Then, advancing, she dares to direct the gaze of her heart even toward him who made the mountains and says: “To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven”—that is, who gladly rests in the saints.

“Like a column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense.” Smoke arises from fire and immediately seeks the higher regions of the air, until it is withdrawn from the sight of those who watch it. Smoke therefore signifies holy desire infused with the fire of divine love. She is not simply compared with smoke but with a column of smoke, because the holy Church, or the soul that loves God, is slender and delicate, attenuated by the disciplines of the Holy Spirit and lacking the coarseness of carnal desires.

Alternatively, she is compared with a column of smoke rather than dispersed smoke because of the unity of the Church, which is one in Christ.

He shows from what source that smoke comes when he adds: “From myrrh and frankincense and every kind of perfumer’s powder.” Myrrh is used to embalm the bodies of the dead, while frankincense is burned in God’s sacrifice. Therefore myrrh signifies the mortification of the flesh, and frankincense expresses the purity of prayers.

The Church is thus likened to a column of myrrh-and-frankincense smoke because the saints strive to please God through the mortification of their flesh and through prayers poured out with a pure and simple heart.

“And every kind of perfumer’s powder,” that is, a collection of all virtues. The spices are said not to have remained whole but to have been reduced to powder, because the deeds of the saints must be examined with great discernment and sifted, as it were, through the sieve of the most subtle consideration, lest anything harsh or inappropriate be found in them, and lest the adversary—manifold in form, and accustomed cunningly to cause harm even through good things—creep in through the virtues themselves. [Col. 1069D]

**Verse 7.** “Behold, Solomon’s bed; sixty strong men surround it, from the strongest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilled in war.” Where this beloved and marvelous woman has ascended is shown when it is added: “Behold, Solomon’s bed,” and so forth.

Although Solomon’s bed may be understood as the repose of that heavenly blessedness in which God rests with his saints, it is more plausibly understood here as the present Church, in which the saints of God, with the tumult of vices quieted, delight in the embrace of Solomon—that is, of the peaceful man. Hence the Psalmist says of Christ: “His place became established in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3).

Solomon’s bed, therefore—that is, the Church—is surrounded by sixty strong men from the strongest of Israel. By the sixty strong men, the order of teachers is understood: they either fortify the Church by preaching or desire, through contemplation, to reach that heavenly blessedness.

The number sixty consists of six and ten: six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty. Six signifies the perfection of a work, because God perfected his works in six days; ten signifies the reward and recompense that will be given to the elect at the end. Thus we read that those who came into the vineyard received a denarius (Matt. 20:10).

The sixty strong men therefore signify, as has been said, the holy teachers, strong and steadfast in spirit. It is added, “from the strongest of Israel”: all who believe in Christ and love Christ are called Israel, that is, “the man who sees God.” The strongest of Israel are those who know how to protect the Church by preaching and defend it from the assaults of demons and the attacks of heretics. They surround Solomon’s bed because the Church has been entrusted to them and must be guarded by their vigilant care.

“All holding swords and most skilled in war.” They hold the spiritual sword, the word of God, concerning which the Apostle says: “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). They are most skilled in war because those who wage war against the rulers and powers of the world, against the governors of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places must be trained in the art of spiritual warfare (ibid. 6:12). This enemy is exceedingly cunning and, both through the subtlety of his spiritual nature and through the long duration of his existence, exceedingly experienced. Against him the saints take up battle. [Col. 1070C]

**Verse 8.** “Each one’s sword is upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night.” The thigh is understood as the propagation of offspring. They therefore have swords upon their thighs who, through fear of God, suppress and restrain all movements of carnal pleasure.

This is “because of the terrors of the night,” that is, because of the hidden snares of the evil enemy, who in the night of this age especially lies in wait for the saints who hold preeminence in the Church, so that, once they have been deceived, he may defile Solomon’s bed—that is, the repose of the saints.

It should be noted that above they are said to hold swords, whereas here they have swords upon their thighs. They hold swords in order to resist their adversaries, overcome them, and pierce heretics and all who contradict sound faith. They have swords upon their thighs in order to care for themselves and restrain the outpouring of carnal pleasures, lest, while preaching to others, they themselves become disqualified (1 Cor. 9:27). [Col. 1070D]

**Verse 9.** “King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon.” What was previously designated by Solomon’s bed is now designated by the litter: namely, the holy Church, in which the saints of God rest as upon a bed and, as upon a bed, recline for the banquets of eternal blessedness and satiety.

“Solomon made the litter from the wood of Lebanon.” Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, whose trees surpass all others in height, beauty, and durability. They therefore signify the saints, shining with the beauty of virtues and hastening toward eternal things.

Lebanon is interpreted as “whitened,” “whitening,” or “whitewashing.” The wood of Lebanon is therefore the saints who have been made white or whitened in baptism and adorned with the beauty of every virtue.

**Verse 10.** “He made its columns of silver.” The columns signify the teachers of that same Church, who support and strengthen it by word and example. Hence it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “James and John and Cephas, who were reputed to be columns” (Gal. 2:9).

These columns are of silver because they shine with the splendor of heavenly speech. “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings” (Ps. 12:7), and so forth. [Col. 1071A]

“A golden back-rest, a purple ascent.” By the golden back-rest, eternal rest is understood, which is promised to the saints in the Church. Yet the ascent to it is purple. The purple ascent is the passion of Christ, because purple resembles the color of blood.

By the purple ascent one reaches the back-rest, because those arrive at the banquet of eternal feasting and the repose of heavenly rest who strive in the present to honor and imitate the passion of the Redeemer worthily. For unless someone imitates Christ’s actions and life, he cannot reach eternal rest.

“He spread it with love in the middle, because of the daughters of Jerusalem.” He spread it with love in the middle because Christ commended his love to all the faithful by suffering for us and preparing rest for us, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “God commends his love in us, because, while we were still sinners, he handed over his Son to death for us” (Rom. 5:8).

Alternatively, the silver columns signify the apostles and apostolic men; the golden back-rest signifies the order of teachers, who, when they promise us the ineffable joys of eternal life, cause us to rest sweetly. This back-rest is rightly called golden because the reward that the saints await is ineffable. Among perishable things nothing is more precious than gold.

The purple ascent signifies the order of martyrs, who, imitating Christ’s passion, shed their blood for him.

“But what shall we do?” says blessed Gregory. “We see that, since we have no merit, we have no place among the teachers or among the martyrs.” It follows: “He spread it with love in the middle.” Let us therefore possess the love with which the middle of this litter has been spread. It is for this reason that love is called the broad commandment, because it prepares eternal salvation for all who observe it.

Let us hold fast to this love effectively. Through it we shall be saved, and this is “because of the daughters of Jerusalem”—that is, because of simple souls who are conscious of no virtue in themselves. The more conscious they are of their own weakness, the more eagerly they strive to love their Savior and Redeemer. [Col. 1071C]

**Verse 11.** “Go out and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon wearing the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the joy of his heart.” This is the voice of the Church inviting faithful souls to contemplate how marvelous and beautiful her bridegroom is.

The daughters of Zion are the Churches; they are also the daughters of Jerusalem—namely, holy souls, citizens of that heavenly city, who enjoy perpetual peace with the angels and contemplate the glory of God through contemplation.

“Go out,” he says, “daughters of Zion”—that is, come out from the turbulent life of this age, so that with an unencumbered mind you may contemplate him whom you love.

“And see,” he says, “King Solomon”—that is, Christ, the true peaceful one—“wearing the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” It is as though he were saying: “Consider Christ clothed in flesh for your sake, flesh that he took from the flesh of his mother, the Virgin.”

He calls the flesh that Christ assumed for us a diadem. In that flesh, when he died, he destroyed the dominion of death; in that flesh, when he rose again, he granted us the hope of rising. Concerning this diadem the Apostle says: “We see Jesus crowned with glory and honor because of his suffering” (Heb. 2:9).

He is said to have been crowned by his mother because the Virgin Mary supplied him with the material of flesh from her own flesh.

“On the day of his betrothal,” that is, at the time of his incarnation, when he joined the Church to himself, “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27); or when God was joined to humanity.

“And on the day of the joy of his heart.” The joy and gladness of Christ is the salvation and redemption of the human race. Thus, in the Gospel, when he saw many flocking to his faith, the evangelist says: “At that hour he rejoiced and said: I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). In the Gospel parable, after finding the sheep, he called his friends and said: “Rejoice with me” (Luke 15:6).

The whole passage may also be referred literally and simply to Christ’s passion. Foreseeing Christ’s passion in the Spirit, Solomon long beforehand admonished the daughter of Zion—that is, the people of Israel: “Go out,” he said, “and see King Solomon”—that is, Christ—“wearing the diadem,” the crown of thorns with which his mother, the Synagogue, crowned him, “on the day of his betrothal,” when he joined the Church to himself, “and on the day of the joy of his heart,” when he rejoiced that through his passion the world was redeemed from the power of the devil.

“Go out,” therefore—that is, come out from the darkness of unbelief—“and see,” that is, understand with the mind, because the one who suffers as a man is true God. Or, alternatively, go outside the gate of your city so that you may see him crucified on Mount Golgotha. [Col. 1072A]

### Chapter IV

**Verse 1.** “How beautiful you are, my beloved; how beautiful you are, and fair.” The voice of Christ repeats twice, “How beautiful you are,” referring to her work and her preaching. In her work, because you do nothing shameful or unworthy of my sight; in her preaching, because you never cease to invite your companions, the daughters of Jerusalem, to contemplate the mystery of my incarnation. [Col. 1072B]

“Your eyes are like those of doves.” By the eyes, the acuity of spiritual senses is understood, by which the Church contemplates divine and eternal things. The Church’s eyes are compared with the eyes of doves because of spiritual grace, since the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove (Matt. 3:16). It follows:

“Besides what lies hidden within”—that is, besides the glory of that heavenly reward which you will receive at the end of the age. Although you contemplate it in the present through faith, it nevertheless lies hidden within; for it cannot be seen in the present but will be perfected in the future.

“Your hair is like flocks of goats that have come up from Mount Gilead.” By the hair of the Church, the Church’s subtle thoughts are understood, by which temporal matters are generally arranged. They are compared with flocks of goats because these animals are clean and graze lying back on rocks or in high places. So the thoughts of the saints, although they are formed in temporal matters for bodily necessity, nevertheless do not depart in their inward intention from heavenly things; even in the care they devote to bodily necessity, they gaze continually, as it were, upon heaven.

We may also understand by the eyes the teachers and preachers of the Church, who hold the highest place in the body of which Christ is the head and see heavenly and spiritual things more than the other members.

By the hair we understand the countless multitude of simple believers established in the lay order. Although they see spiritual things less clearly, they provide great adornment to the Church through their multitude and number.

They are rightly compared with flocks of goats. The goat is appropriate to sinners; through it are understood the communities of the faithful devoted to worldly activities, which cannot be carried out without sin. It follows appropriately: “that have come up from Mount Gilead.”

Gilead is interpreted literally as “heap of testimony,” because when Jacob was departing from Mesopotamia, Laban pursued him and found him on the third day; there they raised a heap of stones as a testimony to their mutual covenant (Gen. 31:46).

Mystically, the heap of testimony is Christ, in whom the multitude of all the saints is established. They are living stones adhering to that true stone of which Peter says: “Coming to him, the living stone, you also, as living stones, are built upon him” (1 Pet. 2:4).

The flocks of goats therefore came up from Mount Gilead because the multitudes of the saints ascend to the heights of virtue and strive in all things to follow Christ’s teaching and commands. [Col. 1072D]

**Verse 2.** “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing.”

Just as by the hair of the Church is understood the innumerable multitude of simple believers, so also by the teeth of the Church are understood its teachers. For with our teeth we chew food, and the holy teachers are rightly likened to teeth, because they break down, by explaining them, the spiritual foods that the simple cannot grasp.

The chief tooth of the Church was Peter, to whom it was said in a vision: “Rise, kill, and eat” (Acts 10:13)—as though it were said: “Kill those whom you convert to the faith” from what they are, that is, so that they may cease to be sinners; “and eat,” that is, transfer or transform them into the body of the Church.

These teeth are rightly compared with sheep shorn and washed in the bath. Sheep are usually washed in running water after shearing, lest unwashed sweat cling to their bodies and produce mange. Thus the holy teachers and masters of the Church are shorn: washed in the bath of baptism, they have lost their fleeces—that is, their possessions and property—for Christ.

What follows, “that have come up from the washing,” applies indeed to all believers, for no one can be a believer without the washing of baptism. But shearing does not apply to everyone, because not all are so perfect that they can give up their possessions for Christ. It applies especially to those who, according to the Lord’s word, sell all they have and give to the poor (Matt. 19:21), and, naked and unencumbered, follow Christ.

Such, then, are the teeth of the holy Church: its preachers and ministers, sheep washed in baptism through innocence, rejoicing in voluntary poverty and the stripping away of possessions.

It follows:

“All of them with twin offspring, and none among them is barren.”

They are preeminent in twin charity and love of God and neighbor, and teach that this should be observed; or else because they preach both faith and works. “None among them is barren”: that is, no one is a stranger to good works.

**Verse 3.** “Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is sweet.”

By the lips of the Church are understood the holy preachers, who are also represented by the teeth. Scarlet has the appearance of blood or fire. The lips of the Church—that is, its holy preachers—are therefore compared with a scarlet thread, because they constantly preach the Passion of Christ, who shed his blood for our redemption.

Or they are likened to a scarlet thread because the preachers burn with love: loving those to whom they devote the words of preaching, and even those from whom they suffer evil. This too is signified by the fact that the Holy Spirit appeared in tongues of fire (Acts 2:3), because he made the apostles both speaking and burning: burning with love and speaking through preaching.

It is rightly called a scarlet thread. A thread binds and constricts the hair, and the holy teachers, through their preaching, bind the multitude of the faithful in the Church into the unity of faith and love and bring them together into a single beauty.

The hair may also signify the subtle thoughts of the mind. We bind the tresses with a scarlet thread when we constrain and restrain our thoughts through the discipline of the fear of God.

“And your speech is sweet.”

The speech of the Church is sweet when the holy teachers recall and proclaim the Passion of their Redeemer and how greatly God has loved humanity, or when they announce the heavenly rewards to their hearers.

“Your cheeks are like a slice of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within.”

We said above that the Church is signified by the cheeks. For when we blush, the redness of blood spreads over the cheeks. A pomegranate has a red rind, while within it is filled with a multitude of seeds; hence it is called a “seeded apple,” or pomegranate.

By a slice of a pomegranate, therefore, is understood the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, which was also represented above by scarlet. One thing is often expressed through different figures.

The cheeks of the Church are therefore compared with a slice of a pomegranate, because the holy teachers reverently commemorate the Passion of their Redeemer and are not ashamed of his cross; indeed, they glory in it, saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). And elsewhere the Apostle writes to his disciple: “Do not be ashamed,” he says, “of the cross of Christ, nor of me, his prisoner” (2 Tim. 1:8).

The cheeks are rightly compared not with a whole pomegranate but with a slice. When a pomegranate is broken, redness appears on the outside and whiteness within. So also, when the holy preachers and teachers proclaim Christ’s Passion, there is, as it were, redness on the outside; but when they demonstrate how great a benefit our redemption has brought forth from it, and that through Christ’s Passion humanity is not only justified from sins but has also merited fellowship with God, what is hidden within is, as it were, white.

The martyrs may also be represented by the cheeks of the Church. They are red through the shedding of their blood, like a pomegranate; but when the pomegranate is broken, whiteness appears within, because after death they shine forth through miracles.

**Verse 4.** “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements.”

The holy preachers and teachers of the Church are the neck of the holy Church. Here the same persons are designated by the neck who above were designated by the eyes or teeth—namely, the holy preachers, who, like necks, transmit accepted food of the word of God to the body for its nourishment and utter the voice of divine preaching to their hearers.

Or the holy teachers are signified by the neck because, just as the head and the other members are joined to the body through the neck, so the holy teachers are mediators between Christ and the other faithful whom they instruct; they join Christ, as it were, to his body, that is, to the Church.

This neck is compared with David’s tower. David, which is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance,” signifies Christ. The whole Church, indeed, is the city of David—that is, of the great King Christ, who is strong of hand because he conquered the devil, according to the Psalmist: “The Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8). He is also desirable in appearance, because, as the Apostle says, “angels long to look into” him (1 Pet. 1:12).

The tower of this city consists of those who surpass the others either in knowledge or in perfection of conduct.

“Which was built with battlements.”

The battlements are the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, from which, like arrows, proceed weapons by which hostile powers are driven back.

“A thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of the mighty.”

The thousand shields signify innumerable defenses of divine protection, by which the holy Church is surrounded and defended. “All the armor of the mighty” means every equipment either of holy conduct or of divine preaching.

The neck of the Church—that is, its preachers and teachers—is rightly compared with David’s tower because they are always, as it were, engaged in war, fighting for the defense of the holy Church.

**Verse 5.** “Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.”

The two breasts of the Church signify the same holy teachers. It is not surprising that one and the same thing is represented in different ways. The holy teachers are eyes because they show those entrusted to them the paths of life they ought to enter. They are teeth because they grind and break up the foods of the divine Scriptures so that they may be chewed—that is, understood—by the simple. They are the neck because they join the head and the members, that is, Christ and the Church.

These teachers, then, are also the breasts of the Church, because they nourish the little ones and simple believers with the milk of the word of God. Thus, speaking to the less advanced, the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, and as infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2).

It is rightly said not simply “breasts,” but, with an addition, “two breasts,” since a woman has neither more nor fewer than two breasts. The holy teachers nourish little ones from both peoples—the Jewish people and the Gentiles—with the milk of the word of God. For Paul also says of himself: “He who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised worked also through me among the Gentiles” (Gal. 2:8).

The two breasts are aptly said to be like two twin fawns of a gazelle. These are the offspring and children of our Savior Jesus Christ, who above was represented by the gazelle. These animals see with exceptional sharpness and climb to higher places with extraordinary speed. So also the holy teachers both see for themselves what ought to be done and show it to others; and, scorning earthly things, they strive to ascend to heavenly ones.

**Verse 6.** “They feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline.”

“They feed among the lilies”: that is, they delight in the purest and brightest meanings of the Scriptures.

“Until the day breathes”: that is, until that eternal day comes, which the Psalmist longed for when he said: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11).

“And the shadows incline”: that is, until the sorrows and disturbances of this age pass away.

“Until the day breathes”—that is, until the day rises. The day will breathe, that is, rise, when that true Sun of righteousness, Christ, appears. Then the shadows will incline: all the clouds of sorrow and the darkness of the present age will pass away.

If we consider the literal meaning itself, the expression beautifully depicts the rising of day and the departure of night. For night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth, which rises beneath the earth as the sun descends; but when the sun again rises above the earth, the shadows incline, that is, night gives way.

They therefore feed among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline, because the preaching and teaching of the holy teachers are necessary only in the present life. In the other life, after the eternal day has appeared and the night of the present age has ended, no one will need to be taught, because all will contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face (2 Cor. 3:18).

Hence the Lord also says through the prophet Jeremiah: “No longer shall a man teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest” (Jer. 31:34).

“I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.”

In myrrh is understood the mortification of the flesh or endurance of sufferings for Christ; in frankincense, the devotion of holy prayers. The mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense are therefore the minds of the saints, exalted through contemplation.

The Bridegroom promises that he will come to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense because he deigns to visit by his visitation those minds that put their members to death with their vices and desires (Gal. 5:24), and that make themselves, through their devotion to holy prayers, a sacrifice pleasing to God.

**Verse 7.** “You are altogether beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you.”

The Bridegroom speaks to his beloved, the bride.

“You are altogether beautiful.” “In every respect,” he says, “you admit no blemish or wrinkle.” For it is not only the teachers and those who are wholly perfect—those who excel in supreme knowledge and contemplation—who are beautiful before the eyes of God. All the simple faithful who are adorned with right faith and good works are also considered beautiful in the eyes of the Bridegroom.

For, as the Psalmist says: “He has blessed all who fear the Lord, both the small and the great” (Ps. 113:13). Therefore he says, “You are altogether beautiful,” not merely one part of you.

We say this not because anyone can be without sin in the present life, since it is written: “No one upon earth is without sin, not even an infant of one day” (Job 14:4). Rather, it is because perfect faith and heavenly desire wipe away every blemish of lesser sin. We are not now speaking of graver sins; those who commit them are no longer the bride of Christ and possess no share in this holy beauty.

For this reason John says: “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:6)—understand, with sin unto death—not that anyone is free from lesser sin, without which this life is not lived.

The Church, therefore, is altogether beautiful insofar as she keeps herself chaste and free from every sin. If she is at times darkened by lesser sin, her former beauty is restored within her by swift repentance and right faith directed toward heavenly desire.

**Verse 8.** “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come.”

Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia. In Hebrew its name is interpreted as “whitening” or “making white”; from the Greek it is interpreted as “frankincense.” Hence above, where it says, “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense,” the hill is understood to be Lebanon.

The Bridegroom therefore calls his bride one made white by baptism, whitened by the splendor of every virtue, and burning with devotion to holy prayers.

He calls her to come—that is, to advance in virtue. God calls the soul not only when he leads it, stripped of the bonds of the flesh, to heavenly rewards; he also exhorts it through inward inspiration to advance in virtue. For as many virtues as the saints advance in, so many steps, as it were, do they take toward God.

He says “come” a third time because he wants her to be perfect in thought, word, and deed.

Or he calls her first to come to him through faith; he calls her a second time to receive, once freed from the body, the reward worthy of heavenly prizes; and he calls her a third time to rejoice on the day of the general resurrection, when she has taken up her body again and is crowned forever with a double garment.

“You shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards.”

They say that Amana is the Cilician mountain Amanus, which is also called Taurus. Senir and Hermon are mountains of Judea in which lions and leopards are said to dwell.

By these mountains are understood the powers of the world—kings and princes—who are exalted like mountains in pride and provide dwellings, as it were, for evil spirits, like lions and leopards.

Evil spirits are called lions because of their pride and leopards because of their fierceness, or also because of their thousand arts of doing harm, since the leopard is a variegated animal.

The Church is crowned from these mountains when the princes of the world are converted to the faith of Christ. She is rewarded for salvation not only because of her own virtues but also because of the conversion of such people.

This may also be understood in relation to the present. The Church is crowned from the summit of these mountains when, after the princes have been subjected to the Catholic faith, the Church that was formerly oppressed is crowned and glorified in Christ—as happened in the time of Constantine, when, after his conversion, the Church was wonderfully glorified.

She is crowned from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards when she converts the proud and all who are savage and deceitful, and receives eternal rewards also for their conversion.

**Verse 9.** “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.”

He calls the holy Church his bride and sister. She is his bride because Christ, having become incarnate, betrothed her to himself and, cleansing her from the filth of sins, joined her to himself through the dowry of the Holy Spirit.

She is his sister because for her sake he deigned to become incarnate and to become her brother, as he said to the women when he rose from the dead: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10).

When he says that his heart has been wounded, he expresses the greatness of the love with which he loves his holy Church. He affirms this by repeating and emphasizing it: “You have wounded my heart,” so that by this repetition he might show how greatly he loves his Church.

He then explains by what she has wounded him.

“With one of your eyes and with one lock of the hair of your neck.”

By the eyes of the Church we understand spiritual perceptions or holy teachers; by the hair, the multitudes of the peoples subject to her, by whom the holy Church is adorned.

The meaning is this: Although you are altogether beautiful, O Church, and although I love you for many reasons, the splendor of your spiritual perceptions and the sincerity of your teachers especially delight me, as does the simplicity of life among the subject peoples who piously and faithfully obey the words of the teachers.

Although above he spoke of the eyes and hair in the plural, here he says “with one eye” and “with one lock of hair” in the singular, so that by this the unity of the holy teachers might be expressed. There is one unity of the heavenly doctrine that they impart to those subject to them. For, as the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5), and likewise there is one devotion among the faithful subject to them.

The statement, “You have wounded my heart,” may also be understood of Christ’s Passion: “You have wounded my heart,” that is, “By your love you caused me to be wounded on the cross.”

It should be noted that he says, “with one lock of the hair of your neck.” For we said that the neck signifies the teachers, and the hair of the Church clings to the neck. Through it, the subject peoples are nourished by the holy teachers, cling to their sound doctrine, and strive to live according to their commands.

**Verse 10.** “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!”

Above we said that the same teachers are represented by the breasts who are designated by the eyes. The holy teachers are breasts because they nourish the humble with simple doctrine; they are eyes when they preach the highest and heavenly things.

He says, therefore: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!” That is, “How beautiful are your teachers!” For their speech excels in eloquence and is precious in the weight of its meanings.

“Your breasts are more beautiful than wine.”

This verse has already been expounded above, where it says: “Your breasts are better than wine.” It should be noted that above the Church praised the breasts of her Bridegroom, saying, “Your breasts are better than wine”; now, in turn, the Bridegroom exalts the breasts of his bride, so that through this the unity of the Church may be commended.

Christ is the head and the Church is his body; the beginning of evangelical preaching excels the legal judgment.

“And the fragrance of your perfumes surpasses all spices.”

The perfumes of the Church are the gifts of heavenly doctrine or even the reputation of the virtues that emanates from the Church. The spices signify the observances of the Law.

The fragrance of the Church’s perfumes therefore surpasses the spices, because the dignity and reputation of evangelical perfection transcend every praise of legal observance.

**Verse 11.** “Your lips drip with honeycomb, O bride.”

A honeycomb is honey in wax. Honey in wax is spiritual understanding within the letter.

The lips of the Church are therefore called a dripping honeycomb because the holy teachers, who are represented by the lips, bring forth spiritual instruction for the education of the faithful.

The lips of the Church are called not merely a honeycomb but a dripping honeycomb. A honeycomb drips when, overflowing with an abundance of honey, it can no longer contain it within its waxen cells.

Divine Scripture is rightly called a dripping honeycomb because it is understood in many ways and explained according to various senses: sometimes according to the letter, sometimes according to allegory, sometimes according to morality, and sometimes according to anagoge—that is, the higher sense.

“Honey and milk are under your tongue.”

Milk is suited to little ones; therefore milk signifies simple doctrine, by which beginners among believers are nourished. Honey, which is believed to be made from the dew of heaven, signifies heavenly and spiritual doctrine, which is suited to the perfect and instructed.

Under the tongue of the Church, therefore, there are honey and milk, because at times she announces heavenly mysteries to the perfect and at times plain and simple things to the inexperienced.

“And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.”

The garments of the Church are the adornments of good works, according to what John says in the Apocalypse: “The fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints” (Rev. 19:8). And in Job it is said: “I clothed myself with righteousness, and it clothed me like a garment and diadem of judgment” (Job 29:14).

We said that frankincense signifies the purity of holy prayers. The garments of the Church are therefore compared with frankincense, because all the works of the Church are, as it were, prayers. In everything she does, she continually entreats the Lord, and in this way what the Lord says is fulfilled: “One ought always to pray” (Luke 8:1).

This cannot always be fulfilled before the Lord in any other way unless our entire life and conduct are such that they are counted as prayer in the sight of God.

Frankincense is a tree of Arabia, resembling laurel in its bark and leaf and emitting a sap like that of the almond tree. It is collected twice a year, in autumn and spring.

For the autumn harvest, the trees are prepared by cutting their bark during the blazing heat of summer. A rich foam then spurts forth and thickens as it congeals; where the nature of the place requires it, a palm-leaf covering receives it. What remains attached to the tree is scraped off with iron; hence the purest frankincense appears to be bark-like—that is, white.

The second harvest is in spring. For it, the bark is cut in winter, and a red substance emerges, inferior to the first. The product of a young tree is believed to be whiter, but that of an old tree more fragrant.

What hangs from it in the rounded form of a drop is called “male” frankincense; the drop expelled by shaking is called manna.

**Verse 12.** “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.”

He calls the Church his sister and bride. From being a servant-girl, he made her his sister, and, having pledged her to himself through the dowry of the Holy Spirit, made her his bride.

This Church is a garden because she produces the shoots of spiritual virtues, which are designated in what follows by the names of spices.

This garden is enclosed because the holy Church is fortified by the help of the Lord her Redeemer and surrounded by the protection of angelic powers; she is open to none of the snares of evil spirits.

This same Church is a sealed fountain: a fountain because she flows with streams of heavenly doctrine, by which all who believe in Christ are washed from sins and given drink through knowledge of the truth.

The fountain is sealed because the word of evangelical faith is secured by the seal of truth, so that neither heretics nor evil spirits can violate or break into the Catholic faith.

This garden, or this fountain—that is, the Church—was first planted or arose in a small corner of Judea. Then, through preaching disseminated throughout the world, she sent forth her garden plots or streams. Hence it follows:

**Verse 13.** “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruit of apple trees.”

The shoots of the Church, as was said, are the growth of faith and the dissemination of preaching. These shoots are a paradise.
