“Paradise” in Greek means “garden” in Latin. The primitive Church, which was like a garden in Judea, sent forth throughout the world many gardens—that is, Churches.

The pomegranates, whose rind is red, signify those who have not only been sanctified by the general baptism but have also been baptized in their own blood through suffering and have become martyrs.

The fruit of apple trees signifies works of virtue, or those who practice the virtues themselves in their conduct.

The shoots of the Church were therefore a paradise of pomegranates because, after the apostles, the martyrs held the first place in the Church. They strove to imitate the Passion of the Lord by suffering themselves.

In a general sense, however, the whole multitude may be understood as a paradise of pomegranates: they are pomegranates because they always keep the Passion of their Redeemer in memory.

And just as a pomegranate contains a multitude of seeds within one rind, so in the Church a multitude of believers is contained within faith in the Lord’s Passion.

Hence the Apostle says: “As many of you as were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3).

**Verse 14.** “Cyprus with nard, nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon.”

Cyprus is an aromatic tree bearing a seed like coriander, namely, white and somewhat shining. It is cooked in oil, from which an extract called cyprus is pressed; a royal perfume is prepared from it.

We read in Exodus that the manna was like white coriander seed (Exod. 16:31). Cyprus and manna therefore have one meaning: they signify heavenly grace, coming from heaven like manna.

Cyprus grows in the garden of the Church when the faithful are taught to prefer heavenly grace to everything else and to hope for salvation through it. No one can be saved by his own virtues, but only by the grace of God.

Nard is a type of the Lord’s Passion. Hence Mary Magdalene anointed Jesus’ head and feet with authentic nard (John 12:3).

Nard is therefore present in the garden of the Church when the saints venerate the memory of the Lord’s Passion and give thanks to him because he loved them so greatly that he accepted death for their salvation and deliverance.

“Nard and saffron.”

Saffron has a flower the color of gold, and therefore signifies charity. Just as gold is more precious than all metals, so charity holds first place among all virtues, as the Apostle says: “Now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13).

Saffron therefore grows together with nard in the garden of the Church when the members of Christ—that is, all the faithful—strive effectively to hold fast to love of God and neighbor.

Saffron is said to cool fiery fevers. So true charity cools the heat of worldly and carnal desire and kindles in the mind love of God and neighbor.

“Calamus and cinnamon.”

Calamus is a short tree, also called cassia, with a purple bark. It signifies the saints who are distinguished in the Church by humility and patience—those who are poor in spirit, whose is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:3).

The purple bark signifies the likeness of Christ’s Passion, which those who are humble in spirit always retain in their hearts, or which those grounded in true humility strive to imitate while keeping it continually in their hearts.

Cinnamon is also a short tree, but of remarkable power and fragrance; it therefore signifies the progress of humility, which is likewise represented by calamus.

Calamus and cinnamon are present in the Church when the saints of God truly hold humility and patience in their hearts and display them outwardly to others.

The fact that calamus has a reddish bark, while cinnamon is ash-colored, signifies that the more the saints of God remember the Passion of their Redeemer, the more insignificant and contemptible they consider themselves in their own eyes. Thus they say with Abraham: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27); and with Job: “Therefore I rebuke myself and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6).

“With all the trees of Lebanon.”

The trees of Lebanon excel in beauty, height, and strength, and therefore signify the teachers and all the perfect in the Church. Above we read that the house of the Church was made from them, as the same Church says: “The beams of our houses are cedars, and our ceilings are cypresses” (Song 1:16), because the holy teachers fortify the Church through their preaching.

Calamus and cinnamon are therefore mentioned together with all the trees of Lebanon in the garden of the Church because the humble and patient, as well as all the perfect teachers, hold the same faith in the Church and await the same blessedness.

“Myrrh and aloe with all the finest perfumes.”

Myrrh is a tree whose sap is called stacte. It is so powerful that whatever is touched by it is preserved unharmed from all decay and worms.

Aloe is a tree of extremely sweet fragrance, so much so that it is burned on altars in place of incense. Its sap, however, is exceedingly bitter and resists decay and worms.

Hence it is also said that at the Lord’s Passion Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloe, about one hundred pounds in weight (John 19:39).

These trees therefore signify continence and chastity of the flesh. For decay usually signifies sexual immorality, according to what the prophet says of certain people: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1:17).

Myrrh and aloe are therefore in the garden of the Church—that is, there are heavenly minds, free from every corruption—hearing the Apostle’s exhortation: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12:14).

“With all the finest perfumes.”

What are the finest perfumes, if not charity? Of it the Apostle says: “I show you an even more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31); and then: “If I speak in the tongues of men and angels but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1).

It is fitting that the finest perfumes are placed after myrrh and aloe, because after continence of the flesh true charity follows—charity which is God, by which God is loved above all things (1 John 4:16).

Those who are held by worldly love—that is, those who still delight in pleasures and enticements—cannot be participants in this charity.

**Verse 15.** “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters flowing forcefully from Lebanon.”

“A fountain of gardens” is the primitive Church herself, who waters the gardens—that is, the Churches disseminated throughout the world—with knowledge of the truth.

She is also “a well of living waters,” because the knowledge of the truth, which is the Church, is like a fountain in some people, where it is open, and like a well in others, where it lies hidden and cannot be perceived plainly.

The difference between a fountain and a well is that a fountain is said to be found both at the bottom and on the surface of the earth, whereas a well is always at the bottom.

The Church is therefore both fountain and well: the mysteries of God are easily grasped in some people, as though they were a fountain; in others they must be drawn out with difficulty, like water from a well.

The living waters signify the mysteries of the Scriptures, which possess within themselves a heavenly power.

By contrast, the teachings of heretics are called cisterns—that is, collections of water—of which the Lord says through the prophet: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2:13).

These flowing waters flow forcefully from Lebanon—that is, they pour forth from the Church, which has been whitened and made bright by baptism and good works, as Lebanon is interpreted.

From this Lebanon—that is, from the Church—they flow; that is, the waters of heavenly teachings issue forth. They do so forcefully, with a certain power by which all the fabrications of heretics are destroyed and overturned.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “The force of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. 45:5)—that is, the power of divine utterances.

**Verse 16.** “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow.”

Having enumerated the virtues of the Church under the name of spices, the Lord—who is the Bridegroom and Redeemer of the Church—knows that the Church will be multiplied through persecutions. He therefore next, as it were, bids persecution itself to come: not by commanding it, but by permitting it.

“Rise,” he says, “north wind, and come, south wind.”

By the north and south winds are understood the blasts of persecutions and disturbances raging against the Church. The north wind is extremely cold, while the south wind is warm. Thus the north signifies terrors and threats, and the south the snares of seductive blandishments. In these two ways the Church is tested: through terrors and through blandishments.

When he says, “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind,” he does not command evils or compel them to do evil; he permits them and gives them the opportunity to rage against the Church, so that through their wickedness the Church may be tested and they may be punished more severely.

For the Lord knows how to bring certain good things out of human evils. Yet he holds the persecution itself under his power, so that they may not rage as much as they wish. Hence it is written: “He gives weight to the winds” (Job 28:25), because he imposes a certain limit upon the blasts of persecution, according to what the Apostle says: “With the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

“Blow through my garden,” he says—that is, “my Church”—“and let its spices flow,” that is, let the fragrance of virtues and the scent of good works proceed from it.

For the more bitterly the Church is shaken, the greater the fragrance of virtue she emits from herself.

# CHAPTER V

**Verse 1.** “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his fruit-trees.”

Hearing that persecution has been called forth, the Church, as though preparing herself against adversity, says: “Let my beloved come into his garden,” that is, “Let Christ, my Bridegroom, come, whom I love with my whole heart, to his Church, so that he may eat the fruit of his trees,” that is, so that he may delight in and be nourished by the good works of his faithful.

For the food of the Lord is our good works. Thus, seeing the faith of the Samaritans—that is, of the Gentiles—he said to his disciples: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John 4:32).

“I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.”

To the Church desiring that the Bridegroom come to her, he replies that he has already done so. “I have already come,” he says. For “I have come” here is not an imperative but an indicative verb in the past tense.

“O my sister, my bride, I have already come into my garden; I have already visited my Church. Indeed, I visit her daily, and I feed upon the fruits of her virtues and enjoy their fragrance. I come to her to correct those who wander, strengthen the weak, confirm the doubtful, and bestow heavenly rewards upon all who are perfect.”

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.”

By myrrh are signified those who ended their lives through martyrdom, or those who crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24).

The spices are the works of holy virtues, fragrant with the scents of good action.

The Lord therefore gathers myrrh with his spices when he cuts off from this life, with the sickle of death, the holy martyrs and the other elect distinguished by good works, and, having brought them to the maturity of good works, stores them in the granaries of the heavenly homeland.

I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk. The holy preachers are signified by the honeycomb and the wine; good hearers, by the honey and the milk. For the preachers are the honeycomb, since by preaching to others they bring forth the secret and innermost mysteries of Scripture as honey from honeycombs. The honey, however, signifies good hearers, because they strive attentively to receive the sweetness of God’s word and to feed upon it with delight. The preachers themselves, who are also the honeycomb, are the wine, because they proclaim the powerful mysteries of Scripture. The milk signifies those hearers who are weak, for whom the mysteries in their plain form are suitable, like milk.

Since, then, the life of all these is directed toward different pursuits, and the Redeemer is nourished and delighted by the good intention of them all, he is said, as it were, to eat the honeycomb with the honey and drink the wine with the milk. We may also refer this to the death of the elect, whom the Lord “eats” when he calls them through death to eternal life and joins them to his body—that is, to the company of the elect already rejoicing in that heavenly blessedness. If we understand this of the death of the saints, we should take as the wine those whose souls already rejoice in heavenly blessedness, and as the honeycomb those who already rejoice in that blessedness in body and soul, such as those who rose with the Lord (Matt. XXVII, 52).

Eat, friends, and drink, and become drunk, dearest ones. The Lord not only rejoices in the progress of the saints; he also exhorts us to rejoice in their virtues [Col. 1081C] and to imitate them: “Eat,” he says—that is, my faithful ones, who are my friends because you do what I command; you are my dearest ones because you love me with perfect charity of heart. “Eat,” therefore, he says, “and drink”—that is, rejoice in the good deeds of the saints and set them before yourselves for imitation.

It should be noted, however, that he says, “Drink and become drunk.” In Scripture, drunkenness is sometimes used for satiety, as it is said of Joseph’s brothers: “They drank and became drunk before him” (Gen. XLIII, 34); and the Psalmist says: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” (Ps. LXIV, 16)—that is, you satisfied and filled it. He therefore exhorts us not only to eat and drink, but also to be satisfied, because there are some who eat and are not satisfied: they listen to divine preaching with pleasure, but forget it carelessly and do not bring what they have heard to the accomplishment of a good work. Those eat and are satisfied who store up in their inner senses the words of life that they hear and strive to fulfill them in action. Of them the Psalmist says: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. XXI, 27).

But if, as was said above, we understand this of the death of the saints, the friends and dearest ones are the angelic spirits, whom the Lord commands to rejoice with the elect when they are transferred from this life to the rest of eternal blessedness, according to what is read in the Gospel parable: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost” (Luke XV, 6).

### Verse 2

I sleep, but my heart is awake. This is the voice of the Church: “I sleep,” because, while my bridegroom grants me a little peace, I rest and do not suffer pressures such as the primitive Church endured. “But my heart is awake,” because, in the peace granted to me, I cling more securely to love for my bridegroom and direct toward him the eyes of my heart. But since this time is not a time of rest, but rather of labor and struggle, the bridegroom again rouses the Church to labor and exhorts her to the contest of preaching.

[Col. 1082A] The voice of my beloved, knocking. The beloved knocks when Christ exhorts his faithful to advance in virtue; or he knocks when he admonishes them to win their neighbors by preaching. There is also a third knocking, by which the Lord knocks upon his elect when, through the distress of illness, he indicates that death is near. Of this knocking the Gospel says: “So that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once” (Luke XII, 36). But in this passage he is said to knock in the sense that he urges the Church to the work of preaching.

Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my dove, my undefiled one. “Open to me, my sister.” She is a sister because she has been made a co-heir of my kingdom; my beloved, because, freed from the yoke of slavery, she has come to know the secrets of my truth; my dove, because she has been sanctified by the gift of my Spirit; my undefiled one, because, through the outpouring of my blood, she has been cleansed from every stain of sins. “Open to me”—that is, come forth from the rest and leisure of sweetness and contemplation to the work of preaching.

[Col. 1082B] For my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights. The head of the Church, as the Apostle says, is Christ (Eph. V, 23). The locks signify the innermost thoughts of the saints, which do not flow loosely and disorderly, but are bound together by the bond of fear and love of God. The dew and the drops of the nights here signify minds that are dark, full of unbelief, and cold. The bridegroom’s head is therefore full of dew when worldly people grow cold toward the love of God, according to what the Lord says: “Because wickedness has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV, 12). And when such people persecute and hate the saints of God, who meditate on heavenly things, the bridegroom’s locks are, as it were, full of the drops of the nights. When such people multiply and burden the Church, the bridegroom admonishes his bride to rise and devote herself to the work of preaching.

### Verse 3

I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? The Church, summoned by her bridegroom to the office of preaching, replies: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” I have stripped myself of the cares and occupations of this world, without which the office of preaching can scarcely, or not at all, be carried out; how can I return again to what I abandoned? For one who prepares to undertake the office of preaching must also provide temporal necessities for his subjects, and this cannot be done without great anxiety.

That the tunic signifies the anxieties and cares of the world, the Lord shows in the Gospel: “Let the one who is on the housetop not come down to take his tunic” (Matt. XXIV, 18). This plainly means: Let the one who stands upon the lofty summit of contemplation not come down to take his tunic—that is, let him not come down to take up the cares of the world, lest he become entangled again in worldly occupations. The Church, therefore, or any holy soul, fears being stripped of this tunic and, while resting in contemplation of her Creator, being clothed in it again and occupied with worldly affairs.

I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? “I have washed my feet”—that is, I have washed with fitting tears of repentance the actions by which I was accustomed never to touch the dust, that is, to engage in earthly things, so that now I desire to think of nothing except divine matters. “How shall I defile them?” That is, how can I return again to thinking about fleeting and earthly things, when now, with my heart occupied yet free, I enjoy the contemplation of divine things?

### Verse 4

My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my belly trembled at his touch. The beloved puts his hand through the opening and touches the belly when, through an inward inspiration of the Creator, he visits the heart and kindles it toward progress in virtue. Or he does so when he recalls us to the memory of his works, so that we may consider that, although he was God, he deigned to become human for us, in order that, by assuming our earthly condition, he might make us heavenly and, by dying for us, grant us eternal life.

When this occurs, the belly trembles, because, when we begin to consider such things, the secrets of our heart are shaken as we begin to be astonished at the greatness of the condescension with which the Creator deigned to accomplish these things for us [Col. 1083A]. That the belly signifies the heart, the prophet shows when he says: “My belly, my belly, I suffer pain” (Jer. IV, 19); and he explains what this means by adding: “The senses of my heart are confused.”

### Verse 5

I rose to open to my beloved. We open to the beloved not only when we receive his coming, but also when we preach to others. Those who had closed their hearts through wickedness we cause, once converted by our preaching, to open the door of their hearts to Christ as well.

It is rightly said first, “I rose,” and then, “to open to my beloved.” For one who wishes to open the hearts of others to Christ by preaching must first rise—that is, be lifted up toward the pursuit of good works—and fulfill in action what he preaches, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should become reprobate (1 Cor. IX, 27). Hence Luke also says of the Lord: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1). He says “to do” first, and then “to teach.”

My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the choicest myrrh. By the hands, with which we work, action itself is signified; by the fingers, the discernment of action, since no member has articulations distinguished to such a degree as the fingers.

The hands of the Church drip with myrrh when her preachers devote themselves to continence and the mortification of their flesh, saying with the Apostle: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (II Cor. IX, 27). Or they do so when they are prepared to die for Christ, as John says: “If Christ laid down his life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (1 John III, 16).

The fingers are full of the choicest myrrh when we carefully discern the work of mortification, asking whether it is performed with a view to the heavenly reward or for the praise of the world. One who fasts for human approval, or devotes himself to works of abstinence or continence, has myrrh in his hands, but not in his fingers, because he does not discern why he is doing it. Of such people the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2). Or the bride’s hands drip with myrrh when they apply themselves to the works of the holy Church, to chastity, or to holy continence.

### Verse 6

I opened the latch of my door to my beloved, but he had turned aside and passed on. The latch of the door is opened when the Church, or any faithful soul, opens her heart to the approaching Creator. But he had turned aside and passed on. Often, when we wish to consider spiritual matters, the more carefully we concentrate, the more the sharpness of the heart is thrown back. Hence Solomon says: “I said, ‘I will become wise,’ but it withdrew farther from me” (Eccl. VII, 24). The Psalmist likewise says: “A person will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Ps. LXIII, 8).

For the more anyone lifts his heart toward divine contemplation through purification of the flesh, the higher he finds what he was seeking to be. He therefore says: “He had turned aside and passed on,” because no one in the present life can comprehend him as he is.

My soul melted when my beloved spoke. “The nearer,” she says, “I sensed the coming of my bridegroom at the touch of his secret inspiration, the more everything in me that was cold grew warm, so that now I desire nothing except to dissolve into tears” [Col. 1083D]. The bridegroom speaks when Christ inspires a holy soul through his inward inspiration, suggesting to her a heavenly desire. When he speaks, she melts, because the more she is breathed upon by heavenly desires, the more she dies to earthly things and becomes, as it were, insensible to the world, living only for heavenly desire.

This is also what is said through the prophet: “Who is blind except my servant? Who is deaf except the one to whom I sent my messengers?” (Isa. XLII, 19).

I sought him, but did not find him; I called him, but he did not answer me. She repeats the cause of her sorrow. The Lord is always present to all who devoutly seek him; he answers those who call upon him—that is, he hears them for salvation. But often he does not answer the faithful soul that longs for him and desires to come to him, so that he may show himself to her in the present as he promises to show himself in the future. Or he does not answer—that is, he does not hear her—in order that each holy person may, at the time he wills, be stripped of the bonds of the body and be caressed in the embraces of his bridegroom.

When the Apostle said, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23), he was, as it were, seeking to cling to his bridegroom and calling him through the desire of his mind. Yet the bridegroom did not answer him, because he did not immediately free him from the body, but allowed him still to be exercised by labors and to toil for the benefit of the Church.

### Verse 7

The watchmen who patrol the city found me; they struck me and wounded me. The watchmen who guard the city are the holy teachers, who patrol the city of God—that is, the Church—keeping vigilant watch over it, so that they may both defend it from adversaries and kindle it toward heavenly desires by their word and example.

They find the bride seeking her beloved when the holy teachers instruct and form a soul intent upon heavenly desires, whether they are present through their word or absent through their sacred writings. “They struck me,” she says, “and wounded me.” The word of God is a sword, as the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. IV, 12). The bride is struck and wounded by this sword when the preacher’s discourse speaks of God and pierces the hearers as with a dart of compunction and love.

The watchmen of the walls took away my cloak from me. This cloak is understood here, as above, as the tunic referred to when she says: “I have taken off my tunic”—the covering, namely, of worldly desires—which the watchmen take away. For whatever love of the present world remains in anyone’s mind, the holy teachers remove entirely and make that person love only Christ, his bridegroom. Such people can say with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

“The watchmen of the walls.” The walls of the city are the holy teachers of the Church. The watchmen of the walls are those who also instruct people capable of presiding over others. Such was Paul, who instructed and guarded Timothy and Titus, who were themselves walls of this city—that is, he exhorted them toward perfection in good work.

### Verse 8

I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love. The daughters of Jerusalem are faithful souls, whether those who are still pilgrims in the present life, those who already enjoy Christ, or those who will one day contemplate Christ face to face. Or the daughters of Jerusalem are citizens of that heavenly city in which there is supreme peace and the blessedness of divine contemplation.

In this passage, however, we should understand the daughters of Jerusalem as souls who desire God but are still engaged in this pilgrimage. The bride therefore adjures the daughters of Jerusalem to tell the bridegroom that she is sick with love when a faithful soul adjures other faithful people who desire God to make known to Christ that she is held by his love and to report this to him.

She rightly says that she is sick with love. For the more she begins to desire heavenly things, the more she grows weak with regard to what belongs to the world. It is no wonder that such people are said to be sick, since the Apostle calls them dead: “You have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ” (Col. III, 3).

Thus the daughters of Jerusalem respond to the bride as she adjures them.

### Verse 9

What is your beloved beyond another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved beyond another beloved, that you have so adjured us? This occurs when one faithful person addresses another faithful person and they mutually suggest to one another words of heavenly desire, by which they kindle each other toward love of things above.

“Tell me,” she says, “now that I desire him, now that I long to reach the vision of my Creator, what is your beloved”—that is, in what manner should Christ be loved? “For some time now,” she says, “I have begun to fear him; but now, with love casting out fear, I desire to hear words by which I may be kindled to love him.”

You, then, who already seek him in love and languish through love for him, tell me: “What is your beloved beyond another beloved?” The beloved beyond another beloved is the Son from the Father, just as God is from God and light from light. Or, “your beloved beyond another beloved” means Christ insofar as he is to be loved, not insofar as he is to be feared. Fear belongs more properly to the imperfect, whom fear restrains from sins; love belongs to the perfect.

She therefore asks what the beloved beyond another beloved is—that is, how Christ should be loved, or what he is toward those who know only how to love him.

### Verse 10

My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands. This is the voice of the responding Church: “My beloved is white and ruddy”: white in virginity, ruddy in his passion. He is white because he was without sin, for he lived without sin: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II, 22). He is ruddy because “he washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I, 5).

Chosen from among thousands. Christ, as human, shone forth by singular grace amid the whole mass of the human race, because through him God purposed to save the human race; he is “the mediator of God and human beings, the human Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II, 5). Concerning him the Psalmist says: “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 3); and Solomon: “I found one man among a thousand” (Eccl. VII, 29)—that is, Christ. And he himself says in the psalm: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. CXL, 10).

He is therefore chosen from among thousands because, from the whole multitude of the saints, he alone was worthy to hear: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

### Verse 11

His head is the finest gold. The head of the bridegroom is God, according to what the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. XI, 3). It is compared with the finest gold because, just as gold is more precious than all metals, so almighty God excels and surpasses all good things made by him. Hence the Lord says: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark X, 18).

The bridegroom’s head is therefore the finest gold because God’s goodness is ineffable and transcends the goodness of all things, since nothing is good except by participation in this supreme good.

His locks are like palm branches. The bridegroom’s locks are the multitudes of the faithful, clinging to God through faith and love, who are compared with lofty palms. The lofty branches of palms are the longer and more excellent branches, sometimes golden in color, curling and always reaching upward, never losing their greenness.

The Church therefore calls the locks of her bridegroom curling and radiant. Some say that “lofty palms” refers to a kind of aromatic tree which in Latin is called *abies* or *spatas*, for in Greek the fir tree is called ἐλάτη (*elatē*). This species is suitable for making ointments. The *abies* mentioned here should not be understood as the large tree suitable for ships and houses, but, as we said, as a kind of aromatic tree.

So much for the literal meaning of “lofty palms.” The bridegroom’s locks are compared with lofty palms because the multitudes of the faithful rejoice in the greenness of faith, are lifted up toward the desire for eternal things, and taste the sweetness of heavenly delight. The more they perceive it, the more they see themselves as sinners and contemptible in their own eyes. Hence it follows:

Black as a raven. The bridegroom’s locks are black as a raven because the multitudes of the faithful are conscious of their own frailty and know that they possess no good from themselves. Or the lofty palms signify hope and victory, while the blackness like that of a raven signifies that they are despised and contemptible amid the pressures of this world.

The saints are lofty palms because, through God’s grace, they strive toward the palm of heavenly victory; they are black as a raven because they recognize that in themselves they are weak and sinful.

The bridegroom’s locks may also be understood as the angelic virtues, which cling especially to God like locks to the head and contemplate him from near at hand. They are rightly compared with lofty palms because they are never bent from the uprightness of their state, but remain undefiled in the dignity of their office. The more they contemplate the glory of their Creator, the more they perceive how worthless every created thing is in comparison with him; therefore they are said to be black as a raven.

### Verse 12

His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk. His eyes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as John shows in the Apocalypse, saying: “I saw a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Rev. V, 6).

They are therefore rightly compared with doves beside streams of water, because the Holy Spirit delights in pure and sincere minds. Doves do not settle upon ponds or marshes, but beside streams of water, because, as was said, the Holy Spirit makes chaste and clean minds his dwelling place. They are “washed with milk” because, as was said, the Holy Spirit is understood under the name of milk—that is, as the grace of God, which is bestowed upon the Church through the Holy Spirit and by which the Church is nourished like infants by milk.

We may also understand the bridegroom’s eyes as the teachers of the Church, who are compared with doves because of their innocence and simplicity. These doves sit beside streams so that they may see the hawk’s approach from afar and guard against it. In the same way, the holy teachers, drenched with the water of baptism, have been whitened by the brilliance of chastity and holiness.

And they sit beside very full streams—that is, beside the overflowing knowledge of Scripture. If we think there is a distinction between streams and very full rivers, it should be said that the streams signify the writings of the Old Testament, while the very full rivers signify the abundant teaching of the holy Gospel. These doves therefore are both beside streams of water and seated beside very full rivers, because the holy teachers continually investigate the mysteries of both the Old and the New Testament.

### Verse 13

His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers. The bridegroom’s cheeks signify Christ’s modest piety, or severity, or the appearance of his face, for joy, modesty, severity, and piety are detected in a man’s cheeks. Thus the appearance of the face of our Redeemer is rightly understood in the bridegroom’s cheeks.

These were his cheeks when he rejoiced in spirit, as the Gospel says; when he wept over the dead Lazarus (John XI, 35); when he grieved over Jerusalem, which was destined to perish (Luke XIX, 41); and on many similar occasions. These cheeks of the bridegroom are compared with beds of spices. For just as well-composed and orderly beds of spices delight the eyes of those who look upon them and offer them the grace of their fragrance, so Christ’s gentleness delighted those who were absent through its reputation and those who were present through its reality, and it summoned them to love him.

These beds are planted by perfumers. The perfumers are the prophets or the apostles, the former describing all these things as future, the latter as already accomplished.

His lips are lilies, dripping with first myrrh. By the bridegroom’s lips are understood the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, which are compared with lilies because they announce the rewards of eternal brightness. They drip with first myrrh because they teach that these rewards are reached through mortification of the flesh [Col. 1086D].

Or the Lord’s lips are compared with lilies because they teach works of chastity and purity. They drip with first myrrh because they indicate that whatever adversities arise must be endured patiently. The Lord’s lips were lilies when, teaching on the mountain, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, blessed are the meek, blessed are the merciful, blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. V, 3, 4, 7, 8, 10). They dripped with first myrrh when he added afterward: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness.”

### Verse 14

His hands are golden, turned on a lathe. In the bridegroom’s hands the action of the Savior is rightly understood. Just as someone works easily on a lathe and needs no rule, so the Savior’s action was easy: whatever he wished, he immediately accomplished, because “he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII, 9). Of him the Evangelist says: “He was as one having his word in authority” (Matt. VII, 29).

They were golden because his action was carried out through the power of his divinity. Divinity is represented by gold because, just as gold surpasses the other metals and is more precious, so divinity surpasses all its works in an ineffable manner.

Full of hyacinths. Hyacinth is a stone the color of the sky. What, then, is understood by hyacinths except heavenly hope and desire? The Lord’s hands are full of hyacinths because all his action awakens us to hope and desire for things above.

Hyacinth is also an aromatic flower of purple color and good fragrance. The Lord’s hands are full of hyacinths because they were pierced by nails on the cross and spattered with the redness of his blood, as though with a purple color. But the former explanation, concerning hyacinth as a stone, is more suitable here.

In another translation, a stone is mentioned. For his hands are said to be turned on a lathe and full of Tharsis. Tharsis is the stone that we call chalcedony.

His belly is ivory. Nothing in the human body is more fragile or more tender than the belly. Therefore, by the belly the fragility of the humanity assumed by Christ is understood. Ivory is the bone of an elephant, an animal said to be most chaste and of an extremely cold nature, and therefore greatly desired by the dragon, which is of a hot nature.

The bridegroom’s belly is therefore ivory because the humanity assumed by the Redeemer admitted no corruption and no stain: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in him” (Isa. LIII, 9). He assumed the fragility of flesh, yet remained entirely free from sin, just as the bronze serpent lifted up by Moses in the desert (Num. XXI, 9) had the form of a serpent but lacked the serpent’s poisonous malice.

Set with sapphires. Sapphire is a stone having the color of a clear sky. Thus, in the vision of the Lord, it is said: “They saw the God of Israel, and beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. XXIV, 10).

By sapphires, therefore, the works of divine Majesty that are accomplished in the flesh are understood. The bridegroom’s belly was set with sapphires because Christ’s humanity shone with heavenly virtues. It is not said to be full of sapphires, but set with them, so that the whiteness of ivory might appear among the sapphires. The Lord worked what belonged to divinity in such a way that he nevertheless accomplished what belonged to humanity, and did not abandon what belonged to divinity.

For Christ’s action is distinguished into divinity and humanity. His hunger, thirst, weeping, weariness, and ability finally to be crucified and die were works of humanity. But his raising the dead, coming to the aid of all who were sick, and raising himself from the dead were unmistakable works of divinity.

### Verse 15

His legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases. The bridegroom’s legs are the journeys of the Savior, by which he deigned to become human and come to us. They are rightly compared with marble columns, because nothing is stronger than marble and nothing is more upright than a column.

The bridegroom’s legs are therefore marble columns because all the Lord’s journeys are both strong and upright. Of his strength the Psalmist says: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Ps. XVII, 6). Of his uprightness, elsewhere: “The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity” (Ps. X, 8); and: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

These legs are founded upon golden bases because everything that was to be done through Christ or in Christ had been preordained and determined by the divine plan before the foundation of the world. Gold, which, as has often been said, is brighter and more precious than the other metals, signifies the purest secret of the divine plan.

The marble columns therefore proceed from golden bases because from the beginning of the world the incarnation, birth, passion, and resurrection of the Savior had been preordained, along with the other mysteries by which the human race would be redeemed. Hence the prophet, praising God, said: “Lord my God, I will honor you; I will sing praises to your name, for you do wondrous things: let your true plan be fulfilled” (Isa. XXV, 1).

His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars. Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, the boundary of Judea toward the north, and it is higher than the other mountains. The trees of that mountain surpass the timber of other forests in height, appearance, and strength.

“Just as,” he says, “Lebanon is higher than the other mountains of the land of Judea, so our Redeemer is more beautiful than all the elect, because he is ‘beautiful in form beyond the sons of men’” (Ps. XLIV, 3). And just as the cedar is more beautiful and taller than the other trees, so he surpasses all the saints from the beginning of the world through the grace of his divinity.

### Verse 16

His throat is most sweet. Above, the bridegroom’s lips signified his words; now, by the throat, the inward sweetness of those words is signified, by which our understanding is refreshed. Hence the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII, 9).

Many can easily understand the Lord’s words, but few are able to penetrate their sweetness—that is, few strive to fulfill God’s commandments out of love and desire.

And he is altogether desirable. It is as though he were saying: Why do I delay by describing him through his individual members? My bridegroom is altogether desirable. “Altogether,” he says, because he is perfect God and perfect human being. He is therefore altogether desirable because he kindles the angels and all the elect with desire for him, according to what the Apostle says: “Into which things the angels desire to look” (1 Pet. I, 12). The more closely he is contemplated, the greater the desire with which he summons those who look upon him to contemplate him.

Such is my beloved, and he is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem. He is beloved because through faith and love I cling to him; he is my friend because, having redeemed me from the bond of sin, he has deigned to make me his friend and one acquainted with his secrets. The more anyone loves him, the more worthy that person becomes of his friendship.

### Verse 17

Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? This is the voice of the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, of the Churches, or also of holy souls. For the Church is Christ’s bride, and the daughters of Jerusalem are that same Church, which consists of the individual souls of the faithful. They therefore say: “Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women?”

Where has your beloved turned aside? We will seek him with you. The bride had earlier adjured the daughters of Jerusalem to tell the bridegroom that she languished through love for him. Those same daughters of Jerusalem had asked what the bridegroom was like, and she had consequently described the form of her bridegroom. Now the daughters of Jerusalem themselves ask where that bridegroom has gone, so that they may seek him with her.

Holy souls do this when they converse with one another about eternal salvation, burning with love for Christ and longing for his appearance; or when they carefully investigate in whose hearts Christ most especially dwells, so that they may be edified by their example and manner of life.

It should be noted that she says, “Where has your beloved gone?” or, “Where has your beloved turned aside?” He turns aside, as it were, for a time while he is being sought, in order to arouse a greater desire to seek him. For this reason he often delays the requests and prayers of the saints, so that they may begin to desire him more ardently.

Thus, when Mary once sought him, he did not immediately show himself to her, but appeared in the form of a gardener (John XX, 15) and finally revealed that he was the one being sought. Christ therefore always hears his elect, but he always seems to turn aside when he does not immediately grant what they ask.

It is rightly said, “We will seek him with you.” For one who seeks Christ without the Church may wander and grow weary, but cannot make progress.

## CHAPTER VI

### Verse 1

My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the bed of spices, to feed in the gardens and gather lilies. We have already learned above what Christ’s garden is: the holy Church, of which it was said earlier, “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride.”

“Christ has gone down,” he says, “to the garden that he himself prepared and cultivated, that he sowed with the shoots of virtues, that he illumined by his grace, and that he defended with the wall of his protection from the assaults of evil spirits.”

He is rightly said to have gone down into his garden. For he wished to be buried in a garden (John XIX, 41), and he first appeared to Mary Magdalene in a garden (John XX, 15), consecrating there, in a certain sense, the first fruits of the Church.

He is said to have gone down when he descended from the higher and heavenly dwelling places into the garden that he himself planted in a lowly place. But he descended for this purpose: that the garden—that is, the Church—might ascend to him. Hence, later, he says of the garden, that is, of his Church: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness?”

“To the bed of spices,” he says. By the bed of spices is understood every faithful soul, cultivated by heavenly discipline, carefully ordered, and squared with the symmetry of its sides.

“To feed,” he says, “in the gardens”—that is, to delight in the pious labors of the saints. For he is nourished by our good works, to such an extent that he himself is refreshed in the poor.

“And to gather lilies,” he says—that is, to gather holy souls, brought by the maturity of virtue to perfect brightness, from this world to himself, and to make them rejoice with him in eternal blessedness. The lilies are holy souls, made white by the pursuit of virtues and by good works.

### Verse 2

“I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me, who feeds among the lilies.”

“I belong to my beloved” implies: I prepare a pleasing pasture for him; and my beloved will grant me the grace of perfection, or the reward of eternal recompense. Or: “I belong to my beloved,” because I prepare a dwelling-place for him within myself; “and my beloved belongs to me,” because he himself dwells in me and makes me dwell in him, just as he says in the Gospel: “I am in you, and you are in me” (John 14:20).

### Verse 3

“You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem.”

The Church was seeking her bridegroom as though he were absent; but, in order to show that he was always present [525] and to demonstrate that he was always near her as she spoke to him and longed for him, he promptly replies: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem.”

You are beautiful because you have neither the stain nor the wrinkle of sin [Col. 1089C], but blossom with every radiance of virtue. “My beloved”: the Church, or every faithful soul. “Sweet and lovely as Jerusalem.” Jerusalem, interpreted as “vision of peace,” signifies that heavenly city in which there is true peace and happiness, because there the saints rejoice in their reward in such a way that they have nothing to grieve over in corruption. Therefore the Church, which is still on earth, or every faithful soul, is sweet and lovely in the likeness of that Jerusalem, because insofar as it can, it imitates that peace.

It continues:

“Terrible as an army drawn up for battle.”

The Church is terrible to the evil spirits, and is ordered like an army drawn up for battle, whenever each of the faithful rightly preserves his own order and vocation. For there are three orders in the Church: teachers, the continent, and the married. These three classes were represented in those three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job. Noah, who guided the ark amid the waves, signifies the holy teachers; Daniel, celibate and chaste, signifies the order of the continent; [Col. 1089D] Job, who had a wife and children, expresses the order of the married.

Therefore the Church is ordered like an army, because each order of the Church stands as if in battle-array against the enemies who are evil spirits, while the holy teachers devote themselves to preaching and instruction. The continent, despising the things that belong to the world, think only of the things that belong to God, and, with their minds free from earthly occupations, devote themselves to God alone. The married devote themselves to almsgiving and to the other good works of active life; and they use the world in such a way that they do not abandon the things that belong to God. This, then, most orderly arrangement of the Church is terrible to unclean spirits, like an army drawn up for war.

Or: the Church is beautiful and lovely as Jerusalem in its virtues, but terrible as an army drawn up for battle, because it does not cease to extend its authority and power to the ends of the whole world. Or: it is terrible as an army drawn up for battle because it is so joined and united by the bond of charity that it cannot be penetrated by any force of the malignant enemy [Col. 1090A] or by any plague of discord. For nothing terrifies evil spirits so much as charity.

### Verse 4

“Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.”

It is as though he said: “I have indeed given you dove-like eyes, by which you might gaze upon me and penetrate most sharply into the mysteries of Scripture; but take care not to direct them toward seeing me now, because while you live in the present life, you cannot do so: ‘No human being shall see me and live’” (Exodus 33:20).

But when, freed from the bonds of the flesh, you have come to me, then you will see me with open vision, and what is promised in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21).

As for the statement that “they have made me fly away,” one must not suppose that God abandons those who seek him and withdraws from them, since he himself commands: “Seek, and you will find” (Luke 11:9). Rather, it should be understood in this way: the more anyone wishes to investigate the divinity of God’s majesty, the more he understands how unsearchable and incomprehensible it is [Col. 1090B]. This is what the Psalmist says: “A human being will approach the deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Psalm 63:7). As though he said: Even if a person raises his heart in order to see God, God will be exalted, because his greatness cannot be comprehended.

“Your hair is like a flock of goats that have appeared from Gilead.”

These verses have often been expounded; but let it not weary us to expound again what did not weary the Holy Spirit to repeat. He placed these verses twice so that we might hold as most certain and stable what we hear confirmed through repetition.

The hair of the holy Church consists in the many and varied subtleties of its thoughts. It is rightly compared to a flock of goats, for the goat is a figure of the sinner. Thus it is commanded in the Law that whoever has sinned through ignorance and has recognized his guilt should offer a goat as a burnt offering for his offense (Leviticus 4:28).

The hair of the Church, therefore, is compared to a flock of goats because all the saints, who are members of the Church, strive to erase every guilt of their thoughts through worthy [Col. 1090C] repentance and the tears of true contrition.

They are rightly said to have appeared from Mount Gilead. Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Through Gilead, therefore, the mind of the saints is signified, since they are a heap of testimony: they bear witness by the clearest signs that they neglect everything belonging to the world and desire God alone.

Gilead may also be understood as the Lord himself and our Redeemer. Gilead is the name both of a mountain and of a city. A flock of goats therefore appeared from Mount Gilead because the Church is founded upon Christ, as he himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:15). He is the heap of testimony, because the multitude of prophets and patriarchs bears witness to him by its deeds and writings.

### Verse 5

“Your teeth are like flocks of sheep that have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and none is barren among them.”

By the teeth of the Church is understood the firm stability of its words. They are rightly compared to a flock of sheep that has come up from the washing, because the words of the Church [Col. 1090D] sound only of innocence and gentleness, retaining nothing foul, nothing shameful or unclean within themselves. They are washed in the washing of sincerity and purity, hearing the Apostle say: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Ephesians 4:29).

They are rightly said all to bear twins, because the speech of the saints sounds and speaks of nothing except what pertains to the love of God and neighbor. The saints should speak only of those things that contribute to the perpetual health of bodies and souls.

### Verse 6

“Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within you.”

We said above that the chaste modesty of the saints is represented by the cheeks, and the mystery of Christ’s passion by the rind of the pomegranate, hearing the Apostle Paul say: “Do not be ashamed of the cross of Christ, nor of me, his prisoner” (2 Timothy 1:8). These things that are outwardly visible are indeed great; but those within are greatest, that is, the things reserved for the saints in the future.

### Verse 7

“There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number” [Col. 1091A].

The queens are the teachers of the holy Church, who rightly draw near to the bed of the eternal King through the bed of faith and knowledge, and bear spiritual children for God.

The number sixty is formed from ten and six. For ten multiplied by six [526] rises to sixty. Ten signifies the divine commandments because of the Decalogue of the Law; six is placed for perfection because God completed his works in six days. The sixty queens, therefore, signify those who excel in perfection of knowledge and work, and who preach solely for love of their Creator and in expectation of heavenly recompense.

This number, sixty, is also formed from twelve multiplied by five: five times twelve, or twelve times five, makes sixty. The sixty queens therefore signify those established in the Church who know how to order chastely the five senses of their body according to the teaching of the twelve apostles [Col. 1091B].

The concubines signify those who do not preach Christ sincerely, but for temporal profits or popular praise. For these too, like the queens, draw near to the King’s bed through knowledge and beget spiritual children; but they remain alienated from the crown of the eternal kingdom.

They are rightly comprehended by the number eighty, for this number is formed from ten and eight. The number eighty is sometimes understood negatively because of four, by which it is multiplied. Four signifies temporal and present things because of the four regions of the world or the four seasons of the year.

The concubines, therefore, are rightly said to number eighty, because, as has been said, they preach for the sake of temporal and visible things alone and care less for spiritual matters. The Apostle spoke of such people: “There are some who proclaim Christ not sincerely,” and so forth (Philippians 1:17–18), until he says: “In this I rejoice, and I will continue to rejoice.”

“Of maidens there is no number.” The maidens are souls already reborn in Christ, who, having laid aside the oldness of the first human being, have been renewed in Christ [Col. 1091C], but are not yet marriageable and are not yet suited to the King’s bed, because they have not yet attained perfection in preaching Christ.

They are without number because the number of souls believing in Christ is infinite and cannot be comprehended by any human being. Nevertheless, all the elect are numbered by God; for with him even the number of the stars is known (Psalm 147:4), and the number of the elect cannot be unknown.

### Verse 8

“My one dove, my perfect one.”

That is: there is one catholic Church spread throughout the whole world. It consists of queens and maidens—or young men—and also has concubines, that is, certain people who are called Christians or teachers in name only.

The Church is one, therefore, because it admits neither division nor schisms. Just as there is one God, one faith, and one baptism (Ephesians 4:5), so there is one universal Church, which is rightly also called a dove, because it has been betrothed and sanctified to Christ by the gift of the Holy Spirit, who appeared in the form of a dove [Col. 1091D].

“She is one to her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her.”

Our mother is that heavenly Jerusalem of which the Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” This Church, therefore, is one to her mother because it is established and formed in this pilgrimage according to the example of that Church which already enjoys Christ; and it strives to reach that blessedness in which it reigns together with Christ.

“The daughters of Zion saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her.”

Those whom above he calls maidens he here calls daughters. Let us understand the queens and concubines here as above. The daughters, queens, and concubines therefore proclaim and praise the Church, because the entire community of the faithful admires the catholic Church. For the Church itself, which consists of many individual faithful, constitutes the catholic—that is, universal—Church.

### Verse 9

“Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn?” [Col. 1092A]

This is the voice of the Synagogue. At the end of the age, when the Jewish people have been converted to Christ through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, it too will admire the Church, saying: “Who is this?”—that is, “How great and what sort of Church is this that comes forth?” This means: that advances from virtue to virtue.

The Church is not said to stand still but to advance, because it is not confined to one place but has occupied the whole world through heavenly preaching. It advances like the dawn because, after the darkness of unbelief has passed, it shows that it possesses the light of truth.

“Beautiful as the moon.”

Physicists say that the moon is illuminated by the sun. And behold, the Church is beautiful as the moon because it is illuminated by the radiance of its bridegroom Christ and shines with his grace.

Or: it is beautiful as the moon in the present life, where at times it grows when peace, tranquility, or security is granted to it, and at times diminishes when crushed by adversities.

“Chosen as the sun.” [Col. 1092B]

In the other life, where it will shine perpetually with joy from the vision of its Creator.

Or: it is chosen as the sun because it strives to imitate that other Sun of whom it is written: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4:2). It imitates this Sun by living in humility, righteousness, and devotion.

“Terrible as an army drawn up for battle.”

It is terrible to the powers of the air, ordered like an army drawn up for battle—that is, united in the unity of charity, so that it cannot be penetrated by any temptations.

### Verse 10

“I went down to the garden of nuts.”

The Church, praised by the Synagogue, replies: “I went down to the garden of nuts.” The garden of nuts is the present life. For just as in a nut a very hard shell appears, while the kernel lies hidden, so in the present life the secrets of our consciences are closed and do not appear until, when the shell of the body has been broken, they are revealed.

The Church therefore descends to the garden of nuts when, through its teachers, it considers the life of individuals. Hence it continues:

“To see the apples of the valleys.”

The apples of the valleys are virtues seasoned with humility. “I went down [Col. 1092C],” it says, “to the garden to see the fruits of the valleys,” that is, to consider the saints, endowed indeed with outstanding virtues but humbled by humility.

“And to see whether the vine had blossomed.”

That is, to consider those who were making progress in the pursuit of holy virtues.

“And whether the pomegranates had budded.”

That is, to seek out also those who are already suited to imitate Christ’s passion. For, as has often been said, pomegranates signify the mystery of Christ’s passion.

The Church therefore considers through its prelates who are growing in virtues, and who are already so perfect that, by imitating Christ’s passion, they are also fit to shed their blood for him. Such were those to whom the Apostle said: “To you it has been granted not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29).

### Verse 11

[527] “I did not know.”

This is the voice of the Synagogue. Seeing such great grace in the Church and contemplating the truth of the Gospel, it grieves that it did not previously know the faith of Christ. As though excusing itself for having been converted so late, it says: “I did not know, O Church of Christ the bridegroom. I did not know,” that is, “I did not recognize such great grace and such great gifts of spiritual virtues bestowed upon you by your bridegroom” [Col. 1092D].

“My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab.”

“I was troubled,” it says, “by great anxiety of spirit because of the Gospel’s sudden preaching.” I knew that the Law and the Prophets had been given by God; and therefore, when I suddenly saw the Gospel being preached, I was troubled because of the chariots of Amminadab.

Amminadab was the great-grandson of Judah, through whom Christ’s genealogy is woven. Amminadab is interpreted as “the spontaneous one of my people,” and therefore signifies Christ, who was spontaneous on behalf of his people: although he was God, he freely became human; although he was Creator and Maker, by his goodness alone he became the portion of his people.

The sense is therefore: “I was troubled because of the sudden preaching of the Gospel, which, like a swift chariot [Col. 1093A], quickly traversed the whole world.” It rightly calls this preaching not a single chariot but chariots, because the preaching of the Gospel rests upon the authority of the four evangelists, and the four Gospels are like the four chariots of the New Testament. Christ himself presides as charioteer, guiding and directing the chariot of the Gospels.

### Verse 12

“Return, return, O Sunamite.”

This is the voice of the Church inviting the Synagogue to faith: “Return, return, O Sunamite.” Return, O Synagogue, from unbelief to faith; return from hatred to love.

Sunamite is interpreted as “captive” or “despised.” Such was the Synagogue before Christ’s coming: captive, namely, in the bond of the devil, and despised by God because it did not recognize Christ, who had been sent for its salvation.

“Return, return, so that we may look upon you,” that is, so that we may behold the beauty of your chastity.

# Chapter VII

[Col. 1093B]

### Verse 1

“What will you see in the Sunamite, except choruses of armies?”

This is the voice of the bridegroom. Hearing that the Synagogue is being invited to faith by his bride, the Church, he says: “What will you see in the Sunamite, except choruses of armies?”

It is as though he said: “You, O bride, grieve over the destruction of the Synagogue and over its coming to faith so late; but the time is at hand when it will be converted, and then you will see in it nothing except choruses of armies”—that is, nothing except harmony in charity and the firm strength of faith, by which it will fight in defense of my faith.

For choruses are groups of singers, whereas armies are groups of fighting soldiers. Choruses of armies will therefore be seen in the Shulammite, because, once converted, the Synagogue will preach Christ harmoniously with the Church and will fight for the faith of Christ to the point of death.

“How beautiful are your steps!”

From this point the bridegroom begins to expound the praises of his bride. It should be noted that he begins to compose her beauty from her steps and ends her praises at her mouth, just as above he had begun from her eyes [Col. 1093C]. He did this either to vary the beauty of the poem or because this arrangement is especially suited to the mysteries.

“How beautiful,” he says, “are your steps!” He saw that the Church did not stand idly in one place but traversed the whole world through swift preaching, and therefore began his praise of it with its steps. For the steps of the Church are the swift preaching of the apostles, through whom the Gospel resounded throughout the whole earth.

“In sandals,” that is, in the examples of the fathers who came before. For sandals are made from dead animals. The sandals of the Church are therefore the examples of the fathers who came before, by which its steps are protected, so that, imitating them, it may walk more securely and without stumbling.

“Daughter of a prince.”

Another translation reads, “daughter of Amminadab.” As was said above, Amminadab is interpreted as “the spontaneous one of my people,” and rightly represents Christ. For the Church is both daughter and bride: daughter because it was redeemed by his blood and regenerated by his baptism; bride because it has been joined to him by the dowry of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1093D].

“The joints of your thighs are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan.”

In the loins, or thighs, Holy Scripture commonly signifies the propagation of a lineage. Thus we read concerning Jacob: “All the souls that came forth from the thigh of Jacob” (Exodus 1:5).

The thighs of the Church therefore signify the spiritual generation of the believing people through the word of preaching and the bath of regeneration. The joints of the thighs signify the union of two peoples in one faith, the Jewish and the Gentile.

This joint is rightly compared to necklaces because the faith of both peoples is manifested especially in works; for “faith without works is dead” (James 2:26). They are fashioned by the hand of an artisan—that is, of almighty God, by whose gift the virtue of good works is granted to believers.

This is the artisan of whom Paul spoke when he recalled the patriarch Abraham [Col. 1094A]: “For he was awaiting the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10).

### Verse 2

“Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking mixed wine.”

The navel is the most fragile part of the body, and therefore through the navel we should understand the fragility of our mortality. A bowl is a large cup with handles on either side.

The navel of the Church is therefore a turned bowl, because the more the teachers of the Church remember their own fragility, the more earnestly they devote themselves to the word of preaching, so that, offering the alms of God’s word, they may themselves obtain mercy from God.

It is rightly called a turned bowl. We work more easily with a lathe, and this signifies the ease of distributing the word or giving alms. Alms should not be given reluctantly or hesitantly, in accordance with what Solomon says: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back; tomorrow I will give it to you,’ when you can give immediately” (Proverbs 3:26).

Moreover, what is made on a lathe does not require an external rule or line, but is completed accurately from within itself. The navel of the Church is therefore a turned bowl [Col. 1094B], because whoever preaches or gives alms ought to do so solely for love and in expectation of heavenly reward.

For whoever preaches or shows mercy to his neighbors for temporal recompense or praise is a bowl, but not a turned bowl. This bowl is never lacking cups, because preaching the word of God is never absent from preachers. The one whom they preach supplies them with cups of knowledge and the strength of steadfastness. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power” (Psalm 68:12).

[528] “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, surrounded by lilies.”

The same fragility that was signified by the navel is shown here by the belly, since the belly is not fortified by the firmness of any bones.

The belly of the Church is therefore rightly compared to a heap of wheat, because the more the saints remember their fragility, the more diligently they devote themselves to producing the fruits of good works. It rightly says not merely “wheat” but “a heap [Col. 1094C] of wheat,” signifying by this the growth of virtues, which, like a heap, rises from lower things to higher by continual increase.

For just as a heap spreads out broadly at its base but contracts and becomes pointed toward the top, so in the Church there are many who live more indulgently, but few who devote themselves to the highest perfection. More are found who give alms from their possessions than those who abandon their possessions for God.

This heap is said to be surrounded by lilies because the saints perform the good things they do out of desire for heavenly brightness and purity. For that heavenly radiance is signified by lilies.

The belly of the Church may also be understood as the divine fountain of baptism, through which the faithful are regenerated into a new creation. This belly is therefore compared to a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies because those regenerated in the baptismal fountain are taught to labor at good works and always to yearn to behold the glory of heavenly radiance.

### Verse 3

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle” [Col. 1094D].

The breasts of the Church, as was already said above, signify the holy teachers, who instruct the little ones—that is, those recently regenerated in Christ—with the milk of clearer and simpler teaching.

They are rightly called two breasts because the faithful are gathered from two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, and are nourished with the milk of spiritual teaching.

These two breasts are said to be like two twin fawns of a gazelle. The two fawns are the two Testaments, upon which all the preaching of those teachers rests. Christ is the one author and promulgator of both Testaments, in accordance with what Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like firmly fixed nails driven deeply, given by one shepherd” (Ecclesiasticus 12:11)—namely, Christ.

The gazelle rightly signifies Christ, because it surpasses the other animals in keenness of sight and speed, and is a clean animal, dividing the hoof and chewing the cud.

Such are the members of Christ, namely the teachers [Col. 1095A]: distinguished by the keenness of their knowledge, and with a speed that abandons earthly things and hastens toward heavenly things; “dividing the hoof,” that is, possessing discernment between good and evil; and “chewing the cud,” that is, meditating continually upon God’s commandments.

### Verse 4

“Your neck is like a tower of ivory.”

The holy teachers, who are signified by the breasts, are also signified by the neck. Through the arteries of the neck the voice proceeds, and by the service of the neck vital nourishment is supplied to the other members. So too the holy teachers announce the words of life to the peoples and nourish them with the food of heavenly doctrine.

The neck of the Church is therefore compared to a tower of ivory because the holy teachers provide that same Church with both beauty and strength. They provide beauty, signified by the whiteness of ivory, by living chastely and sincerely; and they provide strength, signified by the tower, when they fortify the Church against the temptations of the devil and the attacks of heretics.

“Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude” [Col. 1095B].

The same teachers who were signified by the neck are also signified by the eyes. Like eyes, they care for the whole body of the Church and show it the path on which it ought to walk.

These eyes of the Church are compared to pools built at the gate of the city of Heshbon because the holy teachers wash the peoples who believe in Christ in the life-giving bath and refresh them with the drink of saving doctrine.

Heshbon is literally called “daughter of the multitude” because of the multitude of peoples who gather there. Thus the holy Church is rightly called the daughter of the multitude because it daily gathers a multitude of nations.

Heshbon, however, is interpreted as “belt of sorrow.” The eyes of the Church are therefore compared to the pools of Heshbon because the holy teachers, neglecting the fleeting joys of the world, bind themselves with the belt of sorrow. They live chastely and soberly in this world (Titus 2:12) and weep over their sins, so that, mourning in the present world, they may reach true and eternal joys.

These pools are said to be at the gate of Heshbon because no one can enter the Church unless first washed in the water of baptism and unless he drinks from the fountain of saving doctrine. This was also signified by the bronze basin that Solomon placed in the temple portico, so that the priests, when they entered the temple and were about to sacrifice victims, might wash their bodies there (1 Kings 7:23).

“Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon that looks toward Damascus.”

Because by the nose we distinguish foul odors from good ones, the same holy teachers are rightly understood through the nose of the Church. They know how to distinguish skillfully the fragrant doctrine of the catholic faith from the deadly stench of heretical error.

For among the divine gifts distributed through the Holy Spirit it is said: “To another is given, through the Spirit, the discernment of spirits” (1 Corinthians 12:10).

The nose of the Church is therefore compared to the tower of Lebanon because the holy teachers hold the highest place in the Church, standing as if upon Mount Lebanon, and defend the Church against the attacks of evil spirits.

This tower is said to stand opposite Damascus [Col. 1095D]. Damascus is the capital city of Syria, which once fought against the children of Israel because it had very strong and cruel kings.

Damascus is interpreted as “drinking of blood,” or “eye of blood.” It is said that Abel was killed there, and therefore it signifies the powers of this world, which thirst for drinking blood because they delight in the pleasures and enticements of flesh and blood. It also signifies the powers of the air, which thirst for the blood of our souls.

This tower therefore stands opposite Damascus because, fortified by the help of Christ, this Church always resists the devil and his members.

### Verse 5

[529] “Your head is like Carmel.”

The head of the Church signifies the sovereignty of the minds of the faithful. For just as the members are governed by the head, so thoughts are ordered by the mind.

The head of the Church is rightly compared to Carmel. Carmel, also called Carmelus, is interpreted as “knowledge” or “knowledge of circumcision” [Col. 1096A]. The head of the Church is therefore likened to Carmel because it knows that circumcision, once practiced bodily, must now be observed spiritually, in accordance with what the prophet says: “Circumcise yourselves for the Lord in your hearts” (Jeremiah 4:4).

The Jews did not possess this understanding of circumcision, and therefore they are reproved by blessed Stephen, the first martyr, who says: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

It is also written in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 18:45) that Elijah ascended Mount Carmel and there, by praying, watered the dry earth with heavenly rains after a long drought of three and a half years.

This story gives off the fragrance of a beautiful allegory. Elijah, whose name is interpreted as “My God is the Lord,” signifies Christ, who, although he is God and Lord of all and of the whole creation, is specially his own—that is, the proper God and Lord of the Church.

He ascended Carmel when, through his grace, he ascended into the minds of his faithful and through them bestowed the rains of his graces upon the dry world [Col. 1096B].

The head of the Church is therefore rightly compared, as has been said, to Mount Carmel, because the mind of the saints is exalted by a certain manner of life and offers Christ an ascent into itself through progress in virtues.

“And the locks of your head are like royal purple bound in channels.”

If the head of the Church signifies the mind, then by the locks of the head we should understand the thoughts of the mind, which continually proceed from it.

The purple color, which resembles blood, signifies the mystery of the Lord’s passion. Literally, “royal purple bound in channels” signifies wool already dyed purple but not yet drawn out into threads; it is still lying in the channels called in Greek βάτια, in which the blood of shellfish customarily flows and turns the wool purple.

Mystically, these channels signify the humility of the saints. The purple of the eternal King is dyed in them when the saints, imitating the humility of their Redeemer, strive to become conformed to his sufferings, so that they may be changed into the dignity of purple—that is, by laboring for Christ, may deserve to be crowned and reign with Christ [Col. 1096C].

This purple is said to be bound because the inmost hearts of the saints are fixed and established in fear and love of their Redeemer, and can never be separated from his charity.

### Verse 6

“How beautiful and how lovely you are, my dearest, in delights!”

How beautiful you are, namely in faith, and lovely in action, my dearest, in delights.

It was said above of this same Church: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up for battle.” Here, however, it is called beautiful and lovely, dearest, in delights.

These expressions seem almost contradictory. To be ordered like an army drawn up for battle and to be in delights appear incompatible, because delights generally weaken the strength of soldiers.
