But the holy Church does both. It is ordered like an army drawn up for battle because it resists unbelieving heretics and terrifies evil spirits by its holiness and perfection. It is also in delights because it continually tastes the sweetness of heavenly delight upon the palate of the mind, desires to attain it amid the pressures of this world, and longs to be continually satisfied by it.

Therefore one who is such is rightly said to be most dear to its bridegroom Christ.

[Col. 1096D]

### Verse 7

“Your stature is likened to a palm tree.” [Col. 1097A]

The stature of the Church is its perfect uprightness. It is not bent toward vices but remains straight and immovable.

Hence the Psalmist, speaking in the person of sinners, said: “I am bent down and humbled completely” (Psalm 118:107). And the prophet, speaking under the figure of Jerusalem to the soul that has sinned, says concerning the evil spirits: “They humbled you and said to your soul, ‘Bow down, so that we may pass over you’” (Isaiah 51:23).

By contrast, the holy Church stands upright and never consents to be bent, hearing the Apostle say: “Watch, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong, and let everything you do be done in charity” (1 Corinthians 16:13).

And the Lord speaks to the children of Israel: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the prison-house of the Egyptians, so that you might walk uprightly” (Exodus 6:8).

The stature of the Church is therefore likened to a palm tree, because in everything it does it always keeps the heavenly reward in mind. The palm adorns the hand of the victor, and therefore signifies the reward that is to be given to the victorious saints in heaven.

“And your breasts are like clusters of grapes.”

The breasts of the Church, as was said above, are the holy teachers, who nourish those regenerated in Christ with the milk of simple doctrine.

These breasts are likened to clusters of grapes when the same teachers announce more perfect things to the perfect, just as the Apostle, speaking to the more simple, said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as fleshly, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2).

Behold breasts full of milk; these breasts have been changed into clusters of grapes when he says: “We preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, and we speak wisdom among the mature.”

### Verse 8

“I said: ‘I will climb the palm tree and seize its fruits.’”

To show that all this excellence and greatness of the Church’s gifts comes from God’s grace [Col. 1097B], the same bridegroom is introduced as saying: “I will climb the palm tree,” as though he were saying: “From me you have breasts with which to nourish the little ones, and from me also you have clusters with which to offer the more perfect a more perfect teaching, because by my grace I have ascended into you and granted you this perfection.”

“I will climb,” he says, “the palm tree.” The palm signifies the Church, or also the soul of any believer who remembers the Lord his God and says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). She too strives to be victorious over every vice and iniquity.

He is rightly said here to have climbed into the palm, since earlier he is read to have descended into the garden. For the garden and the palm are the same thing, namely, one and the same Church. Yet the Lord descended into her and ascended to her: he descended into her by sending her an abundance of his grace from heaven; he ascended to her by increasing his gifts within her and raising her to higher things, as though by certain stages, through various advances, to higher things [Col. 1097C].

It should also be understood from the nature of the palm that below it is rough, while above it is exceedingly beautiful in the splendor of its leaves and the beauty of its fruits. So too the holy Church below endures the harshness of labors and sufferings for Christ; above, however—that is, in heaven—she awaits the beauty and sweetness of her rewards.

The palm may also signify the tree of the Lord’s cross, upon which our Redeemer ascended for the redemption of the human race and upon which he conquered the enemy of the human race. He therefore says: “I will climb the palm tree,” that is, “through my prophets I have spoken and promised that I would come to suffer and redeem my Church.”

“I will seize,” he says, “its fruits,” that is, I will reward the fruits of good works and labors over which the Church toils. Or, according to my understanding, in which the palm signifies the cross: “I will seize its fruits,” that is, once the triumph of the Passion has been fulfilled, I will come to the glory of the resurrection and grant spiritual gifts to my apostles.

[Col. 1097D] “And your breasts will be like clusters of the vine.”

This has already been explained above. The breasts of the Church are the teachers when they nourish the little ones with simple teaching; but they become clusters of the vine when they announce sublime things to the more perfect. For blessed Paul possessed both breasts and clusters at one and the same time when, speaking of Christ, he said: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ” (Romans 9:5). Behold the breasts, that is, the simple preaching concerning Christ. But these breasts were changed into the sweetest and strongest wine when he added: “Who is God over all, blessed forever.”

### Verse 9

“And the fragrance of your mouth is like apples. Your throat is like the finest wine.”

The mouth and fragrance of the Church are her present preaching, which reaches those absent from her either by report or in writing. The throat, however, is the preacher’s actual voice, which is heard in the present. The fragrance of the Church’s mouth is therefore compared with the fragrance of apples, because the report of her preaching is full of sweetness and grace. Her throat is compared with the finest wine because the very voice of the preachers [Col. 1098A] displayed great power to their hearers.

The fact that the fragrance of apples belongs to what is new, while wine belongs to what is old, signifies that the Church’s preaching possesses all sweetness and grace both in its newness and in its maturity.

“Suitable for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to chew.”

This is the voice of the Church. Hearing herself praised by the bridegroom, she joyfully replies, saying: “Suitable for my beloved to drink,” as though she were saying: “My bridegroom has compared my throat with the finest wine, and that wine is suitable for my beloved himself to drink.” This means the Gospel preaching that he placed in my mouth, which ought to be proclaimed in the world through him and no other. For it was not fitting that the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven should be preached to the world through anyone other than the Mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5).

“And,” he says, “for his lips and teeth to chew.” The lips and teeth of the bridegroom, as was said above, are the holy teachers. That finest wine is therefore to be chewed by the bridegroom’s lips and teeth, because the Gospel preaching [Col. 1098B] handed down by God must be handled and expounded by the teachers.

It is not absurd that, although wine is drunk and not chewed, it is nevertheless said here to be chewed by lips and teeth, since chewing belongs more properly to food than to drink. For the holy teachers chew spiritual wine when they diligently examine the Gospel commandments, investigate them through continual meditation, and discuss them with one another.

### Verse 10

“I belong to my beloved, and his turning is toward me.”

“I belong to my beloved”—understand: I offer him the service of justice and devotion; to him and to no other I promise my faith and service.

“And his turning is toward me” [Col. 1098C], so that in the present he may protect me amid the labors and afflictions of this life, and in the future lead me into the joys of heavenly life.

This may also be the voice of the Synagogue, speaking in the person of the holy Fathers who desired Christ’s coming. It is as though she were saying: “I know that he is always present to me by his spiritual presence, and therefore I desire to serve my beloved with complete devotion; but at last his turning will be toward me, because I desire that at last, as he promised, he may appear to me in my own substance.”

For earlier the bridegroom had said: “I will climb the palm tree,” that is, he had promised that he would come in the flesh and reveal himself to the world as a human being in my substance.

### Verse 11

“Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us stay in the villages.”

This is the voice of the same Synagogue.

“Come, my beloved,” that is, appear through the human being you have assumed. The Psalmist says something similar: “Stir up your power and come” (Psalm 79:3). Isaiah likewise says: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come” (Isaiah 64:1).

“Let us go out into the field.” The field is this world. “Let us go out,” she says, “into the field,” that is, let us preach to the world.

“Let us stay in the villages,” that is, let us announce your faith also to the pagans themselves. Everyone knows that the pagans are called by the word for “village,” because πάγος means “village” in Greek and *villa* in Latin. Hence they are called *Pagani*, because they are far from the city of God.

It may also be the voice of the Church: “Come, my beloved,” as though she were saying: “By the mystery of the Ascension you have already raised the human being you assumed into heaven; but come by visiting me more often with the presence of your divine majesty [Col. 1098D].”

“Let us go out into the field,” in the same sense as above: let us preach the faith of your incarnation to the world.

“Let us stay in the villages,” that is, let us announce your faith even to the pagans who do not know you; and let us not remain there merely in passing, but let us stay until we make them, from pagans, Catholics, and from strangers, your own people.

### Verse 12

“Let us rise early and go to the vineyards.”

“Early” means the dawn of the new grace, when, after the darkness of unbelief had passed, the Gospel began to be preached to the world.

“Let us see whether the vine has flowered,” that is, let us inspect the Church to see whether she has already received the first beginnings of faith.

“Whether the flowers have produced fruit.”

Let us also see whether the flowers produce fruit, that is, whether those who have already believed in Christ are capable of doing good works. The Church sends forth flowers when the faithful first come to faith; the flowers produce fruit when, already through faith and love, she acts well, so that faith itself [Col. 1099A] may not be idle or dead without works. For, as James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:26).

“Whether the pomegranates have flowered.”

The pomegranates, as was said above, have a red or blood-colored rind, and therefore signify the Passion of the Lord or of his members. He therefore says: “Whether the pomegranates have flowered,” that is, whether the saints who are already perfect in faith and works are also capable of imitating Christ’s Passion and suffering for him.

Those pomegranates were the people to whom the Apostle said: “It has been granted to you not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29).

“There I will give you my breasts.”

The breasts of the Church are the teachers who first instruct the faithful in the faith. “When,” he says, “we have gone out to the vineyards, there I will give you, O bridegroom, my breasts,” that is, I will beget spiritual children for you. Hence he adds:

### Verse 13

“The mandrakes have given their fragrance in our gates.”

The mandrake is an aromatic herb whose root [Col. 1099B] resembles the human body. Its fruits have an excellent fragrance, resembling the *Malum Matianum*, which our people call a “ground apple” (*terrae malum*). This herb is highly suitable for medicinal purposes. For it is said that those who suffer from the discomfort of sleeplessness are relieved by drinking its fruit and are able to sleep. It is also said that those who must undergo cutting for medical treatment, if they drink the outer rind of this fruit, do not feel cutting or burning. [531] If anyone wishes to investigate all these things mystically, he will find there spiritual meanings appropriate to the Church.

He therefore says: “The mandrakes have given their fragrance in our gates.” The gates of the Church are the apostles and their successors, because no one enters the city of God—that is, the Church—unless, through the holy teachers, he has been regenerated by the water of baptism and instructed in life-giving doctrine.

Concerning these gates the Psalmist said: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Psalm 86:2).

The fragrance of the mandrakes signifies virtues. The mandrakes therefore gave their fragrance in the gates of the Church [Col. 1099C] when the apostles or their successors spread far and wide the reputation of an exceedingly sweet character and the fragrance of virtues.

For this reason the Church invites her bridegroom to come, because his name is already being proclaimed far and wide through the apostles, and the fragrance of Christ’s preaching is being scattered everywhere.

“All new and old fruits I have kept for you, my beloved.”

That is, “I have kept for you, O my beloved, the commandments and promises of the Old Testament and of the New.” She knew that everything announced in the Old Testament could be fulfilled only through Christ and in Christ, and therefore she said: “I have kept for you new and old fruits,” that is, “I await you, so that through you the things foretold in the Old Testament may be fulfilled in the New [Col. 1099D].”

Hence, already hanging upon the cross in his Passion, after tasting vinegar, he said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). And after the resurrection he said to the apostles: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44).

The new and old fruits may also be understood as the persons of the righteous who lived either in the Old Testament or in the New. The Church therefore says: “I have kept for you new and old,” that is, “I have kept for you the righteous who preceded you in the Old Testament and those who followed in the New, so that through you they might receive the rewards of their labors.”

For none of the righteous was able to enter the kingdom of heaven except through Christ, because he himself first ascended and opened heaven to his members who were to follow.

## Chapter VIII

### Verse 1

“Who will grant you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother? If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me.”

From these words it is understood that this entire divine song is spiritual and that it contains nothing that can be understood according to the literal sense. For what lover ever wished that the one whom she loves should become a little child and her brother, and, having been changed into an infant, suck the breasts of his mother?

It is therefore the voice of that Church which preceded Christ’s coming, which we call the Synagogue, that is, the congregation.

“Who,” she says, “will grant you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother?” The meaning is: “You who are now in the bosom of the Father [Col. 1100A]” (John 1:18), “who will grant that you become human and, being a participant and sharer in my nature, be called my brother?”

For he himself deigned to call the apostles his brothers, saying through the Psalmist: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Psalm 21:23); and after the resurrection he said to the women: “Go and announce to my brothers” (Matthew 28:10).

“Sucking the breasts of my mother,” he says, that is, fulfilling everything that belongs to human nature except sin. In this passage the mother of the Synagogue is understood as human nature itself, from which the Synagogue arose.

“Sucking,” he says, “the breasts of my mother,” that is, enduring everything that belongs to human weakness.

“If I found you outside,” that is, if I saw you openly made human. For he was, as it were, inside when he lay hidden in the bosom of the Father’s majesty; but he was found outside when he became human, showed himself visibly to human beings, and willed that the incomprehensible should be comprehended.

“And I would kiss you.”

“I would kiss you,” she says, that is, I would behold you [Col. 1100B] in a manifest vision, you whom I now hold only in the kiss of faith. At the beginning of this song she desired this, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1), that is, let him now come through himself so that he may appear to me.

For the beloved was kissing the Church, as it were, through the prophets when he promised his coming through them. She therefore desires that he come through himself and kiss her, that is, that he display his presence in his flesh.

“And no one would despise me.”

The Synagogue was, as it were, despised before Christ came, because, devoted to legal observances and living under type and figure rather than in truth, she proclaimed Christ’s coming. But after Jesus appeared and illumined the world by the grace of his coming, no one despised her any longer. Rather, she became terrifying to her enemies like an army in battle array, because she preached Christ throughout the whole world and subjected worldly rule to herself.

It should not seem surprising that we now call the Church the Synagogue, for there is one Church in the preceding and subsequent [Col. 1100C] sections.

### Verse 2

“I will seize you and lead you into the house of my mother.”

“O beloved! By clinging to you through faith and love, I will lead you into the house of my mother.” The mother of the Church is understood here as that heavenly Jerusalem of which Paul says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26).

“I will lead you,” he says, “into the house of my mother,” that is, I will accompany you as you return to heaven after the completion of the mystery of your incarnation and Passion.

He says “I will lead you” in the sense of “I will conduct and accompany you,” because the apostles followed the Lord ascending into heaven with their eyes and watched him with devoted attention until the cloud received him, until the attending angels said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

“There you will teach me.”

This refers to what was said above, where it says, “If I found you outside.” “When,” she says, “I find you outside,” that is, “when I see you in the flesh you have assumed [Col. 1100D], there you will teach me,” because you will answer everything I wish to ask.

For the Lord often anticipated the apostles even when they wished to ask questions and instructed them beforehand (Mark 9).

This may also be joined to the present passage, where he says, “I will lead you into the house of my mother: there you will teach me.” “When,” she says, “you have been received into heaven and have taken me with you into heaven, there you will teach me and lead me into all truth,” something that it is impossible for a human being to attain in the present life.

Hence the Lord promises the apostles, saying: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly” (John 16:25).

Therefore, “there you will teach me” means: you will reveal yourself and the Father to me in an open vision; that is, you will show me your divinity face to face.

“And I will give you a cup of spiced wine.”

Wine signifies the fervor of charity and love. “I will give you,” she says, “wine,” that is, “I will show how fervently I love you.”

And this wine will not be plain [Col. 1101A] but spiced, namely, with good works and virtues. For the love of God, as blessed Gregory says (St. Gregory, *Homily 30 on the Gospels*), is never idle: “If it exists, it accomplishes great things; for if it refuses to act, it is not love.” Spiced wine is therefore love accompanied by action.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14:23). The proof of love is therefore the performance of a work.

“And the new wine of my pomegranates.”

The pomegranate is the same as the *malum punicum*. It is called *malum granatum* because it is full of many seeds, and *malum punicum* because it abounds especially in Africa. For *Punica* itself means Africa.

It has a blood-colored rind and therefore, as has often been said, represents the Lord’s Passion. The new wine of the pomegranates is the love of the holy martyrs, who loved God so greatly that they did not hesitate to die for him.

It is rightly called new wine [Col. 1101B] and not some other kind of drink, because new wine is exceedingly fervent, so that in its excessive heat it boils out and purifies every impurity within it. The Church will therefore give her beloved the new wine of her pomegranates, that is, she will show in the sufferings of the holy martyrs how greatly Christ is loved.

### Verse 3

“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”

By the left hand, as blessed Gregory says, all the prosperous things of the present life are understood (St. Gregory, on chapter 2 of the *Song of Songs*); by the right hand, the blessed future life in heaven is understood.

The Church therefore has the bridegroom’s left hand beneath her head, and his right hand embraces her, because she counts as nothing whatever prosperity in the present age may flatter her with. She despises everything that smiles upon her temporally; and while she strives toward the vision of heavenly blessedness alone, she desires to be embraced by that alone.

### Verse 4

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, do not awaken or rouse the beloved until she herself wishes it.”

The Church contains certain people who have been reborn in Christ’s baptism [Col. 1101C] and are marked by the name of Christianity, yet in conduct and way of life serve the world. They try to disturb the Church, lulled into the sweetest repose, and to rouse her to endure worldly tumult.

Because of the grace of Christ’s mysteries that they have received, these people are called “daughters of Jerusalem” in this passage, although their conduct is contrary to that name.

The bridegroom therefore adjures them not to awaken or rouse the beloved, that is, not to disturb her while she lies in the sleep of the sweetest repose—namely, in contemplation of her Creator—and by their unrest compel her to awaken to the anxieties and cares of the world.

“Until she herself wishes it,” that is, until, after completing the duty of her appointed service by which she serves God in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, she is again reminded by care for bodily weakness to return to the use of the world.

### Verse 5

“Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?”

This is the voice of the Synagogue, marveling at the Church gathered from the nations.

“Who is this,” she says—that is, what sort of person is she, and of what great merit—“who comes up from the wilderness?” She had been abandoned by God [Col. 1101D] through idolatry and ignorance of the truth.

She therefore ascended by the steps of the virtues from the wilderness, that is, from the error of unbelief in which she had for a time been abandoned.

“Overflowing with delights,” that is, abounding in virtues.

“Leaning,” she says, “upon her beloved,” that is, acting with confidence in Christ and referring all her virtues and every good thing to his grace.

She knew that she could accomplish nothing good by her own powers, and therefore says with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

It should be noted that she says “upon her beloved.” The Synagogue alone thought that she possessed knowledge of God, while the other nations were deprived of it in ignorance. For, as the Psalmist says: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75:2).

But the bridegroom and beloved himself responds to the Synagogue’s astonishment with what follows.

“Under the apple tree I raised you up.”

We must understand the apple tree as the Lord’s cross, beneath which the Synagogue was raised up, because she was redeemed from the transgression of original sin and from the power of the devil through Christ’s cross [Col. 1102A]. There she was raised up, having been dead in sins.

He rightly calls it the apple tree, for above he also compared Christ, the beloved, with this tree, saying: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons.”

“There your mother was corrupted; there your mother was violated.”

By the mother and progenitress of the Synagogue he means the greater and more prominent part of the Jewish people, such as the scribes and Pharisees who handed Christ over to Pilate (Matthew 27:2). They ought to have governed and instructed the rest of the people as mother and progenitress. Such also were those who, at the urging of those rulers, wickedly cried out: “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John 19:6).

This mother of the Synagogue was corrupted and violated beneath the apple tree when she bound herself and her descendants by a cruel curse, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25).

For they too were beneath Christ’s cross, though not in faith and devotion, but in invoking upon themselves and their descendants the punishment of cruel vengeance.

[Col. 1102B] ### Verse 6

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.”

“Because,” he says, “I raised you up beneath the apple tree”—that is, “because in my Passion upon the cross I redeemed you”—“set me as a seal upon your heart,” that is, keep me always in your memory, and do not forget how much I endured for your salvation.

“Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart” through faith; “set me as a seal upon your arm” through worthy action.

When we wish to keep something in our memory, we too are accustomed to place a mark upon a finger or arm, so that, reminded by it, we may remember the matter for which we are concerned.

We too ought to place Christ as a seal upon our heart and arm, so that we may always remember him and, believing rightly in him, adorn that faith itself with good works.

If we do this, he too will take us as a seal, as it were, and remember us, in accordance with what he promises Zerubbabel, ruler of Judea [Col. 1102C]: “On that day I will take you, Zerubbabel my servant, and make you like a seal in my presence” (Haggai 2:24).

But if we forget his benefits and do not offer him worthy thanks, he too will forget us, as is said of the wicked king Jeconiah: “If Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring on my right hand, I would tear him away from there” (Jeremiah 22:24).

“For love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as hell.”

Christ’s love is strong as death. Just as death separates the soul from the body, so that it can no longer desire anything or seek anything in the present life, so the love of Christ, when it has truly taken possession of someone, puts that person wholly to death to this age and makes him, as it were, insensible to it. Living only for Christ, he is dead to the world.

The same meaning applies when he says that jealousy is hard as hell. For just as hell never restores those whom it once receives but always retains them, so true love of Christ, once it has received someone, never lets him go.

Hence the Apostle says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness [Col. 1102D], or danger, or the sword?” (Romans 8:35).

The love of Christ may also be understood here as the love with which he loved us, which was strong as death because he loved us so greatly that, although immortal, he accepted death for us.

His jealousy was hard as hell because hell does not know how to show mercy or to be softened toward the punishments of the wretched. So Christ’s love could not cease from mercy or be driven away from love of the human race by any wickedness of his persecutors.

Some refer the words “jealousy is hard as hell” specifically to the Synagogue, which was jealous of the nations and envious of their salvation. In saying this, Christ therefore admonishes her to cease from envy and to rejoice with the Church in her salvation.

“His lamps are lamps of fire and flames.”

That is, the lamps of love are lamps of fire and flames. The lamps of love are the hearts of the saints, in which love dwells as in vessels.

These lamps are therefore both fire and flames: they are lamps of fire because they burn inwardly [Col. 1103A] through love; they are lamps of flames because they shine outwardly through action.

### Verse 7

“Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.”

The waters and rivers are the violent threats of persecutors, or even their flatteries, by which they try to separate the saints from the love of God.

Concerning these the Lord says in the Gospel, speaking of the man who built his house upon a rock: “The rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon a rock” (Matthew 7:25).

Many waters therefore cannot extinguish love, because no tribulation or distress will be able to separate the saints from the love of God.

“If a man were to give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as nothing.”

This verse needs no exposition, for no substance of the world and no wealth amounts to anything in comparison with love.

We read that the saints abandoned their possessions for the love of Christ, yet in comparison with the love of Christ whom they loved, they seemed to themselves to be abandoning nothing [Col. 1103B].

Hence the Apostle, when he abandoned not only earthly possessions but also ancestral traditions for Christ, said: “I consider all these things contemptible and regard them as dung, so that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:8), that is, so that I may acquire his love.

### Verse 8

“Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?”

This is the voice of the beloved addressing the Synagogue concerning the Church of the nations.

“Our sister,” he says, that is, the Church of the nations, “is little, and she has no breasts.” With great condescension, sharing with the Synagogue its name, he says “our sister,” because he assumed flesh from the Jews and therefore, as it were, adapts and equates himself with the Synagogue.

“Our sister is little.” Just as a person’s age is described, so the age of the Church is described. The Church, still being gathered from the nations in the time of the Lord and the apostles, was little, both because the number of believers was small [Col. 1103C] and because she did not yet have breasts—that is, she was not yet able, through preaching, to beget spiritual children for God.

He speaks as though seeking the Synagogue’s counsel: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?”

The address of the Church occurs when God admonishes the soul of each believer either inwardly through hidden inspiration or outwardly through open preaching.

The meaning is: “When through my apostles I address the Church gathered from the nations, what shall we do? How shall we entrust the heavenly commandments to her? Shall we entrust to her only the smallest commandments, or, so that she may become greater, shall we hand over to her the more perfect mysteries of heavenly secrets?”

For almighty God adjusts the word of preaching according to the measure and capacity of the human mind, considering the strength and capacity of the hearer.

But while the Synagogue remained silent, the bridegroom himself answered on her behalf.

### Verse 9

“If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her; if she is a door, let us join it with cedar boards.”

“If,” he says, “our sister is a wall [Col. 1103D], let us build silver battlements upon her.”

It is as though he were saying: “When my apostles begin to preach to the Church gathered from the nations, if the hearers prove to be such that, by reason of their perfection, they can rightly be called a wall—whether because they possess natural intelligence or because they excel in philosophical learning and are able, like a wall, to defend and fortify others—let us build silver battlements upon such a wall, that is, let us add to them the words of the divine Scriptures.”

For, as the Psalmist says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested in fire” (Psalm 11:7).

But if the hearers are such that they cannot resist enemies or repel the weapons coming against them, but are like a door—so that by announcing simple things they can bring some people into the Church and to the faith—such as priests of a lesser rank, who by baptizing in the Church and initiating people into the divine mysteries bring them into the Church, then “let us join that door with cedar boards,” that is, let us set before them the examples of the Fathers who came before [Col. 1104A].

They are like cedars, namely, imperishable wood, because they possess unfading works; and they are spread out like boards in the breadth of knowledge and love.

The breadth of the boards signifies the breadth of the heart, in which there ought to be breadth of love and knowledge, as the Psalmist says: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm 118:32).

With these cedar boards—that is, with the examples of the saints—let us therefore join that door, so that by imitating their examples they may open to others, as a door, an entrance into the Church.

### Verse 10

“I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.”

This is the voice of the Church. When she heard her beloved taking counsel for her salvation, she joyfully replied: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.”

“I am a wall,” she says, because I have been founded upon a firm rock (Matthew 16:18) and made solid by the bond of divine love.

Or I am a wall because I have been built from living and chosen stones, namely, the saints.

“And my breasts are like a tower,” because I contain within me people who [Col. 1104B], in the place of breasts, can nourish others with spiritual doctrine, and, in the place of a tower, can defend and fortify them. Like towers rising above a wall, they surpass the other members in the merit of their doctrine and way of life.

But I possess this neither through my own merits nor through the freedom of my will, but through the gift and grace of my bridegroom.

“From the time when I became before him like one who has found peace.”

That is, from the time when he poured out his blood for me and, by reconciling me to God the Father, destroyed the enmity that existed between God and humanity and made heavenly things peaceful for me.

From the time, therefore, when I found this peace, I became worthy to be a wall and to have breasts in the place of towers.

### Verse 11

“There was a vineyard belonging to the peaceful one,” that is, to my beloved, who is truly peaceful, because through him all things in heaven and on earth have been made peaceful.

Hence he is also called by the prophet “Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). As a figure of this true peaceful one, Solomon—whose name means “peaceful”—the author of this song came before.

To this one [Col. 1104C], therefore, belonged a vineyard, that is, the holy Church.

“In it are peoples.”

He says this in order to show that he is singing of the Church of the nations, not of the Synagogue. The Synagogue belonged to one nation alone, whereas the Church has peoples, because she receives and embraces all nations within her exceedingly capacious bosom.

“He entrusted it to keepers.”

The keepers of this vineyard—that is, of the holy Church—are the prophets, the apostles, and the successors of the apostles.

Alternatively, the keepers of this vineyard in this age are the angelic powers, which guard the Church from the attacks of temptations and demons.

“A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.”

He speaks of strong and perfect men, for *vir* (“man”) is derived from *virtus* (“strength” or “virtue”).

The fruit of the Church is the reward of heavenly life, for which the holy Church does not cease to labor in the present life.

The thousand silver pieces that a man brings for its fruit signify everything that can be possessed in this world. The number one thousand is used to signify the fullness of perfection.

A man therefore brings a thousand silver pieces for the fruit of this vineyard because the saints [Col. 1104D] leave all that is theirs and distribute it to the poor, so that they may obtain the fruit of this vineyard—that is, the reward above.

The Lord says something similar in the parable of the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man, when he finds it, hides, and for joy over it goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44).

### Verse 12

“My vineyard is before me.”

This is the voice of the bridegroom.

“You say,” he says, “that I entrusted my vineyard to keepers; yet the vineyard is always before me, because although I have entrusted it to my keepers, I nevertheless always care for it. I do not cease to be concerned for it, but remain with it until the consummation of the age.”

“Your thousand silver pieces, O peaceful one, and two hundred for those who keep its fruit.”

A thousand silver pieces is understood: the thousand silver pieces that you gave for the fruit of the vineyard belong to your peaceful one.

It is as though he were saying: “O faithful soul, do not doubt the eternal reward for which you gave all that was yours, because your thousand silver pieces [Col. 1105A] belong to your peaceful one,” that is, a certain reward awaits you, and you will truly obtain its fruit.

“And two hundred”—understand, silver pieces—“belong to the peaceful one for those who keep its fruit.”

Just as the number one thousand signifies the fullness of perfection, so the number one hundred signifies the highest perfection, because one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right.

The two hundred silver pieces, which are a doubled hundred, therefore signify those who are perfect in doctrine and holy action, who guard themselves by living justly and piously and also convert others by preaching.

To such people, therefore, belong two hundred silver pieces as their peaceful reward, because a doubled recompense awaits them in heaven. Concerning such people Daniel says: “Those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like stars for everlasting ages” (Daniel 12:3).

The Apostle commands that these people be honored doubly, saying: “Let the presbyters who are among you be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching” (1 Timothy 5:17).

Verse 13. You who dwell in gardens—the friends listen; let me hear your voice.

The voice of the Beloved addressing the bride, that is, the Church: “O Church, you who dwell in gardens,” that is, you who devote yourself to cultivating the shoots of the virtues. For the Bridegroom’s garden is the Church herself, which, as was said above, he frequently promises to visit. The Church therefore dwells in gardens because she continually nourishes the plantations of the virtues. Nor does she set up a temporary shelter there, as though she would soon depart, but dwells there in a fixed habitation.

“Let me,” he says, “hear your voice,” that is, preach the Gospel to those whom you can reach; proclaim the precepts of my law, and likewise announce the promise of heavenly rewards. For this is pleasing and delightful to me: to hear your voice, that is, to hear you announcing the words of eternal salvation.

“But the friends listen to you,” that is, the angelic spirits take delight in hearing your voice. I made them your friends by the shedding of my blood, and appointed them as helpers and protectors against the evil spirits. Or, “the friends,” that is, the spirits of the righteous, whom I took from your company and assumed into the heavenly places. For they rejoice together because of your preaching and the salvation of your brothers. The bride herself immediately responds to her Beloved.

Verse 14. Flee, my beloved, and be like the gazelle and the fawn of deer upon the mountains of spices.

A remarkable response. She is invited to preach, and the Bridegroom wishes to hear her voice; yet she urges her Bridegroom to flee. But the sequence of the mystery is profound. Since Christ’s birth had previously been foretold when she said, “Who will grant that you were my brother, nursing at the breasts?” and since his passion had also been foretold where it was said, “Under the apple tree I awakened you,” she now accordingly urges the Bridegroom to flee—that is, to return with utmost speed through his ascension to the Father.

The meaning is this: “You command me to preach; you wish to hear my voice. Flee, my beloved,” that is, once the mystery of your incarnation and passion has been fulfilled, return to heaven, so that I may begin to think of you no longer as a human being but as God above all things. Then you will hear my voice, because then I shall preach you more freely to the whole world.

This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away” (John 16:7). It was advantageous for the apostles and for the whole Church that Christ should return and withdraw his bodily presence. While he was bodily present, they could not love him spiritually, nor could they think of him—whom they saw as a human being—as the invisible God who is present everywhere. But after he himself ascended into heaven, the Church began to love him spiritually, and thus to think of and preach him as God. This is what the Apostle says: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Cor. 5:16).

Therefore, my beloved, if you wish me to preach you in this manner, flee—that is, depart to the heavenly places. You who were comprehensible through your humanity, become incomprehensible through your divinity.

Nevertheless, do not abandon me in the present without your visitation; deign rather to seek me through your frequent visitation and to allow me to see you often. This is what he says: “Be like the gazelle and the fawn of deer upon the mountains of spices.”

“Just as,” he says, “gazelles and the fawns of deer—untamed animals—avoid human company, yet are frequently seen upon the mountains, so you too, after your ascension, although invisible, deign nevertheless to appear to me frequently through the gift of your grace—and this upon the mountains of spices.”

The mountains of spices are the holy people of God: those who, through the excellence of their holy way of life, are near to heaven and whose fragrance and reputation for virtue spread far and wide. Hence the Apostle says of himself and those like him: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20); and elsewhere: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2:1).

[Col. 1105]

# M. Aurelius Cassiodorus, *On the Institution of Divine Literature* (C, S)

## Preface

[Col. 1105D] 537 When I perceived that the studies of secular literature were burning with intense desire, so that a large part of humanity believed that through them it could attain worldly wisdom, I was moved—I confess—with the deepest sorrow because public teachers were lacking for the divine Scriptures, although worldly authors unquestionably enjoyed the greatest renown through a celebrated tradition.

Therefore, together with the most blessed Pope Agapitus of the city of Rome, I tried to arrange that, just as it is reported to have been established long ago at Alexandria, so now also in the city of Nisibis the school of the Syrians might be diligently expounded by Hebrews; and that, at shared expense, Rome might receive professed teachers of the Christian school, so that the soul might receive eternal salvation and the language of the faithful might be adorned with chaste and most pure eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 1105D] Junilius, an African bishop, also mentions this school of the Syrians at Nisibis in the letter prefixed to his two books *On the Parts of the Divine Law*, addressed to Bishop Primasius. “But you,” he says, “in keeping with your customary practice, first asked whether there was among the Greeks anyone who burned with devotion to the study and understanding of the divine books.” To this I replied that I had seen a certain man named Paul, a Persian by birth, who was educated in the Syrians’ school in the city of Nisibis, “where the divine law is regularly taught by public teachers, just as grammar and rhetoric are taught among us in the schools of secular studies,” and so forth. *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. I, p. 2.]

But since, through the wars raging [ed., “because of”] and the excessively turbulent conflicts in the Italian kingdom, my desire could in no way be fulfilled—for a peaceful undertaking has no place in troubled times—I was found to be compelled by divine charity to prepare these introductory books for you, in the place of a teacher, with the Lord’s help. Through them, as I judge, both the sequence of the divine Scriptures and a concise knowledge of secular literature would be disclosed by the Lord’s gift.

They may perhaps be less eloquent, since they contain not affected eloquence but necessary exposition; yet their usefulness is recognized as great, since through them one learns the sources from which both the salvation of the soul and secular learning are shown to proceed. In them I commend not my own doctrine but the sayings of the ancients—things which it is right for posterity to praise and glorious to proclaim. For whatever is said about the ancients under the praise of the Lord is not considered hateful boasting.

Furthermore, you endure an imposing teacher if you question him frequently; but whenever you wish to return to these books, you will be bitten by no harshness.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us confidently ascend to divine Scripture through the trustworthy expositions of the Fathers, as though by a kind of ladder of vision, so that, raised up by their insights, we may deserve to arrive effectively at contemplation of the Lord. This is perhaps Jacob’s ladder, by which the angels ascend and descend (Gen. 28:12), upon which the Lord leans, extending his hand to the weary and sustaining the tired steps of those who ascend through contemplation of him.

Accordingly, if it pleases you, we must observe the following order of reading: first, after Christ’s beginners have learned the psalms, let them meditate continually upon the divine authority in corrected manuscripts until, with the Lord’s help, it becomes thoroughly familiar to them. This is so that the errors of scribes may not grow into their unpolished minds, since what is known to have been rooted and fixed in the recesses of memory can be extracted only with difficulty.

Happy indeed is the soul that, by the Lord’s generosity, has stored the secret of so great a gift in the recesses of memory; but much happier is the soul that has come to know the paths of understanding through living inquiry. Thus it vigorously drives human thoughts away from itself and occupies itself beneficially with divine utterances.

We remember having seen many people endowed with a strong memory who, when questioned about very obscure passages, solved the proposed questions by examples drawn solely from divine authority, because what is clearly set forth in one book is known to have been stated more obscurely elsewhere. The Apostle Paul bears witness to this: for in large part, in the Epistle called *To the Hebrews*, he clarifies the Scriptures of the Old Testament through the perfection of the new age.

After Christ’s soldiers have therefore filled themselves with divine reading and, strengthened by frequent meditation, have begun to recognize the passages of the books marked at appropriate points, someone may perhaps proceed profitably through the plan of the work that has been established. In it, the matters that must be read are indicated most suitably and briefly in their proper places in these two books. Thus diligent readers may learn which Latin interpreters have explained each matter.

If someone finds that something has been stated carelessly in them, let him—if he knows that language—seek out from the Greek interpreters what has been treated beneficially, so that, once the sluggishness of negligence has been removed from Christ’s school, living knowledge may be sought by minds set aflame.

It is reported, then, that Clement of Alexandria, surnamed Stromateus, and Cyril, bishop of that same city, as well as John Chrysostom, Gregory, Basil, and other exceptionally learned men whom eloquent Greece [ed., “Greek eloquence”] celebrates, explained the divine Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments from beginning to end in the Greek language.

But let us rather follow Latin writers, with the Lord’s help, so that, since we write for Italians, we may seem most suitably to indicate Roman interpreters as well. For each person more readily receives what is narrated in his native language. Thus it may happen that what could not be fulfilled through recent teachers may be accomplished through ancient ones.

Therefore it will be enough to point out to you the most learned commentators, since referring you to such men is rightly shown to constitute a sufficient fullness of instruction. It will also be more beneficial for you not to be imbued with assumed novelty but to be satisfied from the fountain of the ancients. From this it follows that I may instruct you more quickly [mss., “teach you idly”] and instruct you without culpable presumption.

I also judge this kind of instruction useful for us: to educate others in such a way that we may appear to have most suitably avoided the traps of our detractors. In the first volume, therefore, you have teachers of the ancient age, always present and entirely ready, who teach you not so much with their own tongues as through your own eyes.

Therefore, diligent brothers, wisely regulate your desires, learning in order what must be read, imitating those who desire bodily health. For those who wish to be healed by physicians ask what foods they should take first and what they should take at a second meal, lest confused greed burden rather than restore the very slight strength of weak limbs.

In the second book, on the arts and disciplines of the liberal studies, only a little should be sampled. Yet there is less danger of going wrong there, if something is done amiss while the stability of faith remains unharmed. Whatever is found in the divine Scriptures concerning such matters is better understood through prior knowledge.

For it is clear that, as though at the origin of spiritual wisdom, indications of these subjects were sown there, which teachers of secular literature later transferred most prudently into their own rules. We have perhaps demonstrated this at the appropriate place in the exposition of the Psalter.

Therefore, praying to the Lord, from whom comes everything beneficial, read constantly, I beg you, and return to your reading diligently. Frequent and attentive meditation is the mother of understanding.

I am also not unaware that the most eloquent Cassian, in the fifth volume of the *Conferences*, said that a certain old and simple man was questioned about a very obscure passage of divine Scripture and came to know it through frequent prayer by heavenly illumination. What he had not previously learned through human teachers, he explained to those who asked after he had suddenly been filled with divine inspiration.

Similar is the saying of Saint Augustine that he records in the books *On Christian Doctrine* (in the preface): that a barbarian servant, untrained in letters, suddenly read a codex entrusted to him through frequent prayers as though he had been educated in a school through long meditation.

On this matter he goes on to say: “Although these were astonishing miracles, and everything is approved as possible for those who believe” (Mark 9:22), we nevertheless ought not frequently to seek such things, but should preferably remain within the practice of common instruction, lest, when we boldly seek what is above us, we seem rather to incur the guilt of testing the Lord, contrary to his command, where he says in Deuteronomy: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:16). Again, he says in the Gospel: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matt. 12:39), and so forth.

Therefore let us pray that what is closed may be opened to us, and let us never withdraw from the practice of reading. For David too, although he was continually occupied with the law of the Lord, cried out to the Lord, saying: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 118:73). The gift of this matter is exceedingly sweet, for the more it is received, the more greatly it is desired.

Although every divine Scripture shines with heavenly light, and the power of the Holy Spirit clearly radiates within it, I devoted the greatest labor to the Psalter, the Prophets, and the Apostles’ Epistles, because they seemed to me to stir the deepest abysses and to contain, as it were, the citadel and most glorious height of all divine Scripture.

I passed carefully through all nine of these codices of divine authority—as an old man was able—by comparison with ancient manuscripts, while friends read before me. I confess, with the Lord’s help, that I labored greatly over this, so that I might neither fail in measured eloquence [ed., “measured expression”] nor tear apart the sacred books through reckless presumption.

We also believe that this should be mentioned: Saint Jerome, moved by consideration for simple brothers, said in the preface to the Prophets that, for those who had not learned the divisions from teachers of secular literature, he divided his translation by cola and commas, as it is read today.

We too, instructed by the authority of so great a man [ed., “moved by the authority”], judged that this should be followed, so that the rest might be arranged according to divisions [mss., “adorned”]. These provisions are sufficient for the simplest reading, which the aforementioned man, as has been said, arranged by cola and commas in place of divisions, lest we seem to have gone beyond the judgment of so great a man through blameworthy presumption.

The remaining codices, which are not marked with such divisions, I left to be reread and corrected by notaries who would nevertheless attend to the task with diligent care. Although they may not be able to preserve every detail of orthography, they will nevertheless hasten by every means to complete the correction of the ancient codices, as I believe.

For they possess knowledge of their notae, which are known for the most part to touch upon and instruct us in this skill. But so that an ingrained error might be removed to some extent, I arranged in the following book, on the rules of orthography, to set down briefly, according to the capacity of my understanding, certain matters, lest the unpolished presumption of those who correct hastily be handed down for posterity to criticize.

I also prepared, insofar as I could, to find ancient writers on orthography, through whom the manuscripts, even if not entirely corrected, might nevertheless appear improved for the most part. Orthography is generally expressed among the Greeks without ambiguity; among the Latins, however, it is shown to have been left in a state of great difficulty. Hence it now demands great effort from the reader as well.

With the order of the work completed, it is now time for us to come to the most wholesome glory of religious teaching, the light of devoted souls, the heavenly gift, and the joy that will endure without end. In my judgment, this has been briefly indicated in the two books that follow.

## Chapter One: The Octateuch

The first codex of the divine Scriptures is the Octateuch, which began the account of our illumination historically with Genesis. Saint Basil clarified its beginnings in the Attic language. Eustathius [Note: [Col. 1109D] Eustathius’s translation was printed in Paris through the efforts of Nicolas Fabri in a new edition of Saint Basil’s works.]—a most eloquent man—translated it into Latin in such a way that he seems to have matched the talent of that most learned man with the resources of his own eloquence.

He extended it through nine books, up to the creation of the human being. There he disclosed the nature of heaven and earth, of air and waters, and of nearly all creatures, so that what had been omitted in the authority of the text for the sake of brevity might be learned through a fuller, exceedingly detailed, and perfectly clear treatment.

Father Augustine too, disputing against the Manichaeans in two books, carefully expounded the text of Genesis in such a way that he appears to have left almost nothing ambiguous. Thus it happened that, without intending it, the refuted heresy benefited us, since, while it was vigorously defeated, Catholics were instructed more carefully. These books, I believe, we perhaps suitably appended to the aforementioned codex of Basil, so that the text of Genesis might be opened more clearly to readers.

Then Saint Ambrose, being a plain and most delightful teacher, composed six books in his customary style of eloquence and called them the *Hexaemeron*. On the same beginnings, Saint Augustine, an eloquent and cautious disputant, also wrote twelve volumes, adorning them with nearly every kind of learning; he called them *On Genesis Literally*.

Although he treated the same subject on which blessed Basil and Saint Ambrose had shone with the highest praise, nevertheless—as often happens after eloquent men have written—by the Lord’s generosity he brought his work to an entirely different height.

He also wrote thirty-three books against Faustus the Manichaean, where he both refuted Faustus’s most wicked depravity by evident reasoning and again discussed the book of Genesis wondrously. In the same way, the aforementioned man composed two books entitled *Against the Enemy of the Law and the Prophets*, in which he similarly unraveled many questions concerning the divine law.

Against these people he burned with such fervor of devotion that he spoke against them more diligently and vigorously than he argued against other heresies. In the final three books of his *Confessions* he also discussed the exposition of Genesis, confessing the depth of the subject that he had treated through so many repeated explanations.

He also clarified in seven books, with very necessary and syllogistic proof, the questions that could be concealed in the sacred volumes under arduous difficulty. He exerted himself, as an excellent teacher and a man of keen intellect, to ensure that what had been granted for the salvation of souls should not be left unexamined through deadly negligence.

He also wrote seven other remarkable books *On the Modes of Expression*, in which he set forth both the figures of secular literature and many other expressions proper to divine Scripture—that is, expressions not found in common usage. He did this so that, when novel constructions were encountered, the reader’s mind would not be troubled by various difficulties [mss., “pressed”].

At the same time, the outstanding teacher wished to show that general modes of expression—that is, the figures of grammarians and rhetoricians—had developed from these sources, while something had nevertheless been left to them in particular that none of the secular teachers had yet been able to imitate.

It is also said that he composed seven sermons on the seven days of Genesis. We seek them with careful diligence and eagerly desire to find them.

Saint Ambrose likewise published seven books *On the Patriarchs*, which pleasantly unraveled many passages of the Old Testament through questions raised by the events themselves.

Saint Jerome, in one volume, resolved the proposed Hebrew questions concerning the book of Genesis. These questions descend through the Scriptures of both Testaments like a line drawn by a single pen, with equal brilliance. Catholics must necessarily read these works completely, since, once so many questions have been resolved, the text is left entirely plain and brought forth in clear light.

In one volume he also illuminated for us through his Latin translation the explanations of Hebrew names and places, which have been placed in the authority of the ancient books for the great benefit of understanding. He made another book concerning the New Testament, in which that most diligent teacher unraveled questions pertaining to the same law.

Saint Prosper must also be read with diligent care. He comprised three books on the whole of divine authority in 153 titles, after the pattern of the fish that the evangelical nets drew from the stormy depths of this world.

In the Octateuch there are also exceedingly eloquent homilies of Origen in three codices. The judgment of many Fathers identifies him as a heretic. Saint Jerome, however, translated some of his shorter works into Latin in highly eloquent language.

Although the authority of so many Fathers attacks him, in the present time he is also known to have been condemned anew by Pope Vigilius, a most blessed man. Theophilus, pontiff of the Alexandrian Church, convicted as contrary to catholic truth thirty-five of his interpretations that had been distorted by heretical perversity. Epiphanius of Cyprus, likewise, bishop of the Church of Salamis, pursues him with much abhorrence, condemning by episcopal authority his most iniquitous statements, perverted by cunning, and doing so with the deepest grief.

But Saint Jerome indicated with sound judgment in the letter he wrote to Tranquillus how Origen ought to be read (Epistle 76): so that he would neither remove diligent readers from the necessary reading of Origen nor drive the unwary headlong into ruin.

Some have not unjustly said that he should be regarded like dill: while he seasons the dishes of sacred literature, he himself is nevertheless boiled, drained of its juice, and thrown away. Of him it has been conclusively said: “Where he is good, no one is better; where he is bad, no one is worse” [Note: [Col. 1111D] See Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 3; and Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory*.]

Therefore he must be read cautiously and wisely, so that we may draw from him the most wholesome juices without at the same time swallowing the poisons of his unbelief, which are contrary to our life. The saying of Virgil can also appropriately be applied to him: when someone asked Virgil what he was doing while reading Ennius, he replied, “I seek gold in dung.”

Accordingly, in the works of Origen, insofar as I was able to discover them in passing, I marked with the rejection of ἀχρήστων—“useless things”—the passages that were stated contrary to the rules of the Fathers, so that the one who is shown by such a mark to require caution in perverse interpretations might not be able to deceive.

Later writers say that he must be avoided altogether, because he subtly deceives the innocent; but [ed., “because”] if caution is employed with the Lord’s help, his poisonous teachings cannot harm.

I have also left for you, with the Lord’s assistance, if you wish to read them, the homilies of the aforementioned Origen: sixteen on Genesis, twelve on Exodus, sixteen on Leviticus, thirty on Numbers, and four sermons on Deuteronomy. In these there is a highly detailed and subtle exposition; there are also thirty on Joshua and nine on Judges.

As for Ruth, I was unable to find any ancient explanations. I persuaded the most religious presbyter Bellator to compose new ones. In two books he celebrated with abundant praise many things concerning the praises of this woman and of the women who follow her.

I perhaps suitably appended these books to Origen’s expositions, so that the explanation of the entire codex of the Octateuch might be closed with its conclusion complete.

But so that the text of the aforementioned Octateuch might be opened to us in a kind of abridgment, at the beginnings of the books we thought that titles concerning the whole sequence of the reading should be printed, described by our predecessors in their established order. Thus the reader, usefully instructed, may be made attentively receptive and may easily find each matter while searching for it, since he knows that it has been briefly indicated.

## Chapter II: The Book of Kings

In the second codex of Kings, since I could not find an exposition of the continuous text, I wove together fragments of the most eloquent men as though into a single garment, so that, joined together piece by piece, what could by no means be found under a single body might nevertheless be recognized in a collected whole.

I found four homilies of Origen on the first volume. Concerning this book, blessed Augustine also, writing to Simplician, bishop of Milan, resolved six proposed questions.

The first concerns the passage where it says: “And an evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Kings 16:10). The second question from the same book is how it was said: “I regret that I made Saul king” (1 Kings 15:11).

The third asks whether the unclean spirit that was in the medium could have caused Samuel to appear to Saul and converse with him (1 Kings 28). The fourth concerns the second book of Kings, where it says: “King David entered and sat before the Lord” (2 Kings 7:18).

The fifth concerns the third book of Kings, where Elijah says: “O Lord, witness of this widow with whom I dwell, you have done evil in killing her son” (III Reg. XVII, 20). The sixth, in the same book, concerns the spirit of falsehood by which King Ahab was deceived (III Reg. XXII).

We also found in the second book a sermon of that same Saint Augustine on Absalom, who resolved to destroy his father David out of desire for the kingdom. I also found three highly regarded questions of blessed Augustine concerning the same codex.

The first of these, before all the others, concerns the first book of Kings, where David defeated Goliath (1 Kings 17). The second concerns the third book of Kings, Elijah and the widow of Zarephath (III Reg. XVII). The third concerns the fourth book of Kings, where Elisha blessed the deadly spring (IV Reg. II).

Saint Jerome too, writing to Abundantius, explained three other exceedingly obscure questions. The first is why David, who voluntarily went with Achish, king of the Philistines, to attack Saul, killed the man who later announced Saul’s death (II Reg. I). The second is why, when David was dying, he commanded his son Solomon to kill Joab, the commander of his army (3 Kings 2). The third question concerns Shimei, who inflicted intolerable insults of cursing upon the fleeing David, even throwing stones (2 Kings 16).

In the second volume of the same codex I also found one homily of Origen. In the third book of the aforesaid codex, Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, composed a sermon on Solomon’s judgment. Saint Jerome also discussed this passage in his customary exceedingly delightful exposition. We likewise find that Saint Augustine, the most eloquent of men, published a sermon, so that so remarkable an event might be supported by worthy authorities.

Concerning this book, the aforementioned Saint Jerome also wrote to Vitalis, bishop (Epistle 132), explaining how Solomon and Ahaz are said to have fathered sons when they were eleven years into their lives, something that ordinary nature is hardly thought to allow.

Saint Augustine too, in the seventeenth book of *The City of God*, under the fourth title, while that most eloquent disputant speaks among other things about the times of the Kings, explained Hannah’s song in due order.

In the second book of Chronicles I found only one lengthy homily of Origen. Nevertheless, I gathered all these materials into the body of a single codex, so that you might reread them, with the Lord’s help, as commentaries pertaining to these books. I also added blank quires to the codex, so that anything else later found concerning the work mentioned above might be joined to the expositions already described.

In the two aforementioned books of Chronicles—which the Fathers greatly praise for their usefulness and which are known to contain briefly yet most fully an account of past events—since I did not find the ancient titles, I printed new ones at each appropriate place, following the likeness of the preceding titles, as I believe. Thus, through whatever service my wording might provide, the quality of our devotion might be recognized.

## Chapter III: The Prophets

In the third codex, concerning all the Prophets, Saint Jerome first made annotations and explained them suitably and briefly for beginners and children. With the Lord’s help, I recently left these for you in an annotated codex.

In it, formulas of grape-clusters have perhaps been suitably added from the annotations, so that the Lord’s vineyard, filled with heavenly abundance, may appear to have yielded exceedingly sweet fruits.

For those who are mature and already capable of some meditation, the aforementioned man, with Christ the Lord’s generosity, poured forth other lengthy and complete expositions. He makes the obscure and hidden sayings of the Prophets intelligible, sometimes through the variations of translations and sometimes by loosening the knots of riddles, so that the devout teacher opens the great mystery of the heavenly King to human understanding.

He wondrously explained Isaiah in eighteen books. Isaiah, who openly reports the mysteries of Christ and the Church, should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist.

[Col. 1114C] Origen explained Jeremiah, who lamented the ruins of his city in a fourfold alphabet, in forty-five homilies in the Attic language. I found fourteen of these translated [Note: [Col. 1113D] The translator of these fourteen homilies was Saint Jerome, as he himself testifies in the preface to his commentary on Ezekiel and in his book *On Illustrious Men*. These homilies survive among Saint Jerome’s works. Corderius published nineteen Greek-Latin homilies on Jeremiah under the name of Cyril of Alexandria [Col. 1114D]; they are Origen’s. Among them are the twelve translated by Saint Jerome. The distinguished V. C. D. Huet restored them to Origen in his Greek-Latin edition of Origen’s works.] and left them for you.

Saint Jerome is also shown to have commented on Jeremiah in twenty books. Of these we were able to find only six; we are still seeking the remainder, with the Lord’s help.

Saint Jerome explained Ezekiel—whose language in Hebrew is neither entirely eloquent nor especially rustic—in fourteen books. Daniel too, although he is not received among the Hebrews into the prophetic choir but is numbered among those who wrote the *Hagiographa*, is known to have been explained by the aforementioned Saint Jerome in three books.

The remaining twelve prophets, whom ordinary speech calls “minor” because of the brevity of their books, are known to have been commented upon by the aforementioned Saint Jerome in twenty books: Hosea in three books; Obadiah in one; Amos in three; Joel in one; Jonah in one; Nahum in one; Habakkuk in two; Zephaniah in one; Haggai in one; Zechariah in three; Micah in two; and Malachi in one.

So that nothing concerning them might remain ambiguous, he also beautifully clarified how their names ought to be understood in the Latin language through their proper etymologies.

Thus the Lord’s field, plowed as though by certain laborious hired workers and drenched with heavenly dew, granted spiritual fruits by the Lord’s generosity.

Saint Ambrose is also said to have composed commentaries on the Prophets with the customary sweetness of his eloquence. I have not yet been able to find them at all, but I leave them for you to seek with great diligence, so that the multiplied exposition of learned men may provide you with abundant instruction and the soul’s most blessed health.

## Chapter IV: The Psalter

The fourth codex that follows is the Psalter. It is first for us in the labor of the commentators [mss., “commemorators”], but occupies the place of two pairs in the order.

Blessed Hilary, blessed Ambrose, and blessed Jerome treated certain psalms; blessed Augustine, however, treated all of them with exceptionally great diligence and breadth. From these works I have already gathered two decades, with the Lord’s help. Borrowing light from light, as is customary, I have composed some material from Augustine himself, by the Lord’s generosity, so that the saying of the Mantuan poet might truly be fulfilled in me: “And the goose might honk among the melodious swans.”

Here I have mixed in no matter unrelated through digression [ed., “having digressed from its subject”], but, in place of annotations, I have spoken briefly about each passage according to what the character of the text itself required.

If someone should perhaps deign to reread it after such men, he will recognize—as the other Fathers too have stated with unquestionable judgment—that what the teachers of secular literature later transferred into their own studies flowed forth from the divine Scriptures. Whenever the occasion arose, with the Lord’s help, I have shown this as far as I was able, if I am not mistaken.

It is also necessary to read the little book of Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, which he sent to Marcellinus after his illness as a place of sweetest refreshment. It is entitled *On the Book of Psalms*. There, while offering various admonitions, he disclosed the power of the work itself through the most minute analysis, introducing pleasantly the various circumstances of human beings together with their remedies.

For the Psalter is a kind of heavenly sphere, dense with shining stars, and—as I may put it—a most beautiful peacock, painted as though with the circles of its eyes and with a manifold and lovely variety of colors. It is also a paradise of souls, containing countless fruits by which the human mind, gently nourished, may grow rich.

Nevertheless, we judged that the entire body of the Psalms should be written in three codices, fifty psalms in each, so that the quantity of a jubilee year, tripled, might announce to us the promised benefits of remission belonging to the Holy Trinity. And since one codex could prove burdensome to certain brothers, once this distribution had been completed they would receive hope of precious salvation, and many would, with the Lord’s favor, find a salutary abridgment of reading. Let your library therefore possess one of these codices, to which you may turn if textual corruption should perhaps offend you, while the curiosity of the brothers may be satisfied by the portions distributed among them.

## CHAPTER V. On Solomon

The fifth codex is Solomon’s. I found that his first book, which is called *Proverbs*, was divided into four parts. In the prologue to that volume I judged that some observations should be offered concerning these parts, so that its purpose might become briefly known through the divisions mentioned above.

In this book we found Didymus the commentator in the Greek language. He was translated most carefully into Latin, with the Lord’s help, by our friend, the most eloquent man, Epiphanius. Although Didymus was blind in body, blessed Antony, the father of monks, rightly called him “the Seer” (*Videntem*) by prophetic illumination, when with a clear-sighted heart he perceived what he could not behold with bodily eyes.

It is wonderful to say through how many disciplines and arts he was instructed by hearing, since, deprived of bodily sight, he was unable even to inspect the very strokes of the letters. I confess that this seemed almost impossible to me when I read of it, unless it had happened that a certain Eusebius, named thus, came to us from the regions of Asia. He related that he had been blinded at the age of five in such a way that the deepest hollow of the socket indicated that his left eye had been destroyed; while his right eyeball, clouded with a glassy appearance, rolled uselessly in fruitless efforts, without the power of sight.

This man had stored such great authors and such great books in the library of his memory that he could reliably remind readers in which part of a codex they would find what he had mentioned. He retained all the disciplines in his mind and illuminated them with a most lucid exposition. He also explained that the tabernacle and the temple of the Lord had been fashioned in the likeness of heaven. I have suitably adapted these matters, delicately depicted with their proper lines, in a Latin pandect of larger format.

He also wove many mysteries of the Lord into the priestly vestment, asserting that nothing had been placed there idly which did not bear the most beautiful image of some reality. He said that Josephus, Origen, and Jerome had likewise mentioned this in their little works.

What more need be said? By the abilities he displayed in his own person [ed., “example”], he made me believe what was said of Didymus. Instructed also by him, I found many ancient codices that had previously been unknown to me. Yet because he is still held by the error of Novatian perversity, we believe, with the Lord’s mercy assisting, that he must be completed by the illumination of right faith, so that the one whom he caused to learn the Scriptures in his mind may be commanded to possess the integrity of the catholic faith.

The second book of Solomon, which is called *Ecclesiastes*, was powerfully expounded by blessed Jerome. He names it in Latin *Concionator*, “Preacher,” because it speaks to the people, and its speech is directed not specifically to one person but generally to everyone. Our Ecclesiastes, however, is the Lord Christ, who, having destroyed the dividing wall and abolished the hostility of the flesh, made both one (Ephesians 2:14). He declares that the divine commands above all things are to be followed, recalling that everything in this world is vanity of vanities.

Victorinus too, a bishop formerly an orator, discussed some matters concerning this book. In two homilies on the *Song of Songs*, that same holy Jerome, an outstanding enlarger of the Latin language, provided for us—as was his custom—with his credible translation of Origen’s exposition. Rufinus, likewise, the most eloquent translator, explained it at greater length in three books, adding certain passages, up to the command that says: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (*Song of Songs* 2:15).

After these works, Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus [Note: Or rather Philo, ordained bishop of the city of Carpasus on the island of Cyprus by Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, as is read in the Life of that same saint. I saw the Greek text of this commentary in the hands of the distinguished man Em. Bigot, together with the Latin translation mentioned here by Cassiodorus.
