As yet, however, neither has been committed to the press.], briefly encompassed the entire book in one volume in the Greek language. We likewise had this translated into Latin, as we did the others, by our friend, the most eloquent man, Epiphanius, with the Lord’s help.

Therefore I gathered the most diligent commentators on the books mentioned above into a single codex, so that all who had been expositors of one volume might be offered together to readers. Thus Saint Ambrose too, in the third book of *The Patriarchs*, where he speaks about the person of Isaac, discussed many matters profitably and brilliantly.

The oft-mentioned Father Jerome asserts that the book of *Wisdom* was written not by Solomon, as usage maintains, but by a certain most learned Jew, Philo; he labeled it pseudepigraphal because it bears the usurpation of another’s name. The presbyter Bellator testified that he had undertaken an exposition of this volume in eight books, and we preserve it together with his other little works. Father Augustine and Saint Ambrose likewise said some things about it under the title of homilies. Its diction is exceedingly sweet and truly radiant with the dignity of its name.

The aforementioned Jerome states that the book of *Ecclesiasticus* belongs to Jesus son of Sirach, who may be called in Latin “Congregator.” Yet the Fathers placed this distinction between *Ecclesiastes* and *Ecclesiasticus*: *Ecclesiastes* must refer solely to Christ the Lord, whereas *Ecclesiasticus* may properly apply to any just preacher who habitually gathers the Lord’s Church through most holy admonitions.

That the present book has done this is clear. Because of the excellence of its virtues, he calls it *πανάρετον* (*panareton*) (vol. I, preface, p. 115), that is, “capable of all virtues.” Its clarity and Latinity are so great that the text itself serves as its own commentary. Would that what is grasped so quickly by the mind might be rendered equally easily in the quality of one’s actions.

With the help of the Lord, we took care to mark these books with chapter divisions, so that, in such necessary reading—as has often been said—the inexperienced beginner might not be left confused.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Hagiographa

The sixth codex, then, is that of the Hagiographa. It contains eight books and, at its beginning, includes Job, a renowned and glorious lesson in patience. Through the labor of blessed Jerome it deserved to be translated and expounded most carefully into the Latin language, as did many other works [Col. 1118A]. Through his explanations it was shown that, as the Lord deigned to testify concerning him, he had spoken everything blamelessly.

For how many sweet mysteries of words that book contains, as blessed Jerome says in the letter he addresses to Paulinus (Letter 103, near the middle)! “It begins in prose, flows in verse, and ends in pedestrian speech; and it determines all the rules of dialectic by proposition, assumption, confirmation, and conclusion.” If this is so—and it cannot be otherwise than as the authority of so great a man celebrates it—where are those who say that the art of dialectic did not begin with the most holy Scriptures?

Every word in it is full of sacred riddles, propositions, and questions. And, to say nothing of the rest, it prophesies the resurrection of the flesh so clearly that no one seems to have written anything about it either more plainly or more carefully. For it says:

> “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior. I myself shall see him, and my eyes shall behold him, and not another; this hope of mine is stored in my bosom” (Job 19:25).

Saint Augustine also, making notes in the same book, treated it with his customary curiosity. There is also an anonymous writer whose style leads us to suspect that he was blessed Hilary; he arranged commentaries on the book itself. If you read them attentively, they will be able to instruct you carefully.

The book of Job is plainly great, and was written for the consolation and benefit of the human race, since that holy man is shown to have endured such and so many things that every sinner may regard as light whatever he recognizes himself as having to endure.

The exposition of Tobit, in five books; Esther, in six books; Judith, in seven books; and Maccabees, in ten books, was gathered into Latin prose through the labor, as far as possible, of the aforementioned presbyter Bellator. I collected the titles of these books briefly, since it is considered no small means of instruction to indicate in a few words matters dispersed at great length. By these remedies the reader’s mind is introduced and, summoned by them, proceeds through the most salutary sequence of the Scriptures.

Although these books are historical and are founded on a very plain narrative, understand nevertheless that they were written because of the outstanding virtues of their characters: so that they might suitably infuse into our minds patience, hope, charity, courage even in women, contempt for the life of the present age for God’s sake, and the other kinds of virtue that, with the Lord’s favor, flourished there.

In the two books of Ezra I found individual homilies of Origen expounded in the Greek language; they were translated through the labor of that religious man, Bellator. Saint Ambrose too, in the book of *The Patriarchs*, where he himself speaks about the person of Joseph [ed., “Ezra”], mentions the second book of Maccabees by way of example. He disclosed a very large part of it through the sweetest flow of his eloquence, in order to demonstrate endurance.

The books of Maccabees were completed with diligent exposition by our aforementioned friend Bellator, with the Lord’s help, lest so great a work of reading should perhaps be left unexplained—a work that revealed to us such great examples of virtue.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Gospels

The seventh codex of divine Scripture, which is the first of the New Testament and gave us an adorable beginning and a life-giving remedy, shines with the heavenly light of the four evangelists. Saint Jerome discussed the distinctive features of all of them with diligent care; I gathered these into one volume, so that the reader’s attention would not be delayed [ed., “drawn away”] by divided codices.

Blessed Jerome again expounded Matthew in four books, and Saint Hilary also explained him in one volume. Victorinus too, a bishop formerly an orator, discussed some matters concerning him. Saint Ambrose wonderfully expounded Luke. Blessed Augustine illuminated John with a copious and distinguished exposition. He also encompassed, in four books, the harmony of the four evangelists in an exceedingly subtle and necessary discussion.

Eusebius of Caesarea likewise collected the Gospel Canons in a concise abridgment, showing with the truest distinction in which passages they speak of common matters and in which they touch on individual ones. There, as great as the fullness of faith is, so greatly does the marvelous learning of the various commentators flourish.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Epistles of the Apostles

The eighth codex contains the canonical Epistles of the apostles. At the very beginning of my reading I found written commentaries on the thirteen Epistles of Saint Paul. They were considered so famous in everyone’s hands that learned men claimed they had been composed by Saint Gelasius, pope of the city of Rome.

This is what those who wish to defend corrupt matters by the authority of a distinguished name are accustomed to do [Note: Deceivers are accustomed to fabricate an epistle under the name of some famous man, so that the authority of the name may commend what could not be accepted on its own, as Saint Ambrose says in his letter to the Thessalonians, II, chapter 2.].

But through diligent reconsideration of the preceding readings it became clear to us that these were indeed very subtle and brief expressions, but that the poisons of the Pelagian error had been sown there. To keep the heretical error far from you, I purged the Epistle to the Romans as carefully as I could; I left the others, written in a paper codex, for you to correct. This will easily be undertaken, since the example that precedes makes imitation of what follows bolder.

Yet while I was deeply troubled amid these concerns, by divine providence I suddenly found an anonymous codex, marked with notes, which treated the thirteen Epistles of Saint Paul with no undistinguished commentary. Carefully examined [mss., “excerpted”], it will, with the Lord’s generosity, provide you with a sound and secure kind of commentary [Col. 1120A].

As for the Epistle to the Hebrews, which Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, treated in thirty-four homilies in Attic Greek, we had the most eloquent man Mutianus translate it into Latin, lest the continuous order of the Epistles should be suddenly broken by an unbecoming conclusion.

Among the canonical Epistles, Clement of Alexandria, the presbyter who is also called *Stromateus*, explained certain passages in Attic Greek—namely, in the First Epistle of Saint Peter, the First and Second Epistles of Saint John, and the Epistle of James. He spoke many things subtly, but some things carelessly. We therefore had them translated into Latin in such a way that, after certain stumbling blocks had been removed, his purified doctrine could be received more safely.

Saint Augustine too treated the Epistle of the apostle James with his customary diligent curiosity; I left it for you written in a parchment codex. But when great concern about the remaining canonical Epistles was troubling us, a codex of Didymus, written in the Greek style, was suddenly granted to us by the Lord’s favor for the exposition of the seven canonical Epistles. It was translated by Epiphanius, the most eloquent man, with divine assistance.

In the First Epistle of blessed John, Saint Augustine discussed charity at length and wonderfully in ten sermons.

I also found a third codex of the Epistles of Saint Paul, which some say contains very brief notes by blessed Jerome. I likewise left it to you, by Christ’s gift. After these three pairs of commentaries that we have mentioned, Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli, is said to have annotated the Epistles of Saint Paul with examples from the little works of blessed Augustine, so that through another’s mouth he might reveal the secret of his own heart.

He adapted these so suitably to their individual passages that you might rather believe the work to have been completed through the diligence of blessed Augustine. It is remarkable how he clarified one author through another, so that, without mingling any addition of his own words, he appears to have fulfilled the desire of his own heart. With the support of divine grace, this codex is to be sent to you from the African region among the other codices.

Thus the entire order of the canonical Epistles, both those of Saint Paul and those of the various apostles, has been completed by the Lord’s favor. It is also said that blessed Ambrose left an annotated codex of all the Epistles of Saint Paul, completed with a most pleasing exposition. I have not yet been able to find it, but I am seeking it with diligent care.

The annotations on the Epistles, then, have been briefly gathered by certain writers. Now let us say in order—as was also done with the Prophets—who preferred to expound them at greater length, so that the former may appear to have been given for beginners, while the latter was reserved for the mature.

The first of all Saint Paul’s Epistles, and the one recognized as the most remarkable, was addressed to the Romans. Origen explained it in twenty books in the Greek language. The aforementioned Rufinus, however, reducing them to ten books, nevertheless translated them copiously into Latin.

Saint Augustine had begun to expound the Epistle itself. He records that he poured out one book solely on its salutation and— to use his own words—being deterred by the magnitude and labor of the work, turned aside to easier matters. He also wrote to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, and treated certain elevated and carefully considered questions from the same Epistle. We judged that these should be inserted into the aforementioned codex, lest, while a divided exposition is being sought, the reader’s attention should be harmfully delayed.

The same Saint Augustine expounded the Epistle to the Galatians at greater length; Saint Jerome also extended an exposition of it through three books. The same Father Jerome carefully opened up the Epistle to the Ephesians in three books. He also encompassed the exposition of the Epistle to Titus in one volume, and explained Philemon in one book.

As for the remaining Epistles of Saint Paul—namely, the two to the Corinthians, the two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, and the two to Timothy—Saint Jerome is said to have explained them. Much knowledge is thereby conferred, since those who are ignorant come to know what they seek.

We trust that, through the Lord’s mercy, we shall receive these works continuously from the various regions where we have ordered them to be sought. Therefore we must diligently await what we know is to be sent to us. And so, if something from them should perhaps come into the hands of any of you before they arrive, let him take care to transcribe it diligently and add it to the aforementioned expositors, so that, with the Lord’s help and through your labor, the monastery’s library may advance, for which such abundant resources are known to have been prepared.

If, however, our old age should perhaps pass away before these things are completed, by the Lord’s command and with remission of sins—as I beg you to pray—with a wished-for end, the hoped-for material will eventually come to you, as it is worthy to believe.

I also left the Epistles mentioned above, expounded by John Chrysostom in Attic Greek, in the aforementioned eighth cabinet, where the Greek codices have been gathered. Thus, if broader commentaries cannot be obtained in Latin, what can provide the fullest understanding may subsequently be translated from these. In this way, throughout all seventy-one canonical books, as Saint Father Augustine is known to have included them (*On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 8), the expositions of the ancients may, with the Lord’s generosity, be offered to your banquets for consumption like the spiritual fruits of Paradise.

If some doubtful passages should perhaps remain in what has been said, and they have not been able to satisfy you with a thoroughly clear [mss., “complete”] explanation, I do not at all forbid you to consult modern expositors. They must nevertheless be sought carefully among Catholics, since with the passage of time many things are newly infused by divine grace, which may perhaps be shown to have been hidden from the ancient teachers.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse

The ninth codex is known to contain the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse, since this Apocalypse too—that is, the Revelation—is shown to belong to the apostle John.

In the Acts of the Apostles we found commentaries by Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, in the Greek language. Our friends translated them, with the Lord’s help, in two codices containing fifty-five homilies.

The Apocalypse, which diligently leads the minds of readers toward heavenly contemplation and makes them perceive in their minds what the angels are blessed to behold, is conspicuous through the exposition of Saint Jerome. Concerning this book, the oft-mentioned bishop Victorinus also briefly treated certain exceedingly difficult passages.

Vigilius, an African bishop, likewise discussed with a very full and careful account the interpretation of the thousand years contained in the aforementioned Apocalypse, from which a major question arises for certain people.

Ticonius the Donatist also added certain things in the same volume that should not be rejected, but mixed in other things polluted by the dregs of his poisonous doctrine. As much of the useful (*χρήσιμον*) in his good sayings and the useless (*ἄχρηστον*) in his bad ones as I was able to discover in passing, I have, as I believe, suitably attached. We likewise advise you to do this with suspicious expositors, lest the reader’s mind should perhaps be disturbed and confused by the mixture of an abominable doctrine.

Saint Augustine too disclosed much about this volume, more excellently and diligently, in the books of *The City of God*. In our own times the aforementioned Apocalypse was also expounded minutely and carefully in five books through the labor of the blessed bishop Primasius, an African bishop. To these was also appended one book, *What a Heretic Does*, composed with a most cautious argument; these are consecrated offerings in the temple of the Lord, to be presented at the holy altars.

But since we have stated how many expositors we were able either to find among the ancients, or recently to have translated from the Greek language through our friends, or to have newly produced, let us now discuss something about the six methods of interpretation, so that, by returning there more often, we may avoid destructive errors.

## 545 CHAPTER X. On the Six Methods of Interpretation

The first method, after the arrangements of this work have been set out, is to return with attentive mind to the introducers of divine Scripture whom we shall mention later [mss., “whom we found”]—namely, Ticonius the Donatist, Saint Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine*, Hadrian, Eucherius, and Junilius [Note: This author’s works are included in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*]. I gathered these with careful curiosity, so that codices having a similar purpose might be joined together and enclosed in one body.

By forming methods of expression for the sake of explanation, they make intelligible through various likenesses of examples what previously remained closed.

If something has perhaps been omitted by the introducers, then let us diligently seek the expositors of the books, and they begin to open for us what previously remained closed. Next, let us read with the greatest diligence the Catholic teachers, who resolve the most obscure questions after setting forth their propositions.

Fifth, throughout the individual books and Epistles of the various Fathers, the principal passages that they mention by way of example should be noted with diligent care [mss., “after the individual books”]. In this way the books of various Catholic writers may be read through most profitably, since they both properly disclose their intentions and provide us with great knowledge through the questions that arise incidentally among them.

Finally, let conversation with the most experienced elders be sought more frequently. Through their discussions we suddenly perceive what we had not expected, while they diligently report to us what they have been able to learn over their long lifetimes.

It is useful to move through these six methods of interpretation with an eager will rather than to lie inert in irreligious stupor.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Four Accepted Synods

Let us now say how the universal and holy councils strengthened the salutary mysteries of our faith, so that, recognizing there the secret of true religion, we may avoid destructive errors.

The Council of Nicaea is read as having been established first, then that of Constantinople, third the first Council of Ephesus, and fourth that of Chalcedon. The holy Church rightly approves these. They have provided such great lights for our faith that we ought not—if, with the Lord protecting us, we are kept safe—to fall with blinded minds upon any reef of perversity.

For the most holy Fathers, unwilling to tolerate injury to the true faith, also preferred to establish ecclesiastical rules there. They struck down with the divine sword the obstinate inventors of new heresies, decreeing that no one should henceforth introduce new questions, but that those content with the authority of the approved ancients should obey the salutary decrees without deceit or treachery.

There are some who think it praiseworthy to have an opinion contrary to the ancients and to discover something new by which they appear destined to perish.

The codex *Encyclius* is a witness to the Council of Chalcedon. It celebrates its reverence with such praise that it rightly judges it comparable to holy authority. We had this codex, called *ἐνκύκλιον* (*enkuklion*), that is, “the Epistolary of the whole world,” translated from Greek into Latin by the most eloquent man Epiphanius.

But since, with the Lord’s help, we have gathered the sacred writings in nine codices together with their introducers and nearly all their Latin expositors, as was said [mss., “given”], let us now see how the divine law was made known through three systems of division by various Fathers—a law which the universal Church of all regions nevertheless venerates and receives harmoniously.

## CHAPTER XII. The Division of Divine Scripture According to Jerome

According to Saint Jerome, divine authority is divided into two Testaments, namely the Old and the New.

It is divided into the Law: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.

It is divided into the Prophets, which are Joshua son of Nun, Judges, Ruth, Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the twelve books of the prophets.

It is divided into the Hagiographa, which are Job, David, Solomon, Proverbs, Ecclesiasticus, and the Song of Songs.

Then come the *Words of Days*, that is, Chronicles, Ezra, and Esther.

Then the Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

After these follow the Epistles of the apostles: two of Peter, fourteen of Paul, three of John, one of James, one of Jude, one book of the Acts of the Apostles by Luke, and one book of the Apocalypse by John.

It must plainly be understood that Saint Jerome read and corrected the translations of various writers because he saw that they in no way conformed to the authority of the Hebrew. Thus it happened that he transferred all the books of the Old Testament with diligent care into Latin from the Hebrew source and suitably brought them into the form of the twenty-two letters that exists among the Hebrews. Through these letters all wisdom is learned, and the memory of what has been said is preserved in writing forever.

To these were added the twenty-seven books of the New Testament, making forty-nine together. Add to this number the omnipotent and indivisible Trinity, through which these things were made and for whose sake they were foretold, and the number fifty is unquestionably produced. Like a jubilee year, it releases with great piety the benefits that are owed and dissolves the sins of those who repent purely.

Because of the abundance of reading, we judged that this pandect should be written in smaller script in fifty-three quires, so that what extensive reading had spread out, the concentrated density of the writing might gather together.

We must also remember that the aforementioned Jerome arranged his entire translation in the divine authority—as he himself testifies—for the simplicity of the brothers, by cola and commas, so that those who were entirely unable to understand the divisions of secular literature might, supported by this remedy, pronounce the most sacred readings without blame.

## 546 CHAPTER XIII. The Division of Divine Scripture According to Augustine

According to blessed Augustine, divine Scripture is divided into two Testaments, namely the Old and the New.

In the historical books there are twenty-two books: the five books of Moses; one book of Joshua son of Nun; one book of Judges; one book of Ruth; four books of Kings; two books of Chronicles; one book of Job; one book of Tobit; one book of Esther; one book of Judith; two books of Ezra; and two books of Maccabees.

In the Prophets there are twenty-two books: one book of David’s Psalms [ms. Aud., “the Psalter”]; four books of Solomon; one book of Jesus son of Sirach; four major prophets—Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel; and twelve minor prophets—Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Zechariah, Haggai, and Malachi.

In the Epistles of the apostles there are twenty-one: one Epistle of the apostle Paul to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; one to the Galatians; one to the Ephesians; one to the Philippians; two to the Thessalonians; one to the Colossians; two to Timothy; one to Titus; one to Philemon; and one to the Hebrews; two of Peter; three of John; one of Jude; and one of James.

There are four Gospels: according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John.

There is one book of the Acts of the Apostles and one book of the Apocalypse.

Thus blessed Augustine, according to the aforementioned nine codices which the holy Church contemplates, counted the divine Scriptures as seventy-one books in the second book, chapter 8, of *On Christian Doctrine*. When the unity of the Holy Trinity is added to them, the fitting and glorious perfection of the whole book is produced.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Division of Divine Scripture According to the Ancient Translation and According to the Septuagint

According to the ancient translation, sacred Scripture is divided into two Testaments, namely the Old and the New.

It contains Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua son of Nun, Judges, Ruth, the four books of Kings, the two books of Chronicles, one book of the Psalter, and five books of Solomon: Proverbs, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

It contains the Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who is also Angel [Note: In Hebrew, *Malachi* is the same as “Angel,” and so it is rendered by the Septuagint translators, *ἄγγελος*. This led Origen into error, for he wrote that Malachi was not a man but an angel; Saint Jerome charges him with this error. See Quiros on the Bible.].

It also contains Job, Tobit, Esther, Judith, two books of Ezra, and two books of Maccabees.

After these follow the four Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; the Acts of the Apostles; the Epistles of Peter to the nations; the Epistle of Jude; the Epistle of James to the twelve tribes; the Epistle of John to the Parthians; one Epistle of Paul to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; one to the Galatians; one to the Philippians; one to the Colossians; one to the Hebrews; two to the Thessalonians; two to Timothy; one to Titus; one to Philemon; and the Apocalypse of John.

There is also a third division, in another larger codex written in clearer script [ed., “larger”], which has ninety-five quires. In it the translation of the Old Testament by the Seventy Interpreters is contained in forty-four books. To these are appended twenty-six books of the New Testament, making seventy books altogether—perhaps prefigured by the number of palms that the Hebrew people found at the encampment of Elim (Exodus 15:27).

This text, varied through the translations of many writers—as is stated in the prologue to the Psalter—was corrected and arranged with the diligent care of Father Jerome and left in that form. We judged that all three systems of division should be attached to it, so that, when carefully examined and considered, they might appear not to oppose one another but rather to explain one another.

Thus, although many Fathers—namely Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers; Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia; Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus; the Council of Nicaea; and the Council of Chalcedon—did not say contradictory things but different things, nevertheless all adapted the divine books to appropriate mysteries through their divisions.

The same is shown to have been accomplished in the *Harmony of the Evangelists*, where there is one faith concerning the events, but a different arrangement of speech.

But since the aforementioned Father Augustine, in the second book, chapter 15, of the work mentioned above, namely *On Christian Doctrine*, gives this admonition:

> “Latin codices, that is, of the Old and New Testament, must, if necessary, be corrected by the authority of the Greeks,”

and since every translation came to us after the Hebrew source, I have therefore also left you a Greek pandect contained in seventy-five books. It has ninety quires in the aforementioned eighth cabinet, where I gathered other Greek works necessary for various purposes, lest anything necessary for your most holy instruction appear to be lacking.

This number is consecrated by two miracles. For seventy-five souls entered the borders of Egypt from the land of Canaan with the patriarch Jacob (Genesis 46:26); and Abraham was seventy-five years old when he joyfully received the Lord’s promise (Genesis 12:4).

It remains now for us to hasten to explain how we ought to correct the faults of scribes in the divine Scriptures. For what benefit is there in running through many readings while not knowing which things ought probably to be corrected?

## CHAPTER XV. Under What Caution the Heavenly Authority Should Be Read Again
[Col. 1126C] You, therefore, who excel in knowledge of both sacred and secular letters, and whose learning enables you to recognize from common usage what is discordant, should go through the sacred readings in the following manner; for what is known to have been prepared for a simple and less learned congregation must be undertaken by only a few learned men. Therefore, first enter carefully, and then correct the scribal errors, lest you rightly be censured if you attempt hastily to correct others. This kind of correction, as I believe, is exceedingly beautiful and a glorious task for the most learned.

First, then, do not rashly tamper with the 547 idioms of Holy Scripture [ed., *temnetis* (“do not violate”)], lest, when you wish to draw what has been said toward common understanding (God forbid), the purity of the heavenly words be scattered. The idioms of the divine law are its distinctive expressions, which common usage is recognized not to possess. Examples are:

> “According to the innocence of my hands” (Psalm 7:9);

or:

> “From your presence let my judgment come forth” (Psalm 38:13).

> “Give ear to my tears” (Psalm 61:9).

And:

> “Pour out your hearts before him” (Psalm 62:9).

> “My soul clung after you” (Psalm 64:10).

> “You have multiplied to enrich her.”

> “There we shall rejoice in the same thing” (Psalm 65:6).

And:

> “And he inclined from this to that” (Psalm 74:9).

> “He sent Moses his servant, and Aaron, whom he himself loved” (Psalm 104:20).

> “My eyes failed for your word” (Psalm 118:82).

> “Let your hand be, that it may save me” (Psalm 118:137).

Although common usage rejects these and similar expressions, which are thought or shown to be exceedingly numerous, that holy authority nevertheless unquestionably commends them, so that they may not be scattered or destroyed. If you desire to know these matters more precisely [ed., *ea latius*, “more extensively”], read the seven books of Saint Augustine on the *Modes of Expression*, which he composed from the five books of Moses, one book of Joshua, and another of Judges; then you will be able to satisfy your desire concerning this subject with the greatest abundance. In the authority that follows, you will likewise find very many similar examples.

Do not break or alter certain Hebrew names of persons or places by declining them; let the dignified integrity of their own language be preserved in them. Let us change only those letters which can express the quality of the word itself, since each of these names is established as having been assigned, with profound sacramental significance, for the interpretation of something: for example, Seth, Enoch, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth; Aaron, David, and similar names. Likewise, let us leave the names of places—such as Zion, Oreb, Gihon, Hermon, and similar names—with equal devotion.

Third, things that are presented in a good or an evil sense must not be tampered with in any way: mountain, lion, cedar, lion’s cub, cry, man, fruit, cup, calf, shepherd, treasure, worm, dog, and similar terms. Nor are those names to be changed which are employed in place of other names: for example, Satan, who departs from the straight path. “To wash the hands” signifies not to be a participant. “Feet” are used for an action. Frequently “expectation” is used for “hope.” “Once” is proclaimed for an unchangeable decree. “To swear the Lord” [ed., “God”] is said for “to confirm.”

These matters we should desire to have opened up to us by commentators; we should not mutilate any of them through sacrilegious presumption. Nor should those expressions be touched which are occasionally found to have been written contrary to human grammatical art, but which are vindicated by the authority of many manuscripts. For expressions known to have been spoken under the inspiration of the Lord cannot be corrupted. Such are:

> “We have not forgotten you” (Psalm 43:18).

And:

> “Men of blood and deceit” (Psalm 54:14).

> “He constructed a temple.”

And:

> “His head shall be shaved” (Numbers 6:9).

And:

> “His belly shall be inflated,” for “he shall be inflated in the belly.”

And:

> “The spies brought fear to the land which they had explored.”

> “A man, if his wife has transgressed” (Numbers 5:12).

And:

> “They shall place upon the altar all its vessels, in which they minister with them” (ibid., 25).

> “The land in which they dwell in it” (Psalm 23:1).

And:

> “From the hand of the dog, my only one” (Psalm 21:21).

And:

> “The rivers will clap their hands in themselves” (Psalm 97:8).

> “Then all the trees of the forests will rejoice” (Psalm 95:12).

And since the cases and genders of nouns, or the tenses of verbs, sometimes cannot conform to human rules, yet their usage is embraced by ecclesiastical consensus, the authority of two or three ancient and corrected manuscripts should be sought—for it is written:

> “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matthew 18:16)—

and one must not presume to alter what is vindicated by divine speech [Col. 1128A]. Thus, in the twenty-first psalm:

> “For the people who will be born, whom the Lord made” (Psalm 21:32);

and in the Gospel:

> “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Likewise, in the one hundred forty-third psalm:

> “Blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Psalm 143:15);

and similar passages.

Therefore, do not follow in every respect the rules of Latin expression—that is, [perhaps, “as for example”] the *quadriga* of the Messiah—when you are convicted by the authority of ancient manuscripts. For it is sometimes expedient to set aside the formulas of human diction and to preserve rather the measure of divine speech.

In prose, do not correct the head and ending of the heroic verse; that is, do not dare to reject five long syllables and an equal number of short ones. Let a triple trochee be concealed by commendable neglect. Leave entirely alone *iotacisms* and hiatuses of vowels, since what teachers of the liberal arts are known regularly to observe cannot have a place here. Such precautions are suitable among human expressions, but such compositions are in no way to be censured in divine speech. Let the utterance that is known to have pleased God remain everywhere uncorrupted, so that it may shine with its own radiance and not be subjected to the criticism of human preference. These things instruct the simple pleasantly and, on account of their reverence, delight the learned becomingly.

After the foregoing division, where we said that the idioms of the divine law must not be touched, along with the other matters that follow, the subject now prompts us, in the manner of our ancestors, to add this subdivision as well, so that we may proceed more distinctly to the individual parts of the parts. How could the most learned Aristotle have brought his work *On Interpretation* (*περὶ ἑρμηνείας*) to complete clarity, unless he had treated everything while preserving the order of divisions, subdivisions, and further divisions into particulars? Following him, we now state in which matters the errors of scribes are to be corrected.

In words governed by prepositions taking the accusative or ablative, observe carefully position and motion, since scribes ignorant of grammatical art are shown to err especially there. For if you improperly add or remove the letter *m*, the entire expression is confused. Carefully examine the cases of nouns—except for the declensions of *monoptota* [nouns with one form for multiple cases]—and the conjugations of verbs that are not defective, as well as all the parts of speech, provided that sacred authority is not thereby contradicted [Col. 1128D]; preserve them fitted to their proper places, lest, when the order of the expression has been confused, unbecoming disorder possess everything, God forbid.

Do not leave uncorrected *b* written for *v*, *v* for *b*, *o* for *v*, or *n* for *m*, when these have been written defectively contrary to the precepts of orthography. Remove or add an unnecessary aspiration as appropriate. Carefully preserve the cases of nouns and the tenses of verbs wherever you are permitted to do so. For you will frequently find in authoritative texts things that differ from ordinary usage, which you are not permitted to change. In such matters, let the example of corrected manuscripts be preserved.

Correct the remaining things that have been wrongly presumed, since antiquarians [Note: [Col. 1127D] See Sidonius Apollinaris, book 9, letter 16; and the Theodosian Code, book 14, title 9, law 2.] are shown to offend chiefly because they do not know how to serve the Latin language’s mode of expression in an orderly fashion. Do not omit *ae* at the end of an adverb [548]; likewise, do not remove *ae* from the genitive case. We also make many changes plausibly for the sake of euphony, on account of the letters that follow, as in *illuminatio* (“illumination”), *irrisio* (“mockery”), *immutabilis* (“unchangeable”), *impius* (“impious”), and *improbus* (“wicked”).

Remove a superfluous *g* from *gnarratio* (“narration”); for this compound is derived from *gnarus*, that is, “knowing” or “skilled.” When *quod* is a pronoun, it is to be written with *d*, not with *t*; but when it is an adverb of number, it is to be written with *t*, not with *d*. In *quicquam*, the letter *c* should preferably be placed in the first syllable rather than *d*, on account of the euphony which we are instructed to follow. Why say more? Go through the matters that are to be corrected according to the rules of the grammarians, so that the beautiful modulation of articulate speech, stained by foreign letters, may not instead be rendered discordant and unbecoming [Col. 1129B].

Read the ancient orthographers frequently. I have judged that they should be excerpted below, in the thirtieth title, which concerns antiquarians, for the useful instruction of those who need knowledge of scribes; and I have given this book, separately, the title *On Orthography*. Thus it has happened that it is useful for the diligent student to read this section as well, where he learns what he must by no means violate in the sacred Scriptures, while the other section is studied more broadly as necessary, where errors generally presumed are corrected.

If, however, any words are found to have been placed absurdly, they should be corrected fearlessly either from those books which blessed Jerome corrected in his edition of the Seventy Interpreters, or from those which he himself translated from Hebrew; or, as blessed Augustine says, one should have recourse to the Greek *pandect*, which is recognized to contain the whole divine law collected together [Col. 1129C]. Nor should those who can do so hesitate to seek the Hebrew text or its teachers. For it is fitting that the worthy correction should return from the source from which the saving translation came to us.

Our fathers rightly took the greatest care concerning this matter, lest the tunic of the Lord and Savior—which savage soldiers were not permitted to tear—be subjected to unlearned readers. Let the Holy Spirit hear the most sincere things that he bestowed; let that blessed one receive what he conferred. Then he recognizes us as faithful to him, if we do not, through presumption, criticize anything he has said. For how can we wish to be saved if—something abhorrent even to say—we corrupt the saving remedy according to our own will?

But so that you may appear to add ornament to all these things, place in every section the punctuation marks which the Greeks call *θέσεις* (*theseis*), that is, very brief points, both rounded and perfectly plain, as was already said in the preface, except in the translation of Saint Jerome, which is arranged by cola and commas. For they make the speech clear and luminous when, fitted to their proper places—as will be explained below, they shine forth.

What could be better than to proceed with unhindered steps through the sacred senses, to enter subtly into the most salutary veins of instruction, to attach their proper boundaries appropriately to measured speech, and to divide the whole expression into members in such a way that, considered in its parts, each part becomes beautiful? For if our body must be understood through its members, why, when a reading appears to be distinguished according to its parts, should it be left confused?

These punctuation marks, or points, are in fact like paths of the senses and lights of expressions. They make readers receptive, as though they had been instructed by the clearest commentators. The first is the medial point, the second the subdistinction, and the third the full point. Our ancestors are known to have invented them for this reason: so that the spirit, wearied by a long expression, might recover its strength through measured intervals [ed., “decreed intervals”]. If you, eager reader, prefer to learn about them, read Donatus, who can instruct you carefully on this subject in a brief compendium.

We retain the memory that we placed these divisions in the archetypal Psalter, whose obscurities, by the Lord’s favor, we have for the most part clarified by such remedies. Thus the number seven has been completed on both sides, so that it may clearly appear, as I think, both what things we should abstain from and what things we presume to correct in authoritative texts [Col. 1130B]. If, nevertheless, this desire can be assisted in some other way, let it be added to your studies, lest we seem, as human beings, to have omitted something necessary.

Now we must explain how we ought to correct the remaining readings outside the authoritative text. Each corrector should read commentaries on the divine law, letters, sermons, and the books of the ancients in such a way that he joins their corrections to the standards of secular letters. Wherever *paragrammata* [alterations or textual corruptions] are found in eloquent writers, let him correct the defects fearlessly, since these men are to be believed to have composed their words in such a way that they observed the rules of grammatical art which they had learned.

The letters of the Fathers, sermons and books of various authors, as well as homilies and the debates of the faithful with heretics—for these open up different passages of divine Scripture pleasantly and carefully—should be reread with great diligence. Thus, in the Church of the Lord, as though by lamps appropriately lit, everything may shine brightly and splendidly, by the Lord’s favor.

If anything suitable for explaining the divine Scriptures is found in these works, do not hesitate to join it to the divine books, as we are known to have done in the Books of Kings. For many things are found to have been said at greater length by highly approved authors, in the course of another work, about the divine books; these can appropriately be fitted to sacred authority.

Therefore I ask that what we, because of our limited reading, were able to explain inadequately [ed., “too little”], you, nourished by the most abundant reading, complete more perfectly in Christ’s name, both from the books that we have left behind and from those that you may fortunately discover.

I also beg you who presume to correct these texts to strive to make the added letters so beautiful that they might rather be judged to have been written by antiquarians. For in that beauty there ought to be nothing ugly which might later offend the eyes of diligent readers.

Consider, therefore, what kind of charge has been entrusted to you: the benefit of Christians, the treasure of the Church, the light of souls. Strive, then, so that no error may remain in truth, no falsehood in purity, no perversity in the integrity of the letters.

But since we placed nine books of the divine law at the beginning, and, with the Lord’s help, recalled their introducers together with their commentators with as much care as we could; and since, finally, we touched upon the three divisions of the whole divine law handed down by our ancestors; and since we then added how heavenly authority ought to be corrected cautiously, so that presumptuous license might not tear it apart or unbecoming confusion be handed down to the hands of those who come after us—now we must discuss in every respect the power of divine reading, so that each of its proper places may be filled with its own sweetness [ed., “clothed”].

## Chapter XVI. On the power of Holy Scripture

Consider, excellent companions, how wondrously and sweetly the sequence of statements proceeds in the divine Scriptures: ever-growing desire, satisfaction without end, and the glorious hunger of the blessed. There excess is not condemned; rather, frequent insistence is praised.

And rightly so, since from it we learn knowledge of things that bring salvation, and eternal life is granted to those who believe and practice the same things. They describe the past without falsehood; they show the present as more than it appears; they narrate the future as though it were already complete. Truth reigns everywhere in them; divine power shines everywhere; everywhere they disclose what will benefit the human race.

Although these things are so, heavenly truth is communicated to us on earth according to the capacity of our understanding, through parables and propositions, as he himself testifies in the seventy-seventh psalm:

> “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning” (Psalm 77:2).

They also convey to us—as gifts surpassing all others—the worshipful knowledge of the Holy Trinity, which humanity, devoted to idols, blind and tearful, remained ignorant of throughout so many ages: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God, creator and ruler of all creatures, powerful to do whatever he wills in heaven and on earth.

If you seek his mercy, hear it briefly expressed:

> “A helper in tribulations, in the times of distress” (Psalm 45:2).

If you seek his patience, listen:

> “And who can resist your power?”

If you seek his justice, read:

> “For he will judge the world in righteousness” (Psalm 95:13).

His complete presence everywhere is also declared most plainly, when the Psalmist says:

> “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm 138:7–8).

And there are other passages concerning that majesty contained in the sacred readings [Col. 1131D].

Human reason did not discover these writings; rather, heavenly power infused them into holy men. They are rightly understood when the devoted mind believes them to proclaim what is true and useful. What benefit and sweetness will you not find in these writings if you attend to them with the purest light of the mind?

Divine reading is wholly powerful; its word does not fall in vain, nor does the effect promised by the utterance delay. It grants eternal salvation to the obedient and restores everlasting punishment to the proud. Therefore I urge you not only to hear it but to fulfill it through holy works.

At one time it commands love of God and neighbor; at another it teaches you to despise the perishable things of the world; at another it instills the remembrance of that homeland in which you will dwell forever. It commands patience, grants hope, praises profitable humility, constantly condemns destructive pride, and very frequently persuades us to give pious alms.

Then, what is more indulgent than all other acts of mercy, the Judge himself testifies that repentance is acceptable to him, when the most merciful Redeemer even pardons the words with which he is entreated. He terrifies in order to correct; he threatens judgment in order to spare.

And he commands us to live in such a way that we may deserve to be companions of the pious angels, and that what is exceedingly sweet and everlasting may come to pass in us:

> “That God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:18);

and then:

> “That we may see him as he is” (1 John 3:2);

and that we may be filled with the abundance of his glory in such a way that we are no longer wearied by any barrenness of need.

Who, then, would not hasten to obey such commands, except one who is eager to perish eternally in every respect? It surpasses every madness to neglect the commands of one’s Redeemer and fulfill the desires of the most cruel enemy. As many words, so many rewards; as many sentences, so many punishments. Nothing is empty of useful teaching, except when the tongue is silent concerning the mighty works of God.

Would that we never ceased from such things! There would certainly be no room for sins if the restless mind of mortals had no idle time. To these benefits, bestowed with generous mercy, has been added the worshipful and venerable knowledge of the Holy Trinity, which the pagan world, dead in sins, utterly ignored.

549

It remains now that we recall those who have said [ed., “taught”] something worthy of reverence about the Holy Trinity in their books. For the confirmation of our faith and to guard against the snares of heretics, the thirteen books of blessed Hilary should be read. He composed them on the Holy Trinity in language of exceedingly profound and eloquent expression.

The books of Saint Ambrose on the same subject, which he composed for the emperor Gratian, are also very distinguished and written in elegant language. Then the fifteen books of Saint Augustine, which he wrote on the Holy Trinity with extraordinary profundity, should be studied with attentive concentration.

If anyone prefers to touch briefly upon the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and does not wish to weary himself with lengthy reading, let him read the book that Bishop Nicetius composed on the faith. Filled with the clarity of heavenly doctrine, he will be led into divine contemplation in a concise summary. This book has been joined to the volumes of Saint Ambrose which he sent to the emperor Gratian.

O immeasurable mercy and power of the Creator! The heavens were opened; the Holy Trinity, revealed to the hearts of the faithful, shone forth; and paganism, which had usurped honor that belonged to another, departed, refuted by the true Lord [Col. 1132D]!

Also useful for instruction in ecclesiastical discipline are the three honey-sweet books of the aforementioned Saint Ambrose, *On Duties*, as well as blessed Augustine’s single book *On True Religion* and his four books *On Christian Doctrine*. Likewise, his single book *On Christian Combat*, which he composed, is especially necessary for you who, having trampled upon the world, labor in Christian warfare.

Similarly, his work resembling a moral philosophy, which he collected from divine authority for the formation and correction of morals and called the *Mirror*, should be read with great attention.

Let us also pass through, with unwearied diligence, the twenty-two books which Saint Augustine composed *On the City of God*. There the confused city of Babylon, the city of the devil, and splendid Jerusalem, the city of the Lord Christ, are shown in an appropriate contrast for the conversion [ed., “conduct”] of human beings.

He also wrote five questions on the New Testament for the presbyter Honoratus, and eighty-three others composed after remarkable deliberation. If anyone wishes to cleanse his own statements through careful examination and not fall into wrongdoing through heedless presumption, let him pass through the two books of Saint Augustine’s *Retractions* with diligent reading. From them he may adorn himself by imitation and recognize how great an abundance of wisdom divine indulgence bestowed upon that most blessed Father, so that he who perhaps could not be censured by anyone appears to correct himself through the most cautious reconsideration.

It would be lengthy to recall each of that man’s works individually, since a substantial book exists for listing his writings [550]. Although it briefly recalls his statements, it nevertheless extends over many pages of reading.

## Chapter XVII. On Christian historians

After the commentators, there are also various narrators of times and Christian studies. Composed with ecclesiastical seriousness, they proceed through the changes of affairs and the alterations of kingdoms with a truly milky, but very careful, brilliance.

Since they recount ecclesiastical affairs and describe the changes that occur through different periods, they must necessarily educate the minds of readers always in heavenly matters, since they strive faithfully to attribute everything not to random occurrences or the weak powers of the gods—as the pagans did—but to the will of the Creator.

Such is Josephus [Note: [Col. 1133D] Saint Jerome calls Josephus a Greek Livy.], almost a second Livy, extensively developed in his books of *Jewish Antiquities*. Father Jerome, writing to Lucinus of Baetica, stated that because of the work’s length he had been unable to translate it.

Nevertheless, because it is exceedingly subtle and complex, I had it translated into Latin by our friends, with great labor, in twenty-two books. He also composed, with marvelous brilliance, seven other books on the captivity of the Jews. Some attribute their translation to Jerome, others to Ambrose, and others to Rufinus. Since it is attributed to such men, the excellence of its diction is altogether made evident [Col. 1133D].

After these, one should read the history which Eusebius composed in Greek in ten volumes and which Rufinus, with the addition of the events that followed, presents as completed in eleven books.

After Eusebius’s history, Socrates, Sozomenus, and Theodoret wrote subsequent works among the Greeks. With God’s help, we had these translated by the very eloquent Epiphanius into one body of twelve books, so that eloquent Greece might not boast that it possessed something necessary which we judged to have been withheld from us [Col. 1134A].

Orosius, too, the comparer of Christian and pagan times, is available to you if you wish to read him. Marcellinus also composed four books *On the Qualities of Times and the Positions of Places*, with remarkably appropriate expression, and laudably completed the course of his journey; I have likewise left him to you.

Eusebius wrote in Greek the *Chronicles*, which are brief images of histories and very concise recollections of times. Jerome translated him into Latin and carried the work forward excellently to his own times.

The aforementioned Marcellinus of Illyricum followed him. He is said still to have held the office of secretary [mss., “to have governed the secretariat”] of the patrician Justinian [Note: [Col. 1133D] Such is what Constantius says in *The Life of Saint Germanus*, bishop of Auxerre, book 2, chapter 17, concerning the son of Volusianus, who presided over the secretariat of the patrician Segisvultus. On “to hold the secretariat,” see Cassiodorus, book 12, letter 1.]. But, more devoted under better circumstances [ed., “with better diction”], he brought his work, with the Lord’s help, from the reign of the emperor Theodosius to the end [ed., “the beginning”] of the empire of the triumphant Augustus Justinian. Thus he who had earlier been pleasing in the service he had undertaken appeared afterward to be abundantly devoted to Justinian’s authority.

Saint Prosper likewise carried his *Chronicle* from Adam down to the time of Genseric and the plundering of the city of Rome. You may perhaps find other writers who continue after these, since writers of times are not lacking, as succeeding ages continually follow one another.

But when, diligent reader, you have filled yourself with the matters mentioned above and your intellect has been illumined by the divine light, read the book of Saint Jerome *On Illustrious Men*, where he briefly honors and touches upon various Fathers and their works.

Then read the other book, by Gennadius of Marseille, who most reliably identified the writers of the divine law whom he had diligently investigated. I have left these works joined in one body, so that the delay of having to consult different books might not impede the acquisition of knowledge.

For the authors of many venerable readings follow. At one time the most learned men compose books through divine inspiration; at another they console one another through the grace of letters; at another they soothe peoples with the sweetest speech; at another they engage in the most lively disputes with heretics. Some of them thus enter into controversies through individual contests and engage with their judges in glorious debate [perhaps read, “convince them”].

In this way, when each wicked person is destroyed, by the Lord’s favor the most faithful person is thereby strengthened. Then, in that most holy and eloquent choir of the Fathers, you will be able to choose the one with whom you may converse most sweetly.

It is also difficult to say how frequently, when an opportunity arises, they powerfully open up the sacred Scriptures in places most appropriate to them, so that, while passing through, you suddenly learn what you recognize that you had negligently passed over.

## Chapter XVIII. On Saint Hilary

The most learned men, distinguished by varied praise, are witnesses; through them the Church shines like a sky glittering with radiant stars. Among them proceeds Saint Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers, subtle in his exceeding profundity and a most careful disputant. Reverently bringing the deep abysses of the divine Scriptures into the midst, he causes—by God’s favor—what had previously been veiled in obscure parables to be seen by an illumined mind [Col. 1135A].

## Chapter XIX. On Saint Cyprian

It is altogether impossible to encompass how much blessed Cyprian contributes among the other writers—apart from the rebaptism which the usage and reasoning of the Church rejected—like oil flowing into every sweetness, with composed language, a distinguished declamatory style, and wondrous instruction.

How many doubters did he prevent from falling, and how many who had fallen did he strengthen through the firmest preaching? How many confessors did he lead even to martyrdom? And lest he be lesser than his own preaching, he too was adorned, by the Lord’s favor, with the crown of martyrdom.

Among the other bright memorials of his eloquence that he left to us, he composed, with declamatory elegance, a little book expounding the Lord’s Prayer, which is always set against creeping vices like an unconquered shield.

551

## Chapter XX. On Saint Ambrose

Saint Ambrose likewise, a source of milky speech, sharp with gravity and exceedingly sweet in unforced persuasion, possessed a doctrine equal to his life; for the grace of the Divinity smiled upon him through no small miracles.

## Chapter XXI. On Saint Jerome

[Col. 1135C]

Blessed Jerome, too, the outstanding enlarger of the Latin language, gave us so much in his translation of divine Scripture that we scarcely need to approach the Hebrew source, since he is known to have satisfied us with the great abundance of his eloquence and to have produced many books and copious letters [Note: [Col. 1135D] Edition: “to have made blessed through many books and copious letters those to whom he deigned, by the Lord’s favor, to write.”].

Blessed are those to whom he deigned, by the Lord’s favor, to write. Clear, learned, and sweet, with a ready abundance of words, he turns his intellect to whatever subject he chooses. At one time he gently flatters the humble; at another he breaks the necks of the proud; at another he repays his detractors with the necessary sharpness; at another he praises virginity; at another he defends chaste marriages; at another he highly commends the glorious contests of the virtues; at another he censures lapses and wickedness among clergy and monks.

Yet wherever the occasion arose, he interwove examples from the pagans with the sweetest variety, explaining everything and adorning everything, and always proceeding as an eloquent and consistent writer through the various kinds of argument.

For although he sometimes extends certain books with great abundance, the conclusion of his work is always pleasing because of the sweetness of his statements. I do not think that he lived idly at Bethlehem, except so that, in that land of miracles, his eloquence too might shine for us from the East like the sun [Note: [Col. 1135D] Cassiodorus often uses *lampare* for “to shine.”].

He sent a remarkable letter to Paulinus, a presbyter formerly a senator, [Note: [Col. 1135D] Baronius, volume 4, under the year A.D. 394, page 718, Antwerp edition, disagrees and asserts that this Paulinus was different from Paulinus, bishop of Nola.], teaching how divine Scripture should be read with due caution. In it he briefly and wonderfully indicated the power of each book of the Old and New Testaments.

If I had found it earlier, yielding to his eloquence I might perhaps have been content to say nothing about the same subject. But since he wrote one thing and I, in a work already completed, wrote something different, by God’s generosity, I believe that the diligent reader will not be occupied uselessly by this little work as well.

He wrote for a new reader of the divine law who was so learned in secular letters that he had even prudently and elegantly composed a book about the emperor Theodosius [Note: [Col. 1136D] Saint Jerome also mentions this book in his letter to Paulinus *On the Formation of a Monk*, and Paulinus himself in letter 9 to his sister. Gennadius, in his *Catalogue*, calls the work a panegyric on the victory over the tyrants, namely Maximus and Eugenius.].

Nor, as can be understood, did he have at that time writers of his own kind in such numbers that he could urge him to read them in an orderly sequence. For at that time the soldiers of Christ were still laboring with salutary sweat in the gymnasium of divine law, and he himself later wrote many things among them.

Our situation, however, was different. First, we wrote for simple and unpolished brothers who needed instruction, so that through the many authors who have already been made known in our age they might be filled with the fullness of the heavenly Scriptures and might be commendably instructed not so much from us, who are poor in this matter, as from the abundant and ancient Fathers.

But lest anything be lacking to those who have not studied the pursuits of this world, we thought that they should also be briefly instructed, in a second volume, in both the arts and the disciplines of secular letters [Col. 1136C]. Thus the knowledge of worldly letters—which is known to have developed from the divine Scriptures apart from the additions of certain teachers—may also serve simple men.

In this way, neither may reproach seize upon us for novel presumption, nor may some measure of gratitude perhaps arise from the small service of this volume [mss., “from a service that is altogether too small”].

## Chapter XXII. On Saint Augustine

That outstanding teacher, the most blessed Augustine, conqueror of heretics, defender of the faithful, and victor in famous contests, is hidden in some books by excessive difficulty, while in others he is so perfectly clear that he is found acceptable even to children. His evident passages are sweet, while the obscure ones grow rich, filled with great benefits.

If anyone wishes to know the liveliness of his intellect, let him read his books of *Confessions*. There he reports that he grasped, without a teacher, all the mathematical disciplines which others can scarcely approach even under learned interpreters.

He also disclosed our Creed—the guarantor of our faith, the testimony of an upright heart, and the inviolable sacrament of our promise—through frequent exposition [mss., “following exposition”], so that, understanding more deeply what we profess to believe, we might preserve our promises with the greatest care.

One should also read his book in which, after Pope Epiphanius, he summarized various heresies in a concise account. For no sound mind willingly allows itself to fall upon those reefs upon which it knows that another has suffered shipwreck. The opinions of those whom the watchful Church has condemned must be avoided altogether. If anything of this kind is now being presumed, it must be shunned with the greatest caution.

## Chapter XXIII. On Abbots Eugipius and Dionysius
It is also fitting that you should necessarily read the work of the presbyter Eugipius [Note: [Col. 1137D] Concerning him, see Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. VI, under the year of Christ 504, p. 574 of the Antwerp edition.] (see R. P. Chifflet at Ferandus, p. 332), whom we too saw: a man not exceedingly learned in secular literature, but thoroughly versed in the reading of the divine Scriptures. From the works of Saint Augustine he gathered, for our mother Proba, a consecrated virgin, very profound questions and opinions, as well as various subjects, extracting them and collecting them in a single volume with highly necessary arrangement, and set them out in 338 chapters. This book, as I think, is profitably read, since the diligence of a studious man was able to store in one volume what can scarcely be found even in a great library.

### 552

The Catholic Church also continues to produce illustrious men, shining with the splendor of approved doctrines. In our own times there was also Dionysius, a monk, Scythian by nation but wholly Roman in character, highly learned in both languages. By his actions he rendered the justice which he had read in the Lord’s books. He had examined and understood the divine Scriptures with such intense care that, whatever he was asked, he had a suitable answer ready without any delay. He studied dialectic with me and, in the example [mss., temple] of his glorious teaching, spent many years of his life, by the Lord’s favor. I am ashamed to say of a companion what I cannot find in myself. For in him great simplicity was joined with wisdom, humility with learning, restraint in speech with eloquence, so that in nothing did he place himself before even the lowest servants, although he was unquestionably worthy of the conversation of kings [Note: [Col. 1137D] Conversations with kings are held in the highest honor, *Variae*, book III, letter 22.]. May he intercede for us, he who was accustomed to pray with us, so that we, supported here by his prayer, may now be assisted by his merits.

When requested by Stephen, bishop of Salona, he composed from Greek exemplars the ecclesiastical canons [Note: [Col. 1138D] These canons of Dionysius are found in the manuscript compilation of Cresconius’s *Collection of Canons*, as Baronius notes, vol. I of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 58, §24, p. 526.]—matching his own character, for he was straightforward and eloquent—with the great brilliance of his eloquence [ms. Aud., sweetness]. The Roman Church embraces them today with the most renowned usage. You too ought to read them constantly, lest you appear culpably ignorant of such salutary ecclesiastical rules. He also translated many other works from Greek into Latin which may serve ecclesiastical usefulness. He possessed such mastery of Latin and Greek that, whenever he took Greek books into his hands, he could read through them in Latin without difficulty and then reread Latin books in Attic speech; you would have thought that what his mouth poured forth with effortless speed had itself been written in that language.

It would be a long task to recount everything about that holy man, who among his other virtues is shown to have possessed this outstanding quality: although he had given himself wholly to God, he did not disdain to take part in the company of secular people. Extremely chaste, though he saw other men’s wives every day; gentle, though he was buffeted by the mad whirlwind of raging men. He shed tears, moved by compunction, when he heard the chattering words of merriment; he fasted without reproaching those who dined. He took part in banquets so graciously that, when questioned amid bodily meals [Col. 1138B], he always displayed spiritual riches. If, nevertheless, he sometimes ate, he used ordinary foods, though in small quantity. Thus I regard it as the highest form of patience to remain amid human delights while preserving the measure of abstinence.

But, to report the goodness of his mind without cosmetic praise, he was wholly Catholic, wholly and steadfastly attached to the rules of the Fathers [ed., bound to them]; and whatever readers may seek by various paths was recognized as shining forth in his knowledge. Certain wicked men attempt slanderously to attach something to his glorious name, so that their own errors may appear somewhat excused. But he, having now abandoned the perversity of the world and, by the Lord’s favor, having been received into the peace of the Church [ed., buried], must be believed to have fellowship among the servants of God.

I might perhaps still recount the remaining things concerning the holy man which we know through the full truth of our experience; but we must rather carry out our purpose, lest, while we are debtors to another promise, we seem through tedious talk to be reporting something else at excessive length. And so that no deception may harm you in the rules of faith, read the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, which you have at hand, as well as the encyclicals—that is, the letters confirming the aforementioned council. If you run through these carefully, the devices of the wicked will have no opportunity to prevail over you.

## CHAPTER XXIV. With what diligence Holy Scripture should be read together with its interpreters

Let us therefore apply ourselves, and after the introductory books let us diligently proceed through the authoritative works together with their interpreters. Let us follow with devout zeal the paths of understanding discovered through the labor of the Fathers, and let us not hasten with greedy excess toward utterly vain questions. Whatever is found reasonably stated in the most approved commentators, let us unquestionably believe to be divine; but if anything discordant or inconsistent with the rules of the Fathers is found, let us judge that it must be avoided. For the origin of the fiercest error is to love everything in suspicious authors and to wish to defend without judgment whatever one finds in them. For it is written: “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

But, to gather briefly what must be said: everything that the ancient interpreters have stated with probability must be retained with attentive mind. Those matters, however, which they left untreated should first be examined—lest we wear ourselves out with fruitless labor—to see what virtues they possess or toward what practices they may lead us; then we should consider what they wish us to draw from them by reading.

For although a passage may seem extremely clear and shine forth in historical narration, it nevertheless either recommends justice [mss., sorrow], or rebukes impiety; either praises endurance, or condemns the vices of fickleness; either condemns pride, or exalts the goods of humility [Col. 1139B]; either restrains the discontented, or consoles those full of charity; or it recalls something of the kind that encourages upright conduct and, out of reverence for piety, draws us away from wicked thoughts. For if God promised rewards only to the good, his kindness would grow cold through neglect; but if he continually threatened the wicked with destruction, despair of salvation would drive them [mss., provide them] toward vice. Therefore the merciful Redeemer moderated both for our salvation, so that he might terrify sinners by the punishment announced [ms. Aud., from the unwilling woman] and promise the good fitting rewards.

Accordingly, let the mind be raised generally toward the purposes of the books, and let us fix our understanding upon that contemplation which not only sounds in the ears but shines forth to the inner eyes. For even if the account appears simple [Col. 1139C], nothing empty or idle is contained in the divine writings; rather, whatever is said is always directed toward some benefit, to be healthfully drawn from it by the most upright understanding. Therefore, when good deeds are reported, let us immediately rise to imitate them; when deeds deserving punishment are narrated, let us fear to perform such things. Thus we always acquire some benefit if we pay attention to the reason for which they are recounted.

### 553  
## CHAPTER XXV. Cosmography to be read by monks

We reasonably urge you also to survey the knowledge of cosmography, so that you may clearly recognize in what part of the world each place mentioned in the holy books is situated. This will certainly happen if you hasten to read diligently the little book of Julius the Orator [Note: [Col. 1139D] Ausonius, in letter 16 to Probus, prefect of the praetorian guard, mentions Titianus, whom he says wrote *Fables* and calls a master of speech, and shortly afterward mentions Julius. The following words of Capitolinus, speaking of the son of Maximinus Augustus, should be understood of the same man: “He used Julius Titianus as an orator, the son of the elder Titianus, who wrote very fine books about the provinces and was called the ape of his age because he imitated everything.” See the notes of Jacob Sirmond on letter 1 of book I of Sidonius Apollinaris. The book of cosmography commonly attributed to Aethicus is attributed to Julius the Orator in the Thuaneus manuscript.], which I have left for you. He has embraced seas, islands, famous mountains, provinces, cities, rivers, and peoples in a fourfold arrangement, so that almost nothing is absent from the book that is known to belong to the knowledge of cosmography.

Marcellinus also, whom I have already mentioned, should be read with equal care. In four small books he described the city of Constantinople and the city of Jerusalem in a very minute account [mss., with very minute method]. Next, learn Dionysius’s *Pinax*, composed in brief form, so that what you perceive with your ears in the aforementioned book you may almost see with your eyes as you look upon it.

Then, if concern for distinguished knowledge has kindled you, you have the book of Ptolemy, who expressed all places so clearly that you might judge him to have been almost a resident of every region. Thus, remaining in one place—as befits monks—you may traverse in spirit what the journeys of others gathered with immense labor.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On attaching marks

We have also taken care to indicate this, so that our labor might instruct you and, by the Lord’s favor, some sort of gift might adorn your holy zeal: insofar as either old age or weariness from a long journey allowed me to reread, I marked certain books of the Fathers with signs written in red, which are indexes of the books, impressing them, as I think appropriately, at their respective places. For the commentaries on the Octateuch we assigned the mark “Oct.”; for the second book of Kings, “Reg.”; for the third, the Psalter, “Ps.”; for the fourth, Solomon, “Sal.”; for the fifth, the Prophets, “Proph.”; for the sixth, the Hagiographers, “Hag.”; for the seventh, the Gospels, “Ev.”; for the eighth, the Apostolic Epistles, “Ap.”; for the ninth, the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse, “Act. et Aaa.” I always wrote these at the beginnings of the books through which I was able to pass while engaged in the task itself, so that you might recognize them without ambiguity when they are placed in the text, if you carefully run through each page [Col. 1140C].

Then, if you wish—and yet you presume upon extensive reading—imitation of the most approved commentators will readily lie open before you. Thus another kind of exposition, exceedingly sharp and beautiful, will arise, and what perhaps our predecessors did not at all clarify in their commentaries may there be found explained to some extent. We have also marked the idioms of the divine law—that is, its distinctive expressions—with the character “pp.”, so that wherever they are found, the words themselves may not be violated by any presumption.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the figures and disciplines found in the sacred Scriptures and in their interpreters

We have also thought it necessary to remind you that, both in the sacred writings and in the most learned interpreters, we can understand many things through figures, many through definitions, many through grammatical art, many through rhetorical art, many through dialectic, many through arithmetic, many through music, many through geometry, and many through astronomy. It is not without reason, therefore, that we have undertaken to touch briefly, in the following book, upon the arts and disciplines of secular teachers with their divisions, so that those who have learned such things may be briefly reminded of them, and those who perhaps have been unable to read more extensively may learn something from them in concise form. For there is undoubtedly, as it also seemed to our Fathers, a useful knowledge of these matters that should not be rejected, since you find it everywhere diffused through the sacred writings, as through the source of general and perfect wisdom. When these things have been presented and demonstrated there, your understanding is assisted in every way toward comprehension.

Let the work of the ancients, then, be our work, so that what they published at length in many books we may disclose most briefly, as has already been said, gathered together in a second volume. What they diverted toward the exercise of subtle arguments, let us restore, with commendable devotion, to the service of truth, so that what was stealthily taken from it may be honorably returned to the service of right understanding. It is indeed, as I think, a necessary work, but exceedingly difficult in view of its complexity: to attempt to contain in two books the most abundant sources of divine and human literature. Here those verses of Sedulius should be spoken:

> I ask for great things indeed; but you know how to give great things,  
>   
> Whoever grows lukewarm through hoping offends you most.
