## CHAPTER XXVIII. What monks who do not understand the arts set out in the following book should do

But if the simplicity of some brothers is unable to understand what has been extracted in the following book, since almost every brevity is obscure, let it be enough for them to consider summarily the divisions, uses, and virtues of the subjects, so that they may be swept toward knowledge of the divine law by ardent concentration of mind. Through various most holy Fathers they will find means by which they can satisfy their desire with the fullest abundance. Let their affection for reading only be sincere, and their desire for understanding sober. Then salutary perseverance will make learned those whom, at the outset, the profundity of reading frightened; 554 for not only the educated, but also those who do not know letters, receive wisdom from God.

Let us nevertheless understand that prudence is not placed solely in letters, but that God gives perfect wisdom to each person as he wills. For if knowledge of good things existed only in letters, those who do not know letters would certainly not possess right wisdom. But since many unlettered people [mss., “agra mentis,” that is, “from the grace of the mind”] reach true understanding and receive the right faith breathed into them from heaven, there is no doubt that God grants pure and devout minds what he judges beneficial for them. For it is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Psalm 93:12). Therefore we must ask through good deeds and constant prayers that, with the Lord accompanying us, we may come to true faith and the holiest works, where our life is everlasting. For it is written: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

Nevertheless, the most holy Fathers did not decree that the study of secular literature should be rejected, since through it our understanding is instructed in no small degree for the comprehension of the sacred Scriptures—provided that, with divine grace assisting, knowledge of these subjects is sought soberly and reasonably; not so that we place our hope of advancement in them, but so that, passing through them, we may desire that useful and salutary wisdom be granted to us by the Father of lights. For how many philosophers, reading only these things, did not come to the fountain of wisdom, and, deprived of the true light, were plunged into the blindness of ignorance! For, as someone said: “What is not sought by its proper path can never be investigated with complete thoroughness.”

Again, many of our Fathers, educated in such literature and remaining in the law of the Lord, reached true wisdom, as blessed Augustine recalls in *On Christian Doctrine* (book II, chapter 40), saying:

> We do not consider how much gold and silver and clothing Cyprian, the sweetest teacher and most blessed martyr, carried out of Egypt; nor how much Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary carried out; we add Ambrose, Augustine himself, and Jerome, and many other innumerable Greeks.

The most faithful servant of God, Moses, did this also; concerning him it is written (Acts 7:22) that he was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Imitating them, let us hasten, if we can, to read both kinds of learning with the greatest caution and without hesitation. Who would dare to doubt where the manifold example of such men goes before us? Knowing clearly—as has often already been said—that the Lord can grant right and true wisdom, as the Book of Wisdom says: “Wisdom is from the Lord God; it was always with him and remains forever” (Ecclesiasticus 1:1).

Therefore, with all our strength, all our labor, and all our desires, let us seek to become worthy, by the Lord’s generosity, of attaining such a great and lofty gift. This is salutary, profitable, glorious, and everlasting for us—something that no death, no fickleness, and no forgetfulness can separate from us—but which will make us rejoice in eternal exultation with the Lord in the sweetness of our homeland. But if, as Virgil recalls, for some brother

> the cold blood has stood around his heart,

so that he cannot be perfectly educated in either human or divine literature, then, supported at least by some moderate degree of knowledge, let him certainly choose what follows:

> Let the countryside and streams flowing through watered valleys please me.

For it is not foreign to monks themselves to cultivate gardens, work the fields, and rejoice in the fertility of fruit trees. For it is read in the 127th Psalm: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Psalm 127:2).

If authors for this study are sought, Gargilius Martialis wrote most beautifully about gardens [Note: [Col. 1141D] Lampridius mentions him in the *Life of Alexander Severus*, p. 359. Palladius Rutilius, in April, under title 3, writes about gardens: “Martialis asserts a remarkable thing about basil.” Likewise, in March, title 9: “Gargilius Martialis asserted all these things.”], and he carefully explained both the nourishment of vegetables and their properties, so that from reading his commentary each person may, by the Lord’s favor, both be filled and be healed. I have left this work for you among the other books. Likewise, in cultivating fields, in bees, in doves, and also in raising fish, Columella and Aemilianus were among the other reliable authors. Columella, however, proceeds eloquently and fluently through sixteen books on various kinds of agriculture, suited more to the articulate than to the inexperienced, so that students of his work may be filled not only with common benefit but also with the most pleasing feasts. Aemilianus [Note: [Col. 1143D] I think the person meant is the one called Palladius Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus, an illustrious man who wrote books on agriculture, which are still extant in published form. He is also mentioned by Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVII, chapter 1. See what Jacob Sirmond observed about proper names in the Middle Ages in his preface to Sidonius Apollinaris.] also, a most eloquent expositor, discussed gardens, livestock, and other matters in twelve books with the fullest [ed., clearest] explanation. I have left him for you to read repeatedly among the other books, by the Lord’s favor.

Yet when these things are prepared for strangers and the sick, they become heavenly, although they may seem earthly. For what is it to restore the sick with sweet fruits, to nourish them with the offspring of doves, to feed them with fish, or to soothe them with the sweetness of honey? Since the Lord commands even cold water to be offered in his name to the poor (Matthew 10:42), how much more pleasing will it be to give the most delicious foods to various needy people, for whom you may receive in judgment the fruit of multiplied reward! One must not neglect any means by which a person can reasonably be helped.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the situation of the monastery of Vivarium, or Castellum

The site of the monastery of Vivarium invites you to prepare many things for strangers and the needy, since you have irrigated gardens and the nearby waters of the fish-abounding river Pellena. It is regarded as neither threatening because of the magnitude of its waters nor contemptible because of its smallness. It flows to you, regulated by art, wherever it is judged necessary, and is sufficient both for your gardens and for your mills [read: *molendinis*, “mills”]. It is present when desired and, when it has fulfilled your wishes, withdraws into the distance. Thus, in a manner of speaking, it exists as a devoted servant, neither burdensome through importunity [mss., fearful] nor able to be absent when sought.

The seas also lie beneath you in such a way that they are open to various kinds of fishing; and when a fish is caught, it can, whenever you wish, be enclosed in fishponds. For there, with the Lord’s help, we made pleasant enclosures, where a multitude of fish may wander beneath a secure covering [Col. 1143D]. They are so congenial to the caves of the mountains that the fish does not feel itself captured at all: it is free to take food and to hide itself in its accustomed caverns. We also ordered baths to be built, suitably prepared for sick bodies, where the clarity of springs flows in decorously and is known to be most pleasant both for drinking and for bathing. Thus it happens that your monastery is sought by others, rather than that you should rightly desire foreign places. But these things, as you know, are delights of present circumstances, not the hope of the faithful for the future; the one passes away, the other remains without end. Therefore, while placed there, let us transfer our desires rather to those things that make us reign with Christ.

Read attentively and listen willingly to the presbyter Cassian, who wrote concerning the institution of faithful monks. At the very beginning of the holy calling he says that eight principal vices must be avoided. He introduces the harmful movements of the soul so appropriately that he almost makes a person see his own excesses and compels him to avoid them—excesses which previously he did not recognize because of the darkness of confusion. Nevertheless, he was rightly criticized by blessed Prosper concerning free will. Therefore we warn you that, in such matters, you should read him with caution when he goes beyond the proper measure. His statements were so cleansed by Victor, bishop of Martyritanus [mss., Martaritanus], an African, with the Lord’s help, and he added what was lacking, that the palm for these matters may rightly be awarded to him. We believe that he will soon be sent to us from the regions of Africa among the others. He vehemently condemns the remaining types of monks. But you, dearest brothers, with God’s help, choose those parts which he is known to have praised beneficially.

For if, as it is worthy to believe, the custom of coenobitic communities properly educates you in the monastery of Vivarium, with divine grace assisting, and if it should happen that, with your minds purified, you desire something loftier, you have the pleasant seclusion of Mount Castellum, where, like anchorites, you may, by the Lord’s favor, live happily. They are remote places resembling the desert, since they are enclosed by the ancient walls that surround them. Therefore, for those already trained and thoroughly tested, it will be suitable to choose that dwelling, if an ascent has first been prepared in your hearts. Through reading you learn which of the two you are able either to desire or to endure. The only requirement is that, while preserving the uprightness of your way of life, the person who cannot teach others by words should instruct them by the holiness of his conduct.

## CHAPTER XXX. On copyists and the commemoration of orthography

I nevertheless confess my wish: among all the things that can be accomplished among you through bodily labor, the work of the copyists [Col. 1144D] [Note: [Col. 1143D] In the fragment concerning the condemnation of Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, issued by Pope Vigilius: “Sitting in your house, you wrote what you had repeatedly affirmed on oath that you would not do until the appointed time, having copyists hired at a high price.” I think it should be read: “hiring copyists at a high price.” Peter Damian, in a letter cited by Baronius, vol. XI, p. 294: “Although I may perhaps be able to dictate, there is no copyist to transcribe.”] may perhaps please me more, provided they write accurately. For by rereading the divine Scriptures they healthfully instruct their own minds, and by writing the Lord’s commandments they spread them far and wide.

Blessed purpose, praiseworthy diligence: to preach to people by the hand, to open tongues with the fingers, to give silent salvation to mortals, and to fight with pen and ink against the unlawful snares of the devil [Col. 1145A]. Satan receives as many wounds as the copyist [Note: [Col. 1145D] Here Saint Jerome is followed almost word for word in the *Epitaph of Nepotianus*, near the end: “This very thing that I dictate, that is written, that I reread, that I correct, is taken away from my life; the points of the notary are the losses of as many moments of my life.”] transcribes words of the Lord. Stationed in one place, he travels through different provinces by the dissemination of his work. His labor is read in holy places; peoples hear it and learn from it to turn away from an evil will and serve the Lord with a pure mind. Though absent, he works through his work. I cannot say that he is unable to receive a return for so many benefits [ed., benefits of teachers], provided that he is known to accomplish such things not through the ambition of greed but through upright zeal.

A human being multiplies heavenly words, and, in a certain commendable signification, if it is permissible to say so, what the power of the holy Trinity speaks is written by three fingers. O glorious spectacle for those who consider it well! As the reed runs, heavenly words are written, so that from the very thing by which the devil caused the Lord’s head to be struck in the Passion, his cunning may be extinguished. Their praises are further increased by the fact that they seem in some way to imitate the deed of the Lord, who wrote his law—although this is said figuratively—by the operation of the almighty finger. Many things could indeed be said about so distinguished an art; but it is enough to call them scribes who freely serve the Lord and justice [ed., the Lord’s scales].

But lest, when letters are altered, the writers mingle defective words with so great a good, or an unlearned corrector fail to know how to correct errors, let them read the ancient writers on orthography: Vellius Longus; Curtius Valerianus; Papirianus; Adamantius Martyrius, on V and B; the same author on initial, medial, and final syllables; the same author on the letter B when placed in a name in three ways; Eutyches, on aspiration; and also Phocas, on distinctions of gender. I gathered these authors with diligent curiosity, insofar as I could.

And lest the obscurity left in any of the books mentioned disturb anyone, since they are for the most part confused by the intermixture of ancient declensions [ed., their proper parts are confused], I devoted myself with great labor so that, in a separate and carefully arranged book entitled *On Orthography*, the extracted rules might reach you, and, with uncertainty removed, the mind might proceed more freely along the path of correction. We have also discovered that Diomedes and Theoctistus wrote something about this art; if they are found, collect their extracts as well. Perhaps you may find others through whom your knowledge may be better instructed. These authors, however, who have been mentioned, if reread with constant study, cut away all the darkness of ignorance for you, so that what was previously unknown may become known for the most part.

We also added skilled craftsmen for covering the books, so that a beautiful exterior might clothe the beauty of the sacred letters above. In this we perhaps imitate to some extent that example of the Lord’s figurative action: he who judged that those invited to the banquet should be covered with wedding garments in the glory of the heavenly feast. We suitably displayed, I believe, various kinds of workmanship depicted in a single book [Col. 1146A], so that the diligent person may choose for himself whatever form of covering he prefers.

We also prepared for the nightly vigils mechanical lamps that preserve the flames they illuminate, feeding their own fire and, when human service ceases, maintaining for a long time the abundant brilliance of their richest light; in them the richness of the oil does not fail, although it is continually consumed by burning flames.

Nor have we allowed you to remain wholly ignorant of the divisions of the hours, which are known to have been devised for great benefits to humankind. Therefore, I am known to have prepared for you one clock whose indication is given by the brightness of the sun, and another, a water clock, which continuously indicates the measure of the hours by day and night. For frequently, on certain days, the brightness of the sun is absent, and in a marvelous way water on earth performs what the sun’s fiery power, measured from above, carries out. Thus human art has made things that nature divided proceed harmoniously together. In them the reliability of the matter rests upon such truth that you may judge what is accomplished by both to have been arranged through intermediaries. These things, then, have been provided so that the soldiers of Christ, warned by certain signs, may be summoned to perform the divine work as though by the sounding of trumpets.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On monks who care for the sick

I also address you, excellent brothers, who attend to the health of the human body with diligent care and provide the offices of blessed compassion to those fleeing for refuge to holy places: saddened by the sufferings of others, sorrowful over those in danger, pierced by the pain of those entrusted to you [Note: [Col. 1146D] So Paulinus, letter concerning the treasury; Symmachus, book III, letter 39.], and always stunned by personal grief at the calamities of others. As the skill of your art requires [ed., as expertise teaches], serve the sick with sincere devotion, expecting to receive your reward from him who can repay temporal things with eternal ones.

Therefore learn the natures of herbs and investigate the combinations of substances with attentive mind; but do not place your hope in herbs or your well-being in human plans (Ecclesiasticus 38:4). For although medicine is read to have been established by the Lord, he himself makes people well, he who grants life without doubt [ed., life without end]. For it is written: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Colossians 3:17).

If you are not acquainted with the eloquence of Greek literature, you have first of all the herbal book of Dioscorides, who discussed and illustrated the herbs of the fields with marvelous precision. After this, read Hippocrates and Galen translated into Latin: namely, Galen’s *Therapeutics*, addressed to the philosopher Glaucon, and a certain anonymous work which is known to have been compiled from various authors. Next, read Aurelius Coelius’s *On Medicine*, Hippocrates’s *On Herbs and Treatments*, and various other works composed on the art of healing, which, with God’s help, I have left stored in the recesses of our library [Col. 1147A].

## CHAPTER XXXII. Cassiodorus’s exhortation to the monks and abbots Chalcedonius and Geruntius

Therefore, all of you whom the walls of the monastery enclose, observe both the rules of the Fathers and the commands of your own superior, and willingly carry out whatever is salutarily commanded to you; for obeying beneficial commands without any murmuring is the reward of a great recompense.

But I beseech you, most holy men, the abbots Chalcedonius and Geruntius, to arrange everything in such a way that, by the Lord’s favor, you may lead the flock entrusted to you to the gifts of blessedness. Above all, receive the stranger, give alms, clothe the naked, break bread for the hungry; for he must truly be called a consoler who consoles the miserable.

Teach the peasants who belong to your monastery good morals, and do not burden them with the weight of additional payments. For it is written: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). Let them be entirely ignorant of what is commonly associated with peasants: let them not know theft, let them be wholly unaware of worshiping groves, and let them live by an innocent purpose and happy simplicity. In the second place, impose upon them a most pure manner of life; let them frequently come to the holy monasteries, so that they may be ashamed to be called yours without being recognized as formed by your instruction. Let them also know that God graciously pours abundance upon their fields if they faithfully make a habit of invoking him.

A certain city of your own has therefore been given to you, religious citizens. If you live in it harmoniously and spiritually, by the Lord’s favor, you already rejoice in a foreshadowing of the heavenly homeland. Do not love idleness, which you know is hateful to the Lord. The doctrinal instruments of the holy Scriptures are available to you together with their interpreters. They are truly flower-bearing fields and the sweet fruits of the heavenly paradise, from which faithful souls may be healthfully instructed and your tongues equipped not with a fleeting but with a highly fruitful eloquence.

Therefore enter eagerly into the mysteries of the Lord, so that you may be able to point out the way to those who follow; for it is a great burden of shame to have something to read and not know what to teach. And so, mindful of future blessedness, read constantly the lives of the Fathers, the confessions of the faithful, and the passions of the martyrs—whom you undoubtedly find, among other works, in the letter of Saint Jerome addressed to Chromatius and Heliodorus [Note: [Col. 1147D] Baronius, preface to the *Roman Martyrology*, chapter 7, doubts whether it is by Jerome.]—those who flourished throughout the whole world, so that holy imitation, calling you onward, may lead you to the heavenly kingdoms.

Know that crowns are placed not only in the contest of blood or in bodily virginity, but that all who, with God’s help, overcome the vices of their bodies and believe rightly receive the palm of holy reward. But so that, as has been said, you may more easily overcome, with the Lord’s favor, the deadly pleasures and harmful blandishments of the world, and may be, as is read of the blessed, travelers through this age, hasten always to the salutary remedy of the first psalm, so that you may meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night. Then the insolent enemy will find no place when Christ has occupied the whole mind. For Father Jerome also expressed this beautifully, saying (*Letter 4 to Rusticus*):

> Love the reading of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.

Tell me, most prudent men, what is more blessed than to have him favorable whom, when angry, we cannot escape? For if the prefect’s voice is announced by the herald, if we recognize the prefect’s own carriage passing with rattling wheels [Note: [Col. 1148D] The Prefect of the City was conveyed in a carriage. See *Variarum* Book VI, chapter 3], do we not cast away every pleasure of the heart while we fear his appearance and his authority? God thunders through the vaults of heaven, displays lightning in the clouds [Col. 1148B], frequently shakes the foundations of the earth—and, alas, his presence is not feared, though he is known to be wholly and omnipotently present everywhere. Therefore let us not believe the Judge absent, and we shall not come as defendants before his tribunals.

Let the one who sins less give thanks, because he has not been abandoned by the Lord’s mercy so as to plunge headlong into vices. Let the one who has offended greatly entreat him without ceasing; let no one turn to treacherous excuses and deceitful prayers. Let us confess ourselves guilty when we sin outright. Nothing is more foolish than wishing to lie to one who in no way can be deceived. Mercy is ready, if it is sought with a wholly pure mind. There is no worse cause before the gracious Judge than when a subject neglects his own salvation.

[Col. 1148C] Let us therefore pray, dearest brothers, that he who has bestowed such great gifts upon the human race—who deigned to bring back the lost sheep upon his own shoulders and, through the benefit of his incorporation, to break the bonds of sins; who opened the mysteries of faith to the ignorant and estranged, granted baptism, allowed martyrdom, urged the giving of alms, purified us also through the holy instruction of prayer, and commanded us to forgive our brothers’ sins so that he himself likewise might release our debts; who enabled us to convert those who were wandering, so that the bonds of our own error might be loosed; who urged us to seek repentance with the greatest zeal, so that we might possess an abundance of charity toward God and our neighbor—the most merciful Redeemer has also granted communion in his body and blood. Thus [Col. 1148D] the Creator’s mercy may above all be understood, since by such great benefits he has caused us to be absolved, provided that we seek him with a pure heart. May he now add even more to his gifts, illuminate our understanding, and purify our hearts, so that we may be found worthy to know the Holy Scriptures with a wholly pure mind and, with his grace assisting us, fulfill his commandments.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Cassiodorus’s Prayer

Grant, Lord, progress [ed., “profit”] to those who read, and forgiveness of all sins to those who seek your law [Col. 1149A], so that we who desire with great longing to reach the light of your Scriptures may not be obscured by any sins that cast darkness over us. Draw us to yourself by the power of your omnipotence; do not allow those whom you redeemed with your precious blood to wander according to their own will. Do not permit your image within us to be obscured; if it is protected by your favor [ed., “presence”], it is always excellent. Let neither the devil nor ourselves be permitted to overturn your gifts, since everything that strives against you is fragile. Hear us, merciful King, against our sins, and remove them from us before you can justly condemn us because of them in your judgment.

Why does the iniquity within us lie in wait for us? Why do our offenses contend against us? They seek to overthrow your creature, though they possess no stability of substance. Let the devil surely say why he pursues us with insatiable pain. Did we give him the counsel to become proud against you, Lord, and to fall from the blessedness bestowed upon him, when through you he possessed such distinguished signs of power? Let it suffice that he struck us once in Adam. Why does the impious accuser pursue us with daily deceptions? And just as he fell from your grace through his own fault, so he seeks to separate us from that same grace.

Grant, Lord, against the most savage enemy the merciful aid of your protection, so that just as he does not cease to attack our frailty, so, confounded by your strength, he may depart. Do not permit, good King, the most savage enemy who chose gravely to offend you to fulfill his desires against us. Why does he prowl around us like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may strive to devour (1 Peter [Col. 1149C] 5:8)? Once, in holy baptism, we renounced him; once, Lord, we professed our faith in you. Grant that through your protection we may be preserved as you, most high Creator, enabled us to become through the water of regeneration. Since we have begun to belong to you, may we know no other master. We have been redeemed by your grace; with you as giver, may we carry out your commandments.

If you abandon us, that deceiver attacks us; he, unwavering and shameless, is always present, counting his profits in human ruin. He flatters in order to deceive; he incites in order to destroy. Above all, he deceives souls through our bodies, and he spreads himself so fluidly through human desires that he is perceived by scarcely any foresight and by absolutely no deliberation. It would take too long to run through everything. Who could resist such an enemy unless you, Lord, decided to oppose him? For what could he do against us, when he dared to tempt you in our body through deceitful schemes?

Hear us, O guardian [Col. 1150B] of humankind! By your mercy, free us here from him who strives to drag us to Gehenna. May we not share his lot, so that we may share yours, Lord. Vindicate your handiwork from him who destroys it; let him not cause others to be condemned who condemned himself; rather, let him perish with his own followers, since he hastens to destroy everything.

## EPILOGUE

Come now, dearest brothers, hasten to advance in the Holy Scriptures, since you know that, for the abundance of your instruction and with the help of the Lord’s grace, I have gathered together for you such great and such important materials. You who read, now render a return of this work by deigning to entreat the Lord continually for me, since it is written: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16). O immeasurable mercy and power of the Creator, when he promises that it will be useful to all if we pray piously to the Lord for one another!

[Col. 1149]

# M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, ON THE ARTS AND DISCIPLINES OF THE LIBERAL LETTERS (C)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 1149C] The preceding book, completed by the Lord’s favor, contains the *Institution of Divine Readings*; it is known to have been comprised in thirty-three titles. This number is shown to be suited to the Lord’s age, when he bestowed eternal life upon the world dead in sins and granted endless rewards to believers [Col. 1149D]. Now it is time that we should pass through the text of the present book in seven other titles concerning secular learning. This number, nevertheless, revolving continually within itself through successive weeks, extends forever, even to the end of the whole world.

It must plainly be understood that Holy Scripture frequently includes under this number whatever it wishes to be understood as continuous and perpetual. Thus David says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118:164), although elsewhere he confesses: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2). And Solomon says: “Wisdom built her house; she carved out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1). In Exodus also the Lord said to Moses: “You shall make seven lamps and set them upon the lampstand, so that they may shine opposite it” (Exodus 25:37). The Apocalypse likewise mentions this number in various matters (Revelation 1:4, 11, 12) [Col. 1150C]; yet this reckoning leads us toward that eternal time which cannot suffer decay. It is therefore rightly recalled there wherever perpetual time is shown.

Thus the discipline of arithmetic is endowed with dignity, since God, the maker of all things, established his arrangements according to the quantity of number, weight, and measure. As Solomon says: “You have made all things in number, measure, and weight” (Wisdom 11:21). God’s creature is known to have been made according to number, since he himself says in the Gospel: “Even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30). Thus God’s creature was established according to measure, as he himself testifies in the Gospel: “Which of you, by thinking about it, can add one cubit to his stature?” (Matthew 6:27). The prophet Isaiah likewise says [Col. 1151A]: “He measures the heavens with a span and holds the earth enclosed in his hand” (Isaiah 40:12). Again, God’s creature is shown to have been made according to weight, as Solomon says in Proverbs: “He weighed the springs of the waters,” and shortly afterward: “When he established the foundations of the earth, I was with him” (Proverbs 8:28–29).

Therefore, once God’s work had been distinguished, magnificent things were enclosed within a necessary definition, so that, just as we believe that he created all things, we might also learn to some extent how they were made.

From this it is understood that the devil’s evil works are contained neither by weight, nor by measure, nor by number, since whatever iniquity does is always opposed to justice. As the thirteenth Psalm also recalls, saying: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes” (Psalm 13:3). Isaiah likewise says: “They abandoned the God of hosts and walked along crooked paths.” Truly wondrous and supremely wise is God, who distinguished all his creatures by a unique moderation, lest foul confusion possess any of them. Hence Father Augustine argued most minutely in Book IV of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*.

Now let us enter upon the beginnings of the second volume and listen to them somewhat more attentively [Here the manuscripts begin]: “We intend to write briefly for you about the art of grammar, or rhetoric, or some of the disciplines. It is necessary for us to begin with the principles of these matters; and we must first speak about the art of grammar, which is evidently the origin and foundation of the liberal letters.”

A book is called *liber* from *liber*, that is, from the bark of a tree after it has been stripped off and freed [Col. 1151C]; before an abundance of paper, the ancients wrote their poems upon it. We should know, as Varro says, that the beginnings of all the arts arose for the sake of some usefulness.

The word *ars*—“art”—is so called because it binds and constrains us with its rules. Others say that this word was derived from the Greeks, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς, that is, “from the virtue of instruction,” which eloquent men call the knowledge of each good thing.

Second is rhetoric, which, on account of the brilliance and abundance of its eloquence, is considered especially necessary and honorable in civil questions.

Third is logic, which is called dialectic. This, according to what secular teachers say, separates truth from falsehood through exceedingly subtle and concise arguments [Col. 1151D].

Fourth is mathematics, which embraces four disciplines: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy. In Latin we may call mathematics *doctrinal*, “instructional.” Although by this name we can call everything instructional—whatever things these disciplines teach—it has nevertheless claimed this common term for itself in a special way because of its excellence. Thus, when “the Poet” is mentioned, Virgil is understood; when “the Orator” is named, Cicero is meant, although many poets and orators are known to exist in the Latin language. The eloquent Greece likewise celebrates this distinction concerning Homer and Demosthenes.

Mathematics is the science that considers abstract quantity [Col. 1152A]. Quantity is called abstract when, separating it by the intellect from matter or from other accidents, we treat it by reasoning alone. Thus the arrangement of the entire volume has been promised as though by a kind of guide [ed., “path”].

Now let us, with the Lord’s help, render what we have promised through its divisions and definitions, since there is in a certain sense a twofold manner of learning: written description carefully instructs the sight, while what is prepared for the ears enters the hearing. Nor will we be silent about the authorities, both Greek and Latin, through whom the matters we discuss have become clear in exposition, so that the reader who wishes to read diligently, introduced by certain compendia [MSS Reg. and Sang., “appropriate materials”], may more clearly grasp the statements of our predecessors.

# CHAPTER ONE. INSTRUCTION IN THE ART OF GRAMMAR

[Col. 1152B]

Grammar took its name from letters, as the derived sound of the word itself shows. Cadmus is said to have been the first of all to discover only sixteen letters; when he handed them on to the most studious Greeks, they supplied the rest through the liveliness of their intelligence. Helenus and Priscian spoke subtly in the Attic language about their forms and powers. Grammar is the skill of speaking correctly, gathered from illustrious poets and orators [MSS, “authors”]. Its function is to compose diction, both prose and metrical, without fault. The goal of polished speech or writing is to please through unimpeachable skill.

[Col. 1152C] Although authors of earlier times treated the art of grammar in different arrangements and possessed the distinction of honor in their own ages—such as Palaemon, Phocas, Probus, and Censorinus—we nevertheless prefer to bring Donatus forward, since he is especially suited to boys and is considered appropriate for beginners. We have left two commentaries on him, so that what is clear [MS Sanger, “Latin”] in his own work may become clearer through a twofold explanation. We have also found that Saint Augustine wrote some material under the same title, briefly instructing the brothers for the sake of simplicity; we have left it for you to read, so that nothing may seem lacking to the untrained who are being prepared for the heights of such knowledge.

Donatus therefore discusses the following in the second part:

[Col. 1152D] Concerning articulate sound. Concerning the letter. Concerning the syllable. Concerning feet. Concerning accents. Concerning pauses or distinctions. And again, concerning the eight parts of speech. Concerning figures. Concerning etymologies. Concerning orthography.

Articulate sound is struck air, perceptible to hearing, insofar as it lies within itself.

A letter is the smallest part of articulate sound.

A syllable is a combination of letters, or the utterance of a single vowel, capable of measures of time.

[Col. 1153A] A foot is a definite counting of syllables and temporal quantities.

Accent is the skillful pronunciation of the voice, free from fault.

A pause or distinction is a suitable resting-place for measured pronunciation.

The parts of speech are eight: noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, participle, conjunction, preposition, and interjection.

A noun is a part of speech with case, signifying a body or thing either specifically or generally: specifically, as “Rome” and “Tiber”; generally, as “city” and “river.”

A pronoun is a part of speech which, placed in place of a noun, signifies almost the same thing and sometimes takes a person.

A verb is a part of speech with tense and person [Col. 1153B], without case.

An adverb is a part of speech which, added to a verb, explains and completes its meaning, as in “I will now do it” or “I will not do it.”

A participle is a part of speech so called because it shares in part of a noun and in part of a verb. From the noun it receives genders and cases; from the verb, tenses and meanings; from both, numbers and forms.

A conjunction is a part of speech that joins and arranges a sentence.

A preposition is a part of speech which, placed before other parts of speech, either changes, completes, or diminishes their meaning.

An interjection is a part of speech signifying an emotion of the mind through an inarticulate sound.

[Col. 1153C] Figures are transformations of speech or of sentences, introduced for the sake of ornament. Collected by a certain teacher of the art named Sacerdos, they number ninety-eight, although what Donatus placed among faults is included and enclosed within that number. It seems harsh to me also to call faults what are confirmed by the examples of authors and, above all, by the authority of divine law. These figures are common to grammarians and orators, although they are found suitably adapted in both fields.

Something must also be added concerning etymologies and orthography, about which it is certain that others have written. Etymology is either a true or a probable demonstration explaining from what origin words descend.

Orthography is correctness in writing, impaired by no error [Col. 1153D]; it disciplines both the hand and the tongue. Let these brief statements suffice.

Moreover, whoever wishes to know these matters more broadly and fully should read, together with its preface, the book that I prepared through my own diligence: namely, Donatus’s *Art*, into which I inserted one book on Orthography and another on Etymologies, and added a fourth, on the Figures of Sacerdos. Thus the diligent reader may find in one book what he recognizes as assigned to the art of grammar.

But since the statements concerned with the content of the art of grammar are more important, we have taken care to append below, in part, some rules concerning nouns and verbs, which Aristotle alone correctly asserted to be parts of speech.

## ON NOUNS

[Col. 1154A]

The parts of a noun are:

Quality, ποιότης; comparison, σύγκρισις; gender, γένος; number, ἀριθμός; form, σχῆμα; case, πτῶσις.

The parts of a pronoun are:

Quality, gender, number, form, person, [Col. 1154B] and case.

Of nouns ending among us in *-us*, such as *vulgus*, *pelagus*, and *virus*, Lucretius uses *viri*, although it is more correct for the inflection to remain unchanged. The second class consists of those that increase through the oblique cases and end in the letters *-is* in the singular genitive, such as *genus* and *nemus*. Some of these change *u* into *e*, as *olus, oleris* and *ulcus, ulceris*; some into *o*, as *nemus, nemoris* and *pecus, pecoris*. There is uncertainty whether *fenus* and *stercus* change *e* into *o*, since words ending in the syllable *-nus* change *u* into *e*, as in *vulnus*, *scelus*, and *funus*, and we say *funeratos*. The example of *fenus* should not cause difficulty, since it is placed among doubtful genders. Likewise, the ancients said *stercoratos agros*, “manured fields,” not *sterceratos*.

Nouns ending in the letter *s*, when preceded by *n* or *r*, are all of one gender, except those that before the *s* have *r* [Col. 1154C] and sometimes receive *d*, as *socors, socordis*, and sometimes *i*, as *solers, iners*.

In the plural, moreover, except in the genitive and accusative, they are declined alike in all cases. Some end in *-um* in the genitive and *-es* in the accusative, such as *Mars, ars*; some in *-ium*, such as *sapiens* and *patiens*, and for this reason their accusatives end in *-eis*. Most of these nouns are common to all three genders, and in the letter they possess, neuters in the plural nominative also give the genitives of the other genders with which they are common.

Only a few neuter nouns end in the letter *t*, such as *git*, which is indeclinable, and *caput* and *sinciput*. Some, when they say *lac*, “milk,” add *i*, because it makes *lactis*, “of milk.” But Virgil says:

> Milk is not lacking to me, fresh neither in summer nor in winter.

Since no nouns among us end in two mute consonants, the ancients therefore said *lacte* in the nominative.

The letter *x* terminates certain nouns. In all of these, the genitive plural ends in *-ium*; for this reason the accusative ends in *-i* and *-s*. Most, however, have a genitive ending in *-um*, without a preceding *i*, and therefore their accusative ends in *-e* and *-s*; in the remaining forms they agree. For, in the singular, all nominatives and vocatives have a genitive ending in *-is*, a dative in the letter *i*, an ablative ending in *e* or *i*, and an accusative completed and filled out by the addition of *m*. In the plural, however, they end their dative and ablative in the syllable *-bus*.

[Col. 1155A] As for the others, concerning which the ancients disagree, some say *atrocum* and *ferocum*. By what reasoning, then, will all nouns ending in the letter *x* appear to belong to one class? All vowels can precede this letter *x*, as in *capax*, *frutex*, *pernix*, *atrox*, and *redux*. Among these nouns, some have a long vowel in the nominative, some a short one; some agree in the nominative but differ in the oblique cases. Thus *pax* and *rapax*, likewise *rex* and *pumex*, and likewise *nux* and *lux*, vary even in their basic form in relation to *nix* and *nutrix*. Similarly, *nox* and *atrox* agree in their basic form but differ in the oblique cases.

It must also be observed that in declension some of these force the letter *x* into *g*, and others into *c*. Thus *lex* makes *legis*, and *grex* makes *gregis*, as *pix* makes *picis* and *nux* makes *nucis*. In words that are not monosyllables, the letter *x* is invariably changed into *c* in the genitive, as *frutex, fruticis*, and *ferox, ferocis*. But *supellex*, *senex*, and *nix* are declined by a certain privilege contrary to the rule. *Supellex* grows to two syllables, contrary to the rule; *senex* remains disyllabic in the genitive just as in the nominative, although all words ending in *x* increase; and *nix* is changed neither into *c*, like *pix*, nor into *g*, like *rex*, but into a consonantal *u*, which cannot pass into a vowel.

In the plural genitive, however, the singular ablative changes its forms. When it ends in *a* or *o*, it ends in *-rum*; when in shortened *e*, in *-um*; when in lengthened *e*, in *-rum*; when in *i*, in *-um*. The plural dative and ablative ending in *a* become *-is* and *-bus*. These rules are more familiar in the schools; but whenever they end in *-is*, they end in a long syllable; whenever [Col. 1155C] in *-bus*, in a short one. The rules of nouns having been completed, it is fitting next to add the paradigms of the verbs of the first conjugation.

## 561. ON VERBS

The parts of a verb are:

Quality, conjugation, gender, number, form, tense, and person.

The qualities of a verb:

Moods: indicative, ὁριστική; imperative, προστακτική; optative, εὐκτική; subjunctive, ὑποτακτική; infinitive, ἀπαρέμφατος.

The genders of a verb:

Active, ἐνεργητικά; passive, παθητικά; common, κοινά.

Tense, χρόνος:

Present, ἐνεστώς; past, παρεληλυθώς; future, μέλλων [Col. 1156A]; imperfect, παρατάτικος; perfect, παρακείμενος; pluperfect, ὑπερσυντελικός; indefinite, ἀόριστος.

Verbs that end either in the letter *o*, or in *o* preceded by another vowel, have four forms.

Verbs of the shortened second conjugation have twenty forms. Thus all verbs that in the indicative mood, present tense, first person, end in the letter *o* have six forms; these verbal sounds have two forms. Those that end in the letter *o* with no preceding vowel have twelve forms.

Verbs of the lengthened third conjugation that end in the letter *o* in the indicative mood, present tense, first person have five forms. Whatever verbs of whatever conjugation end in the indicative mood, present tense, first person either in *o* with no preceding vowel or in *o* preceded by any other vowel are included in their declension within this number of forms. I shall discuss each of them.

First-conjugation verbs in the indicative mood, present tense, first person end either in the letter *o* with no other vowel preceding it, as *amo*, “I love,” and *canto*, “I sing”; or in *eo*, as *commeo*, “I go back and forth,” and *calceo*, “I shoe”; or in *io*, as *lanio*, “I tear apart,” and *satio*, “I satisfy”; or in *uo*, as *aestuo*, “I boil,” and *continuo*, “I continue.”

First-conjugation verbs in the imperative mood, present tense, end in the lengthened letter *a* in the second person: *amo, ama*; *canto, canta*. In the infinitive mood they end in the syllable *-re*, with the length retained: *ama, amare*; *canta, cantare*. Likewise, first-conjugation verbs in the indicative mood, past tense, completed aspect, with the syllable *-vi* added to the imperative, end with the length retained: *commeo, commea, commeavi*; *lanio, lania, laniavi*; *satio, satia, satiavi*. In the same manner and tense, in the inceptive aspect, with the syllable *-bam* added to the imperative, they end as follows: *commea, commeabam*; *lania, laniabam*; *aestua, aestuabam*. In the first conjugation, in the same manner and tense, in the retrospective aspect, with the syllables *-veram* added to the imperative, the forms end as follows: *commea, commeaveram*; *lania, laniaveram*; *aestua, aestuaveram*. In the first conjugation, in the same manner, in the future tense, with the syllable *-bo* added to the imperative, they end as follows: *commea, commeabo* [Col. 1156D]; *lania, laniabo*; *aestua, aestuabo*.

Those verbs which in the indicative mood, present tense, first person end in the letter *o* with no preceding vowel are expressed in four ways in the indicative mood, past tense, completed and perfect aspect.

The first has a similar rule, as follows. A verb whose first-person indicative present has a vowel in the penultimate position: *amo, ama, amavi, amabam, amaveram, amabo, amare*.

The second changes the final *o* into *i* in the perfect past and shortens the penultimate *e* in the pluperfect: *adjuvo, adjuvi, adjuveram*.

The third has a rule similar to that of the first mode but separates the *a* after removing it: *seco, secavi, secaveram, secabo, secare*. In the completed aspect it makes *secui*, and in the perfect aspect *secueram*.

The fourth is formed by doubling the syllable: *sto, sta, steti, steteram, stabo, stare*. Similar to this is *do, da, dedi, dabam, dederam, dabo, dare*, with the letter *a* shortened contrary to the rule in *dabam*, *dabo*, and *dare*.

Second-conjugation verbs are pronounced as follows: when in the indicative mood, present tense, first person, they end in the letters *-eo*: *video, vides*; *moneo, mones*. Second-conjugation verbs end in the lengthened letter *e* in the second person of the indicative present: *video, vide*; *moneo, mone*. In the infinitive mood, second-conjugation verbs end with the syllable *-re* added to the imperative, with the length retained: *vide, videre*; *mone, monere*. In the indicative mood, past tense, completed and perfect aspect, second-conjugation verbs are declined in seven ways. The first is the one that displays the form of the rule. For this is the form: when a second-conjugation verb in the indicative mood, past tense, perfect, has the syllable *-vi* added to the imperative, with the length retained. The rest are missing in the manuscripts.

# CHAPTER II. ON THE ART OF RHETORIC

The arts are divided into classes. Some are concerned with observation, that is, with the knowledge and assessment of things, such as astrology. Requiring no action, they are satisfied with the understanding of the thing they study; this is called θεωρητική, “theoretical.” Others concern action; their goal is achieved in the action itself, and they leave nothing behind after the act. This is called πρακτική, “practical,” as dancing is. Others concern production; they reach their end in the completion of a work presented to the eyes. We call this ποιητική, “productive,” as painting is.

There are two kinds of discourse: one continuous, called rhetoric; the other concise, called dialectic. Zeno joined them so closely that he said the latter resembled a hand compressed into a fist, and the former a hand spread open.

Nature gave the beginning of speech; observation gave the beginning of art. For human beings, as in medicine, when they saw that some things were healthful and others unhealthful, made an art from observing them.

The ability to speak is perfected by nature, art, and practice. Some add a fourth part, imitation, which we include under art.

There are three things an orator must accomplish: to teach, to move, and to delight. This is a clearer division than that of those who divide the entire work into matters and emotions.

In advising and dissuading, three things must first be considered: what is being deliberated, who the deliberators are, and who is giving advice concerning the matter under deliberation. All deliberation concerns doubtful matters. The parts of advice are the honorable, the useful, and the necessary. Some, such as Quintilian, approve δυνατόν, that is, “the possible.”

## Why the opening speech is called a proem

[Col. 1158A]

The Greeks clearly show that this part comes before entering upon the matter about which one must speak. Either because οἴμη means “song,” and because harpists sing those few things before they begin the formal contest in order to win favor, they called it a *prooemium*, “proem.” Orators likewise marked with the name *proem* what they say beforehand, before beginning their case, in order to win the minds of the judges. Or else, because the Greeks call a road οἶμος, what is placed before entering upon the matter was instituted to be called by this name.

The purpose of a proem is to prepare the hearer so that he may be more receptive to us in the remaining parts. This happens in three ways: if you make him well-disposed, attentive, and teachable. It is necessary to prepare the minds of the judges in the other parts as well, but especially at the beginning [Col. 1158B].

## How the proem differs from the epilogue

Some have thought that past matters are stated in the proem and future matters in the epilogue. Quintilian, however, says that at the beginning the judge’s mercy should be tested more sparingly and modestly, whereas in the epilogue it is permissible to pour out one’s emotions fully, to assume a fictitious speech for the persons involved, to raise the dead, and to bring forward the pledges of the accused—things less customary in proems.

## On narration

Narration is either wholly on our side, wholly on the side of our opponents, or mixed from both. If it is wholly on our side, we should be content with these three aims: that the judge understand, remember, and believe, and consider nothing worthy of criticism.

It should be noted that whenever the outcome of the matter sufficiently reveals what came before, we ought to be content with what enables the rest to be understood. It is better for a narration to have something left over than to lack something; unnecessary things are spoken with weariness, while necessary things are omitted at one’s peril.

When we are going to handle the matter by proof, we shall lightly touch in the narration upon the person, the cause, the place, the time, the instrument, and the occasion. There are often many narrations in a single case. One should not always narrate in the order in which events occurred. Ἐπιδιήγησις, “additional narration,” is used to increase either hatred, pity, or adversity.

The beginning of a narration will be made from the person; if the person is ours, that person should be praised, but if another’s, discredited. The person is presented together with the circumstances belonging to him. The narration ends when the exposition is brought to the point from which a question arises.

## On digressions

An *egressus*, or digression—that is, παρέκβασις—occurs when, after the proposed matter has been briefly interrupted, something is inserted for the sake of pleasure or usefulness. There are many such digressions, which make various excursions throughout the whole case: praise of people and places; descriptions of regions; accounts of certain historical events or even fables.

Indignation, pity, hostility, abuse, excuse, conciliation, refutation of insults, and similar matters, as well as every amplification, diminution, and emotion, and discussions of luxury, avarice, religion, and duties with their supporting arguments, do not appear to be digressions, because they are connected with the case [Col. 1159A].

The Areopagites condemned a boy who was tearing out the eyes of crows. They are thought to have judged nothing other than that this was a sign of a most destructive mind and that, if he grew up, he would bring evil upon many.

## On probabilities

There are three kinds of probabilities.

The first is the strongest, because it happens almost always: for example, that children are loved by their parents.

The second is something like a tendency or expectation: that one who is in good health will reach the next day.

The third is merely not contradictory: that a theft in a house was committed by someone who belonged to the household.

## Where arguments are drawn from

[Col. 1159B] Arguments are drawn from persons, causes, and time. Time has three parts: what precedes, what accompanies, and what follows. If we are prosecuting, our own points must first be confirmed; then those opposed to them must be refuted. If we are responding, we should more often begin with refutation. Eloquence wishes to be rich, splendid, and commanding.

## On the conclusion

The conclusion, which is called the peroration, has a twofold character: it is placed either in the matters themselves or in the emotions arising from them. Repetition and gathering together, which in Greek is called ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, “recapitulation,” and by some Latins *renumeration*, refreshes the listener’s memory and places the entire case before his eyes at once. Thus even if the individual points had been less effective, the mass of them may move him. This must nevertheless be done briefly, touching their main points in passing. It is appropriate when many cases or questions have been inserted; if the matter is brief and simple, it is unnecessary.

## On emotions

There are two kinds of emotion, which the Greeks call ἦθος and πάθος, that is, respectively, something like character and agitated emotion. Πάθος is agitated emotion; ἦθος is mild and composed emotion. The former contains violent movements, the latter gentle ones. Πάθος commands, while ἦθος persuades; the former prevails toward disturbance, the latter toward goodwill. Πάθος is temporary, whereas ἦθος is lasting. Both arise from the same nature, but one is greater and the other lesser: love is πάθος, charity is ἦθος. Πάθος excites; ἦθος calms.

[Col. 1159D] Against opponents, hostility is more effective than abuse, because hostility makes the opponents hated, while abuse makes us hated. There are things which, if they fall from the lips of the unwary, are foolish; when we pretend them, they are thought graceful. A good disputant should be free from the fault of anger, for no emotion is more opposed to reason. Anger usually carries one outside the case, compels one to utter and deserve disgraceful abuse, and sometimes turns one even against the judges themselves. For judgments, words, figures, and stylistic colors are subtler questions, demanding intelligence, care, and practice.

Every conjecture concerns either a matter or a state of mind. [Col. 1160A] Each has three tenses: past, present, and future. Regarding a matter, there are both general and determinate questions—that is, questions not involving persons and questions involving them. A question about a state of mind cannot be raised unless a person is involved; and, when the issue concerns an act, either what was done is called into doubt, or what is being done, or what will be done, and other similar matters.

## On amphibology

The forms of amphibology are innumerable, to such an extent that certain philosophers think that there is no word—or only very few words—that does not signify several kinds of things. For ambiguity arises either in individual words, through homonymy (ὁμωνυμία), or in joined words, through ambiguous construction.

An utterance becomes faulty when a verb is placed between two nouns.

[Col. 1160B] Oppositions, even when they are not contraries but merely unlike, are nevertheless antitheses if they preserve their own form.

A natural question is one that is temporal, as when things that have occurred in the succession of times are narrated. Now let us turn to the divisions and definitions of the art of rhetoric. Since this art is extensive and copious, it has been elaborated by many distinguished writers.

## What rhetoric is

Rhetoric is said to flow from abundant and extended speech. The art of rhetoric, as the teachers of secular literature hand it down, is the science of speaking well in civil questions. An orator, therefore, is a good man skilled in speaking, as has been said, in civil questions. [Col. 1160C] The orator’s duty is to speak appropriately in order to persuade. His end is to persuade by speech, insofar as the circumstances of matters and persons appear to permit in civil questions. Accordingly, we shall now take up certain points briefly, so that, after indicating some of its parts, we may be able to understand almost the entire force and excellence of this art.

According to Fortunatianus, the recent teacher of rhetoric, civil questions are those that can fall within the common conception of the mind—that is, matters that anyone can understand when the question concerns what is just and good. They are divided into a case and a question. A case is a matter containing within itself a controversy set forth in speech, with the intervention of particular persons; a question, however, is a matter containing within itself a controversy set forth in speech without the intervention of particular persons [Note: [Col. 1159D] These are questions such as: whether against this man, whether with this man, whether at this time, whether under this law, whether before this person. Whatever is said in a speech beyond these five parts is a digression [Col. 1160D]. This is παρέκβασις, since one turns aside from the straight path of speaking by inserting any extraneous matter.].

# On the parts of rhetoric

There are five parts of rhetoric:

Invention, Arrangement, Style, Memory, Delivery.

Invention is the devising of true or plausible matters that make a case probable.

[Col. 1161A] Arrangement is the graceful distribution of the matters discovered into an ordered sequence.

Style is the selection of suitable words adapted to the invention.

Memory is the firm apprehension by the mind of matters and words in relation to the invention.

Delivery is the dignified control of voice and body in accordance with the worth of the matters and words.

## On the kinds of cases

There are three principal kinds of rhetorical cases: demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial.

The demonstrative kind occurs when we demonstrate something in which praise and blame are involved—that is, when someone is displayed and recognized through such a description; for example, Psalm 28 and many other passages or psalms, such as: “O Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God,” and what follows.

[Col. 1161C] The judicial kind is that in which the nature of justice and right, and the basis of reward and punishment, is investigated.

The negotiatory kind is that in which what is legally valid according to civil custom and equity is considered.

An absolute case is one that contains within itself the question of right and wrong.

An assumptive case is one that, from itself, supplies nothing firm, but assumes either an external refusal or some form of defense.

Concession occurs when the defendant does not defend what was done, but asks to be forgiven [Note: [Col. 1161D] When everything is conceded to the opponents and the defendant is defended only by humble tears.]—a course which we have found to pertain to penitents (Commentary on the Psalms, cols. 169 and 103 [218 and 258]).

Removal of the charge occurs when the defendant attempts to shift the charge brought against him, and the blame for it, onto another by force and authority.

[Col. 1162A] The deliberative kind is that in which persuasion and dissuasion are involved—that is, what we ought to pursue, what to avoid, what to teach, and what to forbid.

The judicial kind is that in which accusation and defense are involved, or the granting and denial of a reward.

## On the status of cases

“Status” is στάσις in Greek. The statuses of cases are either rational or legal. A status is the matter on which a case rests. It arises from the assertion and rebuttal, or from the constitution of the case.

Some call status constitution, others call it a question, and others call it that which emerges from the question.

The rational statuses, according to the general questions, [Col. 1162B] are four:

Conjecture. Definition. Quality. Transference.

1. The conjectural status occurs when an act alleged by one party is wholly denied by the opponent.

2. The definitive status occurs when we contend that what is alleged is not this particular thing, but establish what it is by applying definitions.

3. Quality occurs when the question is what kind of matter it is; and because the dispute concerns the force and kind of the affair, it is called a general constitution.

[Col. 1162C] A relation of the charge occurs when an act is said to have been lawfully committed because someone had first provoked the injury.

Comparison occurs when it is contended that some other act of another person was honorable or useful, and that it was committed in order that the act under accusation might be carried out.

Purification occurs when the act is indeed admitted, but blame is removed. It has three parts: lack of knowledge, accident, and necessity. Lack of knowledge occurs when the accused denies that he knew something. Accident occurs when it is shown that some force of fortune obstructed the will. Necessity occurs when the defendant says that he committed what he did under the compulsion of some force.

Appeal for mercy occurs when the defendant confesses both that he sinned and that he sinned deliberately, yet asks to be forgiven. This kind can occur only very rarely.

[Col. 1163A] 4. Transference is said to occur when the case depends on the fact that either the person who ought to act does not appear to be the one acting, or that the action is not brought against the person against whom it ought to be brought; or when it is not brought before the persons, at the time, under the law, on the charge, or with the penalty that is required. A constitution is added to transference, since the action appears to require transference and alteration.

There are five legal statuses:

Text and intention—ῥητόν καὶ διάνοια. Conflicting laws. Ambiguity—ἀμφιβολία. Collection, or reasoning—συλλογισμός. Legal definition.

Text and intention occur when the actual words appear to disagree with the writer’s meaning.

[Col. 1163B] The status of conflicting laws occurs when two or more laws appear to disagree with one another.

Ambiguity occurs when what has been written appears to signify two or more things.

Collection, also called reasoning, occurs when something is discovered from what has been written.

A legal definition occurs when the force of a word is investigated, as it were, by a definitive constitution in which that force has been established.

Thus, some have counted both the rational and legal statuses as eighteen. According to Cicero’s Rhetoricians, however, there are nineteen, because he assigned transference principally among the rational statuses. Hence Cicero himself, correcting himself—as was stated above—also applied transference to the legal statuses.

## On controversy

[Col. 1163C]

Every controversy, as Cicero says, is either simple, joined, or based on comparison.

A simple controversy contains one absolute question, in this form: “Shall we declare war on the Corinthians, or not?”

A joined controversy consists of several questions [Note: [Col. 1163D] And if it is joined, one must consider whether it is joined from several questions or from some comparison.], in which several matters are asked, as follows: “Shall Carthage be destroyed, or returned to the Carthaginians, or shall a colony be established there?”

A controversy based on comparison asks which alternative is preferable, or which is most preferable, in this manner: “Should an army be sent against Philip into Macedonia to assist our allies, or should it be retained in Italy, so that our forces against Hannibal may be as large as possible?”

# On the kinds of cases

[Col. 1163D]

There are five kinds of cases:

Honorable, Admirable, Humble, Doubtful, Obscure.

An honorable kind of case is one toward which the listener’s mind immediately inclines without any speech on our part.

An admirable kind is one from which the minds of those who are about to hear have been alienated.

[Col. 1164A] A humble case is one that the listener neglects and does not appear inclined to attend to very closely.

A doubtful case is one in which either the judgment is uncertain, or the case shares both honor and disgrace, so that it produces goodwill as well as offense.

An obscure case is one in which either the listeners are slow, or the case is entangled in matters difficult to understand.

# On the parts of rhetoric

The parts of a rhetorical speech are six:

Exordium, Narrative, Partition, Confirmation, Refutation, [Col. 1164B] Conclusion, or Peroration.

The exordium is a speech that suitably prepares the listener’s mind for the rest of the discourse.

The narrative is an exposition of things done, or represented as done.

The partition, if properly made, renders the whole speech clear and lucid.

The confirmation is the part through which the speech, by argument, adds credibility, authority, and support to our case.

The refutation is the part through which, by argument, the opponents’ confirmation is weakened or overturned.

The conclusion is the ending and determination of the entire speech, [Col. 1164C] where a plaintive appeal to the epilogue is sometimes also employed.

Although Cicero, the outstanding light of Latin eloquence, spread this material abundantly and carefully through various volumes, and appears to have embraced it in two books on the Art of Rhetoric—whose commentaries, composed by Marius Victorinus, I am known to have left for you in my library—

Quintilian too, that outstanding teacher who, after the streams of Tully, uniquely succeeded in fulfilling what he taught, began with the good man skilled in speaking and showed that he must be educated from his earliest years through all the arts and disciplines of noble learning. We have judged that Cicero’s two books on the Art of Rhetoric and Quintilian’s twelve books of the Institutes should be joined together, [Col. 1164D] so that the size of the codex would not grow excessively and so that, whenever either was needed, both might always be readily available.

As for Fortunatianus, the recent teacher who treated this subject subtly and minutely in three volumes, we have perhaps suitably and appropriately reduced him to a small handbook, so that he might remove the reader’s weariness and competently convey what is necessary. Let the lover of brevity read him; for although he did not extend his work over many books, he discussed very many matters with exceptionally acute reasoning. You will find these books collected in a single volume together with his preface.

# On rhetorical argumentation

[Col. 1165]

Rhetorical argumentation is as follows.

[Col. 1165A] 566 Argumentation is so called as if it were speech proceeding from an acute mind.

Argumentation is the speech itself by which we develop a discovered argument in a plausible manner [Note: [Col. 1165D] An argument is an indication of an acute mind which, through probable investigations, establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter, confirming it by examples, as in: “Do not envy evildoers, for they are like grass,” and so forth.].

Induction is a speech by which we obtain the assent of the person with whom the discussion has been undertaken through matters that are not doubtful, whether among philosophers, rhetors, or ordinary speakers.

The proposition of induction is the part that introduces one or several similarities in order to secure assent to the matter.

The inference of induction, also called the assumption, is the part that introduces the matter under dispute, for whose sake the similarities have been employed.

The conclusion of induction either confirms the acceptance of the inference or shows what follows from it.

[Col. 1165B] Reasoning is the speech by which we prove the matter under investigation.

An enthymeme, therefore, is what is translated into Latin as “a conception of the mind,” and what teachers of rhetoric commonly call an imperfect syllogism. For this form of argument consists of two parts: it uses the rule of syllogisms in an abbreviated form to establish what contributes to proof, as in: “If a storm must be avoided, then one must not sail.” Since it is complete when it consists of a proposition and a conclusion alone, this was judged to be more appropriate to rhetors than to dialecticians. We shall speak of dialectical syllogisms in their proper place.

[Col. 1165C] A convincing argument is one that is proved by evident reasoning [manuscript: “proves”], as Cicero did in his speech for Milo: “You therefore sit as avengers of his death, whose life, if you thought it could be restored through you, you would not wish to have restored” [printed edition: “if you could restore it”].

A demonstrative argument is one that compels by a certain demonstration of the matter; thus Cicero in Against Catiline: “Yet this man lives—indeed, he even comes into the Senate.”

[Col. 1166A] A sententious argument is one that presents a general maxim, as in Terence: “Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred.”

An exemplary argument is one that, by comparison with some example, threatens a similar outcome, as Cicero says in the Philippics: “I marvel at you, Antony: you imitate the deeds of those whose ends you do not dread” [M. G.: “do not fear”].

A collective argument occurs when the matters argued are gathered together into one, as Cicero says in his speech for Milo: “The man whom he did not wish to have favored by gratitude, whom he did wish to have favored by someone’s complaint, whom he did not dare to kill under lawful conditions, in a lawful place, and at a lawful time—this man he did not hesitate to kill unjustly, at an improper time, and at the risk of his own life.”

[Col. 1166B] Moreover, according to Victorinus, there is another definition of the enthymeme. An enthymeme is constituted from the proposition alone, as has already been said, as in: “If a storm must be avoided, sailing must not be undertaken.” From the assumption alone, as in: “There are also those who say that the world proceeds without divine administration.” From the conclusion alone, as in: “Therefore the divine judgment is true” [manuscript: “the divine knowledge is true”]. From the proposition and assumption, as in: “If he is an enemy, he kills. But he is an enemy”; and because the conclusion is lacking, it is called an enthymeme. The epicheireme follows.

An epicheireme is, as we said above, a broader digression descending from reasoning, a rhetorical syllogism differing from dialectical syllogisms in breadth and in the extended development of speech; for this reason it is assigned to rhetors.

A three-part epicheirematic syllogism is one consisting of three members: proposition, assumption, and [Col. 1165C] conclusion.

A four-part syllogism consists of four members: proposition, assumption, a proof joined to either the proposition or the assumption, and conclusion.

A five-part syllogism consists of five members: proposition, its proof, assumption, its proof, and [Col. 1167A] conclusion. Cicero constructs one in this way in the Art of Rhetoric: “If deliberative and demonstrative are kinds of cases, they cannot properly be regarded as parts of some kind of case. For the same thing may be a genus for one person and a part for another; it cannot be both genus and part,” and so forth, until the members of this syllogism are complete. But let the reader see how much he can exercise his own ingenuity in the other parts.

The aforementioned Fortunatianus, in his third book, also discusses the orator’s memory, delivery, and voice. A monk nevertheless departs from him with some benefit when he seems not improperly to draw into his own concerns what Fortunatianus usefully adapted for the practice of controversies. He will preserve the memory of divine reading with studied care when he has come to know its force and quality in the aforesaid [Col. 1167B] book; he will conceive the art of delivery in the utterance of divine law; and he will maintain careful attention to the voice in the chanting of psalmody. Thus instructed, he is made fit for holy work, even though he is occupied with secular books.

Now let us proceed in the following order to logic, which is also called dialectic. Some have preferred to call it a discipline, others an art, saying that when it discusses something through apodictic—that is, probable—arguments, it ought to be called a discipline; but when it treats something plausible, as in sophistic syllogisms, it should receive the name of art. Thus it deserves either term according to the character of its argumentation.

# CHAPTER III. ON DIALECTIC

[Col. 1167C] The earliest philosophers possessed dialectic in the arguments of their [Col. 1168A] discourses, but they did not reduce it to the expertise of an art. After them, Aristotle, as a diligent investigator of all disciplines, brought the arguments of this teaching under certain rules, which previously had not been governed by definite precepts. By composing carefully worked-out books, he adorned the school of the Greeks with manifold praise; and since our people could no longer tolerate him as a foreigner, they translated and interpreted him and brought him into Roman eloquence. Varro, in the nine books of the Disciplines, defined dialectic and rhetoric through the following comparison: “Dialectic and rhetoric are like the clenched fist and the open palm in a human hand: the former concludes arguments in brief speech, while the latter ranges over the fields of eloquence in expansive discourse; the former contracts words, the latter extends them.”

[Col. 1168B] Dialectic is sharper for discussing matters, while rhetoric is more fluent for teaching what it undertakes to teach. The former sometimes enters the schools, while the latter continually proceeds into the forum; the former seeks very few students, while the latter seeks large crowds [manuscripts: *frequenter*, “frequently”]. But before we speak of syllogisms, where the usefulness and power of the whole of dialectic are displayed, we must discuss a little about its beginnings, as about certain elementary principles, so that, just as the order distinguished by our predecessors is set out, so also the intention of our arrangement may proceed. It is customary for teachers of philosophy, before they come to explain the Isagoge, to touch briefly upon the division of philosophy. Following that practice, we too rightly believe that it should be presented at the present time.

## The division of philosophy

[Col. 1167D] “Philosophy is assimilation to God, insofar as this is possible for a human being” (Φιλόσοφία ὁμοίωσις Θεῷ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἀνθρώπῳ). Philosophy is the probable knowledge of divine and human matters, insofar as this is possible for a human being. Alternatively, philosophy is the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines. Again, philosophy is meditation on death. This is especially fitting for Christians, who, having trampled upon worldly ambition, live through disciplined conduct in the likeness of their future homeland, as the Apostle says: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 10:3); and elsewhere: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Philosophy is assimilation to God insofar as this is possible for a human being.

[Col. 1168C] The contemplative branch is so called because, having risen above visible things, we contemplate something divine and heavenly, and behold it with the mind alone, insofar as such things surpass bodily perception. The natural branch is so called when the nature of each individual thing is investigated, because nothing is generated contrary to [Col. 1168D] nature in life; rather, each thing is assigned to the uses for which it was produced by the Creator, unless perhaps a miracle is shown to occur by the divine will. The doctrinal branch is the science that considers [manuscripts: “signifies”] abstract quantity. Abstract quantity is that which, separating it by the intellect from matter or from other accidents, we treat in reasoning alone—for example, even and odd, or other things of this kind. The divine branch is so called when we discuss, in some measure and with profound insight, either the ineffable divine nature or spiritual creatures.
