Arithmetic is the discipline of quantity that is numerable in itself. Music is the discipline that speaks of numbers that stand in relation to those found in sounds. Geometry is the discipline of immovable magnitude [Col. 1169A] and of forms. Astronomy is the discipline that contemplates all the courses of the heavenly bodies and the figures of the stars, and investigates, by a searching method, the positions of the stars in relation to one another and to the earth. The practical branch is so called because it seeks to explain proposed matters through their operations. The moral branch is so called because through it an honorable way of life is pursued and institutions directed toward virtue are prepared. The dispensative branch is the wisely ordered arrangement of household matters. The civil branch is that through which the welfare of the entire state is administered. Having treated the divisions and definitions of philosophy, in which everything is contained in general, let us now approach Porphyry’s book entitled the Isagoge.

## On Porphyry’s Isagoge

[Col. 1169B]

Porphyry’s Isagoge treats of genus, γένος; species, εἶδος; difference, διαφορά; property, ἴδιον; and accident, συμβεβηκός.

A genus is that which pertains to species and is predicated of things differing in species with respect to what they are, as “animal.” For the genus “animal” is predicated and signified of each individual species—of human being, horse, ox, and the rest.

A species is that which is predicated of several things differing in number with respect to what they are; for “human being” is predicated of Socrates, Plato, and Cicero.

[Col. 1169C] A difference is that which is predicated of several things differing in species with respect to what they are like; thus “rational” and “mortal” are predicated of human being with respect to what it is like.

568 A property is that by which each species or person is distinguished through a definite addition and separated from every commonality.

An accident is that which occurs and departs without destroying its subject, or those things that occur in such a way that they do not entirely depart. Those who desire to know these matters more fully should read Porphyry’s Introduction. Although he says that he is writing it for the benefit of someone else’s work [printed edition: “of some work”], he nevertheless appears to have formulated such statements not without personal distinction.

## Aristotle’s Categories

[Col. 1169D] Aristotle’s Categories, or Predicaments, follow. Through their various significations, all speech is enclosed in a remarkable manner. Their instruments or tools are three.

The tools or instruments of the Categories or Predicaments are equivocal, univocal, and denominative terms.

Equivocal terms are those whose name alone is common, while, according to the name, the account of the substance is different; for example, “animal,” “a human being,” and “what is painted.”

Univocal terms are those whose name is common and for which the account of the substance is not shown to differ according to the name; for example, “animal,” “a human being,” and “an ox.”

Denominative, that is, derivative, terms are those that receive their designation from something else with only a difference of case in the name [Col. 1170A], as “grammatical” from “grammar,” and “strong” from “strength.”

Aristotle’s Categories or Predicaments are ten:

Substance, οὐσία. Quantity, ποσότης. Relation, πρὸς τί. Quality, ποιότης. Doing, ποιεῖν. Being acted upon, πάσχειν. Position, κεῖσθαι. When, πότε. Where, ποῦ. Having, ἔχειν.

Substance is what is properly, principally, and most fully called substance: it is neither predicated of a subject nor present in a subject, as some particular human being or some particular horse. Secondary substances, however, are those species in which the things principally called primary substances are contained and enclosed, as Cicero is contained in “human being.”

Quantity is either discrete and has parts separated from one another, not communicating according to some common boundary, as a number and spoken discourse; or it is continuous and has parts that meet one another according to some common boundary, as a line, surface, body, place, motion, and time.

Relations are whatever, by the very fact that they are what they are, are said to belong to something else, such as greater, double, possession, disposition, knowledge, sensation, and position.

Quality is that according to which we are called qualified in some way, as good or bad.

Doing is such things as cutting or burning—that is, performing some action. Being acted upon is such things as being cut or burned.

Position is such things as standing, sitting, or lying down. When is such things as yesterday or tomorrow.

Where is such things as in Asia, in Europe, or in Libya. Having is such things as being shod or being armed.

This work of Aristotle must be read attentively, since, as has been said, whatever a human being says inevitably falls among these ten Predicaments. It also contributes to understanding books that are associated either with rhetors or with dialecticians.

## Here begins the Perihermenias, that is, On Interpretation

[Col. 1170D] The exceedingly subtle book Perihermenias follows. It is extremely careful through its various forms and repetitions. Of it was said: “When Aristotle was writing the book Perihermenias, he dipped his pen in his mind.”

In the book Perihermenias, that is, On Interpretation, the aforementioned philosopher treats the following subjects:

The noun, the verb, speech, enunciation, affirmation, negation, and contradiction.

A noun is a significant utterance according to convention, without time; none of its parts is significant when separated, as “Socrates.”

[Col. 1171A] A verb is that which co-signifies time, whose part signifies nothing independently, and which is always a sign of things predicated of something else, as “he thinks” and “he debates.”

Speech is a significant utterance, of whose parts one is significant separately, as “Socrates debates.”

An enunciative speech is a significant utterance concerning something that is or is not, as “Socrates is,” “Socrates is not.”

An affirmation is an enunciation of something concerning something, as “Socrates is.”

A negation is a denial of something concerning something, as “Socrates is not.”

A contradiction is the opposition of an affirmation and a negation, as “Socrates debates,” “Socrates does not debate.”

[Col. 1171B] All these matters are treated and subdivided in the greatest detail throughout the book mentioned above. It is enough for us to have indicated them briefly, since a suitable explanation is found in that work itself—especially because it is known to have been expounded in six books by Boethius, a magnificent man, whose work has been left to you among the other books.

Now let us turn to the species and formulas of syllogisms, in which the minds of noble philosophers are continually exercised.

## On the formulas of syllogisms

There are three formulas of categorical, that is, predicative, syllogisms:

The first formula has nine modes. The second formula has four modes. [Col. 1171C] The third formula has six modes.

The modes of the first formula are nine.

The first mode concludes—that is, gathers from universal affirmative propositions a direct universal affirmative conclusion—as follows: “Everything just is honorable; everything honorable is good; therefore everything just is good.”

569 The second mode conducts [printed edition: “concludes”] from universal affirmative and negative propositions a direct universal negative conclusion: “Everything just is honorable; nothing honorable is base; therefore nothing just is base.”

The third mode concludes from particular and universal affirmative propositions a direct particular affirmative conclusion: “Some just thing is honorable; everything honorable is useful; therefore some just thing is useful.”

[Col. 1171D] The fourth mode concludes from a particular affirmative and a universal negative proposition a direct particular negative conclusion: “Some just thing is honorable; nothing honorable is base; therefore some just thing is not base.”

The fifth mode concludes from universal affirmative propositions a particular affirmative conclusion by conversion: “Everything just is honorable; everything honorable is good; therefore some good thing is just.”

The sixth mode concludes from a universal affirmative and a universal negative proposition a universal negative conclusion by conversion: “Everything just is honorable; nothing honorable is base; therefore nothing base is just.”

[Col. 1172A] The seventh mode concludes from a particular and a universal affirmative proposition a particular affirmative conclusion by conversion: “Some just thing is honorable; everything honorable is useful; therefore some useful thing is just.”

The eighth mode concludes from universal negative and affirmative propositions a particular negative conclusion by conversion: “Nothing base is honorable; everything honorable is just; therefore some just thing is not base.”

The ninth mode concludes from a universal negative and a particular affirmative proposition a particular negative conclusion by conversion: “Nothing base is honorable; some honorable thing is just; therefore some just thing is not base.”

The modes of the second formula are four.

[Col. 1172B] The first mode concludes from universal affirmative and negative propositions a direct universal negative conclusion: “Everything just is honorable; nothing base is honorable; therefore nothing just is base.”

The second mode concludes from universal negative and affirmative propositions a direct universal negative conclusion: “Nothing base is honorable; everything just is honorable; therefore nothing base is just.”

The third mode concludes from a particular affirmative and a universal negative proposition a direct particular negative conclusion: “Some just thing is honorable; nothing base is honorable; therefore some just thing is not base.”

The fourth mode concludes from a particular negative and a universal affirmative proposition a direct particular negative conclusion [Col. 1172C]: “Some just thing is not base; everything evil is base; therefore some just thing is not evil.”

The modes of the third formula are six.

The first mode concludes from universal affirmative propositions a particular affirmative conclusion, both direct and converted: “Everything just is honorable; everything just is good; therefore some honorable thing is good,” or “some good thing is honorable.”

The second mode concludes from particular and universal affirmative propositions a direct particular affirmative conclusion: “Some just thing is honorable; everything just is good; therefore some honorable thing is good.”

The third mode concludes from universal and particular affirmative propositions a direct particular affirmative conclusion [Col. 1172D]: “Everything just is honorable; some just thing is good; therefore some honorable thing is good.”

The fourth mode concludes from universal affirmative and negative propositions a direct particular negative conclusion: “Everything just is honorable; nothing just is evil; therefore some honorable thing is not evil.”

The fifth mode concludes from a particular affirmative and a universal negative proposition a direct particular negative conclusion: “Some just thing is honorable; everything honorable is good; therefore some honorable thing is not evil.”

The sixth mode concludes from a universal affirmative and a particular negative proposition a direct particular negative conclusion: “Everything just is honorable; some just thing is not evil; therefore some honorable thing is not evil.”

[Col. 1173A] Anyone who desires to know these formulas of categorical syllogisms fully should read the book of Apuleius entitled Perihermenias and will learn what is treated there more subtly. Nor should we be wearied by the repetition of words; for, when distinguished and considered, they will, by the Lord’s favor, usefully lead us into the great paths of understanding. Now let us proceed in due order to hypothetical syllogisms.

There are seven modes of hypothetical syllogisms formed with some conjunction.

The first mode is as follows: “If it is day, it is light; but it is day; therefore it is light.”

The second mode is as follows: “If it is day, it is light; it is not light; therefore it is not day.”

The third mode is as follows: “It is not both day and not light; but it is day; therefore it is light.”

The fourth mode is as follows: “It is either night or day; but it is day; therefore it is not night.”

The fifth mode is as follows: “It is either day or night; but it is not night; therefore it is day.”

The sixth mode is as follows: “It is not both day and not light; but it is day; therefore it is not night.”

The seventh mode is as follows: “It is not both day and night; but it is not night; therefore it is day.”

Anyone who desires to know the modes of hypothetical syllogisms more fully should read Marius Victorinus’ book entitled On Hypothetical Syllogisms. It should also be known that Tullius Marcellus of Carthage [Col. 1173C] treated categorical and hypothetical syllogisms—subjects discussed at great length by various philosophers—in seven books, briefly yet subtly. In the first book he discussed, as he himself says, the rule of the collections of dialectical art; what Aristotle had published in many books concerning categorical syllogisms was briefly completed by him in the second and third books; and what the Stoics had treated in countless volumes concerning hypothetical syllogisms was collected by him in the fourth and fifth books. In the sixth he discussed mixed syllogisms, and in the seventh composite syllogisms. I have left this book for you to read.

570 ## On definitions

[Col. 1173D] From here let us approach the most beautiful kinds of definitions. They excel with such dignity that they may be called the greatest ornament of speeches and, as it were, the lights of discourse.

A definition is a speech that encloses the nature of each thing, separated from what it shares with others, through its proper signification. It is formed in many ways and according to many precepts.

The first kind of definition is οὐσιώδης, in Latin substantialis, “substantial.” This is properly and truly called a definition, as in: “A human being is a rational, mortal animal capable of understanding and learning.” For this definition, descending through species and differences, arrives at what is proper and indicates most fully what a human being is.

The second species of definition is called in Greek *ἐννοηματική* (*ennoēmatikē*), and in Latin is termed “notion”: this notion we may call by a common, rather than a proper, name. It is always formed in the following way: “Man is the animal that, through rational conception and exercise, presides over all animals.” For he did not say what man is, but what he does, as though something had been marked out by a sign for recognition. In this and in the remaining cases, the notion of the thing is brought forward—not a substantial definition, as is made clear in that primary explanation; and because that one is substantial, it holds the chief place among all definitions.

The third species of definition is called in Greek *ποιότης* (*poiotēs*), and in Latin “qualitative.” By saying what sort of thing something is, it clearly shows what it is. Its example is as follows: “Man is one who possesses talent, excels in the arts, and has knowledge of things; he either chooses what he ought to do, or, by careful judgment, rejects what is useless.” Through these and similar qualities man is expressed and defined.

[Col. 1174B] The fourth species of definition is called in Greek *ὑπογραφική* (*hypographikē*), and in Latin “descriptive.” By employing a circumstantial account of words and deeds, it declares what a thing is by description. Thus, if we wish to define a pleasure-seeker, we say: “A pleasure-seeker is one who desires unnecessary, costly, and burdensome nourishment, abounds in luxury, and is ready for lust.” These and similar statements define a pleasure-seeker. This species of definition is more suitable for orators than for dialecticians, because it has breadth; it is employed in the same way for good things and for bad.

The fifth species of definition is what we call in Greek *κατὰ λέξιν*, and in Latin “word for word.” It designates the word being sought by another expression, in a single and particular term; and, in a certain way, it declares in one different word what that thing is that has been placed in one word. Thus, “to fall silent” (*conticescere*) means “to be silent”; likewise, when we say that a *terminus* is a “boundary,” or interpret “lands laid waste” as “lands devastated.”

The sixth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ τὴν διάφοραν*, “by difference.” This is when, for example, it is asked what difference there is between a king and a tyrant, and, by adding the difference, each is defined according to what he is: that is, “A king is moderate and temperate, whereas a tyrant is impious and harsh.”

The seventh species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ μετάφοραν*, and the Latins call “by translation” or metaphor. Thus Cicero says in the *Topics*: “A shore is where the wave plays.” This can be handled in various ways: sometimes so as to move the hearer, as in “the head is the citadel of the body”; sometimes to censure, as in “wealth is a long journey-ration for a short life”; [Col. 1174D] sometimes to praise, as in “youth is the flower of life.”

The eighth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατ’ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου*, and the Latins call “by privation of the contrary to what is being defined.” They say, for example: “Good is what is not evil”; “Just is what is not unjust”; and similar statements. This kind of definition is naturally so connected that it joins necessary knowledge to itself in a single comprehension. We should use this type of definition when the contrary is known, for no one proves what is certain from what is uncertain.

The following definitions belong to this species: “Substance is what is neither quality nor quantity nor any accident.” By this type of definition God can be defined. For since we are wholly unable to comprehend what God is, the removal of all existing things—which the Greeks call *ὄντα* (*onta*, “beings”)—circumscribes and removes from our knowledge the cognition of known things, and thereby supplies us with a knowledge of God. Thus we may say: “God is what is neither body, nor any element, nor animal, nor mind, nor sense, nor intellect, nor anything that can be apprehended from these.” When these and similar things have been removed, what God is cannot be defined.

The ninth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ τύπωσιν*, and the Latins call “by a certain imagining.” Thus: “Aeneas is the son of Venus and Anchises.” This always concerns individuals, whom the Greeks call *ἄτομα* (*atoma*). The same occurs in that kind of expression in which there is some shame or fear about naming someone, as in Cicero: “When, obviously, those assassins describe me in this way.”

[Col. 1175B] The tenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *ὡς τύπῳ*, and the Latins call “as it were.” If it is asked what an animal is, one may answer, “A man.” For it is not plainly said that an animal is only a man, since there are countless other animals; but by saying “man,” one designates man as an animal, as it were, although many things fall under the name “animal.” The example given has declared the thing being sought. It is, indeed, the proper function of a definition to declare what the thing being sought is.

The eleventh species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ τὴν ἔλλειψιν*, and the Latins call “by deficiency of the full [amount] from the same genus.” Thus, if it is asked what a *triens* is, the answer is: “That which a *dodrans* lacks in order to be a whole *as*.”

The twelfth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ ἔπαινον*, and the Latins call “by praise.” Thus Tullius says in his speech for Cluentius: “The law is the mind, spirit, counsel, and judgment of the state.” Likewise: “Peace is tranquil liberty.” It can also be made by blame, which the Greeks call *ψόγος* (*psogos*): “Slavery is the worst of all evils, to be repelled not only by war but even by death.”

The thirteenth species is what the Greeks call *κατ’ ἀναλογίαν*, and the Latins call “according to proportion.” This occurs when an inferior thing is defined by the name of a greater thing, as in the statement: “Man is a lesser world.” Cicero used this definition as follows: “They call an edict an annual law.”

The fourteenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *πρός τι*, and the Latins call “relative to something.” Thus: “A father is one who has a son”; “A master is one who has a slave.” Cicero says in the *Rhetorics*: “A genus is that which embraces several parts”; likewise, “A part is that which lies beneath a genus.”

The fifteenth species of definition is what the Greeks call *κατὰ αἰτιολογίαν*, and the Latins call “according to the rationale of the thing”: “Day is the sun above the earth”; “Night is the sun beneath the earth.”

We should understand that the foregoing species of definition have rightly been associated with the topics, since they have been placed among certain arguments and are recalled in some passages of the *Topics*. Let us now come to the topics, which are the seats of arguments, the sources of meanings, and the origins of expressions. Something must be said about them briefly, so that we may recognize both dialectical and rhetorical topics, or the differences between them; and first we must speak about the dialectical topics.

## On Dialectical Topics

[Col. 1176A]

A proposition is an expression signifying what is true or false, as when someone says that the sky is revolving. This is also called an enunciation or utterance. A question, on the other hand, is a proposition brought into doubt and uncertainty, as when someone asks whether the sky is revolving. A conclusion is a proposition approved by arguments, as when someone proves from other matters that the sky is revolving. An enunciation, whether it is stated merely for its own sake or is brought forward to others for proof, is a proposition; when it is questioned, it is a question; when it has been approved, it is a conclusion. Thus proposition, question, and conclusion are the same thing, but they differ in their manner.

An argument is an expression that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter. Argument, however, is not the same as argumentation. [Col. 1176B] The force and reasoning of the judgment enclosed in an expression, when something doubtful is proved, is called an argument; the actual verbal expression of the argument is called argumentation. Thus an argument is the mind and judgment of an argumentation, whereas argumentation is the explanation of an argument through language.

A topic, however, is the seat of an argument, or the source from which a suitable argument is drawn for the question proposed. Since this is so, the nature of each matter must be treated more carefully, and their division must be made according to species, parts, and forms.

First, then, we must discuss the proposition. We have said that it is an expression containing truth or falsehood. It has two species: affirmation and negation. It is an affirmation if someone says, “The sky is revolving”; a negation if someone declares, “The sky is not revolving.” Of these, some are universal, some particular, some indefinite, and some singular.

Universal propositions are such as: “Every man is just”; “No man is just.” Particular propositions are such as: “A certain man is just”; “A certain man is not just.” Indefinite propositions are: “Man is just”; “Man is not just.” Singular propositions are those that propose something concerning an individual and singular person, as: “Cato is just”; “Cato is not just.” For Cato is an individual and singular person.

Some of these we call predicative, others conditional. Predicative propositions are those proposed simply, that is, those to which no force of condition is attached, as when someone simply says that the sky is revolving. [Col. 1176D] But if a condition is joined to this, one proposition becomes conditional from two, as follows: “If the sky is round, it is revolving.” Here the condition makes it understood that the sky is revolving only if it is round.

Since some propositions are therefore predicative and others conditional, we call the parts of predicative propositions their terms. These are the predicate and the subject. By “terms” I mean the words and names by which a proposition is joined together. Thus, in the proposition “Man is just,” these two names—“man” and “just”—are called the parts of the proposition. We also call them terms, one of which is the subject and the other the predicate.

The subject is the term that is lesser, while the predicate is the greater: in the proposition “Man is just,” “man” is less than “just.” For justice can exist not only in man but also in bodily and divine substances. Therefore “just” is the greater term and “man” the lesser; consequently “man” is the subject term, while “just” is the predicate.

Since such simple propositions have one term as predicate and another as subject, the proposition has been called predicative from the privilege of its greater part. It often happens, however, that these terms are found to be equal to one another, as in “Man is capable of laughter”; for “man” and “capable of laughter” are each an equal term in relation to the other. For neither does the capacity for laughter extend beyond man, nor does man extend beyond the capacity for laughter.

In these matters the following necessarily occurs: if the terms are unequal, the greater is always predicated of the subject; but if both are equal, they are predicated of one another with the predication reversed. It never occurs in any proposition that the lesser is predicated of the greater.

It can also happen that the parts of propositions, which we call terms, are found not only in names but also in expressions. For often an expression is predicated of an expression, as follows: “Socrates discusses the nature of philosophy with Plato and his pupils.” The expression “Socrates with Plato and his pupils” is the subject, whereas “discusses the nature of philosophy” is predicated.

Again, sometimes a name is the subject and an expression the predicate, as follows: “Socrates discusses the nature of philosophy.” Here “Socrates” alone is the subject, while the expression “discusses the nature of philosophy” is predicated.

It also happens that an expression is placed as subject and a simple word is predicated, as follows: “Likeness to the higher and divine substances is justice.” Here the expression by which “likeness to the higher and divine substances” is expressed is made subject, while “justice” is predicated. But we have discussed such propositions more carefully in the commentaries that we wrote on Aristotle’s books of the *Peri Hermeneias*.

An argument is an expression that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter; it must always be more familiar than the question. For if unknown things are proved to us, while an argument proves a doubtful matter, what is brought forward to establish the credibility of the question must itself be more known than the question.

Of all arguments, some are probable and necessary; others probable but not necessary; others necessary but not probable; and others neither probable nor necessary.

That is probable which appears so either to everyone, to most people, or to the wise—whether to all of them, to most of them, or especially to those who are best known and most distinguished—or to each expert according to his own field: for example, in medicine to a physician, and concerning the piloting of ships to a helmsman. Also probable is what appears so to the person with whom the discussion is being conducted, or to the person who is judging. In such a case it does not matter whether the argument is true or false, provided that it possesses merely the appearance of truth.

That is necessary which, once stated, is so and cannot be otherwise. It is both probable and necessary, for example: “If something is added to any thing, the whole becomes greater.” No one will dissent from this proposition, and it is necessary that matters stand so.

Probable but not necessary are those propositions with which the mind readily agrees, but which do not possess the firmness of truth, such as: “If she is a mother, she loves.” Necessary but not probable are propositions that must be true as stated, but to which the hearer does not readily consent, such as: “An eclipse of the sun occurs because the lunar body is interposed.”

Neither necessary nor probable are propositions that rest neither on human opinion nor on truth, such as: “Diogenes has horns that he has not lost, since everyone has whatever he has not lost.” Such things cannot even be called arguments, for arguments establish the credibility of a doubtful matter. There is no credibility in what is grounded neither in opinion nor in truth.

[Col. 1178B] It may nevertheless be said that those things too are not arguments which, although necessary, are not at all approved by their hearers. For if credibility is established for a doubtful matter, the hearer’s mind must be compelled, through things to which he himself assents, to approach a conclusion that he has not yet approved. If, then, someone who is judging does not approve things that are merely necessary and not probable, he necessarily will not approve what is produced from such reasoning. Thus it follows from this kind of reasoning that things which are merely necessary and not probable are not arguments.

But this is not so, and this interpretation does not properly understand probability. Things are probable when assent is attached to them spontaneously and freely—that is, when they are approved as soon as they are heard.

[Col. 1178C] Things that are necessary but not probable are first demonstrated through other probable and necessary arguments; once they have been learned and believed, they are brought forward to establish the credibility of another matter about which there is doubt. Such are the speculations, that is, the theorems, considered in geometry. For the propositions put forward there are not of such a nature that the learner’s mind spontaneously assents to them. But since they are demonstrated by other arguments, once they too have been learned and understood, they are brought forward as arguments for other speculations.

Thus they are not probable. Yet, for hearers to whom they have not been demonstrated, they cannot serve as arguments for proving something else, since they are necessary but not probable. Those, however, who have begun to believe them through earlier reasoning—reasoning to which they previously did not assent—can call propositions that admit no doubt arguments.

Since the whole art of reasoning is contained in four disciplines, we must say which of them knows how to use which arguments, so that it may clearly appear to which discipline the abundance of topics and arguments chiefly belongs.

Every method of reasoning is therefore subject to four disciplines and, as it were, their practitioners: the dialectician, the orator, the philosopher, and the sophist. The dialectician and the orator deal with the common material of arguments; for both pursue probable arguments, whether necessary or not. These two disciplines are therefore served by the two kinds of argument that are probable and necessary, and probable but not necessary.

The philosopher and demonstrator, however, deal solely with truth. Therefore it makes no difference whether arguments are probable or not, provided that they are necessary. This discipline likewise uses two species of argument: probable and necessary, and necessary but not probable.

It is therefore clear how the philosopher differs, in his proper inquiry, from the orator and dialectician: in the case of the latter, probability is the object proposed; in the case of the former, truth.

The fourth species of argument, which we showed above could not properly even be called an argument, is assigned solely to sophists. The purpose of the *Topics* is to demonstrate an abundance of arguments that resemble the truth; for once the topics from which probable arguments are drawn have been identified, the material for discussion necessarily becomes abundant and plentiful.

But since, as was said above, some probable arguments are necessary and others not necessary, when the topics of probable arguments are discussed, it follows that necessary arguments are taught as well. Consequently, this discipline is provided principally for orators and dialecticians, and secondarily for philosophers. Wherever all probable arguments are gathered, dialecticians and orators are assisted; wherever probable and necessary arguments are taught, abundance is supplied for philosophical demonstration.

Thus not only the dialectician and orator but also the demonstrator, the producer of genuine argumentation, has something that he can take from the topics proposed, since the tradition of the principles of necessary arguments is mingled with the topics of probable arguments.

Those arguments, however, which are necessary but not probable—and that final genus, namely, what is neither probable nor necessary—are excluded from the consideration of the work undertaken here, except that certain sophistical topics are sometimes introduced for the sake of exercising the reader.

Accordingly, the usefulness and purpose of the *Topics* have been equally disclosed. Through them both the power of speaking and the investigation of truth are increased.

For what benefit does knowledge of the topics provide to dialecticians and orators? It gives their speech abundance through discovery. What does the teaching of the topics of necessary arguments transmit to philosophers? It illuminates, in a certain way, the path of truth.

For this reason the discipline must be investigated and examined further: once it has been grasped through knowledge, it must be strengthened through use and practice. The consideration of topics promises something great, namely, paths of discovery. Those who lack this method attribute such matters entirely to natural talent and do not understand how much is sought through this inquiry, which reduces the power and capacity of nature to an art. But enough of this; let us now explain the remaining matters.

## On Syllogisms

Some syllogisms are predicative, which are called categorical; others are conditional, which we call hypothetical. Predicative syllogisms are those formed from entirely predicative propositions, such as the one I noted above by way of example, for it is woven entirely from predicative propositions.

Hypothetical syllogisms are those whose propositions rest upon a condition, as in this example: “If it is day, there is light; but it is day; therefore there is light.” The first proposition contains this condition: that there is light only if it is day. Therefore this syllogism is called hypothetical, that is, conditional.

Induction is an expression by which a progression is made from particulars to the universal, as follows: “If, in steering ships, the helmsman is chosen not by lot but by skill; if, in driving horses, the charioteer is appointed not by the outcome of chance but by the recommendation of skill; if, in administering the state, chance does not make the ruler, but expertise in governing does; and similarly in many matters, to which it is assigned [ed.: “are inferred”]; and in every matter that someone wishes to be competently governed and administered, the ruler is not assigned by lot but by skill.”

You see, then, how the expression proceeds through individual cases in order to reach the universal. For when it had gathered the examples that a ship, a carriage, and a state are governed not by lot but by skill, it concluded, as though the same were true in other cases as well, that in every matter the foremost person should be appointed not by lot but by skill.

Often, however, an accumulation of many particulars demonstrates another particular, as when someone says: “If neither ships, nor carriages, nor fields are assigned by lot to their overseers, then rulers of public affairs must not be chosen by lot either.” This kind of argument is generally highly probable, even though it does not have the equal firmness of a syllogism. A syllogism proceeds from universals to particulars. If it is constructed from true propositions, it possesses firm and unchanging truth.

Induction has the greatest probability, but it sometimes falls short of truth, as in the following: “Whoever knows how to sing is a singer; whoever knows how to wrestle is a wrestler; whoever knows how to build is a builder.” When many examples have been gathered by similar reasoning, one may infer: “Therefore whoever knows evil is evil.” This does not follow. For a good person cannot lack knowledge of evil; virtue loves itself, rejects what is contrary to it, and cannot avoid vice unless it has recognized it.

From these two principles and kinds of argumentation, as it were, two other modes of argumentation are detected. One is subordinate to the syllogism, the other to induction. In these it is easy to observe that one takes its beginning from the syllogism and the other from induction; yet neither completes a syllogism, nor does the other complete an induction. [Col. 1180D] These are the enthymeme and the example.

An enthymeme is an imperfect syllogism, that is, an expression in which a hurried conclusion is drawn without all the propositions having first been established. Thus someone may say: “Man is an animal; therefore he is a substance.” For he omitted the other proposition, namely, that every animal is a substance. Since an enthymeme strives to prove particulars from universals, it resembles a syllogism. But because it does not use all the propositions that belong to a syllogism, it departs from the nature of the syllogism and is therefore called an imperfect syllogism.

An example is similarly both connected with and distinct from induction. For an example attempts to demonstrate one particular through another particular that has been proposed, as follows: “Catiline ought to be killed by the consul Tullius, since Gracchus was killed by Scipio.” It has been established that Catiline ought to be killed by Cicero because Gracchus was killed by Scipio. The interposition of the individual names shows that both cases are particular, not universal.

Since one particular is approved from another, the thing we call an example possesses a likeness to induction; but since it does not gather several particulars by which to accomplish this, it departs from induction.

Thus there are two principal species of argumentation: one called the syllogism, the other called induction. Beneath these, and as it were flowing from them, are the enthymeme and the example. All of these are derived from the syllogism and receive their force from the syllogism. Whether it is an enthymeme, an induction, or even an example, it derives its credibility above all from the syllogism, as was demonstrated in the earlier *Prior Analytics* that we translated from Aristotle.

It is therefore sufficient to discuss the syllogism as the principal form, containing the other species of argumentation.

It remains now to explain what a topic is. A topic is, as Marcus [manuscripts: Mammius] Tullius holds, the seat of an argument. I shall briefly set out the force of this definition.

The seat of an argument can partly be understood as the maximal proposition, and partly as the difference of a maximal proposition. For there are propositions that are known through themselves, having nothing further by which they can be demonstrated; these are called maximal and principal propositions. There are also others whose credibility is supplied by the first and maximal propositions.

It is therefore necessary that, among all doubtful matters, those propositions hold the most ancient proof which can establish the credibility of other things in such a way that nothing more known than they themselves can be found. For if an argument is what establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter, and must be more known and more probable than what it proves, it is necessary that all arguments receive their greatest credibility from propositions that are so self-evident that they do not require proof from elsewhere.

Such a proposition, however, is sometimes contained within the scope of an argument; at other times it is placed outside it and supplies and completes the force of the argument.

All topics, then—that is, the differences of maximal propositions—must necessarily be drawn either from the terms proposed in the question, namely the predicate and the subject; or they must be taken from outside; or they must lie between these and be situated between both.

Of those topics that are drawn from the terms about which the question is doubtful, there are two modes: one from their substance, the other from what follows upon their substance. Those that derive from substance consist solely in definition. For definition displays substance, and the complete demonstration of substance is definition.

Let us make this clear by examples, so that the whole method of questions, arguments, and topics may be settled. Suppose it is asked whether trees are animals, and let the following syllogism be made: “An animal is an animated, sentient substance; a tree is not an animated, sentient substance; therefore a tree is not an animal.”

Here the question concerns genus. For it is asked whether trees should be placed under the genus of animals. The topic consists in the universal proposition: “That to which the definition of a genus does not apply is not a species of that whose definition it is.” The higher difference of this topic is from definition, and the topic is nevertheless so called.

You see, then, how the entire uncertainty of the question has been drawn [ed.: “has been treated”] through the argumentation of the syllogism by means of suitable and congruent propositions, which preserve their force from the first and maximal proposition—namely, the proposition that denies something to be a species if the definition of the genus does not apply to it.

That universal proposition itself is drawn from the substance of one of the terms placed in the question, namely “animal,” that is, from its definition, which is “an animated, sentient substance.” Thus, in the remaining questions, after the differences of the topics have been mentioned briefly and concisely, one must grasp the property of each with an alert and attentive mind.

This topic, which is drawn from substance, has two modes: arguments are drawn partly from definition and partly from description. Definition differs from description in that definition assumes a genus and differences, whereas description encloses the underlying conception by gathering certain accidents that produce one property, or substantial features joined together apart from a suitable genus.

Definitions made from accidents seem in no way to demonstrate substance. Nevertheless, because true definitions are often stated in such a way that they display substance, propositions taken from description also appear to be assumed from the topic of substance.

Let the following be an example. Suppose it is asked whether whiteness is a substance; the question is whether whiteness is placed under substance as under a genus. We say: “A substance is that which can be the subject of all accidents; whiteness, however, is subject to no accidents; therefore whiteness is not a substance.”

The topic—that is, the maximal proposition—is the same as above: “That whose definition or description does not apply to the thing said to be its species is not the genus of the thing asserted to be its species.” The description of substance does not apply to whiteness; therefore whiteness is not a substance.

[Col. 1182D] The higher difference of the topic derives from the description that we previously placed in the account of substance.

There are also definitions drawn not from the substance of a thing but from the meaning of a name, and applied in this way to the thing being questioned. Thus, if the question is whether one ought to devote oneself to philosophy, the argumentation will be as follows: “Philosophy is the love of wisdom; no one doubts that one ought to devote oneself to this; therefore one ought to devote oneself to philosophy.”

Here it was not the definition of the thing but the interpretation of the name that supplied the argument. Tullius also used this in his defense in the presentation of the same philosophy. In Greek it is called *ὀνοματοποιία* (*onomatopoiia*), and in Latin “the definition of a name.”

I believe we have made clear through evident examples these arguments that are taken from the substance of the terms placed in the question. [Col. 1183A] We must now discuss those that follow upon the substance of the terms.

Their division is many-sided. For many things adhere to individual substances. Arguments are therefore commonly drawn from what accompanies the substance of anything, either from the whole, from the parts, or from causes—whether efficient cause, material cause, or final cause.

An efficient cause is that which moves and operates so that something may be produced. Matter is that from which something is made or in which something is made. The end is that for the sake of which something is made.

Among the topics that are taken from what follows upon substance there are also those derived from effects, corruptions, uses, or, apart from all these, from common accidents.

Since this is so, let us first examine the topic that is taken from the whole.

[Col. 1183B] “Whole” is usually said in two ways: either as a genus, or as that which consists as an integral whole from several parts.

That which is a whole as a genus often supplies arguments for questions in the following way. If the question is whether justice is useful, the syllogism is: “Every virtue is useful; justice is a virtue; therefore justice is useful.”

The question concerns an accident, namely, whether usefulness occurs in justice. The topic is the one that consists in the maximal proposition: “What belongs to the genus belongs also to the species.” The higher topic is from the whole—that is, from the genus, namely virtue, which is the genus of justice.

Again, suppose the question is whether human affairs are governed by providence. We say: “If the world is governed by providence, and human beings are a part of the world, then human affairs are governed by providence.”

The question concerns an accident. The topic is: “What occurs in the whole also belongs to the part.” The highest topic is from the whole, that is, from the integral whole. The thing composed of parts is the world, which is the whole of human beings.

Arguments also arise from parts in two ways: either from the parts of a genus, which are species, or from the parts of an integral whole—that is, of a whole—which are called parts in the proper sense.

Let the question concerning those parts that are species be whether virtue is the disposition of a well-ordered mind. This is a question of definition, namely, whether “the disposition of a well-ordered mind” is the definition of virtue.

We shall therefore construct an argument from species as follows: “If justice, courage, moderation, and prudence are dispositions of a well-ordered mind, and these four are subordinate to one virtue as to a genus, then virtue is the disposition of a well-ordered mind.” [Col. 1183D]

The maximal proposition is: “What is present in each individual part must be present in the whole.” The argument is from the parts—that is, from the parts of the genus, which are called species. For justice, courage, moderation, and prudence are species of virtue.

Likewise, let the question concerning those parts that are called parts of an integral whole be whether medicine is useful. This is an issue concerning an accident. We say: “If driving away diseases, preserving health, and treating wounds are useful, then medicine is useful.”

Often even one part alone is sufficient for the argumentation to stand firm. Thus, if it is doubted whether someone is free, and we show that he has been manumitted either by the census, by a will, or by the *vindicta*, he has been shown to be free; yet other means of granting freedom also existed.

Again, if it is doubted whether something seen from a distance is a house, we say that it is not, because it lacks either a roof, walls, or foundations. Here again the argument has been made from a single part.

We must consider the whole and the parts not only in substances but also in manner, time, quantity, and place. What we sometimes propose in relation to time is a part; but if we propose something simply, it is a whole in relation to manner; if we propose it with some addition, it becomes a part in relation to manner.

Likewise, if we speak of everything in relation to quantity, we speak of the whole; if we select some portion of quantity, we posit a part of quantity. The same applies to place: what is everywhere is a whole; what is somewhere is a part.

Let examples of all these be given together. From the whole to the part in relation to time: “If God always exists, then he exists now.” From the part to the whole in relation to manner: “If the soul [manuscripts: ‘animal’] is moved in some way, then it is simply moved; but it is moved when it grows angry; therefore it is moved universally and simply.”

Again, from the whole to the parts in relation to quantity: “If Apollo the prophet is truthful in all things, then it will be true that Pyrrhus will conquer the Romans.” Again, in relation to place: “If God is everywhere, then he is here also.”

Next comes the topic called “from causes.” There are several causes: those that provide the beginning of motion and bring about an effect; those that receive the forms of species as their underlying subject; those for the sake of which something is done; and that which is the form of anything.

[Col. 1184C] Argument, then, from the efficient cause: if someone wished to show that justice is natural, he might say: “The gathering of human beings is natural; but justice was created by the gathering of human beings; therefore justice is natural.” The question concerns an accident. The maximal proposition is: “Things whose efficient causes are natural are themselves also natural.” The topic is from efficient causes: for whatever is the cause of each thing produces the thing of which it is the cause.

Again, if someone should maintain that the Moors do not possess weapons, he says that they therefore make no use of weapons because they lack iron. The maximal proposition is: “Where the material is lacking, that which is produced from the material is lacking as well.” This is the topic from matter. Both, however—that is, what produces and what receives the act of the producer—are called, by one term, causes; for equally the thing that produces and the thing that receives the action of the agent are causes of the thing produced.

[Col. 1184D] Again, let the proposition be drawn from the end, namely, whether justice is good. The argument will be as follows: “If being blessed is good, justice also is good”; for this is the end of justice, that the person who lives according to justice may be led to blessedness. The maximal proposition is: “Whatever has a good end is itself also good.” The topic is from the end.

From that which is the form of each thing, the argument proceeds as follows: Daedalus could not have flown because he had no wings belonging to a natural form. The maximal proposition is: “Each person can do only as much as his form permits.” The topic is from form.

From effects, corruptions, and uses, the argument proceeds in this way. If the house is good, its construction is good; therefore the house is good. Again, if the destruction of the house is bad, the house is good; and if the house is good, its destruction is bad. Likewise, if riding is good, the horse is good; and if the horse is good, riding is good. The first example is from acts of generation, although it may also be called from effects; the second is from corruptions; the third from uses. The maximal propositions in all these cases are: “Whatever production is good is itself also good, and conversely”; “Whatever corruption is bad is itself good, and conversely”; and “Whatever use is good is itself good, and conversely.”

Arguments are drawn from common accidents whenever accidents are taken that either cannot or ordinarily do not leave their subject. Thus someone might say: “The wise person will not repent, for repentance accompanies a bad deed; but since this is not appropriate to the wise person, neither is repentance.” The question concerns accidents. The maximal proposition is: “Whatever is not present in something cannot be accompanied in it by that which follows from it.” The topic is from common accidents.

The topics that are assumed from the terms themselves placed in the proposition having now been completed, we must next discuss those which, although placed outside it, nevertheless furnish arguments for questions. These are derived either from the judgment of the matter, or from similarities, or from the greater, or from the lesser, or from proportion, or from opposites, or from transference.

The topic that concerns the judgment of the matter is of this kind: we may say that something exists because everyone judges it so, or because most people do, whether those people are wise or thoroughly educated in a particular discipline. An example is that the heavens are revolving, since the wise and those most learned in astronomy have judged them to be so. [Col. 1185C] The question concerns an accident. The proposition is: “What appears so to all, to most, or to learned people cannot be contradicted.” The topic is from the judgment of the matter.

From similarities, the argument proceeds as follows. If it is questioned whether it is proper to a human being to be two-footed, we say by comparison: “The horse possesses four feet, and the human being two feet. But four-footedness is not proper to the horse; therefore two-footedness is not proper to the human being.” The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “If that which is similarly present is not a property, then neither can that which is under inquiry be a property.”

The topic is from similarities. It is divided into two kinds: for similarity consists either in quality or in quantity; in the latter case it is called parity, that is, equality.

Again, from what is greater: if it is asked whether the definition of an animal is “that which can move itself,” we say: “If it is more appropriate for the definition of an animal to be ‘that which lives naturally’ than ‘that which can move itself,’ and if ‘that which lives naturally’ is not the definition of an animal, then neither should the definition of an animal be thought to be the lesser characterization, ‘that which can move itself.’” The question concerns a definition. The maximal proposition is: “If what appears more evidently to be present is not present, then neither will what appears less evidently to be present be present.” The topic is from what is greater.

From lesser things the argument proceeds conversely. If “a two-footed walking animal” is the definition of a human being, and if being two-footed appears to be less a definition of a human being than “a rational mortal animal,” then, since “a two-footed walking animal” is the definition of a human being, “a rational mortal animal” will also be the definition of a human being. The question concerns a definition. The maximal proposition is: “If what appears less evidently to be present is present, then what appears more evidently to be present will also be present.” There are many distinctions among topics that furnish arguments from what is greater and lesser; we have treated them more carefully in our exposition of Aristotle’s *Topics*.

Likewise, from proportion: if it is asked whether magistrates should be chosen by lot in cities, we answer, “Certainly not, since even on ships the helmsman is not appointed by lot.” For there is a proportion: as the helmsman is related to the ship, so the magistrate is related to the city. This topic differs from that drawn from similarities. [Col. 1186B] In the latter, one thing is compared with another; in proportion, however, there is not a similarity of things but a comparison of relationships. The question concerns an accident of proportion. The maximal proposition is: “Whatever occurs in each thing must also occur in its proportional counterpart.” The topic is from proportion.

There are several kinds of topic from opposites. For opposites are opposed to one another in four ways: either as contraries confronting one another; or as privation and possession; or as relatives; or as affirmation and negation. Their distinctions were recalled in the book written on the ten Categories; from them arguments arise in the following ways.

If it is asked, from contraries, whether it is proper to virtue to be praised, I shall answer, “Certainly not, since it is not even proper to vice to be blamed.” The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “Contraries have contrary attributes.” The topic is from opposites, that is, from contraries.

Again, let the question be whether it is proper to those who have eyes to see. I shall answer, “Certainly not, since it can happen that those who see are also blind in other respects.” For in things in which possession is present, privation can also be present; and what is a property cannot depart from its subject. Since sight departs when blindness arrives, it is proved that seeing is not proper to those who have eyes. The question concerns a property. The proposition is: “Where privation can be present together with possession, there is no property.” The topic is from opposites according to possession and privation.

Again, let the question be whether it is proper to a father to be a procreator. I shall answer that this appears correct, because it is proper to a son to be begotten: for as the father is related to the son, so the begotten is related to the procreator. The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “The properties of relatives are themselves related to one another.” The topic is from relative opposites.

Again, let the question be whether it is proper to an animal to move. I shall deny it, because it is not even proper to an inanimate thing [ed.: “in an animal”] not to move. The question concerns a property. The maximal proposition is: “The opposites of opposites ought themselves to be properties.” The topic is from opposites according to affirmation and negation; for “to move” and “not to move” are opposed to one another by affirmation and negation.

From transference the argument proceeds in this way. When, from the terms in which the question has been established, the inquiry is transferred to something else that is better known, and when the propositions in the question are confirmed by proving that other matter, the following occurs. When Socrates was asking what justice could accomplish in each individual, he transferred the entire discussion to the greatness of the commonwealth; and from what justice accomplished in individuals he established that justice too has power. This topic might perhaps appear to be from the whole; but since it does not adhere to the terms about which the proposition is made, and since the matter is placed outside them and is assumed only because it appears better known, it is therefore appropriately called the topic from transference.

This transference also occurs in a name, whenever an argument is transferred from an obscure term to a better-known one. Thus, if it is asked whether a philosopher is envious, and if the meaning of the word “philosopher” is unknown, we transfer the argument to a better-known term and say that one who is wise is not envious; for “wise” is a better-known term than “philosopher.” Enough, then, has been said suitably concerning the topics assumed from outside. We shall now discuss the intermediate topics.

## On the Intermediate Topics

The intermediate topics are derived either from inflection, from cognate terms, or from division.

An inflection is the alteration of a principal noun into an adverb: thus from *justice* comes *justly*; therefore *justice* is the inflected term, while what we call *justly* is an adverb.

Cognate terms are those which proceed from the same source but flow forth in different forms: thus from *justice* come *just* and related forms. These are called cognate with one another and with *justice* itself, and from all of them arguments are readily available. For if what is just is good, and what is done justly is done well, and the just person is good, and justice is good, then these conclusions follow in accordance with the similarity of their proper names.

These topics are called mixed because, when the question concerns justice and arguments are drawn from an inflected or cognate form, they do not appear to be drawn either directly and properly from justice itself or from things placed outside it, but from its inflections—that is, from things derived from it by a slight alteration. These topics are therefore rightly placed midway between those drawn from the things themselves and those taken from outside.

There remains the topic from division, which is treated as follows. Every division is made either by negation or by partition. Thus someone might state: “Every animal either has feet or does not have feet.” By partition, one might divide as follows: “Every human being is either healthy or ill.”

Every division is made either from a genus into species, from a whole into parts, from a word into its proper meanings, from an accident into its subjects, from a subject into its accidents, or from one accident into other accidents. I explained the reasoning of all these matters more carefully in my book composed on division; suitable examples should therefore be sought there for understanding them.

Arguments by division are made both by the separation effected through negation and by that effected through partition. Those who use these divisions either argue by direct reasoning or lead the matter to something impossible or inappropriate, and thus again assume what they had set aside.

Anyone will understand this more easily if he has devoted attention to the earlier *Analytics*. The following examples, however, will provide sufficient knowledge of the matter here.

Let the question be whether time has any origin. Whoever wishes to deny this will establish by reasoning that time did not in any way come into being. He will demonstrate it by direct reasoning as follows: “Since the world is eternal”—let this be granted for the sake of the argument—“and the world could not exist without time, time too is eternal; but what is eternal has no origin; therefore time has no origin.”

If the same conclusion is to be demonstrated by impossibility, it will be stated as follows: “If time has an origin, time did not always exist. There was therefore a time when there was no time; but ‘there was’ signifies time. Therefore there was a time when there was no time, which cannot happen. Therefore no beginning of time has been posited.” For if time began from some beginning, it would follow that there was a time when there was no time—an inappropriate and impossible consequence.

We therefore return to the other side, namely, that time lacks an origin. But when this division by negation is used to derive arguments, it cannot happen that both alternatives exist, since the alternatives are divided by affirmation and negation. Thus, when one is removed, the other remains; and when the other is posited, the first is removed. This is called the topic from division, midway between those ordinarily drawn from the things themselves and those assumed from outside.

For when it is asked whether time has any origin, the argument does indeed assume that an origin exists; from this, through its proper consequence, a syllogism of impossibility and falsehood is drawn from the matter itself under inquiry. Once this has been concluded, we return to the earlier alternative, which must be true, since its opposite leads to something impossible and inappropriate. Thus, because the syllogism is usually constructed from the very matter under inquiry, the topic seems to have been drawn from the things themselves; but because it does not remain there and returns to the proposition assumed, it seems to be taken from outside. Therefore the topic from division is placed midway between the two.

The topics drawn from partition, however, arise in several ways. Sometimes the things divided can exist together. Thus, if we divide a word according to its meanings, all the meanings can exist together: for example, when we say *amplector*, it signifies either an action or a passion, and it can signify both at once.

Sometimes, as in division by negation, the alternatives cannot exist together: for example, “He is healthy or ill.” In the first kind of division, reasoning proceeds either because what is sought is present in all the alternatives or is absent from all, or because it is present in one and absent from another.

We need not labor long in explaining these matters if the earlier *Analytics* or the *Topics* have more carefully trained the reader’s understanding. If it is asked whether *dog* is a substance, and the following division is made—“*Dog* is either the name of a barking animal, or of a sea creature, or of a heavenly star”—and if it is demonstrated in each case that the barking dog is a substance, that the sea creature can also be posited as a substance, and that the heavenly star can likewise be a substance, then it has been shown that *dog* is a substance.

Here the argument will appear to have been drawn from the very terms proposed in the question. In syllogisms of this kind, however, the reasoning may proceed as follows: “He is either healthy or ill; he is healthy; therefore he is not ill”; or, “He is not healthy; therefore he is ill”; or, “If he is ill, then he is not healthy”; or, “If he is not ill, then he is healthy.”

The syllogism has been taken from things outside [mss., inside], namely, from opposites. The entire topic from division is therefore said to be midway between the two: if it is established by negation, it is taken in one way from the things themselves and in another way comes from outside; but if arguments are drawn from partition, they sometimes provide their resources from the things themselves and sometimes from outside.

[Col. 1189B] This, then, appears to be the division of topics given by the Greek Themistius, a most diligent and lucid writer who brings everything back to the capacity of understanding.

Since this is so, I must briefly recall the division of topics, so that it may be shown that nothing remains which is not proved to be included within it. Whatever is questioned in any inquiry will be established by arguments taken either from the very things set forth in the question, or from outside, or from matters investigated as though placed on the boundary between these two.

Beyond this division nothing can be found outside it. If an argument is taken from the things themselves, it must necessarily be taken either from their substance, or from what follows them, or from accidents that inseparably accompany them or adhere to them and cannot—or ordinarily do not—separate or detach themselves from their substance.

Those arguments drawn from their substance belong either to description or to definition, and besides these, to the interpretation of the name.

Those that follow them as though containing their substances are derived from such things as genus, difference, complete form, species, or parts, which stand around the things under inquiry. They are also derived from causes, ends, effects, corruptions, uses, quantity, time, or the mode of subsisting.

That which is properly called an inseparable or adhering accident is included among common accidents. Beyond these, nothing else that could be present in anything can be found.

Having set this out, let us now examine the topics that we earlier said were assumed from outside. For the things assumed from outside are not so separated and disconnected that they do not sometimes look, as it were from an opposing position, toward the things under inquiry. Similarities and opposites are certainly related to the things of which they are similar or opposite, although they are rightly and orderly regarded as placed outside them.

These topics are similarity, opposition, greater and lesser, and the judgment of the matter. Similarity includes both the likeness of things and the relation of proportion. Everything contains some form of similarity.

Opposites consist in contraries, privations, relations, and negations. Comparison of greater with lesser is, as it were, a certain dissimilarity among similar things; for a distinction in quantity among things similar in themselves produces the greater and the lesser. Whatever is separated from something in every quality and in every relation cannot in any way be compared with it.

Arguments drawn from the judgment of the matter provide something like testimony. They are inartificial topics and wholly disconnected, following not the matter itself so much as opinion and judgment.

The topic of transference consists sometimes in equality and sometimes in comparison with what is greater or lesser; for the transfer of arguments and reasons is made either to what is similar or to what is greater or lesser.

The mixed topics that we said arose either from inflections, cognate terms, or division preserve in all cases consequence and incompatibility. Arguments drawn from definition, genus, difference, or causes supply syllogisms with their strength and order chiefly by demonstration; the remaining arguments do so through probabilities derived from dialectic.

The topics that lie chiefly in the substance of the things questioned pertain to predicative and simple syllogisms; the others pertain to hypothetical and conditional syllogisms.

The topics having now been completed, and having been made clear both by definition and by the illumination provided by examples, it remains to explain briefly how these topics are differences among maximal propositions. The matter requires no lengthy discussion. All maximal propositions, or definitions, do not differ in so far as they are maximal; they differ in that some come from definition, others from genus, and still others from different topics. In this respect they rightly differ, and these are called their differences.

## On the Topics

The *Topics* are the seats of arguments, the sources of meanings, and the origins of expressions. It is therefore permissible to define a topic as the seat of an argument, and an argument as a line of reasoning that gives credibility to a doubtful matter.

Arguments are either contained in the very matter under discussion, or are drawn from things somehow related to the matter in question and recognized as derived from other things, or are assumed from outside.

Thus the topics adhering to the matter itself are three: from the whole, from the parts, and from the indication.

An argument is from the whole when a definition is applied to the matter under inquiry. Thus Cicero says: “Glory is praise of rightly performed deeds and the renown of great services to the commonwealth.” “Behold” [ed.: “from itself”]: since glory is a whole, he shows by means of its definition what glory is.

[Col. 1190D] An argument from the parts proceeds as follows: if the eye sees, the whole body does not therefore see.

An argument is drawn from an indication in this way. This is called *etymology* in Greek: “If a consul is one who takes counsel for the commonwealth, what else did Tullius do when he punished the conspirators?”

Arguments are now also drawn from things somehow related to the matter under inquiry and recognized as derived from other things. There are thirteen topics: some from cognate terms, some from genus, some from the form of the genus, that is, from species, some from similarity, some from difference, some from contraries, some from conjunction, some from antecedents, some from consequents, some from incompatibles, some from causes, some from effects, and some from comparison with lesser, greater, or equal things.

First, then, let an argument be drawn from cognate terms. Cognate terms occur when a noun is inflected into a verb, as when Cicero says that Verres “plundered” (*everrisse*) the province; or when a noun is derived from a verb, as when a robber (*latro*) is said to commit robbery (*latrocinari*); or when a noun is derived from another noun, as in Terence: “Beginning is characteristic of madmen, not of lovers.”

An argument from genus occurs when one descends from a general matter to some species, as in Virgil:

> Woman is always changeable and fickle.

Dido too, being a species of woman, could be changeable and fickle.

Or consider Cicero’s argument, descending from genus to species: “Since you ought to keep a careful account of all the provinces and allies, judges, especially of Sicily.”

An argument from species is drawn when a species lends credibility to a general question, as in Virgil:

> Or does not the Phrygian shepherd thus penetrate Lacedaemon?

Since “Phrygian shepherd” is a species, if that one man did this, then other Trojans in general can do it as well.

An argument from similarity occurs when similar things are brought forward, as in Virgil:

> Hand me weapons, for my right hand will not have hurled any in vain  
> Against the Rutulians, nor will they have lodged in the bodies of Greeks  
> On the Trojan plains.

An argument from difference is drawn when things are separated by a difference. Virgil writes:

> You do not see the horses of Diomedes, nor the chariot of Achilles.

An argument from contraries is taken when things that differ are set against one another, as in Terence:

> For if you rebuke the man who brought aid to life,  
> What will you do to the one who has inflicted injury or harm?

An argument derives its force from conjunction when things that are individually weak acquire the force of truth when joined together. For example: “What if he was previously poor? What if he was avaricious? What if he was bold? What if he was the enemy of the murdered man?” Each of these considerations is insufficient by itself; therefore they are brought together, so that the matter may be confirmed by many elements joined together.

An argument from antecedents occurs when something is established from things that happened earlier, as in Cicero’s speech for Milo: “Since he did not hesitate to disclose what he had planned, can you hesitate about what he did?” A declaration came first, and the deed followed; the argument lies in this sequence.

An argument from consequents occurs when something inevitably follows from an established matter, as when a woman has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man.

An argument from incompatibles occurs when what is alleged is destroyed by some contradiction. Thus Cicero says: “This man, then, who was not only freed from danger by you but also enriched with the highest honor, is accused of having wished to kill you in your own house.”

An argument from causes occurs when the matter under discussion is shown to have been possible by common custom, as in Terence:

> I was somewhat afraid earlier, Dave, that you might do to me  
> What the common crowd of slaves is accustomed to do: deceive me by tricks.

An argument from effects is drawn when something is approved from things that have occurred, as in Virgil:

> Fear proves ignoble spirits;

for fear is the cause of a spirit’s being ignoble, and this is the effect of fear.

An argument from comparison is drawn when the reasoning of a judgment is confirmed by comparing persons or causes.

From comparison with the greater, as in Virgil:

> You can arm united brothers for battle.

Therefore, whoever can do this in the case of brothers, how much more can he do it in the case of others?

From comparison with the lesser, as when Publius Scipio, while still a private citizen, killed the chief pontiff Tiberius Gracchus, who was seriously undermining the constitution of the commonwealth.

From comparison with equals, as Cicero says in the case of Piso: it makes no difference whether Piso himself, as consul, harasses the commonwealth with wicked assemblies and destructive laws, or allows others to harass it.

The arguments assumed from outside are those which the Greeks call ἄτεχνα, that is, “inartificial” arguments, because testimony is taken from some external matter to establish credibility.

First, there is the argument from a person—not just any person, but one whose testimony carries weight in establishing credibility; such a person must also be praiseworthy for the integrity of his character.

Authority from nature consists in the greatest excellence. Authority may also come from circumstances such as talent, wealth, age, fortune, skill, experience, necessity, and the coincidence of fortuitous events.

Credibility is sought from the sayings and deeds of ancestors when the words and actions of earlier generations are recalled.

Credibility is also established by torture, after which no one is believed to wish to lie.

## On Syllogisms

The first figure has four modes, which conclude universally or particularly, affirmatively or negatively.

The second likewise has four modes, which conclude negatively, either universally or particularly.

The third figure has six modes, which make affirmative or negative, but particular, conclusions.

The first mode of the first figure is formed from two universal affirmatives and has a universal affirmative conclusion, as follows:

> Every good thing is lovable.  
> Every just thing is good.  
> Therefore every just thing is lovable.

The second mode of the first figure is formed from a universal negative and a universal affirmative and has a universal conclusion, as follows:

> No laughable thing is irrational.  
> Every human being is laughable.  
> Therefore no human being is irrational.

The third mode of the first figure is formed from a universal affirmative and a particular affirmative and concludes with a particular affirmative, as follows:

> Every animal moves.  
> Some human being is an animal.  
> Therefore some human being moves.

The fourth mode of the first figure is formed from a universal negative and a particular affirmative and concludes with a particular negative, as follows:

> No insensible thing is animate.  
> Some stone is insensible.  
> Therefore some stone is not animate.

The first mode of the second figure concludes universally negatively from a universal negative and a universal affirmative, as follows:

> No bad thing is good.  
> Every just thing is good.  
> Therefore no just thing is bad.
