The second mode of the second figure consists of a prior universal affirmative and a later universal negative and produces a universal negative conclusion, as follows:

> Every just thing is equitable.  
> No bad thing is equitable.  
> Therefore no bad thing is just.

The third mode of the second figure, formed from a prior universal negative and a later particular affirmative, collects a particular negation, as follows:

> No stone is an animal.  
> Some substance is an animal.  
> Therefore some substance is not a stone.

The fourth mode of the second figure, formed from a prior universal affirmative and a later particular negative, concludes with a particular negation, as follows:

> Every just thing is upright.  
> Some human being is not upright.  
> Therefore some human being is not just.

The first mode of the third figure concludes a particular affirmative from two universal affirmatives, since a universal affirmative may be converted into a particular affirmative, as follows:

> Every human being is an animal.  
> Every human being is a substance.  
> Therefore some substance is an animal.

The second mode of the third figure is formed from a universal negative and a universal affirmative and produces a particular negative conclusion:

> No human being is a horse.  
> Every human being is a substance.  
> Therefore some substance is not a horse.

The third mode of the third figure, formed from particular and universal affirmatives, concludes with a particular affirmative, as follows:

> Some human being is white.  
> Every human being is an animal.  
> Therefore some animal is white.

The fourth mode of the third figure, formed from a universal and a particular affirmative, concludes with a particular affirmative, as follows:

> Every human being is an animal.  
> Some human being is white.  
> Therefore some white thing is an animal.

The fifth mode of the third figure, formed from a particular negative and a universal affirmative, concludes with a particular negation, as follows:

> Some human being is not white.  
> Every human being is an animal.  
> Therefore some animal is not white.

The sixth mode of the third figure, formed from a universal negative and a particular affirmative, concludes with a particular negative, as follows:

> No human being is a stone.  
> Some human being is white.  
> Therefore some white thing is not a stone.

All the modes of the three figures of categorical syllogisms have been demonstrated, although some have added five other modes to the first figure.

## On Paralogisms

Paralogisms of the first figure arise from a prior universal affirmative and a second universal negative, as follows:

> Every human being is an animal.  
> No animal is a stone.  
> Therefore no human being is a stone.

Because, when the term is changed, both a universal and a particular conclusion—negative and affirmative—will be produced, the same paralogism is rightly judged useless when it is formed from two universal negatives, as follows:

> No stone is an animal.  
> No animal is immobile.  
> Therefore no immobile thing is a stone.

The same paralogism, formed from two particular affirmatives, proceeds as follows:

> Some horse is an animal.  
> Some animal is two-footed.  
> Therefore some horse is two-footed.

Again, from two particular negatives:

> Some human being is not white.  
> Some white thing does not move.  
> Therefore some human being does not move.

Next, if the first proposition is a particular affirmative and the second a particular negative, the result is as follows:

> Some horse is an animal.  
> Some animal is not four-footed.  
> Therefore some horse is not four-footed.

The same applies if the first proposition is a particular negative and the second a particular affirmative:

> Some human being is not a horse.  
> Some horse is immobile.  
> Therefore some human being is immobile.

Likewise, if the major proposition is a universal affirmative and the minor proposition a particular negative, it is a paralogism:

> Every human being is an animal.  
> Some animal is not rational.  
> Therefore some human being is not rational.

But if the major proposition is a universal negative and the minor proposition a particular negative, no syllogism can result:

> No stone is an animal.  
> Some animal is winged.  
> Therefore no stone is winged.

Again, if the first proposition is particular and the second universal, and both propositions are affirmative, there is no syllogism:

> Some stone is a body.  
> Every body is measurable.  
> Therefore some stone is measurable.

Likewise, if the first proposition is particular negative and the second universal negative, there is no syllogism:

> Some animal is not two-footed.  
> No two-footed thing neighs.  
> Therefore some animal does not neigh.

Likewise, if the first proposition is a particular affirmative and the second a universal negative, it does not produce a syllogism:

> Some stone is insensible.  
> No insensible thing lives.  
> Therefore some stone does not live.

Likewise, if the first proposition is a particular negative and the second a universal affirmative, it is a paralogism:

> Some black thing is not animate.  
> Every animate thing moves.  
> Therefore some black thing does not move.

And no syllogism is formed from finite propositions, because the particular propositions are alike.

All propositions are composed in the following ways.

Simple propositions:

> Every human being is just.  
> Some human being is just.  
> Every human being is rational.  
> Some human being is rational.

Contrary propositions:

> No human being is just.  
> Some human being is not just.

Contradictory propositions:

> No human being is rational.  
> Some human being is not rational.

From two infinite terms:

> Every non-human is non-rational.  
> No non-human is non-rational.  
> Some non-human is non-rational.  
> Some non-human is not non-rational.

Likewise, with an infinite subject:

> Every non-human is rational.  
> No non-human is rational.  
> Some non-human is rational.  
> Some non-human is not rational.

Likewise, with an infinite predicate:

> Every human being is non-rational.  
> No human being is non-rational.  
> Some human being is non-rational.  
> Some human being is not non-rational.

Likewise, the propositions that correspond:

> Every human being is rational.  
> No human being is non-rational.  
> Every human being is non-rational.  
> No human being is non-rational.  
> Some human being is rational.  
> Some human being is not non-rational.  
> Some human being is non-rational.  
> Some human being is not non-rational.

Likewise:

> Every non-animal is non-human.  
> No non-animal is non-human.  
> Some non-animal is non-human.  
> Some non-animal is not non-human.

The converse propositions with an infinite predicate:

> Every non-animal is human.  
> No non-animal is human.  
> Some non-animal is human.  
> Some non-animal is not human.

The converse propositions with an infinite subject:

> Every animal is non-human.  
> No animal is non-human.  
> Some animal is non-human.  
> Some animal is not non-human.

Indefinite propositions:

> A human being is just.  
> A human being is not just.

Indefinite propositions with an infinite subject:

> A non-human is just.  
> A non-human is not just.

[Col. 1196A] With an infinite predicate:

> A human being is not just.  
> A human being is not non-just.

With both terms infinite: “A non-man is non-just.” “A non-man is not non-just.”

Singular or individual propositions: “Plato is just.” “Plato is not just.”

From an infinite subject: “A non-Plato is just.” “A non-Plato is not just.”

From an infinite predicate: “Plato is non-just.” “Plato is not non-just.”

From both terms infinite: “A non-Plato is non-just.” “A non-Plato is not non-just.”

## On Rhetorical Topics

Rhetorical discourse has six parts: the proem, which is the exordium; the narration; the partition; the confirmation; the refutation; and the peroration. These parts are the instruments of rhetorical skill, since rhetoric is present in all its forms, and its forms are present in it. Nor will they be present in any other way than by administering what they accomplish. Thus, in the judicial kind of cases, the order of the proem, narration, and the remaining parts is necessary; and they are also necessary in the demonstrative and deliberative kinds.

The work of rhetorical skill is to teach and to move. This is likewise accomplished through nearly the same six instruments, that is, the parts of discourse. But the parts of rhetoric, since they are parts of the skill, are themselves also skills; and therefore they too will use the parts of discourse as instruments.

[Col. 1196C] And in order to operate through these, they will themselves be present in them. For in exordia, unless the five aforementioned rhetorical parts are present—so that the orator may discover, express, arrange, remember, and deliver—he accomplishes nothing. In the same way, nearly all the remaining instrumental parts are useless unless they possess all the parts of rhetoric.

The agent who produces this skill is the orator. His task is to speak appropriately for persuasion. Its end, in the one case, is to have spoken well—that is, to have spoken appropriately for persuasion; in the other, it is to have persuaded. For if something prevents the orator from persuading, he has not thereby failed to attain the end after performing his task. Rather, the person who is connected and related to the task attains the end by performing it. The external result, however, is often not achieved; nevertheless, it does not deprive rhetoric, which is satisfied with its own end, of its honor. These matters are so interwoven that rhetoric is present in its forms, while the forms are present in cases.

[Col. 1196D] The parts of cases are called “statuses.” They may also be called, by other names, “constitutions” or “questions.” They are divided in accordance with the way in which the nature of things itself is divided. But let us begin with the differences among questions, since all rhetorical questions are surrounded by circumstances: either they concern a controversy over some written text, or, apart from a written text, they derive the beginning of their disputes from the matter itself.

Questions contained in a written text can arise in five ways. First, when one party defends the words of the author while the other defends the author’s intention. This is called the status of the written text and the intention.

[Col. 1197A] Second, when laws disagree with one another through a certain contradiction, with one side defending some laws and the other side defending others. This is called the status of conflicting law.

Third, when the written text under dispute encloses an ambiguous meaning, it is called ambiguity, according to its name.

Fourth, when something unwritten is understood in what has been written. Since this is sought through reasoning and a certain consequence of a syllogism, it is called the ratiocinative status, or syllogism.

Fifth, when a text has been written whose force and nature cannot easily become clear unless it has been disclosed by definition. This is called the status of definition in a written text. It is not our present task, or the task of rhetoric, to demonstrate how all these differ from one another. We present these matters for learned persons to contemplate, not for beginners to learn; although we have discussed their differences incidentally in the commentaries on the Topics.

[Col. 1197B] The constitutions that are placed outside a written text, in the controversy over the matters themselves, are divided into distinct kinds, just as the nature of the matters themselves is divided. In every rhetorical question it is asked whether something exists, what it is, and what sort of thing it is; and, on these grounds, whether judgment can be exercised lawfully or according to custom.

But if the fact or matter alleged by the adversary is denied, the question is whether it exists. This is called the conjectural constitution. If it has been established that the act occurred, but it is unknown what the act was, since its force must be shown by definition, the constitution is called definitive. If it has been established both that the act occurred and what its definition is, but its character is being investigated, then, because there is uncertainty as to the genus under which it should be placed, it is called general quality. In this question the consideration of quality, quantity, and comparison is involved. But since the question concerns genus, this constitution must necessarily be divided into several parts according to the form of genus.

[Col. 1197C] Every general question—that is, one in which the genus, quality, or quantity of an act is investigated—is divided into two parts. For the quality of the proposed matter is either investigated with respect to the past, the present, or the future. If with respect to the past, it is called the judicial constitution; if it concerns the present or future time, it is called the deliberative constitution.

The judicial constitution, whose inquiry concerns the past, is divided into two parts. Either the force of the defense lies in the act itself, and it is called absolute quality; or it is assumed from outside, and it is called assumptive constitution.

This latter is divided into four parts: the crime is either conceded, removed, transferred, or, finally, compared. The crime is conceded when no defense of the act is introduced, but pardon is requested. This can happen in two ways: by pleading for mercy or by offering an excuse. One pleads for mercy when one brings forward no excuse. One offers an excuse when the fault of the act is attributed to causes that cannot be resisted or opposed, although these are not persons; for that belongs to another constitution. Such causes are ignorance, accident, and necessity.

[Col. 1198A] The crime is removed when it is transferred from the person who is attacked to someone else. Removal of the crime can occur in two ways: either the cause or the act is transferred. The cause is transferred when it is argued that something was done through another’s power; the act is transferred when it is shown that someone else either could or ought to have done it. These arguments are especially effective when an action is brought against us under the charge that we did not do what ought [mss., “could”] to have been done.

The charge is retaliated when it is conceded [mss., “argued”] that a deed was committed justly against someone, because the person against whom it was committed had often acted unjustly and deserved to suffer what is alleged.

Comparison occurs when the act criticized by the adversary is defended as having been committed for the sake of something better or more useful. But enough on this matter; we must now discuss invention.

## On Invention

Previously we gave the dialectical topics; now we present the rhetorical topics, which necessarily arise from the attributes of the person and of the case.

The person is the one summoned to judgment, whose statement or act is criticized. The case is the person’s act or statement on account of which the person is summoned to judgment. Thus, the entire system of topics is established in these two things. For whatever provides an occasion for criticism does not provide an opportunity for defense unless it tends toward an excusable aspect; accusation and defense alike arise from the same topics.

If, then, a person is summoned to judgment but no act or statement is criticized, there can be no case. Nor can any act or statement be brought to judgment if there is no person. Thus, the entire structure of judgments concerns these two things: the person and the case.

But, as has been said, the person is the one summoned to judgment; the case is the person’s act or statement on account of which the person is made the defendant. Therefore, the person and the case cannot themselves supply arguments, since they are the subjects of the inquiry. Things that are in doubt cannot themselves lend credibility to the doubt.

An argument, however, is a form of reasoning that establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter. The things attributed to persons and cases lend credibility to the case. Sometimes a person lends credibility to a case—for example, if Catiline is believed to have held opinions against the republic because his character was marked by the disgrace of vices. In that instance, the person does not lend credibility to the case merely insofar as he is the person summoned to judgment; rather, he does so insofar as he acquires a certain quality from the attributes of the person.

But, so that the order of matters may become clearer, I think that the circumstances should be discussed.

## On Circumstances

Circumstances are what constitute the substance of a relevant question. For unless there is someone who acted, something that he did, a reason why he did it, a place and time in which he did it, a manner, and also an ability or means, the case will not stand.

Cicero divides these circumstances into two groups. He places the circumstance “who” among the attributes of the person, while he places the remaining circumstances among the attributes of the case.

First, he divides the circumstance “who,” which he attributes to the person, into eleven parts: name, as in “Verres”; nature, as in “a barbarian”; way of life, as in “a friend of nobles”; person, as in “a wealthy man”; pursuit, as in “a geometrician”; accident, as in “an exile”; affection, as in “a lover”; disposition, as in “a wise man”; intention; acts; and speeches. These lie outside the act or statement now brought to judgment.

The remaining circumstances—what, why, when, where, how, and by what means—he places among the attributes of the case. He says that “what” and “why” are connected with the case itself: “why” he places among causes, since the cause of every act is that on account of which it was done.

He divides “what” into four parts: the general outline of the act, as in “the killing of a parent”; before the act, from which amplification is chiefly derived, as in “he rushed forward and seized the sword”; during the act, as in “he struck violently”; and after the act, as in “he buried him in a hidden place.”

Although all these are acts, they nevertheless belong to the case under investigation because they concern the execution of the case. They are not the acts counted among the attributes of the person. Those acts lie outside the case and, by shaping the person, lend credibility to the case in which the charge is involved. These acts, however, being connected with the case itself, belong to the case under investigation.

[Col. 1199B] Cicero places the final four circumstances in the execution of the case, which is the second part of the attributes of cases. He divides the circumstance “when” into time, as in “he did it just now,” and occasion, as in “while everyone was asleep.”

The circumstance “where” he calls place, as in “he did it in the bedroom.” The circumstance “how” he calls manner, as in “he did it secretly.” The circumstance “by what means” he calls ability, as in “with a large army.” Although the natural distinction among these topics is clear from the circumstances of the matters, we shall nevertheless be more helpful if we display their fuller differences from one another.

For when Marcus Tullius proposed that some circumstances were connected with the case itself, while others belonged to the execution of the case, and when, among those connected with the case itself, he counted the circumstance he called “during the act,” the expression itself seems to indicate that “during the act” is the same topic as the one belonging to the execution of the case. But this is not so. “During the act” refers to what was committed at the time when the crime was being perpetrated, as in “he struck.” In the execution of the case, however, we find what encompasses the act before it, during it, and after it. For in all these phases, time, place, occasion, manner, and ability are investigated.

Again, “during the act” is an act—the act being performed is the case. What belongs to the execution of the case, however, is not itself an act but adheres to the act. In those matters, time, occasion, place, manner, and ability are understood to have occurred together with the act. But, as has been said, these are attached to any act and never abandon it in any way, because they are in a certain manner subordinate to the very case that was carried out.

[Col. 1200A] Moreover, what belongs to the execution of the case can exist without what is connected with the case itself. For the place, time, occasion, manner, and ability of any act can be understood even if no one does what could be done in that place, at that time, on that occasion, in that manner, or with that ability. Thus, what belongs to the execution of the case can exist without what is connected with the case itself.

The latter, however, cannot exist without the former; for an act cannot exist apart from place, time, occasion, manner, and ability. These, then, are the matters that consist in the attributes of the person and the case, just as, among dialectical topics, those matters belong to what is inherent in the things under investigation.

The remaining matters, whether attached to the case or following upon the case as carried out, are like those which, among dialectical topics, according to Themistius, partly follow the substance of the thing, partly are external, and partly lie in between; according to Cicero, they are counted among the affections or placed externally.

The matters attached to the case are themselves also those that lend credibility to the question. They are, in a certain way, affections directed toward the matter under investigation and looking back to the case at issue, as follows.

When the seven circumstances counted among the attributes of the person or the case begin to be compared and, as it were, brought into relation with one another—when something containing is referred to what it contains, or to what contains it—there arises either species or genus. If what is referred is something very far removed from it, there is a contrary. If it is referred to its end and outcome, there is an event.

In the same way, they are compared as greater, lesser, or equal. In general, topics of this kind are considered among things that stand in relation to one another. For the greater, the similar, the equally great, and the different are attached to the circumstances counted among the attributes of the case and the person, so that when the circumstances themselves are compared with others, an argument may arise from them concerning the act or statement brought to judgment.

They differ from the preceding topics in that the preceding topics either contained acts or adhered to acts in such a way that they could not be separated from them—for example, place, time, and the other circumstances that do not leave the case as carried out.

[Col. 1200D] The matters attached to the case, however, do not adhere to the case itself; they are added to the circumstances. They provide arguments only when they have entered into comparison. They derive arguments not from contrariety but from a contrary, and not from similarity but from something similar. Thus it becomes clear that arguments among matters attached to the case are derived from relation, and that those matters are attached to the case which are related to the case itself under discussion.

Consequence, the fourth part of the attributes of cases, is neither present in the things themselves nor does it leave the substance of the things, nor is it discovered through comparison. Rather, it either precedes the matter as carried out or follows it. This topic is external.

First, one asks what name should properly be applied to what was done; here the difficulty concerns not the matter but the word. Then the authors, inventors, approvers, and imitators of the act are brought in as support for the argument, entirely from a judgment and a kind of testimony placed externally. Next, one considers what customary agreement, judgment, knowledge, or craft belongs to the matter. Then one considers its nature: what normally happens; whether people customarily approve such a thing on their own authority, unusually and rarely, or whether they customarily find fault with it; and the other matters that commonly follow some act immediately or after an interval. These must be placed externally and tend more toward opinion than toward the nature of the things themselves.

[Col. 1201A] Thus the attributes of cases may be divided into four groups: some are connected with the case itself—these, as was said above, are acts; some belong to the execution of the case—these, as we showed earlier, are not acts but adhere to acts; some are attached to the case—these are placed in relation; and some follow upon the case as carried out—their credibility is derived externally. Enough has been said about rhetorical topics.

Now it must be explained what similarity these topics have to dialectical topics and what difference exists between them. When I have suitably and appropriately shown this, the purpose of the present work will be made clear.

First, then, just as in dialectical topics, according to Themistius, some topics adhere to the matters under investigation, while others are assumed externally and others are placed between the two, so in rhetorical topics some consist in the person and the case, which are the matters disputed by the opposing side; others are external, such as those that follow the case as carried out; and others are intermediate.

The topics closest to the case are those considered among the circumstances; the remaining ones are considered in the execution of the case. Those placed among the matters attached to the case are themselves also situated among the intermediate topics, since they look back upon the case under discussion through a certain affection.

Alternatively, someone may say that the matters attributed to persons, the matters connected with the case itself, and those considered in the execution of the case are like the topics drawn from the very matters that are in doubt in dialectical inquiry. Consequences of the case should be placed externally, while matters attached to it should be placed between the two.

Cicero’s division is similar in the following way. Matters connected with the case itself, and those considered in the execution of the case, adhere to the matters under investigation. Matters attached to the case are placed among the affections. Matters following upon the case as carried out are placed externally.

Alternatively, someone may judge that matters connected with the case itself adhere to the things under investigation; that matters considered in the execution of the case, or attached to the case, are affections; and that matters following upon the case as carried out are external.

The common features are already clear: these topics occur almost equally in both skills, such as genus, part, similarity, contrary, greater, and lesser. Enough has been said about the common features.

The differences are that dialectical topics are also suitable for theses, whereas rhetorical topics are assumed only for hypotheses—that is, questions shaped by circumstances. Just as the skills themselves are distinguished from one another by universality and particularity, so their topics differ in breadth and restriction.

[Col. 1202A] Dialectical topics have the greater breadth. Since they exist apart from the circumstances that make individual cases, they are useful not only for theses but also for arguments placed in hypotheses; and they enclose and surround those topics that consist of circumstances. Thus the rhetorician always needs dialectical topics, whereas the dialectician can be satisfied with his own.

The rhetorician, since he handles cases through circumstances, takes arguments from those same circumstances. These must necessarily be confirmed by universal and simpler arguments, which are dialectical. The dialectician, however, who is prior, does not need the later skill, unless a question concerning a person should arise—for example, when a case surrounded by circumstances happens to arise for a dialectician in proving his thesis. Only then does he use rhetorical topics.

Thus, in dialectical topics, when the situation permits, arguments are taken from genus—that is, from the very nature of genus. In rhetorical topics, they are taken from the genus that is the genus of the matter under discussion, not from the nature of genus but from the actual thing that is the genus.

But for the reasoning to proceed, it depends on the nature of genus having already been understood. Thus, if it is questioned whether someone was drunk, and we wish to refute this, we say that he was not drunk because no extravagance preceded it. This is plainly because, since extravagance is in a sense the genus of drunkenness, if there was no extravagance, there was no drunkenness either.

But this depends upon the other point. For why, if there was no extravagance, could there not have been drunkenness? This is demonstrated from the nature of genus, which dialectical reasoning supplies. Wherever the genus is absent, the species must also be absent, since the genus does not leave the species behind.

The same applies to similarities and contraries, in which the similarity between rhetorical and dialectical topics is greatest. Dialectic investigates arguments from the qualities themselves, while rhetoric investigates arguments from things that receive a quality. Thus the dialectician argues from genus, that is, from the very nature of genus; the rhetorician argues from the thing that is a genus. The dialectician argues from similarity; the rhetorician from something similar, that is, from a thing that has received similarity. In the same way, the former argues from contrariety and the latter from a contrary.

It must also be committed to memory that topics provide arguments commonly to orators, dialecticians, poets, and jurists. But when they prove something specifically, they belong to rhetoricians, poets, and jurists; when they argue generally, it is clear that they belong to dialecticians.

A truly remarkable kind of work: to gather into one whatever the mobility and variety of the human mind could discover through the senses in investigating different cases, and to enclose the free and voluntary intellect. Wherever it turns, whatever thoughts it enters, the human faculty must fall upon something among the matters mentioned above.

It seemed appropriate to us to summarize briefly whose labor brought these matters into Latin expression, so that their authors might not lose their deserved glory and so that the truth of the matter might become fully known to us.

Patrician Boethius translated the *Isagoge*, leaving two commentaries on it. The same patrician Boethius translated the *Categories*, and he himself composed commentaries on it in three books. The aforementioned patrician translated the *Perihermenias* into Latin; he himself treated it in two commentaries with extremely detailed discussion. Apuleius of Madaura briefly unraveled the categorical syllogisms. The aforementioned patrician treated hypothetical syllogisms with the greatest clarity.

[These passages are absent from the manuscripts.]

Cicero translated Aristotle’s *Topics* into Latin in one book. The patrician Boethius, an investigator and lover of Latin literature, explained its contents in eight books. For the aforementioned patrician Boethius also translated the same *Topics* of Aristotle into Latin in eight books.

It should be considered that, since the occasion has now arisen in the rhetorical section, we have touched briefly on the difference between art and discipline, lest the diversity of the names, when confused together, create confusion.

Plato and Aristotle, renowned teachers of secular letters, wished there to be the following difference between art and discipline. They said that art is an operative disposition concerning contingent things, which can also be otherwise; discipline, however, concerns things that cannot happen otherwise.

We shall now come to the beginning of mathematics.

## On Mathematics

Mathematics, which in Latin we may call “the doctrinal discipline,” is the science that considers abstract quantity. Abstract quantity is so called because the intellect separates it from matter or from other accidents—for example, even and odd, or other things of this kind, which we handle through reasoning alone.

It is divided as follows:

[Col. 1203C] Division of mathematics into arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy.

Arithmetic is the discipline of quantity that is numerable in itself.

Music is the discipline that speaks about numbers that stand in relation to those found in sounds.

Geometry is the discipline of immovable magnitude and forms.

Astronomy is the discipline of the courses of the heavenly stars. It contemplates all their figures and investigates, by rational inquiry, the dispositions of the stars in relation to one another and to the earth. We shall explain these matters somewhat more fully in their proper place, so that the power of the matters mentioned may be suitably demonstrated. For now, let us discuss the name “disciplines.”

Disciplines are those subjects which, as has already been said, are never deceived or misled by opinions. They are called by this name because they necessarily preserve their rules. They neither increase through intention nor diminish through subtraction, nor are they altered by other variations. Remaining in their own proper force, they preserve their rules with unchangeable firmness.

When we review them through frequent meditation, they sharpen our understanding, wipe away the mud of ignorance, and—if the health of the mind smiles upon us, by the Lord’s gift—lead us to that contemplative vision.

We should know that Josephus, the most learned of the Hebrews, says in the ninth title of the first book of his *Antiquities* that Abraham was the first to teach arithmetic and astronomy to the Egyptians. Receiving the seeds of these disciplines, they cultivated the remaining disciplines more broadly, being people of exceptionally keen intelligence.

Our holy Fathers rightly urge the most diligent students to read these disciplines, since through them our desire is largely withdrawn from bodily matters, and they make us long for what, by the Lord’s favor, we can behold with the heart alone. Therefore it is time for us to discuss them individually and briefly.

## CHAPTER FOUR. ON ARITHMETIC

Writers on secular letters wished arithmetic to be the first of all the mathematical disciplines, because music, geometry, and astronomy, which follow it, need arithmetic in order to unfold their powers.

For example, music, which has the ratio of the single to the double, needs arithmetic. Geometry, which has the triangle, quadrilateral, and similar figures, likewise needs arithmetic. Astronomy, which has the numbers of points in the movement of the stars, also needs arithmetic. Arithmetic, however, in order to exist, is not known to need music, geometry, or astronomy.

Therefore arithmetic is found to be their fountain and mother. Pythagoras is shown [ed., “is shown”] to have praised this discipline in such a way that he recalled that all things were created by God according to number and measure, saying: “Some things were formed in motion, others in rest,” while nevertheless none of them, apart from those mentioned, had received substance.

I believe that he derived this beginning, as many philosophers did, from the prophetic statement that says: “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21).

Arithmetic thus consists in discrete quantity, which produces kinds of numbers not joined to one another by any common term. Five and ten, six and four, seven and three are not linked to one another by any common term.

Arithmetic is so called because it presides over numbers. A number is a multitude composed of monads, such as 3, 5, 10, 20, and so forth. The purpose of arithmetic is to teach us the nature of abstract number and what happens to it—for example, evenness, oddness, and the like.

### The First Division of Number

[Col. 1205A] An even number is one that can be divided into two equal parts, such as 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and the rest.

An odd number is one that cannot in any way be divided into two equal parts, such as 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and the rest.

An evenly even number is one whose division can be carried out into two equal parts all the way down to the monad. For example, 64 is divided into 32, 32 into 16, 16 into 8, 8 into 4, 4 into 2, and 2 into 1.

An evenly odd number is one that can likewise be divided only into two equal parts, such as 10 into 5, 14 into 7, 18 into 9, and similar numbers.

An oddly even number is one that can be divided into several equal parts, but does not reach the unit. For example, 24 is divided into twice 12, 12 into twice 6, and 6 into twice 3; it proceeds no further.

A prime and simple number is one that can receive only a monadic measure, such as 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, and similar numbers.

A secondary and composite number is one that can receive not only a monadic measure but also an arithmetical measure, such as 9, 15, 21, and similar numbers.

A medial number appears in one respect to be simple and non-composite, but in another respect to be secondary and composite. For example, when 9 is compared with 25, it is prime and non-composite because it has no common number except the monadic one. But when it is compared with 15, it is secondary and composite, since it contains a common number besides the monadic one: namely, the number three, which measures nine as three times three and fifteen as three times five.

### The Second Division: Even and Odd Numbers

An abundant number is one that descends from the even numbers. Although it is even, it appears to possess parts exceeding its quantity. Thus 12 has one-half, 6; one-sixth, 2; one-fourth, 3; one-third, 4; and one-twelfth, 1. Taken together, all these parts amount to 16.

A deficient number is also derived from the even numbers and has a sum of parts less than its quantity. Thus 8 has one-half, 4; one-fourth, 2; and one-eighth, 1. Taken together, these parts amount to 7.

A perfect number is likewise derived from the even numbers. Although it is even, it has all its parts, taken together, equal to itself. Thus 6 has one-half, 3; one-third, 2; and one-sixth, 1. Taken together, these parts produce the number six itself.

### The Third Division of Number

[Col. 1205C] A number in itself is one that is stated without any relation, such as 3, 4, 5, 6, and other similar numbers.

A relative number is one that is compared in relation to others. For example, when 4 is compared with 2, it is called double; likewise 6 with 3, 8 with 4, and 10 with 5. Again, 3 compared with 1 is triple, as is 9 compared with 3, and so forth.

Numbers are called equal when they are equal in quantity, such as two compared with two, three with three, ten with ten, one hundred with one hundred, and so forth.

Unequal numbers are those which, when compared with one another, demonstrate inequality, such as three compared with two, 4 with 3, 5 with 4, and 10 with 6; in general, a greater number compared with a lesser, or a lesser with a greater. When numbers of this kind are compared, they are called unequal.

A lesser number is one that is diminished either by repetition or by the relation of its members or parts.

A greater number is one that contains within itself the lesser number with which it is compared, together with something more. For example, the number five is greater than the number three because it contains the number five, the number three, and two additional parts of it, and so with the others.

A multiple number is one that contains a lesser number twice, three times, four times, or in some other multiplicity. For example, two compared with one is double; 3 with 1 is triple; 4 is quadruple; and so forth.

A submultiple number is one that is contained within a multiple number twice, three times, four times, or in some other multiplicity. For example, one is contained twice in two, three times in three, four times in four, and in other numbers in other multiplicities.

A superparticular number is one in which the greater number contains within itself the lesser number with which it is compared, together with one of its parts. For example, when 3 and 2 are compared, 3 contains 2 and another 1, which is one-half of 2. When 4 and 3 are compared, 4 contains 3 and another 1, which is one-third of 3; and so with the others.

A subsuperparticular number is the lesser number that is contained in the greater together with one of its parts—one-half, one-third, one-fourth, one-fifth, or another part. Examples are 2 compared with 3, 4 with 5, and the rest.

A superpartient number is one that contains the lesser number in its entirety and, beyond this, two, three, four, five, or other parts of it. For example, when 5 and 3 are compared, 5 contains 3 and, in addition, two other parts of it. When 7 and 4 are compared, 7 contains 4 and three other parts of it.

A subsuperpartient number is one that is contained in a superpartient number together with two, three, or more of its parts. For example, 3 is contained in 5 together with two of its other parts; 4 in 7 together with three of its parts; and 5 in 9 together with four of its parts.

[Col. 1207B] A multiple-superparticular number is one that, when compared with a lesser number, contains that lesser number a certain number of times together with one of its parts. For example, when 5 is compared with 2, it contains two twice and one of its parts. The same applies to 9 compared with 4, and to similar numbers.

A submultiple-superparticular number is one that, when compared with a greater number, is contained in that greater number a certain number of times together with one of its parts. For example, when 2 is compared with 5, it is contained in 5 twice together with one of its parts.

A multiple-superpartient number is one that, when compared with a lesser number, contains it a certain number of times together with other parts of it. For example, when 8 and 3 are compared, 8 contains twice three together with two parts of it. When 16 and 6 are compared, 16 contains twice six together with four parts of it.

A submultiple-superpartient number is one that, when compared with a greater number, is contained in that greater number a certain number of times together with some of its parts. For example, 3 compared with 8 is contained twice together with two of its parts; 4 compared with 15 is contained three times together with three of its parts.

### The Fourth Division of the Whole Number

A discrete number is one that is contained by discrete monads, such as 3 by 4, 5 by 6, and the rest.

A continuous number is one that is contained by joined monads. Thus the number three, if understood in magnitude—that is, in a line, an interval, or a solid—is called continuous. The same applies to the numbers four and five.

A linear number is one that, beginning from unity, is written out linearly to infinity. Hence alpha is used to designate lines, since this letter signifies one among the Greeks.

A plane number is one contained not only by length but also by breadth: for example, a triangular number, a square number, a pentagonal number, a circular number, and the others that are always contained in a plane.

[Col. 1208A] A circular number is one that, when multiplied by itself, returns from itself to itself, beginning from itself; for example, five times five, twenty-five.

A solid number is one contained by length, breadth, and height, such as pyramids, which rise in the form of a flame; cubes, such as dice; and spheres, whose roundness is equal in every direction.

A spherical number, however, is one that, multiplied by a circular number, returns from itself to itself, beginning from itself; for example, five times five, twenty-five. Thus a circle, when multiplied by itself, makes a sphere—that is, five times 25, 125.

When these matters have therefore been carefully considered, remember that this discipline is preferred to the others for the reason stated above: in order to exist, it needs no other discipline. The remaining disciplines that follow, as their very nature and power already show, require the discipline of arithmetic in order to exist and endure. Among the Greeks, Nicomachus explained arithmetic diligently. First Madaurensis Apuleius, and afterward the illustrious Boethius, translated it into Latin and made it available for Roman readers. If anyone, as they say, makes frequent use of these works, he is undoubtedly suffused, insofar as is permitted to human beings, with the clearest understanding.

We have also been granted, in large part, to live under this discipline itself: when we learn the hours, when we calculate the courses of the months, and when we recognize the span of the returning year. Through number we are instructed so that we are not confused. Take calculation away from the world, and everything is enveloped in blind ignorance. Nor can one who does not understand the quantity of calculation differ from the other animals. It is therefore as glorious a thing as it is demonstrably necessary to our life, since through it both our substance is learned with complete certainty and the amount of our expenditures is distributed according to a balanced reckoning. Number orders all things. Through it we learn what we ought to do first and what second. Now let us come to music, which is sweet both by its name and by its distinctive power.

# CHAPTER FIVE. ON MUSIC

A certain Gaudentius, writing about music, says that Pythagoras discovered the beginnings of this art from the sound of hammers and the extension of struck strings. Our friend, the most eloquent man Mutianus, translated it into Latin, so that the quality of the work he undertook might reveal his talent. Clement, the presbyter of Alexandria, in the book he published against the pagans, says that music took its origin from the Muses; and he carefully explains for what reason the Muses themselves were invented. These Muses themselves were called ἀπὸ τοῦ μασενεῖν, that is, “from seeking,” because through them, as the ancients wished, the power of songs and the modulation of the voice were sought. We also find Censorinus, who wrote to Quintus Cerellius about his birthday, where he discussed the discipline of music, as well as another branch of mathematics, which ought not to be neglected. It is useful to read him, so that the matters themselves may be stored more deeply in the mind through frequent meditation.

The discipline of music, therefore, is diffused through all the activities of our life in this way [ed., “from creation”]. First, when we obey the commands of the Creator and serve with pure minds the rules established by him. Whatever we say, or whatever inwardly moves us through the pulsations of our veins, is shown to be joined to the powers of harmony through musical rhythms. Music, indeed, is the science of modulating well; and if we conduct ourselves well, we are always shown to be associated with such a discipline. But when we commit iniquities, we do not possess music. Heaven and earth also, and all that is accomplished in them through heavenly governance, are not without the discipline of music, since Pythagoras testifies that this world was formed and can be governed through music.

Music is also deeply interwoven with religion: the ten-stringed instrument of the Decalogue, the ringing of the lyre, drums, [Col. 1209B] the melody of the organ, and the sound of cymbals; and there is no doubt that the Psalter itself was named after a musical instrument, because it contains within it the exceedingly sweet and pleasing modulation of the heavenly powers.

Let us now discuss the parts of music, as they have been handed down by our predecessors. Music is the discipline or science that speaks about numbers which stand in relations to one another in sounds, such as double, triple, quadruple, and similar ratios, which are called “relations.”

There are three parts of music: Harmonic, Rhythmic, and Metric.

[Col. 1209C] Harmonic science is that music which distinguishes high and low in sounds.

Rhythmic science is that which examines, in the coming together of words, whether the sound coheres well or badly.

Metric science is that which recognizes, by a reasoned method, the measures of different meters—for example, heroic, iambic, elegiac, and the rest.

There are three kinds of musical instruments: percussion instruments, stringed instruments, and wind instruments.

Percussion instruments include bronze and silver vessels, or other objects which, struck with metallic hardness, return a ringing sound with sweetness.

Stringed instruments are strands of strings fastened according to an art, [Col. 1209D] which, struck by a plectrum, delightfully soothe the sense of the ears; among them are the various kinds of lyres.

Wind instruments are those which, filled by air blown into them, are brought to life in the sound of a voice, such as trumpets, reeds, organs, panduriums, and other instruments of this kind.

It remains now that we speak about symphonies. A symphony is a proportioning of a low sound to a high, or of a high to a low, producing a melody, whether in the voice, in percussion, or in breath.

There are six symphonies: first, diatessaron; second, diapente; third, diapason; fourth, diapason together with diatessaron; [Col. 1210A] fifth, diapason together with diapente; sixth, disdiapason.

The diatessaron symphony consists in the epitritic ratio and is made from four sounds, from which it receives its name.

The diapente symphony consists in the hemiolic ratio and is made from five sounds, from which it too receives its name.

The third, diapason, is a symphony also called diocto. It consists in the diplasic ratio, that is, the double ratio, and is made through eight sounds, from which it receives its name, whether diocto or diapason: for among the ancients lyres consisted of eight strings. It is therefore called diapason, as though consisting of all the sounds.

The fourth, diapason together with diatessaron, [Col. 1210B] is a symphony that consists in the ratio which the number 24 has to the number 8; it is made from eleven sounds.

The fifth, diapason together with diapente, is a symphony that consists in the triplasic ratio; it is made through twelve sounds.

The sixth, disdiapason—that is, double diapason—is a symphony that consists in the tetraplasic ratio; it is made through fifteen sounds.

A tone is the difference and quantity of the entire harmonic system, consisting in the accent or pitch of the voice.

There are fifteen tones:

Hypodorian, Hypoiastian, Hypophrygian, [Col. 1210C] Hypoaeolian, Hypolydian, Dorian, Iastian, Phrygian, Aeolian, Lydian, Hyperdorian, Hyperiastian, Hyperphrygian, Hyperaeolian, Hyperlydian.

1. The Hypodorian tone is the lowest-sounding of all, and for this reason is also called the lower tone.

2. The Hypoiastian precedes the Hypodorian by a semitone.

[Col. 1210D] 3. The Hypophrygian precedes the Hypoiastian by a semitone and the Hypodorian by a tone.

4. The Hypoaeolian precedes the Hypophrygian by a semitone, the Hypoiastian by a tone, and the Hypodorian by a tone and a half.

5. The Hypolydian precedes the Hypoaeolian by a semitone, the Hypophrygian by a tone, the Hypoiastian by a tone and a half, and the Hypodorian by two tones.

6. The Dorian precedes the Hypolydian by a semitone, the Hypoaeolian by a tone, the Hypophrygian by a tone and a half, the Hypoiastian by two tones, and the Hypodorian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony.

7. The Iastian precedes the Dorian by a semitone, the Hypolydian by a tone, the Hypoaeolian by a tone and a half, the Hypophrygian by two tones, the Hypoiastian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony—and the Hypodorian by three tones.

8. The Phrygian precedes the Iastian by a semitone, the Dorian by a tone, the Hypolydian by a tone and a half, the Hypoaeolian by two tones, and the Hypophrygian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Hypoiastian by three tones and the Hypodorian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony.

9. The Aeolian precedes the Phrygian by a semitone, the Iastian by a tone, the Dorian by a tone and a half, and the Hypolydian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Hypophrygian by three tones, the Hypoiastian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony—and the Hypodorian by four tones.

10. The Lydian precedes the Aeolian by a semitone, the Phrygian by a tone, the Iastian by a tone and a half, the Dorian by two tones, and the Hypolydian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Hypoaeolian by three tones, the Hypophrygian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony; it precedes the Hypoiastian by four tones and the Hypodorian by four and a half tones.

11. The Hyperdorian precedes the Lydian by a semitone, the Aeolian by a tone, the Phrygian by a tone and a half, the Iastian by two tones, and the Dorian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Hypolydian by three tones, the Hypoaeolian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony; it precedes the Hypophrygian by four tones, the Hypoiastian by four and a half tones, and the Hypodorian by five tones.

12. The Hyperiastian precedes the Hyperdorian by a semitone, the Lydian by a tone, the Aeolian by a tone and a half, the Phrygian by two tones, and the Iastian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Dorian by three tones, the Hypolydian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony; it precedes the Hypoaeolian by four tones, the Hypophrygian by four and a half tones, the Hypoiastian by five tones, and the Hypodorian by five and a half tones.

13. The Hyperphrygian precedes the Hyperiastian by a semitone, the Hyperdorian by a tone, the Lydian by a tone and a half, the Aeolian by two tones, and the Phrygian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Iastian by three tones, the Dorian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony; it precedes the Hypolydian by four tones, the Hypoaeolian by four and a half tones, the Hypophrygian by five tones, the Hypoiastian by five and a half tones, and the Hypodorian by six tones—that is, by the diapason symphony.

14. The Hyperaeolian precedes the Hyperphrygian by a semitone, the Hyperiastian by a tone, the Hyperdorian by a tone and a half, the Lydian by two tones, and the Aeolian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Phrygian by three tones, the Iastian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony; it precedes the Dorian by four tones, the Hypolydian by four and a half tones, the Hypoaeolian by five tones, the Hypophrygian by five and a half tones, and the Hypoiastian by six tones—that is, by the diapason symphony; it precedes the Hypodorian by six and a half tones.

15. The Hyperlydian is the last and highest-pitched of all. It precedes the Hyperaeolian by a semitone, the Hyperphrygian by a tone, the Hyperiastian by two tones, and the Hyperdorian by two and a half tones—that is, by the diatessaron symphony; it precedes the Aeolian by three tones, the Phrygian by three and a half tones—that is, by the diapente symphony; it precedes the Iastian by four tones, the Dorian by four and a half tones, the Hypolydian by five tones, the Hypoaeolian by five and a half tones, and the Hypophrygian by six tones—that is, by the diapason symphony; it precedes the Hypoiastian by six and a half tones and the Hypodorian by seven tones.

Hence it is clear that the Hyperlydian tone, the highest of all, precedes the Hypodorian, the lowest of all, by seven tones. In these tones, as Varro records, such a useful power was displayed that it calmed excited [mss., *ut excitaret*, “so that it might arouse”] minds and even drew animals, as well as serpents, birds, and dolphins, to listen to its modulation.

To say nothing, as though they were fables, of the lyre of Orpheus and the songs of the Sirens: what shall we say about David, who rescued Saul from an unclean spirit through the healing discipline of modulation, and in a new manner restored health to the king through hearing—something the physicians could not accomplish by the powers of herbs (1 Sam. 16:23)? Asclepiades, too, a physician reputed by the testimony of our predecessors to have been extremely learned, is recorded to have restored a certain madman to his natural state through a symphony. Many miracles, moreover, were performed among sick people through this discipline. Heaven itself, as we mentioned above, is said to revolve under the sweetness of harmony. And, to embrace everything briefly, whatever is properly accomplished among heavenly or earthly things according to the disposition of their creator is not excluded from this discipline.

It is therefore an exceedingly pleasing and useful form of knowledge, which both raises our understanding toward heavenly things and caresses our ears with its modulation. Among the Greeks, Alypius, Euclid, Ptolemy, and the other writers taught it through a credible system [mss., “instruction”]. Among the Latins, the illustrious Albinus composed a book on this subject in concise form; I remember that we possessed it in the library at Rome and read it carefully. If it has perhaps been carried off in a barbarian incursion, you have here Gaudentius in the Latin translation of Mutianus. If you reread it with attentive concentration, it opens before you the halls of this science. It is also said that Apuleius of Madaura produced a work on the principles of this subject in the Latin language.

Father Augustine also wrote six books on music, in which he showed that the human voice naturally possesses rhythmic sounds and a modulable harmony in long and short syllables. Censorinus, too, discussed subtly the accents necessary to our voice, saying that they belong to the discipline of music; I have left his work transcribed for you among the others.

# CHAPTER SIX. ON GEOMETRY

Now let us come to geometry, which is the contemplative description of forms and also the visual instruction of philosophers. To exalt it with the most celebrated praises, they testify that their Jupiter was a geometer [mss., *geometriare*, “to do geometry”] in his own works. I do not know whether this should be regarded as praise or blame, since what they depict in colored dust they falsely claim that Jupiter performs in heaven. If, however, it is applied reverently to the Creator and almighty God, this statement may perhaps accord with the truth. For the Geometer—if it is permissible to say so—is the holy Divinity, since he grants diverse species and forms to his creatures, which he continues even today to bring into existence; since by his revered power he distributes the courses of the stars; and since by established lines he makes moving things run and establishes fixed things in a definite place. Whatever is well ordered and completed can be related to the qualities of this discipline.

In Latin, geometry is called “measurement of the earth,” because, as some say, Egypt is reported to have first been divided among its own masters by means of the various forms of this discipline. The teachers of this discipline were formerly called surveyors. But Varro, the most learned of the Latins, records that the origin of this name came about as follows: at first, when peoples wandered about [ed., *vacantibus*, “were unoccupied”], human beings established measurements of lands by setting boundaries, thereby providing the benefits of peace. Then they divided the circle of the entire year according to the number of months; hence the months themselves were called months because they measure the year. But after these things had been discovered, eager students, prompted to learn invisible matters, began to inquire how far the moon was from the earth, how far the sun itself was from the moon, and how far the heavens extended up to their summit. He records that the most skilled geometers attained these measurements. He also reports that the measurement of the whole earth was gathered by a credible method. Thus it came about that the discipline itself received the name geometry, which it has preserved through the long ages. Hence Censorinus, in the book he wrote to Quintus Cerellius, described with meticulous care the very distances and the circuit of heaven and earth, distinguished by a number of stadia. Whoever wishes to examine it will learn many of the mysteries of the philosophers through a brief reading.

Geometry, then, is the discipline of immovable magnitude and forms.

Geometry is divided into:

- the plane;
- magnitude capable of being measured by number;
- rational and irrational magnitude;
- solid figures.

Plane figures are those contained by length and breadth.

A numerable magnitude is one that can be divided by the numbers of arithmetic.

Rational and irrational magnitudes are as follows: rational magnitudes are those whose measure we can know; irrational magnitudes are those whose quantitative measure is not known.

Solid figures are those contained by length, breadth, and height. The entire discipline of geometry is treated through these parts and divisions. The multitude of forms, whether earthly or heavenly, is comprehended by this exposition.

Among the Greeks, Euclid, Apollonius, Archimedes, and other reputable writers arose in this discipline. From among them, the same illustrious Boethius produced a translation of Euclid into the Roman language. If it is reread with diligent care, what is covered by the divisions mentioned above will be recognized with clear understanding [ed., “with intelligence and clear truth”].

## Principles of the discipline of geometry

A point is that which has no part.

A line is length without breadth; the ends of a line are points.

A straight line is one that lies equally with respect to its points.

A surface is that which has length and breadth alone. The boundaries of a surface are lines.

A plane surface is one that lies equally along its straight lines.

A plane angle is the meeting of two lines in a plane that touch one another but do not lie in a straight line. [Col. 1214B] When the lines that contain the angle are straight, the angle is called rectilinear. When a straight line standing upon another straight line makes equal angles around itself, each of the equal angles is right, and the line standing upon the other is called perpendicular. An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle; an acute angle is less than a right angle.

A figure is that which is contained by some boundary or by certain boundaries.

A boundary, moreover, is the limit of anything.

A circle is a plane figure contained by a single line, such that all the straight lines drawn from one point among those located within the figure to the circumference are equal to one another. This point is called the center [Col. 1214C] of the circle.

The diameter of a circle is a certain straight line drawn through the center and terminated at the circumference on both sides; it divides the circle into two equal parts.

A semicircle is a plane figure contained by a diameter and by the circumference intercepted by the diameter.

Rectilinear figures are those contained by straight lines.

A trilateral figure is one contained by three straight lines.

A quadrilateral is one contained by four sides; a multilateral is one contained by more than four sides.

[Col. 1214D] An equilateral triangle, therefore, is one enclosed by three equal sides.

An isosceles triangle is one that has only two equal sides.

A scalene triangle is one that has three unequal sides.

Further, among trilateral figures, an orthogonal figure—that is, a right-angled triangle—is one that has a right angle.

An amblygonium is one that has an obtuse angle, wherever the obtuse angle occurs.

An oxygonium—that is, an acute-angled figure—is one in which all three angles are acute.

Among quadrilateral figures, the square is equilateral and rectangular. A figure that is longer on one side is rectangular, but not equilateral.

A rhombus is equilateral but not rectangular.

A rhomboid is placed in the opposite orientation and has equal lines and angles; it is contained neither by right angles nor by equal sides. Besides these, all quadrilateral figures are called trapezia.

Parallels—that is, alternating straight lines—are those placed on the same plane surface which, when extended in either direction, do not meet on either side.

There are five postulates, which are demanded from every point: to draw a straight line from any point to any point; likewise, to extend a finite line continuously in a straight direction; likewise, to describe a circle with every center and at every distance; and for all right angles to be equal to one another; and, if a line cutting two straight lines makes the two interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, for the straight lines extended indefinitely to meet on the side where the angles terminate in less than two right angles.

The common conceptions of the mind are these: things equal to the same thing are equal to one another. If equal things are subtracted from equal things, the remainders are equal. If equal things are added to equal things, the wholes are also equal. Things that coincide with one another are equal.

A gnomon is a parallelogrammatic area consisting of either one of two figures around the same diagonal, together with the two complements.

A smaller magnitude is a part of a greater magnitude when the smaller measures the greater. A greater magnitude is a multiple of a smaller magnitude whenever the whole of the greater is supplied by an integral measurement of the smaller.

A ratio is the relation arising from the comparison of two related magnitudes with one another. Magnitudes are said to have a ratio to one another when, multiplied by one another, they can surpass one another.

The first magnitude is said to maintain the same ratio to the second magnitude as the third does to the fourth when equal multiples of the first and third magnitudes respectively are equal to equal multiples of the second and fourth, or surpass them equally, or are equally surpassed by them, or are equally equal to them—namely, when they are taken in alternate comparison. Things that retain the same ratio are said to be proportional. But when, among equal multiples, a multiple of the first magnitude surpasses a multiple of the second magnitude, while a multiple of the third magnitude does not surpass a multiple of the fourth magnitude, then the first magnitude is said to have a greater ratio to the second magnitude than the third has to the fourth.

Proportionality is found in at least three terms, when the ratios of proportional things are said to be ratios of the same magnitude: antecedents to antecedents and consequents to consequents. [Col. 1216A] When three magnitudes have been constituted proportionally, the first is said to possess a double ratio to the third compared with its ratio to the second. When four magnitudes have been constituted proportionally, the first is said to possess a triple ratio to the fourth compared with its ratio to the second.

To take conversely is for the consequent to stand to the antecedent as the antecedent stands to the consequent.

To take alternately is for the antecedent to stand to the antecedent as the consequent stands to the consequent.

To take by composition is for the antecedent together with the consequent to stand to the consequent itself.

To take by division is for the excess of the antecedent—that by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent—to stand to the consequent itself; that is, for the excess of the antecedent by which it exceeds the consequent to stand to the consequent itself.

To take backward is for the antecedent to stand to the excess by which the antecedent exceeds the consequent, and for the antecedent to stand to the excess by which it exceeds the consequent.

Confused proportionality is so called when the antecedent stands to the consequent as the consequent stands to the antecedent, and as the consequent stands to some other thing, so that other thing stands to the antecedent. This is an equal relation, with the extremes taken while the means are omitted.

# CHAPTER SEVEN. ON ASTRONOMY

[Col. 1216C] Astronomy remains. If we investigate it with a chaste and moderate mind, it also suffuses our senses, as the ancients say, with great clarity. What is it, after all, to ascend in spirit to the heavens, to examine that entire heavenly structure through an investigatory method [ed., *discurrere*, “range over”], and, with the lofty vision [ed., *subtilitate*, “subtlety”] of the mind, to gather in part what the mysteries of so great a magnitude have concealed? For the world itself, as some say, is reported to have been formed into a spherical roundness, so that the diverse circuit of its things and forms might be enclosed within its revolution. Hence Seneca composed a book in agreement with the philosophers, entitled *On the Form of the World*; we likewise leave it for you to reread.

[Col. 1216D] Astronomy, then, the subject of our discussion, is called the law of the stars, because the stars do not in any way know how to stand still or move except as they have been arranged by their Creator—unless perhaps they are changed by the will of the Divinity when some miracle occurs. Thus Jesus son of Nave is read to have commanded the sun to stand still for three hours at Gibeon (Josh. 10:12); in the days of King Hezekiah, the sun is said to have turned back ten degrees (2 Kings 20:11); and at the passion of the Lord Christ, the sun became dark for three hours (Luke 23:44–45), along with similar events. These are called miracles because marvelous things occur contrary to the customary order of things. The stars fixed in the heavens, as the astronomers say, are carried along; the planets, however—that is, the wandering stars—move, though they complete their courses according to a definite determination.

[Col. 1217A] Astronomy, then, as has already been said, is the discipline that contemplates all the courses and forms of the heavenly bodies and investigates, by an examinatory method, the positions of the stars in relation both to one another and to the earth.

The divisions of astronomy are as follows:

- spherical position;
- spherical motion;
- eastern region;
- western region;
- northern region;
- southern region;
- the hemisphere that is above the earth;
- the hemisphere that is said to be beneath the earth;
- the number of the circular motion;
- the advance, or forward motion, of the stars;
- [Col. 1217B] the withdrawal, or retrograde motion, of the stars;
- the station of the stars;
- increase in the reckoning;
- subtraction from the reckoning;
- the magnitude of the sun, moon, and earth;
- eclipse;
- and the other diagrams contained in these subjects.

Spherical position is the means by which the position of the sphere and its condition are known.

Spherical motion is the means by which the spheres move properly.

The eastern region is where certain stars rise.

The western region is where certain stars set for us.

[Col. 1217C] The northern region is where the sun reaches during the longer days.

The southern region is where the sun reaches during the longer nights.

The hemisphere above the earth is the part of heaven that is entirely visible to us.

The hemisphere beneath the earth is, as they say, the part that cannot be seen.

The number of the circular stars is the means by which it is said to be known how much time each star can take to complete its circle, whether in length or in breadth.

The advance or forward motion of the stars is what the Greeks call προτόδισμον (*protodismon*): when a star seems to constrain its customary motion and advances in some way beyond [Col. 1217D] its customary course.

The withdrawal or retrograde motion of the stars is what the Greeks call πόδισμον or ἀναπόδισμον (*podismon* or *anapodismon*), in which a star, while carrying out its motion, also appears to move backward.

The station of the stars is what the Greeks call στίριγμον (*stirigmon*), because, although a star is always moving, it nevertheless appears to stand still in certain places. Varro, too, in the book he wrote on astrology, records that a star was named from standing.

An increase in the reckoning occurs whenever astronomers, calculating according to astronomical rules, appear to add one reckoning to another.

A subtraction from the reckoning occurs when astronomers, calculating according to astronomical rules, judge that one reckoning must be taken away from another.

The magnitude of the sun, moon, and earth concerns the demonstration that the sun is greater than the earth and the earth greater than the moon, by a certain quantity.

A solar eclipse occurs whenever, on the thirtieth day, the moon itself appears to us and the sun is darkened for us through it.

A lunar eclipse occurs whenever the moon enters the shadow of the earth.

Concerning the astronomical discipline, many volumes have been written in both languages. Among them, however, Ptolemy is regarded as preeminent among the Greeks. He published two books on this subject, one of which he called the smaller and the other the greater *Astronomer*. He also established the canons by which the courses of the stars may be discovered. From these, it does not seem absurd, in my view, to learn the climates, to comprehend the lengths of the hours, to determine the course of the moon for the investigation of Easter, and to understand how solar eclipses occur, lest simple people be disturbed by some confusion.

For there are, as has been said, climates—seven lines, as it were, drawn from east to west—in which both different human customs and certain specially distinct animals are born. They were named from certain famous places: the first is Meroe [mss. *Merobis*], the second Syene, the third Catochoras, that is, Africa, the fourth Rhodes, the fifth the Hellespont, the sixth Mesopotus, and the seventh the Borysthenes.

[Col. 1218C] Sundials, too, which are indicated by the brightness of the sun, stand accurately adjusted by certain distinct rules through each region of the climates. The useful diligence of our predecessors, and especially of Ptolemy, is known to have investigated this matter. There is another benefit of such matters that should not be despised: from them we may learn the favorable time for navigation, the season for plowing [ed., *assensuum*, “of assents”], the heat of the dog days, and the threatening rains of autumn. For the Lord has given each of his creatures some power, so that its proper quality may nevertheless be recognized without harm.

The remaining matters that are joined to the knowledge of the stars—that is, to knowledge of the fates—are unquestionably contrary to our faith, and ought to be ignored in such a way that they should not even appear to have been written. Hence the most learned Father Basil, too, treated this matter with the greatest caution and diligence in the sixth book [read: Homily 6] which he called the *Hexaemeron*, removing such concerns from human minds through a most holy discussion. We said that this work should be read at the outset in the *Octateuch*. Father Augustine likewise mentions this in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine* (chapter 29), saying: “Because the foolish fates of those who sing about them are associated with a most pernicious error, such persuasion is more advantageously and honorably despised if it is unknown.”

The exceedingly curious Varro also compared the shape of the world, in his book on geometry, to a long roundness, drawing its form into the likeness of an egg, which is indeed round in breadth but is demonstrably elongated in length. But it is enough for us to think about this art only as much as is read in the sacred Scriptures, [missing in the manuscripts] because it is exceedingly unfitting to follow human opinion here, where we are known to possess, insofar as it is useful to us, divine teaching.

[Col. 1219]

# COMMENTARY ON SPEECH AND ON THE EIGHT PARTS OF SPEECH, ATTRIBUTED TO M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS (C)

[Col. 1219A] 592 Speech (*oratio*) is so called as though from *oris ratio*, “the reasoning of the mouth.” Its parts are counted as eight. Of these, the Peripatetics wished the first two to be called parts in the proper sense: the noun and the verb. The others are, as it were, appendages, since the pronoun performs the function of the noun; the adverb is not complete without the verb; the participle arises from the noun [Col. 1219B] and the verb; the conjunction joins a noun or a verb; the preposition is placed before a noun or a verb; and the interjection is uttered as something inserted into our speech. We have taught that this utterance necessarily consists of a noun and a verb. For since an utterance is by no means complete from the other parts of speech, if we say “before the temple” and do not add “I walk,” the sentence remains incomplete. But when we say “Cicero wrote” or “the orator taught,” the expression is complete in itself from a noun and a verb.

The Stoics, however, say that there are five parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, and participle. Some say that there are more parts of speech, counting the article among them. The article, which the Greeks enumerate among the parts of speech, is included among pronouns in Latin. The interjection, which the Latins enumerate among the parts of speech, is included among adverbs in Greek.

It must be understood, moreover, that cases occur in four parts: the noun, pronoun, participle, and preposition.

[Col. 1219C] Three are declined by cases: the noun, pronoun, and participle. One is declined by tense and persons, namely, the verb. One is declined by tense and case, namely, the participle. Four are declined neither by tenses nor by cases: the adverb, conjunction, preposition, and interjection. But we should not be confused by the fact that Virgil placed *mane*, “in the morning,” an adverb with gender when he said, “When a new morning had dawned.” This word certainly has gender and case, yet no gender exists without a case.

It must be understood that the noun and the adverb have a certain kinship with one another: one may be placed for the other and signify something else, while retaining its own force.
