For just as nouns, when they have been placed for adverbs, take cases—as in *torvum repente clamat*, “he cries out suddenly and fiercely”; *horrendumque resonat*, “and it resounds terribly”; *dulce sapit*, “it tastes sweet”—for one says *hoc torvum, huius torvi*, “this fierce thing, of this fierce thing,” and so forth, and yet they do not lose their cases when placed for adverbs, so conversely adverbs, when placed for nouns and followed by gender, although they assume the meaning of nouns, nevertheless do not lose the rule of adverbs—namely, that they are not declined.

[Col. 1219D] Some ask why Donatus arranged the parts of speech in this order. We answer that he placed the noun first because nothing can exist before a noun; for, if you remove the designation of the noun, you have no way to name the other parts of speech. The pronoun occupies the second place because, depending on the noun, it takes its place. The verb is placed third because, as we said above, it is found together with the noun as a principal part of speech; it could have occupied the second place, however, if the pronoun did not derive from the noun. The adverb is placed fourth because without a verb it does not fully express its meaning. The participle is placed fifth because it is dependent both on the verb and on the noun. The conjunction is placed sixth because, unless the aforesaid parts of speech precede it, it has nothing to join. The preposition is placed seventh because, unless the noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, participle, [Col. 1220A] or conjunction precedes it, it has nothing before which it can be placed; and it is evident that it is placed only before these. The interjection necessarily remains last, because after the noun there can only be a pronoun; after the pronoun, only a verb; after the verb, only an adverb; after the adverb, only a participle; after the participle, only a conjunction; [Col. 1220B] and after the conjunction, only a preposition. Since the interjection is, as it were, inserted among the eight parts of speech, it could be placed only in the eighth position.

# CHAPTER ONE

## On the Noun

The noun is said to be so called as though it were *notamen*, “a marker,” because it makes each thing known to us. A noun is a part of speech with case, signifying a body or a thing either specifically or generally.

The definition of the noun is distinguished from the other parts of speech in the following way. When it is said “with case,” it is separated from the other five parts of speech that do not have case: the verb, adverb, conjunction, preposition, and interjection. 593 Donatus separates it from the other two parts of speech that do have case—the pronoun and the participle—when he says that the noun signifies something specifically or generally; for no pronoun or participle is found to be proper.

[Col. 1220C] A noun may consist of a body or a thing, and may be proper or common, and may have case; but not every noun necessarily contains all five of these features at once. It always contains three. Thus *homo* (“man”) has case, is corporeal, and is appellative; likewise *pietas* (“piety”) has case, is incorporeal, and is appellative. Every noun must have case; therefore Donatus said “a part of speech with case.” He did not say “with cases,” knowing that some nouns are not inflected through all the cases, and that no noun exists that is entirely without cases.

There are nouns with only one case, such as *sponte* (“of one’s own accord”), *tabo* (“with gore”), and *natu* (“by birth”); with two cases, such as *Jupiter*; with three, such as *templum* (“temple”); and with four, such as *ditionis*, *ditioni*, *ditionem*, *ditione*. Their nominative and vocative are not pronounced unless an additional syllable is supplied, as in *conditio* (“condition”). Nouns with five cases cannot be found, because wherever the nominative is absent, the vocative must necessarily also be absent. A noun with six cases is *doctus-magister* (“learned teacher”).

[Col. 1220D] The quality of nouns is divided into two parts: nouns are either proper or appellative. It must be understood, however, that when appellative nouns are applied to individual persons as proper names, they cease to be appellative; thus, if someone is called *Felix* (“Lucky”), because as far as that person is concerned the name belongs to one individual, it is regarded as a proper name.

Proper names cannot be appellative; conversely, appellative names can be proper, except in the case of the names of mountains and rivers, which we sometimes ourselves make appellative—for example, if we call several people *Mercuries*. When we oppose common names to individual persons, propriety is arranged in this way. If names were proper in a strictly individual sense, when we heard “Alexander did this,” we would not ask further, “Which Alexander did this?” But because we know that many people are called Alexanders, we ask which Alexander did it.

We should understand that it is not correctly said that a single human being possesses either an appellation or a designation, but rather a name, such as *Alexander*. Nor is it correctly said that a thing possesses either a name or an appellation, but rather a designation. [Col. 1221A] Nevertheless, we know that the terms *name*, *appellation*, and *designation* are now used indiscriminately.

There are four kinds of proper names. The *praenomen* (“personal name”) is so called because it precedes the name, as in *Publius Cornelius*. The *nomen* (“family name”) comes from the family, as in *Anicius*. The *cognomen* (“surname”) is properly our own name, as in *Sylla* and *Catilina*. The *agnomen* (“additional name”) is taken either from a virtue or from a fault: from a virtue, as *Africanus*, who conquered Africa; from a fault, as *Naso*, because he had a large nose—hence *Ovidius Naso*; or *Sura*, said of a large calf of the leg, as in *Publius Lentulus Sura*.

We must remember that it is not necessary for all four of these kinds of proper names to be found together. Sometimes we find one, as in *Romulus*; sometimes two, as in *Anicius Marcus*; sometimes three, as in *Lucius Cethegus Catilina*; sometimes all four, as in *Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus*.

The order of questioning should therefore be as follows. When we say, “*Africanus*, what part of speech is it?” we should not immediately answer, “It is an agnomen,” but rather, “It is a noun.” Next, when asked what kind of noun it is, we should answer, “It is a proper noun.” Finally, when asked which kind of proper noun it is, we answer, “An agnomen.”

[Col. 1221B] The same procedure applies to the twenty-seven kinds of appellative nouns. If we ask, “*Homo* (‘man’), what part of speech is it?” we answer, “A noun.” Then, “What kind of noun?”—“An appellative.” Then, “What kind of appellative?”—“A specific one.”

We know that names and personal names may consist of three letters, as *Sex. Roscius*; of two, as *Gn. Pompeius*; or of one, as *C. Caius Verres*.

The question arises why we write *C. Caius* when we say *Gaius* and not *Caius*. The reason is that the ancients did not have the letter G; by using C in certain names, they distinguished meaning through pronunciation. We know that certain words ought to have been pronounced differently. Thus, for example, although *gemma* was written with C, they pronounced it *gemma* with the sound of G, since it ought to have been pronounced with G.

[Col. 1221C] These same personal names sometimes become surnames, as when someone is called *Lucius* or *Gaius*. When they belong individually to a person, they are properly called cognomina; when they are placed before cognomina—that is, before proper names—they are called praenomina, as in *Lucius Sylla*. This, however, should not be allowed to override the rule stated above.

The same sort of quibble is found in the question why, although proper names do not admit a plural number, we read *Curios, magnosque Camillos Scipiadas* (“Curii, and great Camilli, Scipios”). We must understand that *Curios* and *Camillos* do not come from the singular *Curius*—“this Curius”—or from *Camillus*—“this Camillus”—but from a multitude of Curii or Camilli. We say *Curios* and *Camillos* because there was not only one Curius or Camillus. If someone has three slaves named Alexanders, he must call them *Alexandros*. These plural cases do not come from the singular *hic Alexander* (“this Alexander”), but from the plural *Alexandri* (“the Alexanders”).

[Col. 1221D] There are twenty-seven kinds of appellative nouns. Some are corporeal, such as *lignum* (“wood”) and *marmor* (“marble”); some are incorporeal, such as *honor* (“honor”) and *medicina* (“medicine”); and some are primary forms, that is, forms from which derivatives and diminutives are made, such as *schola* (“school”), *scholasticus* (“scholastic”), and *scholasticulus* (“little scholastic”).

According to Donatus, there are three degrees of diminution. As nouns are diminished through these degrees, the number of syllables often increases: *scholasticulus*, *scholasticellus*, *scholasticellulus*. Among the ancients, however, the forms were different: *agnus*, *agnulus*, *agnellus*, *agnicellus*, *agniculus*, *agnicellulus*. Donatus observed this and, so that diminution would not proceed offensively to infinity, wished to say that there were only three degrees of diminution.

He often said that the number of syllables increases for this reason: some nouns are found whose number of syllables not only does not increase through diminution, but actually decreases at a later degree, as *homo*, *homuncio*, *homunculus*, *homulus*.

[Col. 1222A] There are also nouns that are diminutive in form. They are considered diminutives because they bear the appearance of diminutive nouns, such as *fabola*, *macula*, *tabula*, and *ferula*. They are not properly diminutives, however—*fabula*, *macula*, *tabula*, and *ferula*—because their primary forms are not found. We must understand that the form of diminutives is gathered more from reading than from grammatical theory.

Some nouns remain wholly Greek and proceed through all their cases according to Greek declension, such as *Euterpe* and *Melpomene*. Some, when they enter Latin, lose everything Greek about them; thus, when a Greek says Ὀδυσσεύς (*Odysseús*), Latin says 594 *Ulysses*. Some, when translated into Latin speech, lose part of their Greek form; these have also been called *notha* (“bastard” or “mixed” forms). The Greek says *Agamemnon*, while Latin says *Agamemno*.

We know that all Greek nouns ending in the syllable *-on*, when transferred into Latin, lose the *n* and change omega into a shortened *o*. Likewise, all Greek nouns ending in *-e*, when they enter Latin, commonly change that *e* into *a*, specifically in the singular nominative, as *Helene*, *Helena*. But since we have spoken of feminine nouns, such nouns do not undergo that change. Other forms that are read differently, or that are transformed in such a way that they cannot sound harsh, are treated differently: thus *Agane* does not become *Agana*, because of the harshness of the sound.

[Col. 1222B] There are nouns by which one thing is indicated through many names; the Greeks call these *synonyms*. Thus, if we wish to signify earth by many names, we say *humus*, *tellus*, *solum*, and *terra*. Conversely, there are nouns by which many things are signified through one name; the Greeks call these *homonyms*. Thus, if we say *acies*, it is uncertain what thing we mean: it may be the edge of the eyes—that is, their gaze or intentness; the edge of a sword—that is, its sharpness; or an army—that is, its battle order.

There are nouns that descend from fathers, mothers, and ancestors, while nevertheless having a Greek meaning. These nouns are called *patronymics*. Masculine patronymics have three rules according to which they end: they end either in *-des*, *-ius*, or *-on*, as *Atrides*, *Atrius*, and *Atrion*. Those ending in *-on*, however, are not used by Latin speakers.

[Col. 1222C] Feminine patronymics likewise have three forms: they end either in *-eis*, *-ias*, or *-ne*, as *Atreis*, *Atrias*, and *Atrine*; thus Virgil has *Nerine Galatea*. It should be carefully observed that Greek patronymics of any gender are better pronounced according to the Greek rule.

There are other nouns called *thetika*, also called possessives. They derive from the rule of patronymics and end, in their likeness, in *-ius*, but they are distinguished in this way: *Evandrius Pallas* is a patronymic; when we say *Evandrius gladius* (“Evandrian sword”), it is possessive. That is one thing, and this is another.

There are other nouns of intermediate meaning, which some have wished to call epithets when added to other nouns, such as *magnus* (“great”) and *fortis* (“brave”). Unless we add *vir* (“man”) or *exercitus* (“army”), they cannot be complete.

Some nouns express quality, such as *doctus* (“learned”), *magnus* (“great”), *felix* (“fortunate”), and *pulcher* (“beautiful”); some express quantity, such as *longus* (“long”), *brevis* (“short”), and *latus* (“broad”); some express nation, such as *Graecus* (“Greek”), *Italus* (“Italian”), and *Gallus* (“Gallic”); some express place of origin, such as *Alexandrinus* (“Alexandrian”) and *Romanus* (“Roman”); some express number, such as *unus* (“one”) and *duo* (“two”); and some express order, such as *primus* (“first”) and *secundus* (“second”).

Just as we say *alius* (“another”) of many and *alter* (“the other”) of two, so we say *primus* (“first”) of many and *prior* (“earlier” or “the former”) of two. [Col. 1222D]

Some are relational nouns, such as *soror* (“sister”) and *frater* (“brother”); so we say *primus* (“first”) of many and *prior* (“earlier” or “the former”) of two. [Col. 1222D] Some are relational nouns, such as *soror* (“sister”) and *frater* (“brother”); for one cannot speak of a sister where there is no brother, or of a brother where there is no sister.

Others are relational in the way they are situated with respect to one another, such as *dies* (“day”), *lumen* (“light”), *nox* (“night”), *tenebrae* (“darkness”), *nigrum* (“black”), and *album* (“white”). Darkness would not be called darkness except in relation to light.

There is a difference between nouns that are simply called relational and those that are relational in their manner of being situated. The former are used in such a way that they are not altogether opposed to one another; in the latter group, however, what is more opposed than light to darkness, day to night, black to white, or left to right? Their comparative degrees are in use: *dexter*, *dexterior* (“right, more right”); *sinister*, *sinisterior* (“left, more left”); *niger*, *nigrior* (“black, blacker”).

Some nouns are general, such as *ars* (“art”) and the like; some are specific, such as *medicina* (“medicine”), *rhetorica* (“rhetoric”), and *grammatica* (“grammar”). Some are verbal nouns, made from verbs, such as *dictor* (“speaker”) and *procurator* (“administrator”).

[Col. 1223A] It must be understood that such nouns are derived from verbs according to the following rule: in the last tense of the gerundial forms, we turn the final letter into *-or*. Thus from *dicendi*, *dicendo*, *dicendum*, *dictum*, and *dictu* (“of saying,” “by saying,” “for saying,” “said,” “in saying”), we make *dictor* (“speaker”), changing *u* into *o* and adding *r*. Likewise, from *procurandi*, *procurando*, *procurandum*, *procuratum*, and *procuratu* (“of administering,” “by administering,” “for administering,” “administered,” “in administering”), we make the noun *procurator* (“administrator”), and the other forms that belong to this pattern.

Moreover, there are nouns whose status as verbal nouns is uncertain. Such is the question whether one should say *cantor* or *cantator*. We affirm that both are formed according to the rule stated above. From *canto* (“I sing”) come the gerundial forms *cantandi*, *cantando*, *cantandum*, *cantatum*, and *cantatu*, from which comes *cantator* (“singer”). Likewise, from *cano* (“I sing”) come *canendi*, *canendo*, *canendum*, *cantum*, and *cantu*, from which comes *cantor* (“singer”).

The question is also raised whether *auctor* (“author”) derives independently or from a verb. We must understand that it arises independently; it does not have the origin of a verb. The word *augeo* (“I increase”) should not mislead us into thinking that *auctor* comes from it. To increase is one thing; to be an author is another.

[Col. 1223B] Every verb must correspond to the noun derived from it, as *scriptor* (“writer”) comes from *scribo* (“I write”), since every writer writes; and *procurator* comes from *procuro* (“I administer”), since every administrator administers.

There is also another rule that prevents this noun from arising from a verb: verbal nouns end either in *-sor*, as *praecursor* (“forerunner”), or in *-tor*, as *scriptor* (“writer”) and *lector* (“reader”). Those ending in *-sor* do not form feminine counterparts in *-trix*; those ending in *-tor*, however, must form feminine counterparts in *-trix*, as *procurator*, *procuratrix*. If *auctor* had come from a verb and ended in *-tor*, it would necessarily have formed the feminine *auctrix*. But since *auctrix* is not used, Virgil confirms the point when he says: “I am the author of seeing.”

Some nouns resemble participles, such as *sapiens* (“wise”), *potens* (“powerful”), *demens* (“mad”), and *clemens* (“merciful”). If they accept comparison, they are nouns; participles do not accept comparison. Thus *lugens* (“mourning”) does not form *lugentior* (“more mournful”), whereas *demens* does form *dementior*, *dementissimus* (“more mad,” “most mad”).

[Col. 1223C] Some forms resemble verbs, such as *comedo*. When they have case, they are nouns; when they have tense, they are certainly verbs. Thus *comedo* means “a moth” if it is a noun; if it is a verb, it is the first-person singular of an active verb of the third conjugation, “I eat.”

The definition of comparison is this: an expression that prefers one thing to another, although others define it differently. Some say that comparison has four degrees: the positive, as *doctus* (“learned”); the comparative, as *tam doctus* (“as learned”); the prepositive, as *doctior* (“more learned”); and the superlative, as *doctissimus* (“most learned”). They say that *doctior* cannot be called comparative because it seems to prefer rather than to compare.

The definition given above is as follows: “Comparison is an expression that, by comparing one thing with another, prefers one to the other.” For it appears that the comparative degree *tam doctus* (“as learned”) does not so much prefer one person to another as make them similar.

[Col. 1223D] The question is asked why the positive degree is so called, when only the other degrees possess the property of comparison. The answer should be that we would not recognize those degrees unless there were another 595 degree that lacked the position of comparison.

The question is also raised concerning the singular nominative case: why is it called a case? The other cases are called cases because they make the noun fall, as *doctus*, *docti*, *docto*, *doctum*, *docto*, *docto* (“learned,” in its various cases). But for this very reason—that nothing would be said to fall unless there were something from which it could fall, and nothing would be inflected unless it had previously been straight—the nominative is called a case because it shows the noun falling through the other cases.

The positive degree has many forms. It may end in *-us*, as *doctus* (“learned”); in *-a*, as *docta*; in *-um*, as *doctum*; in shortened *-is*, as *fortis* (“brave”); in lengthened *-is*, as *dis*, *ditior*, *ditissimus* (“wealthy,” “wealthier,” “wealthiest”); in *-e*, as *forte*; in *-ens*, as *sapiens*; in *-ans*, as *elegans* (“elegant”); in *-ix*, as *felix* (“fortunate”); in *-er*, as *pulcher* (“beautiful”); or in *-es*, as *dives*, *divitior*, *divitissimus* (“rich,” “richer,” “richest”), along with any other forms that we may be able to find.

[Col. 1224A] The comparative, however, has only two patterns. It ends either in *-ior*, as *doctior* (“more learned”) and *melior* (“better”), and has a common gender, except for the one form *senior* (“older”); for one cannot say *senior* of a woman. Or it ends in *-ius*, as *doctius* (“more learned”) and *melius* (“better”). This is the comparative degree of the neuter gender, as *doctius mancipium* (“a more learned slave”) and *melius templum* (“a better temple”).

There is also a comparative degree of the adverb. We say *doctius scripsit* (“he wrote more learnedly”), and *melius fecit* (“he did better”). But when *doctius* is directed toward a noun, it is the neuter comparative; when it is directed toward a verb, it is the comparative of the adverb.

The superlative has three forms: it ends in *-us*, as *doctissimus* (“most learned”); in *-a*, as *doctissima*; or in *-um*, as *doctissimum*. It should not be omitted that when we remove *-rimus* or *-simus* from every superlative, the nature of the positive can be discovered. Thus, from *pulcherrimus* (“most beautiful”), when the final disyllabic ending is removed, *pulcher* remains as the positive. This enables us to recognize nouns whose form is otherwise in question.

[Col. 1224B] The question is whether one should say *acris* or *acer*. It is agreed that both are used today: *acer* of a man, as in Virgil: “Pelops, distinguished by his ivory shoulder, fierce”; *acris* of a woman, as in Horace: “The fierce winter is dissolved.”

Appellative nouns are compared, and those appellative nouns that derive either from quality or quantity are divided into three parts. Those deriving from quality concern the mind, as *prudens* (“wise”) and *honestus* (“honorable”); the body, as *niger* (“black”) and *pulcher* (“beautiful”); or external circumstances, as *fortunatus* (“fortunate”) and *felix* (“happy”). Those deriving from quantity are derived from measurement, which proceeds only from the body, as *longus* (“long”) and *brevis* (“short”).

Not all nouns signifying quality or quantity are compared; rather, those that are compared belong to quality or quantity. A noun of quality may be found that is not compared, such as *mediocris* (“moderate”). Sometimes only one degree is found, sometimes two, sometimes three. But where the comparative is not found, we should place an adverb with the positive to fulfill the function of a comparative, as with *pius* (“pious”), which does not form *pior* but is expressed as *magis pius* (“more pious”).

[Col. 1224C] We must remember to answer as follows when asked, “What is that man like?” Since we have been asked about quality, we name one of the three qualities: “He is learned,” “beautiful,” or “a beggar.” We do not say, on the basis of quality, “He is long” or “short.” When we are asked, “How large is he?” we can answer only from measurement: “He is long,” “broad,” or “short.”

Nor should we be troubled by Virgil’s applying a noun of quantity to the mind: “Great-souled Aeneas.” Here he wished to imitate the Greek; he did not mean that quantity derives from the mind, but that he wished to praise the quality of the mind through quantity.

We recognize anomalous nouns in comparison by this sign: the first syllable that they have in the positive is lost in the comparative. Thus *bonus* (“good”) forms *melior*, *optimus* (“better,” “best”); *malus* (“bad”), *peior*, *pessimus* (“worse,” “worst”); *magnus* (“great”), *maior*, *maximus* (“greater,” “greatest”). It is certain that only these three are defective in comparison.

[Col. 1224D] The positive degree is called complete and absolute because the force of comparison properly belongs to the comparative and superlative degrees, not to the positive. The comparative is often placed in such a way that it signifies more than the superlative, as when we say, “He is more learned than any most learned man.” Sometimes the comparative signifies less than the positive, as if we wished to say, “The Pontic Sea is sweeter than the rest”; for no sea is not only sweeter, but not even sweet. Sometimes the comparative takes on the force of the positive, as in Virgil: “The elder Charon, but his old age was fresh and green for the god.” Here *senior* (“elder”) is used for *senex* (“old”); there was not another Charon in comparison with whom this one would be called older.

There are nouns diminutive in sound but comparative in meaning, such as *grandiusculus* (“rather large”), *maiusculus* (“rather great”), and *minusculus* (“rather small”).

We do not place the five adverbs of comparison—*tam* (“so”), *minus* (“less”), *minime* (“least”), *magis* (“more”), and *maxime* (“most”)—with the comparative and superlative. They are added only to the positive. These adverbs were devised for nouns that cannot have a comparative or superlative. Thus, because *mediocris* does not form *mediocrior*, we say *magis mediocris* (“more moderate”); and because it does not form *mediocrissimus*, we say *maxime mediocris* (“most moderate”).

[Col. 1225A] It is superfluous to add these adverbs to nouns that take a comparative and superlative without them. Thus one should not say *magis doctus* (“more learned”) when one can say *doctior*, or *maxime doctus* (“most learned”) when the superlative *doctissimus* is available.

The comparative degree serves three cases: the nominative, with the particle *quam* (“than”) inserted, as *doctior hic quam ille* (“this man is more learned than that one”); the ablative, as *doctior illo* (“more learned than that one”); and the seventh case, as *doctior ab illo* (“more learned than that one”).

This degree is recognized as serving both the singular and the plural number. Today, however, the comparative is considered best expressed through the seventh case. No one should therefore say needlessly that the seventh case is unnecessary because it signifies the same thing as the ablative. Let him understand that the two differ greatly.

It is one thing to say *illo praesente suscipi* (“to receive something while he is present”), and another to say *ab illo praesente suscipi* (“to receive something from him while he is present”). Through the seventh case, the meaning is that one received something while someone—one does not know whom—was present; through the ablative, the meaning is that one received it from the person who was present.

[Col. 1225B] We must understand that if we wish to prefer one thing to another through the comparative, we may place it before a noun of its own gender or of another gender and say *doctior orator oratoribus* (“a more learned orator than the orators”) and *doctior orator grammaticis* (“a more learned orator than the grammarians”).

When we wish to express preference through the superlative—which properly governs only the plural genitive—we must place it before a noun of its own gender and say *doctissimus orator oratorum* (“the most learned of the orators”) and *doctissimus grammaticus grammaticorum* (“the most learned of the grammarians”).

We should not be troubled by the fact that we read the superlative governing a singular genitive, as in Virgil, *ditissimus agri* (“the richest of the land”) and *fortissimus gentis* (“the bravest of the people”). Although these 596 forms are singular in sound, they are plural in meaning. When we say *ditissimus agri* and *fortissimus gentis*, we must understand that the thing consists of many parts.

The superlative is sometimes found with the same meaning as the positive and is not compared with anything, as when we say *Jupiter Optimus Maximus* (“Jupiter, Best and Greatest”). There are no other Jupiters, one good and another better, in comparison with whom this Jupiter could be called Best and Greatest.

[Col. 1225C] There are six genders of nouns: masculine, as *hic Cato* (“this Cato”); feminine, as *haec musa* (“this Muse”); neuter, as *hoc monile* (“this necklace”); common of two genders, as *hic et haec sacerdos* (“this male or female priest”); common of three genders, as *hic, haec, hoc felix* (“this fortunate man, woman, or thing”); and *epicoenon*, called in Latin *promiscuum* (“indiscriminate”), as *passer* (“sparrow”) and *aquila* (“eagle”).

There is a difference between the common gender and the epicoenon. In the common gender, we vary the article according to sex; in the epicoenon, the noun is the same and there is one article. The epicoenon is defined as a gender in which sex is not easily detected, as *hic piscis* (“this fish”). Although there may be sailors who by skill catch a female fish, because its sex is not distinguished, the article is not changed.

If an expression should occur in which someone, having two sparrows, says, for example, “Mine is male,” and adds, “Yours is female,” he does not commit solecism in gender. If he says *femina tua* (“your female”), after having said *masculus meus* (“my male”), he makes the epicoenon common, as though he were saying *hic et haec passer* (“this male and female sparrow”). But we should understand that the proper expression is: “Let mine be the male and yours the female; this is a sparrow.”

[Col. 1225D] Of the genders, we find two principal genders, masculine and feminine. Everything descends from these two genders. The neuter exists because it is neither masculine nor feminine, as when we say *hoc scamnum* (“this bench”). It is so called because, just as masculine and feminine things either generate or are generated, the neuter does neither.

No one should object by asking why *paries* (“wall”), since it neither generates nor is generated, is masculine. We must understand that with names of this kind, reading or Latin usage assigns the article. Or why, although *mancipium* (“slave”) may be of masculine or feminine gender, is it said to be neuter? When we say *mancipium* without immediately adding *puerum* (“boy”) or *puellam* (“girl”), it is as though it were neither masculine nor feminine, but neuter.

The common gender exists because the articles are changed under one name, whether it signifies a male or a female. The word *omne* (“every” or “all”) signifies masculine, feminine, and neuter because, as we said above, it could not exist unless those two genders existed from which it derived. It comprehends both this and that in one name.

The epicoenon is so called because it is either masculine or feminine with respect to both sexes.

[Col. 1226A] There are also nouns that sound masculine but are understood as feminine, as when we say *Eunuchum comoediam* (“the comedy Eunuchus”). Conversely, some sound feminine but are understood as masculine, such as *Sylla* and *Catilina*. Others sound neuter but are shown to be feminine, as *Phronesium mulier* (“the woman Phronesium”) and *Glycerium meretrix* (“the prostitute Glycerium”). Others, conversely, sound feminine but are neuter in meaning, such as *poema* (“poem”) and *toreuma* (“embossed work”). Others have a masculine sound but a neuter meaning, such as *vulgus* (“the crowd”) and *pelagus* (“the sea”).

There are also nouns that differ in the plural from the gender they have in the singular, such as *hoc balneum*, *hae balneae* (“this bath,” “these baths”); *hic tartarus*, *haec tartara* (“this Tartarus,” “these Tartara”); *hoc caelum*, *hi caeli* (“this heaven,” “these heavens”).

[Col. 1226B] There are nouns of uncertain gender between masculine and feminine, such as *finis* (“end”) and *dies* (“day”). We read: “What end of labors do you grant, great king?” Elsewhere: “This end of Priam’s fates.” Of *dies* he says: “The final day has come,” and elsewhere: “Await this happy day with sorrow.”

There are also nouns of uncertain gender between masculine and neuter, such as *vulgus* (“crowd”) and *frenum* (“bridle”); for *frenus* and *vulgus* are of uncertain gender. We read: “I saw the bridles sounding in the stall,” and: “The bridles of the Pelethronian Lapiths.” *Vulgus* is masculine here: “to scatter ambiguous words among the crowd.” It is neuter here: “the ignoble crowd.”

There are also nouns of uncertain gender between feminine and neuter, such as *buxus* (“boxwood”), *prunus* (“plum tree”), and *malus* (“apple tree”). We read: “The drums call you, and the boxwood”; elsewhere: “the lathe-turned boxwood.” The rest can be recognized from broad reading. When these words refer to fruits, they are neuter; when they refer to trees, they are feminine. Sometimes names of trees are masculine, such as *oleaster* (“wild olive”); for we read, “the sacred wild olive.”

[Col. 1226C] There are also nouns with fixed gender that cannot produce another gender from themselves, such as *pater* (“father”) and *mater* (“mother”); one cannot say *patra* or *matra*. There are mobile nouns, which are either proper and form only two genders, as *Marcius*, *Marcia*, or appellative, as *bonus*, *bona*, *bonum* (“good,” masculine, feminine, neuter).

There are others that are transferred in part into another gender, such as *gallus*, *gallina* (“rooster,” “hen”); *draco*, *dracaena* (“dragon,” “female dragon”); *rex*, *regina* (“king,” “queen”). Since we do not say *gallus*, *galla*; *draco*, *draca*; or *rex*, *rega*, they are said to be neither entirely fixed nor entirely mobile.

They are not entirely fixed because they form *gallus*, *gallina*; *draco*, *dracaena*; and *rex*, *regina*. Nor are they entirely mobile because, when they are converted into the feminine, they retain the likeness of the first syllable.

There are also primary nouns which, when they form diminutives from themselves, change gender. Thus *rana* (“frog”) does not form *ranuncula* but *ranunculus*; and *pistrinum* (“mill” or “bakery”) does not form *pistrillum* but *pistrilla*.

Sometimes diminutive nouns are found that signify more than their primary nouns, as *acus*, *acicula* (“needle,” “small needle”). *Acus* is the needle with which clothes are mended; *acicula* is the needle women use for adorning the head.

[Col. 1226D] Nouns ending in *-a* are either masculine, as *Sylla*; feminine, as *musca* (“fly”); neuter, as *toreuma*, which is Greek; or common, as *rana* (“frog”) and *advena* (“newcomer”). No Latin neuter noun ends in *-a* in the singular nominative, except one, *Thoria*, the name of a river, which is read in Sallust.

Nouns ending in the vowel *e* are either feminine but Greek, as *Agane*, or neuter but Latin, as *monile* (“necklace”). Masculine nouns do not fall under this rule.

There are two foreign nouns ending in the vowel *i*, both neuter: *gummi* (“gum”) and *sinapi* (“mustard”). There are two anomalous forms: *frugi* (“thrifty,” “useful”) and *nihili* (“worthless”).

Nouns ending in the vowel *o* in the nominative are either masculine, as *Cicero*, or feminine, as *imago* (“image”).

Nouns ending in the vowel *u* are neuter only, such as *cornu* (“horn”), *gelu* (“frost”), *tonitru* (“thunder”), *genu* (“knee”), and *veru* (“spit”).

[Col. 1227A] Nouns ending in consonants have multiple rules. Donatus passed over them because Probus has produced a fuller little book on the structure of these nouns.

597 The numbers of nouns are two: singular and plural. A third number, the dual, is also used, but only with two nouns, *duo* (“two”) and *ambo* (“both”). When I say “two have come,” I signify neither one nor many; for, speaking of two, I cannot say “all have come.”

There are also nouns whose singular and plural nominatives are alike, such as *nubes* (“cloud”) and *dies* (“day”); for this reason they are called common in number.

There are also masculine nouns without a plural number, such as *pulvis* (“dust”); one does not say *pulveres*, although we read in Horace: “to scatter nine-year-old dust.”

[Col. 1227B] There are likewise masculine nouns found only in the plural, such as *Quirites* (“Roman citizens”), although we read *hunc Quiritem* (“this Roman citizen”), as in: “Who restored you as a Roman citizen?”

There are feminine nouns found only in the singular, such as *pax* (“peace”) and *lux* (“light”), although we read *has paces* (“these peaces”) and *has luces* (“these lights”).

There are also nouns that are always plural, such as *calendae* (“calends”) and *nundinae* (“market days”). There are neuter nouns that are always singular, such as *pus* (“pus”), *virus* (“poison”), *aurum* (“gold”), and *ferrum* (“iron”).

We must understand that almost everything measured or weighed does not admit a plural number, although usage has already claimed many such forms for itself, as when we say *vina* (“wines”), *mella* (“honeys”), and *hordea* (“barleys”).

There are also neuter nouns that are always plural, such as *haec arma* (“these arms/weapons”) and *haec moenia* (“these walls”); they do not form *armum* or *moenium*. *Saturnalia* does not form *hoc Saturnale*. But if it is a temple, it is declined through both numbers: *hoc saturnale templum* (“this Saturnalian temple”), *haec saturnalia templa* (“these Saturnalian temples”). If it is the noun meaning, as it were, a festival day, it exists only in the plural number.

We should understand that with nouns that do not admit a singular number, we add *uni* for masculine nouns, *unae* for feminine nouns, and *una* for neuter nouns. Thus we say *uni cancelli* (“one set of latticework”), *unae nuptiae* (“one wedding”), and *una moenia* (“one set of walls”), as in Terence: “Make two weddings for me out of one wedding”; and in Sallust: “After these men had assembled within one set of walls.”

[Col. 1227C] We should understand, however, that we speak superfluously when we say *homo unus advenit* (“one man arrived”), since the noun *homo* already signifies one.

There are also nouns singular in form but plural in meaning, such as *populus* (“people”) and *concio* (“assembly”). When we say *populus currit* (“the people is running”), it sounds as though everyone is running, but it nevertheless does not signify the plural number.

Some think that the plural number is superfluous in these nouns, since their singular contains the plural number within itself. Thus we say *hic populus* in the singular and *hi populi* in the plural. Although *populus* signifies a plural number, it refers to one nation; *populi*, however, refers to different nations.

Conversely, there are nouns plural in form but singular in meaning, such as *Papiae* and *Puteoli*. They are not expressed in the plural because there are many Papiae or many Puteoli, but because their singular number has never existed in reading.

[Col. 1227D] How many forms do nouns have? Two: simple and compound.

A noun is simple when, after it has been divided, the division yields nothing Latin, as *medicina* (“medicine”); or when it yields something, it is not like the meaning from which the noun derives.

Thus let us divide *magister* (“teacher”) into *magis*, an adverb of comparison, and *ter*, an adverb of number. When we say *magister*, it is not of the compound form. Although it has been divided into two adverbs, it is nevertheless said to have a simple form, because the division yielded nothing resembling its principal meaning, but something unlike *magister*. Yet *magis* is not an adverb, although it is so divided.

A letter, whenever it occurs in the middle of a word, always passes into the beginning of the following syllable. For this reason the Greeks call it ἀρχικὸν στοιχεῖον (*archikon stoicheion*), that is, “an initial element.”

A noun is compound because, when divided, it yields something Latin or something resembling itself, as *indoctus* (“unlearned”). For two complete forms are found that agree with the meaning of this noun, from which it has been separated.

[Col. 1228A] This compound form is made in four ways: either we find two complete forms, as *suburbanus* (“suburban”); or two corrupted forms, as *municeps* (“municipal citizen”); or a complete and a corrupted form, as *insulsus* (“witless”); or a corrupted and a complete form, as *nugigerulus* (“carrying trifles”).

Some ask why, when Donatus says that nouns are compounded, he adds “from two corrupted forms.” A thing cannot be compound unless it is made either from two complete forms, from a complete and a corrupted form, or from a corrupted and a complete form.

We must understand, however, that a corrupted noun is defined as one that, when separated, can return to its complete form. Indeed, it would not be called corrupted unless it had once been intact. Thus, when we say *municeps*, it is derived from *munera capiens* (“one who receives offices or duties”), but afterward it was corrupted through contraction into a single noun.

Therefore, when we ask, “What form does *municeps* have?” we must not be misled into answering “simple,” supposing that *municeps* has no components, as *paries* (“wall”) does. That is not true. *Paries* is said to have a simple form because, when separated, as we said above, it cannot return to an intact form. Therefore, when we hear that a noun has a simple form, we do not ask further from which forms it is made.

[Col. 1228B] There is a compound word formed from certain complete elements, taking the division itself, but not the same accent or the same metrical foot that the word from which these elements derive possessed. Thus, if someone asks, “What form does *Lucifer* (‘light-bearer’) have?” and says that the noun has a compound form made from a complete and a corrupted form, as though it were derived from *huic luci* (“to this light”), he does not know that in *Lucifer* the syllable *ci* is shortened, whereas in *huic luci* it is lengthened.

With these matters thus established, we must above all understand that, in analyzing a compound form, we should seek no case other than the singular nominative. We must also remember that compound nouns cannot themselves be compounded further, as in *impius*, although Donatus teaches that nouns can be compounded from several elements, as in *inexpugnabilis* and *imperterritus*. In double nouns, one must observe the following: if there are two nominatives, we decline both parts, as in *homo bonus* [Col. 1228C]; if a nominative is followed by any other case, we decline the first part, as in *Dominus servorum*; if any case other than the nominative precedes a following nominative, we decline the second part, as in *jurisperitus*. These rules, however, must be observed in every noun and number, as in *Jupiter Optimus Maximus Capitolinus*.

It must be understood that proper names cannot be compounded; common nouns, however, can be compounded when either they are attested as compounds or, when compounded, they produce a pleasing sound to the ear.

## On the Cases

There are six cases. Why the nominative is called a “case” has been explained above. The ancients [598] treat the nominative and vocative as alike; hence in Virgil too we find:

> *Fluvius regnator aquarum*—“The river, ruler of the waters”—

and:

> *Duc, ait, et Rutulos equites Messapus in armis.*  
> “Lead,” he says, “the Rutulian horsemen in arms, Messapus.”

[Col. 1228D] Hence Donatus also records that these are called the “straight” cases, and the remaining ones oblique. The ablative does not exist among the Greeks, and for that reason some call it the Latin case, while others call it the sixth. Some posit a case which they call the seventh; how much it differs from the ablative, and how necessary it was to posit it, we demonstrated in the preceding discussion.

There are also six case-forms. From them we understand through how many variations nouns are inflected, or how many similar cases each noun possesses. For some nouns retain virtually one and the same pattern throughout all their cases, as when we say: *nequam*, *hujus nequam*, *huic nequam*, *hunc nequam*, *o nequam*, *ab hoc nequam*. Some have two patterns, as *cornu*: the nominative, accusative, and vocative have a shortened *u*, while the genitive, dative, and ablative have a lengthened one. Some have three patterns, as *templum*: the nominative, accusative, and vocative have one pattern, as in *hoc templum, hoc templum, o templum* [Col. 1229A].

Some have four patterns, as *species*: the nominative and vocative have one pattern, as in *haec species* and *o species*; the genitive and dative have one pattern, as in *hujus speciei* and *huic speciei*; the accusative has one, *hanc speciem*; and the ablative has one, *ab hac specie*. Some have five patterns, as *hic doctus*: the nominative alone has one pattern; the genitive another, *hujus docti*; the dative and ablative share one, *huic docto* and *ab hoc docto*; the accusative has one, *hunc doctum*; and the vocative another, *o docte*. Some have six patterns, as *unus*, since it varies in each individual case.

There are also nouns called *aptota* (“uninflected”), not because they have only one case, but because they are not inflected. They are also called *monoptota*, because they preserve similar cases throughout their declension and have no distinct number of their own. For when I say *frugi*, it is uncertain which case or which number I am uttering.

It must also be understood that we decline numbers from one through three. From four through one hundred, declension does not proceed; from two hundred onward to infinity, all are declined, except *mille*, which is not declined in the singular. In the plural, however, although it is written with a single *l*, it is declined.

There are nouns which, when we use them in speech, govern different cases. Some govern the genitive, as *ignarus belli* or *ignarus bellorum*; others only the dative, as *amicus bono*, although Terence joined it with a nominative when he said:

> *Amicus meus summus popularis Getha.*  
> “My friend Getha, a most intimate fellow-citizen.”

Others govern the accusative, but by a figure of speech, as *praescius futura*; it is properly said *praescius futurorum*. Others govern the ablative, as *dignus munere*, *mactus virtute*. Others govern the seventh case, as *secundus a primo*; for we cannot say *secundus primo*, *secundus primi*, *secundus primorum*, or anything similar.

## On the Declensions

[Col. 1229C]

There are five kinds of declension.

The first is that which forms the singular genitive with the diphthong *ae*, in both the masculine and feminine genders, as *hic Aeneas, hujus Aeneae*; *haec musa, hujus musae*. In the neuter gender it is either not found or occurs in such a way that it shares its form with the masculine or feminine gender, as *advena*. This first declension ends the nominative in three ways: it ends either in *a*, *es*, or *as*, as *musa, Anchises, Aeneas*. But when we have stated beforehand that the nominative ends in *es* and the genitive in *ae*, no one should suppose that every noun ending in *a*, *es*, or *as* must necessarily belong to the first declension. Rather, it must be understood that nouns of the first declension necessarily end their singular nominative in one of these letters.

The second declension is that which forms the singular genitive with *i*. It includes the masculine, feminine, and neuter genders, as *Virgilius, Virgilii*; *fraxinus, fraxini*; *prandium, prandii*. It must be clearly understood that in this declension all nouns form the singular genitive with a single *i*, except those ending in *ius*, as *Mercurius, Mercurii*, or in *ium*, as *convivium, convivii*. This second declension ends the singular nominative in five ways: it ends in *er*, *ium*, *eus*, *ir*, or *us*, as *piger, pigri*; *negotium, negotii*; *Tydeus, Tydei*; *vir, viri*; *doctus, docti*. Yet we must not separate the syllables and say *Tydeus, Tydei* in such a way as to make it appear to belong to the fifth rather than the second declension; rather, we must contain it within the single diphthong of that syllable, saying *Tydeus, Tydei*. Greek nouns receive this diphthong; it is not found in Latin nouns. Concerning this declension, we must also point out that not every singular nominative ending in one of these five ways must necessarily belong to the second declension; but every noun belonging to the second declension must necessarily end its nominative in one of these five ways.

The third declension is that which forms the singular genitive with the syllable *is*. It includes the masculine, feminine, and neuter genders, as *Cicero, Ciceronis*; *Juno, Junonis*; *marmor, marmoris*. It also includes the common gender, as *sacerdos, sacerdotis*, and nouns of all three genders, as *demens, hujus dementis*.

This third declension ends the singular nominative in forty-one ways: in *a*, *e*, *o*, *c*, *t*, *al*, shortened *el*, shortened *il*, lengthened *il*, *ol*, shortened *ul*, *an*, shortened *en*, lengthened *en*, lengthened *on*, either quantity of *ar*, shortened *er*, lengthened *er*, either quantity of *or* and *ur*, lengthened *as* and *es*, shortened *es*, either quantity of *is*, shortened *os*, lengthened *os*, lengthened *us*, shortened *us*, shortened *ax* and *ex*, lengthened *ex*, shortened *ix* and *ox*, lengthened *ox*, shortened *ux*, lengthened *ux*, only lengthened *ans* and *ens*, shortened *ons*, lengthened *ons*, and lengthened *uns* [Col. 1230B].

Examples are: neuter *toreuma, toreumatis*; *dulce, dulcis*; *ordo, ordinis*; *lac, lactis*; *caput, capitis*; *tribunal, tribunalis*; *fel, fellis*; *pugil, pugilis*; *sol, solis*; *consul, consulis*; *Titan, Titanis*; *far, faris*; [599] *cadaver, cadaveris*; *ver, veris*; *marmor, marmoris*; *ebur, eboris*; *fur, furis*; *libertas, libertatis*; *miles, militis*; *pes, pedis*; *navis, lis, litis*; *os, ossis*; *os, oris*; *vetus, veteris*; *senectus, senectutis*; *capax, capacis*; *senex, senis*; *lex, legis*; *pix, picis*; *nox, noctis*; *vox, vocis*; *crux, crucis*; *lux, lucis*; *infans, infantis*; *sapiens, sapientis*; *insons, insontis*; *pons, pontis*; *aruns, aruntis*.

It must be understood, however, that all nouns ending in *-ons* and *-ens* form their genitive with *-tis*, except two nouns, *frons* and *lens*. When we mean a part of the head, we say *frontis*; when we mean a leaf, *frondis*. Likewise, if we mean the animal, *lendis*; if the legume, *lentis*. But no one should suppose that *hujus glandis* is correct because it is read that way in Virgil [Col. 1230C]; let him understand that Virgil used it as a nominative. The reader should recognize here that not every noun ending in one of these forty-one ways must necessarily belong to the third declension; but every noun belonging to the third declension must necessarily derive its nominative from one of these forty-one forms.

The fourth declension is that which forms the singular genitive with *us* or *u*. It uses *us* in the masculine and feminine genders, as *hic versus, haec porticus, hujus versus, hujus porticus*; but *u* only in the neuter gender, as *hoc cornu, hujus cornu*; *hoc veru, hujus veru*; *hoc gelu, hujus gelu*, and so forth. This fourth declension ends the singular nominative in two ways, *us* and *u*, as *hic gradus, hujus gradus*; *hoc gelu, hujus gelu*. Here it must be understood that not every noun ending in *us* or *u* must necessarily belong to the fourth declension; rather, nouns of the fourth declension must necessarily have a singular nominative ending in *us* or *u*.

[Col. 1230D] The fifth declension is that which forms the singular genitive with *e* and *i* as separate syllables. It is exclusively feminine, except for *dies*, whose gender is uncertain. The *e* preceding *s* is lengthened in the genitive when the singular nominative has *i* and *es*, as *series, seriei*; it is shortened when a consonant precedes it, as *fides, fidei* and *res, rei*. This fifth declension ends the nominative in one way only: it ends in *es*, as *species, speciei*. Yet not every feminine nominative ending in *es* must necessarily belong to the fifth declension; rather, a noun belonging to the fifth declension must necessarily have a singular nominative ending in *es*.

All nouns, except *aptota*, which sometimes end in consonants, as *nequam*, end their singular ablative either in *a*, as *ab hac musa*; in *e*, as *ab hoc fonte*; in *i*, as *ab hac puppi*; in *o*, as *ab hoc docto*; or in *u*, as *ab hoc fluctu*. Those ending in *a* [Col. 1231A] form the plural genitive in *-rum* and the plural dative and ablative in *-is*, as *ab hac musa, harum musarum, his et ab his musis*. But with some nouns we shorten the rule in order to distinguish gender, as *a filia, filiarum, filiabus*. If we wished to follow Donatus, we would have to say *Romanabus* and *casabus*. But it is established that this is done in those cases which create disputes in wills: if someone has children of both sexes and writes, “I leave this to my sons,” it is uncertain whether he meant sons or daughters. In usage, however, we say *equabus* and *mulabus*; and the rule of correct speech has lengthened this form in nearly these four nouns: *equa, equarum, equabus*; *mula, mularum, mulabus*; *filia, filiarum, filiabus*; *dea, dearum, deabus*. This is the rule of the first declension.

Nouns ending in shortened *e* form the plural genitive in the following way: they lose the *e* and receive *um*, as *ab hoc pariete, horum parietum*. We take this precaution so that no one may object to us: “Why [Col. 1231B] did he say that nouns ending in lengthened *e* form their plural genitive in *-rum*?” For nouns ending in shortened *e* are also found to form it in *-rum*, as *ab hac muliere, harum mulierum*; *ab hoc munere, horum munerum*; *ab hoc funere, horum funerum*. The answer must be given as follows: once the *e* has been removed, whatever consonant is found sounds together in the same syllable. If one joins *-rum* without removing the *e* and says *muliere, mulierum*, the question seems justified. The same applies if someone asks why *ab hoc pariete* becomes *horum parietum*, ending in *-tum* rather than *-um*; why *nomine* becomes *nominum*, with *-num* rather than *-um*; or why *ab hoc codice* becomes *codicum*, with *-cum* rather than *-um*. Yet the *t*, *r*, *n*, and *c* are not added together with *um*; they are natural elements, running through nearly all the cases.

These matters should not trouble us excessively, since the grammarian did not say, “Some nouns end in *-tum* in the plural genitive, some in *-num*, some in *-rum*, and some in *-cum.” Rather, because the rule was not carefully stated [Col. 1231C], this question appears to arise.

It should certainly be understood that one noun contradicts this rule: *ab hoc vase, vasorum, vasis*. For the sake of euphony, three cases have been excepted from the second-declension pattern. The plural genitive, which proceeds in *-rum*, ought to have ended in *-um*, as *horum vasum*; the plural dative and ablative, which end in *-is*, ought to have ended in *-bus*, as *his et ab his vasibus*. But because these forms are harsh to pronounce, the ear rejects them. This is the rule of the third declension—not because all third-declension nouns are declined according to it, but because nouns declined according to it belong to the third declension.

Nouns ending in lengthened *e* form the plural genitive in *-rum* and the plural dative and ablative in *-bus*, as *ab hac re, harum rerum, his rebus*. This rule serves the declension of feminine nouns of the fifth declension, except for *dies*. That noun is shown to be feminine because no masculine noun ends its singular ablative in lengthened *e*. It is shown to be masculine, however [Col. 1231D], by the fact that it forms the adverb *hodie*, as though it were *hoc die*. This is the rule of the fifth declension.

Nouns ending in *i* form the plural genitive by retaining the *i* of the ablative and adding *um*, producing *-ium*; they form the plural dative and ablative in *-bus*. The genitive ending in *-ium* has several sources. It may derive from a singular ablative ending in *i*, which itself occurs whenever the singular nominative ends in *is* and [600] the singular genitive has the same number of syllables with *-is*, as *hic ignis, hujus ignis, ab hoc igni*, although Lucan said *igne viam scandens*. Three nouns are excepted: *mensis*, *juvenis*, and *canis*.

It may also occur when the singular nominative ending in *is* is of common gender, as *hic et haec agilis*. Or it may occur when the singular nominative is neuter and ends in shortened *e*, while its ablative is formed with *i*, so that the noun does not become a *tetraptoton*—a noun with four identical case-forms—as in *hoc nubile*: nominative *hoc [Col. 1232A] nubile*, accusative *hoc nubile*, vocative *o nubile*, ablative *ab hoc nubile*. The nature of neuter nouns does not permit this.

It may also occur when the singular nominative ends in the syllable *-ens*, provided it is a noun. If it is a participle, the form is different: it has a shortened *e*, as *ab hoc parente*. If it is a noun, the ablative ends in *i*, as *ab hoc parenti*. The ancients, however, wished nouns of the third declension to form their singular ablative with shortened *e*, as *hujus rationis, ab hac ratione*.

Some nouns seem to depart from this rule; their authority must therefore not be dismissed, for they contradict it: *vis*, *Tiberis*. One cannot say *ab hac vire* or *ab hoc Tibere*. The aforementioned plural genitive ending in *-ium* may also derive from an ablative ending in shortened *e*. That ablative itself may come either from a singular nominative ending in *-ons*, as *pons, ponte, pontium*, or from a feminine noun, as *ab hac arte, artium* and *clade, cladium*.

[Col. 1232B] It must be understood, however, that not every noun ending in *-ns*, nor every feminine noun whose singular ablative ends in shortened *e*, must necessarily form its plural genitive in *-ium*. Rather, nouns whose singular ablative ends in shortened *e* and whose plural genitive is formed in *-ium* must necessarily derive either from a singular nominative ending in *-ns* or from the feminine gender.

Nouns which formerly formed their singular accusative in *-m*, as *hanc navem, hanc puppem, hanc clavem*, we now say as *hanc navim, hanc puppim, hanc clavim*. In the plural accusative of those nouns which form their plural genitive in *-ium*, we properly use *-eis*; in the nominative we use *-es*, as the plural accusative *has claveis*, with *-eis*, and the plural nominative *hae claves*, with *-es*. Indeed, this avoids ambiguity in speech. If someone says *puppes regunt*, it is uncertain whether the ships are ruling others or whether other ships are ruling. This is the rule of the third declension.

Nouns ending in *o* in the singular ablative [Col. 1232C], as *ab hoc egregio*, form the plural genitive in *-rum*, as *horum egregiorum*, and the plural dative and ablative in *-is*, *his et ab his egregiis*. Two apparent exceptions to this rule are found: *ab hac domo, harum domorum, his et ab his domibus*; likewise, *ab hoc jugero, horum jugerum, his et ab his jugeribus*.

It must be understood, however, that the ancients declined all these nouns in order to remove the difficulty. They said that the fourth declension was *ab hac domu, harum domuum, his et ab his domibus*; and, according to the rule of the third declension, *ab hoc jugere, horum jugerum, his et ab his jugeribus*. Thus the nominative was *hic juger*, and the second-declension form *juger, jugeris* was absent, as with *tuber, tuberis*. In the noun *domus*, however, only the ablative was corrupted, because the word would otherwise have proceeded less faithfully according to the rule of the fourth declension. When the singular ablative was corrupted, the genitive was necessarily corrupted at the same time. In *hoc jugerum, hujus jugeri,* and *ab hoc jugero*, the plural genitive was corrupted: it ought to have formed *jugerorum*, but formed *jugerum* instead [Col. 1232D]. Likewise, the plural dative and ablative, which ought to have formed *his et ab his jugeris*, formed *his et ab his jugeribus*. In these nouns, however, we except these cases not on the basis of any grammatical principle but for the sake of euphony. This is the rule of the second declension.

Nouns ending in *u* in the singular ablative, as *ab hoc genu* and *cornu*, always form the plural genitive in *-uum*, as *horum cornuum*; they form the plural dative and ablative in *-bus*, *his et ab his cornibus*. In the plural dative and ablative, however, these nouns retain the letter *u* in the penultimate syllable, so that when pronounced separately they will not seem to signify something else. Thus, if we wish to mean “limbs,” we say *his et ab his artubus*, lest we confuse *artus* with *artes*. Similarly, one must say *arces, arcibus* and *arcus, arcubus*.

It must be understood that *aptota* do not fall under the rules stated above, because in the singular ablative [Col. 1233A] they either end in consonants, which the nature of the ablative does not permit, as *ab hoc nequam*, or, if they end in vowels, they do not form their plural genitive in *-ium*. Thus *frugi* does not produce *frugium*, nor *nihili* *nihilium*, as *puppi* produces *puppium*.

There are nevertheless singular nouns which do not follow the rule in the plural genitive, as *hic pulvis, horum pulverum*. There are also plural nouns which have no singular ablative and form their plural genitive differently. Thus, in the case of *Vulcanalia*, it is uncertain whether we should say *horum Vulcanaliorum* or *horum Vulcanalium*. It must be understood that whenever such nouns occur, we should compare them with other similar nouns whose declension has taught us the rule, and decline these according to the same principle. For example, if we do not know whether the form is *horum Vulcanaliorum* or *Vulcanalium*, we should set against it the noun *sedile*, whose singular ablative is *sedili*, and begin the declension by comparison: *haec sedilia, horum sedilium*; *haec Vulcanalia* [Col. 1233B], *horum Vulcanalium*. Yet *Vulcanaliorum* could be defended against this rule, on the model of *anciliorum*, as Horace says:

> *Anciliorum nominis et togae oblitus est.*  
> “He forgot the name of the shields and the toga.”

It must be understood that neuter nouns ending in *a* in the plural nominative form their plural genitive in *-ium*, not *-orum*, as *agilia, agilium* and *fortia, fortium*. We must also know that nouns whose gender differs between the singular and plural do not accept the rule of the plural genitive and singular ablative, even though they possess the relevant forms, as *hoc caepe, hae caepae*. Such nouns must be declined according to the method by which we declined those mentioned above: *hae caepae, harum caeparum*. They are nevertheless plural nouns.

Nouns whose gender in the singular differs from that in the plural, as though they belonged exclusively to the plural, do not fall under the rules we have taken from the Greeks, as *poema, thema, schema*. The reason is that the Greeks do not have an ablative from which these nouns could receive such rules, since we find these very nouns declined in the feminine gender [Col. 1233C] by the ancients.

Analogy is the comparison of similar things. It teaches us, when the declension of supposedly similar nouns is brought before us, what we should investigate and establish, and whether the question is sound on the basis of the comparison. Three things are therefore sought in analogy: the characteristics of the nouns, the endings of the syllables, and the penultimate consonants.

Thus, if someone brings forward *lupus* and *lepus*, saying, “Why does *lupus* form *lupi*, while *lepus* [601] forms *leporis*?” we must turn to analogy and investigate whether all the aforementioned elements correspond to one another. If one of them falters, the objection of the person making the challenge is rightly defeated.

Let us therefore examine the elements one by one. *Lepus* is a common noun, and *lupus* is also a common noun. Neither *lupus* nor *lepus* is comparative. *Lupus* is singular, and *lepus* is likewise singular. *Lupus* is a simple form, and *lepus* is a simple form. Both are nominatives. *Lupus* ends in *-pus*, and *lepus* also ends in *-pus*. But since analogy falters in gender alone, one is declined through two genders and the other through one [Col. 1233D].

We must further know that Greek nouns are better pronounced according to their own declension, as *haec Dido, hujus Didos, huic Dido, hanc Didon, o Dido, ab hac Dido*.

The Latin nominative ends either in *a*, as *musa*; in *e*, as *sedile*; in *i*, as *frugi*; in *o*, as *Cicero*; in *u*, as *cornu*; in *l*, as *mel*; in *-um*, as *scamnum*; in *-en*, as *carmen*; in *r*, as *puer*; in *s*, as *doctus*; in *x*, as *pix*; in *t*, as *caput*; or in *c*, as *halec*. The declension of the last word has become doubtful. It is uncertain whether one should say *halec* or *halect*, because no noun ends in *c* except *lac*, and even that word has become a matter of greater uncertainty.

For *lac* cannot be said in that form, lest it produce *lacis* in the genitive; the correct form is *lactis*. Yet in the nominative we do not find the letter *t*. Nor can *lact* be used, since no noun has been found ending in two mute consonants from which *lactis* could be formed [Col. 1234A] by adding *t* to the singular nominative. Only *lacte* remains, as though it were prescribed by grammatical theory: it ends like neuter nouns such as *monile*, *sedile*, and similar words. This is supported by the authority of Plautus, who said:

> *Sicut lacte lactis simile est.*  
> “Just as milk is like milk.”

But although the form is supported not by grammatical theory but by usage and authority, it must nevertheless be understood that today we ought to speak as Virgil spoke:

> *Lac mihi non aestate novum, non frigore defit.*  
> “I lack fresh milk neither in summer nor in the cold.”

## On the Pronoun

The pronoun is a part of speech. It is called a pronoun because, when it is placed in place of a noun, it seems to signify almost the same thing as the noun. It is said to signify “almost” the same thing because, if it signified exactly the same thing, the pronoun would appear to be a superfluous part of speech. It is nevertheless clear that the noun claims the greater share of signification for itself.

The pronoun acquires its force when a noun has preceded it, as when we say: *Cicero defendit [Col. 1234B] Roscium; ipse etiam Syllam*—“Cicero defended Roscius; he also defended Sulla.” Here *ipse* is placed as though we had repeated *Cicero* anew. The pronoun seems to have been invented in place of that noun because of the tedium of repeating the noun.

But no one should turn this into a question by asking why it is called a pronoun. Let him understand that it is so called because it is a word used in place of a noun. If there were no pronoun, the noun would have been gathered into a single expression. But “pronoun” and “noun” are not the same, just as we do not call a *curator* a *procurator*. Donatus separates this part of speech from the others when he says that the pronoun is a part of speech which performs the function of a noun. None of those other three parts of speech performs this function.

This particular part of speech assumes a definite person in only three pronouns, and no more: *ego, tu, ille*. Six properties belong to the pronoun: quality, gender, number, form, person, and case.

Quality is divided in two ways: into those pronouns called definite, because they take persons, and [Col. 1234C] those called indefinite, because they have no limit to their determinate signification. There are seven of the latter: *quis, qualis, talis, quantus, tantus, quotus, totus*.

In this matter Pliny the Elder criticizes the grammarians for calling the accident common, since an accident is one thing and that to which it happens another. They therefore say that the definite pronouns are those which are also persons. When we ask for a definite pronoun, we find *ego*; and when we ask for the first person, we again find *ego*. Thus it turns out that the accident and that which receives the accident are one and the same.

We must understand, however, that such definers erred not so much in reasoning as in the ordering of their words. They said that persons are accidents of pronouns, when they ought to have said that definite pronouns are themselves persons, since indefinite pronouns do not receive persons; indeed, they are never found without persons.

It is nevertheless established that there are only two definite pronouns: *ego* and *tu*. *Ille*, however, is definite when we point out a thing that is present [Col. 1234D]; if it refers to someone absent, it is less than definite, as with *hic*. Pronouns called “less than definite” signify less than definite things. There are six of them: *is, idem, se, ipse, iste, hic*.

For *ipse* cannot be said except of someone already known or of someone who has already been mentioned in speech. When I hear *ipse venit*—“he himself has come”—it is clearly more than definite, even if I no longer see the person being discussed. Yet it is less than definite in the sense that it can give rise to a question, as when someone says *ipse venit* to people who do not know whom they are hearing about.

There are also five possessives: *meus, tuus, suus, noster, vester*. They are so called because through them we indicate that we possess something; no one says *meus* unless there is something that he possesses.

# CHAPTER II

## On the Verb

The verb is so called because it produces a sound when the air is struck. For this reason this part of speech specially took for itself this name, since we use it frequently in speech. In a connected utterance we often find two verbs, one noun or one participle. For example, *Virgilius habet recitare*: “Virgil has to recite.” Here *habet* and *recitare* are two verbs; these are the individual parts.

The verb is a part of speech possessing tense and person. We must understand that a word is most properly a verb when it has person and tense simultaneously. If it has something else, it is not a verb: if it has tense alone, it is a participle; if it has person alone, it is a pronoun; if it has both together, it is a verb.

A verb has either an active or a passive meaning, as *scribo, scribor*: *scribo* is active, *scribor* passive. A neutral and a deponent verb may have either active or passive meaning, as *curro, vapulo, loquor, luctor*. A common verb has both active and passive meaning, as *osculor te*—“I kiss you”—and *osculor a te*—“I am kissed by you.”

The quality of verbs is expressed in moods and forms. [602] [Col. 1235B] Donatus placed these in the wrong order, discussing moods first and forms afterward. We must discuss forms first. Forms properly contain meaning or gender. We must understand that they are called forms because they shape us with respect to each individual matter: through them we show what we are doing. We recognize what a verb signifies through its forms.

The forms of verbs are those which contain meaning; moods, on the other hand, pertain to inflection. How can I know what inflection is unless I first learn what meaning is? Donatus therefore said that what others call forms, they mix with the “genders” or meanings of verbs. A form properly contains meaning or gender. For example, a meditative inflection contains, as it were, the meaning of one deliberating, that is, “I wish to read.” We shall now discuss the individual forms.

Inchoative forms are identified by five rules. They must originate from a neutral verb; they must end in the syllable *-sco*; they must belong to the shortened third conjugation; they must lack the perfect and pluperfect tenses [Col. 1235C]—for what is already completed cannot be inchoative; and they must lack a future participle. Thus no one says *fervesco, fervesciturus*.

Frequentative verbs belong to the first conjugation whenever they end in *-to*, as *lectito, lectitas* and *cursito, cursitas*. Whenever they end in *-so*, they pass into the third conjugation, as *facesso* and *lacesso*. *Consuesco, consuevi* does not seem to be inchoative because it has a perfect tense; for whatever is begun has no past tense.

There are also frequentatives derived from nouns. Here Donatus erred: *patrizat* means the same as “he is like his father.” There is a perfect form, as *sorbeo* and *sugo*; from it a sort of diminutive is formed, *sorbillo* and *sugillo*. Some perfect forms have no source, as *vacillo* and *pitisso*; they do not derive from *pito* or *vaco*. Some resemble inchoatives, as *compesco*. But since it forms *compescui*, it is not inchoative, because an inchoative cannot possess completion.

Inchoatives are formed in *-sco* from a perfect form, as *horreo* [Col. 1235D], which is perfect, while *horresco* is inchoative. Some have no source, as *consuesco* and *quiesco*. Here Donatus erred by calling these inchoative verbs, since they have past forms, *consuevi* and *quievi*. Therefore they are not inchoative either.

It should be noted that the moods themselves have their own meanings. The indicative, as *lego*, is so called because through it I indicate what I say or do. The same applies to the remaining moods, as in *legitur*. The permissive mood ought to be excluded. Why? What purpose is served by positing a mood when we have the future tense, as *legam*?

The infinitive, as *legere*, does not take definite pronouns. No one says *legere a me*, *a te*, or *ab illo*. Donatus therefore taught this rule. The impersonal, however, does take them, as *legitur a me, a te, ab illo, a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*. Some regard this mood as a verbal genus and signification, for the impersonal is thus constituted because every verb receives a verbal genus. Just as I say *ego lego, tu legis, ille legit*, so I say *legitur a me, a te, ab illo*.

[Col. 1236A] These verbs are formed from themselves when they end in *-et*, as *pudet*; no one says *pudeo*. Others derive from elsewhere, as *latet*, which forms *lateo*; thus it receives its inflection, as it were, from another source. We must understand that no participle ending in *-us* is formed from an impersonal verb.

Conjugation is recognized through five features: the verb must be in the present tense, singular number, and indicative mood; in the active it must have before the letter *s* in the second person one of three vowels, namely *a*, *e*, or *i*; and in the passive it must have the same vowels before *-ris*. The first and second conjugations have straightforward rules. Of the third we must understand that, if it has a shortened *i*, it forms the future only in *-am*, as *lego, legam*; if it has a lengthened *i*, it forms it both in *-am* and in *-bo*, as *nutrio, nutriam, nutribo*.

We must understand that the *i* is shortened when the *i* of the second person of the present active passes into *e* in the passive, as *lego, legis; legor, legeris*. When the *i* remains both in the active and passive before the syllable, it is lengthened, as *audio, audis; audior, audiris*. *Odi, sum,* [Col. 1236B] and *possum* are defective neutral verbs.

You should understand that the regular verbs are those which preserve their forms throughout their inflection, as *lego, legebam, legi*, and so forth, and likewise in the passive. *Gaudeo, fio,* and *soleo*, however, change their past tense. They are not true verbs but should be called neutral-passives. Donatus called them this because they are termed unequal. *Cedo* and *ave* are not inflected; we say them as they are found in texts.

Verbs of uncertain meaning are those which we use according to our discretion, as *condio, condis, condior*, and so forth. *Adulor* also receives all participles: *adulans, adulaturus, adulandus*. Some say that verbs have a dual number, that is, a common number, as *leger*, but this is false. No one says *ego leger* or *nos legere*.

There are three distinctions of past tense: the imperfect, which we have just now left behind; the perfect, which we left behind a little while ago; and the pluperfect, which we left behind long ago: *legebam, legi, legeram*.

Donatus says that no first-person singular form ending in *o* can be found in the indicative except those involving the three vowels *e*, *i*, and *u* [Col. 1236C]. There is also a fourth, *o*, but it is Greek, as *boo, boas, boat*, whence comes the line:

> *Reboant silvaeque, et magnus Olympus.*  
> “The forests echo, and mighty Olympus.”

The letter combination *ko* is not prefixed, which is true; but *k* is prefixed, as in *kalendae*.

Some verbs are defective in mood, as *cedo*, meaning “say.” It does not form *cedebam*, although the plural *cedite*, meaning “say,” is found in texts. Others are defective in form, as *facesso*, which has no perfect; for it forms *facio, factito*. Others are defective in conjugation, as *adsum, ades*. Its conjugation cannot be determined, because it has neither *a* before its final letter, nor a lengthened *e*, nor a shortened or lengthened *i*. Others are defective in gender, as *gaudeo, gavisus sum*. Others are defective in number, as *faxo*, for no one says *faximus*. Others are defective in form, as *impleo*. Others are defective in tense, as *ferveo, fervebo*; no one says *ferviturus*. The fact that the same matter is repeated should not confuse us.

# CHAPTER III

[Col. 1236D]

## On the Adverb
An adverb is a word that is associated with a verb, as, for example, in “you acted learnedly”: “learnedly” is the adverb; “you acted” is the verb. Adverbs derive from a noun and a verb, as in *pedetentim* (“step by step”): *pes* (“foot”) is the noun, and *tento* (“I try,” “I proceed”) is the verb. Yet they made an adverb arising from a participle a single part of speech, as *indulgens, indulgenter* (“indulgent,” “indulgently”). Here Donatus was mistaken, for *indulgens* is not a participle, because it has degrees of comparison: *indulgens, indulgentior* (“indulgent, more indulgent”). Some words end in a lengthened *o*, such as *falso*; for it can be an adverb, as in *falso ad me relatum est* (“it was falsely reported to me”) and *falso locutus est* (“he spoke falsely”). It is likewise the dative and ablative case of *falsus*: *huic falso* (“to this false [thing/person]”) and *ab hoc falso* (“from this false [thing/person]”). We are better to call *facile* (“easily”) and *difficile* (“with difficulty”) nouns rather than adverbs, although they are used as adverbs. Otherwise, if they were adverbs, they would form *faciliter* and *difficiliter*; for all nouns that end in *-i* in the singular dative send their adverbs into *-ter*, as *huic sapienti, sapienter* (“to this wise [person], wisely”); likewise, *huic facili, faciliter* (“to this easy [thing/person], easily”).

[Col. 1237A] The rule for adverbs is as follows: a noun ending in *-o* in the singular dative sends its adverb into *-e*, as *huic docto, docte* (“to this learned [person], learnedly”); if it ends in *-i*, the adverb is formed in *-ter*, as *huic sapienti, sapienter*. But authority has weakened this rule. Virgil said *sanguinei lugubre rubent* (“the blood-red [things] glow mournfully”), using *lugubre* for *lugubriter* (“mournfully”); and Terence said *parce ac duriter urgebat* (“he pressed sparingly and harshly”), using *duriter* for *dure* (“harshly”). In the dative they remain as *falso* or *sedulo* (“falsely,” “diligently”), but they form the adverbs *false* and *sedule*. Some form them contrary to the rule, as *a duro, duriter* (“from harsh,” “harshly”); but in such cases this should rather be called usage or art.

*Intus* (“inside”) and *foris* (“outside”), whenever they indicate place, do not take prepositions; for no preposition is separately added to an adverb. No one says *ad intus* or *ad foris* (“to inside,” “to outside”).
