Adverbs also have degrees of comparison: *docte, doctius, doctissime* (“learnedly, more learnedly, most learnedly”). But not all adverbs extend through all degrees. Therefore, to increase their meaning, we join *magis* and *maxime* (“more” and “most”), which indicate increase; to lessen their meaning, *minus* and *minime* (“less” and “least”), which indicate diminution. For just as they are compared, so they are diminished.

Some are derived from the positive degree, as *primum, primule* (“first, somewhat first”), and *longe, longule* (“far, somewhat far”). Others are derived from the comparative, as *longius, longiuscule* (“farther, somewhat farther”) and *melius, meliuscule* (“better, somewhat better”). Such adverbs are not found from the superlative degree; therefore he said that they are rare or nonexistent.

There are also many ambiguous words. An adverb is found in association with a noun in all its parts, as *falso*: in *huic falso* and *ab hoc falso*, it is a noun; but if we say *falso locutus est* (“he spoke falsely”), it is an adverb. Likewise with a pronoun: if you say *cui viro* (“to which man”), it is a pronoun; if you say *qui convenit* (“which is appropriate”), it is an adverb. Likewise with a verb, as *pone*, which we distinguish by accent: when we lengthen its final syllable, it is an adverb; when we shorten it, it is a verb. Likewise with a participle, as *profecto*: it is the affirming adverb *profecto* (“certainly”), as in *profecto audit* (“he certainly hears”). Yet I am more inclined to think that *profecto* is a participle from the verb *proficiscor* (“I depart”).

It is joined with a conjunction, as in *at audi* (“but listen”): here *at* is a conjunction, as in *at illud contigit* (“but that happened”); but, unless I am mistaken, it is an adverb in *at at veni* (“come immediately”), that is, “come at once.” It is joined with a preposition, as *ante* or *propter*: in *ante omnes homines* (“before all men”), *ante* is a preposition; in *ante fecit* (“he did it before”), it is an adverb. In *propter te hoc facio* (“I do this because of you”), *propter* is a preposition; in *ille propter erat* (“he was nearby”), that is, “beside,” it is an adverb. It is joined with an interjection, as *heu!* (“alas!”). If you say *heu! quid contingit?* (“alas! what is happening?”), it is the interjection of one who grieves. In *heu! etiam mensas consumimus* (“alas! we are even consuming the tables”), *heu* is an adverb.

Donatus is correct in saying that we do not add prepositions to the names of cities, as, for example, *Roma venio* (“I come from Rome”), and similar expressions. But authority confuses this rule, for Sallust said *cum Brutus a Roma abierat* (“when Brutus had departed from Rome”). We should nevertheless observe this rule: whenever a nominative ends in the syllable *-us*, we should preferably speak according to the genitive, as *Adrumetus, Adrumeti sum* (“Adrumetus, I am at Adrumetus”); whenever it ends otherwise, we speak according to the dative, as *Carthago, Carthagini sum* (“Carthage, I am at Carthage”). But here too authority creates confusion: Sallust wrote *Narbone consilia Gallorum* (“at Narbo, the plans of the Gauls”), using *Narbone* for *Narboni*; and Virgil wrote *Tyria Carthagine, quae nunc exspectat* (“in Tyrian Carthage, which now awaits”), using *Carthagine* for *Carthagini*.

The preposition *de* is not applied to adverbs. Otherwise it is a solecism if we say *de mane* (“from morning”): *mane* is an adverb, while *de* is a preposition. Nor are we refuted by the adverbs *dehinc* (“henceforth”) and *desubito* (“suddenly”), if they are pronounced with a single accent.

## CHAPTER IV

### On the Participle

The participle is so called as though it were *parti-capium* (“part-taker”), because it claims for itself the rules of two parts of speech. It has properties from the noun and from the verb, as in *hic amans* (“this loving [man]”). It receives two things from the noun: gender and case. When I say *hic amans* (“this loving man”) or *haec amans* (“this loving woman”), there is gender; as for case, it has *hic amans, huius amantis* (“this loving [person], of this loving [person]”), and so forth. From the verb it receives two things: tenses and meanings. Thus *amans* (“loving”) is present, while *amaturus* (“about to love”) and *amatus* (“loved”) are different. It has active meaning, as *docens* and *docturus* (“teaching,” “about to teach”); passive meaning, as *doctus* and *docendus* (“taught,” “to be taught”). From both noun and verb it receives number and figure.

Number belongs to a noun or verb, as *homo, homines* (“man, men”) and *lego, legimus* (“I read, we read”). Figure is of two kinds, as *felix, infelix* (“fortunate, unfortunate”); likewise with a verb, as *scribo, describo* (“I write, I describe”). Therefore participles receive singular number, as *hic legens* (“this reader”); plural number, as *hi legentes* (“these readers”); and figure, because they are simple, as *legens* (“reading”), or compound, as *negligens* (“neglecting”).

Participles properly arise from active and neuter verbs in two tenses, namely the present and the future, as *amans, amaturus* (“loving, about to love”) and *stans, staturus* (“standing, about to stand”). This is correct: for if a neuter verb is declined like an active verb, it properly has these tenses, which the active verb has.

Inchoative verbs have only a present-tense participle, as *horresco, horrescens* (“I shudder, shuddering”); no one says *horresciturus* (“about to shudder”), and similarly in other cases. Defective verbs sometimes have only one tense, namely the past, as *soleo, solitus* (“I am accustomed, accustomed”). *Memini* (“I remember”) has no tense, although it is defective. A defective participle may arise from a non-defective verb, as *studeo, studebam, studui* (“I apply myself, I was applying myself, I applied myself”), and so forth: *studens* (“applying oneself”) is not defective, but no one says *studiturus* (“about to apply oneself”).

To sum up briefly: the participle was said to possess four possible conditions—sometimes only the present tense, as *horrescens* (“shuddering”); sometimes none, as *memini* (“I remember”); sometimes one, as *solitus* (“accustomed”); and sometimes defective participles arise from a non-defective verb, as *lotus* (“washed”) from *lavor* (“I am washed”). Participles are not found from impersonal verbs; no one says *poenitens* (“repenting”).

*Tunicatus* (“clothed in a tunic”) is not a participle, because it does not make the verb *tunicor*; rather, it is a noun. *Pransus* (“having dined”) and *coenatus* (“having supped”) are similar, like *tunicatus*. We call them not only nouns but also participles. For although *prandeo* (“I dine”) does not form *prandeor*, nevertheless *pransus* functions as a noun; and *tunica* (“tunic”) forms no verb at all. Let us therefore call these participles without a verbal origin.

There are words resembling participles which, although they derive from a verb, are nouns because they have no tense, as *furibundus* (“raging”) and *moribundus* (“dying”), since they derive from *morior* (“I die”) and *furio* (“I rage”). But there is another way by which you can understand that these are not participles: present-tense participles change *-s* into *-dus* and form the passive future, as *legens, legendus* (“reading, to be read”). Again, if you remove *-dus* from the end and put *-s*, the present-tense participle is formed: from *legendus* remove *-dus*, and you make *legens*. But *moriens* (“dying”) does not produce *moribundus*; it produces *moriendus* (“to be died,” “destined to die”), for no one says that *moribundus* derives from *morior*.

*Passus* (“having suffered”) and *usus* (“having used”) are both participles and nouns. It is a noun in *usus mei pallii* (“the use of my cloak”); it is a participle in *usus malefacere* (“having used [something] to do evil”).

A participle is defective if it cannot proceed through all tenses, as *coeptus* (“begun”); no one says *coepiendus* (“about to be begun”). Some participles become nouns when they receive composition, as *acceptus* and *incensus* (“accepted,” “kindled”): when they are compared—*incensior, acceptior* (“more kindled,” “more accepted”)—they are nouns.

Adverbs are not formed from participles. Donatus disputed this, and rightly so; he did not provide authority from himself when he said that this had been read by him. No one, moreover, says *videnter* or *legenter* (“seeingly,” “readingly”).

## CHAPTER V

### On the Conjunction

The conjunction is so called because it joins expressions. Conjunctive conjunctions are such as *ego et tu eamus* (“let you and I go”). Disjunctive conjunctions are those that, as it were, separate things or persons: *ego aut tu* (“I or you”). For when I say *ego aut tu*, I separate the meaning, although the words are joined; the speaker does not say, “I will do it, and you,” but rather, “one of the two [will do it].”

Expletive conjunctions are such as, “If you do not want this, at least do that,” as though the conjunction filled out the expression. A prepositive conjunction is *at*, as in *at pater Aeneas* (“but Father Aeneas”); no one says *pater at Aeneas*. Subjunctive conjunctions are such as *primusque Machaon* (“and Machaon first”); not *que primus Machaon*. A common conjunction is *igitur* (“therefore”), because it can be placed anywhere: *igitur hoc facio, facio igitur hoc* (“therefore I do this; I do this, therefore”).

There are conjunctions that can be adverbs. In *ante firmissimum virum accipio* (“I receive [him] before the strongest man”), *ante* is an adverb. It is likewise a conjunction in *an te malus abstulit error?* (“or has an evil error carried you away?”). For even if all the parts can be adverbs, this properly applies to a conjunction.

Conjunctions should be used according to their meanings: causal conjunctions for causes, rational conjunctions for reasoning. The cause comes first, and the reasoning follows. For example, *occido illum, qui habet tunicam* (“I kill the man who has a tunic”) states the cause; *itaque veneno illum occidi, non ferro, ne agnosci possit* (“therefore I killed him with poison, not with iron, so that he could not be recognized”) states the reasoning. The causal expression is: “If I kill him, I will have the tunic”; the rational expression is: “Therefore I killed him with poison, so that he could not be recognized.” But authority alters this distinction, for Virgil also used one conjunction in place of another, saying *subjectisque urere flammis* (“and burn [them] with flames placed beneath”) in place of *ve* (“or”).

## CHAPTER VI

### On the Preposition

The preposition is so called because it is placed before [another word] in speech, as *ante templum* (“before the temple”), not *templum ante*. A preposition either changes something into its opposite, as *felix, infelix* (“fortunate, unfortunate”); fills something out, as *fractus, infractus* (“broken, unbroken”); or diminishes something, as *validus, invalidus* (“strong, weak”), and the other examples given by Donatus.

We have said that a preposition is always placed before; nevertheless, it is found after the word, as *mecum* (“with me”).

Prepositions are either applied to cases and remain separate, as in *apud amicum causatum est* (“the case was pleaded before a friend”): *apud* is not joined to the following word, since no one says the joined form *apudamicum*. Or they serve in word-formation and are joined, as *di-, dis-, re-, se-*; thus *diduco* (“I lead apart”), *distraho* (“I pull apart”), *recubo* (“I recline”), and *secubo* (“I lie apart”).

Therefore prepositions are either word-forming and always joined, or they are separated and joined according to the expression, as *prae me* (“before me”) and *secum* (“with himself”). *In-* and *con-* have the following rule when they precede another consonant: if *f* or *s* follows them, they naturally make the preceding vowel short into a long vowel and give it the accent, as *infula* (“fillet”) and *consilium* (“counsel”).

*Usque* (“as far as”) does not appear to be a preposition, because when it is put before another preposition it is joined to that preposition. If we say *usque ad forum vado* (“I go as far as the forum”), *usque* by itself is not a preposition. The form *circumcirca* (“all around”) is comparable: there one preposition has already been placed before another. *Tenus* (“as far as”) is likewise attached afterward for the sweetness of the sound, as *puppe tenus* (“as far as the stern”); it ought to have said *prae, tenus puppe*.

The remaining prepositions—*super* (“above”) and *subter* (“beneath”)—are joined with the ablative and indicate place, as *super cathedra sedit* (“he sat above the chair”). When we say this, it is *soloecophanes*, that is, an appearance of solecism. *Super* and *subter* govern the accusative; but *super*, whenever it designates someone, governs the ablative, as *multa super Priamo rogitans* (“asking many things about Priam”). *In* and *sub* vary. Thus *in* governs the accusative when we say *in adulterum*, that is, “against the adulterer.” The various examples of these prepositions, whether simple or compound, are those that Donatus appended.

Prepositions alter verbs, as *conficio* (“I complete”), which formerly consisted of *con-* and *facio* (“I make”); or they themselves are altered, as *suffero* (“I endure”), which formerly consisted of *sub-* and *fero* (“I carry”); or they both alter and are altered, as *sufficio* (“I supply”), which formerly consisted of *sub-* and *facio*; likewise *suscipio* and *suspic io* (“I undertake” and “I suspect”), which formerly consisted of *sub-* plus *capio* (“I take”) and *sub-* plus *aspicio* (“I look at”).

The ancients joined prepositions with the genitive, accusative, and ablative, as *crurum tenus* (“as far as the legs”) and *longo post tempore* (“after a long time”). We must know, however, that when a preposition is not placed before another word, or when it changes its case, or when it has no governed case, it ceases to be a preposition and becomes an adverb. Thus in *longo post tempore*, it has changed the case; it ought to have said *post tempus* (“after time”). Again, in *ante fecit* (“he did it before”), it has no governed case.

Separated prepositions do not adhere to other separated prepositions. If someone says *ante juxta eum* (“before beside him”), *ante* is no longer an adverb. They also say that figure belongs to a preposition, as *abs, absque* (“without”); and order, as in *puppetenus* (“as far as the stern”) and *mecum* (“with me”), which are subordinate forms. But we must not break the rule on account of two such matters; rather, we should call these anomalous, that is, outside the rule.

## CHAPTER VII

### On the Interjection

The interjection is so called because, inserted among the other parts of speech, it expresses various emotions of the mind. It may express exultation, as *eia!* (“ho!”); desire, as *o mihi praeteritos referat si Jupiter annos!* (“O, if only Jupiter would bring back my past years!”); reproach, as *o qui res hominumque deumque* (“O you who [rule] the affairs of men and gods”); grief, as *heu!* (“alas!”); or fear, as *ah! ah!* (“ah! ah!”).

Among the Greeks this occurs: they append interjections to adverbs. Among the Latins it does not occur; no one says *Papae feci* (“I did it, oh!”).

[Col. 1239]

# M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, ON ORTHOGRAPHY (C)

## PREFACE

[Col. 1239C] When such matters were being discussed among us, and some dispute arose concerning the *Complexiones* of the Apostles, my monks suddenly began to cry out: “What benefit is there in our learning what the ancients did, or in carefully knowing what your sagacity has taken care to add, if we are altogether ignorant of how we ought to write these things, and cannot reproduce in our speech what we are unable to grasp in writing?”

I replied to them: “The matters of which they speak have been marked out, so that they may both be understood and pronounced as they ought to be. But we must preserve entirely the labor of the ancients, lest we claim to be the authors of those things whose followers we are known to be. And therefore we bring forward the works of twelve authors, which they expressed briefly and fully, so that we may state them more concisely and recall what was said by the ancient authors without any desire for variation. In this way we may appear to satisfy you completely, and the account conveyed by the text of the twelve authors may rest upon firm authority.”

[Col. 1239D] It is now time for us to bring our entire work to its conclusion, so that what has been arranged in a sevenfold conclusion may be more deeply stored in the mind.

1. After the *Commentaries on the Psalter*, in which, with the Lord’s favor, I first devoted myself to the labor of study at the time of my conversion.

2. Then, after the *Institutions* explaining how divine and human readings ought to be understood, completed, as I think, in two books, in which you will find more usefulness than ornament.

3. After the *Exposition of the Epistle Written to the Romans*, from which I removed the corruptions of the Pelagian heresy, and concerning which I also urged those who follow me to do the same in the remainder of the commentary.

4. After the book in which I collected, with the Lord’s favor, Donatus’s grammatical arts together with his commentaries, as well as the book on *Etymologies* and another book by Sacerdos on *Figures*, so that instructed, simple-minded brothers might, whenever necessary, grasp similar statements without confusion.

[Col. 1241A] 5. After the book of headings as well, which I collected from divine Scripture and wished to call the *Memorial*, so that those who dislike lengthy reading might pass briefly through everything.

6. After the *Complexiones* on the Epistles of the Apostles, their Acts, and the Apocalypse, which I traversed in the form of a very brief explanation.

7. I have reached my ninety-third year, with the Lord’s help, in order to examine the most devoted writers on orthography. If I am able to gather from them into one work what has been culled from their writings, insofar as it concerns those whom I have undertaken to abridge, the confusion of the corrector and copyist will, I think, no longer persist, provided he understands it properly.

[Col. 1241B] This is a small work devoted to the treatment of syllables and letters. Sometimes it proceeds from the derivation of nouns, sometimes from the cases of words, sometimes from movement and position, sometimes from the harmony of euphony, and sometimes from the likeness of Greek letters. It establishes what you ought to write and what you should strive to avoid. At times it says that the single letter *l* is correctly written in certain words, but testifies that the sound of the letter *n* can often take its place.

Thus what was previously written with *u* and *o* should now, according to the noble correctness of writing investigated by the surest methods, be written with two *u*s. The present work therefore gives the proper forms: *volnus, vulnus* (“wound”); *i* for *e*, as the ancients wrote *magnai*, while we write *magnae*; *c* for *q*, as the ancients wrote *quum*, while modern writers have judged *cum* more correct; and other matters explained with subtle but necessary distinctions. I have not hurried over them, but have treated them with attentive concentration, so that what you are beginning to learn well you may bring to the perfection of pronunciation without stumbling. For if you have the desire to understand, what you previously sought with delay you will immediately pass through with unhindered speed.

[Col. 1241C] It is surely a glorious study, suited, as it seems, to human and divine letters alike, to write appropriately what you ought to say and to utter what has been written without any ambiguity of error. Articulate speech separates us from animals; the discipline of writing separates us from the uneducated and confused. These two powers therefore claim and defend the complete human being. When these two lights agree with one another, both are correct and both are beautiful; but when they begin to differ, they incur the disgraceful defect of squinting distortion.

Our purpose, then, will be to gather into a single crown what the ancients handed down in a manner suitable to modern usage and to assign it to the most distinguished practical use. Whatever is more appropriate to antiquity, however, should readily be left aside, lest an incongruous labor be undertaken that appears useless to the present age.

Let the fifteenth title of the first book of our *Institutions* explain how heavenly authority ought to be read. There we did not permit the idioms of divine law that conflict with common usage to be dispersed. Here, in the book of *Orthography*, let it be sought more freely and generally how, from the rules of the human arts and with due respect for the authority of our elders, every reading may be made exceedingly elegant and correct.

If anyone should perhaps wish to read the orthographic authors in their own texts, he will find them transcribed. I have left in my monastery, with the Lord’s favor, as many as I was able to find, so that you might test more fully the statements in their own authors, whom we have not thought should be culled merely because of your distaste for them.

I also thought that you should be earnestly reminded to seek out and establish the divisions of meaning with attentive care. Without them, we cannot either read anything properly or succeed in understanding it.

We must know that the grammarian Donatus treated punctuation marks in such a way that he seems to have expressed not their order but rather their functions. For if he had followed the sequence of distinctions according to their recognized degrees, he could not possibly have placed the full stop first and then the middle stop; rather, he would have begun with the subdistinction, followed by the middle stop—both of which always precede rather than follow the full stop. But, as the most learned have clearly judged, we should preserve the following order: first speak of the subdistinction, which is always placed where the sense of a clause is suspended but still expected to be completed, as in *Arma virumque cano* (“I sing of arms and the man”), where the whole work’s meaning has not yet been concluded. Virgil is going to say *arma*, “arms,” and *virumque*, “and the man.” But since *cano* (“I sing”) refers to both, the subdistinction is rightly placed here—that is, after *arma*.

The middle stop is properly affixed in a clause when no expression is lacking, but the sense advances step by step toward a full stop, as:

*Dividimus muros, et moenia pandimus urbis:*  
“We divide the walls and open the ramparts of the city.”

The full stop occurs where a complete sentence ends, as:

*Tantae molis erat Romanam condere gentem.*  
“So great a task it was to found the Roman race.”

Do not suppose that the subdistinction or the middle stop always keeps the precise order we have described, with the subdistinction preceding and the middle stop following. They are placed in suitable locations according to the reason stated above, so that these punctuation marks, properly positioned, may clearly disclose the meaning of the reading to us. If you distinguish the passage otherwise, you unquestionably confuse everything.

These distinctions, or punctuation marks, are called by the Greeks, as Donatus testifies, *θέσεις* (“positions” or “placements”). A period is a pause extending through the length of a complete sentence; its parts are *cola* and *commata* (“members” and “clauses”).

But before we appear to begin the work of *Orthography*, we have judged it appropriate to append, as an example, the preface of the grammarian Phocas. It seems suitable in every respect to our entire work, as though it had been produced by us:

“My art belongs to many whom the ancient ages brought forth,

but a new brevity asserts that you are mine.

Although everything has been explored in the books of the ancients,

to say much briefly is the work of novelty.

Let the young man whom a talkative page frightens

read you—or anyone who is glad to know serious matters in a few words.

Let the traveler seeking distant places not hesitate

to carry you as a companion, bearing much in a small weight.

If anyone wishes to copy you,

he will complain of no loss, nor of the sad burden of thankless labor.

[Col. 1243A] There is something here for everyone to seek. Never will the judgment of an eloquent critic

despise this work, provided envy is absent.”

The authors of *Orthography* have been mentioned. Some of them say similar things in the same order, others in an inverted order, while others describe different matters. It is fitting for us to know all of them completely. Those who say equal things confirm what is common; those who set forth variations, by multiplying their expressions, teach us how we ought to write and speak. Now the order of writing known to have been established by the ancients must likewise be stated.

## CHAPTER I

### These Matters Were Reported by Gnaeus Cornutus on Pronunciation or Orthography

[Col. 1243B] I have noticed that some educated men both pronounce the letter *m* where they ought not and suppress it where they ought not. To prevent this, the matter can be observed if I add at the same time whatever pertains to correct writing and to the division of syllables.

Therefore, if two words are joined, of which the first has a consonantal *m* as its final letter and the second begins with a vowel, the consonant *m* is indeed written in full; nevertheless, in pronunciation it sounds harsh and barbarous. But if the second word has any consonant, or a vowel placed in the position of a consonant, it preserves the sound of the letter *m*. It is an equal and identical fault to pronounce the letter *m* with a vowel and with a consonant.

There is a certain letter shaped like the letter *F*, called the digamma, which seems to have two strokes derived from the letter gamma. Because of its resemblance to this sound, they wished to call joined vowels *digamma-like*, as in *votum* (“vow”) and *virgo* (“virgin”). Therefore a digamma and a vowel ought to have been placed in the first syllable: *fotum, firgo*. The Aeolians did this, as did our own ancients, as the writing in certain books shows.

When Terentius Varro wishes to represent this letter, he writes it as *VA*. Therefore, whatever sound exists in this syllable will be the sound of the letter as well. Today we have compelled the letter *u* to serve two functions: sometimes it is written for the digamma, sometimes for the vowel. It is a vowel when it exists by itself, for in that role it behaves like the other vowels. When it occurs with another vowel, it is the digamma, which is a consonant.

Some think that three vowels can occur under one syllable, which is empty of consonantal structure. They are mistaken if they think this, for nowhere among the Greeks or Latins does a syllable consist of three vowels. Therefore here too there will similarly be a digamma and two vowels.

But a question arises, and some approve writing it with *t*, others with *d*. Among the ancients, I know that *sedum* existed for *sed* (“but”); therefore, after removing the last two letters, we retain the remaining letters, preserving the *d*. Similarly, if the question were how *sat* (“enough”) ought to be written, we would say that it should be written with *t*, since its complete form is *satis*.

The letter *q* is correctly placed when the letter *u* immediately follows it, together with one or more other vowels, so that a single syllable is formed. The remaining words are written with *c*.

[Col. 1244A] Lucius also holds this opinion. [Note: This is Lucius Caecilius Vindex.] Some think that we should serve the ears and write words as they are heard. There is nearly a dispute about correct writing: whether we should write what we hear or what ought to be written. I would not surrender everything to the ears.

There are people who write *cotidie* (“every day”) with *co*, rather than *quotidie*. They may be permitted to err; they would stop if they knew that *quotidie* is derived from *quot diebus*, that is, “from as many days,” or “every day.”

*Qui* (“who,” “which”) is written with the syllables *q-u-i*. If it is divided, as in *si cui* (“if to anyone”), then, like *huic* (“to this person”), it is written with *c*. We shall likewise observe this in other cases: in division, the letter *c* should follow, provided that the pronunciation is according to the ancient form, since the genitive and ablative are not divided.

*Causam* (“cause”) is written with one *s*. Let no one be moved by ancient spelling, for they also wrote *accusare* (“to accuse”) with two *s*s. I find *fuisse* (“to have been”), *ivisse* (“to have gone”), *esse* (“to be”), and *caussasse* (“to have caused”) written with two *s*s. But in this pronunciation I cannot determine how the sound of two consonants is to be heard.

Formerly *vostra* was written with *o*, but today with *e*: *advorsa, adversa* (“adverse”); *pervorsa, perversa* (“perverse”); *votare, vetare* (“to forbid”); *vortex, vertex* (“whirlpool, crown”); *convollere, convellere* (“to tear away”); *amploctere, amplectere* (“to embrace”).

Those who think that *malo* (“I prefer”) descended from the Greek comparative *μᾶλλον* (*mállon*, “more”) and therefore write it with two *l*s are mistaken. It was not translated from Greek; rather, it arose from the custom of the ancients, who first said *magis volo* (“I want more”), then shortened the expression through several elisions: *mage volo*, then *mavolo*, which is extremely common among them. Finally it settled into the form *malo*.

But *malle* (“to prefer”) is written with two *l*s, for it means *magis velle*, “to wish more.” Likewise, *nolo* (“I do not wish”) has one *l*, while *nolle* (“not to wish”) has two: *nolo* is *ne volo* (“I do not wish”), and *nolle* is *ne velle* (“not to wish”). Finally, the words compounded from a verb follow the form of that verb.

Some words are written with two *u*s, and their number of syllables also increases. For when one vowel is joined to another identical vowel, it not only fails to cohere with it but also increases the number of syllables, as *vacuus* (“empty”), *ingenuus* (“native,” “freeborn”), *occiduus* (“setting”), and *exiguus* (“small”). The same division of vowels occurs in verbs: *metuunt* (“they fear”), *statuunt* (“they establish”), *tribuunt* (“they grant”), and *acuunt* (“they sharpen”). Therefore here too *c*, not *q*, must be placed.

The question has been raised whether one should write *lacrumae* or *lacrimae* (“tears”), *maxumus* or *maximus* (“greatest”), and similar words. Terentius Varro reports that Caesar was accustomed to pronounce and write such words with *i*. From this arose the usage established by the authority of so great a man. But in books much older than Gaius Caesar, I find most of these written with *u*: *optumus* (“best”), *intumus* (“deepest”), *pulcherrumus* (“most beautiful”), *lubido* (“desire”), *dicundum* (“to be said”), *faciundum* (“to be done”), *maxumae* (“greatest”), *monumentum* (“monument”), *contumelia* (“insult”), *minumae* (“least”). Nevertheless, it is better, both for pronunciation and for writing, to put the letter *i* in place of *u*, as usage has now inclined to do.

Some have taught that *vineas* (“vines”) should be written with *e* when it refers to those we see in the fields, but that *vinias* should be written with *i* for those beneath which a soldier customarily hides. This distinction is extremely foolish, for military vines were not called that from any other source than their resemblance to those rustic vines.

*Exstinguunt* (“they extinguish”) is written with *u* and *o*. The explanation I gave above concerning the letter *q* must also be understood here: I said that throughout its inflection it ought to have two vowels. Thus *exstinguo* (“I extinguish”) is formed from *ex* and *stinguo* (“I extinguish”), and for this reason *exstinguont* would be the form, although it cannot be pronounced.

*Intervallum* (“interval”) has two *l*s, since *vallum* (“rampart”) itself is written no otherwise; *intervallum* derives from it. Varro says that *intervalla* are the spaces between the heads of the stakes (*valli*) from which a rampart is made; hence other spaces too are called *intervalla*.

The composition of prepositions with verbs beginning with vowels must be observed with somewhat greater care, so that we may know that the final consonants of prepositions do not remain unchanged but are often altered. Thus it is sometimes necessary for the consonants that stand first in verbs or words to become the same in the prepositions; and because of their softness, the letters of the prepositions often cannot be pronounced at all. We distinguish by the sound when this occurs and when it does not.

*Accedo* (“I approach”) has two *c*s; *attuli* (“I brought”) two *t*s; *assiduus* (“assiduous”) two *s*s; *arrideo* (“I smile at”) two *r*s; *apparo* (“I prepare”) two *p*s; *annuo* (“I nod”) two *n*s; *alligo* (“I bind”) two *l*s.

In these forms the consonants are altered not only because of softness but also because the letter *d* cannot sound in any way. Where it does sound, it is written when joined to the consonant *f*, as *adfluo* (“I flow toward”), *adfui* (“I was present”), *adfectus* (“affected”). Against this, *b* does not sound: *offui, offero, offendo* (“I was present, I offer, I offend”). The same occurs with other consonants as well, as in *suggero* (“I bring up”). I have shown above that the digamma has the force of a consonant.

There is a case in which *b*, incredible though it may seem, is forced into *s*, as in *suscipere* (“to undertake”), *sustinere* (“to sustain”), *suspendere* (“to suspend”), and *suscitare* (“to arouse”). What the ancients called *sustollere* (“to lift up”), we call *sustuli* in the past tense.

Likewise, the preposition is formed with the letter *f*: *effluo* (“I flow out”), *effodio* (“I dig out”), *effero* (“I carry out”), and *efficio* (“I accomplish”). It is similarly formed in *escendo* (“I climb out”). In some places, however, the sound is retained, and for this reason it must be written: *exsilio* (“I leap out”) and *exsicco* (“I dry out”). Therefore we shall place the letter wherever it is pronounced.

*Tamtus* and *quamtus* (“so great” and “how great”) ought to have *m* in the middle, since *quam* and *tam* are their sources. Hence *quamtitas, quamtus, tamtus* are the forms. Let no one be moved by the fact that *n* is pronounced; I have already taught above that *n* ought to be pronounced even though *m* was placed in the original spelling.

[Col. 1245D] *Exsilium* (“exile”) is written with *s*, since it is formed from *ex* plus *ire* (“to go”), as though it were *exsolium*, which the Greeks call *ἐξορισμόν* (*exorismón*, “banishment”); the ancients said *exsoles* (“exiles”).

As there is a question whether *h* is a letter or not, so there has never been any doubt that it ought to be placed second after any consonant—a point on which Varro alone is uncertain. He wishes by his authority to establish that *h* should first be placed before the letter that supplies the aspiration, and he tries even more strongly to persuade us of this because he says that it is placed before vowels as well, as in *haeres* (“heir”) and *hircus* (“goat”).

But Varro overlooks the fact that a consonant receives *h* in second position because nothing except vowels can stand before the aspiration. Therefore, whether *h* is joined before or after any such letter, it will not sound. For this is the nature of vowels: whether they have *h* before or after them, in whatever arrangement, they do not obstruct pronunciation.

Moreover, in the book on grammar that Varro wrote, when he discussed letters, he argued that *h* is not among the letters. This is much less surprising than his denial that *x* is a letter as well. I have not yet discovered what he had in mind in this matter; I shall append his own words:

“Some letters both exist and are called letters, such as *a* and *b*; some are called letters but do not exist as such, such as *h* and *x*; some exist but are not called letters, such as φ and ψ.”

Among the ancients, and in Cicero, I read both *vehemens* and *vemens* (“violent”); likewise *prehendo* and *prendo* (“I seize”), *hercule* and *hercle* (“by Hercules”), *nihil* and *nil* (“nothing”). These matters can be observed by usage rather than by reason, especially in words that ought to have aspiration.

The ancients did not always use the letter *y*, but sometimes placed *u* in its place. Therefore, in their books too, I think this spelling should be observed: *Suriam* (“Syria”), *Suracusas* (“Syracuse”), *sumbola* (“symbol”), *sucophantas* (“sycophants”). But in our own writings it must not be corrupted.

I also do not see why we should remove the grace of aspiration from this letter. It is aspirated in itself, and in whatever word it occupies the first position, it is aspirated: *Yacinthus* (“Hyacinthus”), *Yllus* (“Hyllus”), *Ymetus* (“Hymettus”). All the more, aspiration should not be added because among the Latins words are not marked by this letter.

Varro holds that the letter *r*, if placed first, should not be aspirated. “The reader himself,” he says, “must understand that *Rodus*, although it has no *h*, is *Rhodus*; and that *retor* is *rhetor*.” But this observation is unnecessary for the letter *r*, since there are words beginning with *r* that are no less Latin than Greek. Therefore we shall rightly remove or withdraw aspiration from *Roma* (“Rome”), *regina* (“queen”), *rapa* (“turnip”), and *Rodus* (“Rhodes”).

In ancient books *z* is sometimes written and sometimes not. In its place two *s*s were used, as *crotalizo, crotalisso* (“I rattle”); *malacizo, malacisso* (“I soften”), and similarly in other cases. But let those people decide who, while not ashamed to use the complete words of the Greeks, thought it shameful to intermingle Greek letters. For us it is better to use what belongs to another properly than to append what is ours inelegantly.

## CHAPTER II

### These Matters Were Culled from Velius Longus

If *at* is a conjunction, it must be written with *t*, as in:

*At te nocturnis juvat impallescere chartis.*  
“But it delights you to grow pale over nocturnal pages.”

If it is a preposition, it is written with *d*, as in:

*Fando aliquid si forte tuas pervenit ad aures.*  
“If by report anything has perhaps reached your ears.”

Likewise *atque* (“and also”), a compound conjunction, should similarly be written with *t*. The preposition *ad* (“to”) should be written with *d*, as in *ad patrem* (“to the father”), since the ancients often used *apud* for *ad*; after two of its middle letters, namely *p* and *u*, were removed, *ad* remained.

Likewise *quit*, written with *t*, is a verb of the third person. Its first person is *queo* (“I can”), its second *quis* (“you can”), and its third *quit* (“he can”). From these are formed *nequeo, nequis, nequit* (“I cannot, you cannot, he cannot”) and *inquio, inquis, inquit* (“I say, you say, he says”).

Written with *d*, however, it is the adverb *quid* (“why,” “what”), as in *quid faciat laetas segetes* (“what makes the crops glad”), and the words compounded from it: *quidquid* (“whatever”), *siquid* (“if anything”), *aliquid* (“something”), *nunquid* (“surely not?”), and similar forms.

*Id*, written with *d*, is the neuter pronoun from *is, ea, id* (“he, she, it”). Written with *t*, it denotes the third-person verb from *eo, is, it* (“I go, you go, he goes”).

It is also preferred that we write *Delmatia*, not *Dalmatia*, since the name is thought to have been derived from *Delminium* [manuscript: *Delminum*], the greatest city of that province.

*Feriae* (“holidays”) must likewise be written, not *fereae*, because among the ancients they were called *feriae*, not *fereae*.

Both *actuarii* and *actarii* are used. *Actuarii* are generally called those occupied with various acts; *actarii* are called only the writers of records.

Likewise, it is one thing to be a *Cilo*, another to be a *Chilo*. *Cilones* are called men with narrow and elongated heads, and the word has no aspiration. *Chilones*, written with aspiration, are the name given to men with shorter lips; the word is derived from the Greek term *παρὰ τὰ χείλη* (“from the lips”). From this, they also say, *Achilles* received his name.

Conjux, without an *n*, the grammarian Nisus thinks should be written thus, since in the genitive it makes *conjugis*. I, however, think that this letter should not be removed from it, since it expresses the sound of the pronunciation. For although he maintains that a word should not be burdened with superfluous letters, I nevertheless judge that the sound should not be deprived of the letters by which it is conveyed to the ears completely and more fully [ed., “complete and full”].

## CHAPTER III. These rules have been collected from Curtius Valerianus.

The letter *q* is correctly used when the letter *u* immediately follows it, joined to another vowel or vowels [Col. 1247C] in a diphthong, so that it forms one syllable, as in *Quirites*, *quaestio*, *quaerite*. All other cases should be written with *c*, as in *cujus*, *Cumae*, and the rest of this kind.

When *cum* is a preposition, it is written with *c*, as in the following:

> Divisum imperium cum Jove Caesar habet.  
> Caesar shares divided rule with Jupiter.

But when it is an adverb, it should be written with *q*. For the ancients said *quando* and *quum*; for example:

> Quum navis ex Asia venerit.  
> When the ship has come from Asia.

Other adverbs of this kind should likewise be written in the same way, such as *quoquumque* and *ubiquumque*.

*Hujuscemodi* should be written with the letter *c*. [609] The ancients added *-ce* to pronouns, as in *hicce*, *illicce*, *isticce*. When that final letter was removed, the *c* remained, as in *hic*, *illic*, *istic*. But in the genitive alone of the demonstrative pronoun, namely *hujusce*, the same syllable *-ce* still remains intact [Col. 1247D].

Some have thought that *cur* should be written with *c*, saying that the letter *q* cannot be placed where *u* occurs without another vowel, according to the rule given above. Others write it with *q*, because they believe it derives from interrogative adverbs such as *quando* and *quorsum*. Usage, however, has established that *cur* is written with *c*.

The ancients wrote *partubus* and *partibus*, *arcubus* and *arcibus*, *artubus* and *artibus* indiscriminately. We may observe the following distinction: from *partus*, meaning “offspring,” we should write *partubus*; from *partes*, “parts,” *partibus*. Likewise, from *arcus*, “bows,” *arcubus* [Col. 1248A]; from *arces*, “citadels,” *arcibus*; and again, from *artus*, meaning “limbs,” *artubus*; from *artes*, “arts,” *artibus*.

The Greeks have three letters, ζ, ξ, and ψ. Of these we have transferred Ζ into our usage. In place of ξ we use *x*. ψ could not be transferred in any way, but its force has been transferred into *ps*: therefore words written with ψ should be written by us with *ps*. In other cases, words ending in these sounds end either in *-bis* or *-pis*, as in *caeleps, caelibis*; *auceps, aucupis*; *cinips, ciniphis*.

We should also observe the following division of syllables in relation to *bs* and *ps*: wherever *ps* occurs, it cannot be divided; rather, it must be attached to the following or preceding syllable, as though it had the force of a single letter: *apstinui*, *aps* and *tenui*; *apscessi*, *aps* and *cessi*; *apscondo*, *aps* and *condo*. But wherever *bs* occurs, it must necessarily be divided, as in *obstupui*, *obstupeo*, *obsum*, *obstrepo*. Moreover, you will never find *bs* joined together as a syllable, for they cannot form one, even though they may have a vowel before them: they deceive the ear as though they were themselves consonants, as in *trabs*, which we pronounce *trabem*. But if they are placed before a vowel, they cannot be pronounced at all. On the other hand, *ps*, even when placed before a vowel, sounds just as it does among the Greeks, ψ.

I think the same principle should be observed in verbs in which it is uncertain whether the past and future forms should have *p* or *b*. For just as in the cases of nouns the letter *p* changes into *b*, as in *caeleps, caelibis*, so also in the tenses of verbs we see, conversely, *b* changed into *p*: *scribo, scripsi, scripturus*; [Col. 1248C] *labor, lapsus, lapsurus*; *nubo, nupsi, nuptura*.

The letter *z* was not written in ancient Latin books. Instead, two *s*’s were placed for it: *crotalizare*, *crotalissare*. Let those judge who did not blush to use certain complete Greek words in the Latin language, yet thought it shameful to intermingle Greek letters. For it is better to use foreign things well than to append our own inelegantly.

We write *praesto* with *o*; the ancients wrote it with *u*. Nevertheless, it should be pronounced *praesto*, like *sedulo*, *optato*, and *sortito*. Hence also *praestolari*, not *praestulari*. It is not surprising that the ancients used *u* for *o*, since they also used *o* for *u*. Thus they said *poblicum*, where we say *publicum*, and *colpam*, where we say *culpam*.

*Supter* should be written with *p*, not *b*. *Neglegere* should be written with *g*, not *c* [Col. 1248D]. Some thought that *Eutalium*, *Eupolim*, and words of this kind should be written with the letter *y*, because they said they were Greek; but among us the letter *y* is never joined to a vowel.

## CHAPTER IV. These rules have been collected from Papirianus.

[Note: [Col. 1247] Priscianus sometimes cites this grammarian more than the others.]

The syllable *ae*, which we now write as a diphthong at the end of a word, as in *cogitationes magnae*, was written by the ancients with *ai*, so that the genitives could be distinguished from the datives. For the genitive they made the division in such a way that it would not be disyllabic, like the dative, but trisyllabic: *magnai, Asiai, aulai, rugai, ferai* [ms., *frugiferai*].

*Reliquiae* and *reliqui* were written with *c*: just as *relicuus* and *vacuus*, so *relicui* and *vacui*; likewise *mortuus* and *mortui*, *strenuus* and *strenui*. But now *reliquiae* and *exsequiae* are written with *q*.

*Cotidie* is pronounced and written with *c* and *o*, not with *q*, because it is derived not from *quoto die* but from *continenti die*, “on the continuing day.”

When *haud* is an adverb of negation, it ends in the letter *d* and is aspirated at the beginning. But when it is a disjunctive conjunction, it is written with *t*, without aspiration.

*Malo*, meaning “I prefer” (*magis volo*), is written with one *l*. *Malle*, meaning “to prefer” (*magis velle*), is written with two *l*’s. *Nolo*, meaning “I do not wish” (*non volo*), has one *l*. *Nolle*, meaning “not to wish” (*non velle*), has two *l*’s.

At first, *querela* was written by the ancients with one *l*, like *suadela*, *tutela*, *candela*, and *corruptela*. Nevertheless, usage even among them claimed the right to write certain diminutive forms with two *l*’s, as in *capella*, *fabella*, and *tabella*. Now *querella* too is written with two *l*’s.

*Narare* is written with one *r*, as Varro prefers. He followed the etymology of the word, according to which a person who knows and has understood what he ought to say is called *gnarus*. Finally, the compound of the verb is written *ignorare*, with one *r*, not two. Therefore *naratio* ought also to have one *r*.

*Quot*, when it is a numeral, should be written with *t*; when it is a pronoun, with *d*. Thus *totidem* is written with *t* [Col. 1249C], because it is a numeral.

All verbs beginning with the letter *s*, if they are compounds and therefore receive the preposition *ex-*, retain the *s* in writing: *specto, exspecto*; *salio, exsilio*. Other verbs that do not have *s* at the beginning should not be burdened with it: *aestimo, existimo*; *acuo, exacuo*; *agito, exagito*.

We say both *prendo* and *prehendo*, both *hercle* and *hercule*, both *nihil* and *nihili*. But in words that ought to have aspiration, these observations may be followed only insofar as usage permits. Nevertheless, the little book written below on aspiration teaches us this clearly.

*Traps*, from what is called *trabis*, and *urps* should be written with *p* [Col. 1249D], although Varro thinks they should be written with *b*, because they have *b* in the other cases. Yet since the Greek letter ψ could in no way be transferred into our usage, and its force is written with the letters *p* and *s*, it is necessary that wherever Greek ψ sounds in our language—which cannot be avoided—it should be written with these letters, namely *ps*, even though the oblique cases have *b*: *caeleps, caelibis*; *urps, urbis*. Likewise, in other words the same letter is retained: *auceps, aucupis*. Hence it is clear that in these cases we must change *p* and *b*, where both occur with a vowel between them.

The same rule applies to φ, which is composed of *p* and *h*: *cinips, ciniphis*, written with *p* and *s* in the nominative, but with *p* and *h* in the other cases.

*Quicquam*, in the middle, should be written with *c*, not *d* [Col. 1250A]. In compounds, *d* is generally changed into *c*, as in prepositions: *accedo*, *accumulo*.

*Formosus* should be written without *n* in the second syllable, like *arenosus*, *frondosus*, *aquosus*, and *herbosus*. Participles, however, have *n*: *tonsus*, *tunsus*, *mensus*, *pransus*. The ancients had no consistent practice concerning whether they wrote with or without *n*; they generally wrote *tosus*, *tusus*, and *prasus*.

We convert Greek *y* into *u* in some words: *Cymas, Cumas*; *cyminum, cuminum*. In some words we do not convert it: *Syria, Cyriacus, symbolum, sycophanta*.

According to their etymology, we ought to say and write *forfices*. If we derive the word from *filum*, we should use *f*: *forfices*, the shears of tailors. If from *pilus*, we should use *p*: [Col. 1250B] *forpices*, the shears of barbers. If from *capere*, we should use *c*: *forcipes*, because they grasp (*formum*)—the tools of smiths. The ancients called something hot *formum*; hence *formosus*.

Some think that *vulgus*, *vultum*, *parvum*, and *torvum* should not be written with two *u*’s, on the grounds that one vowel joined to another similar vowel not only does not cohere but also increases the number of syllables, as in *vacuus*, *ingenuus*, *occiduus*, *exiguus*, and *perspicuus*, and in verbs such as *metuunt*, *tribuunt*, and *statuunt*.

Velius Longus thinks that those who assume this rule are deceived, because *primitivus*, *adoptivus*, *nominativus*, and other words are written with *u* and *o*. To write one way and pronounce another is the act of a madman. For although they write with *o*, they pronounce with *u*. Moreover, those who hold the contrary view have failed to observe that one *u* repeatedly has the force of a consonant whenever it is used as a consonant. Among the Greeks this is called the digamma. Thus *nominativus* does indeed have two letters *u*, but the first is placed as a consonant and the second as a vowel.

Donatus likewise says that whenever *u* and *i* are placed before themselves or before other vowels, they should be counted as consonants.

Caecilius [ms., Sellius] thinks that *hiemps* should not have *p* because of the letter *m*, since the *m* sounds sufficiently without that letter, or because no trace of it appears in any of the cases. But it is asked whether *sumpsi* can sound without the letter *p*. Since *p* also appears in another declension, when we say *sumptus* and *sumpturus*, it must necessarily be written with *p*.

The prepositions *a*, *ab*, *abs*, and *au* are of one kind, as when we say *a me*, “from me”; *ab illo*, “from him”; *abstuli*, “I took away”; *aufugi*, “I fled away” [Col. 1250D]. We should observe, however, that the preposition *ab* is written whenever it is joined to any part of speech beginning with a vowel, so that the word is not burdened with many consonants. If the word to which it is prefixed begins with a consonant, *ab* should not be used, but only *a*: *a fratre*, *a vicino*, *ab homine*, *ab urbe*.

Among us *abs* should be rejected before nouns with which it enters into composition: we say *ab urbe venio*, not *abs urbe venio*. In compounds, however, it is not to be avoided: *abscondo*, *abstineo*. *Au* likewise should be prefixed to words beginning with consonants.

In a compound, the preposition *in*, when followed by *p*, *b*, or *m*, changes *n* into *m*: *improbus*, *imbuit*, *immut at*. Whenever *g* follows it, it loses the *n*: *ignarus*, *ignotus*, since *gnarus* and *gnotus* are simple forms [Col. 1251A].

The preposition *ad* sometimes retains the letter *d*: *adfert*, *adfuit*; sometimes it changes it: *ammonet*, *amminiculum*. It often happens that certain consonants of verbs or words joined to this preposition are changed. We distinguish by the sound when this occurs and when it does not: *accedo* has two *c*’s, *attuli* two *t*’s, *assiduus* two *s*’s, *appareo* two *p*’s, *alligo* two *l*’s, *annuo* two *n*’s.

There is also a case in which this letter, namely *d*, must disappear: *aspiro*, *aspicio*. No consonant intervenes through *d*; rather, the *d* disappears completely.

The preposition *ex-*, before the letters *b*, *d*, *g*, *l*, *m*, *n*, and before *u* and *i* when they function as consonants, loses the letter *x*: *ebibit*, *edidit*, *egessit*, *elusit*, *emicuit*, *enarravit* [Col. 1251B]. When *f* follows, customary usage changes it into that same letter: *effundo*.

The preposition *ob-* is sometimes written in full, as in *obire*, *oberrare*. Sometimes it changes into the same letter with which the following word begins: *offulsit*, *ommutuit*, *opposuit*. When *u*, placed as a consonant, follows, it is preserved intact: *obversus*, *obvius*.

The preposition *sub-* sometimes preserves the letter *b*, as in *subire*, *subesse*, *subauscultare*. Sometimes it changes into the same letter with which the following verb begins: *sufficit*, *suffigit*, *summovit*, *sumministrat*, *supponit*, *supprimit*, *suggerit*. When the letter *r* follows, it remains intact: *subrado*, *subremigo*, *subrideo*. It is never corrupted when followed by *r*.

[Col. 1251C] *B* changes into *s* before *t* and *c*: *sustulit*, *suscepit*.

The preposition *de-* is either placed in full in compounds, as in *deducere*, *demonstrare*, *detrudere*, or it is corrupted through shortening of the vowel *e*, as in *deorsum*. When it changes into the letter *i*, as in:

> Aera dimovit tenebrosum, et dispulit umbras  
> He dispersed the dark air and drove away the shadows,

it does not derive from the preposition *de* but from *dis-*, as in *distraho*, *dispereo*.

The preposition *dis-* does not lose its *s* before a following *s*, as in *dispicio*. Before *b*, *d*, *g*, *l*, *m*, *n*, and *r*, it loses it: *dibucinat*, *diducit*, *digerit*, *dilacerat*, *dimovet*, *dinoscit*, *diripit*. Sometimes its *s* changes into the following letter, as in *dirumpo*. Before *f*, customary usage changes it into that same letter: *diffundo* [Col. 1251D].

The preposition *re-* is not only placed in full before certain parts of speech, as in *removet*, *refricat*, *respirat*; it also takes the letter *d*, as in *redire*, *redolere*. Sometimes *d* is doubled whenever the following syllable begins with the same letter and one part of the word is completed: thus we say *reddere* with doubled *d*, but *reducere* with a single one.

The preposition *trans-* is sometimes complete: *transtulit*, *transactum*, *transeo*, *transitus*. Sometimes it is shortened: *trajicit*, *traducit*.

The preposition *sine-* is sometimes corrupted by taking on the letter *d*: *seditio*, *sedulo*.

The preposition *pro-*, since it is naturally long, is sometimes corrupted in composition [Col. 1252A], partly by shortening, as in *proavus*; partly by taking on the letter *d*, as in *prodest*, *proditus*, *prodigus*; sometimes it remains intact, as does the word to which it is joined, as in *procuro*. Before *i* and *u*, when they function as consonants, it sometimes loses or changes a letter, as in *providens*; sometimes it takes one on or is shortened, as in *profertur*.

The preposition *circum-*, before vowels, loses the letter *m* in pronunciation but preserves it in writing. But when *i* and *u*, placed as consonants, follow, it is both written and pronounced: *circumvenit*, *circumjacet*.

The preposition *ante-* sometimes remains intact: *anteactum*, *antevenit*, *antecedit*. Sometimes it is corrupted by changing into *i*: *antistat*, *anticipat* [Col. 1252B].

The preposition *inter-*, in a single word before the letter *l*, changes *r* into that same letter: *intellego*. Before other following letters, including vowels, it remains intact in pronunciation: *interius*.

The pronouns *cujus* and *cui* were written with *q*. We, however, have hastened toward brevity in writing and have preferred to smooth away that heaviness.

*Accerso* is written with *c*, and *arcesso* with *r*. But *accerso* means “I summon,” whereas *arcesso* means “I drive away” or “I prohibit.”

The grammarian Gratus thought that *coqui* should be written with *c* in the first syllable and *q* in the second. For we do not say *cocere* but *coquere*, as Virgil says:

> Apricis coquitur vindemia saxis.  
> The vintage is cooked upon sunlit rocks.

The letter *v* is improperly inserted in some parts of speech, as in *urguere*. We say *urgere*, not *urguere*. Virgil has *Urgentur poenis*, “They are pressed by punishments,” written without *u* [Col. 1252C]. Likewise:

> Ungere tela manu, ferrumque armare veneno.  
> To smear the weapons with one’s hand and arm the iron with poison.

It is clear from this that one should not say *unguo*. No verb ending in *-vo*, whether as one word or separated, fails to preserve the same *u* in the past tense: *volvo, volvi*; *eruo, erui*. But *ungo* makes not *ungui* but *unxi*, just as *pingo* makes *pinxi*. Yet we do not necessarily see the letter *u* inserted into the noun formed from this verb so that it cannot be removed, as in Virgil’s:

> Et pingues unguine taedas.  
> And the torches thick with ointment.

In ordinary usage the word is *unguentum*, but it ought nevertheless to be written without *u*.

*Leprosi*, “lepers,” are so called from the excessive itching of the scab itself, and therefore should be written with *p*.

Some write the numeral *mille* with one *l*, because we say *milia*, not *millia* [Col. 1252D]; others more correctly think it should be written with two *l*’s.

## CHAPTER V. From Adamantius Martyrius, on *u* and *b*.

The syllable *va* appearing at the beginning of a noun should be written with the vowel *u* placed in the position of a consonant, since among the Latins this letter has greater force than mute *b*, because it is also a vowel. When it expresses a thicker sound, it passes into the power of a consonant: *vates, vanus, vagus, validus, vacuus*. The exceptions are *basio*, *balineo*, and *baculo*, from which the diminutive *bacillus* is formed.

Nouns whose second syllable ends in the letter *a* are likewise written with mute *b*: *balathro* [Greek ἄσωτος, “profligate”], *balatus* [Greek βληχηθμός, “bleating”], *baratrum*, *barbarus*, and similar words [Col. 1253A].

The shortened syllable *ve*, occupying the beginning of a noun, likewise has the digamma *u* in writing: *venenum, vena, verecundus, venerabilis, vetus, vehemens, vehiculum*. This applies provided that the nouns are not compounds of the adverb *bene*, “well.” Such words are marked with mute *b*, since the regular rule requires the adverb *bene* to be written with mute *b*.

The reason is that certain adverbs clearly derive from nouns. If the singular dative of a noun ends in *-o*, the final *o*, changed into *e*, whether short or long, forms the adverb: *doctus, docti, docto, docte*; *malus, mali, malo, male*. Therefore *bonus, boni, bono* ought also to make *bone*. But lest the vocative be thought an adverb, as in *o bone vir*, “O good man,” it seemed necessary to change the penultimate *o* into *e* as well, so that this adverb might be distinguished from that noun [Col. 1253B]. Thus the adverb *bene* was formed from *bono*. The following rules will show that *bonum* is signified by this letter.

Therefore, if nouns are compounds of the adverb *bene*, they are written with mute *b*: *benignus*, *benevolus*, *beneficus*, at least when derived from *benefacere*, “to do good.” No one is unaware that *venenum*, “poison,” is written with *u*.

We must nevertheless remember that *beatus* does not follow the preceding rule, since no consonant follows its first syllable. Since *vehemens* and *vehiculum* oppose this rule, we point out that aspiration causes the difference, as in many other cases. Here too we see a prefixed *u*, which can be placed in the position of a consonant.

The diphthong *vae* may stand alone, as in *vae misero mihi*, “woe is me, wretched man,” or may be compounded with a noun. In *vaesanus*, “insane,” it is written with the digamma *u* [Col. 1253C].

The lengthened syllable *ve*, likewise situated at the beginning of a noun, is written with *u* as a consonant when the nouns are masculine or neuter: *venator, velum, verum, venabulum*. If they are exclusively feminine, and their origin from a masculine noun is not evident, they are written with mute *b*: *besica, belua, bestia*. This applies provided they are not disyllabic, for they change their spelling in that case: *vena, vespa*, and similar words.

*Beta* is also an exception. The Greeks call it σεῦτλον, “beet”; the same gender distinction could not be maintained in Greek [Col. 1253D].

We also ask why *veritas*, although feminine and exceeding the measure [ed., “nature”] of two syllables, is written with *u*, not *b*. We answer that it is not a noun of the first formation but descends from a changeable gender. Its forms are *verus, vera, verum*, from which the appellative *veritas* is formed. It therefore necessarily preserves the rule of its original form. In the same way, *venatrix* follows the origin of its masculine form.

The syllable *vi*, whether long or short, beginning a noun, is written with mute *b* when it is compounded from the numeral *bis*, that is, “twice.” For the sake of distinction, the numeral *bis* is written with this letter, so that it may be separated from the monosyllabic noun *vis*, which signifies force or necessity: *biceps, bilinguis, biformis, bipatens, biennium, bimum, biga, biduum, bicolor, bipennis* [Col. 1254A], *bijugum*, and similar words.

But if they remain free of the numeral, they have *u* transferred into the power of a consonant: *victor, vinum, vitis, victus, vinitor, vita, vidua, vipera, viator, vitisator*. The exception is *bitumen*, which, although neuter, exceeds the measure of two syllables. *Bile* is also written this way for the sake of distinction. If it means “gall,” it is written with mute *b*; if it means something rejected and of little value, it is written with *u*. *Bibula* is derived from the verb *bibo*, whose rules we shall give later.

The short or lengthened syllable *vo*, preserving the beginning of a noun, is written with the letter *u*, its vowel force having been lost: *voluntas, vorago, vocabulum, vomitus, votum* [612]. The only exception is *bono*, which surpasses the rule because it is divided among three genders, whereas none of the words mentioned above takes the form of the changeable genders [Col. 1254B].

Whether lengthened or shortened, *bu* has mute *b* prefixed: *buxus, buffo, bustum, buccina, bucula*, and all words of this kind. The letter *u* could in no way be prefixed to itself, nor could it be joined to another consonant in the first syllable. But when a dissimilar letter immediately follows, words such as *vultus, vulgus,* and *Vulcanus* are written with the digamma *u*. If the first syllable ends in a consonant, from which the second syllable also begins, it retains mute *b* in writing: *bucca, bulla*, and similar words.

Whenever the syllable *vac* is prefixed, it has the vowel *u* in the position of a consonant: *vacca*, that is, “a draft animal”; *vaccinium*, namely, “the flower.” But *Bacchus*, *bacha*, and *bacchar* are written with *b* [Col. 1254C].

I have found the syllables *bec* and *bic* absent.

I have learned one barbarian word with *boc*: *Bocchos*, which I know has mute *b* in writing. It should be understood that foreign nouns, when drawn into the Latin language, generally retain mute *b*. I say “generally” because some obey Latin rules, as *Massiva*. Although this name is clearly barbarian, it nevertheless preserves the Latin rule in writing, as its proper place will show.

I found the syllable *buc* in only one noun, namely *bucca*, which is written with mute *b*.

The first syllable *val*, when followed by the letter *l*, is written with *u*: *valles*, *vallum*. But *balaena* and *ballistra* are written with *b*. If *l* does not follow, it is marked with mute *b*: *balteus, balbus, balvae*, that is, “doors.”

The exception is the adverb *valde*, since there is no doubt that it was formed by removal of the letter *i*. In my view, *valide* is the complete word. This too derives from a noun: *validus, validi, valido*; therefore it ought to form the adverb *valide*. If we wish to pronounce the word without corruption, it should follow the rule of the first syllable [Col. 1254D].

The syllable *vel*, if it remains alone, is the disjunctive conjunction and is invariably written with *v*. But if it is the beginning of a noun, it has mute *b* in writing: *bellum, bellissimum, bellaria*. The exception is *vellus*, for the sake of distinction. If *vellus* is written with *u*, it is neuter and belongs to the third declension, meaning “wool,” since *vellus, velleris* has this form. But if it is marked with mute *b*, it is masculine and belongs to the second declension, denoting something elegant or clever: *bellus, belli*, meaning “clever” or “playful.”

If the syllable *vil* comes first, it has the vowel *u* in the position of a consonant: *villus*, “a tuft or thread of a garment”; *villa*, that is, “an estate.”

I have found no noun in which *bam*, with other vowels intervening, is pronounced in the first syllable, except in glosses: *bammum*, Greek ὀξυτάριον, “a sharp-pointed object”; and *bambalo*, Greek ψελλιστής, “one who lisps.” These are written with mute *b*.

The syllables *van*, *ven*, and *vin* have the vowel *u* in the position of a consonant: *vannus, ventus, vindicta*.

The prefixed syllable *vap* has the vowel *u* in the position of a consonant: *vappa*, Greek ὑδαρής, “watery.” I have found other vowels placed between *u* and *p* absent [Col. 1255B].

When *ban* begins a syllable, it has mute *b*: *barrus*, Greek ἐλέφας, “elephant”; *bardus*, Greek ἀναίσθητος, “senseless”; *bargus*, Greek ἀφυής, “witless”; *barba*. The only exception is the proper name *Varro*.

The syllables *ver* and *vir*, whether long or short, have the vowel *u* placed as a consonant: *vertex, virgiliae*—Greek πλειάδες, “the Pleiades”—*verbum, virus, virga, virgo, virtus, Virbius*. The sole exception is *berna*. Although I found this noun written with *u*, I heard Mennonius, a man of illustrious memory and a judge of every kind of eloquence, say that he had been reproved by a most eloquent Roman for pronouncing it with this letter. We therefore mark and attempt to explain the distinction as follows.

If *berna* means “born in the home,” that is, Greek οἰκογενής, “home-born,” it is common according to the ancients to two genders, but according to my view to three, and it will be written with mute *b*. If it denotes something temporal, it will be changeable: from *vere* come *vernus, verna, vernum*, as when one says *vernus sol*, “spring sun”; *verna hirundo*, “spring swallow”; *vernum tempus*, “springtime.” In that case it will retain *u* in writing, like its original form.

With these distinctions in place, we may also understand *berna* to refer to someone born among hereditary goods. The preceding discussion shows that *bona*, “goods,” is written with the letter *b* [Col. 1255C].

I have found no noun in the Latin language beginning with the syllable *vor*, whether short or long, except *vortex*, used for *vertex*. Similarly, I remember that the ancients formed *volnus* [*vulnus*].

I have likewise found *bur* absent, except in the proper noun *burra*, which, according to the rule explained above, is known to be written with mute *b*.

I found also the long monosyllabic noun *bes*. It signifies eight ounces, and usage has handed down that it retains mute *b* in writing. I could not find a short form. For although *vesper*, *vestis*, and similar words are written with the vowel *u* in the position of a consonant, according to the rule given above, where we made *bes* long they ought nevertheless to be written with *v*, since the following *s* unquestionably belongs to the next syllable [Col. 1255D].

If *vos* is a pronoun, it is written in the monosyllable with the letter *u*. When it is disyllabic, namely *vobis*, the first syllable is written with *v* and the second with *b*. But when it is the name of a draft animal, as in:

> Procumbit humi bos.  
> The ox sinks down upon the ground,

it has mute *b* in the monosyllabic nominative and vocative. When the word begins to be doubled through the other cases, it retains *b* in the first syllable and *u* in the second: *bovis, bovi, bovem, a bove*. Thus, in the pronoun mentioned above, the contrary letters are shown to have produced the variation.

I found *bat* in only one neuter noun, plural in pronunciation: *battualia*, commonly called *battalia*. We know that it has mute *b* and signifies the exercises of soldiers or gladiators. Hence I think that *battuatores* are called Greek τοὺς βασανιστάς, “those who test or torment.”

*Vit* is written with *u*. I have learned only the monosyllables *vix* and *vox* to be written with the vowel *u* [Col. 1256B]. Latin eloquence knows no other vowels placed before *x*, nor any vowels joined to the letter *b*.

## CHAPTER VI. On the medial syllables, from the same Adamantius Martyrius.

We have treated, as far as we could, without omission, the syllables placed at the beginnings of nouns. I believe it is known to everyone that, if a consonant follows the *b* placed at the beginning of a syllable in any word, it must unquestionably be written: *blandus, gibbus*, Greek κυρτός, “curved”; *braveium*; *latebrae*; *tenebrae*; and all such words. Now the medial syllables will reasonably receive our attention.

The syllable *va*, placed in the middle of a noun, is written with *u*: *avarus, calvare*. The exception is *carbasum*, which I consider more Greek than Latin in origin.

*Ambages* is marked with mute *b*, either because the letter *m* precedes it or because I think the word is composed from two corrupt forms, as though it were *amboactae*. Hence *ambire* is also derived.

Therefore we should mark compound or appellative, transferred, or artificial words—that is, words made from others—in such a way that they follow their original forms, namely their first formations: *novus, novalis*; *rivus, rivalis*; and derivatives from *Alba*, *Albanus*; from *silva*, *silvanus*; from *privo*, *privatum*; from *libo*, *libatum* or *illibatum* [Col. 1256C].

The shortened syllable *ve*, whether alone or joined to a consonant, is marked with the vowel *u* placed as a consonant: *juvenis, alveus, fovea, advena, juvencus, caverna, noverca*, and the preposition *adversus*, except *trabea*. Although *gubernator* is written with mute *b*, I think that this noun is formed from the verb *guberno*. We shall consider its rules later, when we come to the treatment of the letter *b* in its three positions within a noun.

This applies provided the nouns are not diminutives or derivatives. Such words, as we said above, follow their original forms: *liber, libertus, libellus*; *imber, hibernus*; *flabrum, flabellum*; *tabula, tabella*; *taberna, tabernaculum*; *bellator, imbellis* or *imbecillis*; *fabula, fabella*. All these are certainly written with mute *b*, as first forms.

The lengthened syllable *be* is everywhere written with mute *b*: *verbena, rubeta, ambesum, habena* [Col. 1257A]. The exception is *avena*, which means either “reed pipe” or “straw,” for the sake of distinction. *Severus*, because it comes from *saevus*, follows the rule of the syllable *ve* for the sake of its later derivation.

The short syllable *vi* is written with the vowel *u* having the force of a consonant: *Favius, Flavius, avidus, fluvius, civitas, favilla, provincia, exuviae, manuviae, oblivium, diluvium, suavium, lividum, simpuvium*, Greek εἶδος σκεύοις ἱερατικοῦ, “the form of priestly vessels.” The exceptions are the noun *obitum* and the adverbs *subito* and *obiter*. I think that in these words the ancients, because *ob* and *sub* are prepositions, preserved the letter *b* in writing by attaching it not to the medial syllable but to the first syllable.

*Virbius* is removed from the rule because they say that he was made a man twice over. The preceding discussion makes clear that this numeral is written with mute *b*. Some interpret the name as “good man”; others write *virbium*, as though it meant Greek ἥρως ἀναβεβιωκώς [printed *αἰαβεβιωκώς*], “a hero restored to life”;  others interpret him as the god who presides over strength.

Moreover, *ambiguus* is marked with an exception, since when *m*, a semivowel, precedes, the letter *u* never follows as a consonant in the same word. *Quamvis* is opposed to this, but it appears to be a compound, since the latter syllable *vis* is added to many words: *quovis, quorumvis, utrumvis*, and similar forms [Col. 1257B].

We should nevertheless observe whether the pure syllable *es* has ended the nouns. If they are pronounced in this way, the medial syllable is unquestionably written with mute *b*: *abies, scabies, rabies*. But this class is also divided into two. If the word has more than three syllables, it will necessarily be marked with *u*: *illuvies, proluvies, ingluvies, subluvies*.

The syllable *lis* at the end compelled nouns to be written with mute *b*: *nobilis, mobilis, laudabilis, mirabilis, debilis, habilis, effabilis* [Col. 1257C]. The exceptions are *servili*, *civili*, and *ovile*, which derive from *servus*, *civis*, and *ovis*, and from the syllable *vis* by later formation. We shall consider the rules of that syllable later.

Although *habitus, excubiae, probitas, arbitrium, dubium*, and similar words are written with mute *b*, this is because they are formed from verbs. It should be understood that all nouns which have an association with verbs will necessarily also be subject to the rules of verbs, which we shall give in their proper place.

When *bi* is long and penultimate, it is written with mute *b*: *libido, rubigo, tibicen, ambitus, concubina, cubile*. But we must also explain that some of these are shortened in their altered forms: *tubicen, tibia, cubile, cubitus*, and *connubium*. Although they have lost the force of the long syllables, they nevertheless require the same spelling to be preserved in their derivatives.

It should further be understood that if, in compound nouns, a long syllable *vi* falls in the penultimate or antepenultimate position, it is written with the vowel *u* in the position of a consonant: *invitus, divigenus, Lavinia, privilegium*, and similar words. I do not doubt that *privignum* follows this rule, since I think it is formed by removing the letter *e*: *privigenum* seems to our mind the more complete word [Col. 1257D].

We also point out that in derivatives here, as everywhere, we have observed the rules of the original forms: *cervix, cervicale*; *pulvis, pulvinarium*. We shall shortly disclose the rules governing these forms, which arise from the later syllable [Col. 1258A].

The spelling of *convivii* confirms this division of the rules. The syllables of *vivii*, though constituted with different quantities, are marked in the same way, because the first, that is, the antepenultimate syllable, is long and earned the rule mentioned shortly before, where we recalled that a long *vi* in the antepenultimate position must be written with the vowel *u* having the force of a consonant. The remaining syllable, being short, follows the rule given above, where we said that short *vi* placed in the middle of a noun is marked with *u*. I do not think that this division of the rule is unreasonable.

The syllable *vo*, whether long or short and placed in the middle of a noun, is written with *u*: *advocatus, frivolus, devotus, Favonium, divortium*. *Abortu* and *subole* deny the rule, I think, because of the prepositions [Col. 1258B].

The syllable *bu* is most certainly written with mute *b*, as in *tribunal, robustus, vocabulum, stabulum, ebulum, vestibulum, cunabulum, moribundus, furibundus*, and all similar words. *Avunculo* is, however, to be counted less strictly under this rule; hence there is no doubt that it preserves the form of a diminutive or derivative and is shown as though it came from *avus*. The proper place has shown that *avum* is written with the digamma *u*. This concludes the discussion of medial syllables.

## 614 CHAPTER VII. Likewise, by the same Martyrius, on final syllables

It remains to devote attention to the final syllables of nouns.

[Col. 1258C] When a noun ends in the syllable *va*, it is written with *u* if the letter *l* precedes it, or if a naturally long vowel has stood in the penultimate syllable: *silva, malva, ulva, vulva, clava, uva, stiva, oliva, saliva*. The exception is *balbas*, provided that its preceding syllable is written with mute *b*, for the sake of distinction, lest it signify, not doors, but an inexpressible utterance of the voice. For if it is pronounced with mute *b*, it will signify θύρας, or τὸν πυλῶνα ἀμφίθυρον, “doors” or “a gate with doors on both sides”; it is written with the digamma *u* in the final syllable, namely the syllable now under discussion. It signifies *tavellas* [perhaps *tabellas*, “little tablets”]. Persius writes: “Speaking *balva* from the nostril.”

But if this letter, namely *l*, does not precede it, and if the penultimate syllable does not contain one naturally long vowel, mute *b* will properly occupy its place in writing—provided, however, that the nouns have not been formed from the masculine gender: *herba, tuba, turba, larba, δαιμόνιον* (“a demon”), *barba, obba, ποτήριον* (“a cup”), *gleba, pronuba, orba*. *Caterva* and *Minerva* are excepted; as disyllables they exceed the number covered by this rule, since their penultimate syllable is long by position.

The shortened syllable *ve* is without doubt written with *u*, whether the nouns arise from themselves or come from other words: *conclave, suave, sive, quidve*, and similar forms.

I have found no noun ending in *bi* except in dative pronouns and adverbs, which are invariably written with mute *b*: *tibi, sibi, ubi, ibi*; and, in the plural, *nobis, vobis*.
