It must also be understood once and for all that any nouns or pronouns which contain the letter *b* in the singular or plural dative are written with mute *b* in every other case, where that letter does not appear in precisely the same form: *omnibus, similibus, pluribus*, and the like.

[Col. 1259A] A final syllable *bo* is written with mute *b*: *turbo, orbo, bubo,* and *tabo*, although it is pronounced in the ablative case. The sole exception is *pavo*.

Words ending in the syllable *bal* are written with mute *b*, as we know from barbarian or Latin nouns: *Hannibal, Hasdrubal*. I have been unable to find any other vowels placed between *b* and *l*.

We know that the syllables *bam* and *bem*, together with the other vowels in the nominative case, are foreign to the Latin language, except for *novem*. This denotes an indeclinable number and is written with *u*. Certain neuter forms are also to be noted; we shall assign them later to other classes.

Words ending in *bar* and *ber* are written with mute *b* if they do not exceed the number of disyllables, whose penultimate syllable will necessarily be naturally long—that is, if the word is not a trisyllable whose penultimate syllable is not naturally long: *jubar, liber, imber, uber, faber, suber, Calaber, Mulciber*. If, however, they are trisyllabic neuters whose penultimate syllable is naturally long, they are marked with *u* functioning as a consonant: *cadaver, papaver*, and similar words. Although *pulver* is a disyllable, the ancients nevertheless preferred to pronounce a double nominative; for they said not only *pulver* but also *pulvis*. For this reason it is written with *u*.

[Col. 1259B] *Vir* is written with *u* functioning as a consonant: *Semivir, Triumvir*, although these are compounds and not simple forms.

*Vor* is marked with *u*: *livor* and *Mavors*—if, indeed, we think it necessary to place this name here, since some wish to call him not only *Mars* but also *Mavors*, from which they likewise derive *Mavortia*. The exception is *arbor*, since it is also called *arbos*, which usage has taught us to write with mute *b*. *Labor, favor, fervor,* and *pavor*, being formed from verbs, likewise do not reject the rule of their verbs.

A word ending in *bur* retains mute *b* in writing: *ebur, robur*.

The short and determinate syllable *ves* is written with *u* functioning as a consonant: *dives*.

Words ending in the long syllable *bes* retain mute *b* in writing: *labes, tabes, pubes, nubes*, although some have preferred to pronounce the nominative *nubis*.

[Col. 1259D] *Vis* is written with *u* functioning as a consonant: *civis, nivis, clavis, gravis, pulvis, suavis*. Although *scrobis* and *orbis* are written with mute *b*, this is because some have preferred to pronounce the singular nominative without the letter *i*.

*Bos* is written with mute *b*, as is *arbos*, as we recognize from what was recalled above.

If the nouns ending in *bus* are exclusively masculine, they are written with mute *b*: *cibus, nebus, morbus, rubus, globus, nimbus, lembus, lumbus*. The sole exception to be noted is *nervus*, because, if a long *e* is placed before it, it forms a verb. For *enervo*, ἐκνευρίζω, “I enervate,” is called a verbal form. We shall explain its rationale when we discuss the verb.

[Col. 1260A] We shall nevertheless observe that, if these words do not exceed the number of disyllables or do not have a naturally long penultimate syllable consisting of one vowel, they do not change their spelling: *rivus, clivus, acervus, nominativus*, and the rest. But because *coroebus* exceeds the number of disyllables, it is marked with mute *b*. It must be understood that this letter has been retained in writing either because the word is foreign and not Latin, or because it earned a long penultimate syllable not from a single vowel but from a diphthong.

If the forms are variable or of common gender, they are written with *u* functioning as a consonant: *novus, nova, novum; saevus, saeva, saevum; cervus, cerva; curvus, curva, curvum; torvus, torva, torvum; clavus, clava*, although they take a different meaning according to gender; *avus, ava; cervus, cerva; flavus, flava*. The same meaning is likewise followed by another interpretation, unless we wish to write the feminine with mute *b* for the sake of distinction: *calvus, calva*, and *corvus*, a common-gender form; likewise *clavus* in both genders, signifying different things.

*Orbo, gibbo, probo* are removed from the rule, as is *albo* for the sake of distinction. When *albo* signifies the belly, it is written with the digamma *u*; when it signifies a color, it is most certainly written with mute *b*.

It must likewise be understood that forms exceeding the number of disyllables retain the same spelling: *superbus, superba, superbum; acerbus, acerba, acerbum; palumbus*, of common gender, although Virgil used it in the feminine:

> Yet meanwhile, your care for the hoarse dove …

*Protervus* is excepted. *Lascivus* is written with *u*, because it has retained a naturally long penultimate syllable.

And it must be understood that whether the words are disyllabic, or exceed that number, and whether they belong to one, two, or three genders, if they have a long second syllable from the end, they are all written with *u* functioning as a consonant: *rivus, clivus, flavus, positivus, comparativus*, and others.

We must nevertheless remember that the feminine and neuter forms of variable nouns receive the same spelling as their masculine forms: *flavus, flava, flavum; albus, alba, album*, and similar forms. But not all words ending in *-bus* are variable, as we recall having explained at the beginning of this rule when dividing the genders. Some are found only in the masculine gender, such as *cibus, nimbus*; some are masculine and feminine, such as *cervus, cerva*; and some are neuter, such as *aevum*.

It must also be understood that neuter forms which do not arise from later syllabic formations are written with the digamma *u*: *ovum, arvum, hervum*. The exception is *libo*, that is, ποπάνῳ, “a sacrificial cake.” The final syllable of the verb is written with mute *b* because the ancients thought it was derived from *verbero*, “to strike”; we recognize that we explained its rationale above.

The syllables *vax, vex,* and *vix* each have only one word ending in them, as I have found: *vivax, vibex, vervex, cervix*. Their middle syllable is written with mute *b*; those which occur at either side or externally, however, are always represented with *u*. The Latin language admits few other vowels inserted among these consonants [manuscript: “cuts off”]. Those whose resolution was deferred above will be clarified in the following treatise, on the letter *b* placed in three positions within a noun, with appropriate declension.

## CHAPTER VIII. By the same Adamantius Martyrius, on the letter *b* placed in three positions within a noun

We have, as far as possible, dealt sufficiently, I believe, with the letter *b* placed in three positions within a noun. From what has been set forth we can now correctly understand whether anything contrary to the statements should arise. In such a case we must consider whether it differs in gender, in the number of syllables, or in the indication of quantity, or whether it has descended from another part of speech. By observing these points, we shall, I think, make fewer errors.

It remains for us to discuss the letter *b*, which is likewise found in verbs, assigning to the subject, I believe, a complete account of the labor involved. For since a complete sentence is composed from a noun and a verb, I judge it neither necessary to leave this part untouched nor superfluous to labor further upon it. Let us therefore consider briefly, as far as we can, the rules of this part.

Looking at the first person of the indicative mood, namely of the active or even the neuter verb—for just as the active is written, so also is the passive—we find no difficulty in the common and deponent forms. They can more readily be judged from the rules given for nouns and from those that will be set out for verbs. It is beyond doubt that the first syllable of the person follows and retains a form like that of the first syllable of the verbs in common or deponent usage.

The medial syllable is likewise written with *u* placed in the position of a consonant, except in *bajulo* and *bullio*, according to the reasoning that we gave for the first syllable of nouns. For the sake of distinction, *vivo* (“I live”) is written with *u*, but *bibo* (“I drink”) with *b*. I think that *abeo*, “I depart,” *obeo, circumeo, subeo, succedo*, and similar forms are written with *b* because of their prepositions. Usage and ancient custom have likewise handed down that deponent forms retain mute *b* in writing.

As far as our strength permits, we shall attempt to treat the remaining forms under one general rule, while preserving the firm rules given for nouns, even when nouns are transformed into verbs. For just as verbs derived from nouns do not lose the rules of verbs, so nouns placed in the position of verbs cannot be deprived of the rules belonging to their origin.

Therefore, if the past tense of the indicative ends in the syllable *vi*, the medial and final syllables of the first-person present tense are written with *u* placed in the position of a consonant, since every perfect past form ending in *vi*, except *bibi*, is written with *u*: *foveo, fovi; faveo, favi; moveo, movi; paveo, pavi; expaveo, expavi; lavo, lavi; juvo, juvi; servio, servivi*. The exceptions are *lambio, lambibi; ambio, ambibi*, and similar forms, whose spelling has been altered by the preceding letter.

Although *ferveo* forms the perfect *fervi*, written with *u*, to which I myself give the greater assent, *ferbui* will be written with mute *b*, provided that the verbs do not belong to the first conjugation and the first class. For those verbs are always written with mute *b*: *libero, liberas, liberavi; guberno, gubernas, gubernavi; exubero, exuberas, exuberavi; sibilo, sibilas, sibilavi; dubito, dubitas, dubitavi; hebeto, hebetas, hebetavi; titubo, titubas, titubavi; habito, habitas, habitavi*.

*Invito* and *derivo* are excepted, according to the reasoning given above: every first syllable of verbs, except those just listed, is written with *u*, since no one doubts that *in* and *de* are prepositions. *Navigo* and *acervo*—ἐπιπλῶ, “I sail upon,” and σωρεύω, “I heap up”—and similar forms follow the rules given for nouns. This class too is divided into two parts.

If they are disyllabic, they change their spelling: *levo, levas, levavi; servo, servas, servavi; curvo, curvas, curvavi; novo, novas, novavi; ovo, ovas, ovavi*. *Orbo* and *turbo* are excepted. *Turbo*, descending from the noun *turba*, retained the syllable *ba* by right of derivation. I think *probo* is said by removing the letter *r*, since its opposite is called *exprobro*; and for this reason I judge that mute *b* should be added, according to the rule that we remember having given for nouns. We are also confident that *libo* was translated from Greek, namely from λείβω, “I pour.”

Moreover, we ask why the verb *enervo*, which exceeds the number of disyllables and belongs to the first conjugation and first class, is written not with mute *b* but with *u*. In resolving the question, we say that its preposition is long, and therefore it has taken the rule of disyllables.

But since some verbs occur in which the first person has no letter *u* in the final or preceding syllable, whereas the second person contains it—such as *volo, vis; malo, mavis*—and others have it only in the perfect past, though not in their basic form, such as *gaudeo, gavisus sum*; and since again, in the perfect past, which entirely lacks the letter *u*, other persons in other tenses retain that same letter, such as *vivo, vixi*, it must be understood that this *u* is treated in writing as a vowel functioning as a consonant.

If the aforementioned past tense ends in the syllables *bui*, *si*, or *psi*, it will without doubt be written with mute *b*: *praebeo, praebui; jubeo, jussi; scribo, scripsi*, and similar forms.

I believe that we have given a very complete rule concerning verbs, since the final syllable of every imperfect past indicative has mute *b*: *amabam, volebam*; while the final syllable of the perfect past and the penultimate syllable of the pluperfect have *u* placed in the position of a consonant: *amavi, amaveram; volui, volueram*.

The corresponding ending of the future, if the verbs belong to the first, second, or third long conjugation, will likewise be written with mute *b*: *amo, amabo; voco, vocabo; doceo, docebo; moneo, monebo; nutrio, nutribo; audio, audibo*.

We know that the ancients handed down the rule that the final syllables of the subjunctive, or conjunctive, should be written with *u* functioning as a consonant: *volebam, volueram, voluerim, voluissem, voluero*, and similar forms—namely, those verbs whose first person either has *u* functioning as a consonant in the final syllable, such as *levo, privo*, or has no trace of that letter at all in the same place and person, such as *habito, hiberno, amo, doceo*, and similar forms.

For those verbs which have mute *b* in the first syllable of the present tense, as stated, and whose past tense ends in the syllables *bui* or *psi*, seek to retain the same mute *b* in all tenses and moods wherever it occurs.

## CHAPTER IX. Eutychis on aspiration

Although I knowingly passed over many other words relating to aspiration which had not been frequently used by reliable authors, lest I become burdensome through excessive length, nevertheless, since most readers prefer barren brevity to the useful pleasure of extended commentary, I have decided to repeat the same material almost in epitome. Omitting both the testimony of all the ancients and the explanations supplied throughout, I shall once again set out only the bare rules themselves, so that what preceded may satisfy the more diligent and what follows those who dislike greater length.

Every Greek or foreign word preserves among the Romans its own aspiration, both in vowels and in consonants: *Halys, Hecuba, hegio, hieron, Homerus, hymen, hora* (“hour of the day”), *Thibris, Phoebus, chorus, Rhenus, Hannibal*.

All articles beginning with a vowel are pronounced with aspiration: *hic, haec, hoc; hi, hae, haec*, except the vocatives *o* and *a*. Local adverbs are likewise aspirated: *hic, huc, hinc, hac*, unless they are compounded with pronouns: *illic, istic, istaec, istuc, istac*. In that case they lose the aspiration through the collision of vowels. Other compounds also preserve the aspiration between medial vowels: *adhuc, prohibeo*. A few corrupt forms are excepted, which entirely exclude aspiration, as was stated above: *postumus*, as though from *post humatum*, “born after the buried father”; *bimus, trimus, quadrimus*, as though from *bis, ter, quater* and *hieme*; *manubrium*, as though *manu haberium*; *petaeredium*, from “seeking inheritances.” The same thing also happens in certain simple forms: *veho, vexi; traho, traxi; mihi, mi; nihil, nil; prehendo, prendo; vehemens, vemens*, and similar forms, as was previously reported.

Every vowel brought before, divided from, or joined in a diphthong with another vowel loses aspiration: *aeneus, aereus, aeds, aedilis, aeger, Aelius, Aemilius* [edition: *aemulus*], *aequus, aequor, aes, aestimo, aestas, aevum, auceps, audeo, audax, ausus, audio, augurium, augeo, aufero, aulaeum* [edition: *alveum*], *aura, auris, aurum, ausculto, autumo, aut* (the conjunction). The exceptions are *haedus, haereo, haud, haurio, hio, hisco*, and whatever is compounded or derived from these. These are aspirated like the article, as are *heu* and *hei*, which are interjections, and the verb *heiulo*, derived from *hei* or *heu*. *Heus* and *heia* are treated like adverbs or interjections.

Every vowel followed by *b* is pronounced softly: *abies, ebur, ibi, ob, uber*. The exceptions to be noted are *habeo, habes, hibiscus*, and whatever is formed from each of them.

[Col. 1264A] Every vowel followed by *c* is pronounced softly: *acies, ecce, oculus, ocior*, except in articles and adverbs. When it changes, it is followed by an aspirated vowel. In pronouns it is aspirated only in *hic, haec,* and *hoc*.

Every vowel followed by *d* is pronounced softly: *ador, audax, edax, odor, udus*. The exceptions are *hadria* and *hedera*. *Hodie*, being compounded from *hoc die*, “on this day,” has preserved the spelling of the aspirated article.

Every vowel before *f, g, l, n, p, q,* or *u* functioning as a consonant lacks aspiration: *Afer, ager, ala, apis, aqua, ater, avus, affero, egeo, enim, epulae, equus*, and the conjunction *et*; *ignis, iter, opus, otium, ovis, uter, uva*. Concerning *agni apso*, that is, “a fleece,” we spoke above.

[Col. 1264B] Every vowel followed by *l*, except *e*, is pronounced softly: *alea, ales, alo* (“I nourish”), *albus* (“white,” literally “color”), *alga, almus, altus, alvus* (“belly”), *ilex, Ilerda, illico, ille, olor* (“swan”), *oleum, uleus, ulciscor, ulmus, ulna*. The nouns *halo* as a verb, *hilum, hilaris,* and *holus* are exceptions. For when *l* follows *e*, it is generally pronounced heavily: *helluo, heluus, helucus, helops*, and whatever is formed from each of them.

Every vowel followed by *m* is pronounced softly: *amor, amicus, amoenus, amans, amictus, amurca, emo, emax, imus, imo, omen, omasum, omentum, umor, umerus, umidus*. The exceptions are *hamus, Hammon, homo, humus*, and whatever is formed from them.

Every vowel followed by *n* is pronounced softly: *annus, annulus, ensis, inanis, initium, inula, onus, onustus, unus, unicus*. The exceptions are *honor, honestas,* and *Johannes*, as well as foreign and Punic words such as *Hannibal, Hanno, Henna, hinnulus*, and whatever is formed from them.

The vowels *a* and *u* followed by *r* are pronounced softly: *area, aries, aranea, arcus, arma, arduus, artus, aro, urtica, urna*. The exceptions are *hara, harena, harundo*. *Harmonia, Harpyiae,* and *Harpalice* are Greek and are therefore aspirated.

The vowel *e* followed by *r* is pronounced softly: *erus, error, ervum, ergo*, unless *b, n, s,* or a long *e* follows the *r*. Then it is pronounced heavily: *herba, herbidus, herbilis, herbosus*; the proper name *Hernus*, from which comes “the Hernican rocks inhabit”; *hersilia, haeres, haeredium, Herennius*, a proper name; and *Hercules*, formed from Greek by syncope, properly has aspiration. *Heri* is an adverb of time, for the sake of distinction, so that it may not be taken as the genitive of *erus, eri*.

The vowel *i* before *r* is always aspirated: *hircus, hirquitallus, Hirpinus, hirsutus, hirtus, Hirtuleius, Hirtius*, a proper name. The exceptions are a monosyllable such as *ir*, meaning “limb”; forms derived from the movement of the verb, such as *eo, is, irem, ires, ire*; and forms in which *a* follows *r*, which then lack aspiration: *ira, iratus, iracundus, irascor*, and whatever is formed from each of them.

The vowel *o* followed by *r* is pronounced softly: *orbus, orcus, ordior, orsus, orior, oriens, ortus* (“born”). But if another *r* or a *t* follows, this does not arise from the verb’s declension, for in that case *o* is aspirated: *horreo, horror, horreum, hortus, Hortensius*. *Ordeum* is an exception.

[Col. 1265A] The vowels *a, e,* and *u* followed by *s* lack aspiration: *as, assis, astutus, ascendo, aspicio, esca, est, essem, essemus, usus, usura*. The exceptions are *hasta, hastile, hesternus*—for it derives from the adverb *heri*—and the Greek word *Hesperia*.

But *i* or *u* followed by *s*, when *p* or *t* follows the *s*, are pronounced with aspiration: *Hispania, hispidus, historia, histrio, Hister*—whether it is a proper name, a river, or the name of a people—*hospes, hospita, hospitium, Hostilius, hostia*. The pronoun *iste* and compounds formed from it are exceptions. *Os, oris*, from which come *ostendo* and *ostentum*, is pronounced softly, like the other forms which, after *s*, lack *p* or *t*, such as *oscitant*.

## CHAPTER X. These materials have been collected from Caesellius the orthographer

The preposition *con*, when it approaches verbs beginning with vowels, loses the consonant *n*: *aequo, coaequo; eo, coeo; ortus, coortus*. But when it approaches verbs beginning with the digamma—that is, those which retain *u* placed in the position of a consonant—it does not lose the letter *n*: *volvo, convolvo; vinco, convinco*.

The opposite occurs with the preposition *re*. It receives the letter *d* externally when it is joined to a verb beginning with a vowel; but it does not receive that letter *d* when it is joined to the digamma, that is, to *u* placed in the position of a consonant: *ulcero, redulcero; ago, redigo; eo, redeo; voco, revoco; vinco, revinco*.

*Qui*, if it is one syllable, must be written with *q*: *qui homo*, “which man.” If it has two syllables, it is written with *c*, as in *cui homini*, “to which man.” *Aliquunde* ought to be written with *quun*, for its division is *aliquo* and *unde*, that is, “from some place.” Certainly the letter must be *n*, not *m*, because *unde* is written in that way. Likewise *aliquobi* is formed from *aliquo* and *ubi*, that is, “in some place.” These syllables, consisting of the letters *q, u, o*, are not to be excluded, but they must nevertheless be written out in full.

The preposition *re* sometimes doubles the consonants when it is joined to them; this is found especially among the ancients: *duco, redduco; cado, reccido; tuli, rettuli; pello, reppello; do, reddo; lego, rellego*. Hence they write *relliquias* and *relligionem*. I would grant that this spelling ought to be used among poets, although it is also found among ancient orators; for us, however, the elegance and smoothness that constitute the greatest benefit of Latin must now be maintained.

*Tamtus* and *quamtus* ought to have *m* in the middle: from *quam* and *tam* come *quamtitas, quamtus,* and *tamtus*. Let no one be troubled if the sound is absent; for I taught above that *n* ought to be pronounced even though *m* is written.

Whatever verbs begin in the first position with the letter *s* must retain that same *s* when compounded with the preposition *ex*: *salio, exsilio; specto, exspecto*. Other forms should not be burdened with it: *aestimo, existimo* lack *s*, just as *aequo, exaequo*; *peto, expeto* likewise has no *s*. This is readily understood by the distinction: *pecto* is one thing and *specto* another. Therefore, when the verb *pecto*, “I comb,” is compounded, *expecto* has no *s*; but when the verb *specto*, “I use something as a spectacle” or “look at something,” is compounded, *exspecto* necessarily retains *s*, as we stated above.

Likewise, *exscreo* has *s* when the *s* comes from *screare*; without *s* when it comes from *creare*. *Exsilium* too must be written with *s*—for it means “to go out from the soil,” *ex solo ire*—as though it were *exsolium*, which the Greeks call ἐξορισμός, “banishment,” and which the ancients called *exsoles*, whom we call *exsules*. But *extorris* is written without *s*, since it means “expelled from the earth.”

*Exsui* has *s*, for it derives from *sui*, and likewise *insui*, as though meaning “to be inserted into something.” Hence *exsui*, as though meaning “to be sent out” or “stripped bare.” From it come *exsuviae*, and hence *exsuti*, “stripped” or “despoiled.”

*Exire* is written without *s*, since *ire* is simple; and all forms derived from it—*exitus, exitium, exitiale*—likewise have no *s* in the compound. *Exercere* also lacks *s*, because it is composed of *ex* and *arcere*, “to restrain,” as is *exercitus*, “an army,” which is restrained under a fixed discipline; hence *exercitatio*.

*Exscindo* must have *s*, since *scindo* is simple. Likewise *exsculpo* and *exsisto*, since one says *sculpere* and *sistere* as simple forms. *Expurgo* likewise does not require *s*, and in the same way *excedo* and *eximo*. For other prepositions too, the form occurs without this letter: *redimo, interimo, dirimo*. Thus *exemptus* is written like *eximius*, which is as though “removed” and placed outside the others.

*Extremus* also lacks *s*: it derives from *ex*, whence come *extra, extremus, extrinsecus, exter, extrarium*, and any other forms that can be drawn from it. *Exsequiae*, however, have *s*, since *sequi* is simple. *Exiguae* lack *s*, as do *indiguae*, “those in need,” and *exiguitas*, “smallness.” So too *exoletus*, as is made clear by the preposition belonging to the other part: *adolevit* is the form. *Obsolevit* does have *s*, but it is not the *s* of the verb itself; it belongs to the preposition *obs*, as in *abs*: as though from *abolevit*, “it grew old” or “was worn away by age.”

These and similar forms will be recognized in this manner. The remaining forms that are simple and uncompounded will have only *x*, without doubt: *vixi, dixi, vexavi, faxi, uxor, auxilium, examen, axis,* and *exemplum*.

### On the division of syllables

There are two unequal consonants which can nevertheless remain together if they receive a vowel on either side. Equal or unequal consonants follow the latter syllable; single consonants, of course, are divided between the preceding and following syllables. Thus, in *potestas*, the final syllable is *stas*; in *noster*, *ster*; and in *capto*, *pto*. But when there are three, as in *plostrum*, *strum*; *lustrant*, *strant*; *capistrum*, *strum*; likewise *claustrum, rastrum, campestre*, the division is made accordingly. Generally these three consonants have *r* in the third position, while others have the letter *l*: *astula*, and after elision *astla*; *pessulum*. In no other way is unity of syllable granted among three consonants. When the letters are paired, each goes to a separate syllable.

Two equal letters, whether vowels or consonants, do not join together; similarly, they do not form a syllable when they receive a vowel, even though they are unequal: *carpo, dorsum, Porcius*.

A single consonant placed between two vowels follows the second: *Paris, lapis, thuris*. But when a consonant occurs between vowels, as in *digamma*, it adheres to the following vowel of the digamma. I have already said that, except for the letter *g*, no other consonant agrees with syllables of this kind: *solvo, nervo, volvo, larva, pulvis*. Thus, if *tenuis* is trisyllabic, the consonant *n* joins the *u*; if it is disyllabic, the same applies to *belva* and *malva*.

*Dispicio*, a compound verb, raises the question whether it should be written with two *s* or one, and whether it should be divided as *dis* and *spicio*. The basis for its division is clear, since all prepositions must be separated intact: *abstulit*, *abs* and *tulit*; *transtulit*, *trans* and *tulit*; *abscondit*, *abs* and *condit*, and other similar forms.

It must be written with two *s*, not one, because it is composed of a preposition and a verb, just as are *conspicio, aspicio,* and *despicio*. Therefore *disspicio* must be written with two *s* and divided as *dis* and *spicio*. Some, however, think that *dispicio* should be written with one *s*, because the preposition *dis* sometimes loses a letter, as in *diduco, divido, dijudico*. It is better, however, to write *disspicio* with two *s*.

Is *obliviscor* a compound or a simple form? It is certainly a compound; its simple form lies concealed in ancient nouns and monuments. *Livisci* means “to forget,” and *livitus* is what we today say through elision as *oblitus*. Once this has been made clear, anyone will understand fully the division of this verb in writing: *ob* and *liviscor*.

*Pompeiius, Tarpeiius,* and *eiius* must be written with two *i*, both because they are more fully pronounced in sound and because of meter; the syllable will never become long unless it is written with a doubled *i*. We divide this spelling as I stated above.

Now let us consider how their genitives, plural nominatives, and datives are to be written. Some write the forms *Pompei, Tarpei; hi Pompei, Tarpei; his Pompeis, his Tarpeis* with one *i*. Others, slightly more diligent, add a second *i* to these forms. I prescribe that a third *i* also be added. For if, as I taught, the nominative has two *i* in place of two consonants, these cannot disappear in any declension, although modern usage entirely excludes them.

## CHAPTER XI. These extracts have been taken from Lucius Caecilius, the defender

If the letter *m* is placed before vowels at the beginning of words, we shall not pronounce it. When it is placed before consonants or before the Aeolic digamma, for which we use *u* placed in the position of a consonant, we more suitably pronounce the sound of the letter *n* instead of *m*.

When we say *Lucii, magnii, magii* in the singular genitive, it matters which nominatives they have; accordingly, it will matter whether they should be written with two *i* or one. If their nominatives are *lucus, magnus, magus*, they will have one *i* in the genitive, and the plural nominative and vocative, as well as the dative and ablative, will likewise be written with one. But if they are pronounced *lucius, magnius, magius*, they will have two *i* in the genitive: *Lucii, magnii, magii*. Lucilius himself noted this when he distinguished *numerius* from *numero*.

The preposition *cum* is to be written with *c*; the adverb of time *quum*, meaning “when,” is to be written with *q*, for the sake of distinction. Thus Ennius writes:

> With the legions, when the commander sets out.  
> [Manuscript: *imperator* instead of *induperator*.]

*Quujusque* is written with *q*, not *c*, and with *q* it also has another meaning. *Hujusce hominis* means “of this man”; but *quujusque hominis, quujusque ordinis, uniuscujusque hominis,* and *uniuscujusque ordinis* mean “of every man,” “of every rank,” “of each individual man,” and “of each individual rank.”

*Accedo* is written with two *c*; *attuli* with two *t*; *assiduus* with two *s*; *appareo* with two *p*; *annuo* with two *n*; and *alligo* with two *l*. In these forms the consonants are changed not only for smoothness of sound, but also because the letter *d* cannot in any way be heard in them.

The letter *d* is heard and written when joined to the consonant *f*: *adfluo, adfari, adfuturum, adfatus, adfero*. Conversely, *b* is not heard: *offui, offero, offendo*.

## CHAPTER XII. These materials have been taken from Priscian the grammarian

[Note: The modern author Priscian is mentioned above. Perhaps this is the same man whom Dungalus also mentions in his book against Claudius, bishop of Turin. “The other verb,” he says, “which is *colo*, Priscian, on account of the distinction of his most noble intellect, deserved to be called the light of Roman eloquence; he demonstrates that it has a threefold meaning by saying: *Colo* is also understood as ‘I love,’ ‘I inhabit,’ and ‘I cultivate.’”]

Priscian, who in our time was a teacher at Constantinople, is the source from whose first book these materials have been collected.

It must therefore be noted that *hamus*, which the Greeks call ἄγκιστρον, “a hook,” must be written with aspiration. It must also be understood that the Greek *φ* is represented by *ph* in Latin writing only in Greek names: *Orpheus, Phaeton*. In other Latin nouns, however, *f* must be used: *fama, filius, facies*. *Phoebus*, the name by which Apollo is signified, must be written so that *h* follows *p*. Likewise *Herichthonius* [manuscript: *Hiericthonis*] and *hiulcus* must be written with aspiration.

The consonant *b* does not receive aspiration before it, except when the preceding letter is a vowel. *Caelebs*, before its final letter *s*, must be written with *b*, not *u*, since when *u*, a vowel, passes into the power of a consonant, it can precede another consonant.

Aspiration can be placed before all vowels; after consonants, however, it is placed only after four: *c, t, p,* and *r*: *habeo, Herennius, heros, hiemps, homo, humus, Chremes, Thraso, Philippus, Rhodus*. It is attached externally to vowels so that it may sound less strongly; with consonants it is placed internally so that it may sound more strongly.

*Gnatus* must be written with *g* and *n*, as is *gnavus*, because in compounds they retain the *g*: *agnatus* and *ignavus*. *Ecquid* is written with *c* in the first syllable because it means *en quid*, “whether anything,” with the consonant *n* changed into *c*. *Samguis* must be written with *m* in the first syllable in the nominative case; in the other cases, however, it is written with *n*, because the letter *m* changes into *n*.

The letters *b* and *s*, Latin letters corresponding to the Greek letter ψ, may be joined together in one and the same word only at the end of a nominative whose genitive ends in *-bis*: *urbs, urbis; caelebs, caelibis; Arabs, Arabis*.

It must be understood that *surripio* is written with a doubled *r*, not with *b* and *r*; likewise *corripio* and *arripio*, because *b* is also changed into *r*.

The compound verbs *suspicor* and *suspicio*, derived from the adverbs *sursum* or *susum*, are written in the first syllable with one *s*, not two, because a consonant cannot be doubled when another consonant follows, just as it cannot when another consonant precedes—unless it is a mute before a liquid, as in *supplex, suffragor, sufflo, effringo*.

*Quicquam* must be written with *c* in the first syllable, because the letter *d* changes into *c*. *Aggero* and *aggregatus* must be written with *g*, not *d*.

*Harpyia*, which is a Greek name, must be written with Greek *y* followed by Latin *i*, because among the Greeks *y* is a diphthong with *i*.

When *ara* means “altar,” it is written without aspiration; when it means “a pen for pigs,” it is written with aspiration.

## Conclusion
Having therefore gathered together what I found necessarily written among the aforementioned writers on orthography, let us now, with the Lord’s help, bring the book to an end. For it is clear that this was a matter of great usefulness, since it is known to have been treated by so many and such distinguished authors: if anything was omitted by the earlier writers, it is evident that it was supplied by those who followed them.

We must also remember that writers on grammar have often treated orthography, and that writers on orthography have in turn discussed the declension of the parts of speech, although the two subjects may seem to conflict. Grammar treats the declension of the parts of speech; orthography, however, indicates how they ought to be written, identifying what it finds appropriate in the declension of those parts. If you always attend to this in the authors, carefully accepting what is placed in its proper context, you will be troubled by no error. Now lift up your minds, readers, and rejoice that so many ancient authors have come down to you, so that you ought to trust them with unquestioning confidence.

I could indeed add Aquila, Quintilian, and also Avitus, whom some have thought worthy of praise for their expertise in orthography; nevertheless, we are awaiting their arrival very soon in the name of Christ. But there is no need to grant permission to an excessive number, since it has not been established precisely how many preferred to write on the same subject. For if twelve hours are known immediately to complete the day, if twelve months likewise restore the year in its revolving variety, and if twelve heavenly signs enclose for us the fields of the entire circle in a solid roundness, then it ought entirely to suffice for us that I have presented to posterity, for reading, rules extracted from the books of twelve writers on orthography who teach the correctness of writing.

Farewell, brothers, and deign to remember me in your prayers. I have briefly admonished you, among other matters, concerning the power of orthography and the placement of punctuation, which is recognized as exceedingly valuable; and I have prepared, for extensive reading, an abundant guide to how the divine Scriptures ought to be understood. Thus, just as I wished you to be separated from the company of the unlearned, so may divine virtue not allow us to be joined in punitive association with the utterly wicked.

[Col. 1269]

## ON FIGURES AND TROPES, AS WELL AS CERTAIN RHETORICAL DEVICES OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, WHICH ARE FOUND HERE AND THERE IN CASSIODORUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE PSALMS

[Col. 1269C] The divine Scripture, says Cassiodorus (*Preface to the Psalter*, p. 7), exercises its modes of expression in many ways: concise in its definitions, adorned with figures, marked by the propriety of its words, made clear through the combinations of syllogisms, and radiant with the disciplines. Yet it does not receive an alien beauty from them; rather, it confers upon them their own proper dignity. For when these things shine in the divine Scriptures, they are certain and utterly pure; but when they come to human opinions and the most empty questions, they are tossed about by the ambiguous waves of disputation, so that what is always most firmly true here is frequently rendered uncertain elsewhere.

The experts in worldly arts—although it is evident that they arose much later than the beginnings of the divine books—transferred these matters to collections of arguments, which the Greeks call *topica* (τόπικα, “topics”), and to the arts of dialectic and rhetoric. Thus it plainly appears to everyone that what was first given to upright minds for expressing truth was later judged by the pagans to be adaptable to human wisdom. These things gleam in sacred readings like the brightest stars and fittingly illuminate the meanings of things with highly useful brevity.

For Father Augustine also declared the following in Book III, chapter 29, of *On Christian Doctrine*: “Let the educated know that our authors used all the modes of expression which grammarians call by the Greek name *tropos* (τρόπος, ‘figure’ or ‘mode’).” A little later he continues: “Those who know these *tropoi*, that is, the modes of expression, recognize them in the sacred writings, and their knowledge assists them somewhat in understanding them.” He made the same matter exceedingly clear in other books of his. In the books which he entitled *On the Modes of Expression*, he proved that various figures of secular literature are found in sacred writings, while he declared that other modes proper to divine utterances exist which grammarians and rhetoricians have in no way touched upon. Other most learned Fathers among us—namely Jerome, Ambrose, and Hilary—said the same, so that we may appear not presumptuous innovators in this matter, but followers.

But someone may say: “Neither the parts of syllogisms themselves, nor the names of figures, nor the terms of the disciplines, nor anything else of this kind is found at all in the Psalms.” They are plainly found in the power of the meanings, though not in the utterance of the words. Thus we contemplate wine in the vines, the harvest in the seed, leaves in the roots, fruits in the branches, and the trees themselves in their kernels, through the force of perception. We therefore rightly say that things exist when we nevertheless perceive them to be present in potential. The Apostle, moreover, forbids us to be led astray by empty wisdom (1 Corinthians 3:18); but he does not deny that these things are present in the divine writings.

[Col. 1270D] Know therefore, teachers of secular literature, that from here—that is, from Scripture—there flowed figures, arguments of various kinds, definitions, and the teachings of every discipline, since you recognize that in these writings are set down things which you perceive to have been spoken long before your schools.

A figure is a certain shaping of diction removed from ordinary usage, which is always presented to the inner eyes as something bearing a face. Following the tradition of our predecessors, we may call it “display” and “bearing.” P. 16.

[Col. 1271A] **Σχῆμα (*schema*)** is a figure of speech composed with elegance in the arrangement of words. P. 14.

**Τρόπος (*tropos*)** is an expression transferred from the place in which it is proper to another place in which it is not proper. P. 21.

## A

**Αἴνιγμα (*aenigma*)**, that is, an obscure statement, occurs when one thing is said while another is intended: “He spoke of fire, he spoke of lightning, he spoke of mountains, he spoke of the heavens”; through all these things there is one purpose—to proclaim the Lord the Savior. P. 325.

**Αἰτιολογία (*aetiologia*)**, that is, the giving of a reason, occurs whenever an appropriate explanation follows something previously stated: “For this reason my heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh will rest in hope.” P. 54. See pp. 89 and 202.

**Ἀλληγορία (*allegoria*)**, that is, an inversion in which one thing is said and another signified: “Clouds passed before his presence, hail and coals of fire.” Through this figure he explains what those clouds—that is, the preachers—possess. The hail signifies figurative rebukes by which the exceedingly hard hearts of the Jews were struck. The coals of fire signify the burning of charity, by which the minds of the faithful are revived with heavenly fire. Pp. 60 and 101.

**Ἀμφιβολογία (*amphibologia*)**, that is, an ambiguous expression which leaves the meaning in doubt: “They devised plans which they could not establish”—namely, the Jews’ statement, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John 18:14). The statement was true, but uttered with an evil intention. P. 71.

**Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις (*anakephalaiosis*)**, that is, recapitulation, occurs when what was said above at greater length is afterward recalled briefly to memory: “He blessed all who fear the Lord, the small together with the great.” After particular enumerations, he rises to a blessing of generality, in which all who have chosen to serve the Lord with a pure mind are blessed together. P. 388.

**Ἀναδίπλωσις (*anadiplosis*)**, that is, a doubling of an expression, occurs either in a verse or in the repetition of words: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory will enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.” Pp. 82 and 433.

**Ἀναφορά (*anaphora*)**, that is, reference, occurs when one word is repeated at the beginnings of successive clauses: “Though armies encamp against me; though battle rise up against me.” Pp. 89 and 148.

**Ἀναστροφή (*anastrophe*)**, that is, inversion, occurs whenever either the meaning or the words are altered for the sake of elegance: “In the day of my tribulation I cried out to you, because you heard me.” He says that he cried out because he was heard, although the cry precedes the hearing, so that God might be able to hear. Pp. 291 and 449.

**Ἀντίφρασις (*antiphrasis*)**, that is, contrary speech. Through antiphrasis, slander is called “the nursling of the head,” although it rather seeks another’s head and is opposed to it: “Redeem me from the slanders of men.” P. 420.

**Ἀντιπρόσωπον (*antiprosopon*)** occurs when the person of one greatly loved is substituted for an ungrateful person: “For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place.” In place of the sinful nation, the name of the most beloved patriarch was introduced, so that remembrance of the holy man might mitigate the people’s offenses. P. 273.

**Ἀντίπτωσις (*antiptosis*)** occurs when one grammatical case is used in place of another: “As a neighbor, as our brother, so I was pleasing.” In accordance with Latin eloquence, we say that he was pleasing “to a neighbor” and “to a brother.” P. 116.

**Ἀντεισαγωγή (*antisagoge*)**, that is, contradiction: “They said: ‘We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own. Who is our lord?’” P. 45.

**Ἀντιστάθμησις (*antistathmesis*)**, that is, recompense, occurs when someone who has conducted himself either rightly or wrongly receives a corresponding return for his deeds: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy.” P. 441.

**Ἀντονομασία (*antonomasia*)**, that is, something placed in the position of a name, occurs when another name is used in such a way that the necessary person is nevertheless understood: “The King of the virtues of the Beloved.” Here “the Beloved” must be understood as the Father’s Son. P. 221.

**Ἄπευσις** [Note: [Col. 1271D] Thus in the text. Perhaps it should be read as ἀνάπευσις, from the verb ἀναπυνθάνομαι. EDIT.] **and ἀπόκρισις**. *Peusis* and *apocrisis*, that is, inquiry and response, occur when an appropriate answer follows a preceding question: “Why should I fear in the evil day? The iniquity of my heel will surround me.” Pp. 161 and 386.

**Ἀποσιώπησις (*aposiopesis*)**, that is, an expression whose ending is left unspoken, occurs either so that the hearer may be frightened or provoked to desire: “With the hearing of the ear he heard me.” P. 63.

**Ἀποστροφή (*apostrophe*)**, that is, turning aside, occurs whenever speech is repeatedly turned toward different persons: “Now I know that the Lord has saved his Christ.” Pp. 68 and 156.

An **argument** is an indication—or judgment—of an astute mind which establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter through probable investigations. P. 111.

**Argument from accompanying circumstances:** “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, who hope in his mercy.” For fearing the Lord and hoping in him are accompanying circumstances, mutually connected by an unbreakable association. P. 109.

**Argument from antecedents:** “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.” P. 170.

**Argument from causes:** “For behold, you have loved truth; you have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” After so many benefits had been conferred, he says that he ought not to have proceeded to such sins. P. 171.

**Argument from comparison, from the lesser to the greater:** “As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.” Here a human being is understood to have been likened to a deer. P. 141.

**Argument from cognate words:** “They will fail like smoke; they will fail.” These words arise from one another and, having arisen from the same source, are derived in consonant similarity. Pp. 124 and 169.

[Col. 1272C] **Argument from consequents** is spoken of when what precedes is confirmed by the following expression: “Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed; for truths have been diminished among the sons of men.” Pp. 45, 96, and 172.

**Argument from contraries:** “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and I will not enter in with those who do evil.” The council of vanity and the assembly of the innocent are entirely contrary to one another. Pp. 86, 96, and 111.

**Argument from the words and deeds of our ancestors** is spoken of when the weight of testimony is strengthened by the most authoritative witness of the fathers: “O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have declared to us the work that you worked in their days and in ancient days.” P. 146.

**Argument from the outcome** is spoken of when supplication tends toward the result which it recognizes as following from the order of events: “Why do you turn your face and your right hand away from the midst of your bosom forever?” P. 251.

**Argument from genus:** “There all who work iniquity have fallen.” Pride is the genus from which all vices are known to have arisen. P. 120.

**Argument from disposition** is spoken of when someone sins not through ignorance but through malicious intention: “He was unwilling to understand, so as to act well.” P. 119.

**Argument from praise of the injured party** is used so that envy might grow all the more in the enemies, since the holy places had to be devastated through their presumption: “You delivered the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion, in which you dwelt.” Pp. 249 and 316.

**Argument called ‘from necessity’** occurs when very serious causes are stated beforehand, so that a corrected mind may be led to a fruitful confession: “I was turned toward affliction when my spine was broken.” Pp. 104 and 129.

**Argument called ‘from what is necessary’:** “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.” The Lord’s building is necessary, for without him nothing good is brought to the summit of perfection. P. 442.

**Argument called ‘notation’** occurs when a similarity of speech is drawn from the position of a word: “They tested me, and mocked me with mockery.” P. 116.

**Argument from equality:** “Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night.” P. 65.

**Argument from the greater part:** “According to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.” The Lord’s mercy is much greater, although our sins may appear enormous. P. 170.

**Argument called ‘from the person’:** “He will receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Savior.” He wished the merit of the benefit to be recognized through the greatness of the giver. P. 81.

**Argument from a person attributed externally** occurs when someone is either criticized on the basis of wicked associates or praised because of association with the good: “With the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted.” P. 61.

[Col. 1273B] **Argument called ‘from the things themselves’** occurs when we say both that our adversaries have fallen and that we have been raised up: “They themselves were bound and fell, but we have risen and been set upright.” P. 68.

**Argument from time:** “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, because the time for having mercy has come.” P. 340.

**Argument called ‘from torments’** occurs when the minds of the faithful could not be changed by so many evils: “All these things came upon us, yet we did not forget you, and we did not act wickedly against your covenant.” P. 148.

**Argument called ‘exceedingly appropriate’** occurs when the person of someone detestable is represented by a gracious person: “Let the humbled and confounded man not be turned away; the poor and needy will praise your name.” P. 253.

**Ἀστεισμός (*asteismos*)**, that is, urbane expression, composed for the sake of elegance and wit: “The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry.” This seems to belong not to exhortation but rather to mockery. P. 329.

[Col. 1273C] **Αὔξησις (*auxesis*)**, that is, increase, occurs when, by adding certain names in successive clauses, it doubles the increase of the subject: “But you, Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.” Pp. 20, 66, and 272.

## B

**Βραχυλογία (*brachylogia*)**, that is, brief expression, occurs when we encompass many things in few words: “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.” Through this verse and the two that follow, he briefly enumerates the things he professes to reject. P. 166.

## C

**Κακόζηλον (*kakozelon*)**, that is, bad affectation, occurs whenever talent lacks judgment and precipitate haste is deceived by hope of good: “They desired desire in the wilderness, and tested God in the desert.” P. 362.

**Κατάχρησις (*catachresis*)**, properly called misuse, occurs when one lends a thing a name belonging to something else: “Awake! Why do you sleep, Lord?” For it is not fitting for God to arise, since he is never known to be able to sleep. P. 149.

**Χαρακτερισμός (*characterismus*)**, that is, formation or description, occurs when someone is described either by appearance or indicated by his characteristic actions: “His ways are defiled” (that is, the Antichrist’s); “your judgments are removed from his sight; he will rule over all his enemies.” P. 40.

**Κλίμαξ (*climax*)**, that is, gradation, occurs when, once certain steps have been set down, the expression continually increases, whether in praise or blame: “They will pronounce and speak iniquity; all who work injustice will speak.” P. 316.

**Κοινωνία (*koinonia*)**, that is, sharing in counsel, frequently occurs when we mingle words either with adversaries or with helpers: “I trust in the Lord; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee like a sparrow to the mountain’?” P. 43.

**Ἀπὸ κοινοῦ**, that is, “from what is common,” occurs when what was said above responds to what follows: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, O righteous; and glory, all you upright of heart.” Here “glory in the Lord” must be joined to the preceding words. P. 105.

**Concession** occurs when a defendant does not defend what he has done through some dispute, but simply asks to be forgiven: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy,” and so forth. Pp. 169 and 103.

## D

**Substantial definition** is that above which a genus can be found: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” P. 18.

The **second species of definition**, ἐννοηματική (*ennoematike*), is called “notion.” It attempts to show each thing by what it does, not by what it is: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord.” P. 136.

The **third species of definition**, ποιότης (*poiotēs*), that is, qualitative definition, shows clearly what the thing under discussion is by saying what sort of thing it is: “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel.” Pp. 72 and 107.

The **fifth species of definition**, which the Greeks call κατὰ τὴν λέξιν and which in Latin we call “word for word,” occurs whenever we show what each thing is by individual words: “For the word of the Lord is upright.” In a single part of the sentence, what the word of the Lord is has been defined—namely, “upright.” Pp. 107 and 154.

The **seventh species of definition**, which the Greeks call κατὰ μεταφοράν and which the Latins call “by transference,” occurs when we show what a thing is under a brief proclamation: “The law of the Lord is blameless, restoring souls.” P. 65.

The **eighth species of definition**, called in Greek κατ᾽ ἀφαίρεσιν τοῦ ἐναντίου and in Latin “by deprivation of its opposite,” defines something by removing its contrary: “There is none like you among the gods, Lord; and there is nothing according to your works.” P. 291.

The **ninth species of definition**, which the Greeks call καθ᾽ ὑποτύπωσιν and the Latins call “by a certain representation,” occurs when, after a mother or father has been named, our understanding is led to the meaning of an individual person: “The praises of David, the son of Jesse, have failed.” In the title of Psalm 72, p. 244.

The **tenth species of definition**, which the Greeks call ὡς τύπῳ and the Latins call “as it were,” occurs when the combination describing something appears applicable not only to the one thing of which it is said but also to others: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand.” Here “man” is also used of the devil. P. 162.

The **twelfth species of definition**, which the Greeks call κατ᾽ ἔπαινον and the Latins call “by praise,” is: “The works of his hands are truth and judgment; all his commandments are faithful.” In this verse and the following one, the praises of the Lord are described in very beautiful and varied statements. Pp. 381, 383, and 462.

The **thirteenth species of definition**, which the Greeks call κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν and the Latins call “according to proportion,” arises when an inferior thing is defined by the name of a superior thing: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” Here human beings are called gods and sons of God. P. 282.

The **fourteenth species of definition**, which the Greeks call πρός τι and the Latins call “relative,” occurs whenever one name is spoken in such a way that another may be understood from it: “He will call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.’” P. 302.

**Διαφόρησις (*diaphoresis*):** “The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the righteous man has mercy and lends.” Through this figure a distinction is made between the persons of the righteous and the impious. P. 124.

**Διαπόρησις (*diaporesis*)**, that is, doubt, occurs when we are uncertain whether what is sought can be found: “If you observe iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will endure?”

**Διατύπωσις (*diatyposis*)**, that is, expression, is the figure through which the forms and conditions of the things or persons presented are depicted: “My eye is troubled with anger, as are my soul and my belly.” P. 99.

## E

**Ἔκλειψις (*eclipsis*)**, that is, omission, occurs whenever a word is left suspended so that the inquiry may be more vivid: “Remember your word to your servant.” “To your servant” should be understood as: “fulfill your promise.” For if you try to attach what has been said to the preceding words without any addition, the words cannot fit one another. P. 406.

**Ἔμφασις (*emphasis*)**, that is, intensification, occurs when we bring forward some matter amid many collected sorrows, so that we may obtain the judge’s favor by enumerating our calamities: “But now you have rejected and confounded us, and you will not go forth with our armies, O God. You have turned us back,” and so forth. P. 147.

**Ἐνέργεια (*energeia*)**, that is, vivid representation, supplies the action of a thing to incorporeal eyes: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.” Pp. 110 and 257.

**Ἐπανάληψις (*epanalepsis*)**, that is, repetition of a word placed at the beginning of a verse at its end: “God, who will be like you? Do not be silent or restrained, O God.” P. 283.

**Ἐπάναδος (*epanados*)**, that is, repetition of things introduced together: “What is the matter with you, sea, that you fled; and you, Jordan, why have you turned back?” P. 386.

**Ἐνθύμημα (*enthymema*)**, that is, a conception of the mind. A syllogism consists of one proposition and a conclusion: “Because the king hoped in the Lord, and in the mercy of the Most High he will not be moved.” This is explained as follows: “Everyone who hopes in the Lord will exult and rejoice in his mercy. Therefore I too will exult and rejoice in his mercy.” P. 7.

**Ἐπέμβασις (*epembasis*)**, that is, repetition, occurs whenever words are doubled in each successive clause for the greatest elegance: “Many rise up against me; many say to my soul.” Pp. 20 and 73.

**Ἐπεξήγησις (*epexegesis*)**, that is, explanation of what was previously said: “Lord my God, if I have done this; if there is iniquity in my hands.” Pp. 31, 70, and 97.

**Ἐπεξεργασία (*epexergasia*)** occurs whenever two proofs are added to one cause: “For sinners will perish; but the enemies of the Lord, once they have been honored and exalted, will fail; they will fail like smoke.” P. 124.

**Ἐπιχείρημα (*epichirema*)**, that is, execution or confirmation: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” and so forth. We use this argument whenever we attempt to prove the matter under discussion by some example. Pp. 88 and 134.

**Ἐπιδιόρθωσις (*epidiorthosis*)**, that is, correction of what preceded: “My helper, I shall not be moved again.” P. 203.

**Ἐπιμονὴ (*epimone*)**, that is, frequent repetition of a statement, is appropriately used either in praise or in blame and accumulates great force of intensification: “How long, Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will my enemy be exalted over me?” Pp. 47 and 93.

**Ἐπιφώνημα (*epiphonema*)**, that is, an acclamation which bursts forth briefly with a cry after the events have been narrated, ending after everything in a most highly intensified climax: “And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.” Pp. 80 and 102.

**Ἐπιτροχασμός (*epitrochasmos*)**, that is, a swift movement of speech, occurs when it briefly touches upon matters which ought to be expressed at greater length: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing,” and so forth. Pp. 80 and 233.

**Ἐπίζευξις (*epizeuxis*)**, that is, conjunction, occurs when words are doubled in one verse without any intervening word: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night.” Pp. 59 and 117.

**Ἐρώτημα (*erotema*)**, that is, interrogation: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on empty things?” Pp. 16 and 51.

**Ἐρώτησις (*erotesis*)**, that is, interrogation, occurs when someone proposes a question to himself for the sake of exercise and answers it himself: “How does a young man correct his way? By guarding your words.” Pp. 399 and 430.

**Ἐθοποιΐα (*ethopoeia*)** occurs whenever speech is assigned to a particular person: “Preserve me, Lord, for I have hoped in you.” Here the person is the Lord Savior. Pp. 52 and 234.

**Ἐτυμολογία (*etymologia*)** is a brief statement which, through particular correspondences of sound, shows from what name the name under investigation has arisen. P. 12.

**Ἐξαλλαγή (*exallage*)**, that is, exchange or alteration, occurs whenever, contrary to customary usage, either gender or case is changed: “I announced and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number.” Pp. 136, 17, 61, and 173.

**Ἐξεργασία (*exergasia*)** occurs whenever something is proposed briefly and then explained subtly and at greater length: “Mount Zion, expanding the rejoicings of the whole earth, the sides of the north, the city of the great King.” P. 159.

**Ἐξετασμός (*exetasmos*)**, that is, investigation, occurs when, by asking questions, we inquire into several matters separately and apply to each what belongs to it: “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who will stand in his holy place?” P. 81.

## H

**Εἱρμός (*hirmos*)**, that is, continuity, occurs when a sequence of speech preserves its course all the way to the end: “Save me, God, by your name, and deliver me by your power.” Pp. 181 and 392.

[Col. 1276C] **Ὁμοιοτέλευτον (*homoeoteleuton*)** occurs when several expressions end with similar letters: “You have forgiven the iniquity of your people; you have covered all their sins.” Pp. 288 and 302.

**Ὁμοίωσις (*homoeosis*)** is a figure through which the demonstration of a less-known matter is made clear by its similarity to something better known: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters; and as the eyes of a maidservant,” and so forth. P. 435.

**Ὁμοιόπτωτον (*homoeoptoton*)** occurs when different words end in similar sounds: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing, exult, and sing praise.” P. 327.

**Ὑπαλλαγή (*hypallage*)**, that is, exchange, occurs whenever the words that have been spoken are transferred to another meaning: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there was anyone understanding or seeking God.” “To see” means “to make himself seen.” Pp. 49 and 179.

**Ὑπερβατόν (*hyperbaton*)**, that is, suspended word order, occurs whenever the order of the words is extended over a greater distance: “For those who act wickedly will be exterminated.” This verse depends upon what precedes it, where he says: “Do not be envious of the one who prospers in his way.” Pp. 122 and 153.

**Ὑπερβολή (*hyperbole*)** is a figure through which certain things are extended toward an exaggerated magnitude: “I will water my bed with tears.” Pp. 29 and 421.

**Ὑπέρθεσις (*hyperthesis*)**, that is, surpassing, occurs when we attempt, by our judgment, to exceed something known to everyone by reputation: “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds.” Pp. 59 and 172.

**Ὑπεξαίρεσις (*hypexaeresis*)**, that is, exception: “Let his days be few, and let another take his episcopate.” P. 373.

**Ὑπόζευξις (*hypozeuxis*)** occurs when different words are assigned to separate clauses: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and who has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” Pp. 13 and 484.

## I

[Col. 1277A]

**Εἰκών (*icon*)**, that is, an image: “Guard me, Lord, as the pupil of the eye.” Through this figure the Lord compared himself to the pupil of the eye. P. 56.

**Ἰδέα (*idea*)**, that is, form, occurs when, presenting the form of a future matter as though before our eyes, we stir the movement of the mind: “You sit upon the throne, judging equity.” Pp. 37 and 59.

**Εἰρωνεία (*ironia*)**, that is, mockery, occurs whenever something said in the guise of praise is shown to carry the meaning of blame: “He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, since he wants him.” Pp. 73 and 91.

**Ἴσον (*ison*)**, that is, equality, occurs when things alike in parity are joined together with praise or blame: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon.” P. 313.

## L

[Col. 1277B] **Λεπτολογία (*leptologia*)**, that is, subtle expression, occurs when individual matters are indicated minutely and precisely: “You loved wickedness more than goodness; iniquity more than speaking truth.” P. 177.

## M

**Μεταβολή (*metabole*)**, that is, repetition of one matter under varied wording: “Give heed to my words, Lord; understand my cry. Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God.” Pp. 24 and 229.

**Μεταφορά (*metaphora*)**, that is, transference, occurs when a name or verb is moved from the place where it is proper to one in which either the proper expression is lacking or the transferred expression is better than the proper one: “Nevertheless, amid the flood of many waters, they will not approach him.” Pp. 104 and 493.

**Μετάστασις (*metastasis*)**, that is, transference, occurs when we attempt to transfer our guilt to another: “Do not incline my heart toward evil words, to make excuses for excuses in sins.” P. 477.

**Μετωνυμία (*metonymia*)**, that is, renaming, occurs whenever we indicate the meaning of a thing through words that are different, alien, or transferred: “He who dwells in heaven will mock them, and the Lord will deride them.” Pp. 171 and 42.

**Μυθοποιΐα (*mythopoeia*)** occurs when someone is introduced as speaking. P. 21. The Church is introduced as speaking: “When I called,” and so forth.

**Μετριασμός (*metriasmos*)**, that is, moderation, occurs whenever we express a great matter in a moderate account: “Those who saw me outside fled from me; I was cut off as one dead from the heart.” Pp. 100 and 116.

## P

**Παραβολά (*parabola*)**, that is, similitude, occurs when we indicate by means of comparisons what we wish to be understood: “I will open my mouth in parables.” P. 263.

**Παραβολή (*parabole*)**, that is, comparison, occurs when something belonging to a different genus is joined to another in some point of commonality: “And he will be like a tree planted beside streams of water.” Pp. 13, 56, and 219.

**Παράδειγμα (*paradeigma*)** is a narrative which encourages or deters someone by means of examples: “Not so the ungodly, not so.” Pp. 14 and 112.

**Παράδοξον (*paradoxon*)** occurs when an unexpected or unforeseen outcome is introduced: “Nevertheless, your eyes will look upon it, and you will see the retribution of sinners, because you, Lord, are my hope.” P. 310.

**Παρά προσδοκίαν (*paraprosdocia*)**, that is, an unexpected outcome, occurs when one thing is set forth but another is explained: “My God, his ways are undefiled.” P. 62 and 287.

**Παρένθεσις (*parenthesis*)**, that is, insertion, occurs when, in the middle of a meaning, certain words are introduced which seem capable of dividing the order of the sentence: “The works of men: because of the words of your lips, I have guarded difficult ways.” P. 55.

**Πάρισον (*parison*)**, that is, equalization of a statement, occurs when two things are set opposite one another but one is preferred: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands.” Pp. 287 and 312. It also occurs whenever good or evil things are joined together in dissimilar clauses: “For the spirit passed through him, and he will not remain, and he will no longer know his place.” Pp. 345 and 367.

**Παροιμία (*paroemia*):** “I said in the excess of my mind: Every man is a liar.” P. 391.

**Παρονομασία (*paronomasia*)**, that is, a change of name, occurs when similarity of wording stirs the emotion of the hearer: “The merciful and compassionate Lord; patient and abundantly merciful.” Pp. 344 and 408.

**Inquiry** is a figure which does not allow the other person to await a response: “But to the sinner God said: ‘Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take up my covenant upon your mouth?’” P. 167.

**Περίφρασις (*periphrasis*)**, that is, circumlocution: “And he will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.” Pp. 241 and 385.

**Phantasia** occurs whenever the mind of the hearer is led toward the conception of future visions: “He sits in ambush”—he is speaking of the Antichrist—“with the rich in secret places, in order to kill the innocent.” P. 41.

Πεῦσις and ἀπόκρισις, *peusis* and *apocrisis*, that is, inquiry, where both a question is posed and a ready answer follows: “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?” Pp. 35 and 161.

Πλεονασμός, *pleonasmos*, occurs when something superfluous is added: “They set your sanctuary on fire.” In the divine Scriptures this figure is not appropriate, since everything there is useful, everything necessary, and everything perfect. Pp. 250 and 478.

Πολυσύνδετον, *polysyndeton*, is the frequent repetition of a conjunction or of some other word: “May the Lord preserve him, and give him life, and make him blessed, and cleanse his soul on earth, and not deliver him into the hand of his enemy.” Pp. 139 and 283.

Προαναφώνησις, *proanaphonesis*, that is, exclamation, whenever, amid other things that we are saying, we suddenly turn our words toward God: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell, because of the wickedness in their dwellings. But I cried to God, and the Lord heard me.” Pp. 184 and 197.

Προκατάληψις, *procatalepsis*, that is, anticipation: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.” Here he fears the most dreadful sight of his offenses as though he were already standing at the coming judgment. P. 170.

Πρόληψις, *prolepsis*, that is, anticipation: “May the Lord hear you on the day of tribulation.” The prophet, inflamed by the zeal of great charity, wishes for the Catholic Church to receive what he saw could occur only after a long period of time. Pp. 67, 74, and 92.

Προσωποποιΐα, *prosopopoeia*, whenever words are attributed to inanimate things: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voices, because of the sound of many waters.” P. 314.

Προθέσιος παραλλαγή, *prothesios parallage*, occurs when one preposition is placed in the position of another: “I will guard my strength for you.” Here *ad* is used instead of *per*. P. 196.

S

Σαρκασμός, *sarcasmos*, a hostile derision that seems to penetrate as far as the flesh: “And they said: ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’” Pp. 316 and 460.

Σαρδισμός, *sardismos*, is a figure that is always formed through a mixture of languages: “Therefore I shall remember you from the land of the Jordan and Hermonim, from the little mountain. Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts.” Pp. 183 and 199.

Σχέσις ὀνομάτων, *schesis onomaton*, that is, a multitude of nouns joined by different words and signifying one thing: “We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity.” P. 360.

Σωματοποιΐα, *somatopoeia*, that is, attribution of a body, whenever bodies are attributed to incorporeal things: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have embraced one another.” P. 289.

Σύλληψις, *syllepsis*, occurs whenever differing grammatical cases are brought together into a single meaning: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” *Domine* is vocative; contrary to usage, *Dominus*, which is nominative, appears to have been joined to it. P. 34.

Categorical syllogism. “Every just person rejoices in the Lord; everyone who rejoices in the Lord is upright of heart; therefore every just person is upright of heart.” “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you just; and glory, all you upright of heart.” P. 105.

Five-part, or rhetorical, syllogism. The proposition is: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord, for I shall confess to him, the salvation of my countenance.” The proof of the proposition is unquestionably contained in the four verses that follow. Then comes the assumption: “I shall say to God, ‘You are my protector; why have you forgotten me? Why have you rejected me, and why do I walk sadly while my enemy afflicts me?’” The proof of the assumption follows in two further verses. Finally, under the repetition of the first verse, the elegant conclusion of the proposed syllogism is inferred: “Why are you sad, my soul?” etc. P. 144.

Enthymematic syllogism. See *enthymema*.

Συναθροισμός, *synathroesmos*, that is, gathering together, whenever many things and many crimes are joined into one: “Save me, O Lord, because the holy man has failed, because truths have been diminished among the children of men.” Pp. 45 and 78.

Σύγκρισις, *syncrisis*, that is, comparison, when by means of a comparison we demonstrate that our cause is more just than that of our adversaries: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses; but we shall glory in the name of the Lord our God.” Pp. 68 and 87.

[Col. 1280A] Συγχώρησις, *synchoresis*, that is, concession, whenever things are granted to those who importunately demand them, although they cannot contribute to their benefit: “They ate and were exceedingly filled; and he granted them their desire.” P. 267.

Συνδυασμός, *syndyasmos*, *syndesmos*, or, as the manuscripts have it, *syndicasmos*, that is, comparison, when either persons or causes are compared with one another, whether by contrast or by similarity: “The words of the Lord are pure words.” Here the divine words are praised, whereas human speech is criticized above. Pp. 46 and 178.

Συνεκδοχή, *synecdoche*, is a figure that signifies the part by means of the whole: “I will confess to you, O Lord, with all my heart; I will recount all your wonders.” Pp. 37 and 73. It also signifies the whole by means of the part: “Hear my prayer; to you all flesh shall come.” Pp. 211 and 230. It also occurs when, by means of what follows, we can understand what precedes. P. 71.

T

[Col. 1280B]

Ταπείνωσις, *tapinosis*, that is, abasement, whenever extraordinary greatness is compared with very humble things: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.” Pp. 73 and 129. It also occurs when the greatness of something is reduced to a very small measure: “For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed, and like a watch in the night.” Pp. 306 and 339.

Ταυτολογία, *tautologia*, that is, repetition of the same expression: “You have granted him the desire of his soul.” His soul’s desire was as he says in the Gospel: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15). Pp. 69 and 218.

Z

Ζεῦγμα, *zeugma*, that is, conjunction, when many dependent elements are concluded by one verb or one sentence: “Whoever does these things shall not be moved forever.” P. 52.

[Col. 1279]

M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS, ON THE SOUL. (C)

PREFACE

627 When I was already rejoicing in the desired completion of the work I had undertaken, and, having been tossed about through twelve volumes, was being received into the harbor of rest—where, although I had not arrived praised, I had at least arrived freed—my friends’ pleasant company once again pressed me into the sea of reflection, asking me to disclose certain things that I had discovered hidden both in sacred and in secular books, concerning the substance of the soul and its virtues, to which it has been granted to unlock the secrets of such immense matters. They added that it would be exceedingly foolish if we allowed ourselves to remain ignorant of the very thing through which we know so many things, as though it were foreign to us, since it is useful in every respect to know through what faculty we understand. For it is no strange matter to speak about one’s own sense, when nature, questioned, answers for itself; nor does it have to go far in order to succeed in finding itself. The very thing we seek is always with us: it is present, handles the matter, speaks, and—if such a thing is permissible—is unknown amid these very activities.

[Col. 1280C] Therefore it ought to be known, since it is present to itself; for it is placed more fully before us when it is treated with greater subtlety. Since the wise have instructed us to know ourselves, how can it be endured if we remain unknown to ourselves? We desire to know the courses of the planets, contrary to the heavens, and the harmonious movement of the constellations. Some of them remain fixed and lack motion, while others revolve in perpetual motion and never rest at any time. As teachers of the world have attempted to investigate them, these bodies revolve with immeasurable modulation in harmonious delights. Their ringing and united concord produces a sweet-sounding melody.

We also desire to comprehend the height of the ether, the measure of the earth, the rain-bearing clouds or storms of hail, the trembling of the stable earth, the nature of wandering winds, the depth of the fickle sea, the powers of growing herbs, and the complex interweavings of the four elements dispersed throughout the whole body—and yet it must be endured that the soul itself cannot know itself, although it has been granted from above to examine such great matters? We are not seeking anything contentiously [ed., “contentiously”], but modestly desire to know the deepest things. Let us therefore learn first why the soul is so called; then what its definition is. Third, what its substantial quality is. Fourth, whether it should be believed to have any form. Fifth, what moral virtues it possesses, which the Greeks call ἀρεταί, “virtues,” contributed to its honor and glory. Sixth, what natural virtues it possesses, namely, those concerned with sustaining the substance of the body. Seventh, let us discuss the soul’s origin. Eighth, since it is diffused through all the limbs, where it should more properly be believed to reside. Ninth, let us learn about the form and composition of the body itself. Tenth, let the properties of the soul of sinners be disclosed to us through appropriate signs. Eleventh, by what distinction those of the righteous may be recognized, so that we may gather by probable indications what we cannot see with these eyes. Twelfth, in the resurrection—which the truly wise believe in—what is held to happen to each of them, especially we desire to understand, so that the fragile hearts of mortals may be stirred toward the desires divinely promised. Answer these questions for us, with God’s assistance, preserving their order, so that we may easily be instructed and you may deserve to attain the glory of a teacher.

I said that these propositions belong not to the instructions of kings [ms. S. Aud., “laws”], [Note: [Col. 1281D] He alludes to various formulas that he wrote when he was chancellor at the court of the Gothic kings.] which were recently being conducted, but to profound and remote dialogues, which are shown to seek not so much these bodily ears as the attentive and purified hearing of the inner person; nor can one easily speak about the soul itself, because through it we explain countless things.
