For the eye [Note: [Col. 1281D] See Basil, *Homily 9 on the Hexaemeron*, near the end.], which reaches as far as the stars, cannot itself succeed in seeing itself; and our palate, although it perceives different things by taste, does not know what taste it itself possesses. Our nostrils likewise draw in various scents from fragrant bodies, but they do not perceive what they themselves smell like. Finally, although our brain transmits sensation to the other limbs, it is nevertheless said not itself to possess sensation.

How, then, could I discuss such matters while exhausted, when I was already hastening with eager mind toward the end of my labor? Finally, my dear friends, you impose upon me once again the task of thinking about what you know is established by the complete force of the term *cogere*, “to compel,” especially since many have argued about this subject, but it seemed to have been abandoned as almost impossible to explain. Yet since I could not overcome their intellects with many arguments of this kind, and they had resolved not to grant my wish, I, defeated, asked them at least to spare me for several days and not hastily demand what they were imposing upon me, a task full of difficulties [mss. A and N., “what they were obtaining”]. Accordingly, what happened to me was like what happened to Proteus: what he was unwilling to reveal voluntarily, compelled by bonds he was forced to disclose. This nevertheless seemed tolerable [Col. 1282A] because I was being pressed to speak about such a subject—one which, if expressed truthfully with God’s favor, both deservedly refreshes the listener and illumines the mind of one who expounds it well. Therefore, before I enter upon the matter requested, it is necessary first to cut away the similarities of names, like branches confronting us, lest the forest of words with similar sounds appear to weave shadowy images through the path of our discussion.

CHAPTER ONE. Why the soul is so called.

The soul of a human being, therefore, is properly called a soul, but not that of animals, because their life is understood to be established solely in the blood. Since this soul is immortal, it is rightly called *anima*, as though from ἄναιμα, “far removed from blood,” because it is also established that after the death of the body its substance remains complete, as will be explained in its proper place below. Others say that it is called *anima* because it animates and gives life to the substance of its body. *Animus* is said to derive ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνέμου, “from the wind,” because its thought travels about with exceedingly swift movement, in the likeness of the wind. It is stirred by the soul’s appetite according to the character of its desire. *Mens* is said to derive ἀπὸ τῆς μήνης, “from the moon” [Note: [Col. 1282D] The soul is compared with the moon; so too the Church, for the same reason, by Ambrose in his letter against Symmachus, p. 231, and by Glica in *On Animals*, p. 32], which, although it changes through varying phases, nevertheless restores itself through a kind of complete renewal to what it was. At one moment it is diminished by tribulations and, as it were, found obscure; at another it is restored to its natural vigor when joy comes upon it.

The term *spiritus*, “spirit,” is used in three ways. God is truly and properly called spirit: he needs nothing, while all creatures need him; he breathes forth whatever he wills and dispenses all things as he wills; he fills all things, wholly present in the whole, immovable in place, eternal in his turning movement [mss., “will”], and singularly powerful over everything that is highest. We also call spirit a created substance—subtle and invisible to us, immortal, and capable to the extent usefully granted to it. Third, we call spirit that which is emitted and received throughout the whole body, through which the life of mortals is maintained by necessary breathing; it never takes rest but is renewed by continual movement.

Therefore it must be understood that *animus* and *mens* are not properly called the soul; but because these realities excel within the soul, they are sometimes called so by a liberty of expression. Nor is *spiritus* distinctly used in place of *anima*, since this name is shared with other beings—namely, angels, the powers of the air, and whatever things consist in spirit. Nor can that spirit truly be called the soul which is dissolved through the alternation of air, since this is something it shares with animals. It remains, therefore, that the human soul is called, distinctly and meaningfully, a spiritual substance that is in no way consumed by the shedding of blood. Let us now discuss more freely the substance of the soul itself, since we have separated it by necessary distinction from the similarity of names. Therefore, first of all, let us shape, with the utmost care, a pregnant [Note: [Col. 1283D] “Pregnant definition” is apt, for at the end of the following chapter he says: “Behold, that pregnant definition has now given birth.”] [ed., “primary”] definition of the matter, so that whatever consequences may arise from it can easily be recognized by the character of their kind [ed., “parent”].

CHAPTER TWO. On the definition of the soul.

The teachers of secular letters say that the soul is a simple substance, a natural species, distinct from the matter of its body, an instrument of the limbs, and possessing the power of life. But the human soul, as the authority of truthful teachers agrees, is created by God, a spiritual substance proper to itself, the giver of life to its own body, rational and immortal, but capable of turning toward good or evil. It was brought forth like a hatching egg [Lat. *edita*; ed. *editum*], in which the future bird’s life and the pleasing variety of its feathers are contained. Let us now open it into its parts, since it is human custom to learn more easily what, when divided, can shine forth more clearly.

No prudent person is unaware that human souls are made by God, or have been made by him. For everything that exists is either Creator or creature. No created substance, therefore, can be creative, since, in order to exist itself, it needs God and cannot give another the subsistence [ms. S. Aud., “substance”] that it received solely in order to have it. It remains that we must confess most truly that it was created by the Divinity, who alone can create mortal and immortal things. For it is clearly written in Solomon: “And the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Eccli. 12:7). And elsewhere: “I have made every breath” (Isaiah 57:16).

Reasonable and conclusive argument confesses, therefore, that this is a spiritual [ed., “special”] substance, because, although we know that all corporeal things are contained by three lines—length, breadth, and depth—nothing of this kind is shown to be found in the soul. Moreover, although joined to the body and weighed down by its bulk, it carefully considers the ideas of things with anxious curiosity, thinks deeply about heavenly matters, investigates natural things through subtle inquiry, and desires to know lofty things even concerning its Creator himself. If it were corporeal, it would certainly neither discern nor see spiritual things through its thoughts. Let suspicion of its corporeality therefore cease, since in every respect it shows itself alien to the definition of a body and investigates such causes as only the sublime spirit strives to reach. Hence the sacred Scriptures most justly admonish it to despise all visible things of this world: because it is itself incorporeal, so that it may rightly strive toward spiritual things, which it recognizes itself to have been formed to resemble. Its substance is certainly proper to it, since no other spirit assumes flesh in order to suffer or rejoice with its passions.

As we have said, it gives life to its own body, because as soon as it is given, by an ineffable act it loves its own flesh [ed., “loves its own prison”]. For this reason it cannot be free, because it is vehemently affected by the body’s pains; it fears destruction [ms. Aud., “death”], although it cannot die; and it is so anxious about the collapse of its body that you would believe it itself more nearly endures the extremity, although by nature it cannot fail. It also enjoys the most healthful tempering of the flesh, feeds upon the sight of the eyes, delights in resonant sounds, rejoices in the sweetest odors, and is soothed by the necessary pleasure of taste; and although it itself does not consume these things at all, when such things are withdrawn it is nevertheless afflicted with the deepest sorrow, desiring not things naturally suited to itself but things that, when joined to the limbs, are beneficial. Hence vices contrary to reason sometimes creep in, when the soul, by indulging too freely in its beloved body, is known to provide an opening for sin. The life of the body, therefore, is the presence of the soul it has received; death, on the other hand, is shown to be the soul’s departure. Thus we call it day when the sun illuminates it; when the sun has departed, it is called night. The body therefore lives under the soul’s protection and is shown to receive from it the power by which it is able to move itself.

But since this too is recognized as belonging to the kind of life about which we are speaking, it must be understood that, when that fiery vigor has infused itself into the body’s parts and the vital spirit has breathed upon the fleshly matter, if it should perhaps receive some wound, it immediately suffers with it, because it has been substantially inserted everywhere. If its power alone existed and heat alone animated the body [Note: [Col. 1284D] Ed., “unless its power—that is, heat—alone animated the limbs”], it could not suffer with a cut finger, just as the sun is not shown to feel anything if you attempt to cut its rays. It is therefore wholly present in its parts, neither greater in one place nor smaller in another; but [ms. Aud., “nor”] it is more intensely concentrated in some places and more weakly in others, while everywhere it extends with vital intensity. It gathers and unites itself into one; it does not allow its limbs to fall apart or waste away, but preserves them through vital vigor; it distributes suitable nourishment everywhere, preserving in them proper proportion and balance. Moreover, it seems astonishing that an incorporeal thing should be joined to the most solid limbs, and that natures so different should have been brought into one harmony, so that the soul can neither separate itself when it wishes nor retain itself when it recognizes the Creator’s command. Everything is closed to it when it is ordered to remain within; everything is opened when it is commanded to depart. For if the wound inflicts a sharp pain, the soul is not lost without the Author’s command, nor is it preserved without his gift. Hence we frequently see the gravely wounded recover, and again die from slight causes.

Who, moreover, would doubt that reason is present in the human being, when he deals with divine matters, understands human things, is taught by distinguished arts, and is educated in excellent disciplines? This is how he surpasses the other animals in a fitting manner: reason, with its beauty, orders him.

By reason I mean a credible movement of the mind that, through things granted and known, is led toward something unknown, arriving at the secret of truth. Through conjectures and arguments it strives toward what it recognizes to exist in the nature of things. That alone should be called true, pure, and certain reason which is made alien to every image of falsehood. It has therefore been granted to the soul, in a certain way, to grasp its own thoughts and to express them through the service of the tongue in fluent movement [mss., “change”]. Placed in the body, how many things does the soul see without departing from itself! How many different things does it observe around itself! It seems to be stretched everywhere, yet no departure of the soul is demonstrated. It is moved, raised up, and recognized as fluctuating; and, as though running within itself through a great space, it travels about. It does not go out to the causes of things, but through its own processes presents to itself what it observes in thought: sometimes what it has seen with bodily eyes, sometimes what it has conceived through imaginative vision. It thinks distinctly, just as it speaks; through the ordered sequence of sensation it accomplishes nothing [ed., “advances nothing”] when it confounds itself through diversity, because it is proper to Divinity to arrange many things and explain all things simultaneously in fitting measures.

Endowed, therefore, with the abundance of reason, what good things does the soul discover through the gift of the Divinity! It finds the forms of letters, brings forth the uses and disciplines of different arts, encloses cities with defensible walls, produces clothing of various kinds [Jur., “herds”], obtains better fruits through industry, traverses lands, crosses the depths in a winged vessel [ms. Aud., “suitable vessel”], pierces vast mountains for the use of travelers, encloses harbors for the benefit of sailors through lunar arrangement, and adorns the earth with the beautiful ordering of buildings. Who could now doubt its reason, when, illuminated by its Author, it makes visible through art what ought to be praised with universal acclaim? It is now fitting to discuss its immortality.

The authors of secular literature have proved in many ways that souls are immortal, saying: “If everything that gives life to another lives in itself, it is certainly immortal; but the soul, since it gives life to the body, lives in itself; therefore it is immortal.” They also say: “Everything immortal is simple; but the soul is not harmonic, nor does it consist of several parts; rather, it is a simple nature: therefore the soul is immortal.” Again they propose: “Whatever is not destroyed by original contrariety remains perpetually immortal; therefore the soul, since it is simple and pure, is without doubt immortal.” [Col. 1285D] They also add: “Every rational thing that moves itself is immortal; but the rational soul moves itself; therefore it is immortal.”

We, however, easily establish from truthful readings that souls are immortal. For since we read that they were made in the image and likeness of their Author, who would dare to call them mortal contrary to sacred authority? It would rather be shamelessly asserted that they differ from the likeness of their Creator. For how could they be the image or likeness of God if human souls were confined by the limit of death? He who always lives ineffably and always remains ineffably, himself preserving perpetuity, who contains and orders all things, is undoubtedly powerful enough to make immortal things immortal and to give them, according to their measure, a life suited to them.

[Col. 1286A] 630 Someone may say: “How am I like God, since I cannot at all create immortal things?” We think that this should be answered by a comparison of some kind: Can a painting, which resembles us, imitate the things we do? An image can indeed possess some likeness. But it cannot accomplish what the reality accomplishes. We should also recognize the soul as immortal from the fact that it desires to think about immortality: it desires, after the death of its body, to leave behind the fame of its name; it wishes to be praised without end; and with a good conscience it is more deeply concerned about future generations, lest it be stained by what they report. Hence it is established among the more eminent authors that whatever is raised up by the dignity of reason is not crushed by the injury of death. Add that truth openly declares that it will give perpetual punishment to the wicked and everlasting joys to the good, so that it is not right to receive with hesitation what the omnipotent Divinity deigns to promise.

Yet we must understand this immortality of the soul not as one that receives no suffering; for it is subject to change and open to sorrows. Nevertheless, amid every kind of weariness or anxiety, it persists through the benefit of continuity. God alone, however, is singularly immortal, singularly just, singularly powerful, singularly good, and singularly holy. For although these qualities, or qualities similar to them, are said to exist in human beings or angels, they in no way attain the height of his revered power. All lofty virtues are completely and perfectly present in that summit, and from it, by his generosity, they are granted to all creatures according to their measure.

Now we must understand how this immortal soul is thought to live. It lives within itself after the loss of this world, not by breathing spirit as the body does, but with the equal motion attributed to it: pure, subtle, swift, eternal; it sees, hears, touches, and is more effective in its other senses. It no longer understands these things through its parts but knows everything spiritually [ed., “specifically”] as a whole. Otherwise it would be absurd to think that, once free, it is less capable than when burdened by the bulk of its most brutish body. There is no doubt that angels, the powers of the air, and the other beings known to consist of a sublime and immortal substance are capable of understanding such things. It remains that we should now teach, in due order, that it is subject to motion. Would that the matter were uncertain, rather than our easily proving toward which side we so frequently run [ed., “fall”].

Who would doubt that at one moment we are lifted up by joy, at another cast down by sorrow; at one moment gentle through piety, at another terrifying through indignation; now raising our spirits toward virtues, now again declining toward vices? Some things we take up tenaciously, others we reject through forgetfulness; what pleases us now displeases us later. We are built up by the speech of the good and destroyed by conversation with the wicked; and to the extent that we make progress with the upright, to that same extent we know ourselves to become worse with the worst. For if one rigor and one purpose held us firm, neither would good people be made from evil nor blessed people from wicked ones through the benefit of mutability. But so that the cause of this variation [ms. Aud., “truth”] may be recognized more clearly, let us recall—as has been said—that prudence was not granted to us as something immutable. Therefore we are wise when, through divine illumination, we act well; and again we become foolish when we are darkened [ed., “blinded”] by sins that cast shadows over us. Affection, which comes and goes, is always uncertain. God alone is such that for him being is the same as knowing, power the same as living, and willing the same as doing. And rightly so, since all things that are truly good do not come to him but proceed from him.

Therefore this soul, whose origin we have discussed, must not be understood as a part of God, as some people in their irreligious madness have supposed, because it is capable of change; nor as a part of the angels, because it can be joined to flesh; nor as made from air, fire, water, or earth, nor from things joined together by mutual combination. Rather, it is a simple and proper kind of nature, a substance distinct from other spirits, which we must understand to be far more subtle than air and more luminous, since we can look upon air in the ordinary way but cannot behold the soul through the condition of flesh. Natural mobility continually agitates this form as it unfolds its thoughts in the ordinary manner. Hence, when we are relaxed in sleep, when the material of our customary thought has been withdrawn and we have not yet been solemnly attentive to our daily activities, we dream of various things, sometimes through false, sometimes through true, perceptions. It is not enough that, when our senses are asleep, we are deceived by a flying imagination; even while awake we are frequently led away from our contemplation. Often, when we direct ourselves toward prayer with great concentration, we are suddenly drawn away by some unknown game through unexpected thoughts [ed., “inspired thoughts”]. Thus it happens that something adverse, which we did not intend, is suggested to the mind.

It is therefore established that in this unstable and changeable world the soul is turned by its will, that it can lose and regain good things, and that it does not always remain fixed in one firmness of will but changes itself, even against its own purpose, through manifold transformations. Nor do we belong among those who say that souls remember their usual arts and other disciplines rather than learn them [Note: [Col. 1287D] There is no recollection of souls. See Arnobius, book II, p. 519], since they are ready to answer questions when they can arrive at them through the intervention of understanding [ed., “when understanding intervenes”], and they hear new things as though they had learned nothing of them before. Behold, that pregnant definition has now given birth; behold, into the light [if I am not mistaken] the things that had been enclosed have burst forth. Nothing has been left out of the proposed formulation; its method is such that it explains and determines what it intends, so that it appears to have said neither less nor more than it should. Let us now approach, with attentive minds, its substantial quality, which you remember occupies the third place in your question.

CHAPTER THREE. On the substantial quality of the soul.

The authorities have said that the quality of this substance is fiery, because it is always invigorated by mobile ardor and, joined to the body, gives life to its limbs through its heat. They further say this because they report that all heavenly things consist in a fiery vigor—not in this smoky, consumable, and temporal fire, but in one tranquil, nourishing, and immortal. This fire is neither diminished nor increased; it continually remains in the dignity of the origin it has received. It cannot be brought to an end because, unlike the body, it is not compounded from the diversity of several elements. A single and simple thing cannot have an adversary within itself; therefore it always remains, since it contains no conflict in its essence. Thus all created immortal things are said to possess a spiritual substance.

We may also, without impropriety, call it a kind of light because of the image of God, which it is remembered to have suitably received among the conditions of things, insofar as was necessary according to its measure. For God almighty alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16), which the soundness of the mind understands as surpassing all brightness and every object of wonder; but the image possesses some likeness. It cannot, however, possess light as the truth does. That ineffable mystery which we venerate [ed., “fear”], which is wholly and invisibly present everywhere—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one essence and undivided majesty, splendor beyond every radiance, glory beyond every proclamation—which a pure mind devoted to God can indeed perceive in some measure but cannot adequately express: how can one properly speak sufficiently of him who cannot be comprehended by the sense of a creature?

[Col. 1288C] Even if, through excessive piety, we pass beyond the measure of our soul and, through boundless religious devotion, fall silent in lofty thought above ourselves; even if we pass beyond the powers of the heavenly creatures and deeply consider who it is that made such great things by a single command and in a single moment—still, whatever we marvel at is greater, whatever we perceive is more exalted, since the human mind does not penetrate that inscrutable majesty. The single proper response to this power, therefore, is to venerate it because it is unsearchable, not to seek a definitive account of what or how great it is.

Taught by these considerations, we seem not improperly to observe that souls possess a certain substantial light, since it is read in the Gospel: “The light that enlightens every human being coming into this world” [Col. 1288D] (John 1:9). Moreover, when we are engaged in thought, we sense within us something subtle, mobile, and bright, which sees without the sun and sees without an external light. For if it were not itself luminous within, it would not possess such great insight into things. These capacities are not given to darkness. Everything blind grows numb. The lights of the soul are so forceful that they even perceive things absent. Yet souls become much brighter and more unchangeable when, through good actions, they do not depart from God’s grace. For through their contemplative power it is certain, by experience itself, that many difficult things hidden in the secret of nature can be examined and understood. Let us now consider whether souls are believed to have forms, since we have already said that they are incorporeal.

CHAPTER FOUR. Whether the soul has a form.

Before anything else, it is appropriate to learn, from the definition of the ancients, the most truthful account of form itself. By “form,” I mean that which encloses some space with a line or with lines; and it is thus readily understood whether souls can receive form, since it is certain that they subsist through spiritual power. For since every form exists either on a surface or in a body—and a surface exists only in a body, while a body is solid and tangible—whereas it is plainly established that the soul is excluded from these things, it follows [Col. 1289B] that souls must in no way be thought to possess forms, but must remain wholly formless and incorporeal in their nature.

Nor should what the Apostle says about Christ the Lord disturb us: “Who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God” (Philippians 2:6), and so forth. There he wishes “form” to be understood as nature. Otherwise, since God is incorporeal, wholly present everywhere, and incomprehensible, what form could he have possessed? As for what is read in the Gospel (Luke 16:23–24)—that after the setting of this present light Lazarus, in need, was received into Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man, burning and tormented by flames, asked for a drop with which his conflagration might be cooled—it is understood to have been placed there so that the destructive presumption of the human race might recognize what it ought to fear [Col. 1289C]. In reality, the one did not speak with a tongue, which is plainly bodily, nor did the other possess fingers with which he could have cooled the rich man’s fire by means of falling drops. The remaining details contained in the same kind of passage must likewise be understood in this way. For it is a small matter that these things are said of a creature in order to instruct human custom: we even read that the author himself, impassible, immutable, and eternally remaining in one manner, rages, and we have often heard that he sleeps—not because such things can befit the Lord, but so that certain matters may be recognized more easily and briefly through human custom. In the same way, we frequently read that souls, though formless in themselves, receive forms.

Some are also accustomed to be troubled by the question of whether the soul has [Col. 1289D] quantity, since it is clear that it is contained within the human body. But if we bring back into consideration the most truthful definition of quantity, which always briefly accounts for individual things, the truth will readily shine forth as proven. Thus mathematicians describe it with concise precision: every quantity consists either of continuous things, such as a tree, a human being, and a mountain, or of discrete things, such as a chorus, a people, or a heap, and similar things. But since the soul consists neither of continuous nor of discrete things, because it is not a body, it is clear that it possesses no quantity at all; wherever it exists, it neither receives form nor should be said by us to possess any quantity. Nevertheless, we must believe that the Creator can have knowledge of their circumstances and quantities, because he created all things [Col. 1290A] “according to measure, number, and weight” (Wisdom 11:21). These things are truly known to him alone who made them; he who, by wondrous power, sees even our thoughts as though they were visible things; who hears innocent blood crying out (Genesis 4:10); and, finally, who knows all things before they come to be. It is time to come to the moral virtues, which are riches to be sought, and truly the precious wealth of souls—virtues whom the Greeks call *aretai* (ἀρεταί)—by which a good conscience strives to vindicate its purity against bodily uncleanness.

## CHAPTER V. On the Moral Virtues of the Soul

First, justice is set forward as a defense against what is wicked or unjust; and its constitution is known to be such as the ancients wished to define it: justice is a disposition of the soul preserved for the common benefit, assigning to each person his proper dignity [Col. 1290B]. 632 Against confusion and uncertainty, prudence is usefully applied. Prudence, moreover, is the true knowledge of good and evil. Against adversity and prosperity, fortitude is offered as a remedy. Fortitude is the deliberate undertaking of dangers and steadfast endurance of hardships. Against unlawful and fervent pleasures, therefore, temperance comes to our aid as a moderating force. For temperance is firm and measured mastery over lust and the other disordered impulses of the soul.

With these defenses granted through divine assistance, the soul’s salvation is guarded in this mortal world as though surrounded by a fourfold breastplate; and it cannot be attacked by vices, since it has deserved to be fortified by such protection.

[Col. 1290C] But this fourfold splendor of the virtues is completed, so to speak, in a threefold division. The first is contemplation, which extends the edge of our mind toward observing the most subtle things. The second is judgment, which examines the distinction between good and evil through rational assessment. The third is memory, when things observed and deliberated are stored in the innermost recesses of the soul with faithful care, so that we may receive, as in a kind of receptacle, what we absorb through frequent meditation. When our wardrobes are full, they hold nothing more; this treasury is not burdened by being filled, but the more it stores, the more it seeks through the desire to know. We have touched upon the aforementioned parts as though they formed a three-string harmony. For the soul delights in such a number; and Divinity too is known to rejoice in it.

[Col. 1290D] Some are accustomed to raise very subtle questions, saying: If Divinity creates souls that are perfect and rational, why do infants live with their senses apparently inactive, or why are young people found to be witless? But who would not understand that, because of the weakness of infants’ bodies, souls can exercise neither the functions of the senses nor the services of the limbs? It is as though you were to enclose fire in a narrow vessel: it cannot rise to its proper height, because an exceedingly tight obstacle plainly confines it. Each thing appears to possess its own capacity only when nothing opposed to it prevails in hindering it.

So too, what confronts foolish young people is that the soul, because of unequal bodily parts or the thickness of humors contracted through some defect of the mother’s womb, is excessively weakened by an unsuitable dwelling [Col. 1291A] and cannot exercise its power, obstructed by the condition of an inappropriate abode. Even today we see this happening to fools, whom the Greeks call *moriones* (μωρίονες). To speak also of ordinary experience: how many people, when illness comes upon them, or when the brain is overloaded, or when they are confused by torpor of the vital organs, have lost the keenness of their customary wisdom! How many have been changed by a momentary injury! Even the man who is regarded as outstandingly wise, when filled by an ample meal, how easily he becomes dulled by drunkenness, so that you might scarcely believe that the man you see unable to move is the same one who had been arguing with the greatest prudence! Yet I know one thing with absolute certainty: the wise become exceedingly blessed when, through the Lord’s mercy, they are kept free from such adversities. There may perhaps be other causes that seem to oppose a rational soul when it attempts to express its proper movements [Col. 1291B].

In any case, souls do not grow along with infants [Note: [Col. 1291D] See Tertullian, *On the Soul*], nor are different souls allotted to fools by some variation of discernment; rather, just as they continually receive immortality, so they are generally understood to be rational. In infants, reason grows through prolonged reflection, not the soul. Now let us proceed in due order to the remaining matters.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Natural Virtues of the Soul

The ancients wished the natural virtues of the soul to be fivefold. The first is the sensitive faculty, existing in both its parts, which grants us the sense of understanding, through which we perceive all incorporeal things by various forms of imagination. It also makes the bodily senses active—that is, sight, hearing, smell, taste, and [Col. 1291C] touch—by which we perceive hard and soft, smooth and rough things.

The second is the commanding faculty, which orders the bodily organs to perform the various movements it has decided upon: to move from place to place, to utter sounds, and to bend the limbs. We have offered these as examples, so that we may be understood to have mentioned similar things in them.

The third is the principal faculty. When we have withdrawn from every activity and are placed in leisure, we consider something deeper and firmer through the bodily senses at rest. Hence those who have reached maturity of age are judged to possess better understanding: because, as the limbs grow old and the bodily senses are softened, they pass for the most part into deliberation, where, while the mind is more fully occupied, it becomes stronger through the power of concentration. But they again become foolish [Col. 1291D] when they are cast down by excessive weakness, because souls are permitted for a time to follow the necessities of their bodies.

The fourth is the vital faculty, that is, the natural heat of the soul, which, because its fervor must be moderated, gives us life and health by drawing in and releasing the ethereal airs.

The fifth is pleasure, that is, the appetite for good and evil, which the soul desires with delight.

Behold, this part is again unfolded in a fourfold division for the sustenance of the body. The first is the attractive faculty, which draws from nature what it [Col. 1292A] recognizes as necessary for itself. The second is the retentive faculty, which holds onto what has been taken in until useful digestion has been brought about from it. The third is the transformative faculty, which converts and transfers what has been received into something else. The fourth is the expulsive faculty, which, so that nature may be free, drives away what would harm it. We have untied, as was granted us, another knot; we have inclined as though over a sixth hill, so that, once the summit of difficulty had been leveled, we might proceed without stumbling to what remains. Now let us approach the origin of the soul with the greatest caution, since it is full of difficulties.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Origin of the Soul

We read in the account of creation (Genesis 2:7) that, as soon as the body had been formed from the dust of the earth, the Lord immediately breathed into it, and Adam became a living soul. For it is said that he breathed, in order to express [Col. 1292B] the dignity of the work, so that it might be recognized that something extraordinary had been brought forth from his mouth. In reality, his breathing signifies a command and an order. For how can one breathe who neither expels breath nor possesses cheeks, which are plainly bodily? Some, following this view, have said that as soon as human seed has been coagulated into a living substance, souls are immediately created and given to bodies, distinct and perfect. Physicians, however, say that the human and mortal creature receives a soul on the fortieth day, when it has begun to move in its mother’s womb.

There is also an opinion held by some that, just as the all-powerful Creator draws the seed of flesh from our body, so he can generate a new soul from the substance [Col. 1292C] of the soul, so that it may be shown to be guilty through transmission of that original sin which the Catholic Church confesses, unless it has been absolved by the gift of baptism. For how could an infant, who has no desire to sin, be found guilty in any way unless, by some reasoning, guilt appears to have been transmitted in the very origin of the soul? Hence Father Augustine, worthy of praise for his deeply religious uncertainty [edition: devotion], says that nothing should be rashly affirmed, but that this matter belongs to the secret of God, as do many other things that our limited capacity cannot know. This, however, must be believed truly and firmly: that God creates souls, and that by some hidden rationale he most justly imputes to them their liability to the sin of the first human being. For in matters so hidden it is better [Col. 1292D] to confess ignorance than perhaps to assume a perilous boldness, since the Apostle says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34). And again: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9).

But since the course of our discussion has brought us to the point of saying generally that souls are guilty through the transmission of sin, it is fitting to bring forward the soul of Christ the Lord, lest anyone, led astray by a malicious intention, should think that it was bound by a similar condition. Let us therefore hear how its holy origin was prophetically announced [Col. 1293A] to the ever-virgin Mary by a worthy herald. The angel says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35) [Note: Cyprian, *On the Nativity of Christ*: “When the Holy Spirit overshadowed her, the original burning was extinguished,” and so forth]. Who, I ask, could believe that in this majesty of birth there was any guilt of original sin, or suspect any profane offense of the flesh? Without doubt he came without sin, who was to loose the sins of all: conceived through a mysterious inspiration, born of a virgin. He drew nothing from Adam, for he came to conquer [edition: undo] Adam’s evil. The very long rope by which we were bound was broken; the torrent that was carrying us away was dried up there. Death lost its rights when our condition received the life of the Redeemer. For the first human being transmitted destruction to his descendants; Christ the Lord, coming among believers, [Col. 1293B] bestowed the kingdoms of heaven. Through this one he restores the lost state, which through that one had lost its merit [Note: Manuscript Aud., “the lost statutes”; edition, “the soul its condition, which,” and so forth]. Born in glory, he lived without stain. What could he have taken from the one whom he came to destroy by an opposing action? A holy origin was answered by a holy life. He who was born without sin was overcome by no stain of the world. Nature received a true human being, not vices. He rejected what the first-created man had done wrong and assumed the pure human being whom he had created: not taking on sin, but assuming sinful flesh without any violation or pollution.

This digression has become exceedingly pleasing to me, as I strive to remove improper suspicions. But while we pursue another subject, we cannot say much here. It remains for us now, following the order and purpose we have established, to speak about the seat [Col. 1293C] of the soul.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Seat of the Soul

Some have wished the seat of the soul to be in the heart, although the soul is diffused throughout the whole body. They say that the purest blood and the vital spirit are contained there, and consequently maintain that thoughts, whether good or evil, also issue from it. There is no doubt that the soul’s power can operate in this way.

Most people, however, clearly declare that the soul is seated in the head—if it is permissible to say so, though with reverence—in some likeness to Divinity. Although Divinity fills all things with its ineffable substance, Scripture nevertheless confirms that it is seated in heaven. It was fitting that the soul should seek the citadel, since it knew itself [Col. 1293D] to be exalted through heavenly activity, and should dwell above all in such a place, from which the remaining limbs might be governed by suitable direction. The very shape of the head is also an exceedingly beautiful sphere, in which an immortal and rational soul might make for itself a fitting dwelling.

Let us certainly consider bodily things. This mortal fire always tends upward, and because its nature is extremely subtle, it hastens without hesitation toward higher regions. There are also other indications supporting this belief. When the most skilled physicians attempt to restore a human skull shattered by a very serious blow to its former solidity, and frequently touch the membrane [Col. 1294A] that protects the tenderness of the brain because they wish to cleanse it of bloody matter, as soon as it is touched the person falls into such stupor that, even if he is struck heavily elsewhere, he cannot feel it. But as soon as the hand is again withdrawn from contact with the brain, he returns to his customary understanding, recovering voice and sensation and recognizing what is now happening to him. This is not demonstrably the case with other limbs, even when they are hollowed out by deep wounds.

It should also be added that no small signs relevant to this matter appear even in a healthy body. When someone has been inflamed by excessive indignation and has kindled his soul with the heat of thought, he is not troubled by a disturbance of the viscera or by agitation of the chest [Col. 1294B], but is immediately struck by pain in the head. Thus the soul seems to have left the signs of its fatigue there, where it appeared to contend with great force. There too we plainly feel certain waves and greater surges of our soul, so that things absent—of which no one is unaware—come before our eyes. We direct the vigor of the soul toward various parts and many regions, and through imaginative perception it is brought before the judgment of our head, which is known to have been refined through the various parts of the world.

Finally, when we are wholly absorbed in thought, we fix our eyes; the sense of hearing is blocked; taste ceases; the nostrils are free from odors [manuscript Aud., “do not smell”]; the tongue has no voice. In many ways, through such signs, it is recognized that the soul is occupied, in a certain manner, in its own chambers. Thus [Col. 1294C], being situated in an elevated place, as it is thought, and sitting as though upon a tribunal, it is recognized as the governor of its appetites, the judge of good and evil, distinguishing what is uncertain and rejecting what is harmful, whenever the grace of Divinity has shone upon it.

There was indeed in the first human being a natural blessedness, power over free choice, and an unviolated judgment. But deceived by an unhappy transgression and the devil’s fraud, he lost what he had received in order to hand it on to his descendants; and therefore he could not transmit to us what he had lost. Hence came the propagation of destruction; hence the decline of the human race was nourished; hence ignorance opposed to reason, harmful cares, regrettable counsels, obscured understanding, shameful desire, neglect of justice, a thousand falls into wrongdoing, and many things that we share with cattle [Col. 1294D], although Divinity had made us distinct from them.

For, alas, the departure of the sun foretells to us the coming of clear weather; from the movement of the winds we discern future storms; by the course of time we infer the abundance that will come to the ages; sometimes, without knowing it, we promise ourselves joy through the soul’s foresight [manuscript Aud., “through an unknown foreknowledge of the soul”]. But what such thing could the soul have failed to know if its dignity had been preserved? It was justly cast down into ignorance because it stubbornly wished to know what had been forbidden. Now it understands some things through signs or conjectures [Col. 1295A], although it could have known everything without effort. Nevertheless, once purified by holy conduct, it receives, with the help of Divinity, what it lost through the snares of the deceiver. Enlightened by the Creator, it sees what, having been darkened, it cannot recognize by itself.

We have recounted what gifts are demonstrably granted to the soul. But it is appropriate to speak of its temple, since that image of God does not permit it to appear joined to a deformed body.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Structure of the Body

The human being is a tall creature, upright and formed in the image of a most beautiful spectacle, designed to contemplate heavenly and rational things; its harmonious arrangement discloses great mysteries to us. First of all, our head, joined together from six bones, is formed with a rounded concavity in the likeness of the celestial [Col. 1295B] sphere, so that it might contain that most perfect number, six, as the seat of our brain, in whose organ we understand. Hence the eyes are placed like the two most beautiful volumes [edition: lights] of the sacred Testaments. In correspondence with them, all our paired members descend: ears, nostrils, lips, arms, sides, legs, shins, and feet. For in this mystical duality the structure of the whole body is contained; and just as those Testaments look toward one thing and teach one thing, so these functions join together in a single harmony and operation. Yet this equality, united in a most beautiful distribution, lends each part ornament from the other.

There are also single members placed in the middle, lest, by leaning prejudicially [Col. 1295C] toward one side, they should strip the other of its fitting beauty: the nose, mouth, throat, chest, navel, and the descending shaft of the genital organs. These are shown to be praiseworthy and honorable when they remain placed in the middle. To our head, which receives all the senses, the neck is rightly set beneath it like a column, teaching us that holy religion rests in the strongest unity of faith. The tongue also, the most fitting plectrum of our voice, was given to regulate the harmony of our speech, so that articulated words might distinguish us from the confusion of animals.

Nor should it seem pointless that one throat serves two kinds of digestion: namely, so that every understanding of the prudent soul, like food that has been received and digested by the heat of reason [Col. 1295D], may be explained through the two pathways of the Testaments by appropriate processes. And since the human body cannot defend itself by horn, tooth, or flight, as other animals do, a strong chest and arms were granted to it, so that it might defend itself with its hand against an injury inflicted upon it and repel it with the projection of its chest as with a shield.

[Note: The dignity of the genital member. See Gregory of Nyssa, *On Faith*, and Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 13. It is enough to deplore that impious and profane men commit the greatest sacrilege: they turn the worthy and admirable work of God—devised and accomplished by an inconceivable design for the propagation of the race—either toward the most shameful profits or toward the disgraceful acts of obscene lust, so that they seek nothing else from this most sacred thing except empty and sterile pleasure. Add the passage in Deuteronomy, chapter 25.]

Who could doubt that our genital organs [Col. 1296A] were assigned a great ministry [manuscript Aud., “mystery”]? From them, by God’s favor, fruitful human restoration proceeds; from them comes the fact that mortals are not known to suffer extinction, since, when individuals perish, the race can continue to be preserved. It is a seemly member, if it had not been soiled by shameful lust. For what could be more precious than it, if from it the human race descended without guilt? Thus all things were created worthy of praise, if polluting sins had not made them obscene.

This living body is administered and governed by five senses. Although they are shared with animals, they are better distinguished and completed in us by rational judgment. The first is sight, which receives bodily colors through illuminated air [Col. 1296B] and recognizes their individual properties. Sight is, as the ancients preferred to define it, the power of the spiritual soul, going out through the pupil of the eye, reaching things that are not too distant and discerning those to which it can extend: seeing that toward which it is directed in order to see. For if the eyes saw from within themselves, they would undoubtedly see themselves as well. Father Augustine also held this view.

The second is hearing, which receives sounds through hollow and spiral-shaped ears, sounds resounding through the striking of the air, and distinguishes by reason what has been heard. The third is smell, which, taking in various odors, evaluates the force of fragrant bodies through a suitable inhalation, as though it received a kind of invisible smoke through the nostrils. The fourth is taste, by which we recognize the flavor of many things through the palate’s discernment. The fifth is touch [Col. 1296C], which is likewise known to have been assigned commonly to all the limbs.

Touch is more refined in our hands, which were given in a special way to express many of our thoughts collectively. Through them a stronger memory also arises: what we can forget, we retain effortlessly when these hands write it down. They are the craftsmen of the various arts and of almost all our activity. For what good would it do to conceive through the senses something that must be done, if these laboring hands were not able to carry it out?

Nor do I think it should be passed over that our feet and hands are formed with ten digits [Note: [Col. 1296D] Such is the statement written in the *Symbol of the Faith of the Jews*, p. 30: that Moses’ affirmative commandments are 248, as many as the human limbs—that is, bones—are counted by physicians; and that the negative commandments are 365, the number of days in the year], so that the course and activity of our life might contain the mysteries of the heavenly Decalogue, lest we think or do anything contrary to the law of the Lord. The face itself displays indications of wisdom: hidden thoughts emerge in our appearance, and from this it is recognized what sort of soul and will is at work within [Note: Manuscript Aud., “what desires the soul turns over within”].

Our countenance, which is named from the will, is a kind of mirror of its soul, because what cannot be seen in its substance is most clearly revealed through its appearance. How much could also be said about the rest of its limbs [Col. 1297A]! Why is the order of our thirty-two teeth fastened into our gums? Why is our neck joined by seven vertebrae, and our spine by twenty-three joints? Why are twenty-four ribs bent like rays for the protection of the viscera, lest the tenderness of the intestines should too easily be injured by an untimely blow? How suitably do the nerves hold together the whole body in their distribution? How appropriately do the veins irrigate the limbs with nourishing blood? How do the marrow-filled bones strengthen us? Why is it common for our fingernails to continue growing together with our hair? How beautifully and usefully does skin clothe our flesh, so that neither the inner moisture may flow out shamefully nor the beauty of its color perish when its loveliness is withdrawn?

Although the individual limbs appear to perform different services [Col. 1297B] for the body, and one is placed above us, another in the middle, and another at the lowest point, they have come together in such harmony of structure that all are necessary and all are found suitable. As the Apostle says when he unites the Church of God through the devotion of love: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’; nor again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need of your service’; but much more, those members of the body that seem to be weaker are necessary, and those that we think less honorable in the body, upon these we bestow more abundant honor” (1 Corinthians 12:21–23). For God so arranged and distributed the body that the limbs would need one another’s mutual assistance.

But, because of excessive length, this summary statement should be sufficient: no bodily creature was formed with so great a signification [Col. 1297C] of mysteries. For what was to be joined to a rational soul had to be made according to the highest design. O wondrous creature of the supreme craftsman, who arranged the features of the human body in such a way that, if the first human being had not been burdened by the weight of sins, he would not have been stripped of great gifts! What qualities did that free being then deserve to possess, who is now known to retain so many good things despite condemnation?

Yet this flesh, although attacked by various vices and subjected to being torn apart by many wounds, is nevertheless the flesh that sings the heavenly Psalter, that makes glorious martyrs, that, when visited, earned the favor of its Creator, and that received even the life-giving cross of the holy Redeemer. It is rightly believed that it will one day be spiritual, since here too it glories in having been entrusted with so great a gift.

Thus this great nature [Col. 1297D], although exposed through original sin to daily sins, disciplines itself—with divine grace assisting—through fasts, almsgiving, and constant prayers. Thus, when the stains of sins have been cleansed, it prepares a radiant mind so that it may deserve to receive its Creator. It becomes the temple of God, since it has not allowed itself to be a lodging for crimes [Note: Manuscript Aud., “which previously did not deserve to have him as a guest because of its crimes”]. I believe that by divine mercy it was arranged that the body should be subject to the soul, the soul to God, and that the whole should look healthfully toward God the Creator [Note: Manuscript Aud., “and that the whole should receive creation”].

Having completed what needed to be said, it seems appropriate to discuss the signs and indications of souls, since [Col. 1298A], although their substance appears to be one, they are nevertheless separated by qualities that differ greatly. First, let us explain how the habits and behavior of wicked people are revealed, so that those whom we cannot see inwardly may be recognized outwardly through certain indications.

## CHAPTER X. On Recognizing Wicked People

All souls without right faith are therefore exceedingly foul, such as those of philosophers who follow not the law of the Creator but rather human error. Although they appear to be teachers of mortals and strive to polish themselves against the whetstones [manuscript Aud., “rocks”] of the disciplines, they nevertheless do not avoid the rust of superstition. For what madness is it to worship one over whom one is superior, and to believe that one who cannot help himself is able to help others? It does no one any good to have avoided harmful desires, not to have loved enervating luxury, to have fled deceitful falsehood, or to have made himself free from earthly vices, because anyone who makes the rewarder of all good things hostile to himself must labor in vain. Whose commands will he obey if he does not know the giver of the law? He walks without a road, looks without light, thinks without wisdom, and runs with swift step, yet does not find what he has determined to reach.

Such people may flourish for the present, but they are not shown to bear fruit, because their grace did not thrive in the root; it merely boasted in the display of leaves [manuscripts, “lay in the display of leaves”].

Those too belong to the same category who, although they believe correctly [Col. 1298C], are nevertheless polluted by foul crimes, because when they bind themselves to serious sins, they sever themselves from the Creator. Then the immortal soul becomes dead through its own darkness: it begins to love what perishes and to hate what lives; it hates virtues, always desires vices, and, darkened by mournful obscurity, has no pure reason, because it has plunged itself into the whirlpool of perversity. Soon it is taken captive [edition: captured] by the ancient enemy, driven headlong toward vices, and through the allurements of the body it gains victories from its own subjection.

For it is sick and always anxious because of its sins, condemning itself although no one accuses it; so that it may rightly be said that vital death and mortal life have come upon such people. If that merciful one looks upon it and deigns to illuminate the eye of the mind, blinded by bodily excesses, he leads it toward saving [Col. 1298D] repentance and grants it the means of escape—though previously it seemed to have desired only to perish. Then it is happier when it has wept; then it is loftier when it has prostrated itself. Through tears it restores what it had lost through rejoicing; and although it had been invited to the enemy through pleasures, it hastens most successfully, now sorrowful, toward the Lord who saves.

Although human beings are not permitted to behold such souls, they nevertheless disclose their qualities through evident indications, so that we may also recognize those about whom we do not find that we have heard anything.

The face of the wicked is clouded amid every bodily grace. They are gloomy even when they act joyfully, for shortly [Col. 1299A] afterward they repent; abandoned by the impulse of their own pleasure, they suddenly return to sadness. Their eyes are sometimes moved more than necessary; then again, when they are thinking, they become fixed—uncertain, wandering, wavering, timid about everything, dependent on everyone’s will, anxious with cares, restless with suspicions. They anxiously investigate the judgments others form about them, because they have foolishly lost their own judgment. In seeking worldly life, they incur the calamity of infernal death; and while they eagerly desire temporal light, they acquire the darkness of perpetual night. They often leave their accounts unfinished and leap suddenly from one subject to another. Although they do nothing, you would always think them occupied. They live fearfully even when no pursuer troubles them. Their conscience is a punishment to them, and they suffer everything from themselves, although they endure no serious hardship [Col. 1299B] from others. Even their smell is harsh [manuscript Aud., “extremely harsh”], except when they are preserved by the sweetest fragrances. For one who is offended by his own odor must necessarily delight in a foreign one.

Let us come to those faithful souls of the Holy Trinity who retain the apostolic discipline that has been proclaimed and, steadfast in the most glorious will, are truly shown to preserve the likeness of the heavenly image [manuscript Aud., “the heavenly image in the images”].

## CHAPTER XI. On Recognizing Good People

The virtue of holy souls, even in this common life, is already great. For in their sleep they fight down that flesh which wages war against the human race, and [Col. 1299C] they are victorious over themselves while, in their zeal for steadfastness [manuscript Aud., “conscience”], they take delight in inflicting death upon the living body. Woe to the flesh that is not overcome here; for what is conquered in this life will without doubt be crowned in the next.

In the end, the steadfast, pure, and harmless person praises everyone and always accuses himself; and while he pleases everyone, he alone displeases himself. For it is an immense greatness to understand one’s own smallness; and no one can know this unless the wines have already begun to be revealed to him. Such people fly toward heavenly things with all the greater ease the more severely they discipline themselves in human life. They rule the body because they serve the Creator; and while they recognize themselves as insignificant, they escape to the summit of great perfection. They desire to harm no one and always forgive those who harm them. They extend charity even to those who persecute them with criminal hatred.

[Col. 1299D] Such souls—by the Lord’s favor—even command harmful spirits; and those whom the world endures as hostile are overcome by a lesser creature. While still placed in the body, they are stronger than evil angels; while still clothed in flesh, they command the powers of the air; and by divine power they rule over those whose temptations they do not yield to. These, properly speaking, should be called immortal: no remorse tortures them, no sorrow afflicts them, and they cannot reckon against themselves what they are proved to be. They grow rich through poverty; [Col. 1300A] they are joyful in prisons; and amid all this the ages rightly obey them, because they always follow the good. Against persecutors they are always raised up with stronger courage [Note: [Col. 1299D] Ms. Aud.: “Yet amid all this they rightly obey God; and because opposing persecutions always follow the good, they are always raised up with stronger courage.”], when the end of light is for them the beginning of good things; and in eternal blessedness they receive what they have accomplished in temporal life. Thus the souls of the saints, while still dwelling in this world, although they are constrained by the prolonged conflict of their habitation [ed., “scattered”], nevertheless appear to be fellow citizens of the good angels and already, in great part, their companions.

For Moses (Exod. 14:22) opened a land route through the seas, crossing the dwellings of the waters with dry feet; and waves of such magnitude, built up as though on either side, hardened with the strange solidity of a cliff.

Elijah deserved that it should not rain; he also obtained that the desired [Col. 1300B] rain should pour forth (3 Kings 17:1; and James 5:17). One man, through blessed supplications, accomplished what the whole community, when it was suspended, did not deserve to obtain. For to those who purify themselves through a heavenly way of life the power of heavenly mercy is granted [Note: [Col. 1300D] Ms. Aud.: “For these women, who purify themselves … attain virtues through heavenly mercy”], which a human being cannot possess because of original sin. Though created, as they pass through the world they remain continually fixed upon Majesty; and such great works are constantly granted to them that they plainly seem to be miracles.

Elisha opened the eyes of his disciple, who did not see the heavenly army, and struck the enemy forces with blindness (4 Kings 6:17). Some have taken fires away from flames; restored vital warmth to cold corpses; caused fierce lions to gather for the burial of a body; and, in place of a raft, we read that they had men [Col. 1300C] carried by crocodiles. They changed liquid into the hardness of flint; commanded waters to flow from the dryness of rocks; took up live coals with unharmed clothing; commanded the lame to walk on their own feet; ordered the swift sun to stand still. The diversity of nature was made subject to a human word; and they were received into such great favor that even what the world marveled to see serving its Creator could have served them.

Why should we now speak of the power of the voice, when even the touch of their garment bestowed the effect of healing, and the shadow of an apostolic body drove away the danger of death? Thus, through the abundance of their merits, even that which is known to have no substance in itself seemed to heal.

Such a soul is plainly perceived even when its existence is not visible.

[Col. 1300D] Its face is always cheerful and calm, strong in emaciation, adorned with pallor, joyful in constant tears, venerable with its flowing beard, and most pure without any adornment. Thus, through righteousness of mind, people become more beautiful from contrary circumstances: their eyes are joyful and honorably gentle; their speech truthful, penetrating the hearts of the good, eager to persuade everyone to love God, with whose love it is filled. The voice itself is moderate, neither weakened into neighboring silence nor expanded into a robust shout [ed., “robust, with the shout extended”]. It is not broken by harshness, nor moved by accidental joys [ed., “kindled joys”]. In conduct [Col. 1301A] and appearance it is one and the same: a holy temple, a dwelling place of virtues. Its countenance cannot be altered, since it is always proved to strive for steadfastness. Its step too is seen to be neither slow nor swift. It looks upon no one for its own sake, and spares no one for another’s sake [Note: [Col. 1301D] Ms. Aud.: “It blames no one more than itself; it spares no one”]. A persuader toward what is right, teaching without arrogance, free with humility, strict with charity; so that abandoning it is as grievous as unwillingly departing even from life itself [Note: [Col. 1301D] Ms. Aud.: “strict: saying that abandoning God is grievous, and that it is unjust to suffer departure from life itself”]. As a lover of the secret that brings salvation, it is wounded by no lust, inflamed by no contention, puffed up by no pride, and possesses no envy. It says to none of the brethren anything of which it might repent, and hears nothing absurd. It conquers a great crowd of vices by the Lord’s contest [Domini 637; ed., “without a contest”], when the grace of solitude gives support.

Finally, although its tunic is one with the skin in the manner of a second skin, it fills it with the sweetest fragrances; it gives off a scent surpassing the perfumes of wealthy India. One recognizes that the human body has its own aromatics—namely, because, when it is not distended by gluttony, it does not sweat out exceedingly sharp odors. It is easy to perceive whom heavenly power deigns to visit. For our own spirit itself immediately rejoices at such a person and, without being instructed, understands whom it recognizes through heavenly inspiration.

Yet these things are not so astonishing in the stronger sex. But who could adequately describe the greatest virtues of virgins and widows, who are so swept away by holy love toward God’s commandments that they torment themselves with the strength of great patience and, overcoming the weakness of the flesh, attain the crown of martyrdom? We have said much about [Col. 1301C] the soul; we have also spoken of our body about those things that seemed appropriate. Let us now direct the mind’s gaze toward future rewards. For it is fitting that, once the creature has come to know itself, it should hasten with a pure mind toward its Creator.

## CHAPTER XII. What souls do after death, and concerning hope for the future age

Perhaps after this world you ask what our souls do and what their condition remains. We answer as we have gathered from various readings. Death is the dissolution of soul and body, that is, the absence of this present life, wholly ignorant of the desires or necessities of the flesh. For when we have been stripped by the Creator’s command of this light, we simultaneously lose the appetites and weaknesses of the body. We are no longer broken by labor, nor restored by food, [Col. 1301D] nor shaken by the prolonged duration of fasting. Rather, while continually persevering in the nature of our soul, we shall do neither good nor evil; but until the time of judgment we shall either grieve over the wickedness of our past actions or rejoice over the uprightness of our deeds. Then we shall receive the fullest fruit of all our actions, when at the Lord’s voice we are either rejected or admitted to the kingdom of eternity.

In this life, almost peaceful sleep imitates this death, when it lays aside all the desires and ambitions of this world; and the tranquil mind, in the sleep of the spirit, knows nothing of whatever is done here.

[Col. 1302A] For when bodies have received their sex [ed., “their senses”] on the day of resurrection, with the swiftness with which all things were created, what misery it will be for the wretched to be tortured forever and never to fail! They will be delivered to perpetual punishments in such a way that they will be proved always to exist unhappily: pain without end, punishment without respite, affliction without hope, an unchangeable evil. Thus the vicious variety [ms. Aud., “truth”] is punished, so that its condemnation is in no way altered. They are the most wretched of all, both in losing what they love and in continually suffering what they do not want. An age without sweet life; death without a recoverable end; a city without joy; a hated homeland; bitter dwellings; gatherings of the sorrowful; a crowd of mourners. And what is worse than all these confusions, they know that those whom, deceived, they believed to be gods can there [Col. 1302B] be tortured with them. Yet even in that punishment there is diversity according to the quality of their merits. For just as differing blessedness contains the good, so unequal punishment constrains the wicked. Clearly, there will be one perfect age for all. For how could anyone there be younger, where no one grows? Or why should anyone be old, where no one decays? These changes tend toward destruction. Whatever is perpetual is one.

From this, as from a vast river, a turbid little stream of dispute seems to emerge, if eternity is granted to perpetual punishment: since consumption scarcely permits the substance to exist, though it allows it to be restored at no time. But it is entirely superfluous [Col. 1302C] to consider this in reasoning about eternal causes. For there can be a punishment that tortures without diminishing, and a substance that intensifies the sensation of pain without suffering mortal decay [Note: [Col. 1302D] See Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XXI, chapter 4]. Our own soul, after all, is afflicted here by how many tortures, while nevertheless being dissolved by no diminution! Some mountains too are tormented by an excessive conflagration [Note: [Col. 1302D] On burning mountains and the salamander, see *Variae*, Book III, letter 47], yet remain stable amid their flames [ms. Aud., “torment”]. The salamander is restored by fire and renewed by the heat of flame. Certain worms are nourished by boiling waters. Thus that which threatens destruction to some provides nourishment to others. If, amid these mortal substances, such examples strengthen our conviction, what must be believed concerning that eternity where it finds nothing mortal for punishment to consume? There will therefore be for the wretched an inextricable conflagration [Col. 1302D] and eternal burning.

Who could doubt that the gifts of the good are perpetual, when they know that they receive joy and fear no further sorrow; that they deserve a gladness which they know to be continuous? There the mind does not fear its prosperity, but always retains its own exultation in eternity, with prosperity contemplated [ms. Aud., “known”]. They perceive that their blessedness consists in complete security, since they understand that they can no longer sin. There our security is shaken by no change: [Col. 1303A] the fixed mind does not waver, fluctuate, or move; it is so fastened in the stability of such great peace that it cannot bear either to seek or to think of anything apart from that contemplation. Thus what pleases always comes to pass, when there is nothing of which to repent. There we shall be free [ms. Aud., “thither”]—if indeed the Creator’s gift grants it—not dissolved in the torpor of idleness, but intent upon the grace of perfection. Our perception will be filled with the gentlest purity; everything we desire will be tranquil. We shall know without thought and perceive without error. Evil will neither be received from another nor arise outside the will.

We shall have a hunger that delights us; we shall have a constancy of continually loving the Creator and always gazing sweetly upon his glory [Col. 1303B], which the mind cannot grow weary of. There oppressive tedium will not weigh us down, nor feeble change confuse us, since what affects us will be such that it will not allow us to desire an end in anything. Rest that is active, activity that is restful, an unwearied unity of spirit. Then we shall be filled with the knowledge of divine wisdom; the truest understanding of things will not be imbued through laborious disciplines, but revealed in the unworked light of the mind [ms. Aud., “in the strengthened light of the mind”]. There the magnitude of number becomes known; there the distinction of lines is plainly perceived; there the harmony of music is evident; there the movement of the stars is most certain through visual knowledge; there heavenly truth is known by sight. We shall behold God’s wisdom, by what majesty he orders each thing. [Col. 1303C] There we shall see how the Catholic Church was wantonly torn apart by the non-Catholics [ed., “by the perverse”]. There we shall behold her standing as Queen in a golden garment at the right hand of her bridegroom and king (Psalm 44:10). There we shall know how great was the vanity of vanities beneath the sun. There we shall truly see how salutarily we were warned: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10)—for compared with him all things are utterly worthless. He was never otherwise and will never be otherwise; no one can be with him except happily, and no one can be without him except unhappily. Thus, while such knowledge is revolved by the rational and even purified soul, nothing further can be found by it to desire [ms. Aud., “to await”].

We can indeed imagine with what enjoyment the spiritual person is nourished; but what that mode of sweetness is, as it is written, cannot be understood by the mind [Col. 1303D] or explained in words. Blessed are those who have everything they want and are shaken by no adversity. There flesh and soul, established in eternal peace, cannot experience opposition between themselves. There will be limbs that adorn through spiritual harmony, rather than degenerate through carnal desire. Finally, there they will shine with heavenly sobriety, not be polluted in drunkenness by worldly thoughts [ms. Aud., “not be polluted while drunk”]. Their dwellings, as we suppose, will be in the regions above, and they will not desire the earth, whose necessary use they will not have. Therefore their habitation will not be mixed together, as in this world; rather, the elect, separated from the impious, will be divided by the great distinction of places and regions.

The heavenly city, a secure dwelling, a homeland containing everything that delights; a people without murmuring, inhabitants [Col. 1304A] at rest, human beings lacking every need of human affairs. There no greedy hunger troubles anyone, no diseased sickness consumes anyone; no one is ashamed of being naked in freedom; grievous cold does not sadden anyone; heat does not burn the panting body; no one seeks sleep to restore him, where no one is known to be weary. Everything is gentle, everything sweet, everything tranquil, since the world itself, laying aside its harmful disorder, will possess a healthful unity throughout the eternal ages. There will also be continual day and eternal serenity. The sun there is darkened by no cloud, but everything will shine more brightly through the Creator’s grace. For there the blessed have splendor of mind and the light of understanding, so that they may deserve to behold the Creator himself as he is in his majesty.

[Col. 1304B] Therefore the books of the ancients reasonably remind us that the cleansed and improved part, by divine gift, truly contemplates the Creator—namely, that part which bears his image in every respect [ed., “nevertheless bears his image”]. From that source, finally, we shall see what we believe; and from that part we shall contemplate the supreme, exalted, unique reality from which, in any event, we are better. When this globe of the sun shines serenely here, how it caresses the senses of our mind! How much grace earthly light fills us with when it is seen! Flowers when looked upon refresh us with most delightful pleasure. Now we gaze upon the green earth, the blue sea, the purity of the air, and the shining stars with extraordinary delights. If created things provide such great sweetness when they come before our eyes, what is that majesty believed to bestow when it is then seen, since nothing resembling it can be found? [Col. 1304C]

Then we shall perfectly know what we now salutarily believe. For we shall not deserve to perceive it otherwise unless we now confess what is true: namely, the Trinity coeternal, unchangeable, distinct in persons and inseparable, filling all things simultaneously by its substantial power; one threefold and threefoldly simple [ed., “simplable”]; equal in omnipotence, equal in charity, one in nature. This Trinity judges all things together and supremely by its justice, spares together by its mercy, and cooperates together by its power: incomprehensible power, wondrous blessedness, from which all blessed things are blessed, all living things are given life, and all things that subsist are held together. It weighs all things together and distinguishes all things; and for this reason it does not stumble [Col. 1304D] in judging, because it is not deceived in knowing. Though it does not appear, it is present to the good; and though it is absent nowhere, it is absent from the wicked. It is immovable, because it is wholly everywhere; unceasing, because it always accomplishes its wills. It hears itself wholly and sees itself wholly—not looking from some part as though from a limb, but knowing all things on every side as they are through its searching power. It is also said to smell, taste, and walk; but these expressions are attributed to it according to human convention for the sake of our understanding, while by the ineffable [ms. Aud., “unchanging”] power of its majesty it accomplishes all things in a wholly different way.

Holy power, creating and ordering all things, reigns in its own majesty and everlasting glory; incomprehensible, inestimable, and eternal power, it [Col. 1305A] consolidates the heavens with wondrous suspension, fixes the earth above the sea [ed., “void”], gives springs their course, sets a boundary for the sea, flashes serenely, thunders mercifully, and governs the lowest and highest things by the law of its wisdom. For everything subsists in its governance, not abandoned to its own power.
