It grows angry while calm, judges while tranquil, and without any change in it there comes to pass what will overtake the guilt of sinners. Very compassionate toward human affairs, it immediately spares the converted and corrects sinners by waiting for them; and, although it can suffer nothing contrary to itself, it sustains adversity with great forbearance.

How little of that ineffability do we perceive here? There we fully recognize how subject to the sight of its glory are the things we marvel at; to it the greatness of the angels gives service, the exalted principalities minister in their most devoted attendance [Col. 1305B], and innumerable powers obey faithfully and steadfastly—something every excellence of the highest order always requires. What can we now infer concerning its singular power, when we are not even capable of comprehending what we nevertheless do not doubt can obey it? Then, liberated, we understand whom in our madness we attempted to resist, and toward what magnificent things we were summoned, though we seemed to be occupied with such filth. It would be enough to see, even for a moment, what Truth promises that we shall behold forever. There every perversity of questioning is refuted; there what was wrongly believed is overcome by the very voice of truth [Note: [Col. 1305D] Mss. Aud. and de Noa: “the truth itself is concealed by its face”]. A kingdom without end, light without night, a body without vices, life without death; and since everything is directed toward eternity, only destruction will die there. It is great to enjoy these things, but much better that it should not be proved possible to depart from them [Col. 1305C]. Those who are called to the rewards surpass their desires. Then they truly know [639] how happily they were created, those who have reached such great things.

O incomprehensible majesty and mercy! For among the works of creation, by which the world’s expanse is filled with praise of its Maker, nothing is proved to exist more excellent than spiritual substances, which are known to contemplate their Creator with a pure mind. The rest were made for the delight of intelligent beings, but these for their own blessedness, which reveres its Creator.

It is time, having set aside the variety of questions [perhaps “having laid aside”], to gather the immense density of what has been said into certain handfuls, so that, counted up with faithful reckoning, they may be stored in the granaries of memory in concise brevity [Col. 1305D]. First, then, as you remember, most discerning hearers [ms. Aud., “helpers”], we taught that the soul is properly so called in accordance with the consonance of the word’s etymology, separating from it terms which, through similarity of names, could confuse those who heard them. Second, we completed, as was given to us, the definition of this substance together with its explanations. Third, we traversed the matter of its substantial quality. Fourth, we demonstrated how the soul cannot have form. Fifth, its moral virtues were reported, virtues which are bravely set against the vices of this world like certain weapons [Col. 1306A]. Sixth, not a few things were stated [ed., “poured forth”] concerning the soul’s natural virtues. Seventh, we related what has been read concerning its origin. Eighth, we described its seat and judgment. Ninth, we treated the disposition [ed., “arrangement”] of our body. Tenth, the unbelieving soul was displayed together with its signs, insofar as this seemed permitted. Eleventh, we touched upon the luminous mind, full of divinity, as far as our capacity allowed. Twelfth, some things were recalled, by the Lord’s generosity, concerning hope for the future age, so that we may understand that what we believe to be immortal nevertheless has everlasting distributions.

Thus we have closed our little work with the number twelve, which adorned the heavens with the diversity of the signs, composed the year with the beauty of the months, granted the principal winds for the provident arrangement of earthly needs, and divided the spans of day and night into a fitting number of hours [Col. 1306B]—so that this reckoning might rightly be applied to the clarification of the soul, since it is consecrated to the arrangements of so many natural things.

It remains now, most learned men, who flourish in intellect, that, having healthfully crossed beyond the mass of this world [ed., “having salutarily crossed over”], we should swiftly offer ourselves to divine mercy, through which the eyes of those who think are most fully illuminated. Let us understand him; let us love him. And then we truly know our souls, if we gain wisdom from his generosity. For he is the powerful and perfect teacher who both speaks truth to our soul and causes it to behold with an enlightened mind the things he has said. [Col. 1306C] Indeed, in the school of Christ an unteachable heart cannot be found, because whoever gives himself to him with complete integrity of mind can neither fail to know what he seeks nor lose what he has received through pious recompense.

Thus the soul becomes great, precious, and rich when it recognizes that it is poor in itself; powerful if it does not reject the most salutary humility; finally, most happy [ms. Aud., “most faithful”] if it preserves in the flesh what proud angels are proved to have lost in heaven. For no one reaches you, holy Lord, by raising himself up; rather, he ascends after being humbled. Although you are most high, you make yourself nearer to those who bow in supplication. Our humility is acceptable to you. You love what you do not seek for your own sake; you desire what you do not need. For humility is the mother of our life, the sister of charity, the singular protection of the burning [Col. 1306D] soul, the enemy and conqueror of pride; and just as pride through the devil is known to be the origin of crimes, so humility through you is known to be the source of virtues.

You, Lord Christ, wished to ennoble this humility in such a way that you deigned not only to command it but also to receive it. You submitted to judgment in the assumed nature of a human being, although you are to judge the world; you were beaten with scourges, although you exalt and humble kings; you endured hateful spittings upon the face which the angels desire with insatiable longing to see [ms. Aud., “hateful mockeries”; Note: [Col. 1306D] Ms. Aud.: “who … you desire to be seen by the angels”]; you were given gall to drink, although you held the human race so dear that you, Lord of all things, deigned to assume the nature of a servant; [Col. 1307A] you patiently received a crown of thorns, although you fill the earth with the varied flowers of rewards; you submitted to the condition of death, although you granted life to all creatures. Such was the humility in the holy incarnation as is the incomprehensible majesty in the Divinity.

Through you, O wondrous Lord, punishment was made eternal rest, suffering a remedy, and death the entrance to salvation for the faithful. For that which used to extinguish now continually gives life—not unjustly, since that which received human life rightly lost the power of destruction. Given over to disgrace, it remains in honor, because the things that then carried people to the underworld [Note: [Col. 1307D] Ed. and Jur.: “opened the underworld”] now lead them to heaven. [Col. 1307B] Truly, Lord, you who have acted so mercifully are powerful! None of the kings is equal to your needy ones; no purple robes are equal to the nets of your fishermen. When the former drive people into worldly storms, the latter bring them to the shore of eternal security. Poor from what was ours, rich from what was yours. You became a companion of our mortality in order to make us participants in your eternity. You cure pride with humility and overthrow death with death. For you know how to do good through the wicked, turning into assistance what was prepared to cause harm. You judged it more powerful to turn injuries toward benefit than to cut away the causes of evils at the root. For how would the signs of your benefits be recognized if indications were not also shown to the opposing side?

## Cassiodorus’s Prayer

[Col. 1307C] Therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, who bent down so far for us that you deigned to become human, do not allow what you decided in mercy to assume to perish in us. Our merit is your indulgence: grant what I may offer; preserve what you demand, so that you may be willing to crown what you provide. Conquer in us the power of the envious one [Note: [Col. 1308D] Ed., “the envious woman.” Ms. Jur., “the plague of envy, which”], which deceives in such a way that it delights, and delights in such a way that it destroys. It is a sweet enemy and a bitter friend. For you know how the slippery serpent glides in with deadly intent: with its crawling scales it gradually troubles the whole body, and, so that its arrival may not be recognized, it leaves no fixed track marked by its winding movement. It envied—alas!—such great peoples when there were only two; and it still persecutes those temporal beings whom it made mortal through wicked ambition. It ensnares itself, which deceives others [Col. 1307D]; and no one deserves to be corrected who must be condemned for the deception of all [ms. Aud., “because he must be condemned”]. Therefore, may the wicked one not prevail, lest destruction grow strong; may he not exercise dominion over us, who has never bestowed anything, but may your power now possess what it created. Let him grieve that what he made has perished, while he does not see us perish—us whom he wished to destroy.

[Col. 1308A] Lord, because there is nothing in us for you to reward, but there is always in you something to give, rescue me from myself and preserve me in yourself. Attack what I have done, and vindicate what you have made; then I shall be my own when I have become yours. The way without error, the truth without ambiguity, the life without end. Grant that I may hate harmful things and love those that will help. I shall ascribe prosperity to you; I shall always attribute adversity to myself. Since without you I am nothing, let me understand what I am; but let me recognize what I may be with you [mss., “then”]. Let me understand what I am, so that I may be able to reach what I am not. For just as we did not begin to exist apart from you, so without you we cannot progress [ed., “be of benefit”]. Everything nevertheless tends toward ruin that has been separated from the mercy of your majesty. But to love you is to be saved; to fear you is to rejoice; to find you is to have grown; [Col. 1308B] to lose you is to perish. Finally, serving you is nobler than taking possession of the kingdoms of the world—rightly so, since from servants we are made sons, from impious people righteous, and from captives we are restored as free.

Therefore, may the protection of your mercy rise up against our sins—the mercy that is given to the wretched as its very name bears witness—so that, rewarded with a threefold condition [Jur., “a threefold reward”], we may experience the Trinity as propitious toward us. We ask because you command; we knock because you instruct; and you prefer to grant without end, since you continually urge us to ask. O height of mercy! O incomprehensible depth of clemency! Since no one can receive anything if you resist, you attest that you can be constrained by our prayers—rightly so, since we ask the judge not to be summoned to penal judgment and hope through the legislator’s grace to be rescued, lest we be condemned by an enacted statute. [Col. 1308C] To you, holy Lord, King of kings, we say confidently: Forgive our sins and grant us what we do not deserve. Every creature praises you with the goodness of your work. We owe you the fact that we exist; we are also bound to you because we are sustained by your daily gift. We rejoice in this also, most glorious Lord, that we do not ask your benefits in vain. Temper, good craftsman, the instrument of our body so that it may be fitted to the harmony of the mind; do not strengthen it so much that it becomes proud, nor weaken it so much that it fails. You know what is truly measured. Fill your vessels with prosperity in such a way that no capacity is offered to adversity. Let reason rule and the flesh serve, since you alone can bring it about that it may not be injured by the frailty of the body.

[Col. 1308D] But let these things, spoken according to our modest capacity and not according to the greatness of the matters themselves, suffice: for we have said more than we were expected to say, and the nourishing lights of truthful writings have briefly and cautiously taught such things. Those authors could speak of these matters without offense who, purified by divine gift, deserved to conduct themselves in an approved manner.

## [COMPLETIONS]

[Col. 1309]

# APPENDIX TO THE GARETIAN EDITION

## To His Royal Highness John Gaston, Grand Prince of Etruria

### Scipio Maffei

[Col. 1309A] While I hesitated whether to publish now this most excellent monument of so great a writer, as it was urgently demanded that I do, or to postpone it to another time, as I had decided, that thought immediately removed my anxiety and doubt and cut through all hesitation when it occurred to me that I could seize the opportunity provided by its expedited publication to make public a declaration of my most obedient spirit, bound to you by many ties, most serene prince. Ever since I have been happily residing in this capital, you have bound me to you by ties of humanity and clemency, so that I could seek nothing more earnestly or desire anything more fervently than to offer, in whatever way I could, some testimony of my duty and no small indication of my singular devotion.

To this is added the fact that I know well that the greatest reward and unusual distinction will remain attached to whatever works are published under your most auspicious protection: without doubt, they will be read by you, deeply understood, and judged no less sharply than truly and appropriately by the marvelous force of intellect with which you are endowed. The same thing happens with almost every book that comes into your hands [Col. 1309B], for you very often spend several hours reading. How few among the nobles, even of private rank, in our age approve, understand, and embrace this kind of pleasure and recreation?

Certainly, among all those admitted by you into conversation during that celebrated and altogether extraordinary humanity of yours, there has been no one who did not greatly admire your keenness of mind and elegance of intellect, and did not follow them with the highest praise. Foreigners also, and those who have come here from regions very distant from us [Col. 1310A], are accustomed to be addressed by you in their various languages, so that they seem to hear from you not merely the words and proper diction of their speech, but even the pronunciation of their own nation and native cities, and their natural accent.

All these qualities are appropriate—indeed, most appropriate—for one who is to rule Etruria. For throughout every age Etruria has grown in studies and arts, not only brave, as in the days of that earlier Etruria, but learned as well (Virgil, *Georgics*, Book II). We may take an illustration and example of that most distinguished province from this eminent city. For, to pass over ancient matters so often celebrated, it is possible to find in these very times extremely few cities comparable with Florence, whether one considers outstanding men in literary affairs, the resources of the sciences, or the care of ancient monuments.

It is fortunate in very many titles, but in none more than in being ruled by princes who, using paternal rather than royal authority, nourish and foster it in such a way that, while very many Italian cities are gradually declining amid these unfavorable times and the number of their inhabitants is diminishing, Florence itself increases day by day [Col. 1310B] and flourishes happily.

For my part, most serene prince, although I have for several months now enjoyed this climate with extraordinary pleasure and am therefore a participant in this public happiness, I understand very well that, while presenting this distinguished work—until now sought in vain—to you, I am not so much presenting a gift as fulfilling a duty. Nevertheless, I hope that, such is your gentleness and clemency, you will receive me with a cheerful and kindly countenance, and that you will at some time show yourself a supporter and helper of my studies.

## TO THE LEARNED AND HUMANE READER

[Col. 1309]

[Col. 1309B] Why I did not publish this most distinguished little work much earlier, as soon as I first came upon it; why I am now suddenly bringing it out, after I have become engaged in studies far removed from it; where I obtained it; and on what occasion I discovered and brought to light both this manuscript and several others of the greatest value—you, friendly reader, ought to be informed and instructed.

Nearly eight years have now passed since I discovered and excavated, in my own native city, a treasure of ecclesiastical antiquity, which I hope one day, with the help and assistance of Almighty God, to make useful for the advancement of sacred letters and universal learning. The opportunity for investigating and uncovering it was as follows.

I had more than once been conversing with friends about Italian itineraries—that is, those little books which list in each city the things considered rarer and more worthy of observation. Almost everyone who comes from foreign provinces to travel through Italy is accustomed to equip himself with such books and to use them with the utmost confidence. I was pointing out how, in this kind of writing, not only men of no great distinction—who for the most part copy one another—but sometimes even the most eminent and learned men had gone wrong: either presenting an appearance of things very different from the truth, or imagining that anyone staying in a city for only a few days could acquire knowledge of everything in it worthy of notice.

When they spoke particularly of our Verona, I declared that they had been mistaken in more than one place, and I mentioned many things they had omitted which above all deserved to be described and celebrated. [Col. 1310B] To touch on one of the matters that they ordinarily investigate with greater diligence, no one among those travelers has ever named the treasures of the Counts Bevilacqua, collected in the golden sixteenth century [Col. 1310C] and magnificently housed and arranged—even though among them, besides outstanding painted pictures, bronze images, manuscript and printed books, there are about fifty ancient marble statues, and such authentic and distinguished busts of the emperors that they could be regarded as a collection worthy of being viewed and admired even at Rome, let alone at Verona.

I added, however, that the foreign purveyors of such travel-books were not so much to blame for all these omissions as our own carelessness, idleness—shall I say it?—and sometimes even the ignorance and stupidity of our countrymen. Many of them either do not know or ridicule whatever is most excellent, especially whatever concerns knowledge of events and periods; so that, if the things lying before our hands are to become known, it is necessary for people to come from the ends of the earth to investigate and illuminate them.

Taking this as their opportunity, several young men of the greatest ability, who were bound to me by close friendship, began to press me more insistently not to begrudge the preparation of a little book concerning Verona, in which I should endeavor to list and explain everything worthy of remembrance, both for the benefit of visitors and for that of the citizens. Wishing to oblige them, I did not delay in undertaking the little work.

While I was engaged upon it, since I had resolved to indicate whatever more distinguished and rarer manuscript books and ancient documents were preserved among us, the capitulary books came to mind—books of which I had occasionally found mention in several authors. Although everyone in the city agreed, and this had even been handed down by our ancestors, that absolutely nothing remained of that most ancient library, I nevertheless went to the cloisters of the principal church, in order to inspect the place where it had once stood and to see whether at least the old shelves survived.

After searching in vain, I learned from several prudent men that nothing was known about the place, and that neither in their own day nor in the memory of their fathers had anything belonging to the shelves been seen or even heard of. Yet I did not abandon my purpose. For when I reflected that the library had existed not only in the age of Guarino, who had extracted from it the sermons of Saint Zeno, and of Ambrose of Camaldoli, who calls it most famous in his *Hodoeporicon* and saw in it volumes of extraordinary antiquity, but also in the age of Panvinio (*Antiq. Veron.*, p. 153), when great traces of it still survived; and when I considered Saint Charles as well, whom Paulus Manutius celebrates in his dedicatory letter because, having summoned to Verona a manuscript of extraordinary antiquity, he had arranged for Saint Cyprian to be restored—I found it incredible that no remnants should have survived from that time onward.

Accordingly, since among the more distinguished canons of my native city Charles Carinellius excelled both in knowledge of local history and in love of antiquity, I approached him. At that time, in his official capacity, he was also responsible for the archives. I earnestly implored him to search through all the chests, cupboards, and compartments, and to investigate whether any remains of those manuscripts could be found—for even their dust would have been precious to me.

He undertook the search, partly impelled by his own learned nature and partly by the singular affection with which, in keeping with his eminent humanity, he has always honored me. A few days later he came to me with a cheerful face, declaring that he hoped something might be found in a hiding-place which he wished us both to examine.

I hurried immediately to the chapter-house and followed him into a rather dark room. There he showed me a very tall cabinet filled with the writings of the chancellor. Above its cornice, some old papers and certain wooden book-covers, long ago thrown there like *peripsēmata* (περιψήματα, discarded offscourings), seemed to be visible. A ladder was summoned and placed against it. Impatient of delay, I climbed up and found that the top of the storage compartment was not closed by any board but open and hollow, so that it formed, as it were, a spacious chest.

After throwing aside the heap of rubbish and fragments lying above it, I saw the entire hollow filled with books. They seemed, I imagine, to marvel at the unfamiliar daylight which they had not seen for an immeasurable span of time.

But what books, immortal God! The first one I seized and pulled out, without pausing to remove the black, centuries-old dust with which it was buried, shone with large Roman lettering, magnificently and most precisely formed. The second consisted of that swift handwriting which the entire republic of letters now calls sometimes Gothic, sometimes Saxon, sometimes Lombard, and considers to have survived to this day; it is also occasionally called Frankish, with the great P. Mabillon giving currency to the novelty of the name [Col. 1311D]. I, however, shall at some time demonstrate and establish, by arguments that are, unless I am mistaken, irresistible and incontrovertible, that it is purely Roman.

I continued. Books appeared, written only in capital letters or in a script that seemed millenary, though of another form. One came to mind which anyone who believes that the age of a manuscript can be determined from its script would immediately assign to a later period; yet it was written by Thodorus, a reader of the church of Verona, during the consulship of Agapetus, a man of consular rank—that is, in the year of Christ 517.

I was almost beside myself in mind and senses from astonishment, and, while awake, seemed to be dreaming, when I knew that royal libraries had sometimes been commended and illuminated by even one or two codices of such antiquity.

At last Canon Carinellius ordered all the books removed from that tomb to be placed and arranged so that I could examine them. Indeed, after some time, when I had disclosed what I was considering concerning the books and he thought that the matter concerned the chapter and would greatly serve the dignity of the church of Verona, he notified those to whom the matter then belonged, entrusted certain of these revived manuscripts to me for use at my discretion, and allowed them to be carried to my house.

I then bade farewell to various studies, whether already begun or merely contemplated—especially poetic ones. The allure of that discipline had consumed whatever care for the pleasures and follies of flourishing youth had not itself taken from me. I devoted my studies chiefly to these codices. I found many of them, though not all, mutilated, headless, half-consumed, torn—more truly the remains of books than books.

Nor could monuments that had endured an age of ten or twelve centuries, or at least nine, reasonably have emerged in any other condition. Since there are, as it were, two classes of these codices, one marked with a red number and the other with a black one, there are many indications that the parchment of the first class descended from Pacificus, archdeacon of the church of Verona in the ninth century.

Panvinio reported that Pacificus founded a library, either by conjecturing it from the verse of his epitaph, “He had made twice a hundred and three times six books,” or from some tradition that still survived at that time. The same Panvinio argued that this library was the most famous in the whole world (*Antiq. Veron.*, p. 153), evidently from these very traces of it in the monastery of the Canons—traces of which we are now speaking.

That these are the remains of the books which Pacificus either collected or ordered to be written is also confirmed by the fact that one or two of them are said to have been written “while Our Lord Emperor Lothair was reigning.”

To make clear in what year Pacificus died, with what admirable genius he flourished, and how greatly he adorned the church of Verona and our chapter with many distinguished titles—which I shall pursue elsewhere—I shall give the inscription carved in white marble and beautifully placed in the cathedral church. Panvinio, Ughelli, and others published only its first part, omitting eleven couplets which, I have no doubt, were composed by that exceptional man himself to be inscribed one day upon his tomb. I infer this both from the sense of the fifth and especially the thirteenth verse, and because they display a style very different from the preceding rhythmic eulogy. They contain certain flashes both of Latin expression and of poetic elegance such as can be found in no other monument of that age. Compare, for example, the ninth couplet with any compositions of the Middle Ages.

Those who ardently desired to obtain some fruit of this celebrated genius may now welcome, with applause, the elegant epigram which they have had before their eyes every day without recognizing it. By this very epigram our archdeacon indicates that he knew the Hebrew and Greek languages: for he renders his own name in Hebrew and Greek when he calls himself Pacificus, Solomon, and Irenaeus.

I preserve the writing, or orthography, of the stone, assisting the reader only with better and more abundant punctuation.

> Here rests the archdeacon Pacificus,  
> Renowned for wisdom and radiant in appearance.  
>
> [Col. 1312D] No one such as this has been found in our times;  
> Nor do we believe that such a one will ever come.  
>
> Founder of churches, their excellent restorer:  
> Of Zeno, Proculus, Vitus, Peter, and Lawrence,  
> And also of the Mother of God and of George.  
>
> Whatever exists in gold, silver, and other metals,  
> Whatever in different woods and gleaming marble—  
> No one was ever so skilled in such great works.  
>
> He had made twice a hundred and three times six books.  
> No one before him had seen a nocturnal clock.  
> Behold, he invented the device and was the first to construct it;  
> He set forth a gloss of the Old and New Testament,  
> And placed upon the clock an excellent poem of the sphere of heaven.  
> Many other writings and works the wise man will discover.  
>
> He lived thirteen lustra, and more than three years;  
> He was archdeacon for forty-three years.  
> In the twenty-seventh year of Emperor Lothair’s reign,  
> He was released from the burden of the flesh and departed to the Lord.  
>
> [Col. 1313A] He died on the ninth day before the December Kalends,  
> On the holy night which we call the Lord’s Day.  
>
> The priests and excellent ministers mourn as well;  
> At his death, indeed, an innumerable people grieves.  
>
> Holding, as it were, your feet, and bending low,  
> I beg you, readers: pray for Pacificus.  
>
> I ask you, traveler: come and pause here for a little while,  
> And examine my words with your heart.  
>
> What you now are, I was—a traveler famous throughout the world;  
> And what I now am, you too will one day be.  
>
> I pursued the world’s delights with wicked love;  
> Now I am ashes and dust, and food for worms  
> [Note: [Col. 1313D] Read *cibus* (“food”).].  
>
> Therefore remember to care for your soul  
> Rather than for the flesh [Note: [Col. 1313D] Read *carnem* (“the flesh”).]; for this remains, while that perishes.  
>
> Why do you prepare more for yourself? You see how little a chamber  
> Holds me here in repose; so small will yours be  
> [Note: [Col. 1314D] Read *fient* (“will become”).].  
>
> As flowers perish when the threatening wind comes,  
> So your flesh, and all your glory, perishes.  
>
> Reader, I ask you to repay me with a response to this poem,  
> [Col. 1313B] And say, “Grant pardon, Christ, to your servant.”  
>
> “Pacificus, Solomon, and Irenaeus are my names;  
> For him, as you read the inscription, pour forth prayers in your heart.”  
>
> I beseech you: let no pious hand violate the rights of the tomb,  
> Until the angelic trumpet resounds from the citadel above.  
>
> You who lie in the tomb of earth, rise from the dust;  
> The great Judge is at hand, with countless thousands.  
>
> Cast off your sluggishness; lay aside the distaste of your mind.  
> Believe me, brother: from here you will return wiser.  
>
> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 846, Indiction 10.

When I began to investigate what these codices had preserved for us of the writings of the ancients, I found only Christian monuments and ecclesiastical books. In this respect, I must confess, they answered only poorly to the great hope I had conceived, since among so large a number of books there were very few unpublished works.

Nevertheless, I brought to light many things fully deserving of the light of day, and from comparison with published works I learned much that it is greatly in the interest of the Christian and literary republic to know.

“Why then do you suppress them?” someone may ask. “Why do you delay for so many years? Why do you still conceal them?” I wanted you, learned reader, not to be ignorant of this; and it is precisely the matter for which I seem, in a certain sense, obliged to give an account.

The first reason for the delay arose from the very scale and difficulty of the undertaking. In such matters, neither should one who is able hurry, nor can one hurry who wishes to do so. Often many volumes and many heaps of volumes must be read through and examined in order that ten verses may be written with sufficient caution. Comparisons consume an immense amount of time! How many editions and how many collections, from those of Henry Canisius down to the present day, must be thoroughly examined before the unpublished status of so many monuments can be established with sufficient certainty!

The labor would indeed have to be devoured eagerly if that entire stock of mostly rare books were readily available. But with what incredible exhaustion of body, mind, and purse I had to seek out many of them in various cities and summon them from the most distant regions!

It was no small hindrance that an engraver was never available. Although two of the most famous men of our age settled in Verona, I could not make use of one because he does not work at engraving letters, and of the other because he is usually prevented by gout in the hands.

Add to this that I had resolved to establish a manuscript Library of Verona—not only from the capitulary codices but from all the more distinguished manuscripts preserved at Verona. At our place, indeed, they are thought to number none; but in the single Saibantiana library there are twelve hundred. Very few Greek manuscripts were formerly thought to exist; now, through my efforts, a considerable number of these too has been brought together.

I have in mind what would be the most advantageous course: to gather selections from every source, to place a discussion of the ancient writing of the Latins at the beginning, and to construct the final part of the work from selected documents, mostly Veronese. The first class of these would contain documents written on Egyptian papyri, collected and chiefly acquired by me. On that occasion I should like to publish certain new matters pertaining to the critical and diplomatic art, but such things certainly cannot be delivered hastily to anyone.

These delays arose from the nature of the undertaking itself. I caused still greater delays through my own actions and through my earlier pursuits, as well as through the smallness of my equipment—a condition I am not at all afraid to acknowledge, indeed openly to confess.

For when I encountered the capitulary codices, I had not even touched with the tips of my lips the more excellent and deeper ecclesiastical writings. I had merely tasted Greek; I had scarcely seen the elements of Hebrew; only a few months earlier I had made my first attempt at speaking in Latin; and I did not even sufficiently understand the name of criticism, as is commonly the case today.

I therefore had to begin in the very year of life in which my fellow citizen Panvinio ceased his work—that is, after he had died, leaving behind a very long series of immortal volumes prepared.

It is true that P. Abbot Bacchini, to whom I had recourse, and to whom I shall never have an equal opportunity to repay, showed me marvelous shortcuts along so long a road. Yet it was necessary for me to read through the sacred Bible, the councils, and no small part of the Fathers. My studies had been far removed from these matters, as my Italian poems of various kinds, tragedy, erotic treatises, and discussions of poetry sufficiently testify.

The same is true of my Italian writing on the science called equestrian science. Yet I owe it this much: it paved my way at least to the threshold of secular learning, so that I could investigate and make clear by what customs and opinions the Romans and Greeks lived in matters which, as we would say today, concern honor.

I hear that antiquarian investigators have hitherto taken no account of that inquiry, although they seek out with great zeal, and even translate into Latin, discussions of shadowy gods, brooches, and shoes. Yet that investigation, which concerns life and greatly contributes to the purification of morals, should be considered, although more difficult and less well-trodden, far more useful.

To return to the matter at hand: many other things occurred which often drew me away from these codices. I had to contend with the distinguished Christoph Pfaff on matters of the greatest seriousness; I had to set forth at length my opinion, whatever its worth, concerning the method of studies and the proper establishment of a universal school; I had to weave together the history of my native city in ancient times and set forth the metropolitan cities of the Italian regions under the Romans; I had to join a translation to the catalogue of vernacular versions from Latin and Greek authors which I had previously described, and to debate the precedence of coins and stones; and I had to defend with repeated arguments the new opinion I had advanced concerning the generation of lightning.

More events occurred that tore me away not only from manuscripts but from every kind of study. Six months were consumed by public office. My fellow citizens know well how many months I again devoted successfully to the most serene Electoral Prince of Bavaria.

I think I have provided enough reasons why I, who delayed, ought to be readily forgiven, since no blame can be attributed to me in any of these matters. Nevertheless, because I shall again delay for several years, I freely and frankly admit that in this respect I am not wholly free from blame. I turned aside, abandoning so great an undertaking, and gradually slipped into others no less extensive and no less difficult. I shall return to the former only after these have at last been completed and properly adorned.

I shall explain how that came about.

I had resolved to add to the manuscript Library of Verona a supplementary work on unpublished inscriptions found either in our city or in its territory. While investigating and copying ancient stones for this purpose, I became so inflamed by love for monuments of this kind, and so filled with admiration for them, that I was seized by an overwhelming desire to collect into one place those that were scattered, concealed, neglected, and perishing under the harshness of the climate; to display them in a public and secure location; to protect them; and to preserve them whole and uncorrupted for future ages.

As the undertaking progressed more successfully, and distinguished men contributed their assistance, I became eager to search everywhere for as many Greek and foreign inscriptions as I could possibly obtain. Fortune was sufficiently favorable in this matter as well. Since I spared neither labor nor money, the work itself and the more learned citizens began, with a kind of right, to demand from me a *Museum Veronense*, or a special edition of the collected marbles.

When I set my hand to it and encountered extremely distinguished examples, I entered, unexpectedly, upon a discussion of the use and value of inscriptions. Yet as I read through the Gruterian collection, the writers on inscriptions, and the greatest men of letters, who use marbles everywhere—if I may say so with their indulgence—this field appeared to me so buried beneath errors, so sunk in delusions, and still surrounded by such darkness that I thought nothing could be safely accomplished in this subject unless it were furnished with and preceded by a new Critical Art of Inscriptions.

Scarcely had this thought entered my mind when I ceased to be master of myself and no longer governed the direction of my studies. I felt the image and structure of this work and undertaking impressed with such force upon the fibers of my brain [Col. 1315B] that I was altogether compelled to cast aside every other matter or postpone it to another time.

Although I was eager to finish this little book—whatever it might eventually become—as soon as possible, I realized that I had to leave my native city, where diversions would always be available. Therefore, as soon as domestic entanglements permitted, I went to Florence, so that in this dwelling-place of the Muses, and one more agreeable to me in every respect than any other, I might devote myself to that little work.

I willingly confess that this inconstancy, and my desertion from one kind of scholarly labor to another, is not at all praiseworthy but must be condemned, avoided, and censured. I have no adequate defense with which to protect myself. Yet not only in our studies but also in the conduct of life we are guided by some unobserved and hidden connection of things, so that we often do not even perceive our deviations, and sometimes marvel to find that we have gradually arrived where we had never intended to go.

I can also offer this in my defense: amid the many adversities and troubles with which I have often had to struggle, I have preserved the good of freedom entirely intact, so that I am under no obligation whatsoever to give anyone an account of my leisure, whether I devote it to these matters or to those. Indeed, even if I do not bring any of the commentaries I have begun—works that, as I fully understand, greatly exceed my strength—to completion, I shall nevertheless attain the two things I seek uniquely from my studies: to live my life not without pleasure, and meanwhile to do nothing worse.

[Col. 1316A] But why, contrary to what I had decided, am I now taking my hand from the tablet for several days and returning to the manuscripts I had interrupted, by publishing the *Complexiones* of Cassiodorus? And why am I tearing this member away from the body of the Veronese Library? I shall explain briefly.

In this I am complying with the wishes of friends and intimates, whose will and advice I am quite unable to resist when they press them upon me again and again. Through repeated letters they informed me that certain distinguished men in our city had been seized by a sudden and praiseworthy desire to bring into public light whatever unpublished material was contained in the capitulary manuscripts.

Accordingly, when an exceptional man, learned in every field and deserving of esteem both for his rank and for his cultivated character, had come to Verona, his native city, they begged him to take this undertaking upon himself and to bring out of these parchments as many works as he could, as soon as possible. Either they did not know how long I had labored over each of these codices, or they thought that, because I had delayed and suppressed my labors for so long, I had abandoned the undertaking.

My dearest friends therefore asked me urgently and insistently either to set aside everything else and hasten to complete my Library, or at least to communicate some specimen of it, so that at last something might be known of my plan and undertaking.

I complied as far as I could—namely, by immediately beginning to think about publishing a specimen. From among the works that I had transcribed with my own hand and illuminated in one way or another, I selected this little book for several reasons, but chiefly because it could more appropriately be issued separately and constitute a book in its own right.

On rereading my notes, I added some verses in three or four places; otherwise I did not touch what I had previously written. I had begun to comment at length on the version of sacred Scripture used by Cassiodorus, but I am compelled to postpone that work to another time.

Now, however, I flee to the altars—that is, I return once more to my stones. I shall not take up the Veronese codices again for several years, if Almighty God grants me life and health. Whatever others may meanwhile continue to extract and illuminate from them, I shall await willingly and receive gladly, since I know very well that in so arduous and important an undertaking the Christian and literary republic will be served with far greater usefulness and with much greater distinction by anyone else.

## On the Work of the *Complexiones* and the Manuscript to Which They Are Owed

[Col. 1315]

[Col. 1315C] Both the singular genius of M. Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, exercised and demonstrated in many kinds of study, and especially the sacred and Christian-worthy learning that he acquired, are celebrated with such unanimous agreement among the learned that whatever he committed to writing certainly needs no praise and no recommendation to make people seize upon it eagerly.

Among the works he wrote after he had enrolled himself in the monastic militia, he himself mentions, in the preface to the *Orthography*, the *Complexiones* on the Apostolic Epistles, their Acts, and the Apocalypse, which he describes as brief explanations running through the texts.

The most learned man, Johann Albert Fabricius, made a mistake in the *Bibliotheca Latina*, book III, chapter 16, when he stated that these works were mentioned in the preface to the *Variae*, which he had composed much earlier. Cassiodorus completed the *Complexiones* in extreme old age, since after them, at the age of ninety-three and with the Lord’s help, he proceeded to examine the most beloved orthographers. Indeed, from the beginning of the same preface to the *Orthography* we learn that he was prompted to discuss *Orthography* by a certain dispute that arose from the *Complexiones* on the Apostles.

These works had until now been sought in vain and desired, and were commonly listed among the lost. With every hope entirely abandoned, they were mourned as gone forever. Daniel Mollerus says that a small and final part, the section on the Apocalypse, was published, as may be seen in Fabricius’s *Supplement to the Bibliotheca Latina*. Yet although Mollerus identified the edition itself, I suspect that he was deceived. Certainly, among those whom I consulted—and I consulted many by letter—I found no one who had seen it.

The delusion of Wilhelm Crovae, who is cited by Boernerus in the preface to the *Bibliotheca sacra* of Johannes, is beyond doubt: in his *List of Biblical Writers* he believed that the *Complexiones* on the Acts of the Apostles had been published.

But now at last the work appears, and this writing has unexpectedly emerged for the benefit of sacred letters. It is divided into two books, for at the beginning of the Acts one reads: “Here begins Book II.” Trithemius, writing long ago about illustrious Benedictine men, considered it to be divided into sixteen books.

The style is unmistakably that of the other writings of the Senator. In this matter I cannot agree with those who greatly admire it, since I do not know how to love a precipitous and rugged manner of expression. Yet it is the diction and language of its age, and no one should therefore unfairly blame Cassiodorus for it. Nor do books of this kind derive their value from rhetorical elegance.

To some readers this exposition may perhaps seem bloodless and meager, almost even mutilated at times; in it, they may think, piety should be valued more highly than intellectual acuity or doctrinal excellence. Nevertheless, no one will deny that it contains not a few outstanding matters, worthy of the highest regard for various reasons.

Nor do I think I need to labor greatly to show the place that a work composed in the sixth century should hold in ecclesiastical literature, especially since it was written by a celebrated and learned author whom Alcuin (*On Felix of Urgel*, V) and others list among men distinguished for holiness, and whom Bede lists among the sacred Doctors of the Church (Bede, *Commentary on Ezra*).

It is especially remarkable how deeply we are moved, and how we Catholics are stirred by a new spirit of edification, when, discovering something from an ancient monument previously unknown, we find the same doctrines; and when we behold the same teaching, carried down in an unbroken succession from the earliest centuries, confirmed and attested by the most ancient writing as though by a new and irrefragable witness.

In matters of morals and piety as well, you will find much that is excellent in these *Complexiones*. But for learned men to receive them eagerly, it is more than sufficient that they are concerned with interpreting the sacred books of the New Testament and also explain the canonical Epistles, of which scarcely one or two commentaries by the ancients survive.

Even if all the other features by which ecclesiastical books are usually commended were absent, the various readings of the sacred text and the fragments of the ancient version which the work presents would be more than enough to increase its value enormously.

For it is clear, both from the canon and from the hemistichs which the interpreter placed before the chapters, that he did not use the Vulgate, or Hieronymian version, but an earlier one. I have therefore indicated even the smallest discrepancies by adding the Vulgate reading in the margin. These will greatly assist the study and interpretation of the sacred text and will provide an opportunity for many useful and highly serviceable observations.

The fragments of the ancient version excerpted from these *Complexiones* deserve the greater esteem because they are transmitted to us by Cassiodorus—a man exceptionally careful in selecting the best exemplars of the sacred books, as we learn from the *Divine Readings*, and who strongly urged that they be corrected by consulting even their sources.

I have occasionally noted discrepancies in passages that occur more than once within the context of the exposition, although it may be questioned whether they are the actual words of the exemplar or whether the expositor has supplied them paraphrastically or from memory. This suspicion arose for me at one point in the *Complexiones* on the Acts, when certain verses appeared to depart too far from the common text.

The suspicion is weakened, however, by the fact that the very words of the text placed before the exposition sometimes contain hemistichs that might seem to have been added for the sake of explanation or connection. Such is Acts 14:18: “And while they remained there, and taught”; likewise Acts 16:1: “And when they had traveled through these regions.” Yet I have no doubt that the interpreter read these words in his exemplar. Indeed, some Greek manuscript may have preferred either the same readings or similar ones, as Walton’s *Various Readings* especially bears witness.

But let the learned decide these matters. They will also have to note in these *Complexiones* a new and distinctive division into chapters. At that time, as with the correction of sacred books, each person arranged the divisions according to his own judgment.

Learned men have often debated the ancient division into chapters and the stichometry of Holy Scripture. Yet that the labor of one who devotes himself to recovering the ancient writings of the sacred authors is never undertaken in vain is sufficiently demonstrated by even one passage in these *Complexiones* concerning the Trinity.

For a testimony so invincible and irrefragable as this had not yet emerged to defeat or overthrow the Unitarians of our own day. They loudly assert that the verse of the First Epistle of Saint John, chapter 5, by which the most holy Trinity is clearly taught, is for the most part not found in ancient manuscripts and was not read by the ancient Fathers, with the exception of certain Africans.

But Cassiodorus’s interpretation teaches us that it was read by him, and thus establishes that it existed in Roman exemplars. Which Roman exemplars? The most select ones, naturally, and those already regarded at that time as ancient. For in the *Divine Readings* he urged that ancient and corrected codices should be selected with the greatest care for reading Holy Scripture. What should we suppose he did when he undertook not merely to read but also to interpret them?

I scarcely think that in Cassiodorus’s age a codex could have been celebrated for its antiquity if it did not reach nearly to apostolic times, or at least to a period not far removed from them. The degree of correction in the exemplars he used can also be understood from the preface to the *Divine Institutions*, where we learn that he entrusted the other books to copyists for correction but corrected the sacred books himself by hand.

Indeed, he declares that he undertook to discuss *Orthography* for no other reason than to ensure that the sacred Bible should be copied without error.

The parchment book in which this notable monument of ecclesiastical antiquity has uniquely endured displays every sign of exceptional and venerable age, so much so that it may seem not very far removed from the age of Cassiodorus himself.

It is complete and uncorrupted, except for certain pages on which the parchment is either perforated and shows through where it has been eaten away by the ink, or retains only the faintest traces of letters that are disappearing. Taken as a whole, it is also of good quality and, compared with many others, not without the distinction of careful correction. One may often run one’s unimpeded eye over several pages, although afterward errors may appear in clusters somewhere—whether this difference and inconsistency should be attributed to a change of scribe or to the occasional negligence and fatigue of the same one.

To satisfy the taste of the learned age, I present a specimen of the form of the letters and the writing. No distinctive mark of either the scribe or the period is visible.

You have in the first specimen the reason why I have written the author’s name in a new form, and differently from the usual practice. For since, after the invention of the art of printing, no Cassiodorian codex of such great antiquity, so far as we know, has ever emerged and fallen into the hands of editors, we shall owe it chiefly to this work that the true inflection of this name [Col. 1318C] will at last become known: for *Cassiodorius* is more correctly said, as is clear from the threefold testimony of this manuscript. In such matters, certainly, Tertullian’s canon holds: “That is truer which is earlier” (*Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 4). Moreover, it is widely known that gentile names among the Romans very commonly ended in *-ius*. The family of the Cassiodori first arose from the Aurelia gens; afterward, when that gens was again divided into various branches, *Cassidorius* acquired the form of the gentile name, spreading among several families, even though κατ’ ἐξοχήν—“preeminently”—it belonged to the branch that produced our author, *Variae*, book I, letter 4. Fame celebrates those who preceded him as *Cassiodori* (as we have hitherto written the name incorrectly); and although this word appears to run through other branches as well, it is nevertheless established as proper to this family.

I applied the greatest possible fidelity in preparing this edition, and adhered to the manuscript even in minor matters, insofar as this could be done. Whoever is the first to extract and publish an ancient monument from a single exemplar can scarcely show himself sufficiently cautious and circumspect; for he dictates and decrees for posterity what everyone must read. I believed that fidelity, once established as my principle, required me to change nothing—not even when I restored the syntax—and to add nothing of my own, whether to complete a meaning that seemed mutilated or to fill certain lacunae. It is generally easy enough to supply these with words that fit reasonably well; nevertheless, I decided to abstain wherever the very words that have either vanished as the parchment whitened or are missing because it has been eaten away—such as on p. 232 [in this edition, col. 1412]—are not completely obvious and beyond doubt. I shall indicate the emendations, which I have employed only rarely and where it was worth doing so, so that they too may be corrected by others. If critics in former times had done this, we would know the writings of the ancients somewhat better; for by arbitrarily restoring countless passages, they have withdrawn the readings of ancient codices from our sight. It was not only the fidelity that I had proposed to myself in presenting the manuscript that moved me, but also the consistent judgment and wish of learned men, to leave untouched certain forms of writing from which the manuscript never departs—forms which nothing will prevent one from correcting in other editions and bringing into better usage. Among these are *epistula*, *temptare*, *fantastica*, *profeta*, *dicio*, *condicio*, *ammirans*, and others. *Intellegere* is consistently written in this manner, as in very many other ancient codices; this was especially the pronunciation of common and rustic people, as I infer from a passage of Cicero, *On the Orator*, book I, which I understand as referring to these pronunciations: “Cotta is laughed at when he removes the letter *i* and pronounces the *e* very fully; by this pronunciation, Crassus thought that he was imitating not the ancient orators but reapers.”

In this exemplar one finds *caecitas*, *coelum*, *coelestis*; likewise *adicere*, *subicere*, *reicere*. Elsewhere the practice is inconsistent: thus sometimes *seculum*, sometimes *saeculum*; *cena* and *caena*, as among the ancients *scena* and *scaena*. Here *obaedio* occurs almost everywhere, as does *rettulit*. It was tiresome to delay the reader whenever particles such as *non*, *ut*, *quod*, and so forth were either redundant or missing. Let us indicate once here the character and usage of the book, together with its minute emendations; only those initiated into sacred criticism understand what difference it makes to know these things.

First, the book suffers from the customary substitutions of related letters: *peccavimus* for *peccabimus*; *super viam* twice, with an interval left contrary to the usual practice, for *superbiam*; likewise *accedere*, *cadet*, *montes* for *accidere*, *cadit*, *montis*; conversely, *si* and *audiat* for *se* and *audeat*; likewise *adque* and *aliquod*, which occur very frequently, for *atque* and *aliquot*. In the manuscript one finds *inproba*, *conplectens*, *conpunctos*. Further, *opportunae*, *ponitur*, *conversos* occur for *opportune*, *punitur*, *conversus*—mistakes familiar in Cassiodorus’ age. In fact, in *Orthography*, chapter 15, he says: “Do not leave *b* for *v*, *v* for *b*, *o* for *v*, or *n* for *m*, when they have been improperly placed contrary to the rules of orthography.” One often sees *popolus*, *mondissimus*, *iracondia*, a practice attested by more ancient monuments as having been received from an old-established usage.

The codex also reads *piaetas*, *praetio*, *sae*; then, through an obvious error, *patiatur*, *fidelium*, *nobis* for *potiatur*, *filium*, *bonis*. Again, *Dei quae*, *his*, *necesse*, *respicere*, *huc*, *hic* occur for *Deique*, *is*, *nescisse*, *despicere*, *huic*, *sic*. Finally, *se* is found for *esse*, *esse* for *se*, *victum* for *vinctum*, *alibi* for *albi*, *nullis effulsisse* for *nullis se fuisse*, *vita et* for *vitiet*, *subripere* for *subrepere*, *precationibus* for *praecautionibus*, and *impedisset* for *impendisset*. It is astonishing how sometimes a single little letter drives the meaning in the opposite direction, and how, when that letter is added or removed, an entire sentence is restored.

I observed that when the same consonant occurs twice in succession—namely, at the end of one word and the beginning of the next—the scribe often omits the first: *sive unu sive*; *cum ipso semper* for *cum ipsos semper*. Elsewhere, conversely, he inconveniently doubles it: *niger regressus*, *illis suscipere*, where *niger egressus* and *illi suscipere* should have been written. *Regionis* occurs for *religionis*, as it is also written in the Turin codex, from which I published several years ago the beginning of Lactantius’ *Epitome of the Institutions*, never previously seen. Why should I mention having discovered *seddomini* for *se domini*, or *seddicit* for *se dicit*? I learned these things from passages that do not belong to the present place.

There is no time to pursue the phraseologies that anticipate the Italian language. The adverbs *promptissime*, *benigne*, and *devote* are regularly expressed in this little work as *prontissima mente*, *benigna mente*, and *devota mente*. Our author had reproved, in *Divine Literature*, chapter 15, scribes unacquainted with grammatical art because of the letter *m*: if one adds or removes it inappropriately, the entire word is confused. Yet in the manuscript we find *prae passionem*, *de Herosolymam*. These forms flowed from the speech of the uneducated common people, which is known to have been infected with the same solecisms even in an earlier age. Petronius introduces Trimalchio and his companions speaking in the same manner at dinner, in order to catch a laugh from plebeian speech as well: “We know that you are a fool when it comes to letters.”

I have added brief annotations; there was ample scope for dissertations, but then I would have presented not so much Cassiodorus’ work as my own. There was no need to revisit the author’s life after the extensive biography that P. Garetius prefixed to his excellent edition. When I discovered that another biography had been praised by our Cardinal Norisius in his *Apology of the Monks of Scythia*—namely, the one published in French by P. Dionysius of Saint Martha—I finally found it after a long search and read through it.

In book IV, while discussing lost writings, he mentions a *Catena*, or Commentary excerpted from several authors, on the Apostolic Epistles, the Acts, and the Apocalypse. Our *Complexiones* are indicated by this reference; but they could hardly be believed to have been composed in the manner of a *Catena*, since the use of *Catenae* arose long after Cassiodorus’ time. Nor could a commentary have been excerpted from various writers in that age on the Epistles of the Apostles—at least the Catholic Epistles—which very few interpreters had yet touched upon, as I shall discuss in the annotations.

When I was informing learned friends by letter about the publication of this work, the Apostle Zeno—the historian and poet of the most invincible and learned Emperor Charles VI Augustus, and a man equally devoted to letters and to learned men—remarked, among other things that he has written learnedly to me in these very days, how rare copies of these *Complexiones* were even in the Middle Ages. They were wholly unknown, for example, to Notker the Stammerer, a tenth-century writer, as may be inferred from his little work on the interpreters of sacred Scripture, which P. Bernard Pez, a monk of Melk in Austria, recently published in the first volume of the *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*—a work that has not yet been transported to our shores.

It has always been my custom to submit my short writings to the judgment of learned men, and nothing has ever been more welcome to me than being warned when I have made a mistake. When my friend among the closest of friends, Antonio Maria Salvini, an ornament of the age, came upon the passage of my letter in this volume, col. 0000, where I seemed to argue from the word “king” that the reference was not to the Roman emperor, he aptly taught me that this could indeed be proved by other arguments, but not by that one. For it is found that, from the Greek word βασιλέως, which the Greeks customarily use to designate Roman emperors, the name “king” also often adhered to Latin readings, as they are called, with the same meaning. The Greek βασιλέως means “of the king” (and was customarily used of Roman emperors).

[Col. 1319]

# M. Aurelius Cassiodorus’ *Complexiones on the Epistles and Acts of the Apostles, and Also on the Apocalypse* (C)

## Preface

[Col. 1319D] The brief summaries or headings placed at the beginning, by which the text is disclosed to us in a certain abbreviated form (*Divine Reading*, chapter 1), were called by the ancients not only *Titles* and *Chapters*, but also *Breves*. In the collection of ancient Titles published by the most learned Cardinal Thomasius, one manuscript has *Here Begin the Chapters*, while another has *Here Begin the Breves*: see Du Cange’s *Glossary*. Hence in certain manuscripts the index of headings is called a *Breviary*; Suetonius and Pliny also used this word. Seneca says, *Letters* 39: “Commonly it is called a *Breviary*; formerly, when we spoke Latin, it was called a *Summary*.”

The author indicates that these explanations of his could also be called *Breves*, since in them he does not discuss every word but embraces the main points of matters in a brief form. Yet they ought more appropriately to be called *Complexiones*, because the summaries placed before the text are not merely prefatory, but are rather certain paraphrases to be joined to the text, embracing what is contained in it: περιοχαί—“summaries” or “outlines”—of the Apostles, which we may properly call *Complexiones*, since by speaking summarily they embrace various matters that they propose to touch upon, so that the account may neither be judged too expansive nor appear to omit anything compressed by brevity.

Let us therefore have before us a brief and complete narrative of the matter proposed, embracing the main points in a compact form, not discussing every word, but bringing the words, stated summarily, to bear upon their intended meanings. We hasten to lead the reader’s understanding to this study, so that it may reach a deeper understanding, wherever our intention hastens to lead it by an appropriate course.

The difference between *Breves* and *Complexiones* is that *Breves* are a reminder, divided into separate parts, of the matters that follow, whereas *Complexiones* are a joined combination of similar matters. I now make this known to you, reader, having been advised, so that you need not ask another person, while you yourself may learn what we mean with the fullest satisfaction.

[Note: [Col. 1321A] I am not surprised that the primitive letter in this word has been melted away, whether by the author or by the scribe; rather, I am surprised that this defect did not adhere to the common spelling, since otherwise it corrupted similar words. Those forms retained their proper usage in which *m* follows *d*: we write *admoneo*, *admoveo*, *admitto*, just as we write *appono*, *accumbo*, *afflo*, and so forth. But in this book we find *ammonet*, *summovet*, *ammirans*, and *quemammodum*.]

Now let us proceed to explain the text in the name of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1321B] Thus the ancient codex follows the rule for gentile names. See the Preface.]

“Of Cassiodorus Senator, now converted by the Lord’s favor”—[Note: [Col. 1322A] A person who had renounced the world was called *conversus*, “converted.” Thus Saint Benedict speaks in the *Rule*, as does the Council of Arles, canon 11, and so forth. It is reasonable to believe that, in antiquity, whatever he wrote after withdrawing within monastic walls was marked by this addition to his name. Hence perhaps both the praenomen Magnus, or Marcus, is absent, and the name Aurelius is absent, while the designation Senator is retained, by which he was individually identified. For in a later age, when the custom of taking several names became widespread, people generally used the last one.]—the Preface ends.

# M. Aurelius Cassiodorus’ *Complexiones on the Epistles of the Apostles*

## The Epistle of Saint Paul to the Romans

[Note: [Col. 1321D] He does not begin with the Acts. For he did not follow the customary order, or rather Saint Jerome’s canon. Likewise, in *Divine Readings*, dividing the books of the New Testament into three parts, he places all the Epistles—which he calls the Apostolic Catholic Epistles—in the second part, while he relegates the Acts and the Apocalypse to the third. Saint Augustine does the same, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 8. Here is the arrangement:

| Vulgate | Cassiodorus |
|---|---|
| First, Second, and Third Epistles of Saint John |  |
| Acts | Epistles of Saint Paul |
| Epistles of Saint Paul | First and Second Epistles of Saint Peter |
| Epistle of Saint James | Epistle of Saint John to the Parthians |
| First and Second Epistles of Saint Peter | Second and Third Epistles of Saint John |
| Epistle of Saint John | Epistle of Saint Jude |
| Epistle of Saint Jude | Epistle of Saint James to the Dispersed |
|  | Acts |

]

### 1. — Romans I, 1

“Paul, servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle,” and so forth. He appropriately places his name before the Epistles, since he was writing to people absent from him. He also says that he was called by God as an apostle, just as it was said to Ananias: “He is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name among the Gentiles”; and that he was set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised through the prophets concerning his Son, “who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” [Note: [Col. 1322D] Acts IX, 15, Vulgate: “For me this man . . . before the Gentiles . . . his prophets in the holy Scriptures.”]. Through these words he says that he received grace, so that he might preach him among all the Gentiles. Thus, like a learned architect, he establishes the foundations of the Catholic faith at the very beginning by his saving proclamation.

He also blesses the Romans, so that they may receive grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; [Note: [Col. 1322D] He repeats this wherever the name of the Holy Spirit is omitted; and he also confirms it by irrefutable testimonies against Macedonius and other heretics.] here too the Holy Spirit must be understood. For when one or two of the three named persons are mentioned, they are fully understood to indicate the entire Trinity, just as blessed Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts X, 48), whereas the Lord had said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII, 19; Vulgate: “Going therefore, teach”). It is also read in the same book concerning the Holy Spirit alone: “John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts I, 5).

### 2. — Romans I, 8

“First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you,” and so forth. First of all, he gives thanks to God while proclaiming the faith of the Romans, and he testifies that he continually prays for them. He promises that he desires to be able at last to come to them for the strengthening of the faith that was already shown to be shared by them. For he says that he had often desired to come to them, but he testifies that he had been prevented by certain hindering causes—namely, so that he might teach them more fully, as he did the other nations to which he had been appointed, once the truth of the New and Old Testaments had been disclosed. He adds the example of the prophet Habakkuk [Note: [Col. 1322D] P. Possevinus, at the beginning of the *Sacred Apparatus*: “Abacuch,” whom the Septuagint writes *Ambacum* without aspiration. But Saint Jerome, *Prologue to Habakkuk*: “We ought to know that the name of the prophet Habakkuk is corruptly read among the Greeks and Latins; among the Hebrews he is called *Abacuc*.”], that “the righteous person lives by faith” (II, 4). Nor should you be frightened by the depths of sacred matters, since it is chiefly his intention to explain himself in what follows.

### 3. — Romans I, 18

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness,” and so forth. He says that God’s wrath has been manifested against those who, having recognized the heavenly power through his creatures and his immeasurable works, transferred the glory of the incorruptible God to corruptible creatures—that is, they decided to worship human beings, birds, and four-footed animals. While these people considered themselves wise, they were condemned by the blindness of folly, because everything deadly arises from the point at which the author of all things has been abandoned in sacrilegious impiety. For how can a frail creature help if the omnipotence of the Creator is offended? Thus far he has narrated the offense; next comes the punishment of sin.

### 4. — Romans I, 24

“Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their heart,” and so forth. Here he now recalls what sort of punishment befalls those who have withdrawn themselves from the worship of the Lord: namely, those who attempted to despise the incorruptible God, left in the desires and uncleannesses of their heart, stain themselves with mutual disgrace. First, they unlawfully use women contrary to natural usage; the males themselves too, torn by mutual corruption, are subjected to their lusts and to the other vices that a blinded understanding discovers. But he condemns with similar detestation not only those who do these things, but also those who approve them.

### 5. — Romans II, 1

“Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges,” and so forth. He reproves those who rightly judge others while contaminating themselves by the same way of life. For God’s patience mercifully endures those who go astray; but whoever confesses his sins receives glory and honor. Tribulation and distress, however, worthily overtake those who do not consent to the truth. For there is no acceptance of persons with God; only the quality of deeds is to be weighed. For not merely the hearers of the law are pleasing to God, but rather the doers of the law will be justified.

### 6. — Romans II, 14

“For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law,” and so forth. Since the Gentiles, who do not have the law, live according to a naturally ordered disposition, the Jew, because he received the law but neither wished to understand nor to keep it, is held more liable in the judgment of the Lord Christ. For circumcision does not make anyone blessed, but life does—especially since that cutting away of the foreskin is clearly transferred to circumcision of the heart, whose praise is established as coming not from human beings but from God.

### 7. — Romans III, 1

“What advantage, then, has the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision?” He places the Jews before the Gentiles, who had not yet believed at all, since the Jews had received the law of the Lord with devoted hearts. Yet if some of them were disobedient, this cannot annul the divine commands. For although those people perish, the truth of the law remains. He says that human sins commend God’s righteousness, since, when we sin, he is always shown to be most just in condemning us. Those who say otherwise are justly condemned. Therefore he confirms that all Jews and Greeks are under sin. He also proves this by the example of the thirteenth Psalm, saying that no flesh can be justified by the law but by grace. The coming of the Lord Christ proved this, for he bestowed the gifts of his faith upon us who lay under guilt.

### 8. — Romans III, 27

“Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith,” and so forth. He declares that the glory of the Jews, which they seemed to possess through the law, was excluded when the Lord the Savior came, through the law of faith. For a person is not justified by the law of circumcision or by anything similar, but by the law of faith, since there is one God both of the law and of faith.

He then adds the example of Abraham, proving that he found the Lord’s grace not through works but through faith. He adds the testimony of the thirtieth Psalm [Col. 1324B] [Note: [Col. 1323] “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” In the Vulgate it is Psalm XXXI; in the Hebrew sequence and in Jerome’s version, Psalm XXXII.], confirming that those whose sins have been forgiven are blessed. He declares that Abraham was justified not in circumcision but in the foreskin, through faith. His faith clearly appeared when, although the Lord had promised it, he did not hesitate to believe that a son, Isaac, would be born to him and to the aged Sarah. Therefore their righteousness will be like that of those who believe that the Lord Christ, handed over because of human sins and raised for the justification to be conferred upon us, was resurrected.

### 9. — Romans V, 1

“Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” He urges those justified by faith to have peace with the Father, since through Jesus Christ, his Son, they have received the gifts of eternal salvation. They continually increase their hope especially amid tribulations and distresses. Since he says that Jesus Christ died for the ungodly, he promises that he will much more save from wrath those whom he has deigned to justify by his blood. For when Adam sinned, death was inflicted upon the human race, even upon those who are known not to have transgressed the Lord’s commandments as Adam did. But just as death passed through Adam to his descendants, so much more will grace and the gift of eternal life abound for many through the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ.

### 10. — Romans V, 28

“Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one righteousness justification comes upon all human beings.” He continues in the same proof. For he says that the human race received death through Adam, but obtained the rewards of eternal blessedness through the Lord Christ. And just as through the disobedience of one many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one many will be constituted righteous. The law entered in so that the offense might abound; grace came so that destruction might be erased. Therefore whoever has now died to sins must not live in offenses.

### 11. — Romans VI, 3

“Do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” Just as everyone baptized has died to his sins, so, when Christ rises, he is renewed for perpetual salvation. For whoever is recognized as having been planted together with the likeness of his death is likewise declared to be joined to the likeness of his life. On that cross our old person was nailed, so that, renewed thereafter by the gift of resurrection, he might be born anew. For just as Christ died to sin once and lives in the glory of God, so we too, having died to sins, should live in his sanctification, since we are now known to be not under the law but under grace.

### 12. — Romans VI, 15

“What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace?” and so forth. He says that faithful men must serve not sins, since they are no longer subject to the law but to grace. For just as formerly their bodily members served iniquities, so now, having been made spiritual through faith, they ought to live in holiness of purpose. Previously, the end of their service was undoubtedly eternal death; in the present state, however, perpetual joy and security without end are given.

[Note: [Col. 1325C] I have noted this hyperbaton nearly twenty times in these *Complexiones*. Nothing was pursued so diligently in that age, and by this writer, as a certain perpetual rhythm, not without some consideration of meter, as may be inferred from chapter 15 of *Divine Reading*. To preserve that rhythm superstitiously, unusual word order was considered inconsequential, even when it disturbed or inverted the meaning itself. Thus the negative particle is very often moved from its place; the same happens equally to the pronoun *se*, especially when it stands beside the verb *dico*.
