Where one would have expected *dicit gentes gloriari non debere*—“he says that the Gentiles ought not to boast”—one reads *gloriari non dicit debere gentes*—“he does not say that the Gentiles ought to boast.” Where one expected *dicit se bonorum suorum conscium non esse*—“he says that he is not conscious of his own goods”—one finds *conscium se suorum non dicit esse bonorum*. Likewise, *se non dicit in vanum currere* occurs for *dicit se non in vanum currere*; *non decernat horrere* for *decernat non horrere*; *timorem esse in charitate non asserit* for *asserit in charitate timorem non esse*; *non se dicit posse* for *dicit se non posse*; and similar cases.

Traces of this kind of transposition can be seen in other writings of Cassiodorus. In the commentary on Psalm VI: *quoniam non se vult a mortuis rogari*—“because he does not wish himself to be asked by the dead”; on Psalm LXX: *tunc ergo se petit non debere derelinqui*—“then therefore he asks that he ought not to be abandoned”; *Variae*, book V, letter 42: *qui eum non optat evadere*—“who does not wish him to escape.” The fact that this syntax very rarely appears in printed editions, especially in the word order that draws the sentence in the opposite direction, I believe to have resulted from the work of critics, who restored the order of the words. For all who handle manuscript codices know how many things we read differently, against the wishes of the authors. I considered it a religious obligation to change nothing; for the rest, I have judged it more than sufficient to warn the reader about these matters once.]

### 13. — Romans VII, 1

“Do you not know, brothers—for I speak to those who know the law—and so forth.” He indicates the nature of the law by comparing the condition of a man and a woman. For just as, when her husband dies, a woman passes to another without guilt, so, when the law withdraws, one reaches the newness of grace without guilt. Therefore he now says that God must be served in the glory [perhaps “in the grace”], not in the oldness of the letter. For the law provided an occasion for sin: by prohibiting offenses, it continually showed disobedient people to be guilty.

### 14. — Romans VII, 12

“Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good.” Since the law is spiritual, it is necessary that the flesh always offend against it, because, through the fault of original sin, it is shown to desire the condemned lust of the world. Hence the Apostle declares that he has a desire for good but is especially dragged along by the law of sin. Because of this difficulty, God the Father sent his Son, who, having assumed the flesh of sin, might break the bonds of believers.

### 15. — Romans VII, 25

“Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with the flesh the law of sin.” He says that in his will he serves the Lord’s law, but that in the flesh he rather obeys sins. Those who do not walk according to the flesh, however, receive forgiveness from the Lord. For this reason the Father sent his Son: taking the likeness of the flesh of sin, he might dissolve the sins of the world. For he says that the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to the Divinity, produces death; but spiritual understanding, which is always acceptable to God, grants eternal life and salvation. Therefore one must live more fully in the Holy Spirit, who dwells within us when the power of the devil withdraws itself from us. We must consequently walk in holiness of purpose, because those who live spiritually are the children of God.

### 16. — Romans VIII, 15

“For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear,” and what follows. He says that every perfect Christian has received not the spirit of slavery in fear, but the disposition of adoption as sons: he calls that one “Father” whose inheritance he desires with righteous longing. For if we suffer with Christ, we shall deserve to be participants in his glory. Yet present evils are much smaller than future rewards; the former are temporary, while the latter are everlasting.

For our creation [Note: [Col. 1326D] A different reading may have produced a different interpretation. The author seems to explain this passage as referring to our nature. But instead of *all creation*, some understand all inanimate creatures, and others the Gentiles; in this sense the words πᾶσα ἡ κτίσις—“all creation”—also occur elsewhere in the New Testament. Mark XVI, 15: κηρύξατε τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει, “preach the Gospel to every creature”; in Matthew XXVIII, 19, this is expressed as μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη, “teach all nations.”] groans together [Vulgate, verse 22: “every creature groans”] and labors in childbirth until it reaches the point at which it may obtain the promised happiness. He says that this is also what he himself does, although he is known already to have received the first fruits of the Holy Spirit, awaiting the redemption of his body, which is to be granted in the general resurrection.

### 17. — Romans VIII, 24

“For we have been saved by hope. But hope that is seen is not hope.” He proclaims that the divine promises must be endured in hope, because whatever is placed [read: *ponitur*, “is placed,” for *punitur*, “is punished”] in future times is not seen by bodily eyes. The Holy Spirit [Col. 1326C] intercedes for us with ineffable groanings—that is, he causes us to groan so that we may be able to reach the promised rewards. He says that those predestined were called, so that the Lord Christ might be the firstborn among many brothers. And lest fragile human hearts waver in so great a hope, he says that the predestined were called, asserts that the called were justified, and confirms that the justified were glorified. This figure is called *climax*, that is, “gradation,” and he frequently employs it in what follows as well.

### 18. — Romans VIII, 31

“What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” and so forth. He therefore commends the Father’s mercy in all things, for, in order to redeem us, he did not spare his own Son. What good could he deny us, who granted the author of every blessing? He himself intercedes for us, who also sits at the right hand of the Father. There follows also a very extensive and deeply moving promise: no tribulations, persecutions, dangers, or powers of heaven—neither present nor future—can separate us from the grace of the Lord Christ, by which he has deigned to grant such great things.

### 19. — Romans IX, 1

“I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit,” and so forth. He testifies that his love for his fleshly relatives was so great that, which is the extremity of misery, he would rather have wished himself to be separated from Christ than to see the Jews excluded from faith in the Lord. Moses too is read as having said this: “Either forgive this people their sin; but if not, blot me from the book that you have written” [Note: [Col. 1327D] Exodus XXXII, 31–32. Vulgate: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you do not, blot me from your book, which you have written.”].

First, they had been adopted into the glory of sons; then they had been entrusted with obedience to the law, from which the patriarchs too arose; and, surpassing all honors, from them Christ the Lord was born according to the flesh, “who is over all, God blessed forever.” He also says that the children of the promise come to the faith of Christ—not all the children of Abraham, who were indeed born from his seed but did not share the same faith. Examples are given of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and the two brothers Esau and Jacob. But one of these is shown to have been chosen in such a way that he appears to have been preferred to his brother not because of preceding merits but by grace alone, commending the Lord’s gratuitous grace throughout.

### 20. — Romans IX, 14

“What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not,” and so forth. He acknowledges that everything is placed in the Lord’s will, since it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy. He also adds the example of Pharaoh, because God justly carries out by his will whatever he disposes. He raises against himself, from the preceding statements, an opposing question, which he resolves by comparing God to a potter: he says that the potter has power to make one vessel for dishonor and another for honor, so that no one may rise up against God’s will with sacrilegious murmuring.

### 21. — Romans IX, 22

“But what if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known,” [Col. 1327D] [Vulgate: “to make known”] “and so forth.” He shows God’s patience, since God endured the ungodly with great compassion in order to choose holy men from both the Gentiles and the Jews, whom he prepared for everlasting glory. The prophet Hosea provides an example of this. He says that the remnant of the Jews will be converted at the end of the ages, following the example of the prophet Isaiah; and he confirms that this too must take place by another example from the same prophet.

### 22. — Romans IX, 30

“What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness.” He says that the Gentiles grasped righteousness through faith, not through works. The Jews, believing according to the letter and not understanding spiritually, stumbled over the stone of stumbling, which is the Lord Christ. This too is proved by the example of the prophet Isaiah. Therefore, with civic affection for the Jews, he testifies that he prays for them: he bears witness that they indeed have zeal for God, but do not have knowledge of Christ, who is the end of the law and its completing perfection.

### 23. — Romans X, 5

“For Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it.” Moses says that if a person performs the righteousness that comes from the law, he will live by it. Therefore let him believe that the Lord Christ was raised from the dead by the power of his might. For whether Greek or Jew, whoever rightly invokes his name and is not confounded by sacrilegious doubt will be saved. But he denies that the obstinate Jew believes the Gospel, since he has refused to listen to Christ himself. This too is confirmed by the examples of many.

24.---XI, 1. “I say, then: Has God rejected his people? By no means,” and so forth. He does not say that the whole Hebrew people has been despised by the Lord, but that from among them he daily chooses many who may attain the joys of the kingdom to come:

> [Note: [Col. 1327D] Our author, *On Orthography*, chapter 1: “There are those who write *cotidie* with *co*, and they may be allowed to err; they would stop if they knew that *cotidie* is derived from *quot diebus*, ‘from how many days.’ But this is from Gnaeus Cornutus; from Papirianus, chapter 4: ‘*Cotidie* is written with *c* and *o*, as it is pronounced, not with *q*, because it is derived not from *quoto die*, ‘on which day,’ but from *consistenti die*, ‘the established day.’ Which spelling he subsequently preferred, who can say? I have not departed from the manuscript.”]

He confirms this also by readings concerning kingdoms; for just as he says that the elect have obtained the Lord’s grace, so he reports that the unbelieving have been deprived of heavenly light. This is likewise established by the examples of Isaiah [Col. 1328C] and David. He recalls that the Jews indeed stumbled, but not so as to perish utterly. If their offense, when Christ was crucified, is the salvation of the world and the diminution of the riches of the Gentiles, much more will their conversion be an immense joy to the blessed.

25.---XI, 13. “For I speak to you Gentiles: inasmuch as I am indeed the apostle of the Gentiles,” and so forth. The Apostle addresses the Gentiles, saying that he wishes to lead the Jews to emulate them; but he says that the Gentiles ought not to glory because the Jews were rejected on account of their unbelief, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter beneficially. For if their first offering is holy, it is evident that the whole mass is even holier. He makes a most beautiful comparison between the wild olive and the cultivated olive [Col. 1328D], because the grafted branch ought not to glory against the one into which it is understood to have been grafted. For if the Gentiles received an undeserved benefit by the Lord’s gift, how much more can those others be restored by him to the stock from which they once came as the elect!

26.---XI, 25. “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery,” and what follows. He says that the Hebrew people was partially blinded for a time, so that the Gentiles might enter into the Christian faith. But at the end of the age [Col. 1329A] he declares that the Israelite people will be saved by the Lord’s mercy, after the predestined multitude of the Gentiles has believed. For just as the Gentiles did not believe at first, when the Jews received the law, so, when the Gentiles have been saved, the Jews are known to be destined to believe. For God has confined all things under unbelief, so that he might bestow the gifts of his mercy upon all.

27.---XI, 33. “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” and so forth. Filled with admiration at the Lord’s dispensation, he truly exclaims that the things which the Holy Trinity is shown to accomplish are incomprehensible. For all things are “from him,” that is, from the Father; “through him,” that is, through the Son; and “in him,” that is, in the Holy Spirit. And to show that their unity is indivisible, he added: “To him be glory for ever and ever” [in [Col. 1329B] the Vulgate, *saeculorum* is lacking]. Therefore he beseeches the Romans not to be captivated by the pleasures of this age, but to offer their bodies to the heavenly commandments. He also warns that everyone ought to think according to the measure which God, in accordance with his goodness, has distributed to each person, so that he might abolish unlawful presumptions, from which human frailty chiefly falls into sin.

28.---XII, 4. “For just as in one body we have many members,” and so forth. By comparing the members, he teaches that each person, according to the gifts bestowed, ought to serve the Lord Christ within the structure of the ecclesiastical body. He lays down various rules concerning how the faithful people ought to live. Finally, he concludes everything in such a way that no one should repay evil with evil, but that inflicted injustice should rather be overcome by a recompense of goodness [Col. 1329C].

29.---XIII, 1. “Be subject to the higher authorities” [Note: [Col. 1329D] Vulgate: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities.”], and so forth. He says that all must be subject to authorities who command justice, because authority is given by God; and the person who strives to oppose judicial order appears to wish to resist God. He says that a person reasonably fears the authority by which he is proved to be involved in some crime, because of his conscience. For this reason we also pay taxes, because we recognize that we are subject to rulers; for they are God’s ministers when they punish crimes that have been committed.

30.---XIII, 7. “Render to all what is owed,” and what follows. He says that every debt must be repaid through a very full enumeration of obligations, but in such a way that affection for our fellow human beings should always hold us as debtors. For he fulfills all God’s [Col. 1329D] commandments who abides in love of his neighbor, because the fullness of the law is the love shown by guarding one’s brother. He also reminds us that we must rise from the night of this present age, because the Lord’s coming is near; we ought to await it vigilantly through good works. The person who is known to await him is the one shown to overcome the desires of the flesh.

31.---XIV, 1. “Receive the one who is weak in faith,” and so forth. He says that the person who is weak with respect to the sacred Scriptures should be received gently, and that one should not quarrel with him through harsh opposition. By means of a comparison he teaches that some are to be refreshed with vegetables alone, while others are to be satisfied with solid foods. Therefore no one should despise another; rather, the one who truly judges should alone distinguish among all these matters. For the Lord is able to strengthen more firmly in abstinence the person whom we see succumbing through the weakness of the flesh. When he was discussing fasts, he says: “One person judges one day superior to another” (v. 5), so that some of the faithful choose to abstain on the fourth and sixth days [Note: [Col. 1329D] The commentator takes the words “one day superior to another” as an explanation of fasting on the fourth and sixth weekdays. This was thought to have flowed from apostolic ordinance or tradition. See St. Epiphanius, *Haer.* 75.]; but another observes every day, because many are found who purify themselves daily through the offering of abstinence. Yet both do not cease to give thanks to their Lord.

32.---XIV, 7. “For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself,” and so forth. Removing unlawful presumptions from human beings, he says that whether we die or live, we must refer everything to the Lord, who will judge the world. For this reason [read: *ideo*] he redeemed the human race with precious blood, so that he himself might rule over all. The example of Isaiah is also appropriately supplied, since all things serve at his command.

33.---XIV, 12. “Therefore each of us will give an account of himself to God,” and so forth. He rebukes those who, boasting of their abstinence, become a stumbling block to their brothers. He says that nothing is in any way unclean before the Lord, as he himself testifies: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person,” unless perhaps this guilt belongs to those who declare that the foods [Note: [Col. 1330D] He is hinting at the Manichaeans.] which God created for eating are unclean. The Apostle says the same elsewhere: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Tit. 1:15). For the kingdom of God is known to consist not in our food, but in peace and harmony. Although abstinence is good, nevertheless, if it destroys love of one’s brother, it is clearly a sin. He supplies the example of the Lord’s passion, just as Psalm 68 says that he endured reproaches in order that, as a merciful and devout savior, he might fulfill love toward his brothers.

34.---XV, 4. “Whatever was written was written for our correction” [Vulgate: “for our instruction”]. Whatever has been set down in the sacred books, he says, was written for our correction and for the hope of the age to come. Therefore they ought to bear one another’s burdens, just as Christ is known to have taken ours upon himself. He adds the examples of the prophet Isaiah and of Psalm 17, saying that all peoples ought to praise God the Father and the Lord Christ in common fellowship [Col. 1330D]. He also blesses the Romans and celebrates their faith with holy praise. He says that he must admonish them so that their offering may be acceptable to God through the Holy Spirit, who is shown to have been granted to them. Thus the saving unity of the whole Trinity, once recalled, is made known to us.

35.---XV, 17. “Therefore I have my glory in Christ Jesus before God,” and what follows. He says that he has glory in God because, when the Lord came, his preaching, newly established, had filled the Gospel of Christ from Jerusalem and all around as far as Illyricum (v. 19). Then he blesses the Romans, promising that, after he has arranged certain matters in Jerusalem, he will come to them. He asks them not to cease praying for him, so that, once rescued from unbelieving Jews, he may be able to come to them to bring salvation when he has set out for Spain.

36.---XVI, 1. “I commend to you our sister Phoebe” [Col. 1332A], and so forth. To show here also that a good purpose is glorious, he commends and greets highly approved women and various brothers, whose holy works he celebrates with spiritual praise. He warns them to avoid false preachers, lest they overthrow hearts that have been rightly established. He concludes his epistle on the incarnation of the Lord with the same power of preaching with which he began it.

# FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1331]

[Col. 1331A] 1.---I, 1. “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God,” and so forth. Together with his brother Sosthenes he greets the Church of God established at Corinth [Col. 1331B], and all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. In his customary manner he preaches Christ at the very threshold, by whose will he was called as an apostle. He asks that grace and peace be granted to them by divine generosity: he wishes them grace so that they may receive the future words of the Holy Spirit, and peace so that they may rejoice through the power of unity.

2.---I, 4. “I give thanks to my God always for you,” and what follows. First of all he praises their faith and prays that they may persevere blameless until the Lord’s coming. He also beseeches them to preserve the firmness of the teaching they have received and not to think themselves subject to preachers, but to the one Lord Christ, since they recognize that they were baptized not in the grace of Paul, nor of Apollos, nor of Cephas, but of Christ.

3.---I, 14. “I give thanks to God that I baptized none of you” [Col. 1331C], and so forth. The Apostle says that he baptized no others except Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas, because he declares that he was not sent to baptize but to evangelize. This is said by the greater number of interpreters; for the sacrament of baptism was commonly entrusted to all the apostles. Hence it may be understood that they accomplished certain things for the salvation of those who desired it, while they were shown to be occupied with preaching.

He evangelized through heavenly wisdom, not that of the world. For it pleased God, through the foolishness of preaching [as it nevertheless appeared to unbelievers], to save those who believe. Since there are few who are powerful and noble according to the flesh, God chose the lowly, so that no flesh might glory in anything except in the Lord Jesus Christ. As it is written in the prophet Jeremiah: “Let the one who glories glory in the Lord” [Col. 1331D] (Jer. 9:24).

4.---II, 1. “And I, brothers, when I came to you,” and what follows. He says that he came to them not with loftiness of speech but with the power of the message, so that he might show his teaching to be not of this age but heavenly. Thus they too, abandoning worldly things, might ascend to the height of divine contemplation. He also shows how greatly heavenly wisdom is distinguished from human wisdom. For if the Jews had understood the prophetic words, they would never have wished to crucify the Lord of glory. The divine mysteries are profound: just as the spirit of a human being knows the weaknesses that are within that person, so only the Spirit himself knows the depths that are in God. Therefore, in order to speak about God, he asserts that he was endowed not by the spirit of the world [Col. 1332A], but by Divinity [Col. 1332B]. He shows that the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself can be judged by no one. He confirmed this by the example of the prophet Isaiah (v. 15).

5.---III, 1. “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as fleshly people.” In these initial matters he says that he did not disclose to the Corinthians the mysteries of Divinity in their fullness, but rather supplied them, as to little children, with cups of milk. Since they do what belongs to the world, they prove that they have not yet been able to grasp perfect teaching. For while they were thinking carnally, they said, “I am of Paul, I of Apollos” [v. 4; Vulgate: “I of Apollo”], whereas the perfect believer in Christ confesses that he is the servant not of a human being but of Christ.

No one can owe his preacher what he owes God. But the works of human beings, although they are built upon the foundation of Christ, he says must be purified through the tribulations and various necessities of this age [Col. 1332C], just as Father Augustine explained more fully in the book *Enchiridion*.

6.---III, 16. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” and so forth. He confirms that the baptized are God’s temple, because the Holy Spirit dwells in them; they ought to have nothing in common with vices. He especially warns that, if anyone considers himself wise according to the world, he should have recourse instead to divine knowledge, which truly makes people prudent and blessed.

He says that all things belong to the faithful, as he subsequently enumerates; the faithful belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God—this last statement being made with reference to his humanity. He also adds [Col. 1332D] that he does not fear being judged by human beings. But lest this be thought arrogance, he says that he is not conscious of his own goodness, since everything is placed in God’s judgment, where everyone’s deeds are recognized with manifest clarity.

He testifies that the things he said above have been transformed both in himself and in Apollos, his disciple, so that no human presumption might rely on its own powers [Note: [Col. 1331] It seems that *ideo* should be read: perhaps also “the disciple,” to suit the meaning and syntax, with the name *Apollo* treated as indeclinable, as in the Vulgate.]. He wishes them to reign in faith, so that he may rejoice together with them in united love.

7.---IV, 9. “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last,” and so forth. For the sake of the Gospel [Col. 1333A] of Christ, the Apostle says that he is subjected to various insults and necessities, while his spiritual children in Christ are noble and happy. He asks them to persevere in every way in his ways [Note: [Col. 1333D] *Omnino*, or *omnimodo*, “entirely” or “in every way.” This is found not only in Cassiodorius but also in authors of the better age, such as Lucretius more than once.], since they wished him to be the father of their heavenly preaching.

He rebukes those who, puffed up with worldly glory, boasted of themselves, whereas the kingdom of God rests not in empty speech but in power. He also threatens them, lest they compel him to come to them with correction rather than with grace [supply: *magis*, “rather”].

8.---V, 1. “It is generally reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even named among the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 1333D] Vulgate: “It is generally heard that there is fornication,” and so forth, “and such fornication,” and so forth.]. He rebukes the Corinthians for having among them someone joined in marriage to his stepmother, since a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. But he judges that the person who committed such an act should be handed over temporarily to Satan for the destruction [Col. 1333B] of the flesh, so that his spirit may escape the punishments of eternal condemnation at the Lord’s judgment.

He also forbids them to eat even with those who have resolved to conduct themselves impiously. He says that such people must be removed from their midst, lest the rest be defiled by seeing such things. For brothers ought to live according to established rules; but concerning those who are outside, divine judgment has decided.

9.---VI, 1. “Does any one of you dare, when he has a lawsuit against another?” [Vulgate: “when he has a matter against another”], and so forth. He says that the judgment of unrighteous people must be avoided and that the judgment of the saints should rather be sought, since they will also judge the world in the future judgment. He then finds fault with them because they do not endure injury from their brothers but instead attack them with wicked intent.

He also lists the vices whose adherents do not enter the Lord’s kingdom—namely, those who persist in such crimes until the end of life [Col. 1333C]. He declares fornication to be utterly detestable, since it defiles our bodies, which are members of the Lord. For the one who has been bought at a great price ought no longer to serve the devil but Christ.

10.---VII, 1. “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” He says that the highest good is never to have intercourse with a woman. He nevertheless urges married people to abstain for a time so that they may devote themselves to prayer, and afterward to return by mutual consent to marital relations, lest they be overcome by the devil’s temptation. He teaches that this should be done according to concession, not according to command.

For he wishes everyone to be abstinent, as he himself is. But if they cannot abstain, then they should join themselves to their wives [Col. 1333D]. He does not say that those who have entered into one bond of marriage should separate.

11.---VII, 12. “If any brother has an unbelieving wife” [Col. 1334A], and what follows. If a believer has a heretical or pagan wife, he warns that she should not immediately be abandoned but corrected through careful attention. In the same way he says that a woman should be brought to devotion. But if one of them wishes to remain in perverse sects, then it is lawful for the believer to despise that person, because there can be no concord with the obstinate and lost.

He also adds that there is no salvation in uncircumcision or circumcision, but in the commandments of God, which pertain to the New Testament. Moreover, he warns that whether a slave or a free person has been called to the faith, each should persevere in Catholic doctrine without any distinction of status, since at Christ’s judgment the faithful slave is rightly preferred to the unbelieving master.

12.---VII, 25. “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord” [Col. 1334B], and so forth. He praises virginity but also permits marriage. He shows that unmarried persons can think about spiritual matters more easily than married people. Nevertheless, he commands everyone not to love the things of the world, because the form of this age will pass away when its appointed end arrives.

Similarly, he warns parents, saying that the first course is for one who preserves his virgin daughter; the second is to give her to a husband when she has reached the proper maturity. But a woman who has been abandoned by her husband should marry if she cannot abstain; for it is better to be joined in marriage than to be abandoned to the freedom of lust. Nevertheless, he confirms that it is much better for them to remain widows. He asserts that he preaches such instructions by divine counsel.

[Col. 1334C] 13.---VIII, 1. “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols” [Vulgate: “concerning things offered in sacrifice”], and so forth. He says that idols are indeed nothing, but he forbids the eating of meat that appears to have been offered to them, lest the weakness of the brothers fail to abhor what pagans are known to do. Thus the error of believers returns to the point at which guilt begins. Therefore he says that he will never eat anything that can scandalize his most beloved brother, for whose sake the Lord of heaven is known to have been slain in assumed flesh.

14.---IX, 1. “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?” He says that he is an apostle of those whom he had formed through sacred instruction. He had the right to receive food and to marry [Note: [Col. 1333D] Cassiodorius regards it as established that St. Paul did not have a wife, although some have called this into question, especially on the basis of St. Ignatius’ Letter to the Philadelphians. Many things show how early the Christian Church began to move toward celibacy. The nineteenth of the ancient canons called apostolic says: “Of those who, while celibate, have been promoted to the clergy, only readers and singers, if they wish, may take wives”: *ἀναγνώστας καὶ ψάλτας μόνους* (“readers and singers only”). Hilary, a deacon at Rome under Damasus (*On 1 Timothy*, among the works of Ambrose), taught that all our priests and sacred ministers ought to abstain from intercourse with women, because they must be present in the church every day. This was not the case with the Levites of the ancient law, for their service at sacrifices was less frequent, so that several days of purification could precede it. See canon 10 of the Council of Ancyra, and so forth. Our own commentator had said shortly before: “He shows that unmarried persons can think about spiritual matters more easily than married people.”], just as it was also free to the other apostles who remained with their wives.

But he says that he willingly endures everything so that he may appear to bring no offense to the Gospel of Christ. For this reason he says that he does not wish to receive anything from them, although it is known to have been permitted by the Lord [Col. 1334D–1335A], lest the glory of such great labors be emptied by such compensation.

15.---IX, 16. “For if I preach the Gospel” [Vulgate: “if I evangelize”], “there is no glory for me,” and so forth. He says that he evangelizes under a kind of necessity, so that he may be proved to avoid boasting. For he says that he pays a debt if he appears willing to carry out what has been entrusted to him. He declares that he made himself humble to all so that he might win them.

If those who run in the stadium do not cease to abstain in order to receive human prizes, with how much greater zeal should the crown of future blessedness be sought? But he says that he does not run in vain or beat the air with his fists, lest, as would be more miserable than every misfortune, he should preach to others and himself be found rejected.

16.---X, 1. “Now I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud” [Col. 1335B]. He warns the Corinthians to recognize that what happened to the Jews in earlier times pertained to the Lord Christ. He then urges them to fear the severity of their punishments, so that the new people may be kept from similar faults. He also warns them not to tempt the Lord but to hope, so that by his gracious gift they may escape carnal temptations. By his mercy it is brought about that people escape the crimes of this age.

17.---X, 14. “Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols,” and so forth. Just as those who come together in one communion are participants in the Lord’s table, so those who are joined in one superstition are participants in the table of demons. Therefore things divided by a distinct quality cannot be compatible with one another.

[Col. 1335C] Consequently, if someone says that food is sacrificial, it ought not to be touched for the sake of conscience; but if this is not known, it should be eaten in the name of the Lord. For it is written in Psalm 23: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” [Col. 1336A]. Whether one eats, drinks, or does anything else honestly, everything must clearly be done for the glory of the Lord. He also warns them to conduct themselves without giving offense and to please the Church, just as he himself is known to have done.

18.---XI, 1. “Be imitators of me, brothers” [in the Vulgate *brothers* is lacking], “just as I am of Christ,” and what follows. The Apostle warns the Corinthians that, just as he imitates Christ, so the faithful ought to imitate him. This can happen if they seek what can be useful to many, not what can be useful to themselves. He teaches that Christ is the head of the man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ. This statement is rightly understood with reference to Christ’s humanity, so that, once this distinction has been recognized, everything may be considered in its proper order.

He also urges men not to pray with their heads covered [Col. 1336B], because freedom consists in being subject to God [Note: [Col. 1335C] Since the Apostle commanded the Corinthians, once received among Christians, not to pray with covered heads as the Jews did, the interpreter adds that they need fear no mark of servitude on account of uncovered heads, because freedom consists in being subject to God. A cap is otherwise a symbol of freedom on the coin of Brutus.]. But he commands women to supplicate the Lord with covered heads, so that they might declare themselves subject to their husbands.

19.---XI, 16. “But if anyone seems to be contentious, we do not have such a custom” [read: “such contentions”]. He declares that God’s people do not love contention, saying that the ecclesiastical assembly has a desire for peace, not a pursuit of quarrels. Nevertheless, he says that heresies must exist, so that those who are approved may be clearly recognized among them by their manifest purity.

He also rebukes those who, unwilling to wait for the assembly, wish to have the celebration of the Masses individually [Note: [Col. 1335C] Others understand the passage which Cassiodorius interprets as referring to the celebration of Masses as referring to those common meals of the ancient Christians (*ἀγάπαι*), and they think that what is being criticized in them is both contempt for the poor and intemperance. But since our author thinks that those are being rebuked who, unwilling to wait for the assembly, wish to have the celebration of Masses individually, he seems to indicate Masses celebrated within private homes, and one may therefore conjecture that these were already customary in his age [Col. 1335D]. That they were certainly established in the time of St. Gregory is shown by his Letters 42 and 43, in which, to settle a dispute involving the patrician Venantius, he orders the bishop of Syracuse to permit the mysteries of the Mass to be performed in Venantius’ house. Yet they were far from being known in the times of the apostles, when a single Mass was celebrated for the small number of the faithful. Indeed, Apostolic Canon 24 decrees that a presbyter is to be deposed if, having disregarded his bishop, he holds a separate assembly and sets up another altar. Nevertheless, when the interpreter says “unwilling to wait for the assembly,” this can also be understood of those who celebrated Masses in the customary public place but before the faithful had assembled. For in his usage, “to wait” means “to expect”; shortly below he says that one should wait for one another in the spirit of charity, which the Apostle had said in verse 33: “Wait for one another.” In number 10 on the Epistle of James, he says that the judge is not to be awaited, meaning that he is not to be expected.].

He supplies the example of the Lord’s Supper, at which he gave the rule of faith not individually but to all the apostles gathered together.

[Col. 1336C] 20.---XI, 27. “Therefore whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup, the body [Note: [Col. 1336C] This is a new testimony to the Catholic and unwavering doctrine concerning the Eucharistic mystery. The ancient text used by Cassiodorius appears to have presented here “the bread and the cup, the body and blood of Christ”; by this reading, the doctrine clearly handed down in the preceding verses is repeated. I see that my dissertation on Eucharistic consecration, sent to the distinguished P. Benedict Bacchinius and recently printed again at Venice, is once more attacked in a new book published at Tübingen by a most learned man and an eminent professor among the Lutherans, Christoph Pfaff. One may marvel at the wagonloads of learning, as is his custom, heaped together in that volume; but as to the question itself, let the learned men in his own camp judge, after comparison has been made, whether anything I adduced has been shaken even slightly [Col. 1336D]. At some point, when leisure permits, I shall respond to expose and refute certain deceptions. For the present I merely draw attention to this. What was first and chiefly disputed between us was whether the fragments he discovered and published under the name of St. Irenaeus of Lyons truly belong to Irenaeus, as he vigorously argues, or not. The learned men themselves, although alien to our sacred teachings, have not at all rejected or condemned my rejection of them; for this is what I read about these fragments in *Critical History of the Republic of Letters*, vol. 9: “I am not at all surprised that Scipio Maffeius [a distinguished but unrelated work is mistakenly attributed to me here] fought against and rejected them. Frankly, I find his reasons concerning their uncertainty and their conjectural character very plausible and very well founded.”], and the blood of Christ” [Note: [Col. 1336D] Vulgate: “whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.”].

He says that a person who is conscious of right faith and good works ought to partake, lest he appear to seek not so much the forgiveness [Col. 1337A] of sins as his own condemnation. For if we judge ourselves, we are acquitted in the judgment of Divinity.

Therefore, he says that at the celebration of the Mass they should wait for one another in the spirit of charity. If they appeared to approach mute images with reverence, how much more ought they to come to the true God with the purest mind, without blasphemies or contentions? For the Lord Christ must not be approached through blasphemies but honored in the Holy Spirit with the greatest devotion.

21.---XII, 4. “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit,” and what follows. Although there are many varieties of gifts, he confirms that there is one Lord who accomplishes all these things in everyone. He proves this also by the example of the members and the body [Col. 1337B], saying that one member appears to perform one function, the hand performs another, and the foot another, but that they are joined to one another by mutual connection. So in the Church of God, although there are many offices of holiness, all are nevertheless known to be necessary to one another through the union of charity.

22.---XIII, 1. “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels,” and so forth. In this chapter he strongly commends charity, declaring that no virtue is beneficial without it. He also defines what charity rejects and what it pursues. For although other gifts—that is, faith and hope—will come to rest in the age to come, charity alone remains forever. He says that it must be sought above all.

23.---XIV, 2. “For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God,” and so forth. He says that there is a great difference between knowledge of languages [Col. 1337C] and prophecy. Knowledge of languages is not known to everyone, whereas prophecy instructs the churches [Note: [Col. 1337D] While rereading this, briefly drawn away from the ancient stones with which I am now occupied, an excellent and as yet unpublished inscription came to mind. When I publish the Verona Museum, these passages of Cassiodorius will provide some assistance in interpreting it. Hieronymus Baruffaldi, with the generosity characteristic of that distinguished man, gave me an excellent stone as a gift. The inscription is as follows:

[Col. 1338D]

> DACIANA. DIACONISSAQVE. V. AN. XXXXV. M. III. ET. FVIT. F. PALMATI. COS. ET. SOROR. VICTORINI. PRESBRI ET. MVLTA. PROPIIETAVIT CVM. FLACCA. ALVMNA . . . . V. A. XV. DEP. IN. PACE. III. ID. A.

> “Daciana, deaconess, lived 45 years and 3 months. She was the daughter of Palmatus, consul, and the sister of Victorinus, presbyter; and she prophesied much with Flacca, her foster-daughter [lacuna], who lived 15 years and was buried in peace on the third day before the Ides of [the month is uncertain].”]

He says that those who understand are built up by heavenly gifts. He gives examples from musical instruments, because unless what is played on flutes or a trumpet is understood, the hearing cannot be beneficial. By many proofs he teaches that prophecy is the greater gift, and he urges them to devote themselves to it more than to the manifold variety of different languages.

24.---XIV, 13. “Therefore the one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret,” and what follows. He continues to dwell on the same distinction, teaching through many proofs that interpretation of the Lord’s message is more useful than speaking in many languages. He asserts that speech brought forth without understanding is not beneficial prayer. In the same way, if heavenly teaching is not understood, many consider it madness. But if an uneducated person hears someone prophesying and understands what he says, then he falls on his face and publicly declares that the Lord has truly spoken through that person.

25.---XIV, 26. “What then, brothers? When you come together, each of you,” [Col. 1338A] and so forth. He says that great care must be taken by those who teach in the church, so that they may instruct their hearers in the divine commands. If, however, a word of God is revealed to one of those sitting there [Note: [Col. 1338D] The manuscript had: “as to one of those who follow.”], he says that person must not be neglected, since he asserts that the interpretations of the prophets are themselves prophecies. For he says that the understanding of the prophets is subject to the prophets.

He also forbids women to speak in church because of the weakness of their sex. But what they do not know he commands them to learn at home from their husbands, so that, shaped by such a rule, they may obtain both the gifts of knowledge and of modesty.

26.---XV, 1. “Now I make known to you, brothers,” and so forth. He briefly makes known the Gospel which he preached to all. For he says that he delivered to everyone that Christ died for our sins [Col. 1338B] and that he rose from the dead on the third day. Although he appeared after his resurrection to many brothers, he reports that he was also seen by himself, as by one who was least and abortive. He commends the Lord’s grace toward himself with the greatest humility.

Since Christ rose, the resurrection of the dead must not be denied. For all holy teaching is destroyed if this belief is removed from human hearts. He embraces the resurrection in a most beautiful definition, saying that the Lord is the firstfruits of those who sleep.

27.---XV, 21. “For since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also came through a human being.” Just as he says that human beings died through Adam, so through Jesus Christ the resurrection of all the dead will come. Death, however, will be destroyed at the end of the age [Col. 1338C], when the Lord Christ comes. He will always be subject to the Father in the nature of the humanity he assumed, after all things have been subjected to him, so that “God may be all in all” (v. 28).

Those who do not believe these things, as the Apostle John says, will be reckoned under the name of Antichrist. He also raises the words of those who doubt, asking in what body the one who has died will rise. He refutes them by comparing it with the sowing of wheat, saying: If a grain of wheat, when it falls, is reborn renewed, how much more must bodies that have died be restored at the Lord’s command!

28.—XV, 39. “Not every flesh is the same flesh,” and so forth. First he establishes the diversity of all flesh; then, by separating heavenly and earthly bodies, he distinguishes them; finally, in a marvelous account, he foretells how greatly human nature, improved through Christ the Lord, will advance in that resurrection. He describes the mystery of the resurrection itself with an unshakable proclamation. He also urges them, while considering these other matters, to persevere in the faith they have embraced and in good works. He commands that collections for the needs of the saints be made according to custom before it should happen that he came to them; commending some brothers, greeting others, and, so as most completely to strengthen the hearts of believers, declaring anathema at Christ’s future coming upon the one [suppl. *to him*] who does not love the Lord Christ; greeting them and concluding the present Epistle with his customary blessing.

## THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 1339]

[Col. 1339A] 1.—I, 1. “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, through the will of God,” and so forth. He writes with Timothy the brother to the Church of God established at Corinth, including also those who throughout all Achaia persisted in their holy purpose; asking that grace and peace be granted them by God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Although these persons are named, the Holy Spirit is also abundantly mentioned: for one person of the Trinity, when named, fully embraces the whole Trinity.

2.—I, 3. “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and the rest. He says that he was comforted by the Lord in all his tribulation, so that he too might similarly comfort those placed in calamities. For this reason he writes to the Corinthians, so that, just as they were companions in suffering, they might likewise deserve to share in Christ’s consolations. He also reports what evils he endured in Asia, giving thanks to God that through their prayers he was delivered from so great a disaster, so that the faithful too ought to rejoice with one another over the prosperity bestowed.

3.—I, 12. “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience,” and so forth. He says that his glory is the testimony of his conscience, since he testifies that he conducted himself in this world not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of the Lord. He says that the Corinthians are his glory, just as he was also proved to be their apostle. He promises that he had often wished to come to them, but that this was not the fickleness by which his intention had in no way been fulfilled: for all his preaching among them, following the example of the Lord Christ, was firm and not uncertain. Yet, lest he attribute anything to his own powers, he says that it was the work of God’s Son, Jesus Christ, that they were confirmed in everything. For he is the one who both anointed preachers and sealed the hearts of believers.

4.—I, 23. “But I call God as witness upon my life,” and what follows. The Apostle says that he spared them by not coming to Corinth, lest he be burdensome to those who were to be censured for some fault. Yet their grief is the cause of eternal salvation, since disciples become especially pleasing to the Lord when they advance through the correction of their teachers. Teaching patience as well, he asks that the one who is known to have saddened him be spared. He promises that he has therefore forgiven him, lest, in despair, he perish, but rather that, turning back, he may escape the devil’s snare. For he says that it is evident to him by how many deceptions devilish thoughts destroy those who have been temporarily misled.

5.—II, 12. “When I had come to Troas for the Gospel of Christ,” and so forth. He says that grace was given him by the Lord at Troas and in Macedonia, so that a crowd of believers might follow the Gospel of Christ. To some he was the fragrance of death unto death, to others the fragrance of life unto life, drawing an analogy from animals that reach things they desire through the keenness of their sense of smell. He says that those are more truly his letter who held his written preaching in their hearts (III, 2). Nevertheless, he declares that he is not sufficient for such things, but trusts in the Lord’s mercy, who made him competent by revealing the truth of the New and Old Testament; understanding everything not according to the letter but spiritually, because “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.”

6.—III, 7. “But if the ministry of death, formed by letters [Vulgate: ‘deformed by letters’], was in glory on stones.” He compares the written tablets given through Moses with the hearts of those who rightly believe. He says that the former, which were honored until the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ, were emptied when fullness arrived. But the latter, written upon the hearts of the faithful by the power of the Holy Spirit, will be much more firmly established in eternal praise. He confirms this by the argument that follows; and therefore he says that one must persevere in this gift, so that through the truth of preaching we may be acceptable to God and human beings.

7.—IV, 3. “But even if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing.” He says that the hearts of the foolish Jews are veiled, for whom the Gospel’s message does not shine forth. For what can those be said to see for whom Christ the Lord, the image of the Father, does not shine? Believers, although they suffer exceedingly frequent hardships, are nevertheless known to overcome everything with God’s provision. And just as they undergo afflictions for the Lord’s sake, so they will be placed with him in eternal glory. Therefore one ought eagerly to desire his death, so that we may also deserve to receive the rewards of life. For the Apostle says that he underwent every danger so that he might deserve to rise again with them in that recompense of the Lord.

[Col. 1340D] 8.—IV, 16. “Although the one who is outward, our human being, is corrupted, the inner one is renewed day by day” [Note: [Col. 1339] Vulgate: “But although the one who is outward, and so forth, is corrupted, nevertheless the one who is inward,” and so forth]. He says that the outward human being within us is corruptible, but confirms that the inner one can be renewed day by day when a person devotedly approaches the teachings of the Christian faith. Nevertheless, although this outward human being is exposed to harsh necessities in this age, in that resurrection he rejoices, advanced by great hope. And therefore, as long as we are pilgrims in this age, let us please the Lord, so that we may deserve to be acquitted at his judgment, where a person will receive a just recompense for his deeds, whether good or evil.

[Col. 1341A] 9.—V, 11. “Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings; but we are manifest to God.” The Apostle says that he is manifest to the hearts of the Corinthians, not for empty glory but to show himself truthful in speech. He also preaches that the Lord Christ died and rose again, in order to reconcile the lost world to God. For he assumed the flesh of sin on our behalf, so that we might be freed and restored through the gifts of grace. Therefore the Lord must be sought confidently, since it is written in the prophet: “At an opportune time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” [Note: [Col. 1341D] Vulgate: “At an acceptable time,” and Isaiah XLIX, 8: “At a favorable time,” and so forth, “I assisted you”]. For he makes such a promise that we cannot be intercepted.

10.—VI, 2. “Behold, now is the acceptable [Vulgate: ‘favorable’] time; behold, now is the day of salvation,” and what follows. What the Lord’s coming means is defined with great brevity. For he says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” Therefore he says that no occasion of offense should be given to anyone, but that everything, whatever it may be, should be endured patiently, so that the holy people may be acquired for the Lord. Accordingly, to encourage the others, he suitably enumerates the calamities of his sufferings, urging them not to have a share with unbelievers. He makes a sharp distinction between unlike things, since darkness and light cannot in any way agree. He also confirmed this by the example of Numbers and Isaiah.

11.—VII, 1. “Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh.” After receiving the promises, he persuades the most faithful to cleanse themselves from carnal vices and to persevere in sanctification. He rejoices greatly because he sensed that they had been led to repentance and had become sharers both in his sufferings and in his faith. Then, with a necessary distinction, he explains the difference between grief according to God and the grief of the world: the former produces repentance, while the latter sends one to death. He makes clear in the following enumeration how greatly those who were grieved for the Lord’s sake had advanced.

12.—VII, 12. “Therefore, although I wrote” [Vulgate: “I wrote to you”], “not because of the one who did the injury,” and the rest. He says that he wrote not to accuse anyone but to make his concern known to them. He indicates that it was pleasing to him that they had obeyed the brother Titus and received him with a kindly disposition. He also provokes the Corinthians to emulation and praises the Macedonians, who, though poor in resources, are rich in the abundance of faith. And lest an alien praise should again bite them, although they were endowed with many virtues, he says that they were nevertheless complete in their devotion to charity. Therefore he urges them not to appear unequal to others in making the contribution.

13.—VIII, 9. “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and what follows. He continues to persuade them in this way to undertake the contribution, saying: since the Lord, though rich in himself, became poor for us, with how much greater desire ought we to give, when we know that he bestowed divinity upon the human race? Therefore let each person offer according to his ability, without binding himself by any necessity. For that alms is pleasing to God which is shown to have been offered without distress of spirit. He also praises Titus because he did not delay in coming with another brother to build them up; and, in order that he might be well received, he was commended by the Apostle himself. He says that he does not wish to receive the contributions for this reason: lest some scandal concerning the distribution should arise before human beings and God.

14.—VIII, 22. “And with him we sent our brother, whom we have often tested” [Note: [Col. 1341D] Vulgate: “And with them also our brother,” and so forth. Greek: αὐτοῖς, “to them.” Jerome: “also with him”]. Again he reminds them that, in the presence of those who have been sent, the appointed contribution should be prepared, lest their celebrated generosity perhaps prove otherwise. He says that their devotion had stirred very many to imitate what is good, establishing a remarkable rule for almsgiving: each person will reap only as much from it as he appears to have sown in generosity. David’s example is offered for this matter.

15.—IX, 10. “He who supplies seed to the sower, and supplied bread for food” [Note: [Col. 1341D] Manuscript reading: “for food, he will supply.” Vulgate: “will provide for eating”]. He continues to discuss the virtue of almsgiving, saying that God repays much more than those who give money to the needy can give. For those who receive also contribute through their prayers more than they were able to receive. He says that he walks in the flesh, but does not claim to serve the flesh, since he professes that he wishes to destroy the superstitions of the world in such a way that everything must serve the true Lord. He warns that worldly flatteries and blandishments must be avoided in every way.

16.—X, 7. [Note: [Col. 1341D] The first words of verse 7 seem to have been absent from Cassiodorus’s text.] “Look at this: if anyone trusts in himself, let him consider this again within himself” [Note: [Col. 1342D] Vulgate: “You look at what is according to appearance. If anyone trusts in himself that he belongs to Christ,” and so forth]. He forbids anyone to think himself solitary before God; rather, he should recognize himself as a member of the Church. Yet if he himself should wish to boast a little of the authority granted for the building up of all, this does not appear absurd: the honor of a teacher is greater than the devotion of a disciple can be. He also replies concerning those who dispute about him that his letters should be judged according to what his presence can accomplish in completing the work. But he confirms that only those are to be praised who are commended not by themselves but by the Lord.

17.—XI, 1. “Would that you could bear with a little of my foolishness” [Note: [Col. 1342D] From the Greek μικρόν τι, in Italian: “suffer a little of mine,” and so forth. The literal translation may perhaps seem to introduce something foreign. Valtonius’s Polyglot has τῇ.] [Note: [Col. 1342D] Vulgate: “A little of my foolishness,” and so forth]. He begs them to endure his foolishness because, out of zeal for Christ, he desired that the peoples be acquired. For, in the figure of the Church, he says that the people were betrothed to the Lord Christ; but he fears that, with the devil leading them astray, they may be corrupted from the rule of chastity by false preaching. He also asserts that he had been no burden to them in expense, showing in passing what a preacher ought to be. He enumerates his sufferings and deliverances, not to assume vices through boasting, but so that, recognizing such things, they might submit more willingly to Christ the Lord.

18.—XII, 1. [Note: [Col. 1343] I suspect that Cassiodorus did not read the words “If it is necessary to boast, it is not expedient.” Examine the Greek text and consult the context.] “I shall come to visions and revelations of the Lord,” and what follows. He turns to marvelous visions and outstanding revelations, in which he says that he was caught up to the third heaven and learned secret words in paradise that it is not permitted for a human being to speak. Nevertheless, he says that he wishes to boast not in these visions but rather in his weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may always be increased in him. Enumerating various disasters as well, he asserts that in them he labored no less than the other apostles in the holy faith, although it is known that he accepted no financial support from them at all; so that, once this matter was recognized, it might increase their zeal for charity toward him.

19.—XII, 14. “Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not be burdensome to you.” He says that he is ready to come to them, yet he does not presume upon any of their resources. He teaches that children should not store up for parents, but parents rather for their children. He also warns them to live corrected in the Lord, lest, when he comes, he mourn those whom he discovers to have served the devil. He threatens the Corinthians with his rebukes, because, although Christ died in the flesh, he nevertheless lives in the everlasting glory of his divinity, just as all live in him who have chosen to believe in him with a pure mind. Then he says that each person ought to test and judge himself in the faith, to determine whether he can be joined to Christ the Lord. For the one who is not found rejected is recognized as belonging to him.

20.—XIII, 7. “But I pray the Lord” [Vulgate: “But we pray God”], “that you do nothing evil,” and what follows. He says that he prays so that the faithful people may appear glorious before the Lord’s presence—not so that he himself might be praised for their correction, but rather so that they might be praised for their uprightness. He says that he gladly accepts being found weak and humble on account of his sufferings, while they are seen to be noble and powerful in Christ the Lord. Then he says that he deliberately writes such things, lest, when present, he seem to rebuke God’s people harshly. He greets the holy people and adds the greetings of the Churches out of zeal for charity, granting the people his blessing with customary devotion.

## THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 1343]

[Col. 1343C] 1.—I, 1. “Paul, an apostle not from human beings, nor through human beings [Vulgate: ‘nor through a human being’], but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” When he says that he is an apostle made not by human beings but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, he overthrows those who presumptuously called themselves apostles on human grounds. For at that time the Churches were greatly disturbed by false preachers. He greets them together with all the brothers who were with him, and in the greeting itself he blesses them, so that they may be found fit to receive the Lord’s words. And note that the whole Epistle is directed against false preachers who maintained that even those already baptized ought to be circumcised.

2.—I, 6. “I marvel that you are transferring yourselves so quickly from him who called you,” and the rest. He rebukes those who, seduced by false preachers, were departing from the rule of faith they had received. He decrees that if anyone wishes to preach another gospel besides what had evidently been preached by him, let him be accursed, asserting that his revelation was not human but divine. He proves this more fully through the contrary course of his former life, so that the one who had previously been a persecutor of the Church, corrected by the Lord’s will, might appear devoted to his commands. He also says that he came from Jerusalem to see Peter and James; then went to Syria and Cilicia; and returned again to Jerusalem to set out for them the Gospel that he preached among the Gentiles. But those who were striving to confuse the peoples with false preaching, he says, were publicly refuted, so that the truth of the Gospel might appear through evident proofs.

3.—II, 6. “For those who were regarded as something contributed nothing to me” [Note: [Col. 1343D] Vulgate: “Those who were regarded as being something”], and so forth. He says that he did not receive Christ’s Gospel from the brothers, but that it was bestowed upon him by divine inspiration. For this reason he reports that Peter, James, and John gave him their right hands, so that they would preach to the circumcision, while he would preach to the uncircumcision. For he also says that he resisted Peter at Antioch, saying to him: “If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (verse 14). Thus both Hebrews and Gentiles were to be compelled to the grace of faith, not to the strict demands of the Law, which no human being can fulfill. Hence Peter offered an example of great gentleness and patience, so that when such a great apostle was rebuked, he corrected himself [apparently, this should rather be supplied], instead of excusing himself in human fashion through wicked arguments. For he says that he preached grace and commanded grace to be preserved, lest the death of the Lord Christ appear to have been rendered fruitless and void.

4.—III, 1. “O foolish Galatians, who bewitched you?” and what follows. He rebukes the Galatians because, after receiving the doctrine in the grace of Christ and seeing him crucified with their own eyes through apostolic teaching, they had returned again to the works of the Law. He proves this contrary to the Christian faith by examples. The Son of God was crucified in the flesh for this reason: to redeem us from the curse of the Law and to fulfill the promise made to Abraham for those who believe in Christ. For he says that the promise made to Abraham was not made to “seeds” but to his “seed,” clearly showing that the pledge was proclaimed in the Lord the Savior. For if the inheritance came from the Law, which was made four hundred and thirty years later, it certainly would not have come from the promise that preceded it. But since it is established that the promise was made to Abraham long before, it clearly appears that this inheritance did not come from the Law but from grace. For God confined everything under sin through the Law, so that, when Jesus Christ came, the inheritance might be granted through faith.

5.—III, 24. “Therefore the Law was our pedagogue in Christ,” and the rest. He says that, until the Lord’s coming, the fear of the Law was our pedagogue; but after baptism came, he made us his children without distinction of sex or any condition. Through various arguments he proves that they ought not to return to the service of idols, from which they had already been shown to have departed. He also warns them not to listen to false persuaders, since they had shown the preacher the greatest grace and recognized that they had been well instructed. Therefore they act wisely if they strive for better gifts and, even in the Apostle’s absence, advance through divine instruction.

6.—IV, 19. “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you,” and so forth. He continues to rebuke those who wish to be under the Law rather than under grace. He sets before them the fact that Abraham had two sons: one by a slave woman, subject to the flesh, and another by a free woman, known to have been born according to the promise. The former belongs to the Law, the latter to the grace of faith. Why, then, do they wish to choose what is inferior, when they know that they have received what is better? Through examples and arguments he proves the grace of faith to be much better than presumption upon the Law. Therefore they ought to cast away unlawful persuasions, lest the corruption of the whole mass arise from the leaven of iniquity.

7.—V, 10. “I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will think nothing else,” and the rest. He says that he trusts them not to wish to listen any longer to false preachers. He persuades them not to love wicked disputes but to seek God the Lord in one fellowship, since the whole Law is shown to be fulfilled in one saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” He marvelously lays open to them the vices of the flesh and spiritual virtues, warning them that they ought to walk in grace rather than in presumption upon the Law.

8.—VI, 1. “Brothers, even if a person is overtaken in any offense.” He warns that fitting gentleness should be shown to fallen brothers. For we fulfill the Lord’s Law if one person bears another’s burdens. It follows also that the one who is catechized should answer the one who catechizes with moral integrity, so that those whose ears are opened may share the doctrine of faith with their teachers. He adds: “The one who sows in the flesh will reap corruption, but the one who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life” [Note: [Col. 1345] Verse 8. Vulgate: “The one who sows in his flesh will also reap from the flesh,” and so forth; “from the spirit he will reap life”]. Therefore good must be done toward everyone, but kindness must be given especially to members of the household of faith, since the fruit of labor is received in the future judgment. He also explains that false preachers seek to creep in upon them to such an extent that they nullify the cross of the Lord the Savior. For the Apostle glories in that cross, through which he himself has been crucified to the world and the world to him. In Christ, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, but only the perfection of the human being renewed through faith. He professes that he bears the marks of Christ—that is, the standard of the cross—which he endured in various sufferings. He concludes his Epistle with a most holy blessing.

## THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 1345]

[Col. 1345C] 1.—I, 1. “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, through the will of God,” and what follows. He very frequently says that he was called an apostle by the Lord’s will, so that he might overthrow those who sought this honor through human presumption. Therefore he writes to the holy and faithful Ephesians, [Col. 1345D] adding his customary blessing with fatherly charity, so that they may receive grace and peace from the Father and Christ the Lord. Yet here the Holy Trinity is perceived with religious devotion.

2.—I, 3. “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and what follows. First he gives thanks to God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose will he says he was predestined as an apostle. He celebrates the grace of their unity with manifold praise, asserting that the Ephesians too had been filled with the same munificence. Therefore he says that he prays for them to receive excellence of faith and greatness of revelation, so that they may know the secrets of so great a mystery and understand through the truest faith that Jesus Christ sits at the Father’s right hand. The Father appointed him over every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and the other things that are proclaimed about him in a marvelous account.

[Col. 1346D] 3.—II, 1. “And you, when you were dead in offenses,” and so forth. He now teaches again what he first wished them to recognize: they had been dead in their sins under the devil, but now they are shown to have been made alive in Christ. He asserts that this was not granted through human merits but bestowed by divine grace, persuading them most distinctly that this must be believed and held. For those who had previously been far removed among the Gentiles have now been brought near in the blood of the Lord Christ, who gathered the two peoples—the Hebrews and the Gentiles—who had been at odds, into one new human being through his cross, binding them with the bond of peace. Through himself he granted access to the Father to those who believe in one Spirit and one faith.

4.—II, 9. “Therefore you are no longer guests and foreigners, but you are citizens of the saints,” and so forth. He says that they were built up in Christ the Lord, in whom the apostles and prophets themselves were shown to have been constructed. This had previously seemed unknown to the Gentiles, but it is established as revealed to the faithful in the Holy Spirit. He says that this dispensation was now entrusted to him, so that the Gentiles might become co-heirs with the blessed who preceded them in the blood of the Lord the Savior. He says that he was made its minister so that the blessed preaching of the Holy Gospel might run throughout the universal Church. Therefore he asks the Lord that the faith of those who are known to have received such rewards may not fail.

5.—III, 14. “For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and so forth. He says that he asks God the Father, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that Christ may dwell in their hearts, so that they may comprehend the greatness of the Lord and the love of Christ. He also beseeches them to persevere with patience and humility in the rule of faith they have received and to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For the fellowship of right faith is one, and its God is one. He adds that the Son of God gave various gifts to his saints for the building up of the Church, until the future resurrection should come, in which we all rise to the measure of Christ’s stature, though in different sexes [Note: [Col. 1347C] From the Apostle’s words in this Epistle, IV, 13—“that we shall rise into a perfect man”—there were some who maintained that women would rise not in their own sex but in the male sex. Cassiodorus takes the better position and argues against them with an excellent argument. Gelasius I had also cited the same Gospel passage, insisting on this point, *Concilium Labbé*, vol. IV, p. 1257, and had added: “Certainly, if all were to be raised in one bodily form and one sex, there would have been no reason at all for this to be said.”] For when the Lord says in the Gospel, “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew XXII, 30), he clearly shows that males can rise together with females.

6.—IV, 17. “This I say again and testify in the Lord,” and what follows. He urges them not to walk, as they had previously done, in the vanity of the nations. He describes the blindness in which the other nations live, but commands them to put on the new human being in the wisdom to which they were called, who is known to have been created according to God. He presents distinct and clear enumerations of both matters: what must be avoided and what must be pursued. Therefore they ought to imitate the Lord Christ, who offered himself in the fragrance of sweetness for the salvation of all.

7.—V, 3. “But fornication, and every impurity or greed, must not even be named among you” [Vulgate: “in you”]. With perfect instruction he forbids harmful things and persuades them to pursue what is useful. For just as he says that punishment comes upon crimes, so he declares that rewards come upon virtues. He says that what the Lord forbids must be fled, while what he commands must be pursued. And lest anyone attribute any good to his own powers, he warns throughout that we must be subject to God and give thanks to the Lord Christ, who deigns to protect and govern us.

8.—V, 22. “Let women be subject to their husbands as to the Lord,” and what follows. He warns women that they ought to be subject to their husbands, just as he confirms that the Church is subject to Christ. To instill the meaning of perfect charity, he commands the husband to love his wife in the same way that Christ loved the Church, saying that the one who loves his wife cherishes his own flesh. He also instructs children and parents to be joined to one another by mutual duty. He likewise teaches servants and masters how they ought to treat one another. Yet he instructs everyone in general to put on heavenly armor against the devil’s snares. He also says that prayers should be offered for him, so that the freedom of the Holy Spirit may be granted him and he may be found fit to teach. For he says that Tychicus will report to them everything that has happened. He concludes his Epistle with a greeting of charity.

## THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 1347]

[Col. 1347C] 1.—I, 1. “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi.” With Timothy he greets the co-bishops and deacons established at Philippi, wishing them grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He shows that in the Church of God deacons too are to be honored according to their rank.

[Col. 1347D] 2.—I, 3. “I indeed give thanks to our Lord in all remembrance of you always,” and so forth. He promises that he gives thanks to God for them, so that the faithful may remain in mind within the affections of Christ. He indicates that his chains had stirred many to good wishes and others to wicked ambitions. For he says that the pure in heart had embraced the desires of right preaching, while the crooked and ruined had pretended to speak about God so that the Apostle might be burdened more heavily. But in both cases he gives thanks to God, because the name of the Lord was shown to be increasing. He declares that Christ is life for him and death gain.

3.—I, 22. “But if living in the flesh is the fruit of labor for me, and what I should choose I do not know.” He says that he desires to depart from this world so that he may be with Christ, but that, out of zeal for charity, he wishes again to live so that he may strengthen the hearts of the Philippians in Christ the Lord. The essential point is that, steadfast in the Gospel they have received, they should not fear the ambushes of their adversaries, but, preserving the power of charity among themselves, should imitate the Lord Christ, who, although he was almighty God, deigned to become human for our salvation. The Apostle professes that he was equal to the Father not by seizure but by the truth of his nature.
