From this also follows the glory, above all creatures, of the humanity assumed by Christ, whom heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings are known to adore with bent knees.

4.—II, 12. “Therefore, my most beloved” [Vulgate: “my most dear”], “just as you have always obeyed,” and the rest. He warns them that, even in his absence, they ought to be concerned for the salvation of their souls. He declares that God both gives good will and grants what is useful for bringing it to completion. He says that he rejoices over their faith, which will give him glory before the Lord Christ. He promises to send Timothy soon, whom he praises and [Col. 1349A] thoroughly commends. He also says that he has now sent Epaphroditus, who is known to have been restored after a long illness, to the Apostle’s consolation. He too hastened with great desire to see them, and the Apostle earnestly urged that he be received with reverence, since he had not shrunk from many dangers for the preaching of Christ.

5.—III, 21. “Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord,” and what follows. He further warns the Philippians to be cautious concerning false preachers, whom he aptly calls dogs, because they bark rather than speak. He nullifies circumcision of the body but confirms circumcision of the heart, since the former is known to be bound to the Law, while the latter is joined to grace. Nevertheless, he does not assert that he is perfect, but professes that he is striving toward perfection. He says that the faithful are conformed to Christ the Lord if they imitate in every way the one toward whom they strive: “who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (VI, [Col. 1350A] 21). This is so because those who no longer desire sins are immortal and enjoy divine delights. For the blessed have been assigned the condition of those of whom it was said: “They will be like the angels of God” (Matthew XXII, 30).

6.—IV, 1. “Therefore, my most beloved and longed-for brothers, my joy and crown, stand [Vulgate: ‘stand thus’] in the Lord.” He urges the Philippians, whom he rightly calls his crown, to remain firm in the faith they have received. He also commends to his true brother the most holy women, whom he says labored with him and with the other brothers in the Gospel of Christ. He warns them to maintain continual prayer and confidence and thereafter to perform whatever is known to be pleasing to the Lord. He gives them thanks because they consoled him in his tribulations with financial assistance, blessing and greeting them together.

## THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1349]

1.—I, 1. “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” He writes to the Thessalonians with Silvanus and Timothy, who preached the Lord’s Gospel with joined labor. He asks that grace and peace be granted them by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Nor should it be troubling that he is silent about the Holy Spirit. For whether one or two persons of the Trinity are named, as has already been said, they make the perfect Trinity understood, as was said in the Epistle written to the Romans.

2.—I, 2. “We give thanks to God always for all of you, making remembrance of you in all our prayers” [Vulgate: “making remembrance of you”]. He says that he gives thanks to God because the Thessalonians, abandoning the superstition of the Gentiles, received the foundations of the true faith. He reports with what integrity and fatherly affection he conducted himself among them, and he rejoices that they received the Lord’s Gospel not as a human word but as it truly was: the divine word.

3.—II, 14. For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus. He says that they became imitators of the prophets and of the Lord [Col. 1349D] Christ, since they too endured similar things on account of the holy faith. For he says that he himself greatly desired to come to Thessalonica, because they are his glory and crown before God. But for the present he declares that Timothy has been sent, so that he might strengthen them in faith and prepare them for sufferings, which he states will never be absent from the faithful. He adds that he is not sufficient to give God thanks on their behalf, since God is known to have bestowed such love upon them; but may the Lord [Col. 1350B] confirm them in the piety once granted, so that before the Father they may be able to share in Christ and in all the saints.

4.—IV, 1. Finally, brothers, we ask and exhort you in the Lord [Vulg., in the Lord Jesus] always, and so forth. He admonishes the Thessalonians that, just as they have acted until now, so in the future they should guard the faith they have received with devoted minds, adding what they ought always to avoid and what they ought always [Col. 1350C] to seek. He also says that the resurrection of all the dead is likewise to take place; for even those who are found living at that time in the spirit, as he himself was, after bodily death has preceded, will, he says, meet the Lord Christ together in the air. For we all die in the flesh, as it is written: “What man is there who lives and will not see death?” (Psalm 88:49). Yet he testifies that the Lord’s saints will remain with him forever. The day and hour of the Lord’s coming is proclaimed to be unknown to humanity, just as the Lord himself also testifies in the Gospel.

5.—V, 4. But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should seize you like a thief. Those who are children of light will not fear being overtaken by the darkness of sins at the Lord’s coming; nor do those who are armed with the Lord’s commandments and always stand ready sleep, intoxicated by evils [Col. 1350D]. He also admonishes them not to cease treating their preachers with a kindly disposition and to show the other brothers the attentions of charity. They should likewise remind one another of the tradition they have received. He also prays that they may be presented at the Lord’s coming with pure and devout minds. He further adjures them that this Epistle should be read aloud before all the brothers.

# THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 1349]

[Col. 1349D] 1.—I, 1. Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and Jesus Christ. [Col. 1350D] He again greets the Thessalonians together with these brothers, whom he also named in the First Epistle, showing that those who have deserved to share in his labors should be honored in this way, and commending the opening of his Epistle with a holy blessing.

2.—I, 3. We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, and what follows. He praises the Thessalonians for having attained the rule of a sound faith; but he warns them concerning the future, lest the wicked deceive them through some novelty. He says that the Lord’s coming will not take place unless Antichrist is first seen, whose wicked times he describes with remarkable precision. He asserts that the mystery of his iniquity is already at work, but he also declares that the presence of that most wicked one will then be revealed when the Roman empire, which now holds power, has been removed from the midst in due order [Col. 1352A]. Thus, through these indications, the truth of the Lord’s coming is proclaimed as destined to occur.

3.—II, 13. But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, and so forth. He says that he gives thanks to God for them because he has bestowed upon them correct faith and the gifts of eternal salvation. Therefore, he says that the faith must be held with the greatest devotion—the faith which he gloried in having received from them—since he professes that faith belongs not to everyone but to the few. He also prayed for them and again urged them that they ought to pray for him. He further warned that false brothers must be diligently avoided and that they should seek no other rules of faith than those which they had been proved to have received from him, bringing his Epistle to its customary conclusion with a greeting and blessing.

# THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

[Col. 1351]

[Col. 1351B] 1.—I, 1. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and so forth. He writes to the Colossians with Timothy his brother. But when he says “to the saints and faithful,” he shows that the words of the Lord cannot be received by people so long as they are polluted and faithless. He prays that the grace and peace of God the Father and of the Lord Jesus Christ may come upon them. In these two expressions—that is, “peace” and “grace”—he shows how great are the gifts that are repeated with such frequent reiteration.

2.—I, 3. We give thanks to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, and so forth. He gives thanks to God because through Epaphras he learned that they were persevering in the faith they had received, so that, bearing fruit in every good work, they might be found acceptable to the Lord. With wondrous preaching he adds praise of the Father, who was pleased [Col. 1351C] through the blood of his Son to reconcile to himself both the things on earth and the things in heaven, showing that Christ’s holy incarnation benefited all things by wondrous power.

3.—I, 21. And you, although you were once alienated and enemies in his mind [Vulg., in mind], and so forth. He admonishes them that, just as they once lived in carnal vices while alienated, so now they ought to devote themselves to evangelical virtues. He adds his own example, showing how greatly he is weighed down by calamities for their salvation. For now, he says, the mystery of the holy incarnation has been made manifest, which was shown to have been hidden from the ages. He warns that no one should deceive them through the empty wisdom of philosophers, who say that the sun and moon, or the other stars, should be worshiped—although it is beyond doubt that they consist of the elements, since they are also presented to our own eyes. [Col. 1351D] Nevertheless, true authority opposes these people if they do not refer everything to the Lord Christ, in whom dwells all the fullness of divinity (verse 9). For he said “bodily” because the whole fullness of the divine nature dwells in his body [Col. 1352B]. The holy ones who preceded were called “Christs” in figure in former times (Psalm 104:15). But he says that the Colossians were circumcised in heart, not in body; buried together through faith in the Lord’s passion, they are known to have risen with Christ.

4.—II, 13. And you, when you were dead in trespasses, and what follows. Since the Lord’s cross has fastened the old human being to the cross through its passion and has canceled the bond of perpetual death, he forbids the further investigation of certain precepts of the Old Testament. For he says that those things which bring death, not salvation, must be avoided; those who serve Christ ought to desire what belongs to Christ. Therefore, having stripped off the old human being, let us put on the new, which is renewed through the grace bestowed, in the image of him who created him. For in the inner human being neither person, nor sex, nor condition can be found to be different, but Christ the Lord is all things and in all.

5.—III, 12. Put on, therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion [Vulg., mercy]. He sets forth the rules by which one who hastens to embrace the Christian faith ought to walk. He indicates that thanks must be given to God in all our actions. He admonishes men and women, parents and children, masters and servants to render to one another the veneration owed to them. He urges them to persist in prayer, so that the Lord may open to the Apostle the door of preaching, for the proclamation of the Lord’s holy mysteries. He also admonishes them to speak with heavenly wisdom to those who are known to be outside the Church, lest they appear able to irritate rather than to instruct them. Their speech should always be seasoned [Col. 1352D] with salt, so that it may benefit those who hear it and be pleasing to them. After the customary greetings, he commands that this Epistle be read again in the church of the Laodiceans.

# THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 1351]

[Col. 1351D] 1.—I, 1. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus the Lord [Vulg., Jesus, our hope], and so forth. Although in the preceding Epistles he named the Father and the Son, and again in the blessing that follows he mentions the Father and the Son, here alone he says that he became an apostle according to the command of Christ, so that it may clearly appear that one person has been named, just as was already said above [Col. 1353A], while nonetheless the whole Trinity is poured forth. He calls Timothy the son of his faith, whom it is evident was regenerated by the holy Church.

2.—I, 3. Just as I urged you to remain [Vulg., to stay] at Ephesus when I was going into Macedonia, and so forth. He writes to Timothy his disciple so that he may be solicitous concerning the people entrusted to him. They must not follow superfluous doctrines, but must keep firmly in mind those things that have been preached to them, knowing that the law was not established for the just but for criminals. He subsequently enumerates them, since he continually rebukes those who stain themselves with the foulness of crimes. Concerning himself, he relates how much was granted to him through the Lord’s generosity, proving by his own salvation that Christ the Lord came to save sinners. He warns [Col. 1353B] him not to cease persevering in the preaching entrusted to him. Hymenaeus and Alexander abandoned it and suffered shipwreck in the faith; for this reason, he says that they were handed over to the devil, so that they might learn not to blaspheme.

3.—II, 2. I urge, therefore, first of all that supplications be made, and so forth. Writing appropriately to his disciple, he teaches what rule the ecclesiastical order ought to observe. First of all, he commands prayer for kings and authorities, so that, living in peace, we may pass through this life in tranquility. To kindle confidence in prayer, he celebrates the Lord Christ as mediator in holy preaching. He instructs how men and women ought to pray spiritually, adding what bishops, deacons, and subdeacons [Col. 1353C] ought to be, and what they ought not to be. In conclusion, he says that good ministers find great confidence before Christ the Lord.

4.—III, 14. I am writing these things to you, hoping to come to you soon, and so forth. He warns Timothy that his conduct in the Church of God should shine with dignity, lest false preachers deceive the hearts of the simple. In this matter, he says that Timothy ought to be so steadfast that he may offer an example of virtues before all who hear him. He also says with what honor and moderation each person should be treated, praising good stewards and reproving those who have neglected to care for their households, so that he even calls them worse than unbelievers.

5.—V, 9. Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, and so forth. He clearly shows what widows should be chosen and what sort should be avoided. Those who cannot restrain themselves, he commands to marry and bear children, lest they be tempted by the devil’s snares. He declares that presbyters who preside well, especially those who preach the word, are to be honored with double honor; nor should accusers easily be believed against them. He also discusses the other matters embraced by ecclesiastical order. He further warns [Col. 1354B] that the laying on of hands should not be done hastily, lest the one who unwisely promotes him become a partner in another’s sins. Therefore, he says that they must be examined more carefully, lest the reputation of the Church be harmed. He commands servants to honor their masters in every way, especially those who are known to be faithful.

6.—VI, 2. Teach these things and exhort them, and what follows. Gathering together what was said at the end, he says that they must persevere in these matters in every way and avoid the disputes of those whose minds are corrupt. He praises godliness with sufficiency, which is altogether pleasing to the faithful, saying into how many temptations those fall who hasten to become rich in the world, since greed is known to be the root of all evils. He urges them instead to direct their minds toward the virtues he has enumerated [Col. 1354C], so that they may receive eternal rewards from the Lord. He also explains how Timothy ought to admonish the rich of this world, so that in the future they may obtain rather the eternal riches of the Lord. Repeatedly he reminds him to guard the deposit of faith and not to cease avoiding wicked disputes.

# THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 1353]

[Col. 1353C] 1.—I, 1. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and so forth. He says that he was made an apostle by Christ the Lord according to the promise of life, so that it may be understood what reward belongs to those who faithfully deserved to exercise his apostleship. He writes this Epistle to Timothy [Col. 1353D], to whom he appears also to have sent the preceding one. In his blessing, he solemnly places grace and peace, adding mercy in the middle as a kind of amplification of the declaration, because neither grace nor peace can be granted without the Lord’s generosity.

2.—I, 3. I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my ancestors, whom I serve with [V., from my ancestors in] a pure conscience. He promises Timothy that he remembers him day and night in his prayers. He praises him because he remains in the undivided discipline of faith through the emulation of his mother and grandmother. He also warns him not to cease preaching the rule of doctrine he has received [Col. 1354C], nor to be ashamed to do what he knew would bring salvation both to himself and to believers. He wishes that the household of Onesiphorus may obtain the Lord’s mercy on that day of judgment. Onesiphorus was not ashamed to relieve his chains by generous benefactions; in preaching the Gospel, both at Rome and [Col. 1354D] at Ephesus, he supplied him with worthy services.

3.—II, 1. You, therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. He commands Timothy to proclaim without hesitation to the peoples the mysteries of the holy faith that he learned from him. He frequently urges him to avoid contentious and obstinate people, because their speech, accomplishing nothing, spreads like cancer (verse 17). As a preacher of truth, he instructs him what sort of person he should be for teaching, warning him what he should follow and what is to be avoided. Those who are known to be perverse must be corrected with patience, so that they may be freed from the snares of the devil, to which they are held subject.

4.—III, 1. But know this, that in the last [Col. 1355A] times there will be perilous times [Note: [Col. 1355B] Vulg., “that in the last days perilous times will come,” etc.]. Through numerous descriptions he explains what extremely wicked people will be found in the last times. Among them, he says, are those who strive to pour wicked doctrines into women. Yet he says that such people are to be corrupted by the illumination of the truth itself [perhaps: exposed] [Note: [Col. 1355B] I was uncertain whether *depravare*, with an unsuitable meaning, could here convey the same sense as “to remove depravity,” just as *depretiare* among certain medieval writers means the same as “to lower in price.” Since, however, this sense seems to answer the Apostle’s words in verse 9, I think that *declarandos* should be read—that is, “to be exposed” or “made manifest.”]. He also warns that such people must be avoided entirely. But he commands Timothy to remain in the things he has learned and believed. For every Scripture inspired by God is known to be useful for teaching, for reproof, and for instruction, so that the man of God may be perfect and usefully prepared for every good work.

5.—IV, 1. I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead. He places terrifying adjurations before Timothy, commanding him to rebuke the peoples in season and out of season, to reprove them, and to persist patiently with them, so that the word of the Lord may advance through the expansion of preaching. He declares that he himself is continually about to depart from this world and to receive at that judgment the crown of righteousness which the Lord promised to his saints. He also urges Timothy to hasten to come to him quickly with Mark and certain supplies, since he appeared to have been abandoned by those ministers of his. He says that Alexander the coppersmith, an opponent of his preaching, must be carefully avoided, and confirms that the punishment due to him is imminent. After conveying the greetings of many, he himself also admonishes Timothy that he ought to save Christ’s faithful.

# THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

[Col. 1355]

[Col. 1355B] 1.—I, 1. Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Christ Jesus, and so forth. When he calls himself an apostle of Christ, he professes, as has often been said, that he is also an apostle of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, because there is one cooperation, one God, and one power recognized there. But lest it be thought that he bears this title together with false brothers, he says, “according to the acknowledgment of the truth,” which only those deserve to receive who are known to shine with perfect truth [Col. 1355C]. To show that the Son is coeternal with the Father, he also says that Christ, the hope of the promised life, was foretold before eternal times. Thus he teaches that the Lord’s incarnation was announced through the preaching of the prophets and completed in its own time. And lest you should perhaps think him inferior in power, he says, “according to the command of the Lord our Savior” [Vulg., “the command of the Savior”]. He wishes grace and peace to be granted to Titus from God the Father and the Lord Savior.

2.—I, 5. For this reason I left you in Crete, and what follows. He admonishes his disciple Titus what sort of presbyters or bishops he ought to ordain throughout the churches of Crete, lest evil persuaders overturn the hearts of the simple. He specifically says that they must be rebuked, lest, subverted by false preaching, they be transferred to Jewish rites. [Col. 1356B] He professes that all things are clean for the clean, but says that the polluted and unbelieving possess nothing that is perfectly clean, since they confess the Lord with their mouths but deny in their deeds the judge whom they profess as their author.

3.—II, 1. But you, speak what accords with sound doctrine, and so forth. He declares that every age and every condition must be admonished concerning how they ought to conduct themselves in an exemplary manner [Col. 1356C], so that the Lord’s grace may clearly be recognized in all things—he who deigned to die in the flesh for our salvation. He also indicates what can be the most effective form of teaching: let Titus himself live with such moderation that, through his own precautions, he may provide an example, so that the adversary would not dare to say anything evil about one whom he knows to be governed by the holiest discipline. He also explains individually how one who is faithful to Christ ought to conduct himself. He commands him to avoid heretics and further instructs him to come to him at Nicopolis with certain companions, so that, by seeing the Apostle, he may learn how to stand firm in the holy faith with the strongest stability. He concludes his Epistle with a most affectionate blessing.

# THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

[Note: [Col. 1355D] Later, when he writes to Philemon: again, in number 2, “Philimonis.” Since these forms were pronounced ambiguously in ancient times, the spelling is uncertain. Gellius, Book X, chapter 24: “It was customary among the ancients generally to use these letters (e and i) indifferently.”]

[Col. 1355]

[Col. 1355D] 1.—I, 1. Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy the brother, and so forth. At the very beginning he newly joined suffering to his name. And lest it be thought that he was imprisoned for some crime, he added “of Christ Jesus,” showing that these bonds were not criminal but glorious. He writes to Philemon, his brother and fellow worker, together with his brother Timothy. He also mentions Apphia and Archippus in the same greeting. He likewise includes in the same greeting the congregation that appeared to be in Philemon’s house [Col. 1356D], wishing that grace and peace should come to them from the Father and the Lord Christ.

2.—I, 4. I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers. He gives thanks to God after hearing of Philemon’s faith and love, which he had toward the Lord Christ and toward all his saints. With great praise he celebrates Philemon’s works. He also begs him to release Onesimus, formerly his slave, whom he says has become his very heart through faith in the Lord [Col. 1357A], according to the condition owed to him, and to receive him in brotherly love. He says that he will repay whatever Onesimus owed. Yet he trusts that, on account of the Lord’s love [Col. 1358A], Philemon will gladly hear him, and he adds the greetings of certain people.

# THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Note: [Col. 1357D] It should be noted here that Cassiodorus is by no means uncertain concerning the author of this Epistle. It therefore makes no difference that in *Divine Readings*, chapter 8, he praised it without adding the author’s name, nor that he omitted it when listing the expositors and said, “The remaining Epistles of Saint Paul,” etc.—especially since in the same place he also forgot the Epistle to the Philippians, whose Pauline authorship no one doubted. This was sufficiently clear from the preface to *Orthography*, where these words are read: “Paul the Apostle is witness, who for the most part in the Epistle that is written to the Hebrews,” etc. The reason he gives for why the Apostle did not place his name at the beginning had already been offered by Clement of Alexandria in the *Hypotyposeis*, cited by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 14. Below: “they would not receive health”; in *On the Soul*, chapter 11, he attributes the effect of health. On Psalm 70 he also asks for bodily health.]

[Col. 1357]

[Col. 1357A] 1.—I, 1. In many parts and in many ways, formerly God spoke to the fathers in the prophets concerning his Son [Note: [Col. 1358D] The Vulgate, “God speaking,” does not have “concerning his Son.”]. It is customary to ask why this Epistle alone does not contain a greeting, although it appears to have been placed before all the preceding ones. At the very outset he so carefully concealed his name from the Hebrews lest, because of their hatred of his person, they fail to receive heavenly salvation. First joining the Old and New Testaments, he says that the Son of God, foretold through the prophets as being from the seed of David, came in the last times [Col. 1357B]. With inexpressible praise he celebrates his majesty, showing that he is superior to all his creatures through the examples of divine law, since the Father said to none of the angels or to any power of heaven what is clearly foretold concerning him. For if the word spoken through angels is proved to have been fulfilled, what will we deserve to suffer if we neglect the author of the whole gift?

2.—II, 3. Which, having first begun to be proclaimed through the Lord, and so forth. He says that the beginning of salvation was granted when Christ the Lord preached, and that afterward the truth of the holy faith became known through signs and wonders and through his apostles. He returns again to declaring Christ’s omnipotence, which he explains through examples, saying that he was fastened to the cross for the salvation of all. For this reason he never ceases in many places to call them brothers, since he deigned to assume flesh and destroyed through his passion the devil, who held the power of death. Since the assumed humanity grasped not angels but the seed of Abraham, he was rightly called their brother, so that he might exist as the true high priest and mediator of humanity and of God himself. Thus, he who suffered for all is also unquestionably able to help those who are tempted.

3.—III, 1. Therefore, holy brothers, participants in a heavenly calling, and so forth. He urges the Hebrews toward faith in Christ, from whom they are also known to have received the name “brothers.” He places Christ far above Moses, whom they appeared to obey, showing that the creator is much greater than his creature. He joins together highly appropriate examples, so that the Lord’s voice should be heard without hesitation. For the punishment of the ancients is to be feared: they did not enter into his rest because they refused to hear the divine word. But peace and tranquil repose were given to those who obeyed, so that they too might cease from their own labor, just as the Lord rested from his works.

4.—IV, 11. Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest, and what follows. He says that the divine commands must be obeyed, because what is spoken by such great truth cannot deceive. He places his greatest hope in the Lord Christ, because he comes to the aid of our calamities, having endured the cruelty of suffering for us. He adds extremely clear examples and proofs of so great a matter from the divine law. He rebukes those who are known to have forgotten the teaching of the ancient law to such a degree that they must again be nourished with milk like little children [Col. 1358B]. For mature minds need the solid food of preaching, since they are able to exercise sound discernment between good and evil.

5.—VI, 1. Therefore, leaving aside the elementary teaching of Christ, and so forth. He says that it is no longer necessary to deal with the beginnings of faith, but with the remaining matters in which mature perfection is shown. He makes a remarkable comparison with the earth: when it receives rain, it produces pleasant plants for adornment; but if it produces thorns, avenging fire consumes them. Nevertheless, he trusts that they will be raised to imitate those to whom the kingdoms of heaven have been promised. He joins to this the example of Abraham, whose seed the Lord promised with the firmest assurance by swearing an oath, so that, strengthened by this promise, the mind of the faithful might strive toward the innermost places of heaven [Col. 1358C], where our forerunner and high priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, has already entered.

6.—VII, 1. For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, high priest of God Most High [Vulg., of the Most High God], and so forth. At the beginning of this chapter he explains who Melchizedek was, with whom the Lord Christ is compared through great and most subtle arguments. First, because the interpretation of his name—that is, “king of peace” and “king of righteousness”—can apply only to Christ the Lord. Second, because no Scripture at all bears witness to his father or mother, just as Christ’s divinity, as I think, is known to have been without a mother, and his flesh without a father. Third, because neither the beginning nor the end of his life is taught to have been made known, just as the Lord says of himself, “I am Alpha and Omega” [Col. 1358D]. Fourth, because, being made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever. Fifth, the reason is then given why the Psalm did not say “according to the order of Aaron”: namely, so that the transferred priesthood [supply: and] the change of the law—which brought nothing to perfection—might announce that it was to be transformed into the grace of Christ. Thus, through these appropriately explained similarities, Melchizedek is proved to have borne the figure of the Lord Christ.

7.—VII, 19. But the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to the Lord, and so forth. Here he distinguishes between ordinary priests and the Lord Christ. Christ is unique: he was promised through the intervention of the sacrament and is known to have been established forever. Furthermore, every priest first intercedes for his own sins and then presumes to plead for the people. Christ, however, having no sins of his own, confidently intercedes for us. Finally, he alone offered himself for the salvation of all. In him also the promise of the New Testament was made; it is known to have been accomplished in no one else. By saying “new,” he wished to show that what preceded had become antiquated.

8.—IX, 1. The former indeed also had a justification of Holy Scripture [Vulg., ordinances of worship], and so forth. Through the practices previously mentioned, he distinguishes between the New and Old Testaments. He says that the ancient priests approached the holy places in one way, and then the inner Holy of Holies in another; but that the Lord Christ entered the holy places in another manner, accomplishing the glory of eternal redemption. For if the victim of bulls cleansed sins, what will the blood poured out by the immaculate Lord Christ do? Through it he purified the hearts of the faithful for service to God.

9.—IX, 15. And therefore Christ Jesus is the mediator of the New Testament [Vulg. does not have “Christ Jesus”], and what follows. He also proves that the Lord Christ was made mediator of the New and Old Testament, so that the obligation of the Old might be dissolved through the gift of his death [Col. 1359C]. He further teaches that the New Testament was undoubtedly promised even in the ancient solemnities of sacrifices, since he testifies that, with the blood of calves and goats, scarlet wool, and hyssop, both the sacred book and the people themselves were sprinkled. It follows that he suffered once, at the consummation of the ages, so that, as a merciful redeemer, he might continually intercede with the Father for us. For just as it is appointed for human beings to die once and afterward to undergo the Lord’s judgment, so Christ died once, so that he might appear as the one promised to those awaiting him in his judgment.

10.—X, 1. He says that the law is a shadow of future good things [Vulg., “for the law, having a shadow”], and so forth. He says that the law possessed a shadow of future good things, not the image—that is, the truth—of what followed. He shows that the human race could not be saved at all through the blood of sacrifices, but only through the passion of the cross, which came to the aid of the endangered world through its redemption. Having received this confidence, he urges those washed in the font of sacred baptism [Col. 1360A] to approach the Lord Christ, so that the faithful promiser may graciously fulfill his gifts in them.

11.—X, 24. And let us consider one another in the provocation of love, and so forth. He says that God’s grace must be contemplated not through impious divisions but in the brotherly gathering. He threatens the future judgment, which is proved to be already near through the coming of the Lord Christ [Note: [Col. 1359D] We know that the opinion concerning the imminent day of the final judgment, which arose in the age of the apostles, continued for many centuries.]. For if the one who makes Moses’ law void is accustomed to perish, with what punishment must the person be chastised who despises the commandments of love and unity belonging to Christ the Lord? He also warns them not to render empty the sufferings and plundering of their possessions that they have already endured for Christ’s name. Perseverance alone makes Christians perfect, for patience is necessary if the Lord’s promise is to be received.

12.—XI, 1. Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen. First he defines what faith is: belief, namely, in things that are not seen. Then he relates how many were saved through it, by the Lord’s mercy, so that he might incite the unbelieving hearts of the Jews to a similar devotion by considering such great examples of faith. For he speaks of the faith of Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and Sarah. He repeated this so frequently because, since these people believed, the whole Church is known to be blessed in their likeness. Yet all these people have not yet received the promised rewards [Note: [Col. 1359D] I had previously considered whether I should restore *susceperant* (“had received”), but since the same point is repeated in the following section and it is additionally stated that the pious Redeemer would give to all at one and the same time what he is known to have promised to all the faithful, I recognized that Cassiodorus is consistent with himself. In chapter 12 of his book *On the Soul* he transmits the following: “For when, at the Creator’s command, we have passed beyond this light, while continuing perpetually in the nature of our soul, we shall do nothing good or evil, but shall remain until the time of judgment,” etc. You recognize the opinion that has long been heard: namely, that the elect are excluded from the divine presence until their bodies are restored and attain blessedness only after the universal judgment. Our author also touches on the same matter in passing in the *Apocalypse*, number 3; but he would reject it now, if he were alive after the Council of Florence, which, after John XXII had rejected and condemned the opinion, proscribed it in the decree of union.]. But they will receive perfect blessedness in the heavenly city, which the Lord has deigned to prepare for them.

13.—XI, 17. By faith Abraham offered Isaac, so that he might be sacrificed [Col. 1360C] [Vulg., “Isaac, when he was tested”], and so forth. He continues the same enumeration of the faithful. For he speaks of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, the children of Israel, Rahab the prostitute, Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, and Samuel. He also adds the examples of the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms (verse 33) and deserved to find divine grace through various kinds of suffering. Yet they too have not received the promised rewards, so that the merciful Redeemer might give to all at one and the same time what he is known to have promised to all the faithful.

14.—XII, 1. Therefore, since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses laid upon us, and what follows. Having considered the faith of those who came before, he says that, after laying aside sins, we must hasten toward Christ the Lord. For he deigned to undergo the cross for us [Col. 1360D], who sits at the right hand of the Father. Why should we be distressed by lesser sufferings, which nevertheless we know belong to eternal rest? He also warns them that, since they have been called sons, they should endure their father’s chastisements with the greatest gratitude. To this matter he adds the examples of earthly parents [Col. 1361A], whose discipline is indeed considered severe in the present but is known to yield a pleasing righteousness in the future. Therefore, patience must be applied and their steps strengthened, so that they may effectively reach the goal toward which they are striving.

15.—XII, 4. Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God. He says that peace and holiness must be sought in every way, without which no one can see God. He also warns that we must take care lest the works of our impiety go before us upward and make us strangers to the Lord’s inheritance, as he says happened to Esau. After he sold his birthright, Esau indeed shed many tears, but it is not known that he was heard, because of God’s hidden judgment. He also adds the example of Moses, who ordered those who conducted themselves in an unclean manner to be stoned [Col. 1361B]. In this way he draws a contrast between Mount Sinai and the Church of God, since in the Church it is established that Christ was both heard and seen bodily. He says that Christ’s speech must be obeyed with the greatest devotion.

16. — XII, 25. “For if they did not escape when they refused him who was speaking on earth.” Still continuing the comparisons made above, he says: If the Hebrew people could not avoid punishment because they did not obey Moses, what will we suffer if we are seen not to obey the Lord speaking from heaven? He declares his power and greatness both by necessary arguments and by the examples that follow. He also admonishes them how they ought to conduct themselves and what harmful vices they should prefer to shun, [Col. 1361C] asserting that Jesus Christ was seen in the last times, although he always was, is, and will remain throughout the ages of ages.

[Col. 1362A] 17. — XIII, 9. “Do not be carried away by various and foreign teachings” [Vulg., “led away”], and what follows. He entirely forbids various teachings and foreign doctrines to be heard. For it is best to strengthen the heart by the grace of the Lord, not by foods. He also applies the former rite of sacrifices to the likeness of the Lord’s passion: just as the bodies of animals offered for sin were burned outside the camp, so too the Lord Christ, who offered himself for our sins, is known to have been crucified outside the city. But he says that this crucifixion, this reproach, must be desired in every way, so that, going out to him, we may deserve to reach the heavenly city. He persuades them never to forget beneficence and fellowship, for God is pleased by such things. He says that obedience must be shown to those set over them, for the sake of maintaining order, so that they may care for their salvation with joy.

18. — XIII, 18. “But we are confident that” [Vulg., “for we trust that”] “we have a good conscience, desiring to conduct ourselves well in all things.” He testifies that the greatest goodwill is owed to those who conduct themselves well, and says that this must continually be done for them, so that he may hasten toward them with the readiest zeal. He also prays for them, that they may fulfill with a sincere mind the will of God the Father, who brought from the dead the great shepherd, the Lord Christ, to whom be glory throughout the ages of ages. Thus, against those who thought that only the Father should be worshiped, a fitting remedy is briefly conveyed. He indicates that Timothy had been sent to them, through whom he greets the most approved among them in his own words and, with devoted charity, recalls the greetings of the good.

# Seven Summaries of the Canonical Epistles, namely, two of the blessed Apostle Peter, three of John, one of Jude, and one of James

[Note: [Col. 1361D] Commentaries by ancient writers do not flow abundantly upon these Epistles as they do upon the other sacred books of the Bible. Before Cassiodorus, Didymus of Alexandria had explained each one individually; the learned Simonius omitted him in his treatise on expositors of the New Testament. Nevertheless, anyone who consults Didymus’s Latin version, which survives in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, should know that our author borrowed almost nothing from him and used a different and distinctive division.

Clement of Alexandria had also written on four of them, although I suspect that his commentary has perished. For although many accept the fragments that survive under this title in volume III of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, with the distinguished Dupin also inclining toward that view, I cannot be persuaded of it: first, because I see those fragments elucidating the Epistle of Jude, whereas Cassiodorus teaches in *Divine Readings*, chapter 8, that he had explained the Epistle of James in Attic Greek; and second, because more than one error infects them. Our author, moreover, declares in the same place that he removed the stumbling blocks from their Latin version, so that, once purified, its teaching might be imbibed more safely.

Thomas Itigius, introducing Clement of Alexandria’s supplement in his *Bibliotheca Patrum Apostolicorum*, says: “Whether the outlines that survive today are those very ones that Cassiodorus says he corrected himself, we leave for others now to judge.” A work of Saint Augustine on the First Epistle of John survives, but not one on James; this too is commonly omitted from the list of lost works, although, according to Cassiodorus, he treated that Epistle with his customary diligence and care.

Interpreters of these Epistles were ultimately so rare that Cosmas Indicopleustes recorded the following in the sixth century, in Book VII of his *Christian Topography*: “Πάντες οἱ ὑπομνηματίσαντες τὰς θείας γραφὰς οὔτε εἷς αὐτῶν λόγον ἐποιήσατο τῶν καθολικῶν·” — “None of all those who wrote commentaries on the divine Scriptures gave any account of the catholic Epistles.”

Yet even after Cassiodorus the ancient interpreters of the Canonical Epistles are counted as very few, since, if the *Glossa Ordinaria* is left aside, only Bede can be brought forward before Oecumenius. Learned men advise us that Oecumenius’s collection presents us with a Catena drawn from earlier Greek writers. But, as far as the Canonical Epistles are concerned, I do not see from which sources he could have excerpted his commentary, unless we interpret it as collected from the lost works of the Greek Fathers. Cassiodorus, in the preface to *Divine Readings*, informs us that it had become widely known that certain writers had explained the divine Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments from beginning to end in Greek, naming Chrysostom among them, whose abridger is commonly called Oecumenius.

I am scarcely persuaded, however, that, if Chrysostom’s or anyone else’s comments on these Epistles had existed, Cassiodorus could have been unaware of them. He was greatly troubled by his search for some exposition of them (*Divine Readings*, chapter 8), and he arranged for Didymus’s work to be translated from Epiphanius. Rather, I would suppose that this book was for the most part passed over by commentators on the sacred writings, both because its copies may have been comparatively rare and because it was accepted into the canon of sacred Scripture only very late by many churches. [Col. 1364D]

Whatever the truth of the matter, our author must henceforth hold an eminent place among the ancient interpreters of the Canonical Epistles, since he was the first among the Latins to undertake the elucidation of all of them; and, as I believe, the first—or certainly among the first—to call them “Canonical,” even in his book *On the Institution of Divine Literature*, when they were formerly accustomed to be called “Catholic.” They are designated by the name “Canonical” in an ancient prologue, but learned men, on sound grounds, deny that prologue to Saint Jerome. Guilielmus Cave did not notice this when writing about Saint Jerome, nor did the distinguished editor of Saint Cyprian, who reproduces it in full and strongly commends it in his treatment *On the Unity of the Church*.

The editors of Saint Jerome teach that the Council of Laodicea calls them “Canonical” in its catalogue of the divine Scriptures, volume XI, page 1672; but, as I think, this arose from a chance error. For both the Greek text of that catalogue and the Latin translation of Marius Mercator call them “Catholic”; Dionysius does not mention them.]

[Col. 1361]

# Epistle of the Apostle Peter to the Gentiles

[Note: [Col. 1362D] A false title. It could more properly have been entitled “to those in the dispersion,” πρὸς τοὺς ἐν διασπορᾷ, as the Epistle of Saint James is entitled in these *Summaries*, since it too was sent to Jews who had settled outside Judaea. Saint Augustine adopts the order that places Peter’s Epistles before the others, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book XI. See the ancient prologue to the Canonical Epistles.]

[Col. 1361D] 1. — I, 1. “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the chosen sojourners,” and what follows. Joining in the celebration of the institutions of the most holy rule, the Apostle Peter of Jesus Christ also writes to the absent Hebrews who had been scattered by the impious persecution of the Jews [Col. 1363A] and had become sojourners throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, yet had believed in Christ Jesus with a corrected mind. He says that his preaching had been sent to them according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, and in the shedding of the blood of the Lord Christ, so that, following the former custom of sacrifices, the people sprinkled with the Lord’s blood might be cleansed. Thus, in these opening words, both the unity of the triune power and the distinction of the persons are briefly declared. He asks that the grace and peace of the Lord be completed in the fullest abundance.

2. — I, 3. “Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and what follows. Having completed the greeting of the faithful people, mindful of the Lord’s institution, he first gives thanks to God the Father, who, through his great mercy, [Col. 1363B] regenerated us by holy baptism in the hope of eternal life—namely, through the resurrection of the Lord Christ, which is known to have taken place from the dead after three days. He then explains how great are the rewards of this inheritance. He urges us to endure the troubles of the present time patiently, so that at the Lord’s judgment the testing of our faith may be shown to be more precious than gold. For those who believe in him here without seeing him will rejoice when they behold him with immeasurable exultation. Concerning this recompense of rewards, the prophets, searching out the Lord’s hidden matters, said many things. And lest you think that anything was decreed by human will, he teaches that these things were revealed to them through the Holy Spirit, whom the angels desire to see.

[Col. 1363C] 3. — I, 13. “Therefore, girding the loins of your mind, being sober, perfect” [Vulg., “perfectly”], “hope in it.” After revealing to them the great rewards of the promise, he urges them, through strength of mind, to strive toward grace as children, which he shows to have been promised to them at the Lord’s judgment. He admonishes them to remain in a holy purpose, since it is written: “You shall be holy, for I too am holy.” Knowing [Col. 1364A] that they were not redeemed with a corruptible price but with the precious blood of our Lord, who was indeed foreknown before the foundation of the world but manifested in the last times for the salvation of all, they should thus keep the faith and hope of believers fixed upon him.

4. — I, 22. “Purifying your souls for obedience to charity” [Vulg., “in the obedience of charity”], and what follows. Having first explained how faith is to be exercised, he says that they must begin by continually preserving mutual charity for one another in simple love, so that those who have been jointly reborn through the word of the living God may not be separated by any division, and the human mind may not hasten toward worldly vices. By comparison with hay, he shows how perishable our flesh is. But the word of the Lord, [Col. 1364B] by which they are known to have been regenerated, remains forever. Therefore, laying aside the malice of the former time, like newborn rational infants they must desire the beginnings of faith, so that they may advance to salutary growth. For if they have approached the living stone—that is, the Lord Christ—with devoted minds, they too must progress like living stones in the building of the Church, offering acceptable sacrifices to God through Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom the salvation desired by the human race has come. An example is also given from the holy stone itself, through the prophet Isaiah.

5. — II, 4. “To you, therefore, who believe, honor; but to those who do not believe, the stone which the builders rejected has become” [Vulg., “you”; then, “this has become”] “the head of the corner.” Again, Psalm 117 provides an example concerning that stone. A discussion follows, setting believers and unbelievers in opposition: the stone is said to be for the obstinate a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, but for believers an elect race, a holy offspring, a people of acquisition, called from darkness into the perpetual light of holiness. Those who had formerly been outsiders have now become the proper possession of the Lord [Col. 1365A] Christ. And to estrange the inclination of their minds from the world, he teaches them to abstain from carnal desires, which always strive to wound souls. Rather, they should live in such a way that among the nations they may offer examples of good conduct, so that those who now seem to slander them, having observed their conduct, may glorify the Lord when they have been moved to repentance by his visitation.

6. — II, 13. “Be subject” [Note: [Col. 1365D] Didymus had read it this way too; the Latin version may be deceiving us.] “to every human ordinance for the Lord’s sake” [Note: [Col. 1365D] Vulg.: “Therefore be subject to every human creature for God’s sake.”], and what follows. Lest the faith mentioned above should have inflated anyone, he returns to the endurance of patience, so that they should be subject to rulers or governors for God’s sake, whom he is known to have appointed for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Yet he commands this to be done from the freedom of conscience, not performed under the compulsion of fear. He also admonishes servants to obey their masters—not only those who are gentle, but also those who seem harsh—because this is truly the grace of God: not merely to endure what is equitable, but also what is unjust. For we were called by the Lord to such an example, so that we might endure wrongs for the sake of him who chose to accept the cross for us, although he had no stain of sin. Therefore we must turn to our shepherd, who endured death for the salvation of all.

7. — III, 1. “Likewise, those who do not believe the word are won through the conduct of their wives” [Note: [Col. 1365D] Vulg.: “Likewise, let women also be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives.”]. He then comes to the admonition of women, first saying that they should be subject to their husbands, so that those who had not at all believed the holy preaching might instead be brought to repentance by the conduct of their wives. Then he commands them to devote themselves not merely to adornments but to the inner person, who is truly found rich before God. Sarah is given to them as an example; she served Abraham with commendable devotion [Note: [Col. 1365D] *Probabile* in this author means “worthy of approval” or “laudable”; it occurs frequently. In the preface to *Divine Readings*: “through the approved expositions of the Fathers.” This should be noted in this paragraph: the words missing in the prefixed half-verse are to be understood as having been omitted through some error, since the exposition reads, “first saying that they should be subject to their husbands.” I note this so that it may be clear how cautious and circumspect we ought to be in such matters.] He says that they ought to imitate her, through whose emulation of faith they were received into Abraham’s offspring. Likewise, he commands husbands to treat their wives with due honor, as weaker and coheirs of grace, so that each other’s prayer may not be hindered. Finally, he admonishes both sexes to be all of one mind, compassionate, merciful, and humble; not returning evil for evil, but persevering in the grace of blessing to which they were called.

8. — III, 3. “For whoever desires life and loves to see” [Col. 1365D] “good days” [Note: [Col. 1366D] Vulg.: “To love life and to see good days.”] “should restrain his tongue from evil.” Again, he gives a general admonition that we must restrain our tongue from evils, since it is always known to be inclined toward sins. But he says that this alone cannot suffice, since perfection consists in turning away from evils and also accomplishing good deeds eminently. For the Lord looks upon the just, while he fixes his gaze angrily upon the impious. He says that they become blessed if they are torn by some persecution for the Lord’s name. He also says that at all times they must be ready to give an account of their faith with gentleness and holy fear, so that those who disparage the faithful may immediately fall silent once they have perceived the truth.

9. — III, 17. “For it is better, if God’s will should so will it, to suffer while doing good than while doing evil.” He affirms that it is much better for one who acts well to suffer evil than for one who acts badly to be struck according to the quality of his deeds. Thus the Lord, although he had done nothing evil, was put to death in the flesh for our sins, and established for us the pattern of his passion. He also joins to this the example of Noah, because, just as only eight souls in his ark were saved from the destruction of the flood, so the holy people are known to have been freed from the stain of sins through the grace of baptism. For in holy baptism the flesh is not washed of its filth as in an ordinary bath; rather, it is saved through faith in the Lord’s resurrection, who swallowed up death so that we might deserve to share in his life. Therefore, having understood Christ’s resurrection, let us too suffer in the flesh when we abandon sins, so that the remaining time of our life may be spent not according to human desires but according to the Lord’s will.

10. — IV, 3. “For the past time is sufficient for fulfilling the will of the nations” [Vulg., “for the fulfillment”]. He says that the world should consider sufficient the time already elapsed in the wicked will of the nations. Now, however, we must live according to God in the Holy Spirit, who called us from the dead so that we ought to live in his hope. For the Gospel is known to have been preached even to those dead under the law of sin, so that in the general resurrection they may attain the joys of eternal life. Therefore, as the end of the world approaches, we must be prudent and diligent in prayer, having charity among ourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins. He also commands that hospitality and the other good works be provided without murmuring. But he asserts that the word of the Lord must be preached in such a way that the whole attention of believers is directed to the Lord as its author, to whom belong power and glory throughout the ages of ages.

11. — IV, 12. “Beloved, do not be afraid” [V., “Do not be astonished”] [Note: [Col. 1366D] From the Greek μὴ ξενίζεσθε, by which word disturbance is sometimes signified; and disturbance is not far removed from fear. *Geoponica*, Book XI, chapter 46: “for it also astonishes and disturbs.” Bede read, “Do not be astonished.”] “at the burning ordeal that is taking place for your testing.” He strengthens the faithful people, so that they should not be disturbed by the suffering inflicted upon them, since Christ suffered greater things for us than we seem to endure for his faith. Therefore, in such circumstances, we should rejoice here with constancy, so that before him we may rejoice with perfect gladness. He also admonishes that no one should suffer the torments of the world for disgraceful acts or crimes. But if we suffer for the Lord Christ, we shall be placed in eternal blessedness; for no one ought to be ashamed of that by which he knows that he will attain eternal rewards. But if the just and faithful are scarcely saved, surely the sinner and the impious will not stand. Whoever suffers evils here for Christ commends his soul in that judgment.

12. — V, 1. “Therefore, the elders who are among you I exhort, as a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings.” He admonishes presbyters to guard the clergy entrusted to them with diligent and unselfish care, to despise vices, to reject temporal profits, and to place their riches in approved conduct, so that when the chief shepherd appears [Col. 1367B] (verse 4), they may be crowned with the honor of blessedness. He also admonishes the young to be subject to their elders, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Those who humble themselves before Christ will undoubtedly be exalted in his judgment. He says that human anxieties must also be cast upon him, so that he may not cast us out of his kingdom.

13. — V, 8. “Be sober, be watchful; for your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking whom he may devour” [Vulg., “consume”]. He admonishes them to be sober and watchful, because the devil continually attempts to seize them like a bloodthirsty beast. He declares that he must be resisted by faith and good works, since he is overcome when the faithful mind is conquered by no assault. And lest the hearts of the faithful be disturbed by the identification of so great an enemy, he says that the powerful God resists him, and no power can prevail against God. He testifies that he wrote this Epistle through Silvanus, their faithful companion, exhorting and urging them not to cease persevering in the grace of the Lord that had been preached. He also sends greetings from the Church which, from Babylon—that is, from the confusion of this present age—he says is chosen, and through the pious instruction of Mark, his son. He asks that the most faithful in the service of charity be greeted, conferring upon them the grace of his blessing, since they remained in Christ the Lord.

# The Second Epistle of the Same

[Col. 1367]

[Col. 1367B] 1. — I, 1. “Simon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a faith equal” [Vulg., “to those who have obtained with us an equally precious faith”]. Simon is his proper name; Peter is his surname, as the Lord said in the Gospel: “You are Simon, son of John” [Vulg., “son of Jonah”]; “you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated “Peter” (John 1:43). He calls himself a servant because he served the Lord Christ with most humble devotion. He mentions that he is an apostle to indicate the office conferred upon him. For when he says “of Jesus Christ,” as has often already been said, he is known by the mention of one person to indicate the most holy Trinity. And, so that he would not exalt himself above the Lord’s Church, he says that he is writing to those who, by the Lord’s generosity, have received an equal faith. He wishes that grace and peace may be multiplied in the knowledge of the future judgment, where whatever is granted is no longer lost through any deprivation.

2. — I, 3. “As all things of his divine power have been granted to us for life and godliness” [Note: [Col. 1367D] Vulg.: “How his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness,” etc.]. Just as all things have been granted to believers for life and godliness through the recognition of him who called us by his own glory, not by our merits, so that through these promises we may deserve to share in his divinity—as it is said in the Gospel, “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24)—so we too must flee worldly sins. Rather, let us strive to pursue virtue in our faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, godliness in self-control, brotherly love in godliness, and the charity of the Lord in brotherly love. When these things are present in us, we cannot be without fruit in the knowledge of the Lord Christ; rather, we are received into the Lord’s kingdom, [Col. 1368B] which we utterly deserve not to enter by any other means.

3. — I, 12. “For this reason I will not cease always to remind you” [Note: [Col. 1368D] Vulg.: “I will begin always to remind you of these things.”], and what follows. He says that he cannot cease from the established preaching until he leaves them firm and strengthened in faith in the Lord the Savior. [Col. 1368C] He testifies that, as he was instructed by the Lord, he will depart from this world; and therefore, with the most holy affection of a father, he declares that he is taking care to do such things among them that they may be able to retain his memory. He says that he is not going to speak anything about the Lord Christ from invented fables, but that he will speak of what he heard with his own ears and learned through the most certain sight. To this matter he adds the Gospel example: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” He says that he heard this voice with the other apostles while they were with the Lord the Savior on the holy mountain. Thus, by this testimony, those who think that the Father has no Son are refuted.

4. — I, 19. “And we have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend” [Col. 1368D] [Vulg., “more firm, attending to it”]. He praises the example that was given, so that they should always hold it in their hearts as a lamp is prepared in darkness, until Christ comes, by whose incomparable brightness the just will shine. He praises prophecy in general as true, since it was never imparted by human will but by divine inspiration. But with a most suitable conclusion he defines the false prophets, saying that they are lying teachers who, in the hope of the most shameful profit, acquire for themselves the judgment of perpetual damnation.

5. — II, 4. “For if God did not spare the angels who sinned, but thrust them back into infernal prisons” [Note: [Col. 1369C] Vulg., “but, having cast them down, delivered them to Tartarus in the chains of hell.”]. A fitting proof of the preceding statement follows: he did not spare the angels who sinned, but shut them away in gloomy prisons, reserving them to be punished at his judgment. Next, he did not spare the original world, which he had deigned to fashion with his own hands, but destroyed it, together with impious human beings, by the devastation of the flood that came upon it. He condemned Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes in righteous indignation. But [Note: [Col. 1369C] “Let someone more fortunate emend this and restore the text.”] he rescued Noah, the eighth [sic], from the flood, and righteous Lot, deeply grieved, from the society of the shameless, so that by joining such examples together the most holy man might prove both that the impious receive a punishment they deserve and that the righteous are saved through testing.

6. — II, 10. “Especially those who follow the flesh into desires of pollution” [Note: [Col. 1369D] Vulg.: “Especially those who walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness.”]. He reproves those who follow the desires of the flesh and, with sacrilegious intent, despise the dominion of Christ. Recounting their vices in many ways, he says that they rise up against the Lord with proud will, although he is known to have brought sinful angels low. He describes again both their bodily characteristics and their utterly depraved behavior. After many disgraceful acts, he says, they even worshiped images. He marks them by fitting comparisons, recalling that they are dry springs, dark clouds, and turbulences [perhaps “whirlwinds”] driven about, for whom eternal darkness is deservedly prepared. They deceive those who listen and draw them toward the liberty of lust, although they themselves are known to be slaves of sin. He adds a very useful and approved judgment: each person is the slave of the one to whom he is known to be subject.

[Col. 1369C] 7. — II, 20. “For if, having escaped the pollutions of the world, through the knowledge of the Lord” [Vulg., “in the knowledge of our Lord”]. He reproves those who, after receiving the commands of truth, again entangle themselves in the former mire of falsehood. He compares them to those proverbs: “The dog returns to its vomit,” and “the pig returns to wallow again in its own mire.” He says that he has sent them a second Epistle so that they may faithfully hold the traditions of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 1370C] Consider the interpretation of the verse, “so that you may remember,” and the instruction concerning faithfully holding the traditions.], and not turn impiously toward the errors of the Gentiles. Rather, they should desire to do what they know pertains to the commands of Christ the Lord.

8. — III, 3. “Knowing this first, that in the last days scoffers will come in mockery” [Note: [Col. 1370D] Vulg., “that in the last days scoffers will come with deception.”]. He warns that in the last times there will appear those who say: “Where is Christ the Lord, who was promised to come quickly? Behold, so much time has passed, and we know that nothing of the sort has occurred.” He gives the example of the flood: just as the increasing waters filled those aerial heavens and the world then perished from its ordered state, so on the day of judgment those same heavens are to be destroyed again by fire, as we read. By these matters he proves plainly that everything foretold will be fulfilled without any doubt.

9. — III, 10. “But the day of the Lord will come like a thief,” and what follows. He says that the day of the Lord will come suddenly, like a thief, when the heavens rush onward with a great burst of speed and when the elements of the world are to be dissolved by the heat of fire. But when all these things perish and the whole structure undergoes a terrifying transformation, what sort of people ought the faithful then to be, so that they may not encounter such devastation? For since new heavens and a new earth have been promised, in which the promised righteousness dwells, there is no doubt that the things we now see can be dissolved. Therefore, they should not regard the delay of time as in any way hateful to themselves, but should judge that it is working toward their salvation, since they understand that they are being spared so that they may convert.

10. — III, 15. “As also our most beloved” [Vulg., “dearly beloved”] “brother Paul,” and what follows. He praises his brother and fellow apostle, saying: Preserve the truest faith, as the Apostle Paul writes to you, [Col. 1370C] according to the wisdom given to him, searching out profound heights and revealing hidden things. Yet the unlearned and unstable twist these things, as they do the other Scriptures, according to their own will, to their own destruction. But he admonishes those to whom he seems to be writing not to be deceived by the error of the perverse and appear to be overturned from the stability of their faith. Rather, they should advance in the understanding and grace of the Lord Christ, so that they may always increase in good merits.

# Epistle of Saint John to the Parthians

[Note: [Col. 1369D] This Epistle was listed under the same title in *Divine Readings*, chapter 14. The reason for this title cannot be inferred from the Epistle itself. Nevertheless, ancient evidence shows that it was so entitled, besides Saint Augustine’s work *On the Epistle of John* and his *Questions on the Gospels*, and also in the codices of the venerable Cardinal Tommasi, in which we read: “Here begin the chapters of Saint John to the Parthians.” In a certain prologue attributed to Bede, published by Guilielmus Cave, page 403: “Many ecclesiastical writers, among whom is Saint Athanasius, testify that his First Epistle was written to the Parthians.”]

[Col. 1369]

1. — I, 1. “That which was from the beginning” [Vulg., “which was from the beginning”], “which we heard, which we saw with our eyes.” He gives the most certain credibility to his preaching when he says that he reports concerning the Lord Christ not merely what he heard but what he saw. Yet he confirms that he saw things which, according to his Gospel, did not begin in time at all but remained continually in eternity. He says [Col. 1370D] that God is the truest light, and that if anyone wishes to attain knowledge of him, he must live in the brightness of his conscience, since it cannot happen that anyone is filled with his holy light so long as he remains in dark perversity.

2. — I, 8. “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” Lest anyone think that a human being is without sin, although he had always commanded him to walk in the light of the heart, he says that there is no one who cannot offend in some respect. Rather, the person becomes approved who is known to confess his sins to the Lord, so that, when the Lord remits our offenses, he may cleanse us by his mercy. For if we consider ourselves blameless, we make him a liar who said: “God has enclosed all things under sin, so that he may have mercy on all” [Note: [Col. 1371] Romans 11:23; Vulg.: “God has enclosed all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all,” etc.]. He also says that, whenever they sin through the frailty of the flesh, they should immediately return to satisfaction before the Lord Christ, who continually intercedes with the Father for us. Whoever says that he remains in him ought to direct his steps in the manner in which he himself is known to have walked.

3. — II, 7. “I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment, which you had from the beginning.” As far as the divine Scriptures are concerned, he says that he is not preaching anything new, because these things are known to have been foretold long ago in the Law. Yet in this respect the commandment is recognized as new, because what was previously announced now appears to have been fulfilled. The darkness of sins has passed, and the manifestation of light has come through the Lord Christ. Therefore no one ought to hate his brother, for whom he knows that Christ laid down his life. He says that he wrote to elders, younger men, children, and infants, so that they might rejoice in a common charity, since it is clear that their sins have been forgiven on account of the faith they received. Then he says that they conquered the evil one because they have known God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1371C] 4. — II, 15. “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world,” and what follows. He commands that the world not be desired at all, since it is always shown to be opposed to the divine will. Therefore whoever loves the heavenly Father has not loved the darkness of this world. The vices of the flesh and spiritual virtue are far apart. To make them more cautious, he says that it is the final hour, because through deceitful brothers and heretical perversities the wickedness of Antichrist arises. Yet he says that these people went out from the congregation of the saints because they were not worthy to remain with the faithful. He also proves that those who say that Jesus is not the Lord Christ are liars, since whoever denies the Son has certainly also denied the Father.

5. — II, 24. “Let what you heard from the beginning remain in you,” and what follows. He says that they must remain in the faith they received, so that they too may remain in the love of the Father and the Son and obtain his promises—that is, the rewards of eternal life. Therefore one must remain in him, so that at his coming he may not find us estranged. For since he has granted us to be called his children, it is exceedingly impious if we are made strangers to his institutions. Thus we must act so that, when he appears, we may behold him just as he is, through the fullest gift.

6. — III, 4. “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, because sin” [Vulg., “and sin is,” etc.] “is iniquity.” He embraces this with many arguments and diligent proof, saying that we must not be opposed to the Lord Christ if we wish to have a share with him. Since he is spotless and most just, the person who is entangled in the perversity of wickedness utterly separates himself from him. For this reason the Son of God came into the world, to release the ancient sin through an undeserved death. Therefore no one ought to hate his brother, lest he incur the detestable example of Cain, who, through envy of his brother’s good works, slaughtered his own brother by an impious death.

7.---III, 14. “Whoever does not love his brother remains in death” [Vulg.: “Whoever does not love remains,” etc.], and what follows. He declares that whoever does not love his brother is a murderer; and whoever is a murderer cannot possess the life of the blessed. For if someone sees his brother in need and closes his heart of mercy toward him, he cannot obtain mercy from the Lord. For it is clear that one must not love one’s brother with the tongue alone, but by one’s deeds; and if our heart consents to his precepts and commandments, whatever we ask from God we receive without hesitation. The Lord thus remains in us if we fulfill his precepts with a faithful mind.

8.---IV, 1. “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits that are from God” [Vulg.: “Beloved, etc., whether they are from God”]. He says that false prophets are in no way to be believed, but asserts that those to whom faith ought to be given must be tested. For whoever confesses that Christ is the Word made flesh is a true preacher; but whoever dissolves or denies him through heretical perversity is the true Antichrist, since he wishes to destroy that through which the salvation of the world is known to have come about. For since God is love, we truly love him whom no one has seen when we embrace our brothers with mutual affection. His love indeed appeared among us when he sent his only-begotten Son into this world, so that he might rescue us from the snare of death and bestow the gifts of perpetual salvation.

9.---IV, 14. “And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world” [Vulg.: “We testify, etc., as the Savior of the world”]. With the sweetest revelation he repeatedly commends love of God and of one’s neighbor, saying that he had learned that God the Father sent his Son to save the world from its dangers and miseries. Therefore whoever remains in love remains in God, because God is love. For we can have confidence before him if we imitate him in the practice of love. But in order to give this matter the greatest assurance, he declares that there is no fear in love, especially since God first loved us so that we ought to love him. If someone who hates his brother, whom he sees, says that he can love God, whom he does not see, he is altogether lying, since it is an evident commandment that whoever loves God must also love his neighbor.

10.---V, 1. “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God,” and what follows. Whoever believes that Jesus is God has been born of God the Father; he is without doubt a believer. And whoever loves the parent also loves the one born from him, Christ. We love him in this way: when we do his commandments, which do not seem burdensome to upright minds; rather, they conquer the world when they believe in him who created the world.

Three mysteries bear witness to this matter on earth: water, blood, and spirit, which are read as having been fulfilled in the Lord’s Passion. In heaven there are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one God.

[Note: [Col. 1373B] Here is that very celebrated passage of Saint John concerning the Trinity, over which the greatest controversy has been waged down to the present day. I could compose a volume by gathering together what very many learned men have assembled on this question. Those defending the heavenly witnesses, as they call them, receive very strong support from this Cassiodorian work. It thereby becomes clear that the verse was written not only in African codices—as is evident from Eugenius, Fulgentius, Vigilius, Victor, Facundus, and apparently also Cyprian—but also in the oldest and most accurate codices of the Roman Church.
