For since he prescribed with such care to his monks in *Divine Readings* that they should use the finest codices, purified also by comparison with the Greek text, and that in doubtful passages the authority of two or three ancient and corrected codices should be sought, who could doubt that he himself had especially carried out the same procedure?

Those, however, who think that this *pericope*—that is, passage—was once inserted into the Vulgate, or Hieronymian, version must finally surrender and lay down their arms. For it is plainly evident from very many passages of these *Complexiones* that Cassiodorus used a version different from the Hieronymian one, and nevertheless read this *pericope*.

Whenever a passage of Scripture occurs that diverges from the Vulgate, we commonly assert that it was taken from the Old Latin version, usually with excessive confidence. Saint Augustine teaches chiefly in *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, how many translations were once in circulation: “Those who translated the Scriptures from the Hebrew language into Greek can be counted, but the Latin translators cannot be counted at all. For whenever in the earliest times of the faith a Greek codex came into anyone’s hands, and he seemed to possess even a little ability in both languages, he ventured to translate.” No one will doubt that the same thing was done in the Old Testament and in the New.

Nevertheless, the fact that the half-verses which Cassiodorus either cites in this explanation or identifies were truly drawn from the ancient Vulgate, or Old Latin version, nearly proves to me that this version was regarded by the most learned of the ancients as the most approved among the others. I therefore judge that it was undoubtedly used by that learned writer and outstanding investigator of the sacred books, all the more because he was accustomed to seek out the oldest manuscripts of Scripture and compare them with the Greek text. Both the authority of writers and the finest surviving manuscripts testify that the heavenly witnesses were present in that text.

As for why this passage is wholly absent from many of the older Latin codices today, and why several of the Fathers did not have it in their copies, nor Augustine himself read it—although Cornelius a Lapide claims that he did—the reason is readily apparent. It is not merely that, as can be gathered from Saint Jerome’s preface to Joshua, there were in those times among the Latins as many different copies as there were codices; there is a further explanation. I shall show, when discussing ancient inscriptions, that their copyists often omitted an entire line, and not infrequently two, when the same words were repeated after a short interval. It very easily happened that, after copying the earlier words, when they returned their eyes to the stone, they fell upon the later ones and copied what followed. Exactly this happened to some ancient scribe while copying the Epistle of Saint John. Since the words “and these three are one” occurred twice in the same place, his eye wandered and he skipped over the intervening words. One exemplar, however, produces countless copies, and the error of one spreads without limit.

The paraphrase of the words “and these three are one” supplied by our commentator should also be noted, namely: “And these three are one God.” By this paraphrase every suspicion is overturned among those who argue against the common opinion that the words favor the Arians—as though they established unity not in essence but in the manner of bearing witness, by which water, blood, and spirit are equally called one.

Furthermore, in Cassiodorus’s text the verse concerning the earthly witnesses preceded it; learned men have also observed this in certain manuscripts.]

11.---V, 9. “If we receive human testimony” [Vulg.: “the testimony of men”], “the testimony of God is greater.” If we are accustomed to accept the testimony of human beings, we ought to believe the Father’s declaration, who in the presence of many hearers confessed his Son, the Lord Christ, in an irrevocable statement. For whoever does not believe his testimony—something that is impious to say—considers him who spoke the truth to be a liar. Since we possess perpetual salvation in the Lord Christ, whoever refuses to believe in him is recognized as having stripped himself of the gift of salvation.

12.---V, 13. “I have written these things to you” [Vulg.: “I write”], “so that you may know that you have eternal life,” and what follows. In order to strengthen the understanding of believers with the firm root of faith, he says that if their will remains in the preaching they have received, whatever they may wish to ask beneficially from the Lord will be granted to them without hesitation. He also reminds them that they ought to pray for brothers who nevertheless do not commit serious offenses unto death. But concerning those who stain themselves with criminal impiety and persist in the wickedness of despair, he does not say that supplication should be made in any way. Yet lest anyone use the light of understanding as a pretext, he says that the Son of God came into this world and granted us understanding of the truth, warning them not to be deceived any longer by the falsehoods of idols.

## THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE SAME AUTHOR

[Col. 1373]

1.---I, 1. “John the elder to the elect lady and her children,” and what follows. John the elder—because he was advanced in age—writes to the elect lady, the Church,

[Note: [Col. 1373] Inclined toward mystical interpretation, he joins those who think that this “elect” is not a matron but the Church.]

and to her children, whom he had begotten through the sacred font. He says that he loves them not only with the devotion of love but also all the faithful who have learned the Lord’s will, which remains forever. He wishes grace, mercy, and peace to be granted them from God the Father and from his Son Jesus Christ, in truth.

2.---I, 4. “I rejoiced greatly because I found some of your children walking in the truth.” He says that he rejoiced exceedingly because he found the children of the holy Church, to whom he seemed to be writing, walking in the truth, just as the commandment is known to have been received from the Father: namely, that they should believe in his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

He reminds the congregation of the faithful that they should unite with one another in love. For whoever does not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh to save the human race is proved in every respect to be the Antichrist. Whoever remains in the most upright doctrine will rejoice in the blessing of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore he testifies that false prophets ought neither to be greeted nor received, because whoever joins them in any association shares in their crimes. He says that he wished to write many things to them, but since he was preparing to come to them, he reserves what had to be said for his presence, concluding his Epistle once again with a greeting.

## THE THIRD EPISTLE OF THE SAME AUTHOR

[Col. 1375]

1.---I, 1. “The elder to the most beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth,” and what follows. In the preceding Epistle he gave his name and added “the elder”; here he said only “the elder,” since he indicated above who this elder was. He therefore writes to Gaius, whom he rightly loved with the affection of a son, praising and encouraging his resolve in good action.

2.---I, 3. “I rejoiced greatly at the arrival of the brothers who testified to the truth” [Note: [Col. 1375] Vulg.: “When the brothers came and bore witness to your truth”]. He says that he rejoiced because, when the brothers came, he learned of Gaius’s commendable conduct. For it is truly the joy of a good father when he discovers that the way of life of his children is praiseworthy. He praises him for having shown devoted love toward the brothers, especially toward strangers, and he urges him to send such offerings ahead to the Lord, so that he himself may follow more securely. For since they received no support for life from unbelievers, it was fitting that the faithful should assist them.

He says that he wrote on their behalf to a certain Diotrephes, who appeared to exercise leadership over them; but because of his exceedingly evil will, he says that he was not heard. He presents him as someone not to be imitated, since good rather than evil people should be followed. He praises Demetrius, to whom he grants a good testimony together with the truth itself. He reserves the remaining matters that had to be said for his presence, concluding his Epistle with the dearest greeting.

## THE EPISTLE OF SAINT JUDE

[Col. 1375]

1.---I, 1. “Judas, servant of Jesus Christ but brother of James” [Vulg.: “of James, to those who are,” etc.], in the Lord the Father, and what follows. When he calls himself the servant of Christ and the brother of James, he distinguishes himself from Judas the betrayer, whom the hearing of everyone rightly detests. He therefore writes to those beloved in the Lord the Father and called and preserved in Jesus Christ, wishing them to be filled with the Lord’s mercy, peace, and love.

2.---I, 3. “Beloved, making every effort to write to you.” He says that he took commendable pains to write to the faithful concerning their common salvation, so that they would not have to believe false preachers. Yet he testifies that these men had been known to the Lord in predestination: transferring divine grace into heretical lust, they presume to deny our ruler Jesus Christ.

He reminds them that the Lord once liberated the Israelite people from the land of Egypt, but destroyed those who did not believe at all in the indignation of his justice. He also reserves for his judgment the angels who chose to lose the glory of their native dignity, binding them in gloomy chains.

He declares that Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, which sinned grievously by pursuing shameful vices of the flesh, were consumed as an example of eternal fire. He says that danger of perpetual destruction threatens those who blaspheme majesty, to such an extent that, when the archangel Michael disputed with the devil,

[Note: [Col. 1375D] Jerome teaches in his treatise *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that the Epistle of Saint Jude was formerly rejected by many because it takes testimony from the book of Enoch, which is apocryphal. This testimony is cited below, at verse 14. The dispute concerning the body of Moses also seems to have been taken from another apocryphal book, entitled *The Assumption of Moses*. Origen mentions it in *On First Principles*, book III, chapter 2. The commentary attributed to Clement of Alexandria on this passage says: “Here he confirms the Assumption of Moses.” See Sixtus of Siena, book II, who also states in book VII that Saint Jude did not refrain from citing such books, so that he might persuade those to whom he wrote by adducing testimonies even from books that possessed authority among them.

Bede notes on this passage: “We find something similar to this in the prophet Zechariah.” He adds: “There are some who say that the same people of God were called the body of Moses, because Moses himself was a portion of that people; and therefore Jude could rightly say that what he had read had happened to the people had happened to the body of Moses.”]

he did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy against the devil concerning the body of Moses. Then, when the name of the Lord was heard, the devil departed.

3.---I, 10. “But these men blaspheme whatever they were indeed ignorant of” [Vulg.: “whatever they do not know”], and what follows. After setting forth examples of evil and good angels, he returns to those who presume to disparage the Lord Christ. He says that they blaspheme the divinity, which they do not know; but in the things they know naturally—that is, bodily—like irrational animals, they entangle themselves in the mire of perversity.

He proclaims that they are on the way of Cain, that they wander in Balaam’s error concerning the idol, and that they are found in the rebellions of Korah, whom the earth’s vast chasm swallowed up. He defines their wickedness in a brief series of statements. Enoch is given as an example, since he, the seventh from Adam, prophesied that such men would perish at the Lord’s judgment.

4.---I, 17. “But you, beloved, remember the words that were foretold.” He says that they must remember what they heard from the other apostles as well: that deceivers would come in the last times, walking wickedly in their own desires. These are sensual people who do not possess the divine Spirit.

He says that the others, filled with the truest preaching, ought to remain mutually united and make progress in the Holy Spirit, which is known to have been given to them for their advancement. Thus they may reprove some who have been judged, rescue others from the burning of eternal fire, and show mercy to some who are wandering, cleansing their defiled consciences, yet in such a way that they shun their sins as worthy of execration. Thus, at the Lord’s judgment, they may receive the reward of their labor through his abundant mercy, to whom belong honor, power, splendor, and dominion before all ages, now and forever and ever.

## THE EPISTLE OF SAINT JAMES TO THE DISPERSED

[Note: [Col. 1377D] Vulg.: “The Catholic Epistle of Blessed James the Apostle.”]

[Col. 1377]

1.---I, 1. “James, servant of Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes that are in the dispersion, greetings” [Note: [Col. 1377D] Vulg.: “James, of God and of our Lord,” etc.]. The apostle James writes to the twelve Israelite tribes living in dispersion, in accordance with that threat of the Lord which says, “And I will scatter you among all the nations.” Consolation ought especially to be offered to them, since they appeared to be suffering most grievously.

2.---I, 2. “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations.” He says that it should rather be regarded as joy when the temptation of diabolical perversity pursues us, because patience is thereby born in a good mind, and God the Lord deigns to crown it.

Then, like a good physician, he prescribes a salutary remedy: if anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it especially from the one who freely bestows gifts. Yet he says that one must not hesitate in these petitions, because no one can receive who is known to ask with a doubtful mind.

He then admonishes the perversities of human beings: the humble person should rejoice in the blessedness granted to him, while the rich ought to rejoice when he recognizes that he has been humbled, because we see that the riches of this world can pass away like the form of a flowering plant.

He returns again to what he had begun, declaring blessed the person who endures temptation with equanimity, when in that contest of the Lord he is proved to have a crown of life laid up for him.

3.---I, 13. “Let no one, when he is tempted, say, ‘I am tempted by God,’” and what follows. He declares that God is not a tempter of evils, but that each person can be tempted by his own desires. For desire, when it has conceived, produces sin; and sin, when it has been completed, gives birth to death.

And lest human frailty attribute anything good to its own strength, he declares that every good gift and every perfect gift can descend from above, from the Father of lights. From him, through sacred baptism, he says that we have been freely begotten—not by merits—so that we might be the beginning of a new creation.

He also advises that we should be swift to hear but slow either to speak or to anger, because human anger cannot fulfill divine justice. Therefore, casting away malice and uncleanness, we ought to receive the word with gentleness, for it can save us in that resurrection.

4.---I, 22. “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only.” He reminds us that we ought not merely to be hearers of the law but rather its doers. For if anyone is only a hearer of the law, he is like someone who looks at himself in a mirror and, when he has departed, forgets himself and is deceived by his own image. But whoever fulfills the law of freedom in deeds and remains fixed in that same determination will be considered blessed in his action.

If one of the religious is excessively bold in speech, his religion is altogether vain. For conduct is praiseworthy before God if we are not inclined to loquacity but are most diligently prepared to carry out his commandments.

5.---II, 1. “My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with partiality” [Col. 1378C] [Vulg.: “of Christ of glory”]. He says that the faith of the Lord Jesus Christ must not be assessed with partiality, so that the rich are honored while the poor are held in contempt. For it is exceedingly unjust to judge a person not according to merit but according to the amount of his possessions.

Since God chose the poor in this world and made them apostles, it is undoubtedly sacrilege to oppose his judgments. Moreover, since the rich are culpable through their presumption regarding their possessions, it is impious to despise the poor, who are shown to assume nothing of this kind—especially since it is written, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Therefore, if someone observes the whole law but is taught to offend against it in one commandment of love, he becomes guilty of the entire law.

He also adds that strict judgment will be imposed on the person who showed mercy to no one. For when mercy is shown, it undoubtedly triumphs over judgment.

6.---II, 14. “What will it profit, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works?” [Vulg.: “if he does not have works”]. He says that faith without good works cannot save anyone.

[Note: [Col. 1377D] If another proof could be added to the perpetual orthodox doctrine concerning the necessity of good works in adults—which is so clearly established from this Epistle—it would be supplied by this interpretation, in which it is plainly explained that a person can be justified by works, and cannot be saved by faith alone. The same point is made repeatedly: “Only the quality of deeds is to be weighed,” and so forth.

From this it is clear how deceptively and sophistically those proceed who try to force passages into another meaning, passages in which the term “works” denotes Jewish legal observances—as in this very little work: “Abraham did not find the Lord’s grace through works but through faith”; while shortly before it says: “A person is not justified through the law of circumcision or anything similar, but through the law of faith”; and: “He says that the Gentile grasped righteousness through faith, not through works,” followed by: “For the Jews, believing according to the letter and not spiritually,” and so forth.

Elsewhere: “He reproves the Galatians because they had again returned to the works of the law.” This shows what is included under the name “works,” when works are condemned and declared in no way necessary for salvation.]

For if someone asks for alms and is told, “God gives it to you,” the words are indeed faithful, but the Lord’s commands are not fulfilled at all, since he commanded, “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6:30).

He confirms that faith without works is dead by the example of the demons. He again teaches that Abraham’s faith was perfect when he offered his son to be sacrificed upon the sacred altars. He also sets forth the example of Rahab the prostitute, who is known to have been justified not by faith alone but by her deed. In every respect he proves that a person is justified by works and cannot be saved by faith alone.

7.---III, 1. “Do not become many teachers, my brothers,” and what follows. He forbids becoming many teachers, since one is often taught to offend through the boldness of the tongue. For if anyone does not offend in speech, he appears to be perfect and brings his body under control.

Just as we guide horses with bridles, steer ships with rudders, and set great forests ablaze with a small fire, so our tongue is a small member, but it expands with great exultation. Although all beasts can be tamed, the uncontrolled tongue alone cannot be subdued, since through it we bless God and through it we curse the human being who is known to have been made in his image and likeness.

He also draws highly appropriate comparisons: although everything else preserves the order of its nature, the tongue alone cannot remain within the rules of discipline. Therefore whoever is wise should show his conduct in gentleness and moderated wisdom.

8.---III, 14. “But if you have bitter jealousy and contentions in your hearts.” Bitter jealousy is not fitting for perfected men, since such things are proved to be conceived not from above but through diabolical fraud. For where jealousy and contention are, there are instability and every evil work, which divine authority condemns.

But he celebrates saving wisdom with manifold praise: it is granted through heavenly inspiration, sows peace, and is contained in the hearts of the faithful. He declares that wars and quarrels arise from desire, from which the human race is known to suffer.

From this also comes the fact that those who ask wrongly do not obtain the rewards of good things, because whoever is a friend of the world is an enemy of God. Let us therefore be subject to Christ, lest we be justly handed over to the devil, so that he who takes captive may flee from us and he who liberates may draw near.

For if our appearance is changed in affliction and our joy is turned into sorrow, then the Lord exalts us, if he recognizes that we have cast ourselves down before him.

9.---IV, 2. “Do not speak evil of one another” [Vulg. omits “of”], and what follows. Here he teaches that whoever speaks evil of his brother speaks evil of the law and sets himself up as an unjust judge, although there is one Lord, the lawgiver and judge.

He also reproves those who rashly undertake to do something, placing in their own will what is known to have been established in the Lord’s will. He says that such people do not know what may happen when the day arrives; for those who stretch out their pride through wicked arrogance often breathe their last.

Therefore he tells the rich of the world to weep, because the things in which they seem to place their confidence are certainly consumed and perish. He teaches that it is a most serious evil to hoard treasures in the last times, when, with the Lord’s judgment near, the fruit of good action should already be sought. He charges the Jews with having killed the righteous man who is known to have come to them to save them.

10.---V, 7. “Therefore be patient, brothers, until the coming of the Lord,” and what follows. He reminds the faithful that they must be patient until the coming of the Lord, just as the farmers of this world receive the morning and evening fruit according to the season.

He says that the judge should not be endured much longer, since he confirms that he stands before the very gates of the world. He urges them to take the prophets as an example of patience, since they resolved to endure the Lord’s coming long beforehand.

The example of the most holy man Job is also given. By enduring his sufferings he triumphantly conquered them and, with the Lord’s help, overcame the devil’s deceptions. Under a merciful ruler no one perishes except the person who disdains to hope for his own deliverance.

11.---V, 12. “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear,” and what follows. After all his admonitions he gives the faithful a salutary rule, saying that one must not swear under any circumstances. A Christian ought to say that what is is, and that what is not is not.

For if someone is weighed down by another person’s injury

[Note: [Col. 1379D] Baronium discusses at greater length, under the year 63, the force and use of extreme sacramental unction as displayed in this Epistle. But that remedy should be used against injuries is wholly unknown to our writers of chivalric works, as they are called, some of whom I have examined.

Perhaps he understands the passage as referring to bodily illness produced by another person’s injury or violence, for which anointing with oil would seem especially appropriate, also as a form of human assistance. We shall readily be persuaded that this was the author’s meaning if we understand the particle *vel*—“or”—as having been put for *et*—“and.” That usage occurs more than once in these *Complexiones*. Alternatively, *reliqua* may stand for the Greek *τοῦ, et caetera*, “and what follows”: “the priests, or the other leaders,” instead of “and the other leaders.” Such usage is common among medieval writers.]

or is shaken by bodily weakness, he says that a presbyter should be summoned. Through faithful prayer and the application of holy oil, the presbyter is to save the person who appears afflicted. He also promises that sins will be forgiven those who have been visited by either form of prayer. He declares that the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful before the Lord.

Finally, he adds the example of Elijah, who closed the heavens by his word and again opened them when he prayed. He concludes in summary that whoever frees his brother from error dissolves the bonds of his own sins through the devotion of love.

# THE SUMMARIES OF M. AURELIUS CASSIODORUS ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES AND THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN

[Col. 1381]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1381A] Luke, one of the evangelists, who wrote down the Lord’s teaching with heavenly truth, also encompassed the Acts of the Apostles in a faithful narrative, so that the deeds of the blessed might harmonize with the Lord’s commands in concordant grace.

We have encompassed this work in seventy-two chapters,

[Note: [Col. 1381B] The division of the sacred books—whether it was originally introduced by the practice of public readings in Christian assemblies, for the easier citation and discovery of passages, or by expositors and interpreters—was once uncertain and arranged according to anyone’s discretion.

We have noted how different this division is from Jerome’s division into chapters, which our author used in the Apostolic Epistles; the numbers designate sections. The interpreter commonly used divided the book of Acts into twenty-eight chapters, while others divided it into forty, as appears in Oecumenius. Cassiodorus himself divided it into seventy-two, so that it might equal the number of the disciples to whom he seems to extend the name “apostles,” and so that the sacred Acts of the Apostles might be completed with the same number as the number of those chosen.

That the name “apostle” once had a broader application we also learn from the ancient martyrology of Florentius. Cassiodorus was especially pleased by this number. In *Divine Readings*, chapter 13, when speaking of Augustine, who comprehended the divine Scriptures in the reckoning of seventy-one books, he continues: “When you add to these the unity of the Holy Trinity, the complete and glorious perfection of the entire book results.” At that point there is an error not yet noticed. One should read *totius librae*—“of the entire pound”—as will be clear from what follows. Since the scribe did not understand what that word meant there, he removed it and replaced it with *libri*—“of the book.”]

and we have thought it appropriate to note our abbreviation at each individual place, so that the sacred Acts of the Apostles might truly be completed in the same number as those chosen, as the evangelist Luke himself testifies.

For it was fitting that its order should have the quantity of a *libra*,

[Note: [Col. 1381C] I hesitated at this passage, since the manuscript contained only *LIB.*, the other letters having been erased by age and abrasion. When I had gathered my thoughts for a little while, I supplied *librae*, recognizing that the number referred to a pound, which was called “declining” or “western,” either because it had been reduced or because it was used in the West.

It therefore appears that for a long time the custom persisted of designating the number seventy-two by the golden pound. Valentinian the Elder had fixed it in such a way that seventy-two gold solidi made a pound, whereas under Constantine the Great it consisted of eighty-four. See Gothofredus on book VII, title 24, of the *Theodosian Code*, book I.

We read in the acts of the Council of Sinuessa: “All these chosen men are a declining pound who bear witness.” Binius notes that seventy-two witnesses are meant. The names preceding those words are indeed eighty-five; nevertheless, seventy-two witnesses are mentioned below. From this mention of the declining pound it may be inferred that those acts were fabricated long after the time of Pope Marcellinus.]

by which it is proved to have been dedicated to heavenly justice.

Perhaps we have suitably joined the Apocalypse of blessed John to these Acts, because it describes the heavenly kingdom in a wondrous narrative, since such a dwelling will be granted to such men. We have arranged it into thirty-three chapters,

[Note: [Col. 1382B] We see the Apocalypse divided into seventy-two chapters in commentaries bearing the name of Arethas, while the Vulgate version divides it into twenty-two. Cassiodorus divides it into thirty-three, customarily sketching a double reason, for whatever number is given he immediately finds or creates a mystery.

See the preface to the work *On the Arts* concerning the number seven; below, in Apocalypse 4, seven are likewise set forth to indicate perfection.

Dividing Holy Scripture into seventy-five books, he asserts that this number is consecrated by two miracles: the number of Abraham’s years when he joyfully received the Lord’s promise, and the number of souls who entered the borders of Egypt with the patriarch Jacob. See *Divine Readings*, chapter 14.

He concluded the orthography in twelve books because there are twelve hours, twelve months, and twelve heavenly signs. But why he asserts here that thirty signifies the lofty summit of the heavens may be debated by those who investigate the powers and mysteries of numbers.]

and have taken care to divide it according to the years of the Lord Christ. In this arrangement, thirty signifies the lofty summit of the heavens and is associated with the venerable perfection of the Holy Trinity.

It is difficult to compress obscure statements more briefly when what we wish to explain requires fuller treatment. But because Tychonius the Donatist explained this book subtly and carefully,

[Note: [Col. 1382C] In that exposition, *Divine Readings*, chapter 9, teaches that Tychonius handed down some things that should not be rejected, but mixed in other things with the dregs of his poisonous doctrine.]

God providing—he who prepares an antidote for our salvation from poisons—the necessity imposed by our intended brevity requires that some meanings of his novel and perverse doctrine be passed over. We seem thereby not so much to satisfy our reader as to introduce him, since without harm to his understanding he finds in that work what an orthodox and diligent reader seeks.

## THE SUMMARIES OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

[Col. 1381]

1.---I, 1. “I composed the first account, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach,” and what follows. After completing the account of the Gospel, which Luke is recalled to have written after the Lord’s resurrection, he also testifies that he gathered together the Acts of the Apostles, writing to Theophilus, so that the unquestionable perfection of the Christian faith might appear through the most certain testimonies.

He says first that Jesus Christ, about to ascend to the Father, commanded his disciples not to depart from Jerusalem, so that, although they had been baptized, they might be filled with the fullness of the Holy Spirit.

2.---I, 6. “Those who had gathered together therefore asked him,” and what follows. He says that the Lord Christ was asked by those who had gathered together whether the restoration of the Israelite kingdom would take place at that time, which he had promised would come. But it is clear that the determination of that time was withheld chiefly for our benefit. Rather, it was proclaimed to them that on the fiftieth day they would receive the power of the Holy Spirit, so that throughout the whole earth they might bear witness to the mighty works of perfect faith.

3.—I, 9. “And when he had said these things, while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes,” and so forth. Among the words he had spoken above, he suddenly testifies, in the presence of the apostles, that the Lord ascended into heaven; and, lest anyone should believe that such a miracle had been displayed through some fantastic illusion, he says that angels of God stood beside them, saying: “Why are you astonished at this? Thus [he will come] to judge, since he is known to have been taken up from your midst.” Then he says that the apostles returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, where these things had happened, and entered the upper room, where the eleven lived together—he gives their names. They persevered in their prayers with the holy women, Mary the mother of the Lord, and his brothers, so that the one who had appeared to be taken away might not depart from them.

4.—I, 15. “And in those days Peter stood up in the midst of the brothers and said,” and so forth. Then blessed Peter, recalling the example of the hundred-and-eighth Psalm (verse 8), spoke in the midst of the brothers, who numbered about one hundred and twenty: “With Judas the betrayer removed, we ought to think about a twelfth disciple” [supplement: “of”], so that that perfect number might be completed. Then, having set Joseph and Matthias before them, they prayed and cast lots; the choice fell upon Matthias, and he was counted as the twelfth apostle.

5.—II, 1. “When the days of Pentecost were being completed, they were all together in one place” [Vulgate: “And when,” etc., “in the same place”], and so forth. When the fifty days had been completed, as the Lord Christ had promised them, suddenly there came from heaven a powerful sound, with the Holy Spirit arriving; and, while all were sitting in that same house, heavenly fire appeared above their heads, and they spoke in the languages of various nations. When this report had spread, men of different peoples who had gathered in Jerusalem came and were astonished to hear them—although they were Galileans—speaking in the languages of the nations and proclaiming the mighty works of God. Some, looking reasonably upon what had happened, rightly thought that it had been granted by a divine gift; others, foolishly mocking them, attributed it instead to the fault of drunkenness.

6.—II, 14. “But Peter, standing with the eleven, raised his voice and spoke to them,” and so forth. Blessed Peter, standing with the eleven apostles, spoke in a loud voice while everyone was astonished, saying that, since it was the third hour of the day [supplement: “when it was”], they were not, as some supposed, drunk with new wine, but rather filled through the gracious favor of the Holy Spirit. He confirmed this also by the example of the prophet Joel, declaring to them that the knowledge which had been manifested was to be attributed not to drunkenness but truly to divine mercy. Then he rebuked the wickedness of the Jews, who had preferred to crucify the Lord Christ, whom God raised from the dead after he had broken the laws of hell [i.e. the bonds of the underworld]. This too is confirmed by the example of the fifteenth Psalm.

7.—II, 29. “Men and brothers, let me speak boldly to you about the patriarch David,” and so forth. Since the apostle Peter had mentioned David, who was held among the Jews as a venerable prophet, he made him the starting point of his preaching. Yet he proves that David was dead and says that his tomb was among them, although David himself had prophesied that the flesh of the Lord Christ would in no way be subject to corruption. God raised him from the dead, and he received the promises of the Father in complete truth. Peter declares that the gift which was being witnessed had been bestowed by Christ himself; for that he was David’s Lord is proved by the example of the hundred-and-ninth Psalm. By this preaching, he testifies, three thousand men were pierced with remorse [or “convicted,” literally “pierced”] and baptized.

8.—II, 42. “They were persevering in the apostles’ teaching,” and so forth. While those who had been converted remained most devoutly in the teaching they had received, and the apostles repeatedly displayed great miracles, the fear of the Lord and the number of the faithful increased daily. There was great concord among the believers, so that each person sold his own property and whatever a brother needed was duly supplied. They also showed great devotion in assembling at the temple; they took their food in simplicity of heart and with thanksgiving. For this reason the merciful Lord continually increased their number. Peter and John, as they were going up to the temple for prayer, took by the hand a man lame from his mother’s womb and made him walk with strong steps. When the people saw this, they were filled with immeasurable astonishment, and their eagerness to see them increased more and more with heightened devotion.

9.—III, 12. “But when Peter saw this, he answered the people,” and so forth. When the apostle Peter saw the people stirred to eagerness for the faith, he said that attention should not be directed to himself in such deeds, but that the Lord Christ should be glorified, whom they themselves had resolved to crucify. Attributing to them the other things they had done in the Lord’s passion, he said that Christ himself had brought about such deeds as plainly exceeded human powers. He urged them to turn to him before the time of judgment, so that they might deserve pardon for their error. He proved by the testimony of Moses that they had to obey him in all things; for he was the one promised in Abraham’s seed, who could save each person from his own wickedness.

10.—IV, 1. “While they were speaking these words to the people” [the Vulgate does not have “these words”], and what follows. When the rulers, priests, and other leading men of the Jews saw that about five thousand men had believed the apostles, they decided to have them sent to prison, lest the whole multitude believe them. On the following day, after a council had been held, they brought them forward and asked by what power or in whose name they had been able to perform such miracles. The apostle Peter, as was his custom, declared in a clear voice that this miracle had been performed in the name of Christ. He is the stone, as it is read in Psalm 117, the cornerstone, whom the Jews indeed thought ought to be crucified, but God raised from the dead. Then, astonished at the confidence of men whom they did not know to have been educated in letters, and recognizing that they had been with Christ, they were moved by the truth itself and ordered them not to preach any longer in the name of Jesus Christ.

11.—IV, 19. “But Peter and John answered and said,” and so forth. Peter and John therefore answered the priests and the entire council that they ought to obey the Lord’s commands more than human terrors. With steadfast reasoning, they were dismissed from the council because of the people whom they had won over by such an act. When they came to their own people, they told them what had happened. Then, giving glory to God, they said in a loud voice what is written in the second Psalm: “Why did the nations rage?” (Psalm II, 1), and so forth. They also proved that the things written had come to pass in the city of Jerusalem according to the plans foretold, and asked that greater grace for preaching and miracles be granted to them. After this prayer they were filled with the Holy Spirit and preached the word of the Lord with unceasing power. All the believers had one heart and one soul, so that none of them was oppressed by any want; rather, those who possessed something gladly gave it, so that it might benefit everyone in common.

12.—IV, 36. “Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas by the apostles,” and so forth. Here examples of the faithful and the deceitful are given. Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas because he offered the full price, departed unharmed. Ananias, however, together with his wife Sapphira, defrauded the price of the estate that had been sold; they were cursed and surrendered their unhappy souls in the sight of everyone. The men themselves carried him away, and afterward carried away his lifeless wife. As a result, fear increased among all, as did faith and the apostles’ preaching, which continually grew. None of the opponents dared to join them, because popular favor toward them was constantly increasing, especially when the sick were healed by the word of the apostles and those passing by were healed by Peter’s shadow [perhaps: “the shadow of one passing by,” *transeuntis*]. This was done not only by the people of that city, but also by the inhabitants of neighboring cities, as their faith increased.

13.—V, 17. “But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him,” and so forth. When these things became known, the high priest and the rest of the Sadducean sect were filled with great jealousy. They arrested the apostles, set guards over them, and shut them in the public prison. An angel of the Lord opened the doors, led them out, and commanded them, as usual, to teach the people in the temple. The rulers and priests, unaware of this, sent officers to the public prison on the following day. They found the prison carefully guarded, but none of those whom they had shut in the previous day. Then, when others informed them, they learned that the men they were seeking were in the temple proclaiming the mighty works of the Lord to the people. The magistrate therefore went to the synagogue and brought them before the council without using force; again they attempted to prohibit their customary preaching. Then Peter and the apostles, having received confidence, boldly proclaimed the word of the Lord [printed: *elatabant*, “they proclaimed”]. The others were therefore extremely angry and secretly plotted to kill them, since the people were in fear.

14.—V, 34. “But a certain Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law” [Note: “[Column 1385] The Vulgate has *honorabilis*, etc.; to be supplied: ‘Gamaliel, whom,’ etc.”], rose in the council and said. The apostle Paul also praises him. In a public speech he persuaded them to cease persecuting the apostles, saying: “If their preaching is from men, it will undoubtedly fail, as happened with Theudas and Judas the Galilean. But if it is from God, it cannot be destroyed by any power.” Then they had the apostles beaten and sent away, warning them not to involve themselves any further in such preaching. But the apostles preached the word more steadfastly to the nations. Meanwhile there arose a complaint from the Greeks, because their widows were treated with contempt and disgrace in the daily ministry. For this reason seven chosen men were appointed and made deacons, so that such matters might be administered in an orderly and measured way, while the apostles devoted themselves solely to preaching. This honor was also consecrated over them by the laying on of hands. At that time a multitude of priests hastened to obey the Lord.

15.—VI, 7. “A great multitude of priests also obeyed the faith,” and so forth. One of those who had been chosen for the administration of the tables, named Stephen, performed great signs and wonders through the power of the Lord Christ. Since none of the unbelievers could withstand his preaching, false witnesses were brought against him, who said that he had spoken blasphemous words against God and Moses. They set him before the council and wished to question him about such statements. Then, finding an opportunity, he explained the order of the Old Testament which concerned the Lord the Savior, narrating it in accordance with the truth.

16.—VII, 54. “When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart” [Vulgate: *dissecabantur*, “were cut apart”] “and they gnashed their teeth.” Unable to endure Stephen’s preaching, the unbelievers hastened with united purpose toward his destruction. He raised his eyes to heaven and saw the Son standing at the Father’s right hand. When he had spoken this with complete truth, the crowd of madmen rushed upon him; after casting him outside the camp, they overwhelmed him with stones. But while dying, Stephen prayed more for them, that such a crime might not be charged against his persecutors. Paul also consented to this killing, and through him a great persecution arose against the Church established in Jerusalem. After Stephen’s body had been buried amid pious lamentation, the aforesaid Paul devastated the Church of God with as much zeal as he was later to defend it with devotion.

Philip, however, the deacon and another of the seven, went down to a city of Samaria and persistently preached the word of the Lord. He performed many miracles through the power of Christ for the people who desired them, and for this reason the city was filled with great joy.

17.—VIII, 9. “But there was a certain man named Simon” [Column 1387A] “who had previously been a magician in the city,” and so forth. While many were believing, Simon Magus, entirely notorious for his demonic arts, saw such great miracles and himself eagerly sought baptism. But when the Samaritans devoutly received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the hands of the apostles Peter and John, he offered them money so that they too might grant him the power for the grace of the Holy Spirit to be bestowed through the laying on of his hands. Peter rebuked him with a deserved reprimand, saying that he had no share with the faithful, since he believed that the Holy Spirit could be obtained by money. Convicted by this rebuke, he asked with his lips that prayer be made for him, although he did not possess it in his heart. The apostles, meanwhile, did not cease preaching the word of the Lord throughout the many villages of Samaria.

18.—VIII, 26. “But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip,” [Column 1387B] “saying,” and so forth. The angel instructed Philip to go toward the road along which the eunuch of Queen Candace was passing. Returning from Jerusalem, which he had come to worship out of devotion of mind, the eunuch was sitting in his chariot and reading the passage of the prophet Isaiah where it says: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer” [Vulgate, verse 32: “before its shearer, without a voice”], “so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah LIII, 7), and so forth. Then Philip said to him: “Do you think you understand what you are reading?” The eunuch made him climb into the chariot and reveal to him the secrets of the Scriptures. Receiving these with faithful understanding, he saw water along the road and, inflamed by the ardor of his mind, immediately asked to be baptized. When this had been done, the Holy Spirit fell upon the eunuch, and Philip disappeared through a sudden translation. He was found at Azotus, spreading the word of the Lord through his customary preaching.

19.—IX, 1. “But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the Lord’s disciples” [Vulgate: “breathing threats and slaughter”], and so forth. Paul, still intending to harm the faithful of the Lord [Note: “[Column 1387D] So also the Vulgate has it throughout: Acts XVIII, 10, *ut noceat te*, ‘so that it may harm you’; Revelation II, 5, *eos nocere*, ‘to harm them’; plainly from the construction of the verb βλάπτω, *blaptō*, ‘to harm.’ Plautus more than once attached the same case to this verb. In the Latin translation we detect traces of Greek syntax in more than one place: *obumbrabit tibi*, ‘it will overshadow you’; *oriens illuminare his*, ‘the rising one, enlighten them’; *decem millia ad te non appropinquabit*, ‘ten thousand will not approach you’; and in this very verse of Acts, *spirans minarum et caedis*, ‘breathing threats and slaughter,’ from the Greek ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου, where Cassiodorus’s version has *spirans minas et caedes*, ‘breathing threats and slaughters.’”], asked the high priest for letters so that, if he found any preachers of Christ in Jerusalem, he might bring them bound. This request was more truly his own release, without doubt; for on the very journey the Lord said to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” At these words he trembled and fell face down. Struck blind, he entered Damascus led by the hands of others. In that city there was a disciple named Ananias, who was told to go to Paul and restore his sight by laying hands upon him. But Ananias, remembering his former deeds, replied to the Lord that Paul was a persecutor of the Church, so that he had recently received authority from the rulers to bind the Lord’s faithful in chains. The divine clemency answered him that Paul had become a vessel of election, although previously it had known him to be filled with criminal wickedness.

20.—IX, 17. “And Ananias went and entered the house, laid his hand upon him, and said” [Vulgate: “and laying his [Column 1388A] hand upon him, he said”]. Ananias entered to Paul and, by laying on his hands, cleansed his eyes as the scales fell away. He was baptized in the name of Christ and was also restored by taking food, since he had been exhausted by a three-day fast. Then, visited by heavenly mercy and strengthened in Christian teaching, he preached the word of the Lord in the synagogues, happily transformed.

After some days the Jews also armed themselves with plots against him. He was placed in a basket by the disciples, secretly lowered from the wall by a rope, and reached Jerusalem. Presented to the apostles by Barnabas, he reported to them what had happened to him through the Lord’s gift. Then, joined to them in the dearest fellowship, he preached together with them the Lord Christ, whom he had previously thought ought to be persecuted. Therefore the unbelievers hastened to hand him over to death, but the apostles, by holy deliberation, decided that he should be sent away to Tarsus [Vulgate, verse 30: “Tarsum,” Tarsus]. All Judea and Samaria, enjoying peace, grew in the glory of the Lord.

21.—IX, 32. “And it happened that Peter, as he passed through all the places” [Vulgate: “that Peter, as he passed through all the places”], “came down to the saints who lived in Lydda,” and so forth. When Peter came to Lydda, he found there a paralytic named Aeneas, who had been lying on a pallet for eight years. He said to him: “The Lord Jesus Christ heals you” (verse 34), and he was immediately healed. When this miracle had been seen, all who lived in Lydda and Sharon were converted to God.

The woman Dorcas, who devoted herself to almsgiving and holy works and lived in Joppa, died. A message was sent to Peter so that he might come there and display the mighty works of God. The crowd of the poor whom Dorcas supplied with clothing begged him to restore her to them as the mother of the poor. Then Peter prayed on his knees, saying: “Rise in the name of Jesus Christ” [Vulgate, verse 40: “Tabitha, arise”]. He presented her alive to the people who had been summoned. For this reason many believed in the power of the Lord. Thus it came about that Peter remained for many days with a certain Simon the tanner.

22.—X, 1. “There was a certain man in Caesarea named Cornelius,” and so forth. Cornelius, a Gentile living in Caesarea, devoted to almsgiving and prayer, saw in a vision an angel of God saying to him: “Your prayers and almsgiving have come into the Lord’s presence. [Column 1388D] Send to Joppa for Peter, who is lodging in the house of Simon the tanner, so that he may come quickly to save you” [Note: “[Column 1388D] Vulgate: ‘They have ascended as a memorial in the sight of God. And now send men to Joppa and summon a certain Simon who is surnamed Peter. He is lodging with a certain Simon the tanner, whose …’”].

While Peter was in the aforesaid house, about the sixth hour, when he was hungry and wished to taste food, he fell into an ecstasy. He saw a vessel like a white linen cloth in which were all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles, and birds, being lowered from heaven. A voice came to him: “Rise, Peter, slaughter” [Vulgate, [Column 1389A] verse 13: “kill”] “and eat.” A little later: “What the Lord has purified, do not call unclean” [Vulgate, verse 15: “do not call common”]. This happened three times, and the vessel was received back into heaven. For it signified that the peoples of the whole world would believe in the Lord Christ.

23.—X, 17. “While Peter was perplexed within himself about what the vision he had seen might mean,” and so forth. While Peter was astonished and pondering the aforesaid vision, the Holy Spirit said to him: “Behold, men are seeking you, whom Cornelius has sent. Rise and go with them, because they have been sent at my command to seek you” [Note: “[Column 1389D] Vulgate: ‘Behold, three men are seeking you. Rise therefore, go down, and go with them, doubting nothing, because I have sent them.’”].

When Peter went down to them without hesitation, they explained in order the reason for which they had been sent. He received them as guests [corrected reading: “having received them as guests”] and on the following day hurried with them to Cornelius. When Cornelius saw him, he fell at his feet and worshiped him. Peter, preserving humility, prevented this from happening and asked him—although he had already been instructed—why he had summoned him. Cornelius related what the angel had told him while he was praying, waiting to hear from Peter himself, together with the others, what might pertain to the salvation of all.

24.—X, 34. “Then Peter opened his mouth” [Vulgate: “his mouth”] “and said,” and so forth. Peter said: “In truth I have discovered that God is not one who accepts persons, but that in every nation the person who practices righteousness is pleasing to him” [Note: “[Column 1389D] Vulgate: ‘For God is not one who accepts persons; [Column 1390D] but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.’”].

Then, continuing with words of right faith, he preached to them that Jesus Christ was the Lord of all things. The Jews had resolved to crucify him, but after rising from the dead he lived among his disciples for forty days [Column 1389C], together with the other matters required by the order of Christian faith. While he was speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon the believers, and those who had come with Peter rejoiced exceedingly because they saw that such gifts were being granted also among the Gentiles. Then he ordered them to receive the grace of baptism in the name of Christ. When this report spread, the brothers who were in Judea were filled with great joy. Peter, proceeding to Jerusalem, continued to preach the word of the Lord with constant devotion.

25.—XI, 2. “When he had gone up to Jerusalem” [Vulgate: “Peter went up to Jerusalem”], “those who were of the circumcision disputed with him.” When Peter had gone up to Jerusalem, the faithful Jews disputed with him about why he had entered the homes of the uncircumcised and eaten with them. He then truthfully recounted what sort of vision had instructed him and what had been commanded him by the Godhead. When they heard these things, the whole people gave thanks to God, because the Lord Christ had granted both the Gentiles life-giving repentance and the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

26.—XI, 19. “Now those who had been scattered by the tribulation that had taken place” [Vulgate: “and those who indeed had been scattered”], “and so forth.” Those who had been scattered during Stephen’s passion traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews. Yet among them there were some who, after entering Antioch, spoke the words of preaching to the Gentiles. A great multitude of the people believed through them, and news of this reached as far as Jerusalem.

Barnabas, sent by the apostles, approved what had been reported about them. He rejoiced greatly and urged many to remain in the purpose they had undertaken. When Barnabas also heard that Saul was in Tarsus, he went to him. He brought him as far as Antioch, and it is known that he preached with him in the church for a whole year; it is declared that they converted many. It was there that they were first called Christians.

In those days prophets arrived who announced the famine that was to come and that occurred under the emperor Claudius. The disciples are remembered as having sent whatever they could obtain to the brothers living in Judea through the hands of Barnabas and Paul.

27.—XII, 1. “At that time Herod stretched out his hand” [Note: “[Column 1390D] Read *manum* or *manus*. Vulgate: ‘King Herod stretched out his hands.’”] “to afflict certain members of the Church.” King Herod, in impious presumption, killed James, the brother of John, who was preaching the word of the Lord. Seeing that this pleased the Jews, he also sent Peter to prison, assigning sixteen soldiers to guard him with great care. For him the whole Church offered unceasing prayer. On the day before the appointed judgment, an angel visited him, and he is known to have been freed both from the bonds of his chains and from the dangers posed by his guards, so that he thought in his sleep that what was truly happening was a dream. When he came to himself, however, he recognized in manifest reality that the Lord had deigned to free him through his angel.

He came to the house of Mary, the mother of John, where a multitude of the faithful were praying for him. After repeatedly knocking on the door, he finally entered and told them how, when the angel came, he had been released from the bonds of his imprisonment. He instructed them to announce this to James and the other brothers.

28.—XII, 18. “When day had come, there was no small” [Vulgate: “no little”] “disturbance among the soldiers,” and what follows. When day had dawned, a great dispute arose among the prison guards about how Peter had escaped so many human watchmen and so many chains. King Herod, not finding Peter, was extremely angry with the guards, whom he ordered to be brought before him.

He himself went down from Judea to Caesarea [Vulgate: “from Judea to Caesarea.”] Because he was angry with the people, he was appeased by a great supplication after his chamberlain Blastus had been won over. There, dressed in royal clothing and sitting on the tribunal, he spoke exceedingly arrogantly against the Lord. The angel of the Lord struck him because he had not given glory to God, and, swarming with worms, he breathed his last. After these things had been seen, the faith of the Lord increased everywhere.

Barnabas and Saul, taking with them John who was surnamed Mark, left Jerusalem and went as far as Antioch, where a blessed assembly of prophets and teachers was to be seen. The Holy Spirit said to them that they should not hold back Barnabas and Saul, but should permit them to carry out that for which they appeared to have been chosen. Coming to Salamis, they preached throughout the whole island as far as Paphos the word that had been entrusted to them by the Lord’s gracious favor.

Meanwhile they encountered a Jewish false prophet named Bariesus, who tried to oppose them and Paul before Sergius the proconsul [Note: “[Column 1391D] Here you see a man being torn apart and divided into two: from the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, are formed ‘Sergius the proconsul’ and ‘Paul the prudent man.’ In verse 20, *redempto Blasto*, whether from his manuscript or conjecturing a kind of persuasion.”] and Paul the prudent [Note: “[Column 1391D] Vulgate: ‘Who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a prudent man.’”]. But, being restrained by the Lord’s power, he accomplished nothing.

29.—XIII, 9. “But Saul, who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, said” [Vulgate: “gesturing toward him, he said”]. He continues what he began above. In the presence of Sergius the proconsul and Paul the prudent man, the apostle Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, vehemently rebuked Bariesus the false prophet [Column 1391B]. To show that this denunciation had been made out of devotion to the Lord, he said to him: “You will be blind and will not see the sun at all for a time” [Vulgate, verse 11: “not seeing the sun”]. A dark mist immediately came over him and so closed his natural sight that he sought other men’s hands, by whose support he might depart. When the display of this miracle had become known, the judges who saw it were converted, believing that the teaching was truly that of the Most High God, which was shown to be confirmed by such miracles.

30.—XIII, 13. “And when Paul and those who were with him had sailed from Paphos,” and what follows. When Paul and Barnabas, together with the others who had come with them, had sailed from Paphos, they came [*venerunt* is absent] to Perge in Pamphylia and passed through it. From there John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem.

Paul and Barnabas, however, traveling through Perge, came to Antioch of Pisidia. When they entered the synagogue, they heard the prophets and the law being read. The rulers of the synagogue sent to them, asking that if any of them had a word of exhortation, he should speak it, just as they had done in other cities where they had preached the truth entrusted to them.

Then Paul, having made silence with his hand, preached the teaching of the Lord Christ to the people. He demonstrated it through the testimonies of the prophets that were being read, so that by the truth disclosed he might lead them to the fullest faith. He declared that the Lord Christ alone was the one who justifies the severity of the law through the gift of his grace. They had to beware lest, as Scripture warns, they refuse to believe what the truth itself is known to admonish them.

31.—XIII, 42. “As they were leaving, they asked that they speak to them the word of God on the following Sabbath” [Vulgate: “that they speak these words to them”]. As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the crowd of Jews begged them to repeat their words about the Lord Christ when the coming Sabbath arrived.

On the following Sabbath, when the people had gathered most eagerly to hear, some of the Jews, stirred by great zeal, tried to contradict them. Paul and Barnabas answered them: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it, so, as it was commanded us, we turn to the Gentiles” [Note: “[Column 1391D] Vulgate, verse 46: ‘You reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life; behold, we turn to the Gentiles.’”].

When they heard this, the Gentiles received the Christian *daugma* [Note: “[Column 1391D] So the book has it; likewise *plaustrum* and *plostrum*; *Plautia* and *Plotia* are the same family. An old capitulary codex at Verona: *et occisum Aunam*, where *Onam* is usually read in Saint Jerome, Book I Against Jovinian. The praenomen *Aulus* is written *OLUS* on certain stones, as Reinesius and Fabretti attest. *Ou* likewise: an ancient inscription in Gruter, page 506: *JOURE dicendo*. Victorinus, in *Orthography*: hence you read *loucetios*, *nouncios*; on coins, *Fourius*, *Foulvius*, and so forth. See the fragments of laws excavated from bronze tablets by Sigonius and Ursinus.”] [correct reading: *dogma*, “teaching”] with the most ready disposition.

The dissenters, however, in their grief, stirred up respectable women and the leading men of the city, and expelled Barnabas and Paul from their homes. They came to Iconium and converted many to the Lord. Again a sedition stirred up by their adversaries arose against them, but with the Lord’s help it was quickly calmed. Thus it came about that some sided with the apostles, while others certainly sided with the Jews.

32.—XIV, 5. “When an assault had been made by the Gentiles” [Column 1392B] “and the Jews with their rulers,” and so forth. When the sedition stirred up at Iconium had sought to destroy Paul and Barnabas, they fled to Lystra and Derbe, or [*vel* for *et*, “and”] to other regions of Lycaonia. There the entire population was converted to the Christian religion.

At Lystra a certain man had been infirm in his feet from his mother’s womb and lay there. Before everyone, Paul looked at him and commanded in a loud voice, in the name of Jesus Christ: “Rise, sound upon your feet.” When the crowd of Lycaonia saw this, they thought that the men were not human beings but gods, and hurried to offer sacrifices of livestock to them according to the custom of their ancestors.

Then Barnabas and Paul tore their garments and asserted in every way that they were mortal men like the others, but that the Lord Christ, who made heaven and earth and all that is contained within their compass, had accomplished these things by his own power. By this argument they were appeased and were scarcely restrained from the sacrifice they had resolved to offer.

33.—XIV, 18. “And while they were staying there” [the Vulgate does not have the first colon] “and teaching, certain men came from Antioch,” and so forth. While Paul and Barnabas were staying at Lystra amid the great devotion of the citizens, certain extremely wicked Jews arrived. By persuading the crowds, they caused Paul to be stoned and dragged outside the camp as though he were dead.

When he rose with his disciples, he entered healthy, with unconquered confidence, the city from which he had been expelled. On the following day he departed with Barnabas as far as Derbe. There, preaching the word, he converted many to the Lord. From there they returned again to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, strengthening the spirits of the disciples so that they might steadfastly adhere to the rules delivered to them. Having appointed presbyters for them, with fasting they were commended [the printed *praedicati sunt* is uncertain], and they left them to the Lord with a holy commendation.

34.—XIV, 23. “Passing through Ipsidia” [correct reading: “Pisidia”], “they came to Pamphylia,” and so forth. In the same way, they are reported to have proceeded to Antioch, preaching through the various cities. There, after the faithful had been gathered together, they reported how much the Lord had granted to the Gentiles, since he had deigned to reveal to them the fullest truth by opening the door of faith.

But while they remained there for some time, certain false advisers persuaded the Gentiles who had already believed after receiving the preaching that they could not be saved unless they received circumcision, just as the Lord had commanded through Moses. This matter produced dissension among the people. Then it was decided that those established at Jerusalem should be consulted about this question, so that the dispute that had arisen might be brought to an end with their agreement.

As they traveled through the peoples, the cities, and the individual regions, they recounted how much the Lord had granted to the Gentiles. Consequently, great joy increased daily among the brothers.

35.—XV, 4. “When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received magnificently” [the Vulgate does not have “magnificently”] “by the Church.” When Paul and Barnabas had come to Jerusalem with the brothers because of the question that had arisen, they were received by the whole Church with great rejoicing.

There, a dispute again arose between the Pharisees who had already believed and the apostles concerning circumcision. Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, taught that the Gentiles were to be purified not by circumcision but by faith. James the bishop, who was called the Lord’s brother, followed him and confirmed this with substantial arguments and the testimony of the prophet. He said that it was enough for Moses that his name was mentioned with veneration in every synagogue on every Sabbath.

[Column 1393C] 36.—XV, 22. “Then it pleased the apostles, the elders, and the whole Church to choose men and send them to Antioch” [Note: “[Column 1393D] Vulgate: ‘with the whole Church,’ etc.; ‘men from among them,’ etc.”]. The apostles and elders who lived in Jerusalem decided to send Judas, who was surnamed Barsabas, and Silas with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch. Through them they sent a letter of this kind: they should not believe that the law of circumcision was necessary for them, but should merely abstain from idols, fornication, and blood from strangled animals. Remaining in the grace of the Lord, they should be confident that they were rightly established.

### 37.—XV, 30

So, having been dismissed, they went down to Antioch, and so forth. The aforesaid Barnabas and Silas, when they had come to Antioch, delivered the letters to the brothers after gathering the assembly. When it had been read aloud, they rejoiced that the cause of scandal had been removed. Judas and Silas also, since they themselves were prophets, strengthened the hearts of all in this same resolve. After they had remained there for some time, they were dismissed by the brothers to return to those by whom they had been sent. Silas, however, stayed there; Judas alone returned to Jerusalem.

Paul and Barnabas therefore remained in Antioch, teaching the word of the Lord with great zeal. After some days, reminded of their paternal obligations, Paul and Barnabas decided to revisit those regions in which the word of the Lord had been sown far and wide. Then, because of John, who was also Mark [Note: The passage here seems to attest the antiquity of the version to which Cassiodorus adheres. Where the Vulgate reads “John, who was called Mark,” our translator has “who was also Mark,” following the Roman and ancient formula, as the old inscriptions teach. In Rome, in the Justinian gardens: “Felix, who is also Clemens.”], a disagreement arose. Barnabas, taking John, sailed for Cyprus; Paul, taking Silas, departed for Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches so that they might remain firmly established in mind in the traditions of the fathers.

### 38.—XVI, 1

When they had traveled through these regions, he reached Derbe and Lystra [Vulgate: “he reached,” without the preceding words]. As Paul traveled through the nations named above, he reached Derbe and Lystra. There he found a certain Timothy, a disciple born of a Gentile father. Wishing to take him with him, he circumcised him, subtly cutting off the occasion for Jewish opposition. As Timothy passed through the appointed cities, he delivered to them the Christian teachings [sic] that had been established by the other apostles at Jerusalem.

When they wished to go to various cities, the Holy Spirit prevented them from going in one direction and warned them to proceed elsewhere. For when they had come to Troas, Paul saw in a dream a certain Macedonian saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (verse 9). From this they all understood that their journey had been divinely ordered by the evident course of events, and it was necessary for them, rejoicing, to do what the Divinity had deigned to command.

### 39.—XVI, 11

Sailing from Troas, we came by a direct course to Samothrace. Paul and Silas, therefore, having sailed from Troas and traveled through some cities, came to Philippi, which is the first city of that part of Macedonia, a colony [Vulgate: “the first city of the district”]. There a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, believed in Christ; she received the grace of baptism together with her whole household. When the apostles were invited into her house, they made it their lodging for the night.

On the following day, as they were going to prayer, a girl possessed by a pythonic spirit met them. Through her widely known divination she brought her masters considerable profit. While she persistently followed the apostles, Paul commanded the unclean spirit to come out of her, from whom it had held her captive. Then her masters, whose source of gain was the girl’s madness [Note: That is, “profit.” In a letter of King Athalaric to John II: “May ruinous profits be absent from our age.” [Col. 1394D] Also the author of *Rhetorica ad Herennium*, book IV: “There are two things that can move people toward disgraceful profit.” And Ulpian, in *Digest* 30.1.13: “Whatever concerns the adornment or profit of the state.” It is opposed to loss. In the preceding section one should note the excellent reading: “which is the first city of that part of Macedonia,” agreeing both with the Greek text and with Saint Jerome’s version.], stirred up the magistrates and the populace violently against Paul, bringing him into disgrace. They had the apostles beaten with rods, handed over to the jailers, and bound with prison chains.

### 40.—XVI, 25

At midnight Paul and Silas, praying, were praising the Lord. When Paul and Silas, confined in custody, were singing praises to the Lord at midnight, suddenly a great earthquake occurred, so that the foundations of the prison itself were shaken. The doors were also opened, and the bonds of all the prisoners were loosed.

When the jailer realized this, he drew his sword and wanted to kill himself. Paul shouted loudly to him not to harm himself, since he had found all those entrusted to him there. After a light had been brought, he found everyone whom he was seeking. Then he fell at the apostles’ feet and begged to be saved. Having heard the word of the Lord, he believed, and it is understood that he was baptized together with his entire household.

He led them to his dwelling, treated their wounds with ointment, and restored them with a meal. He rejoiced greatly that he and his whole household had received the grace of Christ. The magistrates, shaken also by that earthquake, ordered that the apostles be released from custody. Paul replied: “Although we are Romans and are suffering prison bonds without guilt, we cannot leave secretly, unless those who gave such an unjust order themselves come to lead us out.”

### 41.—XVI, 38

The lictors reported these words to the magistrates, and so forth. When they heard the apostles’ words, the magistrates were thoroughly afraid, because they had declared that they were innocent Romans who had been sent to prison. They went to them and begged them to leave their city unharmed. After this, they came to Lydia and reported one by one to their brothers how much the Lord had done for them.

From there they continued onward and reached Thessalonica. When he entered the synagogue there, he taught them, according to the holy Scriptures, that Christ the Lord had to suffer for our salvation and rise again after three days. Many from among the people, as well as noble women, believed, and are shown to have joined the apostles in faith. The Jews, moved by zeal, stirred up disturbances and drove them out. The apostles came to the synagogue in their customary manner and argued there; and many of the nobles, examining the divine Scriptures with the greatest care, believed in the Lord Christ for the most part.

### 42.—XVII, 13

When the Jews in Thessalonica learned that the word of God had also been proclaimed at Beroea, the Thessalonian Jews, after learning that the apostles were preaching Christ at Beroea, went there and repeatedly incited the people to riot, saying that those who were throwing the whole world into confusion with a new preaching had to be avoided.

Then the brothers decided to send Paul on to Athens, while keeping Silas and Timothy there for a time. When Paul came to Athens, he argued very forcefully in every place, seeing that the city was devoted to idolatry. When this report had become known, certain citizens seized him and brought him to the Areopagus, where an assembly of philosophers had gathered. Some called him a “seed-picker” [Note: The Vulgate at Acts 17:18 has *seminator verborum*, “a sower of words”; the Greek text has σπερμολόγος, *spermologos*. The Athenians were attacking the apostle with an Attic insult. Demosthenes, *On the Crown*: “For if Rhadamanthus or Minos had been the accuser, but not a seed-picker,” and so forth.], while others said that he was a preacher of new demons. Then the thoughtful men, with Paul standing in their midst, desired to hear the teaching that he was spreading far and wide.

### 43.—XVII, 22

Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said, and so forth. Paul, therefore, standing in the middle of the Areopagus, poured forth the honey of heavenly philosophy. He took a most beautiful beginning from the fact that, among their various images, he had found the inscription “TO AN UNKNOWN GOD,” so that they might necessarily seek the one whom they themselves had confessed to be unknown.

He proclaimed in order the Lord Christ, who by all his power made heaven and earth and everything in them. He also convicted them, clearly by examples from their own authors, that since they were the offspring of God, they ought not to worship things made by human hands. When they heard, among other things, about the resurrection of the dead, many believed, while others thought it a falsehood.

After this, departing from Athens, he came to Corinth, where he preached the Lord the Savior to Jews and Greeks and delivered the teachings of the Christian religion.

### 44.—XVIII, 5

When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, they pressed Paul concerning the word [Note: Vulgate: “Paul was occupied with the word.” Greek text: συνείχετο τῷ πνεύματι, “he was constrained in spirit”], and so forth. When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia to Corinth, where Paul was, Paul was teaching the word of the Lord earnestly. But when certain Jews would not listen, he shook out his garments and said to them:

“The blood of Christ the Lord, poured out, shall burden you; but I, as I have been commanded, shall go to the Gentiles” [Note: Vulgate, verse 6: “Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from now on I shall go to the Gentiles.”], to instruct them immediately.

Then he moved to the house of a certain Titus, and there taught Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue. Crispus, together with his entire household and many others, accepted the precepts of the Christian faith.

One night the Lord said to Paul in a dream: “Do not fear the wishes of those who contradict you; I am with you” [Note: Vulgate: “Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent, because I am with you, and no one shall attack you to harm you.”], “and I do not permit anyone to prevail against you.”

Strengthened by this admonition, he remained in the same city for a year and six months, teaching boldly. Because of the new preaching, he was brought by the Jews before the tribunal of the proconsul Gallio. But Gallio, declaring that questions of divine law did not concern him, had them removed and sent away.

After some days, having said farewell to the brothers, Paul came to Ephesus with Aquila and Priscilla. He could not remain there longer, although many urged him to do so, because he was hastening to Jerusalem for the solemnity of Pentecost.

### 45.—XVIII, 21

He departed from Ephesus and went down to Caesarea [Vulgate: “going down”], and what follows. From there Paul departed and went down to Caesarea, where he greeted the assembly of the Church. Afterward he went on to Antioch, remained there for some time, and traveled through the regions of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples so that they might remain in the rules they had received.
