Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man and fervent in spirit, came to Ephesus. While he was speaking boldly with the Jews in the synagogue, Aquila and Priscilla took him aside and instructed him more carefully in the Scriptures of the Lord, after the truth had been made clear to him.

When he wished to go to Achaia, they wrote that the devout people should receive him confidently. As a result, he convincingly and more decisively refuted the Jews.

### 46.—XIX, 1

It happened that, while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having traveled through the upper regions, came, and so forth. While Apollos was at Corinth, it happened that Paul, having traveled through the upper regions, came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples and asked them whether they had received the grace of the Holy Spirit after being baptized.

They declared that they did not know this name at all, but said that they had been consecrated in John’s baptism. When he baptized them with the invocation of the Trinity, the Holy Spirit came upon them, so that they were able to prophesy in different tongues. Paul remained there for three months and preached Christ the Lord in the customary manner.

[Note: *Εὑρών*—“having found”—provides Latin with a new participle, imitating the Greeks. Above he likewise derived *paenisos* from the verb *poenitet*, following μετανενοηκότας. “He asked whether”: this follows the practice of the Vulgate, which renders the Greek εἰ, even when it means “whether,” as *si*. Tibullus appears to use it similarly, book III, elegy 1: “She will tell me whether there is mutual concern between us, or whether it is less.”]

### 47.—XIX, 9

When certain people became hardened and did not believe, and so forth. When certain Ephesians refused to believe out of obstinacy, he separated his disciples from them and argued daily for two years in the school of Tyrannus. He performed many miracles, so that his handkerchiefs were placed upon the sick and they were restored to their former health.

There were seven deceitful brothers, sons of the ruler of the synagogue, who said to those possessed: “I adjure you by Jesus Christ, whom Paul preaches, to come out quickly.” The evil spirit answered them: “I know Jesus, and I know Paul, but who are you? I do not know” [Note: The Vulgate at verse 15 does not have “to come out quickly” or “I do not know.”]

The possessed people then fought against them in a persistent struggle. When this became known, a great multitude of the people believed.

Then those who had pursued occult practices, bringing their books and judging them to be worthless, burned them in the fire. They had been purchased for as much as fifty thousand denarii.

After these things had been completed, Paul sent Timothy and Erastus, the two of them, into Macedonia, while he himself remained for a time in Asia.

### 48.—XIX, 23

At that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the way of the Lord [Vulgate: “there arose”], and so forth. A similar riot arose at Ephesus concerning the Christian religion.

There was a certain Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Diana in the temple. He was accustomed to pay the craftsmen very substantial wages. Seeing that the sacred rites could be utterly overthrown by Paul’s preaching, he strongly incited the aforesaid craftsmen against the apostle and his disciples.

They seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s companions, and dragged them from the theater, where they were preaching the word of the Lord, to be heard by the judges. When Paul wished to enter among the people, the disciples and friends did not permit him to do so—for the entire city was in great confusion—lest the fury of the whole populace attack the man whom they knew to be the author of preaching contrary to their interests.

### 49.—XIX, 33

Then Alexander, having requested silence by a gesture, wanted to give an account to the people. Alexander, one of Paul’s disciples, made a gesture for silence and wished to address the excited crowds. But as soon as they recognized that he was a Jew, lest he say anything against Diana, they spent two hours shouting at the top of their voices, “Great is Diana of the Ephesians.”

The town clerk, fearing that such a great riot would throw the city into confusion, established silence and persuaded the crowds that, if Demetrius and his craftsmen had a case against anyone, they should be heard by the judges after those judges had been pacified. Innocent men, however, who had said nothing against Diana, ought not to be placed in danger of death. Once this reasoning had been accepted, the entire disturbance was calmed.

Then Paul said farewell to the disciples and departed for Macedonia. After teaching many people there, he came to Greece. From there, traveling through the neighboring regions with his disciples, he reached Troas, where they are known to have remained for seven days.

### 50.—XX, 7

On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread [Note: Vulgate: “On the first day of the week, when we had assembled,” and so forth], Paul, intending to depart from Troas the next day, prolonged his discourse until midnight and instructed them with the greatest devotion and gentleness.

It happened that one of the young men, overcome by sleep, fell from the upper room and incurred danger of death [Note: This version notably differs from the Vulgate—or, as I think, notably departs from it. In the common text we read that the young man who fell from the upper room “was taken up dead.” But Cassiodorus reads that he “incurred danger of death”; and shortly afterward, instead of “they brought the boy alive,” he has “he restored him healthy to those who were present.” Yet there will be some who think that this difference should not be attributed to the text but to the translator, who understood “dead” as “lifeless,” and “as though dead,” and who took literally what follows, “his soul is in him,” although these words should be understood as spoken figuratively and almost jokingly, just as Christ Jesus said in Matthew 9:24: “The girl is not dead, but sleeping.”]

Paul embraced him with religious compassion and restored him unharmed to those who were present. After refreshing himself with bread, Paul preached to the people until dawn. From there he set out overland for Assos [perhaps “by the road” is missing]. His disciples, however, sailing as he had ordered them, found Paul in the aforementioned city.

From there they all proceeded together to Mytilene, Chios, Samos, and Miletus. Paul had decided to bypass Ephesus so that he might reach Jerusalem by the day of Pentecost.

### 51.—XX, 17

From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Church. Bypassing Ephesus from Miletus [Note: He very willingly extends the wording: *contradebat*, *promoventes*, *compromittit*, a feature also found in *Divina Lectio*, chapter 24. Plain words, it seemed, would cause the rhythm and that continuous, almost musical modulation of expression to perish. Reversed meanings are sometimes of little concern; thus here *praetermittens*, “bypassing,” means “sending.”], the apostle Paul summoned the bishops of the Church. There he recalled to them with great affection the moderation and humility with which he had conducted himself among them.

He commended the word of the Lord above all things, lest false preachers come and subvert their hearts, causing them to depart through a most dangerous error from the rules they had received. He also declared that he had been a burden to no one in matters of expense; rather, after showing them the affection of a spiritual father, he had fed both himself and his fellow workers with his own hands, since it is clearly more blessed to give than to receive.

He said that, after bidding them farewell, he was departing and would not see them again. When he had said these things, he knelt with the whole congregation and prayed. The weeping of all broke forth loudly. They kissed his neck and mourned him with overflowing affection, because of what he had told them: that they would never again see his face.

### 52.—XXI, 1

When it happened that we sailed, we were torn away from them and came by a direct course to Cos. From there, after many tears, as though forcibly torn away, they came to Cos. Proceeding to Rhodes and Patara, they passed through Phoenicia and Cyprus and reached Tyre.

There they found certain disciples and stayed with them for seven days. Warned by the power of foreknowledge, they told Paul not to hasten up to Jerusalem, since a very severe storm was threatening him there. After prayer and farewell, they came to Ptolemais and from there to Caesarea.

When Paul entered the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the seven whom the apostles had formerly appointed over the distribution of provisions, he found that Philip had four daughters, virgins of the Lord, who prophesied the Lord’s words.

While they were staying there, a prophet named Agabus came from Jerusalem. He took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet with it, and said that the man whose belt it was would be bound in this very way by the Jews and handed over into the hands of the Gentiles.

Then the disciples and the faithful begged Paul to avoid the dangers that threatened him.

### 53.—XXI, 13

Then Paul answered and said [Vulgate: “he answered”], and so forth. Paul warned them, as they wept, not to grieve over his harsh fate. He was ready not only to be bound for the name of Christ but also willingly to be killed.

The disciples replied that they could not restrain him: “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

When they had come to Jerusalem, they were gladly received by the brothers. On the following day Paul went to James and reported to him everything that divine power had accomplished for the Gentiles through his ministry. At this they rejoiced greatly.

They rejoiced with him and gave thanks to the Lord, but they warned him that he ought to be concerned about the Jewish people, because he was strongly suspected by them on the grounds that he taught against the law of Moses that circumcision should be abolished.

They advised him to take four men from among them and enter the synagogue with them after their heads had been shaved. When the Jews learned of this, they would believe that he was saying nothing against the law of Moses.

They said that they had written to those among the Gentiles who had believed, instructing them sufficiently about the matters from which they should abstain and telling them to persevere in the rules delivered to them.

### 54.—XXI, 26

Then Paul, taking the men, was purified on the following day and entered the temple with them. Paul gladly accepted the advice mentioned above. Taking the four purified brothers, with their heads shaved, he entered the synagogue on the following day with confidence.

There he spoke, announcing to them the purification that was necessary until an offering should be made to the Lord for their salvation. After seven days, the Jews from Asia recognized Paul, seized him, and stirred up the people against him, saying that this was the man who persuaded the Gentiles to abandon circumcision, contrary to the law of Moses.

When they had decided to kill him, the tribune of the cohort suddenly arrived with soldiers and centurions and, after hearing the facts, stopped their criminal intent. The tribune rescued Paul from the crowds, bound him with two chains, and ordered him to be taken to the camp.

There the apostle, bound in chains, asked the tribune for permission to address the people. When permission was granted, he made a gesture for silence and spoke to the crowds in the Hebrew language.

### 55.—XXII, 1

“Brothers, hear now the account that I give you,” and so forth [Vulgate: “Brothers and fathers”]. Paul, proceeding with sincerity of heart, recounted in order to the people how he had been chosen by the Lord while he was a persecutor of the Church. He did not conceal his crime concerning the blood of Stephen, speaking with an unshaken mind. But he said that he had heard from the Lord—against whom no one can prevail—that he was to be sent to preach to the Gentiles.

The Jews listened to him up to this point, then began shouting loudly to the tribune that he should be removed from among the living, since he had persuaded himself of such things.

### 56.—XXII, 23

While they were shouting, throwing off their garments, and so forth. When the Jews were causing a riot and throwing dust into the air, the tribune ordered Paul to be taken into the camp. As they were beating him with whips in order to discover the cause of the disturbance, Paul said to the centurion standing nearby:

“See whether it is lawful for you to flog a Roman who has not been condemned” [Note: Vulgate, verse 25: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman, and one who has not been condemned?”]

At these words the centurion was terrified, released him, and halted the tortures that were about to begin. On the following day he ordered Paul and the Jewish council to stand before him, wishing to learn the reason for which he had been handed over.

Then Paul, looking at the Jewish crowds [Note: That is, “gazing upon” them. Elsewhere: “whatever the sun does not look upon,” that is, does not see. In Saint Augustine, a bishop is called *superintendens*, that is, “an overseer”], spoke as follows.

### 57.—XXIII, 1

Looking intently at the council, Paul said, and so forth [Vulgate: “Gazing upon the council”]. When Paul had said at the outset, “Brothers, I have lived before God with a good conscience up to this day,” Ananias the high priest ordered those standing nearby to strike him, as though he were a blasphemer.

Paul answered him openly: “God is going to strike you, whitewashed wall! You sit in the place of judgment and order me to be struck contrary to the law” [Note: Vulgate: “You sit judging me according to the law, and contrary to the law you order me to be struck?”]

When they reproached him for wishing to curse the high priest, he replied that he had not known that the man had been appointed to such an honor.

Knowing that Pharisees and Sadducees, divided by opposing beliefs, were assembled there, Paul proclaimed in a loud voice that he was a Pharisee and that he was undergoing the gravest judgment because of the hope and resurrection of the dead, which they themselves also believed.

At this statement an argument immediately arose among them, and the assembly was dissolved.

### 58.—XXIII, 10

When a great disagreement had arisen and the tribune feared that Paul would be torn apart, and so forth. When a great disagreement arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, the tribune, fearing that Paul would be torn apart by the Sadducees, ordered him to be brought back to the camp.

During the night the Lord said to him: “Take courage, Paul, for just as you have testified about me here, so you must preach my name in the city of Rome” [Note: Vulgate, verse 11: “Take courage; for as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify at Rome.”]

On the following day forty Jews formed a conspiracy and decided to kill Paul. When the son of Paul’s sister heard this, he reported it to him while Paul was in the camp. Paul asked the guards to bring the young man to the tribune. When the young man had told him everything in order, the tribune instructed him to tell no one that he had disclosed this information.

### 59.—XXIII, 23

After summoning two centurions, he said, and so forth. The tribune summoned two centurions and ordered them to take Paul as far as Caesarea to the governor Felix, with armed soldiers, lest it perhaps be believed that he had allowed Paul to be killed by the Jews after accepting money.

He sent Felix a letter in which he truthfully related what had happened. The soldiers carried out what had been entrusted to them. Then the aforementioned governor, after the letter had been read aloud, had Paul kept under guard in Herod’s praetorium until his accusers could come.

### 60.—XXIV, 1

After five days the high priest came down, and so forth. After five days the Jews came to Felix the governor with the orator Tertullus against Paul … [lacuna] di. Then, when both parties had been brought before the court, the orator Tertullus, relying on human eloquence, began to attack Paul maliciously. He claimed that Paul wished to throw the peaceful Jews throughout the whole world into confusion through new teachings. After Paul had been seized, they wished such a great crime to be immediately punished according to their law. The tribune Lysias, he said, had taken him away and was understood to have sent him to Felix’s tribunal.

The remaining Jews testified in a harsh and discordant voice that the things said were true.

### 61.—XXIV, 10

Paul answered when the governor nodded to him, saying, and so forth. After the orator Tertullus had asserted what he wished, having first presented matters that might win the judge’s favor, Paul answered as follows:

He replied that, when he had come to Jerusalem according to the custom of his nation to worship the Lord and to bring alms to his nation, he had caused neither disturbance nor riot. But, when he was detained by the centurions, he said that he had cried out to the people: “Concerning the resurrection of the dead, which you also believe, I stand here to be judged today.”

He maintained that they could not prove any of the things that, in their wickedness, they had fabricated about him. Certainly, since they were present, let them say whether they remembered that anything else had occurred that concerned the disturbance of the city.

Felix the governor postponed hearing them until the arrival of the tribune Lysias. He ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody but allow him rest, and not to prevent anyone from providing him with whatever might serve as his comfort.

### 62.—XXIV, 24

After some days Drusilla, the wife of Felix, who was a Jewess, and so forth [Vulgate: “Felix came with Drusilla his wife”]. After some days, Felix, at the request of his wife Drusilla, had Paul brought before her.

As Paul discussed at length faith in the Lord, justice, chastity, and the coming judgment, Felix, moved by the truth of his preaching, said to Paul: “Go now, and at a suitable time I shall summon you” [Vulgate: “I shall call for you”].

Felix frequently summoned Paul to him, thinking that, in the manner of worldly business, he might receive money from him.

After two years had been completed, Felix received Porcius Festus as his successor. Because he wished to gratify the Jews, Felix left Paul in chains.

When Festus came to Caesarea, he sat on the tribunal after Paul and the Jews who seemed to be pursuing him had been presented before him. Paul testified that he had injured no one, expressing wonder at why he was suffering the hostility of so great a persecution. For this reason he declared that he ought to be sent to Caesar.

Festus answered him briefly: “Since you have appealed to Caesar, you shall go to Caesar” (verse 12).

### 63.—XXV, 13

When several days had passed, King Agrippa and Berenice came down to Caesarea. After several days had passed, King Agrippa and Berenice came to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus. While they stayed with him for some time, Festus recounted to King Agrippa in order what had happened concerning a certain Jew named Paul. Oppressed by the Jews’ wickedness, he said, Paul had appealed to Caesar.

When Agrippa wished to see him, Festus promised that on the following day he would hear him in every respect.

### 64.—XXV, 23

On the following day, when Agrippa and Berenice had come with great pomp, and so forth. On the following day, when Agrippa and Berenice entered the city’s audience hall together with Festus and a very large crowd, Paul was brought into the midst at Festus’s command, so that he might confirm by his own testimony, point by point, the matters he had reported more privately to the king.

After the appeal, Festus stated that Paul had been brought before Agrippa so that, once the truth of the matter was known, he might be sent to Caesar with an explanation of the case.

### 65.—XXVI, 1

Agrippa then said to Paul, and so forth. Agrippa granted Paul the confidence to speak in his own defense. First praising the judge, Paul gathered together from the beginning, with complete truthfulness, the things that had happened to him.

He related how he had persecuted the Christian people; then, when he was going to Damascus, what he had heard after being surrounded by the Lord’s light. Immediately, as was necessary, he obeyed the Lord’s words.

For this reason he declared that he had preached to peoples and nations so that, after being converted and performing works worthy of repentance, they might obtain the rewards of eternal life. Because of this, the Jews had been enraged and decided to kill him. Rescued from their hands by divine assistance, he testified that up to that very time he had preached only what is written in the Prophets and in the other divine Scriptures.

### 66.—XXVI, 19

“Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.” While Paul was saying these things, Festus exclaimed: “You are mad, Paul; your much reading is driving your mind into confusion” [Vulgate: “Your many books are driving you mad.”]

Paul answered him with dignity that he was not mad but was speaking words of truth and sound judgment. For, he said, it was fitting that King Agrippa should know such things, since what had been done publicly could have come to his attention. He also affirmed that Agrippa believed the prophets.

Agrippa answered him cheerfully that, in a short time, Paul wished to make him a Christian. Paul, moved by charity, wished that both Agrippa and all the others who were listening might become as he was, except for his chains.

When the assembly had been dismissed, they spoke among themselves and declared that Paul had done nothing deserving death.

### 67.—XXVI, 32

Agrippa said to Festus, and so forth. Festus then said to Agrippa: “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

Paul was then handed over to the centurion Julius, together with the guards, to sail to Italy. On the second day, as they boarded the ship, they came to Sidon. There the centurion treated Paul kindly and permitted him to go to his friends.

From there they went to Cyprus, then to Lystra; transferred to an Alexandrian ship, they sailed across Crete to Salmone and afterward, after some time, came to Fair Havens (verse 8).

When the sailing season had by then passed, Paul said to his companions that it would be better for them to remain there for the winter, lest they perhaps suffer shipwreck. The centurion, however, disagreeing imprudently, hastened toward Phoenix, which was safer by the position of its harbor.

### 68.—XXVII, 13

When a south wind began to blow, they thought that they had obtained their objective. Having departed from the harbor of Phoenix and thinking that they could keep to their course toward the harbor, they were suddenly met by a contrary and very violent wind called the northeaster.

Then, after the sails had been gathered, the ship began to be carried through the waves. As they passed beyond the island of Cauda, they lost the ship’s boat and, fastening ropes around the ship, tried to save it. But as the winds increased, they were in such danger that for many days they could see neither the sun nor the stars.

Then Paul, recounting the promise of the Lord that he had heard in a dream, encouraged the others. He said that God had granted him all the people traveling with him, in addition to the ship.

On the fourteenth day, while the storm was still raging, the sailors decided to flee. Paul said that none of them could be saved unless the sailors remained on the ship. Then the soldiers cut the ropes and decided that the ship’s boat should be abandoned.

### 69.—XXVII, 33

When daylight began to appear, Paul urged them, and so forth. After the fourteenth day of the storm, Paul urged them to take food, since it was clear that, of the 276 men, not a hair of anyone’s head would be diminished. To encourage the others by his own example, he himself broke bread and ate.

When it became day, they saw a certain bay and steered toward the nearby shore. But when the ship was broken apart by rocks and waves, they decided that everyone should swim ashore. And so it happened: although the ship was lost, they all reached the desired land immediately, unharmed.

70.—XXVIII, 1. “The barbarians showed us no little kindness,” and the rest. When everyone had already reached the shore, while intense cold persisted and they were exhausted by great hunger, the barbarian inhabitants of the region provided the nourishment of human kindness. But when Paul had gathered a quantity of brushwood and placed it on the fire, a viper, which by chance was found there, seized his hand with its teeth. While it hung from his flesh, the inhabitants of the place initially believed him to be a murderer who, after the danger at sea, was thought to have encountered the punishment he deserved. But when he was seen to be unharmed, they believed him to be a god, whom no poison had injured. Then, having also been kindly received by a certain Publius, Paul healed his father, who was suffering from fever and dysentery, by prayer. For this reason, when many who lived on the same island gathered together, those afflicted with various illnesses were healed.

71.—XXVIII, 11. “After three months we sailed in an Alexandrian ship,” and the rest. After three months, then, they boarded an Alexandrian ship and came to Syracuse, a city of the Sicilians; from there to Rhegium [Note: [Col. 1403D] The author may perhaps have approved what he reported from Varro by way of Cornutus, *Orthography*, chapter 1: “If the letter R is placed first, it is not aspirated”; for the reader himself ought to understand that *Rhodus*, although it lacks an h, is *Rhodos*, and that *retor* is *rhetor*.], and from there on foot to the Three Taverns (so-called) [Note: [Col. 1403D] The manuscript had *Tribunus*. The *Three Taverns* are listed in the itinerary along the Appian Way, between Aricia and the Forum of Appius. [Col. 1404D] In the Roman council under Hilary, among the bishops: Lucifer of the Three Taverns. In the Bordeaux Itinerary that name occurs twice, not far from Placentia and near Interamna.]. There Paul was gladly received by the brothers and, having been led into Rome, entered the city. Three days later, after summoning the elders in the synagogue, … a soldier … [Note: [Col. 1404D] This passage is mutilated and corrupt; consult the sacred text]—he set before them in order, by the centurions, the reason for which he had been brought, displaying to them the glorious chain with which he had been bound for the sake of Israel’s salvation.

72.—XXVIII, 21. “But they said to him: We have neither received letters from you, nor … from Judea,” and the rest. The Jews, however, replied to Paul that they had not been able to learn, either by letter or by messenger, what he had recently seemed to be announcing; but they asked him instead to let them learn the things he had preached elsewhere. On the appointed day, when they had come to Paul’s lodging, he spoke about the kingdom of the Lord Christ, whom it was evident had been promised through Moses and the prophets. Some agreed, while others did not believe. Paul rebuked them and cited Isaiah as an example, declaring that the Gentiles would more readily receive the salvation which they themselves had refused to accept. At this statement, a considerable dispute arose among the Jews. Paul, however, remaining for two years in his rented lodging, continually instructed those who came to him about the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ; and although he was bound with iron chains, he daily loosed the bonds of sin from those who believed.

# THE APOCALYPSE OF SAINT JOHN

[Col. 1405]

1.—I, 1. “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known to his servants,” and the rest. A certain prologue is prefixed, so that the dignity of the present book may be briefly indicated. For the apostle John says that a vision concerning the end of the age was shown to him by the Lord Christ; and it is recalled through whom and for what reason it was shown: [Col. 1405B] so that, once such great truth had been revealed, the devout person might receive confidence, while the conscience of unbelievers might discover fear. He also praises the one who chooses to read or preserve these things, so that, invited by such promises, the mind of the devout may be stirred more ardently.

2.—I, 4. “John to the seven churches that are in Asia. Grace to you, and peace,” or the rest. The apostle John says that he is writing to the seven churches established in Asia. He greets them and wishes them peace and grace from the Lord Christ and from the seven angels who are read to stand before the Lord’s throne, just as in the Book of Tobit the angel Raphael said: “I am one of the seven angels who stand before the throne of the glory of God” (Tobit 12). But who this Lord is—“who is, who was, and who is to come”—he reveals in an evident account, [Col. 1405C] declaring him to be the Lord Christ, who redeemed us with precious blood. He also says what he will be like at his second coming and what human beings will see him to be when his power has been revealed. For he confirms, in the very language of divinity, that he is the first and the last and the Almighty.

3.—I, 9. “I, John, your brother and sharer in tribulation,” and the rest. While he was on the island of Patmos, having been happily sent into exile by the emperor Domitian because of the word of the Lord, the apostle says that on the Lord’s day he was admonished by a loud voice to write what he saw and send it to the seven churches whose names are written. Immediately turning toward the voice of the Lord, he saw seven shining lampstands, and in their midst the Lord Christ, whose appearance he explains through mystical figures [Note: [Col. 1405D] Read *contropationes*, from *tropos*, that is, “mode” or “figure”; below, so that the *contropatio* of the allegories made might be preserved.]. For he was clothed in a long robe (*poderes*), which undoubtedly refers to the priesthood. He was girded above the breasts with a golden belt, because the integrity of his deeds shone forth. His head and hair, because they were white, signify the Ancient of Days. His eyes were like a flame of fire, because he penetrates all things with his sight and no one can hide from his heat. His feet were like *aurichalcum*—orichalcum—because in his preaching he is found most powerful and most radiant. His voice was like the sound of many waters, because streams of wisdom proceed from him. Concerning the seven stars he speaks below. From his mouth came a two-edged sword, signifying the mysteries of the New and Old Testaments. His face shone like the sun, [Col. 1406B] because whatever he does not attend to is cast into shadow. Terrified by this vision, he testifies that he immediately fell at his feet. The Lord said to him: “Rise; do not be afraid,” confirming that he was the first and the last and declaring that he possessed the keys of death and the underworld.

Remember, however, that these and other visions of this kind, which the Lord was pleased to reveal to his servants, are shaped temporarily according to the nature of the subject, while the nature of the deity remains in its own excellence. The very nature of divinity, as it is, has not yet been shown to any living human being [Note: [Col. 1405D] See what we noted on page 101 [in this edition, col. 1359, note b].]; after the resurrection, however, it promises to reveal itself as it is to pure hearts.

4.—I, 19. “Write, therefore, what you have seen, and what is, and what must happen after these things.” The Lord Christ now explains to John the mysteries he had seen in the seven lampstands and the seven stars, [Col. 1406C] saying that they are the “splendors” of the seven churches [Note: [Col. 1405D] By this word he signifies angels; he had used it in expressions indicating dignity: “yielding to one splendor alone”; [Col. 1406D] speaking of the patriciate, “yielding to the summit of the consulship alone.”]. But since the multitude of these things is innumerable, seven are given to indicate completeness. Thus he commands that it be written to the angel of the Ephesians—that is, to the bishop—who could genuinely be admonished by written words. He says that he knows his labors and endurance, because he does not wish to tolerate false preachers, but contends that he has neglected charity. He admonishes him, after he has made satisfaction, to return to it, lest his lampstand—which is shown on account of his good works—be taken away as though extinguished. He praises him because he condemns the deeds of the Nicolaitans [Note: [Col. 1406D] On the Nicolaitans, see Epiphanius, Irenaeus, Hilary, Jerome, Clement of Alexandria, Eusebius, and Theodoret]—that is, the most shameful fornications—with the same execration as the Lord. To those who conquer detestable vices a reward is promised: that they may eat from the tree of life established in the Lord’s paradise. From it everyone is spiritually refreshed who is placed in the Lord’s kingdom in everlasting blessedness.

5.—II, 8. “And to the angel of the church of Smyrna write: Thus says the first and the last,” or the rest. He commands that it be conveyed to the angel of Smyrna—that is, to the bishop—for Scripture testifies in the Acts of the Apostles that a bishop is called an angel [Note: [Col. 1406D] The interpretation is sufficiently obvious; the reasoning is sufficiently strange.]. When Peter came and knocked at the door of the apostles, it was said, “It is not Peter, but his angel” (IX, 15). The Lord Christ says that he knows what kinds and how great were the things they endured from unbelieving Jews, although he himself died once and lives forever. Therefore, if he too chooses to persevere to the end, he will receive, when proved, the crown of everlasting life; for whoever conquers the evils of the age will not suffer the destruction of the second death.

He likewise commands that it be conveyed to the bishop of Pergamum: “I know that amid certain depraved practices you have preserved the rule of endurance, so that even while Antipate was suffering martyrdom you were unable to be turned aside by any terror. Yet I have learned that among you there are those who are joined to diabolical depravity. Therefore return more swiftly to the medicine of repentance, lest, when I come in judgment against the obstinate, I be obliged to punish their evils with eternal punishment” (verse 13). To those who conquer the world he promises manna and a white stone, which nevertheless is found to be more precious than all pearls.

6.—II, 18. “And to the angel of the church that is in Thyatira [Vulgate: to the angel of the church of Thyatira], write: Thus says the Son of God,” and the rest. As has already been said, he commands that it be written to the angel—that is, to the bishop—of the church of Thyatira, that the Lord who has eyes like a flame of fire and feet like orichalcum says this, so that nothing may be obscure to him in seeing, nor may he suffer any deficiency in preaching.

He declares that he knows the good things he has done and his exceedingly great charity, but that amid these he is pained by certain offenses caused by his evils. For his congregation, which for the most part has fornicated with the wicked and wishes to bear the name of prophecy—but ought rather to be called Jezebel—unless it is converted, is immediately to be cast onto a bed of sickness, and severe vengeance is to be exacted for its fornications. Then all the churches will know that the Lord repays each person according to the character of his deeds.

He admonishes the others established in the same church to persevere in the rules of faith they have received. To those who conquer he promises that they will rule the nations with an iron rod, just as he says he was granted this by the Father. He also promises such people the glorious resurrection, which he signifies by the mention of the star.

7.—III, 1. “And to the angel of the church that is in Sardis [Vulgate: to the angel of the church of Sardis], write: Thus says he who has the seven spirits of God,” and the rest. The Lord Christ, [Col. 1407D] in whom is the sevenfold Holy Spirit and in whose hand are the seven stars—that is, universal power—commands that this be said to the bishop of Sardis: “In appearance you are alive, but in your works you are dead.” Therefore let repentance come to your aid, so that what has been extinguished in you may revive through the medicine of satisfaction; otherwise you may suffer the arrival of the dreadful judgment like a thief and begin to endure terrible things in your own members.

But since the people of the church live together with differing moral qualities, he says that in Sardis there is a portion of the blessed who obey the Lord’s commands. They will walk continually with the Lord in white garments—that is, in the purest conscience. Thus they will not be erased from the book of life, and their names will be commemorated before the Father and his angels by a praiseworthy confession.

8.—III, 7. “To the angel who is in Philadelphia [Vulgate: And to the angel of the church of Philadelphia write]: Thus says the holy and true one,” and the rest. The Lord, who is girded with the unique power of opening and closing, commands that this be written to the bishop of Philadelphia: “Because you are devoted to me in holy humility, I humble the synagogue—that is, the congregation of Satan—before you, so that it may come to worship the Church which, because of its former pride, used to despise you.”

He also promises to protect him in temptations, when the world has been wearied by various disasters. He encourages him in his endurance to come quickly, lest someone else receive his crown, indicating how great are the things the Lord will bestow upon his faithful.

He also commands that it be conveyed to the bishop of Laodicea that he must be either cold or hot, lest he be vomited from the Lord’s mouth as lukewarm. For since he places confidence in his own powers, he is shown to be more wretched than all the weak. He says that he stands before the door and knocks with repeated blows, so that when each person opens the door of his own heart to him, he may be ready to come to the Lord’s banquet; and, conquering, may sit on the throne of his majesty, just as he himself is known to have sat as victor on the throne of his Father.

9.—IV, 1. “After this I saw a door opened in heaven; and behold, a voice,” and the rest. Called by contemplation of the spirit, John ascended to heaven [Col. 1408C] and looked upon the Lord seated on a throne, to which he joins the colors of gems through figurative language. There twenty-four elders, a number indicating completeness, were seated around the throne in white garments. From the Lord’s seat came flashes of lightning, voices, and thunderclaps. Before it were seven spirits—that is, the angels of God. In the sight of the throne there appeared something like a glassy sea, by which the character of this age is indicated: a sea, because it is driven by waves; glassy, because it is shown to be fragile.

Before the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, which are compared by a certain likeness to the four evangelists. They had six wings [Note: [Col. 1407D] In this sentence he shows that he held the view current among the Hebrews that the age of the world would be bounded by six thousand years. He is consistent with himself: *Various Readings*, book I, letter 10: “For they wished six thousand denarii to constitute a solidus, so that the rounded form fashioned from shining metal might fittingly enclose the age of the world, like a golden sun.” See Lactantius, book VII, chapters 14 and 25.] on account of the age of the world, which is understood to be capable of being completed by that number. They were full of eyes within, signifying that the mysteries of their preaching were profound; and they were continually proclaiming praises to the Lord in exultation.

When the twenty-four elders heard the Lord’s praise, they fell on their faces and worshiped him who lives for ever and ever, themselves likewise offering praises.

10.—V, 1. “And I saw a book in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne, written within and on the back” [Note: [Col. 1408D] Vulgate: “And I saw in the right hand of him who was seated on the throne something written within and on the outside”; Greek text: ὄπισθεν, ‘behind’], and the rest. Amid these things he saw a book in the right hand of the Father seated on the throne, written inside and out, because in the law some things are still hidden while others are known to be manifest. This book was seen to be sealed with seven seals—that is, with the sevenfold Spirit—because the Lord’s mysteries are always unknown until the appointed time.

Then, when an angel proclaimed but could not find anyone worthy to receive and govern it, John was greatly troubled and wept. But one of the elders told him that Christ was worthy to open the book and break its seals. Raising his eyes, he saw a Lamb as though slain, possessing complete power and unimpaired preaching. He received the book to open it, as had been proclaimed. The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders then sounded a new song to him with their harps and bowls full of various fragrances—that is, with the quality of good deeds—saying that he was worthy to be consecrated with such honor, because he had been slain for the salvation of all; he had also bestowed the priesthood generally and promised the faithful the kingdoms of heaven.

The harps signify the integrity of faith and the harmony of works. The bowls full of fragrances signify, as has been said, the prayers and supplications of the righteous.

11.—V, 11. “And I saw and heard, as it were, the voice of many angels around the throne,” and the rest. He also heard the voices of thousands upon thousands of angels proclaiming the praises of the Lord Christ: that he was worthy to receive glory, power, riches, and honor from the Father, because he had suffered, and that every creature should offer him devoted service.

The four living creatures answered them, “Amen.” The twenty-four elders, offering their assent, fell on their faces and worshiped. Then, when the Lamb had opened the first seal of the book he had received, a white horse appeared, indicating a most pure life [Note: [Col. 1409D] This interpretation must be added to the many and diverse interpretations of these figures.]. Its rider held a bow, so that by his penetrating word he might overcome every adversity.

When he opened the second seal, a red horse was shown, bearing the image of the Lord’s shed blood. To its rider a great sword was given, so that he might take away the peace of those subject to him from the earth through great terror and make those who opposed one another destroy each other through mutual conflict.

When the third seal was opened, a black horse came forth. As we suppose, it showed dominion over the impious, when its rider, seated upon it, held a balance in his hand, because such people are undoubtedly to be judged. The four living creatures said to him that wheat and barley should reach the price of a denarius, but that oil and wine should not be harmed.

When the fourth seal was opened, he saw beneath God’s altar the souls of martyrs who were swiftly seeking vengeance. Consolations of patience were given to them, and they were ordered to wait until the number of their fellow servants should be completed.

12.—VI, 12. “And I saw when he had opened the sixth seal [Vulgate: the sixth seal], and behold, there was a great earthquake,” and the rest. When the sixth seal had been opened, he says allegorically that the earth trembled. The sun became black, the moon was darkened with a blood-red eye, and the other things were done which have been foretold as capable of occurring at the end of the world.

Then a multitude of angels and an assembly of the saints—that is, 144 [additional word: thousand], in which number the total of all the blessed is enclosed [Note: [Col. 1409D] He explains below, at no. 20, that what he says about this predetermined number of the sealed is to be applied to all the blessed.]—sounded praises, holding palms and clothed in white garments. They washed their robes in the Lord’s blood and would rejoice in his presence with everlasting happiness. Those who have been filled with the majesty of the Lord Christ would no longer suffer want.

13.—VIII, 1. “And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour” [Vulgate: “the seal,” and so forth, as though “half an hour”]. When the seventh seal had been removed, an angel came before God’s tribunal carrying a golden censer, in which he offered the supplications of the saints, like incense, before the sight of his majesty.

Then the first angel sounded the trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood were thrown upon the earth, so that they burned up a third part of the land. When the second angel sounded the trumpet, a burning mountain was thrown into the sea. As a result, the sea lost a third of the animals and ships that it appeared to contain.

When the third angel sounded the trumpet, a great star called “Absentium” [Vulgate: “Absinthe”] fell from heaven upon a third of the rivers and springs. It made the waters bitter, so that those who drank from them perished. When the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, a third of the sun, moon, and stars became dark, and day lost the same portion together with night.

Then something like an eagle appeared, saying: “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth,” for they would see such great things.

[Col. 1410C]

14.—IX, 1. “And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, and I saw a star fallen from heaven,” and the rest. When the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, a star fell into the shaft of the abyss, and smoke came forth from it, darkening the air and the sun. Locusts then emerged, like scorpions. They harmed neither grass nor tree, but only those who did not have the sign of the cross on their foreheads. Tormented for five months, as though struck by scorpions, they groaned bitterly in their pain.

The position of the locusts is also described as possessing a mystical power to harm; Tychonius explained this more minutely and extensively. He says that a terrible angel presides over them, whose name is Destroyer.

When the sixth angel likewise sounded the trumpet, the angels who had been bound at the river Euphrates were released—four angels. [Col. 1410D] These, terrifying with horses and weapons, are reported to have destroyed a third of humanity, those who did not repent of their deeds.

15.—X, 1. “And I saw another mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud,” and the rest. He reports that he saw another exceedingly powerful angel clothed with a cloud, whose face was like the sun and whose feet were like pillars of fire. He placed his right foot in the sea and his left on the land, and cried out with a loud voice; and they answered … [lacuna] … that he had been admonished.

The angel swore that the world would by no means be prolonged any further, [Col. 1411A] but would end when the seventh angel began to sound the trumpet, just as God’s servants are certainly known to have been so prophesied. He was also instructed to receive a book from the angel. When he swallowed it, it was sweet in his mouth but became bitter in his stomach, because the law of the Lord is pleasant when it is chewed, but becomes bitter when devoured through forgetfulness.

He also received a reed like a rod, by which he appeared to measure the places occupied by the Christian people, while leaving other places for unbelievers to occupy. These are the ones who, at the end of the age, for three and a half years [Note: [Col. 1411D] I have restored the text in this way; the manuscript had *per tressimos annos*. The author is referring to “three days and a half,” XI, 9.], while the Antichrist reigns, will revel in the blood of the martyrs.

Enoch and Elijah are also mentioned: they will lie openly and unburied for three days, until they suddenly appear to be called up into heaven. Their enemies, looking upon them, will be thrown into great terror and will offer glory to God with profound astonishment.

16.—XI, 15. “And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, and there were great voices in heaven,” and the rest. When the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, he reports that voices of those rejoicing arose in heaven, because at last the kingdom of God, which had been awaited, had come and the things that had been promised had been fulfilled.

He briefly touches upon the mother and the Lord Jesus Christ and upon the opposition of the devil, joining things future to things past. He says that God ascended into heaven, while his mother was to be kept for a certain time in more secret places [Note: [Col. 1411D] What is reported here concerning the undefiled mother of the Redeemer should not be accepted, although we may perhaps suspect that Cassiodorus himself spoke mystically, in view of what follows. Who could adequately explain those most hidden coverings of mysteries which, as Tychonius rightly maintained, were spoken as a great sacrament or mystery?], so that he might nourish her there for three and a half years. This, as Tychonius reports, is clearly proclaimed as a great mystery.

[Col. 1411C]

17.—XII, 7. “And there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon” [Note: [Col. 1412D] Vulgate: “There was a great battle in heaven; Michael and his angels fought,” and so forth.]. He reports the battle of Michael and his angels with the dragon, who was hurled down and fell upon the earth, so that he no longer had a place of blessedness. This nevertheless undoubtedly occurred at the beginning of the world.

Then the ranking of the good was established when the devil fell, for he has ever since envied the good who are now faithful; but great woe is pronounced upon earth and sea, because they have received a burden of evil of such great weight.

The mother and the Lord Christ are again mentioned: the devil, believing that he could harm the mother, sent from his mouth an immense river which was thought likely to swallow her. But she was received into a most secure place and escaped the poisons of diabolical fraud. The ancient enemy nevertheless does not cease to persecute those who are known to obey the Lord’s commands.

18.—XIII, 1. “And I saw a beast rising from the sea, having ten horns and seven heads.” In the figure of the Antichrist, a great beast is described as rising from the sea, formed from the various limbs of wild animals in a terrifying image. It is said that for three and a half years [perhaps “three and a half”; Vulgate: 42 months] it will make war against the saints, feeding upon their blood and slaughter. It will speak enormous blasphemies against God. Finally, the impious, who will not possess the Lord’s gifts, will worship it.

This is nevertheless defined generally: whoever wishes to capture another will himself be a captive and will receive the changes of evil with fitting recompense. For the saints suffer evils only for a time, but soon, through the Lord’s favor, they reach their hope.

19.—XIII, 11. “And I saw another beast rising” [Vulgate: “rising from the earth”], “and it had two horns,” and the rest. Another beast is described as rising from the earth in the figure of the devil—that is, of the Antichrist—truly a monster that will lay waste to many who are unprepared.

Then the Antichrist will perform many miraculous signs, so that he may cause an idol, recognized as the product of sacrilegious deception, to be worshiped with great devotion. A condition so savage is also imposed upon the human race that no one may sell to another or buy from another unless he has been marked with the name of the beast—that is, with devotion to it. Then the beast’s proper number is explained by a certain method of calculation.

20.—XIV, 1. “And I saw, and behold, a Lamb standing on Mount Zion” [Vulgate: “And behold, the Lamb was standing upon Mount Zion], “and with him one hundred forty-four” [Note: [Col. 1412D] In this book, a numeral written with a line above it marks thousands; stones are marked in the same way], and the rest. He says that he saw the Lord Christ standing on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred forty-four thousand blessed persons who bore the names of both the Lord and his Father written on their foreheads.

They were polluted by no lie and by no fornication of faith. This, however, is clearly to be applied to all the blessed. They sounded a new song to the Lord, one that could not be sung by another; then they are praised in marvelous succession.

He says that he saw another angel [Col. 1412C] evangelizing various peoples and declaring that God ought to be feared, and worthy … [lacuna] … because the coming of his judgment … [lacuna].

A second angel who followed said that Babylon and the unbelievers had fallen together: Babylon, filled with the wine of fornication, was enduring with its ruined followers the drunkenness of error.

A third angel also said: “If anyone worships the beast and its image” [Vulgate, verse 9: “its image and receives”], he falls into and incurs the wrath of the Lord. A terrifying and fearful description of their punishment follows.

21.—XIV, 13. “And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: Write: Happy [Vulgate: Blessed] are the dead who die in the Lord,” and the rest. A command was given from heaven that he should write what was being said, declaring happy those dead whose labors ended with life.

He also saw a white cloud, upon which the Son of Man was seated. His appearance is formed differently according to the nature of the circumstances; for he will come in the manner in which he was seen by the apostles to ascend into heaven.

At that time he had on his head a golden crown, the most splendid dignity of his majesty, and in his hand a very sharp sickle, by whose authority the wicked generation is to be reaped at the end of the age. When the angel said, “The time has come to reap the harvest, which is known already to have withered,” he thrust his sickle into the earth and cut down the impious with the greatest speed.

Likewise, an angel thrust his sickle into the earth and unhesitatingly cut down its good people, as though they were human beings swollen with wickedness. They were cast into the winepress of God’s wrath and the blood flowed for sixteen hundred stadia; this undoubtedly pertains to a mystical significance.

He also reports that he saw seven angels who possessed seven plagues, which they would inflict by the Lord’s indignation. In the glassy sea mixed with fire stood the martyrs who, by the Lord’s gift, had achieved victory over the devil, and they returned a song to God with great exultation.

22.—XV, 5. “And after these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of martyrdom [Vulgate: tabernacle of witness] was opened in heaven.” [Col. 1413B] When the temple where the martyrs were had been opened, he says that he saw seven angels carrying the plagues they were to inflict upon the unbelieving people. Clothed in white garments and girded around their breasts with golden belts, they received seven bowls in their hands, so that they might pour out over the earth and the rivers various forms of suffering upon those who, scorning the Lord’s voice, served idols and perversities.

Then the glory of the Lord was sung by the mouths of the saints, because a fitting recompense had followed.

23.—XVI, 8. “And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun,” and what follows. The fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh angels poured out the bowls they had received. The earth was struck by such great afflictions that a voice came forth from the Lord saying, “It is done.” Immediately there were voices, thunderclaps, and an earthquake such as, it is agreed, had never occurred from the beginning of the age.

Then, I think, he speaks of the city of God, founded upon belief in the Trinity [Note: [Col. 1413D] From this comes the statement that the city was divided into three parts, verse 19]. And Babylon received what the Divinity had long ago prepared to inflict upon it. All powers and exaltations were removed from their customary condition when the unbelievers, struck and afflicted by enormous hail, began to blaspheme the Lord; so great was the force of the storm that it could not in any way be endured.

24.—XVII, 1. “And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came,” and the rest. One of the angels who had the bowls of the seven plagues promises John that he will show him that Babylonian prostitute, who is famous throughout the whole world.

Then, transported in spirit, he looked upon a woman seated upon the beast, adorned with fine linen, purple, and gems. In her hand was a cup of execration and crime. On her forehead was written: “Babylon, the mother of fornications and the pollution of the whole earth” [Note: [Col. 1413D] Vulgate: “The mystery: Babylon the great, the mother of fornications [Col. 1414D] and of the abominations of the earth.”]. She was also cruelly drunk with the blood of the martyrs and completely filled with the abundance of crimes. He was therefore astonished to see her arranged in so deformed a fashion, although everyone thought her to be the mistress of the earth.

25.—XVII, 7. “After this I saw another angel. Why are you astonished?” [Note: [Col. 1414D] Vulgate: “And the angel said to me: Why are you astonished?” and so forth.] “I will tell you,” and the following. While John was astonished, the angel interprets who the prostitute was whom he had seen seated upon the beast with seven heads and ten horns.

Some wish to understand this as the city of Rome, which sits upon seven hills and possesses the world under a single rule. Others say that the account refers more properly to Babylon, attributing its position not to mountains but to its inflated powers. He says that it will be crushed by the peoples over whom it had previously appeared to rule.

He also reports that ten kings will have power on earth. One of them, who is called the Antichrist, is to be reserved for the end of the age. He intends to prepare a war against Christ, but his wickedness, when the Lord conquers, will collapse.

26.—XVIII, 1. “After this I saw another angel descending from heaven, having great authority.” He also saw another angel descending to the earth, whose brilliance shone throughout the whole world. He said: “That most powerful Babylon has fallen, has fallen, because she did not fornicate by herself, but gave all the nations examples of how to perish.”

Another voice followed, so that the congregation of the faithful might quickly depart from her, lest her ruin engulf the people who believed in the Lord. He says that double recompense must be rendered to Babylon, which had vaunted itself in the presumption of its pride. Then its kings and merchants deeply lament that she, who had believed herself uniquely capable of possessing the world’s goods, perished in an instant.

27.—XVIII, 15. “The merchants of these things, who became rich through her, will also stand far away,” and the rest. The words of those who mourn and reproach Babylon are still related: she had suddenly collapsed, although she had been so powerful in wealth and exalted in authority. They cast dust upon their heads and console the beloved with abundant tears … [lacuna] … and, turning, say: “Rejoice over her, you saints, whom she slaughtered in impious violence, because your blood is known to have been abundantly avenged upon her.”

After this the angel lifted up a great mass and threw it into the sea, saying that Babylon the great would fall with such force. No weddings would ever again be held there, nor would the voices of revelers be heard there in any way, because she had been a receptacle of crimes and an example of every vice from everywhere.

### 28.—XIX, 1. “After this I heard something like the voice of great crowds in heaven,” and so forth.

After what was said concerning Babylon had been fulfilled, a great rejoicing of all the saints, angels, and elders in heaven arose, so that, worshiping the Lord and singing in repeated voices like resounding thunder, they sang “Alleluia,” because he had overthrown the pride of the most wicked harlot with a fitting vengeance. They added a most sweet hymn because the Lord Christ had been joined to his bride, that is, the holy Church. Then the angel said to John: “Write, because these words are the words of God”; and that those who are invited to the Lord’s supper are blessed. When John wished to worship him, he was forbidden, because good angels do not wish to be worshiped, but God.

Then, raising his eyes, he saw the Lord Christ seated upon a white horse. He is described with exceedingly wondrous terror, wearing a garment sprinkled with blood because of the testimony of his Passion. A sharp sword proceeded from him, because his word is proved to be powerful and most effective. As a sign of his humanity, he also had written on his thigh: “King of kings, Lord of lords.”

### 29.—XIX, 17. “And I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying,” and so forth.

The angel was heard by the flying creatures of heaven, that is, by holy men, saying: “Come to the Lord’s supper”—such persons as were fittingly invited to his banquet. And, in order that the correspondence of the allegory might be preserved, he says that the flesh of various animals was to be eaten, as though by the various kinds of people who are to be gathered into the Church.

The devil also appeared with a great army, coming to wage war against the members of the Lord Christ. But he was captured with his false prophet, Antichrist, and plunged into a lake blazing fiercely with fire. The rest of his companions, who had followed the beast, are known to have been slaughtered by the Lord’s sword, and to have furnished food for all the birds, that is, for the saints.

Then the angel descended from heaven and, having seized the dragon, who is Satan, bound him with a chain and cast him into the abyss. He bound him for a thousand years.

> **Note:** He bound him so that he would not confuse the nations that were to believe with unrestricted power. The remaining words are inserted parenthetically. Cassiodorus mentions, *Divine Readings*, chapter 9, that a certain Vigilius, an African bishop, had discussed the interpretation of the thousand years most fully; that work has either perished or still lies hidden. See Augustine, *City of God*, book XX, chapter 7. The statement that this period is reckoned, according to the opinion of many Fathers, from the Lord’s birth seems to refer to an opinion that arose long ago: that in the thousandth year after Christ the whole order of things would be dissolved and Antichrist would come.

This is said by the figure of synecdoche, in which the whole is spoken of through a part, since the precise end of his binding is entirely unknown; nevertheless, by agreement among the Fathers, the period is reckoned from the Lord’s birth. He says that at the end of the age Satan is to be released, when many martyrs and confessors will spring forth at the coming of Antichrist.

He also saw the martyrs of God, who had by no means received the devil’s marks on their foreheads. He calls the first resurrection the resurrection in faith, by which we are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, and in which the second death has no place. The priesthood of the faithful in Christ remains generally until the measure of the appointed time has been completed.

### 30.—XX, 7. “And when the thousand years are finished, Satan will be released from his prison” [Vulgate: “And when the thousand years are completed, and so forth, from his prison”], and so forth.

He says that after a thousand years Satan will come out of his prison, where he is now known to be bound—but this too must be understood as the whole being indicated by a part, since the matter is unknown to human beings—in order to seduce the nations scattered throughout the whole world, so that they may overrun the camp of the saints with impious rule.

Immediately divine fire consumes them and plunges the devil who had incited them into the burning lake, where that cruel beast with his false prophet Antichrist is also said to have been cast. He also saw a white throne and the Lord Christ seated upon it, who, at the future resurrection, restores to each person a fitting recompense for his deeds.

Then, seeing a new heaven and a new earth, he also saw Jerusalem adorned, just as a most beautifully dressed bride is accustomed to be prepared for her husband. And a voice was heard from heaven: “Behold the tabernacle that is promised to exist, where it is granted to human beings to dwell with God; where, with all the sorrow of necessity excluded, eternal joy is known to reign.”

### 31.—XXI, 5. “And he who sat upon the throne said: ‘Behold, I make all things new,’” and so forth.

He says that the Lord Christ told him to write down what he had seen and heard, because he himself is the Α and Ω, making new things and changing those of the past, and granting the water of life to those who thirst. Whoever is faithful to him will possess his inheritance in the place of a son; but the faithless are to be cast into the burning lake, its sulfurous stench congealed, which is most truly called the second death.

One of the angels who, as has been reported, held the seven bowls of the plagues led John onto a high mountain and showed him Jerusalem descending from heaven, most beautiful in the variety of its miracles. Its splendors are compared with the most brilliant jewels. It is described in its entirety so that its beautiful diversity may be applied to the understanding of the great mystery.

### 32.—XXI, 19. “The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, chalcedon,” and so forth.

The wondrous beauty of that Jerusalem is still being described. It is also said to have, in its foundations, in turn the precious gems of the saints. It has twelve gates, always open, corresponding to the number of the apostles. Its street gleams, paved with the purest gold; and all its adornment and every precious object surpass all measure. It is known to shine not from the light of the sun alone, but from its own author.

There nothing polluted, nothing filthy is found. Rather, the river of life proceeds from the Lord’s throne and flows through the middle of the city with transparent brightness. Trees amid groves are said to adorn both its banks, yielding their fruits each month. There will be no night and no want, because the Lord illumines everyone and satisfies everyone.

Finally, he says that those who have kept the sayings of this book with faithful minds are blessed.

### 33.—XXII, 8. “I, John, who heard and saw these things, and when I had heard and seen them, fell down” [Vulgate: “I fell”], and so forth to the end.

When John said that he had heard and seen the words of this book, he wished, in thanksgiving, to worship the angel. But the angel replied that he was his fellow servant, not his lord, and that the one who made heaven and earth should instead be worshiped.

After this he says that the Lord will come quickly and judge each person’s deeds according to their character. He calls blessed those who have cleansed their consciences through good works, so that they may have confidence in the tree of life, that is, in faith in the cross. For all who have defiled themselves with shameful deeds will be excluded from the Lord’s kingdom outside.

Through many different statements he confirms that the Lord is Christ. He solemnly warns that no one should add anything to or subtract anything from this book, which is known to have been granted for the understanding of eternal life. He makes everyone ready, repeatedly testifying that he will come quickly. Amen.

[Col. 1417]

## SCIPIO MAFFEIUS TO NICOLAUS COLETIUS. GREETINGS.

> **Note:** The following letter was inserted in volume V of the recent edition of *Italia Sacra*, in which parchment documents of the chapter of the Veronese church are mentioned. It is reproduced here again because the first printer was deceived in more than one place by a defective and uncorrected exemplar, as will be clear to anyone who compares the texts.

[Col. 1417]

I have learned from your letter that you have at last accepted the force of my reasons, by which I decided to refrain from making a comprehensive examination of Ughelli’s history of the bishops of Verona and from scrutinizing its documents, and that you have reduced your requests to this: that, if I possess anything concerning the older bishops that has been reported neither by Ughelli nor by our historians, and likewise if I should happen to discover a bishop not yet known and still absent from our diptychs, I should immediately communicate it to you. I shall indeed do this briefly.

No monument exists concerning this matter more ancient than a certain rhythmic description of Verona, composed by an anonymous author during the reign of Pepin, son of Charles the Great. Jerome della Corte published the first part in *History of Verona*, book I, from a manuscript chronicle preserved among the Jesuati. Of the remainder, in which the first eight bishops are listed, Perettus cites several words from a very ancient book among the Coelestines at the monastery of Rimini. I encountered some fragments many years ago in a Zenonian codex.

The most excellent portion of this distinguished document would have perished entirely had Father Mabillon not eventually published a complete and finished copy from the library of Lobbes. Ratherius, famous for many writings, had been transferred from that monastery to the see of Verona in the year 928, as Sigebert teaches. When he was later compelled to leave Verona and return for a time to the monastic cloister, he brought that description, together with a plan of our city painted in red, to Lobbes.

In 1713 I arranged, through my brother, then governor of the province of Namur, for that parchment and plan—which would have been of the greatest assistance to Veronese history—to be sought with the utmost diligence. The abbey of Lobbes is scarcely a ten- or twelve-hour journey from Namur. But the attempt was unsuccessful, and the monks complained bitterly that several codices had either been stolen or had not been returned by those who had borrowed them.

Since Mabillon’s *Ancient Analecta*, in whose first volume that rhythmic monument is included, is extremely rare in Italy, I am sending you a copy that I once transcribed faithfully. It is astonishing how useful it is to our history.

This great and illustrious city in Italy, in the region of Venetia, is called Verona, as Isidore teaches, and was so called in ancient times.

It is joined together in a square and strongly fortified with walls; forty-eight towers shine around its circuit, of which eight are lofty and rise above all the others.

It has a high labyrinth, large in circumference, from which one who does not know the way out cannot emerge except by the light of a lamp or by means of a ball of thread.

A broad, spacious forum is paved with stones; at its four corners a great vaulted structure stands, with the remarkable pavement of the streets cut and laid in stone.

Temples of ancient construction were built under the names of the gods: Luna, Mars, Minerva, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and the Sun, who shines above them all.

The tongue cannot describe the appearance of this city. Within it glitters; outside it gleams, surrounded by plates, with common metals gilded in bronze.

There is a great and lofty fortress with strong battlements, and stone bridges founded over the river Adige, whose ends reach in a circle toward the town.

Behold how well it was founded by wicked men who did not know God’s law and worshiped new and ancient images, wooden and stone.

But after the fullness of time came, he incarnated the Godhead by being born of the Virgin, emptied himself, and ascended the gallows.

Then, taken down and given to the most wicked Jewish people, he was placed in a tomb. He remained there for three days; then, rising in triumph, he sat at the Father’s right hand.

When the pagan world learned this, it hastened to believe, because he himself is the God of heaven, the creator of earth, who appeared in the world through Mary’s womb.

From her lineage proceeded martyrs, apostles, confessors, doctors, and most holy prophets, who brought the world into harmony with the Catholic faith.

Thus the Davidic saying was fulfilled: the heavens clearly proclaim the glory of the Most High, from the highest heavens to the ends of the earth.

Euprepius the bishop first preached in Verona; Dimidrianus was second; Simplicius third; Proculus the confessor, an outstanding shepherd, fourth.

Saturninus was fifth, Lucilius sixth, Gricinus the teacher and bishop seventh, and the eighth was the renowned shepherd, confessor, and martyr Zeno.

By preaching, he brought Verona back to baptism; he healed the daughter of Gallus from an evil spirit; and he brought back from the sea oxen, turning away with [lacuna].

Indeed, he freed many from the destructive enemy . . . I cannot tell many of the works of this holy man, which almighty God displayed through him as he came from Syria to Italy.

O happy Verona, enriched and renowned! How you are surrounded by most holy guardians who defend you and drive out the most wicked enemy!

In the east you have the first martyr Stephen, Florentius, Vindemialis, Bishop Maurus, Mamma, Andronicus, and Probus with forty martyrs.

Then Peter and Paul, the apostle James, the forerunner and Baptist John, and the martyr Nazarius together with Celsus, Victor, and Ambrose.

The illustrious martyrs of Christ, Gervasius and Protasius, Faustinus and Jovita, Eupolus, Calocerus, the Lord’s mother Mary, Vitalis, and Agricola.

In the southern regions are Firmus and Rusticus, who once received the crowns of martyrdom among you; their bodies were taken away to the islands of the sea.

When it pleased God, the invisible king, the things among you were renewed through Bishop Hanno, during the reigns of the princes and kings Desiderius and Adelchis.

The holy men who had remained for a long time did not return. The bishop buried their bodies together with spices, galbanum, storax, and [possibly] “argoid,” myrrh, resin, cassia, and the brightest frankincense.

A covered golden tomb is surrounded by heralds; its striped colouring delights human senses, now white, now black, between two purple colours.

Hanno, the illustrious bishop, prepared these things as well as he could. Through his flame, the glory of good works shines from the southern ends of the earth to our boundaries.

In the west, Sixtus and Laurence keep watch; Hippolytus, Apollinaris, the twelve apostles of the Lord, and the most holy great confessor Martin.

No city in Ausonia is now to be praised above you, shining, flourishing, and fragrant from the bodies of the saints, wealthy alone among a hundred cities in Italy.

For Aquileia praises you, Mantua praises you, Brescia, Pavia, Rome, and Ravenna likewise; through you there is passage everywhere to the borders of Liguria.

The most devout king Pepin dwells among you, not forgetting piety or just judgment; acting well, he always makes all things prosper.

Let us sing glory to God, the invisible king, who has adorned you with such mystical flowers, in whose abundance you shine like the rays of the sun.

Do you see how the ancient shepherds are listed, and in what different order?

The anonymous author: Euprepius, Dimidrianus, Simplicius, Proculus, Saturninus, Lucilius, Gricinus, Zeno.

Ughelli: Euprepius, Cricinus, Agapius, N. of unknown name, Saturninus, Lucilius, Diomidianus, Zeno, Proculus.

But neither Ughelli nor our historians nor the compilers of lists have any firm place to stand: they produce no ancient witness and rely upon no monument. The person who several years ago added a history to the Veronese episcopal order placed Dimidrianus sixteenth, Saturninus fourteenth, and Lucilius—or Lucillus—eighteenth. If you ask on what foundation, nothing can be offered.

They produce an inscription for Agapius which anyone would recognize at first sight as something fabricated in recent centuries. Since, therefore, I have found no older or more trustworthy document up to the present day, I would regard it as a sin to depart from the anonymous tradition—especially since there is a second witness, one who preceded the other writers on this subject by more than two hundred years: namely, John, a deacon of the church of Verona. In his *Imperial History*, now lost, he listed the first eight bishops of Verona by the same names and in precisely the same order, as we learn from Panvinius, *Antiquities of Verona*, book IV, chapter 3, who had read that chronicle.

It is not so easy to determine the time in which these men held office. For this reason Panvinius, in the same work, book IV, chapter 7, had written the bare names, in alphabetical order, of many Veronese bishops whose deeds and dates were unknown. Yet after these very words, the editors of the posthumous work added a sequence by an entirely different method and arranged it according to their own judgment.

Nevertheless, I determine the age of three of them, from which the dates of the others may also be conjectured and inferred. First, Saint Proculus, who was present at the martyrdom of Firmus and Rusticus, as is clear from their acts in Mombritius, volume I, page 283. There is no reason to reject these acts, even if they have been interpolated in places. Ruinart did not include them, but he omitted many genuine texts. I myself have read the same account more than once in a Lectionary codex of excellent quality and no ordinary antiquity belonging to the Canons.

In the year 304, therefore, when the holy martyrs suffered under Maximian Herculeus, Proculus presided over this flock. His ancient epitaph—since the other inscriptions celebrated concerning these eight bishops are each of a more recent age—was carved in Parian marble and survives in the confession of his church. Receive it here. It has often been published, but never with sufficient accuracy. Gruterus, on page 1058, properly arranged two poems so that they would conform to meter, but neglected the truth. Panvinius presented it somewhat better, though he too deviated in more than one place. The words are not separated by any interval:

> **HERE I QUICKLY GREW OLD; NOW A LONGER AGE WILL PRECEDE ME.  
> MAY I LIVE LONG IN BETTER YEARS. THE BODY OF PROCLUS, BISHOP,  
> AND OF THE HOLY MARTYRS COSMAS AND DAMIAN, RESTS HERE;  
> THE CONFESSORS, THE RELICS OF MARTIN, WILL REST IN PEACE.**

The age of Lucillus is more easily established, since he signed the Council of Sardica in the year 347. Nor is the date of Saint Zeno unknown, since it is clear from Saint Ambrose’s letter to Syagrius, bishop of Verona, that he held office not long before that time. Ambrose teaches that the consecrated virgin in question had been approved by the judgment of Zeno of holy memory and sanctified by his blessing.
