I know that Baronius, in his notes on the *Martyrology*—followed thereafter in a body by our writers and Ughelli himself—both feared the opinion of the people of Verona concerning the age of Saint Zeno and was overcome by Ambrose’s testimony; in order to reconcile everything, he assigned us two bishops of this name.

But the monuments and ancient parchments of our church, which I have examined, together with a tradition extending over so many centuries, oppose this. The life of Saint Zeno that a certain notary named Coronatus composed derived from the opinion that spread concerning the third century. Mombritius published it, then Ughelli corruptly, and finally Henschenius and Papebrochius. In it our shepherd is said to have flourished during the time of Gallienus. But that document either teems with errors or must be understood differently.

The rhythmic description recently cited presents Saint Zeno as having healed the daughter of Gallus from an evil spirit. Gallienus may indeed have been indicated by that name, as I infer from certain acts; but it may also have been a private individual, for no mark of imperial or Caesarian dignity is present. Coronatus calls his Gallus a king and mentions his royal crown—expressions hardly applicable to the Roman emperor.

The first words after the preface in Ughelli, “in the time of Gallienus,” would indeed indicate an emperor; but they are interpolated and therefore are not found in Mombritius’s better manuscripts, as is usually the case. Papebrochius suspects that some petty king is meant, especially because the Ambrosian Missal contains the words “the daughter of Gallienus the prince.”

To strengthen the learned man’s suspicion, consider these words from the *Life*: “I will not leave this body unless Bishop Zeno comes”; and these: “Then, at the king’s command, the soldiers went to the man of God, for he was sitting upon a stone.” These statements clearly indicate that Zeno was only a short distance from the place where the girl was staying and suffering.

The following words make the matter still clearer: “Then Saint the priest rose, said a prayer, and proceeded to the palace, where the king was being tormented.” Who would say that a man undertaking a long journey was proceeding to the palace? I remember that, when I once reread these passages, it occurred to me that in the *Itinerary of Antoninus* a palace is placed thirty-six miles from this point between Tridentum and Verona. Was some petty king named Gallienus then residing there, ruling in the Rhaetian mountains?

Whatever the truth may be, there is no sufficiently solid reason to compel us to divide the one Zeno into two, since the sermons of our shepherd—of which I shall, God willing, defend a substantial portion elsewhere, despite the futile opposition of the entire learned nation of critics—frequently reveal him as a writer of the fourth century.

What could be clearer than the words in the sermon *On Continence*, in which he expressly teaches that the first times of the Christians were nearly four hundred years earlier? Later editions, which I detest beyond measure, falsified this passage by replacing “four hundred” with “two hundred.” They did so improperly and against all the manuscripts, as well as against the earliest edition in my possession, produced at Venice in 1508.

It is therefore established that, just as the age of Saint Proculus and Lucillus is clear, so too is that of Saint Zeno. From these three bishops we can reach a sufficiently firm conjecture concerning the dates of the other five.

I am truly sorry that I could not say things more agreeable to our clergy. Before Proculus, and therefore before the fourth century, we see only three bishops, and the whole story of the faith being planted in this city during apostolic times, and of Euprepius being sent here by the Apostle Saint Peter, collapses.

But just as I have hitherto devoted myself to truth, so I am determined in the future, as long as breath governs these limbs, to sacrifice to truth alone. Popular tales, as well as little histories usually composed in the sixteenth century, summon the first shepherd of almost every Italian city from the age of the apostles and from the very cradles of the Christian faith, and build up with great elegance a marvelous and unbroken succession of bishops.

Yet anyone who weighs the order and dates of events will see that there were many such cities in which the name of a bishop was not heard before the third century. For the Christian religion could not immediately have been celebrated and taken root in all the municipalities of Italy.

In our own city certainly, which, while the Roman state endured, surpassed all the other cities of this region in population, wealth, and splendor, as I have sufficiently shown in a recent little book, Saint Proculus, at the beginning of the fourth century, hid with a few Christians not far from the city wall through fear of the pagans, as the acts of Saints Firmus and Rusticus teach. Only toward the end of that same century did Saint Zeno bring Verona back to baptism by preaching, as the anonymous author records—that is, he led the greater part of the people back to sound practice.

As for bringing to light bishops not yet recognized, it may indeed seem surprising that anyone should still remain hidden after so much investigation; for it is a much greater fault to insert too many than to omit some. Nevertheless, I shall suggest two.

Among the writers of Brunswick history collected by Leibniz, there is a catalogue of those who were raised from the congregation of canons at Goslar to an episcopal see. William is listed among them as the eleventh provost and afterward as bishop of Verona, whom no one had previously known. That congregation flourished under Henry III, IV, and V. This William may perhaps be placed between Dietbold and Aldegerius, between whom Perettus inserts two bishops rejected by Ughelli.

The second bishop whom I present has never been named in print. I discovered him in a beautiful manuscript missal, complete and uncorrupted among the oldest—but torn, half-destroyed, and scattered—parchments of the cathedral library. In it the order for the blessing of the candle during Holy Week is given:

> “Therefore we beseech you, Lord, on behalf of our people, together with our pope, and with our most illustrious king Otto, and with our venerable bishop Volfkang, and so forth.”

By this prayer our Volfkang emerges from the darkness of oblivion and must henceforth be added to the catalogues. It remains to investigate when he governed our church.

I would scarcely believe that it was under Otto IV, since the book reveals a higher antiquity. The Alemannic name and origin also suggest an earlier date, since from the beginning of the twelfth century native bishops generally resulted from the canonical election of the Veronese clergy.

In my opinion, the phrase “our king Otto” designates the period from the year 983 to 996. Otherwise the name Otto would not have been given without the title of emperor. During that interval imperial dignity was vacant, and Otto III, before receiving the crown and insignia from Gregory V, was called king only.

We shall assign our Volfkang to that same period. Some suspect that he was an intruder, but the ancient and magnificent missal of the Veronese Church that I mentioned proves that he nevertheless held office.

The ecclesiastical history of that century, and especially of that period, is very uncertain, as Ughelli himself observed. I would have disentangled it as I hoped, had the cathedral archive not been suddenly sealed a few years ago for very serious reasons and thereafter opened to no one.

Among the Veronese bishops whom we have so far failed to list, Nottingus also seemed worthy of inclusion. Rabanus Maurus wrote him a letter on predestination against Gottschalk; in the edition of that letter prepared by Father Sirmond he is called a Veronese. But the learned man was misled by an erroneous title, for it is established that Nottingus presided over the Church of Brescia. This was also recently revealed by the distinguished Paulus Galeardus, whom I name with due respect, in his notes on Ughelli, volume IV.

These, my dearest Coletus, are the things I had to report concerning our bishops of earlier times and those not yet discovered. Farewell.

[Col. 1421]

## CASSIODORUS’S SUPPLEMENT

> **Note:** A noble Vatican codex, written in Lombard script in the twelfth century, on page 142 presents an abridgment of the first book of Cassiodorus’s *Institutions of Divine Literature*, occasionally, though rarely, interspersed with material from other authors, among whom Bede appears more than once. One chapter of the aforesaid abridgment, however, corresponding to chapter 16 of Cassiodorus, differs so greatly from the printed edition that it should rather be regarded as a new work. It will therefore appropriately be reproduced here.

*(From Mai’s Roman Spicilegium.)*

[Col. 1421]

[Col. 1421C] For the confirmation of the Catholic faith and to guard against the snares of heretics, the twelve books of blessed Hilary should be read, which he composed on the Holy Trinity in profound and exceptionally eloquent language. The works of Saint Ambrose on the same subject, which he dedicated to the emperor Gratian, should also be read.

The fifteen books of Saint Augustine on the Holy Trinity should be read with careful attention, as well as his book called *On the Definition of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, composed in fifty-five chapters. Its first chapter begins as follows: “We believe that there is one God, the Father, because he has a Son.” Its final chapter reads: “Because of the new legislators of the law, who therefore say that only the soul was created in the image of God.”

There are also two books of the same author to the deacon Peter on the faith of the Holy Trinity, the second of which is divided into forty chapters. The first begins: “Hold firmly and doubt in no way that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God.” The last reads: “Hold firmly and doubt in no way that the Church is God’s threshing floor.”

His one book *On True Religion*; four books *On Christian Doctrine*; one book *On Christian Combat*; and his work resembling moral philosophy, which he collected from divine authority for the formation and correction of morals and called *The Mirror*.

The twenty-two books of the same author *On the City of God* should be read with no less diligence. In them the confused city of the devil, Babylon, and the splendid city of the Lord Christ, Jerusalem, are displayed through the fitting diversity of human conduct.

He also wrote five questions on the New Testament to the presbyter Honoratus, and eighty-three others formed with marvelous deliberation.

The sayings of Saint Athanasius should also be read for the recognition of the truth of the Catholic faith: one letter to Epictetus in four chapters; *On the Sacrament of Faith*; *On the Incarnation of the Lord*; *On the Holy Spirit*; and a letter of his faith sent to Theodosius at Aquileia.

His disputation against Sabellius and Photinus; and another disputation against Arius.

Likewise, Saint Augustine’s *On the Catholic Faith against All Heresies*; his work on which books are to be received into the canon; his work *On Spirit and Soul*; three chapters to Dardanus.

A sermon of the same author *On the Unity of the Trinity* begins as follows: “The birth of the Lord according to the flesh.”

> **Note:** This is sermon 125 in the appendix of the Maurist editors, who perhaps unjustly relegated it among the spurious works.

It ends: “But you who serve the Lord and keep his commandments.”

A one-book treatise of the same author *On the Explanation of the Creed*.

A sermon of the same author *On the Incarnation of the Lord* begins: “We read that holy Moses gave commandments to the people of God.”

> **Note:** I do not know whether this too was unjustly placed by the Maurists in the appendix, number 245.

His work *On the Ten Categories*.

A letter of Cyril, bishop, to John of Antioch.

Another letter of Cyril to Nestorius, the heretical bishop.

The presbyter Faustinus’s exposition of the faith against the Arian heresy.

His work *On the Faith* which the emperor Theodosius briefly ordered to be sent to him.

Four chapters of John Chrysostom.

One chapter of Gregory Nazianzen.

One chapter of Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

Pope Damasus’s exposition of the faith to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch.

Pope Leo’s letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

Another letter of Leo to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem.

Another letter of Leo to the bishops of Palestine.

Another letter of Leo to Pulcheria on the faith.

Another letter of Leo on the faith to the bishops of Constantinople.

Another letter of Leo to the synod assembled at Nicaea.

The order of the acts of the synod held in the city of Chalcedon.

The definition of the Council of Chalcedon.

Pope Leo’s letter to the synod at Ephesus.

Origen’s *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*).

Adamantius’s apology, which Rufinus sent in his own defence to Anastasius, bishop of the city of Rome.

Jerome’s letter to Marcellinus, and *Anapsychia* on the state of the soul.

Another work of Jerome to Pammachius and Maron on the books of Origen.

Pope Gelasius’s exposition on the two natures of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Two books of Saint Faustinus *On the Trinity*.

The exposition of the creed by the presbyter Rufinus to Bishop Laurentius.

One book of Fulgentius *On the Catholic Faith* and *On Ecclesiastical Institutions*.

Three books of Paschasius *On the Holy Spirit*.

Four books of Alcuin *On the Trinity*.

> **Note:** From this we learn that the author of this supplement is at least in part different from Cassiodorus.

Also useful for this subject is the book of Vincent, presbyter of the island of Lérins, which he composed from the books of blessed Augustine and sent to Pope Sixtus; it should be read again.

But if anyone prefers to touch briefly upon something concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and does not wish to weary himself with lengthy reading, let him read the book of Bishop Nicetas, which he wrote *On the Faith and the Incarnation*.

> **Note:** I published these books of Nicetas from a Vatican codex several years ago.

Also the book of blessed Augustine *On the Faith and the Incarnation*, composed in the form of questions and answers.

The three mellifluous books of the aforesaid Saint Ambrose *On Duties* are also useful for instruction in ecclesiastical discipline.

After chapter 23 had spoken of the canons of Dionysius, following those words of Cassiodorus—“The Roman Church embraces”—the Vatican codex continues as follows:

Against various heresies, Saint Augustine, writing to Quodvultdeus, noted each one individually in eighty-nine chapters. Then he composed a book on what each heresy defends, beginning with the Simonians and ending with the Pelagians. In a third work he explains what Eutyches and Nestorius hold. In a final work he treats separately of other heresies. Beginning with the Carpocratians, he ends with the Eutychians.

Pope Epiphanius also wrote books on this subject, wonderfully worthy of reverence.

Philaster, bishop of Brescia, wrote one book on each of the heresies in concise brevity; some attribute it to Jerome.

Bishop Isidore, in his *Etymologies*, although only briefly, nevertheless usefully mentions each of the heresies.

Finally, elsewhere in the codex:

I also found two sermons of the same aforementioned man, Saint Augustine, on the Pythoness, delivered to the people in a basilica.

[Col. 1423]

[Col. 1424B] Ethiopians signify sinners, 252. There are two kinds of affections, 562. What affirmation is, 588. In afflictions one should rejoice in the Lord, 106. When a believer afflicts himself, he escapes God’s anger through chastisement, 298. The more someone has been afflicted here, the more he is to be consoled in the future, 200. The fact that we are afflicted here is attributed to God, 128. Affliction received from neighbors is grievous, 148. See Persecution; Temptation; Tribulation. Hagarenes, that is, newcomers, 283. “Field” is derived from *agere*, “to act,” 369. Columella and Aemilianus wrote about agriculture, 554. See Garden. From what “nourishment” is derived, 109. What allegory is, 80, 105, 328, 331. *Alleluia* is a Hebrew name that has not been adopted by any nation, 494, 496. Why it is placed at the end of certain psalms, 496. Allophyli are foreigners, 371. What a complete alphabet signifies, and what an incomplete one signifies, 487. From what “altar” is derived, 87. The twofold altar, and from what it is derived, 145. See Heretic. Amalek is interpreted as “giving birth” or “grieving,” 178. What ambiguity is, 564. What an amblygonius is, 589. Saint Ambrose published six books on Genesis, which he called the *Hexaemeron*, 539. Seven books on the Patriarchs, 539. Saint Ambrose expounded the Gospel of Saint Luke, 543, and all the Epistles of Saint Paul, 544. See Canticle of Canticles. What friendship is, 130. What a friend is, and from what the word is derived, 130. Aminadab is interpreted as “my people’s willing one,” 527. Ammon, that is, “turbulent people,” 283. The love of the Lord comes to human beings in two respects, 389. The soul languishes from love of God when it puts nothing before love of him, 509. See God. Why love is called sleep, 512. See Charity; Love. Amorite: “exasperation,” 463. The Amorites are called “embittering,” 459. What is two-sided or doubtful, 565. “Angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature, 497. “Angel” is interpreted as “messenger,” 348. What an angel is, and why he afflicts converts, 114. For angels the word of the Lord is his will, [Col. 1425] 346. Angels carry human prayers to God, 78. Unclean spirits desire to be adored, whereas the good angel does the opposite, 325. How we can become angels, 111. What a plane angle is, 589.

What the soul is, 173, 628. Why it is called “soul,” 628. It was created by God, 628. On the origin of the soul, 632. The soul is immortal, 629. It is subject to mutability, 630. The source of the soul’s mutability, 47. The soul has no quantity, 631. It is not corporeal, 628. It is not a part of God, 630. Whether the soul has a form, 631. On the substantial quality of the soul, 630. On the seat of the soul, 633. The soul is wholly present in the parts of the body, 629. On the soul’s natural virtues, 632. On the soul’s affections, 629. Souls do not grow, nor are different souls allotted to fools by any varied distinction, 632. The soul’s fiery quality, 630. Souls possess substantial light, 631. How souls are light, 631. “Soul” properly refers to the human soul, not that of beasts, 628. What souls do after death, 637. What the soul’s moral virtues are, 631. The soul has its own food by which it is fattened, 444. It is satisfied in two ways, 362. It has its own thirst, 142. When the soul thirsts for God, 206. When it is empty and when hungry, 366. The soul’s fatness is knowledge of divine things, 206. In what things the soul is said to be lifted up, and in what things not, 449. Souls without right faith are most foul, 635. The city of the Lord is the devout soul, 334. The Lord preserves only the soul in the saints, 432. Everything is made secure if the soul is saved, 190. Nothing is stronger than saving souls, 221. The soul without the Lord is always captive, 390. Against the soul of the righteous, placed in the hands of the Lord, no power of evildoers can prevail, 415. The soul subject to bodily passion does not lack its own punishment, 356. If the soul clings to the body, it favors sins, and conversely, 402. Who receives his soul in vain, and who does not, 81. The soul must resemble an eagle, 343. By the little garden-bed is understood the soul of each believer, 524. The four powers that serve the vegetative soul, 632.

From what “spirit” is derived, 437. “Spirit” and “mind” are not properly called the soul, 628. What the common conceptions of the mind are, 589. The Lord regards the qualities of souls more favorably than the torment of bodies, 425. We can be bent in body, but not in spirit, 129. The beginning of the year was provided by Janus, whence also *janua*, “door,” 250. What “to announce” means, 136. The Antichrist will abound in all the pomp of the age, 178. The pride of the Antichrist, 40. All the Antichrist’s deeds and words are sins, 42. The Antichrist will have all his paths polluted, 40. The wickedness of the Antichrist is described by a twofold perversity, 41. The Antichrist is the head of all the insane, 283. Why the evils of the Antichrist are permitted by God, 42. The Antichrist is a lion in his lair, 41. Doeg was a figure of the Antichrist, 176. The work of copyists is commended, 548. Praise of copyists, 555. From what “boar” is derived, 276. From what “bees” is derived, 395. The Apocalypse was expounded by Bishop Primasius in five books, 544. Saint Jerome expounded the Apocalypse, while Victorinus and Vigilius Afer, the bishop, expounded certain passages, 544. The error of the Apollinarians is refuted, 54. The errors of the Arians and Apollinarians, 375. See Natures of Christ. The apostles and patriarchs are friends of God, 471. The eyes of Christ, 296. The footprints of Christ, 56. By the servants of God, apostles and prophets are signified, 240. By the watchmen, the apostles and teachers of the Church, 512. By the turtledove, the apostles, 510. By the winds, 459. By the columns, 254. By the heavens, the apostles and prophets, 84. By the beard, the apostles are understood, 455. They are compared with rams, 93; with mountains, 119, 212; with arrows, 442. They are called mountains, 293, 386. They are called arrows, 33. See Court; Christ; Church.

The book of Apuleius entitled *Perihermenias* should be read, 569. From what “water” is derived, 437. Terrestrial water is compared with spiritual water, 13. By waters, peoples are signified, 262. From what “spider” is derived, 307. Noah’s ark and the Ark of the Covenant are types of the Church, 452. What is understood by “bow,” 123. The bow signifies the divine commandments, 43. God’s bow is stretched out for salvation, 173. “Sand” is derived from “dryness,” 471. From what “argumentation” is derived, 566. What argumentation is, 566. What assumptive argumentation is, 564. What an argument is, 111, 571. What is the argument called “notation,” 116. There are many kinds of arguments, 571. There are two modes of argument: the enthymeme and the example; and what they are, 573. What probable arguments are, 572. What a probable argument is, 571. Some arguments are neither necessary nor probable, 572. From what things arguments are drawn, 574, 577, 621, 622. See Rhetoric. From what “ram” is derived, 93. What arithmetic is, 583. Why it is so called, and what its purpose is, 584. Why it consists in discrete quantity, *ibid.* Its divisions, 308. Why it remained among the mathematical disciplines, 584. When it was given, 558. It was handed down by Abraham to the Egyptians, 584. It was expounded among the Greeks and given to Latin culture by Apuleius and Boethius, 586. It was praised by Pythagoras, 584. It must not be neglected, 15. Its uses, 584. In what Arius erred, 8. Arius’s error is destroyed, 393. See Christ; Apollinarian. From what “weapons” is derived, 114. Here to be reproved by many is salvation, 28. From what “art” is derived, 558. What difference there is between art and discipline according to Plato and Aristotle, 583. Nature gave the beginning of speech; observation gave the beginning of art, 562. The arts are divided into three parts, 561. The arts and disciplines of the liberal letters are sown throughout sacred Scripture, 538. What Asaph signifies, 164, 244, 259. Assyrians are interpreted as “those who direct,” 256. What astronomy is, 449, 584, 590. The divisions of astronomy, 590. Ptolemy is regarded as the principal writer on astronomy, 591. It was handed down by Abraham to the Egyptians, 584. Natural astrology is praised, but judicial astrology is rejected, 499. Judicial astronomy is contrary to faith, and knowledge of the fates was condemned by the holy Fathers, 591. It is to be avoided, 239. Saint Athanasius disclosed the powers of the Psalms in his book addressed to Marcellinus, 541. What the court is, and from what the word is derived, 458. The courts of the Lord are the apostles, and why, 322. Who are called “hearers,” 165. Hearers are signified by honey and milk, 520.

How many volumes Saint Augustine wrote for the exposition of Genesis, 539. What questions concerning the Books of Kings he resolves, 540. He is praised for his outstanding exposition of the Psalms, 1. He wrote four books on the harmony of the Evangelists, 543. In the greeting of the Epistle to the Romans he produced one book, 544. He expounded the Epistle to the Galatians, *ibid.* He treated the Epistle of Saint James, 543. In the *Book of the City* he disclosed many things about the Apocalypse, 544. He is praised, 551. See Understanding; Sacred Scripture. “Ear” is derived from “hearing,” 337, 389. “Gold” (*aurum*) is derived from “breeze” (*aura*), 242. What difference there is between *auxesis* and *climax*, 20. What avarice is, 403. It is a conspicuous evil, 133. Avaricious men are called men of wealth, 257.

B

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” 210, 294. The rule of sacred baptism flowed from the Jordan, 241. The Christian people are one nation, born from one baptismal fountain, 283. No one can be a believer without baptism, 515. Through baptism and the satisfaction of confession, sins are expiated, 288. Baptism restores us to Adam’s purity, 170. It is called the water of refreshment, 79. By the womb of the Church the baptismal font is understood, 528. The Church formerly sang Psalm XLI for those being baptized, 144. The Red Sea is a figure of the water of baptism, which came forth mixed with blood from Christ’s side, 251, 279. Just as the people of Israel were saved through the Red Sea, so the Church of the nations is saved through baptism, 507. Why the Flood is set in place of the sacred fonts, 95. From what “barbarian” is derived, 386. Bashan: “confusion,” 459. Bashan is interpreted as “dryness,” 223. Saint Basil composed nine homilies on Genesis in the Greek language, 539, and a book called the *Hexaemeron*, 591.

What the blessed nation is, 108. Everyone wishes to attain blessedness, 398. Blessedness cannot be explained in words, 286. “Blessed” is used in two ways, 12. Existence properly belongs to the blessed, 135. What the blessedness of the saints is, 147. Future blessedness is described, 123, 295. The happiness of the good is declared, 637. The beatific vision, 638. The light of glory is necessary for the beatific vision, 218. What we shall know when placed in glory, 638. Eternal happiness is far better than the present life, 206. Blessedness is compared with an inheritance, 202. The glory of the faithful is suspended until the resurrection, 84, 372, 637. Whoever seeks blessedness here rises before dawn, 442. God’s storerooms are eternal blessedness, 506. A prepared place signifies the kingdom of the Lord, and who will deserve it, 286. The children of the blessed are compared with fresh olive shoots, 444. The first blessedness of the holy soul is to exult in the Lord, 115. The house of the blessed is the mind’s secret place, 383. See Happiness.

The presbyter Bellator expounded the books of Tobit, Esther, Judith, and Maccabees, 543. At Cassiodorus’s urging he composed two books on Ruth and on the other women who follow, 540. When we bless God, we praise his works; when he blesses, he sanctifies us, 400. Those who bless God, 225, 347. The one who blesses is blessing when he sanctifies with continual blessing, 453. The wicked bless in prosperity, but the good also in adversity, 163. The wicked bless with their mouths, not in their hearts, 163. How we can be blessed, 457. What blessing is firm and true, 446. The Lord’s blessing always increases us, 218. The custom among the Hebrews of blessing, 446. See Bishop. The gifts bestowed commend the understanding and memory, 361. No believer forgets a benefit, 412. Why benefits conferred by God should be used well, [Col. 1427] 363. He never ceases to praise God who does not forget the benefits bestowed, 343. Benjamin: “son of the right hand,” 275. What Bethel signifies, 511. Boethius expounded the book *Perihermenias*, 568. There is no satiety of good things, 408. When people are good, 439. Why the good are always a reproach to the wicked, 228. If we wish to attain glory, we must refrain not only from evil but also perform what is good, 112. See Soul; Wicked; Perfect; Holy; Virtue. What the arm signifies, 42, 146, 300.

C
## C

**Chalice**, whence the name is derived, 44, 53. **Slander** is called “the foster-child of the head,” and what it is, 420. **Slanderer**, what he is, 241. **Fields**, whence they are so called, 452. **To sing**, what it is, 71. What it is to sing, exult, and psalm, 327. What a song is, 5, 21. What the new song is, 135, 499. When the voice of singers is pleasing to God, 337. See **To psalm**, **Psalm**.

**Song of Songs.** Why the book is so called, 505. It contains nothing that can be understood according to the literal sense, 531. Origen commented on it, 542. Epiphanius, 542. Saint Ambrose explains much about the Song of Songs in Book III of *The Patriarchs*, 542.

**Head**, from *capere*, “to take,” 379. What is to be understood by “head,” 33.

**Prison**, whence the name is derived, 479. The ancient interpreters understood “prison” in two ways, 479.

**Carmel**, interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision,” 528.

**Flesh**, whence the name is derived, 268. Flesh requires more than the soul, 206. Why our flesh is called the daughter of Babylon, 465. The desires of the flesh are snares, 478. The vices of the flesh are earthly sins, 417. One does not truly live where sin is committed through the weakness of the flesh, 416. Whoever is dominated by the vices of the flesh rolls in dung, 385. See **Vice**. In myrrh, the mortification of the flesh is understood; in frankincense, the devotion of prayers, 516. Our flesh is compared with a turtledove, 285.

Cassian’s book *On the Institution of Monks* should be read diligently, 555. He was censured by blessed Prosper, 555. Victor of Martyritanus cleared him, ibid.

Cassiodorus compared all Scripture with the ancient manuscripts, 538. He abridged the text of the Octateuch, 540. Cassiodorus prefaced the Books of Kings with titles, 540. He is the author of the books *On the Soul* and *Various Letters*, 490. Why he composed the book *On the Institution of Divine Letters*, 537. He composed the book *On Division*, 576, and two commentaries on Donatus’s arts, 559. He had sent [men] into various parts of the world to search out books, 544. Cassiodorus’s most devout prayer to Christ, 639. See **Heretic**.

**Camps**, from *castitas*, “chastity,” 267.

Aristotle’s *Categories* are ten, 568. Why they must be read attentively, 568. The instruments of the categories are three: equivocal, univocal, and denominative terms, 568.

The error of the Catharists, 84.

**Chair**, what it is, 12.

**Whelps**, whence the name is derived, 351.

**Cause**, from *casus*, “fall” or “case,” 246. The parts of causes are called “statuses,” and their divisions, 580. See **Rhetoric**.

**Cedar** is interpreted as “darkness,” 430, 506.

**Neck** is used for pride, 446.

The encyclical codex of the Council of Chalcedon was translated by Epiphanius Scholasticus, 545.

**Canaan** is interpreted as “humble,” 355, and as “evil humiliation,” 459.

**Charity**, in what true charity consists, 47. The law of Christ is charity, 447. The broad commandment is charity, 412. Why, 514. The paths of righteousness are the two commandments of charity, 79. Love of God and neighbor are the Lord’s ways, 61. Charity is placed at the summit of the virtues, 429. Malice embraces the generality of crimes, just as charity embraces that of the virtues, 318. Christ delights among the virtues of the saints, and especially among faith and charity, 511. Charity commends all things, 425. It is stronger than every torment, 426. The fervor of charity is tranquil, 132. The blessed conscience is tested by the fire of charity, 216. The virtue of charity and unity, 437. Through charity the saints become one, 432. Nothing so terrifies evil spirits as charity, 525. After continence of the flesh, true charity follows, 519. Those who love God above all things serve him with joy, 331. Who loves God, 58. Whoever loves God with all his heart leaves no room for vices, 456. When the righteous love God freely, and the impious freely curse him, 373. See **God**, **Love**.

When we love our neighbor as ourselves, 456. Praise of brotherly charity, 456. We ought diligently to do whatever can help another, 383. It is the custom of the saints to grieve over another’s calamities as over their own, 337. A holy man reproves not in anger but [Col. 1428] through love, 477. Love of enemies. See **Enemy**.

Charity and mercy are, as it were, the Father’s wings, 56. Charity is called a nail, 417. By wine the fervor of charity is understood, 531. Charity is compared with spring rain, 47. By coals, prayers kindled by the fire of charity are understood, 430.

**Cherubim**, how the word is to be interpreted, 271, 329.

**Choir**, what it is, 501.

By the anointing of sacred chrism the foreheads of Christians are marked, 467. The face is gladdened by oil when royal chrism is prepared, 350.

The glorious name of Christ, 242. It belongs to Christ’s name faithfully to save those who ask, 482. What is to be believed about the Lord the Savior, 68, 194. To believe in Christ is salvation and glory, 204. Christ is known by his divinity only to the faithful, but by his body merely to unbelievers, 261. How Christ came from the Father and departed from the world, 195. At the Lord’s coming the earth was moved, 59. By “full days” Christ’s first coming is understood, 246. The days before Christ’s coming were ancient days, 133. How many blessings occurred through Christ’s coming, 315. Through Christ’s coming the wounds of the world were healed, 214. The human race was healed through the Lord’s coming, 212. Christ came to us so that we might return to him, 234.

The mystery of the incarnation is explained, 36. At the very origin of the incarnation, divinity was joined to humanity, 73. Divinity assumed humanity without confusion, 19. God made human, 37. The works of God are terrible, especially in uniting human nature to himself, 214. The excellence of the incarnation, 75, 109. The Lord’s magnificence is the incarnation, 34. Nothing is more excellent than the benefit of the holy incarnation, 278. The time of favor is the time of the incarnation, 228. The incarnation can be understood through the Lord’s counsel, 108. It is compared with darkness, 59. Christ became our protector through the mystery of the incarnation, 416. The Lord cared for us when he assumed our humanity, 340. By the incarnation God exalted the human nature which he had predestined to free, 294. Christ stood, as it were, behind a wall when he assumed our flesh, 510. Christ’s assumption of our flesh is proved by the inheritance, 355. Christ, coming into the world, made certain leaps, 510. When Christ came, the obscurity of the divine Word became manifest, 60.

Christ’s temporal birth, 35. What occurred in it, 159. Why Christ says that he was drawn from his mother’s womb, 73. Without a mother in heaven, without a father on earth, 281. It is the Lord’s mercy that he was born of the Virgin Mary, 260. Christ’s temporal birth can be called a visitation, 35. Why we should rejoice in it, 396. Christ appeared to the faithless, but was not given to them, 288.

In Christ there is only one person, 17. Which person Christ is, 20, 52. One and the same person of God and man, 32. In Christ there are two natures but one person, 32, 52, 69, 71, 208. He assumed a perfect human nature, contrary to the Apollinarians, 290. There are two perfect and unconfused natures in Christ, 19, 57, 310. This is proved against the Arians, 473. In him there are two substances, 16, and their operations are expressed, 289. In Christ there are two operations, of divinity and humanity, 523.

Christ is God and man, against the Arians, 140. He is God of gods, 164. He is called the God of truth, 98. God of powers, 286. He is Lord of powers, 156. He is called both Son of David and Lord, 377. He is rightly called the Most High, 215. Why he is not called “man,” 73. Christ alone is by nature Son of God; the saints are sons by grace, 299. He is our end, to which all things must be referred, 182.

Christ is eternal, 243. He is not a new God but coeternal with the Father, 279. Whatever Christ received in time, he acquired according to his humanity, 18. His divinity received nothing by which it might increase, 442. Every creature is subject to Christ, 35. By his power he rules eternally, 215. Christ is the omnipotent King, 319. King forever, 207. Why he is called the King of glory, 82. Christ entered this world especially as King, 223. He was appointed King by the Father, 17. Why he is King, 251. He is truly Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” 239. Christ’s anointing signifies a King and a Priest, 152. Christ is King, Prophet, and Pontiff, 455. Christ is truly Priest, 379. Christ is Priest and victim, 211.

Christ’s soul was exempt from original sin, 633. The Holy Spirit remained in Christ, 3. Christ had no sin, 32. Christ’s humanity admitted no stain, 523. Christ’s first glory was to enter the tabernacle without blemish, 51. He alone walked the immaculate way, 62. Christ’s way alone is good, whereas ours is evil, 122. Christ alone is immaculate in himself; others are so by grace, 398.

Christ’s body is a holy temple, 26. How Christ’s flesh is life-giving, adorable, and saving, 111. His flesh is adorable, 59. The Lord’s body is a garment of the Godhead, 152. How Christ was humbled, 35. When Christ spoke, 136. Why the Lord Christ is called a child, 229. Christ is called beautiful and comely, and why, 508. Whether he was comely in form, 150. Christ is more beautiful than all the elect, 524.

What is meant by Christ’s imperfection, 471. [Col. 1429] Christ is called an orphan, needy, and poor, although he is ruler and Lord of all, 281. Christ is at once rich and poor, 161. Why he is called needy and poor, 138, 231. Rich in what is his own, he became poor for us, 50. A beggar from what is ours, rich from what is his own, 374. What his abundance is, 96.

Christ is called the servant of the Lord, 118. Why, 291. According to his humanity he calls himself the servant of God, 100. Why he calls himself a worm, 73. The humility of Christ’s humanity is expressed, 32. He taught it by words and examples, 639. Christ’s humility possessed beauty and strength, 314. He showed both the way of humility and the discipline of patience, 463. Christ’s gentleness, 141. The acts of Christ’s life are examples, 190. All his activity arouses hope and desire for heavenly things, 523. Christ walked the hard ways of human beings, 55. Why he shed tears, 466. How he wore sackcloth, 116. When he fasted, and with what fast, 116. When he was ill, 96. Why he endured the devil’s temptation, 195. How Christ meditated on the law, 13. He prays to the Father in respect of the humanity he assumed, 97. He asks as man and grants as God, 376. The purity of Christ’s prayer, 20. What he asked, 91. Why he asks the Father for what properly belongs to him, 473. Why Christ is wonderful in the eyes of the faithful but not of the Jews, 396. Why Christ performed miracles, 92. He worked salvation more through preaching than through miracles, 251.

The pagans did not believe that God could suffer, 21. Christ’s passion was a fable to the Jewish nation, 228. What judgment he endured from the Jews, 117. He is white through virginity and red through passion, 522. Why he said, “Look upon my cause, and not upon my punishment,” 117. With what thirst Christ thirsted, 230. Christ says that he was troubled but never despaired, 99. Christ alone desired to die, 69. Christ’s death alone is liberating because it was voluntary, 296. Why Christ chose the death of the cross rather than another death, 75. The end of Christ’s death was unique to him, 223. Why the inscription of the title was not erased during the passion, 186. In Christ’s passion the divinity was not absent, 72. The Lord’s death is described, 190. Christ, as if seated on a throne, absolved the confessing thief, 75. The Savior’s death is called a session, 469. It is called a day of battle, 475. His bed is the most blessed completion of his passion, 451. The whole world mourned Christ’s death, 96. Praise of Christ’s cross, 23. See **Cross**.

It is fitting that he be publicly praised who deigned to suffer for the salvation of all, 392. What instruments of Christ’s passion are preserved at Jerusalem, 295. The fruit of Christ’s passion, 371. Its usefulness, 377. It strengthens God’s servants in afflictions, 140. In the crucified Christ all are crucified, 186. Christ offered himself for the salvation of the whole race, 52. He made everyone’s cause his own, 77. He offered himself as a sacrifice for all, 174. Why, 463. His passion is a sacrifice of righteousness, 174. He freed the human race, which was bound, 229. Christ’s blood redeemed the sins of the whole world, 448. It purifies, but does not stain with blood, ibid. Through Christ, punishment became eternal rest and death the entrance to salvation, 639. He endured reproach in order to instruct us by the example of his patience, 229.

How Christ is said to have been brought down into the dust, 74. In what sense he is said to have descended into corruption, 54. Why Christ did not descend into corruption, 97. Christ’s soul was drawn out of the underworld, 96. He freed his soul from hell, 163. When his soul was freed from necessities, 99. How death was conquered by Christ, 20, 183. Death had to perish, since life invaded its kingdom, 222. When Christ’s flesh blossomed again, 92. The glory of the risen one was the recompense of his passion, 480. By Christ’s death the world was to be saved, but he himself by the resurrection, 290. Christ’s divinity is proved by the resurrection, 371. Why, by rising from the dead, he ascended above the west, 220. The Lord’s resurrection is compared with sleep, 140. Through the resurrection divine power was declared and the hope of believers strengthened, 293. It is the hope of Christians, 96, 149. He strengthened the hearts of the righteous, 480. When the Lord rose, his members received the hope of resurrection, 310.

Christ’s ascension was useful to the apostles and to the whole Church, 534. What reward was given to Christ’s humanity, 442. When Christ was crowned with glory and honor, 35. Christ’s praise is the honor of the whole Trinity, 321. Christ is the Wisdom of God, 351. Through him the Father’s knowledge was made wondrous, 469. He is the peace of God, 288. He is the right hand of the Most High, 261. Christ’s glory is the majesty of the Father, 97. Christ is called the Father’s right hand, arm, salvation, and righteousness because he is consubstantial with him, 327. Christ is the Father’s mercy, 288. The Father’s power, 244. The Father’s hand, 485. His soul is the Father’s sword, 57.

Salvation comes from Christ alone, 31. He alone grants salvation, 490. Christ the Lord is the hope of our salvation, 380. Why Christ is called Savior, 273. It is appropriate to the name “Savior” to save those who are in peril, 361. Through Christ all things were reconciled, 534. Christ is mercy for sinners and life for the faithful, 404. Why Christ is called mercy, 160, 307. Christ is our Ecclesiastes, 542. In him is the fountain of blessing, 152. He is a fountain of waters, 142. From him everlasting water flows, 265.

Christ is the way, guide, and road, 19. The world has no way except the Lord Savior, 206. Christ is the sure way for those coming to the Father, 398. He is the way of truth, 218. He is the way of testimonies, 400. He is the guide of our journey, 222. When he is truly our guide, 98. No one entered the kingdom of heaven except through him, 531.

Through Christ’s first coming the devil was bound and humanity was released, 64. Through the humility [Col. 1430] of Christ the devil’s pride was conquered, 424. When we are with Christ, we fear none of the devil’s snares, 235. Christ conquers the devil in us, 311. See **Devil**.

Why Christ descended into the Church and ascended to it, 529. Praise of Christ’s marriage with the Church, 154. Christ is the foundation and summit of the Church, 158. The people of God are one body of Christ, 436. Christ is said to have foolishness on behalf of his members, 227. Why Christ does not yet reign most fully in his members, 492. Christ is said to suffer what his members endure, 137. Christ calls the world’s evils his own, 296. Christ’s inheritance is the elect, 92. How Christ eats the elect, 520. When Christ judges us to be his own, 297. Who are properly subjected to Christ, 36. If we remember Christ, he too will remember us, 532. See **Church**.

Christ’s regard is our protection, 137. He converts us, 85. He cuts sinners away from their perversities, 301. Every evil is quickly dissolved if it is struck forcefully against Christ, 466. For the righteous Christ is peace, for unbelievers a stumbling block, 288. Christ’s joy is the salvation of the human race, 514. Christ is the right hand of the good, 469. Christ is the strength of our head, 200.

When Christ is produced as our bread from the earth, 349. He is called the bread of heaven and of angels, 266. How he feeds angels and human beings, ibid. See **Eucharist**.

When Christ is near and when he withdraws, 510. The sweetest sleep is to seek Christ, 512. Why he withdraws for a time when he is sought, 524. To seek Christ’s soul is spoken of in a good and in a bad sense, 114. Whoever does not love Christ hates peace, 430. Christ’s enemies delighted over him, 95.

Christ is always set against Adam, 161. Comparison of Christ and Adam, 14. See **Adam**. Christ is to be understood through David, 16. By the diadem, the flesh assumed by Christ is understood, 514. By the sackcloth, his body is signified, 97. The new song signifies the Lord’s incarnation, 106. The thigh signifies the same, 151. By the eighth, the Lord’s second coming is signified, 27. By myrrh, Christ’s passion is represented, 507. By nard, 518. By the cithara, 191. By the purple color, 529. By the purple ascent, 514. By the fragment of a pomegranate, 515. By the does, Christ and the teachers of the Church are understood, 528. By the bridegroom’s cheeks, Christ’s mercy or severity, 523.

Why Christ is compared with a giant, 65, and with does and a fawn of the deer, 510, 511. With a fruitful tree, 13. His wisdom with a torrent, 120. His body with a psaltery, 161, and with the earth, 75. His power with a potsherd, 74. Christ and the devil are compared with a lion under different aspects, 31. Christ is the sun, 351. The true day is unknown to the faithless, 265.

Christ is called the new song, 485. Why he is the “heap of testimony,” 525, and the spiritual rock, 358. Why he is called the cornerstone, 396. The holes in the rock are his wounds, 511. He alone is the mountain in which the Father was pleased, 222. Why he is called the flower of the field and not of the countryside, 508. The sharp arrows are Christ’s words, and why, 151. Christ is called strong in hand, 91. What Christ’s holy seat is, 158. Christ’s eyes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit or the teachers of the Church, 523. His lips are the two Testaments, 53. By his breasts the sweetness of the Gospel is understood, 505. His arms are the prophets and apostles, 62. His feet are the apostles, 75. His crown signifies the gathering of his disciples, 69. His shadow is the protection of the divinity, 509.

Christ’s transformation is to summon the old man to the grace of regeneration, 305. Those who were once called Christ’s, 64, 92. See **Law**, **Synagogue**.

**Christians**, so called from Christ, 68, 243. The patriarchs were Christians in spirit and were called Christ’s, 355. Christians are called the coming generation, 78. The religion of Christ spread throughout the whole world, 34. Christians fill the whole earth, 351. In the Roman world it is now a glory to be a Christian, 200. The Christian people are the Lord’s inheritance, 284. It is an inheritance of acquisition, 108. See **Church**.

Who the true Christians are, 333. The instruction of a Christian consists in two things: turning away from evil and doing good, 125. Every Christian is built upon the rock, that is, Christ, 201. Two things make Christians good, 83. Christians seek only two things, 396. It is not fitting for Christ’s soldier to have idle time, 490. For the faithful Christian there is always day, 467. The Lord’s dwelling is the breast of the Christian and the courts of the Catholic Church, 451. Christians are said to rise in two ways, 68. Whatever a Christian suffers here is refreshed by the thought of blessedness, 49. The greatest affliction of Christians, 142. When oppressed, the Christian then bears fruit, 186. See **Affliction**, **Persecution**, **Tribulation**.

What joy Christians enjoy, 23. What blessings God has promised Christians, 146. Why the Christian people are represented by Jacob, 327. Jacob’s obtaining of the blessing by stealth was a figure of the blessing of the Christian people, 69. The sons of Korah are called Christians, 141, 285. Sheep signify the Christian people, 36. Christ’s servants are compared with sheep, 149. The waters of the sea signify the Christian people, 107. Christians are compared with grapes trampled underfoot, 187.

Saint Chrysostom published commentaries on the Acts of the Apostles, [Col. 1431] which Cassiodorus ordered to be translated, 544. He explained all Saint Paul’s Epistles in the Attic language, 544. He treated the Epistle to the Hebrews in Attic Greek; Mutianus translated it into Latin, 543.

**Cushi**, what the name signifies, 30.

**Scar**, whence the word is derived, 129.

Cicero composed two books on rhetoric, which M. Victorinus commented on, 565.

**Sackcloth**, what it is and what it signifies, 115.

**Circle**, what it is, 325, 589. What the diameter of a circle is, 589. What a semicircle is, 389. Cicero divides circumstances into two classes, 581.

**Cithara**, what it is, 4, 501, 506. By the cithara moral virtues are understood, 493.

There are two cities in this world: one belonging to the Lord, the other to the devil, 464. See **Devil**, **Church**.

Clement of Alexandria explained certain canonical Epistles, 543.

**Furnace**, what it is, 70.

The climates are counted as seven, and what they are, 591.

**Heaven**, whence the name is derived, 388. Some thought that heaven was a living creature, 497. Heaven is in those who conduct themselves in a heavenly manner, 411. Who sets his mouth against heaven, 245. What heaven signifies, 17, 44, 494.

**Thoughts**, whence the word is derived, 138, 490, 628. Our thoughts are called feet, 431. God alone knows the secrets of thoughts, 32. Our house is called a thought proper to us, whose two walls are the two Testaments, 444. Evil thoughts incline toward the lowest earth, 207. It is a twofold evil to conceive wickedness and to bring it openly forth, 245. See **Heart**.

**Joint praise**, what it is, 106, 392.

**Collection**, what it is, 564.

**Dove**, whence the name is derived, 183.

What difference there is between a common noun and an epicene noun, 596.

**Comparison**, what it is, 564. The comparative has only two forms, 595. The degrees of comparison serve three cases, 595.

What the increase of calculation is, 591. What subtraction in calculation is, 591.

Universal councils strengthen the faith, 545. The Fathers and the councils spoke not contradictory but different things, 546.

**Conclusion**, what it is, 30, 565, 566, 571. A conclusion has a twofold basis, 562.

**Concubines**, whom they designate, 562.

**Concupiscence**, what it is, 42. See **Faith**.

**To confirm**, what it is, 123.

**Confirmation**, what it is, 565.

**To confess**, what it is, 254. Confession is called, as it were, *confatio*, “speaking together,” 331. We confess in two ways, 311. There are two confessions: one of praise, the other of repentance, 117, 218, 319, 331. Pious confession begins from the Lord, 233. After true faith holy confession must follow, 391. Those who truly know God descend to humble confession, 104. Whoever confesses his sins gives glory to God, 188. It is a greater glory of God to spare the one who confesses than to preserve one who lives without offense, 359. Confession of weakness moves God’s mercy, 28. Confession of weakness obtains divine gifts, 317. To reveal one’s fault to God is a remedy; to confess is security, 248. Confession repeatedly made to God brings forth salvation, 254. Confession of sins makes the judge favorable, 273. Those who have confessed their sins cannot fear the coming judgments, 218. God alone is the judge who grants forgiveness to the one who confesses, 475. Confession of sins is useless after death, 29. See **Baptism**.

**To be confounded**, what it is, 114, 233. There is a twofold confusion, 381. If we are confounded in this age, we are corrected, 293. When we are prosperously confounded here, 235. Those who bear their confusion, 138.

**Conjecture**, what a simple conjecture is, 564.

**Conjunction**, what it is, 559.

**Conscience**, a pure court of the Holy Spirit, 93. For a good conscience, to sin after forgiveness is a more serious fear, 131.

**To consider**, what it is, 126.

**Counsel**, what it is, 71. Counsel, whence the name is derived, 15, 187. What the spirit of counsel is, 94. A crime is more serious when it is carried out by the counsel of many, 100.

Through Constantine’s conversion the Church was wonderfully glorified, 517.

Why vicious habits are bronze gates, 367. The custom of ruined people, 56.

**Completion** is the perfect fulfillment that completes all the virtues, [Col. 1432] 412. “To complete” signifies both perfection and deficiency, 411.

The contemplation of God is food for spiritual substances, 166.

We must crush ourselves if we wish to be restored, 493.

A continent man is called a king, 108. See **Charity**, **Ecclesiastical Orders**.

**Contradiction**, what it is, 568.

According to Cicero, controversy is threefold, 564.

**To be converted** is permitted in this life, 104. God awaits our conversion at every time, 188. The soul of one truly converted is compared with a spider, 134.

**Heart**, not the brain, is the seat of wisdom, 248. The place of the heart is between the breasts, 507. The heart has a voice, which the divinity hears, 89. Our heart is beneath our tongue, 217. “Heart” is used for “mind,” 350. By the heart the mystery of the mind is understood, 466. “Heart” refers to understanding, 174, 285. What is signified by a double heart and by a single heart? 45. It belongs to God alone to examine our hearts, 32. Those who are upright in heart are joined to the divine rule, 317. Our hearts, not the limbs of animals, are to be sacrificed to God, 174. If we think of God in our heart, we find him there, 110. Who pours out his heart before God, 204. When we open our hearts to Christ, 521. The heart is “high” when it thinks of heavenly things and avoids earthly things, 209.

**Korah** is interpreted as “Calvary,” 141. Korah signifies “baldness” or “bald,” 285.

There are three kinds of things that can be believed, 562. See **Faith**.

Christ’s cross was granted for the salvation of believers, 481. How the Lord’s cross corrected the crooked and distorted world, 323. Christ’s cross is to be adored, 452. ## D
Daemon. See Devil. Damasus means “drink of blood” or “eye of blood,” 528. The punishment of the damned is described, 637. The book of Daniel is counted among the Hagiographa by the Hebrews, 541. David: what the name signifies, 16, 113, 144. How holy David received prophecy, 3. David was anointed twice, 88. Bathsheba signifies the Church; David bore the figure of Christ, 169.

To fall away: what it is, 26. Defectus, “deficiency,” is understood in many ways, 410. To fail: what it is, 99. Definition: what it is, 570. From where a definition arises, 12. What the difference is between a definition and a description, 574. What a substantial definition is, 18. What a legal definition is, [Col. 1433] 564. There are fifteen kinds of definitions, and examples of each are given, 570, 622, 623.

Heavenly delights are described, 220. See Spiritual. Delictum, “offense,” is lighter than peccatum, “sin,” 83. See Flesh; Injustice.

Teeth: from where the word is derived, 21. Supplication: what it is, 29, 134, 201, 564. See Prayer. Derision: what it is, 148. The more the soul is moved by heavenly desires, the more it dies to earthly desires, 521. We live while impious desires die, and conversely, 463. Why holy desire is compared to a little column of smoke, 513. See Flesh.

Sloth is hateful to the Lord, 556. Slanderers are the greatest sinners, 168. Our ancestors called God “from fear,” 72. In the Greek language God is called “fear,” 164. Ten names of God among the Hebrews, 353. Why God is called the Terrible Name, 315. Why he is called great, terrible, and holy, 329. God’s name is believed to be worshiped everywhere, 160. How God is defined by some, 18. God’s true definition is that he has no limit in his perfections, 487. God cannot be defined by genus and differences, 17. Being properly belongs to God, 261. “I am” is the proper verb of divinity, and why, 165. God lives in a unique blessedness, 242. In him there is one power and an undivided majesty, 45. He alone is merciful, compassionate, and patient by essence, 344. All substantial virtues are in God, 424. Light and fountain are opposites among human beings, but in God they are one, 120. God alone exists, 342. God alone is great, 291. When he is called blessed, 64. Why he is called long-suffering, 33. Why he is called strong, 33. Frailty must not be charged to divinity, 290. God properly is, because he has neither past nor future, 306. Before divinity everything present is past and future, 450. God is wholly and presently everywhere, 557. Wholly everywhere, 155. Full everywhere, wholly everywhere, 423. He is confined by no determination of place, 281. Whoever believes him present everywhere sets God before his own sight, 181. God surrounds and penetrates all things, 60. God is wholly present to the good everywhere and absent from the wicked, 439. God is ineffable, 359. He could not be known through human wisdom, 512. The ways of the Lord are incomprehensible, 84. God’s acts can in some measure be grasped by our knowledge, but never his substance, 1491. One may say of God what he is not, but one cannot comprehend what he is, 480. Who are those who know the Lord, 120. Where God is seen, 225. How all creatures confess God, 488. All God’s works are known to human senses as profound, 312. How God is said to see, 17. The Lord’s understanding encompasses all things, 462. Why God can forget nothing, 260. Nothing new occurs contrary to God’s foreknowledge, 364. God knows us not by testing but by foreknowing, 216. He knows our deeds and thoughts even before we exist, 469. Through foreknowledge he distinguishes us, and how, 281. How God speaks to angels and blessed human beings, 346. For God, willing is the same as doing, 489. The Lord’s command does not lengthen time, because his will is its effect, 257. Nothing is impossible for God, 227. To say that something is impossible for God is the gravest sin, 265. In divinity there is no distinction between nature and power, 28. God accomplishes all things by one power, without the senses, 24. God performs by incomprehensible power everything that human beings perform through the senses, 447. God brings all things that have been created to existence, 531. A king is so called from ruling, God from creating, 286. Why all things must be moved by God, 107. Everything created is subject either to the Creator’s permission or to his command, 269. Such is the power of the divine command that all things can obey it even if they cannot understand it, 301. All creatures are shown to obey God’s commands, 265. See Create.

Whatever God has promised will remain forever, 355. The divine sacrament of promise is security, 299. God’s swearing is his promising what is to come, 303. He swears both when calm and when angry, 320.

God is the most equitable judge, 255. Why he is called just, 33. Human justice is temporal, but God’s is eternal, 422. Whatever the Lord judges, he sees, 55. The Lord’s power always either has mercy or judges, 332. It belongs to God’s glory whether he spares or judges, 387. Whoever believes God to be an avenger does not set an evil thing before the eyes of his heart, 333. Why David said, “I will praise your justice,” and not your mercy, 174. How God loves mercy and judgment in this world, 107. The Lord’s mercies endure with eternal stability, 298. How God is merciful and compassionate, 488. All God’s benefits toward us are included in mercy, 198. Without the Lord’s mercy we cannot endure, 461. Its extent cannot be explained, 169. It surpasses all sins, 364. It is a patroness to the weak, 229. He has mercy when he regards his own creature, but condemns when he looks upon our works, 468. When he does not remove a supplication, he grants his mercy, 217. He has mercy as a father, but only on those for whom he is a father, 344. The Lord is our father and also our mother, and why, 90. He is more inclined to mercy than to anger, 260. Whose helper he is, 491. The Lord’s mercy is compared with the variously flowing sky, 344. The Lord’s mercy is compared with a river, 212. See Grace; Mercy.

God is sweet to some, 101, 488. The sweeter he becomes to us, the dearer we become to him, 353. To the impious he is darkness, to the devout he is benevolent, 324. He is called the horn of salvation, 58. Why the Lord’s wonders are not seen by darkened minds, 297. When God teaches goodness, when discipline, and when knowledge, 408. When the Lord remembers a human being, 35. Of which person God is the portion, 248. Why God is called the portion of the devout, 407. God’s face is the gift of all rewards, 475. The Lord’s presence is help, 39. It is a benefit, 44. God’s looking upon someone means that he does not despise that person, 340. Those upon whom he looks favorably he corrects, 251. He looks upon them both in anger and in favor, 420. See Blessedness.

God is said to dwell in many ways, 435. He dwells in the one by whom he is understood, 257. Whatever he inhabits he makes glorious, 87. When he is always in us, we remain saved, 437. All things become bearable when he dwells in the holy, 438. What it means to cling to God, 207. Who is said to stand before God, 25. What it means to await the Lord, 83. Whoever is abandoned by God is deprived of no benefit, 42. When we love the Lord, we find everything in him, 111. See Charity.

How much God’s anger is to be feared, 29. How he is said to become angry, 33. The Lord’s anger is spoken of in two ways, 197. It is only metonymical, 268, 284. It is called the repayment of sins, 17. The Lord is stirred to vengeance when provoked by evil deeds, 27. He is disturbed neither by anger nor by fury, 28. With whom the Lord will be angry forever, and with whom not, 344. What is requested through God’s turning, 28.

What God’s memorial is, 310. What is understood by the Lord’s right hand and what by his left, 432. What is called God’s finger, 35. His shoulders are his wondrous works, 309. Eternal stability is signified by his feet, 378. In what sense he is said to smell, taste, and walk, 368. When we say that God sleeps, 149. God’s hidden things can be understood both in evil and in good, 57. The Creator’s will is called a shield, 26. God is compared with a physician, 493. He is likened to a wax-worker, and in what respect, 108. God is to be blessed at all times, 141. How he can be exalted, 191. He is exalted among the nations and is to be exalted among the Jews, 156. No creature is sufficiently able to complete God’s praises, 351. How he can be celebrated by human beings with new proclamation, 237. The topics of argument from which God can be praised, 487. To recount the Lord’s deeds is to have praised him, 264. Whoever gives God praise makes himself praiseworthy, 225. When we exalt the Lord, we exalt ourselves, 368. It ought to be glorious for us when the Lord’s name is exalted, 354.

Who truly calls upon God, 494. No person ought to be accepted against God, 416. The faithful cannot endure injuries inflicted upon God, 273. Being despised for God’s name is more honorable with him, 287. Whether in prosperity or adversity, our eyes must always be raised to the Lord, 436. When a faithful person looks upon God, 220. God rules those who look upon him with a pure heart, 275. Those who look upon the Lord with a pure mind are the orphan and the widow, 492. It is profound blindness not to have God before one’s eyes, 40. To forget the Lord is an immense crime, 168. What it means to forget the Lord, 39. With what disposition we ought to approach the Lord, 480. Who truly seeks him, 49. The Lord is always present to all who devoutly seek him, 521. Those who follow the Lord are upright in heart, 439. Whenever one comes to God, our youth is rightly said to be renewed, 235. How God is said to withdraw from us, 40. When we become far from him, 319. Whoever is deserted by him is punished and afflicted, 280. Those whom he despises he annihilates, 270. To have the Lord turned away from oneself is the extremity of all evils, 364. Whoever has seen divine things easily despises human things, 83. There is no satiety in divine matters, 89.

“Gods” are improperly called human beings and heavenly powers, 281. The gods of the pagans are called alien gods because they are found with an alienated mind, 280.

The Devil is a spirit, and there are innumerable demons, 351. The devil’s works are contained neither by weight, nor measure, nor number, 558. The devil is never to be restored to grace, 38. He is punished as often as a sinner who has been subdued by him is rescued, 32. At the judgment he will appear condemned before human eyes, 394. Before the Incarnation he held almost the entire human race captive, 115. When his head was crushed, 252. After Christ’s coming the devil was bound, 334. See Christ.

Demons thirst for the blood of souls, 528. The devil with his ministers are persecutors, 418. They are called assailants, 114. In this age there are innumerable snares of demons, 351. The devil’s craft, 339. The enemy is most shameless, 334. He is most cunning, 513. Iniquity and the devil are always lying in wait for us, 557. The devil also habitually harms through good things, 513. Why he hides a snare beside the road, 479. Demons always persist in evil works, 322. Demonic suggestions must immediately be rejected, 334. Whom the devil pursues more fiercely, 130. He especially lies in wait for the holy, [Col. 1435] 513. More intensely near the end of life, 187. Demons rage more savagely against those whom they have been unable to deceive, 418. Why they always surround the faithful, 482. At what time the devil snatches someone away, 31. What he does to us when he has prevailed, 31. Earthly human beings are the devil’s food, not heavenly ones, 352. Whoever follows the devil persecutes himself, 44. To love the Lord is to hate the devil, who is called evil, 326. What weapons are there against the devil? 149. The devil is overcome by weeping, 342. When we are taken from the devil’s power, 31. How he is mocked by angels and faithful men, 352. Demons do nothing to human beings except by God’s permission, 351. No one is tempted by the devil without the Lord’s permission, 352. Why God permits the devil to rage against his servants, 381. Paul asks and is not heard, but the devil was heard, 72. The devil is called prince, 394. Why, 425. The devil and his ministers are called strong, and why, 195. The sinner and sinners are called “of the earth,” 334, 474. The devil is the way of iniquity, 402. And the diabolical act, 473. Why the devil is called the accuser, 240. He is called a human being, 73, 187. A wicked person is understood, 474. He is compared with a moneylender, 374. He is called a soldier, 156. Why he is called a dragon, 352. He is compared with wild beasts, 76. He is called an asp, basilisk, lion, and dragon, 310. He is compared with a pot, 371. He is a hammer, 328. He is the shadow of death, 79. The devil’s city is Babylon, 158. The devil’s cities are unbelieving peoples, 38.

Every method of disputation is subordinate to the dialectician, orator, philosopher, and sophist, 572. Aristotle reduced the arguments of dialectic to certain rules, 366. To praise and proclaim the sayings of the ancients is glorious, 537. Didymus expounded Proverbs, 541, and the seven canonical Epistles, 543. He is praised, 542.

Pagans called days after their gods, 13. “Day” in the singular is frequently used for the whole span of life, 125. What the difference is between temporal and eternal days, 260. Which are to be called our days, 389. What the good days are, 111. Day signifies the righteous; night, earthly human beings, 252. By day joy is declared, by night adversity, 295.

Difference: what it is, 567. Finger has many meanings, 484. Why there are ten fingers on the hands and feet, 634. Dilemma: what it is, 470. “I love”: from where it is derived, 58. Christ’s love is strong as death, 533. The sinner’s oil is the simulated love of words, 477. See Love; Charity.

Dionysius composed ecclesiastical canons, 552. A commendation of Dionysius Exiguus, 552. Diplois is a kind of double cloak, 376. There are two kinds of learning, 559. Disciplines, never deceived by opinions, do not mislead, 584. Who hates discipline, 167. No blessing is granted to those who are discordant, 455. God does not love disagreement, 493. Disposition: what it is, 563.

Rich: from where the word is derived, 163. The actions of the poor and the rich are compared, 77. The peace of sinful rich people is always at war with conscience, 245. When the eyes of the evangelical rich man were lifted up, 449. When the rich of the earth are needy and hungry, 111. They fear the end of life, 162. The pomp of dying rich people is described, 162. Why the rich are not to be feared, 163. Wealth is both good and evil, and how, 205.

One should use divisions and subdivisions, 547. There are two kinds of teachers, 173. Who is learned in divine matters, 402. Teachers ought to be irreproachable, 493. The occupations of very learned men, 550. When teachers are full, 197. When they are fasting, 197. They are the eyes of the Church, 528. Why they are the eyes, teeth, neck, and two breasts of the Church, 516. They are the breasts of the Church, 517. When the breasts are those of the Church, and when they are clusters of grapes, 530. They drive away demons, 508. See Church.

The teachers of the Church are represented by the watchmen who guard the city, 522; by the sixty mighty men, 513; by the eyes, 315; by the teeth, ibid.; by the neck and ivory tower, 528; by the columns, 514; by the walls of the city, 522; and by the woods, 508. They are compared with sheep that have been shorn and washed, 515.

The most effective kind of teaching, 14. There are two most effective instruments of teaching, 125. A certain generation descends from teaching, 442. Christ’s teaching is called bread, 140. The teaching is understood through the fruit of Christ’s womb, 453.

Doech. See Antichrist.

Sorrow: from where the word is derived, 33. Christians eat the bread of perfected sorrow, 442. Deceitful: who is so called, 25, 142. When deceit occurs, 112. Deceitful people are compared with foxes, 207.

Lord. See God.

What the house of the Lord is, 433. What its beauty is, 87. What the goods of God’s house are, 211. The house of the Lord is superior to all palaces, 287. See Church. The Lord’s gifts must continually be requested, 403. Gifts of the Holy Spirit. See Holy Spirit. Why Donatus arranged the parts of speech, 592. [Col. 1436] The error of the Donatists, 202, 218. See Church.

“Until” is used in Scripture for a short time and for eternity, 378. “Until” is used for “forever,” 512. To sleep: what it is, 140. Back: from where the word is derived, 230. Dragon: what it is, 497.

## E

Drunkenness is used in Scripture for satiety, 520. Spiritual drunkenness is described, and its origin is indicated, 120. The praise of spiritual drunkenness, 120.

Churches, in the plural and singular: what they signify, 87. Ecclesia means “assembly” or “gathering,” 499. What the Church is, 21. It is one, that is, catholic, 76. Why it is one, 526. Why Christ’s flesh and the Church are called one, 116. There is one Church in the preceding and succeeding Fathers, 531. From many churches one has been chosen, 511. The Church was also established in the patriarchs, 35. The primitive Church is the fountain of gardens and the well of living waters, 519. What difference there is between the Synagogue and the Church, 281. The Synagogue belonged to one nation, but the Church possesses peoples, 534. Just as Jacob seized his brother’s blessing, so the Church seized that of the Synagogue, 458. Before the coming of Christ her bridegroom, the Church was barren; afterward she became the mother of children, and how, 385. Her age is described, 533. See Synagogue.

Donatus considered the Church local, 242. It has spread throughout the world, 355. It is called great, 137. It blesses the Lord everywhere, 346. The whole body of the faithful admires the catholic Church, 526. See Christians.

From what the Church is constructed, 506. It is formed from different nations, like a crown from different flowers, 199. The Church is founded upon the stability of the earth, gathered from earthly human beings, and founded upon Christ, 348. The Church has a womb, 192. Why it asks that its faith be guarded, 85. It does not know how to speak except what is expedient to believe, 8. Christ is its foundation, 293.

The Church is Christ’s sister and beloved, 520. Christ’s daughter and bride, 527. Christ’s bride and sister, and how, 517. Joined to Christ, she will not depart from him, 277. Why she is called Christ’s widow, 453. Christ always cares for the Church, 534. Why she dwells in Christ’s wounds, 511. She bears Christ’s image, 150. Because Christ dwells in her, she is called the mountain of mountains and holy of holies, 330. The holy Church is Christ’s garden, 534. See Christ.

The catholic Church is the Lord’s bride and handmaid, 392. The Lord’s garment, 347. The Lord’s house, 315. The city of God, 158. The Lord’s inheritance, 24. The children of the Church are the Lord’s inheritance, 442. When the Church’s voice sounds in the Lord’s ears, 511. When she shows her face to God, ibid. What the dignity of the Church is, 153. She enters upon and possesses the Lord’s goods, 24. The praise of the Church, 8. The praise of Christ’s mystical tunic, that is, the Church, 127. The power of the catholic Church is shown, 341. The Church’s glory is the conversion of the daughters of princes, 153. Under the Church’s tongue are honey and milk, 518. What the youth, old age, and extreme old age of the Church are, 237. What her stature is, 529. Why the Church is said not to stand but to advance, 526. Why she is praised for the variety of her garment, 153. When she sends forth flowers, and when flowers bring forth fruit, 530. She is a house of refuge, and why, 98. She is a city of habitation, 369. Who truly inhabits her, 81. The ship of the Church carries believing peoples, 351. Only the innocent and upright cling to the Church; she tolerates the rest with difficulty, 85. Those separated from the Church are alien children, 485. Whatever is done outside the catholic Church is not applied to the praises of the Lord, 395. Whoever seeks Christ without the Church may err but cannot advance, 524.

The Church is tested in two ways, namely by terrors and by pleasant words, 519. She labors in two ways, 204. She is always surrounded by a crowd of slanderers, 376. Her tribulations are described, 187. From her earliest beginnings she endured the fiercest hostilities, 445. The more bitterly she is shaken, the greater the fragrance of virtues she emits, 519. She grows through persecutions and is exalted by humility, 297. She grew when the enemy afflicted her, 60. She is increased by persecutions, ibid. She is black through persecutions but beautiful through virtues, 506. When she is captive and when free, 440. When the Church is vindicated, 64. See Persecution.

The people of the Church are one and poor in Christ, 85. What the humility of the Church is, ibid. She wishes no one a curse in prayer, 26. Her hope is in her members, 23. Her bed is the rest of the present life, 508. When the just desire God’s Church to increase, they desire sinners to be converted, 353. The Church is blessed through the congregation of the saints, 26. The earthly Church is formed according to the example of the heavenly one, 526. The heavenly Jerusalem is the mother of the Church, 531. She is surrounded everywhere by the protection of angels, 511. She rejoices to be fortified by the intercession of the saints, 513.

The Church’s roots are the prophets, 276. The prophets, apostles, and their successors are her guardians, 534. Why the apostles and their successors are called her gates, 531. Her neck is her preachers and teachers, 507, 515. Through the nose the holy teachers are understood, 528. Through the teeth the firm effectiveness of her words is understood, 525. Why her holy teachers are signified by her breasts, 528, 529. Her steps are the swift preaching of the apostles, 527. Her shoes are the examples of the Fathers who proceeded before, ibid.
