The Church is called Zion, 17. She is called the daughter of the multitude, 528. She is called the ark of the Lord’s sanctification, 452. Why she is called the silvered dove, 221. The name winepress applies to her, 34. Why she is called a wall, 533. She is a wine-cellar in which charity is ordered, 509. She is an enclosed garden, and why, 518. The daughters of Zion are the Church, 514. The Church is represented by Noah’s ark, 8, 428, and her innocence by the dove, 508. She is signified by Israel, 50; by the edge of Christ’s garment, 455; by Christ’s seamless tunic, 75, 455; by the tabernacle, 101; by the place of the tabernacle, 142; by Solomon’s bed, 513; by ships, 368; and by the moon, 550. Through the moon and stars she herself and her various orders are signified, 462. Through the cedars of Lebanon the teachers and perfect people who are in her are signified, 519. Through the north and south, the winds of persecution against her are signified, 519. Through the completion of the tabernacle the perfection of the Church is signified, 93.

The Church is compared with the moon, 35. Why she is compared with the sun and moon, 526; with a turtledove, 507; with the eyes of a dove, 514; with the sea, 314; with islands, 324; with a vineyard—one that profits more when dug and multiplies when pruned, 276; with a winepress, 582; with a wineskin, 107; with columns of smoke, myrrh, and frankincense, 513. Her stature is compared with a palm tree, 529. Her belly is compared with a heap of wheat, 528. Her garments are compared with frankincense, 518.

Peter bears the type of the Church; Judas, of Babylon destined for condemnation, 374. The Church of the nations is signified by the prostitute, and by Judah and Tamar, 169. Ecclesiastical flocks are signified by beasts of burden, 494. The steps of the Church are numbered, 160. There are three orders of the Church: teachers, continent persons, and married people, 525. The customs of the Church in processions and communion, 396. The usefulness of books that deal with ecclesiastical discipline, 549. He is foolish who detracts from the Almighty and does not submit to catholic rules, 179.

The author of Ecclesiasticus is Jesus son of Sirach, 542. What the difference is between Ecclesiastes and Ecclesiasticus, ibid. What a solar eclipse is, 591. Eclipse of the moon. See Moon.

Edom means “bloody” or “earthly,” 465. To lead out: what it is, 122. Ephrem means “fruitfulness,” 200. There are two kinds of needy people, 349. Who is precious to God though needy, 77.

Almsgiving: what perfect almsgiving is, 125. How it should be given, 139. It should not be given grudgingly, 527. It should be given to the needy, but especially to holy men, 139. Christ receives it from Christians alone, 457. The reward of the giver of alms, 139. It is most acceptable to God, 153. It is the reconciler of the human race, 139. Elijah means “My God is the Lord” and signifies Christ, 529. Elocution: what it is, 563. Eloquence: what it is, 6. Divine eloquence is enriched by various disciplines and arts, 28. Why the Lord’s utterance is called fiery, 421. It is called water, 60. What the difference is between failing away from the Lord’s utterance and failing in the utterance, 410.

Eman means “his brother,” 295. The Lord’s corrections come to the faithful from an intention of compassion, 307. En-gaddi means “fountain of the kid,” and why it signifies baptism, 508. Enthymeme: what it is, 70, 566. Statement: what it is, 568. Ephrata means “mirror,” 452. Ephrem means “fruitfulness” and “fruitfully,” 264, 270, 275, 371. Epicene: what it is, 596. Epicheireme: what it is, 88, 121, 566.

Epiphanius. See Song of Songs.

What the origin of error is, 552. Errors arise in human beings in three ways, but by no means in Christ, 12. All who sin through some error are transgressors, 417. God said everything and warned about everything, so that we should not wish to err, 490. To be ashamed: what it is, 83. To be ashamed is the condition of one who has been deceived, 110. Learned: from where the word is derived, 18, 307. Food is named from eating, 267. There is one food for all, distributed by the Creator’s generosity, 489. We ought to seek spiritual food, 491. Origen expounded the two books of Ezra, 543.

The Eucharist. In the Eucharist Christ consecrated his body and blood in the distribution of bread and wine, 379. In the sacred mysteries of the highest kind, the Church daily worships the Lord’s body and blood, 467. The Lord’s body and blood are received in holy communion, 212. Here Christ refreshes us through participation in his body, 495. The food of those who fear God is communion in the sacred body and blood, 381. Christ feeds the faithful with his body and blood, 463. The sacrifice of the holy Church is the solemn offering of Christ’s body and blood, 68. The faithful are gathered together through the offering of Christ’s body, 53. Wine gladdens the heart when it has been consecrated into Christ’s blood, 350. How the Lord’s blood intoxicates, 80. Christ is manna in communion, 266. Manna means “What is this?” and is suitably applied to holy communion, 266. Through the failure of David’s praises, the transition from the ancient sacrifices to the offering of Christ’s body is represented, 244. Melchizedek’s offering was received as a prefiguration of the Lord’s body, 423. See Sacrifice.

Euge is the speech of one who praises, 233. Eugippius, an abbot, compiled a book from the works of Saint Augustine and dedicated it to the virgin Proba, 551. Eusebius of Caesarea collected the evangelical canons, 543. The Chronicle of Eusebius was translated by Saint Jerome and brought down to his own times, 550. The history of Eusebius, with Rufinus’s additions, is to be read, 550. Eusebius, blind from childhood, nevertheless became extremely learned, 542. He was held by the Novatian error, 542. The heresies of Eutyches and Nestorius are condemned, 244. See Natures of Christ.

The dignity of evangelical perfection surpasses every praise of legal observance, 517. Evangelical preaching ought to have been announced in the world through Christ, not through another, 530. The four Gospels are like the four chariots of the New Testament, over which Christ presides, 527. The evangelical books are called the heavens, 35. The evangelists are the Lord’s arrows, 60. To exalt: what it is, 98. To shake off: what it is, 412. Exemplifiable: what it is, 566. Perfect men encourage one another through common examples, 454. Exordium: what it is, 27, 565. Expositors: what good they possess, 552. To reproach: what it is, 148. Who is called expelled, 26. What we are awaiting when we await, 135. To exult: what it is, 37, 105. See Blessedness. Face is used for presence, 47. Fastucium: what it is, 7. Fate. See Astronomy. Foolish. See Enlightened.

Faith: from where the word is derived, 267. True faith is the proper light of the saints, 326. What solid faith is, 26. The catholic man remains immovable in faith, 87. Christ’s feet stood where the truth of faith is shown to be founded, 452. Holy men always ask for such things as advance the growth of faith, 274. The heat of faith grows as the heat of desire is diminished, 411. Direction of the heart is the holy rule of catholic faith, 399. All who have believed in Christ are Christ’s seed, 303. Not to believe God is corruption, 179. The Lord sleeps when we grow lukewarm in his faith, 431. Unbelievers are called dead, 297.

Figure: what it is, 16, 589. What plane figures are, 589. What solid figures are, 589. A composite figure is made in four ways, 597.

What faith teaches concerning the Son of God, 17. The Son of God is always equal to the Father, 65. His eternity is explained, 17. He is called the good Word, 150. Why God did not hear many people, but did hear the Son, 73. The Son is the Father’s right hand, 56. See Christ; Word.

Fringes: what they signify, 153. End is spoken of in two ways, 4. What it is, 21. “To the end” is used in two ways, 468. See Psalms. Finitive: what it is, 564. Pipe and cinnamon: what they are and signify, 518. The scourge is understood as divine vengeance, 310. Flame: from where the word is derived, 362. Fountain: from where the word is derived, 224. To fornicate from the Lord: what it is, 248. Fortitude: what it is, 145, 632. He falls under the impulse from whom the Lord’s fortitude is withdrawn, 395. Fortunatianus composed three volumes on rhetoric, 565. Sword: what it signifies, 38, 57, 114. Fraud is so called as if it were “broken faith,” 267. Growling belongs to wild beasts and raging creatures, 16. Bridle: from where the word is derived, 105. To give fruit: what it is, 14. Fruit: from where the word is derived, 14, 369. Grain: from where the word is derived, 23. Ropes: from where the word is derived, 53. Fury: what it is, 28. Fury. See Anger.

## G
Galaad is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” 199, 515, 525. Also “transmigration,” 371. Concerning joy: who come to it and who do not, 441. Gebal, “empty valley,” 283. Groaning: whence the term derives, 29, 129. The groaning of the imperfect and of the perfect is very different, 538. What groaning is to be sought from Christians, 29. Pious groaning is not hidden from God, 129. It is great confidence to groan before our pious Author, 320. Nation: whence the term derives, 18, 272. When the nations were thrown into confusion, 155. They are called “wilderness,” 183. They are compared with the trees of the forests, 323. Genus: what it is, 567. Geometry: what it is, 583. Definition of geometry and its division, 589. Who first used it, 588. Who wrote about it, 589. God is the true geometer, 588. Sword: what it signifies and from what it is called, 123. Why the devil’s sword is wicked, but the Lord’s benevolent, 485. Glory: what it is, 82, 95, 236, 500. Grammar: from where it received its name, 559. What grammar is, ibid. Who wrote more elegantly about grammar, 559. Grace is given freely to all, 287, 344. Without Christ a human being can neither begin nor complete any good, 48. No one can attain any gifts of God by himself, 196. No one can be saved by his own virtues, but only by the grace of God, 518. A person possesses nothing good except what he has received from the Lord, 44. God is good in himself; human beings are good through his grace, 394. Whatever is praiseworthy in us is the work of divine mercy, 366. Without Christ, the true sun, all life is shadowy, 339. God is said to hear only those to whom he deigns to grant his favor, 337. God’s grace is granted in what is shown to exist in the good will of human beings, 252. Grace is the beginning of the good life, without which one lives badly, 339. Prevenient grace is defended against the Pelagians, 171. The Lord’s grace precedes all things, 297. In every good thing we are preceded by the Lord’s grace, 400. God’s good gifts precede us, 222. The Lord’s calling precedes every merit, 27. God freely calls everyone, 61. God freely chose us, 211. No one comes to the Lord’s grace by his own merits, 83. Nothing is to be attributed to human merits, 90. Christ’s grace prepares, assists, strengthens, and crowns us, 287. How the Lord’s mercy both precedes and follows, 80. The faithful are called children of God by grace, not by nature, 282. A human being is restored by grace, though by justice he had rightly been condemned, 238. The sinner’s conversion is freely given, 188. Unless God’s forgiveness has preceded the sinner, he will not acquit the erring person in judgment, 273. Whoever’s right hand is held by the Lord is always acquitted, 247. God’s looking upon someone means liberating and granting grace, 259. The person renewed by grace sings a new song to the Lord, 321. When someone has attained grace, this is called his youth [Col. 1440], 237. Why grace is more pleasing than the law, 286. The breasts are full of grace, 506. Grace is understood through oil, 376. What we call “gratuitous,” 115. Steps signify human actions, 55, 244.

Inheritance: whence the term derives, 18, 53, 270. In former times an inheritance of lands was divided by cords, 53. The difference between human inheritance and Christ’s inheritance, 317. Christ’s inheritance is the predestined multitude of the saints, 53. The lot of the righteous is the Lord’s inheritance, 439. God’s inheritance is established in holy people, 272. Heretics stand beside the rock, not upon the rock as the faithful do, 477. How heretical teachers, standing beside Christ the rock, are drowned, 477. Heretics possess only at the exits, not at the entrances, 486. In what sense they are called Christ’s companions, 506. They consider it praiseworthy to hold opinions against the ancients, 545. How they search the Lord’s testimonies, 398. The custom of heretics is described, 100. Heretical disputations are set forth, 485. Why they seek contentious disputes, 224. Cassiodorus refutes heretics wherever the opportunity arises, 77. God tests us through the contradictions of heretics, 279. Heretics are understood by the foxes that destroy the Church, 511. The tongues of heretics are compared with asps, 474. Heretics are compared with dogs, 76. Heretics imitate the archer, 43. The cisterns signify the teachings of heretics, 519. Heretics and schismatics are called shadows of death, 79. Harmony: what it is, 502, 587. The exceedingly pleasing virtue of harmony exists when the voice agrees with one’s works, 333. Hemisphaerion: what is above the earth, 590. What the hemisphaerion beneath the earth is, 590. Hermon signifies “anathema,” 300, 455. What Hermoniim signifies, 143. Two Herods persecuted Christ, 16. Hesebon is interpreted as “belt of mourning,” 528. Saint Jerome is praised, 557. He translated all the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin, 545. How, 538, 545, 546. He solved many Hebrew questions concerning Genesis, 539. He translated and commented on the book of Job, 542. He expounded Ecclesiastes, 542. He composed commentaries on Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the twelve minor prophets, 541. He explained all the prophets, ibid. He commented on the four Gospels, 543. He commented on the Epistle to the Ephesians, to Titus, to Philemon, and others, 544. The remarkable letter of Saint Jerome to Paulinus, 551. The books On Illustrious Men by Saint Jerome and Gennadius are to be read carefully, 550. See Apocalypse. Saint Hilary is praised, 550. Goat: whence the term derives, 216. History: what it is, 264. “Today” is used in Scripture for perpetuity, 17. Burnt offerings: what they are, 68, 136, 216. What “burnt offerings with marrow” are, 216. Human dignity, 635. The Lord gladly hears what he recognizes as having worked in us according to his own image, 466. Why God is said to have breathed into him, 632. The condition of the first human being before and after sin, 634. God creates us as often as he restores us from the oldness of sin into the new human being, 352. A human being cannot give the price of his own redemption, 162. A human being is a spirit passing through the present world, 345. Every human being except Christ is subject to vanity, 133. Human years are compared with grass that is quickly consumed, 306. A human being is like dust carried away by the wind, 484. What the difference is between human beings and the sons of human beings, 119. Human weakness is compared with hay, 345. Why the human race is compared with hay, 338. A human being is called earthly dust, 14. When human beings became deep mire, 226. When a human being is snow and when wool, 495. The soul alone, or the flesh alone, is used for “the human being,” 211. Our mortal frailty is understood through the navel, 527. The most savage person is compared with a razor, 177. Horeb is interpreted as “Calvary,” 362. Clocks prepared by Cassiodorus, 556. Gargilius Martialis wrote about cultivating gardens, 554. Who is called a guest, 228. What is humble, 565. The trembling of the humble is safer than the presumption of the proud, 353. Only the humble and devout seek God’s presence, 354. Whoever humbles and corrects himself directs his mind, 264. In this world the wicked are raised up, but in the future the humble will be raised, 126. Why God humbles the proud and exalts the humble, 255. Channels signify the humility of the saints, 529. Who are to be called the impious and the wicked, 12, 14, 15, 86. Impiety is the extremity of all evils, 245. Why the Lord is said to know the way of the righteous and not to know the path of the wicked, 15. The custom of criminal people, 56. They do not reach the right way, 46. Why the wicked will not be able to appear before the divine sight, 247. The cries of the wicked at the final judgment are useless, 63. The wicked will be confounded in the future, 147. Their happiness consists only in transitory things, 486. The rising up of the wicked is falling, 247. When a wicked person perishes, the innocent are warned to conduct themselves more cautiously, 193. The wicked are understood through waters and abysses, 348. In what way they are like roses, 284. Sojourner: what it is, 134, 430. The hearts of unbelievers are of stone, 320. To rebuke: what it is, 401. Rebuke makes strong men cautious, 257. Needy: what it is, 585. Spiritual need is more serious than bodily need, 366. Induction: what it is, 566, 572. Infants and sucklings: who they are, 35. Why infants and young people are without understanding, 632. Hell: whence the term derives, 39. Hell is situated beneath the earth, 292. The infernal pit is described, 186. What the nature of infernal fire is, 70. Hell is called a fortified city, and why, 371. How someone descends alive into hell, 184. See Damnation. The minds of unbelievers are called a grave, 297. Why the body of unbelievers is called a house of iniquities, 253. We must not consider as enemies those who benefit us, 468. Why we are commanded to love our enemies, whereas it is devout to hate God’s enemies, 472. A holy conscience prays for enemies so that they may be converted, 30. God gladly accepts prayers made for enemies, 181. Enemies are confounded in two ways, 239. Jabin, that is, “wise,” 284. Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter,” 266. Through Jacob both the Jewish people and the Christian people may be understood, 50. Fasting: from where the term derives, 116. God rejects those who craftily ask to be released from his commandments, 400.

He does not invert the orders of things unless he is the one who made them, 381. Ecclesiastical orders. See *Ecclesiastics, Penance*. Horeb is interpreted as “dryness,” 284. Organ: what it is, 501. The error of the Pelagians, 69. How pernicious it is, 83. Accursed, 98. It is condemned, 53. Objections are answered, 171. See *Original Sin, Grace*. Pilgrim: whence the word is derived, 134. All the books of the divine Scriptures shine with heavenly light and the power of the Holy Spirit, 538. Sacred Scripture is called a lamp, 414. Why it is called light, 7. Ancient orators employed the tropes of Divine Scripture, 7. Aristotle imitated the topics of argument found in Sacred Scripture, 489. From the Scriptures the secular teachings of the saints have flowed, 82. See Art, Eloquence. Sacred Scripture is called the language of God, 256. It is Christ’s garment, 75. The mysteries of the divine Scriptures are the ramparts of the holy Church, 516. The heavenly granary of Sacred Scripture, or storehouse of heavenly things, 490. They are the pastures of the faithful people, 331. [Col. 1455] Why Divine Scripture is called a dripping honeycomb, 517. It is compared with the Lord’s tunics, 548. By living waters it is understood, 519. By spittle it is understood, 109. By a bow, 33. With what diligence Sacred Scripture should be read, 552. Understanding of the divine Scriptures must continually be sought from God, 419. With which book of Scripture beginners ought to begin, 537. See Psalter.

The young understand the divine Scriptures better than the old, 413. The desire of the blessed Agapetus and Cassiodorus to establish public schools at Rome for learning Sacred Scripture, 537. The sacred writings, together with their commentators, collected by Cassiodorus in nine codices, 545. In Cassiodorus’ time the Books of Kings had not yet been commented upon, 540. Through the Sacred Scripture expounded by the Fathers one reaches contemplation of the Lord, 537. See Ambrose, Augustine, Bellator, Cassiodorus, Eloquence of God, Jerome; see also Apocalypse, Ecclesiastes, etc.

Scutum: whence the word is derived, 114. Sehon is interpreted as “temptation of colors,” or “unfruitful tree,” 459, 463. Selmon is interpreted as “shadow,” 221. Seneca composed a book On the Form of the World, which does not exist today, 590. Human old age is compared with the old age of the Church, 312. What is understood by old age, 236. The bodily senses: how many there are and what their functions are, 634. Burial is a duty of piety, 272. Sera: whence the word is derived, 132, 495.

The divine discourse is full of wisdom and prudence, 161. The divine discourse, when meditated upon, nourishes the soul, 79. See Eloquence, Word. Servus, “servant,” is derived from servare, “to preserve,” 418. Who is the Lord’s servant, 419. He always enjoys tranquil peace, 426. Sichima is interpreted as “shoulders,” 199, 371. Signum: whence the word is derived and what it is, 292, 357, 459. The sign of the cross. See Cross. The effect of silence, 135. See Tongue. Similitudo: what it is, 161. Simon Magus: when he walked in wonders above himself, 449. Sina is interpreted as “commandment,” 222. Sion has many meanings, 17. Sion signifies “speculation,” 232, 248, 257, 325, 438. Sion gave birth to all the Churches, 39. Sisara, that is, “exclusion of joy,” 284.

Sol, “sun”: whence the word is derived, 351. The sun has many meanings in Scripture, 506. The sun signifies the wise person, the moon the righteous person, 252. Eclipse of the sun. See Eclipse. When lot is used in Scripture, it signifies some divine judgment, 76. Species: what it is, 567. Spes, “hope”: whence the word is derived, 136. What it truly means to hope, 101. Who truly has hope in the Lord and in his name, 136. Hope in the Lord changes everything for the better, 142. Hope strengthens one for suffering, 390. What the expectation of the saints is, 416. The Lord is the hope of all the ends of the earth, 211. The hope of Christians derives from Christ’s resurrection. See Resurrection of Christ.

Spherical position: what it is, 590. What spherical motion is, 590. The stages of spiritual progress, 213. It is a great sickness to grow weary of spiritual delights, 367. See Spiritual drunkenness, Food.

The Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son, 93, 288. He is Creator, 352. He proceeds from the Father and the Son, 8, 188. Who offers glory to the name of the Holy Spirit, 93. The Holy Spirit is heat from which no one can hide, 65. Why he appeared in tongues of fire, 515. The voice of the Lord repeated seven times signifies the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, 93. The ointments are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 505. The Holy Spirit is designated by the name of oil, 505. Spirit: what it is, 260. Spirit is spoken of in three ways, 628. What the spirit of power is, 94. Unclean spirits are called slanderers, 418. Why unclean spirits are called alien, 374. Spiritual wickednesses must be guarded against with particular care, 31.

Stagna: whence the word is derived, 369. Who are called “standing,” 457. To stand pertains to an utterly steadfast mind, 452. Statues of rulers were placed in the streets for the instruction of memory, 250. The position of the stars: what it is, 591. What the precedence of the stars is, 590. What the removal of the stars is, 591. Study of letters. See Letter.

A fool: who he is, 162, 312. What the custom of fools is, 134. Who is subject to God, 203. Everything sudden is violent, 465. Substance: what it is, 152. Who are to be called proud, 315. Pride is the mother of vices, 401. Every sin is born from it, 102. It is found in every sin, and why, 120. It is called the sickness of the age, 367. It is the devil’s sin, 245. The angel and Adam fell through pride, [Col. 1456] 120. Pride is the greatest offense, 67. The Lord specially curses it, 253. God turns his face away from the proud and removes his grace, 352. The humble draw near to God, while the proud become altogether distant, 467. Why God knows the proud from afar, 467. The creature must not be proud before the Creator, 300. The humble obey the Lord’s commands; the proud swell up through diabolical suggestions, 406. A proud person is mute even if he sings psalms, 253. To climb to the summit of pride is ruinous, 449. The arrogant descend into the depths of Tartarus as far as they thought they could reach the heights, 65. The proud despise the humble, 436. What difference exists between the proud and the servants of God when they are injured, 435. The sacrifice acceptable to God is a slaughtered spirit of pride, 174. The faithful must be avenged at the proper time, lest they be led into pride, 330. Malignant spirits are called lions because of pride, but leopards because of ferocity, 517. Raab signifies pride, 294. The birds of heaven are proud human beings, 36. By the cedars of Lebanon noble and proud kings are understood, 94. A proud person is compared with a horse, 494. By horns the proud are understood, 76. The backbone is used for pride, 103.

Surface: what it is, 589. What a plane surface is, ibid. Superfluous: what it is, 585. Supplantare: what it is, 126. True supplication, 29. See Prayer. Suspicion is unbecoming to a Christian man, 404. Whispering: what it is, 140. Syllable: what it is, 559. On syllables and how they ought to be written, 609, 612, 613 and following. See Orthography. A categorical syllogism: what it is, 13. There are three formulas of categorical syllogisms, 568. An example of a categorical syllogism, 105. What a hypothetical syllogism is, 31, 139. There are seven modes of hypothetical syllogisms, 569. Some syllogisms are predicative, others conditional, and what they are, 572. What a three-part syllogism is, 566. What a four-part syllogism is, ibid. A five-part syllogism, 144, 566. Tullius Marcellus of Carthage composed seven books On Syllogisms, 269. Symphonia: what it is, 587.

Synagogue: what it signifies, 32. Why before Christ’s coming it was called the Shulammite, 527. It was despised before Christ’s coming, but not afterward, 531. It is the mother of the Church, 506. Christ could not dwell in it, 32. It is signified by figs, 510. See Church, Jew.

## T

Tabernacle: what it is, 51. Tabescere: what it is, 421, 472. Temperance: what it is, 632. Why the veil of the Temple was torn during the Passion, 74. Darkness is used in a good sense in Scripture, 59. How the temptations of the righteous and the wicked differ, 280, 374. There are two temptations: one of the Lord, the other of the devil, 86. The faithful always make progress through temptations, 316. Why God tests and tempts, 86. God strikes for salvation, 231. In this life God destroys those whom he decides to build again, 177. See Devil.

Terminus: whence the word is derived, 18. What a boundary is, 589. Terra, “earth”: whence the word is derived, 19. The globe of the earth is enclosed in the form of a wheel, 262. What the face of the earth signifies, 14. What the ends of the earth are, 18. In former times the earth was divided by a stretched cord, 269. Why the earth was given to human beings, 388. When it gave its fruit, 218. Although the earth, like other things, must be renewed, it will retain its name, 125. If we despise earthly things, we are always joyful through God, 278.

The testament of God: what it signifies, 84. How testament is understood in the holy Scriptures, 283. Who are said to establish a testament, 165. Christians ought to rest between the two Testaments, 221. When the two Testaments invoke one another, 143. What God promised in the Old Testament and what in the New, 253. Everything announced in the Old Testament is to be fulfilled through Christ and in Christ, 531. In the New Testament there is mercy; in the Old, truth, 289. Why the New Testament is called eternal, 355, 382. The two abysses are the two Testaments, 143. By the mixed thing the two Testaments are understood, 255. By streams of waters the Old Testament is signified, 523. Greek commentators on both Testaments, 538.

False witnesses: who they are, 115. Testimonium: what it is, 330, 399. What is meant by testimonies, 84. Why the Lord’s testimonies are marvelous, 419. How the Lord’s testimonies contain justice and truth, 421. Thabor is interpreted as “coming light,” 300. Tharsis is interpreted as “contemplation,” 242. Tichonius the Donatist expounded the Apocalypse; its text was corrected by Cassiodorus, 544.

Divine fear, 404. Perfect fear, 417. The spirit of fear of the Lord, 94. Love mixed with dread is the fear of the Lord, 66. Fear of the Lord descends from love, 443. That fear is acceptable to God which is joined with love and pious confidence, [Col. 1457] 494. It belongs to servants to fear, to friends to love, 102. Fear of the Lord drives out another fear, 88. There are two fears that pierce our hearts, namely human and divine fear, 443. The difference between the fear of a carnal person and that of the righteous, 76, 89, 111, 292. Human fear gives distrust; divine fear gives hope, 85. Worldly fear makes people miserable, 383, 443. Fear of the Lord makes blessed, 19, 383. To fear God is unshaken steadfastness, 66. Those who fear God lack nothing, 111. To fear God and hope in him make people blessed, 388. To fear at the proper time is foresight, and conversely, 50. No one fears who has been illuminated by God, 88. Here everything is under fear, 390. See Commandment.

Tone: what it is, 587. There are fifteen tones, 587. See Music. Topaz: what it is, 419. Topics: what they are, 490, 577. Winepress: what it is, 34. Geth signifies a winepress or pressure, 186. Torrents: what they are, 58. “Whole” is spoken of in two ways, 574.

Heretics who do not follow the holy traditions of the Church have spoken falsely, 192. That sweet incense is pleasing to the Lord which has been joined to the traditions of the apostles, 216. An equilateral triangle: what it is, 589. Our tribulation: what it is, 167. The time of tribulation is twofold, but greatly dissimilar, 127. Who are truly troubled in heart, and who are not, 112. When tribulation is distant and when it is near, 74. Why tribulations must be endured patiently, 85. Why the tribulations of the righteous are many, 112. They always enlarge the Church, 22. They are sweet to a holy man, 308. They are gifts to him, 422. They produce continual prayers, 478. They become sweeter than our tears, 339, 294. In them the righteous rejoices, 193. They prick hearts medicinally, 389. For the faithful they are a desired correction, 245. They make God merciful toward us, 155. God exercises through tribulations those whom he has decided to crown, 270. God cleanses those whom he scourges so that, purified, he may receive them; but those whom he does not cleanse he has decided to condemn, 304. The tribulation of Christians extends toward the hope of eternal life, 200. Severe tribulation commonly casts from the mind what one previously believed, 148. In time of tribulation the cry of the heart is raised with all its strength, 366. Tribulation follows those who abandon the author of salvation, 369. By iron hard tribulation is understood, 356. Trilatera: what it is, 589.

The Holy Trinity: what it is, 62. The mystery of the most holy Trinity is explained, 173, 242, 280. The faith that the Church has concerning the Trinity is elucidated, 25. The doctrine of the Catholic Church concerning the Trinity, 8, 188. The Scriptures transmit knowledge of the Holy Trinity, 549. The names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are proper to the Trinity; the remaining names are common, 240. The Trinity alone is called God of gods, 461. It is divided neither in blessedness, nor in power, nor in nature, 453. It wills one thing and works one thing, 190, 451. The eternal Father is Lord, as is the Son, 17. The power of the Father’s omnipotence is declared, 46. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one principle, 378. The Father and Son are called “principle” so that their coeternity may be declared, 378. The Holy Trinity has a communion of words, 95. What is said of one person is often understood as referring to the power of the whole Trinity, 454. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit save, 364. The whole Trinity illuminates, 62. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have a voice, 94. The three persons of the Trinity give testimony, 66. “I am” denotes the Trinity, 166. Those who have written something about the Trinity, 549.

Vital sadness: what it is, 145. The sadness of the age must be fled, and why, 145. It is hostile to the faithful, 144. Trumpet: what it is, 501. There were two kinds of trumpets among the Hebrews, and what they signify, 327. Tympanum: what it is, 501. Tyre signifies distress, 283, 294.

## U

In former times kings, prophets, and pontiffs were anointed, 455. The perfections of unity are enumerated, 15. The arrangement of the universe is marvelous, 34. Urbs, “city”: whence the word is derived, 242. Usury: whence the word is derived, 242. What money is forbidden to be lent at interest and what is not, 51. Uter: what it is, 107. See Church. Uxor, “wife,” is so called as if from “sister,” 444.

## V

Vanity: what it is, 136. Who are vain, 86. What is properly called vain, 22, 178, 484. Everything contrary to truth is vain, 485. Everything becomes vain when compared with better things, 204. Who has not sat in the council of vanity, 86. Venom: whence the word is derived, 49.

[Col. 1458]

The winds signify the souls of the righteous, 347. What kind of correction beating is, 128. The eternal generation of the Word, 379. The generation of the eternal Word is explained, 205. The Word is coeternal with the Father, 185. The nature of the Word is unchangeable, 238. The right hand of the Father is the omnipotent Word, 470. What “the Word became flesh” means, 20. How the Word assumed humanity, 197. Why the Word became flesh, 379. God the Father spoke in the Holy One when the Word became flesh, 199. The humility of the Word in assuming the likeness of sinful flesh, 59. Nothing is more marvelous than that mortal nature, assumed by the Word, should have been placed at the Father’s right hand, 247. The body assumed by the Word is called his footstool, 330. The humanity of the Word cried out to the Lord and was not heard, and why, 72. The king’s reclining was the incarnation of the Word, 507. When the Word comes, not even hardness ought to despair, 496. See Christ, Son of God.

The Word: what it is, 559, 568. Speech ought to be consistent with life, 192. When the Word of God was within and when it was found outside, 531. Who effectively receives the word of the Lord, 494. Those who eat the word of God and are satisfied, 540. Many understand his words, but few penetrate their sweetness, 524. Every harsh saying that is offered against the divine rules like a deadly draught is a harsh word, 309. Those are guilty who hear the Lord’s words and disdain doing them, 477. The sword signifies the Word of God, and why, 151. The word of the Lord is a two-edged sword, and why, 500. The Lord’s words are compared with leaves, 14. See Discourse.

A description of modesty, 148. Truth: what it is, 51. What truth says does not know how to stumble, 382. The one who follows the words of truth cannot be deceived, 298. In a time of joy mercy is to be proclaimed; in a time of sadness, truth, 311. True love curses what can be contrary to truth, 426. Why truth hates vanity, 98. When falsehood speaks against truth, 101. Why the prophet said “truths,” although there is one truth, 45.

Vertex: whence the word is derived, 33. Via, “way”: whence the word is derived, 15, 148. Ways and paths differ greatly, and whence they are called so, 83. What is understood by ways and paths, ibid. When “way” is put in the singular, Christ is understood; when in the plural, the apostles and prophets, 443. The ways of the Lord are his arrangements and wills, which are always just, 489. Christ is our way. See Christ. Vibrare: what it is, 33. Victorinus. See Apocalypse. We are not said to see those things at which we gaze with no delight, and conversely, 333. Nocturnal offices are called vigils, 260. See Office. Vigilius, bishop of Africa. See Apocalypse.

Vengeance: what it is, 273. Vengeance must be reserved for the Lord, 343. God visits with the rod when he exacts strict vengeance, 302. He avenges through scourging when vengeance is exacted from us more lightly, 302. Vinea, “vineyard,” is derived from vines, 276. Wine is love seasoned with action, 532. Vir, “man,” is derived from vires, “strengths,” 12. Virga, “rod”: why it is so called, 18. What the rod signifies, ibid. How the rod and staff console us, 79.

The virtues of virgins and widows are explained, 637. The whiteness of lilies is compared with virginal purity, 511. Virtue: whence the word is derived, 474. The cardinal virtues are perfected through contemplative judgment and memory, 632. As many virtues as the saints advance in, so many steps do they take toward God, 517. Christ knocks when he exhorts his faithful to advance in virtue, 520. We give God the tambourine properly when we cultivate virtues and despise vices, 278. By the wall, the guardianship of heavenly virtues is signified, 511. By the she-goats and stags the virtues of the saints are understood, 509. Virtue is compared with wine, 199. When human virtue is abandoned, 108. See Consummation.

Life. Who are properly said to live and die, 231. What is truly called living, 77. Who are called living, 139. The way of life is unknown to human beings, 482. Human life is a shadow, 484. Only eternal life should be called life, 408. The days of famine signify the time of this life, 124. By the Garden of Nuts eternal life is signified, 526. The beginning of a good life is signified through the East, while through the West the inclination toward bad conduct is signified, 344. One rightly responds through obedience to Christ calling him to a good life, 341. Whoever walks in newness of life will share in Christ, 407. The contemplative and active life are the two eyes, 48. The way of vices is crooked; the way of virtues is straight, 419. Our mind is bound by vices as by certain ropes, 491. All vicious people are blind, ibid. Vices are bitter, 459. A servant of vices does not deserve to have the Lord of the saints, 412. The pleasure of vices produces perpetual death, 77. Those who dominate vices are kings, 18. Blessed is the one who restrains harmful vices, 466. The beginning of progress is to abandon carnal vices, 429. When carnal vices are beginning, they are easily dashed against Christ the rock; not so when they have taken root, 466.

[Col. 1459]

Calves signify the innocent, preachers, and martyrs, 174. A description of the Vivarium, or Castellian, monastery, 534. The calling of God. See Grace. Birds: whence the word is derived, 36. Will: whence the word is derived, 48. The will of God is the perfection of things, 462. In the Lord’s will there is life, 96. Who sees the will of the Lord, 89. Everyone who carries out the divine wills is a minister of God, 318. Arms and shield is the will of the Lord alone, 114. There are two vows of the most faithful Christian, 109. Equal vows are glued together; contrary ones are separated, 333. God judges a pious vow by the result of its action, 104.

[Col. 1460]

Articulate voice: what it is, 559. An unjust voice condemns its authors before it condemns others, 191. Vultus, “countenance”: whence the word is derived, 102. Vultus is named from voluntas, “will,” and why, 635.

## Z

Zabulon: what it signifies, 224. Zeb: what it signifies, 284. Zebee is interpreted as “victim,” 284. Good zeal, 123. It is used in both a good and a bad sense, 421. See Envy. The Ziphaeans: whence they are called so, 180. What they signify, ibid.

[Col. 1459]
